COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR A UNIVERSAL LIBRARY: COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL; OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION EXTANT THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COLLATION WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED after the most extensive editions completed during the past three centuries; FURNISHED WITH SPECIAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING EACH VOLUME OR EACH AUTHOR OF SOME IMPORTANCE; WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY ARRANGED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EVERY PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; EXPANDED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL, YET POSSESSING SOME AUTHORITY in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers wrote on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers commented upon individual Scriptural passages and in what places in their works. A MOST ACCURATE EDITION, EASILY TO BE PREFERRED TO ALL OTHERS, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the thoroughness of correction, both the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient format of the volumes—uniform throughout the whole course of the work—the low price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered together in our library from writings pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

[Col. 0009]

CONTINUATION OF PETER LOMBARD’S *COLLECTIONS ON PAUL*

ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS.

ARGUMENT.

[Col. 0009A]

After the Corinthians had done penance, the Apostle writes them a consoling Epistle from Troas by Titus. Praising them, he urges them toward better things, showing that although they had indeed been grieved, they had been corrected.

CHAPTER ONE.

VV. 1–5.—“Paul, an Apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are throughout Achaia: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we ourselves may be able to console those who are in every affliction, through the encouragement by which we ourselves are encouraged by God; because, as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so also through Christ our consolation abounds.”

“Paul,” etc. The Apostle likewise writes this Epistle to the Corinthians. Some of them, although at first grieved by the preceding Epistle, had afterwards been corrected and had suffered much for Christ’s name. Others among them, however, still stubbornly despised the Apostle and preferred pseudo-apostles to him. Therefore, since some Corinthians had been corrected by the first Epistle, he writes this second Epistle on account of the rest: he repels the pseudo-apostles by exposing the deception of their preaching, while commending himself in many ways. He also reproves those who were stingy in almsgiving [Col. 0009C]. He likewise commands that the corrected fornicator, whom he had handed over to Satan, be received back. [Ambrose] And because even the good among them were being afflicted, he offers himself to them as an example of patience, teaching that they ought not take it bitterly when he himself, for the salvation of others, is daily exposed to dangers and death.

Thus his purpose in this Epistle is to correct the uncorrected, to spur those who have been corrected to further progress, and to humble the pseudo-apostles by commending himself. His method of treatment is as follows: as usual, he begins with a greeting; then, speaking to the perfect, he gives thanks to God for benefits bestowed through grace; afterwards he invites them, by his example, to endure suffering; then, by humbling the pseudo-apostles, he rebukes them, revealing their deceitfulness and commending himself in many ways; finally, a moral admonition is added, together with a repetition of the blessing [Col. 0010A].

In beginning with the greeting, against their false pride he calls himself Paul, and against the presumption of those same persons he calls himself an Apostle, saying: “Paul, an Apostle of Jesus Christ,” not by usurpation but “by the will of God,” not of human beings; for he was neither chosen nor sent by human beings. And “Timothy our brother,” who went with the first Epistle to the Corinthians and reported to the Apostle everything happening among them. He is therefore named here so that they may know that what they do does not escape the Apostle’s notice. Paul, I say, and Timothy write or send this Epistle “to the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints,” that is, with all the holy presbyters, or with all those reborn through the grace of the Holy Spirit, “who are throughout Achaia,” of which Corinth is the capital.

And before all else they greet them in this manner: “Grace and peace be to you,” that is, forgiveness of sins and tranquillity of mind, “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” without whom the Father gives nothing.

“Blessed.” After the greeting, he first speaks to the perfect concerning tribulation, offering himself as an example of patience and of consolation received from God, and turning into praise that which others regard as disgrace. Therefore he says: May God, namely the Creator of all things, “and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” be blessed. Although his glory in himself can neither be increased nor diminished, nevertheless may he be blessed—that is, exalted in his people, among whom he is said to be exalted through their knowledge and progress.

I say, Father of Christ, and through Christ he is also our Father, since we are Christ’s children. He is “the Father of mercies,” fatherly granting us forgiveness of sins, good works, and constancy in tribulation [Col. 0010C]. And he is “the God” who gives all—that is, complete and perfect—consolation, such as it befits God to give to those who suffer for Christ. He rightly says, therefore, “God of all consolation,” that is, perfect consolation, because the consolation is no less than the tribulation.

And that he is the God of consolation is clear from this: he is the one “who consoles us,” his ministers, “in all our tribulation,” that is, of soul and body. He consoles us so greatly that we ourselves, though desolate—that is, deprived of human help—may be able, through the example of our consolation, to console those “who are in every,” that is, any, affliction. I say console “through encouragement,” that is, by such consolation as encourages us to endure greater trials [Col. 0011A]. Hence he adds: “by which we ourselves are encouraged by God,” that is, which God gave not only to console us, but also to encourage us to greater things; and thus our consolation is also able to encourage others.

And truly we can console, “because as the sufferings of Christ,” that is, sufferings inflicted for Christ’s name, or sufferings which we endure in likeness to Christ, “abound in us,” who are, as it were, their place, “so through Jesus Christ our consolation also abounds” no less. For either we are delivered here, or we understand the Father’s love in chastisements, because “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). But all this is for your sake. Hence he adds:

VV. 6–11.—“But whether we are afflicted, it is for your encouragement and salvation; or whether we are consoled, it is for your consolation; or whether we are encouraged, it is for your encouragement and salvation, which works endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer, so that our hope for you may be firm, knowing that, as you are partners in the sufferings, so you will also be partners in the consolation. For we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our tribulation which occurred in Asia: that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were even weary of living. But we ourselves had within ourselves the answer of death, so that we might not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead; who delivered and does deliver us from such great dangers, in whom we hope that he will yet deliver us also, while you too assist by prayer for us, so that from the persons of many faces thanks may be given for us by many on account of the gift which is in us.”

“But whether we are afflicted,” it is for our encouragement and salvation, because by our example God warns us to suffer. Consequently eternal salvation will be ours. Or “whether we are consoled” by hope of the reward, because we understand the Father’s love in chastisements: this too is for our consolation, so that you may hope for the like. Or “whether we are encouraged” to greater things—which comes about either when evils have ended or when the strength of patience is given us—this too is for our encouragement and salvation, namely, that you may be encouraged toward greater things and hope for salvation.

I say, “for salvation, which works,” that is, seeks to work in you—or rather, we seek that it may work in you—“endurance of the same sufferings which we also suffer,” because by our example you ought to endure the same things that we endure. It works so effectively that “our hope,” by which we hope that you will suffer, “may be firm” [Col. 0011D]. I say that we suffer, and this is for you—that is, for your benefit. And it is indeed so, because we know that, just as you are now partners in the sufferings, so in the future you will be partners in eternal consolation, since equal glory will be given in return for our labor.

“For we do not wish”: here he explains his tribulations, so that, when they realize that in comparison with their master they suffer little, they may receive consolation and cease grieving. It is as though he said: I rightly say that we suffer; “for we do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers,” because it benefits you to know about our tribulation. The pseudo-apostles boast of their glory; we, however, boast of the tribulation that occurred to us in Asia. [Ambrose] What do I want you to know about it? That “we were burdened” by the weight of sufferings, and this “beyond measure,” beyond the measure of previous tribulations, and [Col. 0012A] “beyond human strength,” so that we—even we who are accustomed to rejoice in evils—were weary even of living, not merely of speaking or doing other things.

And not only were we weary of living: “we ourselves,” not merely others concerning us, “had,” or received, “the answer,” that is, certainty, “of death,” and this “within ourselves,” because our nature promised nothing but death or failure. He indicates that such an extraordinary violence of wickedness had risen up against the preachers of the faith that death stood before their eyes. For they had been so afflicted that they despaired of their present life.

Yet God permitted us to be afflicted for this reason: “so that we might not trust in ourselves.” For cursed is the one who trusts in a human being, but we should trust only in God, in whom we can safely trust because “he raises the dead.” Compared with that miracle is the fact that he delivered me from those aforesaid dangers. Hence he adds: “Who delivered us from such great dangers,” that is, restored us to safety, “and does deliver us” daily, because God does not deny his protection to his own when they are in need; “in whom,” as we turn toward God with the desire of our minds, “we hope that he will yet,” in the future, “deliver us,” while not only we and others but “you too assist by prayer made for us.”

“So that from many”: it is as though he said: I say that he will yet deliver us, certainly in order that, “from the persons of many faces,” that is, from persons of differing ages converted to God through our preaching, thanks may be given to God for us—that is, for our preaching through which they were converted. What he had said, “from persons of many faces,” he explains by adding: namely, “by many” believers sharing in “the gift which is in us,” that is, possessing the same gift of faith which is in us [Col. 0012C]. By “persons of many faces” he means infants, boys, and all other ages of both sexes.

Or thus: your prayers will help us, so that through many believers thanks may be given to God for us. For what gift are thanks given? Behold: “for the gift which is in us,” that is, for deliverance and other good things. I say, a gift proceeding from persons, that is, from honorable people such as you and others. I say, persons “of many faces,” that is, of discriminations: of distinct merits and diverse virtues. Thus Job’s face was patience, David’s face humility, and Moses’ face meekness.

Or according to another reading. For another translation has: “That in the face of many, for that which is in us,” etc. This reading is understood thus: It is as though he said: Your prayers will help us so that through many thanks may be given to God for us. I say, thanks for “the gift which is in us.” This remains unchanged. I say, let thanks be given “in the face of many,” that is, among many and before many. He says this because God’s grace consoles the Apostles for the sake of many—that is, of all believers—for whose sake his afflictions were also brought upon him. Therefore they—that is, all believers—should give thanks to God for the Apostle’s deliverance.

VV. 12–20.—“For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God, and not in carnal wisdom but in the grace of God, we have conducted ourselves in this world, and more abundantly toward you. For we write to you nothing other than what you have read and known. And I hope that you will know even to the end, just as you have known us in part, because we are your glory, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. And in this confidence I wished first to come to you, that you might have a second grace; and through you to pass into Macedonia, and again from Macedonia to come to you, and by you to be sent onward into Judaea. Therefore, when I had wished this, did I act with fickleness? Or do I consider what I intend according to the flesh, so that with me there may be ‘yes and no’? But God is faithful: our word which was among you does not have in it ‘yes and no,’ but has ‘yes’ in it. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was preached among you through us—through me and Silvanus and Timothy—did not have in him ‘yes and no,’ but ‘yes’ was in him. For however many promises of God there are, in him is ‘yes.’ Therefore also through him is the Amen to God, for your glory.”

“For this is our glory.” It is as though he said: Therefore both you and others ought to pray for us, because our glory, etc. Or connect it thus: Therefore your prayers can help us because this is “your glory,” that is, the thing in which we glory is nevertheless honorable: namely, the testimony, etc. Or connect it thus: Therefore I do not despair of God’s help because my conscience is pure, and I glory in that. Thus he says, “For this is our glory,” that is, this one thing is what we glory in: “the testimony of our conscience,” that is, a conscience pure and free from all pretense, not reproaching us but testifying that “we have conducted ourselves in this world,” where there are so many evils, “in simplicity,” namely, not having one thing in the heart and another on the lips; and “in sincerity,” namely, in the pure truth concerning God, not also preaching observance of the Law. This sincerity and simplicity are “of God,” because they are from God [Col. 0013C].

This is the glory of conscience which he mentioned: simplicity and sincerity. For, just as conscience is a great punishment to the wicked, so it is joy to the godly—not as though they gloried proudly in it, but because they ascribe everything to God. Therefore he rightly does not say, “Our glory is the testimony of another’s malice,” or of lesser grace, but “of our conscience.” Since conscience is hidden, it is not subject to another’s judgment. Therefore let no one presume either to pronounce or to entertain judgment against it.

Thus, I say, we conducted ourselves and acted, “not in carnal wisdom” [Col. 0013D], which is to love pleasures, avoid labors, or preach in accordance with the natures of things and not contrary to them—as the pseudo-apostles preached, whose deceptive preaching, fitted to human understanding, he reproves. We did not conduct ourselves thus, I say, but “in the grace of God,” that is, according as the Holy Spirit freely revealed to me.

“And more abundantly.” It is as though he said: We conducted ourselves simply in this world, but we conducted ourselves more abundantly simply “toward you,” that is, with respect to you or among you. For we yielded our right, because although he received from others, he did not wish to receive from them. “For we write to you nothing other” [Col. 0014A]: it is as though he said: Truly, I observed simplicity toward you more abundantly, because I demanded nothing either in the first Epistle or in this one. This is what he says: “For we write to you nothing other now than what you read” in the first Epistle “and knew” through experience of our deeds.

“And I hope”: it is as though he said: As you have known concerning me thus far, so you will know hereafter. And this is what he says: “I hope that you will know me in the same way even to the end of life.” I say you will know us “just as you have known us in part,” not wholly; for although you know that I abstained, you do not know with how great a love I did this. [Ambrose] Observe that the Apostle hopes they will improve because they had already begun to become better when they recognized his affection for them and gloried in him as children glory in a most beloved father.

“Because we are your glory”: it is as though he said: Truly you will know, because “we are your glory, just as you are ours.” That is, you ought through us to attain eternal glory, and we through your being well instructed [Col. 0014B]; this would not be so if I received from you in a way that caused offense. This glory will appear “on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that is, at the time of judgment, when everything will be open. That is why it is called a day.

“And in this confidence”: it is as though he said: I observed simplicity more abundantly toward you, and “in this confidence,” that is, trusting in this, “I wished,” etc. Or connect it thus: You are our glory and we yours; and “in this confidence,” that is, trusting that we hope to be glorified through one another, “I wished,” etc. Or connect it thus: Some of you have now been corrected; and in this confidence—namely, because the life of certain persons is pure—I wished first to come to you before going to Macedonia. Since the lives of some had been corrected, he wished to see those whom it had been unworthy to see earlier. Therefore, if he did not go when he had wished to, it was not without purpose.

For he wished certain persons among them to understand that it was on their account that he had not carried out his intention; they ought now to take pains to purify themselves. It was not his fault, but theirs, that he did not go. And because he had promised in the former Epistle that he would come and had not come, he seemed false and fickle; this he now excuses. For he did this only because of their fault.

I say that I wished to come so that you, who through the first Epistle had received the grace of right faith, might have through my presence a second grace—that is, confirmation, since you had already possessed faith. I wished to come to you, I say, and “through you,” that is, under your guidance, “to pass into Macedonia,” and again “from Macedonia to come to you,” so that I might confirm you repeatedly, and “by you to be sent onward” [Col. 0014D] “into Judaea,” in order to carry alms to the saints there.

“Therefore, when.” It is as though he said: I wished to come to you for this purpose, yet I did not come. “Therefore, when I had wished this and did not do it, did I act with fickleness?” Did I set aside with the same fickleness, not by reason but by an impulse of mind, what I had proposed? Or do I consider things to be done or left undone “according to the flesh,” so that I proposed this for fleshly advantage and abandoned it because that advantage was absent—so that there might be with me, that is, in my intention, “yes and no,” that is, affirmation and denial regarding the same thing: in other words, falsehood?

[Augustine] For a lie is a false signification of speech with an intention to deceive. Two charges were laid against the Apostle: that he was fickle and that he had abandoned this journey for the sake of greater advantage [Col. 0015A]. [Ambrose] Hence he was also called a liar. He now clears himself, showing that he acted not lightly but deliberately, and did not lie, because when he said it he did not intend to do otherwise. For one who states falsely what he believes to be true is not to be judged a liar: insofar as he is concerned, he does not deceive, but is deceived. [Note: [Col. 0015D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Conversely, the person who says what is true but believes it false lies; nor is the one who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth, while knowing it not to be true, free from lying: by his will he lies.

Or thus, “so that there may be.” It is as though he said: Did I act with fickleness, or do I consider according to the flesh, “so that with me there may be yes and no,” that is, so that I may prefer my will to advantage? [Ambrose] It is as though he said: With me there is not “yes and no,” that is, I did nothing other than what I knew ought to be done, because advantage must be preferred to will.

“But God is faithful,” or “for”: it is as though he said: I should not be believed to have lied in this matter, because I have lied to you in nothing else. And this can be believed because God is faithful, that is, truthful, who promised teachers of truth. If, therefore, I who am his teacher were a liar, he would not be faithful. And because he is faithful, this is clear from the fact that in him, etc.

Or thus: It appears that with me there is “yes and no,” but God, who is faithful—that is, truthful in his promise—is my witness in this: that “in our whole word,” which was our word among you, there is not “yes and no,” that is, falsehood, as there is in the speech of pseudo-preachers. Or, “there is not in it yes and no,” that is, I did nothing other than what I knew ought to be done, because advantage must be preferred to will.

“For the Son of God”: it is as though he said: Truly “yes and no” was not in our word, because in that Son of God—that is, in his preaching—who is the Son of God, Jesus Christ, preached among you through us, namely through me, Silvanus, and Timothy, there was not “yes and no,” that is, falsehood; but there was “yes,” that is, only affirmation of truth. If we were liars, then he would be so too, because we preach only what he taught. Or, in that Son of God there was not “yes and no,” that is, he never willed anything other than what was advantageous. But “yes” was in him, because his will was always joined to advantage.

“For however many.” [Note: [Col. 0015D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] It is as though he said: The Son of God is truthful, and truly so, because however many promises of God there are, “in him is yes,” or, according to another reading, they are truth and [Col. 0015D] fulfillment, because they were manifested and fulfilled in him.

[Note: [Col. 0016D] Augustine, *On Christian Combat*.] Therefore those who say that the Son of God did not assume a true human being, nor was born from a woman, but displayed to those who saw him false flesh and a feigned image of a body, are not to be heard. They rush into this error because they fear what cannot happen: namely, that the truth and substance of God might be defiled by human flesh; and thus they say that truth lied. Yet they declare that this visible sun spreads its rays through every filth and impurity, and keeps them pure and unstained. If, therefore, visible clean things can touch visible unclean things and not be defiled, how much more did invisible and unchangeable [Col. 0016A] truth, assuming the whole human being through the spirit into the soul and through the soul into the body, deliver the assumed whole human being from every weakness without contamination to itself?

Therefore they lie; Christ, the Truth, does not lie, because all God’s promises are in him, namely, “yes,” or also—that is, fulfilled and confirmed. Nor should it be believed that he is a liar through whom the Father appeared truthful. And because God’s promises have been fulfilled through Christ, therefore through him we say “Amen” to God. [Ambrose] This is a word of truth: that is, we say that God is truthful; and the fact that God the Father and Christ are truthful is for our glory, through whom we are thereby proved to preach truth.

VV. 21–23.—“But he who confirms us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; he who also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. But I call God as witness upon my soul that it was in sparing you that I did not come again to Corinth—not because we lord it over your faith, but because we are helpers of your joy. For you stand by faith.”

“But he who confirms us”: I speak of our glory, yet I do not ascribe it to ourselves. Rather, it is God who confirms us Jews “with you,” because the Gentiles too have been confirmed with the Jews. I say confirmed “in Christ,” that is, in the true preaching of Christ. Thus, if you are firm in Christ, this makes us, through whom you are made firm, still more manifest. And it is God “who anointed us” as kings and priests through the Spirit given in baptism. [Ambrose] Hence Peter says: “We are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 0016C].

And it is God “who sealed us,” that is, inscribed us in the book of life. Or, “sealed us,” that is, set us apart from others by the sign of the cross; and “gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts,” that is, the Holy Spirit as the earnest of future glory. For if he has entrusted his Spirit even to those still mortal, there is no doubt that he will grant glory to them once immortal. Or, “he gave the pledge of the Holy Spirit,” that is, gifts which are the pledge that the Holy Spirit is in us.

“But I”: here he explains why he did not go to them as he had said, lest they think themselves despised because he postponed going to them. He intended to go when he found nearly all of them already corrected. For he now speaks to those who seemed willing to correct themselves but did not exert themselves to bring it about. I did not abandon this either through fickleness or for worldly advantage, but “in sparing you”; and concerning this “I call God as witness,” not only against my body but even “upon”—that is, against—my soul, if I lie. Concerning what? Namely, that I did not come to Corinth “again,” beyond the first occasion. Or, “again,” that is, after I had departed from you. And I did this in sparing you, namely, lest I grieve many by reproving them harshly. In this he spared them, lest they turn, in their greater harshness, to sedition [Col. 0016D].

Therefore he first wishes them to be softened and corrected; consequently he did not fulfill what he had arranged either through fickleness or carnal deliberation. For a spiritual person does not carry out what has been arranged when he more wisely plans something for salvation. And lest they take offense as though he were their lord because he had said, “In sparing you I did not come,” he adds: I do not say “in sparing” because “we lord it over your faith,” that is, because your faith endures lordship and compulsion; for it belongs to the will, not to necessity. Rather, I say it because we are, if you are willing to cooperate, “helpers of your eternal joy.” Or, “of your joy,” that is, of your correction, because when corrected they will rejoice.

I rightly spoke of “your faith,” for “by faith,” which works through love, “you stand,” not by lordship.

CHAPTER TWO.

VV. 1–11.—“But I determined this with myself: not to come again to you in sorrow. For if I grieve you, then who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved because of me? And I wrote this very thing to you so that, when I come, I may not have sorrow upon sorrow from those concerning whom I ought to have rejoiced, being confident concerning you all that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much tribulation and anguish of heart I wrote to you through many tears, not that you might be grieved, but that you might know the love which I have more abundantly for you. But if anyone has grieved me, he has not grieved me alone, but in part—not to burden you all. Sufficient for such a person is this rebuke, which was inflicted by the many; so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and console him, lest perhaps one such as this be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Therefore I beseech you to confirm your love toward him. For this also is why I wrote: that I might know the proof of you, whether you are obedient in all things. But whatever you have forgiven anyone, I forgive also. For what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, I have done for your sake in the person of Christ, lest we be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices.”

“But I determined.” It is as though he said: In sparing you I did not come, but “I determined this very thing with myself,” that is, the same thing which I had proposed when I sent the first Epistle: namely, not to come to you again “in sorrow,” that is, so as to grieve you. [Ambrose] Or, not to come again to you in my tribulation, which would be a second sorrow to me, just as it had been when he heard of their sins.

And truly I have sorrow because of your sins, since I have joy because of your repentance. And truly: “For if I grieve you” by correcting or rebuking, in whatever way, whether by letter or in person—something must be supplied here. It is as though he said: And if you grieve me, “who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved because of me?” It is as though he said: No one makes me glad except the one who is grieved because of me—that is, according to my will, namely, by repenting; and this is better accomplished through a letter than in person.

“And I wrote this very thing,” namely, that no one makes me glad except the one who is grieved because of me, “to you now, so that when I come I may not have,” from you, “sorrow,” arising from your lack of correction, “upon sorrow,” which I have for your sins; although concerning you, that is, concerning you, “I ought to have rejoiced,” not only now, but earlier too, when you were grieved and sinned so gravely. The Apostle’s joy, however, is the purification of the people.

I say that I wrote, “being confident concerning you all” that I shall no longer have sorrow concerning you [Col. 0018A], because you will be corrected. See, therefore, that I do not trust in vain: then joy will not be mine with you. And you ought to do what pertains to my joy, because “my joy is the joy of you all,” that is, when I rejoice, you rejoice.

“For,” etc. It is as though he said: I say that I had sorrow, and truly so; for “out of much tribulation,” that is, from many labors, namely watching and praying for you, “and anguish of heart,” namely care and grief, “I wrote to you” the first Epistle, “through many tears,” which showed what was within. Yet I mention this not so that you may be grieved by remembering those things, but so that you may know “what love,” that is, what desire for your correction, I have—or possess.

I say, a love displayed toward you more abundantly than you had thought, because the Apostle loved everyone, including those he rebuked, as himself [Col. 0018B]. For this was why he rebuked them: to show the love with which he loved them, grieving over their sins more than they themselves did. But whoever does not rebuke a brother with this disposition grieves him; for one who does not grieve with his brother insults him. Or: that you may know the love which I have more abundantly in you than that displayed toward others, for whose sake I yielded my right.

But if anyone. [Ambrose] Here he commands that fornicator whom he had judged should be handed over to Satan to be received back, because he had been corrected. As if he were saying: I wrote to you through tears; nevertheless, forgive him. Thus he says: “But if anyone has caused me sorrow,” as that fornicator certainly did, “he has not grieved me only, but you also in part,” that is, not all of you. I say this so as not to burden you all, that is, so as not to impose this burden on everyone [Col. 0018C]: this is said reproachfully. For all ought to have been sorrowful. Or, I say “in part” so as not to burden all of you: he burdens only those who did not grieve over the sin, not those who did grieve, whom he indicates by saying “in part”; although he has grieved both me and you.

Yet for one such as he is, that is, one who has sinned so gravely, this rebuke is sufficient, because such a person would easily despair if he were punished too severely. Although the rebuke, in view of the magnitude of the temptation or in some other respect, may seem an insufficient penalty, nevertheless it is not to be thought slight when it is imposed by many, by whom, when assembled, he was handed over to Satan. [Augustine] He therefore suffers great pain if he sees many horrified by his offence [Col. 0018D]. Thus it is sufficient that he was rebuked by many, so that, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him; for the more persons rebuke him, the more he ought to be forgiven. And comfort him, [Ambrose] by the example of David, who sinned greatly, and of others to whom pardon was granted; and by the words of the Lord speaking through the prophet: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 33). And again: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18).

And rightly he commands that a man afflicted on account of sin be forgiven and helped, because repentance, if it comes from a true disposition—that is, if, once corrected, he immediately grieves in his mind—at once bears fruit. For true repentance is to cease from sin. Therefore forgive and comfort him [Col. 0019A], lest perhaps one such as he, despairing through excessive sorrow—that is, through an overly harsh penance—be swallowed up by the devil, so that he may wish to make use of the world. For this is to be swallowed up: namely, for one in despair to turn to committing sins. Therefore, lest he be swallowed up, I, who could command, beg you to confirm toward him, by forgiving him, the love which you had shown in putting him out; and this you ought indeed to do.

For this reason I also wrote to you: namely, that I might know the proof of you, that is, that I might learn by experience with what disposition you acted, since I had already proved your obedience in part. And that I might know whether you are obedient to me in all things. As if he said: Since I wrote concerning his reception, I also wrote for this reason: that I, having proved you obedient to me [Col. 0019B] in expelling him, might know whether you are obedient in all things.

“But to whom…” As if he said: I beg you to forgive him, and you ought to forgive him; moreover—that is, because—to whom you have forgiven anything, I also forgive. What I say is true: for what I have forgiven, if indeed I have forgiven anything, I did for your sake. I said “if indeed I have forgiven anything” because this was not done rashly or indiscriminately. Therefore, if the master, at the request of his disciples, forgave the sin of one whom they wished forgiven, much more ought the disciples, at the master’s entreaty, to do the same.

And so that he might show before God that it was ratified for the one whom he forgave, he adds: “And I did this in the person of Christ,” that is, as though Christ himself were granting pardon, because the Apostle did nothing apart from God’s Spirit. He says this lest such forgiveness, granted for friends’ sake, should seem ineffective. “That we may not…” [Col. 0019C] As if he said: For this reason we ought to forgive, lest we be outwitted—that is, deceived—by Satan, who might cause him to despair through excessive severity. For he often hurls the weak into despair because of harsher punishments. And rightly do I fear this from him. For we are not ignorant of his thoughts, that is, his devices: those whom he cannot deceive by agreement, he makes harsh by threats.

**Verses 12–17.—**“But when I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest for my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother; but, taking leave of them, I went on into Macedonia. But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus, and through us makes manifest in every place the fragrance of his knowledge; because we are Christ’s sweet fragrance to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. To some indeed a fragrance of death unto death, but to others a fragrance of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not, like very many, adulterating the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God, before God, in Christ we speak.”

“But when I came,” etc. After the digression concerning the reception of the adulterer, he returns to them, showing that, just as it was their fault that he did not come to Corinth, so also his lack of success at Troas resulted from Titus’s being detained among them. Without Titus they could not make progress there, since perhaps Titus could use their language more distinctly [Col. 0020A].

As if he said: Sparing you, I did not come to Corinth. But when I came to Troas to preach the Gospel of Christ, and a door was opened to me—that is, hearts were prepared to receive the Gospel—and this in the Lord, that is, with God cooperating, I had no rest for my spirit, that is, I could not satisfy my desire, because I did not find Titus my brother, who was necessary there. But, being detained among you, he did not come there, as both he and I had agreed.

[Ambrose] And therefore the Apostle could not fulfil his desire: namely, to impart the Gospel fully to them, because of those clamouring against him and rising up against him. Alone he could not accomplish both tasks: instructing the faithful and resisting the clamouring unbelievers. [Note: [Col. 0019D] Aug., *On the Predestination of Knowledge*.] I had no rest, I say; but, taking leave of those who had been converted and in whom a door had been opened, I went into Macedonia.

“But thanks be to God.” Up to this point he has treated of tribulations, inviting them to endure them, and has said through whose fault he had not come to Corinth. Here he begins to commend himself and to abase the false apostles. As if he said: I went to Macedonia, but not fruitlessly, because there I stood forth as a kind of triumphal victor. But I give thanks to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ Jesus, [Ambrose] that is, in the preaching of Christ, who prepares hearts for faith, so that, when unbelief has been trodden down, faith may possess its trophy, while unbelievers become believers. And through us—the true apostles, not through the false—he makes manifest [Col. 0020C] the fragrance of his knowledge: that is, Christ, who, like a fragrance proceeding from the Father, makes him known though he is invisible, just as something which is not seen is known by its fragrance and its location perceived.

Or, “the fragrance of his knowledge” means miracles or words of teaching by which one comes to know him. He makes this known through us, working miracles and preaching words, and this in every place—that is, wherever we preach, throughout the whole world. And rightly did I say “through us,” because we are the sweet fragrance of Christ, most pleasing to God, even if not so to you. The apostles are called Christ’s fragrance because Christ is displayed, not blasphemed, in their life and preaching; as is said of the wicked: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through us” (Rom. 2).

Observe that the Apostle takes his manner of speech from the old law when he says, “a sweet fragrance to God.” For as a legal sacrifice was once called a most pleasing fragrance to God, so now true preaching and the sincere reputation of the apostles are so called.

119. [Note: [Col. 0019D] Id., on Psalm 42.] This sweet fragrance is signified by the naming of certain spices and ointments. For the bride of the Lord says: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” [Note: [Col. 0020D] Id., in a sermon on the birthday of a martyr.] (Song 1). Because of this fragrance the Gospel says that, when the alabaster flask of ointment was broken, the house was filled with fragrance (Mark 14): that is, the world was filled with the good repute and teaching of Christ and the apostles. This fragrance gives life to those who love; it kills those who envy. [Note: [Col. 0020D] Id., on John.] Hence he adds, “Among those who,” etc. [Col. 0021A] As if he said: We are Christ’s sweet fragrance, both among those who are saved by his grace and among those who perish by his judgment; and this with respect both to those who are thereby saved and those who, despising it, perish, because we act with good intention and preach the truth. [Note: [Col. 0021D] Aug., *On Predestination*.] [Note: [Col. 0021D] Id., on John.]

In a wondrous manner it happens that, by one sweet fragrance, the good live and the evil die. How this happens, however, I shall not refuse to disclose to you insofar as the Lord deigns to inspire me. The Apostle, acting well and living well, preached righteousness in word, demonstrated it in deed, and spread his good reputation everywhere, imitating Christ, the teacher of truth. But some loved and others envied. Those who envied the reputation of Christ or Paul perished by the sweet fragrance; those who loved it lived by the sweet fragrance. Therefore do not envy [Col. 0021B], and the sweet fragrance will not kill you. Certainly it was a sweet fragrance by which these lived and those perished. For if there were no brightness in the saints, the envy of the ungodly would not arise. [Note: [Col. 0022D] Id., *On the Birthday of a Martyr*.] The fragrance of the saints began to suffer persecution; but if, by persecuting, they break the vial, the fragrance of the ointment spreads more widely.

“To others,” as if he said, we are a sweet fragrance to God; but to human beings, to some we are indeed a fragrance of death, that is, of envy and evil opinion leading them to eternal death; but to others we are a fragrance of life, that is, of love and good opinion leading them to eternal life. For from our preaching of truth death proceeds for some, [Augustine] when it is heard in unbelief, and they thereby fall into eternal condemnation; [Col. 0021C] for others, life, when it is received in faith and they thereby advance toward eternal salvation.

“And who is sufficient for these things?” As if he said: We are Christ’s fragrance, and through us God performs these things. And who among those false apostles is so sufficient for these tasks as we true apostles are? As if he said: No one. And truly so: for we are not adulterating the word of God, that is, mixing falsehood into it and preaching for our own will rather than for the offspring, as very many do. Here he touches upon the false apostles, who violated truth with corrupt teaching. Of them Isaiah says: “Your wine-sellers mix water with wine” (Isa. 1). [Ambrose] But we speak God’s word from sincerity—that is, from a sincere intention, not for profit and without any mixture of corruption—as we learned from God, who taught us. And [Col. 0021D] we do this before God, that is, for his cause alone, to please him; and in Christ, never going beyond him, as those do who act from the law by preaching legal observances.

## Chapter III

**Verses 1–3.—**“Are we beginning again to commend ourselves? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you or from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all people; made manifest that you are Christ’s letter, ministered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.”

“Are we beginning?” The Apostle knew that they took his self-commendation badly, as they had also done in the first Epistle, as though he were seeking his own glory. He begins to show, against their opinion, that he seeks not his own glory but God’s, saying: “Are we beginning,” as though we were always novices in this, “again,” as in the first Epistle, “to commend ourselves” with these praises, and not God? As if he said: Is there anyone who lays this charge against us? Far be it that we should do this. We do not say these things in vain self-commendation, but are compelled to mention them lest you be deceived by others.

That we do not intend to commend ourselves is clear from this: we never seek letters of recommendation from anyone, nor do we need them. This is what he adds in the form of a question [Col. 0022B]: “Or”—that is, do we need, or do you think that we need—letters of recommendation sent by others to you, or from you to others, as some do, that is, the false apostles, whom no virtue commends? Certainly we do not need them, because you are our letter—that is, our instruction—in whom my knowledge and life are represented to others. Therefore we do not need a letter of recommendation.

And this letter is written in our hearts, because we always care for you. This letter is known by all people, for they know that you were instructed through us; and it is read by the same persons, because in you they learn to imitate us. You are our letter, and you are the same letter. You are made manifest to all as Christ’s letter, because, while you are like me in Christ—Or, you are Christ’s letter because Christ principally wrote you, that is, instructed you, not I; for faith is in you through him as author.

And this letter is ministered by us, because God works in you through our ministry; and it is written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God, that is, the eternal Spirit. What the living one writes lives: that is, the fact that you are a representation of Christ and of me is firmly written in your hearts and will not be erased, whereas what is written with ink is easily erased.

Or, it is written “not with ink,” that is, not with the dark marks of heretical perversity, as the false apostles do, who insert heresies, but with the Spirit of the living God [Note: [Col. 0022D] Id., *On Baptism Against the Donatists*.]: that is, you have been instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured out in hearts and who in the Gospel is called the finger of God [Col. 0022D] (Luke 11). The old law was written with this finger, but there is a difference: that law was written on tablets of stone, while the new law has been poured into hearts.

[Augustine] This law is the love of God. That is the law of works, the letter killing the transgressor; this is the law of faith, giving life to the lover. There, then, the law was set outside, that the unjust might be frightened; here it is set within, that they might be justified. There the finger of God worked on tablets of stone, signifying the hardness of their hearts; here the same finger has worked in human hearts, signifying a ready will and an understanding capable of receiving. Hence he adds: And this [Col. 0023A] letter is written not on tablets of stone—that is, not in hard hearts bearing marks but not feeling them, as in the old law [Note: [Col. 0023D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*]. For stone signifies only a will most hard and inflexible toward God—but on tablets of the heart, that is, hearts made broad by love, and “fleshly,” that is, soft, because they have the power to carry out what is required; and endowed with understanding, because they understand, not stony as though without perception.

**Verses 4–6.—**“And such confidence we have through Christ toward God: not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God, who has also made us sufficient ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

[Col. 0023B] “Confidence.” He said that he does not need letters; now he says that he commends not himself but Christ. As if he said: You are Christ’s letter and ours, but such confidence—that is, confidence to say these things—we have, that is, we refer it not to ourselves but to God. [Ambrose] He says this to show that the ancients did not have this confidence toward God, because their ministry was inferior. And we have this confidence through Christ, through whom this power has been given to us.

I say that we have confidence, and I do not say that we have it because we are sufficient to think even anything good from ourselves—that is, from our own side, as though it defended us. As if he said: Let it proceed from ourselves. Rather, our sufficiency is from God. [Note: [Col. 0023D] Id., *On the Predestination of the Saints*.] Let those who suppose that the beginning of faith is from us and the completion of faith from God attend to and consider these words. For, commending this grace, which is not given according to any merits but produces all good merits, he says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything,” etc.

For who does not see that thinking comes before believing? No one believes anything unless he first thinks it ought to be believed, although believing itself is nothing other than thinking with assent. Therefore, if good thinking is not from us, neither is believing; rather, the sufficiency by which we begin to believe is from God. [Ambrose] See how he places God above apostolic dignity.

“Who has also made us sufficient.” Here likewise is commendation. He commends himself through the dignity of his office, namely that of the Gospel, preferring himself not only to the false apostles who preached carnal observances, but even to Moses himself, the minister of the law. As if he said: Our sufficiency is from God, who also made us ministers of the New Testament; the false apostles are ministers of the Old. Ministers, I say, made perfect in knowledge and life, such as the false apostles are not. Ministers of the New Testament, I say, which does not consist in a letter that merely teaches, but in the Spirit who helps and is given through us, that is, through our ministry.

“For the letter…” As if he said: Therefore God made us ministers of the New Testament through the Spirit, not through the letter, because the letter without the Spirit kills, by causing knowing sin and adding transgression; it incites all the more, especially after Christ’s coming. But the Spirit gives life, because it makes one understand spiritually and fulfil what the letter commands. [Note: [Col. 0023D] Id., *On Baptism Against the Donatists*.]

Observe what he calls the letter that kills, against which he places, as its contrary, the life-giving Spirit. It is certainly the Decalogue written on those two tablets, because “the law entered in, that the offence might abound” (Rom. 5). [Note: [Col. 0023D] Id., in the same work.] Yet these commandments are so useful and wholesome for one who performs them that, unless one performs them, one cannot have life. Therefore the letter is not called killing because the law is evil, but because, while forbidding sin, it does not give life to a person; rather, it increases desire and sin and piles up transgression unless grace sets one free through the law of faith.

It is therefore clear that the oldness of the letter, if the newness of the Spirit is absent, makes people guilty through knowledge of sin rather than frees them from sin. Hence he adds: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1), not because the law itself is evil, but because the good commandment is only demonstrated in the letter, not aided by the Spirit. If that commandment is performed from fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness, it is performed slavishly, not freely; and therefore it is not performed. For no fruit is good which does not rise from the root of love.

[Augustine] But if faith working through love is present, delight in the good arises; this is a gift not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills without the helping Spirit; but when the life-giving Spirit is present, it causes what was written within to be loved, whereas the law written outside caused it to be feared. [Note: [Col. 0024D] Id., *Against Faustus*.] [Col. 0024C] The true bride of Christ understands the difference between letter and Spirit, which are also called, in another way, law and grace. Nor is the law blamed when it is said, “The letter kills,” etc., any more than knowledge is blamed when it is said: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8).

Therefore the law is good when accompanied by grace, just as knowledge is beneficial when joined with love, though without it knowledge kills. Thus the law without grace kills, though it is the power of sin; yet even so it is not evil. For many things are harmful to certain persons although they are not evil. Thus the law, though without grace it does not give life, is nevertheless not evil. [Note: [Col. 0024D] Id., to Anastasius.] When it commands what cannot be fulfilled without grace, it shows the person that he is weak, so that, once his weakness is displayed, he may seek grace. Thus the law leads to faith [Col. 0024D]; faith obtains the more generous Spirit, who pours out the love that fulfils the law. Without the Spirit the human will is not free, since it is conquered by desires. [Note: [Col. 0024D] Id., *On Rebuke and Grace*.]

For we must confess that we have free choice both to do good and to do evil. But in doing evil the will is indeed free; for good, however, it is not free unless it has been set free by him who said: “If the Son shall set you free, you shall truly be free” (John 8).

**Verses 7–11.—**“But if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance—which is being done away—how shall not the ministry of the Spirit be much more in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation is in glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. For what was made glorious has not been glorified in this respect, because of the surpassing glory. For if that which is being done away is through glory, much more that which remains is in glory.”

“But if…” As if he said: God made us ministers of the Gospel, and this ministry will be for us in eternal glory. He proves this from the lesser case, namely the Old Testament. As if he said: It truly will be in glory, because the ministry of death [Augustine]—that is, the old law, which punished the sinner with bodily death, or which brought death upon transgressors [Col. 0025B] whom God’s grace did not help to fulfil righteousness—was *deformata*, that is, “shapelessly formed” or dishonourably fashioned, because according to the letter it commanded unseemly things. Or *deformata* means fully written, if someone understood it spiritually; “on stones,” that is, on tablets of stone in the literal sense, or in hearts hard to understand or love.

It was in glory in Moses, the minister of that law, so that the children of Israel could not direct their sight to Moses’ face, because they were unworthy. For, stained by sin, they could not look upon the face of Moses descending from the mountain after receiving the law on tablets, because his face had become glorious. Hence he adds: “Because of the glory of his countenance,” that is, the brightness of his countenance, which signified that he saw clearly what they could not approach; which glory [Col. 0025C] is being done away, because it immediately passed from Moses and is no longer present in the ministers of the old law.

Or this may be said mystically: by Moses’ face the spiritual understanding of the law is meant; by the glory of his face, the legal observances, which were figures of truth. As if he said: Moses’ law was thus in glory, that the children of Israel—that is, the Jews—could not gaze upon his face, [Ambrose] that is, could not grasp the spiritual understanding of the law, because they did not understand Christ in the law. And this was because of the glory of his countenance, that is, the legal ceremonies performed to signify Christ. But, still carnal, they did not understand Christ in them; this was signified by the veil placed over Moses’ face.

[Augustine] This glory of Moses is done away because the figures attain their end when truth is revealed through Christ. [Col. 0025D] And so Moses’ glory is done away through the law of the Spirit, when people, having received forgiveness of sins and become righteous, can behold God’s glory, as Peter and the others saw on the mountain (Matt. 17). Therefore Moses’ glory is done away because it is a figure, not the truth.

[Ambrose] Moses’ glory is like the stars in the evening, which are then glorious; Christ’s glory is like the rising sun, which obscures the stars. [Note: [Col. 0025D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*.] The glory of Moses’ countenance was a figure of the truth which is done away, because, when the emperor arrives, his images are removed from public view. An image is looked upon where the emperor is not present. [Augustine] But where he is present, the image is removed; the emperor’s presence shines forth.

“How shall not much more,” etc.? As if he said [Col. 0026A]: The ministry of the old law was in glory for Moses; and if that is so, how shall the ministry of the Spirit—that is, of the New Testament, in which the Spirit is given—not much more be in eternal glory? As if he said: This cannot be denied.

“For if…” As if he said: It truly will be in eternal glory because it gives the righteousness of the Spirit who is given in it; this he proves from the lesser case. For if the ministry of condemnation—that is, the Old Testament—is in Moses’ glory: the Old Testament is called a ministry of condemnation because it made all persons transgressors, not giving them life through grace; or because it inflicted temporal death upon sinners. And if so, much more does the ministry of righteousness—that is, the New Testament, through which the Spirit is given, through whom come righteousness and the perfection of virtues—abound in glory, that is, gives abundant [Col. 0026B] glory to its ministers and observers.

[Ambrose] Or, it is more in glory—that is, in praise—to God than the Old Testament, because God’s glory is shown more in salvation than in death. Although he justly condemns what was done under the law, nevertheless it contributes more to praise if he forgives so that the guilty person may correct himself; this he grants by grace in the New Testament.

“For not even…” As if he said: It truly abounds in glory, because in comparison with it the former glory ought not even to be called glory. This is what he says: “For what shone,” that is, Moses, “in this respect,” already mentioned, namely in his face, has not been glorified. Or: it has not been glorified because of the surpassing glory, which belongs to the New Testament, where the pure see God’s glory. That is, compared with this surpassing glory, Moses’ countenance brought no benefit to anyone, but harm—though through their fault, not his. But this glory is far greater; it abounds in grace, so that persons purified by grace, with darkness wiped away, may see God’s glory.

Or read it thus: “What shone is not glory,” that is, it is not glory in this respect, namely with regard to our part. Why? Because of the surpassing glory which is here. For that former glory was as great as ought to be ascribed to a servant; this one is as great as belongs to the Begetter of Christ, because Christ is in the Father’s glory. Thus the difference between Moses’ glory and Christ’s is as great as that between image and truth.

For if that which is being done away—that is, the Old Testament—was through glory, that is, was ministered and received through Moses’ glory, without which it would not be commended, much [Col. 0026D] more that which remains—that is, the New Testament, called remaining because no other testament will succeed it—is in glory: eternal glory for us, because we are ministers of the New Testament and are certain of so great a glory.

**Verses 12–18.—**“Having therefore such hope, we use great confidence. And not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel should not gaze upon his face, which is being done away; but their minds were dulled. For even to this day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is done away in Christ. But even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is laid over their heart. But when he shall have turned to God, the veil shall be removed. Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Spirit of the Lord.”

“Having therefore such hope,” namely of seeing God’s glory, “we use great confidence,” that is, we exercise ourselves in good works, from which confidence grows in us. For we shall see as much as we believe; and because the glory is open, we do not conceal our understanding, as Moses placed a veil by means of legal figures over his face—that is, over the clear and spiritual understanding—whereas we speak openly.

[Ambrose] He placed it so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face, that is, the spiritual understanding of the law, because on account of sin they could not endure it. That veil is now done away, that is, removed, through grace by our expositions. But their minds were dulled: their reason is blunt and cannot penetrate so long as they do not believe. This dullness has come upon them because of unbelief; therefore, when they are converted to faith, the mind’s sight is sharpened so that they may see the splendour of divine light.

“To this day.” As if he said: The Jews’ minds are dulled. And truly so, because not only then, but even to this day—that is, even today, when truth shines clearly—the same veil remains, because they understand no differently now than before Christ’s coming. It remains, I say, in the reading of the Old Testament—that is, while the Old Testament is read to them—and it remains so fully that it has not even been revealed to them that there is a veil [Col. 0027C], which is done away only in Christ, that is, in faith in Christ.

[Augustine] Thus, in Christ’s passion, the veil of the temple was torn, signifying that through Christ’s passion the mysteries of the law and prophecy are revealed. He calls it a veil in respect of prophecy’s operation, so that it should not be understood.

“But even…” As if he said: The veil is removed for those who are in Christ, but a veil is laid over the hearts of those who deny Christ. As if he said: A weight—that is, blindness—is in their hearts, weighing down their reason. This is so although Moses—that is, the Old Testament—is read, that is, expounded to them. And thus two things hinder them from understanding: both a veil, that is, obscurity, lies in the reading [Col. 0027D], and blindness over their hearts. And this is so even to this day, that is, until today.

“But when…” As if he said: A veil lies in the reading of the Old Testament and in their heart; but when one of them turns, by believing, to God—that is, to Christ—the veil will be removed when the Holy Spirit is given, so that it may be understood that wine lies hidden in water. For every prophecy, when Christ is not understood, is something tasteless and foolish.

“Now the Lord is the Spirit.” The order of the words is this: As if he said: I rightly said that the veil is removed through the Spirit, because the Holy Spirit is Lord—that is, able to do what he wills—and by this he enlightens whom he wills [Col. 0028A] and leaves whom he wills in darkness. [Note: [Col. 0027D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] Observe that the Holy Spirit is here called Lord. And lest anyone suppose that the Son is meant by the name “Lord,” and that “Spirit” is said because of an incorporeal substance, he adds: “And where…” As if he said: The Spirit is Lord; and wherever the Spirit of the Lord—that is, of the Son, through whom he is given—is present by indwelling grace, there is freedom: freedom to understand and to act. Therefore the Jews, who do not have the Spirit, cannot understand freely as we can.

Or thus: therefore, when one turns to the Lord, the veil will be removed, because the Lord, namely Christ, to whom they will turn, is Spirit—that is, a spiritual essence. Therefore he gives the law of the Spirit through faith in the mind, and so causes spiritual understanding. Hence he adds: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is,” [Ambrose] [Col. 0028B] that is, the law of the Spirit which the Lord gives, not written in letters but inwardly imparted to souls through faith, there is freedom.

“But we all,” etc. As if he said: They have a veil over their hearts; but we believers, all of us, even the least, with unveiled face—that is, with an unobstructed reason, whereas the Jews have a veil—are beholding as in a mirror, that is, seeing through the mirror of reason, the glory of the Lord, that is, the glorious Lord. [Note: [Col. 0027D] Id., *On the Trinity*, book XV.]

If it is asked what this “beholding” is like, and whence it is so called, one should recall that in a mirror nothing is seen except an image. Wherever there is a mirror, images of things appear. A watchtower (*specula*), however, is that from whose height one looks out upon something farther away. Therefore he says *speculantes* (“beholding”) from *speculum* (“mirror”), not from *specula* (“watchtower”); this is unambiguous in the Greek from which this Scripture was translated into Latin [Col. 0028C]. It is quite clear that he said *speculantes*, that is, “seeing through the mirror of reason—which is the image of God”—not “looking out from a watchtower.” Therefore we strive, through this image, that is, through the reason which we are, that is, in which we were created, somehow to see him by whom we were made, as through a mirror.

But when he adds, “We are transformed into the same image,” he surely means the image of God. By saying “the same,” he means precisely the image which we behold, because the image of God and the glory of God are the same: that is, he takes “image” and “glory” of God as the same thing—[Augustine] the glorious God—just as above, when speaking of the created image, he treated image and glory as identical, saying: “Man indeed is the image and [Col. 0028D] glory of God.” [Note: [Col. 0028D] Id., in the same work.]

“We are transformed,” he says: that is, we are changed from form to form, passing from an obscure form to a radiant form, since even that obscure form is itself the image of God. This is the image in which human beings were created, by which they rule over the other animals. When this creature, the most excellent among created things, is justified from impiety by its Creator, it is changed from a misshapen form into a beautiful form. For nature was good even amid vices. Therefore he adds, “from glory to glory”: namely, from the glory of creation to the glory of justification. Or, from the glory of faith, in which we are children of God, to the glory of sight, in which we shall be like him when we see him as he is.

And he adds, “as from the Spirit of the Lord” [Col. 0029A], thereby showing that the good of so desirable a transformation is bestowed upon us by God’s grace. Yet at some time this image will attain its perfection. A good teacher instructs us to attain it, saying: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding”—that is, looking through the mirror of reason—“the glory of the Lord,” that is, the glorious Lord, “are transformed,” that is, we pass from form to form, [Augustine] tending from the obscure to the radiant, into that same image which is the glory we behold and hope for: so that we may be the image of God, [Ambrose] that is, gods, that is, that we may be like Christ’s glory for ever. As John says: “We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3). [Augustine] I mean that we go from the glory, or brightness, of creation [Col. 0029B] to the glory, or brightness, of justification; or from the glory of faith to the glory of sight. We are transformed, I say, as led by the Spirit of the Lord, because we receive this benefit from the grace of God. [Note: [Col. 0029D] Aug., *On the Trinity*.]

But when, by this transformation, the image has been renewed unto perfection, we shall be like God. [Ambrose] Or thus: “We are transformed,” I say, being transferred from the glory, or brightness, of Moses to the brightness, or glory, of Christ, as by the Spirit of the Lord—as though this glory were such as it befits the Spirit of God to give. For as much glory will be given as it is worthy to be given through the Holy Spirit. For this reason he said, “as from the Spirit of the Lord,” to show that the very glory is given which corresponds to the majesty of the giver.

Or thus: let “Lord” be understood as the Father, and “image” as the Son: we, beholding the glory of God—that is, the Son, who is the glory of the Father—are transformed. This is not altered. We tend into his image, namely that of the Father, the same image with himself—that is, into Christ, who is called the image of the Father. It is the same as him toward whom we tend: namely, so that we may see him in his essence. I mean that we proceed from brightness to brightness, that is, from one clear knowledge to another clear knowledge, as those whom the Spirit of God leads.

## CHAPTER IV

### Verses 1–4

“Therefore, having this ministry, according as we have received mercy, we do not lose heart; but we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking [Col. 0029D] in craftiness, nor adulterating the word of God, but by the manifestation of truth commending ourselves to every human conscience before God. And even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine upon them.”

“Therefore,” etc. As though he said: Because we have such great brightness from the Spirit, therefore we have this ministry—that is, this dignity of ministering the Spirit to others. We have it, I say, not by merits, but according as we have received mercy: that is, through God’s mercy [Col. 0030A]. We do not lose heart because of any adversities, but renounce not only manifest evils but also the hidden things of shame—that is, unclean thoughts. We remove all things foul and defiled which can be done or thought.

I mean that we do not walk in craftiness—that is, in hypocrisy—as the false teachers do, who appear humble; nor do we adulterate God’s word by mixing in falsehood, or by preaching for gain. Rather, we walk in the manifestation of truth, because truth is plainly visible in us. I mean that we commend ourselves—that is, make ourselves worthy of commendation. Without comparing ourselves with our opponents, we so make ourselves commendable that the praise of our truth goes forth. [Ambrose] It reaches not merely the eye, but every human conscience [Col. 0030B], while my intention remains before God—that is, within God’s good pleasure.

Or, I say “before God,” that is, with God as witness, to whom nothing is hidden. [Note: [Col. 0029D] Id., *On the Words of the Gospel*.] He invokes God’s testimony so that he himself may be believed regarding the authority by which he preaches.

Observe the Apostle fulfilling what the Lord said: “Let your light so shine before people,” etc. (Matt. 5); and likewise: “Take heed not to do your righteousness before people, to be seen by them” (ibid.). [Augustine] Thus he wished us to do good works in the sight of people, but only for God’s praise, not our own. Hear the Apostle both doing and teaching each. For he says, “commending ourselves,” to show that he fulfils also the saying, “Let your light shine before people.” And he adds, “before God,” to show that he fulfils also the saying, “not to be seen [Col. 0030C] by people.” For he does not do these things in order to be seen by people.

“And even if.” As though he said: I said that we preach in the manifestation of truth. But if even our Gospel is veiled—[Ambrose] that is, the Gospel preached by us—it is veiled in those who perish; that is, the fault belongs to those who deserved to perish. For it is true that unbelievers do not see the splendour of truth, being deservedly blinded by faithlessness. I say, “in those who perish,” in whom, while they perish through the words of the Gospel, the god of this age—that is, God, who not only governs the good [Augustine] but also casts down the evil according to their deserts—has blinded the minds of unbelievers, turning them away from natural reason. [Note: [Col. 0030D] Id., *To Faustus*.] That is, because they do not believe Christ: he blinded them [Col. 0030D] by giving them what they wanted, that is, by allowing them to do what they wanted, namely not to believe. He does this not through malice but through justice. [Note: [Col. 0030D] Id., *Against an Enemy of the Law*.]

Or the order of the words can be: “In those who are perishing, the true and just God has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age.” Or thus: “the god of this age” means the devil, who is the prince of the world and rules worldly people. Or “god of the age” means pride or gluttony, which blinds the minds of unbelievers—that is, is the reason why they are blinded. He has blinded them so completely that the illumination of the Gospel—that is, the illuminating teaching of the Gospel—does not shine, that is, does not appear, to them. Yet this light is the Gospel of Christ’s glory: that is, the Gospel in which [Col. 0031A] the glory of Christ’s divinity is preached, not merely the weakness of his humanity; namely, that Christ is the image of God the Father because he is from him, and is also equal to him, according to: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

[Note: [Col. 0031D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] It should be known that image, equality, and likeness must be distinguished. Where there is an image, there is immediately likeness, but not necessarily equality. Where there is equality, there is immediately likeness also, but not necessarily image. Where there is likeness, there is not necessarily image or equality. For example, in a mirror there are image and likeness, but not equality, because many things are lacking in the image which are present in the thing from which it has been produced. Sometimes there can also be an image in which there is equality, as is found in parents and children: image, likeness, and equality are found in them, except for the time in which parents precede their children. For the likeness of the Son is expressed from the parent, so that it is rightly called an image; and it can be so great that it is rightly called equality. Sometimes there can also be likeness and equality although there is no image, as in two equal eggs. But Christ is called the image of the Father in such a way that none of these is lacking: he is not only his image because he is from him, and likeness because he is image, but also possesses such equality that not even an interval of time is an obstacle, because God did not beget the Son in time.

### Verses 5–12

“For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus, because God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, himself has shone in our hearts for the illumination of the knowledge of the brightness of God in [Col. 0031C] the face of Jesus Christ. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s, and not from us. In every way we suffer tribulation, but are not distressed; we are in want, but not destitute; we suffer persecution, but are not abandoned; we are humbled, but not confounded; we are cast down, but do not perish. Always carrying about in our body the mortification of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always delivered to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. Therefore death works in us, but life in you.”

“For we do not,” etc. As though he said: I rightly speak of Christ’s glory, for we do not, etc. Or the connection is this: We commend ourselves in the manifestation of truth and do all such things for Christ’s sake. For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord. That is, our preaching is directed neither toward our own glory nor toward our own gain, but toward Christ’s glory. We preach him as our Saviour and Lord; we preach him as Lord. But ourselves, we preach as your servants, that is, your ministers. And this is through Jesus, who has laid this duty upon us.

We do this because God himself has shone in our hearts—that is, he has infused himself, who is light, into us. He who said—that is, who accomplished this by command alone—“Let light shine out of darkness,” which occurred at the separation [Col. 0032A] of the elements. [Note: [Col. 0031D] Id., *Against the Enemies of the Law and the Prophets*.] For from the time when the confused mass of heaven and earth began to exist, before the light was made by which what had been without light was illuminated, it was dark; but afterwards, with the coming of light, what was made was rendered better. In this is signified the disposition of a human being making progress. Hence the Apostle says to believers: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). He did this who, when darkness was over the deep, said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1).

This light signifies the light which is now given to us and, through us, to others. From this it cannot be understood that darkness was eternal, as certain slanderers of the Law accuse the writer of that Law of having held; rather, he shows that it began when he said: “In the beginning God made [Col. 0032B] heaven,” etc. “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (ibid.).

I say, he shone “for the illumination of the knowledge of brightness.” [Note: [Col. 0032D] Id., *On Baptism*, par.] Or: “of the glory of God,” that is, so that we might be enlightened by the knowledge through which we know God to be the light by which our darkness is illuminated.
