For the knowledge of God’s glory is that by which we know him to be the light by which our darkness is illuminated. [Ambrose] Or thus: “for the illumination of the knowledge of the brightness of God,” that is, so that through knowledge of the brightness—that is, the essence—of God we may illuminate others. And he gave this to us in the face of Jesus Christ—that is, through Jesus Christ, who is the face of the Father, without whom the Father is not known.

“But we have.” Up to this point he has dealt with the loftiness of his knowledge; here he deals with the frailty of the flesh, which he attributes to his glory, although it may seem contrary. [Col. 0032C] As though he said: God has shone upon us for the illumination of knowledge, but we have this treasure—that is, this knowledge by which we enrich others—in earthen vessels, that is, in frail bodies. He calls the mystery of God a treasure: it is distributed to believers and hidden from the faithless. This is so that the surpassing greatness may appear to be God’s power and not ours.

“In every way,” etc. As though he said: The vessels are earthen. And indeed they are, because we suffer tribulation in every respect: no manner of affliction is absent. Yet, being conscious of the treasure, we are not distressed in mind. Then he openly enumerates certain afflictions, saying: “We are reduced to want,” that is, we are so poor that necessities are lacking. For *aporos* is Greek, and in Latin it means “poor” [Col. 0032D]. But we are not deprived of our treasure. Or, we are not utterly abandoned by God, because God feeds us. And we suffer persecution from place to place, but are not abandoned by God while he guards the treasure. We are humbled, that is, afflicted, but are not confounded, that is, we are not ashamed. We are cast down into danger of death, but do not perish, that is, we do not cease from good.

In every such circumstance we always carry about—that is, bring before others and show—in our body, not only in our mind, the mortification of Jesus: that is, the death we endure for Jesus, or which Jesus first endured. We do this so that, just as Christ’s death appears in us, [Col. 0033A] the life of Jesus—that is, glory—may also be manifested, even to enemies, not merely in our souls but also in our bodies.

“For we who live.” As though he said: We carry about Jesus’ mortification, and indeed we do, because we who live in virtues, or who are permitted to live a natural life, are always delivered to death, that is, to dangers of death. We endure this for Jesus’ sake—that is, out of love for Jesus—so that Jesus’ immortal and impassible life may also be manifested in our flesh, although it is now mortal. Therefore what we hope for seems impossible. [Ambrose] And the sense is: We are not afraid to die for Christ because of the promised resurrection.

“Therefore death.” As though he said: Since we suffer these things, death works in us, but life in you: that is, death exercises dominion in us, but you tend toward the pleasures [Col. 0033B] of life. Or thus: because through death we shall attain the life of Jesus, death is not useless but works something great in us; but the life in which you delight on earth works eternal death in you. Or thus, taking *operatur* passively: “Therefore death is effected,” that is, because of the hope of Jesus’ life, death is produced in us by the afflictions mentioned above—we allow it to be produced in us—but through this life is produced in you: that is, faith is planted in you, through which you live.

### Verses 13–18

“But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke,’ we also believe, and therefore speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and establish us with you. For all things are [Col. 0033C] for your sake, so that grace, abounding through many, may abound in thanksgiving to God’s glory. Therefore we do not lose heart; but though our outward human being is corrupted, yet our inward human being is renewed day by day. For this present, momentary, light affliction works in us, beyond measure in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory, while we do not contemplate the things seen, but the things unseen. For the things seen are temporal, but the things unseen are eternal.”

“But having.” As though he said: Death always works in us. From this it is clear that we have the same Holy Spirit that the prophets had—a Spirit which is the cause of faith. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.] For the Spirit of grace causes us to have faith, so that through faith we obtain, by prayer, the ability to do what we are commanded. And when he says “the same spirit of faith,” he shows that the faith in the just persons of different times is one and the same. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Id., *On Nature and Grace*.] For the faith which saved the righteous of old saves us also: namely, faith in the mediator between God and human beings. The times, then, have changed, but not the faith, because they believed that Christ would come, suffer, rise, and ascend; while we believe that Christ has come, suffered, risen, and ascended into heaven. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Id., *On John*.]

And he shows that faith saved the righteous of old by saying, “as it is written.” As though he said: We have the same Spirit as they. [Col. 0034A] “Having the same spirit of faith” which they had. I rightly say that they had it. As it is written concerning those fathers, in whose person David says: “I believed fully, and therefore I spoke.” Otherwise he would not have believed fully. [Augustine] For those who are unwilling to speak what they believe do not believe fully. Thus he says, “I believed, and therefore I spoke”; yet he says he spoke because he believed, and thus he did two things, one of which arose as the cause of the other. He believed and spoke, namely, so that faith might not be useless without confession.

Having it, I say, we too believe, as they did, in the life to come; therefore we speak, that is, confess, without fearing evils, because we know that he who raised the Lord Jesus from death will also raise us, so that we may be in the same glory [Col. 0034B] with Jesus. [Ambrose] He says this because of some who denied the resurrection, whom he rebukes also in the First Epistle. And he will establish us in the same glory—that is, he will confirm us so that thereafter we shall not die, nor will death rule over us.

I say, he will establish us with you, because all who share one faith will be in the one house of peace. In it he will establish, I do not say us with ourselves, but us with you, so that you may be not inferior to us but our equals, if you are willing. And I rightly assert this concerning you. For we do all these things for your instruction through our example. All things concern you, so that God’s grace, which abounds in us, may abound through you in others, and through you may abound in many in thanksgiving, so that you and others may give thanks to God. And this is for God’s glory—that is, to show [Col. 0034C] God to be glorious, who wishes no one to be excluded from his gift.

Therefore the Apostle endures all things and faithfully preaches to all, so that he may bring not a few to God’s banquet; for it is an insult to him if few come. For it is a great insult to one who has prepared a rich banquet and invited many if he has few guests.

“Therefore.” As though he said: [123] We do all things for your instruction. Therefore, so that you may imitate us, I say that we do not lose heart in afflictions merely for Jesus’ life; but although our human being—that is, the flesh—the outward one, exposed to evils, is corrupted, nevertheless the inward one—that is, the soul fortified by hope of what is to come, which human fury cannot reach, the image of God—is renewed [Col. 0034D] in the knowledge of God day by day, that is, continually. Or it is renewed day by day, that is, it is continually made purer from vices through the fire of affliction. [Note: [Col. 0034D] Id., *Against Faustus*.]

Observe that although he says “the outward one” and “the inward one,” there are not two human beings, but one, whom God made whole—that is, both what is inward and what is outward. He means the inward human being to be the spirit of the mind, and the outward to be the body and this mortal life; but he made in his image only that which is inward. Therefore he did not make the human being in his image according to the body and bodily life, but according to the rational mind, by which one knows [Col. 0035A] God and is set above all rational beings. Thus not the body alone, but also whatever is shared with cattle, is the outward human being. And the whole human being, in both inward and outward part, grew old through sin and was assigned to punishment.

But now the inward human being is renewed; in the resurrection the outward one also will receive the dignity of a heavenly constitution, so that all that was made may be recreated and restored. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Aug., *On the Trinity*.] But now the outward human being, namely the body, is corrupted more and more the longer this life lasts, whether by age, disease, or other means.

“For this.” As though he said: We rightly do not lose heart, because that portion of our affliction—that is, its smallness—which is present, where there is nothing but desolation, and momentary [Col. 0035B], that is, lasting only a little while, and light to bear, works in us a weight of glory, that is, immeasurable glory. Observe that he sets each thing against its counterpart: weight against lightness, glory against affliction. The weight, I say, is eternal, against what he called momentary; it is beyond measure in comparison with afflictions, against what he called “that portion of affliction”; and it is in sublimity, that is, in heaven, against what he called “present.”

For great reward will be rendered for small labours, and the surpassing greatness of eternal glory will recompense those full of affliction. This works in us, I say, while we do not contemplate—that is, seek—the things seen, but the things unseen. As though he said: Therefore the weight of glory works in us because we seek not earthly but heavenly things. We seek the unseen because the things seen are temporal, that is, passing away, whereas the things unseen are eternal.

## CHAPTER V

### Verses 1–4

“For we know that if the earthly house of our habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this also we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our habitation which is from heaven, if indeed we are found clothed and not naked. For we too who are in this tent groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

“For we know.” As though he said: The weight of glory truly works in us, because it is in our bodies also, not merely in our souls. And this is what he says. The wording proceeds thus: “For we know that we have”—not merely, “we shall have”; we are so certain that we already possess in hope what we shall possess in reality—“a building,” that is, an immortal body fully made firm, from God alone, because it will not be made through human ministry. [Ambrose]

We shall have it, I say, if our house—that is, the mortal flesh in which the soul dwells—of this habitation, where the soul is always disturbed, is dissolved. It is an earthly house, that is, from earth and inclined toward earthly things; it is dissolved, that is, destroyed, for Christ’s sake. The sense is: We know that we shall have an immortal body, even if this mortal body is dissolved through afflictions [Col. 0036A].

He then explains what he called a building, saying: namely, the house of the soul, that is, the immortal body in which, once raised, we shall always be. It is a house not made with hands, that is, not formed by human intercourse, not produced by the work of human generation or increased by human nourishment, but so ineffably constituted; and eternal, because made from eternity—that is, by God’s ordinance, prepared for us from eternity. We shall have it in the heavens, that is, among heavenly beings, namely among angels; or, more properly, it is called eternal because one will remain in it without end.

By this he gives confidence, lest we fear being violently separated from the body by unbelievers, because an eternal dwelling has been prepared in heaven, so that, expelled from a temporal and earthly dwelling, we may be received into an everlasting house [Col. 0036B].

“For in this also.” As though he said: I say that we shall have a house not made with hands, and from this it can be seen that we shall have it. For we groan not only over our present habitation, but also in this—that is, in consideration of this great glory—because of the delay of our desire; which we would not do unless we were certain.

As a figure of this, Achsah, daughter of Caleb, asked her father for the upper spring and the lower spring (Josh. 15), so that we too may shed tears not only for the misery of our present sojourn but also for the delay of heavenly glory. Hence he says here: “In this also we groan.” In what? In this, namely, desiring, in addition to the virtues of the soul, to put on our habitation—that is, our building—which is from heaven, that is, immortal and impassible. The sense is: We groan because, in addition to the renewal of the soul which we have already received, we desire to put on our habitation: that is, for the soul to be given a garment not corruptible from earth but from heaven—that is, immortal and impassible, like heavenly beings [Col. 0036C].

“If indeed.” As though he said: We desire to be clothed, which will certainly happen, but upon this condition: if we are found clothed, namely with virtues, faith, and the rest, when the body has been laid aside; and if we are not found naked of virtues—that is, if, when the body has been laid aside, we have put on Christ and are not naked of him. I say this lest the same thing be thought of the naked.

Or thus: we desire to be clothed with a body at the resurrection, yet only if we are found clothed with the promised glory and not naked. For this is what the saints desire: that when they rise and receive the body, they may not be found naked—that is, alien to the promised glory. For this is necessary: that those clothed with the body may be clothed over with glory, which will be a transformation into brightness.

“For we too.” As though he said: We who are more perfect groan over the delay, because also those who are less perfect and cherish the flesh groan—among whom the Apostle numbers himself—lest they think too little of themselves. And this is what he says:

“For we too,” that is, even we who are less perfect, who are in this tent—that is, who love the habitation of this body, which should not be a cause of concern [Col. 0037A], since it is only a temporary tent—groan, longing for heaven. [Note: [Col. 0037D] Augustine, *City of God*.] I mean that we are burdened, that is, weighed down, by this corruptible body, because now the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind occupied with many thoughts (Wis. 9).

And because the cause of this burden is not the nature and substance of the body but its corruption, we do not wish, if possible, to be stripped of the body, but rather to be clothed also with immortality. This is what he says: “because we do not wish.” [Remigius] As though he said: We are weighed down by the burden of the body, yet we do not wish the body to be stripped off—that is, we would not wish it to be taken from us through death, if it were possible. But we wish to be clothed over, that is, fully clothed, with the robe of immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life—that is, so that the life of immortality may destroy mortality [Col. 0037B], not merely come upon it, etc.

The sense is: We would wish to become immortal, if it were possible, in such a way that immortality itself would now arrive and change us as we are. For although we pass from evils to goods, that transition itself is bitter and has gall and vinegar—that is, something sharp to endure. [Note: [Col. 0037D] Id., on Psalm 88.] And although the body weighs down the soul and has incentives to vices and sinful desires, nevertheless not all evils arise from it, nor should all the vices of an unrighteous life be attributed to the flesh, lest we thereby absolve the devil of all blame, though he has no flesh. Nor was the body’s corruption, which weighs down the soul, the cause of the first sin, but its punishment; nor did corruptible flesh make the soul sinful, but the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible. [Note: [Col. 0037D] Id., sermon on the Nativity of the Apostles.] Therefore those who think that all evils of the soul arise from the body are in error.

Observe that he says that he groans and is burdened under the load of corruptible flesh, yet says: “We do not wish to be unclothed.” [Note: [Col. 0038D] Id., in the same work.] Behold a voice, but not a confession, of punishment. The body is heavy, burdensome, and corruptible; one groans under it, yet it is not gladly abandoned. For by the reason of the mind one first desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but the sense of the flesh recoils and refuses. [Note: [Col. 0038D] Id., *On Natural Grace*.]

This is characteristic of human affection; the soul itself somehow has it in its will: because it loves life, it hates death; and because it does not hate its own flesh, it does not want what it hates to happen to that flesh. If it were possible, it does not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, as the Apostle says: “We do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over.” [Note: [Col. 0038D] Id., *On the Nativity of the Apostles*.]

As though he said: Beneath the earthly tunic I groan; I hasten toward the heavenly one. I want to receive that and to lay aside this. What do you say, Apostle? Will such an injury be done to that great heavenly garment that immortality will come upon you over these rags of mortality and corruption, so that this is below and that above, this within and that without? “I do not say this,” he replies, “not this. Therefore I do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over—not, however, in such a way that corruption remains beneath incorruption, but so that what is mortal in us may be swallowed up by life, so that mortality may be nowhere: neither below nor above, neither within nor without. For [Col. 0038A] death has been swallowed up in victory.”

Or thus: “For we too.” As though he said: We groan over that, namely because we are removed from blessedness; and it is not surprising that we groan over it. For we also groan over this lesser matter, namely that we are stripped of this body. And this is what he says: “For we who are in this tent,” that is, in this dwelling, although we are burdened by it—that is, by the burden of the flesh—groan because of it. [Ambrose] That is, we groan because we do not wish to be unclothed of the body, but to be clothed over with immortality, if this could occur, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life and thus be unable to die any longer.

### Verses 5–10

“But God is the one who accomplishes us for this very thing, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit. Therefore, always confident and knowing that while we are in the body [Col. 0038B] we are away from the Lord—for we walk by faith and not by sight—we are confident and have the good will rather to be away from the body and to be present with the Lord. Therefore we strive, whether absent or present, to please him. For we must all be manifested before Christ’s judgment-seat, so that each may receive the things proper to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.”

But he who. As though he said: We groan with longing for heaven. But it is God who brings us to this very end; that is, God brings this about in us. Or the connection may be taken thus: We do not wish to be stripped of the body; yet God brings this about, that we should desire immortality, as he says: “But he who brings us to this very end,” namely, that we may will immortality, “is God.” Or from the passage, [Col. 0038C] “For we also who.” As though he said: I say that we are to be clothed over, if we are found clothed with virtues; and certainly we pray that, persevering in faith, we may be found clothed with the Holy Spirit. [Ambrose] “For we also who are in this tent,” burdened with sufferings, “groan,” in prayer, “and for this reason,” because we do not wish to be stripped of the Holy Spirit; that is, by groaning we pray this, lest we be stripped of the Holy Spirit, and thus be clothed with glory. Hence he adds: “but we do not wish to be clothed over with the glory of immortality, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” For then we shall be able to be clothed over with the promised glory of immortality, if, when stripped of the body, we have not been deprived of the Holy Spirit.

“But he who.” As though he said: We do not wish to be stripped, but clothed over. But he who accomplishes this [Col. 0038D] very thing in us, that is, who perfects this will in us, is God, who gave us the pledge of the Spirit; that is, he gave us the Holy Spirit as a pledge that this thing will be fulfilled. By this pledge we are certain of immortality, which we shall then possess when, with no enemy remaining, we enjoy ineffable and everlasting peace.

“Therefore, being always confident” [Note: [Col. 0038D] Id., *On Baptism*, par.]. As though he said: God causes us to will immortality, and through the Holy Spirit also makes us certain concerning it. Therefore, that is, for this reason, we are always confident, exercising our accustomed boldness, and knowing this, which surely confirms our confidence. [Col. 0039A] What do we know? That while we are in this mortal body, we are away from the Lord; that is, we are separated from the Lord in sight, though we possess him in mind through faith.

[Ambrose] It is asked, since elsewhere it is written, “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17), why he says here that we are away from the Lord. For if he is everywhere, how then are we away from the Lord? Without doubt he is everywhere, and all things are in him; yet we are said here to be away from him, because, although God is everywhere, he is not seen here as he is in heaven. Therefore, we are away not in faith but in sight. Hence he adds: “For we walk by faith in invisible things,” that is, we tend toward God, “and not by sight,” that is, not by their presence. One who is away from home and walks by faith is not in his homeland, [Col. 0039B] but is already on the road.

[Note: [Col. 0039D] Augustine, *On Psalm* 163.] But whoever does not believe is neither in the homeland nor on the road. Therefore let us walk as though we are on the road, because the king of the homeland himself has become the road. Christ is the king of the homeland, and there is truth. Here, however, he is the road. Where are we going? To Christ. By what way are we going? Through Christ. For he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14). There is illumination by faith, and there is also illumination by sight; at present we are illuminated only by faith, not by sight [Note: [Col. 0039D] Id., *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*]. For it cannot happen to a person still living this mortal life that, once every cloud of bodily images has been removed and dispersed, he should attain the most serene light of unchangeable truth and, with his mind wholly estranged from the habit of this life, cling to it steadily and without turning aside.

“But we are confident.” As though he said: We are confident and know [Col. 0039C] this; confident in mind, we are confident in action. That is, we do not cease from action, even though it be hard; and we have good will, because we are not saddened or do not murmur amid adversities. I say that we desire rather to be away, that is, removed from the body, and present with the Lord, than to remain here. And because we wish to cling to him, therefore in every way we strive to please him, whether away, as now, or present, as when we shall stand before him; that is, we labor so as to please him here and there.

“For we must all.” As though he said: We strive to please him, and this is fitting. For we must all, and so forth. Or the connection may be: We shall be present to him. And this is true, because all of us, good and evil alike, must be made manifest before Christ’s tribunal, that is, before Christ the judge. [Col. 0039D] To what end? So that each one, good and evil alike, may receive, after the analogy of harvesters, the things proper to the body, according as he has done, namely more or less, whether good or evil; that is, may receive what he has done through the body, that is, during the time of the body, since no one merits except while he is in the body.

Another translation confirms this sense, reading: “that each may receive according to what he has done through the body” [Note: [Col. 0039D] Id., *The City of God*]. For he said “through the body,” not because everything is done by the motion of the body, but “through the body,” that is, during the time in which one lived in the body [Note: [Col. 0040D] Id., *Enchiridion*]. For here every merit is acquired by which someone may after this life be [Col. 0040A] either raised up or weighed down.

Even those practices which the Church frequently observes in commending the dead do not benefit everyone. Why? [Note: [Col. 0040D] Id., in the same work.] Is it not according to the difference in the life which each has lived in the body? For while living in the body each also acquired this merit, that such things might benefit him. Therefore, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any alms—are offered for all baptized dead persons, they are thanksgivings for the very good, propitiations for those not very bad; and for the very bad, even if they are no assistance to the dead, they are nevertheless consolations of some kind for the living. But for those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be full remission, or at least so that the condemnation itself may become more tolerable.

“Therefore we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal” (Rom. 14), so that each may receive, [Col. 0040B] after the analogy of harvesters, what he has done through the body. Each one, even children, who, if not through themselves, nevertheless acted through others, since through them they either believed or did not believe, when they were baptized or not baptized. They are judged according to what they did, not according to what they would have done had they lived long. For he says, “according as he has done in the body,” not according as he would have done had he lived long [Note: [Col. 0040D] Id., *Sentences of Prosper*]. Therefore, after this body a person vainly promises himself what he neglected to acquire in this body. And because we shall stand before the tribunal:

## Verses 11–15

“Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but we are manifest to God. And I hope that we are manifest also in your consciences. We do not again commend ourselves to you, but give you an occasion for glorying on our behalf, so that you may have [Col. 0040C] an answer for those who glory in appearance and not in heart. For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us, as we judge this: that if one died for all, then all died; and Christ died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them.”

“Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord,” that is, how chastely God ought to be feared, “we persuade people” to fear, believe, and provide for themselves, because through the perverse speech of certain persons the day of the Lord is called into doubt.

[Ambrose] In this we are manifest to God, that is, approved by him: we are not false apostles, for the Apostle preached what God commanded. “But I hope” [Col. 0040D] As though he said: We are approved by God; and I hope, so far as lies in me, in whom there is no impediment, that we are manifest, that is, approved, also in your consciences, even if you do not confess it with your mouths.

In saying these things we do not again commend ourselves to you; that is, we do not say this arrogantly, just as we did not earlier when we said, “We are not like the many,” and so forth. But in saying such things, we give you an occasion, that is, material for glorying against the false apostles, who glory in themselves through self-exaltation, saying that they were taught by those who were with the Lord. I say, glorying on our behalf, because I, Paul, am an apostle just like those from whom they boast that they learned [Col. 0041A]—something necessary for you, namely so that you may have what you can say to restrain those who glory in appearance, that is, in outward things such as circumcision and other legal observances, and not in heart, that is, spiritual things. Or, they glory in appearance, that is, in the sight of people, as hypocrites do, not in their hearts, so as to check pride by humility of heart.

“For whether.” As though he said: You can certainly glory concerning us, because whatever we do is either for God’s honor or for our neighbor’s benefit. This is what he says: “For whether we are beside ourselves,” that is, if we commend ourselves, in which we are considered senseless, “it is for God,” that is, it is for God’s honor, who has so exalted us. Or: it must be left to God and not judged by a human being. For if he is thought to have spoken proudly—which is as it were madness—when he praises himself while speaking the truth, it must be left to God. For all pride is regarded as a kind of madness. “Or whether we are sober-minded,” so that we do not say lofty things of ourselves, “it is for you,” that is, for your benefit; for, if he is understood to have spoken not boastfully but for the glory of his hearers, it benefits the Corinthians.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Augustine, *On Psalm* 30.] Or thus: “For whether.” He calls an elevation of mind that by which the mind is raised to understand heavenly things. *Ecstasis* is a Greek word; in Latin it may be explained in one word if it is called *excessus*, “an exceeding” or “being carried beyond.” In this exceeding of the mind two things are understood: either terror, or an intentness toward things above, so that lower things somehow slip from memory. All the saints were in this exceeding of mind, to whom the mysteries of God surpassing this world were revealed. Paul speaks here of this exceeding of mind, [Col. 0041C] alluding to himself. As though he said: You may glory concerning us.

[Augustine] “For whether,” that is, by the contemplation of reason I transcend all temporal things, “it is for God,” who alone knows our exceeding. For he sees what we see in the exceeding of mind; it is not for you, who cannot grasp it. [Note: [Col. 0042D] Augustine, *On Psalm* 118.] Therefore he says that he has transcended only for God. For the Apostle, transcending in mind all human frailty, all temporal things of the age, all transient things that vanish through being born and dying, dwelt in heart in a certain ineffable contemplation, where he heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. If [p. 125] he wished always to remain there, he would not lift you up, who cannot see sublime things. What then did he do? He descended [Col. 0041D] and, not ungrateful to him from whom he had received higher things, did not despise lower things for the sake of the weak, but accommodated himself to them.

[Augustine] Hence he adds: “Or whether we are sober-minded,” by condescending, “it is for you,” because we speak in such a way that you can understand. These are the angels of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “You shall see heaven opened and the angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1). Jacob saw these same angels ascending and descending on a ladder (Gen. 28).

“For the love of Christ.” As though he said: It is all for you. For the love of Christ, that is, the love which Christ showed toward us in condescending to us, constrains us [Col. 0042A] to do everything for you. I say, us judging this: that if one alone inwardly without sin, namely Christ, died for all, then all the others are in sin; therefore all are dead.

[Ambrose] And the sense is: We judge this most certainly: if Christ died in love for all, then it is established that all for whom Christ died were dead in Adam, so that he might free them from death. Lest this grace be useless to people, the apostles necessarily commend themselves in order to attract them. For through the glory and merit of the apostles the grace and benefit of Christ are recognized.

Or thus: if one—namely, if one alone, sufficient without all legal observances—died for all, then all died to the old state through him and need no other. Therefore let the Law cease. [Col. 0042B]

[Augustine] Or thus: If one died for all, that is, if Christ, as far as he is concerned, died for all, even though it did not benefit all, then all people are dead, that is, they ought to die for his honor. And Christ also died for all, so that those who live, living by virtues through the remission of sins, may no longer live for themselves—that is, may not attribute the life of virtues to themselves—but for him who died for them, so that they might die to sin, and rose again, so that we might walk in newness of life.

Or thus, so that he speaks of bodily life. As though he said: Therefore he died so that those who now live in the body may no longer live for themselves, that is, for their own private will, but for him, that is, for his will, namely Christ’s, who died and rose again for them; that is, they may live not in hope of earthly things but in hope of the resurrection [Col. 0042C].

## Verses 16–17

“Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh. And even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; the old things have passed away.”

“Therefore,” and so forth. As though he said: And because this is so, therefore from now on—that is, henceforth—we are so certain of eternal glory that we know no one, that is, praise no one who lives according to the flesh, that is, who seeks his own things rather than those of Christ, temporal things rather than eternal ones. Nor should anyone do this, because although we knew Christ according to the flesh, that is, as mortal, and by this thought him to be merely human, now we no longer know him as mortal. [Col. 0042D] That is, although Christ was mortal, and by this I thought him merely human when I was an unbeliever, he is now immortal; and thus we are secure concerning the reward.

And the sense is: For this reason they ought to live for Christ, not for themselves, according to the flesh: although Christ was weak up to the cross—that is, subjected to injury—and did not disdain to become a passible human being and die for us, yet after the resurrection he is no longer weak and mortal, but appears as what he was not thought to be. Hence he himself says: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am” (John 8). He recalls this in order to show with what devotion Christ ought to be served, so that, understanding [Col. 0043A] how much he has done for us, they may serve him more eagerly. Therefore let them render him a return as God, not merely as a human being who suffered for them. And because Christ is no longer according to the flesh, therefore, if anyone is a new creature in Christ—that is, if anyone has been reborn anew in Christ—the old things have passed away for him; and behold, all things have become new for him. That is, mortality has already passed for him in hope, and resurrection will come and new immortality will be given.

[Ambrose] Or thus. “Therefore.” As though he said: Because Christ rose again, therefore from now on—that is, henceforth—we are so certain of the same resurrection that we know no believer to be living, I do not say in actuality but in hope, according to the flesh, that is, according to the corruption of the flesh. For by “flesh” here he means not the substance of the body itself, which Christ possessed after the resurrection and which we shall possess after our resurrection, but the corruption and mortality of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.]

For in his customary manner he reflects upon our future life with such certain hope as though it were already present and held before us—a life which has already been fulfilled in Christ rising again. This life certainly will not be according to the flesh, not because we shall not rise in the same bodily substance, but because we shall not rise in the same quality of corruption, which is here signified by the name “flesh.” Therefore, because he contemplates the life of the risen as though present, he says, “From now on we know no one according to the flesh”; that is, we hold such a sure hope of our future incorruption and immortality that already in this knowledge we rejoice in hope, as though we possessed in actuality the life that will be without corruption, just as [Col. 0043C] Christ’s life is no longer according to the flesh.

Hence he adds: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh,” that is, according to the mortality of the flesh before the resurrection, “yet now,” namely after he rose again, “we know him so no longer,” that is, according to the fleshly quality of corruption, because Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and so forth. Therefore he himself says in the Gospel: “I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer” (John 14); that is, you will never again see me as I now am: you will not see me humble, but exalted; not mortal, but everlasting; not to be judged, but judging. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Augustine, *On John*.]

And again he says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16), [Col. 0043D] that is, you cannot receive the Holy Spirit so long as you persist in knowing me according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0044D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] And because we are in Christ in hope, though not in actuality: therefore, if there is a new creation in Christ, as there truly is—that is, if any people have been renewed through faith in Christ—the old things have passed away for them, and behold all things have become new. For, when renewed by faith, mortality passes in hope and the newness of resurrection is present.

[Augustine] Or thus: “Therefore.” As though he said: Because Christ alone is sufficient for righteousness and life without all legal observances, therefore from this time of grace we know—that is, approve—no one living according to the flesh, that is, living according to fleshly observances. For although, while I was an unbeliever, I understood Christ to have been promised in the Law according to the flesh, namely that he would observe legal ordinances and command their observance, yet now, after conversion, when truth has come, we know that it is not so, but that the shadow must cease and truth be manifested. And because the shadow ought to cease, if any creature has been made new in Christ, the old things have passed away for him—[Augustine] namely fleshly observances and the pleasure of the flesh, that is, the Old Testament and all things pertaining to the old human being: among Gentiles, idolatry; among Jews, bondage to the Law.

## Verses 17–21

“And behold, all things have become new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through [Col. 0044B] Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. For God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their trespasses to them, and placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we carry out an embassy for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God. Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him.”

“And behold, all things have become new,” that is, new things have come: namely the New Testament and all things belonging to the new human being; and the truth of the one God has succeeded. “But all things.” As though he said: I have said that a new creation comes to be in Christ, that is, through Christ, and that old things pass away; nevertheless all things are from God the Father, who reconciled us to himself through Christ, that is, through the incarnate [Col. 0044C] Word, and gave the ministry of reconciliation to us apostles, Christ’s representatives, not to the false apostles.

God reconciled through Christ, something which could indeed be done through Christ; for God the Father, who could do everything, was in Christ. [Ambrose] Therefore Christ could reconcile, because the Father was in him, as he himself says: “The Father is in me, and I in the Father” (John 14). By this it is understood that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. For unity is where there is no diversity; and therefore one is in the other because their image and likeness are one.

I say that he was in Christ, reconciling the world—that is, the elect from the world—to himself. How? Reconciling it in this way: not imputing to them, that is, not punishing eternally in them, their trespasses, both original [Col. 0044D] and actual; and he placed. As though he said: In this way he gave us the ministry of reconciliation, because he placed in us the word of reconciliation, that is, the preaching of faith, by which people are reconciled to God.

[Augustine] And because he placed the word in us, therefore we carry out God’s embassy for Christ, that is, in the place of Christ, who was God’s ambassador. Or, “for Christ,” that is, for Christ’s honor. And therefore we beseech you, as though God were truly exhorting you through us, because he truly speaks in us. What do we beseech? Behold: “Be reconciled to God,” and this for Christ, that is, for love of Christ.

[Ambrose] Or, I beseech you for [Col. 0045A] Christ, that is, in Christ’s place; and you ought, or are able, to do this because God the Father did for us this: him who did not know sin by experience, though he knew it by knowledge—him, I say, Christ—he made sin; that is, him who had not sinned he made sin, that is, a sacrifice for sin. This manner of expression is drawn from the old Law.

[Note: [Col. 0045D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] For the Old Testament custom is to call sacrifices for sins “sins.” Or “sin” means the likeness of sinful flesh. Hence it is said elsewhere: “He condemned sin in sin,” that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh, because God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8). And again it is said: “He died to sin,” that is, to the likeness of sinful flesh, because in dying he was stripped of the mortality of the flesh.

And the sense is: “He made him sin,” that is, mortal. Likewise “curse” is understood as death, which came from the curse, so that what is truly said in the Law may be understood: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. 21). What is “you are cursed”? It is: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Why does he say “everyone”? Because even Christ himself, though he was life, died [p. 126] a true death, not a fictitious one.

Or, he made him sin, that is, caused him to be regarded as a sinner in his punishment. And he did this so that we might become not merely righteous but even righteousness, through whom others might be righteous. I say the righteousness of God, not our own; and this in him, namely in God, Christ, not through another. Or, “that we might become the righteousness of God,” that is, that we might be justified by God, because every perfection is from God alone. [Col. 0045C] And this “in him,” that is, through Christ himself.

Observe that just as, when one reads, “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 3), this does not mean the salvation by which the Lord is saved, but that by which those whom he saves are saved; so when “the righteousness of God” is spoken of, it must not be understood as the righteousness by which God is righteous, but that by which human beings are made righteous, whom he justifies by his grace.

## Chapter VI

### Verses 1–7

“But as fellow-workers, we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: ‘At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.’ Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Giving no offense to anyone, so that our ministry may not be blamed. But in all things let us show ourselves as God’s ministers: in much patience, [Col. 0045D] in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in beatings, in prisons, in tumults, in labors, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in longsuffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left.”

“But as fellow-workers.” As though he said: Christ redeemed and reconciled you. But we, namely those sent by him, helping you, or helping Christ, exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain; that is, lest the grace you have already received should become vain for you. The grace of God is the remission of sins; one receives it in vain who does not afterward exercise himself in good works, [Col. 0046A] or who places confidence in legal observances.

And as though someone were asking, “Does grace exist?” he answers: Certainly it does. For the Lord says in Isaiah: “O human being, I heard you praying for sins at the time of grace acceptable to me or to people; and on the day of salvation, namely when the light was born to the world, namely Christ, I aided you,” or “helped you,” to attain virtues and persevere in good works. Then he explains the prophecy, saying: “Behold.” As though he said: Thus the Lord spoke in prophecy concerning the time of grace, and behold, now is the acceptable time in which health-giving medicine is poured into mortal sicknesses. And in other words he says the same thing: “Behold, now is the day of salvation,” which did not exist under the old Law. Or he says “now” because salvation is given immediately at a believer’s death; it is not delayed until tomorrow or a year later.

[Ambrose] We exhort you—I say you who give no offense to anyone, whether by word or example, for we are so solicitous concerning the salvation of the sick. And we do this so that our ministry, namely the ministry of apostleship, may not be blamed; for it would certainly be blamed if we did this, that is, if we did not set forth in the example of our conduct what we teach in word.

Or thus: “to no one.” As though he said: I say that you must take care not to receive grace in vain—I say you who give no offense to anyone by word or example, so that through you our ministry may not be blamed. “But in all things.” As though he said: Let us offend no one; rather, you as I, let us show—that is, offer—to God ourselves in all things as God’s ministers, [Col. 0046C] because God’s ministers do not flatter people in order to please God, as false apostles do in pursuing gain.

“In much.” As though he said: Let us show ourselves ministers in all things, namely in much patience, so that we are not moved even a little. I say patience exercised in tribulations, that is, afflictions. He then enumerates tribulations individually: in necessities of food or clothing; in distresses, that is, anxiety and fear of mind; in beatings, that is, scourging; in prisons; in tumults, that is, uprisings of people against them; in labors of work, because he worked with his own hands so as not to burden anyone; in vigils, namely by working at night as well in the task assigned to him; in compulsory or voluntary fasts.

But since the saints are assailed with all these hardships, some people find it surprising that the Lord says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke, and you will find rest. For my yoke is easy” (Matt. 11). [Col. 0046D]

For they consider those who have placed their necks fearlessly beneath that yoke and accepted that burden on meek shoulders to suffer such difficult dangers that they seem to be summoned not from labors to rest, but from rest to labor. Someone therefore says: [Augustine] How is the yoke easy and the burden light? And how is it said, “Come to me, you who labor, and I will refresh you,” rather than, “Come, you who are at leisure, so that you may labor”? But it must be understood that, although the saints endure grievous and harsh things, the Holy Spirit is certainly present, who amid the corruption of the outward human being renews the inward one day by day; and, through tasted spiritual rest and the hope of future blessedness, relieves all harsh things. Thus, even amid so many hardships, Christ’s burden is light; inwardly there is rest through the Holy Spirit who gives life, while the hope of the future mitigates everything. For love makes all savage and terrible things easy and almost nothing.

Again, let us show ourselves as God’s ministers in chastity of mind and body, in knowledge of the Scriptures; or, in knowing how one ought to live among the wicked. Or thus: in chastity possessed in knowledge, so that they may know chastely and mingle no adulterated opinion with it. In longsuffering expectation; in kindness, so that we may be gentle and approachable. I say kindness [Col. 0047B] possessed in the Holy Spirit, because we ought to do everything sincerely, so that according to God we may be kind and approachable; not like those who through sweet speech deceive the hearts of the innocent; in unfeigned love, whereas false apostles feign love in order to deceive.

[Ambrose] But love is feigned in those who abandon their brothers in adversity. Again, let us show ourselves as ministers in the word of truth, by preaching or speaking; again, in the power of God, namely so that we may not hope in a human being, or in ourselves if there is any good in us, but attribute it to God. Or, “in the power of God,” that is, in miracles, so that we perform them for benefit, not for boasting; for one who possesses the things mentioned above performs miracles for the conversion of people, as a minister of God.

Again, [Col. 0047C] let us show ourselves as God’s ministers, armed through the weapons of righteousness, that is, through righteousness, which arms us in place of weapons, on the right, that is, amid prosperities lest we be puffed up, and on the left, that is, amid adversities lest we be broken.

### Verses 8–13

“Through glory and dishonor, through evil report and good report; as deceivers, and yet true; as unknown, and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened, and not put to death; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things. Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart has been enlarged. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections. But having the same recompense, I speak as to children: be enlarged also yourselves.”

[Col. 0047D] Again, let us show ourselves as God’s ministers through glory and dishonor; that is, whether we are glorious before people or lowly and despised, so that we are neither inflated by the former nor cast down or grieved by the latter. Observe that glory and dishonor are parts of prosperity or adversity. Or, let us show ourselves as ministers through the glory of the Gospel, so that we preach things that appear glorious and are so, and through dishonor, so that we are not ashamed to preach even those words of the Gospel at which some recoil.

In the same way let us show ourselves as ministers through evil report, whether concerning faith or some other matter, and through good report; that is, if we are defamed for some crime. Or, we have a good report for some good work. Again, let us show ourselves as regarded [Col. 0048A] as deceivers by some, which is certainly false. Therefore I do not simply say “deceivers,” but add “as.” From this comes evil report. And by others we are regarded—not “as true,” but simply “true,” without “as.” As though he said: This is true. From this comes good report. In these things, I say, let us show ourselves so that we are neither proud because of a good estimation nor grieved because of a bad one.

Again, we are regarded as people unknown to God, that is, rejected by God. Yet truly we are known, that is, approved by God. Again, we are regarded by others as dying, that is, falling from vice into vice; and behold, we live through good works, both in others’ opinion and in the reality of the matter. Or he speaks of bodily life and death: we are regarded by some as dying, and behold, we live.

[Ambrose] For their enemies daily thought they would not escape the threats of the wicked. But they themselves are, by God’s help, secure from present and future death. Again: by others we are regarded as chastened, that is, restrained from preaching by words, so that we were thought to yield; by others we are regarded as not chastened, which would be to be put to death. Therefore he puts in its place, “and we are not put to death,” because they were not conquered or yielding. For one is put to death who does not remain in the confession of faith.

Or it may be understood of bodily death: we became as chastened by pressures, because God permitted them to be exercised by pressures so that they might grow in merit; and we were not put to death, because God did not permit them to be killed bodily. Even though many martyrs are killed, [Col. 0048C] the Church nevertheless does not die, but is corrected by adversities.

[Augustine] Again, we were regarded by some as sorrowful because of tribulation. Therefore he adds “as,” because we were not truly sorrowful. Yet we were always truly rejoicing, because this sorrow produces joy. And by others we were so regarded. Again, we were regarded as needy in true and spiritual goods; or, we endured poverty in earthly things. Yet we were enriching [p. 127] many with spiritual riches, and were thus regarded by others.

Again, we were regarded not only as needy, but even as having absolutely no spiritual or earthly good, because they were thought insufficient for themselves; and we possess all things, namely not only spiritual but also temporal things, because those who fear God lack nothing. This was the glory of the apostles: to possess absolutely nothing, to be free from care, and to possess not so much things as their owners, because all things were laid at the apostles’ feet, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 4). [Col. 0048D]

Observe that to certain expressions are added either “as,” “as if,” “just as,” or “as though,” because these pass away as in dreams; but the opposites are set down without “as,” because they are certain. “Your sorrow” has “as”; joy does not have “as.” Why is this? Because joy is a certain reality, while sorrow passes away as in dreams. For if someone recounts a dream, he adds “as,” saying: “I seemed to be sitting, I seemed to be speaking, I seemed to be riding,” and the like. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Augustine, *On Psalm* 38.] Everywhere he says “as,” because what he saw while sleeping he did not find when he awoke.

Our mouth has spoken many and true things, and things from charity, concerning the dignity of our ministry, the truth of the Gospel [Col. 0049A], and the commendation of our person; therefore he adds, “Our mouth.” As though he said: I have said much about ourselves, but in all the foregoing our mouth, O Corinthians, is open to you in the openness, abundance, and truth of its utterances, for your instruction—that is, for your benefit—because all these things were said fully and at length to correct you, O Corinthians, and not from my own pride. As though he said: You are foolish in having abandoned me. Note that the Apostle speaks here freely and from a pure conscience. [Ambrose] For a mind conscious of evil speaks hesitantly, loses its thought, and errs in its words.

“Our heart.” As though he said: I did this because our heart is enlarged—that is, our mind is full of riches and is not ashamed to say what it possesses. Therefore you are not constrained [Col. 0049B] in us; rather, you are constrained in your own affections. That is, if you suffer any narrowness or lack of knowledge or good work, this does not come from us, as you suppose—you who prefer the false apostles to us—but from yourselves, who have pure hearts for understanding and fulfilling.

“But the same.” As though he said: You suffer these constraints from yourselves; but I speak to you as children: be enlarged also yourselves, as we are, in abundance of knowledge and virtues and hope for the future—I mean, you who have the same recompense as we do. And that you may be enlarged:

## Verses 14–18

“Do not be yoked with unbelievers. For what sharing has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What concord, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement, moreover, has the temple of God with idols? [Col. 0049C] For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’ Therefore, ‘Go out from their midst and be separate,’ says the Lord; ‘and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you; and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,’ says the Lord Almighty.”

“Do not be yoked with unbelievers”: that is, do not be partners with the wicked in evil; do not become slaves, having lost your freedom, with those unbelievers who preach carnal observances. If you have already taken up the yoke of the law, do not take it up further.

“For what…?” As though he said: Therefore do not do so, because you are righteous and they unrighteous; thus you ought to share nothing with them. For what sharing [Col. 0049D] is there between righteousness and iniquity? As though he said: None.

“Or what…?” As though he said: Therefore also do not do so, because you are light through knowledge and they are darkness through ignorance. What fellowship has light with darkness? None.

“What concord, moreover…?” As though he said: Again, therefore do not do so, because you are members of Christ and they members of the devil; and Christ and the devil do not agree. He puts it thus: What concord has Christ with Belial—that is, with the devil, who falsely claims to be God? *Belial* is interpreted “apostate,” with whom Christ does not agree, because the former does everything wickedly and Christ does everything well.

“Or what…?” As though he said: Therefore do not do so, because you are believers and they are as unbelievers. What portion has a believer with an unbeliever? [Col. 0050A] None. For as Christ and Belial do not agree, so neither does a believer agree with any unbeliever.

“What agreement, moreover…?” Again, therefore do not do so, because you are the temple of God, in which the Holy Spirit is, while they are those in whom the devil dwells. The temple of God has nothing in common with idols. Thus he says: What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? None. [Ambrose] And you are the temple of God; therefore you ought not share in those who are the temple of the devil. In these words he forbids the worship of idols, which are enemies of God’s temple because they separate people from the one God. By all these arguments he shows that fellowship with the false apostles must be avoided.

“For you are…” As though he said: Therefore you ought not agree with them, because you are the temple of the living God, who will make you live. As the Lord says in Ezekiel (Ezek. XVIII): “I, who am everywhere [Col. 0050B] by my substance, will dwell in them by grace”—that is, I shall cultivate them and make them pure—“and I will walk among them,” that is, I shall walk about in their heart as in a spacious place through charity. For the presence of the divine majesty walks in us if it finds the breadth of charity, though God alone produces this in us.

The sense is: “I will walk among them,” that is, I shall advance them and make them persevere in progress. “And I will be their God,” that is, I shall so benefit them that I may appear to be God. “And they shall be my people,” that is, they shall so obey me that they may appear to be mine and not the world’s.

Or he speaks of Christ’s bodily dwelling among human beings; and Christ says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them,” that is, I shall live bodily among them. Thus Jeremiah says: “He was seen upon earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III). And John says: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). [Col. 0050C] Here Christ is our Lord, and the Church is his people. Hence he adds: “I will be their Lord, and they shall be my people.”

Therefore he wishes them to be separated from every defilement, so that he may receive them as children. Hence he adds: “Therefore,” etc. Here he uses Isaiah’s words as though they were his own. Literally, this was said to the Jews dwelling in Babylon, that they should not associate with the Babylonians among whom they lived. The Apostle applies it spiritually to us.

As though he said: Therefore, because you are God’s temple, go out from their midst, since you are in the midst of their wickedness. But go out not bodily, but spiritually: do not remain silent, [Col. 0050D] but rebuke their crimes. [Note: [Col. 0049D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] The wicked must indeed be endured for the sake of peace; one should not withdraw from them bodily, but spiritually. To go out is to do, as far as one may according to one’s station and without disturbing peace, what pertains to the correction of the wicked. And having gone out, be separated from them, so as not even to consent with them.

Or, “be separated”: that is, stand apart, prepared against them, as formerly you stood ready for them. And the Lord says this to you. As though he said: This does not come from me. “And do not touch what is unclean”: that is, carnal observances and any other unlawful things. As though he said: There must not even be a touch—that is, the delight which is the first movement of mortal sin. A spiritual withdrawal is meant here; likewise, [Col. 0051A] the touch is to be understood as one of the heart, not of the body. [Note: [Col. 0051D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] To be displeased by evil is not to touch it.

For the prophets who spoke these things did not abandon their people; they lived among those whom they rebuked, entered one temple with them, and celebrated the same sacraments. Therefore this is to go out: not to spare with one’s mouth, but to reprove, correct, and warn. This is to be separated: to go against them. This is not to touch what is unclean: not to consent in one’s will. The prophets did all these things.

Therefore we must withdraw spiritually, not bodily, because in separating ourselves bodily from the good on account of the wicked, we commit a greater evil than that which we avoid by not remaining in fellowship with the wicked. [Col. 0051B] [Augustine] Let each person therefore withdraw spiritually from the wicked. God does not impute that person’s own sins, because he did not commit them; nor others’ sins, because he did not approve them; nor negligence, because he did not keep silent; nor pride, because he remained in unity. But if someone withdraws bodily, he is proud and schismatic.

“And I…” As though he said: Do as I have said, and I will receive you, though formerly cast out; and, having received you, I shall be a father to you, giving myself to you; and you shall be to me, namely for my glory and honor, sons—that is, like me—and daughters. He adds this in order to include the weaker sex also. And this says the Lord Almighty—that is, Christ, who can do all that the Father can do.

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–7

“Therefore, having these promises, beloved, [Col. 0051C] let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God. Receive us. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, defrauded no one. I do not say this to condemn you. For I have said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. I have great confidence in you, great boasting on your behalf. I am filled with consolation; I overflow with joy in all our tribulation. For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest, but we suffered every tribulation: conflicts without, fears within. But God, who consoles the humble, consoled us by the coming of Titus—not only by his coming, but also by the consolation with which he was consoled by you, [Col. 0051D] reporting to us your longing, your weeping, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced the more.”

128 “Therefore, having these…” As though he said: Since the Lord commands this and gives so excellent a promise, therefore, having these promises, beloved—namely, that God will dwell in us and receive us—let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh, such as lust, and of spirit, such as anger. Defilement of the flesh is understood in many ways. Therefore he said, “from every,” because carnal vices are many, so that we may flee them all. I mean, let us perfect by good action the sanctification begun in baptism. And let this be in the fear of God, so that we may fear God, who alone accomplishes this.

Or read it thus, according to another text, which does not contain: “And let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh.” [Ambrose] Make the division here. I mean: perfecting the sanctification of the spirit—that is, of the mind—which occurs when we are in the fear of God, that is, when we follow the fear of God. For one who does this without God is holy for the world, not for God.

And if an example is necessary for these things, receive us—that is, take us as your example, not those false apostles. Or read it thus: let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh—that is, from carnal observances—and, nevertheless, perfect the sanctification which belongs to the Holy Spirit, and do this in the fear of God.

Receive us as an example, because we have wronged none of you by haste, as the false apostles do. We have corrupted no one by mixing in falsehood like leaven; we have defrauded [Col. 0052B] no one by fraudulently taking away what was yours, as the false apostles do, who smoothly take away your goods. For the false apostles both harmed them by corrupting their understanding and burdened their purses by the circumvention of serpentine cunning.

But I do not say this to condemn you—that is, to cast you away who have sinned in these matters—but I urge you to correct yourselves. For I love you, as I said before. This is what he adds: “For I have said before that you are in our hearts,” in respect of care and love. I mean, you are there “to die together and to live together”: I love you so greatly that your death in sins seems to be mine, and likewise your life in virtues.

Or: I love you “to die together and to live together,” that is, that you may suffer with me and be crowned with me. Therefore I urge you, because I have great [Col. 0052C] confidence in you: that is, while I consider what is in you, since they had been corrected also through the first Epistle, I therefore boast on their behalf. Hence he adds: “I have great boasting for you before others.” Take care that it is not vain; I also have consolation. Hence he adds: “I am filled with consolation,” having heard of your correction. Through those already corrected he invites others to correction. “And I overflow with joy in every tribulation”: that is, my joy surpasses every tribulation, which was partly in my mind because of your sins. For when he sees progress in those for whom he suffers, he rejoices.

“For even when we came…” [Ambrose] He recounts here what he suffers for the sake of believers, in order to stir them to charity. As though he said: I rightly said “in tribulation,” [Col. 0052D] which is indeed great. For when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no rest. He says that the flesh, rather than the soul, had no rest, because even amid adversities the soul, suffering in the body, rests in hope of the future. It had no rest, I say; rather, we suffered every tribulation, both in body and in soul. And this was because there he drove the Python-spirit from a slave girl (Acts XVI).

And truly every tribulation: for without—that is, in the body—there were conflicts, that is, afflictions; and within—that is, in the mind—there were fears lest the churches should fail. Or, “without” means from the faithless outside the Church, that is, from open enemies: there were conflicts, that is, afflictions. [Col. 0053A] But from the faithful within—that is, within the Church—there were fears lest they should be shaken. Or the fears were from those who were within the Church in body, not mind; in name, not in spiritual reality—that is, from false brethren, because they are harder to endure than those openly wicked. For no plague is more effective than a familiar enemy, and “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X).

“But he who…” As though he said: We suffered so grievously, but God, who consoles those humble in spirit—or “the humble,” that is, the afflicted—consoled us by the coming of Titus, because I received a helper. God consoled us not only by his coming, since the one we longed for arrived, but also by the consolation with which Titus was consoled among you—that is, by your amendment. For I saw Titus consoled [Col. 0053B] among you, and I was consoled. Titus was consoled among you, I mean, while reporting to us your desire for amendment, your weeping over what you had committed, and your zeal—that is, indignation—shown against the false apostles on my behalf, that is, in my defense; reporting these things, I say, so that I rejoiced more at what he reported than I grieved at my tribulation.

### Verses 8–13

“For even if I made you sorrowful by my Epistle, I do not regret it. And even if I had regretted it, seeing that that Epistle, although it made you sorrowful for a time, now I rejoice—not because you were made sorrowful, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance. For you were made sorrowful according to God, so that in nothing you might suffer loss through us. For godly sorrow works repentance unto a lasting salvation; but the sorrow of the world [Col. 0053C] works death. For behold, this very thing—your being made sorrowful according to God—how great a concern it has worked in you; indeed, defense, indeed, indignation, indeed, fear, indeed, longing, indeed, zeal, indeed, vengeance. In every respect you have shown yourselves to be undefiled in the matter. Therefore, even though I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of him who did the wrong, nor for the sake of him who suffered it, but to make manifest before God our concern which we have for you. Therefore we have been consoled.”

“For even if I made you sorrowful…” As though he said: It may be proved from this that I rejoice, because I no longer regret having rebuked you severely in the first Epistle. And this is what he says: even if I made you sorrowful in the first [Col. 0053D] Epistle, I do not now regret it, because you have been corrected—even if I had formerly regretted it, while you were angry. He says this lest he appear inhuman in rejoicing at the sorrow of others.

“Seeing that that Epistle…” As though he said: I do not regret it; rather, I now rejoice, seeing that that Epistle made you sorrowful—that is, although I see that the Epistle made you sorrowful, which initially grieved me and made me regret it. It made you sorrowful, I say, though only for a time, that is, a short time. Hence there is good hope of their correction, and therefore he no longer regrets it but rejoices.

He specifies why he rejoices by adding: “Not because…” As though he said: I say that I rejoice, not indeed because you were made sorrowful against me, but because you were made sorrowful unto repentance: having thus recognized your fault, you repented. [Ambrose] And [Col. 0054A] he says that he rejoices because they were made sorrowful, not with anger, which makes people worse, but with shame, which corrects.

“For you were made sorrowful…” As though he said: I rejoice in this sorrow because it is sorrow according to God. This is what he says: “For you were made sorrowful according to God,” that is, according to God’s will and inspiration, so that in nothing—not even in harsh things—you might suffer loss through us; for everything from us benefits you, even when we rebuke you and make you sorrowful.

“For…” As though he said: Truly, we do not suffer loss; rather, we gain an advantage. For sorrow according to God—namely, when a sinner is sorrowful because he has sinned, when he grieves because he has done what God hates—works repentance, that is, satisfaction, which is effective unto a lasting—that is, eternal—salvation. [Col. 0054B] But worldly sorrow, which does not lead to correction—namely, when a sinner grieves that he has been exposed—works death. Therefore beware of it.

“For behold…” As though he said: Truly, godly sorrow produces repentance unto salvation, because it produces the things that lead to salvation—that is, concern, and so forth. This is what he says: “For behold.” As though he said: You have experienced in yourselves what I say, because this very thing—that is, so small a matter as your being made sorrowful according to God for sin—works in you so great a concern to amend what you have done wrong. This is true, because one who repents is concerned not to sin again.

Nor does it work this alone, but also a defense, so that you defend me even against the false apostles. Or it works a defense because one who repents does not excuse himself but confesses sin; [Col. 0054C] this is to defend oneself against Gehenna. Nor does it work this alone, but also indignation against yourselves for the evil you have done; and not only this, but fear lest such a thing happen in the future; and not only this, but longing to advance toward better things. For one who knows himself to have been deformed by sin longs to be restored; and not only this, but zeal, so that you may imitate me or other good persons. For one who repents has zeal for the accomplishment of good works; but also vengeance, because you punish the sinner, and yourselves as well. For one who repents takes vengeance upon himself for what he has done wrong.

And, to state comprehensively that you have been made sorrowful according to God, in all respects, led by faith, you have shown yourselves undefiled—that is, to be undefiled—in the conduct of Christian business, that is, in performing all the duties of Christian life. Or, “you have shown yourselves”: by punishing the man who committed incest, you showed yourselves undefiled by the matter—that is, by his grave sin in taking his father’s wife, in which you had been defiled by consenting.

“Therefore…” As though he said: And because you are undefiled, it is clear that I wrote to you not principally for their sake, but for the one who acted and the one who suffered wrong. Thus he says: Therefore, even if I wrote to you on their account, I did not do so for the sake of him who committed the wrong—namely, the one who committed incest and carried off his father’s wife—nor for the sake of him, namely the father, who suffered the wrong, that is, whose wife was taken away; but to make manifest [Col. 0055A] our concern for the amendment of all of you. That is, I did this not only for them, but for the correction of all of you.

Or he refers to those whom he says above, in the first Epistle, had inflicted injuries and frauds upon their brethren. He shows that he wrote not more for the sake of those who sinned, that they might be forgiven, than for the sake of the Church, which suffers and is indignant when one person commits insult and fraud. This is what he says: Therefore, even if I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the person who injured—that is, defrauded—his neighbor, nor for the person who suffered fraud, but to make manifest our concern for you. He shows that he has concern for the whole people: that the unjust may be corrected, the defiled sanctified, and the churches reconciled. [Col. 0055B]

129 And I say this before God, that is, with God as witness. “And therefore…” As though he said: Since this was my purpose, and it happened, therefore we have been consoled—that is, we received consolation when you were corrected.

### Verses 13–16

“Moreover, in your consolation we rejoiced still more abundantly because of Titus’s joy, since his spirit was refreshed by all of you. And if in any respect I boasted to him about you, I was not put to shame; but as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting which was made to Titus proved true. And his affections are more abundant toward you as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice that in all things I have confidence in you.”

[Col. 0055C] “Moreover, in your consolation,” which arises from your correction, and in Titus’s joy, we rejoiced more abundantly than we grieved at tribulation—but especially in Titus’s joy. As though he said: In both, that is, your correction and Titus’s joy, we rejoiced more abundantly than we were saddened by tribulation; but more especially in Titus’s joy, because he rejoiced not only over those corrected but also over others whom he hopes to correct.

For his spirit, Titus’s spirit, was refreshed. He now hopes good things from you. It was refreshed by all of you—not because all had been corrected, but because he hopes concerning the rest. And if I boasted anything about you to him, commending you, I was not put to shame; therefore I am not ashamed to be found false. Rather, just as we spoke all things to you in truth—that is, [Col. 0055D] in rebuking, the rebuker’s truth appears when those rebuked amend themselves; for when those corrected change, they bear testimony to the one rebuking them.

Therefore, showing his preaching to be true through their effectiveness, the Apostle says: “Just as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting about you, made to Titus, proved true”—that is, its truth appeared to him; it proved true. Therefore his affections—that is, his innermost charity—are toward you, because a holy man’s affection is fixed upon every good. They are more abundant, I say, than before, because he saw their progress. [Ambrose] Or, more abundant than toward others.

I mean Titus’s affections, as he remembers the obedience of all of you. He shows that Titus praised them because they were eager to obey him. In Titus, however, they reverenced the Apostle. I mean, remembering your obedience: how carefully you received him with fear of heart and trembling of body. And because you acted thus toward him, I rejoice that I have confidence in you—and this in all matters, not only in good will but also in good works.

Observe, however, that here, where he praises them, he incidentally gives prior admonition concerning alms for the saints in Jerusalem, through the example of the Macedonians.
