Aptly, where the corrected are discussed, mention is made of collections, because he does not seek from others to whom it does no good to give their own goods or to persuade them to do so. As though he said: I had no rest in Macedonia, although there a great grace was given to me, which I make known to you. This is what he says:

## Chapter VIII

### Verses 1–8

“Now, brethren, [Col. 0056B] we make known to you the grace of God which has been given in the churches of Macedonia: that in a great testing of tribulation the abundance of their joy was present, and their very deep poverty overflowed into the riches of their simplicity. For I bear them witness that according to their ability—and beyond their ability—they gave willingly, earnestly begging us for the grace and fellowship of the ministry carried out for the saints. And not as we hoped, but they first gave themselves to the Lord, and then to us through the will of God; so that we asked Titus that, as he had begun, so he might also complete in you this grace as well. But as you abound in all things—in faith, speech, knowledge, every earnestness, and moreover in your charity [Col. 0056C] toward us—so may you abound in this grace also. I say this not as one commanding, but through the earnestness of others, testing also the genuine quality of your charity.”

“Now I make known to you, brethren, the grace of God,” that is, God’s free gift. He calls the giving of alms a gift of God. This grace was given to me in the churches of Macedonia. What is it? Namely, that the abundance of their joy was manifest in a great testing of tribulation: they not only were willing to suffer, but experienced suffering; and they rejoiced in it, and, though poor, gave abundantly. Hence he adds: “And their very deep poverty,” etc.

Or: the abundance of their joy was manifest in a great testing of tribulation because they were not scandalized by the tribulation inflicted there upon Paul and Silas. [Ambrose] Rather, they devoutly [Col. 0056D] and joyfully received the word, showing themselves approved by these sufferings. And their very deep poverty—that is, great or very noble poverty—overflowed, through the generosity of their minds, into the riches of their simplicity: it became greater while it sought to give riches. And this they did with a simple mind, not in order to please people. Though scant in material resources, they were rich in giving, because they acted from a private conscience.

I bear them witness because, with no one compelling them, they were willing to give according to their means from their own possessions, and beyond their means, so that they themselves afterward were in need. I mean, they earnestly begged us—when I hesitated to agree to their request—that we would permit them to have the grace and fellowship of the ministry, that is, ministration, [Col. 0057A] which ministry is performed for the saints. That is, they begged that it might be permitted them to give their goods, not as their own but as common goods with which they might minister to others.

And they did not give their goods as we hoped—that is, with the intention we supposed, namely to redeem sins. Rather, they first gave themselves to the Lord, to obey him: amending their former errors and vices of conduct, they devoted themselves to God; then they gave or offered their goods to their brethren. Otherwise, gifts ought not to have been accepted from them, because gifts blind the eyes and weaken the force of authority. Those who give in order not to be rebuked have no fruit from giving. But these people did not give with the purpose that, by redeeming their vices, they should not be rebuked. Rather, they first gave themselves to the Lord by amendment of life.

Then they gave themselves to us by obedience, namely so as to obey us. [Col. 0057B] And this was through God’s will, who wills people to be subject to his vicars. They pressed us so strongly that, stirred by their example, we asked Titus that, just as he had begun to do good among you after seeing you corrected, so he might complete in you not merely other things but also this grace of almsgiving for the saints, so that this grace might not be lacking to you.

I say, “complete this grace in you,” and not in just any manner, but so that you may abound also in this grace of generous almsgiving, just as you abound in all other things: faith, speech—that is, the grace of speaking—knowledge of the Scriptures, every earnestness, since you are earnest in all things, and, moreover, your spiritual charity toward us.

“Not as one commanding…” As though he said: I asked Titus to complete this grace, but I do not say this as one commanding, lest you become transgressors. Or it may be read thus: As though he said: Not only did I ask Titus to complete this grace in you, but I myself also say—not as one commanding—that you should abound in this grace as you abound in all other things, namely faith, and so forth, which are not changed.

“But through the earnestness of others…” As though he said: I do not speak as one commanding; rather, I speak in order to test—that is, wishing to test—the good disposition of your charity: wishing to persuade you to be generous and to act from discernment of mind, not for earthly advantage. And I wish to test and persuade you not merely through other considerations, but also through the earnestness [Col. 0057D] of others, namely the Macedonians, so that you may be like them; or through the earnestness of the poor, for whom you ought to be concerned.

“For you know…” As though he said: You ought to give to the poor, and rightly so, because Christ was concerned for them.

### Verses 9–15

“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, he became poor for your sake, so that through his poverty you might become rich. And in this I give counsel. For this is useful to you, who began not only to do but also to will it from the preceding year. But now complete it also in deed, so that, as the readiness of your will is present, so there may be readiness in accomplishing it from what you possess. For if the will is ready, it is accepted according to [Col. 0058A] what one has, not according to what one does not have. For the purpose is not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but that by equality, at the present time your abundance may supply their need, so that their abundance may also supply your need, that there may be equality, as it is written: ‘He who had much did not have too much, and he who had little did not have too little.’”

You know the grace—that is, the love—of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whose example he exhorts them. You know, I say, this grace of Christ: that, though he was rich as God in his majesty, through whom also all things were made, he became poor for our sakes in the world.

[Note: Col. 0057D, Augustine, in a sermon on the words of salvation.] Observe that he does not say, “He became poor, though he had been rich,” but “though he was rich.” For he took on poverty and did not lose riches: rich within, poor without; God hidden in riches, man appearing in poverty, so that by his poverty you might become rich in spiritual things. Through his poverty, indeed, we cast off the rags of iniquity in order to put on the robe of immortality. Therefore all who believe in poor Christ have become rich. Let no one, then, despise himself. Poor in his cell, rich in conscience, he sleeps more securely on the ground than one rich in gold sleeps in purple. Therefore do not now fear to approach, in your own beggary, him who was clothed with our poverty. He who made himself poor made us rich.

And in this—that is, in consideration of this great benefit of God—I give you counsel: give alms to the poor.

[Col. 0058C] [Augustine] For this is beneficial to you. It is more beneficial to the one who gives than to the one to whom it is done. I speak to you, who began in the first year—that is, in the preceding year—not only to do, but also to will, which is more than doing. But now complete it also in deed, so that you may not only will, but also accomplish it in work.

Or he may mean that some of them had begun to act and others to will. As if he said: I speak to you, who began in the first year not only to will, according to some, but also to act, according to others. For some had willed, and some had begun; but now both groups complete it in work. This is what follows: “But now complete it also in deed, so that, just as the disposition of willing is ready”—that is, just as their choice of the will is ready, because they will from discernment—“so the disposition for accomplishing may be ready.”

[Col. 0058D] [Ambrose] He says this so that their will may appear in action, if it is genuine. I mean, accomplish it from what you have—that is, according to what you possess, whether more or less. For if the will is ready in giving according to what one has, so as to retain necessities, it is accepted to that extent; it is not accepted in giving according to what one does not have—that is, beyond one’s means. Therefore I urge you to give from what you have.

For I do not mean that there should be relief or refreshment for others—that others should live idly from what is yours—while there is affliction for you, that is, poverty. He did not say this because that would not be better. He makes allowance for the weak, whom he urges to give in such a way that they do not suffer want; rather, I mean that your abundance of earthly goods should supply their need, who have forsaken all worldly things. I say, supply it in the present time, which is so brief, and this in equality.

He says this so that each person may share with the saints according to what he has; for no more is required than what one ought to retain for oneself, just as Zacchaeus gave half his goods to the poor (Luke 19). Or: let your abundance supply their need in equality. I do not say this according to strict parity, but so that they may be supported from your possessions, as you yourselves are. This is equality: those who receive spiritual things provide material things. This is the peace of Jerusalem: that bodily works of mercy should be joined to the spiritual work of preaching, and that peace should arise through giving and receiving. Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9).

“And that their abundance.” As if he said: Let your abundance of earthly goods supply their need, so that, conversely, the abundance of their spiritual merits, who devote themselves to divine things, may supply your need.

[Col. 0059B] [Augustine] For those who live in this world do not possess merits sufficient for eternal life unless they are helped by others. But because the poor of Christ, whose is the kingdom of heaven, have made friends and debtors for themselves, through their merits they will obtain what they could not merit for themselves; so that equality may then come about—not that they will not differ in glory, but because all will possess that good and all will have sufficiency. As is written of manna, in a figure of this matter: “He who had much”—namely, collected much manna, that is, had more than a gomor—“did not abound,” because he who had more gave to the needy; “and he who had little”—namely, collected less than a gomor—“did not lack,” that is, did not have less than a gomor, because he received from one who abounded.

[Col. 0059C] But in Exodus it is written thus: “Nor did he who had gathered more have more; nor did he who had prepared less find less” (Exod. 16). This foreshadowed that those having greater merits and those having lesser merits will have the same refreshment at the eternal banquet.

[Ambrose] Or thus: “So that equality may come about.” As if he said: I say that your abundance should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need; so that equality may thus come about, namely, that just as these minister to the saints, so in the future the saints may repay them in turn. As is written of manna, in a figure of this matter: “He who collected much did not abound, and he who collected little did not lack.” The saints have more in the hope of the future; those who are rich in this present time have less. When both are made equal there, then, as the rich here sustain the need of the saints, so there they will be sustained by the benefit of the saints and become rich in the eternal good.

Or thus: “So that equality may come about.” As if he said: Let your abundance supply their need, in such a way that equality may exist in will, even if not in deed; and thus you will receive alike, as is written of manna in a figure of this matter: he who has much and he who has little did not lack. Thus, the rich person who gives much and the poor person who gives little will have an equal reward if their will is equal.

## Verses 16–24

“But thanks be to God, who gave the same concern for you in the heart of Titus; for he indeed accepted the exhortation, but, being more concerned, he went to you of his own accord. We also sent with him our brother, whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the churches. And not only so, but he was also appointed by the churches as companion of our journey in this grace, which is administered by us for the glory of the Lord and our intended will; avoiding this, lest anyone blame us concerning this abundance which is administered for the glory of the Lord. For we provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings. And we sent with them [Col. 0060B] our brother whom we have often proved diligent in many matters, but who is now much more diligent because of his great confidence in you—whether concerning Titus, who is my partner and helper among you, or our brothers, apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ. Therefore show, before the churches, the proof of your love and of our glorying on your behalf toward them.”

“But thanks.” As if he said: I urged Titus to complete this grace, or I myself give you this counsel. But I give thanks to God, who placed in Titus’s heart the same concern which I have: concern to exhort you to abound in this simplicity of almsgiving. And he truly had concern, because he indeed accepted your exhortation; but, being more concerned by his own will than through my exhortation, he went to you.

[Col. 0060C] At first, when asked, he excused himself because of your faults. We also sent with him our brother, namely Luke or Barnabas: Luke, whose praise is in the written Gospel; or Barnabas, whose praise is in the preached Gospel. I say that his praise is throughout all the churches. Not only is his praise in the Gospel, but he was also appointed by the churches of Judaea as companion in our journey—that is, in the preaching by which we travel around the world. He was made a companion in this grace, that is, in this bestowal of alms, which is administered by us—that is, of which we apostles are ministers. This is for the Lord’s glory, so that God may thereby be glorified, and for the fulfilment of our will, which is that you should give well.

[Col. 0060D] I mean the intended will, a will appointed and preordained for us by God; so necessary is it. Or thus: he was appointed companion in our journey—that is, in preaching—namely, in this grace, that is, in the preaching to the Gentiles, which is administered by us, of which I am minister; and this is for the Lord’s glory, so that the Lord may thereby be glorified. He was appointed companion to fulfil our intended will—that is, to complete the preaching to the Gentiles to which I have been appointed.

“Avoiding this.”

[Ambrose] As if he said: We sent these persons mentioned above, avoiding this: lest anyone blame us over this abundance of almsgiving, saying that we defraud them. Or lest anyone blame us concerning this abundance, namely of teaching and miracles, as negligent about the care of the saints; so that it might be said: “He preaches well, but he does not remember the saints, as the other apostles do and as he was commanded.” Thus the Apostle would be blamed if he acted negligently toward the saints. Therefore he makes this provision, so that his concern and foresight may appear.

[Col. 0061A] This abundance, whether of generosity or doctrine, is administered by us—that is, it comes about through our ministry—and this is for the Lord’s glory, so that God may be glorified.

“For we provide.” As if he said: I rightly say, “avoiding,” for we provide that our works may be good, not only before God, so as to please God, but also before people, so as to appear good to people. The Apostle provides what is good before God when he does, concerning the ministry of the saints, what God commands; he provides what is good before people when he sends good persons to urge this work, whose uprightness may move them to give and cause no scandal, lest the Apostle’s good teaching fall into reproach through imprudent ministers.

[Note: Col. 0061D, Augustine, sermon “On Life and Death.”] Observe that the Apostle rightly says that he provides what is good before God and people. For our conscience is sufficient for ourselves; but, for your sake, our reputation ought not to be sullied among you but to have force. There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience benefits you; reputation benefits your neighbor. Whoever, trusting in conscience, neglects reputation is cruel.

“But we sent with them our brother,” Apollos, whom we have often proved diligent in many matters concerning our salvation. But now, when he heard that you had been corrected, he was much more diligent because of the great confidence placed in you—or among you—whether because of Titus, who told him much about you. Thus Apollos, who when first asked by the Apostle and the other brothers had been unwilling to go to them, now went because he heard that they had been corrected.

[Col. 0061C] Titus, that is, is my partner and helper among you—that is, in your conduct. “Or.” As if he said: He went because of his confidence in you, and because of Titus and Luke, with whom he gladly went; or he did this also on account of those others, who are our brothers and apostles of the churches, by whom he had been asked.

Or, according to another reading, with the same sense: “whether through our brothers, apostles of the churches,” who themselves are apostles of the churches. This belongs to the glory of God, of Christ—that is, to Christ’s glory—because in them there is not human glory but Christ’s glory.

“Therefore show the proof,” and so forth. As if he said: Since we sent such men to you, therefore show toward them the proof which is your love and our glorying on your behalf—that is, show them your love, which you have shown to others, and show our glorying about you, which you have shown to be true—by receiving well those whom we sent to you, so that they may find true the good things they heard about you.

[Col. 0061D] [Ambrose] I say, show this before the churches, so that the other churches may know that the good things they heard about you are true. Or, “before the churches,” so that others may take an example from you. “For also”—as if he said: I give this warning concerning their reception.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 0062A]

### Verses 1–7

“For it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry performed for the saints. For I know your ready disposition, on account of which I boast about you among the Macedonians: that Achaia also has been ready since the preceding year, and your zeal has stirred up very many. But we sent the brothers so that our glorying about you might not be made void in this respect, so that, as I said, you may be ready; lest, when Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—lest I say you—should be ashamed in this matter. Therefore I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go ahead to you and prepare this promised blessing, so that it may be ready as a blessing and not as avarice. But I say this: He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessings will also reap from blessings. Let each give as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.”

“For it is superfluous”—that is, unnecessary—for me to write to you concerning the ministry performed for the saints. For I know your ready disposition, on account of which I boast about you among the Macedonians, saying: “Achaia, whose metropolis is Corinth, moved by rivalry with the Macedonians, has been ready since the preceding year; and your zeal,” that is, love and earnestness, “stirs up very many to give alms.”

[Ambrose] For through zeal for the Corinthians, other churches, when they hear that those once entangled in errors afterwards became persons of good will, are stirred to good.

[Col. 0062C] But as though someone should say, “Why then do you send them beforehand?” he says: “But we sent the brothers to exhort you in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I told them you were ready.” I mean, ready, lest this—namely, our whole glorying about you—be made void in this respect, should you prove unprepared. You ought therefore to be ready, lest, when Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we who boast about you should be ashamed—not to say that you would be ashamed, which is greater, that is, ought more especially to be said. For if what he testified about them is not found, both he himself will be ashamed and they will be more deeply confounded.

“In this matter,” that is, in this giving of alms by which the poor are supported. Therefore, lest this happen, I thought it necessary to urge the brothers—namely Luke, Titus, and Apollos—to precede me to you and prepare this promised blessing—that is, this often-promised blessing, namely almsgiving—to be ready when we come. It is rightly called a blessing because it is the cause of eternal blessing.

[Col. 0062D] I mean, ready in this way: as a blessing, namely, so that it may be a work of love and great, not as avarice, so that they grieve over what has been given and what they give is small.

“But I say this.” As if he said: Let them prepare it; but I say this, namely prescribe why you should give generously: he who sows sparingly—that is, gives—will also reap a sparing recompense. He who possesses little and gives little does not sow sparingly if his disposition is ready to give more, should he have more. Observe that he does not say “gives” but “sows,” because giving alms is not losing but sowing: being without something for a time, so as to have more in the future.

[Col. 0063A] And he who sows in blessings, where one’s disposition is weighed more than one’s property, will also reap from God’s blessings an abundant recompense. Therefore let each person give as he has determined—that is, preordained—in his heart, that is, in the counsel of reason; for if they gave unwillingly, it would not benefit them. Whoever gives unwillingly from present embarrassment has no reward. Therefore let each give as he has resolved in his heart that he wishes to give; let him not give in sorrow or under compulsion—that is, sadly or coerced—but freely.

For God loves a cheerful giver—that is, one who gives from good will; God approves and rewards such a giver, not the sorrowful and murmuring one. Whoever gives in order to be free from the annoyance of the petitioner rather than to refresh the distressed heart of the needy loses both the thing and the merit.

[Note: Col. 0063D, Augustine, on Psalm 38.] Whatever good you do, do it cheerfully, and then you do good; but if you do it sadly, it is done by you, not you who do it.

### Verses 8–15

“But God is able to make every grace abound in you, so that, always having all sufficiency in all things, you may abound in every good work; as it is written: ‘He scattered abroad; he gave to the poor; his righteousness remains for ever and ever.’ And he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will provide and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness, so that, enriched in all things, you may abound in all simplicity, which works through us thanksgiving to God. For the ministry of this service not only supplies [Col. 0063C] what is lacking to the saints, but also abounds through many thanksgivings to the Lord, as, through the proof of this ministry, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession in the Gospel of Christ, and for the simplicity of your sharing with them and with all, and in their prayer for you, as they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God in you. Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift.”

“But God is able.” As if he said: I give you this admonition, but God is able. Or the connection is this: I exhort you thus; and do not distrust, because God is able to make every grace abound in you, or in your hearts—not only this grace, but this along with the others, that is, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit—so that you, always having, that is, reckoning that you have, all sufficiency in all things, that is, in every condition of your life, may abound in every good work, that is, in giving alms, as in the rest.

[Col. 0063D] [Ambrose] For one who chooses mere sufficiency can abound in God’s work. Although what one with little gives is small, he nevertheless abounds because it is done with right judgment; for the question is how much is given and with what disposition.

And as though someone asked, “Is this good—namely, the giving of alms?” he answers: Certainly, as it is written in the Psalm: “The righteous person scattered abroad,” not giving everything to one person but distributing among many, “and gave freely to the poor,” not to the rich who could repay.

[Col. 0064A] “And his righteousness”—that is, the reward of his righteousness—“remains for ever and ever,” or eternally, that is, without end. A righteous person is one who regards the goods of this world as common in view of the end of eternal reward. Observe that by this example he invites them to give generously to the saints. For if the reward of one who gives generously to the poor is great, how much greater is that of one who ministers to the saints? For “poor” may include even those who are evil.

“But he who.” As if he said: Not only is life given from this, but he who supplies seed to the sower—namely God—will provide seed from which alms may be given, and bread, that is, life’s necessities, for food, not for superfluity. He will provide so abundantly that he will also multiply your seed, from which you may give more alms. Therefore, let no one be afraid to give through this fear.

[Col. 0064B] And he will increase the fruits—that is, the means and will—for giving alms: I mean the fruits of your righteousness, from which righteousness and life proceed. Righteousness is holiness and a good life, from which come fruits, that is, eternal recompense. The fruits are alms and the will to give; through these virtues will be increased here and glory in the future.

“So that in all things.” As if he said: He will increase both your resources and your will to give to such an extent that, enriched according to your own reckoning in all things—that is, in every condition of life—you may abound in simplicity, that is, generosity performed with a single-minded disposition. I mean every simplicity, that is, perfect generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God. Therefore it ought to be done; that generosity itself is the reason why thanks are given to God, and we are its ministers.

[Col. 0064C] “For,” and so forth. As if he said: Therefore thanksgiving will be given to God for the gift of generosity, because there are many good things in it. This is what he says:

For the ministry of this service of yours not only supplies what is lacking to the saints, but also abounds in thanksgiving made by many, because many thereby give thanks to God. And this is in the Lord—that is, by the Lord’s working, who moved them to give thanks. I say that many will give thanks to God, and this through the proof of this ministry, that is, because they praise this service of ours.

I mean, many glorifying God, not only for your generosity, but also, taking occasion from it, for—or concerning—the obedience of your confession, that is, your faith and confession and all your good. I mean the obedience found in the Gospel of Christ, because you obeyed Christ’s Gospel in submission of mind. They glorify God for the simplicity of your sharing—that is, because you regard your things as common and do this with a single-minded disposition.

[Col. 0064D] Or, “for the simplicity of your sharing,” because others, following your example, share their possessions with others. I mean sharing made with them—that is, the saints previously mentioned—and with all other needy people.

“And in their,” and so forth. As if he said: I mean many also glorifying God for the prayer of those saints made for you; that is, those many likewise glorify God for this, because the saints themselves pray for you.

[Note: Col. 0065D, Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*.] I mean, they long to see you in eternal blessedness, or even here. And this is because of the grace of God—that is, the surpassing love—in you.

“Thanks be to God.” He has treated of the mutual need and the mutual supplying of the need of Christ’s provincials and Christ’s soldiers: from these to those, concerning material goods; and from those to these, concerning spiritual goods. Therefore, as though full of the rich food of holy joys and pouring it forth, he cries: “Thanks be to God.” As if he said: Because so many goods arise from this, I give thanks to God for his unspeakable gift—that is, for the love which he gives to his own, whose usefulness cannot be described. Or, “unspeakable,” that is, a gift which ought to be spoken of.

## Chapter X

[Col. 0065B]

### Verses 1–7

“But I myself, Paul, entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble in appearance among you when present, but bold toward you when absent. But I ask you, lest, when present, I should have to be bold with the confidence by which I am thought to dare against certain persons who suppose that we walk according to the flesh. For, though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds: destroying counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ; and being ready to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled. See the things that are according to outward appearance. If anyone trusts in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: that as he belongs to Christ, so do we.”

“But I myself.” After exhorting the good concerning almsgiving to be given to the saints, he deals with the uncorrected, who followed the false apostles and thought him severe. As if he said: I invite the corrected to give alms; but I, Paul, entreat you others, who prefer false apostles to me. As if he said: Truly humble and not proud is the very one who exhorts others to give alms—the same toward you as toward them.

I entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—that is, if you wish me to be gentle toward you and, should I correct you, to punish you with restraint—as Christ too, even when provoked, showed a gentle disposition and did not exceed moderation in corrections.

[Col. 0065D] I, Paul, am humble in appearance—that is, outwardly, as you say—among you, namely when I am present. “But when absent.” As if he said: When I do not fear that you will do me some harm, I am bold toward you, that is, I act boldly against you, rebuking you sharply.

“But I ask.” Here he says why he entreats them. As if he said: Not only do I entreat you, but I also ask that, when present—that is, when I come—I may not have to dare against certain uncorrected persons; that is, that I may not boldly punish them when present with the confidence by which I am thought to dare when absent. For to the degree that I am thought to be bold when absent, I shall be so in fact when present, unless they amend themselves.

Therefore he asks that he may find them such that he need not be compelled to become angry and dare against them, but may, after the severity already expressed, rejoice with them.

[Col. 0066A] I mean certain persons who suppose that we walk according to the flesh—that is, in the manner of carnal people. “For though we walk in the flesh.” As if he said: They suppose that we walk according to the flesh; we do not, because although we walk in the flesh—that is, live in the flesh, which is frail—we nevertheless do not wage war according to the flesh, that is, for carnal advantage. For we do not exercise the warfare given us by God according to the flesh, that is, for earthly advantage.

And we truly do not wage war according to the flesh, for the weapons of our warfare—that is, the virtues and miracles by which we carry on warfare in preaching—are not fleshly in weakness, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds: that they may destroy the counsels of people or demons fortified by diverse stratagems.

[Col. 0066B] “Destroying counsels.” As if he said: Truly, I can destroy them, for we do destroy them. This is what he says. As if he said: We do not wage war according to the flesh—we who destroy the counsels of people and demons, and every height, that is, profundity of understanding, both of experts in the Law and of philosophers. I mean a height exalting itself against the knowledge of God, that is, knowledge concerning God—for example, when they attack the virgin birth and such matters.

[Ambrose] We also bring every understanding into captivity: we lead captive all who act or think proudly, overcoming those who contradict Christ. We bring them into the obedience of Christ, so that they may humbly obey Christ’s faith, which they had previously opposed.

[Col. 0066C] We are also ready, since nothing reproaches us so as to prevent our daring, to avenge every disobedience. We shall do this when your obedience has been fulfilled—that is, after I recognize that all are obedient from love. For then he avenges disobedience when he condemns it through obedience; then he destroys it when he leads those who resist to faith. And this is a worthy vengeance: that faithlessness should be condemned by those by whom it had been defended.

“See the things that are according to outward appearance,” and so forth. As if he said: I have said many things by which I have shown that you ought rather to follow us than the false apostles; and if what I have said does not suffice to show why you should follow me rather than false apostles, see these other things which are according to outward appearance—that is, as evident as things set before the eyes. For what he will say is clear: if any one of those false apostles—for he speaks of the presumptuous—trusts through something, that is, through faith or something else, that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again carefully within himself, so as not to exceed the force of reason through hatred of us or honor for himself: let him consider that, just as he belongs to Christ, so do we—that is, by whatever means he belongs to Christ, by those same means we do.

[Col. 0066D] Or thus: “See the things that are according to outward appearance.” As if he said: Truly we apostles are such as I have shown above. But consider carefully the works of those who are good only in your sight, lest perhaps they deceive you and you wish to prefer them to us. You ought not to do so, because if any of those presumptuous persons trusts through certain things that he belongs to Christ, let him consider again within himself that, just as he belongs to Christ, so do we: by whatever means he belongs to Christ, by those same means we do. He says this against the proud false apostles, who, presuming upon themselves through the swelling of their minds, set themselves above the Apostle.

### Verses 8–13

“For even if I should boast somewhat more concerning our authority, which the Lord gave us for your edification and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed. But lest I should be thought to terrify you by letters—for some say, ‘His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible’—let such a person consider this: that such as we are in word through letters when absent, such also we are in deed when present. For we do not dare to include or compare ourselves with certain persons who commend themselves; but they, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves. But we shall not boast without measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God apportioned to us, a measure of reaching as far as you.”

“For even if.” As if he said: Truly we belong to Christ as they do. For indeed we belong to Christ more excellently through the authority which they do not have. This is what he says: even if I should boast somewhat more about our authority, namely the apostolate, which the Lord gave to us, not to them, for edification and not for your destruction—that is, so that we may build you up in virtues and not corrupt you by evil teaching or example, as the false apostles do—I shall not be ashamed. For it is true, and it is said not for my own glory but for your benefit.

[Col. 0067C] “But lest,” and so forth. Here he says that, when present, he will fulfil in action what he threatens in words while absent. He says this on account of the statement he had made above, “ready to avenge every disobedience,” lest they suppose that he only threatened while absent and would do nothing when present. As if he said: The Lord gave me this authority for edification and not destruction; yet I shall avenge. They might have thought that he should therefore be gentle because he received authority for edification and not destruction; but he says, contrary to the opinion of some, that he will avenge.

“But lest.” As if he said: I am ready to avenge; nevertheless, because I say this, I am thought to terrify you by letters. And I am truly thought so, since some actually say: “His letters are weighty,” that is, weighty to understand, “and strong” in terrifying; “but his bodily presence is weak,” not daring to exercise severity, “and his speech contemptible,” because, they say, I speak like an unlearned person without arguments.

[Col. 0067D] Observe that he calls bodily presence “weak” in contrast with “strong,” and speech “contemptible” in contrast with “weighty.” But lest I should be thought by you merely to terrify you and not fulfil in deed what I threaten, let one who is such—that is, who holds this opinion of me—consider this. And let you know the same: what I threaten in words I shall fulfil in deeds. He says it thus: just as we are—that is, just as severe we are—in word through letters when absent, so we shall be in deed when present, namely avenging every disobedience; for if we indulged your vices, we would not be building up but destroying.

“For we do not.” As if he said: We shall be in deed such as we are in word, because we are not like the false apostles, who usurp authority for a day and indulge vices.

[Col. 0068A] [Ambrose] This is what he says: We do not include ourselves among certain persons—that is, the false apostles—who, not sent by God, commend themselves by certain arts; God does not commend them. That is, being unworthy, they usurp authority for themselves. In other words: We do not put ourselves in their number so as to usurp authority; rather, chosen by God, we received it, presuming nothing beyond what was granted.

But they, having received no authority but having usurped it, wish to lord it over others, claiming authority for their own name. Nor do we compare ourselves with them so as, like them, to flatter you and indulge your vices—something even one who truly possessed authority might do. We do not do this because we do not dare to include or compare ourselves with them, lest we perish as they do.

[Col. 0068B] We do not do these things; rather, we measure ourselves by ourselves—that is, we examine ourselves in our own consciences, considering whether we have been sent by God, and we usurp nothing other than what has been entrusted to us. For we exercise as much authority as has been granted by its author; we exceed neither measure nor limit. And we compare ourselves with ourselves, because we do what our office requires, which they do not do.

Doing these things, we shall not boast—that is, exercise authority—without measure, that is, beyond our own measure, as those do who boast beyond measure by usurpation. Rather, we shall boast according to the measure of the rule: that is, according to the people measured out to me by God, whose rule I am for their direction, under which measure you stand.

[Col. 0068C] Hence he adds: I mean the measure of reaching, by God’s prompting, as far as you.

[Ambrose] For he was directed by God’s will to evangelize the Corinthians. For each person was assigned those toward whom he was to be directed in preaching, so that individuals might have particular peoples whose faith they might boast of. But all whom he had established in faith belonged to the Apostle’s rule, since he had been sent by God to all. Hence he adds what measure God measured out to us. Whoever therefore resists him resists God who sent him.

### Verses 14–18

“For we do not overextend ourselves as though we did not reach as far as you. For we came as far as you in the Gospel of Christ, not boasting beyond measure in other people’s labors, but having hope, as your faith grows, to be magnified among you according to our rule in abundance; also to evangelize in the regions beyond you, not to boast in another’s rule concerning things already prepared. But let the one who boasts boast in the Lord. For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends.”

“For not.” As if he said: Truly, God has measured it out. “For not” is an overextension. And this is what he says: “For we are not over-extending ourselves, as though we did not reach you” [Col. 0069A]. To over-extend oneself is to extend oneself beyond what is permitted. But we were appointed to you by God who sent us. And truly we do not extend ourselves as though we did not reach you; for we do reach you, since we came even as far as you in the Gospel of Christ, that is, in the preaching of Christ’s Gospel.

[Ambrose] We, I say, are not boasting without measure, that is, in the labours of others—namely, where someone else had laid the foundation of faith—for that would be to boast beyond measure. Rather, we have hope of your growing faith; that is, we hope through your faith, growing from virtue to virtue, to be magnified among others through you, because through you we are proved to be true apostles of such a kind. And we have hope to evangelize according to our rule [Col. 0069B], that is, our allotted realm; that is, according to what has been imposed upon us by God. I say, to evangelize abundantly—not merely in a few places, but also in other places beyond you. Yet we do not hope, that is, we do not expect, to boast within any other person’s rule. Nor are those beyond them under another’s jurisdiction.

He then explains what he meant by “within another’s rule”: namely, in things prepared by other preachers. For he preached to those to whom the message had not been announced, in order that he might seek glory through his own labour.

“But he who boasts.” As if he said: I shall boast in the things stated above and in others; but the whole ground of this boasting is from God. Therefore, “He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord,” following Jeremiah’s admonition; that is, let him attribute his glory and confidence to the Lord [Col. 0069C]. By his grace, the one who has no authority from God cannot do this, since he seeks his own glory.

“For not.” As if he said: Therefore one must boast in the Lord, because the person who commends himself is not approved by God or by men; that is, the one who boasts apart from God, attributing to himself what belongs to God.

Or: “But he who.” As if he said: I shall not boast within another’s rule. Likewise, one who boasts—that is, wishes to exercise authority—should boast in the Lord; that is, he should exercise authority within the measure given him by God, as he ought. For he is not approved by God or by men who commends himself, who preaches without being sent, who is not fit for the task but is presumptuous and reprobate; rather, the approved person is the one whom God commends, that is, whom he shows to be fit and worthy by miracles and powers.

## Chapter XI

[Col. 0069D]

### Verses 1–3

“Would that you bore with a little of my folly! But do bear with me. For I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy; for I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its craftiness, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ.”

“Would that,” etc. As if he said: I boast concerning the authority which appears to be folly; but I wish that you would bear without indignation a little of my folly—that is, of my boasting concerning authority [Col. 0070A], which seems to you and is called folly. Or here he calls “folly” boasting according to the flesh, which he does so that he may not appear inferior to them in that respect. He himself does not value it, but it benefits the Corinthians.

[Ambrose] As if he said: I boast concerning authority; but I wish that you would bear with a little of my folly, that is, of boasting according to the flesh, which seems folly. For it has been said: “Let not your own lips praise you, but those of your neighbour.” This boasting, however, seems to contribute to his praise.

“But do,” etc. As if he said: I desire you to bear with me. But also I command you: bear with me as subjects bear with their superior.

[Augustine] As if he said: Even if I burden you, nevertheless bear it patiently. For I am jealous over you—that is, I love you—with God’s jealousy; that is, for God’s honour, not my own. I am jealous not for the bride of my God [Col. 0070B] on my own behalf, but for God. For I am the friend of the bridegroom. The bridegroom is jealous for his bride; but the friend of the bridegroom is jealous not for himself, but for the bridegroom.

Observe that jealousy (*aemulatio*) is understood in two ways. It is a movement of the mind occasioned by another’s condition, either toward evil or toward good. Here it is a matter of love, not envy, because he loves them with God’s jealousy: that is, a jealousy directed toward God’s honour and inspired by God through his Spirit. By this he shows that what he is about to say is prompted by love for them, so that it may not result in his own praise but in their advancement.

“For I have betrothed you.” As if he said: And truly I love you, because I, who am the bridegroom’s friend, have betrothed you by the ring of faith—not to many, but to one; not to an adulterer, but to a lawful husband, namely Christ, the true bridegroom. You, I say, being a chaste virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Augustine, in the book *Eighty-Three Questions*.] Notice that he descends from the plural to the singular [Col. 0070C], intending us to understand that the whole Church is one virgin, and that in all its true members it preserves virginity of mind, even if not bodily integrity.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] The same, in a certain sermon.] Bodily virginity is an untouched body, and that virginity belongs to few. Virginity of heart is incorrupt faith, and that virginity belongs to all believers. Hence in the Apocalypse: “These are they who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins” (Rev. XIV). By “women” he signified error, because error began through a woman. Therefore he said “virgin” in the singular, because all are one virgin through unity of whole faith, steadfast hope, and sincere love. They are virgin because they are undefiled by the perversity of error and by evil conduct; chaste because they do not possess the heat of evil [Col. 0070D] desire.

“I have betrothed,” I say, “to present you,” that is, that I may present you to God on the day of judgment.

“But I fear.” As if he said: I betrothed you in this manner in order to present you to God; but I fear lest, just as the serpent—that is, the devil—deceived Eve through the serpent, casting her out of paradise, deceived her, I say, by its craftiness, namely by promising false things, so your minds, that is, your understandings, may be corrupted by similar deceits and may fall from the simplicity which is in Christ: that is, from the paradise of Christ’s simple faith, which admits nothing foreign. These Corinthians are like Eve; the false apostles are like the serpent, that is, the devil, who lies in wait through them.

[Note: [Col. 0070D] The same, on John.] The light of faith is like paradise. Therefore, those whose faith is corrupted are cast out of paradise, because they set falsehood before truth. Those who build falsehood in people drive truth from them; they also introduce the devil and thus exclude Christ. For if you say anything against the faith, decay from the serpent’s poison enters, worms of falsehood are born, and nothing remains sound.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] Augustine, on Psalm XXXIII.] Therefore, as our fathers needed patience against the lion, so we need watchfulness against the dragon. Then he compelled; now he teaches. Then he employed violence; now he employs snares. Then he seemed roaring; now he appears slippery and wandering, and therefore difficult to perceive. Hence the Apostle fears lest, as Eve was deceived by the serpent, so the Church may be corrupted by heretics from the virginity of faith which it bears in its heart. Therefore guard now the virginity of your soul; afterwards it is to be made fruitful in the embrace of your bridegroom.

“Fence in your ears with thorns,” therefore, as it is written (Ecclus. XXVIII). For the serpent still whispers and is not silent. What was enacted in that paradise is enacted in the Church. Let no one, therefore, deceive you away from this paradise of the Church. Let it suffice that we fell there; or, having experienced it, let us be corrected.

### Verses 4–9

“For if he who comes preaches another Christ whom we have not preached; or if you receive another Spirit whom you have not received; or another Gospel which you have not received—you would rightly bear with him. For I think that I have been in no way inferior to the great apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not so in knowledge. Yet in every respect I have been made manifest among you. Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself, that you might be exalted? Because I preached the Gospel of God to you freely, I despoiled other churches, receiving wages for your service; and when I was with you and in need, I burdened no one. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked; and in every respect I kept myself free from burden to you and will continue to do so.”

“For if he.” As if he said: I fear lest your minds be corrupted by those false apostles; but you ought not to tolerate them, because they preach nothing different from me, and do so worse than I. Why, then, do you judge us 134 inferior to them? This is what he says: “For if he who comes,” namely, one not sent. Or, “he who comes,” that is, is sold, because he acts for temporal gain, “preaches another Christ whom we have not preached”; that is, even if he preached another Christ more excellent than I—which cannot be—or if through them you received another Spirit, that is, a better Spirit, than you received through us—which certainly is not the case, but rather through us, not through them, you received the Spirit—or if he preached to you another Gospel, that is, another proclamation of redemption, which cannot exist; a Gospel which you did not receive through us, then you would rightly bear with him.

[Ambrose] As if he said: If something different and greater comes to you through them than through us, then you would rightly bear with them. To the Galatians, however, he says “anathema” if they received another gospel. To the Corinthians he says that it would be right to receive another if another were preached; but here “another” means something preferable and greater than what had been handed down by the apostles [Col. 0072A]. To the Galatians, however, he says that they must not receive another, namely one which certainly would not be greater, but contrary.

“For I think.” Above he dealt with false apostles; now he speaks of true preachers, in comparison with whom Paul seemed inferior because he had not been with Jesus. As if he said: If they preached something else, you would rightly bear with them. But because this is not so, you do not rightly tolerate them. And truly it is not so. For I think that I have been in no way inferior in these matters to the great apostles. Thus it is clear that I have done no less than those false apostles, since I have done no less than the great apostles.

The great apostles seemed to these people to be Peter and the others, because they had been with the Lord. Or he says this concerning the false apostles, showing that he has done no less than they. For the Corinthian Church was tossed about by various errors. Some favoured the apostles who had been with the Lord in the flesh, disparaging Paul because he had not been with the Lord; we have discussed this. Others favoured the false apostles, from whom they heard the same things as from the Apostle, expressed in carefully composed words; it is against these that he speaks [Col. 0072B]. As if he said: They preach nothing different to you from what I preach. And because someone might say that, even if they preached the same things, they nevertheless preached better than Paul, he removes that objection. As if he said: They preach neither something different nor something better. For I think that I have done nothing less; that is, I say that I have not then been set at a distance from the great apostles. And truly I have done no less than the false apostles or the true apostles.

“For although I am unskilled in speech,” because I do not adorn words—

[Ambrose] —or because I have an impediment of speech—“yet I am not unskilled in knowledge,” because I know whatever the great apostles know. But when he says “unskilled in speech,” this does not concern the apostles, for they were not eloquent; it concerns the false apostles, who composed their words and whom the Corinthians preferred because of their polished speech. Yet in religion the force of speech is necessary, not the sound of the voice. One unskilled in speech is not guilty before God; rather, the guilty person is especially the one who does not possess knowledge of God pertaining to salvation.

“But in every respect I have been made manifest among you,” because you have experienced what is done through me. Therefore you can and ought to be my witnesses in all these matters concerning the preachers. Thus it is worse that, though you know these things, you prefer them to me.

“Or did I?” As if he said: I have done no less than they; or if I did less [Col. 0072D], did I commit a sin in this? Namely, did I sin because I preached or proclaimed to you the Gospel of God freely, without expense? As if he said: No. The sense is: I did no less for you than they did, but more, because I did it freely. Why are you angry with me and prefer others to me, since this is not a sin but a glory: I preached freely to you?

I, I say, humbled myself by working with my hands, in order that you might thus be exalted from death to life, the false apostles being removed from preaching, and in order that you might not think that you had bought permission to sin. For these two reasons he did not accept the support owed to him.

And as though someone asked, “From what, then, did you live?” he answers: “I despoiled other churches” [Col. 0073A], signifying that he expended no small amount upon them. For when he says “I despoiled,” he signifies that he received and gave much. “I despoiled,” I say, receiving wages from others for your service, that is, so that I could preach to you. And I received nothing from any of you, even when I was in need. This is what he adds: “And when I was with you and in need, I burdened no one” by receiving anything. I was not burdensome, although I was in need and could have accepted support.

“For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what I lacked after the despoiling of the churches.” It was fitting to receive from those who had been well corrected, lest those who sowed well should lose their fruit; for if he did not receive, it might perhaps become a cause of stumbling to them. And, to speak universally, in everything—namely, words and deeds—I kept myself free from burden to you, not only in regard to support; for I did not boast against you of my lineage or do anything of this kind. And henceforth I shall keep myself so, especially by abstaining from the support owed to me.

### Verses 10–18

“The truth of Christ is in me: this boasting shall not be checked in me throughout the regions of Achaia. Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. But what I do, I shall continue to do, in order to cut off the opportunity of those who desire an opportunity, so that in the matter in which they boast they may be found to be as we are. For such false apostles are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers transform themselves as ministers of righteousness, whose end shall be according to their works. I say again—lest anyone think me foolish; otherwise receive me as though foolish, that I too may boast a little—that what I speak, I do not speak according to God, but as in folly, in this matter of boasting. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too shall boast.”

“The truth of Christ is in me.” As if he said: And truly I shall continue to do so, because the truthful Christ speaks in me: namely, this glory of Christ—that I preach freely, that I abstain from lawful things for the sake of your salvation—shall not be checked throughout all the regions of Achaia. And why? Do you think this happens because I do not love you? That is, do you think that I act from hatred, as the false apostles say? God knows that I love you and that I do not act from hatred.

[Ambrose] To make himself believed, he confirms it by oath, calling God as witness to the love [Col. 0073D] which he had toward them. For he was unwilling to receive, not because he did not love them, but all the more because he loved them.

Hence he adds: “But what,” etc. As if he said: I do not do this from hatred of you, but I do it in order to cut off the false apostles’ opportunity—that is, because I love you. This is what he says: “But what I now do, I shall always do, in order by my example to cut off the opportunity of those who seek, through me, an opportunity to take your goods.” For the intention and pursuit of the false apostles was to receive money. Therefore the Apostle refused to receive, lest he give them a model and an occasion for receiving. For he knew that, if they did not receive, they would not preach for long.

Hence he adds: “So that in the matter in which.” As if he said: Therefore I did not receive, in order to cut off the opportunity, so that they might be found to be such as we are—that is, like us. In the matter of being like us, they boast: will they be like us? Certainly.

“For such,” etc. Or thus: “So that in the matter in which they boast,” that is, in receiving, “they may be found as we are,” that is, like us. For their glory lies in extorting money; but since I do not receive, they will not receive either. And truly they will not. For such persons, etc.

Or thus: Therefore I do not receive, so that in the matter in which there is glory—that is, in not receiving—they may be found as we are, that is, not better than we are. And why do they not receive? So that they may appear good. For such false apostles are deceitful workers, cleverly deceiving under the appearance of religion, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ; that is, outwardly showing [Col. 0074B] themselves to be apostles of Christ.

And this is no wonder, for Satan himself, their head, transforms himself into an angel of light; that is, he presents himself as though he were an angel of God—namely Christ—or some heavenly angel, in order to deceive. This also applies to the miseries of this life. For he transforms himself either to tempt those whom it is necessary to train in this way, or to deceive certain persons, as is just.

Great mercy from God is needed for this: lest anyone who thinks that he has good angels as friends should have evil demons as pretended friends, enemies all the more harmful as they are more cunning and deceptive. Nor are the holy and faithful worshippers of the one true God secure from their deceptions and many-shaped temptations [Col. 0074C] in these evil days, when this concern is not useless.

[Note: [Col. 0073D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] This vigilance is needed lest Satan, when he transforms himself, should lead someone astray by deception into harmful things. For when bodily sense deceives, but does not move the mind away from the true and right judgment by which one lives a faithful life, there is no danger in religion. Or, when he pretends to be good and either does or says things fitting for good angels, even if he is believed, the error is neither good, dangerous, nor morbid. But when by such alien things he begins to lead people toward his own ends, great vigilance is needed lest anyone follow him. No one can do this without God; and this very difficulty is useful for this purpose: that no one may place hope in himself, or one human being in another, but only in God. No devout person doubts that this is altogether expedient for us.

And because Satan transforms himself into an angel, it is no great thing if his ministers transform themselves as though they were ministers of righteousness. Their end—namely, the end of Christ’s ministers and Satan’s ministers—shall be according to their works.

“I say again.” As if he said: I said, “Bear with me as foolish”; now I say openly again, lest anyone think me foolish in the glory of spiritual things, since I act for a good purpose. Otherwise, namely, if I am foolish in that spiritual boasting, then receive me all the more as foolish in boasting according to the flesh. He does not simply call himself foolish, but says “as though foolish,” because he is not truly foolish even in this, since he does it for good and himself has no glory in such boasting.

Receive me, I say, as though foolish in this, in order that I too may boast a little [Col. 0075A], that is, according to the flesh, whose boasting is slight.

“What I speak.” As if he said: Therefore I am as though foolish, because what I speak in this matter of boasting—that is, in boasting according to the flesh, which some regard as their substance, loving such things as though they believed that they subsisted by them—I do not speak, as regards the appearance of the words, according to God.

[Ambrose] Before God glory does not arise from the flesh, because humility is glorious before God; whereas these things seem to belong to the swelling of the flesh, in which there is folly. But I speak as in folly. It is folly for someone to praise himself; but because the Apostle does this not for himself but for God, he says “as in folly.”

“For many,” etc. As if someone asked, “Why then do you do this?” He answers: Because many boast, and because you endure them. Thus he says: “Since many boast according to the flesh,” that is, according to things belonging to the flesh, such as nobility and the like, therefore I too shall boast according to the flesh. And it is no wonder if they boast.

### Verses 19–27

“For you gladly bear with fools, being yourselves wise. For you endure it if anyone enslaves you, if anyone devours you, if anyone takes from you, if anyone exalts himself, if anyone strikes you in the face. I speak according to dishonour, as though we had been weak in this respect. In whatever matter anyone dares—I speak in folly—I dare also. Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham’s seed? So am I. Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one less wise: I am more so. In labours more abundantly, in imprisonments more abundantly, in beatings beyond measure, in deaths often. From the Jews five times I received forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I suffered shipwreck; a night and a day I was in the deep sea. Often in journeys: in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers; in labour and hardship, in many watchings, in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.”

“For you gladly bear with fools,” that is, voluntarily, in this boasting—which you ought not to do—although you yourselves are wise, that is, ought to be wise; but you are not. This is proved here from the fact that you endure such persons.

“For you endure” [Col. 0075D] this injury if anyone reduces you—

[Ambrose] —from the liberty of Christ, which is in love, to the slavery of the Law, which makes people serve from fear; and if anyone, presuming on authority, devours you, that is, consumes your possessions; and if anyone takes from you, that is, deceives you with praise in order to devour you; and if anyone exalts himself, that is, boasts of his noble birth; and if anyone strikes you, that is, despises you by reproaching your lineage, and does so to your face, that is, in your presence.

[Augustine, Ambrose] A person is struck in the face when an insult is inflicted upon his mouth. “I say this according to dishonour,” the dishonour which they cast in our teeth. Certain Jews did this: because they were of Abraham’s race, they disparaged those who were uncircumcised and preferred themselves, claiming for themselves nobility of flesh. The Corinthians tolerated them [Col. 0076A] and preferred them to the Apostle.

“As though we.” As if he said: Thus you endure these people and prefer them to us, as though we had been weak in this matter of boasting. Certainly we are not weak in this, because in whatever any of them dares to boast—that is, rashly vaunt himself, for what they do is rash—I also dare; that is, I can dare to boast without rashness.

[Augustine] When I said “in whatever he dares,” I meant that they dare in folly, because what they boast of is folly: in order to appear great, they boast of the flesh. But if the Apostle says anything about himself, he does so not for self-display but in order to humble them.

“Are they Hebrews?” etc. I say that in whatever anyone dares, I also dare, as is evident from these matters. Are they Hebrews in language and nation? So am I. Are they Israelites according to observances? So am I. Are they Abraham’s seed, because they are not proselytes but are of Abraham’s stock? So am I [Col. 0076B]. Are they ministers of Christ? By this they deceived people; and I too am a minister of Christ—indeed, more a minister of Christ.

But I say this as one less wise than I ought to be, because it is not for a human being to praise himself. By this he shows that he was compelled to break out into self-praise. For one who voluntarily recounts matters tending to his own praise does not call himself imprudent.

He then shows how he is more a minister of Christ than they, adding: “In labours.” As if he said: I say that I have shown myself a minister of Christ in more abundant labours, in which I laboured more than they did—indeed, more than the true apostles. He says this because the false apostles too had undergone certain labours so that they might appear to be apostles; but he laboured more.

[Ambrose] Having found the occasion, he also touches upon the true apostles, whom he surpassed in labour [Col. 0076C], lest grace appear less in him.

He then displays his labours in detail, adding: “In imprisonments, I have shown myself a minister of Christ more abundantly than they; and in beatings,” that is, in scourgings beyond the measure of human strength or beyond those endured by others; “in deaths,” that is, dangers of death, “I have often been.” For he endured dangers more frequently than the rest.

He then explains the beatings, adding: “From the Jews five times,” that is, on five occasions, “I received forty lashes less one,” lest they appear merciless. For he was scourged five times by the Jews according to the Law of Moses, receiving thirty-nine blows, as is written in Deuteronomy. Thus what happened five times he relates here in summary: “Three times I was beaten with rods” [Col. 0076D]; this he suffered from Gentiles. Likewise, “once I was stoned,” in a city of Lycaonia. “Three times I suffered shipwreck,” that is, endured it. “A night and a day I was in the deep,” that is, I was held upon the open sea by a storm.

Or, literally: I showed myself a minister of Christ “often in journeys, in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers,” whom the devil stirred up against him on the road when he could not kill him in the city, even though Paul carried nothing which robbers might desire; “in dangers from my own race,” that is, plotted by Jews, because I had abandoned their Law and turned to the Gospel; “in dangers from Gentiles,” because of the preaching of the one God.

Likewise, I was proved a minister of Christ “in dangers in the city,” that is, in the uprisings of citizens against me; likewise, “in dangers in the wilderness,” caused either by serpents [Col. 0077A] or by lack of food; likewise, “in dangers at sea,” which were not from the sea but occurred on the sea, so that this differs from the preceding phrase. Above he called “dangers from the sea” those dangers which came from the sea.

Likewise, I was proved a minister “in dangers among false brothers,” that is, dangers from heretics, who are false brothers, such as those who say that Paul keeps the legal observances but does not readily disclose this to others. Hence elsewhere the Apostle says: “If I still preach circumcision,” etc. (Gal. V).

Likewise, I was proved a minister of Christ in labour of my hands, and in the hardship of illnesses and such things; in watchings undertaken for work or for others. Likewise, I was proved a minister of Christ in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.] When the Apostle recalls that he laboured in hunger and thirst, where then is God’s promise: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI)? For the Lord’s promise seems to have faltered when the Apostle says that he laboured in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] The same, in the same work.] But that physician, to whom we once for all entrusted our whole selves, and from whom we have the promise of the present and future life, knows when to provide and when to withdraw these aids, as he judges beneficial for consoling and training us in this life.

### Verses 28–33

“Besides those things which are outward, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn? If I must boast, I shall boast of the things that concern my weakness. The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for ever, knows [Col. 0077C] that I do not lie. At Damascus, the governor of the people under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me; and through a window I was lowered in a basket through the wall, and thus escaped his hands.”

“Besides those things which are outward,” indeed—

[Augustine] —that is, those which I suffer in my body from persecutors and in other ways—there presses upon my mind my daily burden, which is not relaxed even for one hour. What is it? Namely, concern for all the churches, which proceeds from love.

[Note: [Col. 0077D] The same, on Psalm XXVIII.] Therefore, the greater the love, the greater are the wounds caused by others’ sins. Hence: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. I). If, therefore, the love of life abounds, you will grieve more over a sinner.

See what kind of concern the Apostle has [Col. 0077D]: how paternal, how maternal. It is so great that he says: Who among all the faithful is weak, either in faith or in some virtue, and I am not weak? For I grieve for that person as I do for myself. And who is scandalized by some troublesome tribulation, and I do not burn?

[Note: [Col. 0077D] The same, on Psalm C.] I burn with the fire of love by which I suffer with him. For all who suffer scandal are a frying-pan to those who possess love—that is, to the bones which bear the flesh, that is, to the perfect, because they support and govern the carnal. Hence: “And my bones were crushed as in a frying-pan” (Ps. XXX).

[Note: [Col. 0078D] The same, in the book *Against the Manicheans*.] Observe that he says, “I burn.” Tribulations indeed burn people [Col. 0078A], but they do not burn the good unto destruction; rather, unto purification.

[Augustine] Tribulation, like a biting plaster, burns you but heals you. This affection especially, because it is expressed by the word “I burn,” purifies, because it comes from love.

And when these things are so, if it is necessary to boast—as indeed it is necessary for your sake—I shall boast, not of power or lineage as the false apostles do, but of the things that concern my weakness, although in them there seems to be abasement.

And in order to show as true the things he has said or is about to say, he confirms them by an oath, adding: God, who knows all things, and the Father of Jesus Christ our Lord, whose servant I am and whom you too ought to serve, who is blessed—that is, praised by us faithful—for ever, knows that I do not lie concerning the matters stated above [Col. 0078B], or concerning this thing which I am about to say, namely, what happened to me at Damascus.

What was it? Behold: the governor, etc. Behold, again a weakness is recalled. As if he said: This happened to me at Damascus: the governor of the people under King Aretas, who ruled that people under King Aretas, guarded the city of the Damascenes at the Jews’ instigation in order to seize me, lest I preach any longer. And through a window I was lowered in a basket through the wall by the brothers.

Some say that this was done unworthily, because he was not delivered by God’s help. But divine assistance is not necessary before human help fails; nor should anyone await divine help while he has something he can do, lest he seem to put God to the test. Therefore the Apostle was lowered by the disciples through a window [Col. 0078C] in a basket, in order that he might escape. Hence he adds: “And thus I escaped the governor’s hands.”

[Ambrose] He appears not to have acted like a good shepherd, but like a hireling who does not care for the sheep and abandons them when the wolf comes.

[Note: [Col. 0078D] The same, on John.] But did he not care for the sheep because he fled? Certainly he did. He commended them in prayer to the Shepherd seated in heaven, and by fleeing preserved himself for their benefit. For he had heard from the supreme Shepherd himself: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X).

[Note: [Col. 0078D] The same, *To the Ordination of a Bishop*.] But who would believe that the Lord wished this to be done in such a way that flocks which he bought with his own blood should be abandoned by a necessary minister, without whom they cannot live? Christ himself did not do this when, as a little child, he fled into Egypt carried by his parents, because he had not yet gathered churches which we could say were abandoned by him.

Therefore let Christ’s servants, ministers of the word, do what he commanded or permitted, just as Christ himself fled into Egypt. Let them certainly flee from city to city when any one of them is individually sought by persecutors, so that the Church may not be abandoned by others who are not so sought, but may provide food to fellow servants whom they know cannot otherwise live.

But when the danger is common to all—that is, bishops, clergy, and laity—those dependent upon others [Col. 0079A] must not be abandoned by those upon whom they depend. Therefore either let all move to fortified places, or one who needs to remain must not be left by those through whom the Church’s necessary service must be supplied to them; so that they may either live together or suffer together whatever the master of the household wills them to suffer.

## Chapter XII

### Verses 1–4

“If I must boast, it is indeed not beneficial. But I shall come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ who, fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up, such a one, to the third heaven. And I know such a man—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.”

[Col. 0079B] Likewise, if, beyond what has been said, it is necessary to boast because of the false apostles, I shall proceed to speak—not of matters of weakness, but of visions. I say, if it is necessary to boast, though this is not advantageous in itself, as boasting; yet it is so for your benefit and for the humiliation of the false apostles. And therefore, although I have said much about my labours and weaknesses, I shall now proceed to visions and revelations—that is, secret things which I saw and fully understood, unlike Pharaoh, who saw but did not understand. These are visions of the Lord: that is, concerning the Lord, or which the Lord disclosed. What these visions were he reveals concerning himself, speaking as though of another person. “I know a man.”

[Note: [Col. 0079D] Augustine, On John.] It was the custom of those who furnished us with the sacred Scriptures that, whenever history was narrated by one of them, when he came to himself he would speak as if about someone else. Matthew, John, and Moses did this: thus they spoke of themselves as though they were others. But the Apostle did this in a more unusual way—not in a history, where the narrative of events is undertaken for exposition, but in an Epistle, inserting himself into the sequence of his narrative as though he were a writer of deeds done, rather than a preacher about himself. For truth suffers no loss when the event itself is related and the boastfulness of speaking is in some measure avoided. Indeed, he was recounting what pertained to the praise of God.

Therefore, speaking of himself as though of another, he says: “I know a man abiding in Christ,” that is, conformed to Christ—for otherwise he would not have seen—“such a one caught up to the third heaven.” This happened to that man fourteen years earlier. For fourteen years had already passed between the time when he saw the vision and the time when he recounted it.
