Thus he was now greater in merits; and from his having remained silent for so long, it is evident that he speaks not arrogantly but from necessity. “I know,” he says, “such a man caught up; but I do not know how he was caught up”: namely, whether the soul remained in the body, or was taken up outside the body. But God knows, who was able to do this.

[Note: [Col. 0079D] The same, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.] The Apostle did not know whether, when he was caught up, his soul was in the body, or whether it entirely departed from the body so that the body lay dead, until, after that manifestation had been accomplished, the soul was restored to its lifeless limbs and he who had been altogether dead revived. And whether that separation from the body left the body wholly dead, or whether the soul was present in it after some fashion proper to a living body while his mind was snatched away to see or hear the ineffable things of that vision—this was uncertain.

[Col. 0080A] Therefore perhaps he said, “whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows.” This I do not know; but I know most certainly that such a man was caught up—that is, raised contrary to nature—to the third heaven: namely, the empyrean, which immediately upon its creation was filled with holy angels.

[Ambrose.] It is called the empyrean—that is, fiery—from brightness, not from heat. It is understood that he was caught up beyond all the stars of the world; and therefore what he recounts is magnificent and marvellous. The first heaven is the airy region, whence birds are called “birds of heaven.” The second is the firmament, [Col. 0080B] concerning which Genesis says: “Let there be a firmament”; and “He called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1). The third heaven is spiritual, where angels and holy souls enjoy the contemplation of God. By saying that he was caught up to it, he indicates that God showed him the life in which He is to be seen eternally.

[Augustine.] Or the three heavens are understood as three kinds of vision. The meaning is: “I know such a man caught up,” that is, raised contrary to nature, “to the third heaven,” that is, to knowledge of the Godhead. For the first is bodily vision, when, by God’s gift, certain things are bodily seen which others cannot see: as Elisha saw the unknown hosts when Elijah was taken up. And Belshazzar saw the hand writing on the wall: *mane, thekel, phares* [“numbered, weighed, divided”]. The second heaven is imaginary or spiritual vision, [Col. 0080C] when someone in ecstasy or sleep sees not bodies but images of things by God’s revelation, as Peter saw the vessel. The third heaven is intellectual vision, when neither bodies nor images of them are seen, but the gaze of the mind is fixed by God’s wondrous power upon incorporeal substances. The Apostle was caught up to this vision, so that he might see God Himself in Himself, not in any figure. And this vision is far superior to the other two. Thus, what is seen neither through the body nor imaginatively, but properly, is seen by that vision which surpasses all the others.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] Augustine, in the book On Genesis.] Three kinds of vision occur: one through the eyes, by which the letters themselves are seen; another through the human spirit, by which things near at hand and things absent are thought of; the third through the mind’s direct gaze, by which love itself, when understood, is contemplated. Of these three kinds, the first is clear to all: by it heaven and earth and all things visible to the eyes are seen. Nor is it difficult to explain the second, by which absent bodily things are thought of. For we think about heaven and earth and the things in them which we can see, even while present among them. And sometimes, seeing nothing with the bodily eyes, we nevertheless behold bodily images in the mind: either true ones, as of bodies which we have seen and retain in memory, or fictitious ones, such as thought can form.

[Note: [Col. 0080D] The same, in the same work.] For we think differently about what we know and what we do not know. But the third kind, in which love itself, when understood, is contemplated, contains those things which have no images resembling themselves, which would not themselves be what those things are. For love is seen as present in the form in which it exists; when absent, it is seen otherwise, in some image resembling it. Yet, insofar as it can be discerned by the mind, it is seen more by one person and less by another. A human being, a tree, and other bodily things, however, are seen when present in their own forms and, when absent, are thought of by images impressed upon the mind.

[Col. 0081A] These are the three kinds of vision. The first is called bodily because it is presented through bodily senses; the second spiritual, because whatever is not body yet is substance is rightly called spirit; the third intellectual, from intellect. These three kinds of vision—bodily, spiritual, and intellectual—are to be considered separately.

According to the first vision, Belshazzar saw the hand; and immediately, through bodily sense, the image of the bodily event was impressed upon his spirit. When the seen event had occurred and passed, its image remained in his thought. It was seen in the spirit but not understood; nor was it understood when it was occurring and appearing bodily. Yet it was understood to be a sign; and this came from the operation of the mind, just as the inquiry seeking what it signified was surely conducted by the mind. When this was not discovered, Daniel came and, his mind enlightened by the prophetic spirit, revealed what that sign foretold. He is better called a prophet through this kind of vision, which belongs properly to the mind, than the one who both saw the sign bodily enacted and, by thinking, beheld in his spirit the image of the event after it had passed.

[Col. 0081C] According to the second vision, Peter in ecstasy saw a vessel full of diverse animals and heard the voice: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). Restored to his bodily senses, he beheld by thought in the same spirit what he had seen spiritually and retained in memory. All these things were not bodies, but images of bodies, whether when first seen in ecstasy or when later thought upon. But when it was debated and sought what these things meant, the mind was at work attempting this, though without result until the mind, divinely aided, understood what that vision signified. In what is called intellectual vision are beheld things that are neither bodily objects nor bear any forms resembling bodies: such as the mind itself and [Col. 0081D] every good affection of the soul. For how else is intellect itself seen, except by understanding? In no other way. So too are charity, joy, peace, faith, and such things by which one approaches God; and God Himself, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things.

These three visions have their own order. The second vision is more excellent than the first, and the third than the second. By the third the mind, lifted up, is caught away into that, as it were, region of intelligible things, where it sees clear truth without any image of body, uncoloured by any mists of false opinions. There the virtues of the soul are not active and laborious. For lust is not restrained by the work of temperance; adversity is not endured by the work of fortitude; wickedness is not punished by the work of justice; evils are not avoided by the work of prudence. There the one whole virtue is to love what you see, and the highest happiness is to possess what you love.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] Augustine, in the book On Genesis.] There blessed life is drunk from its fountain; from it something is sprinkled upon human life, so that amid the temptations of this age one may live temperately, courageously, justly, and prudently. For the sake of that vision of truth—as on Sinai, or through spiritual vision, as Isaiah and John saw in the Apocalypse, yet “through appearance, not in a riddle”—every labour is undertaken.

Moses sought by this kind of vision to see God—that is, in the substance in which God is God—whom he had seen in many figures and with whom he had spoken face to face. For there—that is, in that form in which God is—He is seen far more ineffably and immediately, that is, more secretly; and He speaks secrets, that is, reveals them, where—that is, in the brightness of that form—no one living in these bodily senses sees God. This is the third heaven: the vision in which God is seen face to face; and this is paradise, if one may say so, of paradises. For the present Church too is called paradise, and paradise was the place in which Adam lived bodily.

[Col. 0082B] Paul says that he was caught up to that third heaven, but says that he does not know whether this was in the body or with the soul separated. As though he said: “I did not see by human sense; so that, even if he saw while the soul remained in the body, this is not contrary to what the Lord says to Moses: ‘No human being shall see me and live’” (Exod. 33). For then the Apostle did not live as a human being—that is, according to the use of bodily senses—but every human sense was taken away from him.

[Note: [Col. 0081D] The same, To Paulina, On Seeing God.] For the mind itself must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the light of that ineffable vision; nor should it be thought incredible that some saints, not yet so dead that bodies remained to be buried, were granted even this excellence of revelation.

[Note: [Col. 0082D] The same, On Genesis.] Why then should we not believe that God wished to show to so great an Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, when caught up to this most excellent vision, the life in which He is to be seen eternally after this life? And why should this not be called paradise, as it were the region where the soul is well, unless indeed it sees ineffably the very substance of God, the Word of God, and the Holy Spirit? Therefore he adds: “And I know,” etc.

Or thus: by the three heavens are understood [Col. 0082D] three orders of angels according to Dionysius, who establishes three orders of angels, placing three in each order. In the first he places angels, archangels, and virtues; in the second, principalities, powers, and dominions; in the third, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Their third order contemplates God more nearly. The Apostle is said to have seen God in likeness to them. This is the third heaven to which the Apostle says he was caught up: namely, that he might see God as they see Him.

Or, the first heaven is knowledge of heavenly bodies; the second, knowledge of heavenly spirits; the third, knowledge of the Godhead, to which the Apostle was caught up. Note that in the second interpretation we likewise explained the third heaven [Col. 0083A] in this way, but the first and second heavens differently from here; and therefore this interpretation is distinguished from that one.

Then, as though explaining what he meant by “the third heaven,” he adds: “And I know such a man caught up.” Note that he says twice that he was caught up: “whether in the body or outside the body”—that is, whether the soul left the body—“I do not know; God knows.” But this I know: that he was caught up into paradise—that is, into that tranquillity enjoyed by those in the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus he could see what he could never see while impeded by bodily senses.

[Augustine.] For then there occurred a most intense turning-away from the senses of this life. And then he heard “secret words”: that is, he received an intimation concerning God’s hidden essence, as though through [Col. 0083B] words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter—that is, to explain in words.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] Augustine, on Psalm 134.] He did say what could be said to human beings, and kept to himself what could not be said. Therefore, let what we can attain be heard, and let what we cannot be believed. If we said to him, “We beg you, explain to us His greatness,” would he not perhaps reply: “He whom I see is not very great if He can be explained by me”?

[Ambrose.] Then, lest he seem to speak boastfully about himself, commending not himself but the greatness of the matter in himself, he says:

### Verses 5–9

“For such a one I will boast; but concerning myself I will boast of nothing except my weaknesses. For even if I should wish to boast, I would not be foolish, for I would speak the truth. But I refrain, lest anyone think of me beyond what he sees in me or hears from me. And lest the greatness [Col. 0083C] of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a goad of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me. Because of this I begged the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you.’”

For such a vision, or such a man, “I will boast”: that is, I will commend myself. But concerning myself—as a son of Abraham and the like—I will boast of nothing, unless perhaps of my weaknesses: that is, of the tribulations which I suffer. For, as though he said: “I say, ‘I will boast,’ and rightly; for even if I should wish to boast of revelation or weakness, I would not be foolish, though I may seem so.” And truly he would not: “for I would speak the truth,” for your benefit. This he shows subsequently, where he says: “But all things are for your edification.” “But I refrain.” As though he said: “I could boast of many other things, but I refrain”: that is, I recount sparingly, barely a few things, saying, “lest any weak person should suppose me to be beyond what he sees me to be or hears from others concerning me,” when nothing but weakness is seen in me or heard from others who see me. If I had previously reported great and numerous things, weak persons might perhaps think that I was not weak, but an immortal man or an angel, or something of that kind. Therefore he speaks sparingly of himself, lest anyone suppose him to be beyond what he sees or hears: namely, lest because of those great things he should seem not to be a mortal and frail human being.

Or he says this because of detractors, [Col. 0084A] before whom he does not boast magnificently lest they say that he does so from pride rather than truth.

[Ambrose.] The sense is: “But I refrain,” that is, I boast sparingly, lest some detractor suppose that I aspire, in the swelling of pride, to something beyond what he sees in me or hears from me: that is, beyond what the limit of my merits extends to or admits. “And lest,” etc. As though he said: “I refrain from much boasting lest I be thought otherwise; but also, lest I be exalted into pride by the greatness of the revelations, a goad of my flesh”—that is, a goad piercing the flesh—“was given to me by God,” for my benefit.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The same, On Nature and Grace.] Other vices have force only in wrongdoing; pride alone must be guarded against even in right actions. For whenever anyone has made good progress, he is tempted by pride so that he may lose all that progress.

[Note: [Col. 0083D] The same, on Psalm 8.] [Col. 0084B] Therefore it is not surprising that, against this capital vice, the Apostle says that a biting *epithima* [poultice] was applied to him, so that the swelling might be healed. Who then is secure concerning himself?

[Note: [Col. 0084D] The same, On the Words of the Apostle.] How will a lamb go forth secure where a ram fears so great a danger?

What is this goad which was given? “An angel of Satan”: that is, an evil angel sent by God; and for another purpose, it came as sent by Satan.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] The same, Against Faustus.] For the Lord sent it for the preservation of humility; but the devil came in order to bring it to effect. God, however, rightly did not spare him in this, so that He might perfect His power in weakness, giving him an angel that buffeted him. For the devil was not acting so that Paul should not be exalted by the greatness of revelations, or so that God’s power should be perfected.

[Ambrose.] But the righteous man was handed over by God to be buffeted by an angel of Satan—He who, through that angel, handed over the unrighteous to Satan himself.

This remedy, therefore, was given to the Apostle by God so that, pressed by temptations, he might not be exalted. Hence he adds: “To buffet me.” As though he said: “An angel of Satan was given to me, to buffet me”—that is, to restrain every movement of pride by inflicting tribulations and pains.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] The same, on Psalm 130.] For a person is violently drawn and agitated by a certain bodily pain; and bodily pains are commonly inflicted by angels of Satan, though they cannot do this unless permitted. Thus Job also was tested: Satan was permitted to test him and struck him with an affliction. The unclean one was permitted, but the holy man was tested. Thus that angel of Satan [Col. 0084D] was permitted, and came, as though gladly, to buffet the Apostle; but the Apostle was being healed.

Or thus: an angel of Satan was given to buffet me by tempting through lust, as some say. But temptation to which one does not consent is not sin, but material for exercising virtue. Understand this to be said of temptation arising from the enemy, not from the flesh: for the latter is venial sin if consent is not given to it.

“Because of this”—namely, because I was grievously buffeted—“I,” fearing humanly, “three times”—that is, many times—“begged the Lord,” who alone can bring it about [Col. 0085A] that the goad departs from me.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] Augustine, on Psalm 130.] Because the medicine was severe for the sick man, he therefore asked the physician to remove what He had applied, because it was painful. When a physician applies to wounds some perhaps painful and burning *epithima* by which one whose internal organs are swollen must be healed, that person, when he begins to be tormented by the medicine, asks the physician to remove it. But the physician consoles him and urges patience, because he knows that what he applied is useful. So also the Apostle says: “I begged the Lord that the goad might depart”—that is, I asked the physician to remove the painful *epithima* which He had applied to me—but I heard the physician’s voice. And the Lord, providing better for me, said to me through inspiration or through an angel: “O Paul, my grace is sufficient for you”: namely, what I have given you in all respects—that I made you faithful from an unbeliever, an Apostle from a persecutor, one labouring more than all others and seeing secret things. I have also [Col. 0085B] added to you strength to endure the goads. Do not ask that the goad depart.

### Verses 9–13

“For power is perfected in weakness. Therefore I will gladly boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I take pleasure in my weaknesses, in insults, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am powerful. I have become foolish; you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you. For I have done nothing less than those who are apostles beyond measure. Although I am nothing, nevertheless the signs of my apostleship were performed upon you in all patience, in signs, wonders, and powers. [Col. 0085C] For what is it that you had less than the other churches, except that I myself was not burdensome to you? Forgive me this wrong.”

“For,” that is, because, “power is perfected in weakness”: that is, the perfection of virtues is that which has contrary weakness with which it may lawfully contend, because victory is acquired through struggle, and thus virtue is brought to completion.

[Augustine.] Note that the devil is heard when he asks that Job be tested, while the Apostle is not heard when he asks that the goad be removed. God heard the one whom He had determined to condemn, and did not hear the one whom He wished to heal. For even a sick person asks many things of a physician which the physician does not grant. He does not hear according to the patient’s wish, in order that he may hear according to his health. Thus the Lord did not hear [Col. 0085D] Paul according to his wish. It is not a great thing to be heard by God according to one’s wish, but according to one’s benefit. Sometimes God gives in anger what you ask. But when you ask Him for those things which God praises and promises, ask confidently. Such things are granted by a gracious God. But when you ask for temporal things, ask them with moderation, and commit them to Him with fear: that, if they are beneficial, He may give them; but if He knows they are harmful, He may not give them. For the physician knows what harms or benefits; the sick person does not.

“Therefore I will gladly.” As though he said: “And because power is perfected in weakness, therefore not unwillingly but gladly I will boast in my weaknesses, given for this purpose, that the power of Christ may dwell in me”: that is, that Christ’s grace may be confirmed in me. “Therefore,” [Col. 0086A] because weaknesses have been given for this purpose, “I will not only boast of them to others, but I also take pleasure in them”: that is, I delight greatly. He explains the things in which he delights: “in insults of words; in necessities,” that is, lack of necessities; “in persecutions” from place to place; “in distresses,” that is, anxieties of mind inflicted for Christ. And rightly I take pleasure in these things. “For when I am weak” outwardly, “then I am powerful”: that is, I become victorious.

[Ambrose.] For it is true that the Christian conquers when he is thought to perish, and unbelief perishes when it rejoices that it has conquered. The Christian therefore exults when he is insulted, and rises when he is pressed down. In all these commendations I have become foolish—that is, I appear to have become foolish—[Col. 0086B] but through your fault, because you compelled me; for you ought to have commended me against the false apostles. Hence he adds: “For I ought to have been commended by you,” which you did not do. And therefore I was compelled to break out into my own praise. And truly I ought to have been commended.

“For I have done nothing less for you than those”—namely Peter, James, and the others—“who are apostles beyond measure”: that is, in comparison with these, or than those then far removed, who are apostles more worthy than I, as some suppose. But he is not inferior to them either in preaching or in performing signs. He is inferior not in dignity but in time. But if inferiority is to be ascribed to him because of time, then it must also be ascribed to Christ, because John began preaching before Christ, and Christ did not baptize John, but John baptized Christ. Therefore God does not judge in this way.

“Although.” As though he said: “Truly I have done nothing less for you, because, although I am nothing”—that is, though I seem to some people to be nothing—“nevertheless the signs of an Apostle, or of my apostleship, were performed among you”: that is, by God, who is above you. Or, “were performed above you,” that is, beyond what you deserve. As if he said: “Although I appear to some to be nothing, nevertheless, with God as author, I did things that mark me as an Apostle.” These are the signs of my apostleship: namely, that I showed every patience in adversities.

[Ambrose.] He first mentions patience, which pertains to lesser matters, because he bore with them for a long time, like impatient sick persons, so that, having received the power of signs as medicine, he might heal the wounds of their error. Hence he adds: “and in signs.” As though he said: “I also displayed the signs of an Apostle: in signs and wonders,” that is, lesser and greater miracles, “and powers of mind,” namely chastity and other virtues. Or distinguish these three thus: “power” is the genus of signs and wonders—that is, understand every miracle under the name “power”; a sign is that which signifies something at any time and is a kind of wonder; a wonder is that which signifies the future. Or sign and wonder occur in things done contrary to nature. Power, however, occurs in things not done contrary to nature, such as freeing people from illness through laying on of hands and prayers.

“For what is it?” As though he said: [Col. 0087A] “Truly I have done nothing less for you, because through me you have no less than the other churches have through them; indeed, you have more, because I preached to you without charge.” Thus he says: “For what is it that you had less than the other churches?” That is, what did you have less through me than the other churches had through them, except that I myself did not burden you by taking what was yours? If, as unskilled persons, you regard this as an injury, forgive me this injury.

[Ambrose.] As though he said: “This is not an injury, but a good work, for which I deserve praise. If, then, I have offended you by a good work, forgive me.” And because a fool is an accuser of what is good, in order to show that they were unskilled, he asks them forgiveness for the deed for which he deserves praise.

### Verses 14–19

“Behold, for the third time I am prepared to come [Col. 0087B] to you, and I will not be burdensome to you. For I seek not what is yours, but you. For children ought not to lay up treasure for their parents, but parents for their children. But I will most gladly spend and be spent myself for your souls, although, loving you more, I am loved less. But let it be so: I did not burden you; yet, being crafty, I caught you by guile. Did I defraud you through any one of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus defraud you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not follow the same steps? Long ago you think that we are defending ourselves before you. We speak before God in Christ.”

“Behold.” As though he said: “I did not burden you, nor shall I burden you. For when I came the first and second time, I promised and prepared to come. Behold, for the third time I am prepared to come to you.” He did not come a third time, but was prepared to come a third time. “I am prepared,” I say, and I shall indeed come; and then I shall not be burdensome by taking what is yours. He says this lest it appear that he had cunningly not accepted then, so that he might accept more abundantly now.

[Ambrose.] Therefore, against detractors, he shows that he remains of the same intention. “For I seek not what is yours”—namely riches in gold, silver, and so forth—“but I seek to save you”; and this could not otherwise have happened unless I abstained from receiving maintenance. He shows that he was unwilling to take from them in order to win them, so that, understanding that he valued them above money, they might finally recognize his affection toward them.

[Note: [Col. 0087D] Augustine, in a sermon On the Valiant Woman.] The Apostle sought not the gift but the fruit, lest he be thought a seller [Col. 0087D] of the Gospel. Yet he is truly a merchant of his Lord; for he does indeed sell. He gives spiritual things and seeks, not carnal things, but a greater price: the people themselves. Like Joseph selling grain in Egypt, he sought not silver, but made the purchasers royal slaves; and thus he sold the grain which he did not sell. Understand, therefore, this sale as free of charge: someone buys freely. Hence it is said: “You who thirst, come to the water, and buy for yourselves without silver” (Isa. 55). When you buy, you give not silver but yourself; and thus you buy.

“For children ought not.” As though he said: “I do not seek what is yours because, just as carnal children do not lay up treasure for carnal parents, [Col. 0088A] so spiritual children ought not to lay up treasure”—that is, accumulate wealth, though they should supply necessities—“for spiritual parents.” But you lay up treasure for the false apostles. Rather, spiritual parents ought to lay up for spiritual children the riches of eternal life, and should even expend temporal goods, as carnal fathers do for carnal children.

[Ambrose.] Carnal fathers certainly gather goods for their children; and it is fitting that spiritual parents should receive maintenance from their children for the support of life. But here he proves that he did not wish to receive it, so that he may transfer the role of a carnal father to a spiritual one; and he says that he is willing not only to spend his own goods for their salvation but is also ready to die. Hence he adds: “But I will most gladly spend”—not unwillingly—“spiritual things for you, and will also expend temporal things for your needs,” as he said above. “I robbed other churches, receiving support for your ministry”; and after all this I will expend myself, if necessary. Hence he adds: “And I myself will be spent for your souls.”

[Note: [Col. 0088D] The same, On the Epistle.] This is perfect charity: that one be ready to die for one’s brothers. But is it completely perfect as soon as it is born? No: it is born in order to be perfected; once born it is nourished; once nourished it is strengthened; once strengthened it is perfected; when it has reached perfection, it says: “I desire to depart,” etc. (Phil. 1). “Although.” As though he said: “I say that I will gladly be spent, although, loving you more, I am loved less by you than the false apostles are.”

[Col. 0088C] “But let it be so.” As though he said: “Perhaps you grant that I burdened you. I have said that I did not burden you in person. But you object that, being crafty, I caught you by guile—that is, deceived you—that is, extracted much through others, because I could squeeze nothing or little out of you myself. But did I defraud you through any one of those whom I sent to you?”

[Ambrose.] He says this because perhaps they suspected that he had despised their offerings because they were small, in order to obtain greater ones, and that he had therefore sent others to tell them to give more. “But did I defraud them through any of those persons?” This would have happened if they had said: “If you wish to have the Apostle ready, who rejects small offerings, give gifts worthy of him”—so that they might understand this to be the Apostle’s scheme and cunning. Therefore the Apostle, not leaving unspoken what might be alleged against him, shows that in every respect [Col. 0088D] he acted among them not by deception but in simplicity.

“I urged Titus.” As though he said: “I did not do this deceitfully but simply. I urged Titus to come to you, and sent with him the brother, Barnabas or Luke. Did Titus defraud you? Did not Titus and I walk in the same spirit,” that is, with the same intention? “Did we not follow the same steps?” That is, the same actions are called steps because by them it is apparent whether the will is good or evil. Hence: “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7).

“Long ago.” As though he said: “For a long time perhaps you have thought that we defend ourselves before you”: that is, that I say I did not burden you as an accused person offering a defence. But we say this [Col. 0089A] before God—that is, with God as witness; I say this, He who knows that I did not defraud you. Nor do I say this proudly, but in Christ, magnifying this among you.

### Verses 19–21

“For, beloved, all things are for your edification. For I fear lest perhaps, when I come, I shall find you not such as I wish, and I shall be found by you such as you do not wish: lest perhaps there be among you disputes, jealousies, angry resentments, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, puffings-up, seditions; lest, when I come again, God humble me among you and I mourn many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, fornication, and licentiousness which they committed.”

“But all things.” As though he said: “The things I say are true. But all things which I have said, both concerning revelation and concerning tribulation, [Col. 0089B] I have said for your edification, that you may reject the false apostles; I have done all things for you. For I fear lest perhaps, when I come to you, I may find you such as I do not wish: that is, uncorrected. Therefore prepare yourselves, that I may find you such as I wish. And I fear lest I be found by you such as you do not wish: that is, grieving and punishing.

“But I fear lest perhaps there be among you disputes about the merits of leaders, as about baptizers; jealousies, that is, envy among those who have less; angry resentments in demanding restitution and taking revenge; dissensions, that is, the hatreds arising from these; whisperings, when they secretly sow discord; slanders, when someone speaks against one whom he hates; puffings-up, as those who had greater gifts were puffed up; seditions, tumults tending to fighting.

“Lest again.” As though he said: “I fear lest I find you such, lest when I come to you God should again humble me”—that is, afflict me—“among you,” so that I mourn many of those who, after baptism and before the First Epistle, sinned and did not repent—not only of the things already mentioned, but also of uncleanness, namely lust contrary to nature; fornication, which occurs with prostitutes or married women; and licentiousness, which occurs with women free from a husband. “Which they committed”: as though he said, “which they did continually.”

Note that he says, “they did not repent.”

[Note: [Col. 0089D] Augustine, On the Trinity.] To perform repentance it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to the Lord for deeds already done through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with alms cooperating.

[Col. 0089D] [Augustine.] Observe also that people repent of their former sins before baptism, yet in such a way that they are also baptized, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord,” etc. (Acts 2). People also repent if, after baptism, they sin in such a way as to deserve excommunication and subsequent reconciliation, as do in all churches those properly called penitents. There is also the nearly daily repentance of good and humble believers, in which they beat their breasts, saying: “Forgive us our debts,” etc. (Matt. 6). For we do not ask that those sins be forgiven us which we do not doubt were forgiven in baptism, but those which, though small, nevertheless frequently creep in through human frailty. If they are amassed against us, they will weigh us down and overwhelm us just as one great sin would do.

[Col. 0090A] For what difference does it make for a shipwreck whether a ship is covered and overwhelmed by a great wave, or whether water gradually creeping into the bilge fills the ship and sinks it? Therefore fasts, almsgiving, and prayers keep watch, and we do not cease daily to perform repentance, humbling our souls and saying: “Forgive,” etc.

## Chapter XIII
### Verses 1–7

“Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you, and by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. I have foretold, and I foretell, as though present with you, and now absent, to those who sinned before, and to all the rest, that if I come again I will not spare. Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me? He is not weak among you, but is mighty in you. For although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. And we too are weak in him, but we live with him by the power of God among you. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Or do you not know yourselves, that Christ Jesus is in you—unless perhaps you are reprobate? But I hope that you know that we are not reprobate. And we pray to God that you may do no evil, not that we may appear approved, but that you may do what is good, even though we may appear reprobate.”

“Behold, the third time,” etc. As though he said: I fear that I may find you such people; therefore beware, because behold, it is certain that I am coming to you in preparation for the third time. He does not say “third” because he had already come twice, but because he had twice been prepared to come. I say that I shall come, and then “by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand”: that is, every accusation shall stand when supported by two or three approved witnesses. If anything must be investigated in order to judge someone, and if I discover guilt through the testimony of witnesses, I shall not spare, as I foretold twice when I was present, and now foretell as I then foretold twice.

This is what he adds:

> [Note: Col. 0089D, Id., on Psalm IV.] “For I have foretold and I foretell, that if I find them again, I shall not spare those who sinned before the Epistle, and all the rest,” who previously sinned.

Some manuscripts do not have “who,” but it is understood. He says that he will not spare them because, after correction, if they do not amend, they ought not to be spared. And, as I twice foretold this while present, so now also, though absent, I foretell it.

And as though someone should ask, “Will you be able to do this?” he adds: “Do you seek proof of that Christ who speaks in me?” That is, do you wish to test how Christ is able to act, so that I may not say, “I am able,” but rather, “Christ speaks in me”?

[Ambrose] It is the custom of Holy Scripture to attribute to the person of God what he does in us. Thus the Apostle attributes the very act of speaking to him by whose gift he spoke in Christ. Concerning him he adds: “He is not weak in you,” that is, among you, “but mighty in you.”

> [Note: Col. 0090D, Id., On the Trinity.]

That is, he appeared not weak but mighty from what he did among them when he gave gifts, so that, having experienced these things, they could not doubt that they might be punished by him. For they saw the dead raised in his name, demons driven away, hearing restored to the deaf, speech to the mute, walking to the lame, and sight to the blind.

And he is truly mighty: for although he was crucified through our weakness—that is, through human nature—yet he lives by the power of God, that is, by that power whereby he is God. This is the power of divinity. Such indeed was that assumption [of humanity] as made God man and man God.

“And we too.” [Ambrose] As though he said: I rightly say that he lives and was formerly weak; for we also, far inferior to him, “are weak in him,” that is, in imitation of him we suffer many things. Yet, although we are weak, “we shall live in him,” or “with him,” by the power of God: that is, through him we shall have power from God in judging you, both here and in the future.

Or thus: “We are weak in him.” This remains unchanged. But “he lives with him,” that is, in a like blessedness with him. And this is “by the power of God,” which is such “in you,” that is, in your consciences. Another reading agrees with this sense: “toward you,” where the text has “in you.” As though he said: We are weak in him—that is, we suffer many things for him, or in imitation of him, from unbelievers—but through this we shall live with him by the power of God; and thus weakness is toward you who believe, that is, in your estimation. For if they were made weak by unbelievers in the sight of believers, this was not weakness but advancement, because believers thereby become stronger. Therefore the death inflicted by unbelievers is life in relation to believers, because by the power of God they shall rise again in order to live with Christ.

“Test yourselves.” As though he said: Since I shall not spare you and have the power to punish, test—that is, consider yourselves through your deeds, so that each may examine himself. Consider, I say, whether you are in the faith; and if you are in the faith, prove yourselves, whether you are in those good works in which believers ought to be.

Then, as though speaking to those examining themselves, he says, “Or do you not,” etc. As though he said: I say “prove yourselves” because do you not know yourselves—namely, that Christ Jesus, by your earlier instruction, is in you through faith and good works? He is indeed in you, unless perhaps you have become reprobate from that which you formerly possessed.

“But I hope.” As though he said: You will know that Christ is in you, unless you are reprobate. But whatever may be true of you, I hope that from the life which I have lived among you, you will know that we are not reprobate, either from the faith or from authority. Yet we pray to God, without whom no good is possessed, that you may do no evil. The false apostles, on the contrary, desire and pray otherwise concerning you. And we do not pray in order that we may appear approved—that is, powerful among you by exercising authority in punishments—but rather pray that you may do what is good, though we may be, that is, appear, reprobate.

As though he said: We may appear without authority, having nothing to punish. The Apostle prays that, since they act rightly, he may find nothing in them requiring correction, and thus may appear reprobate. For people appear approved when they judge sinners. Therefore, if there are none for them to judge and their authority is unused, they appear, as it were, reprobate.

Observe that he says, “We pray that you may do no evil, but good.”

> [Note: Col. 0091D, Augustine, On Correction and Grace.] This grace of God must be understood—the grace by which alone human beings are delivered from evil, and without which they do no good whatever, whether in thinking, willing and loving, or acting. It does not merely show them what ought to be done, so that they may know it; it also enables them to do lovingly what they know. The Apostle sought this inspiration of good will and action for the Corinthians when he said: “We pray that you may do no evil,” etc. Who can hear this and not confess that it is from the Lord God that we turn away from evil and do good? For the Apostle did not say, “We admonish” or “we teach,” but “we pray,” because he knew that all that he openly did by planting and watering would be of no value unless he who gives growth in secret heard him praying for them.

> [Note: Col. 0092D, Id., Against the Pelagians.] Yet some say that we ought not to ask the eternal Majesty to grant that we walk in the right way, persevere in the commandments, please him in every good work, and the like, because, they say, all this is placed in our own power. Thus, my brothers, they render void, empty, and nullify the blessings which we pronounce over you, as well as our response, “Amen.” What do you say, O new heretic? Do you say that we possess the power not to sin in such a way that we can accomplish this without the aid of divine grace? “Certainly,” he says, “free choice is sufficient for us for this.” Why then did the Apostle say, “We pray”? He could have said, “We admonish,” “we teach,” or “we command.” If he had said this, he would have said something true, because our will also does something. For our will does not do nothing, but it is not sufficient by itself. Yet he preferred to say, “We pray,” in order to commend grace itself, so that they might understand that when they do no evil, they avoid evil not by their own will alone, but fulfill what is commanded by God’s aid. Therefore, when something is commanded, recognize the freedom of the will; when what is commanded is prayed for, recognize the benefit of grace. For both are found in the Scriptures.

### Verses 8–13

“For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. For we rejoice when we are weak, but you are strong. This also we pray for: your perfection. Therefore I write these things while absent, so that when present I may not act more severely, according to the authority which the Lord gave me for building up and not for destroying. Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfected; exhort one another; think the same thing; have peace; and the God of peace and love shall be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.”

“For we cannot.” As though he said: We have authority; but lest it be thought that we can condemn unjustly, he adds, “For we cannot.” As though he said: We are unable to use that authority unjustly. “For we can do nothing against the truth.”

[Ambrose] He says this because authority was not given against justice—that is, so that he might accuse one who lives rightly—but for maintaining truth, namely, that they might punish an enemy of the law.

“For we rejoice.” As though he said: We cannot act against truth, and the result shows this. “For we rejoice”: that is, we are weak, not exercising authority because there is nothing to punish; but you are strong, not fearing judgment because, by doing good and overcoming vices, you avert punishment from yourselves.

And we do not merely rejoice; we also pray for this, namely, “your perfection,” that you may be perfect in all things. Since I wish and pray for this, I therefore write to you while absent, so that when present I may not deal more severely with you than I wish. I could certainly do so if you acted wickedly, according to the power of binding and loosing which the Lord gave me for your building up and not for your destruction: that you may be built up, not destroyed.

Nor does the Apostle destroy when he sometimes rebukes. Those who are rebuked in order to be corrected are not destroyed; rather, when corrected, they are built up.

“Finally.” As though he said: Thus far I have corrected you concerning evil deeds; but henceforth, brothers, rejoice—that is, do what may bring joy. And that you may rejoice, be perfect in faith. You who are greater, exhort those who are lesser to the same thing; and you who are lesser, think the same thing together with those who are greater. And all alike, both greater and lesser, have peace, lest discord arise among you.

If you do these things, the God of love and peace—that is, Christ, who said, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you” (John 13), and again, “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (John 13)—will be with you, helping you.

And so that peace may be among you, greet one another with a holy, not deceitful, kiss. You ought to do this because all the saints likewise desire it, and I command it. This is what he adds: “All the saints greet you,” wishing this for you and, as it were, saying with me: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, Christ freely forgiving sins, through whom we are justified and saved—“and the love of God”—that is, God the Father giving you love.

[Ambrose] It was his love that sent Christ; his glory saves. And “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit,” that is, the Holy Spirit, who is common to the Father and the Son and is the union of both, be with you all: with those corrected, that they may persevere, and with those not yet corrected, that they may be corrected.

Or: “The fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all,” that is, may the Holy Spirit be so with you that he shares and bestows upon you both the grace of Christ and the love of God. For in order that we may possess the grace of salvation which Christ gives, the fellowship of the Holy Spirit brings this about. For he guards those beloved by God and saved by Christ’s grace. Here is an encompassing of the Trinity and a unity of power. It means: May the whole Trinity be with you, granting grace for sins committed and love, so that the perfection of the Three may bring human beings to the completion of salvation. Amen.

## On the Epistle to the Galatians

### Argument

The Galatians are Greeks. They first received the word of truth from the Apostle; but after his departure they were tempted by false apostles to turn to the law and circumcision. The Apostle recalls them to the faith of truth, writing to them from Ephesus.

# Chapter One

### Verses 1–9

“Paul, an Apostle—not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins in order to deliver us from this present evil age, according to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen. I marvel that you are thus so quickly being transferred from him who called you in the grace of Christ to another gospel—which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel besides that which we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone should preach to you a gospel besides that which you received, let him be anathema.”

“Paul, an Apostle,” etc. The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Galatians. The Galatians are Greeks. For the Gauls, coming long ago into a certain province of Greece, mingled with the Greeks. Hence that province was first called Gallo-Greece, then Galatia. Therefore, although Greeks are of sharp intellect, these Galatians were foolish and slower to understand, like the Gauls, who were also unteachable.

They had received the truth of faith and doctrine from the Apostle. But afterward false apostles tempted them to Judaize, using many methods to persuade them to add the law to the Gospel.

[Ambrose, Jerome] They asserted that faith in Christ without bodily observances was insufficient for salvation; that Peter, James, and the others who had been with the Lord had mingled observances of the law with the Gospel; and that Paul himself did one thing in Judaea and preached another among the Gentiles. By these and similar claims they overthrew the Galatians, so that, agreeing with them, they passed over into observances of the law.

Therefore the Apostle calls them back to the truth of Christian faith and evangelical teaching. He writes to them from Ephesus concerning grace, on which he also wrote to the Romans, who likewise revered the law.

[Jerome] But in writing to the Romans, as to wise persons, he used a higher sense and deeper arguments; with these, however, as with persons less wise, he used restrained speech. To them he also says, “O foolish Galatians,” in order to call them back.

Therefore the Apostle’s intention in this Epistle is to bring the Galatians, ensnared by the tricks of false apostles, back to the religion of faith and the truth of the Gospel. His manner is as follows. He begins with a greeting, in which, against detractors who gloried in works of the law, he briefly touches on his own dignity and Christ’s grace, commending his own person, whom the false apostles were disparaging. After the greeting, he rebukes them for fickleness; afterward he commends his own person more fully. Then he disproves the law in many ways, saying that it is not to be observed after Christ, because it not only does not advance righteousness and salvation, but even obstructs them. Finally, he commends the Gospel and faith in Christ, which are sufficient for salvation.

[Ambrose] In giving the greeting, he first commends his own person, saying:

“Paul, an Apostle,” not chosen or sent by human beings—namely, by Ananias, as some said—or by others, as some were chosen and sent by the apostles, and the false apostles by the Jews; nor appointed through a mere human being, but through Jesus Christ and the Lord Father. That is, he was appointed by God the Father through the Son, who is Savior and King. Therefore he is not opposed to God, by whom he was chosen and sent through the Son, as is alleged by those who speak of the abolition of the law.

> [Note: Col. 0095D, Augustine, in the Retractations.] For the charge against him was that he preached things opposed to God, because he abandoned the law given by God.

Or thus: he was not appointed through Christ as man—that is, through Christ in so far as he was human, namely mortal—but through Jesus now wholly immortal, having already risen, who taught him wholly and at once through the Spirit, rather than gradually teaching human beings as a man. Thus he was greater in the very respect in which he seemed to be lesser.

The other apostles seemed greater because they came earlier; he was least because he came last. Yet he appears more worthy for this reason: the earlier apostles were appointed through Christ while he was still human in part, that is, mortal; but Paul, who came last, was appointed through Christ now wholly Lord, that is, wholly immortal, and through the Lord Father, who did this through the Son.

[Augustine] And, to clarify what he meant when he said, “nor through a human being,” he adds: “who raised him from the dead.” Thus he appointed me more worthily through immortal Christ than the others through mortal Christ. By reason of immortality, Christ God is no longer called man; but by reason of the substance of human nature, in which he ascended into heaven, he is also called “the man Christ Jesus,” mediator between God and human beings.

“Paul,” I say, “and the brothers who are with me,” grieving over your seduction: witnesses of my truth, whom you ought to believe. And they are not few, but all. He says this because one who is reproved by many easily recognizes that he has erred.

Therefore all these send this message with me to the churches of Galatia: “Grace be to you,” that is, forgiveness of sins, peace of mind, and reconciliation to God; and this from no other source than God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. He is not lesser than the Father, whom you insultingly equate with the law when you assert that he does not suffice for salvation without the law, any more than the law does without him.

But grace and peace are from him without the law, and may safely be sought from him, because it is he who “gave,” that is, freely offered himself. For there was no other able to open the book except the Lion from the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5). He gave himself because there was no worthy sacrifice to be offered for the blotting out of our sins. He is the beginning of salvation. What place, then, does the law have? None at all.

He also gave himself in order to “deliver” us, as though by force, from sins in which we were entangled and under which we were guilty according to the law; to deliver us from “the age,” that is, from conformity to this world which entices us, namely from the evils committed in the world—such as foolishness, impurity, and weakness. From these he delivers us who is wisdom, holiness, and strength.

[Jerome] I mean the present age, since love takes greater hold on us when eternal things are not seen, and “evil,” because it draws toward wickedness. Observe that the present age is called evil not because this world, created by God, is evil, but because evil things are done in it. In this sense it is said: “The days are evil”; Jacob’s days are “most evil”; “the world lies in the evil one”; the times are perilous; likewise wooded passes full of robbers, a sword by which blood is shed, and a cup in which poison is mixed, are called evil because not only times, but also places and instruments of evil have acquired the infamy of the acts done in them. Thus the age is called evil, from which Christ delivers us.

And in order that what he says of Christ may be firm, he adds, “according to the will.” As though he said: Christ’s giving himself and delivering us was not done because of our merits, but according to the will of God our Father—that is, according to the goodwill of God, who created us and is benevolent. To him, namely Christ and God the Father, one in essence, be glory for this redemption unto ages of ages, that is, forever. As though he said: Those present bear witness to this, and those to come will bear witness. “Amen” is a mark of confirmation.

Observe that in this greeting the Apostle has touched beforehand upon the commendation of himself, what God’s grace can accomplish, and the fact that the law contributes nothing.

“I marvel,” etc. Here he rebukes them for fickleness, because they indiscriminately passed from the Gospel to the law. And because Galatia is said to mean “transfer,” he fittingly takes from the name itself an occasion for this rebuke.

As though he said: Since the aforementioned blessings come from Christ, I marvel that you who were first well instructed are thus—that is, so violently—and so quickly—that is, within so short a time—being transferred by the false apostles, like senseless persons, beyond Christ and into the law.

[Ambrose] Why do I marvel? Because it is astonishing to flee from joy to destruction when one ought to advance gradually. He shows from whom and to what they are being transferred when he adds: “From him,” namely God—that is, from faith in him—who called you when you had turned away, through preaching, “into the grace of Christ,” that is, into the good gifts freely bestowed by Christ. You are being transferred “to another gospel,” namely to the law, which is thought to be a gospel and which, as the false apostles teach it must be observed, is contrary to my preaching. Yet according to the truth of spiritual understanding it is not another.

Therefore he adds: “Which gospel,” that is, the law, “is not another” according to spiritual understanding; nor would it appear otherwise to you unless there were some who trouble you—that is, who disturb the pure fountain of your understanding.

[Augustine] These were the false apostles who said that the law of Moses was a gospel other than Christ’s Gospel. They said this to make the Apostle odious. Such persons “wish to pervert,” that is, strive to turn the Gospel of Christ wholly into law: they wish to turn spiritual things into carnal things.

“But even if.” As though he said: They strive for this. But even if we apostles—not merely they—or an evil or good angel coming from heaven, and thus seeming more credible, should preach to you—that is, announce something to you which appears good—something not, I do not say, greater than, but besides that which I preached to you, true in faith, honorable in practice, and beneficial in faith, let him be anathema.

Observe that he did not say “we” or “an angel,” who may be understood as a good angel, because this had ever occurred; rather, he was so certain of the truth of his Gospel that, even if an angel announced something else, he would not believe him but would anathematize him.

Observe also that he did not say “more than you received,” but “besides what you received.” For had he said the former, he would have prejudiced himself, since he wished to come to some whom he wrote to—for example, the Thessalonians—in order to supply what was lacking in their faith. But one who supplies adds what was lacking, not removes what was present. One who goes beyond the rule of faith does not advance on the way, but departs from the way.

“As,” etc. He argues from the greater. As though he said: Since I would excommunicate even you or an angel, the false apostles ought all the more to be excommunicated. This is the meaning of, “As I have just said concerning you or an angel, so now I say again concerning these, namely the false apostles: if any one of them,” etc.

Or thus: As I formerly foretold this when present with you, so now, though absent, I say again: if anyone, whoever he may be, should preach to you something besides that which you received from me, let him be anathema.

> [Note: Col. 0097D, Augustine, on Psalm CIII.] Why is this so? Because one who preaches something else wishes to rain from his own private source, not from the public fountain. This perhaps a human being, hindered by a carnal mist and brought back from the common source to his own falsehood, may do; but never an angel. Truly, if the angel flowing from his own source in Paradise had not been heard, we would not have been hurled into death. The water placed in the midst was the commandment of God: the water was, so to speak, public, flowing without deceit, stain, or mud. But an angel fallen from heaven came, having assumed a form because he now desired craftily to spread poison. He poured out poison from his own source and spoke from his own: “Taste, and you shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). And they, desiring what they were not, lost what they had received.

> [Note: Col. 0097D, Id., in the Questions.] Here one must consider how “anathema” is spoken of. This word is used for a curse, and is commonly called *devotatio*, “devotion” or dedication to destruction. For scarcely anyone says that he “devotes” himself except while uttering a curse. Hence the statement: “And he anathematized him and his cities; and the name of that place was called Anathema.” From this usage “anathema” has come to seem something detestable and abominable. For, so that the conqueror might take nothing from it for his own use but might assign the whole to undergo punishment, this was to anathematize—what is commonly called *devotare*, “to devote.” The origin of the word is in Greek, from objects vowed and paid—that is, promised and rendered—which were set up high in temples; it is called *apo tou anathene*, “from placing up high.”

### Verses 10–14

“For do I now persuade human beings, or God? Or do I seek to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ. For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which has been preached by me is not according to a human being. For neither did I receive it from a human being, nor did I learn it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ. For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and ravaged it; and I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my own people, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers.”

“For now.” As though he said: I say that one who preaches another gospel should be anathema because do I now persuade human beings or God? That is, I seek honor not from human beings before God, but from God, not human beings.

He says “now” because formerly, when he said that a human being is justified by the law, he proclaimed human glory and God’s grace as useless.

[Ambrose] Here he also suggests that those seducers—the false apostles—did this in order to win praise from the Jews, whom Paul does not fear to offend for the glory of God. When he comes, the law ceases.

Therefore he adds: “Or do I seek to please human beings,” as when I received letters from the chief priests to kill Christians? No. For if I were still pleasing human beings—that is, if I wished to please them as I formerly wished—I would not be Christ’s servant, which I now am. And for this reason I excommunicate them.

> [Note: Col. 0098D, Augustine, On the Sheep.] Observe that he says, “If I were pleasing human beings,” etc. From these words some think that, in living well, a good conscience is enough for them and that they need not care greatly what another thinks of them. But conscience before God is necessary, while one’s manner of life is before one’s neighbor. If this is conducted too negligently, it harms by example. For example, if someone with a good conscience eats food sacrificed to an idol in the presence of a weak person, even though he does this with right belief, nevertheless the conscience of the weak person is disturbed. What good is it if the belly of your conscience has drunk pure water, while the other drinks troubled water because of your negligent conduct? You trouble the waters for others and trample down the pastures; but take care that by negligence in your conduct you do not trouble the water for yourself. Hence elsewhere the Apostle says: “Please all people in all things, as I also please all people in all things” (1 Cor. 10); and again: “Be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God” (ibid.); and again: “We provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings” (Rom. 12).

Someone will say to me: Explain how I am to understand these things which seem different and contrary—what the Apostle says here, “If I were pleasing human beings,” etc., and “Please human beings,” etc. If you listen more calmly, if you do not yourself trouble the water of your mind, I shall perhaps explain it as far as I can.

There are human beings who are rash judges, detractors, whisperers, and murmurers, seeking to suspect what they do not see and even seeking to spread abroad what they do not suspect. Against such people the testimony of our conscience is enough. Neither, when we wish to please others, do we seek—or ought we to seek—our own glory; rather, we seek their salvation, so that they may not err by failing to imitate our good conduct. For then they praise not us, but the Lord who made us such.

Therefore, when we wish to please human beings, we do not seek our own advantage or glory; rather, we rejoice that what is good pleases them, for their benefit and not our own dignity.

> [Note: Col. 0099D, Augustine, On the Sermon on the Mount.] Thus the Apostle rightly said both that he did not please human beings, because in that very matter he had in view pleasing God, and that human beings ought rightly to be pleased—not so that this might be sought as the reward of right actions, but because one could not please God if one did not offer oneself as an example to those whom one wished to be saved.

> [Note: Col. 0100D, Id., On the Sheep.] And, just as these statements in the Apostle seemed contrary, so those sayings in the Gospel also seem contrary. For he said: “Let your works shine before human beings,” etc. (Matt. 5); and again: “Do not perform your righteousness before human beings,” etc. (ibid.). There he rebukes those who display their works in such a way as to place the end of their good works in human praise, counting that praise as the reward of their works. Therefore he says, “in order that you may be seen by them” (ibid.). As though he said: Do not do whatever good you do before human beings in such a way that you may be seen by them—that is, so that being seen by them is itself the end of your good. Do not make your end here; extend your intention further.

“For I make known.” [Ambrose] As though he said: Therefore I do not persuade—that is, I do not please—human beings, but excommunicate persons of this kind, because the Gospel which I preach is not according to a human being.

He says it thus: “I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel which has been preached by me is not according to a human being,” whether as one teaching me or sending me. He says this lest they perhaps doubt. This refers back to what he said above in commending his own person: “not from human beings, nor through a human being.”

And truly it is not from a human being. “For neither did I receive it from a human being,” so that no one chose me to preach the Gospel or imposed the task on me; “nor did I learn it” from a human being teaching me, “but through a revelation of Jesus Christ,” that is, through Christ Jesus making all things manifestly clear.

“For you have heard.” As though he said: Truly, I did not learn from a human being, either before conversion or afterward. You yourselves know from the actions of that time that it was not before conversion. For you have heard of my former way of life, when I was an unbeliever, which I had “in Judaism,” namely while living as a Jew: how, beyond measure beyond others, I persecuted the Church of God by pursuing Christians, and ravaged it, afflicting believers bodily with punishments; and how I advanced in Judaism by fulfilling the law and defending it.

I advanced, I say, beyond many—not elders, but contemporaries of my own, who labored more than elders—and not beyond many proselytes, but those who were of my own people, namely Jews. And though I formerly excelled among them in those legal observances, I have now abandoned them. Therefore you too, following my example, depart from them.

“More abundantly.” As though he said: I advanced in Judaism beyond others; I say also that I was more abundantly zealous than others, an example to others, an imitator of ancestral traditions: traditions added by good fathers, called “my own” because I made them, as it were, my own, serving them zealously, in which service he thought that he was obeying God. For the Apostle had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

[Ambrose] God foresaw his will, or zeal, but saw that knowledge was lacking; and he foresaw him to be fit, because one who was so faithful in a small matter would be more steadfast in a great one. Therefore, that he might be more steadfast in a great matter, he anticipated him by calling him through grace.

### Verses 15–19

“But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not confer with flesh and blood. Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who were before me; but I went away into Arabia, and again returned to Damascus. Then, after three years, I came to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw no other of the apostles, except James, the Lord’s brother.”

When, however, it pleased Him. As though he were saying: Before my conversion it is clear that I did not learn the Gospel; nor did I learn it from a human being afterward, but from God alone. And this is what he says: “When it pleased Him,” namely God, who acted according to His own good pleasure, not according to my merit; who “set me apart,” literally, “from my mother’s womb,” in order that “in me,” that is, in my conversion, He might reveal His Son, that is, show how great the power and goodness of His Son were. Or, “reveal His Son in me,” [Col. 0100D] that is, in my understanding: He called me from an evil way to a good one, not through my merit but through His grace; and He called me precisely for this purpose, “that I might preach Him,” that is, the Son, among the Gentiles. And He who caused me to be born could certainly lead me to this end. For before anyone is born, God knows who and what sort of person he will be. Hence it is written of Jeremiah: “Before I formed thee in the womb, I called thee” (Jer. 1). He who foreknows those who will be before they exist causes them to be born when He wills, so that they may exist; and those already born whom He wills He calls through grace, that they may be righteous, just as He called Paul through grace to proclaim Christ. Therefore, in order to show that the whole matter comes from God—both that he exists and that he is righteous—he says: “He set me apart” [Col. 0101A] “and called me.”

“Immediately,” etc. As though he were saying: He called me and revealed His Son; and immediately I preached, as one instructed by God. Therefore nothing other than what I preach is to be maintained, nor are human beings to be believed, but God who called me. This is what he says: “Immediately I did not confer,” etc.

Or this may be understood mystically: “He set me apart from my mother’s womb.” The mother is understood as the Synagogue; the mother’s womb and inner chambers are the Pharisees, from whose number he was set apart. Thus: “When it pleased Him who set me apart from my mother’s womb,” that is, from the number of the Pharisees, who were the inner circle of the Synagogue, “to reveal His Son in me,” He called me through His grace for the purpose of preaching Him among the Gentiles. This does not change.

“And I immediately did not confer”: [Col. 0101B] he does not say, “I did not confer immediately,” as though he did not then confer but did so afterward; rather, he says, “I immediately did not yield to flesh and blood,” that is, to vices; rather, I rejected vices. Or by “flesh and blood” he means relatives by race, namely the Jews, with whom he did not agree in observing the Law and persecuting Christians.

“Nor did I go up to Jerusalem to the apostles who were before me,” that is, those who had believed before me. Thus it is clear that I did not learn the Gospel from them, since I did not go to them, because one chosen by God had no need of this. “But I went away” to preach the Gospel “into Arabia,” where none of the apostles had preached. “And I returned again to Damascus,” where he himself, though still inexperienced, had preached. “Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter,” not to learn anything from him, but to see him out of apostolic affection, and so that Peter might know that I was to be his fellow apostle. “And I remained with him fifteen days,” received by him as truthful and as a fellow apostle. By this he shows that he disagreed in no way with the other apostles, as his rivals whispered.

“But I saw none of the other apostles.” Thus it is clear that neither did I learn from the others. “I saw no one,” I say, “except James, the Lord’s brother.” This is James the Less, who was called the Lord’s brother because this James was a son of Joseph, who was called Jesus’ father; but this is not accepted, since Joseph is believed to have been a virgin. Another reason must therefore be sought why he was called the Lord’s brother, as were Joseph, Simon, and Jude. Thus the Gospel says: “Behold, [Col. 0101D] thy father and thy mother, and thy brothers,” etc. (Matt. 12).

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Jerome, To Helvidius.]

Therefore, to make clear why they are called brothers, it must be known that Mary, the Lord’s mother, was the daughter of Joachim and Anna, and married Joseph; thus Joseph was the reputed father of Christ. After Joachim’s death, Cleophas, Joseph’s brother, took the same Anna as his wife and begot by her a daughter whom he called Mary. She married Alphaeus, and he begot by her four sons: James, Joseph, Simon, and Jude. After Cleophas died, a certain Salome took the same Anna and begot by her a daughter named Mary; she married Zebedee and had by him sons, namely James, called the Greater, and John the Evangelist. [Col. 0102A] Thus Anna had three husbands and three daughters.

We must now see why James son of Alphaeus was called the Less and the Lord’s brother. He was called the Less in distinction from James son of Zebedee, who was called the Greater, not with respect to time, but because he followed the Lord first. Thus James son of Alphaeus was called the Less because he attached himself to Christ later than the other.

He was called the Lord’s brother, as some hold, because he was the son of Christ’s maternal aunt, [Bede] or because of similarity in holiness, or rather because he was the nephew of Christ’s paternal uncle, that is, Cleophas. For the Hebrews call brothers those joined in full blood-relationship on the fathers’ side. Hence Jerome [Note: [Col. 0101D] Id., Against the Manichaeans.] says that by the Lord’s brothers we should understand this James and his brothers, in these words: “Some, following the absurdities of the apocryphal writings, [Col. 0102B] suppose that the brothers of the Lord standing outside were Joseph’s sons by some little woman; but here we must understand the Savior’s cousins, namely the sons of Alphaeus and of His mother’s maternal aunt: James the Less, Joseph, and Jude.”

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Jerome, To Helvidius.]

For in the divine Scriptures “brothers” are spoken of in four ways: by nature, nation, kinship, and affection. By nature, as Esau and Jacob; by nation, as all Jews are called brothers among themselves. Hence in Deuteronomy: “If [thou hast] a brother who is a Hebrew,” etc. (Deut. 15). And again: “Set over thee as ruler him whom the Lord shall choose, one who is of thy brothers” (Deut. 18). Further, those of one family are called brothers by kinship, when a multitude spreads out from one root; accordingly Abraham in Genesis called Lot his brother, saying: [Col. 0102C] “Let there be no strife between me and thee, for we are brothers” (Gen. 13); and Jacob and Laban are called brothers. Brothers are also named by affection, as all Christians are called brothers, as in: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132). And the Lord says: “Go and tell my brothers” (John 20).

[Augustine] Moreover, all human beings are called brothers in common, because they are born from one parent. I therefore understand those called Christ’s brothers to be so called by the privilege of kinship. James, the Lord’s brother, must be understood either as one of Joseph’s sons by another wife, or as related to Mary his mother.

**VERS. 20–24.**—“But as to the things which I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie. Then I came into the regions [Col. 0102D] of Syria and Cilicia. But I was unknown by face to the churches of Judaea which were in Christ. They had only heard that he who once persecuted us now preaches the faith which he once sought to destroy; and they glorified God in me.”

As to what I now write to you concerning myself, behold, it is clear to all that I do not lie. And I say this before God, that is, with God as witness. The Apostle swears so that what he says, which is beneficial to them, may be believed.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Augustine, On the Epistle of the Apostle James.]

Compelled by necessity, he swears, because unless he did so they would not believe him; and it is not beneficial to them not to believe, indeed it is beneficial that they should believe. And I see that this is more than “Yes, yes; no, no”; but “whatever is more than this is from evil” [Col. 0103A] (Matt. 5). And if it is not from the evil of the person swearing, it is from the evil of the person who does not believe. Therefore He does not say, “If anyone does more, it is evil,” but “what is more is from evil.”

“Then I came” to preach “into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. But I was unknown by face,” that is, by bodily presence, “to the churches of Judaea which were in Christ,” that is, in faith in Christ. From this it is clear that the churches of Judaea did not teach me either; these churches existed on their own, not intermixed with the churches of the Gentiles. “They had only heard of me,” that is, what they had heard of me they had committed to memory: namely, “that he who once persecuted us,” while he was an unbeliever, “now preaches the faith of Christ which he once sought to destroy.”

[Augustine] And because great amazement arises from a difficult matter, he adds: “And in [Col. 0103B] me,” that is, in my conversion, “they glorified,” or magnified, “the Lord,” that is, they proclaimed as great the One who converted me by His grace. Or, “they glorified God in me,” that is, preaching on the basis of my example, or giving thanks to God, through whom I benefited them.

## Chapter II

**VERS. 1–5.**—“Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me. And I went up according to a revelation, and laid before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles. But privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should be running, or had run, in vain. Yet not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Gentile, was compelled to be circumcised; but because of the false brothers secretly introduced, [Col. 0103C] who had slipped in to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce us to slavery. To them we did not yield in subjection even for an hour.”
