“Then after fourteen years” from Christ’s Passion, which years followed his preaching in Syria and Cilicia, when the question had arisen whether the Law ought to be kept or not, “I went up again to Jerusalem.” He does not say “I went,” but “I went up,” according to the geographical position of the land. “I went up,” I say, “with Barnabas,” who was from the Jews, “taking Titus,” who was from the Gentiles. As though he were saying: I had witnesses from both sides, by whom it is clear that it is false that I preach one thing to the Gentiles and another to the Jews.

“But I went up,” not by my own arrangement alone, “but according to a revelation” from God. And I do not say that I learned from them as from superiors; rather, I “laid before” [Col. 0103D] them, as before friends and equals, the Gospel of Christ which I preach among the Gentiles. He did this to establish his preaching, because many were troubled in regard to the Apostle’s doctrine by Jews who caused disturbance.

[Jerome] Therefore, by saying, “I laid it before them,” he shows that he did not have assurance concerning the Gospel unless it was strengthened by the authority of Peter and the others.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Augustine, Against Faustus.]

For the Apostle Paul, called from heaven after Christ’s ascension, would receive no belief at all from the Church unless he communicated with the apostles and compared the Gospel with them, so that it might be evident that he belonged to the same fellowship. But when they knew that he proclaimed what [Col. 0104A] they proclaimed, lived in their communion and unity, and was accompanied by such signs through him as they also performed, then, the Lord thus commending him, he gained authority, so that his words are heard in the Church as though Christ Himself were most truly heard speaking in him. As He Himself said: “I pray not for these only,” that is, for the disciples who were then with Him, “but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John 17). There He intended all His own to be understood: not only those who then existed, but also those who were to come. For all who afterward believed in Him believed through their word, namely the apostles’ word, that is, through the Gospel. Whoever believes in Christ believes the Gospel, which is called their word because it was first and especially preached by them. For it was already being preached by them when Paul received their very word through Christ’s revelation, and received it through that word, though not through them.

When he had received it from God, Paul believed; hence he laid the Gospel before them and received right hands, because he possessed that word with them, though not through them.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] Augustine, Questions on the Gospels.]

For this very comparison displayed one form of doctrine, cleansed of every variety of leprosy. For the lepers whom the Lord is recorded in the Gospel to have healed and sent to the priests so that they might show themselves to them are not unreasonably understood to signify persons who lack knowledge of the true faith and profess various erroneous doctrines. No false doctrine fails to intermingle some truth.

Thus truths disorderly mixed with falsehoods in one doctrine [Col. 0104C] signify leprosy, which changes and blemishes the color of one body in diverse places.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] Augustine, Against Faustus.]

Therefore, in order that the Apostle’s preaching might be shown free from every leprosy of corruption, he compared the Gospel with the other apostles. Otherwise the Church would not believe one who had not been with the Lord.

“But privately.” As though he were saying: I laid the Gospel before them, but “privately,” [Jerome] that is, separately. “I laid it before those who seemed to be something,” that is, to possess some authority; not publicly before everyone, lest a scandal to faith arise among believers from Judaea, who thought the Law ought to be observed.

[Augustine] He also explained the Gospel privately to them after he had already explained it before everyone, not because he had said anything false and was to speak truth privately to the few; but because of the weak, who cannot receive everything, from whom he had withheld things that ought to be said to the perfect. For sometimes it is permissible to withhold a truth.

“Lest perhaps.” As though he were saying: I laid it before them lest perhaps “I should run or had run in vain,” that is, lest I might be thought to have preached uselessly. He calls the work of preaching a race because of his flowing eloquence.

“But not even.” As though he were saying: Not only was I approved in the conference; Titus also, who was with me, though he was a Gentile, “was not compelled,” by their arguments, “to be circumcised”; that is, it could not be forced from me that he should be circumcised, but he was received by the apostles into fellowship uncircumcised. Why then do you [Col. 0105A] Galatians wish to be circumcised? Why do you voluntarily depart from grace and turn to the Law?

“But because,” etc. As though he were saying: Not only was Titus not compelled to be circumcised, but “we did not yield even for an hour,” in any respect, as though convicted concerning the Law, “to their subjection,” so as to submit to those who preached that legal observances were necessary for salvation. But since elsewhere he did yield, as in Timothy’s circumcision, why did he not yield here? He replies and says: “Because of false brothers,” who pretended friendship, “secretly introduced,” [Ambrose] that is, secretly introduced by the Jews into the place where the apostles were. What unbelievers could not accomplish on their own, they attempted through false brothers, whom they had sent in under the appearance of religion in order to spy out what liberty we had in faith in Christ. Hence he adds: “Who,” namely the false brothers, “slipped in,” [Col. 0105B] that is, entered under an appearance of peace and humility, seeking one thing and pretending another, “to spy out our liberty,” so as to accuse our liberty, “which we have in Christ Jesus,” that is, in faith in Christ; not in order to maintain it, but in order by some contention to reduce us to the slavery of the Law, that is, to carnal observances, from which we have been freed through faith in Christ.

If this had occurred, the truth of the Gospel would not have remained among the Gentiles, but all would have Judaized. Therefore here, where he was establishing the authority of his own preaching, he was in no way willing to yield, so that the truth of the preaching might be shown. Note that in all these matters he commends himself and proves that the Law is not to be observed. Hence he adds:

**VERS. 5, 6.**—“That the truth of the Gospel might remain [Col. 0105C] with you. But from those who seemed to be something—whatever they once were makes no difference to me. For God does not accept the person of a man.”

“That the truth,” etc. As though he were saying: This is why we yielded in nothing: that the truth of the Gospel might thus remain with you. For the truth of the Gospel is Christ’s grace. He did not yield here by circumcising Titus lest he give an occasion to those who said that believers could not be saved without that circumcision and boasted, to deceive the Gentiles, that Paul himself held this view.

But where it did no harm, he circumcised Timothy for fear of offending the Jews, lest circumcision should seem to the Jews as detestable to him as idolatry ought to be; whereas God commanded the former to be done, Satan [Col. 0105D] persuaded people to the latter. Therefore he did not do in Titus what he did in Timothy, so as to show that these sacraments ought neither to be sought as necessary nor condemned as sacrilegious.

Or according to another reading. Some Latin manuscripts do not have *neque* (“not even”), and on that reading the passage may be read thus: As though he were saying: Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, but elsewhere we yielded in subjection for an hour, as in Timothy’s circumcision. He gives the reason why he was compelled to do what he did not wish: namely, because of scandal to the Jews, forestalling the slanders of false brothers who were ready to stir up sedition if he ordained that son of a Jewish woman an uncircumcised bishop. This is what he says: “We yielded,” I say, “because of the false brothers who slipped in” where I was with Timothy and others, [Col. 0106A] “who entered to spy out our liberty which we have in Christ Jesus,” that is, in order to reduce us to the slavery of the Law. When they could not accomplish this, they attempted to excite the people against us. Therefore we yielded to their subjection by circumcising Timothy; “we yielded for an hour,” so that the truth of the Gospel might remain among us, which teaches that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision contributes anything, but faith. For this was the case among the Jews: believers circumcised their own sons.

Observe carefully that Ambrose rejects the reading which says that he did not yield even for an hour, since he says that Paul did yield, speaking thus: Titus, he said above, “was not compelled to be circumcised.” Then he adds: “But because of the false brothers secretly introduced,” etc. [Col. 0106B] What do these words now mean except that he yielded for an hour because of them? But if he did not yield because of those false brothers, as is read in some manuscripts, he did not fail to yield by his own will; for he indicated that he would have yielded had they not been present, but he did not yield because of those false brothers secretly introduced. If then one ought not to have yielded, why are they called false brothers, through whose benefit he did not do what ought not to have been done? Therefore, if this is so, they rendered a benefit to the Apostle, because on their account he did not yield, though he ought not to have yielded to the Church. Why then are they called spies, if they wanted him to do what he was going to do anyway? Yet he did not do it because of them. But if he was not going to do it, undoubtedly he did it because of them. The text here indicates that he yielded, and the history cries aloud that this was done. How could he deny that he yielded for an hour, [Col. 0106C] when it is proved that he circumcised Timothy because of the Jews? The person who could defend himself as never having yielded could say that he did not yield even for an hour. For he did not yield even for an hour who never yielded; but if he ever yielded, how did he not yield even for an hour?

Why also does he say that he yielded because of false brothers, if he was going to do it on his own? Either he was going to yield but did not yield because of the false brothers, or he was not going to yield but did yield because of the false brothers. One of these two must be understood. Therefore he yielded unwillingly, not voluntarily, doing because of them what he would not have done on his own; humbling himself to the Law by circumcising Timothy, so that the deceit and scandal of the Jews might cease, for they were ready to stir up uproar and sedition if [Col. 0106D] he received that son of a Jewish woman uncircumcised and ordained him bishop.

[Ambrose] There was no scandal concerning the sons of Greeks, because a letter had been issued by the apostles concerning them, declaring that they need not be circumcised. But believing Jews circumcised their sons; the apostles’ letter neither prohibited this nor said anything concerning them. Thus Titus was not compelled to be circumcised, because he was of Greek or Gentile origin; but Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman, was circumcised because of the spies. By circumcising the one and not the other, it is shown that these legal observances are neither necessary for salvation nor sacrilegious, so that the truth of the Gospel may remain: namely, that in Christ neither uncircumcision nor circumcision has any value, but faith working through love.

“But from [Col. 0107A] those.” As though he were saying: I refer to the comparison of the Gospels in commendation of myself. But “whatever they once were,” that is, how unlearned they were in comparison with me formerly, while they were under the Law and before those who seemed to be something became apostles—those, namely, who seemed to possess authority because they walked with the Lord and were present at His Transfiguration—“makes no difference to me.”

[Augustine] “They seemed,” I say, to the false brothers, because those who seem to be something seem so to carnal people. For they themselves are nothing, even if they are good ministers of God. Christ is something in them, but they are not something in themselves; for if they were something in themselves, they would always have been something. “Whatever they once were”: for they too were sinners and unlearned, it makes no difference to me, that is, it does me no good in this state of misery, because past things neither benefit nor harm. Yet he implies that he surpassed them. For by saying “whatever they once were,” he indicates that in matters of the Law he had surpassed them; but that this had profited them nothing, and therefore legal observances are not to concern the Galatians.

“God,” etc. As though he were saying: This is why it makes no difference to me, because God does not accept the person of a human being, great or small; that is, without respect of persons He calls all to salvation, not reckoning their offenses against them.

**VERS. 7–13.**—“For those who seemed to be something added nothing to me. But, on the contrary, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, as that of the circumcision had been to Peter—for He who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles—and when James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, recognized the grace which had been given to me, they gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcision; only that we should remember the poor, which very thing I was diligent to do. But when Cephas came to Antioch, I withstood him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain persons came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they had come, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews consented to his dissimulation, so that even Barnabas was carried away by them into that dissimulation.”

[Col. 0107D] “For,” or “but.” As though he were saying: This is why I do not return to former things, because the present facts suffice for my commendation: those who seemed to be something, namely Peter and the others who had been with the Lord, “added nothing,” that is, gave nothing additional, to me.

[Augustine] It is clear from this that I am not inferior to those whom the Lord made so perfect that there was nothing they could add to my perfection in the comparison. For He who gave understanding to those who were unlearned gave it also to me.

Or the connection may be made thus: Truly God does not accept the person of a human being; for if He did, I, Paul, formerly impious, to whom such men would add nothing, would not have become what I am; but I did become so. “For to me,” etc.

Or join it thus, reading *autem* (“but”): As though he were saying: It makes no difference to me to relate that, but this I shall say: those who seemed to be something [Col. 0108A] “added nothing to me.” Rather, contrary to the opinion of the plotters, when they saw that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me by the Lord, as to one trustworthy, just as principally as the Gospel of the circumcision had been entrusted to Peter. For Christ gave Paul the ministry of the Gentiles, as He had also given Peter the ministry of the Jews.

[Ambrose] The ministry was nonetheless so apportioned between them that Peter would preach to the Gentiles if occasion required, and Paul to the Jews. “For He who.” As though he were saying: They saw this because He who worked through Peter, that is, gave him all that he had by choosing him for the apostleship of the circumcision, that is, of the Jews, also worked through me, that is, to my honor, among the Gentiles.

“When they had seen,” I say, “and recognized the grace given to me among the Gentiles,” [Augustine] namely how many miracles I had performed and how many nations I had converted, James and Cephas, that is, Peter, and John, who were more honored among the apostles because they were always with the Lord in private settings—those who “seemed to be pillars,” that is, the support of the whole Church, which itself is called “the pillar and ground of truth” (1 Tim. 3), and which Wisdom also built and established upon seven pillars (Prov. 9): by this number either the totality of preachers, since it is customarily used for the whole, or the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit is signified—

when they had seen and recognized this, “they gave right hands” to me and Barnabas as a sign of fellowship, that is, they consented to fellowship and obeyed the Lord’s will, agreeing that I should be foremost in preaching to the Gentiles, as Peter was among the circumcision. [Col. 0108C] And as the other apostles obeyed Peter, so Barnabas obeyed Paul. Thus they were found to disagree with him in nothing, as though, when he said he had received the perfect Gospel, they denied it and wished to add something to him as imperfect.

“That we,” as though he were saying, “should go to the Gentiles”: they gave us right hands for this purpose; “but they to the circumcision only.” They added this: “that we should remember the poor” in Jerusalem, who placed the prices received from selling their possessions at the apostles’ feet. “Remember,” I say, by making collections for their needs. Behold, this shows that they were in need of us.

“Which very thing.” As though he were saying: They instructed us to do this. “Which,” that is, but even before [Col. 0108D] their admonition, I was diligent, that is, I endeavored to do this very thing, no less carefully than they commanded.

At that time, when Peter came to Antioch—although this is not read in the Acts of the Apostles—Paul withstood him to his face. Hence he adds: “But when,” etc. As though he were saying: They added nothing to me, but I added something to Peter, because “when Cephas came to Antioch,” a place of the Gentiles, “I withstood him” as an equal. He would not have dared to do this unless he knew that he would not be inferior. “I withstood,” I say, “him to his face,” that is, pointing out what he did not perceive; and not in secret, but before all whom he was harming. And I did not do this rashly, because “he was blameworthy,” that is, worthy of blame, not for his own sake but for that of others. And truly he was, for the following reason.

[Augustine] [Col. 0109A] Before certain Jews came from James, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, Peter ate with the Gentiles, making no distinction among foods. Those who came from James were zealots for the Law, Christian in name, who honored Christ and the Law as of equal right. Fearing them, he did not mingle with the Gentiles. If that alone had been the case, it would not have been blameworthy, just as Paul himself sometimes yielded to avoid scandal.

[Ambrose] But he erred in this: by his example he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize, while separating himself from the Gentiles and joining himself to the Jews. Hence he adds: “But when they had come from Judaea, Peter withdrew,” secretly, by certain pretexts, from the food of the Gentiles. “And he separated himself,” that is, he formed a flock apart with the Jews, fearing not foods but “those who were of the circumcision,” that is, from Judaea, because they were weak; or, even if they were strong, lest they should be scandalized according to their custom.

Therefore, lest they should be scandalized but might gradually be nourished in faith, he became as a Jew to the Jews, pretending with the weak to think the same thing. “And the rest of the Jews” who were at Antioch consented to his dissimulation, as though he distinguished foods, “so that even Barnabas,” who was with me as teacher of the Gentiles, was led by them, withdrawing from the Gentiles, into that dissimulation [Col. 0109B] of Jewish eating; so that, although he rightly believed that the Law had been abolished for both peoples, nevertheless with the same intention as Peter he withdrew from the Gentiles and pretended to think the same thing as the weak. But this dissimulation was unprofitable to the Gentiles, and therefore Paul rebuked Peter. [Col. 0109C] Hence he adds:

**VERSE 14.**—“But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: If thou, being a Jew, livest as the Gentiles do and not as the Jews do, how dost thou compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

“But when I alone saw that they were not walking rightly,” not as regards their intention, but “according to the truth of the Gospel,” because by this means the truth was lost, in that the Gentiles were made to Judaize, “I said to Cephas before them all,” because it was said for the healing of all, so that all might be healed by his rebuke. It was not useful to correct privately an error that harmed people openly.

[Augustine] To this is added Peter’s steadfastness and love, to whom the Lord said three times, “Feed my sheep” [Col. 0109D] (John 21): he most willingly bore such a rebuke from a later shepherd for the salvation of the flock. This served as a great example of humility, so that in the one who is first the rest might learn to be meek and humble. Peter himself received what Paul did, beneficially through the freedom of love, in the holy and gracious spirit of humble devotion; and so he gave later generations an example all the more holy because it was harder to imitate, so that superiors should not disdain, if perhaps they had departed from the path of rectitude, to be corrected even by inferiors. Thus the praise of righteous freedom shone forth in Paul, and that of holy humility in Peter.

“I said,” then, “if thou, O Peter, though thou art a Jew by nation and descent, livest as a Gentile and [Col. 0110A] not as a Jew,” that is, according to the custom of Gentiles rather than Jews, because he knew that the distinction among foods contributed nothing—behold, one formerly committed to Jewish custom abandoned it—what then ought those who were not so committed, such as the Galatians, to do? Certainly they ought not to adopt it.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] Augustine, To Jerome.]

“If,” I say, “this is so, how dost thou compel the Gentiles,” who think everything they see in thee necessary to salvation, “to Judaize?” He compelled them not by an authoritative command in teaching but by the example of his conduct, and for this he was rebuked. Hence the Galatians should learn, on Peter’s authority, that they ought not to Judaize, since he was rebuked in this matter.

Jerome and Augustine seem to disagree concerning this rebuke, as also concerning observance of legal observances after Christ. For Jerome says that Peter observed those legal observances not because he wished them to be kept after Christ even by Jews—as indeed they ought not to have been—but [Col. 0110B] unwillingly, and by a prudent accommodation, so as not to lose the Jews. He did not sin in this, because he acted with a good intention, even though those who Judaized as though following his example sinned. Nor was the rebuke genuine, because nothing blameworthy was in him; it was an accommodated rebuke, so that by it the Gentiles might know that they ought not to Judaize, seeing so great an Apostle rebuked for this.

Augustine, however, says that Peter observed those legal observances not by accommodation but genuinely, as subject to them, though not placing hope in them. They were to be observed by all Jews; and Peter truly sinned, not by observing them, but by compelling others through his example to Judaize, [Col. 0110C] so that the rebuke was genuine, not accommodated.

For Jerome says:

[Note: [Col. 0110D] Jerome, To Augustine.]

“From this passage the impious Porphyry throws at us Peter’s rebuke by Paul, wishing to fasten upon the former the stain of error and upon the latter that of insolence, and to accuse them both in common of the lie of a fabricated doctrine, because the leaders of the churches disagreed with one another. He certainly does this because he does not understand in what sense Peter is said to have been blameworthy, or the apostle Paul to have withstood him to his face. For both rightly hold that the Law is not to be observed, and that in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to Him; but each, through cautious dissimulation, adopts an accommodation—Peter in withdrawing, Paul in rebuking—in order that Jewish pride and Gentile despair might both be removed. Therefore Peter was not truly blameworthy either to Paul or to those with whom he ate before and from whom he afterward separated himself; nor did Paul insolently withstand him. For Paul could not rebuke in Peter what he himself did, nor accuse a dissimulation of which he himself was guilty. But this rebuke was not genuine, but accommodated; Peter did not sin, nor did Paul rebuke insolently.

“Peter, moreover, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, was the author of the decree that the Law is not to be observed after the Gospel. After the vision of the sheet containing animals of various kinds, he entered Cornelius’s house and ate with Gentiles; he also settled the question on this subject. For when Paul and Barnabas had already converted many Gentiles and had come [Col. 0111A] to Antioch, some who came down from Judaea said: ‘No one can be saved without the Law of Moses.’ Then both parties—Paul and Barnabas and those Jews who said this—went up to Jerusalem to the apostles. Peter said: ‘God gave them the Spirit just as He gave it to us, and made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith. Why then do you now test God by imposing a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through grace, just as they are’ (Acts 15).

“Peter therefore held rightly concerning the abolition of the Law, but he dissembled from fear of the Jews, lest they should abandon the faith because of the Gentiles and he should thus lose his flock. Paul likewise dissembled from a similar fear, as in Timothy’s circumcision; and he who let his hair grow by a vow like the Nazirites cut his head at Cenchreae according to the Law. Later, at Jerusalem, on the advice of James and the presbyters, he was purified according to the Law, entered the Temple, and offered a sacrifice. [Col. 0111B] Behold how he became a Jew to the Jews. Therefore not by an expedient lie but by an honorable accommodation, I—or rather, others before me—have explained both Peter’s separation from the Gentiles and Paul’s resistance to him, so that the prudence of the apostles might be shown and the foolishness of the blasphemer Porphyry restrained.”

[Note: [Col. 0111D] Augustine, To Jerome.]

Augustine, however, says that believers from among the Gentiles were freed from the burden of the Law; but that believers from among the Jews remained subject to the Law and did not sin if they were circumcised and offered sacrifices, provided that they did not place their hope of salvation in these things. Nor did Peter sin if he lived as a Jew; but because by his example he compelled the Gentiles [Col. 0111C] to live as Jews, Paul rebuked him on that point alone, as the teacher of the Gentiles—so that the rebuke may be genuine and not merely dispensational. Otherwise Paul lied. For if Peter did what he ought to have done, Paul lied when he saw him not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. Whoever does what he ought to do certainly acts rightly; and therefore one says something false about him who says that he did not act rightly when he knows that he ought to have acted so. But if Paul wrote truly, then it is true that Peter was not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. For my part, I believe that Peter acted in such a way as to compel the Gentiles to live as Jews. This I read Paul to have written; and I do not believe that he lied. Therefore Peter was not acting rightly here, because it was contrary to the truth of the Gospel for believers in Christ to suppose [Col. 0111D] that they could not be saved without those legal observances. For this was what those believers from the circumcision were maintaining at Antioch.

But I do not believe that Paul acted in this way when he circumcised Timothy, paid his vow at Cenchreae, or, when warned by James at Jerusalem, undertook those legal observances—namely, so as to appear to think that salvation could be given through those observances. Rather, he did so lest he seem to condemn as Gentile idolatry those things which God had commanded to be performed as shadows of things to come. For this is what James says: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are in Judaea who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealots for the Law. For they have heard concerning you that you teach the Jews who are among the Gentiles apostasy from Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom of the Law. What then is to be done? Certainly the multitude must assemble; for they have heard that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon them; take these with you, purify yourself with them, and all will know that the things they have heard about you are false” (Acts 21).

[Augustine] It is not obscure, I think, that James gave this counsel in order that those who had heard these things about Paul might know them to be false—those who, although they had believed from among the Jews, were nevertheless zealots for the Law, wishing it to be observed in such a way as though salvation could not exist in the Gospel for believers without it. They had perceived Paul to be a most vigorous preacher of grace and especially opposed to their purpose. [Col. 0112B] For by the opponents of the new Law—who did not understand with what intention these observances ought then to be kept by Jewish believers, namely, in order to commend the divine authority and the prophetic holiness of those sacraments, not in order to obtain salvation—it was said that Paul, the outstanding preacher of grace, condemned the Law of Moses as sacrilegious and as not written at God’s command. Therefore, wishing to remove the odium of this false accusation, he himself lived as a Jew, showing that the Law was not sacrilegious for Jews, as idolatry is for Gentiles, but was nevertheless not necessary for salvation.

Moreover, the apostles had decreed at Jerusalem that no one should then forbid Jews to live as Jews, although Christian doctrine did not compel even them to do so. [Note: [Col. 0112D] Augustine, *To Jerome*.] Therefore, if after this apostolic decree Peter engaged at Antioch in that dissimulation by which he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews, it is not surprising that Paul pressed him to assert freely what he remembered having decreed at Jerusalem with the other apostles. But if Peter did this before that Jerusalem council, it is still not surprising that Paul wished him not timidly to conceal, but confidently to assert, what he already knew Peter held with him—whether because he had conferred the Gospel with him, because he had received divine instruction on the matter in Cornelius’s calling, or because, before those whom he feared had come to Antioch, Paul had seen him eating with the Gentiles. For we do not deny that Peter held the same view as Paul. [Col. 0112D] Paul was therefore not then teaching him what was true in the matter, but rebuking his dissimulation, by which he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews. For all these things were managed dissemblingly, as though what certain persons said were true: namely, that believers could not be saved without the Law. Peter had fallen into this not by agreeing with that opinion but by dissimulation through fear. Thus Paul truly wrote that he had seen Peter not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, and most truly told him that he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews—something Paul certainly did not do. For Paul truthfully observed those former rites where need required, in order to show that they were not to be condemned; yet he constantly preached that believers are saved not by them but [Col. 0113A] by the grace of faith, lest anyone embrace them as necessary after the Passion and Resurrection. For once faith in the Lord had been revealed, they had lost, as it were, the life of their proper function.

Nevertheless, just as dead bodies must in some manner be carried to burial—not deceitfully but reverently—so these observances were not immediately to be abandoned or thrown aside before the reproaches of enemies like corpses before the bites of dogs. But in the course of time those observances were to be abandoned by all Christians. Whoever among Christians, even if he be of Jewish origin, now wishes to celebrate them is not, as one who digs up sleeping ashes, a pious conductor or bearer of a body, but an impious violator of its burial.

Again, I question and demand of the Apostle Paul himself whether, in what he wrote—namely, that he saw Peter not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel and therefore opposed him because by that dissimulation he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews—he wrote the truth, or whether he lied by some dispensational falsehood. Far be it from us to believe that he acted mendaciously. [Note: [Col. 0113D] Augustine, *Against the Jew*.] For it must altogether be maintained that in the teaching of religion one must by no means lie, and that falsehood must be believed altogether absent from the writers of the Holy Scriptures, lest stewards of Christ suppose that they may lawfully lie for the administration of truth. Therefore the faithful steward Paul undoubtedly shows us faithfulness in writing, because he was a steward of truth, not falsehood. Thus he wrote truly when he said that he had seen Peter not walking rightly [Col. 0113C] according to the truth of the Gospel, and that he had opposed him to his face because he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews. Peter’s and Barnabas’s dissimulation, therefore, was rightly rebuked and corrected, lest it do harm then and become an example for posterity.

Jerome replies to him thus: “You write in your letter that Paul, when he was already Christ’s Apostle, undertook the observances commanded in the Law in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to keep them as they had received them from their parents through the Law, provided that they did not place their hope of salvation in them. And the sum of your position is this: believers from among the Gentiles are free from the burden of the Law, but believers from among the Jews do well if they sacrifice and are circumcised. But if, after the Gospel, one who lives as a Jew does well in sacrifices and the rest, we fall into the heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion, who were anathematized for this very reason: that they mingled the worship of the Law with the Gospel. Since they wish to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither. And if we admit such persons so that they do in the Church of God what they did in the synagogue of Satan, they will not become Christians, but they will make us Jews. You say that the ceremonies of the Law are not deadly to those who are of Jewish origin; I, on the contrary, declare that Jewish ceremonies are certainly deadly to all believers. For Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10). “Again: ‘The Law and the Prophets were until John’” (Luke 16). “Again Jeremiah: ‘I shall complete a new covenant over the house, or for the house, [Col. 0114A] of Israel’” (Jer. 31). “He does not say, for the people of the Gentiles, but for the Jews, that they may not live in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit. Nor are those ceremonies things indifferent between good and evil: if they ought to be observed, they bring salvation; but if they do not bring salvation, they ought not to be observed. You say that observing them is good; I maintain that it is evil—not only for those who have believed from the Gentile people, but also for those who have believed from the Jewish people.”

### Verses 15–18

> “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from among the Gentiles. Yet knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law, except through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the Law. For by works of the Law no flesh shall be justified. But if, while seeking to be justified [Col. 0114B] in Christ, we ourselves too were found sinners, is Christ then a minister of sin? Far be it! For if I rebuild those things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor.”

“We by nature,” etc. Having commended his authority, he now begins to argue by reasons that carnal observances are not to be kept after Christ. He shows that righteousness comes not from the Law but from the grace of faith: first, by the example of himself, the apostles, and Abraham, who were justified by faith; then by the testimony of Scripture; and finally by human custom. Here, then, he begins fully to deal with the rejection of the Law.

As if he said: The Gentiles ought not to live as Jews. And this is true, because we who were strong in the Law know that it does not justify; and therefore, abandoning it, we flee to Christ. He says it thus: “We,” namely I and the other apostles, “are Jews by nature,” that is, not proselytes but Jews by birth, “and are not sinners from among the Gentiles.” As if he said: We are indeed sinners, but not as the Gentiles, who are idolaters and unclean. [Note: [Col. 0113D] Augustine, *On Psalm 105*.] Observe that, just as there is a difference between those who mock and mockers, between those who write and writers, and the like, so Scripture customarily calls “sinners” those who are exceedingly wicked and burdened with grave loads of sins. Jews, in their old pride, gave that name to the Gentiles, as though they themselves were righteous, though they too were sinners.

[Augustine] This term is not customarily used in Scripture of those who, though living justly and laudably, are not without sin. “Yet knowing.” As if he said: We are Jews by nature and not sinners from among the Gentiles, yet we know that a human being—that is, however much a Jew may be under the Law—is not justified by works of the Law, that is, by legal works concerning sacrifices and other figurative observances. In no way is one justified except through faith in Christ Jesus, that is, the faith by which one believes in Christ. And because this is so, we Jews too, like the Gentiles, believe in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0114D] Augustine, *To Bishop Paulinus*.] He does not say “by faith” in order to render good works futile, since God repays each according to his works, but because works come from grace, not grace from works. For faith working through love [Col. 0115A] would do nothing unless the love of God were poured out in us through the Holy Spirit; nor would faith itself be in us unless God gave it. [Note: [Col. 0115D] Augustine, *To Prosper and Hilary*.] Therefore he says that we are justified by faith because it is the first thing, from which the rest are obtained. “That we may be justified by faith,” I say, and in no way by works of the Law, whether they are done before faith or together with faith.

“For this reason”—namely, because a Jew is not righteous by the Law—it is evident that by works of the Law “no flesh,” that is, no Gentile, is justified. For if a Jew is not justified by them, much less is flesh—that is, a sinner from among the Gentiles. “But if,” as if he said: We believe in Christ that we may be justified by faith. “But if”—that is, if we ourselves are found sinners because we seek to be justified in [Col. 0115B] Christ—if you say, and if it is true, that we sinned by abandoning the Law and seeking righteousness in Christ, then he who commands this, namely Christ, is a minister of sin. Is Christ a minister of sin? As if he said: It would be astonishing for anyone to say this. But far be it that Christ sinned in destroying the Law and commanding that it be abandoned!

“For if,” as if he said: Christ certainly did not sin in commanding this, because neither did I sin in abandoning and destroying it. For if I rebuild the things which I destroyed—namely, the pride that boasts in works of the Law—I make myself a transgressor. It may perhaps seem possible to object from these words that, if he now builds up the faith of Christ which he formerly attacked, he makes himself a transgressor. But he did not destroy that faith, for it cannot be destroyed. This pride, however, he had truly destroyed and was destroying; and therefore, if he rebuilt it, he would become a transgressor.

[Augustine] For that person is a transgressor who, after destroying a false thing which can be destroyed, builds it again. But he is not a transgressor who, when he had attempted to destroy a true thing and afterwards recognized it to be true and incapable of destruction, held to it so as to be built up in it.

Or thus: “But if [we are found sinners].” As if he said: I said that righteousness does not come from works of the Law, and this is true. For even we ourselves, who were found greater under the Law—not reputed such by opinion, but proved so by reason—were sinners in it, namely while we served subject to it. This appears from the fact that we are “seeking,” [Col. 0115D] that is, we seek, to be justified in Christ. For why should we seek to be justified in Christ unless we were not righteous in the Law? And if this is so—if we who were perfect in it were sinners by it—then wherever the Law is kept after Christ’s Passion it ministers sin. And if the Law ministers sin, then if Christ now ministers the Law, he ministers sin as well. But is Christ a minister of sin? Far be it! For he is not a minister of sin, and therefore neither is he a minister of the Law—though that might perhaps seem so because he fulfilled it. But far be it that he should be its minister, that is, that he should have administered it by teaching that it must be kept after his Passion. And if Christ is not a minister of the Law, why should you Galatians [Col. 0116A] keep it?

Or thus: “But if.” As if he said: Righteousness certainly does not come from works of the Law, because we ourselves, seeking righteousness in Christ, [Berengar] truly recognized that we could not be justified except by passing over to Christ; we, I say, were found sinners in the Law. And if this is so, as it certainly is, is Christ a minister of sin? That is, does Christ permit and allow us to fall back into what we were? If he permitted, that is, allowed it, he would certainly be for us a minister of sin—that is, of our former condition—as he had been a minister of righteousness to those passing over to him. But far be it! “For if,” as if he said: Christ is certainly not a minister of sin or of the Law; for I, his follower, destroyed the Law by rational teaching and living. And if I rebuild again the things which I destroyed, [Col. 0116B] that is, the Law, I make myself a transgressor—that is, I act contrary to the Law spiritually understood.

### Verses 19–21

> “For I through the Law died to the Law, that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ. Yet I now live—not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. I do not reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died gratuitously.”

“For I through the Law,” spiritually understood, “died to the Law,” lest I live carnally in it. [Augustine] Or, “through the Law,” that is, through the authority of the Law, I abandoned it, being as though dead to it and retaining none of its carnal sense. For it is written in it: “The Lord will raise up a prophet for you from among your brethren; him you shall hear as me” (Deut. 18). And again: “I shall complete a new covenant for the house of Israel” (Jer. 31). And: “Burnt-offerings and sin-offerings you did not require; then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 39); and other such passages.

“I died to the Law,” I say, “that I might live,” not to myself but to God, that is, for the honour of God. This I can do because “I have been crucified with Christ”: that is, Christ’s cross has extinguished in me the ardour of sin, so that through fear of God I no longer stretch out toward it, as though my flesh were fastened with nails. Hence: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). “Yet I live,” as if he said: I have been crucified with Christ, but on that account I live by virtues—that is, I have the strength to act well. I live, [Col. 0116D] I say, “yet not I,” according to the flesh, because I am no longer the sinner that I formerly was. “But Christ lives in me,” that is, Christ’s newness appears in me. And the sense is: [Note: [Col. 0116D] Augustine, *On the Sermon in the Epistle of John*.] The righteousness in me is not my own but Christ’s. Why then is the Law necessary?

“And the life which I now live”: he explains what he had said, what it is, how it is so, and through what means. As if he said: I say that I live. But the life which I now live—that is, my ability to act well in the flesh, which is corruptible and contains an incentive to vices, so that I am not consumed though in fire—I live in faith, that is, it is through faith, not through the laborious works of the Law. I mean faith in the Son of God, whose faith has power because he is the Son of God. And to show that it is not by his own merit but [Col. 0117A] by Christ’s grace that, living in the flesh, he lives in faith, he adds: “who loved me.” Through this love faith has efficacy, and out of love he gave for me, not another sacrifice, but himself alone—he who is so great.

Observe that the Son gave himself, as is said here; and the Father gave him through the Son, as the Apostle says elsewhere: “He who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all” (Rom. 8). If the Father gave up the Son and the Son gave himself, what did Judas do? There was a handing-over by the Father, a handing-over by the Son, and a handing-over by Judas: one event occurred. What then distinguished the Father handing over the Son, the Son handing himself over, and Judas handing over his Master? The Father and the Son did this in love; Judas did it in betrayal. You see that one must consider not what a person does, but with what intention and will he does it. In the same act we find God in whom we find Judas: we bless God, we detest Judas; we bless love, we detest wickedness. God devised our salvation, by which we were redeemed; Judas devised the price for which he sold the Lord; the Son devised the price that he gave for us. Different intention, therefore, makes different deeds, though the thing itself—the restoration—was one, from different sources. If we assess it, we find one person to be crowned, another condemned; one glorified, another detested.

“I do not reject,” as if he said: Because Christ gave himself out of love and justified me, therefore I do not reject God’s grace—that is, I do not receive the Law, which would be to reject grace. [Augustine] Or, according to another reading: “I am not ungrateful for the grace of God,” so as to set another thing alongside it—that is, the Law—and say that righteousness is through the Law. Nor ought I to do so. For if righteousness is through the Law—that is, through the works of the Law in which the Jews trusted—then Christ died gratuitously, that is, vainly and without cause.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–2

> “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth? Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly condemned, and crucified in you. This alone I wish to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law, or by hearing with faith?”

“O foolish Galatians.” [Ambrose] He rebukes them: these are the words of one who is angry and reproves, who by reproving admonishes them to listen more attentively to the arguments that follow. As if he said: Righteousness comes not from the Law but from faith, and Christ gave himself for us out of love. Since all this is established and you were instructed in it, O—he says it in grief—you Galatians are foolish, because you do not even recognize that you have been deceived. And though you were first rightly instructed, who has bewitched you, that you should not obey the truth? For truth presents itself to you, yet you do not believe it. And who has so bewitched you?

He says this by comparison, as if he said: You fail to see what is before your eyes, just as in magical deceptions certain things are shown to human eyes otherwise than they are; these are called “bewitchings.” [Jerome] The common people also call *fascinus* or bewitchment that which harms infants. For certain persons’ eyes are said to burn by their gaze, and this action of theirs is called bewitchment; demons may be enslaved to this sin. Likewise envy burns like a bewitchment. For the envious person harms not only himself, wasting away at another’s prosperity, but also those in whom some good things begin to appear. Hence in the book entitled the Wisdom of Solomon: “The bewitching of wickedness obscures good things” (Wis. 4). Thus it happened that the envious, like bewitchers, harmed the Galatians, newly reborn in Christ, so that the same Galatians, nauseated in the stomach of faith, vomited up the food of the Holy Spirit.

What resulted from this bewitchment he shows by adding: “Before whose eyes,” etc. [Ambrose] As if he said: You have indeed been bewitched, before whose eyes—that is, in whose estimation—Christ was so publicly condemned, [Col. 0118B] that is, sentenced. “And crucified in you,” that is, in your false understandings, Christ was crucified as a mere man, without your salvation. In the eyes and minds of the wise, Christ is seen to have condemned death, the devil, and hell, according to Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death,” etc. (Hos. 13). This is the rod of Moses which, turned into a serpent, devoured the serpents of the magicians. He is the high priest in the Law, at whose death those who had unknowingly shed a neighbour’s blood and therefore, in fear, had gone to a city of refuge were released and made safe from fear. Thus, through Christ’s death, by which the proud one was condemned, our salvation was procured.

This was signified by the ineffable name of the Lord written on the golden plate of the high priest, which was the Tetragrammaton—that is, of four letters: *ioht, he, vau, eth*—meaning, “This one is the beginning of the passion of life”; as though it said: He whose person this legal priest bears is for us, through his Passion, the author and restorer of the life lost through Adam. Hence: “He who ascends above the setting is the Lord; this is his name” (Ps. 67). Christ ascended above the setting of death—that is, he triumphed, condemning the devil and death. But to the eyes of fools he appears merely condemned and, in their judgment, crucified as a man in whom there is no hope of salvation. Therefore Christ lives in the former, but in the latter he is dead.

Or thus: “Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly condemned,” that is, his condemnation was as well known to you as though it had taken place before you; “and crucified in you,” that is, in your understandings was the crucifixion, [Col. 0118D] so that you knew how it took place and what it accomplished.

[Augustine] Or thus: You have indeed been bewitched, before whose eyes—that is, in your presence, while you were looking—that great one, Jesus Christ, was crucified and publicly condemned for you. “And this in you”: you ought not to suffer him to lose his kingdom and inheritance in others, much less in yourselves. Yet he was publicly condemned among you also—that is, he lost his inheritance in you, namely yourselves.

[Berengar] The word “crucified” must be pronounced with the weight of grief; it is added in order especially to move them, when they considered at what price he had purchased the possession which he was losing in them.

Or thus: You have indeed been bewitched, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly condemned: that is, while you abandon Christ Jesus through the Law, Christ is condemned by you as he was by Pilate. In other words, you sin as Pilate sinned in condemning Jesus; and while you consider him insufficient, he is crucified in you—that is, you differ from his crucifiers in no degree in the magnitude of your sin.

“This alone I wish.” After stirring the Galatians by rebuke, he proves to those thus moved that the Law is not to be observed, because all necessary things—namely, the Spirit, [Col. 0119A] righteousness, and blessing—come not from it but from faith. As if he said: Although you are bewitched and foolish, I nevertheless wish to learn this from you, because it is so evident that even fools can teach it. And this alone I wish to know from you, because, even if there were nothing else, this alone would suffice to prove what I intend. What is it? It is evident that you received the indwelling Holy Spirit. Since it is evident that you received the Spirit, did you receive him through works of the Law, where there is labour—works which you never possessed—or through hearing with faith, that is, through faith which comes readily by hearing?

[Augustine] Surely through faith, not through works of the Law. For faith was preached to them by the Apostle, and in that preaching they perceived the advent and presence of the Holy Spirit. For at that time, in the newness of the calling to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit appeared even through perceptible miracles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles. This had happened among the Galatians before those persons came to pervert them. The sense, then, is this: If your salvation were in those works [Col. 0119C] of the Law, the Holy Spirit would not have been given to you unless you had been circumcised. But he was given to you before you possessed the works of the Law.

It should be known that he now treats especially of works that belong to sacraments, which are not necessary where the grace of faith already exists. For the works of the Law are twofold: some are understood as sacraments, others as morals. Circumcision, the Sabbath, new moons, sacrifices, and innumerable observances of this kind belong to sacraments. But “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20), and similar commands belong to morals. If these observances are kept without understanding, they are mere slavery, such as was present among the Jewish people and remains even now. But if they are observed and understood, they not only do no harm but are even useful, if they suit the time—as they were suitably observed by Moses and the prophets for that people, to whom such servitude was still useful, so that they might be guarded under fear. For nothing so terrifies the mind as an uncomprehended sacrament; but one that is understood produces devout joy, and is freely celebrated if the time requires it. If the time does not require it, it is nevertheless read and treated with spiritual delight. Every sacrament, when understood, relates either to contemplation of truth or to good morals. Contemplation of truth is founded upon love and knowledge of God alone; good morals upon love of God and neighbour. On these two hang the whole Law and the Prophets.

### Verses 3–10

> “Are you so foolish that, having begun in the Spirit, you are now being completed in the flesh? Have you suffered so much in vain—if indeed it was in vain? Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so by works of the Law or by hearing with faith? As it is written: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. Know then that those who are of faith are the sons of Abraham. And Scripture, foreseeing that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, proclaimed beforehand to Abraham: ‘In you all nations shall be blessed.’ Therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham. For all who are of works of the Law are under a curse.”

“So foolish.” Again he rebukes them. As if he said: Since the Spirit comes through faith, you are foolish, and so—that is, to such an extent—that, having begun to be instructed by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0120B] having received your beginning from the Holy Spirit, you now, when you are more advanced, seek to be completed in the flesh—that is, by carnal observances. Yet even the beginning of righteousness could not be obtained through them. Thus you confuse the order.

[Augustine] The order is to rise from carnal things to spiritual things, not to fall from spiritual things into carnal things, as has happened to you, because what is not good is not the Gospel when it is proclaimed thus.

“So much,” etc. As if he said: You seek completion in carnal observances, but you are not completed; rather, you lose what you have received. And therefore you have suffered so much in vain, that is, without benefit. Or he says this because they had already endured much for the faith, and in their sufferings had overcome fear through love. Therefore they had suffered so much in vain if they wished to fall away from the love which had enabled them to endure so much and return to the Law.

[Ambrose] “If indeed.” As if he said: I say that you suffered in vain, but I do not state this absolutely, because it is within you—that is, in your power—that, if you wish, it will not be in vain, but rather will benefit you. For something done “in vain” means something superfluous which neither benefits nor harms. But this can benefit you if you come to your senses. He says this lest they despair.

“He therefore who supplies,” etc. He returns to the demonstration which he had begun, showing that just as they did not receive the Holy Spirit through works of the Law, which they had never possessed, but through faith, so he too has power not through those works but through faith to give the Spirit and perform miracles. As if he said: Because you received the Spirit not through works of the Law, which you never possessed, but through faith, does he who supplies the Holy Spirit to you—by ministry, not by authority—and works powers, that is, miracles, among you, namely I, do this through works of the Law or through hearing with faith? Certainly not through works of the Law, but through faith. And if they do not benefit me, who was strong in them, why do you seek them?

That they do not benefit me is made clear by your example. For through yourselves you can see that I, who had the works of the Law, nevertheless received the power to supply the Spirit ministerially, not authoritatively, and to work miracles not through them but through faith. One might doubt concerning him who had been under the Law, but the likeness of these people makes the matter clear. Then he brings forward the example of father Abraham, to whom faith was reckoned as righteousness before circumcision, adding:

“As it is written,” etc. Here he shows that righteousness is from faith. As if he said: Just as the Spirit is from faith, so also is righteousness. For it is written in Genesis: “Abraham believed God,” and that act of believing “was reckoned to him as righteousness,” that is, it was a sufficient cause of Abraham’s righteousness, and of that of others. Here he calls righteousness forgiveness of sins and the observance of a good life.

“Know.” As if he said: Because Abraham is righteous by faith, know therefore that those who are of faith—that is, whose being is from faith, who believe on the basis of faith that they are justified and saved—are sons of Abraham by imitation, that is, righteous.

“And Scripture, foreseeing.” [Augustine] Above he showed that the Spirit and righteousness are from faith; here he shows [Col. 0121B] that blessing comes from the same faith. As if he said: Not only righteousness but blessing also is from faith, because Scripture, introducing God speaking to Abraham, says: “O Abraham, all nations—not Jews only—shall be blessed with eternal blessedness in you” (Gen. 28), that is, in conformity with your faith; because Jews and Gentiles shall be blessed through imitation of that faith by which Abraham was justified even before circumcision. Or “in you,” that is, in your seed, namely Christ.

And lest you turn those words to another meaning, he says that Moses understood them thus, adding, “Foreseeing,” etc. As if he said: Scripture says “foreseeing,” that is, showing that this was foreseen long before it occurred: namely, that God justifies the Gentiles by faith, not by works [Col. 0121C] of the Law. And therefore it proclaimed beforehand to Abraham—that is, showed that it had been proclaimed beforehand to Abraham—that blessing is from faith, saying: “Because in you,” that is, in imitation of your faith, “all nations shall be blessed with eternal blessedness.”

And because the authority of Scripture says this, therefore those who are of faith shall be blessed with faithful Abraham—that is, just as Abraham was blessed through faith. “For all who,” etc. As if he said: I rightly say that those who are of faith shall be blessed. For those who are of works are not blessed but are evil. He says it thus: “For all who are of works of the Law,” like those who think themselves justified through them, “are under the curse” of transgression and cannot escape it. Therefore the saying made to Abraham—“In you all nations shall be blessed”—must be understood only as explained above. [Col. 0121D] It must not be understood, as the Jews wish, as meaning: “In you all nations shall be blessed,” that is, in likeness to your works. For blessing does not come from works of the Law, but curse. This must be understood not of works pertaining to morals, but of works done in those observances. For the Law written upon tablets is useful, containing three commandments concerning love of God and seven concerning love of neighbour; the rest are human ordinances. He proves this by the authority of the Law, adding:

### Verses 10–14

> “For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.’ But that no one is justified before God by the Law [Col. 0122A] is evident, because ‘the righteous shall live by faith.’ But the Law is not of faith; rather, ‘the one who does these things shall live by them.’ Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, becoming a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’ so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

For it is written; as though he were saying: Those who are of the works of the Law are accursed. And this is indeed so, because it is written thus in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is everyone who has not remained,” not merely known, “in all,” not only in some, “the commandments which are written in the book of the Law.” He must remain, I say, so as to do them—that is, not merely to will them, but to fulfil them in deed—which no one is able to do. [Col. 0122B] Hence Peter says: “Why do you test us by imposing a yoke which neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?” (Acts XV.)

And the sense is: as though he were saying, God through Moses did indeed command many things which no one would be able to fulfil; but they were given to humankind as a burden, to subdue the pride of the person who said, “There is no lack of one who may fulfil it; there is only lack of one who may command it.” Therefore all who were under the Law were accursed, because all were guilty of transgression; from this guilt those were absolved who trusted in grace, at least fulfilling the Law spiritually. In this is indicated that a Saviour was to be desired who would put an end to these things and free people not only from other sins, but also from the curse of the Law. Why, then, do the Galatians pass from grace [Col. 0122C] to a curse? As though he were saying: They act foolishly.

“But that”; as though he were saying: From the Law comes a curse; but that righteousness does not come from it is shown by the authority of Habakkuk. This is what he says: “But since no one is justified in the Law”—that is, through works of the Law—“before God,” although they may be justified before deceived human beings, “it is plain” from Habakkuk’s words.

[Augustine] That person is justified before God who worships him gratuitously: namely, not from the desire to obtain something from him besides himself, nor from fear of losing it. For in him alone is our true blessedness. It is plain, I say, from what Habakkuk says: “The righteous person lives by faith.” Someone is righteous by faith, and through this lives the eternal life.

“But the Law”; as though he were saying: Righteousness and life are from faith, but the Law is not from faith, so that its requirements may be fulfilled for the sake of future benefits, but from fear. [Col. 0122D] For it could seem that works of the Law were done from faith, in the hope of receiving through them eternal things, which are the objects of faith. Yet they certainly did not do this, but observed those things from fear of punishment. Hence he adds: “But the one who has done them shall live in them.”

He does not say, “The one who has done it shall live in it,” though he had said, “the Law is not from faith,” so that you may understand that “Law” in this place stands for the very works performed in those observances. Those who lived in these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or something similar. Therefore he says, “The one who has done them shall live in them”: not before God—that is, he shall receive a reward—but so that he may not be punished by that death; otherwise he would be punished.

But the one who lives by faith, when he departs from here, will then possess an immediate reward all the more. Therefore no one lives by faith who either desires or fears the visible things of the present, [Col. 0123A] because faith in God concerns invisible things.

[Ambrose] Or: “The Law is not from faith,” that is, it commands nothing to be believed, but things to be done. The rest is unchanged.

“But Christ”; as though he were saying: From the Law comes a curse, not righteousness; but Christ redeemed us Jews from the curse of the Law, under which we were. Why then, Galatians, are you striving toward the same thing? “Having become,” etc.; as though he were saying: He redeemed us from the curse of the Law. He himself, I say, became—that is, was reckoned—not merely accursed for us, but even a curse. By this expression, in ordinary usage, more is understood than if he were called merely “accursed”: that is, he is understood to be a very great sinner, since he is put to death as a criminal and since, in contempt for him, it is said to the man born blind who had been given sight: “You be that man’s disciple; we are disciples of Moses” (John IX).

“Because it is written”; as though he were saying: He was therefore reckoned a curse because he was suspended on the cross, since it is written in Deuteronomy: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree”—namely, because of his own crimes. [Hieron.] For he is not accursed because he was crucified, but because he has incurred such guilt as to deserve crucifixion—which Christ had not done. Therefore, although he was reckoned such, he was not accursed with the curse of guilt, though he was accursed with the curse of punishment. For there is a twofold curse: that of guilt and that of punishment. Thus *maledictum* (“a curse” or “an accursed thing”) is said in two ways, actively and passively—that is, with respect to guilt and with respect to punishment.

Having therefore shown how this passage may be understood concerning the curse of guilt and the curse of punishment, let us continue. [Col. 0123C] “He became,” etc.; as though he were saying: Christ redeemed us from the liability of transgression, and for this reason truly became for us a curse—that is, mortal. Mortality, however, comes from sin; and therefore it too is called a curse, and anything deriving from it is called accursed.

Lest you shrink back at his saying that Christ is a curse, he confirms it by the authority of the prophet Moses, adding: “Because,” etc. As though he were saying: He truly became a curse because it is written: “Cursed is”—that is, truly dead—“everyone who hangs on a tree.” And truly every person who hangs on a tree is sufficiently miserable. Moses said this literally of those guilty of capital crimes, so that hanging should be enough for one condemned to death, since this punishment was more contemptible and dishonourable than the others.

Therefore Deuteronomy says that one who has been hanged should be taken down in the evening, and states why: because “cursed is [Col. 0123D] everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. XXI).

[Ambrose] As though he were saying: It is enough—or let it be enough—as punishment for a guilty man that he dies hanging and remains there until evening, to be taken down and buried then, lest, if he remained there longer, the disgrace and stain upon his family should be greater. Thus, by this authority it is shown that Christ was not exempt from this curse of punishment, because it is written: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” “Accursed,” that is, dead.

The Apostle therefore confidently says, “He became a curse for us” [Note: [Col. 0123D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*], just as he did not hesitate to say of him, “He died for all.” For to be accursed in this respect is to be dead, because death itself comes from the curse; and every sin is a curse, whether the sin itself which is committed and is followed by punishment, or the punishment itself, which is also called sin because it comes from sin. Christ took upon himself our punishment without liability to guilt, so that through it he might discharge our liability and bring even our punishment to an end.

Hence elsewhere the Apostle says: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that through sin he might condemn sin in the flesh” (Rom. VIII). What he had called “the likeness of sinful flesh,” he also calls “sin” where he says, “through sin,” etc. For because death comes from sin, that flesh, although from the Virgin, was nevertheless mortal; in being mortal, it had the likeness of sinful flesh. Why then should Moses fear to call it a curse when Paul did not fear to call it sin? Certainly the prophet ought to say and proclaim this. Nor should it be regarded as an insult to God that the one hanging on the tree is called accursed. [Col. 0124B] For he hung on the tree in respect of his mortal part. Mortality, however, comes from the curse resulting from the first human being’s sin.

Therefore, if he said, “Death is accursed,” no one would recoil. Likewise, if he said, “Sin is accursed,” no one would be astonished. But what hung on the tree except mortal flesh, whose mortality came from the sin of the old human being?

[Augustine] As a figure of that sin and death, Moses also raised up the serpent in the wilderness upon a piece of wood. For in that figure the death of the Lord was hanging on the tree.

[Note: [Col. 0123D] The same, *Against Faustus*.] Nor is there any greater offence in his having added “to God,” so as to say: “Cursed to God is everyone who hangs [Col. 0124C] on a tree.”

[Jerome] For in Hebrew manuscripts and in our present copies of Deuteronomy it reads, “He is accursed to God.” Yet in ancient Hebrew codices the name of God is not found, and I think that after the Lord’s Passion someone inserted it in order to slander us as people who believe Christ accursed by God [Note: [Col. 0124D] The same, in the same work]. But this does not insult the Lord, who is said to be accursed to God because God hates our sin and death, when he sent his Son to destroy them. What wonder, then, if one who bears in himself what God hates—that is, what he condemns and destroys—is called accursed to God?

He adds, accordingly, “everyone,” Christ included, lest future heretics deny that his death was real. Moses foresaw that heretics would arise and deny the true death of the Lord. Thus they would wish [Col. 0124D] to separate Christ from this curse, so as also to separate him from the reality of death. Therefore Moses cries from afar against heretics yet far in the future: “You evade the issue without cause, O heretics, you to whom the truth of Christ’s death is displeasing. For ‘cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’: not this one or that one, but absolutely everyone, even the Son of God—always living in his righteousness, but dead because of our offences, in flesh assumed from our punishment.”

Thus he is always blessed in his righteousness, but accursed in the death assumed from our punishment.

[Augustine] For when he accepted death from a human being and for human beings, he did not disdain also to accept, from that human being and for that human being, the curse which accompanies death. And therefore “everyone” was added, lest Christ be said not to have undergone real death if he were entirely separated from the curse. A foolish reverence separates Christ from the curse joined to death, and so denies that he truly died, saying that he hung upon the tree in some appearance of false flesh and did not truly pay the penalty of death on the cross.

Against this, the prophet proclaims that he truly died when he says, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,” that is, truly dead. For the punishment of sin comes either from blessing or from curse. But if it comes from blessing, you ought to desire always to remain in the punishment of sin. If, however, you desire to be freed from it, believe that it came from a curse through the justice of the divine sentence which says: “If you touch it, you shall die by death.”

“In the Gentiles”; as though he were saying: [Col. 0125B] He thus redeemed us Jews from the curse of the Law so that even among the Gentiles, who were not under the curse of the Law, the promised blessing of Abraham might come to pass. And this should take place “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ, so that at last we both—Jews and Gentiles—might receive the promise of the Holy Spirit: namely, eternal blessedness, which the Holy Spirit, given as a pledge, promises. We receive it, I say, through faith, not through works of the Law.

### Verses 15–18

> “Brothers, I speak according to human custom: yet no one rejects or adds to a human testament once it has been confirmed. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though to many, but as though to one: ‘And to your seed,’ [Col. 0125C] which is Christ. This, then, I say: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not invalidate a testament confirmed by God so as to nullify the promise. For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from promise. But God granted it to Abraham through promise.”

“Brothers, I speak according to human custom.” Up to this point he has shown, by his own example, that of Abraham, and the authority of the Scriptures, that righteousness comes not from the Law but from faith. Now he demonstrates the same thing through human custom. As though he were saying: I have proved by arguments and authorities that the Spirit, righteousness, and blessedness are given through faith, not through the Law. Now, brothers, I say—that is, I prove—the same thing “according to human custom.” In that custom, though firmness is often absent, a human testament—that is, one made by a human being—is binding upon the person’s heirs, because no one rejects it by saying that it is invalid or improperly made, nor adds further provisions by disposing differently of those matters; rather, it carries authority for all, especially when it has been confirmed by witnesses and by the testator’s death.

Likewise, the testament—that is, the promise—of God is not invalidated by the Law. This the Apostle says subsequently. Had he inserted only this, the application of the comparison would have been easy to understand; but it is somewhat obscured because, before drawing that inference, he states to whom the testament—that is, the promise—was made by God: namely, Abraham. He does this so that the pledge may appear unchangeable from the dignity of both the giver and the recipient.

And this is what he says: “To Abraham.” As though he were saying: Just as a human testament [Col. 0126A] is firm, so also God’s promises are firm. And as though someone asked, “Were any promises made before the Law?” he answers: Certainly they were, because promises were spoken by God to Abraham, whom God would not deceive. He uses the plural, “promises,” because the same thing—eternal blessedness—was frequently promised.

“And to his seed,” Abraham’s seed, that is, Christ. Not that the promise was made to him, but that it concerned him, because the blessing was promised as to be given through him. That this seed is Christ and no other, he notes from the words of the Scripture in Genesis: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” Scripture does not say “in seeds,” as though it meant many—that is, as it would have said if it had intended many—but says “in your seed,” as though of one, that is, as Scripture speaks when it intends one. And that one is Christ. Hence he adds: “who is Christ.” For, says the Apostle, no other can be found who has blessed all nations.

“This, then.” As though he were saying: God promised this to Abraham. This testament, then, confirmed by God through oaths, I say and affirm, is not rendered invalid—that is, false—by the Law. It would be rendered invalid if the blessing were given through the Law. For that promise did not say that blessing would be through the Law, but through the seed. If blessing is through the Law, the seed was promised in vain, and the seed itself came in vain.

Therefore blessing is not through the Law, because it was given long after the promise made to Abraham. If [Col. 0126C] blessing came through it, those of that earlier time—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—would not have possessed it. And he adds: “which Law was made,” that is, given, “four hundred and thirty years” after the promise had been made. Therefore, if the Law justifies, Abraham, who lived long before the Law, was not justified. Since they cannot say this, they are compelled to admit that a human being is justified not through works of the Law but through faith. At the same time, he compels us to understand that all the ancients who were justified were justified by that same faith.

Therefore the Law does not invalidate—that is, it does not weaken—the promise, but indicates that it was still future, and when it would be future. “So as to nullify”; as though he were saying: The Law does not invalidate what was already effective so as to nullify the promise, since then the promise would be false and God a liar.

“For if”; as though he were saying: It would indeed be nullified.
