For if the inheritance—that is, eternal blessedness—is given from the Law, that is, from works of the Law, it is no longer from promise—that is, from what the promise stated. Thus the promise is excluded, and Abraham is disappointed. He then refutes the consequence by adding: “But to Abraham”; as though he were saying: If it is from the Law, it is not from promise; but it is from promise. He shows this in part, because God granted something to Abraham, concerning whom there is no doubt that he possessed it, and it is established that he existed without the Law. He granted it, I say, through a reiterated promise—that is, through faith in Christ, who was often promised.

### Verses 19–20

> “What, then, is the Law? It was imposed because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had made the promise; it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. [Col. 0127A] But a mediator is not of one; yet God is one.”

“What, then, is the Law?” Here a quite necessary question is raised.

[Augustine] For if faith justifies, and the earlier saints were justified before God through it, what need was there for the Law to be given? He introduced this by asking: “What, then?” [Note: [Col. 0127D] Augustine, *Retractions*.] When I formerly expounded this chapter, I thought the punctuation should be arranged so that “What, then?” was the question, followed by the answer, “The Law because of transgression,” etc. This is not inconsistent with the truth, but this punctuation seems better to me: the question is, “What then is the Law?” and the answer follows: “Because of transgression,” etc.

As though he were saying: Since the Law is not for righteousness or blessedness, what then is the Law? That is, why was the Law given by God? What is its usefulness?

[Ambrose] Then, lest it seem to have been given in vain, he explains why it was given, saying: The Law was placed in between, namely, between the promise and the seed to whom the promise was made—that is, between Abraham and Christ—because of restraining transgression: so that people might at least cease to transgress through fear, and at some time do the same things willingly. Therefore it was given in order to train God’s people under the fear of God, so that they might become worthy to receive the promise, which is Christ. [Note: [Col. 0127D] The same, *On the Progress of Human Righteousness*.]

Or it was placed because of transgression, so that a person proudly trusting in his own powers might receive commandments in which he would fail and become a transgressor, and thus seek a liberator and saviour. Therefore the Law was given so that the necks of the proud, whom it would make transgress, might be humbled; so that they who attributed so much to themselves and arrogated so much to their own will as to think free choice sufficient for righteousness might seek a physician, saying, “There is no lack of one who may fulfil it; there is only lack of one who may command it.” [Note: [Col. 0128D] The same, Sermon on the Words of the Apostle.]

Therefore the Law was given to subdue their pride and expose their weakness. It was also given as a scourge to the hard-hearted; it was also given as a sign of future things, so that it might attest the future by figures. Here you have four briefly distinguished reasons for the Law’s being given, which are explained more fully in the Epistle to the Romans, where it says: “The Law entered in besides,” etc. (Rom. V.)

It was placed, I say, to remain until the seed came—that is, Christ. Therefore the Law is no longer to be kept, for God had promised concerning that seed that through him [Col. 0127D] all nations would be blessed. Whoever restores the Law acts against him.

[Ambrose] I say, the Law was “ordained through angels,” that is, through Moses and the other ministers of God; or “through angels,” that is, given to human beings by angelic ministry.

[Augustine] In those angels there were assuredly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and at one time the Father, at another the Son, at another the Holy Spirit, and at other times God without any distinction of person, was represented through them. Note that he does not say “given,” but “ordained”: as though he were saying, given in an ordered manner—namely, between the period of the natural law, by which people were convicted that it could not help them, and the time of grace, before which grace they had to be convicted by the Law.

It was indeed by God’s great counsel [Col. 0128A] that, immediately after the fall of humankind, neither the Law was given nor the Son of God sent. For unless human pride first tested its own powers and claimed sufficiency for the freedom of its own choice, it would judge both that the Law was given superfluously and that the Son of God came in vain. Likewise, unless the written Law had been given, through which a person might prove what he could do, he would judge Christ’s coming superfluous.

Therefore, lest he should have grounds for accusation or complaint, God first left him in the freedom of choice under the natural law, so that he might thus know the powers of his own nature. When he failed there and saw that free choice was insufficient for righteousness, he still did not humble himself to ask for grace. Instead, proudly thinking that the written Law added to natural law was sufficient for him, he cried: “There is no lack of one who may fulfil it; there is only lack of one who may command it.”

Therefore, so that he might be convicted even by this, God gave the Law before sending the Son. The Law uncovered the disease of sin but did not consume it. When it was given, the disease grew strong and weakness increased—not through a defect of the Law, but through the defect of nature and the devil’s assault—so that, when the insufficiency of both laws and one’s own weakness had been recognized, a person might cry out to the physician and seek the help of grace. And so it came to pass. For as weaknesses multiplied, people later hastened to the physician, who came in the form of a servant and healed the wounds of sick humanity.

He is that Samaritan who approached the wounded man who had fallen among robbers and bound up his wounds; the priest and Levite—that is, the old Law and the priesthood—had passed him by without mercy, because the Law brought no one to perfection. [Col. 0128C] He is also that Elisha who sent his staff to raise the son of the Shunammite woman; and when he rose through it, Elisha himself finally came, drew himself together, and fitted himself to the dead boy, and the dead boy arose. He is also that angel at whose descent the water was stirred and one person was healed. He is the almighty Word who came from the royal throne while all things held deep silence.

The first silence was before the Law; the second, under the Law; the third will be in glory. The first was ignorance of the sickness; the second, despair of cure; the third will be the attainment of health. Before the Law, a person did not recognize his disease and therefore kept silent, not seeking a remedy. But when the Law entered in and showed the sick their wounds, silence was immediately broken, and the sick began to seek a remedy. Yet through works of the Law, where there is no salvation, those who wished to be healed could not find what they sought.

At last, therefore, when a person saw that no one was justified through the Law, exhausted as it were by prolonged cries and despairing, he again ceased to speak; the second silence followed. Then the almighty Word of the Father, clothed in the form of a servant, came into the world from the royal throne. The Samaritan approached the wounded man; the Angel of Great Counsel descended into the pool; Elisha came to raise the dead—that is, the Son of the highest King came, by the Father’s permission, from enduring equality of majesty to the cross’s gallows, from the royal throne to the workshop of sin, from heaven’s light to the darkness of the world or of hell, in order to undergo the death of his Passion.

Coming, he spoke peace, gave grace, offered mercy, promised forgiveness; and so, silence having been broken, the sick began with pure faith and true confession, as with loud cries, to demand a remedy and hasten to the physician, through whom their wounds might be healed and their disease cured. But once health has been restored and the blessedness of future immortality granted, nothing further will remain to be asked for; then there will be the third, blessed silence.

Thus the Law was given through angels in an ordered manner and by wise counsel, angels in whom God spoke. Whoever now restores it therefore acts against the order of the angels. I say, the Law was “placed in the hand of a mediator,” that is, in the power [Col. 0129B] of Christ, so that it might remain while he willed and cease when he willed. Therefore one who destroys it acts against him—that is, against Christ, who, being God and human, mediates between God and human beings by reconciling through himself those who had departed from God. [Note: [Col. 0129D] Augustine, on Psalm XC.]

For one is not in the middle except between two. We had departed from the majesty of God and offended him by our sin. The Son of God was sent as mediator, to discharge by his blood the sins through which we were separated from God, and, interposed between us, to redeem us and reconcile us to him from whom we were held estranged by our sins and offences. He is our head; he is God equal to the Father: God, that we might be created; human, that we might be re-created; God, to make us; human, to restore us.

“But a mediator”; [Col. 0129C] as though he were saying: The Law possessed by the mediator belongs only to the Jews; yet the mediator himself is not of one people only—that is, not only of the Jews, who had the Law—but also of the Gentiles. He reconciles not only Jews but Gentiles also to God. Therefore do not seek the Law in order to have the mediator.

“But God”; as though he were saying: The mediator is not of one alone, but he is one—that is, sufficient to reconcile all to God—because he himself is God. Therefore add nothing else to him.

[Ambrose] Or thus: The Law was placed in the hand of the mediator, that is, in the power of Christ, who is the arbiter of two peoples, Jewish and Gentile.

[Ambrose] “But a mediator”; as though he were saying: The Law possessed by the Mediator is of one people, but he himself is not mediator “of one”—that is, he is not the arbiter of one people, but of two peoples in relation to one another—because he made peace between two discordant peoples in himself, the cornerstone. Taking away on the one side the plurality of gods and enslavement to the elements, and on the other the rites of the Law, through which they were at variance, he made them peaceful. “For he himself is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II), creating the two peoples in himself.

But according to these people, Christ is not arbiter of two, who, having been brought into the Law, made one people out of two; and no one is mediator of one people.

“But God”; as though he were saying: Christ is mediator, not the Father or the Holy Spirit; yet there is one God, not many. He says this lest, by preaching Christ as God, he seem to preach one opposed to the one God, since, inasmuch as he is human, he is mediator, but inasmuch as he is God—while the Father is one God—the Father and Son are one God. For “God” is the name of nature and power, which reason teaches remains undivided in Father and Son.

Or this may be said differently: The Law was placed in the hand of a mediator. But a mediator is not of one, as though he were between certain persons or things. A mediator cannot be between God and God, because God is one, but between God and human beings, as between two extremes. Yet he is mediator insofar as he is human. [Note: [Col. 0130D] Augustine, Sermon on the Nativity of John.] For insofar as he is God, he is not mediator but equal to the Father, the same as the Father, one God with the Father.

God is above us and we below him, and many distances lie between, above all the interval of sin, which separates and casts us far away. In this great distance, so that there might be for us a way by which we could come to God, humanity draws near to God and becomes one person, so that he is not a demigod—God in part by being God and human in part by being human—but wholly God and wholly human.

And because the Mediator is between two extremes, it might appear either that Christ was not God or that there were two gods. To this he replies: Although the Mediator is not of one but of two extremes, he is nevertheless God and one with God the Father in divine nature, to whom he mediates in human nature.

[Augustine] For if the Son of God had remained in the natural equality of the Father and had not emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, he would not be the mediator of God and human beings. For the Trinity itself is one God, the same deity enduring in three—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—in eternity and equality of Godhead. Therefore, if Christ according to you, O heretics, has only one nature, show how he is intermediate between us and that nature. For how will he be intermediate if he did not possess both? Unless you posit between God and human beings one who is intermediate in such a way that he is God by reason of the divine nature and human by reason of the human nature, you do not show how human things are reconciled with divine things.

For in coming, he first joined human things with divine things in himself, through the communion of both natures in one and the same person. Then he reconciled all believers to God the Father, when all who loved Christ’s humility by believing and imitated it by loving were healed from the impiety of pride.

### Verses 21–24

> “Is the Law, then, contrary to the promises of God? Far be it! For if a Law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly be from the Law. But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe. But before faith came, we were kept under the Law, shut up unto that faith which was to be revealed. Thus the Law was our pedagogue unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith.”

“The Law, then”; as though he were saying: Since the Law was imposed because of transgression, is the Law therefore contrary to the promises of God, so that their fulfilment might come about otherwise than was promised? Far be it!

[Jerome] It is not hostile to the promise, but confirms it. For if the Law could bestow life and fulfil what the reiterated promise had pledged, the promise would truly seem to be excluded by the Law.

“For if”; as though he were saying: It is truly not contrary to the promises, because life—that is, eternal blessedness—does not come from the Law. For if life came from it, then righteousness would also come from it. He states this as follows: “For if a Law had been given which could give life,” that is, confer life, then righteousness would truly—not merely in opinion—be from the Law.

But righteousness is not from it, because it rather condemns and shuts up under sin. This is what he says: “But Scripture”—that is, the Law itself—“shut up all things under sin.” The Law is called “Scripture” because it remains and is written, or because it does not give the life-giving Spirit but is merely Scripture. [Col. 0131B] And it shut up all things under sin: that is, it completely enclosed the Jews under the dominion of sin. [Note: [Col. 0131D] Augustine, on Psalm XXXIII.] For, overcome by concupiscence and by transgression of the commandment itself, they became guilty.

Or: It shut up all things under sin, that is, it showed that all human beings are shut up under sin. The Law was not given to take away sin, but to show that all things were shut up under sin.

[Augustine] The Law was given so that it might convict a sick person of the disease when he seemed healthy to himself; so that sins might be displayed, not taken away. [Note: [Col. 0131D] The same, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] It was given so that a person might discover himself, not so that the disease might be healed, but so that, as the disease increased through transgression, a physician might be sought. Whoever denies his sickness, therefore, judges the Saviour superfluous. Thus let us praise the Creator in our nature, and seek the Saviour because of the defect inflicted upon us.

[Augustine] Note that here he says the same as in the Epistle to the Romans: “God shut up all things in unbelief, that he might have mercy on all” (Rom. XI).

[Ambrose] Being shut up by sins made known through the Law, they could not excuse themselves, but had to seek mercy. And as though someone, repeating the earlier question, asked, “Why then was the Law given?” he replies: “So that the promise might be given through faith in Jesus Christ to believers.” As though he were saying: God arranged this so that human beings, through their own desires and the Law’s weakness, might hasten to grace and, believing, obtain the promises. [Note: [Col. 0131D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.]

The Law, therefore, was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the Law might be fulfilled. The Law was not unfulfilled through its own fault, but through the fault of the prudence of the flesh. This defect had to be exposed by the Law and healed by grace.

“But before,” or “for,” he speaks specifically of the Jews, showing what benefit the Law afforded them. As though he were saying: The Law shut up all things under sin, but it was nevertheless useful because, before faith came—faith which was as it were spontaneous and invoked no merit—we were kept, not as free persons but as servants, under the Law, that is, under the burden of the Law.

[Augustine] Or, we were kept under the Law as though unwillingly. We were kept, I say, shut up, as though compelled to serve in prisons. Their confinement was the fear of the one God, the knowledge of transgression, and the discovery that they were transgressors of the Law itself. This proved useful, not destructive, to those who believed. For awareness of a greater sickness made the physician be desired more intensely and loved more ardently.

We were kept, I say, so that, accustomed in this way, we might be led to that exceedingly good faith which was to be revealed in Christ’s time, when many things which had earlier been obscure were made clear. For faith was hidden among the ancients, and faith, like grace, is a gift of God. [Note: [Col. 0132D] Augustine, to Amanthus, disciple of the Manichaean.] For what was first ours in faith before grace came? Let no one at all boast that he generated faith from his own understanding, by which he was able to believe God; rather, let him acknowledge that faith was revealed through grace by God to each individual.

[Augustine] If before faith’s revelation the Law had only this stated usefulness, what usefulness did it have after faith? None.

“Thus”; as though he were saying: Because the Law kept us for faith, it was our pedagogue, restraining us like children from unlawful things and directing us to right things by fear of punishments.

[Jerome] A pedagogue is assigned to little children, so that their unruly age may be restrained and hearts inclined to vices may be held back, while tender childhood is trained in studies and, constrained by fear of punishment, prepared for greater things. The very name *paedagogus* is compounded from the notion of leading children, that is, guiding them. The Law was therefore set over a wayward people like a pedagogue, to guard them and prepare them for future faith. Here is the honour of the Law: it guarded them as a pedagogue; but this is no great thing, since it belongs to children, not adults.

It was our pedagogue, I say, and this “unto Christ,” that is, for the instruction of Christ, who instructed for this purpose: that thus, coming to faith as children come to perfection, we might be justified by faith itself, not by the Law. Or, it was our pedagogue “unto Christ,” that is, in carrying out Christ’s commands, so that we might thus be justified by faith. As though he were saying: So long as we were untrained, the Law was our pedagogue.

### Verses 25–29

> “But when faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all children of God through faith which is in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus. But if [Col. 0132D] you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise.”

But when faith came—that is, after the faith previously hidden among the ancients had been revealed—we are no longer, that is, immediately no longer, under a pedagogue: that is, under a coercion unnecessary for those who are free. Or “now” means that in this life we possess this good, that we are no longer under a pedagogue, while in the future we shall possess a greater good.

“For you are all”: as though he said, “For this reason we Jews abandoned the pedagogue in the time of faith: because all of you Gentiles, who did not have the law, are children of God. Therefore, what we abandoned following your example, you are adopting.” As though he said: [Col. 0133A] “You ought not to do this; you are children of God.” You, I say, are so “through faith in Christ Jesus”: that is, one and the same with God, certainly not by nature, but by the bond of charity.

“For as many”: as though he said, “Truly you are in Christ through faith. For as many of every condition or sex as have been baptized into Christ”—that is, into Christ’s institution, in likeness to his death—“have put on Christ”: that is, you have been made conformed to him. This is both an honor to you and a protection against heat.

[Jerome.] That Christ is a garment, moreover, the Apostle explains elsewhere, saying: “Put on our Lord” (Rom. XIII), that is, Christ. [Note: [Col. 0133D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] People put on Christ sometimes as far as receiving the sacrament, and sometimes also as far as the sanctification of life. The former is common to the good and the [Col. 0133B] evil; the latter, however, is peculiar to the good. In this latter putting-on, there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither male nor female: that is, none is more worthy in the faith of Christ because of any of these things. Therefore let no one Judaize, as though he became worthier by this.

“For you are all”: as though he said, “Truly there is none of these things by which anyone is worthier in Christ, because all you Gentiles are one”—that is, not differing in anything. I mean one in Christ Jesus, that is, in Christ’s faith.

“But if”: as though he said, “You are in Christ. But if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed”: that is, righteous through faith, as Abraham was. And if you are Abraham’s seed, what advantage, then, do the Jews have? None. I say that you are Abraham’s seed, and therefore you are [Col. 0133C] heirs of the kingdom. And this is according to the promise—that is, according to faith in Christ who was promised beforehand—not according to fleshly observances.

[Jerome.] Observe that above Christ was called Abraham’s seed, where it is read that the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. But here Christ’s children—that is, all believers—are called Abraham’s seed. Whenever Christ is called Abraham’s seed, it must be understood bodily, namely that he was generated from Abraham’s stock; but whenever we who believe in him are called Abraham’s seed, we must understand the spiritual seed of faith.

## Chapter IV

### Verses 1–5

> “Now I say, as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father. So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons.”

Now I say that the law ought to cease. He proves this first by an analogy from human custom, and then by the authority of the law itself. As though he said: “Now we Gentiles and we Jews are Christ’s, Abraham’s seed, and heirs. But formerly we Jews were under the law while we were children, like an heir to come, appointed by his father, [Col. 0134A] who, while he is a child, is under guardians and stewards and differs not at all from a slave.” Behold again why the law is not to be retained.

This is what he says: “Now I say,” as though he said: “Not only in the ways already stated is it shown that the law is not to be retained, but also by this analogy which I state—that is, set before you.” Namely, as long as the heir is a child in age and knowledge, he differs in nothing from a slave, because he is compelled and has no power over his own affairs, although he is to be lord of all his possessions. Rather, he is under guardians, who defend him against enemies, and stewards, who conduct lawsuits on his behalf and shape his character. This continues until the time appointed—that is, determined—by his father, when freedom over himself and his possessions is granted to him.

For once he is an adult, he has freedom over himself and his possessions; otherwise, he is lawfully disinherited. Indeed, it is true that his fathers made regulations, determined up to what age he ought to be subject, and established at what age, as an adult, he should be emancipated. Thus, while he is a child, he cannot use his freedom or exercise dominion as an heir, but is nearly like slaves in the condition of procurators and advocates.

[Jerome.] By this example he proves that those who were under the law were children with respect to merit, and lacked freedom because of sin. Applying this comparison to them, he adds: “So also we Jews, when we were children in knowledge of God and in strength to resist sin, were enslaved”—[Augustine] both frightened by threats and captured by blandishments—“under the elements,” that is, under the law, which is understood through the elements [Note: [Col. 0134D] Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*], because [Col. 0134C] it is itself the first instruction toward faith and righteousness, just as children begin learning with the elements.

I mean the elements “of the world.” The law is rightly called the elements of the world, because it promised not heavenly and eternal things, but earthly or transitory things, like the world. Or, by “elements” are signified the new moons—that is, lunar days—and the Sabbath, which the Jews observed.

If, therefore, the Jews were under the elements of the world, how did they differ from pagans? [Ambrose.] Pagans do not serve under the elements, but serve the elements themselves. They worship stars, sun, moon, water, earth, and such things. The Jews, however, served God under the elements, because he himself had given them commands to observe new moons, Sabbaths, and such things. Thus by “elements” he means new moons—[Col. 0134D] that is, lunar days—and Sabbaths, which the Jews observed; not because they placed their hope in the elements, as pagans did, but because they worshipped God through these things while they were children and had not reached the time of fullness.

Therefore, as a child is under pedagogue, steward, and guardian before becoming an adult, so the law was a pedagogue to the Jews while they were still children, because it restrained them by fear and compelled them to serve God through commandments. It was also guardian and steward to the Jews, whom God had appointed as heirs, while they were children in knowledge of God and in strength for resisting sins. At that time they were also like slaves: frightened away from evils by legal punishments and urged toward good by promises of temporal benefits. They did not rule themselves, but their vices ruled them; nor did they rule their own things—that is, [Col. 0135A] the eternal inheritance—although God had appointed them lords of these things.

Thus the law served as a guardian to them while, by warning, rebuking, and sometimes punishing them, it defended them against attacks of malignant spirits and the persuasions of Gentiles who would draw them into idolatry. In this way it preserved eternal goods for them, because from among them Christ freed many from hell. It also served as their steward because it conducted their cause well before God, reconciling God to them by sacrifices and expiations. This continued until the appointed time—that is, until Christ’s coming—in which God determined that they should become perfect and free and obtain the inheritance; otherwise, they would be disinherited.

He then speaks of that time: “But when”: as though he said, “When we were children, we served under the [Col. 0135B] elements of the world; but when the fullness of time came”—that is, not by fated necessity but by God’s will alone, after the preceding time had been fulfilled. The fullness of time is the completed period appointed by God the Father for sending the Son.

Or, the time of grace is called the fullness of time because in it the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given fully and the things foretold concerning Christ are fulfilled. When, I say, that time came, God “sent his Son,” that is, made him visible to human beings.

Observe that he says, “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son.” This resembles what John the Evangelist says: “No one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come” (John VII). This means: because he did not will it. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Ambrose, on John.] For the Lord was not born under fate; this ought not to be believed even of you, much less of him through whom you were made. For neither his hour nor ours is anything but his will. Thus he did not speak of an hour at which he was compelled to die, but one at which he deigned to be killed. He awaited the time when he would die because he had awaited the time when he would be born.

Many therefore ask, “Why did Christ not come earlier?” They must be answered that the fullness of time had not yet come, it being governed by him through whom times were made. For he knew when he ought to come, suffer, and do the other things. Yet first a long succession of heralds had to be sent before him. For one who was not insignificant was coming: he had to be proclaimed for a long time and continually maintained in expectation. The greater the judge who was coming, the longer the [Col. 0135D] succession of heralds that had to precede him.

Therefore he says: “When the fullness of time came, God the Father sent his Son, made of a woman.” Observe that he calls him who was uncreated “made.” Thus the Father made him from a woman under the law. When, therefore, he says, “God sent his Son, made of a woman,” he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely in that he was made from a woman. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Augustine, sermon *On the Trinity*.]

For what is the birth of the Son from the Virgin Mary? Certainly, it is the assumption of the form of a servant. What else is it for the Son to be born than to take the form of a servant in the Virgin’s womb? The Father did this, and the Son did it too. The Son, not the Father, was born of the Virgin Mary; but both Father and Son effected the Son’s birth from Mary. Similarly, the Father did not suffer, but the Son did; nevertheless, Father and Son effected the Son’s passion. For the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed over himself. This passion was undergone by one, but effected by both. Thus neither did the Father effect Christ’s birth without the Son, nor the Son without the Father; and likewise with Christ’s passion.

What, then, did Judas do except sin? Let us come to the resurrection. The Father did not rise, but the Son did; nevertheless, Father and Son effected the Son’s resurrection. Behold what it is for the Son to be sent.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] But it is asked from where and to where the Son was sent. “I came forth from the Father and came into this world” (John XVI): this is to be sent. Yet the Evangelist says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John I). Then [Col. 0136B] he adds: “He came into his own.” He was sent to the place to which he came; and if he was sent into this world because he came forth from the Father and came into this world, and was in this world, then he was sent to the place where he already was.

Thus he says in the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. XXIII). If this is understood as spoken of the Father, where could he be without his Word, without his Wisdom, “which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII)? Nor could he anywhere be without his Spirit. Therefore, if God is everywhere, his Spirit too is everywhere. Thus the Holy Spirit was also sent to the place where he already was.

Accordingly, one must carefully inquire how this sending, whether of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, is to be understood. Because this was treated in the Epistle to the Romans according to the capacity [Col. 0136C] of human ability, we touch on it here briefly as we hasten to other matters. Still, if we think soberly and worthily concerning the Son of God, we should understand him to have been sent because the Word of God gave himself to be comprehended by our minds out of that incomprehensible and ineffable secret of profound majesty—not only when he emptied himself, but also when he dwelt in us, as it is written: “I will dwell in them” (II Cor. XVI).

People commonly object that the Son is less than the Father because he was sent. Yet it is plain that he is not less because he was sent. Consider that the Lord Christ says in Isaiah that he was sent by the Holy Spirit. Is the Son therefore less than the Spirit because he was sent by the Spirit? For you have it written that the Son says he was sent by the Father and by his Spirit. You see, then, that the simplicity of the expression does not constitute an injury in being sent.

Therefore God sent [Col. 0136D] his Son, made of a woman. Perhaps the phrase “of a woman” troubles someone, since he did not say “of a virgin”; but let it not trouble him. [Note: [Col. 0136D] Augustine, same work.] Scripture says both, “of a virgin” and “of a woman.” “Of a virgin,” as there: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc. (Isa. VII); “of a woman,” as here. There is no contradiction.

[Augustine.] He used “woman” for “female,” according to Hebrew idiom. Hebrew usage calls women not only those whose virginity has been corrupted, but females generally; as is read of Eve when she was made: “He formed her a woman” (Gen. II), although she had not yet had intercourse with a man.

[Note: [Col. 0137D] Augustine, sermon *On the Trinity*.] Again, do not be offended that he says “made,” although we confess that he was born. For “made” is confessed only of his humanity. God, however, is always making; he does not come to be by being made, but he is made something for someone, as he says: “Lord, you have become a refuge for us” (Ps. LXXXIX), when he became what he had never been made. But the Lord Christ was made man so that he might be man—that is, so that he who was always Creator might be a creature.

[Augustine.] [Note: [Col. 0137D] Augustine, sermon *On the same subject*.] Remaining God, he was made man, so that he might become what he was not, not so that he might cease to be what he was. Thus he says “made” because of his assumption of creaturehood.

And he adds: “Made under the law.” [Ambrose.] The Savior had to be made under the law, so that he might appear circumcised, like the son of Abraham to whom he had been promised, bearing the sign of the one to whom he had been promised. In him circumcision was fulfilled, and therefore its sign now ceases. Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed; we believe that this has now come to pass.

Thus he said “made under the law” because he was circumcised and a legal offering was made for him. Nor is it surprising if he bore even those works of the law from which he was to free those held in servile bondage by them; he also underwent death in order to free others from it. Therefore he was made under the law—that is, under the burden of the law—as under other penalties.

Hence he adds: “That he might redeem those who were under the law,” oppressed and liable, from the devil, destruction, and sins. [Note: [Col. 0137D] Ambrose, on Psalm XXXI.] Observe that he proposed two things, “made of a woman” and “made under the law,” and that, in reverse order, two other things answer them. To “made under the law” he relates: “that he might redeem those who were under the law.” To “made of a woman” he relates the other: “that we might receive adoption.”

As though he said: “For this reason he was made of a woman: that we might receive adoption as sons,” that is, the goods given through grace, through which people become children. Or, “that we might receive the adoption of sons”: that we might share in divine glory. For just as he shares in our nature, so he adopts us to behold his own.

[Augustine.] For we receive adoption because the only Son of God did not disdain participation in our nature by being made of a woman, so that he might be not only the Only-Begotten Son of God, where he has no brothers, but also become the Firstborn among many brothers. He calls it “adoption” so that we may distinctly understand the unique Son of God. We are children of God by favor and condescension; he is Son by nature, being what the Father is.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] God had one only Son, whom he begot from his own substance; but he did not beget us from his substance. For we are creatures whom he did not beget but made; and therefore, to make us brothers of Christ according to our manner, he adopted us. This manner, then, by which God begot us through his Word and grace, when we already existed not as born from him but as created and established by him, so that we might be his children, is called adoption.

Hence: “He gave them power to become children of God,” etc. [Col. 0138A] (John I). Nor did he say “that we might receive,” but “that we might receive back,” to signify that we lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

### Verses 6–8

> “And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father. Therefore you are no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then an heir through God. But then indeed, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods.”

“And because”: as though he said, “Not only we Jews who believe are children of God, but you Gentiles also are children of God.” He proves this from its effect: because God the Father sent the Spirit of his Son—whom the Son also sends—into our hearts, both Jewish and Gentile. This Spirit proves that we are children.

[Col. 0138B] [Ambrose.] To prove that we had been adopted by God as sons, he gave us his Spirit, who displays the Father’s sign in his children, so that, because we would not dare to say this on account of our weakness and unworthiness, he might prompt us to dare to say it. Hence he adds: “crying,” as though he said, “I mean the Spirit who cries—that is, who makes us cry.”

[Augustine.] We would never presume this unless the Spirit taught us. What is it? “Abba,” which means “Father.” [Ambrose.] *Abba* is Hebrew and has the same meaning as *pater*, “father.” Scripture preserves this custom in many places: it sets down a Hebrew word with its interpretation.

[Augustine.] He placed two words, the latter interpreting the former. For *abba* means “father.” It is also elegantly understood that he did not without reason set down words from two languages, both meaning the same thing, because of the whole people called into the unity of faith from Jews and Gentiles: the Hebrew word pertains to Jews, and the Greek word to Gentiles.

[Jerome.] Both words have the same meaning, for the unity of the same faith and Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0138D] Jerome, *On Correction and Grace*.] It should be noted that in Scripture “crying” is not an emission of a loud voice, but is understood as knowledge and intensity of intention. Thus we cry; but the Spirit is said to cry because he causes us to cry.

Therefore he sent the Spirit of his Son, crying “Abba, Father”: that is, making us cry. Observe also that the Spirit is the Son’s Spirit, and observe the Trinity here.

[Note: [Col. 0138D] Augustine, on John.] [Col. 0138D] But perhaps someone asks whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. The Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone. But the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them only, but of both. Hence the Lord says: “The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X). And the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son.” There are many other testimonies by which he plainly shows that the Spirit called Holy Spirit in the Trinity is both the Father’s and the Son’s.

I think that he is properly called the Holy Spirit for no other reason than this: although, when we are asked individually concerning the Father and the Son, we cannot call them anything but spirit, because God is spirit, that name which they share in common must properly be applied to him who is not the Spirit of one of them, but in whom their mutual communion appears. Why, then, should we not believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son, when he is also the Son’s Spirit?

For if he did not proceed from the Son, then after the resurrection, when presenting himself to the disciples, he would not have breathed on them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX). What else did that breathing signify except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him? To this also pertains what he said of the woman suffering from a flow of blood: “Someone touched me, for I perceived power going out from me” (Luke VIII). That the Holy Spirit is called “power” is clear from the angel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I). And when the Lord promised him to the disciples, he said: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV). This is the power of which the Evangelist says: “Power went out from him and healed all” (Luke VI).

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Augustine, Book III, *On the Trinity*.] Although the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Son himself says that he proceeds from the Father, because he customarily refers back to the Father even what is his own, of whom he himself also is. So elsewhere he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John VII). If this means his teaching, which he nevertheless says is not his own but the Father’s, how much more should the Holy Spirit be understood there to proceed from the Son too, where [Col. 0139C] he says that he proceeds from the Father? For the Son, who is God from God, receives from the Father both that he is God and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him.

By saying, “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John XV), and elsewhere, “whom the Father will send in my name” (John XVI), rather than “from me,” Christ shows that the Father is the principle of the whole divinity—or, better expressed, deity.

“Therefore”: as though he said, “Because the Spirit cries in us, ‘Father,’ therefore from the time of grace no one among us who believes in Christ is a slave, serving from fear, but a son, serving from love. And if he is a son, he will also be an heir in the future; and this is through God,” that is, through God’s work and mercy. Or: “I swear this by God.”

“But then,” etc.: as though he said, “You are now sons; you now say ‘Father.’ But then indeed, when you were unbelievers and ignorant of God—and thus you will have some excuse—you served those who are not gods by their own nature, but only by human opinion.”

[Ambrose.] By saying, “who by nature are not gods,” he shows that there is one nature of the true God: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. What is it to be God by nature except to be the true God? Hence elsewhere he says to the apostles: “You turned to serve the living and true God” (II Thess. I). For God is living and true by nature. Therefore the true God is he who is God by nature.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Ambrose, same work.] Thus those could not be true gods to whom this did not naturally belong. Accordingly, the Savior is true God, who is God according to essence.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Didymus, *On the Holy Spirit*.] But heretics say that the Son is not God by nature but is created. They must be answered that if the Son is not God by nature but is a creature, he must not be worshipped at all or adored as God; for the Apostle says: “They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I).

But they will reply: “Why do you worship his flesh, which you do not deny to be a creature, together with his divinity, and serve it no less than the divinity?” I worship the Lord’s flesh—indeed, the complete humanity in Christ—because it has been assumed by the divinity and united to deity, so that I confess not one person and another, but one and the same Son of God, God and man.

Finally, if you separate the man from God, as Photinus or Paul of Samosata does, I neither serve nor believe him; just as, if someone found a royal purple garment or diadem lying on the ground, would he try to worship it? But when a king has put it on, he incurs the danger of death if he refuses to worship it together with the king. So too, in Christ the Lord, if anyone refuses to worship the humanity—not merely by itself or naked, but united to divinity, namely the one Son, true God and true man—he shall die eternally.

### Verses 9–15

> “But now, when you have known God—or rather have been known by God—how do you turn again to weak and needy elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew? You observe days, months, seasons, and years. I fear for you, lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain. Become as I am, because I also am as you are. Brothers, I beseech you: you have done me no wrong. But you know that because of a weakness of the flesh I preached the gospel to you formerly, and you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh; but you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus. Where, then, is your blessedness?”

“But now”: as though he said, “Formerly you served false gods when you did not know the true God. But even now, when truth has been revealed, when you have known—or know—God, and therefore sin more grievously than before, how do you turn again,” etc.? This is the order of the sentence, but he inserts: “or rather, having been known,” etc.

As though he said: “I say, ‘you have known God’; but this is not from yourselves. Rather, you have been approved and loved by God’s grace.” This is what “you have been known by God” means: by his gift he made us knowers of him. Scripture frequently uses this manner of speaking.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Augustine, on Psalm LXII.] Thus the prophetic man says in the Psalm: “So I appeared to you in the sanctuary, that I might see your power” (Ps. LXII). He did not say, “I appeared to you that you might see,” but “that I might see.” Similar is the Apostle’s saying: “But now, when you have known God—or rather, have been known by God.”

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Augustine, *On the Grace of the New Testament*.] He corrected what he had said by adding, “or rather, you have been known by God,” so that we might understand that even our knowing God must not be attributed to ourselves but to his mercy. When God is said to know us, it must be understood thus: he grants us knowledge of himself.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Augustine, *The City of God*.] It is not from ourselves that we know him, but from him. He knew from eternity those whom the Apostle calls “known” at that time; yet he is said to know them at the time when he causes himself to be known, just as he is said to rest when by his gift we rest.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Augustine, *The Literal Interpretation of Genesis*.] God did not first know then those whom he had foreknown before the foundation of the world. Rather, at that time they knew him by his gift, not by their merit or ability. Therefore the Apostle preferred to speak tropologically: he said that they were then known by God when God granted them knowledge of himself, and corrected his own expression as though what he had first said properly had been less correct, rather than permit them to [Col. 0141B] claim for themselves the ability which God had given them.

When, I say, you have known God, how do you turn from faith to the elements—that is, to the elementary law, to the worship of God?

[Jerome.] The elements of God are weak and needy. The law is called weak because it does not justify perfectly; needy because, insofar as it helps, it does so not by itself but in relation to grace. You turn back, I say, as before conversion. But had these Galatians observed the law before conversion? Certainly not, because they were Gentiles and had devoted themselves to the superstitions of idolatry. Therefore he says “again,” because observance of the law, to which they were then devoted, was a sin almost equal to the slavery of idols to which they had been devoted before conversion.

Hence he adds: “to which,” etc. [Augustine.] As though he said: “How do you turn to elements to which you wish to be enslaved anew?” He says “anew” in order to show that the law after Christ did not differ from former idolatry.

“Days”: as though he said, “You wish to serve the elements.” [Jerome.] And truly you do, because you now observe days in the Jewish manner: Sabbaths; the tenth day of the first month up to the fourteenth, when the lamb was sacrificed; from the fourteenth through the twenty-first of that same month, when unleavened bread was eaten; and seven weeks, which they count in Jewish fashion after Unleavened Bread. They observe the days of Israelite Pentecost; also the trumpet-blast on the first day of the seventh month; atonement and fasting on the tenth of that month; and the Feast of Tabernacles (*scenopegia*) on the fifteenth.

“You observe months,” such as new moons. They also keep months because they observe the first and seventh months; “and seasons,” such as the time of the departure from Egypt. They also observed seasons who came to Jerusalem each year, thinking that they fulfilled the Lord’s command: “Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me, and all your males shall appear before your God” (Deut. XVI).

“And years”: namely, seventh years. I think this is said of the seventh year of remission and of the fiftieth year, called by them the jubilee. The Jews at one time could not observe this in its proper sequence because they were oppressed by captivity. When that captivity was ended, they observed in its place the seventh year of the seventh decade, which may be understood either as the sixty-first year, when Cyrus and Darius granted them leave to return from Babylon—whence they returned after seventy years had been completed—or, more probably, as the seventy-first year, which, after returning to Jerusalem, they observed instead of the fiftieth year called the jubilee.

“I fear”: as though he said, “You already do this; but I fear something worse, namely lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain”—that is, uselessly—which will be so if you wholly accept the law. As though he said: “I fear your fickleness, nothing else.”

Or thus: “How do you turn again?” This may be understood of the error of the Gentiles. For in saying, “You turn again to weak and needy elements,” he speaks not to the circumcised but to Gentiles, to whom he writes this Epistle. Nor does he say that they are returning to circumcision or to the law, in which they had never been, but to weak and needy elements, to which they wish once more to be enslaved as before. This must be understood of Gentiles.

[Augustine.] This is indeed a very common error of the Gentiles: in undertaking affairs or awaiting the events of their life and business, they observe days, months, years, and seasons marked out by astrologers and Chaldeans. He rebukes them, saying: “But now, when you have known God, how do you turn again to weak and needy elements, to which you wish to be enslaved anew?”—that is, to superstitious observances of times.

It is clear that he means by “elements of this world” the revolutions of time, administered through the elements of the world—that is, heaven and earth—and through the movements and order of the stars. He calls them weak because they vary in weak and unstable appearance; and needy because they need the supreme and stable form of the Creator in order to exist as they do.

[Ambrose.] Or he calls the elements needy because they need one another in order to govern the world. “Days”: as though he said, “Truly you wish to serve them, because you observe days, months, seasons, and years.” They observe days when they say: “Nothing should be begun on this day.” They observe months when, examining the course of the moon, they say: “Nothing should be started under such a moon.” They observe seasons when they say: “Now is the beginning of spring.” They observe years when they say: “It is a new year; it is the Kalends of January; this or that must not be done.”

But there ought to be no superstition concerning such matters, because whatever is simply done in devotion to God may turn out prosperously. [Col. 0142D] [Augustine.] Observe that the Galatians were subverted in two ways: by turning to the law and by turning to their former errors. Let the reader, therefore, choose whichever interpretation he wishes, provided that he understands that superstitious observances of times concern so grave a danger to the soul that the Apostle immediately adds here: “I fear,” etc. As though he said: “You already do this, but I fear something worse, namely that perhaps I have labored among you in vain.”

[Note: [Col. 0142D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Some matters would be considered very slight, were they not shown by Scripture to be more serious than people suppose. For who would think that someone calling his brother “fool” was liable to Gehenna, unless Truth itself had said so (Matt. V)? Likewise, observing days and seasons would not be considered so grave, unless the Apostle said: “I fear lest perhaps I have labored among you in vain.”

Those observe them who on particular days, months, or years are willing or unwilling to begin something, as though times were lucky or unlucky. Therefore let us not observe such things, lest we hear from the Apostle: “I fear,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Augustine, *To Januarius*.] For he rebukes those who follow constellations, saying: “I shall not set out because the moon is in such a position,” or, “I shall set out so that things may go well, because the stars are so positioned”; “I shall conduct business in this month because that star governs the month”; “I shall not plant a vineyard in this year because it is leap year.” Such people are rebuked, not those who know the natural effects of the elements in the most orderly revolutions of the stars—for example, that they should not sail in stormy weather or should sow in autumn. Of these it was said when they were created in Genesis: “Let them be for signs, seasons, days, and months” (Gen. I).

Be [like me], as though he were saying: “I fear that perhaps I have laboured among you in vain; but be as I am, who have abandoned the Law.” And you ought to be so, because I was once under the Law, as you now wish to be, and I abandoned it not without reason. [Ambrose] Or thus: Be as I am, because I too am, like you, a human being corrected from error; thus you too can be corrected. Or thus: Be as I am, because I, who possessed the Law, am now without the Law, as you are. [Augustine] For though I was born a Jew, I now disdain those carnal things through spiritual judgment.

The Apostle restores the Galatians, whom he has sternly corrected, by praise for what they did well, applying pleasant things after harsh ones, in the manner of a healing physician. As though he said: And you ought to be as I am because, brothers, I beseech you—I say, I beseech you, and can confidently beseech those whom I rightly love—because you have done me no injury, and thus the cause of my enmity is not on your side. By saying this he excuses himself, because the false teachers had said that Paul was an enemy to the Galatians and had not wished to teach them what he preached in other Churches. Refuting this slander, the Apostle removes the ground for enmity when he says, “You have done me no injury.”

“But you know,” as though he said: “You did not injure me; rather, you received me honourably when you had reason to despise me.” And this is what he says: “You know that through weakness of my flesh”—because my flesh was afflicted—“I preached the Gospel to you formerly”; and despite so long a time, you did not despise me. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0143D] “And you did not despise your temptation in my flesh,” that is, me while I was afflicted, through which the devil was testing you, lest you should believe. [Ambrose] For they were tested when the Apostle suffered tribulation in the flesh: whether, out of fear, they would abandon him, or, out of love, embrace him. It was therefore fitting and appropriate for him to remind them of their love, lest they regard him as an enemy, saying: “You know that through weakness of the flesh,” that is, while I was suffering persecution, “I formerly preached the Gospel to you; and you did not despise your temptation in my flesh,” that is, the tribulation which I suffer in the flesh and by which it becomes apparent what sort of people you are, as worthless or contemptible.

“Nor did you reject [me],” [Col. 0144A] so as not to enter into fellowship in my danger. Distinguish between these two phrases: “you did not despise,” namely after conversion, so that I might thereby be of less account; and “you did not reject,” before conversion, so that you might shrink from being converted on that account. “But you received me as an angel of God,” that is, as though an angel of God had come; or, you believed me to be an angel of God. Indeed, I shall say more: “as Christ Jesus,” as though Christ himself had come, who spoke in the Apostle and had therefore come to them.

“Where then is [your blessedness]?” [Augustine] Marvelling at their spiritual conduct, he commends it so that, contemplating it, they may not fall into carnal fear; and because they had changed for the worse, he rebukes them. [Note: [Col. 0143D] Augustine, *On Pastoral Matters*.] Even if they received him as an angel, nevertheless he does not spare cutting or burning, because he seeks not his own interests but those of Christ. He seeks not milk and wool from the sheep—[Col. 0144B] that is, the means of supplying his necessities and the favour of honour—but the salvation of the sheep.

As though he said: And because you acted thus then, where is your blessedness, by which you were called blessed because of your good beginnings and your fervour, as it were, in the stages of progress? As though he said: Be ashamed of having changed. For it is astonishing that you have fallen away from what was good.

### Verses 15–21

> “For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your own eyes and given them to me. Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? They are zealous for you, but not honourably; rather, they want to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them. But be zealous for what is good at all times, and not only when I am present with you. My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you: I would wish to be with you now and to change [Col. 0144C] my tone, because I am perplexed about you. Tell me, you who wish to be under the Law: have you not read the Law?”

“For I bear witness,” as though he said: “You were truly blessed, or you received me as an angel or as Christ.” For I bear witness concerning you that, if it could have been done for the benefit of the Church, you would have torn out your eyes—which are dearer to you than all things—and given them to me, namely for the benefit of my preaching. Therefore there is all the more cause to grieve over you.

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Augustine, *Against the Letter of Gaudentius*.] Observe that he says, “if it could have been done.” Could not that have been done of which the Apostle says that what is not just cannot be done? So too Job says, “Would that I could kill myself” (Job 10); and the Lord says to Lot, “I could do nothing until [Col. 0144D] you enter there” (Gen. 19). [Note: [Col. 0144D] Augustine, *On the Power of God*.] He said that he could not do what without doubt he could do in power, but could not do in justice.

“Have I then become your enemy,” as though he said: Since this is so, is it credible that I have become your enemy by telling you the truth? As though he said: I seem an enemy on this account, because I tell the truth; but if I deceived you, I should be considered a friend, because no one wishes to be reproved when in error. Therefore I seem your enemy because I justly rebuke you.

“They are zealous.” [Ambrose] As though he said: I am not your enemy, but they are zealous for—that is, they profess affection for—you, not honourably, that is, not to your benefit. For “they are zealous” is [used] because they desire not so much that the Galatians should become better as to make them worse and draw them backward [Col. 0145A] through perverse rivalry. Hence he adds: “But they wish to exclude you,” from faith to the Law, or from my love, “so that you may be zealous for them,” that is, look to them in matters of the Law.

“But be zealous for what is good.” As though he said: They wish you to be zealous for them; but you, be zealous—that is, love and imitate—a good person, namely myself and persons of that sort. And do this “in what is good,” that is, love on this account, because virtue and good conduct are in him, not for another reason. Do this always, so that by a persevering course you may reach the end of a good work. For he wishes them always to imitate him. Hence he adds: “and not only.”

[Jerome] As though he said: Be zealous for what is good, namely myself and persons of that sort, and not only when I am present with you; but persevere in what you have received, imitating me even more when I am absent.

“My little children”: here he again begins [Col. 0145B] to show from the Law itself why it must not be retained. As though he said: Imitate me—and you ought to do so—because you are mine. I do not call you sons, but little children, because you are diminished and need stages of perfection. “For whom I am again in labour,” as before: that is, with effort and pain I bring you forth into the light of faith, “until Christ,” whom you have deformed, “be formed in you,” so that you may receive his likeness, which through your own fault you lost.

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Jerome, *On Ezekiel*.] It belongs to very few to weigh what labour there is in the preaching of the Fathers, and with what pains they labour to bring souls to birth in faith and upright conduct. [Note: [Col. 0145D] Augustine, *On the Morals*.] Hence the Apostle, speaking in the person of a mother, says: “For whom I am again in labour.” He had first begotten them through faith in baptism, but afterwards they were deformed by the false teachers and made weak; now he reforms them with pain. Hence he adds: “until [Col. 0145C] Christ be re-formed in you.” For, conceiving faith but not attending to the meaning of faith, they vainly suppose that they possess Christ formed in their souls. Christ is formed in the hearts of believers when the mysteries are unfolded to them in Greek, and what had seemed obscure becomes clear.

Or thus: “until Christ be formed in you,” that is, until through you he appears beautiful to others. This is said more severely than if he had said that they were re-formed in Christ, because in some way it sounds more dreadful in the ears of hearers.

“I would wish, however.” As though he said: I have now used gentle words, calling you brothers and children; but I would wish to be with you now, that they might be confounded by a double begetting: both by their own error and by the Apostle’s shame. Therefore he says, [Col. 0145D] “I would wish to be with you and to change my tone,” that is, [to change it to] rebuke, so that I might say to you things worthy of you which I do not wish to write, lest they remain with you. I would therefore wish to change it, “because I am perplexed about you,” that is, I blush before others on your account.

Knowing that speech has greater force when addressed to those present, the Apostle desires to exchange his apostolic voice, the voice contained in letters, for personal presence. Holy Scripture edifies when read, but is much more useful when changed from writing into speech; for the living voice has great power, a voice resounding from its author’s mouth, uttered and distinguished with the same delivery with which it was conceived in a person’s heart.

[Jerome] The meaning therefore is: [Col. 0146A] Because I am perplexed about you, I would wish, when present, to utter from my own mouth the voice of the letter, so that I myself might rebuke you more severely than usual; for a letter cannot express the voice of one rebuking, cannot sound the cry of one angered, or unfold the pain of the heart by its written characters. For I do not have the fruits which teachers ordinarily have from disciples, and the seed of instruction has been scattered in vain, so that I may say with Jeremiah: “I have neither benefited anyone, nor has anyone benefited me” (Jer. 15). Yet, lest I suffer you to perish and err forever, I shall speak to you out of love. “Tell me,” etc.

Or this text can be read differently, while retaining the same sense. “My little children,” as though he said: Not only do the foregoing points prove that the Law must be abandoned; the authority of the Law itself also shows this. O my little children, tell—that is, answer—me. [Col. 0146B] For the sentence depends thus far, and there is inserted the phrase, “for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you. I would wish, however, to be with you now and change my tone, because I am perplexed about you”; the sense of these words is not changed.

You then, O little children, who wish carnally to be under the Law, tell me—that is, answer me: Have you read the Law, or not? Whichever they choose, they are shown to be foolish. If they have not read it, they ought not to accept what they do not know; if they have read it, it itself proves that it must be abandoned. But if they do not understand it, they are foolish. Therefore he questions them, saying: “Have you not read the Law?” As though he said: You have indeed read it, but have not understood it.

### Verses 22–24

> “For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and [Col. 0146C] one by a free woman. But he who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was by the free woman was born through promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two Testaments. One, indeed, is from Mount Sinai, begetting into slavery: this is Hagar.”

“For it is written that Abraham…” As though he said: This is why I ask whether you have read the Law, because something is written in it which, if you attended to it, would cause you never to return to it. For it is written in Genesis that Abraham had two sons, Ishmael and Isaac: one by the slave woman Hagar, namely Ishmael, and one by the free woman Sarah, namely Isaac. But he who was by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, that is, without any miracle, but by the law of nature. He who was by the free woman, however, was born through promise, [Col. 0146D] that is, miraculously.

Observe that he says, “It is written that Abraham had two sons,” though he had more. [Augustine] For after Sarah’s death he begot others by another wife, namely Keturah; but they do not belong to this signification. Therefore many people who read the Apostle but do not know the book of Genesis suppose that Abraham had only two sons. But the Apostle mentions only these because Scripture sets out the circumstances of each of them particularly, intimating that something eminent was prefigured in them.

Observe also what he adds: “one by a slave woman and one by a free woman.” [Note: [Col. 0146D] Augustine, *City of God*.] He did not distinguish this without purpose. Both indeed were born of Abraham, [Col. 0147A] but by different operation: he who was by the slave woman was born according to the nature of the flesh, because a young woman is accustomed to conceive by an old man. But he who was by the free woman was conceived not through the power of the flesh—for an old and barren woman to conceive by an old man—but through the operation of the God who promised. Thus natural custom, revealing nature, begot the former; promise, signifying grace, gave the latter. There human practice is shown; here divine beneficence is commended.

Ishmael was born, therefore, as human beings are born, by the union of the two sexes according to the customary law of nature. Thus it is said, “according to the flesh,” not because these benefits are not God’s, or because God does not work them—his creative Wisdom reaches, as it is written, “from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). But where God’s gift had to be signified—the gift by which grace freely bestows upon human beings what was not owed to them—it was fitting that the son should be given in a manner not owed by the ordinary course of nature. Although these things occurred thus in the literal sense, yet because the literal sense does not suffice for the higher signification, he adds:

“These things are spoken allegorically,” that is, according to another meaning. [Note: [Col. 0147D] Augustine, on Psalm 103.] Allegory is so called when the words seem to sound one thing and another is signified by their meaning, as here. Abraham is God the Father, who is the father of many nations. For this is said to be the interpretation of the name Abraham: *abba*, “father,” and *ham*, “of many,” with “nations” understood; thereby God the Father is meant. The *r* is inserted for euphony. [Col. 0147C] Thus Abraham is said to be as it were *Abaham*, that is, “father of many nations,” by which God the Father is understood.

The free woman and the slave woman signify the two Testaments. Hence he adds: “For these,” that is, the slave woman and the free woman, “are,” that is, signify, “the two Testaments.” The free woman signifies the New Testament, granting new grace to all through Christ; Hagar, the Old Testament. [Ambrose] In each Testament God begot for himself children who would serve him; but in the Old Testament Jews were begotten as slaves, because they served through fear of punishment and the promise of temporal things. This is what he says: “He who was by the slave woman”—namely, the Jews and all slaves of sin—“was born according to the flesh,” which both shrinks from punishments and loves pleasant things, because they served through fear of punishment and love of temporal things.

But the grace of the New Testament bears [Col. 0147D] free persons, who serve from love—not through the flesh but through God’s work. This is what he says: “He who was born by the free woman,” that is, the free Christian people, begotten by the grace of the New Testament, “was born through promise,” that is, through the power and grace of him who promises, with the figure signifying the truth. For who would believe things impossible according to nature, despise what is pleasant in the present, and hope for what is unseen, unless God’s power worked this in him? Christians are begotten in this manner, and their type went before in Isaac.

For Ishmael signifies the birth of the Jews, or of those who are slaves of sin; Isaac, however, [Col. 0148A] signifies Christians, because they are born into freedom. For the person who receives remission of sins is made free. Behold, the meaning of those words of the Law has been clearly expounded. From this it is shown that the Law which begot into slavery is not to be retained, but the New [Testament], which bears children into freedom.

Hence he adds: “One indeed,” as though he said: The slave woman and the free woman signify the two Testaments. And one was indeed given on Mount Sinai, which is interpreted “commandment.” Its having been given in such a place, that is, on a lofty mountain, signifies either that the Jews were proud of the commandment over against other nations, or that they themselves were proud and puffed up against the commandment itself. This Testament, I say, begets people into slavery because the Jews served from fear, or because they were slaves of sin. This Testament is Hagar, that is, is signified by Hagar. And rightly so: for Hagar is interpreted “alienation,” [Col. 0148B] which fittingly applies because that Testament alienates people from the eternal inheritance.

### Verses 25–31

> “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem which now is, and is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free; she is our mother. For it is written: ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate are many more than of her who has a husband.’ But we, brothers, are children of promise according to Isaac. Yet just as at that time he who had been born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son.’ For [Col. 0148C] the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman. Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, by the freedom with which Christ set us free.”

“For Sinai…” As though he said: The Old Testament truly begets into slavery, because Mount Sinai—that is, the Old Testament given on Mount Sinai—is in Arabia, that is, in humility or affliction, because it afflicted people under carnal observances. For Arabia is interpreted “humility” or “affliction.” And the Old Testament is rightly said to have been given in Arabia, not in the land of promise, where the Jews were, as it were, children, but in Arabia, where they were, as it were, slaves and strangers, because the Old Testament bore not children but slaves and strangers.

Then he compares the Old Testament with the people to whom it was given, saying that the mountain [Col. 0148D] is in every respect joined and similar—that is, the Old Testament given on that mountain is in every respect joined and similar—to the Jerusalem which now is, that is, to the Jewish people which “now is,” that is, which loves earthly things and serves for temporal things. Or: she is in slavery under sin with her children. This is the synagogue which bears children under sin: the whole people is indeed mother, but individuals are children; or the children are proselytes, all of whom serve through fear of punishment.

Therefore the Old Testament is said to be joined and similar to that people because, just as the Old Testament threatened punishments and promised temporal things, so that people served through fear of punishment and love of temporal things. From [Col. 0149A] all this it is clear that the Old Law must not be retained, but the New [Testament], which is above and free—that is, sends us to higher things and makes us free—and which was given to the Church that is above and free. Hence he adds: “But she above.”

As though he said: This synagogue serves through fear or under sin. [Jerome] But that Jerusalem which is above, that is, the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which rejoices with the Lord in hope, is free because she loves and serves out of love. She is our mother, that is, the mother of believers, because individual persons, instructed by her word and example, serve from love. That she is free and mother, he proves by the authority of Isaiah, adding: “For it is written.” As though he said: She is truly free and mother, because it is written in Isaiah: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, [Col. 0149B] you who do not travail, because many children,” etc.

From these words she is shown both to be free and to be mother. Rejoicing, breaking forth, and crying aloud pertain to freedom; “because many children” pertains to motherhood. Isaiah, looking to the time of Christ, addresses the Church of the Gentiles, formerly barren and now fruitful, saying: O Church of the Gentiles, barren, who in the time of the Law did not bear by the power of miracle—who at that time bore almost no one—and who also did not travail, because then you had not even the efforts of labour: rejoice in heart; break forth, that is, outwardly show the joy of your mind; and cry aloud, that is, proclaim your joy to others, because your children, once desolate in childbirth though not in the love of a bridegroom, are many more than those of her, that is, of the synagogue, which has a husband, that is, the Law, for begetting—[Col. 0149C] that is, which carnally bears under the Law.

For the Synagogue had a husband, namely the Law, and was once fruitful in children. But the barren Church, without her husband Christ, without any address from the bridegroom’s word, lay long in the wilderness. But after that other woman received the bill of divorce and turned all the ornaments of her husband into ornaments for an idol, then the husband, when the former girdle had decayed, wove another belt for his loins, another loincloth from the Gentiles. As soon as she was joined to her husband, she conceived and bore. Hence in Isaiah the Lord cries: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out your cords,” etc. (Isa. 54). Likewise: “Is a nation born all at once?”

The Synagogue, therefore, which has a husband, that is, the Law, and the multitude of Gentiles, which is desolate, wandering, and living without any power of the Law, [Col. 0149D] and barren, producing no offspring of any lawful word—these are [the two women]. [Note: [Col. 0149D] Augustine, *City of God*.] For the Church was barren among all nations before this offspring which we see arose. Some Judaizers, however, refer this to the ancient Sarah. But Isaiah would have said this pointlessly concerning ancient Sarah, who had died much earlier.

Or Jerusalem here means the heavenly city, the celestial court. For the city of the saints is above, although in some of those whom it bears here it still sojourns, until the time of its kingdom comes, when it will gather all who rise again in their bodies. Therefore he says of it: “But that Jerusalem which is above,” [Col. 0150A] that is, rejoices with the Lord, “is free” from sin and the punishment of sin, “and is our mother.” The heavenly city is called our mother because we are called to it. It is called heavenly because heaven is its seat; and those whom it bears will be there with it.
