She is truly mother, for it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail.” [Ambrose] The heavenly Jerusalem is called barren because she does not bear according to the flesh, nor travail—that is, suffer pains—but bears spiritually without suffering, crying in joy because she has more children than she who has a husband, that is, the synagogue which bears carnally. Hence he adds: “Because the children of you who are desolate are more numerous.” Desolate by whom? By Adam, who, having forsaken life, followed death, than those of her who has a husband, [Col. 0150B] that is, the synagogue. For Christians are far more numerous than Jews, because Christians have surpassed the number of Jews. [Note: [Col. 0149D] Augustine, *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, 54.]

She is therefore called barren because she is a virgin who bears children not carnally but spiritually through faith alone, and is not said to travail; for one who travails suffers pains. She cries aloud in the joy of human salvation. Earthly Jerusalem, however, is said to have had a husband because she bore carnally. Nature corrupted by sin bears citizens of the earthly city; but grace, freeing nature from sin, bears citizens of the heavenly city. This was signified in Abraham’s two sons, one of whom was born of the slave woman according to the flesh, the other of the free woman not according to nature but through promise.

For nature denies children from a union [Col. 0150C] such as Abraham and Sarah could have had at that age, with the woman’s barrenness added—a woman who could not bear even then, when it was not age that failed fertility but fertility that failed age. [Note: [Col. 0150D] Augustine, *City of God*.] That no fruit of posterity was owed even to persons thus situated signifies that human nature, corrupted by sin and therefore justly condemned, deserved no true happiness in the future. Isaac, born through promise and not through generation, signifies children of grace, citizens of the free city, companions in eternal peace.

And because this was to occur not through generation but regeneration, circumcision was commanded when the son was promised from Sarah. Circumcision therefore signifies nature renewed by putting off its oldness. The command to circumcise all sons, home-born slaves, and purchased slaves testifies that this grace belongs to all. The eighth day also signifies Christ, who rose after the Sabbath; the parents’ names too are changed. Everything sounds forth newness: in the Old Testament the New is shadowed, and in the New Testament the Old is revealed.

“But we.” As though he said: Abraham had two sons, one born according to the flesh, the other through promise. But we, brothers, are children of promise, that is, begotten through grace according to Isaac, that is, in Isaac’s likeness. Isaac is interpreted “laughter,” signifying those who serve in joy, not from [Col. 0151A] sadness or necessity.

“But just as.” As though he said: We are children according to Isaac. But just as at that time he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Holy Spirit—[Note: [Col. 0151D] Augustine, on John.] that is, Ishmael persecuted Isaac, or likewise Esau Jacob—so also now: namely, those born according to the flesh persecute those born according to the Spirit.

Who are those born according to the flesh? Lovers of the world, lovers of the age. Who are those born according to the Spirit? [Origen] Lovers of the kingdom of heaven, lovers of Christ, those desiring eternal life, who give thanks to God. The Jews too are born according to the flesh and persecute us, who are born according to the Spirit, because we keep the Law according to the Spirit, not according to the flesh. Therefore by what we suffer [Col. 0151B] we are proved to be children of promise.

“But what does Scripture say?” As though he said: We suffer from them as Isaac from Ishmael, but this is not to be cared about. [Jerome] For what does Scripture say—that is, what does it report that Sarah said? “Behold: Cast out the slave woman and her son.” I do not think that we can find where Ishmael persecuted Isaac; only this is found: that Sarah was indignant when the son of the Egyptian woman played with Isaac. She saw the boys playing together and said, “Cast out,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Augustine, ibid.] What is this? What harm had Ishmael done to the boy Isaac because he played with him? But that play was mockery; that play signified deceit. Sarah understood that sport, and the Apostle called it persecution. [Note: [Col. 0151D] Augustine, sermon on Hagar and Ishmael.] For the sport of the stronger with the weaker is mockery and deception: knowing that he has other purposes which he intends, he pretends certain things to the boy—that is, to the weak person—while playing with him, and practises frauds.

[Note: [Col. 0151D] Augustine, on John.] So too now those who deceive us through mockery persecute us more. And as Sarah understood that play, so the Church understands this play as persecution. But what did Sarah say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” Thus those belonging to Hagar and Ishmael—that is, the Law and the Jews—have been cast out from the Church and from the Father’s grace; likewise heretics and their children.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] Augustine, on Psalm 119.] All also who seek earthly happiness from the Lord within the Church still belong to Ishmael. They oppose those making spiritual progress, speak ill of them, and have wicked lips and deceitful tongues. Therefore Isaac lived with Ishmael: that is, those who belong to Isaac live among those who [Col. 0151D] belong to Ishmael. The one group do not wish to ascend; the other wish to drag [others] downward. [Note: [Col. 0152D] Augustine, *Against the Pelagians*.] The former wish to fly to God; the latter try to pluck out their wings.

And just as these belong to Ishmael and to the Old Testament, so the ancient ministers of the Old Testament, seeking grace, are children of promise belonging to the New Testament. But when will this “Cast out” occur? It will occur when the threshing-floor begins to be winnowed. Hence he adds: “For the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman,” that is, the evil with the good, Jews with Christians. [Augustine] Just as they are unlike in conduct now, so they will be unlike in the future recompense.

“Therefore.” As though he said: Because we suffer from Jews and other evil persons, as Isaac from Ishmael, therefore, my brothers, we are not children of the slave woman. [Ambrose] For we are not slaves of sin or of the Law, but children of the free woman, namely the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the new people of the kingdom of heaven. We are children of the free woman in no other way than through that freedom: “by the freedom,” that is, through the freedom “with which Christ set us free,” he who was free from sin and obedient out of love. The freedom by which Christ has set us free, therefore, is remission of sins and the justification of faith working through love.

## Chapter V

### Verses 1–4

> “Stand firm, and do not again be held under a yoke of slavery. Behold, I Paul say to you: that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. And again I testify to every person who has himself circumcised that he is a debtor to perform the whole Law. You who are justified in the Law have been emptied of Christ; you have fallen from grace.”

“Stand firm.” Thus far he has shown that the Law ought to cease, both by an analogy from human custom and by the authority of the Law itself. Now he exhorts the Galatians not to wish to subject themselves to the yoke of the Law, and terrifies them with a threat of danger. As though he said: And because you are free through Christ, therefore stand firm in steadfast faith, keeping your foot fixed in freedom. And do not be held under the yoke of slavery, that is, the Law which begets into slavery.

He adds “again,” [Col. 0152C] not because the Galatians had previously kept the Law, but because, while they were subjecting themselves to the yoke of circumcision and legal observances, they were returning as it were to the same forms of worship which they had served in formerly in idolatry. For this slavery of the Law is no lighter than idolatry.

“Behold,” as though he said: Do not be held under the yoke of slavery, not even by circumcision alone, because behold, I Paul, whose authority is well known, say to you: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

[Note: [Col. 0152D] Augustine, to Jerome.] Therefore he deceived Timothy and made Christ profit him nothing. This was said, then, to those who wished to be circumcised because they believed they could not otherwise be saved in Christ. Whoever was then circumcised with this mind, will, and intention, Christ profited him nothing. He therefore reproves those who believed themselves justified in the Law, not those who observed those legal ordinances in honour of him by whom they were commanded, understanding both the reason for which they were commanded as a prophecy of truth and how long they ought to endure.

For those things commanded for the sake of signification, which had necessarily to be abolished as the revelation of grace became more widely known, could justify no one. Yet they were not therefore to be shunned as the devilish sacrileges of the Gentiles, even when the grace already began to be revealed which had been foretold through such shadows.

[Note: [Col. 0152D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] Hence the Apostle circumcised Timothy, born of a Jewish mother and Greek father, and himself observed customs of this kind, not by deceitful pretence but by prudent judgment. For circumcision and the other legal observances were not harmful to those born and brought up in them, though they were no longer necessary for signifying future things. It was more harmful to forbid them as though harmful in those people for whom they ought to endure. But Gentiles, coming from the opposite side, as from a wall, to the same cornerstone, were not to be compelled to such observances.

If any who had come from the circumcision and were still devoted to such sacraments wished voluntarily, like Timothy, to maintain a fitting consistency, they were not to be forbidden. But if they trusted in these things, they were lost, as were the Jews. Hence the Apostle’s statement: “I say to you that, if you are circumcised”—so that you place your hope of salvation in circumcision—“Christ will profit you nothing.”

Those whom the faith now revealed found already imbued with these practices were thus permitted to retain them, lest the practices seem rejected rather than concluded. But they were not to be imposed on Gentiles, lest they seem either not to have been instituted to promise Christ, or still to promise him. Rather, by ceasing, they were now to appear as signs that had belonged to the future; they were to be buried gradually with honour, not shunned as Gentile sacrileges. But afterwards, once buried with honour, they were to be abandoned irreparably by all Christians.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Augustine, to Jerome.] Jerome, however, says that these legal observances after Christ’s passion are harmful to those who observe them, whether they put their hope in them or not, unless they are kept by dispensation. According to this view the passage is expounded thus: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing,” because circumcision now not only does no good but also harms. Before the new preaching began, circumcision had to be observed; but now, with the Law of faith succeeding, circumcision added to a believer profits nothing but harms. For it is a greater evil to become a slave from being free than to be born one.

“I testify.” As though he said: If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing; nor will this alone be your evil, but I again testify—as formerly, before faith—to every person, Jew or Gentile, who has himself circumcised in order to obtain righteousness, that he is debtor to perform the entire Law. [Ambrose] That is, he is bound to fulfil all the legal observances demanded by circumcision. For as baptism requires its own justification, so circumcision requires its own.

He says this so that, frightened by the countless observances written in the Law, they may abstain from the practices to which some wished to subject them, lest they be compelled to fulfil all of them—something which neither the Jews themselves nor their fathers could fulfil, as Peter says.

“You have been emptied.” As though he said: Christ truly will profit you nothing, because you who were formerly full of Christ’s grace have been emptied of Christ, [Augustine] that is, of Christ’s virtues. I mean you who “are justified in the Law,” that is, believe that you are justified; otherwise circumcision would not harm. You have been emptied, I say, and have fallen from the grace to come. [Ambrose] That is, you are unworthy of eternal blessedness. Or, “you have fallen from grace” [Col. 0154A] already possessed, that is, you have lost grace. For whoever wishes to be justified in the Law after faith loses grace, because God’s gift and grace came for this purpose: that, once the burden of the Law had ceased, it might justify believers. Whoever restores that burden loses this grace.

### Verses 5–10

> “For we, by the Spirit and from faith, await the hope of righteousness. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love. You were running well. Who hindered you from obeying the truth? Do not yield assent to anyone. This persuasion is not from him who called you. A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. I am confident concerning you in the Lord that you will think nothing else. But whoever troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.”

[Col. 0154B] **For we.** As though he said: Whoever trusts in the Law loses grace. The contrary may seem to be the case, because we await, from faith, the hope of righteousness—that is, righteousness and hope, namely eternal blessedness. [Note: [Col. 0153D] The same author, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*] Or, “the hope of righteousness” means the hope by which righteousness itself is hoped for. [Augustine] For faith, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, hopes to be renewed and to advance in it. Or, the hope of righteousness is Christ, from whom righteousness itself is hoped for. We await, I say; and we do this by the Spirit—that is, through the Holy Spirit, who does not deceive. [Jerome] He says this lest we should be thought to be deceived.

“For in Christ,” etc. As though he said: I rightly say that righteousness is from faith, because it is not from anything else. For for those who are in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; circumcision is made equal to [Col. 0154C] uncircumcision. For those who desire to live in Christ must seek virtues and flee vices. [Note: [Col. 0154D] The same author, *On the Epistle of John.*] But things intermediate between virtues and vices are neither to be fled nor sought, such as circumcision and uncircumcision, which count for nothing in Christ; rather, what counts is faith—not, of course, an idle faith, since faith without works is dead, that is, it does not save—but faith which works through love of God and neighbor. The work of faith is love itself; without love faith is empty; with love, it belongs to the Christian. [Note: [Col. 0154D] The same author, *Sermons of the Lord.*] The other kind—that is, faith without love—is the faith of a demon. For demons too believe and tremble (James 2); and those who do not believe are slower and worse than demons.

But there is a great difference between believing that Christ exists and believing in Christ. For the demons [Col. 0154D] believed that he is Christ. The person who believes in Christ is one who hopes in Christ and loves Christ.

**You were running.** Here he praises the Galatians, reproves those through whom they were induced to wish to Judaize, and warns them not to agree with such persons. As though he said: Faith working through love is effective, and this was once present among you; for formerly you were running by advancing through works of faith, and doing so well, because you acted from love. [Ambrose] Therefore, who bewitched or hindered you from obeying the truth, which offers itself freely? He testifies that their practice in the works of faith had been good, but that they were hindered by the malice of evil people, so that they might not complete their course with persevering effectiveness. Therefore, urging them to trust none of these people, he adds: [Col. 0155A] “But henceforth do not consent to any of them,” not even by listening to those who urge the observance of works of the Law and thereby prevent obedience to evangelical truth.

**For this persuasion.** As though he said: Will you therefore agree because this persuasion, by which they wish to place you under the yoke of the Law, is from him—that is, God—who called you to life? It is not; it is from the devil. [Augustine] Therefore do not agree, because “a little leaven”—that is, those few sour people who came among them to urge these things—or “a little leaven,” meaning this persuasion, or this circumcision and the few observances of the Law, corrupts the whole lump, that is, the congregation of believers or virtue itself.

The meaning, then, is this: Do not suppose that the snares of a few people should be despised. For a spark is a small thing [Col. 0155B] and, while it is seen, is scarcely seen at all; yet, if it catches hold of fuel and finds sustenance for itself, it consumes walls, very great cities, forests, 158 regions. Likewise leaven seems a slight and worthless thing; but once it has been mixed into flour and has corrupted the whole lump by its power, everything mixed with it passes into its own character. So too perverse teaching, beginning with one person, at first finds scarcely two or three hearers; but gradually it spreads like cancer through the body. And, according to the common proverb: “The scab of one sheep defiles the whole flock.” Therefore, when a spark appears, it must be extinguished; leaven must be removed from the neighboring lump; and a scabbed animal must be separated from the sheepfold. This is what I urge upon you.

And I am confident concerning you, because you were formerly good; and I do not simply say “confident concerning you,” but add “in the Lord,” that is, with God at work. I am confident, I say, that you will think nothing other than what I have taught. He says that he is confident concerning them because they erred not voluntarily but through deception; and thus, now that the true way has been shown, he believes they will readily return.

**But whoever.** As though he said: I am confident concerning you, but the one who troubles you—as though he said: the one who disturbs the pure fountain of your understanding, so that by a reversal of order you become carnal instead of spiritual—will bear judgment. [Ambrose] That is, he will endure condemnation, whoever he may be. Even if he is Abraham’s son according to the flesh, no favor will be shown him. [Jerome] Some say that Paul is covertly attacking Peter, to whom he wrote above that he had withstood him to his face because he had not walked rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. But [Col. 0155D] Paul would not speak with so insolent a curse against the prince of the Church; nor was Peter worthy to bear the judgment for troubling the Church. Therefore it should be understood of someone who either had been with the apostles, or had come from Judea, or had believed from among the Pharisees, or at least was greatly esteemed among the Galatians, so as to bear judgment for troubling the Church. [Ambrose] For just as one who causes an erring person to turn back deserves reward, so one who turns a person walking the right road aside onto a byway incurs condemnation.

### Verses 11–16

> “But I, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still persecuted? Then the offense of the cross has been removed. Would that those who trouble you would even cut themselves off! For you, brothers, were called to freedom; only do not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh, but through the love of the Spirit serve one another. For the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ But if you bite and devour one another, beware lest you be consumed by one another. But I say in Christ: Walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.”

**But I.** As though he said: The one who troubles you will bear judgment. But I do not trouble you, brothers, by preaching legal observances. For if I still preach circumcision, as I once did and as is alleged against me—[Augustine] for it must be understood that the false teachers who wished to persuade the Galatians into this slavery alleged that he preached circumcision elsewhere, but did not wish easily to reveal his own judgment [Col. 0156B] to them—if, I say, I do this, why do I still suffer persecutions? As though he said: I suffer from the Jews for no other cause. [Ambrose] For he endured very frequent persecutions from the Jews because he taught that believers from the Gentiles ought not to be circumcised. [Jerome] And if I preach it, then the offense of the cross has been removed: the Jews would not be angry over the cross if I maintained that circumcision justifies. The preaching of the cross was an offense to the Jews because it abolished Sabbath observance and circumcision; but if he admitted circumcision, it would not be an offense, and they would be at peace with him.

**Would that.** As though he said: They trouble you. And would that those who trouble you might cut themselves off! These words express not so much rage against opponents as love for the Church. For he did not so much curse them as pray [Col. 0156C] for them. [Augustine] Under the appearance of a curse, using an elegant ambiguity, he wishes them good when he says: “Would that those who trouble you would cut themselves off!” Not merely that they be circumcised, but that they be cut off, so that they may become eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven and cease to sow carnal things. For there are some eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. Or thus: They trouble you, but would that those who trouble you might be cut off—not carnally, but lose the power of begetting, so that they may make no progress in you or in others; not merely circumcised but also cut off, so that they possess no power whatever to beget. And I rightly wish this, lest they reduce you to the slavery of the Law.

[Ambrose] For you, brothers, were called by God to freedom, so that you might serve not from fear but from love; and, though you were formerly subject to sins, you might become free by receiving God’s grace. [Augustine] And since this is so, only this is necessary: do not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh. That is, do not abuse freedom by following the desires of the flesh because you are free and the fear of the Law no longer hangs over you; for then you will be slaves. The sense is: Beware lest, upon hearing the name of freedom, you suppose that you may sin with impunity. But through the love of the Spirit—that is, love proceeding from the Holy Spirit—serve one another, for then you will be free. Note that love is not to be possessed through an affection of the flesh, but through the Spirit, so that you may be subject to one another.

**For the whole Law.** As though he said: Love must therefore be possessed, because the whole Law is fulfilled in one saying—that is, in one commandment of love—since the person who keeps that commandment neither does evil nor, so far as he can, fails to do good. In which commandment is it fulfilled? In this: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” This is written in Leviticus. [Ambrose, Augustine] He rightly says that the entire Law is fulfilled in this commandment, even though there are two commandments of love on which the whole Law and the Prophets hang, because love of God is contained in love of neighbor. Thus the perfection of salvation is in this commandment, because God is not loved without one’s neighbor. For how can one who does not love a neighbor whom one sees love God, whom one does not see? (1 John 4.) Again, who can love a neighbor—that is, every human being—as oneself, unless one loves God, by whose command and gift one can fulfill love of neighbor? Therefore, since the two commandments are such that neither can [Col. 0157B] be kept without the other, it is enough to mention one of them.

And note that he says, “as yourself.” Just as a person cannot love a neighbor who does not love himself. But a person does not love himself if he loves iniquity. “For he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10). Note also that he says, “the whole Law.” For both those matters that pertain to good morals and those contained in the sacraments must be referred to love, when they are rightly understood by free persons and not carnally observed by slaves.

**But if.** As though he said: The Law is fulfilled in love of neighbor. But if you bite one another—that is, speak ill of one another in some respect—and devour one another, that is, consume everything by faultfinding out of envy; [Ambrose] or accuse one another, bringing accusations against each other: beware lest you be consumed by one another, the unity of Christian religion having been torn apart through vain glory and vain victory. He touched on this vice because of his discussion of love, since discord is the enemy of love. For through this chief vice of contention and envy, destructive quarrels were nourished among them, by which fellowship and life are consumed.

**But I say.** Having forbidden them the law of deeds, in which there are carnal commands, he now commands them to restrain themselves from the vices of the flesh. He shows how sufficient the faith of Christ is without the Law, because by it they overcome the flesh and its works and follow the Spirit. As though he said: Do not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh, but serve through love of the Spirit. I say that this can be yours in Christ, that is, through faith in Christ, and never otherwise. In that faith [Col. 0157D] walk, that is, advance by doing good works; and do this by the spirit, that is, by reason, or rather by the Holy Spirit. For the human spirit cannot do this by itself. Then you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh—that is, the pleasures which the flesh suggests. He does not say, “You will not do them” or “You will not have them,” because they could not avoid having them; but, “You will not fulfill them.” [Note: [Col. 0157D] Augustine, *Against Julian.*] That is, you will not carry their works out by the consent of your will.

### Verses 17–21

> “For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do whatever things you wish. But if you are led by the Spirit, [Col. 0158A] you are not under the Law. Now the works of the flesh are evident: fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, luxury, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, outbursts of anger, strife, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these. I tell you beforehand, as I told you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

**For the flesh—or, but.** As though he said: I say, “You will not fulfill them,” but this is difficult, because the flesh desires. Or the connection may be made thus: Therefore act in this way, because the struggle is severe. And this is what he says: “For the flesh desires.” As though he said: Being ever new in this respect, it desires against the Spirit. This is evident in the good, in whom the Spirit of God is present.

**But the Spirit.** As though he said: Yet one must not despair, because the spirit—that is, reason aided by the grace of God—desires against the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0157D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle.*] See what kind of war, what kind of conflict, he has set before you: you feel it within yourself. For it is no small vice when the flesh desires against the Spirit; and the virtue contrary to that vice is present when the spirit desires against the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0157D] The same author, in the sermon *On Continence.*]

The flesh is said to desire because the soul acts in this way according to the flesh, just as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, although it is rather the soul that hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For the flesh itself desires nothing except through the soul; but it is said to desire when the soul, by carnal desire, resists the spirit. [Note: [Col. 0158D] The same author, *On Genesis.*] Thus by “the flesh desiring” he means carnal pleasure, which the spirit has from the flesh and through the flesh, in opposition to the pleasure which it has by itself alone. The cause of this carnal desire, however, is not in the soul alone nor in the flesh alone. It arises from both, because without both no pleasure is felt.

**For these.** As though he said: These desire against each other, because they are so opposed to one another that you are not allowed to do whatever good or evil things you wish; and in this conflict one must yield to the better—that is, to the Spirit, by which we will good things, although we do not accomplish all of them. [Note: [Col. 0158D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle.*] For we wish there to be no desires at all, but we do not accomplish this.

**But if by the Spirit.** As though he said: These two fight. But if you are led by the Holy Spirit, the governor and ruler of your spirit—he says this lest they be idle in the struggle—[Ambrose] if, I say, this is so, you are not under the Law, which is laid down for those who err and do evil. But a person who has the Holy Spirit as guide does not err. [Jerome] Observe that he says, “If you are led by the Spirit,” etc. From this it appears that one who is under the Law, not by way of dispensation but truly, as you understand it, does not possess the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0158D] The same author, *To Jerome.*]

It seems to me a great question what it means to be under the Law in the sense censured by the Apostle. He says that those are damnably under the Law whom the Law renders guilty: they do not fulfill the Law, because, ignorant of grace, they presumptuously rely upon themselves in proud self-exaltation. A person is under the Law if he ceases from an evil work because of fear of the punishment threatened by the Law, not because of love of righteousness; he is guilty in will, not yet free and not free from the will to sin, because, if possible, he would wish that there were nothing to fear, so that he might freely do what he secretly desires. [Note: [Col. 0159D] The same author, *On Nature and Grace.*] The meaning is: If you are led by the Spirit, you already have this advantage: you are not under the Law, which instills fear but does not grant love. Therefore this path must now be chosen, by which we are freed from the Law.

**Now the works are evident.** He begins to enumerate the works of the flesh, so that they may understand that, if they consent to the desires of the flesh so as to perform these things, they are then led by the flesh rather than by the Spirit. As though he said: These are opposed to one another; but the works of the flesh are manifest—that is, evil in themselves is evident—which are fornication, namely the work of lust; uncleanness, even if it is not completed in act; or shamelessness, which is contrary to nature, an unchaste manner of life. [Col. 0159B] Luxury is every kind of excess; service of idols; sorceries; enduring enmities; quarrels in words; rivalries, when two people strive for the same thing; anger, namely a sudden storm of the mind; strife, when from anger they strike each other; dissensions, when they form parties in the Church; sects, which in Greek are called heresies; envies, at the good things of others; murders; habitual drunkennesses; excessive revelries; and things like these.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The same author, *The City of God.*] Observe that not all those things enumerated among the works of the flesh, which he called manifest, belong to the pleasure of the flesh; rather, some are vices of the mind, such as enmities and angers. It is also an error to believe that every evil comes to the soul from the flesh. For not all vices of an unrighteous life should be attributed [Col. 0159C] to the flesh, lest we absolve the devil of all of them, though he has no flesh. But by the name “flesh” he signified the whole human being, who falls into these things by living according to himself—that is, according to the flesh. For a human being became like the devil not by having flesh, but by living according to himself, that is, according to man; since the devil too wished to live according to himself when he did not stand in the truth.

To deter them from these things by threatening punishment, he adds: “I now tell you beforehand,” before judgment, while repentance is permitted, “as I told you before,” even before this letter, “that those who do such things will not inherit,” or possess, “the kingdom of God.” [Note: [Col. 0159D] The same author, in the same work.] He does not say, “Those who have done all these things,” or “who have had them all at once,” but “those who do such things,” because even individual things take away the kingdom of God. This apostolic statement would be false if such persons, after however long a time, were to be set free and possess the kingdom of God. But because it is not false, they certainly will not possess the kingdom of God. And if they will never be in the kingdom of God, they will be held in eternal punishment, because there is no middle place where one is not under punishment if one is not restored to that kingdom.

### Verses 22–26

> “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, moderation, self-control, chastity. Against such things there is no Law. But those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. If we live by the Spirit, [Col. 0160A] let us also walk by the Spirit. Let us not become desirous of vain glory, provoking one another and envying one another.”

**But the fruit.** As though he said: The things I have enumerated are works of the flesh, but these that follow are works of the Spirit. Yet he calls them not works but fruits, because they are to be sought for their own sake. This is what he says: “But the fruit of the Spirit”—that is, of the Holy Spirit, or of grace enlightening reason—is love, which calls from earth to heaven; joy, namely purity of conscience and an exaltation of mind over those things worthy of exultation. Of this it is written: “The wicked have no joy, says the Lord.” Peace is when they do not disturb themselves; patience is toward adversaries; long-suffering is in waiting; goodness is sweetness of mind; kindness is generosity with possessions; gentleness is the quality by which a person is not [Col. 0160B] unyielding but rather teachable; faith is certainty concerning invisible things; moderation preserves measure in words and deeds; self-control abstains even from lawful things; chastity rightly uses what is lawful.

Observe that, in his enumeration of the fruits of the Spirit, he set love first as the head of the virtues. For what other fruit of the Spirit ought to hold first place but love, without which the other virtues are not counted as virtues, and from which every good thing is born? [Note: [Col. 0160D] Augustine, *On John.*] Then follow the members born from and connected to this head: joy and peace, and so forth, which cannot profit without it. For one does not rejoice well unless one loves the good in which one rejoices; one has no true peace with anyone unless one loves that person; one is not long-suffering in persevering expectation unless one burns with love; one is not kind unless one loves the person one helps; one is not good except through love; one is not soundly faithful except by that faith which works through love; one is not gentle unless love moderates one; no one restrains oneself from that by which one is disgraced unless one loves that by which one is made honorable. Therefore he rightly commends love so often as though it alone needed to be commanded, since it cannot be possessed without the other qualities by which a person becomes good.

**Against such things.** As though he said: Why should I speak of each individually? The Law, which is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous, is not against such things, but against evils.

**But those who belong to Christ.** As though he said: The Law is laid down against the wicked; but upon the good the cross has been imposed. He says this as follows: Those who belong to Christ, whom it is necessary to follow the Spirit, have crucified—that is, mortified—their flesh, in struggle, with the vices of their deeds and the desires of their appetites. [Note: [Col. 0160D] The same author, in the sermon *On Lent.*] For it accords with our devotion that, as we celebrate the passion of our crucified Lord, we make for ourselves a cross by repressing carnal pleasures. On this cross the Christian ought always to hang during this life, fixed by nails—that is, by the commandments of righteousness—as Christ was fixed to the cross by nails.

**If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit.** What he stated above in general he directs to those to whom he writes, and includes himself among them, thereby showing [Col. 0161A] that he is not telling them something which he himself does not wish to observe. As though he said: Those who belong to Christ act as I have said; and let us, who belong to Christ, walk with the Holy Spirit as guide and author of our freedom. “If” means “since”: since we live by the Spirit—that is, since we have come to this life of grace through the Holy Spirit.

He teaches how we should walk by the Spirit by adding: Let us not become desirous of vain—that is, worldly—glory. Vain glory is wishing to win where there is no reward. Let us not, I say, provoke one another to contention, litigation, and other unlawful things, nor envy one another if we dare not provoke them. Vain glory produces these evils. And it should be known that, although the venom of the ancient enemy is poured into the human heart through every vice, the serpent shakes all its entrails in the zeal of envy, and in impressing this malice stirs up something like a plague. [Cyprian] This jealousy knows no measure, continuing constantly without end, whereas other crimes come to an end. And the more successfully the person envied advances, the more the envious person is inflamed into a greater blaze by the fires of spite. Hence come a threatening face, a grim look, pallor in the face, trembling in the lips, grinding of teeth, furious words and unrestrained insults, hands ready for violence; and even if for the moment they are empty of a sword, they are armed with the hatred of a maddened mind.

## Chapter VI

### Verses 1–4

> “Brothers, even if someone should be overtaken in some transgression, you who are spiritual instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, [Col. 0161C] and so fulfill the law of Christ. For if anyone thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. But let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone and not in another.”

**Brothers, even if someone should be overtaken**, etc. [Ambrose] Up to this point he has spoken to the whole Church of Galatia, indeed to the universal Church, rejecting the Law and commending grace. Now he speaks particularly to prelates, teaching them how to deal with subjects: namely, gently, because they are brothers, even if they are superiors. [Augustine] He addresses those who were stronger so that, through the pride of a good life, they may not think that one ensnared by sin is to be despised and cast aside.

As though he said: Do not do what I have described; but even if someone has been overtaken—that is, has fallen unwittingly so as to be unable to avoid it—and this is no wonder, since he is a human being, that is, weak, overtaken, I speak not of one sinning habitually in many matters, but “in some transgression.” If this occurs, you who are spiritual should not therefore despise him, but instruct the person who is not given over to individual sins and who only occasionally falls, in a spirit of gentleness—that is, reasonably and gently—lest, if you act otherwise, he refuse to endure correction and begin to defend himself lest he seem shameful. Therefore instruct gently, because you are brothers, even though superiors.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Augustine, in the book *Questions on Leviticus.*] Observe that “transgression” is properly said, and what being overtaken is, because he says, “overtaken in some transgression,” so that, once these are understood, you may understand that a brother overtaken in transgression ought to be forgiven. A transgression, perhaps, is turning aside from good. Sin is doing evil. Or, just as in a praiseworthy life it is one thing to turn aside from evil and another to do good, as Scripture admonishes when it says, “Turn aside from evil and do good” (Psalm 36), so in a blameworthy life it is one thing to turn aside from good and another to do evil: the former is transgression, the latter sin.

[Augustine] Sin, therefore, is the committing of evil; transgression is the abandonment of good, as the very name indicates. For what else does *delictum* sound like but “something abandoned”; and what does one abandon when one commits a transgression except the good? Or it may seem that transgression is what is done unknowingly, while sin is what is committed knowingly. Yet they are often used interchangeably, so that [Col. 0162B] sin may be called by the name transgression and transgression by the name sin. [Note: [Col. 0161D] The same author, in the book *Against Lying.*] Being overtaken, however, occurs when, either for a time, what should be done is not perceived, or those who have perceived it are overcome, so that evil is done either when truth is hidden or when weakness compels.

**Considering.** As though he said: Whoever you are, act as I have said, considering yourself, because you too are frail, lest you too be tempted—that is, lest, with God permitting it, you fall into a similar thing. [Augustine] Nothing inclines a person toward mercy so much as the thought of one’s own danger. Thus he did not wish them either to fail in correcting their brothers or to devote themselves to contention. Therefore, lest anyone imagine that he is instructing another even while insolently harassing, mocking, or proudly detesting the sinner as incurable, he says: “Instruct him in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you too be tempted.”

**Bear one another’s burdens.** As though he said: I say, instruct gently, and also bear burdens: let each bear the weaknesses of another. “Burdens” means assist one another through prayers and other such means, as though these were your own load. And so you will fulfill the law of Christ—that is, love. For Christ bore our sins out of love, and he also commanded that we love one another.

**For**, etc. As though he said: Do as I have said. For if anyone acts otherwise, he deceives himself. This is what he says: If anyone thinks—that is, proudly judges in his mind that he is something great in comparison with the sinner—when he is nevertheless nothing of himself, or nothing in comparison with the spiritual person who attributes everything to grace, he deceives himself; that is, he separates himself from [Col. 0162D] truth. His flatterers do not deceive him, but he rather deceives himself, because, although he is more present to himself than they are, he prefers to seek himself in them rather than in himself.

Therefore he adds: **But let each test his own work.** As though he said: Let no one think in that manner; rather, let each person test—that is, carefully examine—his own work, not another’s sin, like the Pharisee who said, “I am not like other men,” and who was righteous not in reality but falsely. Let him test his own work, I say, and thus—[Ambrose] that is, if he considers his own actions, knowing that whatever good he has he has received from God, and that whatever evil there is comes from himself—he will have glory in himself; that is, he will glory in God, whom he has within himself, carrying oil with him. [Note: [Col. 0162D] The same author, *On John.*] [Col. 0163A] And not in another: thus God, who is in him, will be his glory, and nothing else.

Or, “in himself” means inwardly, in his pure conscience: there he will have glory, that is, he will glory and rejoice. “And not in another” means not in another’s praise, namely when another praises him. [Augustine, Jerome] For someone conscious of a good work should not glory in it before another or pour his praise outward, but should glory humbly in himself. [Ambrose] Or thus: if he considers his actions, knowing that no one ought to glory that he has a clean heart, he will have glory in himself and not in another—that is, he will glory in consideration of himself, not another. For he sets himself before no one and judges no one, in order that he may truly be righteous. For one who is truly righteous sets another before himself, because [Col. 0163B] he knows his own evils better than those of another; knowledge of these is his glory. For he rejoices when he recognizes the disease which he desires to heal.

### Verses 5–8

> “For each person will bear his own burden. But let the one who is instructed in the word share with the one who instructs him in all good things. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; but the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

**For each person.** As though he said: I say that each person should test his own work, and this he ought to do, for he will be judged concerning his own work. For each person will bear his own burden—that is, his sin—in punishment. [Col. 0163C] What is said here appears contrary to what precedes, where he says, “Bear one another’s burdens.” But it is not contrary, because the word “burden” is understood in different ways.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Gospels.*] For there are many words which, appropriately used in different places, are understood differently, as here. Unless you take the word “burden” in different senses, you will undoubtedly think him contradictory to himself in words placed so close together: for though shortly before he said, “Bear one another’s burdens,” here he says, “Each person will bear his own burden.” [Note: [Col. 0164D] The same author, *On the Words of the Apostle.*] But there are burdens of shared weakness, of which he spoke above; and burdens of rendering account to God for our deeds, of which he speaks here. The former are shared by being supported with brothers; the latter are borne individually by each person. These burdens are sins. There are therefore some matters in which each bears his own burden, does not bear it with another, and does not cast it onto another; and others that are borne with others and for others.

Again, he says these things with different people in view. For against those who think that a person is defiled by the sins of others, he says: “Each person will bear his own burden.” No one is defiled by another’s sin unless, by consenting to it or imitating it, one makes it one’s own. Again, against the negligent, who care to correct no one because they are secure in the thought that they are not contaminated by other people’s sins, he says: “Bear one another’s burdens.” We bear one another’s burdens of weakness when we patiently endure another’s anger and, when the person who injured us asks, forgive him, [Col. 0164A] and in similar ways.

[Jerome] Or “burden” is understood as a good work. For in Scripture *onus* (“burden”) is taken in both a good and a bad sense. The meaning is: Each person will bear his own burden—that is, on the day of judgment he will offer to God sheaves of his works. Hence: “Those who come shall come with exultation, bearing their sheaves” (Psalm 125). This is understood only of good things. Or it may be said of good and bad alike: Each person, good or evil, will bear his own burden—that is, will receive the recompense of his own works.

But let him share. Above he told spiritual prelates how they ought to conduct themselves toward their subjects; here he speaks to subjects, teaching how they ought to conduct themselves toward their teachers. As though he said: Let prelates conduct themselves as I have said. But let him who is catechized—that is, instructed—even if only by word and not by example, share with him in all the good things which he says, not in evil things if he does them; so that the law may be your guide, not the man. That is, let one who hears the word show himself a partner with the teacher by receiving and putting into practice what he has said. And lest anyone say, “I ought not to do anything unless I see it in him,” he adds: Do not be deceived, for it is an error to say this. And even if you excuse yourselves on that account before people, God is not mocked—that is, he cannot be deceived. [Ambrose] For it is certain that no deception can be practiced upon God; rather, each person receives from him what he deserves. And indeed he is not deceived, because he will repay each according to deserts: Whatever a man has sown.

Or this may be said differently, so as to exhort subjects to give temporal things to the prelates from whom they receive spiritual things. He therefore urges disciples to provide relief for their teachers, saying: Let him who is catechized—that is, instructed—in the word share with him who catechizes him in all his good things; that is, let him make all his goods common with him. For it is a customary precept that the person to whom the word of God is preached should supply necessities to the preacher; and he rightly designated these as “good things,” just as the Lord also, speaking with his disciples in the Gospel, said: “Though you are evil, you know how to give good gifts to your children” (Luke 11). [Jerome] Above all, provision should be made for those who, because of the opportunities of place, time, or any circumstances whatever, are more closely joined to you.

But foreseeing that some would plead poverty and wish to evade the precept, he adds: Do not be deceived; God is not [Col. 0164D] mocked. As though he said: Let no one excuse himself vainly, for God cannot be deceived. He knows our hearts and is not ignorant of our resources. A plausible excuse may appease a human being; it cannot deceive God. [Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome] And indeed he is not mocked, for whatever a man has sown through the labor of this present life, that he will also reap—that is, he will receive the reward of these things. And this is true because he who sows in his flesh, so as to reap from the flesh—that is, he who sows and fosters carnal vices, and who does everything he does, even if some things appear good, in order that he may fare well carnally, and who understands the law carnally—will also reap from the flesh a fitting harvest, namely corruption. For nothing suits the flesh better than [Col. 0165A] corruption. But he who sows in the Spirit, [Ambrose] that is, who gives assent to the Spirit through faith, serving righteousness with charity and understanding the law spiritually, will also reap from the Spirit a fitting harvest, namely eternal life. [Augustine] Observe that man consists of spirit and flesh. Therefore he sows in spirit and flesh. Moreover, even the Christian man is flesh in comparison with the Holy Spirit. It must also be observed that when he says, “he who sows in the flesh,” he adds “his own”; but when he says “in the Spirit,” he does not add “his own.” For carnal seed comes from man, while spiritual seed comes from the Spirit of God. This harvest, however, is promised at the end. Therefore perseverance is necessary in sowing. Hence he adds:

### Verses 9–13

> “But let us not grow weary while doing good; for in due season we shall reap, if we do not give way. Therefore, while we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith. See in what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. For all who wish to make a good appearance in the flesh compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ. For even those who are circumcised do not keep the law; but they want you to be circumcised, so that they may glory in your flesh.”

But let us not grow weary. As though he said: Let prelates conduct themselves toward subjects, and subjects toward prelates, as I have said. But let neither group—namely, prelates and subjects—grow weary in doing good, because one who will not fail in reaping ought not to fail in working. If a man does not set an end to his work, neither will God [Col. 0165C] set an end to his reward. As much as we persevere in works, so much shall we reap in fruits; and as much as the longing of the seeker expands, so much the hand of the rewarder will open itself to the reward. For each will receive as he acts: whoever is vigorous in sowing will be vigorous in reaping.

Hence he adds: For in its own time—that is, at the fitting time—we shall reap, without failing. Observe that he says, “in its own time.” God certainly does not immediately do whatever is prayed for unto salvation; nor does he deny it because he delays it, but grants it in his own—that is, fitting—time. And because we shall reap without failing, therefore, while we have in this life the time for sowing, let us do good. [Jerome] The present life through which we are running is the time of sowing; in it we are permitted to sow whatever we wish. But when it has passed, the time for working will be taken away. Hence: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one will any longer be able to work” (John 9).

Let us do good, I say, to all, so that love may be perfect; but especially to those of the household of faith, that is, to those who belong to our family through faith—that is, to Christians. For eternal life ought to be desired for all with equal love, though the same offices of love cannot be rendered to everyone; these ought especially to be rendered to brothers, because we ought to be more ready and inclined toward good in relation to brothers, since we are members of one another. For if the reins of liberality are loosened toward all, they should be loosened especially toward members of the household—that is, Christians—[Col. 0166A] who have the same Father and are designated by the name of the same teacher. [Note: [Col. 0165D] Augustine, on Psalm 111.] Mercy, then, is to be bestowed upon all; among them the righteous, who are of faith, are to be preferred.

That good should be done even to all our enemies who are wicked and persecute the Church is witnessed by God, who says: “Do good to those who hate you; love your enemies” (Matthew 5). There he plainly shows that the bowels of mercy are not to be closed against sinners, not even if they bear a hostile mind toward us, because they too are human beings. This is confirmed by the example of God the Father, who “makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (ibid.).

Yet some think that alms ought to be given only to the righteous, and that nothing ought to be given to sinners, lest we strive against God if we wish to assist those whom he wishes to punish. They also bring forward testimonies of Holy Scripture. For Scripture says: “Give mercy, and do not receive a sinner; and render vengeance to the ungodly and to sinners. Do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly, because the Most High also hates sinners and will render vengeance to the ungodly” (Sirach 12). Not understanding how these words are to be received, they clothe themselves in detestable cruelty. We must therefore explain to your charity how they are to be understood.

These things were said so that you should not do good to a sinner because he is a sinner, but because he is a human being; so that you may neither be lax in judging nor inhuman in assisting. Thus you will keep both precepts: hate in him what God [Col. 0166C] hates—that is, the fact that he is evil—and rebuke and persecute it, so that you destroy what man has made and preserve what he is. For man made sin, but God made man. And do not receive a sinner in the sense of wishing him to be saved in that in which he is evil; rather, receive him because he is human, so that mercy is closed to no human being and impunity is relaxed for no sinner. Let us therefore pursue in evil persons their own wickedness, and have mercy upon the common condition in those same persons.

See, etc. [Ambrose] After exhorting them to better works, he returns to that which had been dealt with earlier: namely, that legal observances should not be retained. [Jerome] But lest anyone deceive the unsuspecting under his name, he completes the end of the Epistle with writing in his own hand [Col. 0166D]. For from this point to the end he wrote with his own hand. As though he said: So that you may hold the things already said more firmly, see in what sort of writing I have written to you with my own hand, so that you may know that this Epistle was sent by me and thus obey the more readily.

For all who wish. As though he said: It was necessary that I should write, because false teachers are pressing you. And this is the meaning: All who wish to please unbelieving Jews in the flesh—that is, in carnal observances—compel you to be circumcised; they are led by perversity, not by reason. And they do this for one reason only: that they may not suffer from unbelieving Jews persecution of Christ, that is, persecution inflicted for the cross of Christ. [Ambrose] These were false teachers who preached Christ in such a way as also to teach that the law must be kept. They preached the cross in order to receive gain from believers; the law, in order to please the Jews.

[Jerome] Or perhaps he says this because the Romans—namely Gaius Caesar and Octavian Augustus—promulgated laws that Jews, wherever they were, might live according to their own rite and serve their ancestral ceremonies. Therefore, anyone circumcised, even if he believed in Christ, was regarded among the nations as a Jew. But whoever, being uncircumcised, declared by his foreskin that he was not a Jew became liable to persecutions both from Gentiles and from Jews. Those, therefore, who had corrupted the Galatians, wishing to avoid these persecutions, urged circumcision upon their disciples as a defense. For neither Jews nor Gentiles could persecute those whom they saw both circumcising proselytes [Col. 0167B] and themselves observing legal rites.

For even those who are circumcised. As though he said: They truly do this only to avoid persecution; they do not do it out of love for the law. For even those who are circumcised do not keep the law. [Augustine] He means that observance of the law consisting in not killing, not committing adultery, and other such things belonging to good morals. These cannot be fulfilled except through charity and the hope of eternal goods, which are received through faith, as has already been said. But they wish you to be circumcised so that they may glory in your flesh [Ambrose]—that is, in your carnal circumcision, in which you suffer pain—before the Jews, because they make so many proselytes.

### Verses 14–18

> “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation. And as many as shall follow this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. Henceforth let no one trouble me; for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.”

But far be it from me. [Note: [Col. 0167D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] As though he said: They glory in the flesh, but far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Behold: where the philosopher of this world blushed, there the Apostle found treasure; what seemed folly to them became wisdom [Col. 0167D] and glory to the Apostle. [Note: [Col. 0167D] Id., in a sermon on the Passion of Christ.] Therefore do not be ashamed of the cross of Christ. Recall your forehead, so that you may not fear another’s tongue. In order that we might not be ashamed of this cross, we placed it upon the forehead itself—that is, in the dwelling-place of shame. For this reason the cross is fixed upon the forehead of believers, where the seat of modesty is, so that faith may not be ashamed of his name and may love God’s glory more than human glory.

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Id., on John.] Circumcision in hidden flesh is the sign of the Old Testament; the cross on the uncovered forehead is the sign of the New Testament. There is concealment there; here there is revelation. There, beneath a veil; here, with unveiled face. [Note: [Col. 0168D] Id., *On the Words of the Apostle*.] The Lord, moreover, carrying the cross upon his own shoulder in order that we might glory in it, commended it to us in place of a royal scepter. This [Col. 0168A] is great mockery to the ungodly, a great mystery to the devout. Therefore let us not be ashamed of the reproach and disfigurement of Christ, but venerate it. For Christ’s disfigurement gives you form; unless he had been willing to be disfigured, you would not have recovered the form you had lost. He hung disfigured upon the cross, but his disfigurement was our beauty. Therefore let us glory in this disfigurement, whose sign we bear upon our forehead. Let us not be ashamed of this disfigurement, but rejoice with the Apostle, who says that he glories in Christ’s cross.

He could have said, “in wisdom,” “in power,” “in majesty,” and he would have spoken truly. Yet it is a great thing to glory in the wisdom, majesty, or power of God; but it is greater to glory in the cross. This is what the ungodly insults and the philosopher mocks. And as though someone said, “Why do you glory in the cross? [Col. 0168B] What profit is there in it?” [Augustine] Behold the answer: Through him—that is, Christ crucified—the world has been crucified to me, so that it does not hold me, and I to the world, so that I do not hold it. For I desire nothing in the world, nor does it recognize anything of its own in me, as the Lord says: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). The sense is: Through Christ’s cross the desires of the world have no dominion over me; the world no longer presses itself upon me, and I am strong against it.

Observe that he did not say without reason both that the world was crucified to him and that he was crucified to the world. For it often happens that a man does not hold the world in his mind, yet the world binds him by its desires or occupations. The man is dead [Col. 0168C] to the world, while the world, as though living, desires him, striving to carry away into its pursuits one who is intent on something else. But Paul neither desires the world nor is desired by the world, so that among two dead things neither sees the other. Therefore, because Paul neither sought the world’s glory nor was himself sought by worldly glory, he gloried that he was crucified both to the world and that the world was crucified to him.

For in Christ. As though he said: This is why I glory only in Christ: because in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision. As though he said: Foreskin and circumcision are equal before God, but what counts is a new creation—that is, regeneration and new life. For by “new creation” he means new life through faith in Christ. I glory in the cross; and upon all who have followed [Col. 0168D] this rule—that is, this right way of glorying—peace, namely tranquility of mind, and mercy for sins, namely the remission of sins, shall be from God, upon them, the Gentiles, and also upon Israel—that is, the Jews—not carnal Israel, of course, but those who are God’s, that is, spiritual Israel. [Ambrose] For here he indicated two groups upon which the peace and mercy of God remain: believing Gentiles and believing Jews.

And henceforth—that is, from now on. Or, “henceforth,” as two words: “with respect to anything else besides faith,” namely legal observances, let no one trouble me, so that I may again be compelled to write about the same matter. Hence Ambrose says: “He does not wish to be wearied [Col. 0169A] by turbulent disputes concerning a matter that had then been sufficiently expounded.” Or, as it is read in Greek: “Henceforth let no one cause me, or furnish me, labor,” namely so that I should again have the need to labor among you. For one who thinks otherwise than his teacher taught causes labor to his teacher. I say, let no one trouble me—one to whom trouble certainly ought not to be given. For I bear in my body, on behalf of the faithful, the marks of the Lord Jesus—that is, the signs of Christ’s military service, which prove that I am a soldier: sufferings, tribulations, and so forth—which the false teachers do not endure. As though he said: This is what you do not consider.

He called them *stigmata*, as it were marks of punishments resulting from the persecutions [Col. 0170A] that he endured. For a *stigma* is called a puncture or mark made with some iron instrument. The meaning is: trouble ought not to be given to me because I have other conflicts and contests that fight against me through the persecutions which I endure.

Grace. Behold the conclusion of the Epistle, like a subscription, which he uses also in several other Epistles. As though he said: In order that you may hold the foregoing things, may grace—not dissension, not bondage to the law, not strife, not contention—but the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, O brothers, be with your spirit, that is, with your reason, so that you may always understand the truth. Amen. By this Hebrew word he shows that what he has spoken is true.

# Epistle to the Ephesians

[Col. 0169]

## Argument

[Col. 0169B]

The Ephesians are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they persisted in faith. The Apostle commends them, writing from Rome, from prison, through Tychicus the deacon.

# Chapter One

### Verses 1–4

> “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, to all the saints who are at Ephesus and faithful in Christ Jesus: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love.”

[Col. 0169C] Paul, an apostle. The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Ephesians. The Ephesians are Asians; they were not founded in the faith by Paul, but were confirmed in it. For the Apostle did not found them in the faith, but confirmed them, having suffered much for them from unbelievers. After this confirmation they stood firm in faith and good works. The Apostle writes to them from prison at Rome, through Tychicus, a letter of encouragement, since he would not see them again. Knowing them to be good, he does not rebuke them for fault; nevertheless, they had to fear falling back. For one who stands can fall; and because no one is so perfect that he cannot grow, he exhorts them to further progress. So that they might not depart from the faith because of his own tribulations, namely the Apostle’s, and might retain their ordinances, and especially so that perfection might not raise them into pride, he shows from what state and to what worthy state they were called, saying that all benefits bestowed upon them, or upon the apostles themselves, or upon the whole human race, would be bestowed solely through God’s grace.

The Apostle’s intention in this Epistle, therefore, is to strengthen the Ephesians in the good they possess, urge them onward, and also form them in humility and thanksgiving. His method of treatment is as follows: according to his custom, he begins with a greeting. Then he gives thanks to God, first setting forth the benefits granted [Col. 0170B] to the human race, then those specially bestowed upon the apostles themselves, and then showing the Ephesians by whom and to what they have been called. He next shows Christ’s dignity and preeminence; afterward he invites them to patience and charity, commending the unity of faith and of the Church and enumerating gifts of grace. Finally, exhorting them to battle against the rulers of darkness, he describes the armor of Christian warfare.

Therefore, first greeting them and identifying himself by his familiar name, he says: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, not through my merits but by the will of God; and likewise you have through that will whatever good is in you. Paul, I say, writes or commands—or, I Paul write or command—to all who are at Ephesus, saints by the practice of virtues, and faithful by right faith, which is in Christ Jesus. He rightly set down these two things: for a good life is beneficial and believed only if faith is in Christ Jesus; and they are truly saints only if they are faithful in Christ. Or distinguish between “saints” and “faithful,” understanding saints as the greater and more perfect, the faithful as less perfect. Thus he writes to the saints—that is, the perfect—and not to them only, but also to the faithful, who, if they are not saints, are at least sound in faith. And their being saints and faithful is in Christ Jesus, that is, by Christ’s work, not by their own merits.

And in writing he greets them before all else, saying: May the grace of justification and peace [Ambrose]—that is, tranquility of mind and reconciliation with God—be to you from God our Father, through whom all things were created and restored, and from the Lord Jesus Christ, without whom no good things are given to you.

[Col. 0170D] [Haimo] “Blessed”: after the greeting, he begins with thanksgiving, indicating that it comes from God. [Ambrose] For God is blessed by man in one way and man by God in another. The word “blessing” is one, but it must be understood differently according to the appropriateness of the person, just as God and man are both said to make: but God makes effortlessly by a mere act of will, whereas man makes by effort and labor. Thus God is blessed by man when he is exalted with worthy praises; but man is blessed by God when God grants him the gifts of his grace, not because of man’s merits but because of his own mercy.

He says, therefore: Let God be blessed in heart, mouth, and work, by me, by you, and by the good. God, I say, who is Father by generation of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake he benefits us. Who has blessed us. After the thanksgiving, he enumerates the benefits given by God through Christ to the whole human race, and distinguishes two divine preordinations and their effects. One concerns the present, unto righteousness; the other, the future, unto the crown. They are not called two in the sense that God’s predestination, which is God himself, is divided; rather, God’s eternal preordination concerns two things: present righteousness and future glory.

For before the foundation of the world, when no one had merited anything, God preordained that in the time of grace he would separate some from the lost and make them righteous [Col. 0171B] and blameless; he also preordained that he would bring those righteous persons to eternal blessedness. Of these preordinations he fulfills one here, namely by making persons righteous; the other he will fulfill in the future, when all things will be perfected. He begins from that universal consummation, showing its effect and using the past tense for the future because of the certainty of the matter, when he says: Who—God—has blessed, that is, will bless, us, cursed by our merits; that is, he will exalt us in the future by granting immortality.

Hence he adds: With every spiritual blessing—that is, he will exalt us with complete and perfect exaltation, wholly spiritual even in our bodies. Then the bodies will have the nature of spirit, because they will be agile and capable, needing no food, things natural to spirit. I say, with a blessing possessed in heavenly places, that is, in heaven. And this will take place in Christ, that is, with Christ working.

Just as. He set forth the effect of the second preordination, namely that concerning the future; now he sets forth the first preordination, which concerns the present, touching upon its effect. As though he said: He will bless us in the future; and although this seems to be according to merits, it will nevertheless be gratuitous, just as the first preordination is gratuitous, because the merits which precede the future life are from grace and are gifts of God. For God crowns in us his own gifts, not things that originate from us by merit. And this is what he says: He will do this freely, just as he freely chose us by predestining us, and this in him—that is, through Christ himself. He chose us, I say, before the foundation of the world, that is, before we existed.

Therefore lest anyone think souls were eternally with God and then merited something, according to the error of those who say that before these visible things certain holy souls existed and were therefore then chosen, he openly shows this to be false when he says: He chose us before the foundation [Note: [Col. 0171D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*]. How could he choose those who did not yet exist except by predestining them? Therefore he chose us by predestining us; and just as he did not choose us because we were then holy, so neither did he choose us because we would be holy. Rather, he chose us for this purpose: that in the time of grace we might be holy through good works. He did not choose us because we were going to be holy, but in order that we might be holy. For we were going to be such persons because he himself chose us, predestining that through his grace we might be such.

But the Pelagian, resisting the truth, says: God foreknew who would become holy and blameless by the decision of free will; and therefore, in his foreknowledge, he chose them as he foreknew that they would be. “He chose,” he says, “before they existed, predestining as sons those whom he foreknew would become holy; he neither made them holy nor foresaw that he himself would make them holy, but foresaw that they themselves would become such.” The Apostle refutes him by saying: that we might be holy in virtues and blameless from evils and from crime; and this before his sight, not before human beings—that is, inwardly, where he himself sees, not outwardly, where people see. Or, “before him,” that is, so that we may behold him; and he did this not through our merits but in his love. For the love of God did this. [Haimo] Or: I say that we might be holy and blameless, and this in love—that is, through our love by which we love God. [Ambrose] For it may be understood either of God’s charity, by which he loves human beings, or of the charity of human beings themselves, by which they love God.

### Verses 5–10

> “Who predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, in which he has made us gracious in his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which has abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence, so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in [Col. 0172C] him, for the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ—things in heaven and things on earth—in him.”

Who predestined. Having set forth the predestination that concerns the righteousness and holiness of the present life, he here sets forth another predestination concerning eternal life, whose effect he indicated above. As though he said: He chose us so that we might be holy here—he himself, indeed, who predestined us, that is, chose us beforehand by grace alone, by a gratuitous will—for adoption as sons, that is, for the good things which sons will possess. Those who believe in him are sons; and this is what he adds: Through Jesus. As though he said: Their being sons is not through merits but through Jesus Christ.

I say that he predestined us unto this very end: that we should possess the same things as Christ. He predestined us, I say, not according to our own pleasure, but according to the purpose of his will—that is, according to his good will, held long before predestination was fulfilled in us, or set forth and displayed openly to all. I say that he predestined and sanctified us; and this to the praise of the glory of his grace—that is, that we might praise his glorious grace. As though he said: The glory of graces is eternal adoption, in which grace he made us gracious to himself.

Here is indicated the effect of the first preordination, which concerns righteousness. I say, he made us gracious in his beloved Son, for whose sake he loves us. For in loving his Only-begotten Son, he also grants divine gifts through the Son to those whom he loves and to whom the Son wills to give them. In whom: behold, he here shows through whom we have been made gracious, saying: In whom, the Son, we have redemption, so that we may return from the captivity in which we served the devil, sold under sin. We have it, I say, through his blood, which is the price of our redemption. And we have forgiveness of sins in baptism. He shows a double grace: because he both redeemed us and did not impute our sins to us. He bestowed this upon us according to the riches of his grace—that is, according to his rich and abundant grace—because he forgives everything and destroys the whole claim of the enemy.

Which has abounded. Up to this point he has dealt with things bestowed upon the whole human race; now he treats of things he gave especially to the apostles. [Col. 0173B] As though he said: I speak of the riches of grace. Although this grace had abounded among all believers, it superabounded in us apostles, that is, it abounded in us more than in others; for example, in all wisdom, that is, all knowledge concerning divine things, and prudence, that is, forethought concerning temporal things. I say, in all wisdom and prudence, so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will: his will hidden from others, namely that which he willed to do by his secret will.

And he sets forth what that is: namely, to restore all things. And this was not by our merits, but according to his good pleasure—that is, according to his good will, by which he willed to confer benefits and bring aid.
