[Note: [Col. 0173D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*.] He purposed this good pleasure or mystery—that is, he established it long before it came to pass, or offered it openly to all. I say that it was to be fulfilled in him—the Son—namely not in another, that is, in Christ; and not at another time, but in the dispensation of the fullness of times, that is, in the fullness of time ordered by God: the time of grace, in which divine providence reasonably ordered the fulfillment of those things promised and prefigured in earlier times.

For if people had been wholly ignorant, not instructed beforehand, they would not have received Christ; and unless they had first been convicted by the natural and the teaching law, the proud would have despised Christ’s coming. [Note: [Col. 0173D] Id., *Enchiridion*.] Therefore, no one should ask why he willed to fulfill the secret of his will in this time rather than another: namely, to restore—that is, bring back to the first state—all things destroyed by sin, both things in heaven, that is, angels, [Col. 0173D] and things on earth, that is, human beings. This does not mean that Christ died for angels. Rather, whatever among humankind is redeemed and freed from evil through his death is also done, in a sense, for angels, because after the enmities caused by sins between human beings and holy angels, human beings are in some manner restored to favor with them. And from humanity’s redemption the loss caused by that angelic fall is repaired. The holy angels, taught by God and blessed in the eternal contemplation of his truth, know what addition in number the integrity of that city awaits from the human race.

Things in heaven are restored when what fell away from there in the angels is supplied from humanity. [Col. 0174A] Things on earth are also restored when human beings themselves, who are predestined to eternal truth, are renewed from the oldness of corruption. The meaning is: He willed to restore—that is, to supply—things in heaven, namely to fill up the diminished number of angels; and things on earth, namely to renew human beings who had been corrupted by sin. Or, “things in heaven” means the souls of saints already in heaven, and “things on earth” means saints who are still on earth. And this is in Christ, that is, through Christ himself. For Christ’s coming is salvation both for saints who are already with Christ and for those who are yet to come.

### Verses 11–14

> “In whom we also were called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we, who hoped beforehand in Christ, might be for the praise of his glory. In whom you too, when you heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of the possession, to the praise of his glory.”

In whom, etc. Lest the apostles, in whom grace abounds, should seem to have merited something above others, he shows that they, like the others, were called freely and not by merits, saying: In whom—Christ—that is, through whom, Christ, we also, the apostles, like you others, have been called through inward grace; and this not by merits, but by lot, that is, by divine election. [Note: [Col. 0174D] Augustine, on Psalm CXXX.] For the lot is called God’s grace, by which we have been saved. It is rightly called a lot because the choice is not man’s, but belongs to the will of God, who found no merits in us, but called us to salvation by the lot of his will because he willed it, not because we were worthy.

[Augustine] This is the lot by which that seamless tunic of the Lord, woven from above and signifying charity, was obtained when a lot was cast for it: for charity is breathed into us by God’s grace; we were not called by merits. I say, we were predestined beforehand—that is, prepared and chosen by grace—and this not according to merits, but according to the purpose of him who works all things, even the willing of good, also in the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0174D] Id., *On the Predestination of the Saints*.] Thus he himself works so that we may begin to believe. For he chose us not because we believe, but in order that we may believe; and he works all things. And this is according to the counsel of his will, that is, according to [Col. 0174D] his will, which is guided by reason. As though he said: Why he chose us especially for the office of preaching and apostleship we do not know; yet he did it deliberately, not rashly.

[Augustine] And he chose you for this purpose: that we might be to the praise of his glory—that is, that through us others might praise his glory, so that henceforth no one might glory in man by our example. [Ambrose] For what he says is true: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV). Now the praise of God’s glory arises when many are won to faith, just as a physician’s glory arises when he heals many. We apostles, I say, who before all the others to whom Christ was preached and who were converted through him, hoped in Christ, are to be for his praise; and [Col. 0175A] therefore we ought to be such that others may praise through us.

In whom, etc. Having explained the things bestowed on the apostles, he now comes to those which he gave to the Ephesians. As though he said: We hoped in Christ, in whom—Christ—that is, in faith in whom, you Ephesians also are, when you heard—that is, by the fact that you heard—and after you heard, not before. For *when* here denotes both cause and time. You heard, I say, the word of truth, namely, the Gospel of your salvation, which proclaims salvation and calls to salvation. In whom—Christ—that is, through whose working, you also, believing, were sealed—that is, separated from the flock of the devil.

[Jerome] Or: you were sealed, the image of God having been restored in you. Hence: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV). And this was by the Holy Spirit of promise, that is, through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0175B] who had been promised, or who promised the inheritance and is its earnest. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Augustine, in the sermon *On the Vision of God*.] Hence he adds: “Who is the pledge of our inheritance.” For “charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. V). For what does it mean that charity has been poured forth? Behold, God already walks in us by however small an earnest, and so we have received a pledge.

Some manuscripts, however, more correctly have “earnest” (*arrha*); for the interpreters intended to express the same thing. Yet ordinary usage makes some distinction between an earnest and a pledge. For when a pledge is given, it is taken back once that for which it was given has been paid; but an earnest is given when something from the very thing itself is given which is not to be taken away but completed. Therefore, if God has now given us charity through the Spirit as a pledge, must the pledge be taken away from us when the promised reality has been bestowed? Far be it! Rather, he will complete what he has given. For this reason “earnest” is better than “pledge.” He gave us the Spirit, undoubtedly for this purpose: namely, for the redemption of the possession—that is, so that, redeemed by his blood from the right of the enemy, the enemy may no longer rule over us. Let us acquire God, or rather be acquired by God. For he redeemed us in order to possess us, not to lose us. And this is “to the praise of his glory.” As though he said: He also gave us the Spirit for this purpose, that God himself might be praised.

VERS. 15–23.—“Therefore I also, having heard of your faith which is in Christ Jesus and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in [Col. 0175D] the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart being enlightened, that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his strength, which he wrought 164 in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality and authority and power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he subjected all things beneath his feet, and gave him as head over all the Church, [Col. 0176A] which is his body, and the fullness of him who fills all things in all.”

Therefore. Having enumerated the benefits bestowed upon the human race, or upon the apostles, or upon the Ephesians, the Apostle adds what he thinks of the benefits given to the Ephesians: namely, that he gives thanks and prays that more may be added, lest they become proud, but rather press onward. As though he said: When you heard the Gospel, you believed. Therefore, I, having heard of your faith, which is in Christ Jesus—that is, by which you believe in Christ without admitting the Law—and of your love—that is, the works of charity displayed—toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks to God for you. As though he said: I know well what you are like; and therefore I praise, not you, but God, who did this. For thanks are rendered to him who performed the work.

Thus he says: I do not cease [Col. 0176B] giving thanks for you, namely for the good things already possessed, while I also make remembrance of you in my prayers, in which I ask God for further gifts on your behalf. Thus thanksgiving for gifts already given is fittingly placed first. [Note: [Col. 0175D] Id., to Vitalis.] For the one who is to be prayed to in order that he may act is the one to whom thanksgiving must be rendered when he has acted.

Now in my prayers I ask this: that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ and Father of glory—that is, of Christ—may give you, etc. [Haimo] Distinguish: God the Father is both the God of Christ and his Father; but he is Christ’s God according to his humanity, because Christ is man and was born of a woman. Hence he says in the Psalm: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. XXI). [Note: [Col. 0176D] Id., *Against Maximinus*.] This shows that the Father is his God because he became man: for God was born as man from a mother’s womb, and according to his humanity was born of a virgin, so that he who begot him from himself might not only be his Father, but also be the God of him whom he created as man from his mother’s womb. Therefore, he who is Father to the Son from his own womb is his God from his mother’s womb, not from his own. Hence the Lord himself says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John XX).

This, then, is what I say: that the God and Father of Christ may give you the things that follow. As though he said: To obtain these things I do not put forward merits, but the fact that he is the God and Father of Christ. This, I say, I pray: that he may give you, even if you are already wise, a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him—that is, the Holy Spirit, who may give you fuller wisdom concerning heavenly things than you now possess, so that you may know him not obscurely but clearly and without a veil; [Col. 0176D] namely, that he may give, that is, make enlightened, the eyes of your heart—that is, of your reason—which is God’s image, in which you are renewed in the knowledge of God.

Therefore, in his image recognize its maker, who cannot be reached by bodily sense. Do not suppose, then, that God is apprehended by bodily sense; rather, know him with the eyes of the mind and hear him with the ears of the mind. For in the body there are different members: you hear in one place and see in another. But in your heart, where different members are not found, there you hear where you see.

He enlightens the eyes for this purpose: that you may know more fully than you now do what—that is, how great—is the hope of his calling, [Col. 0177A] that is, the thing hoped for to which he calls believers. He says this in order that they may be more zealous; for when they fully know what the reward of believers is, they will become more zealous in cultivating religion. [Ambrose] Then he explains what he has understood by the name “hope,” adding: “And that you may know what are the riches,” etc. This is the hope, for hope receives the thing hoped for. Or it may be understood so that hope is taken in its proper sense, etc.

“That you may know what is the hope of his calling,” that is, how much the hope of eternal life, to which he calls, is worth; and that you may know what is the fulfillment of that hope. This he expresses thus: “and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance,” that is, of the glorious inheritance, namely eternal blessedness, which is called an inheritance because it will be possessed securely and will be shared by all the saints. And that you may also know what is the surpassing greatness [Col. 0177B] of the future glory toward us apostles—that is, that we apostles shall have glory beyond the others—not so that you may stand still and merely possess what you have, but that you may strive toward that greater thing which we shall possess.

For the highest teachers will have some increase of glory beyond that which all will share in common. All will indeed have the same denarius; but “star differs from star in brightness,” and there will be different dwelling places in the Father’s house. Among others shining more brightly, the apostles will sit more highly. Hence, in the tabernacle of the Lord there was made above the table a crown, at once four fingers high and covering the whole table, and above it another, smaller golden crown. By the crown four fingers high which covered the table is signified the glory of eternal life, which all the elect will enjoy, proclaimed in the four books of the Gospel written by the finger of God—that is, by the Holy Spirit—and it was openwork, according to the diversity of merits. The smaller golden crown above it is the perfection of the reward of those who excel as teachers. Therefore the Apostle says, “what is the surpassing greatness of glory toward us.”

This greatness is his power—that is, it is to be given to us by God’s power, we who believed concerning that blessedness according to the working of the might of his strength, which he worked in Christ—that is, according as he worked mightily in Christ, whose members we are; and therefore we believe that we shall possess the same things with him. He worked, I say, in Christ in this way: namely, raising him from the dead and setting him at [Col. 0177D] his right hand, in eternal blessedness.

[Note: [Col. 0177D] Augustine, *On the Christian Conflict*.] Let us not listen to those who deny that the Son sits at the Father’s right hand, asking, “Does God the Father have a right or left side like bodies?” Nor do we think this of God. For God is not bounded and enclosed by any bodily form. But the right hand of God is the eternal blessedness given to the saints, just as his left hand is called the everlasting misery given to the impious. Thus “setting him at his right hand” means showing the man Christ eternally blessed, “in the heavenly places,” that is, in heaven.

The resurrection of the Savior is the model of the saints’ glory, so that in it believers may recognize what has been promised to them. For in like manner they will be raised above the heavens with Christ, as he himself says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII). For his body, which is the Church, will be at that right hand—that is, in that blessedness. Although our body is not there, nevertheless our hope is already there. Therefore, after the resurrection, the Lord commanded his disciples while fishing to cast their nets on the right side; he also said that he would place the lambs at his right hand and the kids at his left.

Or thus: “setting” means establishing firmly that man, Christ, at his right hand—that is, in the judicial seat, in the authority to judge. For since the Father gave all judgment to the Son (John V), he is said to sit at God’s right hand as judge. Hence [Col. 0178B] he says to the Jews: “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of God,” etc. (Matt. XXVI). And he set him in the heavenly places and above every principality and authority and power and dominion—that is, above the rank of these angelic orders—and not only above these four, but also above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come: that is, above everything nameable, whether it is now known or will be known in the future.

He says this on account of the incarnation of the Son of God, so that, having become man, he may also be said to be above all the heavens and above every creature, possessing the name of God by nature, not by adoption. And lest he should seem to preside over every creature by rank alone and not by power, he adds, “and all things.” As though he said: Not only does he preside over all things in rank, [Col. 0178C] but they are also beneath him. And—that is, because—God the Father subjected all things beneath his feet, and subjected them fully to him, so that complete subjection is denoted by the feet. All these things are deservedly subject to him, because they were made through him.

Or, “beneath his feet” means beneath his humanity, which is signified by the feet. For just as the foot is the lower part of the body, so humanity is the lower nature in Christ; even the angels worship it, and all things are subject to Christ the man himself.

“And him.” After commemorating Christ’s dignity, he returns to us, showing that Christ’s dignity concerns us. As though he said: God so exalted Christ, and this exaltation of his pertains to us because he is such a head and we are his body. This is what he says: as though he said, What I have said about Christ pertains to us. And—that is, because—God gave him, who is so exalted, as head, in whom are all the spiritual faculties of the Church, namely the gifts of grace. Him, I say, he gave to be head over all the Church, both that which is in heaven and that which is on earth, while they confess that he is he through whom they were made. For they are subject to him as to a head, from whom they derive their origin. They were made by him according to his divinity, and thus according to his divinity he is head of the Church, according to which he gave him to be head by begetting him before all things.

He is also properly called head according to his humanity, according to which the Church is joined to [Col. 0179A] him both by nature and by grace. For in him was the fullness of grace, “from whose fullness we have received” [Note: [Col. 0179D] Augustine, on Psalm LXXXV.]. Nor could God bestow any greater gift upon human beings than to make the Word through whom he made all things their head, and to fit them to him as members, so that he might be Son of God and son of man, one God with the Father and one man with human beings.

The Church is his body, that is, joined to him by grace and nature; and it is his fullness, that is, completing him so that he may have all his members. And it truly is his fullness because he is the one who is filled up through them. For when those who have returned to confession bend the knee to Christ, he is filled up; for when they depart, he seems to be emptied. He is filled up through them, I say, yet he is all things in all, here or in the future, because the members contribute nothing to him, but he contributes all things to the members. He is said to be all things in all because all things in them are from him, by whose power they are what they are.

## CHAPTER II

VERS. 1–3.—“And you he made alive together with him, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the children of unbelief; among whom we all also once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of the thoughts; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.”

165 And you. Here he recalls their former state—namely, what they were before faith and what they have now become by grace—so that they may humble themselves in the good things they now possess, and so that it may be certain that, if these things have been given to enemies, the things for which the Apostle prays for them will all the more be given to friends: namely, that Christ is the head of the whole Church and of us, because he made us alive together with him when—that is, although—you were dead in trespasses and sins, etc.

Or the connection may be made thus, taking from above the verb which is understood: as though he said, We who have believed have the hope of inheritance, and you—that is, you also believed. But God made us alive together with him when—that is, although—we had formerly been dead. [Ambrose] Or the connection may be made thus: God raised Jesus, and you—that is, he will raise you—when—that is, although—you were formerly, before faith, dead, namely, not even perceiving our evils.

Dead, I say, in trespasses—namely, by omitting what is commanded—and in your sins—namely, by doing what is forbidden. In these trespasses and sins you once, namely before faith, through long practice, walked, turning from one thing to another. You walked, I say, according to the age—that is, the manner of life and appearance—of this world, whose appearance entices us; and according to the prince of the spirit—that is, of spirits. For the singular genitive is used in place of the plural. This is Beelzebub, who is prince of the evil spirits.

Or, intransitively, according to another reading: “according to the prince of spirits.” I say, the prince of the power of this air—that is, he who has power in [Col. 0180A] this dark air, not with human beings in the world, who fell with the apostate angels from the ranks of the higher angels into these dark regions, as into a prison. For the dark air is the hell of demons until judgment. Hence it is said in the Catholic Epistle: “He was shut up in the prisons of the darkness of hell, to be kept for destruction at the judgment.” Therefore he calls the spirit of error the prince of the air because he rules in this air. For he has claimed this region for himself in order to exercise dominion; and because they are so near to us and are invisible spirits, they are to be feared all the more.

These princes still now work, insofar as God permits, in the children of unbelief—that is, in those who distrust eternal things, or whose salvation we despair of; and therefore, once they have been rescued from him, they ought to be grateful to Christ their rescuer. [Col. 0180B] [Note: [Col. 0179D] Id., to Vitalis.] He entered the house of the strong man, who in his dominion possessed the human race, and first bound him—that is, curbed and restrained his power by the stronger bonds of his own power—and thus snatched away whatever vessels he had predestined to snatch away, freeing their will from that one’s power so that, when he does not hinder them, they may believe in this one by free will.

Accordingly, this is the work of grace brought by the second Adam, not of the nature corrupted by the first Adam. But this prince—that is, the devil—rules the children of unbelief according to his own will, though he himself does not have freedom to act as he wishes, but is hardened by his crimes into the greatest malevolence. Hence no person of sound faith believes or says that these apostate angels will ever be converted to their former piety by a corrected will.

But what does this prince [Col. 0180C] work in the children of unbelief except his own evil works—and first and above all, that very distrust and unbelief by which they are enemies of faith, through which he knows they can be cleansed? [Note: [Col. 0180D] Augustine, on Psalm LXXVI.] Therefore, when God is often said to bring them into such obstinacy, he does so not by inciting and inspiring them but by abandoning them, so that they—that is, evil spirits—may work in the children of unbelief. God deservedly and justly permits this.

“In which”—that is, in sins—“we all Jews also, like the Gentiles, once conducted ourselves,” living our life in the desires of our flesh—that is, in the evil concupiscences which arise from the flesh—and also actually doing the wills of the flesh, that is, those things in which the flesh delights, such as sexual immorality and the like; and the will of the thoughts [Col. 0180D] or minds, that is, those things in which the flesh does not delight but the soul devises, such as heretical perversities and the like.

And we Jews, like the rest—that is, the Gentiles—were children of wrath, that is, liable to eternal punishment; and this by nature—that is, through our parents, Adam and Eve—through the original sin transmitted from them. [Note: [Col. 0180D] Jerome, on John, concerning the man born blind.] For blindness befell the first man through sin, from whom we all derive our origin—not only of death, but also of iniquity. Therefore the Apostle says: “We were by nature children of wrath,” that is, children of vengeance, children of punishment, children of Gehenna. In what sense by nature? Because when the first man sinned, vice took root in place of nature. [Note: [Col. 0181D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.]

For the human race was held under a just condemnation, and all were children of wrath. Of this wrath the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe in the Son does not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John III). He does not say “comes,” but “remains.” For everyone is born with this wrath. [Note: [Col. 0181D] Id., on Psalm CI.] This is indeed that wrath with which we were all born, to which we clung in being born: wrath from the propagation of iniquity, from the stain of sin.

And note that human nature in the true and proper sense is called that which was originally created without vice. We use the word in a transferred sense when we call “nature” also that condition in which a human being is born. In this latter sense it is said here: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.” As though he said: Since these things mentioned above were in us as in the Gentiles, let no Gentile despair of becoming equal to the Jews, because we too, like them, were children of wrath.

Since human beings were under this wrath through original sin—and all the more gravely and ruinously insofar as they had added greater or more numerous sins besides—a mediator was necessary, that is, a reconciler who would appease this wrath by the offering of a unique sacrifice. Hence he adds:

VERS. 4–10.—“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of his exceeding charity with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ, by whose grace you have been saved; and raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, that he might show in the ages to come the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; [Col. 0181C] it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them.”

But God. As though he said: Although you were dead, yet God made us alive together: but God, and no other, namely God who is rich in mercy, who forgives actual and original sins. He, I say, did this not on account of merit but because of his exceeding charity with which he loved us—that is, Jews and Gentiles—not only after we had become righteous, but even when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together in Christ, that is, after the likeness of Christ: for just as he cleansed Christ from the oldness of punishment, so he cleansed us from the oldness of guilt.

[Col. 0181D] [Augustine] Or, according to another reading: he made us alive together, namely us Jews, and this in Christ, that is, through the grace of Christ. On this reading, the text is connected with the preceding words thus: “But God,” as though he said, We once conducted ourselves wickedly, but God, who is rich, etc., made us Jews alive in Christ—that is, through Christ’s grace. And just as he made us alive, so likewise he made you Gentiles alive. This is what follows: “By whose grace you Gentiles have been saved,” like us Jews; and he raised both together, that is, he has already raised us with Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0182D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] In hope he declares as already complete what is future, because by certain hope we already hold what will be; therefore he speaks as though it were already completed. Thus he also adds: “And made us sit together,” as judges, us and you, in the heavenly places. He does not vainly but faithfully reckon as already done what he does not doubt will be done. [Augustine] For Christ certainly now sits in the heavenly places, but we do not yet; nevertheless, we hold it by certain hope.

I say that he did this through our being in Christ Jesus, that is, in faith in Christ, “that,” etc. As though he said: He so did these things in hope that he might fulfill them in reality on the day of judgment. He says this thus: “that he might show,” in reality, “in the ages to come,” that is, on the day of judgment, “the exceeding riches of his grace,” that is, the abundant gifts of grace. [Ambrose] For in the future age God’s gift will appear in the reward of believers, “what eye has not seen nor ear heard.” And these are exceeding riches, not merely such as the mind cannot investigate.

Or it may be understood of the present, as though he said: He made us, formerly dead, alive for this purpose: that he might show in the ages to come—that is, to our descendants—the exceeding riches of his grace, that is, the abundant gifts of grace which he bestows here. Then continue both interpretations together, as though he said: The riches, I say, given to you here or in the future, were given not through our merits but in God’s kindness. I say riches which are above us—that is, above our understanding—because we cannot grasp them fully. I say, given in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ.

And I rightly said “in kindness,” for you have been saved by grace—that is, by God’s gratuitous will going before—through faith, because faith cooperates with God’s good will. [Augustine] And this—that is, faith—is not from yourselves, that is, not from the power of your nature, because it is purely God’s gift; not partly from works, so that no one—that is, no person—may boast, that is, exalt himself on account of works.

He did not say this in order that good works done with devout intention should be fruitless, since God renders to each according to his works and there is glory for one who does good. Rather, works are from grace; grace is not from works. It is therefore good for a person not to presume upon the powers of his free will; for the one who thought that he could preserve without God’s help what God had given him went into a far country, lived prodigally, consumed everything, was crushed by misery, and, returning to himself, said: “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke XVIII). He could not have had this good thought unless the most merciful Father had also secretly inspired it within him.

Therefore he rightly says: “And this is not from yourselves, but it is God’s gift, not from works,” lest perhaps you say, “I merited it, and therefore I received it.” [Note: [Col. 0182D] Id., in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Do not suppose that you received by meriting, when you could not merit unless you had received. Grace preceded your merit; grace does not arise from merit, but merit from grace. For if you purchased grace by merit, you did not receive it freely. Grace precedes all merits, so that my merits may follow God’s gifts.

[Augustine] And lest anyone should understand otherwise, especially the arrogant who wish to establish their own righteousness, he explains more plainly, adding: “For we are his workmanship.” As though he said: No one ought to glory in himself, because we, created in Christ Jesus—that is, in faith in [Col. 0183A] Christ—and in 166 good works, are his workmanship, that is, God’s work. Or thus: We are created workmanship, that is, through his workmanship, namely through God’s operation, in Christ Jesus, that is, in faith in Christ, and in good works. Or thus: We are his workmanship. I say, created in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, for good works.

[Haimo] Certainly not that creation by which we were made human beings, but that of which one who was already a human being said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” etc. (Ps. L). [Note: [Col. 0183D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.] By this creation we are formed and created for good works, which God prepared before you could rise up to them. I say, he prepared them so that we might walk in them, making progress, not so that, trusting in grace, we should thereafter be idle.

[Haimo] In these words the Apostle plainly shows God’s very predestination [Col. 0183B] and its effect, that is, the grace which is bestowed. [Note: [Col. 0183D] Id., *On the Predestination of the Saints*.] For he says, “We were created in Christ and for works”: this is grace. But what follows, “which he prepared,” is predestination, because predestination is the preparation of grace. Grace, however, is the very gift which is the effect of predestination. Predestination cannot exist without foreknowledge; but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself would do; but he is also able to foreknow things which he does not do, such as all sins. For even if there are certain sins which are also punishments for sins, as where it is said, “God handed them over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. I), God’s action there is not sin but judgment.

Therefore God’s predestination is toward good, and its effect is good. Thus he who is unchangeably good works and preserves the good human being; and we must always be made and perfected by him, cleaving to him.

VERS. 11–18.—“Therefore remember that you, once Gentiles in the flesh, who were called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh made by hands, were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise and without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus you who were once far off have been made near by the blood of Christ. For he is our peace, who made both one and, [Col. 0183D] breaking down the middle wall of partition, the enmities in his flesh, abolished the law of commandments in decrees, that he might create the two in himself into one new human being, making peace, that he might reconcile both in one body through the cross, killing the enmities in himself; and coming, he preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.”

For this reason. Above he compared Jews and Gentiles, showing that both were under sin; now he shows that the Gentiles had been more unworthy and had endured the reproaches of the Jews, so that, now made equal to the Jews, they may be the more indebted to the grace of God. It is as though he said: “You have the aforesaid good things from God; for this reason—that is, because you have these things, and that you may know that all things are from God’s grace—remember, so that you may be more grateful, that you Ephesians were once,” that is, before conversion, “Gentiles,” that is, such as the Gentiles were: old sinners living “in the flesh,” that is, in carnal things; “you who were called the uncircumcision,” that is, uncleanness. And this was by that circumcision which is not truly circumcision but is called circumcision, because it was made by human hand—not by God—in the flesh, not in the spirit. And remember that you, who are now such persons, were at that evil time “without Christ,” that is, without the promise of Christ, which was then being made to the Jews.

You were also “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel,” with whom—that is, with the Gentiles—the Jews did not associate. [Ambrose] And even if at some time you received the Law and the prophets, you were called, or were, “strangers to the covenants,” that is, outsiders. [Haimo] A *hospes* [guest/stranger] is, as it were, “one whose foot is at the door” (*hostii pes*), because when he was received into a house, the master of the house and the person received placed a foot over the threshold and, giving right hands, swore that his entrance would be peaceful. You were also without the hope of the promise made to the children of Abraham, concerning the eternal inheritance; and “without God,” that is, without knowledge of God, you were in this world, so evil a world.

“But now,” that is, in this time of grace, “you who were once far off”—not in place but in merit, both from God and from Israel in the character of your manner of life—although you were far off, have nevertheless been made near to God and to Jews, not carnal but spiritual Jews. [Col. 0184C] And this is “in Christ Jesus,” that is, through Christ; and not merely in any manner through Christ, but “in the blood of Christ,” that is, through his blood.

In some manuscripts it is found written, “who,” at the point, “you who were Gentiles”; accordingly, the passage is read with suspension until “But now,” while retaining the same meaning, thus: “Remember that you who were once Gentiles,” etc.; “you who were called,” “who were,” etc. “But now, you who were once far off have been made near,” not through yourselves but in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ, and through him not in just any manner but in the blood of Christ. And rightly do I say, “in Christ.” For he himself is our peace—between ourselves, namely Jews and Gentiles, and toward God—he who made the two peoples peaceful with one another and therefore reconciled them.

Hence he adds: “Who made both,” that is, both peoples, “one” in faith and conduct. [Note: [Col. 0184D] Augustine, *Retractations*.] For he himself is the cornerstone, in whom the two peoples, like walls coming from different directions, are joined together as it were in a kiss of peace. He united them by that which follows: “And,” that is, because he “is dissolving the middle wall of the enclosure,” that is, the obstacle which stood between those two peoples—on this side from the Law, on that side from idolatry. He dissolved it by removing the Law from the Jews and idolatry from the Gentiles. This wall is called an enclosure (*maceria*) because it was neither stable nor strong. For an enclosure is a heap of stones without mortar, such as is made [Col. 0185A] around gardens. The wall of the enclosure, then, was one easily destroyed when grace came, which both removed the Law and turned the hearts of the Gentiles away from idolatry. It stood in the middle, so that neither people agreed with the other. But while this wall stood, there were hostilities, anger, and envy between them; these were abolished when the wall was destroyed.

Hence he adds: “And through this he is dissolving hostilities in his flesh,” assumed or offered in sacrifice. “The Law.” Here he explains the wall with regard to the Jewish side. [Haimo] It is as though he said: He, I say, is “annulling the law of commandments,” that is, annulling the old Law insofar as it commanded, namely in its carnal observances, not insofar as it prefigured truth. I say, annulling it “by decrees,” that is, by the Gospel’s precepts, which accord with reason. Therefore he annulled it [Col. 0185B] “that he might create in himself” the two peoples previously separated by the Law, that is, unite them in faith in him. [Ambrose] He, I say, makes peace by destroying hostilities. I say, making it “in one new man,” that is, in himself alone, from whom newness comes and not from elsewhere.

And likewise, he annuls it in order that he may reconcile both to God when they have been set in one body, the Church. [Haimo] It is as though he said: Once hostility has been removed and the Law annulled, he makes peace between them and reconciles both to God the Father. [Ambrose] He reconciles them to God by offering himself for sins and by enlightening through the Gospel; he subsequently shows these two things, adding: He, I say, “killing in himself the hostility” which stood between God and human beings—that is, forgiving sins. But he killed hostility in himself only through the cross, that is, through death. For the death of the Savior benefited all. “And coming,” that is, appearing through the humanity he assumed, he preached the Gospel—if not in his own person, yet in the apostles—to you Gentiles, that peace with God is made through himself. To you, I say, “who were far off from God,” because you were idolaters and without the Law. For no one is far from God by region, but by disposition. Do you love God? You are near. Do you hate God? You are far. And he proclaimed the same peace to those who were near, that is, to Jews who worshipped one God and had received the Law from God.

VERS. 19–22.—“Therefore now you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone, [Col. 0185D] in whom every building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit.”

“Therefore now you are no longer,” etc. It is as though he said: He proclaimed peace, and he also made it; and the effect shows what he has done. For both of us have access, that is, the ability to approach the Father, and this “in one Spirit,” that is, through the same Spirit who is given through Christ to all. And because the Gentiles have access to the Father: therefore, O Gentiles, now—that is, from the time of faith—you are no longer “strangers,” that is, inferior to the Jews in faith, as those formerly received into the Law; nor “foreigners,” that is, persons alien to God. Rather, you are “fellow citizens of the saints,” not of carnal Israel—that is, of the same right and dignity in God’s house as the saints—and “members of God’s household,” that is, his intimates, to whom he reveals mysteries. You have, as it were, been transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem.

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Augustine, *Book of Sentences*.] Two loves make two cities throughout the whole world: love of God makes Jerusalem; love of the age makes Babylon. Let each person therefore ask himself what he loves, and he will discover of what city he is a citizen.

[Haimo] We, I say, are “built upon,” that is, resting upon and advancing from good to better, “the foundation of the apostles and prophets,” that is, Christ, who is the foundation apart from which no one can lay another. Yet the apostles and prophets are also called a foundation. Thus the prophet says [Col. 0186B] in Psalm 86: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” But Christ is the first and greatest foundation: just as he is plainly called the Holy of holies, so figuratively he is the Foundation of foundations. Therefore, if you think of the sacraments, Christ is the Holy of holies; if you think of the flock subject to him, Christ is the Shepherd of shepherds; if you think of the structure, Christ is the Foundation of foundations.

[Ambrose] Or, “upon the foundation,” that is, the teaching, “of the apostles and prophets,” that is, upon the New Testament. And this is true, because what the apostles preached, the prophets foretold as future.

[Augustine] And lest the apostles or prophets, upon whom the city of God is founded, should rest in themselves, he adds: “Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.” [Col. 0186C] For in Christ the whole structure rests upon its primary foundation, on which all this framework depends so that it nowhere falls. This foundation is at the top and not at the bottom, so that the builder may obey [perhaps *pareat*]. Therefore Christ is both foundation and cornerstone; rising from below, he holds the highest place. He is called a stone because of his firmness, since he sustains firmness; chief because he brings to completion; and corner-stone because he joins the two walls coming from different directions, namely those of Jews and Gentiles.

[Augustine] Hence he adds: “In whom,” Christ—that is, through whom, Christ—“every building,” both from Jews and Gentiles, built in faith, “grows” through an increase of virtues. For no one is so perfect that he cannot become more perfect. [Col. 0186D] I say, it grows “into a temple,” that is, until it becomes God’s temple, made so by the removal of vices, “in the Lord,” that is, by the Lord’s working. “In whom,” that is, through Christ, you Ephesians too, like the others, “are built together,” that is, are built in likeness to the others, “into a dwelling-place of God,” so that you may be God’s habitation; and this is through the Spirit at work.

## CHAPTER III

VERS. 1–12.—“For this reason I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles—if indeed you have heard of the dispensation of God’s grace which was given to me for you, that by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote above briefly, so that, as you read, you can understand my insight into the mystery of Christ—which in other generations was not made known to the children of men as it has now been revealed in the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the Gospel, of which I became a minister according to the gift of God’s grace given to me according to the working of his power. To me, the least of all the saints, was given this grace: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God who created all things, so that the manifold [Col. 0187B] wisdom of God may be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the predetermination of the ages which he made in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access in confidence through faith in him.”

“For this reason.” Having shown that peace and reconciliation were made through Christ, he here sets forth through whom they themselves have been built together: namely, because God revealed to Paul that salvation belongs to the Gentiles, sent him to preach, and makes him suffer for them, so that they may be more grateful to God. He begins with the last point, saying: “For this reason,” that is, for this matter pleasing to me, namely that you may be built together; or for fulfilling God’s grace in this matter, “I Paul,” [Haimo] great as I am, am now at Rome, “a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” that is, for Christ Jesus, “and for you Gentiles,” namely because I preached to the Gentiles the word of salvation. “For you,” I say, “if indeed you have heard,” that is, understood, “the dispensation of God’s grace.” It is as though he said: the apostleship was entrusted to me by God for you, he who knows why he chose me for this office.

By this he wishes them to know that, by God’s judgment, he was sent by Christ to preach to the Gentiles the mystery of God’s grace. Or: “if indeed [you have heard] the dispensation of grace which was given to me for you,” that is, the apostleship by which we render different things to different persons. It is as though he said: It is clear that I am imprisoned for you if you know that I am your apostle—which no one is ignorant of. And although I am imprisoned for the apostleship, nevertheless I am so especially for you, because—he means—that dispensation toward you was given to me, because the divine secret was disclosed to me. And this is what follows: “that by revelation,” that is, not obscurely but openly, “the mystery,” that is, God’s secret, “was made known to me by God, as I wrote above briefly,” that is, with brevity, where he said, “He himself is our peace.”

[Jerome] There he touched upon the sum of the mysteries revealed to him in very few words, not so much setting forth everything he knew as showing by the little he said what he left unspoken. Hence he adds: “So that.” It is as though he said: And even if I wrote briefly, I did so plainly, so that you can understand, if you read attentively. What can you understand? “My insight,” that is, my knowledge, “in recognizing the mystery of Christ,” that is, in knowing this secret by which the Gentiles are to be saved through Christ.

This mystery “was not made known in other generations,” that is, in past generations, to any “children of men,” that is, rational beings, as fully as now. Or thus: “in other generations,” that is, in other times, it was not made known to the children of men as fully as—namely, as fully as—it has now, when it seems to be fulfilled, been revealed “in the Spirit,” that is, through the Spirit, to his holy apostles and prophets, the new prophets who interpret the Scriptures and explain the Law. Earlier prophets indeed knew beforehand long ago concerning the Gentiles that they would be called and would become participants in God’s gift. They signified this in many places of Scripture. But this was hidden from them: that this would come to them through faith in Christ without the Law, namely without circumcision, Sabbaths, new moons, and the like.

This, then, is the mystery that has been revealed: that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs” in the future, in the heavenly homeland; [Haimo] “fellow members of the body” now in the Church together with [Col. 0188B] the Jews; and “fellow sharers in his promises,” God’s promises, because the promise made by God to Abraham concerning inheritance and incorporation belongs to them as it does to the Jews. And all this has been done “in Christ,” that is, through Christ, through Christ’s incarnation, “and through the Gospel,” that is, through my preaching. For the incarnation is of no benefit unless it is preached. Of this Gospel I became a minister; for it is not mine, but God’s. Thus no thanks are due to me, but to God. I became a minister, I say, not through my merits but “according to the gift of God’s grace which was given to me according to the working of his power.” For his power is great: it made a persecutor into an apostle. This is equal to any miracle.

Or thus: this is God’s secret, namely that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow sharers in his promise, namely that of God the Father; God gave this gift among the Gentiles “in Christ,” that is, through Christ. And this was “according to the working of his power,” that is, through his powerful work in raising Christ from the dead. This became known “through the Gospel,” that is, after my preaching, of which I became a minister, etc.; these points do not change. [Ambrose] He declares that through preaching the gift of God, which God gives to the Gentiles according to the working of his power, has become known. [Augustine] The working of his power is that he raised Jesus Christ from the dead, conquering death, in whom all were saved without works of the Law.

[Ambrose] Comparing the greatness [Col. 0188D] of this grace with his own smallness, he repeats: “To me,” I say, “the least of all the saints.” He humbles himself when he calls himself least, knowing that humility brings advancement. Therefore he does not call himself least in authority, but is humbler because of his former deeds. For he says that such great grace was given to him that he was granted to make known among the Gentiles a gift unknown in earlier ages. “To me,” I say, the least, “was given this,” that is, this very great, grace: namely, “among the Gentiles,” that is, amid the Gentiles, “to preach the unsearchable,” or immeasurable, “riches,” that is, Christ’s many gifts, which absolutely cannot be understood or searched out.

And “to enlighten,” by preaching and miracles, [Haimo] all who are willing to believe, as by a certain explanation, concerning this matter: namely, that they may understand “what is the dispensation of the mystery,” that is, how wonderful is the fulfillment of the hidden redemption, and from how great a love it has been made. These are the unsearchable riches. For he calls the same thing “mystery” which above he called “riches.” But if these riches are unsearchable, how did the apostle preach them? For an unsearchable thing is one which cannot be comprehended. The answer is that they are unsearchable in their own nature; but through the grace and revelation of the Holy Spirit they are not unsearchable to believers.

I mean the mystery “hidden from the ages,” that is, concealed from the creatures of all ages, and existing “in God,” that is, in God’s knowledge alone—he “who created all things”—“so that it may be made known.” It is as though he said: I was given to preach the Gospel and to enlighten. See how great this is: through this something was added even to the angels, who learned many secrets in these matters. [Col. 0189B] And this is what he says: I say, preaching the Gospel so that God’s manifold wisdom concerning the restoration of human beings may be made known “through the Church,” which receives God’s gifts—that is, through apostles preaching in the Church—to “the principalities and powers,” that is, the various orders of angels, “in the heavenly places,” that is, in heaven, where we too shall be.

For blessed Jerome says that the angelic ranks did not understand the aforesaid mystery fully until Christ’s passion had been completed and the apostles’ preaching had spread among the Gentiles. Hence in Isaiah the wondering angels said: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isa. 63); and in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23). [Jerome] Therefore God’s manifold wisdom was revealed through the Church not only to patriarchs and prophets but also to principalities and powers in the heavens. [Haimo] It is rightly called “manifold,” and in Greek *multivaria* [many-varied], that is, not merely varied but marked by abundant diversity.

[Jerome] Let us see how it is manifold. Christ is immeasurable, yet he is conceived; as an infant he cries in a manger, yet he is praised by angels in heaven; Herod persecutes him, yet the Magi worship him; the Pharisees do not know him, yet the star reveals him; he is baptized by a servant, yet the voice of the thundering Father is heard; he fears to suffer, yet freely comes to the Passion; he wishes the cup to be removed, yet rebukes Peter, who feared the cup. What is more exacting than this truth? Therefore the wisdom of God is called manifold, as though multiple and having many kinds and forms, [Col. 0189D] which the principalities and powers came to know through the Church.

Or thus: “what is the dispensation of the mystery of God”—this does not change. I mean the mystery “hidden from the ages,” not in the ages but in God, “who created all things.”

[Note: [Col. 0189D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.] God has within himself hidden causes of certain events which he did not implant in created things, and which he brings to fulfillment—not through that work of providence by which he established nature so that things exist, but through that by which he administers them wherever he wills, having created them there as he willed. There too is the grace by which sinners have been saved. For they are restored not through nature corrupted by vice but through God’s grace.

For this reason he said that the mystery of grace was hidden, not in the world, where are hidden the rational causes of all things that occur naturally—as Levi was hidden in Abraham’s loins when he was tithed—but in God, where are hidden the causes of things done through grace, or of things miraculously and not naturally done to signify these matters: as when a woman was made from the bone of a sleeping man, and in place of the rib not a rib but flesh was supplied. The first condition of created things did not contain that a woman should thus be made from him; it contained only that this could be done, so that God should not do something by a changeable will contrary to the causes he established by his will. Therefore that it would be done was hidden in God.

[Augustine] Thus the causes of all things which were miraculously done in the order of creation, beyond the customary course of nature, in order to foretell Christ’s coming, were in God; they are believed to have been done through angels administering them. Hence he adds: “That it may be made known,” I say—this mystery “hidden from the ages in God”—yet in such a way that God’s wisdom may be made known from the ages, namely from the beginning of the ages, to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places. Certainly God does not need messengers in order to learn of lower things, as though he might learn these lower things from them; for he knows all things steadfastly and unchangeably. But he has messengers for our sake and for theirs, because it is good for them to stand before God, consult him concerning lower things, and obey his commands. The mystery of the kingdom of heaven, revealed at the fitting time for our salvation, was not hidden from them, so that, delivered from this pilgrimage, we may be joined to their company.

Thus this was hidden from the ages in God, and yet God’s wisdom was made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places, because the Church existed there first; after the resurrection this Church too is to be gathered there, that we may be equal to God’s angels. Therefore it became known to them from the ages, because every creature is not before the ages but from the ages. For the ages arose from the creature itself, and the creature itself is from the ages because it began with them. But the Son is before the ages, through whom the ages were made. Hence Wisdom speaks in person: “Before the ages he founded me” (Ecclus. 24).

It is added, “through the Church, manifold”; and the order of the words is: grace was given to me, namely, to enlighten all through the Church, that is, in the Church, about this matter—what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things. I say, hidden, but in such a way that the wisdom of God may be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places. This wisdom is manifold, not in its own nature, but “according to the predetermination of the ages.” For what is simple in its own nature becomes manifold according to those things which occur in the age and which God predetermined, that is, preordained, since they vary in manifold ways.

[Haimo] And lest the teachers of sacred Scripture seem to contradict one another in the aforesaid statements, what was said can be qualified thus: to those of greater dignity, and through whose ministry these things were announced, they were known in part, as to familiar messengers; but to those of lesser dignity they were unknown. This predetermination God the Father made, that is, preordained to be fulfilled in Christ; or “made,” that is, fulfilled, “in Christ,” that is, in our Lord, that is, through Christ. In him, Christ, since the Father fulfilled it through him, we have boldness against tribulations; or “boldness,” that is, certainty of the future inheritance, and actual access to the Father. And this is “in confidence,” that is, by the merit of confidence held through faith in him.

VERS. 13–21.—“For this reason I ask that you do not lose heart in my tribulations for you, which is your glory. For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may give you, according to the riches of his glory, strength to be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner person, [Col. 0191B] that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, being rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ surpassing knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do all things superabundantly beyond what we ask or understand, according to the power working in us—to him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus through all generations of the age of ages. Amen.”

“For this reason,” that is, because you have access and the other good things aforesaid, “I ask that you do not lose heart,” in faith and good action, “in my tribulations,” that is, because of my tribulations, which are for testing you and constitute your glory if you stand firm in them and do not lose heart. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Augustine, sermon on the words of the Apostle.]

“For this reason.” It is as though he said: I ask you not to lose heart, and therefore I entreat God the Father that grace may cooperate with us. This is what he says: “For this reason,” namely that you may not fall away from faith, “I bend my knees,” etc. [Haimo] Observe that, in saying, “I ask that you do not lose heart,” he shows that they possess the freedom of their own will; but lest they think this sufficient, he adds: “For this reason I bend my knees,” that is, I humble the disposition of my mind. [Ambrose] Or, I bend the outward knees of my body “to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The Greek has only “to the Father.” [Haimo] What has been added in Latin manuscripts, “of our Lord Jesus Christ,” suitably agrees, because he prayed that we might obtain this through the merit of him to whom God is Father properly and naturally, whereas he is our Father by adoption.

“From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named,” that is, by whose ordering we have fathers: angels in heaven who provide for us, and prelates on earth. Note that he does not say, “every fatherhood exists,” but “is named,” because neither human nor angel is truly father as God is, who is Father of all by creation and of believers by re-creation, whom he adopted as sons. For just as God, who alone truly exists and alone is truly good, shares the names of his being and goodness with others, so that they too are called beings and good, so he who alone is Father of all things by creation and of believers by regeneration has given the name of fatherhood to others. Or “is named” means “is capable of being named.” For from him who is Father of all, both angels in heaven and human beings on earth received the designation that they might be called fathers of others.

And note that Christ himself, God’s only-begotten Son by nature, by the benefit of adoption signifies that he is Father, saying: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9); and likewise: “My little children, I am with you a little longer” (John 15). Likewise does the Holy Spirit, through whom the righteous are adopted as sons. A human being, however, is called father either by nature, by the authority of example, or by reason of a benefit.

Therefore I bend my knees to Christ’s Father, “that he may give you, according to the riches of his glory,” that is, according to the abundance of his majesty, “strength,” that is, steadfastness—that is, may he grant you not to lose heart. For from strength comes not losing heart; namely, may he grant you “to be strengthened in the inner person,” that is, may he give you the strength by which you are made strong in the inner person, whom enemies cannot touch. And this is “through his Spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit. And first, may he grant “that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts,” which helps toward this end: that you may be confident of his help while he dwells in you through faith, so that when we have faith we may seem to have him himself.

[Note: [Col. 0191D] Augustine, *On John*.] For faith in us is Christ in us. Your faith concerning Christ is Christ in your heart. Not without reason, when he says, “May he give you strength,” does he add, “and may he grant Christ to dwell in you.” For heretics are sometimes strong, yet Christ does not dwell in them.

“In love.” The order of the words is this: I also pray that, “rooted,” that is, firmly planted in love, like a tree which, the more deeply it is fixed in the earth, the more it draws moisture, grows, and bears richer fruit; and “founded,” in the likeness of a house, because the Holy Spirit dwells in them—you may be able “to comprehend,” that is, to understand perfectly, “with all the saints,” that is, as all saints do.

[Note: [Col. 0192D] Augustine, *On the Grace of the New Testament*.] This is the fellowship of the divine and heavenly commonwealth. Such persons seek not their own interests but those of Christ; that is, they do not pursue private advantages but deliberate concerning the common good, where the salvation of all lies.

What are you to comprehend? “What is,” that is, how great ought to be, “the breadth” of love, which ought to extend even to enemies and to do good cheerfully; for one who gives sorrowfully loses what he gives. [Col. 0192D] [Note: Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Therefore the breadth of love is necessary, lest whatever good you do perish. But because love grows cold when iniquity abounds, length is necessary. Hence he adds: “and what is the length” of love. This is the long-suffering perseverance by which one in some sense endures while standing. Hence: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

“And what is the height” of love. [Augustine] This is what directs the heart upward, so that God may be awaited as reward. For if you do good even to enemies and give cheerfully, you have breadth; and if you persevere in these things to the end, you have length. But if you do not do all these things for the sake of the higher or heavenly reward, you do not have height; and then these are no longer either breadth or length. For to have height is to think of God, to love God, and to love freely him who is himself the helper and himself the one who strives (*conator*); finally, to reckon him himself as the reward, expecting from him no other thing than himself. If you love, you love freely; if you truly love, let him whom you love be your reward.

And “what is the depth” of love: that is, may you understand that it is God’s hidden judgment why he gives to this person and not to that. For from the depth of God’s judgments, which we cannot search out or contemplate, proceeds all that we can do. I see what I can do; I do not see whence I can do it, except because I know it is from God. Why he gives to that one and not to another is too much for me: it is an abyss and a depth.

Thus now love itself is exercised in good works to assist [Col. 0193B] others and is extended even to enemies; and this is breadth. [Note: [Col. 0193D] Augustine, *On the Grace of the New Testament*.] Now it bears adversities through long-suffering and perseveres in what it has truly held; and this is length. It does all this, moreover, for the attaining of eternal life, promised to it on high; and this is height. But this love arises from what is hidden; and this is depth. For depth is God’s will, whose causes are not searched out, by whose grace we have been saved—not from works of righteousness which we ourselves have done, but according to his mercy. For willingly he begot us by the word of truth; and this will is in the hidden place. In awe, as it were, before the depth of this secret, the apostle cries: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11). This is depth. For “height” is a common name for both what is lofty and what is deep; but when it is said of what is lofty, the eminence of exaltation is commended, whereas when it is said of what is deep, the difficulty of investigation and knowledge is meant.

And it should be understood that in these words the figure and mystery of the cross are displayed. For he who died because he willed to die, died in the manner he willed. Therefore he did not choose without purpose such a kind of death, in which he might become for you the teacher of this breadth, length, height, and depth. He who said: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 16). [Note: Col. 0193D, Augustine, *To Januarius*.] The cross is taken up when the deeds of the flesh are put to death by the Spirit; and so long as the body of sin is being destroyed, so long as the outward person is decaying in order that the inward may be renewed day by [Col. 0193D] day, it is the time of the cross. [Note: Col. 0193D, Augustine, in a certain sermon.] Therefore, he in whose power it was to die or not to die, and to die in this way or that, did not choose the cross without purpose, where he might crucify you to this world.

For the breadth of the cross is the transverse beam, where the hands are fastened; this pertains to good works, because there the hands are extended. Its length is in that part of the wood which stretches from the transverse beam toward the earth and is visible from that beam down to the ground: there the body is crucified and, as it were, stands; and this standing signifies perseverance. Its height is in that wood which rises upward from the same transverse beam toward the head; by this is signified the expectation of [Col. 0194A] things above. Its depth, however, is in the part of the wood which does not appear, which, fixed in the earth, is concealed—whence rises that which signifies the depth of gratuitous grace, in investigating which many minds are worn out. [Note: Col. 0194D, Augustine, *To Paulinus, On Seeing God*.]

Thus I am accustomed to understand these words of the Apostle: “I pray that you may be able to understand what is the breadth, the length,” etc.—that is, what is the mystery of the cross. For the understanding of these words is fitted to the sacrament of the cross. The sense is this: What is the breadth in works of charity, which extends even to loving enemies, as Christ did, who prayed for his enemies; this was shown in his cross, stretched broad from right to left, where the hands were fixed, through which works are signified—works which ought to be done cheerfully [Col. 0194B]; and what is the length of charity, namely that it must endure to the end. Hence it is said of Christ: “Having loved his own, he loved them to the end” (John 13). This was signified by the length of the cross from above to below. And what is the height of charity—that is, the goal toward which charity tends, namely eternal blessedness—signified by the upper part of the cross; and what is the depth of charity, which supports the whole, like the part of the cross fixed in the earth, namely in what is hidden and unseen: that is, the mercy of God, which proceeds from God’s hidden judgment, through which charity in us is long and broad, and likewise high. [Note: Col. 0194D, Augustine, *ibid.*]

For from God’s hidden will one person is called to share so great a grace in one manner, another in another manner. Or the depth of [Col. 0194C] charity is the ecclesiastical sacraments, which are profound and unfathomable and are the foundation of charity, without which charity has no power. Therefore, understanding the mystery of the cross, let us be crucified to the world: extending our hands in the breadth of good works; persevering in length to the end; having our heart above, where Christ is; and attributing all this not to ourselves but to his mercy, whose deep judgments weary every investigator.

“To know.” As if he said: I pray that you may also be able to know, in order partly to imitate, the charity of Christ by which he loved us, which surpasses ours, “surpassing human knowledge”—that is, which rises above and exceeds human knowledge, because it cannot be fully known how great was the charity with which he loved us. Or thus: “to know the charity of Christ,” that is, the charity possessed together with the knowledge of Christ is understood to surpass other charity. For charity joined with knowledge—that is, possessed with full knowledge—surpasses other charity, because the better God is understood, the more he is loved. Therefore I pray that you may know these things, so that through these forms of knowledge you may be filled with good, entering into all the fullness of God: so that here you may have fullness of virtues, and afterwards fullness of blessedness.

Some have understood this “fullness of God” in these words so as to suppose that we shall become the very same thing that God is, saying: “If we have anything [Col. 0195A] less than God and are lesser, how shall we be filled into all the fullness of God?” But since we shall be filled, they conclude, we shall surely be equal to God. This error is detestable. For they will not be filled in such a way as themselves to be the full God, but so as to be perfect persons filled with God.

Or thus: I pray that you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of God—that is, to know God as immense and beyond estimation, exceeding all things by the majesty of his power. [Ambrose] When he says this, he signifies that, just as in a sphere the length is as great as the breadth and the height as great as the depth, so also in God all things are equal in the immensity of infinity—indeed, altogether one and the same. The sense is: “What is the breadth,” etc.—that is, what is the immensity [Col. 0195B] of God, exceeding and filling all things, not enclosed within them but containing all things within himself, so that he alone is understood to be ineffable and infinite.

“To know,” etc. After the immensity of the Father, he wishes them to know that Christ’s charity is above human knowledge. Thus: that you may also be able to know that the charity of Christ surpasses human knowledge. For no one can grasp the magnitude of his charity: namely, that God became man; that the righteous one dies for the ungodly; the Lord for servants; the Creator for the creature; and such things. Therefore I desire you to know these things, that you may be filled into all the fullness of God—that is, that by confession and thanksgiving you may render honor to the Son as to the Father, so that there may be in you a full confession of divinity. [Col. 0195C] For then nothing is lacking to the Christian when he thus knows the Father and the Son; otherwise the confession of deity is not complete, because faith is neither complete in the Father alone nor perfect in the Son alone.

“But to him.” As if he said: This I pray for you; but to him who is able to do it be glory. And this is what he says: “But to him who is able to do all things,” that is, to accomplish in you, “far more abundantly than we ask or understand”—that is, more than we know or dare to ask. [Haimo] He says, “ask or understand,” because we understand more than we ask. He is able to do this in us, I say, according to the power working in us—that is, he is able to do it in you here just as he has already done it in us apostles. To him, I say—to him alone, not to a human being, who can do nothing of himself—be glory for the things which he has [Col. 0195D] done in the Church and in Christ Jesus; that is, may he appear glorious for these things, not only in the present age but also through all generations of the age of ages.

Or read the text thus: “But to him who is able to do all these things which I ask,” that is, to accomplish them. He is able, I say, according to the power working in us—working good things in us human beings—far more abundantly than we ask or understand. For God is able to do these things according to the power which works, in which are certain things which no one would ask or understand: namely, that God should become man and die for human beings, and other such things. To him, I say—to him alone—be glory in the Churches and in Christ Jesus. This does not change. [Col. 0196A] Let glory be, I say, through all generations of the age of ages—that is, of the age containing all ages. Amen.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSES 1–6.—“Therefore I beseech you, I, a prisoner in the Lord, that you walk worthily of the calling by which you were called, with all humility and gentleness, with patience bearing with one another in charity; eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all of us.”

“Therefore I beseech.” Up to this point he has shown that all things must be attributed to the grace [Col. 0196B] of God. From here to the end he exhorts concerning morals: first all in common, and afterwards the individual orders. As if he said: Since God can do all things—or that glory may be given to him by you—therefore I, Paul, a prisoner, whom you ought to pity, beseech you. A prisoner, I say, “in the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s sake: that you may walk, advancing from good to better, worthily of the calling by which you were called; that is, walk so that your way of life accords with my preaching. [Haimo] Thus: with all humility, both inward and outward; with gentleness, so that you may be teachable; and with patience in adversities, bearing with one another if trouble arises from a brother; or, “bear one another’s burdens.” [Note: Col. 0195D, Augustine, *To Eudoxius*.] And do this not falsely, nor for earthly [Col. 0196C] advantage, but in charity.

For this is the activity of the straight path, which always keeps its eyes upon God. Such activity is neither broken by business, nor cold, nor turbulent; neither slack, nor rash, nor fleeing, nor headlong, nor lying idle. Walk therefore in this way, and be eager—that is, diligent, cautious, attentive—to preserve, as something most sacred, the unity of the Spirit: that is, ecclesiastical unity, which the Holy Spirit makes, namely that you may be one body through the work of the Holy Spirit. You, I say, living “in the bond of peace,” that is, preserving peace, which is called a bond because this peace is the nourishment of spiritual unity.

This peace exists if we love one another’s goods; if we endure until the final harvest those sins which cannot be uprooted without harm to the wheat, or without hope that those to be corrected may be saved; if we also dispense with works of perfection which may lawfully be done or left undone, lest the weak be scandalized; and so forth.

“One.” As if he said: You ought to preserve the unity of the Spirit, so that you may be one body by helping your neighbor, and one spirit by willing the same thing as God. 170 Or, one spirit with the brothers with whom you ought to will and not will the same things. Or thus: You ought to preserve the unity of the Spirit, because you ought to be one body through the union of many members; you are able to do so because one Spirit dwells in you, by whom we are made one body. [Haimo] For we are made one body because of the fellowship made by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0197A] not without the Father and the Son. [Note: Col. 0197D, Augustine, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.]

Indeed, the Church has received this gift: that remission of sins should occur in the Holy Spirit.
