Although the Trinity accomplishes this remission, it is nevertheless understood as belonging properly to the Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 0197D, Augustine, sermon on Pentecost.] For he is the Spirit of adoption as sons; he is the love and bond of Father and Son. Therefore fellowship belongs to him, by which we are made one body of the only-begotten Son of God.

For as one human body consists of many members and one soul animates all the members—causing the eye to see, the ear to hear, and likewise the other members—so the Holy Spirit contains and animates the members of Christ’s body, which is the Church. And just as a severed member of the human body retains indeed the form by which it is recognized, but does not at all retain the spirit by which it might live apart from unity, so anyone divided from the unity of the aforesaid peace retains the sacrament as a kind of form, but does not live by the Spirit apart from unity. [Col. 0197B] [Note: Col. 0197D, Augustine, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.] In vain, therefore, does one outside boast of the form unless one is inwardly animated by the Spirit.

Because of this fellowship, those upon whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke in the languages of all nations, because the fellowship of the human race is maintained through languages. Thus, through the languages of the nations, this future fellowship of Christ’s members among all nations was prefigured: so that, just as then the person who spoke in the languages of all nations appeared to have received the Holy Spirit, so now the person who stands in the unity of the Church, which speaks all languages, may recognize that he has received the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0197C] “Just as you were called,” etc. As if he said: You ought thus to be one body, just as you were called into one hope of your calling—that is, to one hoped-for reality, which is the effect of calling.

“One Lord.” As if he said: You ought to preserve unity because you have one Lord, not three, for whose differing wills you would have to be at variance. And there is one faith concerning God. Recall that “faith” is said both of that which is believed and of that by which one believes. If therefore faith is here understood as that which is believed, the sense is this: There is one faith—that is, you are commanded to believe the same thing and to act in the same manner, because what is believed by all the faithful is one and the same. Hence Catholic faith is called universal. [Note: Col. 0198D, Augustine, *On the Trinity*.]

[Col. 0197D] Or faith here is understood as that by which one believes. For the things which are believed are one thing; the faith by which one believes is another. Those things are in realities which are believed to be, to have been, or to be future; but this faith is in the mind of the believer, visible only to the person whose faith it is, although it exists also in others—not the same faith itself, but a similar one. There is, therefore, one faith, not numerically but generically, because it is similar in all; just as two people willing the same thing are said to have one will, and two people very alike are said to have one face.

And there is one baptism—that is, equal, whoever gives it, and incapable of repetition. And you have one God—that is, the Creator of all—and Father, through his care and governance. Therefore no one can prefer himself to another, because we have one Creator and Re-creator. [Col. 0198A] He is God above all creatures—that is, preceding all creatures. As if he said: His dignity invites you. And he is diffused through all things, because he is everywhere, and therefore must be feared, since he cannot be escaped anywhere. And he is in all of us by grace, who preserve unity.

And note that this is not said individually concerning any one person, but commonly concerning all—that is, concerning the Trinity—according to the preceding exposition. [Haimo] Or it may be read so as to distinguish the persons. “Who,” etc. As if he said: There is one God and Father, although there are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and this is its sense: He, namely the Father, is above all, because he owes to no one what he is and excels all creatures; and [Col. 0198B] the Son is through all things, through whom all our works are restored and through whom all things were made; and the Holy Spirit is in all us faithful by grace, and in all creatures by essence. Hence: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wisdom 1).

### VERSES 7–10.—“But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift. Therefore he says: ‘Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.’ But what does ‘he ascended’ mean except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.”

[Col. 0198C] “But to each.” He has exhorted them to preserve the unity by which we are all called one body; and, lest unity abolish subordination, he adds that human beings have diverse gifts, which is not contrary to the unity just mentioned. [Ambrose] For the fact that human beings have diverse gifts [Note: Col. 0198D, “Something seems to be missing here.”] is not opposed to unity, but makes us, as it were, one body. But to each of us diverse grace—that is, a gratuitous gift—has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift: according as Christ, the giver, measures out one thing to one person and another to another. Christ, to whom God did not give by measure because he is full of grace, gives to human beings by measure. Measure is a certain division of divine gifts. For one person has one thing, another another; and what this person has, that person does not have.

Therefore, namely in order to prove that [Col. 0198D] Christ as man gives diverse gifts, the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Ascending.” [Note: Col. 0198D, Augustine, on Psalm 77.] As if he said: Truly Christ according to his humanity gives gifts. For the Prophet says that Christ, ascending on high in place and dignity, “led captivity captive”—that is, those whom the devil had held captive from Paradise and had made his own possessions of the world and of hell. Christ made them captive anew when they were led back to heaven. He thus called the human beings themselves “captivity,” because they were held captive under the devil, just as when “the soldiery” is spoken of, those who serve as soldiers are understood. He calls that same captivity captive by Christ, so that the captivity may be blessed. [Col. 0199A] For human beings can be captured for good. Hence Peter was told: “From now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5). They are therefore called captive because they have been captured, subdued, placed under a light yoke, freed from sin, and made servants of righteousness.

And he gave gifts to rational human beings, namely the Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 0199D, Augustine, Book XV, *On the Trinity*.] It is well known that the Lord Jesus, when he had ascended into heaven after the resurrection, gave the Holy Spirit, and believers filled with him spoke in all languages. Yet the Psalm reads thus: “You received gifts in men” (Psalm 67). [Augustine] For many manuscripts, especially Greek ones, have this reading, and we have it thus translated from the Hebrew. The Apostle, however, says “gifts,” as does the Prophet, not “gift.” But although the Prophet said, “You received in men,” Paul, by apostolic [Col. 0199B] authority, preferred to say, “He gave to men,” so that from both expressions, one prophetic and the other apostolic—because each has the authority of divine utterance—the fullest meaning might be conveyed.

For both are true: both that he gave to human beings and that he received in human beings. He gave to human beings as the head to his members; he received in human beings, he himself indeed in his members. Thus Christ both gave from heaven and received on earth: he gave because he is God with the Father; he received because he himself is in his own people in the Church, in which he receives. This is what it means to receive in human beings. Nor should it trouble you that he says “gifts,” not “gift,” although the Prophet agrees with him. Without doubt the Holy Spirit is the gift of God, of whom the [Col. 0199C] Lord said to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God,” etc. (John 4). But both spoke in the plural, “gifts,” because through the gift which is the Holy Spirit many gifts, proper to different persons, are distributed. Not every individual has all gifts: some have these and others those, although they possess the same gift from which the gifts proper to each are distributed—namely, the Holy Spirit. Hence elsewhere: “The one and same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 10), just as one soul acts all things in all the members.

“But what,” he continues the preceding proof—namely, that Christ according to his humanity gives, because the Prophet says that he gave when ascending. The Prophet said, “ascending.” But what is this “he ascended”—that is, what does it mean that he is said to have ascended—[Col. 0199D] except that he first descended, in relation to which he is said to have ascended? [Haimo] He descended, I say, into the lower parts of the earth, that is, to hell; proof of this was given above, because he led away the captivity which he drew out from there. [Ambrose] For they were held in hell by a sentence; but that sentence could not hold the Savior, because he was without sin.

The sequence of the proof is thus: the Prophet says that he gave when ascending; and he called it ascending in relation to descent; thus he implies that he gave also when descending. [Haimo] And it is clear that Christ descended and ascended according to his humanity; therefore he gave according to his humanity. According to his divinity, he who is everywhere [Col. 0200A] does not ascend or descend in place; but according to his soul he descended to hell, and according to body and soul he ascended into heaven; and thus he gave according to his humanity. Take care how you understand that Christ gave according to his humanity, lest this contradict the authority stated above, where it is said that he gives as God. Distinguish it thus: Christ gives according to his humanity—that is, Christ himself, as man, gives—not, however, by virtue of being man, but because he is God who descended. As if he said: Since the Prophet’s words imply this, the one who descended is also the one who ascended—that is, the one who descended to hell is the same as the one who ascended above all heavens.

Or thus, beginning from the place “But what.” As if he said: Christ, ascending—which is according to his humanity—gave gifts. But what is it that humanity ascended? That is, how could humanity ascend, unless [Col. 0200B] divinity first descended into the parts of the earth below the air, in order to be united to human nature? Divinity descended, indeed, not locally but by self-emptying. And because he had said that humanity ascended and divinity descended, lest they appear to be two, he adds: He who descended—that is, God—and he who ascended above all heavens—that is, man—is Christ himself; that is, one and the same person. Hence the Lord says: “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven,” etc. (John 3). [Ambrose] He ascended, I say, in order to fulfill all things that had been foretold of him in the Law and the Prophets. [Haimo] Or all things are filled by his gifts, and thus he filled all things.

[Col. 0200C] ### VERSES 11–14.—“And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others indeed as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness, so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried around by every wind of doctrine, by human wickedness, by cunning directed to the deception of error.”

“And he himself gave some apostles,” namely, successors in his preaching; “some prophets,” who prophesied of future things, or rather interpreters of the Scriptures. [Col. 0200D] [Ambrose] For in the New Testament prophets are called expositors of the Scriptures; nevertheless, at the beginning of the faith some foretold future things, such as Agabus and Philip’s seven daughters. [Haimo] “Others indeed evangelists,” such as Mark and Luke, and the seven deacons under the apostles. For evangelists are deacons, because even though they are not priests, they may nevertheless evangelize. “Others, however, pastors and teachers,” such as bishops, who ought to teach by word and example. Therefore he joined the terms, embracing them as one thing under two names, so that they might understand that teaching belongs to the office of pastors. [Note: Col. 0200D, Augustine, *To Paulina*.] For a pastor is not one unless he has [Col. 0201A] teaching by which to feed the flock.

See how he gave more to some and less to others. He gives to human beings by measure; he himself, however, receives not by measure. He gave all these for the work of ministry: namely, that each might be able fully to perform the work of service entrusted to him. For one person could not perform every task perfectly. This ministry was necessary for the perfecting of the saints—that those who are already holy might be perfected—and for the building up of Christ’s body: that those still alien might be built into Christ’s body.

“Until we all,” etc. As if he said: This preeminence and ordering will endure until, on the day of judgment, all of us who are in the unity of faith—that is, in one and not discordant faith—and in unity of the knowledge [Col. 0201B] of the Son of God—that is, in one and not differing knowledge of the Son of God—or in the unity of knowledge of the Son of God, that is, the virtues by which the Son of God is recognized to be in us, or by which we shall know him in the future; until, I say, all of us may meet one another from the different regions of the world, or meet Christ himself, the head. As if he said: Running in desire toward joy. Until that same thing occurs, this preeminence will endure, but not afterwards; and therefore it must not be borne heavily.

We, I say, advancing and growing “unto a perfect man and unto the measure of Christ’s fullness”—that is, your fullness—growing so that each may be a perfect man. He says that all are to be brought to manhood, not in sex but in perfection of virtue. For they are children in the strength of body and mind. And let each possess the same age, that age at which [Col. 0201C] Christ possessed fullness of years and body, when he departed from this world: this is the measure and limit of age, beyond which nothing naturally increases in a human being. [Haimo] For all shall rise at the same age at which Christ died and rose, whatever their age when they died. And women are included under the name “man” when he says, “unto a perfect man.”

[Note: Col. 0201D, Augustine, *City of God*.] And because all shall rise at the same age at which Christ died, he fittingly did not say “unto the measure of bodily stature,” but “of age.” For each will receive his own bodily measure: either that which he had in youth, even if he died old; or that which he had had; or that which he would have had, if he had died earlier. That age, however, will be the one Christ himself attained—namely, young adulthood, about thirty years. It is not permissible to say that, at the resurrection, a size shall be added to the body which it did not have; nor are larger bodies to be reduced to the size of the Lord’s body. For much of those bodies would perish, although not even a hair is to perish, as the Lord says: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke 21).

[Note: Col. 0202D, Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Nothing removed in any way from the human body shall perish. For in each body that material will be so proportioned that none of it perishes, and he who made what he willed from nothing shall supply what any person lacks. If anything has excessively abounded in some part, it shall be distributed through the whole. For nothing there [Col. 0202A] will be unseemly; whatever shall exist will be fitting. The bodies of the saints, therefore, shall rise without any defect or deformity; nor shall that earthly material which becomes a corpse when the soul departs be restored in the resurrection in such a way that the things which have fallen away, even though they return to the body from which they fell, must also return to the same bodily parts in which they had been. Otherwise the hair and nails would be restored in excessive and unseemly size.

Or it may be understood thus: he calls Christ with his whole body “the perfect man”; this will not be perfect until all the elect are completed. But when the number of the elect is complete, what is said here will occur: “until we meet” Christ the head, “unto a perfect man”—that is, so that we all, namely head and members, [Col. 0202B] may be one perfect man, lacking nothing and requiring no addition. He is perfect because then we shall advance unto the measure of Christ’s full age: a limit, because nothing will then be added to the number or strength beforehand; a measure, because then Christ will more fully possess all, just as he knows all individually, and all in him shall be immortal and blessed with him. Then preeminence will not be necessary.

But until that time he gave the aforementioned ministers for this purpose: that we might no longer, as formerly, be children in understanding and tossed about—that is, wavering through your weakness—and not be carried about, one thing driving another, by every wind of doctrine, that is, corrupt teaching. The teaching of the corrupt is like wind and tempest. [Col. 0202C] [Ambrose] I mean teaching produced by the wickedness of human beings, for which they were created; and produced by cunning—that is, by people malicious in themselves and clever to deceive the simple—whose teaching is devised for the deception of error, so that under a pretext of truth it may deceive more effectively by drawing people into error.

### VERSES 15–22.—“But, doing the truth in charity, let us grow in every way into him who is the head, Christ; from whom the whole body, joined and knit together through every supporting joint, according to the working in the measure of each individual member, makes the body grow for its own building up in charity. Therefore I say and testify in the Lord that you no longer walk as the Gentiles also walk in the vanity of their [Col. 0202D] mind, having their understanding darkened by darkness, alienated from the life of God through the ignorance which is in them because of the blindness of their heart; who, despairing, gave themselves over to unchastity, to the working of every uncleanness, in greed. But you have not so learned Christ, if indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as truth is in Jesus: put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, which is corrupted according to the desires of error.”

“But doing the truth.” As if he said: Let us not be such persons, but rather, actively doing the truth—that is, doing good according to teaching—and doing this in charity, that is, not falsely [Col. 0203A] or from fear, let us grow in affirmation of faith in every respect—that is, in every spiritual gift. And this in him—that is, with him working—who is our head, that is, one who provides for us, and Christ, that is, one able to rule. For *Christ* means “anointed,” and kings were anointed in the Old Testament.

I say, in him, and fittingly so: from whom—that is, through whom—the whole body, that is, the Church, is joined together through faith and knit together by the bond of charity. Hence he adds: “Through every supporting joint.” As if he said: It is joined and knit together through every supporting joint, that is, through faith and charity, which join the members and make them serve one another. I mean support rendered not by will alone but also through action, according to the measure [Col. 0203B] of each member—that is, according to what each member can do by the grace given to it.

And truly the body is joined and knit together through Christ, because he causes the body’s growth—that is, he increases those who are already the body. He alone, I say, is Lord, for the building up of himself, because he builds those who are not the body into his own city or fellowship. And he does all this in charity—that is, out of love. Once this has been accomplished, there will be the measure of age.

“This.” Here he exhorts the Ephesians to guard themselves against the habit of their former Gentile life. As if he said: Because God has provided so many aids for preserving unity, and because you are able to grow and will meet him, therefore I say—not merely “I beseech,” as above, but “I say and testify in the Lord,” that is, I command under the Lord’s witness—this: that [Col. 0203C] now, that is, from the time of faith, you no longer walk, that is, live, as the Gentiles walk, who walk in the vanity of their own mind because they love transitory things. This sensuality suggests it.

Having their natural understanding darkened by darkness, that is, made not a little obscure. And therefore it is less surprising that they walk in vanity than it would be in you, who are enlightened and possess the spirit of life. [Note: Col. 0203D, Augustine, on Psalm LXI.] Everyone who understands is illumined by a certain inward light. There is therefore a certain light within, which those who do not understand do not possess. I say, the Gentiles are alienated from the faith of God, that is, without hope of immortality. Or, from the life of God, that is, from God who is the life of the soul, because God abandons them. [Note: Col. 0204D, Id., in the book of Sentences.] For there are two lives: one of the body, the other of the soul; and as the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. And just as the body dies if the soul abandons it, so the soul dies if God abandons it. The soul, departing from the light of righteousness, the more it seeks something that it may find against righteousness, the more it is driven away from the light of truth and plunged into darkness.

[Ambrose.] I say, alienated through ignorance, that is, because they are ignorant of the life of God—an ignorance remaining in them because of the blindness or hardness of their heart, since they have closed the eyes of their heart to preaching. They too, through their disgrace, despairing of the future life—or, “without feeling,” another reading drawn from the Greek, that is, not grieving for themselves on account of sin—have delivered themselves voluntarily to unrestricted wickedness, to impurity, that is, fornication. And then they have given themselves over to the practice of every uncleanness, so that they have omitted absolutely nothing unclean.

[Jerome.] And this is in covetousness, that is, in vehement and insatiable desire, because they are never satisfied by indulgence, their pleasure knowing no limit, so that they practise shamefulness even beyond the permitted bounds of marriage. Or, as others say, “and covetousness,” or “in covetousness”; and it is understood independently as another vice, so that the sense is: “They gave themselves over to the practice of every uncleanness,” 172 “and gave themselves over to covetousness.” Or thus: I say, they dwell in covetousness; but you—As though he said: The Gentiles thus walk, but you have not learned that Christ is to be imitated [Col. 0204B] in this way. Yet you have heard him, that is, understood his preaching, or heard him speaking inwardly; and you have been taught in him, that is, if you have heard him in such a way that you have been, or are, taught the truth in him, as truth is in Jesus.

[Ambrose.] He says this because there are some in the Church who, under Christ’s name, do not follow the truth of Christ which he taught—namely, “to put off,” that is, that you should put off yourselves, etc. Or, according to another reading: As though he said: This is the truth which he taught, that you should put off yourselves. Therefore put off yourselves, not according to the substance of body or soul, but according to your former manner of life: namely, put off the old man, who is corrupted, even if he takes pleasure. I say, he is corrupted according to desires, not only according to [Col. 0204C] deeds. Therefore put off also the desires of error, that is, desires which come from error or lead to error.

Some suppose that the old man is the body and the new man the soul. But the body is the outward man, the soul the inward; and this newness and oldness take place in the inward man. Therefore, when he says, “put off yourselves,” etc., he does not command that the body be put off, but that life be changed for the better. Thus, if a person follows former vices, he is called old; but if he walks in newness of life, estranged from the error of the world, he is called new. Therefore, in so far as he is corrupted, he grows old. Hence he says, “Put off the old man,” that is, oldness, because it is the inward man that becomes old and is corrupted. He adds that, even if it takes pleasure, it is nevertheless corrupted in the inward man through desires of error: this is oldness. Therefore, so far as it is granted you, put off this oldness [Col. 0204D].

**VERS. 23–27.**—“But be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth. Wherefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth each one with his neighbour, because we are members one of another. Be angry, and do not sin. Let not the sun set upon your anger. Give no place to the devil.”

But be renewed daily in the spirit of your mind, [Haimo.] that is, through the Holy Spirit, who leads to reason. Or, through your spirit, that is, through your mind [Col. 0205A], that is, in a spiritual mind. Or, “through the spirit of your mind,” that is, through the spirit which is mind, or reason, or understanding, or whatever other term may more suitably name it.

[Note: Col. 0205D, Augustine, on Genesis.] The image of God is that by which man rules over the other animals. Created in the knowledge of God, after it became foolish through sin it is renewed in that same knowledge, so that the image may begin to be re-formed by him by whom it was formed.

[Note: Col. 0205D, Id., *The City of God*.] For it cannot reform itself as it was able to deform itself. It was created in the very knowledge of God before it became old through transgression, but after the fall into sin it is re-formed in that same knowledge.

[Note: Col. 0205D, Id., on Genesis.] It is therefore sufficiently shown wherein man was created in the image of God: namely, not in the lineaments of the body, but in a certain intelligible form of the enlightened mind.

[Note: Col. 0206D, Id., *On the Trinity*.] Therefore, when he says, “in the spirit of your mind,” he did not intend two things to be understood there [Col. 0205B], as though mind were one thing and the spirit of mind another; rather, the mind is spirit. A similar expression occurs in “the stripping off of the body of flesh,” that is, flesh which is body.

And put on, in deed, the new man, [Haimo.] that is, assume the likeness of the new man, namely Christ, of whom elsewhere it is said: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13). [Ambrose.] Whoever is conformed to him by the shaping of his mind truly puts him on. For one puts on Christ who is reborn in Christ through faith, emulating the life which Christ handed down. He, the new man—namely Christ—was created according to God, that is, not by human nature but by God’s power.

[Haimo.] For he was conceived in the virginal womb by the work of the Holy Spirit, from the seed of woman and without the seed of man. This [Col. 0205C] was new. Hence Jeremiah: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man in the embrace of her womb” (Jer. 31). I say, he was created in righteousness, namely in universal good action, and in perfect holiness of truth, without hypocrisy; and because he is righteous, good things are to be bestowed universally upon all. And he is truly holy, so that he is holiness itself, as he is righteousness and truth.

Or thus: “who according to God”—as though he said: Be renewed in spirit, which spirit was created according to God, that is, in the image of God, in righteousness indeed and holiness of truth; but by sinning it lost righteousness and holiness of truth. For this reason the image was made deformed and discoloured, but it receives its form when it is fashioned and renewed. Therefore he sets forth, part by part, the old and the new man.

[Augustine.] “Wherefore,” because, namely, the old man is to be put off and the new put on, “putting away falsehood,” which is part of oldness, “speak truth,” which is part of newness, each one with his neighbour—that is, with every person, even a Gentile or a Jew. For every person is a neighbour by the condition of first birth; or, in hope of conversion, every person ought to be considered a neighbour before becoming a Christian. For if you know what he will be before God, perhaps one who is now a Jew, pagan, or heretic will by God’s mercy be so converted to God that he will recline among the saints.

“Because we are,” etc. As though he said: It is fitting to speak [Col. 0206A] truth, because we are members of one another, serving one another. Then he enumerates many parts of the old man from which he dissuades them, and conversely many parts of the new man to which he exhorts them, saying: “Be angry, and do not sin.” As though he said: I unwillingly tolerate what cannot be avoided—namely, that because of anger you do not come to the act of sinning. Therefore, if a movement of the mind arises which, now because of sin’s penalty, is not in our power, at least let reason not consent to it. The Apostle indeed permits anger, which is a human temptation, but forbids bringing anger into effect.

[Haimo.] Or thus: “Be angry” against sinners: this is a natural movement of the mind, which is accustomed to contribute to the improvement of offenders. Therefore he says that one ought to be angry, showing that this anger is good; but he warns them not to sin by exceeding due measure [Col. 0206B], adding, “Do not sin,” by reproving and burdening the sinner too harshly. Hence Solomon: “Do not be excessively righteous, because there is one who perishes in his righteousness” (Eccl. 7). Righteousness therefore must be moderated, so that we may imitate God, who bears with the wicked so that some of them may be corrected.

“And let not the sun set upon your anger,” that is, let anger itself not last until sunset. This is indeed understood simply and temporally: if anger steals upon a Christian through the weakness which we bear, it ought not to be retained long or become yesterday’s anger; it must be cast out of the heart before this invisible light sets.

[Ambrose.] Therefore the Apostle wishes anger not to endure, because, if it endures, opportunity is given to the devil. For an angry person thinks evil thoughts, and thus the devil inserts himself in order to carry out evil deeds. Hence he adds: “Give no place.” Or, better thus: the sun—that is, the brightness of reason; or Christ—“let not [Col. 0206C] set upon your anger,” that is, let it not be darkened for you by anger as though by an intervening mountain. Christ, our sun of righteousness and truth, is he by whose truth the soul is illumined when he dwells in a person through faith. Therefore he says, “Let not the sun set upon your anger,” that is, take care that Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, does not abandon your mind because of anger; for he never dwells with anger. And even if someone provokes you—which is the devil’s temptation—do not give the devil a place by persevering in anger.

[Augustine.] Or thus, so that it may also be understood of good anger: Be angry with yourselves over past sins, which is repentance, and “do not sin,” that is, cease henceforth to sin [Col. 0206D]. As though he said: I want you to be angry so that you may not sin. But with whom ought you to be angry in order that you may not sin, unless with yourselves? For what is a penitent person except one who exacts punishment from himself, so that he may receive pardon? And the sense is: “Be angry, and do not sin,” that is, be indignant with yourselves with such intensity that you cease to sin; for the sun of righteousness does not set upon this anger, but rather shines upon it. Hence he adds: “Let not the sun set upon your anger,” that is, the sun will not set upon your anger; and do not give the devil a place even to enter you, through evil desire or fear.

[Note: Col. 0206D, Augustine, on Psalm CLXI.] For there are two gates through which the devil enters: desire and fear. If you desire something earthly, the devil enters by this gate; if you fear something earthly, he enters by that also. When these are turned to their opposites, God enters by them. For if you desire the kingdom of heaven and fear the fire of Gehenna, you open the gates to Christ, and Christ enters. Therefore those gates must be shut to him and opened to Christ.

**VERS. 28–32.**—“Let him who stole steal no more; but rather let him labour, working with his hands what is good, that he may have whereof to give to one suffering need. Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but if any is good for the edification of faith, that it may give grace to those who hear. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and anger, and [Col. 0207B] indignation, and clamour, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. But be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, as God also in Christ forgave you.”

He who stole—which likewise is a part of the old man—must steal no more, that is, must not take anything away by any fraud. Rather, let each one labour, working not merely through servants but also with his own hands. I say, working not evil works for gain, but what is good, so that he may have not only wherewith to help, but also wherewith to give to one suffering need.

Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, even if it has been conceived in the heart. For in God’s servant all things ought to appear good, and his purity ought not to be stained in any respect. “But if any”—as though he said: Evil speech [Col. 0207C] ought not proceed from the mouth; but neither should even good speech be uttered uselessly. This is what he says: if any speech is good and capable of building up faith, let it proceed in the best and most fitting manner, so that it gives grace, that is, is pleasing to its hearers.

And do not grieve by disobedience the Holy Spirit of God, that is, the preacher of truth; this is to grieve the Holy Spirit, so far as you are concerned. [Note: Col. 0207D, Augustine, on Genesis.] For the substance of the Holy Spirit, by which he is whatever he is, cannot be grieved, since it is eternal and unchangeable blessedness itself. But the Apostle employed a figure of speech 173 by which we speak of things that do not happen to God as though they happened to him, representing him as causing them to happen to us. Therefore we must not maintain that anything of this kind happens to the Holy Spirit, who is unchangeable in himself; but he dwells in the saints in order to fill them with charity, by which he makes them rejoice in others’ progress and grieve over the falls or sins of those in whose faith and piety they rejoiced. This grief is praiseworthy because it comes from the charity which the Holy Spirit pours out. Thus he is said to be grieved because he produces this in his own people, through whose gift they are so good that wicked people grieve them—especially those whom they knew or believed to have been good.

In the same manner of speech God is said to know when he causes us to know, and to rest from the works which he had made very good, because he causes us to rest when we have done good works.

[Col. 0208A] Or thus: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, that is, do not drive him away from yourselves through evil works. When we act well, the Holy Spirit given to us rejoices in us, seeing his admonitions yield profit for us. Therefore he rejoices, that is, he remains in us as an indweller, if we profit by him. Otherwise he is grieved, that is, he abandons us. He is not grieved so as to suffer, since he is impassible; but he is said to be grieved because he withdraws from us. Just as a person is grieved when he is expelled from his own house which he built for himself, so the Holy Spirit is said to be grieved when he is driven out through evil works from the person whom he cleansed for himself in baptism.

“In whom”—as though he said: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, which you ought not to do, because he is the one in whom, that is, by whose grace, you were sealed: as wax by a seal [Col. 0208B], his image having been left in you, that is, the form of newness impressed upon you.

[Haimo, Ambrose.] Or, “you were sealed,” that is, distinguished from the wicked. And this on the day of redemption, that is, of baptism.

[Note: Col. 0208D, Augustine, in the book *Against Lying*.] Let all bitterness—in biting words or deeds—and anger, that is, sudden rage, and indignation, which occurs when one who is inferior exalts himself (this comes from anger), and clamour, that is, contention, which comes from indignation and is the voice of one almost mad; and blasphemy, which is committed against God or the saints—blasphemy by which false things are said about God: let all these, I say, be removed from you, because they can bring destruction unless they are removed. Even if these occur through incidental causes, they must nevertheless be restrained. And because, once these were repressed, evil could remain in the heart, he adds: let them be removed together with every malice of heart.

“Be,” [Col. 0208C] etc. Here again he shows a part of the new man. As though he said: Let those things be removed from you; be kind to one another, that is, generous from your resources; and compassionate, in affection and sympathy of mind, even if there is nothing to give; and forgiving one another the offences committed against you—namely, if one sins against another, forgive him; otherwise God reclaims what he has forgiven. For if one has shown contempt in these matters, without doubt he will revoke the judgment by which he had granted mercy, as is read in the Gospel concerning the wicked servant who was found merciless toward his fellow-servant.

## CHAPTER V

**VERS. 1–6.**—“Be therefore imitators of God, as most beloved children; and walk in love, as Christ also [Col. 0208D] loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness. But let fornication and every uncleanness or covetousness not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor shamefulness, nor foolish talk, nor jesting which is not fitting, but rather thanksgiving. For know this and understand: that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person—which is idolatry—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no one deceive you with empty words; for because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief.”

Therefore, I say, forgive one another, as God [Col. 0209A] in Christ, that is, through Christ, forgave us; and because he forgave, therefore be imitators of God by forgiving one another. Then you will be as most beloved children. And do not merely forgive, but also walk, by the exercise of works, in love, laying down your lives for your brothers if need be. And do this as sincerely as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering to God, when he endured the wrong of spittle, blows, and the like; and as a sacrifice when he was slain on the cross. That sacrifice was not figurative, like the legal sacrifices, but is truly to God an odour of sweetness.

He alludes to the language of the law, because this is he of whom it was said in the law. For those sacrifices were not said to be offered as an odour of sweetness on their own account, but because they signified him who is truly offered as an odour of sweetness, because he was slain for the righteousness which he practised [Col. 0209B] and preserved even unto death.

[Ambrose.] But if Christ’s death was a sweet odour to God, then he willingly accepted his death. Therefore those who crucified him did not sin. But this is not so, because they unjustly killed the righteous one, who was slain and offered according to the will of the Father and his own will.

[Note: Col. 0209D, Augustine, on John.] For what did Judas have in handing Christ over except sin? Yet Christ would not have handed himself over unless Judas had handed him over. Judas handed Christ over; Christ handed himself over. But the former pursued the business of his own sale, the latter that of our redemption. Therefore Judas sinned wickedly; Christ acted mercifully.

But fornication, which is with women free from a husband, and every uncleanness, namely incontinence pertaining to lust, however it is committed; or covetousness, that is, an immoderate desire [Col. 0209C] to possess—let it not even be named among you, that is, let not even a plausible suspicion concerning you exist, as befits saints. Nor let shamefulness be named, as in kisses and embraces; nor foolish talk, such as coarse words; nor jesting, which fools call *curialitas* (“courtly wit”), that is, joking which tends to provoke laughter and is not relevant, that is, does not contribute to usefulness, however much labour may be expended upon it. Rather, let thanksgiving be named among you. Nor ought those things to be named.

For know this by the reasoning of your mind, and understand also that this is what the Scriptures say: every fornicator, unclean person, or covetous person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, that is, in the kingdom of heaven which belongs to the Father and the Son. But observe that, after saying “covetous person,” he added “which is idolatry” [Col. 0209D], equating covetousness with idolatry, because he means the covetous person whose god is money. Or covetousness is equated with idolatry because, as the idolater usurps and claims for himself the honour due to God, so the covetous person usurps for himself and hoards the goods of God which he wishes to be kept for the needy. Or “covetous person” here means an adulterer, who usurps another’s possessions, that is, another man’s wife.

“No one”—as though he said: I say that such persons will not have God’s kingdom, and against what I teach let no one deceive you, promising impunity from God’s mercy or preaching natural necessities. I say, let him deceive you with empty words: all their arguments are empty words.

[Haimo.] Because of this, or because of these things—namely fornication [Col. 0210A] and the other vices mentioned—the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief, that is, the children of the devil, concerning whom we despair; or those who despair of eternal life.

**VERS. 7–17.**—“Therefore do not become partakers with them. For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of light is in all goodness and righteousness and truth, proving what is pleasing to God. And do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to speak of. But all things which are reproved are made manifest by the light; for everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore he says: Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall illumine you. Therefore, brothers, see [Col. 0210B] that you walk cautiously, not as unwise persons but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Therefore do not become imprudent, but understand what the will of God is.”

Therefore do not become partakers, that is, like them, by imitating their deeds; for if you are companions in the deed, you will also be companions in the punishment. Nor ought you to be so. For you were once darkness, that is, sinning through ignorance and children of the devil, prince of darkness; and therefore it is not surprising if those evils were then in us. But now you are light, that is, doing good with discernment and justified by faith and baptism. And you are children of God by adoption, he who is the true light. And this is in the Lord, not in yourselves. You were darkness indeed in yourselves, but you are light in the Lord, who enlightens every person coming into this world [Col. 0210C] (John 1). Therefore he did not add “in the Lord” when he said, “you were darkness,” but when he said, “but now light.” And because you are light in the Lord, walk with the good step of works as children of light—that is, live as children of God, namely holy and without stain.

For this is the fruit of light, that is, these are works of light: to live in all goodness, so that you may be good in yourselves; and in righteousness, so that you do to your neighbours what is just; and in truth, so that you speak what is true. Or he explains goodness in its parts, for righteousness and truth are parts of goodness. The sense is: live in all goodness, and thereby in righteousness and truth, namely live justly and speak truthfully, proving—as though he said: I say, walk, first testing and discerning by reason [Col. 0210D] what is pleasing to God. As though he said: Let all your works be so circumspect that they please God.

“Do not”—as though he said: Walk as children of light, and do not share in the unfruitful works of darkness, namely of evil persons; that is, always be separated in heart from evil persons.

[Note: Col. 0210D, Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] For a time, beware: be joined in body; bear the chaff on the threshing-floor, bear it in the barn. What you bear in the barn you will not have in the granary; the winnower will come, who will separate the good from the evil. There will be a bodily separation, which spiritual separation ought to precede. Therefore he says, “Do not share in unfruitful works,” that is, evil works, lest the wicked have a portion with the good.

“But rather reprove them,” that is, do not be [Col. 0211A] negligent in correcting those who in any way fall under your care, but do so with a gentle spirit. As the Apostle says elsewhere, do this so that correction may sound outwardly terrible, while inwardly the love of gentleness is maintained. Observe that he joins two things: namely, that they do not share by consenting, and that they reprove.

[Note: Col. 0211D, Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] For in these two ways an evil person does not defile you: if you do not consent and if you reprove. The Apostle embraces both, saying: “Do not share,” that is, do not consent, praise, or approve; and because it is little enough not to consent, he adds, “but rather reprove,” that is, rebuke, correct, restrain.

[Ambrose.] And the sense is: Do not consent to the wicked by approving them; do not be negligent by failing to reprove them; and do not arrogantly insult them in pride.

“But the things,” or “for”—as though he said: I say, do not share; nor ought you to, because it is shameful not only to do but even to speak of the things which they do in a hidden place [Col. 0211B], that is, not openly but secretly; and this shows that they are shameful. Or, “in secret,” that is, in thought.

“But all things,” or “for”—as though he said: It is shameful to speak of what they do; nevertheless they must be reproved, because in this way they are often made manifest through confession. This is: all things that are reproved by the light—that is, by good and holy people who are children of light—are often made manifest through confession and repentance; and therefore they must be reproved. For every evil thus made manifest, that is, through confession and repentance, is light, that is, is turned into light, because it is good for sin to be revealed through confession and repentance.

[Haimo.] Or, “is light,” that is, it is not doubtful and cannot be excused when it has been openly stated. Or thus: “For all things”—as though he said: Therefore reprove them, for all things which are reproved by the saints—that is, those evil persons when they are reproved by the saints—are made manifest to themselves, although they are evil.

[Ambrose.] For then they appear sinners to themselves and to others when they are rebuked. Therefore they should be reproved, because in this way they begin to be light. Hence he adds: “everything,” or “for,” “that is made manifest”—that is, an evil person, when he comes to know himself as evil—“is light,” that is, through repentance he begins to turn toward good.

[Haimo, Augustine.] Therefore, because he becomes light, the Holy Spirit says through me: “You who sleep,” [Col. 0211D] that is, who lie torpid in sin and do not know that you are in sins, having forgotten God, “arise” through confession, “and rise up” through satisfaction from the dead, that is, from future condemnation; and Christ, who is the sun of righteousness, will illumine you here through faith and hope, and in the future through sight. And because reproving is profitable:

“Therefore, brothers, see how”—that is, with a certain moderation—“you walk cautiously,” in living and reproving, not as unwise persons, that is, indiscreet persons, but as wise, providing for everything. I say, redeeming the time, that is, preparing for yourselves an opportunity to serve God and attend to divine matters. This is necessary because the days are evil, that is, because there are evil people today [Col. 0212A].

[Note: Col. 0212D, Augustine, in a sermon on the Words of the Gospel.] Days are called evil for two reasons: the wickedness and the misery of people. Otherwise, these days, so far as the succession of hours is concerned, are ordered. They take their turns; they carry on the times. The sun rises and sets; times pass. Times are burdensome to one for whom people are not themselves burdens. Therefore days are called evil, as I said, because of human wickedness and misery; but human misery is common, whereas wickedness ought not to be common. Ever since fallen Adam was driven from paradise, days have never been other than evil. This is shown by the child who is born, because he begins with crying and cannot laugh: as soon as he is born he cries, a prophet indeed of his own calamity. Tears are witnesses of misery; he does not yet speak and already prophesies. What then? That he will be in labour—or will even be afraid, if he is righteous; certainly, placed amid tribulations, he will always fear.

Therefore let us redeem the time. What is it to redeem time? He redeems time who loses, that is, gives of his own, so that he may attend to God rather than lawsuits—as though he gives money for a defect. For you give money and buy bread, wine, or something else; you give and receive, lose something and gain something. Therefore, just as you spend money to buy something for yourself, so spend what is yours to purchase quietness for yourself: this is redeeming the time. Hence the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to contend with you in court and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also,” so that you may have a peaceful heart and not lose the time for attending to your God, from whom he wishes to draw you away by loss and lawsuits.

Or thus: redeeming the time means that what you did too little in one [Col. 0212C] time, restore in another, halving the days which the ungodly do not halve. For some halve their days, others fill them, and others do not even begin them; that is, some die in Egypt, others in the Holy Land. Nor is it surprising if you have done too little, because the days are evil, that is, in this life many hindrances arise and things cannot be done as one wishes.

Therefore, because the days are evil, do not become imprudent, that is, inconsiderate, but rather understand what the will of God is, that is, what pleases God. Seek whom it pleases, so that all things may be done thoughtfully and with moderation, nothing in disturbance and clamour. And you who devote yourselves to this prudence:

**VERS. 18–28.**—“And do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking [Col. 0212D] to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father. Being subject to one another in the fear of Christ. Let wives be subject to their husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church, he himself the saviour of his body. But as the Church is subject to Christ, so wives to their husbands in all things. Husbands, love your wives as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, that he might present [Col. 0213A] her to himself as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind, but that she might be holy and blameless. So also husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself.”

Do not become drunk with wine. For nothing is less fitting for those who ought to rebuke others than to become drunk with wine, [Ambrose] in which there is dissipation—that is, from which an evil impulse proceeds, and so the authority to rebuke is taken away. The sober can confidently rebuke, because good conduct strikes fear into the offender. Therefore one must abstain from wine, in which there is dissipation, and avoid drunkenness, because a belly heated by wine quickly boils over into lust. [Jerome] But be filled with the Holy Spirit—that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit—speaking.

[Col. 0213B] As though he said: In this way you will be able to be filled with the Holy Spirit, if you speak to yourselves—that is, if you understand, and inwardly instruct yourselves, concerning what you say—in psalms, which exhort to good works; and hymns, which speak of God’s praises; and spiritual songs, which concern eternal joy. Therefore they must be understood spiritually, because what they teach is spiritual, and they must be fulfilled in action. Hence he adds: Singing. As though he said: You ought to speak to yourselves—that is, to instruct yourselves concerning these things. And after speaking them, be in actual practice singing—that is, praising God and rejoicing in eternal things, as hymn and song teach—and making melody, by good works, as the psalm teaches; and do this in your hearts—that is, with willing intention. Do all this for the Lord, [Col. 0213C] that is, for the Lord’s honor. [Ambrose] And always give thanks for every gift, or for all things—both prosperous and adverse—to God and the Father: to God, because he creates; and because he is Father of Christ by nature, and our Father by the grace of adoption. Do this, rejoicing in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom he adopted us—that is, through his own Son, through whom we have known him. [Haimo] And be subject to one another: not merely hearers to their prelates, but also prelates to those subject to them, serving them in charity and humbly bearing their care; for even if rank is greater, it is nonetheless a ministerial one. Hence the Apostle says: “I have made myself the servant of all” (1 Cor. 9). Thus it belongs to superiors, while preserving their dignity, to serve, just as it belongs to inferiors [Col. 0213D] to obey. This ordered subjection of both inferiors and superiors ought to be in the chaste fear of Christ, who commanded humility.

Wives. [Ambrose] Up to this point he has spoken generally concerning all; now he gives counsel to the individual ranks. As though he said: Thus far I have admonished generally; beyond these common matters, I say particularly that wives should be subject to their husbands as to the Lord—that is, with the same simplicity with which they are subject to the Lord. So Sarah was subject to her husband and called Abraham lord. And indeed they ought rightly to be subject, since the husband is the head of the wife—that is, her ruler and source, from whom woman took her beginning—as Christ is the head of the Church, its ruler and source. More than this, Christ himself is also the Savior of his body, that is, of the Church, which [Col. 0214A] the husband is not of the wife.

But—as though he said—Christ is the Savior of the Church, which the husband is not of the wife; nevertheless, as the Church is subject to Christ, so wives should be subject to their husbands in all things that are not contrary to God. But you husbands, love your wives, whose heads you are, just as Christ loved the Church, whose head he is. Indeed, he loved it so greatly that he gave himself for it; do likewise for your wives, if need arises. He gave himself, I say, in order to sanctify it by the righteousness of a good life, first cleansing it from sins. [Haimo] He did this by the washing of water sanctified in the word of life—that is, the word through which life is given. When this comes to the element, a sacrament is made, through which the sanctified person receives eternal life. Christ did this so that through it he might present to himself in the future [Col. 0214B] a glorious Church: radiant in soul and body, beautiful in its double robe. I mean a Church having neither now nor then a stain—that is, any grave sin—nor a wrinkle—that is, a mortal sin hidden within, such as deceit. [Ambrose] For duplicity is called a wrinkle. The sense is: having neither stain nor wrinkle, that is, clean and simple.

Or: having neither stain nor wrinkle, because by good action it is clean from stain, and by hope stretched toward the things above. Therefore his garment shone white as snow upon the mountain; this signified the Church cleansed from every stain of sin, which through Christ’s stretching out upon the wood of the cross has been freed from wrinkle and extended in desire toward heavenly things. Or, “having no such thing” means having no sin [Col. 0214C] for which it should be condemned. But—as though he said—I say that he might present to himself a Church having neither stain nor wrinkle, but rather such a Church as may be holy, here through good works, and unstained, that is, through abstinence from evil. Or this concerns the future: then it will be holy, enjoying glory, and unstained through the removal of corruption.

Therefore, as Christ poured out his blood to wash away the Church’s stain, and stretched himself out on the cross to remove its wrinkle, so husbands, if necessary, ought to die for the salvation of their wives and instruct them in the word of life, so that they may present them to God. Likewise husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies—that is, as themselves—because both are one flesh, and the woman is a portion of the husband’s body. I rightly said, [Col. 0214D] that they should love their wives as their own bodies, because whoever loves his wife loves himself: for the wife is the husband’s body, and the husband the wife’s head.

VERS. 29–33.—“For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church, because we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. This is a great sacrament. But I speak concerning Christ and the Church. Nevertheless, let each of you individually love his own wife as himself; and let the wife fear her husband.”

No one, indeed. As though he said: Truly a man ought to love his wife, because she is his own flesh. For no one ever [Col. 0215A] hated his own flesh. Even if a holy person mortifies his flesh, he does not hate it, but the sin within it. Thus one who prefers to be without a body hates not the body but its corruptions and its weight. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*.] Therefore he does not wish to have no body, but an incorruptible and most glorious body. Thus one who, by a certain continence and by labors, disciplines his body does not do so in order not to have it, but in order to have it subdued and prepared for necessary works. I say that no one hates his own flesh; rather, he nourishes it with food and drink and cherishes it with clothing. [Ambrose] Likewise a husband ought not to hate his wife but to cherish her, because she is his flesh and was made from his body.

As. As though he said: A husband should thus love and nourish his wife, as Christ also nourishes and loves the Church as his own flesh. The sense is: [Col. 0215B] A husband ought thus to treat his wife, who is his flesh, because Christ nourishes the Church as his own flesh with the food of his body, and cherishes it with the spiritual garments of commandments, virtues, and good works. [Haimo, Augustine] Christ rightly loves and nourishes the Church as his flesh, because it is his body, and all of us faithful are members of this body: some are of his flesh—that is, the weak, who need to be supported by the strong, as flesh is supported by bones—and others are of his bones—that is, the perfect and strong.

As a figure of this matter, Adam, who was a type of the one to come, when he saw the woman made from his rib, said in Genesis: “This is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2). For just as Eve, made from Adam, drew flesh and bones from him, so we, established by Christ, [Col. 0215C] are some as bones, namely the strong, and others as flesh, namely the weak. Therefore he says, “of his flesh”: that is, we who are weak are so by likeness to the weakness which he had in his humanity.

To show how greatly Christ loved the Church, it is written in Genesis: “Christ, the man, shall leave his Father,” by taking the form of a servant. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Augustine, *On John*.] He does not say this because Christ abandoned or departed from the Father, but because he did not appear to human beings in that form in which he is equal to the Father; and he shall leave his mother—that is, the Synagogue, from which he was born according to the flesh—and shall cleave to his wife, that is, shall join himself to the Church. And the two, namely Christ and the Church, shall be one flesh—that is, one will. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] Certainly Christ and the Church are one flesh, because [Col. 0215D] he who was God with the Father, through whom we too were made, became through the flesh a participant in our condition, so that we might be the body of that head. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Augustine, *On Psalm 138*.] And certainly, if he is the head, he has a body; his body is the holy Church, his bride, to which the Apostle says: “But you are the body of Christ and members” (1 Cor. 12).

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] Therefore the whole Christ is head and body, like a complete man; for woman too was made from man and belongs to man. Thus Christ, by taking flesh [Col. 0216A] from us, in which he might die for us, willed that we should be one with him, our head. [Note: [Col. 0216D] Augustine, *On John*.] Adam sleeps so that Eve may be made; Christ dies so that the Church may be made. While Adam sleeps, Eve is made from his side; when Christ is dead, his side is pierced by a lance so that the sacraments may flow forth through which the Church is formed. [Note: [Col. 0216D] Augustine, *Against the Manichaeans*.] Therefore Christ left the Father, because he did not appear to human beings in the same dignity in which he is with the Father. [Note: [Col. 0216D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.]

And it should be known that Genesis testifies that these words belonged to the first man. But Christ in the Gospel declares them to be God’s words, saying: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave,’” etc. (Matt. 19). Thus you may know that, through the ecstasy of sleep which came upon Adam—in which, entering the sanctuary of God so as to understand the last things, he participated in angelic fashion—he was able to say this divinely [Col. 0216B] as a prophet. And, to show what we ought to seek in these words, lest we seem to have dared to say something merely from our own conjectures, he adds and explains: “This is a great sacrament.” And lest anyone suppose that it lies in husband and wife according to the union of their natural sexes and bodily intercourse, he adds: “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church.”

[Augustine] According, therefore, to the sense in which what was said is understood concerning Christ and the Church, they are no longer two but one flesh; and as they are called bridegroom and bride, so they are head and body. Whether, then, I say head and body or bridegroom and bride, understand one thing. [Note: [Col. 0216D] Augustine, *On Psalm 30*.] For from two there comes to be, as it were, one person—namely, from head and body, from bridegroom and bride. Isaiah commends this wondrous and excellent unity, [Col. 0216C] in which Christ speaks and says: “As to a bridegroom he bound a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament” (Isa. 61).

That which is said literally in Genesis concerning the union of marriage was a sacrament of this spiritual unity. [Haimo] Hence what is said here literally may also be understood literally, thus: as though he said, Because a husband loves his wife, for this reason—that is, because of this love—a man shall leave father and mother and shall cling to his wife. This often happens literally, and the two shall be one flesh—that is, through sexual intercourse, when they are joined together in bodily union. Moses spoke literally of the union of marriage, which is the sign of a great reality, namely the sign of the union of Christ and the Church. Hence he adds: “This is a great sacrament”; “I speak concerning Christ and the Church,” that is, the marital union is the sign of the spiritual unity of Christ and the Church.

Nevertheless. As though he said: Although this is not said merely literally, but is a sign of another reality, nevertheless let each of you individually—that is, each husband—literally love his wife as himself, following the moral teaching of the history. But let the wife not only love but also fear her husband—that is, be subject to her husband.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0217A]

VERS. 1–15.—“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise: that it may go well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth. And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord. Servants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in simplicity of your heart, as Christ; not serving only when watched, as people-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will as the Lord and not human beings, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive this from the Lord, whether slave or free. And you masters, do the same to them, setting aside threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no respect of persons with God. Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might. Put on the armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil; for our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day and, having accomplished everything, to stand perfect. Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, [Col. 0217C] and having shod your feet in readiness for the Gospel of peace.”

But you children, obey, as those subject to your earthly parents; and do this in the Lord—that is, according to the Lord’s faith and righteousness. You ought to do this, for it is just, because it is a commandment of the Law in which the Lord commands this, saying: “Honor your father and your mother.” To honor one’s father is to show him reverence and supply what he needs. This commandment is the first among the commandments concerning human beings, written on the second tablet.

[Note: [Col. 0217D] Augustine, *On the Ten Strings*.] For the Decalogue pertains to the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbor. To the first commandment, love of God, belong three strings—that is, three commandments—because God is Trinity. But to the other commandment, concerning neighbor, belong seven strings—that is, seven commandments. Those three commandments concerning God were written on the first tablet, and the other seven concerning neighbor on the second. Among these, this one is fittingly first, because as God is principally the origin of a human being, so the father is secondarily. To this commandment is added a promise, which is not added to the others. Hence he continues: this commandment is with a promise, namely that it may go well with you in the present life, in bodily and spiritual things, and that you may be long-lived, established in eternal life, upon the land of the living.

And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, because then they will not keep the Law. For in anger one does not recognize [Col. 0218A] what is beneficial. But bring them up while they are children, lest they despise the Law, in the discipline of words and correction by blows, that they may advance in the Lord’s concerns. But you servants, obey masters—not merely spiritual and good masters, but earthly ones as well. Slavery began from sin; for the first cause of slavery is sin, so that one human being should be subjected to another by the bonds of his condition. This occurred only by God’s judgment, with whom there is no injustice, and who knows how to apportion various punishments according to the merits of offenders. [Note: [Col. 0218D] Augustine, *City of God*.]

Obey, I say, with fear—that is, reverence, which children show—and trembling, which servants show. Do so in simplicity of heart, so that your inward will may be what you display outwardly. If you cannot become free from your master, serve freely; for in some measure the person who serves not from deceitful fear but from faithful love makes slavery free, until iniquity passes away and every dominion is abolished. Thus obey simply, as you ought to obey Christ, because he himself commands it for the preservation of humility. Obey, I say, not serving only when watched—that is, while you are seen—as people-pleasers, as those do who seek to please human beings, but as servants of Christ. For when you serve at Christ’s command, you serve not merely a human being but Christ. Do God’s will from the heart: that is, I say that you should serve your masters with good will, as to the Lord—that is, so that you reckon yourselves to be serving God in this and not human beings. Do this, knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive it from the Lord, [Col. 0218C] whether free or slave; for a slave will receive no less than a free person.

And you masters, do the same to them, your servants—that is, show similar good will—remitting to them, if they sometimes err, not only blows but threats also, knowing that their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no respect of persons with God. For the Lord, a just judge, distinguishes cases, not persons. Therefore, by whatever measure one measures, it will be measured back to him.

Finally. After particular commands by which he admonished the individual ranks, he now admonishes all together. [Ambrose] As though he said: Up to this point I have helped you in word and deed; and now, finally—that is, henceforth, in the remaining time to come—brothers, in faith and [Col. 0218D] love, be strengthened against the devil’s war in the Lord—that is, in the Lord’s help—and in the power of his might, because he gives mighty strength to those willing to fight. Indeed, you ought to be strengthened in this way. Put on the armor of God—that is, the virtues—so that you may stand firm against the devil’s snares, because he secretly devises evils. [Haimo] And you must stand, for we have a wrestling contest: the war is close at hand and near; and it is not against flesh and blood only—that is, not against enemies who are visible and frail, or against vices only that arise from flesh and blood—but against principalities, that is, demons ruling over others, and powers, [Col. 0219A] that is, against those who have power even over these rulers of others.

For it is certain that destruction is inflicted upon God’s servants by the devil, whether in person or through his ministers, and his height is great. I say that your struggle is against demons, who must therefore be feared because they rule worldly people. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Augustine, *On Psalm 76*.] Explaining what he had said, he adds: against the rulers of the world—that is, against the devil and his angels, whom he calls rulers of the world because they rule lovers of the world. They do not rule the world that consists of heaven and earth; rather, by “world” he means sinners. Of this world it is said elsewhere: “And the world did not know him” (John 1). They rule such a world, and against them we have perpetual enmity, because they cause even the troublesome people whom we endure: they incite and inflame people, move them as their vessels, and play upon them as instruments. Against them we have a hidden struggle, for which the Apostle arms us.

And lest anyone should suppose that they rule this visible world, he adds what he meant by the name “world”: rulers of this darkness—that is, of sinners—of this evil darkness; that is, they rule those whom they cast headlong into dark works. As though he said: Demons do not dominate the world which consists of heaven and earth, but sinners. And he determines this still more particularly: against spiritual forces of wickedness—that is, against spiritual and wicked enemies. Why must the enemies against whom we wage war be feared? Because they are spiritual and invisible; and because they are wicked. Nor do they fight us for a small matter, but concerning heavenly things, [Col. 0219C] that is, to take away the heavenly inheritance. Or “heavenly things” means the virtues in which we undergo the demons’ combat. Thus: Our struggle is against wicked spirits, whose conflict we experience in heavenly things, that is, in virtues.

Or “heavenly places” means this murky air. [Augustine, Ambrose] The sense is: We have a struggle against wicked spirits, that is, wicked demons, which wicked spirits are in the heavenly places—that is, in this lower air, whence birds are called “birds of heaven.” Our struggle is against such beings, who are rulers; for just as Christ governs and rules those who are light, so the devil casts down and incites to every evil those who are darkness. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Therefore the Apostle exhorts us [Col. 0219D] not to pray against an evil person but rather for him; but to pray against the devil who works with and in that person, and to do whatever we can so that the devil and his angels may be expelled and human beings delivered. For those demons fight like riders upon their horses—that is, human beings. [Note: [Col. 0220D] Augustine, *On Psalm 163*.] Let us therefore kill the riders and take possession of the horses.

Thus we wage war against the rulers of darkness—that is, unbelievers—and this is one battle. [Haimo] But every person has another battle within himself, and this is a heavy and more troublesome war. Whoever emerges victorious in it will immediately overcome those enemies whom he sees, namely the rulers of the world. And if we conquer those [Col. 0220A] who are the princes of wickedness, at whose prompting the vices of the flesh rage against us, then we shall easily overcome all their ministers. Once the leader of an army is conquered, the army is easily put to flight, as is shown in the Book of Judith, where it is narrated that when Holofernes, commander of the army, was killed, the multitude of the forces was turned to flight [and] easily overcome by the Jews.

But to be able to conquer, spiritual armor must be assumed. Therefore, etc. As though he said: Because we have such enemies, and the issue is so great, therefore take up against them the armor of God—that is, that with which God arms his own. Take it up so that you may resist evil and spiritual wickedness in the evil day—that is, in this life, where temptation exists. Otherwise you could not resist, unless you possessed the armor of virtues; and so that, made perfect [Col. 0220B] in virtues, you may stand in every circumstance, both prosperous and adverse. Since the armor of God is necessary, stand therefore manfully whenever you are provoked, having girded your loins—that is, your fleshly desires—with the belt of chastity, binding or restraining them. Do this not in pretense but in truth, so that you truly restrain lust for Christ’s sake, since lust is especially powerful in the loins. Or do this in charity, that is, through charity.

And put on the breastplate of righteousness: let righteousness be your breastplate, each doing what is right, lest an opening lie exposed to the enemy. And have your feet shod: let your affections be fortified with virtues, lest they be pricked by vices. Do this in readiness for the Gospel, so that you may be prepared either to preach the Gospel or to fulfill its commands—the Gospel, I say, [Col. 0220C] of peace, which announces peace between God and human beings. Preachers ought to have these shoes of virtues, lest one who preaches touch the earth with the foot of the mind—that is, act for earthly things. [Note: [Col. 0220D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.] In this sense Mark says that they should be shod with sandals or soles, so that the foot is neither covered nor bare upon the ground: that is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rely on earthly things.

VERS. 16–24.—“In all things taking the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the most wicked one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; through every prayer and entreaty praying at all times in the Spirit, and in the same watching with all persistence and entreaty for all the saints, and for me, that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth [Col. 0220D] to make known with confidence the mystery of the Gospel, for which I serve as an envoy in this chain, so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought. And that you too may know the things concerning me and what I am doing, Tychicus, the most beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make all things known to you. I sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know the things concerning us and that he may comfort your hearts.
