Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption. Amen.”

I say that in all battles you should take up the shield [Col. 0221A] of faith—that is, faith in things which we have not seen—which receives the enemy’s darts and repels them like a shield. For faith is a shield, beneath which, or by which, righteousness—which does not permit the inner person to be pierced—is secure, as beneath the protection of all virtues, which is extended before every weapon and which the devil attacks first. Hence: “Faith, uncertain in the issue of battle, first enters the field for combat.” Take it, then, as a shield, by which you may extinguish all the darts—that is, assaults—of the most wicked one, the devil. These darts are fiery because they inflame from vice to vice.

And take the helmet of salvation, rejoicing in hope of salvation above. For the helmet is eternal salvation, whose remembrance and image envelop the mind lest it fail; and armed with such most splendid weapons—that is, spiritual and unconquerable weapons—you do not yield to the enemy. To strike and drive away that enemy, take also the sword of the Spirit—that is, the sword given by the Holy Spirit. [Note: [Col. 0221C] Augustine, *On Psalm 119*.] This is the word of God. For the word of God is a two-edged sword, teaching about temporal and eternal things, promising consolation concerning the former in the Old Testament and concerning the latter in the New. [Col. 0221B] What is promised to us temporally belongs to one edge of the sword; what is promised eternally belongs to the other. The two are called testaments for this reason: the old promises earthly things, the new eternal things. Concerning this sword the Lord said: “I did not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). This sword is truly sharp, because it separates from the world the person whom it strikes.

And because this armor comes only from grace, he adds: “Through every,” etc. As though he said: Stand in battle, and in it pray through every prayer and entreaty—that is, through all things which ought to be asked in prayer without adjuration, and through all things which ought to be sought with adjuration. Pray, I say, not at stated hours only but at every time, and not merely in words but in spirit—that is, in mind. [Ambrose] A person prays in spirit who prays with a clean conscience and sound faith. A person prays in flesh who makes petition with a polluted mind, intending to sin again, not by accident or surprise, but deliberately.

And in that spirit be watchful—that is, diligent—and not slack, but with every [Col. 0222A] persistence, so that you may persevere in every virtue. Be watchful in entreaty made for all saints and for me: that speech may be given me by God, speech which tribulation does not blunt. Let it be given, I say, in the opening of my mouth—that is, of my discourse—so that I may openly disclose the mystery of the Gospel, that is, the hidden matters of the incarnation and passion, lest the pressure of tribulations, by fear itself, dull the sharpness of teaching. Thus with confidence—that is, freely and without impediment—I may make known that mystery of the Gospel, for which mystery I serve as an envoy, even now at Rome, placed in this chain; for I do not cease from my embassy because of chains. I say that I may confidently make known the Gospel and, with confidence, may dare to speak in preaching the Gospel itself [Col. 0222B] amid every evil, as I ought to speak.

And lest they be shaken when they heard of his tribulations, he says that Tychicus will inform them of all things, adding: “But that you also may know the things concerning me.” He says “concerning” because many tribulations surrounded him, or because they did not touch the inner person. That you may know these things, and what I am doing—that is, how steadfast I am amid them all—Tychicus, my most beloved brother in the faith, will make all things known to you. So that they may willingly and well listen to Tychicus’s words, he commends him, adding: “And he is a faithful minister in the Lord,” that is, in the Lord’s concerns; therefore listen to him. I sent him to you for this very purpose, that through him you may know the things concerning us and that he may comfort your hearts.

And that what I have taught may be done, may peace be to the brothers and love with faith. He wishes them peace, which is the gateway of love, because through peace they will remain in the love which is in faith. May this be from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; and may grace be to you with—that is, also to—all who love our Lord, that is, Christ. I say, who love him in incorruption—that is, in integrity of faith, like a bride who admits no corrupter. Or: may grace be to you in incorruption—that is, in eternal life—with, that is, also to, all who love our Lord, that is, Christ.

## ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0221]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0221D]

The Philippians are Macedonians. Having received the word of truth, they persevered in faith and did not receive false apostles. The Apostle praises them, writing to them from prison at Rome through Epaphroditus.

## CHAPTER ONE

VERS. 1–6.—“Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons. Grace [Col. 0222D] to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks to my God at every remembrance of you, always in all my prayers making petition with joy for all of you because of your participation in the Gospel of Christ from the first day until now, confident of this very thing: that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Christ Jesus.”

Paul and Timothy. The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Philippians. The Philippians are [Col. 0223A] Macedonians who, having received the word of preaching from the Apostle, remained firm in faith and did not receive false apostles. Therefore the Apostle praises them. [Ambrose] They had sent Paul some material support to Rome through Epaphroditus. When he sent Epaphroditus back with this Epistle, he fortified them, though unable to do so in person, against a twofold war: that of persecutors and that of false preachers. He exhorts them to endure every adversity for Christ and, with humility, as Christ himself did; and never to accept the legal observances urged by false apostles.

He does not call himself an Apostle, because they had never thought ill of him or opposed him. He therefore suppresses his rank because they held a right opinion of him. The Apostle’s intention in this Epistle is to exhort the Philippians to patience against tribulations and constancy against false preachers. Its method is as follows. As usual, he first gives a greeting; then he thanks God for them, imploring greater blessings for them, so that by growing in virtues they may arrive at perfection. Then he exhorts them to patience in tribulations by his own example and Christ’s; afterward, that they may guard themselves against the wiles of false apostles. Finally he inserts moral admonition and, near the end, says that he rejoices in the support which they had sent him to Rome through Epaphroditus.

Introducing his greeting, therefore, he says: “Paul and Timothy.” He adds Timothy because he was about to send him to them, thereby in some measure commending him, so that they may readily receive from Timothy the same things that he writes. “Servants of Jesus Christ.” He omits the title of dignity, “Apostle,” because authority was unnecessary when they held a correct opinion of him. He acknowledges his condition, because those who are subject to Christ in chaste fear are truly free. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Augustine, *On John*.]

For just as there are two fears, producing two kinds of those who fear, so there are two servitudes, producing two kinds of servants. There is a fear which perfect love casts out, and there is also a servitude which must be cast out with it. There is another, chaste fear which endures for ever and ever; joined to it is another servitude, by which, in a wondrous and ineffable yet true manner, we are servants so as to be free servants: namely, by chaste fear. To this belongs the servitude that enters into the joy of its Lord, not the servitude of a servant’s fear, which is cast out and does not remain eternally in the house.

He therefore calls himself a servant so that those to whom he writes may themselves endure hardships for the Lord, as servants of Christ, and may stand firm against false teachers. He writes this Epistle to all the saints—that is, those sanctified in baptism—who are at Philippi, a city of Greece founded by Philip, the adoptive father of Alexander, and named Philippi after himself. I say, saints in Christ Jesus—that is, through Christ Jesus at work, or established in Christ, that is, in faith in Christ, namely those who believe that he is also human. He writes to the saints, that is, also to the bishops and deacons. By “bishops” he also means presbyters; for there would not be several bishops in one city, nor would he omit presbyters and descend to deacons. By bishops and deacons he means the greater ranks; by saints, the lesser. The sense is: [Col. 0224A] They write to saints, bishops, and deacons—that is, to lesser and greater alike. By placing the lesser first, he invites them to humility; and by adding the greater, he shows that no one is so perfect before God as not to need this admonition.

Or, Paul and Timothy write to all the saints who are at Philippi, writing also with the bishops and deacons, because they together desired their good. The greeting is placed first in the letter in this form: May grace—that is, remission of sins—be to you, and peace—that is, tranquility of mind and reconciliation with God—from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Thanks, etc.

First he gives thanks to God, by whose providential will all good things happen to all. As if he said: Do the things that you do, because they are such things. Hence: “I give thanks to my God for all of you,” by a special benefit; that is, I praise God because he brings about for me what I desire in you. I give thanks, I say, “whenever I remember you,” that is, as often as I am mindful of you. This I do, indeed, “in all my prayers,” continually offered at suitable times. I give thanks, I say, “for all of you,” namely superiors and subjects. And I do so “with joy,” not grieving over genuine fault, I say, “making supplication,” that is, praying that you may stand firm. I have joy, I say, “because of your fellowship,” which is “in the Gospel of Christ,” that is, because you have shared in the faith and works of the Gospel. Or, you have made your goods common for the advancement of the Gospel; and this from the first day of your conversion until now. Therefore henceforth you must stand all the more firmly, “being confident.” As if he said: I pray [Col. 0224C] that you may stand firm, and I am confident—that is, I trust that you yourselves will do precisely what I pray for, and nothing else; see that it is not in vain. I trust, I say, not in you but in God, because God, who has begun a good work in you by working, will complete it by cooperating. For by cooperating—that is, when God brings something to completion in us—he completes what he begins by working; because, in beginning, he himself works so that we may will, and in completing he cooperates with those who will. Therefore he works so that we may will; when by this we will, and will in such a way as to act, he cooperates with us. Yet without him—whether working so that we may will, or cooperating when we will—we are able to do nothing toward the good works of godliness. He will complete it, I say, “until the day of Christ Jesus,” that is, until the end, when God will be seen. Or, he will complete it in us successively [Col. 0224D] until the day of Jesus Christ, that is, until the common day of judgment.

**178. Verses 7–11.**—“Just as it is right for me to think this of all of you, because I have you in my heart, and because, both in my chains and in the defence and confirmation of the Gospel, you are all partners in my joy. For God is my witness how I long for all of you in the tender affections of Christ Jesus. And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in all knowledge and every discernment, so that you may approve the better things, that you may be pure and without offence for the day of Christ, filled with the fruit of righteousness through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.”

“Just as,” etc. As if he said: Thus I give thanks, pray, [Col. 0225A] and have confidence concerning you, just as it is right for me to think this of all of you; that is, just as it is right for me to desire these things for you. For I ought not to have thought otherwise of persons so good. He explains the reason: because I have you, not merely on my lips, but “in my heart,” that is, in the inmost affection of love, whereby I desire that all of you, even the lesser members, may be partners in the future—that is, that in the future you may be partners in my joy, namely in the reward of eternal life. I desire this while I labour, whether in my chains and in the defence of the Gospel against its assailants, or in the confirmation of the weak in Gospel teaching. The sense is: I remember you and desire good for you, whether I am in chains, knowing that you too are bound; whether I am defending the Gospel, which you too do; or whether I am strengthening the weak in the Gospel.

[Col. 0225B] “For God is my witness,” etc. I pray for all of you because I desire you all to be “in the tender affections of Christ,” namely, to be loved by Christ as though you were his own inward parts. God is my witness of this. This is what he says: “For God is my witness how,” that is, with how great an affection, “I long for all of you in the tender affections of Christ,” that is, in Christ’s inmost love, so that you may be perfectly loved by him. Or: that you may love God and neighbour with the affection with which Christ did, who laid down his life for his brothers. Or this refers to what he said above, when he declared that he desired them to be partners in his joy; here he specifies how he desires it: not through human desire, not through carnal affection, but through Christ’s love. This is what he says: “For God is my witness how I desire all of you to be participants in eternal joy.” I desire this, I say, not with carnal affection, but “in the tender affections of Christ,” that is, in Christ’s love. He says that he desires them with Christ’s love, not human love, so that he may have them as participants in the Lord.

“And this also I pray: that your love may abound more and more,” that is, may increase; and that this may be “in knowledge and every discernment,” namely, that they may know in what matters they ought to love God and neighbour, and, once they know, may have understanding, remembrance, and attentiveness in all things. Thus may your love abound—that is, may it increase so greatly in knowledge that you may “approve,” that is, know how to test and distinguish, not only what is good and what is evil, but also, among good things, which are better. Thus, after testing and discernment, you may be pure in yourselves, that is, without works of corruption; and, with respect to neighbour, [Col. 0225D] without offence. And may this endure until the day of Christ, that is, until the end of life. Since it is not enough to abstain from evil unless what is good is done, he adds: “filled.” As if he said: Not only may you be without evil things, but may you also be filled with the fruit of righteousness, that is, with good works, which are fruit; righteousness itself is a disposition of the soul. Filled, I say, not by your own strength, but through Jesus Christ. Through this, I say, you will pass into the glory and praise of God, that is, into eternal glory, whence you may praise God. Or thus: “filled”—as if he said: I pray that your love and purity may abound, so that through these you may be filled here and in the future with fruit, that is, with the reward of righteousness; and this through Jesus Christ. And may you be filled so abundantly that you may be for the glory and praise of God, that is, that you may be God’s glory and [Col. 0226A] praise, so that it may be said on your account: “God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. LXVII).

**Verses 12–18.**—“Now I want you to know, brothers, that the things which have happened to me have turned out rather for the advancement of the Gospel, so that my chains became manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and among all the rest; and so that many of the brothers in the Lord, made confident by my chains, dared all the more to speak the word of God without fear. Some indeed preach Christ even through envy and contention, but others through good will. Some preach out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defence of the Gospel. But others proclaim Christ out of rivalry, not sincerely, supposing that they will raise affliction for my chains. [Col. 0226B] What then? Provided only that in every way, whether from pretext or from truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice—and I shall rejoice also.”

“Now I want you to know.” Up to this point he has spoken generally, showing his love for them; thereafter he speaks particularly of matters which urge endurance. [Ambrose] Since above he said that he desired them to become partners in his joy, he now indicates to them, as beloved persons, the progress made by his labour, while giving thanks, praying for this on their behalf, and having confidence. “But I want you, brothers, to know,” because I said that you are partners in my joy, namely that “the things which have happened to me”—that is, the abundance of sufferings surrounding me on every outward side—have come “rather for the advancement of the Gospel.” Or, he says “around me” because they do not reach his inward self. They have come for advancement rather than for the harm which the wicked intended. They have come, I say, so that “my chains became manifest in Christ,” that is, so that the usefulness of my chains might appear in Christ, who is proclaimed more because of the chains. [Haimo] Or, “my chains became manifest in Christ,” that is, it became evident that the chains themselves were in Christ for me—that is, for Christ; namely, that I was bound because of him and not for some crime. For since I patiently endure every sort of evil, it is clear that it is not the crime of falsehood which a just retribution assails in me, but rather a certain truth which the courage to endure magnifies. [Jerome] They became manifest, I say, “throughout the whole praetorium,” where the great men assemble, and in all other places.

For when the Apostle, bound at Rome, was confined in prison in the emperor’s house, taught the Gospel, healed the sick, performed many miracles, and many believed through him, he so far succeeded as to make the house of the persecutor into the church of the Redeemer. Then it became manifest in the praetorium and in every place—that is, to the emperor and all consuls, rulers, and lesser persons—that he endured such things for Christ. I endure these things for the Gospel in such a way that many of the brothers, trusting not in themselves but in the Lord because of my chains—that is, on considering my chains—dared more abundantly than before, against their opponents, to speak the word of God without fear. As if he said: By my example they dare to preach confidently, saying: “If one who is bound speaks, why should not we all the more?” For his constancy encouraged many not to fear evangelizing.

Others, however—some different from the former because they are evil—do indeed preach Christ. They do this through envy and contention, that is, because they envy the glory of my apostleship and strive to possess it. Others, different from these because they are good, preach Christ through good will, namely, in order to save others—that is, from love of God and neighbour, and following the example of my good will. Still others are not different from these, because they too are good, and preach Christ out of personal affection for the Apostle, so that they may supply the place of one who is bound, knowing that I am placed in chains “for the defence,” that is, for the defence of the Gospel. Or, “placed” means that I am firm and steadfast in the defence of the Gospel.

But others, different from these because they are evil, proclaim Christ out of rivalry, [Col. 0227B] that is, out of private hatred, because they once disputed with me and were refuted. Lest they should appear to have been corrected, he adds, “not sincerely,” that is, not with a pure mind, but supposing that they will raise affliction for my chains—that is, supposing that if anyone accuses them because of their preaching, they may retaliate against me as its author. Thus these men proclaimed Christ by the craft of pretence, so that they might stir up seditions against the Apostle as their alleged author, since he had gathered many into his fellowship. [Augustine] See: he distinguishes four kinds of teachers, two good and two evil. All proclaim Christ, but not with the same mind. The evil proclaim Christ neither with a simple nor truthful mind; the good do so with a pure mind and sincere faith. Yet all advance the Gospel. Accordingly he says that the evil are to be tolerated, adding:

[Col. 0227C] “What then?” As if he said: Not only I and the other true teachers labour for the advancement of the Gospel, but even the evil do so. Those who preach without a good intention contribute to its advancement and therefore must be tolerated. For what does it matter with what intention they preach, provided only that in every way, whether from earthly pretext or from truth—that is, with a true mind, as the good do—Christ, that is, the truth of Christ and not falsehood, is proclaimed? Some proclaimed the truth even though not in truth, that is, not with a true mind.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Augustine, *On Psalm* XC.] Catering to earthly desires, they proclaimed the King of heaven; they had truth on their tongues but not chastity in their hearts. Yet they are useful to those whom the Lord instructs.

[Note: [Col. 0228D] Id., *On the Words of the Gospel*.] Hence he says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” [Col. 0227D] (Matt. XXIII). They evangelize from pretext, seeking from people their own advantages—money, honour, or human praise—wishing to receive gifts of any kind, and seeking not so much the salvation of the one to whom the message is proclaimed as their own advantage. But the one who hears unto salvation, if he believes in the one whom they proclaim, will gain; the proclaimer will suffer loss, because he proclaims the Gospel, namely right faith, but does not proclaim it rightly. Therefore he is not upright: what is proclaimed is upright, but the one who proclaims it is not upright. Why? Because in the Church he seeks something other than God. If he sought God, he would be chaste. Whoever seeks anything from God besides God does not seek God chastely.

If we investigate the words of the Gospel carefully, we find three persons: the shepherd, the hireling, and the thief. The shepherd proclaims truth in truth. The hireling proclaims truth from pretext, seeking something else; yet he too proclaims Christ. The thief and robber denies and takes away truth. Therefore the shepherd is to be loved, the hireling tolerated, and the robber avoided. Thus the Apostle does not forbid hirelings, but permits them, because they too are useful in some respects. “And in this I rejoice”: now, because Christ is proclaimed from pretext and not only from truth—that is, I now rejoice that the truth of Christ is preached, whatever the intention of those preaching it. And I shall rejoice not only now but afterwards also, namely in the future.

Or thus: Above he said that his tribulations served [Col. 0228B] the advancement of the Gospel; here he says that they bring him joy. As if he said: Evil events produce advancement not only for others, but joy for me. This is what he says: “And in this I rejoice,” namely, that I endure tribulations for Christ; and I shall rejoice also. Therefore I rejoice over my evils, or over the advancement of the Gospel, because from this comes my salvation. This is what he says:

**Verses 19–30.**—“For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, according to my expectation and hope, because in nothing shall I be put to shame, but with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ will be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live in [Col. 0228C] the flesh—this is for me fruit of labour—and what I shall choose I do not know. Yet I am constrained by the two, having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary on your account. And, confident of this, I know that I shall remain and continue with all of you for your advancement and joy of faith, so that your rejoicing in Christ Jesus may abound through me, by my coming to you again. Only live in a manner worthy of the Gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent and hear about you, I may hear that you stand firm in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the Gospel; and that in nothing you are frightened by adversaries, which is to them a cause of destruction, but to you of salvation. And this [Col. 0228D] is from God: because it has been granted to you for Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him, having the same conflict that you saw in me and now have heard of in me.”

“For I know that this.” [Ambrose] Namely, suffering for Christ, or the advancement of the Gospel resulting from my preaching, will come to me in the future unto eternal salvation, though they think it leads to death. It will come about, I say, not only by my own merit but also through your prayer, that is, with your prayer aiding me, and through the supplying ministry of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. [Haimo] That is, through the Holy Spirit, who supports me like a column when I am about to fall; namely, the Holy Spirit gives and supplies aid to me. [Col. 0229A] It will come about for my salvation, a salvation which will correspond to my expectation and hope; that is, it will be as great a salvation as I expect and now hope for. I firmly hope this, because in no condition, whether prosperity or adversity, shall I be ashamed so as in any way to yield from preaching. [Ambrose] He says that he will not be ashamed in anything because both the hope of the promise is great and the thing itself true and honourable.

“I shall not be ashamed,” I say, but “with all boldness,” which, as it has been from the time of my conversion, so is it now while I labour in chains, Christ—that is, Christ’s renown and glory—will be magnified among the nations and in my body, which is the more frail part. He will be magnified, I say, whether through life, granted to me so that I may preach him, or through death, by which I shall give an example of perseverance in him and of dying for him. [Col. 0229B] The sense is: I shall magnify Christ if I live, by teaching; if I die, by leaving an example. “For to me.” As if he said: I shall rightly magnify him through life, because Christ is life to me, since I live for his cause, in order to magnify him and not for anything else. He will be magnified through my death, and rightly so, because death is gain to me, since Christ is the reward of my death. Or, dying itself is gain to me, because through death he is freed from these miseries and passes to blessedness, and by his death gains many for God.

“But if.” As if he said: Christ is life to me so that I may magnify him. For if living is for me the fruit of labour—that is, if so worthy a fruit arises from my work, namely the magnifying of Christ, a work which I perform while I am allowed to live in the flesh—if, I say, this is so, behold, [Col. 0229C] I do not know, that is, I do not know what I should choose, much less what I should desire: whether to die or to live. As if he said: If this fruit did not exist, there is no doubt that I would choose to die, unless I had Christ as my reward. Therefore, Philippians, do not hesitate to die for Christ.

Or thus: “To me, to live.” As if he said: I rightly magnify Christ, whether through life or death, because Christ is life to me, that is, my life here and in the future: here through faith and hope, in the future through sight. For this life he gives up his mortal body, that he may receive it immortal for ever. Hence he adds: To die for Christ is gain to me. “For if.” As if he said: Christ is life to me here and in the future; and this is indeed through good works. For—that is, but—if “to live,” that is, to work well in the flesh, [Col. 0229D] which seems surprising, since nothing but sin dwells in the flesh, “is for me fruit of labour,” that is, a work so fruitful for me that through it Christ is life to me here and in the future: behold, I do not know what I should choose, whether to die or to live.

“For I am constrained,” or “yet I am constrained.” As if he said: Not only do I not know which of the two I should choose, but I am also constrained by two things. Or connect it thus: I do not know because I am constrained by two things, namely by the desire to depart and the necessity of living.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*.] The division should not be made so as to say, “I am constrained,” and then follow with “by two things, having the desire,” namely of departing and remaining in the flesh. For the very wording of the sentence decides the matter, since it follows: “to depart and to be [Col. 0230A] with Christ is far better.” It is clear that he says he has desire for what is best, so that, though he is compelled by two things, he has desire only for one of them and necessity for the other. Therefore the division must be made thus: “I am constrained,” or compelled, “by two things.” Then follows, I say, “having the desire,” or longing, to depart from these miseries, in which I am held as if bound by fetters, and to be bodily present with Christ. And as though someone should ask why he has longing for this rather, he adds: because it is far better with respect to me. And as though it were again asked: Why, then, are you compelled by two things? he adds that there is a necessity to remain, saying: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary on your account,” not on mine. As if he said: That is better for me; this is necessary for you. Therefore I desire the former and do not refuse the latter.

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Id., *On John*.] Some people are imperfect, who die patiently; and some are perfect, who live patiently. One who still desires this life, when the day of death comes, endures death patiently. He struggles against himself in order to follow God’s will; in mind he does rather what God has chosen than what human will has chosen. From his desire for the present life arises a struggle with death, and he employs patience and fortitude in order to die with an even mind: such a person dies patiently. But one who, like the Apostle, desires to depart and be with Christ does not die patiently, but lives patiently; he dies delightfully. See the Apostle living patiently—that is, with patience: here he does not love [Col. 0230C] life, but endures it. Hence he says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ, which is far better.”

[Note: [Col. 0230D] Id., *On Psalm* XCIII.] For remaining in the flesh was weariness to him, and he suffered anguish from two things. He judged one to be best; consequently, as he approached suffering, he gloried more strongly, saying: “I have fought the good fight; henceforth a crown is laid up for me,” etc. (2 Tim. IV).

Or it may be divided thus: “What I shall choose I do not know; for I am constrained, having desire by two things,” namely, to depart and to remain in the flesh. And this is “having desire,” etc., that is, because to depart and to be with Christ is far better, but to remain in the flesh is necessary on your account. And I, confident of this—that it is necessary for me to remain on your [Col. 0230D] account—know that I shall remain, etc.

[Ambrose] See: knowing that being with Christ is better, but that remaining in the flesh is necessary for the instruction of believers and the advancement of the faithful, he chose not what was safer for himself but what was advantageous for many. Thus he shows how great his affection for them was, following that which would make progress through the love which he put before all things. Or thus: “And I know,” not doubtfully, but confident in God’s mercy, namely that I shall remain—that is, not merely for a little while but shall continue for a long time with all of you, lesser and greater—for your advancement, that you may grow in good things, and for the joy of faith, namely, that we may rejoice over your faith, or that [Col. 0231A] you may rejoice in faith as you advance in it, which exists only where conscience is pure. [Haimo] And may you rejoice in such a way that you advance, so that your rejoicing may abound in Christ Jesus, who has done you good by restoring me to you safe and freed from chains; that is, so that you may give abundant thanks to Christ with joy through me, namely through my coming again to you, which will be for your strengthening. I shall certainly come to you if only you live worthily of the Gospel of Christ, that is, of the Lord’s discipline, because according to your merit I shall be granted life for your benefit. And live so worthily that, whether I come and see you, or while absent hear this about you, namely that you stand firm in faith and devotion against adversaries, and this “in one Spirit,” [Col. 0231B] the Holy Spirit, to whom no contrary spirit adheres; and, just as he is one, so you too ought to be of one mind.

Hence he adds: You, I say, being of one mind in will and striving together in deed for the faith of the Gospel, that is, labouring with all your strength to fulfil what faith in Christ requires. For every battle undertaken with one mind produces victory. And after these things, “in nothing be frightened by adversaries,” who terrify you by hardships; this is for them a cause of eternal destruction, but for you a cause of eternal salvation. Moreover, even what you suffer is not from yourselves but from God, because, for the merit of Christ who obeyed the Father, this grace among other graces has been given to you. Hence he adds: because it has been granted to you as a reward, for Christ whom you love. What has been granted? Namely, not only that you should believe in him, but that you should suffer for him.

[Note: [Col. 0231D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*.] Hence the greater glory [Col. 0231C] will be. Therefore both things belong to God’s grace: the faith of believers and the endurance of those who suffer patiently, because he says that both have been granted. You, I say, having the same conflict against enemies as you saw in me when I was present among you, when I was stripped and beaten because of the Pythoness woman, from whom I expelled the evil spirit that brought great profit, or gain, to her masters; and the kind you have now heard of me while I am absent from you. As if he said: I do not exhort you to what I myself shrink from, but to what I fulfil in myself.

**180. Chapter II.**

**Verses 1–8.**—“If therefore there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tender affections of compassion, fill [Col. 0231D] my joy, that you may think the same thing, having the same love, being of one mind, thinking the same thing. Do nothing through rivalry or empty glory, but in humility considering one another superior to yourselves; not each looking to his own interests, but to those of others. For think this in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.”

“If therefore.” He draws an inference from what was said. As if he said: Since suffering is God’s gift, and since I suffer and it is useful, as has been said above, therefore you, who have already caused me to rejoice because of your fellowship in the Gospel of Christ, fill my joy by adding endurance of tribulation and the other things that follow. This is what he says: “If therefore there is any consolation in you in Christ,” that is, if you desire to have consolation in the things of Christ, namely remission of sins and his other gifts; or if you desire to console me; “if any comfort of love,” that is, if you desire the love of the churches, which pray and do good for the brothers, to be comfort and strengthening to you in your adversities.

[Note: [Col. 0232D] Augustine, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*.] “And if there is any fellowship of the Holy Spirit in you,” that is, if you desire to possess the union which the Holy Spirit makes in all believers. Because of this fellowship, those in whom the Holy Spirit first came spoke in the languages of all nations. “And if there are any tender affections of compassion in you,” that is, if there is in you a pious affection from which compassion may proceed, “fill my joy.” I have indeed rejoiced over your faith; now fill my joy by enduring steadfastly.

[Ambrose] Or, according to another reading: “If therefore there is any exhortation in Christ,” that is, if there is among you a true exhortation of hope in Christ, by which we mutually console one another; and if any comfort of common love belongs to you; and if there is any fellowship of the Holy Spirit in you, by which we are joined in one new body; and if there are any tender affections of compassion, that is, an affection of devotion toward me—that is, if I am in your mind as you are in mine—fill my joy. Those things are true if this occurs. The things he listed above are shown to be true by proof if the commands which he gives below are kept; they do not appear to have been proved if what follows is absent, namely if they do not fill his joy and keep the rest. Fill my joy, I say, so that you may not only suffer, but may “think the same thing,” not different things in faith; having the same love toward all, of one mind and one will, thinking the same thing; doing nothing through rivalry, so that one may contend to be preferred to another.

Observe that some among them had been contentious. Or, “nothing through rivalry”: let them speak good things, but not speak in contentious words; doing nothing through empty glory, that is, for the sake of worldly reputation, which is empty. Thus he constrains them, so that if they do not keep these matters they may not appear to be approved in the matters mentioned above; because they are unwilling to appear unapproved in those, they must keep these also, so that they may be perfect. For without doubt some among them were dissenting, restless, contending for vain glory, and breaking the peace of the Church. But live in humility, thinking humbly of yourselves. And be “considering”—that is, judging in your hearts—others to be superior to yourselves, that is, more worthy before God; and do this mutually, each considering the other more worthy. We should not do this by pretending to consider ourselves inferior; rather, we should truly judge that something may be hidden in another by which he is superior to us, even though the good in us by which [Col. 0233A] we seem superior to him is not hidden.

“Not [looking to] what is one’s own.”

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Augustine, *On Eighty-Three Questions*.] Here he teaches how they may avoid rivalry and empty glory, and how they may consider others superior: namely, if they consider not their own goods but those of others. As if he said: In order that they may do the things just mentioned, let not each person consider what goods or evils are his own, but what belongs to others. For those who do not attend only to their own concerns, but also to those of others, can do the things mentioned above—as Christ did, who suffered so much for others. Nothing makes this dutiful service willingly rendered except the thought of how much the Lord endured for us. Hence, in exhorting them, he adds: “For think this in yourselves.” As if he said: I invite you to patience and humility, to seek what belongs to others and not yourselves; and, that you may keep this, take the example of Christ. “For think this in yourselves,” that is, you ought to think in yourselves what was also in Christ Jesus.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Id., in the same work.] Thus, as Christ did not attend to what was his own, but to what was yours, when he assumed flesh and, though without sin, took our sins upon himself, so we too, in imitation of him, should bear one another’s burdens. “Who, being in,” etc. Here he shows in what we ought to imitate Christ, namely humility. But before showing Christ’s humility, he first sets forth lofty things concerning Christ, so that those in whom there is occasion for lowliness may not disdain to be humbled when Christ, so exalted, humbled himself so greatly. He shows his exaltation, saying: Christ, “who, being”—not, I say, having received, but being—“in the form of God” the Father, that is, in the full essence and equality of the Father, considered—that is, most certainly knew—himself equal to God the Father, not committing robbery, that is, not usurping what was not his own, as the devil and the first human being did.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Id., *On John*.] But Christ did not usurp equality with God, because by nature he was truly equal. He was in the equality in which he was born.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Id., *On Psalm* CXXX.] For Christ was equal to the Father, born, not made. Therefore equality was not robbery for him, because by nature he was equal to the one from whom he was begotten. Or: according to his humanity, he did not consider himself equal to God, namely, in such a way as to commit robbery—that is, to presume what was not his own.

“But he emptied himself.” Having shown his exaltation, he adds concerning humility. As if he said: He was equal to God the Father, but although he was in the Father’s form, remaining indeed what he was, [Col. 0233D] he emptied himself. How? Not by emptying his substance, not by changing the form of his deity, but by taking the form of a servant, not by losing the form of God.

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Id., *On John*.] The form of a servant came; the form of God did not depart. Therefore he emptied himself of the greatness of his invisibility by showing himself visible through the assumed form of a servant. For he seems, as it were, to have stripped himself of dignity when the form of a servant was united to the form of God. And lest you suppose that the form of a servant in him, namely Christ, became immortal, he adds: “He was made,” according to the form of a servant—he who [Col. 0234A] was unmade according to the form of God—“in the likeness of men,” that is, mortal and capable of suffering like other human beings.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Id., in the sermon “That …” (title uncertain).] Therefore, through becoming human and emptying himself into the likeness of human beings, Christ himself is both maker and made.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Id., *On the Words of the Gospel*.] See the maker: “All things were made through him” (John I). See the made: “made in the likeness of men.”

We therefore see Christ Jesus both as God and as man: both the maker of things and made among things; both the Creator of man and created man. Christ as God is equal to the Father: as great as he is, so great is he; such as he is, such is he. This is what the Father is—not that this one is the one who is the Father, since he is the Father and this one the Son. But this one is what that one is, because that one is God and this one is God; that one is almighty and this one is almighty; that one is immutable and this one is immutable. Therefore it was not robbery for him to be equal to God [Col. 0234B], because by nature he was begotten and ever begotten, just as he is begotten and ever begotten; and as he is ever begotten, so he is ever equal. Therefore the Father did not beget him unequal, nor add equality to him once begotten; rather, in begetting, he gave it to him, because he begot him equal, not unequal.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] Therefore Scripture not without reason says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son: the former on account of the form of God, the latter on account of the form of a servant. Because of this form he was made less not only than the Father, but also than himself and the Holy Spirit; indeed, he “was made a little lower than the angels” (Heb. 2). Thus he was made man while remaining God. For man was assumed by God; God was not consumed in man. Therefore, with complete reason, Christ the man is less than the Father, while the selfsame Christ God is equal to the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Id., in the *Enchiridion.*] For Christ, the Son of God and God, is man: God from eternity, man in time; God because he is the Word of God, man because a rational soul and flesh were joined to the Word in the unity of person. Since he was the one Son of God, not by grace but by nature, in order that he might also be full of grace he was made the Son of man: one Son of God, and the same Son of man. There are not two Sons of God, God and man, but one Son of God: God without beginning, man from a definite beginning. For just as the number of persons is not increased when flesh is joined to a soul, so that there is one man, neither is the number of persons increased when man is joined to the Word, so that there is one Christ. Accordingly, “God-man” is read, so that we may understand the singularity of this person [Col. 0234D], not suppose that the divinity was changed into flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] For in that assumption neither of the two was converted and changed into the other. Divinity was not changed into a creature, so as to cease being divinity; nor was the creature changed into divinity, so as to cease being a creature.

And in outward appearance. As though he said: He was made in the likeness of men, and also in his outward appearance—that is, in his manner of life—he was found by anyone wishing to test him to be like another man, because he ate, drank, sat, and so forth. Or thus: “Outward appearance” [*habitus*] [Col. 0235A] is said of a thing which is added or happens to another thing in order to be possessed. Yet there is this distinction: some things which happen so as to produce an outward appearance are not changed, but themselves change what they affect while remaining whole and unshaken in themselves; as wisdom, happening to a man, is not itself changed but changes the man, making him wise from foolish. Others happen in such a way as both to change and be changed, as food, which, losing its own form, is turned into the body and changes thinness and weakness into strength and vigor. A third kind occurs when things that happen neither change that to which they happen nor are themselves changed by it, as a ring placed upon a finger; this kind is found very rarely. The fourth kind occurs when things that happen are changed, not from their own nature, but are in some sense formed [Col. 0235B] and take another appearance and form; such is a garment which, when cast down and laid aside, does not have the form it takes on when worn. When put upon the limbs, it receives a form which it does not have when removed. This kind is fitting to the present operation. For God the Son emptied himself, not by changing his own form but by taking the form of a servant; nor was he converted or transformed into man, losing immutable stability. Rather, he who assumed was made in the likeness of men by assuming a true man. [Haimo.] Here, indeed, “likeness” expresses reality.

“And found in outward appearance as a man,” that is, by having manhood he was found to be a man by those to whom he appeared in manhood. What is said, “as a man,” is of the same kind as “as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1): it expresses reality [Col. 0235C]. This outward appearance is not of the first kind. [Augustine.] For the human nature, while remaining in itself, did not change the divine nature; nor is it of the second kind, for man did not change God and was not changed by him; nor of the third, for man was not so assumed that neither he changed God nor was changed by him. Rather it is of the fourth kind. For he was assumed in such a way as to be changed ineffably, more excellently and more closely than a garment when it is put on by a man. Therefore, by the word *habitus* he sufficiently indicated how he said, “made in the likeness of men”: he was made not by migration into manhood, but by outward appearance, when he put on man, whom, by uniting and in some manner conforming him to himself, he would associate with immortality and eternity.

[Col. 0235D] [Note: [Col. 0235D] Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] Therefore the Word should not be understood to have been changed by assuming man, just as limbs are not changed when clothed with a garment, although that assumption ineffably joined the assumed nature to the one assuming it. “Outward appearance,” then, is the assumption of man, like a garment which does not change that which is clothed, to commend the greater humility. And he says: “And he humbled himself,” he who was so high, becoming obedient to the Father, not only by enduring insults and reproaches, but even unto death.

[Note: [Col. 0236D] Id., in a certain sermon.] How great the humility! Christ humbled himself unto the incarnation, unto participation in human mortality, unto the devil’s temptation, unto the people’s mockery, unto spittle and bonds [Col. 0236A], blows, scourges, and unto death. And if this is too little, something must be added concerning the kind of death. It was death—not just any death, but death on a cross, which is more shameful.

[Augustine.] Behold, we have an example of humility, a remedy for pride. Why then do you swell with pride, man? O dead skin, why do you stretch yourself? O foul-smelling pus, why are you inflated? Your prince is humble, and are you proud? The head is humble, and the member proud? Far be it!

“Therefore.” Having shown Christ’s humility, which appeared most fully in the Passion, he now begins to discuss his glory according to his human nature, which took its beginning from his resurrection. For Christ was first humbled by his Passion in order that he might be glorified by his resurrection. Humility is the merit of glory; glory is the reward of humility. But all this [Col. 0236B] occurred in the form of a servant. For in the form of God he always possessed and always will possess glory.

[Ambrose.] Thus he shows here how great a thing humility merits, so that, having trampled down boastfulness, we might seek it more eagerly.

### Verses 9–11

> “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those below—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

“Therefore”: namely, because Christ suffered death so humbly, God the Father exalted him by granting immortality and impassibility. He exalted him, then, according to the human nature, which was made more glorious in the resurrection; and in this respect the divine nature [Col. 0236C] may also be said to have been exalted in manifestation, because it began to be known as what it was. Just as it is said to have been emptied in the assumption of weakness, because what it was did not appear.

[Augustine.] And by grace he gave to Christ the man the name which is above every name: that is, the honor of being called God. He had this even before the resurrection, but after the resurrection what he was was set openly forth, so that men and demons might know it; and a thing is said to come about when it becomes known. Therefore what he had received from conception is said to have been given him after the resurrection because of its manifestation. But the question is: to whom did he give it—to the man or to God? He gave to the man the name above every name, not to God [Col. 0236D]; for when he was in the form of God, he was not lacking in exaltation, nor did heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings fail to bend the knee to him.

But when it says, “therefore he exalted him,” it is sufficiently apparent why he exalted him: namely, because of obedience unto death on the cross. Therefore the form in which Christ was crucified was itself exalted; to it was given the name above every name, so that together with that form of a servant the Only-Begotten Son of God might be named. Therefore this was given to him as man, according to which he was made an obedient Son unto death—the very thing which the same Son of God already possessed, God begotten of God and equal to the Father. For before he rose, indeed even before [Col. 0237A] he became man, was he not the exalted Son of God, the Word of God, God with God?

[Augustine.] Therefore, according to his human nature, it was given to Christ—dead according to the flesh, rising, ascending—that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those below; that is, angels, men, and demons should acknowledge themselves subject to his command. For Christ sits at the right hand of the Father after the resurrection and ascension. This has already happened; we do not see it, but believe and read it. Thus, even in that respect in which Christ was David’s son, he became David’s Lord. For that which was born from David was so honored as to be David’s Lord. Therefore, in the flesh which he received, in which he died, in which he also ascended and sits at the right hand of the Father—in that very flesh, thus honored, thus glorified [Col. 0237B], and changed into a heavenly condition—he is both David’s Son and David’s Lord, the Lord of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those below.

[Ambrose.]

Or, as some think, the name which is above every name was given to the man; but this is fitting in no manner and on no grounds. For this is the Father’s gift: namely, to be Son; and his name above every name is to be God, which is above every name not by appellation alone but by nature. This name was not given to man. For if he received this insofar as he was man, then the Son of God, God himself, gave this name to himself. Why, then, is the Father said to have given what the Son’s divinity could bestow on the man? But perhaps it will be said that, since all things are from God the Father, he is therefore said to have given it. If all things are from the Father [Col. 0237C], why is it not said that he gave all things to his Son through generation, when he begot him equal to himself?

Again, “gave to him” signifies the one who emptied himself, who took the form of a servant. But could man, a weak thing, have emptied himself? [Augustine.] Was he in the form of God before the incarnation? If he was not, he did not take the form of a servant, nor did he empty himself; for the one who was in the form of God emptied himself by taking the form of a servant. Therefore the name of God was not given to man, but to him who is equal to the Father, who emptied himself, and whose all things are from the Father. To him God the Father gave the name which is above every name—that is, to be God by nature—when he was born from him as fully God.

How then does the Apostle say, “Therefore he exalted and gave him [Col. 0237D] the name”? Because after the cross it is manifested what he received from the Father when he was begotten. When his majesty and divinity began to be known by creation after the cross, the Passion, and resurrection, they were revealed to men. “That at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those below.” Here he discloses to whom the name of God was given: to the one to whom every creature bends the knee, that is, to God. But perhaps it is said that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ would be in part true God and in part adoptive God. Yet creation does not bend the knee to an adoptive God, but to the true God, the cause of creation. It is established that Christ, to whom the knee is bent, is true God, not adoptive God.

Finally [Col. 0238A], at the end, every tongue of good and evil persons, willingly or unwillingly, shall confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father—that is, equal to the Father—which some here deny. How can it happen that a man is in the glory of God the Father? Even if he is an adoptive God, a man cannot be in the glory of God the Father. For this belongs to the one born of God: to be in the glory of God the Father is to differ from him in nothing, so that Father and Son have one glory by nature, through common substance and power.

Take care how you understand the foregoing words of the illustrious men Ambrose and Augustine, lest they seem to contradict one another. Know, then, that there is a natural gift and a gratuitous gift. By a natural gift the Father gave the name above every name to God the Son, not to man—that is, to Christ [Col. 0238B] insofar as he is God, not insofar as he is man. Nor was giving anything other than begetting him equal to himself. But by a gratuitous gift he gave it to Christ the man, not to God: for Christ received the name of God by grace not insofar as he is God but insofar as he is man—not by the grace of adoption, but by the grace of union—so that he is not an adoptive God, but the true God to whom every knee bends.

### Verses 12–18

> “Therefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, not in my presence only but much more now in my absence, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good will. But do all things without murmurings and hesitations, that you may be without complaint and simple children of God, without reproach in [Col. 0238C] the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life, to my glory on the day of Christ, because I have not run in vain nor labored in vain. But even if I am poured out upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I rejoice and give thanks with you all. And you likewise rejoice and give thanks with me.”

“Therefore,” etc. [Haimo.] As though he said: Because Christ, being humble, was thus exalted through obedience, therefore, my brothers in faith and love, as you have always obeyed the Lord and me, so now obey—not serving only in my presence, but much more now in my absence, because I am less able to assist you. Work out, that is, merit and prepare by works, your salvation [Col. 0238D], that is, eternal life. And do this with fear of mind and trembling of body, that is, with great and manifest fear, not with presumption. Or, “with fear,” that is, with humility, not proudly, because one who always fears is humble lest he fall; and with manifest trembling.

“For God is”: as though he said, You ought therefore to fear, because it is not you but God who works. For God is the one who works in you both to will what is good and to accomplish the good which you will. And this is according to his good will, not according to our merits.

[Note: [Col. 0237D] Augustine, *On the Gift of Perseverance.*] We therefore will, but God works in us even the willing; we work, but God works in us also the working. It is beneficial for us to believe and say this, because it is devout and true, so that there may be a humble confession [Col. 0239A] and all may be attributed to God.

[Note: [Col. 0239D] Augustine, *Against Julian.*] For unless free choice is aided by God’s grace, not even good will itself can be present in a human being.

“But do all things.” Here he adds patience to humility. As though he said: Not only work with fear, but also do all things without murmuring—that is, not negligently or without devotion—and without hesitations, so that you do not hesitate to suffer for Christ but may be ready. Do all things in such a way that you are without complaint with respect to your neighbor, so that your neighbor cannot complain about you; and with respect to yourselves, be simple, not double-minded, like those who wish to serve two masters. Against this it was said: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6). Simple, I say, as children of God.

[Haimo.] As God is simple, so his children ought to walk with a pure and simple [Col. 0239B] mind. And also, with regard to outsiders, be without reproach, so that there may be nothing in you open to censure. I urge this because you are in the midst of a crooked nation in its works and perverse in its diverse sects: that is, among evil persons who spoil and overturn the right order. They are called a nation because they have not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit. Among them you shine—that is, you ought to shine in teaching and life; indeed, you have been appointed for this purpose, to shine. Therefore it is fitting that you be without reproach.

You shine, I say, as fixed lights in heaven shine in the world; so you are the sun of the world, whom the true light illumines. And this is because you hold the word of life: that is, because you are vessels of the Gospel, just as those things are said to contain the principle of animal life.

He aptly compares the saints to lights [Col. 0239C]. For just as the night does not extinguish the stars of heaven, so worldly wickedness does not darken the minds of believers who cling to the heaven of Holy Scripture.

[Note: [Col. 0240D] Id., from the book of Prosper’s *Sentences.*] And just as the stars, whatever may happen on earth, even if false things are said about them, nevertheless neither bend nor delay their courses in heaven, so the saints, whose “citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3), on account of the evils of the world which they despise or the falsehoods fabricated against them, in no way corrupt the light of the word and the example of life.

Do as I have said. This certainly will be for my glory—not merely for your future glory—on the day of Christ, that is, when Christ is seen. And truly I shall have glory, because I have not run in vain, that is, without fruit, among those easily converted; nor [Col. 0239D] labored in vain among those converted with difficulty. And not only then shall I have glory, but even now I shall rejoice inwardly, in mind, because a sure reward awaits me; and I give thanks to you all, even if I am offered up upon the sacrifice and service of your faith. As though he said: I have already offered your faith and works to God, but even if I myself am offered for you, I rejoice. So also you, if you are sacrificed for me, rejoice. This is what he adds: “And you likewise rejoice and give thanks with me,” that is, give thanks with me, as I do with you, if I am offered up for you.

### Verses 19–30

> “But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be of good courage when I learn how matters stand with you. For I have no one so like-minded who will be sincerely concerned for you. For all seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. But you know his tested character: how, as a son with a father, he served with me in the Gospel. Therefore I hope to send him to you as soon as I see what will happen with me. Yet I trust in the Lord that I myself also shall come to you soon. But I have considered it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus—my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, but your apostle and minister to my need—because he longed for you all and was distressed because you had heard that he was ill. For he was indeed ill, even to death [Col. 0240B], but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but also on me, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow. Therefore I sent him all the more quickly, so that when you see him you may rejoice again and I may be free from sorrow. Receive him therefore in the Lord with all joy, and hold such persons in honor, because for the work of Christ he came near unto death, risking his life, that he might supply what was lacking from you in your service to me.”

“But I hope.” As though he said: I urge this not only by letter, but I also hope in the Lord Jesus—that is, through the mercy of the Lord Jesus—to send Timothy to you. And this soon, so necessary is it that he come, and so attentive is he toward you. I say, “to send,” so that I also may be of good courage when I learn what concerns you [Col. 0240C], just as you will be of good courage when you learn what concerns me. This is why I wish to send him and no other. For I presently have no one so like-minded, that is, no one who so agrees with my will in this matter and who will be so sincerely concerned for you.

For at this time many with the Apostle were hirelings; but there were no sons or shepherds except Timothy. And truly, all seek among you what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ.

[Ambrose.] For they were negligent about the discipline and conduct of the brothers. They did not preach with a devoted mind, but for their own gain. These are hirelings, who are to be tolerated because they have in their mouths the same things as shepherds, who indeed are to be loved. But thieves [Col. 0240D] and robbers who kill are to be avoided.

“But you know his tested character.” As though he said: I shall send him to you, but you should recognize in his life and teaching his tested character—that is, Timothy himself, whom we have tested and found good—because, obedient to me as a son to a father, he served God with me in the Gospel, in which I was able to test him. And because I have tested him, I therefore hope to send him to you as soon as I see what outcome the matters concerning me will have. Yet I trust in the Lord that I too shall come to you soon.

[Haimo.] These things are plain and clear; let us touch on them briefly, that we may dwell upon obscure matters. Meanwhile, however, I judged it necessary to send to you [Col. 0241A] Epaphroditus, my brother in faith, fellow worker in preaching, and fellow soldier in adversities; but your apostle, that is, teacher, and minister of my need, who supplied my necessities. Therefore I wished to send him. There are also other reasons: namely, because he desired to see you all and was distressed, not for himself, but for you, who were grieving on his account. This is what follows: “Because you had heard that he was ill,” that is, weakened by his service, and you were grieving because of this.

“For,” etc. Someone might say: Why was he distressed because they had heard that he was ill, when they might have been deceived? The answer is: because he was ill not only in report, but in reality itself; and their report would thus be confirmed more and more, and their grief increase, unless he came to them quickly.

[Col. 0241B] This is what follows: “For he was indeed ill,” not, certainly, from being beaten, but from sickness; and this was unto death, that is, to the danger of death. But God had mercy on him by healing him—not upon him alone, but also upon me, or us, for whom he preserved him.

[Ambrose.] In this he had mercy on me, lest I should have sorrow from his death upon sorrow from his illness, which was harming you. And because God had mercy on him and us, I sent him to you more quickly than had been intended, so that, upon seeing him, you may again rejoice—for I knew that you grieved over his absence—and I may be free from the sorrow which I had at your grief. And because I sent him, receive him therefore with gratitude, so that by good works you may show that you rejoice in him. I mean joy which occurs in the Lord [Col. 0241C], that is, spiritual joy; and because he is such a person, hold him in all honor.

These matters are complete and need no interpretation. And you ought to do so because, for the work of Christ—that is, in order to do the work which Christ taught and did, who came to minister and not to be ministered to—he came even unto death, that is, to danger of death, not compelled but by voluntary decision, risking his soul, that is, his life, in order to supply what was lacking from you in my service. For you gave the gift, but there was no one to bring it to me from you.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–6

> “For the rest, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is not burdensome to me, but necessary for you. Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers; beware of the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit and glory in Christ Jesus, not placing confidence in the flesh—although I too have confidence in the flesh. If anyone else thinks that he has confidence in the flesh, I have more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee; according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness that is in the law, living without complaint.”

“For the rest.” Up to this point he has chiefly encouraged them against tribulations; henceforth he warns them against false apostles, lest they receive legal observances from them, but believe that Christ’s faith alone suffices. Here he begins to deal with sincerity of faith, as with endurance and certain other matters. Up to this point I have exhorted you. Henceforth—that is, from now on—my brothers in the faith, rejoice in the Lord: that is, have in the Lord the joy of every good, not in fleshly observances. I have indeed said this to you in person, but to write to you the same things that I said in person—namely, that you should rejoice in the Lord alone—is not burdensome to me while absent, but necessary for you against the false apostles who press upon you. He says that it is necessary to write what he had said in person because writing remains longer than speech.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Augustine, *On the Grace of the New Testament.*] Beware—and, in order that you may rejoice in the Lord, beware—that is, recognize them to be dogs, barking not by reason but by habit against unfamiliar truth.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Id., *On the Trinity.*] For this is the nature of dogs: they do not bark at those with whom they are familiar, whether good or bad; but, seeing unfamiliar persons, even innocent ones, they are provoked. He rightly compares them to dogs because, just as dogs follow habit more than reason, so the false apostles maintain the custom of the law and irrationally bark and bite against truth. And beware—that is, recognize them to be evil workers. Evil workers are those who sow the tares of errors over the noble seed of the Gospel and thereby destroy the grain. Beware—that is, recognize them to be not circumcision, as I would say, but mutilation: they are mutilated because they have been cut off from Christ [Col. 0242C]; and they cut off others, that is, separate them.

“For we are.” As though he said: I rightly call these persons mutilation and not circumcision, for we believers alone are truly circumcision. For believers circumcise their heart, so that, with the cloud of error cut away, they may behold and know God the Creator. We, I say, who serve God with that service which in Greek is called *latria*—and this not in flesh but in spirit, that is, by reason free from every hindrance, because spirit rules and flesh is subdued. For one serves God in flesh who hopes to please God through fleshly matters.

[Augustine.] But when flesh itself is made subject to the spirit for good works, we serve God in spirit, we who subdue the flesh so that the spirit may obey God. For spirit rules and flesh is ruled; nor does the spirit rule well unless it itself is ruled.

In some manuscripts we find it written thus: “who serve God the Spirit.” By this it indicates that the Holy Spirit is the one to whom *latria* is rendered—that is, the service due to the Creator alone. There is another kind of service by which we are commanded through charity to serve one another; in Greek it is called *dulia*.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] Id., in a certain sermon.] In many Latin manuscripts, and in all or almost all Greek manuscripts, it is found written thus: “who serve the Spirit of God.” Observe also how, when he did not say, “we have circumcision,” but “we are circumcision,” this is to be understood. The Apostle intended to signify this: We are righteousness, for circumcision is righteousness. Yet he more strongly commends what he says by calling us circumcision, that is, righteousness, than by calling us circumcised, that is, righteous—yet in such a way that, when he says we are righteousness, we are understood to be righteous.

[Haimo.] And we glory especially in Christ Jesus, because Christ alone is our glory. And we are those who have confidence—that is, hope of salvation—in the flesh, that is, in fleshly circumcision or in lineage.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Augustine, in a certain sermon.] He had in view some who place confidence in the flesh. These were those who gloried in circumcision of the flesh and other fleshly observances, as well as in lineage. And lest the Apostle seem unable to place confidence in the flesh and to despise what he does not possess, he adds: “Although I have”—that is, I could have—“confidence in the flesh,” if there were any such confidence. And truly I could more than others. This is what follows [Col. 0243B]: “If anyone else besides me, who deceives you, thinks he has confidence in the flesh,” as though righteous on that account, “I seem more entitled than those false apostles to place confidence in it, because I was circumcised on the eighth day,” from my birth.

As though he said: I was not circumcised when older, but I possess circumcision on the eighth day, as the Law of Moses commands that a man be circumcised on the eighth day with a stone knife—signifying that after the period of seven days, on the eighth, that is, on the eternal day, we shall be perfectly circumcised by Christ the Rock from every corruption of penalty and guilt. And I am of the race of Israel—that is, not a proselyte, not a stranger newly come to the people of God, but born from Jewish parents; and I am not from an inferior tribe, but from the tribe of Benjamin, which was not descended from concubines, and which did not leave the Temple when the division occurred under Solomon’s servant [Col. 0243C]. At that time the royal tribe of Judah, the tribe of Benjamin, and the priestly tribe of Levi remained together, not departing from Jerusalem and the Temple. And, having been born of Hebrew parents, I am a Hebrew.

As though he said: I did not depart from my people. Note that the Hebrews are said to be called from “Abrahamites,” with a letter changed from Abraham, from whom their origin is derived, and not from Heber. Augustine, however, retracts this as follows, saying: “What I said, that their people began from Abraham, is indeed also plausible, so that Hebrews may seem to have been called, as it were, Abrahamites. But it is more truly understood that they are named from the one called Heber, as Hebrews.”

And I am, according to the law—in which I was distinguished—a Pharisee [Col. 0243D], that is, not mingled with the contemptible populace, but set apart from others and eminent by nobility. For certain leading men, as though separated for Jewish nobility and not mixed with the despised populace, were called Pharisees. For this word is said to mean something like “separation,” just as in Latin an *egregius* (“distinguished”) person is said to be one separated from the flock (*grex*). And according to zeal—that is, love for the law—I persecuted the Church of God. For whatever seemed contrary to my law I bore impatiently and pursued fiercely. This was nobility among the Jews, but with Christ humility is sought. Therefore there he was called Saul, from Saul, who was of tall stature; but here [Col. 0244A] he is called Paul, that is, “little.”

And according to righteousness—not true righteousness, but the righteousness which is in the law, which restrains the hands rather than the mind, and makes one serve through fear rather than love—I lived without complaint, that is, without any public outcry made against me.

[Augustine.] Note that he says he lived according to the righteousness of the law; yet elsewhere he says: “Among whom we too all once walked in the desires of the flesh, doing the will of the flesh, and were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. 2). Such was his righteousness according to the law. It was evil to pursue such righteousness, because what in him was without complaint was itself a great ground of complaint against him.

### Verses 7–12

> “But whatever things were gains to me, I counted these losses for Christ. Indeed, I consider all things to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whom I have made all things loss and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ Jesus, the righteousness from God in faith, so as to know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, conformed to his death, if by any means I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead—not that I have already received it or am already perfected.”

But those things which were gain to me, etc. I had all the things mentioned above; but those which were gains to me before Christ, as tokens of truth, I judged—if I were to follow after the truth—to be losses [Col. 0244C], namely, whatever is destructive of good. [Ambrose] And this because of Christ: lest I should show either that Christ’s coming had not yet occurred, or that it was superfluous. For all these things were empty and impediments to approaching grace.

“Nevertheless.” As though he said: I not only judged them so for the sake of obtaining Christ; nevertheless—that is, even if I could not attain him—I consider all things loss for this alone, namely, for the surpassing knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ: that is, the knowledge we have of Christ, surpassing other kinds of knowledge, or which surpasses in him more than in others. Or this wording may be joined to the preceding verse in the same sense. As though he said: I possess all the aforesaid things of the Law; nevertheless—that is, not partly [Col. 0244D], but wholly—I consider them losses, and this because of the surpassing knowledge, that is, of Christ the Lord. This point does not change.

“For whom,” Christ, to be honored—that is, for love and honor of Jesus Christ—I not only consider them losses, but have also made them so, by teaching and by spiritual living, so that it might appear to others that all things are loss. And, what is more, I judge those legal observances not merely to be losses of good things, but even as dung, because they now defile the person who observes them.
