And this in order that in the future I may gain Christ—that is, have Christ as my reward; and that I may be found in him: that is, as a member, to one who considers rationally, in that head—joined to him as his member by love. This cannot happen otherwise [Col. 0245A] unless those things are judged as dung.

How one can be in him as a member, he adds: “that I may be found,” I say, “not having my own righteousness, which is from the Law.” That is the righteousness by which a person fears punishments rather than loves righteousness. For whoever fears, supposes that by his own strength he can fulfill the Law, and does what the Law commands—not by loving righteousness but by fearing punishment—does indeed become righteous according to the righteousness which is from the Law. Of this righteousness it is said elsewhere: “Seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God,” that is, grace (Rom. VIII).

But if righteousness is from the Law, how is it yours? Did you impose the Law upon yourself? [Haimo] God gave and imposed the Law; God commanded you to obey his Law. [Augustine] Yet it is yours because [Col. 0245B], relying upon the Law, you presume by your own will that you can fulfill it, imagining that you perform those legal observances with your hands. “Not having my own,” I say, “but that righteousness which is through faith in Christ,” which obtains from God, removes fear, gives love, and which God alone works in us.

For it is better to be righteous than to be human. Therefore, if God made you human, and makes you righteous—which is better—he did not make you yourself, but made you without you; for you employed no understanding in order to make yourself. Therefore, he who made you without you does not justify you without you. He made you while you did not know; he justifies you while you will. And since true righteousness is from faith, what need then is there of the Law? It must altogether be removed according to the figurative meaning of legal observances. This righteousness which is from faith is from God, not from ourselves. And even if faith and righteousness are ours, this is so insofar as it exists in faith [Col. 0245C]. For just as it was born from faith, so it cannot exist except in faith [p. 184].

Then he adds a commendation of faith by the many things it accomplishes. For it makes one perfectly know God in the other life, whom here one believes by faith; it gives possession of the resurrection—for our resurrection is the power and efficacy of Christ’s resurrection—and in this life it gives fellowship with Christ in suffering. For without faith no one would suffer so much. It also gives conformity to his death: namely, that one may die for Christ, if necessary, as he died for us.

This is what he says: faith, I say, being effective for perfectly knowing him in the future. This seems to be said concerning faith which has no time for working, which is effective only for this. It is also effective for “the power [Col. 0245D] of his resurrection,” that is, for the true efficacy of resurrection, which is the power and effect of Christ’s resurrection. In this life it is effective for fellowship in his sufferings: that is, that we may be Christ’s companions in suffering. This fellowship is from love; this he says concerning faith which has time for working.

“I may be found,” I say, “in him,” I say, “conformed to his death,” namely, that I may die for him if need be, an imitator of his death and passion.

Or thus: “in faith, to know him.” As though he said: One who thinks himself justified in the Law does not acknowledge Christ; but I wish to be justified in the righteousness which is from faith, which is from God, which exists in faith. For what purpose? “To know him”: that is, that I may know [Col. 0246A] him—why he was born and why he suffered. And to know the power of his resurrection: that is, that I may know what the power of his resurrection is, namely, the justification of believers. For we are justified by his resurrection, as though circumcised from the rock. Christ rose for our justification: that is, in order to make us righteous. And that I may know the companions of his suffering: that is, the fruit which comes from fellowship in his sufferings. Therefore, that person knows it rightly who believes that through it he will arrive at the joys of heaven.

“I say, conformed to his death.” This point does not change. “If by any means.” As though he said: I seek to be justified by faith and conformed to the death of Christ. I, I say, am striving, if by any means—for this reason he says this, because it is difficult—that I may meet God, repaying him what he repaid to me, namely, the cup [Col. 0246B] of suffering. Hence the prophet: “What shall I repay to the Lord for all,” etc. (Ps. CXV). I say this as one who for that reason will come to the true and glorious resurrection.

Or: striving, if by any means, etc., to meet Christ in the air at the judgment—coming first to the true resurrection, which is not among the dead but far out from the dead; this belongs only to the saints. Although all will rise on the day of judgment, only the righteous will be gloriously transformed and, carried by angels, will meet the Lord in the air. The wicked, however, will remain on earth until they receive the dreadful sentence of the Judge.

And lest it seem superfluous for the Apostle to suffer so much when he has faith and other goods, he adds: “Not that.” As though he said: Rightly I now labor so greatly for that glory [Col. 0246C], because I do not say that I have already received any share of glory; for if I have received any share of glory, it is nothing compared with what is to come. Or, if I have already received anything of the knowledge of Christ, I do not say that I am already perfect in it. And if this is true of me, what of others?

He says this of himself lest those whom he praises in this Epistle, and in whose faith and devotion he testifies that he rejoices, should be exalted like men by pride; rather, they should labor to add more, as he does, great as he is. For if he who is endowed with such great dignity confesses that he still lacks perfection, how much more ought they to understand that they must labor to attain the merits of justifications and the goal of perfection. Therefore no believer, even if he has made progress, should say, “It is enough for me.”

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Augustine, from the book *Sentences of Prosper.*] For whoever has said this has stopped on the road before the end, which the Apostle, running, looked toward [Col. 0246D] and confessed his own imperfection, seeing one thing in himself and seeking another elsewhere. For he walks by faith, not by sight. Or thus: I strive, if by any means I may come to the resurrection, because it is not true that I have already received the power of the resurrection or that I am already perfect in the knowledge of God.

### Verses 12–14

> “But I follow after, if by any means I may lay hold of that for which I have also been laid hold of by Christ Jesus. Brethren, I do not reckon that I have laid hold; but one thing: forgetting indeed the things which are behind, but stretching myself forth to those which are before, I pursue toward the appointed goal, for the prize [Col. 0247A] of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.”

“But I follow after.” As though he said: I have not received it, nor am I perfect; but I follow—not with bodily steps, but with the dispositions of the mind and the conduct of life—so that I may be able to be a perfect possessor of righteousness. As one advancing by the right path from day to day through spiritual renewal, I have already been made a perfect traveler in that righteousness; for he was a perfect traveler, but had not yet arrived at the perfection of the journey itself.

Therefore he says: I follow, by making progress, striving if by any means I may lay hold: that is, if by some means I may be able perfectly to know Christ, who is supreme blessedness. See how great is the faith which seeks so great a thing. “I may lay hold,” I say, “in that manner of knowledge in which I was laid hold of by Christ Jesus”: namely, that I may see him as he is, just as he sees me [Col. 0247B] as I am.

[Ambrose] Or thus: “I may lay hold,” I say, not by my own merit, but in that by which I was laid hold of by the Lord: that is, through the mercy of God, by which I was sought out and found through God’s foreknowledge.

Or thus: “I may lay hold,” I say, in that manner of seeing in which I have even now been laid hold of by the Lord Jesus: namely, that I may see him in the brightness in which he appeared to me on the road when he took hold of me.

“Brethren,” etc. He explains more plainly what he had said, and specifies what it is that he has not yet laid hold of, but pursues in order to lay hold of it. As though they wondered what he meant when he said, “I have not received it; I am not yet perfect,” he says: “Brethren.” As though he said: I rightly say that I follow in order to lay hold, [Col. 0247C] because I, who know better than you or others, do not reckon that I have laid hold of it, whatever others may think of me.

[Augustine] I do not reckon that I have laid hold of it. One thing: I do indeed have many things, but I do not yet have this one thing—this one thing. “One” is also said in the Psalm: “One thing have I asked of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI). And as though someone said, “What then do you do, Apostle? Have you not yet laid hold? Are you not yet perfect? What then do you do? What do you set before me to imitate?” he says: “The things which are behind.”

Or thus: “I do not reckon that I have laid hold.” Here make the division: I have not laid hold. But I affirm to you this one thing about myself: that, forgetting the things which are behind, but stretching myself out toward those which are before, I also pursue, etc.

Or thus, from the words “brethren”: As though he said: I have not laid hold. And truly, [Col. 0247D] because, brethren, I do not even reckon that I have laid hold; but I pursue, not certainly two or three things, but one—the supreme good, which truly is one, in which are all good things. This is that one thing of which Philip said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV).

“I pursue,” I say—but how? In this way: “forgetting indeed,” that is, consigning to oblivion, “the things which are behind,” namely, the earthly things which I have left; but “stretching myself out toward the things which are before,” that is, toward heavenly things, which are before earthly things, with all my intention and desire for the thing not yet possessed. For he stretched himself toward heavenly things in intention, not in attainment; in purpose, not in possession.

Thus we too should not slip back [Col. 0248A] from what we have already passed over, nor remain in those things to which we have already come. Let us run; let us strain forward. For we are on the way: let us not look back, but stretch forward in purpose and desire.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Augustine, in the *Confessions.*] For the life of a good Christian consists in desire. What you desire, you do not yet see; but by desiring, you become capable, so that when what you desire comes, you may be filled. For just as, if you wished to fill some fold or bag, and know how great the thing to be given is, you would stretch the fold, or sack, or wineskin, or something else, and by stretching it make it more capacious: so God, by delaying the thing, stretches desire; by desire he stretches the soul; by stretching it he makes it capable. Therefore let us desire, because we are to be filled. This is our life: that we may be exercised by desiring. But holy desire exercises us only as much [Col. 0248B] as we cut off our desires from love of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] The same, on Psalm LXXX.] Therefore he says, “forgetting the things which are behind”: that is, all temporal things; and “stretching myself toward the things which are before,” desiring eternal things. For that stretching is the desire for earthly things.

[Ambrose] Or thus: “forgetting the things which are behind,” namely, merits already past—previous deeds—not because they are evil, but because they are small in relation to the merit to be set before one; rather, he stretched toward greater things, so that he might always advance to what is better.

[Augustine] Hence he adds: “stretching myself toward the things which are before,” namely, former evils; “stretching myself toward the things which are before,” that is, toward the promised goods. For past evils must be put behind our backs, [Col. 0248C] so that we may direct our attention to what is promised to us. Therefore we ought to take pleasure neither in past life nor in present life. The mind must be recalled from remembering past evils with a certain pleasure, and from a certain longing to enjoy them, lest we return in heart to Egypt. Therefore forget your past evil life. If vanity once delighted you, let it no longer delight you.

“I pursue,” I say, until I come to the appointed reward: namely, to the prize, that is, the reward appointed and promised to me by God, or toward which I have set myself to run. I say, the prize “of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus”: that is, eternal life, to be given in the heights, to which God calls me through his Son Jesus Christ; and therefore it is a worthy and certain thing.

### Verses 15–16

> “Therefore, whosoever of us are perfect, let us think this; and if in anything you think otherwise, God will reveal this also to you. Nevertheless, to what we have attained, let us think the same thing and remain in the same rule.”

“Therefore, whosoever.” As though he said: And because I run in this way and think thus of myself—namely, that I am still imperfect—therefore you Philippians also think this. But he includes himself among them, saying: “Therefore, whosoever of us are perfect”—[Note: [Col. 0248D] Augustine, on Psalm CXXX.] runners or travelers in comparison with others—“let us think this.”

As though he said: I do not speak to the imperfect, to whom I cannot speak wisdom, who are still fed with milk and not nourished with solid food; [Col. 0249A] but I speak to those who are already called perfect, who eat solid food [Col. 0249A; p. 185] because they understand the equality of the Word with the Father, but do not yet see as they must see face to face. For certain faith somehow begins knowledge. Perfect knowledge is not completed until after this life, when we shall see face to face.

Therefore let us think this: that we may know that the disposition of truly seeking is safer than presumptuously treating unknown things as known.

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] Therefore let us seek as those who will find, and let us find as those who will seek. Concerning things to be believed, let us doubt with no unbelief; concerning things to be understood, let us affirm with no rashness. In the former, authority must be held; in the latter, truth must be sought out.

And it should be known that the righteousness by which the righteous person lives by faith is now true righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0249D] The same, from the book *Sentences of Prosper.*] Although it may not improperly be called perfect in certain righteous persons, according to the capacity of this life, it is nevertheless small in comparison with that great righteousness which the equality of angels will receive. He who did not yet possess the latter, but because of the former which he already possessed was perfect, and because of the latter which he still lacked called himself imperfect: this lesser righteousness produces merit; that greater one, reward. Therefore, whoever does not pursue this one does not attain the other.

[Note: [Col. 0250D] The same, *On the Perfect Righteousness of Man.*] Hence he says: “Whosoever of us are perfect,” that is, run perfectly. “Think this”: that we are not yet perfect, so that we may be perfected there, toward which we now run perfectly; so that, when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial may be destroyed (1 Cor. XIII): that is, it may no longer be partial but whole, because the reality itself, which will be seen, will succeed faith and hope. Love, however, which is greater than these three [Col. 0249C], will not be taken away, but will be increased and fulfilled.

In that fullness, the commandment of love will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul,” etc. (Matt. XXII). For while there remains any carnal desire, God is not loved entirely with the whole soul. Flesh is said to desire only because the soul desires carnally. Then indeed there will be inwardly no sin at all, because there will be no law in the members resisting the law of the mind. Then a person will love God altogether with all the heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; and this is the greatest commandment. Why, then, is this perfection commanded to a person, although no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run rightly unless one knows where one ought to run. [Col. 0249D] And how could one know it unless it were shown by commandments?

“And if in anything.” As though he said: Think as I have said; and if you do this, God will grant you this. But if you now think otherwise than you ought to think, in the future—because now you see through a mirror—God will reveal this also to you, because he will make you know clearly both himself and all other things which you now see obscurely.

Or thus: Think as I have said; and if in anything you think otherwise—that is, imperfectly concerning God and other things—then God has also revealed to you through the Holy Spirit this which you now think otherwise, both concerning God and concerning all things: that is, even this imperfect knowledge.

Or thus: Think as I have said; and if in anything you think otherwise than you ought, like children in understanding—that is, if you suppose that you have perfect knowledge of Christ, if the thought steals upon you that you are something great—God in his mercy will reveal to you that you are thinking wrongly in this very matter, and likewise in other errors.

[Note: [Col. 0250D] The same, on Psalm CXXX.] A tested life will set you free; it will not immediately give the eternal prize. He will do this, I say, if you think humbly and judge yourselves humbly; for whoever remains in Catholic peace, and if he thinks otherwise in anything than he ought, God reveals it to the humble. But if a proud person defends and obstinately asserts this against the peace of the Church, God rejects him, because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. V).

“Nevertheless,” for the present. As though he said: We are imperfect; we now think otherwise; but nevertheless it is necessary that we all think the same concerning that to which we have attained by faith and knowledge, and that we also fulfill it in deed. Hence he adds: “that we may remain in the same rule,” that is, in uprightness of life; and thus God will reveal what we think otherwise.

[Ambrose] Or thus, from “and if in anything”: Think as I have said. And if in anything you think otherwise—that is, if you devise something better for the worship of God—know that this too is God’s gift, because God will reveal these things to you. But lest any presumption arise from this, he adds: “Nevertheless.” As though he said: Even if you think otherwise, nevertheless let us hold fast to that which we have attained: namely, that we may think the same thing and remain in the same rule of faith, doctrine, and life. This is not to think outside the rule of discipline, but what is shared and moderate [Col. 0250C] in evangelical truth and in these things, namely faith and the rule of life.

### Verses 17–21

> “Be imitators of me, brethren, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example. For many walk, of whom I often told you, but now also tell you weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame—those who think earthly things. But our commonwealth is in heaven, from which also we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory, according to the working of his power by which he is also able to subject [Col. 0250D] all things to himself.”

Be imitators, O brethren, [Haimo] both in faith and in love, so that, as I believe, act, and teach, so you too may do. And if you do not have me present, observe—that is, carefully examine and imitate—those who walk in this way, as you have our example: that is, the image of our life, namely those who so believe, live, and teach. Imitate those like me.

[Ambrose] He wants them to be watchful lest they be ensnared by the subtlety of wicked people. Let them note how each person lives and teaches, so that they may join themselves to those in whom they recognize the understanding of their teacher [Col. 0251A].

“For many,” etc. As though he said: I tell you to observe those who walk in this way. For there are many who walk otherwise, not thinking with us concerning the abolition of the Law, but preaching that the Law must be kept together with the Gospel. While I was present among you, I often called them enemies of the cross of Christ. Now I say the same thing, and weeping: both because of their destruction and because of the overthrow of the simple.

He calls them enemies of the cross because those who introduce carnal observances maintain that the cross is superfluous. Their end is eternal destruction: that is, at their end there will be eternal punishment for them. Their god is their own belly. Whatever they do, they do for the belly, as if worshipping the belly itself.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Augustine, from the book *Sentences of Prosper.*] For that is worshipped by a person which is loved more than all other things. Therefore, since God is greater and better than all things [Col. 0251B], he must be loved above all things in order to be worshipped.

[Ambrose] But those make the belly their god who labor over eating as though salvation were in food, or as though the belly were God. “And their glory”—another reading is—“is in their private parts,” that is, they glory in the shameful parts which are circumcised. Those who think such things do so. For this is to think earthly things: namely, to glory in such matters. But one who thinks spiritual things glories in faith, hope, and love.

Or thus: “whose god is their belly,” that is, they make food for the belly into a god when they say that such foods justify people; and their glory is in their shame, that is, in such things as may make them ashamed and blush, while they believe themselves justified through animals. Or, their temporal glory is their shame [Col. 0251C]: [Haimo] that is, it will lead them to eternal shame—those who think earthly things, because in earthly things they understand nothing except what they see, understanding legal observances not spiritually but earthly.

“But our commonwealth.” [Ambrose] As though he said: They walk so wrongly; but our commonwealth, even though we are still on earth, is in heaven, where true hope is: that is, in living and understanding like angels. Therefore, in addition to the benefits we already have, we await God. This is what he adds: we await our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior already of souls and someday also of bodies, to come from there.

When he comes, he will transform. As though he said: This is what we await from him: that, as he has already transformed souls, so he will transform the body of our humiliation, [Col. 0251D] [Haimo] that is, of our lowliness, which through death is humbled into dust and worms. He will transform it so that it will be conformed to the body of his glory: that is, made like his body in the glory which it had at the Transfiguration or at the resurrection. This he can certainly do according to the working—that is, the power of working—by which he can not only transform the body but also subject all things to himself: that is, he can do this according to the power of working by which he has subjected all things to himself, and because he will transform our body.

## Chapter IV

### Verses 1–7

> “Therefore, my brethren most dearly beloved and longed for [Col. 0252A], my joy and my crown, stand firm thus in the Lord, dearly beloved. I entreat Euodia and beseech Syntyche to think the same thing in the Lord. I also ask you, loyal companion, help those women who labored with me in the Gospel, with Clement and the rest of my fellow-workers, whose names are in the book of life. Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people. For the Lord is near. Be anxious about nothing; but in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, let your petitions be made known to God. And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”

Therefore, my brethren most dearly beloved and longed for [Col. 0252B]: that is, whom I greatly desire to see. Or, “longed for”: those who greatly desire to see me; you who are my joy, namely, because I rejoice in your faith and works, and my crown in the future: that is, those through whom I am even now made glad and will in the future be crowned.

[Ambrose] For a disciple victorious in the contest will be worthy of being his teacher’s crown. Stand firm in the Lord in this way, as you know that I and those like me stand, or as you are now and then will be, dearly beloved.

“Euodia,” etc. As though he said: I exhort all, but especially I entreat Euodia and beseech Syntyche, because I fear more for her, to think the same thing that I say, not something else. For what I say is in the Lord: that is, according to the Lord. He also especially entreats these women because these religious women were accustomed to receive preachers.

And, O Germanus—a proper name—you who are a companion, that is, my fellow-worker in preaching the Gospel, I also ask you: help, by strengthening, the women named above, lest they fail. They labored with me in the Gospel by supplying what was necessary for me. And they labored also with Clement and my other fellow-workers, supplying also what was necessary for them.

Their names—that is, the merits and rewards of those who hold to truth—are written in the book of life: that is, in God’s predestination. For, if they are distinct in merits, they will have different dwelling places in the eternal house according to the diversity of merits. Hence: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV). The book of life is God’s predestination, in which all who are to be saved are inscribed.

[Haimo] And the sense is: O Philippians, do not take it grievously that I have not individually named all of you in the Epistle, because even if you are not written in it, you are nevertheless contained in the book of life.

“Rejoice in the Lord always.” The Apostle, rejoicing in their faith and works, desires that they rejoice always in the Lord as they make progress in this pursuit, so that they may be more eager. He repeats it in order to show that he truly rejoices in them with affection. As though he said: Their names are in the book of life.

[Augustine] And so that you may most certainly believe that the same is true of you, rejoice—not for an hour, but always; not in the world, but in the Lord. That is, establish in the Lord, not outside him, everything in which one ought to rejoice.

[Note: [Col. 0252D] The same, *On the Words of the Gospel.*] For just as a person cannot serve two masters [Col. 0253A], so no one can rejoice both in the world and in the Lord. For a friend of this world will be accounted an enemy of God. These two kinds of joys differ greatly and are altogether contrary; they cannot exist together in the same person. Therefore let joy in the Lord prevail until joy in the world is ended. Let the former always increase and the latter always diminish until it is ended.

What is worldly joy? I say briefly: worldly gladness is unpunished wickedness—indulgence in lust, trifling at spectacles, gorging oneself in drunkenness, stinking with indecency, suffering no evil. Behold worldly joy: not being corrected by hunger, fear of war, illness, or any adversity, but committing every evil amid abundance of possessions, peace of the flesh, and the security of a wicked mind. Behold worldly joy.

Therefore it is very great mercy not to leave wickedness unpunished, lest there be joy in the world; and, lest he be compelled at the end to condemn to Gehenna, he deigns now to chastise by the scourge. It is good for us that he helps us by chastising us. Therefore rejoice in the Lord, not in the world: that is, in truth, not in iniquity; in the hope of eternity, not in the bloom of vanity. And this is so necessary for us that I say again: rejoice in the Lord, not merely as some other things are said once.

Do this because this is moderation, and the right measure: that all joy may be in the Lord. Let this moderation be yours, and through you let it be known to all people, so that through you others may learn this.

[Ambrose] Or thus: Rejoice, I say, and let your moderation of conduct—that is, reasonable behavior—be known to all people, both believers and unbelievers: to believers, that they may imitate it; to unbelievers, that they may be unable to find fault and that some may be converted. By their example he wishes others to be won. For when their works shine, there will not be lacking those who imitate their good.

And you ought to do what I have exhorted because the Lord is near: that is, ready to give whatever is needed in spiritual or temporal matters. Therefore be anxious about nothing: that is, fearful about nothing; setting aside worldly anxiety, keep God’s promises before your eyes. But in every prayer and supplication—that is, in prayer made generally for any people and any things, either simply or with adjuration—make your petitions, concerning necessary things which you wish to obtain, with thanksgiving. For whoever wishes to obtain something ought to be grateful for past things.

And let those petitions, I say, be made known to God: that is, let them be so earnest, not lukewarm, that they reach God—that is, are fulfilled. Make the distinction: prayer and supplication are generally made by some for themselves or others and concerning any matters; petition concerns specified necessary things.

Or thus: let your petitions be made known as being with God, through endurance, not with people, through boasting.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Augustine, to Proba, in the book *On Praying to God.*] For this should not be understood as though they become known to God by being with God. This knowledge comes through assiduity in prayer and watchfulness.

Or: let them be made known to the angels [Col. 0254A] who are with God, so that in some sense they may offer them to God, consult concerning them, and bring back to us—openly or secretly—what, by God’s command, they have learned must be fulfilled. Hence the angel speaking to people says: “When you prayed, I offered your prayer to God” (Tob. XII).

For God’s own perfection is sufficient for knowing all things. Yet he has messengers, that is, angels—not to announce to him what he does not know, for there is nothing he does not know—but because it is their good to consult his will concerning their works. This is what is meant when they are said to announce certain things: not so that he learns from them, but so that they announce here from him, through his Word and without bodily sound, whatever they have found in his truth—that is, what they must do, what they must announce, to whom, and when. They are sent by him to whomever he wills.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] The same, in the same work.] They hear everything from him through that Word of his: that is, they find [Col. 0254B] in his truth what they must do and what, to whom, and when they must announce.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The same, *On the Grace of the New Testament.*] Therefore an angel is not said to offer our prayers to God as though God then comes to know what we wish or what we need; he knows all things before they happen just as he knows them after they have happened. But a rational creature obeying God must refer temporal causes to eternal truth, whether by asking what may be done concerning itself or by consulting what it should do. In this it testifies that it itself is not the good by which it is made blessed, but that the immutable good is so, by participation in which it is made wise.

“And the peace of God.” As though he said: I exhort you to make petitions, and to the Lord, without whom human labor is useless, so that prayer may have effect. This is what he says: “And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding,” that is, all intellect—certainly ours, not that of those who always behold the Father’s face, that is, the angels.

Or, if angels too are not understood to be excepted, we take the statement thus: the peace of God, by which God himself is at peace, cannot be known by us as God knows it, nor by any angels; for it surpasses every understanding except his own.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The same, *Enchiridion.*] And the sense is: the peace of God which surpasses all understanding—that is, God, who is supreme peace, which cannot even be thought, and therefore outside him nothing is needed—may guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus: that is, your wills and understandings, so that you understand or desire nothing outside him.

Note that he first spoke of assiduity and watchfulness in prayer, and afterwards adds concerning the guarding of peace [Col. 0254D], because, once assiduity in prayer has been employed, peace then at last guards hearts in Christ. He says this because those who have peace with God do not fear an adverse mind.

### Verses 8–14

> “Finally, brethren, whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovable, whatever things are of good report—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline—think on these things: the things which you have both learned and received and heard and seen in me. Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you. But I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last, at some time, you have flourished again in your concern for me, as you were also concerned. [Col. 0255A] But you had been occupied. I do not say this because of want. For I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know both how to be humbled and how to abound. Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed both to be full and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things in him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you have done well by sharing in my tribulation.”

What remains. Up to this point he has warned against persecutors and false preachers. In conclusion he sets forth the matters that pertain to perfection. As though he said: “Thus far I have admonished you toward endurance and caution. But henceforth, brothers, I exhort you to this: Think upon”—that is, keep in mind—“these things which pertain to perfection: whatever things are true, whatever chaste,” that is, whatever belong to true faith—both because truth is in them and because through them chastity is maintained with God—“whatever are just,” toward one’s neighbor; “whatever are holy,” in one’s own life; and, to say less, “whatever are lovable,” that is, worthy of being loved, such as a modest bearing, humble speech, and the like; and “whatever are of good repute,” because it is fitting that they should be holy and just in such a way that no bad opinion is held of them, but a good one, so that they may benefit others.

[Note: Col. 0255D. Augustine, *Against Julian*.] For our own life is necessary for us; our reputation is necessary for others. Therefore, whoever guards his life from the crimes of shameful deeds does well for himself. But whoever also preserves his reputation for others is merciful. I say, those things which are of good repute, if there is nevertheless any virtue in them, or any praise of Christian discipline. For a good reputation for bodily strength, worldly learning, or other secular things is not to be sought.

Or distinguish it thus: let “if there be any praise” refer to reputation, and “if there be any virtue” to the other matters previously mentioned, in this way: “Think upon whatever things are true,” and so forth, if there is any virtue in them; and think upon whatever things are of good repute, if there is any praise of discipline in them. Think upon these things, I say—all of which you learned while I taught you, and received as worthy to be retained. Again, these things should be thought upon because you also heard them from others, and heard through yourselves that they were in me.

Therefore do these things: do not merely think them, but fulfil them in action. The God who gives peace will be with you, that is, helping you to do these things. “But I rejoiced”: here he recalls that they had often sent him necessities.

[Ambrose.] Thus he shows that his cheerfulness had become more ardent, because in the matter in which they had become negligent, they renewed their efforts with diligence, so that, remembering their apostle, they might send him fruit to be stored in the heavenly granary. As though he said: “I exhort you concerning the future. But concerning the past, I rejoiced greatly—and this in the Lord, not in the gift for the sake of the gift. For at last,” namely after a long time, “at some time,” namely in some period, since they could not do so at all times, “you have blossomed anew”: that is, you have again flourished as formerly, by supplying me with necessities. This ministry is called a flower, because it issues in the fruits of eternal life.

Or: “you have put forth shoots again,” by comparison with trees, because they had withered through barrenness and had faded. “You have blossomed anew,” I say, “so as to show that you feel,” with compassionate mercy, what afflicted me, just as you formerly felt it. I say, you feel it “for me,” that is, for my lowly condition, because your compassion benefits me. Recalling this is effective in stirring them up.

But lest they seem to have ceased for some bad reason, he adds: “You were occupied.” As though he said: “Now you have blossomed anew, but before you were occupied,” that is, hindered by certain adversities. Yet when I say that I rejoiced, I do not say it as though because of want—that is, as though I rejoiced in its relief because I was sad in want through the things given. He shows that he rejoices in their work not on his own account, but because of their progress. For in such matters he is accustomed neither to be sad nor to rejoice. Hence he adds: “For I have learned,” that is, I have acquired the habit, “to be sufficient always,” that is, content with the circumstances in which I am, because I know how to be humbled, since I am not broken by it, and how to abound, since I am not exalted by it.

And I have been instructed by God, not by myself, how I ought to conduct myself everywhere—that is, in every place, before rulers or whoever they may be—and in all things, that is, in every kind of circumstance. I have been instructed to be filled, so that fullness does not harm me; to hunger, so that I do not fail; and to endure want, because I am neither saddened by want nor exultant in abundance, knowing that abundance frequently lifts one up, while want patiently borne acquires heavenly riches. “I can do all things,” and so forth. As though he said: “Not only do I know these things, but I can carry them out through the strengthening of him who taught me.” This is what he says: “I can do all things in him,” that is, through his help, “who strengthens me,” that is, in Christ, who grants me ability.

“Nevertheless”: as though he said, “I do not rejoice in the things given, without which I could do.” [Note: Col. 0256D. The same, in the *Confessions*.] “Nevertheless, you did well,” as far as concerns yourselves; in whatever is just, you act justly, “by sharing your goods with my tribulation.” This is why he rejoices, this is why he is nourished: because they did well, not because his distress was relieved.

### Verses 15–20

> “But you also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the account of giving and receiving except you alone; for even to Thessalonica you sent for my needs once and twice. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the abundant fruit to your account. But I have all things and abound. I have been filled with what was received from Epaphroditus, which you sent as an odor of sweetness, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God. And may my God fulfil your every desire according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. But to God, even our Father, be glory for ages of ages. Amen. Greet every saint in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, but especially those from Caesar’s household. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

“But you know”: you shared with me, but others did not. This is what he says: “You also know, Philippians, that at the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed into Macedonia, no church shared temporal goods with me except you alone.”

[Ambrose.] He recalls this so that they may apply themselves still more to works of this kind, as though worthy of praise. I say, no church shared “in the account of giving and receiving,” so that it might reasonably consider that those who received spiritual things ought to give material things, except you alone. And you did not merely share with me when I preached to you; even at Thessalonica you sent me necessities once and twice for my use, beyond which nothing is to be sought.

“Not that”: as though he said, “I say that you did well, not so that I may be filled, but so that you may not be empty.” [Note: Col. 0257C. Augustine, *On Pastors*.] And this is what he says: “I do not say this because I seek a gift,” that is, that I may be supplied with given things, “but I seek fruit,” that is, a good and right will joined to good action. For he does not rejoice so much that his own necessity has been relieved as he congratulates them on their fruitfulness.

[Note: Col. 0258C. The same, in the *Confessions*.] Distinguish between a gift and fruit. The gift is the thing itself which is given, such as a coin, drink, food, and the like. But fruit is the good work and the giver’s right intention. Thus the Lord in the Gospel does not say simply, “He who receives a righteous man or a prophet,” but adds, “in the name of a righteous man or prophet” (Matt. 10). To receive a prophet or righteous person is the gift in the name of a righteous man or prophet; to do this is the fruit.

A raven and a widow are recorded as having fed Elijah. Yet through the raven he was fed by a gift, not in the name of a righteous man; through the widow, by fruit, for she knew that she was feeding a man of God and fed him for that reason. Therefore I do not seek the gift, but the fruit of the gift, abundant in your account, so that your account may have the grace of the Holy Spirit in return for the work of mercy. He says “abundant,” indeed, because this is a good from which good things proceed.

Or thus: “I seek abundant fruit in your account,” that is, so that the fruit of your righteousness may be abundant when you render an account to God for your deeds. “But I have”: as though he said, “I do not seek a gift; nevertheless I have all that you sent, and I abound—not merely in one thing while needing another, but I have been filled with the gifts received through Epaphroditus, which you sent to me as an odor of sweetness.” For the things you sent please God like a most sweet fragrance. For it is compared to prayer, which is God’s incense. Hence it is said: “Give alms, and it itself will pray for you to the Lord.”

I say, you sent these things, namely an acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God, because this is the sacrifice by which you are enabled to conquer enemies, and which God received graciously.

[Ambrose.] “But my God”: as though he said, “You have filled me; but may my God fulfil your every desire.” As though he said: “As you have done for me, so may it be done for you.” I say, may he fulfil it according to his riches, that is, according to the measure in which he is rich; and he can give more than anyone deserves. I say, may he fulfil it not in earthly things but in eternal glory, and this in Christ Jesus, through whom are all things. Or thus: may he fulfil that which is in glory, which is in Christ Jesus, that is, in Christ’s glory. For Christ’s glory is to fulfil the desires of his own.

“But to God”: as though he said, “May God fulfil them; therefore let thanks be given to him.” This is what he says: “But to God, even our Father, be glory unto ages of ages. Amen.” “Greet every saint,” I say, every saint in Christ Jesus. As though he said: whatever is holy is so through Christ Jesus. “The brothers who are with me greet you; all the saints greet you, but especially those of Caesar’s household.” “All” indicates that they have a more earnest affection toward them. “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit,” that is, with your reason, so that it may always be sound and abound in spiritual things. Amen.

# On the Epistle to the Colossians

[Col. 0257]

## Argument

[Col. 0257D]

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians, and they too had been forestalled by false apostles. The Apostle himself did not visit them, but corrects them also by letter. For they had heard the word from Archippus, who had also undertaken ministry among them. Therefore the Apostle, now in bonds, writes to them from Ephesus through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

# Chapter One

### Verse 1

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy the brother, to those who are at Colossae, holy and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus: grace to you and peace from God our Father. We give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love which you have for all the saints because of the hope laid up for you in heaven, which you heard in the word of truth of the Gospel, which has come to you just as it is in the whole world, and bears fruit and grows, just as among you, from the day when you heard and knew the grace of God in truth, just as you learned from Epaphras, our most beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus for you. He also made known to us your love in the Spirit.”

“Paul, an apostle”: the Apostle writes this letter to the Colossians. The Colossians are Asians, to whom the Apostle himself did not preach, but rather his disciples Archippus and Epaphras. Archippus had undertaken ministry among them; Epaphras, a native of their city, instructed by the Apostle, had confirmed Archippus’s teaching. Thus, while Archippus preached and Epaphras confirmed his preaching, they learned the grace of Christ.

[Ambrose.] But false apostles came upon them, seeking to overthrow them by preaching carnal observances and attempting to ensnare their simplicity with philosophical disputations. When these men came and preached carnal observances, the Colossians came into doubt as to whom they ought rather to believe. Therefore Paul, whose authority was well known, writes from Ephesus as an arbiter, as it were, to judge which things ought rather to be held. He describes Christ and his benefits, showing how he is sufficient for all things. He wholly rejects carnal matters, so that henceforth they may hold the faith of Christ sincerely.

He also instructs them morally, confirming everything which Archippus and Epaphras had taught. His purpose in this letter, therefore, is to establish the Colossians in the same faith and teaching which they had received from his disciples, and to teach that hope must not be placed in anything besides Christ. His manner of treatment is as follows: according to his customary manner, he begins with a greeting. Having given it, he gives thanks for their good qualities; commending their faith and love, he prays that they may be perfected in Christ, whose benefits and primacy according to each nature he commends. Then, recalling the dignity of his own ministry, he warns them not to depart from Christ by being deceived through philosophy or legal ceremonies. Finally, he gives moral instruction both collectively and separately, according to ages, sexes, and conditions. At the end he warns Archippus to be diligent in the ministry he has undertaken.

Introducing the greeting, he says: “Paul,” a name known to all; “an apostle of Jesus Christ,” a title whose dignity is known to all. He rightly calls himself an Apostle here, because he was Apostle even to those to whom he had preached through his disciples. Here is the authority for what is to be said. I say, an Apostle, not through wrath but through the will of God—which false apostles are not. “And Timothy the brother,” a man of great authority, writes these things to the brothers at Colossae, both holy and faithful, that is, both greater and lesser persons. That they are holy and faithful is in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ’s grace, not through the power of the Law.

And in writing he first gives greeting in this way: “May grace be to you,” that is, forgiveness of sins, “and peace,” peace of mind and reconciliation to God, “from God our Father.” “We give thanks,” and so forth. He shows that what they received is good by giving thanks for them, saying: “We give thanks to God the Father,” for since he is both God and Father, he is able and willing. I say, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom every good thing is supplied to us. We do this, I say, while also always praying for you, that you may grow toward what is better, “having heard.”

Here he shows why he gives thanks. The order is this: we give thanks, having heard that your faith is in Christ Jesus, by which you believe that Christ is God and man; and having heard of the love you have—not idle love, certainly, but love shown by the performance of works arising from it—toward all the saints. And this is not for human praise or earthly profit, but because of hope, that is, the thing hoped for, which does not yet appear but is laid up for you from eternity to be given in heaven.

And as though someone should ask, “How then is so hidden a thing hoped for?” he adds: “Which you heard”—so that you might hold it as certain—“in the word,” which must certainly be held because it is “the word of truth of the Gospel,” that is, both wholly true and good news. Therefore do not seek elsewhere the hope which you first understood. You were not the first to have this Gospel, but it came to you through others, nor do you alone possess it. Hence he adds, “Just as,” and so forth. As though he said: “It came to you purely and truly, just as it came through me and others into the whole world, and still remains in the whole world.” As though he said: “You have not been treated less favorably than other churches.”

And since the Gospel is in the world, it bears fruit there, that is, it makes people bear fruit through good works; and it grows, that is, it causes growth in increase of knowledge and in the number of believers. It does not do this because others possess more than you; rather, it does this among you in the same way, and therefore you ought to add nothing. It has been in you from the day on which you first heard through Archippus by believing, and knew by discerning. As though he said: “You did not hear and know it through newcomers, namely the false teachers, but through the first teachers, namely Archippus and Epaphras.” What did you hear? Namely, “the grace of God in truth,” that is, that it is wholly and truly from God.

“Just as,” and so forth: as though he said, “Thus from the first day you heard the truth from Archippus, just as you later learned from Epaphras that it was truth,” Epaphras confirming Archippus’s preaching, “so that in the mouth of two or three,” and so forth (Deut. 19). I say, Epaphras is our most beloved fellow-servant, because he is a preacher with us. He is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus, that is, one chosen by Christ; or one who ministers Christ’s gifts, or offers to Christ the sacrifice of your good works. And this is not for your possessions but for you, that is, for your salvation; because desiring your salvation, he began to assist Archippus. He also made known to us that your love, toward God and neighbor, is grounded in the Spirit, not in the flesh, because you love for spiritual rather than carnal things.

### Verses 9–12

> “Therefore we also, from the day on which we heard, do not cease praying and asking for you that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God, strengthened in every power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering with joy, giving thanks to God the Father, who made us worthy for a share in the lot of the saints in light.”

“Therefore we also”: above he said that he prays for them. Here he shows what he prays. As though he said: “Because you are such people, therefore we also, from the day on which we heard this about you, do not cease praying and asking for you,” as it were through the merits which we offer for you, “that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will,” that is, that you may know fully what God wills and what he does not will. He sets this out in parts: namely, that you may be filled with all wisdom concerning the matters of the active life, and spiritual understanding, that is, knowledge of spiritual things belonging to the contemplative life. It is indeed a great thing fully to know what God wills in all matters of the active or contemplative life.

I say, be filled so that afterwards, by doing good works, you may walk well—that is, perform good works—worthily of God, that is, so that you may be worthy of that reward; namely, so that you may walk through every concern of the active and contemplative life, pleasing God, bearing fruit more abundantly in every good work, and through this purity of life growing in the knowledge of God, that is, in knowledge of the Godhead.

[Ambrose.] He desires that the increase of their works should occur together with knowledge, so that they may not be ignorant of the hope of their faith, that is, the thing hoped for in which they believed. For then they will be firm and steadfast if they consider what has been promised for faith.

“In every”: we pray that you may be filled and advance in this way; and after this progress we pray that you may not fall back. I say, you are strengthened by God in every power, that is, in chastity and the rest. I say, strengthened according to the power of his glory, that is, by him who was able to enlighten you. Or thus: strengthened according to the power of his glory, that is, according to the power with which he who is the brightness of the Father—that is, the Son—is well able to strengthen you; or according to the measure in which he has given you clear knowledge.

I say, remaining in all patience against adversities endured, and in long-suffering amid prolonged labor. And this not from sadness or necessity, but with joy, “giving thanks,” and so forth. Thus far he has said why he gives thanks and what he prays for them. Here he begins to show that the Law does not profit but harms, and that Christ is sufficient for every good; they can know this because he and the other apostles, who had been occupied with legal observances, abandoned them and fled to Christ.

As though he said: “We pray for you. I say, you give thanks to God and Father, who alone can restore, because he is God, and wills to do so because he is Father; who also made you Gentiles, just as us Jews, worthy for a share in the lot of the saints,” that is, for participation in the inheritance which is given by lot to saints, that is, by the divine will.

[Note: Col. 0261D. Augustine, on Psalm 30.] For the will of God is a lot in the human race: with him there is no injustice, but he does all things through justice, even though hidden; through this justice eternal inheritance is given to whom he wills. Thus the inheritance itself is called a lot, because it is given to the saints, namely to patriarchs and prophets, not by merits but by divine election; and therefore it must be sought through grace, not through the Law.

[Ambrose.] For through grace he deigned to call and bring the Gentiles into the promise made to the Jews. I say, he made us worthy, and not in the Law but “in light,” that is, through him who is Light from Light, by whose grace they are enlightened—a thing which the Law could not accomplish. Or: he made us worthy by placing us in light, in clear knowledge; whoever departs from this falls into darkness.

### Verses 13–20

> “Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption and forgiveness of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; because in him all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created. Whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers, all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and all things subsist in him. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he may hold the primacy in all things. For in him it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things unto himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.”

“Who delivered us,” and so forth. As though he said: “He made us worthy in this way: in baptism he delivered us—and likewise you—from the power of darkness,” that is, from the ignorance of sins and from demons, who truly held dominion over us. For the devil and his angels had taken captive those predestined for God’s glory; but expelled by our Redeemer, they who formerly ruled inwardly over unbelievers attack believers outwardly, but do not overcome them.

[Note: Col. 0261D. The same, on Psalm 5.] “And he transferred us” from the world “into the kingdom of the Son,” that is, so that we might be the Son’s kingdom. Of it he himself says: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18). He does not say that it is not here, but that it is not from here, because it journeys indeed in the world, but is not of the world. For he says to his kingdom: “You are not of the world” (John 8), “but I chose you out of the world” (John 15). They were of the world when they belonged to the ruler of the world.

[Note: Col. 0262D. The same, on John.] Or thus: he delivered us from the power of darkness, that is, from hell, in which we were held by the devil both through our own sin and through Adam’s offence; and he transferred us into the kingdom when, raising us from the depths of Tartarus, he brought us into heaven with his true Son. For believers whose devotion is firm in mind, when they depart from the world, are led into heaven by the angel of the Father’s right hand.

I say, the Son “of his love,” namely, the Son whom he loves. Thus he will love us through him; without him we shall be hateful.

[Note: Col. 0262D. The same, Book 15 of *The City of God*.] Consider carefully that he says “the Son of his love.” If the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father demonstrates the ineffable communion of both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called Love who is the Spirit common to both? Otherwise, if in that Trinity the Spirit alone is love, then the Son is found to be the Son not of the Father alone but also of the Holy Spirit. For he did not say “the Son of himself,” though if he had said this, he would have said it most truly. But he says “the Son of his love.” Therefore the Son is also the Son of the Holy Spirit, if in that Trinity the love of God is nothing but the Holy Spirit. Since this is utterly absurd, it remains that not only is the Holy Spirit love there, but that he is properly so called for the reasons about which I have sufficiently spoken.

But the phrase “the Son of his love” must be understood as nothing other than his beloved Son, the Son of his substance. For the Father’s love is his nature and substance, as we have often said. Therefore the Son of his love is none other than he who is begotten from his substance.

“In whom we have,” and so forth. As though he said: “He transferred us into the Son’s kingdom, through whom he also redeemed us.” This is what he says: “In whom, in the Son, we Jews have redemption.” Otherwise we would not go to heaven. Redemption is, after the devil’s power has been destroyed, the capacity for freedom, granted to you through the shedding of his blood—the blood of him who had no sin.

[Note: Col. 0263D. Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] Since the devil rightly held those whom, as guilty of sin, he had bound under the condition of death, he was bound to release these through him whom he punished with death without any desert, though he was guilty of no sin. Overcome by this justice and bound by this bond, the strong man was bound. Therefore there is no need for other sacrifices, because through him we have redemption and forgiveness of sins whenever we sin.

And this was fittingly accomplished through him, because he is “the image of God the Father,” that is, fully like the Father and from the Father.

[Note: Col. 0263D. The same, *On the Ten Strings*.] Therefore he is the image of the Father because he is from him and differs from him in nothing. A human being is not an image of God in the same way. For a human being is the image of the Lord by imitation, but not an image such as the Son is. For the image of God is one thing in the Son and another in a human being, just as the image of a king is one thing on a coin and another in his son. We are the coin upon which God’s image is found; Christ is the Son, who is what the Father is. No image of God ought to be worshipped except the one which is what he is; nor should that image be worshipped in place of him, but together with him.

[Note: Col. 0264D. The same, to Januarius.] I say, he is the image of the invisible God, that is, incomprehensible; he did not begin with creation. Rather, he is “the firstborn of every creature,” that is, he alone was begotten before every creature. Other things are creatures; before all these he was begotten. Here he is shown to be coeternal with the Father. And he was truly begotten before every creature, because in him—that is, through him—all things were created. Here he is shown to be co-omnipotent with the Father, and thus in no respect is the Son less than the Father.

I say, all things in heaven and on earth, visible, such as the sun and moon, and invisible, such as angels and souls: whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers. Even these highest things were made through him. Absolutely all things were created through him, including the elements. Hence all things are also in him, that is, by him as their author they live. Or: all things were created through him, and therefore, before they existed, they were life in him. Or thus: all things were created through him and all things are in him, that is, they do not extend beyond him, because he is immeasurable and therefore cannot be outside his substance.

And he is before all not only in eternity and power but also in dignity: no one is equal to him even according to his humanity. As he created all things, so all things subsist in him, who, poured into all things according to divinity, sustains and governs all things. And being such, even according to human nature, he is the head of his body, namely the Church, which is united to Christ as to its head by grace and nature.

When, therefore, he is called the head of the body—that is, of the Church—this means that he stands in relation to the Church as the head does to the body.

[Note: Col. 0264D. The same, *On Christian Warfare*.] For he provides for the Church and governs it, and in him are all the Church’s spiritual senses, as all bodily senses are in the head. For just as the soul animates and makes alive our entire body, but senses through every faculty in the head, and therefore all things are subject to the head for action, while the head is placed above for deliberation, because in a certain manner it bears the role of the soul itself which deliberates for the body—since every sense appears there—so in the whole people of all saints, as though in one body, the man Christ is head. The Wisdom of God illuminates all these, from Abel to the last righteous person; and this Wisdom was more fully in Christ.

For other wise people are wise in one manner, but the man Christ in another. He does not merely possess the benefit of that Wisdom by which all human beings who become wise are made wise; he also bears its person, being full of its truth and grace. Therefore he is the head of all who receive from his fullness. From this it is apparent that the Wisdom of God, that is, the Word, did not assume that man as it assumes others, but far more excellently and sublimely—as it was fitting that this one alone should be assumed, in whom Wisdom might appear to humanity, as it was fitting that Wisdom should visibly be shown.

For it may rightly be said of other wise persons that they have within themselves the Word of God through whom all things were made; but it cannot rightly be said of any of them, “The Word became flesh” (John 1). Therefore the man who was assumed more excellently bears, as head in whom are all the senses, the person of God’s Wisdom, as the head bears the role of the soul which gives life to the entire body.

But since the Church began from Abel, how is the man Christ head of those who lived then? Properly so, because he who is the Church’s beginning according to divinity—that is, its founder—enlightened, through the power of his divinity and the gift of his mercy, all the righteous who are born from Abel to the last righteous person. He can also be called the Church’s beginning according to humanity, because it is founded upon faith in his humanity.

And rightly: he is head and beginning, that is, ruler and founder, because he is “the firstborn from the dead,” the first of the dead to rise into immortality.

[Ambrose.] For as he was born from God before all things in order to create all things, so again, born as man from the Virgin, he was the first to rise, in order to restore what he had created, so that he might always be first and prince. Hence he adds: “So that through this he may hold the primacy,” that is, dominion, “in all things,” both those earlier and those later, because he can raise others.

And he fittingly holds primacy not only because he is firstborn, but also because it pleased the Trinity that all fullness should dwell in him and that all things should be reconciled through him. That is: it pleased the Trinity that in him the fullness of knowledge and virtues should not merely be present but should dwell, and that all things should be reconciled, namely Jews and Gentiles. Observe that fullness is rightly said to be in him and to remain in him, because he can do all things through himself, so that nothing is excluded which cannot be bestowed through him. Hence he says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5). For as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he wills (ibid.); thus he is shown to be perfect God.

I say, all things tending toward him, who is true and eternal light, that is, eternal truth. Or: “to be reconciled in him”—having been offered to God, it pleased him that all things should be reconciled through him. And he is the one “making peace,” that is, he made peace not freely, nor through another sacrifice, but through the blood of his cross, that is, through the death of his cross, which is a more shameful death. I say, he made peace with things in heaven and things on earth, that is, heavenly and earthly things, because entrance into heaven is open to humanity. Or, “things in heaven” means the saints already in heaven, and “things on earth” means the saints still in this life.

### Verses 21–29

> “And you, when you were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unstained and blameless before him, if indeed you remain founded and steadfast in the faith and immovable from the hope of the Gospel which you heard, which has been preached in every creature under heaven, of which I, Paul, have become a minister. I now rejoice in sufferings for you, and in my flesh I fulfil what is lacking of Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body, which is the Church. I have become its minister according to the stewardship of God which was given to me among you, that I might fulfil the word of God: the mystery which was hidden from ages and generations but now has been made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. Him we proclaim, correcting every person and teaching in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ Jesus. For this I labor, striving according to his working, which works in me in power.”

And you, etc. As though he were saying: “And, to speak especially, you also, O Colossians, he made peaceful and reconciled to God, when—that is, although—you were once alienated from God, that is, having nothing in common with God, and enemies by contradicting him. And this in mind, because you thought that you were acting rightly.” Or, according to another reading, it may be read with the same meaning: “When you were once also enemies of his purpose,” that is, of his counsel, because you did not receive what God commanded through Moses, being devoted to your idols [Col. 0265D]—you, I say, living in evil works.

“But now.” As though he were saying: “You were such once; but now,” and in this time of grace, not at another time, “he has reconciled you” by remission of sins, “in the body of his flesh,” that is, of his frailty, that is, in his passible and mortal body. And this was “through his death.” He reconciled you, I say, “to present you,” for this purpose—that is, that he may at last present or bring you before him—holy in virtues, spotless from sins, and so entirely “unreprovable,” because then no evil will be in them. Unreprovable, I say, “before him,” because he sees all things. Or: he may present you before himself, before whom you will then stand, seeing him as he is, face to face [Col. 0266A]; concerning this there must be no distrust. For if, while mortal and dead, he can reconcile, now immortal he can do all things.

“If indeed,” etc. Here he admonishes them to persevere in faith in Christ and in hope. For this reason he had said so much and such great things concerning Christ: that they might place their hope in him alone, in whom are all good things, and might not think that they should subject themselves to any of the elements or angels. For he alone is to be worshipped, and no one is to be regarded as equal to him.

As though he were saying: “He may present you, I say, yet on this condition: if you remain grounded in faith,” that is, firm and not wavering; “and steadfast,” so that you do not depart through yourselves; “and immovable” when another impels you away “from the hope of the Gospel,” that is, if you are steadfast in hope of the reward promised in the Gospel and immovable from it. If they do these things, they will present them to God. Otherwise Christ does not profit them [Col. 0266B]. [Ambrose.] “Which Gospel you ought to hold, because you have heard,” that is, understood it. And it is better first to turn back: it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.

“This Gospel has been preached,” and remains preached, “in every creature under heaven,” that is, among all human beings who are a new creation, wherever they may be. Or thus: it has been preached in every new creature. This does not change. Yet this new creation is now under heaven, still on pilgrimage, but will at length attain glory. “Of which,” namely of preaching the Gospel, “I, Paul, have become a minister.” Thus you may know that it is true: I, now placed at Ephesus in prison for the Gospel, “rejoice in sufferings,” because believers make progress [Col. 0266C]. “Which I endure for you,” that you may be confirmed in the truth of the Gospel, “and fill up what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ.”

He calls his sufferings Christ’s, because our sufferings, who are Christ’s members, are Christ’s. For the head with the body—that is, the Savior with those to be saved—is as one man, one person. Therefore, if you are among Christ’s members, whatever you suffer from those who are not among Christ’s members was lacking to Christ’s sufferings. [Note: [Col. 0265D] Augustine, on Psalm 61.] It is added, “because it was lacking”: filling up the measure, not overflowing it. You suffer only as much as had to be contributed from your sufferings to the whole suffering of Christ, who suffered in our head and suffers in his members.

Whoever, in this commonwealth, as it were, which belongs to us all, pays according to his measure what he owes, and contributes, according to the possession of our strength, as it were the due quota of sufferings—our complete payment of sufferings will not be made until the world has ended [Col. 0266D].

Or, “what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ” means either those sufferings which Christ endured or those which he commanded me to endure. “What still remains lacking I fill up,” that is, I am ready to suffer. And this I do not in another’s flesh but in my own flesh. Or: what is lacking is not in Christ’s own flesh, but in mine. And I suffer these things “for his body,” increasing it, “which is the Church.” As though he were saying: “I speak of no other body than that which is the Church, whose minister I have become,” that I may minister spiritual things to it.

A minister, I say, “according to the dispensation of God which was given to me among you,” that is [Col. 0267A], I was made a minister for this purpose: that I might at last administer in deed among you, through the grace of the apostolate entrusted to me by God. Or thus: “I became a minister of this Gospel according to the dispensation of God,” that is, according to the grace of the apostolate dispensed to me by God, “which was given to me among you.” For what has been preached to you by my disciples is as much as if it had been preached by me myself.

He says that God through Christ made him a minister of the Gospel among the Gentiles. But for what purpose? He shows: namely, that the mystery undertaken by God may be fulfilled through suitable service—a mystery which had been unknown from ages past: namely, the mystery of birth from God, birth from Mary, the salvation of the Gentiles, and the whole work of Christ. Hence he adds, “that it may be fulfilled.” As though he were saying: “The dispensation was given to me for this purpose, that it may be fulfilled.” And I shall show it fulfilled: “the word,” that is, God’s disposition or ordinance, namely what God preordained concerning you Gentiles—that you should be saved through Christ’s incarnation. He says this lest salvation appear not to have been promised to the Gentiles.

This word is a “mystery,” that is, something hidden. [Note: [Col. 0267D] Augustine, in the *Confessions*.] For although it was known that “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), nowhere was it read: “The Word was made flesh,” etc. (ibid.). These things concern the sacrament, or mystery, of the incarnation. Hence: “You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). “For I have seen certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin, and there I read, not indeed in these words, but with many and manifold arguments altogether persuaded, that in the beginning was the Word and the Word was with God; but that the Word was made flesh, I did not read. Indeed, I investigated in those books the various assertions that the Son is in the form of the Father; but that he emptied himself is not found in them.”

Rightly, therefore, is that Word called a mystery, that is, something hidden: “which was hidden from the ages,” that is, from the beginning of the ages, and was hidden from all generations, not merely from some part of them, except those to whom he revealed it through the Holy Spirit. “But now,” that is, in the time of grace, it has been manifested, not to all, but to his saints, the humble little ones. Nor did it become fully known even to all these, but only to those to whom God willed, from grace alone, “to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery”: that is, the abundant glory of so worthy a mystery, in which there are many things—faith, remission, righteousness [Col. 0267D], gifts of the Holy Spirit, and future blessedness. Therefore he says “riches,” namely, of the mystery existing “among the Gentiles”: which mystery is “Christ in you,” Gentiles; that is, that mystery is Christ’s incarnation, through which the Gentiles are saved. It is thus in you that he may be “the hope of glory,” that is, that through him you may hope for glory without the Law.

“We proclaim him,” that is, such a Christ as saves the Gentiles without the Law. We apostles, I say, are “correcting,” that is, rebuking, not you alone but every person who departs from the truth which he knows; and “teaching every person,” namely those who are ignorant of the truth. Or: we rebuke and convict those who contradict, and teach those who obey. Teaching, I say, “in all wisdom” [Col. 0268A]: we are not blind like the pseudo-teachers, but teach in all wisdom. True wisdom is in the Lord’s teaching, namely when Christ is acknowledged. The Apostle testifies that he does this with great diligence, so that, by instructing a person in this wisdom, he may present that person complete to God.

Therefore he adds: “That we may present,” that is, offer to God as a sacrifice, “every person,” both Jew and Gentile, “perfect,” not in the Law but “in Christ Jesus,” that is, in understanding Christ’s mystery. “In which,” that is, in this matter—namely, that everyone may be perfect in Christ—“I labor, striving” against the rebellious, “according to his working, which works in me with power,” namely the power of miracles. That is: I strive surely against the faithless, being aided by signs of power, through which the life of unbelief is restrained, so that those who contradict by words may yield to power. As though he were saying: God joins miracles to my labor in order to confirm it.

## Chapter II

### Verses 1–3
