> “For I want you to know what great solicitude I have for you, and for those who are at Laodicea, and for all who have not seen my face in the flesh: that their hearts may be comforted, being instructed in charity, and unto all the riches of the fulness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ Jesus, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

“For I want.” As though he were saying: “I report this about myself to you because I want you to know what solicitude I have [Col. 0268C] for you, so that, once you understand it, you may seek to be made perfect in Christ.” And he rightly says “for you.” For he was no less solicitous for those whom he had not seen than for those to whom he preached in person; nor did he love with less affection those whom he had not seen than the others among whom he was present.

And not only for you, but also “for those who are at Laodicea,” because they too had been forestalled by pseudo-apostles; and for those near you, whoever have not seen my face in the flesh, even if they have heard the teaching. And to this end I strive: that they, together with you, may comfort their hearts. They, I say, “instructed in charity,” namely in the charity which God had toward us, who delivered up his Son for us. Whoever considers this can console himself in this misery, because he perceives that, pride having been trampled down through humility, one can return to the homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0268D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*] For pride is the cause of all vices. To convict and remove it, such a remedy came down from heaven: God descended in humility through mercy to human beings exalted through pride, commending clear and manifest grace in that very human being whom he took up with such great charity above his fellows. He did not bring it about by antecedent merits of his own will that he should be so united to the Word of God that, by that very union, he became one Son of God and the same one Son of man. For he had to be one; there would be many if this could occur, not through God’s proper gift but through human free choice. This, then, is especially commended to us for humility [Col. 0269A].

“And instructed in the knowledge of God.” Instructed, I say, by striving through this “unto all the riches of the fulness of understanding,” that is, unto all the abundance of complete understanding, so that they may have a perfect understanding of divine and human things, of the soul and of the heavenly spirits. Otherwise no one ascends to knowledge of God. Therefore he says “riches,” that they may have full understanding concerning all things.

I say, instructed “in the knowledge of God,” not with respect to works, but “in the knowledge of the mystery of God,” so that you may know what is secret and known by few concerning God’s essence—the God, I say, who is the Father of Christ Jesus—so that you may know that the Father is a different person from the Son, although he is one and the same in substance with him. If you seek this knowledge, have recourse to Christ alone, for he is the one “in whom are all treasures,” that is, all abundance, “of wisdom,” concerning divine things, “and of knowledge,” concerning human things. Yet they are hidden. Therefore do not wonder if you are in Christ and have not yet found them, for they are not open to all, but only to those who ask and knock.

Or, without changing the rest, that passage may be read thus: “May their hearts be comforted,” I say, “being instructed in charity and in all riches”—another reading: “full”—“of understanding.” For what purpose? To know Christ, because it is in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0269D] Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] Another reading, that is: “The Word was made flesh,” through which the proud are redeemed by being humbled. “And when I read, ‘The Word was made flesh’ (John 1), in ‘the Word’ I understand the true Son of God; in ‘flesh’ I acknowledge the true Son of man; and I acknowledge both together—God and man—as one person joined by the lavishness of ineffable grace.” [Note: [Col. 0270D] Augustine, *On the Assumed Man.*] Therefore “the Word was made flesh,” which is Christ Jesus [Col. 0269C], and he possesses the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Hence he adds: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.”

These two differ from one another in this way: wisdom is understood as concerning divine things, knowledge as concerning human things. I acknowledge both in Christ: wisdom in him inasmuch as he is the Word with God, and knowledge in him inasmuch as he is human with us. For all that the Word made flesh did and suffered temporally for us belongs to knowledge. But that he is the Word without time and place, coeternal with the Father and wholly everywhere, belongs to wisdom. Therefore Christ is our knowledge; the same Christ is our wisdom. Hence: “Full of grace and truth” (ibid.).

Or, the whole may be read according to another text, which is: “That their hearts may receive consolation, when they have been instructed in charity unto all the riches of the fulness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ Jesus. In whom,” etc. The Apostle wishes to foster their minds in charity and make them ready, through the Epistle, to receive knowledge of the mystery of God, recognizing in Christ the riches of wisdom and knowledge, if Christ is acknowledged as to be worshipped in the fullness of his divinity.

The order is this: “I strive to this end, that their hearts may receive consolation”; this will happen when they have been instructed in love of God and neighbor, and when they have been instructed unto the knowledge of the mystery of God [Col. 0270A] in Christ—that is, unto knowledge of Christ, in whom is every mystery. For every mystery of God’s sacrament is in Christ, so that whoever knows him seems also to possess knowledge of all things. Therefore he adds: “I say, they are striving through this unto all the riches of the fulness of understanding.” For the riches of wisdom and knowledge are found if Christ is acknowledged, because the power of every strength is in him. For all receive from him; hence he is called the head of all, so that all appear to subsist through him.

Hence it is rightly added: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” For every principle of knowledge concerning the whole heavenly or earthly creation is in him who is head and author of all heavenly and earthly things. Therefore whoever knows him should seek nothing further, neither wisdom nor power [Col. 0270B], because he has recognized him in whom are perfect power and perfect wisdom. Whatever is sought elsewhere is found here perfectly.

For what was wiser than Solomon, or more prudent than Daniel? God gave them wisdom above the rest for this reason: that in Daniel and Solomon he might show unbelievers that he is the author of all wisdom. Unbelievers do not think this, because they do not read astronomy, geometry, and such things in the Gospels and prophets. These matters have therefore been despised by our people because they contribute nothing to salvation, but rather lead into error and draw away from God, so that while people study these reasonings of disputations, they do not attend to the care of their souls. But whoever knows Christ has found the treasure of wisdom and knowledge, because he knows what is useful.

[Col. 0270C] ### Verses 4, 8

> “Now this I say, that no one may deceive you by loftiness of speech. For although I am absent in body, yet in spirit I am with you, rejoicing and seeing your order and the firmness of your faith which is in Christ. Therefore, as you have received Jesus Christ our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and confirmed in the faith as you have also learned, abounding in him with thanksgiving. See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.”

“Now this,” etc. Having commended the dignity of his mystery [Col. 0270D], he warns them lest evil conversation and the cunning of iniquity cause their minds to depart from Christ. As though he were saying: “I want you to be instructed. But I say this so that you may not only strive after what you do not yet possess, but that no one, however wise, may deceive you by what appears to be loftiness.” Such subtlety or loftiness, however, is only “of speech,” that is, only in words. For the wise of this world eagerly strive, through a certain art and the minutiae of disputes, to entangle the souls of the simple, in order to draw them away from the hope which is in Christ by the tradition of worldly things.

“For although,” as though he were saying: “Let no one deceive you—and rightly so, for I see in spirit what is being done among you.” [Ambrose.] This is what he means when he says, “For although I am absent from you in body, nevertheless I am with you in spirit,” just as the spirit of Elisha was with Gehazi when he went on the road to Naaman the Syrian in order to receive, in Elisha’s name, things which Elisha had not commanded. How much more could the Apostle see in spirit the things which he mentioned! For there was greater grace in the apostles than in the prophets. Therefore he says, “I am with you in spirit.” For it is given to saints to see distant things in spirit. Therefore let those beware whose actions are not concealed from their teacher.

“I am with you,” I say, “rejoicing and seeing,” that is, because I see “your order,” namely that each of you lives according to his proper order; and seeing the “firmness,” that is, the stability, of your faith which is in Christ, not in the Law. By this he makes them more ready for the Gospel, because he says that he rejoices in the ordered character of their conduct and in the stability of their faith, so that, knowing how God is pleased, they may become firmer in it.

And since you stand well, therefore, as you received Jesus Christ our Lord as the foundation of faith—for your reception was good—so walk: that is, make progress not apart from him but in him. You lesser persons, I say, are “rooted” in the active life, as trees are for bearing fruit; and you greater persons, who are in contemplation, are “built up” above the others, and this “in him,” that is, in the temple of God. Hence, addressing others, as it were: “Walk in the action of giving thanks, confirmed in faith.” Walk, I say, as you have also learned, that is, as you received it—not otherwise—and as you have learned it by knowledge, and you have matter for thanksgiving [Col. 0271B].

You, I say, “abounding” in gifts “in him,” who alone gives increase. And in this walk, see that no one deceives you through earthly philosophy [Ambrose], by which those who desire to be judged prudent in the world are commonly led astray. Adding the same meaning, he says, “through empty deceit.” For earthly philosophy is composed of cleverness and subtle minutiae, and deceives while, through plausible arguments and fabricated matters, its adherents judge nothing so true as what is seen and understood in the elements. This earthly philosophy is “according to the tradition of men” [Note: [Col. 0271D] Augustine, in a certain sermon.], who act according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ—in some respect; that is, it is not ordained by God but handed down by human beings.

For the philosophers, whom he calls “men” [Col. 0271D], handed down that God cannot become a creature; that a human being cannot be born from a virgin; or that one who has died cannot live again. They consider the elements, that is, these visible creatures, in which animals are generated by the mixture of seed, and in which what dies does not live again. Therefore he warns them to avoid this tradition as empty and deceptive. He calls philosophy that which is not ordained by God but arises from the weakness of human reasoning, which confines God’s power within its own awareness, believing that God neither acts nor can act otherwise than carnal reasoning suggests. This must altogether be avoided, because it worships the world rather than God and draws people away from Christ, in whom is the fullness of divinity, because he possesses all that the Father possesses.

Or, when he says “according to the elements,” he touches those who expound idols as though more wisely, saying: “Juno is air; Neptune is sea.” Therefore, after saying “according to philosophy and empty deceit,” he adds “according to the elements of the world,” as though warning that one must beware not merely of any idolaters whatever, but of the apparently more learned interpreters of symbols.

Or, he calls “deceit” what pseudo-preachers say about the Law, and it is called empty because there is no benefit in this falsehood, though there is sometimes benefit in false things. He calls “philosophy” the things by which they seek to prove what they assert. The meaning is: “See that no one deceive you by drawing you to observances of the Law through ‘prophecy,’” that is, through arguments devised for proving or disproving what is said concerning the Law; “and through empty deceit,” namely through that which is proved. Let no one deceive you, I say, acting “according to the traditions of men,” that is, legal observances. For after the truth has been manifested [Col. 0272B], the Law is not a tradition of God but of human beings; and acting “according to the elements of the world,” that is, according to the literal sense, which belongs to worldly things and not to Christ.

### Verses 9–14

> “For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily; and you are filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In whom you have also been circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh, but in the circumcision of Christ; buried with him in baptism, in whom you have also risen through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And you, when you were dead in sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him, forgiving you all sins, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us and contrary to us.”

“For in him,” Christ, “dwells all the fullness of divinity,” that is, all fullness in every respect, so that it is united to him even personally, which is not the case in any creature. [Note: [Col. 0271D] Augustine, *To Dardanus.*] God is indeed present everywhere and wholly present everywhere; nevertheless, he does not dwell everywhere, but only in his temple. Dwelling there, he is possessed more by some, less by others; but of our head alone it is said that “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity,” and this “bodily.”

He does not say this because God is corporeal [Col. 0272D], but uses a transferred term because in the temple made with hands of old he dwelt not bodily but shadowily, that is, by signs prefiguring him. But all those observances were shadows of things to come. [Note: [Col. 0272D] Augustine, *On Genesis.*] Thus he said “bodily” not because divinity is a body, but in comparison with the legal shadows: that is, completely, because all things are fulfilled in him, so that in some manner he is the body and fulfillment of the shadows of the Law—that is, he himself is the truth of those signs.

Therefore, just as the figures themselves were called “shadows” metaphorically, not literally, so, when he says that the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ, he uses a transferred term. Whoever therefore says that carnal observances are necessary says that Christ is not the body of the shadows and that God is not sufficient for all things [Col. 0273A].

Or certainly he says “bodily” because God dwells, as in a temple, in Christ’s body which he took from the Virgin. [Note: [Col. 0273D] Augustine, *To Dardanus.*] What, then, is the difference between the head and the other members, which are also his temple? In our head all the fullness of divinity dwells, so that he is full of every grace; but he does not dwell in the saints in the same manner. For in our body sensation is present in every member, but not to the same degree as in the head. In the head are hearing, sight, smell, taste, and touch; but in the other members there is touch alone. So all the fullness of divinity dwells in Christ because he is the head, in whom are the senses; but in the saints there is, as it were, touch alone, to whom the Spirit is given “by measure.”

Further, there is another thing which plainly distinguishes that head from the excellence of any member: by a certain unique assumption of humanity, that human being was made one person with the Word. For it could not be said, cannot be said, and never will be said of any saint: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1). No saint received the name of the Only-begotten by any presence of grace whatsoever (ibid.). Thus that which the Word himself is before the ages could be said also of him together with the assumed human being. And the total meaning of this is: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily,” that is, truly and solidly.

“And you are.” As though he were saying: “In him the fullness of divinity dwells. And in him, who is so full, you are filled,” with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are not the elements [Col. 0273C]. For the Holy Spirit dwells in believers; this could not be granted to the elements, because it was unfitting that the invisible and incorporeal should dwell in a visible and invisible substance. Therefore let worshippers of the elements hear, come, and believe in Christ, that they may become greater than those whom they now worship.

Therefore he says: “You are filled in him,” you who believe that all fullness dwells in Christ; those who deny this are against Christ. And this Christ is the head not only of human beings but also of angelic principality and power. Therefore he can fill you, who fills the heavenly citizens.

“In whom.” He warned them not to depart from Christ through philosophy; now he warns them not, deceived by pseudo-apostles, to receive the ceremonies of the Law. As though he were saying: “You are filled in him, in whom you have not only been filled with gifts, but have also been circumcised,” that is, cleansed from error and from the world. Circumcised, I say, “with a circumcision not made by hands,” that is, not by a human work. You, I say, remain “in the stripping off of the body of flesh,” that is, stripped of the body insofar as it was flesh—subject to flesh and serving fleshly desires—but now, insofar as it is spiritual, serving the spirit. That is, you serve in the spirit and not in the flesh, converted from earthly things to heavenly, from human things to divine, and from error to divinity.

Or thus: “You have been circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands,” unlike legal circumcision, namely one not made “in the stripping off of the skin”—another reading, “of the flesh”—because there, namely in carnal circumcision, nothing happens except that the skin is removed. Our reading may be understood in the same sense: “not made by hands, in the stripping off of the body of flesh,” that is, of the body which is flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0274D] Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] He did not, therefore, intend two things to be understood, as though flesh were one thing and the body of flesh another; rather, “body” is the name of many things, none of which is flesh, since not every body is flesh. You have not, I say, been circumcised with such a circumcision, but “in the circumcision of Jesus Christ,” that is, in spiritual circumcision, where all vices are cut away, because Christ alone accomplishes this.

“Buried.” Likewise, you have obtained this in Christ because you “were buried in baptism,” that is, baptized in likeness of his burial, so that you may no longer appear to be what you were—old sinners—but new righteous persons; just as Christ, placed in the tomb, was not seen [Col. 0274B]. “In whom,” namely in Christ, “you have also risen,” by walking in newness of life. And this is not through anything else but “through faith in the working of God,” that is, which God works in them. Or, “through faith in the working of God,” that is, through faith in God, concerning whom they believe that, after Christ’s example, he will raise them.

Hence he adds: “Who raised him,” that is, Christ, “from the dead.” He states this first in order to prove that they too will rise immortal. Hence he adds: “And through this you Gentiles also, now in the certainty of hope, he made alive together with him,” that is, made alive in body and soul with Christ, in likeness of him. He made you alive together with him, I say, “when,” that is, although formerly, “you were dead in sins,” not perceiving your evils. He calls “sins” the abandoning of the law of nature.

And you were dead “in the uncircumcision of your flesh,” that is, in original sin, which the uncircumcision signifies. Or, he calls fleshly sins “uncircumcision,” using the sign for what it signifies: that is, fleshly sins from which we must be stripped. [Augustine.] He made the dead alive, I say, freely “forgiving you all sins,” both original and added sins; this is a sign that he will also take away punishment. And he forgave not only you Gentiles your sins, but also remitted to us Jews the transgression which came through the Law.

This is what is meant by: “He himself blotting out the handwriting of the decree,” namely of the Law—that is, the record of transgression arising from the decree, namely the Law. This handwriting “was against us,” for both our conscience and the devil, in order to accuse us, remembered that transgression [Col. 0274D]; and thus that remembrance was against us, harming and tormenting us. But when this too is washed and blotted out in baptism, neither does our conscience fear nor has the devil anything to object. And not only was the handwriting of the decree against us; the decree itself, that is, the old Law, was also against us. Hence he adds “which was.” As though he were saying: “I mean the handwriting of the decree, which decree itself—that is, the Law—was contrary to us, because it did not help but made us more guilty.”

### Verses 14–17

> “And he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross; and stripping principalities and powers, he led them openly in triumph with confidence, triumphing over them in himself. Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival day, or new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ’s.”

And he took this handwriting, or decree, “out of the midst of all,” that is, out of what is common, so that no believer might fear the handwriting or continue to observe the Law. He took it away, I say, fastening that decree to the cross, so that it may now cease, since all the carnal sacrifices of the Law have been fulfilled in the offering of the true Lamb. Who then restores it? As though he were saying: no one ought to restore it.

And as he freed us from the Law and from transgression of the Law, so too he freed the ancient fathers from hell, lest anyone think that they were saved through the Law. This is what follows: “And he himself, stripping principalities,” namely infernal ones, “and powers,” by taking away Abraham, Isaac, and the other righteous persons, “led them away,” his own—that is, he brought them far from this kingdom to heaven. He did so first “with confidence,” that is, with great trust and hope of victory, as God-man without sin, “triumphing,” that is, overcoming them on the cross, namely the infernal princes; and this was not hidden but open. For if anyone considers the perfection of the Church, the ancient enemy is plainly seen to have been defeated. “Triumphing,” I say, in himself offered, not by another sacrifice.

[Note: [Col. 0275D] Augustine, *On the Trinity.*] For by his death, offered for us as the one truest sacrifice, he extinguished every sin on account of which principalities and powers justly held us for punishments to be paid [Col. 0275C]. Therefore, from the very source from which the devil outwardly received power to kill the Lord’s flesh, his inward power by which he held us was slain.

Or thus, from the passage “blotting out,” etc.: as though he were saying, “He forgave you Gentiles all sins; he himself, I say, blotting out also the handwriting of the decree which was against us.” It was God’s decree which he commanded to Adam: “From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Gen. 2). God blotted out the handwriting of this violated decree—that is, its record—when he washed away the first parent’s sin by blood. That record was contrary to us, but he took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross.

Or, he calls Adam’s sin the handwriting which the devil held, as it were, as a bond against us. The decree is the sentence adverse to all human beings, namely that in which it was said: “You shall die by death” (ibid.). But the Lord took away that handwriting. This is what is meant by: “He forgave us all sins.” He himself, I say, “blotting out the handwriting which was contrary to us,” that is, Adam’s sin, of which we were guilty. The handwriting, I say, “of the decree which was contrary to us,” that is, concerning which a sentence contrary to all human beings was pronounced. And he took that handwriting out of the way, fastening it to the cross—not merely other things. Unless he removed this and the other things, we should not be freed from death or hell.

When the innocent one is killed, sin is crucified, that is, put to death. For the cross is not the Savior’s death but sin’s. For when the innocent one is killed, he makes guilty those by whom he is killed; but he kills the sin of the human race, through which he also strips principalities and powers. Hence he adds: “And stripping principalities and powers” of the souls which they held captive—he stripped them of these by washing away those souls’ sins—“he led away principalities and powers,” that is, he expelled them from the Church, so that they could no longer harm the faithful as before.

He did this, I say, after the triumph of the cross, confidently and openly, namely descending to hell with angelic legions. And “triumphing,” that is, conquering, those infernal princes “in himself,” that is, by the presence of his majesty. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Augustine, *Against Faustus.*]

Or according to another reading: “Stripping himself of flesh, he made a public example of principalities and powers, confidently triumphing over them in himself” [Col. 0276B]. By “flesh” in this place mortality is understood, according to the saying, “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15). Through this mortality the powers hostile to us exercised dominion.

By this mortality, therefore, Christ, stripping himself of it in the resurrection, is said to have displayed the diabolical powers that ruled through this mortality, because in himself, our head, he furnished an example which he embraces in the final resurrection in his whole body—that is, in the Church, which is to be liberated from the devil’s power. [Note: [Col. 0275D] Id., *On the Christian Conflict*.] The invisible powers hostile to us are likewise conquered in us where invisible desires are conquered. For when blood without guilt was shed, the written bonds of all sins were erased, by which those who believe in him had formerly been held debtors by the devil. [Col. 0276C] [Note: [Col. 0276D] Id., *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Hence: “Which shall be shed for many.” And because all these things have been granted to us in Christ, therefore henceforth let no one judge you—that is, render you liable to condemnation—in food or drink, whether taken or not taken according to the Jewish rite; or with respect to a part of a feast-day, when it is not celebrated although the Law commands its celebration. That is, let no one condemn you because you observe no part of a feast-day—for example, a new moon or Sabbaths. All these things are a shadow of things to come: that is, certain signs dependent upon the reality, which were then performed as figures of future things. It was then sinful not to observe what was commanded, and one single unobserved command then brought condemnation. [Note: [Col. 0276D] Id., *Against Faustus*.] But now it is not sinful, because then they were commandments, but now they are testimonies. For that was the time for signifying; [Col. 0276D] this is the time for making manifest. Therefore Scripture itself, which then exacted the performance of significant acts, is now a witness to the things signified; and what was then observed for the purpose of foretelling is now recited for confirmation. Thus not eating unleavened bread for the appointed seven days was a sin at that time; but at this time it is not a sin; and so with the rest. For then these were commandments; now they are testimonies and confirmation of the truth. All these things were a shadow. But the body—that is, the truth—of this shadow is Christ’s: that is, it pertains to Christ, because it was fulfilled through him. Or, all these things are Christ’s body: that is, they signify the body [Col. 0277A] of Christ, either that which he took from the Virgin or that which is the Church. And because they are a shadow—

**Verses 18–23.**—“Let no one seduce you, delighting in humility and the worship of angels—things which he has not seen—walking vainly, puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast the head, from which the whole body, supplied and knit together through joints and ligaments, grows with the growth of God. If, therefore, you have died with Christ from the elements of this world, why, as though living in the world, do you decree: ‘Do not touch; do not taste; do not handle’—things which all perish in the very using—according to the commandments and teachings of men, which indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, [Col. 0277B] not in any honor toward the satisfying of the flesh.”

“Let no one seduce you, delighting”: that is, loving to persuade you of things which he has not seen—that is, which he has not understood—namely, the ceremonies of the Law, whose rationale he does not know. Let him not seduce you, I say, by humility and the worship of angels, because they seem like messengers of God by the appearance and lowliness of their religion. These are the means by which people may easily be seduced. And he who does this walks in vain, because whatever he does he loses, since he is without Christ as guide. He is, I say, puffed up—that is, proud—by the mind not of reason but of his flesh, that is, of sensuality; for he understands nothing except what sensuality grasps. This ought to be a cause for shame, not for pride. And he does not hold Christ, the head, full of truth and grace [Col. 0277C] of all the Scriptures, against whom those who preach the Law speak.

From this head—that is, by receiving from whose fullness—the whole body, that is, the Church, is supplied and built up through the ligaments of charity and through the joints of faith, hope, and works, in which believers are joined together and made alike. Distinguish, and assign each thing to its proper term: it is built together into one through the joints, namely because they believe the same things and do the same things; and it is supplied, in mutual service, through the ligaments—that is, through charity, without which the members neither cohere nor serve one another nor live. And thus it grows in virtues and in members. And this is “with the growth of God,” that is, to the measure God has provided. [Ambrose] Or he says, “with the growth of God,” because God is, as it were, increased when people return from error, just as he was diminished when they deserted him. For those who had deserted God through error diminished the abundance of his riches by denying that they belonged to him. But when they return, they bring increase to God, because they are gained from among the lost. [Col. 0277D]

“If therefore,” or “but.” Thus far he has warned those standing firm not to be seduced by false teachers; now he addresses those who observed some things from the Law, dissuading them from the Law in the form of rebuke. It is as though he said: You who stand firm, see that you are not seduced; but you others who have adopted legal observances, tell me: why do you keep the Law? This is what he says: “If you have died”—not by a miserable death, but by a blessed death—“from the elements of the world,” that is, separated from the Law, which is an institution for children who seek worldly things; died, I say, because you are with Christ—why, now that the truth is known and received, do you still, as though living [Col. 0278A] in the world—that is, like Jews who live for the world and not for God—make decrees that legal observances must be kept? You decree, I say, when some say to others: “Do not touch,” and so forth.

Or it may be understood thus: “If therefore.” By “elements” he means the creatures of this world. It is as though he said: Because Christ has erased all offences, therefore, because you are with Christ—that is, because you have received faith in Christ—you have died, that is, have been wholly separated from sin and from the elements of the world, that is, from every superstition and abstinence regarding the creatures of the world.

Or “with Christ” may be understood as “like Christ,” so that the sense is: “If,” he says, “you have died from sin and from the elements with Christ, that is, like Christ, why do you still, as though living for the world, decree that some things must superstitiously be abstained from?” For if formerly, while you were ignorant, you did this, why do you do the same now that [Col. 0278B] the truth has been proclaimed? [Ambrose.] You decree, I say, by saying: “Do not touch these things,” such as a corpse or the place where a menstruating woman has sat; “do not taste,” such as pork or fish without scales; “do not handle,” with a certain studied attention and delight. It is as though he said: You ought not to decree these things. All such things lead to destruction—that is, they lead to death—in their very use: that is, if anyone uses them in a Jewish manner, abstaining from some and using others while believing that he is justified by this. I mean these things now existing according to the commandments and teachings of men, not of God. For after Truth came, God no longer commands these observances to be kept; rather, the Pharisees command them by authority and teach them with arguments.

They are therefore not said to lead to [Col. 0278C] destruction because it is true that they are evil insofar as they were commanded by God; rather, their use and observance destroys because, now that truth has been displayed, they are commandments and teachings of men, not of God. These things have a certain rationale—that is, an appearance of wisdom—because they put forward superstition and humility. Hence he adds, “in superstition.” It is as though he said: They have an appearance of wisdom because they are in superstition—that is, in religion carried beyond measure—and because they are in humility, since those who observe them present themselves as humble. And because they are “not for sparing the body,” since they say that they do not spare the body; and they are “not in any honor,” since they say that they do not care for human honor; and because they are “not for satisfying the flesh,” since they deny themselves many things and call others gluttonous. [Jerome.] [Col. 0278D]

Or thus: “which indeed have an appearance of wisdom.” These legal observances have the appearance of wisdom, not in truth but in superstition—that is, in an excessive falsehood where there is no benefit—namely through worldly wisdom. And they are “in humility,” not that humility which is a virtue, but, as is understood from the Greek, because the mind thinks low things, that is, base and earthly things: that is, they are in the soul’s affection. And they are “not for sparing the body,” because even in those observances there is much labor, which is vain. And they are not “in any honor,” namely of God, whose counsel is said to be made void, nor of the saints, whose faith is overthrown. And they are not “for satisfying the flesh,” because many things are withheld from them.

Or thus: “which indeed have an appearance of wisdom,” that is, those who hand them down think that they possess an account of wisdom. This is because they are in that tradition: “in superstition,” that is, in feigned religion, because they apply the name of religion to human tradition, so that it may be called religion, although it is sacrilege; for whatever is contrary to the Creator has been devised with a sacrilegious mind. Religion there is therefore feigned, so that false things may appear true. And that tradition or religion is “in humility,” because it humbles minds to the earth, lest they rise to things above. And it is “not for sparing the body,” that is, it harms the body whose head is Christ—that is, the Church. And it is not “in any honor” to them, because they have been cut off from Christ the head, giving themselves wholly to the world and fulfilling the mind of the flesh. Hence he adds: “and it is for satisfying the flesh.” For the fattening of the fleshly mind is human tradition, which says that what fleshly prudence hands down is sufficient. [Col. 0279A–B]

## Chapter III

**Verses 1–5.**—“Therefore, if you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on things upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols.”

“Therefore,” and so forth. It is as though he said: Because you have died from the elements, and because these things have no force, therefore, if you have now risen [Col. 0279C]—that is, risen in soul and body: in soul, in actuality; in body, in hope—and this with Christ, that is, after Christ’s likeness, seek and think upon not carnal things, which are signified by carnal observances, but the things above: not above in place, but in the excellence of their worth. [Note: [Col. 0279D] Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*.] Let us not fix our minds upon any part of this world, since we must strip ourselves of the whole of it. Therefore he says: “Seek the things above,” namely spiritual things: either eternal glory or what leads to it. I mean the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God—that is, reigning in equality with the Father. Thus he is in the highest excellence, and therefore it is certain that through him you can attain the heights.

Seek, I say, the things above; and, once found, hold them as delightful. [Col. 0279D] This is what he adds: “Set your minds,” with understanding and charity, on things above; not on things upon the earth—that is, not on things founded in the earth—because you have died to these. Hence he adds: “For you have died.” It is as though he said: Therefore seek things above, not things on earth, because you have died to worldly and perishable things. Your life is now hidden from all who are pilgrims here, but especially from the carnal and earthly; and therefore it must be sought. [Ambrose] It is hidden, I say, with Christ, who is your life; and this life is in God the Father, with whom Christ is one and the same.

But when Christ, who is our life, shall appear—that is, when he shall be revealed to you, so that you may see that he is God with [Col. 0280A] the Father—then you also will appear, to yourselves and to others, standing with him in glory. Observe that in these words of the Apostle are explained the two things which the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the time of the lovers of the world: that it is always ready, whereas his own time and that of his followers are not yet ready. [Note: [Col. 0280D] Id., *On John*.] The time of our glory has not yet come, because summer has not yet come—that is, Christ’s coming, when fruitful trees are distinguished from barren ones. But the glory of the lovers of the world is always ready. Therefore the Apostle says, “Your life is hidden”: that is, your time has not yet come, whereas the time of those who love earthly things is always ready. And he adds, “But when Christ shall appear.” It is as though he said: This is your time. Therefore, when lovers of this age insult us, let us say what [Col. 0280B] Christ said, for he deigned to say this too on our account: “Your time is always ready; my time has not yet come” (John 7).

“Put to death.” After showing arguments concerning Christ’s fullness, he adds a general exhortation to all concerning morals, warning them not to return to their former habit. It is as though he said: You will appear with Christ in glory; therefore put to death your members—that is, the parts of the old man, namely sins. All sins taken together are, as it were, one body; individually, they are members. [Ambrose] Or, “members” means the desires of the members, which are upon the earth—that is, which rule earthly and carnal persons—namely fornication, and so forth. He describes the offences which he calls members so that, after receiving an understanding of truth, they might devote themselves to a good life. For it greatly harms one to know the account of truth and not carry it out in deeds. “He who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes.”

Fornication is every sexual union outside lawful marriage; uncleanness is that which is contrary to nature; lust is burning desire ranging through every sort of shamefulness; evil desire is desire for another’s wife or for another thing; and covetousness, which, if it does not defile the body, nevertheless defiles the soul. It is the service of idols—that is, a vice to be avoided just as idolatry, a similar and equal evil—because it also serves things in place of God. Under one name, however, he forbids two most wicked and impious vices: idolatry and covetousness. He rightly compares covetousness with idolatry, which is not a dissimilar wickedness, because it is the root of all evils and they are almost fulfilled by one act. For just as idolatry strives to take glory away from the one God, so that he alone may not possess the name of deity, so the covetous person reaches out into God’s possessions in order to usurp alone what God made for all. Both, therefore, are hostile to God, because they deny God what belongs to him. [Col. 0280C–D]

**Verses 6–17.**—“Because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief, among whom you also once walked, when you lived in them. But now put away from yourselves all these things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, shameful speech from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off [Col. 0281A] the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him. There is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free; but Christ is all things and in all. Put on therefore, as God’s chosen, holy and beloved, bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience; bearing with one another and forgiving yourselves, if anyone has a complaint against anyone, just as the Lord also forgave you, so you also. But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection; and let the peace of Christ rejoice in your hearts, in which also you were called in one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ dwell in [Col. 0281B] you abundantly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in grace in your hearts to God. Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”

“Because of these things,” namely the evils mentioned above, the wrath of God comes upon the children of distrust—that is, unbelief. What then will become of those whom ignorance does not excuse? It is as though he said: They shall be punished more severely. Among these vices you too once walked, as others did; and therefore it is more shameful if you now return to the same things. [Ambrose] You walked in them, I say, when you lived—that is, when you thought that life consisted—in them. [Col. 0281C] He mentions these things so that they may rejoice that they have escaped them and henceforth beware for themselves.

Hence he adds: “But now.” It is as though he said: Formerly you walked in them; but now, when you have received Christ, you too, like all other believers, put away not only the great vices mentioned above but all other things: anger, which is a sudden movement of the mind. After the greater sins he prohibits the lesser, lest these seem not to be dangerous. He adds indignation at another’s advancement; malice, the effect of anger, namely indignation; for malice is that by which one schemes another’s harm; blasphemy against a brother or against God; and shameful speech, or foul language. Put it away from your mouth, even if it has been conceived in the heart. What need is there to detail each point? “Do not lie to one another,” that is, one to another.

There are those who do not have the habit of drunkenness but are nevertheless occasionally drunk; just as there are those who do not have the habit of lying but nevertheless occasionally lie; and the same happens in other matters. Therefore he prohibits lying even occasionally, and especially habitual lying. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] I say, do not lie—you who strip off the old man, that is, the habit of sins, with his deeds, so that even an act of sin may not occasionally be present. For the old man is nothing other than the old life, which is in sin and in which one lives according to Adam. And put on, with the habit of virtues which is not without deeds, the new man—that is, the rational mind. This new man is renewed in the knowledge of God: he grows more and more and acquires knowledge of God; and that renewal [Col. 0282A] takes place according to the image—that is, in the image—of him who created him, namely, who created the new man in knowledge of himself. [Note: [Col. 0282D] Id., *On Genesis*.]

He sufficiently shows where man was created in the image of God: not in bodily features but in a certain form of the intelligible mind. For just as after the fall into sin man is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created him, so he was created in that very knowledge before he became old through sin. Therefore he is renewed again in the same knowledge. Hence above: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” If therefore we are renewed in the spirit of the mind, and this is the new man who is renewed in the knowledge of God, it is beyond doubt that man is the image of God, or was made in God’s image, not according to the body nor according to any part of the soul whatever, but according to the rational mind, [Col. 0282B] where the knowledge of God is.

This renewal and reformation of the mind is said to take place either “according to God” or “according to the image of God.” It is called “according to God,” as is read in Epistle 195 to the Ephesians, so that it may not be thought to take place according to another creature; it is called “according to the image of God” so that it may be understood to take place in that reality.

This renewal is where the image of God is—that is, in the mind—not because there is one image according to which it takes place and another which is renewed, but because it is the same image. Just as we say that a believer who departs from the body is dead according to the body, not according to the spirit, because he is dead in or according to the body, not in or according to the soul. So someone is called beautiful or strong according to the body, not according to the soul. Note that this image which is renewed in the knowledge of God differs from that image in accordance with which the first man—but not woman—was made. Hence above, in Corinthians: “The man is the image and glory of God, but the woman is the glory of the man” (1 Cor. 11). That image means that, as all things are from one God, so all human beings should be from one man. But this image, which he says is created in the knowledge of God, is in woman as in man.

Or thus: “according to the image.” It is as though he said: I say that you should strip off the old man and put on the new; and what I say is according to the image of him who created him, namely the new man—that is, according to reason, which is God’s image. It is as though he said: I urge [Col. 0282D] upon you nothing except what your own reason counsels. This is the image in which God created man: namely, that he should be rational and always love heavenly things. “Where,” namely in this new man. [Augustine] There is no male and female—that is, no distinction between male and female. For there are males and females according to the body, but not according to the spirit of the mind in which we are renewed according to the image of the Creator. Nor is there Gentile and Jew there—that is, no exclusion or preference of Gentile or Jew. No one is excluded as unworthy, and it neither harms nor benefits anyone before God that they were born from these people or those. Neither is there circumcision or uncircumcision there: that is, no one is more worthy there because he has these things, nor less worthy because he does not have them. Nor is there barbarian and Scythian, slave and free: that is, no one is more worthy or less worthy there because of these. The sense is that in the new man no external difference prejudices anyone: neither differences of sex, nations, observances, languages, nor conditions. But Christ is all things—that is, all the parts of the new man are Christ’s works—and Christ himself is in all believers who are made new through him. [Col. 0283A]

“Put on therefore.” It is as though he said: Because Christ is all things and in all, you therefore, O Colossians, who are as—that is, truly—God’s chosen, namely those whom God chose from eternity, holy through participation in the sacraments, and beloved by God—that is, because you are already holy and because God has loved you—put on bowels of mercy, that is, an affection of compassion toward all. Then follows the exercise of mercy when he adds: kindness, a mind ready to do good; humility, so that you may be humble in heart and bearing; gentleness, so that you may preserve measure in all things; and patience in enduring adversities, bearing with one another, so that one may bear another’s burdens; and forgiving yourselves, if anyone has a complaint against anyone—that is, if one offends another—not merely refraining from judgment but also forgiving. Just as the Lord forgave you, so you too wholly and purely forgive others. [Note: [Col. 0283D] Augustine, *On John*.] In the sacrament of this matter Christ washed his disciples’ feet and said: “I have given you an example, that you also may do likewise” (John 13). Therefore let us forgive one another’s offences, [Col. 0283C] pray for one another’s offences, and thus in a certain manner wash one another’s feet. [Ambrose]

Note that he urges them to do these things so that they may have gain from them, because they lay up merit with God. Fear causes one to abstain from unlawful things, for one fears that, by doing evil, one may be subjected to punishments. The things which he now urges them to do pertain to the increase of merits, for they are done from will, not necessity. He who abstains from unlawful acts has praise; but he who restrains himself even from lawful things has praise and reward.

“But above all.” It is as though he said: Observe all these things. But above all these, have charity—that is, seek charity more zealously than all else. [Col. 0283D] For one must strive more for the virtue which is greater than all. Or: have charity, which is above all these things. For it is the more excellent way, surpassing knowledge and all commandments. [Note: [Col. 0284D] Id., ibid.] This is the Lord’s seamless garment, woven from above; seamless, lest that which reaches unity should ever be ripped apart, because charity gathers all into one. Have charity, I say, which gift—namely charity—is the bond of perfection. For the other virtues make one perfect, but charity also binds all things together lest they fall away.

And let the peace of Christ—that is, the peace which Christ had in himself and commanded to be possessed, or that which he made between God and man—rejoice in your hearts: that is, be in your hearts [Col. 0284A] a cause of rejoicing. This will certainly be so if charity is possessed, for charity has true peace, which it preserves with a pure heart. [Ambrose] Peace may indeed be named even where charity is lacking; but charity always has with it the peace which it makes. In this peace you were called, by it being placed in the one body of the Church. For peace is necessary for the unity of the body, which charity makes.

And concerning all these things be thankful to God, teaching both yourselves and others what you learn through yourselves. And admonishing yourselves concerning what you know, so that teaching may be for those who do not know, and admonition for those who know but are sluggish. Teach and admonish, I say, concerning what is contained in psalms, which treat of morals; hymns, which treat of God’s praises; and spiritual songs, which concern the eternal good. And being taught and admonished by these, sing to the Lord—that is, in honor of the Lord—not only with your lips but in your hearts, that is, with understanding or attentively. And do this in grace—that is, in consideration of God’s benefits.

How they can do these things he set forth earlier in sequence, saying: “Let the word,” and so forth. It is as though he said: In order that you may teach and admonish wisely, let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly, namely in all wisdom, so that you may possess understanding of all the Scriptures. “Whatever,” and so forth. Because above he commanded God to be praised in heart, he now exhorts them to praise and exalt God’s name in words and deeds, so that our words and works may be beyond reproach and the Lord may be magnified, whose disciples are beyond blame through his teaching. It is as though he said: Teach and admonish. [Col. 0284C] Moreover, whatever you do in word or deed, do it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, for Christ’s glory, not your own. And not only what you do in word or deed, but let all things, even thoughts and anything else there may be, be for Christ’s glory.

Or thus: Whatever you do in word or deed, do it. Let everything—that is, what is complete—be ascribed to God. This is what he explains by adding: doing all things in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, for Christ’s glory; you, I say, then truly giving thanks not to the Law but to God the Father through him—through Christ, through whom God gave all things. For then we give thanks to God through Christ if we keep the measure of his commandments.

[Col. 0284D] **Verses 18–25.**—“Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation, lest they become discouraged. Slaves, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not serving only to the eye, as pleasing men, but in simplicity of heart, fearing God. Whatever you do, work from the heart, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you shall receive the recompense of the inheritance. Serve the Lord Christ. For he who does wrong shall receive [Col. 0285A] what he has done unjustly, and there is no respect of persons with God.”

“Wives.” Thus far he has admonished everyone generally concerning morals; now he turns to individual precepts, exhorting different persons separately so that they may serve one another: not only by obeying, as wives serve husbands, children parents, and slaves masters, but also by caring for them, as husbands for wives, fathers for children, and masters for slaves. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Augustine, *in the Book of Sentences of Prosper*.] This is domestic peace: a harmony among cohabitants ordered by God, and clear justice, namely that those who excel in reason should excel in authority. [Note: [Col. 0285D] Id., *On Genesis*.] He teaches this harmony, saying: “Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting,” that is, as fully as God commanded, and this in the Lord, not against the Lord. [Ambrose]

And you husbands, love [Col. 0285B] your wives and do not be bitter—that is, harsh—toward them. By this he softens the rigor of mastery, so that one who prevails in authority over his wife may not use his power too severely. And you children, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing—that is, it pleases God if you obey in all things—provided, nevertheless, that you obey in the Lord. And you fathers, do not provoke your children to indignation against you. Or, according to another reading, “to anger,” lest they become discouraged or faint-hearted, namely unable to endure any longer. He commands fathers to be gentle with their children, lest, being constrained by them, the children transgress against them and offend God. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Id., *in the Book of Sentences of Prosper*.] For anger is an unconsidered thing, such that sometimes even the one who is angry does not spare himself.

And you slaves, obey in all things—but not against the Lord—your masters, not only spiritual [Col. 0285C] masters but also masters according to the flesh, who rule according to the flesh. You, I say, serving not merely to the eye, as though pleasing men rather than God—that is, as though unwilling to please God—but serve in simplicity of heart, that is, with pure intention, so that you may be outwardly what you are in heart. Do this fearing God, whom you cannot deceive. And whatever you do, work not as fearing punishment from God, but from the heart—that is, willingly—as though serving the Lord and not men. For God approves that innocence by which a person becomes innocent not from fear of punishment but from love of justice. For one who does not sin only through fear, although he does no harm to others, nevertheless does very great harm to himself. Feigned innocence is not innocence; feigned equity is not equity, but a double sin, containing both [Col. 0285D] iniquity and pretense.

Work, I say, knowing that for this humility you shall receive from the Lord the recompense of the eternal inheritance; and, despite other masters, serve the Lord of rulers, namely Christ, in what he commands. “For he who…” It is as though he said: You must serve as I have said, and not abandon service because of masters’ cruelty; for whoever does wrong, whether master or slave, shall receive what he has done unjustly. This is because there is no respect of persons with God: no one shall be spared because of his higher rank.

## Chapter IV

**Verses 1–18.**—“Masters, render to your slaves what is just and equitable, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven. Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving; praying also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also bound, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak. Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person. Tychicus, the most beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow-servant in the Lord, will make known to you all things concerning me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that he may know the things concerning you and comfort your hearts, together with Onesimus, the most beloved and faithful [Col. 0286B] brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is happening here. Aristarchus, my fellow-captive, greets you, and Mark, Barnabas’s cousin, concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, receive him; and Jesus, who is called Justus. These are of the circumcision. They alone are my fellow-workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me. Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Jesus Christ, greets you, always striving for you in prayers, that you may stand perfect and full in every will of God. For I bear him witness that he has much labor for you, for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis. Luke, the most beloved physician, and Demas greet you. Greet the brothers in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the church which is in [Col. 0286C] her house. And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you also read the one from Laodicea. And say to Archippus: ‘See to the ministry which you received in the Lord, that you may fulfill it.’ This greeting is in my own hand, Paul’s. Remember my chains. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

…of the Lord, what is just, etc. As if he said: And you, masters, render to your servants what is just in return for their service, and what is equitable by nature: namely, regard them as human beings, knowing that you too have a Lord in heaven, as one who is not powerless. Therefore require of them such things as you would wish to have required of yourselves. Thus do righteous men. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Gospel*.] For the good, living by faith, even while still pilgrims away from that City, serve those whom they seem to command, because they rule not from a desire to dominate but from the duty of providing counsel and benefits.

“Prayer.” As if he said: I have advised the different persons individually; now I advise all of you collectively: persist in prayer, watching in it. As if he said: Persist even by night; or, “watching,” that is, not being sluggish, in prayer concerning future things. I mean you who remain in thanksgiving for past things. Persist, I say, praying also for us, that God may open for us a door for the word—that is, make my mouth open, which was given for this purpose, that the word might proceed from it. Now a mouth is open when it says many and great things. And he shows for what end he wishes his mouth to be opened, saying: namely, to speak the mystery of Christ, that is, to expound that which is secret concerning Christ—his birth, passion, and so forth. Because of this work, namely because I expound Christ’s secrets, I am in chains. I say, “May he open my mouth to speak the mystery,” and so to speak that I may make manifest openly what is hidden from unbelievers, steadfastly and discreetly, as it is fitting for me, who am an Apostle, to speak.

You yourselves also, in the wisdom of God which you possess, walk—that is, make progress toward enlightening those who are outside, that is, outside the Church. One must conduct oneself cautiously among unbelievers, lest they be scandalized, lest an occasion for blasphemy be given them, and lest they be provoked to persecute. Walk wisely, I say, not hindering, but redeeming the time—that is, in various ways preparing an opportunity to preach to them. And when the opportunity has been gained, let your speech always be in grace, that is, such as is pleasing to its hearers. Or, “in grace,” which is to be preached, not in the Law; and let it be seasoned with the salt of wisdom, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person, since an uneducated person must be answered differently from a learned person, and different persons in different ways.

But Tychicus—through whom he is believed to have sent the Epistle—my most beloved brother in faith, faithful minister in preaching, and fellow-servant in adversities, and this in the Lord, that is, for the Lord’s sake, will make known to you all that concerns me: that is, the tribulations which are on every side, or which do not reach as far as the soul. Therefore there will be no need to write them. I sent him to you for this very purpose, that is, for a similar purpose, namely that he might learn what concerns you. [Ambrose.] Therefore take heed for yourselves: when a man sees himself being observed, he ought to take greater heed for himself. I say that I sent him with Onesimus, our beloved and faithful brother, who is one of you; and he, namely Onesimus, and Tychicus will make known to you everything that is happening here.

Aristarchus, my fellow-captive—that is, participant and companion in my labors—greets you; and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, concerning whom you received instructions: concerning Mark or Barnabas, namely that he had departed from me and therefore you should not receive him; but if he now comes to you, receive him. Or: you received instructions that he had returned to me, and therefore, if he comes to you, receive him. Jesus, who is called Justus, also greets you. These aforementioned persons are of the circumcision, yet they affirm with me the same teaching concerning grace. [Col. 0287D] These alone among the Jews are now my fellow-workers in the kingdom of God through preaching; and, while I am placed in tribulation, they are a comfort to me, supplying my place.

Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, not of the Law, greets you. He is always earnest for you in prayers, in which he prays for you that you may stand—that is, persevere—perfect and complete in every will of God: namely, that you may will all that God wills and add nothing beyond what God wills. And he is indeed earnest for you. For I bear him witness that he has great labor for you, not only in praying but in other ways as well. Therefore be earnest for us too, and not only for us but also for those who are in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis.

Luke, the beloved physician and Evangelist, and Demas greet you. Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and especially Nympha, who receives and supports preachers, and the church in her house—that is, her household. And when this Epistle has been read among you, see that it is read also in the Church of the Laodiceans; and let that of the Laodiceans be read to you, or read it yourselves: that is, either the one which I sent them, or the one which they sent me, so that you may see here the answer to those questions. From this passage we understand that the Apostle’s instructions are general and that the Epistles were written for people’s advancement.

And you yourselves, who formerly went astray in spirit, say to Archippus: “See to the ministry,” that is, be diligent concerning the ministry, which you received in the Lord—that is, in matters belonging to the Lord—“that you may fulfil it”: so that, as it ceased through the disobedience of these persons, so through correction it may be girded for action. Note that he admonishes their leader through them themselves: he who received the duty of governing their Church is to be diligent concerning them; and because the Epistle is written for the sake of the people, it is not addressed to the ruler but to the Church.

“Salutation.” As if he said: So that you may know that the Epistle was sent by me, my salutation is written in Paul’s own hand. Before he gives the salutation, he first adds an exhortation, saying: “Remember my chains,” that is, keep in mind why I suffer—namely, because I preach faith alone. He says this so that they may prove themselves such persons that he may not grieve to suffer wrongs for them: that they may suffer simply, or pray for him and supply what is necessary. He then shows what the salutation is, adding: “May the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Amen.”

## FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0287]

197. ARGUMENT

[Col. 0287D]

The Thessalonians are Macedonians who, having received the word of truth, persevered in the faith even amid persecution from their fellow citizens. Moreover, they neither received false apostles nor accepted what was said by false apostles. The Apostle praises them, writing to them from Athens through Tychicus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Verses 1–3

> “Paul and Silvanus and Timothy, to the Church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace. We give thanks to God always for all of you, making remembrance of you in our prayers without ceasing, mindful of your work of faith, labor, charity, and endurance in the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ before God and our Father.”

“Paul and Silvanus,” etc. [Haimo.] The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Thessalonians. Thessalonica is the metropolis of Macedonia, which is a province of the Greeks. The Thessalonians, therefore, are Macedonians who were readily converted by the Apostle and could not be moved away from the truth of the faith either by tribulations or by false preachers. [Ambrose.] The Apostle praises them because, persevering in the grace they had received, they grew in virtues toward the progress of reward by pursuing better things. [Col. 0289B] For they had imbibed so great a spirit of faith that, in hope of future things, they bore dangers with devout courage for Christ’s name even from their unbelieving fellow citizens.

Yet there were among them some idle and meddlesome persons; some also held defective views concerning the resurrection and therefore grieved too rashly over the death of friends; and some of them were fornicators. The Apostle accordingly corrects these persons in this Epistle, exhorts the perfect not to yield to adverse false apostles, and urges them to correct others. [Haimo.] He wrote from Athens. The Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle is to correct the wicked and uncorrected, and to exhort the good to perseverance and to the correction of others. Its method is as follows: in accordance with his custom, he begins with a salutation. Having given it, he thanks God for their good qualities, recalling not only their faith and works but also the manner of their conversion and their endurance of evils. To provoke them more strongly to persevere, he also interweaves an account of his own labors, the truth of the Gospel, his prudent conduct among them, and the depth of his desire to see them. Then he entreats the wicked to refrain from luxury, idleness, and curiosity, and confirms that the dead will rise again. Toward the end is moral instruction.

He begins with the salutation, saying: “Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy.” These were the Apostle’s helpers in instructing them, and they rejoiced together in their progress. Therefore the salutation is placed under their names, though the sense and wording of the Epistle belong to the Apostle alone. These, I say, write to the Church of the Thessalonians, gathered together in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. As if he said: The Church, gathered in the unity of faith, exists through God the Father’s working and through Christ his Son. Before all else they greet them in this manner: “Grace and peace be to you.” Do not expound what has already been expounded, lest you do a thing already done.

[Ambrose.] After the salutation he first strengthens the good, giving thanks to God, from whom all good things come, for their progress, in this manner: “We give thanks to God always for all of you,” because the good things in you are from God. “We,” I say, “making remembrance of you in our prayers,” that you may persist in good. “In prayers,” I say, offered without interruption at the appointed hours. He then shows why he gives thanks, adding: “We,” I say, “mindful of the work”—that is, confession—“of your faith.” For confession is the proper work of faith; and mindful of your labor, which they undertook for themselves and for their neighbors; of the charity exercised toward God and neighbor; and of endurance against evils. This endurance belongs to hope, because hope of glory produces it. They could not have endured such great evils unless hope had strengthened them; and this hope does not disappoint, because it is the hope of our Lord Jesus Christ, who both can and wills to fulfil it. This hope exists before God and our Father, because you are as certain as if you already saw him; and thus he encourages them. Or, it exists before God because it pleases him, not being done for human sight, and because he is its author.

### Verses 4–10

> “Knowing, brothers beloved by God, your election, because our Gospel did not come to you in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and in much fullness, as you know what manner of men we were among you for your sake. And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, receiving the word in much tribulation with the joy of the Holy Spirit, so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. For from you the word of the Lord has been proclaimed abroad, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith toward God has gone forth, so that we have no need to say anything. For they themselves report concerning us what manner of entrance we had to you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God and to await his Son from heaven, whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who delivered us from the wrath to come.”

[Col. 0290C] “Knowing.” As if he said: We give God thanks for these things because we know that he loved you and chose you by grace alone. This is what he says: “We give thanks to God, knowing, O brothers beloved by God, your election,” that is, that you are beloved and chosen by God. We know this from the fact that “our Gospel did not come to you in word only.” [Haimo.] That is, it did not consist merely in an exhibition of words, but came “in power” of miracles, since he performed among them many miracles confirming his teaching; and “in the Holy Spirit,” because through me you received the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and not sparingly, but “in much fullness.” He says this so that they may seem in no respect inferior to the Churches of the Jews, and may rejoice in God’s gift, since he deigned to make them sharers in Abraham’s promise.

“As,” etc. As if he said: We know this invisible divine fact—that you are chosen by God—just as you know this visible fact, namely what kind of persons we were among you: that is, how afflicted we were in your midst, and this for your sake, that is, for your salvation. As if he said: By this also—that we did not shrink from suffering—it is evident for your example that God loved and chose you. [Ambrose.] “And you.” As if he said: We suffered as an example for you, and you became imitators of us and of the Lord, who endured the cross. For they bore reproaches and injuries from their fellow citizens in hope of future things. Hence they are called imitators of the Apostles and of the Lord himself, because the Lord suffered the same things from the Jews, and the Apostles, following the Lord, endured persecutions joyfully because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the Lord’s name.

“You,” I say, “receiving the word in much tribulation”—ours, namely, and yours, because tribulation did not cause you to abandon the word. [Haimo.] “Receiving,” I say, “with the joy of the Holy Spirit,” which the Holy Spirit produced in you, “you became imitators of us,” so that you became a form, that is, an example of confession and teaching, to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia, who through your example do not fear to confess. And you indeed became an example to all. “For from you the word of the Lord has been proclaimed abroad,” that is, from the example of your endurance it came about that others openly preach God’s word.

[Ambrose.] It has been proclaimed abroad, I say, because not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every adjacent and neighboring place, not only the word but your faith—that is, the advancement of faith—has gone forth. This faith is directed to God alone, as in martyrs; it is not the faith of less perfect persons, who also concern themselves with the things of the world. It has gone forth, I say, so that we have no need to say anything about you in order to incite others. For they themselves—that is, all others—report concerning you what kind of entrance we had to you, namely, how afflicted we were when we came to you; and nevertheless how strongly you were converted, although we were afflicted: converted “to God from idols,” to truth from pretence, to one from many.

“You turned,” I say, “to serve the living and true God,” and in serving to await his Son coming from heaven: that is, you turned to God in order to serve God as purely as it is fitting to serve him who is living and true—God in truth, who lives eternally—and in this service to await the vision of God’s Son when he comes, desiring no other gift than to see Christ according to his divinity, whom the wicked will not see. Hence Scripture says: “Let the wicked man be taken away, lest he see the Son of God.” The Father raised this Son from the dead, and by this act made him for his own people the Lord Jesus—that is, the king and savior of his people. This Son “delivered us from the wrath to come,” because in baptism he forgives sin and in the future will free us from punishment.

## CHAPTER TWO

### Verses 1–8

> “For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance to you, that it was not in vain; but, having previously suffered many things and been treated shamefully, as you know, at Philippi, we had confidence in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God amid much anxiety. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor in deceit; but, as we were approved by God to be entrusted with the Gospel, so we speak, not as pleasing men but God, who tests our hearts. For we were never at any time in speech of flattery, as you know, nor under a pretext of greed—God is witness; nor seeking glory from men, neither from you nor from others, although we could have been a burden to you as Apostles of Christ. But we became little ones in your midst, as if a nurse were cherishing her own children; so, longing for you eagerly, we wished to impart to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls, because you had become most dear to us.”

“For you yourselves.” Here he recalls his labors. As if he said: This is why I speak of the kind of entrance we had, and do not set forth its character, because it is unnecessary. For you yourselves, O brothers, know our entrance to you; concerning it you know this: it was not vain, that is, not easy; it was not in worldly prosperity, which is vain; but it was amid much anxiety because of the adversities that we endured. Therefore we had confidence, not in adversities—for we are fragile—but in our God, to speak to you the Gospel of God. You also should do likewise: put confidence in God, not in yourselves.

“We,” I say, before coming to you, “suffered many things and were treated shamefully at Philippi,” as you know. Behold, we suffered before coming to you and afterward as well, so that we might not be permitted to put confidence in ourselves, and our labor thus be vain. [Ambrose.] This oppression which he now recalls he suffered at Philippi because he cast the Pythian spirit out of a girl.
