Or thus: you now know this about our entrance: it was not vain, that is, through no evils did I cease speaking the word of God. This is the mark of a devout and faithful preacher: that he does not fear to speak God’s word under oppression. For he is vain who, through present terror, becomes afraid to preach.

“It was not vain,” I say, “but although we had previously suffered and been treated shamefully at Philippi,” as you know, “and were among you in much anxiety,” that is, greatly anxious, “we nevertheless did not fear, but had confidence in our God to speak to you the Gospel of God.” By these things told about himself, and by their good beginning, he warns them to persevere in patience.

“For our exhortation.” Here he seems to begin speaking against false apostles, recalling the truth of the Gospel. [Haimo.] Then he recalls his prudent conduct among them. As if he said: We rightly had confidence in the Lord, because our exhortation—that is, the preaching by which we exhort others—is not from error, that is, falsehood, but from truth; nor from impurity, such as carnal observances after Christ, or the use of women, and certain other things which some preached; nor “in deceit,” that is, fraud and crafty hypocrisy. For even truth is sometimes preached deceitfully: when it is preached not out of love of truth and concern for the hearers’ benefit, but in order to obtain glory or gain.

It is not in deceit, I say; rather, we speak with truth and a pure intention, as we were approved and chosen by God in order that the Gospel might be entrusted to us, as to faithful persons.

[Note: [Col. 0291D] Augustine, *in the Book of Sentences of Prosper*.] “We speak,” I say, “not as pleasing men,” that is, not seeking to please them, because we do not even have the appearance of one who seeks to please; but as pleasing God, “who tests our hearts,” that is, who makes them approved, so that we may please him rather than men. Unless he himself works this in us, we cannot avoid the contrary. For no one knows what power to harm the love of human glory has, except one who has declared war upon it: although it is easy for anyone not to desire praise while it is withheld, it is difficult not to delight in it when it is offered.

And I truly do not seek to please people. For we were never at any time in speech of flattery, by which others please men, as you know. And our preaching is truly not deceitful, because it is not “under a pretext of greed”: I do not say merely that I did not act in greed, but that I neither did nor said anything which could furnish an occasion for greed. God, who knows hearts, is my witness in this; for it is not equally evident. We pursue neither greed nor glory. That is, we do not seek glory from men, neither from you nor from others, but from God alone.

[Ambrose.] In this he strikes at the false apostles, who wished to commend themselves rather than the Lord’s teaching. But the Apostle, who sought glory not in the present but in the future, made himself humble so that God’s preaching might be exalted. “Although we could.” As if he said: I say that we did not preach under a pretext of greed, although we could, though we were not false apostles, have been a burden to you, so that you would supply us with necessities. We could, I say, as Apostles of Christ. [Ambrose.] He so heavily charges the case against the false apostles that he says he refused what was permitted him—to seek support—in order to repress those who had neither means nor shame in asking. He calls the due of apostolic authority a burden because of the false apostles, who, usurping it without right, demanded it importunately from congregations.

“But we became.” As if he said: We seek none of these things; rather, “we became little ones,” that is, humble, in your midst, that is, toward you all without distinction. [Haimo.] And this for good, and we acted so solicitously “as if a nurse cherishes her own children,” not others’ children. For a woman sometimes nurses others’ children for pay, not out of love; but she nurses her own through affection. Therefore he fittingly says, “as if a nurse cherishes her own children.” This indicates labor, humility, and love, because it is not done for hire. He signifies that he has said this to make his love for them understood, saying: thus, in all our labor, desiring not what was yours but you—that is, desiring your salvation—we eagerly wished to impart to you not only the Gospel of God but also our own souls in defense of the Gospel. And this because you became most dear to us by receiving God’s faith and attaching yourselves well to us. And I rightly say that we became little ones, like a nurse.

### Verses 9–20

> “For you remember, brothers, our labor and toil: working night and day, so that we might not burden any of you, we preached to you the Gospel of God. You are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believed; as you know how, like a father with his own children, we were entreating and consoling each one of you and testifying that you should walk worthily of God, who called you into his own kingdom and glory. Therefore we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of God’s hearing, you received it not as the word of men but, as it truly is, as the word of God, who works in you who believe. For you, brothers, became imitators of the Churches of God which are in Judea in Christ Jesus, because you suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they did from the Jews, who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and persecuted us; they do not please God and oppose all people, forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, in order always to fill up their sins. But God’s wrath has come upon them to the end. But we, brothers, being bereaved of you for a short time—in presence, not in heart—were all the more eager, with much longing, to see your face, because we wished to come to you—I, Paul, indeed, once and again—but Satan hindered us. For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming? For you are our glory and joy.”

“For you remember, O brothers, our labor and toil.” He added this because there can be labor without toil. And I rightly said “toil and labor,” because, working with our hands night and day so that we might not burden any of you by receiving something from him, we preached to you the Gospel of God. He did this also in order to exclude false apostles from preaching.

“For you.” As if he said: We behaved toward you before your conversion just as we did after it. For you are witnesses—and God is witness also—how holily, with respect to you; justly, with respect to one’s neighbor, by rendering what was due; and blamelessly, by doing nothing unlawful, we were present among you who believed, when you still had to be instructed. You know this just as you know this other matter: namely, how we entreated each one of you, entreating you as a father his own children, that is, with as great affection as a father has for his children; and consoling you if any of you was anxious about sin or anything else.

“We testified,” that is, under the testimony of the saints themselves we adjured you, “that you should walk,” making progress, “worthily of God,” following his will in works. Indeed you ought to do this because he is the one who called you by the calling according to his purpose. [Augustine.] He called you, when you were hostile, into his own kingdom and glory: namely, that you might belong to his kingdom, whom he rules here and afterward crowns in glory.

199. “Therefore,” namely because he called us, we too—not you alone—give thanks to God, because God did this. We give thanks, I say, without ceasing. He called you, I say, because you received quickly and firmly. He says it thus: “Because when you received from us the word of God’s hearing,” that is, when you received by hearing alone the word which is from God. Or, “the word of God’s hearing,” that is, the word which we heard from God speaking in us; or, the word in which God is heard. When, I say, you received it, you received it not as the word of men—that is, as though it came from wise men—but as God’s word, as it truly is.

[Ambrose.] For they received the word with such devotion that they demonstrated that they understood God’s teaching to be its source. God works in you, who believe, daily good works, coming through faith into the very thing which you have believed. “For you.” He has said much against the false apostles; here he now warns them not to be moved by their own tribulation or that of the Apostles. As if he said: God works in you, and the result shows this. For you, O brothers, became imitators of the Churches of God which are in Judea, built in Christ Jesus—that is, in faith and the institution of Christ himself—in this respect: you suffered the same things from your fellow countrymen as they who are in Judea suffered from the Jews. The Jews were so harsh that they killed both Christ the Lord and the prophets, and persecuted us, the Apostles of Christ.

They think that in this they serve and please God. Yet they do not please God, and they oppose all people—that is, the salvation of all people—by forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they may be saved. They do this in order always to fill up their sins: that is, by remaining in sins, to bring their own sins and those of their parents to completion, according to the text: “Let the one who is filthy be filthy still” (Rev. 22), and to draw upon themselves the vengeance due for their own sins and those of their parents.

God did indeed allow the Jews forty years after the Lord’s passion for repentance. When these had elapsed and they refused to believe, their sins were completed. Hence the Lord said to them: “Fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matt. 23). But when the Apostle said these things, Jerusalem’s sins had not yet been completed; they were completed when the Romans came. Hence he adds: “For God’s wrath has come.” As if he said: The result shows that they filled up their sins, because God’s wrath—that is, God’s vengeance—has come upon them, oppressing them to the end. God’s wrath is the coming of the Romans, when they were destroyed by sword, famine, pestilence, and captivity. This wrath endures for them until the end of the age, because they will always be captives.

Or, as some manuscripts have it, “God’s wrath has come beforehand”: that is, God’s vengeance came beforehand upon them in this age and will endure to the end. It is said to come beforehand because this temporal punishment precedes the vengeance of the future judgment, in which they will be punished eternally, and afterward the eternal punishment follows. Or he speaks of inward vengeance, by which God punished them through blinding. As if he said: Therefore they fill up—that is, complete—their sins, because the wrath—that is, the vengeance of blindness—has come upon them, oppressing them so that they are blinded; and this continues to the end, that is, to eternal punishment, or until the end of the age, because at the end of the age the Jews will be converted, when Abraham returns to the boys waiting with the donkey.

“But we.” Here he recalls how earnestly he desired to see them. As if he said: You have suffered much. But we, O brothers, bereaved of you—that is, bereaved because of you, not because of ourselves—for a time, that is, before we knew of your steadfastness: we were removed from you in speech, that is, by spoken address, and in sight, that is, in bodily presence, but not in heart, that is, in the affection of love. As if he said: Speech and sight cease because I cannot speak with you or see you; but the heart’s affection and concern never cease.

“We,” I say, “being bereaved, were all the more eager,” more than if you had suffered nothing, and therefore stand firm, “to see your face,” for fuller instruction, so that I might instruct you fully concerning the evils done to you. “We were eager to see,” I say, “with much longing,” in order to exhort you. And we truly were eager, because we all wished to come to you. I, Paul indeed, who care more than the others, wished to come once and again; but Satan, who opposes salvation, hindered us. Therefore take greater care and fear, since God permitted the Apostle to be hindered from coming to them. Their merit will be greater if they stand firm while he is absent.

“For what?” As if he said: This is why I wished to come, or this is why Satan hindered us: for what is our hope in the present, or our joy in the future—that is, the reward which will be common to all the good—or our crown of glory, namely the reward which will belong only to conquerors? Are you not, if you stand before our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, in God’s good pleasure—or because you stand before our Lord, firmly established, are you not, I say, or will you not be, our crown at his coming, that is, when the Lord comes? As if he said: You will be. For it is clear that the perfection of disciples is the joy and crown of teachers.

[Ambrose.] For these are they who will bring forth the fruits of their labors. The teacher’s fruit is the disciple’s obedience; the disciple’s good conduct gives a crown to the teacher when Christ judges. And you will truly then be our crown, for even now you are our glory among the other Churches and our joy among ourselves. And if you are now our glory, what will you be to us before the true Judge?

## CHAPTER THREE

### Verses 1–13

> “Therefore, unable to endure any longer, we were pleased to remain alone at Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s minister in the Gospel of Christ, to strengthen you and exhort you concerning your faith, so that no one might be moved in these tribulations. For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this. For when we were with you, we foretold to you that we would suffer tribulations, as it has happened and as you know. Therefore I too, unable to endure any longer except in order to learn of your faith, lest perhaps he who tempts had tempted you and our labor should become vain. But now Timothy has come to us from you and brought us news of your faith and charity, and that you retain a good remembrance of us, always desiring to see us, as we also desire to see you. Therefore, brothers, we were comforted in you amid all our necessity and tribulation through your faith, because now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord. For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you, for all the joy in which we rejoice because of you before our God, praying night and day more earnestly that we may see your face and supply what is lacking in your faith? May God himself, our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you. And may the Lord make your charity toward one another and toward all people increase and abound, as ours does toward you, in order to strengthen your hearts blamelessly in holiness before God and our Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints. Amen.”

For this reason—namely, because you are our glory, or because we were left desolate on your account—we could no longer bear not knowing your condition, since it was as though a weight lay upon us while I did not know of your steadfastness. We resolved that I and Silvanus should remain alone at Athens, and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s minister [Col. 0297B] in the Gospel of Christ, preaching, to strengthen you by adding whatever you lacked, and to exhort you to stand firm in the good things in which you were, and this for the defence of your faith: so that none of you might be moved from the integrity of the faith by these passing tribulations. For you yourselves. As though he said: No one ought to die because of tribulations, for we have been appointed for this; as he says: “For you yourselves know that we are appointed for this,” that is, for bearing tribulations, appointed by Christ. Or: placed in this, that is, in tribulations, we are steadfast. And truly we are placed in this, for when we were with you, we foretold that we should suffer tribulations, as is evident; and it happened, and you know it. If we foreknew them and did not flee, then you also endure them, knowing these things.

[Ambrose] Therefore, [Col. 0297C] because we too have suffered, lest you should be alarmed on our account—not only for the other reasons stated above—I too, no longer able to bear not knowing what was happening among you, sent Timothy, whom the Apostle had made a bishop, to learn of your faith, lest perhaps he who tempts, that is, the devil, whose office is to tempt, should tempt you, that is, should have deceived you. This was to be feared concerning the weak; and lest your labour, that is, whatever good you have done thus far, should become vain.

“But now,” as though he said, “I sent Timothy to learn of your faith. But now, when Timothy has come to us from you and announced to us your faith and charity amid adversities”—namely, that you have not been moved from faith and the love of God by either your own tribulations or mine—“and that you have a good,” that is, beneficial to yourselves, “remembrance of us,” namely, that we have not become contemptible because of tribulations. You, I say, always desiring to see us, for an example and so that I might rejoice concerning you, just as we too desire to see you. Therefore, because he announced these things—not because of his presence—we who had formerly been desolate were comforted, that is, received consolation, O brethren, in you, that is, on your account, in all our need, that is, want, and tribulation. And he explains how he said “on your account,” adding: through your faith, which we heard to be firm. Or: “through your faith,” I assure you, “we were comforted.” I say, and truly so, because now in this misery we live as though we were in heaven, if you stand upright and firm in the Lord, [Col. 0298A] that is, in faith in the Lord.

“For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you?” As though he said: Truly we have been comforted; indeed, so greatly that we cannot render thanks worthy of it. Nothing is so worthy as to suffice in recompense for the salvation gained by the Gentiles. We, I say, are filled with every joy in which we rejoice—as though he said, a joy that does not quickly pass away—on your account, standing before our God, that is, in God’s good pleasure. We, I say, pray night and day to see your face and to supply what is lacking in your faith: the things which formerly we were unable to teach you, because you were little children. We pray more abundantly than before, because now more could be added to them.

We pray to see you. But may God himself, who is able, and [Col. 0298B] your Father, who wills good, and the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the Father accomplishes all things, direct—that is, make straight and free from obstacles—our way to you. But whether we come or not, may the Lord multiply you in number of believers and virtues, and make your charity, or truth, abound toward one another, among yourselves, and toward all, even enemies, as perfectly as we abound in charity toward you. I say that he may make your charity abound for this purpose: to strengthen your hearts, so that you may be without complaint, namely, that you may not complain of evils. Or thus: that you may be innocent, so that no one can complain concerning you; and that you may be in holiness, that is, in the perfection of virtues. Thus existing before God and our Father, that is, in [Col. 0298C] God’s good pleasure, not for the sight of human beings. You, I say, having your minds set on the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints, that is, as all the saints do. Or, existing before our Lord, that is, in God’s good pleasure, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who will be with all the saints, that is, with whom he will come to judgement. Amen. As though he said: This will truly be so.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSES 1–11

> “Furthermore, then, brethren, we ask and entreat you in the Lord Jesus that, as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you should walk, that you may abound more and more. For you know what commandments [Col. 0298D] I gave you through the Lord Jesus. For this is the will of God: your sanctification—that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire, as also the Gentiles who do not know God; and that no one overreach or defraud his brother in a matter, because the Lord is avenger in all these things, as we foretold you and testified. For God has not called us to uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore, he who despises these things does not despise a human being, but God, who has also given his Holy Spirit in us. But concerning brotherly love, we had no need to write to you; for you yourselves have been taught by God [Col. 0299A] to love one another. For indeed you do this toward all the brethren throughout Macedonia. But we ask you, brethren, that you abound more and more, and make it your aim to be quiet, to attend to your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we commanded you; and that you may walk honourably toward those outside, and lack nothing.”

“Furthermore, then.” Thus far he has urged patience upon the perfect amid their own tribulation or that of others; now he urges purity upon the less mature, exhorting them to continence.

[Haimo] As though he said: Because we abound in charity toward you, therefore, O brethren, we ask and entreat you. It is the Apostle’s custom to repeat or triple words having one meaning, as here. “We ask,” I say, “in the Lord Jesus,” that is, if you love [Col. 0299B] me with him, that you may walk, persevering in good, and that you may abound more and more, that is, grow increasingly in faith and good works. You should walk, I say, precisely as you received from us how you ought to walk, that is, to live and complete the course of this life, in those things without which there is no salvation, and to please God, in those things added by the counsel of perfection. For that person pleases God who adorns right faith with the practice of virtues and perfect action.

[Ambrose, Haimo] Or, according to another reading: “as you also walk, that you may abound more.” The order is: “We ask that you walk”—understand, as you received, by hearing and understanding, from us, that is, from me and Silvanus, how you ought to walk and please [Col. 0299C] God—“as you also walk,” by living rightly; “and we ask that you abound more.” This is unchanged.

“For you know.” As though he said: Therefore I urge you to abound and to please God, because you know what commandments—that is, how honourable and useful—they are which I gave you. I gave them, I say, to human beings through the Lord Jesus. Their author himself commends them, and they are truly good. “For this is the will of God”: this is God’s commandment, this is what God wills, because it benefits you, not him—namely, your sanctification, that is, that you should sanctify yourselves by doing good works, and that you should abstain. As though he said: You who belong to Christ must be far removed from every fornication, both carnal and spiritual. Abstain in such a way that each of you may know how to possess his own vessel, namely, his own body, which is the vessel of the soul, restraining it in the sanctification [Col. 0299D] of virtues and in honour, lest it be dishonoured by some disgrace. Rather, just as one takes care to keep the vessels used in one’s duties clean, so one should strive through continence to keep the workshops of one’s members honourable.

Or thus: “that each may know.” As though he said: Abstain so from what is unlawful that you do not abuse even what is lawful; but let each of you know how to possess his vessel, that is, his wife, ruling over her, and this in sanctification, namely, by abstaining from intercourse, and in honour, namely, by not abusing her shamefully. Let him possess her in sanctification, I say, and not in the passion of desire, so that there may not even be desire, which is a passion and injury of the soul—as the Gentiles do, whom you ought not to resemble, because they are those who do not know God.

And I gave these [Col. 0300A] commandments so that no one may transgress by violence or defraud his brother by deceit in the private matter of a wife, or in any business. Therefore abstain from these things, because the Lord is avenger in all these matters, that is, in fornication, desire, adultery, or fraud. He is avenger, I say, as we foretold you and testified, that is, proved under the testimony of the Scriptures. For, as though he said, this is why these things must be avoided: God did not call us to uncleanness, namely, to serve uncleanness, but to sanctification, that is, to live holy lives. And because God called us not to uncleanness, therefore he who despises these things which we have foretold despises not merely a human being, but God, whose commandments they are, who speaks through my mouth, and who has also given [Col. 0300B] his Holy Spirit in us for their accomplishment.

[Ambrose] Therefore do not despise merely a hearer: he does not dwell in a body subject to sins. Or: “He gave his Holy Spirit in us,” the Apostles, that our authority to rebuke might be greater; it is not safe to act against that authority.

“But concerning brotherly love.” As though he said: It was necessary to write to you concerning the matters stated above; but concerning brotherly love, by which you love the brethren, we had no need to write to you. There was no need to write because you yourselves have been taught by God, that is, by Christ’s own command, saying: “I give you a new commandment” (John 13), “that you love one another.” Or: you have been taught by God through inspiration, or through effect, because he himself has had mercy upon us. And, moreover, there was no need, [Col. 0300C] because you do this, namely, the work of love, toward all the brethren throughout Macedonia.

“But we ask.” As though he said: You practise the work of love; nevertheless, we ask you, O brethren, to abound more in charity, and to make it your aim to be quiet, free from inquisitiveness. Notice that he says, “make it your aim.” As though he said: It is difficult to abandon a habit; nevertheless, compel yourselves also to attend to your own affairs, leaving aside those of others, which is beneficial for the reformation of your life. And work with your hands, which helps you to remain quiet; for that evil comes from idleness. Do these things, then, as we commanded you. Work with your hands so that you may walk honourably toward those outside, and desire nothing from anyone. As though he said: Work must be done, not [Col. 0300D] idleness practised, because it is honourable and like a light to unbelievers. And you will not desire another’s property, much less ask for or take anything.

### VERSES 12–17

> “But we do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve as do the rest, who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself, at a command, at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ will rise [Col. 0301A] first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in clouds to meet Christ in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words.”

“We do not want you,” etc. After exhorting them concerning continence and correcting their inquisitiveness, he confirms that the dead will rise, both through Christ’s resurrection and by his own authority. As though he said: Not only do we want you to know the things stated above, but we do not want you now to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, that is, the dead, because they will rise.

[Haimo] He rightly calls the dead “those who sleep,” because, like sleepers whole and intact, they will quickly rise from the sleep of death, so that you may not grieve inconsolably over the death of friends, as do the rest, that is, unbelievers, [Col. 0301B] who have no hope of resurrection and eternal incorruption. The Apostle admonishes us not to grieve over our beloved dead as do the rest who have no hope. He does not simply say, “that you may not grieve,” but adds, “as do the rest who have no hope,” that is, of resurrection. For it is necessary that you grieve; but when you grieve, let hope console you. For Scripture’s most true custom calls them “those who sleep,” so that, when we hear that they sleep, we may by no means despair that they will awaken.

There is, then, a certain sorrow over the dead whom we love, a sorrow that is in some way natural. Nature shrinks from death, and death would not have happened to humankind had not prior fault existed. Therefore we must be sad [Col. 0301C] when those whom we love leave us by dying. Even if we know that they do not leave us forever, but merely go before us for a little while, to be followed by us, nevertheless death itself—which nature recoils from—when it seizes one beloved, makes the affection of love within us sorrowful. Thus we grieve at the deaths of our own because we must lose them, but with the hope of receiving them again. From one side we are distressed; from the other, consoled. From one side weakness afflicts the mind; from the other, faith restores it. From one side the human condition pains us; from the other, the divine promise heals us.

One may ask how the Lord wept for a dead man whom, at his command, he was immediately to make alive. He did not weep for the dead man whom he himself raised, but for death, which humanity incurred by sinning. For if sin had not come first, death would undoubtedly not have followed. Thus [Col. 0301D] bodily death followed the death of the soul. The death of the soul came first by abandoning God, and the death of the body followed when the soul abandoned it. By the former, the soul voluntarily left God; by the latter, it was compelled unwillingly to leave the body. It is as though it were said to it: “You departed from him whom you ought to have loved; depart from that which you loved.” For who absolutely wishes to die? No one—and so completely no one that it was said to Peter: “Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21). If death had no bitterness, the courage of martyrs would not exist. Therefore he did not simply say, “that you may not grieve,” but added, “as do the rest who have no hope.”

Accordingly, the pomp of a funeral, the procession of mourners, [Col. 0302A] the costly care of burial, and the sumptuous construction of tombs are whatever consolations they may be for the living, not aids to the dead. But there must be no doubt that the dead are helped by the prayers of the holy Church, the saving sacrifice, and alms distributed for their souls, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins deserved. For the universal Church observes what has been handed down by the Fathers: that for those who died in the communion of the body and blood of the Lord, prayer is made when they are commemorated in their proper place at the sacrifice itself, and it is also recalled that the offering is made for them. When works of mercy are performed for the sake of commending them, who can doubt that these aid those for whom prayers are offered to God not in vain? It must not be doubted [Col. 0302B] that these things benefit the departed, but those only who lived before death in such a way that these things can be useful to them after death. For those who departed from their bodies without faith working through love and without its sacraments are vainly served by their own with such offices of piety, since while they were here they lacked faith’s pledge, storing up not mercy for themselves but wrath.

Therefore new merits are not acquired for the dead when their own do some good for them; rather, these subsequent things are rendered in accordance with their preceding merits. For nothing can be done once they have ceased to live here; and therefore, when each person ends this life, he cannot have after it anything except what he deserved in it. Let devout hearts, therefore, be permitted to grieve at the deaths of their beloved with a sorrow capable of healing, and [Col. 0302C] let them shed consolable tears because of the mortal condition; yet let the joy of faith restrain those tears, by which it is believed that the faithful, when they die, at last depart from us and pass into better things. Let there be care, according to one’s means, for burial and the building of tombs, since these are counted among good works in the Scriptures. Those who did such things were commended not only in relation to the bodies of the patriarchs and other saints, but even in relation to the Lord’s own body. Let people, therefore, perform these offices of the final duty toward their own, and these alleviations of their human grief. But let them bestow far more diligently and abundantly on behalf of the dead those things which assist their spirits: namely, offerings and distributions of alms.

[Note: [Col. 0301D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] For God could have granted believers [Col. 0302D] this, that they should not experience even the death of this body. But had he done so, a certain happiness would have been added to the flesh, while the strength of faith would have been diminished. For people would fear this death in such a way that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all. Consequently, no one would hasten to Christ’s glory for the sake of the life to come, but for the removal of death’s annoyance; and faith in Christ would thus in a manner be delicate and self-indulgent. Therefore he bestowed greater grace upon his faithful. For what great thing would it be to believe that one also would not die, when one saw that those who believed did not die? How much greater, stronger, and more praiseworthy it is to believe in such a way that one expects [Col. 0303A] to die, because one will live without end! Hence those dear to a person who survive can console him in the sorrow caused by a friend’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0303D] Augustine, Sermon on the Words of the Apostle.] What wonder if you grieve, when the body which lives by the soul becomes lifeless as the soul departs? He who walked lies down; he who spoke is silent; closed eyes receive no light; ears are opened by no voice; all the functions of the members have ceased. There is no one to move the feet for walking, the hands for working, the senses for perceiving. Is this not the house which some invisible inhabitant adorned? He who is not seen has departed; what remains can be seen with grief. This is the cause of sorrow; but the consolation for this sorrow is what follows:

“For if,” etc. As though he said: You ought not to grieve inconsolably, [Col. 0303B] because we believe that Jesus died. This seems to oppose resurrection, but consider what follows: “and rose again.” And if this is so, we ought to believe that just as Christ died and rose again, so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in death through Jesus, that is, in faith in Jesus. Or, “through Jesus” means those who, always following him, came to the sleep of death. As though he said: He will not only raise those who are found alive, but will also bring the dead about whom you doubt; and even if they have been reduced to ashes, he will bring them, so that they may be with him, immortal and in the same blessedness.

[Haimo] The Apostle says something remarkable: he calls Christ, who now lives and, having risen from the dead, dies no more, “dead”; but he calls the elect [Col. 0303C] who are dead “sleeping.” He calls Christ dead so that, when we hear that he died and rose, we too may hope that we shall rise through the power of his divinity. But he calls the elect sleeping because no one can so easily awaken a companion from sleep as all will be awakened from the sleep of death.

“For this.” As though he said: And truly he will bring them, for the order will be this: those found alive will not precede the dead, although you think that they, rather, are to be brought with Jesus. This is what he says: “For this we say to you by the word of the Lord,” because God taught us this: “that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord shall not precede,” by rising, “those who have slept for a long time.” That is, those among us who will be found alive, and who remain after all the preceding saints [Col. 0303D], or who will remain after the torments of Antichrist—and are therefore most worthy—will not precede the dead. So swift will the resurrection of the dead be.

Notice that he says, “we who are alive.” The Apostle’s words seem to mean that he indicated the day of judgement as coming in his own time. Thus the Thessalonians, reading this Epistle, thought that the day of judgement would come in the Apostle’s time. Hence another Epistle was written, in which he urges them not to be alarmed as though the day of the Lord were at hand. He therefore speaks in the person of the elect who will be found living in the body at the Lord’s coming; and he counts himself among those last ones [Col. 0304A] because he is one body with them, and the Apostles resemble those last ones in sufferings.

And truly those found alive will not precede the dead in resurrection; rather, the dead who are in Christ, that is, who rest again in Christ, will rise first. Christ can do this because he himself is Lord, and he himself will descend in his own person from heaven, locally; or “from heaven,” that is, from what is hidden. He will descend, I say, not humble as before, but with command, that is, with authority: commanding as Lord; and with a voice by which he will say, “Rise, dead!”—the voice, I say, of an archangel, namely, of his own archangel, or of angels, a voice which will cause the dead to rise. Of this voice he adds: “and with a trumpet.” For the great voice of angels will be the trumpet; it is called a trumpet because it will be manifest. Or [Col. 0304B] he is said to descend with a trumpet because he will come openly. Hence: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3).

[Ambrose] Or he says “with a trumpet” because he will come as to war, just as a trumpet sounds in battles, since then he will defeat his enemies; and just as a trumpet sounds for those attacked, so he will summon friends to the solemnity of eternal glory.

That voice, then, will be like a trumpet, awakening his own and terrifying the wicked; and that trumpet will be God’s, that is, Christ’s. Or it will be God’s because God will give it efficacy. I say that the dead will rise first; then we who are alive and remain, that is, those among us who will be alive and left over from Antichrist, will be caught up [202] by angels together with those [Haimo] who have gone before us to rest, in clouds, because clouds [Col. 0304C] will receive them—or us—as a cloud received Christ at his ascension.

[Ambrose] Hence another translator says: “We shall be caught up, with clouds as bearers.” We shall be caught up, I say, to meet Christ in the air. But in that very catching up there will be their death and resurrection, so that the soul, as though leaving the body in sleep, may be restored to it in the same instant.

[Augustine] Yet the Apostle seems, so far as the words are concerned, to affirm that some at the end of the age, when Christ comes and the resurrection of the dead takes place, will not die, but will be found alive and suddenly changed into immortality; but I would prefer to hear wiser persons concerning these words.

[Note: [Col. 0303D] Id., *The City of God*.] For it is commonly asked whether those whom Christ finds alive will never die at all, or whether, in the very instant in which they are caught up to meet Christ, they will pass with wondrous swiftness into immortality. For it must not be said to be impossible that, while borne aloft through the air in that interval, they should die and come to life again.

[Note: [Col. 0304D] Id., in the same work.] The Apostle seems to press us toward the view that those whom the Lord will find alive here will, in that brief interval, both suffer death and receive immortality, where he says: “In Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. 15). And elsewhere: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (ibid.). Why, then, should it seem incredible to us that this multitude of bodies should in some sense be sown in the air, and there immediately live again immortally [Col. 0305A] and incorruptibly, when we believe that the resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of the most ancient corpses will return, with such subtlety as might be called incalculable speed, into members destined to live without end? Nor do we consider them exempt from that sentence in which it was said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), that is, you shall go, having lost life, into that which you were before receiving life. Lifeless, you will be what you were before you were made living.

We, therefore, the elect, shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air, and thus—that is, having become immortal—we shall always be with the Lord. When he says, “and thus we shall always be with the Lord,” this should not be understood as though he had said that we shall always remain with the Lord in the air, for he himself will not remain there either. Rather, “thus” means: having everlasting [Col. 0305B] bodies, we shall always be with the Lord, wherever we are with him.

[Note: [Col. 0305D] Augustine, *On John*.] All souls, when they depart from the world, have different receptions: the good have joy; the wicked, torments. But when the resurrection has occurred, both the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they are tormented with the body.

“Therefore,” etc. As though he said: Because we shall all rise and be with Christ, therefore comfort one another concerning the death of friends, each person the other, with these words of so great a hope. Let sorrow perish where there is such consolation. Let mourning be wiped from the mind; let faith drive out pain. In so great a hope, God’s temple ought not to be sad; there the good Comforter dwells, there the Promiser who does not deceive. “Why,” you may say, “do we mourn a dead person for so long?” Because death is bitter; but the Lord too passed through [Col. 0305C] it. Let us therefore comfort ourselves. But you will say: “Can the human heart fail to feel sorrow for one most dear who has died?” Indeed, it is better for the human heart to be healed while it hurts than, by not hurting, to become inhuman. For Mary sought the Lord and mourned her dead brother.

## CHAPTER V

### VERSES 1–11

> “But concerning times and seasons, brethren, you have no need that we should write to you. For you yourselves know carefully that the day of the Lord comes just like a thief in the night. For when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, as pain upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape. But you, brethren, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you as a thief. [Col. 0305D] For you are all children of light and children of the day. We are not of the night nor of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night. But let us, who belong to the day, be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and charity, and the helmet, the hope of salvation; for God has not appointed us for wrath but for obtaining salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us, so that, whether we watch or sleep, we may live together with him. Therefore comfort one another and build each other up, as you also do.”

[Col. 0306A] “But concerning times.” [Haimo] As though he said: You needed me to write to you concerning the resurrection; but concerning the times, that is, of the Lord’s coming—whether in summer or winter, by day or by night—and concerning the seasons, namely, at what hour of day or night Christ will come, you have no need, O brethren, that I write to you, because I would write nothing except what you know: namely, that he will come secretly. This is what he says: “For you yourselves, by diligently searching the Scriptures, know that the day of the Lord,” that is, the time of the Lord’s coming, is called a day not because it is daytime, but because then all things will be revealed. And it is called the Lord’s because this is the day of human beings acting as they please, but then it will be God’s day in the power of judgement. That day, I say, will come so unexpectedly to the wicked—just as this also happens at each person’s death—like [Col. 0306B] a thief. It comes not in the day, but in the night, when it comes more secretly and people sleep; then it steals everything, so that one who thought himself rich while asleep, when he awakens finds nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0306D] Augustine, Letter to Hesychius.] So many who are quite secure will then find themselves to possess no good thing. For this reason he began to speak of times: to warn them to beware lest they be so caught. It is not necessary, then, to know after how long this will occur, but how it will occur, so that people may take care to be children of light and keep watch with hearts made ready, if they do not wish to be overtaken by that hour as by a thief in the night. For if, in order to avoid this evil—that is, lest the Lord’s hour find someone unprepared like a thief—it were necessary to know the intervals of time, the Apostle would not say that there was no need for him to write this; rather, he would judge that this ought especially to be written. But now he showed that those did not need it for whom it was sufficient to know that the Lord’s hour would come like a thief upon the unprepared and sleeping, and, knowing this, to keep watch.

[Col. 0306C] “For when,” [Augustine] as though he said: Truly he will come like a thief, because he will come unexpectedly. This is what he says: when carnal people—not withered by fear and expectation, but drenched in lust—say, “We have peace now in the present, and security concerning the future,” then sudden destruction will come upon them, that is, the sudden ruin of the day of judgement. For, as is found in the words of the prophet Daniel, Antichrist and his ministers will reign for three and a half years, and Elijah and Enoch will be killed by him, as is found in the Apocalypse. Then there will be such tribulation as has not been [Col. 0306D] before nor will be afterward. Then Antichrist and the greater part of his followers will be killed by Michael. After Antichrist’s death, forty days will be granted to the good who wavered during that persecution for repentance. But Antichrist’s ministers will rejoice during those days, taking wives, celebrating banquets, engaging in various kinds of games, and saying: “Although our prince is dead, now we have peace and security.” When they have said such things, destruction will come upon them as grievous and sudden as pain is to a woman, or to one having a child in the womb. She nevertheless escapes, but they will not escape eternal punishment.

“But you.” [Ambrose] As though he said: The Lord’s day will be unforeseen [Col. 0307A] for them, but not for you, because you, O brethren, are not in the darkness of ignorance and unbelief, so that that day may overtake you like a thief, unto eternal death.

[Haimo] And truly you are not in darkness, for you are all children of light, that is, of faith, and children of God, that is, of virtues. Faith is the light which makes day, that is, the habit of virtues; conversely, darkness is unbelief, and night is the habit of vices. Hence he adds: “And you are not children of night or of darkness.” He added this so that no one might think one could be partly of day and partly of night. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6).

[Ambrose] “Therefore let us not sleep,” etc. He warns us not, secure in the name of the Saviour, to act negligently. Therefore he fortifies us with three defences: faith, hope, and charity.

[Col. 0307B] As though he said: Since we are not children of death, therefore let us not sleep, that is, become sluggish in present things, as do the rest who are devoted to carnal things; but let us watch and be sober. That is, let our mind watch, attending to these passing things, and let us use them soberly, not as though they were our own goods, but as given for our support. For, as though he said, truly we who are not children of night ought not to sleep, because those who sleep with the lethargy of the flesh sleep at night, that is, their vices and sins have brought them to the point that, forgetful of eternal life, they rest in these things. And those who are drunk, using these times immoderately, are drunk at night, that is, they have these things from the night of vices; they have them through the night.

But we who belong to the day, that is, who shine in virtues, should not only watch but be sober, [Col. 0307C] using these things moderately and ready for battle against enemies. Let us be sober in this way: because we are clothed with the breastplate of faith and charity and the helmet, the hope of salvation. He rightly compares faith and charity to a breastplate, and hope to a helmet. For just as a breastplate guards the vital organs, so faith and charity guard you against the desire for earthly things. If we consider that Christ suffered for us, rose again, and prepared life for us—things that are like the connected hooks of faith—and if we also persist in charity, temporal desire will never conquer our minds. Moreover, hope of eternal salvation, tending upward like a helmet surrounding the mind, will not be wounded by temporal desire.

“For God has not,” as though he said: Truly through hope we shall come to salvation, because God has not appointed us for wrath, but for obtaining salvation. That is, God has not placed us in faith and hope so that we may have wrath, that is, eternal punishment, but so that we may obtain salvation through doing good works. For salvation will not be given to the idle. And this is through our Lord Jesus Christ, without whom neither hope nor salvation nor anything else would help us.

[Haimo] Christ died for us so that, whether we sleep—that is, if we have died—or watch, living in the flesh, we may live together with him, that is, joined to him in likeness. “Therefore,” that is, because this hope belongs to us, comfort one another in this misery, those grieving over the death of their own, and build up one another who are ignorant, [Col. 0308A] that is, each person the other, as you already do, so that you may do no less afterwards than you do now.

### Verses 12–22

“But we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who labour among you, who preside over you in the Lord, and who admonish you; that you may hold them in more abundant love because of their work, and be at peace with them. And we ask you, brothers, correct the disorderly, console the faint-hearted, support the weak, be patient toward all. See that no one repays evil for evil to anyone; but always pursue what is good, both toward one another and toward all. Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus in all of you. Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies. [Col. 0308B] But test all things; hold fast what is good; abstain from every appearance of evil.”

“But we ask you.” Up to this point he has spoken generally to all; now he addresses subordinates in particular, morally instructing them concerning the honour to be shown to prelates. [Haimo] As though he said: “All of you do what I have said; but you, lesser brethren, though you are subjects, we ask that you acknowledge—that is, show that you recognize—those who labour among you, that is, in governing and teaching you, and who preside over you in rank; and this in the Lord, that is, by the Lord’s appointment; and who, by the duty of their office, admonish you, so that you may be their equals in right conduct.” Recognize them in this manner, so that you may hold them in love more abundantly than others.

He wishes them to honour presbyters out of love, by supplying their necessities and by showing reverence to their rank. [Col. 0308C] [Ambrose] For what benefit is there in having honour without its practical fruit? Just as riches produce neglect of salvation, so poverty, while it seeks to be satisfied, turns aside from justice. Therefore, in another Epistle he commands that presbyters be honoured with double honour. And if they sometimes rebuke severely or impose punishment, be at peace with them because of their work—that is, knowing that their work requires what they do.

“We ask.” Here he admonishes prelates patiently to bear the wrongdoing and impatience of their subjects when they murmur against them in any matter. As though he said: “These things the lesser ought to do for their superiors; but we nevertheless ask you, prelates and superiors, who are still brethren, to do this: correct the disorderly—that is, the inquisitive and wandering about.” Whoever fails to do this, lest he lose what they used to give him, is a hireling. “And console the faint-hearted,” against adversities or when they despair because of sins; “and support those weak in faith,” as physicians do for healing. And if anything is inflicted upon you in this office, “be patient toward all”; and do not merely endure, but also “see that no one repays evil for evil to anyone.”

As though he said: “Do not withhold good in return for evil, so as to neglect correction.” [Note: [Col. 0307D] Augustine, *On Correction and Grace.*] For evil is then repaid for evil when one who should be corrected is not corrected, but is neglected through perverse connivance. But always, in prosperity and adversity alike, pursue what is good—that is, beneficial. Pursue it, I say, among yourselves mutually and toward all, even unbelievers. And do not merely endure, [Col. 0309A] but “rejoice always,” whatever may happen to you. Hence elsewhere: “Rejoicing in tribulation” (Rom. 12).

Or he says this generally to all: “Rejoice always” in hope, and “pray without ceasing” at fixed hours, even for persecutors. [Haimo] Or, “pray without ceasing,” that is, always live justly and desire eternal things. For a just person never ceases to pray unless he ceases to be just. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Augustine, on Psalm 38.] The person who always acts well always prays. For good desire itself is prayer; and if desire is continual, prayer too is continual. And “in all things,” even adverse things, give thanks to God. For doing all these things is the will of God—that is, it pleases God. I mean the will shown in Christ Jesus, because God taught this through Christ. Or this will of God is shown in Christ, because these things were in [Col. 0309B] Christ Jesus, in whom nothing was displeasing through Jesus Christ. It was not merely shown here, but also fulfilled, in all of you, both superiors and inferiors.

And because it is God’s will that all these things be done, therefore you superiors, who through the Holy Spirit have the gift of understanding, “do not quench the Spirit”—that is, do not conceal the gift of the Holy Spirit, through which you would deservedly lose it yourselves. Another reading agrees with this sense: “Do not conceal grace.” And you subjects, do not despise their prophecies. See what he said: “the Spirit.”

[Ambrose] Or, “do not quench the spirit”: when the Holy Spirit reveals something for the moment, do not prevent someone from saying what he perceives. [Haimo] For God, who opened the mouth of the ass, often reveals through a lesser person what is better. [Augustine] Or, “do not quench the Holy Spirit”—that is, do not exclude him from yourselves by evil deeds. [Note: [Col. 0309D] Augustine, to Boniface.] He does not say this because the Holy Spirit, who is of one substance with the Father and the Son, can be extinguished; rather, insofar as it lies in them, those who act in such a way as to wish him extinguished are deservedly called his extinguishers. Therefore, we quench the Holy Spirit given to us, not as he is in himself, but in ourselves, when by sinning we drive him away from us.

“And do not despise prophecies.” [Haimo] That is, if someone explains the sayings of the prophets and preaches for edification, do not despise or scorn him; nevertheless, do not receive everything indiscriminately. But “test”—that is, examine by reason—all things which are to be tested; for things that are certain do not require examination. And “hold fast what is good,” that is, what is found to be [Col. 0309D] good; “and abstain from every appearance of evil,” that is, from everything which presents the appearance of evil, such as a distorted exposition. As though he said: “If someone presents the appearance of evil, even if it is not evil, do not act rashly.”

[Ambrose] For the spirit of the world is accustomed deceitfully to say good things and, among them, to introduce corrupt things, so that through those things which are good, evil things too may be accepted. Therefore he admonishes them to test all things and to retain whatever is said soberly and well.

### Verses 23–28

“May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly; and may your entire spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord [Col. 0310A] Jesus Christ. Faithful is he who called you, who will also do it. Brothers, pray for us. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord that this Epistle be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

“May the God of peace himself.” As though he said: “I thus admonish prelates and subjects; but may God himself, the giver of peace”—[Haimo] as though he said, “he who can remove disorder”—“sanctify you wholly,” through everything that I have taught, in such a way, namely, that your spirit—of which elsewhere it is said, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4), that is, the mind which serves the law of God—may be preserved entire. That is, may your reason remain unimpaired, by not consenting to the flesh; and may this continue until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, until [Col. 0310B] the end of your life.

And may the soul—that is, the sensitive faculty—be preserved sound, by serving reason; and may the body be preserved blameless, so that you do nothing through its agency of which anyone may complain. [Ambrose] He mentions these three so that the whole human being may be perfect. For sometimes the soul is defiled by an evil thought, while the entire body remains clean; therefore he says that the spirit in a human being must be clean. But if an evil life or thought intervenes, the spirit will not be entire.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Id., in the book *On Perfection.*] Notice that he says “blameless,” not “without sin.” For being without sin is one thing—said in this life only of the Only-begotten One; being blameless is another—something which could be said even in this life of many righteous people, since there is a manner of good life concerning which no just complaint can arise even in this present conduct. For who can rightly complain of a person who wishes evil to no one, faithfully provides for those whom he can help, and harbours no desire to retaliate for anyone’s injuries—so that he may truthfully say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6)?

[Note: [Col. 0310D] Id., in the sermon on the Creed.] Yet precisely by saying here that he is not without sin, he makes this clear. “For we all stumble in many things” (Jas. 3). Again, note that he names the three elements of which a human being consists: spirit, soul, and body—namely, that by which we understand, that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and tangible. These are also called two, because the soul is often named together with the spirit.

[Haimo] Or “spirit” here stands for the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The sense is: “May he sanctify [Col. 0310D] you in such a manner that your spirit may be entire”: that is, that the grace of the Holy Spirit given you in baptism may be kept whole and undefiled, lest it be corrupted, diminished, or driven away by your fault and uncleanness. [Ambrose] For when a person does what the Holy Spirit hates, his grace entirely departs from him, or is diminished. May the soul be kept pure, and the body blameless, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Faithful.” As though he said: “I pray that he may sanctify you and preserve you when sanctified; nor should this be doubted, because God is faithful”—that is, true in his promises—“who called you to life, who will also do it in you”: that is, complete the work of grace by fulfilling his promises. “Brothers, pray for [Col. 0311A] us. Greet on our behalf all the brothers with a holy kiss,” not feigned but holy, which is a sign of love. Greet them, I say, and show them the Epistle. And therefore “I adjure you by the Lord” that “this Epistle be read to all the holy brothers,” that is, those sanctified in baptism. Or, “holy,” that is, perfect, so that they may profit from it, and that you may advance in good works. “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.”

## 204. On the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians

[Col. 0311]

## Argument

[Col. 0311A]

The Apostle writes a second Epistle to the Thessalonians and informs them concerning the last times [Col. 0311B] and the overthrow of the Adversary. He writes this Epistle from Athens through Titus the deacon and Onesimus the acolyte.

## Chapter One

### Verses 1–12

“Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy, to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith grows exceedingly and the love of every one of you toward one another abounds; so that we ourselves glory in you among the churches of God for your patience and faith, and in your works, persecutions, and tribulations [Col. 0311C] which you endure, as an example of the righteous judgment of God, so that you may be considered worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer—if indeed it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give rest with us to you who are afflicted—at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire, inflicting vengeance upon those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. They shall suffer eternal penalties in destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be made wonderful in all who have believed, because our testimony concerning you was believed on that day. For this reason we also always pray for you [Col. 0311D] that our God may deem you worthy of his calling and fulfil every good purpose of his goodness and the work of faith in power, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and Lord Jesus Christ.”

“Paul and Silvanus,” etc. The Apostle again writes this Epistle to the Thessalonians. Since a more severe tribulation had arisen among the Greeks, he again exhorts them to patience, showing God’s righteous judgment: that the good may attain glory and the evil punishment.

[Ambrose] And because in the first Epistle he said certain things about the Lord’s coming and the resurrection of the dead, from which it was thought that the day of the Lord was imminent, he now writes another Epistle in which he signifies the same matters, although obscurely. For he cannot openly speak of the abolition of the Roman kingdom, the appearance and condemnation of Antichrist, and the disorderliness of certain brothers. He also writes that the day of the Lord is not imminent, as it had seemed on the occasion of the earlier Epistle.

[Haimo] When the Thessalonians, while reading the former Epistle, came to the place where the Apostle says, “The dead in Christ shall rise first at his coming; then we who are alive, who have been raised, shall be caught up together with them,” they were troubled and greatly terrified. They thought that the day of the Lord was near and feared that, because they had come late to the faith and were imperfect, they would be condemned with the devil. Having learned this, therefore, he wrote to them that the day of judgment would not come in their own time, lest the Apostle be rejected altogether as a liar in this matter, or lest the devil deceive those awaiting it by some fraud. He also rebukes the disorderly more sharply.

The Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle is to exhort the good and quiet to patience, correct the disorderly, and here somewhat clarify things which he had said obscurely in the preceding Epistle. Its method is as follows: first he greets them; then he gives thanks for their good qualities; afterwards he exhorts them to patience and steadfastness. Then he asserts that Antichrist precedes Christ’s coming, and announces certain, though obscure, signs of Christ’s coming, treating of the abolition of the Roman kingdom and the slaying of Antichrist. Near the end he urges them to correct the inquisitive and idle. He begins his greeting by saying: “Paul, and Silvanus, and Timothy.”

[Ambrose] These are the three in whose name this and the first Epistle are written. They write to the church of the Thessalonians, existing [Col. 0312D] in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. As usual, before anything else he greets them: “Grace be to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.” These matters have been explained above.

[Note: [Col. 0311D] Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will.*] “We give thanks.” Here he gives thanks to God for their good qualities, lest they perhaps be exalted over so great a good which they had from God as though they possessed it from themselves. As though he said: “Hold fast what you have, because it is good; for it we ought always to give thanks to God, and we can never do so worthily.” This is what he says: “Brothers, we must always give thanks to God for you,” from whom these good things come, not from you. I say, give thanks as is fitting, because great thanks ought to be given for great goods.

We ought to give thanks to God because your faith grows exceedingly—that is, beyond what it once was, it grows more and more and does not diminish amid tribulations. And the love of every one of you abounds toward one another, so that the one who is loved may love others, and may show love by mutual services. It grows, I say, and so—that is, it grows to such an extent that we apostles ourselves, who would not glory in a small matter, glory in—that is, concerning—you among the churches of God, to which we offer you as an example. Take care not to become examples of failure. We glory in you, I say, especially for your patience and faith, preserved amid all your persecutions—which are from place to place—and tribulations, that is, torments. You endure these tribulations and persecutions as an example of the righteous judgment of God: that is, these tribulations show what should be given in the future judgment to those who endure and to those who inflict them. [Col. 0313B] For if God punishes sins so severely in the repentant, what will he do to the hardened?

[Note: [Col. 0313D] Augustine, *Against Faustus.*] Therefore he says that the afflictions of the righteous are an example of God’s righteous judgment, so that it may be understood that he will not spare the ungodly, like branches cut off for burning, when he does not spare the righteous, for the completion of their purification. Hence Peter says: “If judgment begins with us, what end will there be for those who do not believe? And if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4).

“You endure,” I say, so that you may be considered worthy—that is, glorious among others—in the kingdom of God, that is, eternal blessedness, or in the present Church which he governs here. [Haimo] And therefore it is called the kingdom of God, for which—that you may be worthy—you not only do good works but [Col. 0313C] also suffer evils. “Of righteous judgment,” I say, “if indeed it is just,” etc.—which is certainly the case.

[Ambrose] Here “if indeed” is not used to express doubt, but affirmation. As though he said: “Because it is just.” Hence another translator says: “Since indeed it is just.” As though he said: “I rightly say ‘righteous judgment,’ since indeed it is just with God”—that is, in the simple and pure nature of God’s justice—“to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give rest with us,” that is, rest equal to ours, “to you who are afflicted.” For what is more just than that those who in this world oppress the good and afflict them with persecutions should suffer in the future what they do, while those who have suffered great affliction for the eternal kingdom should be at rest?

Or thus: “which you endure,” and he is speaking of the present judgment, by which God permits evil people to afflict the good and prosper, while he causes the good to suffer adversities. As though he said: “We glory in your patient endurance of the tribulations which you bear as an example of the righteous judgment of God.” That is, we glory because you endure in such a way that you are an example and instruction to others that God judges justly when he permits his own people to be afflicted and evil people to prosper. For they see you advance from bad things to better things, while those people become worse through prosperity. Thus you are an example to them, lest they become weary when corrected by God, who “scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12), with whom it is just that judgment should begin from his household. Hence Peter says: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” (ibid.), “so that you may be considered worthy [Col. 0314A] of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer.” This does not change.

“If indeed.” As though he said: “I speak of righteous judgment, which may also be seen in respect to present matters, when the good become better and the evil worse. Yet I say ‘righteous judgment’ under this condition: if indeed it is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and rest with us to you who are afflicted.” As though he said: “The judgment by which God judges in the present appears just if the future judgment is considered, where God’s justice is manifestly plain to all when he renders to each according to merits; and by this the present things are finally proved just—namely, if it is just that punishment be given to them and rest to you.” For whoever considers this end does not say that it is unjust for the good to be purified and the evil to become defiled, as each has deserved from his life. David says something similar: “I considered in order to understand this; it was labour before me, until I entered into the sanctuary of God and understood their latter end” (Ps. 72). Yet it can also be seen from present things. Hence he adds: “Nevertheless, because of their deceits you set them in slippery places; you cast them down when they were lifted up” (ibid.).

“At the revelation.” Here he begins to show how dreadful the tribulation awaiting those people will be and how delightful the rest awaiting these people. [Haimo] As though he said: “It is just to give punishment to them and rest to you; and this will surely happen at the revelation”—that is, the manifestation—“of the Lord Jesus,” coming from heaven to judgment with the angels of his power: that is, with angels through whose ministry God’s power will appear, as they choose the good and cast the evil outside. Then there will be glory for these and terror for those.

I mean the Lord Jesus coming “in a flame of fire,” not because he will be surrounded by flame, but in effect, because he will burn his enemies. [Col. 0314C] Or he says “in a flame of fire” because there will be a fire in the world preceding him, occupying as much space in the air as the water occupied in the Flood; it will burn the earth and its gross substance and purify the elect.

I mean the Lord Jesus “inflicting”—that is, bringing—vengeance upon those who do not know God: those who have not received the faith, such as pagans; and upon those who do not obey the Gospel—which ought to be obeyed because it is the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ: that is, those who do not carry out what they have received, such as heretics and false Christians.

[Haimo] For some do not know the law, while others know it. Then he intensifies their punishments, adding: “Who”—both those who know and those who do not know, [Col. 0314D] namely—“shall suffer penalties,” that is, endure them. For “to give” is sometimes used for “to endure,” and this usage is fitting here. A person who suffers gives penalties to the one whom he offended, as it were, pleasing penalties. They shall suffer penalties, I say, not ones ending with the dissolution of body and soul, but eternal penalties in destruction, because they will always feel punishments yet will not entirely perish. I mean that they will then be removed from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power, so that they may not see him and the glory which his power will give to the saints.

And these things foretold will happen when Christ comes to be glorified in his saints, for he will glorify them so that he appears glorious in them. Behold the glory of the saints. And when he comes to be made wonderful in all, even the lesser ones, who believed though they did not have time to work. For he himself will appear bright and wonderful in believers; but he will appear severe to unbelievers when he confines them in eternal punishments.

The brief sense of these words is this: he will come to punish the evil and glorify the good, “because [it] was believed.” As though he said: “Therefore he will give rest with us to you who are afflicted, because our testimony concerning the day”—that is, concerning that day of the Lord’s revelation—“was believed on that day”: that is, you believed whatever we said concerning that day of judgment, the glory of the good, and the punishment of the evil.

[Haimo] Or, “our testimony was believed on that day,” that is, for the sake of that day, so that you may then be delivered. It was believed, I say, “concerning you,” although it was beyond human understanding. Or it was believed in such a manner that it was over you—that is, ruling you—while you did not seek a reason for it.

“For this reason also.” The order of the words is: “On that day, we also always pray for you, that our God may deem you worthy of his calling”: that is, that God may judge you worthy, whom he calls to the kingdom through grace. Or thus: “For this reason,” that is, to avoid the danger of that day, “we also always pray for you”; for the danger of that day must always be avoided by prayer. And we pray that our God may deem you worthy of his calling. This does not change.

And we also pray that meanwhile he may fulfil every purpose of goodness: that is, fully make you willing to will every good thing; and fulfil in you the work of faith, that is, confession, which properly is the work of faith. I say, fulfil it in you “in power” of constancy, namely, so that he may give the constancy by which those who possess it cannot in any way be turned from confession. Or the work of faith is every good thing which faith requires. Thus, “fulfil the work of faith” means fulfil all good things without which faith is dead. And do this in the power of perseverance, namely, that he may give you perseverance to the end.

May it be fulfilled in such a way that the name of the Lord Jesus Christ is glorified in you in this life by widespread renown and honour, and that you are glorified in him in the future; and this not according to your merits, but according to the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, beyond what you deserve, or as the man Christ was glorified.

## Chapter Two

### Verses 1–5

“But we ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly moved from your understanding, nor be alarmed, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by an Epistle purportedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent. Let no one deceive you in any way. For unless the falling-away comes first and the man of sin, the son of perdition, is revealed—he who opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God—you do not remember that, while I was still with you, I told you these things?”

“But we ask you.” [Ambrose] Up to this point he has said that he gives thanks and prays for them; here he determines the matter of the day of judgment, beseeching them not lightly and readily to adopt an opinion about the Lord’s coming as though it were imminent, nor to be alarmed.

[Haimo] As though he said: “Not only do we pray for you, but we also ask you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ to judgment”—that is, if you wish Christ’s future coming to benefit you—“and by the coming of our gathering,” namely that of all the saints—that is, if you wish to be in our gathering. I mean the gathering that will come or tend “to him,” that is, to Christ, so that the eagles may be gathered to the body. Or “to him” means into unity, so that we may be united in mind and body, though now we tend in different directions.

What do we ask? “That you not be quickly moved from your understanding,” that is, from sound understanding. As though he said: “Do not even waver slightly.” For if you are quickly moved, it is because nothing is brought upon you that will last long, since the time is near. “Nor be alarmed.” As though he said: “At the prospect of nearby danger,” that is, “as though the day of the Lord were imminent.”

I say, “Do not be alarmed,” either by an evil spirit: namely, if an evil spirit appearing as an angel of light persuades you of this in a vision; or if someone says that he has learned by a revelation of the Holy Spirit that the day of judgment is imminent. Do not believe it. Nor be alarmed by the speech of some false apostle who expounds this from the Scriptures, nor by an Epistle purportedly sent by us—that is, sent under my name.

[Ambrose] For deceivers are accustomed, in order to mislead, to forge an Epistle under the name of some distinguished man, so that the authority of the name may recommend what could not be accepted on its own account. What does he mean in each case? “Let no one deceive you in any way,” also by some means other than those mentioned, alarming you as though the day of the Lord were imminent.
