[Note: [Col. 0315D] Augustine, to Hesychius.] Not that he does not wish them to be prepared, having their loins girded and lamps burning in their hands, awaiting the Lord’s return from the wedding. For a person’s last day finds each person in the condition in which the world’s last day will overtake him; because as each dies on his own day, so he will be judged on that day. Therefore every Christian must keep watch lest the Lord’s coming find him unprepared. But that day will find unprepared the person whom the final day of this life finds unprepared.

[Ambrose] Therefore he does not merely say, “Do not be alarmed” or “Do not be deceived,” [Col. 0316D] but adds, “as though the day of the Lord were imminent.” He says this lest, in that very disturbance, when they were caught off guard, they should run to pray to the devil. The devil did these things in order that, appearing under Christ’s name, he might cause himself to be worshipped. So that the utterly shameless Satan might not be able to do this, the Apostle sets out in writing the time and signs of the Lord’s coming: the Lord will not come before the Roman kingdom has fallen and Antichrist has appeared.

[Augustine] This is what he adds:

“For unless.” As though he said: “Some wish to deceive you as though the day of the Lord were imminent, but the day of the Lord is not imminent.” [Haimo] For the Lord will not come to judgment unless the departure comes first: that is, unless a nation first departs [Col. 0317A] from the Roman empire; not that the Lord comes immediately afterwards. He speaks covertly concerning the destruction of the Roman empire, lest perhaps, if he said this openly, he should incite them to persecute the Church. Or he says this concerning the spiritual authority of the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] Augustine, *The City of God.*] Or it means departure from the faith. The sense is: “The Lord will not come to judgment unless there first comes the departure of churches from spiritual obedience to the Roman Church, or of people from the faith.”

[Haimo] Some manuscripts have: “Unless the renegade comes first,” which no one doubts was said of Antichrist, whom he calls a renegade, certainly from the Lord God. For if this can deservedly be said of all the impious, how much more of this one? Describing him, he adds: “and unless there is revealed”—that is, made manifest—“the man of sin,” whose hope now precedes him; wholly a man, not God; the servant, author, and fountain of sin: that is, Antichrist, who is “the son of perdition,” that is, the son of the devil who destroys human beings, through whom destruction came into the world. Antichrist is called his son not by nature but by imitation. Or he is called “the son of perdition” because he himself is to perish and destroys others.

He opposes Christ and his members; hence he is called Antichrist. And he “exalts himself”—that is, raises himself—above everything called God, either by false opinion, such as the gods of the Gentiles, or by reason of a benefit, such as saints; or above what is worshipped, such as God the Trinity. I say, he exalts himself so that he sits in the temple of God, that is, in the Church. Or in the temple destroyed by the Romans, which the Jews will then rebuild.

Antichrist will indeed be born in Babylon from the tribe of Dan, according to Jacob’s saying: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path” (Gen. 49). When he comes to Jerusalem, he will circumcise himself, saying to the Jews: “I am the promised Christ.” Then all the Jews will flock to him and rebuild the temple destroyed by the Romans; and he will sit there, saying that he is God.

Or thus: some wish this passage to be understood not only of the ruler himself but of his entire body—that is, the multitude of people belonging to him together with their ruler. They think it more correct to say, as in Greek, not that he “sits in the temple,” but that he “sits as the temple of God”: that is, as if he and his followers were themselves the temple of God, which is the Church; just as one says “he sits as a friend,” that is, in the capacity of a friend. I say, he sits, showing himself as though he himself [Col. 0317D] were God. For just as all the fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ, so in Antichrist fullness of malice and all iniquity will dwell; because in him will be the head of all evils, namely the devil, who is king over all the children of pride (Job 41).

### Verses 6–7

“And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For already the mystery of iniquity is at work; only let him who now restrains continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst.”

## 206. “Do you not,” etc.

As though he said: “You ought to believe what I write to you, because I formerly told you the same things.” This is what he says in question form: “Do you not remember that, while I was still with you, I told you”—in personal speech—“these same things which I now write to you in the Epistle concerning Antichrist’s coming and the day of judgment?”

“And what.” As though he said: “You remember these things; and you also know what now restrains Antichrist”—that is, what delays him, what is the cause of his postponement, why he has not yet come—namely, because the departure has not yet occurred. I say, he restrains him in such a way that he may be revealed—that is, made manifest—in his own time, that is, a time fitting for him and appointed by God, namely after the departure has occurred.

[Haimo] Therefore he rightly says, “in his own time.” [Berengar] For when the accession to the Roman empire and to obedience to the Roman Church has been completed, the departure from both authorities will occur; when that has been fulfilled, the lawless one—that is, Antichrist—will appear. Likewise, when the time of mercy has been completed, during which the fullness of the Gentiles enters [Col. 0318B] the faith, the departure from the faith will be revealed, when the love of many grows cold and iniquity abounds; then Antichrist will come, and thus the day of the Lord will be imminent.

“For the mystery.” As though he said: “He will indeed be revealed in his own time, because already, before his own time, the mystery of iniquity—that is, hidden iniquity—is at work”: that is, evil and hypocritical people who are in the Church. [Augustine] As though he said: “Already in the first beginnings of the accession, iniquity is found, but mystically—that is, covered with the name of piety—so that they wish to be considered ministers of Christ when they are false ones.”

Or thus: “He will indeed be revealed. For the devil is already at work in the mystery of iniquity.” [Haimo] *Mysterium* is Greek; in Latin it means “hidden” and “secret.” [Augustine] Therefore he calls the killing [Col. 0318C] of the saints and the persecution which Nero, their ruler, inflicted upon Christ’s faithful people the “mystery of iniquity”; Nero’s deeds already seemed like those of Antichrist.

[Haimo] It is called a mystery because even then the devil was secretly working through Nero and others in killing martyrs, just as he will then work openly through Antichrist in killing Elijah, Enoch, and many others. [Ambrose] This mystery of iniquity began with Nero, who, at the prompting of his father the devil and out of zeal for idols, killed the apostles. Nero and the others are a shadow of the one to come, namely Antichrist, just as Abel and David were figures of Christ.

Only that he who now restrains, etc. [Note: [Col. 0318D] Id., *City of God*.] Because he said that they knew what restrains, he does not explain it openly. Therefore we, who do not know what they knew, desire—yet are unable—to arrive, with effort, at what the Apostle meant, especially since the things he added make the meaning still more obscure. For what is this: “Only the mystery of iniquity is already at work, until he who now restrains shall restrain, until he is taken out of the way”? Thus I confess that I entirely do not know what he said; nevertheless I shall not conceal the conjectures of men which I have been able to read or hear.

Some conjecture that this was said of the Roman Empire, and that for this reason the Apostle did not wish to write it openly, lest he incur the accusation that he wished ill to the Roman Empire, which was expected to be eternal. Accordingly, they understand his saying, “For the mystery of iniquity is already at work,” to mean Nero, whose deeds already appeared like those of Antichrist. Hence some suspect that Nero himself will rise again and become Antichrist. Others think that he was not even killed, but rather removed, so that he might be thought killed; and that he is concealed alive, in the vigor of the same age in which he was when believed extinct, until in his own time he is revealed and restored to the kingdom. But this great presumption of those who hold such views seems very strange to me.

Yet what he says, “Only that he who restrains,” etc., is not unreasonably believed to have been said of the Roman Empire, until it is removed. The sense is: Only this remains before that lawless one is revealed: that he who now holds the Roman Empire may hold it—that is, that he who now rules may continue to rule—until it is taken out of the way, that is, until that power is removed from the midst of the world, because people from every quarter flowed together to Rome as to their head.

Or thus: only this remains, that he who now holds the faith may hold it, until the faith itself is taken out of the way—that is, until it grows cold.

Or thus: only this remains, that what now holds—namely, the accession to the faith—may hold him back, that is, restrain him, until it is taken out of the way, that is, until that accession itself is removed from the midst.

Or thus: only this remains, that what now holds—namely, the iniquity which is now hidden—may hold him back, that is, restrain him, until the iniquity which is now mystical becomes something ordinary and common: so that a man is no more ashamed to commit adultery, to steal, and to do other such things than he is ashamed to walk or speak.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] Augustine, on the same passage.] Or thus: Some think this was said concerning the evil and hypocritical persons who are in the Church, until they reach [Col. 0319C] such a number as to form for Antichrist a great people. They say that this was called “the mystery of iniquity” because it appears hidden; and that the statement “you know what restrains,” etc., refers to this, when he says, “that he who holds may hold.” They say that the Apostle exhorts the faithful to persevere steadfastly in the faith which they hold, until the mystery of iniquity, now hidden, goes out from the midst of the Church.

The sense is: Only this remains to be done: that he who now holds the faith may hold it—that is, may persevere firmly in it—until the mystery of iniquity is taken out of the way; that is, until those who are now hypocrites in the Church openly depart from it. Of such people Jesus says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2). Therefore, just as many heretics departed from the midst of the Church before the faith, so now all who belong not to Christ but to that final Antichrist will openly depart from it. [Col. 0319D]

Or thus: only this remains, that what now restrains him—namely, the apostasy which has not yet occurred—may restrain him, until that apostasy itself comes out into the open, that is, becomes manifest.

## Verses 8–16

> “And then that lawless one shall be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming; whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with every power, and signs, and lying wonders, and with every deception of iniquity for those who perish, because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved. Therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe lies, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity. But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brethren beloved by God, because God chose us as firstfruits for salvation, in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth; in which also he called you through our Gospel, for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, brethren, stand firm and hold the traditions which you learned, whether by word or by our letter. Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope in grace, exhort your hearts and establish you in every good work and word.” [Col. 0320A–B]

And then—namely, once the departure from the true God has been revealed and the love of many has grown cold, because of the abundance of iniquity, as though a seat had been prepared for him—that lawless one, namely Antichrist, will be revealed, that is, made manifest. He is not to be feared, either now or then, because it follows: “Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth,” that is, with the power of the Holy Spirit, who is called the breath of his mouth because he proceeds from him.

Or: he will slay him by the breath of his mouth, that is, by command and power, namely the force of his command—whether he kills him himself or through Michael. [Haimo] As the teachers relate, he will be killed on the Mount of Olives, in his pavilion and upon his throne, in that place from which the Lord ascended into heaven. After he has been killed, Christ will not come immediately; rather, as is understood from the book of Daniel, forty-five days will be granted to the elect for repentance. How long after that the Lord will come is wholly unknown.

And as the darkness is driven away by the sun’s presence, so the Lord will destroy him—namely Antichrist with all his members—by saying: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 24). He will destroy him, I say, by the brightness of his coming, that is, at his manifest coming. The coming of this Antichrist is according to the working of Satan, because, prompted and assisted by the devil, who will possess him entirely, he will do all these things. Yet he will not be devoid of reason as madmen are, who bear no blame for their evil acts; for if he were afflicted by the devil like a madman, whatever he did would not be imputed to him.

His coming will be [Col. 0320D] in every power of human authority and wealth; with lesser signs and greater wonders, but false ones. For by magical art he will not perform these things truly, but will deceive men by illusion, as Simon Magus deceived the man who, thinking that he was beheading Simon, beheaded a ram in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] Id., *City of God*.] These are also called lies because they confirm a lie—namely, that he is God. It is therefore commonly asked whether they are called lies because they will not be real as they appear, but phantasmal—that is, because he will deceive mortal senses by apparitions, so that he seems to do what he does not do—or because, even if they are real by God’s permission, they will lead to falsehood.

[Augustine] Then [Col. 0321A] Satan will be loosed, and through him Antichrist will work in all his power, wonderfully indeed, but deceitfully. His coming will be with every deception of iniquity for those who perish, because by threats, flatteries, and every other means he will deceive those devoted to perdition.

“Because”—that is, for this reason—“they did not receive the love of the truth,” namely Christ, in whom all the promises are fulfilled; that is, because they did not receive Christ, who showed love to all and fulfilled the truth. [Haimo] They did not receive that love by which, once received, they might be saved.

[Augustine] And therefore, because they did not receive the truth, God “will send them”—that is, permit to come upon them—an operation of error, namely him who is evil itself, because he is the father of all wickedness and iniquity, so that they may believe the lie, namely that Antichrist is God. Thus all who did not believe the truth—that is, Christ, who is truly God—but consented to iniquity, namely to Antichrist openly at last, may be judged; though meanwhile they are judged secretly.

Hence he says: “God will send them,” etc. Because God permits the devil to do these things by his own just judgment, although the devil does them with an unjust and malicious purpose, those who have been judged will be deceived, and those deceived will be judged. But, having been judged by God’s secretly just and justly hidden judgment, they will be deceived. Those who have been deceived, however, will be judged in the final and manifest judgment by Christ, who will judge most justly and has been judged most justly.

“But we.” As though he said: Thus it will be with them; but you will come to salvation, because [Col. 0321C] you received the truth. Therefore we give thanks to God. This is what he says: “But we, brethren beloved by God, ought always to give thanks to God for you, because from eternity God chose us and you as firstfruits of faith,” so that we might believe in Christ and confess the faith not in the perilous final time, but in the primitive Church.

[Haimo] He chose us, I say, for eternal salvation. Or: he chose us apostles as the firstfruits of all believers, because the apostles believed first. And this was for the salvation of all nations. I say that he chose us and you in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit sanctifies in baptism, and in faith in the truth, namely Christ. How they came to faith, however, he then states: Into this faith, just as he chose us freely from eternity, so also freely he called us, though turned away, [Col. 0321D] through our Gospel.

He called us, I say, for the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ: that through faith you may obtain the glory which Christ has. Or, “for the obtaining of our Lord Jesus Christ,” that you may be an acquisition in which Christ is glorified.

“Therefore.” As though he said: Since these blessings belong to us and the day of the Lord is not imminent, therefore, brethren, stand immovable in faith. And in order that you may stand, hold the traditions which you learned from us, even to understanding, whether through present speech or through our letter.

“Now may he himself.” As though he said: I exhort you. But may our God, Jesus Christ himself, and God the Father—his and ours—who is called God by the power whereby he is Creator of all things, and Father by affection, that is, by the sweetness of love, [Col. 0322A] who loved us by giving his Son for us—may he exhort you. Hence he adds: “And gave eternal consolation,” namely Christ, who is consolation to us against the misery of this present age and in the age to come. Or, he gave eternal consolation by promising the kingdom of heaven. And he gave good hope: namely, that from this exile we shall come to our homeland. And this “in grace,” that is, through the grace which he gave, we hope. Or, he gave all these things not by our merit but by his grace. May he, I say, who has already done so many things, exhort your hearts—that is, your wills—and strengthen them against opponents in every good work and good word.

## Chapter III

## Verses 1–18

> “Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of God may run and be glorified, as it is also among you; and that we may be delivered from importunate and evil men. For faith does not belong to all. But the Lord is faithful, who will strengthen you and guard you from evil. And we have confidence concerning you in the Lord, brethren, that you both do and will do whatever we command. May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and the patience of Christ.
>
> “Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, to withdraw yourselves from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: for we were not disorderly among you; neither did we eat bread from anyone without payment, but labored and toiled, working night and day, lest we burden any of you. Not because we did not have the right, but that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitating us. For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat. For we have heard that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work, but meddling in other people’s affairs. Now those who are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they may eat their own bread. But you, brethren, do not grow weary in doing good. If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that person, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.
>
> “Now may the God of peace give you everlasting peace in every place. The Lord be with you all. The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s—which is the sign in every letter: so I write. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” [Col. 0322B–D]

Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of God—that is, the Gospel which God gave us, or which concerns God—may run without hindrance to all nations, so that many may be swiftly converted; and may be glorified, that is, become clear and intelligible to people. Let it run, I say, as it has run among you.

[Ambrose] He exhorts them to pray that God may deign to direct his teaching in an untiring course, and pour it through the mouths of the apostles into the ears of hearers, [Haimo] and [Col. 0323A] from their ears into their hearts, so that it may restrain and calm the disturbances caused by evil people. Hence he adds: “And that we may be delivered from men,” namely from false teachers, lest they deceive us or lay snares for us—from importunate men, that is, shameless in disputation, and evil men, because they preach falsehood.

Or: that we may be delivered from importunate men, namely unbelievers, who resist the word of truth and do not remain in the harbor of peace, and from evil men, namely those who persecute the faithful. I say that we should be delivered, for faith does not belong to all: that is, not all have yet received the faith through me who are to receive it.

Or thus: they truly are importunate and evil. For faith does not belong to all of them: that is, not all importunate persons have faith, because none of them has faith; what they hold is error. But you, who have faith, God will strengthen. Hence follows: “But the Lord is faithful.”

[Note: [Col. 0323D] Augustine, to Vitalis.] Or thus: “For faith does not belong to all.” As though he said: I exhort you to pray that the word of God may run and be glorified, because not all—even though you pray—will believe; only those foreordained to eternal life, predestined to adoption as sons. Yet God, through the prayers of believers, causes those who do not yet believe to believe, in order to show that he himself does it. For no one is so unskilled or so slow of understanding that he cannot see that God commands himself to be asked to do what he does.

[Note: [Col. 0323D] Id., in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*.] It must be understood that the ability to have faith, just as the ability to have love, belongs to human nature; but to possess faith, just as to possess love, belongs to the grace of the faithful. Yet when the will to believe is prepared in some by God, one must distinguish what comes from his mercy [Col. 0323C] and what from judgment. “All the ways” are called “mercy and truth” (Ps. 24). Therefore both the mercy by which he freely delivers and the truth by which he judges justly are unsearchable.

“But the Lord is faithful.” As though he said: Pray that we may be delivered. But God, who is faithful, that is, true in his promises, will strengthen you lest the importunate deceive you, and will guard you from evil.

“But we have confidence.” As though he said: We have not said all this to you, I think, in vain; rather, brethren, we have confidence concerning you in the Lord, who will work in you, that you do and will do whatever we command you. And that this may be so, may the Lord direct your hearts—that is, your wills; that is, may he remove whatever shamefulness is in you. May he direct your wills, I say, so that they may abide in the love of God, [Col. 0323D] namely the love which God gives, or so that you may love God, and in the patience of Christ, namely that you may be patient as Christ also was.

“But we command you.” Here he begins to speak about the meddlesome and idle, warning the good to correct them. As though he said: You will do what we command; but whoever refuses to do it is to be excommunicated. This is what he says: “Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ”—that is, we command by Jesus Christ’s authority, or in honor of Christ, because it honors Christ for a diseased sheep to be excluded—“that you withdraw yourselves from every brother walking disorderly”; that is, do not associate with those who walk disorderly, [Col. 0324A] that is, otherwise than the order of nature requires, and who walk not according to the tradition which they received from us, that is, not according to the teaching we handed down to them.

“For you yourselves.” As though he said: You ought therefore to withdraw yourselves because you yourselves know how—that is, in what respects—you ought to imitate us; and since they do not do these things, you ought to avoid them. And indeed you ought to imitate us, because we are good. He says this as follows: “For we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat bread from anyone without payment,” that is, without our own labor.

Or thus: “For you yourselves know.” As though he said: They certainly do not walk according to our tradition. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us, that is, how I behaved in that wherein I am to be imitated—a thing you do not see in them. As though he said: There is no need for me to explain [Col. 0324B] that tradition to you, because you know it: namely, that I was not disorderly among you, like those who, attending to other people’s business, wander here and there. Nor did we eat bread received from anyone without payment; rather, we lived in labor—the opposite of without payment—and toil. As though he said: That labor went as far as weariness.

We worked night and day, in contrast to what he said above, “from anyone.” We worked, I say, lest we burden any of you. And lest anyone should say that he did not accept payment because he had no right to it, he adds: We did not refrain from accepting it because we lacked the right to receive it, since these persons ought much more to live by their own labor, for they do not have this right. We did not refrain, I say, but in order that we might give ourselves as a pattern for you to imitate [Col. 0324C] us; that is, that you might imitate us and abandon idleness. Behold: here he refrained for one reason, different from that at Corinth. Here he refrained in order to give an example; there, in order to repel false teachers.

[Ambrose] It should be noted that he taught not by words alone but also exhorted by deeds. For it belongs to a competent teacher to fulfill in works what he teaches in words. Even if it is not unknown that the things taught are plainly true, nevertheless, if the teacher begins to neglect them, those who hear will not easily make progress. For deeds persuade more strongly than words. Therefore those who improve through words alone, despite negligent teachers, deserve great praise.

The Apostle was thus a model for those in the people who were slender in means, that they might learn not to lose their independence. Hence Solomon says: “Rarely set your foot in your friend’s house, lest, sated with you, he hate you” (Prov. 25). For one who frequently comes to another’s table, having given himself to idleness, must flatter the person who feeds him, whereas our religion calls people to freedom.

Hence he adds: “For,” etc. As though he said: I worked among you as your example. And rightly so, for I taught that this is what should be done. This is what he says: “For even when we were with you, we gave you this command: If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat.”

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Id., *On the Work of Monks*.] Some say that the Apostle gave this command concerning spiritual works. Otherwise, if he meant bodily work, in which [Col. 0325A] farmers or artisans labor, he would appear to think contrary to the Lord, who says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat” (Matt. 6). But they strive in vain to cast darkness over themselves and others, so that they may refuse not only to do but even to understand what love usefully enjoins, when in many other places in his letters the Apostle teaches most plainly what he thinks on this subject.

For he wishes servants of God to work bodily so that they may have a livelihood and not be compelled by want to ask for necessities. Nor is this contrary to the foregoing saying, “Do not be anxious about what you shall eat.” For this was not said in order that they should not procure, as far as necessity requires, whatever they can honorably procure; rather, it was said so that they should not fix their attention on such things, nor do whatever they are commanded to do in preaching the Gospel for the sake of such things.

“For we have heard.” Here the reason is shown why he mentioned his own labor. As though he said: I give this command because we have heard that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but meddling, with curiosity, in other people’s affairs. In this manner they earn the right to be fed—a practice abhorrent to the Lord’s discipline.

[Ambrose] Their god is their belly, who make shameful provision for their own necessities.

[Augustine] “Now those who are such we command and exhort in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly”—that is, without creating disturbances—“they may eat their own bread,” that is, bread earned by their own labor. But lest on this pretext they should cease to provide for the poor, he added: “But you, brethren, do not grow weary in doing good” to the poor, because even if they work, they may nevertheless still need some things. Therefore he warns those who had the means to supply necessities to servants of God not to become lazy on this pretext. The person who is humane in giving is not censured; rather, the one censured is he who, although able to bear labor, wishes to live idly.

“If anyone.” As though he said: We command them to work, etc. “But if anyone does not obey this word of ours,” commanded to you “through the letter, mark him,” that is, report to me who he is. Or, “mark him,” that is, rebuke him. Or thus: if anyone does not obey our word through your letter, mark him for us, and we will rebuke him severely. “And do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed,” that is, that, rejected by all, he may blush and so submit himself to the Apostle’s commands.

Yet do not [Col. 0326B] regard him as an enemy, so as to hate him; rather, correct him in love as a brother.

[Haimo] May the God of peace give you, here and in the future, everlasting peace in every place, namely both among those of your household and among strangers. And that you may have peace, may God be with you all.

“The greeting in my own hand—Paul’s—is written, which is the sign in every letter.” [Ambrose] “So I write”—how? “May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” Because of forgers of Scripture, he testifies that he personally subscribes the greeting at the end of every letter, so that no letter received under his name may be accepted unless it bears his handwritten subscription.

## On the First Epistle to Timothy

[Col. 0325]

## Argument

[Col. 0325C]

He instructs and teaches Timothy concerning the appointment of bishops and deacons, and all ecclesiastical discipline, writing to him from Laodicea through Tychicus the deacon.

## Chapter I

## Verses 1–5

> “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the command of God our Savior and Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, beloved son in the faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going into Macedonia, so that you might instruct certain persons not to teach differently, nor to give attention to myths and endless genealogies, which furnish questions rather than God’s edification [Col. 0325D] which is in faith. Now the end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.”

“Paul,” etc. [Jerome] The Apostle writes this letter to Timothy. This Timothy was the son of a faithful woman and was born of a Gentile father. Although he was uncircumcised and himself a Gentile, the brothers who were at [Col. 0326C] Lystra and Iconium gave good testimony concerning him. Paul wished him to travel with him and therefore circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places.

[Haimo] He was trained both in the divine Scriptures and in the liberal arts.

[Ambrose] The Apostle made him a bishop and therefore admonishes him to be diligent in ecclesiastical ordination. Paul writes to Timothy, left as bishop in Asia, concerning the episcopal office: how he should resist false apostles; how he should instruct the Church; what kind of presbyters and deacons he should appoint; what their wives should be like; which widows he should honor; and how he should conduct himself in the Church or govern it.

The Apostle’s purpose in this letter is to instruct Timothy about the duty of episcopal dignity. His method is as follows: first he greets him; then warns him to resist false apostles; afterward instructs him concerning episcopal office, teaching what kind of presbyters and deacons he ought to appoint and what their wives ought to be like; then what kind of widows he ought to receive; afterward he instructs him concerning the manner of correction. At the end he warns him to avoid profane novelties. But first he gives the greeting, saying: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus.”

He puts forward the title of dignity so that Timothy, fortified by this authority, may resist false apostles. [Col. 0327A]

[Haimo] I say, an apostle according to the command—that is, according to the command and will—of God the Father, our Savior, and of Jesus Christ, our hope, namely he through whom we hope for glory. Therefore whoever resists the Apostle resists the command of God the Father who saves, and Christ, from whom comes the hope of glory.

He ascribes salvation to the Father and our hope to Christ because the Father gave us salvation through his Son, whom he deigned to send us, and through the Holy Spirit, whom he bestowed upon us in baptism and the other sacraments. Through Christ, moreover, we have hope—that is, expectation—of future blessings; for as he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, so through him we hope for resurrection and ascent into the glory of eternal blessedness.

Paul, I say, writes to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith; and before all else he greets him in this manner: “May grace, mercy, and peace be to you from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.” Observe that in this greeting he sets down three things which he wishes for Timothy, whereas in others he set down only two. Here mercy is understood as what in other letters is called grace, that is, remission of sins. Peace is tranquility of soul and a foretaste of eternal peace. He customarily wishes this to all alike; but the grace which he here adds is wished for bishops: namely, the gift of the Holy Spirit by which God’s ministers are armed.

“As I urged you.” After the greeting, he first begins here with the rejection of false teachers who taught that the law must still be kept.

[Ambrose] As though he said: O Timothy, do thus—namely, do as I urged you, as one equal to you; I do not say “I commanded,” as to one inferior. The Apostle does this because of the affection of love and in order to show Timothy a model of humility. Therefore do this, and no less than as I urged you. What did I urge? That you remain at Ephesus to organize the Church.

[Haimo] Ephesus is the metropolitan city of Asia. When I was going to Macedonia, I urged you to remain there so that you might instruct certain persons who had departed from the Catholic faith—both teachers and lesser persons—that teachers should not teach otherwise than we do, nor subjects attend to the myths of the Jews. They say that the first man had two women, Eve and another from whom, they say, many children were born—a thing which sacred Scripture never relates.

Or, by “myths” he here means the teaching of those who preach that the law together with grace is necessary. For what they say concerning the law is a myth, not reality.

[Ambrose] The bishop entreats his fellow bishop not to allow Judaizing Jews to teach the people otherwise than he had handed down, nor to allow subjects to attend to their myths and genealogies. By these genealogies they recount that they are of Abraham’s and David’s lineage, as though salvation were owed to them; or they recount that Christ is not of David. I say genealogies without end, that is, without a limit, or forbidden by God.

[Augustine] A heretic, indeed an enemy of the law and the prophets, imagines that in this passage the Apostle called the divine utterances myths, as elsewhere when he says: “Avoid profane and old-womanish myths” (1 Tim. 4). Who but a very blind heretic would err so? Why then did the Apostle himself do this, if he indicated that these were old-womanish myths? Why does he say: “Abraham had two sons” (Gal. 4), and other such things?

But the better explanation is that the Jews possess, besides the canonical Scriptures, certain unwritten traditions which they preserve in memory and transmit orally from one person to another. They call these the *Deuterosis*. In them they say that God created two wives for the first man, from whom they weave endless genealogies, producing utterly fruitless questions.

[Haimo] He calls these myths—that is, fictions and inventions—which also include those matters concerning which the Lord said: “You have made the commandment of God void in order to keep your tradition” (Mark 7).

[Augustine] [Col. 0328B] There he rebukes the Jews because they taught their children the impiety of not honoring their parents. But Moses says: “Honor your father and your mother.” Yet you say: “If a man says to father or mother, ‘Corban’—that is, a gift—whatever you might have received as help from me,” then you no longer allow him to do anything for his father or mother, annulling the word of God by your tradition; and you do many things of this kind” (ibid.).

Here Christ plainly shows both that the law which that profane person blasphemes is God’s law, and that the Jews possess traditions distinct from the prophetic and canonical books. The Apostle calls these profane myths and endless genealogies—not, as the heretic thinks, but as the Catholic reader understands.

These myths furnish questions, that is, disputes, rather than the edification of God’s righteousness: they do not build people up in God’s righteousness; and that edification of righteousness is in faith. “But the end”—or, “for.” As though he said: The edification of God’s righteousness is indeed in faith, because from faith comes hope, and from hope comes love, which is the fulfillment of the law. This is what he says: “For the end,” etc.

Or thus: “But the end.” As though he said: They teach and attend to myths and genealogies, but the end and fulfillment of the law is love. Therefore there is no need of other things. This is what he says: “But the end of the commandment”—that is, its fulfillment and completion—“is love.”

“End” means a boundary; it also means consumption. [Haimo] “End” likewise means fulfillment and completion. For bread is said to be finished in one sense, a tunic in another, and a field here or there in yet another. [Col. 0328D] Bread is finished by being eaten; a tunic is finished by being woven; and in each case the word “end” is used. But bread is finished so that it is consumed, whereas a tunic is finished so that it is completed: bread is finished so that it no longer exists, a tunic so that it may be perfect.

Thus charity is the end, that is, the perfection of the commandment—that is, of all the commandments—the fulfilment of which is love; and it is twofold, namely love of God and of neighbour. [Note: Col. 0327D, Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*.] For charity securely possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances, by which we love God and neighbour; it is the root of all good things. Hence: “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. 22). Therefore, if one has no leisure to search all the holy pages, [Col. 0329A] to unfold all the wrappings of discourse, to penetrate all the secrets of Scripture, hold fast to charity, on which all things hang, because the end of all things is love of God and neighbour. No class of things to be loved has been omitted in these two commandments. For although love of God comes first and love of neighbour follows, nothing seems to have been said about love of oneself. But when it was said, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (*ibid.*), love of yourself by yourself was not omitted at the same time.

But one lives holily and justly who has an ordered love: so that he neither loves what ought not to be loved, nor fails to love what ought to be loved; neither loves equally what should be loved less or more, nor loves less or more what should be loved equally. Every human being, insofar as he is a sinner, [Col. 0329B] is not to be loved; but insofar as he is human, he is to be loved for God’s sake. God, however, is to be loved for his own sake, and each person ought to love God more than himself. Likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our own body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake. But since you cannot benefit everyone, you must especially provide for those who, by circumstances of place, time, or whatever other matters, are joined to you more closely as if by a certain lot. Therefore, the sum of all this is that the fulfilment of the law and of all the divine Scriptures is understood to be love of the thing to be enjoyed, and of the thing which can enjoy that thing together with us—that is, of God and neighbour. For we are commanded to love God and neighbour; but there is no need for some further special commandment that each person should love himself. [Col. 0329C]

This charity is love of God and neighbour. [Note: Col. 0329D, Augustine, on Psalm 31.] Love of this world is called covetousness; covetousness is diminished as charity grows. Therefore let covetousness be restrained, and charity stirred up. For charity is the end of the commandment: that is, every commandment is referred to charity. But whatever is done from fear of punishment or from some carnal intention, so that it is not referred to charity, is not yet done as it ought to be done, however much it may seem to be done. Therefore both commandments and counsels are rightly carried out when they are referred to loving God, and one’s neighbour for God’s sake.

“From a pure heart,” etc. Here he defines charity, and not elsewhere, so that it may be defined neither everywhere nor nowhere. As if he said: Charity is the end of the commandment. What kind of charity? That which proceeds from a pure heart, that is, from a pure understanding, so that nothing but God is loved; and from a good conscience, that is, hope. Here “conscience” is used for hope. For the person in whom the prick of an evil conscience remains despairs of attaining what he loves. He hopes who bears a good conscience; but the man whom an evil conscience stings draws himself back from hope. He adds: “and from faith unfeigned,” that is, not pretended—faith in which a person does not invent arbitrary notions for himself, but [faith that is] Catholic. Or, “faith unfeigned,” that is, not made of clay and fragile, but strong against adversities. [Note: Col. 0329D, id., on Psalm 31.]

### Verses 6–17

> “From which things some, having wandered away, have turned aside into empty talk, desiring to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say, nor the things concerning which they make assertions. But we know that the law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this: that the law is not laid down for the just, but for the unjust and insubordinate, ungodly and sinners, wicked and defiled, murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, murderers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound doctrine, which accords with the Gospel of the glory of the blessed God entrusted to me. I give thanks to him who strengthened me, Christ Jesus our Lord, because he judged me faithful, appointing me to ministry—though formerly I was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man. But I received God’s mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief. Yet the grace of our Lord overflowed with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. The saying is trustworthy and worthy of every acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost. But for this reason I received mercy: that in me, the foremost, Christ Jesus might display all patience, as an example for those who are to believe in him unto eternal life. Now to the King of the ages—immortal, invisible, the only God—be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.” [Cols. 0330A–0330B]

“From which things.” Here he rebukes opponents who taught legal observances, saying: “From which”—namely faith, hope, and charity—“some, wandering away, have turned aside into empty talk” about legal matters, supposing that these ought to be observed after Christ, ignorant of the mystery of the Law and the Prophets: namely, that they were to be observed until Christ. These men, I say, desire to be teachers of the law—which is worse—“understanding neither the things which they say,” that is, the things they assert, “nor the things concerning which,” that is, by means of which, they make their assertions, namely the testimonies of the prophets. [Col. 0330C]

Or conversely: they understand neither the things they say in order to prove what they intend, nor the matters concerning which they make these assertions—that is, what they intend to prove. For whenever they begin to be rebuked and convicted concerning their perverse and false opinion, in defence of what they have stated with the most trifling rashness and most manifest falsehood, they recite many words from the holy books, wishing to be teachers of the law, though they understand neither what they say nor the matters concerning which they speak. [Note: Col. 0330D, Augustine, *On Genesis*.]

And lest he should seem to accuse the law, he adds, “But we know.” As if he said: They do not understand, but we do understand; for, to show this in one respect, we know that the law is good. But according to those who understand only carnally, it is not good; for it is good only if someone, whether just or unjust, uses it lawfully—that is, spiritually, as it itself teaches: namely, so that through it he recognizes his disease and seeks a physician.

[Ambrose] He also uses it lawfully who knows that it was given for a time and is to be abandoned under Christ. For the righteous do not need the law for remission, since through Christ they are free from it. And lest he seem again to introduce it, he adds: “knowing also this”—which they do not know—namely, that “the law is not laid down for the just,” that is, not imposed upon him so as to stand over him and rule him. For he is in the law rather than under it and with it, because he is a friend of justice. Its enemy is the person who does not sin through fear of punishment; but its friend is the person who does not sin through love of it, and who then indeed fears to sin. [Col. 0331A]

Or: “the law is not laid down for the just,” that is, it is not given for the righteous person, because he is righteous not from it but from faith. And since he is righteous from faith, what need has he of the law? Yet it was given either to punish the guilty or to restrain one willing to sin. Nevertheless, although the righteous person does not need it, he uses it, so that he may thereby have authority among others and bear witness to future things by deeds. [Note: Col. 0331D, Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.]

But how is the law good if it is not laid down for the righteous? We must understand that the righteous person no longer needs a pedagogue, but the unrighteous person needs one in order to become righteous. [Col. 0331B] There are many ways of using the law lawfully, so that in one respect the righteous person, and in another the unrighteous person, is rightly said to use the law lawfully. For the unrighteous person uses the law lawfully when, understanding why it was given, he is led by its threat, as by a pedagogue, to the grace by which he may become righteous. The righteous person also uses it lawfully when, by maintaining it, he imposes it upon the unrighteous, so that when the disease of ingrained concupiscence begins in them to increase through the stimulus of prohibition and the accumulation of transgression, they may flee to justifying grace; and, delighted through it by the sweetness of justice, may escape the punishment threatened by the letter.

Thus these two statements are neither contrary nor mutually inconsistent: that the law is good and that the righteous person uses it lawfully, yet that it is not laid down for the righteous person, because he has not been justified by it but by the law of faith. The law, I say, is not imposed on the righteous, but upon the unrighteous, who act against the law of nature, and the insubordinate, who are not subject to God although they are rightly admonished by reason. He explains in detail who the unrighteous and insubordinate are: namely, the ungodly, against God; sinners, against themselves and their neighbour; the wicked, to whom wickedness pleases in itself; and the defiled, who consent through some favour or fear. Or: sinners against themselves; the wicked and defiled against their neighbour; murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers—for since the law of nature had become obsolete in these matters, it was restored in writing to restrain them—and murderers, fornicators, men who lie with males, kidnappers, who inflict wounds of any kind upon their neighbours, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound doctrine, namely moral doctrine and the law of nature. [Cols. 0331C–0331D]

This sound doctrine is not contrary to, but according to, the Gospel. For all truth agrees with the Gospel—the Gospel, I say, of the glory of the blessed God, that is, the Gospel which proclaims or bestows glory. This Gospel was entrusted to me as to one who is faithful.

“I give thanks.” Here he shows that evil things had been his under the law, but good things after he left it: namely, that he is faithful and appointed to ministry. Hence he is strong. As if he said: The Gospel was entrusted to me. Therefore: “I give thanks to him who strengthened me,” that is, who made firm my mind, which formerly considered impossible what was preached concerning the Lord’s power, his twofold birth, resurrection, and hope. But he strengthened me so greatly that I believe these things, and that neither death nor life separates me from Christ. [Col. 0332A]

He strengthened me, I say, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore I give thanks because by certain foreknowledge he judged—that is, foresaw—that I would be faithful in him, although I had been unbelieving under the law. He himself appointed me to the ministry of preaching the Gospel. But did these things come to me through the law? No; for I am the one who formerly, while under the law, was a blasphemer against God, a persecutor of the saints, and insolent, inflicting outrage upon those whom I seized. But I received God’s mercy—that is, remission through God’s mercy, not through my own merits—concerning that which I did ignorantly, that is, concerning the sin which I committed in ignorance. [Note: Col. 0331D, Augustine, on Psalm 50.]

Or it may be understood so as to mark a reason: as if he said, “I received mercy the more readily because I acted ignorantly.” Those who sin knowingly, such as David, receive God’s mercy, as do those who sin ignorantly, whose sin is more easily forgiven. I say that I lived in unbelief while I was under the law. For under the law there was ignorance, and consequently unbelief; but now, on the contrary, there are faith and knowledge of the truth. It is evident, then, that he did not abandon his former position from fickleness. [Col. 0332B]

“But [grace] overflowed.” As if he said: I received not only the mercy of remission, but faith, love, and the grace of diverse gifts. And this is what he says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ overflowed,” through which he gave diverse gifts, “with faith and love,” that is, with the perfection of faith and love. For he did not receive mercy without faith and love, because remission of sins is given to no one without faith and love. He says “overflowed,” because the good things were greater than the former evils.

Or thus: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ overflowed with”—that is, in—“the faith and love which are in Christ Jesus,” not in the law; that is, because he not only forgave sins, but also gave faith and love. Of this no one can be doubtful, because Christ Jesus came into this world, so miserable, as passible together with others. [Note: Col. 0332D, Augustine, *On an Apostolic Saying*.] For what purpose? To save sinners of every kind, even little children; because even if they were born of baptized parents, they were nevertheless born of flesh, not of spirit—not of that by which one is renewed.

There was no reason for Christ the Lord’s coming except to save sinners. Remove diseases, remove wounds, and there is no reason for medicine. If the great physician came down from heaven, a great sick man lay throughout the whole world. That sick man is the human race, which wholly perished when the one man sinned, in whom the whole race was. But one came without sin, to save from sin. For “the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19). He came in respect of that whereby he was human. For in respect of that whereby he was God, he was always here: he who said, “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Therefore he was in the world and came. He was here by divine majesty; he came by human weakness. Why did he come? To save sinners. It was not our merits but our sins that drew him from heaven to earth. [Col. 0333A]

Hence: “You shall call his name Jesus” (Matt. 1). Why? Hear: “For he shall save his people” (*ibid.*). From what? “From their sins” (*ibid.*). Do little children belong to this people? They certainly do. Thus believe, with this faith, that little children are brought to the grace of Christ. Why do you tell me, “He is healthy; he has no defect”? Why do you run with him to the physician if he has no defect? If he were healthy, Jesus would not have cried: “Let the little children come to me” (Mark 10)—he who came to save sinners.

And this saying is trustworthy, that is, true, and worthy of acceptance, that is, acceptable because useful—and not of one acceptance only, but of every acceptance, because it saves both body and soul here and in the future: the body in the future, the soul here and in the future. [Col. 0333B; Note: Col. 0333D, Augustine, *On an Apostolic Saying*.]

Or, “This saying is human”—another reading—that I may not call it divine. For if a human being who receives a human being in hospitality is called humane, how much more humane is he who receives a human being in himself. Therefore, although the saying concerning this sacrament is divine, it is nevertheless rightly called human. This saying, I say, is trustworthy—or human—namely that Jesus came into this world, so miserable, to save sinners, “of whom,” that is, among whom, I who had been under the law am the first, that is, the greatest. For I am worse than all, because I was a persecutor, than whom none was worse. No one was fiercer among persecutors; therefore no one was worse among sinners. Thus he was first, not in temporal order but in greatness of wickedness.

“But for this reason I received mercy,” so that Jesus might display in me, the foremost—that is, the greatest sinner. Or, “first,” that is, might display most fully in me. Or, “first,” that is, might display in me before displaying it in other persecutors. What? “All,” that is, perfect patience, by which he endured so much and reserves no wrath for later, as he does toward the ungodly whom he bears with for a long time. He displayed it, I say, as an example for those who are to believe in him: so that, the pattern of my example having been offered, no one who believes in him may despair because of the enormity of his crime. For what will he do for a friend, if he has done this for an enemy? They are to believe, I say, with a view to eternal life—that is, in order that they may have eternal life. [Col. 0333C]

“But to the King of the ages.” As if he said: God has done the foregoing things for us; therefore, for these things let there be honour from creatures and glory in his essence. To whom? [Note: Col. 0333D, Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] To the King of the ages, that is, to the Trinity; immortal, that is, unchangeable; invisible, that is, incomprehensible; the only God, that is, the one who alone is God by nature and alone creates. This is understood of the Trinity itself, not of the Father alone, as some wish, because he did not say “to the Father alone,” but “to the only God.” For the one and only God proclaimed to us is the Trinity itself and the Only-Begotten; since, insofar as he is God with God, and the Holy Spirit in his own nature, [each] is immortal and invisible.

Observe that concerning the only God, who is the Trinity itself, it was not said “the only invisible one,” since there are also certain invisible creatures. Rather, it says, “to the invisible only God,” because there are invisible false gods. [Col. 0334A] Therefore it was said, “to the invisible God.” [Note: Col. 0334D, Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] For there is an invisible creature, yet it is not God for us. Therefore it was said, “to the invisible only God,” so that the order is: “let honour and glory be to the only invisible God”—that is, to him who alone is an invisible God, not to him who alone is invisible.

God is invisible to human beings in his nature, according to the saying: “No one has ever seen God.” This is understood by sound faith of that highest, supremely divine, unchangeable substance in which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and only God. But those visions displayed to the Fathers were made through mutable creation, subject to the immutable God; they were not proper manifestations of him as he is, but signifying manifestations, as was fitting according to the causes and times of things. For God is seen when he wills and as he wills—not as he is, but in whatever form he wills to appear. [Col. 0334B]

In the future, however, they shall see him as he is: that is, the Holy Trinity, which is the one true God, immortal and invisible in its substance. Therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God and King of all ages, namely past, present, and future. But the man assumed by the Word has been king of future ages from the time when he was assumed by the Word; for that man was not king of past ages, because he did not exist. Let there be honour, I say, and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

### Verses 18–20

> “This commandment I entrust to you, my son Timothy, in accordance with the prophecies that went before concerning you, that by them you may wage the good warfare, holding faith and a good conscience. Some, having rejected this, have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme.” [Col. 0334C]

“This commandment.” After demonstrating what and how great are the benefits of God the Father and Christ toward sinners, he shows how ecclesiastical discipline should instruct the people. As if he said: Since all salvation is from Christ and not from the law, therefore, Timothy, to you as one going to war I entrust this commandment, as though you are not permitted to neglect it. I entrust it, I say, in accordance with the prophecies that went before concerning you—that is, in accordance with the knowledge of the prophets which was in you before you were ordained bishop. Or, in accordance with what the Holy Spirit showed me concerning you. [Col. 0334D]

What do I command? That you may wage in deed—that is, in expounding these prophecies and carrying them out in practice—the good warfare, that is, a warfare useful to many: by teaching yourself and others, and by accomplishing in deed what you preach by word. You are capable of doing this well. You, I say, holding right faith and a good conscience, lest one who teaches should be ashamed because he is conscious of an evil life. For it is shameful to do one thing and preach another.

Some, by their disgraceful acts, have rejected this good conscience and have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith, drawing others with them and [remaining] around faith but not within it—that is, they have even lost the faith. [Haimo] Shipwreck means the breaking of a ship. And just as one who suffers shipwreck loses his property and moreover perishes himself, so those who reject a good conscience lose the truth of faith and moreover perish eternally. [Col. 0335A]

Among these—that is, among the false teachers who lost the faith—are Hymenaeus and Alexander. He names them personally in order to remove ambiguity. “Whom I delivered to Satan,” that is, I excommunicated both; you too should excommunicate thus. Observe that he says, “I delivered [them] to Satan,” because that apostolic power employed Satan for the corruption of human beings. For transgressing angels, with their prince the devil, are rightly called agents or officials of divine providence. The devil is called the magistrate of this world; but a magistrate under so great an emperor does nothing except insofar as he is permitted. And the agents and officials of this world do nothing except insofar as the Lord allows. Thus he says, “I delivered [them] to Satan to be afflicted,” because Satan, who afflicts those delivered to him, can do nothing unless permitted. [Col. 0335B]

The Apostle possessed such great power and grace that by a word alone he delivered to the devil those who departed from the faith. This delivery means that the Apostle, moved by their blasphemies, pronounced a sentence against them. But the devil, who is ready for this purpose—to receive into his power those who turn away from God—hears the sentence and seizes them. The Apostle did this not in order that they might perish, but that, corrected in this way, they might learn not to blaspheme and understand that they are bound by punishments because they blasphemed.

Hence in the Gospel the Lord says among other things: “Sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5), showing that bodily infirmities are sometimes inflicted because of sin. And the Lord made clear that they are brought about through the devil as minister, when he said, among many other things: “And ought not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan bound for eighteen years, to be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day?” (Luke 13). Therefore the Apostle says, “whom I delivered to Satan, that through this they may learn not to blaspheme,” so that in this way Satan’s kingdom may be excluded from Satan. [Col. 0335C]

[Augustine] For there is no creature, whether one that remains in the truth and gives glory to God, or one that did not stand in the truth and seeks its own glory, which, willingly or unwillingly, does not serve divine providence. The one that serves willingly does with it what is good; but from the one that does not will this, what is just is done. Yet it is not repaid for that which is justly done through it, but according to the intention with which it acts. For God has not denied free will to rational creatures, yet has retained for himself the power by which he justly orders the unjust. [Col. 0335D]

## Chapter II

### Verses 1–2

> “Therefore I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made for all people—for kings and all who are established in high position—that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity.”

“Therefore I exhort.” [Haimo] Up to this point he dealt with false apostles; here he deals with prayers. Addressing these words to Timothy, he delivered in him a pattern for the whole Church: how it ought to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass and make supplication for all. As if he said: Since Christ came to save sinners, and since you must wage this warfare, therefore teach people to pray, so that what must be done may be obtained.

[Ambrose] And this is what he says: “Therefore I exhort”; [Augustine] or, “I urge first of all,” that is, before all things, that supplications or prayers, prayers, petitions or intercessions, thanksgivings be made. Here the order of the Mass is shown, which is a special kind of prayer. Supplications or prayers are all the things done near to and before the consecration. [Haimo] That is, whatever precedes in the solemnities of the Mass until the point at which the priest begins to consecrate the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood. [Col. 0336A]

[Note: Col. 0335D, Augustine, to Paulinus.] Therefore we understand “supplications” or “prayers” to be those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed. [Haimo] “Prayers” are those which the priest pours forth in the consecration itself of the Eucharist—that is, when what is on the Lord’s table is blessed and sanctified. [Augustine] “Petitions” or “intercessions” occur when the people are blessed by the bishop, who invokes the Lord’s name over them; this was drawn from the Old Testament. For through Moses the Lord says to the priests: “You shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them” (Num. 6).

Or, petitions are made when something is requested as though due, so that what is performed here may be completed in eternal life. Thanksgiving is for things accomplished, and it concludes the whole, as though the whole were from God, as in: “Let us bless the Lord.” Or, supplications are adjurations for difficult matters, such as the conversion of an ungodly person and the removal of evils. Prayers are made when virtues and blessings are sought for those already converted. Thanksgivings are for all things. [Col. 0336C]

I exhort that these be made for all people generally, so that we may follow God’s clemency, by which he wills—that is, provides, exhorts, and urges—that all be saved, even though in justice he reprobates some. Hence Jerome says: “In those who perish he shows judgment, so that in those who are saved he may show mercy.” Or, “for all people,” that is, for people of every class; and especially for kings, even if they are evil, and for all established in high position—such as commanders and counts—even if they are evil. For the Church is to be gathered from every class of people, including those who seem to stray from faith and humility because of worldly ostentation and pride.

Why he wishes prayers to be made for kings and persons in high position, he gives the reason by adding: “that [we may lead] a quiet [life].” As if he said: I wish prayers to be made even for evil rulers because this will also benefit us: so that we may lead a quiet life, free from persecution, and a tranquil one, that is, without any disturbance—a thing beneficial to those weak in the Church. Let us lead it, I say, in all piety, that is, in divine worship and religion, and chastity, that is, integrity of faith. For this is why their peace is necessary to us. [Col. 0336D–0337A]

[Note: Col. 0337D, Augustine, *The City of God*.] We use even Babylon’s peace while the two cities—Jerusalem and Babylon—are intermingled. By faith God’s people are indeed freed from Babylon, yet meanwhile they live there as pilgrims. Therefore the Apostle, inspired by the same Holy Spirit as Jeremiah, who sent a letter to the Jews in Babylon that they should pray for the life of King Nebuchadnezzar and his sons and for the peace of the city, exhorted the Church to pray for kings and all persons in high position, saying: “For in their peace shall be your peace” (Jer. 29).

[Note: Col. 0337D, id., *On Instructing Beginners*.] This, however, figuratively signified that the Church, in all its saints who are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, would be subject to the laws of this age. [Augustine] Therefore the Apostle urges it to pray for them, that they may lead a quiet life. For in the peace of rulers the rest and governance of the churches are preserved. In wars tranquility is scattered, piety grows cold, discipline is loosened; and when it is loosened, the chastity of the weak is violated. [Col. 0337B]

[Note: Col. 0337D, Augustine, *The City of God*.] In Babylon’s peace is our peace, namely the temporal peace common to good and evil while we are held captive among the Babylonians. We are commanded both to serve them and to pay tribute, just as the children of Israel served under the kings of Babylon. But our own proper peace is with God through faith, and it will be with him eternally through sight. And lest anyone suppose that these things should not be done for those through whom the Church suffers, he adds:

### Verses 3–15

> “For this is good and acceptable before God our Saviour, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all; the testimony to this was confirmed in its own times, in which I was appointed a preacher and apostle—I speak the truth, I do not lie—a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth. Therefore I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands, without anger or disputing. Likewise also women, adorning themselves in becoming attire, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, gold, pearls, or costly clothing, but—as is fitting for women professing piety—with good works. A woman should learn in silence with all submission. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be silent. For Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived; but the woman, having been deceived, fell into transgression. Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if she continues in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety.” [Cols. 0337C–0337D]

“This is good,” etc. As if he said: Therefore I urge prayer for all those persons because praying for all is good—that is, useful to the Church—and acceptable, that is, pleasing, before God, since the members of Christ are to be gathered from every class of people. And to remove inequality, he added, “our Saviour,” who, like us, wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth: that is, of Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14).

[Ambrose] If God, who is called omnipotent, wills all people to be saved, why is his will not fulfilled? But in this expression a meaning and a condition lie hidden. Hence Peter says: “All Scripture needs interpretation.” Therefore God wills all to be saved if they come to him. For he does not will in such a way that unwilling people should be saved; rather, he wills them to be saved if they too are willing. Otherwise, he excluded no one from salvation and knowledge. [Col. 0338A]

[Note: Col. 0337D, Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] Or thus: when we read that he “wills all people to be saved,” although it is certain to us that not all are saved, we ought not therefore detract anything from God’s most omnipotent will. For the Omnipotent must not be thought to have willed something to occur which did not occur. Rather, we must understand what is written in this way: “He wills all people to be saved,” that is, no one is saved except one whom he wills [to be saved]. This does not mean that there is no human being whom he does not will to be saved, but that no one is saved unless he wills it. Therefore he must be asked to will it, because it must occur if he wills it.

So we understand also the saying, “Who enlightens every human being” (John 1): not that he enlightens all, but that no one is enlightened except by God. And similarly, “All shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15), because apart from him none are made alive. [Col. 0338B]

Or thus: he who wills all people to be saved does not mean that there was no human being whom he did not will to be saved—for he was unwilling to perform miracles among persons whom he says would have repented had he performed them—but that by “all people” we should understand every class of human beings, distributed through whatever distinctions. The meaning is: He wills all people to be saved, that is, people from every class; because the Church gathers Jews, Gentiles, kings, private persons, rich, poor, learned, unlearned, and whatever other distinctions there are among human beings. The Lord used this manner of speaking when he said to the Pharisees: “You tithe mint, rue, dill, and every herb” (Luke 11), that is, every kind of herb. [Col. 0338C]

[Note: Col. 0338D, id., *On Rebuke and Grace*.] It may also be understood thus: he wills all to be saved, that is, he causes all to will [salvation]; or in whatever other way it can be understood, provided only that we are not compelled to believe that the Omnipotent willed something to be done which was not done. [Note: Col. 0338D, id., *Enchiridion*.] For he cannot will in vain whatever he wills by the will of his essence. [Note: Col. 0338D, id., to Paulinus.]

Or thus: he wills through mercy—that is, he provides, exhorts, and commands—that all people be saved, even though in justice he reprobates some. And lest anyone should suppose that a good life and the worship of one God constitute salvation without participation in the body and blood of Christ:

“One God,” he says, “one mediator,” etc. So that the salvation of all [Col. 0339A] human beings is never accomplished except through the mediator: not the Word who was always God, but the Word made flesh. Attend to the wording and connect it thus: for there is one God. As if he said: Truly, he wills all human beings to be saved, because there is one God, namely the Holy Trinity, creator of all; and there is one mediator between God and human beings—that is, one who, like an arbiter standing in the middle, makes peace—namely Christ Jesus, who was made man for all, in order thereby to be mediator. For he mediates only through being human. This is that arbiter whom Job desired, saying, “that there might be an arbiter between us.”

Now a mediator between God and human beings had to possess something similar to God and something similar to human beings, lest, being wholly like human beings, he should be far from God, or, being wholly like God, he should be far from [Col. 0339B] human beings, and thus not be a mediator.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Augustine, in the *Confessions*.] Therefore Christ, the true mediator between mortal sinners and the immortal righteous one, appeared mortal with human beings and righteous with God. Thus Christ is called mediator between God and man because, between immortal God and mortal man, he is God-and-man reconciling man to God—mediator insofar as he is man. Insofar as he is the Word, however, he is not intermediate, because he is equal to God, God with God, and the one God who is like him. Hence Augustine says: “May the blessed mortality of this intermediary, by intervening, lead us onward—he whom it was necessary neither not to become mortal nor to remain mortal.” For he was made mortal not by any weakening of the divinity of the Word, but by assuming the weakness of flesh.

Good angels cannot be intermediaries between wretched mortals [Col. 0339C] and the blessed immortal One, because they are themselves blessed and immortal with God, and are not mortal or wretched with human beings. Evil angels are intermediaries in a certain way, because they are immortal with God and wretched with human beings; yet they are not true and good intermediaries. For the evil angel, immortal and wretched, places himself between them in order not to allow passage to blessed immortality. Opposite to him is the good Mediator, who both willed to be mortal for a time and was able to remain blessed for eternity. He did not place himself between us so as to prevent our passing into blessed immortality; rather, as mortal and blessed, he placed himself between us so that, mortality having passed away, he might make the dead immortal and the wretched blessed.

[Col. 0339D] Therefore one intermediary is evil, who separates friends; another is good, who reconciles enemies: namely Christ, who gave himself as a ransom. By this it is shown that he wills all to be saved. He gave himself, I say, for all, excluding no one who is willing. The testimony to this matter was confirmed in its proper times; that is, this fact was established by witnesses, namely angels and apostles. Or thus: the testimony to this matter was confirmed in its proper times—that is, witnesses, namely the prophets, went beforehand concerning it, and at the fitting time everything was fulfilled.

For this purpose—that is, for the preaching of this matter—I was appointed by God a preacher and an apostle, which is more. For “preacher” is the name of an activity, whereas “apostle” [Col. 0340A] is the name of a dignity. And in these matters—namely, that Christ gave himself and that I am an apostle—I speak the truth and do not lie, in a matter in which one must believe me, because I am a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth: in the faith which he taught, and in the true commandments of God.

[Note: [Col. 0340D] Augustine, on John.] Or, “in the truth to come,” which is the reality and reward of faith. Do you seek the reward? Let faith go before. For we believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed.

“I desire.” As if he said: Because I am a teacher of the Gentiles, or because prayer is good, therefore I desire men to pray in every place—that is, wherever they may be—not only in church—not sinking down toward earthly things, but lifting up toward eternal things [Col. 0340B] pure hands; that is, the good disposition of a heart which loves God. And this without anger, that is, hatred toward anyone, and without disputation, that is, hesitation. For where there is the storm of anger or hesitation, God is not pleased. Distinguish: anger concerns one’s neighbour; disputation concerns God.

Likewise, I desire women to pray and to lift up their hands, being without anger and disputation, in becoming dress—that is, dress adorning their religious profession.
