I mean women adorning themselves with other virtues, with modesty of countenance, so that they may not have the brazen face of prostitutes; and with sobriety of mind; and not adorning themselves with braided—that is, curled—hair, nor with gold or pearls or costly clothing. Or thus: not adorning themselves with braided hair, gold, or pearls, so that these things are intertwined in their hair. Or, not adorning [Col. 0340C] themselves with costly clothing, so as to devote themselves through all these things, beyond the measure and character proper to their persons, to provoking desire; but rather, through every good work, showing and declaring outwardly the piety of their souls, as befits women.

[Ambrose] Or thus: but let them adorn themselves through every good thing, because this befits women professing piety. For one who wishes to be heard must humble herself, putting away display, in order to move God to mercy. Proud attire neither obtains anything nor causes people to think rightly of its wearer.

“Let a woman,” etc. He has said that the duty of prayer belongs to everyone, and explained how, for whom, why, and that prayer ought to be made everywhere. He now says that the duty of teaching belongs only to men, and determines what sort of men ought to be ordained to it. As if he said: Praying together with men is common to women, but speaking is not. Rather, let a woman learn in silence—that is, without asking questions—what she does not know, with all submission, that is, without presumption, and so forth. But I do not permit a woman to teach a man in the Church. For if she speaks, she more readily incites lust and is herself incited. Nor do I permit a woman to exercise authority over a man by any spiritual preeminence, even if she may do so within her own sex; rather, let her remain in silence, so that she does not converse with her female neighbour.

See: he taught not only that a woman should have humble and respectable dress, but also denied her authority to teach and commanded her to be subject to her husband, so that in both attire and [Col. 0340D] service she may be under the man’s authority, from whom she derives her origin. “For Adam.” He gives the reason why woman is subject: namely, because she was made later and was first in fault. As if he said: I do not permit a woman to rule over a man, but command her to be subject; and the order of creation shows this, namely that woman is subject to man. For Adam was formed first, then Eve; and Adam was not deceived before her, nor in the same manner as Eve. But the woman, deceived with the man’s consent, was in transgression—that is, she caused the man actually to transgress.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Augustine, on Genesis.] Had she ruled, she would have been more easily deceived. Observe that he says Adam was not deceived, though the Apostle calls him a transgressor “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression”; yet he denies that Adam was deceived. Therefore, when questioned, Adam did not say, “The woman deceived me,” but, “She gave [Col. 0341B] to me, and I ate” (Gen. III). The woman, however, said, “The serpent deceived me” (ibid.).

The Apostle properly called that “deception” by which what was being urged, though false, was thought true: namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though he who had made them human beings begrudged them divinity. But even if some desire of making an experiment moved the man, on account of a certain exaltation of mind which could not be hidden from God, the searcher of inward things, when he saw that the woman had not died after eating the food she had received, I nevertheless think that, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, he by no means believed what the devil was suggesting.

Therefore he says that Adam was not deceived first, namely not in the respect in which the woman was deceived: that is, so as [Col. 0341C] to believe this to be true: “You shall be like gods” (ibid.). Rather, he thought that both things could happen: that he might comply with his wife and obtain pardon through repentance. Therefore he sinned less, because he thought of repentance and God’s mercy. For after the woman, deceived, had eaten and given him some that they might eat together, he did not wish to grieve her, whom he believed would waste away without his consolation and, alienated from him, utterly perish. He was conquered not by fleshly desire, which he had not yet experienced, but by a certain friendly goodwill, by which God is often offended lest a friend be offended. The just outcome of the divine judgment showed that he ought not to have acted thus.

Therefore he too was deceived in another manner. Being inexperienced in divine severity, he could be mistaken in thinking the offense pardonable; but by that serpentine trick through which the woman was deceived, I judge that he could in no way have been deceived.

“But she shall be saved.” As if he said: A woman ought not to teach in the Church; nevertheless, she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith.

[Haimo] That is, she receives an increase of salvation if she begets children for God by instructing them daily, so that they remain in faith, in love of God and neighbour, and in the sanctification they received in baptism, with sobriety—that is, temperance against the heat of vices.

Or thus: “But she shall be saved.” As if he said: Even if woman was the cause of sin, she shall nevertheless be saved—not only the virgin and the continent woman, [Col. 0342A] but also the married woman—even if she never ceases from marital intercourse but departs this world while bearing children. She shall be saved, I say, if nevertheless she remains in faith, love, and sanctification, so that beyond her own husband she knows no other man, with sobriety—that is, temperance—so that she uses even her own husband temperately.

Or thus: “But she shall be saved,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Augustine, *City of God*.] These words seem, however, to disadvantage a woman if she has no children, or if the children she has do not wish to remain in good conduct. But elsewhere the Apostle says: “She will be happier, whether virgin or widow, if she remains thus” (1 Cor. VII). Hence, when he says that woman shall be saved through the bearing of children, he may be understood to have figuratively indicated a hidden mystery. The children of the woman are works of the flesh, which are especially accustomed to be exercised in works of mercy. But works of mercy do not benefit pagans, Jews who do not believe in Christ, or any heretics or schismatics in whom faith, love, and sober sanctification are not found. Therefore he adds, “if they remain.”

Otherwise, if it is taken literally, what he says—that woman will be saved through childbearing—seems almost empty. Is not the continent woman saved more? Is not God’s virgin saved more?

[Note: [Col. 0342D] Augustine, on Psalm XXXIV.] But woman is a type of the flesh, Adam of reason, which flies to God on the wings of virtues, like a sparrow to its house. Hence the Prophet: “The sparrow has found itself a house, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII).

[Augustine] The sparrow is reason; the turtledove is flesh, which bears children, that is, good works. Yet these works [Col. 0342C] do not benefit pagans and such people—not merely in faith and love [the syntax of this qualification is uncertain]. This is the turtledove which places its young in the nest and does not cast them down anywhere—that is, it performs good works, but in the nest: that is, in the unity of the Church, in the Catholic faith. This is the one deceived first and which deceives the man: reason is, as it were, deceived through the flesh, just as Adam was deceived through Eve. Yet the flesh shall be saved through the spiritual generation of children—that is, good works—if nevertheless the children, that is, the works, remain in faith, love, sanctification, and sobriety.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–4

> “The saying is faithful: If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work. For [Col. 0342D] a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, well-ordered, prudent, modest, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not violent, but gentle; not quarrelsome, not covetous; but one who governs his own household well, having children subject to him with all chastity.”

This saying which I have spoken, and which I am about to speak, is faithful—that is, true: “If anyone,” etc. He has said that a man may preside, and determines who: namely, one who desires to work and benefit many, not proudly to dominate, and who is blameless. This is what he says: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.”

[Jerome] Truly a work, not a dignity; [Col. 0343A] labour, not luxury; not to rise in eminence, but to descend in humility; to become a servant and minister of human beings for Christ’s sake. Thus, even while setting aside Rachel, fair of face, but not abandoning her, he may enter with Jacob to Leah, bleary-eyed; and may descend with Moses from the mountain to the plains—that is, from the leisure of contemplation to the labour of action.

[Note: [Col. 0343D] Augustine, *City of God*.] No one ought to be so idle that, in that very leisure, he does not consider his neighbour’s benefit; nor so active that he does not seek contemplation of God. In leisure, it is not an inactive occupation that ought to delight one, but either the search for or discovery of truth, so that each may make progress in it and not envy another what he has found. In action, however, one ought not to love honour in this life or power, because all things are vain under the sun, but the work itself that is accomplished through that honour or power, if it is done rightly and usefully—namely, so that it may avail for the salvation of those subject to him. Therefore he says: “If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work.”

[Note: [Col. 0344D] Augustine, *Enchiridion*.] He wished to explain what “episcopate” is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour. For the word is Greek and derives from this: the one who is set over others watches over those whom he governs, namely by caring for them. For *skopos* means “aim”; hence a bishop is called in Latin a *superintendens*, “overseer,” so that he may understand that he is no bishop who loves to preside rather than to benefit. Episcopacy is attention to one’s own life and that of others.

Accordingly, no one is forbidden the study of knowing truth, which belongs to praiseworthy leisure. But a higher position, without which a people cannot be governed, even if it is held and [Col. 0343C] administered as it ought to be, is nevertheless improperly desired. Therefore holy leisure seeks the love of truth; the necessity of love undertakes just business. If no one imposes this burden, one should be free for apprehending and contemplating truth. But if it is imposed, it must be undertaken because love requires it; yet even then the delight of truth must not be abandoned, lest that sweetness be withdrawn and this necessity overwhelm one.

[Augustine] He next describes what sort of bishop he ought to be: “He must.” As if he said: The episcopate is a work which one desires; but in order to be able to work well, the bishop—that is, the man elected for ordination—must be blameless. This is the same as what he says to Titus: “without crime.”

[Col. 0343D] [Jerome] It is almost contrary to nature for anyone to be without sin; but he wishes “blameless” to be understood thus: not liable to rebuke, so that one may be chosen by comparison with whom the rest may be called a flock. “The husband of one wife”: that is, a monogamist after baptism. For if before baptism he had a wife who died, this is not imputed to him, since, being made entirely new, neither sexual immorality nor anything else that occurred before harms him.

“Sober.” For ministers of the temple also are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be burdened by drunkenness, and so that their understanding may always be vigorous and keen. “Prudent” in everything to be done. This is said against those who excuse the foolishness [Col. 0344A] of priests under the name of simplicity. “Well-ordered” in virtues, or in bearing, gait, dress, and ordinary speech. “Modest”: that is, restrained. “Hospitable”: namely, one previously accustomed to this. “A teacher”: namely, one who has the grace of teaching, because an innocent life without speech benefits as much by its example as it harms by its silence. For wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and by a staff. Hence: “Cursed be the dog unable to bark.”

“Not given to wine”: one who does this frequently, because a belly inflamed with wine quickly boils over into lust. Noah exposed his thighs through drunkenness; wines conquered Lot, whom Sodom had not conquered. “Not violent”: that is, not so wrathful and disturbed in mind as to strike, though he ought to be patient and follow him who gave his back to the scourges—that is, Christ. “But gentle”: one who maintains moderation of soul. “Not quarrelsome”: namely, one accustomed to no such conduct. Nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of uncultivated people, who think chattering to be authority and, ready for disputes, thunder haughtily against their subjects. “Not covetous,” like the apostles, who sought nothing beyond food and clothing.

[Haimo] Almost everyone suffers from the disease of covetousness; therefore he commands that a bishop not be covetous, because he would easily depart from justice. “One who governs his own household”—that is, his family—well, not in order to increase wealth or perform other such acts, but so that what he will command the people, he may first require of his own household: namely, having children subject to him in all chastity, lest they imitate the sons of Eli, who slept with women in the entrance of the temple and, regarding religion as plunder, turned what belonged to the sacrifices into [Col. 0344C] their own pleasures.

### Verses 5–6

> “But if anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how shall he take care of the Church of God? Not a novice, lest, lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony even from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach and into the snare of the devil. Likewise deacons must be modest, not double-tongued, not devoted to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain; holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience. Let these also first be tested, and then let them serve, having no crime. Likewise women must be modest, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, [Col. 0344D] governing their children and households well. For those who have served well acquire for themselves a good rank and much confidence in the faith which is in Christ Jesus. I write these things to you, son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon. But if I delay, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth. And manifestly great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the Gentiles, believed in the world, and taken up in glory.”

“But if anyone.” As if he said: He must [Col. 0345A] govern his household well. But if anyone does not know how to govern his smaller household, of which the concern is more familiar, how shall he care for the Church of God, which is larger, where there are so many strangers? In no way.

[Haimo] “Not a novice”: that is, one untrained, newly reborn, newly converted. Few observe this very clear testimony.

[Jerome] For yesterday he was a catechumen, today he is a bishop; yesterday at the theatre, today in the Church; in the evening at the circus, today at the altar; lately a supporter of actors, now a consecrator of virgins.

[Ambrose] He then supplies why he must not be a novice: lest, lifted up in pride, puffed up by the novelty of authority and believing himself worthier than others, as though religion needed him, he fall into the judgment of the devil—that is, fall through arrogance as the devil did.

[Jerome] A priest of a moment does not know humility, the proper treatment of persons, or how to restrain himself. He has not fasted, wept, corrected himself, or distributed to the poor. Those who become masters when they are not yet disciples within the span of an hour fall into arrogance, which is the devil’s fall.

Moreover, he must have good testimony not only from believers but also from those who are outside, that is, unbelievers. This clause corresponds to the beginning, namely that he must be blameless not only before those of his household but also before outsiders—Jews, Gentiles, and heretics—so that those who disparage religion may not dare to disparage his life. Therefore a bishop must be such as has been described, lest he fall into reproach—that is, contempt among unbelievers or believers—and thereby fall into the snare of the devil: that is, into hatred and the other snares of the devil.

“Deacons,” etc. Here he describes what deacons ought to be like. He seems to say nothing about presbyters, but includes them under the title “bishop.”

[Haimo] For unless he took bishops to mean presbyters, he would not pass over them and descend to deacons, of whom he says: Deacons must be modest, not double-tongued, as those who sow discord; not devoted to much wine, that is, not drunkards; not pursuing shameful gain, as those who do this frequently.

[Ambrose] Shameful gain is buying and selling at a higher price. It is shameful for this profession to pursue profit. “Holding the mystery of faith”: namely, knowing what concerning faith is hidden from others. I mean those remaining in a pure conscience. “Let these also first be tested,” for he does not simply say “these,” but “these also.” In this he intimates that bishops ought to be tested. Then, that is, when found to be such persons, having no crime, let them serve.

“Women”: while speaking of deacons, he inserts a statement concerning the women of those who are to be ordained, teaching what sort they should be. He says, therefore: The wives of those to be ordained likewise must be modest in mind and body, not slanderers, as women often are; sober; faithful in all words and deeds. For if they are wicked, the men needed to govern them ought not to be removed.

Observe that, when he commands that bishop and deacon be made holy, he surely does not wish the people to be unlike them, according to what the Lord says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. XI). Therefore he wishes even women, who are in the lowest rank, to be without fault, so that the Church may be pure.

But the Cataphrygians, taking occasion from these words—because, namely, while he speaks of deacons, he speaks of women—say that women deacons ought to be ordained; but this is contrary to authority.

“Deacons”: after the intervening statement about women, he again speaks of deacons: Deacons must be husbands of one wife, whom God has decreed for a man, with whom he is blessed, not with a second wife; governing their children and households—that is, families—well. For such men will serve the Church well, which is certainly a great matter. Those who have served well will acquire for themselves a more excellent rank—namely, that they may become bishops—a good one, beneficial to themselves and other people, and much confidence in eternal glory. And this is in faith—that is, through faith—which is in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0346B] “I write these things to you, son Timothy, hoping to come to you soon.” Yet the things I write are so necessary that, if I delay, I write them in order that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself, according to the different conditions of individuals, in the house of God. Therefore one must act carefully within it because it is God’s house, which is the Church—that is, the gathering of many for worship of the one God. One must act there with all the more care because many people are there.

I mean the Church of the living God, and thus life is in its members; it is the pillar of truth, sustaining truth well within itself lest it collapse, even though it is afflicted; and the foundation—that is, support—of those already wavering and about to fall.

[Haimo] This is evident because it endures so much for Christ. And in the Church there is a sacrament—that is, Christ hidden according to [Col. 0346C] his divinity. For a sacrament is called a hidden thing, that is, a mystery. Therefore the Word of the Father is here called a sacrament; in the nature of divinity, in which he is equal to the Father, he remains invisible. This sacrament is the cause of godliness—that is, of all holy religion and true worship—and therefore the Church must be guarded more carefully.

This sacrament is great because its greatness has no end, and manifestly great because it appeared through preaching and many miracles. Although the sacrament is invisible in itself, it was manifested to the Church.

[Ambrose] Therefore do not be negligent toward her, for whom he did so much. It was manifested, I say, in assumed flesh. He calls Christ-in-the-flesh the sacrament that was manifested. For the Son of God, born as man, who was hidden with God, made himself known to creation by work and preaching. The sense is: He was manifest in flesh—that is, by works and power displayed in the flesh, it became clear who he was that was in the flesh—and he was justified in the Spirit—that is, shown holy and righteous, because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit.

He also appeared to angels, who advanced through what was done here.

[Note: [Col. 0345D] Augustine, on Genesis.] For what is hidden is not made known to angels in God alone; it also appears to them here when it is accomplished and revealed.

[Ambrose] Therefore Christ the man is said to have appeared to angels, no longer in a form of humility but in power. He who had formerly appeared humble through the flesh, having conquered death appeared in majesty. Born as man, he was not merely man. Thus the angels, recognizing the mystery formerly hidden but declared in flesh, bent the knee to him as though giving thanks because they had learned the truth.

“He was preached among the Gentiles.” Behold, again this is great. “And believed in the world,” remaining in the world, so that the world’s unbelief may not be able to obtain pardon for ignorance, just as the Lord says concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have no excuse for their sins” (John XV). “And taken up,” from this mortality, “in glory,” so that he may be above every creature, having the name above every name, to whom every knee bends (Phil. II).

## Chapter IV

### Verses 1–8

> “But the Spirit expressly says [Col. 0347B] that in the last times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and teachings of demons, in the hypocrisy of those who speak lies and have their own conscience branded; forbidding marriage and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by believers and those who know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. By setting these things before the brethren, you shall be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and sound doctrine which you have followed. But avoid foolish and old-womanish fables. Exercise yourself, however, in godliness. For [Col. 0347C] bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.”

“But the Spirit.”

[Ambrose] He does not conceal what the Holy Spirit revealed to him for the instruction and protection of the Church, saying that men of pestilential teaching will arise, so that the Church, forewarned, may be watchful lest it be deceived by such people. As if he said: So worthy is the house of God; but the Holy Spirit clearly says to me in my heart: “Because in the last times”—against which one must now be more watchful—“some,” namely notable persons, “shall depart from the faith.” Hence above: “unless the departure comes first.” Therefore do not lay aside care for the house of God, since it is so exalted, as was said above.

[Haimo] “Some shall depart,” I say, “giving heed,” as though eagerly, to spirits of error, because evil spirits speak in them; and to doctrines, not of human beings indeed, but of demons—that is, of people possessed by demons. I mean people speaking lies in hypocrisy—that is, in pretended religion, that they may deceive more effectively—and having their own consciences branded: corrupted by perverse thought, burned by the fire of evil desire, and openly marked with the sign of falsehood so that all may beware.

A cautery, or *cautere*, is an instrument of iron, said to derive from *cavere*, “to beware,” by which the skin is injured and burned. And so that, of the many lies which they will speak in hypocrisy, some may be set forth by way of example, he adds: [Col. 0348A] “Forbidding.” As if he said: I mean those speaking lies such as this: forbidding marriage—that is, the contracting of marriages—which they say were instituted by an evil author; and commanding abstinence from foods as though unclean, not for the discipline of bodies but in order that they may appear abstinent and good.

[Note: [Col. 0347D] Augustine, against Faustus.] These foods were created by God, not—as those lying princes of darkness say—to be avoided. This is God’s teaching; that is the teaching of demons. He created them, I say, to be received with thanksgiving: that is, that man, for whose sake all things were created, might receive them and give thanks for them. He created them to be received by believers and those who know the truth: that is, those who rightly believe concerning foods and who understand what they believe—which not everyone does.

I mean this truth: that every [Col. 0348B] creature of God is good in its own nature, and nothing which is received—that is, which is customarily received—with thanksgiving is to be rejected. This statement is not contrary to the Old Testament, where certain animals used as food are forbidden. For there certain animals were called unclean, not by nature but by signification. Thus, for example, if one asks concerning a pig and a lamb, both are naturally clean because every creature of God is good. For all natural things are good in their own order; nevertheless, by a certain signification the lamb is called clean and the pig unclean.

And it is indeed true that nothing is to be rejected. For food is sanctified, so that the devil may not harm through it; that is, food becomes holy and wholesome, not harmful to soul or body, through the word of God—that is, through the Son, through whom the Father created—and through prayer. For the Word sanctifies, and prayer obtains. But the devil tempts through food.

By setting forth these things which I have said concerning creatures and marriage—that is, putting them before, or publicly setting them before—the brethren, you shall be a good minister of Christ Jesus in fact and reputation, who can do this well. I mean you, nourished by others with the words of faith and sound doctrine, in conduct, which you have also pursued by your own effort from childhood. Set these things before them.

But avoid foolish fables.

[Haimo] Such fables have no fitness and are empty—that is, without fruit—even if some reasoning seems to be present in them, as in legal matters. Or, “old-womanish” fables are those which old women customarily tell young men. Avoid them. And because avoiding them does not suffice unless one establishes the truth, he adds: “But exercise [Col. 0348D] yourself.” As if he said: Set those things before the brethren, but exercise yourself in godliness—that is, in worship and religion of the Almighty, and in works of mercy.

“For,” etc. As if he said: I urge godliness because bodily exercise, in which you weary yourself through fasting, watching, and abstinence—the restraints of the flesh—is useful for a little unless godliness is added to it.

[Ambrose] It is useful only so far as to avoid certain vices; when these have been avoided, one escapes the punishment due to them, but not every punishment. Godliness, however, which does good works for brethren, avails to win God. For the whole sum of Christian discipline is in godliness and mercy. One who follows them, if he suffers the slippery weakness [Col. 0349A] of the flesh, will without doubt be chastised, yet will not perish. But one who has only bodily discipline will suffer everlasting punishments.

Observe that these words imply that Timothy exercised himself through vigils, fasts, and works, but was not so intent on works of mercy. “But godliness.” As if he said: Bodily exercise is of little use, but godliness, by which a person strives for the salvation of all, is useful for all things, in this respect—that is, because godliness has the promise of the life which now is, so that here one may abound in spiritual goods and have sufficiency of temporal things; and of the future life, so that in the future one may have eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0349D] Augustine, on Psalm CLXIV.] Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “They shall receive sevenfold in this age,” that is, a multiplication of riches and glory, [Col. 0349B] “and in the age to come eternal life” (Matt. XIX). For he does not abandon us even in temporal necessities, as he himself says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. VI). Therefore he says that godliness has the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come: namely, possessing riches and glory here, and eternal life in the future.

Hence Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song II). Elsewhere he likewise says concerning Wisdom itself: “In her right hand are years of life, and in her left are riches and honour” (Prov. III).

### Verses 9–16

> “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance. For in this we labour and are reviled, because we hope in the living God, who is the Saviour of all human beings, especially of believers. Command [Col. 0349C] these things and teach them. Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to believers in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching. Do not neglect the gift which is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; be occupied in them, that your progress may be manifest to all. For attend to yourself and to your teaching; persevere in them. For in doing this, you shall save both yourself and those who hear you.”

“Faithful.” As if he were saying: Godliness has the promise of this present life and of the future one; and this saying concerning godliness is faithful, that is, true, and worthy of all acceptance, because it is useful—as I show in myself. [Col. 0349D] For in this, or rather, because we direct our attention to the fact that godliness has the promise of this present life and of the future, we labor and are reviled—that is, we endure reproaches—because we hope in the living God, that is, in God who gives life, as he has promised, who is the Savior of all human beings. For together with beasts he saves carnal people by bodily preservation, he who makes his sun rise upon good and evil alike (Matt. V). He is, I say, the Savior of all, and especially of believers, whom he saves here and in the future according to body and soul.

“Command.” As if he were saying: Avoid fables, exercise yourself in godliness, and command those who know these things to do the same—namely, to avoid fables and exercise themselves. [Col. 0350A] And teach those who do not know, that they may do likewise; and do these things so maturely that no one may despise your youth, but be an example to believers, so that, seeing your conduct, they may advance through your example. Be an example, I say, in speech, that by your example they may speak cautiously; and in honorable conduct among others; in love of God and neighbor; in faith; and in chastity of mind and body.

[Ambrose] He exhorts him that his progress in every respect should be an example to others, so that in a young man discipline might appear admirable and grave; that his actions might excuse his age; that he might be regarded not as a youth but as an elder; and that older persons might blush if they did not show themselves grave in conduct and morals according to the pattern of this way of life.

But so that you may keep these things, “until I come, attend to reading,” so that you may understand [Col. 0350B] the Scriptures; and, after reading, attend to exhortation for those already willing, and to teaching for those who do not know.

[Haimo] You ought to do this because you were appointed for it. And do not neglect the grace of the episcopate which is in you, which was given to you through prophecy—that is, through the choice of holy persons, in which, from things past, they seem to declare what sort of man he will be.

[Ambrose] Prophecy, therefore, is that by which one is chosen as a teacher who will be suitable in the future. Do not therefore make it void; do not be disobedient to those before whom you bowed your head.

[Haimo] Or here he calls prophecy the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which he foreknew what he would do concerning this man and the others. Therefore he says, “which was given to you through prophecy,” because, by the Spirit of prophecy revealing it, the Apostle knew Timothy [Col. 0350C] to be worthy of episcopal honor. It was given through prophecy, I say, “with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery,” that is, of the presbyters. He used the singular for the plural, because they cannot be fewer than three; and he calls a bishop a presbyter. Or he says “of the presbytery” in the singular because one lays on the hand, while the others assent.

The layings on of hands are those to which mystical words are added, by which the person chosen for this task is confirmed, receiving authority, with his own conscience bearing witness, so that he may dare, in the Lord’s stead, to offer sacrifices to God. Or, according to another reading, “with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery,” because the presbytery is the reason why hands are laid on. Or because the laying on of hands gives the presbyterate to the person ordained.

Meditate upon these things just mentioned which pertain to your office, because [Col. 0350D] you were chosen for them; be occupied in them—that is, carry them out through continual practice—so that your progress may be evident to all, that is, so that no one may fail to recognize that you are advancing in all things. And in order that you may advance, attend—not, I say, to doctrine and then to yourself, but to yourself and to doctrine: first, how you live, and then how you teach. Persist in those things which benefit both you and others. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.

## Chapter V

### Verses 1–10

> “Do not rebuke an elder, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; elderly women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity. Honor widows who are truly widows. But if any [Col. 0351A] widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household and to render a reciprocal return to her parents. For this is acceptable before God. But she who is truly a widow and desolate, let her hope in God and persist in entreaties and prayers night and day. For she who lives in pleasures is dead while living. Command this also, that they may be irreproachable. But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, 216 if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of saints, if she has supplied the needs of those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work.”

“An elder.” As if he were saying: Even if persistence is necessary, it must nevertheless be exercised with discretion. And how should you treat an elder? Namely, one elderly in years or in morals. Do not rebuke him in derogation of the honor proper to him, lest, resenting correction by a younger man, he become more embittered than improved. But exhort him as a father.

[Ambrose] Thus he will receive the admonition more readily.

[Haimo] For an old man may be warned so that he need not afterward be rebuked, which is shameful for an elder. Yet a foolish elder, as blessed Gregory says, must be rebuked very sharply.

[Ambrose] Exhort younger men as brothers, namely with the affection of love, so that, seeing that they are warned out of love, they may correct themselves more readily; elderly women as mothers, so that they may be taught with gentle speech and thus advance honorably; younger women as sisters, so that they may readily receive the discipline of good conduct. [Col. 0351C] Do these things in all chastity, so that not even a gesture may be made against them. In speaking with younger women, a young man is rightly warned concerning chastity.

Honor widows who are nevertheless truly widows—that is, abandoned not only by a husband but also by love of the world—by supporting them from the Church’s resources and cherishing them with consolations.

“But if any.” As if he were saying: Honor true widows, though not all true widows without distinction. Rather, if any true widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her household, in which she will be tested, so that only then may she be worthy to be called a widow of the Church. Merits ought to come first, so that the honor bestowed may appear due. And let her render a reciprocal return to her parents, who have supported her. She ought to do this because this—namely, governing little ones, not merely [Col. 0351D] serving in the Church—is acceptable before God.

“But she who.” As if he were saying: She who has children should govern them. But she who is a true widow and desolate—that is, who does not have a household—should hope, that is, ought to hope, in God; that is, she ought to be received into the Church. And she should persist, that is, ought to persist, in entreaties, which seek the removal of every evil, and prayers, which seek the attainment of good things, night and day. For if she does otherwise, she is dead. Hence he adds, “For,” and so forth. And she ought to be irreproachable in this respect; and he added, “Command this also,” and so forth.

Or thus: He taught that a widow who has children or grandchildren should not easily be admitted to the Church’s support, because, if she has governed her household devoutly and diligently, it is just and necessary that her relatives provide her necessities. But if she is desolate and a true widow, she should be received into the Church. He describes what a true widow is, and this is the definition of a true widow. As if he were saying: Receive a true widow; now this woman is true who is truly a widow and desolate, hopes in God, and persists in entreaties and prayers night and day. A woman truly widowed and desolate—or despised by her own people—hopes in God. For, seeing that she has help from no quarter, she is devoted to God with her whole mind, from whom alone she hopes for aid for life and salvation.

“For,” and so forth. As if he were saying: She who hopes and persists is a true widow; another is not. And this is what he says: “For she who is in the pleasures” of this world, “while living,” in the ordinary life, “is dead” in soul. [Col. 0352B] He signifies that a widow ought to be such, in order to show that she has therefore despised second marriage, so as to devote herself to the Lord’s discipline. For if, under the name of widow, she gives herself to pleasures or luxury, she must be considered dead while living, because it is a kind of imposture to wish to possess the honor of a widow while not obeying God: to do one thing and profess another, while professing religion.

Command these widows not to live in pleasures and to be irreproachable, because they lack worldly occasion for such close attention to activities or manners. He wishes the widow to be such that she cannot be reproached. For, removed from hope of worldly life and from the duty of caring for the body, she has given herself to God, that she may lead an approved life. When the occasions of the world, which are accustomed to open entrances to sins, have been removed, good conduct can remain unharmed.

“But if anyone.” As if he were saying: If a true widow has a household, let her govern it; but if she neglects this, she is worse than an unbeliever. And this is what he says: “But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household,” such as fathers, brothers, and the like, “he has denied the faith” by his works, even if not in words, because he does not love his neighbor; and he is worse than an unbeliever, because the latter has not yet known or professed the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0351D] Augustine, On John.] Note that he says “those of his household,” who are so much one’s own household as parents are to children, or children to parents. Therefore the Master of the saints himself, showing that devoted children ought to expend care upon their parents, set an example in his own person when, from the cross, he entrusted his mother to John and in a manner provided another son in his own place for her (John XIX).

Let the widow, as already stated, who is true and desolate, be enrolled—that is, fed from the Church’s provisions. And let her be of such an age, namely not less than sixty years, at which age the fuel of lust is extinguished; and let her have been the wife of one husband, because of the sacrament mentioned above; having testimony in good works: if she has faithfully raised children; if she has received the poor as guests; if she has washed the feet of holy preachers, whom it was then dangerous to receive.

Let us humbly do for one another what the Most High humbly did. Great is the commendation of humility in this. Brothers do this for one another even in the visible act itself; and those who do not do it with the hand do it in heart. Yet it is much better [Col. 0353A] that it should also be done with the hands, and that a Christian should not disdain to do what Christ did. For in one who bends down to the feet of brethren, an affection for humility is either awakened in the heart or, if already present, confirmed. And if she has supplied the needs of those suffering tribulation in prison or the like. Why enumerate each thing? If she has humbly followed every good work.

### Verses 11–18

> “But avoid younger widows. For when they have lived luxuriously, they wish to marry in Christ, having condemnation, because they have made void their first faith. Moreover, they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome, speaking what they ought not. But I desire younger women to marry, bear children, be heads of households, and give the adversary no occasion [Col. 0353B] for slander. For already some have turned back after Satan. If any believer has widows, let him provide for them, so that the Church may not be burdened, and may have enough for those who are truly widows. Let presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out grain.’ And, ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’”

“But avoid younger widows,” whose blood is hot; that is, take note of their chastity, but do not care for them to such an extent as to admit them to be supported by the Church’s provisions.

[Ambrose] He forbids young widows to be received into this profession, for an unsteady age should not easily be trusted.

“For when.” As if he were saying: Avoid them because this often occurs: when, after a vow of continence, they have lived luxuriously—that is, have indulged in food and other things, have lived a life of pleasures—they do not, I say, marry in Christ, but wish to marry. As if he were saying: Then marrying is not sinful. I say that they have condemnation for breaking faith with their vow.

[Augustine] Hence he adds: “Because they have made void their first faith,” that is, their vow; or the faith of baptism violated in the vow, namely the faith which they professed in baptism, by even wishing to marry.

[Note: [Col. 0353D] Augustine, Against Julian; On Holy Widowhood.] In the marriage bond, indeed, if chastity is preserved, condemnation is not feared; but in widowed continence and virginal excellence the virtue of a greater gift is sought. Once this has been sought, chosen, and offered by vow, not merely entering marriage but even wishing to marry, though she does not marry, is condemnable. For those who vow virginity or widowhood, not only marrying but even wishing to marry is condemnable. To demonstrate this, the Apostle did not say, “When they have lived luxuriously, they marry in Christ,” but “they wish to marry.” “Having condemnation,” he says; and why? He adds, “because they have made void their first faith.” Thus, even if they do not marry, still by wishing to do so, the will which has fallen from its resolve is shown to be condemned, whether marriage follows or does not follow. For the deceit of the resolve is condemned; broken faith with the vow is condemned; such persons are condemned because they have made void the first faith of continence. All such are like Lot’s wife, who looked back.

“Moreover.” As if he were saying: Not only do they look back, [Col. 0354A] but along with the evils mentioned they also learn to be idle, going about from house to house; not merely idle, but talkative and meddlesome, speaking what they ought not—namely, shameful things harmful to religion. Therefore, lest these evils occur, I desire younger widows to marry—which is good—and to bear children—which likewise is good—and to be heads of households—which is likewise good.

[Ambrose] He explains why he said this, adding: and thus to give the adversary no occasion for slander, that is, for speaking evil—the adversary meaning the unbeliever—which is pleasing to him, that is, what the adversary welcomes. For he welcomes speaking evil of us; and I do not desire this without cause.

[Note: [Col. 0354D] Augustine, To Julian.] For already some such women, after their vow of continence, have turned back after Satan—that is, looking backward, they have fallen away from that exalted resolve of widowed or virginal chastity, have perished, and therefore women of this kind should not be received.

But if any believer has young widows in his household, let him supply them with necessities, so that the Church may not be burdened. As if he were saying: If they had no other source, the Church would give them support; nevertheless, they would not be received into the Church. Let the Church not be burdened, I say, so that what the Church has may suffice for those who are true widows.

“He who rules well.” Here he treats of the honor due to presbyters. As if he were saying: Observe what I said concerning widows, and command this also concerning presbyters: that presbyters who rule well in life and teaching should be considered worthy by their subjects of double honor, namely that they should be obeyed spiritually and supplied with outward necessities.

[Ambrose] For good and faithful stewards ought to be honored not only with lofty honor, [Col. 0354C] but also with earthly support, so that they may not be distressed by want of resources and may rejoice in spiritual obedience. For a man becomes more diligent if he is not humbled by poverty; and authority grows in him when he sees that even in the present he receives the fruit of his labor—not so that he may abound, but so that he may not lack. For such should be the reward of one who proclaims the kingdom of God: that he neither be distressed nor exalted. Thus, to receive what is needed to live is a matter of necessity; to supply it is a matter of love. Yet the Gospel is not merchandise, to be preached for such things; for if they sell it in this manner, they make light of a great thing.

Let them therefore receive the support required by necessity from the people, and the reward for their stewardship from the Lord. For it is not repaid by the people as wages to those who serve them in the love of the Gospel, but is given as a stipend, so that [Col. 0354D] they may be fed and able to labor. That double honor is indeed to be given to all presbyters, but especially to those who labor in word—that is, in exhortation of those who know—and teaching of those who do not know.

Then he proves the outward honor by the authority of Scripture, adding: For Scripture says, “You shall not muzzle,” or “put a bridle on, an ox treading out grain”—that is, preachers; that is, you shall not prevent preachers from receiving necessities. And, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. V), by which he may restore his strength in labor.

### Verses 19–25

> “Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three [Col. 0355A] witnesses. Rebuke those who sin before all, that the rest also may have fear. I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to keep these things without prejudice, doing nothing by inclining to one side. Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in other people’s sins. Keep yourself chaste. No longer drink water only, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities. The sins of some people are evident, going before them to judgment; but those of others follow after. Likewise also good deeds are evident, and those that are otherwise cannot be hidden.”

“But against.” Because one who corrects is not usually loved and is therefore readily accused when an opportunity occurs, he warns against this, saying: Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. Two suffice if they are approved by God. He says this because a person of so high an order, acting in Christ’s place, ought not easily to be accused.

“But those who sin”—that is, those proved by this testimony, namely of two or three, to have sinned. Or, “those who sin,” those whose sin is evident: rebuke them before all, so that the rest, whether presbyters or subjects, may have fear.

[Note: [Col. 0355D] Augustine, Sermons on the Gospel.] Let us hear Christ the Lord and Paul his servant. The Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII). The Apostle says: “Rebuke those who sin before all.” A contradiction seems to exist here. The Lord seems to have spoken contrary to his Apostle; but he has not, because he himself spoke in the Apostle as well. Christ therefore said both things: one with his own mouth, the other through the mouth of his herald. Thus it is true that sometimes the one must be done, sometimes the other. But we must discern when one and when the other is appropriate.

Sometimes you ought to rebuke the sinner privately, between yourself and him alone, as the Lord says in the Gospel; sometimes before all, that the rest may fear. If we do one at one time and the other at another, we shall preserve the harmony of the Scriptures and shall not err in acting. But someone asks me: When should I do one, and when the other? Attend and see what we ought to do in each case; but would that we were not sluggish in doing it. When someone sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. Why? Because he sinned against you. What does “sinned against you” mean? You know that he sinned. [Col. 0355D] Therefore, when he has sinned against you—that is, when you know that he has sinned—then rebuke him privately, lest, if you rebuke him publicly, you be not a corrector but a betrayer, as righteous Joseph did when he alone suspected Mary of adultery. But when sin is committed openly, it must be rebuked openly, though a presbyter must not be accused without witnesses.

“I charge you before God,” the Father, and Christ Jesus, who will judge, and his elect angels, whose task is to separate good from evil, that you keep these things which I have commanded and those which follow; and do nothing without prejudice, that is, without prior examination, inclining from justice to one side. As if he were saying: Before doing anything, examine it beforehand; and do not turn away from the examination toward anything other than what the examination discovers. And after all these things, “lay hands hastily on no one”—that is, do not ordain hastily, but test often whether he appears wise and religious, lest you ordain without due consideration. “Nor share by consent in other people’s sins,” which they commit after ordination.

This most certain truth maintains that the sharing in sins which the Apostle forbids must be understood only as consent: a person shares in sins if he flatters them and, though able to correct and rebuke, neglects to do so. And keep yourself, who judge others, chaste.

“Do not”—because he has warned him concerning chastity, he takes this occasion to prohibit the excessive abstinence which Timothy had undertaken. As if he were saying: I say that you should keep yourself chaste; nevertheless, do not continue to drink water only as before, but use a little wine, for thus it does not harm chastity. Use it, I say, because of your stomach, the seat [Col. 0356B] of illness, and your frequent infirmities, namely the attacks themselves. Now he gives him particular counsel in order to guide him by sound teaching.

[Ambrose] For God prudently wishes to be served, not so that people are weakened by excess and afterward require the aid of physicians. Moderation is necessary, so that, if possible, the service once undertaken may gradually advance rather than, through inconsideration, be diminished.

“The sins of some people.” Since he had said, “Do nothing without prior examination,” he determines where preliminary examination is necessary and where it is not, distinguishing good and evil deeds into manifest and hidden. As if he were saying: Examination is needed because, just as some things are manifest and need not be examined, so others are hidden, concerning which judgment cannot be made without prior examination. This is what he says: “The sins of some people,” [Col. 0356C] and so forth.

Or the connection may be made thus: Therefore drink wine, because, even if your good intention does not immediately become clear, it still cannot be hidden, just as with evil things.

[Note: [Col. 0356D] Augustine, On the City of God.] For the sins of some people are manifest. He calls manifest those deeds concerning which it is clear with what intention they are done. These go before judgment, because if judgment follows them, it is not rash. But the sins of others follow after.

[Augustine] Or, they follow after to judgment. The hidden sins follow after, because they too will not remain hidden in their own time, but will become evident on the day of judgment. The same is to be understood concerning good deeds. Hence he adds: Likewise, some good deeds are evident and need not be tested; and those good deeds which are otherwise—that is, not known—cannot be hidden in their own time. Therefore let us judge manifest things; but let us leave hidden things to God’s judgment, because they too, whether good or evil, cannot remain hidden when the time comes for them to be revealed.

Or thus: He treats only of the present human judgment called investigation. As if he were saying: Examination is needed because, just as some deeds are manifest, so others are hidden. This is what he says: “The sins of some people are manifest”; these persons need not be tested, because their sins go before judgment—that is, they are known before they come to investigation. But the sins of others are covered by an appearance of religion and follow judgment, because they appear through [Col. 0357A] investigation. Likewise, some good deeds are evident and need not be tested. And those good deeds which are otherwise—that is, not known—cannot be hidden in investigation, and these must be tested.

## Chapter VI

### Verses 1–10

> “Let all who are slaves under the yoke consider their masters worthy of all honor, lest the name of the Lord and the teaching be blasphemed. But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers, but must serve them all the more, because they are believers and beloved, partakers of the benefit. Teach and exhort these things. If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with godliness, he is proud, [Col. 0357B] knowing nothing, but sickly about controversies and battles of words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, disputes of people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who suppose godliness to be gain. But godliness with sufficiency is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world; doubtless neither can we carry anything away. But having food and coverings, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many useless and harmful desires which plunge people into destruction and perdition. For greed is the root of all evils, which some, desiring, have wandered away from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows.”

“All.” He exhorts slaves not to despise but to honor their masters, saying: And all who are slaves under the yoke of unbelievers, though they may be righteous and wise and appear superior to them, should consider their masters worthy of all honor, serving them well.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Augustine, Questions on Exodus.] It should be known that some have preached that freedom in Christ is common to all. This is certainly true of spiritual freedom, not carnal freedom, as they understood it. Therefore the Apostle here speaks against them, commanding slaves to be subject to masters. Christian slaves, then, should not demand what is said of the Hebrews: “They shall serve six years and be sent away free without payment” (Exod. XXI), which is mystical.

He adds why the Apostle commands this: lest the Lord’s name be blasphemed, as though he were seizing another’s property, and Christian teaching as though it were unjust and preached against the laws. Rather, through the service of believing slaves, unbelieving masters may be converted.

But those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers—that is, equals in Christ—but serve them all the more, because their masters are believers and beloved by God, partakers of their slaves’ present or future benefit. Teach these things to those who do not know, and exhort those who do.

But if anyone teaches otherwise, namely that all should be free, and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ when it is objected to him that Christ said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matt. XXI), and likewise, [Col. 0358A] “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI); and does not assent to our teaching, which accords with godliness—that is, which does not make Christianity hateful—such a person is proud. Pride, not reason, guides him. And therefore he is arrogant and cannot endure to be overcome, since he breaks out into contention in order to seek favor, something avoided by the meek and good.

He knows nothing of what truth contains and is not effective, but is sickly about controversies and battles of words; that is, he is unable to resolve them, but is always occupied with them. Thus he rightly says “sickly”: for by refusing faith he does not wholly die, nor does he recover unto knowledge of truth, but, as though with repeated attacks, he is sickly about controversies and battles of words. For there was a question whether anyone could be a slave, since all were born from the same fathers and Christ redeemed all. Likewise, there seemed to be verbal battles because the Lord says, “If the Son has made you free, you will truly be free” (John VIII). These words seem opposed to the Apostle’s words, but their meaning agrees.

From these battles and controversies arise envies and strifes, because those who have slaves envy and contend; blasphemies against God, because he takes another’s property for himself; evil suspicions, as though we had devised this freedom for gain; and disputes of false preachers against others—namely, people corrupted in mind, whose reason is corrupted and who are deprived of truth, that is, of true knowledge of things and understanding of the Scriptures.

[Col. 0358C] People, I say, who suppose godliness to be gain.

[Haimo] That is, those who perform works of godliness—that is, preach—in order to receive temporal gain from their hearers, because they preach for profit, not for future things.

“But.” As if he were saying: They think godliness is gain, but godliness is a very different gain: godliness with sufficiency is great gain, namely eternal gain. Sufficiency belongs to one for whom his small possessions suffice, when a person desires to have no more than is necessary, as is fitting. For in being born we brought nothing into this world; and it is not doubtful that in dying we can carry away nothing, that is, anything from the world. Hence Job says: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return,” and so forth (Job I).

“Having.” [Ambrose] As if he were saying: Although we brought nothing in and shall take nothing away, these temporal things are not therefore to be wholly rejected. But, having food and clothing with which to be covered, let us be content with these, because whoever reaches beyond them finds evil. Hence he adds: “For those who wish to become rich.”

[Augustine] He does not say those who are rich, but those who wish to be rich, fall into temptation and the devil’s snare by the very act. For there is no kind of evil that does not sometimes arise from greed, since it is the root of all evils.

[Note: [Col. 0358D] Augustine, on Psalm CXXXVI.] Note that this is said to those who wish to be rich but are not. But something else is said in what follows to those already rich: namely, not to be high-minded, but to give to the poor. And he adds: “And [they fall] into many desires,” which riches nourish, [Col. 0359A] useless and harmful, which is worse. He shows how they harm by adding: “These desires plunge people into bodily destruction and the perdition of souls.”

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Augustine, On Genesis.] The universal root of all evils is greed, the desire to have more than one ought. By this the devil fell, and the first human beings. Some books read: “Avarice is the root of all evils,” which properly means love of money. Thus the Greek also has *philargia*, “love of silver/money.” If, then, a book has *avaritia*, which properly means love of money, though it is called the root of all evils, the species is put for the genus, which is greed. Elsewhere Scripture says that pride is the root of all evils (Ecclus. X). These statements do not seem to agree. Yet both should be understood as truly said, if the kinds of sins are considered. For there is no kind of sin which does not sometimes arise from pride, and none which does not sometimes arise from greed. And certainly there is a person who is proud because of greed, and another who is greedy because of pride.

[Augustine] For there is a person who would not be a lover of money unless he thought that through it he would be more eminent; and there is one who would not love eminence unless he thought that through it he would have greater riches. Some, desiring this greed—for one who desires money desires greed—have wandered from the faith, wholly abandoning Christ, and have entangled themselves in many sorrows. This is evident in the avaricious, who endure so many more torments of anxiety as they desire more things, whether things that pass away through use or things which they cannot possess.

[Col. 0359C] ### Verses 11–16

> “But you, O man of God, flee these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life, to which you were called and in which you confessed the good confession before many witnesses. I command you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, that you keep the commandment without stain, irreproachable, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, which in his own times the blessed and only powerful one will show: the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being [Col. 0359D] has seen, nor indeed can see. To him be honor and everlasting dominion. Amen.”

But you, Timothy, because you are a man—that is, rational—and because you belong to God, flee these things. [Ambrose] For nothing is so harsh and so destructive as for a churchman, especially one who holds an exalted position, to devote himself to the riches of this age; for he harms not only himself but also others, to whom he gives a contrary example. But pursue justice, by doing to each person what right requires—which the greedy man does not do; godliness, that you may stoop to help one in need—which the greedy man does not do; true faith. Whoever has a true faith concerning God does not desire to become rich amid miseries, nor does he value the world more highly than God. Pursue [Col. 0360A] the love of God and neighbor, of which the greedy man is wholly devoid; patience and gentleness, which the greedy man lacks, since he neither bears adversities patiently nor is gentle toward another. Fight. That is to say: possess these things in yourself for the sake of others; first fight the contest—as though he said, “Fight continually.” I mean a good contest, namely one that benefits others; that is, fight such a contest as, undertaken with discernment, may benefit others. I mean a contest of faith, namely one undertaken for the faith and for all these things. Lay hold on eternal life; that is, seek nothing but eternal life. You ought to do this, because you were called to it and not to anything else. And this is what he adds: you were called to possess it; and also because you have already confessed before many witnesses—or at [Col. 0360B] your ordination, or in preaching—a good confession, that is, what faith requires.

“I command you.” He gives commands to the ruler of the Church with great watchfulness and foresight. [Haimo] For in Timothy the guardian speaks to all his successors. As though he said: I not only exhort you, but also command you before God the Father, who gave life to all things in which there is life, and thus also to you, and before Jesus Christ, that you may imitate him who, when he was under Pontius Pilate, bore witness—namely, the good confession: that is, when death was imminent, he did not deny the truth, but affirmed what he had said, namely that he was the counsel of God. This was a good and honorable confession. I command you, I say, to keep the commandment—that is, what God and I [Col. 0360C] have commanded you—which is spotless and beyond reproach, because the law of the Lord is undefiled and cannot even fittingly be reproved. Keep it until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; that is, until Christ comes to you in death. This coming of Christ, at his own—that is, fitting—times, the blessed and only mighty one will show to whatsoever saints there are.

[Note: [Col. 0359D] Augustine, Against Maximinus.] This should not be understood of the Father alone, but of God who is the Trinity itself: whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does, and so does the Holy Spirit. Therefore the triune God is meant when he says, “the blessed and only mighty one”; for he alone is blessed and mighty in himself, and he will also make his own people good and mighty, kings of their own selves and lords of their dominions. Hence he adds: “King of kings and Lord of lords,” who alone by nature possesses immortality, [Col. 0360D] that is, immutability, and will bestow it upon his own by grace; and he dwells in light. He says this by likeness: that is, he himself is the light in which his own will share. I mean inaccessible light, because no one approaches it by himself, but only he to whom it is given by God’s gift. The Prophet understood this when he said: “Approach him and he will illuminate [you]” (Eph. V). And that light is thus inaccessible because he himself is the one whom no human being has seen by himself, but sees when made God, as he was speaking of the light. Now he speaks of God himself, because he himself and the light are the same; but neither can a human being see him in this life; afterward, however, he will see him.

[Note: [Col. 0360D] Id., ibid.] Nothing is said here that does not suit [Col. 0361A] the Trinity, because in truth the Trinity is one God: “the blessed and only mighty one, King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality,” because he alone is by nature immutable, since neither by anyone’s grace, but by his own nature, could he or can he be changed by any turning, nor could he or will he be able to sin by any change. But if any rational creature is granted the inability to sin, this belongs not to its own nature but to God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Augustine, On the Trinity.] Therefore God alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being sees or can see; nor should the Son be understood as separated from him, because the Son is eternal life with the Father. [Augustine] Thus he is rightly understood as the one whom, according to the nature by which he is God, no one has seen or can see [Col. 0361B]—but whom one day he will be able to see, if he belongs to those of whom it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). To this God—that is, to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—belong honor from creatures, glory in himself, and dominion, because he can do all things; and he will bestow these also upon his own. And this is forever. Amen.

VERS. 17–21.—“Command the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us all things abundantly for enjoyment: to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, to store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on true life. O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and the objections of knowledge falsely so called, [Col. 0361C] which some, professing it, have fallen away from the faith. Grace be with you. Amen.”

“The rich.” Above he treated those who wish to become rich, saying that they fall into temptation and the devil’s snare. Here he treats those who are rich, warning them not to place hope in riches. And because he had said that evils arise from greed, and had urged the contrary, lest the rich seem altogether rejected, he makes a distinction. As though he said: although the greedy fall into the devil’s snare, the rich are nevertheless not to be wholly rejected; rather, command the rich of this age—for there are also spiritual rich—that is, those who abound in money in this age. What are you to command? Not that they cease to be rich, but that they not be high-minded and not hope in the uncertainty of riches; that is, that they not grow proud from them [Col. 0361D] and not place their hope in them, because they are uncertain. Therefore one should not be proud on their account but afraid.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Augustine, in a sermon On the Words of the Gospel.] Observe that the Apostle did not fear riches, but the disease of riches—that is, pride, which is the worm of the rich. Great is the soul that is not tempted by this disease among riches; great is the person who does not think himself great merely because he is rich. But whoever thinks himself great for that reason is proud and needy: he bursts outwardly in the flesh, but begs in his heart; he is swollen, not [Col. 0362A] full. And lest they suppose that they had lost hope because he had said, “not to hope in the uncertainty of riches,” he added: “But command them to hope in the living God, who provides us all things abundantly”—namely, without diminution—“for enjoyment” in eternity, not merely for use in this life.

[Augustine] For he gives temporal things for use, eternal things for enjoyment: the former, that by them we may do good; the latter, that by them we may become good. But if they ask what they are to do with their riches, command the rich to do good and to become rich in good works; that is, command them to work well, so that they may be rich in works. And command them to give their own goods—and to do so readily, or, thus, to be ready for this. And command them to share; that is, to regard what they have as common property; and to store up for themselves a good foundation, [Col. 0362B] that is, firm virtues, not works alone. And this for the future: that is, for the work not of some present good but of future good, to which riches are sent on ahead, not lost. Command them to do these things so that—that is, when—they may lay hold on true life, namely eternal life, which is not fleeting and vain as this life is.

What more need be said? O Timothy—by the proper name he admonishes him, making him attentive—guard the deposit, namely that which God and I have entrusted to you; avoiding, so that you may be able to guard it, novelties of words—not all novelties, but profane ones, which are contrary to religion, such as *hypostasis*, a term applicable to both person and substance. Under the ambiguity of this term heretics wished to introduce the claim that there are three substances. Other novelties, however, are not to be avoided.

[Note: [Col. 0361D] Augustine, On John.] For certain novelties of words are fitting to the doctrine of religion, such as the very name “Christian,” of which it is written when it first began to be used. For at Antioch, after the Lord’s Ascension, they were first called Christians, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0362D] Id., in the same work.] Against the impiety of the Arians, the Fathers also coined the new term *homoousion*; yet by that name they did not signify a new reality. For *homoousion* is what is of one and the same substance. For if every novelty were profane, the Lord would not have said, “I give you a new commandment” (John XIII); nor would it be called a New Testament, nor would the whole Church sing a new song. And avoid also the objections of knowledge falsely so called; that is, of what is falsely called [Col. 0362D] knowledge. Some who profess this knowledge, laughing at faith as though it were ignorance, have fallen away from the faith, always remaining around the faith and never within it.

[Note: [Col. 0362D] Id., in the same work.] For nothing do these people love so much as promising knowledge and ridiculing, as though it were ignorance, the faith in true things which little children are commanded to believe. And that you may guard these things, may grace be with you. Amen.

## On the Second Epistle to Timothy

[Col. 0363]

### Argument

[Col. 0363A]

He likewise writes to Timothy from the city of Rome concerning the exhortation to martyrdom, every rule of truth, what will happen in the last times, and his own suffering.

## Chapter I

VERS. 1–5.—“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, most beloved son: grace, mercy, and peace from God our Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure conscience, because without ceasing I have remembrance of you in my prayers night and day, desiring to see you, mindful of your tears, [Col. 0363B] that I may be filled with joy, receiving recollection of that unfeigned faith which is in you, which also first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice; and I am certain that it is in you also.”

“Paul, an apostle.” Paul, now about to depart from the world, likewise writes this second Epistle from Rome, from prison, to Timothy, already wearied by weaknesses and adversities: that he may labor steadfastly in the grace of God entrusted to him. He exhorts him to martyrdom in many ways; to persevere in the office of right preaching and holy action; and foretells what will take place in the last times and speaks of his own death.

[Haimo] The Apostle’s intention in this Epistle is to exhort Timothy to the diligent performance of his office and to the crown of martyrdom, and also to add certain matters concerning the episcopal office. Its arrangement is as follows: first he greets him; then he gives thanks for the good which Timothy possesses, where he shows his desire to see him. Afterwards he urges him to preach and to endure martyrdom, by his own example and other means. Then he says what sort of people will exist in the last days, and finally he speaks of the approaching time of his own departure. He begins with a greeting, saying: “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, in whose office you share. Therefore fulfill the work due to that office.” I mean an apostle by the will of God, not through my own merits. As though he said: you too were similarly sent freely, and therefore you are the more bound to preach grace. I am an apostle, he says, and not without hope of reward; indeed, according to the promise of life—not of this life, but that which is [Col. 0363D] in Jesus—I contend lawfully for this promise. I promise it to my followers. Paul, I say, writes an epistle to Timothy, his most beloved son, and before all else greets him thus: may grace—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit by which ministers are armed—mercy—that is, forgiveness of sins—and peace—that is, tranquility of mind and a foretaste of eternal life—be with you from God the Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.

“I give thanks.” He gives thanks for Timothy’s good, commending the grace of faith which is in him. He says therefore: I give thanks to my God because without ceasing I remember you in my prayers—namely, praying for greater gifts for you; that is, I give thanks because you have been so good that I always remember you. This is a wise exhortation to greater things. “My God,” I say, whom I serve—and you too should follow him. I serve, having been taught by my forefathers—that is, by the ancient fathers, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others who worshipped the one God in true faith—for the faith of both is one: that is, of the ancient and modern righteous alike. I serve, I say, with a pure conscience; may yours be so too.
