I, I say, desire to see you night and day, because my sight of you would be your strengthening, and thus I, who rejoice in your goodness, would be filled with joy at your perfection. [Col. 0364B] Hence he adds: “that I may be filled with joy.” As though he said: I desire to see you in order that I may be filled with joy at your perfection, and also because I remember your tears. For Timothy wept when he was dismissed by Paul, being ready to go with him into every danger. What he possessed when present, therefore, let him retain while absent. I, I say, receiving—that is, also holding—the recollection of that unfeigned faith which is in you, that is, not fabricated or fragile; this should remind you of it, since it was firm even in women. Hence follows: this faith also first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and mother Eunice.

[Ambrose] He recalls the sincerity of his parents’ faith in order to make the man stronger. [Haimo] And I am certain that the same faith dwells in you also; therefore let it burn fervently.

VERS. 6–18.—“For this reason I remind [Col. 0364C] you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety. Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner; but labor with the Gospel according to the power of God, who delivered us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time. But it has now been made manifest through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ, who indeed destroyed death and brought life and incorruption to light through the Gospel, in which I have been appointed preacher, [Col. 0364D] apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles. For this reason I also suffer these things, but I am not ashamed. For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day. Hold the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus. Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us. For you know this: all who are in Asia have turned away from me, among whom are Philetus and Hermogenes. [Col. 0365A] May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chain; but when he came to Rome, he diligently sought me and found me. May the Lord grant him to find mercy from God in that day. And how much he ministered to me at Ephesus, you know better.”

“For this reason.” Having commended Timothy’s faith, he exhorts him to preach it without fear or shame. As though he said: for this reason—namely, because you have faith, have been such a person, and have had such good parents—I remind you to rekindle the grace of God, namely the episcopal grace granted you by God, as though lulled asleep by fear, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, and which admonishes you to obey me.

“For God has not.” As though he said: I urge you to rekindle [Col. 0365B] the grace of God, which indeed you can do. For God has given us a spirit of power and love.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] Augustine, On Grace and Free Will.] And this is what he says: for he has not given us—you as well as me—a spirit of fear, by which Peter, troubled, denied Christ. Rather, he wished this fear to be removed from us when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. X). We have not received the spirit of this fear, but of that fear of which the Lord says: “Fear him who can destroy body and soul in Gehenna” (ibid.). For the Holy Spirit gives fear, not of the world, but of God, who can destroy in Gehenna. He has not given, I say, a spirit of fear, but of power—that is, courage against adversities, which drives out fear—which comes from the love of God and neighbor; of this he adds, “and of love,” which sobriety precedes; of this he adds, “and of sobriety,” that is, discernment. Behold, from the highest gift, namely love, he descends to one thing, namely sobriety.

“Therefore do not.” He previously warned him not to fear, for which power is useful. Here he warns him not to be ashamed, for which love and discernment are useful. As though he said: because he has given the spirit of love and discernment, therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord—that is, do not be ashamed to testify to people that the Lord was crucified, because he rose again.

[Ambrose] He teaches that steadfastness must be maintained and that one must not be ashamed in confession. There is nothing in it of which one should be ashamed, because though Christ was seen as a man, by his deeds he nevertheless appeared as God; and though he was crucified, he nevertheless rose from the dead and, as many watched, ascended into heaven when a cloud received him. Where weakness is thought to be, there power appears. Nor be ashamed of me as his prisoner for preaching his Gospel, because there is no shame in this either; rather, labor with me in preaching the Gospel of the cross.

[Haimo] Or: labor with me for the Gospel, that is, for the honor of the Gospel. You can do this according to God’s power; and you ought to do so because he delivered us at the price of his own blood.

[Ambrose] It is fitting, then, to render service in return to the one who delivers us. Since we cannot worthily respond to his benefits, let us at least carry out his embassy faithfully and eagerly. And he called us with his own inward calling, that is, one suited to himself alone, and holy, because he calls us to holy things. He called us, I say, not according to our works, [Col. 0366A] but according to his own purpose and grace; that is, according to what he had indeed foreseen through grace. This grace was given to us in Christ Jesus—that is, it was foreseen that it would be given to us through Christ—before the ages of the world. But it has now been made manifest in its fulfillment through the illumination of our Savior Jesus Christ, that is, through the preaching of Christ which enlightens hearers. He explains what that grace is, adding: Christ indeed destroyed death, both kinds, of soul and body. This is that grace: namely, the destruction of death. Therefore death is not to be feared for Christ’s faith. But he brought life and incorruption to light—that is, incorruptible life. And this through the Gospel, that is, through the preaching of the Gospel. See how necessary the Gospel is, in [Col. 0366B] which—that is, in the Gospel—I have been appointed as a preacher—as though immovable, an active noun—an apostle possessing apostolic authority, and teacher of the Gentiles, daily teaching the nations. For this reason, namely because I preach, I suffer these things which I now endure at Rome; but I am not ashamed—that is, I do not fail or blush. Secure because a great reward has been promised to him for tribulations, he is not ashamed but glories in afflictions. He explains below what these matters concern: “Holding the pattern,” etc.

“For I know.” [Haimo] As though he said: for this reason I am not ashamed, because I know that God is he in whom I have believed.

[Augustine] Or: “I know whom I have believed,” that is, to whom I have entrusted my own concerns, namely Christ. And I am certain that he is able [Col. 0366C] to preserve my deposit: that is, my salvation, which I have entrusted to him, placing it in the hope and faith of him.

[Ambrose] “Until that day,” namely the day of judgment. He is secure in the hope and greatness of the Savior, because what he entrusts to him is safe. He entrusts his salvation to him, so that by suffering here for him, he may find salvation with him when he begins to judge, so that, punishing the unbelievers, he may pronounce this man worthy of eternal life. Or, he is able to preserve my deposit: that is, the Gospel which he entrusted to me, or which I entrusted to him to preserve until that day of my departure.

“The pattern.” Here he shows to what end the foregoing statements about himself tend. As though he said: I labor and persist thus in the office entrusted to me; likewise you, holding the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, not from just anyone—holding, I say, [Col. 0366D] good words with faith and love which is in Christ Jesus, that is, as Christ instituted. Holding these things, I say, by which you can keep them, keep them by diligent performance. Guard the good deposit—that is, the office entrusted to you—which you can do through the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, namely in you as in me.

[Haimo] Some books read, “Hold the pattern.” According to this reading, I connect the passage as follows: as though he said, “Labor with the Gospel; and in order that you may do this rightly, hold the pattern of sound words,” etc. The sense is unchanged. And “guard the good deposit”: here likewise the meaning does not change. “For you know this.” As though he said: therefore you need to guard it, because [Col. 0367A] you know that all those who have turned away from me—that is, departed from me—are now in Asia, among whom are Philetus and Hermogenes, against whom you must especially be on guard.

[Ambrose] Those whom he names were full of pretense: they had been with the Apostle deceitfully, in order to learn something from which they could bring an accusation against him; but after they saw that they had been exposed, they departed from him.

“May he grant,” etc. As though he said: they departed from me, but may the Lord grant mercy to the household—that is, family—of Onesiphorus, an Asian, because he often refreshed me by supplying my necessities. You should imitate him. And he was not ashamed of my chain, like those who departed from me; but when he came to Rome he diligently sought me, that he might be allowed to enter to me, and found me. Therefore may God the Father grant him to find mercy from the Lord—that is, from the Son—on [Col. 0367B] that day of judgment; and not only at Rome, but he also ministered many things to me at Ephesus. You, who were present, know better than many others—or, better than these things.

## Chapter II

VERS. 1–9.—“Therefore, my son, be strengthened in the grace which is in Christ Jesus. And what you have heard from me through many witnesses, entrust these things to faithful people who will be fit to teach others also. Labor as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, that he may please him to whom he has proved himself. For even one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. A laboring farmer ought first to receive from the fruits. Understand what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding [Col. 0367C] in all things. Remember the Lord Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel, in which I labor even to chains, as an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound.”

“Therefore you.” As though he said: because those men have turned away, and you have the example of Onesiphorus, therefore you, my son, be strengthened—especially by the example of Onesiphorus—in the grace of faith and wisdom which must be preserved in you and proclaimed to others. This grace was given in Christ Jesus. And appoint fellow-workers as well. Hence he adds: what you heard from me, confirmed through many witnesses, namely through the prophets, entrust these things to faithful people—that is, those of sound faith—who will be fit in life, knowledge, and eloquence [Col. 0367D] to teach others also. For God’s preaching ought to be entrusted to those who are suitable for that office. And you yourself labor in preaching the Gospel against the enemies of the faith, as a good soldier of Christ. But if you wish to be a good soldier, do not entangle yourself in secular business, since no one serving as a soldier in spiritual matters for God—who cannot be divided between two opposed services, just as no one can serve two masters—entangles himself in any secular business. Or, he calls it secular business especially when someone, as though doing trade, seeks carnal things from spiritual things. And this is the definition of a good soldier: that, therefore, he may be a good soldier, he does not entangle himself in secular business.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] Augustine, in the book On the Work of Monks.] The Apostle says this in writing [Col. 0368A] to Timothy lest perhaps, when Timothy was in need and did not wish to be supported in his daily food by those to whom he ministered the Gospel, and could not labor at bodily work, he might seek for himself some business by which his mind would be entangled. For those too are secular businesses when the mind is occupied by the care of gathering money without bodily labor, as merchants and such people do. For they work by care, not with their hands, and so they occupy their very minds with the anxiety of possessing. Lest Timothy should do this, because in his weakness he could not work, he forbids it, saying: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, that he may please him,” namely God, “to whom he has proved himself”—that is, devoted himself and shown himself worthy through what has gone before in his election.

“For even one who.” As though he said: therefore labor as a good [Col. 0368B] soldier, or therefore let no one entangle himself in secular business, because otherwise the crown is not given unless one serves lawfully as a soldier, so that he is in the contest. For even he who competes in any contest will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully—that is, as the law of the contest requires—which no one can do unless he abstains from everything that may hinder that contest. And as though he might ask: “From what then shall I live, when I cannot dig and am ashamed to beg?” he adds: “A laboring farmer.” As though he said: even if you do not entangle yourself in business, there is nevertheless a way in which you can live, because a laboring farmer ought—Or connect it thus: I say, labor; and although I urge you to labor in this way, nevertheless do not live by your own work, because you are weak and less sufficient for the word of God, because a laboring farmer ought—

[Haimo] namely, the preacher, who in the field of the Church cultivates the hearts of hearers with the hoe of God’s word, first to receive—that is, to take—from the fruits, that is, necessities from his hearers, because “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X). As a farmer or vintner tastes the first fruits of his labor, so the Apostle commands him who is first to take first, and then distribute to the rest.

[Ambrose] For he ought first to supply his own need from what he receives and afterwards minister to others from what remains.

[Haimo] Thus he makes the chaste evangelist, who does not preach in order to sell the Gospel, secure; and he wishes him to understand that taking necessities from those among whom he serves God, [Note: [Col. 0368D] Augustine, in the same work.] and whom he tends as a cultivator tends a vineyard or as a shepherd feeds a flock, is not begging but a right. Timothy, however, was of such great abstinence that, even refraining from what was lawful, he wished to live by the labor of his hands, although the Lord decreed that whoever proclaims the Gospel should live from the Gospel.

“Understand.” As though he said: I say that you should receive necessities from your subjects. And if in this I seem to say things opposed, and contrary to what I myself do, understand what I say; that is, discern what is said and why. For I say that you should receive because you are weak. I refrain because receiving is a cause of scandal to me. Understand, I say, what you can. For God will give you understanding in all things, not in these alone.

“Remember.” [Col. 0369A] [Haimo] As though he said: one who competes lawfully will be crowned; and in order that you may compete lawfully, remember that our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead, born from the seed of David—that is, from David’s offspring.

[Ambrose] And this according to my Gospel, that is, according to my preaching, even if the perverse deny it. He mentions these things not for Timothy’s sake but for the heretics whom he foresaw would come and deny them. In preaching this Gospel I labor even to chains; you should do likewise. I am said to be regarded as an evildoer. Here he notes the insult cast upon him. But the word of God is not bound in me; although the body is bound—that is, although I am bound in body—the word of God is not bound, because I do not cease to teach those who are present by speech and those absent by letters.

[Col. 0369B] VERS. 10–18.—“Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect, that they too may attain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with heavenly glory. The saying is trustworthy: for if we have died with him, we shall also live with him; if we endure, we shall also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself. Remind them of these things, solemnly charging them before God. Do not contend in words, for it is useful for nothing except the ruin of the hearers. But be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a worker without shame, rightly handling the word of truth. Avoid profane and empty talk, for it advances greatly toward impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have fallen away from [Col. 0369C] the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened, and they have overthrown the faith of some.”

Therefore, that is, for the Gospel, or because I remember that Christ rose again, I endure all things, especially hardships, for the sake of the elect, even if I do not benefit everyone, so that they too may obtain with me here the salvation of the soul which is in Christ Jesus, that is, which is accomplished through Christ. And this with heavenly glory, the glory which will be given after this life. As though he said: Here let them obtain the salvation of justification, and after this life heavenly glory. And this saying is faithful, that is, true—namely, that the elect will obtain salvation and glory; and truly so: for those who have died to the world, as Christ died to the old man, and who endure, that is, the martyrs [Col. 0369D], will obtain salvation. And this is what he says: “For if we have died with him,” that is, if we have died to the world or to sins in baptism, as Christ died to the old man, then we shall also live with him, that is, we shall live with him in eternal life. And if we endure tribulations and sufferings for Christ, we shall also reign with him in eternal blessedness.

Or thus: “The saying is faithful”; for if—arrange and connect the text thus—because, in order that you may endure, remember that Christ rose again: for if we have died with Christ in death itself, we shall also live with him; and if we endure in suffering itself, we shall also reign with him in glory. And this saying is faithful. And if we deny him before men, [Col. 0370A] he also will deny you before the Father, saying, “I do not know you” (Matt. XXIV). This is contrary to what he himself says: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X). And if we do not believe that he punishes the wicked, foolishly trusting in his mercy, he nevertheless—namely Christ—remains faithful in his words, and also in what he said: “Whoever does not believe shall be condemned.” And truly he is faithful, because he cannot deny himself, who is truth; he would do so if he did not fulfil his sayings. But his inability to deny himself is praise of the divine will, whereas the fact that some are unable to believe is the fault of the human will.

[Note: [Col. 0369D] Augustine, *On John*.]

These things, then—the things just stated, namely that you should suffer, and so forth—I remind you of, solemnly charging you. Or according to another reading: “Remind them of these things,” [Col. 0370B] solemnly charging those entrusted to you before God, that is, calling God as witness. Do not. As though he said: Do this, but do not dispute about words. For it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of the hearers, because contention can do nothing except overthrow those who hear, while the wordy party seems equal or superior to the Catholic. Contention often produces scruple in those who are less firmly established. For in disputation such points are customarily advanced with a sharpened argument of ill will that they unsettle the minds of foolish brethren. Nor can it fail to happen that contention wrings out something said against conscience, so that a man loses inwardly in his mind while outwardly he comes away the victor. For no one allows himself to be defeated, even though he knows that what he hears is true. Discussion among servants of God, therefore, ought to be a conference, not a quarrel.

But take pains to present [Col. 0370C] yourself to God—this for your own sake—as approved, that is, tested and praiseworthy in the sight of your people—this for your neighbour’s sake—a worker, in performing the works of life, unashamed, namely one who is not ashamed of the Gospel or does not fail, rightly handling the word of truth: that is, according to each person’s capacity, distributing spiritual things to the mature and milk to the little ones. Avoid profane things, such as heresies, and empty talk, namely things without profit, even if they are not so bad; for they harm some people. Hence he adds: “For they make much progress,” that is, they are effective, “toward impiety,” that is, against the worship of God. And their speech, that is, the speech of heretics, spreads like cancer: it advances little by little from a small beginning to something greater, corrupting what is healthy [Col. 0370D] and thus drawing men toward impiety. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus. He discloses their names so that Timothy may especially beware of them; he identifies them as both profane and impious, and as straying from the truth. Hence he adds: “Who have fallen away from the truth,” in which they were formerly; for this reason they are still believed, and are therefore more harmful. Yet they have fallen from it, saying that the resurrection of bodies has already occurred, so that no other may be hoped for. They said this on the occasion of those words contained in the Gospel: namely, “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose again” (Matt. XXVII). And they denied the general resurrection which is still to come.

Or thus, so that it is understood of the resurrection of the soul. For there are two resurrections. The first occurs in the soul, which is made alive through faith and baptism. Hence: “Whoever believes in me shall pass from death to life.” The other will be that of bodies, on the day of judgment. The Apostle here speaks of that resurrection which takes place in the soul through faith when he says: “Saying that the resurrection of minds [Col. 0371A] has already occurred,” in baptism and faith, and that no resurrection of bodies is to come.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] Augustine, *On John*.]

For all sects which promise some religion concede the resurrection of minds in faith; otherwise they would not seem worth hearing. Therefore, wishing to be believed, all those who established a sect of some false religion were unable to deny this resurrection of minds: all agreed concerning it. But [Col. 0371B] many denied the resurrection of bodies, like those whom the Apostle names. And they overturned the faith of some; and therefore they are to be avoided all the more.

### Verses 19–20

> “But the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’; and, ‘Let everyone who invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.’ But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthenware vessels; and some indeed are for honour, but others for dishonour.”

But for this reason one ought not to despair on their account: because the firm foundation of God stands—that is, those whom God has chosen and immovably founded in faith. Whoever perishes was not from it. I say, a foundation having this [Col. 0371C] seal, that is, having this as a sign to friends and enemies: to friends, that they may approach; to enemies, that, terrified, they may flee. Or, “having this seal” means that it has this impressed upon its mind: namely, that “the Lord knows those who are his,” that is, he loves and protects those whom he foreknew as his own. Here is indicated that foreknowledge by which those whom he foreknew would be conformed to the image of his Son he predestined, called, justified, and glorified.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] The same author, *On Baptism*.]

The number of such persons is a locked garden, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with the fruits of trees. From this number some live spiritually and enter upon the surpassing way of charity. Others are still carnal, yet earnestly pursue their progress; and, that they may become fit for the food of spiritual persons, they are nourished with the milk of holy mysteries. They avoid, in the fear of God, things which are evident in depraved conduct even to popular judgment; they firmly hold the carefully investigated rule of faith; and, if they depart from it, they are quickly corrected by Catholic authority, although in its words they still fluctuate, because of their carnal understanding, amid various rushes of images. [Col. 0371D] There are also among that number some who still live wickedly, or even lie in heresies or the superstitions of the Gentiles; and yet even there “the Lord knows those who are his.” For in that ineffable foreknowledge of God, many who seem to be outside are inside, and many who seem to be inside are outside.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] Augustine, *The City of God*.]

Therefore, from among all those who are, so to speak, inwardly and secretly [Col. 0372A] within—that is, those whom the Lord knows—no one is led astray into eternal condemnation. For God knows those who are his: the judgment has not yet appeared, but it has already taken place in God’s knowledge. For he knows who will remain for the crown and who for the flame; he knows wheat and chaff. Then he gives the other part of the seal from the book of Isaiah, adding: “Let everyone who truly names or invokes the name of the Lord depart from iniquity”—even if not from wicked persons with whom he is mingled in the body. Observe that he says, “Let him depart.” For Isaiah, seeing free choice in man, thus admonishes him to depart from iniquity, saying: “Let him depart,” and so forth. And by these things—that a human being departs from iniquity by free choice, and that God protects the one foreknown—it appears to enemies and friends that he belongs to God. [Col. 0372B] This is the seal.

“But in a great house.” As though he said: Some are overthrown, some are sealed; and this is not surprising, because in the great house, that is, in the Church, there are now together not only vessels of gold and silver—that is, good recipients and dispensers of God—but also wooden and earthenware vessels, that is, evil persons. Although they are for dishonour, nevertheless they are useful to the honourable for cleansing. Hence he adds: “And some indeed are for honour,” namely the good, who are cleansed through the wicked; “but others for dishonour,” that is, the wicked, who are the cleansing agent of the good. For just as wooden and earthenware vessels are useful in cleaning silver and gold vessels, so the wicked benefit the progress of the good.

[Note: [Col. 0372D] The same author, *On Baptism*.]

Therefore, the great house is [Col. 0372C] the Church, in which there are vessels of gold and silver—that is, good, faithful, and holy servants of God, scattered everywhere and bound together in spiritual unity, living in the same communion of sacraments—and wooden and earthenware vessels: those who are in the house in such a way that they are not in the house’s structure or its peaceful fellowship, yet are still bodily together with the good. For before the time of the final separation, one must by no means depart from the unity of the Church because of the mixture of the wicked; before the threshing-floor is winnowed, wheat and tares, grain and chaff are together, because the Lord did not permit the apostles to separate the tares from the wheat.

[Haimo] Who, then, would dare do this? Behold: by the golden and silver vessels the good and the elect are understood, and they are the same persons as the vessels for honour, because through the wooden vessels they are raised to the honour and glory [Col. 0372D] of the heavenly homeland. Thus the earthenware and reprobate are understood, and they likewise are the same persons as the vessels for dishonour, because they are plunged into the punishment of condemnation. Or, by golden and silver vessels all good persons are understood, whether they persevere; by wooden vessels all evil persons, whether evil only for a time or obstinate. And of both groups some are for honour, because from among both good and evil persons some are chosen for glory; likewise, from both groups some are for dishonour, because among both good and evil persons some are reprobate.

### Verses 21–26

> “If, therefore, anyone cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified and useful [Col. 0373A] to the Lord, prepared for every good work. But flee youthful desires; pursue righteousness, faith, hope, and charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart. But avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. And a servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all, apt to teach, patient, correcting with meekness those who resist the truth, lest perhaps God may give them repentance for the acknowledging of the truth, and they may return to their senses from the devil’s snares, by whom they are held captive to do his will.”

“If anyone, therefore.” As though he said: Some are for honour, some for dishonour; and because this is one of the two alternatives, if anyone has cleansed himself from these persons who are for dishonour, [Col. 0373B] by departing from their iniquity, not from them, he will be a vessel for honour, sanctified by faith and works; or, sanctified, that is, clean; and useful to the Lord, by gaining others, and ready for every good work. As though he said: He does not perish because he is bodily among them.

“But flee youthful desires.” As though he said: Avoid the profane and empty talk of others; but in yourself flee youthful desires—lust, impurity, and other such things. But pursue righteousness in judgment, true faith, charity toward God and neighbour; or chastity; peace, that is, tranquillity, with those who invoke the Lord from a pure heart, that is, with the faithful. Or thus, “with those”: as though he said, pursue all these things with those, that is, as those do, who invoke [Col. 0373C] the Lord from a pure heart, that is, with a pure conscience. Pursue these things.

But avoid foolish questions, that is, useless questions, and those which are without instruction, that is, in which there is no increase of knowledge, even if they are not foolish. Not all questions must be avoided, but useless ones. And “without instruction”: avoid them, I say, knowing that they generate quarrels, not edification. But a servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, that is, spend his time in disputes. Those who contradict already make enough noise. Therefore, lest God’s servant make noise for himself through a zeal for wrangling and contention, he says: “A servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle,” that is, tractable toward all, even toward evil people, in order to draw them; apt to teach, namely, one who readily teaches or is taught, if necessary, in some matter; patient amid any adversities; correcting with meekness, that is, gentleness of mind, [Col. 0373D] those who resist the truth. For one must not cease from correcting another’s error.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount*.]

It is clear that he wished us neither to be absent from the work of correction nor to devote ourselves to strife. For many people, when awakened from sleep, want to quarrel; or, when forbidden to quarrel, they want to go back to sleep. I say, correcting them, because correction is for this purpose: “lest perhaps,” that is, “so that at some time,” God may give them repentance; or correction is effective then. “Lest perhaps,” that is, if at some time God gives them repentance—

[Note: [Col. 0374D] Augustine, *On Rebuke and Grace*.]

—otherwise correction is of no use unless the heavenly physician looks upon them, that is, unless he makes each person repent of his sin. This repentance is sometimes hindered by shame and by fear of displeasing others, since a person takes more delight [Col. 0374A] in others’ opinion of him than in righteousness, by which each humbles himself in repentance. Therefore, not only when repentance is being undertaken, but also in order that it may be undertaken, God’s mercy is necessary. For Peter to weep bitterly, the Lord looked upon him (Luke XXII).

[Haimo] Therefore the Apostle here says: “May God give them repentance for the acknowledging of the truth,” which they now oppose, so that, once it is known, they may return to their senses from the snares of the devil: that is, they may withdraw from the devil’s errors, by which they are held ensnared, and return to the good so as to taste again the truth. [Augustine] For *resipere*, “to return to one’s senses,” is as it were *re sapere*, “to taste again.” By him, namely the devil, they are not merely bound, but held captive, as though outside their homeland, to carry out his will.

## Chapter III

[Col. 0374B] **Verses 1–9.**—“But know this: that in the last days perilous times will press upon us; and people will be lovers of themselves, covetous, puffed up, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, accusers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, swollen with pride, and lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power. Avoid these also. For among them are those who enter houses and lead captive little women burdened with sins, who are led by various desires, always learning and never coming to knowledge of the truth. Now just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: people [Col. 0374C] corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith; but they will make no further progress.”

“But know this.” As though he said: I said, “Avoid profane and foolish things”; and, in order to avoid them, know that in the last days dangerous or fierce times will press upon the saints. [Augustine] This, moreover, is the cause of the danger: namely, that people will be lovers of themselves, not of God—unlike Peter, who, questioned three times by the Lord, three times confessed that he loved him, saying, “You know that I love you” (John XXI). Therefore the Lord entrusted his sheep to him to feed, because in feeding the sheep true love is shown if one does not seek one’s own interests there, but those of Jesus Christ.

From their loving themselves rather than God, these evils which follow arise as from a root [Col. 0374D]: [Haimo, Augustine] namely, that they will be covetous of money; puffed up against the Lord; proud of honours bestowed on them by their subjects; blasphemers against God through heresies; disobedient to parents, whether natural or spiritual; ungrateful for benefits, like those who return evil for good to those correcting them; wicked in perpetrating grave deeds, as when they exceed the measure of sinning, killing their own souls or those of others; without affection toward anyone, and therefore without compassion for the weak; without peace, that is, disturbing others; accusers, that is, charging others with crimes, or slanderers seeking to stain the reputation of the saints; incontinent in gluttony or lust, [Col. 0375A] not restraining evil desires; savage, that is, cruel, in pursuing quarrels; without kindness, that is, generosity, since they do not know how to assist others; betrayers of another’s secrets, informing the enemies of the godly about what they know should be concealed; reckless or insolent, preserving no modesty in bearing or speech, but shamelessly displaying human shamelessness; swollen with an inflated heart;

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.]

blind, not understanding what they say or the matters of which they speak; lovers of every kind of pleasure more than of God, that is, preferring carnal joys to spiritual ones; indeed having an appearance of piety, that is, of religion, because they possess the same sacraments as the godly, and are therefore dangerous; but denying its power—the power of piety, namely charity—by their deeds. The power of piety is charity from a pure heart, [Col. 0375B] a good conscience, and unfeigned faith. This is the power that nothing conquers: no fire, no waves of the world, no floods of temptation extinguish it.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] The same author, *On Psalm 46*.]

Of this it is said: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII). For just as death, when it comes, cannot be resisted, so nothing in the world can withstand the force of charity. The comparison is given in the opposite direction. For just as death is most violent in taking away, so charity is violent in saving. Or according to another reading, “but they deny its truth,” that is, the reality of piety: the same sense. Avoid such persons. Behold why he began with the last times.

“For among them.” As though he said: I rightly say that you should avoid such persons, because already some are forerunners of these; but more will exist at the end. [Haimo] [Col. 0375C] And this is what he says: “For among them are those who enter houses.” Literally: they entered women’s houses and deceived them. Hence he adds: “And lead captive,” [Ambrose] that is, by crafty and cunning words they seduce first the little women, and through them their husbands, just as the devil first seduced Eve and through her Adam. Or, “they enter houses,” that is, they investigate each person’s property, and those whom they find suitable they lead captive. Hence he adds: “And they lead little women captive,” that is, they seduce easily deceived men as though they were women. I say, little women burdened with sins, and therefore deserving to be seduced. Hence he adds: “Who are led by various desires,” because their desires are always after novelty. “Always learning and never coming to knowledge of the truth,” [Col. 0375D] because they are always walking and never arrive at that way.

[Note: [Col. 0375D] The same author, *On John*.]

But let us always walk in the way until we come to where the way leads. Let us never remain upon it until it brings us to the place where we may remain; and thus, by seeking, we press onward, and by finding, we arrive at something.

“Now just as.” As though he said: Such people deceive, but they always resist the truth. And this is what he says: “Now just as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these too resist the truth.” Jannes and Mambres were two brothers, Pharaoh’s magicians. The Apostle did not find their names in the divine books, but in apocryphal writings, from which this is taken. [Col. 0376A] They resisted Moses up to the third sign, at which they failed, saying, “This is the finger of God.” And just as they resisted Moses, so these, namely heretics, resist the truth: people corrupted in mind, that is, in reason, and reprobate, always such in their works, concerning the faith and never in the faith. But they will make no further progress—namely after these present things—in deceiving, because in a short time they will fail, overcome by Catholics.

### Verses 9–17

> “For their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was. But you have followed my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, long-suffering, love, patience, persecutions, sufferings—such as happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; what persecutions [Col. 0376B] I endured, and from them all the Lord delivered me. And all who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution. But evil people and deceivers will advance toward what is worse, erring and sending others into error. But remain in what you have learned and what has been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned it; and because from your childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation through the faith which is in Christ Jesus. For every Scripture divinely inspired is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, for training in righteousness, so that the person of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work.”

“For their folly”: their folly, which is now thought wisdom, will become manifest to all through good persons, especially [Col. 0376C] through the apostle John, through whom he here predicts that heretics in Asia will be destroyed. It will become manifest, I say, just as the iniquity of those magicians was manifest in the present age through Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] Augustine, *To Januarius*.]

Observe that the defiant spirit of heretics is always restless. By comparing them with Pharaoh’s magicians, the Apostle here declares that they possess the same disposition as Pharaoh’s magicians.

[Note: [Col. 0376D] The same author, *Against Faustus*.]

Jeremiah compares them to the foolish little bird, the partridge, saying: “The partridge cried aloud; it gathered what it had not brought forth; it made riches, not with judgment. In the midst of its days they will leave it, and in its end it will be foolish” (Jer. XVII). The partridge is a contentious creature; similarly, heretics are contentious, not loving to debate, but desiring by any means whatever to prevail through most shameless obstinacy. [Col. 0376D] And just as the partridge cries out and gathers what it has not brought forth, so the heretic finds Christians already born through Christ’s Gospel and makes them his own riches—not with sound judgment but with heedless rashness. For he does not understand that there is the true, salutary, and in a sense native and rooted Christian fellowship. Therefore he has separated those whom he has gathered as his riches; but afterward he is abandoned and is foolish, because he who at first deceived through promises and an exhibition of outstanding wisdom will be foolish—that is, will appear foolish. To those for whom he was initially wise, he will then be foolish [Col. 0377A] when it becomes clear—for his madness will be known to all, as is said here—that “they will make no further progress,” for their folly will be manifest to all.

“But you.” As though he said: They oppose the truth. But you have followed my teaching, that is, you possess knowledge through my teaching. And therefore you can resist them; and you have followed my instruction in good works, my purpose, because you aim where I do; faith in invisible things; long-suffering in awaiting what is promised; love of God and neighbour; patience under adversities; persecutions from place to place; and the sufferings of tortures. “Such as.” As though he said: Such sufferings and persecutions were brought upon you as the tortures that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, and the persecutions which I endured; and from them all. As though he says: I endured persecutions and tribulations, and from them all the Lord delivered me; so he will also deliver you. Nor do I alone suffer: all who desire to live piously, that is, religiously and justly, in Christ [Col. 0377B]—who came to suffer—will suffer persecution, in heart or body, from the devil, [Augustine] or from evil people, or from their own desires, or through grief at sinners.

[Haimo] This always happens, but especially in the Church’s first period; and just as all who desire to live piously suffer persecution, so it is necessary for you also, if you wish to live piously.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] Augustine, *On Psalm 54*.]

The person who lives piously in Christ is one who says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. XI). The weaknesses and scandals of others are persecutions to him.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] The same author, *To Sebastianus*.]

[Col. 0377C] For what so persecutes the life of the good as the life of the wicked? Not only when it compels him to imitate what displeases him, but also when it compels him to grieve over what he sees: for one living wickedly in the presence of a godly person, even if he does not bind the one who refuses consent, nevertheless torments the one who perceives it. Hence: “I saw transgressors, and I wasted away” (Ps. CXVIII). This is the persecution which all godly persons suffer according to the apostolic statement.

“But evil people.” As though he said: The good suffer, but evil persons in themselves and deceivers of others—that is, those whose business this is—will progress toward worse things: namely, they themselves erring from the good and, by the very act, sending others into error.

[Note: [Col. 0377D] The same author, *On Pastors*.]

Such are those who, fearing to offend those before whom they speak, not only do not prepare themselves for impending temptations, [Col. 0377D] but even promise the happiness of this age, which God has not promised in this world. He foretells that troubles upon troubles will come upon the world itself until the end; you promise prosperity. He, to strengthen your heart, came to suffer, die, be smeared with spittle, be crowned with thorns, drink reproaches, and be fastened to wood. He bore all these things for you; you bear nothing for him. But he, strengthening the weak person so that, once he has believed, he may not hope for the prosperity of this world, says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.”

“But remain.” As though he said: The wicked err and send others into error; but you remain firm in what you learned [Col. 0378A] from God or from me, and in what was entrusted to you as to a faithful steward, so that you may proclaim it to others. Remain, I say, knowing, that is, retaining in memory, from whom—or from what true teacher, namely from me—you learned it. And therefore these things should not come into doubt for you. Remain also because from childhood you have known the sacred writings of the Law and the Prophets. Behold the means available to you. Spiritually understood, these writings can instruct you unto the obtaining of salvation through the faith which they themselves teach, the faith which is in Christ Jesus. It is highly significant that knowledge of the Old Testament is beneficial, since there the person and incarnation of Christ are intimated, which avail for human salvation.

“For every Scripture.” As though he said: Truly the Scriptures avail for salvation because they avail for the causes of salvation. For every Scripture of which God is author, inspired [Col. 0378B] divinely into someone—that is, through the Holy Spirit—is useful for teaching the ignorant; for refuting, that is, convincing the negligent of evil; for correction, that is, sharply rebuking those who persist in evil; for training, and this in righteousness, that is, in order to make one righteous, so that the person of God, equipped for every good work, may be perfect. And because you can thus,

## Chapter IV

### Verses 1–6

> “I charge you before God and Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word; press on in season and out of season; refute, entreat, rebuke, in all patience and teaching. For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, [Col. 0378C] but according to their own desires will heap up teachers for themselves, their ears itching; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth but will turn aside to fables. But you, be watchful; labour in all things; do the work of an evangelist; fulfil your ministry; be sober. For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.”

“I charge,” that is, I adjure, you before God, that is, with God the Father as witness, and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living—that is, those who will be found alive, who remain after the torments of Antichrist—and the dead, namely those who will be found dead. Or, “the living” means the righteous and “the dead” the wicked. And by his coming—his first coming, for which you ought to give thanks, or his future coming, which must be feared—and by his eternal kingdom, that you may reign eternally with him: preach the word and press on, [Col. 0378D]

[Note: [Col. 0378D] Augustine, *On the Epistle to the Galatians*.]

that is, preach persistently: in season, as regards those to whom it is pleasing, and out of season for those unwilling to hear. You act in season indeed, but you appear troublesome to the one who does not gladly listen; nevertheless it sometimes benefits him.

[Haimo] Therefore, knowing that what appears troublesome to him is beneficial for him, preserve in your mind a gentle and modest love and concern for his health.

[Note: [Col. 0378D] The same author, *On the Trinity*.]

For although many seem to depart through disturbances caused by me—I say, “press on”—nevertheless, as the power of the word gradually penetrates to the marrow, they are healed. Since Scripture says, “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. X), one must not say that this man [Col. 0379A] has spoken too much, even if the Apostle says, “Press on in season and out of season.” For in brief speech, what is necessary is not excessive.

“And refute” those negligent in sins. Or it may be divided thus: “Press on in season and out of season; refute.” The remaining words are then connected. “Entreat,” that is, adjure those who are willing; “rebuke” those persisting in evil with harsh words; and do this with all patience toward those who resist and teaching toward those who receive, so that you patiently endure those who resist and teach those who receive.

[Haimo] Observe that the Apostle urges patience upon this rather stern man, whereas he urges authority upon Titus, who was excessively patient. “For there will be a time.” As though he said: This is now necessary, namely, that you preach; for a time will come when many will not endure sound teaching, will not even bear to hear it, as though it were a burden to them. Rather, they will heap up for themselves many [Col. 0379B] teachers according to their own desires, that is, teachers who teach what they wish.

[Ambrose] This is a prophecy of the Apostle, who, foreknowing future events, commands that one must press on in teaching, so that the Church might be prepared against what was to come. For he says that there will be people who want to be taught according to their desires, so that they turn away from steadfast and truthful teachers to those who teach them things they are willing to hear. For truth will seem harsh to them, so that, abandoning true teaching, they devote themselves to fables. I say, they will have itching ears, desiring to hear, though not good things; and they will turn their hearing away from truth, which is harsh to them, but turn to fables, taught by the teachers whom they heap up for themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] Augustine, *On John*.]

Solomon wishes these teachers to be understood by the woman of whom he says: “The foolish and bold woman, lacking bread, calls to those passing by, saying: ‘Gladly partake of hidden breads and of the sweetness of stolen waters’” (Prov. IX). For this woman is the vanity of the ungodly, who, though she lacks bread, promises breads: that is, though ignorant of truth, she promises knowledge of truth, which she strives to conceal and, as it were, season through that very concealment so that she may be heard more eagerly. The deceived steal the hearing which she forbids. For this concealment creates, as it were, an itching in the ears of those spiritually committing fornication, just as the itching of lust corrupts in the flesh the integrity of chastity. For wicked teachers season their poisons for the curious by concealment itself, so that people think they say something great because they have a secret, and drink in folly, which they suppose to be knowledge, more sweetly; they listen more gladly to things which are publicly forbidden to be said or believed in the Church. That woman is called not only foolish but also bold because of unlawful and punishable secrets. Under a Christian name she has indeed devised many wicked heresies and invented abominable fables—and would that they were such as are sung in theatres or laughed at in rhythmic buffoonery, rather than such as we grieve that her folly could have invented against God, and marvel at her boldness.

“But you.” As though he said: It will be as I said. But you, while you have time, be watchful in ecclesiastical instruction, in expounding the Scriptures, and labour in all things—that is, in teaching persons of every [Col. 0380A] kind—and do the work of an evangelist: namely, attest in deed what you preach by word, so that “the mouth of the turtledove may be turned toward the armpits,” and there may be pomegranates and little bells at the ends of the hyacinth-coloured tunic. Do this work to such an extent that you fulfil your ministry. Hence he adds: “Fulfil your ministry,” namely your episcopate, in knowledge, life, and teaching. And in order that you may fulfil it, be sober, that is, preserve moderation in all things; by this you will be able to fulfil it, because this virtue moderates all the others. He says this especially lest Timothy afflict himself too severely because of the foregoing command.

“For I.” As though he said: Be watchful, labour, and you ought to act thus because I am already being poured out, that is, I am beginning to be offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice.

[Haimo] We say that *libare* means to taste, to pour out, or to sacrifice.

[Ambrose] [Col. 0380B] From it is formed *delibare*, which is used here for the act of sacrifice itself. He calls his own Passion a *delibatio*, an offering by pouring out. For one who suffers for God’s righteousness is sacrificed to God. Hence he adds: “And the time of my departure,” that is, of my death, “is at hand,” that is, near. And as though someone were to ask, “How do you know this?” he answers: “Behold, because, with God’s grace going before,”

### Verses 7–13

> “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will render to me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his appearing. Make haste to come to me quickly. For Demas has forsaken me, loving this present world, and has gone to Thessalonica; [Col. 0380C] Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in ministry. But I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring with you the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, but especially the parchments.”

“I have fought the good fight” thus far; that is, I have fulfilled what I ought to have done. “And I have finished the course,” that is, I have firmly established it. Or continue it thus: as though he said, “I am soon to depart, but I have fought the good fight” [p. 235] against rebels, as though to say, “I leave you this example.” “And I have completed the course” of my preaching, in which I ran where passage was easy, the Church having been firmly established; and amid all adversities I have kept the faith, which [Col. 0380D] is the head of the Christian religion and cannot be possessed except by God’s mercy, because it is God’s gift. Hence elsewhere he says: “I obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1), not because I was faithful, but that I might become faithful.

[Note: Col. 0380D. Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will.*] Therefore we find the Apostle to have obtained God’s grace with no good merits at all—indeed, with many evil merits—God rendering good for evil. He, now as his Passion drew near, recalls his good merits, after which he receives the crown; yet he had received grace after evil merits, grace which, unless it had first been freely bestowed, would not have made a crown due to him. Therefore his merits are not his as though acquired for him from himself, but are gifts of God.

[Augustine] [Col. 0381A] Observe what he says: “I have fought the fight; I have finished the course.” How could he say this when there still remained for him so great a conflict in his own Passion, which he said was impending over him—a struggle so grievous, for the completion of whose course there was still lacking that point at which the enemy would be fiercer and more cruel? But he says this not as an accomplished fact, but with firm hope, because the one who had revealed to him that his Passion was near had already made him certain and secure of victory in the coming contest and of the completion of the course. Therefore he anticipated what was to come and declared it as though it had happened. Thus we say that all this still had to be accomplished then; but, relying on God’s promise, he spoke of it all as though it had been effected. Therefore, secure concerning the reward, he adds:

[Col. 0381B] “And henceforth,” that is, in the future, “there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness,” which no one may take away. You too may hope for the same. “Which the Lord will render to me on that day,” because he is the righteous Judge.

[Note: Col. 0381D. Augustine, *On Psalm 128.*] Certainly he is righteous in rendering good for good, because he was first merciful in rendering good for evil; yet even that righteousness by which good is rendered for good is not without mercy. And note that he says, “will render.”

[Note: Col. 0381D. Augustine, *Homilies on John.*] For if faith is grace and eternal life is, as it were, the wage of faith, God does indeed appear to render eternal life as something owed. Owed to whom? To the believer, because he has merited it through faith. But because faith is grace, eternal life is grace for grace. “He will render it to me,” I say, “not only to me, but also to those who love his appearing.” The wicked [Col. 0381C] fear his appearing, because there they are to be condemned; but the good love it, because there they are to be saved.

“Make haste.” As though he said: “Because the time of my departure is at hand, hasten to come quickly to me”; and also because those whom I used to have with me I do not now have. For Demas—a proper name—forsook me in time of adversity, loving this present world, and went to Thessalonica. Crescens went to Dalmatia, sent by me for ministry. And Titus went to Galatia, sent by me. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in ministry. But I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring with you the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books which I left there, but especially the parchments, so that I may write my letters there.

According to Haimo, this cloak [Col. 0381D] was given by the Romans to Paul’s father as an insignia when he was received as an associate and Roman citizen. Hence Paul too calls himself a Roman citizen. For the *paenula* was a consular garment, with which Roman consuls were clothed when entering the senate-house. If it is asked how the Apostle came to possess it, I answer that the Romans had this custom when they were acquiring for themselves the monarchy of the whole world: if any people met them with peace and garlands, they granted them freedom, so that their brethren were called and designated Roman citizens; and they gave them power to build a senate-house and to have consuls, just as they themselves [Col. 0382A] had. Therefore Paul’s father, having been transferred from Giscala, a town of Judaea where he had been born, to Tarsus in Cilicia, at a certain time met the Romans as they passed through Cilicia, he himself with the other Tarsians, being a nobleman; and they received them peacefully. Then the Romans granted them the things stated above, and there Paul’s father received the cloak. After his father’s death, Paul retained this garment in remembrance of him.

Or here *paenula* means a scroll of the Law. Hence Jerome says: “I unfold the scroll of the Hebrews, which Paul, according to some, calls a *paenula*.”

### Verses 14–22

> “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils. The Lord will render to him according to his works; you too avoid him. For he strongly resisted our words. At my first defence no one [Col. 0382B] stood by me, but all forsook me; may it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear, because I was delivered from the lion’s mouth. The Lord delivered me from every evil work and will save me into his heavenly kingdom; to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen. Greet Priscilla and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, but Trophimus I left sick at Miletus. Make haste to come before winter. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brethren greet you. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.”

[Col. 0382C] “Alexander.” As though he said: “Those men forsook me; but Alexander the coppersmith”—that is, a craftsman or keeper of the treasury—“showed me many evils,” that is, did them to me at Athens. This is the Alexander previously mentioned as having returned to apostasy, who made shrines of Diana at Athens and stirred everyone up against the Apostle. Hence he adds: “The Lord will render to him according to his works.” He does not say, “May he render,” but “He will render”: this is the word of one foretelling, not of one imprecating. He indicates; he does not wish it.

“You too avoid him, for he strongly resisted my words; and at my first defence,” that is, when I first began to defend the Gospel against him, “no helper stood by me.”

[Ambrose] By saying “at my first,” he implies that he often encountered him; or he calls the pressure and tribulation inflicted upon him a “defence.” For tribulation [Col. 0382D] is a defence for Christians, because it defends them on the day of judgment. “No one stood by me,” I say, “but all my own forsook me. May it not be charged against them,” because it is human to be afraid. Observe that he does not pray for Alexander, who had sinned by attacking the brotherhood out of envy; but he prays that those who had not broken off love, but had yielded through fear, may be forgiven.

[Note: Col. 0382D. Augustine, *On the Sermon on the Mount.*] There is indeed a great difference between those who sin in this way and those who sin in that way.

“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me,” all the more because I was abandoned by men. “He strengthened me,” I say, “so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all nations might hear that I was delivered from [Col. 0383A] the lion’s mouth,” that is, Nero’s. The Lord delivered him from Nero’s hands when he came to Rome, brought there by those who governed Judaea because he had appealed to Caesar. For when he arrived at Rome, he remained for two years in free custody, and afterwards also went on to the nations around Rome.

[Haimo] Or, “from the lion’s hand,” that is, from the devil, who, as Peter says, goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8). Since he cannot remove the Apostle from righteousness, he wishes to take him from life so that he may not benefit others. Because he cannot do this, the Apostle taunts him, saying: “The Lord also delivered me from every evil work and will save me,” leading me into his heavenly kingdom. You too may hope for the same. “To him be glory for ages of ages.” [Col. 0384A] Amen.

[Ambrose] “Greet Prisca and Aquila.” Aquila was Prisca’s husband; the Apostle lodged with them. “And the household of Onesiphorus,” that is, his family. Erastus remained at Corinth; but Trophimus I left sick at Miletus. He names these so that Timothy may visit them as he passes. “Make haste to come before winter,” because of rains and cold; he advises him to come in autumn. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brethren greet you. After the greeting of the brethren, he himself gives greeting, as though subscribing in this manner: “May the Lord Jesus be with your spirit; and take care not to be angered when admonished, but rather may grace be with you,” that is, may our love remain. “Amen,” that is, “May it be so,” or, “What I have said thus far is true.”

## On the Epistle to Titus

[Col. 0383]

[p. 226]

### Argument

[Col. 0383B]

He reminds and instructs Titus concerning the establishment of the presbyterate, spiritual conduct, and the avoidance of heretics who believe in Jewish traditions, writing to him from Nicopolis.

## Chapter One

### Verses 1–4

> “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ according to the faith of God’s elect and the acknowledgement of the truth which is according to godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the ages began; but in his own times he made manifest his Word in the preaching entrusted to me according to the command of God our Saviour—to Titus, beloved son according to the common faith: grace and peace from [Col. 0383C] God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.”

“Paul, servant of Christ,” etc.

[Ambrose] The Apostle writes this Epistle to Titus, whom he made bishop, admonishing him to be diligent in ecclesiastical discipline. Having left Titus as bishop in Crete—a man excessively patient through humility and simplicity—he writes from Nicopolis concerning the episcopal office in an authoritative and commanding manner, setting forth instructions for him by his useful authority. For a bishop ought to have a mother’s tenderness and a father’s severity, so that he may be strong toward the proud and gentle toward the modest; so that, possessing neither the corner of fear nor the brow of arrogance, he may burn and shine. Hence the legal high priest’s garment included scarlet linen, which has the appearance of fire. Fire does two things: it burns and [Col. 0383D] shines. So too the bishop, with the sword of preaching—that is, with fiery speech—ought to burn by biting rebuke and fearful threat, and shine by cherishing with gentleness and promising what is delightful. Therefore manna is said to have hardened by fire and melted in the sun. The episcopal staff pricks at its lower end and [Col. 0384B] extends forward from its upper end, returning into itself, because the ecclesiastical teacher ought to prick with the sword of the word—that is, sharply rebuke sinners, which belongs to the lower end—and direct those corrected forward; yet in such a way that he returns by self-examination to his own conscience, in case he has within himself what he announces to others.

Therefore the Apostle’s intention is to instruct Titus concerning the episcopal office, to admonish him to administer it authoritatively, and to avoid heretics. His method is as follows: first he greets him; then he instructs him concerning the episcopal office, teaching what he should do and what sort of bishops he should appoint in the cities; then how he should instruct various persons according to sex, age, or condition. Afterwards he warns him to avoid heretics. He begins with the greeting, saying: Paul by name, [Col. 0384C] servant by condition—yet not by the wretched slavery of sin, but of God, by a certain nobility, as Moses and David are called servants, and Mary a handmaid—“but an apostle of Christ Jesus.” As though he said: humility does not remove authority and dignity. “An apostle,” I say, “according to the faith of God’s elect,” holding and preaching the faith which God’s elect hold, or by which they are saved, and therefore it must be laboured for; “and according to the acknowledgement of the truth,” which truth is according to godliness, that is, Christ’s religion. He says this because there is also truth in the liberal arts, but it has no bearing upon the Christian religion.

“I am an apostle of Christ,” I say, “and this in hope of eternal life,” that is, by this hoping for eternal life. This [Col. 0384D] is the thing; this is the fruit of the apostolic office. By this he commends the apostolic office as one not to be carried out more sluggishly. God promised this eternal life “before the ages,” or “before eternal times,” which is the same thing—that is, before all times. How?

[Note: Col. 0383D. Augustine, *The City of God.*] He promised it when there were not yet human beings to whom he might promise it, because [Col. 0385A] in his eternity and in his Word, coeternal with him, it was already fixed by predestination. Therefore he promised before times, because in his eternal self it was thus fixed before time existed, which began with created things.

[Note: Col. 0385D. Augustine, *Against the Manichees.*] Therefore we cannot say that there was any time when God had not yet done anything. Thus he says: “Which God promised before the ages.” As though he said: this is no recent promise, but one made before the times of all ages. He adds: “who does not lie,” that is, because he is truthful; by this the promise of life is shown to be certain, and the more certain it is, the more diligent the minister ought to be.

But that it may be more certain, “in his own times,” that is, fitting times, he made manifest his Word, that is, the Son; this is eternal life. He made him manifest, I say, not only by the fact itself, but also [Col. 0385B] in the preaching entrusted to me as to one faithful, in which you, Titus, share. “The preaching has been entrusted to me,” I say, and this “according to the command of God our Saviour,” whom we obey too little in the salvation of human beings if we are in any way negligent. Paul, I say, writes this epistle to Titus, his beloved son according to the common—that is, catholic—faith, not the private faith of anyone. For *catholicon* in Greek is called “common” or “universal” in Latin. And in writing, he first gives greeting in this manner: “May grace and peace be to you from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour.” These things are clear.

### Verses 5–9

> “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might set right what was lacking and appoint presbyters in every city, as I directed you: if anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, having believing children, not under accusation of dissipation or insubordination. For a bishop must be without accusation, as God’s steward: not proud, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict.”

“For this reason.” First he says what Titus ought to do and what sort of presbyters he ought to ordain, beginning thus: “For this reason I left you in Crete,” when I departed from there, “that you might correct evils in sinners,” adding to good things those things lacking for perfection. Observe that, while the Apostle recalls these things, he urges Titus to carry out what he had arranged for him. “And I left you so that you might appoint presbyters”—that is, bishops—in individual cities, so that the burden of pastoral care might more easily be borne when divided among many. “Appoint,” I say, “as I directed you,” that is, such persons as I taught you ought to be appointed: namely, if anyone is—not, I say, without sin, but—without crime, that is, without a criminal sin or criminal infamy. Had he said “without sin,” no minister could rightly be ordained in the Church.

[Note: Col. 0385D. Augustine, *To Boniface.*] For many baptized believers are without crime. But I would say that no one in this life is without sin, not because there remains some sin that is not forgiven in baptism, but because, while we remain in the weakness of this [Col. 0386A] life, deeds do not cease to be committed which are daily forgiven to those who pray faithfully.

[Note: Col. 0386D. Augustine, *Homilies on John.*] However closely you examine even a very righteous person in this life, though he is already worthy of the name “righteous,” he is nevertheless not without sin. Hence John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Yet many righteous persons are expressly called “without complaint,” which is understood as “without crime.” For no just complaint can be made concerning those who have no crime. A crime, then, is a grave sin most worthy of accusation and condemnation, such as murder, adultery, some uncleanness of fornication, theft, fraud, and other such things. When a person begins to be without these, he begins to raise his head into freedom; but this freedom is begun, not perfected.

“The husband of one wife,” after baptism, when neither sexual sins nor any things done before are harmful to the new person. Augustine contradicts this opinion in these words:

[Note: Col. 0386D. Augustine, *On Marriage.*] “They understand more acutely who have judged that not even a man who had another wife while a catechumen or pagan ought to be ordained, because the question concerns a sacrament, not a sin. For in baptism all sins are forgiven. And he who said, ‘If a virgin marries, she does not sin’ (1 Cor. 7), sufficiently made clear that marriage is not sin. But on account of the holiness of the sacrament, just as a woman, even if she was violated while a catechumen, cannot after baptism be consecrated among God’s virgins, so it has not unreasonably seemed that a twice-married man has not sinned, but has lost a certain form of the sacrament, [Col. 0386C] necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the seal of ecclesiastical order. And as the wives of several ancient Fathers signified the Churches to come from all nations, subject to one husband, that is, Christ, so our high priest—that is, bishop—the husband of one wife signifies the unity from all nations subject to one husband, that is, Christ. Therefore, just as it is not lawful to serve two or more masters, so it is not lawful to pass from marriage with one husband into marriage with another, because to apostatize from one God and go to the adulterous superstition of another is always evil.”

Therefore he says: “the husband of one wife,” in whom there is hope of continence and a sacrament. “Having believing children,” that is, children of sound faith, “not under accusation of dissipation or insubordination”; that is, not even accused of dissipation, nor unsubmissive to him. Otherwise he has neither hope of correcting others nor the confidence to address others, being a companion of such persons.

“For it is necessary.” As though he said: “Such a man ought to be appointed bishop.” For it is necessary—that is, required for the administration of the office—that the bishop be without crime, that is, blameless, as God’s steward. When he says [p. 227] [Col. 0386D] “bishop,” he plainly shows that bishops had above been denoted by the name “presbyters.” He must not be proud, not quick-tempered, not violent—that is, not striking others’ minds by speaking otherwise than he ought. Or literally, not fierce, not cruel, not greedy for shameful gain, that is, worldly gain; but hospitable, kind, sober, just toward his neighbour, [Col. 0387A] holy toward God, refraining from unlawful things, that is, from anger, pride, and the rest; lovingly holding the word which is faithful according to doctrine, that is, true. He must possess these qualities so as to be able, by life and knowledge, to exhort the knowledgeable in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict, either by speaking against the truth or by living wickedly.

[Note: Col. 0387D. Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle.*] Those who contradict are not to be understood in one way only. Very few indeed contradict us in speech, but many do so by living badly. For who dares to contradict the truth most openly in speech? Many do not contradict with the tongue, but with their life; to refute them is a great work, a great burden, a steep ascent.

### Verses 10–16

> “For there are many who are also disobedient, vain talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the [Col. 0387B] circumcision, who must be refuted; they overturn whole households, teaching what they ought not for shameful gain. One of their own prophets said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.’ This testimony is true. For this reason rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish myths and commandments of men who turn away from the truth. All things are clean to the clean; but to those who are defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, but both their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess to know God, but deny him by works, being abominable, unbelieving, and reprobate for every good work.”

“For there are.” As though he said: “He rightly spoke of those who contradict.” [Col. 0387C] For there are many unstable and disobedient in themselves, vain talkers toward others, and deceivers by trickery and every kind of fraud; especially those of the circumcision, that is, Jews who taught Judaizing under Christ’s name. For, reborn in Christ, they were not pure Christians, because they wished partly to honour the Law and partly Christ. Of these he adds: “They must be refuted,” because they are those who overturn whole households, that is, an entire family, teaching what they ought not. And they do this for shameful gain, namely, an earthly thing—that is, to acquire earthly things. Or, “for shameful gain,” that is, to make proselytes, as the Lord says to the Pharisees and scribes: “You travel about sea and land to make one proselyte” (Matt. 23).

“One said.” As though he said: “They are truly such as one of their own people said, who knew them.”

[Augustine] This was Epimenides of Crete, in whose books this is found. This man is not found among God’s prophets, nor does his prophecy belong to those utterances of God entrusted to the Jews. Therefore the Apostle did not mention his name, as he customarily mentions God’s prophets, saying, “as David also says,” or “Isaiah”; or, without naming them, says, “as it is written,” and by that is understood a Scripture in which there is God’s authority. But an unlearned man, a rabid dog, dared to say that this man was one of the Jewish prophets, concerning whom [Col. 0388A] the Apostle says: “One of their own said,” because he spoke the truth, even though he was a poet. “A prophet,” I say, of them, not of God, and “their own,” because he accurately disclosed their character. This was plainly said so that he should not be thought a prophet of God. Therefore he was not a prophet belonging to the Jews, but the native prophet of the Cretans, who said: “Cretans are always liars and evil beasts,” that is, thirsty for blood, “and lazy bellies,” that is, gluttonous and therefore lazy. And lest you believe him less because he was a Gentile, the Apostle commends his words, saying: “This testimony is true.”
