It should be known that divine authority may take testimony, wherever it finds it, from whatever source it finds true; as Paul too, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, when speaking to the Athenians, said of God: “In him we live and move and are, as certain among you have said” (Acts 17). And he says concerning the inscription of the Athenian altar: “I found an altar on which was inscribed: ‘To an unknown God’” (ibid.). Thus divine authority takes from wherever it finds what is necessary, but does not thereby confirm that everything written there is to be accepted. Hence it is commanded in the Law that, if Jews bought a Gentile slave, its hair was to be shaved and the growth of its nails cut off, and then it was to be taken for domestic service. Thus, after the vain and superfluous superstitions of the Gentiles and poetic opinions have been shaved and cut away, whatever is found pure ought to be taken up for the service of God’s house. It follows:

“For this reason he teaches.” As though he said: “What they ought not.” “For this reason rebuke them,” not gently as you are accustomed, [Col. 0388C] but sharply, so that they may be sound in faith, that is, believe rightly, not giving heed to Jewish myths of literal observance, in which no one is justified before God, nor to commandments of men. For the commandments of the Law, after the truth has been made manifest, are now commandments of men and not of God—of men who oppose or turn themselves away from the truth of spiritual understanding. For whatever is set against truth is a human intention.

[Ambrose] Therefore he calls what they recount commandments of men and myths, because, ignorant of the Scriptures and of the inward meaning of the words of the Law, they follow the colour, not the flavour. For they think that one must never depart from what Moses handed down, for example, concerning the distinction of foods. Hence he adds: “For all things.” As though he said: “They truly turn away from the truth, because all things granted for human use are clean to the clean,” namely, those who take them with good faith and are just.

[Note: Col. 0388D. Augustine, *Against Faustus.*] They deny this because Moses prohibited certain things in the Law and distinguished clean from unclean things. But he did not intend this to be understood according to the natures which God created, but according to significations. Therefore all things are clean to the clean according to the nature in which they were created. Hence in Genesis: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). Yet according to their significations, some things are unclean to the Jews; nor are all things suitable for us, whether on account of bodily health or the custom [Col. 0389A] of human society. Therefore, when each thing is given its due and maintains its natural order, all things are clean to the clean. But to those defiled by sins and unbelieving—namely, those who do not believe in God or do not believe God—nothing is clean, because they are unworthy of God’s gifts; but both their mind, that is, understanding, and their conscience are defiled. As though he said: their defilement comes not from food, but from an evil understanding and a conscience of sins.

And their mind and conscience are indeed defiled, because they confess in words that they know God, but deny him in works. For John says: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2).

[Note: Col. 0389D. Augustine, *Homilies on John.*] If denial is not only by the tongue but also by works, certainly we find many antichrists who confess Christ with the mouth but differ from him in character. Whoever denies Christ by works is an antichrist. Such are all evil Catholics, who deny him not in words but in works. Therefore do not be as though secure concerning faith; join to right faith a right life, so that you may confess Christ both by saying true things in words and by living well in deeds. For even if you confess him in words but not in deeds, the faith of such conduct is almost the faith of demons.

“Though they are.” As though he said: “They profess to know God, although they are abominable,” that is, hateful to God, “and unbelieving,” that is, not even capable of believing, “reprobate for every good work,” that is, rejected by God, so that they do not have grace for acting well. “But you,” as though he said, “they teach what they ought not.”

## Chapter Two

### Verses 1–8

> “But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine: that older men be sober, chaste, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience; likewise older women, in holy bearing, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, teaching what is good, that they may teach prudence to younger women: that they love their husbands, love their children, be prudent, chaste, sober, attentive to the care of the house, kind, subject to their husbands, so that the word of God may not be blasphemed. Likewise exhort younger men to be sober. In all things show yourself an example of good works: in doctrine, in integrity, in gravity; sound speech beyond reproach, so that one who is on the opposing side may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say of us.”

[Col. 0389D] “But you speak what is fitting for sound doctrine,” that is, the doctrine of sound faith. These are things belonging to good morals: namely, exhort older men to be sober, chaste, so that they may not indulge in lust, prudent, providing what is necessary for faith, sound in faith—that is, having an entire faith; likewise, that they may be sound in love for God and neighbour, in the proper order of charity; and that they may be sound in patience amid temptations and tribulations.

Likewise exhort older women to be holy in bearing, so that their walk, movements, expression, and speech may display holiness; not slanderers, that is, charging others with crimes—as they commonly do to younger women—“not enslaved to much [Col. 0390A] wine.” For there are some women who, when bodily lust has grown cold, have given themselves to wine for pleasure. “Teaching what is good,” [p. 228] not indeed publicly to men, but privately to younger women; yet in such a way that they teach the younger women prudence, namely, to love their husbands. Or distinguish it thus: “Teaching what is good, so that they may teach prudence.” Make the division here. Then follows: exhort younger women to love their husbands, whom they naturally love with a bodily affection, also with chaste love; that is, that they may modestly render their husbands what is due rather than demand it; and that they may love their children not only with bodily but also with spiritual love. Teach them also to be prudent through understanding of mind, chaste through bodily continence, sober in food and drink, attentive to the care of their own household, kind, subject to their husbands, so that [Col. 0390B] they may not, puffed up by riches or nobility, desire to rule over their husbands.

[Jerome] “Subject to their husbands,” I say, so that the word of God, that is, evangelical doctrine, may not be blasphemed, if they have unbelieving husbands, whom they ought to serve more devotedly and rejoice with because of the fear of God, so that, seeing this, they may not blaspheme the Lord’s name.

[Ambrose] Or this may be referred to the older men and to all the preceding matters. As though he said: “Exhort older men, older women, and younger women to conduct themselves as I have said.” They ought to do this so that the Lord’s name may not be blasphemed—which happens if they conduct themselves badly. Likewise exhort younger men to be sober, because youth is accustomed to exceed measure; indeed, it is usually more prone to falling. Therefore it is more beneficially commanded to be restrained by reins, [Col. 0390C] so that, unbridled, it may be governed by divine laws.

That this may be easier, he commands the teacher to be an example, setting before him a model: “In all things show yourself an example of good works,” so that what he teaches by words he may demonstrate in deeds, and those who are profane and enemies of God may be ashamed, seeing that he proves by his deeds that what he teaches is true. Otherwise the shepherd kills the sheep, so far as he is concerned, even if they live. For evil shepherds do not spare the sheep: they not only fail to care for the sick and wandering, but even kill the strong and fat, so far as lies in them. And if the sheep live, they live by God’s mercy; yet, insofar as evil shepherds are concerned, they kill them. How? By living badly and offering an evil example. For when a sheep observes its superior living badly, turning its eyes away from God’s rules and fixing them upon a human being, it begins to say within itself: “If my superior lives in this way, who am I, that I should not do what he does?” Therefore everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he is set, so far as lies in him, kills them. Hence it was said to the servant of God eminent among the members of the supreme Shepherd: “In all things show yourself an example of good works,” namely, in sound doctrine, in integrity [Col. 0390D] of life and body, in gravity, lest you be frivolous but rather authoritative. And let your word be sound and irreproachable, incapable of blame because spoken in the right place and at the right time, so that he who is on the opposing side—that is, who is opposed to you—may be defeated or ashamed, having nothing evil to say of you.

[Col. 0391A] ### Verses 9–15

> “That slaves be subject to their masters, pleasing in all things, not contradicting, not defrauding, but showing all good faith in everything, so that they may adorn in all things the doctrine of God our Saviour. For the grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all people, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and godly in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from every iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works. Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.”

[Col. 0391B] Exhort slaves also to be subject to their masters, whether good or bad. I say, subject in all things that are not contrary to God, and pleasing. Or distinguish it thus: pleasing in all things, not contradicting. In this way they will be able to please—namely, if they do not grumble when their masters command something; not defrauding them of anything due in service, but showing good faith in everything, even the least matters—that they may adorn the doctrine. This he refers to all those mentioned above, namely old men, old women, slaves, and so forth. It is as though he said: Exhort all those aforesaid to conduct themselves as prescribed, so that in all their actions they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior and Lord. He says that the Lord’s doctrine is adorned by good works and faith. For the honorable life of the disciple is the adornment of the teacher or shepherd.

[Col. 0391C] “For it has appeared.” It is as though he said: All must be admonished to adorn it, because Christ was born for all and excludes no one. This is what he says: “For the grace of God and of our Savior God has appeared”—that is, God and our Savior, namely the Son of God. Although he is invisible in the form of God, nevertheless by grace he appeared in the form of a slave. And this was for all people, that is, for the benefit of every class of humankind; without this, his birth would not have benefited us. “Training us” by the example of his life and teaching, in which you ought to follow him—namely, so that you may train others. I say, training us for this purpose: that we, “renouncing,” that is, fleeing, impiety—vain worship and ignorance—and worldly desires, which are suggested by the ruler of this world, may live soberly within ourselves, justly [Col. 0391D] toward our neighbor, and piously toward God, in this very fragile age.

I say, we live “awaiting,” with certainty and concern, “the blessed hope,” that is, eternal glory, and the coming, or manifestation, of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. He will come not in weakness as before, but in glory and power, to give rewards according to merits—he who was so humble in his first coming. He not only trained us, but “gave,” that is, delivered to death, himself for us; through this we are secure concerning hope. I say, he gave himself in order that he might redeem us by his blood from every iniquity, both original and actual, and cleanse in baptism, from guilt and punishment, a people acceptable or peculiar to himself—that is, his own people, followers of every good work. For this purpose Christ redeemed us: that, pursuing a pure life [Col. 0392A] and filled with good works, we might be able to be heirs of God’s kingdom. Speak these things to the ignorant, exhort those who know them, and rebuke the negligent or rebellious; and do this “with all authority,” that is, power, since this is no longer taken harshly when it is known to be done for salvation—yet with such authority that no one despises you because of simplicity.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–15

> “Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to obey their command, to be ready for every good work, to slander no one, not to be quarrelsome, but gentle, showing all meekness toward all people. For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering astray, enslaved to various desires and pleasures, [Col. 0392B] living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another. But when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not from works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he abundantly poured out upon us through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. This saying is trustworthy; and concerning these things I want you to insist, so that those who believe in God may take care to lead in good works. These things are good and useful to people. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, disputes, and quarrels about the law; for they are useless and empty. Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, [Col. 0392C] knowing that such a person has been perverted and sins, being self-condemned by his own judgment. When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis; for I have decided to winter there. Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they lack nothing. Let your people also learn to lead in good works for necessary needs, so that they may not be unfruitful. All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in faith. The grace of God be with you all. Amen.”

“Remind them.” It is as though he said: Although you possess spiritual authority, nevertheless remind them to be subject to rulers, namely kings and governors, and to lesser authorities, [Col. 0392D] and to obey their command—not, indeed, unto evil—but remind them to be ready for every good work, that is, to obey them in the Lord. And remind them to slander no one, even if they are oppressed by such persons.

[Ambrose.] It is as though he said: Remind them to be slow toward evil and ready toward good, knowing what ought to be rendered to each, because a reward is prepared for each. Let them not be quarrelsome, but gentle, showing all meekness toward all people. He wants Christians, whether good or bad, to appear good to all people. For in this way unbelievers can be called to future hope.

“For we too were once.” It is as though he said: We owe this because we too were once what they are; and thus they too will be able to become what we are through the same grace. This is what he says: “For we too were once foolish,” [Col. 0393A] although some among you may have been philosophers; nevertheless they lacked true wisdom. And we were unbelieving, straying through evils, enslaved to the desires of the mind and the various pleasures of the flesh, spending our lives in malice—that is, an evil will to harm—and envy concerning the successes of others; and, even if we were not permitted to harm them, hateful to God or to other people, and hating others in return.

“But when the kindness and love for humankind of God our Savior”—that is, when God our Savior, kind and loving toward humankind, appeared to the world through the flesh, or to us through faith—“not from works,” and so forth. Or thus: when the kindness and love for humankind—that is, the abundant mercy and clemency—of God our Savior appeared, that is, shone upon people, he saved us already in the hope of future salvation, not from the works of righteousness [Col. 0393B] which we had performed.

[Augustine.] For we had done no good works, but according to his great mercy; and perhaps he will likewise act toward those who are still unbelieving. I say, he saved us through the washing of regeneration, that is, through baptism, in which, after the old person has been laid aside, a new person is born; and through the renewal of the Holy Spirit, because day by day we are renewed more and more through the Spirit given in baptism. This Spirit, namely, he poured out abundantly upon us—for the remission of all sins and an abundance of virtues—and this through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, justified by his grace, we may meanwhile in the present life be heirs of eternal life, and this according to hope, although not yet according to possession.

[Col. 0393C] And this saying, namely that Christ saved us and made us heirs, is faithful—that is, true. And concerning the things mentioned above I want you to encourage others, so that many who believe in God may take care to lead others in good works. Or thus: I want you to encourage those who believe in God, that they may take care to lead in good works, either many others or themselves. Therefore I want you to encourage others concerning the foregoing things, because these things are good in themselves and useful to other people.

“But foolish questions.” It is as though he said: Insist upon these matters. But avoid foolish questions, in which there is neither salvation nor useful knowledge; genealogies, that is, enumerations of origins; disputes which they raise from the law—for example, concerning foods which some assert must be distinguished and others deny; and quarrels about the law, such as when, in a corrected Scripture, it seems to teach conflicting or impossible things about the years of Methuselah [Col. 0393D] and other such matters.

For they are useless, that is, without fruit, and empty, [Col. 0394A] that is, false. And do not only avoid these things, but also avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction—that is, after you have corrected him twice. Heretics are those who attack the law by the words of the law.

[Ambrose.] For they establish their own opinion by the words of the laws, in order to confirm the perversity of their minds by the authority of the law. They must be avoided, because if corrected more frequently they would become more practiced in evil. I say, avoid him; why? Because you know that one of this kind—that is, one who is incorrigible—has been perverted, that is, lost, and sins because he sins knowingly, condemned by his own judgment. A person condemns himself by his own judgment when he praises error and censures truth.

“When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you,” to provide meanwhile for the Cretans while you come to me, “hasten to come to me at Nicopolis,” for I have decided to winter there. He tells him to hasten to come after the letter has been delivered because he wishes to see him from affection and to establish him more fully in ecclesiastical discipline.

“Zenas the lawyer.” He says this not because Apollos was more learned, but because Zenas had belonged to this profession in the synagogue. And send on Apollos, because he was well versed in Scripture, diligently—so diligently that they lack nothing; that is, that they have among their own people whatever is necessary for their journey, so that they do not seek from strangers. And as though someone were to ask, “But where will they get the means? Where does Titus have the means to give them provisions for their journey?” he answers: “Let your people also learn,” that is, let the Cretans learn, like others, to excel in good works by giving to ministers. [Col. 0394C] I do not mean for any and every purpose, but for necessary needs, and this so that they may not be unfruitful; otherwise, according to the parable of the tree that does not bear good fruit, they will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

He commands necessary expenses to be given them because it was fitting that those who imparted spiritual things should not lack material things from them. Apollos was bishop of the Corinthians. Because of a sedition stirred up against him by false apostles, he had departed with Zenas, his companion, to Titus, bishop of Crete. But since the Corinthians had now been pacified through Paul’s letters, Paul directs Titus, before he comes to Nicopolis, to send them on so diligently that they lack nothing for the journey.

“All who are with me greet you”: for brevity, he signifies all the greeters together. “Greet those who love us,” not falsely but [Col. 0394D] “in faith,” that is, with faithful affection. Then he greets all generally, saying: “May the grace of God be with you all. Amen.”

## On the Epistle to Philemon

[Col. 0393]

### Argument

[Col. 0393D]

He writes a personal letter to Philemon on behalf of his slave Onesimus, writing to him from prison in the city of Rome through the aforesaid Onesimus.

## Single Chapter

[Col. 0394D]

### Verses 1–6

> “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy the brother, to Philemon our beloved fellow-worker, and to Apphia, most beloved sister, and to Archippus [Col. 0395A] our fellow-soldier, and to the church which is in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers, hearing of your love and faith which you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, that the sharing of your faith may become evident in the recognition of every good work in Christ Jesus.”

“Paul, a prisoner,” and so forth.

[Ambrose.] The Apostle writes this Epistle to Philemon of Colossae, who held no rank of ecclesiastical ministry, but was a praiseworthy layman. He sends him a personal letter on behalf of Onesimus, his slave, who had fled after causing him loss; but Onesimus, having heard the Gospel from the Apostle, was baptized. The Apostle asks forgiveness for him, [Col. 0395B] writing from prison in Rome. The Apostle’s intention is to obtain Onesimus’s pardon from Philemon.

The method is this: first he greets him with his wife and son; then he gives thanks to God for their good qualities, commending their faith and love. Afterwards he entreats Philemon—although he could command him—to spare Onesimus and give thanks to God because he receives him as such a person that he should regard him not as a slave but as a most beloved brother. Then he tells him to prepare lodging for him, since he hopes to come to him.

He begins with a greeting, saying: “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ,” that is, for Christ Jesus. He does not say “apostle,” which is a title of dignity, but “prisoner,” which is a title of humility, because he does not command but entreats. For this is an intercession for Onesimus; therefore, beginning with his own injury, he mentions things belonging to humility in order to give dignity to his Epistle. Just as being bound because of sin is a disgrace, so conversely enduring the chains of imprisonment for Christ is the greatest glory. For at that time he was in custody; therefore he says, “Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” It is as though he said: You ought to pity him and not be a cause of sorrow—which you will be if, being merciless, you torment a son.

“And Timothy the brother,” and so forth. For whose sake also you ought to show pity, they write this Epistle to Philemon, beloved because of the growth of his virtues.

[Jerome.] Or, as it is in Greek, *agapētos*, “worthy to be loved,” namely, one who deserves to be loved; and “our fellow-worker” in the ministry of preaching; and to Apphia, his wife, to whom he writes so that she may entreat her husband concerning this matter, “most beloved sister,” [Col. 0395D] in unfeigned faith; and to Archippus, his son and a minister of the Colossians, so that he too may entreat his father, “our fellow-soldier,” who labors with me in the same warfare; and to the church which is in your, or his, house, that is, his whole household, so that they too may ask him. Before all else he greets them in this way: “Grace be to you,” that is, remission of sins, “and peace” of mind and reconciliation with God, “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

“I give thanks.” After the greeting he gives thanks for Philemon’s good qualities, commending his faith and love. He mentions these in order that the goodness recalled may move him to pardon. He says therefore: “I give thanks to my God, always making remembrance of you in my prayers.” He explains why he gives thanks, adding: “Hearing of your love and faith,” that is, the commendable report of [Col. 0396A] your faith and love. This faith and love you have in the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, or in all the saints, because he believed in and chose Christ, believed in and loved the saints, and through works of faith and love served Christ and the saints.

“That the sharing [*communicatio*] of your faith may become evident.” It is as though he said: You have faith and love in Christ and in the saints, so that the sharing of your faith—that is, your faith sharing in our faith, or what you share with others from your faith—may be manifest. And this is “in the recognition of every good thing in Christ Jesus”; that is, it may be so manifest that by this it is deservedly recognized that every good thing is in you through Christ, that is, the sufficiency of all good things.

Or thus: making remembrance of you, I give thanks in the prayers I have offered that all the operation of your faith—that is, the activity of faith by which you serve Christ and the saints—[Col. 0396B] may become evident in the recognition of every good thing which is in Christ Jesus; that is, with knowledge of the eternal good, so that it might be sought as a reward.

[Ambrose.] For the Apostle prays that his activity may be performed with knowledge of goodness; that is, that he may act with such a mind as to await in the future as his reward Christ himself, not temporal recompense.

### Verses 7–25

> “For I had great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother. Therefore, although I have much confidence in Christ Jesus to command you what is fitting, yet because of love I rather entreat you, being such a one as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus. I entreat [Col. 0396C] you for my son Onesimus, whom I begot in my bonds; he was formerly useless to you, but now is useful both to you and to me. I have sent him back to you; receive him as my own heart. I wished to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf in the bonds of the Gospel. But I wished to do nothing without your consent, so that your good deed might not be, as it were, from necessity, but voluntary. For perhaps he departed from you for a while so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a most beloved brother—especially to me; and how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord! Therefore, if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would me. But if he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, [Col. 0396D] have written this with my own hand: I will repay it—not to mention to you that you owe even yourself to me. Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare lodging for me also, for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you. Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you; and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my hearers. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.”

“For I had great joy.”

[Ambrose.] It is as though he said: I now make this request because I had great joy in my heart and consolation amid adversities in your love. This love was strong not merely as a disposition of virtue in the heart, but also manifested outwardly in deed: namely, because the holy things of the saints—that is, the most beloved children of the saints, or the inward affections of the saints inclined toward you, O brother—were refreshed through you, as you worthily received them and they in some way took breath after their labors. For he supplied necessities to the saints in need; and thus the affection of the saints toward him, resting more fully because he consoled them, was calmed and refreshed.

For this reason, namely, because you serve others and are prompt to do good, you ought much more to serve me. I have much confidence—not, I say, authority—in Christ Jesus, that is, through Christ Jesus, to command you what pertains to the matter, that is, to your benefit. I do not mean against what is lawful. It is as though he said: I have confidence to command what is useful to you and to me. I do not say that I have authority [Col. 0397B] to command you against that which is lawful for you. Having, I say, confidence to command, because of my love or yours, I rather entreat, since you are such a person in life and age as I, Paul, who am old; and for that reason I do not command you but entreat you. Hence above: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father” (1 Tim. 5).

“Now also.” It is as though he said: I say that I am old; not only old, however, but now also a prisoner of Christ Jesus, by which you ought to be moved all the more. I entreat you, I say, concerning my son Onesimus. It is great and praiseworthy if one humbles himself and entreats, not for a lowly man but for an eminent one. My son, whom I begot in faith while I was in bonds. Therefore I love him more tenderly: he who was formerly useless to you while he was unbelieving, taking away your goods, is now useful both to you and to me, serving [Col. 0397C] me and, through me, you; for whatever your slave did for me belongs to you. I have sent him back to you. But receive him—that is, receive him as my own heart, as my most beloved son. Or, “as my own heart,” that is, receive my affection for him as embodied in him.

The Apostle baptized Onesimus, a fugitive fleeing to divine aid, while he was in custody; seeing hope of usefulness in him, he so commends him that he indicates that his own heart is received in him. “I wished to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me in the bonds of the Gospel on your behalf.” But without your counsel, that is, consent, I wished to do nothing, so that your good deed—namely, your slave’s service to me—might not be, that is, might not be, as if from necessity, that is, against your will, but voluntary.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Augustine, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*.] Yet God causes him to will, [Col. 0397D] he who works in us both to will and to work for good will.

“For perhaps.” It is as though he said: Receive him for this reason: his flight was useful. For perhaps he departed from you for a while so that you might receive him forever, namely, here and in the future. By saying “perhaps,” he tempers the assertion. He says this because all human things are uncertain, and another reason may have existed why God arranged or permitted this to happen.

I say, receive [Col. 0398A] him now not merely as a slave, but, in place of the slave he had been before, as a most beloved brother. Or according to another reading: receive him now not merely as a slave, but as a most beloved brother, more than a slave. For brothers are dearer than slaves. I say, he is especially dear to me. How much more, then, than before, or than to me, ought he to be dear to you—both in the flesh, namely because he is your slave, and in the Lord, because he is a faithful brother? Or thus: he is a brother, and especially a brother to me, your teacher.

For Onesimus, having offended his own master, fled to the Apostle so that, his sins having been erased, he might return useful—so useful that he might become equal not merely in merits to his master but a brother to his teacher himself.

[Ambrose.] And lest Philemon, because he was master, should be puffed up against his slave, [Col. 0398B] he humbles him by calling Onesimus his brother, both in the flesh, because we are all from one Adam, and in the Lord through faith. This is what follows: how much more than before is he your brother, both in the flesh through the condition of the first birth, and in the Lord through faith, which cuts off all pride. And because this is so, therefore—that is, for this reason—if you have me, that is, if you wish to have me, as a partner, receive him as you would me; for if you do not receive him, you are not a partner.

“But if he has wronged you in anything or owes you anything, charge it to me.” He now removes every excuse when he says that, if Onesimus has either injured him or owes anything, it must be charged to himself. And that what he says may be believed more fully, he adds: “I, Paul, have written with my own hand; I will repay you,” either here or in the future. I say, I will repay you, “not to mention to you that you owe not merely your possessions but [Col. 0398C] even yourself to me,” for service. It is as though he said: I demand less from you than you owe.

Then an adjuration is added when he says: “Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord,” that is, I shall rejoice concerning you in God’s kingdom if you do what I ask. What is that? Here it is: “Refresh my heart,” that is, my son or my affection, “in the Lord,” that is, for the Lord’s sake. Then he flatters him, saying: “Confident of your obedience, I have written,” knowing that you will do beyond what I say. In flattering him thus, he urges him to do more than is asked. For it often happens that one who sees that others think well of him shows himself better.

Then, to make him more concerned and readier to obey, he indicates that he will come to him, adding: “At the same time prepare [Col. 0398D] lodging for me also.” Or this may move him to pardon. I say, prepare it because I hope, through your prayers, to be granted to you. He says this so that they may obey more readily; absent persons are commonly despised. Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, and Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow-workers, greet you. May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

## On the Epistle to the Hebrews

[Col. 0399]

### Argument

[Col. 0399A]

First it must be said why the apostle Paul, in writing this Epistle, did not preserve his usual practice of setting down either the word of his own name or the dignity of his rank. The reason is that he wrote to those who had believed from the circumcision, being as it were the Apostle of the Gentiles and not of the Hebrews. Knowing also their pride, and himself displaying his humility, he did not wish to put forward the merit of his office. For in like manner the apostle John, out of humility, did not place his own name first in his Epistle for the same reason. Accordingly, the Apostle is said to have sent this Epistle written to the Hebrews in the Hebrew language; preserving its sense and order, Luke the Evangelist composed it in the Greek language after the death of the apostle Paul.

## Chapter I

### Verses 1–7

> “God, who long ago spoke to the fathers in the prophets in many portions and in many ways, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. He, being the radiance of his glory and the exact image of his substance, and sustaining all things by the word of his power, having accomplished purification of sins, sat down at the right hand of Majesty on high. Having become so much better than the angels, he has inherited a name more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did he ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be a Father to him, and he shall be a Son to me.’ And when he again brings the Firstborn into the inhabited world, he says: ‘Let all God’s angels worship him.’ And indeed concerning the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.’”

“In many portions,” or “in many ways,” and so forth. Paul, the eminent teacher and Apostle of the Gentiles, wishing to honor his ministry, as he says in the Epistle to the Romans, “As long as I am Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry, if somehow I may provoke my own flesh to emulation” (Rom. 11), wrote this Epistle to the Hebrews. He treats of Christ’s preeminence according to both natures and of the uselessness of the Mosaic law, demonstrating in many ways that faith in Jesus Christ without legal observances brings righteousness and salvation, whereas legal observances after the Passion not only do no good but actually harm.

He excludes the superstitious tradition of certain Hebrews who, while confessing Christ, thought legal observances must be maintained, and who by their authority had led into this error even certain persons who had come to Christ from Gentile background. Therefore the Apostle, providing for the Gentiles lest they should thereafter be drawn into this error by the authority of the Hebrews, and also provoking the Jews to emulation—which is an honor to his ministry—here commends God’s grace bestowed on believers at this time through Christ the true high priest, showing the law to have been rejected. Finally he also gives moral instruction.

[Chrysostom.] He therefore displays the preeminence of the present time, saying that the Lord sent his only-begotten Son to us and spoke to us in him, in order to raise the minds of his hearers—that is, of the believing Jews to whom he writes—lest, because they had been severely afflicted and crushed by the many evils which had happened to them, they might suppose themselves thereby inferior to others and more miserable. Therefore, to console and raise them up, he declares at the beginning of his Epistle that they have been endowed with greater grace: prophets were sent to the ancients, but the Son to us; servants and fellow-servants spoke to them, but the Lord to us.

Some slanderers of the truth, however, have dared to say that this Epistle is not Paul’s because it does not bear his name in its title and shines with a style far more brilliant and eloquent than the others; they attribute it to Barnabas, Luke, Clement, or Tertullian. But we have a ready answer for them. If it ought not to be called Paul’s because his name is not prefixed, then neither is it to be called the work of any of those persons—indeed, of no one at all—since no one’s name appears in the title. He did not prefix his name to this Epistle as to the others because he was odious to the Hebrews, to whom he appeared to be a destroyer of the laws. Therefore, because he was Apostle not of them but of the Gentiles, he suppressed his name, which was hateful to them, lest the resentment aroused by the name set at the head of the letter should prevent the benefit of reading what followed.

[Jerome.] Knowing also their pride and himself displaying his humility, he wished to set forward the dignity of his rank by naming himself Apostle, but, concealing the merit of his office, being humble before the proud, he did not call himself Apostle lest the proud be offended. That this Epistle shines with greater eloquence than the others is not at all surprising, since it is natural for each person to be more powerful in his own language than in a foreign one. The Apostle composed his other Epistles in a foreign language, namely Greek. But he wrote this one in the Hebrew language; preserving its meaning and order, Luke composed it in Greek after Paul’s death. It is therefore not surprising if it shines with such eloquence of doctrine.

Having therefore refuted the calumnies of opponents of the truth, one must in no way doubt that this too is an Epistle of Paul, in which he intends to show Christ’s preeminence, the sufficiency of faith, and also the insufficiency and uselessness of the law. His method of treatment is as follows. First, he proposes that Christ’s words are to be heard, as are those of the prophets, and even more so by comparing him with and preferring him to the prophets: for God spoke in him just as in the prophets, and he is greater than them. Then he commends him alternately according to each nature, namely the human and the divine. Afterwards he compares him to angels and prefers him to them, inserting much concerning his excellence according to both natures. Then he compares him to Moses and prefers him to him. Next, by many arguments and authorities, he declares that the grace of faith must be preferred to the shadow of the law, Christ’s priesthood to the Levitical priesthood, and the New Testament to the Old; and that his one sacrifice must be preferred to the many sacrifices of the latter, because there is shadow there but truth here. Finally, he gives a definition of faith, commending it by many testimonies. Near the end he adds moral instruction.

First, therefore, comparing him with the prophets, he says: “God, speaking long ago to the fathers in the prophets in many portions,” or “in many ways,” “has in these last days spoken to us in the Son.” Attend to each phrase and compare them with one another. By saying “long ago,” he shows that God’s speaking is not new. “Long ago”—therefore not newly—God, who is unchangeable and who spoke both then and now, joins the present with the past, because the one who spoke then and speaks now spoke to the ancient fathers, who are fathers to us in flesh and in the worship of God; and he spoke “in the prophets.” For they did not speak from themselves, but God spoke in them. They did not speak from their own understanding or discover things by human capacity. When he says “to the fathers in the prophets,” he shows that he spoke to servants through servants, namely through prophets in the time of promise.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Augustine, *On John*.] For the Lord appointed a time for his promises and a time for fulfilling what he promised. The times of promise had prophets inspired and filled with the Word of God, until John. But from him until the end is the time for fulfilling what was promised. The only Son of God was to come to humankind, assume humanity and thereby become human, die, rise again, ascend, sit at the Father’s right hand, and fulfill the promises among the Gentiles. Thus all this had to be prophesied concerning him; it had to be foretold that he would come, so that when he came suddenly he might not be feared with horror, but, having been believed in, might be awaited.

I say, speaking “in many portions,” that is, many times, by many utterances—namely, to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the others, often to the same persons. “And in many ways,” that is, with many modes: at one time through dreams, as to Daniel; at another through an open voice, as to Moses; at another through inward inspiration, as to David. Hence elsewhere it is said: “I multiplied visions, and was represented through the hands of the prophets.” Or “in many ways,” that is, by many and diverse kinds of speech, as by dreams, inspirations, or open voices; “and in many modes,” that is, signifying future things through diverse mysteries of realities. God, I say, speaking long ago, “in these last days,” that is, at the end of times. Or “in these last days,” because after this speaking no other speaking follows “in these days.” It is as though he said: There still remain those who heard and saw. “He has spoken”: speaking of the present, he uses the past tense because the very one who now speaks is he who spoke long ago.

[Chrysostom.] Again note that by saying “long ago” and “in these last days” he indicates something else to us: after a long interval had passed, when we were already near punishment and when all gifts had ceased, then we became more greatly endowed and more worthy. He establishes this wisely, saying: “God has in these last days spoken to us,” the children of those fathers, lest he should be thought to have spoken something different to us from what he said to them—which might have seemed the case if he spoke to another people.

I say, he “has spoken in the Son,” that is, through the only Son, who is greater than the prophets. For he is the Lord, fulfiller, and sanctifier of the prophets. As Christ is both prophet and Lord of prophets, so he is angel and Lord of angels. For he is also called “Angel of Great Counsel,” and Moses was told concerning God: “I will raise him up as a prophet like you” [Col. 0402B] (Deut. 18). If Christ announced nothing, he would not be called an angel; if he prophesied nothing, he would not be called a prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] Augustine, *On John*.] Insofar as he announced the present, he was an angel; insofar as he foretold the future, he was a prophet; insofar as the Word of God was made flesh, he was Lord both of angels and of prophets. Hence he commends him according to both natures, adding:

Whom he appointed. Here he commends Him according to His human nature: for although, with the Father, He possesses all things according to divinity, yet according to humanity He is rightly said to have been appointed heir, according to the words: “I will give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2). And this is what he says: Him—Christ—God the Father appointed as the now unchangeable heir of all things, that is, possessor of every creature. [Col. 0402C] No longer merely “Jacob the Lord’s portion and Israel his share,” but absolutely all the nations of the world. [Chrysostom.] He uses the name “heir” in order to establish and show two things by it: namely, that He is the proper Son, and that no loss can befall Him of the gift bestowed upon Him. Thus, in calling Him heir he indicates that He is Son and never loses anything of all that is given by the Father; and in saying “heir” he also expressed the dispensation of humility. Then he rises to a higher and loftier degree, adding: “Through whom,” as through the Word coeternal with the Father, He made not only eternal things—that is, invisible and immutable things, less known to us—but also the ages, that is, visible and mutable things. Observe how here he follows two sound paths: [Col. 0402D] one recalling us from Sabellius’s impious error, the other from the error of Arian impiety, lest the Father be thought either not to have an Only-Begotten, or the Son to subsist as alien from the Father. For there are some who madly suppose Him alien: this was Arius’s evil opinion. Others endeavor to fabricate, not one Father and another Son, but the same person now Father and now Son. He therefore instructs us with complete reasoning both that He is the Son of God and that He is not alien from Him.

Who, being the brightness. Here he commends Christ according to the divine nature, showing Him to be coeternal and coequal with the Father, and of the same [Col. 0403A] substance with Him, though another in person. We must receive this reverently; and if anything perhaps absurd should occur, we must drive it from the mind’s gaze. For everywhere we need a reverent understanding, but especially when we either speak or hear anything concerning God: neither the tongue suffices to speak of God, any more than of fire, nor does the understanding prevail to comprehend Him. For we understand many things concerning God which we are utterly unable to express; likewise, we say many things which we are not capable of understanding.

For example, we know and say that God is everywhere. Yet we do not grasp by understanding how He is everywhere. Likewise, we know that He is a certain incorporeal power, the cause of all good things; but what this power is, or how it is so, we wholly do not know. There are also certain things which cannot be spoken even though they are grasped in the mind; thus we see Paul himself, in some such matters, as though becoming weak and not presenting complete examples, as here when he says, “Who, being the brightness,” etc. He employs improper names because he could not find proper ones, and uses the likeness of temporal things to show the truth of eternal things—that is, the coeternity of Father and Son—although temporal things cannot be compared with eternal things in a complete comparison. For in eternity there is stability, but in time variation; in eternity all things stand, while in time some things arrive and others succeed.

For what can we find in creation that is coeternal, when we find nothing eternal in it? Find for me an eternal Father in creation, [Col. 0403C] and I will find a coeternal Son. But if you find something eternal in creation, it will suffice for the comparison if we find something coeval. For “coeternal” is one thing, “coeval” another. We call those coeval who have the same measure of time and are not preceded one by another in time; yet we say that both began to exist. And if we can find some coeval things among creatures, still we do not find generator and generated, as in the Trinity, where the Only-Begotten is coeternal with the One begetting Him. For in creatures the generated does not begin at the same time as its generator; but in the Creator the Begetter did not precede the Begotten. Temporal things, then, cannot be compared with eternal things in a complete comparison; nevertheless, by some slender and small likeness, coeval things may be compared with coeternal things.

Let us therefore find coeval things, for Scripture directs us to these comparisons. We read concerning Wisdom itself: “She is the radiance of eternal light” (Wis. 7). Likewise: “the spotless mirror of God’s majesty.” Behold, Wisdom itself is called the radiance of eternal light, that is, the image and mirror of the Father. Let us take our likeness from this, finding coeval things through which we may understand coeternal things, since coeval things can be found among creatures. Using names of temporal things, it says: “She is the radiance of eternal light.” And this is what he says: “the brightness of glory.” For the Son is coeternal with the Father just as brightness is coeval with the fire from which it comes. Fire emits light, and light is emitted from fire. If we ask which comes from which—brightness from fire or fire from brightness—[Col. 0404A] every soul answers me. For God willed to sow in every soul the beginnings of understanding and wisdom. Every soul therefore answers, and no one doubts, that brightness comes from fire, not fire from brightness.

Let us therefore set fire as the Father and brightness as the Son, since we have already stated that we seek coeval things in creatures through which to establish coeternal things in the Creator. If I wish to light a lamp, neither fire nor brightness is there yet; but as soon as I light it, brightness exists together with the fire. Give me fire without brightness, and I will believe that the Father existed without the Son. These things have been said by you as such a great matter could be said; yet they remain ineffable. There can therefore always be One begetting, and always with Him that which has been born from Him. Thus the Son of God is called the brightness of glory because the Father is always His Father, because He has one from whom He is, not because the Father existed first and the Son afterward. For the Father always is, and the Son is always from the Father; the Son is always begotten, the Father always is, and the image is always from Him.

Behold, you could not find coeternal things in creatures, but you found coeval things. Therefore by proportion you understand the Son as coeternal with the eternal Begetter: for what is coeval with the temporal is coeternal with the eternal. Yet observe that, although in these things—fire and brightness—there is coevality, there is not complete equality: for the brightness that streams from [Col. 0404C] the fire shines less brightly than the fire itself. These things therefore possess likeness, but not complete equality. Therefore someone says: “The Son is altogether related to the Father as brightness to fire.” Not altogether: here there is complete equality.

From the proportion of other temporal things, one of which comes from the other, though they are not coeval, the Son is shown consubstantial with the Father. For a human is born from a human and a horse from a horse. Neither is coeval with the other, because the one born is preceded in time by the one from whom it is born; yet that one is human and this one is human, that one horse and this one horse—that is, they are of the same substance, differing in time, not in nature. [Note: [Col. 0403D] Augustine, on the same passage.] Similarly, God the Son is born of God the Father. And since He is coeternal with Him, [Col. 0404D] He is also of the same nature, not less than He, because He is God from God, just as a human born from a human is of the same substance, and a horse from a horse.

Behold, another type of likeness has been introduced. What is found here? What is praised? Certainly, equality of substance is praised here. What is lacking? Equality of time. But in that type of likeness which we gave from the brightness of fire, you do not find equality of nature, but coevality. What is praised there? Coevality. What is lacking? Equality of nature. Join together what you praise. For in creatures something is lacking in the things you praise; in the Creator nothing can be lacking, since whatever you find in creation proceeded from the Creator-Artificer.

In the first type [Col. 0405A] of likeness—that is, in coeval things—you find and praise coevality: in place of coevality ascribe coeternity to God, so that the One begotten may be coeternal with Him by whom He was begotten. From the other type of likeness ascribe to God equality of nature—that equality of nature which you praise in a human. Believe it to be in Him who made humanity: what is born of a human is human, and will what is born of God not be what He is from whom it is born? Therefore all that is praiseworthy in creatures, in which something is at the same time lacking, exists in the Creator, in whom nothing is lacking. Yet there what we find—human and human—are two humans; here, however, Father and Son are one God.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Who is the brightness of glory,” namely, of the Father—that is, He is born from the Father and coeternal with Him, because He is light from light, revealing the Father, and is of the same [Col. 0405B] glory with Him, that is, essence, because He is one and the same with the Father. [Ambrose.] For the Father is glory, and the Son is the same with Him; and, having become human, He makes Him known as a ray makes the sun known. By “brightness” he declared both the nearness of essence and that He makes the Father known to us and illuminates our souls.

“And the figure,” or character, “of His substance,” [Chrysostom] namely, the Father’s: that is, the full manifestation of the Father’s essence, alike in all respects, consubstantial, yet another in person. For by saying “figure of substance” he plainly shows that the Son is personally other than the Father, and that an image differs from the one whose image it is. Yet the Son is equal to the Father, because the Father is not unlike Him, as He Himself says: “The Father is in me” (John 10); “He who sees me sees the Father” [Col. 0405C] (John 14). Observe that these names, “light” and “glory,” are sometimes referred to the divine nature and sometimes to person. And when they are referred to person, they are sometimes referred to the Father and sometimes to the Son. For we say: the Father is light, the Son is light; likewise the Father is glory, the Son is glory. These two are one glory and one light, not two. The Son is called glory from glory, as light from light, principle from principle, and God from God; yet not two Gods, but one; not two principles, but one. “Brightness,” however, and “figure,” like “image,” are properly referred to the person of the Son and are said relatively.

[Chrysostom.] And upholding. Above it was said that [Col. 0405D] through Him He made all things. Here he now ascribes to Him the highest authority, because He governs all things with authority. The sense continues: as all things were created by Him, so they are preserved through Him, who is immutable. [Note: [Col. 0405D] Augustine, in the book of Prosper’s Sentences.] The Creator’s omnipotence is the cause of every creature’s continuing existence. If that power should ever cease from governing the things it made, at once the forms and natures of all things would collapse. Thus the Lord says: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5), showing by this a certain continuance of His work, by which He at once holds together and administers all things, and in which work His wisdom also endures. Of it it is said: “She reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” [Col. 0406A] (Wis. 8). [Note: [Col. 0406D] The same, On Genesis.]

Almighty God—ever the same in immutable eternity, truth, and will—moves the spiritual creature through time; He also moves the bodily creature through time and place, so that by that motion He may govern the natures which He created. When, therefore, He does anything of this kind, we must not suppose that His substance, which is God, is mutable in times and places or movable through times and places. For He is more inward than every thing, because all things are in Him; more outward than every thing, because He is above all things; more ancient than all things, because He is before all things; and newer than all things, because He Himself is after all things, namely after the beginnings of all things.

Therefore, commending His power, the Apostle says: “And He, the Son, is upholding,” [Col. 0406B] that is, containing and governing, “all things by the word,” that is, by the command alone, “of His power,” that is, His power and goodness, which appears no less in governing than in creating. For He holds all things together by His goodness and majesty. [Chrysostom.] Note that “upholding all things by the word” is said by comparison: in saying this, he intended to indicate the ease of His sustaining them, by a metaphor drawn from those who, without any labor, move or accomplish something by word or finger. Thus Christ sustains and governs the mass and magnitude of creation without labor.

Again, observe that, while the Apostle here says Christ holds all things together, above he said that the Father made all things through Him when he said, “through whom He made,” as though He Himself could not make them. For if the Father stretched forth His hand, or if He were some instrument of the Father at work—but if all things are governed by Him, were they not also made by Him? Therefore, heretic, He does not exist as some instrument, as you vainly suppose; nor is the Father said to have made through Him as though He could not Himself make. Rather, as the Father is said to judge through the Son because He begot a Judge, so He is said to work through the Son because He is known to have begotten an Artificer. For if the Father is His cause insofar as He is Father, much more is He the cause of those things which are declared to have been made through the Son.

Making purification of sins, and the rest. After showing His excellence, by which He creates and governs all things, he here commends the goodness of His humility. [Col. 0406D] For he reminds us of the cross, and immediately also of the resurrection and ascension, when he says, “He sits,” etc. What he says here pertains to us, whom He cleanses from sin. As though he said: Christ is the brightness of glory and the figure of substance; though He is such and so great, yet according to His humanity He also makes purification of sins—that is, according to humanity He endured the passion and death of the cross, by which He cleansed us from sins, etc.

“He sits”: after commending Christ through His nature, power, and goodness, he commends Him through dignity. As though he said: He endured the cross in order to cleanse us from sins; and He who was so humbled sits—that is, rests and reigns—exalted at the right hand of Majesty, that is, in equality with the Father, and is placed not in paradise, from which Adam fell, but in the highest places: that is, above all things in place and dignity. For in saying “in the highest places,” he does not confine God to a place, but shows that the human Christ is higher and more eminent than all things; just as by “right hand” he did not give the Lord bodily form but showed a likeness of honor. For the confession shows nothing other than equality of honor.

Contemplate Paul’s wisdom—or rather, marvel at the grace of the Holy Spirit, not Paul’s wisdom. For he did not produce this understanding by his own mind, but the Holy Spirit poured it in. Observe, then, by what steps apostolic wisdom raises them, and how it leads them to the very summit of piety; then, before they should fail and darkness overtake them, see how it recalls them to lower things. At times he speaks of humble matters, and at times proclaims loftier ones; he neither remains always in humble matters nor persists in lofty ones, but, as by certain steps, he is now raised to higher summits and now descends to lower things.

For as one who wishes gradually and little by little to lift some child toward more excellent things does this step by step, ascending from lower things to higher, then, when he has reached the height and sees the child weary from darkness and weakness, after lofty things he lowers him to humbler ones so that he may breathe and refresh his mind; and when restored, raises him again to other lofty matters: so blessed Paul acts toward the Hebrews. He gradually raises them to the knowledge of God, mentioning humble things amid lofty ones, everywhere following in his Master’s footsteps—for He too acted thus. At times He raised His disciples to higher things; at times, for the sake of their weakness, He recalled them to lower things, allowing them to remain in neither state for long. Thus the Apostle acts throughout this whole sequence. First he mentions high things, saying, “in the Son,” where the proper Son is understood, who is above and more excellent than all things. Then he descends to humble things, adding, “whom He appointed heir.” Then he returns to high things, saying, “through whom”; afterward he comes to the degree loftier than all, saying, “who, being the brightness.” Then he speaks of humble things: “making purification of sins”; [Col. 0407D] thence he returns in narration to high things: “he sits at the right hand of Majesty.”

So much better. Here he compares Christ with the angels and sets Him above them. Yet in the Psalm he says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). [Chrysostom.] Here He is said to be better than the same angels; and just as the former statement may be understood according to human nature, so this one might be understood according to divine nature, unless the result were added, which makes clear that he speaks here of Him according to the flesh. For insofar as He is acknowledged consubstantial with the Father’s substance, He was not made but begotten. The discourse therefore concerns Him according to human nature, according to which He was less than the angels in suffering, [Col. 0408A] and greater and better also by the fullness of grace, which the angels themselves receive only in measure.

Therefore Christ Himself says: “Having become so much better,” that is, worthier, “than the angels”—having visibly been made so according to humanity—“as He has inherited,” that is, securely possessed, when He rose and ascended, “a more excellent name,” that is, a more distinguished honor than before; and lest this be thought to be a distinction not above them, he adds: “than they.” For while He was mortal He had a different name, because angels ministered to Him; after becoming immortal, a still more different name, because He became in every respect more honorable and more illustrious than they. Therefore he adds “than they”; or, “has inherited,” that is, has possessed a name of distinction. And this “than they” means a name greatly different from the name of angels: namely, the name above [Col. 0408B] every name, God, or Son of God. This is truly worthier than the name by which they are called angels—that is, messengers. For the name Son denotes proper sonship, not adoption; for unless He were the proper Son, the Apostle could not from this establish the greatness of His honor. The proper Son is begotten from the Father Himself. But if He were Son by grace of adoption, He would be less not only than the Father but also than the angels.

For to which. As though he said: Truly He had a name above the angels. For to which of the angels—not even to the greater ones, nor even after some were confirmed while others fell—did He ever say this: “You are my Son”? Behold, the name “my,” that is, consubstantial, not adoptive. And truly so, because “I have begotten you today,” that is, eternally. He says “begotten,” lest He be thought new, lest He seem to begin only now. [Col. 0408C] He says “today,” lest the generation seem past. For although that day on which Christ was born according to humanity can also be understood, nevertheless, since “today” signifies the present and in eternity nothing is past as though it had ceased to be, nor future as though it were not yet, but only present—because whatever is eternal always is—the words are more divinely understood of the everlasting generation of the Wisdom of God, which the most sincere and catholic faith proclaims. [Chrysostom.] From these words, therefore, he makes clear nothing other than that He was begotten from the very essence of the Father.

And again Isaiah says of the same One, in the person of the Father: “I will be to Him”—that is, for His honor—“a Father, and He will be to Me”—that is, for My honor—“a Son.” This too is always so. But it is said “will be” because all will know it on the day of judgment. For Scripture, by a certain mode of speech, says that a thing is or comes to be when it becomes known. Yet this may also be understood as said according to the flesh. For flesh shares in higher things, just as divinity deigned to share in humble things. [Ambrose.] Thus this is said concerning the incarnation of the Son, as is shown by the phrase “I will be,” signifying the future. God the Father therefore says through the prophet: “I will be to Him,” namely, to the man who will be born of the Virgin, “a Father; and He who will be born will be to Me a Son.” Hence the angel says to Mary: “The holy thing that will be born from you [Col. 0409A] shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

And when He again brings in. [Chrysostom.] He further proves by the authority of Scripture that the Son is worthier than the angels. Observe that Christ calls His coming in the flesh an “exit,” saying: “The sower went out,” etc. (Matt. 13); and likewise: “I came forth from the Father and have come into the world” (John 16). But Paul calls Christ’s advent an “entrance,” saying: “When He brings in.” The assumption of flesh is therefore called both exit and entrance, and rightly so. For we were outside God, like persons bound in chains outside royal halls, who have incurred the king’s displeasure by certain offenses. One who wishes to obtain pardon for such people does not first bring them into the king’s hall; rather, he himself goes out and speaks with them there until he renders them corrected and worthy to be presented before the king. Christ acted in the same way. For He went out to us—that is, assumed flesh—and spoke with us when He made known the king’s commands. Thus, cleansing us from sins and converting us to God, He introduces us, like an excellent Mediator, into the royal hall. [Col. 0409B] Therefore the advent of His flesh is called an exit and an entrance, concerning which he says:

“And again He brings in”: that is, Scripture says that He is to be brought in again. Therefore he says “again,” because it often says that He is to be brought in. He brings in, I say, the Father’s Firstborn—that is, begotten from the Father before all creatures according to deity—into the world, as an heir into his possession. And when He brings Him in, He says. Or thus: the Father Himself again brings the Firstborn [Col. 0409C] into the world; that is, by assuming flesh He made Him visibly appear in the world, though previously He was invisible in the world. He therefore says “again”; this assumption of flesh is called an exit from the Father and an introduction into the inheritance, where He is seen to be adored. Hence he adds: “And when He brings Him in, He says: ‘And let them adore.’”

Or thus: again the Father says concerning the same Son: “When He brings the Firstborn into the world,” that is, when He reveals His Son, who is to be brought even into human hearts through faith. [Chrysostom.] What does He say? “And let all the angels of God adore Him.” Him who suffered and died. For these words are not said of God the Word, but of the assumed man. “Let them adore,” I say: according to His humanity, angels are commanded to adore Christ. From this he shows Him so much better than angels as a master is known to be better than servants. He therefore commanded Christ according to the flesh to be adored by all angels, saying: “Let all the angels of God adore Him,” and they obey His command.

And again the Father says concerning the Son this statement, which indeed pertains to angels: He, the Son, “makes His spirits,” the heavenly angels, that is, His messengers, “and a flame of fire,” that is, the Seraphim, who belong to the higher order, “His ministers.” [Note: [Col. 0409D] Augustine, on Psalm 103.] Although we do not see the appearance of angels—for it is hidden from our eyes—and although they belong to a great commonwealth of the emperor God, nevertheless we know by faith that angels exist, and we read and hold that many have appeared. Angels are spirits; they are not spirits because they are angels, but become angels when they are sent. For “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; “spirit” is the name of their nature. By what it is, it is a spirit; by what it does, it is an angel. Thus “human” is the name of a nature, “soldier” the name of an office. A human becomes a soldier, not a soldier a human. So God the Creator makes angels, by sending them to announce what He commands, out of those spirits whom He created. [Col. 0410A] [Note: Augustine, in the book On the Trinity.] He uses all things according to the immutable purpose of His will, whether good beings through His grace or evil beings through their own will. Accordingly, God’s will is the first and supreme cause of all bodily forms and motions. For nothing visible and perceptible occurs unless it is either commanded or permitted, according to ineffable justice, from the inward, invisible, and intelligible court of the highest Emperor. [Col. 0410B]

[Ambrose.] Or distinguish the passage thus: they are called angels when sent to announce peaceful and mild things; but when sent for vengeance, they are called burning fire, that is, Seraphim. This is what he says: He makes His spirits angels when they announce joyful and mild things, and His ministers like a flame of fire when He sends them to carry out vengeance, as at Sodom and in many other places. And as this occurs literally in creatures, so it occurs figuratively in the Church: there He makes spiritual persons His angels, that is, messengers of His word, and His ministers a flame of fire, because ministers of the Church too are fire when they burn in spirit and consume our vices. [Augustine.] They also tend your hay—that is, your vices—the ministers of God who preach God’s word. [Col. 0410C]

**Verses 8–12.**—But to the Son: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; a scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions. And you, O Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They shall perish, but you shall remain; and all shall grow old like a garment. And like a cloak you shall change them, and they shall be changed.”

But to the Son. Here he commends Christ at once through dignity and power. As though he said: He spoke that which pertains to angels. But the Lord says through the prophet this concerning the Son: “O [Col. 0410D] God, Son, your throne,” that is, kingdom or judgment—of which the Gospel says, “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5)—that is, royal dignity or judicial seat, “remains for ever and ever.” [Ambrose.] For He will reign forever, and the final judgment will stand forever. Hence in the Gospel: “These shall go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25). And rightly does your throne remain. “And,” that is, because, “the scepter of your kingdom,” namely the rule and discipline by which you govern the good and strike or crush the wicked, is a “scepter of righteousness”: a straight and inflexible rule, elsewhere called an iron rod, by which one bent crookedly through perversity is made straight if he wishes to cling to it.

“You have loved.” As though he said: Again, your throne rightly remains because you have loved righteousness from love, that is, every good, and, conversely, have hated iniquity, that is, every evil. Both are not in you together; rather, you love and embrace the one, but hate and pursue the other. “And therefore,” namely, that these might be yours—that you might love righteousness and hate iniquity—He anointed you; or “therefore,” namely, because you loved righteousness and hated iniquity. This reward was therefore given: God, your God, namely the Father, personally—not through ministers—anointed you according to humanity, for deity required nothing.

Observe that “God” is repeated from great affection; or, according to Augustine, one case is vocative and the other nominative, so that the words are: “O God, Son, your God, namely the Father, has anointed you.” In Latin the repeated noun seems to be in the same case, but in Greek there is a most evident distinction: one is understood as nominative, the other vocative. “O God, God has anointed you”: God is anointed by God. Who, then, is the God anointed by God? Understand Christ. For Christ is named from chrism. *Chrisma* is Greek; in Latin it is called *unctio*, “anointing.” The name Christ denotes an anointing; and kings and priests were anointed nowhere else except in that kingdom of the Jews. Thus, by saying that He is an anointed one, he signifies that He is king and priest. God, therefore, has been anointed by God; and God Himself was human in order to be anointed. He was human in such a way that He was God; He was God in such a way that He did not disdain to be human. [Augustine.] [Col. 0411C] Therefore God was anointed, because the human being was God.

But with what oil? With none other than spiritual oil. Hence he adds: “You anointed,” I say, “with the oil of joy,” or gladness, because He was free from sin. Therefore His conscience was joyful. [Note: [Col. 0411D] Augustine, Against Maximinus.] God the Father anointed Him not with visible, bodily oil but with the Holy Spirit, whom Scripture, in its customary figurative manner of speaking, signifies by the name “oil of gladness.” By this anointing, the Son, who so became human that He remained God, was full of the Holy Spirit, as the Gospel reads: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4). Therefore he adds: “Above your companions,” that is, above all saints. [Note: [Col. 0412D] Augustine, on John.] For all saints are His companions, but He alone is uniquely the Holy One of holy ones, uniquely anointed, uniquely the source from which all Christians are anointed.

“And [Col. 0411D] you in the beginning.” [Ambrose.] After discussing the excellence of His humanity, he returns again to demonstrate the Son’s eternity, using the authority of the Prophet, who says this of and to the Son: “And you, O Lord, Son of God, in the beginning of things”—that is, before things existed—“founded the earth,” literally. He says “in the beginning” because the Creator existed before creation without any beginning. As though he said: I know your eternity, by which you precede all that you made, you who said: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3); and “the heavens, together with the earth, are the works of your hands.” He says this as though He worked especially in them. “Hand” means the power of command, that is, the power of will, by which the works were made as He willed. [Col. 0412A]

But they—the heavens, namely the aerial heavens—will perish from what they are when creatures are changed for the better. For the lowest heavens, which perished through the flood, as Peter says, will perish by fire (2 Pet. 3). Water occupied and inundated all this expanse in which birds fly; thus the heavens near the earth certainly perished. Therefore, as to those heavens of which it is said, “the birds of heaven,” there is no doubt that they perished in the flood and will perish by fire. But regarding the higher “heavens of heavens,” whether they too will perish by fire is a more difficult question and a scrupled debate among learned persons. The world’s conflagration will not burn God’s saints: what the furnace of fire was to the three youths, that the burning world will be to the righteous marked by the Trinity.

“But you.” As though he said: The heavens [Col. 0412B] will change, but you will remain. This is said so that, just as He is shown eternal because He is before all things, He may be shown to remain the same after the things changed. And all things—whether the aerial heavens or the earth—will grow old like a garment, that is, as human bodies grow old through long duration. For the human body is, as it were, the soul’s garment. That is said to grow old which is gradually worn away in the manner of a garment, as human flesh is; yet it will be changed for the better. So too the heavens will receive a better form. “And you will change them,” namely the heavens, “like a cloak”: by this he signifies the change of heaven. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Rev. 21). He rightly compares the heavens to a cloak because they encircle the earth. God changes the heavens as easily as a cloak is spread out and folded up; and after their change the heavens will remain. Hence he adds: “And they shall be changed”: that is, once changed, they will so remain, because God’s works will then stand under eternity and will not return to corruption.
