**Verses 12–14.**—“But you are the same, and your years shall not fail.” But to which of the angels did He ever say: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry on behalf of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?

But you, O Son of God, are the selfsame, that is, you are unchangeable—contrary to what was said above, “they shall grow old.” And your years shall not fail, that is, your eternity shall not fail [Col. 0412D]—contrary to what was said, “they shall perish.” The sense is: You neither change nor fail. This was said of the Son; and therefore it also befits God the Son to say, “I am who I am” (Exod. III); and likewise, “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Mal. III). You, heretic, assigned this statement to the Father alone so that the Son might be believed mutable in his substance—as though he had assumed humanity in such a way as to be transformed into a human being. You will not correct so great a blasphemy unless you believe that, in assuming humanity, something was added to the Son which he had not been, while nothing that he was departed or failed.

Or the whole passage may be read mystically, and the words are addressed to the Father, though the Son is also commended therein. [Col. 0413A] As if he said: You, Father, anointed the Son; and you, O Lord Father, by whom the Son was anointed, in the beginning—that is, through your Son, who is beginning from beginning, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII)—founded the earth, that is, established the Church of the peoples, namely, those lesser ones in the Church. And the heavens—that is, the greater ones, such as the apostles—are the works of your hands, because he worked in them, as it were, especially, bestowing more upon them.

And those heavens shall perish, that is, they shall be destroyed by death, and whatever shall be destroyed of itself. But you shall remain in them, that is, your righteousness and those things which you work in them shall remain. And all, namely both greater and lesser, shall grow old, that is, shall gradually decay, like a garment—that is, according to the garment, namely according to the [Col. 0413B] body which surrounds the soul as a garment. And you shall change them like a cloak, that is, according to the body, which you will change into immortality: it shall not be such as it was.

[Augustine] Thus the heavens shall perish and be changed according to their bodies; and they shall be changed not only according to the body but also according to their souls, which will then be more glorious. But you are the selfsame in them through your Son: that is, through the unchangeable form you will be in them because they believed in the Son. And your years shall not fail in them, that is, your eternity.

“To which of the angels?” Again he treats of the glory of Christ’s humanity. [Ambrose] As if he said: Christ is shown to be greater than the angels not only by what precedes, but also by this: because the Father said to him, “Sit,” that is, rest as victor and judge, “at my right hand,” that is, among my greater things, and as my equal according to divinity. Behold: the Father offers shared session to the victorious Son. “Sit,” I say, “until I make your enemies”—which occurs daily while some are converted—“the footstool of your feet,” that is, wholly subjected to you. For in saying “the footstool of your feet,” he signifies complete subjection.

Or by “feet” is understood Christ’s humanity, which is the lower nature in him. The sense is: Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet, that is, subject beneath your humanity, so that they may reverence it and perceive it to be above them. Or: “Sit until I make,” that is, eternally, just as I shall eternally make your enemies the footstool of your feet, that is, subject to the power of divinity. For by the feet is signified [Col. 0413D] eternal stability, which, as it were, stands with its footsteps planted by the power of omnipotence.

“To which of the angels did he ever say this?” He said it to none; for all are spirits, by office ministering servants of the Son, actually sent into service wherever the Son pleases, though they always stand before him who is everywhere. They are sent, I say, for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation—that is, for human beings to whom the inheritance of eternal life is promised. Although they are lesser, the angels serve them at Christ’s command. And is it not so? It certainly is.

[Chrysostom] Understand, therefore, how great an honor is ours: God sends his angels to us as ministers, as to friends. Although there is a great difference between angels and human beings, he has nevertheless made them near to us, because they labor for our salvation, run about for our sake, and perform their office for us. This is the work of angels, the duty of angelic service: that all things should be done for the salvation of their neighbors. Yet this is even more the work of Christ, because he commanded angels, our superiors, to render their ministry for our salvation.

## Chapter II

### Verses 1–5

“Therefore we ought more abundantly to observe the things which we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? Which, having received its beginning of proclamation through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, God bearing witness by signs and wonders and [Col. 0414B] various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit, according to his own will. For God did not subject to angels the world to come, of which we speak.”

“Therefore.” [Chrysostom] After speaking many things concerning the Son of God that serve to commend him, he exhorts those to whom he writes diligently to attend to and preserve what was announced to them through him. All that has preceded tends to this. It is as though he said: Because Christ is greater than the prophets and angels, therefore we ought more abundantly to observe the things which we heard spoken by the Son in the Gospel than those spoken concerning the Law, or by other prophets or angels, who were ministers of the laws.

He nevertheless leaves unmentioned the name “Law,” because he makes this plain in the demonstration which he makes before the praetors. And as though someone were to ask, “Why ought we to do so more?” he adds: “Lest perhaps we drift away,” that is, be punished eternally. We flow away through the punishments of mortal nature; we flow out by adding sins; we utterly flow away into eternal damnation.

He urges the hearing of Christ’s words from the punishment which awaits the negligent. For he proves, from the lesser case, that we shall be punished if we do not observe Christ’s words—namely, from words spoken through angels, which are less worthy than Christ’s words. As if he said: I say, “lest perhaps we utterly flow away,” which will certainly happen. For—that is, because—the word of God spoken through angels to Moses and the others was made firm, that is, true: the Law was confirmed through miracles, threats, and promises, though salvation was not in it. And every transgression, which is doing what is forbidden, and disobedience, which is neglecting what is commanded, received a just recompense—namely, as much as it deserved, according to what it deserved—of reward, so that the character of the punishment corresponds to the character of the deeds.

Attend to every word. He says “every transgression,” to show that punishment must be rendered for individual sins. It is as though he said: Not only will every transgressor, who is guilty of many sins, be punished; but for every transgression or disobedience each shall receive its own punishment. He says “just,” lest justice be thought to perish through mercy.

[Chrysostom] What he calls “recompense” refers to the quantity of punishment, which will be equal to the sin: for as the sin is greater or less, so the punishment will be greater or less. What he calls “of reward” refers to the quality of punishment: thus one who perished through the fire of lust shall be tormented by fire.

“How?” As if he said: If the word of angels was made firm, and if every transgression is punished, how shall we, to whom the Son of God himself—grace through whom salvation exists—has spoken, escape Gehenna if we neglect, even though neglect is less than transgression, so great—that is, unfailing—a salvation made known in the Gospel? It was not so great in the Old Testament: there was a word there, but here there is salvation.

“Which, having received its beginning,” etc. Here he shows that those who despise salvation—that is, Christ’s word, which is the cause of salvation—are without excuse. As if he said: We shall not escape if we neglect salvation.

This salvation received its beginning, not of establishment [Col. 0415B]—for it existed from eternity—but of proclamation. [Chrysostom] And this was through the Lord of angels, namely Christ; hence another edition reads, “through Christ.” Not long after the beginning of its proclamation, it was confirmed to us, namely to the Jews, by those, namely the apostles, who heard from Christ’s own mouth. How? God bearing witness to the authority of the apostles. By what means? By lesser signs, such as driving away diseases, which physicians can do; and by greater wonders, which occur contrary to nature; and by various powers, which do not occur outside nature.

Or he speaks of virtues of the soul: namely, that those who preach are chaste and humble, and possess other such qualities. And by “distributions of the Holy Spirit,” because he gave to some kinds of tongues and to others other gifts. By these things he signifies an abundance of graces that was not among the ancients: neither such great signs nor such diverse prodigies. This shows that they were not believed simply or merely, but through signs and wonders. Therefore, when we believe, it is made clear that we believe not them but God.

The distributions, I say, were made not according to human merit, but according to the will of the Holy Spirit himself—that is, according to the good pleasure of his mercy. Hence elsewhere: “One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. XII).

He did not say merely that those who despise grace confirmed through the apostles, miracles, and gifts are worthy of punishment. Here he says that Christ is powerful to take vengeance and to save his own through the passion of death. As if he said: We truly shall not escape if we neglect Christ’s salvation, since the Jews were punished for not observing the word of angels; for God subjected the world to the Son, which he did not do to angels. Though many things are done in the world through their ministry, all nevertheless look to his rule.

But this—that it should be subjected—shall be to him of whom we speak, that is, Christ. This is what he says: the world, I say, which is to be subjected to him of whom we speak, namely Christ. Or thus: God subjected, not to angels but to the Son, the world that was to come. He says “to come” here as elsewhere he said, “who is the form of the one to come” (Rom. V), speaking of Adam and Christ. With respect to Adam’s times, he calls Christ “to come” according to the flesh; likewise now he calls the world “to come” with respect to Christ. For the world was to come with respect to the Son of God, who always was.

And lest it be understood that he was discussing another world, he adds, “of which we speak.” He adds this so that he would not leave the hearer’s mind wandering in search of some other world. He says, then, that this coming world is subjected not to angels but to Christ. He proves this by the authority of David, who recounts future things as though past, having been admitted to the divine counsels, where even future things are made, according to Isaiah: “Who made the things that are to come.”

But it is fitting first to speak of Christ’s humility, lest his exaltation be doubted because of it; and not only of Christ’s humility, but also of that of the whole human race, showing that humanity is in itself miserable and abject, but exalted by God’s grace. Therefore he adds:

### Verses 6–8

[Col. 0416B] “But someone testified in a certain place, saying: What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet. For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.”

“But someone testified.” As if he said: Not only do I say this; someone also testified to this same thing—namely, one known, eminent, most excellent among the prophets, namely David—in a certain place, namely one known to us and not hidden, of Sacred Scripture, namely in Psalm VIII, saying: “What is man?” This should be read with contempt: “What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man?” etc.

There is a difference between “man” and “son of man,” which the disjunction suggests. Every son of man is a man, but not every man can be understood as a son of man. Adam was a man, but not a son of man. Thus those who bear Adam’s image are called men; but those who bear Christ’s image are more properly called sons of men. The former is called the old man, the latter the new.

Thus “man” here is earthly; the “son of man” is heavenly. The former is far separated from God, but the latter is present to God. Therefore God is mindful of the former as one set at a distance, while he visits the latter whom he illumines with his countenance—that is, with the presence of his grace. “Man,” then, is spoken contemptuously: namely, the earthly sinner.

[Augustine] “What is [man],” as regards this, “that you are mindful of him,” who is, as it were, at a distance, by providing temporal salvation, through which you save humans together with beasts? “Or the son of man,” that is, the spiritual and heavenly man: what is he, as regards this, “that you visit him,” as one infirm, by the presence of grace? And not only the son of man needed to be visited, but also the Son of God; for “you made lower,” namely the Son of God.

Or thus: by “man” understand the good, especially those who existed before Christ’s coming; by “son of man,” Christ. This too is read with contempt in this manner: “A good and righteous man—what is he?” As if he said: Despised, frail, a sinner, as regards the fact that you are mindful of him.

[Ambrose] God is mindful of a human being when he forgives sins. Or “the Son of Man” now arises, that is, from the members he ascends to the head, when he says “the Son of Man,” namely Christ, who was born not from two human beings but from a Virgin. The Son of Man, I say: what is he, as regards this, “that you visit him,” that is, that you visit humanity through the Son of Man himself, as an infirm person through a physician?

Note the propriety of the words. Above he said “mindful,” where he treats of the righteous who lived before Christ’s coming, of whom God was, as it were, mindful when he had mercy from heaven on the patriarchs. Here, however, he uses “visit,” where he treats of the Incarnation, when “the Word became flesh,” when the physician came to the underworld. “You made lower.” As if he said: Through the Son of Man, namely Christ, you visit humanity, and yet you made him—that is, Christ—lower.

Or thus, so that by “man” and “son of man” Christ the man is understood: God was mindful of him in his conception by granting immunity from sin, and visited him in the resurrection by giving the glory of immortality. This is read with admiration: “Man, Christ—what is he?” that is, how great and worthy a thing is he, because you are mindful of him, making him immune from sin? “Or,” that is, “and the Son of Man,” namely that same Christ, who is man from man as God is God from God: what is he, namely, how exceedingly excellent, because you visit him by raising him?

“You made lower.” As if he said: You visited Christ the man. And he needed to be visited because you made him lower through a passible nature. He was made lower when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; therefore on account of the very weakness of flesh which God’s wisdom deigned to bear, [Col. 0417C] and the humiliation of the Passion, it is rightly said, “You made him lower than the angels.” For he was mortal and passible, but only a little lower: though passible, he nevertheless commanded angels, and he was without sin.

But afterwards, in the likeness of a conqueror, “you crowned him,” that is, you surrounded him on every side, “with glory,” in the resurrection and ascension, “and honor,” that is, in sitting with the Father. Or “glory” means the brightness of immortality, and “honor,” that every knee bends to him. “And you appointed him,” establishing him securely, “over the works”—but he adds, “of your hands,” that is, over even the more worthy works, namely humans and angels, which are called works of hands by preeminence.

And he was not only appointed over the works as worthier than they: “you also subjected all things beneath his feet,” that is, to his power and dominion, so that they may adore and reverence him. For he could be superior and yet all things might be granted to him. Therefore he says: “You subjected all things beneath his feet.” For no creature will remain unsubjected to him, to whom even the ruling spirits, so to speak, are subjected.

“For in this,” or “but,” he explains the meaning held by the prophet David in the preceding words. As if he said: David said, “You subjected all things.” But in this, that Scripture subjected all things to him—that is, showed all things to be subject to him—it left nothing unsubjected to him, that is, it excepted nothing from all things. For when it says “all things,” it excludes neither earthly nor heavenly things.

Or thus, according to the continuous wording: “For.” As if he said: I rightly say that the world to come will be subjected [Col. 0418A] to Christ, because in saying, “He subjected all things to him,” Scripture says that all things are subject to him. “It left nothing unsubjected.” The sense does not change. Another text confirms the same sense: “For in saying that he subjected all things, he left nothing unsubjected to him.”

“But now.” As if he said: Scripture says, “You subjected all things,” but not yet are all things subjected to him. Therefore he fittingly said above that the world would be subjected. This is what he says: “But now, although Scripture says ‘all things,’ we do not yet see all things subjected to him voluntarily, which must be subjected.” For every day some are subjected to him; but not all who must be subjected will be subjected until the judgment.

Distinguish when he says, “He left nothing unsubjected.” Here he indicates universal subjection, whether voluntary or necessary. But when he says, “We do not yet see,” etc., here he means only the voluntary subjection of those who faithfully believe in him.

### Verses 9–11

“But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for all. For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, to perfect through suffering the author of their salvation. For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”

“But we see him.” As if he said: We do not yet see all things subjected to him, but one part of the prophecy has already been fulfilled, because we see him, etc.; from this it is evident that the other part will be fulfilled. Therefore do not grieve over adversities.

We see him, I say, who was made a little lower than angels, now Jesus—that is, Savior—and crowned with glory and honor. This was certainly deserved, namely because of suffering—not any suffering, but that of death. Here he begins to show that Christ’s words should be heard not merely because of power or vengeance, but because of the love by which he loved us so as to die for us. Therefore he adds: “So that by the grace of God,” etc.

Or read it thus: We see him now as Jesus and crowned with glory and honor, who was made a little lower than angels, not according to the nature of the human mind, but because of the suffering of death.

[Note: [Col. 0417D] Augustine, *Against Maximinus*.] Angels may indeed be called greater than man, because they are greater than the human being in body and also greater in mind; but this is so only insofar as a corruptible body, by the desert of original sin, weighs down the mind itself. But God alone is greater than the nature of the human mind such as Christ assumed, which could be corrupted by no sin. He therefore disclosed why Christ is said to have been made a little lower than angels when he said, “because of the suffering of death.” He was lower than angels, then, not because of human nature, but because of the suffering of death. But God alone is greater than human nature, which surpasses other creatures through a rational and intellectual mind. He was therefore lower than angels in body, not in mind.

If it seems to you that nothing great is said of God the Father if the form of a servant is greater than that in which angels appear greater, you do not think correctly, nor do you consider what place human nature holds [Col. 0419A] among realities—human nature which was created in the image of God, though no injury was done to it.

[Augustine] When Christ said, “The Father is greater than I,” he placed God the Father above not only his flesh but also the human mind which he bore. This whole is undoubtedly recognized as the form of a servant, because every creature serves the Creator.

“So that by the grace of God.” As if he said: He was made lower than angels, and this was so that the grace of God—that is, he himself who is God’s grace, because he gives freely, or because he was freely given to us—might taste death. Or “by the grace of God” may be taken in the ablative: so that by God’s grace, which man did not deserve, he might taste death. He properly said “taste,” because death is bitter, or because it passed quickly.

[Chrysostom] He remained in it only a short interval and immediately rose, as one who tastes briefly experiences. He tasted death, I say, for all, namely the predestined, who were redeemed and saved through his death. Or: he died generally for all human beings, because the price was sufficient for all. He therefore properly said “for all,” because he died not only for believers but for the whole world. Even if all do not believe, he nevertheless fulfilled what belonged to him.

“For it was fitting.” As if he said: Christ was made lower in order to taste death, and this was most fitting. For it was fitting for him, namely God the Father, for whose glorification all things were made, and through whom all things were made as their author, who had brought many adoptive sons—that is, had foreseen that they would be brought—into glory, to perfect—that is, to bring to completion in the eternal glory of blessedness—what he began in the resurrection, when Christ was raised up in the glory of immortality; what was increased in the ascension, when he ascended to the Father’s right hand; and what will be completed at the judgment, when all things shall be subjected to him and he shall be all in all.

It was fitting, I say, for him to perfect the author of the salvation of those sons, namely Christ, who is Son by nature and whose co-heirs we shall be, we who are sons by adoption. See how great the difference is between us: he is Son, and we are sons, yet there is a difference, because he saves while we are saved; he sanctifies while we are sanctified. Scripture sometimes joins us and sometimes separates us. “Many sons,” it says: here it joins us. “The author of their salvation”: here it distinguishes us.

It was fitting, I say, to perfect him, and this through the suffering [Col. 0419D] of death. That death was most fitting and greatly necessary for healing our misery, because unless Christ died, humanity would not be redeemed, and without redemption would perish. If this were so, all things would have been made in vain. For other things serve humanity, and humanity serves God; and God would be glorified in nothing, though all things were made for this end. His proclamation concerning the sons to be brought would also be false.

“For he who.” He proves that it was fitting for Christ to suffer for our deliverance. It seems unfitting that the author of salvation should suffer; but it does not dishonor him, because he depends on God and is subject to him just as other human beings are. Therefore suffering was fitting for him; why it was necessary he says later at “Since therefore,” etc.

[Chrysostom] As if he said: It was fitting for the Father to perfect Christ through suffering, and it did not dishonor Christ to suffer. For he who sanctifies the predestined, namely Christ, and those who are sanctified through him, namely all of us, alike depend upon and are from one. Behold again how he joins them by saying that they are from one; again, see how great the difference is: he sanctifies, but we are sanctified. Although we are from one, nevertheless there is a great difference. For he is from the Father according to divinity as the proper Son, that is, begotten from his essence; but we are adoptive sons.

### Verses 11–18

“On account of which he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: ‘I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will praise you.’ And again: ‘I will put my trust in him.’ And again: ‘Behold, I and the children whom God gave me.’ Since therefore the children shared in flesh and blood, he likewise shared in the same, that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and might free those who through fear of death were subject to bondage throughout their life. For he nowhere took hold of angels, but he took hold of the seed of Abraham. Hence he had to be made like his brothers in all things, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people. For in that wherein he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able also to help those who are tempted.”

“On account of which.” He proves that all are from one, saying: “On account of which”—that is, because both, head and members, are from the same source—Christ is not ashamed, or embarrassed, although free from sin, to call them brothers, though they have become degenerate through sin. He says in the Psalm: “O Father, I will declare,” or recount after the resurrection, “your name,” that is, the renown and glory of your deity, “to my brothers.” And I, set in the midst of the Church as a pillar, “will praise you.” Or “in the midst of the Church,” that is, throughout the whole world, I will praise you everywhere.

Observe that when he says, “He is not ashamed to call them brothers,” he shows that our brotherhood is not of his nature, but of mercy and humility. He proves through the prophet that we are brothers, lest this be thought something new.

“And again.” By the authority of Isaiah he shows himself to be from God and dependent upon him: “I, Christ, as true man, will put my trust according to my humanity in him,” namely God the Father. He would not do this unless he were from God.

“And again.” He demonstrates both subjection to God and a community of human nature with us, saying: “Behold, I am ready to serve, and my children,” namely the apostles and other faithful persons, “whom the Lord gave me”—as members to their head in the unity of nature and grace. And in this it is clear that they are from God, because I and the children shared in flesh and blood.

“And he likewise shared in the same.” He proved that it was fitting for Christ to suffer if necessary. Here he demonstrates that it was necessary, because the children shared in flesh and blood. As if he said: It is certain that Christ who sanctifies and those sanctified are from God; thus it does not dishonor him to suffer, if this is necessary. But why was suffering necessary? Behold: because the children shared in flesh and blood.

This is what he says, as if he said: He is from the one God together with the sanctified; and because the children who were to be sanctified [Col. 0421A] shared in flesh and blood—that is, in the soul, that is, were corruptible human beings composed of body and soul, the latter being denoted by “blood”—therefore Christ himself also shared in the same: either in the children, because he became a child composed of soul and flesh; or he shared in the same, namely in flesh and blood, that is, the soul. And this “likewise,” that is, in such a manner that he was a passible and mortal human being, able to die. Behold the true brotherhood in Christ, and not a fictitious humanity: that through his death he might destroy him who had the power of death, namely the devil, author of death because author of sin, from which death proceeded.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] This testimony sufficiently shows that even this bodily death came through the devil as its prince and author, that is, from the sin which he persuaded humanity to commit. Nor could he most truly be said to have the power of death for any other reason. Hence he who died without any sin, original or personal, said: “Behold, the prince of this world comes,” that is, the devil who has the power of death, “and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV), namely no sin, on account of which he made human beings die.

Therefore the devil found nothing in Christ on account of which he should die. Yet Christ willed to die for obedience to the Father’s will, having no cause of death from sin under the author of sin, but being made obedient unto death through obedience and righteousness. By this he redeemed us from the devil’s bondage. For we had fallen into the power of the prince of this world, who deceived Adam and made him a slave, and he began to possess us as though we were born household slaves.

But the Redeemer came, and the deceiver was conquered. What did the Redeemer do to our captor? He set a trap: he placed there his cross as bait, his blood. But the devil shed the blood of one who owed him nothing; by this he was commanded to restore those who were debtors. He shed innocent blood and was commanded to release the guilty. Christ indeed shed his blood to blot out our sins. Therefore that by which the devil held us was blotted out by the Redeemer’s blood. For he held us only in the bonds of our sins: these were the chains of captives.

He came, bound the strong man with the bonds of the Passion, entered his house—that is, the hearts in which he dwelt—and carried off his vessels. We are those vessels [which] he had filled with his bitterness, which he offered to our Redeemer in gall. But our Savior, taking away his vessels and making them his own, poured out the bitterness and filled them with sweetness.

Therefore he shared in the children, that is, he became a passible and mortal human being, in order thus to conquer the devil. For unless the one conquering the devil were human, humanity would seem to be taken from him not justly but violently, since humanity had voluntarily subjected itself to him. But if a human being conquers him, the devil justly loses humanity. And for a human being to conquer, God must be in him, making him without sins. For if he were a merely human being, or an angel in a human being, he would easily sin, since it is evident that each nature by itself fell.

The Son of God became man, the Son of Man, passible and mortal, so that through death he might destroy the devil [Col. 0422A] by blotting out the sins through which we were captives under him; and through that same death might free those who, through fear of bodily death, were subject throughout this life to the bondage of the devil and sin.

Here something marvelous is shown: by that through which the devil possessed power, he was conquered; and the weapons which that strong one had used against the world were those by which Christ struck him. In this he suggests the greatness of Christ’s power and skill. Death was the weapon by which the devil conquered, and by it he was conquered by Christ. Hence: “O death, I will be your death” (Hos. XIII). And through it he freed those subject to bondage.

See how great a good Christ’s death accomplishes. He freed those who through fear of death were subject to bondage. Those who feared death were indeed slaves, and endured everything lest they die. But now the saints, who through Christ are to pass into the kingdom, mock at death. Hence the Apostle: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). And blessed Job says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job II).

This is the victory of faith, which would certainly have been lacking if immortality had immediately followed for believers. God could indeed have granted believers that they should not experience even the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain happiness would have been added to the flesh, while the strength of faith would have been diminished. For people fear this death in such a way that they would call Christians happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all. Thus no one would hasten to Christ’s grace for the sake of the blessed life which is to come; instead, people would be thought to believe in Christ more softly, for the renewal of freedom from the affliction of death, and faith would be feeble and weak.

What great thing would it be to believe when one saw that those who believed did not die—believing that one would never die at all? How much stronger it is to believe in such a way that one hopes, though dying, to live without end, following the example of Christ, who after death rose in glory and lives a blessed life without end.

Let us therefore desire Christ’s life, because we possess the pledge of Christ’s death. How will he not give us his good things, who endured our evils? In these lands, in this evil age, what abounds except being born, laboring, and dying? These are the wares of our region. The merchant descended to such merchandise; and since every merchant gives and receives—gives what he has and receives what he does not have—Christ too, in this commerce, gave and received.

But what did he receive? What abounded here except being born, laboring, and dying? And what did he give? Being born again, rising again, and reigning eternally. O good merchant, we give thanks, because you bought us. We drink your blood; we read the Gospel, our legal instrument. We are your servants; we are your creature. You made us; you redeemed us. Someone may buy his slave, but cannot create him. But the Lord Christ both created his servants so that they might exist and redeemed them through death so that they should not always be captives. Thus he tasted death so that the faithful might overcome the fear of death.

[Col. 0423A] For as a physician, having no need to taste foods prepared for a sick person, nevertheless, in caring for or comforting the patient, first tastes the patient’s foods in order to persuade the sick person more readily to take them, so also the Lord, when all people feared death, persuaded them confidently to approach death; and he himself tasted death, having no necessity of dying.

Or thus, “and might free”: he treats of the fear of punishment through which the Jews served under the Law. Once the Law had been annulled through grace, he freed them from the Law’s burden and servile fear. As if he said: Christ became man so that through death he might destroy the devil, and through that same death might annul the Law; and, once it had been annulled, might free them—that is, might make the Jews free through grace.

[Col. 0423B] Those who, through fear of death—of body or of soul—were subject throughout their whole life to the slavery of the Law; that is, they were slaves of the Law through fear of punishments, because through fear of punishments of body or soul they kept the Law. Christ freed them either from hell or from the yoke of the Law. For never. As though he said: He shared in them in order to sanctify and free human beings; and this reason is rightly added, because, if he were not going to free them, he would not share in them. This is apparent in the angels, because “nowhere does he take hold of angels,” that is, nowhere in Scripture is he said to have taken angelic nature upon himself in order to redeem angels. But it is written that he took hold of the seed of Abraham, that is, flesh from Abraham, in order to save his children. [Chrysostom] I do not say “assumed,” but “took hold of”: pursuing that which was fleeing far away. In this [Col. 0423C] may be understood both the dignity of human nature, and the mercy and grace by which he does this, and the care he had for us; for human nature was fleeing before him, and fleeing far away. We were far away; he pursued and took hold of us. This dignity was not granted to angelic nature, that God should be joined to it in one person; and truly it is great, wonderful, and full of astonishment that our flesh should sit on high and be worshipped by angels and archangels. Therefore, as I repeatedly turn this over in my mind, I am carried beyond myself, imagining great things concerning the human race.

Therefore, namely because he took hold of the seed of Abraham, he had to be made like his brothers in every respect: that is, that he should be passible, mortal, and the like—in matters in which he was made like his brothers: namely, that he was born, brought up, grew, [Col. 0423D] suffered, and died. He who above was called the image of the Father’s substance had to be made like God, in order that he might become merciful in the actual exercise of mercy—which he was by nature—and a faithful high priest, that is, a mediator and bridge to God, deceiving no one, offering himself to God as a sacrifice so that he might “repropitiate,” that is, remove by drawing near, the sins of the people.

He is well able to do this. For in that in which he himself suffered—that is, in his lower substance, namely in the flesh in which he suffered under Pilate and was tempted by the devil—[Ambrose: “or experienced,” another reading] he is able also to help those who are tempted. This is said of the incarnate one, who in the flesh he assumed suffered many cruel things and knows by experience what is this [Col. 0424A] tribulation and temptation of those who suffer. He does not know our sufferings only as God does, but also knew them as a human being by experience: because, having been tempted and having suffered many things, he knows how to suffer with others, although as God he is indeed impassible.

And the sense is: He is able to help those who are tempted; that is, with great eagerness he stretches out his hand to sympathize with the tempted, and knows perfectly how to do it. Notice that he says, “tempted.” God tempts, a human being tempts, and the devil tempts. God tempts in order to test; the devil, in order to deceive; a human being, in order to learn what he does not know.

## Chapter III

### Verses 1–11

“Therefore, holy brothers, partakers of the heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who is faithful to him [Col. 0424B] who made him, as Moses also was in all his house. For this one has been deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who built the house has greater honor than the house itself. For every house is built by someone; but God is the one who created all things. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son in his own house. We are that house, if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope. Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested me, put me to the proof, and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with this generation [Col. 0424C] and said: They always go astray in heart. But they did not know my ways, so that I swore in my wrath: ‘If they enter into my rest.’”

“Therefore,” etc. From all that precedes he draws the conclusion: namely, because he is mighty, because he suffered for us, and because he can help. Therefore, O holy brothers, partakers of the heavenly calling—that is, called to heavenly things, to possess the heavenly inheritance with Christ—consider Jesus Christ, by loving him and doing what he commands. For we need no other.

Consider him as the apostle, namely, the one whom God sent to us; and as high priest, namely, the one through whom one goes to God. For high priest and mediator are the same. He is high priest, I say, of our confession: namely, the one whom we confess; or of confession, that is, of the faith in whom we believe. “Who is faithful,” [Col. 0424D] etc. Here he begins to compare Christ with Moses, as above he compared him with the prophets and angels. He compares him with Moses in such a way as to show that he is more faithful than Moses, because he sought not his own glory but the Father’s, and did not conceal his commands.

Comparing him, therefore, with Moses, he says: Christ is faithful, according to his humanity, to him—namely God the Father—who made him from the seed of David according to the flesh. He is faithful, I say, as Moses also was faithful in all, that is, in the whole house of the Jews, which house belongs to him, namely to the Father or to Christ, not to Moses, because Moses was a minister, not a lord.

Or thus: Christ Jesus is faithful to him who made him, namely to God the Father, not only in a certain house but in every house, both of Jews [Col. 0425A] and Gentiles, as Moses was faithful in one. And in every house, I say, belonging to him, namely to the Father or Christ.

“For of greater glory.” As though he said: That Christ was made faithful indicates that this one, namely Christ, was deemed worthy of glory as Moses was; because he was also deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses. Or: he was deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses. He is before Moses in merit, because he merited more than Moses; and he is worthy of so much greater glory as the builder of the house has greater honor in, or from, the house made than the one who administers it as a servant. This must be understood of the spiritual house, not of the Temple or tabernacle but of the people.

Notice that he did not openly say, “Moses [Col. 0425B] is a servant, but Christ is Lord,” but indicated this covertly. For if the people were the house, and Moses himself was of the people, then he was of the house; and we are accustomed to say of a servant, “He is of that man’s house.”

“For every house.” As though he said: I say that he built it, and rightly so: for it cannot make itself but is made by someone. “For every house is built by someone.” Is it therefore built by Christ? Certainly, because God is the one who created all things. And if all things, then also the house. This is what he says: “But he who created both the house and all things is God.” God is the maker of both houses, namely that governed by Moses and that governed by Christ; and since he is acknowledged to be above all things, Christ—because he is God and Creator—is above Moses.

Moses also shows that Christ is worthy of [Col. 0425C] greater glory than Moses, because Christ is the builder of the house, not Moses. Here he shows the same thing by another reason: Christ is Son, Moses servant; Moses delivered carnal things to carnal people, while Christ delivers spiritual things.

As though he said: He is also worthy of greater glory or grace for this reason: Moses indeed was faithful in the whole house, not his own but that of God the Father or Christ, as a servant, who does not love the house as much as he whose own it is. And this was not in order to give grace, but “for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken”: that is, in order to testify to those things which it was fitting to speak to carnal people who could not yet grasp spiritual things. But Christ is faithful as a Son, who is heir, in the house with the [Col. 0425D] Father himself. That house of Christ is we who have been reborn, if we retain firm to the end of life the confidence of hope—that is, hope joined with confidence, not doubtful hope—and glorious hope, namely hope concerning heavenly delight. Then that which is now hoped for will be possessed.

“Therefore”: as above, when he had commended Christ in many respects above the angels and prophets, he added that we ought to keep what we had heard from him; so now, having also commended him above Moses, he begins to frighten them lest, after the likeness of their fathers, they should be unbelieving toward Christ. Afterwards, lest they lose rest, he also encourages them through the favorable time.

As though he said: We are God’s house. Therefore [Col. 0426A] because we are Christ’s in this manner, see, brothers, lest perhaps, etc. The sequence of the words is directed thus far.

Or the order may be: Therefore, because we are Christ’s, do not harden your hearts. And I say this as the Holy Spirit says in David: “Today,” that is, in the time of grace, which was present to David in the Spirit, “if you hear his voice,” namely Christ speaking in person—as indeed you will—“do not harden your hearts.” At one time you heard his voice through Moses and hardened your hearts. He spoke through a herald when you hardened your hearts; now he speaks in person. Let your hearts therefore become soft. He who formerly sent heralds before him deigned to come himself; he speaks here with his own mouth, he who spoke through the mouths of the prophets. If therefore you were hard then, now be soft.

I say, do not harden your hearts by doing as your fathers did in the provocation that took place on the day—that is, on the day of testing in the wilderness. As your fathers were hardened on the day of testing, that is, on one day among the provocations—this testing took place in the wilderness, where they had greater need of help—so you also, in the wilderness of this world, beware lest you test God and perish as those did in the wilderness who tested God.

> [Note: Col. 0425D. Augustine, on Psalm 144.]
>
> You surely remember, brothers, that that people tested God, received discipline, and was governed in the wilderness as by the best rider, by the reins of laws and commandments; nor did he cease to use the rod of correction, by which they were struck for their bitterness. The story is sufficiently well known: they sent [Col. 0426C] scouts to inspect the land, and when they heard from them that there were invincible men there, men of gigantic [239] stature, they forgot God’s power, proved so often, and said: “Let us return to Egypt, to the pots of meat.” Therefore the Lord swore that they would not enter the land of promise, which would be a rest from their labors; and so all perished except two, namely Caleb and Joshua.
>
> It should be known that in this sequence three rests are mentioned: two signifying, and a third signified. One is the Sabbath on which the Lord rested; the second, in Palestine; the third, the true rest, which is in heaven. Of this he speaks here, addressing true Israelites and saying to the faithful, who were to hear Christ speaking: Do not be hard toward Christ speaking, as [Col. 0426D] the Spirit forewarned when speaking in David, lest you suffer things similar to your fathers, who then heard the Lord’s voice through Moses. But you now hear it through Christ himself.
>
> This is what he says: “Do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where”—that is, in which wilderness—“your fathers according to the flesh tested me,” namely the Holy Spirit who was speaking in David. See that they are not your fathers according to the Spirit: they were your fathers according to the flesh, but if you do not imitate them, they will not be your fathers according to the Spirit. “And they proved me,” that is, found me trustworthy; “and,” that is, because, “they saw,” etc. Or: “they proved me,” that is, they inquired out of curiosity whether I could act, and they saw with their eyes my works of great power.
>
> “For forty years,” during which they experienced that I can do all things. Therefore, because they tested me, I was offended—or “unoffended,” another reading, that is, exceedingly and inexorably angry—or “near,” applying the scourges of correction, against this generation, evil as it was. And I said of them: “They always go astray in heart,” that is, by their own deliberate choice, because they sin deliberately. “But they.” As though he said: I gave this warning through the prophet; but although I warned thus, they did not know my ways: that is, they were unwilling to know my works. “Therefore, if they shall enter into my rest,” namely the land of promise—an aposiopesis, meaning: they shall not enter. I say this as I swore, that is, firmly decreed, in my wrath, [Col. 0427B] namely when I was angry. For he sometimes swears when not angry. Yet he is said to be angry by the figure called anthropopathism.

### Verses 12–19

“See to it, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. But exhort one another daily, while it is called Today, lest any of you be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, if indeed we retain firm to the end the beginning of his substance, while it is said: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation.’ For some who heard provoked him, though not all who went out of Egypt through Moses. But with whom was he angered [Col. 0427C] forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter into his rest because of unbelief.”

“See to it,” etc. As though he said: Since rest was denied to your fathers because of unbelief, therefore see to it, O brothers, lest perhaps—that is, something which can easily happen—there be in any of you. He says “in any,” because he does not doubt that among many of them some are perfect. Let there be, I say, a heart of unbelief: that is, an unbelieving heart, so that you think Christ is not sufficient without the Law. This is evil, because in this way a person falls into many [Col. 0427D] sins. [Chrysostom] For unbelief produces a wicked life; thus the soul, coming into the depth of evils, becomes contemptuous. Nor is this a slight matter, because this is to depart from God; and this is to test Christ. Thus he adds: This is a heart departing from the living God. As though he said: Whoever departs from him loses life, because life exists in him alone; conversely, whoever draws near finds life.

But rather exhort, as virtues diminish, yourselves—one another, or each one himself—every day, until, that is, as long as, it is called “Today”: that is, the time of grace concerning which the prophet spoke above in the Psalm, because grace leading believers to salvation is accomplished no less now than when Christ himself was present. For if anyone sins, he can return while it is Today. Let no one, therefore, despair while he lives.

I say, exhort one another, lest any among you be hardened by the devil’s deceit, which is the cause of sin. For know that the devil deceives the one who is hardened; afterwards he falls into sin.

“For we have become partakers.” As though he said: You ought to exhort yourselves and not be hard, because through grace we have become what we were not. [Ambrose] This is what he says: We have become partakers of Christ—that is, having a share with Christ himself in the inheritance—through grace, by which we have been united to him as members to the head. For he is our head, and we have become his members. We are partakers, I say, on this condition: if we retain firm to the end of life, so that we never abandon, the beginning of his substance, [Col. 0428B] that is, the faith which is the beginning of good things, through which God exists in us, through which we are made divine and partake of the divine substance. [Remigius]

We are to retain it to the end, I say, while, that is, as long as, it is said to us: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as”—namely, as your fathers hardened—theirs in that provocation. He adds this concerning the fathers in order to frighten them by their fathers’ example.

“For some.” As though he said: Do not harden yourselves as the fathers did in the provocation. I say this rightly, because some of them, hearing God’s voice in the wilderness concerning the future rest in the land of Palestine, provoked God: that is, they were unbelieving and hard. Therefore they perished. He says this lest anyone suppose it sufficient to hear about rest: they all heard, but not all arrived; only some arrived, those who did not provoke him. Concerning them he adds: “But not all,” that is, not all provoked him, such as Caleb and Joshua and those like them. Not all, I say, who went out of Egypt through Moses; so you have gone out from the darkness of vices and ignorance through Christ.

But with which of those mentioned above, namely those who provoked or did not provoke, was he angered for forty years? He mentions this number of years again because by this number our whole life is signified. For forty signifies the completeness of the ages.

Therefore he is said to have been angered with them for forty years because he is angry with those who sin throughout their life to the end. Then, answering his own question, he adds: “Was he not angered with those who sinned?” As though [Col. 0428D] he said: There is no doubt about it—their bodies, without burial, were cast down for beasts and birds in the wilderness. As though he said: God’s wrath is evident in this. Therefore do not promise yourselves impunity if you are unbelieving.

“To whom, moreover?” As though he said: Not only did he cast down the unbelieving, but he also swore that they would not enter into rest. This is what he says in question form: To whom did he swear that they would not enter, or that they should not enter, into his eternal rest, signified by the land of promise, except to those who did not believe the Lord who promised it to them? To them indeed, and to no others.

“And we see.” As though he said: The Lord swore that they would not enter into rest, and thus we see—that is, openly know that it occurred—that they could not enter eternal rest, just as they could not enter the land of promise, [Col. 0429A] because of unbelief. And because they lost rest through unbelief—

## Chapter IV

### Verses 1–5

“Let us therefore fear lest perhaps, while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any one of us should be judged to fall short. For to us also the good news has been proclaimed, just as to them; but the word heard did not profit them, not being mixed with faith by those who heard. For we who have believed shall enter into rest, as he said: ‘As I swore in my wrath: If they enter into my rest.’ Yet the works were completed from the foundation of the world. For in a certain place he spoke concerning the seventh day thus: ‘And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.’ And again in this place: ‘If they enter [Col. 0429B] into my rest.’”

“Let us therefore fear.” As though he said: If we do not do this through love or fear, let us fear, I say, lest perhaps anyone of us should be judged—by a true judgment, even if he presumptuously thinks otherwise—to fall short of rest. And this, while the promise remains of entering his true rest, which the land of promise signified: that is, if God’s promise, by which he promised entry into heavenly rest, is left behind and despised; or the promise which we make to God in baptism, which, if kept, causes us to enter into rest.

“For.” As though he said: I say, Let us fear, and rightly, because we cannot excuse ourselves as though the matter had not been announced. For, etc.

Or the connection is thus: I say, Let us fear lest anyone among us should suppose that it does not concern us; and it rightly concerns us, for in the time of grace eternal rest has been announced to us also through the Son, just as through the servant the land—and through the figure of the land of promise, heaven—was announced to them. We shall enter by believing, just as they lost it by not believing.

Therefore he adds: “But not,” etc. As though he said: It was announced to them, but the word promised concerning rest did not profit them, being only heard, because it was not mixed with faith: that is, it was not believed, so that the word and faith might be joined together. It was not believed, I say, because of what they heard from the scouts who brought back evil reports.

For after they had left Egypt, travelled a great distance, and received many judgments displaying God’s power in Egypt [Col. 0429D] and at the Red Sea, they formed the plan in the wilderness to send scouts to inspect the nature of the land. When these had gone and returned, they said that the region produced great fruits and invincible, strong men. Those who had sent them were astonished when they heard this and did not believe God’s true promise.

Or thus: the word did not profit them, not being mixed with faith taken from what they had heard from the Lord through Moses, promising them the land of promise.

“For we shall enter.” As though he said: Rest has been announced to you, and the effect proves this: “For we shall enter.” Or the connection is: Truly the word did not profit those who did not believe, because it profits us who believe. For we who have believed shall enter into true rest. We who have believed shall enter, as the Holy Spirit said conversely in the Psalm concerning the unbelieving; from this it is clear that those who believe will enter. What did he say? Namely: “They shall enter into my rest”—an aposiopesis, meaning: they shall not enter—“as he swore in wrath.” For they entered neither Palestine nor true rest; but we shall enter true rest.

“And indeed.” Since he had said that rest was announced, he says when: namely, both before the Law, after the completion of the works of the six days, by the rest of the Sabbath; and under the Law, when it was designated by the land of promise; and in the time of grace, when the Holy Spirit says in David, “Today,” etc.

As though he said: That rest was announced. And indeed, in the designation of that rest, the Holy Spirit spoke, when the completion of that true and signified rest had not yet occurred, because no one had yet obtained it, in a certain—namely, distinguished—place of Scripture concerning the seventh day, through which eternal rest is signified: “God rested on the seventh day,” ceasing from new activity, “from all his works,” so that he might no longer create new works according to kind or matter, but might work from the matter then made and according to the likeness of things then made.

He rested, I say, after works had been completed; after he had begun making them from the foundation of the world—that is, from the time the world began to be established—he was able to rest, because he himself made all things. [Remigius] It should be noted that he says, “the works completed,” which occurred when humankind was made, for whose sake all things were made, and humankind itself was made to glorify God.

God rested on the seventh day. For in six days God made all things in matter or likeness, so that afterwards nothing should be made except from the matter then made or according to the likeness of the things made. On the seventh he rested, which signifies true rest. So too, in the sixth age, Christ was born into the world for labor; on the sixth day and at the sixth hour of the day he suffered. But on the seventh day he rested in the tomb. Thus we too, while we live under the works of the six days, labor; departing from them, we shall rest.

Or, while the same sense of the words remains, it may be read thus: “for” stands in “for he said,” and “it was announced” is understood, as follows: “And indeed.” As though he said: Rest was announced. For the Holy Spirit said in a certain place concerning the seventh day: “And he rested on the seventh day from all his works.” These words do not change. Notice that here he treats of the first rest, which signifies.

“And in this [Col. 0430D] place.” As though he said: There the Holy Spirit touches upon true rest through the sign and figure of the seventh day. And again in this place the Holy Spirit speaks of the same true rest through the sign and figure of rest in the land of promise: “They shall enter,” that is, they shall not enter, “into my rest,” namely the land of promise, which signifies the true rest that Moses promised under a figure. Notice that here he treats of the second rest, which signifies.

“Therefore,” carefully observe what has been said and the order of what follows. Behold, heavenly rest has twice been signified and promised, namely through the seventh day and through the land of promise. And because this is so, therefore again or anew—that is, under the designation of the same rest—the Holy Spirit determines and distinguishes [Col. 0431A] a certain day in which the things foretold may be fulfilled: namely, the distinguished time of grace at Christ’s coming, saying in David, “Today.” For David, in the time of grace yet future, presents the words spoken to the fathers; and he does so after so long a time from when these things were said to the fathers in the wilderness. Thus it is clear that the subject is not the land of promise, which had already long been possessed. In this it is evident that the rest of which David says “Today” is other than that into which Joshua led.

“As already,” etc. As though he said: He determines a certain day by saying “Today,” as has already been said above: “Today,” that is, in the time of grace, “if you hear his voice”—as indeed you will hear it—“do not harden your hearts,” as the fathers did in that provocation. Notice that by saying “a certain day” and “Today,” he treats of the third rest signified, and of when it is given—although obscurely—which has been promised through Christ to believers. Therefore he determines the day of entrance.

### Verses 6–12

“Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again determines a certain day: ‘Today,’ saying in David after so long a time, as was said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterwards have spoken of another day. Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God. For the one who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest, lest [Col. 0431C] anyone fall into the same example of unbelief. For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.”

“It remains,” that is, after the promise, for some—namely, distinguished persons—to enter into it, namely eternal rest, which is signified by the land of promise. Unless David saw that some would enter, he would not determine a day. For David, although he was under the Law, was nevertheless in mind set within the time of grace when he said “Today”; he announced a third time the rest which would be consummated at that time.

And as though someone should ask why it was necessary to say to them, “Do not harden your hearts,” he answers by adding: It was very necessary. “And,” that is, because, [Col. 0431D] those to whom it was first announced did not enter the true rest which the land of promise represented—and which they also did not attain—because of their unbelief.

Or this passage may be read with a different arrangement: “Therefore.” As though he said: Heavenly rest has been promised and signified in both that manner and the other. Therefore it remains for some to enter. And “because” means: because this alone is not sufficient to infer what he is about to infer, he adds another point, namely, “and those,” etc., so that from these two things a third necessarily follows. As though he said: Since some remain to enter, and since those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, therefore he determines a certain day, because it was necessary, saying in David, “Today,” after so long a time from when these things were said to the fathers and the children of Israel had entered the land of promise. Thus it is clear that this is another rest.

“As,” etc. These words do not change. “For if.” As though he said: Truly this is another rest than that into which Joshua led. For if it were that one, David would not speak of another; but he did speak. Therefore it is certain that another exists, into which Christ led, and which was signified by that rest in Palestine.

This is what he says: “For if,” etc. Or the connection is thus: Truly it remains for some to enter, as David determines. “For if Jesus”—that is, Joshua, who led them into the land of promise—“had given them,” that is, if he as leader had prepared and given them, [Col. 0432B] true rest, the Holy Spirit would never, at any time, afterwards—that is, in the present time—have spoken in David about another day, namely the time of grace, when it ought to be given. Or: he would never afterwards have spoken of another rest beyond the land of promise, saying on that day which he had called “Today”; but he did speak of another.

“Therefore there remains,” that is, there is reserved by the promising God, “a sabbath-rest for the people of God who are to come”: that is, the holiday and delight of full repose, signified by the Sabbath on which the Lord rested and which was observed under the Law.

> [Note: Col. 0431D. Augustine, *The City of God*.]
>
> Then we shall be perfectly at leisure, filled with greater grace and filled with God. We shall know perfectly that he is God. There we shall rest and see; we shall see and love; we shall love and praise. Behold what shall be in the end without end. For what other end is ours than to attain the kingdom that has no end?

And truly perfect is the rest which the Lord promises, which was also foreshadowed by the Sabbath rest. For the one who has entered into God’s rest—that is, the rest God promises and gives to his own—has himself rested from the works in which he labored here, as perfectly as God rested from his works.

Because this is so, and because it is true rest, let us therefore hasten to enter that rest through faith and good works, lest anyone—that is, lest any one of us—fall into the same example of unbelief: namely, into the same unbelief in which the fathers were, which is an example to you; hence it is worse if you do not beware. Or: lest he fall into the same example of unbelief, into a punishment such as they deserved through unbelief. He calls it an example so that our mind may be fixed there, lest we likewise fall away.

And to frighten them more, he adds: “For it is living.” As though he said: We ought to hasten into that rest and guard ourselves against the punishment of the unbelieving, because the word of God—that is, the Son of God, who came from royal thrones—is living. The unbelieving think him dead, but he is truly living; and thus you will live in him. The one who judged them is your judge, namely the Son of God; whoever obeys him shall not see death forever. He is effective, that is, powerful to do everything he wills, whether saving or condemning; and being powerful, he is also wise. “And,” that is, because, he is sharper—[Col. 0433A] that is, more discerning—than every two-edged sword: than every faculty that surveys things carnal and spiritual, that is, every carnal or spiritual intelligence.

And he is “reaching,” that is, arriving through complete consideration; the word of God reaches by unconquerable knowledge even to the division, that is, the separation and distinction, of soul—that is, sensibility—and spirit—that is, rationality. For the Son of God knows how sensibility is divided from reason, and how it is divided from itself: when it is more given over to lower things it is lower, and when recalled from them it is more worthy. Likewise, he sees how spirit is divided from itself: when it longs for God, thinking of the divine essence; or when, at a lower level, it considers heavenly things; or when, lower still upon earth, it considers how worldly matters ought rightly to be conducted. He also sees how spirit—that is, reason—is separated [Col. 0433B] from sensibility, when that which is lower in itself, namely in reason, surpasses what is different in the latter.

### Verses 12–16

“Of joints also and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. And no creature is invisible in his sight; but all things are naked and laid open before his eyes, to whom our word is addressed. Therefore, having a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the confession of our hope. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in every respect according to likeness, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach his throne of grace with confidence, that we may obtain mercy and find grace for timely help.”

[Col. 0433C] **“Of joints also.”** As though he said: And he himself reaches even to the discerning of joints and marrow. The “joint” is called the conjunction of sensuality itself and reason, which the Son of God sees—namely, how they cohere with one another in a person, or how this and that, that is, reason and sensuality, agree within their respective distinctions, when the higher distinction of sensuality agrees by consent with the three distinctions of reason, as has already been shown. Or the lower distinction of reason, oppressed and captive, sometimes agrees with the lower distinction of sensuality. “Marrow,” however, being interior, means whatever is more inward or subtle in soul or spirit; this too the Son of God sees. And I say universally, not merely in one respect: he is the discerner of the thoughts [Col. 0433D] and intentions of the heart; that is, he also distinguishes the thoughts of hearts, namely, those which think diverse things in diverse ways. He also distinguishes the intentions of those thoughts—namely, where each tends, whether toward good or toward evil. And, to say more, there is no creature, earthly or heavenly, invisible in his sight, that is, in the presence of his divinity.

Or thus, from the place which says, “and the word of God reaches unto the dividing of soul and spirit”: that is, unto the distinction between carnal and spiritual sins. For by the soul we live with beasts; by the spirit we understand with angels. Therefore carnal sins are understood by “soul,” that is, those committed by bodily act, such as lust; spiritual sins by “spirit,” that is, those of the mind, such as pride. The word of God discerns between carnal sins [Col. 0434A] and spiritual sins; that is, it discerns what each person does, and also with what disposition.

Hence he adds, “of joints also and marrow, and a discerner of thoughts,” etc. Or thus: by “soul” let carnal and evil thoughts be understood, and by “spirit,” spiritual and good thoughts. And the sense is: reaching unto the dividing of soul and spirit—that is, unto the distinction between carnal and spiritual thoughts—“of joints also.” And the order of the words is this: He is also the discerner of thoughts and intentions. This he states more plainly when he adds, namely, “of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.” For by “joints” he means the connections of thoughts, that is, thoughts joined to one another when one follows another. By “marrow” he means their subtle intentions. For [Col. 0434B] if one thought is joined to another, he knows which is according to God and which according to the world. He also knows toward what their intention turns.

“And there is no creature invisible in his sight.” This is unchanged. “But all things.” As though he said: I say that no creature is invisible; rather, all things, heavenly and earthly alike, are naked—that is, uncovered and revealed—and also open—that is, manifest—fully seen in every respect by his eyes, that is, by his vision, namely that of the Son of God. And as though someone should say, “What have all these things to do with you?” he adds: “To whom is our word,” namely, to the Son of God, to whom we must render account for your deeds, thoughts, and intentions.

**“Having therefore.”** Here he begins to treat of Christ the high priest, showing that he is sufficient for all things; how he is more worthy than the old priest, whom he changes, together with the law under him, by his better law; and how necessary he is to us for righteousness and salvation. As though he said: Because the word of God is such, therefore let us hold fast our confession—that is, faith in the heart together with confession by the mouth, so that faith may be in the mouth also. This faith and confession is the cause of our hope, that is, of the future blessedness which we hope for. And rightly ought we to hold it fast, because he himself is our high priest before God, who offered himself insofar as he is man. This is what he says: we, I say, having a great high priest, namely one above all high priests, who has penetrated—that is, fully entered, so that we may follow—[Col. 0434D] not, I say, the Holy of Holies of the Temple, but the heavens: namely Jesus, the Son of God. As though he said: he is also Savior and Son of God.

**“For we have not.”** As though he said: I say that we ought to hold fast, and do so because, although powerful, he is also merciful, having experienced our weakness. This is what he means in saying that we ought to hold fast: for we do not have a high priest who cannot—that is, who does not know how to—have compassion, that is, condescend, as a physician does to a sick person, upon our weaknesses, that is, our frailties. He says this lest they despair because of the things previously said concerning his exaltedness. For although he is so exalted, he can nevertheless have compassion. He says this lest, because he is exalted, he seem to reject them.

**“But tempted.”** As though he said: We do not have one unable to have compassion; rather, he was tempted [Col. 0435A] by the devil and by human beings, because he was mocked and crucified, and therefore can have compassion. He was tempted, I say, through every kind of temptation; and this “in likeness of sinful flesh,” that is, because he was still like human beings in this respect; or “for likeness,” that is, in order to give others an example of enduring similar things—yet being without sin. And therefore he can deliver. For from having been tempted he knows how to have compassion; but from being without sin he has power to deliver. It is impossible for a person who has not experienced affliction, and has not endured all things sensibly, to know the affliction of the afflicted. Christ, however, knows not only because he is God, according to which he knows all things, but because he is man and endured similar things.

**“Let us therefore approach.”** And because we have a high priest who [Col. 0435B] can have compassion upon us, let us therefore approach in faith, intention, and deed with confidence—that is, confidently—although we are sinners, because he is compassionate; not, I say, to the tribunal of judgment, but to his throne of grace, that is, to Christ, in whom grace reigns, so that through him we may obtain mercy, that is, remission of preceding sins, and henceforth find grace for timely help, that is, find grace by which we may be helped not to depart or fall back in this life. For now is the time of help; now is the time of gifts, when those who sin after baptism can through grace find repentance. But when the bridal chamber has been shut, when the king has entered to see those reclining at table, when those worthy of it have come to the bosom of the patriarch, then [Col. 0435C] it will be a time of despair for the wicked. But now, while the contest still continues and the palm hangs before us, one must not despair, but approach with confidence, that is, without doubt, so that timely help may be found through grace. For there is help which is not fitting.

## Chapter V

**Verses 1–7.**—For every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can have compassion on those who are ignorant and go astray, because he himself is surrounded by weakness; and therefore he must, just as for the people, so also for himself, offer for sins. Nor does anyone take the honor [Col. 0435D] to himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself in order to become high priest, but he who said to him: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” As he also says elsewhere: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, he was heard because of his reverence.

**“For every.”** [Chrysostom.] The Apostle now wishes to show that the New Testament is far better than the Old. He does this by arguing at greater length from what preceded and by laying down certain lines of reasoning beforehand. [Ambrose.] And because spiritual things do not lead the weak in the same way as bodily things, he begins [Col. 0436A] to deal with these matters, wishing to show that the New Testament is better than the Old. He sets forth certain features common to Christ and the priests of the old law, certain higher things belonging to Christ alone, and certain lower things suitable only to those priests, as though through him we may obtain all grace and mercy—something demonstrated from the lesser case.

“For every high priest,” according to the law, is taken “from among men,” that is, from the number of human beings, and raised to some higher dignity by which he can help others; he is appointed “for men,” that through him they may obtain mercy from the Lord. He is appointed, I say, “in matters pertaining to God,” namely in offering gifts, victims, and prayers that lead to God; that is, in order that he may offer to God gifts, namely firstfruits and the like, and animal sacrifices [Col. 0436B] for the forgiveness of sins.

**“Who can have compassion.”** As though he said: He is taken from among men, and he is such a one as can, with customary kindness, have compassion upon those who are ignorant, that is, who sin from ignorance, and those who go astray, that is, who sin knowingly. And rightly ought he to have compassion, because he himself, like them, is surrounded by the weakness of sin, [242], unlike Christ.
