Therefore he can help more than the legal priest, who, being surrounded by weakness and therefore weak like others, must offer for himself as well as for them. What necessity this is he explains when he adds: namely, for his own sins and those of others. As though he said: He must offer not only that the righteous may be preserved, but also that he himself and other sinners may be received. This does not apply to Christ. [Col. 0436C] For Christ offered only for his own members.

**“Nor does anyone.”** As though he said: In this respect again that high priest can be of use, and so also Christ: because no one takes the honor to himself, as though it were to be credited to himself, but it belongs to God who calls. But that person rightly becomes high priest who is called by God, that is, who is rightly chosen by God; as Aaron was chosen by the sign of the rod and the burning of his rivals, and shown to be pleasing to God. In these words he strikes at the ambitious, who are not called but thrust themselves forward.

So also Christ as man did not glorify himself by his own virtues, so as to take it for himself—that is, to attribute it to himself. He did not glorify himself, I say, so as to become high priest, as he himself says: “I do not glorify myself” (John 8); but he glorified him [Col. 0436D] in baptism and appointed him high priest. He also spoke to him elsewhere, saying in the Psalm: “You are my Son.” The same thing he was to say to him at baptism and at the Transfiguration. And he adds: “Today I have begotten you,” consubstantial with me, because he is the same as the Father in substance. For the Son was glorified by the Father when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). [Ambrose.] This glorification was foretold long before through the Prophet in the Psalm, where he says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2), through which Christ appears worthy; in that Psalm he is shown as king and priest.

**“As also.”** As though he said: Thus the Father spoke of Christ’s noble birth, just as in another place he speaks of his high priesthood, saying: You, so worthy, are a priest—that is, teaching, praying, and offering. And this is “forever,” not temporarily like Aaron; and “according to the order of Melchizedek,” that is, according to the dignity and rite of Melchizedek’s order, that is, priesthood. He was not temporal, Scripture setting forth neither the beginning nor the end of his life, as a figure of Christ, who has neither beginning nor end. And just as he offered in bread and wine, and once only, so Christ, under the appearance of bread and wine, gave his body and blood to his disciples.

[Note: [Col. 0437D] Augustine, *On Psalm 109*] Christ is a priest not according to that in which, born of the Father, he is God with God, coeternal with the begetter, but because of the flesh he assumed, because of the victim which he offered for us.

And as though someone asks, “What did the high priest do?” he adds: Behold, Christ, in the days of his flesh—that is, of his mortality—offered prayers and supplications [Col. 0437B] to him, namely God, who could save him who prayed from death, that is, raise him again. And because he did this in the time of mortality, what then will he do afterward? Much more. Christ offered these prayers and supplications when his passion was imminent, when he prayed at greater length; and he did it wholly for us, not for himself, because he prayed not from a necessary fear of death but for the sake of our salvation. He offered prayers, I say, “with a loud cry,” that is, with most effectual earnestness, as when he prayed at greater length, and “with tears.” This is not recorded in the Gospel, but it must nevertheless be believed to have occurred. And in offering these things he was heard, because he received in the resurrection and ascension what he sought. And this was “because of his reverence,” that is, as his devotion deserved, because he reverenced [Col. 0437C] God more than all others.

He says this in order that we may be certain of obtaining mercy through him. For from this it is clear that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is now at the Father’s right hand.

Or by Christ’s “prayers and supplications” he means Christ’s actions and life, every action of which was instruction for believers and prayer to God. For whatever Christ did, prayers and supplications were for human beings the shedding of blood; the cry was loud, in which he was heard because of the reverence of that same passion—his reverence being that he suffered without sin out of love alone. Thus he declares that Christ has care for us and displays the excellence of his love.

**Verses 8–14.**—And indeed, though he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and, being made perfect, he became for all who obey him the cause of eternal salvation, called by God high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. Concerning him we have much to say, and it is difficult to explain, because you have become weak in hearing. For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary beginnings of the sayings of God; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a little child. But solid food belongs to the perfect—those who, by habitual practice, have their senses trained to discern good and evil.

[Col. 0438A] **“And indeed.”** As though he said: He was heard, and deservedly so, because although he was the Son of God—one God with the Father in the nature of divinity—nevertheless, insofar as he was man, he learned, that is, experienced, obedience through the things that he suffered. Or, “he learned” means that he voluntarily undertook obedience in the things which he suffered, even unto death. As though he said: He not only offered prayers and supplications, but also obeyed the Father even unto death; and because he obeyed, he was heard, as he indicates by adding: “And therefore he was made perfect,” that is, brought to perfection when he was placed at the right hand of God. And he who was made perfect through the obedience of suffering became the sufficient cause of eternal salvation, that is, eternal glory, for all who obey him; for [Col. 0438B] his passion has such power that it suffices for the salvation of all.

This salvation can rightly come through him because he was called by God, who truly showed this and does not lie, high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. “Concerning whom,” that is, concerning this matter—namely, how he is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron—there is a great discourse, that is, one profound and subtle, and difficult to expound, that is, not suited to explanation for you. For discourse concerning the incarnate Son is difficult to explain.

Or, it is “explicable” because it contains many mysteries requiring exposition: concerning the dignity and eternity of his person; the change of rite and tribe; the excellence and newness of his sacrifice and covenant; the rejection of the law and sacrifices of that time; and many other matters. Concerning these things, as has been said, we have a great discourse, difficult to explain to you—that is, not suited to exposition for you. I do not say this because I cannot explain it, but because you have become weak, that is, feeble in understanding, for hearing—that is, for understanding profound mysteries. Or the connection may be stated thus: I already say that the discourse is great because you have become weak in hearing, that is, in understanding.

**“For.”** Here he inserts a rebuke concerning their weakness, that they may strive to understand the lofty matters concerning Christ. As though he said: You have indeed become weak. For although by this time you ought to be teachers of others, because Christ was proclaimed to you earlier, and because from ancient times you have been trained in the Law and the Prophets, [Col. 0438D] you again need to be taught, from the beginning of your instruction, like children to whom the first letters are given for reading, what are the elementary beginnings of the sayings of God. The beginning of the sayings of God is simple teaching, that is, the creed; its elements are the matters it contains, such as the nativity and passion.

“And you have become,” that is, reduced to such a condition that you need milk, by the likeness of infants, that is, humble speech, and not solid food, which consumes the heart, that is, teaching concerning the hidden things of God.

**“For everyone.”** As though he said: Therefore you have no need of solid food, because you are partakers of milk, that is, simple teaching. For everyone who partakes of milk—which you are—is unskilled in the word of righteousness, that is, in that word suitable to the righteous and perfect. And this is because he is a little child, just as you are tender in faith. The comparison is fitting. For as a little child does not distinguish foods and perishes by taking what is harmful, so the unlearned person, who cannot grasp even the meaning of lesser things, much less of greater—one who does not understand, “The Word became flesh,” how will he understand, “In the beginning was the Word?” For minds still childish and needing to be fed with milk cannot grasp such things. Every discourse on this matter, which seeks not only belief but also understanding and knowledge of what is said, is burdensome; it overwhelms them more easily than [Col. 0439B] it nourishes them.

From this it follows that spiritual persons do not wholly keep these things silent from carnal persons, because of the Catholic faith, which must be preached to all. Yet they should not present them in such a way as to make the truth in discourse more readily wearisome to one incapable of being led to understanding than to enable that person to perceive the truth through discourse.

**“But solid food belongs to the perfect.”** [Note: [Col. 0439D] Augustine, *On John*] As though he said: A little child partakes of milk, but solid food belongs to those perfect in understanding and conduct. Elsewhere he says of this: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). He explains whom he means here by “perfect,” adding: those who have senses, that is, understandings, not merely naturally acute but also trained through habitual practice—that is, because through study and reading of the Scriptures they are accustomed and trained [Col. 0439C] to distinguish good and evil from one another; or good from lesser good, and evil from lesser evil.

Here he shows what solid food is: namely, separating good from evil. This belongs to the perfect, who have trained senses. But persons of weak and untrained mind, unable to do this, must be held by a kind of milk of faith; otherwise, because they do not see invisible things and do not yet understand intelligible things, they are easily led astray by the promise of knowledge into empty and sacrilegious fables. Thus they think of good and evil only in bodily images; they suppose God himself to be some bodily thing; and they cannot help regarding evil as a substance—whereas it is rather a certain defect of mutable substances from the immutable substance, which made those substances out of nothing: that immutable and highest substance which is God. Whoever not only believes this but also understands, apprehends, and knows it with the faculties of the mind exercised upon outward things [Col. 0439D] [243] need no longer fear being deceived by those who, by thinking evil a substance not made by God, make God himself a mutable substance, as the Manichaeans do, or by whatever other plagues deceive in this manner.

## Chapter VI

**Verses 1–3.**—Therefore, leaving the discourse of the beginning of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection, not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the teaching of baptisms, [Col. 0440A] and also of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if indeed God permits.

**“Therefore.”** [Chrysostom.] After sternly rebuking and blaming them because they wished always to learn the same things, he again speaks gently, numbering himself among them and exhorting them to perfection. Therefore, because solid food belongs to the perfect, let us now leave—or release, that is, set aside, since we are already something, although not yet perfect—the discourse of Christ’s beginning, that is, that by which Christ begins to be in us: the teaching concerning the beginning of faith by which untrained persons are to be instructed, such as the creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Let us be carried onward, I by teaching and you by hearing. I say, “Let us be carried,” including myself among you, because I consider your being carried forward as my own carrying forward with you. Let us be carried, I say, to the perfection of Christ, in understanding and good works.

**“Not again laying,”** etc. As though he said: Let us be carried to perfection while laying a foundation. What he previously called the discourse of the beginning he here calls a foundation, because it is first set before those coming to the Christian religion, and what belongs to perfection is built upon it. He divides this foundation into six things, which are the beginning: repentance, faith, baptism, instruction, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment.

As though he said: You, I say, laying the foundation of repentance—that is, laying repentance as a foundation stone—from dead works, that is, from sins; or from the fact that by sinning they rendered their previous good works void. For he calls sins dead works because they kill souls. Hence the Law forbade touching a dead body. For the person who commits sin touches a dead body; or, by pursuing evil, he makes formerly good works dead. Repentance from these is a foundation upon which nothing good is built.

[Note: [Col. 0440D] Augustine, *On Faith and Works*] But what is it to repent of dead works except to repent of things which must be put to death so that we may live?

And laying the foundation of faith—which is toward God, so that they may have all parts of faith and not suppose righteousness to come from elsewhere. Those who seek righteousness in the Law have acted against this. And also the foundation of the teaching of baptisms. He speaks in the plural because there is baptism in water, in repentance, and in blood; for a person is cleansed from sins through repentance or the shedding of blood, just as through the washing of baptism. Yet there is said to be one baptism, because it has one form and cannot be repeated: for the operation of the three persons is one.

Therefore baptism is not said to take place in repentance or blood because the sacrament of baptism is celebrated except in water when the word is added; rather, because the shedding of blood for the name of Christ supplies the place of baptism, as do faith and repentance, but only where necessity, not contempt for religion, excludes the sacrament of baptism. Therefore this saying must be understood thus: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0441A] (John 3); that is, whoever has not been born again by that regeneration by which those are born again who are born of water and the Holy Spirit shall not be saved. But people are born again in diverse ways: some through repentance, some through the shedding of blood, some through baptism. Therefore he said “baptisms” in the plural.

Also, the foundation of laying on of hands: for unless someone believes that through the laying on of hands the Holy Spirit is given for remission and strengthening, he is not founded. And also the foundation of the resurrection of the dead: for unless someone believes that Christ’s resurrection brings about the resurrection of the dead, he has nothing on which to build. And the foundation of eternal judgment, because whatever it determines there will endure forever. Whoever does not believe that judgment has no foundation.

Those whom the Apostle rebuked above did not believe these things completely. For if they knew that all things are forgiven in baptism and that the Holy Spirit is given through laying on of hands, the Law would be superfluous, and they would seek nothing besides Christ, if they knew that through him the dead would rise, be made alive, and be judged. Observe that these six are rightly called a foundation. For just as one introduced to literary instruction must first hear the elements, so a Christian must know these things completely and doubt nothing concerning them, without which life cannot be whole. Therefore whoever converts people to the faith first makes them repent, believe in God, be baptized for the remission of sins, be confirmed through the laying on [Col. 0441C] of hands, and await the resurrection and the day of judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Augustine, *On Faith and Works*] All these things, then, belong to the beginnings of neophytes. Unless all these things have gone beforehand in the foundation, no one can work well. And because all these things are necessary to them, he says, “Let us be carried to perfection.”

“Laying,” I say, “not again,” that is, not as formerly—that is, not as negligently as before, so that, as they fell before, they should fall again. Or thus: Let us be carried to perfection, “not again”—that is, no longer, except now—laying the foundation of repentance, etc.; that is, let us now lay it in such a way that there will be no need to lay it any more. Behold, in these persons he rebukes not only their life but also something else, as people shaken and needing to establish a foundation. The remaining matters are unchanged.

**“And this.”** As though he said: Let us, I say, be carried to perfection, and let us do this—that is, let us be carried to perfection—if indeed God permits, that is, if he grants time for repentance in this life. But lest anyone suppose that a second or third baptism can take place after sin, and that those who have fallen after receiving the sacraments can be renewed through baptism, he adds:

**Verses 4–15.**—For it is impossible to renew again unto repentance those who were once enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and [Col. 0442A] exposing him to public disgrace. For land which drinks the rain frequently coming upon it and produces vegetation useful to those by whom it is cultivated receives a blessing from God; but if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is in burning. But, beloved, although we speak thus, we are confident concerning you of better things, things nearer to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to forget your work and the love which you showed in his name, in that you have ministered to the saints and do minister. But we desire each of you to show the same diligence for the full assurance of hope unto the end, that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience will inherit the promises. For when God made promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, [Col. 0442B] he swore by himself, saying: “Surely I will bless you with blessing and multiply you with multiplication.” And thus, patiently enduring, he obtained the promise.

Impossible. As if he said: I say, “Let us be carried on to perfection,” but let no one suppose that, after falling into sin, one can be renewed a second or third time by baptism. For it is impossible—not merely difficult, lest anyone despair on this account, but impossible, I say—for those who have once been enlightened through faith and baptism and through the Holy Spirit, and who through faith itself have tasted—that is, have received something like a sweet and pleasant taste—the heavenly gift, namely the remission of sins in baptism; and who have also become partakers [Col. 0442C] of the Holy Spirit, possessing kinds of tongues and other gifts; and have tasted the good word of God, that is, Christ’s divinity, or likewise the evangelical teaching which you have tasted; or, likewise, those who have become partakers of the Holy Spirit have tasted the powers of the world to come, that is, they have by hope tasted future impassibility and immortality. And after all these things they have fallen away, that is, have fallen by sinning grievously—for those, I say, who have had even these good things, much less those wholly evil ones—it is impossible, once righteousness has been recovered, to be renewed through baptism, namely to be moved to repentance.

[Remigius] Here the Apostle denies the repetition of baptism, but does not exclude repentance. The meaning is: it is impossible for those who, having received this once, are moved to repentance [Col. 0442D] to be renewed again, that is, baptized—that is, for them to be baptized after repentance. For to be renewed is to be made new; but to make new belongs to the washing. Hence: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102). This takes place in baptism, whose power rests upon Christ’s cross. Hence he adds: “Crucifying again.” As if he said: I mean those who, if they are rebaptized, are crucifying the Son of God again and holding him up to public shame, that is, to mockery. And this is “for themselves,” that is, so far as they are concerned.

[Jerome] They do not actually crucify Christ, but they resemble his mockers and crucifiers, because the one death of Christ consecrated one baptism. This is sufficient against all sins, even subsequent ones, if repentance is performed concerning them, just as that death is sufficient to take away all sins. But one who repeats baptism, as though that one death and the one baptism flowing from it were insufficient, repeats also the death, so that from that repeated death there may come a repeated remission, which is impossible. For just as it is impossible to crucify Christ a second time, so it is impossible to die to sins a second time through baptism. By baptism we have been made conformed to the likeness of his death, and have been buried with him through baptism. Therefore, because in baptism we are conformed to his death and burial, one who supposes that he is baptized a second time crucifies Christ a second time, so far as he is concerned; and this is to hold him up to public shame. For as he died once in the flesh, so we die once to sins in baptism, not a second or third time. Baptism is nothing [Col. 0443A] other than the death and resurrection of the baptized person.

Or thus: “Crucifying again.” This refers to what he said before, “they have fallen away.” As if he said: It is impossible for those who have fallen grievously after baptism to be rebaptized. Therefore they ought to guard themselves lest they fall away; and, lying in sins, they crucify again and hold up to public shame the Son of God, whose grace is despised. And this is “for themselves,” that is, so far as they are concerned. For within themselves they crucify the Son of God and treat him contemptuously, when, despising his grace, they lie in sins. Here is shown the reason why they should not, having abandoned their first faith, fall into sin. They can no longer be rebaptized for the remission of sins; and moreover they despise and publicly shame the Son of God.

For the earth. As if he said: It is impossible for anyone to be rebaptized after falling, because he can drink the rain—that is, Christ’s teaching—by which he may bear fruit only through repentance. This is what he says: “For the earth,” etc.

This passage can also be understood differently: that those who have sinned cannot be renewed through repentance after this life. As if he said: I say that we shall be carried on to perfection, if God gives us time to repent in this life. And I rightly said this; for in the other life it is impossible to be renewed through repentance. This is what he says: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened,” and who have had the good things that follow, and who after all these things have fallen away, to be renewed again—namely after this life—unto, that is, [Col. 0443D] through repentance. For although it is possible here, it is not there. Therefore it is impossible for them to be renewed in the other life through repentance, because it is impossible for them again to be crucifying the Son of God for themselves and holding him up to public shame: that is, because they cannot bring it about that Christ’s crucifixion should avail them again, if they crucified their flesh with its vices and desires—which is possible here, not there. Nor can they hold Christ up for display so as to imitate him in newness of life.

For the earth. As if he said: Truly, in the other life renewal is impossible, because it is only here that it drinks the rain. “For the earth.” Or the connection may be made thus. He said above, “Let us be carried on to perfection,” adding, “And this we shall do”; now he adds that it is right to do this, because the earth—that is, the mind of hearers, namely the soul making progress—drinking, after the likeness of dry earth, [Col. 0444A] rain, that is, holy teaching, the dew of heaven, while the heavens—that is, preachers of the word of truth—rain upon the thirsty earth. The rain, I say, comes from God upon it frequently; for if it is rare, it is insufficient, while if continual, it becomes cheapened. And, watered by rain, it produces vegetation, namely faith and good works, suitable—that is, fitting—not only for those who produce it, but also for those by whom it is cultivated, namely the preachers of those who shall be glorified. These are cultivators of the earth because, with the spiritual ploughshare, they tear up the thickets of sin, and with the sickle of God’s word cut away what is harmful.

Or, “those by whom it is cultivated” means those same persons who cultivate themselves by good works, imitating their elders, according to the saying: “And they produced the fruit of their increase” (Ps. 106), because they imitate their fathers, who begot them in faith. The earth, I say, drinking the rain and producing vegetation, receives a blessing from God: here, an increase of virtues; and in the future, a reward. Otherwise, unless it received blessing from God, it would not produce joyful fruit. Note that by these words the Apostle indicates that those to whom he writes had often drunk, through the Law and the Prophets, the word of heavenly teaching, and yet were not thereby prompt to bring forth the shoots of faith.

But producing. As if he said: Good earth receives blessing. But earth producing openly, so that they may be seen, thorns—that is, sins which prick—and briars—that is, graver sins which prick more sharply; that is, a mind fruitful for evils through its own vice—is rejected by God and near to a curse, that is, damnation. It has not yet fallen under the curse, but is [Col. 0444C] near to it, and it is still possible to return. Its consummation—that is, its end—if it perseveres, is in the burning of eternal judgment or fire.

But we are confident. As if he said: I have rebuked and frightened you harshly; but, beloved, we are confident concerning you of better things than burning, and things nearer to salvation than thorns and briars, though we speak thus harshly, frightening and rebuking. It is as though we do not say these things because we think you are such persons—namely full of thorns—but because we fear that you may be such. I terrify you with words, lest you suffer pain in the reality. Note his words, “we are confident concerning you.” Since he has nothing in the present for which to praise them, he raises them by the hope of future things; through past things he entices and revives their minds toward that hope, strengthens them [Col. 0444D] by recalling former things to their memory, and causes them not to suppose that God has forgotten the good things they did.

Hence he adds: “For God is not unjust.” As if he said: Therefore we are confident concerning you, because formerly you performed many good works, for which, if you repent of evils, God will do good to you. For just as former good things were dead and rendered void by subsequent evils, so those same good things will revive through repentance and further good things following evils. This is what he says: “For God is not unjust so as to forget your good work and the love which you showed,” namely that love from which you performed those good works. And you did all these things “in his name,” that is, for God’s honor.

[Chrysostom] And I rightly spoke of “work,” because you formerly ministered, and still minister, to the saints. This is the work of which I have given great testimony. For he commends three good things in them: that they made all they possessed common to the saints—this is the work; that they did so from love, which gives form to actions—this is eagerness; and that they did so for God’s glory—this is a right and pure intention. Behold the threefold good.

“But we desire.” As if he said: I praise you for past things; but concerning the future I desire good for you. This is what is meant: we desire each one of you to show—that is, to show frequently—until the end of your life the same diligence in ministering to the saints. And this is for the fulfillment of hope, that is, so that what you now hope for may be fulfilled in you in the future. He showed much love toward them and displayed the same concern for each individual: he has equal care for great and small alike, and loves all. Thus we desire you to show [Col. 0445B] diligence, so that you may not become sluggish in this diligence, but imitators of those, namely the saints, who inherit—not by descent, but through faith and patience, that is, by the merit of faith and patience—the promises, that is, possess as an inheritance the often-promised blessedness.

And as if someone should ask, “Have promises been made?” he answers, saying both that they have been made and what they are: “For when God made promise to Abraham,” etc. He knew that the Jews took pleasure in having the promises to the fathers recalled. Therefore, by these praises he now exalts those whom above he had frightened by the example of the hardened. Above all he chose Abraham, whose children they are if they believe.

[Jerome] As if he said: And truly a promise was made. For God, promising Abraham, swore by himself [Col. 0445C] because he had no one greater than himself by whom he might swear. He swore, I say, declaring: “O Abraham, unless I bless you with increase of virtues and multiply you with greatness of glory in future blessedness…” Here is aposiopesis, an unfinished expression. As if he said: If I do not do this, let no one believe me in anything. Or distinguish it thus: “Blessing I will bless you,” namely continually in those who are the stars; “and multiplying I will multiply you,” without end, in those who are the sand. And so Abraham, assured and enduring patiently—that is, waiting a long time patiently amid many adversities—at last obtained the promise, that is, the often-promised blessing, namely eternal blessedness. Here, then, three things are stated: a promise was made to Abraham; it was confirmed by an oath [Col. 0445D]; and it was already fulfilled in Abraham.

## Verses 16–20

> For men swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is the end of every controversy among them for confirmation. Wherein God, willing more abundantly to show unto the heirs of the promise the immutability of his counsel, interposed an oath, that by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us might have most strong consolation; which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, safe and firm, and entering even within the veil, where Jesus, the forerunner, has entered for us, made a high priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.

[Col. 0446A] For men. As if he said: God swore because men swear; by swearing he condescends to human weakness. And therefore he swore by himself, since he had no greater, because men swear by one greater than themselves. This is what he says: The Lord swore by himself because men swear by those greater than themselves, that is, by God, who alone is true of himself. And the end of every controversy, that is, dispute, among them is an oath, effective for confirming the other party. But if a man, who is liable to lie, is believed on oath, how much more should God be believed, who cannot lie?

“Wherein,” that is, on account of this—namely, because such is the practice among men—God, wishing more abundantly to show to the heirs of his promise, that is, those who were to receive what was promised, the immutability of his counsel [Col. 0446B] concerning the elect to be saved by his grace—rightly called God’s counsel, because scarcely anyone knows that human beings are saved through faith in Christ—interposed an oath between the promise and its fulfillment, condescending to the custom of men in order to make them certain.

Notice that he says “more abundantly.” For by the promise he showed abundantly the immutability of his counsel; more abundantly he interposed an oath. He interposed the oath, I say, so that by two immutable things, namely promise and oath, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have in the storms of temptations most strong consolation: namely, that in every adversity it may make us strong, willing to suffer for a time in order to reign eternally. We who, amid adversities, flee for refuge in order to hold fast the hope, not to cast it away because of adversities.

[Ambrose] He flees to hope who, through the hope of blessedness, despises tribulations. I mean the hope already set before us in Abraham and fulfilled; or, more properly, the hope offered to all. This hope we have as an anchor of the soul. For as an anchor holds a ship, so hope holds the soul, lest it be submerged in the sea of this world by consenting to iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] Augustine, on Psalm 102.] Therefore, if you see yourself tossed by waves in this sea, do not break away from the anchor before you enter the harbor. A ship is tossed by waves while at anchor, but it is not cast far from land; nor will it be tossed forever, though it is tossed for a time. Hope, therefore, is the anchor of the soul. Hence he says: “Which we have as an anchor of the soul, safe,” [Col. 0446D] which is not destroyed by the force of tribulations, “and firm,” which does not even waver, “and entering,” that is, causing us to enter, because it introduces us into the reality, even into the inner things of the veil: that is, the inward and veiled blessedness which no one sees as it is in this life. Into these inner things Jesus the forerunner entered, for the purpose of bringing us in; and thus it is clear that we can follow. For this purpose he ran ahead, that we might follow. He is called a runner who is blessed, because no fault hindered him, according to: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18). And elsewhere: “He did not stand in the way of sinners” (Ps. 1). He is a forerunner because he ran before us and for us.

[Col. 0447A] He, I say, was made high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, not according to the order of Aaron. Therefore Christians, whose high priest he is, ought to be superior to Jews in the measure of the difference between Christ and Aaron, and to have a better sacrifice: namely rational service, which leads to heaven—not sheep or oxen, not blood and fat, which are offered according to the flesh, but instead the rational service which must be introduced. What, then, is rational service? That which is offered through soul and spirit, such as the virtues. For God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth (John 4). Behold how God is pleased by sacrifices; therefore let us offer these. Those are the possessions of the wealthy; these are virtues. Those are external; these internal. Anyone may perform those; few can perform these. For by as much as a human being is better than cattle, so much better is this sacrifice than those. Here you offer your own soul in sacrifice; there cattle were offered.

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–3

> For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him—to whom Abraham also divided tithes of all things—first indeed being interpreted king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, which is king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like unto the Son of God, abides a priest continually.

For this Melchizedek, etc. After interposing much concerning their correction, he now begins to pursue that great discourse concerning the sacrifice of Christ [Col. 0447C] which he touched upon above, showing how Jesus is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, as far as the words “made like unto the Son.” As if he said: I prove that Christ is priest according to the order of Melchizedek. For this Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of the most high God, namely one appointed not through man but through God; he met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings.

As is read in Genesis, four kings fought against five and conquered them. Lot lived under the five and was captured by the four. When Abraham heard this, he pursued them with three hundred and eighteen household servants and struck them; he brought back Lot and all the substance which they had taken. Therefore Melchizedek met this Abraham [Col. 0447D] as he returned and blessed him—Abraham. And to him, Melchizedek, Abraham divided tithes of all things; I do not say “gave,” but “divided,” because he presented the choicest portions.

[Jerome] The Hebrews relate that this Melchizedek was Shem, son of Noah; that when Abraham was born he was three hundred and ninety years old; that he came to meet Abraham as his grandson; that he brought out bread for the refreshment of Abraham and his companions; and that, as priest of God, he received tithes. Most say that Salem was Jerusalem, but it was a town in the region of Shechem, which is still today called Salem, where, from the size of its ruins, the palace of Melchizedek is pointed out. Hence in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salem” (John 3).

And he was first called Melchizedek, which is interpreted “king of righteousness.” For *Melchos*, or *Melchi*, means king; *Sedech*, righteous or righteousness; hence Melchizedek, that is, king of righteousness. Then he was called king of Salem, which is king of peace; for Salem is interpreted “peace.” He, I say, was without father and without mother—not because he had none, but because Scripture, in its providence, does not mention them as a figure of Christ; without genealogy, that is, not having offspring; neither having a beginning of days, which Scripture states, nor an end of life, because Scripture is silent concerning these things as a figure of Christ.

[Chrysostom] Therefore he is said not to have these things because it is not written that he had them. In all these things set forth above, however, he was made like the Son of God. And how? Let us consider.

[Remigius] Melchizedek was called Melchizedek; Melchizedek means king of righteousness. This is Christ, who governs his children by righteousness amid the storms of the world. Likewise he is king of Salem, that is, of peace: Christ is this, because those whom he governs here in righteousness, he does not cease to govern in eternal peace. He is likewise priest of the most high God, who offered himself upon the altar of the cross. He also met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings: that is, he meets and comes to each believer, giving grace. After the slaughter of the four principal vices, opposed by four virtues, which enter and rule through the five senses—just as four kings held Lot captive after conquering the five—he blesses him, namely the believer, by giving increase of faith and good work. He also gives bread and wine, that is, his body and blood; fed by these, believers are cleansed from past sins and strengthened for the future. To him Abraham, that is, the believer, gives tithes of all things, that is, attributes all his perfection to him.

[Col. 0448C] Again, carefully observe how what follows applies to Christ.

[Chrysostom] First, indeed, he was called Melchizedek, that is, king of righteousness. This is truly Christ, who makes and rules the righteous. Then, king of Salem, that is, king of peace. This too is truly Christ, who reconciled things in heaven and things on earth. What human being is king of righteousness and peace except Christ? No one. Again, note that he is first called king of righteousness and afterwards king of peace, because Christ first governs his people here in righteousness; afterwards, in the future, he will govern them in eternal peace. He is also without father according to the flesh, and without mother according to divinity; and without genealogy, because he had no children of the flesh; having neither beginning nor end. In all these things there is a likeness between this one and that one.

[Ambrose] [Col. 0448D] And although all the patriarchs and prophets were figures of Christ, Melchizedek was more especially so, because he was not of the Jewish race, as some say. He came beforehand as a type of Christ’s priesthood, he who is called priest according to the order of Melchizedek in many ways: because he alone was both king and priest; because he exercised priesthood before circumcision, so that the Gentiles might not receive priesthood from the Jews, but the Jews from the Gentiles; and because he was not anointed with visible oil, as Moses instituted, but with the oil of gladness and purity of faith. Nor did he sacrifice animals, but dedicated Christ’s priesthood with bread and wine.

He was not truly without father and mother, whereas Christ, according to his two natures, had both Father and mother; but because in Genesis he is introduced as suddenly coming to meet Abraham, and neither before nor after is his genealogy or name found. By this example the Apostle affirms that Aaron’s priesthood had both beginning and end, but that the priesthood of the Church is eternal, both in the past and in the future: because no other preceded before Melchizedek, nor will another succeed after Christ; or, after Christ, no other succeeded formerly and none will succeed in the future. In all things he was made like the Son of God; he remains priest forever, or continually, because Scripture is silent as to another succeeding him. Or, mystically, he speaks through him of Christ’s priesthood. Therefore he remains a priest forever, not in himself but in Christ: that is, his priesthood endures eternally in Christ and in the Church, because another does not succeed him as in the Levitical priesthood.

### Verses 4–10

> Now consider how great this man was, unto whom even Abraham the patriarch gave tithes of the chief spoils. And indeed they of the sons of Levi who receive the priesthood have a commandment to take tithes of the people according to the law, that is, of their brethren, though they also came out of the loins of Abraham. But he whose descent is not counted among them took tithes of Abraham, and blessed him who had the promises. And without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater. And here men that die receive tithes; but there he receives them of whom it is testified that he lives. And, so to speak, Levi also, who receives tithes, was tithed through Abraham. For he was still in the loins of his father when Melchizedek met him.

Now consider. Having recalled certain ways in which Melchizedek is made like the Son of God, that is, Christ, he still dwells upon commending the dignity and excellence of Melchizedek and his priesthood, preferring him to Abraham himself, father of all, and to all Levites. As if he said: Such was Melchizedek. Now consider also from his deeds how great this man was, namely Melchizedek, to whom Abraham the patriarch—that is, prince of our fathers—gave tithes [Col. 0449C] as the lesser to the greater. And he gave them from his chief spoils; this is why it was said above that he “divided.”

[Ambrose] Here Melchizedek is preferred to Abraham, whom the Jews exalt, in whom they glory, and whom the Jews wished to set before Christ, saying: “Are you greater than our father Abraham?” etc. (John 8). And here he compares him with the Levites. As if he said: Consider how great he is in this respect also. For some, indeed, of the sons of Levi receiving the priesthood—for otherwise they would not dare take them—have a commandment in the Law to receive tithes. I do not say simply that they receive tithes; they have a commandment, without whose authority they would never presume to receive tithes—not from some great man or stranger, but from the humble people joined to them by kinship, that is, from their brethren, in whom it is more fitting to place confidence. They receive them, I say, not by unrestricted permission but according to the Law, that is, only as the Law commanded.

But Melchizedek received from the patriarch according to no law, though he was a foreigner, and was in this respect more worthy. “Though,” as if he said: In receiving tithes they are superior, though they also came forth from Abraham’s loins, that is, though they are equal in descent.

[Chrysostom] So great, indeed, is the excellence of priesthood that even those alike in race and having the same ancestor are far more worthy than their brothers. Therefore Abraham the patriarch would not have given tithes to an uncircumcised foreigner unless he were superior. In him the Levitical priests would not have paid tithes, because they were tithed in him.

“But he whose descent…” As if he said: The sons of Levi receive from their brethren, but Melchizedek, whose descent is not counted among them—that is, among the Jews—as if he were a foreigner, without commandment and on his own authority received tithes as superior from Abraham the patriarch, and blessed this very great man, Abraham, who had—that is, to whom had been made—the promises that the nations should be blessed in his seed. As if he said: He blessed him even at the time of his greater dignity. He blessed him, I say, without any contradiction: the lesser is blessed by the greater. Therefore the type of Christ is better than the one having the promises, because what is blessed by another appears lesser according to the common judgment of all and without any contradiction. Even if there is dispute concerning the receiving of tithes—whether the sons of Levi are greater because they receive from their brethren—this point cannot be disputed.

“And here.” As if he said: Consider the dignity in Melchizedek in this respect also. Here indeed, that is, in the Levitical priesthood, mortal human beings receive tithes. But there, where Melchizedek is under discussion, Scripture bears witness—[Col. 0450C] or bears the same witness in many places—that he lives, because it says nothing of his death, as a figure of Christ. For he bore the type of our high priest, whose excellence of power is displayed through Melchizedek’s likeness. Through Melchizedek, in whom the figure of a future reality came beforehand, Christ’s priesthood is distinguished from Levi’s priesthood; and as a figure of Christ it is said that Melchizedek lives.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Augustine, *On John*.] Hence Christ is called a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109), he who offered himself not from any necessity but by the will of his own power.

“And, so to speak.”

[Ambrose] As if he said: Melchizedek is greater than Levi in this respect also, because Levi—that is, the Levitical order—which received tithes from brethren, was tithed, that is, gave tithes [Col. 0450D] to Melchizedek. And this was through Abraham, as through a material cause, so that it may be said by a certain trope, that is, figure of speech; for Levi did not properly give tithes in his own person—he, the circumcised priest, to an uncircumcised man.

“For he was still…” As if he said: I have shown that he was blessed through Abraham. For when Abraham gave tithes, Levi was still in the loins of his father, namely Abraham, when Melchizedek met him—that is, met Levi’s father, Abraham—and therefore Levi was tithed in him. Just as, when Adam sinned, those who were in his loins were tithed; but this does not follow in Christ, although he was in the loins of Adam and Abraham, because he did not descend thence according to the concupiscence of the flesh.

Therefore, although Levi and Christ were in Abraham’s loins according to the flesh when Levi was tithed, they were not tithed together, because Christ was not there in the same manner as Levi was there. Levi was there according to seminal reason, by which he was to come through intercourse into his mother. According to this reason Christ’s body was not there, although Mary’s flesh was there in that respect. Levi was to come from there according to fleshly concupiscence; Christ, however, was to come from there according to bodily substance. For in seed there are both visible bodily substance and invisible reason; both came down from Abraham, or even from Adam himself, to Mary’s body, because that body also was conceived and arose in that manner. But Christ took the visible substance of flesh from the flesh of the Virgin. The principle of his conception, however, came not from male seed but in a wholly different manner, from above.

Therefore, according to what he received from his mother, he too was in Abraham’s loins. He, then, was tithed in Abraham who was in his loins in the same way as Abraham himself had been in his father’s loins: that is, one born from Father Abraham as Abraham was born from his own father through the law in the members resisting the law of the mind and through invisible concupiscence. Although the chaste and good laws of marriage do not permit it to prevail except insofar as they can provide for the continuation of the race. But he was not tithed there whose flesh drew thence not the heat of the wound but the material of the remedy. For since this very tithing belonged to prefiguring the remedy, that in Abraham’s [Col. 0451C] flesh was tithed which was being healed, not that by which it was healed. The same flesh of Abraham, or of the first man himself, possessed together both the wound of transgression and the medicine for the wound. The wound of transgression was the law in the members resisting the law of the mind, which is, as it were, transmitted by seminal reason through all flesh propagated from that source. But the medicine for the wound was that he was assumed from the Virgin from that source, without a work of concupiscence, in bodily matter alone, by the divine manner of conception and formation.

### Verses 11–17

> If therefore perfection were by the Levitical priesthood—for under it the people received the law—what further need was there that another priest should arise after the order of Melchizedek, and not be called after the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also take place. For he of whom these things are spoken is of another tribe, of which no one attended the altar. For it is evident that our Lord sprang from Judah, of which tribe Moses spoke nothing concerning priests. And it is yet more evident: if, after the likeness of Melchizedek, another priest arises, who was made not according to the law of a fleshly commandment, but according to the power of an indissoluble life. For he testifies: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

So, etc. Up to this point he has preferred Christ’s priesthood, which is according to the order of Melchizedek, to the Levitical priesthood. Now he adds [Col. 0452A] that Christ’s priesthood abolishes the Levitical priesthood; and once that is abolished, the Law too must necessarily be abolished, because it was given under that priesthood. As though he said: Since Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, and this priesthood takes precedence over the Levitical one, then, O Jews, answer this if you can: if completion—that is, perfection—came through the Levitical priesthood, because Aaron was of Levi, why was it still necessary, after it had brought completion, for another priest to arise, as David the prophet said—another in rite and tribe, one who would free from sin, which those priests did not do—according to the order of Melchizedek? This would not have been said if that priesthood had been better. And why does he add, “and not according to the order of Aaron,” in any respect? So that you may not suppose that both are to be retained.

As though he said: [Col. 0452B] If the Levitical priesthood brought completion, another would arise according to the order of Melchizedek in vain. But another does arise, as is indicated there: “For when the priesthood is transferred.” He subsequently proves that another arises both by tribe and by rite: by tribe in the words, “For he of whom these things are spoken”; by rite in the words, “And this is yet more evident.” Thus it is clear that another priest arises; therefore the former priesthood did not bring completion.

Attend to the wording, “when transferred.” As though he said: If the Levitical priesthood brought completion, another priest would arise in vain. But another arises; for the priesthood is transferred. And when the priesthood is transferred, a transfer of the Law must also take place. For since both were given together by the same giver and under the same promise, what is said of one must necessarily be understood of the other. Rightly, therefore, when the priesthood is transferred, the Law is transferred. [Col. 0452C] For the people received the Law under that priesthood, because the Law is in the priest’s hand, and through him the Law—which is said to bring completion—is fulfilled.

Or it may be read thus: “If therefore.” [Chrysostom.] Concerning Melchizedek, he showed how much greater he was than Abraham, and proclaimed a great difference. [Ambrose.] Here he now begins to set forth the differences between the Old and the New Testament: the former is imperfect, while the latter is perfect. He proceeds by the direct route, showing that the priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek is better than the Levitical priesthood.

[Chrysostom.] As though he said: Since Christ is according to the order of Melchizedek, answer then, O Jew: if perfection is through the Levitical priesthood—which indeed it ought to be—why was it still necessary for another to arise according to the order of Melchizedek and not according to the order of Aaron? For the people received the Law under [Col. 0452D] that priesthood. [Ambrose.] As though he said: It was not necessary.

“For when transferred.” As though he said: I say that the people received the Law under the priesthood. [Chrysostom.] If, then, there is a transfer of the priesthood, necessarily there is a transfer of the Law, for a priest cannot exist without a covenant, Law, and commandments. Therefore one must pass from the Law to the Gospel. This is what he says: “For when the priesthood is transferred.” As though he said: I say that the Law was given under the priesthood because I thereby note that, when the priesthood is transferred—that is, abolished—the Law too must be transferred, that is, abolished; for it existed only under that priesthood.

[Jerome.] This transfer of the priesthood was prefigured in Samuel, who, [Col. 0453A] although he was not of the Levitical tribe but of the tribe of Ephraim, was chosen priest by the Lord after the rejection of Eli’s sons. The Lord said: “Those who honor me I will honor, and those who dishonor me shall be dishonored.”

“For he of whom,” etc. As though he said: The priesthood is truly transferred; another arises—which amounts to the same thing—both in rite and in tribe. He first demonstrates this from the tribe and afterwards from the rite. As though he said: Another truly arises according to a different “food” [probably OCR-corrupt; perhaps “order”]. For Christ, in whose regard these things are said—namely, “You are a priest for ever,” etc.—is of another tribe, not of Levi. From that other tribe no one stood before the altar, that is, approached the ministry of the altar. And he is truly of another tribe: for it is evident that our Lord, namely Christ, sprang from Judah. The priesthood has been transferred [Col. 0453B] from the priestly tribe to the royal tribe, so that the same person may be priestly and royal, as Melchizedek was king and priest.

Observe the mystery. [Chrysostom.] First it was royal, afterwards it was made priestly; likewise Christ was always king, but became priest when he assumed flesh, when he offered sacrifice.

“In which tribe Moses said nothing concerning priests,” namely, that any person from it should be a priest. And it is still more evident than from the tribe that the priesthood is transferred and another priest arises. For proof from the rite is firmer: although the tribe had been changed in Samuel, the rite had not been changed. And this is indeed evident if—that is, because—another priest arises according to the likeness, that is, the rite, of Melchizedek. [Col. 0453C] For as he offered bread and wine to Abraham, so Christ gave his body and blood to the disciples under the same forms.

I say that another arises, who was not made priest according to the law of a carnal commandment—that is, according to the precept of the Law, which commanded and promised only carnal things—but according to the power of an indestructible life; that is, according to the divinity in him, through which, according to the good pleasure of the divinity, he gives eternal life to his own.

Or thus: he was not made priest according to the law of a carnal commandment, that is, according to the carnal understanding of the Law, so as to act according to carnal observances; but according to the power of an indestructible life, that is, according to the spiritual understanding of the Law itself, by which those who carry it out have eternal life.

[Ambrose.] Behold the difference between priesthood and priesthood: that one is carnal, this one spiritual; that one temporal, this one eternal. The authority proves that he is priest according to the order of Melchizedek. [Col. 0453D] For David bears witness with me—or together with many other Scriptures—that Christ is priest according to the order of Melchizedek. But he more faithfully sets down David’s own words, saying, “For you are.” As though he said: He truly bears witness, for he says, “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

Or thus: I have said, “according to the power of an indestructible life.” For God the Father bears witness by an oath concerning the Son, because he says of him: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

[Col. 0454A]

**VERS. 18–27.—** “There takes place indeed a rejection of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness. For the Law brought nothing to perfection. But there is an introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God. And this was not without an oath. The others indeed were made priests without an oath; but this one with an oath, through him who said to him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever.’ By so much Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant. And the others indeed were made priests in greater number, because death prevented them from remaining. But this one, because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood. Therefore he is also able to save for ever those approaching God through himself, always living to intercede for us. For such [Col. 0454B] a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. He has no need, as the priests do, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people. For he did this once, offering himself.”

“There takes place indeed a rejection.” He has shown from tribe and rite that the priesthood was transferred, and from this it follows that the Law too was transferred. But because the transfer of the priesthood might perhaps not seem sufficient to demonstrate the transfer of the Law, he here adds the cause—a cause satisfying every human mind when people know the reason for a thing. He shows why the Old Testament, though given by God, was abolished [Col. 0454C] and the New substituted: namely, because during the time of its own standing it was weak, and now altogether useless. This also serves to commend the new priest.

He therefore says: “A rejection indeed takes place,” so that there may be room for grace, “of the preceding commandment,” that is, of the old Law. He properly says “preceding,” because another must follow. I say that a rejection takes place, not because of its malignity or wickedness, as the heretics who rise up against me allege, but because of its weakness while it stood: although it did something then, it did not justify fully; and because of the uselessness which it has now. For it is not merely weak but also condemned, if it is retained.

[Augustine.] For after Christ’s coming it was useless to do those things which were formerly done in order to foreshadow these things. [Col. 0454D]

> [Note: [Col. 0453D] Augustine, *Letter to Jerome*.] Circumcision and things of this kind were divinely given to the former people through the Old Testament as signs of things to come, which had to be fulfilled through Christ. Once these had come, those things remained for Christians only to read, for understanding the prophecy that had preceded; they were not, however, to be performed as necessary observances. It would be as though the revelation of God signified by them were still to be awaited as yet to come. Therefore any Christian who now wishes similarly to celebrate them will not be a devout guide or bearer of a body, but an impious violator of a grave, digging up sleeping ashes.

“For the Law brought nothing to perfection.” As though he said: The Law was truly weakened, for at that time it brought no one to perfection [Col. 0455A] in justification. Even if some people were then perfect, they were not so from or through it, but through faith in the One to come.

“But there is an introduction.” As though he said: That Law is rejected; but through the aforesaid high priest there is introduced a better hope, that is, a better Law, through which eternal glory is hoped for. There temporal things were hoped for; here, heaven. “Through which hope we draw near to God.”

“And how great is this?” This concerns the commendation of the new priest: here the dignity of the appointment is discussed. As though he said: We have commended him in many ways, and I add yet another: how great is this—that Jesus was made priest not without an oath? The others, namely the Levitical priests, were made priests without an oath, as men destined at some point to be changed. But this one, [Col. 0455B] namely Jesus, was made priest with an oath made by him—namely God the Father—who said to him, namely Jesus: “You are a priest for ever.” And “for ever”: “The Lord has sworn.” The prophet said this, that is, he confirmed it with unshakable truth. “And he will not repent”: he also said this, that is, he will not alter what he has done.

“By so much,” etc. From praise of the priest he infers a commendation of the Law, saying: “By so much,” that is, through these great facts—that he was made priest with an oath and that through him we draw near to God—it is certain that Jesus has become guarantor, that is, confirmer, of a better covenant than the old one. For as Christ’s priesthood surpasses the Levitical priesthood, so his Law surpasses the old Law. The New Testament is therefore better [Col. 0455C] than the Old, because it promises better things, namely eternal things; the Old promised temporal things.

“And the others.” In this respect again Jesus is more worthy. And—that is, because—the others, namely the Levitical priests, were made priests in greater number according to the Law, because death prevented them from remaining alive. But this one, namely Jesus, because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood.

[Ambrose.] And as he remains, so does the Law which he brought, in which there is true remission and perpetual grace. Because the old Law could not do this, it has been excluded. That he remains for ever, he shows from the high priest: because he is one; which he would not be unless he were immortal, just as under the Law there were many because they were mortal.

Therefore, because he remains and has an everlasting priesthood, he can save for ever those approaching—or the person approaching. Having shown that Christ’s priesthood abolishes the old priesthood and the Law, he commends Christ’s action by contrasting it with the operation of the old sacrifice. As though he said: He can save for ever. He himself, I say, approaches God, not through another high priest or through other victims, [Chrysostom,] but through himself, priest and victim. Jesus himself approaches God through himself as a living victim.

Or, according to another reading, whom can he save? Those approaching God, not through another, but through himself, as he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). [Col. 0456A] Therefore he can save, because he is always living—unlike the others—to intercede for us by presenting himself. In that nature in which he is high priest, namely the human nature which he brought into heaven, he intercedes for us.

“For such.” As though he said: I say that he approaches God through himself, and rightly so. For he is holy inwardly, in the disposition of virtues and mind; innocent in his hands with respect to his neighbor; undefiled in body, through removal from evils. Nor is he merely undefiled: he is also separated from sinners, that is, free from every sin, because he is always without sin. Or, “separated from sinners” means separated from the former priests, unlike whom he is. And he was made higher than the heavens, that is, higher than every heavenly creature, because all angels worship him. Such a high priest was fitting for us [Col. 0456B] who are sons; servants had other high priests.

Since he is such, he does not have a daily need—not that he ever has need, but this is said to remove what applied to the legal priests—to offer sacrifices first for his own sins and then for those of the people, as the Levitical priests do, who were only a figure of this priest. The unchangeable priest did not have this need.

“For he did this.” As though he said: He truly has no such need. For he did this—that is, he made an offering—by offering himself, not for his own sins, but for the sins of the people. And he did so once, because a single offering is sufficient for all and need not be repeated.

[Ambrose.] So great, indeed, is the sacrifice that, although it was offered once and only once, it nevertheless suffices for eternity.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0456C]

**VERS. 1–7.—** “For the Law appoints as priests men who have weakness; but the word of the oath which came after the Law appoints the Son, perfected for ever. Now the chief point of the things being said is this: we have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in heaven, a minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which God pitched, and not man. For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices. Therefore it is necessary that this one too have something to offer. If then he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the Law, who serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was instructed when he was completing the tabernacle. [Col. 0456D] ‘See,’ he says, ‘that you make all things according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain.’ But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by as much as he is mediator of a better covenant, which has been established upon better promises. For if that first covenant had been without fault, a place for a second would certainly not have been sought.”

“For the Law.” As though he said: The Levitical priests have a daily need, but Christ does not; and rightly, because they are weak, whereas he suffices once for all, because he is the perfect Son. This is the meaning: the Law appoints as priests men having the weakness of sinning and dying, and therefore they offered for themselves. But the word of the oath, spoken after the Law through David, appoints as priest the Son himself, who will endure for ever, perfected in grace and truth.

“The chief point.” [Remigius.] [Col. 0457A] Having said a few things about the dignity of this high priest, he briefly gathers together his dignity beyond what he had previously said. A *capitulum* is a brief compendium of many matters, so called because it comprehends the entire sum in brief. As though he said: I have said much concerning him, but now I make a summary of the things being said, containing a worthier praise of Christ than what was stated before.

“Such.” Here the summary begins and ends at “God and not man.” Therefore, making the summary, he says: “We have such a high priest, who”—I do not say merely “sat,” but “sat down with,” because he is God and man, a giant of double substance in whom two natures are united.

“He sat down.” As though he said: For a long time he has rested and reigned according to his divine nature, at the right hand of the throne of Majesty—that is, in equality with the seated Deity, namely God the Father, who rests and judges. According to his human nature, he has been placed in heaven, either above the material heavens or above thrones and dominions. There he is a minister of the holy ones, because he ministers eternal life there to the saints, and ministers from there other good things to those who are here.

[Chrysostom.] “Of the holy things,” I say, and—that is—“of the true tabernacle.” As though he said: He is not minister of shadowy holy things, but of the true tabernacle, which is the souls of the saints, to whom he gives eternal joys in heaven and gifts of grace here. Thus he is minister of the saints here or in the future. God, not man, established that tabernacle, namely the heavenly Church and the present Church.

Notice that he says “at the right hand of the throne of Majesty”: this indicates divine power and majesty. Likewise, notice that he says “minister of the holy things”: this indicates his great mercy and the love he bestows upon us. [Col. 0457C] By these two things, therefore, he is shown to be both powerful and merciful.

Or thus: “He sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty.” This is not altered. He, I say, being in heaven, is minister of the holy things, because there he ministers the glory signified by the Holy of Holies; and minister of the true tabernacle, that is, of the reality which the tabernacle foreshadowed: namely, righteousness in the present Church and glory in the future Church. Both are God’s true tabernacle. God established this true tabernacle so that it may remain for ever. The shadowy tabernacle, however, was not fixed but portable. “And not man”: this is added because God also established the old tabernacle, but through the agency of a human minister.

“For every high priest is appointed [Col. 0457D] to offer gifts,” such as loaves, incense, and things of that sort, “and sacrifices” from animals. Therefore, because every high priest is appointed to offer, this one too—namely Christ—must have something to offer: namely flesh from us, which he had not previously possessed.

“If then,” etc. The wording of this summary is not fully connected and is broken; it therefore introduces obscurity. As though he said: I say that Christ must have something to offer; and since he must have something to offer, that thing must be either earthly or heavenly. Earthly is whatever is offered in carnal things or for carnal things. But his offering is not earthly, because if it were—that is, if what Jesus offered were [Col. 0458A] on earth, namely something carnal—Christ would not even be a priest, much less a high priest. I say he would not be a priest, since there were many who offered gifts according to the Law, that is, upon earth. Thus Christ would offer carnal things superfluously. But lest it seem that Jesus offered those same things more worthily, he adds: “who serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things,” that is, they fully perform all things, as Moses was instructed; and thus Jesus would take up this priesthood in vain in order to offer something carnal. Therefore what he offers is heavenly.

> [Note: [Col. 0457D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] For what could be offered for human beings more suitably than human flesh? What is more fitting for immolation than mortal flesh? What is cleaner for cleansing the faults of mortals than flesh born without any infection of carnal concupiscence in and from a virgin’s womb? And what could be more acceptably offered and received than the flesh of your sacrifice? Thus, since four things are considered in every sacrifice—namely, to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered—the one and true Mediator himself reconciled us to God through a sacrifice of peace, remaining one with him to whom he offered, and one with that which he offered.

[Lanfranc.] Or thus: “If then.” As though he said: Since every priest offers, if there were anyone on earth—that is, if there were an earthly priest capable of cleansing the human race—there would not be any priest according to the order of Melchizedek, since there were sufficiently many who offered gifts according to the Law, namely legal offerings. But because they were mortal and sinful, and therefore unable to cleanse [Col. 0458C] the human race, Christ came, who was sufficient.

Or thus: Since Christ is appointed to offer, he must be either an earthly or a heavenly priest. But he is not earthly, because if he were on earth—that is, if he were an earthly high priest like Aaron—he would certainly not be priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, nor would it have been necessary, since there were, etc. But Christ is priest for ever, not Aaron. For Aaron, because he died, is not priest; but Christ, who lives, is an everlasting priest, not like those who exercise a shadowy priesthood.

Or thus: “If then.” Here the reason is shown why Christ offered himself. As though he said: Christ must offer something; therefore himself. And it is truly necessary for him to offer, because even if there were on earth something that could worthily be offered for the sin of the whole world, there would nevertheless be no priest worthy to offer it, since—even though there were those who offered gifts, etc.—the pure one therefore offered himself as pure.

> [Note: [Col. 0458D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.] For this true sacrifice could not rightly be offered except by one who was righteous and holy. And what priest is as righteous and holy as the only Son of God, who had no need to cleanse his own sins through sacrifice, whether original sins or sins added afterwards?

Or thus: Since every priest is appointed to offer, Christ too offered; and for this reason he ascended into heaven. [Col. 0459A] And this had to happen, because if he were on earth—that is, if he had not yet entered the Holy of Holies, namely the inner places of heaven—he would not be priest, that is, the rite of his priesthood would not be celebrated, while a priest according to Aaron still remained.

[Lanfranc.] Hence he adds: “since there were those who offered gifts according to the Law.” It remains, therefore, that he offer himself and so enter the inner places of heaven. “Who,” etc.: I say, those who offered gifts were such that they serve—that is, fully serve—the copy, namely the figure, and—that is—the shadow of heavenly mysteries. By “heavenly things” he means the Church: one part reigns in heaven, another, which will follow, is a pilgrim on earth. By “copy” and “shadows” he means figures which are a copy and an example in relation to different things.

[Remigius.] [Col. 0459B] A copy is that after whose likeness something is made; an example is what is drawn from it. God showed Moses the reality on the mountain, namely the order of the heavenly court: how the angels obey, praise, and love God; how they love one another and us; how they are concerned for our progress; and other things of this sort, in which they are to be imitated by us. But because a carnal people could not grasp the reality, God commanded Moses to represent it in figures, by which the childish people, being nourished, might someday come to the reality. Thus the reality first shown is called the copy of the figures made in accordance with it.

Again, the figures are called a copy of the reality later fulfilled, because those figures foreshadowed it. In this sense he says: “They serve the copy,” that is, figures foreshadowing the future reality. And because a copy is sometimes the reality rather than a figure, he adds, “and shadow,” because those things were only a shadow of the reality, soon to depart when it arrived.

“They serve,” I say, as the Lord instructed Moses when he was completing the tabernacle, not when he was beginning it but when he had completed it, since he had already expressed many things through figures. But when he could not complete it by himself, he consulted the Lord, who instructed him concerning the figures as concerning reality. What was he instructed? This: [Col. 0459C] “‘See,’ says the Lord, ‘that you make all things.’” “All things” means both the construction of the tabernacle and the sacrifices to be offered in it. “Make them,” I say, “according to this copy,” namely the reality, “which was shown you on the mountain,” because God showed him in a vision on the mountain what he was to make.

“But now.” As though he said: They serve a copy and shadow; but Jesus possesses a better ministry, because he ministers in spiritual things and gives spiritual things. This is now clear, as though he said, since he has been shown not to offer upon earth. This is what he says: “But now,” namely in this last age, Jesus has obtained a better ministry of priesthood than existed under the old Law. It is better by as much as his Law is better than the old Law. Thus he says: “a better ministry, by as much as he is mediator of a better covenant,” because it promises eternal things—mediator, that is, giver standing between God and man.

[Chrysostom.] Here he passes from priesthood and sacrifice to the difference between the covenants, [Col. 0460A] preferring the New to the Old. This New Covenant was established—that is, confirmed to endure—upon better promises than were the promises of the Old Testament.

> [Note: [Col. 0459D] Augustine, *On Psalm LXXXIII*.] If we distinguish the two Testaments, Old and New, the sacraments are not the same in each, nor are the promises the same; yet most commandments are the same.
