For, when examined, nearly all the commandments are found to be the same in the Gospel—the moral commandments, certainly, being the same: “You shall not kill,” and the rest of that kind. But ceremonial matters are not the same, and the sacraments are not the same, because those promised salvation while these give it. Likewise, the promises are not the same: there earthly things were promised, here heavenly things.

“For if,” etc. [Remigius.] He proves that Christ’s covenant is better than the Old, because the latter is not without fault, while this one is without fault. [Col. 0460B] For if that covenant had been without fault—that is, if it perfectly cleansed humanity, if its observers had been blameless—the second would not have been given. But it is given; thus the former is shown to have been imperfect and this one perfect. This is what he says: “For if that first covenant had been without fault, a place,” that is, an opportunity, “for a second would certainly not have been sought” by God, who first instructed gradually through the Law and built through the prophets, so that afterwards he might give the perfect covenant which brought completion.

Notice that he says, “if it had been without fault.” He speaks thus as though it itself has fault, since it commands without grace and makes people transgressors. If we are asked why we do not worship God in the rite in which the Hebrew patriarchs worshipped him:

> [Note: [Col. 0460D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] We reply that God commanded something different for us through the fathers of the New Testament; nor is this contrary to the Old Testament, since the same thing was foretold in it beforehand. For it was thus announced through the prophet Jeremiah. Hence follows:

[Col. 0460C]

**VERS. 8–10.—** “For, finding fault with them, he says: ‘Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will bring to completion upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Judah a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. For this is the covenant which I will establish with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: giving my laws into their mind, and I will write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’”

“For, finding fault with them.” As though he said: If that covenant had been without fault, a place for the second would not be sought; but it is sought. For Jeremiah, finding fault with those who were under the Law, says: “Behold, days are coming,” that is, they gradually draw near. He calls the time of Christ “days,” because, the darkness having been driven away, the light which enlightens every person coming into the world appeared to the world (John 1).

“The Lord says: ‘And I will bring to completion,’” that is, completing, I will give and fulfill the New Covenant, in which what was promised to Abraham will occur. “I will bring to completion,” I say, “upon the house of Israel and upon the house of Judah,” [Col. 0461A] that is, upon the Jews who, after Solomon, were divided into two kingdoms. Upon them he says he will bring the New Covenant to completion, namely so that he may rule them and they may obey him.

“Not according to.” As though he said: I will bring to completion the New Covenant, which will not be according to the covenant he made with their fathers. [Remigius.] That is, it will not concern earthly things like the old covenant, namely the Law given on Mount Sinai. And because he had made a spiritual covenant with certain patriarchs, such as Abraham, he specifies: “On the day when I took their hand.” As though he said: They could not rise from their bed by themselves; or, like a nurse of little children, I took them by the hand “to lead them out of the land of Egypt.” That is, it will not be according to the Law given after the departure from Egypt.

For what he said to Abraham before the Law—“In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22)—he fulfilled in the Gospel. For that was a spiritual promise belonging to grace.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] Behold, it is here prophesied that the Old Testament would not endure, but that there would be a New Testament.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Although this same thing is indicated and foretold in many places, the New Testament itself is not otherwise expressly mentioned. Indeed, in the old books, either nowhere or only with difficulty apart from this prophetic passage is there found a reference to the New Testament under that very name.

Consider carefully, therefore, the difference between the two Testaments, the Old and the New. There is the letter, which alone kills; here is the Spirit, who gives life. That one is old because it does not free from the oldness of sin; this one is new because it renews.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] But if we are asked why we maintain the authority of that covenant whose rite we do not observe, we answer that it must be read and received, lest we extinguish the prophecies; for all those things took place as shadows of future things, as the Apostle says: “These things happened to them as a figure,” etc. (1 Corinthians 10).

Why then does anything of such a kind occur in the document of the Old Testament which we are not commanded to observe in the New Testament, or are even forbidden to observe? One must ask what it signifies, not condemn it; for precisely because it is no longer observed, it is not condemned but is proved fulfilled.

“But because.” As though he said: I took their hand as that of little children. But because they did not remain in the covenant, [Col. 0461D] in it—that is, in the Law given in the synagogue—because they made a calf at Horeb and worshipped a carved image (Psalm 105), see how he found fault with them. Therefore, I say, because they did not remain, “I disregarded them.”

> [Note: [Col. 0462D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] Do not be indignant if I say that you were disregarded, because the Lord says it through me. He openly attributes their failure to remain in God’s covenant to their fault, lest the Law which they then received be judged blameworthy. For it is the Law which Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill; nevertheless, it is not the Law but grace that justifies them. For this is the work of the life-giving Spirit, without whom the letter kills. In what sense, then, is that called the Old Testament and this the New, when the Law is fulfilled through the New Testament? It is because of the fault of the old human being, who is not saved through the commanding and threatening letter. That covenant is called Old, while this is called New, because of the newness of the Spirit, who heals humanity from the fault of oldness.

He clearly explains this by adding: “For this is.” As though he said: I shall truly give a New Covenant, not according to that old one, because this is the covenant which I will establish—that is, establish in order—with the house of Israel, namely all those who see God, not indeed before but after those days predetermined by me. And believe this, because the Lord says it through the Holy Spirit speaking in me: “giving,” or “I will give.”

As though he said: This is the covenant which I will bring to completion: I will give through the Holy Spirit my laws. Behold the covenant. [Col. 0462B] Or, according to another reading: “I will establish the covenant” thus, namely by giving my laws “into their minds,” that is, into their understandings—not on stone tablets as the old Law was written on stone. And I will write them also “upon their hearts,” that is, upon their wills, because they will understand and keep them willingly. I will write them so that they may remain for ever; “upon,” as though he said, because they ought to remain above them and rule them.

> [Note: [Col. 0462D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*.] Here he commends this difference: that God would give his laws into their minds, which belong to the New Testament, and write them in their hearts—not, of course, with ink, as the Apostle says elsewhere, but by the Spirit of the living God.

> [Note: [Col. 0462D] Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*.] That is, by the very presence of the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God. When he is present, charity is poured out into hearts; charity is the fullness of the Law and the end of the commandment.

For because the promises of the Old Testament are earthly, the good of the heart itself is now promised—namely the good of the mind, the good of the spirit, that is, an intelligible good—when it says: “I will give my laws into their mind, and I will write them upon their hearts.” By this he means that they will not fear a Law frightening them from outside, but will love the righteousness of the Law dwelling within them.

Hence this reward is added: “And I will be.” As though he said: I will write my Law in their minds; and thus I will be their God, and they shall be my people. For it will be said: “God is truly in these people, and these are God’s people.” That is, they shall live from me and for me—and this indeed in this [Col. 0462D] world.

### Verses 11–13

“And each one shall not teach his neighbour, and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest; for I shall be merciful to their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more.” But in saying “new,” he has made the former old. And what is becoming old and growing aged is near destruction.

And in the future, no one will teach his neighbour whom he loves, nor his brother whom he loves more dearly, saying, “Know the Lord.” Therefore one will not teach another, because all in the future shall know—[Col. 0463A] that is, shall see—me as I am; this is perfection, so that one, namely, does not teach another.

[Note: [Col. 0463D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter.*] They shall know, I say, from their least to their greatest. It makes no difference if it is said in reverse, namely, “from the greatest to the least,” as it is said, “from the least to the greatest.” This may be understood in different ways: the greater may be called greater either in time or in rank—that is, earlier in time or more eminent in understanding. Thus the greater are understood either as the earlier persons who waited for us later persons in receiving the denarius, or as greater in knowledge or virtue: those who were able, so far as is possible in this life, to understand the incorporeal and unchangeable light, which the lesser could only believe. Therefore, when that which is perfect has come and that which is in part has been done away with (1 Cor. 13), [Col. 0463B] then he who appeared to flesh in assumed flesh will show himself to his lovers. Then all shall know him, from the least to the greatest, because even the least shall then know him perfectly through himself, not instructed by one greater.

[Augustine] This, then, is the difference between the Old and New Testaments: the former was written on stone, the latter in the heart; there the reward is earth, here the vision of God.

Or thus from that point, without changing what precedes: “and no one shall teach.” As if he said: “Therefore I shall be their God, and they shall be my people.”

[Chrysostom] And this will appear as a new thing, which is not recorded as having occurred in the Old Testament: namely, “each one shall not teach his neighbour, and each one his brother,” because what lay hidden in the letter, and what the people learned through the traditions of teachers, the Spirit, coming suddenly, taught to the apostles. [Col. 0463C] And this is what the prophet says: “Each one shall not teach his neighbour, and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’” Why not? Because all shall know him, from the least to their greatest, as is read in the Gospel: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

And therefore I shall do all these things for them in both lives, because “I shall be merciful to their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more,” for eternal punishment. Make the distinction. By “iniquities” he means sins which people commit against their neighbours, and by “sins,” those committed against themselves. Or the terms are the same—that is, “iniquity” and “sin” are here taken for the same thing—but a distinction is made between “I shall be merciful” and “I shall remember”: he is merciful when he does not punish here, and in the future [Col. 0463D] he will no longer remember when he does not punish.

It should be known, however, that in certain books, where we write “of their sins” (*peccatorum*), one finds written “sin” (*peccatum*); and then it is understood of original sin. He explains why he has cited this authority from Jeremiah by adding, “But in saying.” As if he said: The prophet called it “new.” But in saying “new,” he made the former old—that is, he showed it to be old. Or, “he made old”: the former testament became old; and if old, therefore it must come to an end. Hence he adds: “What is becoming old,” as occurs in inanimate things, “and growing aged,” which occurs in living things, “is near destruction”; for obsolescence and old age are heralds of death.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 0464A]

### Verses 1–2

Indeed, the former covenant also had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary. For the first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of loaves, which is called the Holy Place.

“Indeed, it had.” Up to this point he has shown the difference between the Testaments: that the New surpasses the Old and changes it.

[Chrysostom] Now he shows the same thing from the very arrangement of the tabernacle. As if he said: The Old Testament is near destruction; nevertheless, the former testament once had ordinances—not true and spiritual ones, but carnal ones suited to its manner of worship—and it had a sanctuary, not spiritual but earthly, that is, changeable and merely reputed holy, considered holy by human beings. And it truly had an earthly sanctuary, because it had [Col. 0464B] a first and a second tabernacle.

“The first tabernacle was made,” and so on, down to: “which is a parable of the present time.” Since the subject of the tabernacle has arisen, certain matters concerning it should be briefly considered.

It should be known, therefore, that the tabernacle was thirty cubits long, ten cubits wide, and the same in height.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] Augustine, in the book of *Questions.*] It had a veil woven from four precious colours and hung upon four gilded columns. This divided it into twenty and ten cubits: that is, between the Holy Place, which was outside, and the Holy of Holies situated within. For the outer sanctuary was twenty cubits in length; the inner sanctuary—that is, the Holy of Holies—was ten. The Apostle calls the former the first tabernacle, [Col. 0464C] and the latter the second tabernacle.

In the first tabernacle was a golden lampstand. The Apostle, however, says “lampstands” in the plural because, although there was one, it had seven branches. In the middle was a shaft having, in four places, cups, globes, and lilies. From it proceeded branches, three on the right and three on the left, each having in three places cups, globes, and lilies.

There was also in it a square table, like an altar, with four legs. It stood beyond the entrance to the tabernacle. It was made of shittim wood and overlaid with pure gold; it had a golden rim all around, and above it an openwork golden crown four fingers high, and upon that another small golden crown. It also had, at each corner, golden rings, into which [Col. 0464D] poles were inserted so that it could be carried. These were of shittim wood, overlaid with gold. Upon the table were twelve loaves set before God, made of fine flour, all of which were changed every Sabbath. If, however, one was needed before the Sabbath, it could not be taken unless another was immediately put in its place. Over the loaves was a golden dish and a handful of very bright incense.

In the same tabernacle was the altar of incense, where incense was burned upon hot ashes brought there from the altar of sacrifices, which stood outside the tabernacle in the open court. It was square, five cubits wide and equally [Col. 0465A] long.

The first tabernacle is called the Holy Place because of the reverence of that time, and because it signifies the present Church, which is holy. The second is called the Holy of Holies because it was held in greater reverence, and because it signifies the heavenly Church, where there is no sin.

In it were a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered with gold inside and outside. In it were three things: a golden jar containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets upon which the Law was written. Above the ark was the mercy-seat, namely, a slab of the same length and width as the ark. It was a slab of purest gold, called the mercy-seat or oracle, because there the angel of God appeared to Moses, speaking when God was about to be propitious to the children of Israel. [Col. 0465B] Above the mercy-seat were two cherubim, or seraphim—that is, most gloriously ornamented images—gazing at one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat.

The ark was of shittim wood, two and a half cubits in length, one and a half in width, and the same in height. At each side it had golden rings—two on the right and two on the left—in which the poles for carrying it always remained. The poles were of shittim wood, overlaid with purest gold. The mercy-seat was the slab above the ark, of the same length and width, upon which the cherubim stood and toward which they always looked.

[Note: [Col. 0465D] Augustine, in the book of *Questions on Exodus.*] No one except the high priest was permitted to enter this Holy of Holies with blood once a year. And if perhaps necessity ever required it because of [Col. 0465C] the sin of the priest or of the whole synagogue, priests entered the first tabernacle daily to perform the rites of sacrifice.

But all this is a parable and shadow of heavenly things. The first tabernacle is the present Church, rightly called a tabernacle because God is served in warfare there before one arrives in heaven. A tabernacle properly belongs to those engaged in war.

In it is the golden lampstand: Christ, shining in power and wisdom in the midst of the faithful. For they too are golden lampstands, because they shine with wisdom. Gold signifies wisdom. Christ himself is the stem which bears three branches on the right and three on the left, because he is the true vine in which are established three orders of branches, that is, of the faithful. Those who belong to the time of grace are on the right, that is, more worthy; those before grace were, as it were, on the left. These three orders of the faithful are signified in the three men whom Ezekiel saw being saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job—that is, rulers, continent persons, and married persons.

These are also those who, according to the Gospel, are said to be in the field, in bed, and at the mill (Matt. 24). For there it is read: “Two shall be in the field; one shall be taken and the other left. Two shall be in bed; one shall be taken and the other left. And two grinding at the mill; one shall be taken and the other left.” By those in the field are signified rulers, as also by Noah; by those in bed, continent persons, [Col. 0466A] as also by Daniel; and by those at the mill, married persons, as also by Job.

The first part of the shafts was like golden reeds; after that came cups, then little golden globes, and finally lilies. The reeds are saints nourished in the moist places of the divine fountain; they are hollow, to receive and pour forth to others the liquid of grace. They are also the cups when they give others to drink from what they have drunk: namely, wisdom and the knowledge of God. Then come the little globes—that is, persons rounded, perfect, and able to roll against adversity and prosperity, so that nothing holds them back until they come to the lilies of eternal joy, which have neither the angle of fear nor the brow of pride.

Upon these were placed seven lamps: the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which rested most fully in Christ and were distributed among the faithful according to his will.

The table at the entrance is divine Scripture, which abides and is set before those entering.

[Bede] Since it displays eternal joys and how they are reached, it provides the food of life. Upon it were pure loaves, that is, the twelve apostles [251] and their successors, who offer God the incense of prayer. If any one of them dies, another must immediately be substituted in his place; but in the seventh age all shall be removed.

The second place beyond the veil is the heavenly Church, veiled as long as we live here. The censer is Christ, full of the fire of love, always interceding for us. The ark is Christ, in whom are all treasures of wisdom and knowledge, golden on every side because in his thought, word, and deed there is nothing but pure [Col. 0466C] truth. Its length is the perseverance of doctrine, signified by one cubit, and of action, signified by the other cubit; the half-cubit signifies that human understanding is imperfect in relation to its perfection. Its width is the perfection of love; its height, the perfection of hope, toward which we are only halves—that is, imperfect.

The four rings are the four perfect Evangelists, through whom Christ is borne throughout the four parts of the world. To them are always attached the golden poles—that is, preachers shining with wisdom, ever ready against enemies. In the ark is the jar containing manna: the soul of Christ, containing full wisdom, by which even angels are refreshed. The rod signifies Christ’s priestly power. The tablets signify that he is the giver of the Law. The mercy-seat is Christ, who is propitious to us. [Col. 0466D] The two cherubim are all the orders of heaven, united to one another in love and resting in him; although wise, they nevertheless overshadow him as far as lies in them.

Priests entered the first tabernacle daily, completing the sacrifice within, because in the present Church the faithful ought daily to offer themselves, mortifying their flesh with its vices and desires. Into the second, however, the high priest entered with blood once a year: Christ entered the inner places of heaven with the blood of his kindness poured out for the forgiveness of sins, opening to the faithful the gate of paradise formerly closed.

Having treated these matters, attend to the letter. For the tabernacle shows how necessary Christ was, since through all those legal ordinances no one entered heaven. As if he said: The former testament had an earthly sanctuary. And truly so, because it had a first and a second tabernacle. For the first tabernacle was made—that is, the outer sanctuary. Within it was the altar of incense; before its doors, in the open air, stood the altar of burnt offerings. It is called a tabernacle because it endured for a time, made as a figure of this age—that is, of the present Church—in which priests minister daily, kindling the light of doctrine and feeding the people with God’s bread, which is upon the table of sacred Scripture, from the Sabbath of hope to the Sabbath of hope.

[Col. 0467A] In it were the lampstands, the table, and the presentation of loaves, which is called the Holy Place because of the reverence of that time, and especially because it signified the present Church. In it are lampstands—that is, Christ and his faithful, shining with the light of virtue and wisdom—and the table of sacred Scripture, to which the twelve apostles and their successors devote themselves. Or the lampstands are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, shining in the Church. The bread upon the table—that is, the word of sacred Scripture—is ready at the Sabbath of hope, where we are safe in Christ from the storm of this age until the Sabbath of full rest, when hope shall be fulfilled.

### Verses 3–8

[Note: [Col. 0467D] Augustine, in the book of *Questions on Exodus.*] But after the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on every side with gold. In it was a golden jar containing [Col. 0467C] manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat. Of these things it is not now necessary to speak individually. But when these had thus been arranged, priests continually entered the first tabernacle to perform the offices of sacrifices; but into the second, the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own and the people’s ignorance. By this the Holy Spirit signified that the way of the holy places had not yet been revealed, while the first tabernacle still had standing.

But the second tabernacle was beyond the veil, because the veil placed between divided the first from the second. The second tabernacle signifies heaven, into which Christ our priest entered not without blood. Or the tabernacle outside [Col. 0467D] signified the Old Testament. It is a figure of a figure, because it is a figure of the Old Testament. But the tabernacle within signified the New Testament and was a figure of truth, because it is a figure of the New Testament. We do not pursue this allegory according to the sequence of the letter, but according to the preceding exposition.

It is called the Holy of Holies because of the greater reverence of that time, or because it signifies the heavenly Church. It had a golden censer, signifying Christ, full of the fire of love—that is, him through whom the prayers of the saints are offered—and the ark of the covenant, that is, that which contained the covenant, covered with gold on every side, not only outside but [Col. 0468A] also within. It signifies Christ, in whose thought, speech, and action there was nothing but pure truth.

In the ark was a golden jar, namely, a *gomor* containing manna, in remembrance of the ancient benefit. It figures the soul of Christ, full of the wisdom by which even angels are refreshed. There was also Aaron’s rod which had budded, by which Christ’s priestly power is signified; and the tablets of the covenant, upon which the Law was written, signifying that Christ is the giver of the Law.

Or the ark may be understood as Christ’s very flesh, in which is the manna of divinity, and the tablets of the two Testaments, of which Christ is the author, and the rod for priesthood. The jar is the people in whom is Christ, the bread that descended from heaven. For only the people contained in [Col. 0468B] Christ are nourished by the bread of heaven.

Above it, the ark, were the cherubim of glory—that is, two glorious and beautiful angels, gloriously adorned—overshadowing with joined wings the mercy-seat, that is, the slab above the ark. The two cherubim signify the angels of heaven, united in love and full of knowledge.

[Ambrose] For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” The mercy-seat above the ark is Christ, because to Christ himself it was specially given by God the Father that he should be a propitiation for our sins.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] Augustine, on Exodus.] This may also be understood otherwise. For there is a great mystery here. Gold signifies wisdom; the ark signifies God’s secret. The Law, manna, and Aaron’s rod were commanded to be placed in the ark. In the Law are commandments; [Col. 0468C] in the rod power is signified; in manna, grace. For there is no power to perform the commandments except with grace. But because the Law is not fulfilled in every respect by any person making progress, the mercy-seat is above it. God must be propitious for this work; and therefore it is placed above, because “mercy triumphs over judgment” (James 2).

The two cherubim overshadow the mercy-seat with their wings—that is, honour it by veiling it—because these are mysteries; and they look toward each other because they are harmonious. For these are the two Testaments, since cherubim, by interpretation, are the fullness of knowledge. The two Testaments contain this fullness and overshadow the mercy-seat because they either reconcile us to, or commend to us, the mercy of God in which hope rests.

[Augustine] Or by the two cherubim, whose interpretation is “a multitude of knowledge,” the rational creation is signified, namely, the angelic creation. They are two in order to commend the fellowship of love. They overshadow the mercy-seat with wings because they attribute their wings not to themselves but to God—that is, they honour God by the virtues through which they excel. And their faces are directed only toward the mercy-seat because they have no hope except in God’s mercy.

“Of these.” As if he said: The Old Testament had the things which have been enumerated, and other such things. Of these, namely of these things and others like them, [Col. 0469A] it is not now necessary to speak individually, because fewer details suffice for carrying out our demonstration.

“But when these had thus been arranged.” As if he said: We need not speak of those things individually; but this which follows must be said. When these tabernacles had thus been arranged, priests continually entered the first tabernacle, which was lesser—that is, of lesser reverence—and signified the present Church, performing the offices of sacrifices: placing incense within and sacrifices outside. This is what he previously called an earthly sanctuary: earthly sacrifices which do not lead to perfection.

But into the second tabernacle the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood. He often entered without blood, but with blood only once. In part he signifies Christ, who entered heaven once, whom we do not immediately follow. Its annual entry signified that perfection had not yet come.

“Not without blood,” I say, which he might offer for his own and the people’s ignorance. Christ, however, offered for the people; for himself, only in his members. Hence he himself says: “The words of my transgressions,” that is, the transgressions of his body (Ps. 21 [22]). For he calls our sins his own because he assumed them, not in order to possess them but to abolish them.

Observe that he says, “Priests continually entered the first tabernacle,” because here the faithful must sacrifice themselves daily. Otherwise they cannot reach the heavenly homeland. The high priest who entered once a year with blood is Christ, who in the year of favour entered heaven once through his own blood, which he shed for human sins.

“By this signifying.” As if he said: Those aforementioned things were done in the Old Testament, the Holy Spirit signifying [Col. 0469C] by them, he who established that they should be done in this way, that the way of the second holy places had not yet been revealed—that is, that entry into heavenly things was not yet permitted until Christ came. After his coming, heaven is still inaccessible to mortals according to the condition of the body; but formerly it was inaccessible even according to souls. The resurrection, in which access to heaven will be opened through Christ even to bodies, must therefore be patiently awaited.

Or, “the way of the second holy places had not yet been revealed” means Christ, or spiritual understanding. For Christ is the way of the holy ones, leading into heaven; or it is spiritual understanding, by which one ascends into heaven’s inner places.

“While still.” As if he said: The Holy Spirit signified this while the first tabernacle still had standing—that is, while carnal observances still retained their standing. He then explains, by adding the following, that these statements about completing sacrifices in the first or second tabernacle were made according to their signification:

### Verses 9–14

[252] It is a parable of the present time, according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot make the worshipper perfect in conscience, being concerned only with foods and drinks, various washings, and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation. But Christ, having appeared as high priest of future good things, entered once into the holy places through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—neither through the blood of goats or calves, [Col. 0470A] but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption. For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God?

“It is a parable,” that is, a mystical likeness, of the present time—that is, of the time of grace which now exists—according to which parable gifts and sacrifices are offered by figurative priests. Distinguish between sacrifices and gifts. Sacrifices are from animals; gifts are from other things, namely incense, fine flour, and loaves. These are offered according to the parable because [Col. 0470B] they too signify something in the present time.

These gifts and sacrifices cannot make the worshipper of God perfect—that is, fully cleansed—and this according to conscience, that is, inwardly in conscience, even if outwardly in human sight. Or “according to conscience” means with conscience as witness. I say, one serving God only in distinguishing foods and drinks, and in various baptisms—that is, washings—and in other ordinances of the flesh, not of the spirit. All these things were imposed as a burden to restrain transgressions until the time of reformation—that is, until the time of grace, when those who had hitherto been under a pedagogue were to be corrected for the better. Therefore those observances could not make anyone perfect. Yet they ought not to have ceased before that time.

“But Christ.” Here he fully treats of the sufficiency of the one true sacrifice of the New Testament, through which, he says, both the forgiveness of sins—which he touched upon above in Jeremiah’s words—and salvation are conferred. As if he said: These aforementioned legal observances cannot make one perfect; but Christ, appearing as high priest, interceding with the Father for us, or as a giver assisting the faithful, is high priest of good things—not present or carnal goods, but future ones: present righteousness and eternal blessedness, which were future during the time of the Law.

Christ, I say, entered the tabernacle—that is, heaven. By the name of the sign, namely the tabernacle, he designates the thing signified, namely heaven. It is greater because it holds more than the earthly one; and more perfect because eternal [Col. 0470D] blessedness is there. It is a tabernacle not made with hands—not that it was not made by God’s action, but that it was not made by human action. Thus he adds in explanation: “That is, not of this creation,” such as that in the wilderness, that is, of human construction. For the old tabernacle, set up by man, was of that kind; this was made by God in a very different way.

He entered, I say, neither through the poured-out blood of bulls, goats, or calves, as was done in the Old Testament, but through his own blood. He entered the holy places—that is, the heavenly tabernacle, the Holy of Holies, namely the heavenly realm. He entered once through blood, shed once, because it need not be repeated: it is perfect.

Or the tabernacle may be understood as Christ’s flesh, which he offered for us and in which he conquered the devil.

[Col. 0471A]

[Note: [Col. 0471D] Augustine, on Exodus.] For Christ is king and priest. As king he fought for us; as priest he offered himself for us. When he fought for us, he seemed to be defeated; indeed, he then conquered. For he was crucified, and from the cross to which he was fastened he slew the devil; and thus he is our king. What, then, did he offer for us as priest? He found nothing clean in human beings which he might offer; for them he offered himself. Behold the clean, blessed, and true victim. He received flesh from the Virgin’s womb in order to offer it, clean, for the unclean.

He calls this flesh the tabernacle, saying: “Christ, high priest, giver of future good things, entered once into the holy places, neither through the blood of bulls, goats, or calves, but through his own blood.” He, I say, entered through the more perfect and greater tabernacle, not made with hands, [Col. 0471B] that is, not of this creation—that is, through flesh which confers and perfects more good things, and which was conceived and formed without a man’s seed. He stands before the Father to intercede.

I say that he entered the holy places through his own blood, thereby obtaining for us—or Christ obtaining for us—eternal redemption, because those redeemed are eternal. This redemption could not be found in those legal sacrifices.

“For if.” He proves from the lesser that redemption could be through Christ, because through those legal things a bodily cleansing occurred. As if he said: Truly redemption can come through Christ, because the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled—

[Augustine]—which signify the remembrance of Christ’s passion—sanctify persons defiled by contact with the dead; that is, they cleanse from sin, namely from punishment. Thus he adds: “effective for cleansing,” not of the soul but of the flesh, because it frees from the penalty of the Law. For every human soul which had touched a dead person was unclean for seven days; it was purified on the third and seventh days and was clean. Here I see that “defilement” means nothing other than contact with a dead human being.

Or, it sanctifies those defiled, namely by the bodily stain of leprosy, effective for cleansing the flesh—that is, so that the flesh might be cleansed in accordance with the commandment of the Law. But in Christ is perfection. Hence he adds: “How much more?”

As if he said: Even if this is so, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who offered himself to God without blemish—for no other blood is without blemish—[Col. 0471D] cleanse us? “Offered,” I say, through the Holy Spirit, who directed all things to him. Or, “without blemish through the Holy Spirit,” by whom he was conceived and through whom he was free from sin.

It shall cleanse not merely the flesh, but also our inward conscience from dead works—that is, from sins. Whoever touches such works by consenting is defiled, just as one who touched a corpse was defiled; and such a person does not enter heaven, just as the other did not enter the temple, until cleansed from sins. I say, it cleanses in order that we may henceforth serve the living God by righteousness. As if he said: Much more.

Notice that Christ’s blood accomplishes two things: it cleanses from sin, and, by restoring freedom, makes one serve God, who gives life and is life living of himself. Therefore no one who has, or performs, dead works can serve him. Christ grants this deservedly, for those legal observances went before as figures of him. For the goat signifies Christ because of the likeness of sinful flesh; and the bull, because with the horns of the two Testaments he scatters his enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0471D] The same, in the book *Questions on Numbers*.] We must not pass over the red heifer, whose ashes the Law commanded to be made into water for sprinkling and for the purification of those who had touched a corpse. For in it a most evident sign of the New Testament is prefigured. In the book of Numbers the Lord is read to have said to Moses concerning her: “Speak to the children of Israel, and let them bring you a red heifer without blemish, which has no defect in itself and upon which no yoke has been laid. You shall give her to Eleazar the priest, [Col. 0472B] and they shall lead her outside the camp to a clean place and kill her before him. Eleazar shall take her blood and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the testimony. They shall burn her before him: her hide with her flesh, her blood with her dung, shall be burned. The priest shall take cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet, and cast them into the midst of the heifer’s burning. A clean man shall gather the heifer’s ashes and place them outside the camp in a clean place; and it shall be an everlasting ordinance for the children of Israel and for proselytes” (Num. 19). From these ashes water for sprinkling was made, by which persons were cleansed from contact with the dead. For he says: “Every human person who touches a corpse shall be unclean seven days” (ibid.). He [Col. 0472C] “shall be purified on the third and seventh day, and shall be clean; but if he has not been purified, he shall not be clean. Everyone who touches a dead person, and, being defiled by the dead, has not been purified, defiles the tabernacle of the Lord; and that soul shall be cut off from Israel.” Again he says: “A clean man, taking hyssop, shall dip it in the water and sprinkle the house, the vessels, and the persons” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0472D] The same, on Exodus.] The red heifer is Christ’s weak flesh. The female sex is used because of bodily weakness. She is red because Christ’s flesh was bloodied by the Passion. Those who take her from Moses, who is a figure of the Law, are those who, according to the Law, believed that they were killing Christ, because according to them he broke the Sabbath and profaned lawful observances. The heifer is without blemish, because Christ’s flesh was free from sin. For confirmation he repeats this, saying, “which has no defect in itself”; or in order to distinguish the point: although in others who are his members there may be defect, yet in himself there is none. Nor has a yoke been laid upon her, because he was not subjected to iniquity; rather, finding men subjected to it, he set them free, broke their bonds, and possessed the power to lay down his life and to take it up again. She is said to have been given not to Aaron but to Eleazar, because the Lord’s Passion was to come not for the time then present but for the successors of that priesthood. She was led outside the camp; likewise the Lord was led outside the city. And she was led to a clean place, because the Lord had no evil cause. [Col. 0473A] She was killed in Eleazar’s sight; thus Christ’s flesh was killed in the sight of those who were to be the Lord’s priests in the New Testament. He sprinkled her blood seven times toward the front of the testimony, because Christ, according to the Scriptures, shed his blood for the remission of sins. It was toward the front of the testimony because this was declared in no other way than as had been foretold by divine testimony. It was seven times because that number pertains to spiritual cleansing.

She was commanded to be burned outside the camp, I think, because the burning is a sign of the Resurrection. For fire naturally moves upward, and what is burned is transformed into it; moreover, the very word *cremare*, “to burn,” has passed from Greek into Latin, and in Greek is derived from suspension. She is said to have been burned in Eleazar’s sight because Christ’s Resurrection appeared to those who were to become a royal priesthood. Her hide with her flesh, and her blood with her dung, are said to have been burned because not only the mortal substance of Christ’s body, signified by hide, flesh, and blood, but also the insult and rejection by the people, signified by the name “dung,” was transformed into glory, signified by the flame of burning.

Into the midst of the burning the priest casts cedarwood, hyssop, and scarlet. Cedarwood is hope, firmly dwelling in the things above; hyssop is faith, which, though lowly, clings by its roots to the rock. Scarlet is charity, because by its fiery colour it bears witness to the Spirit’s ardour. These three [Col. 0473C] must be cast into the midst of the burning—that is, into Christ’s Resurrection—so that your life may be hidden with him. The ashes, that is, the remains of the burning and killing, are the report which followed Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. A clean man gathered these ashes and placed them in a clean place outside the camp, because this report shone forth especially among those who were not of the fellowship of the Jews, who were clean from the killing of Christ, and outside the observance of Jewish custom. From these ashes water for sprinkling was made, signifying baptism. By it people were cleansed from contact with the dead, because through Christ’s baptism we are cleansed from the iniquity of this dying, or death-dealing, life. Both proselytes and Jews were cleansed by that water, because baptism benefits Jews and Gentiles alike. The water was sprinkled with hyssop, which signifies faith, because hearts are cleansed by faith, and without faith baptism is of no benefit. This was done by a clean man, because the ministers of the Church, who bear the Lord’s person, ought truly to be clean.

**Verses 15–22.**—“And therefore he is the mediator of the New Testament, so that, death intervening for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the case of the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the one who made the testament lives. [Col. 0474A] Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood. For when every commandment of the Law had been read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: ‘This is the blood of the testament which God has commanded to you.’ Likewise he sprinkled with blood both the tabernacle and all the vessels of ministry. And almost all things are cleansed with blood according to the Law, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission.”

And therefore, since Christ offered himself, he is mediator—that is, the one standing between God and human beings—and giver of the New Testament. It is as if he said: He is our High Priest and the giver of the new Law, without which we would neither know what God wishes us to do nor what we should hope for. He is the giver of the New Testament, I say, so that those called by God—that is, chosen from eternity—may receive the promise of the eternal inheritance, that is, the inheritance often promised as eternal. This happens through Christ’s death, without which the Law would not help, intervening—that is, occurring—between the decree and its fulfilment. This death was necessary for the redemption not only of Gentiles but also of those transgressions which were under the former testament—that is, which the Law produced but did not remove. So great indeed was our sin that we could not be saved unless the only-begotten Son of God died for us who were liable to death. Yet in this way he made us worthy of the testament and the promised inheritance, and made the testament firm, [Col. 0474C] as is shown below.

Here is a manifest difference between the Testaments. Between the Old Testament and the New, in which not only the sacraments but also the promises differ, Christ’s Passion is the distinction: in his death it is established that not earthly but eternal things are promised.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Augustine, in the book *On the Evening Sacrifice*.] In the death of the Only-Begotten, great things must be hoped for. Having said that Christ is giver of the New Testament with death intervening, he now proves by the custom of human law that he had to die for its confirmation. For the weak might, because Christ died, fail to believe the promises. Therefore he proves this by human custom. It is as though he said: I rightly said, “death intervening,” for wherever there is a testament, the death of the testator must intervene—that is, occur [Col. 0474D] before confirmation. And indeed, a testament is always confirmed among the dead by the testator’s death; so too the New Testament—that is, the promise of eternal life and evangelical teaching. Both are called the New Testament; both were confirmed by Christ’s death. Therefore, as a testament is confirmed by the testator’s death, so he willed to die in order to establish what he testified that he would give, lest anyone doubt it. Nor could life otherwise be ours: by his death he also confirmed the Gospel in us, so that, because he died for us, we may love his commands and hold them as authoritative; and by death he obtained for us the grace by which we may fulfil them.

“Otherwise.” It is as if he said: A testament is confirmed by death while—that is, as long as—the one who made it lives, for he can change it if he wishes. Hence, because a testament is made firm by death, not even the first testament was dedicated—that is, made firm and strengthened—without blood. This was a figure of the future, namely, that it would be confirmed by Christ’s blood. And indeed the Old Testament was not confirmed without blood. For Moses first read every commandment of the Law to all the people, so as to confirm the whole. Having read it, Moses himself took the mixed blood of goats and calves with water, which signifies the future cleansing through the water of baptism.

[Chrysostom.] For he took water and blood together, because our baptism was there prefigured, as also Christ’s Passion; the two go together, since one is of no avail without the other. Taking it, I say, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, from which he made an instrument for sprinkling, he sprinkled both the book of the Law and all the people, saying: “This is the confirming blood of the testament,” that is, blood shed to confirm the testament which God commanded to you. See how exactly Moses foretold the words which Christ later used at supper, when he gave his body and blood to his disciples. He likewise sprinkled the tabernacle, as he did the book, and all the vessels of ministry—that is, those belonging to the tabernacle’s service—with blood. It was with blood because almost all things are cleansed with blood according to the Law. He says “almost,” because certain vessels were washed with water alone; but within us nothing is cleansed without Christ’s blood. Whatever may be true of other things, remission of sin does not occur in the old Law without the shedding of blood in some sacrifice. This qualification is added because forgiveness of sins was sometimes effected through water for sprinkling made from the red heifer’s ashes, when blood was not being shed; yet it had been shed in the heifer’s immolation.

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Augustine, *Against Faustus*.] Although those sacrifices were imposed more suitably upon a perverse people than offered to a God who desired them, they were nevertheless figures of the truth, which is Christ. By his blood we have been redeemed and cleansed, because without blood there is for us neither cleansing nor God’s propitiation. Therefore, just as Moses took the blood of the aforesaid animals in order to sprinkle and cleanse the aforesaid things with it, so Moses—that is, Christ—having given the new Law, appears to have taken for this work his own blood, mingled with water from his side. He was called a calf because of the power of the cross, with whose horns he scattered the ungodly; and a goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, and because he is a sin-offering. Through water, signifying baptism, he redeemed us by the price of blood. Scarlet wool, being fiery in colour, signifies the fire of Christ’s love. For Christ’s charity is to us the wool from which we make a garment—that is, with which we are clothed. Hyssop, which is effective against swelling of the lungs, [Col. 0476A] signifies Christ’s humility. Through the ardour of love and humility he shed his blood for our redemption. With that blood he sanctified—that is, confirmed—the book, namely the Gospel, and washed the people of believers, saying: “This is the confirming blood of the New Testament, which God commanded to you.” He sprinkled the tabernacle, that is, the Church, of which the Apostle says: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). He sprinkled all the vessels of ministry, that is, those holding offices in the Church, because he redeemed by his blood all the more learned members of the Church, in whom its mysteries are contained; and to the redeemed he gave the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge. All things are cleansed by Christ’s blood, and without it there is no remission of anyone’s sin.

The aforesaid objects may also signify the people of God. For that people is the book, the tabernacle, and the vessels for whom precious blood was shed. For he says: “Which shall be shed for many” (Matt. 26). These are God’s people—that is, the elect—who are spiritually cleansed by blood shed for the remission of sins; other things are not changed.

**Verses 23–28.**—“It was necessary, therefore, that the copies of heavenly things should be cleansed by these; but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these. For Jesus did not enter into sanctuaries made by hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God for us; nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the sanctuary every year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer often [Col. 0476C] from the foundation of the world. But now, once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared through his own sacrifice for the abolition of sin. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this judgment, so Christ too was offered once, to exhaust the sins of many; a second time, without sin, he will appear to all who await him, for salvation.”

254 “It was necessary.” It is as if he said: Since Moses did this and the Law commands it, it was necessary that the copies—that is, the figures of the heavenly things, namely the Church which is led to heaven, that is, the saints of whom it is said, “Your citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3)—should be cleansed bodily by these aforementioned things. But the heavenly things themselves—that is, those signified by them, namely the Church, which, though it is on earth, is nevertheless heavenly—had to be cleansed by better sacrifices than these, that is, by Christ’s sacrifice. Yet he speaks in the plural, “sacrifices,” because Christ is all those sacrifices, since he was signified in all of them.

[Jerome.] Therefore Christ, who was signified in those things, did not need cleansing; but all who belong to him did. Yet his signs, since they performed the service of ministry in the tabernacle, were cleansed with blood. “For Jesus did not enter.” [Remigius] He proves that Christ cleansed the heavenly things—that is, that by his blood he made cleansed human beings heavenly, sharers in heavenly things. For by his own sacrifice he entered heaven. Jesus did not enter sanctuaries made by hands, or those of the saints. Why not? Because those are not [Col. 0477A] the true sanctuaries, but only copies—that is, figures—of the true holy things; and the true priest had to enter not into shadowy things but into the true things. Hence he adds: “But he entered heaven itself,” signified by those things. For what purpose? That he might now—that is, after the consummation—appear before the face, that is, the presence, of God for us; that is, there he intercedes for us, so that God’s presence may be seen as it is, and that he may draw us after himself to see it also.

In these words the Apostle plainly explains the better sacrifices, which are one sacrifice, namely Christ. Note that customary usage would require and approve the text here to be written either, “in sanctuaries made by hands, copies of the true ones,” or, “in a sanctuary made by hands, a copy of the true ones,” as is also found in Greek manuscripts.

“Nor that he should offer himself often.” He has proved that Christ by his sacrifice cleansed the heavenly things; now he proves that the better sacrifices mean that his sacrifice was worthier and more effective than all others, because those sacrifices were repeatedly offered without bringing completion. This one, offered once, brings us back to the homeland, as he now appears before God’s face. Nor indeed does he appear so as to offer himself often—that is, to suffer often on the cross—because, offered once, he is sufficient for all, and there is no need for repetition in every generation. If it had not sufficed for these, neither would it have sufficed for the ancients who likewise had to be redeemed, as he shows below.

“Just as.” It is as if he said: He does not appear in order to offer himself often, as the high priest of the Law enters within the Holy of Holies each year with another’s blood; Christ, however, entered heaven once with [Col. 0477C] his own blood. Consider how great are the differences between the Old and New Testaments. In place of the copy—that is, the temple which was there—here is heaven. The great priest also differs, because he stands ever living before God’s face to intercede for us. There he offered often; here once. There with another’s blood; here with his own. Therefore he is both priest and sacrifice.

“Otherwise.” It is as if he said: I say that he does not offer himself often; otherwise, if he had had to offer himself often, he would have had to suffer repeatedly, beginning from the foundation of the world. That was certainly unnecessary, because his one offering is sufficient.

[Ambrose.] If, offered once, he had not sufficed to exhaust the sins of all who believe in him, he would have had to suffer more often from the foundation of the world. To prevent this, he suffered once at the consummation of the ages. Hence he adds: “But now”: from the aforementioned impossibility it is established that he appeared to the Father through his sacrifice, offered not often but once, for the abolition of sin—that is, so that guilt might be forgiven and vice might no longer rule in us. No other sacrifice could do this. “At the consummation of the ages,” in the last age of the world, in which all things formerly incomplete have been fulfilled; and therefore there was no need for him to begin suffering from the foundation of the world.

“And just as.” Again, this proves that he had to suffer only once, because the law of nature has established this for all human beings. It is as if he said: Natural law also shows what has been proved from the impossibility. For just as it is appointed to human beings by natural law to die once, [Col. 0478A] and after this—that is, after dying once—judgment remains, in which they receive according to their deserts, that is, are judged according to their merits, and it does not remain for them to rise again and die again, so Christ too, by the same necessity and law of nature, was offered not once but often; otherwise he would be more wretched than all human beings. This must not be understood as though he was offered even once from any necessity arising from his own sin; rather, it was by will alone. But as a human being dies once by necessity and the law of nature and dies no more, so Christ, having been offered once by the same law, cannot die again. Nor do we need him to do so, because that one offering suffices to exhaust sins. I do not say the sins of all, but of many, because not all believe. At his second coming, coming for judgment, [Col. 0478B] he will appear to those awaiting him for their salvation, because he died for sins not by necessity but by will. He will appear, I say, “without sin,” namely without the likeness of sinful flesh, but rather in glorious flesh. Or, “he will appear without sin,” that is, so that then he will not be a sacrifice for sin, but justice in rewarding or condemning; and if he will not be a sacrifice even on the day of wrath, much less at other times.

## Chapter 10

**Verses 1–6.**—“For the Law, having a shadow of good things to come and not the very image of things, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually every year, make those who draw near perfect. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshippers, once cleansed, would have had no further consciousness of sin? [Col. 0478C] But in them a remembrance of sins is made every year. For it is impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of bulls and goats. Therefore, when he enters the world, he says: ‘Sacrifice and offering you did not will, but you prepared a body for me; burnt offerings and sin-offerings did not please you.’”

“For the Law, having a shadow.” He has proved that Christ died once; but why even once? Because the Law could not make people perfect; therefore the spotless Lamb had to be offered.

[Chrysostom.] It is as if he said: Christ was offered to exhaust sins, and this was necessary because the Law, having a shadow of the good things to come—that is, an external likeness of the good things which were to come, not the very image of things, which expresses [Col. 0478D] a thing better than a shadow, that is, not the very truth—can never make perfect in virtues and blessed those high priests who draw near each year to the Holy of Holies with the same sacrifices commanded by the Law, which they offer without interruption, that is, even if they offered them unceasingly and always performed them. “Otherwise,” that is, if they were made perfect, those sacrifices would have ceased to be offered, precisely because worshippers cleansed once—that is, perfectly cleansed by one sacrifice—would have no consciousness of sin; whereas, while those sacrifices are always offered, they always have it.

But Christ’s one sacrifice makes perfect. Even if they sin a thousand times, they need no other, because it suffices for all things and washes every consciousness from sin, which the old sacrifice did not do. If the old sacrifice had done this, it would not have needed to be repeated. Just as a medicine, if it is strong, health-giving, and able to restore complete health, accomplishes everything when applied once; but if it is always reapplied, this is manifest evidence that it has brought no benefit: so, because no one was cured by those sacrifices, they were offered repeatedly. Since the first sacrifice availed nothing, it was offered a second time; and since that did no good, another was offered. The frequent offering of sacrifices was not the consuming of faults.

Rather, in those sacrifices offered every year there is a remembrance of sins, because they are offered for sins. Thus it is evident that those offering [Col. 0479B] the sacrifices in which there is remembrance of sins have sin, not release from weakness; accusation, not a manifestation of strength. Therefore God commanded those sacrifices always to be offered, in order to display weakness and to preserve the memory of sins.

What, then, of us? Do we not offer every day? We certainly do offer.

[Chrysostom.] Yet even if we offer daily, we do it in remembrance of his death; and this sacrifice is one, not many, because it was offered once only.

[Ambrose.] This sacrifice is an image of that one: we always offer the same thing; nor are many Christs offered by many people, but Christ is one everywhere—whole here and whole there. Everywhere it is one body that is offered; therefore there is one sacrifice, not many. Our high priest offered the cleansing sacrifice; we offer that same sacrifice, and, though offered then and now, it can never be consumed. What we do is the remembrance of the sacrifice. It is not repeated because of its own weakness, because it perfects the human being, but because of ours, because we sin daily. Therefore in the legal sacrifices there was remembrance, not abolition; but here there is the deletion of sins, the perfection of virtue, and the disclosure of our weakness. It is celebrated for two reasons: for our weakness, as has been said, and so that greater love of Christ may be impressed on our minds when we recall how much he did for us.

“It is impossible.” It is as if he said: In those sacrifices we acknowledge that we are in sin; for it is impossible for sins to be removed by the blood [Col. 0479D] of bulls and goats. “Therefore,” and so forth. It is as if he said: Since Christ’s sacrifice suffices and the Old Testament does not make perfect, therefore God, entering the world—that is, becoming human, by which he became visible in the world—speaks to the Father in words or deeds: “O Father, from the time of the Passion you did not will sacrifice from animals or offering from other things; but you prepared for me a body, which is above all sacrifices—that is, you gave me a fitting and suitable body, without sin, yet capable of suffering and mortal, able to be offered for the redemption of all.” The signs were therefore removed because the truth was presented. When the time came for them to be removed, they were removed and the truth came.

The Lord was never delighted in those odours except through the faith and desire of the one offering. Yet he commanded them to be offered to himself rather than to idols; he imposed them as servitude, not as justification, and so that they might be figures of the future. Of their rejection he adds: “Burnt offerings,” which seemed worthier than other sacrifices because they were wholly burned, “and sin-offerings did not please you.” For some sacrifices were not offered for sin. Those, I say, which were worthier than the others, did not please you once the truth came.

[Jerome.] From the time of the Passion, in which all sacrifices reached completion, they began to displease God.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Augustine, on Psalm 30.] Before then he never abolished them, but was subject to them when he was presented in the temple with sacrifices. In those figures the truth was foretold. Many celebrated the figures of the future reality knowingly, but more did so ignorantly; they had to cease when the reality had been presented. Hence follows:

**Verses 7–17.**—“Then I said: ‘Behold, I come. In the head of the book it is written of me: to do your will, O God.’ Having said above, ‘Sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings, and sin-offerings you did not will, nor did they please you, though they are offered according to the Law,’ then I said: ‘Behold, I come to do your will, O God.’ He removes the first in order to establish that which follows. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. Every priest indeed stands daily ministering and frequently offering the same sacrifices, which cannot remove sins. But this man, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at [Col. 0480C] the right hand of God, henceforth awaiting until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified. And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us. For after he said: ‘This is the testament which I shall make with them after those days, says the Lord: giving my laws in their hearts, and I shall write them upon their minds’; and, ‘Their sins and iniquities I shall remember no more.’”

Then, namely when I saw that all those things displeased you and that a body fit for this purpose had been given to me, I said: “Behold, without any delay I come to offer myself.” He is himself both offerer and offering. He willed the Church’s daily sacrifice to be the sacrament of this reality. The ancient sacrifices were multiple and varied signs of this true sacrifice. By those many sacrifices this one was signified, as though one thing were said in many words, so that it might be strongly commended without weariness. All sacrifices gave way to this highest and true sacrifice, so that remission of sins might occur in the priest and sacrifice himself, that is, through the man Christ. Thus he says: “I come to offer myself, to do and fulfil your will,” namely so that what the Law could not do may be fulfilled through me, because you are my God insofar as I am human. Therefore I come to fulfil your will. For thus it is written—that is, decreed—of me in the head of the book, that is, in the counsel of the Godhead which is my head. I am the book of the human race, in which all may read what is necessary for them; and therefore there is no need for the Law. Or, “it is written in the head of the book,” that is, in the first Psalm, “Blessed is the man,” which is called the head of the Psalter.

“Having said above.” Here the Apostle explains what he understands by that Scripture. It is as if he said: That authority not only indicates that the old sacrifices did not make people perfect, but, if its words are carefully noted, that Christ’s sacrifice alone also brought about the abolition of the Old Testament and the establishment of the New. For above the Prophet said: “You no longer willed offerings, burnt offerings, and sin-offerings, nor did they please you,” although they were offered according to the Law. He says this lest they should seem displeasing because they were not offered according to the Law. Having said this, he adds: [Col. 0481B] “Then I said: Behold, I come to do your will, O God.” In saying this, he removes the first sacrifice, and with it the Old Testament given through Moses, in order to establish as firm that which follows, namely the new sacrifice, and with it the New Testament, that is, the Gospel.

By that will—that is, by his offering, made according to God’s will—we have been sanctified, that is, reconciled to God through cleansing from sins, namely through the once-made offering of the body of Jesus Christ. Therefore, once this has been established, the former falls, because it could not accomplish this.

“And every priest.” He further explains the power of this sacrifice. Lest it should seem that blood offered once a year by high priests was less effective, while daily sacrifices offered by priests made people perfect, he adds this. It is as if he said: The high priest who offers yearly does not attain completion; likewise every priest of the Law stands by, as a servant, daily ministering prayers and many gifts, and frequently offering the same animal sacrifices, because they do not cleanse completely. Hence he adds: “Which can never”—that is, at no time, however often they may be performed—“remove sins from the conscience.” Note that ministering belongs to servants, while sitting belongs to lords. Therefore the Apostle shows those priests to be servants, but Christ to be Lord, whom he subsequently says sits.

“But this man,” namely Christ, whose sacrifice is sufficient, having offered one sacrifice for the sins of all, a sacrifice able to save by completed obedience, sits—that is, [Col. 0481D] rests and reigns—forever at the right hand of God, that is, among the higher goods. He need not labour again or offer again. He is rightly able to bring perfection because he deserved such exaltation. He sits, I say, henceforth—that is, with respect to what remains, namely the glory of the good and punishment of the evil—awaiting, not so that he suffers anything because of an imperfection in himself or his own, but without suffering himself he delays and bears patiently until his enemies are made the footstool of his feet; that is, until they are wholly subjected to him and are shown to be subject to him. He can do this even now; but he endures until the common judgment, when his enemies will truly be his footstool. Though they now resist him and do not seem subject, then all will see that they are subject to him, under whose rule they will endure punishments.

“For by one offering.” He offered only one sacrifice because there is one offering, and by it he sanctified the elect from sin. He perfected those sanctified in every virtue. And this is forever, that is, for as long as this age endures.

“And the Holy Spirit bears witness.” It is as if he said: Not I alone affirm this, but the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us—that is, confirms our words concerning sanctification. “For after he said”: it is as if he said, He truly bears witness, for what he promises is true and he commands nothing but what is just. After the Holy Spirit had said in Jeremiah, “This is the New Testament which I shall make with them after those days, says the Lord,” he added, “Giving my laws in their hearts.”

It is as if he said: After he stated that which does not suffice for our proof, he added these other words which strengthen both points we have made: “Giving my laws,” which pertains to perfection; and again, “I shall remember their sins no more,” which pertains to sanctification. Thus by Jeremiah’s authority he confirms both things he had said. Read the text thus: “I shall make,” I say, “the testament by giving my laws,” not as I gave them to the fathers on stone tablets, but in their hearts—that is, their understandings—and I shall write them upon their minds—that is, their wills—namely my commandments. He does not say merely “I shall write,” but “I shall write upon,” because those laws exceed human powers, so that no one could fulfil them except with the help of grace. Here it is said that he perfects in virtues. Then he adds concerning sanctification, saying: “And their sins,” committed against themselves, “and their iniquities,” committed against their neighbour, [Col. 0482C] “I shall remember no more,” that is, after the time of grace, I shall not remember them for eternal punishment, ever again, not even in the future. Here it is said that he sanctifies.

Or distinguish the text in this way, while retaining the same meaning: After he said, “This is the testament which I shall make with them after those days, says the Lord,” he said, “I shall make it by giving my laws in their hearts and writing them upon their minds”; he then added, “And their sins and iniquities I shall remember no more.” Therefore a sacrifice is no longer necessary, as he makes clear in what follows.

**Verses 18–33.**—But where there is remission of these things, there is no longer an offering for sin. Therefore, brethren, having confidence for entry into the holy places through the blood of Christ, [Col. 0482D] by the new and living way which he inaugurated for us through the veil, that is, his flesh, and having a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience and our body washed with pure water. Let us hold unwaveringly the confession of our hope, for he who promised is faithful. And let us consider one another so as to provoke love and good works, not abandoning our assembly, as some are accustomed to do, but encouraging one another—and this all the more as you see the Day approaching. For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire that will consume the adversaries. Anyone who sets aside the law of [Col. 0483A] Moses dies without any mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as unclean the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” And again: “The Lord will judge his people.” It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God. But remember the former days, in which, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings: on the one hand you yourselves were made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations; on the other, you became companions of those who were so treated.

**256. But where there is.** Here he shows that not only can it be seen from this authority that Jesus sanctifies and perfects, but also that after the time of [Col. 0483B] grace an offering for sin is no longer to be made, because remission has been effected. As though he said: “Behold, remission of sins is here said to have been made; but where there is now remission of these things, an offering for sin is not to be made,” that is, the legal offering ceases.

“Therefore, having.” Having completed his great discourse concerning the high priest, his new law, and sacrifice—which he preferred to the old institutions—he adds a moral instruction. In it he exhorts them to many things, but especially to faith, patience, peace, purity, and brotherly love; and he draws the conclusion from all the foregoing. As though he said: “Because one sacrifice perfects, and because it is for us—namely, or. m. [sic]—and because such a great difference has been shown, since those things are lesser and these greater.” [Chrysostom.]

Therefore, brethren, we have confidence for entry into the holy places through the blood of Christ; that is, [Col. 0483C] we are certain that we shall enter the heavenly Holy of Holies through Christ’s blood. Christ, who first ascended, inaugurated this way for us—that is, this entrance—and through this we are certain concerning ourselves. It is a new way, because no one entered before him; and a living, that is, enduring and passable, way, because afterward it was closed to none of the faithful. He opened that way, and kept it passable.

“Through the veil,” that is, through his flesh. It is called a veil because the flesh itself veiled and concealed the divinity. Or it is called a veil because it is received by believers under the veil of faith. As though he said: That way remains passable because believers receive, as provision for their journey, Christ’s flesh veiled from every sense. Bread is seen, yet it is truly the flesh of Christ. [Col. 0483D] This is so that the merit of faith may be increased, since faith has no merit where human reason—that is, human sense—offers proof by experience. Therefore, through the veil, that is, through the flesh received under a veil, the way remains passable; and it remains so because that priest always intercedes for us.

Hence he adds: “And [having] a priest”—namely Christ, great above all—“over the house,” that is, the people, of God; and having this confidence, let us draw near. Or thus: “And a great priest.” As though he said: “We have this confidence, and having it, and having a great priest over the gift of God”—namely, one who always lives to intercede for us—“let us draw near to the entrance of the holy places, with a true heart,” that is, with a true and unfeigned understanding. And if this cannot be so, at least let us draw near “in fullness [Col. 0484A] of faith,” that is, in full faith. For none of these things—the priest or the sacrifice—is now visible.

This is both what we ought and what we can do, because we have had our hearts sprinkled, that is, cleansed by spiritual sprinkling from an evil conscience, namely from a consciousness of wickedness. The former people, however, had only their bodies washed; whereas we have had our body washed with pure water, that is, bodily sin—namely original sin, contracted through the concupiscence of the flesh—has been washed away by the water of baptism. This shows that not faith alone but a good life with virtues is required.

He then exhorts them to those things that accord with faith, adding:
