“Let us hold.” [Ambrose.] As though he said: “Whatever may happen, let us hold unwaveringly”—so that we do not turn aside to earthly things—“the confession of our hope,” which [Col. 0484B] concerns eternal things; that is, let us hold the confession and the hope which is its cause. This hope is not empty and does not put to shame. For God, who promised the things for which we hope, is faithful—that is, true in his promises. And as God is faithful in his promises, so he wishes us to be faithful to him in ours.

Let us hold, I say, and “consider one another,” one person, namely, another—not in order to envy or plot against him, but for the provoking of inward love and of good works: so that one may be stirred by another’s example to love and to do good. The sense is: Let us have faith and confession with respect to ourselves; and let us consider one another—the perfect exhorting the less mature, and the less mature imitating the perfect.

Let us consider one another, I say, not abandoning, in time of persecution, [Col. 0484C] our assembly, that is, those gathered with us in faith, as some among you are accustomed to do. Either from fear of persecution they yield, or, in their own presumption, they withdraw from sinners or the imperfect in order to appear righteous. He therefore censures those who break the unity of love, as though they could not dwell among others because of their holiness, when rather they ought by their example to encourage others. Hence he adds: “But rather encouraging them.” One who stands alongside another in labor encourages the laborer, because the sight of a fellow-worker lightens toil, as happens on a journey.

And let us encourage one another all the more as you see the day of recompense approaching through suffering. As though he said: “The nearer you are to the end and to the reward of recompense, [Col. 0484D] the more earnestly persevere, lest anyone be lacking through your fault.”

“For if we sin willingly.” As though he said: “Love must surely be maintained and evils abandoned. For if we sin willingly”—that is, if we remain in the will to sin—“there remains no sacrifice for sins,” that is, Christ, who is the sacrifice, does not profit us for sins. “There remains no [sacrifice],” I say, now, namely in this present life; from which it follows that neither does one remain in the future. “There remains no [sacrifice],” I say, after receiving the knowledge of the truth, that is, after we have come to the faith through which some are secure, as though they could never perish.

Observe that he does not say “those wishing to sin,” but “those sinning willingly.” A voluntary sinner is one who persists in something; one who merely wills does so for a time. By this he means those who persevere until the end. [Chrysostom.] [Col. 0485A]

Or thus: “There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,” that is, Christ, who is the sacrifice for sins, will not again be immolated. There remains no place for a second sacrifice, as under the old law sacrifices for sin were given to be offered repeatedly. For Christ is not to be immolated again for sin: what was done once does not need to be done a second time. Rather, there is need to remain in faith and truth. If you do not do this, judgment of condemnation awaits you unless you are renewed through repentance. Therefore he adds:

“But a fearful [expectation].” Yet it must be known that some arise here, taking occasion from these words to abolish repentance, as though through repentance a sinner could not rise again after a fall a second, third, or subsequent time. But in this passage he does not exclude repentance [Col. 0485B] or the propitiation effected through repentance. He is not so hostile to our salvation; rather, he excludes a second baptism. For he does not say, “There is no further repentance or remission,” but “sacrifice,” that is, a second cross, when one was sufficient. He wishes us not to expect this further, but to repent.

“But a fearful [expectation].” As though he said: “No sacrifice remains for sins, but there remains a certain fearful expectation of judgment.” This is the present punishment, and “a zeal of fire,” that is, an assault—an attacking fire—which will consume Christ’s adversaries. He proves this from the lesser case. For anyone who makes void, that is, transgresses, the law of Moses and is convicted by two or three witnesses dies without any mercy, by the death prescribed by the law. [Jerome.] [Col. 0485C] What then will those do against whom angels, saints, and their own conscience will bear testimony? As though he said: “They will be punished far more severely.”

Hence he adds: “How much worse punishments, then, do you think he deserves who has trampled underfoot the Son of God,” that is, despised him, if he believes that Christ is not sufficient for salvation but that animals are; and who has regarded as unclean the blood of Christ, confirmer of the New Testament, as though it could not cleanse sin. Yet by that blood he was sanctified, that is, received remission, and thus sins grievously against it.

For he regards Christ’s blood as unclean who believes sins to be forgiven through fleshly observances, from which Christ’s blood draws us back. In this way it is defiled, and it defiles us if it draws us back from that through which remission comes. And he insults “the Spirit of grace,” that is, the Holy Spirit freely given, or the Spirit who gives grace. He insults the Spirit when he ascribes to fleshly observances the remission which the Spirit himself effects, or when through evil living he casts the Spirit away from himself.

Or, the person who sins freely without fear and repentance tramples Christ underfoot; and one who partakes of him unworthily regards the blood as unclean if, after being cleansed by it, he returns to his vomit and neglects repentance. He wrongs the Spirit if he does not receive his benefit gratefully. [Col. 0485D]

“For we know.” As though he said: “Such a person will truly be punished, for we know him”—that is, how true and powerful is he who said: “Reserve for me vengeance for your injuries, and I will repay.” If he avenges injuries done to others as well as his own, and Scripture again says that the Lord will judge his people by cleansing them and separating them from the wicked, how much more will he punish [Col. 0486A] his enemies.

“It is dreadful.” As though he said: “The Lord will punish his enemies, and not lightly. Therefore it is dreadful to fall into the hands of God,” that is, he falls who does not take heed but is caught suddenly. I mean the living God, who is always effective and powerful to do what he wills.

“But remember.” Just as the best physicians, when they have cut others and increased pain by the incision, bring consolation and remedy with gentler medicines, soothing the place where pain is and restoring the troubled soul, so the Apostle acts. After he has shaken and terrified their souls, he restores them by praise of their former conduct, recalling their earlier good works so that he may more readily stir them to what remains. As though he said: “But in order that you may not fall into the hands of God, remember the former days.” As though he said: “You have believed for a long [Col. 0486B] time, and are therefore more practiced. In those days, after you were enlightened by the faith for which tribulation came, you endured a great contest of sufferings.” For sufferings were as though contending against them, in order to force out their patience and faith. If they endured while inexperienced, it is shameful if they now fail.

Their sufferings arose partly from their own pains, partly from the pains of others with whom they suffered. Hence he adds: “And on the one hand.” As though he said: “You endured a great contest—and a great contest indeed—because, on the one hand,” that is, in one part of the contest, namely in your own reproaches and tribulations, you yourselves became a spectacle to all, which is most grievous. Reproach is grievous; but it is more grievous when one becomes a spectacle to all and is not reproached in secret. [Col. 0486C]

“But on the other hand,” that is, in the other part of the contest, namely in the pain you felt for others, you became companions of those so treated—that is, of those who suffered continually, whose example you ought to follow; in other words, you had compassion on the apostles and others of this kind. The sense is: You endured the contest of suffering both in your own sufferings and in compassion for the sufferings of others. **257** These are the two forms of suffering that contended against you, and you truly became their companions.

**Verses 34–39.**—For you also had compassion on prisoners, and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have a better and abiding possession. Therefore do not lose your confidence, [Col. 0486D] which has a great reward. For you have need of patience, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a very little while, and he who is to come will come and will not delay. But my righteous one lives by faith; and if he draws back, my soul will not be pleased with him. But we are not children of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul.

“For you also had compassion on prisoners,” who could not procure necessities for themselves, supplying them with what was needed; for this reason, when your own possessions were taken away, you had compassion on them. And this is what follows: “And you accepted the plundering of your possessions.” As though he said: “This was God’s gift.” And you accepted it with joy because you hoped for better things, namely eternal ones. Hence he adds: “You,” I say, “knowing that you have [Col. 0487A] a better and abiding possession,” that is, eternal life.

“Do not [lose it].” As though he said: “Since you have suffered thus and have trusted in a better and abiding possession, do not, through impatience, lose your confidence.” It will not merely have a great reward in the future; it already has it while it hopes. Therefore its loss is no slight matter. But in order that you may not lose it, you need this one thing: patience. For patience is necessary for us.

Here he shows how confidence is not lost: namely, if patience is maintained. For the Lord says: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). Therefore he says patience is necessary for us, so that by it, doing God’s will, you may receive in the future the promise—that is, [Col. 0487B] the promised life—which you sow here.

“For yet.” As though he said: “Patience must be maintained, for the tribulation is not long, though it is severe.” This is what he says: “For yet a very little while,” that is, for a short time, “and a little,” that is, suffering is not to be endured very intensely; and soon he who is at some time to come, the rewarder, will come and will not delay. For in martyrs, after death, glory is immediately given where there is nothing to be purged that might delay them from glory.

“But my righteous one.” Here he says that salvation is given through faith alone if the necessity of suffering does not arise. To confirm this, he introduces the words of God speaking through the prophet Habakkuk. As though he said: “Not only the person who suffers, but also the person who has faith alone, if suffering is not imminent, will be saved; for the Lord says [Col. 0487C] through the prophet: ‘My righteous one,’ that is, one righteous before me, ‘lives by faith’: through faith he will live in the future, in the eternal life which faith merits.” See how much faith avails, since it alone saves.

He shows by the contrary that one lives by faith: if one withdraws from faith, one does not live. Hence he adds: “But if he withdraws.” Or thus: “But my righteous one.” As though he said: “The Lord will come and will not delay. Meanwhile the Lord says: ‘My righteous one,’ namely one made righteous by me, not by fleshly observances, lives by faith, not by sight. Therefore let him not seek his crown here, but bear his labor.”

“But if.” As though he said: “Life truly comes from faith, because faith is the gaining of the soul—and truly so. For if anyone withdraws, my soul,” that is, God’s will, [Col. 0487D] “will not be pleased with him.”

“But we.” As though he said: “The person who withdraws from faith will not live. But we are not children of withdrawal unto destruction,” that is, of apostasy through which the soul is lost, because they had not yet entirely apostatized but had been begotten by faith. Hence he adds: “But we are children of faith, which avails for gaining [the soul]; and therefore they ought not now to withdraw from faith.”

Or: “We are not children of withdrawal unto destruction,” that is, children of unbelieving pagans who are to perish, “but [children] of faith unto the gaining of the soul,” that is, children of the faithful prophets whose faith leads to the gaining of the soul.

## Chapter XI

**Verse 1.**—Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

“Now faith.” Because he has begun to speak about faith, he shows [Col. 0488A] its dignity and use by defining faith and by the illumination of many examples. Here is praise and commendation of faith. In its description he notes three things: what faith effects in us, that it is the foundation of all good things, and that it concerns things not seen. We have discussed it fully in the Epistle to the Romans; therefore let us touch on it briefly.

As though he said: “The righteous lives by faith. Now faith is the substance of things hoped for,” that is, the cause which will at some time make hoped-for things subsist in us. That is to say: it will make us attain future goods. Faith is properly called “substance,” because it underlies things hoped for and causes them to exist in the believer in the other life. It is also the foundation of all good things, which no one can alter; without it there is no good [Col. 0488B] building.

Or, “faith is the substance of things hoped for,” that is, it causes the things hoped for already to exist in the believer’s heart even in this life. [Chrysostom.] For through faith future goods are already, as it were, in us, because it makes those unseen things concerning which faith properly speaks subsist in our souls. Faith does not concern things seen, but knowledge.

This is faith’s praise: what is believed is not seen. Thus Thomas, to whom it was said, “Because you have seen, you have believed” (John 20), did not believe what he saw: he saw one thing and believed another. He saw a man; he believed God. He beheld and touched living flesh which he had seen dying, and believed God hidden in that very flesh. Therefore he believed in his mind what he did not see by means of what appeared to his bodily senses. If things that are seen are said to be believed—as when each person says that he has believed his own eyes—this is not the faith built up in us; rather, from things seen there is produced in us the belief of things unseen.

And faith is “evidence,” or conviction, of things not apparent; that is, a foretoken, certainty, and proof of things that do not appear. If anyone doubts them, they are proved through faith, as the future resurrection is still proved because the patriarchs, apostles, and other saints so believed. Faith, therefore, is proof of things not yet present; because if one considers what Abraham and others received by the merit of faith, one can believe and hope the same concerning oneself.

**Verses 2–4.**—For by it the elders received testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were fitted together by the word of God, so that visible things came to be from invisible things. By faith Abel offered God a much greater sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks.

“For by it.” As though he said: “Faith is truly the cause of hoped-for things, because it is the cause of righteousness, through which such things are to be hoped for.” This is what he says: “For by it,” that is, because of this faith, “the elders,” that is, the ancient fathers, received from God or from human beings testimony of righteousness, because God testified on account of faith that they were righteous. He calls them elders not because of their age, but because they were the predecessors of these people. Thus it is clear that faith is not new, since the ancients held it.

“By faith we understand.” He uses examples in praise of faith and to show that faith does not concern visible things. As though he said: “Faith is evidence of things not apparent; that is, we must believe what does not appear. Thus we understand by faith alone that the ages were fitted together,” that is, wisely ordered, “by the word of God,” that is, by God’s command, so that visible things were formed from invisible things, that is, from unformed elements.

Before God arranged the forms of all things in their places and stations by an ordered distinction, there were darkness and invisible elements; but in their separation light came to be. Therefore the first matter was made confused and unformed, from which all distinct and formed things were to be made. I believe that the Greeks call it *chaos*. [Note: [Col. 0489D] Augustine, *Against the Manichees*.]

Therefore God is rightly believed to have made all things from nothing. Even if all formed things were made from that matter, this matter itself was nevertheless made from nothing. Moses signified it when he said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” etc. (Gen. 1). By the names “heaven” and “earth”—the things that would later come from it—he signified the unformed and confused matter, called *chaos*; that is, he used the names of visible things because of the weakness of little children, who are less able to grasp invisible things.

And then there was darkness, that is, the absence of light. For darkness is not a thing, but the absence of light itself; just as silence is not some thing; just as, in a body, where there is no covering, there is said to be nakedness; and just as emptiness [Col. 0489C] is not something, but a place where no body is is called empty. This same unformed matter was also called “earth invisible and unformed”: earth, because among all the elements of the world earth is less beautiful than the rest; invisible because of darkness.

The same unformed matter was also called water, over which the Spirit of the Lord moved, just as the will of an artisan moves over things to be fashioned. That matter was called water because all things that grow on earth—animals, trees, herbs, and the like—begin to be formed and nourished from moisture. The same matter was also called the abyss because it was confused, mixed together, and without form.

Thus all these terms—heaven and earth; earth invisible and unformed, **258** and the abyss with darkness; and water over [Col. 0489D] which the Spirit moved—designate that unformed matter, in order that an unknown thing might be made intelligible to the less learned by familiar terms, and not by one term alone. For if it had been expressed by one term, people would have thought it to be what they were accustomed to understand by that term.

Under all these names, then, was signified that unseen and unformed matter, which could be neither seen nor touched under any form, from which God made the world. The Apostle signifies this when he says “visible things.” But when he says “from invisible things,” he signifies that unformed nature.

Or, by “invisible things” is signified the invisible world which existed in the wisdom of God, after whose likeness this visible world was made. [Note: [Col. 0490D] Augustine, *On Genesis*.] These visible things, indeed, did not exist before they were made. How, then, were things that did not exist known to God? And again, how could he make things that were not known to him? For he made nothing in ignorance. Therefore, he makes them by knowing them; he does not know them once made. Accordingly, before they were made, they both were and were not: they were in God’s knowledge, but not in their own nature.

I do not dare say that they became known to God in one way when he made them and in another way when he knew them in order to make them; with him there is no change or shadow of turning (James 1). Therefore he says, “so that visible things came to be from invisible things,” that is, from the intelligible world which existed in God’s wisdom. This is God’s disposition by which he ordered all things, so that these visible things might come to be according to the invisible exemplar that was in God’s mind. [Col. 0490A]

“By faith [Abel offered] a much greater [sacrifice],” or “a greater [sacrifice] by much,” because the ancient fathers received testimony of righteousness through faith. He gives another example in commendation of faith. As though he said: “The elders received testimony of righteousness by faith, as is clear in this case: Abel, by faith,” that is, by faith in invisible things, “offered God a much greater sacrifice,” that is, one more acceptable and of greater value than Cain’s.

Or: Abel offered to God a sacrifice “by much greater faith than Cain,” because Abel was righteous by faith. Hence he adds: “Through that faith he deserved to be righteous,” and received testimony of this fact. Hence Jesus himself says: “From the blood of righteous Abel,” etc. (Matt. 23). He received testimony, I say, God himself bearing witness even to his gifts, because he received them—that is, approved them—as was shown when he consumed them with heavenly fire.

“And through it, though dead, he still speaks,” that is, he still provides us matter for speech, so that we may offer his faith as an example. Death did not extinguish the renown of his faith: his faith was so great that death did not extinguish it. He comforts these people by the faith and patience of the preceding fathers. Therefore he says that Abel still speaks, because by his example he admonishes others to be righteous. Death indeed killed him, but it did not kill along with him his glory and memory.

**Verses 5–12.**—By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, and he was not found because the Lord translated him. For before his translation he had testimony that he had pleased God. But without faith it is impossible to please God. For one approaching God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. [Col. 0490D] By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things not yet seen, moved by fear prepared an ark for the salvation of his household; through it he condemned the world and was appointed heir of the righteousness that is by faith. By faith Abraham, who was called, obeyed in going out into the place which he was to receive as an inheritance, and went out not knowing where he was going. By faith he sojourned in the land of promise as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise. For he awaited the city having foundations, whose designer and builder is God. By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power for the conception of seed, even beyond the time of age, because she considered him faithful who had promised. [Col. 0491A] Therefore there sprang from one man—and him as good as dead—as many as the stars of heaven in multitude and as the innumerable sand upon the shore of the sea.

“By faith.” Here he gives another example in praise of faith, saying: “By faith,” that is, by the merit of faith, Enoch was translated into paradise, from which Adam was expelled, so that he might not see death—not merely that he might not feel it, but that he might not even, as it were from afar, see it in others. “And he was not found.” Scripture says this lest he be thought to be in some part of the world. Therefore he was not found because God translated him, who could hide him from everyone’s sight.

“Before [his translation],” etc. As though he said: “He was truly translated through faith, because through faith he was righteous; and he truly pleased God through faith.” This is what he says: “For before his translation he had testimony,” that is, [Col. 0491B] the righteous testified that he had pleased God. And he truly pleased God through faith: “For without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God.” Faith from God is necessary, because no one pleases God without it.

And truly no one can please God without faith because one cannot even approach him. For anyone approaching God must believe this: that God exists. “To be” properly belongs to God because he exists immutably; and one must believe that he is a rewarder of those who seek him. What use, then, is the law to him? Notice that no one could ever be saved without this faith. Yet this faith does not suffice for salvation.

“By faith.” He gives another example from Noah in commendation of faith, saying: Noah, having received an answer from God concerning things not yet seen, and moved by fear, prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. And he did this by faith, that is, through faith, because he believed God when he said, “The end of all flesh has come,” even though he saw no signs of the flood. He so believed what he did not see that, fearing, he built the ark; through it—namely, through faith or through the ark—he condemned the world, that is, showed it worthy of condemnation, because when it saw the ark being built, it did not believe.

And Noah himself was appointed heir of the righteousness which is by faith, that is, he was righteous by faith like his fathers. For unless he had been righteous, the Lord would not have commanded this of him.

“By faith,” etc. Here he comes down to the fathers of the Jews, showing that in them and in those before them all righteousness had its origin from faith. He gives the example of Abraham thus: “By faith,” that is, through faith, he who is now called Abraham, though formerly called Abram, obeyed in going out [Col. 0491D] into the place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out not knowing where he was going. [Augustine.] He so trusted the God whom he obeyed when he said, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” etc. (Gen. 12).

But Abraham had already done this: for this command was given to him after he had already departed from the land of the Chaldeans and had settled in Mesopotamia. The Lord did not command him to remove his body from his land, but to uproot his mind, lest he should wish to return. For he had not gone out in his mind if he was held by the desire to return; this desire, by God’s command and help and Abraham’s obedience, had to be cut away.

By faith in a better land, that is, eternal life, Abraham sojourned in the land of promise; and although it had been promised to him, he lived in it as in a foreign land and in tents. Hence he adds: “He sojourned,” I say, “in tents, living with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the same promise,” that is, as Isaac and Jacob lived there. For they did not live together at the same time. [Col. 0492A]

“For he awaited.” As though he said: “Why did Abraham live there in this way? Because he awaited the heavenly city having foundations, because it is stable and firm, whose designer and builder is God.”

“By faith Sarah herself,” though barren, in her own person and not through a substitute, received power, that is, fertility, for the conception of seed, even when she was beyond the time of age—that is, though barren and advanced in years—by this faith indeed, because she believed him faithful who had promised. She had first laughed, and although this was from joy, it was not yet with full faith; but after the angel’s words she was strengthened in faith. Abraham, too, laughed when the son was promised to him; but his laughter was one of wonder and joy, not doubt.

“Therefore,” namely because she believed God faithful, “there sprang from one”—from Sarah’s womb, or from the one father Abraham—and this one, namely the womb or Abraham, “as good as dead.” The womb of Sarah is said to have been dead with respect to conception by an elderly man. Or Abraham himself is said to have been dead for begetting by an elderly woman. For both were old, but she was also barren and had already ceased to have menstrual blood. Therefore she could no longer give birth, even had she not been barren.

For an elderly woman, even if she still has the customary female flow, cannot bear a child by an elderly man, though she can by a young man. An elderly man, however, can beget by a young woman, as Abraham after Sarah’s death was able to beget by Keturah, who was young, because he found her age vigorous. Thus Abraham’s body is said to have been already dead in this respect: at that age he could not beget by every woman who was still of childbearing age. Therefore his body was dead with respect to something, but not with respect to everything. [Col. 0492C]

From one, I say, so many sprang forth, “as the stars of heaven in multitude.” This refers to the good, who are compared to stars because of the light of virtues and their multitude; and “as the innumerable sand by the shore,” that is, the beach, “of the sea.” This refers to the wicked, who are compared to sand because of their instability and number. The sea is the Gentile world; the shore of the sea is the practice of the Gentiles. Some Jews were made near to you, but they were not wholly within Gentilism. [Col. 0492D]

**Verses 13–20.**—All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they are strangers and sojourners upon the earth. For those who say such things show that they seek a homeland. And if they had remembered the one from which they had gone out, they certainly had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better one, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. By faith Abraham, when tested, offered Isaac; and he who had received the promises was offering his only-begotten son, concerning whom it had been said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called,” reckoning that God is able even to raise from the dead. Hence he received him also in a figure. By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come.

In accordance with faith. As if he were saying: I have set forth the examples of certain persons in order to commend faith. And rightly so indeed: for all these, except Enoch, who was translated, died in faith—that is, adhering to faith—not having received the promises in their fullness during this life. Or thus: all these died without receiving the promises upon earth. And this was according to their faith. For they hoped that heavenly things, not earthly things, had been promised them; they did not receive them here. I say, the promises; rather, they were looking upon them as to be fulfilled from afar, namely after death at Christ’s coming, and greeting them—that is, rejoicing in and applauding the promises, though they were distant.

[Col. 0493B] He uses a metaphor drawn from sailors, who glimpse at a distance the cities they desire and, before entering them, greet them in anticipation. For, by a nautical metaphor, he says: “Greeting them,” that is, rejoicing in and desiring them, as sailors do when they see cities afar off. And therefore they were confessing—that is, they confessed—that they were strangers and sojourners dwelling upon the earth. Strangers are those who have nothing in a foreign country; sojourners, those who are not natives of the country. These men confessed that they were not of this world and had nothing in the world; therefore they confessed it.

For those who say this, namely that they are strangers and sojourners, indicate that they are seeking a homeland—that is, they make it understood that they seek another homeland, as they themselves were able to signify. And lest anyone suppose that they sought the country from which they had departed, he adds: “And if indeed they had remembered that country from which they came out, they certainly had opportunity to return.” But now it is clear from their unwillingness to return that they seek a better country, that is, a heavenly one. And because they seek this, God is not ashamed—that is, does not blush—to be called their God, namely the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who is called the God of angels.

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Augustine, Against Julian.]

In these men he is honoured, just as through the wicked he is blasphemed. Therefore he willed to be called their God, as though he were God of them alone, though he is God of every creature. Certainly he bestowed so great an honour upon them not without reason, but because he knew in them a sincere and outstanding love, and because in these three patriarchs he brought to completion the great and wonderful mystery of his future people.

For they begot children by free women and unto freedom: Abraham by Sarah, Isaac by Rebekah, Jacob by Leah and Rachel; and unto servitude, as Esau was begotten by Isaac through Rebekah, to whom it was said: “You shall be the servant of your brother” (Gen. XXVII). And by maidservants they begot not only unto servitude, as Abraham begot Ishmael by Hagar, but also unto freedom: Jacob, by Bilhah, begot Dan and Naphtali, and by Zilpah Gad and Asher.

Thus also among God’s people, good and free persons are born through spiritual and good persons, as through Paul those to whom he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV); and evil slaves, as Simon Magus was born through Philip.

[Col. 0494A] And through carnal slaves are born not only evil persons, into a damnable slavery, who imitate them, but also persons into praiseworthy freedom, to whom it is said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. XXIII). Whoever wisely recognizes this mystery among God’s people preserves unity of spirit and the bond of peace to the end, cleaving to some and tolerating others.

“For he prepared.” As if he were saying: They do not seek heaven without reason, nor is he undeservedly unashamed to be called their God, because he has prepared for them a city in which they shall be fellow citizens.

By faith also in invisible things Abraham offered Isaac—not in anger, but willingly—when he was tested by God; that is, when God showed what sort of man he was, as an example to others. For God did not test Abraham as one ignorant of his faith,

[Col. 0494B] but so that Abraham himself and the world might know the unity and firmness of his faith. And he offered his only-begotten son, in whom—that is, with respect to whom—the promises had been made to him, to whom it had been said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called.”

As if someone should ask, “How then did he believe God truthful?” he adds: “Considering that God is able even to raise him from the dead,” just as he is able to make him from nothing.

[Ambrose.]

Abraham did not hesitate to believe when the promise was made, nor did he hesitate to offer when the offering was demanded. His right hand was raised for the sacrifice, that he might die whose heart had been raised in faith, that he might be born. The religion of the believer was not contrary to the devotion of the obedient man. For the devout father faithfully holding the promise which had to be fulfilled through this son whom God commanded to be killed did not doubt that one offered in sacrifice could be restored to him, since one who had been given beyond hope could be given again. He did not raise for himself a question as though concerning contradictory and mutually opposed words of God—God promising that a son would be born, and afterwards saying: “Kill your son for me.” Rather, there was in his heart an unshaken and unfailing faith, by which he believed that God, who had enabled him to be born from aged parents, was also able to restore him from death.

[Augustine.]

Therefore, namely because he had such great faith, “he received him in a parable,” that is, not only in fact but also in signification. For he understood that Christ was signified: Christ’s divinity does not die, but the ram caught by its horns among the thorns—that is, Christ’s flesh suffering among the Jews, upon the horns of the cross—could be offered to God amid Jewish thorns before the crowning.

[Col. 0494D] “By faith Isaac also blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come,” things not yet seen as possessed. Isaac had faith by which he believed not only that the better man would be blessed, but also that the Christian people would supplant the Jews’ blessing.

## Verses 21–31

“By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, and worshipped the top of his staff. By faith Joseph, when dying, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel, and gave command concerning his bones. By faith Moses, when born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful; and they did not fear the king’s decree. By faith Moses, when he had grown up,

[Col. 0495A] refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of temporary sin, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of Egypt. For he looked to the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the king’s wrath; for he endured as though seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and the outpouring of blood, lest he who destroyed the firstborn should touch them. By faith they crossed the Red Sea as through dry land; which the Egyptians experienced and were swallowed up. By faith the walls of Jericho fell after being encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with the unbelievers, having received the spies in peace.”

Likewise Jacob, when dying, having faith concerning things not seen, blessed each of Joseph’s sons, namely Ephraim and Manasseh, because, with his hands crossed, he gave each his own blessing; and by placing his right hand upon Ephraim and his left upon Manasseh, he set the younger before the elder. “And he worshipped the top,” or “upon the top,” of his staff.

Why did he worship upon the top of Joseph’s staff? Perhaps he had taken the staff from his son when that same son swore to him; and while holding it, after the oath had been spoken and before returning it, he immediately worshipped God. For he was not ashamed to bear for a little while the emblem of his son’s authority, where the staff prefigured a great future reality, namely the kingdom of Christ to come among the Gentiles. The sense is: he worshipped God, namely standing upright and leaning upon the top—that is, the summit—of his staff.

Or, mystically, omitting “upon”: he worshipped his summit, that is, Christ, through whom Joseph had dominion and the staff of discipline in Egypt.

[Col. 0495C] Or: he worshipped upon the top of his staff, that is, for Christ’s kingdom—that is, he prayed for Christ’s future kingdom among the Gentiles, Christ who was signified in Joseph.

Likewise Joseph, when dying, through faith concerning future things, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, in which the redemption of believers from sins was signified, and he did so through faith in the future resurrection. He commanded concerning his bones, adjuring the children of Israel to carry them into the land of promise and bury them in the tomb of his fathers, namely in the double cave, in which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other patriarchs were buried, where Adam and Eve rested. They wished this because they foresaw that Christ would be born in that land,

[Col. 0495D] so that they might rise again with him.

Likewise Moses, from the time he was born, was hidden by his parents for three months, and this through faith—that is, through the faith of his parents, who believed that God would accomplish something great through him, since he was so beautiful in form. Hence he adds: “Because they saw that he was a beautiful child,” for from birth a great grace of beauty had been poured into him, not by nature but by God’s gift. For this reason his parents did not fear the king’s decree, by which he had commanded that every male child of the Hebrews be killed.

Likewise Moses, when he had grown up, by faith—that is, through faith in invisible things—refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with God’s people than to have the carnal enjoyment of temporary—that is, passing—sin. For he judged it sinful to rejoice

[Col. 0496A] in the king’s palace while his brethren were afflicted; and it is an act of the greatest faith to despise pleasure. I say, esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of Egypt—that is, considering it greater to bear Christ’s reproach than to abound in Egyptian wealth.

[Chrysostom.]

He calls “the reproach of Christ” either what Moses suffered for Christ, or what he signified by representing Christ in his own person, or what Moses endured from his brethren whom he wished to deliver, just as Christ endured it from his own people whom he had come to redeem. For they said to Christ: “You have a demon” (John VIII). They said to Moses: “Do you wish to kill us, as you killed the Egyptian?” Yet he bore this patiently, as Christ did. For he looked to the eternal reward of those who endure patiently, or to the Rewarder, to whom he was going.

Moses also, by faith, left Egypt, leading out the children of Israel, not fearing the king’s wrath. This seems contrary to the fact that, after killing the Egyptian, he departed from there into the land of Midian. But when he first fled into Midian, it was not fear but faith, because he believed that he would be delivered by God. He did not wish to remain there lest he should provide a cause of boasting by casting himself openly into danger and thus putting God to the test, which is devilish. For as long as the saints have something they can do, they ought not to test God but to withdraw; as the Lord himself made way, who also commanded his own, saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. X).

“Invisible,”

[Col. 0496C] that is, as if he were saying: For this reason he did not fear, because he endured the invisible one—that is, God, whom he did not see—as though seeing him; and he trusted in him, awaiting what he had promised, and therefore did not fear.

Likewise Moses, by faith—that is, through faith—kept the Passover, which was the cause of passing over. He did so with this faith: because he believed that the people would be saved, namely both they from Pharaoh and we from the devil. And he observed the outpouring of blood, with which they smeared both doorposts and the lintel of the house, lest the smiting angel, who destroyed the firstborn of the Egyptians, should touch them, being driven back by the blood. This was certainly done as a figure of those to be delivered through Christ’s blood.

Likewise, by faith—that is, through faith by which they believed God’s promise—they passed through the Red Sea as through dry land. And lest this seem to have happened by chance and not through faith,

[Col. 0496D] or lest it seem an illusion, he adds: “Which the Egyptians experienced and were swallowed up.” Thus through baptism believers pass over with sins remitted, as though the Egyptians, together with the devil the prince of darkness, had been drowned.

By the faith which the children of Israel had, the walls of Jericho also fell, when the circuit of seven days had been completed by the Levites bearing the ark of the Lord and sounding bronze trumpets. Thus the obstacles of this world fall at the voices of preachers while, in this time, the Church is renewed—or set in motion—with Christ as leader, encircling the whole world like Joshua.

Likewise Rahab, though she was a prostitute, did not perish with the unbelievers. And this was through faith, namely because she believed that the land would be given by God to the Jews and therefore received their spies. Hence he adds: “Receiving the spies in peace.”

[Col. 0497A] What then ought you to do, who have heard the prophets and Christ? Certainly you ought, by believing, to receive the two Testaments through the apostles, like spies sent by Christ; and thus you will not perish with the unbelievers.

## Verses 32–35

“And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises. They stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were strengthened from weakness, became mighty in war, put to flight the armies of foreigners, and women received their dead raised to life.”

“And what?” As if he were saying: I have spoken of many deeds of faith and set forth many examples of believers. And what more shall I say, if I would pursue each thing done through faith? As if he were saying: They are innumerable. For the time of this epistle, or the time of my life, would fail me if I were to tell of Gideon—how, having received from the Lord the sign of the fleece, he went against the Midianites with three hundred men and defeated them by night—and of Barak, of whom it is read in the book of Judges that, when Jabin king of Canaan was oppressing the children of Israel, Deborah the prophetess, who at that time judged Israel, commanded Barak son of Abinoam to take ten thousand fighters. He did so and was to go against Sisera, commander of Jabin’s army; but he said that he would go if she herself went with him. Therefore she went with him.

[Col. 0497C] The Lord threw into terror Jabin’s army, which Sisera had assembled by the torrent of Kishon. Sisera fled to the tents of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. There, while he lay hidden asleep, Jael drove a tent-peg struck with a hammer through his brain and into the ground, and he died. And behold, Barak came pursuing Sisera; Jael went out to meet him and said: “Come, and I will show you the man whom you seek.” When he entered, he saw Sisera lying dead (Judg. IV). Thus God humbled on that day Jabin, king of Canaan, before the children of Israel.

And of Samson, who, as is read in the book of Judges, greatly afflicted the Philistines. And of Jephthah, who, when he went to battle against his enemies, vowed to the Lord that, if the Lord granted him—or he attained—triumph over his enemies, upon returning he would offer to the Lord whatever first came to meet him; and his daughter met him, and he sacrificed her. Jephthah is not praised for killing his daughter, but because by faith, with God’s help, he overcame his enemies.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Augustine, The City of God.]

Abraham, however, is not merely not accused of the crime of cruelty; he is even praised under the name of piety, because he wished to kill his son not wickedly but obediently. And it is rightly asked whether Jephthah’s killing of the daughter who came to meet him ought to be regarded as commanded by God, when he had vowed to God that he would sacrifice whatever first met him as he returned victorious from battle. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for having caused the collapse of the house to crush himself together with his enemies, except because the Spirit had secretly commanded this, the Spirit who performed wonders through him.

And of David, Samuel, and the other prophets, who through faith conquered

[Col. 0498A] kingdoms and wrought righteousness—that is, just judgment.

[Chrysostom.]

And although he declined to say what each one had done, he nevertheless states the things that some accomplished by faith. He wisely avoids recounting the histories lest he prolong his discourse. Touching briefly upon certain matters, he neither remained altogether silent nor became tiresome by speaking. He avoided density and length, lest he weary the hearer.

“And obtained,” by faith, “promises,” that is, the things promised, such as victory and other things. Many promises were made, to David, Abraham, and others. “They stopped.” As if he were saying: They conquered not only men but also beasts, because they stopped the mouths of lions, as Daniel did. The plural is used for the singular, as in what follows, where he says: “They were sawn asunder.” For Daniel alone is meant as having shut the lions’ mouths, and Isaiah alone was sawn asunder; just as in the Psalm a plural is used for the singular, where it is said: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together as one” (Ps. II). For “kings” is said of Herod, and “princes” of Pilate.

[Col. 0498B] “They quenched the violence of fire,” as did the three children cast by Nebuchadnezzar into the fiery furnace; “and escaped the edge of the sword,” that is, the army girded with the sword, as Joshua, David, and many others did; “were strengthened from weakness,” as Hezekiah and Job; “became mighty in war,” that is, in battle, as Joshua, Judas Maccabaeus, and others; and they often put the armies of foreigners—that is, enemies—to flight. Women also received their dead returning from resurrection, that is, restored to life, as happened through Elijah and Elisha.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] The same author, in The Grace of the New Testament.]

It should be observed that in the Old Testament temporal prosperity was often shown as granted to the patriarchs in the things mentioned, and in other such matters. In the New Testament it is not the time for such things. Previously God gave such things belonging to the old human being, so that it might be understood that, besides him, there is another who also grants abundantly that earthly prosperity which belongs to the old human being. But in Christ, the new human being, he promises new things to the new: namely, eternal things.

Therefore he himself wished to suffer before his enemies and to die mocked, as though abandoned by God, so that the grace of the New Testament might be commended, by which we might learn to seek another happiness and, for the sake of the eternal, despise temporal happiness. He endured persecutors and raging enemies even to death, while they mocked him as though he were a proud man conquered and crushed.

[Col. 0498D] But when he raised his own flesh and restored it to the sight and touch of the disciples, and ascended into heaven in their sight, he built them up and showed with most evident truth what they ought to expect. Therefore James, distinguishing the endurance of the Old and New Testaments, says: “You have heard of Job, and you have seen the end of Christ” (Jas. V). As if he were saying: Endure temporal evils as Job did; but for such endurance do not hope for the temporal goods that were restored to him in greater measure. Rather, hope for the eternal things that went before in Christ.

## Verses 35–40

“But others were stretched out, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others indeed experienced mockings and scourges, moreover also chains and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tested, died by the slaughter of the sword. They wandered about in *melotes* [garments], in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes in the earth. And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God having provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.”

“But others.” Behold, he has said above how great were the things they did through faith. Now he says how great were the things they suffered for faith.

[Col. 0499A] As if he were saying: Those things were accomplished through faith; but these things were endured for faith. Others, namely, were stretched upon the rack and other instruments of torture, not accepting present deliverance—that is, escape from their enemies’ hands—that they might obtain resurrection, that is, eternal life, better than that deliverance, that is, liberation. Or: that they might obtain a resurrection the better in proportion as they suffered more.

[Chrysostom.]

For the more a person suffers, the more gloriously he will be crowned. But others experienced mockings and scourges, and moreover chains and prisons. By saying “moreover,” he indicates that these were suffered by the same persons. They were stoned, as Jeremiah in Egypt and Ezekiel in Babylon; they were sawn asunder, as Isaiah; they were tested by promises; they died in the slaughter of the sword, that is, were killed by the sword, as Uriah and Josiah.

[Note: [Col. 0499D] Augustine, The Grace of the New Testament.]

Behold, from this it is clear that among those fathers of the Old Testament, although such instances were rare, there nevertheless were examples of endurance even unto death, from the blood of Abel to

[Col. 0499C] the blood of Zechariah. The Lord says that their blood will be required of those who persist in the wickedness of their fathers, by whom they were killed. And in the New Testament there has not been, nor is there, any lack of a multitude of good believers who abound in this temporal prosperity and experience in it the goodness and mercy of God the Giver.

Then he still adds other examples of the endurance of the ancients, saying: “They wandered about” through many parts of the world “in sheepskins.” A *melota* is a garment of camel’s hair. Or *melotus* is an animal also called a badger, whose skin is called a *melota* and is very shaggy. “And in goatskins,” as Elijah and others; needy of necessities; distressed in anxiety of mind; afflicted by labours. “Of whom,” that is, of whose manner of life,

[Col. 0499D] “the world”—that is, lovers of the world—“was not worthy.” And therefore these persons are not to be deemed contemptible because of their tribulations. Or: “Of whom the world was not worthy,” that is, they were so contemptible in the eyes of men. As if he were saying: They were not thought worthy to dwell among them. “Wandering in deserts,” as Mattathias and his followers; and before him Elijah and the sons of the prophets under Jezebel; “and in mountains, caves, and holes in the earth.” Distinguish: caves are naturally formed; hollows are formed by some accident.

“And all these.” As if he were saying: The ancient faithful did such great things through faith, or suffered such great things for faith. Yet all these, approved by the testimony of faith—that is, by what faith testified concerning them—had not yet received the promise,

[Col. 0500A] that is, the complete blessedness of body and soul, namely the two robes, although each had received one. God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected—that is, completed—without us, but in the common joy of all, so that the joy of each might be greater. For although they have received one robe apiece, they will not have the double robe until the common resurrection, so that the consummation of all the faithful may occur together.

Or: those earlier persons did not immediately receive the promise, namely the life permitted to them until Christ. Why not? Because God provided something better: namely, that he should assume our nature and exalt them with us more gloriously. Hence he adds: “So that they should not be perfected without us,” that is, enjoy rest and the vision of God. And if they held fast to faith who waited so long for rest, much more ought we to hold fast, who receive it immediately.

## Chapter XII

## Verses 1–17

“Therefore we also, having such a great cloud of witnesses laid upon us, laying aside every weight and the sin surrounding us, let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame, and sits at the right hand of God’s throne. For consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, lest you grow weary, failing in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin, and you have forgotten the consolation that speaks to you as to sons, saying: ‘My son, do not neglect the Lord’s discipline, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For whom the Lord loves he chastens; and he scourges every son whom he receives. Persevere in discipline. God presents himself to you as to sons.’”

“Therefore we also.” After commending faith, he returns to the point at which he had begun, exhorting them to their homeland in many ways, especially by Christ’s own example. As if he were saying: Since others have endured. Therefore—as if he were saying, for this reason, as also for other reasons—we have so great a cloud of witnesses, that is, so great a multitude of saints. They are witnesses of faith, and, like a cloud, refresh us by their example in the heat of tribulation and rain doctrine upon us.

[Col. 0500D] This cloud has been set before us as an example of faith and deeds. First laying aside every weight of sins that is already present, and the sin that surrounds us—that is, sin which surrounds and threatens us even if it has not yet entered us. Or, laying aside the weight, namely the weariness produced by tribulations, so that we may no longer be weary of suffering; and the sin surrounding us, that is, renouncing the sins which encircle us on every side, girded and made ready through endurance.

Why should we not run without hesitation to the contest of martyrdom? Because it is set before us. Let us run, I say, looking to the author of faith in the present and to Jesus, our finisher in the future. As if he were saying: Because he is so great a giver of faith, we ought to run;

[Col. 0501A] and because he brings us to full blessedness, and because he himself suffered. Hence he adds: He, having eternal joy set before him, to which one comes through suffering, endured the cross, despising shame—that is, setting aside human disgrace. Thus we too, with eternal joy set before us, ought to run, putting shame behind us.

Or: with the joy of a temporal kingdom set before him, he instead endured the cross, despising shame. For the crowds wished to seize him to make him king (John VI); but he did not wish this, because he himself was the way of humility.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] Augustine, On Instructing Beginners.]

For Christ the man despised every earthly good, in order to show that it should be despised; and he endured every earthly evil which he commanded men to endure, so that happiness might not be sought in the former nor unhappiness feared in the latter. Born of a mother who, although she conceived untouched by a man and remained always untouched, was nevertheless betrothed to a carpenter, he extinguished all pride of carnal nobility. Born in the city of Bethlehem, which was small among all the cities of Judea, he did not wish anyone to glory in the eminence of an earthly city.

[Col. 0501B] Though he was the source to whom all things belong, he was poor, lest anyone be exalted by earthly riches. He did not wish to be made king by men, because he showed the way of humility to the wretched. He hungered, though he feeds all; he thirsted, though he is the spring of those who thirst; he was wearied by the journey, though he made for us the way to heaven; he became mute and deaf, though through him the mute spoke and the deaf heard; he was bound, though he looses the bonds of the weak; he died, though he raised the dead. Therefore let us suffer like things for love of him.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] The same author, in the same work.]

For the law is then fulfilled when whatever it commands is done, not from desire for temporal things, but from love for him who commanded.

“For consider.” As if he were saying: Jesus’ endurance of the cross ought to encourage us, because he also endured this lesser thing, namely contradiction. As if he were saying: Look to Jesus who endured the cross. For consider, so that you may follow him, him who endured—not in his members, but against himself, that is, in his own person—such, that is, so vehement, contradiction amid every adversity, and this from sinners, which is exceedingly unworthy. Consider, I say, so that, attending to these things, you may not grow weary in any adversities, failing in your souls.

[Col. 0501D] As if he were saying: Even if the body fails, let the spirit stand firm. To fail is to deny the faith through fear of tribulation. For you ought not to fail: “You have not yet resisted unto blood,” that is, unto the shedding of blood, although you have lost your possessions.

[Note: [Col. 0501D] The same author, On the Words of the Apostle.]

There is no more perfect love in this life than that to which the holy martyrs attained, who contended against sins unto blood. Therefore it is an injustice in the Church to pray for a martyr, when we ought to commend ourselves to the martyr’s prayers; prayer is made for other dead persons.

You, I say, are striving against sin, that is, unbelief or any other sins; and this is good.

[Col. 0502A] And for this reason again you ought not to fail, but still to do the same. And—that is, because—you have forgotten the consolation, namely Christ consoling in Scripture? As if he were saying: You ought not to forget. This consolation, that is, Christ the Consoler, speaks to you as his sons, that is, sons of Christ from whom consolation comes. He speaks, I say, saying: “My son”—these are Christ’s words in Solomon’s Proverbs—“do not neglect the Lord’s discipline,” that is, the tribulations by which you are instructed by the Lord; “nor grow weary unto failure when you are rebuked by him,” who purges sins. And you ought not to grow weary when rebuked; “for whom the Lord loves,” in order to crown him, “he chastens,” that is, he makes chaste through correction. “And he scourges every son whom he receives,” that is, whom he is to receive into the eternal inheritance.

[Col. 0502B] He adds: “Every,” even the innocent person who is without all sin. Therefore, if anyone is excepted from the suffering of scourges, he is excepted from the number of sons.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The same author, On Pastors.]

That only-begotten one, born from the Father’s substance, equal to the Father in the form of God, the Word through whom all things were made, had nothing in himself for which he might be scourged. Yet he clothed himself in flesh so that he might not be without scourging. He who scourges the only-begotten without sin leaves unscourged the adopted son who has sin? The only-begotten, without sin but not without scourging, set before us an example in his sufferings.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] The same author, on Psalm LXXX.]

Therefore we ought not be troubled when any saint suffers grievous and undeserved things, if we have not forgotten what the Just One and Holy of Holies endured. Observe here both the justice and the mercy

[Col. 0502C] of God: his justice lies in his scourging; his mercy lies in his receiving. Observe also that he does not say, “Everyone who is scourged is a son,” but “Every son is scourged.” Otherwise no one is received. And because he scourges every son, therefore persevere in discipline to the end, bearing it patiently; and you ought to do so, because in giving discipline he presents himself to you as to sons—that is, he shows himself to be a father.

He proves this by a human comparison, adding:

## Verses 7–14

“For what son is there whom his father does not correct? But if you are without discipline, in which all have become participants, then you are adulterous children and not sons. Moreover, we have had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? For they indeed instructed us for the few days of a time, according to their own will; but he does so for what is useful, that we may receive his sanctification. Now all discipline at the present time seems to be not of joy but of sorrow; yet afterwards it will yield the most peaceable fruit of righteousness to those trained by it. Therefore lift up the slack hands and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no one who limps may go astray, but rather may be healed. Pursue peace with all and holiness, without which no one shall see God.”

For what son is there whom his father does not correct? That is, to whom he does not give discipline, so that he may not withdraw mercy. [Note: Col. 0503D, Augustine, on Psalm 89.] He strikes the obstinate in order to restore the inheritance. If you have rightly heard or recognized the Father’s promises, do not fear being scourged, but being disinherited. Run beneath the hand of the Father who scourges; for while he scourges, he trains you for the inheritance. Do not think perversely and childishly, saying: “My father loves my brother more, whom he permits to do whatever he wishes, than he loves me; for if I move against his command, I encounter stripes.” Rather rejoice under the stripes, because the inheritance is being reserved for you; for the present he spares those whom he will also condemn eternally.

“But if you are outside.” As though he said: You who are sons, remain under discipline. But if you are outside the discipline in which all God’s sons have become participants, then you are adulterers—that is, illegitimate sons—and not legitimate ones. Or, “adulterers,” that is, the devil’s possession and not sons of God. Note that he who begets by adultery is not rightly called a father, because those begotten by him are not called legitimate sons.

“Then.” Here again it is shown why they ought to be under discipline. As though he said: From what has been said, it is clear that you ought to persevere in discipline. “Then,” that is, the same may also be understood from what follows: namely, that we had fathers of our flesh—not of our souls—as instructors, and we reverenced them. To reverence is to render honor with fear. Shall we not, then, much more obey the Father of spirits, that is, of souls, which are not derived from matter, as bodies are from fathers? “And we shall live.” As though he said: We ought also to obey him because through him we shall live eternally.

“Whereas they.” Here another reason is shown why God must be obeyed: namely, because they—the fathers of the flesh—trained us only for the time of a few days, and this according to their own will, that is, in the things they wished, namely vain things. But he, the Father of spirits, trains us for what is useful—that is, for faith and a good life. He trains us, I say, if we are receiving sanctification, that is, if we receive his discipline which sanctifies us. Or thus: he trains us for what is useful, namely in receiving—that is, so that we may receive—his sanctification, that is, his purity.

“But every.” [Chrysostom.] Here he states what they might object, in order to answer it. As though he said: Remain under discipline; but it is true that every discipline—[Col. 0503D] [Augustine] not, certainly, that which takes its name from learning and may be called knowledge, but that correction which is for sins—[Note: Col. 0503D, Augustine, *On the Trinity*]. For discipline, which in Greek is called *paideia*, is instruction through troubles, when someone suffers evils for his sins in order that he may be corrected; this is what is meant here. For there is a discipline which takes its name from learning and can be called knowledge, and which in Greek is called *epistēmē*. Every discipline, I say, for the present does not seem to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; yet this is not really so, if one now considers future things. But afterward—that is, in the other life—God will render, to those trained by that discipline, the fruit of righteousness, that is, the fruit by which righteousness is merited. This fruit [Col. 0504A] will not be like the fruit of this world, which is never in tranquillity, but will be most peaceful—that is, possessed in complete repose: peace beyond which there is none greater.

“Therefore,” namely, that you may have such fruit, raise up your hands—that is, the affection of charity with which you formerly embraced God—which are now slack, that is, sluggish in almsgiving; and your loosened knees—that is, the strength by which one stands firmly upon one’s knees, which has been weakened through cooling charity—raise them upward toward God, so that you neither grow numb through idleness nor hesitate through weakness. And make straight paths for your feet—that is, for your faith—so that your faith may proceed rightly, confessing what it believes and, if need be, suffering for it. Faith is rightly called a foot because it bears the whole person. Make them so straight that no one—that is, that no person—may stray from the way of uprightness [Col. 0504B], that is, deviate from the true life of faith, as does the person who accepts carnal observances; for this is to stray. And let no one be lame—that is, let him not limp, like one who wavers through fear of suffering—but rather be healed, if he has strayed or feared.

Or straight paths for the feet are a right intention in works. Thus: “Make straight paths for your feet.” [Haimo.] That is, have a right intention in your works, so that no lame person may stray in a good work from the way of uprightness, that is, from right intention; but rather may be healed from sins by acting with good intention.

“And pursue peace with all.” As though he said: Endure so greatly that you have peace even with your persecutors; this peace is love and concord. And [Col. 0504C] pursue holiness, that is, perfection in works, because faith alone is insufficient. Or, holiness means chastity of mind and body. Hence: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Without it—namely, peace and holiness—no one will see God. They are so necessary that by striking the eye we extinguish it. [Note: Col. 0504D, Augustine, in a sermon on the vision of God.] See how he frightened the lover of good, not the one who fears evil. He says, “Without it no one will see God”: he frightens you by the very thing you desire. It is one thing to fear punishment, another to love righteousness. If you do no evil through fear of Gehenna, you indeed have faith unto life, because you believe that God’s judgment is to come. I rejoice at your faith, but I still fear your wickedness. Therefore let peace and holiness be in you, without which God will not be seen. For we shall have no means of seeing God [Col. 0504D] if, by striking it, we have extinguished that very eye within ourselves. Let us be peacemakers, so that we may be recognized as sons; let us be pure in heart, so that we may see God. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. Blessed are the pure in heart,” etc. (ibid.).

## Verses 15–19

“Seeing to it lest anyone fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness, springing up, hinder, and through it many be defiled; lest anyone be a fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. For know that afterward also, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he had sought it with tears. For you have not approached [Col. 0505A] a tangible and accessible fire, and a whirlwind, and darkness, and a storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words.”

“Seeing to it.” As though he said: I exhort you to peace and patience; and do not doubt that you can be so patient, because God’s grace is at hand. But beware lest you fall short of it. This is what “Pursue peace” means. You, I say, giving careful attention lest anyone—not only yourselves—fall short of God’s grace. As though he said: Let your concern be not only for yourselves but also for others. Attend diligently and consider lest any one of you fall short of grace, which the merit of human perversity often repels. You can retain grace in this way: beware lest any root—that is, an evil thought—of bitterness, that is, harmful delight, from which [Col. 0505B] bitterness arises, springing up—that is, coming to consent and action—hinder that grace; and through that bitterness, not only the person in whom it is found but also many others may be defiled by his example. Therefore it is serious.

[Haimo.] The root of bitterness is an evil thought, because just as a bitter root does not produce sweet fruits but fruits like itself, that is, bitter ones, and a sulphurous spring produces water unfit for drinking, so an evil thought produces not sweet fruits—that is, love and good action—but bitter ones, through which the way to heaven is obstructed. Then he shows in detail how they should take heed lest a root of bitterness spring up, identifying some among them in the matters concerned, when he adds: “Lest anyone,” etc.

As though he said: Be watchful lest anyone among you [Col. 0505C] be a fornicator by holding carnal observances together with faith, like a concubine; this is spiritual fornication. [Haimo.] Or profane—that is, wholly neglecting faith and alienated from God. For *profanus* is said as though *procul a fano*, “far from the shrine,” that is, from God’s temple: entirely irreligious. “Like Esau.” Or literally: lest anyone be a fornicator or profane person like Esau. For among the Jews there were some followers of Esau, both in fornication and in gluttony. Esau is called a fornicator because, against the will of his father and mother, he took foreign wives. He is called profane because he became a glutton, that is, a slave of the belly; hence he sold his birthright for red lentils. Therefore he adds: “Who for one meal [Col. 0505D] sold his first things,” or “his birthright,” that is, the dignity of the firstborn.

[Chrysostom.] Here “birthright” means the honor and dignity of the priesthood, because before Aaron’s priesthood all firstborn sons were priests, as Shem was. This was their dignity: they received a larger portion from their father’s property and inheritance, were more richly arrayed in splendid clothing, and received the blessing. See how far Esau was from religion. For his belly he gave up the blessing. The Apostle recalls his deed in order to dissuade them from resembling him. “For know,” lest you be like Esau, “that he was rejected.” For know that, afterward also, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected by God, Isaac confirming the blessing he had bestowed upon Jacob [Col. 0506A]. Thus these persons must beware lest, when after death they ought to receive the blessing, they be rejected and repentance avail them nothing; for then repentance will be fruitless. Esau’s case prefigures this, and it did not benefit him.

Therefore he adds: “For he did not.” [Haimo.] As though he said: He truly lacked the blessing. For he found no place for repentance—[Chrysostom], that is, for pardon and for obtaining the blessing through repentance—not because he did not repent, but because he did not repent as he ought, saying: “The days of mourning for my father Isaac will come, and I will kill my brother Jacob” (Gen. 27). He did not find it, I say, although he sought that blessing with tears—not genuine tears. For those tears flowed more from indignation against God and grief over lost honor than from humility and true repentance.

[Col. 0506B] He had said and warned that no one should fall short of grace in the ways he had set forth. No one ought to fall short, for grace is prepared. This is what he here shows: “For you have not approached” the harshness of the Law, which he describes, so that the sweetness of grace may be understood by contrast. For it is the custom of those comparing one thing with another to lower one and diminish the other, so that the eminence of the other may thereby shine more clearly. Thus the Apostle, by comparing the things which were in the Old Testament, declares ours greater and better.

Describing, therefore, their harshness, he says: “You have not approached a tangible fire,” that is, a fire which can be touched, “and accessible,” namely, one approached by bodily movement; but you have approached the Holy Spirit, who is a fire consuming sins [Col. 0506C], and whom one reaches not by bodily movement but by the spirit of the mind. “And you have not approached a whirlwind.” A whirlwind is a force of winds with hail and rain. These things occurred literally when the Law was given. The whirlwind signifies the onrush of vices, which exercised greater domination through the Law; now, however, through grace one comes to the calmness of virtues. Or the whirlwind signifies the threat of the Law itself: “If anyone does this or that, let him die.” “And darkness.” Darkness is the obscurity of fire and smoke, signifying that the Law was obscure. For darkness signifies obscurity of mind, whereas now understanding is clear. “And a storm,” which is greater than a whirlwind, that is, a tempest that drives one in whatever direction. This [Col. 0506D] is the bondage of sin in actual operation, which through the Law drew human beings along; now there is rest from imperfect vices. [Chrysostom.] Or the storm signifies the Law’s very punishment. “And the sound of a trumpet,” a signal calling to battle, which signifies the movements of desire, extinguished not through the Law but through grace.

[Haimo.] Or the trumpet sound signifies the presence and coming of almighty God. Hence the same Apostle elsewhere, speaking of Christ’s coming for judgment, says: “At the trumpet of God he will descend—he will descend from heaven,” that is, amid the voice of angels. These things occurred literally at the giving of the Law, so that the hearts of the Jews, prone to sin, might be converted and they might not dare to transgress the Law. This terror is not found in the Gospel. “And the voice [Col. 0507A] of words.” The voice of words is understood as not God’s own voice but that of angels. For God spoke to Moses through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel.

## Verses 19–24

“Those who heard it excused themselves, lest a word be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was commanded: ‘Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.’ And so terrible was the sight that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’ But you have approached Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and God the Judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and the sprinkled blood which speaks better than Abel.”

That voice of trumpets and angels: those who heard it begged that no word might be spoken to them, that is, that God might not speak to them, saying to Moses: “Speak to us yourself; let not the Lord God speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. 20). They were struck with excessive fear. For they could not bear what was said, that is, they could not endure the angel’s voice because of fear, seeing all Mount Sinai smoking, seeing storms and thunder, and hearing trumpet sounds. They were told to stand far from the mountain, because “if even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned”—with hail—as the Lord had commanded, saying: “Let the children of Israel keep far from the mountain, because if a human being or beast touches the mountain, it shall be killed with hailstones” (Exod. 19). And so [Col. 0507C] terrible was the sight that they did not dare either to hear or to approach the mountain. For Moses also said: “I am terrified and trembling.”

[Haimo.] It was exceedingly terrible, since it terrified Moses; and if Moses was terrified, how much more, surely, were the others terrified.
