It should be known that this voice of words signifies the Law’s command and threat, which the people considered burdensome and unbearable, because it was command alone without assisting grace. “For they could not bear what was commanded,” because without grace they were insufficient for keeping the Law’s commandments; and it was said: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” The mountain is divinity; the beast is the failure of reason, which occurs when a word of blasphemy against God is uttered; to touch is to offend. Thus the person who offends God by blasphemy touches the mountain as a beast [Col. 0507D], and the Law commands without mercy that he be stoned. But if he wishes to return in the Church, he is received mercifully.

Moses was terrified there because the harshness of the Law was so great that the imperfect were frightened, since there was no assisting grace there. But now the command is not burdensome even to the imperfect. The yoke is sweet and the burden light, through the charity poured into hearts by the Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 0507D, Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*.] Observe, then, the difference: there, after Passover, which was celebrated on the first day by the sacrifice of the lamb, God descended upon Sinai in fire, terrifying the people standing at a distance and writing with his finger on stone, not on the heart. But here the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, came where the faithful were gathered together, in tongues of fire; he did not terrify them from afar, but rather sat upon each one of them. A sound indeed was suddenly made from heaven, as though a violent wind were blowing; it sounded, but no one was afraid. There were fire and smoke there; here, serene fire.

“But you have approached.” [Haimo.] These words depend on what was said above, where he declares what they have approached. After setting aside those former things, he does not posit their opposites, which are understood by contrast, as explained above, but the reward which follows from them, so that by this he may more strongly persuade them to retain grace. As though he said: You have not approached such harsh things. But you have approached Mount Zion, that is, those who behold God from on high; to behold him is a great [Col. 0508B] reward. And you have approached—that is, “and” means “that is”—the city of the living God, that is, the God who gives eternal life to his citizens, because God dwells in them and gives them life: namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, the vision of heavenly bread; and the assembly of many thousands of angels, whose companions you will be. He says “many” because blessedness will be greater with more companions.

And you have approached the Church of the firstborn, that is, the apostles who first believed, to whose faith those people were joined. These apostles are enrolled in heaven. He says this by analogy with the ancient “enrolled fathers,” because their names are written in the book of life. It is as though he said: Do not doubt that you will reach the angels, because your predecessors have reached them. This is what he means by “who are enrolled [Col. 0508C] in heaven”: they are written with those who are in heaven, that is, written in their order.

Then he adds another reward, saying: “And God, Judge of all,” that is, Christ, to whom the Father gave all judgment; you too will judge with him. “And spirits,” or “of spirits,” or “spirit”: the textual versions differ, but proceed thus: “and the God of the spirits of the righteous made perfect,” that is, God, who will be the possession of the spirits of the righteous made perfect, when he will be all in all (1 Cor. 15). He will indeed be the possession of others too, but more especially of the perfect; and by this he urges them toward perfection. Or: you have approached the spirits, that is, the souls of righteous persons made perfect, whose companions they had been in faith and works; or the spirit of righteous persons made perfect, that is, the Spirit who makes righteous persons perfect, [Col. 0508D] through whom, moreover, they possess all these things. He adds, saying: “And you have approached Jesus, mediator of the new covenant,” that is, the giver who stands between God and human beings, through whom they can become companions of angels. For what God promised seemed incredible: that human beings, from this mortality, corruption, abjection, weakness, and dust, would become equal to the angels of God.

God did not merely give human beings Scripture so that they might believe; he also set forth as mediator of their faith not just any prince or angel, but his only Son, in order that he might show and provide, through the Son himself, the way by which he would lead us to that ineffable immortality and equality with angels. [Col. 0509A] It was too little for God to make his Son the demonstrator of the way; therefore he made him the way, that we might go through him. The physician was sent, but the sick person did not recognize him and therefore killed him; yet the sprinkled blood of the physician proved to be medicine for the sick person. He came to visit; he was slain to heal.

Therefore he added: “And you have approached the sprinkling of Christ’s blood,” that is, the cleansing effected by Christ’s blood. [Chrysostom.] As though he said: They possess all these things through Jesus, who gave the New Covenant, and through Christ’s blood, which speaks better than Abel’s blood speaks; for this blood cries out for pardon, Abel’s for vengeance; this cries out for salvation, Abel’s for condemnation. This blood also implores life and forgiveness for persecutors, the Lord saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know [Col. 0509B] what they are doing” (Luke 23). Note that Abel, who was the first person unjustly killed, stands for all others whose blood could secure no remission; much less, therefore, could the blood of animals do so. But Christ’s blood did, and for that reason is said to speak better. Or certainly it speaks better, that is, makes us speak better: namely, that Christ is the Son of God, by whom we were redeemed, rather than Abel’s blood, which makes us say that Abel was a righteous man and was sacrificed as a figure of Christ.

## Verses 25–29

“See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if they did not escape when they refused him who spoke upon earth, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven. His voice then shook the earth; but now he promises, saying: ‘Yet once more [Col. 0509C] I will shake not only the earth but also heaven.’ But his saying ‘yet once more’ signifies the removal of things that are shaken, as of things made, so that those things which are immovable may remain. Therefore, receiving an immovable kingdom, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire.”

“See.” [Haimo.] As though he said: Since you have approached God, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s, therefore see that you do not refuse—that is, despise—Christ speaking through the Gospel, because he prohibits carnal things and commands spiritual ones. For if they—namely, your fathers—did not escape, that is, did not escape punishment, when refusing him—that is, Christ—who spoke [Col. 0509D] to them upon earth, that is, who commanded earthly things, namely carnal observances, through Moses and promised earthly things; or, if you refuse Moses or an angel, who speaks upon earth, that is, of earthly matters: much more shall we not escape if we turn away from Christ, who speaks to us from heaven, that is, speaks spiritual things to us and promises eternal things.

Nor ought we to refuse him, because he is the same one whose voice then—when he spoke from earth, giving the Law on Mount Sinai—shook the earth in order to threaten them lest they refuse. Now, he does not merely threaten but promises. Therefore you ought much less to refuse him. He promises, I say, saying: “Yet once more I will shake,” as is read in Haggai, “not only the earth but also heaven,” namely the lower, aerial heaven. Thus Scripture calls birds “birds of heaven,” meaning all, or nearly all, this windy air which Scripture calls heaven or heavens. It means these lower heavens, not the higher ones where the sun, moon, and stars are placed. Scripture here says that they shall be shaken and elsewhere that they shall perish, owing to some great transformation of themselves.

He explains the sense of this authority from Haggai, saying: But in saying “yet,” adding “once,” he declares the removal of movable things. As though he said: They have already been shaken, but I shall shake them again; and he can do this because he made them. Hence he adds: “as of things made.” As though he said: He can shake them as his own works. By adding “once,” he indicates that he will shake them in such a way that afterward they remain eternally immovable according to what they themselves are, that is, according to their essential being [Col. 0510B]; for whatever they will be, whether in their principal essences or in forms externally received, in that respect they will be immovable. Therefore “once” indicates that they shall no longer be shaken, while “yet” indicates that they are to be shaken.

“Therefore.” As though he said: Since God promises an immovable heaven and earth, it is clear that we, receiving now in hope and afterward in reality an immovable kingdom, have grace—that is, faith, hope, and charity with holy action—without which we could not reach that promised reality; but through it we receive that immovable kingdom. Therefore let no one fall short of grace. Or according to another textual reading, “let us have.” As though he said: Since he promises immovable things, therefore, receiving an immovable kingdom, let us have grace, that is, let us give thanks to God for everything, murmuring at nothing, because in this way God is well served. Hence he adds: “By which grace let us serve, pleasing God.” And let this be with fear, because he is God—that is, fearing him as God and Judge of all—and with reverence, that is, with love of honor, because he is Father—that is, loving him as Father.

“For.” As though he said: Truly, through grace we can please him; for God—that is, the Holy Spirit, who is grace and a gift made ours because he is freely given to us—is fire, because he is the love of the Father and the Son, consuming all sins. The Spirit is called a consuming fire because he consumes the rust of sins and raises human hearts to charity. By purifying us and making us serve [Col. 0510D] in virtues, he makes us pleasing to God.

## Chapter XIV

## Verses 1–6

“Let brotherly love remain among you. And do not neglect hospitality. For through it some pleased God by receiving angels as guests. Remember those in bonds as though bound with them, and those who suffer hardship as though you yourselves also dwell in the body. Let marriage be honorable in all things, and the marriage-bed undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Let your conduct be free from avarice; be content with what you have. For he himself said: ‘I will not leave you nor forsake you.’ Thus we may confidently say: ‘The Lord is my helper; I shall not fear what man may do to me.’”

“Love.” From this point the Apostle gives them moral instruction. As though he said: Since charity must be possessed, therefore let brotherly charity remain among you; that is, let charity be among you, because you are brothers, so that you may love one another as brothers. “And do not neglect hospitality.” He says “neglect” because they had practiced it before being despoiled of their possessions. It is right, I say, that you not neglect it. [Haimo.] For through it some pleased God by receiving angels as guests, as Lot received them, not knowing that they were angels, though knowing that God was in them.

[Note: Col. 0511D, Augustine, in the book *Questions*.] Hence another translation reads: “For through this some, though unaware, received angels as guests,” as Abraham and Lot did: not knowing them to be angels, but thinking them human beings in whom God was and spoke. Abraham indeed rendered services of humanity which could not be necessary except to weak flesh. It is astonishing if he did not suppose that they were human beings, though he understood that God spoke in them, certain signs of majesty being present and apparent, as Scripture testifies that they often appeared in God’s human servants. But afterward he learned that they were angels, when, as he watched, they went into heaven. Likewise Lot, who met the angels and worshipped with his face to the ground, seems to have understood that they were angels; but again, when he invited them to bodily refreshment, which mortal persons need, he seems to have thought that they were human beings. Therefore the same may be said here as was said of the three who came to Abraham: certain divinely given signs showed that they were sent, though they were nevertheless believed to be human beings. He therefore offered hospitality to them as holy people of God, because he knew that God was with them, even as Abraham himself did not know them to be angels. Abraham knew God to be in the three, and Lot in the two. When they spoke with them in the singular number, they thought them human beings, while they provided them, as needy persons, with human refreshment.

“Remember.” Here he exhorts them to another good, namely to assist those imprisoned by providing for them. As though he said: Besides guests, remember also, by doing good, those bound for faith in Christ; sympathize with them as though you yourselves were bound, and thus sympathize with and help them as though you were bound with them. And remember those who suffer hardship, those upon whom hardship is impending, as though you too remained in the body, through which you have experienced what sufferers need. [Haimo.] The meaning is: Help those in bonds and those who suffer, as you would wish help to be given to yourselves when bound and suffering.

“Let marriage also be honorable,” not meretricious, “among all,” so that a lawful wife may be taken at proper times for the love of children, because one must abstain from her at definite times. And let the marriage-bed be undefiled—that is, let there be among you no adultery, no stain of fornication. For God will judge [Col. 0511D] fornicators and adulterers—that is, eternally condemn them—although some think otherwise, saying that God does not care about sins of the flesh.

Let conduct—that is, life—be without avarice, that is, without stinginess in giving. He exhorts them not to be miserly with what they have, and to be content with present possessions. By this he exhorts them not to be covetous of what they do not possess. [Col. 0512A] [Chrysostom.] A miser is one who is stingy in giving; a covetous person is one who is eager in receiving. He says this because perhaps, after they had lost their own property, they wished again to gather riches, which he here forbids. But lest they perhaps say, “What shall we do if the necessary means of support fail us?” he immediately adds consolation, employing testimony from the book of Joshua. For the Lord Almighty himself said to Joshua son of Nun: “I will not leave you,” that is, without giving what is necessary, “nor forsake you.” The person who perished from hunger would be forsaken. But since this does not happen, no one should be covetous.

[Haimo.] After Moses’ death the Lord said this to Joshua: “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you. Be strong and courageous; I will not leave you nor forsake you” (Josh. 1). He says this to everyone who hopes in him as Joshua did. He promises it to us if we place our hope in him. This promise is not for the miserly and covetous, but for those who hope in God. Therefore he adds: Thus, namely, he is with us, so that we may confidently say: “The Lord is my helper,” supplying what is necessary; and therefore, “I shall not fear what man may do to me,” even if he takes away what is mine. Under the name “man” every adversary is understood, even the devil, because he is called “man” from his work of deceiving a human being. Since it would take too long to speak of each matter individually, he exhorts them to follow their teachers, saying:

## Verses 7–14

“Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Considering the outcome of their manner of life, imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and for ever. Do not be led away by diverse [Col. 0512C] and strange teachings. For it is best that the heart be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not profited those who walk in them. We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For here we have no abiding city, but we seek the city to come.”

“Remember,” in order that you may imitate, “your leaders,” because they were good, namely the apostles and their successors. Therefore remember them, because they are those who spoke [Col. 0512D] the word of God to us. Consider their end so that you may imitate them in death, if necessary dying for Christ as they did; imitate their faith in the conduct of a good life and in perfect faith.

“Jesus Christ.” [Haimo.] This relates to the preceding statement, where he testified that God said, “I will not leave you nor forsake you.” It could have seemed to them that this promise applied only to Joshua. The Apostle answers this by saying that Christ will help them as he helped Joshua. As though he said: The promise is not to be doubted, because Jesus Christ, who yesterday—that is, in the past—helped Joshua, is the same today—that is, in the present—helping you and other faithful people, and will help in the future, for ever—that is, without end.

“Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings,” because through grace it is lawful to use all foods. [Jerome.] Some preached that it was not sinful to abound in foods, but that this was good. Others superstitiously said that one must abstain from certain foods which the Law forbids while allowing others; by distinctions and observance of foods they deceived many. Against all of these the Apostle argues here, saying: “Do not be led away by diverse teachings,” namely teachings diverse from your own, that is, different ones, “and strange,” that is, foreign ones. Do not be drawn away from the truth.

Such persons are aptly compared to lepers, who, lacking knowledge of the true faith, profess various erroneous teachings. They do not conceal their ignorance, but parade it as supreme expertise, bringing it into public view and displaying boastfulness of speech. [Col. 0513B] There is no false doctrine that does not intermingle some truth. Truths disorderly mixed with falsehoods in one disputation or narrative, appearing as though in a body of one color, are compared to leprosy, which variegates and stains human bodies with different colors. Such people must be avoided, as the Apostle teaches here: “Do not be led away,” I say, for it is best to strengthen the heart by grace—namely, that you may have perfect faith, believing that all things are clean to the clean—and not by varieties, abundance, and distinctions of foods.

Hence he adds: “And not by foods,” that is, not by distinctions or by abundance of food, “which have not profited those who walk in them,” that is, those who observe and distinguish foods and devote themselves to abundance of food. [Col. 0513C] The sense is: You ought to strengthen your heart by grace, which permits all things by releasing from the Law, and not devote yourselves to the observance or abundance of foods, which have not profited for salvation those who walk in them—not those who merely sustain themselves by them, I mean, but those who persistently occupy themselves with them, either distinguishing foods or indulging too abundantly. [Chrysostom.] Abstinence by which one abstains from sin is indeed beneficial; but that observance concerning foods has profited nothing—faith, however, has. Likewise, to abound in gifts of grace is beneficial; but to overload the stomach with a mass of foods is harmful.

**“For we have.”** Again, here he shows that one should not be zealous for distinctions among foods or for an abundance of foods. As though he said: Truly, one ought not to be zealous for distinctions among foods, for we have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat—that is, the observances of the Law [Col. 0513D], such as those who distinguish foods and keep other legal practices of this kind. He denotes these by the name of “tabernacle,” because they were established for a time.

Or thus: One should not be zealous for an abundance of foods because we have an altar—that is, Christ’s body—through faith in which prayers and offerings are accepted, and which is consecrated and received upon the altar. Those who serve the tabernacle have no authority, that is, no permission, to eat of it: those, namely, who wholly serve the tabernacle, that is, bodily pleasure and abundance of food. The body is rightly called a tabernacle, because one is to remain in it only for a time; and therefore one ought not to serve it in its desires.

[Haimo] Here the Apostle recounts the practice of the Law, its mystery, and its spiritual meaning. For it was commanded by the Law that on the tenth day of the seventh month from the Passover feast [Col. 0514A], that is, on the feast of propitiation, they should take a calf and a goat and sacrifice them within the camp. Their blood was to be carried by the high priest alone into the Holy of Holies, to pray for the people. But their flesh was to be carried outside the camp and burned there; and no one serving the tabernacle was permitted to eat of it.

Spiritually, however, those two animals, namely the calf and the goat, represent the Lord and Savior. For he is the calf which the merciful Father sacrificed at the return of the prodigal son. He is the goat offered for sinners. That high priest also, who entered the Holy of Holies with the blood of those animals to pray for the people, bore the type of Christ, who entered the inner places of the heavenly homeland with the blood of his passion, to intercede for the faithful.

Those animals were sacrificed [Col. 0514B] within the camp, but their flesh was burned outside the camp. So too our Redeemer was sacrificed in Jerusalem, as though within the camp, by the cries and judgment of the Jews; but his flesh was burned outside Jerusalem upon the cross by the fire of passion. For when he was condemned to death, while the Jews cried, “Crucify him” (John 19), he was in some manner sacrificed, so far as they were concerned. Hence Mark says that he was crucified at the third hour (Mark 15); for at the sixth hour he was raised upon the cross.

The altar upon which the flesh was burned outside the camp is the altar of the Church, where Christ’s body is consecrated daily. Therefore we have the altar of the Church, where the Lord’s body is consecrated, and those who serve the tabernacle [Col. 0514C]—that is, the body—have no authority to eat from it: namely, fornicators, adulterers, drunkards, and all who serve the pleasures and desires of their flesh. “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

I think enough has been said concerning how these things pertain to the Lord. But because he himself is the head of all the elect, all the elect may also be understood by the flesh of those animals. Therefore, just as Christ was outside the camp, so also his own people, outside the camp—that is, outside the manner of life of worldly and carnal people—set ablaze by the fervor of the Holy Spirit, consume whatever is carnal, transitory, and lustful in themselves, by afflicting themselves and mortifying their bodies with their vices and desires, or even by enduring martyrdom for Christ’s name.

Their blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest [Col. 0514D]; that is, their praiseworthy life is presented to God the Father through Christ, the true priest, who is our advocate, interceding for us. Or their blood is brought into the holy places when their souls are borne to heaven with the triumph of their passion. They are also fittingly [p. 266] consumed upon the altar, because all holy martyrs are offered to God upon the altar of faith. They fulfill all these things through faith, believing that God will reward them; and carnal persons who love the world do not dare to approach them—as though he said: those who serve the tabernacle.

To fulfill this mystery Jesus suffered outside the camp, as is said afterward. But first, referring to the same legal custom in its spiritual sense, he adds: **“For the bodies of those animals.”** By a twofold allegory—one of the Old [Col. 0515A] Testament and the other of the New Testament, that is, by an allegory arising from a twofold history—namely, the Old and New Testaments—he proves that Christ’s body is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle, that is, the body. For to signify this, the bodies of animals were formerly burned outside the camp; and for this reason Christ suffered outside. And we, who desire to be cleansed from sin by his body and blood, ought to forsake the delights and pleasures of the tabernacle and to endure reproaches and afflictions.

First he proves this through an allegory from Old Testament history, in this way: As though he said: Truly, those who serve pleasures cannot share in Christ’s body and blood, because the bodies of these animals are burned, signifying a memorial, outside the camp—that is, outside the delights and pleasures of the body. Christ’s body, which is profitable, is signified by the bodies of those animals; and his blood is signified by the blood of those animals, whose blood is carried into the holy places for sin by the high priest. Likewise Christ’s blood is offered through himself as high priest—that is, Christ himself is offered to the Father; he is signified not only by the calf and goat but also by the other animals offered according to the Law.

And Christ is rightly signified by these corporeal animals. For he is a lamb, by reason of meekness and innocence; a goat, because of the likeness of sinful flesh, since his flesh was capable of suffering and death; a ram, because he drove away vices by the twofold horn of charity; and a bull, by the strength of the resurrection. What is burned becomes ashes. By ashes is understood remembrance of a past event [Col. 0515C]; to be outside the camp is to depart from fleshly pleasures.

Therefore, for those who are outside the camp—that is, outside bodily delights—the bodies are burned; that is, Christ’s body is made an object of remembrance, signified by the bodies of those animals that were burned. For if anyone lives voluptuously, he does not possess an effective remembrance of Christ. His blood, however, is signified by the blood of those animals carried by the high priest into the Holy of Holies, because Christ was offered to the Father by himself as high priest, so that we might thus enter the heavenly holy places.

Or the text may be read thus, with nearly the same meaning: As though he said: Truly, those who serve the tabernacle cannot share in Christ’s body and blood, because the bodies of these saints [Col. 0515D] are burned—that is, afflicted by fasts and other labors—outside the camp, that is, outside fleshly pleasures; theirs is the blood of the animals which is brought into the holy places for sin by the high priest. That is, Christ’s blood is signified by the blood of those animals, because Christ’s blood benefits only those who enter the heavenly holy places through it. The whole meaning is this: Christ’s blood benefits only those who abandon pleasures and afflict the body.

Then, by an allegory from the New Testament, he proves the same point, adding: **“Therefore”**—that is, to signify this same thing, namely, that we should live outside carnal desires—“Jesus also suffered outside the gate,” precisely in order that he might sanctify his people, not through their merits but through [Col. 0516A] his blood. The gate of the city is the body’s sense faculties, in none of which Christ sinned. Therefore he suffered outside fleshly pleasures, so that, by his example, we too might suffer outside fleshly desires, having shut the door of the senses against vices.

And because Christ suffered for us, the Apostle exhorts us to imitate him, saying, **“Let us therefore go forth.”** As though he said: Since he suffered outside the camp in order to sanctify us, let us therefore go forth through faith and charity, outside the camp, mortifying the members of our bodies with their vices and desires, to imitate him. Let us, I say, patiently bear, as he did, his reproach—that is, the passion of the cross, which seems a reproach to unbelievers but is sanctification and redemption to us.

And we ought to go outside the camp. “For we do not have here an abiding city,” that is, an abiding body in this [Col. 0516B] condition; “but we seek the city to come,” namely, the body according to its future condition. Therefore, that we may attain the future city and bear the reproach:

**Verses 15–19.—“Through him therefore let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name. But do not forget beneficence and sharing; for by such sacrifices God is won. Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who must render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not groaning; for this is not profitable for you. Pray for us. For we are confident that we have a good conscience, desiring in all things to conduct ourselves well. And I urge you the more earnestly to do this, that I may be restored to you more quickly.”**

“Through him,” that is, through Christ, who is for us the way from whom we receive an example for martyrdom, let us always offer to God sacrifices of praise. This is expressed through what properly belongs to it: “the fruit of lips confessing his name”; that is, let us confess his name. This is the praise of God and a fruitful sacrifice, because through it others are drawn to faith. Therefore, you who fear God, praise him, that you may worship him freely. Learn to love him whom you fear, and you will be able to praise him whom you love.

For people fearing him under the Old Testament, because of the letter that terrifies and kills, not possessing the life-giving Spirit, ran with sacrifices to the Temple and, as a figure of Christ’s blood by which we are redeemed—although ignorant of what was prefigured—offered bloody victims. But now, in the grace of the New [Col. 0516D] Testament, a special sacrifice of praise is offered, by which God is honored, and of which that visible sacred sign was the sign of an invisible sacrifice.

**“But do not forget beneficence.”** Having disposed of the perverse opinion concerning food, he returns to urging good conduct. As though he said: Do not merely do the things already mentioned, but do not forget beneficence—that is, generosity toward others. A beneficent person is called generous and a distributor of alms. Hence beneficence means generosity in almsgiving; and sharing means charity, through which all things are considered common. As though he said: Even if your property has been taken away, nevertheless give alms out of what you have. This is what he said above: “not forsaking your assembly.”

**“For by such sacrifices.”** As though he said: Therefore do not forget them, because by such sacrifices, namely gifts of alms, [Col. 0517A] God is won, not by those ancient legal sacrifices. For by alms enemies are conquered, sins are extinguished, and life is obtained. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matt. 9).

Again: **“Obey your leaders,”** with regard to commands, so that you may do what the Church commands through them. **“And submit to them,”** so that you may show them reverence. We must indeed obey prelates and preachers insofar as their teaching, morals, and devotion are sound. But if they have deviated from the path of uprightness, we should not do what they do but what they say—unless perhaps they also err in their teaching. Hence the Lord says: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). They possess rank even though their lives are corrupt; and therefore attend not to their life [Col. 0517B] but to their speech.

**“For they.”** As though he said: You ought therefore to obey because they keep watch—that is, they are concerned for you by preaching, giving good example, and providing outward necessities. As though he said: Since they must render an account for your souls, obey, so that they may do these things—that is, keep watch and care for you—with joy, gladness, and cheerfulness of mind because they see you making progress, and not groaning, that is, with murmuring and sorrow.

[Ambrose] We surely do these things with joy when we see everyone advancing in God’s words. For then the laborer works in the field with joy, when he looks at the tree and sees fruit; when he looks at the crop and sees abundance, he then understands that he has not labored without cause, has not bent his back without cause, has not worn out his hands without cause, and has not endured cold and heat without cause. Therefore he says, “that they may do this with joy and not groaning.”

**“For this,”** namely, that they should groan, is not profitable for you, because their care will then not benefit you if they sigh sadly on your account because you make no progress. Note that he says, “it is not profitable for you.” I do not say, “It is not profitable for them,” for it benefits them to bear witness concerning you. Those leaders, when they are saddened by your evils, profit from that sorrow and it benefits them; but it is not profitable for you. Therefore, let leaders and subjects labor together in the Lord’s field, so that together they may rejoice in the reward.

Or thus: “that they may”—you ought therefore to obey them, so that on the day of judgment they may do this, that is, render an account to God for you with [Col. 0517D] joy, being secure in hope of the true reward, and not groaning. [Chrysostom] That is, not anxious or hesitant concerning our condemnation. “For this,” that they should render an account for you with groaning, is not profitable for you.

**“Pray for us.”** He rebukes the proud exaltation of mind of certain bishops, who disdain to ask their subjects to pour out prayers for them. Pray, I say, for we are confident that we have a good conscience—that is, a good disposition concerning the past—desiring in all things, not only among Gentiles, to conduct ourselves well in the future also, among both Jews and Gentiles. He says this because the Apostle was accused by some of neglecting his own people. But he shows that he has a good disposition toward all, namely Jews and Gentiles: he rejoices in their past good deeds and wishes them better things in the future.

Hence he says, “We have a good conscience.” As though he said: Our conscience [Col. 0518A] accuses us in nothing; nor are we conscious that we have laid snares for you, uttered anything deceitfully, or acted for the sake of gain. Therefore do not form a malicious judgment of us—for perhaps he was accused in such matters.

**“And I urge you the more earnestly.”** As though he said: I tell you to pray for me. But I urge you more earnestly to do this, namely, to pray for me, that I may be restored to you more quickly. As though he said: I ask you to do this not only for my own sake, but especially for your humility’s sake: namely, to pray for me.

**Verses 20–25.—“Now may the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the blood of the eternal covenant, [Col. 0518B] equip you with every good thing to do his will, working in you what is pleasing before him through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen. But I urge you, brothers, to bear with the word of exhortation; for I have written to you in very few words. Know that our brother Timothy has been released; if he comes soon, I shall see you with him. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. The brothers from Italy greet you. Grace be with you all. Amen.”**

**“Now may the God.”** As though he said: I exhort you to good; but may God, who is able to equip you because he is the giver of peace—that is, so that vices may not disturb you—he who brought back from the dead, that is, raised from the tomb, which is properly the place of the dead, our Jesus Christ, the great shepherd of the sheep, that is, of the humble, who became shepherd “by the blood of the eternal covenant,” that is, through the shedding of his own blood, by which he confirmed the New Testament, called eternal because no other shall succeed it—may he, I say, who did this, equip you, that is, make you fit, with every good thing, that you may will and also accomplish in deed his will, that is, the things which he himself wills.

May he equip you, I say, by working in you that which is pleasing before him, because no good comes from yourselves, but he himself works it. For you can possess no good unless he goes before and follows after. May he work good in you, I say, and this through Jesus Christ, not through carnal observances. To him—to Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, not to carnal observances—be, or is, glory for ages of ages, that is, [Col. 0518D] without end. Amen: a confirmation.

[Haimo] As though he said: Thus it shall be, or thus it is true, as I have said. **“But I urge you, brothers, to bear patiently the word of exhortation.”** [Chrysostom] That is, this epistle, which is consolation and entreaty—not, I would say, admonition, which is as though directed to the sluggish. [Haimo] It is consolation, however, for those who are faint-hearted. And you ought to bear it patiently.

[Chrysostom] “For I have written in very few words,” fearing to be burdensome to you. As though he said: No one can reject the length of the discourse. [Haimo] For this was what his adversaries did; and therefore he touches upon it indirectly.

**“Know”** [Chrysostom], also by serving and honoring, **“our brother Timothy,”** namely, my fellow-apostle and fellow-worker in preaching, released by me to undertake the journey he wished, or sent out to preach [Col. 0519A], or perhaps released from the prison in which he had previously been held. “If he comes sooner,” that is, quickly, “I shall see you.” By this he makes them more attentive and more gentle.

**“Greet all your leaders and all the subject saints,”** that is, those sanctified in baptism. As he writes generally to all, so he sends good wishes generally [Col. 0520A] to all, namely leaders and subjects. For to greet is to wish salvation. “All the brothers from Italy greet you.” From this observe that he wrote from Rome. “Grace,” that is, cleansing from sins and God’s other gifts, “be with you all. Amen.”

[Col. 0519] **End of the Collections of Peter Lombard, Bishop of Paris and Master of the Sentences, on all the Epistles of the Apostle St. Paul. Printed by Ascensius, 1535, in the month of October.**

[Col. 0519]

# The Four Books of Sentences of Peter Lombard of Novara, Surnamed the Master of the Sentences, Bishop of Paris, Truly Restored to Their Former Splendor by John Aleaume, Professor of Theology at Paris

## Notice

[Col. 0519B] We publish the four books of the *Sentences* in print according to the most recent and especially accurate edition, namely the Antwerp edition of 1757, prepared by the distinguished John Aleaume, professor of theology at Paris. With the utmost care he ensured that not only the book, but also the chapters of every author cited by the Master, should be set before the reader’s eyes. Anyone who considers the incredible and rugged difficulty of the passages, all of which previous editions had left thorny and neglected, will judge how greatly this excellent man has deserved of students of theology.

An old and likewise very carefully corrected edition, printed at Paris in 1538 in what are called Gothic characters, was also of no small assistance to us. All know the *Sentences* of Peter [Col. 0519C] Lombard, in which that author has with wonderful concision and skill embraced the sum of all theology from Holy Scripture, passages and decrees of the orthodox Fathers, and has reconciled their apparent disagreements by a clear method and singular lucidity of expression.

He accomplished this with such success [Col. 0520B] that he nearly put an end to the disputed cavils of empty dialectic and diminished the deceptive arts of disputation with which the schools of scholastic theologians had hitherto resounded. Hence afterward the custom prevailed everywhere, under the famous watchword, “to follow the leader and swear by the Master’s words.”

Yet certain defects occur in this work. That celebrated theologian sometimes omits questions of great importance, while developing many questions weighty in his own age but more often useless in ours. And while he pursues figurative senses through argument, he neglects to establish the asserted doctrine by firm weight of reasoning. These faults, however, will readily be pardoned in Peter if one considers the time in which he lived and observes that, except perhaps one or two persons, he was the first to gather the whole of theology into one body, as it were. Certain opinions not commonly held by all are also reproached in him; these we shall append below at the end of the work.

# Prologue of Peter Lombard to the Books of the Sentences

[Col. 0521]

[Col. 0521] Desiring to put something from our poverty and scantiness, with the poor widow, into the treasury of the Lord, we have presumed to climb steep heights and undertake a work beyond our strength. We place confidence for its completion and reward for the labor in the Samaritan, who, after producing two denarii for the healing of the half-dead man, promised to repay in full whatever should be spent beyond them.

The truthfulness of the promise delights us, but the immensity of the labor terrifies us. The desire to make progress urges us on, but the weakness of failing discourages us (*from Augustine, On the Trinity*, book 3, prologue); yet zeal for God’s house conquers it. Inflamed by that zeal, we have endeavored to fortify—or rather to show fortified—our faith against the errors of carnal and merely natural people with the shields of David’s tower; to open up the hidden things of theological inquiry; and to impart, according to the measure of our understanding, knowledge of the Church’s sacraments (*from Augustine in the same passage cited; from Hilary, at the beginning of On the Trinity*, book 10).

We could not rightly resist the wishes of studious brothers, who demand that we serve their praiseworthy studies in Christ with tongue and pen; Christ’s charity drives this chariot-team within us. Yet we do not doubt that every utterance of human speech has always been subject to the calumny and contradiction of rivals. For when impulses of will differ, the judgment of minds also differs; so that although every statement is perfected by the reason of truth, nevertheless, while one thing seems good or pleasing to some and another to others, error of impiety resists truth, whether not understood or offensive, and the envy of the will protests. This the god of this age works in the children of unbelief: they do not subject their will to reason or devote effort to learning, but strive to fit the words of wisdom to what they have dreamed, pursuing not the reasoning of truth but of their own preference. An unjust will incites them not to an understanding of truth but to the defense of what pleases them; they do not desire to be taught the truth but turn their hearing away from it to fables.

Their profession is to seek out what they prefer rather than what ought to be taught; they do not desire what ought to be taught, but fit doctrine to their desires. They have an appearance of wisdom upon the surface. For the abandonment of faith is followed by lying hypocrisy, so that piety may be in their words although conscience has lost it. By every falsehood of speech they render even their feigned piety impious, seeking to corrupt the holiness of faith by the institutions of false doctrine and to instill into others an itching of ears under the novel dogma of their own desire. Eager for contention, they wage war without truce against truth.

For between the assertion of truth and the defense of what pleases them there is a stubborn struggle, while truth maintains itself and the will of error defends itself. Therefore, desiring to overthrow their church, hateful to God, and to stop their mouths lest they pour out the poison of wickedness upon others, and desiring to raise the lamp of truth upon the lampstand, we have, by God’s help, composed this volume amid much labor and sweat. It is founded on testimonies of truth established forever and divided into four books.

In it you will find examples and teaching of the elders. In it, through a sincere confession of the Lord’s faith, we have exposed the deceit of viper-like doctrine, embracing a way of demonstrating truth and not uncertain of the danger of an impious confession, using a measured moderation between the two (*from Augustine, prologue to On the Trinity*, book 3). Wherever our voice echoes that of the Fathers, it has not departed from their boundaries.

Therefore this labor ought not to appear superfluous to anyone who is idle or very learned, since it is necessary to many diligent persons and many unlearned persons, among whom I too am included. In a brief volume it gathers the opinions of the Fathers and appends their testimonies, so that one who seeks need not unfold a multitude of books when brevity offers without labor what is sought (*from the same passage cited above*).

In this treatise I desire not only a devout reader but also a free critic, especially where a profound question of truth is being considered—a question which would that it had as many discoverers as it has opponents! That what is sought may be found more easily, we have prefixed the headings by which the chapters of the individual books are distinguished.

# Book I. On the Mystery of the Trinity

[Col. 0521]

## Distinction I

[Col. 0521]

1. As we have repeatedly and carefully considered the contents of the Old and New Law, God’s grace going before us, it has become clear that the treatment of sacred Scripture is concerned chiefly with things or signs. For, as the excellent teacher Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, every doctrine concerns either things or signs; but things too are learned through signs.

Strictly speaking, “things” here are those which are not employed to signify something else; while “signs” are those whose use consists in signifying. Of signs, some have their whole use in signifying and not in justifying; we use these only for the sake of signifying something, as in certain legal sacraments [Col. 0522]. Others not only signify but confer that which helps inwardly, as the evangelical sacraments do. From this it is clearly understood what are here called signs: namely, those things which are employed to signify something.

Every sign, therefore, is also some thing. For that which is not any thing, as Augustine says in the same work and passage, is altogether nothing. But conversely, not every thing is a sign, because it is not employed to signify something. Since the earnest and modest contemplation of theologians is directed toward these matters, it will observe that divine Scripture preserves the prescribed form of teaching. Therefore, with God as our guide, we must discuss these things in order to open for ourselves some approach to understanding divine realities. We shall first discuss things, and afterward signs.

## He treats of things in general

2. Therefore, concerning things, one must consider what Augustine says in the same work (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 3): some things are to be enjoyed, others used, and others enjoy and use. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed. By those which are to be used, we are helped and, as it were, supported while moving toward blessedness, so that we may reach and cling to those things which make us blessed. But the things which enjoy and use are ourselves; we are, as it were, placed between the two kinds, together with angels and saints.

To enjoy (*frui*) is to cling in love to something for its own sake. To use (*uti*) is to refer that which comes into use to the attainment of that which is to be enjoyed. Otherwise, it is misuse, not use; for an unlawful use ought to be called abuse or misuse.

The things which are to be enjoyed are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet the Trinity is one supreme reality, shared by all who enjoy it—if indeed it ought to be called a reality and not rather the cause of all realities; if indeed it ought also to be called a cause. For a name suitable to so great an excellence cannot easily be found, unless it is better said that this Trinity is one God.

The things which are to be used are the world and the creatures in it. Hence Augustine says in the same work, book 1, chapter 5: “This world is to be used, not enjoyed, so that the invisible things of God may be understood through the things made” (Rom. 1:20), that is, so that eternal things may be apprehended from temporal things. Again, in the same work, chapter 4: “Among all things, only those are to be enjoyed which are eternal and unchangeable; the rest are to be used, so that we may attain the enjoyment of those.” Augustine also says in *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapter 10: “We enjoy the known things in which the will, delighted in them for their own sake, comes to rest; but we use those which we refer to something else which is to be enjoyed.”

## Again: the difference between enjoying and using, understood otherwise than above

3. It should be noted, however, that in *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapter 11, Augustine takes *use* and *enjoyment* otherwise than above, saying: “To use is to take something into the power of the will. To enjoy is to use with joy, not now of hope but already of the thing itself. Therefore everyone who enjoys uses; for he takes something into the power of the will with the end of delight. But not everyone who uses enjoys, if he seeks what he takes into the power of the will not for its own sake but for another.”

Observe that Augustine seems to say that only those enjoy who rejoice in the reality and no longer merely in hope. Thus in this life we seem not to enjoy but only to use, where we rejoice in hope; although it was said above that to enjoy is to cling in love to something for its own sake, and in this manner many even now cling to God.

## Resolution of matters which appear contradictory

4. Therefore we resolve these statements, which seem to contradict one another, by saying that we enjoy both here and in the future; but there, properly, perfectly, and fully, where we shall see by direct vision that which we enjoy. Here, however, while we walk in hope, we indeed enjoy, but not so fully. Hence in *On the Trinity*, book 10, chapter 10: “We enjoy the known things in which the will rests.” Again, in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 30, Augustine says: “The angels, enjoying him, are already blessed; and we desire to enjoy him also. And insofar as we already enjoy him in this life, whether through a mirror or in an enigma, we both endure our pilgrimage more tolerably and desire more ardently to bring it to an end.”

## Another resolution

5. It may also be said that one who enjoys even in this life possesses not merely the joy of hope but also the joy of the thing itself, because he already delights in what he loves and thus already possesses the thing in some measure.

It is established, then, that we ought to enjoy God and not use him. For, as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, you enjoy that by which you are made blessed and in which you place hope so as to attain it. The same author says concerning this in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 31: “We say that we enjoy that thing which we love for its own sake, and that only that thing is to be enjoyed by us by which we are made blessed; the rest are to be used” (Augustine, same book, chapter 33).

Yet *enjoy* is frequently said where one uses with delight. For when that which is loved is present, it also brings delight with it. But if you pass through this delight and refer it to that in which one must remain, you use it; and improperly, not properly, you are said to enjoy it. But if you cling and remain in it, making it the end of your joy, then you are truly and properly said to enjoy it. This must not be done except in that Trinity—that is, the supreme and unchangeable good.

## Whether human beings are to be used or enjoyed

6. Since human beings, who enjoy and use other things, are themselves things, the question arises whether they ought to enjoy themselves, use themselves, or both. Augustine responds thus in *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 22: “If a human being is to be loved for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for something else, we use him” (Jer. 17). But it seems to me that he is to be loved for something else. For that which must be loved for its own sake constitutes the blessed life, whose hope also consoles us at this present time. Yet hope must not be placed in a human being, because cursed is the one who does this (the sole chapter).

Therefore, if you consider carefully, no one ought even to enjoy himself, because he ought not to love himself for his own sake but for the sake of that which is to be enjoyed. This should not seem contrary to what the Apostle says in speaking to Philemon: “Yes, brother, I will enjoy you in the Lord.” Augustine resolves this thus in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 33: “If he had said only, ‘I will enjoy you,’ and had not added ‘in the Lord,’ he would seem to have placed the end of love and hope in him. But because he added ‘in the Lord,’ he showed that he had placed the end in the Lord and that he enjoyed the same.” For when, as Augustine says in the same place, you enjoy a human being in God, you enjoy God rather than the human being.

## Here it is asked whether God enjoys or uses us

7. But since God loves us, as Scripture frequently says—and Scripture strongly commends his love toward us—Augustine asks in the same work, chapter 38, how he loves: whether as using or as enjoying. He proceeds thus: If he enjoys, he needs our good, which no sound-minded person would say. For the Prophet says: “You have no need of my goods.” For every good of ours either is himself or comes from him. Therefore he does not enjoy us but uses us. For if he neither enjoys nor uses, I do not find how he loves us.

Yet he does not use us in the way that we use other things. For we refer the things which we use to the end that we may enjoy God’s goodness; but God refers his use of us to his own goodness. For he has mercy on us because of his goodness, while we have mercy on one another because of his goodness. He has mercy on us so that we may enjoy him; but we have mercy on one another so that we may enjoy him. For when we have mercy upon someone and care for someone, we act indeed for that person’s benefit, and we consider that benefit (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, chapter 30). Yet our own benefit follows, since God does not leave unrewarded the mercy we extend to others. This reward is supreme: that we may enjoy him.

Again, because he is good, we exist; and insofar as we exist, we are good (*from the same book*, chapter 32). Moreover, because he is just, we are not wicked with impunity; and insofar as we are wicked, to that extent we also are less. Therefore, the use by which God uses us is referred not to his benefit but to ours; to his goodness alone (*from the same work*, chapter 32).

## Whether virtues are to be used or enjoyed
8. Here it must be considered whether virtues are to be used or enjoyed. Some hold that they are to be used, not enjoyed; and they support this by Augustine’s authority. For, as was stated above (no. 5 of this first distinction; see *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. 1, ch. 33), he says that nothing is to be enjoyed except the Trinity, that is, the highest and immutable Good. They also say that virtues are not to be enjoyed because they are not to be loved for their own sake, but for the sake of eternal blessedness. But that which is to be enjoyed is to be loved for its own sake. They prove, however, by Augustine’s authority that virtues are not to be loved for their own sake, but solely for blessedness. In book 13 of *On the Trinity*, he says against certain persons:

> Perhaps the virtues, which we love solely for the sake of blessedness, dare to persuade us not to love blessedness itself; and if they do this, we certainly cease also to love the virtues, when we do not love that for the sake of which alone we loved them.

By these words Augustine seems, in chapter 8, to show that virtues are to be loved not for their own sake, but solely for blessedness. If that is so, then they are not to be enjoyed.

Others, on the contrary, hold that virtues are to be enjoyed, because they are to be sought and loved for their own sake. They support this by Ambrose’s authority, who says on the passage in the Epistle to the Galatians, “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience,” etc.: “Here he does not name works, but fruits, because they are to be sought for their own sake.” But if they are to be sought for their own sake, then they are also to be loved for their own sake (ch. 5).

Desiring, therefore, to remove this apparent conflict of authorities, we say that virtues are to be sought and loved for their own sake, and yet for the sake of blessedness alone. They are indeed to be loved for their own sake because they delight their possessors with a sincere and holy delight and produce spiritual joy in them. Nevertheless, one must not stop here but go farther; the movement of love must not remain here, nor must this be its terminus. Rather, this must be referred to that highest Good, to which alone one must wholly cling, because it alone is to be loved solely for its own sake, and beyond it nothing is to be sought; for it is the supreme end.

Therefore Augustine says (in no. 5, and in *On Christian Doctrine*, ch. 33) that we love virtues solely for blessedness—not because we do not love them for their own sake, but because the very fact that we love them is referred to that highest Good, to which alone we must cling and in which we must remain, and in which the end of joy must be placed. Therefore virtues are not to be enjoyed.

But someone may say: To enjoy is to cling lovingly to something for its own sake, as was stated above. Therefore, if virtues are to be loved for their own sake, they must also be enjoyed. To this we reply that, in that definition, where it says “for its own sake,” this must be understood as “solely for its own sake”: that it be loved only for itself, not referred to something else, and that the end be placed in it. As Augustine showed above in chapter 1, saying: “If you cling to it and remain there, placing the end of joy in it, then you may truly and properly be said to enjoy it.” This is not to be done except in that Trinity, that is, in the highest and immutable Good.

Virtues, therefore, are to be used, and through them the highest Good is to be enjoyed. We say the same concerning good will. Hence Augustine says in book 10 of *On the Trinity*: “Will is that by which we enjoy.” Likewise, we enjoy through virtues, not virtues themselves—unless perhaps some virtue is God, as charity is; of this will be treated later, distinction 71, book 1.

### Epilogue

9. The sum, then, of all that has been said since we began to treat specifically of things is this: some things are to be enjoyed; others are to be used; and still others enjoy and use. Among those things which are to be used, there are also certain things through which we enjoy, such as virtues and powers of the soul, which are natural goods. Before treating of signs, we must discuss all these matters; and first the things which are to be enjoyed, namely the holy and indivisible Trinity.

## DISTINCTION II. ON THE MYSTERY OF TRINITY AND UNITY

1. This too must be held by true and devout faith: that the Trinity is one and the only true God, as Augustine says in book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This Trinity is said, believed, and understood to be of one and the same substance or essence. It is the highest Good, seen by minds most thoroughly purified. For the gaze of the human mind is too weak to remain fixed in so excellent a light unless it is cleansed through the righteousness of faith.

Likewise, in book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapter 10: “I do not approve what I said in a prayer: ‘O God, who willed that only the pure should know the truth’; for it may be answered that many who are not pure also know many true things.”

Therefore, concerning this supremely great and most excellent matter, we must speak with modesty and fear, and listen with the most attentive and devout ears, when the unity of the Trinity is investigated—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing is sought with greater labor, and nothing is found with greater fruitfulness.

Accordingly, everyone who hears or reads what is said concerning the ineffable and inaccessible light of the Godhead should endeavor to imitate and observe what the venerable teacher Augustine says of himself in book 2 of *On the Trinity*:

> I shall not be reluctant, wherever I am uncertain, to inquire; nor ashamed, wherever I err, to learn. Whoever therefore hears or reads this: where he is equally certain, let him proceed with me; where he is equally uncertain, let him inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back. Thus let us together enter upon the way of charity, tending toward him of whom it is said in Psalm 10: “Seek his face always.”

### What was the intention of those who wrote on the Trinity

2. All Catholic writers, as Augustine says in the same first book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, who have written about the Trinity, which is God, have intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and, in inseparable equality, are one God: so that there is unity in essence and plurality in persons. Thus they are not three gods but one God, although the Father begot the Son, and therefore the Son is not the one who is the Father; and the Son was begotten by the Father, and therefore the Father is not the one who is the Son; and the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of Father and Son, coequal with both and belonging to the unity of the Trinity.

Let us therefore hold that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God, as Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*. Yet the Father himself is not the Son, nor the Son himself the Father, nor the Holy Spirit himself either the Father or the Son. For the essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, which the Greeks call *homoousia* (ὁμουσία), “same substance”: in it the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is other, the Son other, and the Holy Spirit other.

### What order should be observed when discussing the Trinity

3. Moreover, as Augustine teaches in the first book of *On the Trinity*, it must first be demonstrated by the authorities of the Holy Scriptures whether the faith is so constituted. Then, against talkative reasoners—more arrogant than capable—Catholic arguments and fitting analogies must be used for the defense and affirmation of the faith. Thus, by satisfying their inquiries, we may instruct the gentle more fully; and if the others cannot discover what they seek, they may complain of their own minds rather than of truth itself or of our assertion.

### Testimonies of the saints concerning the Trinity

4. Let us therefore bring forward the authorities of the Old and New Testaments by which the truth of divine unity and Trinity may be demonstrated. First let the very beginnings of the Law present themselves, where Moses says, Deuteronomy 6: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” Likewise, Exodus chapter 20: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you shall have no other gods besides me.” Here he signified the unity of the divine nature. For, as Ambrose says in the first book *On the Trinity*—that is, *On Faith*, book 1—“God” is the name of nature, while “Lord” is the name of power.

Again, elsewhere God, speaking to Moses, says, Exodus 3: “I am who I am; and if they ask my name, go and say to them: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’” For in saying, “I am,” not “We are,” and “He who is,” not “We who are,” he most plainly declared that there is one God only.

In the Song of Exodus, chapter 15, it is also read: “The Almighty Lord is his name.” He does not say “Lords,” wishing to signify unity. The Lord also simultaneously displayed plurality of persons and unity of nature in Genesis chapter 1 when he said: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness.” By saying “Let us make” and “our,” he displayed plurality of persons; by saying “image,” unity of essence.

For, as Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*, if in the nature of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there were only one person, it would not be said, “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness.” For when he says “in [the] image,” he shows that there is one nature in whose image humanity was made; but when he says “our,” he shows that the same God is not one person but several persons. [Col. 0527]

### He expressly shows that there is neither solitude, diversity, nor singularity there, but likeness

5. Hilary also says in book 3 of *On the Trinity* that these words signify that in the Trinity there is neither diversity nor singularity or solitude, but likeness and plurality or distinction. He says:

> He who said, “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness,” showed, by saying “image” and “our likeness,” that they are mutually like one another. For an image is not solitary, nor is likeness directed toward itself; nor does likeness allow diversity to be introduced between two, so that one is made unlike the other.

Likewise, the same author in book 4, near the end:

> He wished this meaning to be understood more fully as not being referred to himself alone, when he said: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness.” For the declaration of fellowship removes the understanding of singularity, because fellowship cannot belong to one who is solitary by himself; and again, the solitude of one who is solitary does not admit “Let us make”; nor does anyone say “our” to one foreign to himself. Therefore each expression—namely, “Let us make” and “our”—just as it does not allow him to be solitary and the same, so neither does it signify him as different from himself or foreign to himself. “I shall make” and “my” suit one who is solitary; “Let us make” and “our” suit one who is not solitary. Each expression signifies that he is neither merely solitary nor different or diverse. We too must confess him as neither solitary nor diverse. Thus God is found to act toward an image shared by him with God, and toward the same likeness, so that neither the expression of the agent permits an understanding of solitude, nor does the action directed toward the same image or likeness allow a diversity of divinity.

In these words Hilary intended plurality of persons to be understood by the term “fellowship,” and he indicated that by “fellowship” or “plurality” something is not posited, but something is removed. For when plurality or fellowship of persons is spoken of, solitude or singularity is denied. When we say that there are several persons, we signify that there is not one person alone.

Therefore Hilary, wishing these things to be understood subtly and soundly, says: “The declaration of fellowship removed the understanding of singularity”; he does not say, “It posited something.” Likewise, when we speak of three persons, we remove singularity and solitude, and signify that the Father is not alone, the Son is not alone, and the Holy Spirit is not alone; and that there are not merely the Father and Son, nor merely the Father and Holy Spirit, nor merely the Son and Holy Spirit. But this will be treated more fully below (distinction 19), where it will also be shown in what respect the three persons are called similar, and whether there is in any way diversity or difference there.

### He returns to what he had begun, in order to introduce other authorities

6. But now let us return to our purpose and introduce other authorities of the saints to show the plurality of persons and the unity of the divine essence.

Moses says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1), signifying the Father by “God” and the Son by “beginning.” And where we say *Deus*, “God,” the Hebrew text has *Heloym* [*Elohim*], the plural of the singular *hel* [*El*]. Therefore, because it does not say *hel*, “God,” but *heloym*, which can be translated “gods” or “judges,” this is referred to plurality of persons.

The saying which the devil uttered through the serpent also seems to belong to this: “You shall be like gods.” The Hebrew here has *heloym*, as though he said: “You shall be like divine persons.”

David also, that greatest of prophets and kings, who sets his understanding above that of others when he says in Psalm 67, “I have understood beyond the elders,” shows the unity of the divine nature when he says in Psalm 80: “The Lord is his name”; he does not say “Lords.” Elsewhere, likewise showing both his unity and eternity, he says in the person of God: “Israel, if you listen to me, there shall be no new god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god.”

One of these expressions, as Ambrose says in book 1 *On the Trinity*—that is, *On Faith*, book 1, chapter 5—signifies eternity; the other, the unity of an undifferentiated substance, so that we may not believe that the Son or the Holy Spirit is later than the Father or of another divinity. For if the Son or Holy Spirit is later than the Father, he is new; and if he is not of one divinity, he is foreign. But he is not later, because he is not new; nor is he foreign, because the Son is born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.

Elsewhere, also insinuating the distinction of persons, David says (Psalm 66): “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.” Elsewhere he also says: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.” For the threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons; while it discloses the unity of essence when it adds, in the singular, “him.”

Isaiah likewise says in chapter 6 that he heard the Seraphim crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God.” By saying “holy” three times, he signifies the Trinity; by adding “Lord God,” unity of essence.

David also plainly intimates the eternal generation of the Son, speaking in the person of the Son: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Psalm 2). Of this ineffable generation Isaiah says, chapter 53: “Who shall recount his generation?”

In the book of Wisdom, moreover, the Son’s eternity with the Father is shown, where Wisdom speaks thus:

> The Lord possessed me from the beginning of his ways. Before he made anything from the beginning, I was ordained from eternity. Before the earth was made, the abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived. The springs did not yet exist, nor mountains or hills, and I was being brought forth. He had not yet made the earth and the foundations of the world; when he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he set the foundations of the earth in balance, I was with him, composing all things, and I delighted day by day, playing before him.

Here is a fitting testimony concerning eternal generation, by which Wisdom herself bears witness that she was conceived and brought forth—that is, begotten—before the world, and exists eternally with the Father. She also says elsewhere (Ecclesiasticus 24): “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature.”

The prophet Micah likewise simultaneously intimated the Word’s eternal generation and his temporal generation from Mary, saying in chapter 5: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth one who shall be ruler in Israel; and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” [Col. 0528]

### Particular testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit

7. We also have explicit testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament. For Genesis reads (chapter 1): “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” And David says in Psalm 138: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” In the book of Wisdom, chapter 1, it is said: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit; for the Spirit of wisdom is gracious.” Isaiah likewise says in chapter 61: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me.”

### On testimonies of the New Testament

8. Now, after the testimonies of the Old Testament concerning faith in the holy Trinity and unity, let us turn to the authorities of the New Testament, so that truth may be known “in the midst of two living creatures,” that is, the two Testaments; and that the coal may be taken with tongs from the altar to touch the mouths of believers.

The Lord Christ openly intimates the unity of the divine essence and the Trinity of persons when he says to the apostles: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” He says “in the name,” indeed, as Ambrose says in book 1 *On the Trinity*—that is, *On Faith*, book 1, chapters 1–2—not “in the names,” in order that unity of essence may be shown. By the three names which he adds, he declares that there are three persons.

He himself also says: “I and the Father are one.” As Ambrose says in the same work, he said “one” so that no distinction of power or nature might be made; and he added “are,” so that you may recognize the Father and the Son—that is, so that it may be believed that the perfect Father begot a perfect Son, and that Father and Son are one not by confusion of person but by unity of nature.

John also says in the First Catholic Epistle: “There are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one.” Likewise, in the beginning of his Gospel, he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Here he openly shows that the Son always and eternally existed with the Father—as one distinct person with another.

The Apostle also openly distinguishes the Trinity, saying, Galatians 4: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts”; and elsewhere, Romans 8: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus [Col. 0529] dwells in us,” etc. Again, elsewhere he most clearly commends both Trinity and unity, saying, Romans 8: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory.” “From him,” Augustine says in book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, is said with reference to the Father; “through him,” with reference to the Son; “in him,” with reference to the Holy Spirit. But because he does not say “from them,” “through them,” and “in them,” nor “to them be glory,” but “to him,” he indicated that this Trinity is one God.

But since almost every syllable of the New Testament harmoniously intimates this truth of ineffable unity and Trinity, let us cease the accumulation of testimonies on this matter and show, by appropriate reasons and analogies, as far as our weakness permits, that it is so.

## DISTINCTION III. HE BEGINS TO SHOW HOW THE CREATOR COULD BE KNOWN THROUGH CREATION

1. The Apostle says, Romans 1, that “the invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made,” as are also his eternal power and divinity. By “creation of the world” humanity is understood, on account of the excellence by which it surpasses other creatures, or on account of the correspondence it has with every creature.

Therefore humanity could see, and indeed did see, the invisible things of God with the understanding of the mind through the things that were made—that is, through visible or invisible creatures. For humanity was aided by two things: namely, by nature, which was rational; and by works made by God, so that truth might be made manifest to humanity. Therefore the Apostle said: “Because God revealed it to them”—namely, when he made works in which some indication of the craftsman shines forth.

### The first reason or way by which God could be known

2. For, as Ambrose says, so that God, who is invisible by nature, might also be known from visible things, he made a work which by its visibility manifested its maker; so that through what is certain, the uncertain might be known, and he might be believed to be the God of all who made what it is impossible for a human being to make.

Therefore they could know, or did know, that he who made those things—which no creature can make or destroy—is above every creature. Let any strength of a creature come forward and make such a heaven and earth, and I shall say that it is God. But because no creature can make such things, it is evident that he who made them is above every creature; and thus the human mind could know that he is God.

### The second reason by which he could be known, or the manner in which they knew him

3. By another method too, under the guidance of reason, they could know, and indeed did know, the truth of God. For, as Augustine says in *The City of God*, the greatest philosophers saw that no body is God, and therefore transcended all bodies in seeking God. They also saw that whatever is mutable is not the supreme God or the principle of all things; and therefore they transcended every soul and mutable spirit. Then they saw that everything mutable can exist only from him who exists immutably and simply. Therefore they understood that he made all these things and could be made by none.

### The third reason or method

4. They also considered that whatever exists among substances is either body or spirit; and that spirit is something better than body, but that he who made spirit and body is far better.

### The fourth method or reason

5. They also understood that bodily form is perceptible by the senses, while spiritual form is intelligible; and they preferred intelligible form to sensible form. By “sensible” we mean things capable of being perceived by bodily sight and touch; by “intelligible,” things capable of being understood by the vision of the mind.
