Therefore, since both body and mind appeared to them more or less beautiful, and yet, if they could lack all form, would be wholly nonexistent, they saw that there is something by which these were made beautiful, in which there is the first and immutable—and therefore incomparable—form. They most rightly believed that to be the principle of things which was not made and from which all things were made. [Col. 0530]

See by how many methods the truth of God could be known. Therefore, although God is one simple essence, consisting of no diversity of parts or accidents, the Apostle nevertheless says in the plural, “the invisible things of God,” because the truth of God is known through the things made in many ways. For from the permanence of creatures the eternal Creator is understood; from their greatness, his omnipotence; from their order and arrangement, his wisdom; and from their governance, his goodness. All these things pertain to demonstrating the unity of the Godhead.

### How a trace of the Trinity appears in creatures

6. It remains now to show whether, through the things that have been made, any indication, however slight, of the Trinity could have been had. On this Augustine says in book 6, chapter 6, of *On the Trinity*:

> It is necessary that, while seeing the Creator by understanding through the things that have been made, we should understand the Trinity. For a trace of this Trinity appears in creatures. Things made by divine art display in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. For each of these created things is one thing—for example, bodily natures and capacities of souls; and is formed by some kind of shape, such as figures or qualities of bodies, and doctrines or arts of souls; and seeks or maintains some order, such as the weights or positions of bodies and the loves or delights of souls. Thus in creatures there shines forth a trace of the Trinity.

For in that Trinity are the highest origin of all things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed delight. The highest origin, as Augustine shows in *On True Religion*, is understood as God the Father, from whom are all things, from whom are the Son and Holy Spirit. The most perfect beauty is understood as the Son, namely the Father’s truth, in no respect unlike him, whom we worship with the Father and in the Father. He is the form of all things made from the beginning and referred to unity.

Yet all these things would neither be made by the Father through the Son nor remain preserved within their proper ends, unless God were supremely good: he did not begrudge any nature, which was good from him; and, that it might remain in the good itself, he gave some as much as they willed, others as much as they were able. This goodness is understood as the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of Father and Son. Therefore it is fitting that we worship and hold fast this gift of God, equally immutable with Father and Son.

Thus, through contemplation of creatures of one substance, we understand the Trinity: one God, the Father, from whom we are; the Son, through whom we are; and the Holy Spirit, in whom we are—namely, the principle to which we return, the form which we follow, and the grace by which we are reconciled. That is: God, by whose authorship we were created; his likeness, through which we are restored to unity; and peace, by which we adhere to unity.

That is, God who said in Genesis 1, “Let there be light”; the Word through whom everything that exists substantially and naturally was made; and the gift of his loving-kindness, by which what was made from him through the Word pleased him and was reconciled to its maker so that it should not perish.

Thus it has been shown how the image of the Trinity is in some degree indicated in creatures. Yet through contemplation of creatures a sufficient knowledge of the Trinity cannot be, and could not be, obtained without the revelation of teaching or inward inspiration. Therefore the ancient philosophers saw truth as through a shadow and from afar, failing in their contemplation of the Trinity, like Pharaoh’s magicians at the third sign, Exodus 8. Nevertheless, through the things which have been made, we are aided in faith in invisible things.

### How the image of the Trinity is in the soul

7. Now let us come to the discussion in which we discover the image of the Trinity in the human mind that knows God, or can know him. For, as Augustine says in book 14 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, nevertheless the image of him than whom nothing is better must be sought and found where our nature has nothing better—namely, in the mind.

Even in the mind, before it becomes a participant of God, his image is found. For although it is disfigured through the loss of participation in God, the image of God nevertheless remains. For the mind is the image of God precisely insofar as it is capable of him and can participate in him. Let us therefore seek in it the Trinity which is God.

For behold: the mind remembers itself, understands itself, and loves itself. If we perceive this, we perceive a Trinity—not God himself, certainly, but the image of God. For here appears a certain trinity of memory, understanding, and love. Let us therefore treat especially these three: memory, understanding, and will.

These three, as Augustine says in book 10 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 21, are not three lives but one life; nor three minds but one mind, one essence. Memory is spoken of in relation to something, and likewise understanding and will or love are spoken of in relation to something. But life is spoken of in reference to itself, as are mind and essence. Therefore these three are one insofar as they are one life, one mind, one essence; and whatever else they are each called in reference to themselves, they are also called together not in the plural but in the singular. But they are three insofar as they are referred to one another.

### How they are equal, because each comprehends all things, entirely  
*(From Augustine, book 10 of* On the Trinity, *chapter 11)*

8. They are equal not only each to each, but also each to all; otherwise they would not comprehend one another. But they do comprehend one another. For each is comprehended by each, and all are comprehended by each. For I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; I understand that I understand, will, and remember; and I will that I will, remember, and understand.

### How memory comprehends all three in their entirety

9. I remember at the same time all of my memory, understanding, and will. For whatever I do not remember of my memory is not in my memory; but nothing is so much in memory as memory itself. Therefore I remember it wholly. Likewise, whatever I understand, I know that I understand; and I know that I will whatever I will; but whatever I know, I remember. Therefore I remember all my understanding and all my will.

### How understanding comprehends all three in their entirety  
*(Augustine, cited passage)*

10. Likewise, when I understand these three, I understand them all together in their entirety. For there is nothing intelligible which I do not understand except what I do not know. But what I do not know, I neither remember nor will. Therefore, whatever intelligible thing I do not understand, I consequently neither remember nor will. Whatever intelligible thing I remember and will, I consequently understand.

### How will comprehends all three in their entirety

11. My will also comprehends all my understanding and all my memory when I use all that I understand and remember. Therefore, since each comprehends both all and the entirety of the others, the whole of each is equal to the whole of each other and to all the wholes together. These three are one: one life, one mind, one essence.

Behold, the human mind is an image, although unequal, of that highest unity and Trinity in which there is one essence and three persons. Here “mind” is understood as the soul itself, in which that image of the Trinity exists. But, properly speaking, as Augustine says in book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, mind is not the soul itself but what is more excellent in it, as the term is often understood.

This too must be known: memory concerns not only absent and past things but also present things, as Augustine says in book 14 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 14; otherwise it would not comprehend itself.

### In what sense are these three said to be one and one essence?

12. Here we must carefully consider in what sense the preceding statement is to be understood: that these three—memory, understanding, and will—are one, one mind, one essence. This does not seem true in the strict sense of the words. For mind, that is, rational spirit, is a spiritual and incorporeal essence. But these three are natural properties or powers of the mind itself, and differ from one another; for memory is not understanding or will, nor is understanding will or love.

### That they are also mutually predicated relatively

13. These three are also referred to one another, as Augustine says in book 9 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3. For the mind cannot love or remember itself unless it also knows itself. For how does it love or remember what it does not know? Thus, in a wonderful manner, these three are inseparable from one another; nevertheless, each of them, and all together, is one essence, although they are spoken of relatively in relation to one another. [Col. 0532]

### Here is explained what was asked above: how these three are called one

14. But now we must see how these three are called one substance. This is because they exist substantially in the soul or mind itself, not as accidents in subjects, which can be present or absent. Hence Augustine says in book 9 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> We are admonished, if we can in any way see it, that these exist substantially in the mind, not as in a subject, as color exists in a body; for although they are mutually spoken of relatively, nevertheless each exists substantially in its own substance.

See in what sense those three are said to be one or one substance. Whoever, Augustine says in book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, keenly perceives these three as naturally established by God in the mind, and sees what a great thing occurs in it, by which the eternal and immutable nature can be remembered, beheld, and desired—for it remembers through memory, beholds through understanding, and embraces through love—such a person truly finds the image of that highest Trinity.

### That in this likeness there is unlikeness  
*(From Augustine, book 15 of* On the Trinity, *chapter 20)*

15. Nevertheless, let such a person beware of comparing this image, made by the Trinity, with that Trinity itself in such a way as to think it wholly similar. Rather, even in this whatever likeness, let him perceive a great unlikeness as well.

### First unlikeness  
*(From the same book, chapter 22)*

16. This can be shown briefly. A single human being remembers, understands, and loves through these three; but that human being is neither memory, understanding, nor love, but possesses them. Therefore one human being possesses these three, but is not himself these three. In the supreme simplicity of the nature which is God, however, although God is one, there are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and these three persons are one God.

Thus the Trinity itself is one thing, and the image of the Trinity in another thing is another. Because of this image, that in which these three are found—namely, the human being—is also called an image. Just as both the panel and the painting upon it are called an image, though the panel is called an image because of the painting which is on it.

### Second unlikeness  
*(From Augustine, book 15 of* On the Trinity, *chapter 7)*

17. Again, this image—the human being possessing those three—is one person; but that Trinity is not one person, but three persons: Father of the Son, Son of the Father, and Spirit of Father and Son. Thus, in this image of the Trinity, these three do not constitute one human being, but belong to one human being. In that highest Trinity, however, of which this is an image, those three are not things belonging to one God, but are one God; and those persons are three, not one person.

For those three are not a human being, but belong to a human being or are in a human being. But can we say that the Trinity is in God in such a manner that something belongs to God and yet is not God himself? Far be it from us to believe this! Let us therefore say that there is in our mind an image of the Trinity, but a slight and imperfect one, which bears the likeness of the highest Trinity in such a way that it is in very great measure unlike it.

But it must be known that this trinity of the mind, as Augustine says in book 14 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12, is not the image of God merely because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can also remember, understand, and love him by whom it was made.

### Another designation of the trinity in the soul: mind, knowledge, and love
18. The Trinity in the soul, which is the image of that supreme and ineffable Trinity, may also be distinguished in another way and by other names. For, as Augustine says in Book 11 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, mind, its knowledge, and love are three certain things. For the mind knows itself and loves itself; nor can it love itself unless it also knows itself. Mind and its knowledge are two certain things, as is stated in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7. Likewise, mind and its love are two certain things. Therefore, when the mind knows itself and loves itself, there remains a trinity: mind, love, and knowledge. Here “mind” is understood not as the soul, but as that which is more excellent in the soul.

Although these three are distinct from one another, they are nevertheless said to be one, because they exist substantially in the soul.

How mind is understood in the place of the Father, knowledge in the place of the Son, and love in the place of the Holy Spirit.  
(From Augustine, Book 9 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12.)

19. The mind itself is, as it were, a parent, and its knowledge is, as it were, its offspring. For when the mind knows itself, it begets knowledge of itself, and it alone is the parent of its own knowledge. The third is love, which proceeds from the mind itself and its knowledge, when the mind knows itself and loves itself; for it could not love itself unless it knew itself. It also loves its pleasing offspring, that is, its own knowledge; and so love is a certain embrace of parent and offspring.

That knowledge is not less than mind, nor love less than both.  
(From the same work of Augustine.)

20. Nor is the offspring less than the parent, since the mind knows itself as greatly as it is; nor is love less than parent and offspring—that is, than mind and knowledge—since the mind loves itself as greatly as it knows itself and as greatly as it is.

That these three are in themselves.  
(From the same book, chapter 5.)

21. These individual things are also in themselves: for the loving mind is in love, love is in the knowledge of the one who loves, and knowledge is in the mind that knows. Behold: in these three there appears some sort of trace of the Trinity.

How the mind, through these things, advances to the understanding of God.

22. Therefore the rational mind, considering these three and the one essence in which they are, stretches itself toward contemplation of the Creator; and it sees unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity. For it understands that there is one God, one essence, one principle. It understands that, if there were two, either both would be deficient or one would be superfluous. For if one lacked something possessed by the other, supreme perfection would not be there. But if one lacked nothing possessed by the other, then, since all things were in one, the other would be superfluous. Therefore it understood that God, the author of all things, is one; and it saw that he is not without wisdom, as though he were a foolish thing. It therefore understood that he has wisdom, begotten from himself; and because he loves his wisdom, it understood that love too is there.

Here concerning the unity of the supreme Trinity.

23. Therefore, according to this consideration, as Augustine says in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, let us believe that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, the maker and ruler of all creation; and that the Father is not the Son, nor the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son, but that they are a Trinity of persons mutually related. For, as he himself says in *On Faith, to Peter*, the nature or essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, but not their person. For if the person were one in the same way as the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, the Trinity would not truly be called a Trinity. Again, the Trinity would indeed be real, but the Trinity itself would not be one God, if Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are distinguished from one another by the properties of their persons, were also distinguished by diversity of natures. But the faith of patriarchs, prophets, and apostles proclaims that the one God is Trinity.

Therefore, in that holy Trinity, there is one God the Father, who alone essentially begot from himself one Son; and there is one Son, who alone was essentially born of the one Father; and there is one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from Father and Son. But one person cannot do all this: that is, beget itself, be born of itself, and proceed from itself. For, as Augustine says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, there is nothing that begets itself in order to exist.

## DISTINCTION IV. HERE IT IS ASKED WHETHER IT SHOULD BE GRANTED THAT GOD BEGOT HIMSELF.

1. Here is a question quite necessary. For it is certain, and incontrovertibly true, that God the Father begot the Son. Therefore it is asked whether it should be granted that God [Col. 0534] begot God. For if God begot God, it seems that he begot either himself as God or another god. But if he begot another god, there is not only one God. If, however, God begot himself, then something begot itself.

In answer, we say that it is sound and catholic to grant that one begot one, that God begot God, because God the Father begot God the Son. It is also written in the Creed: “Light from Light, true God from true God.” But as for the addition, “Therefore he begot himself as God or another god,” we say that neither should be granted. That he did not beget another god is clear, because there is only one God. And that he did not beget himself Augustine shows in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, saying: “Those who think it belongs to God’s power that he himself should beget himself err all the more, because God not only is not so, but neither is any spiritual nor bodily creature. For there is nothing that begets itself in order to exist.” Therefore it must neither be believed nor said that God begot himself.

Another question on the same matter.

2. Yet the talkative reasoners construct a further argument, saying: “If God the Father begot God, he begot either God who is God the Father, or God who is not God the Father. If he begot God who is not Father, then there is God who is not God the Father. Therefore there is not only one God. But if he begot God who is God the Father, then he begot himself.”

In reply, we distinguish the proposition which they put forward in this way: “If God the Father begot God, he begot either God who is God the Father, or God who is not God the Father.” For this can be understood rightly or wrongly. The answer must therefore be as follows. “God the Father begot God who is himself the Father”: we say this is false. We grant the other proposition, namely, that he begot God who is not the Father. Yet he did not beget another God, nor is he who was begotten another God than the Father, but one God with the Father.

But if it is added, “He begot God who is not God the Father,” we distinguish, because this can be understood in two ways. “He begot God who is not God the Father,” namely God the Son, who is the Son and not the Father, though he is God: this meaning is true. But if it is understood thus, “He begot God who is not God who is Father,” this meaning is false. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same God; and conversely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

The opinion of certain persons who say that the three persons are one God and one substance, but not conversely—namely, that one God or one substance is three persons.

3. Certain opponents of the truth grant that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—or the three persons—are one God, one substance; yet they refuse to grant that one God or one substance is three persons. They say that the divine substance is predicated of the three persons, but not the three persons of the divine substance.

But the catholic faith holds and proclaims both that the three persons are one God and one substance, essence, or divine nature, and that the one God, or divine essence, is three persons. Hence Augustine, in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, says: “God himself is rightly understood as Trinity, blessed and alone powerful.” See how explicitly he said, “God himself [is] Trinity,” in order to show both that God himself is Trinity and that the Trinity is God himself.

Likewise, in the same work: “In those words of the Apostle,” he says, “where, speaking of Christ’s coming, he says: ‘whom the blessed and only powerful [one] shall show, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality,’ etc., neither the Father nor the Son nor the Holy Spirit is specifically named; but ‘the blessed and only powerful [one],’ that is, the one and only true God, who is the Trinity itself.” Here too he openly says that the one only true God is the Trinity itself; and if the one God is Trinity, then one God is three persons.

Likewise, in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8: “We say not three gods, but one God, to be that most excellent Trinity itself.” Likewise, in the book called the *Enchiridion*, addressed to Lawrence, chapter 9: “For a Christian, it is enough to believe that the cause of created things, visible and invisible, is none other than the goodness of the Creator, who is the true and one God [Col. 0535]; that there is no nature which is not either he himself or from him; and that he is Trinity, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Likewise Augustine, in his sermon *On Faith*, chapter 7: “We believe one God to be the one Trinity of the divine name.” The same author, in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*: “We say that God alone is the Trinity itself.”

Behold: by these and many other authorities it is plainly shown that it must be said and believed that one God and Trinity are one substance, three persons; just as, conversely, the Trinity is said to be one God and the three persons are said to be one substance.

He returns to the foregoing question: whether God the Father begot himself as God or another god.

4. Let us now return to the foregoing question, in which it was asked whether God the Father begot himself as God or another god. We say that neither is to be granted. Augustine nevertheless says, in Letter 66 to Maximus the physician, that God the Father begot another self from himself, in these words: “In order that the Father might have a Son from himself, he did not diminish himself, but so begot from himself another self that he remained wholly in himself and was in the Son as great as he was when alone.”

This may be understood thus: he begot from himself one other than himself—not another god, certainly, but another person. Or, “he begot another self,” that is, he begot another who is what he himself is. For although the Father is other than the Son, the Son is not something other than the Father, but they are one.

## DISTINCTION V. HERE IT IS ASKED WHETHER THE FATHER BEGOT THE DIVINE ESSENCE, OR THE ESSENCE ITSELF BEGOT THE SON; WHETHER ESSENCE BEGOT ESSENCE; OR WHETHER THE ESSENCE NEITHER BEGOT NOR WAS BEGOTTEN.

1. After this, it is asked whether it should be granted that the Father begot the divine essence, or that the divine essence begot the Son, or that essence begot essence; or whether the divine essence neither begot nor was begotten at all. Agreeing with catholic writers, we say that the Father neither begot the divine essence, nor did the divine essence beget the Son, nor did the divine essence beget the divine essence. Here, by “essence” we understand the divine nature, which is common to the three persons and wholly present in each.

Therefore it must not be said that the Father begot the divine essence, because, if the Father were said to have begotten the divine essence, the divine essence would be spoken of relatively to the Father, or would be used in place of a relative term. But if it were spoken of relatively, or used in place of a relative term, it would not signify essence. For, as Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, what is said relatively does not signify substance.

Second reason.

2. Again, since God the Father is the divine essence, if he were its begetter, he would surely be the begetter of the thing which he himself is; and thus the same thing would have begotten itself, which Augustine denies in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, as we showed above.

Third and stronger reason.

3. Again, if the Father is the begetter of the divine essence, then, since he himself is the divine essence and is God, he is and is God by that which he begets. Therefore it is not what is begotten that is God from the Father; rather, the Father is and is God by that which he begets. And if this is so, the begotten is the cause to the begetter that he is and that he is God, rather than the begetter being the cause to the begotten.

By similar reasoning Augustine proves, in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, that the Father is not wise by the wisdom which he begot. For if he is wise by it, he is by it; for to be is the same for him as to be wise. And if to be is the same for him as to be wise, then the Father is not wise through that wisdom which he begot. For what else do we say when we say, “For him, to be is the same as to be wise,” except: “He is by that by which he is wise” (ibid.)? Therefore, whatever is the cause to him that he is wise is also the cause to him that he is. If, then, the wisdom which he begot is the cause to him that he is wise, it is also the cause to him that he is. But no one would ever say that wisdom, begotten by the Father, is the cause to the Father by which he is; for what could be more insane?

Thus, if the Father begot the essence by which he is, the essence which he begot is the cause to him that he is. Therefore he did not beget that essence which he is. For in that simplicity, as Augustine says, because to be wise is not one thing and to be another, wisdom there is the same as essence. Therefore what we say of [Col. 0536] wisdom, we say of essence. Thus, just as he did not beget the wisdom by which he is wise, so neither did he beget the essence by which he is. For he is wise by wisdom and powerful by power; likewise, he is essence itself. And the same wisdom and power are essence. It is therefore clear from what has been said that the Father did not beget the divine essence.

Augustine seems to oppose this.

4. But Augustine appears to say the contrary in his single book *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 3: “When God begot the Word, he begot what he himself is—not from nothing, nor from some matter already made and created, but from himself, what he himself is.” Likewise: “God the Father, who most truly both willed and was able to reveal himself to minds that would know him, begot, in order to reveal himself, what he himself is who begot.”

See: in these words he plainly says that God the Father begot that which he himself is. But what he himself is is nothing other than the divine essence. Therefore it appears that he begot the divine essence.

We answer that these words must be understood thus: the Father begot from himself that which he himself is, namely the Son, who is what the Father is. For what the Father is, the Son also is; but the one who is Father is not the one who is Son.

He treats the other parts of the question.

5. So too it must not be said that the divine essence begot the Son. For since the Son is the divine essence, the Son would be the thing by which he is begotten, and thus the same thing would beget itself. Likewise, we say that the divine essence did not beget essence. Since the divine essence is one supreme thing, if the divine essence begot essence, the same thing would have begotten itself. This is altogether impossible. Rather, the Father alone begot the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from Father and Son.

Passages that seem contrary to the foregoing.

6. But what Augustine says in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, appears contrary to the foregoing: “For God, to be is to be wise; hence Father and Son together are one wisdom, because [they are] one essence; and separately, wisdom from wisdom, just as essence from essence.” In these words Augustine plainly says “wisdom from wisdom” and “essence from essence,” where he seems to mean that wisdom begot wisdom and essence begot essence.

The same author says in *On Faith, to Peter*, chapter 15: “Believe Christ the Son of God, that is, one person of the Trinity, to be true God in such a way that you do not doubt that his divinity was born from the nature of the Father.” Here he appears to say that the Son’s nature was born from the Father’s nature.

The same author says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20: “The Son is called counsel from counsel and will from will, just as substance from substance and wisdom from wisdom.” Here too he appears to say that substance was begotten from substance and wisdom from wisdom.

But we determine this as follows: “wisdom from wisdom” and “substance from substance” mean that the Son, who is wisdom and substance, is from the Father, who is the same substance and wisdom; and the Son, who is divinity, was born from the Father, who is divine nature. To put it more explicitly: we say that the Son, wisdom, is from the Father, wisdom; and that the Son, substance, was begotten from the Father, substance, and by the Father, substance.

That this is how it should be understood Augustine shows near the end of Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, saying: “The Father himself is wisdom; and the Son is called the wisdom of the Father, just as he is called the light of the Father; that is, just as light from light, and both one light, so ‘wisdom from wisdom’ is to be understood, and both one wisdom and one essence.” Likewise: “Christ is called the power and wisdom of God because, from the Father who is power and wisdom, he himself too is power and wisdom; just as he is light from the Father who is light, and he is the fountain of life with God the Father, the fountain of life.”

Therefore the Son, wisdom, is from the Father, wisdom, just as the Son, light, is from the Father, light; and God the Son is from God the Father, so that each separately is light, each separately God, each separately wisdom, yet together they are one light, one God, one wisdom. See how clearly Augustine explains in these words in what sense the foregoing expressions and similar ones are to be received—namely, when “substance from substance” or “substance begot substance” is said.

What seems contrary to the foregoing explanation.

[Col. 0537]

7. Yet the following, said by Hilary in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the beginning, also appears contrary: “The Son has nothing except what is begotten; and the wonder of the begotten honor is in the honor of the begetter.” Therefore, since the Son has essence—for the whole divine essence is in him—it appears that the divine essence itself was begotten.

Likewise, near the end of Book 5, he says: “The birth of God cannot fail to possess the nature from which it came forth; for nothing other than God subsists which does not subsist from God and from no other source.” Here he says that God’s birth came forth from nature; and thus, from these words and those cited above, it appears that the nature of God both was begotten and begot.

He says this more openly in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*: “We confess that the only-begotten God, remaining in the form of God, remained in the nature of man. We neither merge the unity of the servant-form into the nature of the divine unity, nor, conversely, proclaim the Father to be in the Son by a bodily suggestion; but [we proclaim] that a nature begotten from him and of the same kind naturally has within itself a begetting nature, which, remaining in the form of the nature begetting itself, received the form of nature and bodily weakness. For the nature of God had not failed so as not to be; rather, remaining in itself amid the lowliness of earthly birth, it had assumed for itself the nature of God, exercising the power of its own kind in the condition of assumed humanity.”

See: here he openly says that nature begot, that nature was begotten, and that nature assumed nature—something denied by many.

Likewise, in the same work: “Is it an insult to the only-begotten God that the Father is for him the unbegotten God, when from the unbegotten God the only-begotten birth subsists in an only-begotten nature?” Here too he speaks of an only-begotten nature.

How Hilary’s foregoing words are to be understood.

8. But because he intends these words to be understood rightly, he himself says in the middle of Book 4: “The meaning of statements must be drawn from the causes for making them; for the thing is not subject to the expression, but the expression to the thing.”

These words may therefore be understood as follows. “The Son has nothing except what is begotten,” that is, he has nothing, insofar as he is God, except what he received by being born; and in being born he possessed in himself the Father’s subsisting nature. Hence Hilary adds near the end of Book 5: “The one begotten has the same nature as he who begot him, yet the one born is not the one who begot. For how could he be the Father himself, if he has been begotten? But the one who has been begotten subsists in those very things in which he who begot is wholly present, because he who was begotten is not from elsewhere; and therefore what subsists in and from one is not referred to another.”

“And so, in the generation of the Son, the unchangeable God begetting unchangeable God is accompanied, if I may so speak, by his own nature; nor does the perfect birth of the unchangeable God from the unchangeable God abandon his own nature. Therefore, when we understand the nature of God to subsist in him, let us understand that, since God is in God, there is no other God besides him who is God. For he is God, and God is in him. Thus the truth of the nature of God the Father is shown to be in God the Son, when the one who is God is understood to be God in him. For one is in one, and one is from one.”

That it is read that the Father begot the Son from his own substance, and that the Son is of the Father’s substance.

9. It is also said, and frequently read in Scripture, that the Father begot the Son from his own substance. Thus Augustine, in *On Faith, to Peter*, chapter 2, says: “God the Father, begotten by no God, once begot from his own nature, without beginning, the Son—God equal to himself and coeternal with the same divinity by which he himself is naturally eternal.” See: Augustine here says that the Son was begotten from the Father’s nature.

But the nature of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one. Therefore, if the Son was begotten from the Father’s nature, he was begotten from the nature of the Son and Holy Spirit—indeed, from the nature of the three persons.

Likewise Augustine, near the end of Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19, says that Christ is the Son of the Father’s substance and was begotten from the Father’s substance. Treating the Apostle’s words concerning God the Father—“Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love”—he says: “‘The Son of his love’ means nothing other than his beloved Son, the Son of his substance. For the Father’s love, which is in his ineffably simple nature, is nothing other than his very nature and substance, as we have often said and are not weary of repeating. Accordingly, the Son of his love is none other than he who was begotten from his substance.”

See: Augustine here openly says that the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance and is the Son of the Father’s substance.

Likewise Augustine, in Book 3 against the heretic Maximus, chapter 14, asserts that God’s substance begot the Son and that the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance, saying: “Filled with carnal thoughts, you do not think that the substance of God begets the Son from itself unless it suffers what the substance of flesh suffers when it gives birth. You err, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God [Matthew 22]. For you in no way conceive the true Son of God if you deny that he was born from the substance of the Father. For he was not already the son of a man and, by God’s gift, made the Son of God—born from God by grace, not by nature. Or perhaps, even if he was not the son of a man, he was already some sort of creature and was transformed, by God’s action, into the Son of God? But none of these is so. Therefore he was born either from nothing or from some substance. But lest we should think you believe the Son of God to be from nothing, you affirm that you do not say that the Son of God is from nothing. Therefore he is from some substance; and if not from the substance of the Father, tell us from what substance. But you will not find one. Therefore do not hesitate to confess with us that Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, is from the Father’s substance.”

The same author, in the same work: “Certainly we read that we may be in his true Son, Jesus Christ. Tell us, then, whether this true Son of God, distinguished by a certain property from those who are sons by grace, is from no substance or from some substance. ‘I do not say,’ you reply, ‘that he is from no substance; nor will I say that he is from nothing.’ Therefore he is from some substance. I ask: from what? If he is not from the Father’s substance, seek another; if you find no other, acknowledge the Father’s substance and confess the Son to be *homoousios*—of the same substance—with the Father.”

The same author, in the same work: “I confess that God the Father begot incorruptibly altogether; but he begot what he himself is.” Likewise: “I say what must often be said: either the Son of God was born from some substance or from none. If from none, then from nothing—which you no longer say. But if from some substance and yet not from the Father’s substance, he is not the true Son. If, however, from the Father’s substance, Father and Son are of one and the same substance. Yet you refuse to have the Son of God begotten from the Father’s substance, while granting that he is neither from nothing nor from some matter but from the Father. You do not see how necessary it is that one who is not from nothing, nor from any other thing, but from God, can only be from God’s substance and be what God is, from whom he is: God born from God; for another did not exist earlier, but coeternal nature is from God.”

Gathering the substance of the foregoing, he explains in what sense these statements must be received.

10. From the words set out above, it appears to be suggested that the divine substance begot the Son; that the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance; that coeternal nature is from God; and that the Father begot what he himself is. But what he himself is is the divine essence; and thus one might think that the divine essence begot.

These statements trouble us greatly. As to how they ought to be understood, I would rather hear it from others than set it forth myself. Yet, so that I may speak without prejudice or rashness, they may be understood in this sense: “Coeternal nature is from God,” that is, the Son, coeternal with the Father, is from the Father, and is therefore the same nature as he, or of the same nature.

Augustine confirms this meaning immediately afterward, as though explaining what he had said. Having said, “Coeternal nature is from God,” he adds: “The Son is not other than that from which he is,” that is, he is of one and the same substance. Then, in the same book against Maximinus, he makes it clearer that this is the understanding to be taken from the preceding words: “This Trinity is of one and the same substance, because the Son is not from some material or from nothing, but from him from whom he was begotten; likewise the Holy Spirit is not from some material or from nothing, but is from him from whom he proceeds.”

By these words he plainly shows that the Son is said to be from the Father’s substance because he was begotten from the Father [Col. 0539], so that he is of the same substance with him; and the Holy Spirit is said to be from the substance of Father and Son because he proceeds from both, so that he is of the same substance.

That neither Son nor Holy Spirit is from nothing, but from something—not, however, from matter.

11. From those words it is also shown that the Son and Holy Spirit are not from nothing but from something, though not from material. Hence Hilary too says in Book 12 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the middle: “Since the only-begotten God was born, he bears witness to the Father as author. Since he was born from one who remains, he was not born from nothing; and since he was born before time, in being born he transcends every understanding.” Here it is plainly said that the Son was not born from nothing.

Likewise, the Holy Spirit must not be said to be or to proceed from nothing, because the Son was born from the Father’s substance—that is, he is from the Father, with whom he is of the same substance and is the same substance.

In this sense, too, the statement “The Father begot what he himself is” must be understood: that is, he begot the Son, who is what the Father is. Augustine shows that this is how it should be understood in Book 1 against Maximinus, near the middle: “The Father begot what he is; otherwise the Son is not true, if the Son is not what the Father is.” Likewise, “the substance of God begot the Son” means that the Father, substance, begot the Son, who is the same substance and of the same substance.

Augustine shows that this is how it must be understood when he says to Maximinus: “As you say, ‘Spirit begot Spirit,’ so say, ‘Spirit begot Spirit of the same nature or substance.’ Likewise, as you say, ‘God begot God,’ so say, ‘God begot God of the same nature or substance.’ If you believe and say this, you will no longer be accused on this matter.”

By these words he explains how the preceding statements should be understood. Similarly, “the Son was born from the Father’s substance,” or “the Father begot the Son from his own nature or essence,” means that from his nature and essence the Father begot a Son of the same substance and nature, who is the same essence and nature. Similarly explain “Son of the Father’s substance” and “Son of the Father, substance”: that is, he is Son of the Father who is substance, with whom the Son is the same substance, because the Son is consubstantial with the Father.

This meaning is also supported by Augustine’s words in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12: “We say three persons of the same essence, or three persons [who are] one essence. But we do not say three persons from the same essence, as though essence were one thing there and person another.” These words show that a person must not be said to be from essence except in the sense stated above.

This meaning is also confirmed by what the same author says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*: “Just as our knowledge differs from God’s knowledge, so our word, which is born from our knowledge, differs from that Word of God which was born from the Father’s essence.” This is as though I said, “from the Father, knowledge,” “from the Father, wisdom”; or, more explicitly, “from the Father, essence,” “from the Father, knowledge,” “from the Father, wisdom.”

Accordingly, in this sense the Word of God the Father, his only-begotten Son, wholly like and equal to the Father, is rightly called God from God, light from light, wisdom from wisdom, essence from essence: because he is altogether what the Father is, though not the Father; for this one is Son, that one Father.

Why the Word of the Father is called Son by nature.

12. Hence God’s only-begotten is called Son by nature, because he is of the same nature as the Father and is the same nature with the Father. Thus Hilary, speaking of Christ in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, says: “He is Son by nature, because he has the same nature as he who begot him.”

## DISTINCTION VI. WHETHER THE FATHER BEGOT THE SON BY WILL OR BY NECESSITY; AND WHETHER GOD IS WILLING OR UNWILLING.

1. Furthermore, it is customary to ask whether the Father begot the Son by will or by necessity. On this Orosius says to Augustine: “Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?” But [the answer is] neither by will nor by necessity. For there is no necessity in God, and will could not precede wisdom. Therefore, as Augustine says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20, the dialectic of Eunomius, from whom the Eunomian heretics arose, is ridiculous. Unable to understand—and unwilling to believe—that the only-begotten Son of God, the Word of God, is Son by nature, that is, begotten from the Father’s substance, he said that the Son is not Son of nature or substance, but Son of God’s will. He wished to assert that a will comes to God by which he begets the Son, just as we sometimes will something which we did not previously will; and for this reason our nature is understood to be changeable. Far be it from us to believe this of God.

Therefore let us say that the Word of God is Son of God by nature, not by will, as Augustine teaches in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20. There he commends a certain catholic replying to a heretic, saying: “A certain man answered very shrewdly a heretic who craftily asked whether God begot the Son willingly or unwillingly. For if he answered ‘unwillingly,’ there would follow the most absurd misery in God; but if ‘willingly,’ the heretic would immediately conclude what he intended, namely that the Son is not of nature but of will. But the catholic most watchfully asked him in return whether God the Father is God willingly or unwillingly. If he answered ‘unwillingly,’ there would follow a great absurdity and misery, and it is great madness to believe this of God. But if he said ‘willingly,’ the reply would be: ‘Therefore he himself is God by his own will, not by nature.’ What then remained except that he should be silent, seeing himself bound by an indissoluble chain by his own question?”

From what has been said, it is taught that it should not be granted that God is God by will or necessity, or willingly or unwillingly; likewise, that he begot the Son by will or necessity, willingly or unwillingly.

Objection to the foregoing.

2. But against this the following objection is raised. The will of God is God’s nature or essence, because for God to be is not one thing and to will another; and therefore, just as the essence of the three persons is one, so too is their will one. Therefore, if God is God by nature, he is also God by will; and if the Word of God is Son of God by nature, he is Son by will as well.

This is easily refuted. For God’s foreknowledge, or knowledge by which he knows or foreknows good and evil, is the divine nature or essence; and his predestination, or will, is the same divine essence. Nor is knowing and willing anything other for God than being. Yet, although God’s knowledge and will are one and the same, not everything said of will is said of knowledge, nor conversely; nor does God will by his will all that he knows by his knowledge. For by his knowledge he knows both good and evil, whereas by his will he wills only good. God’s knowledge and foreknowledge concern both good and evil; but will and predestination concern good alone. Yet knowledge and will, foreknowledge and predestination, are one and the same in God.

Thus, although God’s nature and will are one, the Father is said to have begotten the Son by nature, not by will; and to be God by nature, not by will.

How the statements “The Father is God neither unwillingly nor willingly” and “He begot the Son neither willingly nor unwillingly” are to be understood.

3. Yet the foregoing statements—that God the Father is God neither willingly nor unwillingly, and that he begot the Son neither unwillingly nor willingly, whether by will or by necessity—seem to me to be understood in the sense of a preceding or added will, in the way Eunomius understood it. For God is not God by a preceding or efficient will, nor is he willing before being God; nor did he beget the Son by a preceding or added will. Nor did he beget the Son by first willing and then begetting; nor by first begetting and then willing. Nevertheless, he begot willingly, just as he begot as powerful, begot the Son as good, and begot as wise, and so forth.

For if the Father is said to have begotten the Son wisely and in goodness, why not willingly as well, since for God to be willing is the same as to be God, just as to be wisdom is the same as to be God? Therefore let us say that the Father begot the Son willingly just as he begot wisely, but not by a will preceding or added.

Augustine explains this meaning and confirms it when, commenting on the Epistle to the Ephesians, he says: “Of the Son of God, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ, it is written that he was always with the Father, and the Father’s will never preceded him in order that he might be; and he is Son indeed by nature.”

## DISTINCTION VII. HERE IT IS ASKED WHETHER THE FATHER COULD OR WILLED TO BEGET THE SON.

1. Here some are accustomed to ask whether the Father could or would generate the Son. For if, they say, he could or would generate the Son, then he could and would do something which the Son neither willed nor could do; for the Son neither could nor willed to generate a Son. To this sophistry we readily reply: To be able or willing to generate the Son is not to be able or willing to do some thing subject to power or will. Yet there is a certain power or will—namely, the ability or will to generate the Son—and therefore the meaning of the proposition “to be able or willing to generate the Son” must be distinguished from “to be able or willing something.” For the generation of the Son is not one of those things subject to divine power and will; nor is it something among all things or belonging to all things, but above all things and before all things. For he neither willed nor could do so before he generated, just as he did not exist before he generated; for he existed eternally, and he generated eternally. We may also see this from a similar case. The Father can be Father and wills to be Father; but the Son cannot and does not will to be Father. Therefore it does not follow that the Father can or wills to be something which the Son cannot or does not will to be; for to be Father is not to be some thing, but to be relative to something, as will be shown below.

### He adduces certain words of Augustine that may perplex the reader.

2. But we are greatly troubled by what Augustine says in his book *Against Maximinus*. Maximinus maintained that the Father was more powerful than the Son because the Father generated the Son, God the Creator, whereas the Son did not; and he said that the Father could generate, but the Son could not, and was therefore superior to the Son. Replying to this, Augustine seems to say that the Son also could generate, wishing to show that the Father is not superior to the Son. His words are these:

> Far be it that the Father is more powerful than the Son for the reason you suppose: because the Father generated the Creator, while the Son did not generate the Creator. For it was not that he could not; rather, it was not fitting.

See and attend carefully to these words: “For it was not that he could not; rather, it was not fitting.” For he seems to say that the Son could generate, but that it was not fitting; and thus he could do what it was not fitting that he should do. Why it was not fitting, Augustine adds, saying:

> For the divine generation would be without measure if the generated Son should generate a grandson for the Father; since that grandson too, unless he generated a great-grandson for his grandfather, would, according to your wonderful wisdom, be called powerless. Likewise, if he did not generate a grandson for his grandfather and a great-grandson for his great-grandfather, he would not be called almighty by you; nor would the succession of generation be completed if one were always born from another. And no one would bring it to completion unless one Almighty One were sufficient. Thus the nature of the Father generated an almighty Son; it did not make him.

### An objection to the foregoing words of Augustine.

3. Some think that this cannot stand—namely, that the Son could have generated. For if the Son could generate, he could be Father; and if he could be Father, then he could be Father either of himself, or of the Father, or of the Holy Spirit, or of some other. But not of another, since no other has always existed. Not of the Father, since the Father is unbegotten and incapable of being begotten. Not of himself, since no thing can generate itself. Nor of the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit could not be born. For if he could be born, he could be Son, and thus could be mutable.

### Here it is asked how these words are to be understood.

4. How, then, is the preceding statement to be understood: “For it was not that he could not generate, but that it was not fitting”—as though he could, but it was not fitting? It is not clear to us how this is true; and therefore it would rather be passed over in silence, unless the insistence of those asking compelled me to say something about it.

### Here the sense in which the words are to be accepted is explained.

5. It may therefore be understood thus: “For it was not that he could not, but that it was not fitting”; that is, it was not owing to any impotence in himself that the Son did not generate, but it did not belong to him to do so. So God the Son is not God the Father, yet this is not owing to any impotence in himself. Likewise the Father is not the Son, and this is not owing to an impotence in the Father. But Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, asks: whence, then, is it that the Father cannot be the Son, or the Son the Father? Certainly not from impotence; rather, the Father is Father by the property of generation, by which it is fitting that he not be Son; and the Son is Son by the property of birth, by which it is fitting that he not be Father. These properties will be treated more fully later, in Distinction 26 of this first book.

### Whether the Father is naturally able to generate the Son, and whether this is some power also present in the Son.

6. Again, some ask whether the Father is naturally able to generate the Son, and whether this is some power that is in the Son. We answer that the Father is able only by nature; for his power is his nature or essence. But they say: if he is able to generate, then he has a power of generating. Yet the Son does not have the power of generating, if he cannot generate. Therefore the Father has some power which the Son does not have.

This does not follow. For the Son has altogether the same power as the Father: the power by which the Father could generate and the Son could be generated. For the power in the Son by which he could be generated is the same power as that in the Father by which he could generate.

But an objection is made: to be able to generate is one thing, and to be able to be generated another, because generating and being generated are different things. Here a distinction must be made. If, when you say, “To be able to generate is one thing, to be able to be generated another,” you mean a different power by which the Father is able to generate and another by which the Son is able to be generated, the understanding is false. But if you mean that the Father has one property or notion by which he is begetter, and the Son another by which he is begotten, the understanding is true. For the Father has one property by which he is Father, and the Son another by which he is Son.

### How the statement “the Son has, or does not have, the power of generating” is to be understood.

7. Likewise, when it is said, “The Son does not have the power of generating which the Father has,” this can be understood in two ways. If it is said that the Son does not have the power of generating which the Father has—that is, the power by which he is able to generate, so that he has generated or may generate as the Father does—this is true. But if it is understood thus—that the Son does not have the power by which he can be generated or be begotten, although the Father has that same power by which he has generated or may generate—it is false.

Similarly, it is said: “The Father has the power by which he can be Father, but the Son does not have the power by which he can be Father”; and conversely, “The Son has the power by which he can be Son.” Therefore the Father has some power which the Son does not have, and conversely. Far from it: for the Father’s power by which he can be Father is the same as the Son’s power by which he can be Son. So also the will by which the Father wills to be Father, and not Son, is the same will by which the Son wills to be Son, and not Father. And the Son’s will by which he wills to be begotten and the Father to have generated is the same as the Father’s will by which he wills to be begetter and the Son to have been begotten.

## DISTINCTION VIII. ON THE TRUTH, PROPRIETY, IMMUTABILITY, AND SIMPLICITY OF GOD’S ESSENCE.

1. We must now treat of the truth—or propriety—immutability, and simplicity of the divine nature, substance, or essence. Thus God is, as Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, without doubt substance, or—if this is a better term—essence, which the Greeks call οὐσία (*ousia*, “being” or “essence”). For as “wisdom” is named from being wise, and “knowledge” from knowing, so “essence” is named from being. And who is more truly than he who said to his servant, in Exodus 3: “I am who I am”; and, “Say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’”? He alone is truly and properly called essence, whose essence knows neither past nor future. Hence Jerome, writing to Damasus, says:

> God alone, who has no beginning, possesses the name of true essence; because, in comparison with him who truly is, because he is immutable, mutable things are as though they were not. For that of which it is said “was” is not; and that of which it is said “will be” is not yet. But God alone is, who knows neither having been nor being to come. God alone, therefore, truly is; compared with whose essence our being is not.

### How Jerome’s words are to be understood.

2. Here we must carefully observe how Jerome’s words are to be understood: “God alone is, and does not know having been or being to come.” They seem to deny that “was” or “will be” can be said of God, allowing only “is”; yet we frequently find it written of him: “He was from eternity,” “he always was and will be for ages,” and similar expressions. Hence it seems that not only “was,” or “is,” or “will be” should be said of God.

For if only “was” were said, he might be thought to have ceased to be. If only “is” were said, he might be thought not always to have been, but to have begun to be. If only “will be” were said, he might be thought not to exist now. Let it therefore be said that he always was, is, and will be, so that it may be understood that he neither began, nor ceased, nor will cease to be.

On this Augustine says, commenting on John:

> Although “is” is properly said of an eternal thing, “was” and “will be” are rightly said of it with reference to us: “was,” because it never ceased; “will be,” because it will never fail; “is,” because it always is. It has not passed away, as though it did not remain; nor will it be, as though it had not been. Therefore, although our speech changes according to times, words of every tense are truly said of him who has not been absent, is not absent, and will not be absent at any time. Thus it is not surprising that Truth, speaking of the Spirit of truth, said in the future tense, John 16: “Whatever he hears, he will speak”; that is, he will hear from him from whom he proceeds. His hearing is his knowing, and likewise his being. Therefore, from whom he has essence, from him he has hearing—that is, knowledge—which is nothing other than essence. “He will hear,” therefore, was said of him who has heard, and hears—that is, who has always known, knows, and will know.

Here Augustine says that words of every tense are said of God, though “is” is said properly. Jerome’s statement must therefore be understood thus: God “does not know having been or being to come, but only being”; that is, when God is said to have been or to be about to be, one must not understand that he has passed away or is future, but that he exists simply, without any temporal movement. Although substantial verbs of different tenses are said of God—such as “was,” “will be,” “is,” and “was being”—they do not distinguish temporal motions: past, future, imperfect past, perfect past, or pluperfect past. Rather, they simply signify the essence or existence of his divinity.

God alone, therefore, is properly called essence or being. Hence Hilary says in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*: “Being is not an accident in God, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the property of his natural kind.”

### On immutability.

3. The essence of God alone is also properly called immutable, because it neither changes nor can change. Hence Augustine, in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, says:

> Other essences or substances receive accidents by which some great or however extensive change comes about in them. But nothing of this kind can happen to God; and therefore the one substance or essence which is God alone is immutable, to whom being belongs most fully and most truly. For what changes does not preserve true being itself; and what can change, even if it does not change, can cease to be what it was. Therefore only that which not only does not change, but absolutely cannot change, is most truly called being—that is, the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Therefore the Apostle, speaking of God, says in 1 Timothy 5: “Who alone has immortality.” For, as Augustine says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, although the soul is in a certain sense said to be and is immortal, the Apostle would not have said, “God alone has immortality,” unless true immortality is immutability, which no creature can possess, since it belongs to the Creator alone. Hence James says, chapter 1: “With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning”; and David, Psalm 101: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same.”

Therefore Augustine says, commenting on Genesis, that God is moved neither through places nor through times, whereas the creature is moved through places and times. To be moved through times is to be changed through affections; but God can be changed neither by place nor by affection. He says through the prophet, Malachi 3: “I am God, and I do not change.” He alone is immutable, and therefore is rightly said alone to have immortality.

For in every mutable nature, as Augustine says *Against Maximinus*, change itself is in some respect a death, because it makes something in it cease to be what it was. Thus even the human soul, which is called immortal because in its own manner it never ceases to live, nevertheless has a kind of death: if it lived righteously and sins, it dies to righteousness; if it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin—to say nothing of its other changes, which it would take too long to discuss here.

The nature of the heavenly creatures could die, because it could sin. For angels sinned and became demons, of whom the devil is prince; and those who did not sin could have sinned. Whenever a rational creature is granted inability to sin, this comes not from its own nature but from God’s grace. Therefore God alone, as the Apostle says, has immortality: not by anyone’s grace, but by his own nature he neither could nor can be changed by any conversion, nor could nor can sin by any change.

Accordingly, as Augustine says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, we ought, though it is difficult, to contemplate and know the substance of God as making mutable things without any change in itself and creating temporal things without any temporal motion of its own. Thus the essence of divinity alone is truly and properly immutable; without changing itself, it created all natures.

### On simplicity.

4. That same essence alone is properly and truly simple, in which there is no diversity, variation, or multiplicity of parts, accidents, or forms of any kind. Augustine teaches in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, how that substance is simple:

> Observe first why every creature is multiple and in no way truly simple; first the bodily creature, then the spiritual. A bodily creature is composed of parts, such that one part is smaller and another larger, and the whole is greater than any individual part. In each body, moreover, size is one thing, color another, and shape another. For the same color and shape can remain when the size is diminished; and the same shape and size can remain when the color changes. Thus the nature of a body is proved to be multiple, and in no way simple.

### Here he shows how the spiritual creature too is multiple and not simple.  
*(From the same work, Book 6, chapter 6.)*

5. A spiritual creature also, such as the soul, is simple in comparison with the body; but apart from comparison with the body it is multiple and not simple. It is called simple in relation to the body because it is not spread out by mass through spatial extension, but is wholly present in every body, in the whole of it and in each of its parts. Thus when something occurs in any very small part of the body that the soul perceives, even though it does not occur in the whole body, the soul nevertheless perceives it wholly, because the whole soul is not unaware of it.

Yet even the whole soul does not possess true simplicity. For to be skillful is one thing, to be dull another; to be keen another; to have memory another; desire one thing, fear another, joy another, sorrow another. These and innumerable other such things can be found in the nature of the soul, some without others, some in greater and some in lesser degree. It is clear that the soul’s nature is not simple but multiple. For nothing simple is mutable, whereas every creature is mutable. Therefore no creature is truly simple.

God, however, though he is called multiple, is nevertheless truly and supremely simple. For he is called great, good, wise, blessed, true, and whatever else may fittingly be said; but his greatness is the same as his wisdom. For he is not great by bulk, but by power; and his goodness is the same as his wisdom, greatness, and truth. Nor is his being blessed one thing and his being great, wise, true, good, or simply being, another.

### How God, though simple, is nevertheless called multiple.

[Col. 0545]

6. Here it must be carefully noted: since Augustine says that God alone is truly simple, why does he call the same God multiple? He does not say this because of a diversity of accidents or parts, but because of the diversity and multitude of names said of God. Although these names are many, they signify one thing—namely, the divine nature. For they are not understood, when said of that immutable and eternal substance incomparably simpler than the human mind, as they are when said of creatures.

Hence Augustine says in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4:

> In God, to be is the same as to be strong, wise, or just, and whatever you may say of that simple multiplicity or multiple simplicity by which his substance is signified. But for the human mind, to be is not the same as to be strong, prudent, or just; for a mind may exist and possess none of these virtues.

### God’s simplicity is so great that he falls under none of the categories.

7. Augustine shows in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, that in the divine nature there is no diversity of accidents and no mutability whatever, but perfect simplicity:

> Let us understand God, as far as we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, presiding without position, containing all things without habit, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet fully discover what God is, should nevertheless reverently take care, as far as he can, not to think anything of him that he is not.

If you attend closely, these words and those preceding show that the categories of dialectical art do not apply at all to God’s nature, which is subject to no accidents.

### That God is called substance not properly, but improperly.

8. Therefore he is not properly called substance, as Augustine shows in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapters 4 and 5:

> As essence is named from being, so we call substance from subsisting—if indeed it is fitting to say that God subsists. For this is correctly understood of those things in which, as subjects, there are things said to exist in a subject, as color or shape in a body. A body subsists, and is therefore substance. Thus mutable things that are not simple are properly called substances. But if God subsists so that he can properly be called substance, something is in him as in a subject, and he is not simple. Yet it is impious to say that God subsists and underlies his goodness, and that this goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and that God himself is not his goodness, but that goodness exists in him as in a subject.

It is therefore evident that God is called substance improperly, so that essence may be understood by the more usual name; “essence” is said truly and properly, so that perhaps God alone ought to be called essence. For he alone truly is, because he is immutable.

### That there is nothing in God which is not God.

9. The simplicity and purity of this essence are so great that there is nothing in it which is not itself, but the possessor and that which is possessed are the same. Hence Hilary says in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*:

> God, who is life, does not subsist from composites; nor is he who is power held together from weak things; nor is he who is light fitted together from dark things; nor is he who is spirit formed from dissimilar shapes. Everything that is in him is one.

The same author says in Book 8 of *On the Trinity*:

> God is not composed in a human way, as though one thing in him were what is possessed by him, and another were he who possesses it. Rather, the whole is one nature: perfect, infinite, not constituted from dissimilar things, but living in its entirety through itself.

On this same point Boethius says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*:

> Accordingly, that is truly one in which there is no number, nothing in it other than what is in it; for it cannot become a subject.

Augustine too, in *On Faith and the Creed*, chapter 3, says: “In God’s substance there is nothing which is not substance”—as though substance there were one thing and something happening to the substance another. Rather, whatever can be understood is substance. These things may easily be said and believed, but cannot at all be seen except by a pure heart.

Again Augustine, in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 9, says: “In the nature of each of the three, that which has is what it has, as in an immutable and simple substance.” Hence Isidore says: “God is called simple, either because he does not admit what he has, or because he is not one thing and what is in him another.”

Though the divine nature is of such great simplicity and purity, there is nevertheless in it a Trinity of persons. Hence Augustine says in Book 11 of *The City of God*:

> We do not call the nature of the supreme good simple because the Father alone is in it, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone; nor because it is only a Trinity of names or a subsistence of persons, as the Sabellians thought. Rather, it is called simple because it is what it has—except that each person is said relatively to another and is not that other. For the Father has the Son, to whom he is related, yet he is not the Son; and the Son has the Father, yet he is not the Father. But in respect of what is said of himself and not of another, he is what he has: for example, he is called living in respect of himself by having life, and that life itself is he.

Thus this nature is called simple because the possessor is not one thing and that which it possesses another, as happens in other things. For that which has liquid is not liquid; a body is not color; nor is a soul wisdom. We have thus set forth, according to the capacity of our weakness, how great are the identity, unity, immutability, simplicity, and purity of the divine substance.

## DISTINCTION IX. ON THE DISTINCTION OF THE THREE PERSONS.

1. Let us now proceed to the distinction of the three persons. Let us therefore hold, as Augustine teaches in *On Faith to Peter*, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Yet the Father is not the one who is the Son; nor is the Son the one who is the Father; nor is the Holy Spirit the one who is the Father or the Son. For the essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; in it the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

### On the Son’s coeternity with the Father.

2. For the Son was begotten by the Father, and is therefore another; yet the Father did not exist before the Son, for the three persons are coeternal with one another.

### Argument of the Arians.

3. But against this the heretic says, as Ambrose reports in Book 1 of *On Faith*, addressed to Gratian, chapter 15, about the middle: “Everything born has a beginning; therefore, because the Son was born, he has a beginning and began to exist.” This was said by the mouths of heretics. For Arius himself, as Augustine recalls in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, is reported to have said: “If the Son is Son, he is born; if he is born, there was a time when the Son was not.”

### Augustine’s Catholic response.

4. Whoever says this does not understand that the Son, though begotten, is eternal with God, so that the Son is coeternal with the Father—as the brightness generated and diffused from fire is coeval with it, and would be coeternal if the fire were eternal. (Augustine, same passage.)

### Augustine’s counterargument against the heretic.

5. Again Augustine says, Book 6, chapter 1: If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and if God was never without power and wisdom, then the Son is coeternal with God the Father. But the Apostle calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Therefore either there was no time when the Son was not, or God at some time did not have power and wisdom—which is madness to say. It is evident that he has always had wisdom; therefore he has always had the Son.

### Ambrose’s response to the same objection, supported by authority.

6. Ambrose likewise responds to this Arian question in the following way, in *On Faith to Gratian*, [Col. 0547] about the middle of chapter 5:

> I confess, I say, that the Son was born; I shudder at what remains of impiety. For it is written in the Old Testament, Isaiah 44—to name only one passage among many—“Before me no other God was, and after me none shall be.” Who says this, then: the Father or the Son? If the Son, he says, “Before me no other God was.” If the Father, he says, “After me none shall be.” The one has no predecessor and the other no successor. For they are known reciprocally in one another: the Father in the Son, and the Son in the Father. For when you say “Father,” you also indicate his Son, because no one is father to himself; when you name “Son,” you also confess the Father, because no one is son to himself. Thus the Son cannot be without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. Therefore the Father always is, and the Son always is.

### Ambrose’s invective against the heretic.  
*(Book and chapter cited.)*

7. Again, tell me, I say, heretic: was there ever a time when almighty God was not Father, while still being God? For if he began to be Father, then he was first God and afterward became Father. How, then, is God immutable? For if he was first God and afterward Father, he was plainly changed by the addition of generation. But may God avert this madness.

### It is ineffable how the Son is, yet does not have a prior Father; just as the manner of generation is unintelligible and ineffable.

8. But you ask me, Ambrose says, how, if the Son is Son, he does not have a prior Father. I in turn ask you when or how you think the Son was generated. For it is impossible for me to know the secret of that generation. The mind fails; the voice is silent—not mine alone, but that of the angels also. It is above powers, above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, and above every understanding; for it is written in Philippians 4: “The peace of Christ is above every understanding.” And if Christ’s peace is above every understanding, how is so great a generation not above every understanding? Therefore put your hand over your mouth: it is not permitted to search out the heavenly mysteries. It is permitted to know that he was born; it is not permitted to investigate how he was born. I may not deny the former; I fear to inquire into the latter. For that generation is ineffable; hence Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?”

### Some presume to investigate the sequence of generation.

9. Yet some, trusting in their own ingenuity, say that this generation can be understood, and make other similar claims, relying on Jerome’s authority in his commentary on Ecclesiastes: “In the Sacred Scriptures, *who* is very often used not for the impossible but for the difficult,” as in the passage, “Who shall declare his generation?” But Jerome does not say this in order to imply that the eternal generation of the Son can be fully understood or explained by any mortal, but because something concerning it can be understood or said. Some, however, take the statement to concern Christ’s temporal generation.

### Whether the Son should be said always to be generated, always to have been begotten, or always to be begotten.
