10. Here it may be asked, since the Son’s generation from the Father has neither beginning nor end, because it is eternal, whether it should be said: “The Son is always being generated,” or “The Son has always been begotten,” or “The Son will always be begotten.”

On this Gregory says in Book 29 of the *Morals on Job*, chapter 1:

> The Lord God Jesus, in that he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before times; or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly that he was always born. But we cannot say, “He is always being born,” lest he seem imperfect. Yet, in order that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born”: “born,” in order to indicate perfection, and “always,” eternity. Although, by calling him perfect, we depart far from an expression of that truth, since what has not been made cannot properly be called perfect; yet, stammering as we can, let us sound forth the lofty things of God. And the Lord, condescending to the language of our weakness, says: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” [Matthew 5].

On the passage of Psalm 2, “Today I have begotten you,” Augustine speaks thus concerning this generation of the Son:

> Although by his saying “today” we may understand that day on which Christ was born according to his humanity, nevertheless, because “today” signifies presence, and in eternity there is neither anything past, as though it had ceased to be, nor anything future, as though it were not yet; but only the present, because whatever is eternal always is—the text is nevertheless divinely understood concerning the everlasting generation of the wisdom of God.

By these words Augustine shows that the Son’s generation is always present, neither past nor future, because it is eternal. Therefore he said, “I have begotten,” lest it be thought new—that is, lest it appear to have begun; and he said “today,” lest the generation appear to be past. From the prophet’s words, therefore, as John Chrysostom says, nothing else is made clear except that the Son has always been begotten from the very essence of the Father.

### Origen seems to say the contrary, for he says that the Son is always generated by the Father.

11. Origen, however, says in his commentary on Jeremiah that the Son is always generated by the Father:

> Our Savior is the wisdom of God; wisdom is the brightness of eternal light; therefore our Savior is the brightness of glory. But brightness is not born once and then ceases. Rather, whenever the light from which brightness arises has arisen, the brightness of glory also arises. Thus our Savior is always being born. Hence he says in the Book of Wisdom: “Before all hills the Lord generates me,” not, as some wrongly read, “generated me.”

By these words Origen openly shows that it can and ought rightly be said: “The Son is always being born.” This seems contrary to Gregory’s preceding statement: “We cannot say, ‘He is always being born.’”

### He explains Gregory’s preceding words, lest the teachers be thought to contradict one another.

12. But lest such great authorities seem to contradict each other in so great a matter, let us interpret Gregory’s words favorably:

> The Lord Jesus was born from the Father before times; or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly, “always born.”

But in what sense is this—namely, that the Son was always born—said more truly than the statement that he was born from the Father before times? For sincere and Catholic faith maintains and proclaims the latter just as it does the former. Why then does he say, “more truly,” when both are equally true? Unless he meant that this is said with greater clarity and force in expressing the truth than the other statement.

For by these words every avenue for the slanderous sophistries of heretics is closed, since Christ’s generation according to divinity is shown to be without beginning, without end, and perfect. But the truth is not always made so plainly manifest by saying, “The Son was begotten from the Father before times,” or “The Son is always being born from the Father.” Therefore Gregory says that we cannot say, “He is always being born”—that is, not so fittingly, not so suitably for an explanation of the truth. Yet it may be said if it is understood soundly: for the Son is always born from the Father, as Origen says, not because that generation is repeated daily, but because it always is. “He is always being born,” therefore, means that his birth is everlasting.

### That the Son is always generated is confirmed from Hilary’s statements.

13. Hilary likewise says in Book 7 of *On the Trinity* that the Son is born from the Father:

> God is living, and he is the power of a living eternal nature; and that which is born from him in the mystery of his knowledge could not be anything other than living. For when he says, “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,” he teaches that life is in him through the living Father.

Here you have that the Son is born from the Father. Again, in the same work, when Christ says, John 6: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself,” he testified that all his living reality comes from the Living One.

> What is born living from the Living One has the advance of birth without newness of nature. For what is generated living from the Living One is not new, because it is not from nothing. And life which receives birth from life must, through unity of nature and the mystery of perfect birth, both live in the Living One and have living life in itself.

Here again you have that the living Son is generated from the Living One. Again, in the same work:

> In God, all that is lives; for God is life, and nothing can be from life except living. This does not arise by derivation, but by the power of birth. Thus, while all that is lives, and all that is born from him is power, the Son has birth, not alteration.

Here too he says that the Son is born. Again, in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*: “The Father grants to the Son to be as great as he himself is; to him he imparts, through the mystery of birth, an image of unbegotten being, generating him from himself in his own form.” Here he says that the Father generates the Son.

### He briefly teaches what should be conceded concerning this.

14. Let us therefore say that the Son was born of the Father before time, and is always being born of the Father; yet it is more fitting to say that he has always been born. Let us confess that he is eternal and coeternal with the Father—that is, with his Author. For the Father is the Author of the Son by generation, as will be shown below. Therefore, as the Father is eternal, so too the Son is eternal; but the Father is without an author, whereas the Son is not, because the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten. And, as Hilary says in *On the Trinity*, book 6, it is one thing eternally to exist always without an author, another to be coeternal with the Father—that is, with the Author. But where the Father is Author, there is also birth; for, as birth is from an author, so birth from an eternal Author is eternal. Everything which always exists is eternal; yet not everything eternal is also unbegotten, because that which is born from eternity possesses an eternal existence as something born. But that which is not born is, with eternity, not born; whereas that which is born from the Eternal—if it has not been born eternally—then the Father will no longer be an eternal Author. Therefore, if anything should be lacking in eternity to him who was born of the eternal Father, that same deficiency cannot ambiguously be said to be lacking to the Author; for if begetting is infinite for the begetter, being born is likewise infinite for the one being born. No interval between the birth of God the Son and the generation of God the Father is admitted even by thought: for there is generation in birth, and birth in generation; since without both, neither exists. Therefore both are without an interval between themselves.

### The heretic’s argument

15. But the heretic will object: “Everything that has been born did not always exist, because it was born in order that it might exist.” No one doubts that things born in human affairs at one time did not exist. But it is one thing to be born from one who has not always existed, another to have been born from one who always exists. In the former case, he who is father has not always existed, nor has he always been father; and he who is not always father has not always begotten. But where the Father always is, the Son always is. Therefore, if it belongs perpetually to God the Father that he is always Father, it must belong perpetually to the Son that he is always Son. How, then, can it enter our understanding that he did not always exist, when it belongs to him always to be that which has been born? We therefore confess God, the Only-Begotten, as born—but born before time: neither existing before being born, nor born before existing. For to be born when one already was is not to be born, but to alter oneself through being born. This surpasses human sense and worldly understanding; the reasoning of human intelligence cannot grasp it, but it is the confession of faithful wisdom.

## DISTINCTION X. HERE THE HOLY SPIRIT IS TREATED OF; FIRST, HE IS SAID TO BE THE LOVE OF THE FATHER AND THE SON.

1. Now, after the eternity of the Son, let us discuss the Holy Spirit, insofar as God grants us to see it. The Holy Spirit is the love, charity, or affection of the Father and the Son. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 17, says:

> The Holy Spirit belongs neither to the Father alone nor to the Son alone, but to both; and therefore he makes known to us the common charity by which the Father and Son love one another.

### That the Holy Spirit is properly called love, and yet the Trinity is love

2. John, however, says in the First Catholic Epistle, chapter 4: “God is charity.” He did not say, “The Holy Spirit is charity.” Had he said this, the statement would have been more definite, and no small part of the question would have been settled. But because he said, “God is charity,” it is uncertain and must therefore be investigated whether God the Father is charity, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or God the Trinity itself, since the Trinity too is not three gods, but one God. On this point Augustine says in the same book:

> I do not know why, just as wisdom is said of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and all together are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, charity should not likewise be said of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, all together one charity. Yet no one should judge us improper for calling the Holy Spirit charity, since both God the Father and God the Son can be called charity; just as the Word of God is properly called also the Wisdom of God, although both the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom.

### As the Word of God is properly called wisdom, though the whole Trinity is called wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called charity, though the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called charity  
*(From the same book and chapter, somewhat below.)*

3. If, therefore, one of these three should properly be called charity, who is more suitable than the Holy Spirit? Thus, in that highest and simple nature, substance is not one thing and charity another; rather, substance itself is charity, and charity itself is substance, whether in the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit. Yet the Holy Spirit is properly called charity. By these words Augustine plainly says that in the Trinity charity is sometimes referred to the substance, which is common to the three persons and wholly present in each; sometimes it is referred especially to the person of the Holy Spirit. Similarly, God’s wisdom is sometimes understood as the divine substance and sometimes, properly, as the Son. This is found to occur in many cases.

### He establishes by examples that the same names are used both properly and universally

4. By many examples it can be shown that many terms are used universally and are also applied properly to particular things. For example, by the name “Law” all the utterances of the Old Testament are sometimes signified together; but sometimes “Law” properly denotes the law given through Moses. Many other examples are available, but prolixity is to be avoided where the matter is clear. Therefore, just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name of wisdom, although both the Holy Spirit and the Father are universally wisdom itself, so the Holy Spirit is called charity by his proper designation, although the Father and Son are universally charity.

### He adduces authority that the Son is properly called wisdom

5. But the Word of God—that is, the Only-Begotten Son of God—was openly called God’s wisdom by the Apostle, who says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” We find where the Holy Spirit is called charity if we carefully investigate the Apostle John’s words. After saying, “Let us love one another, because love is from God,” he added: “And everyone who loves has been born of God, because love is God.” Here he made clear that he called that love God which he said was from God. Therefore love from God is God. But since both the Son is born from God the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, it is rightly asked which of them is here meant to be called love. For the Father alone is God in such a way that he is not from God; therefore the love which is God in such a way as to be from God is not the Father himself, but either the Son or the Holy Spirit.

But in what follows, after John had recalled God’s love by which he loved us, and had from this urged us to love one another so that God might dwell in us—since he had certainly called love God—he immediately, wishing to say something more plainly on this matter, says: “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” The Holy Spirit, therefore, of whom he has given us, causes us to abide in God and him in us; and love does this. Therefore that God is love. Therefore God the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God, is signified where we read, “God is love,” and “love is from God.”

By these words Augustine plainly says that the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father and the Son; and he develops the discussion so far that he seems to have said not only that the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father and Son love one another and love us, but also that by which we love God. Whether he himself is the charity by which we love God will be explained below, in Distinction 17.

### He returns to show what he had proposed: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father is loved by the Son and the Son by the Father

[Col. 0551]

6. Let us now attend to showing what we began to show: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the affection or love of the Father and the Son, by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father. Jerome, commenting on Psalm 17, says of this:

> The Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the love which the Father has toward the Son and the Son toward the Father.

Augustine likewise says at the end of *On the Trinity*, book 6, chapter 4:

> In all things the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance. Therefore the Holy Spirit also subsists in the same unity and equality of substance.

### What the Holy Spirit is is here made clear

7. For whether he is the unity of both, or holiness, or charity, it is manifest that he is not something belonging to one of the two, by which each is joined: by which the Begotten is loved by the Begetter and loves his Begetter, and by which they preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, not by participation but by their own essence, nor through the gift of some superior being, but through what is proper to themselves. Here you have that the Holy Spirit is that by which the Son is loved by the Father and the Father by the Son, and by which those two preserve the unity of peace.

Therefore, as Augustine says in the same sixth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> Whatever it may be, there is something common to the Father and the Son. That communion itself is consubstantial and coeternal. If it may suitably be called friendship, let it be so called; but it is more aptly called charity. And this too is substance, because God is substance and God is charity. Therefore there are three, and no more: one loving him who is from him, one loving him from whom he is, and love itself. If this love is nothing, how is God substance?

### That, just as the Holy Spirit is common to Father and Son, so he has as his proper name one that is in a way common to Father and Son

8. Here it should be noted that, just as in the Trinity the Holy Spirit is specially called charity, which is the union of the Father and Son, so he properly bears a name which in a certain manner applies commonly to the Father and Son. Hence Augustine, near the end of *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 19:

> If the charity by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father displays their ineffable communion, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called charity who is the Spirit common to both? For it is more soundly believed and understood that not only is the Holy Spirit charity in that Trinity, but that he is not without reason properly called charity because of the things already said. Likewise, he alone is not Spirit or holy in that Trinity, for the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy; yet he is not without reason called the Holy Spirit. For he who is common to both is properly called that which both are in common. Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit alone is charity in that Trinity, then the Son is found to be Son not only of the Father but also of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle says of God the Father, Colossians 1: “He transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his charity.” If, then, there is no charity of God in that Trinity except the Holy Spirit, the Son is also Son of the Holy Spirit. But since this is utterly absurd, it remains that the Holy Spirit is not the only charity there, though for the reasons I have sufficiently discussed he is properly so called.

## DISTINCTION XI. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT PROCEEDS FROM THE FATHER AND THE SON

1. Here it must be said that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son—something many heretics have denied. That he proceeds from both is proved by many testimonies of the divine utterances. For the Apostle says, Romans 8: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts.” Here he is called the Spirit of the Son. And elsewhere, Romans 8: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.” The Son himself says of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel, Matthew 10: “Whom I will send to you from the Father.” He is called the Spirit of the Father where we read, John 14: “If the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you.” And Christ himself says, in the same place, Matthew 15: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks.” And elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name.” And in another place the Son himself says of the Holy Spirit: “He proceeds from the Father.” By these and many other authorities it is shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

### That the Greeks do not grant that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son

2. The Greeks, however, say that the Holy Spirit proceeds only from the Father and not from the Son. They say this because Truth, speaking in the Gospel which contains the complete faith about the procession of the Spirit, mentions only the Father: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father.” They say it also because in the principal councils held among them their creeds were established with appended anathemas, so that no one might be permitted to teach or preach differently concerning faith in the Trinity than what is there contained. In these creeds, although the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father and not from the Son, whoever adds that he proceeds from the Son incurs an anathema; and thus they accuse us of being liable to anathema.

They further add, in support of their opinion and as testimony to our condemnation, the Creed of Faith which Leo III, according to the tradition of the aforesaid councils, had copied onto a silver tablet and placed behind the altar of Saint Paul, leaving it to posterity “for the love,” as he himself said, “and safeguard of the orthodox faith.” In that creed only the Father is mentioned in the procession of the Spirit, in these words: “And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is to be adored and glorified,” etc. This is the creed sung in the Mass, issued at the Council of Nicaea, at the end of which is appended: “Whoever teaches otherwise or preaches differently, let him be anathema.” The Greeks therefore say that we have been anathematized because we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, which is not contained there. For the words which, according to us, read, “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son,” were added by the Latins: namely, “and the Son” (*Filioque*).

### Reply, in which the foregoing is determined

3. We explain the words, “Whoever teaches otherwise or preaches differently,” as meaning: whoever teaches what is contrary or preaches in a contrary manner, let him be anathema. “Otherwise,” therefore, is used for “oppositely,” as the Apostle also uses it in Galatians 1: “If anyone proclaims another gospel”—that is, a contrary one—“let him be anathema.” He does not say, “If anyone adds.” For if he said that, as Augustine says, *Thessalonians*, chapter 3, he would pass judgment against himself, since he wished to come to some persons to whom he wrote—as to the Thessalonians—to supply what was lacking in their faith. But one who supplies what was deficient adds; he does not take away what was present. One who transgresses the rule of faith does not walk in the way, but departs from the way.

To what they object from the Gospel, we answer thus: since Truth says there that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, he does not add “alone,” and therefore does not deny that he also proceeds from himself. But he names the Father alone because he customarily refers even what belongs to himself back to the Father, since he has it from him.

### That the Greeks agree with us in meaning, though they differ in words

4. Yet it should be known that the Greeks confess that the Holy Spirit is the Son’s as well as the Father’s, because the Apostle says in Galatians 4, “the Spirit of the Son,” and Truth says in the Gospel, John 16, “the Spirit of truth.” But since it is nothing other than for the Holy Spirit to be the Father’s or the Son’s than to be from the Father and the Son, they seem to agree with us even in this conclusion of faith, although they disagree in words.

### By Greek authorities he shows that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son

5. Hence certain Catholic doctors among them, understanding that the preceding expressions—by which the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Son and to be the Son’s—have one and the same meaning, professed that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. Thus Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith: “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, neither made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.” Here he plainly says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Didymus also, their greatest teacher, says after the middle of book 2 of *On the Holy Spirit* that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son:

> The Savior, who is Truth, says in John 16: “For he will not speak from himself,” that is, not without my will and that of the Father, because he is inseparably united with me and with the Father’s will; for he is not from himself, but is from the Father and from me. For the very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father and from me.

Again Didymus, in the same book:

> The Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot hear from the Son speaking things that he does not know, since he himself is what is brought forth by the Son—that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth, the Comforter flowing from consolation.

For Cyril, bishop, in a letter addressed to Nestorius, says:

> The Spirit is understood in himself insofar as he is Spirit and not Son; yet he is not alien to the Son. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and he flows from him as from God the Father.

John Chrysostom likewise says in a homily on the exposition of the Creed:

> This is the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, who distributes his own gifts as he wills.

The same author says in another homily:

> It must be believed that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son. We say that this Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son and proceeds from the Father and the Son. Believe this, lest evil conversations corrupt good morals.

Here, then, we have plain testimonies from Greek doctors showing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore let every tongue confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

## DISTINCTION XII. WHETHER THE HOLY SPIRIT PROCEEDS EARLIER OR MORE FULLY FROM THE FATHER THAN FROM THE SON

1. Again, since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, it is asked whether he proceeds earlier or more fully from the Father than from the Son. The heretic attempts to show that he does, arguing as follows: “If the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father, he proceeded either when the Son had already been born or when the Son had not yet been born. If he proceeded when the Son had already been born, then the Son was born before the Holy Spirit proceeded; therefore the Son’s birth preceded the Holy Spirit’s procession. But if he proceeded from the Father before the Son was begotten, he proceeded before the Son had been begotten.”

### Augustine’s reply to the first question: whether he proceeded earlier from the Father than from the Son

2. Augustine replies to these and similar questions, more laborious than fruitful, in *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 26:

> In that supreme Trinity, which is God, there are no intervals of time through which it could be shown, or even asked, whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterwards the Holy Spirit proceeded from both. Could we then ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father when the Son was born, or had not yet proceeded, and, after the Son was born, proceeded from both? Such questions absolutely cannot be asked there, where nothing begins in time in order to be completed later in time. Therefore, whoever can understand the Son’s generation from the Father without time should understand the Holy Spirit’s procession from both without time.

By these words the question concerning whether the Holy Spirit proceeded earlier from the Father than from the Son is resolved.

### Here the second question is treated: whether he proceeds more fully or more greatly from the Father than from the Son

3. We must now consider the second question: whether the Holy Spirit proceeds more fully or more greatly from the Father than from the Son. We answer that, just as he does not proceed earlier from the Father than from the Son, so he does not proceed more fully or more greatly from the Father than from the Son. Augustine nevertheless says in *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 17, that the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father:

> Not without reason, in this Trinity, is only the Son called the Word of God; only the Holy Spirit, the gift of God; and only God the Father he from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit principally proceeds.

You have heard that the Holy Spirit principally proceeds from the Father. But lest this disturb you, he immediately explains the sense in which he said it:

> I added “principally” because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son; but the Father gave this also to the Son—not to a Son who already existed and did not yet possess it, but whatever he gave to the Only-Begotten Word, he gave by begetting him. Thus he begot him so that the common gift might proceed also from him, and so that the Holy Spirit might be the Spirit of both.

He himself has explained, therefore, how the Spirit principally proceeds from the Father: not because he proceeds earlier or more greatly from the Father than from the Son, but because, although he proceeds from the Son, the Son has this very thing from the Father.

### In the same sense the Holy Spirit is also said properly to proceed from the Father

4. In the same sense he is also said properly to proceed from the Father. Thus Jerome, in *An Exposition of the Catholic Faith and of the Nicene Creed*, says: “We believe in the Holy Spirit, who properly proceeds from the Father.” Again: “We find in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is true God and properly from the Father.” And again: “The Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit properly and truly proceeds from the Father.” Here he plainly says that the Holy Spirit is properly from the Father and properly proceeds from the Father. This must not be understood as though he proceeded earlier or more fully from the Father than from the Son, but because the Father has from himself, and not from another, that the Holy Spirit is from him and proceeds from him. The Son, however, has this not from himself but from the Father: that the Holy Spirit is from him and proceeds from him.

### In the same sense the Holy Spirit is said to be and to be sent from the Father through the Son

5. Perhaps in accordance with this understanding the Holy Spirit is also said to be sent through the Son and to be from the Father through the Son. Thus Hilary, speaking to God the Father of the Holy Spirit and the Son in *On the Trinity*, book 12, says:

> In your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you and is sent through him.

Again:

> Your Only-Begotten, born from you before time, remains such that your Holy Spirit is from you through him. Though I do not grasp this by understanding, I nevertheless hold it in faith. For I am dull in your spiritual matters.

Again, in the same work:

> Preserve, I pray, this devotion of my faith, that I may always retain what I professed in the creed of my regeneration: namely, that I may worship you as Father and your Son together with you, and may merit your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your Only-Begotten.

Here he plainly says that the Holy Spirit is both sent and is from the Father through the Son. This must not be understood as though he were sent or existed in a lesser way from the Father through the Son, but because he is from the Father and the Son and is sent by both; yet the Son has from the Father this very thing, that the Spirit is from him and is sent by him. Hilary therefore intended to signify this by making a distinction in his expression, so as to show that authority is in the Father.

For this reason Truth too, showing the Father to be the Author of the procession by which the Spirit proceeds from the Son, said in the Gospel: “He proceeds from the Father,” although the Holy Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son. Hence Augustine asks in *On the Trinity*, book 15:

> If the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, why did the Son say, “He proceeds from the Father”? Why do you suppose, except because he customarily refers even what is his own to him from whom he himself is? Thus he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.” If here his teaching is understood, though he did not call it his own but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit be understood there to proceed from him when he says, “He proceeds from the Father,” so that he does not say, “He does not proceed from me.” From him from whom the Son has that he is God—for he is God from God—he certainly has that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from him. Therefore the Holy Spirit has from the Father himself that he proceeds from the Son as he proceeds from the Father.

> Accordingly, whoever can understand, when the Son says, “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself,” that the Father did not give life to a Son who already existed without life, but begot him without time in such a way that the life which the Father gave the Son in begetting him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it—let that person also understand that, just as the Father has in himself that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him, so he gave the Son that the same Spirit should also proceed from him; and both are without time.

Thus the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father in such a way that he is understood also to proceed from the Son, to be from the Father and the Son. For if the Son has everything that he has from the Father, he certainly has from the Father that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. But no times are to be imagined there, with a before and after, because there are none at all.

## DISTINCTION XIII. WHY THE HOLY SPIRIT, THOUGH HE IS FROM THE FATHER’S SUBSTANCE, IS NOT SAID TO BE BEGOTTEN OR A SON, BUT ONLY TO PROCEED

1. After this we must consider, insofar as such people as we are can understand, why, although the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is from the Father’s substance, he is not said to be born but rather to proceed, and why he is not called Son. Augustine explains in *On the Trinity*, book 15, why the Holy Spirit is not called or is not born, and therefore is not Son:

> If the Holy Spirit were called Son, he would certainly be called the Son of both; and that is utterly absurd. No son is son of two persons except of a father and a mother. Far be it from us to suppose anything of that sort between God the Father and God the Son. Therefore he would most absurdly be called Son of both—that is, of the Father and the Son. For he would be called Son of both if both had begotten him, a thought abhorrent to every sound mind. Therefore he is not begotten from both, but proceeds from both as the Spirit of both.

These words show why the Holy Spirit, though he is from the Father, is not called begotten or Son.

### Since the Holy Spirit is not called begotten, why is the Son said to proceed?

2. Since the Holy Spirit is not called begotten but only proceeding, it is commonly asked why the Son is not called only begotten but also proceeding. For he himself says in the Gospel of John, chapter 16: “I proceeded—or went forth—from God, and came into the world.” Therefore not only the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but the Son also. To this we say that, although each proceeds from the Father, they do so differently. For the Holy Spirit, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 5, proceeds from the Father not in the manner of one born, but in the manner of one given, or as a gift. The Son, however, proceeds by being born; he went forth as begotten. Hence it becomes clear why the Holy Spirit is not also Son, although he too goes forth from the Father: the Spirit is not called Son because he was not born as the Only-Begotten was, nor made so that by God’s grace he might be born into adoption, as we are.

### That we cannot distinguish between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit

3. While we live here, however, we are unable adequately to distinguish between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit. Therefore Augustine, replying to Maximinus when he revived the preceding question—asking why the Holy Spirit was not called Son although he was of the Father’s substance—says:

> You ask me: if the Son is of the Father’s substance, and the Holy Spirit also is of the Father’s substance, why is one Son and the other not Son? Here is my reply, whether you grasp it or not: the Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father. But the one is begotten, the other proceeding. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father, from whom he is begotten; but the other is the Holy Spirit of both, since he proceeds from both. Yet because he was speaking of him as from the Father, he said, John 15, “He proceeds from the Father,” because the Father is the Author of his procession: he begot such a Son and, in begetting him, gave him that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him. For unless the Spirit proceeded also from him, he would not have said to the disciples, John 20, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” nor have given him by breathing upon them; thus, by breathing openly, he showed that he was secretly giving what proceeds from himself as well.

> For if he were born, he would certainly be born not from the Father alone or the Son alone but from both, and without doubt would be called Son of both. But since he could in no way be Son of both, it was not fitting that he should be born from both. Therefore the Holy Spirit is of both, proceeding from both.

### Here he says that he cannot distinguish between these two

4. Who, speaking of that most excellent nature, can explain what difference there is between being born and proceeding? Not everything which proceeds is born, although everything born proceeds. Just as not everything two-footed is a human being, although everyone who is human is two-footed. This I know; but I do not know, cannot, and am not able to distinguish between that generation and this procession. Therefore, since both that and this are ineffable—as the prophet Isaiah says of the Son, chapter 53, “Who shall recount his generation?”—so it is most truly said of the Holy Spirit: “Who shall recount his procession?”

Let it therefore suffice for us that the Son is not from himself but from him of whom he was born; that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds; and that he proceeds from both, as we have already shown. Above we have discussed, as seemed appropriate, how the Holy Spirit is from God and yet is not the Son himself, because he is said to be from God by proceeding, not by being born.

### Whether the Holy Spirit ought to be called unbegotten

5. We must now consider whether, since the Holy Spirit is not begotten, he ought to be called unbegotten. We say that the Holy Spirit ought to be called neither begotten nor unbegotten. Hence Augustine says to Orosius:

> Certain faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we seem to affirm two Fathers; but if we call him begotten, we are charged with believing in two Sons.

For as the Son alone is called begotten, so the Father alone is called unbegotten, because he is not from another. Thus Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 25:

> The Father alone is not from another. Therefore he alone is called unbegotten—not indeed in the Scriptures, but in the custom of those disputing and expressing as best they can speech concerning so great a matter. But the Son is born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and jointly from both. Therefore, though we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, neither do we dare call him unbegotten, lest someone suppose from this term either two Fathers in that Trinity or two persons who are not from another.

By these words he plainly shows that the Holy Spirit should be called neither begotten nor unbegotten.

### Jerome says that the Holy Spirit is unbegotten, which appears contrary to the preceding

6. Jerome, nevertheless, in the *Rules of Definitions against Heretics*, says that the Holy Spirit is unbegotten:

> The Holy Spirit is not the Father, but is unbegotten and unmade. He is not the Father, because he is of the Father and in the Father; he has procession from the Father, not birth. Nor is he the Son, because he is not begotten.

Here the Holy Spirit is said to be unbegotten, which appears contrary to Augustine’s preceding words.

### Resolution: they spoke according to different meanings of the term

7. But to remove this apparent contradiction, we say that Jerome understood the term *unbegotten* (*ingenitus*) differently from Augustine. Augustine understood *unbegotten* as one who or that which is not from another, and in this sense it is said only of the Father. Jerome, however, uses *unbegotten* to mean “not begotten”; in this sense it can be said of the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit is not begotten.

### Jerome’s words show in what sense he called the Holy Spirit unbegotten

8. That Jerome understood it in this way is shown by the words he uses in the same treatise, where he makes the following division:

> Everything that exists is either unbegotten, begotten, or made. Thus, there is that which is neither born nor made; there is that which is born and not made; there is that which is neither born nor made; there is that which is made and not born; there is that which is made, born, and reborn; and there is that which is made and born but not reborn. Let us now assign a subsistence to each of the foregoing categories. That which is neither born nor made is the Father, for he is not from another. That which is born and not made is the Son, who was begotten from the Father, not made. Again, that which is neither made nor born is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father. That which is made and not born is heaven and earth and the other inanimate things. That which is made, born, and reborn is the human being. That which is made and born but not reborn is the animals.

By these words Jerome shows that he understands *unbegotten* to mean “not begotten.” Otherwise the preceding division—“everything that exists is either unbegotten, begotten, or made”—would not be true. Moreover, in carrying through this division, when assigning the unbegotten category, he everywhere says “not born.”

## DISTINCTION XIV. THAT THE HOLY SPIRIT HAS A TWOFOLD PROCESSION

1. Furthermore, it must be carefully noted that the Holy Spirit has a twofold procession: an eternal procession, ineffable, by which he proceeds eternally and without time from the Father and the Son; and a temporal procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son in order to sanctify the creature. And just as from eternity he proceeds jointly and simultaneously from the Father and the Son, so too in time he proceeds jointly and simultaneously from both to the creature, not separately from the Father into the Son and from the Son to the creature. Hence Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 15:

> The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify the creature; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave the Son that, just as he proceeds from himself, so he should also proceed from the Son.

### The temporal procession of the Holy Spirit is treated specifically
2. But concerning the temporal procession, Bede speaks thus in his homily for the first Sunday after the Ascension: “When the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and is also sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and also proceeds from the Son, because his mission itself is his procession.” By these words he plainly shows that the bestowal of the grace of the Holy Spirit is called his procession or mission. But since the bestowal or giving is only temporal, it is evident that this procession or mission too is temporal.

Augustine likewise indicates this temporal procession of the Holy Spirit in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 26, saying: “The Holy Spirit proceeded from Christ when, after the resurrection, he breathed upon the disciples, in these words of John 20: ‘When Christ had risen from the dead and appeared to the disciples, he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,”’ so as also to show that he proceeds from himself; and he himself is the power which went out from him” (as is read in the Gospel, Luke 6) “and healed them all.” And, in order to show that this procession of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the bestowal or giving of the Holy Spirit himself, he added, on John 20: “After the resurrection the Lord Jesus gave the Holy Spirit twice: once on earth, for love of neighbour, and again from heaven, for love of God; because through that gift charity is poured out in our hearts, Acts 2, by which we love God and neighbour.”

### That some say that the Holy Spirit himself is not given, but his gifts are

3. There are some, however, who say that the Holy Spirit, God himself, is not given, but that his gifts are given—gifts which are not the Spirit himself. As they put it, the Holy Spirit is said to be given when his grace is given, although he himself is not what is given to human beings. They say that Bede meant this in the preceding words, in which he says that the Holy Spirit proceeds when his grace is given to human beings—as though not he himself, but his grace, were given.

But Augustine plainly says, in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 26, that the Holy Spirit himself, who is God, is given:

> “We ought not to doubt that it was this same Holy Spirit whom Jesus gave when he breathed upon them, concerning whom he immediately says, Matthew 28: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ He is therefore the one who was also given from heaven on the day of Pentecost. How, then, is he not God who gives the Holy Spirit? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God?”

See: in these words he plainly says that the Holy Spirit—that is, God himself—is given to human beings by the Father and by the Son.

Ambrose also plainly shows, in Book 1 of *On the Holy Spirit*, that the Holy Spirit, who is God and the third person in the Trinity, is given to us and poured into and instilled in our minds:

> “Although many are called spirits, because it is written in Psalm 103 [104], ‘Who makes his angels spirits,’ yet the Spirit of God is one [Col. 0558]. This one Spirit, therefore, was received both by the apostles and by the prophets; as also the vessel of election says, Acts 9: ‘For we have drunk one Spirit’—as though he were one who cannot be divided, but is poured into souls and enters into the faculties of sense, in order to quench the burning heat of worldly thirst. This Holy Spirit is neither of the substance of bodily things nor of the substance of invisible creatures.”

By these words he plainly says that the Holy Spirit himself, who is not a creature, is poured into our minds.

Again, in the same book, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 5:

> “Every creature is changeable, but the Holy Spirit is not changeable. Why should I hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit too has been given, when it is written in Romans 5: ‘The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us’? Though inaccessible by nature, nevertheless, because of his goodness, he can be received by us, filling all things with power, yet shared only by the righteous. He is a simple substance, rich in powers, present to each person, distributing from his own to each, and wholly present everywhere. Therefore the Holy Spirit is uncircumscribed and infinite; he poured himself into the minds of the separated disciples, and nothing can deceive him. Angels were sent to a few persons; but the Holy Spirit was poured out upon peoples. Who, then, can doubt that what is poured simultaneously into many, yet is not seen, is divine? Therefore there is one Holy Spirit, who was given to all the apostles, although separated from one another.”

Here Ambrose plainly says (Sermon 43, Volume 10) that the Holy Spirit, who is a simple substance and one, is given to many.

The same is also established by another authority, on Romans 5: namely, that the Holy Spirit, who is equal to the Son, is given to human beings. For Augustine says in *On the Words of the Apostle*:

> “‘The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.’ By whom is he given? By him who gave gifts to human beings. What gifts? The Holy Spirit, who gives a gift such as he himself is. Great is his mercy: he gives a gift equal to himself, because his gift is the Holy Spirit.”

From these and many other authorities already set forth, it is plainly shown that the Holy Spirit, equal to the Father and the Son, is given to us; yet for that reason he is not less than the Father and the Son. Hence Augustine says, near the end of the final chapter of *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit is not to be judged less because both the Father sent him and the Son.”

### Whether holy persons and prelates of the Church give, or can give, the Holy Spirit: here it is shown that they do not give him

4. Here it is asked whether holy persons also give, or can give, the Holy Spirit to others. If they give him to others, then, since his giving was above called a procession, the Holy Spirit seems to proceed or be sent from them. But the Creator is not sent or does not proceed from a creature. It follows, therefore, that they neither give nor can give the Holy Spirit.

Hence Augustine says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*:

> “No disciple of Christ gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed, indeed, that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they did not themselves give him. The Church still observes this practice even now in her prelates. Finally, Simon Magus, offering money to the apostles, Acts 8, did not say: ‘Give me also this power, that I may give the Holy Spirit’; but, ‘That whomever I lay hands upon may receive the Holy Spirit.’ For Scripture had not previously said, ‘Simon saw that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit’; but it had said, ‘Simon saw that through the laying on of the apostles’ hands the Holy Spirit was given.’”

See: by these words Augustine shows that neither the apostles nor other prelates of the Church gave or give the Holy Spirit.

### That they cannot give the Holy Spirit is taught here

5. Moreover, he says in the same book that they cannot give him, adding:

> “It is written of Christ that he received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and poured him out; in this both natures are shown, namely the human and the divine. For he received as man; he poured out as God. We, however, can indeed receive this gift according to our measure; but we certainly cannot pour it out upon others. Rather, that this may happen, we call upon God over them, from whom it is effected.”

By these words he expressly says [Col. 0559] that we cannot pour out the Holy Spirit upon others—that is, give him to others.

### What seems contrary to this

6. But what the Apostle says of himself in Galatians 3 seems contrary to this: “He who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you.” See: he plainly says that he supplied the Spirit. But this must be understood as said by the Apostle, not because he possessed the power and authority to give the Holy Spirit, but because he exercised a ministry in which the Holy Spirit was given by God.

For Augustine, commenting on that same passage, Volume 4, explains the Apostle’s words thus:

> “Faith was preached to them by the Apostle; and in that preaching they had experienced the coming and presence of the Holy Spirit. For at that time, in the newness of the invitation to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit was also made manifest by sensible miracles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles.”

Here he plainly shows how the Apostle supplied the Holy Spirit to them: certainly not by himself sending him into them, but by preaching to them faith in Christ. When they received that faith, visible signs showed that the Holy Spirit was in them. Thus human beings, however holy, cannot give the Holy Spirit.

## DISTINCTION XV. WHETHER THE HOLY SPIRIT GIVES HIMSELF

1. Here it must be considered, since the Holy Spirit is given to human beings by the Father and the Son—which is his temporally proceeding from both, or being sent—whether he also gives himself. If he gives himself, then he proceeds or is sent from himself.

We answer that the Holy Spirit is both God and gift, or thing given; and therefore he gives and is given. He gives insofar as he is God; he is given insofar as he is gift or thing given. But since the giving or bestowal of the Holy Spirit is an operation of God, and the operation of the three persons is common and undivided, the Spirit is given not only by the Father and the Son, but also by himself.

Hence Augustine says, in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 9, that he gives himself:

> “Just as the body of flesh is nothing other than flesh, so the gift of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the Holy Spirit. Therefore he is the gift of God insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given. But with himself he is God, even if he is given to no one; for he was coeternal God with the Father and the Son before he was given to anyone. Nor is he less than them because they give and he is given. For he is given as God’s gift in such a way that, as God, he also gives himself. For he cannot be said not to have authority over himself, of whom it has been said: ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills.’”

See: he plainly says that the Holy Spirit gives himself. For if the Holy Spirit cannot give himself, while the Father and the Son can give him, then the Father and the Son can give something which the Holy Spirit cannot. Again, if the Father and Son give the Holy Spirit but he himself does not give, then the Father and Son perform something which the Holy Spirit does not perform. Therefore the Holy Spirit gives himself.

But if he gives himself, then he also proceeds and is sent from himself, which is certainly true. For the temporal procession or mission of the Holy Spirit is his very bestowal, and is an operation of God. Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds temporally from himself and is sent from himself, because he is given by himself.

### It is not strange that the Holy Spirit is said to be sent or to proceed from himself, since the Son also is said to be sent by himself

2. Nor should you wonder that the Holy Spirit is said to be sent or to proceed from himself. For Augustine likewise says of the Son, in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, that he was sent not only by the Father but also by himself and by the Holy Spirit. He asks how the Son or the Holy Spirit can be sent, when each is everywhere as God.

For, Augustine says, both are read to have been sent. Of the Holy Spirit it is written, John 14: “Whom the Father will send in my name”; and again, John 16: “If I go, I will send him to you.” And the Son says of himself, John 16: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world.” The Apostle says, Galatians 4: “God sent his Son.” But in the prophet Jeremiah 23 it is written in the person of God: “I fill heaven and earth.” Therefore God is everywhere; therefore the Son is everywhere, and the Holy Spirit likewise is everywhere. Thus the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent to the place where they already were [Col. 0560].

### How the mission of each is to be understood

3. Therefore it must be asked how the mission of the Son or Holy Spirit is to be understood. For Augustine says in the same book, chapter 5: “The Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent, but the Son and the Holy Spirit are.” Let us first see how the Apostle says that the Son was sent, Galatians 4: “God sent his Son, made of a woman”; where he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely in being made of a woman.

Accordingly, he could not be sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit, because the Father is understood to have sent him when he made him from a woman; and he certainly did not do this without the Holy Spirit. See: here he says that the Son was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit.

### That the Son was sent by the Holy Spirit is confirmed by authorities

4. Augustine says in the same place that authorities confirm that the Son was sent by the Holy Spirit. Christ himself says through Isaiah 48: “Now the Lord and his Spirit have sent me.” Concerning this, Ambrose says in Book 3 of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 1:

> “Who is it who says, ‘The Lord and his Spirit have sent me,’ except he who came from the Father in order to save sinners—that is, Christ? Therefore both the Father sent the Son and the Holy Spirit.”

The same author says in the same work, chapter 2:

> “He was given by the Father, as Isaiah says, chapter 9: ‘A child has been born to us, and a Son has been given to us.’ I dare also to say that he was given by the Spirit, because he was sent by the Holy Spirit. For the Son of God says, Isaiah 61: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me, sent me to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives,’ and so forth. When he read this from the book of Isaiah, he said in the Gospel, Luke 4: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing,’ thereby showing that it had been spoken of himself. He rightly said, ‘upon me,’ because as Son of Man he was both anointed and sent to preach. For according to his divinity the Spirit is not upon Christ, but in Christ.”

By these words Ambrose shows that the Son was sent and given to us not only by the Father, but also by the Holy Spirit.

### That the Son was also given by himself

5. Then he shows that the Son was also given by himself, saying in the same book, chapter 2:

> “Since prophecy did not specify by whom the Son was given, it is shown that he was given through the grace of the Trinity, so that the Son himself also gave himself.”

See: he says here that the Son gave himself because the Trinity gave him. But if the Son was given by himself, then he was sent by himself and proceeded from himself. This is certainly true and must be granted, since his mission is a divine operation.

### That the Son is sent by himself

6. Augustine maintains that he is sent by himself in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> “Perhaps someone may compel us to say that the Son was also sent by himself, because both Mary’s conception and her childbirth are an operation of the Trinity. But someone says: ‘How did the Father send him, if he sent himself?’ I answer by asking him to say: How did the Father sanctify him, if he also sanctified himself? For the Lord says both, John 10: ‘Whom the Father sanctified and sent into this world’; and elsewhere, John 17: ‘For their sake I sanctify myself.’ Again I ask: How did the Father hand him over, if he handed himself over? For both are read. I believe he will answer, if he is sound in judgment, that the Father and the Son have one will and an inseparable operation.

> “Thus, then, let him understand that the incarnation and birth from the Virgin, in which the Son is understood to have been sent, were brought about inseparably by the one and same operation of the Father and the Son, with the Holy Spirit not excluded. Therefore the same Son was sent by the Father and the Son, because the Father and his Word caused him to be sent—that is, caused the incarnate one to appear to human beings. For he was not sent by changing place, since he was in the world.

> “Accordingly, the invisible Father, together with the invisible Son who was with him, is said to have sent that same Son by making him visible. If, however, he had become visible in such a way as to cease to be invisible with the Father—that is, if the substance of the invisible Word had been changed and transformed into a visible creature—then the Son would be understood to have been sent by the Father in such a way that he would be found only sent, and not also sending with the Father. But since the form of a servant was received while the form of God remained unchangeable, it is clear that the Father and Son, though not appearing, caused what appeared in the Son: that is, the same Son was visibly sent by the invisible Father together with the invisible Son.”

### A summary of what is established by the foregoing

7. From the foregoing it is plainly shown that the Son was sent by the Father, the Holy Spirit, and himself; and that this mission is the incarnation—that is, his becoming human, by which he appeared visibly. This is the common work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### The question why he says, “I did not come of myself”

8. But an objection is made: if the Son was sent by himself, why does he say in John 8, “I did not come of myself”? Augustine answers this in the previously cited chapter of *On the Trinity*, saying that this was spoken according to the form of a servant. According to that form he did not cause himself to be sent—that is, he did not effect the incarnation—but it was not spoken according to the form of God.

### Whether the Son was sent only once or is sent often

9. Here it is asked whether the Son was sent only once, or whether he is sent often. For if the Son’s mission is only his incarnation, then, since he was incarnate only once, he seems to have been sent only once. But if he is sent often, then there is another mission of his besides the incarnation. What is it? Is his eternal generation to be called his mission, or must another mission be sought?

### That the Son is said to be sent in two ways

10. We answer that, apart from his eternal and ineffable generation, the Son is said to be sent in two ways. According to that generation, some think that he could also be called sent; but more fittingly and truly, according to it he is called begotten.

Apart from it, then, he is said to be sent in two ways: either when he appeared visibly to the world clothed in flesh, or when he so communicates himself to devout souls that he is perceived and known by them. Augustine plainly distinguishes these two modes of mission in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20:

> “The Son is not called sent merely because he was born of the Father, but because he appeared to this world: ‘The Word was made flesh.’ Hence he says, John 16: ‘I came forth from the Father and came into the world’; or because, in time, he is perceived by someone’s mind, as is said of Wisdom, Wisdom 9: ‘Send her forth from your holy heavens and from the throne of your greatness, that she may be with me and labour with me’—that is, teach me to labour. And then she is sent to each person when she is known and perceived by someone, insofar as she can be known and perceived according to the capacity either of a rational soul advancing toward God or of one made perfect in God.”

### That according to one mode he was sent once, and according to the other often; and according to one he was sent to be human, and according to the other to be with a human being

11. See: the two modes of the Son’s mission have been distinguished. According to one, the Son of God was sent only once; according to the other, he has been sent often and is sent daily. For according to one he was sent to become human, which happened only once. According to the other, he is sent to be with a human being, when he is daily sent to the saints; and he was sent even before the incarnation—to all the saints who came before, and also to the angels.

Hence Augustine, speaking of the Son, that is, of the Father’s Wisdom, says in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, the same chapter:

> “Wisdom is sent in one way to be with a human being; in another she was sent to become human. She communicates herself to holy souls and makes them friends of God and prophets, just as she also fills the holy angels. But when the fullness of time came, she was sent not to fill angels, nor to become an angel, nor to be with human beings or in human beings, as she was formerly in the patriarchs and prophets, but in order that the Word himself might become flesh—that is, human.”

### That according to one mode he is said to be sent into the world, and according to the other not

12. Further, it should be noted that, although the Son is sent in these two ways, according to one he is said to be sent into the world and according to the other he is not. For he is said to be sent into the world in the mode in which he visibly appeared to the world. Hence Augustine says in the same book and chapter:

> “When he is perceived in time by someone’s mind, he is said to be sent, but not into this world; for he does not appear sensibly—that is, he is not present to bodily senses. For we too, insofar as we grasp something eternal by the mind, are not in this world; and the spirits of all the righteous, even while living in the flesh, insofar as they discern divine things, are not in this world.”

From the foregoing it is clear that, apart from his ineffable generation, the Son is sent in two ways: when he appeared visibly, or when he is invisibly perceived by the mind.

### Why is the Father not said to be sent when he is known by someone, as the Son is?

13. Here it is asked why the Father is not said to be sent when he is known by someone in time, as the Son is. We answer that in him is the authority of the principle: he has no one from whom he is, whereas the Son and Holy Spirit are from him. For the Father, as Augustine says in the same book and chapter, is “the principle of the whole divinity,” or, better expressed, “of deity,” because he is the principle of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

For Augustine says in the same work, near the end of chapter 21:

> “If God the Father had willed, he too could have appeared visibly through a creature subject to him; nevertheless, it would be utterly absurd for him to be called sent either by the Son whom he begot or by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him. Fittingly, however, he is called sent who appeared in the flesh; and he is called sender who did not appear in it.”

### Some heretics thought the Son and the Holy Spirit less than the Father because they are said to be sent

14. For this reason certain heretics thought that, since the Father is not sent but the Son and Holy Spirit are, the Father is greater, while the Son and Holy Spirit are less; and that the Father, as greater, sent each of the others as lesser. Augustine refutes this in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, replying to them:

> “The Son is not to be judged less because he was sent by the Father; nor is the Holy Spirit to be judged less because both the Father and Son sent him. Whether these things are understood because of a visible creature, or rather because of the authority or manifestation of a principle, they are not set down in Scripture because of inequality, disparity, or dissimilarity of substance.”

Thus the Father is not said to have sent the Son or the Holy Spirit because he was greater and they were less, but chiefly in order to indicate the authority of the principle, and because they appeared in visible creation whereas he did not. See: it has been shown what the mission of the Son is and in what ways he is sent.

## DISTINCTION XVI. ON THE MISSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, WHICH OCCURS IN TWO WAYS: VISIBLY AND INVISIBLY

1. We must now consider, concerning the Holy Spirit, what is his temporal procession—called mission or giving—apart from that ineffable and eternal procession by which he proceeds from the Father and Son, and not from himself. We answer that, just as the Son is said to be sent in two ways, one in which he appeared visibly and the other in which he is invisibly perceived by pure minds, so the Holy Spirit is said to proceed, be sent, or be given in two ways by the Father, the Son, and himself: one visibly and the other invisibly.

For he was given through the manifestation of a visible creature, as on the day of Pentecost and at other times; and he is given daily in an invisible manner, by entering into the minds of believers.

### First, he treats the mode of mission that occurs visibly

2. Let us first treat that mode of mission which occurs in visible appearance. Augustine says of it in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> “It is easy to understand why the Holy Spirit too is said to have been sent. For at a particular time a form of created thing came into being in which the Holy Spirit was visibly shown: either when he descended in the bodily form of a dove upon the Lord himself, or when, on the day of Pentecost, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and tongues divided as though of fire appeared to them, and rested upon each [Col. 0563] of them. This operation visibly displayed and presented to mortal eyes was called the mission of the Holy Spirit—not that his very substance might appear to them, for he, like the Father and the Son, is invisible and unchangeable; but that, by outward sights, human hearts, stirred by the temporal manifestation of his coming, might be turned toward the hidden eternity of him who is always present.”

By these words Augustine explains the mode of mission visibly exhibited, although the Spirit himself is not seen in his own nature. He was not more present in those creatures than in others, but he was present in them for another purpose: so that, by coming through them to human beings, he might be shown to be in those to whom those creatures came. For the Holy Spirit did not then come or descend into human beings by temporal movement; rather, the temporal movement of the creature signified the spiritual and invisible infusion of the Holy Spirit. To state it more plainly: the inward and spiritual mission, or giving, of the Holy Spirit—which is now to be discussed—was shown through that bodily exhibited mode of the Holy Spirit’s mission.

### Since the Son is less than the Father according to the created form in which he appeared, why is the Holy Spirit not similarly less?

3. But first it must be asked: since the Son is said to be less than the Father according to the mission in which he appeared in a created form, why is the Holy Spirit not likewise called less than the Father, since he too appeared in a created form?

Augustine plainly shows, in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19, that the Son is less than the Father according to the form in which he appeared by being sent:

> “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, Galatians 4—so small that he was made. Therefore he was sent in that he was made. Let us therefore confess that he was made less; and less insofar as he was made; and made insofar as he was sent.”

See: the Son, insofar as he is sent—that is, made—is less than the Father. Why, then, is the Holy Spirit not said to be less than the Father, though he too assumed a creature in which he appeared? Because the Spirit assumed the creature in which he appeared differently from the Son. The Son assumed it through a union of person; the Spirit did not. For the Son took a human being in such a way that he became human; but the Holy Spirit did not take the dove in such a way as to become a dove.

On this Augustine says in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6:

> “Therefore nowhere is it written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father, because the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the same manner as the Son of Man was assumed, in whose form the person of God the Word was manifested—not as though the Word of God were possessed by him as by other holy and wise persons, but because he himself was the Word. For ‘the Word in flesh’ is one thing, and ‘the Word made flesh’ another; that is, the Word in a human being is one thing, the Word as a human being another. For ‘flesh’ stands for ‘human being’ in John 1: ‘The Word was made flesh.’ Therefore the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed as that flesh and human form from the Virgin Mary was assumed. For he did not bless the dove, that wind, or that fire and unite it with himself in the unity of person forever.”

From the foregoing it has been plainly shown in what respect and why the Son is said to be less than the Father, while the Holy Spirit is not.

### That the Son, insofar as he became human, is less not only than the Father but than the Holy Spirit and even than himself

4. It should be noted that the Son, insofar as he became human, is said to be less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit and even than himself. Augustine shows in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, that he is said to be less even than himself according to the form of a servant:

> “People have erred by transferring to his eternal substance things said of Christ according to his humanity, such as what the Lord himself says, John 14: ‘The Father is greater than I.’ Truth says this because of the form of a servant; in this respect the Son is even less than himself. For how did he not become less even than himself, when he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, Philippians 2? He did not, however, take the form of a servant so as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father. Therefore, in the form of God, the Only-begotten of the Father is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he is even less than himself. Thus Scripture rightly says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood because of the form of God; the latter because of the form of a servant.”

On the same subject Augustine says in Book 2 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1:

> “The Son of God is equal to the Father according to the form of God in which he exists, and less than the Father according to the form of a servant which he received; in that form he is found less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit, and not only this, but even less than himself.”

Therefore, as Augustine says in his work *Against Maximinus*, he was made less not only than the Father but also than himself and the Holy Spirit, and was “made a little lower than the angels.” Thus the Son of God, as he says in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7, is “equal to God the Father by nature, less by condition,” that is, in the form of a servant which he received. These authorities plainly show that the Son, according to the form of a servant, is less than the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit.

### Hilary speaks differently: namely, that the Father is greater, yet the Son is not less

5. Hilary, however, seems to say that the Father is greater than the Son, yet that the Son is not less than the Father. For the Father is called greater because of authority, since in him is the authority of generation. According to this, he says in John 14: “The Father is greater than I.” And the Apostle says, Philippians 2: “He gave him the name that is above every name.” Thus, when he says, “The Father is greater than I,” it is as though he said, “He gave me the name.”

Hilary says in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*:

> “If the Father is greater by the authority of giving, is the Son less by the acknowledgment of the gift? The giver, then, is greater; but he to whom oneness of being is given is no longer less, for he says, John 10: ‘I and the Father are one.’ If it is not given to Jesus to be confessed in the glory of God the Father, he is less than the Father. But if it is given to him to exist in the glory in which the Father exists, then you have both that the Father is greater in the authority of giving, and that they are one in the acknowledgment of what is given. Therefore the Father is greater than the Son, and plainly greater: he gives him to be as great as he himself is; he imparts to him, through the mystery of birth, the image of his own unbegotten being; he begets him from himself in his own form.”

You have heard, reader, what Hilary says on this point. Wherever his words occur, note them carefully and understand them devoutly.

## DISTINCTION XVII. ON THE MISSION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, BY WHICH HE IS SENT INVISIBLY

1. Let us now proceed to explain the mission of the Holy Spirit by which he is invisibly sent into the hearts of believers. For the Holy Spirit himself, who is God and the third person in the Trinity—as was shown above—proceeds temporally from the Father, the Son, and himself; that is, he is sent and given to believers. But what this mission or giving is, and how it occurs, must be considered.

### Something necessary to this explanation is first set forth: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbour

2. In order that this may be taught more intelligibly and perceived more fully, something very necessary must first be stated. It was indeed said above, and demonstrated by sacred authorities, that the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son, by which they love one another and us. To this must be added that this same Holy Spirit is the love or charity by which we love God and neighbour. When this charity is in us so as to make us love God and neighbour, then the Holy Spirit is said to be sent or given to us. And whoever loves the very love by which he loves his neighbour, loves God in that very act, because that love itself is God—that is, the Holy Spirit.

### He confirms this by authorities

3. But lest in so great a matter we appear to introduce anything of our own, let us strengthen what has been said by sacred authorities. Augustine says of this in Book 8 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7:

> “It follows that whoever loves his neighbour loves love itself especially. But God is love; therefore it follows that he loves God especially.”

Again, in the same work:

> “God is love, as the Apostle John says in his First Epistle, chapter 4. Why, then, do we go and run about seeking him in the heights of heaven and the depths of earth, when he is with us, if we are willing to be with him? Let no one say, ‘I do not know what to love.’ Let him love his brother, and let him love that same love. For he knows the love by which he loves more than the brother whom he loves. See: you can now have God more known to you than your brother—indeed, more known, because more present, more inward, and more certain. Embrace love, which is God; and embrace God by love. Love itself is what joins together all good angels and all servants of God in the bond of holiness. Therefore, the more sound we are from the swelling of pride, the fuller we are of love. And with what is one full, if full of love, except God?”

By these words Augustine sufficiently shows that the very love by which we love God or neighbour is God. But more plainly still he adds in the same book:

> “Let us observe how greatly the Apostle John commends love. ‘Whoever loves his brother,’ he says, First John 2, ‘remains in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him.’ It is plain that he placed the perfection of righteousness in love of one’s brother. For one in whom there is no stumbling-block is certainly perfect. And yet he seems to have said nothing about love of God; but he would never have done this unless he intended God to be understood in that very brotherly love. For a little later in the same Epistle, chapter 4, he says quite plainly: ‘Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God; and everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love has not known God, because God is love.’ This sequence plainly enough declares that this same brotherly love—for brotherly love is that by which we love one another—is proclaimed on the authority of John to be not only from God but also God.
