Therefore, when through love we love our brother, through God we love our brother; and it cannot be that we do not especially love that same love by which we love our brother, since God is love. Again, whoever does not love his brother is not in love; and whoever is not in love is not in God, because God is love.”

See: he plainly says that brotherly love is God.

### That, although brotherly love is God, it is neither the Father nor the Son, but the Holy Spirit alone
4. But since fraternal love is God, it is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Holy Spirit, who is properly called love or charity in the Trinity. Hence Augustine, in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19: “If among God’s gifts nothing is greater than charity, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more consistently than that he himself is the charity which is called both God and from God? For thus 1 John 4 says: ‘Love is from God.’ And shortly afterward: ‘God is love.’ There he makes clear that he called God that love which he had called from God; therefore God is love from God.” Again, in the same chapter, John, wishing to speak more openly on this matter, says: “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” Therefore the Holy Spirit, of whom he has given to us, causes us to abide in God and him in us; and love does this. Therefore he himself is God-love. Thus he is signified where we read, “God is love.” From these things, therefore, it is evident that the Holy Spirit is charity.

### That “God is charity” is not said causally, as “You are my patience and my hope” is said

5. But lest someone perhaps say that “God is charity” is said by way of expressing a cause—namely, because charity is from God and is not God himself—just as it is said, “God is our patience and hope,” not because he himself is these things but because they are from God, Augustine answers this objection, showing in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17, that this is not said causally as those expressions are. He says: “We must not say that charity is called God not because charity itself is some substance worthy of God’s name, but because it is God’s gift; just as it was said to God, ‘You are my patience.’ Certainly ‘You are my patience’ was not said because our patience is God’s substance [Col. 0566], but because it comes to us from him. Hence Psalm 61: ‘From him is my patience.’ For the very manner of speech in Scripture easily refutes this interpretation. For ‘You are my patience’ is of the same kind as ‘Lord, my hope’ and ‘My God, my mercy,’ and many similar expressions. But it is not said, ‘Lord, my charity,’ or ‘You are my charity,’ or ‘God, my charity’; rather, 1 John 4 says, ‘God is charity,’ just as John 4 says, ‘God is spirit.’ Whoever does not distinguish this, let him seek understanding from the Lord, not an explanation from us. For we can say nothing more plainly: therefore God is charity.”

From what has been said it is clear that the Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbor; thus it is easier for us to show how the Holy Spirit is sent or given to us.

### How the Holy Spirit is sent or given to us

6. For he is then said to be sent or given when he is in us in such a way that he causes us to love God and neighbor, so that we abide in God and God in us. Hence Augustine, indicating this manner of mission, says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 70: “God the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God, when he has been given to a person, kindles that person to love God and neighbor, and he himself is love. For a human being has no source from which to love God except God.”

Behold how the Holy Spirit is given or sent to us insofar as he is called “given” or “gift.” Augustine commends this gift, explaining more openly in the same book how it is given: “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured out into our hearts, as the Apostle says in Romans 5, through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. There is no gift of God more excellent than this. It alone distinguishes the children of the kingdom from the children of perdition. Other gifts also are given through the Spirit, but without charity they are of no benefit. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is imparted to someone so far as to make that person a lover of God and neighbor, he is not transferred from the left hand to the right. Nor is the Holy Spirit properly called a gift except on account of love. Whoever does not have this love, even if he speaks with all tongues, has prophecy, all knowledge, all faith, distributes all his possessions, and gives up his body so that it may be burned, gains nothing from it (3 Cor. 13). How great, then, is that good without which such great goods bring no one to eternal life! But love or charity itself—for both are names of one thing—leads to the kingdom. Therefore love, which is God and is properly from God, is the Holy Spirit, through whom God, who is charity, is poured out into our hearts, and through whom the whole Trinity dwells in us. Therefore, most rightly, the Holy Spirit, since he is God, is also called the gift of God. What else should this gift properly be understood as but charity, which leads to God and without which no other gift of God leads to God?”

Here it is made clear what was said above: namely, that charity is the Holy Spirit and the most excellent gift; and how this gift—that is, the Holy Spirit—is given to us: namely, when he is imparted to someone in such a way, that is, has such being in someone, as to make that person a lover of God and neighbor. When he does this, he is said to be given or sent to that person; and then that person is said properly to possess the Holy Spirit.

### Whether it should be granted that the Holy Spirit increases in a human being, or is possessed or given more or less

7. Here the question arises: if charity is the Holy Spirit, and charity itself increases and decreases in a human being and is possessed more or less at different times, should it be granted that the Holy Spirit increases or decreases in a human being, or is possessed more or less? For if he increases in a human being and is given and possessed more or less, he seems mutable; but God is altogether immutable. Therefore it seems either that the Holy Spirit is not charity, or that charity does not increase or decrease in a human being. Again, charity is given to one who does not possess it so that he may possess it, and to one who possesses it so that he may possess it more fully. Thus, if the Holy Spirit is charity, he is given to one who does not have him so that he may have him, and to one who has him so that he may have him more fully. But how is he given to one who does not have him, when, as God, he is wholly everywhere and wholly in all creatures? And how is he given or possessed more fully without a change in himself?

### Reply to the first question

[Col. 0567]

8. To these questions we reply that the Holy Spirit, or charity, is utterly immutable: he neither increases nor decreases in himself, nor does he in himself admit of more or less. But in a human being—or rather, for a human being—he increases and decreases, and is given or possessed more or less, just as God is said to be magnified and exalted in us, although he is neither magnified nor exalted in himself. Hence the Prophet says in Psalm 63: “Let a human being draw near to the deep heart, and God shall be exalted.” On this passage an authority says: “God becomes great not in himself but in the human heart.” [Note: [Col. 0567] In the ancient text, this is attributed to Cassiodorus.] Thus the Holy Spirit is given to a human being, and, once given, is given more abundantly—that is, increased—and is possessed more or less, while he nevertheless remains immutable.

### Reply to the second question

9. Although he is wholly everywhere and in every creature, nevertheless many do not possess him. For not all possess the Holy Spirit in whom he is present; otherwise irrational creatures too would possess the Holy Spirit, which the piety of faith does not admit.

### He confirms both replies by authority

10. But, in order that what we have said may be more certain, let us confirm it by authority. Augustine shows, commenting on John, that the Holy Spirit is received more or less, increases for a human being, is given to one who does not have him, and is given to one who has him so that he may possess him more fully:

“Without the Holy Spirit, it is certain that we cannot love Christ or keep his commandments; and we are able to do and accomplish this in proportion as we receive him less, and more fully in proportion as we receive him more fully. Therefore he is not promised in vain not only to one who does not have him, but also to one who has him: to one who does not have him, that he may have him; to one who has him, that he may have him more fully. For unless he were possessed less by one person and more fully by another, the holy Elisha would not have said to the holy Elijah, in 4 Kings 2: ‘May the Spirit that is in you be doubled in me.’ But to Christ, who is the Son of God, the Spirit was not given by measure, John 3. For Christ the man, mediator between God and human beings, is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit. That he is the only-begotten Son of God, equal to the Father, belongs not to grace but to nature. But that the human being was assumed into the unity of the person of the only-begotten Son belongs to grace, not nature. To others, however, the Spirit is given by measure; and what has been given is added, until each person’s proper measure is filled according to the measure of that person’s perfection.”

Here you have expressly that the Holy Spirit is given or received more or less, that he increases when given to a human being, and that he is given both to one who has him and to one who does not have him, because the Holy Spirit is charity, which is given to one who does not have it and increases and advances in one who has it. Indeed, to speak more truly and more properly, the human being sometimes advances or declines in it; and then charity itself is said to advance or decline, although it neither advances nor declines in itself, because it is God. Hence Augustine, in Homily 9 on the Epistle of John, says: “Each person proves how much charity has advanced in him—or rather, how much he himself has advanced in charity. For if charity is God, it neither declines nor advances. Thus charity is said to advance in you because you advance in it.”

This is how it should be understood when the Holy Spirit is said to increase in us: namely, because we advance in him; and likewise with other such expressions.

### That some say that the Holy Spirit is not the charity by which we love God and neighbor

11. It was said above that the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father and the Son, by which they love one another and us; and that he himself is the charity poured out into our hearts, Romans 5, for loving God and neighbor. All Catholics grant the former: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father and the Son. But most deny that he himself is the charity by which we love God and neighbor. For they say: “If the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father and Son and also ours, then the charity by which God loves us and that by which we love him are the same charity. But the authorities of the saints seem to deny this.”

For Augustine says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “From where comes love except from where faith itself comes—that is, from the Holy Spirit? For it would not be in us unless it were poured out into our hearts through the Spirit. But the charity of God is said to be poured out into our hearts, not that by which he himself loves us, but that by which he makes us his lovers; just as the justice of God is called that by which we are made just by his gift; and the salvation of the Lord, that by which he saves us; and the faith of Christ, that by which he makes us faithful.”

These words seem to show a distinction between the charity by which God loves us and that by which we love. And just as our justice is called God’s, not because he is just by it, but because he makes us just by it, likewise faith and salvation, so the charity in us seems to be called God’s charity not because he loves by it, but because he causes us to love by it.

Again Augustine says, in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17: “When John had mentioned God’s love—not that by which we love him, but that by which he himself loved us and sent his Son as deliverer for our sins.” Here too he seems plainly to separate the love by which we love God from that by which he loves us. Therefore, they say, if the Holy Spirit is the love by which God loves and by which we love, there are two loves—indeed, two distinct things—which is absurd and far from the truth. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not the love by which we love, but only that by which God loves us.

### Reply to the foregoing, determining the authorities

12. To this we reply by determining the words of the aforesaid authorities as follows: “The charity of God is said to be poured out into our hearts, not that by which he loves us, but that by which he causes us to love,” and so forth. By these words the charity by which God loves us is neither separated from nor shown different from that by which we love; rather, since it is one and the same charity and is called God’s charity, Scripture is shown to call it God’s charity for different causes and reasons. For it is called God’s charity either because God loves us by it or because he makes us his lovers by it.

### Determination of the first authority

13. Therefore, when the Apostle says in Romans 5, “The charity of God is poured out into our hearts,” it is not called God’s charity as that by which he loves us, but as that by which he makes us love; that is, there it is called God’s charity not because God loves us by it but because he makes us his lovers by it. And that it can be called God’s charity on this ground—because it makes us love—is shown by a similar kind of expression: just as the justice of God is called that by which he justifies us, the salvation of the Lord that by which he saves us, and the faith of Christ that by which he makes us faithful.

### Determination of the second

14. Likewise we explain the other authority, where he says that God’s love is mentioned, “not that by which we love him, but that by which he himself loved us,” as though he said: He mentions God’s love, not insofar as we love God by it, but insofar as he himself loves us by it.

### They raise another objection

15. But, they say, another point is more pressing. Augustine said above, in chapter 32 of *On the Spirit and the Letter*, that love is from the Holy Spirit, from whom faith also comes. Therefore, just as faith is not the Holy Spirit from whom it comes, neither is charity. How, then, is the Holy Spirit charity, if charity is from him? For if it is from him and he himself is it, then the Holy Spirit is from himself.

To this we say: the Holy Spirit is not indeed from himself, but he nevertheless gives himself to us, as was said above; for the Holy Spirit gives himself to us. In this sense it was said that charity is from him in us, yet charity itself is the Holy Spirit. Faith, however, is from the Holy Spirit and is not the Holy Spirit, because it is merely a gift or thing given, not God who gives.

### That they introduce other arguments and authorities to prove the same point

16. They also introduce other arguments to show the same thing: namely, that charity is not the Holy Spirit, because charity is an affection of the mind and a movement of the soul, whereas the Holy Spirit is not an affection of the soul or movement of the mind, since the Holy Spirit is immutable and uncreated. Therefore charity is not the Holy Spirit.

### That charity is a movement or affection of the soul

17. They confirm by authorities that charity is an affection of the soul and movement of the mind. Augustine says [Col. 0569] in Book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*: “By charity I mean a movement of the mind toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake.” Again, in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 1, volume 1, discussing the Apostle’s words in Romans 8:11, “Neither death nor life will be able to separate us from the charity of God,” he says: “The charity of God here means the virtue which is the most upright affection of our soul, which joins us to God and by which we love him.”

These words express that charity is an affection and movement of the soul; consequently, it does not seem to be the Holy Spirit.

### Reply determining the authorities

18. To this we say that it is said in the same way as “God is our hope and our patience,” because he makes us hope and endure. Thus charity is called a movement or affection of the soul because through it the soul is moved and affected to love God. But do not be surprised that charity, although it is the Holy Spirit, is called a movement of the mind, since in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 8, it is said of the Spirit of wisdom: “Who reaches from end to end, who is a mobile act, certain, undefiled.” This is not said because wisdom is something mobile or some act, but because by its immovability it reaches all things—not through local motion, but by being always everywhere and contained nowhere.

Thus charity is called a movement of the soul not because it itself is a movement, affection, or virtue of the soul, but because the mind is affected and moved through it, as though it were a virtue. But if charity is the Holy Spirit, who works in each person as he wills, and through him the human mind is affected and moved to believe, hope, and the like, just as it is moved to love, why is charity called a movement or affection of the mind toward loving, but not similarly toward believing or hoping?

To this it may rightly be said that charity—that is, the Holy Spirit—works the other acts and movements of the virtues through the mediation of the virtues whose acts they are: for instance, the act of faith, that is, believing through faith as its means; and the act of hope, that is, hoping through hope as its means. For through faith and hope he performs the stated acts. But the act of loving—that is, to love—he works by himself alone, without the mediation of any virtue. Therefore he performs this act differently from the other acts of the virtues. Hence Scripture speaks differently of this act and the others, specially attributing this act to charity.

Therefore charity truly is the Holy Spirit. Hence Augustine, discussing the Apostle’s preceding words in the same work, calls charity the good than which nothing is better, and thereby signifies that it is God, saying, volume 9, tractate 14: “If no thing separates us from his charity, what could be not merely better but even more certain than this good?” Behold, he says that nothing is better than charity. Therefore charity is the Holy Spirit, who is God and God’s gift, or thing given; he distributes gifts to individual believers, yet he himself is not divided, but is given undivided to each. Hence Augustine, where John says that the Spirit is not given to Christ by measure, says: “To others, however, not the Spirit himself but his gifts are distributed.”

### Whether it should be granted that gifts are given through the Gift

19. Here it is asked: since the Holy Spirit, through whom gifts are distributed, is himself the Gift, should it be granted that gifts are distributed and given through the Gift? To this we say that through the Gift which is the Holy Spirit, gifts proper to each person are distributed, while all the good possess the Gift himself in common. Hence Augustine says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19: “Through the Gift which is the Holy Spirit, many gifts, which are proper to particular persons, are distributed in common to all the members of Christ. For not every individual has all gifts, but some have these and others those, although all possess the Gift himself through whom gifts proper to each are distributed—that is, the Holy Spirit.” Here he plainly says that gifts are given through the Gift.

## DISTINCTION XVIII. WHETHER THE HOLY SPIRIT IS CALLED “GIFT” AND “GIVEN,” OR “BESTOWED,” FOR THE SAME REASON

1. Further, it must be carefully considered: since the Holy Spirit is called both Gift and Given, whether both names belong to him for the same reason—which may indeed seem to be the case.

### Why this seems to be so

[Col. 0570]

2. For since to give the Holy Spirit and to bestow the Holy Spirit are the same thing, it seems that the Holy Spirit is called Given and Gift for the same reason. Augustine also seems to signify this in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19, when he says: “The Holy Spirit is God’s Gift insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given; but in himself he is God, even if he is given to no one.” Here he plainly says that the Holy Spirit is called Gift because he is given. But if he is called Gift only because he is given, he was not Gift from eternity, because he is given only in time.

### Answer: why the Holy Spirit is called Given or Bestowed

3. To this we say that the Holy Spirit is called both Gift and Given, or Bestowed; but he is called Given or Bestowed only because he is given or bestowed, and this he has only in time.

### Why he is called Gift

4. But he is called Gift not merely because he is bestowed, but from the property which he possessed from eternity; hence he was Gift from eternity. For he was eternally Gift, not because he was given, but because he proceeded from the Father and the Son. Hence Augustine says in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*: “As for the Son, to be born is to be from the Father; so for the Holy Spirit, to be God’s Gift is to proceed from the Father and the Son.”

Here it is plainly shown that the Holy Spirit is Gift because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, just as the Son is from the Father because he was born from him. For the Son’s being from the Father and the Holy Spirit’s being from the Father are not the same: that is, the Son is not said to be from the Father by the property by which the Holy Spirit is so said. The Son is said to be from the Father because he was begotten by him; but the Holy Spirit is said to be from the Father and the Son because the Holy Spirit is the Gift of the Father and Son—that is, because he proceeds from both. For he is called Spirit in the same respect in which he is called Gift; and Gift in the same respect in which he is proceeding.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11: “The Holy Spirit, who is not the Trinity but is understood in the Trinity, is relatively named when he is properly called the Holy Spirit, since he is referred both to the Father and to the Son, because he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son; but the relation itself does not appear in this name. It does appear when he is called the Gift of God, for he is the Gift of the Father and Son because he proceeds both from the Father and from the Son.”

These words plainly show that the Holy Spirit and Gift are said by the same relation: Gift, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore the property by which he is called Holy Spirit or Gift is procession; this we shall discuss more fully later along with the others. Since, therefore, he proceeded from both from eternity, he was Gift from eternity. Thus the Holy Spirit is not called Gift merely because he is bestowed, for he was Gift before he was bestowed.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit always proceeds, and proceeds not in time but from eternity. But because he proceeded in such a way as to be capable of being bestowed, he was already Gift before there was anyone to whom he might be bestowed. For ‘Gift’ is understood differently from ‘bestowed’: a gift can exist even before it is given, but something bestowed cannot in any way be so called unless it has been given. Therefore the Holy Spirit is eternally Gift, but temporally bestowed.”

These words plainly show that, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from eternity, so he is Gift from eternity—not because he was bestowed by the Father upon the Son or by the Son upon the Father, but because from eternity he proceeded as capable of being bestowed.

### The question: to whom was he capable of being bestowed?

5. But it is asked to whom he was capable of being bestowed: to the Father and the Son, or only to us, who did not yet exist. If he was not capable of being bestowed upon the Father and the Son but only upon us, and was Gift because he proceeded as capable of being bestowed in that way, then it seems that the Son too was always Gift for the same reason, because from eternity he proceeded from the Father as capable of being given to us in time; for Isaiah 9 also says of the Son that he was given to us.

To this we say that the Holy Spirit proceeded as capable of being bestowed only upon us, not upon the Father or Son, just as he was given only to us. And the Son was truly given to us, and from eternity proceeded from the Father not merely as capable of being bestowed, but as begotten, though also capable of being given. He proceeded [Col. 0571], then, as begotten and as capable of being bestowed; but the Holy Spirit proceeds not as begotten but only as Gift. Yet he was always Gift not only because capable of being bestowed, but because he proceeded from both and was capable of being bestowed.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 14, near the end: “In that God was going to give him, he was already Gift even before he was given, and therefore capable of being bestowed; but he is capable of being bestowed differently from the Son. For he is given differently and proceeds differently from the Son. The procession of the Son is generation, or birth; but the procession of the Holy Spirit is not birth; both, however, are ineffable.”

### That as the Son received by being born not only that he might be Son, but also that he might be essence, so the Holy Spirit received by proceeding not only that he might be Gift, but also that he might be essence

6. It should be noted that just as the Son received by being born not only that he might be Son, but that he might be altogether, and that he might be the very substance, so the Holy Spirit, by proceeding from the Father and Son, received not only that he might be the Holy Spirit or Gift, but also that he might be altogether and might be substance. This he certainly did not receive from being given; for since he is given only in time, if he had this from being given, he would have received in time that he might exist.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 15: “The Son has by being born not merely that he may be Son, but that he may be altogether.” Therefore it is asked whether the Holy Spirit has from being given not only that he may be Gift, but that he may be altogether. If only because he is given—that is, if he has being only because he is given—just as the Son by being born has not only that he may be Son, which is said relatively, but that he may be the very substance, how then was the Holy Spirit already the very substance, since there was no one to whom he might be given before he existed? Therefore it is not from being given but from proceeding that he has both that he may be Gift and that he may be essence; just as the Son received not from being given, but by being born, not merely that he might be Son but that he might be essence.

Hence Augustine says in Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 26: “Just as generation from the Father grants the Son essence without any beginning of time and without mutability of nature, so procession from both grants the Holy Spirit essence without any beginning of time and without any mutability of nature.”

### That from the foregoing it seems that the Son is essence by birth, and the Holy Spirit essence by procession, not merely Son and Holy Spirit

7. Here a question arises: if the Son has by being born not only that he may be Son but that he may be essence, and the Holy Spirit has by proceeding not only that he may be Gift but that he may be essence, then the Son is essence by birth and the Holy Spirit is essence by procession. Yet chapter 2 says that the Father is not Father in the respect in which he is God, nor the Son Son in the respect in which he is God, nor the Holy Spirit Gift in the respect in which he is God; for, as Augustine says in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, these names show their relations, not their essence. We shall discuss this more fully later.

Replying briefly, we say that the Son is not essence by birth but only Son, nor is the Holy Spirit essence by procession but only Gift; yet both received that they might be essence: the former by being born, the latter by proceeding. For, as Hilary says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, near the end, the Son is not God from God by diminution, extension, or derivation, but subsists by birth from the power of nature into the same nature; and the Holy Spirit subsists by procession from the power of nature into the same nature.

### Explanation of Hilary’s words

8. This may be understood thus: from the Father, who is unbegotten power, the Son has by birth—that is, by being born—and the Holy Spirit has by procession—that is, by proceeding—the same nature that the Father has. Hence the same author, expressing himself more clearly, explains what he had said, declaring a little later in the same place: “The birth of God cannot fail to possess the nature from which it proceeded. For that which subsists not from elsewhere than God subsists as nothing other than God.”

These words explain how the statement should be understood: “Generation from the Father grants essence to the Son, and procession from both grants essence to the Holy Spirit.” It is not because the Son is essence, nor the Holy Spirit essence, by personal property; rather, both the former by being born and the latter by proceeding have the same essence, whole and entire, which is in the Father.

### That the Holy Spirit is called Gift and Given according to the two aforesaid modes of procession

9. From the foregoing it is clear that the Holy Spirit is eternally Gift and temporally Given or Bestowed. From this appears the distinction of the twofold procession discussed above. For according to one procession he is called Bestowed or Given; according to the other, Gift.

### As Gift he is referred to the Father and Son; as Given, to the one who gave and those to whom he was given

10. Insofar as he is eternally Gift, he is referred to the Father and Son; but insofar as he is called Given or Bestowed, he is referred both to the one who gave and to those to whom he is given. He is said to belong to the one who gives and to those to whom he is given.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 14: “What is given is referred both to the one who gave and to those to whom he gave. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father and Son who gave him, but also ours who have received him. Therefore he is both the Spirit of God who gave him and our Spirit who received him—not that spirit of ours by which we exist, for that is the spirit of the human being which is within that person, although we have certainly received even that spirit which is called human; but this and that are called ours in different ways. For one thing is what we received in order that we might exist; another is what we received in order that we might be holy.”

That the Holy Spirit is called ours, Scripture shows. For it is written of John that he would come “in the Spirit of Elijah.” Here the Spirit which Elijah received—namely, the Holy Spirit—is called Elijah’s Spirit. And the Lord says to Moses, Numbers 11: “I shall take from the Holy Spirit whom I have already given you.” Here too he is called Moses’ Spirit. It is plain, then, that the Holy Spirit is called our spirit because he has been given to us, and indeed given so that we might be holy. But the created spirit was given so that we might exist.

### Whether the Son, since he has been given to us, could be called ours as the Holy Spirit is

11. Here it is asked whether the Son also, since he has been given to us, is or can be called ours. We answer that the Son is called our bread, our redeemer, and the like; but he is not called our Son, because “son” is said only relatively to the one who begot him. Therefore he cannot be called our Son, but only the Father’s Son.

In being called Given, however, he is referred both to the giver and to those to whom he is given. Thus the Holy Spirit too, although Scripture—as said above—calls him our spirit, your spirit, or that person’s spirit, as was said of Moses and Elijah, is nevertheless nowhere in Scripture called “our Holy Spirit,” “your Holy Spirit,” or “that person’s Holy Spirit,” but “our spirit,” “your spirit,” or “that person’s spirit.” For the Holy Spirit is called Spirit in the same respect in which he is called Gift; and both are said relatively to the Father and Son, by an eternal relation.

If, however, he is ever called our gift, “gift” is understood as “bestowed” or “given.” But when “Gift” is understood in the sense in which the Holy Spirit is called the Gift of the Father and Son, not of a human being, then the Son too cannot under that designation be called ours, so as to be called our son, just as the Holy Spirit is not called our Holy Spirit. Yet the Son is called our bread, and the Spirit our spirit: the former our bread because, given to us, he refreshes us; the latter our spirit because he is breathed into us by the Father and Son and breathes in us as he wills.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*: “That which is born from the Father is referred to the Father alone when it is called Son. Therefore he is the Father’s Son and not ours. Yet we say, ‘Give us our bread,’ Matthew 6 and Luke 11, just as we say ‘our Spirit.’”

### Whether the Holy Spirit is referred to himself

12. After this it is asked whether the Holy Spirit is referred to himself. This seems provable from what has been said. For if what is given is referred to the one who gives it and the one to whom it is given, and the Holy Spirit is given by himself, as was said above, then he is referred to himself. We postpone the determination of this question [Col. 0573] until later, when we treat matters which are said relatively of God in time, among which “given” and “bestowed” are included.

## DISTINCTION XIX. ON THE EQUALITY OF THE THREE PERSONS

1. Now that, to the measure of our ability, we have set forth the coeternity of the three persons, it remains to say something concerning their equality. For Catholic faith affirms that the three persons are coeternal and coequal. The Son is equal to the Father in all things, and the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son. For, as Augustine teaches in *On Faith to Peter*, briefly explaining how equality is to be understood, “none of them either precedes another in eternity, exceeds another in magnitude, or surpasses another in power; for the Father is neither prior nor greater than the Son or Holy Spirit, insofar as the unity of the divine nature is concerned; nor is the Son greater than the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the nature of the Father and Son is eternal and without beginning. Therefore we rightly believe and call the three one God, because the divinity of the three persons is altogether one eternity, one immensity, and one by nature.”

Here Augustine briefly identifies wherein the equality of the three persons consists: namely, that none surpasses another in eternity, magnitude, or power.

### That eternity, magnitude, and power in God are one, though presented as though distinct

2. Although these are listed as though distinct, in God they are one: namely, the simple and immutable divine essence. Hence Augustine says in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1: “He is not great by one thing and God by another; rather, he is great by that by which he is God, because for him being great is not one thing and being God another.” For his magnitude is the same as his power, and his essence is the same as his magnitude. Therefore Father and Son together are one essence and one magnitude.

Likewise, the power of God is the divine essence. Hence Augustine says in Book 7 of the *Confessions*: “God’s will and power are God.” The eternity of God likewise is the divine essence. Augustine shows this in commenting on the Psalm passage, “Your years are through generation and generation”: “There is a generation of generations which does not pass away, gathered from all generations—that is, from the saints. In it will be the years of God which do not pass away, that is, the eternity of God. For the years of God are not one thing and he himself another; rather, the years of God are God’s eternity. And eternity itself is God’s substance, having nothing mutable.”

Let us therefore hold firmly that one and the same thing is the divine essence, God’s eternity, power, and magnitude; and yet Scripture customarily presents these and similar things as though distinct. In these words Augustine therefore briefly embraced the equality of the three persons, because none surpasses another in eternity, magnitude, or power. That none of the three persons exceeds another in eternity has been shown above, where the coeternity of the three persons was set forth.

### Here concerning magnitude: that none of the persons exceeds another in it

3. It remains, then, to show that none exceeds another in magnitude or power; and let us first consider magnitude.

### That one Person is not greater than another, nor two greater than one, nor three or two greater than one.

4. It must therefore be known that the Father is not greater than the Son, nor is the Father or the Son greater than the Holy Spirit; nor are two Persons together anything greater than one, nor are three together anything greater than two. Nor is the essence greater in three than in two, nor in two than in one, because it is whole in each. Hence John Damascene says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 6:

> We confess that the whole nature of the Godhead is perfectly in each of its hypostases, that is, Persons: wholly in the Father, wholly in the Son, wholly in the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father is perfect God, the Son perfect God, and the Holy Spirit perfect God.

### How the Father is said to be in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Holy Spirit in both, and each in each.

5. Hence the Father is said to be in the Son, and [Col. 0574] the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both, and each in each. Thus Augustine, in *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 1, says:

> On account of the unity of nature, the whole Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit; likewise the whole Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. None of these is outside any of the others, on account of the unity of the divine nature.

Here he discloses this to some extent. For so great a mystery cannot be fully revealed by a human being: namely, the sense in which each of the Persons is said to be wholly in the others.

Accordingly Hilary, investigating these matters more deeply, says in book 3 of *On the Trinity*:

> The Lord’s saying brings obscurity to many when he says, John 14, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”; and not without reason. For the nature of human understanding does not grasp the rationale of this statement, nor can any human comparison furnish an example suitable to divine realities. But what is unintelligible to a human being is possible for God. We must therefore recognize and understand what this means: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me”—if indeed we are able to grasp it as it is—so that the reasoning of divine truth may establish what the nature of things is thought incapable of allowing.
>
> Therefore, that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father is the perfect fullness of divinity in both. For the fullness of divinity is in the Son. What is in the Father is also in the Son; what is in the Unbegotten is in the Begotten: one is from the other, and both are one. That is, the one who is from the other, having nothing that is not also in him from whom he is, is not two but one—one distinct person in the other—because what is in both is not different, so that they may be one in our faith. Each is not the other, nor are both the same person; yet neither do we confess something different, because the fact that God is born from God allows him to be neither the same nor something other. Therefore we confess both the likeness of power and the fullness of deity to be the same in both, because Truth says, John 14, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”
>
> For the Son received all things from the Father. If he received a part of the one who begot him, neither would be perfect: the one from whom something departed would lack it, and there would be no fullness in one constituted from a portion. Thus neither would be perfect if the one who begot lost his own fullness and the one who was born did not attain it.

Let us therefore confess that the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and God in God, as Hilary himself says in book 7 of *On the Trinity*: not through a double conjunction of compatible kinds, nor through an inherent nature of a more capacious substance, but through the united likeness of nature, through the birth of a living nature from a living nature: while the reality does not differ, while birth does not degrade the nature of God, while nothing other than God is born from God; while in these there is nothing new, nothing foreign, nothing separable.

These words, so far as human weakness permits, explain in what sense Christ said that he was in the Father and the Father in him. In the same sense, the Holy Spirit is understood to be in both, and each Person to be in each, since in each is the same fullness of divinity and the united likeness of nature. For the divine nature is not greater in any of these Persons; these three Persons are of one and undifferentiated nature. Therefore one is said to be in another, as stated above.

Hence Ambrose, explaining for us the meaning of the preceding words in his exposition of 2 Corinthians 5, says:

> By this it is understood that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. For unity is where there is no diversity.

Thus, by the testimonies of three illustrious men—Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose—who agree in the same revelation of the Holy Spirit speaking in them, those willing to believe devoutly are shown, though as through a mirror and in an enigma, 1 Corinthians 12, how the statement is to be understood that the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, or the Holy Spirit in both.

### He returns to what he began: to show that one does not surpass another in greatness.

6. But now let us return to our purpose and persist in the undertaking, showing that none of the three Persons surpasses another in greatness. For none is greater than the others; nor are two anything greater than one, nor three than two; nor is God greater than each of them, because each is perfect and that perfection has no possible increase.

### That none of the Persons is a part in the Trinity.

[Col. 0575]

7. None of the three Persons is a part of God or of the divine essence, because each of them is true and full God, and is the whole and full divine essence. Therefore none of them is a part in the Trinity. Hence Augustine says in book 3 *Against Maximinus the Heretic*, ch. 10:

> Do you think that God the Father, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, cannot be one God? For you fear that the Father may be a part of one God composed of three. Do not fear this, for in the unity of the Godhead no division into parts occurs. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; that is, the Trinity itself is one God.
>
> “Then,” you say, “God the Father is a part of God.” Far be it. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three Persons; and these three, because they are of one substance, are one, and are supremely one, where there is no diversity of natures and no diversity of wills. For if they were one in nature but not one in agreement, they would not be supremely one. But if they were unlike in nature, they would not be supremely one. Therefore these three, because they are one through the ineffable conjunction of deity by which they are ineffably joined, are one God.
>
> Therefore whoever is one among the three cannot be a part of the Trinity. In the Trinity, therefore, which is God, the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and these three together are one God. One is not a third part of this Trinity; nor are two there anything greater than one, nor are all of them anything greater than each individually, because its greatness is spiritual, not bodily. Let the one who can receive this receive it, Matthew 19; but the one who cannot, let him believe and pray that he may understand what he believes. For what is said through the prophet Isaiah, ch. 7, is true: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.”

By these words he plainly shows the undifferentiated greatness of the three Persons. Again, in the same work:

> You indeed said that one God is not composed of parts, and you wish this to be understood of the Father alone. “He,” you say, “is unbegotten, simple power.” Yet in this simple power you seem to enumerate many things when you say, “God begot God, the good begot the good, the wise begot the wise, the merciful begot the merciful, the powerful begot the powerful.” Are goodness, wisdom, mercy, and power, then, three parts of the one power which you called simple? If you say that they are parts, simple power is composed of parts. And, by your definition, this simple power is one God; therefore you say that God is composed of parts.
>
> “I do not say that,” you reply; “they are not parts.” If, then, in the one Person of the Father you find things which appear multiple, yet do not find parts because there is one simple power, how much more are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one God because of their indivisible deity, three Persons because of the proper characteristic of each, and not parts of one God because of the perfection of each? The Father is power, the Son is power, the Holy Spirit is power. You speak truly in this; but in refusing to allow the power begotten from power and the power proceeding from power to have the same nature, you speak falsely—against right and catholic faith.

These words plainly teach that the three Persons are not parts of God or of the divine essence. None of them is to be called a part of the Trinity, nor is one in any respect greater than the others.

### When we say that three Persons are one essence, we do not predicate as a genus of species, nor as a species of individuals; for essence is not a genus and Person a species, nor essence a species and Person an individual.

8. It must here be added that the equality of the three Persons and their undifferentiated greatness are so complete that, when we say the three Persons are one essence or substance, we do not predicate this either as a genus of species or as a species of individuals. For the divine essence is not a genus and the three Persons species; nor is the divine essence a species and the three Persons individuals.

Augustine plainly demonstrates this with probable and irrefutable arguments in book 7 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 6:

> If essence is a genus and Person a species, as some think, three substances ought to be named, just as three Persons are named. For just as animal is a genus and horse a species, three horses are named, and likewise three [Col. 0576] animals. The species is not named in the plural and the genus in the singular there, as though one were to say, “Three horses are one animal”; rather, just as three horses are called by the specific name, so three animals are called by the generic name.
>
> Therefore, since we confess three Persons to be one essence, not three essences, whereas three horses are called three animals, not one, it is clear that essence does not signify a genus, nor Person a species.

### Here he proves that it is not spoken as a species of individuals.

9. But if they say that *Person* does not signify a species, but something singular and individual, and that *essence* is understood as a species—so that Person is not said as “human being,” but as “this human being,” or as Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or any other who can be pointed out while present with a finger—then the same reasoning refutes them also. For just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called three individuals, so too they are three human beings and three animals. Why then, if we reason in these terms of genus, species, and individual, are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit not called three essences in the same way that they are called three Persons?

### He proves the same in another way.

10. Augustine also proves the same in another manner, in the same book and chapter: namely, that the divine essence is not a genus and the Persons species, nor essence a species and the Persons individuals.

> One essence does not have species, just as one animal does not have species. Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three species of one essence; therefore the divine essence is not a genus. Nor is the divine essence a species and the Persons individuals, as a human being is a species and Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are individuals. For if essence is a species, as human being is, then, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are not called one human being, so the three Persons are not called one essence. Thus we do not speak in this manner according to genus and species.

### Nor are three Persons called one essence according to material cause.

11. It should further be noted that the divine essence is not the matter of the three Persons, as Augustine teaches in the same book and chapter. Thus, three Persons are not said to be one essence as though they had one common and identical matter, as we would call three statues one gold if they were made from the same gold.

But we do not say that the Trinity is three Persons and one essence, or one God, as though three things subsisted from one matter. For in three equal statues there is more gold in all three together than in each alone, and less gold in one than in two. But there is nothing whatever of this kind in the essence of the Trinity. Therefore we do not call three Persons one substance or essence according to material creation, as three statues are called one gold.

### Nor are three Persons called one essence as three human beings are one nature or of one nature.

12. To this must also be added that we do not say the three Persons are one essence, or of one essence, as Augustine says in the same book and chapter, in the way we say that any three human beings of the same sex, the same bodily constitution, and the same disposition are one nature or of one nature.

For in such things, one human being is not as much as three human beings together, and two human beings are something more than one human being, just as we said of statues. But it is not so in God. For the Father and Son together are not a greater essence than the Father alone or the Son alone; rather, those three Persons together are equal to each individually.

From what has been said, it is clear that the three Persons are called the divine essence neither according to material cause, as three statues are one gold; nor according to similarity of constitution, as three human beings are of one nature; nor as a genus is predicated of species, or a species of individuals—that is, as what contains is predicated of what is contained, or the greater of the lesser.

### Matters which seem contrary to the foregoing.

13. Yet certain teachings handed down in the writings of some catholic interpreters of Sacred Scripture seem contrary to these points. In them the divine essence appears to be signified as something common and universal, like a species; [Col. 0577] while the three Persons are three particulars, three individuals differing in number.

Thus John Damascene, greatest among the Greek doctors, says in the book which he wrote *On the Trinity*, and which Pope Eugenius caused to be translated:

> Common and universal terms are predicated of their particular subjects. Therefore substance is common, but hypostasis—that is, Person—is particular. It is called particular not because it has a part of the nature, but because it is particular in number, as an atom—that is, an individual. For hypostases appear to differ in number, not in nature.

Again, book 3, ch. 4:

> Substance signifies the common and comprehensive species of hypostases alike in species—*homoideōn*, that is, Persons alike in species—such as God and human being. But hypostasis indicates an individual: that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Peter, Paul, and the like.

Here he plainly says that substance is universal and hypostasis particular; that God is a species as human being is; and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are individuals like Peter and Paul because they differ in number. These statements appear wholly to contradict Augustine’s foregoing position. What, then, are we to say to these things? Certainly, we can and must say that the teachings which Augustine set forth above are to be held without any hesitation.

### That what John says can be soundly understood, and how.

14. Yet these statements, although on the surface of their wording they seem to sound somewhat alien to the faith, can nevertheless be soundly understood—namely, that the substance of God is a species or universal and that the Persons are individuals. They greatly require a devout reader and interpreter.

In explaining them, I would rather be silent and listen to others than, by speaking, provide ill-disposed people an occasion for detraction. Nevertheless, it seems to me that his statement, “Substance is common, and hypostasis particular,” can be understood as follows. When these terms are said of God, he does not take them as they are taken in philosophical discipline, but speaks by analogy with what philosophers say.

Thus, just as in philosophy that is called common or universal which is predicated of many, while that is called particular or individual which is predicated of one alone, so this divine essence is called universal because it is said of all the Persons together and of each separately. But each individual Person is called particular because it is predicated neither commonly of the others nor individually of any other.

Therefore, owing to the analogy of predication, he called God’s substance universal and the Persons particulars or individuals. For the same reason, he called this same divine essence the common and comprehensive species of Persons alike in species. Just as the species “human being” is predicated of its individuals—Peter, Paul, and others—and they do not differ in that species but agree in every respect, so God is predicated of the three Persons, who do not differ in deity but agree in every respect.

Perceiving this analogy between eternal and temporal things, John transferred to eternal realities the names *universal* and *particular*, which properly belong to temporal things. Augustine, however, seeing the greater dissimilarity than similarity between the matters mentioned, removed those names from the excellence of the Trinity.

### In what sense he said that the Persons differ in number.

15. John says that hypostases differ in number, not in nature. In saying that they do not differ in nature, he speaks most truly and without difficulty. But when he says that they differ in number, care must be taken as to how this is understood. For things are said to differ in number in different ways.

### The ways in which things are said to differ in number, and the sense in which this may apply to the Persons.

16. Some things are said to differ in number when they differ such that this is not that, nor anything which that is or which is in it. Socrates and Plato differ in this way, as do the things philosophers call individuals or particulars. The three Persons cannot be said to differ in number in this sense.

Things are also said to differ in number when, in enumeration or counting, they are not joined to one another but distinguished from one another; as when, speaking of certain things, we say one, two, three. Perhaps it was in this sense that John said hypostases, that is, Persons, differ in number. For we may say: “The Father is one”; “the Father and Son are two”; and “the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three.” Likewise: “This Person is one”; “this and that are two”; and “this, that, and the other are three.”

More fittingly, however, those three Persons are said to be distinguished only by their properties, distinction 26; their distinction according to properties will be treated in what follows. But now let us return to what we began, repeating what has been said so that, by turning it over more often, it may become more familiar.

### That one Person is not greater than another, nor three together than one; and this is shown by catholic reasoning.

17. It must therefore be known that there is such equality in the Trinity, as Augustine says in book 8 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 1, that not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but even the Father and Son together are not anything greater than the Holy Spirit, nor is any Person something less than the Trinity itself.

That this is so must, insofar as possible, be demonstrated in some way. Therefore, says Augustine in the same work, ch. 2, let us attend, so far as the Creator himself assists us, to how two or three Persons in this Trinity are not anything greater than one of them.

### He employs an exceedingly subtle argument to show that this is so.

18. What is called great there is not great from anything other than that by which it truly is, because there greatness itself is truth, and truth is essence. Therefore what is not truer is not greater there. But the Father and Son together are not truer than the Father alone or the Son alone. Therefore the two together are not anything greater than each individually.

And because the Holy Spirit also exists equally truly, the Father and Son together are not anything greater than he, because they are not truer. Again, in the essence of truth, to be true is to be; and to be is to be great. Therefore to be great is to be true. Whatever is equally true there is equally great. Therefore what has no more truth there has no more greatness; and what is not truer has no more truth.

But one Person is not truer than another, nor two than one, nor three together than each individually. Therefore one has no more truth than another, nor two than one, nor three together than each individually. Thus the Trinity itself is not anything greater than each individual Person there, but is as great as each; for where truth itself is greatness, what is not truer is not greater.

Here, by an appropriate method and catholic reasoning, the undifferentiated greatness of the three Persons has been shown: one is not greater than another, two are not anything greater than one, and three together are not anything greater than each individually.

### God should not be called triple, but triune.

19. Furthermore, although God is called triune, he ought not to be called triple. For there is no triplicity where there is supreme unity and undifferentiated equality. Thus Augustine says in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 7:

> God is not to be thought triple merely because he is triune; otherwise the Father alone, or the Son alone, would be less than the Father and Son together. Since, therefore, the Father alone, the Son alone, and the Holy Spirit alone are each as great as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, God is in no way to be called triple. For the Father with the Son and Holy Spirit is not greater God than each one of them, because that perfection has no possible increase. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each perfect; and each is called perfect God. Therefore he should be called Trinity rather than triple.

### That bodily realities are not as the Trinity is.

20. In bodily realities, one thing is not as much as three together, and two things are more than one. But in the supreme Trinity, one Person is as much as three together, and two are as much as one. They are infinite in themselves, and there is no end to their greatness.

Thus is made plain what was said above: how each is in each, all are in each, each is in all, all are in all, and one is in all and one is all. We have now sufficiently shown [Col. 0579] how no Person in the Trinity surpasses another in greatness.

## DISTINCTION XX. HAVING SHOWN THAT NO PERSON SURPASSES ANOTHER IN GREATNESS, HE NOW SHOWS THAT ONE DOES NOT EXCEL ANOTHER IN POWER.

1. It remains to show how none of these Persons excels another in power, so that, just as the greatness of the three is one and undifferentiated, their power too may be shown one and undifferentiated.

It must therefore be known that the Father is not more powerful than the Son, nor is the Son or Father more powerful than the Holy Spirit. Nor do two or three together have greater power than each individually, because the Father and Son together can do no more than the Holy Spirit alone. Nor can these three together do more than each individually, because the Son received by being born, and the Holy Spirit by proceeding, the omnipotence which the Father possesses. Augustine establishes this by probable arguments and authorities in book 3 *Against Maximinus*, who said that the Father was better and more powerful than the Son.

### That the Son cannot do less than the Father.

2. Augustine says in the same work, ch. 12:

> He who says, John 16, “All that the Father has is mine,” has nothing less than the Father. For if he has something less in power than the Father, not all that the Father has is his. But all that the Father has is his. Therefore the Son has as great a power as the Father; therefore he is equal to the Father. For one who has received cannot be unequal to the one who gave.
>
> But this is your view of power: the Son is powerful, but the Father more powerful—so that, according to your teaching, one powerful being could generate or beget another powerful being, but the Omnipotent could not generate the omnipotent. Therefore the Father has omnipotence which the Son does not have; and if this is so, the Son’s statement, “All that the Father has is mine,” is false.

### The heretic admitted this truth, from which he proceeded to falsehood.

3. “But,” you say, “the Father received power from no one, whereas the Son received it from the Father.” We too confess that the Son received power from him from whom he was born powerful. But no one gave power to the Father because no one begot him. For by begetting, the Father gave power to the Son, just as by begetting he gave to him whom he begot from his substance all that he has in his substance.

### Augustine’s question, by which he presses the heretic.

4. But the question is whether the Father gave the Son power as great as his own or a lesser power. If as great, the Omnipotent is understood to have begotten not merely a powerful Son but an omnipotent Son. But if lesser, how are all the things that the Father has the Son’s? If the Father’s omnipotence is not the Son’s, then undoubtedly not all that the Father has is the Son’s. But all that the Father has is the Son’s; therefore the Father’s omnipotence is also the Son’s. Therefore the Father is not more powerful than the Son.

### He proves in another way that the Son is equal to the Father.

5. Again, he proves in another way that the Son is equal to the Father, against Maximinus, book 3, ch. 7:

> You say that the Father begot a Son less than himself; in this you also detract from the Father. For if he begot his only Son as less than himself, either he could not or he would not beget one equal to himself. If you say that he would not, you have said that he is envious; but if he could not, where is the omnipotence of God the Father? The matter is entirely reduced to this point: God the Father either could not or would not beget a Son equal to himself. If he could not, he is found weak; if he would not, envious. But both are false. Therefore the Son is truly equal to the Father. Thus the Father begot a Son equal to himself, and from both proceeds the Holy Spirit, equal to both.
>
> For if the Father, as Augustine says in book 3, ch. 15, *Against the Same Man*, could beget his own form in its fullness in the only Son but did not beget it in its fullness, but as lesser, you are compelled to call the Father envious. Therefore he begot a Son who is full God and equal to himself.

### By an analogy he shows that the Father did not beget the Son as lesser.

6. He demonstrates this through a human analogy, saying in book 3, ch. 15:

> If a human father could, he would beget an equal son. Who then would dare say that the Omnipotent could not do this? I add also that, if a human being could, he would beget a son greater and better than himself. But nothing can be greater or better than God. Why then, as you say, did God not beget an equal Son? He required no years through which equality might be completed, nor did he lack omnipotence. Or perhaps he did not will it? Then, God forbid, he was envious. But he was not envious; therefore he begot a Son equal to himself. Let us therefore believe that the Son is equal to him.

### He states the heretic’s opinion in order to destroy it.  
*(From the same work, book 3, ch. 18.)*

7. But perhaps you say: “The Father is greater than the Son precisely because, though begotten by no one, he nevertheless begot an equal.” To this I will reply promptly: rather, the Father is not greater than the Son because he begot one equal to himself.

For this is a question of origin—who is from whom—but equality concerns what sort of being, or how great a being, each is. That is to say: the question which asks who is from whom pertains to origin; the question which asks what sort of being, or how great a being, someone is pertains to equality.

Nor, when the Son is said to be begotten by the Father, is inequality of substance shown, but an order of nature—not an order by which one was prior to the other, but one by which one is from the other. Therefore equality or inequality does not exist there according to the fact that the Father begot, the Son was begotten, or the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; for one Person is not called equal or unequal to another on that basis.

Thus, as briefly as we could, the equality of the Trinity and its one and identical substance have been shown above: namely, how none of the three Persons exceeds any other in eternity, greatness, or power.

## DISTINCTION XXI. THE QUESTION: HOW CAN THE FATHER ALONE OR THE HOLY SPIRIT ALONE BE SPOKEN OF, WHEN THEY ARE INSEPARABLE?

1. Here a question arises from what has been said. For it was stated above that the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is as great as those three together; and that two or three Persons together are not anything greater than one Person alone.

Augustine therefore asks, in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 7, how these things can be said soundly, since neither the Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit is alone. Rather, the Son is always and inseparably with the Father, the Father with the Son, and the Holy Spirit with both. For these three Persons are inseparable.

Augustine answers in the same work:

> We call God the Father alone, not because he is separated from the Son or the Holy Spirit, but because, in saying this, we signify that they are not Father together with him; for the Father alone is Father. This is not said because he himself is alone—that is, without the Son or Holy Spirit—but because the Son and Holy Spirit are excluded from sharing the property of fatherhood.
>
> Likewise, when it is said, “The Son alone is Son,” or “The Holy Spirit alone is Holy Spirit,” the Son is not divided from the Father, nor the Holy Spirit from both; rather, the Father and Holy Spirit are excluded from sharing the filial property, and the Father and Son from sharing the property of procession.
>
> Therefore, when it is said, “The Father alone is as great as those three together,” the word *alone* does not separate the Father from the others. The sense is rather: the Father alone—that is, the Father who is Father in such a way that neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is Father—is as great, and so forth.

Understand similarly when it is said, “The Son alone is,” or “The Holy Spirit alone is.” Thus the Father alone is spoken of, as Augustine says in the same work, book 7, ch. 9, because no one but he is Father there; the Son alone, because no one but he is Son there; and the Holy Spirit alone, because no one but he is Holy Spirit there.

### Whether it may be said, “The Father alone is God,” “the Son alone is God,” or “the Holy Spirit alone is God”; or, “the Father is God alone,” or “the Holy Spirit is God alone.”

2. After this, it is asked whether, just as one says, “The Father alone is Father,” or “the Son alone is Son,” one may say, “The Father alone is God,” or “the Son alone is God,” and likewise of the Holy Spirit; or, “the Father is God alone,” “the Son is God alone.”

We say in reply that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called, and are, one God; and that this Trinity together is properly called God alone, just as it is called wise alone and powerful alone. But in our own wording we ought not, it seems, to say “the Father alone is God,” or “the Father is God alone”—and similarly of the Son and Holy Spirit—unless a statement of authority is encountered.

Hence Augustine says in book 7 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 9:

> Since we have shown how the Father alone or the Son alone can be spoken of, we must consider the statement by which it is said that the Father is not alone the one true God, but that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the one true God.

Here you have that the Father alone is not to be called the true God. Again, in the same work:

> If someone asks whether the Father alone is God, how shall we answer that he is not, unless perhaps we say that the Father is indeed God, but not God alone? But let us call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit God alone.

Here too you have that the Father ought not to be called God alone. Some, however, wish to take *alone* only as part of the subject here, while, if it occurs in the predicate, they grant that the Father is God alone. But Augustine’s words seem to show that the whole Trinity should properly be called God alone.

And this Trinity, as Augustine says *Against Maximinus*, is understood when the Apostle says, 1 Timothy 6, “the blessed and only powerful one”; Romans 16, “to the only wise God”; and 1 Timothy 1, “to the invisible only God.” These expressions are not to be understood of the Father alone, as Maximinus and other heretics contended, but of the Trinity. So too: 1 Timothy 6, “who alone has immortality.” For according to right faith, the Trinity itself is one God alone—blessed, powerful, wise, and invisible. Hence Augustine says in the same work:

> Since the Trinity is one God, this is to be our solution to the question: let us understand the only wise God, the only powerful God, as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who is one and only God.

### How the Trinity is called God alone when it is with holy spirits and souls.

3. But again it is asked how we call the Trinity itself God alone when it is with holy spirits and souls. Augustine replies in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 7:

> We call the Trinity God alone, although it is always with holy spirits and souls; but we call it alone because nothing other than the Trinity itself is God. For those beings along with it are not God, nor is anything else; but the Trinity itself alone, not they or anything else, is God.

### Even if the preceding statements were said of the Father alone, the Son and Holy Spirit would not thereby be excluded.

4. Yet, as Augustine says, even if the preceding statements were said of the Father alone, the Son or Holy Spirit would not thereby be excluded, because these three are one, 1 John 5. Thus in Revelation, ch. 19, it is said of the Son that he has a name written which no one knows except himself. The Father or Holy Spirit is not thereby separated. And when it is said, Matthew 11, “No one knows the Father except the Son,” the Father or Holy Spirit is not thereby separated, because they are inseparable.

At times the Father and Son are named and the Holy Spirit is unmentioned, Luke 10; as Truth, speaking to the Father, says, John 17: “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent, [as] the one true God.” Why then, Augustine asks in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, ch. 9, did he omit the Holy Spirit? Because it follows that wherever one is named—such as Father and Son—the peace adhering to the one with such great concord is also understood, although not mentioned. Therefore, when one of these is named, the others too are understood, as occurs in many places in Scripture.

## DISTINCTION XXII. ON THE DIFFERENCE OF THE NAMES WHICH WE USE IN SPEAKING OF GOD.

1. After the foregoing, it seems to us that we must discuss the diversity of the names which we use when speaking of the ineffable Unity and Trinity. Next, it must be shown in what ways anything is said of it. Let us therefore hold especially this: that certain names pertain distinctly to the individual persons, as Augustine says in Book 9 *On the Trinity*—names which are said only of the individual persons; [Col. 0582] while certain others signify the unity of essence and are said both separately of each person and commonly of all. Still others are said of God figuratively and by likeness. Hence Ambrose, in Book 2 *On the Trinity*, says: “So that faith may shine forth more purely, a threefold distinction appears necessary. For there are certain names which plainly display the property and person of the Godhead, and there are others which express the manifest truth of the divine majesty; while others are said of God figuratively and by likeness. Thus indications of property are generation, Son, Word, and the like; of eternal unity, wisdom, power, truth, and the like; and of likeness, brightness, character, mirror, and the like.”

He adds to the foregoing that some names befit God temporally and are said relatively.

2. To these it must be added that, as Augustine says in Book 5 *On the Trinity*, certain names befit God in time and are said in relation to creation. Some of these are said of all the persons, such as Lord, Creator, refuge; others, however, are not said of all, such as bestowed, given, sent.

He adds concerning the name *Trinity*.

3. Moreover, there is one name which is not said separately of any person, but of all together: namely, *Trinity*. It is not said according to substance, but indicates, as it were, a collective plurality of persons.

Concerning other names which befit God temporally and are not said relatively.

4. There are likewise certain names which befit God in time and are not said relatively, such as made man, incarnate, and the like. Behold, we have set forth six kinds of names which we use in speaking of God; each of these must be discussed.

That names which pertain to the individual persons are properly said relatively; whereas those which signify unity of essence are said absolutely, both of individual persons and commonly of all persons, and in their totality are understood in the singular, not the plural.

5. We must know, therefore, that those names which properly pertain to the individual persons are said relatively to one another, as Father and Son, and the Holy Spirit, the gift of both. But those which signify unity of essence are said absolutely; and those which are said absolutely are certainly said substantially, both commonly of all and separately of the individual persons, and in their totality are understood in the singular, not the plural: as God good, powerful, great, and the like. But what is said relatively is not said substantially. Hence Augustine, in Book 5 *On the Trinity*, chapters 6 and 8, says:

> Whatever is said absolutely is said substantially of that most excellent and divine sublimity. But whatever is said in relation to something is not said substantially, but relatively. And such is the power of the same substance in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of the individual persons absolutely is understood in their totality not plurally but singly. For we say: “The Father is God,” “The Son is God,” and “The Holy Spirit is God”—and no one doubts that this is said according to substance. Yet we do not say that this Trinity is three gods, but one God. Thus the Father is called great, the Son great, and the Holy Spirit great; yet not three great ones, but one great one. Likewise, the Father almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty; yet not three almighty ones, but one almighty one. Therefore, whatever is said of God absolutely is likewise said of the individual persons, and is said together of the Trinity itself not plurally but singly. And since for God to be is not one thing and to be great another, but for him to be is identical with being great, therefore, just as we do not say three essences, so neither do we say three greatnesses, but one essence and one greatness.

That God is great by that greatness by which he is God; likewise concerning goodness and everything said according to substance.

6. For God is not great by a greatness which is not himself, as though he participated in it; otherwise that greatness would be greater than God. But nothing is greater than God. Therefore, he is great by that greatness which he himself is. Consequently, neither do we say three greatnesses, but one greatness; nor three great ones, but one great one, because God is great not by participation in greatness, but is great by himself, who is great, because he himself is his own greatness. The same must be said of God’s goodness, eternity, and omnipotence, and indeed of all things which can be predicated of God substantially, by which he is spoken of absolutely—not figuratively or by likeness, but properly—if indeed anything can properly be said of him by a human mouth.

Behold, he has plainly taught that names signifying the unity of divine majesty are said absolutely of God, that is, without relation; that they are said commonly of all persons and severally of each; and that in their totality they are understood not plurally but singly. But those names which properly pertain to the individual persons are said relatively, not substantially. For, as Augustine says in the same work, whatever is properly said of an individual person in the Trinity is in no way said absolutely, but reciprocally in relation to another person or in relation to creation. It is therefore clear that such names are said relatively, not substantially.

## DISTINCTION XXIII. CONCERNING THE NAME “PERSON,” WHICH, ALTHOUGH SAID ACCORDING TO SUBSTANCE, IS NEVERTHELESS UNDERSTOOD IN THE TOTALITY PLURALLY, NOT SINGLY.

1.
