To the foregoing must be added that, although all names said of God according to substance are said of all the persons in their totality singly and not plurally, as was shown above, there is nevertheless one name—namely, *person*—which is said according to substance of the individual persons and is understood in their totality plurally, not singly. For we say: “The Father is a person,” “The Son is a person,” “The Holy Spirit is a person”; and this is said according to substance. Yet it is not said: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person,” but “three persons.” Thus this name is excepted from the aforesaid rule governing names said of God according to substance; for although it is said absolutely and according to substance, it is nevertheless understood in the totality plurally, not singly.

Authority that *person* is said absolutely and according to substance.

2. That *person* is said according to substance, Augustine shows in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, saying in chapter 6: “For God, to be is not one thing and to be a person another, but they are altogether the same.” Again: “In this Trinity, when we speak of the person of the Father, we say nothing other than the substance of the Father. Therefore, just as the substance of the Father is the Father himself—not by that whereby he is Father, but by that whereby he is—so the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself. For person is said absolutely, not in relation to the Son or Holy Spirit, just as God, great, good, just, and the like are said absolutely. And just as for him to be is identical with being God, great, and good, so for him to be is identical with being a person.”

Here you have expressly that *person* is said according to substance, so that when it is said, “The Father is a person,” the meaning is, “The Father is the divine essence.” Likewise, when it is said, “The Son is a person,” or “The Holy Spirit is a person,” it means: the divine essence.

Why Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not called one person, as they are one substance and one God.

3. From this arises a difficult, though not useless, question: why these three are not called one person, just as they are one essence and one God. Augustine carefully treats and suitably explains this question in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, saying thus in chapter 6:

> Why do we not call these three together one person, as we call them one essence and one God, but call them three persons, although we do not call them three gods or three essences? Because we wish to preserve at least one term for that signification by which the Trinity is understood, lest, when asked what the three are, we remain altogether silent, though we confess that they are three. Therefore, when it is asked what three, as Augustine says in Book 5 *On the Trinity*, chapter 9, human speech labors under a truly great poverty. Yet “three persons” has been said, not in order to express the matter, but lest we be altogether silent. For the excellence of the ineffable reality cannot be explained by this term.

Here he shows why *persons* is said in the plural: namely, so that by this one name we may answer those who ask about the three.

Why the Latins have said “three persons,” and the Greeks “three hypostases” or “substances.”

4. By this necessity not only Latin speech, but Greek also, suffering almost the same poverty of terms in this matter, is constrained. Hence Augustine, explaining what Greeks and Latins have said by necessity about the ineffable Trinity, says in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 4:

> For the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some manner be able to speak, the Greeks have said: one essence, three substances—that is, one *ousia*, three hypostases. For Greeks understand “substance” differently from Latins. Latins, however, have said: one essence or substance, three persons, because in our language, that is, Latin, essence is ordinarily understood no differently from substance. And so that it might be understood at least in a riddle, it pleased them to speak thus, so that when it was asked what the three are, something might be said—those three which true faith declares to be three, since it does not say that the Father is the Son and the Holy Spirit, namely the gift of God; nor does it say that the Holy Spirit is either Father or Son. Therefore, when we ask what the three—or what the three persons—are, we strive to find some name that may encompass these three. But none comes to mind, because the surpassing eminence of the Godhead exceeds the capacity of ordinary speech. For God is thought more truly than he is spoken, and he exists more truly than he is thought.

What is signified by the expression “three.”

5. Since, therefore, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three, let us ask what three they are and what they have in common. They cannot be called three fathers, because only the Father there is Father; nor three sons, since neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit is Son; nor three Holy Spirits, because the Holy Spirit, in the proper meaning by which he is called the gift of God, is neither Father nor Son. What, then, are the three? If they are called three persons, that which is person is common to them. Certainly, because the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Holy Spirit is a person, they are called three persons. We therefore say three persons because that which is person is common to them. From the foregoing it can plainly be understood by what necessity the Latins have said “three persons,” although *person* is said according to substance. Hence that which is person—that is, this name *person*—is common to the three.

Why we do not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods, as we say three persons, although that which is God is common to them, because the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.

6. But here one asks: since we say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons because that which is person is common to them—that is, because the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Holy Spirit is a person—why do we not likewise say three gods, since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God? Namely, because Scripture contradicts the latter, whereas it does not state the former but neither does it contradict it. Hence Augustine, raising and resolving this question, says in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 4:

> If we say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons because that which is person is common to them, why do we not also say three gods? Certainly, as was said above, because the Father is a person, the Son a person, and the Holy Spirit a person, they are called three persons. Since, then, the Father is God, the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God, why are they not called three gods?

He has raised this question; attend to his answer, which follows:

> Is it because they are not called three gods since Scripture does not say “three gods”? But neither does any text of Scripture mention three persons. Is it because the necessity of speaking and disputing has allowed us to say three persons—not because Scripture says it, but because Scripture does not contradict it? But if we were to say three gods, Scripture would contradict us, saying in Deuteronomy 6: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

Behold the resolution of the question why we say three persons rather than three gods: namely, because Scripture does not contradict the former.

Another question: why we do not say three essences, as we say three persons, although Scripture does not contradict it.

7. Yet another question arises here, which Augustine immediately adds, saying in the same book and chapter:

> Why is it not permissible to say three essences, when Scripture, just as it does not say this, likewise does not contradict it? But if you say that, because of the unity of the Trinity, three essences are not said but one essence, I ask why, because of the same unity of the Trinity, one person is not said rather than three persons. For just as the name essence is common to them, so that each one individually is called essence, so the term person is common to them. What remains, then, except that we confess that these terms were produced by Greeks and Latins out of the necessity of speech, against the snares or errors of heretics? When human poverty tried by speaking to bring before human minds what it holds about God in the inward chamber of the mind, whether through devout faith or through any understanding whatever, it feared to say three essences, lest some diversity be understood in that supreme equality. Again, it could not say that there were not three somewhats; for because Sabellius said this, he fell into heresy. Therefore it sought what it might call the three, and said three persons, or, according to the Greeks, three substances.

Just as we say three persons, so Greeks say three substances, which they call hypostases, understanding substance differently from us.

8. For what must be understood concerning persons according to our usage must be understood concerning substances according to Greek usage. Thus they say three substances, one essence—that is, three hypostases, one *ousia*—just as we say three persons, one essence or substance. Yet they too, if they wished, just as they say three substances, three hypostases, could say three persons, three *prosōpa* (πρόσωπα). But they preferred that expression because perhaps it is more fitting according to the usage of their language.

That in the Trinity there is neither diversity nor singularity or solitude, but unity, Trinity, distinction, and identity.

9. Now, I think, it has been sufficiently shown why we say three persons, and why we do not likewise say three gods or essences: because in the one case Scripture stands in the way, and in the other the notion of diversity; for there is absolutely no diversity there, just as there is no singularity or solitude, but unity and Trinity. Hence Augustine, in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, says:

> Human poverty, seeking what it might call the three, said three persons or substances. By these names it did not intend diversity to be understood, but it refused singularity; so that not only unity might be understood there from the expression “one essence,” but also Trinity from the expression “three persons.”

Hilary likewise, in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, near the end, says:

> The Lord says in John 4: “He who sees me sees the Father also.” When this is said, singularity and the notion of one alone—that is, of a solitary being—are excluded. For the statement signifies neither a solitary being, while the confession nevertheless teaches an undifferentiated nature. For the Father was seen in the Son through the unified likeness of nature. The begotten and the begetter are one; they are one, yet not one [person]. Therefore the Son is neither solitary, nor singular, nor unlike.

Again, in the same work:

> Just as it is impious to believe in two gods in the Father and Son, so it is sacrilegious to proclaim the Father and Son as a singular God. There is nothing new in them, nothing diverse, nothing alien, nothing separable.

Augustine also says, in the *Book of Questions on the Old and New Law*, tome 4, question 122, Book 5, chapter 2, near the end: “God is one, but not singular.” Likewise Ambrose, in *On the Faith*, says: “What is of one substance cannot be separated; and since God is not a God of singularity but of unity, when he is called one, the Trinity of the Godhead is by no means excluded. Therefore he is proclaimed as one not by reason of singularity, but by reason of unity.”

From the foregoing it is shown that God must be confessed neither as singular, nor diverse, nor unique, nor solitary, [Col. 0586] because singularity or solitude excludes the plurality of persons, while diversity removes unity of essence. Diversity introduces a separation in the Godhead; singularity takes away the distinction of the Trinity. Therefore Ambrose, in Book 2 *On the Faith*, chapter 2, says: “The equality is neither diverse nor singular: it neither confounds Father and Son, as the Sabellians do, nor separates Father and Son, as the Arians do. For Father and Son have distinction, but not separation.” Again in the same work: “Father and Son are one in Godhead; there is no difference of substance there, nor any diversity. Otherwise, how could we call God one? For diversity makes many.”

It is therefore clear from the foregoing that there is no diversity in the Trinity. If, however, one sometimes finds in Scripture the expression “three diverse persons,” or the like, “diverse” means distinct.

That God ought not to be called multiple.

10. And just as there is no diversity in the Trinity, so neither is there multiplicity. Therefore God should not be called multiple, but triune and simple. Hence Ambrose, in Book 1 *On the Faith*, chapter 2, says: “In Father and Son there is one Godhead, not discordant; and what is one is not confused, nor can what is undifferentiated be multiple. Therefore God is not multiple.”

## DISTINCTION XXIV. WHAT IS SIGNIFIED BY THE TERMS “ONE” OR “A,” “TWO,” “THREE,” “TRIUNE” OR “TRINITY,” “MANY” OR “PLURALITY,” “DISTINCTION” OR “DISTINCT,” WHEN WE USE THEM IN SPEAKING OF GOD.

1. Here we must carefully inquire, since there is neither diversity nor singularity, neither multiplicity nor solitude in the Trinity, what is signified by the terms one or a, two, three, triune or Trinity, many or plurality, distinct or distinction, when one says “one God,” “two persons,” “three persons,” “many persons,” “the persons are distinct,” or “a distinction of persons,” “a plurality of persons,” “a trinity of persons,” and the like. For in saying this we seem to posit in God quantities of number and a multitude or multiplicity of things. Let us therefore endeavor to indicate what these signify there, with the one of whom we speak himself disclosing it.

These terms are said more to exclude what is not in God than to posit something.

2. If we attend carefully to the words of the authorities set forth above, in order to grasp the meaning of what has been said, the use of these terms seems to have been introduced more in order to remove and exclude from the simplicity of the Godhead things which are not there than in order to posit anything.

What is signified by “one” when “one God” is said.

3. For when “one God” is said, a multitude of gods is excluded; no quantity of number is posited in the Godhead. It is as if one said: “God exists, and there are not many or several gods.” Hence Ambrose, in Book 1 *On the Faith*, chapter 2, says: “When we say one God, unity excludes the number of gods; nor does it posit quantity in God, because neither number nor quantity is there.”

In what sense it is said: “One is the Father,” or “one is the Son.”

4. Likewise, when it is said, “One is the Father,” or “One is the Son,” and the like, the meaning is that there are not many fathers or many sons; and so also in similar cases. Again, when we say that there are many persons, we exclude singularity and solitude; we do not posit diversity or multiplicity there. It is as if one said: “We confess persons without solitude or singularity.” Hence Hilary, in Book 4 *On the Trinity*, says:

> God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” I ask now whether you suppose that God spoke to himself alone, or whether you understand this speech to have been addressed to another. If you say that he was alone, you are refuted by his own words, when he says “Let us make” and “our.” For the profession of companionship removes the notion of singularity and solitude, because there can be no companionship for one who is solitary; nor does the solitude of one who is alone admit “Let us make”; nor would he say “our” to one alien to himself.

Observe, reader, these words, and see that by the term *companionship* he signified plurality; the profession of companionship, therefore, is a profession of plurality, which he made by saying “Let us make” and “our,” for both are said in the plural. Yet by this profession of plurality he did not posit diversity or multitude, but denied solitude and singularity. Thus, when we say many persons or a plurality of persons, we exclude the notion of singularity and solitude.

What is signified by the number three when three persons are said.

5. Likewise, when we say three persons, by the term denoting three we do not posit a numerical quantity in God or any diversity, but signify that understanding must be directed to none other than Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus the meaning of the statement “There are three persons,” or “They are three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit”—is this: not the Father alone, not the Son alone, nor the Father and Son alone are in the Godhead, but the Holy Spirit also, and no one other than these. Similarly, not merely this person, or that person, or this and that person, is there, but this and that and that person, and no other. Augustine appears sufficiently to indicate that this is perhaps the proper understanding when he says that by that term he did not intend diversity, but rejected singularity.

What is meant by “two,” when “two persons” is said, or “the Father and Son are two.”

6. Likewise, when it is said, “The Father and Son are two,” we do not posit there a quantity of duality, but signify that there is not the Father alone nor the Son alone, but Father and Son, and this one is not that one; and so also in other such cases. Likewise, when we say, “The Father and Son are two persons,” we signify that not the Father alone is a person, nor the Son alone a person, but the Father is a person and the Son is a person, and this person is not that person.

In what sense distinction in the persons, or distinct persons, is said.

7. When, however, we say “distinct persons,” or “there is distinction in the persons,” we exclude confusion and commingling and signify that this one is not that one. When we add, “The persons are distinct in their properties,” or “differ in their properties,” we signify that this person and that person are different by their respective properties. And when we say “one and another,” we do not posit diversity or alienation there, but exclude Sabellian confusion.

How distinction is understood there.

8. Likewise, when persons are called discrete, or when there is said to be discreteness among the persons, we mean the same thing. For *discreteness* is understood there in the same way as *distinction*. It is fitting to say that there is discreteness or distinction there, but not diversity, division, or separation. Hence Ambrose, in Book 1 *On the Trinity*, says: “The Father is not himself the Son, but there is an explicit distinction between Father and Son.”

How Trinity is understood there.

9. When Trinity is said, it appears that the same thing is signified as when three persons are said. Thus, just as it cannot be said, “The Father is three persons,” or “The Son is three persons,” so it ought not to be said, “The Father is the Trinity,” or “The Son is the Trinity.”

This seems contrary to the foregoing.

10. We must not omit that, although it was said above that God must be confessed neither singular nor multiple, and this was confirmed by the authorities of the saints, Isidore seems to hold the contrary view when he says: “A distinction must be made between Trinity and unity. Unity is simple and singular, but Trinity is multiple and numerable, because Trinity is the unity of three.” Behold, he calls unity singular and Trinity multiple and numerable. To this we reply that he understood *singular* as others understand *one*, and *multiple* and *numerable* as others say *triune*.

## DISTINCTION XXV. WHAT IS SIGNIFIED WHEN “THREE PERSONS” OR “TWO PERSONS” IS SAID IN THE PLURAL.

1. Furthermore, we must consider, since the name *person*, as stated above, is said according to substance, what is meant when it is used in the plural—“three persons” or “two persons”—and when it is said, “The person of the Father is one, the person of the Son another, and the person of the Holy Spirit another.” For if in these expressions the term *person* conveys the meaning of essence, we appear to confess several essences and therefore several gods. But if it does not bear the meaning of essence there, then this name has one meaning when it is said, “The Father is a person,” or “The Son is a person,” and another when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” or “The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another,” and the like.

That “the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another,” or “three persons,” seems to be said according to essence, just as when it is said “the Father is a person,” “the Son is a person.”

2. For, as Augustine said above, *person* is said absolutely, and for God to be a person is identical with being, just as for him to be is identical with being God. It is therefore clearly inferred that we predicate the divine essence when we say: “The Father is a person,” “The Son is a person,” “The Holy Spirit is a person”—that is, the divine essence. And altogether one and the same thing is signified by the name *person*, namely the divine essence, when it is said, “The Father is a person,” and “The Son is a person,” as is signified by the name God when it is said, “The Father is God,” “The Son is God.” Likewise, the same thing is signified when it is said, “God is God,” and “God is a person.” For by each name the divine essence is understood, because each is said according to substance.

But when it is said, “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” what do we signify by the name *person*? Essence? This seems so if we examine carefully Augustine’s words quoted above. For he said above that we say three persons because that which is person is common to the three; and again, because the Father is a person, the Son a person, and the Holy Spirit a person, they are called three persons. Therefore, the name *person* seems to retain the same meaning when “three persons” is said as it has when it is said, “The Father is a person,” “The Son is a person,” and “The Holy Spirit is a person.” For, as Augustine shows, “three persons” is said because that which is person is common to them. Therefore that which is common to them—that is, to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—appears to be signified by the name *person* when “three persons” is said.

It also seems possible to show in another way that it is said according to essence even when used in the plural.

3. It also seems possible to show in another way that by the name *person* essence is signified when “three persons” is said. For, as Augustine said above, we say three persons by necessity, so as to answer those asking “What three?” or “What three things?” Therefore, when it is asked “What three?” or “What three things?” the reply “three persons” is appropriate. But when it is asked “What three?” or “What three things?” the question is asked through *what* concerning essence. For what those three are cannot be found except as essence. Therefore, if we answer the question correctly, in answering we must signify essence; otherwise we shall not show what the three are. But if in answering we signify essence, then we understand essence itself by the name *person* when “three persons” is said.

The opinion of some who think that essence is signified by the name *person* when we say three persons.

4. Some think that essence is signified by the name *person* when “three persons” is said, because Augustine says in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, that three persons are said because that which is person is common to them. Thus they understand the statement in this way: “The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons,” that is, they are three who have in common that which is person; that is, they are three, each of whom is a person, that is, an essence. But how, according to this understanding, will it be said: “The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another”? They likewise wish to understand this as meaning that the Father is one, the Son another, while having in common that which is person.

They confirm this with Augustine’s authority, who says in Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 1: “We say three persons of the same essence, or three persons, one essence; but we do not say three persons from the same essence,” as though essence were one thing there and person another. By this authority and by the preceding arguments they attempt to establish that in the aforesaid expressions the name *person* signifies essence.

But what will they answer to what Augustine himself says in *On Faith to Peter*: namely, that the Father is other in person, or personally; the Son other personally; and the Holy Spirit other personally? For how is the Father other personally, the Son other personally, and the Holy Spirit other personally, if they are altogether alike in being a person—that is, if *person* conveys only the meaning of essence? We therefore think that this can more fittingly be explained otherwise, according to the authorities of Catholic doctors.

That the name *person* is understood in the Trinity in three ways; and this is a useful and Catholic teaching concerning person and persons.

5. We must know, then, that the name *person* conveys several meanings, not merely one. And, as Hilary says in the middle of Book 4 *On the Trinity*: “The meaning of utterances must be taken from the reasons for speaking them, because the thing is not subject to speech, but speech to the thing.” Therefore, distinguishing the reasons for using this name, *person*, we distinguish its meaning. We say that this name, *person*, is properly said according to substance and signifies essence, as Augustine showed above in Distinction 23, when it is said: “God is a person,” “The Father is a person.”

Yet by a certain necessity, as Augustine said above, this name was transferred so as to be said plurally, “three persons,” when the question was asked, “What three?” or “What three things?” There it does not signify essence—that is, the divine nature common to the three persons—but substances or hypostases according to the Greeks. For the Greeks, as Augustine says above (in the same passage, that is, Book 7 *On the Trinity*, chapter 4), understand *substance*, that is, hypostasis, differently from us. We call essence or nature “substance”; but we call persons what they call substances, that is, hypostases. Thus we understand persons as they understand substances or hypostases; but they understand hypostases differently from the way we understand substance. Therefore, we understand persons differently from substance. When, therefore, we say three persons, we do not signify essence by the name *person*. What, then, do we mean by three persons? We mean that there are three persons, that is, three substances—namely, three beings—for which the Greeks say three hypostases.

He shows that Augustine’s words agree with this view.

6. This interpretation is supported by Augustine’s foregoing words if they are understood more deeply. Because the Father is a person, that is, essence; and the Son a person; and the Holy Spirit a person; therefore they are called three persons, three substances, three beings. For they could not be called three substances or beings unless each one of them were a person, that is, an essence. Therefore, because that which is person, namely essence, is common to them, they are rightly called three persons, that is, subsistences or subsisting beings; so that, by reason of the essence which is common to them, they may truly and properly be understood as subsistences or beings.

Therefore Augustine, distinguishing the reasons for the expressions, says that three persons are one essence or are of the same essence, but not from one essence, lest person be understood there as one thing and essence another. For three persons—that is, substances—are one essence and of one essence, but they are not one person or of one person, although *person* is sometimes said according to substance. For if this were said, confusion would arise among the persons.

Here he responds to their objection, by which they endeavor to prove that persons are understood according to essence, because we answer “three persons” to those asking “What three?” or “What three things?”

7. To their claim that, when “What three?” or “What three things?” is asked, essence is being asked about because what those three are cannot be found except as essence—and thus they wish to induce us to understand essence by the name *person* when we answer “three persons”—we reply as follows. It is unquestionably true that no one thing can be found which those three are except essence. For those three are one, that is, the divine essence; hence Truth says in John 10: “I and the Father are one.” Nevertheless, when “What three?” or “What three things?” is asked, the question is not asked concerning essence, nor does *what* there refer to essence.

Rather, since the Catholic faith professed that there are three, as John says in the First Catholic Epistle, chapter 5: “There are three who bear witness in heaven,” the question was asked what those three were: that is, whether they were three things, what three things they were, and by what name those three things might be signified. Therefore, through necessity of speech, the name *person* was devised as an answer, and “three persons” was said.

### What Is Meant Here by “Three Things” and “One Thing”

**8.** Nor should it disturb you that we speak of “three things.” In saying this, we do not posit a number of different things in the Trinity; rather, we call them three things in such a way as to confess that they are the same one supreme thing. Hence Augustine, in Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 3, volume 3, says:

> The things to be enjoyed make us blessed; therefore the things to be enjoyed are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And this same Trinity is one certain supreme thing, common to those who enjoy it—if indeed it is a thing and not rather the cause of all things. For a name suitable to so great an excellence can hardly be found, except that this Trinity is better called one God.

Therefore, just as three things are spoken of, and these are one thing, so three subsistences are spoken of, and these are one essence. Behold, it has been shown what is meant by the name “person” when we say “three persons.”

### In What Sense It Is Said: “The Person of the Father Is One, That of the Son Another, That of the Holy Spirit Another”

**9.** Let us now consider whether the statement, “The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, that of the Holy Spirit another,” is made according to the same principle and reason. This can certainly be understood correctly in the following sense: the subsistence or hypostasis of the Father is one, the subsistence of the Son another, and the subsistence of the Holy Spirit another; and: the Father is one subsistence, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another.

### How These Statements Are to Be Understood: the Father Is One in Person, the Son Another, and the Holy Spirit Another

**10.** Next, it is asked whether the following is understood according to the same principle: “The Father is one in person; the Son another in person; the Holy Spirit another in person”; or, “The Father is one personally, the Son another personally, the Holy Spirit another personally.” We answer that, although it can be understood in the same way, yet the wording more fittingly gives it a different sense: here, by the name “person,” the property of the person is understood. The meaning is thus: the Father is one in person, or personally—that is, by His own property the Father is other than the Son, and by His own property the Son is other than the Father. For the hypostasis of the Father is distinguished from the hypostasis of the Son by the paternal property; and the hypostasis of the Son is differentiated from the Father by the filial property; while the Holy Spirit is distinguished from both by the property of procession.

### How, in This Sense, the Same May Be Understood in the Statements Above

**11.** In the preceding statements “person” may also rightly be understood in this sense when it is said: “The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another”—that is, the property by which the Father is Father is one, that by which the Son is Son another, and that by which the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit another. Thus some also wish to understand “property” by the name “person” when three persons are spoken of. But it is better, when we say “three persons,” to understand subsistences or hypostases. From what has been said, it follows that the name “person” has a threefold meaning in the Trinity. In one usage it conveys the meaning of essence; in another, that of hypostasis; and in another, that of property.

### He Shows by Authorities of the Saints What He Has Said

**12.** We have clearly shown above, from Augustine’s statements, that “person” is sometimes said according to substance and signifies essence. But it must be shown from the authorities of the saints that it is also understood as hypostasis and as property, lest we seem to have ventured to say something on the basis of our own conjectures [Col. 0591].

On this subject Jerome, in his *Exposition of the Catholic Faith* addressed to Damasus, says:

> There is absolutely no rank in the Trinity, nor anything which can be called lower or higher; but the whole Godhead is equal in the perfection of itself, so that, apart from those terms which indicate the property of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most worthily be understood of all three. And just as, refuting Arius, we say that the Trinity has one and the same essence or substance, and confess one God in three persons; so also, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons marked by their properties. We do not say that the Father is Himself His own Father, the Son Himself His own Son, or the Holy Spirit Himself His own Holy Spirit; rather, the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. For we confess not merely the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons—or, as the Greeks express it, the hypostases, that is, the subsistences. Nor does the Father ever assume the person of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, nor does the Son or the Holy Spirit receive the name and person of the Father; but the Father is always Father, the Son always Son, and the Holy Spirit always Holy Spirit. Thus they are one in substance, but distinguished in persons and names.

Here Jerome plainly says that properties are persons, and persons are substances. Hence what we have said becomes evident: namely, that by the name “person” both hypostasis and property are signified. John Damascene likewise says that persons are hypostases, and calls them real beings, saying in Book 1 of *On the Orthodox Faith*:

> In the Godhead we confess one nature and three hypostases truly existing—that is, persons.

## DISTINCTION XXVI. ON THE PROPERTIES OF THE PERSONS; BUT FIRST ON THE TERM “HYPOSTASIS”

**1.** We must now say something concerning the properties of the persons, which we have frequently mentioned in this treatise. But first let us hear what Jerome says concerning the term *hypostasis*. He says that poison lies hidden under this name; but he says this insofar as heretics used it to deceive the simple, namely, both for person and for essence. Thus, whether one hypostasis only or three were said, they might lead the less learned into error, since this term was not then so widely current among Catholics, nor was its meaning so fixed as it is now.

Therefore Jerome says that this term should not then be used without distinction or explanation—that is, at the time when controversy was being conducted with heretics. Thus he writes on the Catholic faith to Pope Damasus:

> The leader of the Arians demands of me, a Roman, the novel term *hypostasis*. We ask what they think is meant by three hypostases. They say: three subsistent persons. We answer that this is what we believe. The meaning does not suffice them; they demand the very word itself, because I know not what poison lies hidden in its syllables. We cry aloud: if anyone does not confess three hypostases, that is, three subsistent persons, let him be anathema. But if anyone, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*—that is, essence—does not ascribe one hypostasis to the three persons, he is alien from Christ; for, in speaking of three hypostases, he attempts under the name of piety to maintain three natures. Let it suffice us to say one substance and three perfect, equal persons; let us be silent about hypostases, if you please. This name is not free from suspicion when meanings differ in the same word. Or, if you think it proper that we should say three hypostases together with their explanations, we do not deny it. But believe me: poison lies beneath honey. For Satan transforms himself into an angel of light. 2 Corinthians 11.

By these words he does not deny that the term *hypostasis* may be used; rather, he shows that heretics had misused it. Against them caution was needed in distinguishing its meaning. Otherwise he would contradict himself, since above he confesses three hypostases.

### On the Properties of the Persons and Their Relative Names

**2.** Let us now consider the properties of the persons, which in Scripture are also usually called notions or relations [Col. 0592], in that holy Trinity. We repeat this subject so that it may be more firmly impressed upon our heart.

Augustine says at the end of chapter 10 of his book *On Faith, to Peter*:

> To beget is one thing; to be born is another; and to proceed is another than to beget or to be born. Hence it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. It is proper to the Father alone, not merely that He Himself is not born, but that He has begotten one Son; proper to the Son alone, not merely that He Himself has not begotten, but that He is born from the essence of the Father; and proper to the Holy Spirit, not merely that He Himself is neither born nor begets, but that He alone proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Here he briefly assigns the three properties of the three persons, of which one is not another. For this is what he signified when he said: “To beget is one thing; to be born another; and to proceed another.” That is, generation is one property or notion, birth another, and procession another; these are called by other names paternity and filiation. The names of the persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—designate these properties. They are relative names and are said in relation to one another, because they denote relations which are not accidental to God, but exist eternally and immutably in the persons themselves. Thus not only are the titles relative, but the relations or notions themselves exist in the realities themselves, namely, in the persons.

### Not Everything Said of God Is Said according to Substance; Some Things Are Said according to Relation, Yet Nothing according to Accident

**3.** It should therefore be known that not everything said of God is said according to substance, since some things are said according to relation. Relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable. Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> Nothing is said of God according to accident, because nothing happens to Him. Yet not everything that is said of God is said according to substance.

And in chapter 4 of the same book:

> In created and mutable things, whatever is not said according to substance remains to be said according to accident. But in God nothing at all is said according to accident, because nothing in Him is mutable or liable to be lost. Yet not everything said of God is said according to substance; for something is said in relation to something else, as Father in relation to Son and Son in relation to Father. This is not an accident, because the one is always Father and the other always Son—and always so, because the Son has always been begotten and never began to be Son. If He had at some time begun to be, or at some time ceased to be, Son, He would be so called according to accident. And because the Father is not called Father except because He has a Son, and the Son is not called Son except because He has a Father, these things are not said according to substance but in relation to one another. Yet they are not said according to accident, because both being called Father and being called Son are eternal and immutable for them.

These words plainly show that some things are said of God according to substance, others according to relation, yet nothing according to accident. They also show that the Father’s property is that He has a Son, and the Son’s property that He has a Father. Therefore, when Augustine says that being called Father and being called Son are eternal and immutable, he means that the property by which the Father is Father and the property by which the Son is Son are eternal and immutable, because the Father is always Father and the Son always Son.

Hence Hilary, assigning the properties of the persons, says in the middle of Book 12 of *On the Trinity*:

> If it is always proper to the Father that He is always Father, it must always be proper to the Son that He is always Son. For where there is always a Father, there is always also a Son; therefore, one who is not always Father has not always begotten.

And again in the same book, a little before the middle:

> In the case of God born, it is manifest that being Son is proper to Him.

### Why It Is Said to Be Proper to the Only-Begotten That He Is God’s Son, Although Human Beings Also Are Sons of God

**4.** Here it is asked how being the Son of God, or begotten from God, is said to be proper to God born, since human beings too are called and are sons of God, according to Psalm 81: “You are all sons of the Most High.” And concerning the people of Israel the Lord says to Moses in Exodus 4: “Israel is my firstborn son” [Col. 0593].

But the difference is great. Human beings are sons of God by creation, not by the property of birth. But God the Son is Son by the property of origin and by the reality of birth, not by creation or adoption. Moreover, human beings exist before they are sons of God: they become sons of God; they are not born sons of God.

Hence Hilary, showing that God alone who is born is the Son of God by the property of origin, and distinguishing Him most clearly from human beings who are sons of God, says in Book 22 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the beginning:

> To the true Father, He alone who is born from Him is truly Son; and we indeed are sons of God, but by creation. For we were once children of wrath, Ephesians 2; but we have been made sons of God by adoption rather than being born as such. And because everything which comes to be did not exist before it came to be, we, who were not sons, are made so. Previously we were not sons, but through grace we were made so: not born nor begotten, but acquired. God acquired us for Himself, and in this sense is said to have begotten us. For we never find God’s begetting sons stated with the meaning of a proper property. A human being is made a son of God by adoption, not by generation; and this is not a property but a designation. Consequently, he is not truly a son, because he is neither said to be properly born nor has he always been a son. But the only-begotten God was never at any time not Son; He was not something before being Son; nor is He anything other than Son. Therefore He who is always Son is Son, by the property and reality of birth, of Him alone who begot Him; and He alone who begot Him is His Father, because just as the former is Son by origin, so the latter is Father by generation.

### That Man Is Called a Son of the Trinity, and the Trinity May Be Called the Father of Human Beings

**5.** But the human being who is a son of God by creation is the son not of the Father alone, but also of the Son and of the Holy Spirit—that is, of the entire Trinity. The Trinity itself may be called his Father.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11:

> The Trinity cannot be called Father, except perhaps figuratively in relation to the creature, because of the adoption of sons. For what is written, Deuteronomy 6, “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God,” must certainly not be understood as excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit. We rightly call this one Lord our God also our Father, who regenerates us by His grace.

Hilary likewise says in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, a little after the middle:

> God is Father to all through faith—to those to whom He is Father through that faith by which we confess Jesus Christ to be the Son of God.

It has thus been shown why being Son is said to be proper to God who is born: namely, because He alone is properly said to be born. Hence Hilary says in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the beginning:

> When the Lord says, John 17, “Glorify your Son,” He testifies that He is Son not by name alone, but also by property. We are sons of God, but this Son is not such a son. For He is true and proper Son by origin, not adoption; by reality, not designation; by birth, not creation.

### That the Holy Spirit Is Properly Called the Gift of God, Because He Is Gift by Property, as the Son Is Son by Birth; and That in Both Ways He Is Said Relatively and according to the Same Relation

**6.** The same must be said of the Holy Spirit, who is properly called the gift of God, although there are many other gifts of God. But the Holy Spirit is gift by an immutable and eternal property, just as the Son is Son by property. He is called gift in the same respect in which He is called Holy Spirit; and by each name He is certainly said relatively. “Holy Spirit” and “gift” are said according to the same relation, although that relation is not as evident in the name “Holy Spirit” as in the name “gift.”

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11:

> The Holy Spirit, who is not the Trinity but is understood to be in the Trinity, is said relatively insofar as He is properly called Holy Spirit, when He is referred to the Father and the Son; for He is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, though the relation itself does not appear in this name. But it appears when He is called the gift of God. For He is the gift of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and from the Son. Therefore the Holy Spirit is a certain ineffable communion of the Father and the Son [Col. 0594]. And perhaps for this reason He is so called, as we have already said—and it is no burden to repeat it—because the same designation can apply to the Father and the Son. For He is properly what they are in common: the Father too is spirit, and the Son too is spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy. Therefore, so that the communion of both may be signified by a name applicable to each, the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of both, is so called.

Here you have why the Holy Spirit is properly called gift; that both “gift” and “Holy Spirit” are said relatively; and that He bears as His proper name one which belongs commonly to the Father and the Son, though separately. It must be known that when the Father or Son is called spirit or holy, neither term is said relatively, but according to substance.

### Whether the Father, the Son, or the Trinity Itself May Be Called Holy Spirit

**7.** Here one may ask whether the Father, the Son, or the Trinity itself can be called Holy Spirit, just as each separately is called spirit and holy. On this Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11:

> The Trinity can in no way be called Son. But it can indeed universally be called Holy Spirit, according to what is written in John 4: “God is spirit.” Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, since they are one God, and since God is certainly holy and God is spirit, can be called both Trinity and Holy Spirit. Yet in that case “Holy Spirit” is not said relatively but according to essence, because the Holy Spirit properly so called—who is not the Trinity but is in the Trinity—is said relatively.

### Some Think That the Holy Spirit Is Not Said Relatively to the Father and the Son Because the Terms Do Not Reciprocally Correspond; but They Are Wrong

**8.** Some nevertheless think that “Holy Spirit” or “gift” is not said relatively to the Father or the Son. For, they say, if these terms are said relatively to each other, their respective terms should correspond reciprocally: just as the Father is called Father of the Son and the Son is called Son of the Father, so the Father should be called Father of the Holy Spirit or of the gift, and the Holy Spirit or gift should be called Spirit or gift of the Father.

But this is not so with all relatives. Not all things said relatively have terms that reciprocally correspond to each other. Hence Augustine, refuting their opinion, says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12:

> Do not be troubled because we said that the Holy Spirit—not the Trinity itself, but He who is in the Trinity—is said relatively, although the name of that to which He is referred does not correspond to Him reciprocally. For we call Him the Spirit of the Father, but we do not in turn call the Father the Father of the Holy Spirit, lest the Holy Spirit be understood as His Son. Likewise we call Him the Spirit of the Son, but we do not call the Son the Son of the Holy Spirit, lest the Holy Spirit be understood as His Father. For this occurs in many relative terms: a word cannot be found that reciprocally corresponds to them. Thus, when we call Him the gift of the Father and the Son, we cannot call the Father the father of the gift or the Son the son of the gift. But, so that the terms may answer one another reciprocally, we call Him the gift of the giver and the giver of the gift, because in this case a customary term could be found, whereas in the other case it could not. Therefore, when we say “gift of the giver” and “giver of the gift,” we say both terms relatively and reciprocally. Yet God was not a giver except in time, although the Holy Spirit is gift and is so from eternity.

## DISTINCTION XXVII. WHETHER AUGUSTINE AND HILARY ASSIGN THE SAME PROPERTIES; AND WHETHER THESE ARE WHAT ARE CALLED PATERNITY, FILIATION, AND PROCESSION

**1.** Here it may be asked whether the properties assigned above by Hilary—namely, that the Father is always Father and the Son always Son—are the same properties that Augustine distinguished above when he said that it is proper to the Father that He begot the Son, proper to the Son that He was begotten by the Father, and proper to the Holy Spirit that He proceeds from both. Further, it may be asked whether these are the same as those called paternity, filiation, and procession.

It seems that the properties set forth by Hilary are not the same as those set forth by Augustine. For if they are the same, then for the Father to be Father and to have begotten the Son are the same [Col. 0595]—a point which some indeed concede. But if this is so, then whoever is a father has begotten a son. Therefore, if the divine nature is Father, it has begotten a Son; but if it has not begotten, it is not Father. Yet who would dare say either that the divine nature itself begot the Son or that it is not itself Father? But if it is itself Father and has not begotten the Son, then to say that something is Father and to say that it begets a son are not the same. Thus the property cannot appear to be one and the same.

### Answer, Showing That They Are the Same Properties

**2.** Without prejudice to others, we answer that each author has indicated the same properties, though in different words. What Hilary says must be understood thus: “It is proper to the Father that He is always Father,” that is, the Father’s property is that by which He is always Father. But He is always Father because He has always begotten the Son. Likewise, it is proper to the Son that He is always Son, that is, the Son’s property is that by which He is always Son. But the Son is always Son because He has always been begotten. Therefore the property by which the Father is Father is that He has always begotten; and this same property is called paternity or generation. The property by which the Son is always Son is that He has always been begotten by the Father; and this same property is called filiation, begetting, birth, or capacity for birth. Likewise, the property by which the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit or gift is that He proceeds from both; and this same property is called procession. Thus the same properties have been signified in the foregoing statements.

### How It Is Not Entirely the Same to Say That Something Is Father and That It Has Begotten or Has a Son; and Similarly of the Others

**3.** Nevertheless, it does not seem to us altogether the same to say that something is Father and that it has begotten the Son; or that something is Son and that it has a Father; or that it is Holy Spirit and that it proceeds from both. Otherwise Father would not be a name of hypostasis—that is, of person—but only of property; and likewise Son and Holy Spirit. Then the three persons would not be signified by the three names.

Therefore we say that the name Father not only denotes relation, but also signifies hypostasis—that is, subsistence; and likewise Son and Holy Spirit. But the terms for the relations—namely, paternity, filiation, procession, or begetting, being begotten, proceeding—signify only the relations themselves, not the hypostases; as does “having a Father.”

For example, when we say, “God is Father,” by the name Father we both indicate a relation and signify the divine hypostasis. The meaning is: God, or the divine essence, is Father—that is, the one who has begotten, that is, the hypostasis which has a Son. Similarly: God is Son—that is, a begotten hypostasis, or one having a Father. Likewise: God is Holy Spirit—that is, the hypostasis proceeding from both, or the one who proceeds.

But when we place the names of relations in the predicate, we signify the notions themselves only, not the hypostases; for example, when we say, “God has begotten,” that is, has a Son; and “God has been begotten,” that is, has a Father. Then the subjects must be understood as hypostases only, not as the essence, which is determined by those properties.

### That the Properties Determine the Hypostases, Not the Substance, That Is, the Nature

**4.** Each of these properties belongs properly to one particular person, and through them the persons are determined and differ from one another, though they do not depart from one another. Hence John Damascene says:

> The hypostases do not differ from one another according to substance, but according to characteristic idioms—that is, determining properties. But the characteristic features—that is, the determining features—belong to the hypostases, not to the nature; for they determine the hypostases.

Again:

> We say that the divine hypostasis of the Word exists without time and eternally, simple, possessing everything that the Father possesses, and is *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with Him; differing from the paternal hypostasis in the manner and relation of birth, yet never departing from the paternal hypostasis.

Expressing the personal properties more clearly, he says in the same Book 3, chapter 7:

> We recognize the distinction of the hypostases—that is, the persons—in three properties: paternal, filial, and processional. The hypostases themselves are inseparable and undivided from one another, and united without confusion; for they are three although united, and divided without separation. For each hypostasis is perfect and possesses its own proper property, namely, its own manner of existence; but they are united in substance and neither are distant from nor depart from the paternal hypostasis.

Here you have the three distinct properties which above were signified in different ways.

### That There Are Other Names of the Persons Signifying the Same Properties: Namely, Begotten, Begetter, Word, Image

**5.** It must not be omitted here that, just as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are names of persons and designate personal properties, so also there are other names of persons—that is, names signifying the persons themselves, denoting their properties, and denoting the same properties as the names just mentioned. They too are relative terms: begetter, begotten, Word, image.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6:

> We must see that “begotten” signifies the same thing as “Son.” For He is Son because begotten; and because Son, certainly begotten. And as Son is referred to Father, so begotten is referred to begetter; and as Father is referred to Son, so begetter is referred to begotten.

Again, in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2:

> Word is understood of the Son alone, not of Father and Son together, as though both were one Word. For Word is said as image is said. Father and Son together are not image; the Son alone is the image of the Father, just as He alone is Son.

Again, in Book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2:

> Word, insofar as He is wisdom and essence, is what the Father is; insofar as He is Word, He is not what the Father is, because the Word is not the Father, and Word is said relatively, as Son is.

Again, in the same work:

> As Son is referred to Father, so Word is referred to Him whose Word it is when it is called Word. Therefore He is not called Word in the same respect in which He is called Wisdom, because Word is not said of itself but is said only relatively to Him whose Word it is, as Son is said relatively to Father. For He is Son in the same respect in which He is Word, and Word in the same respect in which He is Son; but Wisdom in the same respect in which He is essence and one wisdom.

Again, in the same work:

> The Father Himself is not the Word, just as He is not the Son or image. But what could be more absurd than for image to be said of itself?

Again, in Book 5, chapter 1:

> Son is said relatively; Word and image are said relatively; and in all these names He is referred to the Father. But the Father is called none of these.

### A Brief Summary of the Meaning of the Foregoing

**6.** It has plainly been shown that, just as Son or begotten is said relatively to Father, so Word and image are said relatively; and that He is called Word or image in the same respect in which He is called Son—that is, Word and image are said by the same property or notion as Son. But He is not called Wisdom or essence in the same respect in which He is called Word, because He is not called Wisdom by the notion by which He is called Word. For Wisdom is said according to essence, not according to relation.

### A General Rule concerning What Is Said Absolutely and What Is Said Relatively: Whatever Is Said Absolutely Is Said of Both Together, but Not So in the Foregoing Relatives

**7.** A certain general rule must be observed here concerning what is said absolutely and what is said relatively of the Father and the Son. For, as Augustine says in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2, whatever is said absolutely is not said of one without the other; that is, whatever is said which manifests their substance is said of both together. Therefore the Father is not God without the Son, nor the Son without the Father; but both together are God. Yet both together are not Father, nor both together Son, Word, or image.

### Whether “God,” “of God,” and Such Expressions Are Said according to Substance

**8.** Here it is asked whether, when “God of God,” “light of light,” and such expressions are used, they are said according to substance; for it is certain that they are not said according to relation. If they are said according to substance, however, both—namely, Father and Son—are said together, and according to the foregoing rule “God of God” and “light of light” can be said.

We answer that although “God,” “light,” “wisdom,” and similar terms are said according to substance [Col. 0597] and are never taken relatively, they are nevertheless sometimes taken for relatives—that is, for persons—though not relatively. Thus, when it is said, “God begot God,” we take one occurrence for the Father and the other for the Son. Similarly when it is said, “God of God,” “light of light.” In other expressions as well, names of essence are frequently used to signify persons, as when it is said, “God was born,” “God died,” “God suffered,” where the Son alone is signified. Thus “God of God” and similar phrases are also understood of the Son alone.

Hence Augustine, asking how such expressions are said, states in Book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2:

> How is “light from light” said of God? For both are not together God of God; rather, the Son alone is from God, namely the Father. Nor are both together light of light; rather, the Son alone is from the Father, who is light.

### That “That One from That One” Is Said Only by Names of Substance, Not by Names of Persons

**9.** It must be known that “that one from that one” is said only by names of substance, although in such cases those names do not signify substance. But by the same names of persons, “that one from that one” is never said—for example, “Word from Word” or “Son from Son”—because names of this kind could not belong to different persons.

Augustine says this, though obscurely, in the same book:

> Only in the case of what both are not together can that one not be said to be from that one; that is, we cannot use only a name which does not belong to both together to show one from one. Thus “Word from Word” cannot be said, because both are not Word; nor “image from image,” nor “Son from Son,” because both are not Son or image.

And just as names of substance sometimes convey separately the meaning of the persons, so they sometimes convey the meaning of the whole Trinity together. Hence Augustine says in the same book:

> In the name Father, the Father Himself is pronounced by Himself; but in the name God are the Father Himself, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—as when it is said: “No one is good except God alone,” because the Trinity is one God alone.

## DISTINCTION XXVIII. THAT NOT ONLY THE THREE AFORESAID PROPERTIES ARE IN THE PERSONS, BUT ALSO OTHERS WHICH ARE SIGNIFIED BY OTHER NAMES, SUCH AS “UNBEGOTTEN”

1. Moreover, it must be considered that not only the three aforesaid properties or notions are in the persons, but also others which are denoted by other names. For this name *unbegotten* (*ingenitus*) is also said relatively of the Father alone, and it designates a notion other than “father” or “begetter.” For to be Father and to be unbegotten are not the same; that is, the Father is not called Father by the same notion by which he is called unbegotten. For Father, as was said above, is said according to the property of generation, whereas unbegotten is said according to the property of unoriginateness (*innascibilitas*). Therefore the Father differs from the Son by the authority of generation; he also differs by the property of unoriginateness, that is, because he is unbegotten.

Hence Augustine, distinguishing between the property by which he is called Father and that by which he is called unbegotten, says as follows in *On the Trinity*, book 5, chapter 6:

> To say “unbegotten” is not the same as to say “Father”; for even if he had not begotten a Son, nothing would prevent his being called unbegotten. And if anyone begets a son, he is not thereby unbegotten; for begotten human beings beget others. Therefore he is not called Father because he is unbegotten. Thus, although both are said of God the Father, the notion by which he is understood as begetter is one thing, and that by which he is understood as unbegotten another. For “begetter” is said in relation to the begotten, that is, the Son. But when “unbegotten” is said, it indicates not what he is, but what he is not. This must be made clear by examples. By saying “unbegotten,” it is here indicated that he is not a Son; but “begotten” and “unbegotten” are fittingly said, whereas “Son” is the Latin term. Yet ordinary usage does not permit one to say “not Son”; nevertheless, if one says “not Son,” nothing is lost to the understanding, just as, if one says “not begotten” in place of “unbegotten,” nothing else is said. Therefore, in matters of this kind, we must consider not what the usage of our language permits or does not permit us to say, but what understanding of the things themselves becomes evident. Therefore let us now say not only “unbegotten” [Col. 0598], but also “not begotten,” which has the same force. Are we then saying anything other than “not Son”? The negative particle *not* does not cause what is said relatively without it to be said substantially when it is prefixed; it merely negates what was affirmed without it. Thus, in other categories, when we say, “He is a human being,” we signify substance. Therefore one who says, “He is not a human being,” does not state another category, but merely negates that assertion. As, therefore, I affirm according to substance, “He is a human being,” so I deny according to substance when I say, “He is not a human being.” But if “begotten” has the same force as “Son,” then “not begotten” has the same force as “not Son.” Yet we negate relatively when we say “not begotten.” And what is “unbegotten” but “not begotten”? Therefore, when “unbegotten” is said, one does not depart from the relative category. For just as “begotten” is not said of itself, but indicates that it is from a begetter, so, when “unbegotten” is said, it is not said of itself, but indicates that it is not from a begetter; nevertheless, both are said relatively. But what is predicated relatively does not indicate substance. Therefore, although “begotten” and “unbegotten” are different, they do not indicate different substance; for as Son is related to Father, and not-Son to not-Father, so begotten must be related to begetter, and not-begotten to not-begetter.

Behold, he clearly shows that “unbegotten” is said relatively and is understood of the Father alone. The notion by which he is called unbegotten is one thing; that by which he is called Father is another. And when he is called unbegotten, this has the same force as “not begotten” or “not Son.”

### Whether, as the Father alone is called unbegotten, he ought to be called not begotten or not Son

2. Therefore it is commonly asked whether, just as the Father alone is called unbegotten, so he alone ought to be called not begotten or not Son—so that even the Holy Spirit may not be called not Son or not begotten. Some think that the Father alone ought to be called not begotten or not Son. They say that, just as the Holy Spirit is not called unbegotten, so he should not be called not begotten or not Son. Certainly, it ought to be said and believed that the Holy Spirit is not begotten and is not a Son; but he ought not to be called “not begotten” or “not Son.”

Others, however, think that although the Holy Spirit cannot be called unbegotten, he may nevertheless be called not begotten or not Son. They say that Augustine’s earlier statement—that “unbegotten” has the same force as “not begotten” or “not Son”—was made in order to show the etymology of the word, not on account of its manner of predication.

### What the property is according to which the Father is called unbegotten

3. But if you wish to know what property it is according to which the Father is called unbegotten, hear Hilary call it *unoriginateness* (*innascibilitas*). In book 4 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the end, he says:

> There is one from one, namely, the begotten from the unbegotten, with the property in each respectively both of origin and of unoriginateness. Therefore, since the understanding of the persons is signified in the Scriptures and the meaning of unoriginateness and nativity is distinguished, God is not to be supposed solitary. Thus the distinction or differentiation of persons is set forth in the Scriptures, but nowhere a distinction of nature.

### The Arians sought to prove that the Father and the Son are of different substances because the one is unbegotten and the other begotten; Ambrose, replying to them, said that he had not read this name in the divine Scriptures

4. Nor ought it to be passed over in silence that the Arians sought from this to prove that the Father is of one substance and the Son of another, because the former is called unbegotten and the latter begotten, since to be unbegotten and to be begotten are different. Therefore Ambrose, replying to their question, says in chapter 8, volume 2, that he has not read this name, “unbegotten,” in the divine Scriptures. Thus he says in *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*:

> Since certain persons have lately heard us say that the Son of God who was begotten cannot be unequal to the Father who begot him, although the one was begotten and the other begot, because essence or generation belongs to nature, they think that, against [Col. 0599] that question, speech has been closed off to them. Yet, with blameworthy evasiveness, they turn their steps back at the same point, imagining that a change in the question comes about through a change of expression, and saying: “How can the unbegotten and the begotten be of one nature and substance?” Therefore, to answer the question put to me, first of all I nowhere find “unbegotten” in the divine Scriptures; I have not read it, I have not heard it. Of what instability, then, are people of this sort, who say that we employ things which are not written, although we say what is written, while they themselves object what is not written? Do they not contradict themselves and undermine the authority of their own accusation?

Observe, reader, that Ambrose did not wish to employ the name “unbegotten” because of heretics. So we too ought to pass some things over in silence because of the snares of slanderers, though Catholic and devout readers may safely believe them. For there are certain things that are not of such religious importance and authority that one must always be occupied with confessing and receiving them; rather, they can sometimes be passed over in silence. Yet they are not of such perversity that, when it is opportune, we are not free to employ them.

### Whether to be Father and to be Son are different

5. Moreover, it is commonly asked, since it was said above that to say “unbegotten” is one thing and to say “Father” another, and that begotten and unbegotten are different, whether similarly to be Father and to be Son are different, or the same.

To this we say that, in the same sense in which begotten and unbegotten are called different, and in which to say “begotten” and “unbegotten” is said not to be the same, one may say that to be Father and to be Son, or to be Holy Spirit, are not the same but different. For the Father is not Father by the same notion by which the Son is Son, or by which the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit. In this sense, therefore, we concede that to be Father is one thing and to be Son another: because the notion by which the Father is Father is one thing, and that by which the Son is Son another.

But if you transpose the words and say, “It is one thing for the Father to be, another for the Son to be,” the sense changes, and therefore this is not conceded. For the meaning would be as though one said: “That by which the Father is—not Father, indeed, but is—is one thing; that by which the Son is—not Son, indeed, but is—is another”; and that is altogether false. For the Father is by that whereby the Father is God, that is, through essence or nature; and the Son is God by that whereby the Father is God. Therefore the Son is by that whereby the Father is; thus to be Father is the same as to be Son. But to be Father and to be Son are not the same.

Hence Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity*:

> Although to be Father and to be Son are different, the substance is nevertheless not different, because this is not said according to substance but according to relation; yet this relation is not an accident, because it is not mutable.

Behold, he calls to be Father and to be Son different; this must be understood according to the account given above, namely, because the notion by which he is Father is one, and that by which he is Son another. For Father is not called Father, nor Son Son, according to essence, but according to relation.

### How Wisdom is said to be begotten or born: whether according to relation or substance

6. It should also be known that, as the Son alone is called Word or Image, so he alone is also called Wisdom born or begotten. Therefore it is asked whether this is said relatively; and, if it is said relatively, whether it is according to the same relation by which he is called Word and Image.

On this Augustine says in book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2:

> Let us take what is said when “Word” is said as though “born Wisdom” were said, so that he may be Son and Image. And when these two words are said, “This is born Wisdom,” in the one word, namely “born,” Word, Image, and Son are understood. In all these names essence is not indicated, because they are said relatively. But in the other word, namely “Wisdom,” essence is also shown, because it is said of itself; for Wisdom is wise through itself, and its being is to be wise. Hence Father and Son together are one Wisdom, because they are one essence.

Take care, reader, how you understand what Augustine says here. For he seems to say that, when “born Wisdom” is said, “Wisdom” signifies essence and “born” indicates relation. If this is so, we are compelled to say that the divine [Col. 0600] essence is born, which conflicts with what has been said above.

But to this we say that in the one term, that is, “born,” the same notion is understood which is denoted when Word and Image are said. In the other term, namely Wisdom, essence is shown—that is, it is shown that the Son is essence, because Wisdom is said according to essence. Therefore, when “born Wisdom” is said, it is to be understood that he who is born is essence. Yet there “Wisdom” does not produce the understanding of essence, but of hypostasis; just as, when Word or Son is said, a hypostasis with its property is understood. Likewise, when “born Wisdom” is said, the same thing is understood: namely, a begotten hypostasis.

Therefore Augustine carefully says that the same thing is to be understood when Word is said and when born Wisdom is said: that is, the same relation and the same hypostasis in which that property inheres. This also supports what we said above: namely, that when Father, Son, or Holy Spirit is said, not only those properties are signified, as when paternity or filiation is said, but also the hypostasis together with its properties.

### That “image” is sometimes said according to essence

7. It should also be known that, although it was said above that Image is said relatively of the Son, like Word or Son, it is nevertheless sometimes found said according to substance. Thus Augustine, in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 1, says that the divinity and image of the Holy Trinity, according to essence, are one—the image after which man was made. Hilary too, in book 5 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the beginning, says:

> Man is made after the common image; the name does not differ, the nature does not differ. For there is one form after which man was created.

These words show that “image” sometimes conveys the understanding of essence; and then it is said of itself, not relatively.

## DISTINCTION XXIX. ON “PRINCIPLE”: THAT IT IS SAID RELATIVELY AND DENOTES A MANIFOLD RELATION

1. There is, moreover, another name denoting a manifold relation: namely, *principle* (*principium*). For principle is always said in relation to something. The Father is called principle, the Son is called principle, and the Holy Spirit is called principle, but differently.

For the Father is called principle in relation to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Hence Augustine says in book 4 of *On the Trinity*:

> The Father is the principle of the whole divinity, or, if it is better said, deity, because he himself is from no one. For he does not have that from which he is or from which he proceeds; but from him both the Son is begotten and the Holy Spirit proceeds.

He is therefore not called the principle of the whole deity as though he were the principle either of himself or of the divine essence, but because he is the principle of the Son and the Holy Spirit, in each of whom the whole divinity is.

The Son is called principle in relation to the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit is called principle only in relation to creatures; and the Father, the Son, and the Trinity itself together are also called principle in relation to creatures, and each person is called the principle of creatures.

Therefore the Father is principle without principle; the Son is principle from principle; the Holy Spirit is principle from both, that is, from the Father and the Son.

### That from eternity the Father and the Son are principle, but the Holy Spirit is not; indeed, he began to be principle

2. The Father is from eternity the principle of the Son, and the Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit, because the Son is from the Father and the Holy Spirit from both. But the Holy Spirit is not principle from eternity; rather, he began to be principle, because he is called principle only in relation to creatures. Therefore, when creatures began to exist, the Holy Spirit also began to be their principle.

Likewise, the Father and Son, together with the Holy Spirit, began to be one principle of creatures, because creatures began to exist from Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These three are called not three principles but one principle of all creatures, because they are the principle of things in one and the same manner. For things are not from the Father in one way and from the Son in another; they are from them altogether in the same way.

Therefore the Apostle, understanding this Trinity to be one principle of things, says: “From him, through him, and in him are all things.” But when we hear that all things are from God, as Augustine says in *On the Nature of the Good*, we must understand all natures and everything that is natural. [Col. 0601] For sins, which do not preserve nature but corrupt it and which arise from the will of sinners, are not from him.

Therefore, of all things that exist naturally, the Father with the Son and Holy Spirit is one principle; and this began to be. From eternity, however, the Father is principle of the Son through generation, and Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit.

Hence Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity*:

> Father is said relatively, and “principle” is likewise said relatively. But Father is said in relation to the Son, while principle is said in relation to all things that are from him. And the Son is called principle. For when he was asked, “Who are you?” he replied: “The Principle, who also speak to you” [John 8]. But is he the principle of the Father? By no means. Rather, in calling himself principle, he wished to show himself as Creator; just as the Father is principle of the creature, because all things are from him.
