But when we say both that the Father is principle and that the Son is principle, we do not say that there are two principles of the creature, because Father and Son together are one principle in relation to the creature, as they are one Creator. But if everything which remains in itself and begets or makes something is the principle of the thing which it begets or makes, we cannot deny that the Holy Spirit too is rightly called principle, because we do not separate him from the name of Creator; for it is written of him that he works, and certainly he works while remaining in himself. For he is not changed or transformed into any of the things which he makes. Therefore the Holy Spirit is one principle with Father and Son in relation to the creature—not two or three principles.

Behold, Augustine clearly shows that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle of created things; that is, they are principle in one and the same manner. And he sufficiently reveals that manner: namely, because they make all things; and because these three work in the same way, they are called one principle.

### Here he shows how the Father is principle of the Son, and how he and the Son are principle of the Holy Spirit

3. Then, continuing in the same book, he shows how the Father is called principle in relation to the Son, and how he and the Son are called principle in relation to the Holy Spirit. He says that the Father is principle of the Son because he begot him, and that Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit proceeds or is given by both:

> If that which begets is principle in relation to that which is begotten, then the Father is principle in relation to the Son, because he begot him. But whether the Father is principle also in relation to the Holy Spirit, because it is said, “He proceeds from the Father,” is no small question. If this is so, he will be principle not only of that which he begets or makes, but also of that which he gives and which proceeds from him. Therefore, if that which is given or proceeds has as its principle the one by whom it is given or from whom it proceeds, it must be confessed that the Father and the Son are principle of the Holy Spirit—not two principles, but, just as Father and Son are called one Creator and one Lord relatively in relation to the creature, so they are one principle relatively in relation to the Holy Spirit. But in relation to the creature Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one principle, as they are one Creator and one Lord.

Here you have that the Father is called the principle of the Son because he begot him. Therefore, by the same notion by which he is Father, he is called the principle of the Son: namely, by generation, according to which he is also called the Son’s author.

Hence Hilary says in book 4 of *On the Trinity*:

> By the very fact that he is called Father, he is shown to be the author of him whom he begot, bearing a name which indicates both that he is not to be understood as having proceeded from another and that the one who was begotten is taught to have subsisted from him. The Church knows one unoriginated God; it knows the only-begotten Son of God. It confesses that the Father is free from origin; it also confesses the origin of the Son from a beginning, but from the unbegun: born not through himself but from him who is from no one, born eternally, taking his nativity from the Father’s eternity.

Here a profession of faith has been set forth, but the rationale of the profession has not yet been explained. It must therefore be sought: namely, how one should understand his statement that the Son’s origin is from a beginning, while the Son himself is not from a beginning but from the unbegun. He immediately clarifies how he understood “beginning,” saying that the origin of the Son is from a beginning—as though saying: Do not understand the Son’s origin to be from a beginning as if the Son himself had a beginning, but because he is from the unbegun, that is, from the Father, from whom are all things.

For although the Son is principle from principle [Col. 0602], it must not be conceded that the Son has a principle. And although the Son is principle from principle, while the Father is principle not from principle, the principle from principle is not a principle without principle. Just as the Son is not the Father, yet they are not two principles but one, so Father and Son are not two creators but one Creator.

### Since Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, whether this is by the same notion

4. Father and Son are one principle not only of creatures, as was said above, but also of the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is commonly asked whether the Father is principle of the Holy Spirit by the same notion as the Son, or whether the notion by which the Father is called principle of the Holy Spirit is one thing and that by which the Son is so called another.

We answer that, since Father and Son are called principle of the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit proceeds or is given from both, and since he does not proceed or is not given differently from the Father than from the Son, it may soundly be understood that Father and Son are called principle of the Holy Spirit by the same relation or notion. But if one asks what that notion is which “principle” denotes here, we do not have a name for it. It is not paternity or filiation; rather, it is a certain notion belonging to Father and Son, according to which Father and Son are from eternity one principle of the Holy Spirit.

But Father or Son is called giver, as was said above, in time, just as the Holy Spirit is called given or bestowed.

## DISTINCTION XXX. ON THOSE THINGS WHICH ARE SAID OF GOD TEMPORALLY AND RELATIVELY ACCORDING TO ACCIDENT: WHICH HAPPENS NOT TO GOD BUT TO CREATURES

1. There are certain things which are said of God from time and belong to him temporally without change in himself. They are said relatively according to accident—not an accident which happens to God, but one which happens to creatures—such as Creator, Lord, refuge, given, or bestowed, and the like.

Augustine says of these in book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13:

> Creator is said relatively in relation to creature, as Lord in relation to servant. Likewise, let no one be troubled that, although the Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and Son, something is nevertheless said of him from time, such as what we have called “bestowed.” For the Holy Spirit is eternally gift, but temporally bestowed. And if one is not called lord except when one begins to have a servant, then this appellation too is relative to God from time. For the creature of whom he is Lord is not eternal. Therefore, his being Lord is not eternal, lest we be forced to say that the creature also is eternal, since he would not have ruled eternally unless it too had served eternally. But as there cannot be a servant who has no lord, so neither can there be a lord who has no servant.

### Objection: that he is not Lord from time in respect of time, which is not from time

2. But someone may here say that this appellation by which God is called Lord does not belong to him from time, because he is Lord not only of things which began from time but also of that thing which did not begin from time, namely, time itself. Time did not begin from time, because there was no time before time began; and thus he did not begin to be Lord from time.

To this it may be said that, although he did not begin from time to be Lord of time, he nevertheless began to be Lord of time, because time was not always. And he began from time to be Lord of man.

Augustine continues in the same book:

> Whoever may arise who says that God alone is eternal, while times are not eternal on account of their variety and mutability, yet that times themselves did not begin in time, because there was no time before times began, and thus that it did not happen to God in time that he was Lord, because he was Lord of times which certainly did not begin to exist in time—what will he answer concerning man, who was made in time and whose Lord he certainly was not before man existed? Surely, for God to be Lord of man happened from time. And, to remove every controversy, surely he began from time to be your Lord or mine, since we began to exist [Col. 0603] only now. How then shall we maintain that nothing is said of God according to accident, except because nothing happens to his nature whereby it is changed? Thus those relative things are accidents which occur with some change in the things of which they are said; as friend is said relatively. For one does not begin to be a friend except when one begins to love. Therefore some change of will occurs, so that one is called friend. But when a coin is called a price, it is said relatively; yet it was not changed when it began to be a price, nor when it is called a pledge and the like. Therefore, if a coin can so often be called relatively with no change in itself—so that neither when it begins to be called so nor when it ceases is there any change in its nature or form as a coin—how much more readily should we understand this of that immutable substance of God: that something may be said relatively of him in relation to a creature, so that, although it begins to be said temporally, nothing is understood to have happened to God’s substance, but only to the creature in relation to which he is said to be something! Thus too he is called our refuge. For God is called our refuge relatively, in relation to us; and he becomes our refuge when we flee to him. Does something then come to be in his nature which was not there before we fled to him? Rather, some change comes about in us, who become better by fleeing to him; but none occurs in him. So he begins to be our Father when through his grace we are reborn—he who gave us power to become children of God. Therefore our substance is changed for the better when we become his children. Likewise, he begins to be our Father, but with no change in his own substance. Therefore whatever God begins to be called temporally which he was not called before is plainly said relatively; but it is not an accident of God, as though something happened to him, but an accident of that in relation to which God begins to be called something relatively.

From this it is plainly shown that some things are said of God temporally in relation to creatures without a change in the Godhead, though not without a change in the creature. Thus the accident is in the creature, not in the Creator. And the appellation by which the creature is called relatively is relative to the Creator and denotes the relation which exists in the creature. But the appellation by which the Creator is called relatively in relation to the creature is indeed relative, but denotes no relation which comes to be in the Creator.

### Here is resolved the question whether the Holy Spirit is called given in relation to himself, since he gives himself

3. Here the question raised above may be resolved. It was asked, since the Holy Spirit is called given or bestowed—and what is given is related both to the giver and to the one to whom it is given—and since the Holy Spirit gives himself, whether, when he is said to be given or bestowed, he is said relatively in relation to himself.

Answering this question, we say that the Holy Spirit is called given or bestowed relatively, both in relation to the giver and in relation to the one to whom he is given. But the giver or donor is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, we do not say that the Holy Spirit is related to himself. Rather, the appellation “given” or “bestowed” is related both to giver and recipient, because nothing can be called given unless it is given by someone and to someone.

But when the Holy Spirit is said to give himself or to be given by himself, he is indeed said relatively in relation to the one to whom he is given, and the appellation is relative; the change occurs in the one to whom he is given, not in the giver.

## DISTINCTION XXXI. HOW THE SON IS CALLED EQUAL TO THE FATHER: WHETHER ACCORDING TO SUBSTANCE OR RELATION; AND SO TOO “SIMILAR”

1. Moreover, since the three persons are coequal with one another, it must be considered whether this is said relatively or according to substance; and, if relatively, whether equality is to be considered according to relation or essence; and further, what equality itself is.

To this we say that, just as nothing is similar to itself—for, as Hilary says, likeness is not to itself—so neither is anything called equal to itself. Accordingly, just as similar, so equal is said relatively. Therefore the Son is called equal to the Father relatively, and the Holy Spirit equal to both. Yet the Son is equal to the Father, and the Holy Spirit to both, because of the supreme simplicity and unity of the essence. [Col. 0604] Therefore the Son is equal to the Father according to essence, not according to relation.

Hence Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6:

> Let us ask in what respect the Son is equal to the Father. He is not equal to the Father in respect of that by which he is said in relation to the Father to be Son. It remains, then, that he is equal in respect of that which is said of himself. But whatever is said of itself is said according to substance. It remains, therefore, that he is equal according to substance; therefore the substance of both is the same.

Again, in book 6, chapter 4:

> It is enough to see that the Son cannot in any way be equal to the Father if in any respect—namely, in anything belonging to the signification of his substance—he is found unequal. Therefore the Son is equal to the Father in all things and is of the same substance.

The Holy Spirit also is equal to Father and Son, and equal in all things, because of the supreme simplicity of that substance. From these things it is clear that the Son is equal to the Father according to substance, and the Holy Spirit to both; the appellation alone is relative. Therefore the equality of Father and Son is not a relation or notion, but natural unity and identity.

### Here it is asked how he is called similar and what likeness is

2. We say the same about “similar” and likeness. For when the Son is called similar to the Father, he is indeed called so relatively; but he is similar to the Father because of unity of essence. Therefore the appellation alone is relative, whereas likeness is the undifferentiated essence.

Hence some reasonably think that by the name equality or likeness nothing is positively posited, but something is removed: thus the Son is called equal to the Father because he is neither greater nor less than him, and this because of unity of essence. Likewise, he is called similar because he is neither different, nor alien, nor unlike in any respect; and this because of the simplicity of essence. Therefore the Son is not equal or unequal to the Father, nor similar or dissimilar, insofar as he is begotten from the Father; rather, he is equal and similar according to substance.

### On the statement of Saint Hilary, in which he sets forth what is proper to the persons in the Trinity

3. Nor should it be omitted here that the illustrious Hilary, assigning the properties of the persons, says that in the Father there is eternity, in the Image form, and in the Gift use. These words are so difficult that Augustine labored intensely to understand and explain them, as he himself shows in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 10:

> Someone, wishing to set forth as briefly as possible what is proper to the individual persons in the Trinity, said: “Eternity is in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift.” Since he was a man of no slight authority in interpreting the Scriptures and defending the faith—for Hilary set this down in his books *On the Synods*, not far from the beginning—I have examined, to the extent I can, the hidden meaning of these words: Father, Image, Gift; eternity, form, and use. I do not think that, in the term “eternity,” he had anything in view except that the Father does not have a father from whom he exists, whereas the Son is from the Father both in order to exist and in order to be coeternal with him. For if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, the image is made equal to it, not it to its own image. In that image he called the form, I believe, on account of its beauty, where there is such congruity and primary equality and primary likeness—differing in no respect, in no way unequal, and in no part dissimilar, but corresponding in identity to him whose image it is. There is the primary and supreme life, for which to live and to be are not different but the same; there is the primary and supreme intellect, for which to live and to understand are not different but the same single thing, as a perfect Word; nothing is lacking to it; and it is, as it were, the art of the omnipotent and wise God, full of all the living and immutable intelligible principles. All are one in it, just as it is one from the One with whom it is one. There God knows all things which he made through it.

### Why the Holy Spirit is called “use”  
*(Augustine, On the Trinity, book 6, chapter 10)*

4. There is, moreover, an ineffable embrace of the Father [Col. 0605] and the Image, which is not without enjoyment, charity, and joy. Therefore that love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if indeed it can be worthily called by any human word—was briefly called “use” by him; and in the Trinity it is the Holy Spirit, not begotten, but the sweetness of begetter and begotten, who with immense generosity and abundance floods all creatures according to their capacity.

Thus these three seem to be defined reciprocally by one another, and they are infinite in themselves. Whoever sees this, even in part or through a mirror in an enigma, should rejoice in knowing God and give thanks. But whoever does not see it should strive through the piety of faith to see, not through blindness to slander; for God is one, yet Trinity.

Here you have how Hilary’s foregoing words are to be understood, although they are of such depth that even with this explanation human understanding can scarcely grasp them in any measure. For the explanation itself which Augustine has given here contains much difficulty and ambiguity.

### That according to this exposition the three properties of the persons are not distinguished there  
*(Augustine, ibid.)*

5. For according to the foregoing exposition, the three properties assigned above are not distinguished here; rather, the hypostases themselves are shown as distinct from one another. Yet by the name eternity the same property seems to be designated as is denoted by the name “unbegotten.”

But let us see what he means when he says: “If an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, the image is made equal to it, not it to its own image.” For he seems to say that the Son, who is the Father’s Image, is made equal to the Father, but not the Father to the Son. Yet in Scripture the Son is called equal to the Father and the Father equal to the Son. But the Son has from the Father that he is equal to him; the Father does not have this from the Son. Nevertheless, the Son is fully and perfectly equal to the Father—that is, he is an image equal to him whose image he is.

### Why Hilary is said to have assigned the proper characteristics of the persons in the foregoing words, although the properties are not expressed there

6. Hilary is therefore said to have assigned what is proper to the persons in the foregoing words because he used relative names of the persons, namely, Image and Gift. These are said relatively of the persons and denote the properties by which the persons are distinguished. For the Holy Spirit is called Gift relatively, just as he is called donation.

Nevertheless, according to Augustine’s foregoing exposition, Hilary did not signify the properties themselves by the other three names, except by the name eternity alone. By it he intended to be understood not paternity itself, but the notion by which the Father is called unbegotten.

### That Augustine denotes the distinction of these same persons in other words, without expressing the three properties
7. It must also be known that Augustine, wishing to show the distinction of these same three persons without expressly naming those three properties mentioned above, says in *On Christian Doctrine*:

> In the Father there is unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the harmony of unity and equality. And these three are one: all things are one because of the Father, all things equal because of the Son, all things connected because of the Holy Spirit. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—each one of them—is God, and all together are one God; each one is a full substance, and all together are one substance. The Father is neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit; the Son is neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. Rather, the Father is Father alone, the Son Son alone, and the Holy Spirit Holy Spirit alone. The same eternity belongs to the three, the same unchangeability, the same majesty, the same power.

In these words the distinction of the three persons is clearly indicated.

### Why unity is attributed to the Father and equality to the Son

8. But many are troubled by the fact that he attributes unity to the Father and equality to the Son. For since unity is spoken of according to substance, it exists not only in the Father but also in the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the equality of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and the same [Col. 0606]. Why, then, is unity attributed to the Father and equality to the Son? Perhaps unity is attributed to the Father, according to Augustine, for the same reason that eternity above was attributed to him according to Hilary: namely, because the Father exists in such a way as not to be from another; because he begot the Son as one God with himself; and because the Holy Spirit proceeds from him as one God with him. Unity, therefore, is said to be in the Father because there is no other from whom he exists. For he is not from another, nor is there from him, from eternity, any person or thing that is not one with him: for the Son and the Holy Spirit are one with the Father. Hence Truth says, John 10: “I and the Father are one.”

### Why the Father and Son are called one, or one God, but not “one person”: things of the same nature may rightly be called one simply and with a qualification, whereas things of different natures cannot be called one unless it is stated in what respect they are one

9. Here it must be said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are rightly called one and one God, but not “one [person].” For two or more things may rightly be said to be one if they are of one essence and have one nature. But “one” in the masculine or feminine cannot be said of distinct things unless one adds what they are one in; with this addition it may rightly be said of things both of one substance and of different substance.

Hence Augustine says in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3:

> I do not know whether it is found in the Scriptures that things of different natures are said to be one. But even if several things are of the same nature and think differently, they are not one insofar as they think differently. Therefore, when “one” is said without adding in what respect they are one, and several are called one, this signifies the same nature and essence, neither divided nor discordant.

Thus Paul and Apollos, 1 Corinthians 3, who were both human beings and held the same view, are called one when it is said: “He who plants and he who waters are one.” But when what they are one in is added, something made one from several things may be signified, even if they are of different natures. Thus soul and body certainly cannot be called one—for what is more different?—unless what they are one in is added or understood, namely, one human being.

Hence the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 6: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.” He did not say, “He is one,” or, “They are one,” but adds “spirit.” For the spirit of a human being and the Spirit of God are different in nature; yet by cleaving to God, the human spirit becomes one spirit with God because it becomes a participant in his truth and blessedness. If, then, things of different substances are rightly said to be one spirit, how much more rightly are those of one substance said to be one God?

Therefore Father and Son are one, certainly according to unity of essence, and one God. In this the Arian heresy is condemned, which, as Augustine says in *On Heresies*, refuses to hold that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one and the same substance and nature—or, more explicitly, essence, which in Greek is called *ousia*—but declares the Son to be a creature. So too is the Sabellian heresy condemned, which, as Augustine says in the same book, maintained that Christ himself was both Father and Holy Spirit, so that the Trinity would be a trinity of names without the substance of persons.

As Augustine says in his commentary on John, Truth demolishes both plagues by saying: “I and the Father are one.” Hear and observe both expressions, “one” and “are,” and you will be delivered from Charybdis and Scylla. For his saying “one” frees you from Arius; his saying “are” frees you from Sabellius. If “one,” then not different; if “are,” then Father and Son. For he would not say “we are” of one person, nor “one” of things different in substance.

Let the Sabellians, then, be ashamed, who say that he who is the Son is himself the Father, thereby confusing the persons. They are also called Patripassians, because they say that the Father suffered himself. The Arians, however, say that the Father is one thing and the Son another, not one substance but two: the Father greater, the Son lesser. Do not say this, Catholic. Sail, then, through the middle; avoid both dangerous sides, and say: “The Father is Father; the Son is Son; the Father is another, the Son another, but not another thing—indeed the very same thing—because they are one God.” Thus it has been shown why unity is said to be in the Father, although the three are one.

### Why equality is said to be in the Son, although the equality of the three is one

[Col. 0607]

10. Let us now see why equality is said to be in the Son, although the supreme equality of the three is one. This was perhaps said because the Son was begotten by the Father as equal to the one begetting him, and equal to the gift proceeding from both; and therefore those three are said to be equal because of the Son. For the Son has from the Father that he is equal to the Father and to the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit has from both that he is equal to each. Yet we say this without the arrogance of assertion and without prejudging a fuller understanding, preferring, in the exposition of words so obscure, to listen to those more learned than to impose something upon others.

### Why the harmony or connection of both is said to be in the Holy Spirit

11. That the harmony of Father and Son is said to be in the Holy Spirit, and that through him all things are connected, is easier to understand if we recall to mind what was set forth above. For, on the authority of the saints, it was said above that the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father. The Holy Spirit is therefore rightly called the connection or harmony of Father and Son, and through him all things are connected.

Hence Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 11: “The Holy Spirit of both is a certain consubstantial communion of Father and Son.” Again, in book 7 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3: “The Holy Spirit is the supreme charity joining the two together and joining us to them.”

## DISTINCTION XXXII. WHETHER THE FATHER OR THE SON LOVES THROUGH THE HOLY SPIRIT, SINCE FOR GOD TO LOVE IS THE SAME AS TO BE

1. Here a question arises from what has been said. For it was stated above and shown by the authorities of the saints that the Holy Spirit is the communion of Father and Son, and the love by which Father and Son love one another. Therefore it is asked whether the Father or the Son loves through the Holy Spirit.

According to the authorities cited above, this must indeed seem to be affirmed, since they show that the Holy Spirit is that by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter. But, on the other hand, if the Father or Son is said to love through the Holy Spirit, he seems to exist through the Holy Spirit, because for God to be is not one thing and to love another, but the same thing. For, as Augustine says in book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5, whatever seems to be said according to qualities in that simple nature must be understood according to essence—for example, good, great, immortal, wise, loving, and the like. Therefore, if the Father or Son loves through the Holy Spirit, he seems to exist through that Spirit; and he loves not only through his own essence but also through the gift.

### This question is insoluble and exceeds human understanding; here authorities seem to conflict

2. Since this question contains the height of excessive profundity, we answer only what Augustine appears to indicate: namely, that Father and Son love one another and preserve unity not only by their essence but by their own proper gift. Although this has been set out above, it is not burdensome to repeat it, since this is useful.

Augustine says in book 6 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 5:

> It is clear that neither of the two is that by which both are joined together: that by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter, and by which they preserve the unity of peace, not by participation but by their essence, nor by the gift of some superior being but by their own proper gift.

See: here he says that they preserve unity by their essence and by their gift. Again, Augustine says in book 5 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7: “Who in that Trinity would dare to say that the Father loves neither himself, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit except through the Holy Spirit?” Here he clearly shows that the Father does not love only through the Holy Spirit; yet he does not simply say that the Father does not love through the Holy Spirit.

### Whether the Father is wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, just as he loves by the love proceeding from him

3. Moreover, it must be carefully examined whether the Father is wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, who is the Son alone. This seems provable by analogy. For if [Col. 0608] the Father loves by the love proceeding from him, why is he not wise, or does he not understand, by the Wisdom or Understanding whom he begot?

Augustine says that this question seems pressing because the Apostle wrote, 1 Corinthians 1, that Christ is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God.” There it is asked whether the Father is the Father of his Wisdom and Power in such a way that he is wise by the Wisdom whom he begot and powerful by the Power whom he begot.

But far be it that this is so. For if in God to be is the same as to be wise, the Father is not called wise through the Wisdom whom he begot; otherwise she would not be from him, but he from her. For if the Wisdom whom he begot is the cause of his being wise, she is also the cause of his existence. This cannot occur unless she begets or makes him; but no one could in any way call Wisdom the begetter or creator of the Father. What could be more insane? Therefore the Father is himself the Wisdom by which he is wise. The Son, however, is called the Wisdom of the Father and the Power of the Father, not because the Father is wise or powerful through him, but because the Son is Wisdom and Power from the Father’s Wisdom and Power. From this it is clear that the Father is not wise by begotten Wisdom, but by himself, unbegotten Wisdom.

### Whether the Son is wise by begotten or unbegotten Wisdom

4. After this, some commonly ask whether the Son is wise by begotten Wisdom or by unbegotten Wisdom. For if he is not wise by begotten Wisdom, neither is he wise by himself; but if he is wise by begotten Wisdom, he does not seem wise by unbegotten Wisdom, and thus does not seem to be wise from the Father, although he has all things from the Father.

We answer that the Wisdom of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, just as their essence is one, because in the simplicity of that nature Wisdom is essence. Yet the Son alone is begotten Wisdom, and the Father alone unbegotten Wisdom; and begotten Wisdom is from unbegotten Wisdom, or from unbegotten Wisdom. Since there to be is the same as to be wise, it follows that begotten Wisdom is wise from unbegotten Wisdom.

Therefore the Son is not called God’s Wisdom as though he alone understands or is wise for himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit. For Augustine says in book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7:

> If the Son alone understands there for himself, the Father, and the Holy Spirit, we return to that absurdity: that the Father is not wise from himself but from the Son; that Wisdom did not beget Wisdom, but that the Father is called wise by the Wisdom whom he begot. For where there is no understanding, there cannot be Wisdom. Therefore, if the Father does not understand for himself but the Son understands for the Father, then the Son surely makes the Father wise. And if for God to be is the same as to be wise, and his essence is the same as his Wisdom, then it is not the Son who has essence from the Father—which is true—but rather the Father who has essence from the Son; this would be most absurd and utterly false.

Therefore God the Father is wise by his own Wisdom, which he himself is; and the Son, the Wisdom of the Father, is wise from the Wisdom who is the Father, from whom the Son was begotten. So too the Father understands by his own Understanding, which he himself is; for one who did not understand could not be wise. But the Son, the Father’s Understanding, was begotten from the Understanding who is the Father, and from whom he also understands.

Accordingly, the Father is Wisdom and the Son is Wisdom, and both are one Wisdom; yet the Father alone is unbegotten Wisdom and the Son alone begotten Wisdom. The Father is not one Wisdom and the Son another Wisdom, but they are one and the same Wisdom. So the Father is unbegotten God and the Son begotten God; nor is begotten God unbegotten God. Yet for this reason the Father is not one God and the Son another God: both are one God, though not one person. For the begotten is another and the unbegotten another, but not another God; indeed, both are one, or one God. Thus begotten Wisdom is not unbegotten Wisdom, but begotten Wisdom is other than unbegotten Wisdom; nevertheless, they are not another Wisdom, but one and the same Wisdom.

### Whether the Son is wise by himself or through himself

5. From what has been said, it is clear that the Son is not wise from himself or of himself, but from the Father and through the Father. Yet it is commonly asked whether the Son is wise by himself or through himself.

Some say that the phrase bears several meanings and must therefore be distinguished. Thus, when you say that the Son is wise by himself or through himself, the statement is true if you understand that he is wise by his own nature and essence; but it is false if you understand that he is wise from himself or of himself. Others simply grant such expressions without qualification: “The Son is Wisdom through himself, but not from himself or of himself”; “the Son is God through himself and exists through himself, but not from himself or of himself.”

They support this with the words of Hilary, who says in book 9 of *On the Trinity* that the Son acts not from himself but through himself:

> This is the unity of the nature which you oppose, heretic: the Son acts through himself in such a way that he does not act from himself, and does not act from himself in such a way that he acts through himself. Understand the Son as acting, and the Father as acting through him. He does not act from himself, since the Father is shown to abide in him. He acts through himself, since according to the Son’s birth he himself does the things that please him. He would be weak in not acting from himself unless he acts from God; and he would not be in unity of nature if he did not act through himself in the things he does and in which he is well pleased.

Therefore, they say, just as the Son acts through himself but not from himself, so he should be called wise through himself but not from himself. Likewise, they say, he is God through himself, or should be called such, and exists through himself, but not from himself or of himself.

### Whether there is only one Wisdom of the Father

6. After this, some commonly ask whether there is only one Wisdom of the Father. They strive to prove that there is not, as follows. “The Son,” they say, “is the Father’s begotten Wisdom, by whom the Father is not wise. Therefore there is a Wisdom of the Father by whom he is not wise. But there is also the Father’s unbegotten Wisdom, and by her the Father is wise. Therefore there is a Wisdom of the Father by whom he is wise; and she is not that Wisdom of the Father by whom he is not wise. Therefore there is not only one Wisdom of the Father. Again, unbegotten Wisdom is Wisdom of the Father, and begotten Wisdom is Wisdom of the Father; but unbegotten Wisdom is not begotten Wisdom. Therefore there is not only one Wisdom of the Father.”

We reject these and similar arguments as sophistical, far removed from truth, and obvious to all skilled in theology to be unworthy of reply. Yet we add this: there is only one Wisdom of the Father, but she is called “Wisdom of the Father” in more than one way. The Wisdom whom he begot is called the Father’s Wisdom, and the Wisdom by whom he is wise is called the Father’s Wisdom. Thus the reason for the designation differs. The former is called the Father’s because he begot her; the latter is called the Father’s Wisdom because by her he is wise.

Nevertheless, there is only one Wisdom of the Father, because begotten Wisdom is the same Wisdom as that by which he is wise—whether that by which he is wise is understood as the person of the Father or as the essence of the Father. For the person of the Father, meant when “unbegotten Wisdom” is said, and the person of the Son, signified when “begotten Wisdom” is said, are one and the same Wisdom: namely, the divine essence understood as common to the three persons.

### In the Trinity there is love which is the Trinity, yet the Holy Spirit is love which is not the Trinity; therefore there are not two loves—likewise concerning Wisdom

7. Just as in the Trinity there is love which is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, namely the very essence of deity, yet the Holy Spirit is love who is not Father or Son, there are not therefore two loves in the Trinity. For the love which is properly the Holy Spirit is the love which is the Trinity, though he is not himself the Trinity; just as the Holy Spirit is the essence which is the Trinity, though he is not himself the Trinity.

So also in the Trinity there is Wisdom who is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, namely the divine essence; yet the Son is Wisdom who is not Father or Holy Spirit. There are not therefore two Wisdoms there, because the Wisdom who is properly the Son is the Wisdom who is the Trinity, though he is not himself the Trinity; just as the Son is the essence which is the Trinity, though he is not himself the Trinity.

### By the same reasoning by which the Father is not said to be wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, it seems that neither Father nor Son should be said to love by the love proceeding from both

8. Moreover, it must be carefully noted that, by the reasoning according to which the Father is not said to be wise by the Wisdom whom he begot, it seems necessary to say that the Father does not love [Col. 0610] the Son, nor the Son the Father, by the love proceeding from both—namely, the love which is properly the Holy Spirit. For just as for God to know is the same as to be, so for him to love is the same as to be.

Therefore, just as the Father is denied to be wise by the Wisdom whom he begot—because, if he were called wise by her, she would be understood to be not from him but he from her—so it seems that one should not grant that Father or Son loves by the love which is the Holy Spirit alone. For if the Father or Son loves by that love, the Holy Spirit seems not to be from Father and Son, but Father and Son from the Holy Spirit, because there to love is the same as to be.

Yet it was said above, and established by Augustine’s authority, that in the Trinity there are three: one loving him who is from him, one loving him from whom he is, and love itself; and neither of the two is that by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter. These words clearly signify that the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father by that love which is neither of them but the Holy Spirit alone. Since, then, there to love is the same as to be, how is it said that Father or Son does not exist by the love by which one loves the other, when the Father is denied to be wise by the Wisdom whom he begot lest he be understood to exist by her?

### This question too is inexplicable and surpasses human weakness

9. I confess that this question is difficult, especially since it arises from the preceding matters, which seem to involve a similar argument. In considering it, the weakness of my understanding is troubled; I prefer to report what the saints have said rather than to introduce something myself. For Hilary says, in the middle of book 1 of *On the Trinity*: “The best reader is one who awaits the understanding of statements from the statements themselves rather than imposing it upon them; who reports rather than contributes; and who does not compel the statements to appear to contain what he had presumed before reading ought to be understood.”

Therefore, when our discourse concerns the things of God, let us grant to God knowledge of himself and serve his words with devout reverence. Let the pious reader diligently investigate the meaning of these statements, in case he may be able to discover some rationale for them. Once that is known, perhaps the foregoing question may in some measure be explained.

For my part, without resolving this question but excluding error, I profess that it is not said that the Father loves the Son, or the Son the Father, by the love proceeding from both—which is neither of them but the Holy Spirit alone—as though Father or Son existed by that love. Rather, the Father loves the Son by that love in such a way that the Father also loves by himself, through the love which he himself is; and likewise the Son. But this is not so that the Father and Son do not love by themselves, but only through that love. “Who,” Augustine says, “would dare to suppose or affirm these things concerning that Trinity?”

Nevertheless, we leave this question for the reader’s diligence more fully to judge and resolve, being less adequate to the task.

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. WHETHER THE PROPERTIES OF THE PERSONS ARE THE PERSONS THEMSELVES OR GOD, THAT IS, THE DIVINE ESSENCE

1. After what has been said, it must be considered more deeply and investigated more subtly whether the properties by which the persons themselves are determined are the persons themselves and are God—that is, the divine essence—or whether they exist in the persons in such a way that they are not persons and therefore not the divine essence.

No one dares deny that properties are in the persons, since authority openly declares that property is in the persons and unity in the essence. Above, too, we established by many testimonies of the saints that the persons are distinguished and determined by properties, and we expressed those same three properties by their proper names. Since, then, the properties by which the persons themselves are determined and differ have existed from eternity, how could they exist if they were not in them? And how could they be in them without themselves being persons, unless there were multiplicity there?

Accordingly, just as we confess that the properties are in the persons, so we confess that they are persons and the divine essence. As we declared above on Jerome’s authority—lest it be burdensome to recall it—he says in his exposition of the faith:

> Avoiding the heresy of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressed under property. For we confess not merely names but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences.

See: he plainly says that the persons are distinguished by properties and that the properties themselves are persons. We cite his words here briefly because we gave them more fully above.

### That the properties are the divine essence

2. When we discussed above the simplicity of deity, we clearly showed by the authorities of the saints—Augustine, Hilary, Isidore, and Boethius—that God is altogether whatever he has in himself, except that the Father has the Son and is not the Son, and the Son has the Father and is not the Father; and that in the nature of the three, whoever has is what he has; and that everything there is one and is one life. We do not repeat those passages now, lest we weary the reader.

Therefore, if the properties are there, each of them is that in which it is, and each is one and the same life. Let us therefore confess both that the properties are in the three persons and that they are themselves persons and the divine essence.

### Authority establishes that property is nature

3. Hilary shows that property is also the divine nature when he calls the Son’s birth nature. Hence he says in book 7 of *On the Trinity*: “The nature of each does not differ; Father and Son are one. Therefore the birth has this character of mystery: that it embraces in itself both name, nature, and power, because birth cannot be that nature from which the Son is born.”

Again, in book 6: “Birth is property; it is truth.” Again, in book 7 he says that the birth of nature must be understood as existing in the nature of God. For above he had said that it is proper to the Father always to be Father, and proper to the Son always to be Son, signifying that the Father’s property is Father and the Son’s property is Son.

By these and many other authorities it seems clearly signified that the Son’s property is the Son, and therefore God; likewise the Father’s property, and that of the Holy Spirit.

### Some deny that the properties are persons and the divine nature, and why

4. Some deny this. They indeed say that properties are in the persons, but deny that they are the persons themselves. They say that the properties exist in the persons or in the divine essence in such a way that they are not inwardly present, as are those things said of God according to substance, such as goodness and justice, but are externally attached; and they strive to prove this by arguments.

“For,” they say, “if properties are persons, the persons are not determined by them.” Against this we say that the persons also differ by themselves, as Jerome says above, speaking of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: “They are one in substance, but distinguished in persons and names.”

But they add again: “If the properties themselves are the divine essence, then, since the three persons do not differ in essence, neither do they differ in properties. For how does the Father differ from the Son by being divine essence, when they are one in essence?”

### A response to the foregoing, supported by authority

5. To these novel doctrines and human inventions I reply with the words of Hilary:

> What is demanded is immeasurable and incomprehensible. It lies beyond the meaning of speech and beyond the reach of thought. It cannot be uttered, attained, or grasped. The nature of the thing itself exhausts the signifying power of words; impenetrable light blinds the contemplation of the mind; that which is contained by no limit exceeds the capacity of understanding. Therefore there is failure in my understanding and stupefaction in my intelligence; in speech, however, I confess not merely weakness but silence. It is exceedingly dangerous to say anything concerning matters so great and hidden beyond the heavenly prescription, so that speech about God goes beyond God’s own definition. The form of faith is certain. Therefore nothing is to be added, but a limit must be set to boldness: whatever is investigated beyond this is not understood.

### How wicked heretics press their case by adding further arguments

6. Yet the perversity of heretics, stirred by the prompting of diabolical deceit, does not yet rest, but adds this in so great a question: “If paternity and filiation are in God or in the divine essence, then the same thing is Father and Son to itself. For where paternity is, there is Father; and where filiation is, there is Son. If, then, one and the same thing has paternity and filiation in itself, it itself begets and is begotten.”

In saying this, they are drawn into the Sabellian heresy, extending the Father into the Son, since they make him both Son and Father to himself. But if they deny that paternity and filiation are in the one essence of God, how then do they say that paternity and filiation are God? By these and other sharp arguments they seek to uphold their opinion and dissect the form of truth.

### A response to their objection: the properties are not in the divine essence in exactly the way in which they are said to be in the hypostases

7. Resisting their audacity and guarding against their ignorance, we shall dare to say something on this matter. Paternity and filiation are not said to be in the divine substance in exactly the way in which they are in the hypostases; in the hypostases they are present in such a manner that they determine them. As John of Damascus says in book 3 of *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 6: “The characteristic idioms”—that is, the determining properties—“belong to the hypostasis and not to the nature; for they determine the hypostasis and not the nature.”

Therefore, although paternity and filiation are in the divine essence, because they do not determine it, one cannot therefore say that the divine essence both begets and is begotten, or that the same thing is Father and Son to itself. For property determines the person in such a way that by one property one hypostasis is begetting, and by another a different hypostasis is begotten. Thus the same does not beget and is begotten, but one begets the other.

### It is asked how properties can be in the nature without determining it

8. But perhaps you will ask: since these properties cannot be in the persons without determining them, how can they be in the divine essence in such a way that they do not determine it? I answer you here too with Hilary, in book 1 of *On the Trinity*, not far from the beginning:

> I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I shall nevertheless take comfort. The archangels do not know; the angels have not heard; the ages do not comprehend; the prophet did not perceive; the Apostle did not ask; the Son himself did not disclose it. Let the distress of complaints therefore cease. Let no human being suppose that by his own understanding he can attain the mystery of generation.

Yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit must be understood without qualification. The understanding of these words stands at this limit: the Son is from the Father; he is the only-begotten from the unbegotten, offspring from parent, one from one; the nature of deity is not one thing in one and another in the other, because both are one. Begin by believing this; pursue it; persist in it. Though I know that you will not arrive at its end, I shall nevertheless rejoice that you advance. For one who devoutly pursues infinite things, even if he does not attain them, nevertheless makes progress as he goes forward.

But do not insert yourself into that secret and hidden mystery of unimaginable birth; do not plunge into it, presuming to comprehend the summit of understanding. Rather, understand that these things are incomprehensible. By these and many other passages it is clearly shown to us that we are in no way permitted to search out the divine majesty, impose a law on power, or prescribe a limit to the infinite.

### The authorities by which they support their opinion that the property of Father or Son is not God

9. Nevertheless, driven by a spirit of impatience, they do not desist, but try also to support their opinion with authorities of the saints. By these they intend to show that the property by which the Father is Father and that by which the Son is Son are not God.

For this purpose they introduce Augustine’s words, volume 2, on Psalm 68, “And there is no substance,” where he says:

> God is a certain substance. Thus we are also built up in the Catholic faith so as to say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance. What does “of one substance” mean? Whatever the Father is insofar as he is God, this the Son is, this the Holy Spirit is. But insofar as he is Father, he is not that which, or that by which, he is. For “Father” is said not with reference to himself but to the Son; whereas “God” is said with reference to himself. Therefore that which, or that by which, he is God is substance. And because the Son is of the same substance, without doubt the Son is God. But because the Father is Father not according to substance but in relation to the Son, we do not say that the Son is Father as we say that the Son is God.

From these words they say that it is signified that the Father’s property or the Son’s property is not God or the divine essence. For when Augustine says that that by which God is God is substance, but that by which he is Father is not substance, they say that he plainly shows that what makes God God is substance, whereas what makes him Father is not substance. Likewise, when he says, “The Father is not that which he is,” he shows that the Father is not Father by being substance. For he did not simply say, “The Father is not that which he is,” but said, “When he is Father, he is not that which he is,” signifying that that by which he is Father is not that by which he is, namely essence.

By interpreting the passage in this way, they make their own inventions seem true to the simple and unwary. But we say that these words must be understood otherwise. For in saying, “That by which he is God is substance, but that by which he is Father is not substance,” Augustine intended this: essence is God, and substance by deity. For he is substance by that by which he is God, and conversely, the one whose deity is substance and whose substance is deity. But the Father is not substance insofar as he is Father—that is, he is not substance by that by which he is Father—because he is Father by the property of generation, by which he is not substance. Yet Augustine did not deny that this property itself is substance.

Likewise, what he says, “When he is Father, he is not that which he is,” must be understood thus: he is not Father by that which, or by which, he himself is—that is, essence—but by a notion or relational property.

### They also use other words of Augustine to maintain that the properties of the persons are not God’s substance

10. They also press strongly the words of Augustine quoted above: that the Word, insofar as he is Wisdom and essence, is what the Father is; insofar as he is Word, he is not what the Father is. “If,” they say, “the Word is not what the Father is insofar as he is Word, then that by which he is Word is not that by which the Father is Father. Therefore the property by which the Word is Word is not what the Father is; therefore it is not the divine essence.”

To this we say that, although the Word is not what the Father is insofar as he is Word, nevertheless the property by which he is Word is what the Father is—that is, the divine essence—but it is not the hypostasis of the Father.

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. THE OPINION OF SOME WHO SAY THAT PERSON AND ESSENCE OR NATURE ARE NOT THE SAME, AND THAT THE SAME ESSENCE CANNOT BE FATHER, SON, AND HOLY SPIRIT
1. To the foregoing must be added that certain men of perverse understanding have rushed into such madness as to say that God’s nature is not identical with person or hypostasis, maintaining that the same essence cannot be Father and Son without a confusion of persons. “For,” they say, “if the essence which is the Father is the Son, Father and Son are identical with one another. If you call this thing Father, seek another thing which you may call Son. But if you seek no other, and call the same thing both, the same one both begot and was begotten.” For these and similar reasons, they divide nature from person, so that they do not admit that the one simple nature of the Godhead is three persons.

They attempt to defend this by Hilary’s testimony. In Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, asking whether, when the Apostle names “the Spirit of God” and “the Spirit of Christ,” he signifies the same thing by both expressions, he says:

> The preacher to the Gentiles, wishing to teach the unity of nature in Father and Son, says, Romans 8: “The Spirit of God is in you; but if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus,” and so forth. We are all spiritual if the Spirit of God is in us; but this Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ. And when Christ’s Spirit is in us, the Spirit of him who raised Christ is in us. And when the Spirit of him who raised Christ is in us, and Christ’s Spirit is in us, nevertheless the Spirit in us is not other than God’s Spirit. Distinguish, therefore, O heretic, the Spirit of Christ from the Spirit of God; and distinguish the Spirit of Christ, who was raised from the dead, from the Spirit of God, who raised Christ from the dead. Since the Spirit of Christ who dwells in us is the Spirit of God; and the Spirit of Christ who was raised from the dead is precisely the Spirit of God, who raises Christ from the dead. And now I ask whether, in “the Spirit of God,” you think nature is signified, or a thing belonging to nature. For nature is not the same as a thing belonging to nature: just as man is not the same as that which belongs to man, nor fire the same as that which belongs to fire; and accordingly God is not the same as that which belongs to God.

[Col. 0614]

On the occasion of this statement, the aforementioned heretics have taught that person and God’s nature are not identical, asserting that God’s nature is not three persons. In the preceding words of Hilary they understand “a thing belonging to nature” to mean a person, and “nature” to mean the divine nature. Thus they say that Hilary asked the heretic whether he thought that nature or a thing belonging to nature was signified by “the Spirit of God,” in order to show that nature must be distinguished from a thing belonging to nature—that is, from person.

### Here he teaches how the context of the passage itself answers them, how the foregoing words should be understood, and that the Holy Spirit is a thing of the one nature of Father and Son, and is that very nature.

2. Some say this because they have not considered with reverent care the context of Scripture. When it is considered, one may perceive how Hilary made the foregoing statement. For later in the same sequence he shows that “the Spirit of God” sometimes signifies the Father, as when it is said, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me”; sometimes the Son, as when it is said, “In the Spirit of God I cast out demons,” showing that he casts out demons by the power of his own nature; and sometimes the Holy Spirit, as there: “I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh.” He says this was fulfilled when, after the Holy Spirit had been sent, the Apostles spoke in every language.

Then he plainly shows why he made this distinction, that in the preceding words of the Apostle the same Holy Spirit was signified, and that the Spirit himself is a thing of the one nature of Father and Son:

> These things have been demonstrated for this reason: that whatever direction heretical falsehood might take, it might be enclosed within the bounds of truth. For Christ dwells in us; and, when he dwells, God dwells. And when the Spirit of Christ dwells in us, no Spirit other than the Spirit of God dwells there. But if Christ is understood to be in us through the Holy Spirit, we must nevertheless know this Spirit of God to be the Spirit of Christ; and, since by God’s nature nature itself dwells in us, the nature of the Son is believed not to differ from that of the Father, when the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of God, is shown to be a thing of one nature. Therefore I now ask: how are they not one by nature? The Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, is sent by the Son, and receives from the Son. But all that the Father has belongs to the Son. Therefore, the Spirit who receives from him is the Spirit of God, and the same Spirit is the Spirit of Christ. He is a thing of the Son’s nature, but that same thing is also of the Father’s nature; he is the Spirit of God who raised Christ from the dead, and the same Spirit is the Spirit of Christ who was raised from the dead. Does Christ’s nature differ in any respect from God’s nature, so that it is not the same, if it can be maintained that the Spirit who is God’s is not also Christ’s? Therefore the Spirit of God is in us, and the Spirit of Christ is in us; and when Christ’s Spirit is present, God’s Spirit is present. Thus, since what is God’s is Christ’s and what is Christ’s is God’s, Christ cannot be anything different from what God is. Therefore Christ is God, one with God in the Spirit, according to John 10: “I and the Father are one.” In this, Truth teaches that there is unity of nature, not the solitary character of union.

See: if you attend carefully to these words, you find that the Holy Spirit is called a thing of the Father’s and Son’s nature; and he is said to be God’s nature itself where it says: “By God’s nature nature itself dwells in us,” if Christ is in us through the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, in the Trinity, nature and a thing belonging to nature must not be distinguished as they are in created things. For, as Hilary says in the middle of Book I of *On the Trinity*, “There is no comparison of earthly things with God; and if examples of comparisons are sometimes brought forward, let no one suppose that they contain in themselves, absolutely speaking, perfect explanatory force. For one must not speak of God according to human understanding.”

### That he said, “Nature is not the same as a thing belonging to nature,” with reference to created things.

[Col. 0615]

3. Therefore, looking to the nature of created things, he says: “Nature is not the same as a thing belonging to nature,” adding examples from creatures themselves. Then, showing that it is erroneous to measure the Creator by the standard of creatures, he adds: “And accordingly God is not the same as that which belongs to God”; as though he said: If you think about the Creator in the manner of creatures, you are compelled to confess that God is not the same as that which belongs to God. But this is impious to say, since the Spirit of God is God and the Son of God is God.

### That God is not something other than his own things, in such a way that they are in him; for some things are in him and others are not.

4. Therefore these statements concerning God are not to be understood in bodily ways, as he adds in the same sequence. There, refuting the opinion of those who suppose that God is one thing and what belongs to God another, and that God’s nature and a thing belonging to that nature are different—as in creatures—he plainly teaches that God is not other than that which belongs to God, nor God’s nature other than his own things, in such a way that they are in him:

> When a human being, or something like one, is somewhere, he is not elsewhere, because that which he is is confined, in the form of his nature, to the place in which it is. Thus, in order that he may be everywhere, he must be standing somewhere. But God is a living power of immeasurable might, which is nowhere absent and nowhere lacking; which teaches that it is wholly present through its own things, and signifies that its own things are nothing other than itself, so that where its own things are present, it may be understood that God himself is present through them. Yet he must not be thought, in a bodily manner, to be somewhere and not also everywhere, since he does not cease to be in all things through his own things. And those things which are his are not other than what he himself is. These things have been said for the understanding of nature.

By these words it is plainly signified—if you understand, O heretic—that the divine nature is not other than those things which are its own in such a way that they are in it; and that God is in all his things through those that are in him. For his own things also include those which are not in him, namely all creatures; and his own things include those which are in him, namely the three persons, who are of the same nature and are the same nature. As we established above by Augustine’s testimony, he says that the three persons are of one essence, or are the same essence, but not from the same essence, lest essence be understood as one thing and person as another.

Yet we do not deny that a distinction must be made in the manner of understanding when “hypostasis” is said and when “essence” is said, because the latter signifies what is common to the three, whereas the former does not. Nevertheless hypostasis is essence, and conversely. Let us therefore confess that the three persons are one and the same according to essence, while differing in their properties.

Hence Augustine, Book VIII, on the previously cited passage of Psalm 68, says:

> You ask what the Father is. The answer is: God. You ask what the Son is. The answer is: God. You ask what Father and Son are. The answer is: God, God. When asked about each separately, answer “God.” When asked about both, answer not “gods” but “God.” It is not so among human beings. For there is there such unity of substance that it admits qualification but does not admit plurality. Therefore, if it is said to you, when you say that the Son of God is what the Father is, “Surely then the Son is the Father,” answer: “I said that the Son is what the Father is according to substance, not according to that which is said in relation to another. For ‘God’ is said with reference to himself; ‘Son’ is said with reference to the Father. Again, ‘God’ is said with reference to himself of the Father; ‘Father’ is said with reference to the Son. What is called Father with reference to the Son is not the Son; what is called Son with reference to the Father is not the Father; but what is called Father with reference to himself is what both Father and Son are—that is, God.”

### Whether one may say “one God of three persons” or “three persons of one God,” as one says “one essence of three persons” and “three persons of one essence.”

5. Here one must consider: since God is the divine essence, and the one God is said to be three persons just as the one essence is said to be three persons, may one soundly say, “one God of three persons” and “three persons of one God”? In such expressions, the usage of Scripture seems to be imitated. There one frequently finds: “One essence of three persons,” and “three persons of one essence.” But nowhere do I recall reading “one God of three persons” or “three persons of one God.”

[Col. 0616]

I think the holy teachers avoided this lest it perhaps be understood of the divine persons as similar expressions are understood when used of creatures. For one speaks of “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” and “the God of every creature.” This is said because of the primacy of creation, or the privilege of grace, and the creature’s subjection or servitude. Since, therefore, there is nothing created, serving, or subjected in the Trinity, the faith has not admitted such a form of expression in speaking of the Trinity.

Likewise, conversely, God’s essence is not said to be the essence of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, or any creature, lest we seem to confuse the natures of Creator and creature.

### Although power, wisdom, and goodness are said of God according to substance in Scripture, these names are nevertheless sometimes distinctly referred to the persons.

6. From the foregoing it is clear that, like essence, power, wisdom, and goodness are said of God according to substance. What is said of God according to substance belongs equally to the three persons. Therefore the power, wisdom, and goodness of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one; and these three are the same power, the same wisdom, the same goodness.

Thus it is evident that the highest perfection is in the Trinity. For if power, wisdom, or goodness were lacking there, it would not be the highest good. But because there is perfect power, infinite wisdom, and incomprehensible goodness there, it is rightly said and believed to be the highest good.

Although power, wisdom, and goodness are altogether one and the same in God, Sacred Scripture frequently refers these names distinctly to the persons: power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit. Why this is done is not an idle matter to investigate.

### Why this is done—namely, why power is attributed to the Father and wisdom to the Son.

7. Therefore the wisdom of sacred speech has taken care to do this, lest we measure God’s immensity by the analogy of a creature. Sacred Scripture had said that God is Father and that God is Son. A man heard this—a man who had seen a human father but had not seen God the Father—and began to think that the Creator was as he had seen creatures to be. These names have been transferred from creatures to the Creator; among creatures, a father is prior to his son, a son later than his father, and antiquity in the father is commonly thought to imply decay, while later origin in the son implies an imperfection of understanding.

Therefore Scripture meets this by calling the Father powerful, lest he seem prior to the Son and thus less powerful; and by calling the Son wise, lest he seem later than the Father and thus less wise.

### Why goodness is attributed to the Holy Spirit.

8. The Holy Spirit too was called God, and God was said to have a Spirit; and this appeared almost to be a name of pride and swelling. Consequently the human conscience fears to approach God as stern and cruel. Scripture therefore moderated its language by calling him the good Spirit, lest he who is gentle be thought cruel.

This does not mean that the Father alone is powerful or more powerful, the Son alone wise or wiser, or the Holy Spirit alone good or better. The power, wisdom, and goodness of the three are one, just as their essence is one. Therefore, just as the Son is called *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with the Father, so he is also called co-omnipotent.

### Concerning the name *homoousion*: where it was received into authority and what it signifies.

9. Here it must not be passed over that Augustine, in Book III *Against Maximinus*, says concerning the term *homoousion*, frequently used by Latin writers:

> Father and Son are of one and the same substance. This is that *homoousion* which, at the Council of Nicaea, was established by the authority of Truth through the Catholic Fathers against the Arian heretics. Later, at the Council of Rimini, heretical impiety, under the heretical emperor Constantine, attempted to undermine it because the novelty of the word was understood less fully than it ought to have been—though the ancient faith had produced it—and because many were deceived by the deceit of a few. But not long afterward, when the freedom of the Catholic faith prevailed and the force of the term had been understood as it should be, that *homoousion* was extended and spread far and wide in the soundness of Catholic faith. For what is *homoousion* except “of one and the same substance”? What, I ask, is *homoousion* except “I and the Father are one” [John 10]? Therefore it is not to be avoided among the unfamiliar expressions of secular speech.

[Col. 0617]

### Concerning names said of God metaphorically and by likeness.

10. Moreover, it must be known that, in setting out the distinction of names, among other things which we have carefully expounded above, we have said that certain terms are said of God metaphorically and by likeness: such as mirror, radiance, character, figure, and the like. Concerning them I briefly offer the devout reader what I think, so that, considering the character of the likeness, he may draw a Catholic understanding of these sayings from the reasons for using them.

### He confesses that he has set forth nothing worthy of the ineffable excellence of the Trinity, and proceeds to other matters.

11. We have now said much concerning the mystery of the unity and Trinity that is supreme and ineffable. Yet we confess that we have handed down nothing worthy of its ineffability; rather, its knowledge has been made wondrous to us, and we have been unable to attain to it.

## DISTINCTION XXXV. CONCERNING CERTAIN THINGS SAID OF GOD ACCORDING TO SUBSTANCE WHICH REQUIRE SPECIAL TREATMENT: NAMELY, KNOWLEDGE, FOREKNOWLEDGE, PROVIDENCE, DISPOSITION, PREDESTINATION, WILL, AND POWER.

1. Since above we have discussed and said much concerning those things which are commonly said of God according to substance, some of them nevertheless require special treatment. We must now treat of these: knowledge, foreknowledge, providence, disposition, predestination, will, and power.

It must be known, then, that God’s wisdom or knowledge, though one and simple, receives many diverse names because of the various states of things and different effects. For it is called not merely knowledge, but also foreknowledge or providence. Knowledge or providence concerns not future things only, but all things: both good and evil. Disposition concerns things to be done; predestination concerns all who are to be saved and all good things by which they are delivered here and crowned in the future.

For God predestined human beings from eternity, choosing them for good; and he predestined good things for them, preparing those good things. That he predestined persons, the Apostle shows when he says, Romans 8: “He predestined those whom he foreknew to become conformed to the image of his Son”; and Ephesians 1: “He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish.” That he prepared good things for them, the prophet Isaiah shows, chapter 46, saying: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you,” or “who wait for you.”

Therefore from eternity he predestined certain persons to be good and blessed—that is, he chose that they should be good and blessed; and he predestined good things for them—that is, he prepared them. Providence concerns things to be governed, and seems indeed to be understood in the same way as disposition. Yet providence is sometimes taken for foreknowledge.

Wisdom or knowledge, however, concerns all things: good and evil, present, past, and future; and not temporal things only, but eternal things also. For God does not know temporal things in such a way that he does not know himself. Rather, he alone knows himself perfectly, and in comparison with his knowledge every creature’s knowledge is imperfect.

### Whether knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, or predestination could have been in God if nothing were going to be.

2. Here it must be considered whether knowledge, foreknowledge, disposition, or predestination could have been in God if nothing were going to be. Since foreknowledge concerns future things, disposition things to be done, and predestination things to be saved, if nothing were future—if God were going to do nothing or save no one—there seems to have been no foreknowledge, disposition, or predestination in God. But God could have foreknown no future things; he could have created nothing, and thus saved no one. Therefore foreknowledge, disposition, or predestination could have been absent from God.

Some object to this as follows. “If God’s foreknowledge could have not been in God from eternity, then it could have failed to be. But if it could have failed to be, since God’s foreknowledge is his knowledge and his knowledge is his essence, then that which is his divine essence could have failed to be from eternity.” They make the same objection about disposition and predestination, which are the divine essence.

They add further arguments in these terms: “If God could fail to foreknow—that is, to know, and to be—he could therefore fail to be. Again, since being God who foreknows and being God are identical, if he could fail to foreknow, he could fail to be God. But he could fail to foreknow if he could foreknow nothing; and he could foreknow nothing because he could make nothing.”

[Col. 0618]

### Reply: foreknowledge, disposition, and predestination are spoken of, as it were, relatively to future things or things to be done.

3. To this we reply, according to the measure of our understanding, as follows. Foreknowledge, disposition, and predestination appear to be said with reference to something. For as Creator is said relatively to creature, so foreknowledge or foreknowing appears to refer to future things, disposition to things to be done, and predestination to things to be saved.

Nonetheless, “Creator” is said relatively in such a way that it does not signify essence. But “foreknowledge” or “foreknowing” is said both in relation to future things and as designating essence; likewise disposition and predestination.

Therefore, when it is said, “If nothing were future, there would be no foreknowledge in God,” or “God would not foreknow,” the reason for the statement must be distinguished, because the grounds of speaking are diverse. If, then, you say, “If nothing were future, there would be no foreknowledge in God,” or “he would not foreknow,” and you mean that there would be nothing subject to his foreknowledge, from which it could be called foreknowledge or he foreknowing—both terms being used because of future things—this understanding is true. But if you say it because there would be no knowledge in him by which he foreknows future things, or because he would not be God who foreknows future things, the understanding is false.

The same qualification must be applied to the expressions: “God’s foreknowledge could fail to be,” “he could fail to foreknow,” and “God could fail to foreknow some things.” They mean: it could be the case that no future things were subject to his knowledge, and hence he could not be called foreknowing or said to foreknow, nor could his knowledge be called foreknowledge. Yet he himself, and his knowledge, would be no less present. But he could not be called foreknowing, or said to foreknow, nor could his knowledge be called foreknowledge, if no future things were subject to his knowledge. The same applies to disposition, predestination, and providence. For these, as has been said, refer to temporal things and concern temporal things alone.
