### That God’s knowledge concerns not temporal things only but eternal things also.

4. Knowledge or wisdom, however, concerns not temporal things only but eternal things also. Therefore, even if nothing were future, the same knowledge that is now in God would still be in him; it would not be less than it now is, nor is it greater than it would be. From eternity God knew the eternal, and everything that was to be; and he knew it unchangeably.

He knows past and future things no less than present things, and by his eternal and immutable wisdom he himself knows all that is known. For, as Ambrose says, “Every principle of supreme and eternal wisdom is in him, because his immeasurable knowledge comprehends all wisdom and essence.”

### Why all things are said to be in God, and why what has been made is said to have life in him.

5. For this reason all things are said to be in God and to have been from eternity. Hence Augustine, Book V, chapter 18, on Genesis, volume III, says:

> Before these visible things were made, they were not; how, then, were things which were not known to God? And again: how could he make things unknown to him? For he made nothing in ignorance. He made them known; he did not come to know them when made. Accordingly, before they were made, they both were and were not. They were in God’s knowledge; they were not in their own nature. But I dare not say that they became known to God in one way when he made them and in another way when he knew them in order to make them; for with him there is no change, nor shadow from turning.

Here you have that these visible things were in God’s knowledge before they were made. In this sense, therefore, all things are said to be in God, and everything made is said to be life in him—not because creature is Creator, or because these temporal things are essentially in God, but because they are always in his knowledge, which is life.

### That for the same reason all things are said to be present to him.

6. Hence all things are said to be present to him: not only things that are, but also things that have passed and things that are future, according to Romans 4: “He calls those things which are not as though they were.” For, as Ambrose says in *On the Trinity*, “he knows things which are not as he knows things which are.”

For this reason all things are said to be in him, or with him, or present to him. Thus Augustine, Book V, chapter 8, volume VIII, on the passage of Psalm 49, “And the beauty of the field is with me,” says:

> It is with me because with God nothing has passed away and nothing is future. All future things are with him, and things already past are not withdrawn from him; all are with him in a certain ineffable knowledge of God’s wisdom.

Here Augustine explains in what sense such statements are to be understood: “All things are present to God”; “all things are in God,” or “with God,” or “with him”; or “in him, life.” They are so said because the ineffable knowledge of all things is in him.

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. WHETHER IT SHOULD BE GRANTED THAT ALL THINGS ARE IN GOD’S ESSENCE, OR IN HIM THROUGH ESSENCE, AS ALL THINGS ARE SAID TO BE IN GOD’S KNOWLEDGE OR FOREKNOWLEDGE.

1. A question is commonly raised here. Since all things are said to be in God’s knowledge or foreknowledge, or in God through knowledge, and since his knowledge or foreknowledge is the divine essence, should it be granted that all things are in the divine essence, or in God through essence?

We answer that God’s knowledge is indeed his essence, and that his foreknowledge, in which all things are, is his knowledge. Nevertheless, not everything that is in his foreknowledge or knowledge should be said to be in his essence. For if this were said, those things would be understood to be of the same essence as God. For that is said to be in God through essence which is the divine essence, which is God.

Thus God has with himself in his foreknowledge things which he does not have in his own nature. Hence Augustine, volume X, Sermon 11, *On the Words of the Apostle*, says:

> “He chose us before the foundation of the world.” Who is sufficient to explain this? Those who do not exist are chosen; nor did he who chose not exist, nor did he choose in vain. Yet he chose, and he has as chosen those whom he is going to create and choose; he had them with himself, not in his own nature but in his foreknowledge. Those to whom the promise was made did not yet exist; yet they too were promised, to whom the promise was made.

Here he plainly says that God had the elect with himself before the foundation of the world, not in his own nature but in his foreknowledge, although his foreknowledge is nothing other than his nature, because his foreknowledge is his knowledge. Yet when he says “not in his own nature,” this can be referred to the elect: that is, not in their nature. For he had them with himself from eternity, not in their own nature, since they did not yet exist, but in his foreknowledge, because he knew them as though they existed.

### Whether evils should be said to be in God, where all good things are, since both are in his knowledge and foreknowledge; for he knows all things.

2. After the foregoing, the question arises: since all things are said to be in God not through the essence of nature but through the knowledge of science, and since God knows good and evil, should evils simply be said to be in God, or to be in God through knowledge?

For God knows, and has always known, all things, good as well as evil, even before they happened; and from eternity he foreknew that they would be. Therefore, since we said that all good things are in God because of the foreknowledge of knowledge, the same reasoning seems to require us to say that all evils are in him, since he has always known them and they have been present to him through knowledge. For God foreknew from eternity that some would be evil, and, as Augustine says, he foreknew their wickedness but did not prepare it.

Since, therefore, he knows everyone’s sins, should they be understood to be included in the general statement in which the Apostle says, Romans 11, that all things are in God? “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.” But who, except one mad, would say that evils are in God? For those things are understood to be in God which are from him and through him. But those things are through him and from him of which he is the author; and he is the author only of good things. Therefore only good things are from him and through him; hence only good things are in him, and evils are not in God.

Although he knows evils, he does not know them altogether as he knows good things. He knows evils, therefore, as though from far off, as the Prophet says, Psalm 137: “And he knows lofty things from afar,” that is, pride. And elsewhere, speaking to God concerning evils, he says: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things.” Explaining this, Augustine says: “The hidden things are sins, which are hidden from the light of your truth.”

But how are sins hidden from the light of divine truth if they are known by God? For if he did not know them, how would he judge concerning them and condemn the wicked for them? Elsewhere the Prophet says: “For he is absent neither from the east nor from the west.” Explaining this, Cassiodorus says: “God is absent neither from good persons nor evil persons, but is present to all and knows all.”

God therefore knows good and evil through knowledge; but he knows good things also through approval and good pleasure, whereas he does not know evils in this way. Hence Cassiodorus, on Psalm 16, says: “Sins are hidden from God because he does not know them,” that is, does not approve them. And in this sense Augustine said that they are hidden from God’s light. In his work *Against Helvidius* he also indicates that God’s knowledge is understood in various ways:

> If you refer it to knowledge, God does not fail to know any persons or things; yet at the judgment he will say to certain persons, “I never knew you.” By this expression, however, their rejection is indicated.

See: God is said not to know what he does not approve, what does not please him. Thus what we have said is shown to be true: God knows good things in a manner in which he does not know evil things. He knows both alike, indeed, in the same manner so far as bare knowledge is concerned; but he knows good things also by approval and good pleasure.

[Col. 0620]

### Here he explains why good things alone are said to be in God, and not evils.

3. This is why good things alone are said to be in God, not evils; the former near, the latter far off. Although certain things are said to be in God because of the presence supplied by knowledge, and God knows good and evil, he knows evils only through bare knowledge, while he knows good things not only through knowledge but through approval and good pleasure. Things are said to be in God because of such knowledge—namely, because he knows them in such a way as to approve them and to be pleased by them; that is, he knows them in such a way as to be their author.

### That “all things are from God,” “through him,” and “in him” mean the same thing.

4. Therefore, if we examine closely, “all things are from God,” “through him,” and “in him” seem to mean the same thing. Hence Ambrose, Book II *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 12, says:

> We have said above that these three expressions—“from him,” “through him,” and “in him are all things” [Romans 11]—are one. When he says that all things are through him, he does not deny that all things are in him. All these expressions have the same force: “with him,” “in him,” and “through him”; and one and similar thing, not contrary things, is understood in them.

Here you have that Scripture says that all things are in him, through him, from him, and with him in the same sense. Since all things are said to be from God or through him for the same reason—not only because he knows them but because he is their author—it follows that they are said to be in God for the same reason: namely, because he knows them and is said to be their author, “for in him we live and move and are.”

Since he is the author only of good things, good things alone are rightly said to be in him, just as they are from him and through him. Therefore, although all things—good and evil—are in his knowledge or foreknowledge, only good things, of which he is the author, are said to be in him. Hence Augustine, in *On the Nature of the Good*, says:

> When we hear that all things are from God, through him, and in him, we must certainly understand all natures and everything that exists naturally. For sins, which do not preserve nature but corrupt it, are not from him; all sins arise from the will of those who sin.

Here it is plainly said that only good things are included in that general statement.

[Col. 0621]

### That all things are from the Father, through the Father, and in the Father; and the same must be said of the Son and the Holy Spirit, although a distinction is made because of the persons.

5. Moreover, it must be known that although a distinction of persons is indicated when it is said, “from him,” “through him,” and “in him,” nevertheless all things are from the Father, through the Father, and in the Father. The same must be understood of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Hence Augustine, Book I *On the Trinity*, chapter 10, says:

> The Apostle’s statement, “From him, through him, and in him,” must not be understood confusedly: “from him,” because of the Father; “through him,” because of the Son; “in him,” because of the Holy Spirit. But take careful heed: because he said “from him” intending the Father, do not understand all things to be from the Father in such a way as to deny that all things are from the Son or from the Holy Spirit. For it may rightly be said that all things are from the Father, through the Father, and in the Father; likewise the same must be said of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

### That not all things which are from God are also from his substance; but the converse is true.

6. This also should be added: not everything said to be from God should also be said to be from his substance. For, as Augustine says in *On the Nature of the Good*, chapter 27, “from him” does not altogether signify the same as “from his substance.” What is from his substance can be said to be from him; but not everything which is from him can be said to be from his substance, because it is not from his substance.

For heaven and earth are from him because he made them, but they are not from his substance, because they are not from his substance. Just as if a man generates a son and makes a house, the son is from him and the house is from him; but the son is from his substance, whereas the house is from earth and wood, not from him.

### He gathers together briefly what has been said.

7. From the foregoing it is clear that all things, good and evil alike, are in God’s knowledge or foreknowledge; but evils are not there in every way in which good things are. Good things alone, not evils, are in God, just as they are from him and through him. The sense in which these statements must be understood has been explained. It has also been shown that what is other than God is not properly said to be from his substance. But all things of which he is the author are said to be from him.

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. THE WAYS IN WHICH GOD IS SAID TO BE IN THINGS.

1. And since it has been shown in part how all things are said to be in God, it seems fitting to add here in what ways God is said to be in things—if indeed the human mind can worthily conceive this even in part, or language suffice to express it. It must therefore be known that God, always existing unchangeably in himself, is in every nature or essence by presence, power, and essence, without being bounded; in every place, without spatial circumscription; and in every time, without changeability. Moreover, he is in holy spirits and souls more excellently, dwelling there by grace; and most excellently in the man Christ, “in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily,” as the Apostle says. For in him God dwelt not by the grace of adoption, but by the grace of union.

Lest anyone presume, because these matters exceed the capacity of human understanding, to charge them with falsehood, it seems to me that they should be fortified by the authorities of the saints. Blessed Gregory, on the Song of Songs [Note: [Col. 0621] This is not found in his work on the Song of Songs, but accords in sense with Ezekiel], says: “Although God is present to all things in a common manner by presence, power, and substance, nevertheless he is said to be in a more intimate manner by grace in those who consider more keenly and faithfully the wonderful character of God’s works.”

On this same matter Augustine, in his book *On the Presence of God*, addressed to Dardanus, says: “Since God is an incorporeal nature and unchangeably living, abiding in himself with eternal stability, he is wholly present to all things and wholly present to each individual thing. Yet those in whom he dwells possess him according to the diversity of their capacity, some more, some less; these he builds for himself, by the grace of his goodness, as a temple most beloved by him.”

Hilary too, in Book 8 of *On the Trinity*, teaches most plainly [Col. 0622] that God is everywhere. “God,” he says, “is a living power of immeasurable might, who is absent nowhere and lacking nowhere; he teaches that he is wholly present through his works, so that wherever his works are, he himself may be understood to be. Nor, because he is somewhere, should he be thought to be there in a bodily manner and not also everywhere, since he does not cease to be in all things.”

Ambrose, in *On the Holy Spirit*, proves that the Holy Spirit is not a creature because he is everywhere, which is proper to divinity. He says: “Since every creature is bounded by fixed limits of its nature, how can anyone dare to call the Holy Spirit a creature, when he has no circumscribed and determinate power, but is always in all things and everywhere? This is certainly proper to divinity and lordship.” The same author, in the same work: “It belongs to the Lord to fill all things, who says: ‘I fill heaven and earth.’ If, therefore, he who fills heaven and earth is Lord, who can judge the Holy Spirit to be devoid of lordship and divine power, when he has filled the world and—what is greater—has also filled Jesus, the Redeemer of the whole world?”

From these and many other authorities it is plainly shown that God is everywhere in every creature by essence, presence, and power.

### That he is not merely present in the saints, but also dwells in them; for he does not dwell wherever he is

2. He also dwells in the saints, in whom he is by grace. For he does not dwell wherever he is; but wherever he dwells, there he is. He dwells only in the good, who are his temple and his seat. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah 66:2: “Heaven is my throne, and earth is my footstool.” For God dwells and reigns in the elect, who are heaven, because they devotedly obey his will; but he tramples the wicked, who are earth, with the severity of judgment.

Hence in the Book of Wisdom the soul of the righteous is called the throne of wisdom, because God is present in the righteous more specially than in other things—though he is wholly present in all of them. As Augustine says, vol. 2, Epistle 28, to Jerome, *On the Origin of the Soul*, the soul is wholly present at once through all the parts of the body, neither smaller in smaller parts nor greater in greater parts; yet it operates more intensely in some and more weakly in others, although it is essentially whole in every individual part of the body.

So too, although God is essentially and wholly in all things, he is said to be more fully in those whom he inhabits; that is, in those in whom he is so present that he makes them his temple. Such persons are already with him in part here, but perfectly in blessedness. The wicked, however, although they are where he is, for he is absent nowhere, are nevertheless not with him.

Hence Augustine, vol. 9, Tractate 111 on John 17: “It was not enough to say, ‘Where I am, let them also be’; but he added, ‘with me,’ because the miserable can be even where he is, who is absent nowhere. But the blessed are with him, because they are blessed only by being with him: they enjoy him and see him as he is. The wicked, however, are not with him; and the blind who are in the light are not with the light. Nor are even the good now so with him as to see him by direct sight, although they are with him in some manner through faith.”

How God dwells in the good you will be able to understand in some measure from what was said above when the temporal procession of the Holy Spirit was discussed. There it is explained, though only in part—for “we know in part and we prophesy in part”—how the Holy Spirit dwells in us, and he does not dwell without the Father and the Son.

### Where God was or dwelt before there was a creature

3. But if you ask where God dwelt before the saints existed, we say that he dwelt in himself. Hence Augustine, Book 3, chapter 21, *Against Maximinus*: “God dwells in his temple,” that is, in the saints, who are God’s temple, now walking by faith and someday to be God’s temple by direct sight, just as the angels are even now God’s temple. But someone will say: “Before God made heaven and earth, before he made the saints, where did he dwell?” God dwelt in himself; he dwells in you, and he is in himself. Therefore the saints are not God’s house in such a way that, if it were removed, God would collapse. Rather, God dwells in the saints in such a way that, if he departed, they would collapse.

### Here he briefly teaches many things confirming what has been said

[Col. 0623]

4. It must also be known that, as Augustine says in his book to Dardanus, vol. 2, Epistle 57, it can only be said most foolishly that the Holy Spirit has no place in our body, when our soul fills that whole body. It is said even more foolishly that the Trinity can be cramped somewhere, so that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot be somewhere together.

But far more wonderful is this: although God is wholly present everywhere, he nevertheless does not dwell in all things. Who, moreover, unless he entirely ignores the inseparability of the Trinity, would dare suppose that the Father and Son can dwell in someone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, or that the Holy Spirit can dwell in someone in whom the Father and Son do not dwell? We must therefore confess that God is everywhere by the presence of his divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of indwelling. Because of this indwelling grace, we do not say, “Our Father who art everywhere,” though this too is true, but, “Who art in heaven” (Matthew 6), that is, in the saints, in whom he is in a certain more excellent manner.

### That God dwells in some who do not yet know God, and not in some who know him

5. This too is wonderful: as Augustine says in the same work, God is the indweller of some who do not yet know God, and not of some who do know God. For those who know God but do not glorify him as God do not belong to God’s temple. But little children sanctified by Christ’s sacrament and regenerated by the Holy Spirit, who are not yet able to know God, do belong to God’s temple. Therefore those others were able to know him without possessing him, while these were able to possess him before knowing him. But those are most blessed for whom to possess God is to know him.

Here Augustine explains in some measure how God dwells in someone: that is, how he is possessed, namely when he is in someone in such a way as to be known and loved by that person.

### How God is wholly everywhere by essence cannot be understood by the human mind

6. From what has been said it is clear that God is wholly everywhere by essence and dwells in the saints by grace. Although it has been shown above, however slightly, on what ground he is said to dwell in certain persons, the order of the discussion would now demand an explanation of how he is everywhere and wholly present by essence—were not the loftiness and immensity of this consideration utterly beyond the grasp of the human mind.

Chrysostom says the same in his commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Just as we understand many things about God which we are wholly unable to express, so we say many things which we are not capable of understanding. For example, we know and say that God is everywhere; but how he is everywhere we do not grasp by the intellect. Likewise, we know that there is a certain incorporeal power which is the cause of all good things; but what it is, or what manner of thing it is, we utterly do not know.”

### The opinion of some who presume to show how God is everywhere by essence, power, and presence

7. Nevertheless, some, presuming to measure the immeasurable by their own intellect, have taught that this should be understood as follows: God is said to be everywhere by essence, not because God’s essence itself is properly in every place and every creature, but because every nature and everything that exists naturally, wherever it may be, has being through that essence—and so does every place in which it exists.

They likewise say that God is called everywhere by presence or power because all places and the things in them are present to him, and he never ceases to work in them. For the places themselves and whatever is in them could not remain unless he preserved them. Therefore, they say, God is said to be in them by substance because by the power of his own substance he causes both places and all things in them to exist.

But although what they assert is true in explaining the meanings just mentioned, nevertheless the words that say that God is everywhere by essence should be believed to contain more than a living human being can comprehend.

### That, although God is in all things, he is not defiled by the impurities of things

8. The same persons also commonly ask how God can be substantially present in all things without being touched by the defilement of bodily filth. This is so frivolous a question that it does not deserve an answer, since even a created spirit cannot be defiled by bodily impurities, even those of a leper or of one however polluted.

The sun too pours out its rays without defiling itself over places and bodies that are not merely clean but also unclean and foul with filth. Human beings and certain other things are infected by contact with such things; but the rays of the sun remain undefiled and uncontaminated while touching them. It is therefore no wonder that the utterly simple and unchangeable divine essence fills all places and is essentially present in all creatures, yet is neither defiled nor touched by the filth of any thing.

Hence Augustine, in *On the Nature of the Good*: “Although all the things which God has implanted are in God, those who sin do not defile him.” Of his wisdom also, “which reaches mightily from end to end,” it is said: “It reaches all things because of its purity, and nothing defiled enters into it.” Some fear what cannot happen: namely, that the truth and substance of God may be defiled by human flesh. Yet they proclaim that this visible sun scatters its rays through every kind of refuse and filth, and that the rays remain clean and pure.

If, therefore, visible clean things can touch visible unclean things without being defiled, how much more can invisible and unchangeable Truth do so. Finally, let them answer what they think should rather be said of God: that he is nowhere by essence, or that he is everywhere, or that he is somewhere but not everywhere. But who would dare say either that the divine essence is nowhere, or that it is somewhere and not everywhere? For if it is somewhere in such a way as not to be everywhere, then it is local.

Therefore it is wholly everywhere: it contains all and penetrates all; it can neither be divided because of its simplicity, nor stained because of its purity, nor in any way comprehended because of its immensity. Hence Augustine, Book 1, chapter 10, *On Christian Doctrine*: “God is everywhere; we draw near to him not by places but by actions.”

### That God is everywhere and in every time, yet is neither local nor circumscribable, and is moved neither by place nor time

9. Although the divine nature is truly and essentially in every place and every time, it is nevertheless not moved through places or times, nor is it local or temporal; rather, it is moved by affection and cognition. It is not local because it is not at all circumscribed by place: it is not in one place in such a way that it is not in another. Nor does it have dimensions as a body does, whose beginning, middle, and end, front and back, right and left, above and below, are assigned according to place, and which by interposing itself produces distance and surrounding space.

For Scripture calls something local or circumscribable in two ways, and conversely not local or uncircumscribable: either because it possesses dimensions of length and breadth and produces spatial distance, as a body does; or because it is defined and determined by a place, since, being somewhere, it is not found everywhere. The latter applies not only to a body but to every created spirit.

Every body, therefore, is local in every respect. But a created spirit is local in one sense and not local in another. It is called local because it is bounded by the definition of a place: when it is wholly present somewhere, it is not found elsewhere. But it is not local in such a way as to possess dimensions or produce spatial distance. For if many spirits were here, they would not thereby make the place so cramped that it could no longer contain bodies.

Accordingly Augustine attributes change of place to a body, not to a spirit. Although a spirit passes from place to place, it does not do so in such a way as, being circumscribed by dimensions, to make distance by its own interposition, as a body does.

### What it is to be changed according to time

10. To be changed through time is to be varied according to interior or exterior qualities which are in the thing itself that is changed: as when it undergoes a succession of joy, sorrow, knowledge, or forgetfulness, or a variation of form or of some exterior quality. This change which occurs according to time is a variation of qualities occurring in a bodily or spiritual creature; and for this reason it is called time.

### The opinion of some who say that created spirits are moved in place and are not local

11. Concerning change of place, however, a great dispute is carried on among those who investigate the matter. For there are some who say that no spirit can in any way be changed in place, wishing universally to remove place from every spirit. For they maintain that place consists only in dimension and circumscription, and say that only what receives dimension and produces distance in a place is local or in a place. They say that Augustine held this view, attributing change of time only to a spiritual creature, but change of both place and time to a bodily creature.

### Here he answers them

12. But, as we said above, a thing is called local or circumscribable in two ways: either because it receives dimension and produces distance, or because it is bounded by a limit of place. Both apply to a bodily creature, but only the latter to a spiritual creature. For, as we said above, a bodily creature is local or circumscribable in that it is determined by the definition of a place and, by receiving dimensions, produces distance. A spiritual creature, however, is enclosed only by the definition of a place, since it is somewhere in such a way that it is not elsewhere; yet it neither receives dimensions nor produces distance in a place. For if many spirits were here, they would not make the place so cramped that it could not contain bodies.

Therefore Augustine attributes change of place to a body, not to a spirit, because although a spirit passes from place to place, it does not do so in such a way that, being circumscribed by dimensions, it produces distance by its own interposition, as a body does.

### Conclusion from the foregoing: created spirits are in some manner local and circumscribable, but God’s Spirit is wholly uncircumscribable

13. Created spirits, therefore, are in a place and pass from place to place; they are in some manner local and circumscribable, though not in every respect in which bodily creatures are. But the uncreated Spirit, who is God, is indeed in a place—and in every place—yet is wholly nonlocal and uncircumscribable.

Hence Bede, commenting on Luke, says: “When angels come to us, they outwardly perform their ministry while inwardly standing before God in contemplation. For although an angel is a circumscribed spirit, the supreme Spirit, who is God, is uncircumscribed, and within him the angel moves wherever it is sent.” Here it is said that the angelic spirit is circumscribed, but that the Spirit who is God is uncircumscribed.

Elsewhere Ambrose, showing the difference between the uncreated and created spirit, says in Book 1, chapter 1, *On the Holy Spirit*, speaking thus in *On the Trinity*: “Isaiah said that one of the seraphim was sent to me. The Holy Spirit too is said to be sent, but a seraph is sent to one person, whereas the Spirit is sent to all. A seraph is sent in ministry; the Spirit works the mystery. A seraph passes from place to place, for it does not fill all things but is itself filled by the Spirit.” Here it is plainly shown that angels are in some manner local.

### Repeating the preceding points, he confirms by authorities that God is everywhere without local movement

14. Let us therefore confess that the divine nature, because of its immensity, is absent nowhere; that it alone is wholly nonlocal and wholly uncircumscribable, enclosed by no place; and that it reaches from end to end—not through spatial extension or local movement, but through the immensity and immobility of its essence.

Hence Augustine, Epistle 57, to Dardanus, says: “We should not suppose that God is diffused throughout all things by spatial magnitude, as smoke or this light is diffused. Rather, consider two wise persons, one of whom is physically larger than the other but not wiser: wisdom is one; it is not greater in the larger person, smaller in the smaller person, or smaller in one than in two. So God, effortlessly ruling and containing the world, is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly in both, contained by no place, but wholly everywhere in himself.”

The same author, commenting on the Psalmist’s words, “He runs swiftly,” says: “It belongs to the Word of God not to be in a part but to be everywhere through itself. For this is the wisdom of God, which reaches mightily from end to end, not by local movement but by its own immobility. Just as if a mass of stone fills a certain place, it is said to reach from one end of that place to the other, although it does not abandon one end by occupying the other. That Word therefore has no local motion, and that Wisdom is solid and everywhere.”

From what has been said it is clear that God is everywhere by essence in such a way that he is neither diffused by spatial magnitude nor occupies one place by abandoning another, because he has no local movement. Therefore Augustine, wishing to exclude from God’s purity every local movement and every local circumscription, says rather that all things are in him than that he is somewhere; yet he does not say that God is a place, since he is not in a place.

In Book 20 of the *Eighty-Three Questions*, Augustine says: “God is not somewhere. Whatever is somewhere is contained by a place; whatever is contained by a place is a body. But God is not a body; therefore he is not somewhere. Yet because he is, and is not in a place, all things are rather in him than he is somewhere. Yet they are not in him in such a way that he himself is a place. For a place is a space occupied by the length, breadth, and height of a body; and God is no such thing. Therefore all things are in him, and he is not a place, nor is he in a place. Nevertheless, the temple of God is called God’s place, though improperly, not because he is contained by it. Nothing is understood as this temple better than a pure soul.”

Here Augustine says that God is not in a place; but this must be understood to mean that he is not in a place locally, that is, because he has neither circumscription nor local movement.

### Objection apparently proving that God changes place

15. The following objection is commonly made: Creatures come to exist which did not exist before, and God is in them whereas he was not in them before. Therefore he is where he was not; and so he seems changeable.

But although each day he begins to be in creatures in which he was not before, because they did not exist before, this occurs without change in himself. In the same way, he began to be in the world which he made, yet without change in himself; and similarly he ceases to be in things in which he formerly was, without change in himself. Yet he does not himself leave a place; rather, the place ceases to exist.

### Epilogue explaining why he entered upon the foregoing discussion

16. It now seems sufficiently demonstrated how all things are said to be in God and God in all things. We undertook this discussion almost incidentally, because the matter around which our discourse was occupied seemed to require it. For we were discussing the knowledge or wisdom of God; and, when we said that God knows all things, the question arose whether all things are said to be in God because of the knowledge he has of all things, or whether Scripture says this for another reason. The occasion of this question led us into the preceding discussion.

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. HERE HE RETURNS TO THE SUBJECT, REPEATING WHAT WAS SAID ABOVE IN ORDER TO ADD FURTHER MATTERS

1. Let us now return to our subject and continue the discussion begun. Above it was said that God’s foreknowledge concerns only future things, but all future things, both good and evil. Knowledge or wisdom, however, concerns not only future things but also present and past things; nor only temporal things but eternal things as well, because God knows himself.

Here an unavoidable question arises: whether knowledge or foreknowledge is the cause of things, or things are the cause of God’s knowledge or foreknowledge. For God’s foreknowledge seems to be the cause of those things subject to it, and to impose upon them necessity of occurrence. For no future things would have been future unless God had foreknown them, and they cannot fail to occur when God has foreknown them. But if it is impossible for them not to occur because they have been foreknown, then the foreknowledge by which they have been foreknown seems itself to be the cause of their occurrence.

It is impossible for them not to occur once they have been foreknown, because if they did not occur despite having been foreknown, God’s foreknowledge would be mistaken. But God’s foreknowledge cannot be mistaken. Therefore it is impossible for them not to occur when they have been foreknown. Thus foreknowledge seems to be the cause of what has been foreknown.

The same is said concerning knowledge: because God has known certain things, therefore they exist. Augustine seems to support this view in Book 5, chapter 13, *On the Trinity*: “God did not know these things from some point in time. Rather, before any beginning he foreknew all future temporal things, including what we would ask of him and when, and whom he would hear or not hear, and concerning what matters. But he knew all creatures, spiritual and bodily, not because they exist, but they exist because he knew them. For he was not ignorant of what he was going to create. Since, therefore, he knew, he created; he did not know because he created, nor did he know things when created otherwise than he knew them when they were to be created. For nothing was added to his wisdom from them; rather, when they came into existence as and when they ought, that wisdom remained as it was.”

Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “Before they were created, all things were known to him; so also after they have been completed.” By these words Augustine seems to imply that God’s knowledge or foreknowledge is the cause of things which occur, when he says that they exist because God knows them.

The same seems also to say this in Book 6. “When times pass away and succeed one another,” he says in the same chapter, “nothing passes away or succeeds in God’s knowledge, by which he knows all that he has made through it. For created things are not known by God because they have been made; rather, they have been made because they are unchangeably known by him.” And here again he seems to indicate that God’s knowledge is the cause of things which occur, saying in chapter 10: “God did not know them because they were made; they were made because God knew them.” Therefore God’s knowledge or foreknowledge seems to be the cause of the things he knows.

### He shows the unacceptable consequences that would follow if knowledge or foreknowledge were said to be the cause of all things subject to it

2. But if this is so, then it is the cause of all evils, since all evils are known and foreknown by God. This is far from the truth. For if God’s knowledge or foreknowledge were the cause of evils, God would certainly be the author of evils, which is wholly false. Therefore God’s knowledge and foreknowledge are not the cause of all things subject to them.

### That future things are not the cause of God’s knowledge or foreknowledge

3. Nor are future things the cause of God’s foreknowledge. Although they would not be future unless foreknown by God, they are not foreknown because they are future. For if this were so, something external to and distinct from that which is eternal would be its cause; the Creator’s knowledge would depend upon creatures, and the created would be the cause of the uncreated.

Origen, however, in volume 4, Book 7, on the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 8, says: “A thing will not be because God knows that it will be; rather, because it will be, it is known by God before it happens.” This seems to conflict with Augustine’s words cited above. Here future things seem to be indicated as the cause of foreknowledge; there, foreknowledge as the cause of future things.

### What should be maintained from the foregoing, with a determination of the authorities

4. Wishing therefore to remove this apparent contradiction, we say that future things are in no way the cause of God’s foreknowledge or knowledge; nor are they foreknown or known because they are future or have occurred. Thus we explain Origen’s saying, “Because it will be, it is known by God before it happens,” as meaning: “What will be is known by God before it happens, and it would not be known unless it were going to be.” Thus no cause is indicated there except a condition without which it would not occur.

Likewise, we say that God’s knowledge or foreknowledge is not the cause of things which occur except as a condition without which they do not occur, provided that “knowledge” is referred only to awareness. But if the term “knowledge” includes good pleasure and disposition as well, then it can rightly be called the cause of those things which God does.

For, as stated above, Book 15, chapter 13, God’s cognition or knowledge is understood in two ways: either as awareness alone, or as awareness together with good pleasure. Augustine perhaps understood it in the latter way when he said, Homily 51, volume 9: “They exist because he knows,” that is, because it pleased him who knows, and because he who knows disposed them.

This interpretation is supported by the fact that Augustine there treats only of good things—namely, creatures and the things God does. God knows all these not only by knowledge but also by good pleasure and disposition. Therefore, in that passage God’s cognition is understood as signifying not merely awareness but also God’s good pleasure.

God knows and foreknows evils before they occur, however, by awareness alone and not by good pleasure. For God foreknows and foretells even things which he himself will not do, just as he foreknew and foretold the unbelief of the Jews, but did not cause it. Nor did he compel them into the sin of unbelief because he foreknew it; nor would he have foreknown or foretold their evils unless they were going to have them.

Hence Augustine, on John: “God, foreknowing future things, foretold through the prophet the unbelief of the Jews, but did not cause it. Nor would he have foreknown their evils unless they possessed them. For he does not compel someone to sin because he knew beforehand the future sins of human beings. He foreknew their sins, not his own. Therefore, if the things he foreknew are not theirs, he did not foreknow truly. But because his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, without doubt it is not another but the very persons whom God foreknew to be sinners who sin. Therefore, if they had wished to do good rather than evil, they would not have been foreseen by him who knows what each person will do as destined to do evil.”

These words plainly show, if carefully considered, that God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of the evils it foreknows. For he does not foreknow them as things he will do, nor as his own acts, but as the acts of those who are going to do or possess them. Therefore he foreknew them by awareness alone, not by the good pleasure of authorship. Hence we are given to understand, conversely, that God foreknows good things as his own, as things which he will do, so that in foreknowing them there is at once his awareness and the good pleasure of authorship.

### Objection to the assertion that God’s foreknowledge cannot be mistaken

5. To the statement made above, namely that God’s foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, some commonly object as follows: God foreknew that this person would read, or something of that sort; but it may happen that this person does not read. Therefore it can be otherwise than God foreknew; therefore God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken—which is wholly false.

Certainly something may fail to occur even though it has been foreknown to occur; yet God’s foreknowledge cannot thereby be mistaken. For if it did not occur, it would not have been foreknown by God to occur.

But they press the question further, saying: Either it can happen otherwise than God foreknew, or not otherwise. If not otherwise, then all things happen necessarily. But if otherwise, then God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken or changed. Yet it can happen otherwise, because it can happen otherwise than it does happen; but it happens as it was foreknown. Therefore it can happen otherwise than it was foreknown.

We reply that the expression “It can happen otherwise than God foreknew,” and similar expressions, admit more than one meaning; so too do these: “What God foreknew can fail to be,” “What God foreknew cannot fail to be,” and “It is impossible that all things which occur should not be foreknown.”

For these may be understood jointly, with a condition implied, or separately. If you understand, “It cannot happen otherwise than God foreknew,” as meaning, “The two cannot both be true at once: that God foreknew it would happen in this way, and that it happens otherwise,” you understand correctly. But if you understand it separately, as saying that this thing cannot occur otherwise than it does occur, and otherwise than God foreknew it would be future, this is false. For it can occur otherwise than it occurs, although God foreknew that it would occur in this way.

Likewise concerning the other proposition: “It is impossible for that which God foreknew, or while God foreknew it, not to occur.” If understood jointly, it is true; if separately, false. So too: “It is impossible that everything which occurs should not be foreknown,” that is, “The two cannot both be true: that it occurs and that it has not been foreknown.” This sense is true. But if you say that God could not have failed to foreknow everything which occurs, this is false. For he could have brought it about that it did not occur, and thus that it was not foreknown.

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. WHETHER GOD’S KNOWLEDGE CAN INCREASE OR DECREASE, OR BE CHANGED IN ANY WAY; FOR BOTH SEEM CAPABLE OF PROOF
1. Furthermore, it is customary to ask whether God’s knowledge can be increased or diminished; for each alternative seems capable of proof. That divine knowledge can be increased or changed is proved as follows: God can know what He never knows. There is someone who will not read today, yet it can happen that he reads today; for he can read today. But nothing can happen which cannot be known by God. Therefore God can know that this person will read today; therefore He can know something which He does not know; therefore His knowledge can be increased or changed. And it likewise seems capable of being diminished. For there is someone who will read today, and God knows that he will read. Yet it can happen that he does not read; therefore God can fail to know that this person will read; therefore He can fail to know something which He knows; therefore His knowledge can be diminished or changed.

To this we reply that God’s knowledge is altogether immutable: it can neither be increased nor diminished. For, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapters 13–14, God’s knowledge is Wisdom itself, and Wisdom is God’s very essence or substance; because in the wonderful simplicity of that nature, to be wise is not one thing and to be is another, but what it is to be wise is also what it is to be. Thus the Word knows all that the Father knows; but for Him, knowing is from the Father, just as being is. For there, knowing and being are one. Therefore, just as the Father’s being is not from the Son, so neither is His knowing. Accordingly, in uttering Himself, as it were, the Father begot a Word altogether equal to Himself. For He would not have spoken Himself wholly and perfectly if there were anything less or more in His Word than in Himself. Thus the Word is altogether what the Father is, yet He is not the Father, because the one is Son and the other Father. Father and Son therefore know one another: the former by begetting, the latter by being begotten. And everything that is in their knowledge, wisdom, and essence, each of them sees simultaneously—not bit by bit or one by one, as if their gaze alternated from here to there and back again, seeing this thing and then that, so that one could not see certain things without failing to see others. Rather, each sees all things at once, and there is nothing among them which He does not always see and know. Therefore His knowledge is incapable of loss and unchangeable.

Our knowledge, however, is capable of loss, change, and reception, because for us being is not the same as being wise or knowing. Consequently, just as our knowledge is unlike God’s knowledge, so our word, which is born from our knowledge, is unlike that Word which was born from the Father’s knowledge. This authority clearly demonstrates that God’s knowledge is altogether unchangeable, just as God’s essence itself is altogether unchangeable; and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit simultaneously know and see all things. Therefore, just as the divine essence cannot be increased or diminished, neither can divine knowledge. Yet it is granted that God can know what He does not know, and can fail to know what He knows, because something could be subject to His knowledge which is not now subject to it, and something which is subject to it could fail to be so, without any change in that knowledge itself.

### Objection: whether God can newly, or in time, know or foreknow something

2. Some object here as follows: if God can know or foreknow something which He has never known or foreknown, then He can know or foreknow something in time. We reply: God can indeed know or foreknow everything that He can do, and He can do what will never happen. Therefore He can know or foreknow what will never happen, and neither is, nor was; yet He does not know or has not known it, nor foreknow or has not foreknown it, because His knowledge concerns only things which are, were, or will be [Col. 0630], and foreknowledge only future things.

And although He can know or foreknow what never is or will be, nevertheless He cannot newly, or in time, know or foreknow anything. He can certainly know or foreknow what never is and never will be, though it has not been known or foreknown by Him from eternity; yet He cannot begin to know or foreknow it. Rather, He can now know or foreknow it in the same way as He could have known or foreknown it from eternity. For if it is said that He can now know or foreknow what He did not know or foreknow from eternity—in such a manner that He did not know or foreknow it from eternity, as though both could be true at once—this is false. But if you say that He can now know or foreknow what He did not know or foreknow from eternity—that is, that He has the power, eternally and now, of knowing or foreknowing something, though it is not foreknown and will not occur—this is true. Therefore He cannot newly, or in time, know or foreknow anything, just as He cannot newly, or in time, will something; although He can will what He has never willed.

### Whether God can know more things than He knows

3. Again, some say that God can know more than He knows, because He can know everything that He knows, and He can make some things which never will be; and He can know those things, for He cannot make anything unknown to Him. If all things now existing existed, and He made certain other things which neither are nor will be, He would certainly know all those things, and would know more than He now knows. Yet His knowledge could not be increased, because this entire change could occur without any mutability of His knowledge. It is therefore evident that God’s knowledge is altogether immutable and cannot be increased or diminished, though the things subject to it can change.

### What seems opposed to the statement made above, that God always and simultaneously knows all things

4. But what was said above—that God always sees all things simultaneously—seems to conflict with Jerome’s statement in his *Exposition of Habakkuk*: “It is absurd,” he says, “to reduce God’s majesty to this: that He should know, moment by moment, how many gnats are born, how many die, what is the number of fleas and flies, how many fish swim in the waters, and similar things. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God that, while we thrust His providence even down to the lowest things, we do injury to ourselves by saying that His providence over irrational beings is the same as over rational beings.”

Here Jerome seems to say that God has no knowledge or providence of those tiniest things. If this were so, then He would not always and simultaneously know all things. We must therefore understand that statement to have been made in this sense: Jerome denies that God knows such things alternately or separately, or that He has known them through different moments of time in the way that, through successive moments, some of them perish and others begin. Nor does He provide for these and other irrational creatures as He does for rational creatures. For, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 9, “Is God concerned for oxen?” And just as God is not concerned for oxen, so neither is He concerned for other irrational creatures. Yet Scripture says, Wisdom 12, that He has care for all things.

Therefore He has providence and care universally for all that He created, so that each thing has what is due and fitting to it. But He has a special providence and care for rational beings, to whom He gave commandments, prescribed the law of right living, and promised rewards. He does not have this providence and care for irrational beings. Thus the Apostle says that God is not concerned for oxen; nevertheless, He provides for and cares for all—that is, He governs all, makes His sun rise upon all, and gives rain. God therefore knows how great is the number of fleas, gnats, flies, and fish, and how many are born and die; but He does not know this moment by moment. Rather, He knows all things simultaneously and once for all. Nor does He know them in such a way as to have the same providence for irrational and rational beings—that is, as though He provided for irrational creatures in exactly the same way. For He gave rational beings commandments and assigned angels for their guardianship.

### Brief summary of the foregoing, with some additions

5. Therefore, just as God knows immutably all things which were, are, and will be, both good and evil, so He also foreknows all future things, both good and evil.

## DISTINCTION XL. WHAT PREDESTINATION IS, AND HOW IT DIFFERS FROM FOREKNOWLEDGE

[Col. 0631]

1. Predestination concerns saving goods and persons to be saved. For, as Augustine says in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10, predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge. Foreknowledge, however, can exist without predestination. For by predestination God foreknew those things which He Himself would do; but God also foreknew those things which He Himself would not do—that is, all evils. He predestined those whom He chose; but He reprobated the rest—that is, He foreknew that they would sin and suffer eternal death.

### Whether any of the predestined can be damned, or any of the reprobate saved

2. None of the predestined seems able to be damned, nor any of the reprobate able to be saved. Hence Augustine says in *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 13: “In the Apocalypse [Revelation], chapter 3, it is said: ‘Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown.’ If another is not to receive it unless this person loses it, then the number of the elect is fixed”; that is, it cannot be increased or diminished.

Some object to this, seeking to prove that the number of the elect can be increased and diminished, as follows: God could fail to bestow grace on those upon whom He does bestow it, and could withdraw it from those from whom He does not withdraw it. If He did so, they would certainly be damned. Therefore these persons, who nevertheless will be saved, could be damned; thus the number of the elect could be diminished. Likewise it could be increased, because grace could be bestowed upon those on whom it is not bestowed, by which they would be saved. Therefore those who will be damned without grace could be saved if grace were received; thus the number of the elect could be increased.

We reply that it is said—and truly said—that the number of the elect cannot be increased or diminished because both cannot be true at once: namely, that someone should be saved and not predestined, or that someone should be predestined and be damned. The implicit conjunctive understanding makes the statement true, and the impossibility real. But if it is understood simply, the impossibility is not admitted; as when it is said: “A predestined person can, or cannot, be damned,” and “A reprobate person can be saved.” In these and similar expressions, the meaning of the statement must be judged from its formulation. One understanding results if these statements are taken conjunctively, and another if they are taken disjunctively, as was explained above in the discussion of foreknowledge.

For if, in saying, “A predestined person cannot be damned,” you mean, “It cannot be that he is predestined and damned,” you speak truly, because you understand it conjunctively. But it is false if understood disjunctively, as if you meant that the person whom I call predestined cannot be damned; for he could have failed to be predestined, and then would be damned.

### How they still press the question

3. Yet they persist, proceeding by conjunctive reasoning thus: “It cannot be that someone is predestined and damned. These two cannot both be true at once. But one of them cannot fail to be true, namely that this person is predestined—for he has been predestined from eternity—and he cannot now fail to be predestined. Therefore, since it is impossible for both to be true together, and impossible for one not to be true, it seems impossible for the other to be true—namely, that he be damned. If so, then it cannot be that he is not saved.”

In resolving this question I would rather hear others than teach. Yet we say that a similar question can be raised concerning foreknowledge. Therefore we give one answer both here and there, saying that the proposition on which this entire question rests must be qualified: “It is impossible for one of these two not to be true, namely, that this person is now predestined; for he has been predestined from eternity.” For when it is said, “This person cannot now fail to be predestined,” or “It cannot be otherwise than that he is predestined,” this can be understood conjunctively or disjunctively. It cannot be that he has been predestined from eternity [Col. 0632] and is not now predestined; nor can it be that he is predestined and is not predestined. Yet it could from eternity have been the case that he was not predestined, and he could from eternity not have been predestined.

And just as God could from eternity have failed to predestine him, so some grant that even now God can have failed to predestine him. Therefore God can from eternity have failed to predestine him; therefore this person can have failed to be predestined. But if he had not been predestined, he would not now be predestined; therefore he can now fail to be predestined. They say the same of foreknowledge and of things foreknown—something which they by no means grant with respect to the actions or works of God and human beings. For once something has been done or said, they do not grant that it can fail to be, or fail to have been; rather, it is impossible that what has been done or said should not be, or should not have been, referring possibility or impossibility to the nature of the thing that exists. But when God’s foreknowledge or predestination is under discussion, possibility is referred to God’s power, which always was and is the same, because in God predestination, foreknowledge, and power are one.

### What God’s reprobation is, in what respects it is considered, and what is the effect of predestination

4. Since predestination is the preparation of grace—that is, the divine election by which He chose whom He willed before the foundation of the world, as the Apostle says in Ephesians 1:8—reprobation, conversely, must be understood as the foreknowledge of the wickedness of certain persons and the preparation of their damnation. For just as the effect of predestination is the grace by which we are justified in the present, aided to live rightly and persevere in good, and by which we are made blessed in the future, so God’s reprobation—by which from eternity, in not choosing them, He reprobated certain persons—is considered in two respects. One He foreknows and does not prepare, namely iniquity; the other He foreknows and prepares, namely eternal punishment.

Hence Augustine, writing to Prosper and Hilary, says: “This rule must be held unshaken: sinners are foreknown in their sins, but not prepared for them; punishment, however, is prepared.” For God, as Augustine says in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, prepared in His foreknowledge His good things for whom He willed, and undoubtedly foreknew that He would give them to all those to whom He gives them. God also, as Fulgentius says, prepared eternal fire for the wicked—namely for those whom He justly prepared to undergo punishments—yet He did not prepare them to commit sins. For God prepared what divine justice would render, not what human wickedness would commit. He did not prepare the saints for receiving righteousness in the same way as He prepared the wicked for losing righteousness; for He was never the author of perversity.

Therefore, just as God’s predestination properly is the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered, so God’s reprobation is the foreknowledge of malice in certain persons which will not end, and the preparation of punishment which will not terminate. And just as the effect of predestination is the bestowal of grace, so in a certain way hardening seems to be the effect of eternal reprobation. Yet God does not harden, as Augustine says in volume 4, letter 15, to Sixtus, by imparting malice, but by not imparting grace; for they are not worthy of it. Those to whom it is not imparted are neither worthy of it nor merit it; rather, they are worthy and merit that it not be imparted. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 9: “God has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills,” calling mercy predestination, and especially the effect of predestination—that is, the bestowal of grace—but calling hardening the deprivation of grace.

For, as Augustine says in book 1, volume 4, to Simplicianus, one must not understand God’s hardening as though He compelled anyone to sin. Rather, He does not grant some sinners the mercy of His justification; for this reason He is said to harden them—because He does not have mercy on them, not because He drives them to sin. He does not have mercy on those whom, by a justice most hidden and far beyond human understanding, He judges that grace ought not to be granted. The Apostle does not explain this justice but marvels at it, saying in Romans 11: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!”

## DISTINCTION XLI. WHETHER THERE IS ANY MERIT FOR HARDENING AND MERCY

1. If we seek the merit of hardening and mercy, we find merit for hardening, but no merit for mercy. For there is no merit of mercy, lest grace be made void if it is not freely given but rendered in return for merits. Therefore God has mercy according to grace, which is freely given; but He hardens according to judgment, which is rendered according to merits. From this it may be understood that, just as God’s reprobation is His unwillingness to show mercy, so God’s hardening is His not showing mercy: not that He inflicts anything by which a human being becomes worse, but merely that He does not confer that by which one would become better.

From these things it is plainly shown what the Apostle meant by mercy and hardening, and that mercy invokes no merit, whereas hardening is not without merit. Here “mercy” denotes predestination, especially its effect; but “hardening” does not denote God’s eternal reprobation itself, for that has no merit, but the deprivation or withdrawal of grace, which is in some sense an effect of reprobation. Reprobation is sometimes nevertheless used for hardening, just as predestination is used for its effect, namely the grace bestowed. For grace bestowed upon a person for justification is an effect of predestination.

Since there are no merits for the grace bestowed upon a person for justification, still less can there be any merits for predestination itself, by which God chose from eternity whom He willed. Neither are there merits for reprobation, by which from eternity He foreknew that some would be wicked and damned, just as He chose Jacob and reprobated Esau. This was not because of merits which they then possessed, for they had none, since they did not yet exist; nor because of future merits which He foresaw, did He choose the one or reprobate the other.

### The opinion of some, once held by Augustine but later retracted

2. Some nevertheless held that God chose Jacob because He foreknew that he would be such a person as would believe in Him and serve Him. Augustine says that he himself once thought this, in book 1 of the *Retractations*, where in chapter 23 he clearly shows that, if election were based on future merits, election would no longer be by grace. Therefore he was not chosen by God because he would be such a person; rather, through such election he was made such a person. Augustine says:

> “While discussing what God chose in the not-yet-born child, of whom He said that the elder would serve, and what He likewise reprobated in that elder, also not yet born, I brought my reasoning to this point, so as to say: God therefore did not choose anyone’s works in foreknowledge, works which He Himself was to give; but He chose faith in foreknowledge. He chose the person whom He foreknew would believe in Him, in order to give him the Holy Spirit, so that through doing good works he might also attain eternal life.”

Here Augustine plainly says that God chose him not because of works, but because of faith, by which He foresaw that he would believe. Yet, since there is merit in faith as well as in works, Augustine retracted this, saying:

> “I had not yet examined carefully enough, nor had I yet discovered what the election of grace is of which the Apostle says, Romans 11: ‘The remnant shall be saved by the election of grace.’ Certainly it is not of grace if it proceeds from merits, so that what is given is no longer given according to grace but is instead rendered as a debt according to merits. Likewise, what I immediately said follows: for the same Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 12, ‘The same God works all things in all.’ But it has never been said, ‘God believes all things in all.’ And afterwards I added: ‘What we believe, therefore, is ours; but the good we do is from Him who gives the Holy Spirit to believers.’ But I surely would not have said this if I had known that faith itself is found among the gifts of God which are given in the same Spirit. Therefore both are ours because of the freedom of the will, and both are given through the Spirit of faith and charity. And what I said a little later—‘For it is ours to believe and to will, but it is His to give believers and those who will the capacity to work well through the Holy Spirit, by whom the love of God is poured into our hearts, Romans 5’—is indeed true, but the same rule applies. Both are His, because He prepares the will; and both are ours, because they do not occur except with our willing.”

Therefore even the merit of faith comes from God’s mercy. God therefore did not choose anyone from eternity because of faith or any merits, nor did He in time bestow the grace of justification because of them; rather, in His free goodness He chose them in order that they might be good. Hence Augustine says in book 1 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 18: “He chose us not because He foreknew that we would be such, but in order that we might be such through the election of His grace itself, by which He bestowed grace upon us in His beloved Son.”

### A statement Augustine makes elsewhere seems contrary to this

3. Yet what Augustine says in book 33 of the *Questions*, question 98, seems contrary to this: “God has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills. But this will of God cannot be unjust, for it arises from most hidden merits. For even though sinners, because of the general sin, have become one mass, there is nevertheless some diversity among them. Therefore there precedes something in sinners by which, though they are not yet justified, they are made worthy of justification. And in other sinners there likewise precedes something by which they are worthy of dullness [hardening].”

Here Augustine seems to say that God’s very will, by which He chooses some and reprobates others, arises from merits, though most hidden—that is, that because of merits He willed to choose some and reprobate others; and that because of merits the grace of justification is bestowed on some but not others, and thus they are made dull. But what he meant is unknown, unless perhaps he intended what was said above, which he later retracted. For he immediately adds some other points in the same place which he openly discusses in book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 23; this will be clear to anyone who reads both passages. Hence it is likely that he also retracted this point in the preceding passage.

Some, however, understand the statement in this sense: not that anyone is predestined because of merits, or merits the grace of justification, but that some are not so wicked as to deserve that grace not be imparted to them. For no one can merit the grace of God by which one is justified; yet one can merit that it not be bestowed, so as to be utterly rejected. Indeed, some have descended into such a depth of wickedness that they deserve this and are worthy of it; while others live in such a way that, although they do not merit the grace of justification, they nevertheless do not deserve to be wholly rejected or to have grace withdrawn from them. Thus Augustine said that in some sinners there precedes something by which they are worthy of justification, and in others something by which they are worthy of dullness. But this is frivolous.

### The false opinion of some who discuss God’s hidden things carnally

4. Many, seeking to give an explanation of this depth and attempting, according to the conjectures of their own hearts, to comprehend the unsearchable profundity of God’s judgments, have wandered into fables of vanity. They say that souls sin above in heaven and, according to their sins, are sent to bodies as their due recompense and enclosed in bodies worthy of them as though in prisons. Such persons followed their own thoughts; desiring to dispute about God’s depth, they themselves were turned into a depth. They say that souls formerly dwelt in heaven, did some good or evil there, and were cast down into earthly bodies according to their merits.

But the Catholic faith rejects this because of the Apostle’s plain statement in Romans 9: “When they were not yet born, nor had done any good or evil,” etc. Faithful ignorance is therefore better than rash knowledge. He therefore chose whom He willed by free mercy, not because they would become faithful, but in order that they might be faithful; and He gave them grace not because they were faithful, but in order that they might become so. For the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 7: “I received mercy in order that I might be faithful”; he does not say, “Because I was faithful.” Grace is indeed given also to a believer, but it was first given so that the person might be a believer. In the same way, He reprobated whom He willed, not because of future merits which He foresaw, but by a justice altogether right and removed from our understanding.

### Question

5. But it is asked whether, just as God is said to have chosen some persons in order that they might become good [Col. 0635] and faithful, so it should likewise be granted that He reprobated some in order that they might become wicked and faithless, and hardened them in order that they might sin. This must by no means be granted. For reprobation is not the cause of evil in the way that predestination is the cause of good; nor does hardening make a human being evil in the way that mercy makes one good.

### Whether God always knows and foreknows, and always has known and foreknown, what He once knows or foreknows

6. Moreover, we must consider whether God always knows and has known, and foreknows and has foreknown, all things which He once knows or foreknows; or whether He formerly knew or foreknew what He does not now know or foreknow. We answer first concerning foreknowledge, saying that He foreknew many things which He does not now foreknow. For since His foreknowledge concerns only future things, once things which were future become present or pass away, they cease to be under God’s foreknowledge, though they always remain under His knowledge.

God therefore foreknew from eternity all things which were future, and He does not cease to foreknow them except when they cease to be future. Nor, when He ceases to foreknow things which He formerly foreknew, does He know them less than He knew them before. For it is not through a defect in God’s knowledge that He is said formerly to have foreknown things which He does not now foreknow, but because of the meaning of the word “foreknowledge.” To foreknow is to know something before it happens. Therefore God cannot be said to foreknow except what is future.

### Here concerning knowledge: God always knows what He once knows

7. Concerning knowledge, however, we speak differently. God always knows everything that He ever knows; for every item of knowledge which He ever has, He always had, has, and will have. But the following objection is made: He formerly knew that this man, who has now been born, would be born; now He does not know that he will be born. Therefore He knew something which He does not now know. Likewise: He knew that the world would be created; now He does not know that it will be created. Therefore He knew something which He does not now know. And infinitely many similar cases can be stated.

But we reply that He now knows the same thing concerning this man’s birth and the world’s creation which He knew before they occurred, though His knowledge must be expressed then and now in different words. For what was then future is now past. Therefore the words must change in order to indicate the same thing. Thus, when speaking at different times, we designate the same day by the adverb “tomorrow” while it is still future, “today” while it is present, and “yesterday” when it is past. Accordingly, before the world was created, God knew that it would be created; after it was created, He knows that it has been created. Yet this is not different knowledge, but entirely the same knowledge concerning the world’s creation.

Likewise, the ancient fathers believed that Christ would be born and die, while we believe that He has been born and died; yet we and they do not believe different things, but the same things. For, as Augustine says, the times have changed and therefore the words have changed, but not the faith. Let us therefore hold without doubt that God always knows all that He ever knows.

## DISTINCTION XLII. ON GOD’S OMNIPOTENCE: FIRST, WHY HE IS CALLED OMNIPOTENT

1. We must now treat of God’s omnipotence. The first question that arises is how God is truly called omnipotent: whether because He can do all things, or only because He can do what He wills. That God can do all things is established by many authorities. Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “God can indeed do all things, but He does only what accords with His truth and justice.” Again in the same work: “God could have made all things at once, but reason—that is, will—forbade it.” There he called God’s will “reason,” because God’s will is reasonable and utterly just. Therefore it must be confessed that God can do all things.

### How God is said to be able to do all things, when we can do many things which He cannot

2. But it is asked how He can be said to be able to do all things, since we can do some things which He cannot. For He cannot walk, speak, and do similar things wholly foreign to the nature of divinity, since an incorporeal and simple substance cannot possibly possess the instruments required for them. I think the answer is that such actions—walking, speaking, and the like—are not foreign to God’s power but pertain to it. Although God cannot possess such actions in Himself—for He cannot walk or speak and the like—He can nevertheless perform them in creatures: for He causes a human being to walk, speak, and do such things. Therefore these actions do not diminish the divine power, because the Almighty can do even this.

### Objection concerning other matters

3. But there are certain other things which God cannot do at all, such as sins: He cannot lie; He cannot sin. Yet nothing is thereby taken away from or derogated from God’s omnipotence if He is said to be unable to sin, because this would not be power but weakness. If He could do this, He would not be omnipotent. Therefore the fact that He cannot do these things must be attributed not to impotence but to power. Hence Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 15: “It is a great power of God not to be able to lie.” For some things are counted as powers in certain beings, but not in others; and things praiseworthy in some are blameworthy in others. Therefore God is not less powerful because He cannot sin, since no one who can do this can in any way be omnipotent.

### Another objection concerning other matters

4. There are also some other things which God cannot do, and therefore He seems unable to do all things. For He cannot die or be deceived. Hence Augustine says in *On the Creed*: “God Almighty cannot die, cannot be deceived, cannot become miserable, nor can He be conquered.” Far be it from the Almighty to be able to do these and similar things. For if He could be subject to such passions and defects, He would by no means be omnipotent. Therefore He is shown to be omnipotent because these things cannot come near Him; yet He can perform them in others.

### That God’s omnipotence is considered under two aspects

5. Therefore, to attentive consideration, His omnipotence appears under two aspects: that He does everything He wills, and that He suffers absolutely nothing. In both respects God’s omnipotence is most truly proclaimed, because nothing can bring upon Him a corruption to be suffered, and nothing can introduce an impediment to what He does.
