It is therefore evident that God can suffer absolutely nothing and can do all things except only those which would injure His dignity or detract from His excellence. Yet in this He is not less omnipotent, for to be able to do such things would not be ability but inability.

Therefore let no one presume to call God powerless in any respect, because He can do everything that belongs to power to be able to do; and for this reason He is truly called omnipotent.

### Certain authorities teach that He is called omnipotent because He can do whatever He wills

6. Yet some authorities teach that He is truly called omnipotent because He can do whatever He wills. Thus Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 96: “He is truly called omnipotent for no other reason than that He can do whatever He wills, and the effect of the omnipotent will is not hindered by the will of any creature.” Again, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “God cannot do unjust things because He Himself is supreme justice and goodness. But He is omnipotent, not because He can do everything, but because He can bring about whatever He wills, so that nothing can resist His will so as to prevent its fulfilment or hinder it in any way.” John Chrysostom says in a homily on the exposition of the Creed: “God is called omnipotent because no inability can be found in His power,” as the Prophet says, Psalm 113: “He has done whatever He willed.” Therefore He is omnipotent in that He can accomplish everything that He wills. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 9: “Who resists His will?” These authorities seem to show that God is called omnipotent only because He can do everything that He wills, not because He can do all things.

### Clarification of the foregoing authorities

[Col. 0637]

7. But it may be said in reply that Augustine, when he says, “The Almighty is not called so because He can do all things,” and so forth, took “all things” in such a broad and general sense that it included evils, which God neither can nor wills. He therefore did not deny that God can do everything which it is fitting for Him to be able to do. Likewise, when he says, “He is truly called omnipotent for no other reason than that He can do whatever He wills,” he does not deny that God can also do things which He does not will. Rather, against those who said that God willed many things which He could not do, Augustine affirms that God can do whatever He wills and that He is truly called omnipotent for this reason alone: because He can do whatever He wills.

But take care how you understand this: does He do whatever He wills Himself to be able to do, whatever He wills to do, or whatever He wills to happen? If you say that He is called omnipotent because He can do whatever He wills Himself to be able to do, then Peter, or any blessed saint, could likewise be called omnipotent: for each can do whatever he wills himself to be able to do, and can do whatever he wills to do. For he wills to do only what he does, and wills to be able to do only what he can do. But he cannot do everything that he wills to happen. He wills those who are to be saved to be saved, yet cannot save them.

God, however, can do everything that He wills to happen. If He wills something to happen through Himself, He can do it through Himself, and does so through Himself; thus He made heaven and earth through Himself because He willed it. But if He wills it to happen through a creature, He works through that creature; thus He makes houses through human beings and similar works of craftsmanship. God indeed has power from Himself and through Himself; but a human being or angel, however blessed, does not have power from himself or through himself.

### Objection
8. But perhaps you will say: Neither the Son of God nor the Holy Spirit can be able of himself; the Father alone can. For he can be able of himself who exists from himself; but the Son, because he is not from himself but from the Father, cannot be able of himself but from the Father; and the Holy Spirit is from both. To this we reply: although the Son cannot be able of himself, nor work from himself, he nevertheless can and does work through himself; and so too the Holy Spirit. Hence Hilary, in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*: “This is the unity of the nature which you oppose, heretic: that the Son so acts through himself that he does not act from himself; and so does not act from himself that he acts through himself.” He is said to act and to be powerful through himself because he possesses the same natural power as the Father, by which he is powerful and acts. But because he has it from the Father and not from himself, he is therefore said to be able and to act from the Father, not from himself. A human being or an angel, however, has a gratuitous power by which he is powerful. Therefore God the Trinity is truly and properly called omnipotent because through himself—that is, by natural power—he can bring about whatever he wills to happen, and whatever he wills himself to be able to do. For he wills no thing to happen which he cannot accomplish through himself or through creatures; nor does he will himself able to do anything which he cannot do. He wills himself able to do everything which he wills to happen, but he does not will everything which he wills himself able to do to happen; for if he willed it, it would happen, since nothing can resist his will.

## DISTINCTION XLIII. THE OPINION OF CERTAIN PEOPLE WHO SAY THAT GOD CAN DO NOTHING EXCEPT WHAT HE DOES

1. Yet some people, glorying in their own judgment, have attempted to confine God’s power within limits. For when they say, “God can do as far as this, and no further,” what else is that but to enclose and restrict his infinite power within a measure? They say: “God cannot do anything other than what he does; nor can he make better what he makes; nor can he omit anything among the things he does.” They try to support this first opinion of theirs with plausible arguments, fabricated reasons, and also testimonies of sacred authorities, saying: “God cannot do except what is good and just to be done; but it is not just and good for him to do except what he does. For if it is just and good for him to do something other than what he does, then he does not do everything which it is just and good for him to do. But who would dare say this?”

### Second argument

2. They add further: “He cannot do except what his [Col. 0638] justice requires.” But his justice does not require that he do except what he does; therefore he cannot do except what he does. And that same justice requires that he not do what he does not do; but he cannot act against his justice. Therefore he cannot do any of those things which he leaves undone.

### Reply to the preceding statement

3. We reply to these arguments by making clear the twofold meaning of the words and unravelling what they have entangled. “God cannot do except what is good and just,” that is, he cannot do except that which, if he did it, would be good and just: this is true. But he can do many things which are neither good nor just, because they neither are nor will be, neither are rightly done nor will be done, because they will never be done. Likewise, as to the second objection: “He cannot do except what his justice requires,” and, “He cannot do that which his justice requires not to be done.” We say that the word “requires” is not fittingly predicated of God, nor is it properly understood; and those expressions have a twofold meaning. For if you understand, “He cannot do except what his justice requires,” that is, except what his just will wills, you speak falsely. For the justice of God himself is understood as his most equitable will. Thus Augustine understands the Lord’s words in Genesis to Lot, Genesis 19: “I cannot do anything until you enter there,” explaining: “He said that he could not do what he undoubtedly could do by power, but could not do by justice”—as though he could indeed have done it, but did not will to do it, and that will was just. But if by these words you understand that he cannot do except what, if it were done, would accord with his justice, you speak truly. In the same way distinguish the statement: “He cannot do what his justice requires him not to do,” that is, he cannot do what he himself, who is supreme justice, does not will to do: this is false. But if by these words you understand that he cannot do what cannot accord with his justice, you speak truly.

### Their third argument

4. They add other arguments, saying: “God cannot do except what he ought to do; but he ought not to do except what he does. For if he ought to do other things, then he does not do everything that he ought to do. But if he does everything that he ought to do, and cannot do except what he ought to do, then he cannot do except what he does. Again, either he ought to leave what he leaves undone so as not to do it, or he ought not. If he ought not, he does not rightly leave it undone. But if he ought to leave it undone, then he ought not to do it. Now if he ought not and it is not fitting, it is not necessary for him to do it; and if it is neither fitting nor necessary for him to do it, then he cannot do it. Therefore he cannot do except what he does; nor can he leave undone what he does without doing it, because he ought to do it; and what he ought to do, he cannot leave undone.”

But, as it seems to me, this word “ought” contains poison. For it contains a manifold and tangled meaning, and it is not properly applicable to God, who is not our debtor, except perhaps by promise; whereas we are debtors to him because of what we have committed. But so that the poison may be removed, distinguish the sense of the word: “God cannot do except what he ought,” that is, except what he wills, is false; for in this sense he himself may be said to owe something because he wills it. But if it is said, “He himself cannot be said to owe anything because he wills it.” [The text appears to repeat or interrupt the argument here.] But if it is said, “He cannot do except what he ought,” that is, he cannot do except what, if he did it, would fittingly accord with him, it is true.

They further add, saying: “He does nothing or leaves nothing undone except for an optimal and rational cause, though hidden from us, according to which he ought to do and leave undone what he does or leaves undone. For there is within him a reason by which he does these things and leaves those things undone; and this reason is eternal and always abiding, apart from which he cannot do or leave anything undone. Therefore, while that reason remains, he cannot leave undone what he does, nor do what he leaves undone; and thus he cannot do except what he does.”

We reply to this by determining the ambiguity of the expression. When it is said, “There is in God an optimal reason or cause by which he does all that he does and leaves undone what he leaves undone,” this is indeed true: for in him is a most equitable and most upright will, by which he does and leaves undone what he wills, against which he cannot act and apart from which he cannot act. Certainly he would not act against it or apart from it [Col. 0639] if he left undone the things he does, or did the things he leaves undone. But, while the same reason and cause remained, he could have done other things and left these undone. Therefore, although there is within him a reason by which he does some things and leaves others undone, he can nevertheless, according to that same reason, leave undone what he does and do what he leaves undone.

They also add: “There is reason for his doing what he does and not other things; and he cannot do except what there is reason for him to do; and thus he cannot do except what he does. Again, there is reason for his leaving undone what he leaves undone; and he cannot fail to leave undone what there is reason for him to leave undone; and thus he cannot fail to leave undone what he leaves undone.”

To this we say that the expressions are ambiguous and must therefore be determined. For if, when it is said, “He cannot do except what there is reason for him to do,” you understand that he cannot do except things which are rational, and things which, if done, would be rational, the meaning is true. But if you understand that he cannot do other rational and good things except those which he wills and does, the interpretation is false.

They add another point, saying: “If God can do something other than what he does, then he can do what he did not foreknow. And if he can do what he did not foreknow, he can act without foreknowledge, because he does everything which he foreknew that he would do, and does nothing which he did not foreknow. But if it is impossible for anything to occur apart from his foreknowledge, then everything foreknown must occur. Therefore it is in no way possible for anything other than what occurs to occur; therefore God cannot do except what occurs.” This question concerning foreknowledge, however, can readily be settled by what was said above when foreknowledge was being discussed.

### They use authorities to support their opinion

5. These investigators, who “have failed in searching out searches,” attach to these arguments the testimonies of the saints. Augustine says in Book 1 of *On the Creed*, chapter 1: “God cannot do only what he does not will.” From this it seems that he cannot do anything except what he wills; but he wills only what he does, and thus he seems unable to do except what he does. But this must be understood thus: God cannot do only what he does not will himself able to do.

The same author, addressing God in Book 7 of the *Confessions*, chapter 4, says: “You are not compelled unwillingly to do anything, because your will is not greater than your power; but it would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself.” From this it appears that God cannot do more than he wills, just as he does not will more than he can do. For as will is not greater than power, so power is not greater than will. Accordingly, they say that as he does not will more than he can do, so he cannot do more than he wills.

But we say in reply that neither is will greater than power nor power greater than will, because power and will are one and the same reality—namely, God himself, who would be greater than himself if will were greater than power, or power than will. Nor does this authority deny that God can do more than he wills, because more things fall under his power than under his will. Let us therefore confess that God can do more things which he does not will, and can leave undone what he does. To hold this more certainly and firmly, let us establish by the testimonies of Scripture that God can do more than he does.

Truth itself says, according to Matthew 26: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” These words plainly indicate that both the Son could ask what he was not asking and the Father could provide what he was not providing. Each, therefore, could do what he was not doing.

Augustine also says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 95: “The will of the Almighty can do many things which it does not will and does not do; for he could have made twelve legions of angels fight against those who seized Christ.” Again, in the same work: “Why were miracles not done among certain persons which, if they had been done, those people would have repented, while they were done among people who were not going to believe? Then what is now hidden will not be hidden. Nor, indeed, did God unjustly refuse that they be saved, since they could have been saved if he had willed it. Then, in the clearest light of wisdom, what the faith of the devout now holds before it sees it by manifest knowledge will be seen: how certain, unchangeable, and efficacious is the will of God, which can do many things and does not will them, but wills nothing which it cannot do.”

The same author says in Book *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 7: “[Col. 0640] The Lord raised Lazarus in the body. Should it be said that he could not raise Judas in mind? He certainly could, but he did not will to do so.”

These and many other authorities plainly teach that God can do many things which he does not will. This may also be proved by reason: God does not will to justify all human beings, yet who doubts that he can? Therefore God can do something other than what he does; yet if he did something else, he would not thereby be someone else. And he can will something other than what he wills; yet his will can in no way be other, new, or mutable. Even if he can will what he never willed, he can nevertheless will it not newly, nor by a new will, but only by an eternal will. For he can will what he has been able from eternity to have willed; he has the power both now and from eternity to will what nevertheless he neither now wills nor willed from eternity.

## DISTINCTION XLIV. WHETHER GOD CAN MAKE SOMETHING BETTER THAN WHAT HE MAKES

1. It remains now to examine whether he can make something better than what he makes. These investigators commonly say that God cannot make the things he makes better, because if he could make them better and did not do so, he would be envious and not supremely good. They try to establish this by analogy. Augustine says in Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 50: “Because God could not beget one better than himself—for nothing is better than God—he had to beget one equal to himself. For if he willed it and could not, he is weak; if he could and did not will it, he is envious.” From this it is confirmed that he begot the Son equal to himself. By analogy, they wish to say that if God can make a thing better than he makes it, he is envious.

But this analogy is invalid, because he begot the Son from his own substance. Therefore, if he could beget one equal to himself and did not beget one, he would be envious. But he can make better the other things, which he does not make from his own substance.

### The question by which they are pressed

2. But here I ask them to answer why they say that some thing, or even the whole universe of things, in which a greater perfection is expressed, cannot be better than it is. Is it because it is supremely good, such that no perfection of goodness at all is lacking to it? Or because it itself cannot receive the greater good that it lacks? But if it is called supremely good in such a way that no perfection of good is lacking to it, then the creature is made equal to the Creator. But if it cannot be better because it cannot receive the further good that it lacks, then this very inability is a defect, not a perfection; and it can be better if it is made capable of a better good—which he who made it can do. Therefore God can make a better thing than what he makes.

Hence Augustine, volume 2, Book 11, *On Genesis*, chapter 7: “God could have made a human being such that he could neither sin nor will to sin; and if he had made such a one, who doubts that he would have been better?” From what has been said it is clear that God can both make things other than those which he makes and make the things he makes better than he makes them.

### Whether he can make what he makes in another or better way

3. After this we must consider whether he can make the things he makes in another or better way than he makes them. If the mode of operation is referred to the wisdom of the maker, no other or better mode can exist. For he cannot make anything differently or better than he makes it—that is, by another wisdom or a greater wisdom; for he cannot make anything more wisely than he makes it. But if the mode is referred to the thing itself which God makes, we say that another and a better mode can exist. In this respect it may be conceded that he can make the things he makes better and differently than he makes them, because he can bestow upon some a better mode of existing and upon others another mode.

Hence Augustine, in Book 13 of *On the Trinity*, says that another mode of our deliverance was possible for God, who can do all things; but no other was more fitting for the healing of our misery. Therefore God can make some of the things he makes in another and better way, some in another but equally good way, and some even in a less good way than he makes them—provided that the mode is referred to the quality of the work, that is, of the creature, and not to the wisdom of the Creator.

### Whether God can always do everything that he once could do

4. Furthermore, it is commonly asked whether God can always do everything that he once could do. Some think that he cannot, saying: God could become incarnate, could die, rise again, and do other such things which he now cannot do. Therefore he could do things which he now cannot do, and so he had a power which he now does not have; hence it appears that his power has diminished.

To this we say that, just as he always knows everything that he has at some time known, and always wills what he has at some time willed, and never loses any knowledge or changes any will which he has had, so he can always do everything which he has at some time been able to do, and is never deprived of any of his power. Therefore he is not deprived of the power of becoming incarnate or rising again, although he cannot now become incarnate or rise again. For just as he was once able to become incarnate, so he can now be incarnate; in this the power regarding the same thing is shown. For as he once knew that he would rise again, and now knows that he has risen, so there is not one knowledge in having known the former then and another in knowing the latter now, but wholly the same knowledge. And just as he once willed to rise again, and now wills that he has risen, in which the will concerning one thing is expressed, so he was once able to be born and rise again, and now he is able to have been born and to have risen again; and this is power regarding the same thing. For if he could now be born and rise again, it would not be the same ability.

For verbs of different times, uttered at different times and joined to different adverbs, express the same meaning. Thus, speaking now, we say, “This man can read today”; tomorrow we shall say, “This man can have read,” or, “He could read yesterday.” In every case, power concerning one thing is shown. But if, speaking at different times, we use verbs and adverbs of the same time, saying today, “This man can read today,” and tomorrow, “This man can read today,” we say that he can do not the same thing but different things.

Let us therefore confess that God can always do whatever he was once able to do—that is, that he has all the power which he once had, and power concerning every thing concerning which he once had power. But he cannot always do everything which he was at some time able to do [Note: [Col. 0641] Here the Master is contradicted by most modern doctors]: he can, indeed, do or have done what he was once able to do. Likewise, he has and wills whatever he has willed—that is, every will which he had he also has now—yet he does not will everything which he at some time willed to be or to happen; rather, he wills it to have been or to have happened. The same must be said of God’s knowledge.

## DISTINCTION XLV. ON THE WILL OF GOD, WHICH IS GOD’S ONE AND ETERNAL ESSENCE, AND ON ITS SIGNS

1. We must now say something about the will of God, insofar as the weakness of our understanding permits. It must be known, therefore, that “will” or “willing” is said of God according to essence. For to will something is not one thing for him and to be another; rather, they are altogether the same. And just as for him to be good is the same as to be God, so for him to be willing is the same as to be God. For the will by which he is always willing is not an affection or movement—which cannot occur in God—but the divine *ousia* by which God is willing, and likewise in similar expressions.

### Although willing and being are the same for God, God cannot be said to be all that he wills

2. Although for God to will is the same as to be, it must not therefore be said that God is all the things that he wills. Some people, who think wrongly concerning God’s will, object to us: “If for God to will is the same as to be, then when we say that God wills everything he makes, we say that he is everything he makes. Otherwise, in this statement the word ‘will’ does not signify the same as the word ‘be’ signifies when it is said of God. And if that is so, ‘will’ is not always said of God according to essence. But if it is sometimes not said according to essence, in what way is it said of God? For it is never said relatively.”

We reply that although for God to will is altogether the same as to be, he nevertheless cannot be said to be all that he wills. So likewise, for God to be is the same as to know, yet he cannot be said to be all things in the way that he is said to know all things. [Col. 0642]

### The meaning of the statements “God knows” or “God wills”; likewise, “God knows all things” or “God wills something”; and what is predicated of God in them

3. Wherever God is said to know or to be knowing, to will or to be willing, these are said of him according to essence. For when it is said, “God knows,” “God wills,” “God is knowing,” or “God is willing,” the divine essence is predicated of him, and God is affirmed to be. But when “all things,” “something,” or “some things” is added, and it is said, “God knows all things,” or “God wills something” or “some things,” the divine essence is indeed predicated, but not simply and absolutely: rather, all things are shown as subject to the knowledge which he himself is, and something or some things are said to be subject to the will which is likewise himself. Thus the sense is: “God knows all things,” that is, God is he to whose knowledge, which is his own essence, all things are subject. Likewise: “God wills these or those things,” that is, God is he to whose will, which is himself, these or those things are subject. Therefore God is called willing, or is said to will, according to the essence whose will is eternal and immutable essence—although the things subject to it vary and pass away—and which cannot be unjust or evil, because it is God.

### God’s will is the supremely good cause of all things which naturally exist; its cause is not to be sought, because it has none, being eternal

4. This supremely good will, then, is the cause of everything that occurs naturally, or has occurred, or will occur; no cause preceded it, because it is eternal. Therefore its cause should not be sought. For whoever seeks its cause seeks something greater than it, whereas nothing is greater than it.

Hence Augustine, in Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 28: “Whoever asks why God willed to make the world seeks the cause of God’s will. But every efficient cause is greater than what is effected. Nothing, however, is greater than the will of God. Therefore its cause should not be sought.”

The same author says in the book *Against the Manicheans*: “If anyone should say, ‘What pleased God in making heaven and earth?’ one must answer: Those who desire to know God’s will seek to know the causes and will of God, even though God’s will is itself the cause of all things that exist. For if God’s will has a cause, there is something preceding God’s will, which it is impious to believe. Therefore to one who says, ‘Why did God make heaven and earth?’ one must reply, ‘Because he willed.’ For God’s will is the cause of heaven and earth; and therefore God’s will is greater than heaven and earth. But one who says, ‘Why did he will to make heaven and earth?’ seeks something greater than God’s will; but nothing greater can be found. Let human rashness therefore restrain itself and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist.”

Behold: these authorities plainly show that God’s will has no cause, and therefore its cause ought not to be sought.

### God’s will is the first and supreme cause of all things

5. Therefore, as Augustine says, volume 4, in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, the will of God is the first and supreme cause of all forms and motions. For nothing happens which does not proceed, according to ineffable justice, from the inner and intelligible court of the supreme ruler. For where does the wisdom of Almighty God fail to accomplish what it wills? It “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). It makes not only things which, by the persistence of custom, admit no wonder, but also things which seem wonderful because of the rarity and unusual character of their occurrence: such as eclipses of the heavenly lights, earthquakes, monstrous births of animals, and the like. None of these occurs without God’s will, though this is not apparent to most people. Therefore it pleased the vanity of philosophers to attribute them to other causes also, since they were wholly unable to perceive the cause higher than all the rest—namely, the will of God.

Thus God’s will alone is the first cause of health, sickness, rewards and punishments, graces and recompenses. This alone, therefore, is the source from which whatever exists has arisen; and it itself has not arisen, but is eternal.

### The ways in which “God’s will” is understood

6. Here we must not pass over the fact that sacred [Col. 0643] Scripture customarily speaks of the will of God in various ways; nevertheless God’s will is not diverse, but the language about the will is diverse, because it understands diverse things by the name “will.” For will is truly and properly called that which is in him and is his essence. It is one, admits neither multiplicity nor mutability, and cannot be unfulfilled. Of it the Prophet says, Psalm 113: “The Lord has done all that he willed.” And the Apostle, Romans 9: “Who has resisted his will?” And Romans 12: “That you may discern what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” This will is rightly called God’s good pleasure or disposition.

### God’s will is figuratively called command, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation; hence Scripture speaks of “wills” in the plural

7. Sometimes, however, by a certain figure of speech, something is called God’s will which is not properly his will: namely, command, prohibition, counsel, as well as permission and operation. Therefore Scripture sometimes speaks of the wills of God in the plural. Thus the Prophet says, Psalm 110: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills.” Although there is but one will of God, which is himself, it nevertheless says “wills” in the plural because God’s will is understood in various ways and for different things, as has been said.

Likewise, because of the many effects of mercy and justice, the same Prophet speaks in the plural, Psalm 88: “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord”; and Psalm 18: “The righteous ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts.” Yet in God there is one mercy and one justice, and mercy itself is one and the same as justice—namely, the divine *ousia*.

### Why command, prohibition, and counsel are called God’s will

8. Although command, prohibition, and counsel are three things, each is nevertheless called God’s will because they are signs of the divine will. In the same way signs of wrath are called wrath, and signs of love are called love. God is called angry, yet there is no wrath in him: only the external signs by which he is shown to be angry are called his wrath. This is a figure of speech according to which what is said is not false; but the truth of what is said is veiled beneath the cloud of trope. According to these tropes diverse wills of God are spoken of, because the things called God’s will by trope are diverse.

### Where God’s will is understood as command and counsel

9. “Will” may be understood as God’s command and counsel, as in Matthew 6: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth”; and Matthew 12: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.” Many things are done against this will. Hence Augustine, volume 3, in Book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 13: “The unbelieving act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel.”

### God does not will that human beings do everything which he commands, or fail to do everything which he prohibits

10. Even if these things are called God’s will because they are signs of the divine will, it should nevertheless not be understood that God wills every thing to be done which he commands anyone to do, or every thing not to be done which he has forbidden. For he commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, yet did not will it; nor did he command it in order that it might be done, but in order that Abraham’s faith might be tested. And in the Gospel he commanded the man who had been healed to tell no one; but the man proclaimed it everywhere, understanding that God had not forbidden this because he did not will his work to be proclaimed, but in order to provide humankind with a model for avoiding human praise.

### On permission and operation, where they are called God’s will

11. God’s permission and operation are likewise called God’s will. Augustine understands it thus in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 95, saying: “Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it to happen or by doing it himself. Nor should it be doubted that God acts well even when he permits whatever happens badly to happen; for he permits these things only by God’s just judgment, and certainly everything that is just is good.”

Here we plainly have God’s [Col. 0644] operation or permission called his will, when he says that nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, thereby including all good and evil things that occur. Therefore he expressly distinguishes the manner in which he says that God wills, lest willing good and evil should be understood in the same way. He adds: “Either by permitting it to happen”—this he says with reference to evils—or “by doing it himself”—this with reference to goods. For he permits evils to happen but does not do them; whereas he himself does good things. Thus he said that God wills, because, while not willing evils, he permits them, and while willing goods, he works them. For this reason permission and operation are called God’s will.

### The five things stated above are called God’s will tropologically; the reader must therefore distinguish everywhere which one is intended

12. The five things stated above are called God’s will by trope because they are signs of the one and immutable divine will, namely, God’s good pleasure. The reader must therefore carefully distinguish, wherever Scripture mentions God’s will, in which sense it should be understood: whether as God’s good pleasure or as one of its signs. Great discernment is required in understanding the divine will, because both God’s good pleasure is his will and a sign of his good pleasure is called his will. But his good pleasure is eternal, whereas the sign of his good pleasure is not; his good pleasure accords with the effects of things, and the effects themselves do not depart from it. For everything which he wills to happen by his good pleasure happens, and whatever he does not will to happen does not happen at all. But this is not so with the signs: for God commands many people to do things which they do not do, forbids things which they do not avoid, and counsels things which they do not carry out.

## DISTINCTION XLVI. CERTAIN STATEMENTS SEEM TO CONFLICT WITH THE PROPOSITION THAT GOD’S WILL, WHICH IS HIMSELF, CANNOT BE FRUSTRATED

1. Here a question arises. It has been said above, and supported by authorities, that the will of God—which is himself and is called his good pleasure—cannot be frustrated, because by that will he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, and, according to the Apostle’s testimony, nothing resists it. The question, therefore, is how we should understand what the Apostle says of the Lord in 1 Timothy 2: “Who wills all human beings to be saved.” Since not all are saved, but more are condemned, it certainly appears that what God wills to happen does not happen, human will obstructing God’s will.

The Lord likewise, rebuking the impious city in the Gospel, says, Matthew 23: “How often I willed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” These words likewise seem to say that God’s will was overcome by human will, and that the Most Powerful could not do what he willed because the utterly weak, by refusing, obstructed him. Where, then, is that omnipotence by which, according to the Prophet, he “has done all that he willed” in heaven and on earth? And how does nothing resist his will, according to the Apostle, if he willed to gather Jerusalem’s children and did not do it? These statements seem very strongly to conflict with what was said above.

### Solution: how “I willed to gather, and you were unwilling” should be understood

2. But let us hear the solution, and first consider how the Lord’s saying should be understood. As Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 97, resolving the question just stated, it was not said in the sense that the Lord willed to gather Jerusalem’s children and what he willed did not occur because she herself was unwilling. Rather, she herself was unwilling for her children to be gathered by him, yet, though she was unwilling, he himself gathered all her children whom he willed. For in heaven and on earth he did not will some things and do them, while willing other things and not doing them; rather, he did all that he willed.

Thus the sense is: “How often I willed to gather your children, and you were unwilling!” That is: “All those whom I gathered, I did so by my ever-effective will, though you were unwilling.” Behold, it is clearly established that the Lord’s words do not conflict with the preceding statements.

### How “Who wills all human beings to be saved” should be understood

3. It remains to see how the Apostle’s preceding [Col. 0645] words also do not contradict what was said before, when he says of God, “He wills all human beings to be saved.” On account of these words many have departed from the truth, saying that God wills many things to happen which do not happen. But this must not be understood as though God wills some people to be saved who are not saved. For who would be so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn into good the evil wills of human beings—whichever wills he chooses, whenever he chooses, and wherever he chooses?

Certainly the Psalm’s statement, “He has done all that he willed,” would not be true if he had willed certain things and had not done them; and what is more unworthy, he would not have done them because human will prevented Almighty Will from accomplishing what it willed. Therefore, when we hear and read in sacred Scripture that he wills all human beings to be saved, we must not for that reason detract anything from God’s all-powerful will. Rather, we should understand the written words, “He wills all human beings to be saved,” as though it said that no human being is saved except one whom he himself wills to be saved—not that there is no human being except one whom he wills to be saved, but that no one becomes saved except one whom he wills to save. Therefore he must be entreated to will it; and it must happen if he wills it.

For one must not believe that the Almighty willed something to occur which did not occur. Thus also John 1, “He enlightens every human being coming into this world,” is understood: not because there is no human being who is not enlightened, but because no one is enlightened except by him. It may also be understood in another way, provided that we are not compelled to believe that the Almighty willed something to occur which did not occur. For, without any ambiguity, as Truth declares, he has done in heaven and on earth all that he willed; certainly he did not will to do whatever he did not do.

From these points it is plainly shown that God, by the will which is himself, does not will something to happen which does not happen, nor something not to happen which does happen.

### Whether evils occur by God’s will or against his will

4. Therefore, since it is established that all good things which occur occur by his will—things which could in no way occur if he did not will them to occur—it is rightly asked whether all evils which occur, that is, sins, occur by God’s will, or whether they occur against his will. On this matter different people, holding various opinions, are found to contradict one another. Some say that God wills evils to exist or to occur, though he does not will evils. Others say that he wills neither for evils to exist nor for them to occur. Yet both groups agree in this: they confess without qualification that God does not will evils. Both rely on reasons and authorities to support their assertion.

### Why Some Say That God Wills Evils to Exist or to Occur

5. Those who say that God wills evils to exist or to occur support their position in the following ways. “For,” they say, “if he willed that evils should not exist or occur, they would by no means exist or occur. For if he wills them not to exist or occur, yet cannot bring this about—namely, that they do not exist or occur—then something resists his will and power, and he is not omnipotent, since he cannot do what he wills; rather, he is powerless like ourselves, who sometimes cannot do what we will. But since he is omnipotent and powerless in no respect, it is certain that evils cannot occur or exist except with his willing it. For how could evil be done by anyone against his will and while he is unwilling, when it is written in Romans 9: ‘Who has resisted his will?’ Augustine also said above that it must happen if he wills it. But he wills evils either to occur or not to occur. If he wills that they not occur, they do not occur; but they do occur; therefore, he wills them to occur.

“Again, it is good that evils exist or occur; otherwise, the supremely good God would not permit them to occur.” Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 96: “Although those things which are evil, insofar as they are evil, are not good, nevertheless it is good that there should be not only good things but also evil things. For unless it were good that evil things should exist, they would by no means be permitted to exist by the omnipotent Good; for undoubtedly, as easily as he does what he wills, so easily does he prevent what he does not will from existing.”

Unless we believe this, our confession is endangered, since we profess faith in the Father almighty. Behold, [Col. 0646] here you have it stated openly that it is good for evils to exist. But God is the author of every good, and he wills every good that exists to exist. Therefore, since it is good for evils to occur or exist, he also wills evils to occur or exist. Such are the arguments and authorities, among others of this kind, used by those who say that God wills evils to exist or occur.

### Here He Sets Out the Arguments of Those Who Say That Evils Do Not Occur or Exist by God’s Will

6. But those who say that evils do not occur or exist by God’s will respond to the foregoing arguments as follows. They say that God neither wills evils to occur nor wills them not to occur; rather, he is not unwilling that they occur, but merely does not will them to occur.

For if he willed them to occur or exist, he would certainly cause them to occur or exist, and thus would be the author of evils. But he is not the author of evils, as the authorities of the saints attest. Therefore evils do not occur by his will. Again, if he were unwilling that evils occur, or if he willed that they not occur, and yet they did occur, he would not be omnipotent, since his will would be impeded in its effect by the human will.

Therefore they do not grant that God wills evils to occur, lest he be understood to be the author of evils; nor do they grant that he wills evils not to occur, lest he seem powerless. Rather, they say only that he does not will evils to occur, so that he may be shown to be not the author but the permitter of evils.

Thus the Evangelist, John 1, after showing that God is the author of all good things by saying, “All things were made through him,” subsequently denies that he is the author of evils by saying, “And without him nothing was made”—that is, sin. He did not say that sin was made through him, or while he was unwilling and opposed, but only “without him,” that is, without his will, because sin does not occur by his will.

Therefore evils occur neither with God willing nor with God unwilling, but with God not willing them; for it is not subject to God’s will that evil should occur or not occur, but that he should permit it to occur. For it is good to permit evils to occur; and indeed, while willing, he permits them—not willing evils, but willing to permit them to occur—because evils are not good, nor is their occurrence or existence good.

### How Augustine’s Statement, “It Is Good That Evils Occur,” Is to Be Understood

7. Yet Augustine’s statement—“It is good that evils occur,” and “evils would not be permitted by the omnipotent Good to occur unless it were good that they should exist”—they maintain was made for this reason: God draws good things out of the evils that occur, and would not permit them to occur unless he made some good out of them.

Hence Augustine, in the same book, *Enchiridion*, chapter 11, clearly indicating that the preceding words have this meaning, says: “God almighty, whose power over things is supreme, being supremely good, would in no way permit any evil to exist in his works, unless he were so omnipotent and good that he could bring about good even from evil.” Again, in the same work, tome 3, chapter 17: “God judged it better to make good things out of evils than to permit no evils at all.”

It is in this sense, then, that the statement was made, and it is true: “It is good that evils occur,” because from the evils that occur there comes goodness—that is, benefit—to the good, “who are called saints according to his purpose.” For, as the Apostle says, all things, even evils, work together for good for such persons, because they benefit them, though they harm others who do them.

Thus Scripture also sometimes calls an evil good. As Jerome says, tome 9, *Commentary on Mark*, chapter 14: “The evil of Judas was good—namely, for us.” Yet if something is good for this person or that, it does not follow that it is good simply speaking; what is good simply speaking is good in itself and for the one doing it.

### A Fourfold Understanding of “Good”

8. For there is something which is good in itself and for the person for whom it is done, but not good for the one doing it: as when aid is given to a poor person, but not for God’s sake. There is also something good in itself and for the one doing it, but not for the person for whom it is done: as when truth is preached for God’s sake to someone who does not obey. And there is something good in itself, for the one doing it, and for the person for whom it is done: as when truth is preached for God’s sake to a believer. Hence the Apostle says: “We are a sweet savour unto God: to some, a savour of life; to others, a savour of death.”

There is, however, another thing which is neither good in itself, nor beneficial to the one doing it, but harms and condemns that person unless he repents: namely, evil. Yet it has some usefulness. For as Augustine says in *Enchiridion*, chapters 10 and 11: “All things have been created good by the supremely, unchangeably good Trinity [Col. 0647]; not supremely or unchangeably good, but nevertheless good, each individually. Yet taken all together, they are very good, because from them all consists the wondrous beauty of the universe. In it even that which is called evil, being well ordered and placed in its own location, more strikingly commends the good things, so that they may please more and be more praiseworthy when compared with evils.”

### How Evils Benefit the Universe, and Benefit Their Doers Through Their Own Evils or the Elect Through Evils Suffered from Others

9. From this it is clear that some good results from the evils that occur, since good things are more pleasing and are regarded as more praiseworthy. Even to the persons doing evils, good sometimes results from the evils which they do, if they are saints called according to the purpose. For, as Augustine says, tome 7, in *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 9, God so completely makes all things work together for good for such persons that, if any of them stray and wander from the path, he makes even this itself advance them toward good; for they return more humble and more instructed, as Peter did.

Likewise, those evils which the faithful endure devoutly at the hands of the wicked, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, benefit them: either for the removal of sins, or for the exercise and testing of righteousness, or for demonstrating the misery of this life. Thus Job felt God’s hand, and the Apostle the thorn of Satan; and each made good progress, because each bore evil well.

### From the Foregoing He Concludes That It Is Good for Evils to Occur in Many Ways

10. If anyone carefully attends to what has been written, it is easy for him to understand that good things arise from evils, and that the statement, “It is good for evils to occur or exist,” was made with reason—not because evil is good, or because it is good for evil to be done. For it is not good for evil to be done by anyone, because it is not good that anyone should do evil.

For if this were good, then God, who is the author of every good, would certainly be its author. But if God is the author of this, then a human being does evils with God as author, and so becomes worse with God as author. And if a human being becomes worse with God as author, then the person becomes worse with God willing it. For to say that something is done with God as author is the same as to say that it is done with God willing it. But a human being does not become worse with God as author, and therefore not with God willing it.

Augustine, tome 4, *Questions*, book 33, question 3, plainly establishes this by an argument from the lesser, saying: “No human being becomes worse with any wise human being as author; for this fault is so great that it cannot befall a wise person. But God surpasses every wise human being; much less, therefore, does a human being become worse with God as author. For God’s will surpasses by far that of a wise human being. But when one says ‘with him as author,’ one says ‘with him willing’; therefore it is a defect of the human will by which a human being becomes worse. Since, as reason teaches, this defect is far removed from God’s will, from whom must it be sought?”

Behold, Augustine plainly says that a human being does not become worse with God as author or willing it, but through the defect of his own will. Therefore it is not with God as author that evil is done by anyone; and consequently evils do not occur with God willing them.

### That There Is No Cause in God Why a Human Being Becomes Worse

11. Next, Augustine himself, in question 4, asks what is the cause by which a human being becomes worse, and asserts that it is not in God. In the same book he says: if a human being becomes worse, the cause is either in the person himself, in another, or in nothing. If it is in nothing, there is no cause. If it is in another, it is either in God, in some other human being, or in that which is neither God nor human. But it is not in God, for God is the cause only of good things. Therefore it is in the human being, or in that which is neither God nor human, or in nothing.

From this it is plainly shown that it is not good for a human being to become worse, because God is not the cause of that thing, since he is the cause only of good things. And if it is not good for a human being to become worse, then it is not good for evil to be done by him; therefore God does not will evil to be done by him.

### Another Proof That Evils Do Not Occur with God as Author

12. Again, it is also shown in another way that evils do not occur with God as author—that is, with God willing them—because he is not the cause of tending toward non-being. For to tend toward non-being is evil, and he is not the author of evil. But one who does evil tends toward non-being. Therefore it is not with God as author that anyone does evil.

Therefore it is not good that anyone does evil, because God is the author only of good [Col. 0648]. Augustine, in the same book, question 21, at the beginning and end, explains this plainly as follows: “He who is the author of all things that are, and to whose goodness it belongs that everything which is should exist, is the cause only of good. Therefore he is not the author of evil; and consequently he himself is the supreme good, from whom not to fall away in any respect is good, while to fall away is evil. Therefore he is not the cause of falling away—that is, of tending toward non-being—who, so to speak, is the cause of being; for he is the author of all things that are, which, insofar as they are, are good.”

Here you have it plainly: to fall away from God, who is the supreme good, is evil; therefore to do evils is evil; therefore evils do not occur with God as author or willing them.

### The Sophistical Objection of Certain Persons, by Which They Endeavour to Prove That the Occurrence of Evils Is from God

13. It has now been sufficiently shown that evils do not occur with God as author. Yet certain people, proceeding sophistically and therefore hateful to God, try to prove that the occurrence of evils is from God as author in this way: “It is true that evils occur. But every truth that exists is from the truth, which is God. Therefore it is from God that evils occur.”

That every truth is from God they confirm by Augustine’s authority, *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 1, where he says: “Every truth is true through truth; but truth is God; therefore every truth has God as its author.” But it is true that evils occur or exist; therefore, with God as author, evils exist or occur.

### The Reply, Which Grants That Every Truth Is from God and Exposes the Sophism

14. We can easily answer them; though what they say seems unworthy of an answer. For every truth is from God, as Augustine says. Ambrose agrees with him, tome 4, exposition on 1 Corinthians 12. Discussing the Apostle’s statement, “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit,” he says that whenever truth is spoken by anyone, it is from the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, since it is true that evils occur, this truth expressed by the statement “evils occur” is from God. But it does not follow from this that it is from God that evils occur. For if that were said, God would be understood to be the author of evils. That this inference is plainly false is shown by a similar argument: God forbids theft to occur; but it is true that theft occurs; therefore he forbids truth. The conclusion does not follow.

### He Approves That Side of the Question Which Says That God Does Not Will Evils to Occur

15. Leaving aside these and other empty arguments of this kind, and adhering to the sounder side of the foregoing question, which is more fully approved by the testimonies of the saints, let us say that God does not will evils to occur; yet neither does he will them not to occur, nor is he unwilling that they occur. Therefore everything which he wills to occur does occur, and everything which he wills not to occur does not occur. Yet many things occur which he does not will to occur, such as all evils.

## DISTINCTION XLVII. THAT GOD’S WILL IS ALWAYS FULFILLED IN REGARD TO HUMAN BEINGS, WHICHEVER WAY THEY TURN

1. God’s will is always effective, so that everything he wills comes to pass and nothing he does not will comes to pass. His will is always fulfilled in regard to a human being, whichever way that person turns. For, as Augustine says, nothing established in free choice surpasses God’s will. Even if a person acts against his will, nevertheless nothing should be thought to happen against that will which he himself is, as though he willed something to occur and it did not occur, or did not will it to occur and it did occur.

For that will, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, is always fulfilled either concerning us or by us. It is fulfilled concerning us, but we do not fulfill it when we sin. It is fulfilled by us when we do good, for we do it because we know that it pleases God. Thus God always fulfills his own will concerning a human being, because a person does nothing from which God does not bring about what he wills.

For God does not will that any human being should sin. But if a person sins, he wills to spare the repentant person so that he may live; whereas he wills to punish the person who perseveres in sins, so that the obstinate may not escape the power of justice. Just as he prepared some from eternity for punishment, so he prepared others for glory; and these are “the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” [Col. 0649] (Psalm 110 [111]).

Yet these works are wisely sought out: so that, when angelic and human creatures sinned—that is, did not what he willed, but what they themselves willed—he might nevertheless fulfill what he willed even through that same will of the creature by which what the Creator did not will was done. For, being supremely good, he makes good use even of evils: for the damnation of those whom he justly predestined for punishment, and for the salvation of those whom he graciously predestined for grace.

For as far as they themselves were concerned, they did what God did not will; but as regards God’s omnipotence, they could in no way bring this about. Indeed, precisely in doing against his will, his will was accomplished concerning them. Moreover, the great works of the Lord are sought out according to all his wills, so that in a wondrous and ineffable manner nothing happens apart from his will, even when it happens against his will; for it would not happen if he did not permit it. And he certainly does not permit it unwillingly, but willingly; nor would the good God permit evil to be done unless, being omnipotent, he could also make good out of evil well.

These words plainly show that God’s eternal will is always fulfilled concerning a human being, even if that person acts against God’s will. But one must carefully consider how, in the foregoing, something is said to occur against God’s will, although it does not occur apart from it; and how the statement, “As far as they themselves were concerned, they did what God did not will; but as regards God’s omnipotence, they could in no way bring this about,” is to be understood. For these statements seem contrary to those above, where it was said that nothing resists his will.

### Here He Explains That “God’s Will” Has Been Taken Above in Different Senses

2. But, as we said above, God’s will is understood in different ways. If this distinction is carefully noted in the preceding statements, no contradiction will be found there. For when he says that even what happens against God’s will does not happen apart from his will—which will is God himself and is eternal—he intends in the preceding words that God’s signs be understood, namely, prohibition and permission.

For many things occur contrary to God’s command or prohibition, but do not occur apart from his permission. All evils occur by his permission, yet occur apart from his eternal will, which he himself is. Thus Augustine, tome 8, says on Psalm 16 [17], at the words, “Let not my mouth speak the works of men.” By “works of men” he means evil things, which occur apart from God’s will, which he himself is, but not apart from his permission, which he himself is not.

Yet permission itself is called God’s will, because God willingly permits evils to occur. They occur also contrary to his precept or prohibition, but not contrary to his will, which he himself is—unless they are said to occur against that will because they occur apart from it. For nothing occurs against it in such a way that he wills it to happen and it does not happen, or does not will it and it happens.

Augustine clearly noted this where he said: “As far as they themselves were concerned, they did what God did not will; but as regards God’s omnipotence, they could in no way bring this about.” It is as though he said: they acted against God’s command, which is called a will, but they did not act against God’s omnipotent will. For they had power to do the former, but not the latter. Thus, through what they did against God’s will—that is, his command—his will was fulfilled concerning them: namely, his eternal will by which he willed them to be condemned.

Hence Gregory, *On Genesis*: “Many carry out the will of God while striving to alter it, and, resisting his counsel, they serve it; for they advance that ordering of his which opposes human endeavor.” Here it is plainly shown that, while the wicked resist God’s counsel and command, which is called God’s will, they do those things through which his will, which he himself is, is fulfilled—a will called disposition or good pleasure.

For, as Augustine says, tome 3, chapter 102, in the *Enchiridion*: “However many may be the wills of angels and human beings, good or evil—whether willing what God wills or something other than what God wills—the will of the Almighty is always unconquered. It can never be evil; and even when it inflicts evils, it is just. And certainly what is just is not evil. Therefore God almighty either has mercy on whom he wills through mercy, or hardens whom he wills through judgment; he does nothing unjustly, does nothing except willingly, and does whatever he wills.”

### A Summary of the Foregoing, with the Reason Why God Commanded All Persons to Do Good and Avoid Evil Though He Did Not Will This to Be Fulfilled by All

3. From the foregoing it is clear that God’s will, which he himself is, is always unconquered and is frustrated in no respect, but is fulfilled in all things. But his counsel and command, or prohibition, are not fulfilled by all those to whom they are proposed and given.

Nor did he command good things to all, forbid evils, or counsel what is best, because he willed all persons to do the good things he commanded or avoid the evils he forbade. For if he had so willed, they would certainly have done so, since his will can in no respect be overcome or impeded by a human being. Rather, he did so in order to show his justice to human beings and to make the wicked inexcusable; finally, so that the good might receive glory for obedience and the wicked punishment for disobedience, as he prepared both from eternity.

Therefore, he willed certain persons, though not all, to do or avoid the things which he commanded or prohibited for all. He also issued some personal commands, in both the Old and New Law, which he did not will to be performed by those to whom he gave them: for example, to Abraham concerning the sacrifice of his son, and in the Gospel to certain persons whom he healed, when he commanded them to tell no one.

## DISTINCTION XLVIII. THAT SOMETIMES A HUMAN BEING WITH A GOOD WILL WILLS SOMETHING OTHER THAN GOD WILLS, AND SOMETIMES WITH AN EVIL WILL WILLS WHAT GOD WILLS WITH A GOOD WILL

1. It should also be known that sometimes the will of a human being who wills the very thing God wills to occur is evil, and sometimes the will of a human being who wills something other than God wills is good. For a human will to be good, one must consider what it is fitting for that person to will, and for what end.

There is such a great difference between God’s will and a human being’s will that, in some matters, it is fitting for God to will one thing and for a human being to will another. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 101: “Sometimes, with a good will, a human being wills something which God does not will by a will far better and far more certain; for his will can never be evil. For example, a good son may wish his father to live, whereas God in his good will wishes him to die. Again, it may happen that a human being wills with an evil will what God wills with a good will: for instance, an evil son may wish his father to die, and God may also will this. The former wills what God does not will; the latter wills what both he and God will. Yet the filial devotion of the former, though willing something different, is more in harmony with God’s good will than is the impiety of the latter, though willing the same thing.”

For it makes a great difference what it is fitting for a human being to will, what it is fitting for God to will, and to what end each refers his will, if it is to be approved or disapproved. One may will a good thing which it is not fitting for one to will; and one may will a good thing which it is fitting to will, but not refer it to the right end, and therefore the will is not good.

### That God’s Good Will Is Fulfilled Through the Evil Will of Human Beings, as Happened in Christ’s Passion; There Something Was Done Which God Willed with a Good Will and the Jews with an Evil Will, Though They Also Willed Something Which God Did Not Will

2. Nor should this be omitted: sometimes God’s good will is fulfilled through the evil will of a human being. This occurred in the crucifixion of Christ, whom God willed to die with a good will, while the Jews crucified him with an impious will.

The Jews, with an evil will, willed something which God willed with a good will—namely, that Christ should suffer and die. But they also willed something else which God did not will: namely, to kill Christ. This was an evil action and a sin. God did not will the action of the Jews, but he did will Christ’s passion. Thus Christ himself says to the Father in Psalm 138 [139]: “You have known my sitting down”—that is, “You have willed and approved my passion, for it pleased you.”

Therefore the whole Trinity willed that Christ should suffer, yet did not will that the Jews should kill him; because God willed Christ’s punishment, but not the Jews’ guilt. Yet he was not unwilling; for if he had been unwilling, it would not have occurred.

### Objection

[Col. 0651]

3. But the following objection is raised. If God willed Christ to suffer, then he either willed him to suffer at the hands of the Jews or did not. If he willed that Christ should not suffer at the hands of the Jews, then, since Christ did suffer, what God willed not to occur did occur. But if he willed him to suffer at the hands of the Jews, then he willed him to be killed by the Jews; therefore, he willed that the Jews should kill him.

In reply, we say that it must simply be granted that God willed Christ to suffer and die, because his passion was good and was the cause of our salvation. But when it is said, “He willed him to suffer or be killed by the Jews,” a distinction must be made. If it is understood thus—“He willed Christ to undergo the passion or crucifixion inflicted by the Jews”—the sense is true. But if it is understood thus—“He willed that the Jews should kill him”—it is false.

For God did not will the action of the Jews, which was evil, but he willed the good passion; and this will was fulfilled through the evil wills of the Jews. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 101: “God certainly fulfills some of his good wills through the evil wills of wicked human beings. Thus through the ill-willed Jews Christ was killed for us by the good will of the Father. This was so great a good that the Apostle Peter, when he did not wish it to happen, was called Satan by the very one who was killed.”

Here you have it plainly: it was a great good that Christ was killed; and because Peter did not wish this good, he was rebuked.

### Whether It Was Right for Good Men to Be Pleased That Christ Should Suffer: It Was Pleasing in View of Our Redemption, but Not in View of His Torment Itself

4. This resolves the question commonly asked: whether holy men ought to have been pleased that Christ suffered or was killed. They ought indeed to have been pleased in view of our redemption, but not in view of his torment itself. Therefore they willed and ardently desired Christ to die for humanity’s deliverance and for the fulfillment of the divine will, but they did not will it with delight in his affliction itself.

Thus they rejoiced and grieved over the same thing; but they rejoiced for one reason and grieved for another. They willed Christ to die for humanity’s redemption, [Col. 0652] and yet their hearts were variously moved concerning his death for different reasons.

### How One Should Think About the Sufferings of the Saints: Whether We Should Will or Not Will Them

5. If it is asked whether one should think in the same way about the sufferings and martyrdoms of the saints, we say that there is some difference between the passion of the Head and that of the members. Christ’s passion is the cause of our salvation; this is not so of any saint’s suffering. For we have been redeemed by no one’s passion except Christ’s. The sufferings of the saints did indeed benefit not only those who suffered but also other faithful persons; nevertheless, they are not our redemption. For this could be accomplished only by the passion of him who is God and man.

Therefore the devout minds of believers willed and desired Christ’s passion to occur, as they believed it would occur. But we may will and not will the sufferings of the saints, and either response may be made with a good will, provided we set before ourselves right ends.

For someone who was pleased at Paul’s suffering because he saw that Paul’s reward was thereby increased and prepared seems to have had a good will—a will consonant with Paul’s own, since he desired “to depart and be with Christ.” But someone who wished Paul to escape suffering and to evade the hands of the wicked from compassionate piety also had a good will.

Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 101: “The good wills of the devout faithful, who did not wish the apostle Paul to go to Jerusalem lest he suffer there the evils foretold by Agabus, appeared good. Yet God willed him to suffer this for the preaching of Christ’s faith, exercising Christ’s martyr. Nor did he fulfill his good will through the good wills of Christians, but through the evil wills of the Jews. Those who did not will what he willed belonged more to him than did those through whom, while willing, what he willed was done, because they did the very thing which God willed with an evil will, though God willed it with a good will.”

The same occurred in Christ’s passion. For the Jews and the devil willed the same thing that God willed—namely, that Christ should die—but they willed it with an evil will, whereas God willed it with a good will. Nevertheless, they willed the action which God did not will.

# BOOK TWO: ON THE CREATION AND FORMATION OF BODILY AND SPIRITUAL THINGS, AND VARIOUS OTHER MATTERS PERTAINING TO IT

[Col. 0651]

## DISTINCTION I. IT SHOWS THAT THERE IS ONE PRINCIPLE OF THINGS, NOT SEVERAL, AS SOME HAVE THOUGHT

[Col. 0651]

1. In setting forth the creation of things, Scripture shows at its beginning that God is the creator and the source of time and of all visible and invisible creatures, saying in Genesis 1: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” By these words Moses, inspired by the Spirit of God, declares that the world was made by God the creator from one beginning, refuting the error of some who supposed that there were several principles without a beginning.

Plato, indeed, held that there were three principles: God, the exemplar, and matter itself—uncreated and without beginning—and that God was, as it were, an artisan rather than a creator. For a creator is one who makes something from nothing. Properly speaking, to create is to make something from nothing; whereas to make is not only to produce something from nothing, but also from matter.

Thus both human beings and angels are said to make certain things, but not to create; and they are called makers or artisans, but not creators. For this name properly belongs to God alone, who makes some things from nothing and some things from something. He is therefore creator, craftsman, and maker; but he has retained the name of creation as properly his own, while communicating the other terms also to creatures. In Scripture, however, “creator” is often used in the sense of “maker,” and “to create” in the sense of “to make,” without distinction of meaning.

### That These Words—“To Act,” “To Make,” and the Like—Are Not Said of God in the Same Sense in Which They Are Said of Creatures

[Col. 0652]

2. Nevertheless, it should be known that the words “to create,” “to make,” “to act,” and others of this kind cannot be said of God in the same sense in which they are said of creatures. For when we say that he makes something, we do not mean that he has any movement in acting or any passion in laboring, as commonly happens to us; rather, we signify some new effect of his eternal will—that is, that by his eternal will something begins newly to exist.

Therefore, when he is said to make something, it is as though one said that something newly happens or exists according to, or through, his will; so that nothing new happens in him, but something new comes to be, as it had been in his eternal will, without any movement or change in himself.

But we are said to be changed in working because we are moved; for we do nothing without movement. God, then, is said to act or make because he is the cause of things newly existing, while by his will new things begin to exist which did not exist before, without any agitation in himself. Thus “action” cannot properly be said of him, since every action consists in movement, while in God there is no movement.

Just as certain things happen by the heat of the sun, without any movement or change having occurred in the sun itself or in its heat, so new things have being by God’s will without change in the Author, who is the one, sole, and universal principle.

Aristotle, however, posited principles, namely matter and form, and a third principle called the efficient cause; and he held that the world always exists and always has existed.

### He Teaches What Is Catholic Doctrine

3. The Holy Spirit, then, overthrowing the error of these and similar thinkers and handing down the teaching of truth, signifies that God created the world at the beginning of times and existed eternally before time. Thus it commends his eternity and omnipotence, for to will is to do for him; because, as we said above, new things come into existence through his will and goodness.

Let us therefore believe that the cause of created things—heavenly and earthly, visible and invisible—is none other than the goodness of the Creator, who is the one true God. His goodness is so great that, being supremely good, he wills others to participate in his own blessedness, by which he is eternally blessed—a blessedness which he sees can be shared and cannot at all be diminished by being shared.

Therefore, the good which he himself was and by which he was blessed, he willed to be communicated to others by goodness alone, not by necessity; because it belongs to the supremely good to will to benefit, and to the supremely omnipotent to be unable to harm.

### Why Rational Creatures Were Made

4. Since no one can be a participant in his blessedness except through understanding—and the more it is understood, the more fully it is possessed—God made a rational creature to understand the supreme good, to love it by understanding it, to possess it by loving it, and to enjoy it by possessing it.

He distinguished this creature in such a way that one part remained in its purity and was not united to a body—namely, the angels—while another part was joined to a body—namely, souls. Thus rational creation was distinguished into incorporeal and corporeal: the incorporeal is called an angel, while the corporeal is called a human being, subsisting from a rational soul and flesh. The first cause of rational creation, therefore, was God’s goodness.

### Why Human Beings or Angels Were Created

5. Therefore, if it is asked why a human being or angel is created, the answer can be given briefly: because of God’s goodness. Hence Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 32: “Because God is good, we exist; and insofar as we exist, we are good.”

### For What Purpose Rational Creatures Were Created

6. And if it is asked for what purpose rational creatures were created, the answer is: to praise God, to serve him, and to enjoy him. In these things the creature itself advances, not God. For God is perfect and full of supreme goodness; he can neither be increased nor diminished. Therefore, the fact that a rational creature was made by God must be referred to the Creator’s goodness and to the creature’s benefit.

### A Very Brief Answer When It Is Asked Why or for What Purpose Rational Creatures Were Made

7. Therefore, when it is asked why or for what purpose rational creatures were made, the briefest answer is: for God’s goodness and for their own benefit. For it is beneficial to them to serve God and enjoy him. Thus angel or human being is said to exist for God, not because God the Creator and supremely blessed One needed the service of either, for he does not need our goods (Psalm 147); but so that the creature might serve him and enjoy him, for to serve him is to reign. Thus it is the servant who benefits by serving, not the one who is served.

### As Human Beings Were Made to Serve God, So the World Was Made to Serve Human Beings

8. And just as human beings were made for God—that is, to serve him—so the world was made for human beings, namely, to serve them. Thus the human being was placed in the middle, so that he might both be served and himself serve; so that he might receive both kinds of service, and the whole might flow back to the human good—both the service received and that rendered.

For God so willed himself to be served by human beings that by this service it is not God, but the human being serving, who is helped. And he willed the world to serve human beings, so that human beings might similarly be helped by it. Thus the whole good of the human being consisted both in what was made for that person and in that for which the person was made.

For, as the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 3, all things are ours: namely, things above us, things equal to us, and things below us. The things above us are ours for enjoyment, as God the Trinity; the things equal to us are ours for companionship, namely the angels. Although they are now superior to us, in the future they will be equal to us. Even now they are ours because they are for our use, just as the possessions of masters are said to belong to servants, not by ownership but because they are for their use.

The angels themselves are said in certain places of Scripture to serve us when they are sent into ministry for our sake.

### How Scripture Sometimes Says That Human Beings Were Made for the Restoration of the Angelic Fall
9. Scripture also sometimes states that man was made for the restoration of the angels’ fall. This should not be understood as though man would not have been made if an angel had not sinned, but because, among the other causes—namely the principal ones—this too was a secondary cause.
