Thus the higher and equal beings are ours. The lower beings also are ours, because they were made to serve us.

### Why man was so constituted that the soul is united to the body

10. It is also commonly asked, since the soul would seem to possess greater dignity if it remained without a body, why it was united to a body. To this one may first answer: because God willed it, and no reason for his will is to be sought. Secondly, it may be said that God willed it to be joined to a body in order to display in the human condition a new example of the blessed union between God and the spirit, in which he is loved with the whole heart and seen face to face. For a creature might think that it could not be united to its Creator with such closeness as to love and know him with its whole mind, unless it saw a spirit—the most excellent creature—united in such love to something most lowly, namely flesh, which is from the earth, that it cannot be constrained to wish to leave it. This is shown by the Apostle when he says, 2 Corinthians 5: “We do not wish to be unclothed of the body, but to be further clothed”; by this it is shown that the created spirit is united to the uncreated Spirit by ineffable love.

Therefore, as an example of the future fellowship which was to be brought to completion between God and the rational spirit in the latter’s glorification, he joined the soul to bodily garments and earthly dwellings. He made clayey matter quicken to living sensation, so that man might know that, if God could join the so dissimilar natures of body and soul into one alliance and so great a friendship, it would by no means be impossible for him to raise the lowliness of a rational creature, though far inferior, to participation in his glory. Therefore, because the rational spirit was, by way of example, humbled in part to fellowship with an earthly body, divine providence added this, lest it should seem too greatly depressed thereby: afterward, with that same body glorified, it would be raised to fellowship with those who had remained in their purity. Thus what it had received in a lesser measure when created, by the dispensation of its Creator, it would afterward receive in a glorified state through the grace of that same Creator.

Thus God our Creator, disposing rational spirits in various lots according to the choice of his will, assigned a dwelling above in heaven to those whom he had left in their purity; but to those whom he had joined to earthly bodies he assigned a habitation below on earth. He imposed upon both a rule of obedience, so that the former might not fall from the state in which they were, and the latter might rise from the state in which they were to that in which they were not. God therefore made man from a twofold substance, composing the body from earth but making the soul from nothing. Souls are also united to bodies so that, serving God in them, they may deserve a greater crown.

### After the mystery of the Trinity, we must discuss the threefold creature, and the more worthy of these, namely the angelic creature

11. From what has been set forth, it is evident that rational creature was divided into the angelic and the human: one of these is wholly spiritual, namely the angelic; the other is partly spiritual and partly bodily, namely the human. Since, therefore, we must treat of these—that is, of spiritual and bodily creature, rational and non-rational—it seems fitting first to speak of rational and spiritual creature, that is, of angels, so that our reasoning may turn from contemplation of the Creator to knowledge of the more worthy creature, [Col. 0655] and then descend to the consideration of bodily creature, both that which is rational and that which is not rational. Thus instruction concerning the uncreated Trinity’s mystery may be followed by instruction concerning threefold creature and the things compounded and contingent upon it.

## DISTINCTION II. MATTERS TO BE CONSIDERED CONCERNING ANGELIC NATURE

1. Concerning angelic nature, then, these matters must first be considered: when it was created; where; and what it was like when first created. Then, what it became through the turning-away of some and the turning-toward of others. Something must also be said concerning its excellence, orders, diversity of gifts, offices and names, and many other matters.

### He first says when angels were made, in which authorities seem to conflict with one another

2. Certain authorities seem to indicate that angels were created before every creature. Hence Ecclesiasticus 1: “Wisdom was created before all things.” This is understood of angelic nature, which Scripture often calls life, wisdom, and light. For that Wisdom which is God was not created. The Son, the Wisdom of the Father, is begotten, not made or created; and the whole Trinity is one Wisdom, which is neither made nor created, nor begotten nor proceeding. Therefore that statement must be understood of angelic life, of which Scripture says that it was made “before all things.”

But elsewhere Scripture, Genesis 1, says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” And in the Prophet, Psalm 101: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.” A certain contradiction seems to arise from these assertions. For if Wisdom was created before all things, all things seem to have been made after it; thus heaven and earth seem to have been made after it, while Wisdom itself was made before heaven and earth. Likewise, if in the beginning God created heaven and earth, nothing was made before heaven and earth, nor was Wisdom itself made before heaven and earth. Since, therefore, these statements seem contrary, and it is not permissible to suppose that there is any contradiction in divine Scripture, let us seek the understanding of the truth.

### What must be maintained, by resolving the authorities set forth above

3. It seems, therefore, that this must be maintained: spiritual creature, that is, angelic creature, and bodily creature were created simultaneously. This is the sense in which Solomon’s saying may be taken: “He who lives forever created all things simultaneously”—that is, spiritual and bodily nature. Thus the angels were created earlier in time than that bodily matter of the four elements; and yet Wisdom was created before all things, because, although it does not precede in time, it does in dignity.

That bodily and spiritual creature were created simultaneously is plainly shown by Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, tome 3, book 1, chapter 1. He says that by heaven and earth spiritual and bodily creature are understood, and that these were created “in the beginning,” namely, of time; or “in the beginning” because they were the first things made.

### Nothing was made before heaven and earth—not even time; for they were created with time, but not from time

4. Nothing, indeed, was made before them; nor was time made before spiritual nature, namely angelic nature, and before bodily nature, namely that undifferentiated matter of the four elements. For these were created with time, but not from time, nor in time. Likewise time itself was not created in time, because there was no time before heaven and earth existed. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 5, chapter 6, says that God was Lord before time existed and did not begin to be Lord in time, because he was Lord of time when time began to exist; nor indeed did time begin to exist in time, because there was no time before time began.

### Bodily and spiritual creature began simultaneously with time and with the world

5. Bodily and spiritual creature, therefore, were made simultaneously with time, and simultaneously with the world. Angelic creature did not exist before the world, because, as Augustine says, tome 3, book 5, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, chapter 19: “No creature was created before the ages, but from the ages with which it began.” [Col. 0656]

Jerome, however, tome 9, on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 1, seems to hold another view, saying: “Not yet six thousand years of our time have been completed; and how many eternities before this, how many times, how many beginnings of ages must we suppose there were, in which angels, thrones, dominions, and the remaining orders served God without changes or measures of times, and at God’s command stood firm!” Relying on these words, some have said that temporal time began with the world, but that before the world there existed eternal time without change; and in it they maintain that the angels, at God’s command, stood immutably and timelessly and served him.

But we, according to the capacity of our understanding, approve more readily what was stated earlier, while preserving reverence for mysteries, in which nothing should be rashly asserted. We judge that Jerome said this not as expressing his own view, but as reporting the opinion of others.

### Where angels were immediately after their creation: namely, in the empyrean, which, as soon as it was made, was filled with angels

6. It has now been shown when angelic nature was created; we must now consider where it was made. The testimony of certain authorities clearly shows that before the fall angels were in heaven, that some fell from there because of pride, while others, who did not sin, remained there. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel, Luke 10: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.”

This heaven is not the firmament made on the second day, but the resplendent heaven called the empyrean—that is, “fiery,” from brightness rather than heat—which, as soon as it was made, was filled with angels. It is above the firmament. Some interpreters of sacred Scripture understand this empyrean to be the “heaven” mentioned when Scripture says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” “By heaven,” says Strabo, “he does not here mean the visible firmament, but the empyrean—that is, the fiery or intellectual heaven. It is so called not from burning heat but from brightness, and as soon as it was made it was filled with angels.” Hence Job 38: “Where were you when the morning stars praised me?” and so forth.

Bede also says of this: “This higher heaven, set apart from the revolution of the world, was filled with holy angels as soon as it was created. The Lord testifies that they were made in the beginning together with heaven and earth, saying: ‘Where were you when the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God rejoiced?’ By ‘morning stars’ and ‘sons of God’ he calls the same angels of God. For the heaven in which the luminaries were placed was made not in the beginning but on the second day.”

From these passages it is clear that all the angels were in the empyrean before the fall of some of them, and that angels were created simultaneously with the empyrean heaven and with the unformed matter of all bodily things.

### The matter of visible things and the nature of invisible things were created simultaneously; each was in some respect unformed and in some respect formed

7. Therefore the matter of visible things and the nature of invisible things were created simultaneously; each was unformed in some respect and formed in some respect. For just as the confused and mingled matter of bodily things—which the Greeks called *chaos*—at that first beginning of creation possessed the form of confusion but lacked the form of distinction and differentiation, until afterward it was formed and received distinct species; so spiritual and angelic nature was formed at its creation according to its natural condition. Yet it did not possess the form which it would afterward receive through love and conversion toward its Creator; rather, it was unformed without that form.

Hence Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 1, chapter 1, explaining the preceding words of Genesis in various ways, says that “heaven” signifies the unformed nature of spiritual life, as it can exist in itself when not turned toward its Creator, in whom it is formed; while “earth” signifies bodily matter without every quality that appears in formed matter.

### How Lucifer can say, according to Isaiah, “I will ascend into heaven and be like the Most High,” when he was already in heaven

8. Here one commonly asks: if angels were in the empyrean heaven as soon as they were made, how could Lucifer say, as is read in Isaiah 14: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt [Col. 0657] my throne, and I will be like the Most High”? But here he calls God’s exaltation “heaven,” to which he wished to make himself equal. The meaning is: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with God.

## DISTINCTION III. WHAT ANGELS WERE LIKE WHEN MADE, AND THAT FOUR THINGS WERE ATTRIBUTED TO THEM AT THE VERY BEGINNING OF THEIR CREATION

1. We have shown where angels were immediately after their creation. It now follows to investigate what they were like at the very beginning of their creation. Four things appear to have been attributed to angels at the beginning of their existence: simple essence—that is, indivisible and immaterial essence; personal distinctness; understanding, memory, and will or love, through reason naturally implanted; and free choice, that is, the free capacity of the will to incline either to good or to evil. For through free choice they could turn by their own will to either alternative, without violence or compulsion.

### Whether all angels were equal in three respects: wisdom, essence, and freedom of choice

2. Here it must be considered whether all were equal in their spiritual substance, rational wisdom, and freedom of choice, which belonged to all. The first consideration concerns substance; the second, form; the third, power. For person is substance; wisdom, form; and choice, power. Subtlety of nature pertains to substance; keenness of understanding to form; and capacity of rational will to power.

Accordingly, those rational essences which were persons, spirits, simple by nature, and immortal in life, are rightly understood to have possessed differing degrees of subtlety of essence, perspicacity of wisdom, and freedom and capacity of choice—just as bodies possess some difference in essence, form, and weight. Some have a better and more worthy essence and form than others; some are lighter and more agile than others.

In this manner we must believe that those spiritual natures received, at the beginning of their creation, differences suited to their purity and excellence in essence, form, and capacity. By God’s wisdom some were established lower and others higher, with greater gifts granted to some and lesser to others, so that those who then excelled others in natural goods might afterward also preside over them through gifts of grace. Those created more subtle by nature and more keen in wisdom were also endowed with greater gifts of grace and made superior to others in rank. But those made less subtle by nature and less keen in wisdom received lesser gifts of grace and were established lower, through the wisdom of God who orders all things in equitable proportion.

Difference is likewise to be observed in the capacity of choice, according to the differing strength of nature and the differing power of knowledge and understanding. Just as differing vigor and subtlety of nature do not entail weakness, and lesser wisdom does not introduce ignorance, so inferior freedom imposes no necessity upon the will of choice.

### What angels possessed in common and equally

3. As angels differed in the matters just mentioned, so they also had certain things in common and equally: that they were spirits, indissoluble, and immortal was common and equal to all. But they differed in subtlety of essence, understanding of wisdom, and freedom of will. Only he who made all things in weight, number, and measure could comprehend and assess these intelligible distinctions among invisible natures.

### Whether angels were created good or evil, just or unjust; and whether there was any interval between creation and their fall

4. Another matter appears worthy of investigation, and is commonly asked by many: whether angels were created good or evil, just or unjust; and whether there was any interval between their creation and fall, or whether they fell without delay at the very beginning of creation.

### The opinion of some who say that angels were created in wickedness and fell without any delay

5. Some have thought that the angels who fell were created evil, that they did not turn to wickedness through free choice, but were made wicked by God himself; and that there was no interval between creation and fall, but that they apostatized from the beginning. They also maintain that the others were created fully blessed. They support their opinion by Augustine’s authority, *On Genesis*, book 1, chapter 16, where he says:

> “Not without reason may it be thought that the devil fell at the beginning of time, and never at any time lived peaceably and blessedly with the holy angels, but apostatized immediately. Hence the Lord says, John 1 [sic]: ‘He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth’; so that we may understand that he did not stand in the truth from the time when he was created, though he would have stood if he had wished to stand.”

Likewise, in the same work, book 1, chapter 19 at the end and chapter 20 at the beginning:

> “It should not without reason be thought that the devil fell from the very beginning of his time or creation, and never stood in the truth. Hence some suppose that he was not bent into this wickedness by free choice but was created by God in it, according to the saying of blessed Job, 40: ‘This is the beginning of God’s creature, which God made to be mocked by his angels.’”

> **[Note: [Col. 0658] This text is not found in the Book of Job according to the Vulgate edition, but according to the Septuagint translators.]**

And the Prophet says, Psalm 103: “This dragon which you formed to mock him.” They take this as though he were first made evil, envious, and a devil, rather than corrupted by his will.

Those who say that the angels who fell were created evil and fell without delay employ these and other testimonies. They also maintain, on Augustine’s authority, that those who remained steadfast were created perfect and blessed. For Augustine, commenting on Genesis, says that “heaven” signifies spiritual creature, which has always been blessed from the beginning in which it was made.

### The probable opinion of others, who say that all angels were created good and that there was some brief interval between creation and fall

6. Others, however, hold that all angels were created good, and were good at the very beginning of creation—that is, without fault—and just, that is, innocent; though not just in the sense of possessing the exercise of virtues. For they had not yet been endowed with the virtues which were added to those who stood firm in their confirmation through grace, while others became proud by free choice and therefore fell.

They also say that there was some brief interval between creation and fall or confirmation. During that brief time all were good, not through the exercise of free choice but through the benefit of creation. They were such as could stand—that is, could avoid falling—through the goods of creation, and could fall through free choice. For they could sin or not sin; but they could not advance to merit life unless grace were added, which was added to some in their confirmation.

To establish this, they use Augustine’s testimony. Commenting on Genesis, he says that angelic nature was first created unformed and called “heaven”; afterward it was formed and called “light,” when it turned toward its Creator and clung to him in perfect love. Thus it was first said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and afterward added: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” In the first passage the creation of unformed spiritual nature is addressed; in the second, its formation.

Reason also opposes those who say that angels were created evil. The best Creator could not be the author of evil. Therefore all that they had from him was wholly good; and it was wholly good because it was wholly from him. In this way it is proved that all angels were good when first made, though with the goodness received by beginning nature.

### He adduces Augustine’s proof against those who say angels were made evil; he also determines the meaning of Job’s words which they had cited for themselves

7. Therefore Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, chapter 1, refuting the opinion of those who think angels were created evil, proves by authority and reason that they were created good. He also explains how the foregoing words of blessed Job, which they had cited for themselves, [Col. 0659] should be understood. Commenting on Genesis, he says:

> “God made all things very good; therefore he made the nature of angels good. Since it is unjust for God to condemn in any creature what he created without any merit [on that creature’s part], we must believe that it is not nature but the evil will which is to be punished. Nor is the angel’s nature signified when it is said, ‘This is the beginning of God’s creature,’ and so forth. Rather, it signifies the aerial body which God fitted to such a will; or God’s very ordering, by which he made him, even against his will, useful to the good; or the making of the angel himself, because although God foreknew that he would become evil by will, he nevertheless made him, foreseeing how much good he would bring about from him by his goodness.”

He is therefore called God’s creature because, although God knew that he would become evil by will and harm the good, he nevertheless created him so that he might benefit the good through him. He did this so that he might be mocked. For he is mocked when his temptation contributes to the progress of the saints. Likewise, evil men, whom God created while foreseeing that they would become evil, are nevertheless created for the benefit of the saints; they are mocked when the saints’ progress is afforded through their temptation. But he himself is “the beginning” because he precedes in antiquity and primacy of wickedness.

This mockery is inflicted upon evil angels and evil human beings through evil angels, because God subjects evil angels and evil people to them, so that they can do harm not as much as they strive to do so, but as much as they are permitted. Thus he plainly shows how the aforementioned words of Job should be understood, and affirms that angelic nature was created good.

### He explains how the Lord’s preceding words should be understood, clearly teaching that angels were created good and fell after creation

8. Augustine then explains how the Lord’s words cited above should be understood, and also defines his own preceding statements, saying plainly that angels were created good and fell after creation, with some very brief interval intervening. Thus he says, book 11, chapter 23:

> “The view that the devil never stood in the truth, never lived a blessed life, but fell from the beginning, should not be understood so as to suppose that he was created evil by the good God, as though one said that he had not fallen from the beginning. For he did not fall if he was made such—that is, evil; from what could he fall? Therefore, having first been made, he immediately turned himself away from the truth, delighted in his own power, and did not taste the sweetness of blessed life. He did not disdain a life which he had received, but lost it by refusing to receive it. Therefore he could not have foreknown his fall, because wisdom is the fruit of piety. Yet, as soon as he was made, he fell—not from what he had received, but from what he would have received if he had wished to submit to God.”

Here he plainly declares that angels were created good and fell after creation; and there was some interval, however exceedingly brief. Origen confirms this, commenting on Ezekiel, tome 2, homily 1:

> “The serpent, the enemy opposed to truth, nevertheless did not from the beginning, nor immediately, crawl upon its breast and belly. Just as Adam and Eve did not sin immediately, so the serpent too was at one time not a serpent when it dwelt in the paradise of delights; for God did not make wickedness.”

He plainly says that it fell after creation, with a brief interval intervening. Therefore the words appear to be understood thus: “He was a murderer from the beginning,” or a liar—that is, immediately after the beginning, when he promised himself equality with God and killed himself, he who in the Gospel is called “man”; and “he did not stand in the truth,” because he was not in it, but from the beginning of time—that is, immediately after the beginning of time—he apostatized.

The statement may also be understood thus: “He was a murderer or liar from the beginning,” that is, from the time man was created, whom he cast down into death through envy and deceitfully seduced. From what has been said, therefore, it is clear that all angels were created good, and that after creation some fell from the good which they would have possessed had they remained steadfast.

### The threefold wisdom angels possessed before their fall or confirmation

9. Here it is commonly asked what wisdom they possessed before fall or confirmation. They possessed a threefold natural knowledge, by which they knew that they had been made, by whom they had been made, and with whom they had been made. They also possessed some knowledge of good and evil, understanding what they ought to seek [Col. 0660] or reject.

### Whether they possessed any love of God or mutual love of themselves

10. It is also commonly asked whether they had any love of God or mutual love of themselves, just as they had memory, understanding, and intelligence, by which they nevertheless loved God and themselves in some measure, though they did not thereby merit anything.

## DISTINCTION IV. DID GOD CREATE ANGELS PERFECT AND BLESSED, OR WRETCHED AND IMPERFECT?

1. After this, we must consider whether God created angels perfect and blessed, or wretched and imperfect. One may answer that they were created neither in blessedness nor in wretchedness. For they could not be wretched before sin, since wretchedness comes from sin. If there had been no sin, there would have been no wretchedness.

Nor were those who fell ever blessed, because they were ignorant of their own outcome—that is, of their future sin and punishment. If they had foreknown their fall, either they wished to avoid it but could not, and thus were wretched; or they could have avoided it but would not, and thus were foolish and malicious. Therefore we say that they did not foreknow their outcome, nor was knowledge given them of what would happen to them.

The good angels, however, those who remained steadfast, perhaps foreknew their blessedness. Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 17: “How, among the angels, was one blessed who did not foreknow his future sin and punishment?” But one asks why he did not foreknow it. “Perhaps God did not wish to reveal to the devil what he would do or suffer; but he wished to reveal to the others that they would remain in the truth.”

By these words Augustine seems to signify that the angels who fell did not foreknow their fall and therefore were not blessed; while the angels who remained steadfast foreknew the blessedness to come to them and were certain of it in hope, so that in a certain sense they were already blessed. And indeed, if this were so, the latter could be said to have been blessed at that time, unlike the others, who did not know their outcome.

### Augustine said this as an opinion and inquiry, not as an assertion: that the good angels who remained steadfast had foreknowledge

2. But Augustine says this more by way of opinion and inquiry than assertion. Accordingly, opposing this opinion, he immediately adds: “But why were those distinguished from the others, so that God did not reveal to these what concerned them, while he did reveal it to the others, when he is not an avenger before anyone is a sinner? For he does not condemn the innocent.”

Here he seems to suggest that God revealed neither the future evil to those who would sin nor the future good to those who would remain. Therefore neither those who fell nor those who remained steadfast were blessed until their consummation, since they could not be blessed if they were not certain of blessedness or if they were uncertain of damnation. Hence Augustine says in the same work: “To say of angels that they could be blessed in their own kind while uncertain of damnation or salvation, and without hope of being changed for the better, is excessive presumption. For how can those be blessed whose blessedness is uncertain?”

### He gathers the substance of what has been said, confirming that all angels before confirmation or fall were not blessed—unless blessedness means the state of innocence in which they were before the fall

3. It follows from the foregoing that the angels who fell were never blessed, unless one understands “blessedness” as the state of innocence in which they were before sin. Those who remained steadfast either foreknew their future blessedness through God’s revelation, and thus were in some measure blessed through the certainty of hope; or they were uncertain of their blessedness, and thus were blessed in no other way than the rest who fell. But the latter view seems more probable to me.

### Answer to the question whether angels were created perfect or imperfect: they were perfect in one respect and imperfect in another

4. As to the question whether they were created perfect or imperfect, it may be said that they were perfect in one [Col. 0661] way and imperfect in another. For something is not called perfect in only one sense, but in several.

### “Perfect” is said in three ways: according to time, according to nature, and absolutely

5. “Perfect” is said in three ways. Something may be perfect according to time, perfect according to nature, or universally perfect. Perfect according to time is that which has everything that time requires and that is fitting to possess at that time; in this way angels were perfect before confirmation or fall. Perfect according to nature is that which has everything owed or expedient to its nature for glorification; in this way angels were perfect after confirmation, and the saints will be perfect after the resurrection. Universally and supremely perfect is that to which nothing is ever lacking and from which all good things proceed; this belongs to God alone. The first perfection, therefore, belongs to created nature; the second, to glorified nature; the third, to uncreated nature.

### He briefly reviews the foregoing, adding what angels were like in conversion and turning-away

6. We have shown what angels were like in creation: namely, good and not evil; just—that is, innocent; perfect in one sense but imperfect in another. But they were not blessed until confirmation, unless, as has already been said, blessedness is understood as that state of innocence and goodness in which they were created.

## DISTINCTION V. CONCERNING THE CONVERSION AND CONFIRMATION OF THOSE WHO STOOD FIRM, AND THE TURNING-AWAY AND FALL OF THOSE WHO FELL

1. After this, consideration leads us to inquire what they became when they were divided through turning-away and conversion. For immediately after creation some turned toward their Creator, while others turned away. To turn toward God was to cling to him in charity; to turn away was to hate or envy him. For pride, by which they wished to make themselves equal to God, is the mother of envy.

In those who turned toward God, God’s wisdom began to shine as in a mirror, and by it they were enlightened; but those who turned away were blinded. The former were turned and enlightened by God through grace added to them. The latter were blinded not by an infusion of wickedness, but by the withdrawal of grace, from which they were left destitute—not because grace already given was withdrawn, but because it was never added so that they might turn.

This, therefore, is the conversion and turning-away by which those who were good by nature were divided: some became good above that natural good through righteousness; others, by its corruption through fault, became evil. Conversion made them just; turning-away made them unjust. Both were acts of the will, and the will in both cases was free.

2. For all possessed free choice, which is the free power and capacity of rational will. They could by will choose whatever they wished and by reason judge—that is, distinguish; and free choice consists in these things. They were not created willing either to turn away or to turn toward God, but capable of willing one or the other. After creation, by spontaneous will, some chose evil and others good. Thus God “separates light from darkness,” as Scripture says—that is, good angels from evil. And he called the light day and the darkness night, Genesis 1, because he enlightened the good angels by his grace but blinded the evil.

### After creation, something was given to those who stood firm by which they might turn toward God: not by any merit, but through cooperating grace

3. If it is asked whether, after creation, something was conferred on those who turned toward God by which they might turn—that is, love God—we say that cooperating grace was conferred on them, without which rational creature cannot advance to the merit of life. For it can fall by itself, but cannot advance without assisting grace.

### What grace the angel needed, and what grace it did not need

4. The angel did not need grace by which it might be justified, because it was not evil; but it needed grace by which it might be helped to love God perfectly and obey him. Grace by which the ungodly person is justified—that is, by which an ungodly person becomes godly, an evil person good—is called operative grace. Cooperating grace, however, is that by which one is helped effectively to will the good, to love God above all things and do good, to persevere in good, and the like—matters to be discussed more fully later. Therefore cooperating grace was given to the angels who remained steadfast, through which they turned so as to love God perfectly. They turned, therefore, from the good they possessed without losing it to a greater good which they did not possess. This conversion was effected by grace cooperating with free choice; this grace was not added to the others who fell.

### Whether this should be imputed to those who turned away

5. Therefore some commonly say that it should not be imputed to those who turned away and did not turn toward God, because they could not turn without grace; yet grace was not given to them, and it was not their fault that it was not given, because no fault had yet preceded in them. To this one may answer that grace was not added to those who received it on account of their merits; otherwise it would no longer be grace, if it were given on account of merit existing before grace.

### By what fault grace was not given to those who fell

6. But that it was not given to the others was their own fault, because, though they could have stood firm, they were unwilling to do so until grace was added—whereas the others remained steadfast until, when the former fell through pride, grace was added to the latter. The fault of those who fell can therefore plainly be discerned in this: without grace, which they had not received, they could not advance; yet through what had been given them in creation they could have avoided falling—that is, they could have stood firm—because nothing compelled them to fall. Rather, they turned aside through their own spontaneous will. Had they not done so, what was given to the others would surely also have been given—
to/for/by these [persons or things].

### That the angels were blessed in their very confirmation; but whether they merited it through the grace then given to them is uncertain, for different authorities hold different views on this.

7. Here it is commonly asked whether the angels were blessed in their very confirmation, and whether they in any way merited that blessedness. Many authorities attest that they were blessed in their confirmation itself, and this must therefore be held as certain. But whether they merited that blessedness through the grace then given them is uncertain. Some hold that they merited it through the grace received in confirmation, and say that merit and reward existed in them simultaneously: merit did not precede reward in time, but in causal order. Others, however, maintain that they did not merit, through the grace then bestowed, the blessedness which they received in confirmation. They say that grace was then conferred upon them not for meriting, but for living blessedly; and that they were not then given a good by which they might merit, but one by which they might enjoy happiness. What they then received as a reward, they say that they merit through services rendered to us, in obedience and reverence toward God. Thus reward preceded merits. I confess that this latter opinion pleases me more.

## DISTINCTION VI. THAT SOME OF THE GREATER AND SOME OF THE LESSER ANGELS FELL; AMONG WHOM ONE WAS HIGHER, NAMELY LUCIFER.

1. Moreover, it should be known that, just as some of both the greater and lesser angels remained steadfast, so some of each rank fell. Among these was one more excellent than all the others who fell; nor was anyone among those who remained more worthy than he, as the testimonies of authorities show. For Job says, chapter 40: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.” And in Ezekiel, chapter 28, it is written: “You were the seal of likeness, full of knowledge and perfection; you were beautiful amid the delights of God’s paradise.” Explaining this, Gregory says, *Morals*, book 31, chapter 24: “The more subtle his nature, the more clearly is the likeness of God’s image shown as impressed upon him.”

Likewise, in Ezekiel, chapter 25, it is written: “Every precious stone was his covering”; that is, every angel was, as it were, his covering, because, as Gregory says, Homily 34 on Isaiah: “In comparison with the others he was brighter than the rest.” Hence he was called Lucifer, as Isaiah testifies, chapter 14: “How have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” and so forth. This is not to be understood as one order, but as one spirit, who, according to the testimony of Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, book 1, chapter 12, after he had been created, considered the eminence of his nature and the depth of his knowledge, and grew proud against his Creator—to such an extent that he wished to make himself equal even to God. [Col. 0663] Thus Isaiah says, chapter 14: “I shall ascend into heaven above the stars of heaven; I shall exalt my throne, and I shall be like the Most High.” He wished indeed to be like God, not by imitation, but by equality of power.

### Whence and to where he was cast down through the merit of his pride.

2. By the desert of such great pride he was cast down from heaven—that is, from the empyrean, where he had been with the others—into this darksome air, together with all the companions of his wickedness. For, as John says in Revelation, chapter 12, the dragon, falling from heaven, drew with him a third part of the stars. That Lucifer, greater than the others, did not fall alone, but with him fell many others who consented to him in evil; and this darksome air received them as they fell for its habitation. This was done for our testing, so that it might furnish us an occasion for exercise. Hence the Apostle says, Ephesians 6: “Our struggle is against the principalities and powers of this world, and against the rulers of these darknesses, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places”; because demons, who are spiritual and wicked, dwell in this turbulent air near us, which is called heaven. Hence the devil is called the prince of the air (elsewhere, of the world), John 14.

### That they were not permitted to dwell in heaven or on earth.

3. They were not permitted to dwell in heaven, because it is a bright and pleasant place; nor on earth with us, lest they afflict human beings too severely. But, according to the teaching handed down by the Apostle Peter in his second canonical Epistle, they are in this darksome air, which has been assigned to them as a prison until the time of judgment. Then they will be cast down into the abyss of hell, according to Matthew 25: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

### That some demons rule over others and have other kinds of precedence as well.

4. And just as among the good angels some rule over others, so also among the evil angels some are set over others and others are subject to others. As long as the world lasts, angels rule angels, demons rule demons, and human beings rule human beings. But in the future every precedence will be abolished, as the Apostle teaches, 1 Corinthians 15. They also have greater or lesser forms of precedence according to the measure of their greater or lesser knowledge. Some preside over one province, others over one person, and some even over one vice. Thus there is said to be a spirit of pride, a spirit of lust, and the like, because the demon is especially able to tempt persons by that vice from which it takes its designation.

For the same reason riches are called by the demon’s name, namely *mammon*. Mammon is the name of a demon; by that name riches are called in the Syrian language. This does not mean that the devil has power to give or take away riches from whomever he wishes, but that he uses them for the temptation and deception of human beings.

### Whether all demons are in this darksome air, or whether some are in hell.

5. It is commonly asked whether all are in this darksome air, or whether some are already in hell. It is probable that some demons descend daily into hell, leading souls there to be tormented; and it is not far from the truth that some are always there, perhaps taking turns, to hold and torment souls there. That the souls of the wicked descend there and are punished there is clear from the fact that Christ descended into hell in order to bring out the righteous who were held there. For if the righteous descended there, much more did the unrighteous; and, as authority has handed down, when he brought forth the righteous, he left the wicked there. For he bit hell, but did not swallow it up.

### Some think that Lucifer was confined in hell after he tempted Christ and was defeated; they say that he tempted and conquered the first human being.

6. Concerning Lucifer, some are of the opinion that he has been confined there and now has no access to us for tempting us, because Revelation, chapter 20, says: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison; and he will go out and deceive the nations.” This will occur in the final time of Antichrist, when there will be such great tribulation that, if possible, even the elect might be shaken, Matthew 24. [Col. 0664]

They say that he was confined there from the time when he tempted Christ in the wilderness or in the Passion and was defeated by him. They think that he tempted and conquered the human being; and that secondly he tempted God, but was defeated by him, and was therefore confined in hell. Others think that, from the time he fell, he was plunged there because of the gravity of his sin.

### That Lucifer does not have the power which he will have in the time of Antichrist.

7. But whether he has been plunged into hell or not, it is credible that he does not have the power of access to us which he will have in the time of Antichrist. At that time he will act deceitfully and violently; perhaps this is why he is then said to be released, because then power will be given to him by God to tempt human beings, which he does not now have.

### That demons once defeated by saints do not thereafter approach others.

8. The power to tempt others also seems to be taken away from those demons which are defeated by saints living justly and chastely. Hence Origen, volume 1, Homily 15 on the Book of Joshua, chapter 12 of that work, says: “I think indeed that the saints, resisting these instigators and conquering them, diminish the army of demons, as though they kill very many of them; nor is it thereafter lawful for that spirit which has been defeated by some saint through chaste and modest living to attack another human being again.”

Some think this is to be understood only of the vice in which it was overcome: thus, if it tempts a holy man concerning pride and is defeated, it may no longer tempt either him or another person concerning pride.

## DISTINCTION VII. THAT GOOD ANGELS ARE CONFIRMED BY GOD THROUGH GRACE SO THAT THEY CANNOT SIN; AND THAT EVIL ANGELS ARE SO HARDENED IN EVIL THAT THEY CANNOT LIVE WELL.

1. It was said above that the angels who remained steadfast were confirmed through grace, and those who fell were abandoned by God’s grace. The good angels have indeed been confirmed through grace to such an extent that they cannot sin. But the evil angels are so obstinate through malice that they cannot have a good will, or will rightly, even though what they sometimes will is good. For they sometimes will something to happen which God wills to happen; and that thing is certainly good and just to happen. Yet they do not will it with a good will.

### That both have free choice, yet cannot be bent toward both alternatives.

2. But since neither can the good sin nor the evil will or do good, it seems that they no longer possess free choice, because they cannot be bent in either direction, whereas free choice bears itself toward both. Thus Jerome says in his treatise on the Prodigal Son: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all other things, since they possess free choice, can be bent in either direction.” Here he seems to say that every creature established in free choice can be bent toward good and evil. If this is so, then both good and evil angels can be bent toward both; therefore the good can become evil and the evil good.

To this we say that the good are confirmed by such great grace that they cannot become evil; and the evil are hardened in malice to such a degree that they cannot become good. Yet both possess free choice: the good choose good and reject evil, not by some compelling necessity but through their own spontaneous will, though aided by grace; and likewise the evil, abandoned by grace, avoid good and pursue evil by spontaneous will. The evil possess free choice, but one that is depressed and corrupted, unable to rise toward good.

### That after confirmation the good have freer choice than before.

3. But after confirmation the good possess a choice much freer than before. For, as Augustine teaches in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 105, they do not lack free choice because they cannot will evil; indeed, choice which cannot be enslaved to sin is much freer. Nor should a will be blamed—or said not to be a will, or not to be free—because the blessed so will to be blessed that they not only do not wish to be miserable, but cannot at all will it. Therefore good angels cannot will evil [Col. 0665] or will to be miserable; and they possess this not from nature but from the benefit of grace.

Before the confirmation of grace, angels could sin; some did sin and became demons. Hence Augustine, volume 6, book 3 *Against Maximinus*, chapter 12: “The nature of heavenly creatures could die, because it could sin. For angels sinned and became demons, of whom the devil is prince; and those who did not sin could have sinned. And whenever it is granted to a rational creature that it cannot sin, this belongs not to its own nature but to God’s grace. Therefore God alone is he who, not by anyone’s grace but by his own nature, could not, cannot, and will not be able to sin.”

Here it is indicated that angels could sin before confirmation but cannot sin after confirmation. Their ability to sin came from free choice, which is natural to them; but their present inability to sin comes not from nature—that is, from free choice—but from grace. By this grace, free choice itself can no longer be enslaved to sin.

### That after confirmation angels cannot sin by nature as they could before; not because their free choice has been weakened, but because it has been confirmed.

4. Therefore after confirmation angels cannot sin by nature as they could before—not because their free choice has been weakened by grace, but rather because it has been so confirmed that through it a good angel can no longer sin. This certainly does not arise from free choice, but from God’s grace. Therefore Jerome’s statement, “All other things, since they possess free choice, can be bent in either direction,” must be understood according to the state in which they were created. For both human being and angel were created such that each could be bent toward either alternative. But afterward the good angels were so confirmed through grace that they cannot sin, and the evil were so hardened in vice that they cannot live well.

Likewise, Isidore’s statement must be understood thus: “Angels are changeable by nature, unchangeable by grace.” By nature, at the beginning of their condition, they could change toward good or evil; but afterward through grace they were so devoted to good that they cannot change away from it. Grace, not nature, prevents this.

### That evil angels have not lost their keen perception, and the ways in which they know.

5. Although evil angels are thus hardened through malice, they have not been utterly deprived of keen perception. For, as Isidore teaches, *On the Supreme Good*, book 1, demons are vigorous in knowledge by a threefold sharpness: the subtlety of their nature, experience of times, and revelation from heavenly spirits.

Augustine likewise says, book 2 *On Genesis*, chapter 17, at the end: “Evil spirits are permitted to know certain true things about temporal matters: partly through subtlety of perception, partly through experience of times—being more cunning because of the great length of their lives—and partly because holy angels, by God’s command, reveal to them what they themselves learn from almighty God. At times these same foul spirits also predict, as if by divination, what they are going to do.”

### That magical arts operate through the devil’s power and knowledge; and that this power and knowledge are given him by God either to deceive the wicked, admonish, or test the good.

6. Through their knowledge and power magical arts too are practiced. Yet it is not so much knowledge as power that has been given them by God: either to deceive the deceived, to admonish believers, or to exercise and prove the patience of the righteous. Hence Augustine, book 3 *On the Trinity*, chapter 7: “I see what may occur to a weak mind: namely, that these miracles too are performed by magical arts. For Pharaoh’s magicians made serpents and other things. But it is still more remarkable how the magicians’ power, which could make serpents, wholly failed when they came to the tiniest flies, namely gnats, by which Egypt was afflicted in the third plague. There the magicians failed, saying: ‘This is the finger of God.’

“From this it is given to be understood that even the transgressing angels themselves—the aerial powers cast down from the dwelling-place of that lofty ethereal purity into this lowest darkness, as into a prison of their own kind—through whom magical arts can do whatever they can do, [Col. 0666] nevertheless cannot have power to do anything unless power is granted from above. It is granted either to deceive the deceived, as in the case of the Egyptians; and it was given even to the magicians themselves, so that in the working of those spirits by which the deeds were done they might seem admirable, yet might be condemned by God’s truth; or to admonish believers not to desire as something great the ability to do such things—for which reason these matters have also been handed down to us in Scripture; or to exercise and make manifest the patience of the righteous.”

### That the matter of visible things does not obey transgressing angels at their will.

7. We must not suppose that this matter of visible things obeys these transgressing angels at their will. Rather, it obeys God, from whom this power is given insofar as the Immutable One judges.

### That they are not creators, although magicians made frogs and other things through them; only God is Creator.

8. Nor should those evil angels be called creators because magicians made frogs and serpents through them; for they did not themselves create them. Certain hidden seeds of all things which come to birth bodily and visibly lie concealed in the bodily elements of this world; God originally placed them there. Therefore he is the Creator of all things because he is the Creator of invisible seeds. For whatever things, in coming to birth, emerge before our eyes receive from hidden seeds the beginnings of their advance, the growth appropriate to their size, and the distinctions of their forms from original patterns, so to speak.

### Just as parents are not called creators of their children, nor farmers of crops, so neither good angels nor evil angels are creators, although creatures come to be through their ministry.

9. Therefore, just as we do not call parents creators of human beings, or farmers creators of crops, although God’s power works inwardly to create these things through motions externally applied by them, so it is not right to think that either evil or good angels are creators. Yet, through the subtlety of their perception, they know the seeds of these things, which are more hidden from us, and secretly scatter them by suitable combinations of the elements. Thus they provide occasions both for things to be generated and for their growth to be hastened.

But the good do these things only insofar as God commands, and the evil do them unjustly only insofar as he justly permits. For the wicked have an unjust will through malice, but receive power only justly—either for their own punishment or for that of others: the punishment of the wicked or the praise of the good.

### Just as God alone brings about the justification of the mind, so he alone brings about the creation of things, although a creature serves externally.

10. Therefore, just as none but God can form our mind by justifying it, although even human beings may externally preach the Gospel—not only the good through truth, but also the evil through occasion—so God works inwardly in the creation of visible things. But external operations and contemplations, or occasions, are supplied by angels, good as well as evil, or even by human beings. These, however, are supplied by human beings with proportionately greater difficulty, because they lack the subtlety of senses and mobility of bodies possessed by angels, being encumbered by earthly and sluggish limbs.

Hence, the easier it is for angels of whatever sort to draw together proximate causes from the elements, the more remarkable is their speed in works of this kind. Yet no one is creator except the one who principally forms these things, and no one can do this except the one Creator, God. For it is one thing to create and administer a creature from the innermost and highest hinge of causes, which God the Creator alone does; it is another, according to the powers and capacities distributed by him, to apply some external operation, so that what is created may come forth then or then, in this way or that. For all these things were already created originally and primordially in a certain texture of the elements, but later emerge when suitable opportunities are received.

### That evil angels can do many things through the vigor of their nature which they cannot do because God or good angels forbid them—that is, because they are not permitted.

11. It should also be known that [Col. 0667] evil angels can do certain things through the subtlety of their nature, but cannot do them because God or good angels forbid them; that is, because they are not permitted by God or good angels to do them. Certainly those who made frogs and serpents could have made gnats. But there are things they cannot do even if superior angels permit them, because God does not permit them.

Hence Augustine, book 3 *On the Trinity*, chapter 9: “By God’s ineffable sovereignty it happens that evil angels, who could do something if they were permitted, cannot do it precisely because they are not permitted. For no other reason occurs to explain why those who made frogs and serpents could not make gnats, except that the greater dominion of the prohibiting God was present through the Holy Spirit. This too the magicians confessed, saying: ‘This is the finger of God.’

“But what they can do by nature yet cannot do because of prohibition, and what they are not allowed to do by the condition of their very nature, is difficult—indeed impossible—for a human being to discover. We know that a human being can walk, and that even this cannot be done if it is not permitted; but that one cannot fly even if permitted. So too those angels can do certain things if they are permitted by more powerful angels under God’s command; while other things they cannot do even if permitted by those angels, because he does not permit it, from whom they have this measure of nature, and who also often does not permit through his angels things which he has granted them the capacity to do.”

## DISTINCTION VIII. WHETHER ALL ANGELS ARE BODILY, AS SOME HAVE THOUGHT; WITH WHOM AUGUSTINE SEEMS TO AGREE, SAYING THAT ALL ANGELS BEFORE THE FALL HAD SUBTLE AND SPIRITUAL BODIES, BUT THAT IN THE FALL THE BODIES OF THE EVIL WERE CHANGED FOR THE WORSE SO THAT THEY COULD SUFFER IN THEM.

1. Among learned persons there is also a question whether all angels, both good and evil, are bodily—that is, whether they have bodies united to them. Some think so, relying on Augustine’s words. He seems to say that before confirmation or fall all angels had aerial bodies, formed from a purer and higher region, suited for acting but not for suffering. Such bodies were preserved for the good angels who remained steadfast, so that they could act in them but could not suffer. They are so subtle that mortals cannot see them unless they are clothed over with some grosser form; when this is assumed they are seen, and when it is laid aside they cease to be seen.

But in their fall the bodies of evil angels were changed into the inferior quality of denser air. For just as they were cast down from a more worthy place to a lower place—that is, into darksome air—so their subtle bodies were changed and transformed into inferior and denser bodies, in which they could suffer from the higher element, namely fire.

Augustine seems to have held this view in his work *On Genesis*, saying: “Demons are called aerial animals, vigorous by the nature of aerial bodies; nor are they dissolved by death, because in them the element more suited to acting than to suffering prevails. Moisture and earth provide aptitude for suffering; air and fire, for acting. It is no wonder that transgressing angels, with their prince—now the devil, then the archangel—were after sin cast down into this darkness. Nor is it surprising if, by punishment, they were changed into an aerial quality in which they can suffer from fire. Yet they were permitted to hold only the dark regions of the air, which serve as their prison until the time of judgment.”

By these words Augustine seems to hand down what some think concerning the bodies of angels. Others, however, maintain that he said this not as his own opinion but as a report of others’ opinion; they wish to judge this from his own words, in which he says, “Demons are called aerial animals,” not, “They are aerial animals.” That is, “Some were saying this.” But they say that he taught the dwelling-place of the darksome air, into which they were cast, not as an opinion but as an assertion of fact, as the distinction of his phrasing shows.

They also say that many Catholic writers have agreed in this matter and have unanimously taught that angels are incorporeal and have no bodies united to them, though they sometimes assume bodies, prepared by God, [Col. 0668] in order to fulfill the ministry enjoined on them by God. When they have completed it, they lay them aside. In these bodies they appeared and spoke to human beings. Sometimes they spoke in God’s person, without distinction of any person; at other times in the person of the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

### That God appeared in those ancient bodily forms.

2. Nor should it be doubted that God appeared to human beings in bodily forms, as Augustine demonstrates in book 2 *On the Trinity*, comparing different Scriptural testimonies by which he proves that God appeared to human beings in bodily figures; and that sometimes speech was made by them in God’s person without distinction, and sometimes under a distinction of persons.

### On the intricate question which Augustine raises: whether a new creature was formed to display these bodily appearances; or angels already existing were sent; and, if they themselves were sent, whether, while preserving the quality of a spiritual body, they assumed some bodily appearance from denser matter, or changed their own body into a form suited to their action.

3. But where he asserts that God appeared to human beings in bodily images, he proposes an intricate question which he does not resolve. He asks whether, in those bodily appearances, some creature was created solely for that work, in which God might appear to human sight; or whether angels already existing were sent in such a way that, remaining in their spiritual bodies, they assumed from the bodily matter of the lower elements some bodily appearance, which, fitted upon them like a garment, they changed into any true bodily forms; or whether they changed their own body into forms suited to their actions by a power given them by God.

For Augustine says thus, book 3 *On the Trinity*, question 3, chapter 1: “It must be asked, concerning those ancient bodily forms and visions, whether a creature was formed solely for this work, in which God was shown to human sight as he then judged fitting; or whether angels already existing were sent so as to speak in God’s person, assuming for the use of their ministry a bodily appearance from bodily creation; or whether they changed and transformed their own body, which they do not serve but rule as subject to them, into whatever forms they wished, adapted and suitable to their actions, according to the power bestowed on them by the Creator.

“But I confess that the question exceeds the powers of my inquiry: whether angels, while the quality of their spiritual body remains, working more secretly through it, assume a body from the denser lower elements, which, fitted to them like a garment, they change and transform into any bodily forms, themselves real—as real water was changed into real wine by the Lord—or whether they transform their own proper bodies into what they will, adapted to what they do. But which of these is the case—for I am a human being—I cannot grasp by any experience, as the angels who do this can.”

Observe, reader, that he does not solve the question proposed, but leaves it unresolved: whether the angels who were sent, retaining their own spiritual bodies, clothed themselves over with some denser appearance in which they could be seen, or whether they changed and transformed their very body into whatever appearance in which they wished to be seen. In these words Augustine seems to attest that angels are bodily and have their own spiritual bodies.

### That God has never appeared to mortals in the form in which he is God.

4. Leaving these matters as too profound and obscure, let us hold this without doubt: God has never appeared to mortals in the form of his essence, as he says to his servant Moses, Exodus 33: “No human being shall see me and live.” And the Gospel, John 1, says: “No one has ever seen God.” For nothing visible exists which is not mutable. Therefore God’s substance or essence, because it is in no way mutable, is in no way visible through itself. Consequently, it is evident that all the things seen by the fathers when God was presented to them were made through created things. [Col. 0669] Though we do not know how God made them through ministering angels, we nevertheless say that they were made.

Therefore I dare confidently to say that neither God the Father, nor his Word, nor his Spirit—who is one God—is in any way mutable by that whereby he is and is himself; and, consequently, is much less visible.

### Whether demons enter human bodies substantially, or enter into human minds.

5. It also seems most worthy of consideration whether demons, whether bodily or incorporeal, enter substantially into human bodies and insinuate themselves into their souls; or whether they are said to enter because, by God’s permission, they exercise there the effect of their malice, oppressing and harassing them, or drawing them into sin according to their own will. The Gospel plainly declares that they enter human beings and, having been expelled, depart from them, when it recounts that demons entered certain persons and were cast out by Christ. But whether they entered substantially, or are said to have entered on account of their evil effect, is not altogether clear.

On this Augustine says, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 83: “We do not believe that demons enter substantially into the soul through an energic operation, but that they are joined to it by application and oppression. But to enter into a mind belongs only to him who created it, who, subsisting incorporeally by nature, is capable of his own work.” Here it seems to be indicated that demons do not substantially enter or penetrate human hearts.

Bede, too, commenting on Acts of the Apostles, chapter 5, where Peter says to Ananias, “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” says that it should be observed that nothing can fill the human mind as to its substance except the creative Trinity, because the soul is filled with created things only in respect of operation and the prompting of the will. Satan fills someone’s heart not by entering into him and into his perception, nor by entering the gateway of the heart—for that power belongs to God alone—but by cunning and deceitful deception, drawing the soul into the effect of malice through thoughts and incitements to vices, of which he is full. Satan therefore filled Ananias’s heart not by entering, but by inserting the poison of his malice. The same unclean spirit, expelled from the hearts of believers by the flame of virtues while teachers of truth contend, pours in the poison of persecution.

These authorities show that demons do not substantially enter human hearts, but are said to be expelled from them because of the effect of their malice, when they are not allowed to harm them.

## DISTINCTION IX. ON THE DISTINCTION OF THE ORDERS: WHAT AND HOW MANY THEY ARE.

1. After what has been said, it remains to learn what Scripture hands down concerning the orders of angels. In many places it declares that there are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. In these orders there are found three groups of three, with three orders in each group, so that the likeness of the Trinity may be shown as impressed upon them. Thus Dionysius teaches that there are three orders of angels, placing three in each: three higher, three lower, and three middle orders. The higher are seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle, dominions, principalities, and powers; the lower, virtues, archangels, and angels.

### What is called an order, and the rationale of each name.

2. Here we must consider what is called an order; then whether the distinction among these orders existed from creation itself. An order is a multitude of heavenly spirits who resemble one another in some office of grace, just as they agree in the gift of natural endowments. For example, seraphim are called those who burn with charity beyond the others; for *seraphim* means “burning” or “kindling.” Cherubim are those who excel others in knowledge; for *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” A throne means a seat; but thrones are called, as blessed Gregory says, Homily 34 on Luke 15, those who are so filled with divine grace that God sits in them and through them decrees and directs judgments.

Dominions are called those who transcend principalities and powers. Principalities are those who arrange the things to be done by those subject to them and preside over them in carrying out the divine mysteries. Powers are those who have received more powerfully than the others in their order the capacity that hostile powers may be restrained under their authority, lest they be able to tempt human beings as much as they wish. Virtues are those through whom signs and miracles are frequently performed. Archangels are those who announce greater matters; angels, those who announce lesser matters.

### That these names are given to them not for their own sake but for ours; they are taken from gifts of grace possessed not exclusively but preeminently, and from their chief gifts they are named.

3. These names are given to them not for their own sake but for ours. Those who are known to themselves by contemplation become known to us by their designations. The individual orders are named from gifts of grace which are given to them in participation not exclusively, but preeminently. For in that heavenly court, where there is fullness of good, although certain things are given preeminently, nothing is possessed exclusively. All things are in all, though not equally; for some possess more sublimely than others what nevertheless all possess.

Although the higher orders have received all gifts of grace more sublimely and perfectly, they have received their names from their chief gifts, leaving the remaining names to the lower orders for their designation. Thus seraphim, the order considered most excellent, has received both love and knowledge of divinity and the other gifts of virtues more sublimely and perfectly than all the others; nevertheless, that highest order receives its name from its more excellent gift, namely charity. For charity itself is a greater gift than knowledge. Likewise, to know is greater than to judge, for knowledge informs judgment. Therefore the second order is named from the second gift, namely knowledge of truth: that is, cherubim. The same is to be understood of the others.

The excellence of the orders is therefore assigned according to the excellence of their gifts. Yet, as Gregory says in Homily 34 on the Gospels, “Those gifts are common to all.” For all burn with charity and are full of knowledge; and so also with the others. But the higher orders have received these gifts more excellently than the others, as has already been said, and are named from them. Hence Gregory says: “In that highest city, each order is designated by the name of the thing which it has received more fully as a gift.”

### A question arising from Gregory’s words.

4. But here the following question arises: If each order is named from that gift which it possesses more fully, then the cherubim surpass all others in knowledge, because they are named from knowledge. But the more one loves, the more one knows. For, as authority teaches, there each one knows in proportion as he loves. Therefore the seraphim surpass not only in charity but also in knowledge. Accordingly, that authority seems to be understood in this way: the comparison is not made with all the orders, but with certain ones, namely the inferior orders. For that order has not received knowledge more fully than the seraphim as a gift, but more fully than the other orders which are inferior. Nor is each order named from everything which it has received more fully than others, but from one of the things which it has received. Or the comparison may be referred, not to the orders themselves, but to other gifts; and not to all other gifts, but to certain ones. For just as human beings, though they possess several gifts, possess some more excellently than others, so perhaps angels also are more powerful in certain endowments and less so in certain others.

### Whether the orders were thus distinct from the beginning of creation

5. It remains now to inquire whether these orders too were thus distinct from the beginning of creation. That they were distinct from the first beginning of their creation seems to be suggested by the testimony of authority, which teaches that some fell from each order. For that Lucifer was of the highest order; none more worthy than he was created. The Apostle also names the principalities and powers of darkness, showing that some fell from those orders; although they carry out their ministry in evil, they have nevertheless not been wholly deprived of the names of their orders [Col. 0671].

But this does not seem able to stand. For at that time they did not burn with charity, nor were they powerful in wisdom, nor did God sit in them; for if they had possessed these things, they would not have fallen. Therefore they were not then cherubim, seraphim, or thrones. To this we reply that, before the fall of some, these orders did not exist, because they did not yet possess the gifts in participation of which they agree. But when some fell, certain gifts were added to others; and the same gifts would have been conferred upon those who fell if they had remained steadfast. Therefore Scripture says that some fell from each order, not because they had been in the orders and afterward fell, but because, had they remained steadfast, some of them would have been in each order. They had differing ranks both in subtlety of nature and in keenness of form, just as those who remained steadfast did. For, as we said above, some were created higher and some lower: higher, those made more subtle in nature and more keen in wisdom; lower, those made less subtle in nature and less keen in understanding.

But only he who disposed all things in number, measure, and weight could weigh these invisible differences among invisible beings: that is, he who is in himself measure, setting a limit to every thing; number, giving every thing its form; and weight, drawing every thing toward stability—that is, limiting, forming, and ordering all things.

### Whether all angels of the same order are equal

6. Moreover, it must be considered whether all angels of the same order are equal. Some have held that they are; but this is neither probable nor worthy of assertion. For Lucifer, who belonged to the company of the higher angels, was himself more worthy even than those who had been created more excellent than others. From this it is understood that, had he remained steadfast, he would have been in the highest order and would have been more worthy than the others of that order. For just as there is one order of apostles and another of martyrs, yet among the apostles some are more worthy, and likewise among the martyrs some are higher than others, so it is rightly believed to be so also in the orders of angels.

### How Scripture says that a tenth order is to be completed from human beings, although there are only nine orders

7. It should also be noted that a tenth order is said to be restored from human beings. But since there are only nine orders, and there would not have been more even if those who fell had remained steadfast, readers wonder how Scripture can say that a tenth order is to be completed from human beings. For Gregory, Homily 34 on Luke, chapter 15, says that human beings are to be assumed into the order of angels: some into the order of the higher angels, namely those who burn more greatly with charity; others into the order of the lower angels, namely those who are less perfect. From this it is apparent that a tenth order is not to be formed from human beings, as though nine orders were angelic and the tenth human; rather, human beings are to be placed in the angelic orders according to the quality of their merits.

Thus, when it is read that a tenth order is to be completed from human beings, this may be understood in the following sense: from human beings there will be restored that which fell among the angels, from whom so many fell that a tenth order could be made. On this account the Apostle says, Ephesians 1, that all things in Christ are to be restored, “the things in heaven and also the things on earth,” because through Christ the human race has been redeemed, and from it comes the repair of the angelic ruin. Yet a human being would be saved no less if an angel had not fallen.

### That human beings are assumed according to the number of the angels who remained, not those who fell

8. For human beings are admitted to blessedness according not to the number of those who fell, but to that of those who remained. Hence Gregory, Homily 34: “That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings; and we believe that as many of the human race will ascend to it as angels happened to remain there.” As it is written in the Song of Deuteronomy, chapter 32: “He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.”

### Some say that human beings are to be restored according to the number of fallen angels

9. Yet some think that human beings are restored according to the number of angels who fell [Col. 0672], so that that heavenly city may neither be deprived of the number of its own citizens nor rule with a greater abundance. Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 29, seems to hold this view, not asserting that more human beings are saved than angels fell, but that no fewer are saved. Thus he says:

> “The heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, the city of God, shall not be deprived of any number of her citizens, or perhaps shall reign with an even more abundant company. Nor do we know the number either of the holy human beings or of the unclean demons; in whose place the children of the Catholic mother, who appeared barren on earth, succeeding, shall remain without any limit of time in that peace from which they fell. But the number of those citizens—whether it is, was, or will be—is in the contemplation of that Craftsman who calls the things which are not as though they were” [Romans 4].

See: he expressly says that no fewer human beings are saved than angels fell; but he does not assert that more are saved.

## DISTINCTION X. WHETHER ALL THE HEAVENLY SPIRITS ARE SENT; TWO OPINIONS AND THE AUTHORITIES ON WHICH THEY RELY

1. It must also be investigated whether all those heavenly spirits are sent out to announce external matters. Some think that within that multitude there are some who go forth for an office, while others always stand within. As it is written in Daniel, chapter 7: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and a million stood before him.” Likewise Dionysius, in the *Hierarchy*, which is called “sacred rulership,” says concerning the precedence of the spirits: “Those higher ranks never withdraw from the innermost realities, because those that are preeminent never have the exercise of an external office.” Those who deny that any angels except the lower ones are sent rely on these authorities.

### Objection against them
