2. Against them is objected what Isaiah says, chapter 6: “One of the seraphim flew to me”—an order which is highest and most excellent. Therefore, if angels are sent from that order, it is beyond doubt that angels from the other orders are also sent. The Apostle likewise says, Hebrews 1: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into service?” By these testimonies some maintain that all angels are sent. Nor should it seem unworthy that even the higher angels are sent, since he who is creator of all descended to these lower things.

### Question: If all are sent, why is only one order designated by the name angels?

3. Here a question arises: if all are sent and are God’s messengers, why is only one order among the nine designated by the name of angels? Some answer that all are indeed sent, but some are sent more frequently and, as it were, by an assigned office—those properly called angels or archangels. Others, namely the greater spirits, are sent more rarely, when some occasion arises outside the ordinary dispensation. When they undertake the ministry of angels, they also take the name. Hence Psalm 103: “You make your angels spirits, and your ministers”; for those who are spirits by nature sometimes become angels, that is, messengers.

### Some believe Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael belonged to the highest order; these are names of spirits, not orders

4. And they think that Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael belonged to the highest order. Michael means “Who is like God?”; Gabriel, “Strength of God”; Raphael, “Medicine of God.” These are not names of orders, but of spirits. Some say that each of these is properly and singularly the name of one spirit. Others say that it is not the name of one particular and determined spirit, but now of this one, now of that one, according to the character of the matters which they are sent to announce or perform. Likewise, certain names of demons are thought by some to belong properly to one demon, while others regard them as common to several.

For the devil—so called in Greek, and interpreted “accuser” or “one flowing downward”—is called in Hebrew *Satan*, that is, “adversary.” He is also called *Belial*, that is, “apostate” and “without yoke”; he is also called *Leviathan*, that is, “their addition.” You will find many other names which either belong properly to one spirit or are common to several [Col. 0673].

### How those who say that all angels are sent explain the foregoing apparently opposing authorities

5. Those who maintain that all angels are sent explain the aforementioned authorities—namely those of Daniel and Dionysius—as follows. The higher ranks are said to stand before God and never withdraw from the innermost realities, not because they are never sent, but because they go forth to external matters very rarely. Nor do they then withdraw from those innermost realities; rather, they always stand in God’s presence and contemplation, as do those who are sent frequently.

### Whom others say are sent and whom they say are not sent, with their explanation of apparently opposing authorities

6. Others, however, say that the three highest orders—cherubim, seraphim, and thrones—so stand before the Creator that they do not go out to external matters. The three lower orders are sent outward; while the middle three stand between the two groups, not merely in dignity or place but also in office, because they receive the divine command from the higher orders and convey it to the lower. Therefore, since the highest announce God’s command to the middle, the middle to the lowest, and these to human beings, all rightly ought to be called angels.

For this reason perhaps the Apostle says that all spirits are ministers of the Son and are sent into service; by “all” he embraces not every individual order, but individual angels from the lower orders. They explain Isaiah’s statement through the words of Dionysius by saying: “Those spirits who are sent receive the designation of those whose office they perform.” Thus they say that the angel sent to Isaiah in order to cleanse and burn the prophet’s lips was of the lower order; but perhaps he was called one of the seraphim because he came to burn and consume Isaiah’s sins.

## DISTINCTION XI. THAT EVERY SOUL HAS A GOOD ANGEL ASSIGNED FOR ITS GUARDIANSHIP, AND AN EVIL ANGEL FOR ITS EXERCISE

1. It should also be known that good angels are appointed for the guardianship of human beings, so that each of the elect has an angel specially assigned for that person’s progress and protection. Hence in the Gospel, Matthew 18, Truth, forbidding offense against the little ones, says: “Their angels always see the face of the Father.” He calls them their angels because they have been assigned for their guardianship.

On this passage Jerome, volume 9 of the *Commentaries*, book 3, on Matthew 18; Tobit 5, distinction 6 and 8, a; Acts 12b, teaches that every soul has an angel assigned to its guardianship from the beginning of birth, saying: “Great is the dignity of souls, that each one has from the beginning of its birth an angel assigned for its guardianship.” Gregory likewise says that each person has a good angel assigned for protection and an evil angel for exercise.

For although all good angels desire our good and labor together for the salvation of all, nevertheless the one assigned to someone’s protection especially urges that person toward good, as is written of Tobias’s angel and of Peter’s angel in the Acts of the Apostles. Likewise, although evil angels desire human evil, the angel assigned for a person’s exercise incites that person more strongly toward evil and presses more forcefully to do harm.

### Whether one angel is assigned to each person, or one to several

2. It is commonly asked whether individual angels are assigned to individual human beings, or one angel to several for protection or exercise. But since the elect are as numerous as the good angels, it is evident that all good and evil human beings together are more numerous than the good angels. And since the elect are as numerous as the good angels, good angels are more numerous than evil angels, and evil human beings are more numerous than good; there is no doubt that good human beings are more numerous than evil angels, and evil human beings are more numerous than either evil angels or good angels.

### Confirmation that one angel is assigned to several human beings, either simultaneously or at different times

3. Therefore it must be said that one and the same angel, good or evil, is assigned to several human beings for protection or exercise, whether at the same time or at different times [Col. 0674]. We say “at the same time or at different times” because some think that all human beings living at any one time can each have their own good or evil angel. For although the number of all human beings who have been, are, and will be, counted together, is greater than the number of angels, human beings succeed one another as they die and thus are never all in this life at the same time; angels, however, never die, but all exist together. Thus it may be that each human being, while in this life, has an individual good or evil angel assigned for that person’s guardianship or exercise.

But whether this is so or not, there is no doubt that each person has an angel assigned to that person, whether the angel is assigned simultaneously to several or individually to one alone. Nor is it surprising that one angel should be assigned to several human beings for protection, since the guardianship of several is assigned to one human being, so that each may be said to have that person as lord, bishop, or abbot.

### Whether angels advance in merit or reward until the judgment

4. Moreover, it must be considered whether good angels advance in reward or merit until the judgment. Some think that they advance in merits and daily merit more and more, because they daily serve human needs and labor for human advancement. These same persons also think that they advance in reward, namely in knowledge and love of God. For although, as they say, they received eternal and perfect blessedness at their confirmation, their blessedness nevertheless increases daily because they love and know more and more.

Their charity, by which they love God and us, is both merit and the reward of merits: through it they merit by the services rendered to us from it, and they advance in blessedness; and this same charity is reward, because by it they are blessed.

### They confirm what they say by authorities

5. They confirm by testimonies of the saints that angels advance in knowledge and thereby in blessedness. Isaiah, chapter 63, speaks in the person of angels admiring the majesty of Christ ascending: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” And Psalm 24: “Who is this King of glory?” From these passages it is apparent that angels knew the mystery of the incarnate Word more fully after its fulfillment than before. And, just as they advanced in knowledge of this mystery, these writers say that they advance in knowledge of the Godhead.

The Apostle plainly teaches that they advanced in knowledge of such a mystery, saying in Ephesians 3:6: “[That] the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God [may be known], so that the manifold wisdom of God may be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places.” On this passage Jerome, volume 9, says that the angelic dignities did not understand the aforesaid mystery fully until Christ’s passion had been completed and the apostles’ preaching had spread among the nations.

### Augustine seems to oppose Jerome in this view

6. Augustine, commenting on the same passage of the Epistle, seems to contradict this. He says: “The mystery of the kingdom of heaven, which was revealed at the fitting time for our salvation, was not hidden from the angels. Therefore that aforementioned mystery was known to them from the ages, since every creature exists not before the ages but from the ages.”

Observe, reader, that these distinguished doctors seem to disagree on this point. Therefore, that every contradiction may be removed, let us, following Haymo, explain the foregoing words thus: let us say that the angels of higher dignity, through whose ministry these things were announced, knew them in part from the ages, as familiars and messengers; but that they were unknown to angels of lower dignity until they were fulfilled and foretold through the Church; and that then they were perfectly known by all angels.

It is therefore established that all angels have advanced in knowledge of divine mysteries according to the progress of time. Hence those writers not incongruously say that the knowledge and blessedness of angels increase until the future consummation, when they will be so perfect in knowledge and blessedness that they will neither increase nor diminish further.

### The opinion of others who say that angels have not advanced in certain of the matters mentioned above

7. Others, however, say that at their confirmation angels were endowed with such love and knowledge of the Godhead that they have not advanced, nor will advance, further in these. They have nevertheless advanced in knowledge of external things, such as knowledge of the mystery of the Incarnation and similar matters, but not in contemplation of the Godhead. For they do not understand, nor will understand, the Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity more fully than they received it at their very confirmation.

They likewise say that angels have not advanced in charity after confirmation, because their charity was not afterward increased. Thus they say that angels have not advanced in merits, but this as regards the power of meriting, not as regards the number of merits. For they have afterward done many good things which they had not then done; but the charity from which those acts proceeded has not increased. By it they merited as much before those acts were added as afterward when they had been added. Yet what the others said above seems more probable: namely, that angels advance in knowledge and other things until the judgment.

### Certain authorities seem to oppose the more probable opinion

8. Yet the words of certain authorities seem to oppose this. For Isidore says, *On the Supreme Good*, book 1, chapter 12: “Angels know all things in the Word of God before they happen.” But he did not say that all angels know all things perfectly, and therefore he did not exclude their advance in knowledge. Gregory, in the *Dialogues*, chapter 5, says: “What can they not know there, where they know him who knows all things?” He seems here to say that angels know all things and that there is nothing of which they are ignorant. But this should be understood of those things the knowledge of which makes the knower blessed, such as those belonging to the mystery of Trinity and unity.

## DISTINCTION XII. AFTER CONSIDERING THE ANGELS, THE TREATISE TURNS TO THE CREATION OF OTHER THINGS, ESPECIALLY TO THE DISTINCTION OF THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS

1. Let what has been said about the condition of angelic nature suffice. It remains to set forth some matters concerning the creation of other things also, and especially the distinction of the works of the six days. When God created angelic spirits in his wisdom, he also created other things, as the Scripture cited above, Genesis 1, shows. It says that in the beginning God created heaven, that is, angels, and earth, namely the matter of the four elements, still confused and unformed, called by the Greeks *chaos*; and this existed before every day.

Then God distinguished the elements and gave to each thing, according to its kind, its own proper and distinct forms. He formed these not all at once, as some of the holy Fathers thought, but through intervals of time and the six revolutions of days, as others held.

### That holy interpreters seem to have delivered almost opposing accounts of this: some saying all things were made at once in matter and form, others through intervals of time

2. Some of the holy Fathers, who searched the words and mysteries of God with exceptional penetration, seem to have written almost opposing things on this subject. Some taught that all things were created at once in matter and form; Augustine seems to have held this. Others judged and asserted more strongly that the first crude and unformed matter, containing the mixture and confusion of the four elements, was created; afterward, through the intervals of six days, the classes of bodily things were formed from that matter according to their proper forms.

Gregory, Jerome, Bede, and many others commend and prefer this view. It also seems more consonant with the Scripture of Genesis, from which our first knowledge of this matter came.

### How bodily things were created through intervals of time

[Col. 0676]

3. According to this teaching, then, let us examine the order and manner of the creation and formation of things. As was mentioned above, in the beginning God created heaven, that is, angelic nature—though still unformed, as some think—and earth, that is, that confused matter of the four elements. Moses called it “earth,” as Augustine says, volume 1, book 1, *On Genesis against the Manichees*, chapter 7, because earth is the least beautiful of all the elements. It was empty and unordered because of the mixture of all the elements.

He also calls the same matter “the deep,” saying, “And darkness was upon the face of the deep,” and so forth, because it was confused and mixed, lacking a distinct form. The same unformed matter was also called “water,” over which the Spirit of the Lord was borne, just as the will of an artisan is borne over the things to be made. For what he had begun to form and perfect lay subject to the good will of the Creator, who, as Lord and maker, presided over the fluid and confused matter so as to distinguish it into various forms whenever and however he wished.

This matter was called water because all things which grow on earth—whether animals, trees, plants, and the like—begin to be formed and nourished from moisture. That unformed matter was called by all these names so that an unknown thing might be indicated to the less learned by familiar terms, and not by one term alone. For if it were signified by one word alone, people would suppose it to be the thing which they were accustomed to understand by that word.

Thus under these names was signified that confused and unformed matter, which could neither be seen nor touched in any form: it was indicated by the names of visible things which were to come from it, because of the weakness of beginners, who are less able to grasp invisible things. And there was then darkness, that is, the absence of light. For darkness is not something; it is simply the absence of light. Thus silence is not some thing, but where there is no sound there is said to be silence. Nakedness too is not some thing; rather, where a body lacks covering, there is said to be nakedness. Likewise emptiness is not something, but a place is called empty where there is no body, and emptiness is the absence of a body.

### In what sense darkness is said not to be something, and in what sense it is said to be something

4. Observe that Augustine here says darkness is not something, although elsewhere darkness is placed among creatures which bless the Lord. Hence it is said, Daniel 3: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness.” Therefore it should be known that darkness is understood in different ways: either as the absence of light, as Augustine understood it above, in which sense it is not something; or as darkened air, or a dark quality of the air, in which sense it is a created thing.

Therefore he says that darkness was then upon the face of the deep because light did not yet exist. If it had existed, it would have been above and spread over it. But God had not yet adorned his work with the grace of light, which was afterward formed on the first day.

### Two matters must here be considered: why that confused matter was called unformed, where it came into being, and how far upward it extended

5. Before we treat this matter, two questions present themselves for examination. First, why is that confused matter called unformed: because it lacked every form, or for another reason? Second, where did it come into existence, and how far upward did it extend?

Briefly answering the first question, we say that this first matter was not called unformed because it had absolutely no form, since no bodily thing can exist without any form whatsoever. Rather, we say it may fittingly be called unformed because, existing in a certain confusion and mixture, it had not yet received the beautiful, manifest, and distinct form which we now see. Thus that matter was made in a form of confusion before the form of ordered arrangement. In the form of confusion all bodily things were created materially together and at once; afterward, in the form of ordered arrangement, they were ordered in six days [Col. 0677]. Thus the first matter proposed for examination has been resolved: why that matter is called unformed.

### Here he answers the second question

6. It remains to explain the second question: where that matter existed and how far in height it extended. Making no rash assertion, we say that when that first mass of all things was created, it appears to have come into being in the very place where it now exists in formed condition. This earthy element existed in one place, the same central place, while the other three were mixed together in one confusion. They enveloped it on every side in the manner of a kind of cloud, so that what it was could not appear.

The other three, confused together in one mixture and suspended all around, extended upward as far as the summit of bodily nature now reaches. And, as some think, that mass extended beyond the region of the firmament. In its lower part it was denser and coarser; in its upper part, thinner, smoother, and more subtle. From that thinner substance some think came the waters which are said to be above the firmament. Such was the appearance of the world in the beginning, before it received form or arrangement.

### Having shown what the appearance of the world was at its very beginning, he begins to set forth the distinction of the works of the six days

7. It remains now to follow in order how that arrangement was completed. In six days, as the Scripture of Genesis teaches, God distinguished and reduced to their proper forms all the things which he had made materially together. He completed his work on the sixth day; and afterward on the seventh day he rested from all his work—that is, he ceased to make a new creature. For in six days he distinguished six classes of things, and afterward made nothing which is not contained in one of them.

Yet he worked afterward, as Truth says in the Gospel: “My Father has worked until now, and I work.”

### On the four modes of divine operation

8. For, as Alcuin says on Genesis, God works in four ways. First, in the Word, disposing all things; second, in the unformed matter of the four elements, creating it from nothing. Hence Ecclesiasticus 18: “He who lives for ever created all things together”—that is, he created all the elements, or all bodies materially, together. Third, through the works of the six days, he distinguished the various creatures. Fourth, from primordial seeds, no unknown natures arise, but known natures are repeatedly renewed so that they do not perish.

## DISTINCTION XIII. WHAT THE FIRST WORK OF DISTINCTION WAS

1. The first work of distinction was the formation of light, as the Scripture of Genesis shows. After recalling the unformed state of things, it began their ordering with light, adding: “God said, LET LIGHT BE; and light was made. And he divided the light from the darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night. And evening and morning were made, one day.” Fittingly, the adornment of the world began with light, by which the other things that were to be created might be seen.

### What kind of light it was: bodily or spiritual

2. If it is asked what sort of light that was, whether bodily or spiritual, we answer what we read as handed down by the saints. Augustine says that the light may be understood either bodily or spiritually. If it is understood spiritually, angelic nature is meant. It was first unformed, but afterward formed when, turning to the Creator, it clung to him in charity. The creation of its unformed state was signified above, as was said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Here, however, its formation is shown when he says: “Let light be, and light was made.”

Thus angelic nature was first darkness and afterward light, because it first had formlessness and imperfection, then the perfection of formation; and in this way God divided light from darkness. For, as Augustine says on Genesis: “The formlessness and imperfection of this creature existed before it was formed in love of the Creator. But it was formed when it turned to the unchangeable light of the Word” [Col. 0678].

But if that light was bodily—which is certainly probable—it is understood to have been a luminous body, like a bright cloud. It was formed not from nothing but from pre-existing matter, so that it might be light and possess the power of shining. With it the first day arose, because before light there was neither day nor night, though time existed.

### That light was made where the sun appears, and could shine in the waters

3. If it is asked where that light was made, since the deep covered the whole height of the earth, it may be said that it was made in those regions which are now illumined by the daylight of the sun. Nor is it surprising that light can shine in waters, since they are often illumined even by the activity of sailors, who, submerged in the depths, illuminate the water about them by releasing oil from their mouths. The waters were much thinner in the beginning than they are now, since they had not yet been gathered in one place.

Thus that light was made which performed the function and held the place of the sun; moved in its course, it distinguished night and day. It is therefore likely that light first appeared where the sun, carried around in its daily course, now appears: so that, traveling in the same path and first descending toward the west, the light made evening; then, returning to the east, it illumined dawn, that is, morning. Thus God divided light and darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night.

### That “day” is understood in different ways

4. Here it should be noted that “day” is understood in different ways in Scripture. That light which illumined the darkness during those three days is called day; the illumination of the air itself is also called day. A day is also a period of twenty-four hours, as it is understood when it is said: “Evening and morning were made, one day.”

This should be distinguished as follows: evening occurred first, then morning; and so one complete day of twenty-four hours existed. It was a natural day, because it had evening but not morning. For morning is called both the end of the preceding day and the beginning of the next: it is dawn, which has neither full light nor complete darkness. Thus the first day did not have a morning, because no day had preceded it to be ended at the beginning of the following day; and especially because, once light appeared, a full and splendid day immediately existed over the earth, since it began not from dawn but from full light, and was completed by the morning of the following day.

Hence Bede, on Genesis: “It was fitting that day should begin from light and extend to the morning of the following day, so that the works of God might be signified as having begun from light and as completed in light.” The remaining days, however, had morning and evening; each began with its own morning and extended to the morning of the next day.

### On the natural order for reckoning days, and that introduced for a mystery

5. This is the natural order for distinguishing days: days are distinguished and counted from morning to morning. Later, however, for a mystery days began to be counted from evening to evening, and the day was joined with the preceding night in the reckoning, whereas according to the natural order the preceding day ought to be joined to the following night. For through sin humanity fell from light into the darkness of ignorance and sins, and then through Christ returned from darkness to light. Hence the Apostle, Ephesians 5: “We were once darkness, but now light in the Lord.”

Therefore the first day, beginning not with dawn but with full light, and after evening, as the light gradually set, receiving the morning of the following day, was completed. Hence Bede: “When the light was setting and gradually, after the span of daylight, was entering the lower regions, evening occurred, just as it is now accustomed to occur by the course of the sun. Morning occurred when that same light returned over the earth and began another day, and one day of twenty-four hours was completed.” During those three days the night was entirely dark; after the stars were created, it was brightened by some light.

### Why the sun was made if that light sufficed
6. It is commonly asked why the sun was made, if that light was sufficient to make the day. To this it may be said that perhaps that light illumined the higher regions, and [Col. 0679] that the sun had to be made for the illumination of the lower regions. Or rather, it was made because, once the sun had been made, the brightness of the day was increased. For the day afterward shone with a much more abundant light than before. But if it is asked what became of that light, since it now does not appear, it may be said either that the body of the sun was formed from it, or that it is not in that part of heaven in which the sun is; not because it itself is the sun, but because it is so joined to it that it cannot be distinguished.

### How the statement “God said” is to be understood: whether God said it with the sound of a voice, or otherwise

7. Moreover, it must be investigated how the statement, “God said,” is to be understood: whether he said this temporally, or with the sound of a voice, or in some other way. Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 1, chapter 2, teaches that God spoke neither temporally nor with the sound of a voice; for if temporally, then mutably. And if the voice of God is said to have sounded corporeally, there was neither a tongue by which he might speak, nor anyone who needed both to hear and to understand. Therefore the voice of God is rightly referred to the nature of the Word, through whom all things were made. Thus, “God said, Let there be,” etc., not temporally and not with the sound of a voice, but in the Word coeternal with himself—that is, he begot the Word timelessly, in which it was, and in which he ordained from eternity that it should come to be in time; and in him it was made.

### How it is to be understood that the Father works in the Son, or through the Son, or in the Holy Spirit

8. Here it is commonly asked how the statement is to be understood that the Father works in the Son, or through the Son, or in the Holy Spirit. For Scripture frequently sets this before us; as in Psalm 103: “You made all things in Wisdom, O Lord,” that is, in the Son; and Genesis 1: “In the beginning,” that is, in the Son, “God created heaven and earth.” And Hebrews 1 says: “Through whom he also made the ages.” Moreover, on that passage of Psalm 32, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established,” etc., Augustine says that the Father works through his Word and the Holy Spirit. How, then, is this to be understood?

Certain heretics supposed that the Father, as an author and craftsman, employed the Son and the Holy Spirit in the operation of things as though they were instruments, taking from the foregoing words an occasion for error. Pious faith rejects this as blasphemous and contrary to sound doctrine. Therefore Scripture is not to be understood as frequently declaring that the Father works in the Son or through the Son as though the Son could not act unless the Father extended his right hand to him, or as though the Son were some instrument of the working Father. Rather, by these words it intended the Father to be understood as working with the Son and the Holy Spirit, and as doing nothing without them.

### The heretic objects to this explanation

9. But the heretic says that, by this reasoning, it could equally have been said that the Son works through the Father or in the Father, and that the Holy Spirit works with both or through both, because the Son works with the Father and the Holy Spirit with both. The brief answer is that this, and not the other, was said in order to display authority in the Father. For the Father does not act from the Son, but the Son from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both. Thus the Son too is read to work through the Holy Spirit, because he works with the Holy Spirit, who has from the Son himself the power to work.

### Another explanation of the foregoing

10. This may also be understood otherwise: the Father is said to work in the Son or through the Son because he begot the maker of all things. Just as the Father is said to judge through him because he begot the Judge, so likewise either the Father or the Son is said to work through the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit, maker of all things, proceeds from both.

Hence John Chrysostom, in his exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews, says:

> Not as the heretic vainly supposes, did the Son exist as some instrument of the Father; nor is the Father said to have made through him as though he could not himself make. But just as the Father is said to judge through the Son because he begot the Judge, so he is said to work through the Son because it is agreed that he begot him as maker. For if the Father is his cause, insofar as he is Father, he is much more the cause of those things that were made through the Son.

These things have been said concerning the work of the first day.

## DISTINCTION XIV. ON THE WORK OF THE SECOND DAY, ON WHICH THE FIRMAMENT WAS MADE

[Col. 0680]

1. God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.” And he divided the waters that were below the firmament from those that were above the firmament. It should be known that here, as Bede says in his commentary on Genesis, the creation is described of that heaven in which the stars are fixed. Beneath it are waters in the air and on the earth, and above it are other waters, of which it is said: “You cover its upper regions with waters.” The firmament, therefore—that is, the starry heaven—is in the middle; and it may be believed to have been made from waters. For crystal, a stone possessing great firmness and transparency, is made from water.

But if anyone is troubled by the question how waters, fluid by nature and prone to fall downward, can remain above heaven, let him remember what is written of God: “Who binds the waters in his clouds.” He who binds beneath heaven waters temporarily held in the vapors of clouds can also suspend waters above the sphere of heaven, not by vaporous thinness but by icy solidity, lest they fall. What they are like, and for what purpose they were created, is known by him who created them. Thus these words have shown that heaven was made—namely, that heaven in which the stars are fixed, that is, the heaven above the air—and from what material, namely waters; and also what the waters above that heaven are like, namely solid like ice.

### Others hold that this heaven is of a fiery nature; Augustine agrees with them

2. Some, however, say that the heaven beyond the regions of the air is of a fiery nature, maintaining that above the air there is pure fire which is called heaven. They conjecture that the stars and luminaries were made from this fire, and Augustine appears to agree with them. But Augustine asks, without deciding, whether by the name “firmament” heaven beyond the air is meant here, or the air itself. Yet he seems rather to approve the interpretation that the heaven which exceeds the regions of the air is meant here.

He says that the waters above that heaven are drawn up in vapor and suspended in the lightest drops, just as this cloudy air draws waters up in vapor by the exhalation of the earth, holds them suspended in tiny particles, and afterward pours them down as rain when they have gathered into denser masses. Therefore, if water, as we see, can be reduced to such minute particles that it is carried in vapor above air, which is naturally lighter than water, why should we not believe that it likewise rises above that lighter heaven in finer drops and lighter vapors? But however they may be there, we do not doubt that they are there.

### What shape the firmament has

3. It is also commonly asked what shape heaven has. But although our authors knew it, the Holy Spirit was unwilling to say it through them, except insofar as it benefits salvation. It is likewise asked whether heaven stands still or moves. “If it moves,” they say, “how is it a firmament? If it stands still, how do the stars fixed in it move around?” Yet it may be called a firmament not because of its standing still, but because of its firmness or because it is an impassable boundary for the waters. But if it stands still, nothing prevents the stars from moving and circling around.

### Why Scripture was silent about the work of the second day, which it mentioned in the other days

4. After this it is commonly asked why it is not said here, as in the works of the other days: “God saw that it was good.” Some sacramental mystery is indicated here. Perhaps it was not said because, although it was so in fact as on the other days, the number two is the beginning of otherness and a sign of division.

### On the work of the third day, when the waters were gathered into one place

5. It follows: “God said: Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” The gathering of the waters into one place is the work of the third day. All waters below heaven were gathered into one basin, so that the light which during the preceding two days had surveyed the waters with clear brightness might shine more brightly in the pure air, and so that the earth, which lay hidden under its covering, might appear; and that which had been muddy with waters might become dry and fit for plants. For on the same day the earth brought forth green grass and trees bearing fruit.

But if [Col. 0681] it is asked where the waters were gathered which had covered all the space up to heaven, it could have happened that the earth subsided and provided hollow regions in which it received the surging waters. It may also be believed that the primordial waters were thinner, so that they covered the lands like mist, but were thickened by their gathering and thus could easily be brought into one place. And although it is certain that there are many seas and rivers, nevertheless the waters are said to have been gathered into one place because of the continuity or union of all waters on the earth, since all rivers and seas are joined to the great sea. Therefore, although it has said that the waters were gathered into one place, it subsequently speaks in the plural of “gatherings of waters,” because of their many branching bays, all of which have their origin in the great sea.

### On the work of the fourth day, when the luminaries were made

6. It follows: “God said: Let luminaries be made in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night.” During the preceding three days the structure of this universe was arranged and apportioned among its parts. For when light had been formed on the first day to illuminate everything, the next two days were assigned to the uppermost and lowest parts of the world: namely, the firmament, air, earth, and water. For on the second day the firmament was spread out above. On the third, when the masses of waters had been gathered within their receptacles, the earth was uncovered and the air cleared. Thus the four elements of the world were distinguished and ordered in their places during those days.

But in the three following days those four elements were adorned. For on the fourth day the firmament was adorned with sun, moon, and stars. On the fifth, air received birds and waters fish as their ornaments. On the sixth, earth received cattle, creeping things, and beasts; and after all these, man was made from earth and upon earth—yet not for earth, nor on account of earth, but for heaven and on account of heaven.

### The adornment of heaven is treated first, just as its making was treated first

7. Therefore, because heaven surpasses the other elements in beauty and was made before the others, it is adorned before the others on the fourth day, when the stars are made. They were made so that the lower region might be illumined by them, lest it be dark for its inhabitants. Provision was made for human weakness, so that, as the sun moved round, human beings might enjoy the alternation of day and night, because of the need to sleep and wake. Likewise, lest night should remain unadorned, the moon and stars were provided as a consolation for those who might be compelled to work at night, and because there are certain animals that cannot endure light.

But how the further words, “Let them be for signs, and seasons, and days, and years,” are to be understood is commonly asked. For it seems to be said as though seasons began on the fourth day, whereas the preceding three days were not without time. Therefore, by the “seasons” produced through the stars we should understand not intervals of duration, but changes in the condition of the air, since such things are produced by the movements of the stars, as are the days and years with which we are familiar. For they are signs of fair and stormy weather; and they are for seasons, because through them we distinguish the four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Or they are for signs and seasons, that is, for the distinction of hours, because before they were made the order of times, the noon hour, and any other hour were marked by no signs. These things were made on the fourth day.

## DISTINCTION XV. ON THE WORK OF THE FIFTH DAY, WHEN GOD CREATED FROM THE WATERS FLYING AND SWIMMING CREATURES

1. God also said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping creatures with living souls, and birds above the earth,” etc. The work of the fifth day is the formation of fish and birds, by which two elements are adorned. From the same matter, namely water, he created fish and birds, raising the winged creatures into the air and consigning the swimming creatures to the deep.

### On the work of the sixth day, when the animals and creeping things of earth were created

2. It follows: “God said: Let the earth bring forth living souls—cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth—according to their kinds,” etc. The work of the sixth day is described when the earth is said to be adorned with its animals.

### Whether poisonous animals became harmful after sin, or, though made harmless, began to harm because of sin

[Col. 0682]

3. It is commonly asked concerning poisonous and destructive animals whether they were created after sin as a punishment for human beings, or whether, having been created harmless, they began to harm sinners. Certainly it may be said that, had man not sinned, creatures would have harmed him in no respect. They began to harm for the punishment and intimidation of the vicious, or for the testing or perfecting of virtue. Thus they were created harmless, but became harmful because of sin. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 3, chapter 15.

### Whether small animals were created then

4. There is likewise a question concerning certain small creatures: whether they were created in the first establishment of things, or afterward arose from corrupted substances. For many are produced from the defects of moist bodies, from exhalations of the earth, or from corpses; some also from the decay of woods, plants, and fruits. Yet God is the author of all. It may be said that those which arise from animal bodies, especially dead ones, were not created with the animals, except potentially and materially. But those which arise from earth or water, or from things which arose when the earth put forth vegetation, may not unfittingly be said to have been created then. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 3, chapter 14.

### Why man was made after all other things

5. After all things had been created and arranged, man was made last, as lord and possessor, and as one who was to be set above all things. Hence Genesis 1 continues: “God saw that it was good, and said: Let us make man in our image,” etc.

But before treating of the creation of man, let us set forth more fully and clearly what we briefly touched upon above. For, as we said earlier, Catholic interpreters are found to disagree concerning this distinction of things. Some say that things were created and distinguished according to their kinds over the intervals of six days. Since the letter of Genesis seems more strongly to support their view, and since the Catholic Church more highly approves it, we have therefore carefully taught thus far how, from that common matter first made without form, the kinds of bodily things were afterward separately formed through the course of six days.

But others think that they were not made over intervals of time, but that they came forth into existence, formed all at once. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, book 4, endeavors by several arguments to show this, saying that the four elements existed from the beginning in the form in which they now appear, and that heaven was adorned with stars. Some things, however, were then made not formally but materially, and were afterward formally distinguished with the passage of time: such as plants, trees, and perhaps animals. Therefore they say that all things were made at the beginning of time, but some formally and according to the kinds which we see them possess, such as the greater parts of the world, while others were made only materially.

But, they say, Moses, speaking to a crude and carnal people, moderated his manner of speech, speaking of God by analogy with a human being who completes his works over delays of time, although God made his works all at once. Hence Augustine says: “Moses therefore relates separately that God made those works, because what God could make all at once could not be said all at once by man.” Again: “Scripture could divide by the times of speaking what God did not divide by the times of working.” Those who, adhering to these and similar authorities, say that the four elements and the luminaries of heaven were formed all at once and had those six days mentioned by Scripture, call those six days six kinds of things—that is, distinctions—which were made all at once, partly formally and partly causally (*book 1, chapter 15*).

### How it is to be understood that God rested from all his work

6. We must now say something concerning the rest of the seventh day. It is written in Genesis 2 that “God completed his work on the seventh day, and rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had accomplished.” God is said to have rested on the seventh day not as though wearied by working, but he rested from all work because he ceased making a new creature. For “to rest” [Col. 0683] means “to cease”; hence Revelation, chapter 4, says: “They had no rest, saying: Holy, Holy, Holy”—that is, they did not cease speaking.

God, then, is said to have rested because he ceased making kinds of creatures, since he created no new ones thereafter. Yet, as Truth himself says in the Gospel, the Father works with the Son even now: namely, in administering the same kinds that were then established. For the Creator’s power is the cause of subsistence for every creature. Therefore the saying of John 4, “My Father works until now, and I work,” indicates the continuous administration of the whole creation. Thus he rested on the seventh day, so that he would make no further new creature whose matter or likeness had not preceded it; but he works even now, so that he does not cease to sustain and govern what he created. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 4, chapter 12.

### How it is to be understood that God completed his work on the seventh day, since on that day he rested from all his work  
*(Augustine, Genesis 1;* Enchiridion, *chapters 10 and 11)*

7. But it is asked how God is said to have completed his work on the seventh day, since he rested from all work on that day and made no new kind of thing. Another translation has: “God completed his works on the sixth day.” This presents no difficulty, because what was made on that day is manifest, and the completion of all things was perfected on that day, as Scripture shows when it says: “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good.”

All things were indeed naturally good, having no defect in their own nature; and the individual things which God created are good. But all things together are very good, because the wonderful beauty of the universe consists of all of them. Within it even that which is called evil, when rightly ordered and placed in its own location, makes the good stand out more prominently, so that good things please more and are more praiseworthy when compared with evils. Thus the completion of the works occurred on the sixth day.

Therefore the foregoing question arises: how is God said to have completed his work on the seventh day, as the Hebrew text has it, though he is not said to have created anything new on that day? Unless perhaps he is said to have completed his work on the seventh day because he blessed and sanctified that day, as Scripture adds: “He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it.” For blessing and sanctification are works, just as Solomon performed a work when he dedicated the Temple.

### What the blessing and sanctification of the seventh day are

8. God is said to have sanctified and blessed that day because he endowed it, above the others, with a mystical blessing and sanctification. Hence the Law says, Exodus 20: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” This is why, in counting days, we proceed to the seventh and say that there are seven days, by whose repetition all time is conducted: not because there is an eighth day distinct from them, and a ninth, and so on with the rest, but because the kinds of things were distinguished in six days, and on the seventh—although no new kind of thing was established—there was nevertheless a certain new state, as it were, of the sanctification of the works and the rest of their maker.

The passage may also be explained thus: “God completed his work on the seventh day,” that is, he saw it completed and perfected.

## DISTINCTION XVI. ON THE CREATION OF MAN, WHERE IT MUST BE CONSIDERED WHY MAN WAS CREATED, HOW HE WAS ESTABLISHED, WHAT HE WAS LIKE AND HOW HE WAS MADE; THEN HOW HE FELL; AND FINALLY HOW HE WAS RESTORED—MATTERS WHICH MUST BE EXAMINED

1. Having passed through the matters which we set forth above concerning the creation of man, we now undertake to carry them into effect and explain them in order. Here the following matters appear to require consideration: why man was created; how he was established; what he was like and how he was made; then how he fell; and finally how and by what means he was restored.

We have dealt above, according to the measure of our ability, with the first and second of these—that is, the cause of human creation and the manner of man’s establishment. It remains, therefore, to discuss what he was like and how he was made. In Genesis, chapter 1, we read: “Let us make man in our image [Col. 0684] and likeness,” etc. In saying “Let us make,” the single operation of the three persons is shown; while in saying “in our image and likeness,” the one and equal substance of the three persons is displayed. For this is spoken in the person of the Father to the Son and the Holy Spirit, not, as some suppose, to the angels, because the image or likeness of God and of angels is not the same.

### That “image” and “likeness” are understood here differently by different persons: by some as uncreated, by others as created and uncreated; either as the essence of the Trinity, or as the Son and Holy Spirit

2. In this place, “image and likeness” is understood either as uncreated—that is, the essence of the Trinity, to which man was made—or as created, in which man was made and which was created along with him. Bede seems to have understood the uncreated image, which is God, when he says that God and the angels do not have one image, but the three persons do; and therefore the speech there concerns the persons, not the angels.

Yet “image” is used improperly, because an image is spoken of relatively to another thing whose likeness it bears and which it was made to represent, as an image of Caesar bore his likeness and in some way represented him. Properly speaking, however, that is called an image according to which another thing is made, just as an example is properly called that which is taken from something else, and an exemplar that from which something is taken. Nevertheless, one term is sometimes improperly used for the other; thus the essence of the Trinity is also understood less properly as “image,” if indeed it is understood in this passage under the name of image. (Bede, *On Genesis*.)

### The opinion of those who thought that the Son is here understood by “image and likeness”  
*(Augustine, On the Trinity, book 7, chapter 6, at the end)*

3. The Son, however, is properly called the image of the Father, as we said above in the treatise on the Trinity. Hence there were some who made the distinction in such a way that they understood the Son by “image” in this passage, while they said that man was made not as image but “in the image.” The Apostle refutes them when he says, 1 Corinthians 11: “Man indeed is the image and glory of God.” For when this image, that is, man, is said to be made “in the image,” he is not said to be made, as it were, in relation to the Son; otherwise it would not be said, “in our image.” How could he say “our,” when the Son is the image of the Father alone?

There were also others who treated these matters more keenly, understanding the Son by “image” and the Holy Spirit by “likeness,” since he is the likeness of the Father and the Son. They therefore supposed that “our” was said in the plural with reference only to likeness, while with respect to image “my” was to be understood. They taught that man is both image and made in image and likeness, and is the image of the Image and of the Likeness.

### He does not approve their opinion, but teaches that the image and likeness of God must be sought and considered in man, so that “image and likeness” are understood as created

4. Nevertheless, although this distinction does not seem altogether reprehensible, because it does not flow from the midst of the mountains—that is, from the authorities of the saints—it is more fitting that the image and likeness of God be sought and considered in man himself. Man, therefore, was made in the image and likeness of God according to his mind, by which he surpasses irrational creatures: in the image according to memory, understanding, and love; in likeness according to innocence and justice, which naturally exist in the rational mind.

Or the image is considered in the knowledge of truth, and likeness in the love of virtue; or image in all the other respects, likeness in the essence, because the soul is both immortal and indivisible. Hence Augustine, volume 2, *On the Greatness of the Soul*, chapter 1: “The soul was made like God because God made it immortal and indissoluble.” Image, therefore, pertains to form; likeness to nature.

Thus man was made, according to the soul, in the image and likeness not of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit separately, but of the whole Trinity. Accordingly, man is said to be the image of God according to the soul because the image of God is in him. Just as both the panel and the painting on it are called an image, but because of the painting that is on it the panel too [Col. 0685] is called an image, so likewise, because of the image of the Trinity, even that in which the image is found is called by the name of image. (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 2, at the end.)

### That man is called image and “in the image,” whereas the Son is image, not “in the image”

5. Therefore man is called both image and “in the image”; but the Son is image, not “in the image,” because he is begotten and not created, equal and unlike in no respect. Man was created by God, not begotten; not equal through parity, but approaching him by a certain likeness. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 7, chapter 6, at the end:

> We read in Genesis: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” He said “Let us make” and “our” in the plural; and these must be understood from relative terms, so that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are understood to make man in the image of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, that man might subsist as the image of God. But because that image was not made altogether equal, as not having been born from him but created by him, it is so called image that it is also called “in the image”; for it is not equal by parity but approaches by a certain likeness. The Son, however, is image but not “in the image,” because he is equal to the Father. Man, therefore, is said to be “in the image” because of his unequal likeness. And “our” is said so that man may be understood as the image of the Trinity, not equal to the Trinity as the Son is equal to the Father.

Thus it has been shown in what respect man is like God: namely, according to the soul. Yet in his body he has a certain characteristic that indicates this, because his stature is upright. By this his body accords with the rational soul, since it is raised toward heaven. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 6, chapter 12; and *On Genesis against the Manichees*, book 1, chapter 17, at the end of the first volume.

## DISTINCTION XVII. ON THE CREATION OF THE SOUL: WHETHER IT WAS MADE FROM SOMETHING OR NOT; WHEN IT WAS MADE; AND WHAT GRACE IT HAD IN ITS CREATION

1. Here several questions are commonly raised concerning the soul’s origin: from what it was created, when it was created, and what grace it possessed in its creation. Just as man’s formation according to the body is described when it is said, “God formed man from the mud of the earth,” so the making of the same man according to the soul is described when it is added: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” God formed the body from the mud of the earth, into which he breathed a soul. Or, according to another text, “he blew” or “breathed upon.”

This does not mean that he breathed with a mouth, or formed the body with bodily hands; for God is Spirit and is not composed of bodily features. Therefore we must not think carnally that God formed a body with bodily hands, or breathed a soul with his mouth. Rather, he formed man’s body from the mud of earth by commanding and willing—that is, he willed and commanded by his Word that it should be so—and “breathed into his face the breath of life,” that is, he created the substance of the soul in which man might live, not from any bodily or spiritual material, but from nothing.

### The opinion of certain heretics who thought the soul to be from the substance of God  
*(Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 7, chapters 2 and 3)*

2. Certain heretics thought that God created the soul from his own substance, obstinately adhering to the words of Scripture which say “he breathed” or “breathed upon,” etc. “When a human being blows or breathes,” they say, “he emits breath from himself. Therefore, when God is said to have blown or breathed a breath into man’s face, he is understood to have emitted the human spirit from himself—that is, from his own substance.”

Those who say this do not understand that “he breathed upon” or “he blew” is said figuratively—that is, he made the breath of man, namely the soul. For to blow is to make breath, and to make breath is to make a soul. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah, chapter 57: “I made every breath.” Therefore those who think the soul is a part of God must not be heard. For if this were so, it could be deceived neither by itself nor by another; nor could it be compelled either to do or to suffer evil; nor could it be changed for better or worse. The breath by which God gave life to man was therefore made by God, not from God, nor [Col. 0686] from any material, but from nothing.

### When the soul was made: whether before the body, in the body, or outside the body  
*(Augustine, book 7, chapters 25 and 27)*

3. But whether the soul was made before the body, in the body, or outside the body is a difficult question even among learned persons. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, teaches that the soul was created without a body together with the angels, and afterward came to the body. It was not compelled to become embodied, but naturally willed this—that is, it was so created as to will it, just as it is natural to us to will to live. But to will to live badly belongs not to nature but to a perverse will.

Others say that the soul of the first man was created in the body, explaining those words thus: “He breathed into his face the breath of life,” that is, he created the soul in the body, so that it might animate the whole body. Yet the face is specifically mentioned because this part is furnished with senses for beholding higher things. But whatever may be thought concerning the soul of the first man, concerning other souls it must be held with complete certainty that they are created in the body; for God infuses them by creating, and creates them by infusing. It must also be said that that soul was not created so as to foreknow whether its future action would be righteous or unrighteous. (*Ibid.*, chapter 26.)

### At what age God made man  
*(Augustine, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, book 6, chapters 13 and 14)*

4. It is also commonly asked whether God made man suddenly in mature adulthood, or by completing him and increasing his ages, as he now forms him in the womb of his mother. Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis, says that Adam was immediately made in mature adulthood. This occurred according to higher, not lower, causes—that is, according to the will and power of God, which he did not bind to the kinds of nature. In this manner Moses’ rod too was changed into a serpent.

Such things do not occur contrary to nature except for us, to whom another course of nature has become known; for God, however, what he does is nature. Therefore God did not do this contrary to his own ordering. For in the first condition of created causes there was the possibility that man might be made in this way, though there was no necessity that he be made in this way. For this was not in the condition of the creature, but in the good pleasure of the Creator, whose will is necessity. For whatever he wills and foreknows will necessarily come to pass.

Many things will occur according to lower causes, however, which will not occur in God’s foreknowledge. But if they are to occur otherwise there, they will rather occur as they are there, where he who cannot be deceived foreknows them. Thus, if Adam was made not according to lower causes—because it was not in the seminal causes of things that he should be made in this way—but according to higher causes, then this was not an operation against nature, because in the natural causes of things there was the possibility that he might be made in this way. (*The same book*, chapter 17.)

### That man was created outside Paradise and placed in Paradise; and why this was done

5. God took man thus formed, as Scripture teaches in Genesis 2, and placed him in the Paradise of delight, which he had planted from the beginning. By these words Moses plainly indicates that man was created outside Paradise and afterward placed in Paradise. This is said to have been done because man was not to remain there; or so that this might be attributed not to nature but to grace.

Paradise is understood as a local and bodily place in which man was placed. For there are three general opinions concerning Paradise: one of those who wish it to be understood only bodily; another of those who wish it to be understood only spiritually; and a third of those who understand Paradise in both ways. I confess that the third pleases me: that man was placed in a bodily Paradise, which may be understood to have been planted from that beginning when, after the waters had been removed, God commanded the whole earth to produce plants and trees.

Although it bears a figure of the present Church or of the future Church, it must nevertheless be understood literally as a most delightful place, rich in fruitful trees, vast, and made fertile by a great spring. What we call “from the beginning,” the old translation calls “toward the East.” Hence they maintain that Paradise is in the eastern region, separated from the lands inhabited by human beings by a great intervening expanse of sea or land, and situated on high, extending as far as the lunar sphere, so that not even the waters of the Flood reached it. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 8, chapter 1.

### On the trees of Paradise, among which were the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil

[Col. 0687]

6. In this paradise there were trees of various kinds, among which one was called the tree of life, and another the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The tree of life, as Bede and Strabo teach, was so called because it had divinely received this power: whoever ate of its fruit would have his body strengthened in stable health and perpetual soundness, and would not decline or fall into deterioration through sickness or the weakness of age. But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil received this name not from its nature, but from the event that followed afterward. For that tree was not evil; rather, it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, after the prohibition, transgression was to occur in connection with it, through which man would learn by experience what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Therefore the name was not imposed because of the fruit growing from it, but because of the event that followed the transgression.

Before touching this tree, man knew good and evil: good through prudence and experience, but evil through prudence alone. He also came to know evil by experience when he unlawfully took the forbidden tree, because through experiencing evil he learned what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. If, however, the first parents had been obedient and had not sinned against the command, the tree would nevertheless still have been called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, since this would have resulted from touching it if it had been unlawfully taken. Thus he was forbidden a tree which was not evil, so that keeping the command itself might be good for him and transgression evil.

Nor can the magnitude of disobedience’s evil be better considered than in this way: namely, when a man is understood to have become guilty because he touched a thing while forbidden to do so—a thing which, if he had touched it without prohibition, would neither have made him sin nor caused him to suffer punishment. If you touch a poisonous herb after being forbidden, punishment follows; and if no one had forbidden it, the same consequence would follow. Likewise, a thing is forbidden whose touching harms not only the person touching it, but also the person who forbids it, such as another person’s money: it is forbidden because it is harmful to the person who forbids it. But when something is touched which harms neither the toucher if it is not forbidden, nor anyone else if it is touched, and is nevertheless forbidden, this is so that the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience may be displayed in themselves. Thus the first man incurred punishment through a thing that was good, in order to show that punishment comes not from an evil thing but from disobedience, just as the palm of victory comes from obedience. (Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 8, chapter 6, at the end; and the same book, chapter 3.)

## DISTINCTION XVIII. ON THE FORMATION OF WOMAN

1. In the same paradise God also formed woman from the substance of man. For after the paradise had been planted, man placed in it, and all the animals brought to him and designated by their names, Scripture adds, Genesis 2: “God cast a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, He took one of his ribs and formed it into a woman.”

### Why He created man first and afterward woman from man, rather than both at once

2. Here it must be considered why He did not create man and woman together, as He did the angels, but first man and then woman from man. This was so that there might be one source of the human race, whereby both the pride of the devil might be confounded and human humility exalted by likeness to God. For the devil had desired to be a principle other than God. Therefore, in order that his pride might be crushed, man received as a gift what the devil perversely sought to seize but could not obtain. And in this the image of God appeared in man: just as God is the originating principle of creation for all things, so man is the originating principle of generation for all human beings. God also willed that all should be from one man, so that, knowing that they all came from one, they might love one another as though they were one.

### Why woman was formed from the man’s side, rather than another part of his body

3. Although woman was made from man for these reasons, she was formed not from just any part of the man’s body, but from his side, in order to show that she was created for the fellowship of love; lest, if she had been made from his head, she might seem to be set above the man in dominion, or, if from his feet, to be subjected to slavery. Therefore, since she was prepared for man neither as mistress nor as servant, but as companion, she was to be brought forth neither from his head nor from his feet, but from his side, so that he might recognize that she was to be placed beside him, whom he had learned was taken from his own side. [Col. 0688] (Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 9, chapter 13.)

### Why the rib was taken from him while sleeping rather than awake

4. Not without reason was the rib, from which woman was formed as an aid to man in generation, taken from the man while he slept rather than while he was awake. This was to show that he felt no pain in it, and at the same time to display the marvelous work of divine power, which opened the side of the sleeping man without rousing him from the repose of sleep. In this work, too, the sacrament of Christ and the Church was prefigured, according to Ephesians 5. For as woman was formed from the side of the sleeping man, so the Church came forth from the sacraments which flowed from Christ’s side as He slept on the cross—namely, blood and water—by which we are redeemed from punishments and washed from sins.

### That woman was made from that rib, without an extraneous addition, by God’s power, as the five loaves were multiplied in themselves

5. It is also customary to ask whether woman was made from that rib without the addition of any extraneous matter; this has not pleased some. Yet if God had added external material to complete the woman’s body, that addition would have been greater than the rib itself; and so woman ought rather to be said to have been made from that added material than from the rib itself, from which she would have received more parts of her substance. It remains, then, that the woman’s body must be said to have been made from the substance of that rib alone, without any external addition, multiplied within itself by divine power. This was indeed the same miracle by which, later, five thousand men were fed from five loaves multiplied by Jesus through a heavenly blessing.

It must also be known that although the formation of woman took place through the ministry of angels, the power of creation is not thereby to be attributed to them. For angels cannot create any nature; therefore neither can they form a rib into a woman, nor supply flesh in the place of the rib. This is not because they do nothing toward the creation of something, but because they are not therefore creators, any more than farmers are creators of crops or trees. God alone—that is, the Trinity—is Creator. Thus woman was made by God, even if the rib was ministered by angels.

### Whether woman was made thus according to higher or lower causes; that is, whether the seminal principle contained this result—that she should be made thus—or only the possibility that she might be made thus, while the cause of her actually being made thus was in God alone

(Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 9, chapter 15, and the same book, chapter 1.)

6. But it is asked whether the principle which God created together with the first works contained the necessity that woman be made from man’s side according to that principle, or only the possibility that she might be so made. To understand this, one must know that the causes of all things are eternally in God. For that a human being, a horse, and things of this kind should be made in this way has been eternally in God’s power and disposition. These are called primordial causes because they are not preceded by other causes, but themselves precede other causes; they are causes of causes.

And although divine power, disposition, and will are one, and therefore the principal cause of all things is one, Augustine nevertheless speaks in the plural of the primordial causes of all things in God because of their diverse effects. He introduces the comparison of an artisan, in whose design lies the character which a chest will have. So too, in God the cause of every future thing preceded it.

In creatures, however, there are causes of some things, but not of all, as Augustine says. For God implanted seminal principles in things, according to which some things come forth from others: from this seed such a grain, from this tree such a fruit, and so forth. These too are called primordial causes, although less properly, because they have before them the eternal cause, which is properly and universally first. But they are called first with respect to certain things—namely, those which proceed from them. They are also called primordial because in the first establishment of things they were implanted by God in things. [Col. 0689]

And as creatures are changeable, so these causes too can be changed; but the cause which is in the unchangeable God cannot be changed.

### A most useful distinction among the causes of things: some are in God and in creatures, while others are in God alone

7. The causes of all things are in God; but the causes of some things are both in God and in creatures, while the causes of others are in God alone. The causes of the latter things are said to be hidden in God, because it is in the divine disposition that this or that should occur, though it is not contained in the creature’s seminal principle. Those things which occur according to a seminal cause are said to occur naturally, because the course of nature has become known to human beings. Other things occur beyond nature, and their causes are in God alone.

Augustine says, in *On Genesis*, book 9, chapter 18, at the end, that these are things which occur through grace, or which occur not naturally but wonderfully in order to signify such things. Among these he places the making of woman from the man’s rib, saying as follows in the same book, chapter 1: “That woman had necessarily to be made in this manner was not established in created things, but hidden in God. Every course of creation has natural laws. Above this natural course the Creator retains with Himself the power to make anything different from what its natural principle contains: namely, that a dry rod should suddenly bloom and bear fruit; that a barren woman should give birth in old age; that a she-ass should speak; and things of this sort. Yet He gave to natures that these things also might be possible from them, not that they might occur within their natural motion. Therefore God has hidden within Himself causes of certain future events which He did not implant in created things; and He fulfills them not by that work of providence through which natures subsist in being, but by that through which He governs them as He wills, having created them as He willed.” (Augustine, same book, chapter 18.)

Therefore, for all things which were wrought miraculously, rather than by the natural motion of things, in order to signify grace, the causes were hidden in God. One of these was that woman was made from the side of a sleeping man. The first establishment of things did not contain that woman should be made thus, but that she might be so made, lest God should be thought to do something by a changeable will contrary to the causes which He Himself voluntarily established.

### On the soul of woman: it is not from the soul of man, as some thought who said that souls are transmitted by propagation

(Augustine, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, book 10, chapter 1.)

8. Just as woman’s body was derived from man’s body, some supposed that her soul was propagated from man’s soul, and that all souls except the first arise by transmission, like bodies. Others thought that all souls were created together from the beginning. But the Catholic Church teaches neither that souls were made together nor that they are produced by transmission; rather, they are infused into bodies conceived and formed through intercourse, and are created in being infused.

Thus Augustine, in *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, tome 3, chapter 14, says that human souls are not among the intellectual natures created at the beginning, nor were they created all together, as Origen imagines; nor are they sown in bodies through intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latin writers affirm. “But we say that the body alone is conceived through the union of marriage, while only the Creator knows the creation of the soul; and that, by His judgment, the body is coagulated, compacted, and formed in the womb; and that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being, consisting of soul and body, may live in the womb and emerge from it alive, complete in human substance.”

Jerome also, in tome 8, condemns under the bond of anathema those who say that souls arise by propagation, citing the authority of the Prophet, Psalm 12: “Who fashioned their hearts individually.” “The Prophet sufficiently indicates,” he says, “that God does not make soul itself from soul, but creates souls individually from nothing.”

## DISTINCTION XIX. ON THE FIRST STATE OF MAN BEFORE SIN, NAMELY WHAT HE WAS LIKE IN BODY AND SOUL

1. Many questions are commonly asked concerning man’s first state before sin: what man was like before he sinned, both in body and soul; whether mortal or immortal, passible or impassible; concerning the end of the lower life and the transition to the higher; the manner in which children would have been propagated; and many other things which are not useless to know, even if they are sometimes sought from curiosity. But before pursuing matters concerning the quality of the soul, let us consider his bodily condition, the manner of the propagation of children, and certain other points.

Thus the first man, according to the nature of his earthly body, was in one respect immortal, because he was able not to die; and in another respect mortal, because he was able to die. For in that first state he had both the ability to die and the ability not to die. This was the first immortality of the human body: the ability not to die. In the second state, after sin, he had the ability to die and the inability not to die, because in that state there is a necessity of dying. In the third state he will have the ability not to die and the inability to die, because the impossibility of dying belongs to that state; this will be by grace, not by nature.

In the first state man’s body was animal—that is, requiring the nourishment of food. Therefore man is said to have been made into a living soul, not a spiritual one; that is, into a soul giving life to the body, which was still animal rather than spiritual, since it required food in order to live through the soul. He was made, therefore, into a living soul—that is, one giving life to the body, though by the support of food. At that time the body was mortal and immortal, because it could die and could not die.

After sin, however, it became dead, as the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin”—that is, it contains within itself the necessity of dying.
