But in the resurrection it will be spiritual, namely, agile and not needing food; and immortal, not as it was in the first state, namely capable of not dying, but also incapable of dying. Hence Augustine, on Genesis: “The Apostle says: ‘The body indeed is dead because of sin,’ and so forth. Before sin the body was formed from the mud of the earth as an animal body, not as the spiritual body with which we shall rise. For it will be renewed from its former state, not into the animal body that it was, but into something better—that is, spiritual—when this mortal body puts on immortality, into which Adam would have been changed had he not, by sinning, deserved the death of the animal body. The Apostle does not say, ‘The body is mortal because of sin,’ but ‘dead.’ For before sin it was mortal and immortal, because it could die and could not die. But ‘not being able to die’ is one thing, and ‘being able not to die’ another. Thus through sin it became not mortal, as it had been, but dead—which it would not have become had it not sinned. For this body is not animal as the first man’s body was, but is already worse, for it has the necessity of dying.” (Augustine, same book, chapter 24.)

Here Augustine plainly states that before sin man’s body was mortal and immortal, though not as it will be in the resurrection. On this same matter Bede says, on Genesis: “We must not believe that before sin bodies were dead as they are now. For the Apostle says, ‘The body is dead because of sin’; but although they were animal and not yet spiritual, they were nevertheless not dead—that is, not bodies which necessarily had to die.”

### Whether the immortality which man possessed before sin belonged to the condition of nature or was a benefit of grace

2. Here it is customary to ask: since the first man had a body mortal and immortal, did he possess both from the condition of the body’s nature? Or was one a benefit of grace—namely immortality, that is, the ability not to die? It may be said that he had one from the body’s nature, namely the ability to die; but the other, namely the ability not to die, was his from the tree of life—that is, from the gift of grace. Therefore Augustine, book 6, chapter 25, on Genesis, says: “In a certain sense man was created immortal; this was his from the tree of life, not from the condition of nature. He was mortal by the condition of the animal body, immortal through the Creator’s benefit. For he was not immortal in such a way that he could not die at all, as he will be only when he has become spiritual.”

He plainly says that man possessed the ability not to die not from nature but from the tree of life. On this account some say that unless he used that tree of life, he would not live forever, because he would sin. For he would sin if he did not use that tree, since he was commanded to eat from every tree of paradise except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Therefore, just as he sinned by eating what was forbidden, so too he would sin if he did not eat what was commanded.

### If he had not been commanded to eat from that tree, and used the other trees but not it, could he have avoided death?

3. But it is still asked: if he had not been commanded to eat from the tree of life, and used the others but did not eat from it, could he have avoided death? If he would live forever without using that tree, then the ability not to die was not his from that tree. But if he could not live forever, then it was his from that tree.

Some say that if he had not been commanded to eat from that tree, and used the other trees but did not eat from it, he would live forever. They thus explain Augustine’s statement above, “It was his from the tree of life, not from the condition of nature alone,” as though it meant that it was his not from nature alone, but also from that tree. Others, however, think that his ability not to die came from the tree of life, not from nature. For he is said to have been able not to die because he could use that tree, by eating from which he would not die.

### Augustine’s question: how man was made immortal

4. Concerning this immortality of man, and what it was like—[Note: [Col. 0691] On this see the *Ordinary Gloss* on Genesis 1, “Let us make man,” etc.]—Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 3, chapter 2, raises the question in this way: “It is asked how man was made immortal in contrast to the other living creatures, and how he received food in common with them. But the immortality of the flesh which we received in Adam is one thing, and that which we hope for in the resurrection through Christ is another. That man was made immortal so that he could not die if he did not sin, but would die if he sinned; whereas the children of the resurrection will no longer be able either to sin or to die. Our flesh will then not need the refreshment of food, because no deficiency will be possible. Adam’s flesh before sin was created immortal in such a way that, assisted by nourishment, it was free from death and pain. Thus human flesh was made immortal and incorruptible in such a way that it might preserve its immortality and incorruption through observing God’s commands. Included among these commands was that he should eat from the permitted trees and abstain from the forbidden one. By the food of these trees he would preserve the gifts of immortality, until, through bodily growth, he reached the age pleasing to the Creator; and, after the offspring had multiplied at God’s command, he would take from the tree of life, by which he would be made perfectly immortal and would no longer require the sustenance of food.”

### A summary statement of the meaning of the preceding words

5. By these words Augustine seems to teach that the flesh of the first man possessed in itself an immortality to be preserved through the nourishment of food until the time of its translation into a better state, when he would eat from the tree of life and become entirely immortal, so that he could not die.

### What seems to follow from the foregoing: man was in a certain manner immortal by the condition of his nature, but would not become wholly immortal unless he partook of the tree of life

6. Therefore some say that he had from nature an immortality by which he was able not to die, which could be preserved by eating the other trees but could not be brought to completion except by receiving the tree of life. Augustine seems to hold this view in *On Genesis*, book 8, chapter 5, when he says: “I add also that that tree supplied such food that the human body would be strengthened in stable health—not as from other food, but by a hidden infusion of healthfulness.” Here he seems to suggest that although the body could be sustained by other foods, through this food it would be strengthened in unfailing health.

From this it seems to follow that, just as man had in his nature a certain mortality—namely, an aptitude for dying—so he had in his nature a certain immortality, that is, an aptitude by which, aided by food, he could not die. But if he had persevered, [Col. 0692] the perfection of immortality would have been his from the tree of life. Those who maintain this view should carefully inquire how the earlier words of Augustine, in which he says that man was immortal by the tree of life, do not conflict with this position.

## DISTINCTION XX. ON THE MANNER OF THE PROCREATION OF CHILDREN IF THE FIRST PARENTS HAD NOT SINNED, AND WHAT SORT OF CHILDREN WOULD HAVE BEEN BORN

1. Next it must be considered how the first parents would have procreated children if they had not sinned, and what sort of children those children would have been. Some think that the first human beings could not have come together in paradise for the begetting of children except after sin, saying that intercourse cannot occur without corruption or stain. But before sin neither corruption nor stain could exist in man, since these followed from sin.

It must be said in reply that, if the first human beings had not sinned, they would have come together in paradise by bodily union without any sin or stain. There would have been an undefiled marriage-bed and intercourse without concupiscence. They would have governed the genital members as they did the rest, so that they would feel no illicit motion there; and just as we apply other bodily members to other things—for instance, the hand to the mouth—without the heat of lust, so they would have used the genital members without any prurience of the flesh. For this deadly sickness clung to the members of human beings as a consequence of sin.

Thus they would have begotten children in paradise through undefiled intercourse and without corruption. Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 3, chapters 10 and 3, says: “Why should we not believe that before sin the first human beings could have governed their genital members for procreation just as we use our other members in every activity without the prurience of pleasure? For it is not incredible that God made those bodies such that, had they not sinned, they would govern those members as they do their feet; neither would they sow seed with ardor nor give birth with pain. But after sin they deserved that motion which marriage regulates and continence restrains. For weakness prone to the ruin of shamefulness is received within the honorableness of marriage; and what is an office for the healthy is a remedy for the sick. Indeed, after their expulsion from paradise they came together and begot children; but in paradise they could have had honorable marriage and an undefiled bed, without the ardor of lust and without the labor of giving birth.”

### Why they did not have intercourse in paradise: two solutions

(Augustine, same book, chapter 4)

2. Why, then, did they not come together in paradise? Because immediately after woman’s creation the transgression occurred, and they were expelled from paradise. Or because God had not yet commanded them to come together, and divine authorization could be awaited where concupiscence did not press them. God had, however, given the command, because He foresaw their fall, from which human beings were to be propagated. Here you have an explicit account of the manner of the propagation of children.

### The end of that lower life: whether, after children were born, they were to be transferred by succession or all at once

3. Concerning the time when they would be transferred to the spiritual and heavenly life, Scripture hands down nothing certain. It is therefore uncertain whether, once children had been born and the full justice of human duty completed, the parents would be transferred to a better state—not by death but by some change—or whether the parents would remain in a certain state of life, using the tree of life until the children reached the same state, and then, when the number was completed, all would be transferred together to better things, so as to be like the holy angels in heaven.

Augustine discusses this ambiguously in *On Genesis*, book 8, chapter 4, saying: “The first human beings could have begotten children in paradise, not so that children would succeed parents who had died, but while the parents remained in a certain state and received vigor from the tree of life. Their children would be brought to the same state, until, when the number was complete, their animal bodies would pass without death into another quality, in which they would serve the ruling spirit altogether and live by the spirit alone, which gives life, without bodily food. Or the parents could yield place to their children, so that the number might be completed by succession; and, after they had begotten children and fulfilled the due order of human office, they would be transferred to better things, not by death but by some change.”

Here we have an account of man’s transition to better things, but it is left uncertain to us whether all would be transferred at once or by successive generations. [Col. 0693]

### What sort of children they would have begotten: whether they would possess mature bodily stature and the use of their members, as the first man did when created

4. If it is asked what sort of children man would have begotten if he had not sinned—namely, whether, just as the first man was immediately created complete in bodily nature and use of his members, his children also would have been complete from the very beginning of birth, able to walk, speak, and do everything—it may be answered that children had to be born small because of the need of the maternal womb. But whether, immediately after birth, they would have had mature stature and use of their limbs; or whether, while small and young, they could have exercised the functions of their members; or whether they would have acquired mature stature and use of their limbs over intervals of time in the manner that now occurs, we have no determination from authoritative sources.

### Augustine’s ambiguous words, though he seems to imply that even small children could use their members’ functions

5. On this question Augustine [Note: [Col. 0693] Book 1, *On the Baptism of Infants*, otherwise called *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, chapter 37, tome 7.] speaks ambiguously. “It moves us,” he says, “whether, if the first human beings had not sinned, they would have had children such as could use neither tongue, hands, nor feet. For perhaps, because of the need of the womb, it was necessary that children be born small. Yet although a rib is a small part of the body, He did not for that reason make the man’s wife small; hence the Creator’s omnipotence could also have made her children large immediately upon birth. But, leaving this aside, He could certainly have granted them what He granted many animals, whose young, though small, nevertheless run and follow their mother as soon as they are born. By contrast, a human being at birth has feet not fit even for walking, nor hands capable even of scratching; and although the breasts lie beside him, the newborn is more able to cry in hunger than to suck. This weakness of flesh suitably accords with the weakness of mind.”

These words seem to imply that even small children would have been capable of using their members’ functions.

### The not unreasonable opinion of some that children would have been born small and grown in stature and other respects over time as they do now, without this being attributable to defect

6. But since Augustine makes no assertion on these questions, some have not unreasonably thought that the children of the first parents would have been born small and thereafter, through intervals of time, would have acquired growth in stature and use of their limbs according to the same order by which we now see human birth governed. Thus they would have awaited the age for walking and speaking, as we do now. This, of course, would not be attributed to defect but to the condition of nature, just as they could not wholly abstain from food, though that too arose not from defect but from the condition of nature.

### An objection from those who seek to prove that they could have lived without food

7. The following objection is raised: If they had not sinned, they would not have died; but they would not have sinned if they had not eaten; therefore they could have lived without food. But, as we said above, they would have sinned not only if they ate from the forbidden tree, but also if they did not use the permitted ones, because they were commanded to refrain from that tree just as they were commanded to eat from the others. Moreover, they would have acted against natural reason, because they understood that they should eat from them, and naturally desired to do so.

Another objection is raised: Since hunger is a punishment for sin, if they had not sinned, they would not have experienced hunger; but without hunger eating would appear superfluous. Hence some think that before sin they had no need of food, because they could not become hungry if they had not sinned. To this it may be said that hunger truly is a deficiency and a punishment of sin. For it is an immoderate appetite for eating, to which man would not have been subject had he not sinned. Yet undoubtedly he would have sinned unless he forestalled this deficiency by food. For he had a natural and moderate appetite, which had to be satisfied in such a way that he did not experience the deficiency of hunger. [Col. 0694]

Therefore, just as it arose not from defect but from the condition of nature that before sin man needed food, so it would arise not from defect but from nature if the human condition, which in its beginning—that is, in the first parent—was initiated in perfection, should in subsequent propagation advance from smallness to greater things, so as to acquire over intervals of time growth in bodily stature and use of its members.

### Whether, as regards bodily stature, children would also have been born small in mental capacity, progressing over time in understanding and knowledge of truth; or whether they would have been perfect in these matters immediately upon birth

8. Since this opinion concerning the human body is neither absurd nor unsuitable, it is commonly asked whether the same should be thought concerning the soul’s understanding and knowledge of truth: namely, whether those born without sin would be imperfect in mental perception and understanding, advancing in these through time until perfection; or whether immediately upon being created they would receive perfection of understanding and knowledge.

Those who think that children born small would progress over time in bodily stature and use of their members do not deny that, at the beginning of birth, the same children would be imperfect in understanding and would advance through time in perception and knowledge until perfection.

### Some object against their opinion

9. Some object by saying: If they did not possess perfection of perception and understanding immediately after birth, ignorance would be in them; but ignorance is a punishment of sin. Yet those who say this have not considered carefully enough that not everyone who does not know something, or knows something less perfectly, is immediately to be called ignorant or said to be in ignorance. Ignorance is not so called except when a person does not know what ought to be known rather than left unknown. Such ignorance is a punishment of sin, when the mind is darkened by fault and so cannot know the things it ought to know.

### On man’s translation to a better state, and on two goods, one given here and the other promised

(Augustine, *On the Sacraments*, book 1, part 2, chapter 6)

10. Such was man’s condition before sin with respect to the body. From this state he was to be transferred, together with all his posterity, to a better and more worthy state, where he would enjoy the heavenly and eternal good prepared for him in heaven. For just as man is composed of a double nature, so from the beginning the Creator prepared two goods for him: one temporal, the other eternal; one visible, the other invisible; one for the flesh, the other for the spirit. And because what is animal comes first and what is spiritual afterward, He first gave the temporal and visible good; but He promised the invisible and eternal good, setting it forth as something to be sought by merits.

For preserving what He had given and meriting the other good which He had promised, He added a command of obedience to the natural reason implanted in the creation of the human soul, by which it could discern between good and evil. By observing this command man would not lose the gift and would obtain the promise, so that through merit he might come to the reward.

## DISTINCTION XXI. ON THE DEVIL’S ENVY, BY WHICH HE APPROACHED TO TEMPT MAN

1. Therefore, when the devil saw that man could ascend by obedience and humility to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride, he envied him. And because the devil had first fallen down through pride, through the zeal of envy he became Satan—that is, an adversary. Hence he tempted the woman, in whom he knew reason to be less vigorous than in the man. For his malice, timid in testing strength, attacked human nature in that part in which it appeared weaker, so that if perhaps he gained some advantage there, he might afterward approach more confidently to assault—or rather overthrow—the other part, which was stronger.

Therefore he first tested the woman while she was alone, so that in her he might first try the whole force of his temptation.

### Why he came in another form
2. But because he could not harm him by force, he turned to deceit, so that he might trip up by guile the human being whom he could not overcome by strength. Yet, lest his deceit be too evident, he did not come in his own appearance, lest he be openly recognized and thus repelled; and again, lest his deceit be too hidden—a deceit against which no precaution could be taken—and the human being seem at once to suffer an injury if God permitted him to be so circumvented that he could not guard against it, the devil was permitted indeed to come in another form, but in one in which his malice could be detected. Therefore, that he did not come in his own form was due to his own will; but that he came in a form suited to his malice was brought about by God. Thus he came to the human being in a serpent—though perhaps, if he had been permitted, he would have preferred to come in the form of a dove. But it was not fitting that the malignant spirit should make hateful to humankind that form in which the Holy Spirit was to appear. Therefore the devil was permitted to tempt only through a serpent, so that by what was outwardly present the woman might perceive the cunning of the tempter; for the devil was tempting through the serpent, in which he spoke.

Accordingly, the serpent is said to have been more cunning than all the animals of the earth because, as Augustine says, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 2, evil angels, though cast down by pride, are nevertheless by nature superior to all beasts because of the excellence of reason; although the serpent may be called most wise, not because it had a rational soul, but because of the devilish spirit. It is therefore no wonder if the devil, filling the serpent with his spirit, as he used to fill prophets, had made it the wisest of all beasts. Yet the devil did not choose it for tempting; rather, he tempted through whichever animal he was permitted to use. Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 1: “We must not suppose that the devil chose the serpent through which to tempt; rather, when he desired to deceive, he could do so only through whatever animal he was permitted to use. For the will to harm belongs to each being from itself, but the power belongs to God.”

The devil spoke through the unaware serpent as he speaks through the possessed or the frenzied. For he used the serpent as an instrument, moving its nature to utter the sounds and signs of words by which he might reveal his will. Thus the serpent neither understood words nor was made rational; nevertheless, it was called most cunning because of the devil’s craftiness. It spoke as Balaam’s ass spoke; but this was diabolical, whereas that was angelic, for good and evil angels work in similar ways. Here it is commonly asked why the woman was not horrified by the serpent. Because, knowing it to be a creature, she thought that it had received even the function of speech from God. (*Ibid.*, chapters 27 and 29.)

### On the manner of temptation

3. The temptation occurred in this manner. The proud enemy, standing before the woman, does not dare to proceed directly to words of persuasion, fearing detection; rather, he approaches her by a question, so that from her response he might gather how he could proceed in malice. “Why,” he says—Genesis 3—“did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman answered him: “We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die.”

In these words she gave the tempter an opening when she said, “lest perhaps we die.” Therefore the devil immediately said to the woman: “You shall not die at all; for God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” Observe the order and progress of human ruin. First God had said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death”; then the woman said: “Lest perhaps we die”; finally the serpent said: “You shall not die at all.” God affirmed it; the woman spoke it as though doubting; the devil denied it. Therefore she who doubted departed from the one affirming and drew near to the one denying.

### On the devil’s cunning: to persuade more easily, he removed the evil and doubled the promised good

4. In order fully to support his persuasion [Col. 0696]—that is, to persuade freely the evil he intended—he removed by denial the evil which the woman feared and added a counter-promise. Moreover, that his persuasion might be accepted more quickly, he doubled the promise. Advising one act of eating, he proposed two rewards: promising likeness to God and knowledge of good and evil. Here he tempted the human being in three ways: by gluttony, in the persuasion to eat, when he said, “on whatever day you eat”; by vain glory, in the promise of divinity, when he said, “you shall be like gods”; and by avarice, in the promise of knowledge, when he said, “knowing good and evil.”

Gluttony is an immoderate eagerness for food; vain glory is the love of one’s own excellence; avarice is an immoderate desire to possess, which concerns not only money but also eminence and knowledge, when exaltation is sought beyond measure.

### On the two kinds of temptation

5. Moreover, it should be known that there are two kinds of temptation: inner and outer. Outer temptation occurs when evil is visibly suggested to us from without by a word or some sign, so that the person to whom it is made may turn toward consenting to sin; and such temptation comes only from the adversary. Inner temptation occurs when evil is invisibly suggested to us within; and this temptation sometimes comes from the enemy, sometimes from the flesh. For the devil too invisibly suggests evils, and from the corruption of the flesh there arises an unlawful movement and a slight titillation.

Therefore temptation arising from the flesh does not occur without sin; but temptation from the enemy, unless consent is given to it, involves no sin, but is material for the exercise of virtue. For the inner temptation of the flesh is conquered with greater difficulty, because the attacker within is strengthened against us from what is our own. Thus the man who fell when assailed by outer temptation alone deserved a punishment so much the graver as he had been overthrown by a lighter impulse. Nevertheless, because he had some, though slight, occasion for falling, he could through grace be helped toward pardon, so that he who had fallen through another might be raised through another. Therefore, one who had an instigator to evil did not unjustly have a restorer to good.

But because the devil sinned without anyone’s temptation, he ought not to be helped by another in order to rise, nor could he rise by himself; and therefore his sin was beyond remedy. Human sin, however, as it had its beginning through another, so fittingly had its remedy through another.

### Why man, rather than the angel, was redeemed

6. Furthermore, angelic nature was not redeemed because it had not wholly perished, but had in part remained steadfast. Human nature, however, had wholly perished; and therefore, lest it perish utterly, it was redeemed in part, so that the angelic loss might thereby be made good. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 29:

> It pleased the Creator and Governor of the universe that, because not the entire multitude of angels had perished by abandoning God, that part which had perished should remain in perpetual perdition, while that part which had remained with God when the other abandoned him should rejoice in the certainty of its everlasting happiness. But the rational creature that existed in human beings, because it had wholly perished in sins and punishments, could be restored in part, so that what that fall had diminished might be supplied to the fellowship of angels. For this has been promised to the saints: that they shall be equal to the angels of God.

### That the commandment was not given to the man alone  
*(Augustine, On Genesis, book 8, chapter 16)*

7. It must also be noted that the commandment does not seem to have been given to the man alone, since the woman herself testifies that it was commanded to her as well, saying, “God commanded us,” and so forth. Yet above it is read that, before the woman was made, God said to the man: “Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” He did not say, “Do not eat,” in the plural. Perhaps because he was going to make the woman from the man, he thus gave the command so that the commandment might pass through the man to the woman; for the woman, who was subject to the man, ought to receive the divine command only through the mediation of the man. Hence the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 14: “If women wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home.”

If it is asked how those who had not learned by growing up among speakers or by instruction could speak or understand someone speaking, we answer [Col. 0697] that God had made them such that they could speak and could learn from others, if there were others. Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 8, chapter 16, at the end.

## DISTINCTION XXII. ON THE ORIGIN OF THAT SIN

1. Here it seems necessary to investigate carefully what was the origin and root of that sin. Some think that a certain self-exaltation preceded in the human mind, by which he consented to the devil’s suggestion. Augustine seems to intimate this in *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 5, saying:

> We must not suppose that the human being would have been cast down unless a certain self-exaltation requiring restraint had first existed in him, so that through the humility of sin he might learn how falsely he had presumed concerning himself, and that nature is not in a good condition if it departs from the One who made it.

Again, in the same work, book 11, chapter 30:

> How could the woman have believed the tempter’s words, that she had been forbidden something good and useful, unless there existed in her mind that love of her own power and proud presumption concerning herself, which had to be exposed or destroyed through temptation? Finally, not content with the serpent’s persuasion, she looked upon the tree as good for eating and beautiful to behold; and, not believing that she could die from it, she perhaps thought that God had said this for the sake of some symbolic meaning. Therefore she ate, and gave to her husband also—perhaps with some persuasion, which Scripture leaves to be understood. Or perhaps persuasion was unnecessary, since the man did not see her dead after taking that food.

Therefore, just as the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent, so neither was he permitted to tempt the man except through the woman; so that, as God’s command passed through the man to the woman, the devil’s temptation might pass through the woman to the man. But in the woman, who was rational, he did not himself speak as in the serpent; rather, it was his persuasion—although inwardly he assisted it by prompting—which he carried out outwardly through the serpent (Augustine, book 1, dictum 2, chapter 27).

From the foregoing, the manner and progress of temptation are indicated; and likewise what we said above appears to be suggested, namely, that some self-exaltation and presumption in the human mind preceded the temptation.

### Objection against those who say that self-exaltation preceded in the mind

2. But if this was so, then the human being did not first sin through another’s suggestion, since authority teaches that the devil’s sin is incurable because he fell not through suggestion but through his own pride, whereas the human being’s sin is curable because he fell not by himself but through another, and therefore could rise through another.

Accordingly, Augustine’s foregoing words call for a devout and careful reader. We can soundly understand them as follows: the human being would not have been cast down into the act of that sin—namely, into eating the forbidden tree and, through the devil’s temptation, into these miseries—unless a self-exaltation needing restraint had preceded, not indeed the temptation, but the sinful deed. For the sequence was this: in tempting, the devil said, “If you eat, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” On hearing this, a certain self-exaltation and love of her own power immediately crept into the woman’s mind. From this it pleased her to do what the devil advised, and she indeed did it.

Therefore she sinned through suggestion, because temptation preceded, from which self-exaltation arose in her mind; this was followed by the sin in deed and by the punishment of sin.

### What the woman’s self-exaltation was

3. Such self-exaltation certainly existed in the woman’s mind: she believed and wished to possess likeness to God with a certain equality, thinking true what the devil said. Therefore Augustine especially mentions the woman, saying: “How could the woman believe the devil unless proud presumption concerning herself existed in her mind?” And what follows there—namely, “which had to be exposed or destroyed through temptation”—must be referred to the woman, so that it is understood that the woman, not the self-exaltation, was to be exposed or destroyed through temptation, and so forth.

### What the man’s self-exaltation was: whether he believed and wished what the woman did

4. It is commonly asked whether such self-exaltation and love of one’s own power existed in the man as in the woman. We answer that Adam was not deceived in the manner [Col. 0698] in which the woman was. For he did not think true what the devil suggested. Yet he may be believed to have been deceived in that he thought the offense venial when it was deadly. But he was neither deceived first nor deceived in the same matter as the woman—namely, so as to believe that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because, if they touched it, they would become like gods.

Nevertheless, some self-exaltation could have existed in his mind immediately after the temptation, from which he wished to try the forbidden tree when he did not see the woman dead after she had taken that food. Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 42:

> Although the Apostle shows that Adam was a transgressor, saying, Romans 5, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” he nevertheless denies that he was deceived when he says, 1 Timothy 2, “Adam was not deceived, but the woman.” Thus, when questioned, he did not say, “The woman deceived me,” but, “She gave to me, and I ate.” But the woman said, “The serpent deceived me.” The Apostle properly called that deception through which what was being urged, though false, was thought true: namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods—as though he, who had made them human beings, begrudged them divinity. Yet, even if some desire to make trial of it stirred the man because of a self-exaltation of mind which could not be hidden from God, when he saw that the woman had not died after taking that food, I do not think that he, if he was already endowed with a spiritual mind, believed in any way what the devil suggested.

(*Same book and chapter.*)

### Which sinned more: Adam or Eve?

5. From this it can plainly be perceived which of them sinned more, Adam or Eve. The woman seems to have sinned more, for she wished to usurp equality with divinity and, raised up by excessive presumption, believed that it would come to pass. Adam, however, did not believe this; and he thought of repentance and God’s mercy when, complying with his wife, he consented to her persuasion, unwilling to grieve her or leave her estranged from himself lest she perish, judging the offense to be venial rather than mortal.

Hence Augustine, in the same book and chapter:

> The Apostle says, “Adam was not deceived.” This can certainly be understood as meaning that he was not deceived first, or in the same matter as the woman: namely, so as to believe true the words, “You shall be like gods.” But he thought that both could occur: that he might comply with his wife and obtain pardon through repentance. Therefore he sinned less, because he thought of repentance and God’s mercy. For after the deceived woman ate and gave him some so that they might eat together, he did not wish to grieve her, whom he believed would waste away without his consolation and, being utterly estranged from him, perish; not because he was overcome by carnal lust, which he had not yet experienced, but through a certain friendly goodwill. It often happens through this that God is offended lest a friend be offended—something which the just outcome of the divine sentence showed he ought not to have done. Thus he too was deceived in another sense. For, being inexperienced in divine severity, he could be mistaken in thinking the offense venial; but I do not think that he could in any way have been deceived by that serpentine deception through which the woman was deceived.

From this it is understood that the woman sinned more, since in her was the presumption of greater swelling pride; she also sinned against herself, her neighbor, and God, whereas the man sinned only against himself and God. It is further inferred that the woman sinned more because she was punished more severely; to her it was said: “In pain you shall bear children,” Genesis 3, and so forth.

### What seems to oppose the foregoing view

6. But Augustine appears to say the contrary in *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 1, concerning the man and woman excusing their sin:

> Adam said, “The woman whom you gave me gave me from the tree, and I ate”; he does not say, “I sinned.” For pride has the ugliness of shame, not the humility of confession. Nor does the woman confess her sin; rather, she refers it to another, saying, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” They differed in sex, but were alike in haughtiness.

Here Augustine says that the woman had the same haughtiness as the man; therefore they were equally proud and sinned equally.

This may be resolved by saying that each had equal haughtiness in excusing the sin, and also in eating the forbidden tree; but their haughtiness was unequal—and much greater in the woman—in that she believed and wished to be like God, which the man did not. Yet it is nevertheless read of the man also that he wished to be like God. For Augustine says, commenting on Psalm 68: “Then I repaid what I had not seized”: “Adam and Eve seized, presuming upon divinity as did the devil; they wished to seize divinity and lost happiness.” Again, commenting on the words, “O God, who is like you?”: “Whoever wishes by himself to be as God perversely wishes to be like God: as the devil, who refused to be under him; and the human being, who as a servant refused to be held under the commandment, but wished, as it were, to be like God with no one ruling him.” Again, in volume 8, on the passage of the Epistle, “He did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized”: “For he did not usurp what was not his own, as the devil and the first human being did.”

### The view of some: Adam desired to be like God, but did not believe it possible

7. Therefore some think that Adam too desired to be like God, though he did not believe that this could happen; and therefore he knew that what the devil promised was false. And although he coveted equality with divinity, he did not burn with desire to the same degree, nor was he moved by such great ambition as the woman, who thought it possible and therefore was more proud in desiring it. Perhaps some momentary impulse of ambition moved the man, but not so that he thought it would be true or possible.

Others think that Adam is said to have wished this because the woman, who was taken from him, wished it. For just as, they say, sin is said to have entered the world through one man—that is, through human nature—although the woman sinned before the man, because it entered through the woman who was made from the man; or rather, it is said to have entered through the man because, even if the woman had sinned, the human race would by no means have perished corrupted by sins if the man had not sinned. Therefore the man sinned less than the woman.

### Objection to the claim that the man sinned less

8. But the following objection is commonly made: as Isidore says in *On the Highest Good*, book 2, chapter 17, sin is committed in three ways—through ignorance, weakness, and deliberate intent (*industria*). It is more serious to sin through weakness than through ignorance, and more serious through deliberate intent than through weakness. Eve, however, seems to have sinned through ignorance because she was deceived; Adam, on the other hand, through deliberate intent, because he was not deceived, as the Apostle says.

To this we answer that, although Eve sinned through ignorance in this respect, that she thought true what the devil advised, nevertheless she knew that this was God’s command and that it was sinful to act against it. Therefore she could not be excused from sin by ignorance.

### That one kind of ignorance excuses and another does not

9. For there is an ignorance which excuses the sinner, and an ignorance of such a kind as does not excuse. There is vincible ignorance and invincible ignorance. Every excuse is removed where the commandment is not unknown.

### On the threefold ignorance that excuses and that which does not

10. There is a threefold ignorance: that of those who do not wish to know although they can, which does not excuse, because it is itself sin; that of those who wish to know but cannot, which excuses and is a punishment of sin, not sin; and that of those who simply do not know, neither refusing nor intending to know, which fully excuses no one, though perhaps it results in a lesser punishment.

Hence Augustine, *To Valentinus* [Note: [Col. 0699] Volume 7, *On Nature and Grace, against the Pelagians*, chapter 17]:

> Excuse is taken away from those who know God’s commandments—the excuse which human beings commonly derive from ignorance. And although it is more serious to sin knowingly than unknowingly, we should not therefore flee into the darkness of ignorance, so that anyone may seek excuse in it. For not to know is one thing; not to wish to know is another. In those who refused to understand, ignorance itself is sin; but in those who could not understand, it is the punishment of sin. But the ignorance which belongs not to those who refuse to know, but to those who simply do not know, excuses no one in such a way that he does not burn in eternal fire [Col. 0700], though perhaps in such a way that he burns less.

Therefore the woman had no excuse from ignorance, since she both knew the commandment and did not fail to know that acting otherwise was sinful. (Volume 7, chapter 3.)

### From what the consent to that sin proceeded, when human nature was uncorrupted

11. It is also commonly asked: since human nature was without fault, from what did consent to evil proceed? It may be answered that it proceeded from the free choice of one’s own will. For the cause of becoming worse existed both in another and in the person himself: in another, because it was in the devil who persuaded; in the person himself, because he consented by the will of free choice. And since free choice is good, that evil consent proceeded from a thing that was good; and thus evil flowed from good.

We shall treat this more fully in what follows, when we investigate the origin of evil and in what thing it comes to exist.

### Whether the will preceded that sin

12. But if it is asked whether a will preceded that sin, we say that the sin consisted both in the will and in the act. The will preceded the act, but no other evil human will preceded that will itself. From the devil’s persuasion and the human being’s choice there arose that evil will by which he abandoned justice and began iniquity; and that will itself was iniquity.

## DISTINCTION XXIII. WHY GOD PERMITTED THE HUMAN BEING TO BE TEMPTED, THOUGH HE KNEW THAT HE WOULD FALL  
*(Augustine, On Genesis, book 11, chapters 4 and 9)*

1. Furthermore, it is commonly asked why God permitted the human being to be tempted when he foreknew that he would be deceived. But it would not be praiseworthy for a human being to be able to live well merely because no one urged him to live badly, since he had in his nature the ability, and in his power the capacity, not to consent to one who urged him, with God’s help. And it is more glorious not to consent than to be unable to be tempted.

Some also object: “Why did God create those whom he foreknew would be evil?” Because he foresaw what good he would make from their evils. For he made them in such a way as to leave them the means of doing something; and if they did anything blameworthy, they would find him working praiseworthily from them. They have their evil will from themselves, but from him a good nature and a just punishment.

It is therefore vainly said: “God ought not to have created those whom he foreknew would be evil.” For he knew that they would benefit the good and would justly be punished for their evil will. They add that he ought to make a human being such that he would not wish to sin at all. We grant indeed that a nature which would not wish to sin at all is better. Let them also grant that the nature which was made such that it could avoid sin if it wished is not evil, and that it is justly punished when it sins by will rather than necessity. Therefore, since this nature is good and that one better, why should he not make both, so that he might be more abundantly praised for both? The latter is the nature of holy angels, the former that of human beings.

Again, they say: “If God willed it, those persons too would be good.” We grant this as well; but he preferred that they should be what they themselves willed: the good not without fruit, and the evil not without punishment. Again, they say: “God could turn their will to good, because he is omnipotent.” Indeed he could. Why did he not do it? Because he did not will it. Why did he not will it? He himself knows. We ought not to be wise beyond what is proper (same book, chapter 7).

### What man was like in respect of the soul, and concerning human knowledge before sin

2. In respect of the soul, the human being was rational, possessing discernment of good and evil. It is also reasonably thought that, immediately upon being created, he received knowledge of created things and knowledge of truth such as suited his original perfection; and that he did not advance to it through study or some instruction over intervals of time, but received it from the beginning of his creation by divine gift. (*Same book*, chapter 10.)

### That before the fall man had threefold knowledge: of things made for his sake, of the Creator, and of himself

3. The first human being before the fall was endowed with threefold knowledge: namely, of things made for his sake, [Col. 0701] of the Creator, and of himself. That the human being received knowledge of things is clear from the fact that it was neither the Creator himself nor any angel, but the human being, who gave names to all living creatures; thus it was shown that the human being himself possessed knowledge of each one.

God gave him both knowledge and foresight of all things created for him and to be governed and ordered by him, and entrusted their care to him because, as the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 9: “God does not care for oxen.” God entrusted to the human being care and providence for these and other animals, so that they might be subjected to his dominion and governed by his reason; so that he might know how to provide what was necessary for those from whom he was to receive benefit. The human being did not lose this knowledge by sinning, any more than he lost the knowledge by which the necessities of the body were provided. Therefore Scripture does not instruct the human being about such matters, but about the knowledge of the soul which he lost by sinning.

### On knowledge of the Creator

4. The first human being is also believed to have possessed knowledge of the Creator. For he knew by whom he had been created, not by that mode of knowing which is acquired merely through hearing, in which an absent God is sought by believers, but by a certain inward inspiration through which he contemplated God’s presence. Yet he did not know him as excellently as the saints will see him after this life, nor as enigmatically as we see in this life.

### On self-knowledge

5. Furthermore, that same human being seems to have received such knowledge of himself that he did not fail to know what he owed to one above him, to one equal to him, and to one below him. He also understood his own condition and rank: what sort of being he had been made, how he ought to conduct himself, what he ought to do, and what he ought to avoid. If he had not possessed knowledge of these matters, he would not have been guilty of transgression, nor would he have known himself.

### Whether man foreknew the things that would happen to him

6. But if it is asked whether the human being had knowledge of things that were going to happen to him—that is, whether he foresaw his own fall and likewise foreknew the good things he would have possessed had he remained in obedience—it may be answered that he was commanded more concerning what was to be done than he was shown concerning what would happen. For he received knowledge and a command concerning the things to be done, but did not have foreknowledge of things to come. Therefore the human being did not foreknow his fall, as we have also said concerning the angel. Augustine affirms this in *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 17, using the reasoning we set out above. Let this be enough concerning human knowledge as it pertains to the first state.

## DISTINCTION XXIV. ON HUMAN GRACE AND POWER BEFORE THE FALL

1. We must now carefully investigate what grace or power the human being had before the fall, and whether through it he could stand or not. It should therefore be known that, as we said concerning the angels, the human being was given in creation the help of grace, and was granted a power by which he could stand—that is, not depart from what he had received. But he could not make such progress that, by the grace of creation without another grace, he could merit salvation.

By that help of the grace of creation he could indeed resist evil, but he could not bring good to completion. Yet in a certain manner he could live well through it, since he could live without sin; but without another assistance of grace he could not live spiritually, so as to merit eternal life. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 107:

> If the human being was made upright, so that he could remain in that uprightness, not without divine help, and could become perverse by his own choice, whichever he chose, God’s will would be done either by him or concerning him. And because he preferred to do his own will rather than God’s, God’s will was done concerning him.

Again, in the same work:

> The human being first had to be made such that he could will both good and evil: not without result if good, and not without punishment if evil.

Likewise Augustine, volume 7, in *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 10, chapter 105, and chapter 11 at the end, says:

> If this help had been lacking to either angel or human being when they were first made, since their nature was not made such that it could remain if it wished without divine help, they would certainly not have fallen through their own fault; for the help without which they could not remain would have been absent.

Again, in the same book and chapter:

> God had given the human being a good will, for in that will he had made him upright; he had given help without which he could not remain in it if he wished, and through which he could remain. Yet he left it to his own choice whether he would will this.

Again, in the same work: “He had received the ability, if he willed, but he did not have the willing by which he could do so; for if he had had it, he would have persevered.”

These testimonies clearly show that the human being received uprightness and a good will in creation, together with help by which he could stand; otherwise he would not appear to have fallen through his own fault. (*Same book and chapter.*)

### What was that uprightness and goodness of will in which he was created?

2. But how did the human being possess an upright and good will if he could not merit life through it? Because at that time he willed nothing evil by it, and for a time he willed to stand, though not perseveringly; and therefore the human will was then upright and good.

### Objection to the claim that man could not make progress

3. Against our statement that the human being could not make progress or merit by the grace of creation, the following objection is commonly made: by the help of the grace of creation he could remain in the good which he had received. Therefore he could resist temptation. But to resist temptations and evil suggestions is merit and a good worthy of reward; and every meritorious good is progress. Therefore by the grace of creation he could make progress without the addition of another grace.

We answer that resisting evil and not consenting to temptation would not have constituted merit for him, even if he had not consented, because nothing in him impelled him toward evil. Similarly, it was not merit for the angels who did not fall that they stood—that is, did not fall. For us, however, it is sometimes merit if we do not do evil but resist it, precisely where there is a cause that moves us to do it, because through the corruption of sin our steps are inclined to fall. But where no cause intervenes that impels us toward evil, we do not merit by turning away from it. For turning away from evil always avoids punishment, but does not always merit the crown.

### On the help given to man in creation, by which he could stand

4. Here we must consider what was that help given to the human being in creation, by which he could remain if he willed. It was certainly freedom of choice, immune from every stain and corruption, together with uprightness of will and the integrity and vigor of all the soul’s natural powers.

### On free choice

5. True free choice is the capacity of reason and will by which good is chosen with grace assisting, or evil with that same grace withdrawing. It is called “free” with respect to the will, which can be bent toward either alternative; but “choice” (*arbitrium*) with respect to reason, to which that capacity or power belongs, and whose function is to distinguish between good and evil. Sometimes, possessing discernment of good and evil, it chooses what is evil; sometimes it chooses what is good. But it does not choose what is good unless aided by grace; evil, however, it chooses by itself.

For there is in the rational soul a natural will by which it naturally wills good, although weakly and faintly unless grace helps it. When grace comes, it helps and raises the will so that it may effectively will good. By itself, however, it can effectively will evil. Therefore that power of the rational soul by which it can will good or evil, while discerning both, is called free choice. Brute animals do not possess it because they lack reason; nevertheless, they possess sensation and the appetite of sensuality.

### On sensuality
6. For sensuality is a certain lower power of the soul, from which arises the movement directed toward the bodily senses and the appetite for things pertaining to the body. Reason, however, is the higher power of the soul, which, so to speak, has two parts or functions, a higher and a lower. [Col. 0703] In its higher part it attends to beholding or consulting things above; in its lower part, it attends to the ordering of temporal things. Whatever, then, occurs in our soul, upon consideration, that is not shared with beasts pertains to reason. But whatever you find in it shared with animals pertains to sensuality. And where, as we proceed step by step in considering the parts of the soul, something first occurs that is not shared with beasts, there reason begins.

Augustine teaches this in Book 12 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 1, saying:

> Let us see where there is, as it were, a boundary between the outer and inner human being. Whatever we have in the mind in common with cattle is rightly said to belong to the outer human being. For not only the body is reckoned the outer human being, but also a certain life joined to it, by which the bodily frame and all the senses flourish, with which one is equipped for perceiving external things. Therefore, as we ascend inward by certain steps of consideration through the parts of the soul, where something begins to occur which is not shared by us with beasts, there reason begins, where the inner human being can now be recognized. (*ibid.*, ch. 8)

But the higher part of reason clings to beholding or consulting eternal reasons; the lower portion turns aside to governing temporal things. That attention of reason by which we contemplate eternal things is reckoned as wisdom; whereas that by which we make good use of temporal things is reckoned as knowledge (*same book*, ch. 4). Yet when we discuss the nature of the human mind, we discuss one thing, and we do not divide it into these two things which we have mentioned except according to their functions. The carnal or sensual movement of the soul, which is directed toward bodily senses, is common to us and to animals; it is separated from the reason of wisdom, but is adjacent to the reason of knowledge (*same book*, ch. 12).

### That the order of sinning or falling in us is such as it was in the first human beings

7. Nor should this be passed over: the order and progression of temptation in one person now is such as it first occurred then in our first parents. For just as then the serpent urged evil upon the woman, and she consented, then gave it to her husband, and sin was thus completed; so now in us the sensual movement of the soul stands in place of the serpent, the lower portion of reason in place of the woman, and the higher portion of reason in place of the man.

This is the man who, according to the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 11, is called the image and glory of God; and this is the woman who, according to the same Apostle, is called the glory of the man. Between this man and this woman there is, as it were, a spiritual marriage and a natural bond, by which the higher portion of reason, as the man, ought to preside and rule, while the lower portion, as the woman, ought to be subject and obey. Therefore, according to the Apostle, the man ought not to have a covering, but the woman ought.

And just as among all living creatures no helper like himself was found for the man, but one was taken from him to be formed for him in marriage; so also among those parts of the soul which we have in common with animals, no helper like our mind is found. Hence Augustine, Book 12 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 3:

> That part of us which is so occupied in dealing with temporal actions that it is not shared by us with cattle is indeed rational; but it is, as it were, drawn from that rational mind by which we cleave to intelligible and unchangeable Truth, and assigned to dealing with and governing lower things. For just as among all animals no helper like himself was found for the man, unless one were taken from him to be formed in marriage; so for our mind, by which we consult the Truth above, there is no helper like it for the use of temporal things—so far as the nature of humanity requires—drawn from those parts of the soul which we have in common with animals. (*same book and chapter*)

Therefore our rational element is not separated into a divorce from unity, but, as though derived for the help of fellowship, it is apportioned in its own function. And just as the two, male and female, are one flesh, so our understanding and action—or reason and rational appetite, if these can in some way be expressed more significantly—are embraced by one nature of the mind. [Col. 0704] Thus, as it was said of them in Genesis 2, “The two shall be one flesh,” so it may be said of these: “Two in one mind.” From these words it can plainly be understood how an image of that marriage exists in the human soul, and how these three things exist spiritually in each of us: namely, man, woman, and serpent.

### How temptation is completed in us through those three

8. It remains now to show how sin is completed in us through these three. Here, if careful attention is given, one may recognize what mortal and venial sin are in the soul. For just as there the serpent persuaded the woman, and the woman the man, so in us the sensual movement, when it has conceived the enticement of sin, suggests it as a serpent to the woman—that is, to the lower part of reason, or the reason of knowledge. If this part consents to the enticement, the woman eats the forbidden food. Afterwards she gives the same thing to the man, when she suggests the same enticement to the higher part of reason, that is, to the reason of wisdom. If this consents, the man too tastes the forbidden food with the woman.

Therefore, if the enticement of sin is present only in the movement of sensuality, the sin is venial and very slight. But if the lower part of reason consents, so that it is held merely by delight in the thought, without a will to carry it out, the woman alone has eaten, not the man. By his authority the will is restrained, so that it does not proceed to the deed. But if a full will to carry it out is present, so that, if opportunity is available, it may be brought into effect, the man too eats, because the higher part of reason has consented to the enticement; and then it is a grave and damnable sin.

But when the woman tastes without the man, this is sometimes mortal and sometimes venial sin. For, as has been said, the woman tastes without the man when sin is held with such delight in thought that its commission is not decided upon; or when the man sets a certain limit and measure upon sin, so that the woman may not proceed into sin with unbridled freedom. Therefore, if the sin is not retained long in the delight of thought, but is repelled by the man’s authority as soon as it touches the woman, it is venial. But if it is retained long in delight of thought, even though the will to carry it out is absent, it is mortal; and for it both man and woman—that is, the whole person—will be condemned, because even then the man did not restrain the woman as he ought. He may therefore be said to have consented.

### A recapitulation stating the sum

9. Therefore, to state the sum briefly: when sin is conceived in the soul in such a way that one resolves to do it, or even carries it out—some sins frequently, others once only—or when it is held long in delight of thought, it is mortal. But when it exists only in the sensual movement, as we said above, it is very slight, because reason does not then take delight in it.

I said above, however, “some frequently, others once only,” because there are certain things which condemn if they are done even once, or if one resolves to do them; while others do not condemn unless they are done more often, or their performance is resolved upon—as in the case of an idle word and similar matters.

Augustine sets this forth in Book 12 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12:

> Just as in that marriage of the first human beings the serpent persuaded them to eat, but the woman did not eat alone; she gave to her husband, and they ate together: so also in a certain hidden marriage which is conducted and recognized within one person, when animal sense introduces some enticement to the reason of knowledge—which is occupied, through its quickness in reasoning, with acting in temporal matters—the serpent then, as it were, speaks to the woman. To consent to this enticement is to eat from the forbidden tree. But if this consent is content merely with delight in thought, while by the authority above the bodily members are so held back that they are not presented to sin as instruments of unrighteousness [Romans 6], then, I think, it must be understood as though the woman alone had eaten from the forbidden tree.
>
> But if, in that consent, a particular sin is so resolved upon that, if there is power, it is also fulfilled in deed, the woman must be understood to have given her husband forbidden food to eat with her. For sin cannot be resolved upon in the mind not only pleasantly to be imagined, but also effectively to be committed, unless that attention of the mind to which belongs the supreme power either of moving the members to action or restraining them from action [Col. 0705] yields to evil action.
>
> Nor indeed, when the mind delights merely in thought concerning unlawful things—not deciding that they should be done, but nevertheless holding and willingly cherishing things which ought to have been rejected as soon as they touched the mind—must this be denied to be sin; but it is far less than if it is also resolved to be completed in deed. Therefore, forgiveness must also be sought for such thoughts, the breast must be struck, and it must be said: “Forgive us our debts” [Matthew 6].
>
> For just as in those first two human beings each bore his or her own person, and therefore, if the woman alone had eaten forbidden food, she alone would certainly have been punished with the penalty of death; so it cannot be said that, within one person, if thought alone willingly feeds on unlawful delights from which it ought immediately to turn away, and evil deeds are not resolved upon but are nevertheless sweetly retained in remembrance, the woman can be condemned without the man. Far be it from us to believe this. (*same book and chapter*)

For here there is one person, one human being, and the whole person will be condemned unless these sins of thought—which are experienced without a will to act, but with a will to delight the mind in such things—are forgiven through the Mediator’s grace. [Note: [Col. 0705] Augustine, vol. 1, Book 2, *On Genesis*, ch. 14.]

He also says the following on the same subject in his book against the Manicheans:

> The Apostle says, Ephesians 2: “According to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the children of unbelief.” Does he, then, visibly appear to them, or approach and work upon them as though in bodily places? Rather, in wondrous ways he suggests through cognition whatever he can; and these suggestions must be resisted. For we are not ignorant of his devices [Note: [Col. 0705] The Vulgate edition has “thoughts.”] [2 Corinthians 2].
>
> For how did he approach Judas when he persuaded him to betray the Lord? Was he seen by him in places or with these eyes? But surely it is said: “He entered into his heart” [John 13]. A person repels him if he guards the paradise of the mind. For God placed the human being in paradise “to cultivate and guard it” [Genesis 2]. For, just as it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs, chapter 4, “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed,” into which that persuader of perversity is certainly not admitted, nevertheless he deceived through the woman.
>
> For neither can our reason be led to consent to sin unless delight has been stirred in that part of the soul which ought to obey reason as its ruling husband. In each one of us, too, nothing else happens when a person falls into sin than what then happened in those three—the serpent, woman, and man. For first there is a suggestion, either through thought or through bodily senses: by seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, or smelling. When that suggestion has occurred, if our desire is not moved toward sin, the serpent’s cunning is excluded. But if it is moved, it is as though the woman has already been persuaded. Yet reason sometimes restrains and checks even desire when it has been stirred, with manly firmness. When this occurs, we do not fall into sin but are crowned through a certain struggle. But if reason consents and determines that what lust has stirred up should be done, the human being is expelled from all blessed life, as from paradise. For sin is then imputed even if the deed does not follow, when conscience is held guilty through consent.

### Why these things were said concerning the parts of the soul

10. We have inserted these matters concerning the parts of the soul so that the nature of the soul itself may be more fully known, and so that it may be understood according to which part of itself free choice exists in it: namely, according to reason, in which every mortal sin is committed, though not every venial sin—specifically, the venial sin which exists only in the movement of sensuality.

### That “sensuality” is often understood otherwise in Scripture than above—namely, so that the lower part of reason is also meant by that name

11. Nor should it be passed over in silence that in Scripture the name “sensuality” often means not only that part of the soul which we share with cattle, but also the lower part of reason, which attends to the ordering of temporal things. The careful reader should attentively observe this in passages of Scripture where sensuality is mentioned.

## DISTINCTION XXV. HE RETURNS TO THE CONSIDERATION OF FREE CHOICE

1. Now let us return to the matter proposed: the treatment of free choice. The philosophers, in defining it, called it “a free judgment of the will,” because that power and capacity of will and reason, which we said above is free choice, is free toward either alternative, since it can freely be moved toward this or toward that. Therefore choice is called free with respect to the will, because it can be moved voluntarily and carried by spontaneous desire toward things which it judges, or is capable of judging, to be good or evil.

### That free choice concerns only the future, and not every future thing

2. But it should be known that free choice does not refer to the present or the past, but to contingent future events. For what is present is determined, and it is not in our power that it should be or not be when it is. It can cease to be, or become something else afterwards; but it cannot not be while it is, nor be something else while it is—that is, while it is what it is. But whether this or that shall be in the future pertains to the power of free choice.

Yet not all future things come under the power of free choice, but only those which can happen or not happen through free choice. For if someone wills and intends to do something which is in no way in that person’s power, or which would equally happen without that person’s intention, that person has no free choice in the matter.

### That the foregoing description of free choice does not fit God or those who have been glorified

3. Indeed, according to the foregoing account, free choice seems to exist only in those who can change their will and turn toward contrary things: those, namely, in whose power it is to choose good or evil and, according to that choice, to do or omit either. Accordingly, free choice could exist neither in God nor in all those who have been strengthened by such grace of blessedness that they can no longer sin.

But that God has free choice Augustine teaches in volume 5, Book 22 of *The City of God*, final chapter:

> Surely, is God himself to be denied free choice because he cannot sin?

Ambrose likewise says in *On the Trinity*: “Paul says, 1 Corinthians 12, that one and the same Spirit works all things, distributing to each as he wills”—that is, according to the judgment of free will, not in obedience to necessity.

### How free choice is understood in God

4. But free choice is understood differently in the Creator than in creatures. God’s free choice is called his most wise and omnipotent will, which does all things as it wills, not by necessity but by free will. Therefore Jerome, observing that free choice is not in God as it is in creatures, seems to exclude free choice from God himself. In a homily to Pope Damasus, in volume 3, on the prodigal son, he says:

> God alone is one into whom sin does not fall and cannot fall. All other things, since they possess free choice, can be turned in either direction.

By saying “all other things,” he indicates that free choice as it exists in other things does not exist in the same way in God.

### That the angels and saints who are already blessed have free choice

5. But the angels and saints who now live happily with the Lord, and have been so confirmed by the grace of blessedness that they neither will nor can turn toward evil, are not without free choice. Hence Augustine, Book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 30, says:

> Just as the first immortality, which Adam lost by sinning, was the ability not to die, so the first free choice was the ability not to sin; the final free choice will be the inability to sin.

The same author says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 105:

> It was fitting that the human being should first be made able to will both good and evil. But afterwards that person will be such as to be unable to will evil; nor for that reason will the person lack free choice. For free choice will be far freer when it can in no way serve sin. Nor is the will absent, nor should it be called unfree, by which, being blessed, we so will to be blessed that we not only do not will to be miserable but are wholly unable to will it. Therefore, just as our soul now has the capacity to reject unhappiness, so it will always have the capacity to reject iniquity. But the order had to be observed by which God willed to show how good a rational creature is which can also sin, although better is that which cannot sin.

See how these words plainly affirm that after confirmation in blessedness there will be in a human being free choice by which one cannot sin; it now exists in the angels and in the saints who are with the Lord. It is certainly freer in proportion as it is more immune from sin and more inclined toward good. For the farther anyone stands from that slavery of sin of which it is written in John 8, “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin,” the freer is that person’s judgment in choosing good. Hence, if one looks carefully, choice seems to be called free because it can desire or choose, without compulsion and necessity, what it has decided upon through reason.

### The difference in freedom of choice according to different times

6. From what has been said it is clear that the first freedom of choice was greater than the second, and the third far greater than either the second or the first. For the first freedom of choice was that in which one could sin. The final freedom will be that in which one will be able not to sin and unable to sin. The intermediate freedom is that in which one can sin and cannot not sin: before restoration, even mortally; but after restoration, at least venially.

### The four states of free choice in the human being

7. Four states of free choice can be identified in the human being. Before sin, nothing hindered the good and nothing impelled toward evil. The human being had no weakness toward evil and had help toward good. Then reason could judge without error, and the will could desire good without difficulty.

But after sin, before the restoration of grace, the human being is oppressed and overcome by concupiscence, has weakness in evil but does not have grace in good; and therefore can sin and cannot avoid sin, even damnably. After restoration, however, before confirmation, the person is oppressed by concupiscence but not overcome. There is indeed weakness in evil, but grace in good, so that one can sin on account of freedom and weakness, and can avoid sin unto death on account of freedom and assisting grace. Yet one does not have an absolute ability not to sin, or inability to sin, because weakness has not yet been perfectly consumed and grace has not yet been fully perfected.

But after confirmation, when weakness has been completely consumed and grace perfected, the person will be able neither to be overcome nor oppressed, and will then have the inability to sin.

### The corruption of free choice through sin

8. Hence it is clear that, besides the other punishments for that sin, the human being incurred punishment in the corruption and oppression of free choice. For through that sin the natural goods in the human being were corrupted and the gratuitous gifts taken away. This is the one who was wounded and stripped by robbers [Luke 10]: wounded in natural goods, of which the person was not deprived, since otherwise restoration could not take place; but stripped of gratuitous gifts, which had been added to natural goods by grace.

These are the good gifts and perfect presents. Some of them were corrupted by sin—that is, the natural goods, such as native ability, memory, and understanding; others were removed—that is, gratuitous gifts—although natural goods too are from grace, for they belong to God’s general grace. Yet this distinction is often made when the term “grace” is applied to the species rather than the genus.

Thus freedom of choice was corrupted by sin and partly lost. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 30:

> By using free choice badly, the human being lost both himself and it. For when sin was committed through free choice, sin became the conqueror and free choice was lost. For whoever is overcome is made the slave of the one who overcomes him [2 Peter 2].

See: he says that the human being lost free choice, not because after sin the human being did not possess free choice, [Col. 0708] but because the person lost freedom of choice—not all freedom, but freedom from misery and sin.

### The three modes of freedom of choice

9. For freedom is threefold: freedom from necessity, from sin, and from misery. Choice is equally free from necessity both before and after sin. Just as then it could not be compelled, so neither can it now. Therefore the will is rightly judged by God, since it is always free from necessity and can never be compelled. Where there is necessity, there is no freedom; where there is no freedom, neither is there will, and therefore neither merit. This freedom exists in all, both evil and good persons.

There is another freedom, from sin, of which the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 3: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom”; and Truth says in the Gospel, John 8: “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free.” This freedom liberates from slavery to sin and makes servants of righteousness; just as, conversely, the slavery of sin makes people free from righteousness. Hence the Apostle says in Romans 6: “Having been freed from sin, you were made servants of righteousness”; and again: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.” The human being lost this freedom by sinning.
