Therefore Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 30, says that by using free choice badly the human being lost both himself and it, because through sin freedom was lost—not freedom from necessity, but from sin. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” [John 8].

### Who possesses this freedom, namely freedom from sin, and through what means

10. Only those now possess this freedom from sin whom the Son frees and restores through grace. This is not to say that they are altogether without sin in this mortal flesh, but that sin does not rule or reign in them. This is true and good freedom, which brings forth the good slavery of righteousness. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 30, says:

> No one will be free for doing righteousness unless, freed from sin, that person has begun to be a servant of righteousness. This is true freedom because of delight in right action, and at the same time pious servitude because of obedience to the commandment.

There is another freedom, not true, joined to evil slavery: freedom to do evil, where reason dissents from the will, judging that what the will desires ought not to be done. But for doing good, reason agrees with the will; therefore there is true and pious freedom. Augustine says of freedom toward evil and evil slavery in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 30:

> What freedom can slaves—that is, those enslaved to sin—possess except when it delights them to sin? For one serves freely who willingly performs the will of his master; and therefore the person who is the slave of sin is free to sin.

### Question whether freedom toward evil is the freedom of choice itself, or another freedom

11. Here it may be asked whether this freedom by which a person is free toward evil is freedom of choice. If it is freedom of choice, it is certainly good, since freedom of choice is a natural good. Some hold that it is freedom of choice itself, always good, but through slavery to sin is freer and more inclined toward evil; and therefore it is said not to be true freedom, because it is directed toward evil. Others think that this freedom toward evil, which Augustine mentioned above, is not freedom of choice itself, but a certain propensity to sin and crookedness arising from sin, and is evil.

### Another question: whether freedom toward good is freedom of choice itself

12. Likewise, it is commonly asked whether that true freedom which exists for doing righteousness is freedom of choice itself. Some say that it is the same freedom, restored by grace; with grace assisting, it is free toward good, but without grace it is not free toward good. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter cited:

> This freedom for doing good will never belong to a human being enslaved and sold under sin unless the one who says in John 8, “If the Son sets you free, you will be truly free,” redeems that person. Before this begins to occur in a human being, how can anyone boast of free choice who is not yet free to do good?

See: he plainly shows that free choice is liberated through grace, so that a person may do good through it. Therefore they say that the true freedom for doing good, of which Augustine has spoken above, is the freedom of choice itself, freed and assisted by God’s grace. Others think that it is not freedom of choice itself but another kind of freedom which, through grace and free choice, begins to exist in the human mind when God acts and the person is restored.

### A definite resolution of both questions: freedom toward good and toward evil is freedom of choice

13. But we judge it more fitting that both the freedom by which one is free toward evil and that by which one is free to do good are freedom of choice itself. For it receives different names from different causes. Before it is restored by grace, it is called freedom for doing evil; but when restored through grace, it is called freedom for doing good. For before grace the will is free toward evil, whereas through grace it becomes free toward good.

Therefore the human will is always free in some manner, but it is not always good. It is not good unless it has been freed from sin; nevertheless, it is free from necessity. Hence Augustine, *On Grace and Free Choice*, addressed to Valentinus, chapter 15, volume 7:

> The will in us is always free, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good.

### Freedom from misery

14. There is again freedom from misery, of which the Apostle says in Romans 8: “Creation itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” The human being possessed this freedom before sin, because he was free of every misery and troubled by no affliction; and will possess it more fully in future blessedness, where one cannot be miserable. But in this life, which lies between the first sin and final confirmation, no one is free from misery, because no one is without sin’s punishment.

### He repeats concerning the corruption of free choice in order to add further points

15. From what has been said, it now appears how free choice was diminished or corrupted through sin: before sin, the human being had no difficulty or hindrance from the law of the members in doing good, and no impulse or instigation toward evil. But now, through the law of the flesh, one is hindered from good and urged toward evil, so that one cannot will and accomplish good unless freed and aided through grace; because, as the Apostle says in Romans 7, sin dwells in the flesh.

Therefore, although free choice is always free and belongs to every individual, it is not equally free in good and evil, or toward good and evil. It is freer in good, where it has been liberated, than in evil, where it has not been liberated. And it is freer toward evil, which it can do of itself, than toward good, which it cannot do unless it is freed and assisted by grace.

### Freedom arising from grace and freedom arising from nature

16. Freedom from sin and misery, then, comes through grace; freedom from necessity comes through nature. The Apostle notes both freedoms, that of nature and that of grace, in Romans 7 when, speaking in the person of an unredeemed human being, he says: “Willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good.” It is as though he said: “I have the freedom of nature, but I do not have the freedom of grace; therefore perfection in good is not present in me.”

For the human will, which one possesses naturally, cannot be raised to an effective willing or practical accomplishment of good unless it is freed and assisted by grace: freed so that it may will, and assisted so that it may accomplish. For, as the Apostle says in Romans 9, willing does not belong to the one who wills, nor running—that is, working—to the one who runs, but to God who has mercy, who works in us both to will and to do good. Human will or action does not summon this grace; rather, grace itself precedes the will, preparing it to will good, and assists the will once prepared so that it may accomplish it.

## DISTINCTION XXVI. ON OPERATING AND COOPERATING GRACE

1. This is operating and cooperating grace. Operating grace prepares the human will to will [Col. 0710] good; cooperating grace helps it not to will in vain. Hence Augustine, in *On Grace and Free Choice*, addressed to Valentinus, chapter 17, volume 7:

> By cooperating in us, God completes what he begins by operating; for he acts so that we may will when he begins, and he cooperates with those who will when he completes. Therefore he acts so that we may will. But when we will, and will in such a way that we accomplish, he cooperates with us. Yet without him—whether operating so that we may will, or cooperating when we will—we can do nothing in works of piety.

These words sufficiently make clear what operating grace is and what cooperating grace is. Operating grace precedes the good will: through it the human will is freed and prepared to become good and to will good effectively. Cooperating grace follows the will already made good, assisting it.

Hence Augustine says against Julian the heretic, who claimed that a good will arises from free choice alone and that a human being can will and perform good without grace through free choice:

> The Apostle expressed a clear judgment in commendation of grace when he said: “It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” If you had considered this, Julian, you would not have extended the merits of the human will against grace. For God does not have mercy on someone because that person willed and ran; rather, that person willed and ran because God had mercy. For the human will is prepared by God, and human steps are directed by the Lord [Psalm 36].
>
> Therefore he fittingly says: “It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” Not because this occurs without our will, but because our will does no good unless it is helped by God. Hence elsewhere the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 15: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” He does not say this because he did no good, but because he would do no good if grace did not assist him.

These testimonies plainly indicate that the human will is preceded and prepared by God’s grace so that it becomes good, not so that it becomes a will; for will existed even before grace, but it was not a good and upright will.

### What will is

2. Augustine himself defines will thus in volume 6, *On Two Souls*, chapter 10:

> Will is a movement of the mind, with no one compelling it, either not to admit something or to obtain it.

But so that it may not admit evil and may obtain good, it is preceded and prepared by God’s grace. Therefore the Apostle, commending preceding and following grace in Romans 9—that is, operating and cooperating grace—carefully said: “It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy”; and not conversely: “It is not of God who has mercy, but of the one who wills and runs” (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 32).

For if, as some have held, the saying is understood thus—“It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy”—as though it meant, “The human will alone is insufficient unless God’s mercy is also present,” then the converse is said: “God’s mercy too is insufficient unless the human will is also present.” Thus, if the former statement is rightly made because human will alone does not accomplish this, why is the contrary statement not also rightly made—“It is not of God who has mercy, but of the human being who wills”—when God’s mercy alone does not accomplish it? For a human being cannot believe or hope unless one wills; nor can one attain the prize unless one runs by will.

It remains, therefore, that the statement is rightly understood in this way: that the whole is attributed to God, who precedes the human good will and prepares it to be assisted, and assists it once prepared; he precedes the unwilling person so that the person may will, and follows the willing person so that the person may not will in vain. [Note: [Col. 0710] Augustine, vol. 4, Book 1, *To Simplicianus*, about the middle, question 2.]

See: these words and the preceding ones clearly teach that the human will is prepared and preceded by God’s grace so that it may will good, and is assisted so that it may not will in vain.

### That a good will follows grace

3. Therefore good will follows grace; grace does not follow will. Hence Augustine, writing to Pope Boniface against the Pelagians, says:

> When faith obtains justification, according as God has allotted to each a measure of faith, no human merit precedes God’s grace; rather, faith itself merits to be increased, so that, when increased, it may merit to be perfected, with the will accompanying, not leading; following as an attendant, not going before. [Col. 0711]

[Note: In volume 2, Epistle 106, in the Gloss on Romans 5: “Having therefore been justified.”]

Here you plainly have that grace precedes the merit of a good will; and that good will itself follows grace as an attendant, not as a forerunner.

### What grace precedes the will—namely, faith with love
4. And if you attend carefully, you are likewise shown what that grace is which precedes and prepares the will—namely, faith together with love. Thus Augustine, in the same letter, discussing how we are justified by faith and yet gratuitously (for the Apostle says both things: “Justified by faith,” Rom. 5, and “Justified freely by his grace,” Rom. 3), says:

> He said this so that faith itself might not grow proud and say to itself: “If we are justified by faith, how is it freely? For what faith merits, why is it not rather repaid than given?” Let no faithful person say this; for when he says, “I have faith, so that I may merit justification,” he is answered: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). For the faith by which you have been justified was freely given to you.

Here it is plainly shown that faith is the cause of justification, and that it is itself the grace and benefit by which a person’s will is preceded and prepared. Hence Augustine says, in the *Retractations*, chapter 9, toward the middle:

> The will is that by which both sin is committed and right living is pursued. But the will itself cannot live rightly and piously among mortals unless God’s grace frees it from the slavery by which it is enslaved to sin, and assists it to overcome vices. And unless this benefit, by which it is freed, preceded it, it would now be given according to merits and not by grace, which is certainly given freely.

Therefore a person’s good will is preceded by that benefit of grace through which it is freed and prepared. This benefit is rightly understood as the faith of Christ, as Augustine plainly shows in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 106:

> After that fall, free choice must be liberated from the slavery of sin. Nor is it liberated at all through itself, but through the grace of God alone, which is established in faith in Christ, so that the will may be prepared.

See: he plainly says that the grace through which free choice is freed and the will prepared is established in faith in Christ. For, as he says in chapter 117, faith in Christ obtains what the law commands.

### That the good will preceded by grace precedes certain gifts of God

5. Yet this same will precedes certain gifts of grace. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 32:

> A person’s good will precedes many gifts of God, though not all. But in those gifts which it does not precede, it is itself present and itself assists; for both statements are read in the holy Scriptures: “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58 [59]); and, “The mercy of God will follow me” (Ps. 22 [23]). For it precedes one unwilling, that he may will; it follows one willing, lest he will in vain. Why are we urged to pray for our enemies who are unwilling to live piously, unless God may work willing in them? And why are we urged to ask, that we may receive, unless what we will may be done by him through whom it was brought about that we should will? Hence the Apostle says, Rom. 9: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.”

From this it appears that a person’s good will precedes certain gifts of God, because assisting grace accompanies it; and that it is preceded by other gifts, because operative grace precedes it—namely, faith together with charity.

### What seems contrary to the foregoing: namely, that faith appears to be said to arise from the will

6. Yet one must not overlook that Augustine, tome 9, tractate 26, at the beginning, seems to indicate that faith comes from the will. On the Apostle’s words, Rom. 10, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” he comments on John as follows:

> Therefore the Apostle did not simply say, “One believes,” but, “One believes with the heart”; because a person can do other things unwillingly, but cannot believe except willingly. He can enter a church and approach the altar unwillingly, but he cannot believe unwillingly.

Likewise, on Genesis, chapter 24, where Laban and Bethuel said, “Let us call the girl and ask her will,” the expositor says that faith belongs to the will, not to necessity.

In reply, we say that these statements are not to be understood as meaning that faith proceeds from the human will, since faith is properly God’s gift, as the Apostle says, Eph. 2, and since the good merits of a person begin from it. For by faith, as Augustine says on Psalm 67 [68], the ungodly person is justified—that is, is made godly from ungodly—so that faith itself may thereafter begin to work through love; and from this all good merits begin.

Rather, these words were said because faith exists only in one who wills to believe. Faith precedes such a person’s good will, not in time but in cause and nature. Hence Augustine fittingly said above that good will is present in those gifts which it does not precede, and itself assists: it assists the gifts by which it is preceded, when it consents to them for the accomplishment of good; and it is present in them because it is not temporally preceded by them.

### He adds further points that make the question more difficult: namely, that thought of the good precedes faith

7. Moreover, this question is sharpened and pressed more forcefully by Augustine’s words in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 2, tome 7, where he discusses the Apostle’s saying, 2 Cor. 3: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything as from ourselves”:

> Let those who think that the beginning of faith is from ourselves and faith’s completion from God attend to this and weigh these words. For, commending the grace which is not given according to any merits but produces all good merits, he says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything good,” namely, from ourselves. But who does not see that thinking comes before believing? For no one believes anything unless he has first thought that it ought to be believed. Therefore, if thinking what is good is not from ourselves, as the Apostle here teaches, neither is believing—although believing itself is nothing other than thinking with the assent of the mind.

Here he seems to suggest that good thought precedes faith, and thus that good will precedes faith rather than being preceded by it; this seems contrary to what was said above. To this we reply that sometimes good thought or will precedes faith; but it is not that good will or thought by which one lives rightly. For this does not exist without faith and charity.

For, as Augustine says to Anastasius, Letter 144, tome 2, without the Spirit a person’s will is not free when it is overcome by desires (Gal. 5); it is not free for good unless it has been liberated. But it is not liberated unless charity is poured into hearts through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5). The will is not free unless grace frees it through the law of faith; that is, it is not free without faith working through love. And that is sufficiently and truly good. For no fruit is good which does not rise from the root of charity. But if faith working through love is present, delight in the good results.

### A full discussion of that thought of the good which precedes faith

8. That thought or will which precedes faith, charity, and the other means of justification does not suffice for salvation, nor does one live rightly by it. By this will one desires that good will which is a great good; but this will is not such a good. Therefore that will or thought is one thing, and this another. And just as the former precedes the latter, so understanding goes before the former.

Thus Augustine, distinguishing these things in his exposition of Psalm 118 [119], “My soul longed to desire,” says at the end of his exposition of that psalm, tome 8:

> “It longed to desire,” he says—not, “It desired.” For we sometimes see by reason how useful God’s ordinances are; but, hindered by weakness, we sometimes desire them. Therefore understanding flies ahead; a slow effect, or no effect at all, follows. We know the good, yet taking action does not delight us; and we desire that it may delight us. Thus this man formerly longed to desire the things which he saw were good, wishing to possess delight in those things whose reason he could see. He therefore shows by what steps, as it were, one reaches them. First, one must see that they are useful and honorable; then, desire for them must be longed for; finally, as grace advances, their performance must delight—the performance of things whose reason alone delights.

Observe this order of graces, distinctly set out here by Augustine: understanding of good things precedes desire for them, and this desire precedes the delight which comes through faith and charity. Once this delight is possessed, the will by which one lives rightly is truly good. It is a companion of faith, not its precursor.

Whoever considers Augustine’s foregoing words according to this distinction will perhaps notice no contradiction in them. Such a reader will also recognize that, even before the preceding and operative grace by which a good will is prepared in a person, certain things come first from God’s good grace and free choice, and certain things even from free choice alone. Yet by such things a person neither merits life nor the grace by which he is justified.

For no merits precede the reception of that grace which heals the human will, so that once healed it may fulfil the law. It is the grace by which an ungodly person, who had been ungodly, is justified and made righteous. But punishment, not grace, is due to the merits of the ungodly; nor would that grace be grace unless it were bestowed freely. It is bestowed freely because we had previously done no good thing by which we might merit it.

We do not, however, deny that before this grace and apart from this grace many good things are done by a person through free choice, as Augustine teaches in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, in the *Replies against the Pelagians*, where he says that people cultivate fields, build houses, and perform many other good things through free choice without cooperating grace.

### Whether operative and cooperating grace are one and the same grace

9. Here it must be considered: since it has been said that through operative and preceding grace a person’s will is freed and prepared to will the good, and through cooperating and subsequent grace it is assisted so that it does not will in vain, are these one and the same grace—that is, one gift freely given—which operates and cooperates? Or are they different: one operative and the other cooperating?

To some it seems, not without reason, that they are one and the same grace, the same gift, the same power, which both operates and cooperates; but because of its different effects it is called both operative and cooperating. It is called operative insofar as it frees and prepares a person’s will to will the good; cooperating insofar as it assists that same will not to will in vain, namely, so that it may perform a good work. For grace itself is not idle; rather, it merits increase, so that, increased, it may merit completion.

### What this grace is, and how it merits increase

10. But if it is asked how this preceding grace can merit to be increased and perfected, since no merit exists without free choice; and what that grace itself is—whether a virtue or not; and, if a virtue, whether an act or not—then, in order that this may be made plain, one must first state that there are three kinds of goods. For some are great, others least, and others intermediate, as Augustine says in the first book of the *Retractations*:

> The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods. The forms of any bodies whatsoever, without which one can live rightly, are least goods. But the powers of the soul, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods.

Likewise, *On Free Choice*, book 2, chapter 19, tome 1:

> No one makes bad use of virtues. But of other goods—that is, intermediate and least goods—anyone can make not only good but also bad use. Therefore no one makes bad use of virtue, because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly. But no one uses something badly by using it well. The goodness of God has granted that not only great goods but also intermediate and least goods should exist.

Here you have the three kinds of goods distinguished.

### Among which goods is free choice found?

11. But the question is, among which goods is free choice included? Augustine says this in the first book of the *Retractations*, chapter 9, at the end:

> Free choice of the will is found among the intermediate goods, since we can also use it badly; nevertheless it is such that we cannot live rightly without it. But its good use is now virtue, which is found among the great goods, of which no one can make bad use. And since great, intermediate, and least goods are from God, it follows that the good use of free will, which is virtue and is numbered among the great goods, is also from God.

Consider carefully what has been said and compare it together; in this way what was asked above will become clear. He indeed said that the work of virtue is the good use of those goods which we can also fail to use well—that is, the intermediate goods—among which he placed free choice, whose good use he also called virtue. If that is so, then virtue is not the work of virtue, as he said above, because virtue is one thing and its work another.

## DISTINCTION XXVII. WHAT VIRTUE IS, AND WHAT ITS ACT OR WORK IS

1. Here we must see what virtue is, and what its act or work is. Virtue, as Augustine says, is a good quality of the mind by which one lives rightly and of which no one makes bad use; God alone produces it in a person. Thus it is God’s work alone, as Augustine teaches concerning the virtue of justice in his exposition of Psalm 118 [119], “I have done judgment and justice.” In tome 8, sermon 26 on that psalm, he says:

> Justice is a great virtue of the soul, which no one but God produces in a person. Therefore, when the prophet says in the person of the Church, “I have done justice,” he intended not the virtue itself, which a human being does not produce, but its work.

Here it is plainly indicated that justice in a person is not a human work but God’s; the same must likewise be understood of the other virtues.

### He says the same concerning faith: it is not from a human being but from God alone

2. For when writing to the Ephesians about the grace of faith, the Apostle likewise maintains that faith is not from a person but from God alone, saying: “You are saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; for it is the gift of God.” The saints explain this as follows: namely, this faith is not from the power of our nature, because it is wholly God’s gift.

Here too it is plainly taught that faith is not from the freedom of choice, or from the choice of the will. This agrees with what was said above: that preceding or operative grace is a virtue which frees and heals a person’s will. Hence Augustine says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 9, tome 3:

> We are justified not through free will but through the grace of Christ; not because it occurs without our will, but because our will is shown weak through the law, so that grace may heal the will and the healthy will fulfil the law.

### Concerning the grace that frees the will: if it is virtue, virtue is not from free choice, and thus is not a movement of the mind

3. Therefore, if the grace which heals and frees a person’s will is one virtue or several virtues, then, since this grace is not from the choice of the will but rather heals and prepares it to be good, it follows that virtue is not from free choice and therefore is not a movement or affection of the mind. For every movement or affection of the mind is from free choice: the good is from grace and free choice, but the bad from free choice alone.

For Augustine says in the first book of the *Retractations*, chapter 15, and in tome 6, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, book 2, chapter 11: “A human being was able to fall voluntarily and by free choice, but not likewise to rise again.” Likewise, in *On Two Souls*, chapter 12, tome 6:

> If souls lacked a free movement of mind to do and not to do, and if, finally, no power of refraining from their action were granted them, we could not hold them accountable for sin.

Here it is plainly shown that a movement of the mind, whether toward good or evil, is from free choice. Therefore, if grace or virtue is a movement of the mind, it is from free choice. But if it is from free choice, even partly, then God alone does not make it without human cooperation.

For this reason some writers, not without learning, teach that virtue is a good quality or form of the mind, which gives form to the soul. It is not itself a movement or affection of the mind; rather, free choice is assisted by it in order that it may be moved and raised toward good. Thus a good movement or affection of the mind arises from virtue and free choice, and from this a good external work proceeds.

As rain waters the earth so that it may sprout and bear fruit—yet the rain is neither earth, shoot, nor fruit; the earth is neither shoot nor fruit; and the shoot is not fruit—so the rain of divine blessing, that is, grace, is freely poured into the soil of our mind, namely, the free choice of the will. This grace is inspired by God alone, not by a human being together with him. By it the human will is watered so that it may sprout and bear fruit: that is, it is healed and prepared to will the good, insofar as grace is called operative; and it is assisted to do the good, insofar as grace is called cooperating. This grace is not unfittingly called virtue, because it heals and assists the weak human will.

### In what sense good merits are said to begin from grace, and of what grace this is understood

4. Therefore, when good merits are said to arise and begin from grace, this may mean grace which freely gives—that is, God—or, rather, freely given grace, which precedes the human will. For it would not be a great matter to say that these things are from God, from whom all things are. Rather, it is his freely given grace from which good merits begin. And when they are said to be from grace alone, free choice is not excluded, because there is no merit in a person except through free choice.

But in the earning of good merits the primacy of causation is ascribed to grace, because grace itself is the principal cause of good merits: by it free choice is awakened and healed, and the human will is helped to be good.

### That good will is principally from grace, and is itself grace, as is every good merit

5. That good will is itself both God’s gift and a human merit—indeed, a merit of grace—because it is principally from grace and is grace. Hence Augustine, tome 2, Letter 105, to the presbyter Sixtus: “What is a person’s merit before grace, when grace alone produces in us every good merit?”

For from grace, as has been said—the grace which precedes and heals human choice—and from choice itself, a good affection or good movement of mind is produced in a person’s soul. This is the first good merit of the human being. For example, from the virtue of faith and a person’s choice there is generated in the mind a certain good and rewardable movement, namely, believing itself. So also from charity and free choice another good movement arises, namely loving, a very good movement. The same is to be understood of the remaining virtues. These good movements or affections are merits and gifts of God, by which we merit both their own increase and other things subsequently added to us here and in the future.

### In what sense faith is said to merit justification, and similarly other virtues

6. Therefore, when faith is said to merit justification and eternal life, this means that it merits them through the act of faith. The same is understood of charity, justice, and the rest. For if faith itself—the preceding virtue—were said to be an act of the mind which is merit, it would then originate from free choice. Since this is not so, faith is called a merit because its act is merit, provided charity is present; without charity neither believing nor hoping is a merit unto life.

Thus it plainly follows that charity is the Holy Spirit, who gives form to and sanctifies the qualities of the soul, so that through them the soul may be formed and sanctified. Without charity, a quality of the soul is not called virtue, because it cannot heal the soul.

### On the gifts of virtues, and the grace which is not merit but produces merit

7. Therefore, through the gifts of virtues we are good and live justly, and through grace, which is not merit but produces it. Yet our merits—namely good affections, their progress, and good works, which God rewards in us—do not arise without free choice; and these very things are God’s gifts. Hence Augustine, to the presbyter Sixtus:

> When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than his own gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0715] Letter 105, tome 2; and tome 6, exposition of Psalm 98 [99], toward the middle; and exposition of Psalm 102 [103], not far from the beginning.]

Thus eternal life, which at the end is rendered by God in accordance with preceding merits, is rightly called grace as well, because both the merits for which it is rendered are not from us but have been produced in us through grace, and life itself is freely given. It is not freely given because it is not given for merits, but because the merits for which it is given were themselves given through grace.

### He summarizes in order to add further points

8. From the foregoing, we may now in some measure recognize how preceding grace merits increase and other things; what it itself is, whether virtue or something else; and, if it is virtue, whether it is an act or not. For it has been shown above, according to the view of some, that it is virtue, because virtue is not an act but its cause, though not without free choice.

Thus Augustine’s earlier statement that the good use of free choice is virtue can be understood to mean the act of virtue. Otherwise he would seem to contradict himself, since above he also said that the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can fail to use well, among which he placed free choice. But if the good use of free choice is the work of virtue, then it is not virtue itself. Therefore, when he said that its good use is virtue, by the name “virtue” he meant the use of virtue itself.

### That the same use belongs to virtue and free choice, but principally to virtue

9. Certainly the same good use arises from virtue and from free choice, but principally from virtue. This good use is to be numbered among the great goods. But that preceding grace, which is also virtue, is not the use of free choice; rather, the good use of free choice comes from it. It is from God to us, not from ourselves.

But the good use of choice is both from God and from us, and therefore is a good merit. There God alone operates; here God and the human being operate. This merit proceeds from that most pure grace, as the Apostle observed when he said, 1 Cor. 15: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” and, “His grace in me was not empty.” On this passage Augustine says in *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapters 5 and 6, tome 7:

> He rightly names grace, for God first gives grace alone, and gives nothing but grace, since only evil merits precede. But after grace, good merits begin. And, to show free choice as well, he adds: “And his grace in me was not empty.” And lest the will itself be thought capable of any good without God’s grace, he adds: “Yet not I alone,” namely, not I without grace, “but the grace of God with me,” that is, with free choice. Plainly, when grace has been given, our good merits begin to exist; yet they exist through grace, because if grace is lacking, a person falls.

### The opinion of others is set forth here, who say that virtues are good uses of free choice, that is, acts of the mind

10. Others say that virtues are good uses of natural powers, though not all good uses: only those inward uses which are in the mind. The outward uses performed through the body they say are not virtues, but works of virtues. Therefore Augustine’s statement that the work of virtue is the good use of natural powers they understand of outward use; but his statement that the good use of free choice is virtue and is numbered among great goods they understand of inward use.

They maintain that virtues are nothing other than good affections or movements of the mind, which God produces in a person and not the person. For although those movements belong to free choice, they cannot exist unless God frees and assists it through his operative and cooperating grace. They understand this grace as God’s gratuitous will, because God is the one who works in us both to will and to perform the good.

### The authorities by which they maintain that virtues are movements of the mind

11. They establish that virtues are movements of the mind by testimonies of the saints. Augustine says, tome 3, chapter 10, on John: “What is faith? Believing what you do not see. But believing is a movement of the mind.” Likewise, in book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*: “By charity I mean a movement of the mind.”

But if charity and faith are movements of the mind, then virtues are movements of the mind. Others reply that Augustine’s foregoing statements must be understood as follows: “Faith is believing what you do not see,” that is, faith is the virtue by which what is not seen is believed. Likewise: “Charity is a movement of the mind,” that is, charity is the grace by which the mind is moved to love.

That these and similar statements ought to be understood in this way is inferred from what Augustine says elsewhere. For in book 2 of the *Questions on the Gospels*, chapter 39, he says: “Faith is that by which things not seen are believed, which is properly called faith.” Likewise, tome 4, *On the Trinity*, book 13, chapter 2: “The things believed are one thing; the faith by which they are believed is another.”

From these words they argue as follows: believing is one thing; that which is believed is another. But it has been said that faith is that by which one believes. Therefore believing is not faith, because believing is not that by which one believes. They add also: Virtue is God’s work alone, which he alone produces in us; therefore it is not a use or act of free choice. But believing is an act of free choice; therefore it is not virtue.

Both sides rely upon the foregoing and other arguments and testimonies. I leave the judgment between them to the careful reader’s examination, and hasten on to other matters.

## DISTINCTION XXVIII. HE REPEATS THE FOREGOING IN ORDER TO ADD FURTHER POINTS, SETTING OUT A DEFINITE ACCOUNT OF GRACE AND FREE CHOICE AGAINST THE PELAGIANS

1. But we must hold firmly and without hesitation that free choice, without preceding and assisting grace, does not suffice to obtain salvation and righteousness; nor is God’s grace summoned by merits preceding it, as the Pelagian heresy taught.

For Augustine says in the first book of the *Retractations*:

> The new heretics, the Pelagians, so assert free choice of the will that they leave no place for God’s grace, which they maintain is given according to our merits.

The Pelagian heresy, the most recent of all, arose from Pelagius the monk. These people are such enemies of God’s grace—by which we have been predestined and by which we have merited to be delivered from the power of darkness—that they believe a person can fulfil all the divine commandments without it.

Indeed, when Pelagius was reproved by the brethren because he attributed nothing to the aid of God’s grace for carrying out God’s commandments, he did not put grace before free choice, but deceitfully subordinated it, saying that grace is given to people so that through grace they may fulfil more easily what they are commanded to do through free choice. By saying “more easily,” he intended people to believe that, though with greater difficulty, they could nevertheless fulfil God’s commands without grace.

They say that the grace of God, without which we can do no good, consists only in free choice. Our nature received it from God without any preceding merits of its own. God assists us only by his law and teaching, so that we may learn what we ought to do and what we ought to hope for; but he does not assist us by the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that we may do what we have learned ought to be done.

Accordingly, they admit that knowledge, by which ignorance is expelled, is given to us by God; but they deny that charity, by which one lives piously, is given by God. Thus knowledge, which inflates without charity, is God’s gift, while charity itself, which builds up so that knowledge may not inflate, is not God’s gift.

They also destroy the prayers which the Church offers, whether for unbelievers and those resisting God’s teaching, that they may be converted to God; or for believers, that God’s faith may increase and that they may persevere in it. For they contend that people receive these things not from God but from themselves, saying that the grace of God by which we are delivered from ungodliness is given according to our merits. They also assert that infants are born without any bond of original sin.

### Here he states the arguments by which they support their error, using Augustine’s words against him

2. To establish their claim that a person can fulfil all commands through free choice without grace, they employ arguments such as these: “If a person cannot do what is commanded, its failure cannot be imputed to that person unto death, as you yourself, Augustine, maintain in *On Free Choice*.” [Note: [Col. 0717] Book 3, chapter 18, tome 1; and *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 67, tome 7, book 1, chapter 9.]

“You ask: ‘Who sins in what cannot in any way be avoided?’ But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided.”

Pelagius used this testimony of Augustine while disputing against him—indeed, against grace itself—as Augustine recalls when retracting this and similar statements in the *Retractations*:

> In these and similar words of mine, because God’s grace was not mentioned, since it was not then under discussion, the Pelagians think that we held their opinion. But they think this in vain. For the will is that by which sin is committed and right living is pursued; but unless it is freed by God’s grace and assisted to overcome vices, mortals cannot live rightly.

See: Augustine plainly establishes in what sense he made that statement, refuting the enemies of grace.

### Augustine cites another testimony which Pelagius used in his own support

3. Likewise Pelagius relied against grace upon Augustine’s words in *On Two Souls*, chapter 12, and in the *Retractations*, chapter 15: “To hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do is the height of injustice and madness.”

On hearing this, Pelagius leapt up and said: “Why then are infants, and those who do not have grace—without which they cannot fulfil the divine commandments—held guilty?”

But Augustine explains in the *Retractations*, replying to Pelagius, on what occasion he had said this. He had said it against the Manichaeans, who contend that there are two natures in a human being: one good, from God; the other evil, from the race of darkness, which was never good and cannot will good. If this were so, it would not seem imputable to that nature if it did not do good.

### He adds another statement which appears to contradict God’s grace

4. Elsewhere Augustine also says something which seems contrary to the grace by which we are justified. For he says in *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, chapter 26, tome 6:

> Unless a person changes his or her own will, that person cannot do good; and the Lord teaches that this lies within our power when he says, Matt. 22: “Either make the tree good, or its fruit good,” etc.

Augustine shows in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 22, that this is not contrary to the grace of God which we preach. For it is within a person’s power to change the will for the better; but that power does not exist unless it is given by God, of whom it was said, John 1: “He gave them power to become children of God.” Since what we do when we will is within our power, nothing is so much within our power as the will itself; but the will is prepared by the Lord. Thus he gives power in this manner.

### Another statement of the same author, which appears contrary

5. Likewise one must understand his statement in the same work: namely, that it lies in our power to deserve either to be grafted in by God’s goodness or to be cut off by his severity. For nothing is within our power except what follows our will; and when the will is prepared by the Lord, the work of piety becomes easy, even when it had been impossible and difficult.

### Another testimony

6. In his exposition of certain propositions from the Epistle to the Romans, Augustine also inserts some statements which seem opposed to this doctrine of grace. He says:

> Our believing is ours; but the good we do belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to believers.

And a little later:

> Believing and willing are ours; but to give believers and willing persons the ability to work well through the Holy Spirit belongs to him.

Augustine explains how these should be understood in the *Retractations*:

> It is indeed true that the good which we do is from God; but the same rule applies to both willing and doing. Both belong to him, because he prepares the will; and both are ours, because neither happens except when we will. I certainly would not have said those things if I had then known that faith itself is found among the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

### He adds yet another apparently contrary statement

7. Careful attention must also be given to Augustine’s statement in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, tome 7:

> The capacity to have faith, like the capacity to have charity, belongs to human nature; but having faith, as having charity, belongs to the grace of the faithful.

This was not said as though faith or charity could be possessed through free choice; rather, the human mind has a natural aptitude for believing and loving, and, being preceded by God’s grace, it believes and loves—something it cannot do without grace.

### By Jerome’s testimony he establishes what must be held concerning grace and free choice; three heresies are introduced: those of Jovinian, Manichaeus, and Pelagius

8. Therefore we must hold concerning grace and free choice without doubt what Jerome teaches in the *Explanation of the Catholic Faith to Pope Damasus*, refuting the errors of Jovinian, Manichaeus, and Pelagius:

> We confess free choice in such a way that we say we always need God’s help. Both those who, with Manichaeus, say that a person cannot avoid sin, and those who, with Jovinian, assert that a person cannot sin, are in error. Each removes the freedom of choice. But we say that a person can always both sin and not sin, so that we may always confess ourselves to possess free choice. This is the faith which we have learned in the Catholic Church and have always held.

## DISTINCTION XXIX. WHETHER A HUMAN BEING BEFORE SIN NEEDED OPERATIVE AND COOPERATING GRACE
1. After this, it must be considered whether man before sin needed operating and cooperating grace. To this we briefly reply that he needed not only cooperating grace but also operating grace—though not in every mode in which operating grace works; for it works by freeing and preparing the human will for good. Man therefore needed it, not in order that it might free his will, which had not been enslaved to sin, but in order that it might prepare it effectively to will the good, which he could not do by himself. For he could not merit good without grace, as Augustine clearly teaches in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 106, vol. 3:

> Human nature lost through free choice that immortality in which it was able not to die. But it will receive through grace that immortality in which it will not be able to die—the immortality which, had it not sinned, it would have received through merit; although even then no merit could have existed without grace. For although sin lay within the power of free choice alone, free choice was nevertheless not sufficient for acquiring or retaining righteousness unless divine assistance were supplied.

These words sufficiently show that before sin man needed operating and cooperating grace. For he did not have the means to move even a foot without the aid of operating and cooperating grace; he nevertheless had the means by which he could stand.

### That man possessed virtues before the Fall

2. Moreover, it is commonly asked whether man possessed virtue before the Fall. Some think that he did not, attempting to prove it thus: they say that he did not have justice, because he despised God’s command; nor prudence, because he did not provide for himself; nor temperance, because he desired what belonged to another; nor fortitude, because he yielded to a wicked suggestion. Replying to them, we say that he indeed did not possess these virtues when he sinned, but possessed them before then and lost them at that time. This is established by many testimonies of the saints.

For Augustine says in a certain homily: “Adam, having lost charity, was found evil.” Again: “When the prince of vices overcame Adam, made from the clay of the earth in the image of God, armed with chastity, ordered by temperance, radiant with charity, he stripped the first parents of those gifts and such great goods, and at the same time destroyed them.”

Ambrose also says of this same matter, to Sabinus, vol. 3, epistle 41: “When Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind clung to God.” On the Psalms he likewise says that man before sin, most blessed, “breathed the ethereal air.” But how could he have been most blessed without virtue? Augustine too, in Book 11, near the end of ch. 42, on Genesis, says that Adam before sin was endowed with a spiritual mind. Therefore there must be no doubt that man before sin shone with virtues, but was stripped of them through sin.

### On man’s expulsion from paradise

3. As punishment for that sin, he was also cast out of paradise into this place of miseries, as is read in Genesis, ch. 3: “Now, therefore, lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take from the tree of life and eat, and live for ever, God sent him out of the paradise of delight.” These words seem to imply that he would never have died if afterwards he had taken from that tree.

### How the words “lest he take from the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever” are to be understood

4. But since through sin he already had a mortal body, those words may be understood as follows. God, speaking in anger concerning proud man, says: “See lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand,” etc.—that is: “Take care, you angels, lest he eat from the tree of life, of which he is unworthy; from which, if he had persevered, he would have eaten and lived for ever. But now, because of disobedience, he is unworthy to eat.” And as he spoke in word, so he carried it out in deed. For God sent him from the paradise of delight to a place suitable to him; just as, often, when an evil man has begun to live among good people, if he refuses to change for the better, he is driven from the fellowship of the good, weighed down by the burden of evil habit.

### On the flaming, turning sword placed before paradise  
*(Augustine, On Genesis, Book 11, ch. 40)*

5. So that he could not approach it, God placed before paradise cherubim, and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life. According to the letter, this may be understood in this way: through the ministry of angels, a fiery guard was stationed there. For it should be believed that this was done in the visible paradise through heavenly powers, so that through angelic ministry there might be there a certain fiery guard. Yet this was not without purpose, but signified something concerning the spiritual paradise.

For *cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”; this is charity, because “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13). The flaming sword, however, signifies temporal punishments, which are turning because times are changeable. Therefore these were set before paradise to guard the tree of life, because one does not return to life except through the cherubim—that is, through fullness of knowledge, namely charity—and through the turning sword, that is, through endurance of temporal sufferings.

### Whether man ate from the tree of life before sin

6. It may be asked whether man ate from the tree of life before sin. Augustine says of this in Book 2 of *On the Baptism of Infants*:

> The first human beings are rightly understood to have abstained, before the devil’s evil persuasion, from forbidden food and to have used the things permitted to them.

[Note: Col. 0720. Elsewhere this work is called *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, against the Pelagians*, ch. 21.]

These words show that they took from the tree of life before sin, since they were commanded to eat from every tree of paradise except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

### Why they were not made immortal if they ate from the tree of life

7. Why, then, were they not clothed with perpetual soundness and blessed immortality, so that they would not be changed for the worse by any weakness or age? For that tree is said to have possessed this power by nature. But perhaps it did not confer this unless it was frequently eaten from. It could therefore have happened that he ate from it once and not more often, though he is understood to have remained in paradise for some time. For Scripture says that he was put to sleep there when a rib was taken from his side and a woman formed from it; and the animals were brought before him, to which he gave names.

## DISTINCTION XXX. THAT THROUGH ADAM SIN AND PUNISHMENT PASSED TO HIS DESCENDANTS

1. In what precedes it has been indicated, though only in part—for we are not sufficient to explain it perfectly—how the first man sinned and what punishment he suffered for sin. To this must be added that sin together with punishment passed through him to his descendants, as the Apostle shows, saying in Romans 5: “As through one man sin entered into this world, so death passed into all men.”

### Whether that sin was original or actual

2. Here we must first consider what that sin was: namely, whether original or actual. If it is understood of original sin, it must then be carefully investigated what original sin is, why it is called original, and how it passed, or passes, into all.

Some have thought that this should be understood of Adam’s actual sin, maintaining that the Apostle meant this when he says below: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so,” etc. They say: “The Apostle clearly expresses by the very name that the sin which entered the world through one man was disobedience.” But disobedience is actual sin.

### How they say it entered the world

3. They say that it entered the world not by transmission of origin but by likeness of transgression; and they say that all sinned in that one man because that one man provided all with an example of sinning. Certain heretics, called Pelagians, thought wrongly in this way. Augustine recalls them in *On the Baptism of Infants*:

> It should be known that certain heretics called Pelagians said that the sin of the first transgression passed to other human beings not by propagation but by imitation. Therefore they refuse to believe that original sin is forgiven in infants through baptism, vigorously maintaining that there is no original sin at all in those being born. But they are told that, if the Apostle had intended sin by imitation rather than propagation, he would name as its prince not Adam but the devil, of whom it is said in Wisdom 2: “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world.” And because Scripture does not wish this to be understood as occurring by propagation but by imitation, it immediately adds: “But those who are on his side imitate him.” Indeed, all who transgress God’s command through disobedience imitate Adam. But one thing is an example to those who sin by will, and another is an origin to those born with sin.

Therefore Adam’s sin must not be understood as having passed into all merely by an example for imitation, but by the defect of propagation and origin.

### Here he explains that the sin which passes to descendants is original sin

4. And that sin which passed into all through Adam, as Augustine plainly attests, is original sin, transmitted through his corrupted flesh to those generated in concupiscence.

### Here it is investigated what original sin is

5. This must be carefully investigated. For holy teachers have spoken of it obscurely, and scholastic teachers have held differing views. Some think original sin is the liability to punishment for the first man’s sin—that is, the debt or obligation by which we are bound and liable to temporal and eternal punishment because of the first man’s actual sin. They say that eternal punishment is owed by all for that sin unless they are freed through grace.

According to their opinion, original sin must be said to be neither guilt nor punishment. They acknowledge that it is not guilt; nor can it, according to them, be punishment. For if original sin is the debt of punishment, and a debt of punishment is not itself punishment, then original sin is not punishment. Some of them also admit this, saying that in Scripture original sin is often called *reatus*, “liability”; and by *reatus* they understand, as stated, obligation to punishment. They assert that original sin is said to be in infants because infants are liable to punishment for that first sin, just as, in accordance with legal justice, children are sometimes exiled for the sin of an unjust parent.

### He proves by authorities that original sin is guilt

6. But that original sin is guilt is taught by many testimonies of the saints. On Exodus, ch. 13, where it is said, “You shall exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep,” Gregory says: “We are all born in sins, and conceived from the pleasure of the flesh; we have drawn original guilt along with us, and through it we become entangled in sins by our own will.” Behold: he says that we draw original guilt, from which it is clear that original sin is guilt.

Augustine likewise, in *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 4, vol. 7, says concerning this same matter:

> All, as the Apostle says in Romans 3, have sinned—certainly either in themselves or in Adam—because they are not without sin, whether it be what they contracted originally or what they added through evil habits. For the sin of the first man killed not only himself but the whole human race, because from him we received both condemnation and guilt.

The same author, on Psalm 50, at the verse, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities,” says:

> What is sown from a dead body is born with the bond of original sin and death. Therefore David says that he was conceived in iniquities, because in all human beings iniquity and the bond of death are drawn from Adam. For no one is born except bearing punishment and the desert of punishment. But the desert of punishment is sin. Therefore everyone born through the concupiscence of the flesh draws sin.

Original sin, then, is the guilt which all conceived in concupiscence draw.

Hence it is written in *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that every human being conceived through intercourse of man and woman is born with original sin, subject to ungodliness and death, and for this reason born a child of wrath by nature; from which no one is freed except through faith in the mediator between God and men.”

By these and other authorities it is clearly shown that original sin is guilt and is drawn from parents by all who are begotten in concupiscence.

### What is called original sin: namely, the tinder of sin, that is, concupiscence

7. It remains now to see what original sin itself is. Since it is not actual sin, it is not an act or movement of soul or body. For if it is an act of soul or body, it is certainly actual sin. But it is not actual sin; therefore it is not an act or movement. What, then, is called original sin? The tinder of sin (*fomes peccati*), namely concupiscence or concupiscibility, which is called the law of the members, the sickness of nature, the tyrant in our members, or the law of the flesh.

Thus Augustine, in *On the Baptism of Infants*, vol. 7:

> There is in us concupiscence, which must not be permitted to reign. There are also its desires, which are actual concupiscences: they are the weapons of the devil, which arise from the sickness of nature. This sickness is a tyrant that moves evil desires. Therefore, if you wish to be the victor over the tyrant and find the enemy unarmed, do not obey evil concupiscence.

These words sufficiently show that concupiscence is the tinder of sin.

### That by “concupiscence” is understood the tinder of sin, and what is called the tinder of sin

8. By the term “concupiscence” he signified not the act of desiring but the primal defect, when he called it the law of the flesh. Hence the same author, in a treatise *On the Words of the Apostle*, says:

> There is always conflict in the body of this death, because the very concupiscence with which we are born cannot be ended as long as we live. It can be diminished daily, but it cannot be ended. What, then, is this concupiscence with which we are born? It is certainly a defect which makes the infant capable of desiring and also makes the adult actually desirous. For just as in the eye of a blind person, in the night, the defect of blindness exists but does not appear, and one cannot distinguish between the sighted and the blind except when light comes; so in a child the defect does not appear until the time of more advanced age arrives.

From this we are given to understand what original sin is: namely, the defect of concupiscence which entered through Adam into all born in concupiscence and corrupted them. Hence Augustine, vol. 7, *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book 1, chs. 9 and 10:

> Besides the example of imitation, Adam also infected within himself all who would come from his stock with the hidden contagion of his fleshly concupiscence. Hence the Apostle rightly says: “In whom all sinned.” The Apostle says this carefully and without ambiguity. For whether it is understood as “in which man” or “in which sin,” it is sound. For all sinned in Adam as in their material source, not merely by his example, as the Pelagians say. For all were that one man: that is, they were materially in him. It is thus clear that all sinned in Adam, as in a mass. For he himself, corrupted through sin, begot all who were born under sin. Therefore, just as all were made sinners from him, so all are rightly said to have sinned in that one sin which entered the world; because, just as they cannot be free from that one man, so they cannot be free from that one sin unless they are absolved from its liability through Christ’s baptism. Other sins, therefore, are personal sins, in which only those whose sins they are commit sin; but this is the one sin in which all sinned—that is, by which all were made sinners.

### What is the sin in which all sinned: namely, original sin, which proceeded from disobedience

[Col. 0723]

9. This is original sin, by which all conceived in concupiscence are born sinners; it flowed forth from Adam, or from his disobedience, and migrated into his descendants. Hence the Apostle subsequently says that many were made sinners through the disobedience of one man—which is actual sin. But when he says that through one man sin entered the world and that all sinned in it, this must be understood as said of original sin.

### In what sense it was said, “Through the disobedience of one, many were made sinners”

10. Therefore the statement, “Through the disobedience of one, many were made sinners,” must be understood in this sense: from Adam’s disobedience—that is, from Adam’s actual sin—proceeded the original sin by which all are born sinners, so that it was in him and passed into all.

### That original sin was from Adam and is in us

11. Augustine, responding to the heretic Julian, who maintained that there is no sin in infants, plainly asserts that original sin proceeded from Adam’s will and entered the world through his disobedience.

For Julian asks by what means sin is found in an infant:

> This one who is born does not sin; the one who begot him does not sin; the one who created him does not sin. Through what cracks, then, among so many safeguards of innocence, do you imagine sin has entered?

Holy Scripture replies: “Through one man sin entered into the world”; “through the disobedience of one,” says the Apostle. What more does he seek? What could he seek that is clearer?

Julian likewise says: “If sin entered into the world through man, sin is either from will or from nature. If it is from will, it is an evil will that produces sin; but if from nature, nature is evil.” To this I answer: sin is from will. Perhaps he asks whether original sin is from will. I answer: original sin too is wholly from will, because it was sown from the will of the first man, so that it was in him and passed into all.

[Note: Col. 0723. In Book 2 to Valerius, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 28, vol. 7.]

### Objection of some against the statement above that all human beings were in Adam

12. Against what we have said, that all human beings were in Adam, some adherents of words object as follows: “Not all flesh derived from Adam could have existed in him simultaneously, because it is of much greater quantity than Adam’s body was. Nor did that body contain as many atoms as the number of human beings descended from him. Therefore,” they assert, “it is not true that the substance of each person was in the first parent.”

### Reply, explaining how they were in Adam according to seminal reason, and how they descended from him by the law of propagation

13. It may be answered that all which naturally exists in human bodies is said to have been in the first man materially and causally, not formally. It descends from the first parent by the law of propagation; it has increased and multiplied within itself, no external substance passing into it; and it will rise again in the future.

It receives nourishment from foods, but foods are not converted into human substance—that is, into the substance descending from Adam through propagation. For when Adam begot his children, he transmitted some small part of his substance to their bodies: that is, something small was divided from the mass of his substance, and the son’s body was formed from it and increased by its own multiplication, without the addition of an external thing. From that substance, thus increased, something is separated from which the bodies of descendants are formed. In this way the order of procreation proceeds by the law of propagation to the end of the human race.

Thus it is plain to those who understand carefully and clearly that all were in Adam bodily according to seminal reason, and descended from him by the law of propagation.

### It is proved by authority and reason that nothing external is converted into the human substance which is from Adam

14. That nothing external passes into the nature of the human body is indicated by Truth in the Gospel, saying in Matthew 35 [probably 15]: “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the belly and is expelled into the privy.” This can also be shown by reasoning in the following manner.

A child who dies immediately after birth will rise in that stature which he would have had if he had lived to the age of thirty, unhindered by any bodily defect. From where, then, will that substance, so small when dead, be so large at the resurrection, unless by its own multiplication within itself? It follows that even if he had lived, that substance would have increased not from elsewhere but within itself. This is like the rib from which woman was made, and like the Gospel loaves.

We nevertheless do not deny that food and fluids pass into flesh and blood; but they do not pass into the true substance of human nature which descends from the first parents and which alone will exist in the resurrection. The remaining flesh, into which foods pass, will be laid aside at the resurrection as superfluous, though it is built up by nourishment from foods and other things.

## DISTINCTION XXXI. HOW ORIGINAL SIN PASSES FROM PARENTS TO CHILDREN: WHETHER ACCORDING TO THE SOUL, THE FLESH, OR BOTH

1. It remains to investigate how sin is transmitted from parents to children: whether according to the soul alone, according to the flesh, or according to both. Some thought that original sin is drawn according to the soul, and not according to the flesh alone, because they believed that not only the flesh but also the soul was derived by transmission. For just as in the generation of offspring the child’s flesh is substantially drawn from paternal flesh, so they believed that the soul of the begotten person was essentially derived from the soul of the begetter. Thus, just as corrupted flesh is sown from corrupted flesh, so they say that a sinful soul, infected with original corruption, is drawn from a sinful soul.

### He condemns the preceding opinion, says that sin is transmitted through the flesh, and explains how

2. But the catholic faith rejects and condemns this as contrary to truth, admitting that not souls but flesh alone is derived by transmission, as we said above. Original sin, therefore, is drawn from parents not according to the soul but according to the flesh alone.

For original sin, as we said above, is concupiscence—not an act, but a defect. Hence Augustine: “Concupiscence itself is the law of the members or of the flesh; it is a certain morbid affection, or sickness, which stirs unlawful desire, that is, fleshly concupiscence, called the law of sin.” It is said to remain in the flesh not because it arises in the soul, but because through the corruption of the flesh it arises in the soul.

### He explains the cause of the flesh’s corruption, from which sin arises in the soul

3. For flesh was corrupted in Adam because of sin, to such an extent that, although before sin man and woman could unite without the stimulus of lust and the heat of concupiscence, and their marriage-bed was undefiled, after sin bodily union cannot occur without lustful concupiscence. This is always a defect, and is also guilt unless excused by the goods of marriage.

Therefore the flesh that is to be formed into the body of offspring is conceived in concupiscence and lust. Hence the very flesh conceived is polluted and corrupted in sinful concupiscence. When the soul is infused, through contact with that flesh it draws a stain by which it is defiled and made liable: namely, the defect of concupiscence, which is original sin.

### That sin is said to be in the flesh because the corruption of the flesh is the cause of sin

4. For this reason sin itself is said to remain in the flesh. The flesh, then, which is sown in lustful concupiscence possesses neither guilt nor an act of guilt, but the cause of guilt. Thus, in what is sown there is corruption; but in what is born there is the defect of concupiscence.

Hence Ambrose, vol. 4, commentary on Romans, ch. 7, says:

> How does sin dwell in the flesh, when it is not a substance but the privation of good? Behold: the first man’s body was corrupted through sin, and that very corruption remains in the body by the condition of the offense, retaining the force of the divine sentence given in Adam; by association with it the soul is stained by sin. Therefore sin is said to dwell in the flesh through that which remains as the cause of its occurrence. This is the law of the flesh.

The same author says:

> Sin does not dwell in the soul but in the flesh, because the cause of sin is from the flesh, not from the soul. For the flesh is from the origin of sinful flesh, and through transmission all flesh becomes a cause of sin. But the soul is not transmitted, and therefore does not have in itself the cause of sin.

Augustine likewise shows in a sermon *On the Words of the Apostle* that the soul contracts sin from the flesh, saying, vol. 10: “The defect of concupiscence is what the soul has contracted, not from itself, but from the flesh. For human nature was not originally established by God’s work with a defect; rather, by the free choice of earlier human beings it was wounded by a defect that came upon it. Thus there is in the flesh not good but the defect by which the soul is infected.”

### Whether the cause of original sin, which is in the flesh, is guilt, punishment, or something else

5. Here it is commonly asked whether the cause of original sin, said to be in the flesh, is guilt, punishment, or something else. It cannot be guilt, because guilt is not in an irrational thing. For if guilt were in the flesh before the infusion of the soul, it would be either actual or original. But actual guilt is not there; nor is it original guilt, because it is itself the cause of original sin. But if it is punishment, what punishment is it? Passibility, mortality, or another corruption; for it is agreed that these defects are present in flesh.

### Here is explained what the foulness drawn from the lust of those uniting is, which may be called a defect or corruption

6. It may be said in reply that a manifold defect of the flesh, and especially a certain pollution which the flesh contracts, while being conceived, from the heat of the parents’ intercourse and their lustful concupiscence, is the cause of original sin. This may rightly be called a defect or corruption of the flesh. This foulness seems greater in flesh transmitted through concupiscence than in the flesh from which it is transmitted.

That a defect or corruption is in the flesh before the soul’s conjunction is proved by its effect: when the soul is infused, it is stained by the flesh’s corruption, just as one recognizes a defect in a vessel when wine poured into it turns sour.

### By analogous examples he shows that it is not absurd to say that children draw sin from parents who are themselves cleansed

7. So that we may not wonder or be troubled in mind on hearing that children draw original sin from parents already cleansed of that sin through baptism, Augustine indicates through various analogies in *On the Baptism of Infants* that this can occur:

> Just as the foreskin is removed by circumcision, yet remains in the one whom circumcised persons beget; and just as chaff, separated with such great care by human labor, nevertheless remains in the grain born from cleansed wheat: so the sin cleansed from parents through baptism remains in those whom they beget. For they beget from that which they still draw as old; not from that by which the law has advanced them in newness among the children of God. Parents do not generate children according to that generation by which they have been born again, but rather according to that by which they themselves were first carnally generated.

### Why it is called original: summary

8. It has now been shown what original sin is, and how it passes from parents to children and through the flesh into the soul. From this it is also apparent why it is called original sin: namely, because it is transmitted from the defective law of our origin in which we are conceived, namely the lustful concupiscence of the flesh, as was said above.

For we do not draw sin simply because we are conceived from flesh derived from Adam, since Christ’s body too was formed from the same flesh which descended from Adam. But Christ’s conception was accomplished not by the law of sin—that is, not through the concupiscence of the flesh—and therefore his flesh was not sinful; indeed, it was accomplished by the operation of the Holy Spirit. Our conception, however, does not occur without lust, and therefore is not without sin.

Augustine clearly shows this in *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, in the middle of the second [book], vol. 3:

> Since the intercourse of parents is not without lust when man and woman unite with one another, the conception of children born from their flesh cannot be without sin. It is not propagation that transmits sin to infants, but lust; it is not the fruitfulness of human nature that makes human beings be born with sin, but the foulness of lust which human beings possess from the utterly just condemnation of that sin.

Therefore blessed David, because of original sin by which the children of wrath are naturally bound, says in Psalm 50: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me.”

It is thus apparent that original sin is transmitted from the law of conception, because unless conception occurred in the flesh in this manner, the soul would not draw the defect of concupiscence from its union with the flesh.

### Objection of some who attempt to prove that sin is not transmitted through the law of intercourse

9. But this is opposed as follows. In conception itself, where sin is said to be transmitted, flesh is propagated; yet, according to natural philosophy, the soul is not infused then, but only after the bodies have been formed. Moses too clearly indicates this in Exodus, ch. 21, where he says concerning the striking of a pregnant woman: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and causes a miscarriage, if the offspring is still unformed, he shall be fined money; but if it is formed, he shall give life for life.” “Formed” is understood as animated by its own soul; “unformed,” as not yet possessing a soul.

Therefore, when flesh is propagated at conception, the soul is not yet infused. How, then, is sin transmitted there, since sin cannot exist where there is no soul?

It may be answered that sin is said to be transmitted in that conception not because original sin is then present there, but because the flesh there contracts that from which sin arises in the soul when it is infused. And both are called conception: both when the flesh is propagated and receives the form of a human body, and when the soul is infused; this is sometimes also called birth. Hence it is said: “What has been born in her.” Properly speaking, however, birth is the bringing forth into the light.

## DISTINCTION XXXII. HOW ORIGINAL SIN IS FORGIVEN IN BAPTISM, WHEN THE CONCUPISCENCE CALLED ORIGINAL SIN REMAINS AFTERWARD

1. Since it has been said above that original sin is the defect of concupiscence, and since it has been explained how it is drawn from parents and why it is called original, it remains to investigate how it is forgiven in baptism, when the concupiscence which existed before baptism remains even afterwards. It therefore appears either that original sin is not concupiscence or that it is not forgiven in baptism.
