For fleshly concupiscence remains, as Augustine says in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book 1, ch. 25, vol. 7, in “the body of this death”; we are commanded not to obey its sinful desires. Yet this concupiscence is daily diminished in those who advance and live continently.

But although concupiscence remains after baptism, it nevertheless does not rule and reign as before. Rather, through the grace of baptism it is mitigated and diminished, so that afterward it cannot rule unless someone restores strength to the enemy by following concupiscences. After baptism it does not remain as a ground of liability, because it is not imputed as sin; it is only the punishment of sin. Before baptism, however, it is both punishment and guilt.

### That original sin is forgiven in two ways: by its own diminution and by the removal of liability
2. Original sin is therefore said to be remitted in baptism for a twofold reason: because through the grace of baptism the vice of concupiscence is weakened and diminished, so that it no longer reigns unless strength is restored to it by consent; and because its guilt is dissolved. Hence Augustine, in *On the Baptism of Infants*:

> By baptism grace brings it about that the old man is crucified and the body of sin destroyed; not so that the concupiscence diffused through and inborn in this living flesh is suddenly consumed and ceases to exist, but so that it does not harm one who has died, though it was present in him when born. For if after baptism he lives, he has concupiscence in the flesh against which to fight, and, with God’s help, to overcome—provided that he has not received His grace in vain. Therefore baptism does not confer this, except perhaps by an ineffable miracle of the Creator: that the law of sin which is in the members be utterly extinguished and cease to exist. Rather, it confers that whatever evil has been done, said, or thought by a human being is wholly abolished and regarded as though it had never occurred; while concupiscence itself, once the bond of guilt has been loosed—the bond by which the devil held the soul through it and separated it from its Creator—remains for the struggle. [Col. 0727]

Behold, by these words he plainly shows that it is remitted in baptism not because it does not remain after baptism, but because its guilt is abolished in baptism.

Then the same author shows that it is also remitted in baptism in this way: because by baptismal grace concupiscence itself is moderated and diminished. In the same book he says:

> The law of the flesh, which the Apostle calls sin when he says, Rom. 6, “Let not sin reign in your mortal body,” does not remain in the members of those reborn from water and the Holy Spirit as though no remission of it had taken place, where a wholly full remission of sins is effected. Rather, it remains in the oldness of the flesh as conquered and slain, unless by some unlawful consent it should in a manner revive and be recalled to its own kingdom and dominion.

Here it is plainly suggested that concupiscence is weakened in baptism, and for this reason too is said to be remitted—not only because its guilt is there dissolved. Scripture teaches this manner of remission by many other testimonies as well.

For Augustine says against Julian:

> The law which is in the members is a defect of the flesh, arising from the punishment of sin and from the propagation of death. But this law which is in the members has been remitted by spiritual regeneration, and remains in mortal flesh. It has been remitted because the guilt has been dissolved by the sacrament through which believers are reborn; yet it remains because it produces desires against which even believers struggle.

The same author, in a sermon *On the Concupiscence of the Flesh*, says:

> Through the grace of baptism and the washing of regeneration, the very guilt of concupiscence with which you were born has been dissolved, together with whatever evil you previously consented to through evil concupiscence, whether in thought, speech, or action.

The same author, in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, says:

> Although the concupiscence of the flesh is no longer reckoned as sin in the regenerate, nevertheless every offspring that is born is bound by original sin.

Likewise:

> The concupiscence of the flesh is remitted in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not reckoned as sin. For this is not to have sin: not to be guilty of sin.

Therefore, just as other sins pass away in act while remaining in guilt, such as homicide and the like, so conversely concupiscence may pass away in guilt while remaining in act. From what has been said it is clearly shown how original sin is remitted in baptism.

### On the defilement which the flesh contracts through the lust of intercourse: whether it is washed away in baptism

3. Here it is commonly asked whether the flesh itself is cleansed in baptism from that defilement which it contracted at conception from lustful concupiscence. Some think that, just as the soul is purified from guilt, so too the flesh is cleansed from that pollution: so that, just as the mystery of baptism is accomplished by two things, namely water and the Spirit, so two things are purified there—the soul from guilt, namely, and the flesh from that contagion. This too is probable.

Others, however, think that only the soul is cleansed there, and that the flesh is not purified from that defilement. But if that defilement remains until the procreation of children, which occurs through the concupiscence of the flesh, then the nature of the flesh seems to be corrupted increasingly. The flesh of the offspring appears more corrupted than that of the parent, because, with the flesh retaining the pollution it had from conception, the offspring is derived in a polluted condition and is conceived in concupiscence, by which it too is defiled; and thus it is contaminated from a double cause. Hence the flesh’s pollution seems greater in the offspring than it was in the parent.

To this they reply that, although the offspring’s flesh is begotten from defiled flesh and conceived in the concupiscence of seed, it nevertheless contracts no greater defilement than the flesh from which it is begotten possessed. Even if, however, the flesh of the offspring is more foul and unclean, and therefore more corrupted than that of the parent, they say that truth is not thereby prejudiced. For they maintain that it is not absurd if the nature of the flesh is transmitted more corrupted in later generations, nor that the soul is thereby further infected from the more corrupted flesh. [Col. 0728]

### From what author this concupiscence comes—namely, God or another

4. Further, it is commonly asked whether the concupiscence which remains after baptism, and is only a penalty, whereas before baptism it was both penalty and fault, comes from God as its author or from another. We answer briefly: insofar as it is a penalty, it has God as its author; but insofar as it is fault, it has the devil or man as its author.

### By what justice this sin is imputed to a soul clean at creation, when it cannot avoid it

5. It is also commonly asked by what justice an innocent soul created by God is held liable for that sin, since it is not within its power to avoid it. For it is not committed through free choice, because the soul is not prior to being subject to that sin.

To this some say that the soul is guilty of that sin, although it was created clean by God, because when it is infused into the body it delights together with the flesh, and thereby contracts sin. But if this were so, it would be called actual rather than original sin.

It may more rightly be said that this sin, which the soul unavoidably contracts from the corruption of the body, is imputed to it because, as Augustine says, *City of God*, book 14, chapter 3, tome 5: “The corruption of the body which weighs down the soul was not the cause of the first sin, but its penalty; nor did corruptible flesh make the soul sinful, but the sinful soul made the flesh corruptible.”

### Whether that sin is voluntary or necessary

6. It may also reasonably be asked whether original sin should be called voluntary or necessary. It may be called necessary because it cannot be avoided. Hence the Prophet says: “Deliver me from my necessities.” Yet it is not incongruously called voluntary, because it proceeded from the will of the first man, as Augustine shows in *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 15:

> That which is called original sin in infants, although they do not yet exercise free choice of the will, is not absurdly called voluntary, because, having been contracted from the first man’s evil will, it has become in a manner hereditary.

### Why God joins the soul to the body, knowing that it will thereby be stained and therefore damned

7. But if it is asked why God, who made the soul itself without stain and knows that through union with the body it will contract the stain of sin and may at some time be separated from that body before baptism and so be damned, nevertheless joins it to the body: we answer that this proceeds from the height of God’s judgments, and that God does not act unjustly in doing so.

For He fittingly continues without alteration to preserve the order of the human condition which He established in the beginning, even though human sins have intervened: forming bodies from matter originally made without defect, creating souls from nothing, and completing the human being by their union. Therefore, since both natures of the human being were established by God without defect, although they have been corrupted through sin of their own accord, the unchangeable God ought not for that reason to change the primordial law of the human condition or cease from multiplying humankind.

### Whether the soul before baptism is such as God creates it

8. Some here commonly ask whether the soul before baptism is such as God creates it. They try to prove that it is not, as follows: the soul is created in a body, by union with which it is stained by sin. Therefore, as soon as it exists it has sin; nor did it exist before it had sin. Therefore it is not such as God creates it. For it is created by God innocent and without defect, yet it is never such.

One may answer that it is not wholly such as God made it. God made it good and bestowed goodness upon it without corruption. This is called the natural goodness which it received from its Creator in creation. It did not utterly lose that goodness through sin, but possessed it in a corrupted condition; nevertheless God made it without defect. For unless the soul were a good thing, evil could not exist in it, since evil cannot exist except in a good thing, as will be said below.

Therefore the soul is not altogether such as it was when created by God. It is like a person with polluted hands who does not possess an apple such as I gave with clean hands; for I gave it clean. [Col. 0729]

### Whether souls are equal from creation in natural gifts

9. It is likewise reasonably asked whether all souls are equal from creation, or whether some excel others. Many think, not without reason, that from creation itself some excel others in natural gifts: that one is more subtle in essence than another and more capable of understanding and remembering, being endowed, for example, with a keener mind and more penetrating intellect. This is not implausibly said, since it is known to have been so among angels.

Although some possess greater natural gifts than others, yet those who depart from the body before baptism receive an equal punishment, and those immediately after baptism receive an equal crown, because keenness or slowness of intellect does not determine reward or punishment in the future.

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. WHETHER INFANTS ORIGINALLY DERIVE THE SINS OF ALL PRECEDING FATHERS, AS THEY DERIVE ADAM’S SIN

1. To what has been said, it seems necessary to add the question whether the sins of preceding fathers pass to infants, just as we have said that the transgression of the first man redounded to all who are carnally begotten. And if the sins of parents pass to infants, whether those of all who have existed from Adam down to them do so, or those of some and not all.

### What Augustine seems to say on this in the *Enchiridion*

2. Augustine discusses this ambiguously in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 47, tome 3. For he seems to approve the view that the sins of preceding parents are imputed to infants, though not those of all who have existed from Adam, lest infants be burdened by an unbearable and excessive load of eternal punishment; but only those of the parents who preceded them by four generations. He confirms this with the words in which the Lord says in Exodus 20: “I am God, visiting the iniquities of the fathers unto the third and fourth generation”; as though the sins only of their nearest parents, and not others, were imputed to infants. This would be through the moderation of divine mercy. There, chapter 44.

### He presents the arguments of those who say that parents’ offences pass to infants

3. Those who hold this view confirm that infants are held not only by the transgression of the first man, but also by others, from the fact that infants as well as adults are said to be baptized for the remission of sins. David, though begotten in lawful marriage, says in Psalm 50: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me”; he does not say, “in iniquity” or “in sin.” Hence they think that not only the one original sin, but also the several sins which may be found in Adam’s sin, and the other sins of parents, are imputed to infants.

### That several sins are found in the one first sin

4. Augustine indicates in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 45, that several sins may be noted in Adam’s actual sin:

> Several sins may be understood in the one transgression of Adam, if it is divided, as it were, into its parts. For pride is there, because man preferred to be under his own power rather than God’s; and sacrilege, because he did not believe God; and homicide, because he cast himself headlong into death; and spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; and theft, because forbidden food was appropriated; and avarice, because he desired more than ought to have sufficed him; and whatever else may be found in this one sin.

Then, concerning the sins of preceding parents and whether they are imputed to infants, he argues more by conjecture than assertion, saying as follows, *ibid.*, chapter 49:

> It is not implausibly said that infants are bound by the sins of parents, not only of the first human beings, but also of their own parents from whom they were born. For that divine sentence, Deut. 5, “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children,” holds them before regeneration, to such an extent that even one begotten from lawful marriage says, Psalm 50: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me.” He did not say “in iniquity” or “in sin,” though that too could rightly have been said, but preferred to say “iniquities” and “sins,” because in that one sin which passed into all human beings—and is so great that by it human nature was changed into a necessity of death—there are found, as I discussed above, several sins and also other sins of parents. Though these cannot so alter nature, they bind children by guilt unless the grace of God comes to their aid (*Enchiridion*, chapter 47).  
>
> But concerning the sins of other parents, through whom each person succeeds in his own generations from Adam himself down to his own father, it may reasonably be debated whether one who is born is implicated in the evil acts of them all and in their multiplied original offences, so that each person is worse off the later he is born. Or whether God threatens descendants with the sins of their parents to the third and fourth generation because, in the moderation of His mercy, He does not extend His wrath further with respect to the faults of progenitors; lest those to whom the grace of regeneration is not given be weighed down by an excessive burden in eternal damnation itself, if they were compelled to contract originally the sins of all their preceding parents from the beginning of the human race and pay the punishments due for them. Whether anything may or may not be discovered concerning so great a matter by more careful examination and treatment of the Holy Scriptures, I do not dare rashly to affirm.

Behold, it becomes clear to the reader that Augustine said the foregoing not as assertions, but in reporting differing opinions. [Col. 0730]

### He shows that Augustine would contradict himself if he held this view

5. Otherwise Augustine would appear to contradict himself, since in the same work, chapter 93, he calls the punishment of infants who are held only by original sin the mildest of all, in these words:

> Certainly the mildest punishment will be theirs who, beyond the sin which they contracted originally, have added no further sin; and among the rest who have added further sin, each will have a more tolerable damnation there in proportion as he has had less iniquity.

Here he plainly says that the punishment of infants is the lightest of all punishments. If this is so, then they are not bound by the sins of preceding parents, except Adam’s. For if they were eternally punished for their parents’ actual sins as well as their own original sin, they would no longer be punished less, but perhaps more, than their parents themselves.

Therefore infants will be damned not for their parents’ actual sins, nor even for the first parent’s actual sins, but for the original sin which is derived from their parents. For it they will suffer no other punishment of material fire or the worm of conscience, except that they will lack the vision of God forever. Therefore infants are bound by one sin, not several.

Hence Augustine also explains in the same work, chapter 44, the points by which that opinion seems to be supported—namely, that Scripture sometimes signifies that sins and iniquities exist in infants, using the plural number:

> Because in Scripture the plural number is often signified by the singular, as in Num. 21: “Pray therefore to God, that He may take away the serpent from us”; it does not say “serpents,” though the people suffered from them. And conversely the singular is signified by the plural, as in the Gospel, Matt. 2: “For those who sought the child’s life are dead”; it does not say, “he is dead,” although it was speaking of Herod. And in Exodus 32: “They made golden gods,” though they made one calf, of which they said: “These are thy gods, Israel.” Thus the one original sin is signified by the plural when we say that infants are baptized for the remission of sins and are conceived in sins or iniquities.

### Whether Adam’s actual sin is graver than other sins

6. Here it is commonly asked whether Adam’s sin of transgression, from which original sin proceeded and in which several sins were noted above, was graver than other sins. To some this seems so, because that sin changed the whole of human nature. Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 48:

> That one sin, committed in a place and condition of such great happiness, is so great that in one man the whole human race was originally and, so to speak, radically damned.

The same author says in *City of God*, book 14, chapter 12:

> That command was violated with so much the greater injustice because it could have been observed with greater ease. For concupiscence had not yet resisted the will itself, as later occurred as a penalty of transgression.

Those who say that this sin was graver than the other sins of other people employ these and other authorities. They also endeavor to show it by reason as follows: that sin did more harm than any other, because it corrupted the whole human race and surely subjected it to death—something effected by no other sin. Therefore that sin had a greater evil effect than any other.

### Reply against them, showing that other sins are greater than it

7. To this one may say that, although that sin changed human nature into the necessity of death and spread guilt through the whole human race, it should nevertheless not be thought graver than sin against the Holy Spirit, which, as Truth says in Matt. 12, is forgiven neither in this world nor in the world to come.

That it corrupted the whole human nature is not because it was graver than all other sins, but because it was committed by man at a time when the whole human nature existed in one man, and therefore was wholly corrupted in him. It produced a greater evil effect with respect to the many defects flowing from it, but not with respect to eternal punishment; for it did not deserve a punishment graver than that which many later deserved through other sins. Indeed, we believe that others earned a wrath more severe than Adam earned.

### Whether this sin was forgiven the first parents

8. But if it is asked whether that sin was forgiven the first parents, we say that through repentance they obtained pardon. Hence Augustine says in *On the Baptism of Infants*:

> Just as those first parents, by later living justly, are believed through the Lord’s blood to have been freed from final punishment, though they did not in that life merit restoration to paradise; so too the flesh of sin, even when sins have been remitted, does not immediately merit, if a person has lived justly in it, not to suffer the death which it derived from the propagation of sin.

### That parents’ sins are visited upon children, and that what God says in Exodus and Ezekiel is not contradictory

9. Although infants are not bound by parents’ sins except Adam’s, it must nevertheless not be denied that parents’ sins redound upon children. Thus the Lord says to Moses in Exodus 20: “I am a mighty and jealous God, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation, upon those who hate me.” These words plainly suggest that God repays the sins of fathers upon the third and fourth children.

Yet this seems opposed by what the Lord says in Ezekiel 18:

> What is this proverb that you use among yourselves, saying: “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge”? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be used by you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

By these words God seems through the prophet to correct what He had wrongly said in the law. For if He repays parents’ sins unto the third and fourth generation, God’s justice seems to require that one person sin and another be punished. How can it be just that one should sin and another pay the penalty for sin?

### Resolution showing the harmony of the foregoing authorities

10. But, as Jerome says, tome 5, in his explanation of Ezekiel chapter 8: lest the Law and the Prophets—that is, Exodus and Ezekiel—or rather God Himself, who spoke both here and there, appear to differ in judgment, let us note the end of that Exodus statement. For after saying, “I repay the iniquities of the fathers upon the children,” He adds, “upon those who hate me.” By this He plainly shows that children are punished not because their fathers sinned, but because, through a sort of hereditary evil, they likewise hate God.

Therefore what the Lord says in Exodus, as Jerome explains, does not mean what many suppose, nor is it like this proverb, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes,” and so forth. Jerome, commenting on that passage of Ezekiel, and Augustine, commenting on the Psalm, “O God, be not silent concerning my praise,” judge that the Exodus passage must be understood of children who imitate their fathers’ sins. God is said to repay the fathers’ sins upon them because He punishes them for imitating their fathers’ sins, not because their fathers sinned.

Thus God does not correct through the prophet what He had previously said in the law, but explains how it ought to be understood. Hence He rebukes those who understood it perversely and said, “The fathers have eaten,” and so forth. [Col. 0732]

### Why He spoke of the third and fourth generation, and why He mentioned fathers only

11. Nevertheless, if that passage concerns imitators of evil persons, why did He mention only the third and fourth generation, when in every generation those who imitate their fathers’ sins are guilty? And why did He mention fathers, when all who imitate the sins of any evil persons are likewise evil?

But He named fathers especially because children are most accustomed to imitate fathers, whom they especially love. He mentioned the third and fourth generation because parents sometimes live so long as to have children of the third and fourth generation; seeing their fathers’ iniquities, these become heirs of their impiety through imitation. In this way what is said in Exodus is rightly understood literally.

### How the Exodus passage should be understood mystically

12. That it must also be understood mystically is shown by its being called a parable. For if it is a parable, as Jerome says, it sounds one thing in words and contains another in meaning. Thus some expound it as follows. They say that the father in us is the light stir of the senses, namely the first movement of suggestion or thought; the son, if thought has conceived, is sin, in which the woman’s consent and delight are signified; the grandson, if you have brought into act what you thought and conceived, or have resolved to bring it into act, in which the man’s consent—or the completion of sin—is signified; and the great-grandson, if you have not only done it but gloried in it. This is the fourth generation, not because three have preceded it, but because it is counted fourth from the first motion, which is as it were the father.

Therefore God will not punish eternally the first and second impulses of thoughts, which the Greeks call *propatheiai*—“pre-passions”—and without which no human being can exist. But He will punish if someone resolves to do what has been thought, or refuses to correct what has been done: these are mortal sins, the third and fourth generation.

### How it is proved that the first motion is not punished eternally

13. To prove, as Jerome says, that the first impulse of thought is not eternally punished by God, one should adduce Genesis 9. For Ham sinned in mocking his father’s nakedness, yet it was not he but his son Canaan who received the sentence: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be the servant of his brothers.” What justice is there in the father’s sinning and the son’s being punished? But this event occurred in mystery.

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. MATTERS TO BE CONSIDERED CONCERNING SIN

1. After the foregoing, certain matters concerning actual sin must be considered by careful inquiry: namely, what was the origin and cause of the first sin, whether it was a good thing or an evil thing; then, in what thing sin exists and in how many ways it comes to be; and the differences among sins themselves.

### What was the first origin and cause of sin

2. The first cause and origin of sin was a good thing, because before the first sin there was nothing evil from which it could arise. For when it had an origin and cause, it had it either from good or from evil. But evil did not previously exist; therefore it arose from good.

For sin first arose in the angel, and afterwards in man. And what was the angel except a good nature created by God? The evil which was in the angel did not arise from God, nor from anything other than the angel; therefore it arose from good. Hence Augustine, in his *Replies against the Heretic Julian*, to Julian’s statement, “If sin is from nature, then nature is evil,” says:

> I ask him to answer, if he can. It is clear that all evil works, like evil fruits, arise from an evil will, as from an evil tree. But from what does he say that the evil will itself arose, if not from good? For if from an angel, what is an angel but a good work of God? If from a human being, what was that human being but a good work of God? Indeed, what were these two before an evil will arose in them, except a good work of God and a good and praiseworthy nature? Therefore evil arises from good, and there was nothing else from which it could arise except good. I say, therefore, that no evil preceded the evil will, but that it had its origin from good.

Here it is plainly said that the first cause and origin of evil was a good nature. At the same time it is shown of which sin it was the cause, namely, of evil will.

### That evil will was the secondary cause of evils

3. But that evil will of angel and man is also the cause of subsequent evils: namely evil works and evil wills. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 23, tome 3:

> We must not doubt at all that the cause of the good things that concern us is nothing other than the goodness of God; but the cause of evil things is the will of mutable good falling away from immutable good—first the angel’s, then man’s. This is the first evil of a rational creature: that is, the first privation of good.

Here you have that the first will of mutable good—that is, of angel and man—falling away from immutable good, that is, God, is the cause of evil things concerning us, because it is the cause both of sins and of the punishments by which human nature is afflicted. Therefore the first origin and cause of sin was good; the second was the evil which arose from good.

### In what thing sin exists: whether in a good thing or an evil thing; and that it exists only in a good thing

4. Having shown the origin of evil, it remains to see in what thing evil exists: whether in a good thing or in an evil thing. Whoever thinks rightly and keenly understands that evil exists only in good—that is, in a good nature. For evil is corruption or privation of good; but where there is no good, there can be no corruption or privation of good. Therefore sin can exist only in a good thing.

For just as bodies are corrupted by diseases and wounds—which, as Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 11, are privations of the good called health—so all defects of souls are privations of natural goods. For what else is called evil except privation of good? It is evil for good to be diminished; yet however greatly it is diminished, something must remain so long as nature remains. For the good which is nature cannot be consumed unless nature itself is consumed.

When nature is corrupted, its corruption is evil because it deprives it of some good. For if it deprived it of no good, it would do no harm. But it does harm; therefore it removes good. So long, then, as nature is corrupted, there is good in it of which it may be deprived. Thus there is nothing called evil if there is no good; but good wholly free of evil is uncorrupted good. When evil is present, however, the good is spoiled or defective; and no evil can ever exist where no good exists.

Hence the striking conclusion follows: because every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, when a defective nature is called an evil nature, nothing else seems to be meant than that evil is what is good, and that nothing is evil except what is good. In this connected argument it is plainly suggested that evil cannot exist except in a good thing; and it is also manifestly said, however paradoxical this may seem, that what is good is evil. [Col. 0733]

### What follows from this: that when a human being is called evil, a good thing is called evil

5. From this it follows that when one says “an evil human being,” one means nothing other than an evil good. Hence Augustine adds in the same work:

> What is an evil human being except an evil nature? For a human being is a nature. Now if a human being is some good because he is a nature, what else is an evil human being except an evil good? Yet when we distinguish these two things, we find that he is not evil because he is human, nor good because he is unjust; but good because he is human, evil because he is unjust. Therefore every nature, even if defective, is good insofar as it is nature; insofar as it is defective, it is evil.

### That the dialecticians’ rule concerning contraries fails in the case of good and evil

6. Accordingly, in the case of these contraries called evil and good, the dialecticians’ rule fails, by which they say that two contraries cannot simultaneously belong to the same thing. No drink or food is at once sweet and bitter; no body is at once white and black in the same respect. And this is found in many, indeed nearly all, contraries: they cannot coexist in one thing.

Yet although no one doubts that good and evil are contraries, they can not only coexist, but evil cannot exist at all without good and except in good things. Indeed, if there were no good in which evil could exist, evil could not exist at all, because corruption would have neither a place in which to subsist nor something from which to arise unless there were something that could be corrupted; for corruption is nothing other than the destruction of good. Therefore evils arose from goods and do not exist except in goods. Nor was there anything from which any evil nature could arise except the good nature of angel and human being, from which evil will first arose. (*Ibid.*, chapter 15.)

### He makes an epilogue before passing to other matters

7. From these things it is made clear what we said above must first and second be investigated: namely, what was the origin of evil, and in what thing it exists. The foregoing testimonies prove that it arose from a good thing and subsists in a good thing.

### An objection from the prophecy saying: “Woe to those who call good evil!”

8. To the statement that evil is what is good, some object thus: if we say that good is evil, we fall under that prophetic sentence in Isaiah 5: “Woe to those who call good evil, and evil good!” Therefore, if we wish to avoid this curse, we must by no means say that good is evil, or conversely.

Augustine resolves this in the same work:

> What is said in the prophecy must be understood of the things by which people are evil, not of the people themselves. Therefore whoever calls adultery good falls under that prophetic condemnation; and so does one who calls an evil human being good, or an unjust person good. For whoever says that a human being, insofar as he is human, is evil, and that goodness is injustice, condemns God’s work, which is the human being, and praises the human defect, which is injustice. (*Enchiridion*, chapters 13 and 19.)

## DISTINCTION XXXV. WHAT SIN IS  
*(Against Faustus, tome 6, book 22, chapter 27)*

1. After this we must consider what sin is. Sin is, as Augustine says, everything said, done, or desired that is against the law of God.

The same author, in *On the Two Souls*, says: “Sin is the will to retain or attain what justice forbids.”

Both definitions concern actual and mortal sin, not venial sin. The first description shows sin to be an evil will, or corrupt speech and action—that is, an evil act both inward and outward. The second shows it to be only an inward act. For will, as was said above, is a motion of the mind; therefore it is an inward act.

Ambrose too, tome 4, in *On Paradise*, chapter 8, says:

> What is sin except transgression of the divine law and disobedience to the heavenly commandments? Therefore sin is in the transgressor, but fault is not in the commander. For sin could not exist if there had been no prohibition. But if sin did not exist, perhaps not only vice but also virtue would not exist, since virtue could neither subsist nor excel unless there had been certain seeds of vice.

Behold, Ambrose defines sin as transgression of the law and disobedience.

### He presents differing opinions concerning sin
2. Accordingly, on the occasion of this diversity of expressions, very many have held differing views concerning sin. Some say that only an evil will is sin, and not external acts; others, that both will and acts are sin; others, denying both, say that all acts are good and are from God and from God as their author, while evil is nothing, as Augustine says on John. [Note: [Col. 0735] Vol. 9, tractate on John, chapter 1]: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” that is, sin, which is nothing; and people become nothing when they sin. Augustine also said above that evil is a deprivation of good, or a corruption of good. And in book 83 Questions, question 36, he says: “The highest evil has no measure; for it lacks every good. But measure is something good. Therefore it does not exist, because it is contained under no form; and this entire name ‘evil’ has been devised from the deprivation of form.” Likewise, in vol. 3, *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 56, it is said that evil or wickedness was not created by God but invented by the devil, who himself was created good. Augustine also, in vol. 6, in the book *Against the Manichaeans*, ch. 8, shows what sin is, saying: “What is sinning but erring in the precepts of truth or in truth itself?” If people do not do this voluntarily, they are unjustly judged sinners. What, then, amid so great a variety, is to be maintained or said?

### The true position concerning sin is set forth

3. It may indeed be said, and ought freely to be taught, that sin is an evil inward and outward act: namely, evil thought, speech, and deed. Yet sin consists especially in the will, from which, as from an evil tree, evil works proceed as evil fruits.

### The teaching of some who say that an evil will and act, insofar as they exist, are natures and therefore good; but insofar as they are evil, are sins

4. Some, however, carefully attending to Augustine’s words, which he uses above and elsewhere in Scripture, quite intelligently teach that an evil will and evil acts, insofar as they exist or insofar as they are acts, are good; but insofar as they are evil, they are sins. They say that every will and act is a good nature made by God, insofar as it is an act or will, and is from God as author; but insofar as it occurs disorderly and contrary to God’s law, and lacks its due end, it is sin. Thus, insofar as it is sin, it is nothing. For it is no substance and no nature.

### By authorities they prove that all wills and acts are good insofar as they exist

5. They prove that every will and action is good insofar as it exists from Augustine’s statement, vol. 4, in *83 Questions*, question 21: “God is the cause only of good; accordingly he is not the author of evil, because he is the author of all things which exist; and these, insofar as they exist, are good.” Likewise, in the same place, question 27, proving that nothing occurs by chance in the world, he says:

> Whatever happens by chance happens rashly; whatever happens rashly does not happen by providence. Therefore, if some things happen by chance in the world, the universe is not governed by providence. If the universe is not governed by providence, there is some nature or substance which does not belong to the work of providence. But everything which exists, insofar as it exists, is good. For that is the highest good by participation in which other things are good; and everything mutable is good, insofar as it exists, not through itself but through participation in that good—which we also call divine providence. Therefore nothing happens by chance in the world.

They rely on these testimonies to show that everything which exists is good insofar as it exists. Thus the same Augustine, vol. 3, in book 1 of *On Christian Teaching*, ch. 32, says: “He exists supremely and originally who is altogether unchangeable; and all other things which exist could not exist except from him, and they are good insofar as they have received being.”

### What follows from the foregoing

6. From the foregoing it is gathered and inferred that, if an evil will and an evil action exist, they are good insofar as they exist. But who denies that an evil will and an evil action exist? Therefore an evil will or action, insofar as it exists, is good; and likewise, insofar as it is a will or action, it is good. But it is evil through a defect, and this defect is not from God and is not anything. Augustine, vol. 4, seems to have noted this in *83 Questions*, question 3, saying: “A defect is a will by which a human being becomes worse; and this defect, as reason teaches, is far removed from the will of God.” From this passage they prove that a will, insofar as it is defective, is not from God; insofar as it is defective, it is sin, they say, insofar as it has neither due order nor due end. So too an action, insofar as it proceeds from evil, lacks order, and tends toward evil.

### Another proof that every act is good insofar as it exists

7. Again, they prove in another way that every inward or outward act is good insofar as it exists: an evil act could not exist unless it were a good thing, because no thing is evil unless that same thing is good. Thus Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 13: “Every nature is good; nor would any thing be evil unless the thing itself which is evil were a nature. Therefore evil cannot exist unless there were some good.” Although this seems absurd to say, the connection of the reasoning compels us to say it.

From the foregoing testimonies they maintain that all acts, insofar as they exist, are good things; nor is anything evil—that is, sin—unless the same thing is in some respect also good. They declare God the author of all things which exist, insofar as they exist; and they say that all things whatsoever exist by his will, and that, insofar as they exist, they are natures.

### Objection to those who say that all acts are good insofar as they exist

8. The following is objected to them: If all things which exist are good insofar as they exist, and are natures, then adultery, homicide, and similar things, insofar as they exist, are good and are natures, and occur by God’s will. But if this is so, then those who do such things do good deeds—which is utterly absurd.

They reply as follows: adultery, homicide, and the like do not signify acts simply, but defects of acts. The acts themselves of adultery and homicide, insofar as they exist or insofar as they are acts, are from God and are good natures; but not insofar as they are adultery and homicide. Therefore, they say, it does not follow that, if the acts which are homicides and adulteries are from God, homicides and adulteries are from God.

### Another objection of theirs against the same persons

9. Again, they are challenged in another way: If nothing is evil which is not a nature or a good thing, how, then, are failures to believe in God, failures to go to church, and the like sins, since these are not natures—indeed, are not at all? For not going to church, not believing, and the like are not things or entities.

They reply that, in these and similar expressions—which seem simply to signify privations and to posit nothing, because they are stated negatively—something is truly posited, and acts are signified by them. Not believing in Christ, they say, is unbelief; and by the name “unbelief” an evil act of the mind is signified. Likewise, when it is said, “Not going to church is evil,” the contempt of the person who does not go is signified—that is, an evil will or intention. For this is turning aside from good, and is therefore evil; just as, conversely, turning aside from evil is good. Therefore, just as turning aside from evil posits something, namely the will and intention of avoiding evil—for what is wholly nothing cannot be good—so turning aside from good signifies something, namely the will and intention of evil. In this sense that general definition of mortal sin which Augustine set out above is true: “Sin [Col. 0737] is a saying,” etc.

### Whether an evil act, insofar as it is sin, is a deprivation or corruption of good

10. One may also ask them: since sin, as was said above, is a deprivation or corruption of good, and every evil act is sin, is it a deprivation or corruption of good insofar as it is sin, or not? For if, insofar as it is sin, it is a corruption of good, then, since the corruption or deprivation of good is a punishment for human beings, it is a punishment insofar as it is sin. If this is so, then insofar as it is sin it seems to be good and to be from God. But if it is not a corruption insofar as it is sin, then one asks in what respect it is a corruption. For if it is a corruption, and not insofar as it is sin, then, since it is not good except insofar as it is sin, it is a corruption or deprivation of good insofar as it is good.

They reply also to this that an evil act is a deprivation or corruption of good not insofar as it exists, nor insofar as it is good, but insofar as it is sin. Yet insofar as it is sin it is not a punishment, or anything from God. For, as is gathered from Augustine’s foregoing words, sin is called a corruption or deprivation actively, not passively. Evil or sin is called a corruption of good because it deprives a good nature of some good. For if it deprived it of no good, it would not harm it, as Augustine said above. But it does harm; therefore it takes away good. Yet it does not harm except insofar as it is sin; therefore, insofar as it is sin, it deprives of good. Thus, insofar as it is sin, it is a deprivation or corruption of good.

### How, insofar as sin is nothing, it can corrupt or remove good

11. But since sin is nothing insofar as it is sin, how can it corrupt or take away good? Augustine teaches you this in *On the Nature of Good*, saying: “Abstaining from food is not a substance; yet if the substance of the body abstains altogether from food, it languishes and is weakened. So sin is not a substance, yet by it the nature of the soul is corrupted.”

### That sin is properly a corruption of the soul, and how

12. Sin—that is, guilt—is properly a corruption of the soul. If one asks in what respect the soul can be corrupted, this is made clear in the parable of the man who fell among robbers, who wounded and stripped him, Luke 10. For a person falls among robbers when, through sin, he is delivered into the devil’s power; and then through sin he is stripped of gratuitous goods, that is, virtues, and wounded in natural goods. These are reason, understanding, memory, and intelligence, and the like; through sin they are darkened and impaired. Through sin he is also deprived of that good by participation in which the other goods are good; and he is deprived of it all the more as he removes himself further from it.

### How a human being removes himself from God—namely, through the dissimilarity which he produces, that is, sin

13. A person removes himself from God by sin, not through spatial distance, because God is wholly everywhere and present to all, and all things are in him, as Augustine says in *83 Questions*, question 20, vol. 4; and he himself is not a place. Yet the temple of God is improperly called God’s place, not because God is contained by it, but because he is present in it and dwells there; and this is understood to be the pure soul. Therefore through sin a person becomes distant from God not spatially, but because he departs from God’s likeness; and he is farther away in proportion as he becomes more unlike him.

But, as Augustine says in *83 Questions*, question 23, vol. 4, those things which are like God by participation can acquire dissimilarity. Likeness itself, however, can in no respect be dissimilar from anything. Hence, since the son is the likeness of the Father, he cannot in any respect be unlike the Father. Whatever things are like God are so by participation in that likeness, and they can acquire dissimilarity. Nothing makes a person so unlike God as sin does.

Since sin is a deprivation or corruption of the good which is in the soul, it is also a deprivation or corruption of the good of the body. Thus it deprived the human body of the benefit of that immortality and impassibility [Col. 0738] which it possessed before sin.

### Is punishment a deprivation of good?

14. It is commonly asked whether punishment too is a deprivation or corruption of good. The answer is easy if what was said above is recalled. We have said that deprivation or corruption of good is understood actively or passively—that is, according to agency or effect. Therefore both sin and punishment are called a deprivation or corruption of good: sin according to agency, because it deprives or corrupts good; punishment according to effect, that is, according to suffering, which is the effect of sin. For guilt is one thing and punishment another: the one is God’s, namely punishment; the other is the devil’s or the human being’s, namely guilt.

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. THAT SOME THINGS ARE AT ONCE SINS AND PUNISHMENTS OF SIN; SOME ARE SINS AND CAUSES OF SIN; AND OTHERS ARE SINS, CAUSES, AND PUNISHMENTS OF SIN

1. It must nevertheless be known that some things are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sins. Hence Augustine, on the passage of Psalm 57, “Fire fell upon them, and they did not see the sun,” says: “Fire is understood as pride, desire, and anger. Few see these punishments; therefore the Apostle especially mentions them in the Epistle to the Romans, where he enumerates many things which are sins and punishments of sin.” For between the first sin of apostasy and the final punishment of eternal fire, the intervening things are both sins and punishments of sin.

Gregory likewise, commenting on Ezekiel, says: “For one who despises and refuses to repent, God sets a stumbling-block, so that he may strike more heavily.” For “a sin which is not swiftly removed through repentance is either sin and cause of sin; or sin and punishment of sin; or at once sin, cause, and punishment of sin.” Hence Moses says, Genesis 15: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete.” David says, Psalm 68: “Add iniquity upon their iniquity.” And another prophet, Hosea: “Blood touched blood,” that is, sin was added to sin. Paul likewise says, Romans 1: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonourable passions,” etc. And again, 1 Thessalonians 2: “That they may always fill up their sins.” John too is told through an angel, Revelation 22: “Let the one who is filthy become filthy still.” From these testimonies it is gathered that a sin can be both sin and punishment of sin.

### From the foregoing a question arises: whether, insofar as it is sin, it is a punishment of sin  
(*On Free Will*, ch. 18)

2. It is therefore rightly asked whether, insofar as it is sin, it is a punishment of sin. This does not seem so, since every punishment of sin is just. Hence Augustine says in the *Retractations*: “Every punishment of sin is just and is called a penalty.” Therefore, if a sin which is both sin and punishment of sin is a punishment of sin insofar as it is sin, then, since every just punishment comes from the justice of God, it seems to be just and to proceed from God insofar as it is sin.

They answer that sin is called a punishment of sin because, through the sin into which a person falls, deservedly on account of a preceding sin, when God abandons him, a good nature is corrupted. Eternal fire, for example, is called the punishment of evil persons because they are tormented by it; yet the torment itself of evil persons is not fire, but is produced in the human being by fire. In the same way, nature is corrupted through sin, and the good of nature is diminished; and that diminution and corruption of good is suffering and punishment. It is not essentially the sin itself through which it comes about. But it is called sin, as stated above, because through sin, as soon as a person sins, that corruption occurs in the person; yet it occurs through God as author. For that punishment or suffering, which is a corruption of good, is from God. Its material and cause, so to speak, is sin, which is not from God.

Augustine, vol. 7, appears to have noted and understood this in this sense when he says in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 10: “By predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do. But God also foreknew what he himself was not going to do, namely all evils. For although there are certain things which are sins in such a way that they are also punishments of sin, according to that statement of the Apostle, ‘God gave them over [Col. 0739] to passions,’ etc., nevertheless sin is not God’s doing, but judgment is—namely, punishment.” For in Scripture punishment is often understood by the name “judgment.”

To attentive readers, he seems here to indicate that things which are sins and punishments of sin belong to God, not insofar as they are sins, but insofar as they are punishments. For after he had said that God would not do certain evils, namely sins, because it might be objected that some sins are also punishments of sin, and every punishment of sin is just and therefore from God, he added the remaining words in order to determine in what respect he does, or does not, do them.

According to the foregoing interpretation, sins are rightly called punishments. Hence the Apostle, Romans 1, calls them dishonourable passions, because, as the authority says, although certain sins give pleasure, they are nevertheless passions of a nature that ought not to be named, because nature is corrupted through them.

### Although every sin may be called punishment, not every sin is a punishment of sin

3. Although in this sense every mortal sin can be called a punishment, not every sin can be called a punishment of sin. For a punishment of sin, as stated above, is that whose cause is another preceding sin. A sin is called a punishment of sin in relation to a preceding sin, just as it is called a cause of sin in relation to a following sin. Hence the same sin may be both cause and punishment of sin: the punishment of one sin and the cause of another. For, as Gregory says in the *Morals*: “A sin not washed away by repentance immediately draws, by its own weight, into another.” Hence it is not only sin but also a cause of sin, because the subsequent sin arises from that guilt.

A sin arising from sin is not only sin but also a punishment of sin, because by a just judgment God darkens the heart of the sinner, so that he falls into further sins on account of the preceding sin’s desert. The one whom God was unwilling to free, he struck by abandoning him. Accordingly, as Augustine says, vol. 7, book 5 *Against Julian*, ch. 3: “This is a punishment of preceding sin, and yet it too is sin. For by the judgment of the most just God they were given over,” as the Apostle says of some, “whether by abandonment, or in another explicable or inexplicable way, to dishonourable passion, so that crimes might be punished by crimes, and the penalties of sinners might be not only torments but also increases of vices.” Therefore those sins which the Apostle enumerates, because they arise from pride, are not only sins but also punishments. From this it is now clear that some sins are also punishments and causes of sin; that sin is a punishment of sin which has a preceding sin as its cause; and that sin is a cause of sin which is the merit of a subsequent fault.

### The foregoing seems to signify that the very same things which are sins are also punishments of sin

4. But when he says that crimes are punished by crimes, he seems to suggest that the things which are sins are essentially punishments of sin—that is, penalties for sin. To this they reply that these and similar statements are made according to the foregoing rationale and must therefore be understood according to the explanation already given. For the meaning of statements must be taken from the reasons for making them. (Hilary, book 4 *On the Trinity*, not far from the middle.)

### What conflicts with truth if someone says that sins themselves are essentially punishments of sin

5. Yet it is thought that no prejudice is done to the truth if one says that the very things which are sins are essentially, so to speak, punishments—that is, penalties—of preceding sins, which are just and are from God. Nevertheless, they are not from God insofar as they are sins; nor are they punishments of sin insofar as they are sins. Yet insofar as they are sins, they are deprivations of good, but, as said above, they are called deprivations causally and actively.

### He clearly shows that certain sins are a punishment of sin, and that punishment itself is just and from God

6. Augustine, vol. 1, clearly teaches that some sins are punishments, and that this punishment itself is just and from God, in the *Retractations*, ch. 9, and in *On Free Will*, book 3, ch. 18. He says that some evil things are done [Col. 0740] by human beings from necessity, and that the same things are just punishments of sin:

> There are certain blameworthy things done from necessity, where a person wishes to do rightly and cannot. Hence the Apostle’s statement, Romans 7: “The good that I will, I do not do; but the evil that I hate, this I do.” And that statement, Genesis 2 [materially uncertain citation; probably Galatians 5]: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish.” But all these things arise from that condemnation of death. For if this is not a punishment of the human being, but nature, none of these things are sins. For if, in doing them, one does not depart from the manner in which the human being was naturally made, then one surely does what one ought. But if a human being is not good because he is such, and does not have it in his power to be good—whether because he does not see what sort of person he ought to be, or because he sees it and cannot be what he sees he ought to be—who can doubt that this is a punishment? Every punishment, if it is a punishment of sin, is just and is called a penalty. But if a punishment is unjust—since no one doubts that it is a punishment—it has been imposed on a human being by some unjust ruler. But since it is madness to doubt God’s omnipotence and justice, this punishment is just and is inflicted for some sin. For no one ruling unjustly could either snatch away a human being while God was ignorant, or extort from him against his will, as from one weaker, that an unjust punishment should torment a human being. It remains, therefore, that this just punishment comes from the condemnation of the human being.

By these and many other testimonies it is taught that certain things are both sins and, essentially, punishments of sin. Augustine, book 3 *On Free Will*, ch. 18, vol. 8.

### Certain things which are undoubtedly sins and punishments, such as anger and envy

7. Moreover, it must in no way be doubted that some sins are punishments without any qualification, such as envy, which is sorrow at another’s good, and anger. These too are sins, not insofar as they are punishments. The same must also be thought concerning desire, fear, and similar things. Hence Augustine says in *83 Questions*, question 77, vol. 4:

> Every disturbance is a passion; every desire is a disturbance. Therefore every desire is a passion. But whenever a passion is in us, we suffer through that very passion. Therefore, whenever desire is in us, we suffer through that very desire; and we suffer through it insofar as it is desire. But every passion, insofar as we suffer it, is not sin.

The same applies to fear. For it does not follow that, if we suffer fear, it is therefore not sin; many sins are things which we suffer, but not insofar as we suffer them.

### A statement of Jerome seems to conflict with Augustine’s foregoing words

8. It should be carefully noted that Jerome’s statement in the *Explanation of the Faith*, vol. 4, addressed to Pope Damasus, Distinction 28 of this Second Book, seems to conflict with Augustine’s words set out above—that some evil and blameworthy things are done from necessity. Although it has been given above, it is worth repeating that it may be more fully understood:

> We condemn the blasphemy of those who say that something impossible has been commanded to a human being by God, and that God’s commandments can be kept not by individuals but only by all collectively.

And shortly afterward:

> We say that those who, with Manichaeus, say that a human being cannot avoid sin are in error, just as are those who, with Jovinian, assert that a human being cannot sin.

Jerome plainly says that it is an error to say that a human being cannot avoid sin. But one who says that some things are done from necessity says that some things cannot be avoided. Therefore, since Augustine says this, either what he teaches seems to be erroneous, or what Jerome says seems not to be true.

### Resolution, from the teaching of the saints, removing the contradiction

9. To this it may be said that Augustine taught this according to the condition of this misery—to which ignorance and difficulty belong, as he says in book 13 of *On Free Will*, ch. 18, and which have descended from just condemnation—and there he included venial sins as well. Jerome, however, speaks only of mortal sins, which every person enlightened by grace can avoid; or else he says this concerning the human being in the condition of free choice before sin.

### He gives a summary before passing on to other matters

10. We have set out sufficiently carefully the opinion of those who say that all acts are good natures and are good insofar as they exist. In this treatment we inserted certain matters which are not to be understood as coming only from their position, because they are held without hesitation by all who think in a Catholic manner. We have also supported with authoritative testimonies and arguments the teaching of those who say that all acts are good in their essence—that is, insofar as they exist—while some are sins insofar as they occur disorderly.

They add that some acts are good not only in essence but also in kind—for example, feeding a hungry person, an act belonging to the class of works of mercy. They call other acts absolutely and perfectly good: those commended not only by their essence or kind, but also by their cause and end, such as acts which proceed from a good will and attain a good end.

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. THE OPINION OF OTHERS WHO SAY THAT EVIL ACTS ARE IN NO WAY FROM GOD, NOR GOOD EITHER IN THAT THEY EXIST OR IN ANY OTHER WAY

1. There are also many others who think very differently concerning sin and act. They maintain that an evil will and evil act are sins and in no respect good; nor are they from God as author in any respect, because they occur without God. For, as the Evangelist John says, chapter 1, “Without him nothing was made,” that is, sin, which is said to be nothing—not because an evil action or will, which is something, does not exist, but because it separates people from true being, draws them to evil, and thus leads them to non-being. For those who depart from participation in the highest good, which alone truly and properly exists, are rightly said not to exist. Augustine therefore says, vol. 9, tractate 1 on John, that sin is nothing and that people become nothing when they sin.

For this reason, those who say that sin removes a person from true being maintain that sin is nothing. They call an evil will, action, or speech sin because these are transgression and disobedience and are done against God’s law. Yet they exist, but are from the human being or the devil, not from God. They say that they are in no way from God, whether insofar as they exist or in any other respect.

### How they explain Augustine’s foregoing words: “Everything which exists is good insofar as it exists”

2. They also teach that Augustine’s words, in which he says that everything which exists is good insofar as it exists and has God as its author, must be understood only of nature or substances. By “substance” and “nature” they understand substances themselves and what they naturally possess, namely what is created together with them. Thus the soul naturally has understanding, intelligence, will, and the like. This is gathered from Augustine’s foregoing words, where he calls a human being a good nature and an evil human being an evil nature.

According to this assertion or interpretation, evil acts are not natures or substances; nor, indeed, are good acts. Augustine seems certainly to imply this in the *Retractations*, ch. 30, distinguishing substances or natures from good or evil actions. Explaining how a statement that he made in *On True Religion* should be understood, he says: “This was said concerning substances and natures. For the discussion there concerned these, not good actions and sins.” Here he plainly seems to distinguish natures or substances from actions or sins.

Therefore the aforesaid teachers maintain that inward or outward actions are not natures or substances; and if they are evil, they are sins and are not from God. Augustine appears to observe that evil acts are not natures in his first answer against the Pelagians [Note: [Col. 0741] The work called the *Hypognosticon against the Pelagians*, at the end, vol. 7], saying: “The works of the devil, which are called vices, are acts, not things.” In the fourth answer, [Col. 0742] in the same place, at the beginning: “No evil is a nature, but an act incidental to something through a defect of good. Therefore what is not a nature God did not make, because everything he made is a nature.” Likewise, in the same place: “Everything that is good by nature God made from nothing, not the devil.”

### Accordingly, some things from which people are evil are not from God

3. From this it is gathered that there are some things which are not from God, and through which people are evil. They likewise concede this, relying on Augustine’s words quoted above. In the *Enchiridion*, ch. 19, explaining the prophet’s words, Isaiah 5, “Woe to those who call good evil,” Augustine says that this is to be understood of the things through which people are evil, not of persons themselves. Therefore there are things through which people are evil.

But that through which a person becomes worse is not from God, because, as Augustine says in vol. 4, book *83 Questions*, question 3: “A human being does not become worse with God as author.” Therefore God is not the author of the things through which a human being becomes worse. Yet, as has been said, there are things through which people become evil, because these things are sins. Therefore Scripture testifies in many places that God is not the author of evils—that is, of those things which are sins.

### Their foregoing position is opposed by the statement: “God is not the author of evils”

4. In this statement the position of the former group is rightly opposed. They say that God is not the author of things which are evil insofar as they are evil, but insofar as they exist; and they say that insofar as they are evil, they are nothing. What wonder, then, if God is said not to be the author of them insofar as they are nothing, since no one can be the author of nothing?

Accordingly, when it is said that God is the author of all things which exist, they want good things to be understood. These they call good which naturally exist. And they say that things naturally exist not only when they are substances or are created together with substances, as they explained above, but whenever they do not deprive nature of good. Thus, according to them, Scripture has multiple senses wherever it speaks of nature, substance, or things naturally existing.

But Augustine, vol. 8, commenting on Psalm 68, “There is no substance,” speaks of substance in such a way as to seem to agree with the foregoing position:

> By substance is understood that by which we are whatever we are: human being, beast, earth, sun—all these are substances. By the very fact that they are natures, they are called substances. For what has no substance is absolutely nothing; therefore substance is to be something. God made the human being a substance, but through iniquity the human being fell away from the substance in which he was made. Iniquity itself is not a substance. For iniquity is not a nature fashioned by God, but a perversity made by the human being. All natures were made through him; iniquity was not made through him, because iniquity is not a substance. In that hymn of the three children, every creature praising God is mentioned. For all things praise God—but the things God made. There the serpent praises God, but not avarice. All creeping things are named there, but not any vices. For we have vices from ourselves and from our own will, and vices are not substances.

Let the defenders of the foregoing positions attend carefully to these words, and they will be able to grasp the rationale and meaning of statements where Scripture mentions nature or substance. But we leave judgment concerning these positions to the discretion of the prudent reader, to whom we have fully given knowledge of both views, hastening on to discuss the matters still remaining.

### That when it is said, “God is not the author of evil,” sin and not punishment is understood

5. Although all Catholic writers agree on this point—that God is not the author of evils—care must nevertheless be taken not to include punishments along with sins indiscriminately under the name “evils.” For God is the author of punishments, as he himself says through the prophet, Amos 3: “There is no evil in a city which God has not done.” Likewise, Isaiah 45 says in God’s own person: “I am God, creating evil and making good.” Here he is said to have created and made evil; but by “evil” punishment is understood, [Col. 0743] not sin. Conversely, when it is said that God is not the author of evils, by “evil” sins are understood.

Therefore Augustine, who had said, vol. 4, in book 1 of *83 Questions*, ch. 26, question 21, that God is not the author of evil, explains in book 1 of the *Retractations* how this should be understood:

> Care must be taken lest what I said be understood wrongly: “God is not the author of evil,” though he is the author of all things which exist, because insofar as they exist, they are good. Let no one suppose from this that the punishment of evils is not from him, though it is certainly evil for those who are punished. Rather, I said this as Scripture says, Wisdom 1: “God did not make death,” although elsewhere it is written, Ecclesiasticus 11: “Death and life are from the Lord.” The punishment of evil persons, therefore, which is from God, is indeed evil for the evil; but it belongs among God’s good works, because it is just that evil persons should be punished, and everything just is certainly good. Thus God is said not to have made death because he did not make that for which death is inflicted, namely sin.

You have heard, reader, the reason for these statements, from which a sound understanding is established when it is said: “God is not the author of evil,” and “God did not make death.”

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. ON THE WILL AND ITS END, BY WHICH THE WILL ITSELF IS JUDGED
1. After the foregoing, we must discuss the will and its end. It should therefore be known that, as Augustine says, a will is known from its end to be either right or perverse. Now the end of a good will is blessedness, eternal life, God himself. But the end of an evil will is something else—namely, evil pleasure, or some other thing in which the will ought not to rest. The Prophet indicates the good end when he says: “I have seen the end of every consummation,” etc. Therefore charity, whose commandment is broad, is the end of every consummation—that is, of every good will and action—to which every commandment must be referred. Hence Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, book 11, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, vol. 3: “All divine commandments are referred to charity.” Of this the Apostle says, 1 Timothy 1: “The end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned.” Thus the end of every commandment is charity; that is, every commandment is referred to charity. But whatever is done either from fear of punishment or from some carnal intention, so that it is not referred to charity, which is love of God and neighbour, is not yet done as it ought to be done, however much it may seem to be done. For then the things God commands, and those which he urges by counsel, are rightly done when they are referred to love of God and neighbour. These words plainly indicate what is the right end of a good will or action: namely, charity, which is also God, as we showed above.

### That God is the end of every good action because he is charity; and that not only the Holy Spirit, but also Christ and the Father, are this end; nor are these three ends, but one.

2. Therefore, whoever sets charity before himself as his end sets God before himself as his end. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 10, that Christ is “the end of the law unto righteousness to every one that believeth.” And Christ is rightly called the end of the law unto righteousness, because, as Augustine says in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*, “in Christ the law of righteousness is not consumed but fulfilled.” For every perfection is from him and in him; nor is there anything beyond him to which hope may extend itself. Christ is the end of the faithful; when the intention of one who runs has reached him, it has nowhere further to go, but possesses that in which it ought to remain. Therefore the right and supreme end is God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are not three ends, but one end, because they are not three gods but one God.

### That all good wills have one end, and yet some good wills obtain diverse ends.

3. But it is asked whether all good wills have only one end. On this Augustine says in book 11 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6:

> Different wills have their own proper ends; yet these are referred to the end of that will by which we desire to live blessedly and to attain that life which is not referred to anything else, but is sufficient in itself to the one who loves it. Thus the will to see has vision as its end; and the will to see a window has the vision of the window as its end. But another will is that of seeing passers-by through the window; its end likewise is the sight of the passers-by. To this end the aforesaid wills are also referred.

Again, in the same place: “Wills are right, and all bound together with one another, if that to which they are all referred is good. But if it is perverse, they are all perverse. And therefore the connection of right wills is a sort of path by which people ascend to blessedness, a path traversed, as it were, by definite steps. But the entanglement of perverse and distorted wills is a bond by which the one who does this will be bound, to be cast into outer darkness,” Matthew 22.

These testimonies of authorities clearly show that among the faithful there are many right wills having their own and diverse ends, and nevertheless one and the same end, because all are referred to the one who is the end of ends, of whom we spoke a little earlier. Perhaps the converse is likewise true among evil persons.

### Certain things seem contrary to this opinion.

4. Nevertheless, the statement that certain right wills of the faithful obtain diverse ends and are yet referred to one end seems opposed by Augustine’s warning elsewhere that we must not establish two ends for ourselves. Thus he says in *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, vol. 4, chapter 24:

> We ought not to preach the Gospel in order that we may eat, but to eat in order that we may preach the Gospel; so that food may not be the good which is sought, but a necessity added in order that the other may be fulfilled. “Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you,” Matthew 6. He did not say: “First seek the kingdom of God, and then seek these things,” although they are necessary; but he said: “All these things shall be added unto you,” that is, they shall follow if you seek those things, lest, while seeking these things, you turn away from the other; or lest you establish two ends, seeking both the kingdom for its own sake and these necessities for its sake. Therefore we ought to do everything solely for the kingdom of God, and not contemplate bodily reward either by itself or together with the kingdom of God.

Here he plainly says that we should not establish two ends for ourselves, but only one, namely the kingdom of God, although above he had said that various good wills have their own distinct ends.

### Here it is shown how the foregoing statements, though they appear to do so, do not conflict.

5. Yet the person who attentively fixes a single eye upon the preceding words sees that they do not conflict. For he who said that we should not establish two ends for ourselves, but should do everything for the kingdom of God, himself first stated that we ought to eat in order to preach the Gospel. But when we do this, we make the Gospel the end of that action; and we also refer that end to the kingdom of God. For we eat for the Gospel’s sake, and we eat and preach the Gospel for the kingdom of God’s sake. Therefore in eating we establish two ends for ourselves. But do we sin by doing so? Far from it. For he himself advises us to do this, if we carefully examine his words.

Therefore, when he says that we should not establish two ends for ourselves, he means ends tending in different directions—namely, ends of which one is not referred to the other. Likewise, when he says that everything should be done solely for the kingdom of God and that temporal reward should not be contemplated along with it, this must be understood as meaning that we must not seek or contemplate temporal reward together with the kingdom in such a way that we seek it not for the kingdom’s sake but for its own sake. Rather, we should seek the kingdom for its own sake and those things for the kingdom’s sake, as he himself teaches.

For if we ask eternal life, and also ask temporal things from God, Luke 12, we do not offend if we ask for them on account of eternal life. Nor does the left hand then know what the right hand does, Matthew 6, because we contemplate temporal reward not for its own sake but for the kingdom of God, so that the left hand may be under the head and the right in the embrace, Song of Songs 2. Otherwise, if we seek these temporal things for their own sake just as we seek eternal things, the left hand is mingled with the right. Therefore, although the Lord said, Matthew 6: “Take heed that ye do not your righteousness before men, to be seen of them,” elsewhere he says, Matthew 5: “Let your good works so shine before men, that they may glorify your Father which is in heaven.” Therefore everything must be done for God, so that we refer to him everything we do and the ends of all our actions.

### On the difference between will, intention, and end.

6. It is also commonly asked what the difference is between will, intention, and end. To this it may be said that will and end are distinguished in a certain and evident way.
