For will is that by which we will something; but the end of the will is either the thing that we will, by which the will itself is fulfilled, or rather another thing for the sake of which we will that thing. Intention, however, is sometimes taken for will and sometimes for the end of the will; and the diligent and devout reader should endeavour to distinguish these where they occur in Scripture.

The end of the will is good or evil pleasure, which each person strives to attain. Hence Augustine, on the verse of the Psalm, “Searching the hearts and reins,” says:

> God alone searches hearts, that is, what each person thinks; and reins, that is, what delights each person; because the end of care and thought is delight, which each person strives by care and thought to attain.

And shortly afterwards:

> Our works, which consist in words and deeds, may be seen by human beings; but only God sees with what disposition they are done and what end they seek to attain. When he sees that the heart is in heaven and that we delight not in the flesh but in the Lord—that is, when thoughts are good and their ends are good—he directs the righteous person.

On another passage of the Psalm, namely, “In this snare which they have hidden, their foot has been caught,” he says: “The foot of the soul is love. If it is perverse, it is called cupidity or lust; if right, it is called charity. By it the soul is moved as it were toward the place to which it tends, that is, toward good or evil delight, which it rejoices to have reached through love.”

Therefore, as was said above, the end of the will means both that which we will and that for the sake of which we will it. Intention looks to that for the sake of which we will, while will looks to that which we will. For example, if I wish to feed a hungry person in order to obtain eternal life, the will is that by which I wish to feed the hungry person, whose end is the feeding of that hungry person; but the intention is that by which I wish thus to attain life. The supreme end, however, is life itself, to which the other end is referred.

### Whether that intention is a will.

7. But it is asked whether such an intention is a will; and, if it is a will, whether in this action the will by which I wish to feed the hungry person and that by which I wish to possess eternal life are one and the same will. Such an intention certainly seems to be a will. For just as the will by which I wish to relieve a poor person is a will, so also the will by which through that deed I wish to possess life is a will. And the will by which I wish to possess life seems to be one will, while that by which I wish to help a poor person is another. But the latter is referred to the former. For even if this pleases us so that the will rests in it with some delight, it is not yet the thing toward which one tends; but this is referred to that, so that the latter is reckoned as the citizen’s homeland, while the former is reckoned as the refreshment or lodging of a traveller. Augustine, book 11 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6.

And these wills are affections or movements of the mind, by which one tends toward the homeland as though by paces or steps. Therefore, just as, according to Augustine’s teaching cited above, the will to see windows is one will, while the will joined to it—namely, the will to see passers-by through the windows—is another, so to some it seems that the will to give alms to a poor person is one will and the will to possess life another. Others, however, think there is one will in both cases, but that a plurality of objects gives rise to the description of a plurality of wills. But whichever of these may be true, this is beyond dispute: a will is judged from its end to be right or perverse, sinful or gracious; and the term “intention” sometimes means the end and sometimes the will.

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. SINCE WILL IS AMONG THE THINGS WHICH A HUMAN BEING POSSESSES NATURALLY, WHY IS IT SAID TO BE SIN, WHEN NO OTHER NATURAL THING IS SIN?

1. Here a rather necessary question arises from the preceding discussion. For it was said above that will is naturally present in human beings, as are understanding [Col. 0746] and memory. But those things which are natural to human beings, however much they are corrupted, do not cease to be good, because vice cannot utterly consume the goodness in which God made them. For example, understanding or reason, native ability, and memory, although darkened and corrupted by vices and sins, are nevertheless good and are not called sins. Augustine clearly shows this concerning reason, which is the image of God in which we were made, in book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8:

> This is the image in which human beings were created, by which they rule over the other animals; this creature, most excellent among created things, when justified by God, is changed from a deformed form into a beautiful form. For even amid vices, nature was good.

This image is reason or understanding. Since, then, will belongs to natural things, why is it not always good, even if it is sometimes subject to vices? Those who say that all things, insofar as they are, are good answer this easily. They assert that will itself, insofar as it exists, or insofar as it is will, as we stated above, is good; but insofar as it is disordered, it is evil and sin.

One may reasonably ask them here: if will, insofar as it is disordered, is sin, why are understanding, reason, native ability, and the like not sins when they are disordered? For they too are disordered, just as will is, when they do not tend toward a right end and their acts are transgressions. They answer that the term “will” sometimes means the power, namely the natural capacity of willing, and sometimes the act of that power. The power itself, naturally implanted in the soul, is never sin, just as neither the power of remembering nor that of understanding is sin. But the act of this power, which is called will, is sin when it is disordered.

### Why the act of the will is sin, if the acts of other powers are not sins.

2. But it is still asked why the act of this natural power is sin, if the acts of other powers are not sins—for example, the power of remembering, whose act is remembering, and the power of understanding, whose act is understanding. They answer that the act of will is of another kind than the act of memory or understanding. For this is an act directed toward acquiring something or refusing to admit something; it cannot concern evil things without being evil. For to will evil things is evil, but to understand or remember evil things is not evil. Although some of them also not improperly assert that these acts are sometimes evil. For one sometimes remembers evil in order to do it, and seeks to understand truth in order to know how to attack it.

Thus the foregoing question is answered by those who teach that all things are good insofar as they exist. But those who say that evil wills are sins and are in no way good answer more briefly, saying that the act of will is not among natural things, but only the power itself and the capacity of willing, which is always good and exists in everyone, even in little children, in whom its act is not yet present.

### How the statement is to be understood: “Even a human being who is a slave of sin naturally wills the good.”

3. Moreover, it is commonly asked how Ambrose’s statement should be understood, in volume 4 of his commentary on Romans 7: “For what I will, that I do not; but what I hate, that I do.” For he says that a person subject to sin does what he does not will, because he naturally wills the good. But this will always lacks effect unless the grace of God assists and liberates it.

If a human being is subject to sin, he indeed wills and performs evil, because he is a slave of sin and willingly does its will, as Augustine said above, chapter 18. How, then, does he naturally will the good? Is it the same will—that is, the same movement—by which he willingly serves sin and by which he naturally wills the good? If it is not the same will, then which of these is the will that, when a person is justified, is freed from the slavery of sin? For, as we discussed above, God’s grace liberates and assists the human will: it prepares the will to be assisted and assists it when prepared. But which is this will? Is it the will that naturally wills the good [Col. 0747], or that which willingly serves sin, if indeed there are two wills?

A profound question has been posed, and different people settle it by different interpretations. Some say that there are two movements: one by which a person naturally wills the good. Why is it called natural, and why naturally? Because such was the movement of human nature in its first condition, in which we were created without vice, and which is properly called nature. For the human being was created upright in will. Hence it is written in *On Faith to Peter*, volume 3, chapter 25:

> Hold most firmly that the first human beings were created good and upright, with free choice, so that, if they wished, they could sin by their own will; and that they sinned not by necessity but by their own will.

Therefore a person is rightly said naturally to will the good, because he was created with a right and good will. For the higher spark of reason—which, as Jerome says, could not be extinguished even in Cain—always wills the good and always hates evil.

> [Note: [Col. 0747] In the commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 1, on the passage: “And sparks as the appearance of glowing bronze”; volume 5.]

But they say that there is another movement by which the mind, abandoning the higher law, subjects itself to sins and takes pleasure in them. This movement, they say, rules and reigns in the human being before grace is present; it suppresses the other movement, although both arise from free choice. When grace comes, however, that evil movement is crushed, and the other, naturally good movement is liberated and aided so that it effectively wills the good. Before grace, however, although a person naturally wills the good, one ought not simply to grant that he has a good will, but rather an evil one.

Others say that there is one will—that is, one movement—by which a human being naturally wills the good and, through vice, wills evil and delights in it. Insofar as he wills the good, he is naturally good; insofar as he wills evil, he is evil.

## DISTINCTION XL. WHETHER ALL ACTS SHOULD BE JUDGED FROM THEIR END, SO THAT THEY MAY BE CALLED SIMPLY GOOD OR EVIL.

1. After this, it seems proper to add a discussion of acts: whether they too, like will, should be judged good or evil from their end. For although, according to some, all acts are good insofar as they exist naturally, they should not all simply be called good, nor are all rewardable; rather, some are called simply evil, just as others are good. For those acts are simply and truly good which accompany a good cause and intention—that is, a good will—and tend toward a good end. But those which have a perverse cause and intention ought simply to be called evil.

Hence Ambrose says: “Your disposition gives your work its name.” And Augustine [Note: [Col. 0747] Vol. 1, in *On Offices*, book 1, chapter 3; vol. 8, preface to that Psalm], on Psalm 31:

> Let no one reckon his good works before faith. For they seem to me to be like great strength and very swift running off the road; for where faith itself was absent, good work was absent. For intention makes a work good, and faith directs intention. Do not pay too much attention to what a person does, but to what he has in view when he does it, to what destination he directs the sinews of excellent steering.

These testimonies seem to indicate that works are good or evil by disposition and end. They agree with what Truth says in the Gospel, Matthew 7: “A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can an evil tree bring forth good fruit.” By the name “tree” is meant not the nature of the human mind but the will. If it is evil, it produces not good works but evil ones; if it is good, it produces good works, not evil ones.

### Whether all human works are good or evil by disposition and end.

2. But it is asked whether all human works are good or evil by disposition and end. Some think so, saying that all acts are indifferent, so that none is good or evil in itself; rather, every act is good by a good intention and evil by an evil one. According to them, any act whatever can be good if performed with a good intention.

Others, however, think that some acts are evil in themselves, so that they can only be sins, even if they have a good cause; and that some are good in themselves, so that they do not cease to be good even if they have an evil cause. They confirm this by Augustine’s testimony that the good is sometimes not done well. For what someone does unwillingly or under compulsion, he does not do well, because he does not do it with a good intention. Thus Augustine says, volume 8, tractate 8 on 1 John:

> Servile fear is not in charity. In it, although God is believed, he is not believed in; and if a good thing is done, it is nevertheless not done well. For no one does well unwillingly, even if what he does is good.

Here you have that someone does not do well something which is good. Therefore he does what is good with an intention that is not good. They therefore maintain that certain works are such that they are so good that they cannot be evil, however they are done; and, conversely, certain works are so evil that they cannot be good, whatever their cause. But there are other works which are good or evil according to their end or cause; and to these they apply the testimonies of the saints which say that the judgment of works is to be assessed from disposition or intention. They set forth this threefold distinction of acts.

### Augustine seems to hold another opinion: human works are good or evil by intention and cause, except for certain acts which are sins in themselves.

3. But Augustine teaches most plainly in *Against Lying*, chapter 7, volume 4, that all acts are to be judged good or evil according to intention and cause, except certain acts that are so evil that they can never be good, even if they appear to have a good cause:

> It matters greatly for what cause, to what end, and with what intention anything is done. But things known to be sins must not be done under any pretext of a good cause, under any apparently good end, or with any seemingly good intention. Indeed, human works which are not sins in themselves are now good, now evil, if they have good or evil causes. Thus, providing food for the poor is good if it is done from mercy and with right faith; and marital intercourse is good when it is undertaken for the sake of begetting children, if it is done with the faith that those begotten may be regenerated. But these things are again evil if they have evil causes: for example, if a poor person is fed for boasting, or a wife is approached for lust, or children are begotten not to be brought up for God but for the devil.

> But when works are sins in themselves, such as thefts, fornications, and blasphemies, who would say that they ought to be done for good causes, or that they are not sins—or, what is still more absurd, that they are just sins? Who would say: “Let us steal from the rich, so that we may have something to give to the poor”; or, “Let us give false testimony, not so that innocent persons may thereby be harmed, but rather saved”? For there are two goods here: that the needy person should be fed and that the innocent person should not be punished. Or who would say that adultery ought to be committed so that, through the woman with whom it is committed, a man may be saved from death? Why do we not also suppress true wills and substitute false ones, lest inheritances come to those who do no good, but rather to those who assist the needy? Why should those evil things not be done for these good things, if they are not evil when done for these good things? Why should not a good man seize wealth from unclean prostitutes, whom fornicators enrich, in order to distribute it to the needy, if no evil is evil when done for a good purpose? Who would say this except someone trying to overthrow human affairs, morals, and laws? For what crime could not be said to be capable of being rightly committed, not only with impunity but even gloriously, so that punishment need not be feared but reward may be hoped for, if once we agreed, in evil acts, to ask not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is done for good causes should not itself be judged evil?

> Yet justice rightly punishes the person who says that he took superfluities from a rich man in order to provide for a poor man; and the forger who corrupts another’s will so that the heir might be one who gave generous alms rather than one who gave none; and the person who admits that he committed adultery in order, through the woman with whom he committed it, to save a man from death.

> But someone will say: “Then is a thief who steals from a merciful motive to be regarded as equal to every thief?” Who would say this? But neither of the two is good because one is worse. For worse is the one who steals from covetousness than the one who steals from pity. Yet if every theft is sin, every theft must be avoided. For who would say that one ought to sin, even though one sin is graver and another lighter?

In the same book, chapter 8: “But now we are asking which act is sin and which is not, not which is graver or lighter.”

Reader, consider the quoted words with the full attention of your mind; they provide no useless exercise. You will recognize that an act is sin when it has an evil cause; yet not only then, because there are certain acts which, even if they have a good cause, are nevertheless sins, as was set forth above. From this it seems to follow that will or action is not always judged evil by its end, as in those things that are sins in themselves. For when someone performs these for some good cause, the action seems to have a good end. The will is not evil because of its end, nor does the action become evil because of the will; rather, the will becomes perverse because of the action.

Among such acts some place the action of the Jews, who in crucifying Christ thought that they were rendering service to God. For they say that the Jews set before themselves a good end, namely service to God; yet they maintain that their will and action were perverse. But in Augustine’s foregoing words no exception is made regarding good acts: every good will is good by its end, and every good action is good by end and will. But not every evil will is evil by its end, nor is every evil action evil by end and will. Every action having an evil cause is evil, but not every action having a good cause is good. Therefore, when disposition is said to give a work its name, this rule is universally true in good works; but among evil works, those that are evil in themselves are excepted. Thus all human works are judged good or evil according to intention and cause, except those which are evil in themselves—that is, those which cannot be done without transgression.

### Some say that the foregoing acts cannot be done with a good end.

4. Yet some contend that these acts never have a good cause. Whoever steals another’s goods in order to give them to the poor, they say, does not steal for a good purpose. For it is not good to distribute another’s goods to the poor. Whoever offers God a sacrifice from robbery, according to the authority of Ecclesiasticus 34, does the same as one who sacrifices a son in his father’s presence or offers God a sacrifice of flesh. For the offering of the ungodly is abominable to God. Likewise, they say that saving a person from death through adultery is evil. Although saving a person from death is good, they maintain that saving someone in this manner is evil.

Therefore they say that Augustine, in the preceding passage, moderated his language and spoke cautiously when he said that things known to be sins must not be done under any “apparently good end” or “seemingly good intention.” For he did not simply say “a good end” and “a good intention,” but added *quasi* (“apparently”) and *velut* (“seemingly”), because such acts are not done with a good end or good intention, but with an intention which appears good and an end which is thought good but is not. Nor, they say, did Augustine state this because those acts do not have evil causes; rather, because they have causes that appear good but are evil.

## DISTINCTION XLI. WHETHER EVERY INTENTION OR ACTION OF THOSE WHO LACK FAITH IS EVIL.

1. Since, as was said above, intention makes a work good and faith directs intention, it may rightly be asked whether every intention and every work of those who do not have faith is evil. For if faith directs intention and intention makes a work good, where faith is absent there seems to be neither good intention nor good work. This is not unreasonably maintained by some, who say that all actions and wills of a person without faith are evil, though they would be good if faith were present. Hence the Apostle says, Romans 14: “Whatever is not of faith is sin.”

Explaining this, Augustine says in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*, chapter 105, distinction 38: “The entire life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good; where knowledge of eternal truth is lacking, there is false virtue even in the best morals.” And James says in his Catholic Epistle, chapter 2: “Whosoever offends in one point,” namely charity, “is guilty of all.” Therefore, whoever lacks faith and charity, every action of his is sin, because it is not referred to charity. For, as Augustine noted above, whatever is not referred to charity is not done as it ought to be done; and therefore it is evil. Hence the person who lacks charity does not keep the commandments, because without charity none of the commandments is kept.

Therefore Augustine, commenting on the Epistle to the Galatians, says: “The Apostle calls keeping the law, Romans 13, not being drunk, not killing, not committing adultery, and other such things pertaining to good morals; these cannot be fulfilled without charity, faith, and hope.” Therefore the person who does not have faith and charity fulfils no commandment and performs no good work. For, as the Apostle says, Hebrews 11, it is impossible to please God without faith. Therefore things done without faith are not good, because every good thing pleases God.

### Objections to the foregoing opinion from Augustine’s words.

2. To this is objected what Augustine said above: namely, that under servile fear, even if a good thing is done, it is nevertheless not done well. “For no one does well unwillingly, even if what he does is good.” Here he says that a good thing is done, though not well, by someone who lacks charity. For one who fears servilely is devoid of charity; yet Augustine says here that he does good, but not well.

Again, on the passage of Psalm 83, “The turtledove hath found a nest for herself, where she may lay her young,” in *Confessions*, book 1, chapter 12, he says that Jews, heretics, and pagans perform good works because they clothe the naked, feed the poor, and do such things; but they do not do so in the nest of the Church, that is, in faith, and therefore their young are trampled underfoot.

They answer that such deeds done without charity are called good works not because they are good when so done—which Augustine plainly taught above—but because they would be good if done otherwise. They are good in their kind, but evil in disposition.

### The opinion of others on the foregoing question—whether every action of those who lack faith is evil.

3. Others, however, who make a threefold distinction of acts, maintain that all works done for the support of nature are always good. But when Augustine says that they are evil if they have evil causes, this should not be understood as meaning that the acts themselves are evil, but that those who perform them with an evil end sin and are evil. Likewise, they explain the other statement, “intention makes a work good and faith directs intention,” by saying that “good” there means what is rewardable unto life, not that this alone is a good work; indeed there are many other good works, though not good in the same sense. For “good” is understood in many ways: as useful, as rewardable, as a sign of good, as an appearance of good, as lawful, and perhaps in other ways.

Only that intention which faith directs is rewardable unto life; but, they say, it is not the only good intention. For if a Jew or an evil Christian, led by natural compassion, relieves the need of a neighbour, he has done good, and the will by which he did it was good.

### Here are set forth certain passages of Augustine which he retracted, not as wrongly stated, but while explaining the sense in which he stated them.

4. After this, we must investigate how Augustine’s statement is to be understood, volume 1, *On True Religion*, chapter 14: “Sin is voluntary evil to such an extent that it is in no way sin if it is not voluntary.” Explaining the meaning of this statement in *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 13, Augustine says:

> This definition may seem false; but if it is carefully examined, it is found to be most true. For one must understand that sin which is sin only, not that which is also the punishment of sin—namely, the first sin of man, which was sin and the cause of sin, but not punishment. Yet even those sins which are not improperly called involuntary, because they are committed either by those who do not know or by those who are compelled, cannot in every respect be committed without will. For the person who sins in ignorance certainly does by will what he thinks ought to be done, although it ought not to be done. And the person who, because the flesh lusts against the spirit, does not do the things he wills, indeed lusts unwillingly and in that respect does not do what he wills; but if he is overcome, he consents willingly to lust, and in that respect does nothing except what he wills. And the original sin which exists in little children was contracted from the first evil will of man. Therefore what I said was not false: “Sin is voluntary,” etc.

Behold how that statement should be understood: either concerning the first sin of man or, generally, concerning all mortal sins. Although some of these are called involuntary—namely, those committed through ignorance or weakness—they may nevertheless in that respect be called voluntary, because they are not committed without will.

### Another passage.

5. The meaning of the further statement which he published in volume 6, in the book *On the Two Souls*, chapter 10, must also be investigated. He says: “Sin is nowhere except in the will.” He defines this quite plainly also in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 15, saying: “This statement of ours—that sin is nowhere except in the will—may be thought false, since the Apostle says, Romans 7: ‘What I do not will, that I do,’ etc. But the sin which is nowhere except in the will must be understood chiefly as that which was followed by just condemnation, namely, the first sin of man.” In the same book *On the Two Souls*, chapter 10, he also set forth another point worthy of consideration. For he says: “One sins only by the will”; and he defines the will itself thus: “Will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, either to admit or not admit something, or to obtain it.”

Explaining the reason for this statement and disclosing its meaning, he says in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 15: “This was said so that, by this definition, one acting willingly might be distinguished from one acting unwillingly, and thus the intention might be referred to those who, in paradise, by sinning, made the beginning of evil, being compelled by no one—that is, by free will. For they knowingly acted against the commandment, and that tempter persuaded them that it should be done; he did not compel them. For one who sinned unknowingly may not improperly be said to have sinned unwillingly; although he too acted unknowingly, he nevertheless acted willingly. Thus even such a sin could not exist without will; but there was there a will for the deed, not a will for sin—though that deed was sin. For what was done was what ought not to have been done. But whoever sins knowingly, if he can resist without sin one compelling him to sin and nevertheless does not do so, certainly sins willingly; for one who can resist is not compelled to yield. Therefore it is most true that sin cannot exist without will.” From these passages it is clear how the foregoing statements should be understood.

### That an evil will is voluntary sin

6. But if every mortal sin is voluntary, and an evil will is a mortal sin, it is evident that it itself is voluntary sin. For what, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0751] Vol. 1, in *On Free Will*, chapter 12; and *Retractations*, book 1, chapters 9 and 22], is so much situated in the will as the will itself? Therefore an evil will is rightly called voluntary sin, since it consists in the will. For will, as Augustine says in the same work, is the first cause of sinning; otherwise no sin is the first cause of sinning, nor is there anyone to whom sin may rightly be imputed except the sinner. Therefore it is imputed rightly to no one except the will. This, however, must be understood of actual and mortal sin. Nor did Augustine intend by these words to show anything else, as he himself says in the *Retractations*, except that the will is that by which one sins and by which one lives rightly.

## DISTINCTION XLII. WHETHER EVIL WILL AND EVIL ACTION IN THE SAME PERSON AND CONCERNING THE SAME MATTER ARE ONE SIN OR SEVERAL

1. Since, then, evil will and action are sin, it is customary to ask whether, in the same person and concerning the same matter, these two are one sin or distinct sins. Thus, if someone steals by will, he has an evil will, which is sin, and an evil act, which likewise is sin. These two, however, are distinct: namely, will and action. But are they distinct sins, or one? Some say that they are one sin; others say that they are distinct sins, because, since these two are admittedly distinct, either they are called two distinct sins, or they are two distinct things which are not sins.

Others answer them that these two are distinct things, but not sins [Col. 0752]. For they are not sins, but one sin, because one transgression or disobedience is committed in both, whether one wills or acts; and there is one contempt involved, though lesser when sin is contained in the will alone, and greater when action is added to the will. Thus the sin becomes greater, but not more numerous, when the will is committed to the deed.

### Another objection against the same view

2. But the same persons are still challenged: if those two are only one sin, then when someone, having first conceived an evil will, subsequently performs the deed, he is guilty of nothing except that for which he was guilty before performing the deed, when sin still consisted in the will alone. For no one is guilty of eternal death except because of sin; but by acting he has committed no sin other than that which he had previously committed by willing. Therefore, by sinning in act, he does not become liable to condemnation for anything other than that for which he had previously been liable when he sinned by will alone.

To this they too answer, saying that the thief is indeed made guilty only on account of sin; and although his will and action are one sin, nevertheless by sinning in act he is made guilty for something other than that for which he was guilty when he sinned by will alone—namely, for the act, which is other than the will, though not another sin.

### Another objection against the same view

3. Again, they press the question further, saying that these two are distinct sins because they are transgressions of distinct commandments of the law. For the action of theft is forbidden by one commandment of the law, namely: “You shall not steal”; and the will to steal by another, namely: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” Since these are two distinct commandments by which the two things are forbidden, it is clear that the two are distinct transgressions; therefore, distinct sins.

To this they also say that the commandments by which these two things are separately forbidden are indeed distinct, as Augustine teaches on Exodus. Nevertheless, in failing to observe them, only one transgression is incurred and one sin contracted, although two distinct things are prohibited by them. Conversely, there are two commandments of charity, by which two things are commanded to be loved; yet one charity is commended to us in them.

### Whether sin committed by someone remains in that person until repentance

4. Furthermore, it is customary to ask: when a sin has been committed by someone’s will, and both the will to do it and the action have passed away, but true repentance has not yet taken place, does that sin remain in him until he repents? It seems not to remain, because the will which previously existed no longer exists, nor does the action; for he neither wills nor does what he formerly willed and did.

But it must not be ignored that sin is said to be in someone, and to pass away, in two ways: namely, in act and in guilt. It is in someone in act while that which is sin itself—such as an action or a will—is in the sinner. It is in him in guilt when, because of it, whether it has passed away or is present, the human mind is defiled and corrupted, and the whole person is bound over to everlasting punishments. Except for original sin, sin is never in anyone in act without also being in guilt; but after it has passed away in act, it must be understood as remaining in guilt.

### The senses in which *reatus* is used in Scripture

5. In Scripture, *reatus* (“guilt” or “liability”) is understood in several ways: as fault, as punishment, and as an obligation to temporal or eternal punishment. For if sin is mortal, it binds us to eternal punishment; if venial, it binds us to temporal punishment. There are, indeed, two kinds of sins: mortal and venial. Mortal sin is that through which a person merits eternal death. For a crime, as Augustine says, is that which is worthy of accusation and condemnation. Venial sin, however, is that which does not burden a person to the point of liability for perpetual death; nevertheless, it merits punishment, but is easily forgiven.

### On the modes of sins, which are variously assigned

6. The modes of sins have various distinctions in Scripture. There sin is said to be committed in two ways: by desire and by fear, as Augustine teaches [Col. 0753] on Psalm 79, at the words: “Burned with fire and dug down.” By these two modes, he says, all mortal sins are included. He calls “burned with fire” those which arise from desire burning wrongly; and “dug down” those which arise from fear humbling wrongly—that is, when someone desires what ought not to be desired, or fears what ought not to be feared.

Elsewhere sin is said to occur in three ways: by thought, word, and deed. Hence Jerome, on Ezekiel: “There are three general kinds of transgression to which the human race is subject. For we sin either in thought, in speech, or in deed.” Sometimes a fourth mode is added to these, namely habit; this was signified in Lazarus, four days dead. A human being is also said to sin against God, against himself, and against his neighbor. Against God, when he thinks wrongly concerning God, like a heretic; or rashly and unworthily presumes to appropriate things belonging to God, by participating in the sacraments; or when, by swearing falsely, he makes God’s name contemptible. He sins against his neighbor when he unjustly harms his neighbor; but against himself when he harms himself and no one else.

### How transgression and sin differ

7. Sin also has varied names. Sin is also called transgression (*delictum*). And transgression perhaps is, as Augustine says in the *Questions on Leviticus*, a turning aside from good; sin is doing evil. For it is one thing to turn aside from good, another to do evil. Sin, therefore, is the perpetration of evil; transgression is the abandonment of good, as the very word itself shows. For what else does *delictum* sound like but “something left behind” (*derelictum*)? And whoever leaves something, what does he leave except the good? Or transgression is what is done unknowingly, while sin is what is knowingly committed. Yet sin is indiscriminately called by the name of transgression, and transgression by the name of sin.

### On the seven principal vices

8. Furthermore, it must be known that there are seven capital or principal vices, as Gregory says on Exodus: vain glory, anger, envy, acedia or sadness, avarice, gluttony (*gastrimargia*), and lust; which, as John Chrysostom says, were signified by the seven peoples who held the land of promise promised to Israel. From these, as from seven springs, all the deadly corruptions of souls flow forth. They are called capital because all evils arise from them. For there is no evil which does not derive its origin from one of them.

### On pride, the root of every evil

9. Yet all evils arise from pride—both these and others—because, as Gregory says, pride is the root of all evil. Of it Scripture says, Ecclesiasticus 10: “The beginning of every sin is pride,” which is love of one’s own excellence. It has four species, as Gregory says. The first is when someone attributes to himself the good which he possesses. The second, when he believes it has been given by God, but nevertheless on account of his own merits. The third, when he boasts of having what he does not possess. The fourth, when, despising others, he wishes to appear singularly distinguished. Pride is therefore rightly called the root of every evil.

But this seems opposed by what the Apostle says, at the end of 1 Timothy: “Covetousness is the root of all evils.” For if covetousness is the root of all evils, so is pride. How, then, is pride the root and beginning of every sin?

### In what sense both pride and covetousness are called the root of all evils

10. But both statements are rightly understood if the two expressions are taken to include the kinds of individual sins, rather than individual instances of kinds. For there is no kind of sin which does not sometimes proceed from pride, nor any which does not at times descend from covetousness. Some people, indeed, become proud through covetousness; and some become covetous through pride. For, as Augustine says, there is a person who would not be a lover of money unless he thought that by it he would become more eminent; and therefore, in order to excel, he desires riches. In such a person covetousness arises from pride. And there is another who would not love to excel unless he thought that by it he would possess greater riches. Therefore he strives to excel because he loves to possess riches. In him pride—that is, love of excellence—is born from covetousness. It is clear, therefore, that covetousness sometimes arises from pride, and pride sometimes from covetousness [Col. 0754]; and so each is rightly said to be the root of every evil.

## DISTINCTION XLIII. ON SIN AGAINST THE HOLY SPIRIT, WHICH IS ALSO CALLED SIN UNTO DEATH

1. Moreover, there is a certain kind of sin, more grave and abominable than the rest, which is called sin against the Holy Spirit. Concerning it Truth says in the Gospel, Luke 12: “Whoever shall sin against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither here nor in the world to come.” And John says in the First Catholic Epistle: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” For whoever sins against the Father shall be forgiven; and whoever sins against the Son shall be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither here nor in the world to come.

But the question is: what is this sin against the Holy Spirit, or sin unto death? Some say that it is the sin of despair or obstinacy. Obstinacy is the persistence of a mind hardened in wickedness, through which a person becomes unrepentant. Despair is that by which someone utterly distrusts God’s goodness, judging his own wickedness to exceed the greatness of divine goodness, like Cain, who said, Genesis 4: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon.”

Both are called sin against the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son, and the kindness by which they love one another and us—a kindness so great that it has no end. Therefore those are rightly said to sin against the Holy Spirit who think that their wickedness surpasses God’s goodness and consequently do not undertake repentance; and those who cling to iniquity with a mind so obstinate that they resolve never to abandon it and never to return to the goodness of the Holy Spirit, abusing God’s patience and presuming excessively upon God’s mercy. Wickedness pleases them for its own sake, just as goodness pleases the devout. These sin through excessive obstinacy and presumption, judging God not to be just. The former, through despair, judge God not to be good, thereby removing, in this most stormy sea of iniquities, the harbor of divine forgiveness into which they might retreat amid the waves. By that very despair they add sins to sins, saying that there is no mercy and that necessary condemnation is due to sinners.

### Whether every obstinacy is sin against the Holy Spirit

2. But it is asked whether every obstinacy of a mind hardened in wickedness, and every despair, is sin against the Holy Spirit. Some say that every obstinacy and every despair is sin against the Holy Spirit. If this is so, that sin is sometimes forgiven, because many even of the most obstinate and despairing are converted, as Augustine says on the words of Psalm 14: “I shall turn [them] into the depths of the sea,” that is, those who had been most despairing; and there: “He sends forth his ice like morsels,” that is, he makes the obstinate teachers of others. Their conversion is also clearly shown where he says, Psalm 67: “Who brings forth prisoners in strength, likewise also those who exasperate, who dwell in tombs.”

According to these people, that sin is called unforgivable not because it is never forgiven, but because it is forgiven only rarely, with difficulty, and scarcely at all. For ice is not melted except by a vehement blast of wind.

Others teach, however, that not every obstinacy or despair is called sin against the Holy Spirit, but only that which is accompanied by impenitence; and they also call impenitence itself sin against the Holy Spirit. But because Augustine says that impenitence is sin against the Holy Spirit when someone is so obstinate that he does not repent, it must be considered whether obstinacy is one thing and impenitence another sin in him, or whether they are the same thing, committed in different ways.

According to these people, that sin is called unforgivable because it is never forgiven. Hence Augustine also says that this sin alone cannot merit pardon; and Jerome, that one who sins in such a manner cannot worthily repent. Thus John rightly says: “I do not say that anyone should pray for it,” because one who sins thus cannot be helped by the prayers of the Church either here or in the future, having a heart hardened like a stone, as is written concerning the devil. After this [Col. 0755] life, those who are exceedingly evil cannot be helped by the merits of the Church.

### That sin against the Holy Spirit is understood differently

3. There is also another explanation of this sin. Augustine, defining it in the book *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, says: “Sin unto death is when, after knowing God through the grace of Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is inflamed by the fires of envy against that very grace by which he was reconciled to God. Perhaps this is sinning against the Holy Spirit, a sin said not to be forgiven—not because it ought not to be forgiven if the sinner repents, but because the stain of that sin is so great that he cannot submit to the humility of entreaty, even if, compelled by an evil conscience, he acknowledges and renounces his sin; as Judas, when he said, ‘I have sinned,’ more readily ran in despair to the noose than sought pardon in humility. Because of the greatness of their sin, such persons must be believed already to have this disposition as a consequence of the condemnation of sin.”

Here is given a certain explanation of sin against the Holy Spirit, or sin unto death: it is said to be an attack upon the brotherhood after knowledge, and envy against grace after reconciliation. This can be understood as a species of obstinacy. Yet Augustine, recalling this definition in *Retractations*, book 1, chapter 9, makes clear that something should have been added there, and that he had not stated it as an assertion. He says: “I did indeed confirm it, because I said that this was my opinion. Yet it should have been added: if he ends this life in this criminal perversity of mind. For no one, however wicked his present condition in this life, ought to be despaired of; nor is prayer imprudently made for one of whom there is no despair.”

These words indicate that the sin described by the preceding definition should be called sin unto death, or sin against the Holy Spirit, only when it does not have repentance as its companion. No sinner in this life should be despaired of, and therefore prayer should be offered for everyone. Hence 1 John 5, “I do not say that anyone should pray for it,” seems to be understood thus: we should not pray for someone who has sinned unto death or against the Holy Spirit after he has ended this life. But while he is in this life, we ought neither to judge his sin nor despair of him, but pray for him.

Thus Augustine says in *On the Words of the Lord*, concerning impenitence, which is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, volume 10, sermon 11, after the middle: “This impenitence, or impenitent heart, cannot be judged while anyone lives in this flesh. For no one should be despaired of as long as God’s patience leads him to repentance. Today he is a pagan; today he is an unbelieving Jew; today he is a heretic; today he is a schismatic. What if tomorrow he embraces the Catholic faith and follows Catholic truth? What if those whom you mark as being in some kind of error and condemn as wholly despairing repent before they finish this life, and find true rest and life in the world to come? Therefore judge no one before the time” (1 Corinthians 4).

From this it is shown that one should pray for individual sinners in this life and despair of none, since anyone may be converted while still in this life. For it cannot be known of anyone whether he has sinned unto death or against the Holy Spirit except when he has departed this life—unless perhaps this has been wonderfully revealed to someone by the Holy Spirit. From what has been said, it may in some degree be understood how sin against the Holy Spirit is to be taken: namely, envy against grace attacking the brotherhood of the impenitent. This indeed seems to be obstinacy, and every obstinacy and despair of the impenitent. It should be noted, however, that not everyone who does not repent can be called impenitent, because impenitence properly belongs to the obstinate and, as some maintain, also to the despairing.

### Another explanation of sin against the Holy Spirit

4. Ambrose also gives a definite explanation of this sin against the Holy Spirit in volume 2, *On the Holy Spirit*, book 1, chapter 3, at the end. He says: “Consider carefully why the Lord said, Matthew 12: ‘Whoever blasphemes against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever blasphemes [Col. 0756] against the Holy Spirit shall be forgiven neither here nor in the future.’ Is the offense against the Son one thing and that against the Holy Spirit another? As dignity is one, so is the injury one. But if someone, deceived by the appearance of Christ’s human body, thinks something too slight concerning Christ’s flesh—less than is fitting—he is guilty, but is not excluded from pardon. But if someone denies the everlasting dignity, majesty, and power of the Holy Spirit, and thinks that demons are not cast out by the Spirit of God but by Beelzebub, there can be no exhortation to forgiveness where there is the fullness of sacrilege.”

Here it is explained quite plainly what sin against the Holy Spirit is. It seems to agree with Augustine’s description, in which that sin is called envy against grace attacking the brotherhood. For one who, after knowing the truth, denies the truth of the Holy Spirit and calls his works those of Beelzebub is undoubtedly envious of God’s power, goodness, and grace.

Therefore the distinction of these words should not be understood as though the offenses against the three Persons were divided, but as distinguishing kinds of sins. Sin against the Father is understood as that committed through weakness, because Scripture frequently attributes power to the Father; sin against the Son, as that committed through ignorance, because wisdom is attributed to the Son; the third has been explained. Therefore one who sins through weakness or ignorance easily obtains pardon, but not one who sins against the Holy Spirit. Since the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Three are one, why power is more often assigned to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit has been stated above.

## DISTINCTION XLIV. ON THE POWER OF SINNING: WHETHER A HUMAN BEING HAS IT FROM HIMSELF, FROM THE DEVIL, OR FROM GOD

1. After the foregoing, a question worthy of consideration arises: is the power of sinning from God, or from ourselves? Some think that the power of acting rightly is from God, but that the power of sinning is not from God but from ourselves or from the devil; just as an evil will is not from God in us, but from ourselves and from the devil, whereas a good will is from God alone.

For God clearly shows that the beginning of good will and thought is not born in a human being from himself but is divinely prepared and bestowed, because neither the devil nor any of his angels, since they were cast down into this darkness, has been able or will be able to recover a good will. For if it were possible that human nature, after turning away from God and losing the goodness of its will, could regain it from itself, angelic nature could do this much more readily, since the less it is weighed down by the burden of an earthly body, the more it would be endowed with this capacity. Therefore neither human nor angel can possess a good will from himself, though he can possess an evil one. Similarly, they argue concerning power, reasoning by analogy with will concerning the power of good and evil: that the former is from God, not the latter.

### By authorities he proves that the power of sinning is from God

2. But numerous testimonies of the saints show beyond doubt that the power of evil is from God, from whom comes every power. For the Apostle says, Romans 13: “There is no power except from God.” This must be understood not only of the power of good, but also of evil, since Truth says even to Pilate, John 19: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above.”

For the malice of human beings, as Augustine says, has in itself the desire to harm; but it does not have the power unless God gives it. Therefore, before the devil took anything from Job, he said to the Lord, Job 1: “Put forth your hand”—that is, give power—because even the power of those who harm exists only from God. As Wisdom says, Proverbs 8: “By me kings reign, and tyrants hold the earth by me.” Hence Job says of the Lord, chapter 34: “He causes a hypocrite to reign because of the sins of the people.” And God says of the people of Israel, Hosea 13: “I gave them a king in my anger.”

For the will to harm can arise from a human being, but the power does not arise except from God, and this according to a hidden and fitting justice. For through power granted to the devil, God makes the righteous his own. Gregory also says in the *Moralia*: “The exaltation of pride, [Col. 0757] not the order of power, is culpable. God grants power, but the malice of our mind devises the arrogance of power. Therefore let us remove what is ours, because it is not just power but wicked action that is condemned.” By these authorities and many others it is clearly shown that no one has power, whether for good or evil, except from the just God, even if his justice is hidden from you.

### Whether one must ever resist authority

3. Here a question arises which must not be passed over in silence. It was said above that the power of sinning or harming is not possessed by a human being or the devil except from God. But the Apostle says, Romans 13, that whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. Therefore, since the devil has the power of evil by God’s ordinance, it seems that his power should not be resisted.

But it must be known that the Apostle there speaks of secular authority, namely kings, rulers, and the like. They are not to be resisted in those things which God commands to be rendered to them, namely taxes and the like. But if some ruler or the devil commands or urges anything against God, then resistance is required. Hence Augustine, determining when authority should be resisted, says in *On the Nature of the Good*: “If authority commands something which you ought not to do, then certainly disregard that authority, fearing the greater authority. Consider the ranks of human affairs themselves. If an administrator commands something, must it be done if he commands contrary to the proconsul? Again, if the proconsul commands one thing and the emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must serve the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, disregarding the emperor, one must obey God.”

Therefore let us resist the authority of the devil or of a human being when it suggests something against God; in doing so, we do not resist God’s ordinance but obey it. For God has commanded that in evil matters we obey no authority. Now let us apply the full attention of our minds to understanding and examining those matters which pertain to the mystery of the incarnate Word, so that, by God’s revelation, we may be able to say even a little about things ineffable.

# BOOK THREE. ON THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD

[Col. 0757]

## DISTINCTION I. ON THE INCARNATION OF THE WORD AND OTHER MATTERS PERTAINING TO IT

[Col. 0757]

1. When, therefore, the fullness of time came, as the Apostle says, Galatians 4, “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children of God.” The time of fullness is called the time of grace, which took its beginning from the coming of the Savior. This is the time of mercy and the year of favor, in which grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1. Grace, because through charity what was commanded in the law is fulfilled. Truth, because through Christ’s coming the promise of human redemption made from ancient times is presented and accomplished.

Therefore the sending of the Son is the Incarnation itself. For in this he was sent: that he appeared visibly to the world in human form, as has been sufficiently discussed above.

### Why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh

2. It must be carefully noted why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, was incarnate. For the Son alone assumed a human being. This he did by a fitting order and by the profound counsel of God’s wisdom: so that God, who had created the world in his wisdom, according to Psalm 103, “You made all things in wisdom, O Lord, things in heaven and things on earth,” might restore it in that same wisdom.

This is the woman in the Gospel, Luke 15, who lights a lamp and finds the tenth coin which had been lost: namely, the wisdom of the Father. She kindled the earthen vessel of human weakness with the light of her divinity and restored the lost human being, marked with the king’s name and image. The Son was also sent rather than the Father because it was more fitting that he who is from another should be sent than he who is from no one. The Son is from the Father; the Father is from no one. For, as Augustine says in book 4 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 20, volume 3: “For he has no one from whom he is.”

Therefore, as the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so fittingly the Father sent and the Son was sent. For God’s Word is fittingly sent by him whose Word it is. He is sent by him of whom he was born. What is begotten is sent. But the Father, who sent, is from no one; therefore the Father was not sent, lest, if he were sent, he should be thought to be from another. Thus the Son, who is from the Father alone, was sent first; and afterwards also the Holy Spirit, who is from the Father and the Son. But the Son alone was sent in flesh, not the Holy Spirit, just as neither was the Father. This was done so that he who in divinity was God’s Son might in humanity become a human being’s son. The Father or Holy Spirit did not put on flesh, lest one should be the Son in divinity and another in humanity, and lest the same should be Father and Son if God the Father were born of a human being.

Hence Augustine says in *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “Neither the Father assumed flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, so that he who was in divinity God’s Son might himself become, in the human being, the human being’s son; lest the name of son should pass to another who was not son by eternal generation. Therefore the Son of God became the Son of Man: by the truth of nature the Son of God, born from God; and by the truth of nature the Son of Man, born from a human being. Thus the truth of the begotten one might possess the name of son in each birth by being born—not by adoption and not by appellation—so that one Son might be true God and true man. Therefore we must not say two Christs or two sons, but God and man, one Son. For this reason we also call him Only-begotten: remaining in two substances, as the truth of nature granted him, with the natures neither confused nor mixed, as the Timotheans wish, but united in fellowship.”

Here you have why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh.

### Whether the Father or the Holy Spirit could have been incarnate, or can be now

3. If, however, it is asked whether the Father or the Holy Spirit could have been incarnate, or can be even now, the sound answer may be given that both formerly could and now can assume flesh and become human: both the Father and the Holy Spirit. For just as the Son became human, so the Father or the Holy Spirit could and can do so.

### Whether the Son, who alone assumed flesh, did anything which the Father or the Holy Spirit did not do

4. But perhaps someone may say: since the works of the Trinity are undivided, if the Son assumed flesh, then the Father and the Holy Spirit did also. For if the Son assumed flesh and the Father or the Holy Spirit did not do this, then not everything which the Son does is done also by the Father and the Holy Spirit. But the Father, the Son, and the Spirit of both work all things together, equally and harmoniously. Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 13, chapter 11.

To this we say that the Son does nothing without the Father and the Holy Spirit, but the operation of these three is one, undivided and dissimilar in no respect. Yet the Son, not the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh. Nevertheless, the Trinity effected the assumption of flesh itself, as Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, volume 3: “We were reconciled through the Son alone according to the flesh, but not to the Son alone according to divinity. For the Trinity reconciled us to itself in that the Trinity itself made only the Word flesh.”

Therefore the Trinity effected the assumption of flesh, but for the Word, not for the Father or the Holy Spirit. For if the Father had effected an assumption of flesh for himself, and the Son for himself, or if the Father had effected it for the Son and the Son for the Father, then their operation would no longer be the same but divided. But just as the unity of substance of the Three is inseparable and undivided, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, chapter 4, so also is their operation. Nevertheless, Catholic theologians have not taught that the Trinity itself was born of the Virgin, crucified, and buried, but the Son alone; nor that the Trinity itself descended upon Jesus in the appearance of a dove, but the Holy Spirit alone; nor that the Trinity itself said from heaven, “You are my Son,” Mark 1, but that it was the voice of the Father alone addressed to the Son—although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, just as they are inseparable, also work inseparably.

This too is my faith, because this is the Catholic faith. Therefore, although the Son alone assumed flesh, he nevertheless effected the Incarnation itself together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

## DISTINCTION II. WHY HE ASSUMED THE WHOLE OF HUMAN NATURE, AND WHAT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD BY THE TERM “HUMANITY” OR “HUMAN NATURE”

1. Since in man the whole of human nature had been corrupted by vice, he assumed the whole of it—that is, soul and flesh—in order to heal and sanctify the whole. That by the term “human nature” or “humanity” soul and flesh are meant is plainly taught by Jerome in his *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, where he says to Pope Damasus:

> Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, so that we may say that there are two perfect and complete substances, namely divinity and humanity, the latter consisting of soul and body.

See how plainly he shows that soul and body are meant by the name of humanity. These are the two things which the Son of God is understood to have assumed wherever he is said to have received man, humanity, or human nature. Therefore those err who maintain that, wherever Christ’s humanity is mentioned, “humanity” signifies not a substance but some property from which a man is named.

John Damascene says: “It must be known that the name of divinity and humanity represents substances and natures.” For “nature” is not understood in Christ as it is when one says that all human beings have one nature. The same John clearly demonstrates this, assigning a different sense to the expression when human nature is named in Christ and when the nature of all human beings is said to be one. For he says:

> When we say that human beings have one nature, we must understand that we do not say this by considering the relation of soul and body. For it is impossible to call the Lord’s body and soul, compared with one another, of one nature. But because there are very many human persons, and all receive the same definition of nature—for all are composed of soul and body, all participate in the nature of soul, and all possess the substance of body—we call the common species of many differing persons one nature; each person, that is, having two natures and existing perfectly in the two natures of soul and body.

> But in the Lord Jesus Christ there is no common species to be found; for no other has been made, is, or ever will be. Rather, Christ is from divinity and humanity, and in divinity and humanity became both God and perfect man.

Therefore God assumed the whole human nature—that is, soul and flesh—and their properties or accidents: not flesh without a soul, nor a soul without reason, as heretics wished, but flesh and soul with its senses. Hence John Damascene says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 60:

> The Word assumed everything which God planted in our nature: namely, a body, an intellectual soul, and their idioms [proper attributes]. For he who is whole assumed the whole of me, that he might bestow salvation upon the whole of me. For what is not assumed is not healed.

### On the union of the Word and flesh through the mediation of the soul  
*(Augustine, On the Christian Conflict, chapter 18)*

[Col. 0760]

2. Therefore the Son of God assumed flesh and soul, but flesh through the mediation of the soul: the Word of God was united to the flesh through the medium of the intellect. For the divine essence is of such subtlety and simplicity that it was not fitting for it to be united directly to a body formed from the clay of the earth, except through a rational essence.

That union is so inexplicable that even John, sanctified from the womb, confessed that he was not worthy to loosen the strap of Jesus’ sandal, because he was not capable of investigating and explaining to others the manner of that union. Therefore those must not be heard who say that the Son of God did not take on a true man, nor was born of a woman, but displayed to those who saw him a false flesh and a simulated appearance of a body. They rush into this error because they fear that the truth and substance of God might be defiled by human flesh. Yet they proclaim that this visible sun scatters its rays through every filth and impurity of bodies and preserves them clean and undefiled.

If, then, visible clean things can touch visible unclean things without being defiled, how much more did the unchangeable and invisible Truth, assuming the soul through the spirit and the body through the soul, assume the whole man without any change in itself and free him from all infirmities! Here he says that the Wisdom of God assumed the soul through the spirit and the body through the soul. For the spirit is the higher part of the soul and approaches God through a greater likeness than does the soul itself—that is, the same soul according to its lower part—and the soul more than the body. Thus it is not unfitting to say that the soul was assumed through the spirit and the body through the soul.

### That the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously; nor was the flesh conceived before being assumed

3. But if it is asked whether the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously, or first the soul rather than the flesh, or the flesh rather than the soul; and whether that flesh was first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and afterwards assumed: it is most truly and without any ambiguity said that, from the moment God assumed man, he assumed the whole, and united soul and flesh to himself simultaneously. Nor was the flesh first conceived and afterwards assumed; rather, it was assumed in being conceived, and conceived in being assumed.

Hence Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 16:

> Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was received by the Word; rather, that the Word, God himself, was conceived by his assumption of his own flesh, and that the flesh itself was conceived by the incarnation of the Word.

The same writer, *On the Trinity*, book 1, final chapter:

> He would not be the Mediator of God and men unless he were the same God and the same man, one and true in both; and the whole Trinity, whose will and operation are one, made that servant-form which the Son alone assumed. The flesh was not first received in the Virgin’s womb and divinity afterwards came into the flesh; but as soon as the Word came into the womb, preserving the truth of his own nature, he became flesh and perfect man—that is, he was born in the reality of flesh and soul.

Gregory also says in the *Morals*: “At the angel’s announcement and the Spirit’s coming, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately within the womb the Word was flesh.”

## DISTINCTION III. CONCERNING THE FLESH ASSUMED BY THE WORD: WHAT IT WAS BEFOREHAND, AND WHAT IT WAS WHEN ASSUMED

1. A question is also raised concerning the flesh of the Word: before it was conceived, was it subject to sin, and was it assumed by the Word in that condition? In accordance with the harmonious testimony of the saints, it may safely be said—and must be believed—that it had previously been subject to sin, like the rest of the Virgin’s flesh; but that by the operation of the Holy Spirit it was so cleansed that it was united to the Word free from every contagion of sin. Only punishment remained, not by necessity, but by the will of him who assumed it.

The Holy Spirit, preceding her, also entirely cleansed Mary from sin and even freed her from the tinder of sin [*fomes peccati*], [Col. 0761] either by wholly removing that tinder itself, as some hold, or by weakening and attenuating it so completely that afterward no occasion whatever for sinning remained for her. He also prepared in the Virgin the power to conceive without a man’s seed.

The words of the Gospel teach this. Addressing the Virgin, the angel says, Luke 1: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” And: “That holy thing which will be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” The holy Virgin answered: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.”

Explaining this, John Damascene says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 2:

> After the holy Virgin’s consent, the Holy Spirit came upon her, according to the Lord’s word spoken by the angel, cleansing her and preparing her both to receive the divinity of the Word and to conceive. Then the Wisdom and Power of God Most High, existing in itself—that is, the Son of God the Father, *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial—overshadowed her as a divine seed. From the most holy and pure blood of that Virgin he united to himself flesh of our ancient lump, animated by a rational and intellectual soul; not sowing it, but creating it through the Holy Spirit. Therefore at once there was flesh, at once flesh of God the Word, at once flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul.

From this it clearly appears what we said above: namely, that the flesh of the Word was conceived and assumed simultaneously, and that this flesh—indeed, the whole Virgin—was purified from every stain of sin by the preceding action of the Holy Spirit. She was granted the power to conceive in a new manner, so that in the Virgin’s womb the conception of God and man might take place without intercourse with a man and without the lust of one conceiving.

For that flesh which God deigned to unite to himself from the Virgin was conceived without fault and born without sin. Yet do not suppose that this flesh was of a heavenly, aerial, or any other nature; rather, it was of the same nature as the flesh of all human beings. *(Augustine, On Faith to Peter, chapter 2, middle.)*

### He confirms by authority that from that time the Virgin was free from sin

2. That the holy Virgin was from that time free from every sin is plainly shown by Augustine in *On Nature and Grace*, chapter 26:

> With the exception of the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, for the honor of the Lord, I wish no question at all to be raised when sins are under discussion. For we know that more grace was bestowed upon her for overcoming sin in every respect, since she merited to conceive and bear him whom it is certain had no sin. With this Virgin excepted, if all holy men and women could be gathered together and were asked whether they had sin, what would they answer except what John says in chapter 1: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves”?

> But that Virgin was uniquely anticipated and filled with grace, so that she might possess as the fruit of her womb him whom the whole universe has had from the beginning as its Lord; so that what was born from the lineage of the first man might derive from it an origin only of the race, not of guilt.

### Why Christ was not tithed in Abraham as Levi was, although the flesh he assumed was subject to sin in Abraham

3. Since that flesh, whose singular excellence cannot be expressed in words, before it was united to the Word had been subject to sin in Mary and in the others from whom it was transmitted by propagation, it may reasonably seem that it was subject to sin in Abraham, whose whole flesh was subject to sin.

Hence it is commonly asked why Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham, but not Christ, when both were in Abraham’s loins in a material sense at the time when Abraham was tithed and gave tithes to Melchizedek. The Apostle says that Levi was tithed in Abraham as in his material cause. For by that tithing, just as Abraham is shown to be inferior to Melchizedek, to whom he personally paid tithes, so also is the Levitical order, which was in Abraham according to seminal principle and descended from him through the concupiscence of the flesh.

But Christ was not tithed, because although he was there according to the flesh, he did not descend from there according to the common law—[Col. 0762] namely, through the lust of the flesh. Likewise all sinned in Adam, Romans 5, but not Christ.

Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 10, chapter 19:

> Just as those who were in Adam’s loins sinned when Adam sinned, so those who were in Abraham’s loins were tithed when Abraham gave tithes. But this does not follow in Christ, although he was in the loins of Adam and Abraham, because he did not descend from there according to the concupiscence of the flesh.

Therefore, although Levi and Christ were both according to the flesh in Abraham’s loins when he was tithed, they were not tithed alike, because Christ was not there in the same manner in which Levi was there. *(Ibid., chapter 20.)* Levi was there according to the seminal principle by which he was to come through intercourse into his mother. Christ’s flesh was not there according to that principle, although Mary’s flesh was there according to that same principle. Therefore he was tithed in Abraham who was in Abraham’s loins in the same way that he was in his own father’s loins—that is, who was born from father Abraham as that other was born from his own father: according to the law of the flesh and invisible concupiscence. *(Ibid., chapter 2.)*

### In what sense Christ’s flesh is said in Scripture not to have been sinful but to have been like sinful flesh; and why it was not bound by sin in Christ

4. Therefore Christ is rightly said to have assumed the firstfruits of our mass, because he received not sinful flesh but the likeness of sinful flesh. For God sent his Son, as the Apostle says in Romans 8, “in the likeness of sinful flesh.” The Word assumed flesh like sinful flesh in punishment, but not in guilt, and therefore not sinful.

All other human flesh, however, is flesh of sin. His flesh alone is not flesh of sin, because his mother conceived him not by concupiscence but by grace. Yet it has the likeness of sinful flesh through passibility and mortality, because he hungered, thirsted, and experienced such things. Therefore, although his flesh is the same flesh as ours, it was not made in the womb as ours is. For it was sanctified in the womb, born without sin, and he himself never sinned in it.

Thus it is like ours in punishment, not in the quality of sin, because it utterly did not possess the defilement conceived from the movement of concupiscence, nor was it born from carnal pleasure. Therefore he came to an immaculate body, conceived apart from lustful concupiscence. It did not contain in itself the vice which in others is the cause of sin, nor did he sin in it. Thus the flesh of the Word is truly said not to have been bound by sin in Christ.

### Some seem to oppose the opinion that Christ’s flesh was not conceived before it was assumed

5. The view stated above—that the flesh of the Word was not conceived before it was assumed—seems to be opposed by what Augustine says on John, where chapter 2 reads: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews said: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it in three days?”

Here, Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 4, chapter 5, that this number corresponds to the perfection of the Lord’s body, because, according to physicians, the form of a human body is completed in so many days. On the occasion of these words, some have dared to say that the form of the Lord’s body was completed during that number of days, as are other bodies, and distinguished by the outlines of its members; and that immediately afterward the Word united flesh and soul to himself. In this way, they say, that number corresponds to the perfection of the Lord’s body.

But there is another explanation of that statement, from which a sound understanding of the words arises. Augustine did not say this because, as soon as that flesh had been sanctified by the work of the Holy Spirit and separated from the rest, it was united with its soul to the Word of God, so that it might be perfect and true God and perfect and true man. Rather, he said it because, in the very moment of the conception and union of God and man, the differentiation of the Lord’s bodily members was so fine and small that it could scarcely be perceived by human sight; but during the days mentioned by Augustine it was completed and made discernible.

Therefore the Word was incarnate, as John Damascene says at the end of *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 7, without departing from his own incorporeality. He was wholly incarnate and wholly uncircumscribed. He is diminished and contracted bodily, yet is divinely uncircumscribed; his flesh is not coextensive with his uncircumscribed divinity. Thus, he who was above all things was in all things and was in the womb of the holy Mother of God, yet in her by the act of incarnation.

## DISTINCTION IV. WHY THE INCARNATION, WHICH IS A WORK OF THE TRINITY, IS MORE OFTEN ATTRIBUTED IN SCRIPTURE TO THE HOLY SPIRIT, AND WHY CHRIST IS SAID TO HAVE BEEN CONCEIVED AND BORN OF HIM

1. Since, as was treated above, the Incarnation of the Word is truly the operation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it seems worthy of inquiry why Scripture more frequently attributes this work to the Holy Spirit and records that Christ was conceived and born of him.

The operation of the Incarnation is not more often attributed to the Holy Spirit because he alone accomplished it without the Father and Son. Rather, it is because the Holy Spirit is the love and gift of the Father and the Son; and by God’s ineffable love the Word was made flesh, and by God’s ineffable gift the Son of God united the servant-form to himself. Therefore the frequent naming of the Holy Spirit does not exclude the Father or the Son from that work. On the contrary, when one is named, the three are understood, as often happens in other works.

Accordingly, Augustine, raising this question, resolves it in this way in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 38:

> Since the whole Trinity made that creature whom the Virgin conceived and bore, although it pertains to the person of the Son alone—for the works of the Trinity are inseparable—why is the Holy Spirit alone named in its making? Or, whenever one of the three is named in any work, is the whole Trinity understood to work? This is indeed true, and can be taught by examples.

You have heard the question proposed and its solution or explanation.

### In what sense Christ is said to have been conceived and born of the Holy Spirit

2. But we should not linger over this. For this point raises a difficulty: how is Christ said to have been born of the Holy Spirit, when the Son is in no way the Son of the Holy Spirit?
