Shall we say that the Holy Spirit is the father of the man Christ, so that God the Father begot the Word and the Holy Spirit begot the man, from which two substances Christ would be one: Son of God the Father according to the Word and Son of the Holy Spirit according to his humanity, because the Holy Spirit begot him from the Virgin mother as his father?

Who would dare to say this, when it is so absurd that no ears of believers could bear it? Therefore, though we confess that Christ was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, it is difficult to explain how he is not the Son of the Holy Spirit but is the Son of the Virgin, although he was born both of him and of her.

Undoubtedly, he was not born of the Holy Spirit as of a father; but he was born of the Virgin as of a mother. Nor should it be granted that whatever is born from something must immediately be called that thing’s child. To set aside the fact that from a human being a son is born in one way, hair in another, and a louse or worm in another—none of which is a son—and to set these aside because they are improperly compared to so great a matter: certainly those born of water and the Holy Spirit would not rightly be called children of water. Rather, they are called children of God the Father and of Mother Church.

So Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, yet he is not the Son of the Holy Spirit. Conversely, it does not follow that everyone called the son of someone is also said to have been born of that person, as in the case of those who are adopted. People are also called children of Gehenna, not because they were born from it but because they are prepared for it.

Since, then, something may be born of another without being its child; and, conversely, not everyone called another’s child is born of the one whose child he is called, this manner in which Christ was born from Mary as a son and from the Holy Spirit not as a son teaches us about the grace of God. By that grace, without any preceding merits, at the very beginning of his nature, when he began to exist, the man was joined to the Word of God in so great a unity of person that the same one was Son of God and son of man, and son of man and Son of God. Thus, in the assumption of human nature, grace itself became in some manner natural to that man, by which he could admit no sin.

This grace is signified through the Holy Spirit because he is God in such a way as properly also to be God’s gift. Therefore, by saying that Christ’s birth was from the Holy Spirit, Scripture shows nothing other than the grace of God by which, in a wonderful and ineffable manner, he was joined and bound to the Word of God, and filled bodily with divine grace.

### Another reason why he is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit

3. It may also be said that Christ, according to his humanity, was born of the Holy Spirit because the Spirit made him. For insofar as he is man, he too was made, as the Apostle says, Galatians 4. Therefore he is said to have been conceived and born of the Holy Spirit, not because the Holy Spirit was seed for the Virgin—for the seed of the birth was not taken from the substance of the Holy Spirit—but because that which was united to the Word was assumed from the Virgin’s flesh by the grace of God and the operation of the Holy Spirit.

In the Gospel, Matthew 1, Mary is accordingly said to have been found with child by the Holy Spirit. Ambrose, explaining the sense of this statement in *On the Holy Spirit*, book 2, chapter 5, says:

> What is from something is either from its substance or from its power. It is from substance, as the Son is from the Father or out of the Father, and as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. But it is from power, as all things are from God. How then did Mary have in her womb by the Holy Spirit? If it were from his substance, then spirit would have been changed into flesh and bones. Certainly not. But if the Virgin conceived through his operation and power, who would deny that the Holy Spirit is the author of the Lord’s incarnation?

### Why the Apostle calls Christ “made,” though we confess that he was born

4. But one may ask: since we profess that the Savior was born, why does the Apostle call him “made from the seed of David” in Romans 1, and elsewhere, Galatians 4, “made from a woman,” since to be made is one thing and to be born another? He meant something, then, by this expression.

Since the Lord’s flesh was not formed and made into a body in the Virgin’s womb from human seed, but by the operation and power of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says “made,” not “born.” For it is one thing to generate through mixed seed and congealed blood, and another to produce not by mixture but by power. Human beings can generate children, but they cannot make them.

The Apostle therefore says “made,” not “born,” lest his birth—which was without male seed—be thought similar to ours, which is brought about through the mingling of seeds. Yet when the Apostle said “made,” he added “from the seed of David,” because although no human seed intervened in the Virgin’s conception, nevertheless Christ was formed from flesh which derives from seed; and therefore he is rightly said to have been made from the seed of David.

## DISTINCTION V. WHETHER A PERSON OR NATURE ASSUMED A PERSON OR NATURE; AND WHETHER THE NATURE OF GOD WAS INCARNATE

1. Furthermore, since the preceding material establishes that the Word of God assumed flesh and soul together into the unity of person, it must be asked which of the following should preferably be affirmed: that person assumed person, nature assumed nature, person assumed nature, or nature assumed person. And should the divine nature be said to be incarnate, just as God incarnate and the Word incarnate are rightly said?

This inquiry, or line of questioning, is, according to the testimonies of sacred authorities, partly involved and perplexing, but partly explicit and clear. For it is certain and unquestionably true that neither nature assumed person nor person assumed person; rather, person assumed nature. This is proved and established by the appended testimonies and teachings of the saints.

Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*:

> God the only-begotten, when he was conceived, received the reality of flesh from the Virgin; and when he was born, he preserved the integrity of virginity in his mother.

And shortly afterward:

> Thus God received human nature into the unity of person, so that, humbling himself through mercy, he filled the womb of the incorrupt Virgin, from whom he was to be born.

Therefore that God received the servant-form—that is, the nature of a servant—into his own person. Again: “God the Word received not the person of man, but nature.” Again: “The only-begotten Son of God was incarnate by assuming flesh and a rational soul, in order to cleanse human flesh and soul.”

By these and many other authorities it is plainly shown that neither nature assumed person nor person assumed person, but person assumed nature.

But regarding the fourth part of the question—whether nature assumed nature—there is a thorny question even among learned men. For those who have been distinguished in authority and more learned than others in sacred Scripture seem to differ widely in this matter; and they seem to disagree not only with others but even with themselves, as the following chapters show.

For it is read in the Second Council of Toledo:

> The Word alone was made flesh and dwelt among us. Although the whole Trinity accomplished the formation of the assumed man, since the works of the Trinity are inseparable, the Son alone received man into the singularity of his person, not into the unity of the divine nature—that is, into what is proper to the Son, not into what is common to the Trinity.

Again, in the Second Council of Toledo:

> We believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be God of one substance. Yet we do not say that the Virgin Mary gave birth to the unity of this Trinity, but only to the Son, who alone assumed our nature into the unity of his person. It must also be believed that the whole Trinity effected the incarnation of this Son of God. Yet the Son alone received the servant-form into the singularity of his person.

These statements seem to imply that person alone, not nature, assumed nature. For if that which is common to the Trinity did not receive man, then the divine nature, which is common to the three persons, did not receive him.

This seems opposed by Augustine’s statement in *On Faith to Peter*:

> Christ’s divinity is not alien to the nature of the Father, according to John 1: “In the beginning was the Word”; nor is his humanity alien to the nature of his mother, according to the statement: “The Word was made flesh.” For that nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin, in order to be born of the Virgin.

This authority seems to teach that the divine nature assumed the human nature. We may be greatly troubled by his saying that it was eternally begotten from the Father, unless perhaps “nature” is here understood to mean person. Otherwise, if we say that the nature common to the three persons was begotten, we encounter what we discussed above in the treatise on the Trinity, where we said that nature did not beget nature but person begot person. For if nature begot nature, since the Trinity’s nature is one and the same, the same thing would have begotten itself. Augustine denies that this is possible.

But elsewhere we find certain evidence showing that nature assumed nature. Augustine says in the first book *On the Trinity*:

> Christ also made himself lesser, by receiving the servant-form. For he did not receive the servant-form in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father, so that the same only-begotten Son of the Father is in the servant-form and in the form of God; because the form of God received the servant-form.

If the form of God received the servant-form, then without doubt nature received nature. For by the name “form” nature is signified, as Augustine plainly teaches in *On Faith to Peter*:

> When you hear concerning Christ that he was in the form of God, you must recognize and hold most firmly that by the name of form the fullness of nature must be understood. Therefore he was in the form of God because he was always in the nature of God the Father, from whom he was born.

Hilary likewise says in *On the Trinity*, book 12: “To be in the form of God means nothing other than to remain in God’s nature.” You have learned that the name “form” conveys the meaning of nature; and you have heard that the form of God assumed the servant-form. Consequently, the divine nature assumed human nature.

Jerome also plainly suggests this in the *Explanation of the Faith*, saying to Damasus:

> The Son of God suffered not in appearance but truly, according to the saying: He suffered in that which could suffer—that is, [Col. 0766] not according to the substance which assumed, but according to that which was assumed.

From this it is apparent that the divine substance assumed the human.

Moreover, if Augustine’s words set above are carefully considered, they seem to indicate that the Word alone was made flesh and that the divine nature alone assumed human nature. Augustine says, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, at the end:

> The Trinity reconciled us to itself by this: the Trinity itself made only the Word flesh. In this the unchangeable truth of divine and human nature remains, so that, just as his divinity which he has from the Father is always true, so also his humanity, which the supreme Divinity bears united to itself, is always true and unchangeable.

See that he says that only the Word was made flesh and that humanity is united to divinity. Earlier he likewise said that the servant-form was assumed by the Son alone, although the whole Trinity made it.

It is now easy to recognize how various and manifold the teachings of the authorities have been concerning the question proposed. Therefore later writers who read them, taking occasion from the foregoing, offer diverse and contrary opinions.

### What should be held on this matter

2. We, however, wishing to exclude every charge of falsehood and contradiction from the sacred pages, and entertaining no suspicion of a perverse meaning regarding orthodox Fathers and Catholic doctors, agree in saying both that the person of the Son assumed human nature, and that the divine nature was united to human nature in the Son, united it to itself, or assumed it. Therefore it is also truly called incarnate.

When it is said that the Son alone received the servant-form, this does not exclude the divine nature from the assumption of the servant-form; rather, it excludes the other two persons, namely the Father and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the other statement—namely, that what is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity, received man—must be understood in this way: the divine nature united human nature to itself properly in the hypostasis of the Son, not commonly in the three persons.

This interpretation is confirmed by John Damascene’s words in *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 6. He plainly affirms that the whole divine nature was incarnate in one hypostasis, saying:

> In the humanization of God the Word, we say that the whole and perfect nature of divinity was incarnate in one hypostasis—that is, united to human nature—and not part to part. For we say that the whole nature or substance of divinity is united to the whole human nature. The nature is the same in each hypostasis, that is, in each person. When we say that the nature of the Word was incarnate, according to the blessed Fathers, namely Athanasius and Cyril, we mean that divinity was united to flesh, and we confess one incarnate nature of God the Word. But the Word possesses both what is common to the substance and what is proper to the hypostasis, that is, the person.

From this it is manifestly shown that the divine nature was incarnate. Therefore it is truly said also to have assumed human nature.

### Whether the divine nature ought to be called “made flesh”

3. But it is asked whether the same divine nature ought to be called “made flesh,” just as the Word is called “made flesh.” For if to be incarnate is the same as to be made flesh, it seems that it ought likewise to be said to have been made flesh, just as it is called incarnate.

To this we say: if that expression were found in sacred Scripture, it would be understood in the same sense as when the divine nature is said to be incarnate. But because authority is silent on that phrase, and because the manner of speaking would seem excessively emphatic if the divine nature were called “made flesh,” I think it better to be silent about it or deny it than rashly affirm it, lest, if it were said, it should be thought to signify the convertibility of one nature into another.

From the foregoing it is beyond doubt that the person of the Word—or the divine nature—assumed the nature of man, namely flesh and soul, but not a human person. But if the divine nature assumed human nature, why is it not said to have become man or to be man, as the Word of God is?

It may be said in reply that the Son of God is called made man or is called man not merely because he assumed man, but because he received him into the unity and singularity of himself and his person. The divine nature, however, received man—that is, united the form of man to itself—but not into its own singularity and unity. For while the property and distinction of the two natures were preserved, the singularity of the person remained. Therefore the divine nature is not called man or made man in the same way as the Son of God. Some, nevertheless, grant both expressions without distinction.

### Why he did not assume a human person, although he assumed man

4. He did not assume a human person because that flesh and that soul were not united as one person which he might assume; for when the Word was united to them, no person was constituted from them. Rather, they were united to one another at the same time as to the Word.

Yet those two, namely soul and flesh, were united to each other by one union, and were united to the Word by another. For the union of that soul with the flesh is one thing, while the union of the Word with that soul and flesh is another. Therefore the Word of God assumed not a human person but a nature, because no one composite person consisting of that flesh and soul existed for the Word to assume; rather, by assuming he united them, and by uniting them he assumed them.

### An objection against this, by which some seek to prove that person assumed person
5. Here some object that a person assumed a person. For a person is an individual substance of a rational nature, and this is the soul. Therefore, if he assumed a soul, he also assumed a person. But this does not follow, because a soul is not a person when it is personally united to another thing, but when it exists by itself; for, separated from the body, it is a person, like an angel. But that soul was never without being joined to another thing. Therefore, when it was assumed, a person was not assumed.

They also try to prove in another way that the Word of God assumed a person, because he assumed some man. For he assumed the man Jesus Christ; therefore, he assumed some man. Now Augustine, in the *Exposition of the Creed*, declares under an anathema that he assumed the man Jesus Christ, saying: “If anyone says and believes that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.” He also uses expressions of this kind in many passages of Scripture: “That man was assumed by the Word”; “That man was made Christ.” And the Prophet, speaking to God of the man Christ, says in Psalm 54: “Blessed is he whom you chose and assumed,” etc. From these it seems to follow that some man was assumed by the Word, and thus that person was assumed by person.

But because it is wicked to say or think this, the foregoing expressions and others like them must soundly be understood in this sense: that Christ-man, or that man, or a certain man, is said to have been assumed by the Word or united to the Word, not because the person of a man was assumed or united to the Word, but because that soul and flesh were so assumed and united to the Word—in which the person of God and man subsists—that, when Scripture in expressions of this kind mentions “the assumed,” “the united,” “a certain one,” or “some one,” you must look to human nature, not to a person.

Accordingly, when one asks, without citing an authority, whether someone or some man was assumed by the Word or united to the Word, no answer should be given without a distinction of meaning, since the question as posed is equivocal. The questioner's insistence should instead be resolved thus: if you ask concerning the person of a man, I answer, No; if concerning human nature, I say, Yes.

## DISTINCTION VI. ON THE MEANING OF THESE EXPRESSIONS: “GOD WAS MADE MAN,” “GOD IS MAN”; WHETHER BY THESE EXPRESSIONS GOD IS SAID TO HAVE BECOME SOMETHING, OR TO BE SOMETHING, OR NOT TO BE SOMETHING

1. From what has been said there arises a question of very great usefulness, but of excessive difficulty and complexity. Since it is established from the foregoing and from many other testimonies, and all Catholics unanimously confess, that God was made man and that Christ is true God and true man, the question is asked whether, by these expressions—“God was made man,” “the Son of God was made the Son of man,” “God is man,” and “man is God”—God is said to have become something or to be something, or something is said to be God; and whether it is equally fitting to say, “Man was made God” and “the Son of man was made the Son of God,” as the converse is said; and, if these expressions do not say that God became something or is something, what is the meaning of these expressions and similar ones. In explaining this profundity and expounding this scrupulous question, learned persons are found to differ greatly.

### The opinion of some is reported

2. Some say that in the very Incarnation of the Word, a certain man, constituted of a rational soul and human flesh—of which every true man is constituted—began to be God, not by the nature of God but by the person of the Word; and God began to be that man. They also grant that that man was assumed by the Word and united to the Word, and yet is the Word. For this reason they teach that God is said to have been made man, or to be man: because God was made—that is, began to be—a certain substance subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; and that substance was made—that is, began to be—God. This was not by a migration of nature into nature; rather, with the property of each nature preserved, it came about that God was that substance and that substance was God.

Hence it is truly said: “God was made man”; “Man was made God”; “God is man”; “Man is God”; “the Son of God is the son of man”; and conversely. Although they say that this man subsists from a rational soul and human flesh, they nevertheless do not confess that he is composed of the two natures, divine and human, nor that those two natures are his parts; rather, they say that only soul and flesh are his parts.

### Authorities by which they support their opinion

3. Lest they seem to speak only from their own understanding, they fortify this opinion with many testimonies. Augustine says in Book 13, chapter 19, of *On the Trinity*: “When one reads, ‘The Word was made flesh,’ in the Word I understand the true Son of God; in the flesh I recognize the true son of man; and both together are one person—God and man—joined by the generosity of ineffable grace.”

The same, in chapter 38 of the *Enchiridion*: “Christ Jesus is God from God, but man was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. Each substance, divine and human, is the one Son of God the almighty Father, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds; both are one, but one on account of the Word and the other on account of the man: not two sons, God and man, but one Son of God” (*ibid.*, ch. 35). “God without beginning; man from a definite beginning.”

The same, *ibid.*, chapter 36: “What did human nature in Christ the man merit, that it should be singularly assumed into the unity of the person of the only Son of God? What good will, what good works preceded, by which this man merited to become one person with God? Was he previously a man, and was this singular benefit bestowed upon him, so that he might singularly merit God? Certainly, from the moment he began to be man, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and this one and only Son. Therefore the Word of God, because from the time flesh was assumed by him it was surely made God; so that, just as any individual man is one person, namely rational soul and flesh, so Christ may be one person, Word and man.”

The same, Tractate 78 on John: “Let us recognize the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and the human, by which he is less than the Father. Yet both together are not two, but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity and not a Trinity. And therefore Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.”

Likewise, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*: “What did that man merit, that, being assumed by the Word coeternal with the Father into unity of person, he should be the only-begotten Son of God? What good preceded in him, that he should attain this ineffable excellence? By the action and assumption of God the Word, that man, from the moment he began to exist, began to be the only Son of God.” Likewise: “Any man becomes a Christian by grace in the same way as that man was made Christ by grace from the beginning.” The same, in Book 13 of *On the Trinity*: “The grace of God is commended to us in the man Christ. For neither did he attain, by any preceding merits, that he should be joined to the true God by so great a unity and become, with him, one person, the Son of God; but from the moment he began to be man, from that moment he is also God. Hence it was said, John 1: ‘The Word was made flesh.’”

Hilary likewise says in Book 10 of *On the Trinity*: “We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word, nor are we ignorant that the Son of man was constituted from soul and body.” They use these and other authorities who say that a certain man composed of rational soul and flesh was made God, but by grace, not by nature. For that man had by grace alone, not by merits or nature, that he should be God or the Son of God, and that he should possess all the knowledge and power possessed by the Word with whom he is one person. Yet in the preceding authorities it is read not only that that man is one person with the Word and is the Word itself, but also that rational soul and flesh are the same person, and are Christ and God.

### The opinion of others

4. There are others who agree with these in part, but say that that man consists not merely of rational soul and flesh, but of human and divine nature—that is, of three substances: divinity, flesh, and soul. They confess that this is Jesus Christ and that he is one person only. Before the Incarnation, however, he was merely simple; but in the Incarnation he became composite from divinity and humanity.

Nor is he therefore another person than before; but whereas previously he was the person of God only, in the Incarnation he also became the person of man—not so that there were two persons, but so that one and the same person was the person of God and man. Therefore the person which was previously simple and existed in one nature only subsists in two natures and from two natures; and the person which was God alone became also true man, subsisting not only from soul and flesh but also from divinity. Yet that person ought not to be called a made person, although he is called a made person of man.

Thus that person became, as some hold, something subsisting from soul and flesh; but it did not become a person, substance, or nature. Insofar as it is that subsisting thing, it is composite; but insofar as it is the Word, it is simple.

### Authorities also cited which prove this opinion

5. On this Augustine says in the Book of Prosper’s *Sentences*: “By every means we strive to prove that the sacrifice of the Church consists of two things and is effected from two things: the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, the body of Christ. So too the person of Christ consists and is effected from God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man. For every thing contains within itself the nature and truth of those things from which it is made.”

On the same matter John Damascene says in Book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapters 5 and 7: “In our Lord Jesus Christ we recognize two natures, but one hypostasis composed from both. Therefore Christ was incarnate, taking from the Virgin the first-fruits of our lump, so that the hypostasis itself existed in the flesh—the hypostasis of God the Word—made composite and formed, whereas previously it had been the simple hypostasis of the Word. It is composite from two perfect natures, divinity and humanity, so that it bears the characteristic and delimiting property of the divine sonship of God the Word, by which it is distinguished from the Father and the Holy Spirit; and the characteristic and delimiting properties of flesh, by which it differs from the mother and from other human beings.”

Likewise, in the same book, chapter 3, in the middle of the chapter: “We confess one hypostasis of the Son of God, perfectly existing in two natures, divinity and humanity; and that the same hypostasis was incarnate; and that these two natures are preserved and remain in him after the union, not placing each separately and according to parts, but united to each other in one composite hypostasis. For we call the union substantial, namely true and not imaginary; substantial, however, not because the two natures complete another thing, namely one composite nature, but because they are united to each other in one composite hypostasis of the Son of God. We determine that the same substantial difference remains: what was created remains created, and what was uncreated remains uncreated; what was mortal remains mortal, and what was immortal remains immortal; what was circumscribed remains circumscribed, and what was uncircumscribed remains uncircumscribed; and the one shines forth indeed in miracles.”

Augustine likewise says in *On the Trinity*: “Just as according to divinity there is one nature of Father and Son, so also according to humanity there is one nature of mother and Son. Therefore from both substances, both divinity and humanity, one and the same Jesus Christ is God, the Son of God and of man, true God and likewise true man.” Again, in Book 13 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17: “Human nature could be joined to God in such a way that from two substances one person might be made. And thus he now consists of three: God, soul, and flesh.”

They support themselves with these and many other authorities, who say that Christ’s person is composite or made, or consists of two natures or three substances.

### A third opinion of others

6. There are also others who, in the Incarnation of the Word, deny not only that a person is composed from natures, but even deny that some man, or indeed any substance, was there composed or made from soul and flesh. They say rather that those two things, namely soul and flesh, are united to the person or nature of the Word in such a way that no nature or person is made or composed from those two, or from these three; but the Word of God is clothed with those two as with a garment, so that he might fittingly appear to mortal eyes. He is therefore said truly to have been made man because he received the reality of flesh and soul.

Those two are also said to have been received into the singularity or unity of his person, not because those two, or anything composed from them, is one person with the Word or is the Word, but because, when those two were added to the Word, the number of persons was not increased so as to make a quaternity in the Trinity; and because the very person of the Word, which was previously without a garment, was not divided or changed by assuming the garment, but remained one and the same, unchanged.

They say that God was made man according to *habitus*—that is, according to an acquired clothing or condition. For by receiving man, God is said to have been made man; and on account of the man received, God is said truly to be man; and on account of God who assumed him, man is said to be God. For, they say, if “God is man” or “man is God” were understood essentially, then, if God had assumed a human being of the female sex, a woman would essentially be God, and conversely. But God could have assumed a human being of the female sex; therefore a woman could be God, and conversely. (Gregory, *On Ezekiel*.)

### Authorities adduced by which this opinion is strengthened

7. So that these too may not seem to put forward merely their own view, they confirm what they say by producing testimonies. Augustine says in *On the Grace of the New Testament*: “Just as the number of persons is not increased when flesh is added to soul so that one man exists, so the number of persons is not increased when man is added to the Word, so that the one man Christ exists. Thus “God is man” is read, so that we may understand the singularity of this person, not suspect that divinity was changed into flesh.”

Again, while treating the Apostle’s words, Philippians 2, “He was found in appearance as a man,” he plainly shows in Book 83 of the *Questions*, question 73, that God is said to have been made man, or to be man, according to *habitus*:

“We speak of *habitus* in many ways: either as a habit of mind, such as the grasp of learning established by practice; or as a habit of body, as when we say one person is stronger than another; or as a habit of things externally fitted to the limbs, as when we say that someone is clothed or shod, and the like. In all these kinds it is evident that *habitus* is said to be in that thing which happens to or is added to something in such a way that it can also not have it. This name, however, is derived from the verb *habere*, ‘to have.’ Therefore *habitus* is said to be in that thing which happens to us or is added to us so as to be had.

“Nevertheless, there is this difference: some things that happen or are added so as to produce a *habitus* are not changed, but themselves change those things to which they are added, while remaining whole and unshaken in themselves; as wisdom, when added to a person, is not itself changed but changes the person, making a wise person out of a foolish one. Other things happen or are added in such a way that they both change and are changed, as food which, losing its own form, is turned into the body; and we, refreshed by food, are changed from thinness and weakness into strength and vigor. A third kind occurs when those things which happen or are added neither change the things to which they happen nor are themselves changed by them, as a ring placed on a finger; this kind is found very rarely. A fourth kind occurs when those things which happen or are added are changed, not from their own nature, but by receiving another appearance and form; as a garment which, when cast off and laid aside, does not have the form which it assumes when worn. For, worn upon the limbs, it receives a form which it did not have when unworn. This kind suits the present comparison.

“For the Son of God emptied himself, Philippians 2, not by changing his own form, but by taking the form of a servant; nor, having lost immutable stability, by being turned or transformed into man, but by being made in the likeness of men. He himself, the one who assumed, by assuming a true man, was found in appearance as a man; that is, by having man he was found to be man—not to himself, but to those to whom he appeared in man. And by saying ‘as a man,’ he expresses reality. Therefore by the name *habitus* the Apostle sufficiently indicated in what manner he said, ‘made in the likeness of men’: because he was made not by transformation into man, but by *habitus*, when he clothed himself with man, joining him to himself and, in a certain manner, conforming him so that he might associate him with immortality and eternity. Therefore the Word should not be understood to have been changed by assuming man, just as limbs clothed with a garment are not changed—although that assumption joined the assumed being ineffably to the one who assumed him.”

By these words Augustine seems openly to indicate that God is said to have been made man according to *habitus*. Wishing also to express the manner of the Incarnation itself, he says, in Book 4 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 21, or the last chapter:

“If one asks how the Incarnation took place, I say that the very Word of God was made flesh, that is, was made man; yet he was not turned or changed into that which he was made, but was clothed with flesh so that he might appear fittingly to fleshly persons. This occurred in such a way that there is there not only the Word of God and the flesh of man, but also the rational soul of man. And this whole is called both God on account of God, and man on account of man. If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be cleansed by faith through abstaining from sins and doing good works; for these matters are difficult.”

The same, in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 2: “Although the Son of God is eternal and true God, for us he was made true and complete man. He is true in this: that this God has true human nature; he is truly complete in this: that he assumed both human flesh and a rational soul.” Again, later in the same work: “The assumption or emptying of the supreme God was nothing other than the assumption of the servant’s form, that is, human nature. Therefore both forms are in Christ, because both substances are true and complete in Christ: divine nature and human nature.”

The same, in *Against Maximinus*: “Although he was invisible in himself, he appeared visibly in the man whom he deigned to assume from a woman.” Again in the same work: “We believe that Christ the Lord assumed true man, and that in him the invisible appeared visibly to men; that in him he lived among men, in him endured human things from men, and in him taught men.”

Hilary likewise says in Book 10 of *On the Trinity*: “How was the Son of God born from Mary, except because the Word was made flesh; namely, because the Son of God, though he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant? Yet we confess him one and the same, not by a falling away of God but by an assumption of man; and that he was found both in the form of God because of the divine nature, and in the form of a servant from the conception of the Holy Spirit, according to the *habitus* of man. That *habitus* was not merely that of man, but ‘as of man’; nor was that flesh flesh of sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh,” Romans 8.

You have heard three opinions set forth according to differing views, and testimonies adduced for each.

## DISTINCTION VII. HAVING SET FORTH THE OPINIONS AND PRODUCED THE TESTIMONIES, HE PURSUES THE MEANINGS OF THE PROPOSED EXPRESSIONS ACCORDING TO EACH OPINION, FIRST ACCORDING TO THE FIRST

1. According to the first opinion, then, God is said to have been made man, and man made God, because God began to be a certain rational substance which he had not previously been; and that substance began to be God, and possessed this by grace, not by nature or merits. Hence Christ, insofar as he is man, is rightly said to have been predestined to be the Son of God.

But the following objection is made to this opinion: if that substance began to be God, and God to be that substance, then some substance is God which was not always God; and some substance is God which is not divine substance; and God is something which was not always. This they too grant, relying on the testimony of Origen, who says: “Without doubt he was made what he was not before”; but he adds, “according to the flesh.” According to God, however, he existed before, and there was not a time when he was not.

This opinion can also be opposed in many other ways. We pass these over, leaving the exercise of inquiry to the reader, and hasten on to other matters.

### Here he explains the second opinion and the sense of the same expressions

2. In the second opinion of this distinction, the reasoning appears to be as follows: when it is said, “God was made man,” it is understood that he began to subsist from two natures, or three substances. Conversely, “Man was made God,” because that which subsists in two natures began to be God; or rather, “Man was made God,” and conversely, is said because God assumed man and man was assumed by God. Hence Augustine says in *On the Trinity*: “Such was that assumption as made man God and God man.”

But the meaning varies when it is said, “God is man,” and “man is God.” God is said to be the person subsisting in two natures and from two natures; and the person subsisting in two natures and from two natures is said to be God—that is, the Word or divine nature. For a simple person or a nature can be predicated of a composite person. But, as John Damascene says, “nature” and “person” are not the same thing.

### In what sense they say Christ was predestined

3. These say that Christ was predestined insofar as he is man—that is, insofar as he subsists from two substances, soul and flesh. For with respect to the nature of divinity, he was not predestined. Therefore he was not predestined insofar as he subsists in it or by it, but insofar as he subsists in the other two substances, soul and flesh; that is, insofar as he is man.

### How the earlier authorities, which seem to oppose this opinion, are explained

4. They also interpret the authorities which support the first opinion and seem to contradict this one. Thus, when it is read that “that man was assumed by the Word in the singularity of person” or “made one person with the Word,” this is understood of human nature, which was united to the Word in the singularity of person: that is, the same person which previously existed and was simple remained unchanged, although composite, without increase in the number of persons.

They say, however, that the manner of this composition differs from that in other human beings, because this composition is from three substances, whereas that of other persons is from two. They also deny that human nature is a person or the Son of God; and just as they say that the same one is man and God, son of man and Son of God, so they say that he is one and the same—not one thing and another, just as he is not one person and another.

### He sets forth certain things which seem contrary to the foregoing

5. But the matters contained in the following chapters seem contrary to these. Augustine says, in Tractate 69 on John: “The Word of God is one thing, man another; but the Word was made flesh, that is, man. Therefore the person of the Word is not one and the person of man another, since both are Christ and one person.”

The same, *To Felicianus*, chapters 11 and 12: “The Son of God is one thing, the son of man another; but not another person.” Likewise: “The Son of God is one thing from the Father, another from the mother.” The same, in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*: “Since the Son is both God and man, God is one substance and man another.”

### How they answer these

6. They interpret these statements as follows. When it is said, “the Word of God is one thing, man another,” or “God is one substance, man another,” Christ is signified to be of one nature insofar as he is man and of another insofar as he is God; and the nature by which he is man is one thing, while that by which he is God is another.

For John Damascene says, in Book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, at the beginning of the chapter: “The natures are united to each other without conversion and without alteration: neither does the divine depart from its own simplicity, nor is the human either changed into the nature of divinity or divided into nonexistence, nor from the two is one composite nature made. For a composite nature cannot be *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial, with either of the natures from which it is composed, since one is completed from the other; just as a body composed of four elements is called neither fire, nor air, nor earth, nor water, nor is it said to be *homoousios* with any of these.

“If, therefore, according to the heretics, Christ after the union existed as one composite nature, he was changed from a simple nature into a composite one; and he is neither *homoousios* with the Father, who exists in a simple nature, nor with the mother; and he will be called neither God nor man, but Christ alone. This name, ‘Christ,’ will then be not the name of his person’s nature, but of the one composite nature according to them. But we do not teach that Christ is of one composite nature; and we say that this name, ‘Christ,’ is a name of person, not *monotropon*, that is, not said in one way only, but signifying two natures, divinity and humanity. From divinity and humanity we confess that he both is and is called perfect God and perfect man, the same one, from two natures and in two natures.”

Thus the Son of God is said to be one thing and the son of man another, because he is of one substance or nature insofar as he is the Son of God and of another insofar as he is the son of man; not because the Son of God and of man himself is those two distinct things, namely two distinct natures.

### He confirms the interpretation by authority

7. For Hilary plainly says in Book 9 of *On the Trinity*: “Since the son of man is not one thing and the Son of God another—for the Word was made flesh—and since he who is the Son of God is himself also the son of man, I ask who was glorified in this son of man?” He expressly says that the Son of God is not one thing and the son of man another. From this the foregoing interpretation is strengthened and approved.

### He also notes other words of authorities to interpret them

8. What has also been said—“both are Christ and one person”—may move the reader, as may Augustine’s statement in Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 24: “Because the form of God took the form of a servant, both are God, both are man. But both are God on account of God who assumed, and both are man on account of man who was assumed.”

And the same in *On the Gift of Perseverance*: “Whoever is faithful believes that in him true human nature was so exalted by God the Word who assumed it, that the one who assumed and that which was assumed were one person in the Trinity, that assumption ineffably bringing about the reality of one person in God and man.”

But if the one who assumed and that which was assumed are one person, then human nature and the Word are one person. They maintain, however, that all these statements were made in this sense: both are called Christ and one person because one Christ and one person subsists in both. Likewise the assumed is called one person with the one assuming because the assumed is associated with the one assuming in unity of person—that is, such that the unity of person remained. This does not mean that flesh and soul are one God; for, as Jerome says, “the Word is God, not the flesh assumed.” And Ambrose says in Book 3 of *On the Holy Spirit*: “One thing is that which assumed, another that which was assumed.”

### Here he sets forth an authority which seems very greatly opposed to this opinion

9. There is another statement which seems very greatly to oppose this opinion. Augustine says in Book 1 of *Against Maximinus*: “Christ is one person of twofold substance, because he is both God and man; yet neither God nor man can be called a part of this substance. Otherwise the Son of God, God, before he assumed the form of a servant, was not whole, and he grew when man was added to his divinity.”

See: he says that God is not a part of that person. Thus it appears that that person does not consist of God and man. To this they reply that that person does not consist of God and man as a whole consists of parts. For the parts of a whole are so joined that something which did not previously exist is constituted from them. But the human and divine natures are not united in Christ in that way. The manner of this union, which is not a union of parts, is inexplicable.

Some nevertheless think that “God” there signifies person, because Augustine was dealing with the three persons, none of which he said was a part of the Trinity, just as God is not a part of this person. If it is understood of person, it is manifest that person is not part of person.

The second opinion and its explanation have been carefully set forth. The authorities adduced under the third opinion, which must now be considered, oppose it in no respect, or only slightly.

### The third opinion: the meaning of the foregoing propositions

10. In this opinion, then, “God was made man” is said because he received man; he is said to be man because he has man, or because he is one having man; “man was made God” because he was assumed by God; and man is God because the one having man is God.

Therefore, when it is said, “God is man,” either the *habitus* is predicated, or the person—but as humanated. Cassiodorus seems to show that the humanated person is predicated when he says: “He became, if I may so speak, humanated God; even in assuming flesh he did not cease to be God.” Yet this may be understood in different ways: either God was made humanated, or Christ was made humanated God; for either may soundly be said.

Therefore, when it is said, “God was made man,” there are multiple meanings according to these writers: it may be understood that he assumed human nature, or that the humanated Word began to exist. Yet if the humanated Word began to exist, it does not follow that the Word began to exist; nor, if God was made the humanated Word, does it follow that he was made the Word. Just as one may say of someone, “Today this man began to be good,” or “was made a good man,” yet he did not today begin to be a man or become a man.

### In what sense, according to these, Christ is said to have been predestined

11. According to these writers, Christ is said, insofar as he is man, to have been predestined to be the Son of God, because it was predestined by God from eternity and conferred upon him in time by grace that he himself, God-man, should be the Son of God. For he did not always possess this, but received it in time by grace.

Augustine seems to have noted this in *To Prosper and Hilary*: “Jesus was predestined so that he who, according to the flesh, was to be the son of David, should be the Son of God in power.”

[Note: [Col. 0774] In the book elsewhere called *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 15.]

These writers also understand it according to *habitus* when Christ is said to be less than the Father insofar as he is man—that is, insofar as he has man united to himself. Hence Augustine, volume 3, Book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7: “God the Son is equal by nature to God the Father, lesser by *habitus*.” For in the form of a servant he is less than the Father; in the form of God he is equal to the Father. Because they hold that the Incarnation must be understood according to *habitus*, they teach that one should say “God humanated,” not “man deified.” Hence John Damascene, Book 3 of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 2: “We do not say that a man was deified, but that God was made man.”

### Why “the Lordly man” should not be said

12. Although “man is God” is said, it is nevertheless not fitting to say “the Lordly man” (*homo dominicus*). Hence Augustine, in Book 1, chapter 19, of the *Retractations*: “I do not see whether the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and men, may rightly be called ‘the Lordly man,’ since he is certainly Lord. To say this, indeed, I had read among certain Catholic interpreters. But wherever I said it, I wish I had not said it. For afterward I saw that it should not be said, although it might in some respect be defended by the same reasoning.”

According to these writers, the person of the Son is also said to exist in and from two natures according to adhesion or inherence: one adheres to him, the other is in him.

### Why the foregoing is insufficient for knowing this question

13. We have treated the question above with sufficient care, according to the opinions of different persons, without assertion or prejudice. Nevertheless, in a matter so great and so difficult to know, I do not want the reader to think that this discussion of ours ought to suffice for him. Rather, let him read other treatments, perhaps better considered and handled; and let him examine with a more alert and intelligent mind, if he can, the matters which may trouble him here.

Let him firmly hold this: that God assumed man, and man passed into God—not by a changeability of nature, but by God’s condescension—so that neither God was changed into human substance by assuming man, nor man, when glorified, into God’s divine substance; for change or mutability of nature brings about diminution and abolition of substance.

## DISTINCTION VIII. WHETHER THE DIVINE NATURE OUGHT TO BE SAID TO HAVE BEEN BORN OF THE VIRGIN

1. After these matters one must inquire whether it should be granted of the divine nature that it was born of the Virgin, as it is said to have been incarnate in the Virgin. It seems indeed that it should not be said to have been born of the Virgin, since it was not born of the Father. For a thing which is not begotten of the Father does not seem to be born of the mother, lest something should possess the name of sonship in humanity which it does not possess in divinity.

Yet it seems possible to prove that it was born of the Virgin, because if for God to be born of the Virgin is to assume man, then it seems that the divine nature should be said to have been born. Augustine says thus in *On Faith to Peter*: “Eternal and divine nature could not be temporally conceived and born from human nature unless, through the conception of true humanity, the ineffable divinity in itself received a true temporal conception and birth. Thus eternal God was truly, according to time, both conceived and born of the Virgin.”

By this authority it seems to be suggested that divine nature was conceived and born of the Virgin. But if the words are carefully noted, it is understood rather to concern the person, which without doubt ought to be said to have been born both of the Father and of the mother.

## On the Twofold Nativity of Christ, by Which He Was Born Twice

2. It is commonly asked whether Christ should be said to have been begotten twice, just as he is called the Son of God and of man. To this one may answer that Christ was born twice and had two births. Thus Augustine, in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, not far from the beginning: “God the Father begot from his own nature the Son, God equal and coeternal with himself. This same only-begotten God was born a second time: once from the Father and once from the mother. For the Word of God was born of the Father; the Word made flesh was born of the mother. Therefore one and the same Son of God was born before the ages and was born in time; and both births belong to the one Son of God: the divine and the human.”

John Damascene likewise says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 7, in the middle: “We therefore venerate two births of Christ: one from the Father before the ages, which is beyond cause, reason, time, and nature; and one in the last times, for our sake, according to us, and above us. For our sake, because it was for our salvation; according to us, because he was born as a man from a woman and after the period of conception, namely nine months; above us, because he was born not from seed but from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin, above the law of conception.” From these passages it is plainly apparent that Christ has two births and that the same one was born twice.

## DISTINCTION IX. ON THE ADORATION OF CHRIST’S HUMANITY: WHETHER THE SAME ADORATION OUGHT TO BE OFFERED TO HIS HUMANITY AND HIS DEITY

1. Further inquiry must be made whether Christ’s flesh [Col. 0776] and soul ought to be adored with one and the same adoration as the Word—namely, that called *latria*. For if *latria* is offered to the soul or flesh—*latria* being understood as the service or worship due to the Creator alone—then, since Christ’s soul or flesh is merely a creature, what is due to the Creator alone is offered to a creature. Whoever does this is reckoned guilty of idolatry.

For this reason, some think that Christ’s flesh or soul should not be adored with the adoration called *latria*, but with that called *dulia*, which they say has two kinds or modes. There is one kind of *dulia* that can be offered to any creature; and there is another that ought to be offered to Christ’s humanity alone, and to no other creature, because Christ’s humanity is to be venerated and loved above every creature. Yet it is not to be so venerated that the worship due to the divinity is offered to it—a worship consisting in love, the offering of sacrifice, and reverence. In Latin this is called *pietas*; in Greek, Θεοσέβεια, that is, “worship of God,” or εὐσέβεια, that is, “good worship” or “piety.”

### The Opinion of Others, Who Teach That One Adoration Is to Be Offered to Both

2. Others, however, hold that Christ’s humanity should be adored with one adoration together with the Word, not for its own sake but for the sake of him whose footstool it is and to whom it is united. The humanity itself is not to be adored alone or nakedly, but together with the Word to whom it is united; nor for its own sake, but for the sake of him to whom it is united. Nor can one who does this be judged guilty of idolatry, because he serves neither a creature alone nor the creature for its own sake, but the Creator with, and in, his humanity.

On this point John Damascene says, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book 3, chapter 8:

> Christ has two natures, differing in reason and mode, yet united according to hypostasis. Therefore Christ is one, perfect God and perfect man, whom we adore with the Father and the Spirit in one adoration together with his undefiled flesh—not by saying that the flesh is not to be adored. For it is adored in the one hypostasis of the Word, which hypostasis was begotten; we do not offer reverence to a creature. Therefore we adore it not as bare flesh, but as united to the divinity in one hypostasis of God the Word, the two natures being brought together. I fear to touch the coal because of the fire joined to the wood. I adore both natures together in Christ my God because of the divinity united to the flesh. For I do not add a fourth person to the Trinity, but confess one person of the Word and his flesh.

These words seem to indicate that Christ’s humanity should be adored with one adoration together with the Word.

Augustine also says, in the sermon on the Lord’s words, “Let not your heart be troubled” (John 14):

> Heretics say that the Son is not God by nature but a creature. To them it must be answered that, if the Son is not God by nature but a creature, he ought not to be worshipped at all or adored as God, since the Apostle says: “They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator” [Rom. 1]. But they will reply and say: “Why is it that you adore together with the divinity his flesh, which you do not deny to be a creature, and serve it no less than the divinity?” I adore the Lord’s flesh—indeed, the complete humanity in Christ—because it was assumed by the divinity and united to the divinity, so that I may confess not one person and another, but one and the same Son of God, both God and man. Finally, if you separate the man from God, I neither believe in him nor serve him. It is as if someone were to find royal purple or a royal diadem lying on the ground: would he try to adore them? Yet when the king has put them on, a person incurs the danger of death if he refuses to adore them together with the king. Thus, if anyone refuses to adore in Christ the Lord the humanity—not alone or bare, but united to the divinity, namely the one Son, true God and true man—he will die eternally.

The same author, commenting on Psalm 98, where it is said, “Adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy,” says:

> It must be understood that in Christ there is earth, that is, flesh, which is adored without impiety. For he received earth from earth, because flesh is from earth; and he received flesh from Mary’s flesh. This flesh, assumed by the Word of God, is adored by us without impiety, because no one eats his flesh unless he has first adored it. But the one who adores does not look upon the earth, [Col. 0777] but rather upon him whose footstool it is, for whose sake he adores.

By these authorities the solution of the foregoing inquiry is set forth.

## DISTINCTION X. WHETHER CHRIST, INSOFAR AS HE IS MAN, IS A PERSON OR SOMETHING

1. Some also commonly ask whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is a person or even something. Arguments are advanced from both sides of this question. Those who maintain that he is a person reason as follows. If, insofar as he is man, he is something, then he is either a person, a substance, or something else. But he is not something else; therefore he is either a person or a substance. If he is a substance, then it is either rational or irrational; but it is not an irrational substance; therefore it is rational. But if, insofar as he is man, he is a rational substance, then he is a person, because this is the definition of person: an individual substance of a rational nature. Therefore, if insofar as he is man he is something, then insofar as he is man he is a person.

But conversely, if insofar as he is man he is a person, he is either the third person in the Trinity or another person. But he is not another person; therefore he is the third person in the Trinity. And if, insofar as he is man, he is the third person in the Trinity, then he is God.

On account of these difficulties and others, some say that Christ, as man, is neither a person nor anything—unless perhaps *according to* expresses the unity of person. For *according to* has several senses. Sometimes it expresses a condition or property of the divine or human nature; sometimes the unity of person; sometimes it denotes a state or disposition; sometimes a cause. Let the careful reader note the rationale of this distinction and store it in the recesses of memory, lest its senses be confused whenever discourse concerning Christ occurs.

### Even If Christ, Insofar as He Is Man, Is Called a Rational Substance, It Does Not Therefore Follow That He Is a Person Insofar as He Is Man

2. Yet the conclusion introduced in the preceding argument does not follow: that if Christ, insofar as he is man, is a rational substance, therefore he is a person. For even Christ’s soul is a rational substance, yet it is not a person, because it does not subsist by itself, but is joined to another thing. Moreover, that description of person was not given for the three divine persons.

### Another Proof That Christ Is a Person Insofar as He Is Man

3. They still strive to prove in another way that Christ, as man, is a person: Christ, insofar as he is man, was predestined to be the Son of God; but he is that which he was predestined to be; therefore, if he was predestined insofar as he is man to be the Son of God, then insofar as he is man he is the Son of God.

To this one may answer that Christ is what he was predestined to be. For he was predestined to be the Son of God, and he truly is the Son of God. But insofar as he is man, he was predestined to be the Son of God, because according to his humanity he has this through grace. Yet he is not, insofar as he is man, the Son of God—unless perhaps *according to* expresses unity of person, so that the meaning is: “He who is man is the Son of God.” But that he, being man, is the Son of God, he has by grace. If, however, a causal meaning is intended, the statement is false: for it is not because he is man that he is the Son of God.

### Whether Christ Is an Adoptive Son Insofar as He Is Man, or in Another Way

4. If it is asked whether Christ is an adoptive son insofar as he is man, or in any other way, we answer that Christ is not an adoptive son in any respect, but only a natural Son; for he is Son of God by nature, not by the grace of adoption.

He is not, however, called Son by nature in the same way that he is called God by nature. For he is not Son by that by which he is God: he is Son by the property of nativity, but God by the nature of divinity. Yet he is called Son by nature, or the Son of nature, because he is naturally Son, having the same nature as he who begot him.

But he is not an adopted son, because he was not first something else and afterward adopted as Son. We are called adoptive sons because, though born children of wrath, we were made children of God through grace [Eph. 1]. Christ, however, was never not the Son of God; therefore he is not an adoptive son.

### Objection: That He Is an Adoptive Son

5. But the following objection is raised. Christ is the son of man, that is, of the Virgin, either by grace, by nature, or in both ways. If by nature, then either by divine or human nature. But not by divine nature; therefore he is either the son of man by human nature or not by nature. If not by nature, then by grace alone; and even if by human nature, he is no less so by grace. Therefore, if he is the son of man by grace, he seems to be an adoptive son: thus he is the natural Son of the Father and the adoptive son of the Virgin.

To this one may answer that Christ is the son of the Virgin both by nature, or naturally, and by grace; nevertheless he is not the adoptive son of the Virgin, because he is called the Virgin’s son not through adoption but through union. For he is called the Son of the Virgin because, in the Virgin, he assumed a man into unity of person; and this was by grace, not by nature.

Hence Augustine, commenting on John, chapter 2, not far from the middle, says: “That the Only-Begotten is equal to the Father is not by grace but by nature. But that a man was assumed into the unity of the person of the Only-Begotten is by grace, not by nature.” Therefore Christ is the adoptive son neither of God nor of man; but he is Son of God naturally, and Son of man naturally and by grace.

That he is naturally the Son of man Augustine shows in *On Faith to Peter*: “That God who is naturally the only-begotten Son of God the Father became naturally the Son of man.” That he is not an adoptive son and yet is Son by grace is proved by the following testimonies.

Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0778] Book 1 of the *Commentary on Chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Ephesians*, on the passage, “Predestining in love,” etc.; in volume 9, far after the beginning]:

> It is written concerning Christ Jesus that he was always with the Father, and that the Father’s will never preceded him so that he might come to be. He indeed is Son by nature; we, however, by adoption. He was never not Son; we, before we existed, were predestined, and received the Spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.

Hilary also says, in book 3 of *On the Trinity*:

> When the Lord says, “Glorify your Son,” he testified that he is the Son of God not by name alone but also by property. We are sons of God, but this Son is not such a son. For he is the true and proper Son by origin, not adoption; by reality, not designation; by birth, not creation.

Augustine too, commenting on John, says: “We are sons by grace, not by nature; but the Only-Begotten is by nature, not by grace.” Is this also to be referred to the Son himself with respect to his humanity? Certainly.

Ambrose likewise, in book 1 of *On Faith*, chapter 9 and at the end, says: “Christ is Son not by adoption but by nature. We are called sons by adoption; he is so through the reality of nature.”

From these passages it is plainly shown that Christ is not Son by the grace of adoption. This is the grace meant when Augustine asserts that he is not Son by grace. For by grace—not of adoption but rather of union—the Son of God is the Son of man, and conversely.

### Whether the Person or the Nature Was Predestined

6. Next, if it is asked whether the predestination mentioned by the Apostle concerns the person or the nature, it may soundly be said both that the person of the Son, who has always existed, was predestined according to the assumed man—namely, that he himself, being man, should be the Son of God—and that human nature was predestined to be personally united to the Word of the Father.

## DISTINCTION XI. WHETHER CHRIST IS A CREATURE, CREATED, OR MADE

1. It is also commonly asked whether it should simply be said and granted that Christ was made, created, or is a creature. One may answer that saying this simply and without qualification is less fitting. And if it is sometimes stated simply for brevity’s sake, it must never be understood simply.

For, as Augustine says in book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 13: “When we speak of Christ, the prudent, diligent, and devout reader ought to understand what is said, according to what, and for what reason.” In book 1 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 6, he shows that Christ, or the Son of God, was not made and is not a creature:

> “In the beginning was the Word,” and “the Word was made flesh”; and “all things were made through him.” He says “all things” only of the things that were made, that is, of every creature. Thus it is plainly apparent that he through whom all things were made was not himself made; and if he was not made, he is not a creature. But if he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance which is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. But if the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a made substance; and if he is a made substance, not all things were made through him. But all things were made through him; therefore he is not a made substance, but with the Father is one unmade substance.

Again in the same work:

> If the Father made the Son, whom the Son himself did not make, then not all things were made through the Son. But all things were made through the Son. Therefore he himself was not made, so that with the Father he might make all things that were made.

The same author says in the *Eighty-Three Questions*: “Whatever God the Father made through the Son is called a creature; the Son cannot be called a creature, because all things were made through him.”

Ambrose, in book 1 of *On Faith*, says: “Let us prove that the Son of God is not a creature. For we have heard in the Gospel that the Lord commanded his disciples: ‘Preach the Gospel to every creature.’ He who says ‘every creature’ excludes none. Where, then, are those who call Christ a creature? For if he were a creature, he would command the Gospel to be preached to himself, and he would be subject to futility, because, as the Apostle testifies, ‘every creature is subject to futility’ [Rom. 6]. Therefore Christ is not a creature but the Creator, who entrusts to his disciples the office of teaching the creature.”

### The Impiety and Punishment of Arius

2. Arius is recorded to have held this impiety: that he made Christ a creature. Therefore Arius’s entrails were poured out, and he burst open in the middle, having fallen face-down, his foul mouth—by which he had denied Christ—being defiled by them.

By these and many other testimonies we are taught that we ought not simply to confess that Christ was made or is a creature. But with a qualification it may rightly be said that he was made according to the flesh or according to his humanity, so that being made is attributed to the humanity, not to God.

For Ambrose says, book 1 of *On Faith*, chapter 9: “God was not made; but God, the Son of God, was born. Afterwards, according to the flesh, he was made man from Mary. For ‘God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law’ [Gal. 4]. He says ‘his Son,’ that is, not one among many. When he says ‘his,’ he signifies the property of eternal generation. Afterwards he declares him ‘made of a woman,’ so that the making might be ascribed not to the divinity but to the assumption of a body. Thus he says ‘made of a woman’ because of the assumption of flesh; ‘under the law’ because of the observance of the law. One generation does not prejudice the other, nor does flesh prejudice divinity. For the eternal God received the mystery of incarnation—not divided, but one, and one in both, namely in divinity and body. For he is not one person from the Virgin and another from the Father, but the same one in one manner from the Father and in another from the Virgin. Yet he who was made according to the assumption of our nature was not made according to the substance of eternal life; him we read to be the firstborn. Firstborn, because no one was before him; only-begotten, because no one is after him.”

From this it is clearly taught in what sense the statement that Christ was made should be understood, whether said simply or with a qualification: namely, so that creatureliness is referred not to the assuming God but to the assumed man.

For there can be no creature in God, as Ambrose says, book 1 of *On Faith*, chapter 7:

> Was Christ made by a word? Was Christ created by a command? And how can creatureliness be in God? For God is of a simple nature, not a joined and composite one; nothing happens to him by accident, but in his nature he possesses only what is divine.

Therefore, even if Christ is called a creature according to his humanity, he should not simply be predicated to be a creature. Nor from the fact that Christ is said to be a creature according to his humanity can anyone proceed in this manner of argument: “If Christ, insofar as he is man, is a creature, then he is either rational or not; either God or not God,” attempting thereby to prove that Christ is something non-divine, because whatever he is, he is so according to his humanity. Therefore, if according to his humanity he is some non-divine substance, he is certainly something non-divine.

But no sound argument proceeds from figurative modes of expression. The expression by which Christ is called a creature, whether simply or with an addition, is figurative.

## DISTINCTION XII. WHETHER THAT MAN HAS ALWAYS EXISTED OR BEGAN TO EXIST

1. After these matters, it is asked whether that man began to exist or always existed, just as we state simply that Christ, or the Son of God, has always existed and did not begin to exist.

On this Augustine says, commenting on John: “At some time the Son of God had what the same Son of God as man did not have, because he was not yet man.” Again, in the same place: “Before the world existed, neither we nor he himself—the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and men—existed.” The same author, commenting on the Psalms: “Though our Christ may be a recent man, nevertheless he is eternal God.”

Elsewhere it is read that that boy created the stars. Christ says that he is the beginning and that he existed before Abraham. Without contradicting any of these or other authorities, we say that that man, insofar as he is man, began to exist; insofar as he is the Word, he has always existed.

Here an answer must not be given without a distinction. Augustine himself employs such a distinction in several places, saying that all things were made through Christ insofar as he is the Word, but that insofar as he is man he himself was made and glorified. Therefore, if you look to the person, confidently say that that man has always existed; but if to the nature of man, grant that he began to exist.

### Whether God Could Have Assumed Another Man, or One Not from Adam’s Race

2. It is also commonly asked whether God could have assumed another man, or one from somewhere other than the race of that Adam. One may soundly answer that he could have assumed another soul and another flesh, because that soul and flesh were assumed by the Word of God through grace alone.

For Augustine says, book 13 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 19: “Among things arising in time, that is the supreme grace: that a man is joined to God in unity of person.” Therefore God could have assumed another soul and another flesh, and indeed flesh from somewhere other than the race of Adam.

Hence Augustine, in the same work, chapter 18:

> God could therefore have assumed a man from elsewhere, in whom there would be a mediator between God and men, not from the race of that Adam who, by his sin, bound the human race; just as he created the man whom he first created not from the race of anyone. Therefore he could have created another man, whether in this or any other manner he wished, through whom the conqueror of the first man might be conquered. But he judged it better to assume a man from the very race that had been conquered, through whom he might conquer man’s enemy. Yet he did so from a Virgin, whose conception was preceded by the Spirit, not flesh; faith, not lust. The lust of the flesh by which the others are conceived, who inherit original sin, played no part; but virginity was made fruitful by believing, not by sexual union.

From these words it is plainly shown that God could have assumed another man, and one from elsewhere.

### Whether That Man Could Have Sinned or Could Have Failed to Be God

3. Therefore it is not without reason asked whether that man could have sinned or could have failed to be God. For if he could have sinned, he could have been condemned. If he could have been condemned, he could have failed to be God. Therefore, if he could have sinned, he could have failed to be God, because being God and being able to will iniquity cannot coexist.

Here a distinction is necessary: whether the question concerns the person or the nature. If it concerns the person, it is plain that he could neither sin nor fail to be God. But if the nature is under discussion, one must ask whether it is considered as united to the Word or as not united to the Word, though still existing: that is, whether it is considered insofar as it was united to the Word, or insofar as it could have existed without being united to the Word.

For there is no doubt that that soul, existing and united [Col. 0781] to the Word, could not sin; and it is unquestionably true that the same soul, if it existed without being united to the Word, could sin.

### The Objection of Some: That Even When United It Could Have Sinned

4. Some, however, attempt to prove that even when united to the Word it could sin, because it possesses free choice and thus can be bent in either direction. This is frivolous. For angels too possess free choice, yet by grace they have been confirmed by God so that they cannot sin. How much more, then, that man, to whom the Spirit was given without measure.

They also adduce an authority to prove the same point. For it is written in the book of Wisdom: “He could have transgressed, and did not transgress; he could have done evil, and did not do it.” But this should be understood in reference to the members, or partly of the head and partly of the members. Of the head: he did not transgress and did not do evil. Of the members: they could transgress and do evil.

### Whether God Could Have Assumed Human Nature in the Female Sex

5. Some also ask, though inquisitively, whether God could have assumed human nature in the female sex. Some think that he could have assumed a human being in the female sex, just as he assumed one in the male. But it was done more suitably and fittingly that he should be born from a woman and assume a man, so that the liberation of both sexes might be shown.

Hence Augustine, volume 4, in the *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 11: “Human liberation ought to have appeared in both sexes. Therefore, because it was necessary to assume a man, since that sex is more honorable, the liberation of the female sex also followed. Hence it appears that that man was born from a woman. Therefore the Wisdom of God, which is called the only-begotten Son, having assumed a man in the womb and from the womb of a Virgin, displayed the liberation of humankind.”

## DISTINCTION XIII. WHETHER CHRIST, ACCORDING TO HIS HUMAN NATURE, COULD AND DID ADVANCE IN WISDOM AND GRACE

1. Further, it must be known that Christ, according to his humanity, received from the very moment of conception the fullness of grace. The Spirit was given to him without measure, and in him “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” [Col. 2].

Augustine says, volume 2, in the letter to Dardanus, at the end, that this fullness dwells in him so that he is full of every grace. It does not dwell in the saints in the same manner. Just as sensation is present in the individual members of our body, but not to the same extent as in the head—for in the head are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, whereas in the other members there is touch alone—so in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells, because he is the head in which all the senses are found. But in the saints there is, as it were, touch alone; to them the Spirit is given by measure, since they have received from his fullness.
