They received from his fullness not according to essence but according to likeness, because they never received that same grace essentially in a similar manner. That boy, therefore, was full of wisdom and grace from his very conception. Hence Jerome rightly says: “The Lord performs a new thing upon earth: a woman shall encompass a man,” because he was perfect in the Virgin’s womb, not only in soul and flesh, but also in the wisdom and grace with which he was full.

### An Authority That Seems to Oppose This

2. Yet this position seems opposed by what is read in Luke’s Gospel, chapter 2: “Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men.” For if he advanced in wisdom and grace, he does not seem to have possessed from conception the fullness of grace without measure.

To this one may soundly answer that, according to his humanity, from conception he received such fullness of wisdom and grace that God could not confer a fuller measure upon him. Yet he is truly said to have advanced in wisdom and grace, not indeed in himself but in others, who advanced through his wisdom and grace while he disclosed to them more and more, according to the progress of his age, the gifts of wisdom and grace.

Hence Gregory, homily 11 on Luke chapter 2, says:

> According to human nature he advanced in wisdom—not because he himself, who remained full of the Spirit of wisdom from the first hour of conception, became wiser over time, but because over time he gradually displayed to others the wisdom with which he was full. According to human nature he advanced in age, from infancy to youth. According to human nature he advanced in grace, not by receiving through the passage of time what he did not have, but by disclosing the gift of grace which he possessed. He advanced before God and men because, insofar as he disclosed to men, as his age advanced, the gifts of grace and wisdom that were present in him, he stirred them to the praise of God; and thus he advanced toward God the Father in the praise of God, and toward men in their salvation.

Therefore he advanced in wisdom and grace in others, not in himself. Hence in the same Gospel, John 1, that boy is declared to be full of wisdom and grace. Thus he is said to have advanced in wisdom and grace just as an ecclesiastical ruler is said to advance in the care entrusted to him when, through his diligence, others advance.

### What Ambrose Says Seems Contrary to the Foregoing

3. Elsewhere, however, it is found written that he advanced according to human understanding just as he advanced in human age. Ambrose says in *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*:

> God assumed the perfection of human nature. He assumed human understanding, but he was not puffed up by fleshly understanding. By human understanding he said that his soul was troubled; by human understanding he hungered and asked; by human understanding he advanced, as it is written in Luke 2: “Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace.” How did the wisdom of God advance? Advance in age and advance in wisdom belong not to the divine but to human nature. Therefore he mentioned age so that you might believe that this was said according to his humanity. For age belongs not to divinity but to the body. Therefore, if he advanced in the age of man, he advanced in the wisdom of man. But human understanding advanced; and because it is understanding, therefore it is wisdom. What understanding advanced? If human, then it itself was assumed through increase; if divine, then it is mutable through advance, for whatever advances is changed for the better. But what is divine does not change. Therefore what changes is not divine. Human understanding, therefore, advanced. He therefore assumed human understanding. The power of God could not be strengthened, nor could God grow, nor could the height of God’s wisdom be filled. Therefore the wisdom being filled was not God’s but ours; for how could he be filled who descended in order to fill all things? Through what understanding, moreover, did Isaiah say, chapter 8, that the boy did not know father or mother? For it is written: “Before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the spoils of Samaria.” The Wisdom of God is not deceived concerning things future and hidden. But infancy, lacking knowledge, through human ignorance does not know what it has not yet learned. Yet I fear, I say, that if we assign two principal understandings or a twofold wisdom to Christ, we divide Christ. Do we divide him when we adore both his divinity and his flesh? Do we divide him when we venerate in him the image of God and the cross? Certainly the Apostle, who said of him, “Although he was crucified from our weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” [2 Cor. 13], himself said, “Christ is not divided” [1 Cor. 1]. Do we divide him when we say that he assumed a rational soul capable of our understanding? For God the Word himself was not in his flesh in place of a rational soul capable of understanding; rather, by assuming a rational soul capable of our understanding—a soul that was human and of the same substance as our souls—and flesh like ours and of the same substance as our flesh, he was also perfect man.

### The Meaning of the Foregoing Words

4. These words of Ambrose must be examined with devout care. In one respect they instruct and enlighten ignorance; badly understood, they provide fuel for error.

For they plainly teach that in Christ there are two principal understandings, or a twofold wisdom. Yet the unity and singularity of person is not thereby divided. Rather, according to the two natures, he has two wisdoms: one uncreated but begotten, which he himself is; the other not begotten but created and bestowed upon him through grace.

For Isaiah testifies of him, chapter 11: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding rests upon him.” Therefore, through the Spirit of wisdom and understanding—that is, through wisdom and understanding freely given by the Holy Spirit—Christ was wise according to his soul. But according to God he was wise through the eternal wisdom which is God.

And just as, insofar as he is God, he is good by the natural goodness which he himself is, and just by the natural justice which he himself is, so he is wise by the natural wisdom which he himself is. But his soul, just as it is good and just by freely given goodness or justice, which neither he nor the soul itself is, so is wise by freely given wisdom, which it itself is not.

Although there is a twofold wisdom in Christ, there is nevertheless one and the same person. Insofar as he is God and of divine nature, he is wise by unbegotten wisdom—namely, eternal wisdom, which is the Father—and by wisdom that is not unbegotten, which is common to the three Persons. Yet this is not a twofold wisdom, because there are not two different wisdoms: unbegotten wisdom, which is the Father alone, and wisdom which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are commonly.

But insofar as the same person is man—that is, according to the assumed man, or insofar as he subsists from soul and flesh—he is wise by freely given wisdom. Therefore he is wise by human and by divine understanding.

### How the Statement “Human Understanding Advanced” Is to Be Understood

5. But on what ground should the meaning of that saying, “human understanding advanced,” be taken? For Ambrose seems plainly to indicate that Christ advanced according to human understanding, and that his infancy lacked knowledge and did not know father and mother. Yet neither the Church accepts this nor do the foregoing authorities permit it to be understood in that way.

But it may soundly be understood to mean that Christ is said to have advanced with respect to what people saw and to the manifestation of his understanding. Therefore human understanding advanced in him by manifestation and in the opinion of other people. In the same way he is said not to have known father and mother in infancy because he conducted and bore himself as though he lacked knowledge.

## DISTINCTION XIV. WHETHER CHRIST’S SOUL HAD WISDOM EQUAL TO GOD, AND WHETHER IT KNOWS ALL THAT GOD KNOWS

1. Here it must be asked, since Christ’s soul was wise by freely given wisdom, whether it had wisdom equal to God’s, or possessed—or possesses—knowledge of all things; that is, whether it knows all that God knows.

Some hold that it has neither knowledge equal to God nor knowledge of all that God knows, because a creature is equal to the Creator in nothing. Therefore, since that soul is a creature, it is equal to the Creator in nothing, and consequently not in wisdom. Therefore it does not have wisdom equal to God’s and does not know all that God knows.

Again, if that soul has wisdom equal to God’s, then God does not have a greater sufficiency in every good than his creature. They also adduce authorities to prove this. For the Prophet says in Psalm 138, in the person of the assumed man: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me, and I shall not be able to attain it.” Cassiodorus explains this by saying: “The truth of the human condition is shown, because the assumed man cannot be equalled to the divine substance, either in knowledge or in anything else.”

The Apostle also says, 1 Corinthians 2: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, who alone searches all things, even the depths of God.” By these and many other arguments and authorities they maintain that Christ’s soul has neither knowledge equal to God’s nor knowledge of all that God knows. For if it knows all that God knows, then it knows how to create the world and also knows how to create itself.

### Response Containing the Definitive Resolution of the Question
2. In reply to these persons, we say that the soul of Christ, through the wisdom freely given to it in the Word of God, to whom it is united—and therefore understands perfectly—knows all that God knows; yet it cannot do all that God can do, nor does it comprehend all things as clearly and distinctly as God does. Thus it is not equal to the Creator in knowledge, although it knows all that He knows; nor is its wisdom equal to the wisdom of God [Col. 0784], because that wisdom is far more excellent and apprehends all things more worthily and perfectly than the wisdom of that soul. Therefore God has a greater sufficiency in knowledge than that soul, which is more excellent than every creature.

But the Apostle’s statement which they cite, 1 Corinthians 2, “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, who alone searches all things,” supports us. For the Apostle immediately adds: “But we have the Spirit of God,” in order to show that through the Spirit of God, whom he possessed, he knew the deep things of God. But that soul possessed the Spirit of God above all others: “To him the Spirit was not given by measure,” as John the Evangelist says, chapter 3. Therefore it possessed the gifts of the Holy Spirit without measure, and consequently wisdom also. That soul, therefore, knew all things. For if it knew some things and not others, it would not have knowledge without measure. But it had knowledge without measure; therefore it knows all things.

Fulgentius also, in a certain sermon, adduces many considerations by which he asserts that that soul possesses knowledge of all things, using the Apostle’s authority when he says: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.” This can also be proved by reason as follows: no one knows anything that his soul does not know. But Christ, by the admission of all, knows all things; therefore his soul knows all things.

As to the objection, “If it knows all things, then it knows how to create the world or itself,” we answer that it possesses knowledge of creating the world, but not the power; and it possesses knowledge of creating a soul, and knows how God created it. Therefore it has knowledge of itself as created, but not of itself as to be created, because it is not to be created but has been created.

### Why God did not give it power over all things as He gave it knowledge

3. But if it is asked why God did not give it the power to do all things, as He gave it knowledge, one may answer: because it is naturally capable of knowledge, and therefore knowledge was suitably given to it without measure, since it is naturally capable of it. But the power to do all that God does was not given to it, lest it be considered omnipotent and therefore God.

Nevertheless, perhaps God could not even bestow upon it the power to do all things, although He gave it power to do certain things which it could not otherwise do. Thus the soul of Christ knows in the Word of God all that God knows—a Word which, because it is united to it, it contemplates more clearly and immediately than any creature; and in that Word angels too know both the things of God and future things.

### How certain words of Ambrose on Luke are to be understood

4. But if that soul does not have as great a power as God, and if the assumed man does not have as great a power as God, how then is Ambrose’s statement on Luke to be understood, where the angel says of the Virgin’s Son who was to be born: “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High”? “He shall not,” he says, “be great because he was not great before the Virgin’s childbirth, but because, as man, he was to receive in time the power which the Son of God naturally possesses, so that man and God might be one person.”

See: he expressly says that the man was to receive in time the power which the Son of God naturally possessed. But if the man was to receive that power, it must have been either the person or the human nature that received it. Not the person, because the person always possessed and possesses it; therefore the nature. If the nature, then the soul; for it is evident that the flesh could not receive it.

To this we say that the statement must be understood of the person, but not insofar as it is the person of God—rather, insofar as it is the person of man. For there is one person of God and man, of the Son of God and the son of man. Insofar as it is the person of God, it always and naturally possessed omnipotence; but insofar as it is the person of man, it did not always exist. Therefore the person which had always been the person of God was to become the person of man; and insofar as it was to become the person of man, it was to receive in time the power which it had always and naturally possessed insofar as it was a person. According to this distinction, that statement and similar ones can be understood soundly. This distinction is necessary in many articles of disputed questions against the tangled verbosity of certain persons. But where the facts are clear, controversy about the facts is futile.

## DISTINCTION XV. THE DEFECTS OF HUMANITY WHICH CHRIST ASSUMED IN HUMAN NATURE

[Col. 0785]

1. Nor should it be passed over that the Son of God assumed a passible human nature: a passible soul and a passible, mortal flesh. For, in order that He might be proved to possess a true body, He assumed bodily defects—hunger, thirst, and the like. And in order that He might be proved to possess a true soul, He assumed defects of the soul, namely sorrow, fear, pain, and the like.

Every sensation belongs to the soul. For flesh does not feel; rather, the soul feels, using the body as an instrument. Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 12, chapter 24, tome 3: “The body does not feel, but the soul feels through the body, which it uses as a messenger in order to establish within itself what is reported from without.” Therefore, just as the soul sees or hears what is outside through the body as through an instrument, so also through the body it feels certain evils which it would not feel without the body, such as hunger, thirst, and the like. Hence these are rightly called defects of the body. But it feels certain other things not through the body, indeed even without the body, such as fear and the like. The soul, therefore, feels pains, some through the instrument of the body and others not through it.

Christ assumed true defects of humanity just as He assumed true human nature, though not all of them. He assumed defects of punishment, but not of fault; nor even all defects of punishment, but all those which it was fitting for Him to assume as man and which did not derogate from His dignity. For just as He became man for man’s sake, so for man’s sake He assumed human defects. He assumed what was ours in order to bestow what was His upon us, and to take away our defect. He assumed our oldness in order to infuse His newness into us. He assumed our single oldness, that is, punishment, in order to destroy our double oldness, that is, punishment and fault.

### How the statement of Pope Leo is to be understood

2. Hebrews 4 teaches that our Lord assumed in Himself every one of our infirmities except sin. Unless this is understood only of those things which it was fitting for Him to assume for us and which did not dishonor Him, it is shown to be false. For He did not assume any ignorance, although there is a kind of ignorance which is a defect but not a sin, namely invincible ignorance. Vincible ignorance, however, is sin, provided it concerns things which it is useful for us to know. There are some things the knowledge of which brings no benefit, or ignorance of which does not impede salvation; perhaps ignorance of such things is not a defect.

Yet it is evident that in us there are ignorance and a difficulty in willing or doing good, which belong to our misery. Hence Augustine, in book 3 *On Free Choice*, chapter 18; book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 9, tome 1; and book 7 *On the Good of Perseverance*, chapter 11, says: “To approve false things as true, so as to err unwillingly, and, because of the resistance and torment of the bond of the flesh, to be unable to refrain from lustful works, is not the nature of the human being as created, but the punishment of the human being as condemned. From this misery, most justly inflicted upon sinners, the grace of God delivers us; for by free will man could fall voluntarily, but could not rise again. To this misery belong ignorance and difficulty, which every human being suffers from the beginning of birth; and no one is delivered from this evil except by God’s grace.”

Here Augustine plainly says that the ignorance by which a person unwillingly approves falsehoods as truths, and the difficulty by which one cannot restrain oneself from evil, belong to our misery and are a punishment of humanity. Christ, however, did not have these. Therefore He did not assume every defect of our infirmity except sin.

### That such ignorance and difficulty are not sin

3. But perhaps someone will say that these are sin. Against him stands what Augustine appears to teach: namely, that God could without blame have endowed man before sin, at the beginning of creation, with these as natural properties. Thus he says in the *Retractations*: “Even if ignorance and difficulty had been natural to man from the beginning, God would not even then be blameworthy, but praiseworthy.”

But if man had naturally possessed these at the beginning, would they have been defects and punishments in him? If defects, or if punishment had been imposed upon him before sin, God would seem to have dealt unjustly with him if he felt punishment before fault. Therefore we rightly say that these would not have been defects or punishments if they had been naturally infused into man. Similarly, before sin, when man had not yet received grace, inability to make progress was not a defect or punishment for him. But after he received grace, through which he could make progress and for a time did progress, and afterward lost it through his own fault—and lost with it the power of making progress—it became a defect and punishment for him not to be able to make progress, namely, not to be able to avoid evil and do good.

Therefore Christ assumed all our defects except sin which it was fitting for Him to assume and beneficial for us that He should assume. For there are many kinds of illnesses and bodily defects from which He was entirely free. He assumed the defects which He had: either to demonstrate true humanity, as fear and sorrow; or to accomplish the work for which He came, as passibility and mortality; or to raise our hope from despair of immortality, as death. But He assumed these defects not through the necessity of His condition, but through the will of compassion.

He had true defects, as we do, but not from the same cause. For we contract these defects from original sin, as the Apostle indicates when he says, Romans 8: “The body indeed is dead because of sin,” that is, it has within itself the necessity of dying. Christ, however, did not possess such defects from sin, because He was conceived, born, and lived on earth without sin. Rather, solely by the will of compassion, He transferred into Himself from what was ours a true infirmity, just as He assumed true flesh—which He could have assumed without any infirmity, just as He assumed it without fault.

### By authorities he proves, against those who deny it, that Christ truly felt pain and fear according to His humanity

4. But because some are found to have held erroneous opinions about the experience of Christ’s human nature in the Passion, maintaining that Christ the man endured only a likeness and image of passion and pain, but felt absolutely no pain or passion, let us, by testimonies of authorities convicting them, make indubitable what we said above.

The prophet Isaiah says, chapter 53: “Surely He bore our infirmities and carried our pains.” Truth Himself says in the Gospel, Matthew 26: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” And Mark 14 also reads: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed.” The Prophet likewise says in Christ’s person, Psalm 87: “My soul has been filled with evils.” Explaining this, Augustine says, tome 8, in his exposition on the same verse: “Christ’s soul was filled not with vices and sins, but with human evils, that is, pains, by which it has compassion on the flesh. For bodily pain cannot exist without the soul. But the soul can suffer pain even when the body does not suffer pain.”

He assumed these affections of human infirmity, just as He assumed flesh itself and death, not through the necessity of the human condition but through the will of compassion.

Ambrose also, tome 2, book 2 *On Faith*, chapter 3, says: “It is written, Matthew 26: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.’ Therefore Christ is afraid; and while Peter is not afraid, Christ is afraid. Peter said, John 13: ‘I will lay down my life for you’; Christ says, John 12: ‘My soul is troubled.’ Both are true and full of reason: both that he who is inferior is not afraid, and that He who is superior bears the affection of one who fears.”

The same author, in the same work, chapter 5, at the end: “As man He is troubled, as man He weeps, as man He is crucified; through human nature He was weary and rose again. His power is not troubled; His divinity is not troubled; but His soul is troubled, according to the assumption of human frailty. For He who assumed a soul also assumed the soul’s capacity for passion. For insofar as He was God, He could neither be troubled nor die.”

The same author, in the same work, chapter 3, a little earlier: “He assumed my sorrow; and I confidently call it sorrow, I who proclaim the cross. As man He had sorrow, which He assumed with my affection; He has compassion on me, He is sorrowful for me, He suffers pain for me [Col. 0787]. Therefore He suffered for me and in me, who had nothing in Himself for which He should suffer. Thus, Lord Jesus, You suffer my wounds, not Your own, because You suffer not for Yourself but for me.”

Jerome also, to Damasus, tome 4, in the *Explanation of the Faith*, says: “We say that a passible man was assumed by the Son of God, while the divinity remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered not merely in appearance but truly, all that Scripture testifies concerning Him, but according to that which could suffer—namely, according to the assumed substance. Therefore, although the person of the Son assumed a passible man, nevertheless His indwelling, according to His own substance, suffered nothing; as must be confessed of the whole Trinity, which is impassible.”

From these and other authorities it is clear that Christ assumed a man truly capable of suffering, and in him assumed the defects and affections of our infirmity; but He did so by will, not by the necessity of His condition.

### Here he sets forth passages which seem opposed to what has been said

5. Nevertheless, certain statements are found in the treatises of the saints which seem contrary to what has been stated. For Augustine, on Psalm 21, “I shall cry out and You will not hear,” tome 8, second exposition, seems to teach that Christ neither truly feared nor was truly sorrowful, saying:

“How does He say this, He who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found [Isaiah 53]? Yet He says it to us, concerning His body. For He bore the person of His body, that is, the Church. Thus elsewhere also, Matthew 26, when He said, ‘Let this cup pass from me,’ He speaks for us—unless perhaps it be thought that He feared to die. But the Lord did not truly fear to suffer, He who was to rise on the third day, when Paul burned with longing to be dissolved and to be with Christ [Philippians 1]. Nor is the soldier stronger than the commander. The soldier, about to be crowned, rejoices to die; and does the Lord who is to crown him fear death? But, representing our weakness, He said these things for His weak ones who fear death: it was their voice, not the Head’s.”

Jerome likewise says: “Let those be ashamed who think that the Savior feared death and, through dread of the Passion, said: ‘Let this cup pass from me.’” (*On the Gospel of Matthew*, at the beginning of the commentary on chapter 26, tome 8.)

### Resolution of the authorities

6. So that no contrary discrepancy may be thought to exist in Holy Scripture, we say that the words of these authorities are to be understood in this way: not that they remove from Christ the reality of fear and sorrow, or the first stirring of these affections (*propassio*), but that they remove the necessity and full passion of fear and sorrow.

For Christ had true fear and sorrow in human nature, but not as we do, who are His members. Because of our sin, we are necessarily subject to these defects; in us they exist both as *propassio* and as full passion (*passio*), whereas in Christ they existed only as *propassio*. For just as certain stages are distinguished in sins—*propassio* and *passio*—so also in penal effects. Sometimes someone is affected by fear or sorrow in such a way that the mind’s understanding is not thereby moved away from rectitude or contemplation of God; then there is *propassio*. But at other times it is moved and disturbed; then there is *passio*.

Christ, however, was not so disturbed in soul by fear or sorrow that He departed in any degree from rectitude or contemplation of God. In this sense, when it is said that He either feared or was sorrowful, the statement must be understood. Hence Jerome, commenting on Matthew chapter 26, nearly in the middle, where it reads, “He began to be sorrowful and distressed,” says: “To prove the truth of the assumed man, He was truly sorrowful; but passion did not dominate His mind—rather, there was *propassio*. Hence it says, ‘He began to be sorrowful.’ For it is one thing to be sorrowful, another to begin to be sorrowful.” That is: a person is sorrowful in one way through *propassio*, and in another through full passion.

Accordingly, according to this distinction, Christ is sometimes said not truly to have feared and sometimes truly to have feared, because He had real fear and sorrow, but not according to full passion nor from the necessity of His condition. Hence Augustine, tome 8, *Exposition on Psalm 93*, after the middle, wishing for these reasons to establish the meaning of the statements, says that Christ did not truly fear or grieve, and immediately afterward that He had true sorrow:

“Signifying in Himself the weak, the Lord said: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.’ For the Lord did not truly fear to suffer, He who was to rise on the third day, when Paul burned with longing to be dissolved and to be with Christ. This man rejoices because he is to be crowned, and is the Lord sorrowful when He is to crown him?” Here he seems to remove sorrow and fear from Christ. But immediately he adds: “Yet He assumed sorrow as He assumed flesh. For He was sorrowful, as the Gospel says, Mark 14. For if He was not sorrowful when the Evangelist says, ‘My soul is sorrowful,’ and so forth, then neither, when it says ‘Jesus slept,’ did He sleep; nor, when it says that He ate, did He eat. Thus nothing sound remains, and it may even be said that His body was not real. Therefore everything written concerning Him is true and happened. Therefore He was sorrowful; but by His will He assumed true sorrow, just as by His will He assumed true flesh.”

You plainly see that he would contradict himself in these words unless he distinguished the different grounds of the statements, from which their meaning must be drawn. For if the interpretative ground of the foregoing statements is distinguished, no contradiction arises.

### Certain very obscure passages of Hilary, which seem contrary to the common view

7. Yet the words of Hilary cause more difficulty and raise a harder question. He seems to teach that blows, wounds, and the like fell upon Christ in such a way that they did not inflict the pain of suffering: as a weapon drawn through water, fire, or air does the things it does when drawn through living bodies—since it pierces and punctures—but nevertheless causes no pain, because those things cannot experience pain. So he says that Christ’s body received the force of punishment without the sensation of punishment; for just as our body does not have such a nature that it can tread upon waves, so Christ’s body, he says, did not possess the nature of our pain, because it did not have a nature capable of suffering pain.

For he says as follows in book 10 *On the Trinity*:

“The only-begotten God assumed a true man according to the likeness of our human being, without ceasing to be God. Although in Him a blow might fall, a wound be inflicted, knots be tied tight, or suspension raise Him up, these things indeed brought the force of suffering, but did not inflict the pain of suffering; like a weapon piercing water, puncturing fire, or wounding air. It indeed inflicts upon all these the actions proper to its nature, so as to pierce, puncture, and wound; but the suffering inflicted upon them does not retain its own nature in them, since it is not in their nature for water to be pierced, fire punctured, or air wounded, although it belongs to the nature of a weapon both to wound, puncture, and pierce.

“Christ suffered when He was struck, suspended, and died; but the suffering which rushed upon His body was indeed suffering, yet did not exercise the nature of suffering, since punishment raged in its penal ministry, while the power of His body received within itself, without sensation of punishment, the force of punishment raging against it.

“Certainly that body of the Lord possessed the nature of our pain, if our body has it in its nature to tread upon waves and walk above the floods, and not to be barred by the obstacles of a closed house. But if the nature of the Lord’s body alone is to move upon wet places, stand upon liquid things, and pass through constructed barriers, why do we judge flesh conceived of the Holy Spirit according to the nature of the human body? That flesh is from heaven, and that man is from God: He had a body capable of suffering, and He suffered, but did not have a nature capable of feeling pain.”

The same author says in the same book:

“Let us see whether that sequence of sufferings permits us to understand an infirmity of pain in the Lord. Setting aside the reasons from which heresy attributes fear to the Lord, let us compare the events themselves as they occurred. For fear cannot be signified in the words of one whose confidence is continuously displayed in deeds. Therefore, according to the heretic, He seems to have feared the Passion. But through the error of this ignorance, Peter is both Satan and a stumbling block. Or did He fear death, He who went forth to meet armed men, and in whose body there was infirmity, at whose approach the ranks of persecutors, struck with terror, fell backward with their bodies cast to the ground? What infirmity, then, do you believe ruled in that body whose nature possessed such great power?

“But perhaps He feared the pain of wounds. Tell me, you defender of the Lord’s infirmity: what terror did the nail penetrating His flesh hold for Him who restored a severed ear by touch alone? Does the hand that performs these things suffer pain from the nail and feel the wound—He who left no pain from the wound in another? Is He sorrowful through fear of flesh to be pierced, whose touch heals flesh after it has been cut?”

The same author, in the same tenth book:

“Therefore, from comparing the power of His sayings and deeds, it is plainly shown that in the nature of His body there was no infirmity of bodily nature; and that Passion, although inflicted upon His body, did not impart to His body the nature of feeling pain. For although the form of our body was in the Lord, the form of our defective infirmity was not in the body which the Virgin brought forth from conception by the Holy Spirit.”

You have heard, reader, Hilary’s words, by which he seems to exclude pain. But if, casting off an attitude of spiritual dullness and impiety, you carefully attend to the foregoing and consider the context of Scripture itself, you may in some measure grasp the reason and force of his words, and will not venture to impugn their meaning.

For he is understood to have said that the pain of suffering did not befall Christ, and that the power of Christ’s body received in itself the force of punishment without sensation of punishment, because He did not have in Himself the cause and merit of pain. He appears to have noted this where he says: “Not having a nature capable of feeling pain.” Therefore His flesh is not to be judged according to the nature of our body; and suffering did not exercise dominion in Him. Likewise, He did not have a nature capable of fear or sorrow, because He did not have such a nature as contained a cause of fear or sorrow. Thus there was no necessity of fearing in Him, as there is in us; nor was there in Him a nature of pain, as there is in us.

Nevertheless, he consequently asserts that sorrow existed in Him, but that its cause was not His own death, but the failure of Peter and the other apostles. For he says that Christ was sorrowful not because of death but until death, in these words:

“I ask what it is for Christ to be sorrowful until death, and what it is to be sorrowful because of death. For ‘to be sorrowful because of death’ and ‘to be sorrowful until death’ do not have the same meaning. Where sorrow is because of death, death is the cause of sorrow; but where sorrow is until death, death is not the cause of sorrow but its end. Sorrow was not assumed from God because of death, so that it might be removed through death. Therefore He is not sorrowful for Himself, but for those who would be in scandal because of the weakness of the flesh; He warns them to pray that they may not enter into temptation, though they had earlier promised that they would not be scandalized.” (*Ibid.*, a little below.)

## DISTINCTION XVI. WHETHER THERE WAS IN CHRIST A NECESSITY OF SUFFERING AND DYING, WHICH IS A GENERAL DEFECT

1. From the foregoing there arises a question: for it was said above that Christ assumed our defects in Himself except sin. But there is a certain general defect of humanity which is not sin—namely, the necessity of suffering or dying. Hence our body is called not only mortal but also dead, because it possesses not merely an aptitude for dying but also a necessity of dying. Therefore it is asked whether such necessity existed in Christ’s flesh.

There is no doubt that He possessed an aptitude for dying; this was present even in man before sin, when it was not a defect in him. Therefore that mortality was not then a defect in man, because it belonged to his nature. Hence some rightly teach that such mortality in us is not a defect; but the necessity of dying or suffering is a defect, which is also called mortality or passibility. For a person is now called passible or mortal not merely because of an aptitude, but because of a necessity.

But was this defect in Christ’s flesh? And since His soul was passible before death, did it possess a necessity of suffering? For if a necessity of suffering or dying existed in Christ, He would not seem to have assumed our defects solely through the will of compassion.

To this it may be said that Christ assumed these defects, as He did the others, by will and not through the necessity of His nature—namely, the necessity of suffering in His soul, and at once the necessity of suffering and dying in His flesh [Col. 0790]. Yet He did not have this necessity through the necessity of His condition, because He was free from sin; rather, by His will alone He accepted it from our infirmity, “placing His tent in the sun,” that is, under temporal changeability and toil.

Hence an authority—the Gloss on chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Hebrews—says that, just as it is appointed to other human beings by right and by the law of nature to die once, so Christ too was offered once, by the same necessity and law of nature, and not often. It does not say “by the law of nature” because He drew this defect from the nature of His own condition; for it does not arise in us even from nature as first instituted, but from nature corrupted by sin. Therefore this defect is called natural because it has become established, as it were, in place of nature, being spread through all.

### The states of humanity, and what Christ took from each

2. Here it should be noted that Christ took something from every state of humanity, since He came to save all. There are four states of humanity: the first, before sin; the second, after sin and before grace; the third, under grace; the fourth, in glory.

From the first state He took freedom from sin. Hence Augustine, explaining John the Evangelist chapter 3, “He who comes from above is above all,” says that Christ came from above, that is, from the height of human nature before sin; because the Word of God took human nature from that height, since He did not assume the fault whose punishment He assumed.

But He assumed punishment and the other defects from the second state; from the third, the fullness of grace; and from the fourth, inability to sin and the perfect contemplation of God. For He possessed simultaneously certain goods of the present life and goods of the heavenly homeland, just as He possessed certain evils of the present life.

## DISTINCTION XVII. WHETHER EVERY PRAYER OR WILL OF CHRIST WAS FULFILLED

1. After these matters, one must consider whether Christ willed or prayed for anything which did not come to pass. This can seem likely from what He Himself said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what You will.” Here He seems to distinguish His own will from the Father’s will.

### Christ’s wills according to His two natures

2. Therefore there must be no doubt that Christ had distinct wills corresponding to His two natures: namely, a divine will and a human will. Human will is either the inclination of reason or the inclination of sense-appetite (*sensualitas*); and the soul has one inclination according to reason and another according to sense-appetite, although both are called human will.

By the inclination of reason, He willed the same thing as by the divine will—namely, to suffer and die. But by the inclination of sense-appetite He did not will it; indeed, He recoiled from it. Yet in Him the flesh did not desire against the spirit or against God. For, as Augustine says in book 10, chapter 12, *On Genesis Literally*: “There is no little fault when the flesh desires against the spirit.”

But the flesh is said to desire because the soul does this in accordance with the flesh, just as the soul hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For flesh desires nothing except through the soul. It is said to desire when the soul, through carnal desire, resists the spirit, possessing against the delight which the spirit has a carnal delight arising from and concerning the flesh. The cause of this carnal desire, however, lies neither in the soul alone nor in the flesh alone; it arises from both, because such delight is not felt without both.

Such conflict and struggle, therefore, could in no way exist in Christ’s soul, because carnal desire could not exist there. It was also God’s will, and agreeable to reason, that He should will this according to the flesh, so that the truth of His humanity might be demonstrated. For He who assumed human nature had to undergo what belongs to it.

Accordingly, just as in us there is a twofold inclination, that of the mind and that of sense-appetite, so there had to be a twofold inclination in Him as well: so that by the inclination of the mind He would will to die, and by the inclination of sense-appetite He would not will it, as happens in holy persons. For Truth Himself says to Peter, John 21:18: “When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish”—namely, to death [Col. 0791].

Explaining this, Augustine, tome 9, tractate 123, at the end, says that Peter was led unwillingly to that hardship, came to it unwillingly, but overcame it willingly; and he retained the inclination of weakness by which no one wishes to die, an inclination so natural that not even old age took it from Peter. Hence the Lord also said: “Let this cup pass from me,” but the force of love overcame it.

Therefore in Christ according to His humanity, and in His members, there is a twofold inclination: one of reason, informed by charity, by which someone wills to die for God’s sake; the other of sense-appetite, close to and joined with the infirmity of the flesh, by which death is shunned. For, as Augustine says, Paul by the reason of his mind desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, but the feeling of the flesh recoils and refuses. This is characteristic of human inclination: one who loves life hates death. According to this inclination Christ did not wish to die, and did not obtain what He asked according to this inclination.

### By authorities he proves that there were diverse wills in Christ
3. Therefore, from the human affection which he derived from the Virgin, he willed not to die and prayed that the cup might pass away. Hence Bede: “He prays that the cup may pass, because he was man, saying: ‘Father, let this cup pass from me.’ Behold, you have the human will expressly stated. Now observe the upright heart: ‘Yet not what I will, but what you will.’” Hence elsewhere, John 6: “I came not to do my own will”—namely, that which I assumed temporally from the Virgin—“but the will of him who sent me,” namely, that which, being eternal, I had with the Father. Here he openly says that there were two wills in Christ, according to which he willed different things.

Jerome likewise, on that passage in Mark 14, “The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak,” indicating that two wills are expressed here, says: “This is against the Eutychians, who say that there is only one will in Christ. But here he shows the human will, which, because of the weakness of the flesh, declines the Passion; and the divine will, which is ready to accomplish the dispensation.”

Augustine also [Note: [Col. 0791] First sermon of the exposition of Psalm 32, on the words, “Praise befits the upright,” vol. 8.] maintains two wills in Christ, saying: “As far as God is from man, so far is God’s will from the will of man. Hence Christ, bearing man, showed a certain private will of man, in which he represented both his own will and ours—he who is our head, and to whom we belong as members. ‘Father,’ he says, ‘if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.’ This was the human will, willing something proper to itself and, as it were, private. But because he wills man to be upright and directed to God, he adds: ‘Not what I will, but what you will.’ As though he said: ‘See yourself in me, because you can will something proper to yourself while God wills something else. This is conceded to human frailty.’”

The same writer elsewhere, on Psalm 93, after the middle, says: “In his Passion Christ expressed in himself two wills according to his two natures. For he says: ‘Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me.’ Behold, you have the will of man, which he immediately directs to the divine will when he says: ‘Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.’”

Ambrose likewise, in Book 12 *On the Faith*: “It is written: ‘Father, if it be possible, remove this cup from me.’ These are Christ’s words; but consider how and in what form they are spoken. He bears the substance of man; he has assumed human affection. Therefore he speaks not as God, but as man. Indeed, he assumed my will. It is my will which he called his own when he said: ‘Not as I will, but as you will.’ But when he said, in John 16 and 17, ‘All things that the Father has are mine,’ because nothing is excepted, unquestionably the Father’s will is the same will that the Son has. Christ’s will is the same as the paternal will. Therefore the Father and the Son have one will. But the will of man is one thing, and the will of God another; so that you may know that life belongs to the will of man, whereas Christ’s Passion belongs to the divine will, so that he might suffer for us.”

These testimonies plainly teach that there are two wills in Christ. Because Macarius, archbishop, denied this in the Constantinopolitan synod, he was condemned. And it was from the human affection of sensibility, indeed—not of reason—that he willed and asked for what he did not obtain. Nor did he ask in order that he might obtain it, because he knew that God would not do [Col. 0792] that; nor did he will it by the affection of reason or by the will of his divinity. Why, then, did he ask? That he might provide his members with an example, when distress is imminent, of crying to the Lord and subjecting their own will to the divine will: so that, if they are saddened when affliction knocks, they may pray for its removal. But if they cannot avoid it, let them say what Christ himself said. Therefore it was not foolishness that Christ, crying out, was not heard for bodily salvation. He asked for something good—namely, that he should not die; but it was better that he should die, and this is what occurred.

### On Ambrose’s Statement That Christ Doubted in His Human Affection

4. Moreover, the words of Ambrose, by which he seems to indicate that Christ, according to human affection, doubted the Father’s power, trouble us not a little. Thus he says in Book 2 *On the Faith*: “Concerning whom does he doubt—concerning himself or concerning the Father? Certainly concerning him to whom he says, ‘Remove [it],’ he doubts by human affection. For God does not doubt concerning the Father, nor does he fear death. Nor does the prophet doubt, who asserts that nothing is impossible to God, Psalm 134: ‘He has done all things whatsoever he willed.’ Will you place God below men? The prophet does not doubt, and do you believe that the Son doubts? Therefore he doubts as man; he spoke as man.”

By these words he seems to imply that Christ doubted, not insofar as he is God or the Son of God, but insofar as he is man, by human affection. This may be understood in the sense that he did not himself doubt, but acted in the manner of one doubting and appeared to men to doubt.

### Words of Hilary Expressing a View Far Different from the Foregoing

5. Nor should it be ignored that Hilary [Note: [Col. 0792] Book 10 *On the Trinity*, fairly far from the beginning, but before the middle.] seems to maintain that Christ prayed not for himself but for his own followers when he said, “Remove this cup from me,” just as he feared not for himself but for them; nor, indeed, did he will that he himself should not undergo the Passion, but that the cup of suffering should pass from his followers. Thus he says:

“If the Passion was to glorify him—as, when Judas had gone out, he said, ‘Now the Son of Man has been glorified’—how could fear of the Passion have made him sorrowful, unless perhaps he was so irrational as to fear suffering death, which would glorify him in suffering? But perhaps he was thought to have feared so greatly that he prayed for the cup to be removed from him, saying: ‘Father, remove this cup from me,’ Mark 14. For how could he, through fear of suffering, pray that what he was hastening to accomplish through devotion to the dispensation should be removed from him? For it is not fitting that one should be unwilling to suffer who wills to suffer. And when you recognized that he willed to suffer, it would have been more reverent to confess this than to burst forth into such impious folly as to maintain that he prayed not to suffer, when you recognized that he willed to suffer.

“Therefore he was not sorrowful for himself, nor does he pray that the cup pass from himself for his own sake, but for his disciples: lest the cup of suffering fall upon them—a cup which he prays may pass from him, lest it remain in them. For he does not ask that it not be with himself, but that it pass from himself. Then he says, Luke 22: ‘Not as I will, but as you will,’ signifying in himself a sharing of human anxiety, but not distinguishing from himself the judgment of the will he held in common with the Father. Therefore he wills the cup to pass for the sake of men, by which all the disciples were to be tested; and therefore he prays for Peter, that his faith may not fail.

“Knowing, therefore, that all these things would cease after his death, he is sorrowful until death; and he knows that this cup cannot pass unless he drinks it. Therefore he says, Matthew 26: ‘My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.’ He knows that, when the Passion had been completed in himself, the fear of the cup would pass—a fear which could not pass unless he drank it; nor could the end of terror succeed terror except when the Passion had been completed, because after his death the scandal of apostolic weakness would be driven away through the glory of miracles.”

Reader, attend to these words with devout care, lest they become vessels of death to you.

## DISTINCTION XVIII. WHETHER CHRIST MERITED FOR HIMSELF AND FOR US, AND WHAT HE MERITED FOR HIMSELF AND WHAT FOR US

1. Nor should Christ’s merit be passed over [Col. 0793]. Some are accustomed to say concerning it that he merited not for himself but only for his members. He did indeed merit for his members redemption from the devil, sin, and punishment, and the opening of the kingdom, so that, once the fiery sword had been removed, the entrance might stand open and free. But he also merited for himself the glory of impassibility and immortality, as the Apostle says in Philippians 2: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross; on account of which God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name.”

The Apostle plainly says that Christ was exalted by the glory of impassibility because he was humbled by the obedience of suffering. Therefore the humility of the Passion was the merit of exaltation, and exaltation the reward of humility. Hence Augustine, explaining the foregoing chapter, says: “For Christ to be glorified by resurrection, he was first humbled by suffering. Humility is the merit of glory; glory is the reward of humility. But all this was done in the form of a servant. For in the form of God glory always was and always will be.”

Likewise Ambrose, discussing the same chapter, says: “Here it is shown what humility merits, and how great a thing it merits.” From these testimonies it is evident that through the humility and obedience of his Passion Christ merited the glorification of his body; and not that alone, but also the impassibility of his soul. For before death his soul was capable of suffering, just as his flesh was mortal; but after death, by the merit of humility, his soul too was made impassible and his flesh immortal. Whether the soul was made impassible when the flesh was made immortal—namely, at the very moment of resurrection—is not certain to us on authoritative grounds. But either immediately after its separation from the flesh the soul was endowed with impassibility, or at the resurrection, when the flesh flowered anew.

### That Christ Merited for Himself from His Conception What He Merited through His Passion

2. Christ merited this not only when, obedient to the Father, he underwent the cross; from his very conception, from the time he became man, through charity, justice, and the other virtues—in the fullness of which he was created as man—he merited for himself just as much as he later did through endurance of martyrdom. For there was in him such fullness of spiritual gifts that he could not advance in them; and therefore his soul could not become better than it had been from the beginning of its creation, because he could not advance in merits.

Hence Gregory, on Exodus 25, says: “Christ had absolutely no capacity, with respect to the merit of his soul, by which he could make progress; but in the members—which we are—he progresses daily.” Therefore by the gibbet of the cross he did not merit more for himself than he had merited from conception through the grace of virtues. He did not, then, progress with respect to the merit of his soul in the strength of merit; nevertheless, he did progress in the number of merits. For in the Passion he had more merits than at conception; but the more numerous merits were not greater in their meriting power than the fewer ones had been earlier.

Therefore from conception he merited not only the glory of the body’s impassibility and immortality, but also the impassibility of the soul. By what means? By perfect obedience and will—which he did not first possess then, nor possess in greater measure when he began to suffer and die. For from the time he was man, he was obedient, perfect, and good as man.

That soul, therefore, possessed some good in itself after death which it did not possess before. Was it then happier or better than before? Far be it that it was better, since it was neither holier nor more richly endowed with grace. Nor was it happier in contemplation of God, wherein blessedness chiefly consists. Yet it may be said to have been happier in this respect: that it was free from every misery. From this it cannot simply be inferred that it was happier.

### On What Is Written in Philippians 2: “He Gave Him the Name Which Is above Every Name”

3. He merited not only glory of impassibility and immortality, but also that the name above every name should be given to him—namely, the honor of being called God. Yet he had this name before death. For the Son of God had the name of God, insofar as he is God, eternally by nature; insofar as he truly became man, he had it in time by grace.

Nevertheless Augustine [Note: [Col. 0794] In Book 2, *Against Maximinus*, chapter 5; and Book 3, chapter 2. See the Ordinary Gloss on Philippians 2.] says that this name was given to the man, not to God, because he possessed that name when he existed only in the form of God. But when it is said, “On account of which he exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name,” it sufficiently appears why he exalted him—that is, because of obedience—and in what form he was exalted. For in the form in which he was crucified, he was exalted; and in that form the name was given to him, so that, together with the very form of a servant, he should be called the only-begotten Son of God. This was given to him as man which he, the same person, already possessed as God.

Therefore by grace he received this: that he, being man or subsisting in the form of a servant—that is, in soul and flesh—should be called and should be God. But did he merit this at that time? For it was stated above that this man did not merit so great a good. How then is it said here: “On account of obedience this name was given to him”? It should be understood according to that very common scriptural figure by which a thing is said to happen when it becomes known. After the resurrection, what had existed beforehand was set in plain view, so that humans and demons might know it. Therefore God gave him, after the resurrection, the manifestation of that name; but he merited that manifestation by the obedience of his Passion, since by obeying in suffering he was exalted in rising again, and through this the name was manifested.

The Lord himself used this same figure after the resurrection when he said, Matthew 28: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me”—not because he received it then for the first time, but because the power which he had before was then manifested.

Moreover Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0794] Vol. 4, Commentary on chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Philippians, in the middle; and cited in the Ordinary Gloss on the same passage of Paul.] says that that name was given to God, not to man. According to the surface of the words, he appears opposed to Augustine; but their meanings do not conflict, although they have a different sense. For Ambrose understands it as said of the natural gift by which the Father, in eternally begetting the Son, gave him the name above every name—namely, God by nature—because from eternity he begot the Son, fully God and equal to himself. Yet the Apostle says that this name was given to Christ on account of the obedience of the Passion. But it must be understood in the manner of speech set out above.

### Whether Christ Could Have Possessed Those Things without Any Merit

4. But if it is asked whether Christ could have possessed, without any merit, that glory of immortality and impassibility and the manifestation of the name of God, it may rightly be said that he could have assumed human nature as glorious as it was at the resurrection. He could also have made his name known to human beings in another way. But, being a passible man as he was, he could not arrive at that glory without merit. He could indeed arrive at it without the merit of suffering, because, once mortality had been consumed, he could be clothed in the glory of immortality; but not without the merit of justice, charity, and the other virtues.

For Christ could not be man without possessing the fullness of virtues and grace. Nor, when clothed in the sackcloth of mortality, could virtues be present in him without his meriting through them. Therefore, possessing these virtues as a passible and mortal man, he could not fail to merit the glory of immortality. Thus, having become mortal, he could not attain the glory of impassibility and immortality, and the manifestation of the divine name, without merit. Yet he could attain these without the merit of the Passion, because through the Passion he merited nothing for himself which he had not already merited through the virtues.

### On the Cause of Christ’s Death and Passion

5. Why, then, did he will to suffer and die, if the virtues sufficed for him to merit those things? For you, not for himself. In what way for me? So that his Passion and death might be for you both example and cause: an example of virtue and humility; a cause of glory and freedom; an example of obedience to God even unto death; and a cause of your liberation and blessedness.

For by enduring death and suffering he merited for us [Col. 0795] what he had not merited by what preceded—namely, entrance into paradise and redemption from sin, punishment, and the devil. Through his death we obtained these things: redemption and adoption into the glory of children. For by dying he became the sacrificial victim of our liberation.

But how did he redeem us from the devil and from sin through death, and open the entrance to glory? God had decreed in mystery, as Ambrose says, that because of the first sin a human being should not be admitted into paradise—that is, should not be admitted to the contemplation of God—unless there should be in one man such humility as could benefit all who belonged to him; just as in the first man there was such pride as harmed all who belonged to him.

But among human beings none was found through whom this could be fulfilled except the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who opened the book and loosed its seals, fulfilling in himself all justice—that is, the most complete humility, than which none can be greater. For all other human beings were debtors, and scarcely did each person’s own virtue and humility suffice for that person. Therefore none of them could offer a sacrifice sufficient for our reconciliation. But Christ the man was a sufficient and perfect sacrifice, who humbled himself far more, in tasting the bitterness of death, than that Adam had exalted himself in pride by enjoying with harmful delight the eating of the forbidden tree.

Therefore, if the pride of that man was the ruin of all, sending him himself out of paradise and closing the gate to others, much more was Christ’s humility—by which he tasted death—able, once God’s decree had been fulfilled, to open the entrance of the heavenly kingdom to all his own and erase the written bond of the decree. For, as Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0795] In the Ordinary Gloss on chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Hebrews.]: “So great was our sin that we could not be saved unless the only-begotten Son of God died for us, who were debtors to death; but thus he made us worthy of the covenant and of the promised inheritance.”

This should not be understood as though he could not have saved us in another way than through his death, but because by no other sacrifice could the entrance to the kingdom be opened for us and salvation be accomplished, except through the death of the Only-Begotten, whose humility and patience were, as stated, so great that by his merit the entrance to the kingdom might stand open to those who believe in him.

Great things, therefore, were granted to us in the death of the Only-Begotten, so that we may return to our homeland, just as formerly those who had fled to a city of refuge could safely return to their own homes upon the death of the high priest. Thus it has been shown, to some extent, how through Christ’s death the entrance to the kingdom has been prepared for us.

## DISTINCTION XIX. HOW HE REDEEMED US FROM THE DEVIL AND FROM SIN THROUGH DEATH

1. Let us now ask how, through his death, we were redeemed from the devil, sin, and punishment. We were freed from the devil and from sin through Christ’s death because, as the Apostle says in Romans 5, “we have been justified in his blood.” In being justified—that is, freed from sin—we have been freed from the devil, who held us in the bonds of sins.

But how were we freed from sins through his death? Because through his death, as the Apostle says in Romans 8, the charity of God is commended to us—that is, God’s outstanding and praiseworthy charity toward us appears in this: that he delivered his Son to death for us sinners. When the pledge of such great love toward us has been displayed, we too are moved and kindled to love God, who has done such great things for us; and by this we are justified—that is, freed from sins, we are made righteous. Therefore Christ’s death justifies us when through it charity is awakened in our hearts.

We are also said in another way to be justified through Christ’s death, because through faith in his death we are cleansed from sins. Hence the Apostle, Romans 3: “The righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ.” And again in the same place: “Whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood,” that is, through faith in his Passion. Thus, long ago, those who looked upon the bronze serpent erected on wood were healed from the bites of serpents [Col. 0796], Numbers 2. Therefore, if with the gaze of right faith we look upon him who hung upon the wood for us, we are released from the bonds of the devil—that is, from sins—and so are liberated from the devil, so that after this life he may find in us nothing to punish.

For by his death, as one most true sacrifice, Christ extinguished every fault by which the devil held us for the payment of punishments, so that in this life he may not prevail over us by tempting us. Although he tempts us after Christ’s death in the ways in which he tempted before, he nevertheless cannot conquer as he conquered before. For Peter, who before Christ’s death denied him when frightened by the voice of a maidservant, Luke 22, did not yield after the death when brought before kings and governors. Why? Because the stronger one—that is, Christ—coming into the house of the strong one, Luke 11, that is, into our hearts, where the devil dwelt, bound the strong one: he restrained him from seducing believers, so that temptation, which is still permitted to him, may not be followed by seduction.

Therefore in Christ’s blood—he who paid what he had not taken, Psalm 68—we have been redeemed from sin, and through this from the devil. For, as Augustine says in Book 2 *On the Baptism of Infants*, otherwise called *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 30, vol. 7: “The invisible hostile powers are conquered in us where invisible desires are conquered. For when blood without fault was shed, the written bonds of all faults were erased, by which those believing in him had formerly been held as debtors by the devil.” Hence: “Which shall be poured out for many.” Therefore we were redeemed through him, in whom the ruler of this world found nothing.

Hence Augustine, Book 2 *On the Baptism of Infants*, otherwise called *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, chapter 30, vol. 7, setting forth the cause and manner of our redemption, says: “The devil found nothing in Christ for which he should die; but Christ willed to die according to the will of the Father, having no cause of death from sin, but tasting death from obedience and justice, through which he redeemed us from the slavery of the devil. For we had fallen into the ruler of this world, who deceived Adam and made him a servant, and began to possess us as though born slaves. But the Redeemer came, and the deceiver was conquered.

“And what did the Redeemer do to our captor? He stretched out his cross as a trap; he placed there his blood as though bait. But the devil shed that blood, not the blood of a debtor, and by this he withdrew from the debtors. For he shed his blood for this purpose: to blot out our sins. Therefore that by which the devil held us was blotted out by the Redeemer’s blood. For he held us only in the bonds of our sins; these were the chains of captives. He came, bound the strong one with the bonds of his Passion, entered his house—that is, the hearts in which he dwelt—and snatched away his goods, namely us, whom he had filled with his bitterness. But our God, snatching away his goods and making them his own, poured out bitterness and filled them with sweetness, redeeming us from sins through his death and granting adoption into the glory of children, Romans 8.”

### Why God Became Man and Died

2. Therefore he became a mortal man in order that by dying he might conquer the devil. For unless the one who conquered the devil were man, it would appear that man, who had voluntarily subjected himself to the devil, was taken away from him not justly but violently. But if man conquered him, the devil manifestly lost man by right. And for man to conquer, it was necessary that God be in him, making him free from sins. For if he were merely man, or an angel in a human being, he would easily sin, since it is evident that each nature by itself fell. Therefore the Son of God assumed a passible man, in whom he tasted death, by which he opened heaven to us and redeemed us from slavery to the devil—that is, from sin, for slavery to the devil is sin—and from punishment.

### How and from What Punishment Christ Redeemed Us through Death

3. From what punishment? From temporal and eternal punishment. From eternal punishment, indeed, by remitting the debt; from temporal punishment he will free us completely in the future, when the last enemy, death, is destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15. For we still await the redemption of the body. But with respect to our souls we have already been redeemed in part, not wholly: from guilt, not from punishment; nor wholly even from guilt. For we have not been redeemed from it in such a way that it does not exist, but so that it does not reign, Romans 6.

### How He Bore Our Punishment, 1 Peter 2

[Col. 0797]

4. He is also said to have borne our sins—that is, the punishment of our sins—in his body upon the tree, because through his punishment, which he bore on the cross, every temporal punishment owed for sin by those converted is wholly remitted in baptism, so that none is exacted from the baptized; and it is diminished in penance. For the punishment by which the Church binds penitents would not suffice unless Christ’s punishment cooperated—he who paid for us.

Hence the Apostle says that the sins of the righteous who lived before the coming were held in God’s forbearance until Christ’s death, for the showing of his righteousness at this time. Here, then, it has plainly been explained how and what Christ merited and obtained for us through death.

### Whether Christ Alone Ought to Be Called Redeemer, as He Alone Is Called Mediator

5. Hence he is truly called Redeemer of the world and Mediator of God and human beings. But in Scripture the Son alone is called Mediator, whereas sometimes the Father or the Holy Spirit is also called Redeemer. This is on account of the exercise of power, not on account of the display of humility and obedience. For in respect of the exercise both of power and of obedience, the Son is properly called Redeemer, because in himself he fulfilled the things through which we are justified, and he effected that justification itself by the power of divinity together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore he is Redeemer insofar as he is God, by the exercise of power; insofar as he is man, by the effect of humility. And he is more often called Redeemer according to his humanity, because according to it and in it he undertook and fulfilled those sacraments which are the cause of our redemption. Therefore the Son is properly called Redeemer.

### On the Mediator

6. He alone is called Mediator, not the Father or the Holy Spirit. Of him the Apostle says, 1 Timothy 2: “One mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus”—that is, through his humanity, as one placed in the middle, he is an arbiter for establishing peace, that is, for reconciling human beings to God. This is the arbiter whom Job desires: “Would that there were an arbiter for us!” For, as the Apostle says, Romans 5, we were reconciled to God through Christ’s death.

This should not be understood as though Christ reconciled us to God in such a way that God began to love those whom he had hated, as one enemy is reconciled to another, so that those who had previously hated one another might afterward be friends. Rather, we were reconciled to a God who already loved us. For God did not begin to love us from the time we were reconciled to him through the blood of his Son; he loved us before the world, before we were anything.

How then were we reconciled to a God who loved us? Because of sin we had enmity against him, though he had charity toward us even when we exercised enmity against him by working iniquity. Thus we were enemies of God in the way sins are enemies of justice. Therefore, once sins are forgiven, such enmities end, and we are reconciled to the righteous one, who himself justifies us.

Christ, therefore, is called Mediator because, being in the middle between God and human beings, he reconciles them to God. He reconciles them by removing human offenses from God’s sight—that is, by blotting out sins, by which God was offended and we were his enemies. But since sins are blotted out not by the Son alone but also by the Father and the Holy Spirit, and their blotting out is our reconciliation to God, why is the Son alone called Mediator? For we read that the Father reconciled the world to himself. The Apostle says, 2 Corinthians 5: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” Since, then, he reconciles, why is he not called Mediator? Because he is neither in the middle between God and human beings, nor did he possess in himself those sacraments by faith in and imitation of which we are justified—that is, reconciled to God.

Therefore the whole Trinity reconciled us by the exercise of power, namely by blotting out sins; but the Son alone did so by fulfilling obedience, in whom those things were accomplished according to human nature through which those who believe and imitate are justified. (Augustine, Book 13 *On the Trinity*, chapter 16.)

### According to Which Nature He Is Mediator

7. Hence he is called Mediator according to his humanity, not according to his divinity. For he is not mediator between God and God, because there is only one God, but between God and man, as between two extremes, since one cannot be a mediator except between things. Therefore he is Mediator insofar as he is man. For insofar as he is God, he is not Mediator but is equal to the Father, the same as the Father, one God with the Father.

He mediates between human beings and God the Trinity according to human nature, in which he undertook those things through which we are reconciled to God the Trinity. According to that same nature he has something like God and something like human beings, as was fitting for a Mediator, lest, being altogether like human beings, he should be far from God, or, being altogether like God, he should be far from human beings, and so should not be Mediator.

Thus the one Mediator, Christ, between mortal sinners and the immortal righteous one, appeared mortal with human beings and righteous with God: drawing near to us through weakness, to God through righteousness. Therefore he is rightly called Mediator, because between the immortal God and mortal man he is God and man, reconciling man to God—insofar as he is man. But insofar as he is the Word, he is not in the middle, because he is one God with the Father.

Therefore, if Christ according to you, O heretics, has only one nature, in what respect will he be in the middle? And unless he is in the middle in this way—that he is God by reason of the nature of divinity and man by reason of the nature of humanity—how are human things reconciled in him with divine things? For, coming first, he united human things to divine things in himself through the conjunction of both natures in one person. Then through his death he reconciled all believers to God, when all who, by believing, loved Christ’s humility and, by loving, imitated it were healed from ungodliness. (Augustine, vol. 1, *Confessions*, Book 19, chapter 42.)

Thus it has been indicated to some extent why Christ alone is called Mediator of God and human beings; according to which nature he mediates, namely the human; and to whom he mediates, namely to God the Trinity. For through death he reconciled us to the Trinity, through which he also redeemed us from slavery to the devil. For, as 1 Peter 2 says: “We were redeemed not with corruptible gold and silver, but with the precious blood of the immaculate Lamb.”

## DISTINCTION XX. THAT GOD COULD HAVE LIBERATED MAN IN ANOTHER WAY, AND WHY HE CHOSE THIS ONE RATHER

1. If it is asked whether God could have liberated man in some other way than through Christ’s death, we say that another manner was possible to God, to whose power all things are subject; but no other manner was more fitting for healing our misery, nor ought there to have been one. For what so greatly raises our minds and frees them from despair of immortality as this: that God so valued us that the Son of God, unchangeably good, remaining what he was and receiving from us what he was not, deigned to enter into fellowship with us and, by dying, bear our evils?

There is another reason why he willed to liberate us in this manner rather than another: because in this way the devil is conquered by justice, not by power. And how this occurred I shall explain as I can. By a certain justice of God, the human race was delivered into the devil’s power, the sin of the first man passing originally to all and binding all by its debt. Hence all human beings from their origin are under the devil’s ruler. Therefore the Apostle says, Ephesians 2: “We were by nature children of wrath”—by nature, that is, as nature has been corrupted by sin, not as it was rightly created in the beginning.

But the manner in which man was delivered into the devil’s power must not be understood as though God did this or commanded it to be done, but only that he permitted it—though justly. For when God abandoned the sinner, the author of sin immediately invaded him. Yet God did not restrain his mercies in his anger, nor did he lose man from the law of his power when he permitted him to be in the devil’s power; for the devil is no more outside God’s power than outside his goodness. For neither devil nor human being could subsist in any kind of life except through him who gives life to all things.

Therefore God did not abandon man so as not to show himself God to him; rather, even amid penal evils he bestowed many good things upon the wicked, and at length drew out from the devil, through forgiveness of sins granted by Christ’s blood, the man whom the commission of sins had subjected to the devil. Thus the devil was conquered by justice, not by power.

But by what justice? By the justice of Jesus Christ. And how was he conquered by it? Because, finding in Christ nothing worthy of death, he nevertheless killed him. And surely it is just that those debtors whom he held should be set free when they believe in him whom he killed without any debt at all.

He did not will to conquer by power because the devil, through the vice of his perversity, is a lover of power and a deserter and assailant of justice. Human beings imitate him especially in this: neglecting justice, or even hating it, they strive more for power and rejoice either in obtaining it or burn with desire for it. Therefore it pleased God to conquer by justice rather than by power, and to rescue man in such a way that man might learn to imitate him.

Afterward, in the resurrection, power followed, because he who had died returned to life, never afterward to die. But would not the devil have been conquered by fullest right if Christ had willed to deal with him by power alone? Certainly; but Christ set aside what he could do in order first to do what was fitting. Therefore the justice of humility liberated man, whom power alone could most justly have liberated.

### On the Case between God, Man, and the Devil
2. For if those three should come to trial, namely God, the devil, and man, the devil and man would have nothing to say against God.
