For the devil would be convicted of wronging God, because he both deceitfully led away and forcibly held His servant, namely man. Man likewise would be convicted of wronging God, because he despised His commandments and enslaved himself to another’s dominion. The devil would be convicted of wronging man, because he first deceived him by a false promise and afterwards injured him by bringing evils upon him. Therefore, insofar as he himself was concerned, the devil held man unjustly; yet man was justly held, because the devil never deserved to have power over man, whereas man deserved through guilt to suffer the devil’s tyranny. Therefore, if God, who had authority over both, had wished to liberate man by power, He could most rightly have liberated man by the force of command alone; but for the reason previously stated He chose to employ the justice of humility. When He was crucified in mortal flesh, we were justified—that is, by the remission of sins we were rescued from the devil’s power; and thus the devil was conquered by Christ’s justice, not by power. But how our sins were remitted in His blood has been explained above. (Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 13, ch. 14.)

### On Christ’s handing over, said to have been effected by the Father and the Son, by Judas and by the Jews

3. Christ, therefore, is priest and likewise victim, the price of our reconciliation. He offered Himself on the altar of the cross not to the devil, but to the Trinity, for all as regards the sufficiency of the price, but only for the elect as regards its efficacy, because He effected salvation only for those predestined. Of Him it is also written that He was handed over by the Father, that He handed Himself over, and that Judas and the Jews handed Him over. He handed Himself over because He voluntarily entered upon His Passion; and the Father handed Him over because He suffered by the will of the Father—indeed, of the whole Trinity. Judas handed Him over by betraying Him, and the Jews by inciting it. The act of Judas and the Jews was evil, while the act of Christ or the Father was good; the work of Christ and the Father was good, because the will of the Father and Son was good. The work of Judas and the Jews was evil, because their intention was evil.

There were different deeds or works there—that is, different acts—yet one event or deed, namely the Passion itself. Therefore doctors sometimes join together, in that event, the Father, the Son, Judas, and the Jew; at other times they distinguish them. For, looking to the Passion, they call it their one work; attending to their intentions and acts, they discern distinct deeds. Hence Augustine says: “The handing over was effected by the Father; the handing over was effected by the Son; the handing over was effected by Judas: one thing was done. What then distinguishes them from one another? The Father and the Son did this in love, but Judas in betrayal. You see that one must consider not what a person does, but with what will he does it. In the same deed we find God and Judas: we bless God, we detest Judas, because God devised our salvation. Judas devised the price for which he sold the Lord; the Son, the price which He gave for us. Therefore a different intention makes things different, although there is one event arising from different agents.”

See: he says that there was one event there [Col. 0800], yet different deeds, because there was one Passion there but different acts—the evil acts of Judas and the Jews, by which they brought about Christ’s Passion, which is good and is God’s work. (Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm 93*, vol. 8; *Homilies on the First Epistle of John*, homily 7.)

### That Christ’s Passion is called the work of God and of the Jews, and how

4. Christ’s Passion is therefore called the work of the Jews because it resulted from their acts, and the work of God because it took place with Him as author—that is, because He willed it. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 0800] *On the Unity of the Trinity*, addressed to Optatus, against Felicianus, ch. 14, vol. 6]:

> No one takes Christ’s soul from Him, because He has power to lay it down and to take it up again, John 10. Here you have the author of the work: He will lay down His soul. Here you have the author’s work. And, to state the matter generally, whenever Christ suffers anything in the flesh, it is the work of its author; for, because He endures it by His own will and not under another’s compulsion, He Himself is the author of the work.

But since Christ’s Passion is God’s work and therefore good, and Judas and the Jews brought it about, the question is whether one ought to grant that they did good there. A distinction must be made. It may be said that they did good because good resulted from their acts, namely Christ’s Passion; and likewise that they did not do good but evil, because their action was not good but evil.

## DISTINCTION XXI. WHETHER, IN CHRIST’S DEATH, SOUL OR FLESH WAS SEPARATED FROM THE WORD

1. After the foregoing, it must be considered whether, in Christ’s death, either soul or flesh was separated from the Word. Some have thought that, in death, the flesh was divided from the divinity just as it was from the soul. For, they say, if the soul, as an intermediary, united the flesh to the divinity—as was noted above—then, when the flesh was divided from the soul, it was also divided from the divinity. For it could not be separated from the soul, through which it was united to the Word, without being divided from the Word. But it was divided from the soul in death; otherwise there would not have been a true death there. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0800] Vol. 8, distinction 2, book 3, ch. *Assumpsit*, sermon 2, on Psalm 48, “Like sheep set in hell”]:

> The death which people fear is the separation of soul from flesh. But the death which they do not fear is the separation of soul from God. Both were administered to man at the devil’s persuasion.

Therefore, if there was true death in Christ the man, the soul—and consequently the divinity—was divided from the flesh.

To this plausible argument they add the testimony of authority. For Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0800] Vol. 4, Commentary on Luke ch. 22, on the words, “Father, into Your hands I commend my spirit”], treating Christ’s abandonment—when upon the cross He cried with a loud voice, “My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”—says: “The man cries out, about to die through separation from the divinity. For since divinity is free from death, death certainly could not be there unless life departed, since life is divinity.” Here he seems to teach that in death divinity was separated from the man; unless it had departed, that man could not die. They refer this to the flesh, which they say was separated from God.

We answer that this separation must be understood as the abandonment signified by the words, “Why have You forsaken me?” How then was Christ forsaken by the Father when, upon the cross, He cried that He was forsaken? God had not withdrawn from the man in such a way that the union of God and man was dissolved. Otherwise there was a time when Christ, still alive as man, was not God, since while still living He cried that He was forsaken, not that He would be forsaken. Therefore, if that abandonment is understood as a dissolution of union, the dissolution of God and man occurred before Christ had died. But who could say this?

Let us therefore confess that God in a certain manner abandoned that man in death, because for a time He exposed Him to the power of His persecutors, not exercising His power to defend Him from dying. Divinity separated itself because it withdrew protection, but did not dissolve the union. It separated itself outwardly, so as not to be present for defense, but inwardly it did not fail in union. If it had not restrained its power there but had exercised it, Christ would not have died. Christ died with the divinity withdrawing—that is, by not displaying the effect of its power in defending Him.

This is the scapegoat, ἀποπομπαῖος, which, after the other goat was sacrificed, was sent into the wilderness, as is read in Leviticus. For the two goats signify Christ’s humanity and divinity. Thus, when the humanity had been sacrificed, Christ’s divinity went into the wilderness—that is, into heaven. Hence Hesychius says: “In the wilderness,” that is, “in heaven,” the divinity is said to have gone at the time of the Passion, not by changing place, but by restraining its power in a certain manner, so that the ungodly might complete the Passion. It therefore went away—that is, it restrained its power—and bore our iniquities (Isa. 43), not in order to possess them, but in order to consume them; for God is a consuming fire (Deut. 4). From these statements it is sufficiently shown that Ambrose’s preceding words must be understood as we have stated.

### They introduce another authority to the same effect

Others likewise rely upon an authority in asserting that, in death, divinity withdrew from the man according to the flesh. For Athanasius says [Note: [Col. 0801] Book 6, called *On the Blessedness of the Son of God*, addressed to Theophilus]:

> Accursed is he who does not confess that the whole man assumed by the Son of God, having been assumed anew, rose again from the dead on the third day. So be it, so be it.

“If,” they say, “the man whom He assumed in the Incarnation was assumed anew in the Resurrection, then He laid him aside in death; therefore divinity was separated from humanity in death.”

We answer that, if in these words “assumption” is understood as the assumption effected by union, then in the Resurrection He united anew to Himself not the flesh alone but the whole man, that is, soul and flesh; for Athanasius says not simply that “man,” but that “the whole man,” was assumed. Therefore He laid aside the whole man in death, that is, soul and flesh. But who, except an enemy of truth, would say that the soul was laid aside by the Word? Yet unless they admit this, namely that the whole man was assumed, that authority—which says that the whole was assumed—does not support them.

It must therefore be understood that Athanasius said this against the unbelief of those who denied Christ’s Resurrection, thinking that He who alone is free among the dead was held by death. Therefore he curses the person who does not confess that the whole man, having been assumed anew, rose again—that is, that Christ joined the soul anew to the body; and that, when those two were newly joined in the Resurrection, He truly lived as man as He had before death. For in death the soul was separated from the flesh; nevertheless, although Christ is said to have died, neither was separated from the Word of God.

### By authorities he proves that the flesh was not divided from the Word in death

3. As Augustine teaches, *On John*, tractate 57, vol. 9, discussing the Lord’s saying, “I lay down my soul, that I may take it again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down; I have power of myself to lay it down and to take it again,” He says here that the soul was sent forth. By whom was it sent forth? It was not sent forth by itself, because it did not lay itself down; nor did the Word lay down the soul or the flesh. Therefore the flesh laid down the soul, but by the power of the divinity remaining in it. Thus by the power of the divinity the soul was divided from the flesh, but neither was divided from the Word of God.

Hence Augustine, *On the Unity of the Trinity*, addressed to Optatus, ch. 14:

> From the time when the Word assumed man—that is, flesh and soul—He never laid aside the soul, so that the soul should be separated from the Word; but the flesh laid down the soul when He expired, and when it returned He rose again.

Death, then, for a time separated flesh and soul, but neither from the Word of God. The flesh therefore lays down and takes up the soul, not by its own power, but by the power of the divinity dwelling in the flesh. Here it is clearly taught that neither soul nor flesh was divided from the Word of God in death in any way that dissolved the union.

Hence Augustine, against Felicianus:

> Far be it that Christ experienced death in such a way that, so far as He was concerned, life lost life! For if this were so, the fountain of life would have dried up. He therefore experienced death through participation in the human affection which He voluntarily assumed; He did not lose the power of His nature, by which He gives life to all things. Thus in the tomb Christ did not abandon His flesh by dying with it, just as in the Virgin’s womb He formed it by being born with it. He therefore died without life departing, just as He suffered without power perishing. No one takes His soul from Him, because He has power to lay it down and to take it up again.

Here also you have that Christ did not abandon the flesh in death, that life did not depart from the dead one, and that He voluntarily gave up His spirit rather than having it wrested from Him by another. Hence Ambrose, *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, ch. 5: “Christ sent forth His spirit; yet, as though arbiter of laying aside and taking up the body, He sent it forth. He hung upon the cross and set all things in motion. But whence did He send it forth? From the flesh. Whither did He send it forth? To the Father.”

### In what sense Christ is said to have died and suffered

4. When the soul departed, Christ’s flesh died; and because the flesh died, Christ died. For just as God is said to have died when the man died, so the man is said to have died when the flesh died. The separation of the soul was the death of the flesh. Therefore, because of the flesh united to the Word, which died, God is said to have died; and because of the flesh and soul, both of which felt pain, God is said to have suffered, although divinity is free from every pain.

Hence Augustine says: “The Word became flesh so that through the flesh the heavenly bread might pass to infants; and according to this very fact the Word was crucified, yet He was not changed into man; rather, man was changed in Him, in order that he might become better than he had been. Therefore through that whereby He was man God died, and through that whereby He was God man was raised and rose again. Whatever the man suffered cannot be said not to have been suffered by God, since God was man. How can you say that you have not suffered an injury if your garment is torn, although your garment is not you? Much more, therefore, whatever the flesh united to the Word suffers must be said to be suffered by God, although the Word could neither die, decay, nor change. But whatever of these He suffered, He suffered in the flesh.”

Ambrose likewise says, in *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*: “What the flesh of the Word suffered, the Word remaining in the flesh referred to Himself by reason of the assumed body, so that He might be said to suffer because the flesh suffered; as it is written, 1 Peter 4: ‘Christ having suffered in the flesh.’”

Here it is taught on what ground God or the Son of God is called to have suffered or died: not because He experienced death insofar as He is God, but because the flesh united to Him died. In this sense Augustine says, in his sermon *On Faith*: “If anyone should say and believe that God the Son of God suffered, let him be anathema.” Explaining from what understanding this statement must be taken, he immediately adds in the same place: “If anyone should say that in the Passion God the Son of God felt pain, and not only the flesh together with the soul which He had assumed, let him be anathema.”

Thus it may rightly be said that God died and did not die; that the Son of God suffered and did not suffer; that the third Person suffered and did not suffer; that the Word was crucified and was not crucified. For according to one nature He suffered; according to the other He was impassible. Hence Ambrose, *On the Holy Spirit*, book 3:

> This is the general faith: Christ is the Son of God and born of a Virgin; the Prophet describes Him as a giant in Psalm 18, because He is one of two forms and twofold natures, sharing in divinity and body. The same one suffered and did not suffer; died and did not die; was buried and was not buried; rose and did not rise. He rose according to the flesh, which had died, not according to the Word, which always remained with God.

## DISTINCTION XXII. WHETHER CHRIST WAS MAN IN DEATH

1. Here the question is raised whether Christ was man during those three days of death. This does not seem so to some, because He was dead and a dead man is not a man. They further add that, if He was then man, He was either mortal or immortal; but not mortal, because He was dead, nor immortal, because this applied only after the Resurrection.

We answer that although man had died, God was nevertheless man in death; yet He was neither mortal nor immortal, and nevertheless He was truly man. Such subtleties [Col. 0803] have their place in created things, but the sacrament of faith is free from philosophical arguments. Hence Ambrose, *On Faith*, book 1, ch. 5, at the end: “Remove arguments where faith is sought. Let dialectic now be silent even in its own schools; fishermen are believed, not dialecticians.”

We therefore say that in Christ’s death God truly was man, and yet dead; and that the man was neither mortal nor immortal, because He was united to soul and flesh which were separated from one another. For God is called man, or man God, on a different ground than Martin or John is called man. God is called man, and conversely, because of the assumption of man—that is, soul and flesh. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, ch. 13: “That assumption was such as to make God man and man God.”

Therefore, since that assumption did not fail through death, but God remained truly united to man, and man to God, as before, then God was man and conversely, because He was united to soul and flesh; and the man was dead because the soul was divided from the flesh. He was dead because of the separation of soul and flesh, but man because of His perpetual union with both. Yet He was not man in such a way as to subsist from soul and flesh joined together. Before death He was man in the same manner in which any other person is called man, and He was so after the Resurrection. But in death He was man only because of His union with soul and flesh, and dead because of the division between those two.

### Whether Christ was man somewhere in death, and whether wherever He is He is man

2. Here the question is raised whether Christ was man somewhere in death, and whether, wherever He is, He is man. We answer that He was not man wherever He was; nor is He now man wherever He is. For He is everywhere according to His divinity, but not everywhere man, because He is not everywhere united to humanity. But wherever He is according to humanity, there He is man.

At the time of death He was everywhere according to God, and in the tomb according to man, and in hell according to man; but in hell according to the soul alone, and in the tomb according to the flesh alone. Therefore in the tomb He was man because He was united to humanity, though not to all of it, because only to the flesh; and in hell He was man because He was united to humanity, though not to all of it, because only to the soul.

But if in hell He was united only to the soul, and in the tomb only to the flesh, then in neither hell nor the tomb was He united to both soul and flesh. How then is He said to be man there or here? What is the basis for this statement? Because by one and the same union He was united to the soul in hell and to the flesh in the tomb. Thus He was united to those two, then separated, just as He had been before their separation—that is, before death.

But an objection is made. If Christ had assumed only soul or only flesh, He would not have been true man; He was true man because He assumed both. Therefore, wherever He did not have flesh and soul united to Himself, He was not true man there. But during death He had those two truly united nowhere: neither in the tomb, nor in hell, nor elsewhere. Therefore He was man nowhere.

We answer that Christ certainly would not have been true man if He had not assumed flesh and soul. Yet because, after assuming them, He laid aside neither, but continuously retained with each the same union which He contracted in assuming them, He is not improperly said to be man wherever He is united to soul, flesh, or both, because there He was made man. Therefore He was man in the tomb and man in hell, because Christ was made man in both places and retained one and the same union with soul and flesh, though separated. At one and the same time Christ lay in the tomb and descended into hell; but He lay in the tomb according to the flesh alone, and descended into hell according to the soul alone.

Hence Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2; *On John*, tractate 78, at the end: “Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ, but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb? Christ, but in the flesh alone; because Christ is in each of these. We confess Christ in all these things and in each one.” From this it is clearly shown that Christ was united to the flesh [Col. 0804] lying in the tomb just as He was to the soul in hell. Otherwise, if He were not united to the dead flesh, He would not be said to have lain in the tomb in it.

The soul therefore descended into hell; the flesh lay in the tomb; Wisdom remained with both. As Ambrose says in *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, ch. 5, Wisdom poured upon those placed in hell the light of eternal life. There shone the true light of Wisdom; it illumined hell, but was not confined in hell. “For what place is there for Wisdom?” Of it it is written, Job 28: “Man does not know its ways, nor is it found among men.” Of it the deep says, “It is not in me”; the sea says, “It is not with me.” Therefore Wisdom is neither in time nor in place, and death must not be attributed to it. For upon the wood hung the flesh, not that divine substance which works all things. Nevertheless, we confess that Christ hung upon the wood and lay in the tomb, but in the flesh alone; and that He was in hell, but in the soul alone.

### That Christ is wholly everywhere, but not wholly one thing; as He is wholly man or wholly God, but not wholly man or wholly God

3. At that same time He was wholly in hell, wholly in heaven, wholly everywhere. For that eternal Person was not greater where He had flesh and soul united to Himself together than where He had only one of them; nor was He greater where He had both together, or only one, united to Himself than where He had neither united to Himself. Therefore Christ was wholly and perfectly everywhere.

Hence Augustine, against Felicianus, *On the Unity of the Trinity*, addressed to Optatus, ch. 14: “Christ did not leave the Father when He came into the Virgin: wholly everywhere, perfectly everywhere.” Therefore at one and the same time He was wholly in hell and wholly in heaven. Among the dead was the resurrection of the dead; above the heavens was the life of the living: truly dead, truly living. In Him the assumption of mortality underwent death, while divinity did not lose life. Thus the Son of God neither endured death in the soul nor experienced it in His majesty; yet through participation in weakness the King of glory was crucified.

From this it appears that Christ was at the same time wholly in the tomb, wholly in hell, wholly everywhere; as now He is wholly wherever He is, but is not wholly one thing. He was not the whole in the tomb or in hell, although He was wholly there, just as Christ is wholly God and wholly man, but is not wholly God or wholly man, because He is not only God or only man, but both God and man. For “whole” refers to nature, while “wholly” refers to hypostasis; just as “another thing” and “something” refer to nature, whereas “another person” and “someone” refer to person.

Hence John Damascene, *On the Faith*, ch. 7, at the end: “Christ is wholly perfect God, but He is not wholly God. For He is not God only, but also man; and wholly perfect man, but not wholly man. For He is not man only, but also God. ‘Whole’ represents nature; ‘wholly,’ hypostasis. Just as ‘another thing’ belongs to nature and ‘another person’ to hypostasis, so also do expressions of this kind.”

### Whether what is said of God or the Son of God may be said of that man or of the Son of Man

4. It is also commonly asked whether it may fittingly be said that the Son of Man, or that man, descended from heaven or is everywhere, as the Son of God or God is said to have come from heaven and to be everywhere. We answer that, if the meaning of the statement is referred to the unity of person, it may certainly be said; but if it is referred to the distinction of natures, it must by no means be granted.

Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 1: “Christ, God and man, is one person. Therefore it is said: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except He who descended from heaven,’ and so forth. Therefore, if you attend to the distinction of substances, the Son of God descended and the Son of Man was crucified; but if you attend to the unity of person, the Son of Man descended and the Son of God was crucified.”

Because of this unity of person He not only said that the Son of Man had descended from heaven, but also that He was in heaven while speaking upon earth. Because of that same unity the God of glory is said to have been crucified, although He was crucified only in the form of a servant—not according to that whereby He is the God of glory and glorifies His own. Yet the God of glory is rightly said to have been crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of flesh. Let the prudent, diligent, and devout reader therefore understand what is said because of what, and according to what [Col. 0805]. Let these remarks concerning the strap of the Lord’s sandal suffice, lest the bones of the king of Edom be consumed to ashes.

## DISTINCTION XXIII. WHETHER CHRIST HAD FAITH AND HOPE AS HE HAD CHARITY

1. Since it has been asserted above that Christ was full of grace, it is not superfluous to inquire whether He had faith and hope as He had charity. For if He lacked these, He does not seem to have had fullness of graces. But in order that this question may be explained more clearly, something must be set forth concerning each of these matters, beginning with faith, according to the measure of which the Apostle commanded every person to think.

### What faith is

2. Faith is the virtue by which things not seen are believed. Yet this must not be understood of everything not seen, but only of those things which, as Augustine says, pertain to religion to believe. For there are many things which, if a Christian is ignorant of them, need cause no fear, because he does not thereby depart from religion.

### In how many senses faith is spoken of

3. Faith is understood in three senses: as that by which one believes, and it is a virtue; as that which is believed, and it is not a virtue; and as that in which one believes, which is different from that by which one believes. Hence Augustine says, *On the Trinity*, book 13, ch. 2: “The things believed are one thing; the faith by which they are believed is another. The former exist among realities which are believed either to be, to have been, or to be future; the latter exists in the mind of the believer and is visible only to the one whose it is. Yet both are denoted by the name faith: namely, both that which is believed and that by which it is believed.”

That which is believed is called faith, as in the Athanasian Creed: “This is the catholic faith, which unless each person believes firmly and faithfully, he cannot be saved.” But the faith by which one believes, if it is joined with charity, is a virtue, because charity, as Ambrose says on the Epistle to the Romans, is the mother of all virtues and gives form to them all; without it no true virtue exists. Therefore faith working through love is the virtue by which unseen things are believed. This is the foundation that cannot be altered, as the Apostle says; placed as a foundation, it permits no one to perish. Hence Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “The foundation is Christ Jesus—that is, faith in Christ, namely the faith which works through love, through which Christ dwells in hearts, and which permits no one to perish.” No other faith is the foundation. For faith without love is empty; faith with love belongs to the Christian; the other belongs to the demons. “For even the demons believe and tremble.” Yet it makes a great difference whether one believes that Christ is the Christ, believes Christ, or believes in Christ. For the demons believed that He is Christ, but they did not believe into Christ. (Augustine, vol. 10, sermon 61, *On the Words of the Lord*.)

### What it is to believe in God, to believe God, or to believe God to be God

4. To believe in God is one thing; to believe God is another; to believe that God exists is another. To believe God is to believe that what He says is true. Even evil persons do this, and we believe a human being, but not into a human being. To believe that God exists is to believe that He is God; even evil persons do this. To believe in God is, in believing, to love; in believing, to go into Him; in believing, to cleave to Him and to be incorporated into His members. By this faith the ungodly person is justified, so that thereafter faith itself may begin to work through love. For only those works are to be called good which are done through love of God. That love itself is called the work of faith.

Therefore the faith possessed by demons and false Christians is a quality of mind, but an unformed one, because it is without charity. For the Apostle shows that evil persons have faith while lacking charity, saying, 1 Corinthians 12: “If I have all faith but do not have charity,” and so forth. This faith may also be called a gift of God, because even in evil persons there are certain gifts of God. (Augustine, vol. 8, *Exposition on Psalm 67*.)

### Whether the unformed quality of mind in an evil Christian becomes a virtue when he becomes good

5. But if it is asked whether that unformed quality [Col. 0806], by which an evil Christian believes everything that a good Christian believes, remains when charity is added and becomes a virtue, or whether it is eliminated and another quality succeeds which is a virtue: either may be said without danger. Yet it seems to me that the quality which was present before remains and becomes a virtue through the accession of charity.

### In what sense faith is called one

6. Although faith is spoken of in various senses, we must nevertheless confess one faith, as the Apostle says, Ephesians 4: “One Lord, one faith.” Whether faith is taken as that which is believed or as that by which one believes, it is rightly called one faith. If it is understood as that which is believed, it is called one faith because we are commanded to believe the same thing, and the thing believed by all the faithful is one and the same. Hence it is called catholic—that is, universal—faith.

But if faith is taken as that by which one believes, it is called one not because it is numerically one in everyone, but according to kind—that is, similarity. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 13, ch. 2: “Faith, which makes those who possess it faithful and those who do not possess it unbelieving, is common to all the faithful, just as a face is said to be common to many people, although each has his own. For faith is not one numerically but by kind; when it is in one person, it is also in others, not the same faith but a similar one. Because of this similarity we call it one rather than many, just as the will of persons desiring the same thing is called one will, although each has his own will; and the faces of two very similar persons are called one face.”

### That faith is properly concerned with things not seen, although it is seen by the person in whom it exists

7. It should also be noted that faith properly concerns only things not apparent. Hence Gregory, in a homily on Ezekiel: “Things that are apparent do not have faith, but knowledge.” Likewise, when Paul says, Hebrews 11, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not apparent,” that is truly said to be believed which cannot be seen. For what can be seen can no longer be believed. Thomas saw one thing and believed another: he saw the man and confessed God, saying, John 20, “My Lord and my God.”

Augustine likewise says, *On the Trinity*, book 13, ch. 1: “Each person sees faith itself to be in his own heart if he believes, or not to be there if he does not believe. It is not seen as bodies are seen with bodily eyes, and, through the images of them retained in memory, are thought about even when absent; nor as things which we do not see but of which we somehow form a thought from things we see and commit it to memory; nor as a human being, whose soul, although we do not see it, we infer from our own, and, from bodily movements, contemplate him in thought as we have learned by seeing. Faith is not seen in this way by the one in whose heart it is; rather, he possesses certain knowledge of it. Therefore, although we are commanded to believe because we cannot see what we are commanded to believe, nevertheless, when faith is in us, we see it in ourselves. For faith in absent things is present, faith concerning things outside is within, faith concerning things not seen is seen; and it itself comes to exist temporally in human hearts, and perishes from them if believers become unbelievers.”

These words plainly teach that faith itself is seen in the human heart by that same person—not bodily, not imaginatively, but intellectually—while nevertheless it concerns absent and unseen things. For, as Augustine says elsewhere, *On John* 27, tractate 27: “We believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is to believe what you do not see; truth is to see what you have believed.” Faith is thus rightly called evidence or conviction concerning things not apparent, because if faith exists, from it one is convinced and shown that certain non-apparent things exist, since faith concerns only things not apparent.

### Definition of faith

8. For the Apostle says, Hebrews 12: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence,” or “conviction,” “of things not apparent,” because through faith the things now hoped for subsist in us even now, and in the future they subsist through experience. Faith itself is proof and conviction of things not apparent, because if anyone doubts concerning them, they are proved through faith—for example, the future resurrection is still proved because the patriarchs and other saints so believed. Or it is proof and certainty that certain things not apparent exist, as was said above. Yet faith is properly called the substance of things hoped for because it underlies the things hoped for, and because it is the foundation of good things, which no one can alter.

### Whether that definition applies to hope
9. If, however, it is asked whether this definition suits hope, either answer may safely be granted. If it is said to suit it, there are also several other respects in which faith and hope differ; yet it may without impropriety be said to belong to faith alone, and not to hope, because faith alone is called a foundation—not because faith, as a virtue, can exist without hope and charity. Hence Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 8:

> Faith working through love certainly cannot exist without hope; nor love without hope; nor hope without love; nor either without faith. And faith without love is of no benefit. Yet something may be believed which is not hoped for; but nothing can be hoped for which is not believed.

Therefore believing, which is the act of faith, naturally precedes hoping, which is the act of hope; for unless something is believed, it cannot be hoped for. For something is believed which is not hoped for. Hence Scripture very often states that faith precedes hope and hope follows faith—not because the virtue of faith precedes the virtue of hope in efficacy or causation, but because the act of faith naturally precedes the act of hope. Some also concede this concerning the very virtue of faith: that it naturally, though not temporally, precedes hope.

Thus faith alone is rightly called the foundation of all virtues and good works. But it is not the foundation of charity, because it is not the cause of charity; rather, charity is the cause of the virtue of faith itself. For charity is the cause and mother of all virtues: if it is absent, the other virtues are possessed in vain; if it is present, all are possessed. For charity is the Holy Spirit, as was set forth above in Book I of the *Sentences*, distinction 17. Therefore charity is the cause of all virtues; no one of the virtues is its cause, because it surpasses all gifts.

Hence Augustine, in his treatise *On the Praises of Charity*:

> Consider the gifts of the Church, and you will recognize that the gift of charity surpasses them all; like oil, it cannot be pressed down to the bottom, but rises above.

Faith, therefore, is neither its cause nor its foundation. Gregory, however, says in his commentary on Ezekiel that unless faith is first held, one can by no means attain to spiritual love. For charity does not precede faith, but faith charity, because no one can love what he has not believed, just as no one can hope for it.

But this may be understood as said of faith which is not a virtue. Such faith frequently precedes both hope and charity. Or it may be understood of the act of faith, which perhaps naturally precedes the act of charity, as it does the act of hope. This is indicated by the words quoted above, if carefully noted, and also by what he adds:

> Unless you believe the things you hear, you will not be kindled to love the things you hear.

This applies only to things unseen, as we said before. Hence Chrysostom:

> Faith causes the things not seen to subsist in our soul; properly speaking, faith concerns these things, for faith does not concern things seen, but recognition does.

*Homilies on the Epistle to the Hebrews*, Homily 21, at the end.

## DISTINCTION XXIV. HOW THE WORDS “THAT WHEN IT HAS HAPPENED, YOU MAY BELIEVE” ARE TO BE UNDERSTOOD

1. Here the question arises: if faith concerns only things unseen, how does Truth say to the apostles in John 14, “Now I tell you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe”? This seems to imply that their faith concerned things done and seen.

Augustine raises and resolves this question as follows, in Tractate 79 on John:

> What does this mean, “that when it has happened you may believe”? This is the praise of faith: that what is believed is not seen. For even Thomas, to whom it was said in John 20, “Because you have seen me, you have believed,” did not believe what he saw. He saw and touched the living flesh which he had seen dying, and he believed [Col. 0808] that God was hidden in that flesh. He therefore believed with his mind what he did not see, through that which appeared to the bodily senses. But if visible things are said to be believed—as everyone says that he has believed his own eyes—this is not the faith built up in us. Rather, by means of things seen, it is brought about in us that the things not seen are believed.

From this it is plainly understood that faith properly concerns things not apparent. Nor is that the faith by which we are built up in Christ when, in ordinary speech, we say that we believe what we see.

Elsewhere, however, Augustine says that faith concerns present things. This will be in the future, when through direct sight we contemplate the God who is present. Yet this is not properly called faith, but truth:

> There is a faith by which things not seen are believed. Yet there is also a faith of things, when belief is given not to words but to the things themselves as present. This will be when the Wisdom of God offers himself to the saints to be contemplated through manifest sight. But this is not properly called faith; rather, it is faith’s reward, to which one arrives by believing, so that the righteous person may pass from faith in words to faith in things.

### Whether Peter had faith in the Passion when he saw that man suffering

2. If, however, it is asked whether Peter had faith in the Passion when he saw with his eyes the man Christ suffering, we say that he did have faith in the Passion—not insofar as he believed that a man was suffering, for he saw this, but insofar as he believed that the one suffering was God.

For it was not the virtue of faith that a man was believed to suffer and die; a Jew who saw it also believed that. Rather, it was faith that believed the sufferer to be God. Hence Augustine, on the passage in Psalm 101, “He answered him in the way of his strength”:

> The praise of faith is not that it believes that this man died, which even a pagan believes, but that it believes him glorified and true God.

Faith, then, believes God to be man, and man to be glorified. Thus Peter’s faith was not to believe that that man was dying, which he saw with his eyes, but to believe that the one dying was God. Nor is our faith meritorious in believing that that man died, which even a Jew believes, but because we believe that the man who died was God.

### Whether some things are known which are not believed

3. After this, the question is usually raised whether, since faith concerns things not apparent and unseen, it concerns only things unknown as well. For if it concerns only unknown things, it seems to concern only things that are not known.

But it should be understood that, since one kind of seeing is interior and another exterior, faith does not concern things subject to external sight. Yet it does concern things grasped in some way by interior sight. Some are grasped in such a way that they are understood, though not as they will be in the future; others are not. For since faith comes by hearing, not only external but also internal, it cannot concern something wholly unknown.

Faith itself does not pertain to bodily sense, as Augustine says in Book XIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 2:

> Although faith is in us by hearing, it does not pertain to the bodily sense called hearing, for it is not a sound; nor does it pertain to any bodily sense, because this is a matter of the heart, not of the body.

Therefore some things are believed by faith which are understood by natural reason; others are believed which are not understood. Hence the Prophet says, Isaiah 7, according to the Septuagint: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.”

Augustine makes the distinction plainly:

> There are some things which, unless we understand them, we do not believe; and others which, unless we believe them, we shall not understand.

Yet no one can believe in God unless he understands something, since faith comes by hearing preaching. The same author says in *On the Trinity*:

> Certain faith in some manner begins knowledge; but certain knowledge is not perfected until after this life.

Ambrose likewise says:

> Where there is faith, there is not immediately knowledge; where there is knowledge, faith precedes.

From these statements it is clear that certain things are believed which are not understood or known unless they are first believed; while certain things are sometimes understood even before they are believed. Yet even then they are not understood now as they will be known in the future. And now, too, through the faith by which hearts are cleansed, they are understood more fully; for unless God is loved through faith, the heart is not cleansed so as to know him.

Hence Augustine, in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4:

> What is it to know God except to behold him with the mind [Col. 0809] and to apprehend him firmly? But before we are able to discern and apprehend God as he is apprehended by pure hearts, the heart cannot be cleansed unless he is loved through faith, so that it may be fit to see him.

Here you plainly have that God cannot be known unless he is first loved in belief. Yet above it was said that no one can believe in God unless something is understood. From this it follows that some things to be believed cannot be known and understood unless they are first believed; that some things cannot be believed unless they are first understood; and that those same things are more fully understood through faith.

Nor are the things believed before they are understood wholly unknown, since faith comes by hearing. They are, however, unknown in part, because they are not known. Thus what is unknown is believed, though not wholly unknown, just as what is unknown is also loved. Hence Augustine, in the same place, chapter 4:

> Something can be known and not loved. But whether what is not known can be loved, I ask. If it cannot, no one loves God before knowing him. But where are those three—faith, hope, and charity—except in the mind that believes what it does not yet know, and hopes for and loves what it believes?

Therefore what is unknown is loved, but it is nevertheless believed.

## DISTINCTION XXV. ON THE FAITH OF THE ANCIENTS

1. To what has been said must be added the question of faith’s sufficiency for salvation. Faith seems to have advanced, in accordance with the progress of time, for those who preceded Christ’s coming and those who follow it, just as knowledge advanced. For faith is called great in respect of knowledge, the number of articles, constancy, and devotion.

There is, however, a certain measure of faith without which salvation could never exist. Hence the Apostle says, Hebrews 11: “Whoever approaches God must believe that he is, and that he rewards those who hope in him.” But it is asked whether believing this was sufficient for salvation before the coming and before the Law.

In the time of grace, it is certainly clear that this is insufficient, for one must believe all things contained in the creeds. But it does not seem to have been sufficient either before the coming or before the Law, because the authorities of the saints testify that no human being, before or after, has been saved without faith in the Mediator.

Hence Augustine, volume II, Letter 157 to Optatus:

> That faith is sound by which we believe that no human being, whether older or younger, is delivered from the contagion of death and the obligation of sin contracted in the first birth, except through the one mediator between God and humanity, Jesus Christ, 1 Timothy 2. By the most saving faith in this man, who is also God, those righteous persons too were saved who, before he came in the flesh, believed that he would come in the flesh. For their faith and ours are the same. Therefore, since all righteous persons, whether before or after the incarnation, neither lived nor live except by faith in Christ’s incarnation, undoubtedly what is written in Acts 4—that there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved—has availed for the salvation of the human race from the time when it was corrupted in Adam.

The same author, volume VII, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 7:

> No one is delivered from the condemnation brought about through Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ.

The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*:

> The same faith in the Mediator which saves us made the righteous persons of old safe—little ones together with great ones. For as we believe Christ to have come in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe him to have died, so they believed that he would die; as we believe him to have risen, so they believed that he would rise; and both we and they believe that he will come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

Gregory, on Ezekiel:

> Both those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” because all the elect who could be in Judea, as well as those now in the Church, believed and believe in the Mediator between God and humanity.

These and many other testimonies clearly teach that salvation has never been granted to anyone except through faith in the Mediator. Whoever approaches God must therefore believe what the Apostle said above; but this is not enough.

### On the faith of the simple

2. What then is to be said of those simple people to whom the mystery of the Incarnation had not been revealed, but who piously believed what had been handed down to them?

It may be said that there was no righteous or saved person to whom revelation had not been given—either distinct or veiled, open or in mystery. It was distinct for Abraham, Moses, and other greater persons, who possessed a differentiated knowledge of the articles of faith. It was veiled for simple persons, to whom it had been revealed that they must believe what those greater persons believed and taught, though they did not possess a clear differentiation of those matters.

So, too, in the Church there are persons of lesser capacity who cannot distinguish and specify the articles of the Creed, yet believe all that is contained in the Creed. For they believe what they do not know, possessing veiled faith in mystery. In the same way, even now those of lesser capacity adhered in belief, through the revelation of faith given to the greater persons, to those to whom they in a sense entrusted their faith. Hence Job 1: “The oxen were ploughing, and the asses feeding beside them.”

The simple and lesser persons are the asses feeding beside the oxen, because, by humbly adhering to the greater persons, they believed in mystery what those persons also taught in mystery. Such, perhaps, was the widow of Zarephath.

### What belief concerning the Mediator was sufficient before Christ’s coming

3. But it is asked: since the ancients had no salvation without faith in the Mediator, any more than people today do, were they required to believe everything concerning the Mediator which we now believe?

Some hold that it was sufficient for them to believe only four things: namely, his birth, death, resurrection, and coming for judgment. They infer this from Augustine’s words quoted above, where he enumerated these four points.

Others hold that, provided they had faith in the Trinity, faith in the mystery of the Incarnation was sufficient if they believed that the Son of God would be born of a human being and would judge. They take proof of this from John the Baptist, who, according to Gregory’s exposition in Homily 6, seems in the Gospel to have doubted concerning Christ’s death and descent into hell when he asked through his disciples, Matthew 11: “Are you he who is to come, or should we expect another?” As if he said: “Will you yourself descend into hell, or will you send another for these mysteries?”

Some, however, say that he did not doubt out of ignorance but out of piety; that is, he presented himself as doubting, not because he did not know, but because, out of compassionate feeling for Christ, he expressed wonder at his humility.

### On the faith of Cornelius

4. The question is also commonly raised whether Cornelius had faith in the Incarnation, since the angel said to him in Acts 10: “Your alms have been accepted, and your prayers have been heard.” For if he did not have faith in the Incarnation, then he possessed righteousness without faith in the Incarnation, since it is written of him that he was righteous and feared God. But if he had faith in the Incarnation, why then was Peter sent to him?

It may safely be said that, just as he had faith in the unity of God by revelation, so he had faith in the Incarnation; but he did not know that the Son of God had already become incarnate. Peter was therefore sent to him to announce to him that the Son of God had now been born and to confer upon him the sacrament of regeneration.

Thus he had faith in the Incarnation, but he did not know whether it had occurred or was still future. In this way he came by faith to works, and by works was more firmly established in faith. For, as Gregory says, one comes by faith to works; Cornelius too came by faith to works. He believed in one God, but did not know that his Son had become incarnate. His works pleased God through faith, for without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God.

Augustine, however, says that Cornelius was told by the angel, “Your alms and your prayers have been accepted,” before he believed in Christ; yet he gave alms and prayed not without some faith. For how could he call upon one in whom he did not believe? But if salvation could exist without faith in Christ, Peter, the architect of the Church, would not have been sent to him.

Notice that he says salvation cannot exist without faith in Christ, and yet that Cornelius was heard before he believed in Christ. This may be understood to mean: before he knew that Christ, in whom he believed in mystery, had become incarnate.

### On the equality of faith, hope, charity, and works, in a certain respect

5. Nor should this be omitted: faith, hope, charity, and action are, in a certain respect, equal in the present life. Hence Gregory, in his final homily on Ezekiel:

> While we live in this life, we find faith, hope, charity, and action to be equal among us. For as much as we believe, so much we love; and as much as we love, so much confidence do we draw from hope. For each believer believes as much as he hopes and loves; and acts as much as he believes, loves, and hopes.

Nevertheless, charity is said to be greater than hope and faith, because, when the vision of God is attained, hope and faith pass away, but charity remains. And charity is the mother of all virtues. It is not placed after faith and hope because it arises from them, but because after them it will remain increased. For “charity never fails,” 1 Corinthians 13.

The equality stated above must properly be understood with reference to the intention of the interior acts. Yet the Apostle’s statement in 1 Timothy 1 seems contrary to what is said here and above—namely, that charity is not from faith and hope, but the reverse: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.”

Expounding this, Augustine, Book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, at the last chapter, takes “heart” for understanding and “conscience” for hope:

> Charity is the end of the commandment when it proceeds from a pure heart, that is, a pure understanding, so that nothing but God is loved; and from conscience, that is, good hope; and from unfeigned faith, that is, faith not pretended.

Thus charity seems not to precede faith and hope, but faith and hope charity. Understand this teaching, then, not as meaning that faith and hope precede charity—the mother of all good things—either in cause or in time, but because charity cannot exist in anyone without them, whereas they can exist without charity, although faith or hope without charity is not devout. Charity is therefore said to proceed from faith and hope because it comes to no one without them.

## DISTINCTION XXVI. ON HOPE: WHAT IT IS

1. Hope is the virtue by which spiritual and eternal goods are hoped for; that is, awaited with confidence. For hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, arising from God’s grace and preceding merits—either merits of hope itself, which charity naturally precedes, or merits of the thing hoped for, namely eternal blessedness. For to hope for something without merits may be called not hope but presumption.

### What hope concerns

2. Like faith, hope concerns invisible things. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 8: “We call faith the belief of things not seen.” Hope too is described in Romans 8: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?”

In respect of not seeing, the things believed and the things hoped for are common to faith and hope. Yet faith differs from hope not only in name but also by a rational distinction. Faith concerns evil things as well as good, since both good and evil things are believed, and this with good, not evil, faith. Faith also concerns things past, present, and future. We believe Christ’s death, which is already past; we believe his session, which is now present; we believe that he will come to judge, which is future.

Likewise faith concerns future things and things belonging to others. For each person believes that he exists, has begun to exist, and certainly has not existed eternally. We also believe many different things about other people which pertain to religion, and likewise about angels.

Hope, however, concerns only good things, only future things, and things that pertain to the person said to entertain that hope.

### Return to the preceding question: whether faith and hope existed in Christ

3. It remains to investigate whether faith and hope existed in Christ—the question with which this discussion began. Some, not without learning, hold that faith as a virtue and hope were not in him, just as they are not in saints already made blessed or in angels. Yet the saints believe and hope for the future resurrection, and angels believe the same; nevertheless, faith or hope is not a virtue in them, because they enjoy God through direct vision and behold in God’s Word the future resurrection and judgment, not in a mirror or enigma, but with utmost clarity.

For if their belief in the future resurrection means that they truly have faith, then after the judgment, when it is completed, they will likewise be said to have faith because they will believe it to be past. But just as then they will believe and yet will not possess the faith that makes believers, because they will not believe without knowledge—a knowledge not enigmatic but through direct vision—so now they believe and hope for the resurrection, and yet do not have faith, because in believing they know.

For that which is perfect has come to them, and that which is partial has been abolished. Knowledge has come, and faith has been abolished. Direct vision has come, and hope has ceased.

So too Christ, in whom were the goods of the homeland, did indeed believe and hope for the resurrection to occur on the third day, and for it he prayed to the Father; yet he did not possess faith as a virtue or hope, because he had not an enigmatic and mirror-like but an utterly clear knowledge of it. He did not know it more perfectly as past than he understood it as future.

Christ nevertheless hoped, as he says in Psalm 30: “In you, Lord, I have hoped.” Yet he did not possess faith or hope as a virtue, because through direct vision he saw what he believed.

Of the ancient fathers, however, who were held in the underworld until the Passion, it may fittingly be said that they possessed faith and hope as virtues, because they believed and hoped that they would see God through direct vision, in the manner in which they did not then see him. For knowledge of God through direct vision was not open to them before Christ’s Passion; when that was completed, they passed from faith to direct vision.

## DISTINCTION XXVII. ON THE CHARITY BY WHICH GOD AND NEIGHBOR ARE LOVED, WHICH IS IN CHRIST AND IN US

1. Although Christ did not possess faith and hope, he nevertheless possessed love insofar as he was human—love so great that none greater can be. Out of surpassing charity he laid down his life for friends and enemies. For he had in his heart the charity which he displayed to us in deed, so that the example of this display might instruct us to love.

Here something must be said about charity, and about the manner and order of loving God and neighbor.

### What charity is

2. Charity is the love by which God is loved for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake, or in God. It has two commandments: one concerning the love of God, which is the greatest commandment in the Law; and the other concerning love of neighbor, which is like it.

The first is: “You shall love God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your soul,” written in Deuteronomy 6. The second is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets, Matthew 22. The end of the commandment is love; and it is twofold, namely love of God and love of neighbor.

### Whether God and neighbor are loved by the same charity

3. Here it is asked whether God is loved by the same love by which one’s neighbor is loved, or whether the love of God and that of neighbor are different loves.

Certainly the love by which God and neighbor are loved is one and the same: it is the Holy Spirit, as was said above, because God is charity. Hence Augustine:

> John says: “He cannot love God whom he does not see, who does not love the brother whom he sees.” But if he loved with spiritual charity the person whom he sees with human sight, he would see God, who is charity itself, by the inner sight by which he can be seen. Therefore, how can one who does not love the brother whom he sees love God, who is the love itself of which the person who does not love his brother is devoid?

We love God and neighbor by one and the same charity; but we love God for God’s sake, while we love ourselves and our neighbor for God’s sake. But if God’s charity and love of neighbor are one and the same, why is it called twofold? Because there are two beloved objects: God and neighbor. For although charity is one, it loves two different things, namely God and a human being or angel.

For this reason there are two commandments: although the same charity is commended by both, different things are commanded to be loved. Hence Augustine:

> I think that the Holy Spirit was given twice—once on earth and again from heaven—so that the two commandments of charity, namely love of God and love of neighbor, might be commended to us. Charity is one, and the commandments are two; the Spirit is one, and the gifts are two. For no charity loves the neighbor except that which loves God.

Thus we love God by the same charity by which we love our neighbor. But because God is one thing and neighbor another, although they are loved by one charity, perhaps the commandments are therefore said to be two, one greater and one lesser; or it is because two motions take place in the mind when God and neighbor are loved. The mind is moved to love God and also moved to love its neighbor, but much more toward God than toward neighbor. (Augustine, Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8, and in the sermon *On the Ascension*.)

### On the manner of loving

4. Next let us consider the manner of each love. This rule of love, says Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 25, was divinely established: that you love God for his own sake with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself—that is, unto that end and for that reason for which you ought to love yourself.

You ought to love yourself in the good and for God’s sake; therefore your neighbor must be loved in the good, not in evil, and for God’s sake. “Neighbor” must be understood to mean every human being, because there is no one with whom one ought to act wickedly.

Therefore one who loves human beings either because they are righteous or so that they may become righteous ought to love them in God or for God’s sake. So too one ought to love oneself in God or for God’s sake: that is, because one is righteous or so that one may become righteous.

For one who loves oneself otherwise loves oneself unjustly, because one loves oneself in order to be unjust—therefore in order to be evil; and so one no longer loves oneself. For “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul.”

Thus the manner of loving must be commanded to a person: namely, how one ought to love oneself so as to benefit oneself. But it is madness to doubt that one loves oneself and wishes to benefit oneself. The manner is prescribed when it says, “as yourself”: love your neighbor unto the end for which you love yourself.

If, therefore, you ought not to love yourself for your own sake, but for the sake of him in whom lies the most upright end of your love, let no other human being take offense if you love that person also for God’s sake.

Truth indicates the manner of this love when he says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you”—that is, unto the end for which I have loved you, namely, that you may be children and have life. (Augustine, Homily 65 on John, before the middle.)

### On the manner of loving God

5. The manner of loving God is indicated when it is said: “with all your heart,” that is, with all your understanding; “with all your soul,” that is, with all your will; “with all your mind,” that is, with your memory—so that you direct all thoughts, all your life, and all your understanding toward him from whom you have what you direct toward him.

In saying this, he left no part of our life that ought to be idle; whatever comes into the mind should be drawn to that place toward which the impulse of love runs. To love God for his own sake is the manner of loving God; and these, as some hold, are the two ways of loving God. (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 22.)

### On fulfilling that commandment

6. That commandment is not wholly fulfilled by a human being in this mortal life, but in part and not wholly, because we love in part, just as we know in part. But in the future it will be fulfilled wholly. Hence Augustine:

> [Col. 0813] Augustine, volume VII, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness, against Coelestius*, before the middle. While there remains any carnal concupiscence, God is not loved altogether with the whole soul. The flesh is said to desire only because the soul desires carnally. But when that which is perfect comes, so that that which is partial may be destroyed—that is, so that it may no longer be in part but wholly—charity will not be taken away but increased and fulfilled. In that fullness the commandment of charity will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. Then the righteous person will be without sin, because there will be no law resisting the mind. Then indeed you shall love God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind. This is the greatest commandment.

(Ibid., somewhat above.)

### The question why the commandment is given

7. But why is this perfection commanded to a human being when no one possesses it in this life? Because one does not run rightly if one does not know whither one ought to run. And how would this be known if it were not shown by commandments? (Ibid., at the earlier passage.)

Here, then, you have why this commandment is given even though it cannot be wholly fulfilled here. Yet it is fulfilled in part, namely according to the perfection of the way. For one perfection belongs to the person running, another to the person who has arrived. This commandment is fulfilled by the runner who loves God before all things and above all things, though the runner does not yet fulfill it completely. (Augustine, in the same work, somewhat below.)

### That one commandment is contained in the other  
(Augustine, Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 7)

8. Although there are two commandments of charity, one is often put for both, and not without reason, because neither God can be loved without neighbor nor neighbor without God. Hence the Apostle says that every commandment of the Law is summed up—that is, contained and fulfilled—in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

And Christ mentions love of neighbor more particularly when he says, John 13: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” Here the greater commandment, the love of God, seems to have been omitted. But those who understand rightly find both in each commandment: for one who loves God cannot despise the person whom God commanded to be loved; and one who loves a neighbor—what does that person love in the neighbor except God?

This is the love distinguished from every worldly love, which the Lord distinguished when he said, “As I have loved you.” For what did he love in us except God—not the God whom we possessed, but that we might possess him, as a physician loves the sick? And what does the physician love in them except the health which he desires to restore, not the illness which he came to drive out?

Thus let us also love one another, so that, as far as we can, we may mutually draw one another, through love, toward possessing God within us. (Augustine, volume IX, Tractate 65 on John 13, “A new commandment,” etc.)

### What ought to be loved with charity

9. But let us now inquire what ought to be loved with this love. For, as Augustine says, not all things which are to be used are to be loved, but only those which either are associated with us by a certain fellowship directed toward God, such as a human being or an angel; or which, being related to us, need our service through God’s benefit, such as the body. The body must be commanded to be loved so that it is cared for with order and prudence. (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 23, at the beginning.)

## DISTINCTION XXVIII. WHETHER BY THAT COMMANDMENT WE ARE ORDERED TO LOVE OUR WHOLE NEIGHBOR AND OUR WHOLE SELVES
1. Here it may be asked whether, in that commandment concerning love of neighbour, we are commanded to love the whole neighbour—that is, soul and body—and likewise our whole selves. To this we reply that every kind of thing to be loved is contained in those two commandments. For, as Augustine says in Book 1, chapter 23, of *On Christian Doctrine*, there are four things to be loved: one which is above us, namely God; another which we are, namely ourselves; a third which is beside us, namely our neighbour; and a fourth which is below us, namely the body. No commandments needed to be given concerning the second and fourth—that is, that we should love ourselves or our own body; but God and neighbour are commanded to be loved. For no commandment is needed in order that each person should love himself. However far a person falls away from truth, love of his own body remains to him, “for no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5). For righteous men who afflict their bodies do not hate the body, but its corruptions and its burden.

Here Augustine seems to teach that we are not bound by commandment to love ourselves or our own body. But if this is so, not every kind of thing to be loved is contained in those two commandments. For since we ought to love both ourselves and our body, what need was there for a commandment, when it is written in Psalm 10: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul”? But no special commandment concerning this was to be given; nor was it necessary to convey it by a separate commandment, that each should love himself or his body, because it is contained in that commandment: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” For there you ought to understand both the whole neighbour and your whole self.

Hence Augustine says in the same work, chapter 24: “If you love your whole self—that is, soul and body—and your neighbour, that is, soul and body (for a human being consists of soul and body), no class of things to be loved is omitted from these two commandments. For since love of God comes first, and the prescribed manner of loving him is apparent, and love of neighbour follows, nothing seems to have been said about love of yourself. But when it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself,’ love of yourself by yourself was not omitted at the same time” (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book 1, chapter 26).

See how he expressly says here that the commandment contains not only love of neighbour, but also love of oneself; and love of the whole neighbour and of the whole self. From this it appears that the statement concerning the second and fourth—that is, concerning love of ourselves and of our body—that no commandments were to be given, must be understood as meaning no special and separate commandments. For the whole is contained in that one commandment; and because we love, by natural law, both what we are and what is below us yet pertains to us—a law which exists even in beasts. Therefore we received distinct commandments concerning that which is above us and that which is beside us. In one of these commandments is contained love of what we are and of that which is below us.

The human mind is so constituted that it never fails to remember itself and never fails to love itself. Yet because one who hates someone strives to harm him, the human mind too is not improperly said to hate itself when it harms itself. For, without knowing it, it wills evil to itself when it does not think that what it wills harms it; nevertheless it wills evil to itself when it wills what harms it, according to Psalm 10: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul.” Therefore, whoever knows how to love himself loves God. But whoever does not love God does not love even himself, although this is naturally implanted in him; nevertheless he is not improperly said to hate himself when he does what is contrary to himself and pursues himself as though he were his own enemy.

### Whether love of the angels is contained in that commandment

2. Here a question also arises concerning angels: whether love of angels belongs to that commandment concerning love of neighbour. For the Lord showed, in the parable of the man left half-dead, that he excluded no human being when he commanded love of neighbour, calling him neighbour who acted mercifully toward that man. He then adds: “Go, and do likewise.” And we are to understand as neighbour one to whom an office of mercy must be rendered if he is in need, or would have to be rendered if he were in need.

Who does not see that no one is excluded to whom the office of mercy is not to be denied, when it is extended even to enemies by the Lord’s words: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you”? It is therefore clear that every human being is to be regarded as a neighbour. But the term “neighbour” is relative; and no one can be a neighbour except to a neighbour. It follows, therefore, that both the person to whom and the person by whom the office of mercy is to be rendered are rightly called neighbours.

It is thus clear that holy angels also are included in the commandment of love of neighbour, since they render us such great offices of mercy. Hence the Lord also willed to be called our neighbour, as he showed in the parable of the wounded man; and in the Prophet, Psalm 34: “As a neighbour and as our brother, so I was well-pleased.” But because the divine substance is more excellent and above our nature, the commandment concerning love of God is distinguished from love of neighbour. Therefore, although God bestows every benefit upon us, he is not included under the name of neighbour in that commandment; for we ought not to love him as ourselves, but more than ourselves, with all heart and soul.

Christ, however, insofar as he is human, must be loved as ourselves; and love for him according to his humanity is contained in that commandment. According to his humanity we ought to love him more than ourselves, but not as much as God; because, insofar as he is human, he is less than God.

### In what ways “neighbour” is said

3. Here it should be noted that “neighbour” is said in different ways: by the condition of original birth, by hope of conversion, by nearness of kinship, and by the relation involved in rendering a benefit.

## DISTINCTION XXIX. ON THE ORDER OF LOVE: WHAT SHOULD COME FIRST AND WHAT AFTERWARD

[Col. 0816]

1. After the foregoing, we must discuss the order of charity, because the bride says in Song of Songs 2: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar, and ordered charity within me.” Let us therefore consider what ought to be first and what afterward; for one sins who acts out of order. To know what one must do but not to know the order in which it must be done is not perfect knowledge. For ignorance of order disturbs the form of merits.

Augustine sets forth the order of love when he says in Book 1, chapter 27, of *On Christian Doctrine*: “A person has ordered love when he neither loves what ought not to be loved, nor fails to love what ought to be loved; nor loves equally what ought to be loved less or more, nor less or more what ought to be loved equally. Every sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; and every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake; but God for his own sake. God is to be loved for his own sake more than every human being, and each person ought to love God more than himself. Likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our own body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake; and a human being can enjoy God together with us, whereas our body cannot, because the body lives through the soul, through which we enjoy God.”

You have heard something concerning the order of charity: it is expressly stated that we ought to love God more than all human beings or ourselves, and the soul of another human being more than our own body. In the enumeration of the four objects of love given above, that which is above us is placed first; secondly, that which we are; thirdly, that which is beside us; fourthly, that which is below us. By the order of this enumeration, an order of loving seems to be indicated. It is not clear, however, whether we ought to love all human beings equally, and as much as ourselves, or less.

### Are all human beings to be loved equally?

2. Therefore a question is often raised on this point; it is made perplexing by the various statements of the saints. Some seem to teach that all are to be loved with equal affection, but that a distinction must be observed in effect—that is, in rendering service. Hence Augustine says in Book 1, chapter 28, of *On Christian Doctrine*: “All human beings are to be loved equally; but since you cannot benefit all, you must give chief care to those who, by opportunities of place, time, or any other circumstances, are more closely joined to you, as though by a certain lot. For you should regard it as your lot that someone is more closely attached to you in temporal circumstances; hence you choose rather to give to him.”

Likewise, on the Epistle to the Galatians: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith,” that is, Christians. Eternal life is to be desired for all with equal love, although the same offices of love cannot be shown to all. These should chiefly be shown to the brethren, because they are members of one another and have the same Father, namely God. On these and other testimonies rely those who say that all human beings are to be loved equally in the affection of charity, though differently in the rendering of works.

### Arguments which seem to oppose this

3. Against this stands the commandment of the Law concerning love of parents: “Honour your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth” (Deut. 5). Why, then, would this have been specially commanded concerning parents unless they were to be loved with greater love? But they say that this refers to outward rendering, in which parents are to be preferred. Hence he said “honour,” not “love.”
