There also stands against it what Jerome says on Ezekiel: namely, that according to the order of charity, as it is written in Song of Songs 2, “He ordered charity within me,” after God, the Father of all, one should also love one’s father according to the flesh, and mother, son and daughter, brother and sister. Ambrose also, explaining the order of love on the text, “He ordered charity within me,” says: “The charity of many is disordered: what is first, they place third or fourth. First God is to be loved; second, parents; then children; afterward members of the household,” [Col. 0817] “who, if they are good, are to be preferred to evil children. In accordance with this, in the Gospel he assigns what is proper to the love of each: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength, and your neighbour as yourself’; and enemies not with all one’s strength, nor as oneself, but simply. For it is enough that we love them and do not hate them.”

See how the preceding statements plainly indicate what distinction is to be maintained in the affection of charity: that we should love human beings with differing, not equal, affection—God before all; ourselves second; parents third; then children and brethren; afterward members of the household; and finally enemies. But those people say that what is said above about the order of love should be referred to the rendering of works, which ought to be shown differently to neighbours: first to parents, then to children, afterward to members of the household, and finally to enemies. God, however, is to be loved before all things both in affection and in the rendering of service.

### That some teach that neighbours ought to be loved as much as ourselves

4. Some of them also teach that neighbours are to be loved in the affection of charity as much as we love ourselves. They confirm this by Augustine’s authority, who says at the end of Book 8, chapter 8, of *On the Trinity*: “Let that question no longer trouble us: how much charity we ought to bestow upon a brother, and how much upon God. Incomparably more upon God than upon ourselves; but upon a brother as much as upon ourselves. Now we love ourselves all the more insofar as we love God more.”

From this and from the preceding testimonies of Augustine, they maintain that all human beings are to be loved equally by us and as much as ourselves; but God more than ourselves, and our body less than ourselves or our neighbours. Nor do they say that an order of loving is assigned in the foregoing enumeration of things to be loved, but only the things which are to be loved.

### According to others, not all are to be loved with equal affection

5. But because Ambrose’s preceding words seem, to careful readers, to explain an order of loving according to affection rather than according to effect, others—not without learning—say that a differing order has been established not only in the performance of works but also in the affection of charity: so that before all we love God; second, ourselves; third, parents; fourth, children or brethren and the like; afterward members of the household; and finally enemies.

Augustine’s statement that all are to be loved equally and that eternal life is to be desired for all with equal love can be understood such that equality refers not to affection but to the good wished for them: for in charity we ought to wish for all that they may merit equal goods. Thus the Apostle says in 2 Corinthians 7: “I wish all human beings to be as myself.” The perfection of those greater than themselves is to be desired for the lesser, so that they too may become perfect and thus merit equal blessedness. Or “with equal love” means that all are to be loved with the same kind of love.

Likewise, his statement that we ought to love brethren as much as ourselves can be understood to mean that we should love brethren toward as great a good as ourselves: that we should wish them as great an eternal good as we wish for ourselves, though not with as great an affection. Or there *as much as* denotes likeness, not quantity.

### The question concerning good and evil parents: how they are to be loved

6. It is also commonly asked whether, if our parents, children, or brethren are evil, they are to be loved more or less than other good people who are not joined to us by this tie. It seems that good persons not joined to us by flesh ought to be loved more than evil persons joined to us by flesh but united to us by the glue of charity in the heart. For the union of hearts is holier than that of bodies. Hence Bede, on the Lord’s words in Matthew 2, “My mother and my brethren are those who do the word of God,” says: “He does not neglect his mother wrongfully, nor is his mother denied, since she is acknowledged even from the cross; but the bonds of minds are shown to be more religious than those of bodies.”

Nevertheless, this is a difficult question, and we must not resolve it fully here as we hasten to other matters. For we are moved by those words in which he commands that enemies be loved not with all one’s strength nor as oneself, but simply: “It is enough that we love them and do not hate them.” This should not be understood as though it were enough for you to love an enemy, but not as yourself, [Col. 0818] since you ought to love all, both friends and enemies, as yourself. Rather, to show the degrees of loving God, neighbour, and enemy—who is nevertheless a neighbour—the Lord uses distinct expressions when he says, in Matthew 22: “You shall love God with all your strength, and your neighbour as yourself.” He does not say, “with all your strength,” in order to show that a neighbour is to be loved less than God. He also says, in Luke 6: “Love your enemies”; but he adds neither “with all your strength” nor “as yourself,” but says it simply. For it is enough that we love them and do not hate them—that is, it is enough to say that we should love them and not hate them—not because we ought not to love them as ourselves, since they are neighbours, but because it is enough if we love them less than other neighbours, as this manner of speaking suggests.

### Augustine’s question in the *Retractations* (Book 1, chapter 10, middle)

7. It is also commonly asked why the Lord commanded us to love enemies when elsewhere he commands us to hate parents and children (Luke 14). We must say in reply that two things are to be loved in a human being: nature and virtue; but vice and sin are to be hated. Therefore parents, insofar as they are evil, are to be hated; and enemies, insofar as they are human beings, are to be loved. Let us then love enemies so that they may be gained for the kingdom of God, and hate relatives if they hinder us from the kingdom of God; and in all alike let us love the nature which God made.

### On the degrees of charity

8. It should also be known that there are different degrees of charity: charity beginning, advancing, perfect, more perfect, and most perfect. Hence Augustine, in the fifth tractate on the Catholic Epistle of John, shortly before the middle, says: “This is perfect charity: that someone should be ready even to die for the brethren. But is it wholly perfect as soon as it is born? No: it is born in order to be perfected; once born, it is nourished; once nourished, it is strengthened; once strengthened, it is perfected; when it has reached perfection, it says, ‘I desire to be dissolved,’ etc.” (Phil. 1).

Here the progress and perfection of charity are plainly indicated. Truth itself also commends that perfection, saying in John 15: “No one has greater love than this, that one should lay down his life for his friends.” This was certainly said of the work of love, since no effect of love is greater than to lay down one’s life for others. Nor should the words “for his friends” trouble you: whoever lays down his life for friends lays it down also for enemies, so that they may become friends.

## DISTINCTION XXX. WHETHER IT IS BETTER TO LOVE FRIENDS THAN ENEMIES, OR THE REVERSE

1. Here it is commonly asked which is preferable and of greater merit: to love friends or to love enemies. But this comparison is entangled. If love of friends alone is compared with love of both friends and enemies, the resolution is clear. But if one asks, in a single person who simultaneously loves friend and enemy, which of these comes first, the answer is obscure. For it concerns a movement of the mind, regarding which judgment is not easy for us: whether there is one and the same movement toward friend and enemy, but more intense toward the friend; or two movements, one toward the enemy, called more difficult, and the other toward the friend, seeming more fervent. It is not improperly thought that the more fervent one is better. Or if it is one and the same movement, it is not wrongly judged stronger where it is more ardent.

Augustine nevertheless seems, in chapter 73 of the *Enchiridion*, to hold that loving an enemy is greater than loving a friend, because he says that loving enemies and doing them good belongs to the perfect; and that this is not fulfilled by as great a multitude as is heard in the Lord’s Prayer when it is said in Matthew 6: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” For he says that this promise is fulfilled by many who do not yet love enemies. He says:

“It is a great thing to be kindly disposed and beneficent toward one who has done you no harm; but it is much greater, and belongs to the most magnificent goodness, that you should also love your enemy, and toward one who wishes you evil and, if able, does it, should always will and do whatever good you can, hearing Jesus say in Matthew 5: ‘Love your enemies [Col. 0819] and do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you.’ But although this belongs to the perfect sons of God, toward which every believer ought to stretch himself and bring the human mind, by praying to God and by striving and wrestling with himself, to this disposition; nevertheless, because so great a good does not belong to as great a multitude as we believe is heard when it is said in prayer, ‘Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors,’ without doubt the words of this promise are fulfilled if a person who has not yet advanced so far as to love an enemy nevertheless, when asked by someone who has sinned against him to forgive him, forgives him from the heart—he who wishes to be forgiven himself when he prays and says, ‘as we forgive our debtors.’ Whoever asks forgiveness from a person against whom he has sinned, if he is moved by his sin to ask, is not yet to be counted an enemy, so that it should be difficult to love him, as he was when he was practising hostilities. But whoever does not forgive one who asks and repents must not suppose that his own sins are forgiven by the Lord, because Truth cannot lie. After teaching the prayer, Truth commended this sentence placed within it, saying in Matthew 6: ‘If you forgive people their sins, your Father will forgive you also. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your sins.’”

Here it seems to be maintained, as we have already said, that it is a greater virtue to love an enemy and do him good than to love one who has done us no harm, or a friend. If someone refuses to grant this simply, saying, “A friend is loved more intensely than an enemy, and therefore that love is greater than this,” let him determine the matter according to the preceding interpretation, saying that the comparison there is between the love by which a friend alone is loved and that by which both friend and enemy are loved.

But what follows moves us more: namely, that he says the number of those who love enemies is not as great as the number heard when it is said, “Forgive us our debts,” etc. Here he gives us to understand that sins are forgiven by God to someone who does not love an enemy, if he nevertheless forgives a brother who asks and has sinned against him. But since sins are not forgiven to an adult unless he has charity, it follows that a person who does not love an enemy has charity. How, then, is every human being understood under the name of neighbour in the commandment, “You shall love your neighbour as yourself”? For if every human being is a neighbour, then an enemy is also a neighbour; therefore we are commanded to love enemies. And because that commandment is general for all, we are commanded to love all human beings, even enemies.

Some, wishing to maintain simply what is said here, qualify that commandment, saying that the perfect are commanded to love every human being, even an enemy, whereas this is counsel for the less mature. They say that the less mature are commanded to love those who have done them no harm and not to hate enemies. But it is better understood that all are commanded by that precept to love everyone, even enemies; the authorities given above and many others support this interpretation.

The last statement of Augustine must be understood as spoken of perfect charity, which belongs only to the perfect: they not only love friends but love enemies perfectly and do them good. This perfection of love does not belong to as great a multitude as is heard in the Lord’s Prayer; and it is indeed a great thing and a mark of exceptional goodness to love an enemy perfectly. Thus, when he says that the words of that promise are fulfilled by one who has not advanced so far as to love an enemy, this must be understood of perfect love.

## DISTINCTION XXXI. WHETHER CHARITY, ONCE POSSESSED, IS LOST

1. Nor should this be passed over: some assert that charity, once possessed by someone, cannot fail, and that no person to be damned ever possesses it. They support this teaching with the following testimonies. The Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 13: “Charity never fails.” Augustine also says:

> [Note: [Col. 0819] Augustine, *To Count Julian*; also found in *On Penance*, distinction, chapter 2.]

“Charity which can be abandoned was never true.” Likewise: “Charity [Col. 0820] is the proper and singular fountain of good things, in which no stranger shares. All who will hear, ‘I never knew you’ (Matt. 7), are strangers. Scripture says of this fountain, Proverbs 5: ‘Let the fountain of living water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you.’ But if those who will hear that voice are strangers, then those to be damned do not share in this fountain.”

Likewise Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 0820] Volume 9, tractate 8 on chapter 4 of the Epistle of John, after the middle, on Song of Songs 8.]

“Charity is rooted: be secure; no evil can proceed from it.”

Likewise Gregory says in the *Morals*: “Love is strong as death. Love is compared to the power of death because it utterly kills, from love of the world, the mind which it has once seized.”

Likewise Augustine, Volume 9, in the first tractate on the Epistle of John, at the end: “The invisible anointing is charity, which, in whomever it is found, will be a root for him. It cannot wither in the burning sun; it is nourished by the sun’s heat and does not wither.”

Likewise Bede, on John, chapter 1: “It must be asked how it could be a special sign of recognizing the Son of God that the Spirit descended upon him and remained. What great thing is it for the Son of God that the Spirit is said to remain in him? It should be noted that the Spirit always remained in the Lord; but among the saints, so long as they bear a mortal body, he remains in part continually, and in part departs in order to return. He remains with them so that they may apply themselves to good works; but he withdraws for a time, so that they may not always have the power to heal the weak, raise the dead, cast out demons, or prophesy. Thus he remains continually so that they may possess virtues, so that they themselves may live wonderfully; he comes for a time so that they may also shine forth to others, by signs of miracles, as to what they are inwardly.”

Likewise Gregory, Homily 5 on Ezekiel: “In the hearts of the saints, the Spirit always remains according to certain virtues; according to others, he comes intending to depart and departs intending to come. In those virtues without which life cannot be attained, he remains in the hearts of his elect. But in those through which the power of holiness is displayed, as in the performance of miracles, he is sometimes present and sometimes withdraws.”

Likewise Ambrose, in the *Morals*, on the Epistle to the Romans: “Charity is feigned if it abandons one in adversity.”

These statements appear to suggest that charity, once possessed, is not lost. Therefore some have rushed into the previously mentioned audacity, saying that charity is not possessed by those to be damned and cannot be lost by anyone who has possessed it. But reason and authority refute them. For some are good for a time and afterward become evil, and conversely. Hence Christ says that the names of some were written in the book of life, though they afterward went back. But he calls them written not according to foreknowledge, but according to their present righteousness, which they then served; because they were then worthy of that good which those foreknown to possess it are recorded as having.

Hence Ambrose says:

> [Note: [Col. 0820] Volume 4, on chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans, on the passage, “Because the elder shall serve the younger.”]

“Grace was given to some for use, as to Saul and Judas, and to those disciples to whom the Lord said in Luke 10: ‘Behold, your names are written in heaven’; and afterward they went back. But he said this because of the righteousness which they served, because they were good. For often those who will be good are first evil; and sometimes those who will become and remain evil are first good. For this reason they are said to be written in the book of life and to be erased.”

### Explanation of the foregoing authorities

2. But the Apostle’s statement, “Charity never fails,” does not help them at all. Displaying the dignity of charity, he says that it does not fail because it will exist here and in the future; whereas faith, hope, and knowledge will be brought to an end. Likewise, the statement that charity which can be abandoned was never true refers not to the essence of charity but to its effect: charity which is abandoned does not make a person truly blessed or bring him to the true good.

Strangers—that is, those to be damned—do not share in this fountain at the end, because they do not persevere. Yet this and the other things said about charity can also be understood of perfect charity, which only the perfect possess and which, once possessed, is not lost. But the beginnings of charity sometimes grow and sometimes fail; for there are beginnings of virtue, progress, and advancement. The one who understands that parable distinguishes these degrees: “The kingdom of God is as if a man should cast seed into the ground and sleep, and rise, and the seed should sprout and grow,” etc. (Mark 4).

Therefore, if perfect charity is so rooted that it cannot be lost, charity which is beginning or advancing can nevertheless be lost, and is often lost. But while it is possessed, it does not allow its possessor to commit mortal sin. Augustine shows this when he says: “Since covetousness is the root of all evils and charity the root of all goods” (1 Tim. 6), “they cannot both exist at the same time; unless one has been uprooted, the other cannot be planted. Someone strives in vain to cut off the branches if he does not also strive to uproot the root.”

### Why faith, hope, and knowledge are said to be brought to an end, but not charity, although charity too is partial

3. It must also be observed how faith, hope, and knowledge are said to be brought to an end because they are partial, while charity is not, although it too is partial. For we love partially—that is, imperfectly—just as we know partially, as Hesychius says on Leviticus. Since, then, everything partial is brought to an end, why is charity excepted, when it is said never to fail?

Charity too is partial, as the saints often teach, because we now love partially. Therefore it too will be brought to an end insofar as it is partial, because imperfection will be removed and perfection added. Charity itself will remain, increased, together with its act and manner of loving: namely, that you love God for his own sake with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself. But the manner of imperfection will be eliminated. Faith and hope, however, will be utterly brought to an end. Knowledge, in its present act and manner, will be removed, but not in its own essence. For the virtue of knowledge itself will remain, though it will have a different use and manner.

### Whether Christ observed the prescribed order of charity

4. It remains now to inquire whether Christ, insofar as he was human, observed the prescribed order of loving. If so, he loved every human being as himself. Therefore he wished life for all and willed all to be saved; yet not all are saved, and so what he wished has not come to pass.

But it must not be overlooked that in him charity existed according to the manner of the homeland, not of the wayfarer’s path; and that he fulfilled the order of love observed in the homeland, not on the way. For those who are in the homeland—that is, who have already been made blessed—are so devoted to God’s righteousness that nothing pleases them except what pleases God. Accordingly, they love and will the salvation only of those whom God wills to be saved, and love them alone as themselves. Thus Christ too loved only the elect as himself and desired their salvation.

## DISTINCTION XXXII. ON GOD’S CHARITY

1. To the foregoing must be added something concerning God’s love, by which he loves us; and this is none other than that by which we love him. God’s love, moreover, has been seen to be divine; and by the same love the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit love themselves and us, as we discussed above. And although his love is immutable and eternal, he nevertheless loves one more and another less.

Hence Augustine says: “God’s love is incomprehensible and immutable: by it God loves in each of us what he has made, just as he hates what we have made. Thus, in a wonderful and divine way, even when he hates, he loves us.” This may indeed be understood of all. Who, then, can worthily express how greatly he loves the members of his Only-begotten Son, and how much more he loves the Only-begotten himself?

It is also said of him in Wisdom 11: “You hate none of the things which you have made.” From these statements it is understood that God loves all his creatures, because it is written, “You hate none of the things which you have made”; and likewise, in Genesis 1: “God saw all the things which he had made, and they were very good.” If all that he made is good, and he loves every good, then he loves all that he made. And among these he loves rational creatures more; and among them, still more those who are members of his Only-begotten Son; and the Only-begotten himself far more than all.

### In what sense he is said to love this or that more or less

[Col. 0822]

2. But since God’s love is immutable and therefore is neither intensified nor diminished, if it is asked why he is said to love this more and that less, and why he is said to love everything, we say that God’s love, like peace, surpasses all human understanding, so that human understanding can scarcely rise at all to grasp such exalted things.

Nevertheless, it may be understood that God is said to love all the things he has made because he approves them all insofar as they are his works. Nor did they please him then, or before, or more, when they were made—that is, before they came to be; rather, from eternity all pleased him, no less than after they began to exist. But when he is said to love some rational creatures—that is, human beings or angels—more and others less, this does not signify mutability in his charity, but that he loved some for greater goods and others for lesser; some for better uses and others for less good uses. For all our goods come to us from his love.

Therefore from eternity he loved, and even now loves, some of the elect more and others less, because in his love he prepared greater goods for some and lesser goods for others; and in time he bestows greater goods upon some and lesser upon others. Hence he is said to love these or those more or less.

### That God’s love must be considered in two ways

3. God’s love is considered in two ways: according to essence and according to effect. According to essence it admits neither more nor less, but only according to effect; so that those are called more loved for whom he prepared a greater good in his love from eternity and grants it in time, and those less loved for whom he does not prepare and grant so much.

For the same reason, when some are converted and justified, they are said then to begin to be loved by God—not because God can love anyone with a new love. Rather, with eternal love he loved before the foundation of the world all whom he loves. But they are said then to begin to be loved by him when they receive the effect of God’s eternal love, namely grace or glory.

Hence Augustine says in Book 5, chapter 16, of *On the Trinity*: “Far be it that God should love anyone temporally, as with a new love which was not previously in him; for with him past things have not passed away, and future things are already done. Thus he loved all his saints before the foundation of the world, just as he predestined them. But when they are converted and find him, they are said then to begin to be loved by him, so that this may be said in a way capable of being grasped by human feeling.”

Likewise, when he is said to be angry with the evil and gracious toward the good, they change, not he; just as light is harsh to weak eyes and gentle to sound eyes, by their change, not by its own. Thus, when someone begins through justification to be God’s friend, that person changes, not God.

### Whether someone is loved by God more or less at one time than at another

4. But if it is asked of someone whether he is loved by God more at one time than at another, the meaning of love must be distinguished. If it is referred to the effect of love, this may be granted; but if to the essence of love, it must be denied.

### Whether God loved the reprobate from eternity
5. But concerning the reprobate, who are prepared not for life but for death, if it is asked whether one ought to grant that God loved them from eternity: we say that this is to be granted without qualification only of the elect—that God loved from eternity those whom he prepared for righteousness and for the crown. But of the non-elect, it is to be granted without qualification that he hated them, that is, reprobated them; as is read in Malachi 1: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” Yet it must not be said without qualification that he loved them, lest they be understood to be predestined; but with an addition it may be granted: he loved them insofar as they were to be his work—that is, such persons as, and the persons whom, he was going to make.

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. ON THE FOUR PRINCIPAL VIRTUES

1. After the foregoing, we must discuss the four virtues called principal or cardinal, namely [Col. 0823] justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance. Concerning these Augustine says, in *On the Trinity*, book 14, chapter 9:

> Justice consists in helping the distressed; prudence, in guarding against snares; fortitude, in enduring hardships; temperance, in restraining depraved pleasures.

Of these it is said in the Book of Wisdom, chapter 8: “She teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and truth.” By sobriety he means temperance, and by truth he means fortitude. These are called cardinal virtues, as Jerome says, by means of which one lives well in this mortal life and afterwards attains eternal life. They were and are present most fully in Christ, from whose fullness we have received. In him they had the same functions that they have in the homeland, and also certain functions belonging to the way.

Nevertheless, whether these virtues—which begin to exist in the mind, though the mind was still a mind before it possessed them—cease to exist when they have brought it to eternal things, is a question of some difficulty. Some have thought that they will cease; and, indeed, when this is said of three of them—prudence, fortitude, and temperance—it seems to have some plausibility. Justice, however, is immortal; and when we live blessedly in the contemplation of the divine nature—which created all other natures and established them—justice will be perfected in us rather than cease to be. Nothing is better or more lovable than that nature; and to be subject to it as ruler is the part of justice. Therefore justice is altogether immortal, nor will it cease in that blessedness; rather, it will be such and so great that it cannot be more perfect or greater.

Perhaps the other three virtues also will exist in that happiness: prudence, with no longer any danger of error; fortitude, with no suffering to endure from evils; and temperance, with no resistance of lusts. Thus prudence there will consist in preferring or equating no good with God; fortitude, in clinging to him most firmly; temperance, in taking delight in no harmful defect. But what justice now does in aiding the distressed, prudence in avoiding snares, fortitude in enduring hardships, and temperance in restraining depraved pleasures, will not exist at all there, where there will be no evil. These functions of the virtues, therefore, necessary for this mortal life—as is faith, to which they must be referred—will belong to things past.

Here Augustine states plainly, at the beginning of *On the Trinity*, book 14, chapter 9, that the aforesaid virtues will exist in the future, though they will then have functions other than those they have now. Bede agrees with him in his commentary on Exodus, chapter 26, saying:

> The pillars before which the veil was stretched are the powers of heaven, illustrious in four outstanding virtues: fortitude, prudence, temperance, and justice. These are maintained otherwise in heaven by angels and holy souls than here by the faithful.

Bede then assigns the functions of those virtues according to the present and future states, following Augustine in the assignments given above.

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. ON THE SEVEN GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

1. We must now treat of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. First we must consider whether these gifts are virtues; second, whether they will cease in the future, either all of them or any of them; and then whether all these gifts were present in Christ.

Ambrose shows that these gifts are virtues and will not cease in the future, calling them seven virtues and saying that they are present most abundantly in angels. Thus in *On the Holy Spirit*, book 1, chapter 20 and the last chapter, at the beginning of the chapter:

> That heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God, is not washed by the channel of any earthly river. Rather, the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the fountain of life—of whom we are satisfied by a brief draught—seems to flow forth more abundantly in those heavenly spirits, boiling over in a full stream of seven spiritual virtues. For if a river, overflowing the raised banks of its channels, floods over, how much more does the Holy Spirit, surpassing creation, gladden that heavenly nature of the angels with a more copious abundance of sanctifications, when he touches the secret places of our mind as though they were lower regions!

Then, explaining “sanctifications,” he adds a little below:

> By these sanctifications is signified the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues, which Isaiah enumerates, saying, in chapter 11: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.”

[Col. 0824] Therefore, the Holy Spirit is one river, but there are many streams of spiritual gifts. Although many spirits are spoken of, such as the spirit of wisdom and understanding, and so forth, there is nevertheless one Spirit of God, 1 Corinthians 12, the disposer of his own freedom, distributing all things to each person according to the authority of his will.

Here it is expressly taught that the seven gifts are virtues and sanctifications of faithful minds, and that they will not cease in the future, since they are also in angels.

### That those seven gifts were in Christ

2. Isaiah also shows that these same gifts were in Christ, saying in chapter 11:

> A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.

### What seems to conflict with the foregoing

3. Yet what Bede says on the fear of the Lord in his commentary on Proverbs seems to conflict with this—namely, that every fear will cease in the future. For he says, on that passage, Proverbs 17, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom”:

> There are two fears of the Lord: servile fear, which is the beginning of wisdom, and friendly fear, which accompanies the perfection of wisdom. Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom because one who begins to be wise after wrongdoing is first corrected by divine fear, lest he be punished; but perfect charity casts this fear out, 1 John 4. Holy fear of the Lord succeeds it, remaining for ever and ever, Psalm 18; charity does not exclude this fear, but increases it. By it a son fears lest he offend, even in the smallest matter, the eyes of his most loving father. Both will cease in the future; but charity never fails.

But Augustine, commenting on Psalm 5, “I shall worship toward your holy temple in your fear,” says that the fear of God will cease:

> The fear of the Lord is a great safeguard for those advancing toward salvation, but it is cast out in those who have arrived. For they no longer fear a friend, when they have been brought to that which was promised.

These authorities signify that fear will not exist in the future. But if fear will not exist in the future, then neither will the seven gifts exist, nor do they now exist in angels or in holy souls.

In resolving the apparent contradiction of the foregoing authorities, we say that those seven gifts are now in angels and in holy souls living in blessedness, and will be in us in the future; but they will not all have the functions or offices which they now have. For example, filial fear now makes us fear lest we offend the one whom we love and lest we be separated from him; it also makes us revere him. In the future, however, it will make us revere him, when we shall not fear separation or offense. Therefore the fear of separation or offense is not now in angels or holy souls, nor will it be in us in the future; but reverence will be: reverence mingled with the submission of love. This was also in Christ, as the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, speaking of Christ, chapter 5: “He was heard because of his reverence.” Some nevertheless contend that fear in Christ and in angels exists only according to its effect.

### A full distinction of fears

4. Since the occasion has arisen to treat of fear, it must be known that there are four fears: worldly or human fear; servile fear; initial fear; and chaste, filial, or friendly fear.

Worldly fear, as Cassiodorus says on Psalm 127, occurs when we fear suffering bodily dangers or losing worldly goods, and because of this commit sin. This fear is evil; it is abandoned with the world at the first stage. The Lord forbids it in the Gospel, saying, Matthew 10 and Luke 12: “Do not fear those who kill the body,” and so forth.

Servile fear, however, as Augustine says on Psalm 127, is when a person refrains from sin through fear of hell. By it he fears the presence of the Judge and punishments, and does whatever good he does from fear—not from fear of losing the eternal good which he does not love, but from fear of suffering the evil which he dreads. He does not fear losing the embraces of the most beautiful Bridegroom; he fears being cast into hell. This fear is good and useful, though insufficient. Through it a habit of righteousness gradually arises, and initial fear succeeds it, when that which was hard begins to be loved. Thus servile fear begins to be excluded by charity. Chaste or friendly fear then succeeds it, by which we fear lest the Bridegroom delay, depart, be offended, or be lost to us. This fear comes from love. Servile fear is indeed useful, but does not remain forever; and this divine fear is a companion through all the stages.

### Collection of the foregoing

5. Notice that four fears are distinguished here, whereas above Bede said that there are two. But Bede omitted worldly fear, and under the name “servile” included the two which we have here distinguished: servile and initial fear. He called friendly fear chaste.

Augustine likewise plainly distinguishes servile and chaste fear when he expounds the passage in Romans 8, “For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as children of God,” saying:

> Two fears are indicated here: one which is in perfect charity, namely chaste fear; the other which is not in charity, namely servile fear. In the latter, although one believes God, one nevertheless does not believe in God; and although one does what is good, one nevertheless does not do it well. For no one does well unwillingly, even if what one does is good.

### He treats more fully of chaste and servile fear, sometimes touching on initial fear

6. Augustine discusses these same fears more fully, saying:

> Someone begins to believe in the day of judgment; if he begins to believe, he also begins to fear. But because he still fears, he does not yet have confidence on the day of judgment; for perfect charity is not yet in him. But if perfect charity were in him, he would not fear. For perfect charity would produce perfect righteousness, and he would have no basis for fear; indeed, he would have something like a desire for iniquity to pass away and for the kingdom of God to come. Therefore fear is not in charity. But in what charity? Not in charity that has begun. In which, then? In perfect charity. Therefore perfect charity casts fear out. Let fear begin, then, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” For fear, as it were, prepares a place for charity. But once charity begins to dwell there, the fear which prepared a place for it is driven out. For as charity increases, fear decreases; and as charity becomes more inward, fear is cast out. Greater charity, less fear; lesser charity, greater fear. But if there is no fear at all, there is no way for charity to enter. Just as we see thread introduced by a bristle when something is being sewn: the bristle enters first, and unless it comes out, the thread does not follow. So fear first occupies the mind; but fear does not remain there, because it entered in order to introduce charity.

### What seems contrary to the foregoing

7. There is, however, another statement which appears contrary to this, if it does not have a devout interpreter. For Psalm 18 says: “The chaste fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever.” It shows us a certain eternal fear—but chaste fear. Now, if it shows us eternal fear, does this Epistle, 2 John 4, contradict it when it says: “Fear is not in charity; but perfect charity casts fear out”? The former was spoken through John, the latter through David. But do not suppose the Spirit to be different. If one breath fills two pipes, can one Spirit not fill two hearts and move two tongues? If two pipes, filled with one spirit—that is, one breath—sound in harmony, can two tongues filled with the Spirit of God sound discordantly? Indeed, there is a certain harmony there, a certain concord; but it requires an attentive rather than an idle hearer.

Behold, the Spirit of God moved two tongues. From one we heard: “Fear is not in charity”; from the other we heard: “The chaste fear of the Lord remains for ever and ever.” What is this? Do they disagree? No. Clear your ears; attend to the melody. It is not without reason that “chaste” was added here but not added there. For there is a fear called chaste, and another not called chaste. Let us distinguish these two fears and understand the harmony of the pipes. How do we distinguish them? Let your charity attend.

There are people who fear God because they may be sent to hell, perhaps to burn with the devil in eternal fire. This is the fear which introduces charity, but it comes in such a way as to go out. For if you fear God because of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you thus fear; you do not desire good things, but avoid evil things. Yet because you avoid evils, you correct yourself and begin to desire good things. And once you begin to desire good things, chaste fear will be in you. What is chaste fear? To fear lest you lose those very good things any further; to fear God lest he depart from you. But when you fear God lest his presence abandon you, you embrace him and desire to enjoy him. (Augustine, *Tractates on the Epistle of John*, tractate 9, vol. 6.)

### He shows by the comparison of two women how the two fears differ

8. You cannot explain better the difference between these two fears than by imagining two married women. Let one wish to commit adultery but fear being condemned by her husband. She fears her husband because she still loves wickedness; her husband’s presence is not welcome but burdensome to her, and, if she perhaps lives wickedly, she fears that her husband may come. Such are those who fear the day of judgment.

Make the other love her husband and owe him chaste embraces, wishing to stain herself with no adulterous impurity. She desires her husband’s presence. The first fears, and the second fears. Let them now be asked why they fear. The first will say: “I fear my husband lest he come.” The second will say: “I fear my husband lest he depart.” The first will say: “I fear my husband lest he condemn me.” The second will say: “I fear my husband lest he abandon me.”

Place these things in the mind, and you will find the fear which charity casts out, and the other, chaste fear which remains for ever and ever. Perfect charity casts out that fear because it has torment: the conscience of sins is tormented, and justification has not yet taken place. There is something there to tickle the mind, to prick it, to spur it on. That fear spurs; but charity enters, healing what fear wounds. Chaste fear produces security in the mind.

We have heard two pipes, John and David, sounding in harmony. The former speaks of the fear of God by which the soul fears being condemned; the latter of the fear by which the soul fears being abandoned. The former is the fear which charity excludes; the latter is the fear which remains for ever and ever. [Note: [Col. 0826] Augustine, same tractate; and vol. 2, Epistle 120, to Honoratus, *On the Grace of the New Testament*, chapter 21.]

In these preceding words Augustine plainly shows what chaste fear is, what servile fear is, and how they differ. He also indicates initial fear, which is neither entirely servile nor entirely chaste, but, as it were, intermediate: it has something of servile fear and something of chaste fear. For it makes one serve partly from fear of punishment and partly from love of righteousness, by which we fear punishment and fear to offend. This fear is in charity that has begun, not in perfect charity. And as charity increases, this fear decreases with respect to fear of punishment—that is, with respect to that which makes one fear punishment and with respect to the torment of conscience. For the more we love, the less we fear.

This fear is indicated in Augustine’s words where he does not deny that fear is in charity that has begun, but only in perfect charity. This could not be said of servile fear, because, as he himself said above, servile fear does not remain when charity comes; nor does charity enter unless that fear first goes out. Nor does anyone in that fear believe in God, even though he believes God; nor does he act well, even if what he does is good. Therefore that fear is not in even incipient charity, because everyone who has charity, though not perfect charity, both believes in God and performs good works. Therefore the fear which Augustine granted to exist in incipient charity, and which he said decreases as charity grows, is not servile fear, but initial fear—which he denies to be in charity only when that charity is perfect.

### That servile and initial fear are called the beginning of wisdom, but differently

9. It must nevertheless be known that each fear—servile and initial—is called in different passages of Scripture, Proverbs 1 and 9 and Ecclesiasticus 1, “the beginning of wisdom.” You will find this to be so if you carefully observe the passages of Scripture in which the fear of the Lord is mentioned. Yet servile fear is called the beginning of wisdom for one reason and initial fear for another.

Servile fear is called the beginning of wisdom because it prepares a place for wisdom [Col. 0827] and leads to wisdom; yet it does not remain with wisdom, but instead goes out. Initial fear, however, is called the beginning of wisdom because it is in wisdom that has begun: when someone begins to have it, he begins to have wisdom and charity. Hence each fear is also sometimes called initial, as you may find in various passages of Scripture.

Each fear is also sometimes called servile, because initial fear itself, which is in charity that has begun, contains something servile—namely anxiety about punishment—just as it contains something chaste, namely fear of offending and of being separated.

### On Augustine’s statement that chaste fear is eternal

10. We must also carefully note that Augustine says above that chaste fear is eternal. This confirms the foregoing position: namely, that the spirit of fear will exist in the future, like the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, but will not have every function which it now has. For it will then make us revere God, not fear separation from him or deprivation of him. That fear was therefore also in Christ, but according to the function it will have in the future among the saints. For Christ did not fear separation from God or offense against God, but revered God above all things.

### Whether the fear of punishment which was in Christ was servile, initial, or another kind

11. Since fear of punishment was in Christ, the question arises whether this fear was worldly, servile, or initial. We say that none of these was in Christ, because worldly fear is evil, as was said above, and is abandoned with the world at the first stage; while servile or initial fear is not present in perfect charity. Therefore none of these fears was in Christ.

What, then, was the fear by which he feared punishment? That fear may be called natural or human fear, which is present in all human beings and by which death is dreaded and punishment feared. This fear is called natural not because it came to human beings from nature as it was first established—for that fear was not joined to human beings, nor was it among their natural goods—but because it comes to all from nature corrupted through sin, in which corruption has become ingrained as though it were natural; and this fear is an effect of sin, as was stated above.

## DISTINCTION XXXV. HOW WISDOM AND KNOWLEDGE DIFFER

1. After the foregoing, we must carefully consider how wisdom differs from knowledge. Augustine says of this in the middle of *On the Trinity*, book 14, chapter 1:

> Philosophers, discussing wisdom, defined it by saying: “Wisdom is knowledge of divine and human things.” I too do not deny that the knowledge of both kinds of things—that is, divine and human—may be called both wisdom and knowledge. But according to the Apostle’s distinction, 1 Corinthians 12, where he says, “To one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” this definition must be divided, so that the knowledge of divine things is properly called wisdom, whereas the knowledge of human things properly receives the name of knowledge.

> Yet I do not assign to this knowledge whatever can be known by a human being in human matters, where there is a great deal of superfluous vanity and harmful curiosity. I assign only that by which the most health-giving faith which leads to true blessedness is generated, nourished, defended, and strengthened. Very many faithful persons do not possess this knowledge, although they possess faith itself to a great degree. For it is one thing merely to know what a person ought to believe in order to attain the blessed life; it is another to know how this very thing may assist the devout or be defended against the impious. This is properly called knowledge.

Concerning these same two virtues Augustine also, in *Enchiridion*, chapter 2, setting out their difference on the Psalm, says:

> Wisdom differs in some way from knowledge, as holy Job testifies. Defining each in some manner, he says, chapter 28: “Wisdom is piety; knowledge, however, is abstaining from evils.” Here he uses piety to mean the worship of God, which in Greek is called *theosebeia* (Θεοσέβεια). It consists in knowing and loving that which always exists and remains unchangeably: God. But abstaining from evils is prudently living in the midst of a depraved generation.

Likewise, plainly distinguishing these two, he says in *On the Trinity*, book 12:

> Action, by which we make good use of temporal things, differs from the contemplation of eternal things. The latter is assigned to wisdom, the former to knowledge—although that which belongs to wisdom may also be called knowledge, as the Apostle states in 1 Corinthians 13 when he says, “Now I know in part”; by this knowledge he undoubtedly intends the contemplation of God.

The difference, therefore, is that wisdom belongs to contemplation, whereas knowledge belongs to action. Here it is plainly shown how the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of knowledge differ: wisdom is assigned to divine things, knowledge to human things.

And, as Augustine teaches in the middle of *On the Trinity*, book 13, chapter 19, we recognize both in Christ: both the divine reality and the human reality; and therefore we have wisdom and knowledge concerning him. For when John 1 is read, “The Word was made flesh,” in the Word is understood the true Son of God, while in the flesh the true son of man is recognized. Likewise, when it is said, “We saw him full of grace and truth,” let us refer grace to knowledge and truth to wisdom. For wisdom and knowledge were present in Christ in fullness, and we possess knowledge and wisdom concerning him who is God and man.

### How wisdom differs from understanding

2. Having shown the difference between knowledge and wisdom, let us see how wisdom differs from understanding. These two differ in that wisdom properly concerns eternal things and is directed toward contemplating eternal Truth. Understanding, however, concerns not only eternal things but also invisible and spiritual things which have arisen in time. By it the supreme nature which made all natures—that is, the divine nature—is considered; and the spiritual and invisible natures after it, such as angels and all good affections of souls, are perceived.

The difference, therefore, is that by wisdom the Creator alone is perceived, whereas by understanding both the Creator and certain creatures are perceived. Again, by understanding we apprehend intelligible things only; but by wisdom we not only apprehend higher things but also delight in things apprehended. Thus these three—understanding, knowledge, and wisdom—may be distinguished. Knowledge serves the right administration of temporal matters and good conduct among the wicked. Understanding serves the contemplation of the Creator and invisible creatures. Wisdom serves the contemplation and delight of eternal Truth alone.

### That the understanding and knowledge discussed here are not those which human beings possess naturally

3. It should be noted that the understanding and knowledge called gifts of the Holy Spirit are different from the understanding and knowledge naturally present in the human soul. For the former are virtues infused by grace into the minds of the faithful, enabling them to live rightly. The latter human beings possess naturally by the benefit of creation, though from God. But through the virtues called gifts of the Holy Spirit, these natural powers are renewed and assisted. Thus, for example, natural understanding, darkened by sin, is renewed and assisted in understanding through a certain virtue and grace called the spirit of understanding. Likewise, through the virtue called the spirit of wisdom, the faculty of reason is assisted and raised to contemplate and delight in truth.

### That this wisdom belongs to God, but is not the wisdom which God is

4. It must also be known that the wisdom of which we are now speaking is not that Wisdom of God which, as Augustine says at the beginning of *On the Trinity*, book 14, chapter 1, is God; rather, it is human wisdom, though wisdom according to God and his true and chief worship. Therefore, if the human mind worships God, whose capacity it has been made by him and in whom it can participate, it thereby becomes wise—not by its own light, but by participation in that supreme light. This human wisdom, then, is also God’s wisdom; but it is not God’s in such a way that God is wise by it. For God is not wise by participation in himself, as the mind is wise by participation in God. So too “the righteousness of God” is called not only that righteousness by which he himself is righteous, but also that which he gives to a human being when he justifies the ungodly.

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. ON THE CONNECTION OF VIRTUES, WHICH ARE NOT SEPARATED

[Col. 0829]

1. It is also customary to ask whether the virtues are so joined to one another that they cannot be possessed separately by anyone, but whoever has one has all. Jerome also says of this in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 56: “All the virtues adhere to one another, so that whoever lacks one lacks all. Therefore whoever has one has all.” This indeed is probable. For since charity is the mother of all virtues, wherever the mother herself—that is, charity—is, all her children, that is, the virtues, are rightly believed also to be present.

Hence Augustine says in Tractate 83 on John: “Where charity is, what can be lacking? But where it is not, what can be of benefit?” Why, then, do we not say, “Whoever has this virtue has all,” since charity is the fullness of the law? The more charity is in a person, the more that person is endowed with virtue; the less it is present, the less virtue is present; and the less virtue is present, the more vice is present.

2. But whether someone possesses all virtues equally, or whether some flourish more and others less in a person, is a question. Some think that one person has some virtues more and others less, as patience shone forth in Job, humility in David, and gentleness in Moses. They also grant that someone merits more through one virtue than through another, insofar as he possesses it more fully than the other. Yet they do not say that anyone merits more through any virtue than through charity; nor that anyone possesses any virtue more fully than charity. Thus they say that some virtues are more, others less, in a person; but none is possessed more fully than charity, which produces the rest. They say that these are the many “faces” mentioned by the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 1: “From the persons of many faces,” and so forth.

Others state more truly that all virtues are alike and equal wherever they are present, so that whoever is equal to another in one virtue is equal to that same person in all. Hence Augustine says at the beginning of *On the Trinity*, book 6, chapter 4:

> The virtues which are in the human mind, although each is understood in a different way, are nevertheless in no way separated from one another. Thus, whoever are equal, for example, in fortitude, are equal also in prudence, justice, and temperance. For if you say that these persons are equal in fortitude but that one excels in prudence, it follows that the other’s fortitude is less prudent; and consequently they are not equal even in fortitude, because the former’s fortitude is more prudent. You will find the same regarding the other virtues if you examine them all by the same consideration.

From this it is clear that all virtues are not only connected but also equal in the human mind. Therefore, when someone is said to excel in a particular virtue—as Abraham in faith, Hebrews 11; Job in patience, James 5—this must be understood according to their outward exercises or by comparison with other persons: because he exhibits especially the habit of humility, or performs especially the work of faith, or carries out in particular the work of one of the other virtues. Hence he is said to abound in that virtue before the others, or to excel singularly among other persons, in this sense: according to the character of outward acts.

In another place Augustine says that one virtue is greater in someone, another less; and that one virtue is present and another absent. For he says in his Epistle 29 to Jerome:

> Your very clear disputation has sufficiently shown that our authorities—indeed, truth itself—did not approve the equality of all sins, even if this is true of virtues. For even if it is true that whoever has one virtue has all virtues, and whoever lacks one lacks all, sins are not therefore equal. For where no virtue exists, nothing is right; yet one thing may still be more depraved than another, and one distortion more distorted than another.

> But if, as I think is truer and more in accord with the sacred Scriptures, the dispositions of souls are like the members of a body—not because they are seen in locations, but because they are felt in affections—and one is illuminated more, another less, while another entirely lacks light, then surely, according as each person is affected by the illumination of devout charity, more in one act, less in another, and not at all in some act, he may be said to have one virtue, not to have another, to have one more, and another less. For charity is greater in this person than in that; and thus we may rightly say, as regards charity which is piety, that there is some virtue in this person and none in that; and that in one person chastity is greater than patience, and greater today than yesterday, if he progresses in it; and that he does not yet have continence, though he has no small mercy.

> And, to state briefly and generally the conception which I have of virtue: virtue is charity by which one loves what ought to be loved. This is greater in some, less in others, and absent in others. But while a human being lives here, there is in no one a charity so complete that it cannot be increased.

This seems to indicate that someone may be said to have one virtue more than another because charity makes him more effective in the act of one virtue than of another; and because of the difference in acts, the virtues themselves are said to be possessed more or less. Someone may even be said not to have a certain virtue, although all are possessed together and equally with respect to the habit of the mind or the essence of each virtue. In act, however, one virtue is possessed more, another less, and another not at all. Thus, a just man using marriage does not possess continence in act, though he possesses it in habit.

Why then are sins not called equal? Perhaps because one who sins more grievously acts more against charity, and one who sins more lightly acts less against it. For no one sins except by acting against that which is the fullness of the law, Romans 13. Therefore James 2 rightly says: “Whoever has offended in one point has become guilty of all”—that is, he acts against charity, on which all things depend.

### He returns to charity, in order to add how the whole law depends upon it
3. Since there are two commandments of charity, on which, as stated above, the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22), we must consider how this is so, since the Law and the Prophets contained many ceremonial commands which, if they belonged to the sanctification of charity, would seem not yet to have had to cease. But because they were instituted not for the sake of justification, which charity effects, but as a figure of things to come and as a burden imposed, they ceased like a shadow when the truth became clear. Nevertheless, both the ceremonial precepts, according to the spiritual meaning which they contain, and all moral precepts are referred to charity. For all relate to the ten commandments written on the tablets, in which the sum of all things is briefly embraced and from which the rest flow forth; just as in the Lord’s discourse eight virtues are set first, to which the rest are referred. And as the other precepts are referred to the ten commandments of the Decalogue, so the ten themselves belong to the two commandments of charity. Therefore all things belong to the two commandments of charity, because they are fulfilled through charity and ought to be referred to charity as to their end.

Hence Augustine, in the final chapter of the *Enchiridion*: “Charity, by which we love God and our neighbor, possesses the whole greatness and breadth of the divine utterances”; it is the root of all good things. Hence Truth says, Matt. 22: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets.” Therefore, if there is no leisure to search all the holy pages and unfold all the wrappings of the sayings, hold fast to charity, on which all things hang, because it is the perfection and end of all things. For then commandments and counsels alike are rightly performed when they are directed to loving God and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. But what is done through fear of punishment or from some carnal intention, so that it is not referred to charity, is not yet done as it ought to be, though it may appear to be done. For one who does not sin through fear of punishment is an enemy of justice; but one who does not sin through love of justice is its friend. Therefore this is the sum of all things: the fullness of the Law and of all divine Scriptures is to be understood as love of God and neighbor. (Aug., *Letter to Anastasius*, Ep. 144; idem, *On Christian Doctrine*, bk. 1, ch. 35.)

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. ON THE TEN COMMANDMENTS, AND HOW THEY ARE CONTAINED IN THE TWO COMMANDMENTS OF CHARITY

1. We must now consider the division of the Decalogue, which is fulfilled in the two commandments. The Decalogue contains ten commandments, the ten-stringed psaltery [Col. 0831]. They are so distributed that the three on the first tablet concern God—namely, the knowledge and love of the Trinity—while the seven on the second tablet concern love of neighbor.

### On the first commandment

2. The first commandment on the first tablet is: “You shall have no strange gods; you shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness,” and so forth. Origen calls these two commandments; Augustine (*On the Ten Strings*, one book, ch. 5) calls them one. For the words already spoken, “You shall have no strange gods,” are more fully explained by the prohibition against worshipping fabricated things—namely, an idol or the likeness of some thing.

Origen says that these two differ thus: an idol is that which has nothing resembling itself; a likeness, however, has the appearance of some thing. For example, if someone makes in gold, wood, or another material the figure of a serpent, bird, or another thing and sets it up for worship, he has made not an idol but a likeness. But one who fashions an appearance that the eye has not seen, but which the mind has devised for itself—for example, if someone gives a dog’s or ram’s head to human limbs, or gives a single human figure two faces—makes not a likeness but an idol, because he makes what has nothing resembling itself. Hence the Apostle says, 1 Cor. 8: “An idol is nothing in the world.” For its appearance is not taken from any existing things, but is something found by an idle and curious mind. A likeness, however, is formed from something existing in heaven, on earth, or in the waters.

Augustine explains, “An idol is nothing in the world,” in this way: among the creatures of the world there is no form of an idol. God made the material, but human folly gave it its form. Whatever has been made was made naturally through the Word; but the human form in an idol was not made through the Word, just as sin was not made through the Word. Rather, it is nothing, and human beings become nothing when they sin.

But the question arises how the form of an idol is here said not to have been made through the Word, when elsewhere we read: “Every form, every joining together, every harmony of parts was made through the Word.” This is variously resolved by different writers. Some say that every form and everything that is, insofar as it is, is from God; and that the form of an idol, insofar as it exists or insofar as it is a form, is from God, but not insofar as it is an idol—that is, insofar as it has been set up for worship. For in this there is not a creature, but a perversion of a creature. Thus, what is sin, insofar as it is sin, is nothing; and when human beings sin they become nothing, because they are separated from Him who truly is. Hence Jerome: “What is not from God, who alone truly is, is said not to be.” And therefore sin, which draws us away from true being, is called nothing or non-being.

Others say that every form which exists naturally, and everything which exists naturally, is from God; but the form of an idol is not natural, because it does not preserve the justice of nature. For that is said to exist naturally which serves, and does not resist, the justice of the simple nature which is God, and which does not corrupt created nature.

The second commandment is, Exod. 20: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” which literally means: you shall not swear the name of God for nothing. Allegorically, however, it commands that you should not think Christ, the Son of God, to be a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity, but rather equal to the Father.

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” where, literally, Sabbath observance is commanded. Allegorically, however, you are commanded to hope for rest, both here from vices and hereafter in the contemplation of God, from the Holy Spirit—that is, from charity and God’s gift; not that the Holy Spirit accomplishes this without the Father and the Son. Indeed, the Church received this gift, that in the Holy Spirit remission of sins might take place. Although the Trinity accomplishes this remission, it is nevertheless said to belong properly to the Holy Spirit, because he is the Spirit of adoption as sons. He is the love and bond, or communion, of Father and Son. Therefore our justification and rest are more often attributed to him.

These are the three commandments of the first tablet, concerning God. The first, concerning the worship of one God, belongs to the Father, in whom there is unity or authority; the second to the Son, in whom there is co-equality; and the third to the Holy Spirit [Col. 0832], in whom there is the communion of both.

### On the commandments of the second tablet

3. On the second tablet were seven commandments concerning love of neighbor. The first of them refers to one’s carnal father, just as the first commandment of the first tablet refers to the heavenly Father. It is Deut. 5: “Honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land”—namely, the land of the living. Parents are to be honored by being shown due reverence and supplied with necessities.

The second is: “You shall not kill,” where, according to the letter, the act of homicide is forbidden; but according to the spirit, even the will to kill. Hence this commandment receives an addition in the Gospel, according to the letter, because the letter of the Gospel expressly states what the letter of the Law did not express. The letter of the Gospel expresses the spiritual understanding—that is, the understanding possessed by spiritual people and according to which one lives spiritually. The letter of the Law expresses the carnal sense—that is, the sense possessed by carnal people and according to which one lives carnally—and to this an addition was made.

The third is: “You shall not commit adultery,” that is, you shall not have intercourse with anyone outside the covenant of marriage; for the whole is understood from a part. Under the name of adultery, therefore, every illicit sexual union and every unlawful use of those bodily members must be understood as forbidden.

The fourth is: “You shall not commit theft,” where sacrilege and every act of robbery are forbidden. Augustine says, in Question 71 on Exodus: He who forbade theft did not permit robbery; rather, by the name of theft he intended every unlawful appropriation of another’s property to be understood. Sacrilege is committed in three ways: when one takes either something sacred from something sacred, something non-sacred from something sacred, or something sacred from something non-sacred. “Sacred” means whatever has been devoted to divine worship, such as a church or church property.

Usury, which is included under robbery, is also forbidden here. Hence Jerome, in a letter on Psalm 54: “There is no difference between seeking usury, cheating, or robbing. Lend to your brother, receive what you gave, and seek nothing beyond it; for an excess is reckoned as usury.” For usury, Augustine says, occurs when a person demands more in a loan or in any matter whatever than he received. Again Jerome, Question 3 on Ezekiel, chapter 14: “Some think that usury exists only in money; but they should understand that usury is called excess—namely, whatever exceeds what was given. Thus, if in winter we give ten measures and at harvest receive fifteen.”

But if a question is raised concerning the children of Israel, who at the Lord’s command borrowed gold and silver vessels and valuable garments from the Egyptians and carried them away—whether they committed theft—we say that those who did this in obedience to God’s command did not commit theft and did not sin at all. Hence Augustine: “The Israelites did not commit theft, but rendered service at God’s command. For God commanded it—he who gave the Law.” Thus an officer of a judge kills without sin the person whom the law commands to be killed; but if he does it of his own accord, he is a murderer, even if he kills one whom he knows is to be put to death by the judge. Yet the weak, who deceived the Egyptians from greed, were permitted rather than commanded to do this to people who justly suffered such things.

An objection is raised: even the good sinned in this action, because they transgressed the natural law with which the Gospel and the Law of moral command agree: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another.” Truth wrote this upon the human heart; and because it was not being read in the heart, he repeated it upon tablets, so that, when the voice was externally applied, it might return to the heart and there find what it read without. They therefore seem to violate this law in that act, doing to others what they did not wish done to themselves. But “unjustly” must be understood there: do not do unjustly to another what you do not wish unjustly done to yourself. Otherwise a judge violates it when he punishes a guilty person, not wishing something similar to be done to himself.

Likewise, the Lord’s words in Matt. 7, “Whatever you want people to do to you,” and so forth, must be understood concerning good things which we ought to render one another. [Note: [Col. 0832] Augustine, vol. 6, bk. 22, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, ch. 71.]

[Col. 0833] The fifth commandment is, Luke 6: “You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor,” where the crime of lying and perjury is forbidden. It is also commonly asked whether every lie is forbidden. Some say that only the lie is forbidden which harms and does not benefit the person to whom it is told. For such a lie is not “against one’s neighbor”; and this seems to be why Scripture added that phrase. But there is a great question concerning lying, which cannot quickly be explained. (Augustine, vol. 5, *On Exodus*, Question 72, at the end.)

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. ON THE THREEFOLD KIND OF LYING

1. It should nevertheless be known that there are three kinds of lies. Some lies are spoken for someone’s safety or advantage, not from malice but from kindness, as the midwives and Rahab lied. There is another kind of lie made in jest, which does not deceive. For the person to whom it is said knows that it is said jokingly. These two kinds of lies are not without fault, but not with great fault. Yet it does not suit the perfect to lie, even for someone’s temporal life, lest they kill their own soul for another’s body. They may conceal the truth, however, but must not state what is false: thus, if someone does not wish to betray a person to death, he should conceal the truth but not speak falsely.

The third kind of lie proceeds from malice and duplicity and must be very carefully avoided by all. [Note: [Col. 0833] Augustine, vol. 8, *On Psalm 5*, at the verse “You destroy all who speak lies,” not far from the beginning of the exposition.]

These words seem to indicate that lies made in jest or for someone’s safety are venial sins for the imperfect; but for the perfect, a lie told for another’s advantage is damnable. The same may be thought concerning a jesting lie, especially if it is repeated.

Augustine teaches in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 22, that the lies of the midwives and Rahab were venial: “Perhaps the midwives were rewarded not because they lied, but because they saved the infants; and because of this mercy their sin was venial, though not nonexistent. Thus Rahab was saved because she saved the spies, for which her sin was venial.” But no one should suppose that pardon may likewise be granted in other sins if they are committed for the saving of human beings, for many detestable evils follow from such an error. We may also benefit someone by stealing, if the poor person to whom something is given perceives the advantage and the rich person from whom it is taken perceives no loss. Likewise we may benefit someone by adultery, if a woman seems likely to die of love unless intercourse is granted her, and, if she lives, is to be purified by repentance. Yet such adultery will not therefore be denied to be a grave sin.

It should also be known that there are eight kinds of lies, as Augustine teaches, vol. 4, *On Lying*, ch. 14. They must be carefully noted, so that it may be clear which lie is venial and which damnable.

The first and capital lie, to be avoided at all costs, is that which occurs in religious teaching; no one should be induced to it by any cause. The second is a lie which benefits no one but harms someone. The third benefits one person while harming another. The fourth proceeds solely from the desire to lie and deceive, and is the greatest lie. The fifth is told from the desire to please, in pleasant speech. Once all these have been avoided, there follows the sixth kind, which harms no one and benefits someone: for instance, if one knows that another’s money is to be unjustly taken and lies that he does not know where it is. The seventh harms no one and benefits someone: for instance, if someone, unwilling to betray to death a person being sought, lies. The eighth harms no one and benefits someone by protecting that person from bodily defilement. In these cases, the less a person sins by lying, the farther he is from the first kind.

But whoever thinks that some kind of lie is not a sin deceives himself shamefully, since he judges it honorable to deceive others. Therefore flee every kind of lie most earnestly, because no lie is from God.

### What a lie is

2. Here we must see what a lie is and what it is to lie [Col. 0834]; then whether every lie is sin, and why. A lie, Augustine says, is “a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving.” [Note: [Col. 0834] Vol. 4, *Against Lying, to Consentius*, ch. 12, at the end; and *Enchiridion*, ch. 18.] Therefore, for there to be a lie, something false must be uttered and uttered with the intention of deceiving. For this is the evil proper to a liar: to have one thing shut up in the heart and another ready upon the tongue.

### What it is to lie

3. To lie, however, is to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind, whether that thing is true or not. Therefore everyone who speaks a lie lies, because he speaks contrary to what he thinks—that is, with a will to deceive. But not everyone who lies speaks a lie, because someone sometimes lies while saying what is true, just as, conversely, someone may be truthful while saying something false.

Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 18: “Certainly no one who says a falsehood which he thinks true should be judged a liar; for, insofar as he is concerned, he does not deceive, but is deceived. Therefore the person who carelessly believes false things and regards them as true is not to be charged with lying. On the contrary, the one who says what is true while thinking it false lies. For as regards his mind, he does not speak truth, because he does not say what he thinks, although what he says is found to be true. Nor is the person free from lying who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth but knowingly lies in will.”

It is commonly asked whether, if a Jew says that Christ is God while not so thinking in his mind, he speaks a lie. What he says is not a lie, because, though he holds otherwise in his mind, what he says is nonetheless true; and therefore it is not a lie. Yet he lies by saying what is true.

Augustine indicates that every lie is sin. “It seems to me,” he says in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 18, “that every lie is sin; but it matters greatly with what intention and about what matters each person lies. For the person who lies with an intention to benefit does not sin in the same way as one who lies with an intention to harm; nor does one who sends a traveler by lying along a different road do as much harm as one who corrupts the way of life by lying.”

Moreover, every lie must be called sin because a person ought to say what he holds in his mind, whether it is true or merely thought true and is not so. For words were instituted not so that human beings might deceive one another by them, but so that they might convey their thoughts to one another’s knowledge through them. Therefore to use words for deception, rather than for that for which they were instituted, is sin. Nor should any lie be thought not to be sin because we may sometimes benefit someone by lying; for, as stated above, we may benefit someone by stealing and adultery as well. Nor can we say that a lie exists only when someone is harmed. When a person knowingly speaks a falsehood, it is a lie whether someone is harmed or no one is harmed.

See, then, that every lie is sin.
