Yet the words of Psalm 5, “You destroy all who speak lies,” are not to be understood of every lie; nor are the words of Wisdom 1, “A lying mouth kills the soul.” Nor does this commandment seem to forbid every lie, nor does the preceding definition include a jesting lie.

### Where error involves danger, or does not

4. It should also be known that in some matters we are deceived with great evil, in others with little evil, and in others with none. In matters in which it makes no difference for attaining God’s kingdom whether they are believed or not, or whether they are considered true or false, whether they exist or not—in such matters, to err, that is, to think one thing instead of another, should not be judged sin; or, if it is sin, it is the least and lightest kind.

And some things are true, though they may not appear so, which must be believed if one is to attain eternal life. Although error must be avoided with the greatest care not only in major matters but also in minor ones, and although no one can err except through ignorance of things, it does not follow that everyone who does not know something thereby errs. Rather, a person errs if he thinks that he knows what he does not know. For he approves falsehood as truth, which is characteristic of error.

Nevertheless, it matters greatly in what matter a person errs [Col. 0835]. Some things are better unknown than known. Again, error has sometimes benefited some people—but on the road under their feet, not on the road of morals.

It is also commonly asked whether Jacob lied when he said he was Esau, while thinking otherwise in his mind. Augustine says concerning this, *Against Lying, to Consentius*, ch. 10: “What Jacob did at his mother’s prompting in order to deceive his father, if carefully considered, seems not to be a lie but a mystery. For he intended to obey his mother, who knew the mystery through the Spirit; and therefore Jacob is excused from lying because of the intimate counsel of the Holy Spirit which she had previously received.”

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. ON PERJURY

1. We must now consider perjury. Perjury is a lie confirmed by an oath. The question is raised whether there is perjury where there is no lie. Some think so on the authority of Jerome, who says, in his commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 4, at the beginning: “It should be noted that an oath has three companions: truth, judgment, and justice. If these are absent, it will not be an oath but perjury.” But where a falsehood is sworn, truth is absent. Therefore, if a falsehood is sworn, even without an intention to deceive, it seems to be perjury because truth is absent.

Others hold that there is no perjury where there is no lie; and that, just as one may sometimes speak falsely without lying, so one may swear falsely without perjury. Perhaps the Apostle said something false when he promised that he would come to the Corinthians, 1 Cor. at the end; yet he did not incur, as was charged against him, the guilt of lying, because he thought so in his mind. Even if he had confirmed it by oath, he would not have incurred perjury, because, insofar as he was concerned, he spoke truth; and if he had added an oath, insofar as he was concerned, he would have sworn truth, although events occurred otherwise than he had said.

Thus, just as a person is not a liar unless he thinks otherwise in his mind than he says, whether the thing is so or not, so some hold that no one is made perjured unless he thinks otherwise in his mind than he speaks, whether the thing is so or not.

### On the threefold mode of perjury

2. But the better view is that a person commits perjury both when he swears a falsehood with an intention to deceive, when, believing false that which is true, he swears, and when, believing true that which is false, he swears. Hence Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 28, not far from the beginning: “People swear falsely either when they deceive or when they are deceived. Either a person thinks true what is false and swears rashly; or he knows or thinks it false and nevertheless swears to it as true, and still swears wickedly.”

The two perjuries he mentions differ. Suppose someone swears to what he thinks true: he thinks true what he swears to, and yet it is false. He does not commit perjury from his mind, but is deceived. He takes as true what is false; he does not knowingly interpose an oath concerning a false thing. Give another person who knows something is false and swears as though what he knows false were true: you see how detestable this beast is. Give still another who thinks something false and swears as though it were true, and perhaps it is true. To make this clear: “It is raining in that place.” You ask a person, and he says that it has rained; and at that time it is raining there, but he thinks that it has not rained. He is perjured. It matters how the word proceeds from the mind: the tongue is not made guilty unless the mind is guilty.

These words clearly teach that a person commits perjury in three ways, as we said above: when he knowingly swears a falsehood; when he swears what is true while believing it false; or when he swears what is false while believing it true. But this last does not seem to be perjury, even though it is called perjury, because a falsehood is sworn; the person who swears thus does not seem guilty of perjury, because his mind is not guilty, and therefore neither is his tongue. On the contrary, his mind is guilty because he presumes to swear to what he has not clearly ascertained to be true.

Therefore not every perjury is a lie, and not everyone who commits perjury lies. But everyone who swears while lying commits perjury, and everyone who swears a falsehood, whether lying or not, commits perjury. Yet when someone swears what is true while thinking it false, the question is raised: what is the perjury there? [Col. 0836] The signification of his words is true, because he unknowingly speaks truth. Therefore the signification itself is neither falsehood nor a lie, because it is true; and what is true does not seem to be perjury.

To this we say: to speak thus—namely, contrary to one’s mind, under the attestation of an oath—is perjury. Therefore lying with an oath added is perjury. Perjury, then, is either: swearing while speaking a falsehood with an intention to deceive; swearing while speaking a falsehood without an intention to deceive; or swearing while speaking truth with an intention to deceive.

An objection is raised: if everyone who swears a falsehood commits perjury, then a person who promises someone, under a fixed term, to give something but does not do so has committed perjury from the moment he swore, because he swore falsely. For it was not going to happen as he swore. It can be answered that not everyone who swears something false commits perjury from the moment he swears, as does the person presently under discussion. Rather, when he changes his intention or exceeds the time-limit, such an oath becomes perjury in guilt.

### Whether swearing is evil

3. If it is asked whether swearing is evil, we say that sometimes it is evil and sometimes it is not. To swear voluntarily and without necessity, or to swear falsely, is a great sin. But to swear from necessity—namely, either to establish innocence, to confirm compacts of peace, or to persuade hearers of what is useful to them—is not evil, because it is necessary for them.

Hence Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, bk. 1, and in his *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*: “An oath is to be made in necessary matters, since people are slow to believe what is useful to them. An oath is not good; yet a necessary oath is not evil—that is, it is not to be sought as a good, nor is it to be avoided as an evil when it is necessary.” For swearing is not contrary to God’s command. But the Lord is understood to have prohibited swearing in such a way that, insofar as a person himself is concerned, he does not swear. Many do otherwise, holding an oath in their mouth as though it were something great and pleasant. The Apostle knew the Lord’s command and yet swore. We are forbidden to swear from desire or from delight in swearing.

Therefore, when Christ says in the Gospel, “But I say to you, do not swear at all,” he is understood to command that no one should seek an oath as a good, lest habitual swearing cause him to fall into perjury. What he adds in Matt. 5, “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no,’” is good and to be desired. But “what is beyond this is from evil,” that is, if you are compelled to swear, know that it arises from the necessary weakness of those to whom you are commending something; and that weakness is certainly an evil. Hence we daily pray to be delivered from it, saying, “Deliver us from evil.” Therefore he did not say, “What is beyond this is evil.” You do not do evil when you make good use of an oath; rather, it is from the evil of the person who does not otherwise believe—that is, from weakness, which is sometimes punishment and sometimes both punishment and guilt. There the Lord forbade evil, urged good, and permitted what is necessary.

### On an oath made by creatures

4. It is also asked whether it is lawful to swear by a creature. This seems not to be so, since it is written in the Law, Deut. 9: “You shall render your oaths to the Lord”; and Christ commands in the Gospel, Matt. 5, not to swear at all, either by heaven, by earth, by Jerusalem, or by one’s head.

The Jews, as though little children, were permitted to swear by the Creator and commanded that, if it happened that they swore, they should swear only by the Creator and not by a creature. For in swearing by angels and elements they honored creatures with veneration; and it was better that this honor be rendered to God than to creatures. He therefore forbade this to the weak; but he did not forbid it to the holy, who worshipped only the Creator in creatures. Hence Joseph swore by Pharaoh’s welfare, reverencing God’s judgment in him, who had been placed in the lowest condition.

Christ, however, forbade swearing by creatures lest something divine be believed to reside in them, for which reverence would be owed to them; or lest people, in swearing falsely by them, think themselves not bound by the oath. (Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, ch. 5, at the end.)

### Which oath binds more: one made by God, or one made by the Gospel or by creatures?

[Col. 0837]

5. If it is asked who is more bound, one who swears by God or one who swears by the Gospel or creatures, we say: the one who swears by God, because these holy things were made by God. Hence Chrysostom: “If there is some cause, one who swears by God seems to do a small thing; but one who swears by the Gospel seems to have done something greater.” To them it must be said: “Fools, the holy Scriptures were made for God’s sake, not God for the Scriptures’ sake; likewise creatures were made for God’s sake.”

### What it means to say, “I swear by God”

6. Here it is asked what it means to say, “I swear by God.” It means to call God as witness. For the Apostle swore when he said, Rom. 1: “God is my witness,” as if he had said, “By God, it is so.” Hence Augustine, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 28: “It is ridiculous to think this: if you say ‘By God,’ you swear; if you say ‘God is my witness,’ you do not swear. For what is ‘By God’ except ‘God is my witness’? Or what is ‘God is witness’ except ‘By God’?”

What, then, is it to swear, except to render right to God when you swear by God—the right, namely, of truth and not falsehood? Again, I say to your charity: one who swears falsely by a stone commits perjury, because he calls as witness not the stone, which does not hear, but its Creator. Therefore to swear by any creature is to call its Creator as witness.

There is also a most grave kind of oath, made through imprecation: for example, when someone says, “If I did that, may I suffer this,” or “May this happen to my children.” This is also the sense sometimes intended when someone swearing says, “By my health,” or “By my children,” and the like: for he binds this to God. Hence Augustine, in the same sermon: “When someone says, ‘By my health,’ he binds his health to God. When he says, ‘By my children,’ he pledges them to God, so that what proceeds from his mouth may come upon their heads: if true, true; if false, false.”

Just as a person swearing thus sometimes binds this to God, so one swearing by God calls God himself as witness. Therefore in every oath either God is called as witness, or a creature is bound and pledged to God. Thus to swear is either to call God as witness or to pledge something to God. Therefore to swear by any creature is to call its Creator as witness.

### On those who swear by false gods

7. After this it is asked whether one may rely upon the faith of a person who has sworn by demons or idols. Augustine says on this matter, vol. 2, Letter 154 to Publicola, at the beginning: “I first want you to consider whether, if someone swore by false gods and did not keep faith, he would not seem to you to have sinned twice. Certainly he sinned twice: because he swore by those by whom he ought not to have sworn, and because he acted contrary to the pledged faith which he ought not to have pledged.”

Therefore a person who relies, not for evil but for good, on the faith of one known to have sworn by false gods does not join himself to the sin of the one who swore by demons, but to his good agreement by which he kept faith. And without doubt it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by false gods than deceitfully by the true God. For the holier that by which one swears, the more punishable is perjury.

### An oath carelessly made is not to be kept; neither is an unjust vow or promise

8. It remains to consider whether every oath must be fulfilled. If someone has sworn something to another contrary to faith and charity, and keeping it would result in a worse outcome, it ought rather to be changed than fulfilled. Hence Ambrose, *On Duties*, bk. 22, ch. 4: “It is sometimes contrary to God’s duty to fulfill a promised oath,” as Herod did.

Likewise Isidore, *Book of Sentences*, chapter “It Is Not To Be Observed”: “In evil promises, break faith; in a shameful vow, change your resolve. Do not do what you vowed carelessly; a promise fulfilled by wickedness is impious.” Again: “An oath by which evil is carelessly promised is not to be observed—for example, if someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity in remaining with her. For it is more tolerable not to fulfill the oath than to remain in fornication.”

Likewise Bede: “If we happen carelessly to swear something which, if kept, would result in a worse outcome, let us know that it should freely be changed by more salutary counsel; and that, under pressing necessity, we ought rather to commit perjury than, in avoiding perjury, turn aside into another and graver crime. For David swore by God to kill the foolish man Nabal; but at the first intercession of Abigail, a prudent woman, he withdrew his threats, recalled his sword into its sheath, and did not grieve that he had incurred any guilt by such perjury.”

Again Augustine, Sermon 22: “That David did not fulfill his oath by shedding blood was greater piety. David swore rashly, but by greater piety did not fulfill his oath.” From these and many other passages it is shown that some oaths are not to be kept. Whoever swears in this manner sins gravely; but when he changes his course, he does well. Whoever does not change sins twice: because he swore unjustly, and because he does what he ought not to do.

### Whether one who does not do what he carelessly swore is perjured

9. It is commonly asked whether one who changes his course ought to be called perjured. Bede above called such an oath perjury. John, apocrisiary of the eastern sees, also said: “The saying of our father Sophronius signifies that it is better for one swearing to commit perjury than to keep an oath in the breaking of holy images.”

But such an oath not kept is called perjury, and the person who does not fulfill what he swears falsely is said to commit perjury—not because he is guilty for failing to observe it, but because he swore something unjust, by which he is guilty, as is the person who commits perjury.

### On one who swears through verbal cunning

10. It should also be known that, by whatever verbal artifice someone swears, God, who is witness of conscience, nevertheless receives it as the person to whom the oath is made understands it. Such a person becomes guilty in two ways: he both takes God’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbor by deceit. (Isidore, *Sentences*, bk. 2, distinction 22, ch. 2, “Whatever.”)

### On one who compels another to swear

11. It is also asked whether a person sins who compels someone else to swear. Augustine says, *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 28, not far from the end: “For one who demands an oath, it matters greatly whether he does not know that the other will swear falsely, or knows it. If he does not know and says, ‘Swear to me,’ so that he may have confidence in him, it is not a sin, though it is a human temptation. But if he knows that the man has acted thus and compels him to swear, he is a murderer.”

Again, in his sermon on the Beheading of John: “One who provokes a person to swear, knowing that he will swear falsely, surpasses a murderer; for the murderer is about to kill a body, but that person a soul—indeed, two souls: that of the person whom he provokes to swear and his own.”

### From the Council of Orléans

12. The holy synod decreed that, except for making peace, all faithful persons should approach the sacramenta—that is, oaths—while fasting.

## DISTINCTION XL. ON THE SIXTH AND SEVENTH COMMANDMENTS OF THE SECOND TABLET
1. The sixth commandment is: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife.” The seventh is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor his servant, nor his maidservant,” and so forth. Yet the commandment not to covet one’s neighbor’s possessions seems to be one and the same as that which says, “You shall not steal”; and the commandment not to covet a wife seems to be one and the same as that which says, “You shall not commit adultery.” For the commandment against stealing could have been understood in that general prohibition in which one is commanded not to covet one’s neighbor’s property; and in the saying, “You shall not commit adultery,” this too could have been understood: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” But in those two commandments against adultery and theft, the acts themselves are identified and prohibited; whereas in these final commandments, desire itself is prohibited. Thus the former differ greatly from the latter. Hence, in the Gospel an addition is made to the commandment against adultery, in Matthew 5, where every desire to commit adultery is prohibited. But since the desire for another’s wife and for another’s property is here forbidden, why is the Law said to restrain the hand and not the mind? This is said of the Law with respect to ceremonial matters, not moral matters; or because the Law does not contain a general prohibition of every deadly desire, as the Gospel does.

### What the killing letter is

[Col. 0839]

2. But if it is asked which “killing letter” the Apostle means, in 2 Corinthians 3, it is certainly the Decalogue. It is not called the killing letter because the Law is evil, but because, by prohibiting sin, it increases concupiscence and adds transgression unless grace sets one free—a grace which does not abound in the Law as it does in the Gospel. Or this may be understood according to their carnal interpretation. Therefore the Law is good, and yet it kills without grace, since it is the power of sin that commands what cannot be fulfilled without grace. But grace was lacking, and therefore the letter was killing.

The letter of the Gospel differs from the letter of the Law because their promises differ: there, earthly things are promised; here, heavenly things. Their sacraments likewise differ: those merely signified, whereas these confer grace. Their commandments also differ in ceremonial matters. For in moral matters they are the same, but are contained more fully in the Gospel. You have heard the ten strings of the psaltery imposed upon both sexes, which are to be struck with charity, so that the beasts of vices may be slain.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0839]

## DISTINCTION I. ON SACRAMENTS AND SACRAMENTAL SIGNS

1. For the Samaritan, drawing near to the wounded man, applied the bindings of sacraments for his healing, because God established the remedies of the sacraments against the wounds of original and actual sin. Concerning them, four matters first present themselves for consideration: what a sacrament is; why it was instituted; in what it consists and is made; and what difference there is between the sacraments of the old and new law.

### What a sacrament is  
*(Augustine, City of God, book 10, chapter 55; On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 1.)*

2. A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. Yet “sacrament” is also said to mean a sacred secret, as “the sacrament of divinity,” so that a sacrament may be both the sacred thing signifying and the sacred thing signified. But here we are treating of sacrament insofar as it is a sign.

Likewise, a sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace. A sign, however, is a thing which, beyond the appearance that it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into thought through itself. Of signs, some are natural, such as smoke signifying fire; others are given. Among the given signs, some are sacraments and some are not. For every sacrament is a sign, but not conversely.

A sacrament bears the likeness of the thing of which it is a sign. For if sacraments did not have a likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not properly be called sacraments. For a sacrament is properly called that which is so a sign of God’s grace and a form of invisible grace that it bears its image and exists as its cause. Sacraments, therefore, were instituted not merely for signifying, but also for sanctifying.

For those things instituted only for signifying are merely signs and not sacraments, such as the carnal sacrifices and ceremonial observances of the old Law. These could never make their offerers righteous, because, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 9, “The blood of goats and bulls and the sprinkling of the ashes of a heifer sanctified the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh,” not of the soul. For that defilement was contact with a dead person. Hence Augustine, *Questions on Numbers*, chapter 33: “I understand no other defilement cleansed by the Law than contact with a dead human being. Whoever had touched him was unclean for seven days, but was purified according to the Law on the third and seventh days; and thus was clean, so as then to enter the Temple.”

Those legal rites also sometimes cleansed from bodily leprosy. But no one was ever justified by works of the Law, as the Apostle says in Romans 4, even if those works were done in faith and charity. Why? Because God imposed them for servitude, not for justification, and so that they might be figures of things to come, preferring that they should be offered to himself rather than to idols. Those things, therefore, were signs, yet also sacraments, although they are often called sacraments less properly in Scripture, because they were signs of a sacred thing which they indeed bestowed. The Apostle calls “works of the Law” those things instituted solely for signifying or as a burden.

### On the reason for the institution of sacraments

3. Sacraments were instituted for three reasons: for humiliation, instruction, and exercise.

They were instituted for humiliation, so that, while a human being reverently subjects himself by the Creator’s command to insensible things which by nature are beneath him, he may please God more through this humility and obedience, and may merit before him. By God’s command he seeks salvation in things beneath himself—not indeed from them, but from God through them.

They were also instituted for instruction, so that the mind might be taught, through what is outwardly seen in a visible form, to know the invisible power that is within. For the human being who before sin saw God without an intermediary became so dulled through sin that he cannot grasp divine things unless trained by human ones.

Likewise, they were instituted for exercise, because, since a human being cannot be idle, a useful and healthful exercise is set before him in the sacraments, through which he may avoid vain and harmful occupation. For one engaged in good exercise is not easily captured by the tempter. Hence Jerome advises: “Always do some work, so that the devil may find you occupied.”

### On the threefold kind of exercise

4. There are three kinds of exercises. One pertains to the building up of the soul; another to the support of the body; another to the destruction of both. Therefore, although God could give grace to a human being without sacraments—for he has not bound his power to them—he instituted sacraments for the reasons stated above.

There are two things in which a sacrament consists, namely words and things: words, such as the invocation of the Trinity; things, such as water, oil, and the like.

### On the difference between the old and new sacraments

5. It remains to consider the difference between the old and new sacraments, calling “sacraments” those things which formerly signified sacred realities, such as sacrifices, offerings, and the like. Augustine briefly states their difference in his letter to Rusticus, *On the Form of Living*: “Because those only promised and signified, whereas these give salvation.”

### On circumcision

6. Yet among those sacraments there was a certain sacrament, namely circumcision, which conferred the same remedy against sin that Baptism now provides. Hence Augustine, in his exposition of the title of Psalm 73; to Valerius, book 2 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 11, near the end; and on Luke 2, “And when the days were fulfilled,” etc.:

“From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God—which was then a seal of the righteousness of faith—it availed for the cleansing of original and old sin in adults and children, just as Baptism began to avail for the renewal of the human being from the time it was instituted.”

Likewise Bede says: “Circumcision under the Law accomplished against the wound of original sin the same aid of saving healing which Baptism is accustomed to accomplish in the time of revealed grace; except that they could not yet enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom. Nevertheless, after death, comforted in blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, they awaited with happy hope the entrance into the peace above.”

These authorities plainly teach that, from the time it was instituted, circumcision bestowed upon children and adults from God the remission of original and actual sin, just as it is now given through Baptism.

### On men before circumcision, and women before and after it

7. It is asked what remedy against sin was available to men before circumcision, and to women before and after it. Some say that sacrifices and offerings availed them for the remission of sin. But it is better to say that those descended from Abraham were justified through circumcision; women, however, through faith and good works—through their own, if they were adults, or through those of their parents, if they were little children.

Those before circumcision, if little children, were justified through their parents’ faith; but their parents through the power of sacrifices—that is, through the spiritual reality which they understood in those sacrifices. Hence Gregory, *Morals*, book 4, chapter 2: “What the water of Baptism avails among us, that among the ancients either faith alone accomplished for little children, or the power of sacrifice for adults, or the mystery of circumcision for those descended from Abraham’s stock.”

### On the institution and reason for circumcision

8. Here it must be said in whom circumcision was instituted, why it was instituted, and why it was changed into Baptism. Abraham was the first to receive the command of circumcision, as a test of obedience. Circumcision was commanded not to him alone, but also to his seed—that is, to all Hebrews. According to the Law, it was performed on the eighth day with a stone knife, upon the flesh of the foreskin.

Circumcision was given for several reasons: first, so that Abraham might please God through obedience to the command, though Adam had displeased him through transgression. It was also given as a sign of Abraham’s great faith, for he believed that he would have a son in whom the blessing of all would come about. Further, it was given so that by this sign that people might be distinguished from the other nations.

Circumcision was commanded to be performed upon the flesh of the foreskin because it was instituted as a remedy for original sin, which we derive from our parents through the concupiscence of the flesh—a concupiscence which rules especially in that part. And because the first human being felt the guilt of disobedience in that part, it was fitting that there he should receive the sign of obedience.

### Why on the eighth day and with a stone knife

9. It was performed on the eighth day with a stone knife because, in the general resurrection and the future eighth age, through Christ the Rock every corruption will be cut away from the elect; and through Christ’s resurrection, accomplished on the eighth day, the soul of each believer in him is circumcised from sins. Thus that sacrament has two meanings.

### Why circumcision was changed into Baptism

10. Circumcision was changed into Baptism because the sacrament of Baptism is more universal and more perfect, being enriched with fuller grace. For there sins alone were forgiven; neither assisting grace for doing good, nor the possession or increase of virtues, was bestowed there as in Baptism. In Baptism sins are not only abolished, but assisting grace is also conferred and virtues are increased. [Note: “The Master is not upheld here.”]

Hence it is called “water of refreshment,” because it makes the dry fruitful and bestows greater abundance even on those already bearing fruit. For however righteous one may be when approaching Baptism through faith and charity already possessed, there one receives more abundant grace; but this was not so in circumcision. Thus for Abraham, already justified by faith, circumcision was only a seal and conferred nothing inwardly upon him.

### On children who died before the eighth day

11. But if it is asked whether children who died before the eighth day—before which circumcision was not performed under the Law—were saved or not, the same answer may be given as is held concerning children who die before Baptism: they are known to perish. [Note: “Here the Master is not upheld.”]

Hence Bede, on Luke: “He who now cries out terribly and beneficially through his Gospel, John 3, ‘Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of God,’ long ago cried out through his Law, Genesis 17: ‘The male whose foreskin’s flesh has not been circumcised—that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has made my covenant void.’”

Perhaps, however, under the Law, when death was urgently impending before the eighth day, they circumcised children without sin, just as Baptism is now administered in the Church.

## DISTINCTION II. ON THE SACRAMENTS OF THE NEW LAW

1. Let us now proceed to the sacraments of the new Law: Baptism, Confirmation, the blessing of bread—that is, the Eucharist—Penance, Extreme Unction, Orders, and Marriage. Some of these provide a remedy against sin and confer assisting grace, as Baptism does; others are only a remedy, as Marriage; others strengthen us by grace and power, as the Eucharist and Orders. [Note: “Here the Master is not upheld.”]

### Why they were not instituted immediately after humanity’s fall

2. But if it is asked why these sacraments were not instituted immediately after the fall of humankind, since righteousness and salvation are in them, we say that the sacraments of grace were not to be given before the coming of Christ, who brought grace; for they received their power from his death and passion. Christ, however, did not will to come before humankind had been convicted by the natural and written Law that neither could help it.  
*(Hugh, book 1, part 2, chapter 8.)*

### That the sacrament of Marriage existed before sin

3. Marriage was instituted before sin—not indeed as a remedy, but as a sacrament and an office. After sin, however, it became a remedy against the corruption of carnal concupiscence, concerning which we shall treat in its proper place.

### On Baptism

4. Let us now consider the sacrament of Baptism, which is the first among the sacraments of new grace. John foretold Christ’s Baptism by his own baptism. He is read as the first to baptize, but in water, not in the Spirit, as he himself says: “I baptize you in water unto repentance.” For he washed bodies alone and did not cleanse from sins. John’s baptism was unto repentance, not unto remission; Christ’s Baptism, however, is unto remission.

For John, in baptizing people, summoned them to repentance; and he taught those whom he baptized to repent, according to the saying: “They came to John in the Jordan, confessing their sins.” But in John’s baptism forgiveness of sins was not given; it was given in Christ’s Baptism.

### What use John’s baptism had

5. What use, then, was John’s baptism? It prepared people for Christ’s Baptism by the practice of being baptized. But it is asked why it was called John’s baptism, as Truth says in Matthew 21: “Whence is John’s baptism?” Because there John’s operation was only the outward, visible act of washing, not the inward, invisible grace of God at work.

Yet that operation of John was from God, and that baptism was from God, not merely from a human being. But it was called a human being’s baptism because nothing occurred there which a human being did not perform. If it is asked whether it was a sacrament, this may readily be granted in the sense in which the legal signs are called sacraments. For John’s baptism signified a sacred reality, namely Christ’s Baptism, which is not only of repentance but also of forgiveness of sins.

### On the form of John’s baptism and those baptized by him

6. Here it must be considered whether those baptized by John were baptized again with Christ’s Baptism, and what form of words John used. Those baptized by John who did not know that the Holy Spirit existed and placed their hope in his baptism were afterwards baptized with Christ’s Baptism. John’s baptism, however, was given in the name of the One to come.

Hence Jerome, on Joel, commentary on chapter 2: “Whoever says that he believes in Christ and does not believe in the Holy Spirit does not yet have clear eyes.” Therefore, those baptized by John in the name of the One to come—that is, of the Lord Jesus—who said, “But we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit,” were baptized again; indeed, they received true Baptism.

But those who did not place their hope in John’s baptism and believed in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were not baptized afterwards. Rather, when the apostles laid hands upon them, they received the Holy Spirit. [Note: “Here the Master is not upheld.”] Others, however, who did not believe in this way were baptized with Christ’s Baptism, as stated above.

Hence Jerome, in the Letter *On the Husband of One Wife*: “Those who did not know the Holy Spirit when they received baptism from John were baptized again with Christ’s Baptism, as stated above, lest anyone from the Jews or Gentiles should suppose that water without the Holy Spirit could suffice for salvation.”

Ambrose also says of this in book 1 of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 3: “Some denied that they knew the Holy Spirit, though they said that they had been baptized with John’s baptism, who baptized in the name of the coming Jesus, not in his own name. Therefore these persons, because they had been baptized neither in Christ’s name nor with faith in the Holy Spirit, could not receive the sacrament of Baptism. Thus they were baptized in Christ’s name; and Baptism was not repeated in them, but renewed.”

## DISTINCTION III. WHAT BAPTISM IS

1. After this it must be considered what Baptism is, what its form is, when it was instituted, and the reason for its institution. Baptism is called immersion, that is, the outward washing of the body performed under the prescribed form of words. For if washing takes place without the word, there is no sacrament there; but when the word is joined to the element, a sacrament comes into being. This does not mean that the element itself becomes the sacrament, but that the washing performed in the element becomes so.

Hence Augustine, volume 9, tractate 80 on John: “Baptism is consecrated by the word. Take away the word, and what is water but water? The word comes to the element, and a sacrament comes into being.” Whence comes this great power of water, that it touches the body and washes the heart, except through the working of the word—not because it is spoken, but because it is believed? For even in the word itself, one thing is the passing sound, another the power remaining within.

Thus the sacrament of Baptism consists in two things: the word and the element. Therefore, even if other things instituted for the adornment of the sacrament are absent, it is nevertheless a true and holy sacrament if the word and element are present. For in this sacrament and in others, some things are customarily done for the beauty and dignity of the sacrament; other things pertain to its substance and cause. The word and the element belong to the substance of this sacrament; the rest pertains to its solemnity.

### On the form of Baptism

2. But what is that word which, when joined to the element, makes a sacrament? Truth teaches you the form of this sacrament in the final chapter of Matthew, when he says to the disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The invocation of the Trinity, therefore, is called the word by which Baptism is consecrated; and this is the form of words under which Baptism is administered.

Hence Pope Zacharias, to Bishop Boniface, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *In synodo*, says: “It was most firmly commanded in the synod of the English that anyone who had been immersed without invocation of the Trinity should not possess the sacrament of regeneration.” This is altogether true. If anyone has been immersed in the baptismal font without invocation of the Trinity, he is not a complete Christian unless he has been baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, it is read in the Acts of the Apostles that the apostles baptized in the name of Christ. But, as Ambrose explains in book 1 of *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 3, the whole Trinity is understood in this name. For when you say “Christ,” the Father by whom he was anointed, he himself who was anointed, and the Holy Spirit through whom he was anointed are understood.

Hence Pope Nicholas, in reply to the inquiries of the Bulgarians: “You state that many have been baptized by a certain Jew, and ask what should be done concerning this. Certainly, if they were baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or in the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, they have been baptized; for the two are one and the same, as Ambrose explains.”

### Whether Baptism may be administered in the name of the Father alone or of the Holy Spirit alone

3. Here it is asked whether Baptism would be valid if it were said “in the name of the Father” alone, or “of the Holy Spirit” alone, just as it is said “in the name of Christ.” Ambrose, in the same place, seems to say that if the mystery of the Trinity is held in faith and one person alone is named, the sacrament is complete; and, conversely, if all three are named but one thinks wrongly of any of them, the mystery of the Trinity becomes empty.

For he says: “Where the full sacrament of Baptism is not present, neither a beginning nor any form of Baptism is to be regarded as present. But it is complete if you confess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. If you deny one, you overthrow the whole. And just as, if you include one in your speech—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—yet in faith deny neither Father, Son, nor Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is complete, so also, though you name Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, if you diminish the power of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, every mystery is empty. For when it is said ‘in the name of Christ,’ the mystery is fulfilled through the unity of the name; nor is the Spirit separated from Christ’s Baptism, because Christ baptized in the Spirit.”

### Ambrose’s question

4. Let us now consider whether, just as we read that the sacrament of Baptism is complete in Christ’s name, nothing is lacking for the fullness of the mystery if the Holy Spirit alone is named. Let us follow the argument: one who has named one has signified the Trinity. If you say “Christ,” you designate both the Father by whom the Son was anointed, and the one who was anointed, namely the Son, and the Holy Spirit by whom he was anointed. For it is written in Acts 10 that this is Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.

And if you say “Father,” you likewise indicate his Son and the Spirit of his mouth, provided that you also grasp this in your heart. And if you say “Holy Spirit,” you name God the Father, from whom he proceeds, and his Son, whose Spirit he is. Hence, so that authority may be joined to reason, the Lord says in Acts 1: “But you shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit,” by which he indicates that we may rightly be baptized in the Holy Spirit.

### He briefly reviews the foregoing interpretation, with a qualification of a certain statement

5. From these things you have plainly understood that true Baptism is administered in Christ’s name. Hence it nevertheless seems to be implied that true Baptism may be given in the name of the Father alone or of the Holy Spirit alone, provided that the one baptizing holds the faith of the Trinity, which Trinity is understood in any one of these names.

But if someone, believing perversely and intending to introduce error, names only one of the three, he does not complete the mystery. When Ambrose says that the mystery is empty where the three have been named if the baptizer diminishes the power of Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—that is, if he thinks wrongly concerning the power of any of them and does not believe in the one power of the Three—this must be understood of someone who neither intends nor believes that he is baptizing. Such a person lacks not only faith but also the intention of baptizing.

Therefore, one who baptizes in Christ’s name baptizes in the name of the Trinity, which is understood there. Yet it is safer to name the three persons, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; not “in the names,” but “in the name,” that is, in the invocation or confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For the whole Trinity is invoked there, so that it may work invisibly there through itself, just as it works outwardly and visibly through ministry. But if “in the names” is said, there is no sacrament, because the form of Baptism is not preserved.

### On the institution of Baptism

6. There are differing views concerning when the institution of Baptism began. Some say that it was instituted when Christ said to Nicodemus, in John 3: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. Others say that Baptism was instituted when he said to the apostles, in Luke 10: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

But he said this to them after the resurrection, commanding them concerning the calling of the Gentiles. Before his Passion he had sent them out two by two to preach in Judaea and baptize, saying in Matthew 10: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles.” Baptism had therefore already been instituted, since they baptized and preached at the same time.

### The form in which the apostles baptized before Christ’s Passion

7. But if it is asked in what form the apostles baptized at that time, one may safely say: in the name of the Trinity, namely in the form in which they later baptized the Gentiles. This form may be understood to have been handed down before the Passion, although it is not written. Therefore Christ did not first give them that form when he sent them to evangelize the Gentiles; rather, having handed it down earlier when he sent them into Judaea, he repeated it when he sent them to the Gentiles.

It is more suitably said, therefore, that the institution occurred when Christ was baptized by John in the Jordan. He underwent this by divine dispensation, not because he wished to be cleansed, since he was without sin, but because by contact with his pure flesh he gave the waters regenerative power, so that whoever should afterwards be immersed, with the name of the Trinity invoked, might be cleansed from sins. Thus Christ’s Baptism was instituted then, with the name of the Trinity invoked; in it the Trinity, whose mystery was there made known, baptizes the human being inwardly.  
(*On Consecration*, distinction 4: *Nunquam aqua*.)

### Why it is performed in water alone

8. This sacrament is performed only in water, not in any other liquid, as Christ says: “Unless one is reborn,” and so forth. Therefore it is commanded to be performed uniformly in water, so that it may be understood that, as water washes dirt from the body and clothing, so Baptism, by cleansing, wipes away the stains of the soul and the filth of vices.

Or this is so that no one might be excused by poverty, as might happen if it were performed in wine or oil; and so that a common material for baptizing might be found among all people. Water signified this, flowing from Christ’s side, just as blood was the sign of the other sacrament. Therefore Baptism cannot be consecrated in any liquid other than water.

### On immersion and how often it should be done

9. If it is asked how immersion should be performed, we answer plainly: either once or three times, according to the varying custom of the Church. Hence Gregory, Letter 41, to Bishop Leander:

“Concerning triple immersion in Baptism, no truer answer can be given than what you yourselves have judged. Since in one faith diverse custom does no harm to the holy Church, and since in three subsistences there is one substance, it can in no way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in Baptism either three times or once. For in three immersions the Trinity of persons may be signified, and in one the singularity of the Godhead. We, however, who immerse three times also signify the sacrament of the three days’ burial.”

Accordingly, it is permitted to immerse not only three times but also only once. Yet one immersion is permitted only where such is the Church’s custom. If someone begins doing this where the custom is otherwise, or maintains that immersion ought to be done only once, he renders himself blameworthy.

Hence Haymo [Note: Chapter 14, on the Epistle to the Romans, on the words: “Let every person abound in his own understanding”]: “Cyprian abounded in his own understanding when he immersed little children once in Baptism, because he diligently fulfilled in good works what he understood, abounding in them, although in this he sinned unknowingly. But because he abounded in good works, afterwards corrected by God he abounded in a higher understanding, immersing them three times.”

Here we have that one who immersed once sinned. But this was because the custom of that Church was otherwise, or because he maintained that only one immersion should be performed. Augustine says of triple immersion, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter *Postquam*: “After we have promised to believe, we immerse our heads three times in the sacred font. This order of baptizing is celebrated with a twofold signification of mystery. For you were rightly immersed three times, since you received Baptism in the name of the Trinity. You were rightly immersed three times because you received Baptism in the name of Christ, who rose from the dead on the third day. For that thrice-repeated immersion expresses a type of the Lord’s burial.”

It is thus clear that those to be baptized ought to be immersed three times; nevertheless, if they are immersed only once, they receive true Baptism. And one who immerses only once does not sin unless the Church’s custom opposes it, or unless he maintains that it ought to be done only in that manner.

### When circumcision lost its power

10. It is also customary to ask whether circumcision lost its power immediately upon the institution of Baptism. To this we say that all legal observances ended in Christ’s death. From then on, circumcision lost its power, so that it subsequently did not benefit its observers but rather harmed them. Yet it could benefit until the offering of the true victim. For if the legal observances had ended before the Passion, Christ would not, as it approached, have eaten the old Passover with his disciples.

### On the cause of Baptism’s institution

11. The reason for the institution of Baptism is the renewal of the mind: that the person made old through sin may be renewed through the grace of Baptism. This occurs by the putting away of vices and the bestowal of virtues. For each person is thus made new when, sins having been abolished, he is adorned with virtues. The abolition of sins drives away ugliness; the addition of virtues brings beauty. This is the reality of this sacrament, namely inward cleansing.

### Whether Baptism opened heaven, which circumcision did not open

12. If it is asked whether Baptism opened heaven, which circumcision did not open, we say that neither Baptism nor circumcision opened for us the entrance to the kingdom, but the sacrifice of the Savior did. Had it been offered in the time of circumcision, the people of that time would have entered the kingdom. The reality of this sacrament, therefore, is justification.

## DISTINCTION IV. THAT SOME RECEIVE THE SACRAMENT AND ITS REALITY, OTHERS THE SACRAMENT BUT NOT ITS REALITY, AND OTHERS THE REALITY BUT NOT THE SACRAMENT

1. Here it must be said that some receive the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament; some the sacrament but not the reality; and some the reality but not the sacrament. All little children who are cleansed in Baptism from original sin receive both sacrament and reality together, although some deny that sins are forgiven in Baptism to little children who will perish, relying upon Augustine’s statement in *On the Baptism of Little Children*: “The sacraments effect what they signify only in the elect.” They do not understand that this must be taken thus: although the sacraments effect remission in others, they do not effect it for their salvation, but only for the elect.

For Augustine plainly says that sin is remitted through Baptism to all little children in Baptism. In the *Enchiridion*, chapter 43, he says: “From the newly born infant to the decrepit old man, just as no one is prohibited from Baptism, so there is no one who does not die to sin in Baptism. But little children die only to original sin, while adults die also to all the sins which they have added by living badly to that which they contracted by being born, unless the enormity of their life prevents it.”

Some likewise who are baptized with faith receive both sacrament and reality.

### On those who approach deceitfully
2. But those who approach without faith or deceitfully receive the sacrament, but not its reality. Hence Jerome, in his Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 16, on the words, “You were not washed with water”: “There are washings among pagans and heretics, but they do not wash unto salvation. Even in the Church, those who receive Baptism without full faith receive not the Spirit but water.” Augustine likewise says, at the beginning of his Exposition of Psalm 77: “The sacraments were common to all the Jews, but grace, which is the power of the sacraments, was not common to all. So now Baptism is common to all who are baptized, but the power of Baptism—that is, grace itself—is not.” Likewise, in the book *On the Remedy of Penance*, chapter 2: “Every person who has already become master of his own will, when he approaches the sacrament of the faithful, cannot begin the new life unless he repents of the old. From this repentance only little children are exempt when they are baptized.”

By these and other testimonies it is plainly shown that, in Baptism, grace for the remission of sins is not bestowed upon adults without faith and true repentance; for remission is not given in Baptism even to little children without another’s faith, since they cannot possess faith of their own. Therefore, if anyone approaches deceitfully, without true contrition of heart, he receives the sacrament without its reality.

Yet Augustine seems to say that even one who approaches deceitfully, and who also harbors hatred toward a brother, has all sins forgiven at the very moment of Baptism, and that they immediately return after Baptism. But he does not say this affirmatively. Rather, comparing that opinion with the preceding view, he says thus in [Col. 0847] Book 1 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 12:

> “For those who are baptized with a false heart, either sins are not forgiven at all, because ‘the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit’ [Wisdom 1]; or, having been forgiven at that instant through the power of the sacrament, they are again brought back through deceit. Thus both statements may be true: ‘As many of you as were baptized into Christ’ [Gal. 3], etc.; and, ‘The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit’ [Wisdom 1]: so that the holiness of Baptism clothes him with Christ, while the ruin caused by deceit strips him of Christ. For the Lord plainly teaches, in the case of that servant from whom his master demanded the debt which he had forgiven because the servant refused to forgive his fellow servant, that forgiven sins return where brotherly charity is absent. Thus the grace of Baptism is not prevented from forgiving all sins, even if brotherly hatred remains in the mind of the person whose sins are forgiven. For the guilt of yesterday and whatever remains is discharged; even the very hour and moment before Baptism, and in Baptism itself, are discharged. Thereafter, however, he immediately begins to be guilty not only of subsequent days, but also of past days, hours, and moments, since all that had been forgiven returns.”

But, as stated, he did not say this as an assertion. This is evident from what he says in the same book: “If one comes deceitfully to Baptism, his sins either have been forgiven or have not been forgiven: let them choose whichever they wish.” Clearly, if one attends carefully, Augustine said this not by asserting it, but by raising a question and reporting others’ opinion. For a little later in the same place he says: “Baptism begins to avail for salvation when that deceit has departed through true confession; while it persisted in the heart through wickedness, it did not allow the cleansing of sins to take place.” Therefore sins are not forgiven to one who approaches deceitfully.

### How the words “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” are to be understood

3. It is therefore asked how this is to be understood: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” It may be said that those who are baptized into Christ—that is, in conformity with Christ—put on Christ, whom they possess dwelling in them by grace: just as they die to the oldness of sin, so Christ died to the oldness of punishment. Or it may be resolved differently. For we are said to put on Christ in two ways: either by receiving the sacrament, or by receiving its reality. Hence Augustine, Book 5 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 24:

> “People put on Christ sometimes as far as receiving the sacrament, sometimes as far as sanctification of life. The former may be common to good and bad alike; the latter belongs properly to the good and devout.”

Therefore all who are baptized in Christ’s name put on Christ, either according to reception of the sacrament or according to sanctification of life.

### Concerning those who receive the reality but not the sacrament

4. There are also others, as we stated above, who receive the reality but not the sacrament. Those who shed their blood for Jesus’ name receive the reality, even if not the sacrament. Hence Augustine, in the same work, chapter 22:

> “Whoever dies for confession of Christ without having received the washing of regeneration, it avails for the forgiveness of sins as much as if he had been washed in the sacred font of Baptism.”

You have heard that suffering undergone for Christ’s name supplies the place of Baptism. Nor does suffering alone fulfill Baptism’s role: faith and contrition do so as well, where necessity excludes the sacrament. Augustine plainly teaches this when he says that suffering sometimes fulfills the role of Baptism:

> “From the thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said, ‘Today you shall be with me in Paradise’ [Luke 23], blessed Cyprian draws no slight proof in Book 4 *On Baptism*. As I consider this again and again, I find that not only suffering for Christ’s name can supply what was lacking to Baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if in the constraints of time one cannot obtain help in order to celebrate the mystery of Baptism. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name, but for the deserts of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed, but believed while suffering. How much faith avails, even without the sacrament of visible Baptism—as the Apostle says, ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ [Rom. 10]—is made clear in that thief [Col. 0848]. But this is fulfilled invisibly when not contempt for religion but an exigency of necessity excludes the mystery of Baptism. Baptism can indeed be present where conversion of heart is absent; conversion of heart can indeed be present without Baptism having been received, but not where Baptism is despised. Nor can conversion of heart to God be called such in any way when God’s sacrament is despised.”

Here you have that not only suffering but also faith and contrition confer remission where the sacrament is not despised—as is shown in that thief, who was saved without Baptism not by suffering but by faith.

But some say Augustine retracted this. He did indeed retract the example, in Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 18, but not the proposition. For he says in Book 4: “When I said that suffering could take the place of Baptism, I did not put forward a sufficiently suitable example in the case of that thief, because it is uncertain whether he had not been baptized.” Thus it is established that some are justified and saved without Baptism. Hence Ambrose, *On Valentinian*: “My heart grieves, to use the language of prophecy, because I have lost one whom I was to regenerate; nevertheless, he did not lose the grace which he sought.”

### Matters which seem to oppose the foregoing

5. But this appears to conflict with what the Lord says in John 3: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.” If this is universally true, the things set forth above do not seem true. But it must be understood of those who can be baptized but scorn to be so. Or it may be understood thus: unless someone is reborn by that regeneration which occurs through water and the Holy Spirit, he will not be saved. Yet this regeneration occurs not only by Baptism, but also by repentance and blood.

Hence an authority says that the Apostle spoke of “the foundation of baptisms” in the plural because there is Baptism in water, in blood, and in repentance. This is not said because the sacrament of Baptism occurs otherwise than in water, but because its power—that is, sanctification—is given not only through water but also inwardly through blood or repentance. Reason also supports this. For if Baptism suffices for infants who cannot believe, much more does faith suffice for adults who wish to be baptized but cannot. Hence Augustine: “You ask which is greater, faith or water? I do not hesitate to answer: faith. If then what is less can sanctify, can not what is greater—that is, faith, concerning which Christ says, ‘Whoever believes in me, even though he die, shall live’—do so?”

But some say that no adult can believe in Christ or possess charity without Baptism, unless he sheds blood for the Lord; and they introduce the testimonies below. Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 3, says: “From the time when the Savior said, ‘Unless one is born again,’ etc., no one can receive eternal life without the sacrament of Baptism, except those who shed their blood in the Church.” Likewise: “We believe that no catechumen, though he die amid good works, has eternal life, except through martyrdom, in which all the sacraments of Baptism are fulfilled.” Likewise, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 4: “We believe that for the baptized alone there is a way of salvation.”

But what he said inadequately in these passages, he supplied in the other chapters set forth above. Thus these statements must be understood so as to except only those who have time in which to be baptized. For if anyone who has faith and charity wishes to be baptized but cannot because necessity intervenes, the goodness of the Almighty supplies what was lacking to the sacrament. For while a person is able to discharge the obligation, he is bound unless he does so; but God does not impute against him what he can no longer do but nevertheless wills to do. God has not bound his power to the sacraments.

That invisible sanctification is present and beneficial to some without a visible sacrament Augustine plainly teaches in his commentary on Leviticus, saying that invisible sanctification has been present and profitable to some without visible sacraments. Visible sanctification, however, which occurs through a visible sacrament without the invisible one, can be present but cannot be beneficial. Yet the visible sacrament must not therefore be despised, because one who despises it cannot be sanctified invisibly.

Thus Cornelius and those who were with him, already sanctified by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0849], were baptized [Acts 10]. Nor is visible sanctification to be judged superfluous because invisible sanctification came first. Therefore invisible sanctification can exist and be beneficial without the visible; but visible sanctification which extends only to the sacrament cannot be beneficial without invisible sanctification, since all its usefulness lies there. Simon Magus’s visible Baptism did not benefit him [Acts 8], because invisible sanctification was absent; but it benefited those in whom invisible sanctification was present. Nor does another’s faith avail an infant as much as an adult’s own faith.

For infants, the Church’s faith does not suffice without the sacrament. If they die without Baptism—even if they are being brought for Baptism—they will be condemned, as is demonstrated by many authorities of the saints. Let this one authority suffice. Augustine says, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 7:

> “Hold most firmly that infants who begin to live even in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or who, having been born of their mothers, depart this world without the sacrament of Baptism, are to be punished with eternal punishment. For although they have not had sins of their own actions, nevertheless by conception in carnal concupiscence they have contracted original sin.”

And just as infants who die without Baptism are counted among the unbelievers, so those who are baptized are called believers and are not separated from the fellowship of believers when the Church prays for departed believers. They are believers, therefore, not by virtue but by the sacrament of faith. Hence Augustine:

> “Although infants do not yet possess that faith which also consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of faith itself, that is, Baptism, makes faith: just as it is answered that he believes, so he is also called a believer—not by assenting to the reality itself in his mind, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.”

(Augustine, vol. 2, Letter to Boniface, question 22.)

### What Baptism benefits those who approach with faith

6. It is also commonly asked concerning those who, already sanctified by the Spirit, approach Baptism with faith and charity: what does Baptism confer upon them? For it seems to bestow nothing on them, since by faith and contrition, with their sins already forgiven, they have been justified. To this one may rightly say that they are indeed justified by faith and contrition—that is, cleansed from the stain of sin and released from the debt of eternal punishment—yet they are still bound to temporal satisfaction, by which penitents are bound in the Church.

But when they receive Baptism, they are cleansed both from any sins which they may have contracted in the meantime after conversion and released from external satisfaction. Helping grace and every virtue are increased in them, so that they may then truly be called a new person. The tinder of sin is further weakened in them. Therefore Jerome says that the faith which makes believers is given or nourished in the waters of Baptism: for it is sometimes given there to one who lacks it, and is given to one who already has it so that he may have it more fully. The same is to be understood of other gifts. Therefore one who approaches clean becomes cleaner there, and to everyone who has, more is given there.

Ambrose shows that all external satisfaction is remitted there, commenting on Romans 11, “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance,” and saying:

> “The grace of God in Baptism does not require groaning or weeping or any work, but freely forgives everything.”

[Note: Col. 0849, vol. 4, not far from the end of the commentary on Romans, chapter 12.]

This must indeed be understood of outward groaning or weeping. For no adult is renewed without inward repentance; but the outward satisfactions and afflictions—the penitents’ austerities—are remitted there. Baptism therefore confers much even on one already justified by faith. For in approaching Baptism, he is borne like a branch by a dove into the ark: he was previously inside by God’s judgment, but now is also inside by the Church’s judgment.

But since sin is deleted in Baptism and external satisfaction is not charged, why is the penal condition to which we have been subjected because of sin not removed? The saints teach that this is so because, if people were released from punishment through Baptism, they would regard that release as the price of Baptism, rather than the eternal kingdom. Therefore, though the guilt of sin has been removed, temporal punishment remains, so that the life which will be free of every punishment may be sought more earnestly. It also remains in order to furnish the believer matter for struggle and an occasion for victory: he would not conquer unless he fought, nor would he fight if [Col. 0850] he became immortal in Baptism. (Same source, Book 1, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 24.)

### Of what reality Baptism, given to one already righteous, is a sacrament

7. If it is asked of what reality that Baptism is a sacrament which is given to one already righteous, we say that it is a sacrament both of the reality which preceded it—namely, the remission previously given through faith—and of the remission of temporal punishment or of sin, if there is any, should something be committed in the meantime; and also of the newness and every grace bestowed there. For it is the sign of every reality of which it is the cause.

Nor should you wonder that the reality sometimes precedes the sacrament, since it sometimes follows much later, as in those who approach deceitfully. When they later repent, Baptism will begin to benefit them; in them Baptism was the sacrament of the sanctification which they possess through repentance. But if they never repent or depart from their deceit, of what reality is the Baptism received by them a sacrament? It may be said: of the reality which would occur there if their wickedness did not prevent it.

### Whether infants receive in Baptism the grace by which they can make progress at a later age

8. It is also commonly asked whether infants receive in Baptism grace by which, when they reach the time of using free choice, they can will and do good. For concerning adults who worthily receive the sacrament, there is no doubt that they receive operating and cooperating grace. Yet this becomes fruitless for them if, through free choice, they later commit mortal sin; by the desert of sin they lose the grace bestowed upon them. Hence they are said to do injury to the Holy Spirit and to drive him away from themselves.

But concerning infants, who do not yet use reason, the question is whether in Baptism they receive grace by which, when they reach a more mature age, they can will and do good. It seems that they do not receive it, because that grace is charity and faith, which prepares and assists the will. But who would say that they have received faith and charity? Yet if they have not received grace by which they can act well when adults, then grace given in Baptism does not suffice for them in this state, and they cannot now be good through it unless another grace is added. If that grace is not added, this is not their fault, because they have been justified from sin.

Some think that operating and cooperating grace is bestowed upon all infants in Baptism as a gift, not in its use, so that when they reach a more mature age they may obtain use from the gift, unless by free choice they extinguish the use of the gift through sin. Thus it is their own fault, not a deficiency of grace, that they become evil: being able by God’s gift to have good use, they refused it through free choice and chose evil use.

## DISTINCTION V. THAT BAPTISM IS EQUALLY HOLY WHEN ADMINISTERED BY A GOOD OR A BAD PERSON, TO A GOOD OR A BAD PERSON

1. After this it must be known that the sacrament of Baptism is administered by good and bad ministers, just as it is received by good and bad persons. Baptism administered by a better person is not better; Baptism administered by a less good person is not less good; nor is it bad when administered by a bad person. Nor is a greater gift bestowed in Baptism administered by a good person, nor a lesser gift in Baptism administered by a bad person: it is equal, because it is not a human gift but God’s. This is fully made clear by the testimonies set below.

Augustine, in his fifth tractate on John, says: “Baptism is such as he is in whose power it is administered, not such as he is through whose ministry it is administered.” Likewise, Book 2 *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapter 6: “It can certainly happen that some have true Baptism and do not have true faith.” Likewise, in the sixth tractate on John:

> “If, among good ministers, one is better than another, the Baptism administered through the better is not better. What is administered even through a bad person is in no way bad, because the same Baptism is given. Thus God’s gift is equal through unequal ministers, because it belongs not to them but to him.”

Likewise, in the same work, tractate 5, after the middle:

> “When a bad person baptizes, what is given is one thing, and it is not unequal because the ministers are unequal, but is alike and equal because this is he who baptizes.”

Likewise, in the same place:

> “[Col. 0851] I say, and we all say, that those through whom Baptism is administered ought to be righteous; they ought to be righteous ministers of so great a judge. Let the ministers be righteous if they wish. But if those who sit in Moses’ seat do not wish to be righteous, my master makes me secure—namely, Christ, of whom the Holy Spirit says, ‘This is he who baptizes’ [John 1].”

Likewise, in the same place, tractate 5, not far from the end:

> “Those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized. Therefore, if a drunkard, murderer, or adulterer baptized anyone, if it was Christ’s Baptism, Christ baptized. I do not fear the adulterer, drunkard, or murderer, because I look to the dove, through whom I am told: ‘This is he who baptizes.’”

Likewise, at the end of the fifth tractate on John: “A murderer administered Christ’s Baptism; this sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer.”

Likewise, in the book *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 3, near the end:

> “If anyone in any heresy or schism receives the sacrament of Baptism in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, he receives the sacrament whole. But he will not possess salvation, which is the power of the sacrament, if he possesses that sacrament outside the Catholic Church. Therefore he ought to return to the Church, not to receive again the sacrament of Baptism—which no one ought ever to repeat in any person—but to receive life in the Catholic communion. For Baptism cannot benefit one outside the Church. For Baptism can benefit each person there where almsgiving can benefit him: namely, in the Church.”

Likewise, Isidore, bishop of Rome: “It is not the person baptizing whom God judges, but the Spirit of God who supplies the grace of Baptism, even though the one who baptizes is a pagan.”

In these passages you clearly see that true Baptism is bestowed upon good and bad people and by good and bad people; and yet it is equally holy, and its gift equal in good recipients, whether they are baptized by good persons or bad.

### On the power and ministry of Baptism

2. Ministers possess only the ministry, not the power of Baptism. For Christ reserved the power to himself. John recognized this when he saw the dove descending upon Christ. Hence Augustine, in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, commenting on the first chapter of John:

> “What did John the Baptist know? The Lord. What did he not know? That the power of the Lord’s Baptism would pass from the Lord to no human being, while the ministry would indeed pass on; the power from the Lord to no one, but the ministry to good and bad alike. Let not the dove shrink from the ministry of bad persons; let it look to the Lord’s power. What does a bad minister do where the Lord is good? ‘Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase’ [1 Cor. 3]. If the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil; but Christ’s gift is not contaminated. What flows through him is pure. Water passes through a stone channel to the beds; nothing grows in the stone channel, but the garden produces abundant fruits.”

(Augustine, tractate 5 on John, after the middle of tractate 1.)

Therefore not only good but also bad persons have the ministry of baptizing; but neither has the power of Baptism. Christ gave the ministry to servants, but retained the power for himself. If he had wished, he could have given that power to servants, so that a servant might administer his own Baptism, as it were in his own stead. He could have established his power in one or several servants, so that the force in a servant’s Baptism would be as great as that in the Lord’s Baptism. But he did not will this, lest a servant place his hope in a servant.

The servant baptizes as a minister; the Lord baptizes as one possessing power. If he had given this power to servants—so that what belonged to the Lord belonged to them—there would be as many baptisms as servants. Just as “John’s baptism” was spoken of, so one might speak of Peter’s or Paul’s baptism. To prevent this, the Lord retained the power of Baptism for himself and gave its ministry to servants. Therefore, if a servant says that he baptizes, he speaks correctly, but he baptizes as a minister. Consequently it makes no difference whether a good or bad person baptizes.

Thus no one says, “My Baptism,” though he may say, “my Gospel” or “my wisdom,” even though these too are from God and differ among persons. One person works better than another in preaching the Gospel, and one is wiser than another. But no one can be said to be baptized more or less than another, whether baptized by an inferior or a superior minister.

### What was the power of Baptism which Christ could have given to servants

[Col. 0852]

3. Here it is asked what that power of Baptism was which Christ reserved for himself and could have given to servants. Most hold that it was the power to forgive sins in Baptism. But the power to forgive sins which is in God is God. Therefore others say that he could not have given this power to any servant, because he could give no one the power to be what he himself is, or to possess the essence which he possesses, to whom being is identical with being able.

For they say: if he could give this power to someone, he could give that person power to create creatures, since the latter is no greater a power than the former. To this it may be said that he could have given them a power to forgive sins, though not the identical power by which he himself is powerful: rather, a created power through which a servant could forgive sins.

[Note: Here the Master is not maintained.]

Yet the servant would not be the author of remission but the minister, and not even then without God as author. Just as, in the ministry he possesses the power outwardly to sanctify, so in the ministry he might possess the power inwardly to cleanse. And just as he performs the external act with God as author, who works that outward act with him, so he would cleanse inwardly with God as author, who would use the servant’s word as a kind of ministry.

Likewise, God could create certain things through someone, not through him as author, but as a minister with and in whom he works, just as he himself works in our good works and we work also: neither he alone nor we alone, but he with us and in us. Yet in doing those works we are his ministers, not authors. Therefore he could have given a servant the power to forgive sins in Baptism: that is, so that in inward cleansing the servant would work with the Lord—not the servant without the Lord, nor the Lord without the servant, but the Lord with and in the servant—just as the Lord works with the servant in the outward ministry.

Hence both the Lord and the servant are said to sanctify; but the Lord by invisible grace, the servant by the visible sacrament. Therefore Augustine, commenting on Leviticus:

> “The Lord says: ‘I am the Lord who sanctifies.’ And it was also said of Moses in Exodus 19: ‘And you shall sanctify him.’ But Moses sanctifies through visible sacraments, by ministry; whereas the Lord sanctifies by invisible grace, through the Spirit, where lies the whole fruit of visible sacraments. Without this sanctification, visible sacraments are of no benefit.”

If anyone can explain this better, I do not begrudge him.

## DISTINCTION VI. WHO MAY LAWFULLY BAPTIZE
