1. Let us now add who may lawfully baptize. Isidore says of this in Book 2 *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “It is established that Baptism has been entrusted to priests alone. Its ministry is not lawful even for deacons to perform without a bishop or presbyter, unless the utmost necessity of sickness compels it while they are far away; and this is permitted even to faithful laypersons.” From the Fifth Council of Carthage. Likewise: “A woman, even if holy, must not presume to baptize unless necessity compels.”

It is commonly asked whether those baptized by heretics ought to be rebaptized. To this we say briefly: whoever baptizes, if the form handed down by Christ is preserved, administers true Baptism; therefore one who receives it must not be rebaptized. Hence Bede:

> “Whether heretic, schismatic, or criminal, whoever baptizes in confession of the Holy Trinity: one baptized by us Catholics cannot validly be rebaptized, lest the confession and invocation of the Trinity appear to be nullified.”

Likewise Augustine:

> “Although there is one Baptism both of heretics—namely, those who baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and of the Catholic Church, nevertheless those baptized outside the Church receive Baptism not unto salvation but unto destruction. They possess the form of the sacrament but deny its power. Therefore the Church does not rebaptize them, because they were baptized in the name of the Trinity, and that is the form of the sacrament.”

Likewise: “To rebaptize a heretic who has received these signs of sanctification is altogether a sin; but to rebaptize a Catholic is a most enormous crime.”

From these things it is plainly gathered that even those baptized by heretics, when the character of Christ has been preserved, must not be rebaptized, but only [Col. 0853] reconciled by the laying on of hands, in order that they may receive the Holy Spirit and as a sign of detestation of heretics.

There are, however, certain doctors, such as Cyprian and some others, who seem to say that Baptism cannot be administered by heretics and that those said to have been baptized by them must be rebaptized when they come to the Church. But this is true of those who presume to baptize outside the Church’s form. Cyprian nevertheless seems there to have departed from the truth when he says of a heretic: “How can he sanctify water when he himself is unclean, and when the Holy Spirit is not with him? Since the Lord says in the Law, ‘Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean,’ who can give what he himself does not possess?”

Augustine suggests that Cyprian said this through ignorance:

> “The glorious martyr Cyprian, who in his excessive detestation of them refused to recognize Baptism administered among heretics or schismatics, had such great merits following him even to the triumph of martyrdom that both the shadow cast over him was dispelled by the light of the charity in which he excelled, and whatever still had to be fought against was removed by the sickle of suffering. Nor are we, who recognize the truth of Baptism and the wickedness of heretics, for that reason better than Cyprian, any more than we are better than Peter because we do not compel Gentiles to Judaize.”

### That no one is baptized in the maternal womb

2. It must also be known that although there is a threefold immersion because of the mystery of the Trinity, it is nevertheless counted as one Baptism. Nor must it be unknown that no one can be baptized in the maternal womb, even if the mother is baptized. Hence Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, chapter 24:

> “Those who are in their mothers’ wombs cannot be baptized because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ; nor can regeneration be said to occur in one whom generation has not preceded.”

Likewise Augustine, to Dardanus: “No one can be born again before he has been born.”

But if Jeremiah and John the Baptist, who are read to have been sanctified from the womb—and, as some think, Jacob as well—are raised in objection, we say that, if sanctification there is understood as inward cleansing, it must be regarded as among the miracles of divine power. Augustine says this, speaking ambiguously on the matter:

> “If the use of reason and will was so hastened in that child that, within the maternal womb, he could already know and believe what in other infants age must await before they can do so, this must be regarded as among the miracles of divine power and not drawn into an example for human nature. For when God willed it, even a beast of burden spoke.”

Likewise:

> “Of Jeremiah it is written: ‘Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you.’ Yet that sanctification by which we become God’s temple belongs only to those who have been reborn. For unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter God’s kingdom. But no one is reborn unless he is first born. Therefore that sanctification may be understood according to predestination.”

Here he seems to speak doubtfully. He also says: “It was not said that the infant believed in the womb, but that he leaped for joy; and Elizabeth does not say, ‘He leaped for joy in faith,’ but ‘He leaped for joy in my womb.’ This sanctification may have been an indication that a greater reality was to be known, not a reality known by the infant.” He speaks without assertion about this sanctification, not determining how it should be understood: whether it is a sign of a future reality or the reality of justification wrought by the Spirit.

But it is better to say that they were justified in the womb beyond the common law, and anticipated by grace, with all sins forgiven; this too is taught by many testimonies of the saints.

### Whether Baptism is valid when the words are pronounced incorrectly

3. It is also commonly asked whether Baptism is valid if those words are pronounced incorrectly. Zacharias writes to Boniface:

> “Your messengers reported to me that there had been a priest in that province who was wholly ignorant of Latin. When baptizing, unaware of Latin speech and mangling the language, he would say: ‘I baptize you in the name of the Fatherland, and the Daughter, and the Holy Spiritess’ (*in nomine Patria, et Filia, et Spiritus sancta*). Because of this you considered rebaptizing. But if the one who baptized, introducing neither error nor heresy, had said this merely through ignorance of Roman speech while mangling the language, we cannot agree that they should be baptized anew.”

### Pope Leo

[Col. 0854]

4. Furthermore, it must be known that, in the case of those concerning whom no evidence survives among relatives, household members, or neighbors from whom it could be learned that they were baptized, action should be taken to ensure that they are reborn, lest they perish. In their case, reason permits what is not shown to have been done to appear to be repeated. What is not known to have been conferred ought to be conferred upon them, because rash presumption does not intrude where there is careful piety.

### Concerning one who is immersed in play

5. It is also commonly asked concerning one who, joking like an actor, is nevertheless immersed with mention of the Trinity: whether he has been baptized. Augustine does not decide this in volume 2, Letter 23 to Boniface, saying:

> “If the entire act were performed playfully, theatrically, and in jest, whether Baptism so administered should be approved, I would judge that divine judgment should be sought through the miracle of some revelation, invoked by prayer.”

Yet it seems to the learned that this was not Baptism. Thus, when people are immersed in a bath or river in the name of the Trinity, it is nevertheless not Baptism, because the act is not done with the intention of baptizing. For in this and other sacraments, just as the form must be preserved, so there must be the intention of celebrating it.

Nor should this trouble you: some bring infants to Baptism not with the faith that they may be regenerated by the Spirit unto eternal life, but because they think they will receive temporal health through this remedy. The infants are not for this reason not regenerated, even though they are not offered by those persons with this intention.

### That there were two times at which persons were baptized

6. It must also be recognized that two seasons are to be observed for the baptism of the elect, namely Easter and Pentecost, so that the sacrament of Baptism is celebrated on the Saturday of Easter or Pentecost. But those pressed by the necessity of death or danger must be baptized at every time.

### On the response of godparents
7. Moreover, all who come to Baptism ought to profess their faith and explain what they have come to the church to seek. Hence the person to be baptized is asked: “What have you come to the church to seek?” If an adult, he answers for himself: “Faith,” that is, the sacrament of faith and instruction. Likewise, when questioned point by point, he answers that he believes in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. But if he is an infant, unable to believe or speak, another answers on his behalf. Hence Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book 2, chapter 24: “Infants are baptized while another makes the profession, since they do not yet know how to speak or believe. Just as another professes for the sick, mute, or deaf while they are baptized, so also must it be done for penitents.” But if another answers for one who is able to answer, it is not valid in the same way, as has been said. He is of age; let him speak for himself.

But if it is asked in what sense one says for an infant, “I believe,” or, “I seek faith,” we say that this should be understood of the sacrament of faith: he is said to seek it when he is brought to the church, and to have faith when he is baptized. Thus the sense of “I seek faith” is: “I am ready to receive the sacrament of faith”; and of “I believe”: “I receive the sacrament of faith”; that is: “This infant is ready to receive the sacrament of faith.” Hence Augustine, Letter 23 to Boniface: “To believe is nothing other than to have faith; and therefore, when it is answered that the infant believes, though he does not yet possess the effect of faith, it is answered that he has faith because of the sacrament of faith, and that he turns to God because of the sacrament of conversion.”

But it is still asked in what sense it is answered for an infant: “I believe in God the Father, and in Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit.” Is this said concerning the sacrament of faith or concerning faith as an inward disposition? If concerning the sacrament, why are the persons individually distinguished by name? But if concerning the disposition of faith, how is it true, since the infant lacks it? Or is the infant pledged to do this when he has grown up, just as he is pledged to renounce all the pomps of the devil? If, having become an adult, he does not keep this, is he bound, or is the sponsor?

Certainly, it may also be said that a pledge is made for the infant that, if he reaches a more mature age, he will both renounce the pomps of the devil and hold the sound faith whose sacrament he now receives. The infant for whom this pledge is made will be bound by it, [Col. 0855] not the sponsor—provided that the sponsor has done, so far as lies in him, what is necessary for the surety to be fulfilled; for a godparent is required to show diligent concern for the person for whom he has pledged himself. On this Augustine says: “You have given the most certain surety, by which you promised to renounce the pomps of the devil.”

## On Catechism and Exorcism

8. This questioning and response concerning faith takes place in the catechism, to which exorcism is added. For catechism and exorcism take place before Baptism; after the catechism follows exorcism, so that the hostile power may be driven out from one who has already been instructed in faith. *Exorcism* is called in Latin from the Greek an “adjuration”; *catechism*, “instruction.” To catechize is to instruct, for example concerning the Creed and the rudiments of faith. To exorcize is to adjure, as in: “Come out of him, unclean spirit.” The *symbolum* [Creed] is a sign or a collection. It is a sign because by it believers are distinguished from unbelievers; a collection because the sufficiency and completeness of the whole faith are gathered there.

Catechism and exorcism belong to neophytes, and ought rather to be called sacramentals than sacraments. A *neophyte* means a novice or beginner; and one recently converted to the faith, or untrained in the discipline of religious life, is called a neophyte. These therefore precede Baptism, not because Baptism cannot be true without them, but in order that the candidate for Baptism may be instructed in the faith, may know to whom he henceforth becomes indebted, and that the devil’s power in him may be diminished.

Hence Rabanus: “Before Baptism, the office of catechizing ought to come first in a person, so that the catechumen may receive the rudiments of faith and know to whom he henceforth becomes indebted.” Likewise Augustine: “Infants are breathed upon and exorcized, so that the devil’s power may be driven from them, lest he now strive to overthrow them and prevent them from obtaining Baptism.” Therefore it is not God’s creature that is breathed upon or exorcized in infants, but the devil, that he may withdraw from the human being.

## DISTINCTION VII. ON CONFIRMATION

1. We must now add something concerning the sacrament of Confirmation, whose efficacy is commonly questioned. Its form is clear: namely, the words spoken by the bishop when he signs the baptized upon their foreheads with sacred chrism. This sacrament cannot be performed by anyone other than the highest priests; nor is it read that, in the time of the apostles, it was performed by any others than the apostles themselves. It cannot or ought not to be performed by any except those who hold their place. For if it should be undertaken otherwise, it is held void and without effect, and shall not be reckoned among ecclesiastical sacraments.

Priests may touch the baptized on the breast, but may not sign them with chrism on the forehead. The efficacy of the sacrament is the gift of the Holy Spirit for strengthening; he was given in Baptism for remission. Hence Rabanus: “By the laying on of the hand of the high priest, the Paraclete is bestowed upon the baptized person, that he may be strengthened through the Holy Spirit to preach to others what he himself obtained in Baptism.” Likewise: “All believers ought, after Baptism, to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, that they may be found fully Christian.”

### Melchiades, in a Letter to the Bishops of Spain

2. “Know that both are great sacraments, but one must be held in greater veneration, since it is conferred by greater persons.” Behold, he calls Confirmation the greater sacrament; perhaps not because it confers greater efficacy and benefit, but because it is conferred by persons of greater dignity and is performed upon a more dignified part of the body, namely the forehead; or perhaps because it supplies a greater increase of virtues, although Baptism has greater power for remission.

This seems to be suggested by Rabanus when he says that, in the anointing of Baptism, the Holy Spirit descends in order to consecrate a dwelling for God; but in this sacrament the same Spirit’s sevenfold grace comes into a person with all fullness of holiness and virtue.

This sacrament ought to be received by fasting persons and administered to fasting persons, as should Baptism also, unless necessity compels otherwise. Nor ought it to be repeated, any more than Baptism or Orders. No sacrament is to be treated with injury; and this is thought to occur when that which ought not to be repeated is repeated. But whether any sacraments, or none, can be repeated is a question. For Augustine plainly says concerning Baptism and Orders that they ought not to be repeated: “Both are sacraments, and are given with a certain consecration—the one when a person is baptized, the other when he is ordained. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church, because neither is to be treated with injury.” This must undoubtedly also be maintained concerning Confirmation. But whether the others may or ought to be repeated will be discussed later.

## DISTINCTION VIII. ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE ALTAR AND THE EUCHARIST

1. After the sacraments of Baptism and Confirmation follows the sacrament of the Eucharist. By Baptism we are cleansed; by the Eucharist we are brought to completion in the good. Baptism extinguishes the burning heat of vices; the Eucharist spiritually refreshes. Hence it is excellently called *Eucharistia*, that is, “good grace,” because in this sacrament there is not merely a proof of power and grace, but the whole one is received who is the fountain and origin of all grace.

Its figure came beforehand when God rained manna upon the fathers in the wilderness, who were fed daily with the food of heaven. Hence: “Man ate the bread of angels” [John 6]. But those who ate that bread then died. This living bread, however, which came down from heaven, gives life to the world. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That bred worms when reserved for the next day; this is free from all corruption. Whoever receives it reverently shall not see corruption.

That manna was given to the ancients after the crossing of the Red Sea, where the Hebrews were delivered when the Egyptians had been drowned (Exodus 16). So too this heavenly manna ought to be given only to those who have been reborn. That bodily bread led the ancient people through the wilderness to the land of promise. This heavenly food carries the faithful, passing through the wilderness of this age, up to heaven. Hence it is rightly called *viaticum*, because, refreshing us on the way, it brings us as far as our homeland.

Therefore, just as in the Red Sea the figure of Baptism came beforehand, so in manna came the signification of the Lord’s body. These two sacraments were shown when blood and water flowed from Christ’s side, because Christ came through the blood of redemption and the water of washing to redeem us from the devil and from sin, just as he delivered the Israelites through the blood of the paschal lamb from the destroyer and through the water of the Red Sea from the Egyptians.

Melchizedek also displayed the rite of this sacrament when he offered bread and wine to Abraham. Hence, as Ambrose says in *On the Sacraments*, book 4, chapter 3, it is made clear that Christian sacraments are earlier than Jewish ones.

### On the Institution of the Sacrament

2. Here four further matters require consideration: the sacrament, its institution, its form, and its reality. The Lord instituted the sacrament when, after the typical lamb, he gave his body and blood to the disciples at supper. Hence Eusebius of Emesa: “Because he was about to remove the body he had assumed from their eyes and carry it up to the stars, it was necessary that on the day of the supper he should consecrate for us the sacrament of his body and blood, so that through the mystery there might continually be worshipped what had once been offered as the price.”

### On the Form

3. Its form is what he there uttered, saying: “This is my body”; and afterwards: “This is my blood.” When these words are spoken, the conversion of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood takes place; the rest is said in praise of God.

Hence Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book 4, chapter 4: “This sacrament is effected by Christ’s word, because Christ’s word changes the creature; and thus from bread Christ’s body comes to be, and wine mixed with water and put into the chalice becomes blood through the consecration of the heavenly word. By what words is the consecration effected? Attend to the words: ‘Take and eat of this, all of you; this is my body’; and again: ‘Take and drink of this, all of you; this is my blood’ [Matthew 26]. Through everything else that is said, praise is rendered to God and prayer is offered beforehand for the people and for kings.”

Likewise Augustine: “It must be believed that the sacraments are effected in those words of Christ; everything else is nothing other than praises, or entreaties and petitions of the faithful.” Behold what the institution [Col. 0857] and form of this sacrament are.

Here it is worthy of consideration why he gave this sacrament to the disciples after supper. The Lord Jesus, about to depart to the invisible realities of his Father’s majesty, celebrated the typical Passover with his disciples; wishing to entrust to them a memorial, he gave them his body and blood under the appearance of bread and wine, in such a way as to show that the sacraments of the old law—among which the chief was the sacrifice of the paschal lamb—were ended in his death, and that the sacraments of the new law were substituted, among which the mystery of the Eucharist excels.

He gave it after the other food also so that this one sacrament might be more firmly impressed upon the disciples’ memory and thereafter be frequently observed by the Church. But he did not thereby establish a rule for the future that it should be received after other foods; rather, it ought to be received by fasting persons, as the Apostle teaches, in order that it may be judged distinctly—that is, distinguished—from other foods. The Lord left its arrangement to the apostles.

Hence Augustine, Letter 118 to Januarius: “It is apparent that, when the disciples first received the Eucharist, they did not receive it fasting. Yet for this reason the universal Church must not be accused because it is always received by fasting persons. For the Holy Spirit determined that, in honor of so great a sacrament, the Lord’s body should enter the mouth of a Christian before other foods; and therefore this custom is observed everywhere. For it does not follow, because the Lord gave it after food, that people who have dined or supped ought to receive it, as those did whom the Apostle rebukes. For the Savior, in order to commend more strongly the depth of that mystery, wished this to be the last thing impressed upon the hearts and memory of the disciples from whom he was about to depart to his Passion. But he reserved for the apostles, through whom he was to order the churches, the teaching of the order in which it should thereafter be received.”

### On the Sacrament and Its Reality

4. Let us now see what is sacrament there, and what is reality. A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace. Therefore the appearance of bread and wine that is seen there is the sacrament—that is, the sign of a sacred reality—because, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, it causes something else to come into knowledge. The appearances therefore retain the names of the things that previously existed, namely bread and wine.

This sacrament has a twofold reality: one contained and signified; the other signified but not contained. The reality contained and signified is Christ’s flesh, which he drew from the Virgin, and the blood which he shed for us. The reality signified but not contained is the unity of the Church in the predestined, called, justified, and glorified. This is twofold: Christ’s flesh and blood.

Hence Jerome, commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Christ’s flesh and blood are understood in two ways: either as that flesh which was crucified and buried, and that blood which was shed by the soldier’s lance; or as the spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, John 6: ‘My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink’; and: ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’”

Therefore three things must here be distinguished: one which is sacrament only; another which is sacrament and reality; and a third which is reality and not sacrament. The sacrament and not the reality is the visible appearance of bread and wine. The sacrament and reality is Christ’s own flesh and blood. The reality and not the sacrament is his mystical flesh.

Moreover, that visible appearance is a sacrament of the twofold reality, because it signifies both realities and bears an explicit likeness of each. For just as bread, above other foods, refreshes and sustains the body, and wine gladdens and intoxicates a person, so Christ’s flesh spiritually refreshes and nourishes the inner person more than other graces. Hence Psalm 22: “My intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!”

It also bears a likeness to the mystical reality, which is the unity of believers. For just as one bread is made from many grains, and wine from many grapes flows together into one, so ecclesiastical unity consists of many persons among the faithful. Hence the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 10: “Though many, we are one bread and one body,” etc.

Hence Augustine, *On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit*: “The Church is called one bread and one body because, just as one bread is made from many grains and one body [Col. 0858] is composed of many members, so the Church is joined together from many faithful persons through love binding them together. Christ consecrated this mystery of our peace and unity upon his table. Whoever receives this mystery of unity and does not maintain the bond of peace receives this mystery not for himself but against himself.”

Christ’s own body, taken from the Virgin, is also a sacrament of this reality; for just as Christ’s body consists of many most pure and spotless members, so the fellowship of the Church consists of many persons free from the stain of grave sin. In figure of this, the ark of the Lord was made of *sethim* wood, which is incorruptible and resembles white thorns.

## DISTINCTION IX. ON TWO WAYS OF EATING

1. And just as that sacrament has two realities, so there are also two ways of eating: one sacramental, by which the good and the evil eat; the other spiritual, by which the good alone eat.

Hence Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord*, and *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “What It Is to Eat Christ”: “What is it to eat Christ? It is not merely to receive his body in the sacrament; for many receive it unworthily. Rather, it is to remain in him and to have him remaining in oneself. For he eats spiritually who remains in the unity of Christ and the Church which the sacrament signifies. For one who is at discord with Christ neither eats Christ’s flesh nor drinks his blood, even though he daily receives, unto his own judgment, the sacrament of so great a thing.”

Augustine, distinguishing spiritual eating from sacramental eating, says in Tractate 25 on John: “Why prepare your stomach and teeth? Believe, and you have eaten. For to believe in him is to eat the bread and wine. Whoever believes in him eats him.”

Likewise, Tractate 26 on John and *On the Remedy of Penance*; *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “How”: “How is Christ eaten? As he himself says, John 6: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ If he remains in me and I in him, then he drinks; but whoever does not remain in me, nor I in him, even if he receives the sacrament, acquires great torment.”

Likewise, *On Consecration*, distinction 2: “No one should doubt that then a person becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when he becomes a member of Christ. Nor is he deprived of fellowship in that bread and cup even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body; for he is not deprived of the benefit of that sacrament when he is found to possess that which the sacrament signifies. For in that sacrament he commended his body and blood to us, and he made us ourselves into that body. For we too have become his body.”

Likewise, *On the Sacraments of the Faithful*: “Whoever is at discord with Christ does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, although he daily receives, to his own judgment, the sacrament of so great a thing.”

### On the Error of Those Who Say That Only the Good Receive Christ’s Body

2. Some people, reading these and similar words about spiritual eating with dull hearts, have been so enveloped in the darkness of error that they have presumed to say that Christ’s body and blood are received only by the good and not by the evil.

But it must undoubtedly be maintained that the good receive them not only sacramentally but also spiritually; the evil receive them only sacramentally—that is, under the sacrament, namely under the visible appearance, they receive Christ’s flesh taken from the Virgin and the blood shed for us, but not the mystical flesh, which belongs only to the good. This is proved by the testimonies set forth below.

Gregory: “In sinners and in those who receive unworthily there are indeed the true flesh and true blood of Christ, but in essence, not with saving efficacy.”

Likewise Augustine, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Because He Suffered,” paragraph “Our Lord”: “Many receive the Lord’s body unworthily; of them the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 11: ‘Whoever eats and drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’ By this we are taught how greatly we must beware of receiving a good thing badly. For behold, evil results when good is received badly; just as, conversely, good resulted for the Apostle when evil was received well, namely when Satan’s thorn was patiently endured. Therefore evils benefit the good, as Satan’s angel benefited Paul; and holy things harm the evil. To the good they are for salvation; to the evil, for judgment. Hence whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself—not because that thing is evil, but because an evil person receives badly what is good.”

The same author, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, in book 4 of the *Dialogues*, on John, Tractate 26, after the middle: “A person who receives Christ’s body unworthily does not make what he receives evil because he himself is evil, nor, because he receives it not unto salvation, does he receive nothing. For the Lord’s body and blood were no less present in those to whom the Apostle says: ‘Whoever eats unworthily,’ etc.”

By these and many other testimonies it is plainly shown that even the evil receive Christ’s true body and blood, but sacramentally, not spiritually.

### On the Interpretation of Certain Ambiguously Stated Words

3. In accordance with these two ways of receiving, the meaning of certain ambiguously expressed words must be distinguished. Augustine says in his Tractate on John 6, after the middle: “The good person receives the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament; the evil person receives the sacrament and not the reality.” Here he calls Christ’s own body, born from the Virgin, the sacrament; and his spiritual flesh the reality. The good person, therefore, receives both kinds of Christ’s flesh; the evil person receives only the sacrament—that is, Christ’s body under the sacrament—and not the spiritual reality.

Likewise, book 5, chapter 8, of *On Baptism against the Donatists*: “The one who does not eat eats, and the one who eats does not eat, because one who does not eat sacramentally sometimes eats spiritually, and conversely.” Those who eat spiritually are said to receive the reality of flesh and blood because they possess its efficacy, namely remission of sins. This seems to be what is prayed for when it is said: “Bring about in us, Lord, we pray, through your sacraments what they contain, so that what we now perform under the appearance we may receive in the reality of the things.”

By “reality of the things” he means their efficacy, as though saying: “Through these sacraments grant that, just as we receive Christ’s flesh sacramentally, so we may receive it spiritually.” Or the priest asks that Christ, who is now truly received under the appearance of bread and wine, may someday be received in manifest vision, as he is in the essence of his divinity.

It is therefore established that the good and the evil receive Christ’s body; but the good unto salvation, the evil unto destruction. (Gregory, in an Easter homily.)

## DISTINCTION X. ON THE HERESY OF OTHERS WHO SAY THAT CHRIST’S BODY IS NOT ON THE ALTAR EXCEPT AS A SIGN

1. There are others who exceed the madness of the preceding group. Measuring God’s power by the manner of natural things, they oppose the truth more boldly and dangerously, asserting that Christ’s body or blood is not on the altar, nor is the substance of bread or wine converted into the substance of flesh and blood; rather, they say Christ meant, “This is my body,” as the Apostle meant when he said, “The rock was Christ.”

For they say that Christ’s body is there only sacramentally, that is, as a sign, and that it is eaten by us only as a sign. They take their occasion for error from the words of Truth, from which the first heresy arose among Christ’s disciples. For when he said: “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he shall not have eternal life,” they, not understanding, said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” And they went back. When they had departed, he instructed the twelve who remained:

“It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Have you understood them spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood them carnally? Even so, they are spirit and life, but not there. Understand spiritually what I have spoken. You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink the blood which those who crucify me will shed. I have commended to you a certain sacrament; understood spiritually, it will give you life. But the flesh profits nothing.”

There are also other passages that supply fuel for their madness. Augustine says, in his exposition of Psalm 54, not far from its end: “Until the age is ended, the Lord is above; yet the Lord, who is Truth, is also here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place, but his truth is spread everywhere.” Likewise, in Letter 57 to Dardanus, near the beginning: “Christ is one person, God and man: everywhere in respect of that by which he is God; in heaven in respect of that by which he is man.” He also says, Matthew 26: “You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” These and other passages are used by the aforesaid heretics to maintain their error.

### Determination of the Foregoing

2. All these passages must be understood in the same way. For these words do not deny that Christ’s true body is received by the faithful or is present on the altar. Rather, through them Truth instructed the apostles, and us in them, that he would give us his body and blood not divided into pieces—as those disciples who turned back supposed—but whole; and not visibly in human form, but invisibly under the appearance of bread and wine.

Augustine confirms this meaning, saying in the Letter to Irenaeus: “The very body, indeed, and not the body as it appeared, is eaten; the very body indeed invisibly, not visibly.” Likewise: “And if it must be celebrated, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.”

So also it must be understood that Christ’s body is in one place, namely visibly in human form. For his truth, that is, his divinity, is everywhere; and his truth, that is, his true body, is also upon every altar wherever it is celebrated. So too the saying, “You always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me,” must be understood according to his bodily presence, namely that by which he associated with them. Likewise, he is in heaven in respect of that by which he is man, namely visibly; but invisibly he is on the altar, because he does not appear in human form but is covered by the appearance of bread and wine. Hence his flesh, which truly is on the altar, is called invisible. But because it does not appear in its own form, it is called invisible.

For Augustine says in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*: “This is what we say and strive by every means to demonstrate: that the sacrifice of the Church is made up of two things and consists of two things—the visible appearance of the elements, and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Thus Christ’s person also consists of and is made up of God and man, since Christ is true God and true man; because every thing contains in itself the nature and truth of those things of which it is composed. But the sacrifice of the Church is composed of two things: the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Therefore Christ’s body itself is both sacrament and reality of the sacrament.”

Behold, he called Christ’s flesh invisible because it is received and handled covered under the appearance of bread; and in the same place he called Christ’s body both sacrament and reality. This confirms what we said above. He then adds what moves the reader still more:

“His flesh is that which we receive in the sacrament, covered under the appearance of bread; and his blood is that which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine. The flesh, namely the sacrament of the flesh, and the blood, namely the sacrament of the blood, signify, by flesh and blood both invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, Christ’s body visible and tangible, full of grace and divine majesty.”

### What Is the Meaning of the Foregoing?

3. Attend carefully to these words, because Augustine here employs a trope by which things that signify receive the names of the things they signify. Here the visible appearance of bread is called by the name of flesh, and the visible appearance of wine by the name of blood; while Christ’s flesh is called invisible and intelligible because, under that appearance, flesh is not seen but understood; and so too with the blood.

Therefore invisible flesh is said to be the sacrament of visible flesh because the appearance of bread—according to which Christ’s flesh is not seen as flesh—is the sacrament of visible flesh; for by invisible flesh, that is, by the appearance under which Christ’s flesh is not seen as flesh, Christ’s body is signified, which is visible and tangible where it appears in its own form. The same must be understood concerning the blood.

Augustine confirms this meaning by explaining how the foregoing should be understood, since he had spoken obscurely. He subsequently says that bread is called Christ’s body, though it is truly the sacrament of Christ’s body which was placed upon the cross; just as the immolation performed by the priest’s hands is called Christ’s Passion, not in the reality of the thing, but by the mystery of signification; and just as the sacrament of faith is called faith.

This sufficiently answers the heretics and their objections, who deny that Christ’s true body is on the altar and that bread is converted into body or wine into blood by mystical consecration, saying: “Who would dare to eat his Lord? Who would also dare to say that Christ’s body is daily formed from matter or substance which was not the Virgin’s flesh?”

### He Proves by Authorities That Christ’s True Body Is on the Altar and That Bread Is Converted into It

4. They raise these and similar objections, following the law of nature in the divine mystery; the testimonies below refute their unbelief.

For Truth says, Matthew 26: “Take; this is my body.” Likewise Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 9: “If Elijah’s word had such power as to bring fire down from heaven, will Christ’s word not have such power as to change substances? Of the works of the whole world it is written: ‘He spoke, and they were made,’ etc. Therefore the Word—that is, the Son—who could make from nothing what did not exist, cannot change the things that exist into what they were not? For it is no less to create than to change the new natures of things.”

Likewise, in the same work: “If we seek the order of nature, a woman joined with a man was accustomed to give birth. It is therefore clear that the Virgin gave birth outside the order of nature, and that what we effect is the body from the Virgin. Why, then, do you seek the order of nature here in Christ’s body, when the birth itself from the Virgin was outside nature?”

Likewise, in the same work: “Before the blessing, another appearance is named; after consecration, the body is signified. Before consecration it is called something else; after consecration it is called blood. You say, ‘Amen,’ that is, ‘It is true.’ Let the heart perceive what the word declares.”

Likewise Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*: “In the appearance of bread and wine which we see, we honor invisible realities, that is, flesh and blood. Nor do we weigh these two appearances in the same way as before consecration, since we faithfully confess that before consecration they are bread and wine, which nature formed; but after consecration, Christ’s flesh and blood, which the blessing consecrated.”

Likewise Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 4: “The bread on the altar is ordinary bread before the sacred words; when consecration has been added, from bread Christ’s flesh comes to be. But how can what is bread be Christ’s body? By consecration, which is effected by Christ’s word.”

Likewise, in a sermon *On the Words of the Gospel*: “If there is such force in the Lord’s word that things which did not exist begin to exist, how much more effectual is it that things which existed should remain and be changed into something else? Thus what was bread before consecration is now Christ’s body after consecration, because Christ’s word changes the creature; and so Christ’s body comes to be from bread, and wine mixed with water and put into the chalice becomes blood through the consecration of the heavenly word.”

Likewise Augustine: “Just as Christ’s true flesh is created without sexual intercourse through the Holy Spirit, so by the same Spirit Christ’s body and blood are consecrated from the substance of bread and wine. Christ’s body is both reality and figure: reality, when Christ’s body and blood are made from the substance of bread and wine by the power of the Holy Spirit; figure, in what is outwardly perceived.”

Likewise Eusebius of Emesa: “The invisible priest changes visible creatures, by his word and secret power, into the substance of his body and blood.”

From these and many other authorities it is established that Christ’s true body and blood are on the altar; indeed, the whole Christ is there under each species, and the substance of bread is converted into his body and the substance of wine into his blood.

## DISTINCTION XI. ON THE MODES OF CONVERSION

1. But if it is asked what kind of conversion this is—formal, substantial, or of another kind—I am unable to define it. Yet I know that it is not formal, because the appearances of the things that existed before remain, along with taste [Col. 0862] and weight. To some it seems substantial, who say that substance is converted into substance in such a way that this essentially becomes that. The authorities cited above seem to agree with this understanding.

### Objection

2. But others object to this position as follows: “If the substance of bread or wine is substantially converted into Christ’s body or blood, then every day some substance becomes Christ’s body or blood which was not previously body; and today something is Christ’s body which was not so yesterday; and Christ’s body is daily increased and formed from matter from which it was not made at the conception.”

This may be answered as follows: Christ’s body is said to be effected by the heavenly word not because that body, formed at the Virgin’s conception, is thereafter formed anew, but because the substance of bread or wine, which had not previously been Christ’s body or blood, becomes body and blood through the heavenly word. Therefore priests are said to effect Christ’s body and blood because, through their ministry, the substance of bread becomes flesh and the substance of wine becomes Christ’s blood. Yet nothing is added to Christ’s body or blood, nor is Christ’s body or blood increased.

### Augustine, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*
3. But if you ask how this can be done, I answer briefly: the mystery of faith can beneficially be believed, but it cannot beneficially be investigated. Therefore, that Christ’s body is not increased by the change of bread into it, nor his blood by the conversion of wine, must be ascribed to the will and power of him who brought forth that same body from the Virgin. Thus that substance comes to be without any increase of his body.

Some nevertheless do not grant that the substance of bread ever becomes Christ’s flesh, although it becomes Christ’s flesh; just as flour became bread and water became wine, yet one does not say, “Flour is bread,” or “Water is wine.” Others, however, grant that what was bread or wine is, after consecration, body and blood; yet it does not follow that “Bread is Christ’s flesh,” or “Wine is blood,” because the substance of bread or wine, after it has become Christ’s flesh or blood, is no longer the substance of bread or wine, but flesh and blood.

Accordingly, a distinction seems necessary when one says: “The substance of bread,” or “that which was bread,” is now Christ’s body. For bread remaining as bread is not Christ’s body; but, having been changed into that which it has become, it is Christ’s body. Nor do we say that the substance of bread or wine is the material of the Lord’s body or blood, because his body is not formed from it as from matter; rather, it itself is formed into that body and becomes it. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 3, chapter 4:

> We call Christ’s body that which, taken from the fruits of the earth and consecrated by a mystical prayer, we receive in remembrance of the Lord’s passion. Although it is brought by human hands to that visible appearance, it is not sanctified so as to be so worthy a sacrament except through the invisible working of the Spirit of God.

### Some maintain that the bread is said to pass into Christ’s body

4. Some explain that conversion in this way: beneath those accidents under which the substance of bread and wine formerly existed, after consecration there is the substance of body and blood; yet it is not affected by those accidents. Thus they maintain that the bread is said to pass into Christ’s body because where bread was, Christ’s body is now. But if this is so, what becomes of the substance of bread and wine? They say that it is either dissolved into pre-existing matter or reduced to nothing.

Others have thought that the substance of bread and wine remains there, and that Christ’s body and blood are also there; and that for this reason that substance is said to become this one, because where this is, that is also. This is astonishing. They also call the very substance of bread or wine a sacrament. But that no substance is there except Christ’s body and blood is clearly shown from what has been said and what follows.

For Ambrose says, *On the Sacraments and Allegories*:

> This bread which we receive in the mystery, I understand, of course, to be that which was formed by the hand of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb and baked by the fire of suffering upon the altar of the cross. For the bread of angels became the food of human beings.

[Col. 0863] Hence Truth says in John 6: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven”; and again: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world.” From these two statements it is clearly to be understood that that bread and this bread are not two breads but one bread; one flesh undoubtedly becomes one body. It is truly that very body, that very body which was taken from the Virgin, rose again, and ascended into heaven.

Likewise Gregory, in his Easter homily:

> What believer can doubt that, at the very hour of immolation, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, angelic choirs are present in Christ’s mystery, things highest and lowest are joined together, and one reality is made from invisible and visible things?

The same author:

> At the same instant, it is caught up to heaven by the ministry of angels, to be joined to Christ’s body, and is seen upon the altar before the priest’s eyes.

As the divinity of the Word fills the whole world, so that body is consecrated in many places. Yet there are not many bodies of Christ, but one body and one blood. Therefore, whether one receives more or less of it, all receive Christ’s body equally and wholly intact. After consecration, then, the substance of bread or wine is no longer there, though the appearances remain. For there is the appearance of bread and wine, as also their taste. Hence one thing is seen and another understood.

### Why under another appearance

5. Christ delivered his flesh and blood under another appearance, and ordained that they should thereafter be received, for three reasons.

First, so that faith might have merit, since faith concerns things not seen; for faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof by experience. Second, lest the mind recoil from what the eye sees, since we are not accustomed to eat raw flesh and drink blood. Since it is not permissible for Christ to be devoured with the teeth, he commended his flesh and blood to us in a mystery. Third, lest unbelievers mock the Christian religion.

Hence Augustine, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Under a Figure*:

> Nothing is more reasonable than that we receive a likeness of blood, so that truth may not be absent and yet no ridicule may arise from pagans because we drink the gore of a slain man. Therefore, lest this happen, and lest we feel, as it were, a certain horror even of blood, we receive the sacrament in a likeness.

From the foregoing it is now clear why the Lord celebrated this sacrament under another appearance, and why he instituted its celebration by us under this appearance.

### Why under two appearances

6. But why is it received under two appearances, when Christ is wholly present under either? So that he might be shown to have assumed the whole of human nature in order to redeem it wholly. Bread refers to flesh; wine to the soul, because wine produces blood, in which physicists say the seat of the soul is located. It is therefore celebrated under two appearances so that Christ’s assumption of soul and flesh, and our liberation in both, may be signified.

For what we receive avails for the protection of body and soul, as Ambrose says in his commentary on chapter 10 of the First Epistle to the Hebrews: Christ’s flesh is offered for the salvation of the body, but his blood for our soul, as Moses foreshadowed: “The flesh is offered for our body, the blood for the soul.” Yet Christ is received under each appearance, and what is received under each avails for both, because Christ is received under each. But if he were received under only one, it would signify that it avails only for the protection of one—namely, soul or body—not equally for both.

Yet under each appearance Christ is wholly received; neither is more received under both appearances nor less under one alone. For, as Hilary says, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Where the Part Is*, the same principle applies to Christ’s body as was prefigured in the manna. Of it Exodus 16 says: “He who had gathered more had no excess, and he who had prepared less had no lack.”

Although whole Christ is received under both appearances, the bread is converted only into flesh, and the wine only into blood. Nor should these be called two sacraments, but one, because the same thing is received under both appearances. Nor should the sacrament be repeated, because the blessing is not repeated over the same appearance. Nor should other substances be offered in the sacrifice of truth, [Col. 0864] because Christ’s body or blood cannot be consecrated from other substances.

### Why water is mixed in

7. Water must be mixed with the wine because water signifies the people redeemed through Christ’s passion. Therefore, according to the command of the canons, the Lord’s chalice must be offered with water mixed into wine, because we see the people understood in the water and Christ’s blood shown in the wine. When water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined to him in whom it believes. This union of water and wine is so mixed in Christ’s chalice that the mixture cannot be separated. For if someone were to offer wine alone, Christ’s blood would begin to exist without us.

### Pope Julius

8. But if it is asked whether what is performed is invalid when water is omitted, hear what follows in the same canon:

> The Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone, unless both are mixed together.

Likewise Cyprian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *You Must Not*, and chapter *As in Sanctification*:

> The Lord’s chalice is not water alone or wine alone, unless both are mixed together; just as the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone or water alone, unless both have been united and compacted into the solid unity of one bread.

Yet if someone, not intending to introduce heresy, omitted water through forgetfulness or ignorance, the sacrament does not seem to be invalid; but that person is to be severely rebuked. For the Church of the Greeks is said not to add water. This also seems inferable from Cyprian’s words. For he says, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *And Scripture*:

> If any of our predecessors, whether through ignorance or simplicity, did not observe what the Lord taught us to do by both example and instruction, pardon from the Lord’s indulgence may be granted to his simplicity. But we cannot be forgiven, since we have now been instructed by the Lord to offer the Lord’s chalice mixed with wine, according to what the Lord offered.

This seems to mean that someone who, through simplicity or ignorance, offers wine without water does consecrate the sacrament. Water, however, can by no means be offered without wine in the sacrifice; nor can bread be offered unless it is made from wheat; nor wheat grain unless it has been made into bread, because Christ both calls himself bread and compares himself to a grain of wheat.

Therefore, the earlier statement that wine alone cannot be offered must be qualified, for it admits an exception: it cannot be offered unless this is done simply or ignorantly; or “cannot” means “ought not.” Yet some think this universally true. It is also inferred from what has been said that Christ gave his disciples wine mixed with water. But he gave a body such as he then possessed: namely, mortal and capable of suffering. We now receive him immortal and incapable of suffering; yet it has no greater efficacy.

The Eucharist administered by intinction ought not to be given to the people as a substitute for communion, because Christ is not read to have given dipped bread to any of the disciples except Judas. Then Judas did not receive Christ’s body, but bread alone; he had previously received Christ’s body and blood together with the other disciples.

## DISTINCTION XII. IN WHAT THE ACCIDENTS ARE GROUNDED

1. But if it is asked concerning the accidents which remain—that is, the appearances, taste, and weight—in what subject they are grounded, it seems to me preferable to confess that they exist without a subject rather than that they exist in a subject. For no substance is there except that of the Lord’s body and blood, which is not affected by those accidents. Christ’s body does not possess such a form in itself, but the form in which it will appear at the judgment.

Those accidents therefore remain, subsisting through themselves, for the rite of the mystery and for the support of taste and faith; by them Christ’s body, possessing its own form and nature, is covered.

### On the breaking and division

2. It is also customary to ask whether the breaking and division that appear to take place there are real; and, if there is real breaking, of what thing it is, or in what thing it takes place. Since no substance other than Christ’s is there, if that breaking occurs in any substance, it seems to occur in Christ’s body. But, on the other hand, since that body is incorruptible—being immortal and incapable of suffering—it seems impossible for it to occur in it.

For Christ rebuked the carnal understanding of the disciples, who thought that Christ’s flesh was to be divided into parts like other flesh and torn apart by bites. Therefore some hold that there is no breaking there as appears; it is said to be broken because it appears to be broken. They are met with Ambrose’s saying: “Nothing false is to be supposed in the sacrifice of truth”; nor is it like the tricks of magicians, in which the eyes are deceived by some illusion so that they see what is not.

To this they reply: sight neither deceives us nor is deceived; it would do so if it were believed to be broken as it appears. Nor is it an illusion, because it is done for the benefit of faith, not for deception—just as Christ showed himself to two disciples on the road in the appearance of a traveler. Yet he did not possess such a form; rather, their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him.

### Another opinion

3. Others say that, just as the appearance of bread is there but the thing whose appearance it is, or in which that appearance exists, is not there, so there is a breaking there that takes place in no thing, because nothing is broken there. They say that this is brought about wonderfully by God’s power: there is breaking where nothing is broken.

### Another opinion

4. Others maintain that Christ’s body is essentially broken and divided, yet remains whole and incorruptible. They assert that they infer this from Berengar’s confession. Before Pope Nicholas and many bishops, he confessed that the bread and wine placed upon the altar are, after consecration, not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of Christ, and that they are sensibly handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful—not merely under the sacrament, but in truth.

### The more probable opinion

5. But because Christ’s body is incorruptible, it may reasonably be said that this breaking and division occur sacramentally not in the substance of the body but in the appearance of bread, so that real breaking and division occur there—not in the substance of the body, but in the sacrament, that is, the appearance.

Do not marvel or scoff if accidents appear to be broken while existing there without a subject, although some maintain that they are grounded in the air. There is real breaking and division there, which takes place in bread—that is, in the appearance of bread. Hence the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 16: “The bread that we break,” because the appearance of bread is broken and divided into parts, while Christ remains whole and is entirely present in each individual part.

Hence Augustine, in a sermon *On the Words of the Gospel*:

> When Christ is eaten, life is eaten. But who would dare to eat his Lord? Yet Truth, inviting us to eat, says in John 6: “He who eats me lives because of me.” Christ is not killed so that he may be eaten, but gives life to the dead. When he is eaten, he refreshes; he is not diminished. Eaten, he lives, because slain, he rose. Nor, when we eat, do we make parts of him—although in the sacrament this is done.

Likewise, *On Consecration*, distinction 2:

> The faithful know how to eat Christ’s flesh: each receives his own part; hence the graces themselves are called “parts.” He is eaten in parts and remains whole and entire; he is eaten in parts in the sacrament and remains whole and entire in heaven; he remains whole and entire in your heart. Therefore these are called sacraments because in them one thing is seen and another understood: bread and a chalice are seen, as the eyes report; but what faith, which must be instructed, requires is this: the bread is Christ’s body, the chalice is blood.

From these things it is understood that the breaking and parts seen to take place there occur in the sacrament—that is, in the visible appearance. Therefore Berengar’s words must be distinguished in this way: Christ’s body is said to be handled sensibly by the priests’ hands not only in the sacrament but in truth; but it is broken and ground by teeth truly indeed, yet only in the sacrament. Thus the grinding and division are real, but whole Christ is in every part.

Hence Jerome, in a certain sermon, also found in *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Each Receives*:

> Each receives Christ the Lord, and in each [Col. 0866] portion he is whole; he is not diminished by the individual portions, but offers himself whole in each.

Likewise Hilary: “Where the part of the body is, there the whole is.”

### What those parts signify

6. Pope Sergius teaches what those parts signify, saying, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Threefold*:

> Christ’s body is threefold. The portion offered and placed into the chalice represents Christ’s body now risen; the portion eaten, his body still walking upon earth; the portion remaining upon the altar until the end of the Mass signifies the body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in their tombs.

As those parts bear a mystical meaning, so also the breaking represents Christ’s passion and death. Hence he himself says in Luke 22: “Do this in remembrance of me,” that is, in remembrance of my passion and death. For, as Ambrose says, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *Not This One*:

> Because we have been set free in Christ’s death, we ought, in eating and drinking his flesh and blood, to be mindful of this. But let everyone take care not to receive unworthily, for such a person eats judgment upon himself. For this is not bread that goes into the body, but bread of eternal life, which sustains the substance of our soul. Therefore live in such a way that you deserve to receive every day, and do not approach unworthily. The unworthy person is one who celebrates the mystery otherwise than Christ handed it down, or who approaches while bearing mortal sin. Therefore, even if sins are daily, provided they are not mortal, before you approach forgive your debtors. If you forgive, you will be forgiven; and thus approach confidently. For it is saving bread, not poison. If you approach in this way, you eat spiritually. For the one who brings innocence to the altar eats spiritually.

### Whether this is a sacrifice, and whether Christ is repeatedly sacrificed

7. Next it is asked whether what the priest performs is properly called a sacrifice or immolation, and whether Christ is sacrificed daily or was sacrificed only once. A brief answer may be given: what is offered and consecrated by the priest is called sacrifice and oblation because it is the remembrance and representation of the true sacrifice and holy immolation made on the altar of the cross.

Christ died once upon the cross and was there sacrificed in himself; but he is sacrificed daily in the sacrament, because in the sacrament there is a recollection of what was done once. Hence Augustine, on Psalm 20:

> We are certain that Christ, risen from the dead, now dies no more, etc. Yet lest we forget what was done once, it is enacted in our remembrance every year—namely, whenever Easter is celebrated. Is Christ killed whenever this happens? No; the annual remembrance only represents what was done long ago, and thus moves us as though we saw the Lord upon the cross.

Likewise, in Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*:

> Christ was sacrificed once in himself, and yet is sacrificed daily in the sacrament.

This must be understood thus: in the manifestation of his body and the distinction of his limbs, he hung only once upon the cross, offering himself to God the Father as an efficacious sacrificial victim of redemption for those whom he predestined.

Likewise Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> In Christ a victim powerful for salvation was offered once. What then of us? Do we not offer every day? Although we offer daily, it is done in remembrance of his death; and there is one victim, not many. How is it one and not many? Because Christ was sacrificed once. This sacrifice is an image of that one; the very same thing, always the very same thing, is offered. Therefore it is the same sacrifice. Otherwise, because it is offered in many places, it would be said: “There are many Christs.” No: Christ is one everywhere, wholly present here and wholly present there. As what is offered everywhere is one body, so there is also one sacrifice. Christ offered the victim; we now offer that same victim, but what we do is a remembrance of the sacrifice. It is not repeated because of any weakness in it, since it perfects the human being, but because of our weakness, since we sin daily.

From this it is inferred that what takes place on the altar is and is called a sacrifice; that Christ was offered once and is offered daily, but differently then and differently now; and also what power this sacrament has: namely, remission of venial sins and the perfection of virtue.

### On the reason for its institution

8. This sacrament was instituted for two reasons: for the increase of virtue, namely charity, and as a remedy for daily weakness. Hence Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, book 4, chapter 6:

> If Christ’s blood is poured out for the remission of sins whenever it is poured out, I ought always to receive it, since I always sin; I ought always to have medicine.

Likewise Augustine, to Januarius, in the same place:

> This oblation is repeated daily, although Christ suffered once, because we daily sin with sins without which mortal weakness cannot live. Because we fall daily, Christ is mystically sacrificed daily for us. For he gave us this sacrament of salvation so that, because we sin daily and he can now die no more, we may obtain remission through this sacrament. He himself is eaten and drunk daily in truth, yet remains whole and alive.

Likewise: “It is called the mystery of faith because you must believe that our salvation consists there.”

But if it is asked whether communion should be received daily, hear what Augustine teaches concerning this, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53:

> I neither praise nor blame receiving the Eucharist daily; nevertheless I urge communion on every Lord’s Day. If, however, the mind is disposed toward sinning, I say that it is made more burdened by receiving the Eucharist than cleansed. Even if someone is stung by sin, yet has no further will to sin and makes satisfaction by tears and prayers, let that person approach confidently; but I say this of one not burdened by mortal sins. If not more often, people should communicate at least three times a year, unless perhaps someone is prevented by grave sins: namely, at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas. Therefore all who do not wish to be excluded from the thresholds of the church should communicate.

(Pope Fabian, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter *If Not*.)

## DISTINCTION XIII. WHETHER HERETICS AND EXCOMMUNICATED PERSONS CONSECRATE THIS SACRAMENT

1. It is also commonly asked whether corrupt priests can consecrate this sacrament. To this it may be said that some, although corrupt, truly consecrate: namely, those who are within the Church in name and sacrament, though not in life. For it is effected not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator. Hence Augustine, in *On the Lord’s Body*:

> Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, nothing greater is accomplished by a good priest and nothing less by a bad one; for it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. For it must be believed that the sacraments are consecrated in Christ’s words. As he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself, through the Holy Spirit, makes his own flesh and blood.

Likewise Gregory:

> Some think that communion of the body is less sanctified if it is performed through the office of those whose life appears base in their eyes. Alas, into what great snare they fall, believing that divine and hidden mysteries can be made more sanctified by some persons than by others, when one and the same Holy Spirit throughout the whole Church invisibly both sanctifies those mysteries by working and blesses them by sanctifying!

It is called a mystery because it has a secret and hidden dispensation; a sacrifice, as it were a sacred act, because it is consecrated for us by mystical prayer in remembrance of the Lord’s passion. A sacrament occurs in a celebration when a thing is done in such a way that we receive something of the thing signified. Baptism, chrism, and Christ’s body are sacraments; they are called sacraments because beneath the covering of visible things divine power more secretly works the salvation of those same sacraments. Hence sacraments are so called from secret powers or sacred things.

The sacrament of bread and chalice is called in Greek *Eucharistia*, in Latin interpreted “good grace”; and what is better than Christ’s body and blood? Therefore, whether it is administered within the Church by good or bad ministers, it is nevertheless a sacrament, because the Holy Spirit gives life. It is neither enlarged by the merits of good administrators [Col. 0868] nor diminished by those of bad ones. This must be said and maintained concerning the Lord’s body, and likewise concerning Baptism and Chrism: divine power works more secretly in them, and this power or authority is divine alone, not an efficacy belonging to human beings.

But those who are excommunicated or publicly marked by heresy do not appear able to consecrate this sacrament, even if they are priests, because no one says in the consecration itself, “I offer,” but “We offer,” as though speaking in the person of the Church. Therefore, although other sacraments may be celebrated outside the Church, this one does not seem able to be so celebrated.

Augustine also seems to teach this in a sermon *On Christ’s Body*, saying:

> Recall the name and observe the truth. It is called *missa* [Mass] because a heavenly messenger comes to consecrate the life-giving body, according to the priest’s words: “Almighty God, command these things to be carried by the hands of your holy angel to your altar on high,” etc. Therefore, unless the angel comes, it cannot rightly be called a Mass. For if a heretic should dare to usurp this mystery, does God send an angel from heaven to consecrate that person’s offering—especially when through the prophet he has threatened them with these words: “I will curse your blessings”? If Truth declares that it will curse their blessings, what will become of the victim? Shall we then say that it can be blessed by one whom we know will be cursed by God along with his blessing? For if God curses the blessings of heretics and a schismatic blesses, which of them will prevail? Can the blessing of one cursed reduce to nothing the utterly true words of God who threatens?

From this it is inferred that a heretic cut off from the Catholic Church cannot consecrate this sacrament, because the holy angels who attend the celebration of this mystery are not present when a heretic or schismatic presumptuously undertakes to celebrate it. For it is not permissible to doubt that, wherever the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are performed, an assembly of heavenly citizens is present.

In the completion of this mystery, it is necessary both that the prescribed form be observed and that the proper order be present—namely, that there be a priest and that intention be applied, so that he intends to do that thing. But if he does not believe about that mystery as truth requires, can he intend to consecrate it? And if he does not intend it, does he consecrate?

Some say that even one who does not think rightly about the mystery can intend—not indeed to consecrate that mystery, which would already require correct belief, but to do what others do when they consecrate; and thus intention is present. Even if the intention of consecrating that mystery is said to be absent, nevertheless, since he intends to say and do the things that others do, the mystery is fulfilled.

It may also rightly be said that Christ’s body is not received by brute animals, even if it appears to be. What, then, does a mouse receive, or what does it eat? God knows.

We have briefly touched upon certain matters concerning this heavenly mystery, which Catholics must faithfully maintain. Whoever contradicts these is judged a heretic.

### What makes a heretic, and what a heretic is

2. But lest you be ignorant of what makes someone a heretic, or what a heretic is, hear briefly what the holy doctors teach on this point. Hilary says:

> There have been many who accepted the simplicity of heavenly words, but not the plain sense of truth itself, interpreting them otherwise than the force of the sayings required. For heresy arises from interpretation, not from Scripture; and the meaning, not the wording, becomes the offense.

The same author, in book 8: “The meaning of an interpretation is the matter at fault.”

Jerome says that heresy is incurred through words uttered without order.

Augustine, defining what a heretic is, says:

> A heretic is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—and especially for the sake of his own glory and pre-eminence—creates or follows false and novel opinions.

## DISTINCTION XIV. ON PENANCE
1. After these matters, we must treat of Penance. Penance is necessary for those who are far from God, that they may draw near. For it is, as Jerome says, the second plank after shipwreck: because if anyone has stained by sinning the garment of innocence received in Baptism, he can restore it by the remedy of Penance. The first plank is Baptism, in which the old man is put off [Col. 0869] and the new put on; the second is Penance, by which we rise again after a fall, when the returning oldness is driven away and the lost newness is resumed. Those who have fallen after Baptism can be renewed through Penance, but not through Baptism. A person may repent repeatedly, but may not be baptized repeatedly. Baptism is only a sacrament; but Penance is called both a sacrament and a virtue of the mind. For there is an inward Penance and an outward Penance. The outward is a sacrament; the inward is a virtue of the mind; and each is a cause of salvation and justification. Whether, however, every outward penance is a sacrament—or, if not every one is, which ought to be designated by this name—we shall investigate in due course.

John’s preaching began with Penance, when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is drawing near.” What the herald taught, Truth himself afterward preached, beginning his discourse with penance. Penance is so called from punishing, by which a person punishes the unlawful deeds that he has committed. The virtue of penance is conceived through fear. Hence Isaiah: “From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and brought forth the Spirit of salvation.” Penance, as Ambrose says, is to grieve for past evils and not to commit again the things that must be grieved for. Likewise Gregory: To repent is to weep for sins previously committed and not to commit what must be wept for. For one who laments some sins in such a way as nevertheless to commit others either does not yet know how to do penance or is pretending to do it. For what good is it if someone weeps for sins of lust while still panting after the fires of avarice?

Some, clinging rather forcefully to these words, contend that one who truly repents can thereafter no longer sin damnably; and that, if he sins gravely, true penance did not precede. They reinforce this position with other testimonies as well. Isidore says: “He is a mocker and not repentant who still does that for which he repents; he seems not to entreat God as one subject to him, but proudly to mock him. The dog has returned to its vomit, and the penitent person to sin.” Many pour out tears unceasingly and do not cease from sinning. “I see some receive tears for penance while lacking the disposition of penance; because, through instability of mind, they now shed tears at the remembrance of sin, and now, when the practice revives, repeat what they had wept for.” Isaiah says of sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” He is washed and clean who both laments past sins and does not again commit what must be lamented. He is washed but not clean who laments what he has done yet does not abandon it, and after tears repeats what he had bewailed.

Likewise Augustine: “Penance is empty when subsequent guilt defiles it. Lamentations profit nothing if sins are repeated. It is of no avail to seek pardon for evils and to commit the evils anew.” Likewise Gregory: “He who laments deeds committed yet does not abandon them subjects himself to a heavier punishment.” Likewise Ambrose: “There are persons who think penance ought to be performed repeatedly; such people indulge themselves in Christ. For, if they truly performed penance in Christ, they would not think it should afterward be repeated; for as there is one Baptism, so there is one Penance.”

They use these and many other passages to maintain their opinion. But Ambrose says: “This is true penance: to cease from sin.” And again: “It is great progress to have renounced error.” For to strip off and reform minds steeped in vices belongs to perfect virtue and heavenly grace. Therefore it can properly be defined thus: Penance is the virtue or grace by which we grieve for and hate the evils committed, with the purpose of amendment, and do not wish to commit further the things that must be lamented; because true penance consists in grieving in the mind and hating vices. Hence the words quoted above—“to repent is to weep for past deeds and not to commit what must be wept for”—can rightly be understood so that they refer not to different times but to the same time: namely, that at the time when a person bewails evils committed, he does not commit, by will or deed, things that must be bewailed. This is suggested by the following words: “For one who thus laments some things,” etc.

Hence Augustine says: “Care must be taken lest anyone suppose that those abominable crimes—whose perpetrators will not possess the kingdom of God—are to be committed daily and redeemed by alms. For one’s life must be changed for the better, and through alms God is to be propitiated for past sins; he is not, as it were, to be bought off so that one may always be permitted to commit them with impunity. For he has given no one a license to sin, even though in mercy he wipes away sins committed, provided that fitting satisfaction is not neglected.” Likewise Pope Pius: “It profits a person nothing to fast and pray and perform other religious works unless the mind is recalled from wickedness.”

Therefore, whoever so recalls his mind from evils that he laments what he has committed, does not wish to commit what must be lamented, and does not neglect satisfaction, truly repents. Nor is penance for that reason not true because perhaps afterward he will sin, not deliberately, but by chance or through weakness. But he is a mocker and not repentant who so bewails what he has committed that he does not cease to commit, by will or deed, things that must be lamented.
