Likewise, one who after tears repeats what he bewailed is washed for a time but is not clean; that is, that cleansing is not sufficient for his salvation, because it is momentary rather than persevering.

Likewise, the statement, “Penance is empty when subsequent guilt defiles it,” must be understood thus: it is empty, that is, lacking the fruit of that penance which subsequent guilt defiles. For its fruit is avoidance of Gehenna and attainment of glory. For through that subsequent sin, that penance and the other previous good works are rendered dead, so that they do not receive the reward which they deserved when they were done and which they would have if sin did not follow. But if penance is performed for the subsequent sin, both the preceding penance and the other previous good works revive—but only those that proceeded from charity. For only those things are alive which are done from charity. Therefore, if they are rendered dead through subsequent sins, they can revive through subsequent penance. But things done without charity are produced dead and empty, and therefore cannot revive through penance.

The same is to be understood of the statement, “Lamentations profit nothing,” etc., and of the statement, “It is of no avail,” etc. For if sins are repeated, the preceding lamentation profits nothing for salvation or pardon at the end, because nothing remains of purity of life: either forgiven sins return, as some hold, when they are repeated; or, if they do not return, yet, though they have been erased, a person is made guilty and unclean through ingratitude, while still entangled in sins requiring expiation, as though the sins already erased were returning. Yet concerning this—whether sins return—we shall speak more fully later. Similarly, it is of no avail for obtaining salvation or possessing purity of life to seek pardon for wrongs and commit wrongs anew.

Thus also must be understood what the same Augustine says elsewhere: “Penance is a kind of vengeance on the part of one who grieves, always punishing in himself what he grieves to have committed.” And below: “One must grieve daily for sin, as the force of the very word declares. For to repent is to hold punishment, so that one may always punish in oneself, by avenging it, what one committed by sinning. But he holds punishment who always takes vengeance for what he grieves to have committed. Therefore penance is vengeance, always punishing in oneself what one grieves to have committed. What remains for us except to grieve in this life? For where grief ends, penance also fails. But if penance ends, what remains of pardon? Let a person rejoice and hope in grace as long as he is sustained by penance. For the Lord says: ‘Go, and sin no more.’ He did not say, ‘Do not sin,’ but rather, ‘Let not even the will to sin arise within you.’ How will this be observed unless grief is continuously preserved in penance? Yet let a person always grieve and rejoice in grief; and let it not be enough that he grieves, but let him grieve from faith, and not grieve that he has not always grieved.”  
(Augustine, *Soliloquies*; *On Punishments*, distinction 3, chapter *Inanis*; *On Penance*, distinction 3, *Qui admissa*; *On Penance*, book 2, chapter 10, vol. 1, on the Epistle to the Corinthians; *Enchiridion*, chapter 70; *On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter *Nihil prodest*; *On True and False Penance*, chapter 8, middle.)

### Determination of the Meaning of the Sayings

2. What I said above must be understood of the penance of the perfect, or of penance sufficient for salvation—namely, that penance is vengeance always punishing what it has committed, and other statements of this sort. But the saying, “If penance ends, nothing of pardon remains,” may be taken in two ways. For if, according to the understanding of some, forgiven sins return, it is easy to understand that nothing of pardon remains, because forgiven sins are repeated. For just as one who is manumitted from slavery into freedom is truly free for a time, yet afterward is recalled into slavery because of an offense, so through penance sins are truly forgiven, yet through an offense that is repeated they return again. But if they are said not to return, it can still properly be said in this way that nothing of pardon remains: not because forgiven sins are imputed again, but because through ingratitude a person is made guilty and unclean as though they returned.

### On Solemn and Single Penance

3. But what Ambrose says, *On Penance*, distinction 3, chapter *Reperiuntur*—“There are persons,” etc., and “As there is one Baptism, so also there is one Penance”—is to be understood not according to the general practice but according to the special practice of the Church, concerning solemn penance, which among some people, once performed, is not repeated. Likewise the other statement of Ambrose, *On Penance*, distinction 3, final chapter, § *Poenitentia ergo*: “Penance once undertaken but not truly performed both takes away the fruit of the former and loses the use of the subsequent,” is to be understood of solemn penance.

Solemn penance, then, as Ambrose says in the same place, is that which is done publicly outside the church, in ashes and haircloth; it is imposed only for more serious, horrible, and public offenses. And it is not to be repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament, lest it become cheap and contemptible to people. Hence Augustine, in Letter 54 to Macedonius: “Although it has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble penance be granted once in the Church, lest the medicine become cheap or less useful to the sick—a medicine that is more beneficial in proportion as it is less contemptible—yet who would dare to say to God: ‘Why do you still spare this person, who after the first penance has again bound himself in the snares of iniquity?’”

Origen also says of this solemn penance, which is imposed for more serious crimes: “If some mortal fault should overtake us which does not consist in a mortal crime or blasphemy against the faith, but in a fault of speech or conduct, this fault can always be repaired, and one is never forbidden to do penance for such a matter. But it is not so with more serious crimes. For in more serious crimes, the opportunity for penance is granted only once. Ordinary sins, which we incur frequently, always admit penance and are always redeemed.” By “ordinary” he means venial sins, and perhaps certain mortal sins less grave than others, which, as they are frequently committed, are also frequently redeemed through penance. But for more serious crimes penance is performed only once, namely solemn penance. For if those sins are repeated, penance is repeated too, but not solemn penance—though this is not observed in certain churches.

### He Proves by Authorities That Sins Are Forgiven Not Only Once but Repeatedly through Penance

4. That Penance is not performed only once, but is repeated frequently, and that through it pardon is repeatedly granted, is proved by many testimonies of the saints. Augustine says, in *On True and False Penance*, chapter 5, writing against certain heretics who said that Penance was useful only once for those sinning after Baptism:

“Unbelievers still press their case, thinking beyond what is fitting—not soberly, but exceeding the measure. They say: ‘Even if Penance is effective for those who sin once after Baptism, its repetition will not benefit those who sin often; otherwise forgiveness would be an inducement to sin.’ For they say: ‘Who would not sin continually, if he could continually return through Penance?’ They make the Lord an encourager of evil if he helps those who always sin, and claim that sins please him because grace is always ready for them. But they are mistaken. For it is clear that sins greatly displease him who is always ready to destroy them. If he loved them, he would not always destroy them.”

Likewise, in Letter 54 to Macedonius: “Human wickedness sometimes advances so far that even after Penance has been performed and after reconciliation with the altar, people commit offenses either similar or more serious. Yet God makes his sun rise even upon such persons, nor does he grant them less abundant gifts of life and health than he granted before. And although that place of Penance is not granted them in the Church, God nevertheless does not forget his patience toward them. If someone of their number were to say to you: ‘Tell me whether it benefits future life at all if, in this life, I despise the enticements of most alluring pleasure; if I torment myself in repentance more severely than before; if I weep more abundantly; if I live better; if I support the poor more generously; if I burn more ardently with charity’—which of you is so foolish as to say to that person: ‘These things will profit you nothing hereafter; go and at least enjoy the sweetness of this life’? May God avert such monstrous and sacrilegious madness.”

Likewise John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of One Who Has Fallen*: “Such, believe me, such is God’s compassion toward human beings: he never despises penance if it is offered to him sincerely and simply. Even if someone has reached the utmost extremity of evils, yet wishes from there to return to the way of virtue, God gladly receives and embraces him, and does everything to restore him to his former state. And what is still more excellent and eminent: even if someone cannot complete the entire course of satisfaction, he nevertheless does not reject penance performed in however small a measure and for however brief a time; he receives even that, and does not allow the reward of even the slightest conversion to be lost.”

This same point can also be established by examples. For David, through penance, obtained pardon both for adultery and for homicide; yet afterward he sinned gravely in numbering the people, as the overthrow of the multitude showed. But this is remarkable: he offered himself to the angel striking the people, saying, 1 Chronicles 21: “What has this flock done? Let your hand be against me and against my father’s house.” By this act, one thought unworthy of absolution was immediately judged worthy of sacrifice. Nor is it surprising that by such an offering of himself for the people he obtained pardon for his sin, since Moses, by offering himself for the error of the people, wiped away sins.

By these and many other testimonies it is clearly shown that through penance we rise from sins not only once but often, and that true penance is performed often. For, as the Apostle says, Hebrews 10, when we sin voluntarily, no second sacrifice remains for sins—that is, because Christ had to suffer only once; nor does a second Baptism remain. But a second, third, and subsequent penance does remain, as John Chrysostom says in Homily 20 on this passage:

“We must know,” he says, “that some, on the occasion of these words, rise up and take away penance, as though a sinner could not through penance rise again after a fall a second, third, or subsequent time. But even here he does not exclude penance, nor propitiation, which is often made through penance; rather, he excludes a second Baptism and sacrifice.”

## DISTINCTION XV. THAT ONE ENSNARED BY SEVERAL SINS CANNOT TRULY REPENT OF ONE UNLESS HE REPENTS OF ALL

1. And just as the error of those who do not think penance must be performed repeatedly, and who deny that sinners can often rise from a fall through it, is refuted by the foregoing authorities, so by those same authorities the contrary position of those is demolished who assert that a person ensnared by several sins can truly repent of one and obtain its pardon from the Lord without repentance for another. They also attempt to establish this by authorities.

For the prophet Nahum says, chapter 1: “God will not judge twice for the same thing”; or, as others have translated: “A double affliction shall not arise.” Therefore, they say, if someone has confessed one of two or several sins to a priest, and has completed, in satisfaction, the penance imposed on him by the priest for that sin, while keeping the others silent, he must no longer be judged for that sin for which he satisfied according to the judgment of the priest, who acts in the Church in Christ’s place. Therefore, if he is judged for it again, God judges twice for the same thing, and a double affliction arises.

But this must be understood only of those who are changed for the better by present punishments and thus persevere; no double affliction shall arise against them. But those who become harder and worse amid scourges, like Pharaoh, attach eternal punishments to present ones, so that temporal punishment is for them the beginning of eternal penalty. Hence Augustine: “A fire has been kindled,” etc.; that is, God’s vengeance will begin here and burn until final condemnation. [Col. 0873]

This should be noted against those who say that the statement, “God will not judge twice for the same thing,” applies to all scourges, because some are corrected here by scourges, while others are punished both here and eternally. For scourges occur in five ways: either that the merits of the righteous may be increased through patience, as in Job; or for the preservation of virtues, lest pride tempt them, as in Paul; or for correcting sins, as with Miriam’s leprosy; or for God’s glory, as in the man born blind; or as a judgment of punishment, as with Herod, so that what follows in hell may be seen here, according to the words: “Crush them with a double crushing, O Lord.”

Therefore Nahum’s authority does not compel us to think that all who are punished temporally are not to be punished further by God. For although Jerome says on the same passage that the Egyptians and Israelites were punished temporally by God so that they would not be punished eternally, it must nevertheless not be understood generally of all. For he says: “Know that God punished temporally for sins the human race by the flood, the Sodomites by fire, the Egyptians by the sea, and the Israelites in the wilderness, so that he would not punish them eternally, because God will not judge twice for the same thing. Therefore those who have been punished will not afterward be punished; otherwise Scripture lies, which it is wicked to say.”

### What Is the Meaning of the Foregoing?

2. Attend, reader, to these words, and beware of understanding them universally of all; rather, understand them only of those who did penance amid the very scourges, believing in the God of the Hebrews. Although this penance was brief and momentary, God nevertheless did not reject it. But Jerome shows in the same place that those who are not corrected by temporal scourging are punished eternally afterward, when he discusses a believer caught in adultery who is beheaded. There he shows that light sins are purged by brief and temporal punishment, while great sins are reserved for long-lasting and eternal punishments. He says:

“Someone may ask here: if a believer caught in adultery is beheaded, what happens to him afterward? Either he will be punished, and the statement ‘God will not judge twice for the same thing’ is false; or he will not be punished, and adulterers should desire to be punished here by a brief penalty so that they may escape eternal torments. To this we reply that God, as he knows the measures of all things, so also knows the measures of punishments; the sentence of the judge does not forestall him, nor can the power be taken from him to inflict afterward punishment on a sinner. A great sin is expiated by great and long-lasting torments. But if someone has been punished temporally—as the Israelite who cursed, and the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath—such persons are not punished afterward, because a light fault has been compensated by present punishment. For a light fault is compensated by a light punishment.”

Jerome sufficiently indicates here that grave sins are punished heavily both here and eternally in the future when no penance is performed amid the scourges; whereas light sins punished here receive compensation through a light penalty. We do not doubt that this occurs in the good, and perhaps it occurs thus in the wicked also.

It is now sufficiently clear that the prophecy adduced by them does not support those who say that pardon for one sin is granted through penance to a person who keeps another crime in reserve. They bring forward other authorities as well. Gregory says: “The Lord rains upon one city and does not rain upon another; and he rains upon the same city in part and leaves it dry in part. When one who hates his neighbor corrects himself of other vices, one and the same city is rained upon in part and remains dry in part; for there are some who, though they cut off certain vices, persist grievously in others.” Likewise Ambrose, Homily 10: “The first consolation is that God does not forget to show mercy; the second is through punishment, where, even if awareness is lacking, punishment makes satisfaction and brings relief.”

They also argue from reason: If a person who confesses one sin while concealing another completes the satisfaction imposed by the priest, then, if later converted he confesses the concealed sin, will penance be imposed upon him for both? This seems far from reason and from the Church’s practice, which imposes penance twice on no one for the same sin unless it is repeated. Therefore that was a satisfaction worthy of the sin, and the sin consequently seems to have been erased.

### How the Foregoing Must Be Understood

3. The answer to these points may be as follows. Gregory’s statement, “The Lord rains,” [Col. 0874] etc., must be referred not to pardon of guilt but to abandoning a wicked deed. Thus a part of the city is said to be rained upon because the person now ceases from the act and delight of the sin to which he formerly was enslaved, not because he has its pardon. Such continence, by which a person is recalled from the act of sin, is called rain, because this is instilled into the heart from the fountain of God’s grace, either so that the person may gradually come to penance or so that he may be punished less by God, having accumulated greater torment for himself through more prolonged delight in and practice of sin.

But if this rain is referred to remission of guilt, it will seem contrary to the Gospel sentence. For if, because of the lack of mercy by which one does not show mercy to one’s neighbor, even sins already forgiven are repeated for punishment, much more is it shown that sins not yet forgiven are reserved for punishment because of hatred for one’s brother. And if a person who has been made master of his own will cannot begin a new life, as Augustine says, unless he repents of the old life, how shall one attain the newness of pardon who has not put off the oldness of hatred?

Likewise Ambrose’s statement, “Even if awareness is lacking, punishment makes satisfaction,” etc., is not to be understood of faith by which God is believed in, but of consciousness of the offense. For awareness is lacking when consciousness of sin is absent. Since no one understands all faults, there is sometimes sin in a person of which he has no awareness. Hence the Apostle: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified.” Therefore, when a person is scourged for a sin of which he is unaware, if he bears the punishment patiently and humbly embraces it, thinking that perhaps he has a sin he does not understand and is being punished by God for it, that punishment makes satisfaction and relieves the burdened person.

As for the objection concerning that satisfaction—if it was not satisfaction, it must be imposed again; but if it need not be imposed again, it was satisfaction; and if it was satisfaction, it obtained pardon—it may be answered that it was not satisfaction because the person did not produce worthy fruits of penance. For satisfaction of penance, as Augustine says in the book *On Penance*, is to cut off the causes of sins and not to grant them entrance through their suggestions.

The same Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 75: “Certainly, those who live wickedly and do not care to correct such a life and conduct, yet do not cease amid their very crimes to give alms frequently, flatter themselves in vain on the ground that the Lord says, Luke 11: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.’ For they do not understand how widely this extends. There are many kinds of almsgiving, and when we perform them, we are helped. Not only one who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and similar things, but also one who grants pardon to a petitioner gives alms; one who corrects with a blow someone over whom he has authority, or restrains him by some discipline, or prays that his sin may be forgiven, gives alms, because he offers mercy. For many benefits are bestowed even upon unwilling persons when their benefit, rather than their will, is considered. But greater still is that alms by which we forgive from the heart what anyone has sinned against us. For it is a less great thing to be benevolent toward one who has done you no evil. It is far greater to love even your enemy, and always to will good—and, as far as you can, to do good—to one who wishes you evil and, if able, does it.

“Are we then to understand the Lord’s saying, ‘Give alms, and all things are clean for you,’ to mean that all things are clean for those who do not believe in Christ if they give these alms? For whoever wishes to give alms in an ordered manner ought to begin with himself and give them first to himself. For almsgiving is a work of mercy, and it has been said most truly, Ecclesiasticus 30: ‘Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.’ Therefore let not those deceive themselves who, through most lavish alms of their produce or money, think to buy impunity for themselves while remaining in sins which they love so much that they wish to dwell in them. But whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul, Psalm 10, verse 6; and one who hates his own soul is not merciful but cruel to it. For by loving it according to the world, he hates it according to God. Therefore, if he wishes to give it alms by which it may be cleansed, let him hate it according to the world and love it according to God. By this alms, which a person ought first to give himself, the inner things are cleansed.”

Exhorting them to this, Christ says, Matthew 23: “Cleanse the things that are within.” For nothing is clean to the unclean, but their mind and conscience are defiled, as the Apostle says. All, however, whom faith does not cleanse are unclean—the faith by which Christ is believed in, of whom it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.” But lest Christ seem to reject those alms given from the fruits of the earth, he says: “These things you ought to have done”—namely judgment and the love of God—“and not to have omitted those,” that is, alms from earthly produce.

From these points it may be understood that those who remain in mortal sin, even though they give lavish alms, nevertheless do not make satisfaction through them, because they act disorderly, not beginning with themselves. Nor is such a work properly called almsgiving while they prove cruel to themselves and do not please God. Therefore, that must not be called satisfaction for sin which someone performs for one sin while persisting in another. For fasting, praying, and doing other good works profit nothing unless the mind is recalled from sin. And if at some time, after conversion, he confesses the concealed sin to the priest, satisfaction must be imposed upon him for both, because he did not make worthy satisfaction for the first.  
(*On Penance*, distinction 3, *Nihil prodest*, Pope Pius.)

### According to Some, It Was Satisfaction

4. Yet some think that there was satisfaction, but fruitless while the person persisted in another sin; nevertheless its fruit will be received and it will begin to profit when he repents of the other sin. For then both sins are forgiven, and the preceding satisfaction, which had been dead, is made alive; just as Baptism first becomes effective for one who approaches deceitfully when the pretense departs from the mind through penance.

To support this opinion, they bring forward authorities. Augustine says, *On True and False Penance*, chapter 14, at the end: “It is pious to believe, and our faith requires, that when Christ’s grace has destroyed a person’s former evils, it also rewards his good deeds; and when it has destroyed what it did not find its own, it loves the good which it planted in the sinner.” Likewise Jerome, commenting on Haggai 1, “You have sown much,” etc.: “If you should at times see someone, amid many sins, performing certain righteous works, God is not so unjust that, because of many evils, he forgets a few good things; rather, he will make him reap and gather into barns what he sowed in good ground.”

But we understand these sayings of one who at one time does good works in charity and is good, while at another time is evil and commits many sins. Thus we must not understand that he performed righteous works amid many sins as though he committed sins and righteous works at the same time; rather, he did both at different times. For unless he were good when he did good works, he would not be said to have sown in good ground. Therefore, after the evils committed after good works have been destroyed, the earlier good works, namely those done in charity, which subsequent evils had rendered dead, are made alive by penance for those evils and are rewarded.

Hence the Apostle, Hebrews 6: “Laying the foundation of repentance from dead works,” calling previous good works “dead works,” since through subsequent sin they were dead, because by sinning these persons made their previous good works void. Just as these works are made void by sinning, so they revive through penance and begin to avail toward the merit of eternity. Similarly, God loves the good that he planted in the sinner—that is, in one who sinned after that good work; he was not simultaneously sinning and doing good, because God would not love the work of such a person so as to reward it.

This may also be understood of good works performed by someone while he is wicked and persists in mortal sin, either for a time or until the end. Such works are said to be rewarded by God and not forgotten, not because they avail toward eternal life, but toward suffering the punishment of the Last Judgment more tolerably. Thus Augustine says of faith and other things possessed without charity, *On Penance*, distinction 3, *Quid ergo*, paragraph *Potest etiam*, in the book *On Patience*:

“If someone lacking charity—which belongs to the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace by which the Church is held together—being established in some schism, suffers tribulations, hunger, persecution, flames, beasts, or even the cross itself rather than deny Christ, out of fear of Gehenna, these things are by no means to be blamed; indeed, even this patience is to be praised. For we cannot say that it would have been better for him to suffer none of these things by denying Christ than to suffer them by confessing him. But perhaps it should be judged that the judgment awaiting him will be more tolerable than if, by denying Christ, he had suffered none of these things. Thus the Apostle’s words, 1 Corinthians 13, ‘If I deliver my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing,’ are to be understood as meaning that it profits nothing for obtaining the kingdom, though it may avail toward undergoing the punishment of the Last Judgment more tolerably.”

And below: “These things were said because of charity, without which true penance cannot exist in us; for in the good, there is the charity of God, which endures all things.”

### He Briefly Reviews the Sum of What Has Been Said, in Order to Add Further Points

5. From these points it is shown that good works performed without charity indeed avail toward experiencing a more tolerable punishment, but not toward obtaining life. Ezekiel says, chapter 33, that the works which a person performs in charity, if afterward he falls and does not rise again, are not in God’s remembrance: “If the righteous turns away from righteousness and commits iniquity, shall he live? None of the righteous deeds which he had done shall be remembered; he shall die in his sin, and the righteous deeds he did shall not be remembered.”

In explaining this passage, Gregory, book 1, Homily 11, says: “This above all must be considered by us: when we commit evils, we call past good deeds to mind without cause; for in committing evils there ought to be no confidence in past good deeds.” This must be understood to mean that previous good works give no confidence for receiving life, though they may give confidence for a milder punishment; otherwise it would conflict with Augustine’s authority quoted above. Therefore good works done without charity, accompanied by mortal fault which subsequent penance does not erase, avail toward experiencing a milder punishment, not toward the fruit of life.

### He Brings Forward Other Authorities against Those Who Say That Penance Can Be Performed for One Sin While Another Is Concealed
6. I think a sufficient answer has been given to those who maintain that repentance may be made for one sin and pardon granted while another is retained in affection or not disclosed in confession. They are refuted not only by the authorities already cited, but also by those which follow. For Augustine says, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 9:

> There are many who repent of having sinned, yet nevertheless wholly reserve for themselves certain things in which they take pleasure. They do not observe that the Lord freed from the devil at the same time both the mute and the deaf man, thereby teaching us that we are never healed except from all sins. For if he had wished sins to be partly retained by one who had seven demons, it could have profited him if six had been expelled; but he expelled seven, in order to teach that all crimes must be cast out together. Again, when he cast a legion of demons out of another, he left none at all among them to possess the person set free, showing that, even if sins are a thousand, one must repent of them all. The Lord never healed anyone whom he did not completely free. For on the Sabbath he healed the whole man, because he freed both his body from every infirmity and his soul from every contagion, indicating that the penitent person must grieve at once for every sin. For I know that the Lord is an enemy to every criminal person. How, then, will one who retains one sin receive pardon for another? He would obtain pardon without the love of God, without which no one has ever found grace. For he is God's enemy while he persists in offending him. Indeed, it is a certain impiety of unbelief to hope for half a pardon from him who is righteous and is righteousness. For he would then find grace without true repentance. True repentance endeavors to bring the confessor back to the purity of Baptism. Therefore the person who truly repents ought to wash away whatever defilement he has contracted after Baptismal cleansing, at least with the tears of his mind; but one is sufficiently hard whose eyes do not disclose his mind's grief. Let him know, then, that he is culpably hard who mourns losses of time or the death of a friend, but does not show grief for sin in tears. Therefore, whoever repents, let him repent entirely.

The same author, there, ch. 10:

> You who repent—if you truly repent and are not mocking—change your life; be reconciled to God. You do penance, bend your knees, and laugh: you ridicule God's patience. If you do penance [Col. 0877], you are sorry; if you are not sorry, you are not penitent. If, then, you are sorry, why do you do what you did wickedly? If you are sorry to have done it, do not do it. If you still do it, certainly you are not penitent.

Likewise Innocent II:

> We admonish our brethren not to allow the souls of laypeople to be deceived by false penitences and drawn into hell. A repentance is plainly false when, several sins being disregarded, repentance is made for one alone; or when repentance is made for one in such a way that one does not depart from another.

He repeats the subject of true repentance in order to add something.

7. From what has been said, a clear understanding of true repentance or satisfaction emerges. That repentance is true which abolishes sin; and this is done only by that repentance which corrects wrongdoing, which brings hatred both of the crime committed and of committing it, together with a desire to make satisfaction.

Judas, indeed, is recorded to have repented without obtaining pardon, because by such repentance he did not correct his crime. Hence Jerome, commenting on Matthew 27, “What is that to us?” says:

> Judas's late repentance profited him nothing, since by it he was unable to correct his crime. Thus, when a brother sins against a brother in such a way that he cannot amend what he has sinned, he may be forgiven; but if the deeds remain, repentance is vainly undertaken in words.

This is what is said of that most unhappy man in Psalm 108:

> “And let his prayer become sin,”

so that he not only could not amend the wickedness of his betrayal, but added the crime of his own homicide.

Take care how you understand the words, “so that he may be able to amend what he has sinned,” and so forth. “Amendment” here does not mean compensation for a thing taken away, but reproach and abhorrence of the offense, together with the desire to make satisfaction. For someone may unjustly deprive another of something which he cannot restore, such as an eye, life, and things of that kind; yet if he repents of the sin with a desire for fitting satisfaction, he receives pardon.

Nor should anyone suppose that a person who has unjustly taken another's property which he can restore can repent of that sin and obtain pardon unless he restores what was taken. “For as long as the thing on account of which the sin was committed is not restored, when it can be restored, repentance is not being done but feigned” (Augustine, Letter 2, to Macedonius).

## DISTINCTION XVI. ON THE THREE THINGS TO BE CONSIDERED IN REPENTANCE

1. In the perfection of repentance, however, three things must be observed: compunction of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Hence John Chrysostom:

> Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure everything: in his heart, contrition; in his mouth, confession; in his work, complete humility. This is fruitful repentance: as we offend God in three ways—namely, in heart, word, and deed—so we make satisfaction in three ways.

For there are three kinds of sin, as Augustine says in *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, somewhat before the middle: in the heart, in deed, and in habit or word, as it were three deaths. One is as though in the house: namely, when the heart consents to lust. The second is as though already carried outside the gate, when consent proceeds to an act. The third occurs when the mind is weighed down, as by a mass, through the force of evil habit, or is armed with the shield of harmful self-defense, as though already stinking in the tomb.

These are the three kinds of dead persons whom God is recorded to have raised. This threefold death is therefore met by a threefold remedy: contrition, confession, and satisfaction.

Compunction is commended to us in Joel 2: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments.” Confession, in Proverbs 18: “The righteous man, at the beginning of his speech, is his own accuser.” For the person truly confesses who accuses himself, who imputes evil to himself in abhorrence. And in Psalm 61: “Pour out your hearts before him.” And again, James 5: “Confess your sins to one another.” Satisfaction is commanded by John, when he says in Matthew 3 and Luke 3: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance”; that is, the quality and quantity of punishment should correspond to the quality and quantity of guilt. The fruit of good work ought not to be equal for one who has sinned not at all or less grievously and for one who has fallen more seriously.

Therefore discernment is very necessary for the penitent, so that he may do what Augustine sets forth when he says:

> Let him consider the nature of the crime: its place, time, persistence, and the variation of persons; by what temptation he committed it; and the manifold carrying-out of the vice itself. For one who has committed fornication must repent [Col. 0878] according to the eminence of his state or office, according to the manner of the prostitute, according to the nature of his act, and according to how he performed the shameful deed: whether in a sacred place, whether at a time appointed for prayer, such as festivals and times of fasting. Let him consider how long he persisted, and mourn that he sinned persistently; and how great an assault overcame him. For there are some who are not merely overcome, but freely offer themselves to sin; they do not await temptation, but anticipate pleasure. Let him consider with himself in how manifold a practice of vice he sinned pleasurably. All this variety must be confessed and mourned, so that when he has recognized what his sin is, he may quickly find God favorable to him. In discerning the aggravation of sin, let him discover at what age, with what wisdom, and in what rank he was. Let him dwell upon each of these points and perceive the measure of the crime, cleansing every quality of vice with tears. Let him mourn the virtue which he lacked meanwhile. For one must grieve not only because one sinned, but because one deprived oneself of virtue. Let him also mourn because, by offending in one point, he became guilty of all, as James 2 says. For the person who, though full of virtues, did not fear God at all proved ungrateful. In this respect every sinner becomes more culpable in proportion as he is more acceptable to God. Thus Adam sinned more greatly because he abounded in every good. In another way, too, one who offends in one point becomes guilty of all, because every virtue suffers injury from a single vice. Let him place himself wholly under the judgment and authority of the priest, reserving nothing of himself for himself, so that, at the priest's command, he is prepared to do everything for the recovery of his soul's life which he would do to avoid bodily death—and this with desire, because he regains everlasting life.

Augustine, *On True and False Penance*, chs. 14 and 15:

> For one who is to be immortal ought joyfully to do what, if destined to die, he would do to defer death. Let him always entreat God; let him offer God his mind and contrition of heart; then let him give, insofar as he can, from his possessions, and then, if he offers anything, let him offer it securely. “The Lord had regard for Abel and for his gifts” [Genesis 4]. He says first, “for Abel,” and then, “for his gifts.” Therefore the almsgiving of the giver must be assessed by the judgment of the heart. The question is not how much, but with what mind and affection he gives what he can. Therefore, whoever wishes to redeem his sins by an offering of temporal goods must first offer his mind.

Augustine, there, ch. 15. Let him also beware lest, led by shame, he divide his confession within himself, wishing to disclose different matters to different priests. For some conceal from one what they reserve to reveal to another. This is self-praise, tends toward hypocrisy, and results in perpetual deprivation of the pardon which they think they can attain piecemeal.

Let him also beware lest he approach the Lord's body before he is strengthened by a good conscience, and let him grieve that he does not yet dare receive the saving food for which he greatly longs. Let one who wishes to attain the perfect grace of remission also refrain from games and worldly spectacles.

These are fruits worthy of repentance, freeing the captive soul from its snare and preserving it in freedom. And below:

> Let the soul seek worthy fruits, though not fruits worthy of repentance. There are fruits worthy of virtues which are insufficient for penitents. For repentance demands more grievous things, so that through grief and groans it may obtain life for one who is dead.

From these statements it is shown what are fruits worthy of repentance, by which true satisfaction is fulfilled; and that not all worthy fruits are fruits worthy of repentance. This is to be understood of repentance for more serious crimes. For what suffices for those who sin less gravely or only slightly does not suffice for those who sin gravely.

### What false satisfaction is

2. And just as there are fruits worthy of repentance and true satisfaction, so also there are unworthy fruits and false satisfaction—that is, false repentance. Hence Gregory, *On Penance*, distinction 5, chapter *False*:

> We call false those penitences which are not imposed according to the authorities of the saints in proportion to the nature of the crimes. Therefore, if a soldier, merchant, or person devoted to an occupation which he cannot pursue without sin, comes to repentance entangled in graver offenses; or if one unjustly retains another's property; or bears hatred in his heart: let him recognize that he cannot perform true repentance unless he abandons his business or [Col. 0879] occupation, casts hatred from his heart, and restores the goods which he unjustly took. Yet let him not despair. Meanwhile we exhort him to do whatever good he can, so that God may enlighten his heart unto repentance.

Since repentance is both inward and outward, what is true and what is false in each is sufficiently evident from what has preceded.

### On the three acts of repentance

3. To the foregoing must be added that repentance is performed in three ways: before Baptism, namely for former sins; after Baptism, for the graver sins committed afterward; and the daily repentance for venial sins, which belongs even to the humble and perfect. Hence Augustine, Homily 50, *On the Usefulness and Necessity of Penance*, and *On the Medicine of Penance*, ch. 2:

> There are three acts of repentance, which your instruction recognizes with me. One is that which gives birth to the new person, until through Baptism there comes cleansing from all past sins. For no one who is master of his own will can begin a new life unless he repents of the old; children are exempt from this when they are baptized, because they cannot yet use free choice, though the faith of those who present them benefits them for the remission of original sin. The second act of repentance is after Baptism, and is performed for those sins contained in the law of the Decalogue. Thus people repent before Baptism of prior sins, yet in such a way that they are also baptized, as Peter says, Acts 2: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord,” and so forth. They also repent if, after Baptism, they have sinned in such a way as to deserve excommunication and later reconciliation. There is also the daily penitential punishment of good and humble believers, in which we strike our breasts, saying, Matthew 6: “Forgive us our debts,” and so forth. We do not mean that those debts which we do not doubt were forgiven us in Baptism are to be forgiven again, but those small yet frequent sins which creep in through human frailty; if gathered against us, they will weigh us down and crush us just like one great sin. For what difference is there, for a shipwreck, whether a ship is covered and overwhelmed by one great wave, or whether water gradually entering the bilge through the fault of the negligent fills the ship and it sinks? Therefore let fasting, almsgiving, and prayers keep watch. When we say, “Forgive us our debts,” and so forth, we declare that we have something to be forgiven; and, humbling our souls with these words, we do not cease to perform daily repentance.

### On satisfaction for venial sins

4. Augustine indicates what satisfaction is sufficient for venial sins, saying thus in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 71:

> For daily, brief, and slight sins, without which this life cannot be lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction. For theirs is the saying, “Our Father who art in heaven,” and so forth. This prayer completely removes these least and daily sins. It also removes those sins from which the life of the faithful departs, even though it was wickedly lived but has been changed for the better through repentance. Just as it is truthfully said, “Forgive us our debts,” so it must also be truthfully said, “As we forgive our debtors”; that is, let what is said be done, since itself it is an almsgiving wholly to forgive those who ask pardon.

From these and the other preceding passages it is now easy to understand what satisfaction must be rendered for venial sins. The Lord's Prayer, together with fasting and almsgiving, suffices—provided that some contrition first precedes and confession is added if opportunity is available. This confession will be treated later.

For more serious sins, these things also must be employed in satisfaction, but much more intensely and strictly, because, as Augustine says in *On the Medicine of Penance*, ch. 5, and Homily 50, *On the Usefulness and Necessity of Penance*, “To perform repentance, it is not enough to change one's conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to the Lord for what has been done through penitential sorrow, the groaning of humility, the sacrifice of a contrite heart, and the assistance of almsgiving.”

## DISTINCTION XVII. THREE QUESTIONS ARE PROPOSED: FIRST, WHETHER SIN IS FORGIVEN WITHOUT CONFESSION

[Col. 0880]

1. Here a multiple question arises. First, whether, without satisfaction and oral confession, sin is forgiven to someone through contrition of heart alone; second, whether it is enough for someone to confess to God without a priest; third, whether confession made to a faithful layperson is valid.

Even among learned people divergent views are found on these matters, because the doctors appear to have handed down various and almost opposite teachings concerning them. Some say that no one is cleansed from sin without oral confession and satisfaction in deed, if he has the opportunity to perform them. Others say that, before oral confession and satisfaction, God forgives sin in contrition of heart, provided the person has the intention of confessing. Hence the prophet says, Psalm 31: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin.”

Explaining this, Cassiodorus says in the Ordinary Gloss: “‘I said,’ that is, I resolved within myself that I would confess, and you forgave. Great is God's mercy, who forgave sin upon a promise alone! For an intention is accounted as an action.”

Likewise Augustine:

> He has not yet uttered it, but promises that he will utter it, and God forgives; because this very saying is a certain utterance in the heart. The sound is not yet in the mouth for a human being to hear the confession, but God hears.

Likewise: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite heart,” and so forth. Elsewhere it is also read, Psalm 31: “At whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he shall live and shall not die.” It does not say, “when he has confessed with his mouth,” but “when converted, he has groaned.” Hence it is understood that, even while the mouth is silent, we sometimes obtain pardon.

Likewise, those lepers whom the Lord commanded to show themselves to the priests were cleansed on the way, before they came to the priests. From this it is suggested that, before we open our mouths to priests—that is, confess our sins—we are cleansed from the leprosy of sin.

Lazarus, too, was not first brought out of the tomb and then raised by the Lord. Rather, raised within, he came forth alive, in order to show that the resurrection of the soul precedes confession. For no one can confess unless raised, because from one dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes. Therefore no one confesses unless restored to life. But no one is raised unless released from sin, because sin is the death of the soul; and as the soul is the life of the body, so God is its life.

By these and many other authorities it is proved that before confession or satisfaction, sin is forgiven through compunction alone. Those who deny this labor to explain these texts and, in order to undermine this position and establish their own opinion, introduce testimonies of authorities.

For the Lord says through Isaiah: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified.” Likewise Ambrose: “No one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed the sin itself.” The same says: “Confession frees the soul from death; confession opens paradise; confession grants the hope of salvation, because one who is unwilling to confess sin during his life does not deserve to be justified. That confession frees us which is made with repentance. True repentance is grief of heart and bitterness of soul for the evils which each person has committed.”

Likewise John: “No one can receive the grace of God unless he has been cleansed from every sin through the confession of repentance and through Baptism.”

Likewise Augustine:

> Perform repentance such as is performed in the Church. Let no one say to himself, “I do it secretly, because I do it before God; God knows and forgives me because I do it in my heart.” Then was it said in vain, “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven”? Then were the keys given in vain? Then we make Christ's word void.

Job says: “If I was ashamed to confess my sins in the sight of the people.” Likewise Ambrose: “A fault is pardonable when confession of sins follows it.”

Likewise Augustine, on Psalm 68, “Let not the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me”:

> The pit is the depth of iniquity. If you fall into it, it will not close its mouth over you if you do not close your mouth. Therefore confess and say, “Out of the depths I have cried to you, O Lord,” and so forth, and you will escape. It closes over the one who despises while in the deep; from one dead, as from one who does not exist, confession perishes.

Likewise: “No one receives remission of the punishment due to him, however much more severe it is than the punishment he pays, unless he pays some punishment, however slight and far less than he owes.” For God's abundance of mercy is imparted in such a way that the justice of discipline is not set aside.

Likewise Jerome:

> Let the sinner weep for his own offenses or for those of the people, enter the church from which he had departed because of sins, and sleep in sackcloth, so that he may compensate by austerity of life for past delights through which he offended God.

By these and other authorities they endeavor to maintain that no one is cleansed from sin without confession of the voice and some payment of punishment.

### Which opinion should preferably be accepted

2. What, then, should be thought and maintained concerning these matters? It may certainly be said that sins are wiped away through contrition and humility of heart without oral confession and payment of an outward penalty. For from the moment someone, with a compunct heart, resolves to confess, God forgives, because there is then confession of heart, though not of mouth; through it the soul is inwardly cleansed from the stain and contagion of the sin committed, and the debt of eternal death is remitted.

Therefore the things said above concerning confession and repentance must be referred either to confession of heart or to outward punishment. Thus Augustine's statement that no one is said to obtain pardon unless he first pays some, however small, punishment for sin must be understood either of outward punishment or as referring to those who despise or neglect it; likewise the saying, “Let no one say, ‘I do it secretly,’” and so forth. For some neglect or are ashamed to confess their sins during life and therefore do not deserve to be justified.

For just as inward repentance has been commanded to us, so too have oral confession and outward satisfaction, if opportunity is present. Hence one who does not have the intention of confession is not truly penitent. And just as forgiveness of sin is God's gift, so repentance and confession, by which sin is erased, cannot exist except from God, as Augustine says: “He who confesses and repents already has the gift of the Holy Spirit, because confession of sin and compunction cannot arise in a human being from himself. For when each person is angry with himself and displeased with himself, this is not without the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore the penitent must confess sins if time permits; nevertheless, before there is confession in the mouth, if the intention is in the heart, forgiveness is granted.

### Whether it is enough to confess to God alone

3. Let us now consider the second part of the question: whether it is enough to confess sins to God alone, or whether one must confess to a priest.

Some have thought it sufficient if confession is made to God alone, without priestly judgment and the confession of the Church, because David said: “I said: I will confess to the Lord; and you forgave,” and so forth. He did not say, “to the priest,” yet he says that his sin was forgiven.

Likewise Ambrose:

> Peter therefore wept because fault had crept upon him. I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read of his tears; I do not read of his satisfaction. But what cannot be defended can be washed away. Tears wash away an offense which shame prevents from being confessed by the voice. Weeping provides both for pardon and for modesty.

Bishop Maximus says the same thing.

Likewise John Chrysostom:

> I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly or accuse yourself before others; rather, I want you to obey the Prophet who says, “Reveal your life to God.” Therefore confess your sins before God, the true judge; declare your offenses in prayer, not with your tongue but in the recollection of your conscience; and then at last hope that you may obtain mercy. If you keep your sins continually in mind, you will never harbor evil against your neighbor in your heart.

The same author:

> Speak of your sins daily, so that you may erase them. But if you are ashamed to tell them to someone, speak of them daily in your mind. I do not say that you should confess them to your fellow servant, so that he may reproach you. Speak of them to God, who heals them. For even if you do not tell him, he does not fail to know them: he was present when you committed them; when you committed them, he knew. Does he wish to learn them from you? You were not ashamed to sin, and are you ashamed to confess? Speak in this life, so that in the other you may have rest; speak while groaning and weeping. Your sins are written in a book; let your tears be the sponge for your sins.

Likewise Prosper, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *Moreover Those*, and *On the Contemplative Life*, ch. 7:

> Those whose sins are hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor made public by others, if they are unwilling to confess or amend them, will have as avenger the God whom they have as witness. But if they become their own judges and, as it were, avengers of their own iniquity, and here inflict upon themselves a voluntary punishment of most severe correction, they will exchange eternal punishments for temporal ones and extinguish the fires of eternal flame with tears flowing from true contrition of heart.

And below, in the same place:

> They will more easily appease God who either disclose their crime by their own confessions or, though others do not know it, pronounce upon themselves a sentence of voluntary excommunication; separated from the altar at which they ministered—not in intention, but in office—they mourn their life as though dead. They may be certain that, reconciled to themselves by the fruits of efficacious repentance, they will receive from God not only what they lost, but also the joys of the heavenly city.

Those who contend that it is enough to confess sins to God without a priest rely on these authorities. They say that if someone fears to reveal his fault to people, lest he thereby incur reproach or others be encouraged to sin by his example, and therefore keeps silent before a human being but reveals it to God, he obtains pardon.

### That it is not enough to confess to God alone if opportunity is present, provided one can confess to a human being

4. But that confession must be made to priests is established not only by James 5, “Confess your sins to one another,” and so forth, but also by many other testimonies.

For Augustine says in Homily 50, *On the Usefulness and Necessity of Penance*:

> Let a person judge himself voluntarily while he can, and change his conduct for the better, lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged by the Lord against his will. And when he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of most severe medicine, yet most useful, let him come to the bishops through whom the keys of the Church are administered to him. As a good son now beginning to be such, preserving the order of the maternal members, let him receive from the rulers of sacred things the measure of his satisfaction, devout and humble in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart. Yet let him do what benefits not only his own salvation but also provides an example to others: if his sin consists not only in his own grave evil but also in such great scandal to others, and the bishop judges this expedient for the Church's good, let him not refuse to do penance in the knowledge of many or of the whole people, lest through shame he add swelling to a lethal wound. When the wound of sin and violence of the disease are so great that the remedies of the Lord's body and blood must be deferred by the bishop's authority, each person ought to withdraw from the altar to perform repentance and be reconciled by the same authority.

Likewise Pope Leo, *On Penance*, distinction 1, chapter *Manifold*:

> God's manifold mercy so comes to the aid of human falls that the hope of life is restored not only through Baptism but also through repentance. Thus the supports of the divine will are ordained so that people cannot obtain God's pardon except through the prayers of priests. For Christ gave this authority to the rulers of the Church: to impose penitential satisfaction upon those who confess, and, after cleansing them by wholesome satisfaction, to admit them to communion in the sacraments through the gate of reconciliation.

Likewise Augustine, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10:

> Whoever repents, let him repent entirely and show his grief in tears. Let him present his life to God through the priest; let him anticipate God's judgment through confession. For the Lord commanded those being cleansed to show their faces to the priests, teaching that sins must be confessed in bodily presence, not disclosed in writing. He said, “Show your faces”—and all of you; not one person for all, nor appoint another as a messenger to offer to God on your behalf the offering established by Moses. But you who sinned must yourselves blush. For shame itself has a part in remission. The Lord commanded this in mercy, so that no one might repent in secret. For in personally speaking to the priest and overcoming shame [Col. 0883], a person obtains pardon for his crime through fear of the God whom he has offended. What was criminal in its commission becomes pardonable through confession; and, even if it is not immediately cleansed, what he committed as mortal becomes pardonable. For the person who, mastering shame, withheld none of the things he committed from God's messenger has offered much satisfaction. For God, who is merciful and just, as he preserves mercy in justice, so also preserves justice in mercy. To forgive sins to a sinner is an act of mercy; but the just God must show mercy justly. For he considers whether the person is worthy, not only, I say, of justice, but even of mercy. Justice alone condemns; but the one who seeks grace through spiritual labor is worthy of mercy. The mind labors in enduring shame. And because shame is a great punishment, one who is ashamed for Christ becomes worthy of mercy. Hence it is clear that the more persons to whom one confesses the shamefulness of one's crime in hope of pardon, the more easily one obtains the grace of remission. For the priests themselves can do more and be more lenient toward those who confess.

Likewise Pope Leo, *On Penance*, distinction 1:

> Although the fullness of faith that does not fear to blush before people because of the fear of God seems praiseworthy, yet because not all sins are of such a kind that those seeking repentance do not fear their publication, this objectionable custom must be removed, lest many be excluded from remedies of repentance because they are ashamed or fear to reveal their deeds to enemies who may strike them under legal provisions. For confession is sufficient when it is first offered to God and then also to the priest, who approaches as an intercessor for the offenses of penitents. For then more people can be summoned to repentance if the confessor's conscience is not made public to the ears of the people.

From these and many other passages it is shown beyond doubt that confession must first be offered to God and then to the priest, and that one cannot otherwise attain entrance into paradise, if opportunity is available.

### On the third point: whether it is enough to confess to a layperson
5. But now, before we answer the authorities set forth above which seem to contradict these points, let us consider the third question. For what the second question contained—namely, whether, without confession and the judgment of a priest, it were enough to confess to God alone—has been resolved and established by the foregoing testimonies: it is not enough to confess to God without a priest; nor is one truly humble and penitent if one does not desire and seek the priest’s judgment. But is confession to one’s companion or neighbor of equal value, at least when a priest is unavailable?

Certainly, one may say in reply that a priest’s examination must earnestly be sought, because God granted priests the power of binding and loosing; and therefore those whom they forgive, God also forgives. Nevertheless, if a priest is lacking, confession must be made to a neighbor or companion. But everyone should take care to seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose. For such a person ought to be the one who judges the crimes of others.

Hence Augustine, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10:

> Whoever wishes to confess sins in order to find grace should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, because he has been negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by the one who mercifully warns and seeks him; lest both fall into the pit which the foolish man refused to avoid.

So great, therefore, is the power of confession that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to one’s neighbor. For it often happens that a penitent cannot be ashamed before the priest, since neither time nor place affords access to the priest whom he desires. And although the person to whom he confesses has no power to absolve, he nevertheless becomes worthy of pardon through his desire for a priest, when he confesses his crime to a companion. For the lepers were cleansed while they were going to show themselves to the priests, before they reached them. Hence it is clear that God looks upon the heart when a person is prevented by necessity from reaching the priests.

Thus Augustine, in the same place:

> Often indeed they seek them while healthy and cheerful; but while seeking them, they die before they arrive. Yet the mercy of God is everywhere; he knows how to spare even the righteous, though not as swiftly as if they were absolved by a priest.

In the same work, ch. 11:

> Therefore, whoever confesses to a priest should confess to the best priest he can find; and if the sin is hidden, it is enough to bring it to the knowledge of the priest. For, at the raising of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, only a few were present who saw: for she had not yet been buried, had not yet been carried outside the gate, had not yet been brought forth from the house into public notice. He raised within the house her whom he found within, leaving only Peter, James, and John, and the girl’s father and mother—by whom the priests of the Church are figuratively represented. But concerning those whom he found outside, one should observe how he raised them. For the crowd wept after the widow’s son; Martha and Mary wept, pleading for their brother; and the crowd that followed Mary also wept. In this we are taught that, for those who sin publicly, not their own merit but that of the Church suffices.

Augustine, in the same work, ch. 12:

> Let the penitent therefore strive to be within the Church and to tend toward the unity of the Church. Unless the unity of the Church comes to his aid, unless it supplies by its prayer what the sinner lacks, the soul of the dead man will not be snatched from the enemy’s hands. For it must be believed that all the prayers and alms of the Church, and works of righteousness and mercy, assist one who acknowledges his death unto conversion. Therefore no one can worthily repent unless he is sustained by the unity of the Church. Therefore let no one seek priests who, through some fault, have been separated from the unity of the Church.

From these passages the point of the preceding question is sufficiently clarified and resolved. A wise and discerning priest must be sought, one who possesses judgment together with authority; but if he happens to be unavailable, confession should be made to a companion.

Bede, however, on James 5, distinguishes between the confession of venial and mortal sins in commenting on the passage, “Confess your sins to one another.” For he says:

> We should disclose daily and light sins to our equals, but graver sins to a priest; and we should take care to purge them for whatever time he commands, because sins cannot be forgiven without the confession of amendment. Yet graver sins must also be disclosed to equals when a priest is unavailable and danger presses. Venial sins, however, may be confessed even to an equal when priests are available; and this suffices, as some hold, provided that the priest is not omitted out of contempt. Nevertheless, it is safer and more perfect to disclose sins of both kinds to priests and seek from them counsel for healing, since the power of binding and loosing has been granted to them.

### Here he explains how the authorities mentioned above are to be understood.

6. Therefore, since from these and many other testimonies it is plain and unquestionably established that sins must first be confessed to God and then to a priest, and, if he is unavailable, also to a companion, the passage from John Chrysostom cited above, *On Penance*, distinction 1, ch. *Quos aliquando*, near the end, must not be understood as though someone who has the opportunity may refrain from confessing to a priest. Rather, it means that where the crime is hidden, it is enough to tell God alone through the priest, and only once. Nor ought what is hidden to be made public before many people. This is what he indicated by saying: “I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly.”

For just as a public offense requires a public remedy, so a hidden offense is cleansed by secret confession and hidden satisfaction. Nor is it necessary that what we have confessed once to a priest be confessed again; but before the true Judge we must continually confess it with the tongue of the heart, not of the flesh.

Hence the same John, in the same work, ch. *Nunc autem*, says:

> But if you remember your sins and frequently pronounce them before God’s sight and pray concerning them, you will erase them more quickly. But if you forget them, then you will remember them unwillingly when they are made public and brought forth before the sight of all friends and enemies and of the holy angels.

Likewise, Ambrose’s statement, *On Penance*, distinction 1, ch. *Lacrymae*—“Tears wash away the offense which shame prevents one from confessing aloud; it must be referred to public penance”—is to be understood in this way. There, showing the power of tears and confession, he intended to signify that hidden tears and secret confession, such as is made to a priest alone, wash away an offense which someone is ashamed to confess publicly.

But when he says that he has read of Peter’s tears, not of his satisfaction or confession, he does not thereby exclude these things. For many things were done which were not written; and perhaps the institution of confession, which now exists, had not yet been established.

Likewise Prosper’s statement, “If they become their own judges, they will change eternal punishments” [Col. 0885], and the other, “They will more easily make God favorable to themselves who either reveal their crime by their own confessions or, while others do not know, pronounce upon themselves a sentence of excommunication,” must be referred to public confession and satisfaction. For the right of binding and loosing has not been given to priests alone if anyone may, at his own discretion, bind himself by a penalty or sentence of excommunication and reconcile himself to God or the altar without priestly judgment—a practice wholly opposed to ecclesiastical institution and custom.

Therefore, if you have sinned publicly, confess publicly that you are guilty and make amends. But if you have sinned secretly, do not remain silent even so; yet I do not say that you should make it public. For silence concerning sin arises from the pride of the heart. A person hides his sin in order not to be considered outwardly what he has already shown himself to be in the sight of God; and this springs from the fountain of pride. For it is a form of pride to wish to appear righteous while one is a sinner. And that person is shown to be a hypocrite who, after the manner of the first parents, either attempts to minimize his sins through evasive words or, like Cain, seeks to suppress them by keeping silent.

Where pride and hypocrisy reign, humility has no place. But without humility no one may hope for forgiveness. Therefore, where confession is kept silent, pardon for the crime is not to be hoped for. It is now entirely clear how detestable silence concerning sin is, and conversely how necessary confession is.

For confession is the testimony of a conscience that fears God. Whoever fears God’s judgment is not ashamed to confess sin. Perfect fear removes every shame; confession of sin involves shame, and that very shame is a heavy punishment. Therefore we are commanded to confess our sins, so that we may endure shame as punishment; for this itself is part of the divine judgment. If, then, it is asked whether confession is necessary when sin has already been removed through contrition, we say that it is a certain punishment for sin, like satisfaction in deeds. Through confession, moreover, the priest understands how he ought to judge concerning the offense. By it also the sinner becomes more humble and more cautious.

## DISTINCTION XVIII. ON THE PRIEST’S FORGIVENESS

1. Here it is commonly asked: if sin has been entirely forgiven by God through contrition of heart, from the moment when the penitent had the intention of confessing, what is thereafter forgiven him by the priest? For I see by what bond he binds him—namely, that of temporal punishment—but not from what he absolves him. Therefore I ask.

Before repentance of heart, the soul of the guilty person bears the stain and foulness of sin and remains bound by the bond of eternal punishment. But if, before confession, God himself, without the ministry of a priest, through contrition of heart entirely remits both the debt and inwardly cleanses the soul from the contagion and foulness of sin, what then does the priest cleanse? What does he forgive? Where are those keys which the Lord gave to Peter and his successors, saying in Matthew 16: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” etc.: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also,” etc. [Luke 5?]

But in order that the preceding question may be more fully explained, let us, as it were, cast the net deeper and discuss these keys and their use.

### On the keys

2. These keys are not bodily but spiritual: namely, the knowledge of discernment and the power of judging—that is, of binding and loosing. By these the ecclesiastical judge, who has the right of loosing just as he has that of binding, ought to receive the worthy and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom.

Hence Ambrose, *On Penance*, distinction 1, ch. *Verbum Dei*:

> The Lord willed the right of loosing and binding to be equal, since he permitted both under equal conditions. Therefore one who does not have the right of loosing does not have that of binding either.

And below:

> It is certain that the Church is permitted both; heresy has neither. For this right has been granted to priests alone. Therefore the Church rightly claims this for herself, because she has true priests; heresy cannot claim it, because it does not have true priests.

### On the use of the keys

[Col. 0886]

3. The use of these keys is manifold: namely, to discern those to be bound and those to be loosed, and then to bind or loose them. For, as Gregory says, one who binds or looses the unworthy deprives himself of his own authority—that is, makes himself worthy of deprivation.

### Whether a priest can forgive or retain sins

4. But it is asked whether a priest can loose a person from sin—that is, from guilt—so as to wipe away the stain of guilt, or whether he can remit the debt of eternal death.

Some have thought that, since a sinner is held bound in two ways, as stated above—namely, by the contagion and blindness of the mind, and by the debt of future punishment—one is healed by God and the other loosed by the priest. For through sin a person suffers certain inward darknesses and stains, and unless he is freed from them, he will be cast into outer darkness. When he is freed from them, however, he is raised from the death of sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you.”

For Christ alone, not the priest, raises the soul; and, having driven away its inner darknesses and stains, he enlightens and cleanses it—the one who washes the face of the soul. But they maintain that he granted priests the power to remit the debt of eternal punishment. They assert that this is signified in the raising of Lazarus: Christ first gave him inward life by himself, then ordered him to come out, and commanded the apostles to loose him while he was still bound. For, as they say, Christ himself inwardly cleanses the soul from the darkness and stain of sin, but gave priests the power to loose the bond of eternal death.

Others, however, say that God alone, not the priest, remits the debt of eternal death, just as he himself inwardly gives life to the soul. Yet they do not deny that the power to forgive and retain sins was entrusted to priests, to whom it was said, John 10: “Whose sins you forgive,” etc. For just as Christ retained for himself the power of Baptism, so also that of Penance. Therefore, just as he inwardly enlightens the soul by his grace, so he simultaneously remits the debt of eternal death. For he himself covers the sins of penitents; and he covers them when he does not reserve them for punishment. Therefore he covers them when he remits the debt of punishment.

That he himself covers them Augustine clearly says in expounding Psalm 31: “Whose sins are covered,” that is, concealed and abolished. For if God has covered sins, he has not wished to take notice of them; and if he has not wished to take notice of them, he has not wished to exact punishment—that is, to punish—but to forgive. Thus he calls sins covered by God so that God does not see them—that is, does not punish them eternally. For God’s seeing sins is his imputing them for punishment. But turning his face away from sins is not reserving them for punishment.

Likewise Jerome, in his commentary on the same Psalm:

> Those whose sins God forgives, he covers, so that they may not be revealed in judgment.

Likewise Cassiodorus, on the same Psalm, on the words, “Blessed is the man who,” etc.:

> Of those who have grave sins, God imputes them to some; to others he does not impute them through mercy.

From these passages it is clearly shown that God himself looses the penitent from the debt of punishment; and he looses him when he inwardly enlightens him by inspiring true contrition of heart. Reason supports this judgment and authorities attest it. For no one is truly pierced with grief for sin, possessing a contrite and humbled heart, unless he is in charity. But one who has charity is worthy of eternal life. No one, however, is worthy simultaneously of life and death. Therefore he is not then bound by the debt of eternal death. For he ceased to be a child of wrath from the moment he began to love.

From that moment, therefore, he is loosed from wrath, which does not remain upon one who believes in Christ, but upon one who does not believe. Therefore he is not afterward delivered by the priest to whom he confesses from eternal wrath, from which he was already delivered through the Lord from the time when he said, “I will confess.”

Therefore God alone inwardly cleanses a person from the stain of sin and looses him from the debt of eternal punishment. Through the prophet Isaiah 43 he says: “I alone blot out the iniquities and sins of the people.” Likewise Ambrose says: “The Word of God forgives sins; the priest is a judge. The priest indeed performs his office, but exercises no rights of power.”

Likewise Augustine, Tractate 121 on John:

> No one takes away sins except God alone, who is the Lamb taking away the sins of the world. He takes them away both by forgiving what has been done, by helping so that they are not done, and by leading to the life in which they cannot be done at all.

[Col. 0887]

By these and many other testimonies we are taught that the Lord alone, by himself, forgives sins; and just as he forgives the sins of some, so he retains the sins of certain others.

### That priests also forgive and retain sins, in their own manner

5. Yet we do not therefore deny that priests have been granted the power of forgiving and retaining sins, since Truth clearly teaches this in the Gospel. Hence Augustine says, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10:

> The charity of the Church, which is poured out through the Holy Spirit into the hearts of those who share in it, forgives the sins of those who belong to it; it retains the sins of those who do not.

The same author says:

> Priests can spare those who confess; for those whom they forgive, God forgives. For he presented Lazarus, raised from the tomb, to the disciples to be loosed, thereby showing that the power of loosing was granted to priests. For he said, Matthew 16: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven,” etc.; that is: I, God, and all ranks of the heavenly court, and all the saints in my glory, praise with you and confirm those whom you bind and loose.
