He did not say, “Whom you suppose that you bind and loose,” but “those upon whom you exercise the work of justice or mercy.” But I do not acknowledge your other works upon sinners.

The same author, *On the Baptism of Little Children*, book 6:

> When sins are forgiven to one truly converted to God, they are forgiven by those to whom he is joined by that true conversion. The Holy Spirit forgives them, the Spirit who has been given to all saints united to himself by charity, whether they know one another bodily or not. Likewise, when someone’s sins are retained, they are retained by those from whom that person is separated through perversity of heart, whether bodily known or unknown. For all the wicked are spiritually separated from the good.

See: here he says that sins are forgiven or retained by holy persons, and yet says that the Holy Spirit forgives them. What is still more worthy of consideration, he also says that God forgives sins only by himself or through saints. For he says:

> God gives the sacrament of grace even through the wicked; but grace itself only through himself or through his saints. Therefore he brings about the forgiveness of sins either by himself or through the members of his dove, to whom he says: “If you forgive anyone, it shall be forgiven.”

See how various are the teachings handed down by the doctors concerning these matters; and what is to be maintained amid such great diversity? We may safely state and hold this: God alone forgives and retains sins; yet he granted the Church the power of binding and loosing. But he binds or looses in one way, and the Church in another. For he alone himself forgives sin: he both cleanses the soul from its inward stain and looses it from the debt of eternal death.

### How priests bind or loose from sins

6. But he did not grant this to priests, although he did give them the power of loosing and binding: that is, of showing persons to be bound or loosed. Thus the Lord first restored the leper to health by himself and afterward sent him to the priests, so that he might be shown clean by their judgment. Likewise, he presented Lazarus, already given life, to the disciples to be loosed. For although someone may be loosed before God, he is not regarded as loosed in the face of the Church except through the judgment of a priest.

Therefore, in loosing or retaining guilt, the evangelical priest acts and judges in the same way as the legal priest formerly did with those contaminated by leprosy, which signifies sin. Hence Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew 16, where the Lord says to Peter, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven,” says:

> Some people, not understanding this passage, assume something of the arrogance of the Pharisees, so that they think they can condemn the innocent or loose the guilty, whereas before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is considered. In Leviticus the lepers are commanded to show themselves to the priests; the priests do not make them leprous or clean, but discern who is clean and who is unclean.

Thus here also it is plainly shown that God does not always follow the Church’s judgment, which sometimes judges through deception and ignorance; but God always judges according to truth. In forgiving or retaining guilt, evangelical priests possess the same legal right and office that legal priests formerly possessed under the Law in treating lepers.

Thus priests forgive or retain sins when they judge and show sins to have been forgiven or retained by God. For priests place the Lord’s name upon the children of Israel, but he himself blesses, as is read in Numbers. Jerome noted above this manner of binding and loosing.

7. Priests also bind when they impose the satisfaction of Penance upon those who confess. They loose when they remit some part of it or admit to communion of the sacraments those cleansed by it; Pope Leo noted this manner above. In this sense priests too are said to forgive or retain sins. Hence Augustine said above, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10: “Those whom they forgive, God forgives,” etc.

For they exercise a work of justice upon sinners when they bind them by a just punishment; they exercise a work of mercy when they relax some part of it or reconcile them to sacramental communion. They cannot perform other works upon sinners. And it should be noted that those whom they bind by the satisfaction of penance they thereby show to be loosed from sins, because penitential satisfaction is imposed upon no one unless the priest judges him truly penitent. Upon others, however, they do not impose it; and thereby they judge that their sin is retained by God.

That this belongs to the keys Augustine shows when he says in his book *On Penance*:

> He frustrates the keys of the Church who performs penance without the judgment of a priest, if he seeks pardon for his crime without confession by the mouth.

There is also another manner of binding and loosing, exercised through excommunication. When someone, according to canonical discipline, having been summoned three times to correct a manifest offense, despises making satisfaction, he is cut off by the Church’s sentence from the place of prayer, from communion in the sacraments, and from the fellowship of the faithful, so that he may be ashamed and, converted by shame for his crime, repent, so that his spirit may thus be saved, as in 1 Corinthians 5. But if, professing repentance, he comes to his senses, he is admitted to the communion previously denied and reconciled to the Church.

This is the Church’s anathematization. It inflicts this punishment on those properly struck by it because God’s grace and protection are further withdrawn, and they are left to themselves, so that they may freely fall into the destruction of sin. Greater power to rage is also granted to the devil against them. Likewise, the prayers of the Church and the assistance of its blessings and merits are thought to be of no avail to them.

### How, according to these modes, the saying “Whatever you loose,” etc., is to be understood

8. According to these modes of binding and loosing, how is the saying in Matthew 16 true: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” etc.? For sometimes priests show persons to be loosed or bound who are not so before God; and sometimes by the punishment of satisfaction or excommunication they bind or loose the unworthy; they admit the unworthy to the sacraments and prevent the worthy from being admitted.

But this must be understood concerning those whose merits demand that they be loosed or bound. For then the priest’s sentence is approved and confirmed by the judgment of God and of the entire heavenly court, when it proceeds with such discernment that the merits of the accused do not contradict it. Therefore all whom priests loose or bind, applying the key of discernment to the merits of the accused, are loosed or bound in heaven—that is, before God—because a priestly judgment so rendered is approved and confirmed by divine judgment.

Therefore those whom the sentence of the Church strikes according to their merits are harmed, and they are outside before God. But one who has not deserved it is not harmed by the Church’s sentence unless he despises it. Hence Origen, on Leviticus, Homily 14, on chapter 24:

> Whoever departs from truth, faith, and charity thereby goes out from the camp of the Church, even though he is not cast out by the bishop’s pronouncement. Conversely, someone is cast out by an unjust judgment; but if he has done nothing to deserve expulsion, he is not harmed. For sometimes one who is cast out is within, and one who is outside appears to be retained within.

See what the use of the apostolic keys is, and how great it is. It has now been shown in part how priests forgive or retain sins. Yet God retained for himself a certain singular power of forgiving or retaining, because he alone, by himself, looses the debt of eternal death and inwardly cleanses the soul.

### What the inward darkness and inward stain are

9. Here it is asked what that stain is, and what those inward darknesses are, from which God inwardly cleanses the soul when he instills true repentance. Regarding darkness and inward gloom, it is rather easy both to understand and answer.

For when someone sins mortally, he is deprived of the grace of virtue, if he previously had it, and suffers an impairment of natural goods. Hence the understanding is dulled and the whole inward person is darkened; thus the mind is enveloped, as it were, by a certain gloom, which gloom is the punishment of sin. God drives this away when he instills repentance, through which he restores lost goods and repairs what has been impaired. Hence the Prophet says, Psalm 147: “He scatters the mist like ashes.”

But what is the stain of sin from which he washes the soul? Consider someone who wished to commit murder and carried it out. Once it has been done, he ceases both to wish and to perform it; yet he does not truly and humbly repent, nor does he intend to confess. What stain, then, remains in his soul? The evil will was indeed the stain of that soul, but it has passed away. It is also a stain if he despises repentance; but this is another sin, distinct from the preceding one. What stain, then, remains, from which he is cleansed in Penance?

The soul remains polluted until it repents, just as it was when the perverse will was in it. For just as a person who touches a corpse or another unclean thing is as polluted after touching it, until washed, as he was while touching it, so after the act of sin the soul remains as polluted as it was in the very act of sin. For it remains as far from God through dissimilarity—God who is the life and purity of the mind—as it was while committing the sin.

Therefore that very dissimilarity which is in the soul through sin, and is an alienation from God, is understood to be the soul’s stain, from which it is cleansed in Penance. But God alone does this, for he alone raises and enlightens the soul. Priests cannot do this, although they are physicians of souls. Hence the Prophet says, Psalm 87: “Will physicians raise the dead and confess you?” Augustine, expounding this, says:

> Good teachers are rightly called physicians, because by their ministry they can heal the living, but cannot raise the dead. For the dead live again only through God’s grace.

## DISTINCTION XIX. WHEN THESE KEYS ARE GIVEN, AND TO WHOM

1. Having shown what the apostolic keys are and what their use is, it remains to investigate when these keys are given, and to whom. These keys are given through the ministry of a bishop to someone at his promotion to the priesthood. For when he receives priestly order, he receives these keys at the same time.

But it does not seem that all priests, or priests alone, possess these keys, because many possess the knowledge of discernment before sacred ordination, while many lack it after consecration. One may rightly say that not all priests possess one of these keys—namely, the knowledge of discernment—and this is a cause for grief and lamentation. For many, although undiscerning and devoid of the knowledge in which they ought to excel, presume to receive the rank of priesthood while unworthy of it in life and learning. They possess neither before nor after priesthood the knowledge to discern who should be bound or loosed. Therefore they do not receive that key in consecration, because they always lack knowledge.

But those endowed with the knowledge of discernment before priesthood, although they possess discernment, do not yet possess a key in themselves, because they are unable by it to close or open. Therefore, when a person is promoted to the priesthood, he is rightly said to receive the key of discernment, because the discernment he already possessed is increased and becomes a key in him, so that he may now use it to close or open.

### Whether all priests possess the other key, namely, the power of binding and loosing

2. Since it is now established that not all priests possess both keys, because most lack the knowledge of discernment, the question remains concerning the other—that is, the power of binding and loosing—whether all priests possess it.

For some think that this power has been granted only to those who observe both the teaching and the life of the apostles. For, they say, the Lord promised those keys to Peter and his imitators alone. They also use authorities to support their opinion. They say that Augustine meant this when he stated above, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, book 5, ch. 21: “God brings about forgiveness of sins either by himself or through the members of the dove.” The same author also says that sins are forgiven or retained by saints.

Likewise, Augustine, on Exodus, ch. 120, where one reads of the golden plate, “But the golden plate was always upon the priest’s forehead,” says:

> This signifies the confidence of a good life; and the person who possesses it truly and perfectly—not by signification but in reality—as a priest, can alone take away sins.

Likewise Gregory, in *Gospel Homilies*, Homily 27:

> Those alone, while placed in this flesh, have the power of binding and loosing, like the holy apostles, who maintain both their example and their teaching.

Likewise, from Origen’s statements:

> This power was granted to Peter alone and to Peter’s imitators. For whoever imitates Peter’s footsteps rightly possesses the power of binding and loosing.

Those who assert that the power of binding and loosing was granted only to priests who shine in life and teaching like the apostles rely upon these and other testimonies.

### The truer opinion of others

3. But it seems to others—and I confess that this opinion pleases me—that this key, namely the power of binding and loosing, is given to all priests, though they do not possess it rightly and worthily unless they observe apostolic life and teaching. Nor do the authorities cited above deny that wicked priests possess this power; rather, they signify that only those endowed with apostolic life and teaching use this power worthily and rightly. For only imitators of the apostles can bind and loose worthily and rightly.

And forgiveness or retention of sins is accomplished worthily and rightly only by the Lord or by the saints in whom the Holy Spirit dwells. Yet it is also accomplished through those who are not saints, though not worthily or rightly. For God gives his blessing to one who worthily seeks it even through an unworthy minister.

That all priests possess this power Jerome testifies in commenting on the Gospel passage where the Lord said to Peter, Matthew 16: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” For, he says:

> The other apostles have the same judicial power; and the whole Church possesses it in bishops and presbyters. But Peter received it specially so that all may understand that whoever separates himself from the unity of faith and fellowship of the Church can neither be loosed from sins nor enter heaven.

Likewise, Augustine shows that a priest, even if wicked, nevertheless conveys grace by virtue of his office’s dignity. In his book *Questions on the Old Testament*, he says:

> The Lord said in Numbers 6 to Moses and Aaron the priests: “Place my name upon the children of Israel, and I, the Lord, will bless them,” so that he may convey to people through the ministry of the ordained person the grace entrusted to him. The will of priests cannot harm or benefit, but the merit of the person seeking blessing does.

But let us observe from this how great is the dignity of the priestly office and order. It is said in John 11 concerning the utterly wicked Caiaphas, among other things: “He did not say this of himself; but because he was high priest that year, he prophesied.” By this it is shown that the Spirit of graces follows not the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission. Thus, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he is ordained, so that he may perform the ministry of his office. But it belongs to God to grant the effect of blessing.

From this it is clearly shown that the order is not deprived of the power of imparting grace because of the minister’s unworthiness.

Yet Hesychius seems to oppose Augustine’s judgment. In his commentary on Leviticus 9, book 2, he says:

> Priests bless not by their own power but because they bear the figure of Christ and, on account of him who is in them, bestow the fullness of blessing. Nor is only he who has received the priesthood competent to confer blessing; whoever has Christ in himself and bears his figure through good conduct, like Moses, is competent to do so.

See: here you have that not only a priest but everyone in whom Christ dwells confers blessing. But one kind of blessing belongs only to priests; another is commonly bestowed by all good persons. Finally, those priests in whom Christ dwells are said to bestow the fullness of blessing, not because they alone convey grace, but because they alone do this lawfully and worthily.

Nor does a priest’s evil life harm those subject to him if they do the good things which he says. Hence Gregory says:

> Many, while scrutinizing the lives of priests more than their own, fall into the pit of error, giving too little consideration to the fact that priests’ lives would not harm them if they humbly gave heed to the good admonitions of priests.

### On what is written in Malachi: “I will curse your blessings”

4. But the preceding judgment—that the grace of blessing is conveyed even through the ministry of an evil priest—seems to be opposed by the threat which the Lord makes through the prophet Malachi, ch. 2, against evil priests: “I will curse your blessings.” And elsewhere, Ezekiel 13: “Woe to those who give life to souls that do not live, and put to death souls that do not die!” For if the Lord curses their blessings, and if the souls to which they give life do not live, how is the grace of blessing conveyed through them?

But some refer the chapter, “I will curse,” etc., to heretics who have been cut off from the Church and to excommunicated persons, whose blessings become curses for those who follow their errors. They explain the other statement, “give life,” etc., as concerning all those priests who presume to bind or loose without the key of knowledge and the form of a good life. But no one ought to exercise the priestly office unless free from the faults which he judges in others; otherwise, he condemns himself.

### What an ecclesiastical judge ought to be like
5. But what sort of person one appointed as judge of others ought to be, Augustine describes as follows, saying in *On True and False Penance*, chapter 20:

> The priest to whom every sinner is presented, before whom every sickness is set, must not be liable to judgment in any of those things in which he is ready to judge another. For one who judges another, while himself liable to judgment, condemns himself. Let him therefore know himself, and cleanse in himself what he sees others bring before him; let him beware that he has cast away from himself whatever he finds harmful in another. Let him heed that whoever is without sin should be the first to cast a stone at her [John 8]. For this reason he set the sinful woman free: there was no one who could justly cast the stone. How could one stone her who knew that he himself deserved to be stoned? For no one was without sin; from which it is understood that all were guilty of a criminal offence, since venial sins were remitted through ceremonies. Therefore, if there was sin in them, it was criminal. Hence it is utterly clear that the crime of priests is detestable when they do not first judge themselves before binding others. Let the spiritual judge take care that, just as he has not committed the crime of wickedness, so he is not without the gift of knowledge. He must know how to recognize whatever he ought to judge. For judicial authority requires that he discern what he is to judge. Thus, as a diligent investigator, let him wisely ask the sinner about what he may perhaps not know, or may wish to conceal out of shame. Once the offence is known, let him not hesitate to investigate its circumstances: place, time, and the other matters mentioned above. When these are known, let him be kindly, ready to raise the sinner up and to bear the burden with him. Let him have gentleness in affection, discernment amid diversity, teach perseverance, and beware lest he fall and thereby justly lose his judicial authority. Although penance may obtain grace for him, it does not immediately restore him to his former authority. Although Peter was restored after his fall, and the authority of office has often been restored to fallen priests, it need not be granted to all as though by rule. There is an authority that grants it and, as it were, commands it. There is another authority that does not grant it but forbids it; these do not conflict with Scripture, but agree with it. For when there are so many who fall that they defend their former dignity by appeal to authority and virtually make for themselves a practice of sinning, this hope must be cut off. But if there is a case in which these considerations do not apply, those who sin may be restored.

Thus far Augustine, in the above-cited chapter 10 [Col. 0892]. From this it is sufficiently clear what a priest who binds and looses others ought to be: namely, discerning and just. Otherwise he often kills souls that do not die and gives life to those that do not live, and thus falls under the judgment of the curse.

But the saying in Malachi, “I will curse your blessings,” whether it is understood as spoken only concerning heretics and the excommunicated, or concerning all priests who presume to bless while lacking life and knowledge, may be understood thus: “I will curse your blessings,” that is, the things you possess in those blessings, because I shall make them turn for you into a curse rather than a blessing. For even if they bless the holy, they do not do so from a true heart; and therefore their blessing is turned into a curse for them. Or: “I will curse your blessings,” that is, what is blessed by you will be cursed by me, because they bless those acting unjustly and flatter sinners, provided that they are rich. (Jerome, near the beginning of his commentary on Malachi, chapter 2.)

## DISTINCTION XX. CONCERNING THOSE WHO REPENT AT THE END

1. It must also be known that the time for repentance lasts until the final moment of life. Hence Pope Leo, *On Penance*, distinction 7:

> No one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, because what is deferred through distrust caused by age is sometimes accomplished by maturer counsel.

Augustine, however, writes as follows concerning those who defer repentance:

> If someone placed in his final necessity wishes to receive Penance, and receives it and is immediately reconciled, and then departs this life, I confess to you that we do not deny him what he asks; but we do not presume that he departs well. If he departs safely, I do not know. We can give Penance; we cannot give assurance. Do I say that he will be damned? No; but neither do I say that he will be saved. Do you therefore wish to be freed from uncertainty? Do penance while you are well. If you do this, I tell you that you are secure, because you did penance at the time when you were able to sin. If you wish to do penance when you can no longer sin, it is your sins that have left you, not you them.

Again:

> There are two possibilities: either you are forgiven or you are not forgiven; which of these will happen to you I do not know. Therefore hold fast to what is certain, and leave aside what is uncertain.

But why did Augustine say this, when repentance performed at the end is called in Psalm 140 an “evening sacrifice,” which was more acceptable under the Law; and when, on whatever day God is called upon, he is present, and at whatever hour the sinner groans and turns back, he shall live and not die? Augustine said these things because of those who put off repentance until the end of life; for then they seem to repent not from love of God, but from fear of death, as though under compulsion.

Thus the same writer, in *On True and False Penance*, chapter 17, almost explaining why he had said the foregoing, says:

> Let no one wait until he is unable to sin. For God seeks freedom of choice, so that deeds committed may be blotted out; not necessity but love; not fear alone, because a human being does not live by fear alone. Therefore one who repents late must not only fear the Judge but also love him, because no one can be saved without love. Thus the penitent must not fear punishment only, but be anxious for glory. If such conversion should occur to anyone even at the end, one must not despair of his forgiveness. But since so righteous a conversion is scarcely or rarely found, one must fear for the late penitent, especially when the children whom he loved unlawfully are present, and wife and world call him back to themselves. Late repentance commonly deceives many. Yet because God is always powerful, he is also always able, even in death, to help those whom he pleases. Therefore, since fruitful repentance is the work not of a human being but of God, his mercy can inspire it when he wills and reward in mercy those whom he can condemn in justice. But because many things impede and draw back the sick person, it is dangerous and close to destruction to defer the remedy of repentance until death. Yet great is the person to whom God then inspires—if there is such a person—true repentance. But even if one thus converted lives and does not die, we do not promise that he will escape every punishment. For he must first be purified by the fire of purgation [Col. 0893], who deferred the fruit of conversion to another age, according to Augustine, *ibid.*, chapter 18.

This fire, though not eternal, is nevertheless grievous in a wondrous manner; for it surpasses every punishment that any person has ever suffered in this life. Never has so great a punishment been found in the flesh, although martyrs suffered remarkable torments and many wicked persons have often endured such great penalties.

From this it is sufficiently shown how dangerous it is to defer repentance until the end of life. Yet if true repentance is found even then, it frees the person and obtains life for one who is dying; though not so as to ensure that he suffers no punishment, unless perhaps the intensity of his groaning and contrition is sufficient for the punishment of the offence. Therefore, although it is difficult for repentance that comes so late to be true—when suffering binds the limbs and pain overwhelms the senses, so that a person can scarcely think of anything—it is still better late than never. For repentance, even if it comes at life’s final gasp, heals and frees. The thief’s repentance was very late, but forgiveness was not late. Yet although the thief deserved pardon at the end for every crime, he did not thereby give the baptized authority to sin and persist in sinning.

### Concerning those who do not complete penance here

2. But if the question is raised concerning those who do not complete penance in this life—whether they will pass through the fire of purgatory in order to complete there what they did less fully here—we say that the same judgment should be made concerning them as concerning those who repent at the end.

For if their contrition of heart and reproach of their offence are so great as to suffice for the punishment of sin, they pass free from other punishments into life, even though their penance was incomplete; for they have repented perfectly and groaned in heart. But those who are not so contrite in heart and do not groan sufficiently for sin, if they depart before completing their penance, will experience purgatorial fire and will be punished more severely than if they had completed their penance here.

For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God [Hebrews 10]. Since God is merciful and just, out of mercy he forgives the penitent, not reserving sin for eternal punishment. Yet in justice he does not leave an offence unpunished. Either a human being punishes it, or God does: the human being punishes it by repenting; God, by exacting punishment. And there is both inward and outward penance. If inward repentance is so great that it is sufficient vengeance for sin, God, who knows this, exacts no further punishment from the one who so repents. But if inward repentance is not sufficient for the punishment of sin, and outward penance is not completed, God, who knows the kinds and measures of sins and punishments, adds sufficient punishment.

Therefore let each person strive so to correct offences that after death it will not be necessary to endure punishment. Augustine, *On True and False Penance*, chapter 18:

> Certain mortal sins are venial in penance; yet they are not healed at once. A sick person would often die if he were not treated, yet he is not healed immediately upon treatment. He remains ill, though he will live, whereas before he was going to die. But whoever dies unrepentant dies utterly and is tormented eternally. For if he were always to live, he would always sin.

### Concerning one upon whom an undiscerning priest imposes a light penance

3. But if the question is raised concerning one who has completed the satisfaction imposed upon him, though it was not proportionate to the sin through a priest’s ignorance or negligence—whether, when he departs this life, he is free from every punishment—I give the same answer as I gave above concerning one who did not complete penance. If the lament of inward grief is so great as to suffice for the punishment of sin, he is entirely freed. But if inward grief together with the imposed penalty is insufficient, God will add punishment.

That inward grief sometimes suffices for the punishment of sin, we have certain proof in that thief, Luke 23, who by contrition and confession of mind alone deserved to enter paradise immediately upon his conversion. But because the ministers of the Church cannot measure the degree of contrition, since they have not been given to understand the secrets of hearts, they establish laws of penance for all alike: for those who grieve more and those who grieve less over sin.

Their chief effort ought to be directed to recognizing, so far as is lawful, the sorrow of heart, and imposing satisfaction according to its degree. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 65:

> In the practice of penance, where an offence has been committed such that the offender must be separated even from Christ’s body, one must consider not so much the measure of time as that of grief. “For God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” [Psalm 50]. But because the grief of one heart is often hidden from another and does not come to another’s knowledge except through words or any other signs—although it is manifest to him to whom it is said, “My groaning is not hidden from thee” [Psalm 37]—the periods of penance are rightly established by those who preside over the churches, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which sins themselves are forgiven; for outside it they are not forgiven. For it has received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, without whom no sins are forgiven.

Likewise Jerome, *On Penance*, distinction 1:

> The canons do not prescribe with sufficient explicitness a measure of time for doing penance for each individual crime, so as to state separately how each is to be corrected. Rather, they determined that it should chiefly be left to the judgment of an understanding priest, because before God the measure of time is not worth as much as the measure of grief, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices. Therefore they command that periods of penance be shortened in accordance with the faith and manner of life of the faithful penitents, and lengthened in accordance with negligence; though for certain offences fixed modes of penance have nevertheless been imposed.

### That satisfaction is not to be imposed upon the dying, but made known to them

4. It is also commonly asked whether the rule of satisfaction ought to be imposed upon the dying. On this Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, says in his *Penitential*, 26, question 7:

> From the sick who are in danger of death, a pure confession of sins is to be sought. Yet the quantity of penance is not to be imposed on them, but made known to them; and, if they should die, the burden of penance is to be lightened by the prayers of friends and the giving of alms. But if they recover, let them diligently observe the manner of penance imposed by the priest. For others, penance is to be determined according to the character of the sin, at the discretion of those who preside.

Hence Pope Leo, 26, question 7:

> Periods of penance must be established with moderation by your judgment, according as you perceive the souls of converts to be devout. You must likewise take account of old age and consider the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses.

### In necessity, penance or reconciliation must not be refused

5. It must also be known that in a time of necessity, penance or reconciliation must not be denied to penitents. Hence Pope Leo, *ibid.*, question 6:

> To those who, under the pressing urgency of necessity and danger, implore the aid of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction must be forbidden nor reconciliation denied; for we can neither set limits to God’s mercy nor prescribe its times. And if they are so burdened by some illness that they cannot at the present moment signify what they requested a little before, the testimony of faithful persons standing by ought to benefit them; and let them receive together the benefit of penance and reconciliation.

Likewise Pope Julius, *ibid.*:

> If a priest denies penance to those who are dying, he shall be guilty of their souls; for the Lord says, Ezekiel 18: “When he has turned, then he shall be saved.” For true confession may occur at the final time, because God is the examiner not only of time but also of the heart, as the thief proves.

### That a priest must not reconcile without consulting the bishop, except under compelling necessity

6. Yet a priest ought not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless extreme necessity compels it. Hence the Council of Carthage, 26, question 6:

> A priest shall not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, unless the bishop is absent or extreme necessity compels it. Whoever’s public crime has disturbed the whole city, hands are to be imposed upon him before the apse, that is, at the entrance of the church.

Likewise Aurelius said, 26, question 6, chapter *If He Commands*:

> If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the priest ought not consult the bishop, but should reconcile the person in peril without his command.

But without consulting the bishop a priest cannot reconcile the excommunicated or public penitents. Hence in the Second Council of Carthage, *ibid.*, it was decreed that chrism, reconciliation of penitents, and consecration of virgins should not be performed by priests. Likewise, a priest is not permitted to reconcile anyone at a public Mass; nevertheless the consecration of virgins may be performed by a priest with the bishop’s consent. Hence the same Second Council of Carthage, *ibid.*:

> A priest shall not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop; but he shall never make chrism.

Just as a priest may consecrate virgins by command of the bishop, so also he may reconcile penitents.

### Whether the offering of one forestalled by death while hastening to penance is to be received

7. But if a question is raised concerning someone who, hastening to penance, could not find a priest and so died: whether his offering ought to be received, we say that it should. Hence the Council of Apanensis, 26, question 6:

> If anyone has died without having confessed, but has a good testimony and could not come to a priest, because death overtook him at home or on the road, let his relatives make an offering for him at the altar and give a ransom for captives.

## DISTINCTION XXI. CONCERNING SINS REMITTED AFTER THIS LIFE

1. It is also commonly asked whether any sins are remitted after this life. Christ shows in the Gospel that some are remitted after this life, where he says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” From this, as the Fathers hand down, it is understood that certain sins are forgiven in the future.

For certain faults are remitted in this age; and certain small ones even in the future—sins which indeed burden persons after death, but are remitted if they are worthy, if by good deeds in this life they have merited that these be remitted to them.

Augustine also says concerning those who build wood, hay, and straw that the combustible structures they have built, which people carry with them, will find the fire of temporary tribulation burning them. Thus he says in book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 26:

> After the death of this body, until one comes from purgatorial fire to the day of condemnation and reward, if during this interval the spirits of the dead who built wood, hay, and straw are said to suffer such a fire—which others do not feel, because they have not carried structures of that kind—so that they may find the fire of temporary tribulation consuming venial sins, I do not refute it, because perhaps it is true. But because it is said, “He shall be saved, yet as through fire,” that fire is treated lightly. Yet that fire will be more grievous than anything a human being can suffer in this life.

Here it is plainly indicated that those who build wood, hay, and straw carry with them certain combustible structures, that is, venial sins, which are burned in the corrective fire. Hence it is certain that certain venial sins are wiped out after this life.

### That some are purified more quickly and others more slowly in the fire

2. In that purgatorial fire, some are purified more slowly and others more quickly, according as they have loved these perishable things more or less. Hence Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 69:

> After this life it is not unbelievable that some believers are saved through a certain purgatorial fire, more slowly or quickly according as they have loved perishable goods more or less. Thus the Apostle did not distinguish without reason those three things—wood, hay, straw—which are built by those who, although they do not seize another’s property, nevertheless cleave with some love to things allowed to human weakness. According to their ways of loving, they will endure the fire either longer, as wood; less long, as hay; or least of all, as straw. But those who build upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stone are secure from both fires: not only from that eternal fire which will torment the impious for ever, but also from the corrective fire by which certain persons who are to be saved will be purified. [Col. 0896]

### Objection

3. Here an objection may be raised: if wood, hay, and straw mean venial sins, and no one is so perfect as not to sin venially, then those who build gold, silver, and precious stone also build wood, hay, and straw; therefore they will pass through fire.

We answer that not everyone who sins venially builds wood, hay, and straw; just as, conversely, not everyone who contemplates God, loves his neighbour, and performs good works builds gold, silver, and precious stone. Yet gold signifies contemplation of God, silver love of neighbour, and precious stone good works.

But those who build wood, hay, and straw do contemplate God, love their neighbour, and perform good works; yet they do not build gold, silver, and precious stone. For one builds these latter who does those three things in such a way as to think on the things of God and how to please God, not the world. Wood, hay, and straw, however, may be understood as such desires for secular things, although lawfully allowed, that they cannot be lost without pain of mind.

Therefore, the one who thinks about worldly matters and how to please the world builds these things; he who is held to his wealth by a certain carnal attachment, though he does many benefits from it and contrives no fraud or robbery for its sake. From this it is clear that the same person does not build both these things and the former things at the same time.

For that former building belongs only to the perfect, who do not think of pleasing the world but God alone. Although they sometimes sin venially, sin is consumed in them by the fervour of love as a drop of water in a furnace of fire; therefore they never carry combustible material with them.

This lower building belongs to the less perfect, who think of pleasing not God alone but also the world, though they put God first. If they put the world first, they would not build upon the foundation but destroy it. Therefore the carnal attachments by which they are devoted to houses, spouses, and possessions, while preferring nothing to Christ, are signified by those three things. Such attachments do not enter the minds of the perfect, though they admit other venial sins.

But in the hearts of the less perfect these attachments sometimes endure to the end. They pass on with such structures, but these are dissolved in the fire. Yet by the merit of the foundation they themselves will be saved, though they will experience a most grievous punishment. From this it appears how great mercy God displays here and how great severity he exercises there, since for the same sin he punishes far more severely there than here. (Augustine, *Enchiridion*; likewise *On Faith and Works*, chapter 16.)

### The opinion of some, with an objection

4. But perhaps you will say that Gregory’s statement, distinction 25, chapter *What It Is Here*, book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 139—that certain light things are to be forgiven in the future—must be understood as concerning the punishment of sin, not sin itself. For if a person has true repentance, all sins are forgiven; perhaps punishment nevertheless remains. Therefore, if one dies truly penitent, one passes on without sin. But if one is not truly penitent at death, one bears a stain which will never be wiped away. Now one who builds wood, hay, and straw truly repents, because he is good, has charity, and passes from this life in charity; therefore he passes without sin—this conclusion does not follow.

For it is true that he is good, has charity, and truly repents; yet he passes on with venial sin, which Penance has not wiped away. For Penance wipes away only that sin which a person abandons. Yet a person often does not abandon such a sin in this life, and nevertheless is truly penitent, although not repentant of every venial sin.

For someone may repent of every mortal sin and every venial sin except one or several venial sins; just as someone may have charity and yet one or several venial sins. This cannot occur at all in the case of grave sins. For someone may be good and possess charity, while still loving these secular things with a certain attachment of desire; such a person may be overtaken by sudden death. He dies in that earthly attachment and yet will be saved, though he did not free himself from it here; therefore after this life he will be purified from it. It is therefore certain that certain sins, namely light ones, are forgiven after this life.

But if the authorities had wished that statement to be understood of the punishment of sin, why would they have mentioned light sins rather than grave ones, since the uncompleted punishment even of grave sins remains after this life?

### What benefit general confession has

5. After this, it must be considered what benefit there is in that confession in which the individual sins committed by each person are not specified. Certainly it may be said that every grave sin ought to be specified in confession at least once, unless some have slipped from the mind. But because no one understands all offences, confess at least generally those of which you have no memory, and thus you have concealed nothing of your crimes.

Venial sins, however, as Augustine says in response 5 against the Pelagians, are innumerable; it is sufficient to confess them generally, unless some have been frequently repeated. Yet it is more perfect to specify even these, if you can. Therefore general confession is made daily in the Church, namely for the venial sins that we commit daily, and for those deadly sins of which we have no knowledge.

Hence Augustine:

> The penitent speaks truth to God when he conceals from him none of the crimes he has committed—not because God would be unaware even if he concealed them deliberately, but because God wishes truth to be spoken to him by the penitent, so that he may obtain pardon. But if some have slipped from the mind, he confesses truth to God when he says generally: “God, who knowest the secrets of the heart, my works and offences are not hidden from thee; I pray thee to grant pardon for them.” And this is the truthfulness of the confessor which God loves.

Hence Psalm 50: “Behold, thou hast loved truth.” Here it is indicated that general confession also wipes out mortal sins of which one has no awareness.

### Let no one confess sins that he has not committed

6. Just as a penitent ought not conceal sin, since that is pride, so neither, for the sake of humility, should he confess himself guilty of what he knows he has not committed. For such humility is incautious and makes him a sinner. Hence Augustine, *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 29:

> When you lie for the sake of humility, if you were not a sinner before you lied, by lying you become what you had avoided being. For truth is not in you unless you call yourself a sinner in such a way that you know yourself also to be one. Truth itself is that you say what you are. For how can there be truth where falsehood reigns?

### Concerning the penalties for a priest who reveals a penitent’s sins

7. Let a priest beware of revealing to others the sins of those confessing to him; otherwise he is to be deposed. Hence Gregory, *On Penance*, distinction 6:

> Before all things, a priest must take care not to recount to anyone the sins which are confessed to him—not to relatives, not to strangers, nor, heaven forbid, for the sake of any scandal. For if he does this, he is to be deposed and shall proceed in shameful pilgrimage for all the days of his life.

The assertion that a penitent should choose a priest who knows how to bind and loose appears contrary to what is found in the canons: namely, that no one should presume to judge another’s parishioner. But it is one thing to despise one’s own priest through favour or hatred, which the canons forbid; it is another to avoid a blind guide, which Urban advises, lest, if a blind person lead a blind person, both fall into the pit.

For Urban II says, 16, question 1:

> It has pleased us that henceforth no priest may receive for penance anyone entrusted to another priest without the consent of the one to whom he was first entrusted, except because of the ignorance of the one to whom he first confessed. Whoever attempts to act contrary to this shall be liable to the peril of his rank.

## DISTINCTION XXII. WHETHER FORGIVEN SINS RETURN

1. Since it has been established above by many authorities that in true contrition of heart sins are forgiven before oral confession or satisfaction by works, even for one who has at some point fallen again into grave sin, the question is raised: if after contrition of heart one scorns to confess, or falls into the same or a similar sin, do forgiven sins return?

The resolution of this question is obscure and perplexing: some assert, while others deny, that sins once forgiven are subsequently charged again for punishment. Those who say that forgiven sins return support themselves with the following testimonies.

Ambrose says, *On Penance*, distinction 4:

> Forgive one another if one sins against another; otherwise God reclaims what he has forgiven. For if he is despised in these matters, without doubt he will revoke the judgment by which he had granted mercy; as is read in the Gospel concerning the wicked servant who was found merciless toward his fellow-servant.

Likewise Rabanus:

> God handed the wicked servant over to the torturers until he should pay the whole debt, because not only the sins which a person committed after Baptism will be charged against him for punishment, but also the original sins which were forgiven him in Baptism.

Likewise Gregory:

> From the Gospel sayings it is clear that if we do not forgive with all our heart what is sinned against us, that also is again exacted which we rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance.

Likewise Augustine, on Luke, book 4, chapter 47:

> God says, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven”; if I have forgiven first, forgive even afterwards. For if you do not forgive, I shall call you back and charge against you whatever I had forgiven.

Again:

> Whoever, forgetful of the divine benefit, wishes to avenge his own injuries, will not only fail to deserve pardon for future sins, but even past sins, which he believed had already been forgiven him, will be charged against him for punishment.

Likewise Bede:

> “I shall return into my house,” etc.: that verse must be feared, not expounded, lest the fault which we believed extinguished in us overwhelm us while we are careless and unoccupied.

Again:

> Whatever depravity of heresy or worldly desire seizes a person after Baptism will immediately cast him down into the depths of every vice.

Likewise Augustine:

> The Lord teaches most plainly in the Gospel that forgiven sins return where fraternal charity is absent, in that servant from whom the master demanded the debt he had forgiven because the servant would not forgive his fellow-servant’s debt.

Those who say that forgiven sins, if charged again, simply return, rest upon these authorities. Against them it is objected: if someone is again punished for a sin concerning which he repented and received pardon, this does not appear just. If he is punished because he sinned and did not amend, the justice is clear. But if what had been forgiven is demanded again, then either there is injustice or justice hidden from us.

Moreover, God appears to judge twice concerning the same matter, and a double tribulation to arise—which Scripture denies. But it may be said in answer that neither does a double tribulation arise nor does God judge twice concerning the same matter. This would occur if he punished again after worthy satisfaction and sufficient punishment; but one who did not persevere did not make satisfaction worthily and sufficiently.

For he ought to have maintained continual memory of sin, not in order to commit it but in order to avoid it. He ought not to have forgotten all God’s benefits, which are as numerous as remissions of sins. Therefore he ought to have considered as many gifts of God as his own evils, and given thanks for them to the end. But because, ungrateful, he returned to his vomit like a dog, he killed his former good works and recalled forgiven sin, so that God, who had forgiven sin to him when humbled, may afterwards impute it to him when proud and ungrateful.

### The opinion of others

2. But because it seems discordant that forgiven sins should be imputed again, some hold that no one is punished by God again for sins once forgiven. Rather, forgiven sins are said to return and be imputed because, through ingratitude, a person is made guilty and sinful in the same manner as before. Thus what had been forgiven is said to be exacted because one who is ungrateful for forgiveness received becomes as guilty as he was before.

Approved teachers support both sides of the question. Therefore, prejudging neither side, I leave judgment to the diligent reader, adding that it will be safe for me and close to salvation to eat crumbs beneath the table of the masters.

### What is sacrament and what is reality here

3. After the foregoing, it remains to investigate what in the act of Penance is sacrament and what is the reality. For a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing. What, then, is the sign here?

Some, such as Grandulf, say that the sacrament here is what is performed only outwardly, namely outward penance, which is a sign of inward penance, that is, contrition and humility of heart. If this is so, not every evangelical sacrament produces what it signifies. For outward Penance does not produce inward penance; rather, inward penance is the cause of outward.

But, they say, this must be understood of those sacraments instituted in the New Testament, such as the sacrament of Baptism, Confirmation, and Christ’s Body. But the sacrament of Penance, like that of Marriage, existed even before the time of grace, from the beginning of humankind. For both were instituted in the first parents.

Again, if outward Penance is sacrament and inward Penance the reality of the sacrament, the reality more often precedes the sacrament than the sacrament precedes the reality. But this too is not incongruous. For even in other sacraments that produce what they signify, this often occurs.

Others say that outward and inward Penance are sacrament—not two sacraments, but one—just as the species of bread and wine are not two sacraments but one. And, as in the sacrament of the Body, so also in this sacrament they say that one thing is sacrament only, namely outward Penance; another is both sacrament and reality, namely inward penance; and another is reality but not sacrament, namely forgiveness of sins. For inward penance is both the reality of the sacrament, that is, of outward Penance, and the sacrament of remission of sin, which it signifies and effects. Outward Penance likewise is a sign both of inward penance and of forgiveness of sins.

## DISTINCTION XXIII. CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF EXTREME UNCTION

1. Besides what has been stated, there is another sacrament, namely the anointing of the sick, which is performed at the end of life with oil consecrated by a bishop.

There are three kinds of anointing. There is an anointing performed with chrism, called the principal anointing, because in it the Paraclete is given principally. Thus, because of the abundance of grace, it contains two blended liquids: oil, namely of conscience, and balsam, of good reputation. Chrism is called *chrisma* in Greek and *unctio* in Latin.

Yet not every oil sanctified for anointing is called chrism, but only that which is mixed with balsam, with which the heads of kings and bishops are anointed; with which also the priest anoints the baptized on the crown of the head, and the bishop anoints on the forehead those to be confirmed through laying on of hands.

There is another anointing by which catechumens and neophytes are anointed on the breast and between the shoulder-blades when receiving Baptism. The third anointing is what is called the oil of the sick; it is this that is now under discussion.

### By whom this sacrament was instituted

2. This sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick is said to have been instituted by the apostles. For James says, chapter 5: “Is any among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the Lord will relieve him; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him.” In this it is shown that this sacrament was instituted for a twofold purpose: namely, for the remission of sins and for the alleviation of bodily infirmity. Hence it is clear that one who receives this Anointing faithfully and devoutly is relieved both in body and soul, provided that he desires to be relieved in both. But if it is perhaps not expedient for him to have bodily health, he obtains in this sacrament the health of the soul.

And, as in the other sacraments, so also in this one, the sacrament is one thing and the reality of the sacrament another. The sacrament is the outward Anointing itself; the reality of the sacrament is the inward anointing, accomplished through the remission of sins and the increase of virtues. And if this sacrament is omitted through contempt or negligence, it is dangerous and damnable.

### On repeating this sacrament

3. Some ask whether this sacrament may be repeated, since Baptism and certain other sacraments, once received, are not repeated. Augustine, in the book *Against Parmenian*, says that a sacrament is not to be repeated and that no injury is to be done to a sacrament; but he says this where he treats of the sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and [Col. 0900] Ordination. Hence that statement does not seem to be taken generally, but concerning Baptism, Confirmation, and Ordination, which are in no way to be repeated, because Baptism, Confirmation, and Ordination are given only once, not more often.

But the sacrament of the altar, of Penance, and of Marriage seems often to be repeated: for the sacrament of the Body is received frequently, penance is often performed, and marriage is often contracted. Why, then, cannot anointing likewise be repeated? If the illness does not return, the medicine should not be repeated. But if the illness cannot be restrained, why should the medicine be prohibited? Just as prayer can be repeated, so anointing too seems capable of repetition: for James mentions both there, and each cooperates with the other in bestowing relief upon body and soul. Why, then, is it denied that anointing over a sick person can be repeated in order to obtain repeatedly health of mind and body, when, because of infirmity, the same prayer must often be repeated?

Some, however, wish the statement that a sacrament is not to be repeated to be understood of every sacrament, namely, according to the whole of that which pertains to the sacrament. They say that certain sacraments may be received more than once, while others may not. Yet those received more often are not repeated in their entirety, as are the sacrament of the altar and anointing. Although they are received often, since the same host or the same oil is not blessed again, the sacrament is not repeated to its injury.

But someone will say: In that manner Baptism too is not repeated, even if someone is baptized frequently, so long as the same water is not blessed again. They reply that the blessing of water by which Baptism is performed is different from the blessing of bread and oil. Baptism may also be celebrated in water not blessed, because that blessing is made only for reverence and decorum, not by the power of the sacrament. But the Body of Christ cannot be made except from consecrated bread, nor can that anointing be performed except with oil consecrated by a bishop. Therefore that consecration appears to pertain to the efficacy of the sacrament.

Likewise, in marriage each person is blessed only once, not repeatedly. For, as Ambrose says in the Gloss on 1 Corinthians 9, “Let her marry only in the Lord,” and in his commentary on the same chapter, one is blessed with a first, not a second, wife. Therefore, if, when it is said that a sacrament is not to be repeated and that no injury is to be done to it, you refer the reason for this statement to the consecration of the thing by which the sacrament is performed, it is generally true of every sacrament. But if you refer it to receiving the sacrament, it is true of some that they are not repeated through frequent reception, but not of certain others, because they are frequently received—as is this sacrament of anointing, which in almost every Church is often repeated.

## DISTINCTION XXIV. ON ECCLESIASTICAL ORDERS

1. Let us now proceed to the consideration of sacred ordination. There are seven grades or orders of spiritual offices, as is plainly handed down from the sayings of the holy Fathers and shown by the example of our Head, Jesus Christ, who displayed in himself the offices of all, and left these same orders to be observed by his body, which is the Church. They are seven because of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; those who do not share in it approach ecclesiastical grades unworthily. But those in whose minds the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured out, when they approach ecclesiastical orders, are believed to receive a fuller grace in that very promotion to a spiritual grade. (Hugh, book 2, chapters 3, 4.)

### What kind of persons are to be admitted to the clergy

2. Such clerics are to be chosen for spiritual ministry as can worthily handle the Lord’s sacraments. For it is better for a bishop to have a few ministers who can worthily perform God’s work than many useless ones who impose a heavy burden upon their ordainer. Ministers of Christ ought to be such that they are adorned with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, so that, from their teaching and manner of life, that same grace may be poured into others, lest the heavenly pearls of spiritual [Col. 0901] words and divine offices be trampled beneath the feet of a filthy life. (Pope Clement, distinction 23.)

Therefore, in the sacrament of the sevenfold Spirit there are seven ecclesiastical grades: door-keepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, deacons, subdeacons, and priests. Yet all are called clerics, that is, those allotted a share. For the tonsure is the sign by which they are marked as sharing in the allotted portion of divine ministry. The tonsure signifies royal dignity, because to serve God is to reign. Therefore ministers of the Church ought to be kings, so that they may govern themselves and others. To them Peter says, 1 Peter 2: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” etc.

The top of the head is bared, so that their mind may be shown to be free for the Lord, contemplating with unveiled face the glory of God. For the summit of the head is the eminence of the mind; the baring of the head is the unveiling of the mind. A cleric ought not to be ignorant of God’s mysteries. The hair is also cut back to the uncovering of the senses, namely, the eyes and ears, to teach that vices springing up in heart and deed must be cut away, lest the mind be impeded from hearing and understanding God’s word; for keeping that word, a crown will be rendered above.

The practice of ecclesiastical tonsure seems to have arisen from the Nazirites, who first preserved their hair, then, because of the continence of their life, shaved their heads and placed their hair in the fire of sacrifice. Hence the practice arose that those devoted to divine worship should appear, like Nazirites—that is, holy persons—with their hair laid aside. (Hugh, *On the Crown and Tonsure*, book 2, part 3.) Thus it is said to Ezekiel, chapter 5: “Son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and beard.” We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that Priscilla and Aquila did this. Paul too, and certain other disciples of Christ, did so.

Rightly, then, persons established in any of these grades are called clerics. Explaining their names and the reasons for their names, Isidore says in book 7 of the *Etymologies*: “We believe that *clerus* and *clerici* are so called because Matthias was chosen by lot, whom we first read to have been ordained by the apostles. For *cleros* in Greek is called in Latin ‘lot’ or ‘inheritance.’ Therefore they are called clerics because they belong to the Lord’s lot, or because they have God as Father.” More generally, all who serve in the Church are called clerics; their grades and names are these: door-keeper, reader, and so forth.

### On door-keepers

3. Door-keepers, also called gatekeepers, were chosen in the Old Testament to guard the Temple, lest anyone unclean enter it. They are called door-keepers because they preside over the doors of the Temple. Holding the key, they guard everything within and without; and, exercising judgment between good and evil persons, they admit the worthy and reject the unworthy. Hence, when they are ordained, the bishop gives them the keys of the Church and says to them, *On Consecration*, distinction 23, chapter “The Door-keeper”: “Act in such a way as persons who must render an account to God for the things opened by these keys.”

The Lord undertook this office in his own person when, having made a whip of cords, he drove those selling and buying from the Temple. For, signifying that he himself was the door-keeper, he says in John 10: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he shall be saved; and he shall enter and go out and find pasture.”

### On readers

4. The second grade is that of readers. Readers are so called from reading, just as psalmists are named from singing psalms. The former proclaim to the people what they ought to follow; the latter sing and stir the minds of hearers to compunction—although some readers pronounce so mournfully that they drive certain people to grief and lamentation. They are also called announcers, because they announce beforehand and at a distance, since their voice ought to be so clear as to fill even the ears of those far away.

It belongs to the reader to recite the readings and proclaim to the people what the prophets foretold, so that in church he may read prophecies and lessons as part of his office. Hence, before the people’s eyes, the bishop hands him the book of divine readings and says: “Receive it and be a herald of God’s word. If you faithfully fulfill your office, you will have a share with those who have ministered God’s word well.”

One promoted to this grade should be trained in literary knowledge, [Col. 0902] so that he understands the meaning of the words, knows the force of the accents, and reads distinctly, lest by confused pronunciation he deprive his hearers of understanding. He should notice what is to be read declaratively and what interrogatively, and where a division should be made in the sentence. For failure to observe these matters confuses understanding and provokes others to laughter. The reader’s voice ought to serve ear and heart.

Christ fulfilled this office in Luke 4, when, in the midst of the elders, he opened the book of Isaiah and read distinctly so as to be understood, chapter 61: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc. From this readers are given to understand that those who announce God’s word to others ought to shine with spiritual grace. This order seems to have received its form and beginning from the prophets, to whom Isaiah 58 says: “Cry aloud; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet.” (Isidore, distinction 21, chapter “Clerics”; distinction 25, chapter “After the Readings”; distinction 23, chapter “The Reader”; Hugh, book 2, part 3.)

### On exorcists

5. The third order is that of exorcists. *Exorcists* is translated from Greek into Latin as “those who adjure” or “rebuke.” For over catechumens and those who have an unclean spirit they invoke the name of the Lord, adjuring the spirit through him to depart from them. It belongs to the exorcist to retain the exorcisms by memory and to lay hands upon the possessed and catechumens during exorcism.

He who commands unclean spirits ought to possess a clean spirit; and he should cast from his own heart the evil one whom he casts from another’s body, lest the remedy which he applies to others fail to benefit himself and it be said to him: “Physician, heal yourself,” Luke 4. When ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand the book of exorcisms, and it is said to them, distinction 13, chapter “The Exorcist”: “Receive, and have the power of laying hands upon the possessed or catechumens.”

The Lord exercised this office when he touched with his saliva the ears and tongue of the deaf and mute man, saying, Mark 7: “Ephphetha,” that is, “Be opened”; thereby teaching us that we ought spiritually to open the ears of human hearts for understanding, and their mouths for confession, so that, when the demon has been driven out, the Holy Spirit may take possession of his vessel. Christ also exercised this office when he healed many demoniacs. This order seems to descend from Solomon, who discovered a certain mode of exorcism by which demons, when adjured, were driven from possessed bodies. Those assigned to this office were called exorcists. Of them Christ says in the Gospel, Matthew 12: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons”—that is, your exorcists—“cast them out?” (Isidore, distinction 21, chapter “Clerics”; distinction 25, chapter “After the Readings.”)

### On acolytes  
(Isidore, same place)

6. Acolytes follow in the fourth place. *Acolytes* is Greek; in Latin they are called candle-bearers, from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered. For then lights are kindled and carried by them—not to dispel the darkness of the air, since the sun shines at that time, but to signify joy, so that under the figure of bodily light that Light may be shown of which John 1 reads: “There was the true Light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.”

It belongs to the acolyte to prepare the lights in the sacristy. He carries the candle; he prepares for the subdeacons the cruet with wine and water presented for the Eucharist. When they are ordained, after being instructed by the bishop how they ought to act in their office, they receive from the archdeacon a candlestick with a candle and an empty cruet. The Lord testifies that he holds this office when he says, John 8: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness.” Those in the Old Testament who trimmed the lamps of the lampstand and lit them with heavenly fire, to illuminate the northern darkness, represented the form of this office.

### On subdeacons  
(Isidore, same place)

7. The fifth order is that of subdeacons. In Greek they are called *hypodiacones*, whom we call subdeacons, and they are thus named because they are subject to the commands and offices of the Levites. They receive in the Temple the offerings from the faithful and bring them to the Levites to be placed upon the altars. Among the Hebrews they were called *Nathinnaei*, that is, those serving in humility.

It belongs to the subdeacon [Col. 0903] to bring the chalice and paten to Christ’s altar and hand them to the Levites, serving them; likewise to hold the cruet, basin, and hand-towel for bishop, presbyters, and Levites, providing water for washing hands before the altar. The law of continence is imposed upon them because, approaching the altar, they carry the vessels of Christ’s Body and Blood. Hence they ought to fulfill Isaiah 62: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord.” It also belongs to them to place upon the altar only as much of the offerings as may suffice for the people, and likewise to wash the corporals and the coverings beneath them.

When ordained, they receive from the bishop’s hand an empty paten and chalice; from the archdeacon, however, a cruet with a basin and a hand-towel. The Lord exercised this office when he girded himself with a towel, poured water into a basin, washed the disciples’ feet, and dried them with the towel. (Hugh, book 2, part 3, chapter 9.)

### On deacons

8. The order of deacons occupies the sixth place, on account of the perfection of the number six. In the Old Testament this order received or derived its name from the tribe of Levi. They are indeed also called Levites. For the Lord commanded Moses, after the ordination of Aaron and his sons, that the entire tribe of Levi should be ordained for the ministries of divine worship and consecrated to the Lord; that it should serve on behalf of Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle; that its members should carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; keep watch around the tabernacle; and, during the transport of the tabernacle, take it down and set it up again. (Hugh, same work, chapter 15.)

They were also commanded to serve in the tabernacle from twenty years of age and upwards, a rule which the holy Fathers established in the New Testament, since this age is strong for bearing burdens. Levites are therefore named after their ancestor: the Levites sprang from Levi, through whom the mysteries of the mystical sacrament were performed in the Temple.

In Greek they are called *diacones*, in Latin *ministri*, “ministers,” because as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of ministry belongs to the deacon. It belongs to the deacon to assist priests and minister in all that is done in Christ’s sacraments—namely, in Baptism, Chrism, the paten and chalice; also to bring and arrange the offerings on the altar; to set the Lord’s table in order and clothe it; to carry the cross; and to preach the Gospel and Epistle to the people. For, just as readers are commanded to proclaim the Old Testament, so deacons are commanded to proclaim the New.

To him also belongs the office of prayers and the recitation of the names of catechumens. He warns the people to give ear to the Lord; he gives peace and makes the proclamation. What was appointed for this order by Moses is also represented in the New Testament when a stole is placed upon the deacon’s left shoulder and the chasuble is folded on days of fasting, because whatever labor and endurance is borne in this life is, as it were, carried on the left, until rest is possessed on the right—that is, in eternity. (Isidore, *Etymologies* 7; distinction 21, chapter “Clerics”; distinction 25, chapter “After the Readings.”)

This order was established by the apostles when, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, they chose seven men full of the Holy Spirit for this office and, after prayer, laid hands upon them. Hence the custom arose that in every mother church seven deacons should stand around Christ’s altar like seven pillars. These are the seven angels sounding trumpets in the Apocalypse; the Apostle, writing to Timothy, teaches what sort of persons they ought to be.

When ordained, the bishop alone lays hands upon them, because they are appointed to ministry. He places the *orarium*, that is, the stole, upon their left shoulder, so that they may understand that they have received the Lord’s sweet yoke, by which they are to subject things pertaining to the left to divine fear. They also receive the text of the Gospel, so that they may understand themselves to be heralds of Christ’s Gospel. Before ordination, however, they should be tested, as the Apostle teaches, and then minister, having no charge against them.

Christ exercised this office when, after supper, he distributed to his disciples the sacrament of his flesh and blood, and when he stirred the sleeping apostles to vigilance, saying, Matthew 26: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation.” (Isidore, same place, distinction 21.)

### On presbyters

[Col. 0904]

9. The seventh order is that of presbyters. *Presbyter* is Greek and means “elder” in Latin. They are called presbyters not merely because of age or worn-out old age, but because of the honor and dignity they have received; for they ought to excel among the people in prudence of character and maturity of conduct. Hence it is written: “Venerable old age is not long-lived, nor counted by the number of years. For the gray hairs of a human being are understanding, and the age of old age is an unstained life.”

They are also called priests because they give what is sacred. Although they are priests, they do not possess the summit of pontifical office as bishops do, because they neither sign the forehead with chrism nor give the Paraclete; the reading of the Acts of the Apostles shows that these belong to bishops alone. Hence among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, because this is a name of dignity, not of age.

The name *sacerdos* (“priest”) is compounded from Greek and Latin: “one who gives the sacred,” or “sacred leader.” As *rex* (“king”) is so named from ruling, so *sacerdos* is called from consecrating; for he consecrates and sanctifies. A priest is called an *antistes* (“one who stands before”) because he stands first; he is first in the order of the Church.

It belongs to the presbyter to make on God’s altar the sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood, to say prayers, and to bless God’s gifts. When ordained, their hands are anointed so that they may understand that they have received the grace of consecrating and ought to extend works of charity to all. They also receive the stole, which covers both sides, because they ought to be armed with the weapons of righteousness against adverse and prosperous circumstances. They also receive a chalice with wine and a paten with hosts, so that by this they may know they have received the power of offering sacrifices pleasing to God. (Isidore, same place.)

This order took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. For through Moses God established high priests and lesser priests. By God’s command Moses anointed Aaron as high priest and his sons as lesser priests. Christ also first chose twelve disciples, whom he called apostles; the greater pontiffs in the Church act in their place. Then he appointed another seventy-two disciples, in whose place presbyters stand in the Church.

But among the apostles Peter stood forth as chief. The supreme pontiff is his vicar and successor; hence he is called “apostolic,” and also pope, that is, “father of fathers.” The Apostle, writing to Timothy, shows what kind of presbyter should be chosen, where by the name “bishop” he means presbyter.

Christ exercised this office when he offered himself upon the altar of the cross, being at once priest and victim; and when, after supper, he changed bread and wine into his Body and Blood. Thus, having spoken briefly of the seven grades of the Church, we have indicated what belongs to each. Although all are spiritual and sacred, the canons nevertheless judge that only two are to be called sacred orders in the eminent sense: the diaconate and the presbyterate, because the primitive Church is read to have had these alone, and because we have an apostolic command concerning these alone. For the apostles ordained bishops and presbyters in individual cities. We also read that Levites were ordained by the apostles, of whom blessed Stephen was the foremost. But the Church instituted subdeacons and acolytes for itself as time went on.

### What is here called an order

10. If it is asked what this is which is here called an order, it may properly be said to be a sign, that is, a certain sacred thing by which spiritual power and office are conferred upon the person ordained. Thus a spiritual character, where there is a promotion to authority, is called an order or grade. And these orders are called sacraments because, in receiving them, a sacred reality—that is, grace—is conferred, which the things there performed signify.

### On names of dignities or offices

11. There are also certain other names, not of orders, but of dignities or offices. *Bishop* is the name both of a dignity and of an office. The word *episcopate* is so named because one made bishop “oversees,” that is, takes care of those subject to him.
