For *episcopēo* in Greek is called *intendere*, “to direct one’s attention,” in Latin. *Episcopi* in Greek are translated in Latin as “watchers.” For a watcher is a superior in the Church, so called because he watches and observes the manners and life of the peoples placed beneath him.

A pontiff is the chief of priests, as it were the way for those who follow; he is also called high priest. For he makes Levites and priests and arranges all ecclesiastical persons. (Isidore, distinction 21, chapter “Clerics.”)

### On the fourfold order of bishops

12. The order of bishops is fourfold: patriarchs, archbishops, metropolitans, and bishops. *Patriarch* in Greek means “highest of fathers,” because he occupies the first, that is, apostolic, place—as do the Roman, Antiochene, and Alexandrian patriarchs; but the Roman is supreme over all. *Archbishop* means chief of bishops, for *archos* in Greek means “chief” in Latin. Metropolitans are so named from the measure of cities. For they preside over individual provinces and cities, and the other priests are subject to their authority and teaching. The care of the whole province is entrusted to these bishops.

All the orders designated above are called bishops. Note that by the name “archbishops” he seems above to have meant primates, and by “metropolitans” those whom we now call archbishops. This distinction seems to have been introduced from the pagans, who called some of their *flamines* simply *flamines*, others *archiflamines*, and still others *protoflamines*. The priests of the gentiles were called *flamines*. They had on their heads a cap in which was a short rod with something of wool on top. Since they could not bear this in hot weather, they began merely to bind a thread upon their heads; for it was unlawful for them to sit with bare heads. Hence they were called *flamines* from the thread (*filum*) which they used, as though *filamines*. But on feast days, after laying aside the thread, they put on the cap as a sign of the eminence of the priesthood.

*Vates* (“seers” or “bards”) are so called from the force of mind; the term has several meanings. At one time it means priest, at another prophet, at another poet. A singer is one who modulates the voice in song. There are two kinds: the precentor and the succentor. The precentor leads the voice in song; the succentor responds in singing afterward. A *concentor* is so called because he sings in harmony. But one who neither harmonizes nor sings together will not be a concentor.

Having treated these matters briefly, Christ’s ministers must be admonished that, just as they excel in the dignity of order, so they may surpass others in holiness of life, so that the people entrusted to them, instructed by their discipline, may gladly obey them and may progress day by day by imitating those from whom they receive the divine sacraments and hear the solemnities of the Mass.

The Mass is so called either because the victim is sent forth, whose commemoration is made in that office; hence it is said, “*Ite, missa est*”—that is, “Follow the victim that has been sent to heavenly things, going after it”; or because a heavenly messenger comes to consecrate the Lord’s Body, through whom the victim is borne to the heavenly altar. Hence it too is called “the Mass.”

## DISTINCTION XXV. ON THOSE ORDAINED BY HERETICS

1. It is also commonly asked whether heretics cut off and condemned by the Church can confer sacred orders, and whether persons ordained by them, upon returning to the unity of the Church, ought to be reordained. The words of teachers, which appear to disagree greatly, make this question perplexing and almost insoluble.

For some seem to teach that heretics cannot confer sacred orders, nor can those apparently ordained by them receive grace. Innocent says, *On the Dispensation of Sacred Orders*, question 1, that Arian clerics do not seem to be received with the dignity of priesthood or any ministry; to them he permits Baptism alone, provided it is received in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He also says that they cannot give the Holy Spirit whom they have lost; that those ordained by heretics have a wounded head; that one who has lost honor cannot give honor; and that the recipient has received nothing, because in the giver there was nothing he could receive.

He also teaches that persons coming [Col. 0906] from heretics are to be granted only lay communion through the laying on of hands, and that none of them is to be appointed even to the lowest rank of clerical honor. Gregory too, in book 3 of the *Dialogues*, says that the Arian consecration is sacrilegious when communion is received from their hand.

Cyprian too, in the Letter against Heretics, says: “All things whatever heretics do are carnal, empty, and sacrilegious; their altars are false and unlawful, and their priesthoods and sacrifices sacrilegious. Like apes, which, though not human beings, imitate human form, they claim for themselves the appearance and authority of the Catholic Church, although they themselves are not in the Church; and although sacrilegious, they administer priesthood and set up an altar. Yet an offering cannot there be sacrificed where the Holy Spirit is not; nor does the Lord benefit anyone through the pleas and prayers of one who has violated the Lord himself.”

Jerome likewise asserts that everything offered by heretics is defiled in the Lord’s sight, because, although such things appear holy in their outward form, since they are handled by one who is defiled, all are defiled. The same author: “God hates the sacrifices of heretics and casts them away from himself; and whenever they have gathered in his name, he abhors their stench and closes his nostrils.” The same: “They offer sacrilegious bread,” etc.

Leo too testifies that outside the Church priesthoods are neither valid nor sacrifices true. He also says that, through a most cruel madness, the light of all sacraments was extinguished from the Alexandrian see: the offering of sacrifice was interrupted, the consecration of chrism failed, and all the mysteries withdrew themselves from the parricidal hands of the impious.

By these and other testimonies it seems to be established that ecclesiastical sacraments—especially those of the Body and Blood, Ordination, and Confirmation—cannot be administered through heretics.

### Authorities adduced which seem to conflict with those above

2. On the other hand, others seem to hold that sacred orders, like Baptism, can be conferred even by heretics who have been cut off; and that those baptized and ordained there by heretics, when returning, are not to be ordained again, just as they are not to be baptized again.

Hence Augustine: “Concerning even condemned heretics, what some say—that one who departs from the Church does not lose the Baptism he received, but loses the right to give what he received—plainly appears empty in many ways. First, because no reason is shown why a person who cannot lose that Baptism should be able to lose the right of giving it. For each is a sacrament, and each is given to a person by a certain consecration: the one when he is baptized, and the other when he is ordained. Therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church.

“For when persons coming from that party, even their superiors, were received for the good of peace after the error of schism had been corrected, if it seemed necessary that they should carry out the same offices they had performed, they were not ordained again. But, as Baptism remained intact in them, so Ordination remained intact, because the fault lay in their severance, which is corrected in the unity of peace, not in the sacraments, wherever they are found.

“And when it seems expedient to the Church that their superiors, on coming to Catholic fellowship, should not exercise their offices there, the sacraments of Ordination themselves are nevertheless not taken from them but remain upon them. Therefore hands are not laid upon them, lest an injury be done, not to the person, but to the sacrament itself. And as there is in Baptism a right by which it can be conferred through them, so in Ordination there is a right of conferring it: each indeed to their own destruction. But it is one thing not to possess something, another to possess it destructively, and another to possess it beneficially.”

The same author: “Concerning those separated from the unity of the Church, there is now no question that they possess it and can give it; but they possess it destructively and give it destructively, because they are outside the bond of peace. Injury must be done to neither sacrament. Just as one who departs from unity does not possess it rightly, but nevertheless possesses it, and therefore it is not restored when he returns, so too one who departs from unity does not give rightly, but nevertheless gives; and therefore what one receives from him is not repeated when he comes to unity.”

The same author: “It is one thing not to possess something, another not to possess it lawfully or to usurp it unlawfully. Therefore the sacraments of Christ and the Church are not not sacraments because they are used unlawfully not only by heretics [Col. 0907] but also by all the impious; rather, those persons must be corrected and punished, while the sacraments must be recognized and venerated.”

Likewise Gregory: “What you say—that one who has been ordained should be ordained again—is very ridiculous. For just as one baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one consecrated once cannot be consecrated again in the same order.”

By these and other authorities it seems to be affirmed that Christ’s sacraments remain in all impious persons, even in heretics who have been cut off and condemned, together with the right to confer them. For they can confer them, though destructively; and those on whom they confer them are not to be ordained again—points which seem, on the contrary, to conflict with the foregoing.

### Resolution of the foregoing apparent contradiction among authorities
3. Some resolve this as follows. They say that heretics who, after receiving priestly or episcopal anointing, depart from the Church retain indeed the right to confer Baptism, but, once they have been cut off and condemned by the Church, do not have the power to confer holy Orders or to consecrate the Lord’s body—just as a deposed bishop has no power to confer holy Orders, although he has not lost the faculty of baptizing. What Augustine says, they understand as said of heretics who are divided from the truth of faith and unity of doctrine not by a judgment of the Church but by the perversity of their own opinion. Although such persons are heretics, they nevertheless have the right to ordain and consecrate. Those ordained by them before their public severance, even if they have openly gone out with them and have been condemned by judgment of the Church, are not to be ordained again if they return. And wherever one reads of persons ordained by heretics that they may minister while retaining their orders, or that they are not to be ordained again, this, they say, must be understood of persons of this kind. For after they have been cut off and condemned by the judgment of the Church, they maintain that the right to ordain and consecrate is withdrawn from them, as from the deposed or excommunicated.

Others, however, say that sacraments celebrated by heretics who have been cut off, according to the form of the Church, are true and valid, because those departing from the Church have not lost the right to ordain and consecrate; and those so ordained by heretics are not to be ordained again when they return. But things done by heretics otherwise than in the Church are false and void; and those who appear to be ordained by such persons receive not an office but a wound. According to this distinction, therefore, the doctors speak variously on these matters.

Others say that the same sacraments may be celebrated by cut-off heretics as by Catholics, provided that the form of the Church is preserved by them; and that sacraments celebrated by them are, in themselves, true and valid, but with respect to their effect false and void. Thus they are void and false both in those who administer them wrongly and in those who receive them wrongly, because they do not bestow what they promise and are believed to confer. They are also called condemnable, because they are unto judgment for those who give or receive them unlawfully. They are called defiled, not in themselves, but because of the unworthy handling of heretics. Thus Gregory calls Arius’s communion an “execration,” and Innocent calls Bonosus’s ordination a “condemnation”: not because they are such in themselves, but because they make those who give or receive them wrongly such persons. So also Jerome calls their sacrifices “bread of mourning,” not in themselves but with respect to their effect.

Some maintain that heretics ordained in the Church retain the right of ordaining and consecrating even when separated from it. But those who, being in schism or heresy, have been ordained and anointed by such persons lack that right. Therefore, when they wish to ordain, they inflict a wound rather than confer grace.

### On simony: whence it is named, and what it is

4. Concerning simoniacs, however, there can be no doubt that they are heretics; yet before a sentence of deposition they both ordain and consecrate. Although those are properly called simoniacs who, after the manner of Simon Magus, wish to obtain priceless grace for a price, those who receive payment for sacred ministry after the manner of Gehazi ought to be called Gehaziites. Yet all alike, both givers and receivers, are called simoniacs, and both are struck by the same sentence.

### On those knowingly ordained by simoniacs

5. There is nevertheless a difference between those who are knowingly ordained by simoniacs [Col. 0908] and those who are ordained in ignorance. For those who knowingly permit themselves to be consecrated—indeed, execrated—by simoniacs, have an utterly void consecration. But the ordination of those ordained by simoniacs whom they do not know, at the time of ordination, to be simoniacs, and who are then regarded as Catholics, is mercifully tolerated. (Pope Urban, 1, question 1.)

### On those who say that they purchase material things, not spiritual things

6. But if some object that they are not buying consecrations, but the things themselves which result from consecration, they are shown to be wholly irrational. For whoever sells one of these two things, without which the other cannot be had, does not refrain from selling either. (Paschal, question 3, chapter *Si quis objecerit* [“If anyone should object”].)

### Distinction among simoniacs

7. The distinction of simoniacal heresy is threefold. Some are simoniacally ordained by simoniacs; some are simoniacally ordained by non-simoniacs; others are non-simoniacally ordained by simoniacs. Hence Pope Nicholas, 1, question 1:

> We establish a decree concerning the threefold simoniacal heresy: that is, concerning simoniacs who simoniacally ordain or are ordained; concerning simoniacs simoniacally ordained by non-simoniacs; and concerning simoniacs non-simoniacally ordained by simoniacs. Simoniacs simoniacally ordained, or simoniacal ordainers, shall fall from their proper rank according to the canons. Simoniacs likewise simoniacally ordained by non-simoniacs shall similarly be removed from office. But simoniacs non-simoniacally ordained by simoniacs we mercifully permit, through laying on of hands, to remain in office according to the needs of the time.

This is to be understood of those ordained by simoniacs while ignorant that they are simoniacs. It is not guilt for a crime, but ordination by a simoniac, that makes these persons simoniacs.

### Pope Alexander on those forcibly ordained by simoniacs or heretics

8. Similarly, when Pope Alexander decrees that simoniacs are altogether to be condemned and deposed, this must be understood with the qualification: unless someone has been forcibly compelled. For Innocent says, 1, question 1, concerning persons forcibly ordained by these or by any heretics, that they may have some appearance of excuse if they immediately depart from them and renounce their most wicked assembly.

### Pope Nicholas’s decree concerning the age of those to be ordained

9. “The sacred canons,” he says, distinctions 77 and 78, “have decreed that a subdeacon is not to be ordained before fourteen years of age, nor a deacon before twenty-five, nor a priest before thirty. Thereafter, if he is worthy, he may be elected to the episcopate; and we likewise command that this be observed.” Likewise Fabian: “If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he is by no means to be ordained a priest, even if he is very worthy; for the Lord himself was baptized at thirty years of age, and then began to teach.”

## DISTINCTION XXVI. ON THE SACRAMENT OF MARRIAGE: ITS INSTITUTION AND PURPOSE ARE SET FORTH

1. Whereas the other sacraments took their beginning after sin and because of sin, the sacrament of Matrimony is read to have been instituted by the Lord even before sin—not, however, as a remedy, but for an office or function. For Scripture relates, in Genesis 2, that when a sleep had been sent upon Adam, one of his ribs taken, and a woman formed from it, the man, spiritually understanding the purpose for which the woman had been made, prophetically said after his ecstasy: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh; therefore a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

### On the twofold institution of marriage

2. The institution of marriage is twofold. One institution was made before sin in Paradise, for its function: there the marriage-bed would be undefiled and the marriages honorable; they would conceive without passion and give birth without pain. The other was made after sin, outside Paradise, as a remedy, to avoid unlawful movement. The first was so that nature might multiply; the second, so that nature might be preserved and vice restrained. For before sin God said, in Genesis 1, “Increase and multiply”; and after sin, when almost all human beings had been destroyed by the Flood. That marriage was instituted before sin for its function, but granted after sin as a remedy, Augustine attests when he says, *On Genesis*, book 9, chapter 7: “What is for the healthy a function is for the sick a remedy.” For the infirmity of incontinence, which is in flesh dead through sin, is received into the honorability of marriage lest it fall into the ruin of shameful acts. But if the first human beings had not sinned, they and their descendants would have come together without the stimulus of the flesh and the heat of lust. And just as some good work is worthy of reward, so their intercourse would have been good and worthy of reward. But because, through sin, the law of deadly concupiscence has adhered to our members—without which no bodily union occurs—evil intercourse is blameworthy unless excused by the goods of marriage.

### When marriage is contracted by precept, and when by indulgence

3. The first institution had a precept; the second, an indulgence. For we have learned from the Apostle that marriage was granted to the human race for avoiding fornication. Indulgence, however, because it does not choose better things, has a remedy, not a reward; whoever declines from it deserves destructive judgment. What is granted by indulgence is voluntary, not necessary; otherwise, one who did not do it would be a transgressor. And it may rightly be understood that the first human beings before sin were given this command: “Increase and multiply.” They were bound by it even after sin, until multiplication had taken place; after that, marriage was contracted by indulgence. Thus after the Flood, by which almost the entire human race was destroyed, Noah’s sons were commanded: “Increase and multiply.” But once humankind had multiplied, marriage was contracted by indulgence, not by command.

### In what ways “indulgence” is understood

4. Indulgence is understood in various ways: as concession, remission, and permission. In the New Testament there is permission with respect to lesser goods and lesser evils. Marriage is among the lesser goods: it does not merit the palm of victory, but serves as a remedy. Among the lesser evils—that is, venial sins—is intercourse undertaken because of incontinence. Marriage, then, is indulged, that is, granted; but such intercourse is permitted, that is, tolerated, in the sense that it is not forbidden.

### That marriage is good

5. There were certain heretics, called Tatianists, who detested marriage. They wholly condemn marriage, make it equal to fornications and other corruptions, and admit into their number no man or woman who makes use of marriage. That marriage is a good thing is proved not only from the fact that the Lord is read to have instituted it between the first parents, but also because Christ attended the wedding at Cana of Galilee and commended it by a miracle, turning water into wine; he also afterward forbade a man to dismiss his wife except for fornication. The Apostle too says, 1 Corinthians 7: “A virgin does not sin if she marries.” It is evident, therefore, that marriage is a good thing; otherwise it would not be a sacrament, for a sacrament is a sacred sign. (Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 25; Hugh, *Four Books of Sentences*, chapter 3.)

### Of what reality marriage is a sacrament

6. Since Marriage is a sacrament, therefore, it is a sacred sign, and a sign of a sacred reality: namely, the union of Christ and the Church, as the Apostle says. “It is written,” he says, in Ephesians 5: “‘A man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,’” Genesis 2. “This is a great sacrament; but I speak of Christ and the Church.” For as spouses are united both by the agreement of their minds and by the union of their bodies, so the Church is joined to Christ by will and nature: by will, because it wills the same as he; by nature, because he took his form from human nature. Thus the bride is joined to the bridegroom spiritually and bodily—that is, by charity and by conformity of nature. Marriage is a figure of both unions. The consent of spouses signifies the spiritual union of Christ and the Church, which occurs through charity; the mingling of the sexes signifies that union which occurs through conformity of nature.

### How the statement is to be understood: “That woman does not belong to marriage with whom there is no union of the sexes”

7. For this reason, some doctors have said that a woman who does not experience bodily union does not belong to marriage. Augustine says, 27, question 2, chapter *Non est*: “There is no doubt that that woman does not belong to marriage with whom there is shown to have been no mingling of sex.” Likewise Pope Leo, in the same place, chapter *Cum societas*: “Since the fellowship of marriage was so instituted from the beginning that, apart from the mingling of the sexes, it does not have in itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that that woman does not belong to marriage in whom there is shown to have been no nuptial mystery.” Likewise Augustine: “Marriage is not complete without mingling of the sexes.”

If one takes this according to the surface of the words, one is led into so great an error as to say that marriage cannot be contracted without bodily union, and that there was no marriage between Mary and Joseph, or that it was not perfect—a thought it is impious to entertain. For it was holier and more perfect precisely insofar as it was freer from bodily activity. The statements set above must therefore be understood in this sense: not that a woman with whom there has been no mingling of the sexes does not belong to marriage, but that she does not belong to a marriage which bears the explicit and complete figure of the union of Christ and the Church. Such a marriage figures the union of Christ and the Church that consists in charity, but not the union that consists in conformity of nature. Therefore that marriage too contains a type of the union of Christ and the Church, but only of that union by which the Church is joined to Christ in charity, not of that by which the members are united to their Head through the assumption of flesh. Yet marriage is no less holy for this reason, because, as Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, “in marriage the holiness of the sacrament is of greater force than the fruitfulness of the womb.” Marriage is also a sign of the spiritual union and affection of minds by which spouses ought to be united to one another. Hence the Apostle says, Ephesians 5: “Husbands, love your wives as your own bodies.”

## DISTINCTION XXVII. WHAT MUST BE CONSIDERED IN MARRIAGE

1. After this, it must be considered what Marriage is; what is its efficient cause; the purpose for which it ought to be contracted; what are the goods of marriage; how through them bodily intercourse is excused; and which persons are lawful for matrimony. There are also many other matters to be considered in Marriage, which we shall touch upon briefly.

### What marriage is

2. Marriage or matrimony, then, is the marital union of a man and woman between lawful persons, maintaining an indivisible partnership of life. To the indivisible partnership of life belongs this: that neither can profess continence or devote himself or herself to prayer without the consent of the other; that the marital bond remains between them while they live, so that they may not unite themselves with others; and that each renders to the other what is due to the other. This definition includes only the marriage of lawful and faithful persons.

### On the consent which effects marriage

3. The efficient cause of Matrimony is consent—not just any consent, but consent expressed in words; not consent concerning the future, but concerning the present. For if they consent regarding the future, saying, “I will take you as my husband,” and, “I will take you as my wife,” that consent does not effect Matrimony. Likewise, if they consent in their minds but do not express it in words or by other certain signs, such consent does not effect marriage. But if they state in words what they nevertheless do not will in their hearts, provided that neither compulsion nor deceit is involved, the obligation of those words by which they consent, saying, “I take you as my husband,” and “I take you as my wife,” makes Matrimony.

### He proves by authorities that consent alone makes matrimony

4. That consent makes Matrimony is proved by the following testimonies. Isidore says: “Consent makes Matrimony.” Likewise Pope Nicholas: “According to the laws, the consent alone of those whose union is in question is sufficient; if that alone should perhaps be lacking in a marriage, all the other things celebrated, even intercourse itself, are frustrated.” Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily 32 on Matthew chapter 19: “It is not intercourse that makes marriage, but will; and therefore separation of bodies does not dissolve it.” Likewise Ambrose, in his second exposition on Matthew: “It is not the deflowering of virginity that makes Marriage, but the marital compact.” From these it appears that consent—that is, the marital compact—makes Matrimony; and from that point there is Marriage, even if bodily union neither preceded nor followed.

### When marriage begins to exist

5. The testimonies of the saints prove that, from the very betrothal at which the marital compact is expressed, they are spouses. Ambrose says, in the same place, chapter *Cum initiatur*, and in book 27 of *On Virgins*: “When marriage is begun, the name of marriage is assumed; when she is joined to a man, there is marriage—not when she is known by a man’s union.” Likewise Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 9, chapter 8: “They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital intercourse is not yet known between them.” Likewise Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 11: “She is called a wife from the first pledge of betrothal, though he had not known her by intercourse and was not going to know her. Nor was the designation of wife either false or deceitful where no mingling of flesh had occurred or was going to occur. Therefore, in that faithful marriage both deserved to be called Christ’s parents: not only she as his mother, but also he as his father, as the husband of his mother—yet both in mind, not in flesh.” From these passages it is plainly indicated that from the time when voluntary and marital consent intervenes—which alone makes Marriage—the betrothed man and woman are true spouses.

### According to some, there is no marriage before bodily union; they are bridegroom and bride

6. Some nevertheless maintain that true marriage is not contracted before the bringing home of the bride and bodily union, and that persons are not truly spouses before the mingling of the sexes occurs. From the first pledge of betrothal, they say, the man is a bridegroom and the woman a bride, not a wife. They say that bridegrooms and brides are frequently called spouses not because they are so, but because they will be so, having made to each other the pledge of that future reality. They hold that the words of the preceding authorities must be understood accordingly.

### The reasoning on which they rely

7. They argue that there is a great difference between a bride and a wife from the fact that, before bodily union, a bride may choose the monastery without consulting or obtaining the consent of her bridegroom; after she has done so, the bridegroom too may take another woman. But a married man or woman can neither observe continence except by common consent, nor enter a monastery unless both profess continence together. That a bride may choose the monastery is proved by authorities of the saints. Pope Eusebius says, 27, question 7, chapter *Desponsatam*: “A betrothed girl may not lawfully be given by her parents to another man; nevertheless, she may choose a monastery for herself.” Likewise Gregory, chapter *Decreta*, 27, question 2, paragraph 2: “Legal decrees have never imposed any penalty whatsoever upon a betrothed woman who wishes to convert.” Jerome also relates that Macarius, foremost among Christ’s hermits, after the wedding feast had been celebrated and when he was about to enter the marriage-chamber in the evening, left the city, crossed the sea, and chose the solitude of the desert for himself. Blessed Alexis likewise, called by divine grace from his wedding, left his bride and began to serve Christ naked. These examples make clear that bridegrooms may profess continence without the consent of their brides, and conversely.

### That a married man or woman cannot profess continence without the other’s consent

[Col. 0912]

8. This is in no way permitted to married persons. A husband cannot adopt a way of life of greater perfection without his wife’s consent, nor conversely. Hence Gregory, 2, question 2, chapter *Sunt qui*, writing to the patrician Theotista:

> There are those who say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion. But it must be known that, although human law has allowed this, divine law has forbidden it. Yet if both agree to live a continent life, who would dare to condemn this? For we know that many saints both formerly lived a continent life with their spouses and afterward passed to the governance of the holy Church. But if the woman does not follow the continence desired by the husband, or the husband refuses that desired by the wife, the marriage cannot be divided, because it is written, 1 Corinthians 7: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.” Likewise, “The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”

Likewise, 27, question 2, chapter *Agathosa*, and the four following chapters:

> Agathosa, bearer of this letter, complained that her husband had entered a monastery against her will. Therefore we command your experience diligently to investigate whether perhaps he converted with her consent, or whether she herself promised to change her life. If you find this, provide that he remain in the monastery, and compel her, as she promised, to change her life. But if none of these things is so, and you have not learned that the aforesaid woman has committed any former crime of fornication—for which a wife may lawfully be dismissed—then, lest his conversion, with his wife left in the world, become an occasion of destruction for him, we will that you restore her husband to her, even if he has already been tonsured, setting aside every excuse; for no reason permits a husband to dismiss his wife except fornication. For after man and woman are made one body through the union of marriage, it cannot be that one part converts and the other remains in the world.

Likewise, from the eightieth synod, 27, question 2, chapter *Si quis*: “If a married man wishes to convert to a monastery, he is not to be received unless he has first been released by his wife, who professes chastity.” Such persons, then, follow Christ without fault after leaving the world if they have a mutual consent to chastity. Likewise, if husband and wife mutually agree to separate solely for religious life, this is by no means to be done without the bishop’s consent, so that they may be established in places separately assigned by him. For when the wife is unwilling, or either of them is unwilling, marriage is not dissolved even for such a reason.

Likewise Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*: “If you abstain without your wife’s consent, you grant her permission to commit fornication; and her sin will be imputed to your abstinence.” Likewise Pope Nicholas, cited above: “Queen Theutberga wrote to us that she wished to lay aside royal dignity and marital union and desired to be content with private life alone. We wrote to her that this could not be done otherwise unless her husband Lothair chose the same life.”

From these passages it is clear that married persons cannot choose a monastery, profess continence, or take up a religious habit without mutual consent; and, if they do so, they ought to be recalled. But betrothed persons may choose a monastery without mutual consent. Therefore, it seems that there is no marriage between bridegroom and bride. Accordingly, they maintain that from the first pledge of betrothal they are called spouses not by the reality of the present but in hope of the future, because from the pledge which they owe each other in betrothal they subsequently become spouses.

The authorities cited above, which assert that consent makes marriage, they wish to understand thus: marital consent or compact does not make marriage before intercourse, but in intercourse. For just as defloration of virginity does not make marriage unless a marital compact has preceded it, so neither does a marital compact make marriage before bodily union is present. Thus from the marital compact bridegroom and bride arise before intercourse; in intercourse they truly become spouses. For the marital compact makes her who was previously a bride become a wife in intercourse.

### Reply to the foregoing, with determination of the preceding points

9. To this we reply as follows. Sometimes a betrothal occurs in which there is a mutual promise by man and woman to contract marriage, but there is no consent in the present tense. There is also a betrothal containing present consent—that is, a marital compact—which alone makes marriage. In the betrothal, then, in which there is a promise to contract marriage, they become only bridegroom and bride, not spouses; and such betrothed persons may profess continence and choose a monastery without mutual consent. But in the betrothal in which there is present consent, marriage is contracted; and from the first pledge of that betrothal they are called true spouses. According to this distinction of betrothal, the doctors speak variously concerning betrothed persons.

### How “bride” is understood in the following chapters

10. Sometimes they call “brides” women who have had that kind of betrothal in which there was a present marital compact; and these women are true spouses. Hence Gregory, 27, question 2, chapter *Si quis uxorem*:

> If anyone has betrothed or endowed a wife, although he may afterward be unable to take her as his wife because the day of death intervenes first, nevertheless no one of her kin may take her in marriage; and if this is found to have been done, they are to be completely separated.

Likewise Pope Julius, in the same place, chapter *Si quis desponsaverit*:

> If anyone has betrothed or endowed a wife and, whether through the prior intervention of death or through the onset of certain circumstances, has not known her, neither his brother nor any one of his kin shall ever take the same woman as wife at any time.

Likewise Gregory, in the same place, chapter *Qui desponsatam*:

> Whoever takes as wife the betrothed girl of his neighbor, let him and all who consent with him be anathema, because according to God’s law he is decreed to die. For it is not contrary to divine law to call brides “wives,” as in the Gospel, Matthew 1: “Take Mary your wife.” And in Deuteronomy: “If anyone violates another’s bride in a field or any place, or brings her into his house, let him die, because he has violated his neighbor’s wife”—not one who was already a wife, but one who was to become a wife through her parents.

From this it is gathered that some brides are spouses before the mingling of the sexes. But perhaps one is troubled by what is said at the end of the chapter: “not one who was already a wife, but one who was to become a wife.” This should not be understood as though she were not truly a wife once the marital compact had intervened, but because she had not yet been brought home and the marital act, namely marital intercourse, had not occurred.

### That “bride” is understood differently in these other chapters

11. A bride is also a woman betrothed to a man in such a manner that no present consent has intervened, but only a promise of the future. In this sense is to be understood the decree from the Council of Tibur, 27, question 2, chapter *Si quis sponsam*:

> If anyone violates his son’s bride, and afterward his son marries her, the father thereafter is to have no wife, nor the woman a husband; but the son, who did not know of his father’s crime, shall take another woman.

If she had been a wife—which indeed would have been so if a marital compact had intervened in the betrothal—the bridegroom would not be permitted to take another. But the penalty of not marrying is imposed strictly upon adulterers so that others may be frightened. Likewise, from the same source:

> A certain man betrothed and endowed a wife, but could not have intercourse with her. His brother secretly violated her and made her pregnant. It was decreed that, although she could not be the lawful wife of her betrothed man, the brother could not have the woman betrothed to his brother; but the adulterer and adulteress should indeed undergo punishment for fornication, while lawful marriages are not to be denied them.

This must be understood of that betrothal in which there was no present marital consent; otherwise they would not be permitted to enter other marriages. Likewise this is to be understood, from the Council of Toledo: “It has been established by the holy assembly that, if anyone abducts another’s bride, he is to be punished with public penance and remain without hope of marriage. But if she did not consent to the same crime, she is not to be denied permission to marry another.” It is clear that she was betrothed without a present marital compact, and therefore was not a wife; while her bridegroom lived, she was not denied permission to marry another.

For there are certain nuptial compacts concerning the future, from which persons are called bridegrooms and brides but do not thereby become spouses. And there is a marital compact in the present tense which makes a bridegroom and bride spouses as well. Both compacts are sometimes called betrothal or espousals; properly speaking, however, espousals are certain solemn nuptial compacts.

### Why brides are not immediately given over

12. Concerning nuptial compacts in which there is only a promise of the future, Augustine says, in the same place, book 2: “It was instituted that brides already promised should not immediately be given over, lest a husband regard cheaply the woman given whom he, as bridegroom, had longed for while she was delayed.”

### Which bride is a widow on the bridegroom’s death, and which is not (27, question 2)

13. It must be known that a bride promised only in the future does not remain a widow when her bridegroom dies, because he had not been her husband. Hence, if anyone marries her, he is not prohibited from ascending to holy orders, because he has not married a widow. For the husband of a widow, just like a bigamist, is prohibited from becoming a priest. No one is excluded from holy orders because of such a union.

### One who marries another’s bride after his death may approach holy orders

14. In this sense must be understood what Pope Pelagius says concerning one who, after her bridegroom’s death, takes his bride as wife: “So far as this point is concerned, there is nothing,” he says, distinction 34, final chapter, “in canonical institutions to hinder his promotion to holy orders.” But if such a bride had been one between whom and her bridegroom present consent had intervened, then upon his death she would have remained a widow; one joined to her in marriage could no longer approach holy orders, since he had married a widow. There is therefore no doubt that present consent alone effects marriage, and that from that point they are called true spouses. Therefore, after such consent, if either joins himself or herself to another, even if bodily union follows there, that person must be restored to the prior union.

## DISTINCTION XXVIII. WHETHER FUTURE CONSENT WITH AN OATH MAKES MARRIAGE

1. Here it must be asked whether consent concerning the future, even with an oath added, effects marriage. For example, if someone promises or even swears to another that he will marry her at an agreed time, and she promises or swears that she will marry him, does such a promise make them spouses? If, changing intention, one or both pass to a union with another, is the compact of the second union to be broken because of the prior promise supported by an oath?

Consider that promising is far different from doing. One who promises does not yet do the thing. Therefore, one who has promised to take some woman as wife has not yet taken her as wife; and she who has promised to marry has not yet married. How, then, can those who do not yet contract marriage, but promise on oath that they will contract it in the future, be called spouses? Again, if by force of an oath concerning the future they immediately become spouses, why do they swear that they will do in the future what they accomplish in the present? Again, if they immediately become spouses as soon as they swear, then they accomplish the thing when they swear that they will accomplish it. Therefore I say that at that point marriage does not exist, but is promised for the future.

But if he afterward marries a wife and she marries a husband, marriage exists on both sides and cannot be dissolved. The preceding falsehood or perjury, therefore, must be corrected by penance, but the subsequent marriage is not to be dissolved. It is otherwise when an oath is confirmed by the attestation of present marital consent: after such consent, if someone joins himself or herself to another, even if offspring are produced, that later union must be annulled and the person restored to the prior union.

### Things which seem contrary to the foregoing
2. But the following provision handed down by the laws seems to conflict with the preceding view: “If anyone, having touched the divine Scriptures, swears to a woman that he will have her as his lawful wife, or even if he gives such an oath in an oratory, she shall be his lawful wife, even though no dowry and no other written instrument has intervened.” But this indicates what ought to be done or to be, not what then comes to pass. For by that oath she does not then become his wife; rather, she ought to become so because an oath has been sworn [Col. 0915]. This statement may also be understood of an oath where they consent in the present tense and mutually receive one another.

The statement that consent alone makes marriage also seems to be opposed by what Pope Evaristus says: “A marriage does not otherwise become lawful except through those who are seen to have authority over the woman and by whom she is guarded. A wife is to be sought and betrothed by her parents, endowed according to the laws, blessed by a priest—as is customary—guarded by attendants of the bridal chamber, and solemnly received.” He cites 30, question 4, chapter *Si quis*; and determines the matter in 30, question 5, chapter *Aliter*. Likewise, 30, question 5: “Know that marriages are lawful in this way; those otherwise presumed are not marriages but adulteries or fornications, unless their own will has supported them and lawful vows have come to their aid.”

This is not to be understood as though a lawful marriage could not exist without the things enumerated, but because without them it lacks the fitting adornment and proper dignity. For in the celebration of this sacrament, as in others, some things belong to the substance of the sacrament, such as present-tense consent, which alone suffices to contract marriage; while other things belong to the adornment and solemnity of the sacrament, such as the giving by parents, the blessing of priests, and the like. Without these, marriage is lawfully made as regards its force, though not as regards the propriety of the sacrament.

Thus, without these things, people come together not as though they were lawful spouses, but as adulterers or fornicators—as do those who marry secretly. Indeed, they would be fornicators unless their will, expressed in present-tense words, supported them, for this makes a lawful marriage between them. For even secret present-tense consent, expressed in words, makes a marriage, although the contract is not honorable; but the marriage is not legally confirmed by consent given secretly. For if one leaves the other, he or she is not compelled by the judgment of the Church to return and live together as with a spouse, since a contract made secretly cannot be proved by witnesses. But if those who consented secretly to one another publicly profess that same consent by their will, then certainly their own will supports them, and lawful vows come to their aid in confirming the marriage that had previously been contracted secretly. Therefore, will expressed in words secretly supports the making of a marriage; expressed openly, it supports its confirmation and strengthening, so that the Church may freely judge the matter if expedient.

### What is the object of that consent: carnal intercourse, cohabitation, or something else?  
(27, question 2, chapter *Subjiciat*, § *Cum ergo inter istos*; Augustine, *On Holy Virginity*, chapter 5.)

3. Here it is asked: since present-tense consent makes a marriage, consent to what thing is it—carnal intercourse, cohabitation, or both? If consent to cohabitation makes marriage, then a brother may contract marriage with his sister, or a father with his daughter. If it is consent to carnal intercourse, then there was no marriage between Mary and Joseph. For Mary had resolved to remain a virgin unless God commanded otherwise; as she seems to have said to the angel: “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” That is: “I have resolved not to know a man.” For it was not necessary to ask how she could have a son merely because she did not then know a man, but because she had resolved never to know one. Bede says, commenting on Luke 1, that she had determined to remain a virgin. Therefore, if afterward she consented to carnal intercourse contrary to her resolution, she appears to have become guilty of breaking her vow in intention, even if not violated in act.

Let us say, therefore, that consent to cohabitation or to carnal intercourse does not make marriage, but consent to a conjugal partnership, expressed in words according to the present tense. Thus, when a man says: “I take you as mine—not as mistress, not as servant, but as wife.” For woman was given neither as servant nor as mistress; therefore, from the beginning she was formed neither from the highest part nor from the lowest, but from the man’s side, for the sake of conjugal partnership. Had she been made from the highest part, namely the head, she would seem to have been created for dominion; but if from the lowest, namely the feet, she would seem subject to servitude. But because she is taken neither as mistress nor as servant, she was made [Col. 0916] from the middle, that is, from the side, because she is taken into conjugal partnership.

Therefore, when they come together in such a way that the man says, “I take you as my wife,” and the woman says, “I take you as my husband,” these words, or others signifying the same thing, express consent—not to carnal intercourse or bodily cohabitation, but to conjugal partnership. From this it follows that they must live together, unless perhaps, for the sake of religion and by equal vow, they separate bodily, whether for a time or until the end.

## DISTINCTION XXIX. COERCION EXCLUDES CONJUGAL CONSENT

1. Conjugal consent must be free from coercion. Coerced consent—which should not even be called consent—does not make a marriage. Pope Urban testifies to this in 31, question 2, chapter *De neptis*, writing to the holy king of Aragon in these words:

“Concerning the marriage of your niece, whom, when necessity pressed, you confirmed under a pledge of faith that you would give to a certain knight: guided by equity, we have decreed this: if she wholly refuses that man—as is said—and persists in the same will utterly to deny that she will marry him, do not in any way compel her, unwilling and resisting, to be joined in marriage to that man.”

Likewise, in the same place, chapter *Si verum*: “If it is established as true what the envoys of Prince Jordan have reported to us, namely, that he himself, compelled and grieving, betrothed his daughter—unwilling, weeping, and resisting with all her strength—to Raynald: since the authority of laws and canons does not approve such betrothals, lest this seem excessively harsh to those ignorant of laws and canons, we temper our judgment as follows. If the prince, with his daughter’s assent, wishes to bring to completion what has been begun, we permit it. But if not, let our legate hear both parties; and, if there is nothing on Raynald’s side further to hinder it, let him receive from Jordan himself an oath establishing that these things are as stated. And we, following the written laws and canons, henceforth do not forbid the said daughter of Jordan, if she wishes, to marry another man in the Lord alone.”

From these texts it is clear that marriage is made between consenting and willing persons, not between those who resist and are unwilling. Yet those joined unwillingly and under coercion, if later, after some time, they cohabit without contradiction or complaint while having the opportunity to leave or object, seem to consent; and that subsequent consent supplies what the preceding coercion had taken away.

### In the book of the *Pandects*

2. A person is proved to consent when he or she does not plainly object, according to the saying: “In their betrothals the consent of those is to be required whose consent is desired in their marriages.” Nevertheless, a daughter is understood to consent to her father unless she plainly dissents. Likewise, betrothals, like marriages, are made by the consent of the contracting parties. Therefore, as in marriages, so in betrothals the daughter of the head of household must consent; if she does not oppose her father’s will, she is understood to consent.

## DISTINCTION XXX. CONCERNING ERROR THAT INVALIDATES CONSENT

1. Not only coercion impedes or excludes consent; error does so as well. Yet not every error invalidates consent. One error concerns the person, another fortune, another status, another quality. Error as to person occurs when this man is thought to be that man, but is another. Error as to fortune occurs when one thought rich is poor, or conversely. Error as to status occurs when one thought free is a slave. Error as to quality occurs when one thought good is bad.

Error as to fortune or quality does not exclude consent to marriage. But error as to status invalidates conjugal consent; this status will be discussed later. Error as to person likewise admits no conjugal consent. Thus, if someone seeks a noble woman in marriage, and another, ignoble woman is delivered to him in her place, there is no marriage between them, because the man consented not to this woman but to another. It is as if someone promised to sell me gold, but offered me brass in place of gold and thereby deceived me [Col. 0917]. Would I be said to have consented to brass? I never wished to buy brass; therefore I did not consent to it, because consent belongs only to the will. Therefore, just as error concerning the material excludes consent, so does error concerning the person in marriage.

But an objection is raised concerning Jacob, who had served seven years for Rachel and was given Leah in her place. Did error as to person exclude marriage, since he consented not to Leah but to Rachel? What occurred there is not improperly handed down as having been enacted in mystery. Yet, although consent did not precede, it followed. Nor are they judged fornicators because of the intercourse that preceded consent, since he knew her with marital affection and she rendered the debt with wifely affection, believing herself lawfully joined to him by the law of primogeniture and her father’s commands. He is also excused because this was so done by God’s counsel in mystery.

Even today, a man would be excused if, without his knowledge, his wife’s sister entered his bed and offered herself to him. Although she is to be judged permanently incapable of marriage, the man who knew her in ignorance is excused, as is proved by an analogous case. For if the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light, is believed to be good, the error is not dangerous.

That the man did not consent to that woman is shown by a parallel. If some heretic calling himself Augustine or Ambrose offered himself to a Catholic and summoned him to imitate his faith, and the Catholic assented, to whose doctrinal position would he be said to have consented? Not to the sect of heretics, but to the soundness of faith which that heretic falsely claimed to possess.

But error as to fortune does not exclude consent. A woman who marries a poor man believing him rich cannot renounce her former condition, although she was mistaken. Nor does error as to quality: if someone marries a prostitute or a defiled woman whom he thinks chaste or virgin, he cannot dismiss her.

### On the marriage of Mary and Joseph

2. Something must be added to what has been said concerning the nature of the consent that passed between Mary and Joseph. It may safely be believed that not only Mary but Joseph also had resolved within himself to wish to preserve virginity unless God commanded otherwise; and that they so consented to conjugal partnership that each understood of the other, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, that the other wished to preserve virginity unless God inspired otherwise. But they had not expressed that will in words. Later they did express it, and they remained virgins (Augustine, book 24, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, chapters 8 and 9).

Mary therefore consented to marital partnership, but not to carnal intercourse unless God should specifically command it. Indeed, she consented to marital union also by God’s counsel, because she wished to preserve virginity; and therefore she would not otherwise have consented to conjugal partnership unless she had received God’s intimate counsel. Augustine says of this in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*:

“Blessed Mary resolved in her heart to keep a vow of virginity, but did not express the vow with her lips. She subjected herself to the divine ordering; she resolved to persevere as a virgin unless God revealed otherwise to her. Entrusting her virginity, therefore, to the divine ordering, she consented to carnal intercourse—not desiring it, but obeying divine inspiration in both matters. Later she expressed this with her husband in words, and each remained in virginity.”

### That their marriage was perfect

3. Between them, as Augustine says, 27, question 2, there was a perfect marriage: perfect indeed, not in its signification, but in holiness. For marriages of those who preserve continence by equal vow are holier. Hence Augustine says: “What you both vowed to God by equal vow and consent, you both ought steadfastly to have fulfilled. If he fell from that resolution, you at least should persevere. Your husband had not ceased to be your husband because you both abstained alike from carnal union; rather, you remained spouses all the more holy because you kept in concord the more holy commitments.”

Therefore, the marriage of Mary and Joseph was perfect in holiness. It was also perfect according to the threefold good of marriage: faith, offspring, and sacrament. Every good of marriage, Augustine says in the same place, chapter 11, was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: faith, offspring, sacrament. “We recognize the offspring [Col. 0918] as the Lord himself; the faith, because there was no adultery; the sacrament, because there was no divorce. Only marital intercourse was absent there, because it could not occur in the flesh of sin without the shameful concupiscence of the flesh which results from sin; and he who was to be without sin chose to be conceived without it.”

Although marital intercourse did not occur, they nevertheless were truly spouses in mind, not in flesh, and likewise parents. Ambrose, however, says that marriage is made perfect through carnal intercourse: “In every marriage,” he says in *On the Patriarchs*, chapters 11 and 12, “a spiritual union is understood; the bodily union of those joined confirms and perfects it.” But marriage must be understood to be perfected by bodily union not as to the truth or holiness of marriage, but as to its signification, because then it more perfectly figures the union of Christ and the Church.

### On the final cause of marriage

4. Having explained what is the efficient cause of marriage, it remains to show for what reason marriage is customarily or ought to be contracted. The principal final cause of contracting marriage is the procreation of offspring. For this reason God instituted marriage between the first parents, to whom he said in Genesis 1: “Increase and multiply,” etc. A secondary cause, after Adam’s sin, is the avoidance of fornication. Hence the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 7: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.”

There are also other honorable causes, such as reconciliation of enemies and restoration of peace. There are further, less honorable causes for which marriage is sometimes contracted: for example, the beauty of a man or woman, which often impels hearts inflamed by love to enter marriage so that they may fulfill their desire. Gain and possession of riches are also frequently a cause of marriage, as are many other motives easily discerned by anyone who considers the matter carefully.

Nor should one agree with those who say that a union contracted for these less honorable causes is not a marriage. For it is evident from what has been said that marriage is made by mutual consent expressed in present-tense words, even if love drew them to it. Jacob provides an example: he loved Rachel, beautiful in face and lovely in appearance, and loving her greatly said: “I will serve you for Rachel seven years.” Likewise, Deuteronomy reads: “If you see among the captives a beautiful woman, and love her and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house,” etc.

### That an evil end does not contaminate the sacrament

5. Even if marriage is contracted for an improper end, when the appearance of the contracting party moves the mind, the marriage is still good, because a person’s evil life or perverse intention does not contaminate a sacrament. The marriage of Mary and Joseph, however, had other special causes: that the virgin might be sustained by the comfort of a husband; that the birth might be concealed from the devil; and that Joseph might be a witness to her chastity, defending her from the disgrace of suspicion, lest she be condemned as an adulteress.

## DISTINCTION XXXI. CONCERNING THE THREE GOODS OF MARRIAGE

1. After this, it must be said what the goods of marriage are and how they excuse intercourse. There are principally three goods of marriage. Augustine says, commenting on Genesis, book 9, chapter 7: “The good of marriage is threefold: faith, offspring, and sacrament.” In faith, care is taken that, after the marriage bond, intercourse is not had with another man or woman. In offspring, that it be received lovingly and brought up religiously. In sacrament, that marriage not be separated and that neither the dismissed husband nor the dismissed wife be joined to another, even for the sake of offspring.

### On the twofold separation

2. Separation is twofold: bodily and sacramental. Spouses may be separated bodily because of fornication, or by mutual consent for the sake of religion, whether for a time or until the end. But they cannot be separated sacramentally while they live, if they are lawful persons. For the marriage bond remains between them, even if, having departed from one another, they adhere to others.

Hence Augustine says in book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 10: “The rights of marriage once entered into remain so fully between living persons that they are spouses to one another even when separated, rather than to the others to whom they have attached themselves.” Likewise: “A certain marital bond remains between living persons which neither separation nor union with another can remove; just as an apostate soul, departing as if from the marriage of Christ, does not lose the sacrament of faith received in the washing of regeneration even though faith has been lost. It would be restored to the returning person if it had been lost on departing. But the person who has departed possesses it as an increase of punishment, not as a merit of reward” (ibid., chapter 11).

Likewise: “If persons have agreed by mutual consent to abstain forever from the use of carnal concupiscence, far be it that the marriage bond between them should be broken. Rather, it clings more firmly, insofar as they maintain between themselves commitments to be kept more dearly and more harmoniously—not through pleasurable bodily bonds, but through the affectionate wills of their minds” (Hugh, *Four Books of Sentences*, chapter 5).

Observe that the third good of marriage is called “sacrament,” not because it is marriage itself, but because it is a sign of the same sacred reality: the spiritual and inseparable union of Christ and the Church.

### These three goods are not present in every marriage

3. It must be known that some contract marriage in which these three goods do not accompany it. Faith is absent where a husband has intercourse with another woman, or a wife with another man. Yet this good adheres to marriage such that, if present, it commends marriage more; if absent, it does not thereby destroy it. A woman who commits adultery is not for that reason not a wife; indeed, if she were not a wife, she would not be an adulteress. When this happens, fault is committed, but the sacrament is not annulled.

Likewise, the good of offspring is not present in all spouses. Some preserve continence by equal vow; others cannot generate because of age or another cause. Nor do all those who receive offspring possess the good of offspring. For the good of offspring is not the offspring itself, nor hope for offspring unrelated to religion—rather, directed to hereditary succession, as when someone desires heirs to an earthly possession. It is the hope and desire by which offspring is sought in order that it may be formed by religion. Many, therefore, have offspring yet lack the good of offspring; their marriage does not thereby cease to be a marriage.

But sacrament adheres so inseparably to the marriage of lawful persons that without it marriage seems not to exist, because the marriage bond always remains between living persons, so that even when divorce occurs because of fornication, the firmness of the marriage bond is not dissolved (Hugh, *On the Sacraments*, part 11, chapter 8). But where marriage is not contracted between lawful persons, that good called sacrament is absent, because the union of such persons may be dissolved; this will be discussed later.

Augustine shows that marriage exists between persons who come together with conjugal affection, not for offspring but to satisfy lust, and that they are called spouses rather than fornicators. He says in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 5:

“It is customary to ask, when a man and woman—neither being another’s husband or wife—are joined to one another, not for begetting children but, because of incontinence, solely for intercourse, on condition that neither she does this with another nor he with another, whether they should be called married. Perhaps it may not unreasonably be called a marriage if this arrangement pleases them until the death of one of them, and if they do not avoid the generation of offspring, though they were not joined for that reason—so as either not to wish children to be born to them, or even to act by some evil deed to prevent their birth. But if either or both of these conditions are absent, I do not find how we can call these unions marriages. For if he has taken a woman for a time, until he finds one worthy of his rank or resources to bring into marriage, he is an adulterer already in intention—not with the woman whom he seeks to find, but with this woman with whom he lies in such a way that he has no marital partnership with her.”

Thus, those who come together solely for intercourse are called spouses, provided that they do not avoid the generation of offspring by some evil stratagem.

### On those who procure drugs of sterility

4. But those who procure drugs of sterility are not spouses [Col. 0920], but fornicators. Hence Augustine says in book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 15:

“Sometimes this lustful cruelty, or cruel lust, proceeds so far as even to procure drugs of sterility; and if these accomplish nothing, it somehow extinguishes or expels conceived fetuses within the womb, wishing its own offspring to perish before living, or, if it was alive in the womb, to be killed before birth. Certainly, if both are such, they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not through marriage but rather through sexual defilement. But if both are not such, I dare to say: either she is in some way her husband’s prostitute, or he is his wife’s adulterer.”

### When those who procure abortion are murderers

5. It is customarily asked concerning those who procure abortion: when are they judged murderers and when not? The expulsion of the fetus pertains to homicide when it has been formed and possesses a soul, as Augustine maintains in his commentary on Exodus, 32, question 2, chapter *Quod vero*: “But the law did not wish an unformed fetus, in which there is no living soul, to be reckoned as homicide.”

Augustine also says in *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, chapter 32, that an unformed fetus has no soul; therefore a monetary penalty is imposed, and life is not rendered for life. But a soul is given to the body once it is formed; it is not born at the conception of the body, derived with the seed. For if a soul from a soul exists with the seed, many souls perish daily whenever seed, through emission, does not advance to birth. First the house must be built, and then its inhabitant introduced. Therefore, before the features have been put together, where would the soul be?

Likewise Jerome, in his epistle to Algasius, among the questions, question 4: “The seeds are gradually formed in the womb; and for so long it is not reckoned homicide, until the elements, completed, receive their forms and members.” Here it is evident that those who procure abortion are murderers when the fetus has been formed and ensouled.

### On the excusing of intercourse effected by these goods

6. Therefore, when these three goods concur together in a marriage, they avail to excuse carnal intercourse. Even when spouses, preserving marital faith, come together for the sake of offspring, intercourse is so excused that it has no fault. But when the good of offspring is absent, although faith is preserved, and they come together because of incontinence, it is not so excused that it has no fault; rather, it has venial fault.

Hence Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapters 6 and 7: “Marital intercourse for the sake of begetting has no fault; intercourse to satisfy concupiscence, yet with one’s spouse for the sake of marital fidelity, has venial fault.” Likewise Hugh, *Four Books of Sentences*, chapter 4: “That married persons, overcome by concupiscence, use one another beyond the need of begetting children, is included among those debts for which we say every day: ‘Forgive us our debts,’ etc.” Matthew 6.

But where these goods are absent, namely faith and offspring, intercourse does not seem defended from sin. Hence in the *Sentences of Sextus Pythagoricus*, 32, question 1, chapter *Origo quidem*, it is read: “Every excessively ardent lover of his own wife is an adulterer.” Likewise Jerome, in the same place: “A wise man loves his wife by judgment, not by passion; the impulse of pleasure does not rule in him, nor is he rashly borne into intercourse. Nothing is more shameful than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress. Those who say they are joined to wives for the sake of the human race should at least imitate cattle: once a wife’s womb has swollen, they should not destroy their children, nor present themselves to their wives as lovers, but as husbands.” Likewise: “In marriage, acts for the begetting of children are allowed; pleasures taken from the embraces of prostitutes are condemned in a wife.”

### On how the Apostle’s indulgence is to be understood

7. But if intercourse undertaken for the sake of offspring lacks fault, what does the Apostle permit “by way of indulgence”? For he says, 1 Corinthians 7: “But I say this by way of indulgence.” To whom is pardon granted except to one at fault? Some also wish by this to prove that marriage is sin. But, as stated above, one indulgence is of concession, another of permission.

The Apostle had spoken of marriage and of carnal intercourse; and he referred the statement “But I say this by way of indulgence” to both. Marriage is indulged by concession, as is marital intercourse occurring only for the sake of offspring. But intercourse beyond the need of generation because of incontinence is indulged by permission, because some fault is present, though slight. Therefore it is not commanded or conceded, but permitted, because it is not praiseworthy but venial.

Augustine says this in *On the Words of the Apostle*: “Perhaps someone will say: ‘If the Apostle granted pardon, then marriage is sin. For to whom is pardon granted except to a sinner?’ Certainly, what he permitted to weakness by way of pardon, I dare say is sin. For in granting pardon, the Apostle has in view intercourse of married persons, in which there is the evil of incontinence. The evil of incontinence is that a man knows his wife even beyond the need of begetting children; yet the good of marriage is also there. It does not follow that marriage is evil because incontinence is evil. Where intercourse occurs apart from the intention of generation, it is not good; this good is not culpable because of that evil, but that evil becomes venial because of the good of marriage. The Apostle does not reproach marriage, but the evil of incontinence.”

Likewise Augustine, in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 10: “Marriage does not compel intercourse that is not for the sake of offspring, but obtains its forgiveness—provided, however, that it is not so excessive as to hinder the times owed to prayer, nor transformed into the use that is contrary to nature. For intercourse necessary for generation is blameless, and that alone is marital intercourse. But intercourse which goes beyond necessity obeys not reason but lust; and it pertains to a spouse not to demand this, but to render it to the other spouse lest he or she commit fornication. But if both are subject to such concupiscence, they do something that does not belong to marriage; marriage does not urge this offense, but pleads for it. Marital honor, indeed, is chastity; faith in begetting and rendering the carnal debt is the work of marriage.”

This is what the Apostle defends from every sin when he says, 1 Corinthians 7; Augustine, chapter 4 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, volume 7: “A virgin does not sin if she marries.” Therefore, since intercourse with the intention of generation, which properly belongs to marriage, is not culpable, what does the Apostle concede by way of pardon except that spouses claim the debt of the flesh, not from a will to propagate, but from the pleasure of lust? Yet this pleasure incurs fault not because of marriage, but receives pardon because of marriage. Therefore, excessive indulgence is conceded by way of pardon. For this reason marriages are praiseworthy even in this respect: because, on their account, they cause forgiveness of what does not belong to them. For the intercourse by which concupiscence is served is not undertaken to produce the offspring that marriage seeks.

Therefore marriage is wholly good in its own kind, because it preserves fidelity of the marriage bed, joins the two sexes for the sake of receiving offspring, and abhors the impiety of separation (Augustine, *Against Julian the Heretic*, chapters 21 and 22). Even an unbelieving spouse cannot harm the holiness of marriage; rather, the believing spouse benefits the unbelieving one, as the Apostle teaches.

From these texts it is shown that the holiness and good of marriage defend from sin spouses who come together only for the sake of offspring, or who render the debt when it is demanded. For if marital intercourse could not take place without sin, the Lord would not have commanded them after the Flood to join together, saying in Genesis 9: “Increase and multiply,” when they could no longer unite without carnal concupiscence (Hugh, *Four Books of Sentences*, chapter 4).

### That not every delight of the flesh is sin

8. But perhaps someone will say that every carnal concupiscence and delight present in intercourse is evil and sin, because it comes from sin and is disordered. We say that this concupiscence is always evil because it is shameful and a punishment for sin, but it is not always sin. A holy man is often delighted in the flesh by something, such as resting after labor or eating after hunger; yet such delight is not sin unless it is immoderate. So also the delight occurring in marital intercourse, where the three goods are present, is defended from sin (Hugh, same place).

Blessed Gregory, however, seems to hold otherwise: namely, that carnal union cannot occur without sin. He says, 33, question 4: “A man sleeping with his own wife should not enter a church unless he has washed with water.” Although different nations of men think differently about this matter and appear to observe different practices, the custom of the Romans has always been, from ancient times, after union with one’s wife, to seek purification by washing and to refrain for a little while from entering a church. In saying this, we do not judge marriage to be a fault; but because even lawful union with a wife cannot take place without fleshly pleasure, one must refrain from entering the sacred place, because pleasure itself can in no way exist without fault.

### The author determines the authority

9. To prevent this from conflicting with the foregoing, it must be understood of those who do not come together for the sake of offspring, whose pleasure is not without sin. Few, indeed, can be found who still experience carnal embraces and who do not sometimes come together apart from the intention of begetting offspring. Whenever this occurs, one must refrain from entering a church.

That this is how the passage is to be understood Gregory subsequently shows in the same place: “But if anyone uses his wife not carried away by desire for pleasure but only for the sake of creating children, he certainly is to be left to his own judgment, whether concerning entering the church or receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body. For we ought not forbid someone to receive who, placed in fire, does not know how to burn. But when not love of begetting offspring, but pleasure rules in the act of union, spouses should have in their union something to lament. Then, however, a man who has washed with water after union with his wife may receive even holy communion, when, according to the determination already given, he has been permitted to enter the church.”

## DISTINCTION XXXII. CONCERNING THE RENDERING OF THE CARNAL DEBT

1. It must also be known that although in all other matters a man is set over a woman as the head over the body—for “the man is the head of the woman,” 1 Corinthians 11—in rendering the debt of the flesh they are equals. Therefore the Apostle commands each alike, in this matter, to be subject to the other, saying, 1 Corinthians 7: “Let the husband render the debt to the wife; likewise also the wife to the husband. For the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.”

For neither the woman has authority over her own body in relation to another man, nor the man in relation to another woman. Nor does the man have authority to practice continence, nor the woman, without mutual consent. Rather, each has authority over the other’s body, so that one may not lawfully deny the debt to the other who asks it. In this they are equal: neither man nor woman may give his or her body to another; rather, in this matter they are mutually indebted, lest an occasion for sinning be given. By this, the man’s dominion is not taken away, but abuse is.

For married persons owe one another not only the fidelity of intercourse between their sexes for the sake of begetting children—which is the primary fellowship in this mortal life—but also a kind of mutual servitude in receiving one another’s weakness, in order to avoid unlawful intercourse.
