Thus, even if continence pleases one of them, it cannot be practiced except with the other’s consent. For neither has authority over his or her own body for this purpose. This is so true that neither husband nor wife may deny the other what is fitting, whether for begetting children or because of weakness and continence, lest through this they fall into condemnable corruptions.

To render the marital debt is no crime; to demand it beyond the need of generation is a venial fault. But to commit fornication or adultery is a punishable crime. (Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapters 6 and 7.)

### That neither can practice continence except by mutual consent
2. That a husband may not practise continence without his wife’s consent is proved by the following testimonies. For Augustine says, on Psalm 45: “If the husband says, ‘I now wish to practise continence,’ but the wife does not wish it, he cannot do so. For what you will, she does not will. Must she, through your continence, become a fornicator? If she marries another while you are alive, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish such harm to be compensated by such a gain.” [Col. 0923] Render the marital due; and, if you do not demand it, render it. God will reckon it to you as perfect sanctification if you do not demand what is owed you, but render what you owe your wife.

The same author, following the Apostle’s words: “Even if the husband had wished to practise continence and you had not wished it, he would have been obliged to render you the due; and God would have imputed continence to him, if he yielded not to his own weakness but to yours, lest you fall into adultery.” Therefore whoever, out of compassion for his wife’s weakness, renders the due does not demand it; or, if because of his own weakness he takes a wife, grieving rather that he could not remain without a wife than rejoicing that he has taken one, he confidently awaits the last day.

The same, to Armentarius, Letter 45: “There can be only one reason why we should not merely fail to urge you to fulfil what you vowed, but should even forbid you to fulfil it: namely, if perhaps your wife, through weakness either of mind or flesh, refused to undertake this with you. For married persons ought not to make vows of this sort except by common consent and common will; and if it has been done rashly, the rashness is more to be corrected than the promise fulfilled. For God does not require a person to fulfil a vow made from another’s property; rather, he forbids one to usurp what belongs to another.”

The same Augustine, in *On Adulterous Marriages*, ch. 14: “The Apostle did not wish spouses mutually to deprive one another of the carnal due, even for a time in order to devote themselves to prayer, except by consent.”

The same, in *Questions on Numbers*, book 4, 3, 59: “It is clear that the Law intended woman to be subject to her husband in such a way that none of her vows made for the sake of abstinence should be performed by her unless the husband authorized them by permitting them. For although the Law intended it to count as the husband’s sin if he first permitted and afterwards forbade it, yet it did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because she had first been permitted by her husband. It called it the husband’s sin because he refused what he had earlier granted; nevertheless it did not thereby command the woman, when her husband had first granted it and afterwards forbidden it, to disregard him.”

From these passages it appears that neither husband nor wife can offer continence to God without common consent, nor ought either to deny the other the due. But if either releases the other from his or her right, can that person afterwards recall the other to the former obligation? For Augustine above seems to have intended this. Some think that a wife who, remaining in her husband’s house, has vowed or promised continence with his permission cannot fulfil it when he forbids her, because of the husband’s dignity, since he is the head of the wife. But this is better understood in the case where the husband grants the wife permission to vow continence and forbids her to fulfil it before the vow is made. But if she has changed her habit, she cannot be recalled, according to the following: “He who has allowed his wife to take the veil shall not take another wife, but shall likewise be converted.” (Council of Rheims, 23, q. 5.)

### At what times intercourse should cease

3. Although the marital due must always be rendered when demanded, it is not lawful to demand it on every day. Hence Augustine, in *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, ch. 127: “For a Christian it is sometimes lawful to have intercourse with his wife, and sometimes not. On days of processions and fasts it is sometimes unlawful to have intercourse; for one must abstain even from lawful things, that what is requested may more readily be obtained.”

The same: “Whenever either the days of the Nativity or the other festivals arrive, abstain not only from intercourse with concubines but also from your own wives.”

Likewise Ambrose: “If a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children, it seems that not much time is granted for that very use, since feast days, days of processions, and the very course of conception and childbirth according to the Law show that the use of the flesh ought to cease at certain times.”

### Jerome seems to disagree with what has been said

4. Yet the statement that rendering the marital due is not a sin seems opposed by what Jerome says in a certain sermon, 33, q. 4, *Sciatis*: “Whoever renders the due to his wife cannot be free for prayer, nor eat the flesh of the Lamb.” Likewise: “If the loaves of proposition could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives, how much more can the bread which came down from heaven not be violated and touched by those who shortly before clung in marital embraces! Not because we condemn marriage, [Col. 0924] but because, at the time when we are to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we ought to abstain from carnal acts.”

This chapter seems chiefly to concern ministers of the Church, who were not permitted to celebrate sacred offices and mysteries at the time of marital embrace, when even the presence of the Holy Spirit is not given. Hence the same author says, on Matthew, 32, q. 2: “Lawful marriages are indeed free from sin; nevertheless, during the time when marital acts are performed, the presence of the Holy Spirit will not be given, even if the person performing the office of generation seems to be a prophet.”

### At what times marriages are not to be celebrated

5. Times must be observed not only in carnal activity but also in celebrating marriages, according to the following, 38, q. 4, ch. *Non oportet*: “It is not fitting to celebrate marriages from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, nor during the three weeks before the feast of St John, nor from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany. If this is done, they shall be separated.”

Likewise Pope Nicholas, in his response to the Bulgarians, 33, q. 4, ch. *Nec uxorem*: “I judge that it cannot in any way be fitting either to take a wife or to contract marriages during the season of Lent.”

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. ON THE DIFFERENT LAWS OF MARRIAGE

1. Here the question is raised concerning the ancient fathers, who are read to have had several wives or concubines simultaneously: whether they sinned. To this we say that, according to the diversity of times, a varied dispensation of the Creator is found. For from the beginning of time marriage was instituted only between two persons, namely Adam and Eve, God saying through Adam’s mouth, Genesis 2: “A man shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Marriage would have been contracted only between two throughout the whole succession of ages, according to the manner of that first institution, had the first human beings remained in obedience.

After their union, their sons and daughters were joined together in marriage, but one man only with one woman. Brothers were then united with sisters because there were no other women or men to whom Adam’s sons or daughters could be joined. Lamech is read to have been the first of all to have had two wives simultaneously; and he is reproved for this, because he is said to have done it in order to satisfy carnal pleasure.

Later, when almost all people were serving false gods and only a few remained in the worship of God, God saw fit that several women should be joined in marriage to one man, lest, if those few failed, the worship and knowledge of God should fail. Thus Abraham, while his wife was alive, went in to a handmaid and begot a child by her. Jacob also joined himself to free women and handmaids; and Lot’s daughters used their drunken father. For when, with all the rest abandoned to idolatry, the Lord had chosen Abraham and his children as a people especially his own, the multiplication of the people of God was rightly sought through the fertility of many women, because the succession of religion lay in succession of blood. Hence under the Law the barren woman, who left no seed upon the earth, was cursed. For this reason marriages were also assigned to priests, because succession in the family is succession in office.

Therefore Abraham or Jacob did not sin because, besides a wife, he sought children from a handmaid. Yet, by their example, it is not lawful for anyone to seek fertility from any woman outside the marital due, since their marriages are equal to the virginity of our own time, while the immoderate use of marriage in our time almost imitates the shamefulness of the fornication of that time.

Augustine says thus concerning this, in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 15: “It was not a sin for the ancient righteous men to use several women; nor did they do this against nature, since they did it not for wantonness but for begetting; nor against custom, because such things were done at that time; nor against a command, because it was forbidden by no law.”

The same, 33, q. 4, ch. *Objiciuntur Jacob*: “Jacob’s four wives are objected: what was custom was not a crime. Thus the patriarchs had intercourse with their wives in receiving their seed, not through a desire to accomplish pleasure, but through provident care to propagate succession; just as the Apostles delighted with their teaching among their hearers who admired them, not from greed for obtaining [Col. 0925] praise, but from love for sowing truth.”

The same elsewhere, in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 14: “In ancient times, while the mystery of our salvation was still veiled, the righteous contracted marriages for the duty of propagation, not conquered by lust but led by piety; and they could and would much more easily have practised continence. Yet they made use of wives, and one man was permitted to have several; they possessed them more chastely than any one of those who now has a single wife, among whom we see what the Apostle permits as a concession. For they had them for the work of begetting, not for the sickness of desire.”

Likewise Ambrose, 32, q. 4, ch. *Dixit Sara*: “Sarah said to Abraham, Genesis 16: ‘Behold, the Lord has shut me up so that I do not bear children. Go in therefore to my handmaid, that you may make a son by her.’ And so it was done. Consider first that Abraham lived before the Law of Moses and before the Gospel. Therefore Abraham did not transgress the Law, but preceded it; for it did not yet appear to be forbidden. Secondly, consider that he did not set aside the marriage bed for fellowship with a handmaid, inflamed by any heat of wandering lust or captivated by the beauty of a wanton form; rather, he did so from zeal for seeking posterity and propagating offspring. Even after the Flood the human race was sparse; religion too was sparse. Finally, the daughters of holy Lot also had this purpose of seeking offspring, lest the human race fail; and so, for the sake of a public service, it veiled a private fault.”

Likewise Augustine, in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 15: “Although the righteous man desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ, nevertheless he takes food, not through a desire to live but from the duty of prudent care, so that he may remain as necessary for others. So it was dutiful, not lustful, for holy men to have intercourse with women by the right of marriage. What food is to the preservation of a human being, intercourse is to the preservation of the human race; and neither is without carnal pleasure. Yet when this pleasure is moderated and, through restraining temperance, brought back to natural use, it cannot be lust. But what unlawful food is in sustaining life, fornication or unlawful intercourse is in seeking offspring; and what excessive appetite is in lawful food, that is the venial intercourse of married persons.”

### John’s virginity is not preferred to Abraham’s chastity

2. Augustine shows that virginal chastity is not superior in merit to Abraham’s marital chastity, saying in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 31: “Just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and Abraham, who begot children. For John’s celibacy and Abraham’s marriage served Christ according to the distribution of times; but John had continence in practice, Abraham in disposition alone. The chastity of celibates is indeed better than that of marriage; Abraham had one of these in practice, both in disposition. For he lived chastely and as a married man. He could have been chaste without marriage, but at that time it was not fitting.”

Likewise Jerome, 32, q. 4, ch. *Quis ignoret*: “Who does not know that, under God’s exalted dispensation, all his saints of former times had the same merit as Christians now have? As Abraham formerly pleased God in marriage, so virgins now please him in chastity. He served the law and time of his own day; let us also serve the law and time of ours, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.”

From these passages it appears that the holy fathers before the Law had several wives or concubines without sin. Scripture now calls these women wives, now concubines. Rachel and Leah, however, were both wives, not concubines.

### Objection

3. If someone objects that those fathers did not preserve the fidelity of the marriage bed, we say that in this they did preserve marital fidelity: they had intercourse not with other women but with their own wives or handmaids. Thus far was the practice in this matter before the Law.

In the time of the Law, however, Moses forbade carnal intercourse with one’s mother, stepmother, sister, niece, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, daughter-in-law, and certain others. He permitted divorce by the giving of a bill of repudiation, in which the husband wrote the reasons for repudiating his wife. He permitted a man, after giving the former wife a bill, to take another. Christ says that this was permitted because of the hardness of their hearts—not that discord might be approved, but that homicide might be removed. Evils were permitted lest worse evils occur; and by permitting this, God did not display his justice but diminished the sinner’s guilt.

### To whom it was permitted to have several wives, or not

4. But was it lawful under the Law to have several wives? Hear what is written in Deuteronomy, ch. 17: “The king shall not have very many wives, lest they entice his heart.” On this passage Augustine says, book 5 on Deuteronomy, ch. 27: “It is clear that Solomon transgressed this command. David, however, had several and did not transgress the command. For a king was permitted to have several, but not to multiply very many wives that might entice his heart. Yet, when it is added, ‘lest his heart be lifted up,’ it seems that foreign women are prohibited. Nevertheless, the multiplication of wives is prohibited generally. A king was permitted to have several, but not to multiply them.”

But when the time of fullness came, in which Christ’s grace was spread everywhere, the law of marriage was restored to its earlier and more honourable institution: one man is joined to one woman in the figure of Christ and the Church. The choice of an office is no longer sought in succession of lineage, but in perfection of life and sincerity of knowledge; virginity is preferred to fertility, and continence is enjoined upon priests.

### On virginity of mind and flesh

5. Virginity of mind is better than virginity of flesh. Hence Ambrose, in book 2 of *On Virgins*: “It is more tolerable to possess a virgin mind than virgin flesh. Both are good, if both are possible; if not, at least let us be chaste not for human beings but for God. A virgin may be prostituted, but she cannot be made an adulteress; brothels do not disgrace chastity, but chastity even removes the disgrace of a place.”

The same: “The flesh cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted.” Likewise Isidore, in the *Synonyms*: “The body cannot be corrupted unless the soul has first been corrupted; for, when the soul has been cleansed from contagion, the flesh does not sin.”

At the end of this chapter it is explained in what sense it is true that the body cannot be corrupted unless the soul has first been corrupted—namely, by sin. Augustine’s statement in *On the Good of Marriage*, ch. 16, should also be noted: “Just as it is holier to die of hunger than to eat food sacrificed to idols, so it is holier to die without children than to seek offspring through unlawful intercourse. But wherever human beings are born, if they do not follow their parents’ vices and rightly worship God, they will be honourable and saved. For seed from whatever human being is God’s creature; it will go ill for one who uses it badly, but it will never itself be evil.”

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. ON LAWFUL PERSONS

1. It remains to consider which persons are lawful for contracting marriage. Persons are judged lawful according to the ordinances of the Fathers, which differ. Some were lawful before the Law, others under the Law, others in the time of grace. Likewise, in the primitive Church some persons were lawful who are not lawful now.

Among those who are now lawful or unlawful, some are fully lawful, some wholly unlawful, and some intermediate. Fully lawful are those to whom no vow of continence, sacred order, kinship, disparity of worship, condition, natural frigidity, or anything else presents an obstacle. Wholly unlawful are those rendered so by a vow, order, kinship, or disparity of worship. Intermediate persons are neither fully lawful nor wholly unlawful because of frigidity or condition. For if such persons are joined in ignorance, they may remain together if certain causes arise, and be separated if those causes are absent.

### On separating the frigid

2. Concerning those who, because of frigidity, cannot render the marital due, Gregory advises that they remain together (33, q. 1, ch. *Quod autem interrogasti*). But if the woman complains, saying, “I wish to be a mother and bear children,” he decreed that each of them should swear, with the seventh hand of kinsmen, that they had never had carnal intercourse; then the woman might contract a second marriage. But the man, who is of a frigid nature, should remain without hope of marriage.

For he says: “You asked concerning those who are joined in marriage and cannot have intercourse, whether he may take another woman or she another man. Of them it is written: if a man and woman join themselves and afterwards the woman says of her husband that he cannot have intercourse with her, if what she says can be proved by a just judgment, let her take another; but if he has taken another, let them be separated.”

Likewise, in the same place: “You asked concerning those who say that, because of a frigid nature, they cannot have intercourse with one another while rendering the service of the flesh. If a man cannot use her as a wife, he has her as a sister. But if he wishes to sever the bond of marriage, let each remain unmarried; for if he could not naturally be compatible with this woman, how will he suit another?”

Likewise: “If the man wishes to take another wife, the reason is plainly evident: prompted by the devil, he has conceived the fuel of hatred and held her in loathing; therefore he schemes to put her away by the falsehood of a lie. But if the woman complains and says, ‘I wish to be a mother and bear children,’ each of them, with the seventh hand of kinsmen and touching the most holy relics, shall state under oath that they were never joined by a mingling of flesh so as to become one flesh. Then the woman seems able to contract a second marriage—I say this because of the weakness of their flesh (Romans 6). But the man who is of a frigid nature shall remain without a wife. If he too has taken another wife, then those who swore shall be held guilty of perjury, and, after performing penance, shall be compelled to resume their former marriages.”

This is to be observed when both confess the same thing. But if the husband asserts that he has rendered the due to his wife and she denies it, the question rightly arises to whom greater credence should be given. The following has been decreed concerning this: “If anyone has thus taken a wife and has had her for some time, and the woman says that he has never had intercourse with her, while the man says that he has, the husband’s truth shall stand, because the man is the head of the woman” (Ephesians 5). This was decreed concerning natural incapacity.

### On those prevented from intercourse by spells

3. Concerning impediment by sorcery, the following is decreed and must be maintained: if intercourse does not take place through the acts of sorceresses and magicians, those to whom this happens are to be exhorted, with contrite and humbled spirit, to make confession to God and the priest of all their sins, to make satisfaction to the Lord by tears, prayers, and fasts, and to seek healing through exorcisms and the other safeguards of ecclesiastical discipline administered by ministers of the Church. If they cannot be healed, they may be separated.

But once they have sought other marriages, they cannot, while the persons to whom they were subsequently joined are living, be reconciled to the former spouses whom they left, even if the capacity for intercourse is restored to them (Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, 33, q. 3). What is contained at the end of this chapter should be understood as said more from strict rigor than from canonical equity. Or it should be understood to mean that they cannot be reconciled to their former spouses except by the judgment of the Church, by which the separation had been made.

### An addition concerning the insane

4. Those who are insane cannot contract marriage while they are in madness. Hence Fabian, 32, q. 7: “Neither an insane man nor an insane woman can contract marriage; but if marriage has been contracted, they are not to be separated.” Likewise Pope Nicholas, in the same place: “Those who contracted marriage while sound, and afterwards one or both of them suffer madness, frenzy, or some other infirmity: their marriages cannot be dissolved because of such infirmity.” The same must likewise be understood concerning those blinded by enemies, mutilated in their limbs, or carried off by barbarians.

### On those who sleep with two sisters

5. Concerning those who sleep with two sisters, or women who sleep with two brothers, one must consider what the canons decree. “He who sleeps with two sisters, where one of them was formerly his wife, shall have neither of them; nor shall those adulterers ever be joined in marriage” (Council of Orléans).

Likewise: “He may not render the due even to his own wife, whom he has made unlawful to himself by knowing her sister. Nor, after his wife’s death, may he be joined in marriage to the adulteress.” [Col. 0928]

Likewise Pope Zachary, in the same place: “You have lain with the sister of your wife. If you have done so, have neither woman. And if your wife was not aware of the crime and does not wish to practise continence, let her marry in the Lord whom she wishes. But you and the adulteress shall remain without hope of marriage and do penance as long as you live.”

The words “let her marry whom she wishes” must be understood to apply after her husband’s death. Hence Gregory, in the same place: “Those who discover their wives in adultery: neither the husband nor the wife may take another wife or husband while both are alive. But if the adulteress has died, her husband may marry if he wishes; but the adulteress may never marry, even if her husband has died; rather, all her days she must offer the lamentations of penance.” Here the adultery meant is that committed with the husband’s kinsman or the wife’s kinswoman.

### A wife is not to be dismissed because of any bodily blemish or deformity

6. It should also be known that a husband may not dismiss his wife because of any bodily infirmity or blemish, nor conversely; rather, each ought to provide assistance to the other. Hence Augustine: “If anyone has a wife who is barren, deformed in body, weak in limb, blind, lame, deaf, or afflicted by diseases, labours, and pains—or anything else, except fornication, that can be imagined as exceedingly horrible—he should endure it for the sake of fellowship and fidelity.”

## DISTINCTION XXXV. HUSBAND AND WIFE ENJOY THE SAME RIGHT

1. It should also be noted that, although the Lord permits a husband to dismiss his wife because of fornication, the same permission is not taken away from women (Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*). Hence Jerome, *On the Death of Fabiola*: “The Lord commanded that a wife not be dismissed except for the cause of fornication; and if she is dismissed, that she remain unmarried. Whatever is commanded to men consequently extends to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained.”

Likewise: “Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men; the same servitude is assessed under equal condition.” From this it is shown that a woman may bring an action against her husband concerning fornication, just as a husband may against his wife.

Hence Pope Innocent, 32, q. 5: “Christian religion condemns adultery in both sexes by an equal rule; but women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, whereas men more freely customarily report their adulterous wives before priests. Therefore women, once their crime is disclosed, are denied communion; but no man whose offence remains hidden is readily excluded merely upon suspicions, though he too will be removed if his disgraceful act is discovered.”

### That an adulterer cannot dismiss a fornicating wife unless he is himself free from fornication, and conversely

2. If it is asked whether an adulterer can dismiss an adulteress because of fornication, we say that an adulterous wife cannot be dismissed by her husband unless he too is free from fornication, and conversely. Hence Augustine, book 1 of *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*: “Nothing is more unjust than to dismiss one’s wife because of fornication when one is oneself convicted of fornication. For that saying confronts one: ‘In judging another, you condemn yourself’ [Romans 2]. Therefore whoever wishes to put away his wife because of fornication must first be cleansed from fornication; and I say the same concerning a woman.”

The same, book 2 of *On Adulterous Marriages*: “Husbands are indignant if they hear that adulterous men suffer punishments equal to adulterous women, though men ought to be punished much more severely, inasmuch as it belongs more to them both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example.” From this it appears that an adulterer cannot dismiss an adulteress, and conversely.

### That those separated for fornication can be reconciled

3. If someone free from fornication dismisses a fornicating spouse, that person cannot be joined to another, but must practise continence or return to the dismissed spouse; and the same applies to a woman. Hence the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 7: “To those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.” And he adds concerning the husband: “Let not the husband dismiss his wife.”

But Ambrose says, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, 32, q. 7: “Therefore he does not add concerning the husband what he says concerning the woman, because a husband is permitted to take another.” But this is believed to have been inserted into Ambrose’s book by falsifiers. For Augustine plainly says, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, that what was stated concerning the wife must be supplied concerning the husband: “Why does he not add concerning the woman what he had previously stated concerning the man, unless he wishes a similar rule to be understood? Thus, if he dismisses her—which is permitted because of fornication—let him remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife.”

The same: “If she is not permitted to marry while the husband from whom she departed is alive, nor he to take another while the wife whom he dismissed is alive, much less is it lawful to commit unlawful fornications with anyone whatsoever.”

The same, in the same place: “In order that a wife not be easily dismissed, the Lord excepted only the cause of fornication; all other troubles, whatever may arise, he commands to be endured courageously for marital fidelity and chastity. And he called adulterous the man who takes a woman dismissed by her husband.”

From this it is shown that, if separation occurs because of fornication, neither husband nor wife can enter another union. They may, however, be reconciled and live together as before, if the one who dismissed the other wishes to call the dismissed spouse back.

### Passages which seem contrary to the foregoing

4. Yet John Chrysostom says, 32, q. 1: “Just as one who dismisses a chaste woman is cruel and unjust, so one who keeps a prostitute is foolish and unjust. He who conceals his wife’s crime is a patron of shamefulness.”

Likewise Jerome, in the same place, ch. *Dixit Dominus*: “When a woman divides one flesh into another and separates herself from her husband by fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she make her husband too subject to a curse, Scripture saying, Proverbs 18: ‘He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and without understanding.’”

The same, writing to the priest Amandus concerning a certain woman who, while her husband was alive, married another, says, 34, q. 2: “I speak a new thing—indeed, not new but old, confirmed by the authority of the Old Testament. If the woman leaves her second husband and wishes to be reconciled to the first, she cannot be.”

### Determination

5. But all these passages must be understood concerning a woman who refused to withdraw from adultery or to erase her sin through penance. If the husband knowingly endures this, he appears to consent (32, q. 1). For if she chooses to persist in adultery, her husband will be considered a patron of shamefulness and guilty of procuring prostitution, unless he wishes her to be charged as guilty of adultery. But if she withdraws from sin and cleanses it through penance, she may be reconciled to her husband.

Hence Augustine, to Pollentius, 32, q. 1: “What seems hard to you—that a spouse should be reconciled after adultery—will not be hard if faith is present. Why do we still count as adulterers those whom we believe have been healed by penance?”

The same, in *On Adulterous Marriages*: “Reconciliation of marriage will be neither shameful nor difficult, even after adulteries committed and cleansed, where through the keys of the kingdom of heaven forgiveness of sins is not doubted to take place—not so that, after divorce from her husband, the adulteress may be recalled, but so that after union with Christ she may no longer be called an adulteress.”

Likewise Gregory, in the book called *The Pastor*: “He ought to receive the sinful woman who has done penance, but not often.”

Likewise Hermas, in *On Adulterous Marriages*: “If a husband knows that his wife has sinned, and the woman has not done penance but remains in her fornication and he lives with her, the husband will be guilty and a participant in her sin. But if the dismissed woman does penance and wishes to return to her husband, he ought to receive the sinful woman who has done penance, but not often.”

### On those who have previously defiled themselves by adultery

6. It is also customarily asked whether a woman previously defiled by adultery may be taken in marriage. Pope Leo says concerning this, 31, q. 1, ch. *Nullus*: “Let no one take in marriage a woman whom he has previously defiled by adultery.”

Likewise, from the Council of Tibur, in the same place, ch. *Relatum*: “It has been reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man violated another’s wife by fornication and moreover gave the adulteress an oath that, after the death of his lawful wife, if he survived, he would take her as his wife; and this was done. Therefore we forbid and anathematize such a union.” [Col. 0930]

These and other authorities forbid those who previously stained themselves by adultery to be joined in marriage. But Augustine appears to argue against this, saying in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. *Denique*: “Finally, after the death of the man with whom there was a true marriage, marriage may be made with the woman with whom adultery had preceded.” Likewise: “It is evident that lawful marriages may indeed be made between persons unlawfully joined, when an honourable agreement follows.”

### Determination

7. But this final authority speaks of concubines, maintaining that concubines may pass to the honourable agreement of marriage if they wish to preserve chastity and fidelity. Augustine’s first authority concerns those who have repented of their sin, neither plotted their husband’s death nor, while the husband was alive, received from their adulterer a pledge that he would take them in marriage if he survived. Those who do these things are forbidden to be joined by the authorities previously cited.

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. WHETHER A WIFE MAY BE SEPARATED FROM HER HUSBAND BECAUSE OF A DISPARITY OF CONDITION, AND CONVERSELY

1. We must now consider whether condition can divide a marriage. We say that a freeborn woman is not forbidden to marry a slave; but if she does not know him to be of servile condition, she may freely dismiss him when his slavery is discovered, according to the following from the council at Vermerie: “If a freeborn man takes another’s female slave as wife, believing her freeborn, and that woman is afterwards reduced to servitude, he should redeem her from slavery if he can; if he cannot, he may take another if he wishes. But if he knew that she was a slave and afterwards approved of her, he should have her as his lawful wife.”

Likewise, from the same source: “If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he is a slave, let her have him; for we all have one Father in heaven, and there shall be one law for man and woman.” When it says that she knew him to be a slave, it gives us to understand that, if she did not know him to be a slave, she is not compelled to remain with him. For if she suffers deception concerning status, she is not compelled to cleave to one by whose fraud she has been deceived. But if the man knew the woman’s condition, or conversely, he cannot dismiss her.

Hence Pope Zachary, 29, q. 2, ch. *Si quis liber*: “If any free person takes a female slave in marriage, he has no permission to dismiss her, if they were joined by the consent of both, except because of fornication.” This concerns those whose respective condition is known when they are joined.

### On the union of a male and female slave belonging to different masters

2. It is also asked whether there is marriage between a slave of one master and a female slave of another. The following was decreed concerning this in the Council of Chalon: “It has been reported to us that some, by a certain arbitrary presumption, dissolve the lawful marriages of slaves, without attending to that saying, Matthew 19: ‘What God has joined, let no human being separate.’ Therefore it has seemed good to us that the marriages of slaves are not to be dissolved, even if they have different masters, but that, continuing in one marriage, they should serve their own masters.”

This is to be observed in cases where there has been a lawful union and it occurred by the will of the masters. Notice the end of this chapter, where it seems to be implied that marriage cannot be contracted between a male and female slave without their masters’ consent, or that, if contracted, it is not valid. Some nevertheless think that marriage can take place between them without the masters’ knowledge.

### On a husband who makes himself a slave in order to be dismissed by his wife

3. It should also be noted that if a woman has taken a free man as her husband and he makes himself another’s slave in order to furnish a reason for separation, neither may he dismiss his wife nor may she be reduced to slavery because of the marriage bond. Hence the following from the Council of Tibur: “It was reported to the holy synod that a freeborn man took a freeborn woman as wife and, after the begetting of children, made himself the slave of someone else as a pretext for divorce. The question was asked whether he must necessarily retain his wife; and, if he retained her, whether she too should be subjected to slavery. It was judged that the wife must by no means be dismissed; but that, by Christ’s law, the woman must not be reduced to [Col. 0931] slavery, since he made himself a slave without the consent of his wife, who had taken him as a free husband.”

### On the age of those contracting marriage
4. It must also be known that, according to the laws, boys under fourteen years of age and girls under twelve cannot enter into marriage. If they have entered into a union before the aforesaid ages, they may be separated, even though they were joined by the will and consent of their parents. But those who, having been joined in childhood, after reaching the years of puberty do not wish to offend, but to remain in the union, thereby become spouses, and thereafter cannot be separated. Likewise, 30, question 2, paragraph *Sponsalia*: “Betrothals cannot be contracted before the seventh year; for they are contracted by consent alone, which cannot intervene unless it is understood by one or the other party what is being done between them.” We have dealt with those two matters, with the addition of certain others, by which marriage can be dissolved; yet it need not always be dissolved. We must now add matters that make persons altogether ineligible, and first, Order.

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. IN WHAT ORDERS MARRIAGE CANNOT TAKE PLACE

1. There are, then, certain orders in which marriage cannot in any way be contracted; and, if intercourse has occurred, a separation takes place: namely, the priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate. In other orders, however, marriage is permitted, unless they have assumed the religious habit or made a vow of continence. Hence Pope Leo, distinction 32, chapter *Seriatim*:

> The Roman Church permits clerics, readers, doorkeepers, exorcists, and acolytes, if they are found outside a vow and religious habit and do not wish to profess continence, to take a virgin as wife—not a widow or a repudiated woman—because thereafter they will be unable either to be promoted to the subdiaconate, or, if a layman has taken a wife other than a virgin, or is a bigamist, to be admitted to the clerical order.

Likewise, from the Council of Carthage:

> It has been decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons must also abstain from their wives; if they do not, they are to be removed even from ecclesiastical office.

But it does not compel the other clerics to this. Likewise Pope Leo, distinction 31, chapter *Lex continentiae*:

> The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. While they were laymen or readers, they could lawfully take wives; but when they attained the aforesaid ranks, what had formerly been permitted to them began no longer to be permitted.

Likewise, in the Sixth Synod, distinction 38, chapter *Si quis*:

> If any of those approaching the clerical order wishes to be joined to a woman by the law of marriage, let him do this before the order of subdiaconate.

Likewise Pope Callixtus, distinction 28, chapter *Presbyteris*:

> We utterly forbid presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and monks to keep concubines or contract marriage. We judge also that marriages contracted by persons of this sort must be dissolved, and that the persons must be reduced to penance, in accordance with the determinations of the holy canons.

Likewise Gregory, distinction 28, chapter *Nullum*:

> Let bishops presume to make no one a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been approved before he undertakes that ministry.

### On Those Who Kill Their Wives

2. To these must be added the matter of killers of their wives, concerning whom Pope Nicholas writes to Radulf, Archbishop of Bourges, 23, question 2, chapter *Interfectores*:

> Those who kill their wives without judicial process—since you do not add that the wives were adulteresses or anything of that kind—what else are they to be considered but murderers? Accordingly, they must be reduced to penance, and marriage is utterly denied them.

Here Nicholas seems to permit husbands to kill their wives for adultery or some similar cause; but ecclesiastical discipline ought to strike criminals with a spiritual sword, not a material one. Hence the same Nicholas:

> Among these matters, Your Holiness has taken care to add this question: if a man’s wife has committed adultery, whether her husband may kill her according to worldly law. But the holy Church of God is never bound by worldly laws; it possesses no sword except a spiritual one.

Likewise Pope Pius, 33, question 2, chapter *Quicumque propriam*:

> Whoever kills his own wife without legal process and without cause, [Col. 0932] and takes another, must lay aside arms and perform public penance; and if he proves contumacious, let him be anathematized until he consents.

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. ON VOW

1. Let us now consider vow. A vow is a kind of attestation of a voluntary promise, which ought properly to be made to God and concerning things that belong to God. Yet there are also vows of fools, which must be broken.

### On the Different Kinds of Vows

2. It should be known that one kind of vow is common and another particular. A common vow is that which everyone makes in Baptism, when they promise to renounce the devil and his pomps. A particular vow is when someone voluntarily promises to preserve virginity or continence, or something similar. Again, one particular vow is private and another solemn. A private vow is made in secret; a solemn one in the sight of the Church.

Again, if a private vow is violated, it is a mortal sin; but to violate a solemn vow is both sin and scandal. Those who make a private vow of continence ought not to contract marriage, because by contracting it they sin mortally. Yet, if they have contracted it, they are not to be separated, because what was done secretly cannot be proved. But those who make a solemn vow cannot enter marriage at all: for them, not only marrying but even wishing to marry is damnable.

Hence Augustine, to Julian, *On Holy Widowhood*:

> If chastity is preserved in the marital bond, condemnation is not feared; but in widowly continence and virginal excellence, the virtue of a greater gift is sought. Once that gift has been sought and chosen and a vow has been offered, it is now damnable not only to enter marriage but even, though one does not marry, to wish to marry.

Jerome, chapter *Voventibus*:

> For those who vow virginity or widowhood, not only marrying but even wishing to marry is damnable.

The Apostle demonstrates this. Writing to Timothy, First Epistle, chapter 5: “Avoid younger widows; for when they have lived wantonly, they wish to marry in Christ.” That is: when, after a vow of continence, they have lived a life of pleasures, I do not say that they marry, but that they wish to marry “in Christ,” as though there were then no sin. But he shows that there is sin by adding: “having condemnation”; and he adds why: “because they have made void their first faith.” This is so even if they do not marry, yet do wish to do so, so that the will which has fallen away from its resolve is shown to be condemned, whether marriage follows or not. For the betrayal of their purpose is condemned; such women are condemned because they have made void their first pledge of continence—that is, their vow, or, in the violation of their vow, the faith which they professed in Baptism. But if they are condemned for the will to marry, it is clear that, if they have carried that will into effect, the act must be annulled and they must be compelled to return to their former purpose.

Hence Gregory, to Boniface:

> Concerning widows who have departed from their purpose of widowhood, about whom you have consulted us: I believe you know from St Paul that, unless they are converted, they have long since been condemned. By apostolic authority we judge that they must be condemned and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the church, until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or unwillingly, to the good which they began.

### On Unveiled Virgins

3. Concerning virgins not veiled, if they go astray, we have the following decree from our predecessor Pope Innocent, 27, question 1, chapter *Haec vero*:

> Those who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed that they would remain in a virginal purpose—even if they were not veiled—must, if at any time they marry, perform penance, because their promise was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is customarily dissolved for no reason, how much more can this promise, which they have pledged with God, not be dissolved without punishment!

Likewise:

> If unveiled virgins are punished in this manner by public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction is made, how much more must widows—who are of more mature age and judgment, have assumed the religious habit, and then apostatized and returned to their former vomit [Col. 0933]—be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the church and from the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction is made, and be handed over to prisons.

From these passages it appears that virgins or widows bound by a vow of continence, whether veiled or not, can in no way enter marriage. The same must likewise be understood of all who have vowed continence. For what was permissible before becomes impermissible after the vow.

Nor should it be omitted that Pope Innocent, in the same place, chapter *Quae Christo*, decreed concerning widows and maidens who marry Christ spiritually that, if afterward they publicly marry, they are not to be admitted to penance unless the men to whom they joined themselves have departed from this world. For if this principle is observed in every case—so that any woman who marries another while her husband is living is considered an adulteress, and is not granted permission to do penance unless one of the two has died—how much more must it be maintained in the case of a woman who had first joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and then passed over to human marriage!

Observe that marriage seems not merely to be denied to such women, but even the place of penance. Yet this should not be understood as though women who desire to perform worthy penance are ever to be excluded from penance. Rather, those women are not to be admitted to penance who refuse to withdraw from an incestuous union, because after undertaking a religious purpose, she who neglects to return to the habit of her profession cannot be reconciled to God through penance. The man to whom she had joined herself will have died when she has utterly withdrawn from his unlawful embraces. Therefore, when it is said that they are not to be admitted to penance unless those to whom they joined themselves have departed from the world, “from them” must be understood. For their husbands depart from the world and die to them when these women estrange themselves from their desire; the comparison that follows explains and confirms this sense.

### That Adultery Is a Great Evil

4. When a man and woman have been lawfully joined, it is certain that, while one is living, the other cannot pass to another union; otherwise adultery is committed. Concerning this Pope Clement says, 32, question 6, chapter *Quid in omnibus*:

> What sin is graver than adultery? In punishments it holds the second place, while the first is held by those who stray from God. Adulterers therefore sin most gravely; fornicators gravely; but incestuous persons more gravely than all these. Yet all of them are surpassed by those who sin against nature.

Hence Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*:

> The evil of adultery surpasses fornication and is surpassed by incest. For it is worse to sleep with one’s mother than with another man’s wife; but worst of all these is what is done against nature—for example, if a man uses a woman’s member for a purpose for which it was not granted. This is done execrably with a prostitute, but more execrably with a wife.

### On Those Who Return after Long Captivity

5. Here the question is raised concerning those women who, thinking their husbands to have been killed, or never to be freed from captivity or unjust domination, passed into marriages with others. If those thought to have perished return, must the women be restored to them? Have the second husbands committed fornication, and are the women guilty of adultery? Pope Leo says of this:

> We must believe that the bonds of lawful marriages are to be restored; and, once the conditions brought about by hostility have been removed, what was taken from each person must lawfully be restored to that person. Care must be taken that each receives what is his own. Yet the man who assumed the place of a husband believed no longer to exist is not to be judged culpable or considered an invader of another’s right. Thus many things belonging to persons led away into captivity may have passed into another’s possession, and yet it is altogether just that they be restored when those persons return. Therefore, if husbands return after long captivity and persevere in love for their wives so that they desire the wives to return to their union, what necessity brought about must be forgiven and judged blameless, and what fidelity requires must be restored. But if certain women have been so captivated by love for their later husbands that they prefer to cling to them rather than return to their lawful union, they deserve censure, so that they are deprived of ecclesiastical [Col. 0934] communion, since in a matter capable of excuse they have chosen the defilement of crime.

Let them therefore return to their marital state. For just as women who refuse to return to their husbands must be regarded as impious, so those who return are deservedly praised. From this it is shown that those who are joined in such a way, believing the husband to have been killed, have some excuse for sin through ignorance; and that only the first union is lawful, not the second—though there is pardon if it is free from the reproach of evil will.

But if someone, leaving a wife in his own country, goes to a distant land and takes another wife, and then, moved by repentance, wishes to dismiss her, asserting that he has another wife who is alive, while the Church—which does not know whether what he asserts is true—does not permit it: the question arises whether there is marriage in this second union. It may rightly be said that there is no marriage and that the woman is excused from guilt through ignorance, while the man has committed adultery. But once, wishing yet unable to return to the first wife, he is compelled by the Church’s discipline to keep the second, he begins to be excused, by obedience and fear, for rendering the marital due to the woman who asks for it—though he himself ought never to demand it from her. The same judgment should be made concerning other cases of this kind.

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. ON DIFFERENCE OF RELIGION

1. Next we must consider difference of religion. This is one of the causes that make persons ineligible to contract marriage. A Christian may not enter marriage with a pagan or a Jewish woman, since even in the Old Testament faithful men were forbidden to take unbelieving wives. The Lord says in Exodus 34: “You shall not take wives from the daughters of foreigners for your sons, lest they lead them away after their gods.” In accordance with this command of the Lord, Ezra separated marriages of Jews with foreigners. The same is also observed in the New Testament.

Hence Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book and chapter 21:

> Let not a woman marry except a man of her own religion, nor let a man take such a wife. For this, as you say, the Lord commands, the Apostle teaches, and both Testaments prescribe.

Likewise Ambrose, in the book *On the Patriarchs*:

> Take care, Christian, not to give your daughter to a pagan or a Jew; take care not to take for yourself a pagan woman, a Jewish woman, or a foreign woman—that is, a heretic, or any woman alien to your faith—as wife.

Likewise, from the Council of Urban:

> If any man has carnal intercourse with a Jewish woman, or a Christian woman with a Jew, or a Jewish woman with a Christian, whoever commits so great an enormity is immediately to be separated from the Christian community.

From these and many other testimonies it appears that marriage cannot be contracted by those who differ in religion and faith.

### On Marriage of a Believer and an Unbeliever, and of Two Unbelievers

2. This, however, seems to be opposed by what the Apostle says about unequal marriages, 1 Corinthians 7: “I speak, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away; and if any woman,” etc. But Augustine, in the same book and chapter, clearly shows that this is one matter and the former another:

> There the question concerns marriages of believers and unbelievers which are contracted while they remain in differing religion and faith. But the Apostle deals with those who were of one and the same unbelief when they were joined. Yet when the Gospel came, one believed without the other. Do you understand what I mean? Pay attention, that I may explain the matter itself more carefully. Behold: two spouses were of one unbelief when they were joined. None of the questions belonging to that command of the Old and New Testaments, by which a believer is forbidden to join marriage with an unbeliever, applies to them. They are already spouses, and both are still unbelievers. They remain such as they were when they were joined. Then a preacher of the Gospel comes; one of them, man or woman, believes, but in such a way that the unbeliever consents to live with the believer. The Lord does not command the believer to put away the unbeliever to whom he or she was thus joined. Nor does the Apostle command the believer to do so; rather, he counsels it, so that if anyone acts otherwise, that person is not a transgressor—just as he also counsels concerning virgins. He gives this admonition because there is an opportunity of gaining the other, when it is lawful to leave but not expedient. For that which is lawful is not expedient when it is permitted [Col. 0935] indeed, but its use brings an impediment to the salvation of others—as in the departure of the believer from the unbeliever. The Lord does not forbid it, because before Him it is not unjust; but the Apostle advises through the counsel of charity that it not be done, so that no one may be bound in this matter by the necessity of a command, but may act freely by the will of counsel.

From this it is shown that there is marriage among unbelievers and that the Apostle’s counsel does not conflict with the Lord’s command, by which He commands a believer not to join marriage with an unbeliever, and, if they have been joined, to separate. For it is read that Ezra the prophet—or rather, the Lord through him—commanded the Israelites to put away foreign wives, through whom they were going after foreign gods; those women were not being won to God through their husbands. He rightly gave this command, because through Moses the Lord had commanded that no one take a foreign wife. Therefore, rightly, at the Lord’s command, they put away those whom they had taken contrary to the Lord’s prohibition. For, as Ambrose says, 28, question 1, chapter *Jussit*: “That which has been done outside God’s decree is not to be considered marriage; but when it is recognized, it must be corrected, as when a believer is joined to an unbeliever.”

But, as Augustine says in the same book and chapter:

> When the Gospel began to be preached to the Gentiles, it found Gentiles already joined in marriage to Gentiles. If both did not believe, but one, man or woman, did, and the unbeliever consented to live with the believer, the believer ought neither to have been forbidden by the Lord to put away the unbeliever nor commanded to retain the unbeliever. The believer ought not to have been forbidden, because justice permits departure from a fornicator. And the fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can that person’s chastity with a spouse be called true, because whatever is not from faith is sin—although the believer has true chastity even with an unbelieving spouse, who does not have true chastity. But the believer ought not to have been commanded to put the other away, because both Gentiles had not been joined contrary to the Lord’s command. Thus justice permitted the believer to put away the unbeliever; but, because of free benevolence, what was lawful was not to be done.

It is plainly evident both that there is marriage among unbelievers and that the Apostle speaks of those who were joined in unbelief, after which one converted to the faith, while the unbeliever also consents to live with that person. The Apostle counsels the believer not to dismiss the unbeliever because perhaps the unbeliever will be saved through the believer.

### On Spiritual Fornication, for Which a Spouse May Be Dismissed

3. Yet the believer may lawfully dismiss the other, because in an unbeliever there is fornication, if not of the body, at least of the mind. For the Lord made an exception for the cause of fornication. We are compelled to understand fornication in a general and universal sense, not merely bodily fornication but also spiritual fornication. Augustine says concerning it, in Gloss 1: “Idolatry and every harmful superstition are fornication.” The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed for the cause of fornication, but did not command it. Thus He gave the Apostle room to exhort that whoever wishes need not dismiss her; yet the believer may lawfully dismiss her. For if fornication of the flesh is detestable in a spouse, how much more is fornication of the mind—that is, unbelief!

### For What Faults a Spouse May Be Dismissed

4. But if you ask whether a spouse may be dismissed for any fault other than unbelief or idolatry, attend to what Augustine says, 27, question 1:

> If unbelief is fornication, and idolatry is unbelief, and avarice is idolatry, it must not be doubted that avarice too is fornication. Who, then, can separate any unlawful desire from the category of fornication, if avarice is fornication?

From this it is understood that a man may without sin put away his wife, and a wife her husband, not only because of unlawful desires committed in sexual crimes with other men or women, but because of any desires whatsoever that cause the soul to stray from God’s law and to be corruptly ruined. Likewise, a wife is most rightly dismissed if she says to her husband: “I will not be your wife unless you gather riches for me by robbery, or unless you practice your customary procuring,” or if she demands from her husband anything else criminal or shameful. Then the man, if he is truly repentant and has faith working through love, will cut off the member that causes him to stumble. (*Augustine, On Faith and Works*.)

From these statements it is apparent that not only unbelief but every desire that corrupts ruinously and shamefully is spiritual fornication, through which a husband may dismiss his wife, or a wife her husband. [Col. 0936] Yet the Apostle counsels that a believer not dismiss an unbeliever who wishes to cohabit and does not seek to draw the believer away from God.

### Whether a Believer May Take Another Wife When an Unbeliever Departs or Is Dismissed

5. Here the question is raised whether, if a believer dismisses an unbeliever, or an unbeliever departs from a believer, the believer may take another wife. Authority seems to testify that, while the first wife is alive, he cannot take another. For Ambrose, explaining the Apostle’s words, says, 28, question 5:

> Otherwise, if you separate from one another, put away spouses who wish to live with you, and join yourselves to others, you are adulterers; and your children born from that union are unclean, that is, illegitimate.

Likewise, 28, question 2:

> If anyone had a virgin wife before Baptism, he cannot have another while she is alive after Baptism. For crimes are forgiven in Baptism, not marriages.

### Statements That Seem Contrary to the Preceding

6. But Ambrose testifies to the contrary, to Hilary:

> If the unbeliever, says the Apostle, departs, let that person depart. For a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases, because reverence is not owed to one who abhors the author of marriage. For a marriage without devotion to God is not ratified; and therefore it is not sin for the person dismissed for God’s sake to join himself or herself to another. For contempt of the Creator dissolves the right of marriage with respect to the one who is left, so that such a person is not accused for joining another. But the unbeliever who departs sins both against God and against marriage; nor is marital fidelity to be preserved toward one who withdrew in order not to hear that Christ is the God of Christian marriages. But if both believe, marriage is confirmed through the knowledge of God.

### Determination

7. Observe that these statements may seem contrary to the foregoing, so that Ambrose appears to contradict himself. But a distinction must be made: it is one thing to dismiss someone who wishes to cohabit, and another to be dismissed for God’s sake by one who abhors the name of Christ. In the former case the law of benevolence is not observed; in the latter truth is preserved. Therefore, though one may dismiss a spouse who wishes to cohabit, one may not take another while that spouse lives. But one need not follow a spouse who departs, and may take another while that spouse lives. Yet this must be understood only of those joined to one another in unbelief.

But if both have converted to the faith, or if both believers were joined in marriage and afterward one departed from the faith and left the spouse out of hatred for the faith, the one dismissed will not accompany the one who departs, but cannot take another while that spouse lives, because there had been a ratified marriage between them, which cannot be dissolved. (28, question 2.)

### Some Say There Is No Marriage among Unbelievers, and Why

8. Nevertheless, there are some who maintain that there is no marriage among unbelievers, because their union is neither ratified nor lawful. It is not ratified because it can be dissolved; nor is it lawful because the Apostle says, Romans 14: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.” But their union is not from faith and therefore is sin. Therefore it is not marriage, because no marriage is sin. Augustine also says that there is no true chastity of an unbeliever with a believer.

But chastity is denied to be true, not because the marriage of unbelievers is not true, but because it lacks that threefold good which excuses intercourse and merits reward. Likewise, the Apostle’s statement, “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” must not be understood to mean that everything done by unbelievers is sin; rather, everything done against faith—that is, against conscience—is done wrongly and builds toward Gehenna. Or: in everything that an unbeliever does, that person sins, not because he does it, but because he does not do it in the manner in which he ought, referring it to its proper end. (28, question 1.)

### That the Marriage of Unbelievers Is Lawful but Not Ratified, and Why

9. Therefore the marital union existing among unbelievers is lawful marriage, but not ratified. It is lawful because it is between lawful persons, but not ratified because it is without faith. The marriage of believers, however, is both lawful and ratified, provided that the persons are eligible.

Augustine testifies that the union of unbelievers is lawful when he says in *On Faith and Works*: “A wife joined in lawful fellowship [Col. 0937] is left without any fault if she is unwilling to remain with her Christian husband.” It is also proved from the fact that the Apostle counseled an unbeliever converted to the faith not to dismiss the unbelieving spouse; he would not do so if there were not a lawful marriage between them. A marriage is lawful when it is contracted by legal institution or by the customs of a province, and not contrary to the Lord’s command. (Hugh, *Sentences*, book 4, chapter 9.)

## DISTINCTION XL. ON CARNAL AND SPIRITUAL KINSHIP; FIRST, ON CARNAL KINSHIP

1. It remains now to say something concerning kinship. One kinship is carnal and another spiritual. Let us first consider carnal kinship and affinity. Therefore blood-relatives or relatives by marriage in the seventh degree, or closer, ought not to be joined. Hence Gregory, 35, question 3:

> We decree that each person must observe the line of descent as far as the seventh generation; and, as long as persons know themselves to be close relatives by affinity or consanguinity, we forbid their approaching marital union. If they do so, let them be separated.

Likewise Pope Nicholas, in the same place:

> Let no one take a wife from his own blood relationship before the seventh generation, or as long as the kinship can be known.

Likewise, from the Council of Lyons:

> Let no one take wives from among relatives of his own blood through the seventh degree.

By these authorities and many others, unions of blood relatives are prohibited through the seventh degree.

### On Calculating Degrees of Consanguinity

2. Isidore explains how degrees of consanguinity are to be calculated, *Etymologies*, book 9, chapter 3:

> The series of consanguinity is divided into six degrees in this manner: let the son and daughter—that is, brother and sister—themselves be the trunk. Once these have been separated on either side, these little branches issue from the root of that trunk: grandson and granddaughter, the first; great-grandson and great-granddaughter, the second; great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter, the third; great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter, the fourth; *trinepos* and *trineptis* (great-great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-great-granddaughter), the fifth; the grandson of a *trinepos* and the granddaughter of a *trineptis*, the sixth.

Observe that Isidore gives only six degrees, because he does not count the trunk among the degrees. Others, however, who give seven degrees, count the trunk among the degrees. For degrees of consanguinity are calculated in different ways. Some place the father in the first degree and children in the second; others call children the first degree, denying that there is a degree of kinship between father and son, since father and son are one flesh. Therefore, authorities that prohibit the restriction of consanguinity through the seventh degree place the father in the first degree. But those who prohibit it through the sixth degree call children the first degree. Thus, because of this difference, the same persons are found in the sixth and seventh degree.

He places the father in the first degree who says that brothers are in the second. Pope Zachary calculates in this way, saying in the same place:

> We calculate degrees of kinship thus: my brother and I are one generation and make the first degree. Again, my son and my brother’s son are the second generation and make the second degree; and so with the remaining successions.

There is no difference in meaning between those who calculate six degrees and those who calculate seven, although there seems to be a difference in the number of degrees. For the last generation, if counting begins from brothers, is found to be the seventh.

### Why Six Degrees Are Calculated

3. Why Isidore calculates six degrees, he himself explains in the same place, chapter 6:

> When consanguinity, gradually separating itself by the ranks of descendants, has extended to the last degree and has ceased to be proximity, then for the first time the law admits it into the bond of marriage and in a sense begins to call back the one fleeing away. Consanguinity has been established through the sixth degree of lineage because, just as the succession of the world and the human condition ends in the six ages of the world, so proximity of lineage is bounded by the same number of degrees. Within these six degrees all names of relationship are contained; beyond them neither affinity can be found nor succession further [Col. 0938] extended.

According to others, seven degrees are calculated so that, after seven degrees, bridegroom is joined to bride, just as, after this life—which is conducted through seven days—the Church will be joined to Christ.

Here, however, there arises the fact that Gregory, when Augustine, bishop of the English, asked him in what generation persons ought to be joined, replied as follows, 35, question 3:

> A certain Roman law permits the son and daughter either of a brother and sister, or of two full brothers, or of two sisters, to unite. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot arise from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that faithful persons may lawfully join one another in the fourth or fifth generation.

But much later the same Gregory, when Felix, governor of Messina in Sicily, asked whether he had written to Augustine that marriages contracted by English persons in the fourth generation should not be dissolved, gave among other things this explanation in the same place:

> Know that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English, I wrote specially, not generally, for the English people themselves, who had recently come to the faith, lest through fear of stricter requirements they should fall away from the good which they had begun. Nor did I write this to them so that, once they had been established in the faith, if they were found within their own consanguinity they should not be separated, or should be joined within the line of affinity—that is, through the seventh generation.

## DISTINCTION XLI. ON DEGREES OF AFFINITY

1. We must now consider affinity. Gregory says of it, 35, question 5:

> Further, concerning affinity, which you say is the kinship that pertains to a man on the wife’s side, or to a wife on the husband’s side, the reason is clear: because, if according to the divine declaration my wife and I are one flesh, undoubtedly the kinship of my relatives and hers becomes one relationship for both of us. Therefore my wife’s sister and I are in one and the first degree; but her son is in the second degree from me, and her granddaughter in the third. The same must be done reciprocally in the remaining successions. I ought to regard the wife of a relative in any degree just as I would regard a woman of the same degree within my own kinship. This, of course, applies equally to my wife regarding the relatives of her husband in every degree of kinship. Those who think otherwise are antichrists.

Likewise Pope Julius, 35, question 3, chapter *Aequaliter*: “A man is joined equally to his own blood relatives and to the blood relatives of his wife.” Likewise Isidore, in the same place, chapter *Sane consanguinitas*:

> The consanguinity which must be observed in respect of one’s own husband must also be observed, under the law of marriage, in the wife’s kindred, because it is established that the two are one flesh. Therefore both kinds of kinship are common to them.

Likewise Pope Julius, in the same place, chapter *Nullum*:

> We permit no one of either sex to take a wife from among the relatives of his own blood or of his wife, through the seventh generation, or to be joined in the stain of incest. For just as no Christian may take a spouse from among his own blood relatives, so neither may he take one from among his wife’s blood relatives, because of the unity of the flesh.

Likewise Gregory, in the same place, chapter *De affinitate*:

> It has been decreed that affinity arising from consanguinity must be observed through the degrees of kinship as far as the seventh generation. For inheritance of property, established by legal determinations of documents, extends succession through the seventh degree of heirs. For they would not succeed unless this were owed to them from the stock of kinship.

These authorities indicate both what affinity is and through what degree it must be observed—namely, through the seventh.

### Various Traditions Concerning Affinity
2. But others seem to permit marriage to be contracted in the fifth degree among persons related by affinity, and even in the fourth degree, if it has been contracted, not to have it dissolved. For Pope Fabian says, in the same place, chapter *De propinquis*:

> Concerning relatives who come into affinity through husband and wife: after the death of the wife or husband, let them be joined in the fifth degree; if they are found in the fourth, let them not be separated. But in the third degree of relationship, it is not lawful to take another’s wife after his death. A man is equally joined in marriage [Col. 0939] to those who are his own blood-relatives and to the blood-relatives of his wife after her death.

Here marriage between relatives by affinity is permitted in the fifth or fourth degree. Pope Julius likewise says, in the same place, chapter *Et hoc quoque*:

> It has been established that no one shall take in marriage his father’s widow, his brother’s widow, or his son’s widow; nor shall anyone take as wife the widow of his wife’s blood-relatives down to the third generation. But if they are found in the fourth or fifth degree, let them not be separated.

See how variously the authorities speak concerning the observance of affinity. Some decree that it must be observed to the seventh degree; others do not dissolve marriages contracted in the fifth or fourth degree. Yet the former seem to set forth the strictness of truth, the latter a merciful dispensation. For the Church can grant a dispensation in unions of persons related by affinity down to the third degree, just as Gregory granted a dispensation in the fourth degree of consanguinity.

Nor should this be passed over: Gregory wrote to Bishop Venerius, 35, question 10, chapter *Fraternitatis*:

> You have decided to consult the Apostolic See whether a woman joined in marital intercourse to a man unrelated to her becomes connected to his kindred; whether, when he has died, that kinship remains; whether under another husband the terms of relationship are dissolved; or whether children born to her may lawfully enter into a union with the kindred of the former husband. If they become one flesh, how can either belong more closely to one party without belonging to the other? It must be believed that this cannot happen at all. Moreover, when one has died, affinity is not erased in the survivor; nor can another marital union dissolve the affinity created by the former union. Nor is it fitting that offspring of the second union should enter into the affinity-group of the former husband. Therefore, if anyone, by sacrilegious and rash presumption, seeks to extinguish relationship in a deceased person, or under another spouse to destroy the terms of affinity, or believes that children born from another union may lawfully be joined to the kindred of the former spouse, he denies the word of God and denies the force of what was said in Genesis 2 and Matthew 19: “The two shall be one flesh.”

Here he forbids, if the first husband has died and his wife marries another, the children born of the second husband to marry wives from the kindred of the former husband. For through their mother the children belong to the kindred of her former husband, with whom their mother had become one flesh.

Pope Innocent says the same, 25, question 10, chapter *Si qua mulier*:

> If any woman has proceeded to second marriages and has borne offspring from them, that offspring can in no way attain membership in the kinship-group of the former husband.

This, however, is to be observed to the seventh degree of kindred, but especially to the third and fourth, as stated above.

### Whether there is marriage between persons separated by known consanguinity

3. It must be known that the Church separates persons united within the aforementioned degrees of consanguinity. But if they have been joined ignorantly in the sight of the Church, and afterwards, when their consanguinity has been proved, are separated by its judgment, the question arises whether that union was a marriage.

Some think that it was not a marriage, because the persons were not legally eligible; yet they are excused from wrongdoing through ignorance, and it is treated as if it were a marriage, because they came together in good faith and through the hand of the Church. Hence their children are considered legitimate. Others say that it was a marriage, although the persons were not legally eligible, because the canons call such unions marriages when dealing with persons whose union is to be dissolved upon the testimony of blood-relatives.

Thus Pope Urban, 35, question 6, chapter *Si duo viri*, says:

> If two or three men establish consanguinity by oath, or if perhaps the parties themselves confess it, the marriages shall be dissolved. But if neither occurs, the bishops shall adjure them by the faith of Christ to confess openly whether they recognize themselves as blood-relatives. If they separate themselves by the judgment of the bishops, they shall not be forbidden to contract other marriages.

The same pope, to Richard, bishop of Genoa, in the place cited above, chapter *Notificamus*:
