> We notify you that, when three or two of the closer relatives of the person accused have established this relationship by oath, [Col. 0940] or if two or three of the elder Genoese, to whom this relationship is known, being of good reputation and truthful testimony, free from affection, fear, payment, and every evil motive, have established the foregoing, the marriages shall without delay be dissolved. No one shall accuse strangers of consanguinity or compute consanguinity in a synod, but rather the relatives to whose knowledge it belongs. But if the entire line of descendants has failed, the bishop shall make canonical inquiry from the elder and more truthful persons to whom the whole relationship is known; and if it is found, they shall be separated.

Here are specified the accusers or witnesses by whose testimony the union of blood-relatives—called a marriage—is to be dissolved. (Pope Fabian, in the same place, chapter *Consanguinitatis*.)

### A useful distinction: what fornication, defilement, adultery, incest, and abduction are

4. Here it must be said that fornication is one thing, defilement (*stuprum*) another, adultery another, incest another, and abduction (*raptus*) another.

Fornication, although it is the general term for every unlawful sexual act performed outside marriage, is understood more particularly of intercourse with widows, prostitutes, or concubines. *Stuprum*, properly speaking, is the unlawful deflowering of virgins. Adultery is the violation of another’s marriage-bed; whence it is called adultery as though it were access to another’s bed. Incest is sexual misuse of blood-relatives or relatives by affinity. Thus those who sexually misuse their own blood-relatives or relatives by affinity are called incestuous.

Abduction occurs when a girl is violently carried away from her father’s home in order that, after being violated, she may be kept as a wife. If it is established that violence was inflicted either upon the girl or upon her parents, the offender is punished with death; but if he flees to a church with the abducted girl, he obtains exemption from death by the privilege of the Church.

The following statement of Alexander should also be added:

> That your wife’s brother or sister are called your relatives is due to equivocation and to the necessity of common usage rather than to any ground of kinship. For a brother’s wife is more properly called a *fratrissa* than a relative. A husband’s brother is called a *levir* [brother-in-law]. The wives of two brothers are called *janitrices*, as if entering through the same door. A husband’s sister is called a *glos* [sister-in-law]. But a sister’s husband has no special name, nor does a wife’s brother.

(36, question 1, chapter *Lex praeteritorum*, paragraph *Sed non omnis*; 35, question 5, chapter *Quod autem frater*.)

## DISTINCTION XLII. ON SPIRITUAL KINSHIP

1. We have said something, though less adequately than might be wished, concerning the celebrated question of degrees of kinship. Let us now add something concerning spiritual kinship, which likewise prevents persons from being legally eligible to enter marriage.

There are three kinds: consanguinity, affinity, and spiritual siblinghood. Consanguinity exists between those united according to the line of descent; affinity between those not united by descent itself but connected through descent. For example, the wife of my brother’s son, who is not of my lineage, becomes related by affinity to me—and I to her—through that man who is of my lineage. Spiritual closeness exists between godfather and godmother, and between persons where one has lifted the other from the sacred font or held that person at catechization or Confirmation. It also exists between a man’s children by flesh and his spiritual children. (Hugh, *Sentences*, book 4, chapter 13.)

### Who are spiritual children

2. Spiritual children are those whom we lift from the sacred font or hold at catechization or Confirmation. The spiritual sons and daughters are also those whom persons baptize in the sacred Baptism with the formula of triple immersion. A woman who confesses her sins to a priest is also called that priest’s spiritual daughter.

Thus Pope Symmachus, 30, question 1, chapter *Omnes quos*, says:

> All whom we receive in penitence are our spiritual children just as much as those whom the water of Baptism has regenerated, whether we received them or baptized them under the formula of triple immersion.

Sylvester likewise warns that no priest should approach his penitential daughter, because it is written:

> All whom we receive in penitence are our children just as those received in Baptism; intercourse with any of all these is criminal.

That godfather and godmother cannot marry one another, nor can a spiritual father or mother marry a spiritual daughter or [Col. 0941] son, is taught from the Council of Mainz, 30, question 7, chapter *De eo*:

> Concerning what you asked: whether someone has taken his goddaughter as wife; concerning one who has had intercourse with his spiritual mother; and concerning one who baptized his own son, while his wife received him from the font, in order that the marriage might be broken up, if afterwards they cannot remain in such a union—this is the answer. If anyone has taken his goddaughter or godmother in marriage, we judge that they must be separated and subjected to severe penance. But if lawfully married spouses—or one of them, or both—have deliberately done this, so as to receive their own child from the font, it is good if they wish to remain unmarried. But if not, severe penance shall be imposed upon the deceiver, and they shall remain together. If the violator of the marriage covenant survives, he shall be punished with the most rigorous penance and remain without hope of marriage.

From this it is clear that a person cannot marry his goddaughter or godmother; and, if this has been presumed, they must be separated. But persons lawfully joined are not to be separated merely because one of them deceitfully lifted their child from the font.

Nicholas confirms this, saying, 30, question 7, chapter *Nosse*:

> You desire to know whether a woman who has lifted from the sacred font the son of a man, born by another woman, may afterwards be joined to that same man. We decree that they may be joined, because according to the sacred canons no spouse ought to leave the other spouse under any pretext of religion unless both consent; as the Apostle commands, 1 Corinthians 7: “Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time,” etc. Therefore the Council of Chalon said that certain women, some through negligence and others fraudulently, had held their own children before bishops for Confirmation in order to be separated from their husbands. We therefore judged it fitting that, if any woman through negligence or fraud has held her child before a bishop for Confirmation, she shall do penance as long as she lives because of the deception or fraud; nevertheless, she shall not be separated from her husband.

Likewise Pope John, 30, question 7, chapter *Ad limina*:

> A man named Stephen came to the thresholds of Saint Peter and made known to our episcopal office that, when his son was at the point of death and had not yet been washed in the water of Baptism, he baptized him because the absence of priests compelled him, and received him with his own hands. For this reason, your reverence judged that the aforesaid man ought to be separated from his wife. This must by no means be done, for Scripture says, Matthew 5 and 19: “What God has joined, let no human being separate.” And the Lord commands that a wife not be dismissed except for the cause of fornication. Relying on so great an authority, we declare that he must not be dismissed and that what necessity imposed must be judged blameless. For the work of baptism is freely permitted to faithful lay persons if necessity requires it. Therefore, if the aforesaid man, seeing his son dying, washed him in the water of Baptism lest he allow his soul to perish eternally, in order to rescue him from the power of death, he is praised for having done well. Accordingly, we judge that he shall remain joined without penalty for as long as he lives to his wife, who had long since been lawfully united to him, and that he ought not to be separated on this account.

These and many other authorities teach that spouses are not to be separated if, after their lawful union, one has lifted the other’s child from the font or held that child at Confirmation.

### What seems opposed to the foregoing

3. Yet what the same pope says in the same place seems opposed to this:

> A deacon of your holiness has come to us bearing a letter stating that, on the preceding Easter Saturday, because of the great press of people, certain men and women unknowingly received their own children from the font. You therefore desire to know whether, on this account, husbands and wives ought to return to the use of their own marriage-bed or not. Distressed by the matter, we inquired into the sayings of our predecessors and found in the archives—that is, the repositories—of the Apostolic See that such things had already happened in many churches. When their bishops asked this Apostolic See whether husbands and wives should return to their own bed, the holy fathers of blessed memory—Pope Julius, Innocent, and Celestine—presiding in the church of the Prince of the Apostles with the consent of very many bishops, wrote and confirmed the following: that in no way should the men and women who had received their children for this reason resume marital life, [Col. 0942] but that they should separate, lest, at the devil’s urging, such a vice gain strength.

Likewise:

> If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before a bishop for Confirmation, he shall be separated from his wife and shall never take another.

But these statements were either made as a warning—not because this ought actually to be done, but in order that the act itself might be most carefully avoided—or they must be understood of persons who reciprocally received one another’s children from the font before becoming spouses. Yet, in accordance with the preceding authorities, it must be held without qualification that, whether a woman has received from the font her own child or merely her husband’s child, she is not for that reason to be separated from her husband; and the same must likewise be understood concerning a husband.

### On the union of spiritual, adoptive, or natural children

4. Pope Nicholas testifies that spiritual or adoptive children cannot be joined to natural children, saying as follows in his replies to the Bulgarians, 35, question 5:

> A person ought to love the one who received him from the sacred font as a father. Between spiritual brothers and children there is a gratuitous and holy fellowship, which must not be called consanguinity but regarded as spiritual closeness. Therefore I judge that a lawful marriage cannot take place between them, because the venerable laws do not permit marriages to be contracted between those who are children by nature and those who are children by adoption.

Likewise:

> If marriage is not contracted between those whom adoption joins, how much more ought those whom rebirth through the heavenly sacrament of the Holy Spirit binds to refrain from carnal cohabitation with one another!

### Whether children born before or after godparenthood may marry

5. Some wish this to be understood only of those children through whom their parents became co-godparents. But concerning other children, born before or after the godparenthood, they allow that they may be lawfully and legitimately joined. Pope Urban II seems to agree, saying:

> To the matters concerning which your belovedness has consulted us, this answer seems proper: that Baptism is valid if, under pressing necessity, a woman baptizes a child in the name of the Trinity; and that sons or daughters of spiritual parents, born before or after their godparenthood, may lawfully marry, apart from that person through whom they became co-godparents.

### Pope Paschal

6. But Paschal II, in the same place, forbids the marriage of children born after the godparenthood, writing to Bishop Regino:

> After a son has been received from the font, or after a spiritual daughter has been received, those born from the godfather or godmother cannot be joined in marriage.

The following should also be noted, as it is read in the Council of Tibur, in the same place:

> If anyone, by chance and through such an accidental occurrence, has taken in marriage the daughter of his spiritual godmother, let him retain her after more mature deliberation, and duly devote himself honorably to the lawful marriage.

### Whether someone may marry two godmothers, one after another

7. It is also commonly asked whether, after his wife’s death, a man may marry his wife’s godmother. Pope Nicholas writes thus concerning this to the bishop of Constantinople, 30, question 4:

> Your holiness asks us whether anyone may have two godmothers, one after the other. In this matter you ought to remember that it is written: “The two shall be one flesh.” Therefore, since it is clear that man and woman become one flesh, it follows that the man becomes co-godfather to the woman whose co-godmother was his wife; and thus the man cannot be joined to that woman who was his co-godmother, with whom he had become one flesh.

But the following from the Council of Tibur seems contrary:

> A man who has a spiritual co-godfather whose son he has received from the font, while his own wife is not a co-godmother, may, after his co-godfather has died, take that man’s widow as wife, since no spiritual generation separates them.

Likewise, from the letter of Pope Paschal, in the same place:

> After the death of his wife, no reason or authority seems to forbid a man from being joined in marriage with his wife’s co-godmother. For through union of the flesh one does not pass into union of spirit.

But it should be understood that Nicholas’s authority concerns a man who rendered the marital debt to his wife after she had become his godmother. The other authorities concern a man whose wife, after being abandoned by her husband, becomes his co-godmother and is not carnally known by her husband after that spiritual kinship; or, rather, they concern a man whose wife dies before she is carnally known by him.

### Whether husband and wife may jointly hold a child

8. It is also commonly asked whether a wife should receive a child in Baptism together with her husband. Urban says on this matter, in the same place:

> No authority appears or is found to forbid a wife from receiving a child together with her husband in Baptism. But, in order that the very purity of spiritual parenthood may be preserved free from every stain and reproach, we decree that neither of the two should presume jointly to undertake this. Since he has committed a grievously wicked crime who married two godmothers or two sisters, great penance must be imposed upon him.

### On second, third, and subsequent marriages

9. It should also be known that not only first and second marriages are lawful, but third and fourth marriages are not to be condemned either. Thus Augustine, 51, question 1, chapter *Deus masculum* and the following chapter, says:

> The Apostle permits second marriages as altogether lawful. But people commonly raise a question about third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages. Yet who would dare to determine what I do not see the Apostle himself determining? For he says: “If her husband falls asleep, let her marry whom she wishes.” He does not say first, second, third, or any particular number; nor should we determine what the Apostle does not determine. Thus, to answer briefly: I ought neither to condemn such marriages nor to remove the shame associated with their number; nor do I dare, contrary to the sense of human modesty, to say that women may marry as often as they wish; nor, from my own heart and apart from scriptural authority, to condemn marriages of any number.

Jerome testifies to the same effect, in the same place, chapter *Aperiant, quaeso*:

> I now cry aloud with a free voice: that a twice-married woman is not condemned in the Church—indeed, not even a thrice-married woman; and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth or sixth husband as a second.

Nevertheless, the Apostle excludes twice-married men from priestly honor. But he does this not because second marriage is a fault, but because of the force of the sacrament: that the husband may be the husband of one woman, as the one Church is of the one Christ.

Yet the Council of Caesarea seems to imply that second marriage is a sin:

> It is not fitting for a presbyter to dine at the wedding of persons in a second marriage; for since the twice-married person needs penance, what presbyter could give approval to such marriages?

But this may be understood of someone thought to have plotted against his first wife out of desire for a second; or it may be said on account of the sacramental sign, which is not preserved in a twice-married man.

Ambrose also says, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians, that only first marriages were instituted by the Lord, while second marriages are permitted. First marriages are solemnly celebrated under God’s blessing; second marriages even now lack glory.

## DISTINCTION XLIII. ON THE CONDITION OF THE RESURRECTION AND JUDGMENT

1. Finally, something must briefly be said concerning the condition of the resurrection, the manner of those who rise, the day of judgment, and the character of mercy. I cannot satisfy every question customarily raised on this subject. Yet no Christian ought in any way to doubt that the flesh of all who have been born and will be born, who have died and will die, will rise again (Augustine, *Enchiridion*).

For Isaiah says, chapter 26: “The dead shall rise, and those who are in the tombs shall rise.” And the Apostle says, 1 Thessalonians 4:

> We do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest, who have no hope—namely, hope of resurrection. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For we say this to you in the word of the Lord: we who live, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not go before those who sleep. For the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of an archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven; and the dead in Christ shall rise first. Then we who live, who remain, shall together with them be caught up in clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord.

In these words both the truth of the resurrection and the cause and order of those rising are most clearly indicated.

### On the voice of the trumpet

[Col. 0944]

2. The cause of the resurrection of the dead will be the voice of the trumpet, which all will hear at the coming of the Judge; by its power the dead will be awakened and rise from their tombs. Hence the Prophet says, Psalm 67: “He will give to his voice a voice of power,” that is, the effect of raising the dead. And John the Evangelist says, chapter 5:

> The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.

If it is asked whose or what sort of voice that will be, the Apostle says that it will be the archangel’s—that is, Christ’s own voice, since he is the prince of the archangels. Or it will be the voice of one angel or several angels. It is also called a trumpet because it will be manifest, and the last trumpet because none will follow it.

This trumpet, as Augustine says in *On the Grace of the New and Old Testament*, is the cry mentioned in the Gospel, Matthew 25: “At midnight a cry was raised: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.’” By the name “trumpet” some evident and glorious sign is understood. What the Apostle calls the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God is called in the Gospel the voice of the Son of God and a cry; the dead will hear that sign and rise.

### On midnight

3. He is said to come at midnight, as Augustine says in the place cited above, not with reference to an hour of time but because he will come when he is not expected. Thus, at midnight—that is, when it will be very dark, namely hidden—he will come. For the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night.

Nevertheless, it may not inappropriately be understood that he will come at the time of midnight; for, as Cassiodorus says in his commentary on the Octonary, at that time the firstborn of Egypt were struck, and at that time also the bridegroom is to come. In many passages authors also attest that Christ’s coming is called the day of the Lord not because of the character of the time but of events, because then the thoughts and counsels of each person will be laid open. Hence in Daniel, “The Ancient of Days sat, and books were opened before him.” The books are the consciences of individuals, which will then be opened to others. Then this will be fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed.”

When the supreme Judge comes, not only will the darkness of the air be illuminated, but the hidden things of hearts will be made manifest. By divine power, therefore, every person’s good and evil deeds will all be recalled to memory and be seen by the mind’s gaze with marvelous swiftness; conscience will either accuse or excuse the person, and by its testimony that person will be condemned or saved.

### Whether the elect will then remember earlier evils

4. Here it is asked whether the elect will then retain the memory of earlier evils as they do of goods. Certain authorities seem to teach that the good will then have no memory of preceding evils—that is, sins or sufferings. For Isaiah says, chapter 65: “I create new heavens and a new earth; former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they arise upon the heart, but you shall rejoice for ever.” Again, in the same place: “Former distresses have been given over to oblivion and are hidden from our eyes.”

Explaining these words as referring to the future, Jerome says:

> Former evils will be given over to oblivion, because perhaps in the future the memory of one’s former manner of life will be utterly erased when eternal goods succeed, lest it be any part of evil to remember former distress.

But these and similar passages can be understood in such a way that they do not exclude memory of earlier evils, but remove from that memory distress and injury. For their memory will not make the saints sad or dim their blessedness, but will make them more grateful to God. Thus Gregory says on Psalm 88:

> How can one sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord who does not remember misery? And how can blessedness be complete if remembrance of guilt touches the mind? Yet we often happily remember sad things, and, when healthy, remember pains without pain; thus we are more happy and grateful.

From this it appears that, if the saints remember former evils in the future, that memory will nevertheless not be punishment to them or detract from glory, but will lead to thanksgiving. But if it is asked whether sins committed by the elect will then become known to all, just as the evils of the condemned will be known to all, I have not read this expressly stated in Scripture [Col. 0945]. Hence it may not unreasonably be thought that sins covered and erased here through repentance will there also be concealed from others, whereas other sins will be disclosed to all.

### On those found alive

5. It is commonly asked whether those whom Christ finds alive will never die at all, or whether, at the very instant when they are caught up to meet Christ, they will pass to immortality with marvelous swiftness. For it must not be said to be impossible that, while borne upward through the air, they should both die and revive within that interval.

The Apostle seems to press us toward the interpretation that they will undergo death and receive immortality in a small interval, when he says, 1 Corinthians 15: “All shall be made alive in Christ.” And elsewhere, in the same chapter: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.” Why should it seem incredible to us that this multitude of bodies should in some way be sown in the air and immediately there be restored to immortal and incorruptible life, when we believe that the resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye and that the dust of bodies dead from most ancient times will return with such swiftness to limbs destined to live without end?

But I would rather hear teachers speak concerning these matters. If, therefore, we believe that the saints found alive at Christ’s coming and caught up to meet him will, in that same rapture, leave their mortal bodies and immediately return to them immortal, we shall suffer no difficulty in the Apostle’s words, if we understand generally what is said in 1 Corinthians 15: “We shall indeed all rise,” namely both good and evil; “but we shall not all be changed,” namely into the festal glory of resurrection.

Ambrose likewise says, commenting on “For the Lord himself”:

> In the very rapture of those found alive, there will be death and resurrection, so that the soul, as if in sleep, departs from the body and is restored to that same body in an instant.

On the other hand, Jerome, writing to Marcella, seems to testify otherwise, saying in Letter 4 that, at the end of the age when Christ comes, some will not die, but, being found alive, will suddenly be changed into immortality. Which of these views is truer is not for human judgment to determine.

### How Christ is understood to be judge of the living and the dead

6. To this must be added that the saying that Christ will judge the living and the dead is understood in two ways. Either “the living” means those found alive at his coming, although they die in the rapture, and “the dead” those who had died before; or “living” and “dead” mean the just and the unjust. (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 55.)

### How all are incorruptible

7. Since from what has been said it may soundly be believed that all will rise, it must also be believed that all will rise incorruptible. This does not mean impassible, since the reprobate will suffer eternal death; rather, they will lack no bodily member and possess every member of the human body, though they will not be clothed with glory and the hope of impassibility.

## DISTINCTION XLIV. ON THE AGE AND STATURE OF THOSE WHO RISE

1. Some also inquire and ask whether all will rise in the same bodily age and stature. Some have thought that all will rise according to the measure of Christ’s age and stature, because the Apostle says, Ephesians 4: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the age and fullness of Christ.” But those words assign to the risen not the same stature, but the same age.

For all will rise at the same age at which Christ died and rose, whatever age they were when they died. He used “man” not to distinguish sex but to signify the perfection of strength which they will then possess. Yet not all will receive the same bodily stature.

Thus Augustine says, book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 14:

> He did not say “to the measure of body or stature,” but “of age,” because each shall receive the measure of body which that person had in youth, even if he died old, or would have had if he had died before reaching it. But the age will be that which Christ attained, namely youth, about thirty years. For Christ was thirty-two years and three months old [Col. 0946] when he died and rose again. It is not permissible to say that, in the resurrection, bodily size will be added which it neither possessed here nor would have possessed by long life; nor are larger bodies to be reduced to the measure of the Lord’s body. For much would perish from those bodies, although not even a hair is to perish, as the Lord says, Luke 21: “Not a hair of your head shall perish.”

### That whatever belonged to the substance and nature of the body will rise, and in the same bodily part

2. Earthly matter, from which the flesh of mortals is created, is not lost to God. But however it may be dissolved into dust or ashes, scattered into vapours and breezes, changed into the substance of any other bodies or even into the elements themselves, or transformed into the food and flesh of animals or human beings, it will in an instant return to that soul whose flesh it first animated so that it became human, grew, and lived.

Therefore, the earthly matter which becomes a corpse when the soul departs will not be restored in the resurrection in such a way that the parts which decay and are changed into various kinds of things must return, even though they return to the body from which they decayed, to the same bodily parts where they were. Otherwise, if the hair removed by such frequent cutting returns as hair, and the nails repeatedly cut back return as nails, the unwarranted and indecent excess imagined by people who reject the resurrection of the flesh will confront them.

Rather, just as if a statue of any fusible metal were melted by fire, crushed to powder, or mixed into a mass, and an artisan wished to restore it from that material and quantity, it would make no difference to its integrity which particle of matter was restored to which member of the statue, provided that the restored object recovered the whole from which it had been made: so God, the wonderful and ineffable artificer, will with marvelous swiftness restore our flesh from the whole of that from which it existed. Nothing will affect its complete restoration whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is changed into flesh and recalled into other bodily parts, since the providence of the artisan ensures that nothing unbecoming occurs. For there will be nothing unbecoming there; whatever will be there will be fitting, because it will not be there if it is not fitting. (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 88; Hugh, *On the Sacraments*, book 2, part 1, chapter 19; Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 90.)

### That the saints will rise without every deformity

3. This is to be understood concerning the bodies of the saints, of whom Augustine immediately adds in the same work, chapter 91:

> Therefore the bodies of the saints will rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as without any corruption, burden, or difficulty. In them there will be as much ease as happiness; and for this reason they are called spiritual, though without doubt they will be bodies, not spirits.

From this it appears that all who rise will have one age, namely youth; but their stature will differ, namely the stature each had in youth or would have had if death had come earlier. Nothing from the substance from which human flesh is made will perish; rather, the natural substance of the body will be restored by the gathering together of all previously scattered particles. The bodies of the saints, too, will rise without any defect, shining like the sun, with all deformities they had here cut away.

### Whether the wicked will then have the deformities they had here

4. It is commonly asked concerning the reprobate whether they will rise with the deformities they had here. Augustine does not affirm this but leaves it uncertain, saying in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 2:

> All who are not delivered through Christ from that mass of perdition which came about through Adam will also rise, each with his own flesh, but in order to be punished with the devil and his angels. But whether they will rise with whatever defects and deformities of their bodies they bore in them—why should we labor to investigate this? For the uncertain condition or beauty of those whose condemnation will be certain and everlasting ought not to trouble us.

See: he does not decide [Col. 0947] whether the bodies of the reprobate will then have the deformities they had here.

### That the bodies which will then burn will not be consumed
5. But if the question is raised concerning the bodies of the wicked—how they burn in fire and are not consumed—Augustine, *City of God*, book 21, chapters 1 and 3, establishes by various examples that they burn in everlasting fires and are not consumed by that burning; just as the soul, by whose presence the body lives and can suffer pain, cannot die. For this will then be true in the bodies of the damned which we know to be true now in the souls of all.

Whether demons are burned by bodily fire.

6. It is also commonly asked whether demons burn in bodily fire. Augustine answers this question in his commentary on Genesis and in *City of God*, book 21:

> Why should we not say that, although in wonderful yet true ways, even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of bodily fire, if the incorporeal spirits of human beings can even now be enclosed in bodily members, and then will be bound indissolubly by the bonds of their bodies? That Gehenna which is called the lake of fire and sulphur will be bodily fire, and will torment the bodies of the damned, whether human beings or demons: solid bodies in human beings, aerial bodies in demons. For there will be one fire for both, as Truth says.

If it is asked what kind of fire this is or where it will be, Augustine answers thus in *City of God*, book 20, chapter 16:

> What eternal fire will be like, and in what region of the world or of created things it will exist, I think no human being knows, unless perhaps one to whom the divine Spirit has revealed it.

Whether souls without bodies feel bodily fire.

7. Since it is established that souls will be tormented by material fire in their bodies, it is commonly asked whether, in the meantime, before the resurrection of bodies, the souls of deceased reprobates are burned by material fire. On this point Julian, bishop of the church of Toledo, following Gregory’s sayings, wrote as follows in *Dialogue* 4, chapter 18:

> If the incorporeal spirit of a living person is held in a body, why should it not also be held after death in a fiery body? We say that a spirit is held by fire so that, by seeing and feeling the torment of fire, it may be punished. That the soul suffers the torment of fire not only by seeing it but also by experiencing it is gathered from the Gospel, Luke 16, where the rich man, after death, is said by the voice of Truth to have been buried in hell. That his soul is held in fire he indicates when he entreats Abraham, saying: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.” Therefore, when Truth declares that the sinful rich man is damned in fires, what wise person would deny that the souls of reprobates are held in fires?

Especially since Augustine teaches that the human soul has a likeness of a body, saying thus in his commentary on Genesis, book 12, chapter 33:

> Whoever refuses to acknowledge that the soul can have a likeness of a body, and indeed of bodily limbs, can deny that there is a soul which in dreams sees itself walking, sitting, or being carried here and there by walking or even by flight. This does not happen without some likeness of a body. Therefore, if it bears this likeness even among the dead—a likeness not bodily but similar to a body—then it also seems to exist in places not bodily, but similar to bodily places, whether in rest or in pains.

It is also read in the writings of Cassian that souls are not idle and do not feel nothing, since that rich man cries out that he is tormented by flame in hell. Hence it is proved that the souls of the dead are not only not deprived of their senses, but also do not lack these affections: namely hope, sorrow, joy, and fear; and that, from those things reserved for them in that general judgment, they already begin in some measure to taste beforehand.

Concerning miscarried fetuses and monsters.

8. It must also be investigated whether miscarried fetuses and monsters will rise again, and in what condition. Augustine says of this in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 85:

> A question arises concerning miscarried fetuses, which have already been born within their mothers’ wombs, but not in such a way that they can yet be born again. For if we say that they will rise again, what is said can somehow be tolerated concerning those already formed. But who would not be more inclined to think that the unformed perish, like seeds that have not been conceived [Col. 0948]? Certainly, it can be carefully investigated and disputed among learned people when a human being begins to live in the womb, and whether there is some hidden life which does not yet appear through the movements of a living being. For it seems excessively rash to deny that embryos have lived which are for that reason cut up limb by limb so that they may be expelled from pregnant women’s wombs, lest the mothers also die if they are left dead there. But from the time a human being begins to live, from that time he can also die; and when dead, wherever death may have happened to him, I cannot discover how he would not belong to the resurrection.

Nor will monsters which are born and live, however quickly they die, either be denied resurrection or be believed to rise in that same condition; rather, their nature will be corrected and restored. Far be it from us to suppose that the two-limbed being, reported by most trustworthy brethren who saw him recently born in the East, and concerning whom Saint Jerome left a written account, will rise as one doubled human being rather than as two human beings, as would have occurred had twins been born. Thus also all other beings called monsters because of excessive deformity will be restored in the resurrection to the form of human nature (*ibid.*, chapter 87).

## DISTINCTION XLV. CONCERNING THE DIFFERENT RECEPTACLES OF SOULS

1. Furthermore, it must be known that, as Augustine says in his commentary on John, tractate 49, when all souls depart from this world, they have different receptions: the good have joy, but the evil have torments. When the resurrection has occurred, the joy of the good will be greater and the torments of the evil more severe, when they are tortured together with their bodies.

From these matters it is shown that the joy of the saints will be greater in and after the resurrection than it was before; and that the souls of the saints will have different receptacles. Of these Augustine says in his work *On the Words of the Apostle*:

> The period lying between a person’s death and the final resurrection contains souls in hidden receptacles, according as each is worthy either of rest or of distress, according to what it received in the flesh while living.

Concerning suffrages for the dead.

2. Nor must it be denied, as Augustine says in *Enchiridion*, chapter 19, that the souls of the dead are relieved by the devotion of their living relatives, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these benefit only those who, while they lived, merited that they might subsequently benefit them. For there is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so evil that these things are of no benefit to it. Yet there is a condition so good that it does not require them; and again there is one so evil that, once it has passed from this life, it cannot be helped even by these things.

Therefore all merit is acquired here, by which someone may after this life be burdened or relieved. Let no one hope, when dead, to obtain from God what he neglected here. Therefore, the practices which the Church frequently observes for commending the dead are not contrary to that apostolic statement in Romans 14: “We shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, so that each may receive according to the things done through the body,” namely, good or evil. For while living in the body, each person also acquired this merit: that these things might benefit him; for they do not benefit everyone. And why? Solely because of the difference in the life which each person led in the body.

Therefore, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any other alms—are offered for all the baptized, they are thanksgivings for the very good; for those not very evil, they are propitiations. But for the very evil, although they are no aids to the dead, they are nevertheless consolations of some kind to the living. Those whom they benefit are benefited either so that there may be full remission, or at least so that damnation itself may be more tolerable.

Therefore, by the prayers of the holy Church, the saving sacrifice, and the alms offered for their spirits, there is no doubt that the dead are helped, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins have deserved. For this has been handed down by the Fathers and is observed by the whole Church: that, for those who died in the communion [Col. 0949] of the Lord’s body and blood, prayer is made when they are commemorated in their proper place at the sacrifice, and it is also mentioned that this is offered for them. There must therefore be no doubt that these things benefit the dead—but such persons as lived before death in such a manner that they can be useful to them after death.

For those who departed from the body without faith working through love and without its sacraments are vainly served by their own people with offices of such devotion, since, while here, they lacked its pledge, storing up not mercy for themselves but wrath. Therefore, when their relatives do some good on their behalf, no new merits are acquired for the dead; rather, these consequent things are rendered to them because of what preceded. For when each person finishes this life, he cannot have after it anything except what he merited in it.

Behold for whom and in what manner those things which the Church frequently does for the dead are beneficial. They assist the moderately evil toward mitigation of punishment; the moderately good, toward full acquittal—those who do not have merits of such perfection that they do not need to be helped through the poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, whom they made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity. Others have such perfection that they do not need these helps: such are the apostles and martyrs. For, as Augustine says:

> It is an injury to pray in the Church for a martyr, when we ought to be commended by his prayers.

But prayer is made for other dead persons. (Augustine, in the sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*, and in the Gloss on 1 Thessalonians 4, “We do not wish you…”)

Concerning the offices of burial.

3. Concerning the pomp of funerals, Augustine says:

> The pomp of the funeral, the procession of obsequies, and costly care in burial are consolations of some kind for the living, not aids to the dead. For if an expensive burial benefits an ungodly person, a cheap burial, or none at all, would harm a godly one. A crowd of servants gave splendid obsequies, in the sight of human beings, to that rich man clothed in purple; but the ministry of angels gave far more splendid obsequies, in the sight of the Lord, to that poor man covered with sores, whom they carried not to a marble tomb but to Abraham’s bosom.

Nevertheless, care should be taken to bury the dead and construct tombs, since these are counted among good works in the Holy Scriptures. Those who did these things were praised not only in the case of the bodies of the patriarchs and other saints, but also in the case of the Lord’s own body. Let people therefore fulfill toward their own the duties of the last service and the alleviations of their human grief. But let them provide with much greater observance those things which aid the spirits of the dead: namely, offerings and prayers. (*Sermon on the Words of the Apostle*; *City of God*, book 1, chapter 12; and *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 2.)

Concerning two equally good persons, one of whom has more aids after death.

4. A question is commonly raised concerning two persons, one rich and the other poor, equally but moderately good, who need the aforesaid suffrages and equally deserve to be helped after death. Yet special and common prayers are made for one, the rich person, and many distributions of alms; for the poor person, however, only common distributions and prayers are made. The question is therefore whether the poor person is helped as much by fewer aids as the rich person by more ample ones.

If he is not helped equally, he is not recompensed according to his merits. For he deserved to be helped equally, since they were equally good. But if the poor person receives as much suffrage as the rich, what did those things specially done for the rich contribute to him? It may certainly be said that the general and special suffrages did not avail him more than the general suffrages alone availed the poor person. Yet the special suffrages benefited the rich—not toward something else or something greater, but toward the same end as the general ones, so that one benefit might be received from several different causes.

It may, however, be said differently: those more numerous aids afforded the rich person a quicker, not a fuller, acquittal. (*Sermon on the Words of the Apostle*, book 1.)

By what suffrages moderately good persons found at the end will be helped.

5. But the question is again raised concerning a moderately good person who needs such suffrages and who, if saved, departs together with the rest at the very moment [Col. 0950] of the consummation. No further sacrifice, prayer, or alms is offered for him; nor did he possess merits of such perfection as not to require these suffrages. Will he then be saved? I think that, as one passing through fire, he will be saved by the merits and intercessions of the heavenly Church, which always intercedes by prayer and merit for the faithful until Christ is complete.

How glorified saints hear the prayers of suppliants, and how they intercede with the Lord for us.

6. But perhaps you ask whether saints hear the prayers of suppliants and whether the vows of petitioners come to their knowledge. It is not incredible that the souls of saints, who rejoice in the hidden place of God’s face through the illumination of true light, understand in his contemplation those things which take place outside, insofar as they concern either their joy or our help. For just as our petitions become known to angels, so also to saints who stand before God, in the Word of God whom they contemplate.

Hence angels are said to offer our prayers and vows to God, not because they inform him, but because they consult his will concerning them. (Hugh, *On the Sacraments*, book 2, part 16, final chapter.) Thus Augustine, in *On Praying to God*:

> Our petitions become known to the angels who are with God, so that in some manner they may offer them to God and consult him concerning them; and what they learn, by God’s command, must be fulfilled, that they may report to us, openly or secretly. Hence the angel says to human beings, in Tobit 12: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer to God.”

God’s own perfection is sufficient for knowing all things. Yet he has messengers, that is, angels—not to announce to him what he does not know, for there is nothing he does not know, but because it is good for them to consult his truth concerning their works. This is why they are said to report certain things to him: not so that he may learn from them, but so that they may themselves, through his Word and without bodily sound, announce even what he wills, being sent by him to whom he wills. They hear all things from him through that Word of his—that is, they find in his truth what they must do, and what they must announce, to whom and when. (*On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 13.)

For when we pray to him, we do not instruct him; for, as his Word says, “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Nor did he know this only in part; rather, without beginning he foreknew all temporal future things, including what and when we were going to ask of him, and whom he would hear or not hear, and concerning what matters. Therefore an angel is not said to offer our prayers to God as though God then comes to know what we wish or need—he knows all these things before they happen, as he knows them after they have happened—but because a rational creature must refer temporal causes to eternal Truth, whether by asking what may be done concerning itself or by consulting what it should do. (Augustine, *ibid.*, continuously; also in *On the Grace of the New and Old Testament*, and on Philippians, “Rejoice.”)

The statement made concerning angels is attributed to the souls of saints.

7. But if angels learn from God through his Word our petitions, and what must or must not be fulfilled concerning them, why should we not believe that the souls of saints who contemplate God’s face understand in his truth the prayers of human beings, and which should or should not be fulfilled? Hence God is said to hear certain persons’ prayers not only when he brings them to effect, but also when he makes known to the court of angels and holy souls what will or will not happen concerning them; and what they know to be in God’s will, they also will. For they are so devoted to the heavenly will that they can will nothing beyond his will.

The saints therefore intercede with God for us both by merit, insofar as their merits assist us, and by affection, insofar as they desire our prayers to be fulfilled. Yet they do this only after learning what must be fulfilled in the will of God. We pray, therefore, that they may intercede for us: that is, that their merits may assist us and that they themselves may will our good, since when they will it, God wills it, and so it will occur.

From the foregoing it is clear that God deals with certain persons more mercifully than their sins have deserved—namely, the moderately evil, who are helped by the suffrages of the Church.

## DISTINCTION XLVI. WHETHER MITIGATION OF PUNISHMENT IS GIVEN TO THE VERY EVIL

1. But here the question is raised concerning the very evil: whether they too experience God’s mercy through some mitigation of punishments, so that they are punished less than they have deserved. Some maintain that they will have no relief from punishment. They confirm this by the authority of James, who says in chapter 2: “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not done mercy.”

Augustine also, *on the octonary*, 19, Matthew 5, says: “Mercy is here; judgment is in the future.” Distinguishing how all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, he says:

> Toward the saints, all God’s ways are mercy; toward the wicked, all are truth. For in judging he gives aid, and thus mercy is not lacking; and in showing mercy he fulfills what he promised, lest truth be lacking. But toward all whom he liberates and condemns, all his ways are mercy and truth, because where he does not show mercy, the truth of vengeance is given.

By saying “where he does not show mercy,” he indicates that God does something where he himself does not show mercy. But against this is set what Cassiodorus says on Psalm 50, speaking of God’s mercy and compassion: “These two things are always joined to God’s judgment.” Therefore even in the punishment of the wicked there is no justice without mercy. The same author, on Psalm 100, says of judgment and mercy: “These two are joined together in mutual fellowship. In them he briefly includes all God’s works.”

Augustine likewise, in the *Enchiridion*, replying to those who contend that the punishments of the reprobate will have an end, rejects their opinion while affirming that reprobates are to be punished forever, yet without denying that their punishments are in some measure mitigated:

> In vain do some, through human sympathy, pity the eternal punishment and unceasing perpetual torments of the damned, and consequently refuse to believe that they will be so. They do not indeed oppose the divine Scriptures, but, according to their own inclination, soften everything harsh and bend the sentence toward something milder, supposing that what is said in them is more terrible than true. For, they say, “God will not forget to show mercy, nor will he restrain his mercies in his anger” [Psalm 76]. This is indeed read in the psalm, but it is understood concerning those who are vessels of mercy [Romans 9], since they too are delivered from misery not by their merits but because God shows mercy. Or, if they think this applies to all, it does not therefore follow that they should suppose the damnation can end for those of whom it is said, Matthew 25: “These will go into eternal punishment,” lest in this way the happiness of those concerning whom the contrary is said—“But the righteous into eternal life”—be thought to have an end.
>
> But let them suppose, if this pleases them, that the punishments of the damned are in some measure mitigated at fixed times. For thus it can be understood that God’s wrath remains in them—that is, damnation itself. For this is called God’s wrath, not a disturbance of the divine mind—so that, in his wrath, that is, while his wrath remains, he does not restrain his mercies: not by ending eternal punishment, but by applying or interposing reliefs among the torments. For the psalm does not say, “to end his wrath,” or “after his wrath,” but “in his wrath.”
>
> If that alone existed—alienation from the kingdom of God and deprivation of the great abundance of God’s sweetness—it would nevertheless be so great a punishment that no torments known to us could be compared with it, even if that were eternal and these lasted for however many ages. Therefore the everlasting death of the damned will remain without end; and it will be common to all, just as the eternal life of all the saints will commonly remain.

Thus he here affirms that the punishments of the reprobate are not to end, while not rejecting the assertion that some relief may be applied to their suffering. Hence it may fittingly be said that God, although he could justly do so, will not in the future punish the wicked altogether as much as they have deserved, but will remit to them something of the punishment, however evil they may be.

It determines the preceding authorities.

2. Therefore, the statement that “judgment without mercy will be for the one who has not done mercy” can be understood to mean that the judgment of damnation will be rendered to one who did not show mercy, because he was without mercy. Or judgment will be rendered to him without mercy that liberates and saves, though he will nevertheless experience God’s mercy in some alleviation of punishment.

Thus, when it is said, “Mercy is here; judgment is in the future,” it is not denied that there will be an effect of mercy in the future, both in the elect, who through mercy will be freed from every misery, and in the reprobate, who will be tortured less than they deserved. But God’s mercy is rightly said to occur here, and judgment in the future, because here God has mercy in many ways in which he will not then have mercy. For he now calls and justifies sinners, which he will not do then; and then, repaying each according to his merits, he will judge openly, whereas he now judges secretly.

His secret judgment, as Augustine says, is understood as the punishment by which each person is either exercised for purification, warned toward conversion, or, if he despises it, blinded toward damnation. Therefore God’s secret judgment is called punishment, by which he judges through purifying, converting, or blinding. God’s judgments are also sometimes called his dispensations concerning all things. Hence Romans 11: “How incomprehensible are his judgments!” And Psalm 35: “His judgments are a great abyss.”

But the judgment by which he will judge in the future is understood as the judge’s sentence, by which the threshing floor will be winnowed: that is, the good will be locally separated from the evil by the ministry of angels; these will be led into life, and those sent into punishment, though they are now mingled together.

Concerning God’s justice and mercy.

3. But how did Cassiodorus above say that God’s justice and compassion—that is, mercy—are two things always joined to God’s judgment? God’s justice and mercy are not two things, but one thing: one divine essence, as has been shown above by many authorities. For to God, being merciful is not other than mercy, nor being just other than justice, but precisely the same. Nor is being merciful different for him from being just, nor mercy from justice; they are altogether the same, because these are said of God essentially, not denominatively.

Why, then, does Scripture say that some works of God are works of mercy and others of justice? For if God’s justice is mercy, whatever are works of mercy would seem to be works of justice, and conversely. The answer may be as follows: in those forms of speech by which distinctions are made between such works, so that some are attributed to mercy, others to justice, and others to goodness, the words do not express a diversity of the underlying reality; rather, they show a variety of meanings and effects in creatures.

For when God is called just or justice, the divine essence is predicated, and it is also indicated that he is the distributor and judge of merits. Likewise, when he is called merciful, the divine essence is predicated, and in addition it is indicated that he is the deliverer of the miserable. Similarly, when he is called good, the divine essence is predicated; and when he is called God, it is further shown that he is the author of all good things. Likewise, when he is called God, the divine essence is predicated, and he is shown to be one to be feared.

Therefore certain works are called works of mercy and others works of justice, not because the divine essence does not perform both, or because both are not works of the divine essence, which is called mercy and justice; but because some display him as judge and equitable distributor, while others display him as one who has compassion. He is called *merciful* (*misericors*) in nature, but *one who shows mercy* (*miserator*) in manifestation.

In some works, therefore, the effect is said to be one of mercy, and in others one of justice—not because, if referred to the essence, God’s justice produces one thing and his mercy another, but because from certain effects he is understood as judge and from others as one who has compassion; or, as some prefer, as just and merciful. But on this account the question arises how he is shown to be just by some works and merciful by others, since being just and being merciful are the same for him. For if he is called just and merciful in the same respect, then by the work through which he is understood to be just, he is also understood to be merciful, and conversely.

But I said above that, when God is called just and merciful, the same divine essence is signified and the same thing is predicated according to it, while certain distinct things are also understood. For by this we understand him to be one who shows mercy and a just judge. Origen clearly demonstrates this when he says:

> Christ is everything that belongs to God: he is his wisdom, his strength, justice, holiness, prudence, and truth. But although he is one in the underlying reality, he is named by different terms because of the variety of meanings. For wisdom signifies one thing, justice another. When wisdom is named, it is understood that he instructs you in the disciplines of divine and human things; when justice is named, he is indicated as the distributor or judge of merits. Likewise, when prudence is named, he is understood as teacher and demonstrator of good, evil, and neutral things.

It proves from authorities that certain things are attributed to justice, others to mercy, and others to goodness.

4. That some works are attributed to mercy, others to justice, and others to goodness is easy to find in the Scriptures. The matter is plain concerning mercy and justice; concerning goodness and mercy it is less evident. But Augustine teaches, on Psalm 135, that those works properly belong to mercy by which some are delivered from misery; whereas not only these, but also the creation and governance of natural things, belong to goodness. He says:

> It belongs to mercy that God cleanses from sins and delivers from misery; but it belongs to goodness that he created heaven, earth, and all things very good, that they might exist.

The same author, on Psalm 32, says:

> The heavens do not need mercy, where there is no misery; but on the earth human misery abounds, and God’s mercy superabounds. Therefore the earth, not the heavens, is full of human misery and God’s mercy. The heavens do not need mercy, but they do need the Lord to govern them. For all things need the Lord, both miserable and happy: without him the miserable are not raised up, and the happy are not governed.

Again, elsewhere, on the words “Remember me according to your mercy,” he says: “Mercy is toward the miserable; goodness, toward anyone whatsoever.” Yet mercy is sometimes taken broadly so as to mean goodness.

How all the ways of the Lord are called mercy and truth.

5. After this, it must be considered in what sense all the ways of the Lord are called mercy and truth. This admits of several explanations. For “all the ways of the Lord” by which he comes to us, as Augustine says on Psalm 24, are understood as the two advents: the first, in which he displayed manifest and manifold mercy toward us; and the second, in which, examining merits, he will display justice.

“All the ways of the Lord,” that is, the ways by which we ascend to the Lord, are also justice, by which we turn away from evil, and mercy, by which we do good. For every good merit is included in these two. But since Cassiodorus, on Psalm 100, has said above that all God’s works are included in these two, the question may reasonably be raised whether these two are mutually joined in every work of the Lord.

Some have held that these two do not concur in every work of the Lord, speaking according to effect; for according to essence mercy is not divided from justice, but is one. Yet according to effect, they say that mercy and justice are not in every work of the Lord. They acknowledge mercy alone in some works, justice in others, and mercy and justice in still others. Nevertheless, they acknowledge that the Lord does everything he has made mercifully and justly, referring the rationale of this assertion to God’s will, which is justice and mercy, not to the effects of mercy and justice present in things.

Others, however, think that, just as God is said to perform all his works justly and mercifully, so it should be granted that in every work of God there are justice and mercy—that is, clemency—according to effect or sign. For there is no work of God in which there is not an effect or sign of equity and clemency, whether hidden or manifest. At times clemency or kindness is manifest and equity hidden; at other times, the reverse.

## DISTINCTION XLVII. CONCERNING THE SENTENCE OF JUDGMENT

1. It is also commonly asked: How will the sentence of judgment be delivered? [Col. 0954] But this cannot be clearly explained. Scripture does not openly determine whether it will be pronounced in words—Matthew 25: “Come, blessed ones,” and “Go, cursed ones”—or whether it will occur through the judge’s power, with each person’s conscience bearing witness, so that the effect of the judge’s power is said to be signified by his speech.

Likewise, the words in the same place, “I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and similar statements, many think will be expressed more in consciences than in words, because the Apostle teaches that the mystery will be completed “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” But they refer this only to the condition of the resurrection, not to the judgment; others maintain that the sentence of judgment, the rebukes of the wicked, and the rewards of the good will be expressed in words.

That the saints will judge, and how.

2. Christ will not judge alone; the saints also will judge the nations with him. For he himself says to the apostles in Matthew 19: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” Nor should it be thought that Christ promised this only to the twelve apostles. For where will Paul sit, who labored more than all, if no more than twelve will sit there? Therefore, by the twelve thrones is understood the perfection of the tribunal—that is, the whole body of those judging: all the perfect, who, leaving all things, followed Christ. By the twelve tribes is understood the whole body of those to be judged.

The saints will judge them not merely through cooperation, but also through authority and power. Hence Psalm 149: “Two-edged swords in their hands,” that is, the sentence concerning good and evil is in their power. But if it is asked what their power or authority in judging will be, I think it cannot be known before it is seen, unless someone has learned it through divine revelation.

Concerning the orders of those who will be judged.

3. There will be four orders in the judgment. For there are two parties: the elect and the reprobate, as Gregory says in the *Moralia* on Job, book 26, chapter 24. Yet two orders are contained under each party. Some are judged and perish; some are not judged and perish; some are judged and reign; and some are not judged and reign.

Those are judged and perish to whom, by the Lord’s accusation, it will be said in Matthew 25: “I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth. Those are not judged and perish to whom the Lord says in John 3: “Whoever does not believe is already judged.” For their condemnation is known and certain to the whole Church; and therefore they are said not to be judged then, because they will come into the presence of the strict Judge with the open condemnation of their unbelief.

But those who have a profession of faith without works will be judged and perish: that is, they will be rebuked in order to perish. Those, however, who did not possess even the sacraments of faith will not hear the judge’s rebuke directed against them, because, already condemned by the darkness of their unbelief, they do not deserve to be reproved by the indictment of him whom they despised. At least those who held his faith in word will hear the judge’s words. But those who were unwilling to maintain his reverence even in words will not receive even the words of the eternal Judge in their condemnation. Therefore the former are called to be judged, but the latter not to be judged.

On the side of the elect, some are judged and reign: namely, those who wipe away the stains of life with tears and cover them over with the addition of almsgiving. To these, standing at his right when the Judge comes, he will say: “I was hungry and you gave me food.” Others, however, are not judged and reign: those who by the power of perfection transcend even the precepts of the law. For they are not content merely to fulfill what the law commands, but also strive to fulfill what is counseled toward perfection.

Of these the Prophet says, Isaiah 3: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people.” And Solomon, speaking of the bridegroom of the Church, says in the final chapter of Proverbs: “Her husband is noble in the gates when he sits with the elders of the land.” And Job says, chapter 36: “He does not save the wicked, and he grants judgment to the poor.” Therefore these are rightly not held under the general judgment, but come as judges, because in their lives they overcame the general precepts and, leaving all things, followed Christ. He rightly grants judgment to the poor, because the more they were despised in this world in great humility, the more they will then grow to a greater height of power.

Of such persons it is said in Revelation 3: “To the one who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne.” The conquering Lord sat with the Father on the throne because, after the struggle of his passion and the palm of resurrection, it became clear to all that he was equal to the Father. But for us to sit on the Son’s throne is to judge by the power of that same Son. For because we receive the primacy of judging from his power, we sit, as it were, upon his throne.

From these matters it is clear that even the more perfect saints will judge with Christ by power, and why some are called to be judged and others not to be judged.

Concerning the order of judgment and the ministry of angels.

4. But since we read in the Gospel that the Lord will send his angels, who will gather out of his kingdom all scandals and will cast the wicked into the furnace of fire; and likewise, Matthew 13: “The angels will go out, and will separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, and will cast them into the furnace of fire”; and likewise, Matthew 24: “He will send his angels with a trumpet, and they will gather the elect from the four winds”; and the Prophet says, Psalm 49: “Gather to him his saints”—there can be no doubt that these things will be fulfilled through the ministry of angels. For when the Lord comes for judgment, fire will go before him, by which the face of this world will be burned up; and heaven and earth will perish, not in their substance but in their appearance, which will be changed—the aerial heaven, indeed, not the ethereal heaven. For the fire at the judgment will rise as high as the waters rose in the Flood.

That fire will be destruction for the wicked who are found alive, but not for the good, as Augustine says, *City of God*, book 20, chapter 18. For the saints, this conflagration of the world will be what the furnace was for the three children. If anything in them needs purging, it will be purged through that fire. To others, however, it will cause no distress at all. Once the world has been purified by fire and the Lord has come for judgment, that great voice will be uttered by which all the dead will rise; and then, through the ministry of angels, the threshing-floor will be winnowed, because the good will be gathered there from the four quarters of the world by angelic service. By that same service they will be caught up to meet Christ in the air, according to 1 Thessalonians 4, while the reprobate remain upon the earth which they loved.

Then those proclamations addressed to the good—“I was hungry, and you gave me food”—and those rebukes of the wicked—“I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matthew 25, etc.)—will be pronounced, whether in an audible voice or in some other manner. Finally, the sentence upon both groups will be declared there: “Come, you blessed”; and, “Go, you cursed,” etc. Through the ministry of angels, with God’s power cooperating, the wicked will be cast into the furnace of fire—that is, into hell.

### Whether demons will preside over human beings for punishment after the judgment

5. It is commonly asked whether, after the judgment, demons will preside in hell over the wicked in order to punish them—demons whom Scripture calls executioners and torturers of souls. The Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 15, that Christ will then abolish every rule, authority, and power. For while the world endures, angels preside over angels, demons over demons, and human beings over human beings. But when all have been gathered, every prelation will cease.

Hence some think that after the judgment demons will not have power to torment human beings as they do now. They maintain that demons are tormented by the power of God without the agency of a creature; likewise, they say that reprobate human beings there will be subjected to eternal torments not by the action of demons but solely by divine power. Yet the authority cited above does not compel this view. Although it asserts that then neither demons will preside over demons nor human beings over human beings, it does not determine whether demons will preside over human beings in order to torture them. Hence some think that demons will stand over human beings as torturers in punishment, just as they stood over them as instigators in sin.

## DISTINCTION XLVIII. ON THE FORM OF THE JUDGE

1. It is also commonly asked in what form Christ will judge. He will judge, certainly, in the form of a servant; this form will appear to all at the judgment, so that the wicked may see him whom they pierced. But the wicked will not see his divinity. Hence Isaiah, chapter 16: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God.” They will see his humanity so that they may fear; but they will not see his divinity, lest they rejoice. For divinity cannot be seen without joy.

### In what condition he will then appear in the form of a servant

[Col. 0956]

2. But since it is certain that he will appear in human form, the question is whether he will appear in that glorious form in which he truly is, or in the form in which he appeared during the Passion. Some think that he will be seen by the wicked as the one whom they crucified—that is, weak. For Scripture says: “that they may see him whom they pierced.” But Augustine plainly says, in his commentary on John and in his treatise *On the Trinity*, book 1, chapters 16 and 17, that the glorified form of a servant will then be seen by both good and wicked alike:

> When the good and the wicked see him judging in the glorified form of a servant, the wicked man will be taken away so that he may not see the brightness of God as God is; that brightness only the pure in heart will see, and it will be eternal life to them.

Therefore Christ’s glorified human form will be seen by all. Hence Christ is said to be the one who will judge because he is the Son of Man. For so we read in the Gospel of John, chapter 5: “And he gave him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” This does not mean that he will judge by the power of his humanity, or that he alone, apart from the Father and the Holy Spirit, will carry out judgment. Rather, he alone will be seen judging in the form of a servant by both good and wicked.

Therefore, when it is said that the Father judges no one but has given all power to the Son, this is not to be understood as though the Son alone judges and not the Father. It means that the Son’s human form will appear to all at the judgment—not in a weak form, but a glorious one. He will judge by the power of divinity, not apart from the Father and the Holy Spirit; and he will appear terrifying to the wicked and gentle to the righteous. For he will be terror to the wicked and light to the righteous.

### Why Christ is said to raise bodies according to the form of a servant

3. Just as Christ is said to judge according to the form of a servant, for the reason stated above, so he is also said to raise the bodies of the dead according to his humanity, although he will raise them by the power of divinity, not of humanity. Yet this is said for the reason that in his humanity he assumed that which is the cause of our resurrection—namely, his Passion and resurrection. Therefore the resurrection of the dead is ascribed to him according to his humanity.

Hence Augustine says: “Through the Word, the Son of God, the resurrection of souls takes place. Through the Word made flesh, the Son of Man, the resurrection of bodies takes place.” Again: “It is not the Father, but the Son, who judges and raises bodies, according to the dispensation of humanity, in which Christ is less than the Father. In that he is the Son of God, he is life which gives life to souls; in that he is the Son of Man, he is judge.”

See: he is said to raise bodies and to judge according to the form of humanity. He is said to judge because that form will appear to all at the judgment; and to raise the dead because in that same form he assumed the merit and cause of our resurrection, and because according to that same form he will give the voice by which the dead will rise from their tombs and come forth. As God, he gives life to souls—and not the Father alone; for not only is the Father life, but the Son with him, and the Holy Spirit, are the same life, which pertains to the soul and not to the body. For the body does not perceive the life of wisdom, but the soul, which is illuminated by eternal light.

Although, therefore, Christ gives life to souls, raises bodies, and judges through the power of divinity, it is nevertheless neither idle nor without reason that the giving of life to souls is attributed to him according to the form of God, while judgment and the resurrection of bodies are attributed to him according to the form of a servant.

### On the place of judgment

4. Some think that the Lord will descend for judgment into the valley of Jehoshaphat, because he speaks thus through the prophet Joel, chapter 2: “I will gather all nations and bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and there I will contend with them.” In the exposition of this chapter one finds the following:

> Some understand this childishly: that the Lord will descend for judgment into the valley on the side of the Mount of Olives. This is frivolous, because he will sit not upon the earth but in this region of the air, opposite the place of the Mount of Olives, from which he ascended.

And, as John Chrysostom says, angels will bear before him the sign of the cross. Hence Truth says in the Gospel, Matthew 21: “And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear,” etc. Now *Jehoshaphat* is interpreted “the judgment of the Lord.” Therefore all the wicked will be gathered into the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, of the judgment [Col. 0957] of the Lord. But the righteous will not descend into the valley of judgment, that is, condemnation; rather, they will be raised in the clouds to meet Christ.

### On the condition of the heavenly lights and of time after the judgment

5. When the Lord comes for judgment in great strength and power, the sun and moon are said to be darkened, not because they are deprived of their own light, but because the brightness of a greater light comes upon them. The powers of heaven, that is, the angels, are also said to be moved—not through fear of condemnation or any disturbance of dread, but through a certain amazement at what they will see. Hence Job, chapter 16: “The pillars of heaven tremble at his coming.”

Before the day of judgment, however, the sun and moon will suffer eclipse, as Joel testifies, saying in chapter 2: “The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” It is called great because of the great things that will then occur.

When a new heaven and a new earth have been made, then the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, as Isaiah testifies, chapter 30: “And the light of the sun will be sevenfold,” that is, like the light of seven days. For the sun will shine after the judgment as brightly as it shone in the first creation during the seven days before the sin of the first human being. The light of the sun, moon, and other stars was diminished through the sin of the first human being; but then the sun will receive the reward of its labor, because it will shine sevenfold.
