Then there will be no alternation of day and night, but day only.

Hence Zechariah, chapter 14: “And there will be one day, known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there will be light.” For then there will not be the present variation of day and night, but continuous day and light. Isaiah nevertheless seems to say that the sun and moon will not then shine, speaking to the assembly of saints: “There will no longer be for you,” he says in chapter 60, “a sun to give light by day, nor will the brightness of the moon illumine you; but the Lord will be your everlasting light.”

But by these words he does not deny that the sun and moon will then shine; rather, he signifies that they will provide no use of light to those who will then be in eternal blessedness. For, as Jerome says in book 10 on the same passage, “the service of heaven and earth, sun and moon, will cease for us, and the Lord himself will be light to his own forever.”

That saying of Isaiah may also be understood thus: the sun and moon will then have neither rising nor setting as they do now. Hence Isidore, as though explaining Isaiah’s statement, says, book 1, chapter 5: “After the judgment the sun will receive the reward of its labor. Hence the Prophet: ‘It will shine sevenfold’; and neither sun nor moon will come to its setting, but they will remain in the order in which they were created, lest the wicked, placed in torments beneath the earth, enjoy their light.” Hence Habakkuk, chapter 3: “The sun and moon stood in their order.”

See: he plainly says that the sun and moon will then shine, but remain fixed; there also he indicates that hell is beneath the earth. But if one asks what use the light of the sun and moon will then have, I confess that I do not know, because I do not remember having read it in the Scriptures.

## DISTINCTION XLIX. ON THE DIFFERENCE OF DWELLING-PLACES IN HEAVEN AND HELL

1. After the resurrection, when the universe has been brought to completion and the judgment accomplished, the two cities will attain their respective ends: one, Christ’s; the other, the devil’s; one, of the good; the other, of the wicked—each, nevertheless, comprising angels and human beings. The former will lack the will to sin, and the latter the ability to sin; neither will have any condition of dying. The former will live happily in eternal life; the latter will endure unhappily in eternal death, without power to die, because both conditions are without end. Yet among the former, in blessedness, one will remain more eminent than another; among the latter, in misery, one will remain more tolerably than another (Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 111).

From this it appears that, just as the good will be glorified differently—some more, some less—so too the wicked will be punished differently in hell. For just as in the Father’s house, that is, in the kingdom of heaven, there are many dwelling-places, that is, differences of rewards, so in Gehenna there are different dwelling-places, that is, differences of punishments. Yet all will suffer eternal punishment, just as all the elect will have the same denarius, which the householder gave to all who worked in the vineyard.

By the name *denarius* something common to all the elect is understood—namely, eternal life, God himself, whom all will enjoy [Col. 0958], though unequally. For just as there will be differing glorification of bodies, so there will be differing glory of souls. One star differs from another—that is, one elect person differs from another—in brightness of mind and body. Some will contemplate God’s presence more nearly and more clearly than others; and this difference in contemplation is called a diversity of dwelling-places.

Therefore the house is one, that is, the denarius is one; but there is a diversity of dwelling-places there, that is, a difference of brightness. For the one and highest good is the blessedness and life of all—God himself. All the elect will fully enjoy this good, but some more fully than others. They will enjoy it by seeing face to face, not in a mirror and enigma. To possess life, therefore, is to see life—that is, to know God in his manifest reality. Hence Truth says in the Gospel, John 17: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent, as the one and only true God.” That is to possess life: to know you is not the same as the knowledge which you are, but through knowledge to possess the good which you are, namely life.

### Whether all human beings wish to be happy

2. It is also commonly asked concerning blessedness whether everyone desires it and knows what true blessedness is. Augustine discusses this in *On the Trinity*, book 13, chapter 4, as follows:

> It is strange, when the will to obtain and retain blessedness is one in all, that there should nevertheless be such a diversity of wills concerning blessedness itself; not because anyone does not will it, but because not all know it. For if all knew it, it would not be thought by some to consist in virtue of mind, by others in bodily pleasure, and by still others in this thing or that thing elsewhere. How, then, do all love what not all know? Who can love what he does not know, as I argued above? Why, then, is blessedness loved by all and yet not known by all? Perhaps all know what it is, but not all know where it is, and that is the source of the dispute? Or perhaps it is false that we have assumed as true: that all human beings wish to live happily?
>
> For if living happily is, for example, living according to virtue of mind, how does one who does not will this wish to live happily? Have we not said more truly: that person does not wish to live happily because he does not wish to live according to virtue, which alone is living happily? Therefore not all wish to live happily; indeed, few wish this, if living happily consists only in living according to virtue of mind, which many do not wish. Will this then be false, a point about which not even Cicero doubted? For he says in the *Hortensius*: “Certainly we all wish to be happy.” Far be it from us to say that this is false.
>
> What then? Must it be said that, even if living happily is nothing other than living according to virtue of mind, nevertheless the one who does not will this wishes to live happily? This indeed seems exceedingly absurd. It is like saying: “The person who does not wish to live happily wishes to live happily.” Who could hear such a contradiction? Who could endure it? Yet necessity drives us to it if it is both true that all wish to live happily and that all wish to live in the only way in which one lives happily.
>
> Perhaps we can escape these difficulties by saying that living happily is nothing other than living according to one’s own pleasure, and that therefore it is not false that all wish to live happily, because all wish to live in the way that pleases each one. But this is certainly false. To will what is unfitting is to be most miserable. Nor is it as miserable not to obtain what one wishes as it is to obtain what one ought not to wish. Who is so blind as to say that someone is happy because he lives as he wishes? Surely, even if he were miserable, he would nevertheless be less miserable if he had been unable to possess any of the things he wrongly wished for. For a person is made miserable by an evil will alone; but he is made more miserable when the desire of an evil will is fulfilled.
>
> Therefore, since it is true that all human beings wish to be happy, desire this with most ardent love, and seek whatever else they seek on account of it; since no one can love what he wholly does not know either in what it is or what it is like, nor fail to know what he knows that he wishes: it follows that all know the happy life. All who are happy have what they wish, although not all who have what they wish are thereby happy. But those who either do not have what they wish [Col. 0959], or have what they do not rightly wish, are thereby miserable. Therefore no one is happy except one who both has all that he wishes and wishes nothing wrongly. For that person lives happily who lives as he wishes and wishes nothing evil.
>
> Therefore, since the happy life consists in these two things, although a person may be good amid evils, he is not happy unless all evils have ended. When one who is faithful and good amid these miseries passes from this life to the happy life, then what cannot in any way be true now will truly be so: a human being will live in the way he wishes. For there he will neither wish to live evilly, nor wish for anything that will be lacking, nor lack anything that he will wish for. Whatever is loved will be present, and what is absent will not be desired. Everything that is there will be good, and the supreme God will be the supreme good; and, what is altogether most blessed, it will be certain that this will always be so.
>
> All human beings wish to be happy. All see in their own hearts that they wish to be happy; yet not all possess the faith by which blessedness is attained.

(*Ibid.*, chapters 3 and 7.)

### Whether one person knows something about God that not all understand there

3. It is also commonly asked whether someone of greater merit, such as Peter, knows something about God that someone of lesser merit, such as Linus, does not know. It seems to many that all the elect jointly know all things concerning God that pertain to blessedness, though in differing degrees. For nothing knowable in God appears greater or more worthy than understanding him as three and one. Yet all will then know this by direct vision. It follows, therefore, that nothing pertaining to blessedness is unknown to any of the blessed.

Thus all will see all those things the knowledge of which serves blessedness, but they will differ in their manner of seeing. One will shine more, another less.

### On equality of joy

4. It is also commonly asked whether they are unequal in joy, as they differ in the brightness of knowledge. Augustine says concerning this in *The City of God*:

> There will be many dwelling-places in one house, namely, various degrees of reward; but where God will be all in all, there will be equal joy even amid unequal brightness, so that what each possesses will be common to all, because the glory of the head of all will also belong to all through the bond of charity.

From this it is understood that all will have equal joy, even though they have unequal brightness of knowledge, because through the charity that will be perfect in each, every person will rejoice as much in another’s good as if he possessed it in himself. But if the joy of all is equal, it seems that the blessedness of all is equal—which is clearly not so. One may answer that blessedness would be equal if joy were equal in such a way that knowledge also were equal; but since that will not be so, equality of joy will not produce equality of blessedness.

“Equal joy” may also be understood in this way: equality does not refer to the intensity of the affection with which they rejoice, but to the totality of the things over which they will rejoice. For whatever one rejoices over, all will rejoice over. (*On Virginity*, chapter 26.)

### Whether the blessedness of the saints will be greater after the judgment

5. After this, it is commonly asked whether the blessedness of the saints will be greater after the judgment than it is meanwhile. Without any hesitation, one must believe that they will have greater glory after the judgment than before; for their joy will be greater, as Augustine has testified above in his commentary on Hosea 6, and their knowledge will be fuller.

Hence Jerome, on Genesis, book 12, chapter 35: “When the judgment has been completed, God will show the elect a fuller glory of his brightness.” If anyone is troubled by the question why the spirits of the dead need to receive their bodies at the resurrection, if supreme blessedness can be granted them without bodies, it is a difficult question and cannot be fully determined by us.

Yet there is no doubt that the human mind, when withdrawn from bodily senses, and after death when it has laid aside the flesh itself, cannot see the unchangeable substance, that is, God, as the holy angels see it—whether because of some other, more hidden cause, or because it has a certain natural desire to govern the body, by which it is in some manner delayed and does not proceed toward that [Col. 0960] highest heaven with its whole attention until that desire is at rest.

Moreover, if the body is such that governing it is difficult and burdensome, as is this corruptible flesh, the mind is much more turned away from that vision of the highest heaven. Therefore, when it receives this body no longer animal but spiritual, made equal to the angels, it will possess the perfect condition of its nature: obedient and commanding, enlivened and enlivening, with such ineffable ease that what was a burden will be its glory.

## DISTINCTION L. WHETHER THE WICKED WILL SIN IN HELL

1. Here a question arises from what has been said. For above Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 111, speaking of the wicked condemned in hell and the good glorified in heaven, said that neither the good will have the will nor the wicked the ability to sin. This is clear concerning the good. But concerning the wicked, from whom he does not remove an evil will, one asks how it can be true that they cannot sin; indeed, how it can be true that they do not sin, when they have an evil will.

Some maintain that this will is not sin but punishment only. Others admit that it is sin, but say that through it they merit no punishment, because that is not a place for meriting. They therefore say that this sin is not a meritorious cause of punishment, but the punishment for evil merit which preceded in this life.

Augustine says of this in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 3, section 26:

> God gave human beings the time for acquiring eternal life in this life alone, in which he also willed repentance to be fruitful. Repentance is fruitful here because here a person can lay aside wickedness, live rightly, change his will and at the same time change both his merits and his works, and do what pleases God. Whoever does not do this in this life will indeed have repentance in the world to come for his evils, but will not find forgiveness in the sight of the Lord. For although there will be the sting of repentance, there will be no correction of the will.
>
> Their iniquity will be blamed by such persons in such a way that justice can in no manner be loved or desired by them. Their will will be such that it always possesses within itself the punishment of its own malignity, yet can never receive an inclination toward goodness. For just as those who will reign with Christ will have no remnants in themselves of an evil will, so those allotted to the punishment of eternal fire with the devil and his angels will have no further rest and will in no way be able to have a good will. And just as the co-heirs of Christ will be given perfection of grace unto eternal glory, so malignity itself will increase punishment for the companions of the devil, when, assigned to outer darkness, they will be illuminated by no inward light of truth.

(*Enchiridion*, chapter 111.)

From this it appears that the reprobate in hell will bear repentance in such a way that they do not abandon their perverse will through it. That malicious will will increase their punishment, though they will not thereby merit punishment, because no one merits except in this life.

### Why they are called outer darkness

2. Here one may ask why the darkness in which the wicked will be enveloped in Gehenna is called outer darkness. It is because then the wicked will be wholly outside both bodily and spiritual light—namely, God. For now, although they suffer darkness through blindness of mind, they are not wholly outside God’s light, nor are they deprived of bodily light.

Augustine says of this in his commentary on Psalm 6:

> The wrath of God will be present also in the judgment, and it is present here in blindness of mind, when the wicked are given over to a reprobate sense. There will be outer darkness, because then sinners will be wholly outside God. For what is it to be wholly outside God except to be in utmost blindness, since God dwells in inaccessible light? This darkness already begins here in the sinner when he is shut out from God’s inward light, but not wholly while he remains in this life.

See why the sinner is said to suffer outer darkness there, and not here: there he will be entirely excluded from God’s light, which is not so here. But how is this exclusion to be understood? Is it because they will not see God face to face? But no one here sees God face to face either. Is it by the dissimilarity which sin makes between God and human beings? But here too many are made distant from God by grievous sins. Is it because they hate God, so that they wish God not to exist? But here too many hate God, concerning whom it is written, Psalm 73: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually.”

What, then, is that removal? Outer darkness may rightly be understood as a certain malignity of hatred and will, which will then grow in the minds of the reprobate, and as a certain forgetfulness of God. For they will be so afflicted and disturbed by the pains of inward and outward torments that they will scarcely, rarely, or never call their mind back from these pains to think anything about God. Like persons pressed beneath an excessive weight, they become so stupefied and disturbed that for the time being they do not extend themselves to another thought; rather, the force of thought tends where the violence of pain is felt.

But in this life no one is so evil as to be wholly cut off from thought of God, because no one loses the desire for blessedness or that certain love of the good which a rational creature possesses by nature. Augustine says that the reprobate will suffer those outermost and deepest darknesses after the judgment, contrasting them with the rich man who, placed in hell, lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham and Lazarus in his bosom. Compelled by the comparison, he confessed his evils, so far as even to beg that his brothers be forewarned; this is said to have occurred before the judgment. But after the judgment the wicked will be in deeper darkness, where they will see no light of God to whom they might make confession.

### Whether the souls of the condemned know what occurs here

3. Further, it is commonly asked whether the souls of the reprobate now tormented in hell know what happens in this life to those belonging to them, and whether they grieve in any manner over the misfortunes of those dear to them. Augustine mentions this question in his commentary on Psalm 168, partly explaining it and partly leaving it unresolved. He says:

> Someone will ask whether any sorrow touches the dead concerning what happens after death to those belonging to them, or how the spirits of the dead know the things that take place around us. I answer that this is a great question and not to be discussed at present.

Yet it may briefly be said that the dead have concern for those dear to them, as is read of the rich man who, while suffering torments among the dead, lifted up his eyes to Abraham and among other things said, Luke 16: “For I have five brothers; send someone from the dead to testify to them, lest they too come to this place of torment.” For the dead have concern for the living whom they know to be alive, since they see them neither in the places of punishment, where the rich man was without his brothers, nor in the repose of the blessed, where he recognized Lazarus and Abraham, though far off. Yet it does not follow from this that they know what joyful or sorrowful things happen here to those dear to them.

### How the account of Lazarus and the rich man is to be understood

4. But if anyone asks how the account of Lazarus and the rich man is to be understood, let him hear Augustine’s answer in *On Genesis*, book 8, chapter 5:

> If anyone thinks that souls stripped of bodies are contained in bodily places, though they are without bodies, there will not be wanting persons who support him and contend that the thirsty rich man was in a bodily place, and that the soul itself had fashioned a bodily tongue and desired a drop from Lazarus’s finger. But it is better to doubt concerning hidden things than to argue about uncertain things. I do not doubt that the rich man is in punishment and the poor man in refreshment. But how the rich man’s tongue, Lazarus’s finger, the flame of hell, Abraham’s bosom, and things of this kind are to be understood is scarcely discovered by the gentle, and never by the contentious.

[Col. 0962]

### Whether the good and the wicked see one another

5. It is also commonly asked whether those in hell and those in glory see one another in turn. As the saints teach, before the judgment the good see the wicked and the wicked see the good. But after the judgment the good will see the wicked, while the wicked will not see the good. Hence Gregory, on the passage “And it came to pass,” Homily 40:

> The unbelievers, placed below before the day of judgment, behold above them the faithful at rest, whose joys they are afterwards unable to contemplate.

### On the chasm between the good and the wicked

6. But since the saints see the wicked in torments, are they not moved by some compassion toward them? Do they not wish them to be freed from their torments? Recall what Abraham answered the rich man in the Gospel, Luke 16: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot, nor can any cross from there to here.”

What is that chasm between the good and the wicked except righteousness on one side and iniquity on the other, which cannot in any way be joined? For the saints are so devoted to God’s justice that they cannot cross over to the reprobate in any compassion, and no intercession for them is made among the saints. How then are some said to wish to cross from there to them but not to be able? Because if God’s justice permitted it, their deliverance would not be burdensome to the saints. Or they are said to wish and not to be able, not because they actually wish and cannot, but because even if they wished, they could not help them.

Gregory says of this in his commentary on Luke:

> Just as the reprobate wish to pass from punishments to the glory of the saints and cannot, so the righteous, in their merciful minds, wish to go to those placed in torments in order to free them, but cannot; because although the souls of the righteous possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, now joined to the justice of their Creator, they are bound by such rectitude that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.

### That the sight of the punishment of the wicked does not diminish the glory of the blessed

7. Finally, it is asked whether the punishment of the reprobate, when seen, tarnishes the glory of the blessed, or contributes to their blessedness. Gregory says of this in Homily 40 on Luke 16:

> In the mind of the righteous, the sight of the punishment of the reprobate does not darken blessedness; for where compassion for misery will no longer exist, it will be unable to diminish the joy of the blessed. And although their own joys suffice for the righteous, they nevertheless see the punishments of the wicked for a greater glory, which they escaped through grace; for those who see God’s brightness can see nothing done in creation that they are unable to see.

Nor is it remarkable that the saints, already immortal, should see the reprobate through the understanding of the mind, since even mortal prophets were granted to see all these things. Therefore the elect will go forth—not by changing place, but through understanding or manifest vision—to behold the torments of the wicked. Seeing them, they will not be affected by sorrow but filled with joy, giving thanks for their own deliverance when they behold the unspeakable calamity of the wicked (Jerome, book 8, chapter 66, on Isaiah).

Hence Isaiah, describing the torments of the wicked and expressing the joy of the good at their sight, says in the final chapter: “They will go forth”—that is, the elect—“and will see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished; and they will be unto the satiety of vision for all flesh,” that is, for the elect. “For the righteous will rejoice when he sees vengeance,” Psalm 57.

Let it suffice for the writer—though not for the hearer—to have recalled these matters concerning the feet of him seated upon the lofty throne, which the seraphim covered with two wings: the writer who, beginning from the face of the seated one, arrived by a guiding path through the intermediate parts as far as the feet.

# ARTICLES IN WHICH THE MASTER OF THE SENTENCES IS NOT HELD IN COMMON BY EVERYONE

[Col. 0961]

## IN THE FIRST BOOK

[Col. 0961]

First: that the charity by which we love God and neighbor is the Holy Spirit. Distinction XVII, chapter II; or [Col. 0962], that the charity which is love of God and neighbor is not something created.

Second: that numerical names spoken of God are said [Col. 0963] only relatively. Distinction XXIV, chapter *Et si diligenter*. Or: that these numerical names, *threefold* and *Trinity*, signify not position but only privation.

Third: that “similar” and “equal” are likewise said of God privatively. Distinction XXI, chapter *Et hoc idem*.

Fourth: that God can always do whatever he was at any time able to do, and wills whatever he has willed, and knows whatever he has known. Distinction XLIV, chapter *Praeterea quaeri solet*.

## IN THE SECOND BOOK

First: that angels did not merit blessedness through grace given to them; but that reward preceded merit, and afterward they merited through services rendered to the faithful. Distinction V, chapter *Hic quaeri solet*. Or: that reward preceded merit for angels, and that merit must follow in respect to the substantial reward.

Second: that angels advance, up to the judgment, both in merit with respect to the essential reward and in the reward itself. Distinction XI, chapter *Praeterea illud*.

Third: that charity is the Holy Spirit, namely, that which informs and sanctifies the qualities of the soul. Distinction XXVII, chapter *Cum igitur*.

Fourth: that in the reality of human nature nothing extrinsic passes over; rather, what descended from Adam through propagation, increased and multiplied, will rise at the judgment. Distinction XXX, penultimate chapter.

To this the response is either that nothing from foods passes into the reality of human nature, whether through generation or through nourishment.

## IN THE THIRD BOOK

First: that a soul stripped from the body is a person. Distinction II, chapter *Hic opponitur a quibusdam*.

Second: that Christ is fittingly said both to have died and not to have died, to have suffered and not to have suffered. Distinction XXI, final chapter.

Third: that Christ was a dead human being during the three days. Distinction XXII, chapter I.

## IN THE FOURTH BOOK

First: that the legal sacraments did not justify, even if performed with faith and devotion. Distinction I, chapter *Non igitur*.

Second: that before sin, the human being saw God without an intermediary. In the same Distinction, chapter *Triplici*.

Third: that circumcision did not confer grace for acting well, nor virtues for increase; but was effective only for the remission of sins. In the same Distinction, chapter *Duo igitur*.

Fourth, that infants who died uncircumcised before the eighth day perished, and that, in a case of necessity, they could be circumcised earlier. Same distinction, chapter “But if.”

Fifth, that certain sacraments of the New Law were instituted only as remedies, such as marriage. [Col. 0964] Distinction II, chapter I, “Now concerning the sacraments.”

Sixth, that those baptized with John’s baptism, if they did not place their hope in it, were not to be baptized with Christ’s baptism. Distinction II, final chapter, “Here it must be considered.” Or alternatively: John’s baptism together with the laying on of hands was equivalent to Christ’s baptism; so that one baptized with John’s baptism was not to be baptized again.

Seventh, that God could give a creature the power to create and to wash inwardly—that is, to forgive sins. Distinction V, final chapter, “Here it is asked what it is.” Or thus: that God could give others the power of baptizing inwardly, and that a creature could receive this power; and likewise that God can communicate to a creature the power of creating, and create through a creature as through a minister. Distinction V.

Eighth, that degraded schismatics, heretics cut off from the Church, and excommunicated persons do not have the power to consecrate Christ’s body. Distinction XIII, chapter “But those persons.”

Ninth, that a brute animal does not receive the true body of Christ, even if it appears to do so. Distinction XIII, chapter “That also indeed.”

Tenth, that the knowledge of discernment, insofar as it denotes the habit of knowledge, is a key. Distinction XIX, chapter I.

Eleventh, that simoniacal bishops who have been degraded cannot confer orders. Distinction XXV, chapter “Concerning simoniacs.”

Twelfth, that the second husband of a woman not carnally known by her first husband is, by his knowledge of her, a bigamist and is barred from orders. Distinction XXVII, final chapter.

Thirteenth, that a man who knows his wife’s sister is not obliged to render the marital debt to his wife when she demands it. Distinction XXXIII, chapter “Concerning these persons.”

Fourteenth, that a man who, while his wife was alive, took another woman in a foreign country, and who, upon coming to his senses, wishes to dismiss her but cannot—if he is compelled by the Church to remain with her and render the marital debt because he is not believed—begins, according to the Master, to be excused by obedience and fear, and is obliged to render the debt if it is demanded. Distinction XXXVIII, final chapter.

Fifteenth, that sins which have been erased are not made known to others at the judgment. Distinction LXIV, chapter “Here it is asked whether [this applies] to the elect.”

To the foregoing errors we shall add the following proposition, condemned after the author’s death by Pope Alexander III: namely, “Christ, insofar as he is man, is not something.” By this expression the distinguished author certainly intended to signify that Christ … is not something **absolute which constitutes a person**; yet his meaning was not sufficiently clear from the words stated above.

## At an Uncertain Year of the Twelfth Century: The Four Books of Sentences of Master Bandinus, Most Learned Theologian

In these books the whole sum of theology and a compendium of our faith are treated purely, plainly, and methodically; now published much more correctly than before, for the benefit of all students of Christian piety. Arguments have been added to the individual books, indicating what each book contains. (Louvain, at the press of Peter Colonaeus, sworn bookseller, 1557. With the privilege of the royal majesty for four years.)

[Col. 0965]

## Peter Colonaeus to the Benevolent Reader, Greetings

Under the happy auspices of the most pious and ever-August Emperor Maximilian of illustrious memory, Christian reader, the four books of theological *Sentences* by Bandinus, a most learned and very ancient theologian, were published at Vienna nearly forty years ago. In them that author, thoroughly practised in sacred letters, set forth briefly, but carefully and precisely and in a style not without elegance, the sum of all theology and a compendium of our faith.

When a friend placed a copy of them at my disposal, and I observed that they greatly pleased all who saw them because they explained, in the most artfully arranged, pure, plain, and methodical way, the teaching of religion that lies scattered far and wide through the Scriptures, I thought it would be no small service if, after the countless errors of the first printer—who, given the character of that age, was excessively sleepy and unpolished—had been removed by the judgment and diligence of learned theologians, I caused the now corrected Bandinus to appear publicly in more elegant type, so that as many persons as possible might more easily enjoy so great a treasure.

At first, indeed, I had decided to publish separately for the use of students only this author’s first little work, which concerns the Trinity, so that students might infer from it what judgment ought to be made concerning Bandinus: an ancient indeed, learned, and very concise teacher, but hitherto seen by few. But when this little book had scarcely been completed and read by students, they did not cease most eagerly to demand all the rest as well, which they had no doubt were composed with no less skill and concision. In complying with them, we have spared no great expense of our own.

Therefore, benevolent reader, accept kindly this labour and expenditure of ours, wholly devoted to your studies; farewell; and, if you can, assist our endeavours by rescuing from bookworms and moths copies, hidden in libraries, of these little books and of Bandinus’s other works not yet published—especially old handwritten copies. Farewell again.

[Col. 0965]

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the unconquered and magnanimous Emperor MAXIMILIAN, Caesar Augustus, Benedict Chelidonius, abbot of the Scots at Vienna, his tireless servant, wishes happiness.

That those devoted to wisdom ought to govern commonwealths if they are to stand secure is the judgment of Plato, most pious Caesar Maximilian. How true and useful this is, not to mention Greek and Latin history, the histories of barbarian peoples also show. Yet a wise mind—the guide and commander of mortal life—seems to me truly wise only if it is religious.

Hence it comes about that wisdom, which the Greeks call philosophy, which, as Seneca testifies, forms the mind, orders life, and, as ruler of our actions, points out what ought to be done and omitted—being knowledge not only of human but also of divine things—has an indissoluble kinship with religion. Whoever is imbued with it lives rightly and acts prosperously. To such a person every fortune is despised, and heaven itself serves. If you entrust such a person with the administration of the state, it is a most beautiful empire to behold.

The ancient Romans, not unaware of this, frequently joined the pontifical dignity to the imperial height. That august majesty is called sacred even to this day. In respect of such sanctity, the ancients—among whom, besides what was publicly administered, nothing against an enemy was, in their opinion, successfully undertaken without auspices—asserted that the Roman commonwealth grew as great as we know it to have been. Yet their religion was not sacred but abominable, their wisdom foolish, and their superstition profane.

We, therefore, who have been instructed not in heathen but in orthodox piety, and who invoke not Mars but Christ for our fortunes: since events have occurred in your time which no preceding age has seen and which all posterity will admire, being so immediately advantageous to the public and almost unbelievable unless seen with one’s own eyes, why should we not think that they too should be attributed to your most sacred auspices?

I pass over the new institutions of military discipline which your enemies have experienced in many ways, and by which their stubborn pride has been constantly subdued under your arms from youth even to old age, as your countless triumphs testify—triumphs which John Stabius, historian of your majesty, assembled into the great arch that he calls triumphal. At your command, we translated his Commentary from German into Latin.

I pass over the new and astonishing engines of war devised through you, endowed in all things with divine ingenuity: machines at whose thunder and lightning even the Alps might tremble and collapse, and against which nothing can prevail. Meanwhile, how great has been your zeal for peace, for whose sake you have undertaken all your wars, may be gathered from the fact that, by the great artifice of your mind, you have brought so many kings and princes into your alliances and family connections, especially recently at Vienna.

For then we saw assembled there, summoned by you from the whole Roman world, as many eminent men clad in purple and gold chains as no age anywhere records to have gathered together. We described that most illustrious assembly—worthy to be celebrated in everlasting memory—in two books of heroic verse and presented them to your most sacred hands. These things, I say, I pass over, and deliberately, because they surpass not only my powers but themselves as well.

For these reasons I see fulfilled in you that Virgilian saying by which the same poet embraced the ideal ruler:

> Remember, Roman, to rule the peoples by your command:
>
> These shall be your arts: to impose the custom of peace,
>
> To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.

I shall come to one thing alone, which surpasses the destinies of all rulers from the beginning of the world. We know that Bacchus and Hercules brought very remote nations into their dominions; likewise Pompey and Julius, and many other Roman rulers, conquered a great many peoples, though not unknown to us, and added them to Roman dominion. But about the time of your birth, and thereafter under your most valiant father as emperor, and later under your own most valiant rule, another world of lands and other peoples, unknown in any former age and not even dreamed of, came into Christian dominion: the Spaniards, and especially the Portuguese—whose people provide your maternal lineage—surpassing both tropics and the furthest ocean, that of the antipodes, by maritime exploration, almost insane, if one may say so.

In these same times there also came to light a new kind of writing, hitherto, I think, unknown even to Pallas herself: that which we call printing (*chalcographia*). By its occasion those outstanding talents now flourish widely, letters increase, and libraries everywhere are filled up even in emulation of Philadelphia. Whoever should wish worthily to recount these individual matters and many others besides—rightly attributable to your destiny and auspices—would require a summer’s day, a hundred tongues, and a voice of iron.

Nor could one who attempted even selectively to tell of the extensive splendour of your most ancient lineage, which we read descends from the great Ham, its continuance down to your descendants—than whom the whole world now possesses nothing more precious—and its royal pedigrees, avoid being as anxious about finding an end as about the beginning. He would summon Calliope to his aid, and Apollo himself, from whom no history lies hidden; yet he would laugh at his own efforts, however strenuously made, as futile.

Let us pass over the rest of your line, celebrated everywhere with the highest praises: Charles, an image most like yourself, thunderbolt of tyrants, now king of the West and soon, through your efforts, of the East—whom it is right to call Catholic. Who among mortals does not know him to be a most mighty increase of your glory? Who could pursue him with praises worthy of him? Ferdinand, younger in age but equal in character, born likewise for sceptres, is known as a brother most worthy of his brother. Each is an outstanding emulator of your virtues: the one raises immense joy among all Christians through the excellent hope he offers of himself, the other by the reality itself.

For these and many other most great gifts of glory, divinely granted to you as to a singularly exalted prince, and especially for the worship of the Christian religion, which you zealously aid and most courageously defend, our Bandinus—long ago discovered at Medlik among the many other very ancient volumes there, and brought to light by Lord Sigismund, a man distinguished by excellent character and the finest studies, master of the arts called liberal, and vigilant abbot of the same monastery—most joyfully presents himself, with me as his guide; and he attributes to your happy auspices his eventual liberation from a long imprisonment.

Happy indeed: for the practice, adopted in boyhood, of living justly and piously has become your nature. No one is now stronger or wiser than you, no one more prudent, upright, or holy; no one more merciful to the conquered or more devoted to letters, which you understand excellently. Deign, most sacred Caesar, to favour him: small indeed in bulk, but full of the holy doctrines of our religion. From him, in the opinion of myself and many other persons not unlearned, that Peter Lombard seems to have developed his great four-part work.

Likewise, deign to enroll us among the most ready servants of your majesty—us who judge it a most beautiful honour to serve so great a prince, and the safest protection to enjoy so great a patron—among the number of your dependants, whom you always count as your best.

At the Scots monastery in Vienna, 1518.

[Col. 0967]

## Letter of the Same Author to Abbot Sigismund

To the most reverend father and lord, Lord SIGISMUND, abbot at Medlik, a man most distinguished in letters and religion, bound to him by a most welcome friendship and deserving of the highest respect: Brother Benedict Chelidonius, abbot of the Scots at Vienna, sends greetings.

[Col. 0969] While recently dining with you, most worthy Abbot Sigismund, and with several other professors of humane letters, conversation was held, as is your custom, concerning the literary disputation lately conducted at Vienna between Dr. John Eck, doctor of sacred theology, and the Viennese doctors of that same faculty, before a very great gathering of learned persons. I too, as on very many previous occasions, was invited, in accordance with the long-standing familiarity I have enjoyed with your paternity.

At the mention of Dr. Eck, we turned in memory to the very ancient handwritten codices filling your library, which you newly built. From their number, your reverence produced an old book entitled *The Book of Sentences of Master Bandinus*, discovered a few days earlier through Dr. Eck’s indication. Since we all unanimously judged it worthy of publication, you, best of fathers, entrusted to me—then somewhat less occupied, because you were wholly constrained by domestic concerns—the task of reviewing it and correcting it, which it very greatly needed.

I, owing much to your paternity both because of your great goodwill and because of your many benefits, undertook this task readily, relying more on boldness than skill. I took with me for the work Martin Milius, a regular canon and then parish priest of our monastery, a man abundantly equipped for every branch of letters. To the extent possible, I divided it in the manner of Peter Lombard, delivered it from errors—of which it was more full than a leopard of spots—and finally annotated most of the passages from authorities.

While reading, therefore, I discovered with complete certainty that Peter himself, in his four books, used our Bandinus in order. For Peter, in his fourth book, which concerns the sacraments, discusses confirmation—although only slightly, yet to some extent. If Bandinus had abridged him, as some have supposed, he would not have passed over that sacrament so completely as he did, since the subject was necessary to his purpose.

Dr. Eck appears to support our judgment in his book on the disputation held by him at Vienna, whose words I shall append below. I have recently found something similar concerning Gratian also, in order to establish the truth by an example, with due reverence nevertheless for both men. For John Hessus, the highly esteemed associate of the most reverend bishop of Wrocław and of Charles, duke of Silesia, a most learned man and my compatriot, assured me that he had heard from a certain George of Spalato, likewise most learned, secretary to the duke of Saxony, that in a monastery in Thuringia called the Valley of Saint George there was kept a book by Isidore of Seville containing synodal constitutions and judgments of the Fathers. From this, whatever Gratian was, he assembled the greater part of his *Decretum*.

After long and extensive investigation, both in histories and through the experience of the most learned men George Collimitius, doctor of medicine and astronomy; Sebastian Vunderlius, licentiate of laws; Masters Ambrosius Salser and Andrew of Mergentem; and also by letter from John Eck, I have discovered nothing concerning what man Bandinus was or what was his fortune. Unless he had left this monument of his intellect behind him, he might perhaps lie buried in eternal oblivion. Let us therefore, since we possess nothing certain concerning the author, be content with the work. It is now under the printers’ hands and, as you commanded, will come forth into public as quickly as possible. Farewell, abbot famously devoted to letters.

Given at the Scots monastery in Vienna, the first day of July 1518.

Reader, observe what the most distinguished Lord John Eck, doctor of sacred theology, thinks of Master Bandinus in the book which he published on his disputation held at Vienna. These are his words:

“We came to Medlik, the distinguished monastery of Saint Benedict. While, at our lodging, my travelling companions tended their bodies and horses, I, because of my love for humane letters, went up to the monastery to inspect its paper furnishings [its books]. There I found many manuscripts. But I was especially delighted by Master Bandinus’s theological summary. When I had read it more carefully, I discovered that, except for elegance of style, he differs little or not at all from Peter Lombard, Master of the *Sentences*; thus he treats each proposition most learnedly, and even in the same order as the Master.

“For I immediately compared book with book, and in more than one place. Consequently, no small doubt arose in me as to which of them was the cuckoo, passing off another’s offspring as his own.

[Note: [Col. 0969] “This doubt as to which of these two owed his work to the other is resolved by a codex of Upper Altaich (*Ober-Altaich*), written in the thirteenth century, large quarto, in which Bandinus’s work is clearly and affirmatively called ‘An abridgment, faithfully made, of the Book on the Sacraments of Master Peter, Bishop of Paris.’” D. B. PEZIUS, Dissertation in vol. I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, pp. XLV–XLVII.—See the literary notice prefixed to the works of Peter Lombard, in the preceding volume, col. 22. PATRISTIC EDITION.]

“For Peter has for so many centuries been accepted as the certain and principal author of this summary. Bandinus’s codex, on the other hand, is extremely ancient, kept in a most ancient monastery, and composed in such a form that one might more easily have added something than removed something.”

Thus Eck.

[Col. 0969]

# Master Bandinus’s Book on the Most Holy Trinity, Which Is the First Book of the *Sentences*

*Outline (Περιοχή).*—In this first book—as also in all the rest—Bandinus, a man, as his writings plainly show, thoroughly versed in sacred letters and in the reading of the orthodox Fathers, employs remarkable concision and clarity. [Col. 0971] Beginning with a general subject-matter, as it were, of the whole of Scripture, he treats as concisely and clearly as possible, in a lucid method drawn from these very sources, of the most holy Trinity: teaching that God is one in essence and three in persons; then how these persons are distinguished from one another and derive their origin one from another, while being in reality equal in eternity, greatness, and power. Finally, he briefly treats and clearly resolves various abstruse but very pleasant and no less useful questions concerning God’s knowledge, providence, predestination, power, and will.

[Col. 0971A]

## Distinction I. The General Subject-Matter of the Whole of Scripture: Things and Signs. What a Thing Is; What a Sign Is

Concerning divine things [Note: [Col. 0971D] Compare Distinction I of Peter Lombard.], desiring, with heaven’s favour, to hand down some compendium to students, we are first instructed that there are two things in which the teaching of God is chiefly concerned: namely, things and signs. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0971D] Book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 2.], “All teaching concerns either things or signs.” Things are those that are not employed for signifying something else; signs, however, are those whose use lies in signifying, such as the sacraments of both laws.

### Division of Things. The Use of the Division. What It Is to Enjoy; What Is to Be Enjoyed; What Is to Be Used; What It Is to Use

With the help of God, the Lord of knowledge, we undertake to treat these two matters: first things, then signs. Augustine says of things [Note: [Col. 0971D] Chapter 3, in the same book.]: “Some things are to be enjoyed, others are to be used, and others enjoy and use.” By the things to be enjoyed we are made blessed. These are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and yet the Trinity itself is one supreme reality.

To enjoy is to adhere in love to some thing for its own sake. This is known to apply only to the Trinity. The things to be used are those by which we are assisted so that we may adhere to the things that make us blessed: namely, the world and the creatures in it. We are to use them so that, through the things that have been made, God’s invisible things may be beheld as understood—that is, so that eternal things may be grasped from temporal things (Rom. 1). For to use is to refer what comes into one’s use to the attainment of that which is to be enjoyed. Finally, the things which enjoy and use are the holy angels [Col. 0971C] and ourselves, established as intermediaries, as it were, between the two classes.

### Whether Human Beings Are to Be Enjoyed

But it is asked whether human beings ought to enjoy one another. Augustine answers thus [Note: [Col. 0971D] Chapter 22 of *On Christian Doctrine*.]: “If a human being is to be loved for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for the sake of something else, we use him.” Therefore a human being does not seem to be loved for his own sake, because blessed life is constituted in that which is loved for its own sake and which alone we enjoy. Even its hope consoles us in this present time. But hope is not to be placed in a human being. Therefore one is not to enjoy another human being, nor even oneself.

But it is objected that the Apostle says to the Romans (15): “If I shall first have enjoyed you in part.” Certainly, “in the Lord” must be supplied, as he says to Philemon [Col. 0971D] (20): “Yes, brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord.” Finally, when you enjoy a human being in God, you enjoy God rather than the human being, as Augustine says.

[Col. 0972A]

### Whether God Enjoys Us

Likewise, it is asked whether God enjoys us. Augustine denies it [Note: [Col. 0971D] In the same Book I of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapters 31 and 32.], because he does not need our good. For the prophet says: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15). Therefore he does not enjoy us but uses us; otherwise, if he does not even use us, I do not see how he loves us. We too use one another, but otherwise than he does. For he uses us by showing mercy, so that we may fully enjoy him; but we use one another by cooperating, so that we may fully enjoy him.

### Whether the Virtues Are to Be Enjoyed

Nor are the virtues to be enjoyed, because we love that which we enjoy, as has been said, only for its own sake; but we love virtues for the sake of blessedness, not for their own sake. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0972D] *On the Trinity*, Book 13, chapter 8.]:

> “Perhaps the virtues, which we love for the sake of blessedness alone, presume so to persuade us that we do not love blessedness itself. If they do this, we certainly cease also to love the virtues themselves when we do not love that for the sake of which alone we love them.”

But against this is objected what Ambrose says in his *Letter to the Galatians* [Note: [Col. 0972D] It is not found in Ambrose’s commentaries, but in the interlinear gloss.]: “The Apostle calls these works not virtues but fruits, because they are to be sought for their own sake.” If this is so, then they are to be loved for their own sake and not merely for blessedness.

It should, however, be known that virtues are also to be loved for their own sake, because they delight their possessors piously and holily and distress them in nothing. Yet one must not stop there; rather, through them, as through certain aids, we advance further, seeking something in the attainment of which alone the end of joy and delight—namely, being blessed—is set before us. This is the supreme and unchangeable good, God the Trinity. It was in this sense that virtues were said to be loved for the sake of blessedness alone. Therefore virtues are to be used, and through them—not enjoyed as themselves—the supreme good is to be enjoyed. We say the same of the will and all the powers of the soul. Such is the division of things already set forth.

Therefore, with the help of the very one of whom we speak, let us first treat those things which are to be enjoyed: namely, the most holy and undivided Trinity.

## Distinction II. On the Most Holy Trinity

Thus, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0972D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.], this must be held with true and devout faith: that the Trinity is the one and only true God, namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This Trinity is called, believed, and understood to be of one and the same substance or essence, which is the supreme good.

[Col. 0973A]

### The Trinity Must Be Discussed Reverently

Let us treat this most excellent subject with modesty and fear; and let us hear with most attentive and devout ears. For nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing is sought with greater labour, and nothing is found more fruitfully.

Moreover, in this matter let everyone strive to imitate Augustine speaking of himself: “I shall not grow weary of inquiring wherever I hesitate; nor be ashamed to learn wherever I err.” [Note: [Col. 0973D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 3.]

### The Intention of Those Who Have Written on the Trinity

It should further be known that all Catholic writers on this subject have intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance and, in inseparable equality, one God; [Col. 0973B] so that unity in essence and plurality in persons may be taught. Therefore they are not to be believed to be several gods, but one God.

Accordingly, let us hold, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0973D] *On Faith, to Peter*.], that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet that the Father is not the same person as the Son, nor the Son the same person as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same person as either the Father or the Son.

### The Order in Which the Trinity Must Be Treated

Furthermore, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0973D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 2.], this subject must be handled in this way: first, it must be shown from the Scriptures whether faith is thus constituted; then, against the talkative, one must proceed with Catholic arguments and fitting likenesses for the assertion and defence of faith, so that by satisfying their investigations [Col. 0973C] we may instruct the modest more fully. But if the former cannot find what they seek, let them complain of themselves rather than of truth itself, or of our definition or assertion.

### Testimonies of the Old Testament Concerning Divine Unity and Trinity: Unity of Nature

Let us therefore bring forward the authorities of the Old and New Testaments, by which the truth of unity and Trinity may be demonstrated. First, let the very beginnings of the Law come before us. Moses says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, God is one” (Deut. 6). Again: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 20). Here the unity of the divine nature is asserted. For “God” and “Lord,” as Ambrose says, are names of nature and power. [Note: [Col. 0974D] Book I, *On Faith*, chapters 1 and 2.]

Again, elsewhere: “I am who I am”; and, “He who is sent me to you” (Exod. 3). By saying “I am,” not “we are,” and “he who is,” not “we who are,” he most plainly declares the unity of the divine substance.

### Trinity of Persons

The Lord also simultaneously shows plurality of persons and unity of nature when he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). For when, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0974D] *On Faith, to Peter*.], he says “let us make” and “our,” he shows that the same God has not one but several persons. But by saying “in [the] image,” he shows that there is one nature in whose image man was made.

Again, when it is written, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” [Col. 0974A] (Gen. 1), it should be known that the Hebrew text has *eloym* where “God” is written. This is the plural of the singular *el*, and is interpreted “gods” or “judges.” Therefore, because Moses said *eloym*, not *el*, he indicated the plurality of persons.

The following passage is also referred to this: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 1), for which the Hebrew again has *eloym*, as though to say: “You shall be like the divine persons.” Finally David, the greatest of prophets, “understanding above the elders” (Ps. 118), bears witness to the unity of the divine nature when he says: “The Lord is his name” (Ps. 67), not “lords.” He also intimates the distinction of persons by saying: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32); and, “May our God bless us; may God bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66). The threefold confession of God expresses [Col. 0974B] the Trinity of persons; while his addition, “him,” reveals the unity of essence. Likewise Isaiah says that the Seraphim cry: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God” (Isa. 6). By saying “holy” three times, he plainly distinguishes the Trinity; by adding “Lord God,” unity.

### Old Testament Testimonies Concerning the Son’s Eternal Generation from the Father

Moreover, David, speaking in the person of the Son, shows the divine generation in the passage: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). Concerning this Isaiah says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53). Concerning this generation Clement writes in his first letter to Bishop James: “This secret origin, together with his own Son, is known to him alone who begot him.”

God is not to be investigated by us but believed, since we do not know even within ourselves how we think: namely, how our wisdom, talent, or understanding, counsel, or mind generates a word. It is enough, then, to know that light begot radiance, as the Prophet says: “In the splendours of the saints, from the womb before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109). And elsewhere: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him” (Baruch 3).

In Wisdom also she says concerning herself: “Before the earth was made, I had already been conceived; the springs, mountains, and hills not yet existing, and I was being brought forth” (Prov. 8). Again: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24). Here are plain testimonies concerning the eternal generation.

### Testimonies Concerning the Temporal Generation

Micah, however, gives testimony to both generations of the Word, the temporal and the eternal, as follows: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah; from you shall come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5).

### Testimonies Concerning the Holy Spirit

Scripture also testifies specifically concerning the Holy Spirit in Genesis: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). And David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit?” (Ps. 138). And in Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1). And Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc. (Isa. 61).

[Col. 0975A]

### Testimonies of the New Testament Concerning the Same Matters

So that truth may be known “in the midst of two living creatures,” and a coal may be taken from the altar by tongs, to touch the mouths of the faithful, let us set forth testimonies of the New Testament also concerning the divine Trinity and unity.

Thus the Master of truth says: “Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). By saying “in the name,” not “in the names,” Ambrose says, he declares the unity of essence; by the three names which he gives, he declares that there are three persons. [Note: [Col. 0975D] Book I, *On Faith*, chapter 12.]

Again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). “He said ‘one,’” Ambrose says, “lest there be a distinction of nature or power.” [Note: [Col. 0975D] Same place.] He added “we are,” so that you may recognize the Father and Son.

John also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [Col. 0975B] (John 1), plainly showing that the Son is eternally with the Father, as one person with another. Again elsewhere: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5).

The Apostle likewise distinguishes Trinity and unity here: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory” (Rom. 11). “From him,” Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0975D] Book I, *On the Trinity*, chapter 6.], is said with reference to the Father; “through him,” with reference to the Son; “in him,” with reference to the Holy Spirit. This is the Trinity. But by not saying “to them be glory,” but “to him,” he shows that this Trinity is one God.

Since nearly every syllable of the New Testament consistently suggests this, omitting to introduce further testimonies, let us show, by arguments and fitting likenesses according to the capacity of our weakness, that it is so.

## Distinction III. The Creator Could Be Known through Creation in Three Ways

“The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1)—that is, by the human being, who, as the Apostle says, was aided by two things in knowing the invisible God: namely, rational nature and external works, in which the judgment of the artisan shines forth to some degree.

For Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 0975D] In the commentary on the Letter to the Romans, chapter 1, “That which is known of God.”]: “So that God, who is invisible by nature, might also be known from visible things, he made a work which manifested its maker by its visibility—a work impossible for a human being or any creature to make.” It is therefore evident that he who made creation is above every creature; and through this the human mind could know that he is God.

The philosophers also knew that he had made all things and had himself been made by no one. For they saw that every substance is either body or spirit; that the latter is better than the former; but that far better still is he who is the maker of both. Therefore they most rightly believed him to be the first principle of things: one who was not made and from whom all things were made.

The truth of God is known through the things that have been made in many ways; hence the Apostle speaks in the plural of “the invisible things of God” [Col. 0976A], although the divine essence is simple and one (Rom. 1). From the perpetuity of creatures God the Creator is understood to be eternal; from their magnitude, omnipotent; from their arrangement, wise; from their governance, good. Thus through all these things a human being could come to know the unity of the Godhead.

### How the Trinity may be known through creatures

An indication or trace of the Trinity could likewise be found through created things. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0976D] *On the Trinity*, Book VI, ch. 10]:

> All these things made by divine art display in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. For every created thing is one thing, is formed by some kind of shape, and seeks or maintains some order.

Behold, such a trace of the ineffable Trinity appears in creatures. For in that supreme reality the source, or unity, of all things is the Father [Col. 0976B]; the most perfect beauty of all things is the Son; and their most blessed delight is the Holy Spirit. Thus, through the things that have been made, we are aided in faith concerning invisible things.

### How the image of the Trinity is in the soul

Finally, these matters may be understood more fully in the human mind, which is an image of the Godhead. For although, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0976D] *On the Trinity*, Book XIV, ch. 8], the human mind is deformed through the loss of participation in God, the image of God nevertheless remains precisely because it is capable of Him and can participate in Him. Because it remembers itself, understands itself, and loves itself: if we discern this, we discern a Trinity. We have not yet found God, indeed, but we have found the image of God—namely memory, understanding, and will. These, therefore, are both three and one. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0976D] Book XIV, ch. 8], they are not three lives, but one life.

They are also spoken of relatively, as Augustine says. For the mind cannot love itself or remember itself unless it also knows itself. For how does it love or remember what it does not know? The same must be said of the others. But the mind itself, or life, is spoken of in relation to itself.

### How those three are equal

Accordingly, they are equal not merely each to each, but each to all. For I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; I understand that I understand, will, and remember; and I will that I will, remember, and understand.

### How those three are called one

But how are these called one mind, when they seem rather to be called powers of the mind [Col. 0976D]? Namely, because they exist substantially in the mind itself. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0976D] *On the Trinity*, Book IX, ch. 4]:

> We are instructed that these exist substantially in the soul, not as in a subject, as colour exists in a body. For although they are spoken of relatively to one another, each is nevertheless substantial in its own substance.

Thus, in a wondrous way, these three are inseparable from one another; and each one of them, and all of them together, are one substance, as has been said.

### In what respect the created Trinity differs from the uncreated Trinity

[Col. 0977A] Although through these things the created trinity is seen to resemble the uncreated Trinity, it is nevertheless unlike it in many respects, as is readily shown upon reflection. For here there is one human being who possesses these three things. Yet he himself is not these three things, nor are these three things one human being. There, however, one God is three persons, and the three persons are one God. Again, here there is only one person, whereas there are three persons there: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Finally, here none of these three is the human being; there, each of the persons is fully and perfectly God.

Therefore our mind differs greatly from the uncreated Trinity. This mind is indeed the image of God, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0977D] *On the Trinity*, Book XIV, ch. 12], not only because it remembers, understands, and loves itself, but also because it can remember, understand, and love Him by whom it was made [Col. 0977B]. By this it is able to understand unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity. For it understands that there is only one principle of things; because, if there were several, either all would be insufficient or all besides one would be superfluous. It judged that principle not to be foolish, and thus understood that wisdom exists there; and when it loves that wisdom, it rightly perceives that love also exists there. It is therefore clear how our mind resembles God, and likewise how, through it, the unity and Trinity of the Godhead could become known to humankind.

### On the unity of the Trinity. A firm argument for confirming the Trinity

Therefore, according to the signification of the things stated above, let us believe that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in nature and three in persons. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0977D] *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 1]:

> The nature or essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, but the person is not one.

For if the person were one as the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, a Trinity could not truthfully be spoken of. Likewise, the Trinity would indeed be real, but the Trinity itself would not be one God, if Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as they are distinct from one another by the property of their persons, were also differentiated by diversity of natures.

Let us therefore maintain that in that holy Trinity there is one Father, who alone begot the Son; one Son, who alone was born from the Father; and one Holy Spirit, who alone proceeds from both. All this cannot belong to one person—namely, to beget oneself, to be born from oneself, and to proceed from oneself [Col. 0977D].

## Distinction IV. Whether God may properly be called begotten

Here, then, a question arises: did God beget Himself? For it is certain that God begot God, because the Father begot the Son and each is God. The argument proceeds thus: if God begot God, then He begot either God Himself or another God. If another, there is not only one God. But if Himself, then some thing begot itself. Augustine contradicts this, saying [Note: [Col. 0977D] *On the Trinity*, Book XV, ch. 20]:

> Those who suppose it belongs to God’s power that He should have begotten Himself err the more, because not only is God not so [Col. 0978A], but neither is any creature: for there is no thing which begets itself.

Augustine nevertheless seems to oppose himself where he says [Note: [Col. 0978D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 1], “God the Father begot Himself as another.” This is rightly understood thus: that is, from Himself He begot another person; or, He begot another—namely, the Son—who is the very same thing that He is.

The analogy below, however, counters the foregoing inference—namely, “If God begot God, then either Himself as God or another”: “The Son of God began to be a human person; therefore, either the very human person He Himself is, or another.” Since both alternatives are absurd, neither is to be admitted. The same must be said of similar cases.

Yet they press the same question in different words: “God the Father begot God; therefore He begot either God who is God the Father, and so appears to have begotten Himself; or God who is not God the Father, and so appears to have begotten another God” [Col. 0978B]. Although this may be conceded in a Catholic sense, because the expression “God the Father” is not said according to substance but is personal, nevertheless, to empty out every obstinate objection, we advise that the proposition “God the Father begot God who is not God the Father” be qualified by the force of its relation. Thus, if “who” is referred simply to God, it produces a false statement; but if it is referred to the begotten God, it appropriately gives a true statement. For God the Father is the same God as the begotten God; nevertheless, God the Father is not the begotten God, since otherwise one person would be another—which be far from us.

## Distinction V. Whether the divine essence may properly be called begotten [Col. 0978C] or said to have begotten

The next question is whether the Father begot the divine essence, whether the essence itself begot the Son, whether essence begot essence, or whether none of these is so.

That the Father begot the divine essence seems to follow from Augustine’s words: “When God begot the Word, He begot that which He Himself is” [Note: [Col. 0978D] In Letter 66 to Maximinus the physician]. Again: “God the Father, who both willed and was able most truly to make Himself known to minds capable of knowing Him, begot, in order to make Himself known, that which He Himself is who begot.” But He Himself is nothing other than the divine essence; therefore He seems to have begotten it.

But we say that the foregoing statements must be understood thus: the Father begot that which He is—that is, the Son, who is what the Father is, though not the one who is Father. For the Father is one, the Son another, but they are not another thing.

### Proof that the essence was not begotten

[Col. 0978D] That the Father did not beget the divine essence is proved in three ways. First: if He begot it, He is said relatively to it. But if this is so, the name “divine essence” does not signify substance. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0978D] *On Catholic Faith and the Creed*, ch. 3]: “What is said relatively does not signify substance.”

Second: if He begot it, then, since He Himself is the divine essence, He begot Himself—the impossibility of which has already been stated.

Third: if He begot it, the begotten would be the cause of the begetter, rather than the begetter the cause of the begotten, in order that the Father might be and might be God; for the divine essence is God the Father and is, and is God.

Likewise, it must be said [Col. 0979A] that the divine essence did not beget the Son, because it is not said relatively to Him.

Nor did essence beget essence, for the reason already given: the same thing does not generate itself. Yet Augustine appears to oppose what we say. He writes [Note: [Col. 0979D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book VII, chs. 1–2]: “As essence from essence, so wisdom from wisdom.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0979D] In *On Faith, to Peter*]: “Believe Christ, the Son of God, to be true God, so that you may not doubt that His divinity was born from the Father’s nature.”

These statements, and any similar ones, must be understood thus: “as essence from essence,” and so forth—that is, as the Son, who is essence, is from the essence of the Father, so the Son, who is wisdom, is from the Father, who is wisdom. That this is the proper explanation may be inferred from Augustine’s words: “Christ is called the power and wisdom of God because, from the Father who is power and wisdom, He too is power and wisdom” [Col. 0979B; Note: [Col. 0979D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 3].

Hilary also seems to state the contrary [Note: [Col. 0979D] *On the Trinity*, Book IV, near the beginning]: “The Son possesses nothing except what is begotten.” But the Son also possesses the divine essence—for it is wholly in Him—and therefore that essence too appears to be begotten. He says more plainly [Note: [Col. 0979D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, and Book IX, ch. 2]:

> We do not proclaim the Father to be in the Son by a bodily insinuation, but [proclaim] that a nature begotten from Him, of the same kind, has naturally in itself the nature that begot it.

Behold: by these words he manifestly says that God’s nature was begotten and begot. Yet, as he himself says [Note: [Col. 0979D] About the middle of Book IV], the meaning of statements must be taken from the reasons for making them. For the thing is not subject to speech, but speech is subject to the thing.

These words may therefore be received faithfully as follows. “The Son possesses nothing except what is begotten”: that is, the Son possesses nothing, inasmuch as He is God, except what He received by being born [Col. 0979C]. Again, “we proclaim a nature begotten from Him, of the same kind,” and so forth: that is, we proclaim that the Father, who is nature, is naturally in the Begotten—that is, in the Son begotten by Him—who is the same nature that the Father is. Hence Hilary says: “The Begotten has the same nature as He who begot Him” [Note: [Col. 0979D] Book V of the same work].

### What it means to say that the Father begot the Son from His own substance

One frequently encounters the statement that the Father begot the Son from His own nature. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0979D] *On Faith, to Peter*; *On the Trinity*, Book XV, ch. 19, near the end; [Col. 0980D]]: “God the Father, begotten from no God, once begot God the Son from His own nature without beginning.”

Again, Augustine, on the words “Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of His love,” says: “The phrase ‘the Son of His love’ means nothing other than His most beloved Son, that is, the Son of His substance” [Col. 0979D]. For the Father’s love, which is in His nature, is nothing other than that nature and substance itself; and therefore the Son of His love is He who was begotten from His substance.

Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Against Maximinus*, Book III, ch. 14] that the substance of God begot the Son:

> Filled with carnal thoughts, you do not suppose that the substance of God begets the Son from itself unless it undergoes what the substance of flesh undergoes when it begets. You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matt. 22).

These words plainly seem to say that the nature or substance of God begot the Son. But lest these and similar statements be vessels of death for us rather than vessels of life, we warn that they should always be brought back to the straightforward sense which is a friend of truth. Without prejudice, then, we say that what seems to be said of nature or substance must be referred to the persons. The authors expressed these matters not by names of the persons but by the name of nature itself, thereby teaching us that the three persons are of the same nature and substance, and, as Hilary says, are immutably and individually three. Hence Augustine says in the same work: “This Trinity is of one and the same substance” [Note: [Col. 0980D] *Against Maximinus*, Book III].

[Col. 0980B]

## Distinction VI. Whether the Father begot willingly or unwillingly. The Father begot by nature

The further question is whether the Father begot the Son by will or by necessity; whether God begot unwillingly or willingly.

That He begot by will appears capable of proof as follows: the Father’s nature and His will are identical. But you concede that nature begot; therefore will also begot. Yet this is easily refuted by an analogous case. For His knowledge and will are likewise identical; but it does not follow that whatever happens with His knowledge also happens with His will.

Nor did He beget by necessity, because, as Augustine says, it would be great misery and absurdity to assert that God begot by necessity [Note: [Col. 0980D] *On the Trinity*, Book XV, ch. 20]. We therefore say that He begot neither willingly nor unwillingly—plainly in the sense of a will preceding or following the begetting, as Eunomius supposed [Note: [Col. 0980D] Also in *To Orosius*, 4, vol. IV; Dialogue 65, *Questions*, 4, 7].

For the will to beget in the Father and the Begotten Himself existed together from eternity, as Augustine says: “The Son of God was always with the Father, nor did the Father’s will precede Him so that He might exist” [Col. 0980C; Note: [Col. 0980D] As above]. According to this meaning, then, we say that the Son is Son not by will but by nature; and as the Father is God by nature, not by will, so also are the Son and the Holy Spirit.
