Because Eunomius could not understand this and would not believe it, he called the only-begotten Son of God a Son not of nature but of will. Augustine says that this dialectic is indeed to be ridiculed [Note: [Col. 0980D] *On the Trinity*, Book XV, ch. 20]. Therefore it must be maintained that the Father did not beget the Son by will, because the will to beget the Son did not precede Him; nor by necessity, lest we speak absurdly of God; but He begot by nature. For, as Hilary says [Col. 0980D], the Son is Son by nature, since He possesses the same nature as He who begot Him.

## Distinction VII

Since, as has been said, Father and Son are one and the same essence, it must likewise be held that the power of each is one and the same. For there, to be is altogether identical with to be able. Hence it is certain that whatever the Father can do, the Son can do as well.

But a difficult question arises on this point. If the Son can do whatever the Father can do [Col. 0981A], then the Son can beget, because the Father can do this. This is disproved by an analogy: whatever the Father is, the Son also is; therefore the Son is Father, because the Father is Father. This does not follow, because being Father is not for the Father to be something, but to be related to something. Accordingly, perhaps it may be said without irreverence that the Father’s ability to beget is not His ability to be something. For, as “Father” is relative, so also is “to beget.”

The question is pressed more strongly by Augustine’s words against the heretic Maximinus, who maintained that the Father was more powerful than the Son because the Father could beget and did beget the Son, God the Creator, whereas the Son could not. Augustine replies [Note: [Col. 0981D] Book III, ch. 12]:

> Far be it that the Father should be more powerful than the Son, as you suppose, because the Father begot the Creator whereas the Son did not beget the Creator. For it was not that He could not, but that it was not fitting.

If you consider this carefully, he seems to say that the Son could have begotten, but that it was not fitting. Why, then, was it not fitting? Augustine adds:

> Divine generation would be unrestrained if the begotten Son begot a grandson for the Father. For that grandson likewise, unless he begot a great-grandson for his grandfather, would, according to your wonderful wisdom, be called powerless. Similarly, unless that one begot a grandson for his grandfather and a great-grandson for his great-grandfather, you would not call him omnipotent. Nor would the succession of generation be completed if one were always born from another. For no one would bring it to completion, unless one omnipotent being were sufficient. [Col. 0981B]

We therefore think that the preceding statement, “For it was not that He could not, but that it was not fitting,” should be understood thus: the Son did not beget, not through incapacity, but because it did not befit Him, for the reason already stated. Just as the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father, nor can either be so. This does not result from the incapacity of either, but because it does not befit the Father to be the Son or the Son to be the Father.

Augustine says, in reply to Maximinus asking why the Father cannot be the Son or the Son the Father [Note: [Col. 0982D] Augustine, *To Maximinus*]:

> Certainly not from incapacity; but the Father is Father by the property of generation, by which it is fitting that He not be the Son; and the Son is Son by the property of birth, by which it is fitting that He not be the Father.

Thus the Father begets, not through incapacity, but by the property of generation, by which it is fitting that He not be begotten [Col. 0981D]. And the Son is begotten by the property of birth, by which it is fitting that He not beget.

### The Son could not beget

Finally, it is proved that the Son could not beget. For if He could beget, He could be Father. But if He could be Father, He would be father either of the Father, of Himself, of the Holy Spirit, or of another. He could not be father of another, because no other could have existed from eternity. Nor could He be father of the Father, because the Father is unbegotten and incapable of being born; nor of Himself, because no thing can generate itself; nor of the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit cannot be born, otherwise He would be mutable. It remains, therefore, that the Son could not beget.

### How Father and Son possess the same power

[Col. 0982A] The question set forth must therefore be resolved as follows: whatever the Father can do, the Son also can do—that is, whatever is subject to the Father’s power is likewise subject to the Son’s power, because their power is altogether the same. By things subject to power we mean those things which follow from that power. But generation, or begetting, neither precedes nor follows power, for it exists with it from eternity.

But if it is granted that being able to beget is being able to do something, the objection is made: the Father has this ability which the Son does not have; therefore the Father has some ability which the Son does not have. The reply is by analogy: the Father has this being which the Son does not have—namely, being Father; therefore the Father has some being which the Son does not have. This is false. For all and the whole being of the Father is altogether also the being of the Son [Col. 0982B].

We say, then, that the power of Father and Son is precisely the same, although not everything said of the Father is said of the Son in the same respect. This is clear in an analogous example. The same marriage wholly belongs to these two persons; yet in respect of it the man is called husband and not wife, whereas the woman is called wife and not husband. Or, to state it more plainly: the will of the Father and Son is altogether the same; yet the Father wills that the Father be Father, and not the Son; and the Son wills that the Son be Son, and not the Father. Thus the power of Father and Son is the same; yet the Father can beget and not be begotten, while the Son can be begotten and not beget.

Nor is it unsound if someone says that the Father’s ability to beget is spoken of not from power alone [Col. 0982C], but also from the property of generation. Since this does not belong to the Son, it is no wonder if the ability to beget does not belong to Him.

### In what sense the Son has the power of begetting

But if it is said, “The Son has the power of begetting,” distinguish the statement thus. “He has the power of begetting,” that is, to beget or to be able to beget: this is false. But He has the power of begetting by which He is begotten, or can be begotten.

It is true impersonally. Thus, “You have knowledge of writing,” meaning knowledge by which you know how to write, is false; but meaning knowledge by which writing is known, it is true.

We also say that in the course of the foregoing objection—“Whatever the Father can do, the Son also can do; but the Father can beget; therefore [Col. 0982D] the Son can beget”—the word “can” is understood differently in the major proposition than in the assumption or conclusion. So the words “God” and “is,” placed in different contexts, signify differently. For example: “Everything that God the Father is, God the Son is; but the Father is God begetting; therefore the Son is God begetting.” This does not follow. Likewise: “Whatever the Father is, the Son also is; but the Father is begetting; therefore the Son is begetting.” This does not follow. The reason is that the words “God” and “is” signify essentially in the propositions, but thereafter signify personally as well.

Thus the foregoing question is resolved in many ways. It is truly believed and understood that the Son cannot beget but can be begotten, whereas the Father can beget [Col. 0983A] but cannot be begotten.

## Distinction VIII. On the truth of the divine essence

We must now discuss the truth of the divine essence. God is therefore, without doubt, substance—or, more properly, essence—which the Greeks call **οὐσία** (*ousia*, “essence”). For just as *sapientia* (“wisdom”) is derived from *sapere* (“to be wise”), and *scientia* (“knowledge”) from *scire* (“to know”), so *essentia* (“essence”) is derived from *esse* (“to be”).

And who is greater than Him who said, “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3)? He, I say, is truly and properly said to be, whose essence knows neither past nor future. Hence Jerome writes to Marcella [Note: [Col. 0983D] Jerome touches on this there, and also writes to Damasus; but the wording is found in Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VII, ch. 1]:

> God alone, who has no beginning, possesses the name of true essence. For that of which it is said, “was,” is not; and that of which it is said, “will be,” is not yet. But God simply is: He does not know to have been or to be going to be.

Therefore God alone truly is; in comparison with whose essence our being is nothing [Col. 0983B].

Yet the statements frequently found in Scripture seem to stand against this: “God was from eternity,” “was always,” “and will be for ages,” and others of this kind. Augustine too says, commenting on John [Note: [Col. 0983D] Tractate 99 on John 16]:

> Although “is” is properly said of an everlasting reality, according to our manner of speech “was” and “will be” are rightly said. He was, because He never ceased; He will be, because He will never cease; He is, because He always is. He has not passed away, as though He did not remain; nor will He be, as though He was not—which is not said of us in this way.

Understanding Jerome according to these words, we say: “He does not know to have been or to be going to be,” that is, He has not passed away and will not cease to be; but He simply is, because He always is [Col. 0983C].

For although substantive verbs of different tenses are said of God, they do not distinguish temporal movements but simply indicate the essence of the Godhead. God alone, therefore, is properly and naturally called essence or being. Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 0983D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, near the beginning]: “Being is not an accident in God, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the property of His natural kind.”

### God is immutable

The essence of God is properly immutable, because it neither changes nor can be changed. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0984D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 2]:

> Other essences or substances admit accidents through which change occurs in them. But none of these can happen to God; and therefore His substance or essence alone is immutable.

### Every creature is mutable

Accordingly, the Apostle says of God, “who alone has immortality” (1 Tim. 6), meaning that immutability which no creature can possess, since it belongs to the Creator alone. Hence the Apostle James says: “With whom there is no change or shadow of turning” (Jas. 1). And David: “You will change them, and they shall be changed; but You are the same” (Ps. 101). And elsewhere: “I am God and I do not change” (Mal. 3).

But every creature is subject to mutability, which, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0984D] *Against Maximinus*, Book III, ch. 12], is a kind of death to the creature itself, because it causes something in it not to be which previously was. Even the human soul, though immortal because in its own mode it never ceases to live, nevertheless has its own death: if it lived righteously and sins, it dies to righteousness; if it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin—to say nothing of its other changes. Even the nature of heavenly creatures could die, because it could sin. For some angels sinned, and those who did not sin could have sinned. But nothing of this kind can happen to God. Therefore, since God alone is properly immutable, He alone is truly immortal.

[Col. 0984B]

### The simplicity of God

The same divine essence is properly and truly simple, because in it there is no diversity, variation, or multiplicity of parts, accidents, or any forms whatsoever. This does not occur in any creature. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0984D] *On the Trinity*, Book VI, ch. 6]:

> A bodily creature consists of parts, so that one part is greater and another less, and the whole itself is greater than any part. In it, moreover, magnitude is one thing, colour another, shape another; all these make multiplicity in a body.

A spiritual creature likewise is multiple. For although the soul, in comparison with the body, is simple, because it is not spread part by part through regions of space but is wholly present wherever it is [Col. 0984C], nevertheless true simplicity is not found even in it. For being skilled is one thing, being dull another, being keen another, being mindful another; and since these and innumerable other qualities can be found in the soul’s nature, it is clear that the soul is not simple but multiple, since none of these things is the soul itself, but the soul possesses them.

Finally, whatever is in God is God; and thus His simplicity is evident, especially since the possessor and what He possesses are the same. For we do not call the nature of the highest good simple merely because the Father alone is in it, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone—that is, because this trinity of names, or subsistence of persons, is alone—as the Sabellians thought [Note: [Col. 0984D] Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XI, ch. 10]. Rather, it is called simple because it is what it possesses, except in those things in which each person is spoken of relatively to another and is not that other.

For the Father has the Son, to whom He is related, yet He is not the Son. And the Son has the Father, yet He Himself is not the Father. But in that in which He is said in relation to Himself, not in relation to another, He is what He possesses. Thus He is called living by possessing life, and that very life is Himself—something which does not occur in other things. For that which possesses liquid is not liquid; nor is a body colour; nor is the soul wisdom [Col. 0985A], but only its possessor. Accordingly, God alone is truly and properly simple.

### God is spoken of in many ways

Yet God is spoken of in many ways: as wisdom, justice, prudence, holiness, and whatever else may worthily be said of God. This is because God operates in things in diverse ways, not because there is any multiplicity in Him. For although the underlying reality, God, is one, He is named by many terms in accordance with the variety of meanings.

Wisdom signifies one thing, knowledge another, justice another, and so with the rest. God is wisdom because He instructs concerning the disciplines of divine and human things; He is justice when He is understood as judge and distributor of merits; He is prudence when He is known as the doctrine or discernment of good and evil, true and false, or neutral things [Col. 0985B]. Further, He is holiness because He is the foundation and confirmation of all things.

These and similar predicates of God must be understood apart from any reference to accidents. Augustine likewise warns us [Note: [Col. 0985D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 1]:

> Let us understand, as far as we can, God as good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, presiding without position, containing all things without circumference, wholly everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without undergoing change in Himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this manner, even if he has not yet altogether found what God is, nevertheless piously takes care not to think something of Him which He is not.

### God’s simplicity is so great that He is subject to no category

[Col. 0985C] Therefore God is subject neither to the laws of the categories nor to accidents. Hence He is not properly called substance. For we call *substantia* from *subsistere* (“to subsist”), which is rightly said of those things in which there are subjects and things said to exist in a subject, as colour in a body; but it is impious to say this of God. Therefore God is called substance only improperly; more properly and truly, He is and is called essence.

## Distinction IX. On the personal properties of Trinity and unity

Now, turning to the distinction of persons, we must confess that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father. For since the Son was begotten by the Father, the Father is certainly one, and the Son another [Col. 0985D; Note: [Col. 0985D] Augustine, *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 1].

### On the Son’s coeternity with the Father

Yet the Father did not exist before the Son, as the heretic falsely alleges; for the three persons are coeternal with one another. Scripture says: “Before me no other God was, nor shall there be after me” (Isa. 43). If these are the Father’s words, He says that there is no other God after Him; if they are the Son’s, He says that there is no God before Him. Thus neither has one before Him nor the other one after Him.

Further, if the Father existed before He had the Son [Col. 0986A], then the addition of generation changed the Father; this is blasphemy [Note: [Col. 0985D] Ambrose, *On Faith to Gratian*, Book II, ch. 5, about the middle]. Again, since the Son is the wisdom and power of the Father, if the Father was at some time without the Son, then the Father was also at that time without His wisdom and power—something no less irreverent than foolish to say [Note: [Col. 0986D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, ch. 1].

### An apt comparison

It is certain that the Son is coeternal with the Father, just as the radiance diffused from fire is coeval with it and would indeed be coeternal if the fire were eternal. But this, like the generation itself, is ineffable. Hence Isaiah says: “Who shall declare His generation?” (Isa. 53). He means the divine generation, not the human, although the latter too is in large measure beyond expression. The former, however, is wholly beyond expression, because, although the Son is said to be begotten by the Father, neither apostle nor prophet nor angel knows in what manner [Col. 0986B].

### Whether the Son should be said always to be begotten, or always to have been begotten

The question is raised whether it should be said, “The Son is always being born.” Gregory says of this [Note: [Col. 0986D] *Morals*, Book XXIX, ch. 1]:

> We cannot say of the Lord Jesus, “He is always being born,” lest He appear imperfect. But in order that He may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both “always” and “born,” so that “born” pertains to perfection and “always” to eternity.

### Origen appears to contradict the foregoing

Origen, however, appears to contradict these words [Note: [Col. 0986D] *On Jeremiah*, Homily VI, on ch. 11 throughout: “They returned”]:

> Our Saviour is the radiance of glory. He is not born once and then ceases, but arises as often as the light from which He is born has arisen. Thus the Saviour is always being born [Col. 0986C].

### Reconciling Origen and Gregory

Reconciling the apparent disagreement of such great men in so great a matter, we think that each author found something objectionable in ordinary usage of speech. For when we say, “The reading is always being read,” ordinary usage indicates the incompleteness of the reading; Gregory, denying this of the Only-begotten, says, “We cannot say, ‘He is always being born.’” He clearly shows that this is what he meant by adding, “lest He appear imperfect.”

Similarly, when a reading has been read, we say, “I read it long ago, but have now ceased to read it”; by our way of speaking we signify this. Origen, rejecting such a sense in the birth of the Word, asserts its perpetuity by saying, “The Saviour is always being born.” He plainly makes this clear when he first states, “He is not born once and then ceases” [Col. 0986D].

Therefore, while employing different modes of speech in order to exclude different errors, they affirm that the Son’s birth is from eternity both perfect and everlasting.

But, says the heretic, everything that has been born has not always existed, because it was born in order that it might exist. To him we say: no one doubts that this holds true in human matters. There, indeed, neither was he who is father always in existence, nor is he who once came to be father always father. Therefore neither has he always begotten. But where there is always a father, there is always a son [Col. 0987A; Note: [Col. 0987D] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book XII, gives this answer].

What is proper to the Father and to the Son. — If, then, it is always proper to God the Father that he is always Father, it must always be proper to the Son that he is always begotten. Therefore we confess the Only-Begotten as begotten: neither existing before he was begotten, nor begotten before he existed. This indeed surpasses human sense and worldly understanding; human reason cannot comprehend it, but it is the profession of faithful wisdom.

DISTINCTION X. On the personal procession of the Holy Spirit. — Let us now, with his own granting, discuss the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit, then, is the love or affection of the Father and the Son, by which each is united to the other; by which the Begotten is loved by the Begetter, and loves his Begetter. They are so not by participation but by their own essence; nor by the gift of some superior being, but by their own gift, “preserving the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). For he is not the Spirit of the Father alone or of the Son alone, but of both. And therefore they make known to us the charity by which they love one another in common. [Note: [Col. 0987D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 5.]

The Holy Spirit is properly called charity. The whole Trinity is charity. — He is properly called charity, because, since he is that by which the Father and Son mutually love one another, he manifests their ineffable communion. What, therefore, is more fitting than that he should properly be called charity who is the Spirit common to both? [Note: [Col. 0987D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 16.] Yet we do not say this in such a way as to deny that the Father and Son are charity. For just as the only Word of God is properly called wisdom, although both the Holy Spirit and the Father are, in common, wisdom itself, so the Holy Spirit is properly termed charity, although the Father and Son are in common charity. The Word is called wisdom by the Apostle, who says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 8). Likewise, the Holy Spirit is called charity in John’s epistle; for he says: “God is charity” (1 John 4). Augustine clearly proves that this is properly to be understood of the Holy Spirit.

The third person is properly called the Holy Spirit. — Moreover, he himself is properly called the Holy Spirit. For although the Father and Son are Spirit, and each is holy, it is nevertheless not without reason that he himself is properly called the Holy Spirit. For he who is common to both is deservedly called, in a proper sense, what both are in common. [Note: [Col. 0988D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 17.]

DISTINCTION XI. That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. — He who is the Spirit of the Father and the Son proceeds from both, as is proved by the testimonies of Scripture. For the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4). And elsewhere: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). The Son himself also testifies concerning him thus: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. 18). And elsewhere: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15). From these and similar passages it is evident that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son—a fact which many heretics have denied.

What the Greeks think. The principal councils determined concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. — The Greeks, however, do not acknowledge that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, being led by the following arguments: namely, that when Truth says, “the Spirit who proceeds from the Father,” he mentions the Father’s name alone and not the Son’s. Likewise, in their Creed the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, but not also from the Son. These statements, I say, were made in the principal councils, with anathemas appended, in such a way that no one is permitted to teach or preach anything other concerning the faith of the Trinity than what is contained there. Hence they even dare to charge with the bond of anathema those whom they know confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

The author’s confession concerning the procession of the Spirit. — But we, confessing this eternally, certainly confess the Truth—that the Spirit proceeds from the Father—yet we do not confess that he so proceeds from him as to deny that he proceeds also from the Son.

He answers the first objection of the Greeks. — The reason why he names the Father alone is that he is accustomed to say that what is his is not his own, but to refer it to the Father, as where he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7). He says this, certainly, not in denying it of himself, but in showing that the authority of the principle is in the Father.

[Col. 0988C] He answers the second objection. — The other point which they make [Note: [Col. 0988D] In the councils of the Greeks.] must be understood by its contrary, so that the sense is: “No one may say anything else,” that is, anything contrary. Thus the Apostle writes to the Galatians: “If anyone,” he says, “should preach another gospel”—that is, a contrary gospel, as Augustine explains—“let him be anathema” (Gal. 1). He did not say, “if anyone should add,” otherwise he would have prejudiced himself, since he wished to come to certain persons in order to supply what was lacking in their faith. But one who supplies what was said insufficiently does not say something contrary to what was said.

It should certainly be known that, although in the present matter the Greeks disagree with us in wording, they do not differ in meaning. For they confess that the Spirit is the Son’s, although not that he proceeds from the Son, because it is written: “the Spirit of the Son” (Gal. 4). But we faithfully believe it to be one and the same thing: that the Spirit is the Son’s and that he proceeds from him.

Even by the testimony of the Greeks themselves it is taught that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. — This is proved by the testimony of Greek teachers. For Athanasius says in the Creed: “The Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is not made, nor created, nor begotten.” Likewise Christ says: “For he will not speak from himself, because he will receive from what is mine” (John 16).

Likewise Cyril [Note: [Col. 0988D] In the letter addressed to Nestorius.]: “The Spirit is not alien to the Son; for he is called the Spirit of truth, and flows forth from him, as from God the Father.” [Col. 0989A] Likewise Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 0989D] In a certain homily on the exposition of the Creed.]: “We say that the Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son.” Thus, with the Greeks corrected by the testimony of their own teachers, let every tongue confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

DISTINCTION XII. Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds earlier or more fully from the Father than from the Son. — Yet he does not proceed earlier and later from either of them, as the heretic raves. For in that supreme Trinity there are no intervals of time, without which there can be no earlier and later at all. Nor does he proceed more fully from one than from the other, because, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, so he proceeds from the Son.

Wherever it is read that he proceeds properly or principally from the Father, this is said in the sense that the Father has from no other but from himself that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. Thus Jerome [Note: [Col. 0989D] In the exposition of the Catholic faith.] uses “properly”: “We believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, who is from the Father and proceeds.” Augustine [Note: [Col. 0989D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 17.] uses “principally” in these words: “Not without reason in this Trinity is none called the Word of God except the Son, none the gift of God except the Holy Spirit, and none the one from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally except God the Father.”

But he himself explains that this is to be understood as we have said, when he adds: “I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father gave this also to him; whereas no one gave this to the Father.” Therefore he confesses that the Spirit proceeds principally from the Father.

On the difference between the Son’s procession from the Father and that of the Holy Spirit. — The Son also proceeds from the Father, as he himself testifies: “I proceeded from God and came into the world” (John 8). Yet he proceeds differently from the Holy Spirit. For the Holy Spirit, as Augustine says, proceeds from the Father not as born, but as given or as gift. The Son, however, proceeds by being born and goes forth as begotten. Between this procession and that one, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0989D] *Against Maximinus*.], “I do not know how to distinguish; I cannot do it; I am unable. For both are ineffable.” For just as the prophet, speaking of the Son, says, “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53), so of the Holy Spirit it may most truly be said: “Who shall declare his procession?”

[Col. 0989D] DISTINCTION XIII. Why the Holy Spirit is not called begotten or Son. — Finally, although the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, he is nevertheless called neither begotten of both nor Son. For no one is called the son of two persons except of a father and mother. Far be it from us to suppose anything of that sort between God the Father and God the Son!

The question whether the Holy Spirit may be called unbegotten. — The Holy Spirit, however, is not called unbegotten. Hence Augustine writes to Orosius: “The certain faith declares that the Holy Spirit is to be called neither begotten nor unbegotten.” Although we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, we nevertheless do not dare to call him unbegotten, lest in this term someone suppose either two fathers in that Trinity or two who are not from another. Jerome, however, seems to disagree. [Note: [Col. 0989D] In the rules of definitions against heretics.] For he says: “The Holy Spirit is not Father, but unbegotten and unmade.”

Solution by a distinction. — Yet each of them used the word *unbegotten* in a different sense. Augustine [Note: [Col. 0990D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 26.] calls unbegotten that which is not from another, as he makes clear when he says, “or two who are not from another.” Jerome, however, calls unbegotten that which is not born, as is proved by the universal division of things which he sets forth. “Everything that exists,” he says, “is either unbegotten, made, or begotten.” Pursuing this in discussion, he explains what he had called unbegotten as “not born,” adding the Holy Spirit as an example.

DISTINCTION XIV. On the twofold procession of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit himself is given to us. — The Holy Spirit proceeds both eternally, jointly from the Father and the Son, and temporally, likewise jointly from both, in order to sanctify the creature. That is, when he is poured into human souls and enters into their faculties in order to sanctify them, as the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5).

For the Holy Spirit himself—the third person in the Trinity himself—is given to us, as Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0990D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 26.]: “We ought not to doubt that the same Holy Spirit was given when Jesus breathed upon the disciples, concerning whom he immediately said: ‘Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit’” (John 21). And below, concerning the same: “How, then, is he not God who gives the Holy Spirit? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God? Though inaccessible in nature, he is nevertheless receivable by us because of his goodness, filling all things with his power; yet he is shared only by the righteous.”

And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0990D] Ambrose, in the book *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 5.]: “Angels were sent to few persons; but the Holy Spirit was poured out upon peoples. Who then can doubt that what is poured out upon many at once and is not seen is divine?” Augustine also says [Col. 0990D] [Note: [Col. 0990D] *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon 3.]: “Great is the mercy of him who gives a gift equal to himself, because his gift is the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore these and many other authorities clearly show that the Holy Spirit himself, not merely his gifts, is given to us—something which certain people, misled by Bede’s authority, refuse to believe. For he says [Note: [Col. 0990D] Homily for the Sunday after the Ascension.]: “When the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to human beings, the Holy Spirit is certainly sent and proceeds from the Father and the Son, because his mission is his very procession.” To this we answer that either he ought not to bring prejudice against such great authorities, or what he says must indeed be understood differently. Thus the Holy Spirit is sent and given to us; yet he is not thereby to be judged inferior because the Father and the Son send him. [Note: [Col. 0991D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book IV, final chapter.]

Whether the Holy Spirit is given by human beings. — Moreover, it should be known that the Holy Spirit is not given by human beings. For, since his giving has above been called procession, if the Holy Spirit were given by human beings, the Creator would surely proceed from, or be sent by, a creature—which is absurd. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0991D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*.]: “No disciple of Christ gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they themselves did not give him. The Church still observes this custom in her bishops.” And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0991D] *Ibid.*]: “We can indeed receive this gift according to our measure, but certainly cannot pour it out upon others. Rather, in order that this may happen, we call upon God, who accomplishes it, over them.”

But the Apostle’s statement concerning himself is raised as an objection: “He who supplies the Spirit and works miracles among you” (Gal. 3). Yet this must be understood as said by the Apostle not by an authority of power, but by the ministry of preaching. For while he preached to them, they had visibly received the Holy Spirit. Faith had been preached to them by the Apostle, and in that preaching they had perceived the Holy Spirit’s coming. For at the new invitation to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit was also made manifest by perceptible miracles.

[Col. 0991C] DISTINCTION XV. That the Holy Spirit gives himself. — The Holy Spirit also gives himself. For, since the giving of the Holy Spirit is an operation of God, and the operation of the three persons is common and undivided, the Holy Spirit is surely given not only by the Father and the Son but also by himself. Augustine says of this [Note: [Col. 0991D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 19.]: “The Holy Spirit is given as God’s gift in such a way that he also gives himself as God. Nor can it be said that he is not in his own power, of whom it is said: ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills.’” Thus it is evident that the Holy Spirit is given by himself.

On the mission of the Son also by himself. — Here it should be considered that, although there are three persons in the Trinity, the Father alone is nowhere read to have been sent, but the Son and the Holy Spirit are. The Son was sent by the Father, as the Apostle says: “God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4), where he sufficiently shows that the Son was sent precisely by being made of a woman. He was sent by the Holy Spirit, as Isaiah says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord anointed me; he sent me to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim release to captives” (Isa. 61). And he was sent by himself as well. For Isaiah has: “A Son has been given to us” (Isa. 9). Since the prophet does not specify by whom the Son was given, he is shown to have been given by the grace of the Trinity. Hence the Son himself also gave himself, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0991D] *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 6.]:

“Since the Father and the Son have one will and an inseparable operation, therefore the same Son was sent by the Father and the Son, without the Holy Spirit being separated; because it was brought about by the Father and his Word that he should be sent—that is, that, incarnate, he should appear to human beings.”

But if this is so, why does he say, “I did not come of myself” (John 8)? This was said according to the form of a servant, according to which he did not cause himself to be sent—that is, he did not effect the incarnation—but according to the form of God.

The Son is said to be sent in two ways. — Finally, Augustine distinguishes two ways in which the Son is sent, saying [Note: [Col. 0992D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 20.]: “The Son is not said to be sent merely because he was born of the Father, but either because he appeared to this world, the Word having been made flesh. Hence he says: ‘I went out from the Father and came into the world’ (John 16); or because he is apprehended in time by someone’s mind, as was said of Wisdom: ‘Send her out from your holy heavens, and from the throne of your majesty, that she may be with me and labor with me’” (Wis. 9).

Augustine’s words explained. — According to the first mode, then, he was sent once, into this world, and in order that he might be human. According to the other, he is sent often: not into this world, nor in order to become human, but in order to be with a human being. Augustine makes this clear, saying [Note: [Col. 0992D] *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. 20.]: “He is sent in one way in order that he may be with a human being; the Wisdom of the Father was sent in another way in order that she might be human. For she passes into holy souls and makes them friends of God. But when the fullness of time came, she was sent not in order to be with human beings, as she had formerly been with the patriarchs and prophets, but in order that the Word himself might become flesh, that is, human.”

DISTINCTION XVI. Insofar as the Son is human, he is less than the Father, the Holy Spirit, and himself. — Finally, insofar as he was made human, the Son is less than the Father. For he himself says: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14). Truth says this because of the form of a servant, according to which he is also said to be less than the Holy Spirit and than himself. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0992D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 1.]:

“He did not receive the form of a servant in such a way as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father. Therefore, in the form of God, the Only-Begotten of the Father is equal to the Father; but in the form of a servant, he is even less than himself—that is, the Son of God, equal to the Father according to the form in which he exists, is according to the form which he received found less not only than the Father, but also than the Holy Spirit, indeed even than himself. Nor only this: he was also made somewhat lower than the angels.”

That the Father is greater than the Son, and yet the Son is not less than the Father. — Hilary [Note: [Col. 0992D] Book IX, *On the Trinity*.], however, appears to say that even according to the form of God the Father is greater than the Son because of the authority of generation, yet that the Son is not less than the Father. His words are these:

“Certainly the Father is greater than the Son by the authority of the one giving, since he gives him to be as great as he himself is; he imparts to him, by the mystery of birth, the image of unbegottenness, whom he begets from himself in his own form. Thus the giver is greater, but the one to whom one being is given is no longer less. For he says: ‘I and the Father are one’” (John 10).

See, reader, Hilary’s words carefully, wherever they occur; note them diligently and understand them reverently.

The Holy Spirit is sent in two ways, visibly and invisibly. — [Note: [Col. 0993D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book II, ch. 2.] The Holy Spirit likewise is read to have been sent visibly and invisibly. He was sent visibly when, in time, some form of a creature was made in which the Holy Spirit was visibly displayed: whether when he descended upon the Lord himself in the bodily form of a dove; or when, on the day of Pentecost, there suddenly came a sound from heaven as though a violent wind were being borne along, and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and it settled upon each one of them. This operation, visibly expressed and set before mortal eyes, was called the visible mission of the Holy Spirit.

Why, although the Son is called less than the Father because of the human form in which he appeared, the Holy Spirit is not likewise called less. — But it is asked: if the Son, insofar as he was sent, was made less than the Father, why is the Holy Spirit not said to be less than the Father, though he too assumed a creature in which he appeared? Because the Spirit assumed the creature in which he appeared differently from the Son. The Son assumed it by union; the Spirit did not. For the Holy Spirit did not beatify that dove, that wind, or that fire, nor unite it to himself eternally in the unity of his person, as the Son of Man was assumed. In that form the person of God’s Word was represented, not in order that the Word might be in flesh—that is, in a human being—but in order that the Word might be flesh, that is, human. For “flesh” stands for “human being” in the statement: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1). Therefore it is nowhere written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit and that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father.

DISTINCTION XVII. On the invisible mission of the Holy Spirit. — We must say how the Holy Spirit is invisibly sent. But in order that this may be set forth more intelligibly, let us first state that the Holy Spirit is brotherly love. Augustine teaches that this is so:

[Note: [Col. 0993D] Here Bandinus and Lombard are not accepted when they teach that the Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbor.]

“Let no one say, ‘I do not know what to love.’ Let him love his brother, and let him love that same love. For he knows better the love by which he loves than the brother whom he loves. Behold, he can now have God better known to him than his brother: clearly better known, because more present, more inward, more certain.”

Augustine also proves the same point more openly by John’s example. For John says: “Let us love one another, because love is from God; whoever does not love has not known God, because God is love” (1 John 4). This connection clearly and openly declares that this very brotherly love by which we love one another is not only from God but also is God. Therefore, when we love a brother through love, we love a brother through God. Brotherly love, then, is God.

That the Holy Spirit is simply called charity. — But lest you suppose that this was said causally, as in “God is my patience” (Ps. 70), Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0994D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 17.]: “It is said to God, ‘You are my patience,’ not because our patience is God’s substance, but because it comes to us from him. Hence: ‘Our patience is from him’” (Ps. 61). But we shall not say that charity is called God in this manner. For it is not said, “God is my charity,” or “You are my charity,” as it is said, “God is my hope,” “You are my patience.” Rather, it is said: “God is charity” (1 John 4:8), just as it is said, “God is spirit.”

That God the Holy Spirit, not the Father or the Son, is properly called charity. — Since brotherly love is God, it is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Holy Spirit, who is properly called affection or charity. For if among God’s gifts nothing is greater than charity, and there is no greater gift of God than the Holy Spirit, what is more consequent than that he should be the charity which is God and from God, as was stated above? Whoever does not discern this should seek understanding from the Lord, not an exposition from us. For we cannot say anything more plainly.

[Col. 0994C] How the Holy Spirit is sent so that God may be given to us. — Therefore the Holy Spirit is said to be sent and given when he is in us in such a way as to make us love God and neighbor, whereby we remain in God and God in us. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0994D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 17.]:

“God the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God, when given to a human being, kindles him to love God and neighbor. For he himself is love, through whom God-charity is poured into our hearts, through whom the whole Trinity dwells in us. Accordingly, since the Holy Spirit is God, he is most rightly also called God’s gift. And what is this gift, properly speaking, to be understood as but charity?” [Note: [Col. 0994D] Here Bandinus does not hold this in common, nor does the Master.]

The following objection is made to these statements. Charity is given to one who does not have it. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is charity, he is given also to one who does not have him. But how is he given to one who does not have him, when he, as God, is everywhere? Certainly he is everywhere and wholly in every creature. Yet there are many who do not have him; for not everyone has the Holy Spirit in whom he himself is present. Otherwise even brute animals would have the Holy Spirit, which the piety of faith does not admit.

Does charity increase and diminish? — Charity also increases and diminishes, and thus is mutable—an absurd assertion. In answer we say that this should not simply be granted, but with this addition: namely, “for us” or “in us,” in whom charity increases or diminishes; or the Holy Spirit, as God, can be exalted in us, but certainly not in himself. Hence: “A human being shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). Cassiodorus says here that God grows great not in himself but in the human heart. Yet, to speak more truly, charity does not increase in us; rather, we increase in it. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0995D] Homily 9 on the Epistle of John.]: “Let each person test how much charity has advanced in him—or, rather, how much he himself has advanced in charity. For if charity is God, it neither advances nor declines.”

Whether brotherly charity is God. — Certainly, some concede that God is charity but deny that brotherly charity is God. Misusing the writings of the Fathers, they absurdly maintain that the charity by which God loves us is one thing and that by which we love him another. For they say that Augustine writes [Note: [Col. 0995D] Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 32.]:

“God’s charity is said to be poured out into our hearts, not that by which he himself loves us, but that by which he makes us his lovers; just as the Lord’s salvation is so called because he saves us, and the faith of Christ because he makes us faithful.”

To them it must be said that Augustine did not mean by these words that there are different charities of God. Rather, since charity is one and the same, he indicated the different respects in which it is called God’s charity in Scripture. For charity is called God’s charity either because God loves us by it or because by it he makes us lovers of himself. Therefore the meaning of the foregoing words is this: “Charity”—that is, in the Apostle—is called “the charity of God” (Rom. 5), not insofar as God loves us by it, but insofar as by it he makes us lovers of himself. In order to show that this could be said with such a meaning, he gave analogous forms of speech: “the Lord’s salvation, by which he saves us,” and so forth.

Whether there is one charity or another. — Again, they say, Augustine writes elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0995D] Book XIII, *On the Trinity*, ch. 17.]: “When John had mentioned God’s love, not that by which we love, but that by which he himself, he says, loved us.” By this they wish to assert distinct loves. But, referring even these words to the preceding meaning, we say that they should be understood thus: John mentioned God’s love, not insofar as we love God by it, but insofar as he loves us by it.

It is argued from reason that the Holy Spirit is not charity. — Pressing the point more strongly, they say: “Whence comes love, if not from the same source as faith itself—that is, from the Holy Spirit? But if charity is from him and he is that charity, then the Holy Spirit is from himself.” We, however, confess that the Holy Spirit is from himself, but not without qualification, since then he would seem to be said to exist without a principle. Rather, “for us” must be added: namely, for us to whom the Holy Spirit gives himself. In this sense it is also true that charity is from the Holy Spirit.

They prove the same point differently. — Further, still contradicting the truth, they say: “If the Holy Spirit is charity, then he is a movement and affection of the soul, since charity is this.” For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0995D] *On Christian Doctrine*, book III, ch. 10.]: “I call charity the movement of the soul toward enjoying God, oneself, and one’s neighbor, for God’s sake.” Likewise, where it is said, “Nothing shall be able to separate us from the charity of God” (Rom. 8), Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0996D] Augustine, book I, *On the Morals of the Church*, ch. 11.]: “The charity of God here means the virtue which is the most rightly ordered affection of our soul.”

To this we say that this is said not by a property of essence but with reference to efficient causality. For just as God is called our hope and patience, not because he is these things but because he produces them, so charity is called a movement or affection of the soul because through it the soul is moved and affected toward loving God. Therefore, having rejected the cold and empty slander of the enemies of truth, we freely confess that charity is the Holy Spirit. Let them be angry that he is God and God’s gift, through whom many gifts proper to each individual are distributed.

DISTINCTION XVIII. Whether for the same reason the Holy Spirit is called gift and given. The Holy Spirit is called gift in one way, given in another. — He is called both gift and given, but for different reasons. He is called gift because he proceeds; he is called given because he has been given. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0996D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 15.]:

“The Holy Spirit is the gift of the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from both. The Holy Spirit always proceeds, and not in time. But because he so proceeded as to be able to be given, he was already a gift before there was anyone to whom he might be given. For ‘gift’ is understood differently from ‘given.’ A gift can exist even before it is given; but something given cannot in any way be called such unless it has been given.”

Therefore the Spirit is eternally gift, but temporally given.

In what respect the Holy Spirit is gift and in what respect given; and to whom this is referred. How the Holy Spirit is ours. — Accordingly, insofar as the Holy Spirit is gift, he is referred to the Father and the Son. But insofar as he is given or bestowed, he is referred both to the one who gave and to those to whom he is given. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0996D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 14.]:

“What has been given is referred both to the one who gave and to those to whom he gave. Thus the Holy Spirit is called not only the Spirit of the Father and Son who gave him, but also ours, who received him.”

As it is written of John that he came “in the spirit of Elijah” (Luke 1). Likewise the Lord says to Moses: “I shall take from your spirit and give to them” (Num. 11), speaking of the Holy Spirit, whom he had already given to Moses.

How the Son is called ours. Whether the Holy Spirit is called our gift. — But it is asked whether, since the Son has been given to us, the Son can be called ours. We answer that he is called our God, our Redeemer, and so forth, but not our Son. For since Son is said only relatively to the one who begot him, he is called the Father’s Son alone, not our Son. Nor is the Holy Spirit called our Holy Spirit, or our gift, since both expressions are said by an eternal relation only to the Father and the Son. Hence nowhere in Scripture is it found that he is called our Holy Spirit, or your Holy Spirit, or his Holy Spirit.

For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0997D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 14.]: “That which is born of the Father is referred to the Father alone when it is called Son. Therefore he is the Father’s Son, not ours. Yet we say, ‘Give us our bread,’ just as [we say] ‘our Spirit.’ For the Son is our bread, because he refreshes us; and the Holy Spirit is our Spirit, because he is breathed forth by the Father and the Son and breathes within us as he wills.”

Comparison of the Son and the Holy Spirit. — Finally, it should be known that, just as the Son has by being born that he exists altogether, so the Spirit has it by proceeding. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0997D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 15.]: “The Son has by being born not only that he is Son, but that he exists altogether. Just as generation from the Father grants essence to the Son, so procession from both grants it to the Holy Spirit.” But we do not say this to mean that the Son is essence by birth or that the Holy Spirit is essence by procession, since elsewhere it is said [Note: [Col. 0997D] Book XV, *On the Trinity*, ch. 26.] that the Father is not Father in the same respect in which he is God; nor is the Son Son in the same respect in which he is God; nor is the Holy Spirit gift in the same respect in which he is God.

DISTINCTION XIX. On the equality of the three persons. — For by these names their relations are shown, not their essence. But just as the Son by being born received from the Father everything whereby he exists eternally, so the Spirit by proceeding received from both. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Augustine, book VII, *On the Trinity*, ch. 2.]

After the discussion of the coeternity of the three persons, it remains to speak of their equality. For the Catholic faith asserts that the three persons are coequal just as they are coeternal. Augustine teaches wherein this equality is to be recognized, saying [Note: [Col. 0997D] *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 1.]: “None of these either precedes another in eternity, exceeds another in greatness, or surpasses another in power.” Although these three matters are enumerated as if distinct, they are nevertheless the same in God: namely, the divine essence.

Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0997D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 1.]: “He is not great in one respect and God in another. For his greatness is the same as his essence.” Likewise: “The will and power of God are God himself.” Likewise, God’s eternity is his very substance, containing nothing mutable. Therefore in these three terms Augustine briefly comprehended the equality of the three persons. [Note: [Col. 0998D] Book VII of the *Confessions*, ch. 40, on Psalm 101.]

### That one Person is not greater than another

Just as none of the three Persons precedes another in eternity, as has been said, so neither does one exceed another in greatness. The Father is not greater than the Son, nor greater than the Holy Spirit. Nor are two or three Persons together something greater than one; nor is the essence greater in two or three than in one, [Col. 0998A] because it is wholly present in each. Hence John of Damascus says [Note: [Col. 0998D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book III, ch. 6]: “We confess that the whole nature of the Godhead exists perfectly in each of its ὑποστάσεων (*hypostaseōn*), that is, Persons. Therefore the Father is perfect God, the Son perfect God, and the Holy Spirit perfect God.”

Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0998D] *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 1]: “Because of the natural unity, the whole Father is in the Son and in the Holy Spirit; and likewise the whole Holy Spirit is in both.” Thus also the Father is said to be in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. Hilary makes this still clearer when he says [Note: [Col. 0998D] *On the Trinity*, Book III]:

> The Lord’s saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14), causes obscurity for many. It must certainly be understood that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father: the perfect fullness of divinity is in both. For the Son received everything from the Father. If he received from the Father a portion of him who begot him, neither is perfect; for something would be lacking to the one from whom it departed. Nor would fullness be in one constituted from a portion. Since this is absurd, let us confess both the likeness of power and the fullness of Godhead to be the same in both. For Truth says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14).

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit is understood to be in both, and each of the Persons to be in each, in this sense: the same fullness of divinity and likeness of nature are shown to exist in the individual Persons.

### DISTINCTION XX. That one Person does not surpass another in power

Likewise, the Father is not more powerful than the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor are two or three together more powerful than each of them individually. Augustine proves against Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0998D] Book III, ch. 12], who said that the Father was more powerful than the Son, that the Father is not more powerful than the Son:

> “All things whatsoever the Father has are mine,” says the Son (John 16). But the Father has omnipotence. Therefore it belongs to the Son; consequently the Son is equal to the Father.

If this is denied, Augustine proves it thus against the same man [Note: [Col. 0998D] Book III, ch. 7, *Against Maximinus*], who falsely said that the Son was less than the Father:

> You say that the Father begot a Son less than himself, and thereby you disparage the Father as well. If he begot his only Son as less, then either he could not or he would not beget one equal to himself. If you say that he could not, he is found weak; if that he would not, he is found envious. No one dares say either. Therefore the Son is truly equal to the Father.

Nor does it matter if perhaps you say that the Father is more powerful and greater than the Son because he received power from no one and was not begotten, whereas the Son has both from the Father. For this is a question of origin—who is from whom; but equality concerns what a thing is like or how great it is. Therefore equality or inequality does not exist there on account of the fact that the Father begot, the Son was begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; rather, an order of nature is demonstrated.

Finally, let us add a brief summary in confirmation of what has been said: there, greatness or power is nothing other than truth. Therefore, if none is truer than another, it follows by clear reasoning that none is greater or more powerful either.

### DISTINCTION XXI. The difference among the names by which we speak of God

We must now add something concerning the names by which we speak of God. Some of them belong to God eternally, others temporally. Of those which belong eternally, some express a property of the Godhead and may be called personal, such as generation, Son, and Word. Others show the unity of the divine majesty, such as wisdom, power, truth, and the like. Still others are said of God figuratively, through likeness, such as radiance, mirror, and the like.

Of those said of God temporally, some are relational and are said of all the Persons, such as Lord and Creator. Some are not said of all, such as bestowed, given, and sent. Other names are said temporally, but not relatively and not of all, such as incarnate, made human, and the like. There is besides a certain special name, belonging to the mode of thought: it is neither personal nor essential, but as it were collective of all the Persons. It is not said of any one Person by itself, but of all together: namely, Trinity.

### DISTINCTION XXII. In how many ways names are said of God

Although there are so many differences among the aforesaid names, we must maintain that all names signifying unity of essence are said of God in himself and substantially, of each individual Person separately, and, in the totality, in the singular rather than the plural. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0999D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, chs. 6, 8]:

> Whatever is said of God in relation to himself is said alike of the individual Persons and at the same time of the Trinity itself, not plurally but singularly. Thus the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; yet we do not say that this Trinity is three gods, but one.

The same may be said of similar names, and also of those which are said temporally and relatively of all the Persons. But those which belong properly to the individual Persons are sometimes said relatively, never substantially. Hence whatever is properly said of an individual Person in the Trinity is in no way said in relation to itself, but reciprocally in relation to another Person or in relation to a creature. It is therefore plainly said relatively, not substantially: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0999D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 11].

### DISTINCTION XXIII. Divine substantial names in particular

This name *person* too is said of God in himself and according to substance. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0999D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, ch. 6]: “To be God is not one thing, and to be a Person another, but altogether the same thing.” Again: “The Father is called a Person in relation to himself, not in relation to the Son or the Holy Spirit, just as he is called God, great, and good in relation to himself. And just as it is for him to be what it is to be God, great, and good, so it is for him to be what it is to be a Person.”

But if this is so, why do we call these three—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—three Persons rather than one Person, although we say not three gods but one? Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0999D] ibid.]:

> Because we wish to preserve at least one word for the meaning by which the Trinity is understood, lest we be entirely silent when asked what the three are. For we confess that there are three, since it is written: “There are three who bear witness in heaven” (1 John 5). Yet when it is asked, “What three?” human language suffers a profound poverty.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 9.] No name occurs by which we may properly encompass these three. Therefore devout faith adopted for this point of doctrine a word taken from other contexts, by which it might express what it holds concerning God in the inner chamber of the mind, and by whatever understanding, provided it be devout, might somehow answer one asking, “What three?”

For three Persons are spoken of, not in order to state precisely what is being asked, but lest we be altogether silent. For the surpassing excellence of divinity exceeds the capacity of ordinary speech. God is more truly conceived than spoken; indeed, he is more truly than he is conceived.

On account of this necessity, then, this name is excepted from the rule concerning names said substantially of God. For although it is said in relation to itself and substantially, it is received in the totality not in the singular but in the plural. For we confess not one Person but three Persons. The Greeks too, constrained by the same poverty of speech, say three hypostases and one οὐσίας (*ousias*), that is, three substances and one essence. Nor should it trouble anyone that they say three substances, whereas we say only one: in the idiom of their own language, they understand the word *substance* differently from us.

#### In the Trinity there is neither multiplicity nor singularity

Although there are three Persons, as has been said, there is absolutely no diversity or singularity there, but unity and Trinity. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1000D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, ch. 4]:

> Human poverty, seeking what to call three, said “three Persons” or “three substances.” By these names it did not intend diversity, but it rejected singularity, so that not only unity might be understood there from the saying “one essence,” but Trinity also from the saying “three Persons.”

Likewise Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1000D] *On Faith*, Book II, ch. 2]: “Equality is neither diverse nor singular: it neither separates Father and Son with the Arians, nor confounds Father and Son with the Sabellians. For Father and Son have distinction, not separation.”

Therefore, if one happens to find a statement that there are three distinct Persons, “distinct” must there be understood as “differentiated.” Likewise, there is neither triplicity nor multiplicity in God. Therefore he must not be called triple or multiple, but triune and simple. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1000D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 2]: “God must not be thought triple because he is Trinity.” And Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1000D] *On Faith*, Book II, ch. 2]: “What is one is not confused; what is undifferentiated cannot be multiple.”

God, therefore, is not multiple but simple and one. None of the three Persons is a part of him, since each is true and perfect God. Hence Augustine says:

> In the Trinity the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and at the same time these three are one God. Nor are all of them something greater than each one, because their greatness is spiritual, not bodily. Let the one able to receive this receive it (Matt. 19); but let one who cannot believe and pray, that he may understand what he believes. For what is said through the prophet is true: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7).

#### How three Persons are called one God or of one essence

It must further be known that the three Persons are one God, or of the same essence, not by material causation, as three statues are one gold; nor by similarity of composition, as three human beings are said to be of the same nature. For in three statues there is more gold taken together than in each one. But in the three Persons the essence is not greater than in each individual Person. Again, in three men there is not only one man, but two and three men, whereas in the Trinity there is only one God.

Nor is this according to the logic of the categories—namely, that essence should be understood as genus and the three Persons as species, or that one essence should be regarded as species and the three Persons as individuals. For if we discuss these matters according to genus, species, and individual, then three essences would be said just as three Persons are said; just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are three individuals, so too three men and three animals are spoken of.

Yet the following statement of John of Damascus seems contrary to this: “Substance,” he says [Note: [Col. 1001D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book III, ch. 2; see M[aster], Distinction 19], “signifies the common and encompassing species of ὁμοειδῶν ὑποστάσεων (*homo-eidōn hypostaseōn*), that is, Persons alike in species—for example, God or man. Hypostasis, however, indicates the individual: namely, Father, Son, Holy Spirit, Peter, Paul, and the like.”

John must, however, be understood to have said this not according to the reality of a property, but because of the similarity of predication. For just as “common” is what is said of several things and “individual” what is said of one alone, so also the divine essence is said of all the Persons. But any one of them is predicated not of another, but only of itself.

#### How the Persons differ in number

The same John added something which should not be passed over in silence. He says that the hypostases are said to differ in number, not in nature. To understand this correctly, note that there is one number by which things are numbered—an accidental property—and another which is numbered, namely, the things themselves that are countable.

Thus the hypostases differ in number: that is, they are distinct from one another as countable things, so that you can count in this way: the Father is one; the Father and the Son are two; the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three. Yet they do not differ by number as an accidental property, as though the unity in one Person were different from the unity in another; for the same unity, namely the divine essence, is ineffably in all.

### DISTINCTION XXIV. What a numerical term signifies in divine matters

Those carefully examining the authorities of the saints should know that the use of numerical words—such as one, two, three, and the like—was introduced not to posit something in the simplicity of Godhead, but rather to remove what is not there.

#### What “one” signifies when we speak of God

For when “one God” is said, the plurality of gods is excluded by “one”; no quantity of number is posited in the Godhead—as though one said: God exists, and there are not many gods. Hence Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1001D] *On Faith*, Book I, ch. 2; and Book III, *On the Holy Spirit*, [Col. 1002D] ch. 14]:

> When we say only one God, unity excludes a number of gods; it does not posit quantity in God, because neither quantity nor number is there.

Likewise, when it is said, “The Father is one” and “the Son is one,” the reason for this saying is that there is a Father and a Son, not many fathers or sons. So too with similar expressions.

#### What is signified by “several”

Again, when we say that there are several Persons, we exclude solitude and singularity; we do not posit diversity or multiplicity there. It is as though we said: we confess the Persons without solitude, diversity, or singularity. Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1002D] *On the Trinity*, Book IV, about the middle, on Genesis 1]:

> God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” I ask whether you suppose that God was speaking alone to himself, or whether you understand this speech to have been addressed to another. If you say that he was alone, you are refuted by his own words: “Let us make” and “our.” Thus, by the profession of plurality, he did not posit diversity or multitude, but denied solitude and singularity.

So also, when we say three Persons, by the name of the number three we do not posit diversity, but indicate that our understanding must be referred to none other than Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that singularity may be shown not to exist there. The sense is this: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three Persons; that is, not merely this Person or that, nor merely this and that, but this, that, and that are in the Godhead—and no others. Augustine clearly shows that this is the proper understanding when he says [Note: [Col. 1002D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 4]: “By these names he did not intend diversity, but rejected singularity.”

#### What “two” signifies

Likewise, when it is said that the Father and the Son are two, the meaning is that there is not merely the Father or the Son, but Father and Son; and this one is not that one.

#### What is signified by “distinct” and “discrete”

When we say that the Persons are distinct or discrete, we exclude Sabellian confusion and indicate that this is not that. So too, when it is said, “The Person of the Father is other than that of the Son,” by *other* we indicate not separation but the distinction of each one’s own property. For Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1003D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 2]: “Father and Son have distinction, not separation.”

#### What is signified by the name “Trinity”

The name *Trinity* appears to signify the same thing as the expression “three Persons.” Therefore, just as none of the Persons is “three Persons,” so none of them is the Trinity.

### DISTINCTION XXV. What is signified

Let us further consider whether, since the name *person* is said according to substance, its plural use signifies the same thing. Some who think so endeavor to prove it as follows. When, they say, it is asked, “What three?” or “What three things?” the fitting answer is, “Three Persons.” But through the question *what?*, the essence is asked about. Therefore, if we answer that question correctly, we must signify the essence by answering with the name *person*.

They add that Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1003D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, ch. 4] that three Persons are so called because that which is *person* is common to them. But nothing is common to them except the essence. If this is so, however, how may it be said, “The Person of the Father is other than the Person of the Son,” as though the essence were other?

They say this must be understood in the following way: “The Father is other than the Son,” though they have in common that which is person. They confirm this by Augustine’s authority, when he says [Note: [Col. 1003D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, ch. 6]: “We say three Persons of the same essence, or the same essence; not from the same essence, as though what is essence were one thing there and what is person another.” They therefore think that “person” belongs in every respect to the three Persons.

[Col. 1003C] But if this is so, how will Augustine’s statement in *On Faith, to Peter* stand: “The Father is other in Person, or personally; the Son other personally; the Holy Spirit other personally”? Therefore let us seek another meaning, in accordance with the authorities of the saints.

When it is asked, then, “What three?” or “What three things?”, one must know that the question is not about the essence, nor does *what?* there refer to essence. Since Christian faith confesses that there are three, because it is written, “There are three who bear witness in heaven” (1 John 5), it asks what those three are—that is, by what name it may designate those three. Thus faith, constrained by poverty of speech, answered, “Three Persons”; not, I say, understanding essence by this name, but subsistences or hypostases, in Greek usage.

Indeed, these three may the more properly be called three Persons, that is, subsistences, because that which is person—namely essence—is common to them. For they could not themselves be called three true subsistences unless each one were true essence.

#### The sense in which the Person of the Father is other than that of the Son

It may as readily as correctly be understood in what sense it is said, “The Person of the Father is other than that of the Son”: that is, the subsistence or hypostasis of the Father is other than that of the Son; or, the Father is one Person and the Son another—that is, the Father is one subsistence or hypostasis and the Son another. Understand the same concerning the Holy Spirit.

But although Augustine said [Note: [Col. 1003D] Augustine, *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 1], “The Father is one in Person or personally; the Son another personally,” this can be said in the same sense. Yet we think that in this passage the name *person* is more suitably understood as a personal property. The sense is: the Father is other in Person, or personally—that is, the Father is Father by his own property, and is other than the Son.

#### The threefold meaning of the name “person”

Thus this name *person* has a threefold meaning in the Trinity. At times it signifies essence, at times property, and at times hypostasis. That it signifies essence is clearly established above from Augustine’s words. That it signifies property is shown by Jerome, who says [Note: [Col. 1003D] *In an Explanation of the Creed, to Damasus]: “We confess not merely the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the Persons; or, as the Greeks express it, the hypostases, that is, subsistences.” That it signifies hypostasis John of Damascus states thus [Note: [Col. 1004D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book III, ch. 5]: “In the Godhead we confess one nature and three hypostases, that is, Persons, existing in truth.”

### DISTINCTION XXVI

It should further be noted that heretics used the term *hypostasis* to deceive the simple, because it was sometimes said in place of *person* and *essence* [Note: [Col. 1004D] See the beginning of Distinction XXVI]. Therefore, as Jerome advises [Note: [Col. 1004D] *In the Letter to Damasus*], when the expression is suspect, one must either remain silent against heretics or use it with their own explanations.

#### The properties of the Persons: why they are called properties, notions, and relations

Let us now examine the properties of the Persons, which are also often called notions or relations. First let us discuss generation, nativity, and procession. They are called properties because through them the proper characteristics of the Persons are assigned. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1004D] *On Faith, to Peter*, chs. 1–2]:

> It is proper to the Father that he begot one Son. It is proper to the Son that he was born from the essence of the Father. It is likewise proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from Father and Son.

They are also called notions, because through them the Persons are known—that is, distinguished from one another. The same things are also called relations, because by them the Persons are referred to one another. These are not accidental to God, but exist in the Persons eternally and immutably. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1004D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, chs. 4–5]:

> Nothing in God is said according to accident; yet not everything said of God is said according to substance. For he is said in relation to something, as Father in relation to Son and Son in relation to Father. This is not accidental, since the one is always Father and the other always Son. And the Father is not called Father except because he has a Son, nor is the Son called Son except because he has a Father. These things are not said according to substance, but reciprocally.

Finally, Hilary, assigning what is proper to Father and Son, says: “If it is always proper to the Father that he is always Father, it must always be proper to the Son that he is always Son” [Note: [Col. 1005D] Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book XII, middle of the book]. Again: “For God who is born, it is manifestly proper that he is Son” [Note: [Col. 1005D] the same Hilary, a little before the middle].

### DISTINCTION XXVII. Whether Augustine and Hilary assign the same properties

But it is asked whether Hilary and Augustine have expressed the same properties. If this is granted, then to be Father is the same as to have begotten the Son. But if that is so, whoever has the one has the other. Yet the divine nature is Father; therefore it begot the Son—which is not rightly said.

Answering this question without prejudging a sounder interpretation, we say that where Hilary said, “It is proper to the Father that he is always Father,” the name *Father* must there be understood to signify hypostasis with a relational determination.
