The sense is: “It is proper to the Father that he is always Father,” that is, that he always begot. Hilary himself explains this meaning when he adds: “Therefore, one who is not always Father did not always beget.”

But when the divine nature is called Father, *hypostasis* is used without a relational determination; or, more plainly, it is not said relatively. The sense is: “The divine nature is Father,” that is, the hypostasis which is Father. Understand this likewise of the names *Son* and *Holy Spirit*.

#### Diversity of divine names: whether it is the same to say that something is Father and that it begot the Son

Finally, some terms signify hypostases together with relations, such as begetting, born, proceeding, and the like. Others signify relations alone, such as generation, nativity, procession, and the like. All of these are said both of the Persons and of the divine nature. Other terms signify only determinations, such as to beget, to be born, to proceed, and the like; these are said only of the Persons and never of the divine nature. For properties determine only Persons, not nature.

Hence John of Damascus says [Note: [Col. 1005D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, Book III, ch. 6]: “The hypostases do not differ from one another in substance, but by their characteristic idiomata—that is, determining properties. The characteristic, that is, determining properties belong to the hypostases and not to the nature.”

For this reason, it seems that it is not altogether the same to say that something is Father and that it begot the Son; or that something is Son and has a Father; or that it is Holy Spirit and proceeds from both [Note: [Col. 1005D] Compare with the Master, Distinction 26].

#### How a human being is a Son of the Trinity

The statement of Hilary [Note: [Col. 1005D] *On the Trinity*, Book XII, a little before the middle], that for God who is born it is proper that he is Son, clearly seems contrary to the fact that human beings too are and are called sons of God, according to: “You are all sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81); and, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4).

But human beings are sons of God by creation; the Only-begotten is Son by the property of birth. Hence the same Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1006D] *On the Trinity*, Book XII, near the beginning]: “We indeed are sons of God, but by creation, because we were made by grace, not born; acquired, not begotten. For a human being is God’s son by adoption, not by generation.”

#### How the Trinity is Father of humankind

It must be known that the whole Trinity is also called the Father of humankind. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1006D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 11]:

> The Trinity cannot be called Father, except perhaps figuratively in relation to creation, because of the adoption of sons. For him whom we rightly call our one Lord God, we shall also rightly call our Father because by his grace he regenerates us.

It is certain that the Only-begotten is Son of God properly and by nature, while human beings are sons by grace. Likewise, although the gifts of God are many, the Holy Spirit is properly called the gift of God because he is so called by an eternal property or relation, which is plainly evident in the name *gift*. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1006D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 11]:

> The Holy Spirit, who is not the Trinity but is in the Trinity, is understood in that he is properly called the Holy Spirit; but he is called relatively when he is referred to Father and Son. The relation itself, however, does not appear in this name; it appears when he is called God’s gift.

Nor should it trouble anyone that these names do not correspond reciprocally to Father and Son. This occurs in many relatives, where no term is found by which they can answer one another reciprocally. Therefore, when we say “the gift of the Father and the Son,” we do not say “the Father of the gift” or “the Son of the gift.” But so that these may reciprocally correspond, we say “the gift of the giver” and “the giver of the gift.” Yet God was not a giver except temporally, although the Holy Spirit is gift eternally.

#### The names “Word” and “image”

There are also other names said relatively to the Father with the same notion as *Son*, such as *Word* and *image*. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1006D] *On the Trinity*, Book VII, ch. 2]: “He is called Son in the same respect in which he is called Word, and Word in the same respect in which he is called Son.” Again [Note: [Col. 1006D] ibid., ch. 3]: “Son is said relatively; Word and image are also said relatively.” In all these names he is referred to the Father; but the Father is called by none of them.

[Col. 1006D] Finally, names of essence, such as God, light, and the like, are never said relatively. Yet they are sometimes used in place of relational names—that is, in place of Persons—as when it is said, “God from God, light from light.” One is then used for the Father, the other for the Son.

### DISTINCTION XXVIII. The name “image”

Yet *image* sometimes signifies the essence, as in: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1007D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, at the beginning; and *On Faith, to Peter*, ch. 10]: “Man is made in the common image.” And Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1007D] *On the Trinity*, Book IV, not far from the end]: “There is one image of the Trinity, in whose image man was made.”

It should also be noted that being Father and being Son differ only in relation. Therefore, though being Father and being Son are different, the substance is not different, because this is not said according to substance but according to relation.

#### The name “unbegotten”

It is also necessary to know that the Father is called unbegotten by a property other than that by which he is called begetter. Thus, although both are said of God the Father, one notion makes him understood as begetter and another as unbegotten. The latter is unbegottenness. Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1007D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 7]: “There is one from one—that is, begotten from unbegotten—by the property, in each respectively, both of origin and of unbegottenness.”

But according to this notion he is referred to the non-begetter. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1007D] *On the Trinity*, Book IV, ch. 20]: “As Son is referred to Father, and non-Son to non-Father, so begotten must be referred to begetter, and unbegotten to non-begetter.” For what is unbegotten except not begotten?

### DISTINCTION XXIX. The name “principle”

#### What it is to be a principle in relation to creatures

There is another name, namely *principle*, which is always said relatively, though in several ways. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are each called principle, but differently. The Father is principle in relation to the Son, because the Son is begotten from him; and in relation to the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit proceeds from him. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1008D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 13]: “The Father is the principle of the whole Godhead”—that is, of the Son and Holy Spirit, in each of whom the whole Godhead is present.

But the Son is principle of the Holy Spirit because the Spirit proceeds from him. The Holy Spirit, however, is principle only in relation to creatures. Thus the Father is principle without principle; the Son is principle from principle; and the Holy Spirit is principle from both. Moreover, the Father is eternally principle of the Son, and Father and Son are principle of the Holy Spirit; but the Holy Spirit is not eternally principle: he is principle temporally. Since he is principle only of creatures, he began to be their principle when creatures began to exist. So too the whole Trinity began to be principle in relation to creatures.

To be principle in relation to creatures is to be Creator. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1008D] *On the Nature of the Good*, ch. 28]: “When he was asked, ‘Who are you?’ he answered, ‘The Principle, who also speak to you’” (John 8). In this he intended to show himself as Creator.

#### The Trinity is one principle, not three

But these three are not three principles but one, because they operate in things in one and the same way, so that they may exist. Understanding this, the Apostle says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11). By “all things,” understand natures and those things which exist naturally, not sins, which corrupt nature and arise from the will of sinners.

#### How the Father is principle and author of the Son

The Father is called principle in relation to the Son because he is begetter. For if the begetting one is principle in relation to what is begotten, the Father is principle in relation to the Son because he begot him. In the same way the Father is also called the Son’s author. Hence Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1008D] *On the Trinity*, Book IV, not far from the beginning]:

> By the very fact that he is called Father, he is shown to be the author of him whom he begot. He has that name by which he is understood not to be made perfect from another, and by which he who was begotten is shown to have subsisted from him.

#### Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit

We must likewise confess that Father and Son are one principle of the Holy Spirit, not two. For just as Father and Son are called one Creator and one Lord in relation to creation, so they are one principle relatively to the Holy Spirit. Both are called principle in relation to the Holy Spirit because the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Nor does he proceed from the Father in a different way than from the Son.

It may indeed be understood that Father and Son are called principle of the Holy Spirit by the same eternal relation—a relation for which we have no name.

### DISTINCTION XXX. Things properly said of God temporally

There are also certain names which belong to God temporally and are said of God relatively, such as Creator, Lord, refuge, and the like. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1008D] *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 13]: “Creator is said relatively to creature, just as lord is said to servant. This relative appellation, then, belongs to God temporally. Otherwise we are compelled to say that creation is eternal, because he would not be eternally lord unless it also eternally served.”

Just as there cannot be a servant unless there is a lord, so there cannot be a lord unless there is a servant. These things are said of God according to an accident which exists not in him but only in the creature. Therefore God is called these things without change in himself, as appears in a lesser case.

For when a coin is called a price, it is said relatively; yet it was not changed when it began to be a price, nor when it is called a pledge, and so forth. If this is so in these least matters, we must with much greater force believe concerning that unchangeable substance of God that something is said of him temporally, while he is changed in no respect.

Thus the designation by which a creature is referred to its Creator places the relation in the creature itself. But the designation by which Creator is referred to creature is merely a relative designation, marking no property in God.

#### The Holy Spirit is called given relatively and temporally

In the same way, the Holy Spirit is called given or bestowed, relatively and temporally.

Whether the Holy Spirit is said relatively with reference to himself. — But if it is asked whether the Holy Spirit is said relatively with reference to himself, because Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1009D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 14] that “is given” is referred both to the one who gives and to the one to whom it is given, and the Holy Spirit gives himself: we answer that the Holy Spirit is not referred to himself, because the giver is the Trinity and the recipient is the creature. Or we say that there is no inconsistency if here he is said to be referred to himself, since the designation “given” or “bestowed,” as regards the giver, marks no property, but only as regards the recipient. For if it marked a property as regards the giver, then it could not be referred to itself; for thus it would be said to differ from itself. This would not be effected by a designation alone, but by a property.

## DISTINCTION XXXI. On the Meaning of the Relative Terms “Similar” and “Equal”

Moreover, in the Trinity “equal” and “similar” are spoken relatively, since, as Hilary says [Note: [Col. 1009D] *On the Trinity*, book III, not far from the end]: “Just as nothing is similar to itself, so neither is anything called equal to itself.” Yet they are not said according to relation, but according to substance. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1009D] *On the Trinity*, book V, ch. 6]: “The Son is not equal to the Father in virtue of the fact that he is said in relation to the Father. It remains, therefore, that he is equal according to that which is said of himself, that is, according to substance.” Thus, in these terms the designation alone is relative; but equality and similarity in the three persons are the supreme and undifferentiated simplicity of the divine substance.

Another explanation of “equal” and “similar.” — Some, moreover, say that these names do not posit something but remove something: thus the Son is called equal to the Father, as though he were neither greater nor less than him; and similarly, similar, as though in nothing different or dissimilar. This is plainly a quite orthodox statement.

How Hilary indicates the properties in the Trinity of persons. — Nor should it be passed over that Hilary, indicating the properties of the persons, says [Note: [Col. 1009D] *In the Book on Synods*]: “Eternity is in the Father, form in the image, use in the gift.” Augustine does not think that Hilary should be followed in the term “eternity” [Note: [Col. 1010D] *On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 10, explaining Hilary’s words], except in this respect: that the Father does not have a Father from whom he is. Further, in the image he named “form,” I believe, because of beauty, where there is primary equality and such correspondence that it answers in identity to the one whose image it is. But the delight, or ineffable blessedness, of the Father and the image—if it can worthily be expressed in human speech—is what he briefly called “use.” “Gift” means the same as “donation.” The gift is the Holy Spirit. Whoever sees this in part or through a mirror, let him rejoice in knowing God and give thanks. But whoever does not see it, let him strive through devotion to see it, not through blindness to slander it.

How Augustine distinguishes the properties of the persons. Unity is assigned to the Father, equality to the Son, concord to the Holy Spirit. — Augustine also, distinguishing the proper characteristics of the persons, says [Note: [Col. 1010D] *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, ch. 1]: “In the Father is unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the concord of unity and equality. And these three are all one because of the Father; all equal because of the Son; all connected because of the Holy Spirit.”

Accordingly, unity is assigned to the Father according to Augustine, perhaps for the same reason that eternity was assigned to him above according to Hilary. Or it is also because the Father is the one principle of the whole Godhead. Since he is one God, he gave to the Son born from himself and to the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself that they should be one and the same God with himself. Thus all things are one because of the Father.

Equality is assigned to the Son because he is the image of the Father. But if an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, the image is made equal to it, not it to its image. The Son perfectly fulfills that of which he is the image [Col. 1010B], and therefore is equal to it. The Holy Spirit is also given by the Son to be equal to himself and to the Father. By this, then, both points are made clear: how these three are equal because of the Son, not from the Son. We state these things, without prejudice to a better understanding, with fear.

But concord is assigned to the Holy Spirit, which may be understood more easily. For he is the ineffable love of the Father and the Son. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1010D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 3]: “The Spirit is the highest charity, joining the two and joining us to them.” Therefore all things are rightly said to be connected because of him. Hence it is said that he contains all things in wisdom.

## DISTINCTION XXXII. Whether the Father or the Son Loves through the Holy Spirit; How This Is to Be Understood. The Father and Son Love by the Holy Spirit

From these matters, since it was also said above, “The Holy Spirit is that by which the begotten is loved by the begetter, and loves his begetter” (Wisdom 1), it seems that the Father and the Son are the Holy Spirit, because in the Trinity to be is nothing other than to love. But we say that the statement “the Father and the Son love by the Holy Spirit,” that is, through the Holy Spirit, is rightly made, just as Augustine above says that all things are connected through the Holy Spirit. But if it is said that they love *by the Holy Spirit*, that is, from the Holy Spirit, it is said falsely; for thus the authority of principle would be placed in the Holy Spirit.

Or, as it is said that the Father is equal to the Son through the Son, not indeed from the Son, so likewise here. Or we say that “to love” does not signify “to be” there, just as “love” in the Trinity does not always signify essence. Thus Augustine proves it [Note: [Col. 1010D] *On the Trinity*, book VI, ch. 5]: “God is love.” For the statement that the begotten is loved by the begetter through the Holy Spirit appears to be said relatively. But if it were said absolutely, “The Father or the Son loves, or is loving, by the Holy Spirit,” then, I think, it would be said substantively. Since this never occurs, I think that this itself supports the meaning stated above. If this is so, the question is empty, since it is one thing in the Trinity for the Father to love by the Holy Spirit and another for the Father to love the Son by the Holy Spirit.

Two questions. Whether the Father is wise by the begotten wisdom. — It is asked whether the Father is wise by the begotten wisdom. This seems to follow from what the Apostle says: that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” that is, of the Father (1 Corinthians 1). If this is so, it follows that the Father is that wisdom, because there “to be” is the same as “to be wise.”

Whether the Son is wise by the begotten wisdom. — Likewise it is asked whether the Son is wise by the begotten wisdom. This seems to have to be granted; otherwise he does not appear wise through himself, since he alone is the begotten wisdom. But if it is granted, the inconsistency stated above is incurred. To this we say that neither the Father nor the Son is wise by begotten wisdom, but by unbegotten wisdom, which is the Father alone. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1011D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 7]: “God the Father is wise by that wisdom which he himself is [Col. 1011B]; and the Son, the wisdom of the Father, is wise from the wisdom which is the Father, from whom he is begotten.” The same must be said of one who understands and understanding.

How the Son is called the wisdom and power of God the Father. — Moreover, the Son is called the wisdom and power of the Father, not because the Father is wise or powerful through him, but because the Son is wisdom and power from the Father’s wisdom and power. Yet, lest we be thought to assert several wisdoms on this account, we confess only one wisdom in the Trinity, though it is not said in only one way. Wisdom is called begotten or unbegotten; begotten wisdom is not unbegotten wisdom, yet there is only one wisdom, just as there is only one God. He is called begotten and unbegotten; the begotten is not the unbegotten; yet he is one and the same God alone [Col. 1011C].

Whether the Son is wise through himself. — Likewise it is asked whether the Son is wise through himself. We distinguish: if “through himself” means “from himself,” it is said falsely; but it is truly said “through himself,” that is, through his own self. Thus the Son is said to act not from himself but through himself. Hence Hilary [Note: [Col. 1011D] *On the Trinity*, book IX, after the middle]: “Heretic, this is the unity of the nature which you oppose: that the Son acts through himself, yet does not act from himself; and that he does not act from himself in such a way that he acts through himself.” Accordingly, when he says, “He does not act from himself,” he removes from him the authority of principle; but when he says, “He acts through himself,” he confesses in him the unity of nature.

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. Whether the Properties of the Persons Are the Persons Themselves or God. That the Properties Are the Persons

Finally, it must faithfully and firmly be maintained that the properties of which we have thus far treated are in the persons, because it is written: “In the persons is property, and in the essence unity” [Note: [Col. 1011D] The Church, in the Preface on the Trinity]. And they are the persons themselves; otherwise there would be multiplicity in God. Certainly, we have above established by manifest truth that whatever God has from eternity is God, except relations. Therefore Jerome expressly says that the persons are distinguished by properties, and that the properties themselves are persons [Note: [Col. 1011D] *In the Exposition of the Creed to Damasus*]: “Avoiding the heresy of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressed under property. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names, that is, persons.”

Yet there are some who do not tremble to deny this with sacrilegious thought and ill-omened speech, adding something more blasphemous: namely, that the properties are indeed in the persons, but not inwardly; rather, they are fastened to them outwardly. We do not doubt that this ridiculous claim bursts forth from the madness of their presumption.

They strive to prove their fancy thus: “If the properties are persons, the persons do not differ from the properties.” Against this we say that the persons are also said to differ from one another in themselves. Hence Jerome, speaking of these three, says [Note: [Col. 1012D] Place cited above]: “They are one in substance but distinguished in persons and names.” The properties themselves are also the divine essence. Hence Hilary says of one of them [Note: [Col. 1012D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, in the middle of the book]: “The birth cannot fail to be that nature from which the Son is born.” Yet the persons differ not by divine essence but only by properties. This is indeed truly said, but how it is so is neither grasped nor comprehended. For the nature of the thing itself exhausts the significance of words.

The enemies of truth also rise up and say: “If paternity and filiation are the same thing in the divine essence, therefore the Father is the Son; and thus the same thing both begets and is begotten.” That this is heretical speech is more than manifest. But those who say this should also have been warned above that properties determine not natures but only persons. It is not burdensome to repeat here what has once been said, so that by more frequent consideration it may become more familiar.

“For characteristic idioms,” says John [Note: [Col. 1012D] Damascene, book III, *On the Orthodox Faith*, ch. 6], “are the determining properties of hypostasis, not of nature.” But they ask: “How are the properties in the essence and yet do not determine it, when they are in the persons in such a way that they determine them?” We say that this must firmly be held; but as to how it is so, we should not be ashamed to confess that we do not know, with Hilary also saying [Note: [Col. 1012D] *On the Trinity*, book I, not far from the beginning]: “I do not know; I do not inquire; yet I will console myself: the archangels do not know, the angels have not heard, the ages do not comprehend, the Prophet did not perceive, the Apostle did not inquire, the Son himself did not disclose it. Let the anguish of complaints therefore cease.”

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. Why the Father Is Distinctly Called Powerful, the Son Wise, and the Holy Spirit Benign

Moreover, it should be known that power, wisdom, and benignity, although they belong to the three persons because they are said according to substance, are nevertheless often assigned by Scripture distinctly to the persons: power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and benignity to the Holy Spirit. This is not without purpose.

For the names “father” and “son,” taken from creatures, commonly suggest that the father is prior to the son and thus imply deficiency in the father through age; while the son is later than the father and thus imply imperfection of understanding in him. When these names are transferred to the Creator, Scripture intervenes lest human weakness measure the hidden God by the likeness of a creature [Col. 1013A]. It calls the Father powerful, lest he seem prior to the Son and therefore less powerful; and the Son wise, lest he seem later than the Father and therefore less wise. This is not because the Father alone is powerful or more powerful, nor because the Son alone is wise or wiser.

Likewise, the name “Spirit” commonly suggests harshness and severity. Therefore, lest man think anything of God that would make him fear to approach God, Scripture tempers its language by calling the Spirit benign—not because the Spirit alone is benign or more benign.

On names spoken of God metaphorically. — Finally, it should be known that “mirror,” “splendor,” “figure,” and similar terms that are said of God metaphorically are by no means spoken to express the property denoted by those names, but in order that some spiritual understanding may be gained from the reasons for so speaking, which the devout reader should draw out in their respective places.

## DISTINCTION XXXV. On the Knowledge of the Unbegotten God in Himself. God’s Knowledge Has Many Names

Although much has been set forth above concerning those things said of God according to substance, a special treatment must nevertheless be given to certain of them: namely, knowledge, God’s will, and power. God’s knowledge, though one and simple, receives different names because of the different effects of created things. It is called foreknowledge, disposition, providence, and predestination.

Foreknowledge and providence concern future things only, both good and evil; disposition concerns things to be done; providence, things to be governed; predestination, those to be saved and their goods, by which they are here delivered and in the future crowned. Hence the Apostle: “He chose us before the foundation of the world, that we might be holy and blameless” (Ephesians 1). And the prophet: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isaiah 64; 1 Corinthians 2).

But if this is so, it seems that, if future things had not existed from eternity, neither foreknowledge nor any of the other things would have been in God, and thus neither would essence; for in God essence is the same as foreknowledge. Likewise, if future things had not existed from eternity, God would not have foreknown, and thus would not have existed, since for him to foreknow is the same as to be. To this we say that the name “foreknowledge,” and each of the things mentioned, signify essence and are said relatively to future things. Since they are thus twofold, the statement “If there were no future things, there would not be foreknowledge in God”—that is, there would not be knowledge in God which is foreknowledge—is false.

But if it is said that there would be knowledge in God, but not knowledge comprehending future things, it is true.

Likewise distinguish the statement: “If there were no future things, God would not be foreknowing.” Say the same of the rest. For even if nothing of this sort were said of God because no future things existed from eternity, there would nonetheless be in God knowledge concerning all things, both good and evil, temporal and eternal [Col. 1014A].

Hence Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1013D] Ambrose, *On Genesis According to the Letter*, ch. 18]: “Every plan of the supreme and eternal wisdom is in him, because his immeasurable wisdom comprehends all wisdom and essence.” For this reason all things are said to be in God from eternity.

Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1013D] *On Faith*, book V, ch. 8]: “Before these visible things came to be, they were and were not: they were in God’s knowledge; they were not in their own nature. For he made them known, not as things made.” Hence it is said: “What was made, in him was life” (John 1), not because the creature is the Creator, but because it is always in his knowledge, which is life.

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. How Things Are in God

Accordingly, it is said that he “calls things that are not as though they were” [Col. 1014B]. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1013D] On the passage of Psalm 49]: “The beauty of the field is with me.” All things are with him by a certain ineffable knowledge of the wisdom of God.

But since God’s knowledge and his nature, or essence, are the same, it is asked whether all things are in God’s nature. No, for Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1014D] *On the Words of the Apostle*, sermon 11]: “He has the elect with himself, but not in his nature, rather in his foreknowledge.” But since the nature of God and knowledge are altogether the same, what does it mean that all things are said to be in knowledge and not in nature? Perhaps this is one reason: the name “nature” simply posits essence, whereas “knowledge” indeed posits the same thing but is not said altogether without reference to things knowable.

It also follows that not everything which is in God’s knowledge is said to be in his love, because these names—love, knowledge, and the like—having been transferred from creatures to the Creator on account of the various conditions of things, are said with different relations to the things themselves. Because of these relations, we need not say by one name everything we say by another. For example, all things are in God’s knowledge because nothing escapes the fullness of his awareness. But not all things are in his love, because he is not found to bestow the gift of grace on all.

Whether evils ought to be said to be in God. — But since all things are in God through knowledge, it is asked whether we should grant that evils are in God. For God knows all things, both good and evil. Surely, who but a madman would grant that evils are in God? Therefore the expression “God knows” must be distinguished according to the variety of knowable things.

For God knows certain things only as existing, whether past or future, in such a way that he neither approves them nor is pleased by them. Hence he is said to know them from afar, as it is written: “He knows the lofty things from afar” (Psalm 138). Accordingly he will say to some: “I never knew you” (Matthew 7). Things of this kind are not said to be in God, because he does not grant them the authority to exist.

Therefore only those things are said to be in God of which he is the author: namely, good things, which are from him, and in him, and through him, as Scripture says (Romans 11). These three, as Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1014D] *On the Holy Spirit*, book III, ch. 12], are one with respect to the causative authority by which things that exist are enabled to exist.

This should not, however, be understood indiscriminately, because the Apostle set it down for the distinction of the persons: saying “from him” because of the Father, “through him” because of the Son, and “in him” because of the Holy Spirit. Yet believe this in such a way that you refer all three to each individual person. For all things are from the Father, through the Father, and in the Father; and the same applies to the Son and the Holy Spirit. Yet it should be noted that “from him” is said more generally than “of him.” Heaven and earth are from him, but not of him, since they are not from his substance. Thus both a son and a house made by him are from a man; but only the son is of the man.

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. How God Is in Things and in Bodily Places

Having stated how things are in God, it seems proper to ask [Col. 1015B] how God is in things. It should therefore be known that God alone was in himself before created things existed. When heaven and earth were created, he filled them. Hence: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23). Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1015D] *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, ch. 10]: “God is everywhere; we draw near to him not by places but by actions.”

How God is generally in things and specially in the saints. — God is therefore present, powerful, and essential in all things generally; but in the saints specially, namely through indwelling grace. Hence Gregory [Note: [Col. 1015D] *On the Song of Songs*, ch. 61]: “Although God is present in all things in a common way by presence, power, and substance, still he is present more familiarly through grace in those who consider more keenly and more faithfully the wondrousness of God’s works. Thus they know him and love him [Col. 1015C]. And therefore God is said to dwell in them.”

Hence: “Heaven is my seat, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66). And elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1015D] Gregory, *In the Book of Wisdom*, ch. 7]: “The throne of wisdom is the righteous soul.” For this reason we do not say, “Our Father who art everywhere,” although this too is true, but “who art in heaven,” that is, in the saints.

How God dwells in some who do not know him. — God also dwells in some who do not yet know him, such as little children confirmed by the sacrament of Christ, whom he builds for himself as a temple most beloved through the grace of his goodness.

How God is in Christ. — God is also in the man Christ in a more excellent manner, because not by adoption but by union; for in him the fullness of divinity dwells bodily. Thus God is in Christ excellently, in the saints mercifully, and everywhere ineffably. But we cannot explain how he is so. For we understand many things about God which we are wholly unable to speak; and we also speak many things which we are not capable of understanding.

How God is everywhere and yet is not defiled by filth. — But since God is everywhere, how is his nature not defiled by filth? How frivolous this is is proved even in the created spirit and is plainly mocked by the rays of the sun [Col. 1016A].

That he is not changed through places and times. What it is to be changed through time and place. — Although God is everywhere and at every time, he is not moved through places and times; this belongs only to creatures. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1015D] *On Genesis*, book VIII, chs. 22–23]: “The Almighty, ever the same in unchangeable eternity, will, and truth, moves the spiritual creature through time and the bodily creature through time and place; nevertheless, his substance, by which he is God, is not changed by times and places.”

To be changed through time is to vary according to qualities. What is local is changed through place, and this occurs in two ways. Something is called local when, by the interposition of itself, it produces distance between surrounding things because of its dimensions; this is proper to a body. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1015D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 20]: “Place is the space occupied by a body in length, height, and breadth.” Something is also called local when it is bounded merely by place—that is, when it is somewhere in such a way that it is not everywhere. This also belongs to an angel. Hence Bede [Note: [Col. 1016D] On Luke, “I am Gabriel”]: “An angel is a circumscribed spirit; but the supreme Spirit is uncircumscribed, within whom the angel runs wherever he is sent.” Likewise Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1016D] *On the Spirit*, book I, chs. 6 and 10]: “A seraph passes from place to place, for it does not fill all things.” Nothing of this sort belongs to God, for he neither produces distance by the interposition of himself nor is he somewhere in such a way that he is not everywhere. For it has been proved above that God is everywhere.

Yet he should not be imagined to be diffused throughout all things by a spatial magnitude, as this light or the earth is; rather, as the same wisdom is equally in two wise persons, one of whom is greater than the other in body, while wisdom is neither greater in the larger nor smaller in the smaller, nor less in one than in two: so God is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, wholly in both, and wholly everywhere. [Note: [Col. 1016D] Augustine, Letter 57 to Dardanus.] Therefore God is not changed through places and times, because he is not varied by any qualities. Nor is he moved because he is in more creatures today than yesterday; for in this respect it is not he but only creatures that are changed, by beginning to exist or by ceasing to exist.

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. Whether God’s Foreknowledge Is the Cause of Future Things

Now, returning to the preceding matters, let us ask whether God’s knowledge, foreknowledge, and providence are the cause of future things. If they are, it seems impossible that what has been foreknown should not occur; for it is impossible for God’s foreknowledge to be mistaken. But it would be mistaken if the things foreknown did not occur.

Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1016D] *On the Trinity*, book XV, ch. 13]: “He does not know all creatures because they are, but they are because he knows.” Again elsewhere [Note: [Col. 1016D] *On the Trinity*, book VI]: “These created things are not known by God because they have been made; rather, they have been made because they are immutably known by God.”

Whether God’s knowledge is the cause of evils. God compels no one to sin. — But if this is said, God’s knowledge seems also to be the cause of evils, since he knew them before they happened. This is absurd. We answer: it is impossible for what has been foreknown not to occur—that is, it never happens otherwise. But the word “because,” as used by Augustine, is not causal but consequential, so that the meaning is: “He does not know because they are; but they are because he knows,” that is, God’s knowledge did not follow the existence of things, but their existence followed God’s knowledge.

Augustine himself explains this when he immediately adds: “For he did not fail to know what he was going to create.” Or Augustine understood this of good things [Note: [Col. 1017D] Homily 53 on John], of which God is indeed the cause, not of evils, which knowledge alone comprehends and of which he is not the author, since they are not his own [Col. 1017B]. Therefore God does not compel anyone to sin because he foreknew human sins that would occur; for he foreknew their sins, not his own.

Whether good things created by God are created necessarily. — But since God is the cause that good things exist, are good things made by necessity? If so, they do not merit, since every merit rests in the will. And the Prophet says: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Psalm 53). We say that God is the efficient or disposing cause of good things insofar as they exist, but does not impose necessity. For what would this mean if, freedom of choice being extinguished, he produced any good things even against our will?

That future things are not the cause of God’s knowledge. — It is clear, therefore, how God’s knowledge is not the cause of future things. Yet future things are in no way the cause of his knowledge, since neither a temporal thing can be the cause of the eternal nor a creature the cause of the Creator. Origen nevertheless says [Note: [Col. 1017D] On Romans 7]: “Something will not be because God knows it will be; rather, because it will be, it is known by God before it happens.” But understand this thus: it would not be known by God as future unless it were future.

Whether God’s foreknowledge can be mistaken. — Although God’s foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, some prove the contrary in this way: something may fail to occur when its occurrence was foreknown, or may occur when it was not foreknown that it would occur. If that happened, God’s foreknowledge would be mistaken. But although this objection is answered in many ways, we say that something was foreseen only in the way in which it would occur.

Moreover, the statement “It is impossible for it to occur otherwise when it has been foreknown, foreseen, and so forth” must be determined according to conjunction and disjunction. If you understand it thus—that both cannot be true at the same time, namely, that God foreknew this to happen thus and that it happened otherwise—it is true. But if you say, “This cannot happen otherwise than thus, as God foreknew beforehand that it would happen,” it is false.

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. Whether God’s Knowledge Can Increase or Decrease

Likewise it is asked whether God’s knowledge can increase or decrease. This seems to be proved as follows: he could do what he was never going to do; and if he did it, he would know it. Likewise, God could fail to do what he is going to do; and if he never did it, he would not know it either.

But we say that God’s knowledge, which is the divine essence, cannot increase or decrease, since in God being is nothing other than knowing. Things known, however, can increase or decrease without change in God’s knowledge. The reason why it cannot increase or decrease is this: God’s knowledge would then increase or decrease only if God began to know or not to know something—which is impossible [Note: [Col. 1017D] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chs. 13–14].

But some say: “If God can know something which he has never known, he can begin to know something.” We say this does not follow, and the proposition itself should not be received without dividing the sense of conjunction and disjunction. For example, if you say, “He can know what he has never known,” that is, “He can now know something which he has never known,” this is false—as though both could be true at once. But if you say it disjunctively, “God can know this, but it is nevertheless true of that thing that he has never known it,” the proposition is true.

Therefore God has knowledge of all things, present, past, and future. Nor should Jerome’s statement disturb us [Note: [Col. 1018D] In the Exposition of Habakkuk]: “It would be absurd to reduce God’s majesty to this, that he should know at every single instant how many gnats are born and die, and what is the number of fleas or flies.” He said this not to remove such things from God’s knowledge, but to warn us not to suppose that God exercises the same providence over rational and irrational beings.

## DISTINCTION XL. On Predestination and Reprobation

Finally, something must be said concerning predestination. Predestination, therefore, is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge. It concerns only those who are to be saved and is called election. But foreknowledge without predestination concerns those who are to be damned and is called reprobation.

Whether one predestined can be damned, or one reprobated saved. — Next it is asked whether one predestined can be damned, or one reprobated saved. No, because the number of the elect can neither increase nor decrease. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1018D] Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*], on the words of Revelation, “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Revelation 2): “If another will not receive it unless this man loses it, the number of the elect is certain”—that is, it cannot increase or decrease.

But it is objected: every salvation is from grace, and what is freely given could fail to be given. If this happened, the number of the elect would decrease. Again, grace for meriting can be given to anyone and preserved to the end; if this happened, the number of the elect would increase. But this is impossible; therefore the former consequence does not follow either. Indeed, observe carefully that in objections of this sort the antecedent is frequently possible while the consequent is impossible. For example: “If God now knows what he has never known, then without doubt he begins in time to know something.” The antecedent is possible; the consequent is by no means so. You will find the same regarding providence and similar matters.

Moreover, the reason why the number of the elect cannot increase or decrease is plain. It would increase only if someone now began to be predestined; it would decrease only if someone then began to be reprobated. But both are impossible for God.

Yet such statements occur according to the senses of conjunction and disjunction. Thus, “It is impossible for one predestined to be damned”—that is, it is impossible for both to be true at once, that he is predestined and is damned—is true. But if you say, “It is impossible for this man to be damned; but this man is among the predestined,” it is false. The same judgment applies to similar cases.

Predestination concerns two things; reprobation, two things. Effects of predestination and likewise of reprobation. — Furthermore, predestination is considered with respect to two things: grace, by which we are now justified, and glory, by which we are made blessed. Likewise reprobation concerns two things. One God foreknows but does not prepare, namely iniquity; the other he also prepares, namely eternal punishment.

Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1019D] *On the Good of Perseverance*, ch. 14]: “Predestination properly is the preparation of God’s benefits.” Thus God’s reprobation is the foreknowledge in some persons of malice that will not end, and the preparation of punishment that will not terminate. As mercy is the effect of predestination, so hardening is the effect of reprobation. Hence the Apostle: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9). By “mercy” he means the bestowal of grace; by “hardening,” the deprivation of that grace.

Augustine, to Sixtus [Note: [Col. 1019D] Letter 105]: “God hardens not by imparting wickedness, but by withdrawing grace.” Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1019D] *To Simplician*, book I]: “Just as God’s reprobation is unwillingness to show mercy, so hardening is unwillingness to show mercy, so that he does not inflict upon a person that by which the person becomes worse, but only does not dispense that by which the person becomes better.”

## Distinction XLI. Whether predestination and reprobation arise from our merits

There are immediately two things in sinners: love and hatred.—Finally, there is no merit for God’s mercy, lest grace be emptied of its character; for if it is not given freely but rendered for merits, it is no longer grace. But sin is the merit of hardening. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Book I to Simplicianus*]: “He has mercy according to grace, which is given freely; but he hardens according to judgment, which is rendered according to merits.” Yet there is no merit for eternal election and reprobation, as the Apostle plainly says concerning the two men, Jacob, namely, elected, and Esau, reprobated: “not from works, but from him who calls,” when they had not yet been born, it was said, “The greater shall serve the lesser” (Mal. I; Rom. IX).

Augustine seems indeed to contradict the foregoing when he says [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 68]: “‘He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.’ But this will of God cannot be unjust. For it arises from the most hidden merits, because, although sinners have made one mass through the general sin, nevertheless there is not no diversity among them. Therefore something precedes in sinners by which, although they are not yet justified, they are made worthy of justification [Col. 1020A]. And likewise something precedes in other sinners by which they are worthy of dullness.”

But we say that he retracted this when he also retracted that statement [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Retractations*, Book I, ch. 23]: “God chose faith in foreknowledge, knowing also that faith itself is found among the gifts of God”—which he had not known previously. If he did not retract this, then, with pardon granted in advance, we dare to say that perhaps he called “most hidden merits” the high and profound judgments of God, by which each person, before he exists, merits God’s hatred or love. So we are accustomed to say that Christ’s death benefited even those not yet born, and merited salvation for them.

Those by which they merit hatred are God’s most just judgments, removed from our understanding; but that by which they merit love is grace alone. Hence Jerome: “God did not act unjustly in having Esau, willingly hated, hated; nor in loving Jacob, loved by grace without merit; because not without some most hidden merit, by which Esau himself merited God’s hatred and Jacob his love—though they themselves had not merited these things, since they were not yet born.” These two things are immediately present in sinners: by one, namely love, they are worthy of justification although not yet justified; by the other, namely hatred, they are worthy of dullness although not yet made dull. If this is well said, we praise God; if not, we are not ashamed to confess that we do not adequately grasp Augustine here.

Difference between predestination, etc.—It must indeed be known that predestination, knowledge, election, foreknowledge, and reprobation are spoken only from eternity; mercy, justification, dulling, and hardening only in time; whereas God’s love [Col. 1020C] and hatred signify neither from eternity nor in time.

Finally, it must be known that reprobation is not the cause of evil coming to be, as predestination is the cause of good. For foreknowledge is the cause of standing firm for many, but the cause of falling for no one.

### God always knows what he has once known

But since God’s foreknowledge concerns only future things, once they cease to be future, God also ceases to foreknow them. This does not indicate any deficiency in God’s foreknowledge, but rather a deficiency or change in the things of which it is foreknowledge. Thus God once foreknew many things which he does not foreknow now. For we must most firmly believe that he now knows everything which he once knew, or will know in the future.

Yet the following objection is raised: if he now knows whatever [Col. 1020D] he knew and will know, then he knows that Christ is going to be born and that Antichrist is alive, since he knew the former and will know the latter. But we say that God now knows precisely the same thing concerning Christ’s birth and Antichrist’s life that he knew or will know. The change of times indeed compels God’s knowledge concerning these matters to be expressed in different words, as appears in a similar case. For we designate the same day, because times have changed, by saying “tomorrow,” “today,” and “yesterday.”

Likewise, the same faith possessed by the ancient and modern fathers is expressed in differing formulations because of the change of times. What they confess as yet to come, we confess as having come; but [Col. 1021A] the faith is the same. Hence Augustine: “The times have changed, and therefore the words have changed, but not the faith.”

Or we say that the inference is not properly made: “God knew that this man would be born; therefore God now knows that this man will be born,” because *would be born* does not signify the same time. Therefore infer instead: “Thus God now knows that at some time this man was going to be born.” The judgment is the same in comparable cases.

## Distinction XLII. On God’s omnipotence

Let us now consider God’s omnipotence, which is considered under two aspects: namely, that he does everything he wills, and that he suffers absolutely nothing that he does not will. For Scripture says: “He did all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. CXIII [114/115]). Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1021D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 69]: “He is truly called Omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of the will of the Omnipotent is not hindered by the will of any creature.”

The same author says [Note: [Col. 1021D] *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 5, §3 and end]: “He is omnipotent not because he can do all things, but because he can bring about whatever he wills.” He cannot commit sin, lie, and the like, because being able to do such things belongs rather to weakness. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1021D] *On the Trinity*, Book XV, ch. 4]: “It is a great power of God not to be able to lie.” Similarly, he cannot suffer what he does not will, because he cannot be deceived, become miserable, and the like: to be able to undergo these things is weakness.

Finally, walking, eating, and similar acts are not so entirely foreign to him. Although they are by no means fitting to the divine essence, God nevertheless performs them in creatures. But take care how you understand Augustine’s foregoing words, namely, “he can bring about whatever he wills.” For if you say “whatever he wills [Col. 1021C] to do,” or “whatever he wills himself to be able to do,” in this sense an angel or any blessed person could be called omnipotent, since he wills to do nothing except what he does and wills, nor to be able to do anything except what he can do. Therefore, so that this applies to God alone, say: “He can bring about whatever he wills to come about,” either by himself, as heaven and earth, or through a creature, as good works and products of art. No saint either will be able or has been able to do this.

## Distinction XLIII. In what respects God can do more than he wills

It must be known that God can do more than he wills. Hence: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. XXVI). Here it is plainly apparent both that the Son could have asked what he did not ask, and that the Father could have provided what he did not provide.

Augustine also says [Col. 1021D] [Note: [Col. 1022D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 95]: “The will of the Omnipotent can do many things which it neither wills nor does.” For he could have made twelve legions fight against those who seized Christ. Again [Note: [Col. 1022D] *ibid.*], what the faith of the pious now holds will then be seen in the most brilliant light of wisdom: how certain and immutable God’s will is—a will which can do many things and does not will them, but wills nothing that it cannot do. Again, he says [Note: [Col. 1022D] *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 7]: “He raised Lazarus in body; could he not have raised Judas in mind?” Certainly he could, but he did not will to do so.

He sets forth another opinion and refutes it.—Yet, against this truth, so manifest, some attempt to confine God’s power [Col. 1022A] within a measure, saying that God can do nothing other than what he does, nor omit anything among those things which he does, in this manner: “God cannot do anything except what it is good and just for him to do. But it is not just and good for him to do anything except what he does. Otherwise stated: he cannot do anything except what his justice requires. But his justice does not require him to do anything except what he does. Therefore he cannot do anything except what he does. And the same justice requires that he not do what he does not do. But he cannot act against his justice. Therefore he cannot do any of the things he leaves undone.”

These assertions have several meanings. “God cannot do anything except what it is good and just for him to do,” that is, he cannot do except that which, if he did it, it would be good and just for him [Col. 1022B] to do—this is true. But if one says, “He cannot do except what he does do, which assuredly is good and just for him to do,” this is false.

We also distinguish the other proposition, although the word *requires* in relation to God is not free from difficulty: “He cannot do except what his justice requires him to do,” that is, except that which, if it came about, would be fitting to his justice—this is true. But if it means, “He cannot do except what he does, which surely accords with his justice,” it is false. The same applies to similar statements.

Again they say: “God cannot do except what he ought to do; but he ought to do nothing except what he does.” But we say that “ought” is improperly said of God, because he owes us nothing whatever except by promise. But what he promised was in no way a matter of necessity, but of grace. Accordingly distinguish as follows: “He cannot do except what he ought,” that is, except what he promised—this is false. But “he cannot do except that which, if he did it, would accord with his justice”—this is true.

They add also: “He cannot do or leave undone anything except what there is reason for him to do or leave undone. But this alone is what he does or leaves undone.” But distinguish this too after the pattern of the foregoing: “He cannot do or leave undone except that which, if he did or left it undone, there would be reason for him to do or leave it undone”—that is, whatever things are not subject to his will belong among things not willed—this is true. But if it means, “He cannot do or leave undone except what he does or leaves undone, for which assuredly there is reason for him to do or leave it undone,” it is false [Col. 1022D].

Finally, let us briefly be warned that all doubts of this sort, when resolved conditionally, are true; but simply stated, they are false.

Still more laboriously than fruitfully, they continue: “If God can do something other than what he does, then he can do what he did not foreknow. If this is so, he can act without foreknowledge—which is absurd.” This has indeed become clear according to the manner of conjunctive and disjunctive expressions defined above: “He can act without foreknowledge,” that is, “he can do something which he did not foreknow”—is true. But “without foreknowledge,” that is, [Col. 1023A] “he can so do something that he did not foreknow it, and yet does it”—is false.

They also misuse Augustine’s authority, when he says [Note: [Col. 1023D] *On the Creed*, Book I, ch. 1]: “This alone God cannot do: what he does not will.” By this it seems that he cannot do anything except what he wills. But he wills nothing except what he does; and thus he seems unable to do except what he does. But they should know that this was said as though the discussion concerned only things which God does not will, not all things. It is as if Augustine had said: “Whatever God cannot do, he does not will.” From this it does not follow: “Therefore whatever he does not will, he cannot do.” It is like saying: “Only what is not an animal is not a human being.” Yet not everything which is not a human being is not an animal.

Or we say this more simply: “This alone he cannot do which he does not will,” that is, [Col. 1023B] he does nothing unwillingly; in other words, whatever is not subject to his will belongs among things not willed—this is true. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1023D] *Confessions*, Book VII, ch. 4]: “You are not compelled unwillingly to anything, because your will is not greater than your power.” Understand this to be true with regard to what subsists, not with regard to the objects of power and will.

## Distinction XLIV. Whether God can make better things than those he makes

They also say that God cannot make things better than those which he makes. For if he could and did not make them, he would be envious. In this they misuse what Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1023D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 50]: “God ought to have begotten him whom he begot as his equal. For if he willed it and could not, he is weak; if he could and would not, he is envious.”

This was well said, because when he begot from his own substance, [Col. 1023C] he could not beget either one better than himself or one less good. But other things which he makes from elsewhere he could make better, and less good. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1024D] *On Genesis according to the Letter*, Book II, ch. 7]: “God could have made man such that he could neither sin nor will to sin; and if this were so, who would doubt that he would have been better?”

Finally, if it is asked whether God can make better things than he makes in another or better manner, we say: if “manner” refers to God, as though he could make them by another or better wisdom, this must be denied. But if it refers to the things created themselves, as though he could make other or better things, it must certainly be granted, as was said above. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1024D] *On the Trinity*, Book XIII, ch. 10]: “Another manner of our liberation was possible to God, but none more fitting for healing our misery.”

[Col. 1023D] Whether God can now do whatever he could formerly do.—Further, it is asked whether he can now do whatever he could formerly do. This seems not to be so, because he could formerly die and rise again, which he cannot do now. Here we must say what we said above concerning knowledge: namely, that he can now have formerly died and risen again. For changed times compel a change of expression while the meaning remains altogether the same.

Therefore we confess that God can always do whatever he was once able to do; that is, that he possesses every power which he once possessed. Yet he cannot always do what he was at some time able to do. Just as he has all the knowledge [Col. 1024A] and will that he has ever had, but does not now know to be, or will, all that he formerly knew to be and willed.

## Distinction XLV. On God’s will

Something must now be said concerning God’s will. To will is said of God according to his essence, for to be willing is the same for him as to be God. Nor is will in God an affection or movement, as it is in a creature, but simply the divine *usia* [οὐσία, essence]. Yet not whatever God wills is himself, just as God’s being is the same as his knowing, although God is not whatever he knows.

### The meaning of “God knows” and “God wills”

Understand, however, the meaning of these expressions: “God wills,” “God knows,” “he is willing,” and “he is knowing”; that is, God [Col. 1024B] is he whose essence is his will and knowledge. Likewise, “God knows all things” means: God is he to whose knowledge, which is his own essence, all things are subject; just as “God wills this or that” means: God is he to whose will, which is his essence, this or that is subject.

### God’s will is the first cause of all creatures

This supremely good will, therefore, is the cause of all things which naturally have been, are, and will be. But it has no cause. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1024D] *On the Trinity*, Book III, ch. 4]: “God’s will is the first and supreme cause of all forms and motions.” For where does God’s wisdom—which reaches mightily from end to end and sweetly orders all things—fail to accomplish what it wills? (Wis. VIII.)

Thus it is the first cause [Col. 1024C] of health, sickness, rewards, punishments, graces, recompenses, and, finally, of all wonders, including those things which occur wonderfully without astonishment, as ancient miracles do.

### What God’s will is

Properly speaking, God’s will is this: being divine *usia* [οὐσία, essence], it is immutable and cannot remain unfulfilled. Hence: “The Lord did all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. CXIII [114/115]); and the Apostle: “Who has resisted his will?” (Rom. IX). It is rightly called God’s good pleasure.

### That several things are called God’s will

Yet several things, each of which is called God’s will not properly but according to figures of speech, are called God’s will: God’s command, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation. In this sense the Prophet says in the plural: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills” (Ps. CX [111]). So also, because God’s mercy and justice have many effects, though there is only one mercy and justice, namely the divine *usia*, Scripture speaks in the plural: “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXVIII [89]); and elsewhere: “The justices of the Lord are right” (Ps. XVIII [19]).

Thus command, prohibition, and counsel are called God’s wills because they are signs of the divine will, just as future judgment and God’s scourge are called God’s wrath because they are signs of wrath, although wrath cannot be attributed to God. [Col. 1025A] Finally, “will” may be understood in this manner in: “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. VI); and: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. XII). This will is mutable and is often unfulfilled. For God commands many people things which they do not do; he prohibits things which they do not avoid; he counsels things to which they pay no heed. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1025D] *On the Spirit and the Letter*, ch. 33]: “Unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel.”

### God does not always will what he commands to be done, nor what he forbids to be avoided

Indeed, God himself does not always will to be done what he commands. He did not will Isaac to be sacrificed, although he commanded it; he wished only to test Abraham’s faith (Gen. XXII). Likewise, he does not always will what he forbids to be avoided. For after healing a sick man, he told him to tell no one [Col. 1025B] (Mark I), not because he wished him to remain silent, but rather because he wished to set an example and decline personal praise.

## Distinction XLVI. On God’s permission and operation

Permission and operation too are called God’s will. Thus Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1025D] *Enchiridion*]: “Nothing happens unless the Omnipotent wills it to happen—either by permitting it to happen, as evils, or by himself doing it, as good things.” These are called God’s wills because he permits them. But God permits evils to occur, willing to draw good out of them; he works good things, namely those which he wills to exist.

### Whether God’s will is always fulfilled

But God’s will does not seem always to be fulfilled, since the Apostle says: “God wills all human beings to be saved” (Rom. [Col. 1025C] IX; I Tim. II); yet not all are saved, because they are unwilling to do what brings salvation. Again, the Lord says, addressing the impious city: “How often I wished to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. XXIII). It seems as though, because she was unwilling, God’s will was not fulfilled.

But the Apostle’s statement is not to be understood as though there were no human being whom he did not will to be saved, but that no one is saved unless he wills that person to be saved. Understand likewise: “God enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I), not because there is no person who is not enlightened, but because no one is enlightened except by him.

The Gospel passage is not to be understood as though your will had impeded my will; rather, it means: all those whom I gathered by my ever-effective will, I gathered although you were unwilling [Col. 1025D] (Matt. XXIII).

### Whether God wills evils to exist

It is asked whether God wills evils to exist. This seems so to some, who argue as follows: God either wills evils to occur or wills them not to occur. If he wills them not to occur, they do not occur, for nothing resists his will. But they do occur. Therefore he wills evils to occur.

Otherwise: God wills everything that is good. But it is good that evils exist. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1025D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 96]: “It is good not only that good things exist, but also that evils exist. For unless it were good that evils too should exist, they would in no way be permitted to exist by the good Omnipotent.”

Others reply that one should not say in this way that God wills evils to happen, or wills them not to happen, but only that he does not will evils to happen. As for the saying proposed from Augustine, namely that the occurrence of evils is good, they say that *good* there is used in the sense of *useful*, as Jerome also says: “Judas’s evil was good for the good,” that is, for those to whom the benefit of salvation came from it. For God produces good from evils. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1025D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 72]: “God judged it better to make good things out of evils than to permit no evils to exist.” Thus it is good that evils exist—that is, useful.

This applies only to those saints who are called according to his purpose. For to such persons, as the Apostle says, all things work together for good (Rom. VIII), even evils. If they occur, they advance toward good, because after a fall people return more humble [Col. 1026B] and become more cautious, as Peter did. Evils inflicted by wicked persons also benefit them for the correction of sins and the exercise and preservation of justice, just as Job felt God’s hand and the Apostle Satan’s thorn; and each advanced because he bore evil well.

Finally, God does not will evils to occur; for if he did, God too would be the author of evils, since his will is authority. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1026D] *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 3]: “When something is said to be done by that author, it is said to be done by that person’s will.” The Evangelist also, professing God to be the author of good things, says: “All things were made through him” (John I). Excluding evils, he adds: “Without him was made nothing,” that is, sin. But he did not say “with him unwilling,” or “willing,” or “against his will,” but “without him,” that is, without his authority.

Again [Note: [Col. 1026D] *ibid.*, q. 4]: “God is not the cause by which a human being becomes worse; he would be if he willed evils to occur, through which a human being becomes worse. But God is the cause only of good things.”

## Distinction XLVII. That God’s will is always fulfilled concerning us or by us

God’s will is always done by the creature’s will. He examines the meaning of the foregoing words. God does not always will his commands to be done.—It must also be known that God’s eternal will is always fulfilled concerning what we do. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1026D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 106 and following]: “That will is always fulfilled either concerning us or by us. It is fulfilled concerning us, though we do not fulfill it, when we sin. It is fulfilled by us when we do good. For we do it because we know that it pleases God.”

Therefore a human being does nothing from which God does not [Col. 1026D] bring about what he wills. For if someone sins, God wills to spare the penitent so that he may live, and to punish the impenitent so that the obstinate person may not escape the power of justice. Thus, through that same will of the creature by which what the Creator did not will was done, he himself fulfills what he wills, using even evils well. For by the very fact that the creature acted against his will, his will has been brought about from that action.

Yet, lest these matters leave room for error, recall the distinction of will set out above, so that one may say: through the creature’s acting against God’s command, his eternal will has been brought about—that is, fulfilled—concerning that creature, by which he willed to condemn it. Hence Gregory, commenting on Job, plainly says [Note: [Col. 1027C] *Morals*, Book VI, ch. 11, on Job V, “Who takes the wise”]: “Many carry out God’s will in the very things by which they strive to change it, and, resisting his counsel, they serve it, because what results from human endeavor serves his providential ordering.”

It must also be known that God commands all persons to do what ought to be done and forbids them what ought to be avoided, although he does not will each individual to act accordingly. He does this in order to show his justice to all, so that the good may receive glory through obedience, while the wicked, rendered inexcusable through obstinacy, receive punishment. Finally, in each Testament he personally commanded and forbade many things, not because he willed them to be done in that way, but for a hidden reason which the diligent and devout reader will discover in its respective places when God reveals it.

## Distinction XLVIII. Sometimes a person of good will wills something other than God wills

Finally, we must be warned that sometimes a person’s will is good when he does not wish something to happen which God wills, provided that the end is pious. Hence Augustine, speaking of the Apostle, says [Note: [Col. 1028C] *Enchiridion*, ch. 101]: “The wills of pious believers appeared good when they did not want the apostle Paul to go to Jerusalem (Acts XXI), lest he suffer there the evils foretold by the prophet Agabus; and yet God willed that he should suffer this.”

Sometimes too a person’s will is evil when he wills the same thing as God—that is, on account of an impious end. Thus the Jews willed the same thing as God, namely that Christ should be killed. Yet God’s will in this was good because he willed it piously; theirs was evil because they willed it impiously.

[Col. 1027C] It must be noted here that God willed only that Christ be killed by the Jews; he did not will [Col. 1028A] that the Jews should kill him. Just as Christ willed that what he had foretold concerning Peter should be fulfilled; he did not will Peter to fulfill it, otherwise he would have willed Peter to deny him.

Nor should the statement “God willed Christ to be killed by the Jews” be understood without distinction. It is true if it means that he willed Christ to suffer death inflicted by the Jews. But if it means that he willed the Jews to kill him, it is false. Or, as seems better, one should say that God willed the Lord to be killed, but not by any person or persons, although this could not happen without them. So he wills someone to repent, yet does not in any way will that person to have sinned, although repentance cannot exist without sin.

But if it is asked whether the saints ought to have been pleased that Christ suffered, we say: certainly, with respect to humanity’s liberation, but by no means with respect to his suffering itself. One of them, even abhorring it through piety rather than doubt, asked as though in doubt: “Are you he who is to come, or are we to wait for another?” (Matt. XI).

Again, it is asked whether the suffering of holy martyrs ought to please us. We say: certainly, with respect to the crown prepared for them to receive. Yet we may worthily not wish it, when through compassionate piety we desire that they should avoid suffering and escape the hands of wicked persons. Thus we may piously both will and not will the sufferings of the saints. Hence it is pious to weep for Martin, and pious to rejoice for Martin. Therefore every will is good that is directed toward a right end, which must be assessed solely by zeal for God according to knowledge [Col. 1028C].

[Col. 1027] End of the book on the Trinity, which is the first book of Bandinus’s *Sentences*.

[Col. 1027]

# Master Bandinus’s Book on the Creation of the World and the Fall of Man, Being the Second Book of the *Sentences*

*Outline.*—After Bandinus, in the first book, briefly and clearly expounded God’s power and nature—as far as these can be perceived and communicated by a human being—he transfers his inquiry in this second book, by a most fitting method, to things created by God. First, after a preliminary discussion of the principles of things, he sets forth the creation, nature, condition, fall, ranks, and ministries of angels. Then, having explained the creation of the world—which was completed and ordered in the work of six days—he undertakes a special treatment of humanity, teaching that humanity was formed in God’s likeness, placed in paradise, and there seduced through the Devil’s envy by the woman. Finally, taking occasion from Adam’s fall, Bandinus treats with great learning many matters: free choice, grace, both original and actual sin, other varieties of sins, the seven capital vices, sin against the Holy Spirit, and venial sins.

[Col. 1027D] ## Distinction I. There is one principle of things, not several

Plato has three principles; Aristotle has three.—We have thus far treated, as far as the usefulness of brevity permits, matters known to pertain to the mystery of the divine unity and Trinity [Col. 1028D–1029A]. Let us now proceed to the consideration of creatures [Note: [Col. 1029D] Compare the first distinction of Peter Lombard, *Sentences*, Book II].

Scripture, set forth by the finger of God, indicates at its beginning that God is the Creator of all things which naturally exist, apart from himself, when it says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I). By saying “in the beginning,” rather than “in the beginnings,” and likewise by saying “God” and “created,” it refutes the folly of philosophers who believed that not only one—as is taught here—but several primary principles of things exist without a beginning. Plato thought there were three: God, the exemplar, and matter. Aristotle, however, said that there were two, matter and form, and a third called the agent. He also said that the world had always existed [Note: [Col. 1029D] Near the end of the second book *On Generation* and of the eighth book of the *Physics*].

What is Catholic teaching. What a creator is. What it is to create. [Col. 1029B] Difference between God and an angel. Why God made rational creatures.—Having rejected those views, we confess that God alone is the one principle and Creator of things. A creator is one who makes something from nothing, or out of nothing. Strictly speaking, to create is to make something from nothing. In this God, who makes, differs from human beings and angels who make: what they make, they make not from nothing but from something.

Moreover, when they make something, a movement of operation is present; this cannot at all exist in God. For God works not by movement but solely by will, so that “God makes” may truly be said to mean that, according to his will, something newly comes forth. Such is the goodness of this will that he wished others, in time, to share in his blessedness, in which he alone has been blessed from eternity—a blessedness which he saw could be communicated and could not at all be diminished. But since it cannot be shared except through understanding, God made the rational creature, which might understand the highest good, love it by understanding it, possess it by loving it, and enjoy it by possessing it.

Distinction of rational creature. Why and for what purpose the rational creature was made. Why the soul is united to the body.—Finally, he divided it into the incorporeal creature, which is an angel, and the corporeal creature, which is the soul possessing flesh or a body: this is the human being. Therefore angel and human being were made for God’s goodness. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1030D] *On Christian Teaching*, Book I, ch. 13]: “Because God is good, we exist.” The creature was made, moreover, to serve and enjoy God.

Thus, when briefly and rightly asked why and for what purpose the rational creature was made, we answer: for God’s goodness and for the creature’s benefit.
