That statement found in Augustine—that humanity was made for the restoration of the angelic fall [Note: [Col. 1030D] Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXII, ch. 1; and *Enchiridion*, ch. 29]—must not be understood as though humanity would not have been made had the angel not sinned. Rather, among the other reasons known to God, this was one reason when he made humanity.

If it is asked why God united the soul to the body, when it seemed worthier remaining in its own purity, one must answer: because he willed it. No cause of his will is to be sought, because it has none. Or perhaps we may dare to say that he did this so that in the human condition he might present an example of the blessed union between God and the creature in eternal life. For lest perhaps the creature should think that it could not be united to the Creator so far as to love him with all its power, it seemed fitting that the most excellent creature, namely spirit, should be united in such great love to the lowest creature—that is, flesh, which is from mud—that it could not be compelled to will to leave it. Hence the Apostle says: “We do not wish to be unclothed of the body, but to be clothed over” (II Cor. V).

Or souls are united to bodies so that, serving the Lord in them, they may deserve a greater crown. For thereby, together with the very body in which they served, they will in the future be made equal to the angelic nature, [Col. 1030B] concerning which it remains for us next to dispute.

## Distinction II. On angelic nature in particular

The time of angelic creation.—As we are to treat of angelic nature, let us consider when it was created, where, what it was made like, and in what respect perfected; and also its orders, offices, names, and several other matters. It is established that the angel was made before every other creature, as it is written: “Wisdom was created before all things” (Ecclus. I). This must be understood of angelic nature, which is often called life, wisdom, and light in Scripture. For God’s Wisdom, who is God himself, is uncreated.

But how can this be? Elsewhere Scripture says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I), and: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth” (Ps. CI [102]). Certainly, if he created the earth in the beginning, nothing was made before it. But if the angel was first of all, then it is also proved that he was made before the earth.

### How wisdom was created before all things

Therefore, lest any contradiction seem to exist in such weighty pronouncements, we should maintain that spiritual and corporeal creatures were made simultaneously. Hence Solomon says: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. XVIII), that is, spiritual and corporeal nature. Augustine likewise says [Note: [Col. 1030D] Augustine, *On Genesis*, Book II, ch. 1] that spiritual and corporeal creatures are understood by “heaven” and “earth,” and that these were created “in the beginning,” namely at the beginning of time, or “in the beginning” because they were made first.

Nevertheless, wisdom was created before all things because, although the angel does not precede in time, he does precede in dignity. Or it is said to have been created “before all things,” not with regard to essence, but with regard to the differentiation of form. Spiritual nature is believed to have received a distinct form in the first moment of its creation, unlike corporeal creation, which God made during six days. For it was first made unformed and confused—that is, without differentiation of form. Hence, according to the Greeks, it was called *chaos* and *hyle* (χάος and ὕλη). We do not rashly assert this, but set it forth while preserving reverence for the mysteries.

[Col. 1031A] ### Where angels were created

Accordingly, angels were created in heaven. Hence the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke X). Here “heaven” is not understood as the firmament, made on the second day, but as the empyrean—that is, the fiery heaven, so called from its brightness rather than its heat. Once made, it was immediately filled with angels. Hence Bede says [Note: [Col. 1031D] *On Genesis*]: “That highest heaven, which is removed from the world’s revolution, was, as soon as it was created, filled with holy angels. The Lord testifies that they were created in the beginning together with heaven and earth, saying: ‘Where were you when the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God shouted for joy?’” By “morning stars” and “sons of God” he means the same angels.
calls.

But if the angels were made in heaven, how does Lucifer say: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, [Col. 1031B] and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)? But there he calls “heaven” God’s exalted height, with which he wished to make himself equal. The sense is: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with God.

DISTINCTION III. What kind of beings the angels were when made. The angels were not created equal.—We must also believe that the angels were created after receiving four benefits from their Founder and Creator: namely, so that they might be simple in essence, distinct in person, rational in intelligence, and free in will—thus existing from the outset able to incline either to good or to evil. We must not suppose that all were created equal in these respects. For just as there is some difference among bodies even in their first condition, so also in spiritual [Col. 1031C] creatures there must be believed to have been a manifold difference appropriate to their condition. Hence Lucifer was made more excellent than the rest. Thus Ezekiel says: “Every precious stone was your covering” (Ezek. 28). Again: “The fir trees did not equal his height; the plane trees were not equal to his branches” (Ezek. 31).

In what respects angels differ.—They differ, then, in subtlety of nature, keenness of knowledge, and freedom of will. Thus those who then surpassed others in natural gifts likewise presided over them through gifts of grace, being established as more excellent in rank. But those created less subtle and less keen in wisdom received lesser gifts of grace and were established as inferior, by the equitable ordering of the wisdom [Col. 1031D] of God, who arranges all things. Yet a difference in subtlety of nature does not bring weakness; lesser knowledge does not introduce ignorance of wisdom; nor does an inferior freedom impose necessity upon anyone’s will.

How angels were created good; how just. There was an interval between creation and confirmation.—It must also be firmly maintained that the angels were created good, not indeed through the exercise of free choice, but through the benefit of creation; and just, not through the practice of virtue, but through the innocence of their nature. For they were made [Col. 1032A] such that they could sin and could refrain from sin, if they wished. And this they did: some by falling, others by remaining steadfast. Hence Genesis says: “God made all things very good” (Gen. 1). Therefore he made the nature of angels good.

It is also faithfully believed that there was some interval between creation and the fall, on the basis of what Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1031D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XII, chapter 23]: “The angel, having first been made, immediately turned himself away from the truth, delighting in his own power.” By saying “first,” he indicates an interval. Likewise Origen [Note: [Col. 1031D] *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 1, on “I saw something like an appearance”]: “Just as Adam and Eve did not sin immediately, so too the serpent was at one time not a serpent.” For God did not make malice; by these words he affirms that, after their good creation, an interval also intervened.

Moreover, it is clear that an interval occurred between creation and confirmation. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1032D] *On Genesis*, book I, chapters 2, 3, 4, and 6] that the angelic [Col. 1032B] nature was first called “heaven” when it was created, but afterwards “light” when it was formed and turned toward its Creator, namely to praise God. Thus it was first said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”; then: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Gen. 1). That is, the angels were confirmed.

Yet the contrary seems to follow from what Truth says in the Gospel: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8). But this must be understood as meaning from the beginning of the human being’s creation, whom, immediately after he was made, the devil envied and brought down into death by seducing him. Or “from the beginning” means after the beginning. Or understand it as from the beginning of confirmation, not from the first condition. For it is not irreligious to say that an angel has a twofold beginning, just as a human being has a twofold [Col. 1032C] birth.

An objection is likewise drawn from Augustine [Note: [Col. 1032D] *On Genesis*, book XXI, chapters 19 and 20], who says that it should not without reason be thought that the devil fell from the very beginning of his condition. Hence some think that he was not bent toward this malice by free choice, but was created by God in it, according to the text: “This is the beginning of God’s creation, which God made so that the devil might be mocked by his—that is, God’s—angels” (Job 40).

But Augustine himself makes clear elsewhere that, according to others, he had said this [Note: [Col. 1032D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book XI, chapter 23]: “The view that the devil never stood in the truth must not be understood so as to suppose that he was created evil by the good God; otherwise it would be said that he did not fall from the beginning. For he did not fall if he was made such. From what, indeed, would he fall? Therefore, having first been made, he immediately turned himself away from the truth, delighting [Col. 1032D] in his own power; and he did not taste the sweetness of blessed life. He did not, of course, despise it after receiving it, but lost it by refusing to receive it.”

Finally, the phrase drawn from Job, “the beginning of God’s creature,” is explained thus: it signifies not nature, but an aerial body, which God fitted to such a will; or “creature” means God’s own ordering, by which he made the devil, even unwillingly, useful to the good; or it means the making of the angel himself, because, though God foreknew that he would become evil, he nevertheless made him, foreseeing how great goods he would bring forth for the elect from him. He is called “beginning” because he precedes others in antiquity [Col. 1033A] and in primacy of malice. Hence Job says: “He is called king over all the children of pride” (Job 41).

DISTINCTION IV. Whether angels were made blessed.—We must not, however, concede that the angels were made blessed. Although Augustine at first entertained differing opinions concerning the good angels, he finally gave this warning [Note: [Col. 1033D] *On Genesis*, book XI, chapter 14]: “To say of the angels that they could be blessed in their own kind, while uncertain of damnation or salvation and having no hope that they would be changed for the better, is excessive presumption.”

Concerning the evil angels he explicitly denies this, saying [Note: [Col. 1034D] Book XI, *On Genesis*, chapter 17]: “How was he blessed among the angels who had no foreknowledge of his future punishment and sin?” This is proved as follows. If he foresaw it and wished to avoid it but could not, then he was miserable. Thus misery preceded sin and did not follow it—[Col. 1033B] which is false, since it arises from sin. Finally, if he could avoid it and did not wish to, he was foolish, which again is false. For angels were made knowing what they were, from whom they were, and with whom they were; they also had knowledge of good and evil, and the love by which they loved God and themselves. This was not the love of charity but natural love, by which we also, without fault, love things we possess, such as a horse or a book.

On confirmation and fall. “Perfect” is said in many senses. What integrity is; what blessed brightness is; supreme perfection.—It must be maintained that angels were perfect in one respect, yet created imperfect in another. A thing is perfect according to its condition, for example, [Col. 1033C] when nothing belonging to the due condition of its creation is lacking, as when a human being is born whole. In this sense the angels were made perfect. There is also perfection according to progress, when nothing is lacking from progress; in this sense angels will be perfect only after confirmation, and saints after the resurrection. There is also that which never lacked and never will lack anything: God alone. The first perfection, then, belongs to created nature and is called integrity. The second belongs to glorified nature and is called blessed brightness. The third belongs to uncreated nature and is called supreme and universal perfection.

DISTINCTION V. The confirmation of those who stood and the fall of those who fell.—Finally, using freedom of choice—which is free power and the capacity of a rational will—some chose good and were turned toward God; others [Col. 1033D] chose evil and were thus turned away from God. To turn toward God was to cling to him in charity. To turn away from God was to envy charity. For grace cooperating with free choice was given to those who stood, by which they were effectively helped to will and do good and to persevere in it; this was to turn toward God. Yet they did not need operating grace. For this is the grace by which the ungodly person is justified and becomes godly. But they were not evil, and therefore did not need justification.

Whether turning away from God is imputed to the evil angels.—But since they could not turn toward God without grace, some think it should not be imputed to those who fell that they were not turned toward him. For, they say, [Col. 1034A] it was not their fault that grace was not given to them, since no fault had preceded it. But we say that no preceding fault prevented grace, except the fault involved in falling. For they were able to stand as the others did, since nothing hindered them from standing and nothing impelled them to fall. Their fall, therefore, was a manifest fault, for which grace was not given.

On the blessedness of those who stood, and whether they merited it.—Thus, once confirmed, they immediately became blessed. It is commonly asked whether some merit preceded the reward of blessedness. This seems so to some, if not temporally, at least causally; they say that the holy angels received simultaneously the grace of merit and of reward. But we think it more faithfully believed that merit followed, and that only then did they receive the grace by which they would live blessedly [Col. 1034B]; yet afterwards, through services continually rendered to their Creator, they merited—and have merited—the reward received at the beginning.

DISTINCTION VI. Lucifer was higher among the angels who fell.—But did those who fell immediately become miserable? Among them one, as the head of malice, was more eminent. Thus Job says: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). And Ezekiel: “You were the seal of likeness, full of knowledge and perfection; you were beautiful amid the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). Hence in Isaiah he is called Lucifer: “How,” he says, “have you fallen, O Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14).

Whence and how they fell. Demons near to us.—Driven out of the empyrean heaven, where they had been made, they fell into this dark air. [Col. 1034C] Thus Revelation says that the dragon, falling from heaven, drew the third part of the stars with him (Rev. 12), because that Lucifer fell, with all who consented to his malice, into this air. Hence the Apostle says: “Our struggle is against the rulers and powers of this air, and against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6), because demons, spiritual by nature and wicked by malice, dwell in the air near us. Peter likewise says: “They are kept in dark air,” which has been assigned to them as a prison until the time of judgment (2 Pet. 2). Then they will be driven down into the abyss of hell, according to: “Go, you accursed” (Matt. 25). Yet all this is for our sake: with them set before us on the way, tested through them as through fire and water, we may pass [Col. 1034D] into refreshment.

Evil angels descend daily into hell.—That some demons descend daily into hell in order to lead souls there for torment is most true. Nor is it far from the truth that some are always there, taking turns by allotted shifts, detaining and tormenting souls. That the souls of the wicked descend there is evident from the fact that Christ, descending into the lower regions, brought out the just while leaving the wicked there. For “he bit hell; he did not swallow it up” (Hos. 13).

Demons once conquered by saints cease to tempt others.—It should also be known that unclean spirits [Col. 1035A] overcome by saints who live justly and chastely are deprived of the power to tempt. Origen says [Note: [Col. 1035D] Volume I, homily 85 on the book of Joshua]: “I indeed think that saints, resisting these inciters and conquering them, diminish the army of demons, or kill as many of them as possible; and it is no longer permitted to the spirit that has been overcome by some saint through chaste and modest living to attack another person again.” Some understand this to mean that it is not permitted to tempt a person concerning the vice in which it was defeated.

DISTINCTION VII. Good angels cannot will evil, nor evil angels good.—Furthermore, it should be known that good angels have been so confirmed through grace that they cannot will or do evil. Likewise the evil are so hardened by malice that they cannot will or do good. An objection to this is taken from Jerome, [Col. 1035B] who says [Note: [Col. 1035D] In the treatise *On the Prodigal Son*, to Pope Damasus, at the end]: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur. All other things, since they have free choice, can be turned in either direction.” But he must be understood to have said this according to the simple nature of free choice, according to which even angels can change, not according to the consolation of grace or its deprivation, according to which they are wholly unable to change. Hence Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1035D] Book I, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 12]: “Angels are mutable by nature, immutable by grace.” Augustine likewise says [Note: [Col. 1035D] *Against Maximinus*, book III, chapter 12]: “God alone is unable to sin by no grace but by his own nature. Therefore, whenever a rational creature is granted inability to sin, this belongs not to its own nature but to God’s grace.” In this sense we also say that whatever rational creature cannot do good does not have this from nature, but from its own [Col. 1035C] malice.

The confirmed good have freer choice than before. On the ranks of angels.—The good do not therefore lack free choice, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1035D] *Enchiridion*, chapter 105], because they cannot will evil. Far freer is the choice that cannot serve sin, by which good is voluntarily chosen and evil rejected. So too the evil have free choice, corrupted by malice to such an extent that they cannot serve righteousness; by it they voluntarily avoid good and always follow evil.

Angels, both good and evil, also have ranks over one another. They likewise preside over cities, provinces, and persons, as Daniel and many passages of Scripture testify. Evil angels also preside over individual [Col. 1035D] vices. Hence there is said to be a spirit of pride and of lust. Thus riches are called by the demon’s name *mammon*, not because they belong to him, but because one of them uses them more especially than the others for deceiving human beings. Likewise, good angels must be believed to preside individually over virtues.

On the knowledge of demons. Threefold demonic knowledge. Magical arts come from demons.—Although evil angels are thus hardened by malice, they are not altogether deprived of keen perception. For, as Isidore [Note: [Col. 1036D] *On the Supreme Good*, book I, chapter 12] and Augustine [Note: [Col. 1036D] *On Genesis*, book II, chapter 17] teach, they possess a threefold sharpness of knowledge: subtlety of nature, experience of times, and reports from higher spirits. Through their knowledge and power magical arts are also practiced. Thus Pharaoh’s magicians made serpents and frogs in Egypt through them (Exod. 8). But demons must not be thought creators of these things, any more than parents are creators of children or farmers of crops. For God alone is the one Creator of all things. From him all these things which, when suitable opportunities arise, come before our eyes, have been created within a certain interwoven structure of the elements, as though certain seeds had been placed there. From these, as from original principles, they take the beginnings of their emergence and the growth proper to their size [Col. 1036B] and distinction of forms. Both good and evil angels, knowing these seeds through subtle perception, draw forth suitable things from hidden seeds—and then nature operates through the fitting tempering of the elements—secretly scatter them, and thus provide occasions for things to be generated and their growth accelerated. Yet God’s power always works inwardly; therefore he alone is Creator.

Why demons have been given knowledge and so great a power of operation.—This knowledge and power were given to demons by God, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1036D] *On the Trinity*, book III, chapter 7]: either to deceive deceivers, such as the Egyptians themselves; or to warn the faithful not to desire such abilities as something great; or to exercise and test the patience of the just.

[Col. 1036C] The power of demons is restricted.—Moreover, it should be known that they cannot do whatever they can do by subtlety of nature, because the higher power of God or of angels does not permit it. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1036D] *On the Trinity*, book III, same chapter], no other reason appears why those who made frogs and serpents could not make gnats, except that the greater dominion of God, prohibiting them through the Holy Spirit, was present. This the magicians themselves confessed when they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8).

DISTINCTION VIII. Whether angels have bodies. Even if angels had bodies, they would not for that reason be bodily.—It is also commonly asked whether angels have bodies. Although some think that they do not, [Col. 1036D] Augustine nevertheless seems plainly to maintain that they have bodies, when he discusses the ancient bodily forms in which God was shown to human sight. Among other things, he says [Note: [Col. 1036D] *On the Trinity*, book III, chapter 1]: “Angels were sent to speak in the person of God. But I confess that the strength of my inquiry is exceeded as to whether, while the spiritual quality of their own body remains, they assume something from the denser lower elements, or transform their own prior bodies into whatever [Col. 1037A] is suitable to their purpose.” He likewise appears to say, in *On Genesis* [Note: [Col. 1037D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book III, chapter 10], that all angels had bodies at creation, in which they could not suffer; these were preserved for the good angels after confirmation, but altered for transgressors, so that they could suffer. Finally, even granting that angels have bodies, it does not follow that they are bodily, because our souls also have bodies yet are not bodily.

Whether demons substantially fill the human heart. God alone enters the mind. In what way Satan is said to fill the heart.—Finally, it should be known that demons enter human bodies by God’s permission, to oppress and afflict them. Thus the Gospel recounts that demons entered certain persons and were expelled by Christ [Col. 1037B] (Matt. 4 and 8; Mark 1; Luke 4, 9, and 11). But they do not substantially enter anyone’s heart. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1037D] Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 33]: “We do not believe that demons enter the soul substantially through energetic operation—that is, an inwardly effective operation—but that they are joined by application and oppression. But entering the mind belongs only to him who created it.” Likewise Bede says [Note: [Col. 1037D] On Acts 5, “Why has Satan tempted your heart?”]: “It should be noted that nothing can fill the human mind according to its substance except the creating Trinity; for the soul is filled with created things only according to operation and the rectitude of its will.” Satan fills someone’s heart, then, not by entering into that person and into his perception—for this is the power of God alone—but by craftily drawing [Col. 1037C] the soul into an inclination toward malice through thoughts and incitements to vices. In this manner he filled the heart of Ananias and Judas (John 13; Acts 5).

DISTINCTION IX. On the orders of angels. Nine orders of angels. Dionysius establishes only three orders.—It remains to consider how many orders of angels there are; what an order is and why it is so called; and whether they were distinguished in this way from creation itself. Scripture frequently declares that there are nine orders of angels: angels, archangels, principalities, powers, virtues, dominions, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. Some, however, such as Dionysius [Note: [Col. 1038D] Book I, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*], teach only three orders, placing three within each, so as thereby to suggest that the image of the Trinity exists in the angelic order.

[Col. 1037D] What an order is, and the meaning of each name.—An order is a multitude of heavenly spirits which resemble one another in some gift of grace, just as they agree in receiving natural gifts. Thus Seraphim, interpreted as “burning” or “kindling,” are those who burn more than others in charity. Cherubim, interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” are those who surpass others in knowledge. So with the other orders.

The individual orders. How they are named from gifts of grace.—The individual orders are also named from gifts of grace which were given to them not exclusively but pre-eminently. Hence Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1038D] Homily 34 on the Gospels]: “In that heavenly city, each order is designated by the name of the thing which it possesses more fully as a gift.” “More fully” should be understood either in relation to the orders subject to it, or in relation to other gifts which the same order received less fully. And just as not all in the order of apostles or martyrs are equal, so too this must be understood of the orders of angels.

Whether they were distinguished in this way from creation itself.—It seems that they were so distinguished from creation itself, because Scripture says that some fell from every order. Yet this cannot stand. For if they burned in charity as seraphim, excelled in knowledge as cherubim, and God sat in them [Col. 1038B] as in thrones, and likewise with the other orders, they could not have fallen. But it should be known that from creation itself the angels had differing ranks, both in fineness of nature and clarity of form, so that some were superior, some inferior, and some intermediate. It is in this sense, therefore, that some are said to have fallen from each of the orders. Or it is said because, if those who fell had remained steadfast, some of them would have been confirmed in each of the orders.

In what sense a tenth order is said to be completed from human beings.—Scripture also says that a tenth order is completed from human beings. But how is it called a tenth order when we have above stated that there are only nine? Especially since Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1038D] Homily 34 on the Gospel, Luke 15] that human beings [Col. 1038C] are to be assumed into the orders both of inferior and superior angels. It is not said as though there were a tenth order of human beings and nine of angels. Rather, it is because the fall of angels will be repaired from human beings: either as many fell as could make one order, as it were a tenth; or as many fell as remained in any one order. Hence the Apostle says that all things in heaven and on earth are to be restored in Christ (Eph. 2).

Human beings will be saved according to the number of those who stood, not of those who fell.—Yet human beings are believed to be saved according to the number not of those who fell but of those who remained. Hence Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1038D] In the place cited above]: “That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings; and we believe that as many of the human race ascend to it as there are angels known to have remained there.” As it is written: “He established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. 32).

DISTINCTION X. Angels are sent from every order. Confirmation from the lesser.—It may also be faithfully believed that heavenly spirits from every order are sent to announce these outward matters. Hence the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for ministry?” (Heb. 2). And in the Psalm: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103). Isaiah also says: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. 9); this is the highest order. Nor [Col. 1039A] should it seem unworthy if even higher angels are sent, since the Son of God himself was sent to these lower things.

Others think differently because it is written in Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him,” apparently in these outward matters; they say this was said of the lower orders. And: “Ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7); this is said of the higher orders, as of those who never depart from God in service. Hence Dionysius says [Note: [Col. 1039D] Chapter 7; and quoted verbatim by Gregory, Homily 34]: “In the heavenly hierarchy, which is called sacred rule, those higher hosts never depart from the innermost things, because those which are pre-eminent never have the exercise of an outward office.” But this should be understood of regular office: their order is not characterized by that office. Yet on occasion, when a cause arises outside the common dispensation, they are sent because of the importance or signification [Col. 1039B] of some greater matter.

DISTINCTION XI. From birth, one angel is assigned to every person for guardianship.—Furthermore, it should be known that one good angel is assigned to every human being for guardianship, and one evil angel for spiritual exercise. Hence Gregory says that each person has one good angel assigned for protection and one evil angel for spiritual exercise. Concerning good angels, Truth, forbidding offence against little ones, says: “Their angels always see the face of the Father” (Matt. 18). Jerome says there [Note: [Col. 1039D] On Matthew, at the passage cited]: “Great is the dignity of souls, that each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel appointed for its protection.”

Whether individual angels are assigned to individual persons, or one angel to several persons.—Finally, it may without offence be believed either that individual angels are assigned to individual persons, or that one angel is assigned to several, at the same or at different times. Nor should it be wondered that one angel is assigned to guard several persons, since the care of several persons may be assigned or entrusted even to one human being.

Whether angels advance in merit or reward. A reconciliation of the apparent controversy among the teachers.—Finally, it should faithfully be said that good angels advance in merit until the day of judgment, because they daily serve the welfare of human beings and strive for their progress; by this they merit. They also advance in reward, that is, in love. For they advance in knowledge, and the more they know, [Col. 1039D] the more they love. Isaiah testifies that they come to know more, speaking in the person of angels who knew less of the mystery of the incarnate Word: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). And the Psalm: “Who is this king of glory?” (Ps. 23). The Apostle also says: “What is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, so that the manifold wisdom of God may become known through the Church to principalities and powers in heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

Although Augustine says there [Note: [Col. 1039D] Originally in *On Genesis*, book V, chapter 16] that the angels [Col. 1040A] were not ignorant of the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, they did not understand it fully. Hence Jerome says in the same place [Note: [Col. 1039D] Jerome, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 3] that the angelic dignities did not understand the aforesaid mystery clearly until the apostles’ preaching had spread among the nations. From this it is evident that angels advance in knowledge. Nor does this conflict with what Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1040D] *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 3, and *Morals*, book XX, chapter 3]: “What can they not know there, where they know the One who knows all things?” For he says that they are ignorant of nothing without which blessedness does not exist. These are matters pertaining to the mystery of unity and Trinity.

On the distinction of the works of the six days. What is signified by “earth.”—After treating angelic nature, it remains to consider the other things. For in the beginning God created not only heaven—that is, angels—[Col. 1040B] but also earth (Gen. 1), that is, the confused matter of the four elements. This, Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1040D] *On Genesis against the Manichees*, book I, chapter 7], was called earth because it is the least beautiful among the elements. It was also called the abyss, as Scripture says: “And darkness was upon the face of the abyss” (ibid.), because it was joined together, lacking distinct and luminous form. It was also called water, over which the Spirit of the Lord was borne, as the will of an artisan over prepared material. It was also called water because whatever grows in the earth begins to be formed and nourished from moisture. This matter was created before every day; afterwards it was distinguished, as individual things received their proper species. This was not done all at once, as some of the Fathers seem to teach, but through the course of six days, as the Catholic faith [Col. 1040C] maintains.

Why the earth is called formless.—In considering this distinction, let us first explain why that matter is called formless, where it came into being, and how far upward it extended. Matter is called formless not because it lacked all form; that could not be, since it was a body. Rather, it had not yet received the beautiful, fitting, and distinct form that we now see. It was therefore first made arranged in a form of confusion, and second in a form of distinction.

On the modes of divine operation.—Finally, it seems worth noting what Alcuin taught concerning this passage. “God works in four ways,” he says [Note: [Col. 1040D] On Genesis]: “first, by disposing all things in the Word; second, by creating uniformly in matter; third, by distinguishing through the works of six days; fourth, by repeatedly renewing things, not as new but as known, lest they perish.”

Where that matter came into being, and how high it extended.—Accordingly, if it is asked where it came into being while confused, we believe faithfully that it came into being where it now subsists in formed condition. It extended upward as far as the summit of bodily nature now reaches. Indeed, as some maintain, that mass extended beyond the firmament [Col. 1041A]; it was denser in its lowest part, but thinner and lighter at its highest. They say that waters are from that part which are said to be above the firmament. Such, then, was the appearance of the world in the beginning, before it received the distinction made in six days.

DISTINCTION XIII. The distinction of the first day.—The work of the first day, therefore, was the formation of light. Accordingly Scripture says: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light; and he divided the light from the darkness” (Gen. 1). The adornment of the world fittingly began with light, by which the other things to be created might be seen [Note: [Col. 1041D] Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chapter 9].

What that light was.—This light may be understood spiritually, namely as angelic nature, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1041D] *On Genesis, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapters 3–5]: it was first darkness when created without form, but was made light when turned toward its Creator and clinging to him in charity. Or it may be understood as bodily light—which is more probable—like a luminous cloud, with which the day began.

Where the light was made.—It may be believed to have been made where the solar body is now situated. For it took the place of the sun until the third day; borne about in motion, it distinguished night and day, just as the sun is now carried in its daily course and makes the same distinctions. And he called the light day, and the darkness night.

In how many senses “day” is used. The order in reckoning days.—Finally, “day” is used in many senses. For it means light itself, as stated above; the illumination of the air, as often occurs; and [Col. 1041C] a period of twenty-four hours, according to the saying: “And evening and morning came, one day” (Gen. 1). This should be understood thus: evening came first, when, its daytime course completed, the light was turning toward setting; then came morning, namely of the second day, when the same light, having revolved in its nighttime course, returned to its rising. For the first day had no morning—that is, dawn—but began in full light and ended in the morning of the second day. The reckoning was therefore such that day came first and night followed, and this continued until the time of the Lord’s burial. This is not without mystery: through sin, humanity fell from the light of righteousness into the darkness of ignorance. But from the Lord’s resurrection, the day is reckoned from evening to evening, [Col. 1041D] so that night precedes and day follows—also as a mystery, because through Christ humanity returns from darkness to light. Hence the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Why the sun was made. How the statement “God said” should be understood. How God works in the Word and through the Word.—If, then, it is asked why the sun was made when that light made the day, it may be said that that light illuminated the upper regions but not the lower; therefore the sun was made, so that either that light remains joined to it in the same part [Col. 1042A] of heaven, or perhaps the body of the sun was formed from it [Note: [Col. 1041D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book I, chapter 11].

It should be known that God did not say in time, “Let there be light,” because he did not speak changeably, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1041D] *On Genesis*, book I, chapters 2 and 9]; nor did he speak with a sound of voice, since he had no tongue with which to speak. It is therefore referred to the nature of the Word: he spoke not with a sound of voice but in the Word coeternal with himself; that is, he begot the Word, in whom he disposed from eternity what he would make in time through that same Word. For the Father works in the Word and through the Word, as Scripture frequently says, not as an artisan works through an instrument, but because he begot the maker of all things. Hence Chrysostom says [Note: [Col. 1041D] In the exposition of the Epistle to the Hebrews, homily 2, [Col. 1042D] chapter 1]: “Just as the Father is said to judge through the Son because he begot a judge, so he is said to work through the Son because he is known to have begotten a maker.” Or, to work through the Son means to work [Col. 1042B] with the Son. Yet the Son is not similarly said to work through the Father, though he works with the Father, in order to preserve the Father’s authority as principle. The same should be understood concerning the Holy Spirit.

## Distinction XIV. On the distinction of the second day, on which the firmament was made. Of what material the firmament was made.

God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters” (Gen. 1). That is, the waters which are in the air and on the earth from those which are above the firmament. Of these it is said: “You cover its upper regions with waters” (Ps. 103). Here, however, the subject is the starry firmament, which may be believed to have been made from waters, like crystal, as Bede testifies [Note: [Col. 1042D] On Genesis, in various places; John Damascene, *On the Orthodox Faith*, book II, ch. 6.]; although others say that the heaven extending beyond the region of the air is of a fiery nature. Augustine also seems to support them [Note: [Col. 1042D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book II, ch. 3.]: “Yet, whichever of these is believed, faith is not harmed.” But what the waters above the firmament are like, and for what purpose they were created, is known by him who created them.

### Why it is called a firmament

Finally, it is called a firmament not because of its fixed position, but because of its firmness and because it forms an impassable boundary for the waters.

### Why God was silent concerning the goodness of the things created on the second day

It should also be observed that on this day, as on the others, one does not read: “God saw that it was good.” This is not because it was not so, but in order to commend some mystery. Perhaps it was done because of the rejection of the number two, which is the beginning of otherness and division.

### On the distinction of the third day

The distinction of the third day was the gathering of the waters into one place. For God said: “Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1). It could have happened that the earth, sinking down, provided hollow places to receive the surging waters, and thus dry land fit for grasses was made.

### Where the waters were gathered

All waters are said to have been gathered into one place on account of the great sea, from which they flow forth and to which they return. They are also called “gatherings of waters” because of its many inlets and the numerous channels branching from the same sea.

You have, then, how on the first day light was created, to illumine all things; on the second, the firmament was made, to divide waters from waters; and on the third day, when the masses of water had been gathered within their receptacles, the earth was revealed and the air made clear. Thus the elements were distinguished during the first three days; during the next three, those same elements were adorned. This we must now consider.

### On the adornment of the fourth day, when the luminaries were made

The adornment of heaven on the fourth day, then, was the creation of the luminaries. For God said: “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night” (Gen. 1). By these provision was made for human beings, so that, as the sun moved in its course, they might enjoy the succession of day and night. They were also comforted by the moon and stars, lest night remain unadorned. Concerning these it is further said: “And let them be for signs and seasons, and days and years” (ibid.). This is said not because the seasons first began on the fourth day, but because they serve as signs of fair and stormy weather, and ordinarily distinguish days and years and the four seasons of the year: spring, summer, winter, and autumn.

## Distinction XV. On the adornment of the fifth day

The adornment of the fifth day was the creation of living creatures from the waters. Thus God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds above the earth” (Gen. 1). By these two elements were adorned: the air by birds and the waters by swimming creatures.

### On the adornment of the sixth day

On the sixth day the earth also was adorned with beasts. Hence God said: “Let the earth bring forth the living soul, cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds” (Gen. 1). All these were created harmless, but because of sin many became harmful.

### On the creation of man

When all things had thus been arranged, as we have briefly indicated, man was made last and introduced into the world as lord and possessor of all things. Hence it follows: God, who had seen that it was good, said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). We shall now treat of his creation, but first complete our discussion of the seventh day.

### On the adornment of the seventh day

Scripture therefore says: “God completed his work on the seventh day, and rested from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2), that is, which he had brought to perfection.

### How God is understood to have rested

Finally, God is said to have rested, not as though weary from working, but by ceasing to make new creatures. Thus also in the Apocalypse it is understood: “They had no rest,” it says, “saying, ‘Holy’” (Rev. 4); that is, they did not cease saying “Holy.”

### How God is understood to have completed his work on the seventh day. The blessing of the seventh day

But how is he said to have completed his work on that day, when he is read to have done nothing on it? Perhaps because on that day he blessed and sanctified it, as Scripture testifies: “He blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Gen. 2), and this was an act of working. So Solomon performed a work when he dedicated the temple. He is said to have sanctified that day because he endowed it, above the others, with a mystical blessing. Hence in the Law: “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day” (Exod. 20). Or, “God completed his work on the seventh day” means that he saw it to be perfect and complete.

## Distinction XVI. On the creation of man. How man was made

Having proceeded through the foregoing matters, let us consider the creation of man, investigating how and what kind of man was made; then how man fell; and thirdly how he was restored. In Genesis, then, one reads: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). By saying “let us make,” the one operation of the three Persons is shown; by saying “our,” the equal substance of the three Persons is shown or indicated. For here the Father speaks to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, not to angels, because God and angels do not have one image or likeness.

### What kind of man was made. In what image and likeness are considered

Finally, man was made in the image of God according to the mind, on account of memory, understanding, and love. He was made according to likeness on account of innocence and justice, which are naturally present in the human mind. Or image consists in all the other faculties, while likeness consists in the essence of the soul, because it too is immortal and indivisible. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1043D] In *On the Greatness of the Soul*, ch. 2.]: “The soul was made like God because God made it immortal and indissoluble.” Image, therefore, pertains to form; likeness to nature.

### How man is called the image of God

Man is also called the image of God. Hence the Apostle: “Man is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11). This is properly said of the mind, yet it is said of the human being in whom that image itself resides. Thus both a painting and the board on which the painting is found are called an image.

### Man is called both image and “in the image” of God; the Son is image alone

It should also be noted that man is called both image and “in the image”; the Son, however, is called image only. Augustine explains why [Note: [Col. 1044D] *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 6, at the end.]: “Man is called image in such a way as also to be ‘in the image,’ because he is not equal by parity but draws near by a certain likeness. The Son, however, is image, but not ‘in the image,’ because he is equal to the Father.” Behold: according to the property of his mind, man is like God; his body also indicates this, since it is upright toward heaven.

## Distinction XVII. On the creation of Adam’s soul

Accordingly, the making of Adam’s body and soul is described when it says: “God formed man from the slime of the earth,” with regard to the body; and again: “He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2), with regard to the soul. Or, according to others, “he blew” or “breathed upon.” This is not to be understood as having been done with bodily hands or jaws, but as brought about by willing and commanding. For God is spirit, not body; he has done whatever he willed. He breathed in, that is, he made a breath, not from his own substance. For to breathe is to make breath, that is, a soul. Hence through Isaiah (57): “I made every breath,” that is, every soul.

### How the soul is created

According to Augustine, God made Adam’s soul with the angels and without a body [Note: [Col. 1045D] Ch. 57, according to the Septuagint translation; *On Genesis*, book VII, chs. 25 and 27.]. According to others, it was created in the body, in order that it might animate the whole body. He expressly names the face because, above the other parts of the body, it is adorned with the senses. But whatever may be held concerning Adam’s soul, concerning other souls one must hold that they are created in the body: for in creating, God infuses them, and in infusing, creates them.

### At what age was Adam created, and where? Whether paradise is bodily. Description of paradise. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil. How man knew good and evil. How disobedience is best understood

Adam was created at the age of a man, as Augustine says on Genesis [Note: [Col. 1045D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VI, ch. 13.]. Man was not made in paradise but outside it, and was then placed in paradise, as Scripture teaches: “The Lord took man and placed him in the paradise of delight, which he had planted from the beginning” (Gen. 2). By this was signified that man ought to advance to better things.

This paradise is understood as a local, bodily place. It may be said to have been planted “from the beginning” at that beginning when God commanded the earth to bring forth plants and trees [Note: [Col. 1045D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VIII, ch. 3.]. Or “from the beginning” means in the east; hence the ancient text says “toward the east.” There is there a most pleasant place, made fertile by a great spring and adorned with fruit-bearing trees of various kinds. Among these is one tree called the tree of life, because it was divinely given this power: whoever ate its fruit would have his body strengthened in stable health and perpetual soundness, and would not decline for the worse or fall into decay.

There is also there the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. It was not so called because the tree was evil, but because through the prohibition transgression was destined to occur there, by which man would learn through experience what lay between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Before touching this tree, man knew good by experience and prudence, but evil only by prudence. Once he had appropriated what was forbidden, he knew evil also through experience. Nor is it better understood how great an evil disobedience is than when man is understood to have become guilty because he touched a thing prohibited, though it would not have harmed him if it had not been prohibited. For if you touch a poisonous thing after being forbidden, the punishment itself seems to follow not so much from the prohibition as from the nature of the thing. But when you touch a good thing after being forbidden, it is shown that punishment arises from disobedience alone, just as reward arises from obedience.

## Distinction XVIII. On the formation of woman

Finally, in paradise God formed woman from the substance of man, as Scripture says: “God cast Adam into sleep; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and built it into a woman” (Gen. 2).

### Why was woman made from the side of man?

Woman was made from the side of man, not from his head or feet, because she was being prepared neither as his mistress nor as his servant. If she had been made from his head, she would seem to be set above man for dominion; if from his feet, to be subjected to servitude. But she was made from his side, to show by this that she was created for fellowship in the man’s love and as an aid to generation [Note: [Col. 1046D] From Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 13.].

### Why Adam was created first and Eve not at the same time

She was not made at the same time as the man; rather, the man was first alone, and she was afterward made from him, so that the image of God might appear in man. For as God is the principle of all creation, so Adam is the principle of generation. In this also the pride of the devil is checked, since he wickedly wished to usurp being a principle.

### Why woman was made while man slept. That the soul is not propagated by descent

Woman’s creation when sleep had been sent upon Adam was a sacrament of Christ and the Church. For just as woman was formed from the side of the sleeping man [Note: [Col. 1046D] From Augustine, *The City of God*, book XII, ch. 26.], so the Church came from the sacraments which flowed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross (John 19): washed from sins by water and blood, redeemed from punishments. Thus the woman’s body was derived from the man’s body; but the same cannot be understood of the soul, which is not propagated by descent. Jerome [Note: [Col. 1046D] On Psalm 32.] binds with the bond of anathema those who say that souls are propagated by descent, adducing the prophet’s authority: “He who fashioned their hearts individually” (Ps. 32). Here, he says, the prophet sufficiently indicates that God does not make soul from soul, but creates souls individually from nothing.

## Distinction XIX. On the state of man. On man’s first state, namely before the Fall. On man’s state after the Fall

Here a threefold consideration concerning the state of man presents itself: what man was like before sin, after sin, and what he will be like in the resurrection. In the first state, man had the ability to die and the ability not to die. In the second state, namely after sin, he had the ability to die and the inability not to die. In the third state, he will have the ability not to die and the inability to die.

Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1046D] On Genesis, book VI, chs. 19 and 24.]: “The body first formed from the slime of earth was animal, not spiritual—the kind of body with which we too shall rise. Before sin, it was both mortal and immortal, because it could die and could also not die. Through sin it became subject to death.” As the Apostle says, this body is not mortal as the first man’s body was, but worse, because it has the necessity of dying (Rom. 5; 1 Cor. 15). It will be changed into a spiritual body and will no longer be able to be dissolved when it has put on immortality. For the children of the resurrection will no longer be able either to sin or to die.

### Whence Adam’s immortality before sin came

Adam’s flesh before sin seems to have been immortal by a condition of nature requiring support, preserved both by nourishment from food and perfected by eating from the tree of life. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1047D] *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. 19.]: “Before sin Adam’s flesh was created immortal in such a way that it was preserved by nourishment from the other trees, from which he was commanded to eat, until, having reached the age pleasing to the Creator, he should by God’s command take from the tree of life; made perfectly immortal by it, he would no longer require the nourishment of food.”

Nor is this contradicted by Augustine’s statement [Note: [Col. 1047D] On Genesis, book VI, ch. 25.]: “In a certain way man was created immortal; this was his through the tree of life, not through the condition of nature.” The Lord’s words about Adam after sin accord with this view: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3).

Yet some still object, believing that the first parents did not need food before sin. They say: “If they had not sinned, they would not have died; but they would not have sinned if they had not eaten, because they could live without nourishment.” To them it is said that they would have sinned not only by eating what was forbidden, but also by failing to use what was allowed. For both were commandments: to use these things and to abstain from that one. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1048D] In the passage cited above in *Questions on the Old and New Testament*.]: “Both were contained in the commandments: that they should eat of what was granted and abstain from what was forbidden.”

Again, if they had not sinned, they would not have felt hunger, since hunger is a penalty of sin. But without hunger they would have eaten superfluously. The response is this: hunger is indeed a penalty of sin, for it is an immoderate appetite for eating. Man would not have been subject to it had he not sinned. Yet he would have had a natural and moderate appetite, which had to be satisfied even before sin.

## Distinction XX. Why did the first parents not have intercourse in paradise?

The first parents, having been created, did not have intercourse in paradise. Either because, once woman had been created, they immediately transgressed and were expelled; or because God had not yet commanded them to unite, and divine authorization could be awaited where concupiscence did not trouble them.

### Where the first parents begot children. How they would have begotten before sin

After they were expelled from paradise, however, they begot children. Honorable marriage and an undefiled marriage-bed could not have existed there without the heat of lust or the labor of childbirth. For it must be believed that before sin they could have controlled their generative members, as they did their other members in any act, without any itching of pleasure. But after sin they deserved that motion which marriage rightly orders and continence restrains. For weakness, inclined toward the ruin of shamefulness, is received into the respectability of marriage; and what would have been a duty for the healthy becomes a remedy for the sick.

### What would have been the nature of children begotten before sin. What must be held concerning the soul’s understanding

It may be asked whether, if they had begotten children before sin, those born would immediately have been perfect in bodily stature and mental understanding, like Adam when he was created, or would have advanced through intervals of time as people do now. Certainly, no authoritative determination of either view occurs, except perhaps that infants had necessarily to be born, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1048D] *On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, ch. 37.], because of the needs of the womb.

But this is certain: this weakness of the flesh—namely, that a human being at birth has neither feet fit for walking nor hands even suited to scratching—properly corresponds to a weakness of mind. It is otherwise with the young of many animals, which run immediately after birth and follow their mother.

Finally, if someone should say that they would have advanced in soul through an interval of time, he would not thereby be compelled to admit that ignorance, which is the penalty of sin, could have existed in them before sin. For not everyone who does not know something, or knows it less perfectly, is at once ignorant; ignorance is not spoken of except when something which ought to be known and not unknown is not known. Such ignorance is a penalty of sin. But man’s state before sin was such, as has been said, that if he had not sinned he was to be transferred, with all his posterity, to the love of everlasting blessedness.

## Distinction XXI. On the devil’s envious temptation

The devil, seeing that through humility man could ascend from where he himself had fallen through pride, envied him and therefore approached in order to tempt and cast him down. But because his malice is timid in tempting virtue, he chose not the man, in whom he knew reason to be stronger, but the weaker woman.

### Why did the demon come in another form? On the manner of the temptation

Lest his deceit be perceived, he wished to come not in his own form but in another’s. God therefore permitted him to take the form suited to his malice, namely that of a serpent, through which he might tempt. Filling it with his spirit, the devil, as Augustine says, made it the wisest of all beasts. Thus it is said: “The serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. 3). This was not through a rational soul, but through the devil’s spirit with which it was filled, for he is most wise.

In this form, then, he stood by the woman, saying: “Why did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman replied: “Lest perhaps we die” (ibid.). By this reply she opened the way for seduction; and so he immediately added: “You shall not die at all. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (ibid.).

### Man was tempted in three ways. What are gluttony, vain glory, and avarice?

Here the devil tempted man in three ways: gluttony, vain glory, and avarice. He tempted through gluttony by persuading him to eat, saying: “On whatever day you eat”; through vain glory by promising divinity, saying: “You shall be like gods”; and through avarice by promising knowledge, saying: “Knowing good and evil.” Gluttony is an immoderate craving for food; vain glory is a craving for one’s own excellence; avarice is an excessive desire to possess, which concerns not money alone but everything pursued beyond measure.

### On the order and progress of human ruin

Observe here also the order of human ruin. First God affirmed, saying: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” Then the woman said doubtfully: “Lest perhaps we die.” Third, the devil denied it, saying: “You shall not die at all.” Thus the doubter departed from the one affirming, and, in order to perish, drew near to the one denying.

## Distinction XXII. On human sin

Finally, seeing the tree to be beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating, and believing the serpent’s words, she ate and gave to her husband (Gen. 3). At the devil’s suggestion, both sinned in this.

### Did a lifting-up in their minds precede the Fall?

Yet it seems that their sin preceded the temptation, because Augustine says concerning Genesis [Note: [Col. 1049D] Book II, ch. 5.]: “It should not be thought that man was cast down unless a certain self-exaltation to be subdued had first existed in him.” Again [Note: [Col. 1049D] *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book II, ch. 30.]: “How would the woman have believed the tempter’s words unless love of her own power and proud confidence in herself had been present in her mind?”

If this is so, man did not first sin at another’s suggestion. Yet authority teaches that the devil’s sin is incurable because he fell not by suggestion but by his own pride, whereas man’s is curable because he fell not through himself but through another, and therefore could rise through another [Note: [Col. 1049D] Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, in the passage previously cited.]. To this we reply that the self-exaltation did not precede the temptation, but the act of forbidden eating. For events occurred in this order: the temptation of the seducer came first; the self-exaltation of the mind in man followed; third came the transgression of disobedience.

### What was the self-exaltation in each person? In what Adam was deceived

The woman’s self-exaltation was such that she wished to possess God’s likeness, believing the devil’s statement, “You shall be like gods,” to be true. This self-exaltation was not at all in the man, nor was he deceived, as the Apostle says—not believing the devil’s suggestion to be true (1 Tim. 2), namely, that God had prohibited touching the tree because he knew that they would become like gods if they touched it.

Certainly, when Adam saw that the woman, having taken that food, had not immediately died bodily, as he supposed, some self-exaltation at once attached itself to his mind, by which he too desired to try the forbidden tree. For Adam was not deceived, as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 3), in the respect in which the woman was deceived—namely, in believing the statement “You shall be like gods” to be true. But he was deceived in thinking that the sin would be pardonable. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1049D] *On Genesis*, book II, ch. 42.]: “Adam, inexperienced in divine severity, could be deceived in this, that he believed the offense would be pardonable.”

### The opinion of some that Adam also sought to be like God

Moreover, it seems that the man too wished to be like God. Where it is said, “What I did not seize, I then paid back,” Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1049D] On Psalm 68, on the words “What I did not seize.”]: “Adam and Eve seized; presuming like the devil, they wished to seize divinity and lost blessedness.” Again, on the words, “O God, who shall be like you?” (Ps. 82): “Whoever wishes through himself to be like God perversely desires to resemble God, as the devil did, who would not be under him; and as man did, who, as a servant, would not be held by the commandment but wished to be, as it were, God, with no one ruling him.” Again, on Paul’s words to the Philippians (2), “He did not consider equality with God a seizure”: “Because he did not usurp what was not his own, as the devil and the first man did” [Note: [Col. 1050D] Augustine, tractate 17 on John 5, “but he also called God his Father.”].

To this they say that Adam desired this because the woman taken from him desired it. But then how did sin enter the world through one man? They reply: because it entered through the woman made from the man. For the woman sinned before the man.

### Which of them sinned more?

To some it seems better to say that Adam too desired to be like God; but because he did not believe that it could happen, he was not inflamed as much as the woman, who thought it possible. Thus she was prouder in her ambition. The man, therefore, sinned less than the woman.

### That the man sinned less than the woman

The man is also understood to have sinned less because, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1050D] On Genesis, book II, ch. 24.], he thought about forgiveness, repentance, and God’s mercy. For he thought both might happen: that he could comply with his wife and obtain forgiveness through repentance. The same seems evident from the fact that the woman sinned against herself, against God, and against her neighbor; the man only against himself and against God. It also appears because the woman was punished more severely, when she is told: “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3).

### An objection to the statement that the man sinned less

Augustine seems opposed to this [Note: [Col. 1050D] On Genesis, book II, ch. 35.], speaking of those who excuse sin: “For this reason Adam does not confess his sin, but says: ‘The woman whom you gave me gave me, and I ate’ (ibid.). The woman also does not confess, but transferring blame to another says: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate’ (ibid.). Though unequal in sex, they sinned with equal arrogance”—that is, with equal pride. They therefore sinned equally.

But distinguish these three sins of the parents in the matter of our ruin: the sin of transgression, the sin of excuse, in which they sinned equally because their knowledge and pride were equal; and the sin of self-exaltation, in which, because their ambition differed, as was said, one sinned more or less than the other.

It is also objected that, since there are three ways of sinning, as Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1051D] *On the Highest Good*, book VI, ch. 17]—namely through ignorance, weakness, and deliberate intent—and since it is more serious to sin deliberately than through ignorance, Adam seems to have sinned more, since he sinned knowingly and was not deceived. The woman, however, was deceived, as has been said, and thus seems excusable through ignorance.

The reply is that Eve’s ignorance cannot be excused, because she could have known but would not. For she was endowed with reason and knowledge, especially since she knew that she had received the command against the devil’s persuasion. She herself says: “God commanded us” (Gen. 3). The excuse of ignorance is taken away, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1051D] To Valentinian.], from those “who know God’s commandments.”

### On three kinds of ignorance

Finally, one ignorance is affected: that of those who can know but do not wish to know; in them it is itself a sin. Another is unwelcome to those who have it: namely, those who wish to know but cannot; in them it is a penalty of sin, not sin itself. Another is simple ignorance: that of those who simply do not know; in them too there is sin.

Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1052D] As above.]: “It is one thing not to know and another not to wish to know; for in those who were unwilling to understand, ignorance itself is sin, whereas in those who could not, it is the penalty of sin.” Yet the ignorance of those who simply do not know excuses none so completely that they do not burn in eternal fire, though perhaps it causes them to burn less. Affected ignorance is conquerable; unwelcome ignorance is unconquerable; simple ignorance is partly conquerable, and so is imputed for punishment, and partly unconquerable, and so excuses from a greater punishment.

## Distinction XXIII. Why God did not make man better, as people ask

Someone here asks why God made man such that he could be seduced. In this he should know that man was treated more magnificently. For man, being made in this way, had in his nature the ability, and in his power the will, not to consent to one persuading him, with God’s help; and it is more glorious not to consent than to be incapable of temptation.

It is also asked why God created those whom he knew would become evil. Namely, because he foresaw what good he would bring about from their evils. He knew that they would benefit the good; therefore he did not create them in vain.

### Why God did not create man incapable of sin

It is also asked why God did not make man such that he would not sin; or, if he sinned, why God did not restore him to a better state when he could have done so. To these and similar questions, which are asked too inquisitively, even an unlearned person may answer: “He certainly could have. But why did he not? Because he did not will it. Why did he not will it? He knows. Do not inquire,” because it is written: “Do not be wise beyond what is fitting” (Rom. 12). Nor does the vessel say to the potter: “Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9).

### On man’s threefold knowledge before the Fall. How man had knowledge of the Creator. That man had knowledge of creatures. He had self-knowledge

Before the Fall, man was endowed with threefold knowledge: of the Creator, of created things, and of himself. He knew the Creator, though not so perfectly as the saints will know him in the future, when with unveiled face they shall know. Nor did he know him in an enigma, as we now see, but by a closer understanding through which he contemplated God’s presence.

He also had knowledge of things, as is evident from his giving names to all living creatures, which had been created for him and were to be governed by him. Accordingly, he had self-knowledge as well, understanding what he owed to his superior, equal, and inferior. For he would not be guilty of transgression if he had not known this.

### Whether man foreknew his own fall

If it is asked whether he knew beforehand future events concerning himself, we say that duties to be performed were prescribed to him more than future events were disclosed. Thus man did not foreknow his own fall, just as we say of the angel.

## Distinction XXIV. On man’s grace and power before the Fall. On the help given to man in creation by which he could stand

Here it must be known that man was created with an upright will, and was given help by which he could remain in that uprightness. Yet he could not merit salvation unless another grace were given to him. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1052D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 107.]: “If man was made upright, so that he could remain in that uprightness, yet not without God’s help, then if this had been absent from angel or man when they were first made, he certainly would not have fallen by his own fault.”

That help consisted in freedom of choice, immune from every corruption; in uprightness of will; and in the integrity and vigor of all natural powers. But against what we have said—that through these things man could not advance without another grace—it is objected: through the assistance of the grace of creation man could remain in good; therefore he could resist evil, and if he had done so, this would have been advancement for him and a merit unto life.

We reply that resisting evil then becomes a merit unto life only when a cause is present which urges us to do this—as sin’s corruption is now, though it was not then in man. Otherwise, what is seen in angels would not be merit, since for them standing firm was not merit. For turning away from evil always avoids punishment, but does not always merit the crown.

## Distinction XXV. On free choice. What is free choice? Why “free”? Why “choice”?

Let us now discuss free choice: where it is, what it is, why it is so called, whose it is, and to what it pertains. Free choice is in will and reason. It is a faculty of will and reason: called “free” because of the will, which cannot be compelled; and “choice” because of reason, which judges and discerns between good and evil. Thus it is called free choice because it is led freely and spontaneously either to choose good—though not without the help of grace—or to evil, for which it is sufficient in itself.

### That the foregoing definition does not suit God or the glorified

According to this definition, free choice does not seem to exist in God, since God cannot choose evil. Hence Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1053D] In the homily *On the Prodigal Son*, to Damasus.]: “God alone is one in whom sin cannot occur; all other beings, since they possess free choice, can be inclined in either direction.” Likewise it does not seem to exist in the glorified, who cannot will evil. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1053D] *The City of God*, book XXII, ch. 30.]: “The first free choice was the ability not to sin; the last, the inability to sin; the middle, the ability to sin and the ability not to sin.”

### That free choice exists in God. Free choice exists in the glorified. Choice will be freer when it cannot sin

Nevertheless, free choice is in God. Hence Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1053D] In *On the Faith*, book II, ch. 3.] says on the words, “Dividing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12): “That is, according to the judgment of free will, not according to the service of necessity.” Therefore the divine will itself, which does all things not by necessity but freely, as it wills, is free choice in God.

Free choice also exists in the glorified. Hence Augustine [Note: [Col. 1054D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 105.]: “Man will not lack free choice, because he will be such that he cannot will evil. Indeed, the choice that cannot at all serve sin will be far freer; nor is the will either nonexistent or not to be called free because we so desire to be blessed that we not only do not wish to be miserable, but cannot in any way whatever wish it.”

Therefore, if free choice belongs both to God and to human beings, both now and in the future, it seems to be so called because without compulsion it can choose whatever reason has decided ought to be chosen.

[Col. 1053C] General description of free choice. On the fourfold condition of free choice. — Here note the four conditions of man with respect to free choice: before sin, namely, when nothing impelled him toward evil and nothing hindered him from good; after sin and before restoration, when he is pressed down and conquered by concupiscence; after restoration but before confirmation, when, because of weakness, he is pressed by concupiscence but, because of grace, is not conquered; and after confirmation, when he will neither be pressed nor conquered. Then weakness having been utterly consumed and grace brought to completion, he will receive every freedom.

On the threefold freedom. Freedom from necessity; freedom from sin; freedom from misery. — There is freedom from necessity, from sin, and from misery. Freedom from necessity [Col. 1053D] is that by which free choice is always free, since it is located in the will, which cannot be compelled. Freedom from sin is that by which we are made servants of righteousness; hence the Apostle: “Having been freed from sin, you have become servants of righteousness” (Rom. VI). Freedom from misery is that of which it is said: “The creation itself also shall be freed from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII).

Free choice possessed this entire freedom also before sin. But, corrupted through sin, while retaining the first freedom, which belongs to nature, it lost the subsequent ones, which belong to grace. For free choice is the man who, descending from [Col. 1054A] Jerusalem to Jericho, was wounded in his natural endowments and stripped of gratuitous goods (Luke X). Hence Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 1054D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 30:] By using free choice badly, man both lost himself and subjected free choice itself wholly to the slavery of sin.

On the inequality of the freedom of choice. That there are two freedoms. Bad freedom; good freedom. — It is therefore clear from the reasoning given above that free choice exists always and in every person; nevertheless, it is not equally free in all. In the wicked it is free simply through that freedom which is from necessity. In the redeemed it is freer, by reason both of that same freedom and of freedom from sin; hence it is said to have been liberated in them. In the glorified, however, it will be freest, possessing complete freedom toward good, not toward evil.

Accordingly, in itself it is free, but not equally toward [Col. 1054B] good and evil. For it is freer toward evil, which it can do of itself, than toward good, which it cannot do unless grace assists. Thus it is clear that there are two freedoms of free choice: bad freedom, namely, and good freedom. Bad and untrue freedom is present when reason dissents from the will, judging that what the will desires ought not to be done. Good and true freedom, however, is present where reason agrees with the will.

Yet we are not here discussing several freedoms essentially, but one and the same freedom. We do not divide it into these two things mentioned except according to its functions. Just as one individual man, identical with himself, is at one time good and at another bad, as though he were one person and then another.
