The objects to which free choice applies. — It must now be understood that free choice does not concern things present [Col. 1054C] or past. For what is or was is so determined that it is not within free choice, when it is or was, either to be or not be, or to have been or not to have been. It concerns only future things, yet not those whose occurrence or non-occurrence is not within its power, but only those which it can choose, by the freedom of the will, to be or not to be, whether good or evil.

## DISTINCTION XXVI. What the will is. On operating and cooperating grace.

The will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either rejecting or attaining something. But that it may not admit evil and may attain good, the grace of God both precedes and follows it. Hence the Apostle: “It is not of one who wills nor [Col. 1054D] of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

This is not said as though the human will alone, without God’s mercy, were insufficient for good. For conversely one might say: “It is not of God alone who shows mercy, but of the human will,” since God’s mercy alone does not accomplish it. It is said, then, in order that the whole may be attributed to God, who both prepares the good human will for assistance and assists it once prepared. For he anticipates the unwilling person so that he may will, and follows the willing person so that he may not will in vain.

That the good will accompanies grace. — It is therefore evident from these things that, by itself, the human will does not [Col. 1055A] efficaciously will good without God’s grace. The will follows this grace: grace precedes, with no merit summoning it. Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] Augustine, Epistle 106 to Boniface:] No human merit precedes the grace of God; rather, grace itself merits to be increased, so that, when increased, it may merit also to be brought to perfection—with the will accompanying, not leading; following at its heel, not going before.

What is the grace that precedes the will. — This grace is faith in Christ, which obtains what the law commands. It also justifies, as the Apostle says: “Having been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Rom. V). It precedes and thus frees from the slavery of sin, so that one may live devoutly in Christ. Hence Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 106:] After the fall, free choice itself must be freed from slavery to sin. It is not freed at all through itself, but only through the grace of God, placed in faith in Christ, [Col. 1055B] so that the will itself may be prepared.

From these things it is evident that a good will comes from faith.

That faith seems to proceed from the will. — Yet faith appears to arise from the will, because the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. X). Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] On John, Tractate 26:] He does not simply say “one believes,” but “with the heart one believes,” because a person can do other things unwillingly, but cannot believe unless willing.

Likewise, commenting on Genesis, where Laban and Bethuel said, “Let us call the girl and ask her will” (Gen. XXIV), a certain interpreter of Genesis says:

> [Note: [Col. 1055D] Book I, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 2:] Faith belongs not to necessity but to the will.

But these and similar statements are not made because faith proceeds from the will, but because faith does not come except to one who [Col. 1055C] wishes to believe; and grace precedes that person’s good will, not in time, but in authority and efficacy.

This question, however, is made more difficult by Augustine’s words when he treats the text: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything as of ourselves” (II Cor. III). “Who,” he says, “does not see that thinking comes before believing? For no one believes anything unless he has first thought that it ought to be believed.” From this it seems plainly evident that the thought of good, which belongs to the will, precedes faith, and therefore that a good will precedes faith rather than being anticipated by it—apparently contrary to what was said above.

We reply that thought of good or will indeed precedes faith, but not the will by which one lives rightly. One arrives at the latter in this order: understanding of the good comes first; desire for it follows; [Col. 1055D] third comes good will, or delight. Augustine makes this distinction in the passage, “My soul has longed to desire your justifications” (Ps. CXVIII [in the Latin numbering; Ps. 119]):

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] Augustine on Psalm CXVIII:] “It has longed to desire,” he says, not “it has desired.” For we sometimes see by reason how useful God’s justifications are, yet we do not desire them. Understanding therefore flies ahead; affection follows slowly, or not at all. We know the good, yet are not delighted to do it; and we desire that it may delight us.

He therefore shows the stages by which one comes to them. The first is to see how useful they are; [Col. 1056A] next, to long for their desire; finally, as grace advances, to be delighted by their performance. If you attend to this, the whole question vanishes. For, in order that you may live devoutly, you first understand the good; second, you consider that it comes not from yourself but from God; third, you are delighted to act, when the will has already been made good through faith and charity. That will alone is the means by which one lives rightly, and it accompanies faith rather than preceding it.

Nevertheless, that same will precedes certain gifts of grace, namely, those which follow the justified person. Hence Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 32:] The good will of man precedes many gifts of God, but not all. Those which it does not precede are in it itself, and it assists in them, because it is not preceded by them even in time, and consents with them toward good.

On the three kinds of goods. — That what has been said may become clearer, [Col. 1056B] it must be known that some goods are greatest, some least, and some intermediate. The greatest goods are those by which one lives rightly and which no one uses badly. The least are those without which one can live rightly. The intermediate goods are those without which one cannot live rightly, but which one can use either well or badly. Hence Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] *Retractations*, Book I:] The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods. Bodily forms, without which one can live rightly, are the least goods. The faculties of the mind, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. In short, no one uses virtues badly; but one can use other goods either well or badly. Moreover, no one uses virtue badly because the work of virtue is the good use of those things which we can also use badly. But no one uses something badly while living well.

[Col. 1056C] The goods among which free choice belongs. — Free choice belongs among intermediate goods, because we can use it badly and because we cannot live rightly without it. Its good use, therefore, is the work of virtue. Wherever it is read that the good use of free choice is virtue, “virtue” is there taken for its work.

## DISTINCTION XXVII. On virtue and its merit. Faith is from God, not from man.

Virtue, then, as Augustine says, is a good quality of the mind by which one lives rightly and which no one uses badly, and which God alone works in man. Thus Augustine says of righteousness in the passage:

> [Note: [Col. 1056D] *On Free Choice*, Book II, ch. 18:] “I have executed judgment and righteousness.” Righteousness is a great virtue, which none but God produces in man; and therefore, when he says, “I have done righteousness,” he intended not virtue itself, which man does not produce, but its work.

The same is said of the other virtues. Accordingly the Apostle says of faith: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves” (Eph. II). For it is God’s gift; that is, faith is not from the power of your nature, because it is purely God’s gift.

This is called operating grace because it heals the will and prepares it for good; and it is called cooperating grace because it helps the will in doing good. From this grace, too, merits arise. Hence Augustine, writing to the presbyter Sixtus, says:

> [Col. 1057A] [Note: [Col. 1057D] Epistle 105:] What is man’s merit before grace, when grace alone produces all our good merit?

How good merit is established in man. — Merit comes from grace and free choice in this way: just as a good act or affection of the mind is produced from faith and free choice—namely, believing, which is the first merit—so likewise, from charity and free choice comes loving; and so with the rest. Through these merits the virtues merit both their own increase and, for us, justification and life.

On the gifts of the virtues. — Yet these merits are given by grace, similar in authority to their source. Hence they too are called grace. Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] To the presbyter Sixtus, Epistle 105:] When God crowns our merits, he crowns nothing other than [Col. 1057B] his own gifts.

Hence eternal life, which is rendered to merits, is called grace because it is freely given—not freely given because it is not given to merits, but because the merits themselves, to which it is given, are given through grace.

Another opinion concerning virtue, and its reasoning. — Others, however, say that virtues are the good uses of natural powers, inward and outward, and call the acts performed through the body “works of the virtues.” They are moved to this opinion because Augustine says, commenting on John:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] Tractate 40:] What is faith? To believe what you do not see.

And likewise:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] *On Christian Doctrine*, Book III, ch. 10:] I call charity a movement of the mind.

From this they argue: if charity and faith are movements of the mind, then virtues are movements of the mind. But these statements must be understood as being made through the cause: charity [Col. 1057C] is a movement of the mind, that is, the virtue by which the mind is moved to love; and faith is believing what one does not see, that is, the grace by which one believes what is not seen. For what is believed, that by which one believes, and believing itself are different things.

Finally, if virtue were a movement of the mind, it would no longer be from God alone, as was demonstrated above, but also from free choice, from which, Augustine’s words show, every movement of the mind arises:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] *On the Two Souls*, ch. 12:] If souls lack, by free choice, the movement of mind for doing or not doing, and if, in short, they are given no power to refrain from their own act, we cannot hold them guilty of sin.

Therefore virtue is not a movement of the mind. For if it were, then free choice would be good from virtue—which is true no longer—but virtue would be from good [Col. 1057D] free choice—which is false.

## DISTINCTION XXVIII. On the heresy of the Pelagians.

Finally, something must be added concerning the Pelagian heresy, which opposes grace. This most recent of all heresies arose from Pelagius, a monk. Hostile to grace, it holds that without grace a human being can fulfill all the divine commandments. It says grace is given to people so that they may more easily [Col. 1058A] fulfill through it what they are commanded to do through free choice. It also destroys the prayers which the Church offers, whether for unbelievers that they may be converted, or for believers that they may persevere, by teaching that people possess these things not from God but from themselves. It also asserts that infants are born without the bond of original sin.

The Pelagians’ argument against Augustine. — As the Pelagians said these things, they argued against Augustine from his own words as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 1057D] *On Free Choice*, Book III, ch. 18:] If a human being cannot do what is commanded, it ought not to be imputed to him unto death, as you yourself, Augustine, say. “Who,” he says [Note: [Col. 1057D] *Retractations*, Book I, ch. 9], “sins in what cannot be avoided? But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided.”

But Augustine says that he spoke this concerning the will—as if to say: Who sins unto death through necessity, rather than [Col. 1058B] through the will? For it is by the will that one sins and lives rightly; but unless it is freed by God’s grace, one cannot live rightly by it.

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] Augustine, *On the Two Souls*, ch. 12.]

Likewise: “To hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do is utter madness.” Why then are infants, and those who do not have grace, without which they cannot fulfill the commandments, guilty? But Augustine had said this specifically against the Manichaeans:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] *Retractations*, Book I, ch. 15.]

They said that there are two natures in man: one good, from God; the other evil, from the race of darkness—to such an extent that man could not will the good. If that were so, it would not seem imputable to him that he did not do good.

Finally, Augustine seems in many places to oppose this doctrine of grace. For he says:

> [Col. 1058C] [Note: [Col. 1058D] *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Mani*, ch. 26:] It lies within human power to change the will for the better.

Likewise:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] The same work, ch. 27:] It lies within our power that we may deserve either to be grafted in by God’s goodness or to be cut off by his severity.

Likewise: “To believe and to will are ours; but the good that we do is God’s.” But he himself explains how these statements should be understood:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] Augustine, *Retractations*, Book I, ch. 23:] The rule is the same for both willing and doing. Both are God’s, because he prepares the will. And both are ours, because neither happens except when we will.

Therefore, with every faithless error removed, let us hold without hesitation concerning grace and free choice what Jerome teaches:

> [Note: [Col. 1058D] *Exposition of Faith to Pope Damasus*, beginning, “We believe in God”:] Free choice exists in such a way that we say we always need God’s help; and those err who, with Mani, say that man cannot avoid sin, just as those err who, with Jovinian, assert that man cannot sin. Each removes freedom of choice. But we say that man can always both sin and not sin. This is the faith which we have learned in the Catholic Church.

## DISTINCTION XXIX. Whether man before sin needed operating grace.

After this, it must be understood that man, even before sin, needed operating grace—not in order that [Col. 1059A] he might be freed from sin by it, but in order that he might be prepared efficaciously to will the good. Hence Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 10:] Even then no merit could have existed without grace; for although sin depended solely on free choice, free choice was not sufficient for acquiring or retaining righteousness unless divine help was afforded.

Whether man before the fall possessed the virtues. — It must likewise be understood that before sin man possessed charity and the virtues, as is proved by these authorities. Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] In a certain homily on Genesis:] Adam, having lost charity, was found evil.

Likewise: “Before sin Adam was endowed with a spiritual mind.” Likewise: “When Adam was alone, he did not transgress, because his mind clung to God.”

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] Ambrose, to Sabinus.]

Likewise: “Before sin, man, most blessed, breathed the ethereal air.”

> [Col. 1059B] [Note: [Col. 1059D] Ambrose on the Psalms.]

Therefore he possessed virtues, which he lost through sin; for this reason he was cast out of paradise, the Lord saying: “See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. III). This is not said as though he would have lived forever had he eaten. Rather, the Lord spoke in the manner of one angered with the proud man; the sense is: “Take care, you angels, lest he eat from the tree of life, of which he is unworthy—though, had he remained and eaten of it, he would have both eaten and lived forever.”

On the flaming sword before paradise. — So that he might not be able to approach it, God placed before paradise the Cherubim and a flaming, turning sword. This may be understood literally: through the ministry of angels a fiery guard was placed there. Spiritually, however, the transmitted text is syntactically defective: “unless through charity, which is the fullness of knowledge, [lacuna] temporal punishments (sic), which also are changeable because they change with time, one does not return to life.”

## DISTINCTION XXX. That Adam’s sin made all guilty.

Finally, when Adam sinned, both sin and punishment likewise passed through him to his descendants. Hence the Apostle: “Just as through one man sin entered into this world, so death passed into all human beings” (Rom. V). The Pelagians wrongly thought this was said of imitative sin. For if he had meant the sin of which Wisdom says, “Through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. [Col. 1059D] II), the Apostle would not have named Adam, but the devil, its prince. Those who belong in part to the devil imitate him. Therefore the Apostle speaks not of that sin, but of propagated or original sin, which passed through Adam to all who are generated by concupiscence.

What original sin is. — Many have held various opinions about this. Some thought that it is neither guilt nor punishment, but liability, debt, or obligation by which we are assigned, as a matter of penal right, to punishment for the first man’s sin—as if by a law of the age. Sometimes [Col. 1060A] children are punished for their father’s crime, which they did not themselves incur.

But that it is both guilt and punishment is proved by these authorities. Gregory says:

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] These words are found in the gloss on Exodus XIII, “The firstborn,” etc.:] All conceived through the pleasure of the flesh have contracted original guilt with us.

Augustine likewise says:

> [Note: [Col. 1059D] *On Nature and Grace*:] The sin of the first man killed not only himself, but the whole human race, because from him we received both condemnation and guilt together.

The same author says: “No one is born without bringing with him punishment and the desert of punishment, which is sin.”

> [Note: [Col. 1060D] Augustine on Psalm L: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities.”]

Original sin is called the tinder of sin, that is, concupiscence. — This is not a movement or act of soul or body, but the tinder of sin, called concupiscence, the law of the flesh and of the members, the weakness of nature, and also the tyrant that is in our [Col. 1060B] members. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1060D] *Sermons on the Words of the Apostle*, Sermon 12:] There is concupiscence in us, which must not be allowed to reign, as also its desires, which are actual concupiscences and arise from the weakness of nature. But this weakness is the tyrant that moves evil desires.

What is meant by concupiscence. How original sin passes from fathers to children. Why sin is said to be in the flesh because of the corruption of the flesh. — This concupiscence is not the act itself of desiring, but the vice with which we are born. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1060D] *Against Julian*, Book VI, ch. 7:] What is the concupiscence in which we are born? It is certainly a vice, which makes an infant capable of desiring and an adult actually [Col. 1060C] desirous.

Therefore we transgress not only by imitating Adam, but are also born sinners from him. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1060D] *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book I:] Besides the example of imitation, Adam, by the hidden contagion of his carnal concupiscence, infected in himself all who would come from his stock.

Hence the Apostle says: “In whom all sinned” (Rom. V), that is, in that man, in whom all existed as if in their material source; or “in whom,” that is, in which sin. Accordingly, the Apostle says that through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners.

This must be understood thus: from Adam’s actual disobedience original sin arose—that is, carnal concupiscence—so as to exist in him and pass into all through propagation, which belongs to the flesh, not the soul. In the soul this sin dwells by reason of corruption, not by guilt. Hence Ambrose says:

> [Note: [Col. 1060D] On Romans, ch. VII:] How does sin dwell in the flesh, when it is not a substance but a privation of good? Behold: the first man’s body was corrupted through sin, and that very corruption remains in the body; by fellowship with it, the soul is stained by sin. Therefore sin is said to dwell in the flesh because the cause of the fact remains in the flesh.

Likewise: “Sin does not dwell in the soul but in the flesh, because the cause of sin is from [Col. 1061A] the flesh and not from the soul; because the flesh, by its origin from sinful flesh, is the cause of sin. For through propagation all flesh becomes a cause of sin, but not the soul.”

> [Note: [Col. 1061D] The same Ambrose, a little below.]

But an objection is made: if only the flesh, and not the soul—which is infused much later—is from propagation, sin does not seem to be transmitted in the flesh, since that which is contracted is not sin, especially since sin cannot exist in an irrational thing, such as flesh is before it is joined to the soul.

But it must be understood that sin is in the flesh before the soul is joined to it by cause, not by effect. Nor does this inference follow: “If that which is transmitted in the flesh is not sin, therefore sin is not transmitted in the flesh.” For what is conceived in the womb is not yet a human being, and yet a human being is conceived in the womb; nor is what is sown in the field a crop, and yet a crop is in the field.

Whether the cause of original sin is punishment or guilt. — Thus sin is there only in its cause, which is not guilt but punishment—namely, pollution and foulness contracted from the heat of intercourse. When the soul is immediately infused, its contagion makes the soul guilty, as liquid immediately turns sour or moldy from a defect in the vessel.

How sin passes through propagation. — From these points it is now clearly apparent how sin passes through propagation. We are not born sinners merely because flesh is derived from Adam, but because it is derived in a defective manner through lust. While man and woman mingle with one another, their intercourse cannot be without lust. Therefore the conception of their children [Col. 1061C] born from them cannot be without sin. It is not propagation but lust that transmits sin to infants; not nature’s fertility but the foulness of lust.

From this it is clearly suggested why the Lord’s flesh was not sinful: it descended from Adam according to a law different from ours. For it was conceived of a virgin not by the corruption of lust, but by the power of the Holy Spirit.

## DISTINCTION XXXII. How original sin is called voluntary.

Finally, this sin is voluntary because it proceeded from the will of the first man. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1061D] *Retractations*, Book I, ch. 15:] What is called original sin in infants is not absurdly termed voluntary, because, having been contracted from the evil will of the first man, [Col. 1061D] it has become hereditary.

It is, however, necessary because it cannot be avoided. Hence the Prophet: “Deliver me, O Lord, from my necessities” (Ps. XXIV [Ps. 25]).

What kind of soul is joined to a defiled body. — But since this is so, by what justice is a soul created pure by God bound by it? I answer: because the body is corrupted through its own defect, not because the soul delights with the flesh when it is infused, as some suppose. For then the sin would no longer be original, but actual. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1061D] *The City of God*, Book XIV, ch. 3:] The corruption of the body that weighs down the soul was not the cause of the first sin but its punishment; nor did corruptible flesh make the soul sinful, but the sinful soul [Col. 1062A] made the flesh corruptible.

Whether the soul before baptism is such as it was when created. — Though the soul is created by God without defect, before baptism it is nevertheless never wholly such as it was at creation. For immediately upon being infused it is stained: just as, if you had polluted hands, you would never have fruit such as that which I gave you with clean hands.

Why God joins an innocent soul to a harmful body. Whether souls are equal in natural gifts from creation. — Yet God is not to be blamed for joining an innocent soul to a body, knowing that it will thereby be stained and condemned unless it is regenerated. This belongs to his hidden justice.

Moreover, it is not implausibly said that some souls are created superior to others in natural [Col. 1062B] gifts, since it is agreed that this was so among angels. Yet this is neither a merit for punishment nor for life, since quickness or slowness of intellect does not determine reward or punishment in the future.

How original sin is remitted in baptism, yet concupiscence remains afterward. — This sin is dissolved in baptism with respect to its liability. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1062D] *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book I, ch. 39:] Grace accomplishes this through baptism: the body of sin is destroyed, so that concupiscence spread through the flesh may not harm one who has died [to sin], though it was present in him when born.

Nevertheless, it is not wholly consumed in baptism, for it remains after the act in the members. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1062D] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book I, chs. 25–27:] The concupiscence of the flesh is forgiven in baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it is not imputed as [Col. 1062C] sin.

Therefore, just as other sins pass away in act but remain in liability—as homicide and the like—so, conversely, concupiscence can pass away in liability and remain in act. For it remains in the oldness of the flesh, not to reign, but to lie as one overcome. It daily diminishes in those who are making progress and are continent, until it is slain—unless it comes to life again through unlawful consent. It also remains because it produces desires against which the faithful fight. Therefore, what before baptism was both punishment and guilt is afterward punishment only.

How offspring contract original sin from cleansed parents. — Although this concupiscence is not imputed to the regenerated, nevertheless every offspring that is born is bound by original sin, derived even from cleansed parents. This is no wonder. For how is the foreskin removed by circumcision, yet remains in the one begotten by the circumcised? How also does chaff, which is separated with such care, remain in the grain born from purified wheat? So sin, cleansed in the parents through baptism, remains in the children whom they have begotten.

## DISTINCTION XXXIII. That it is Adam’s sin, not that of other parents, which is imputed to children.

Finally, it must be understood that only Adam’s sin, not the sin of other parents, is imputed to children. This is proved from the fact that [Col. 1063A] those to whom the grace of regeneration is not granted, and who die immediately after birth, are owed the mildest punishment. Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1063D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 93:] Their punishment will be the mildest who have added no sin beyond original sin.

If this is so, then children are not bound by the sins of all their parents. For if they were punished for those sins as well as for their own original sin, their punishment would no longer be less, but perhaps greater than that of the parents themselves. This agrees with the Prophet’s statement: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, but the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII).

Yet this appears contrary to what the Lord says in the Law: “I am a mighty and jealous God, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XX). The person who carefully considers what is added there understands that these are not contrary—namely, “of those who hate me.” By this, as Jerome says, [Col. 1063B] it is clearly shown that children are punished not because their fathers sinned, but because, like them through a kind of hereditary evil, they hate God.

> [Note: [Col. 1063D] Jerome on Exodus.]

The Law speaks of children who imitate wicked fathers. It names them particularly because children especially tend to imitate the fathers whom they especially love.

> [Note: [Col. 1063D] On Ezekiel, ch. 18.]

It also mentions only the third and fourth generation because fathers sometimes live until they beget third or fourth children; seeing their fathers’ iniquity, these become heirs of their impiety by imitation.

[Col. 1063C] That this must also be understood mystically is shown by the fact that in Ezekiel it is called a parable: “What is this, that among you you turn a parable into a proverb?” (Ezek. XVIII). The father, then, as some say, is the first point of a thought; the son is the conception of sin, namely, the consent and delight of the woman. The grandson is the completion of the deed, or the consenting man’s resolve to complete it, or the perpetration of sin. The great-grandson is perseverance in what you have done.

God will not punish eternally all the first and second impulses of thoughts, which the Greeks call *propatheiai* (προπαθείας, “pre-passions”), and without which no one can exist. But if someone resolves to do the things he has thought, or refuses to correct what he has done, these are mortal sins and the third and fourth generation.

[Col. 1063D] Nor is the statement, “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L [Ps. 51]), troubling, as though it referred to several sins. For, as Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1063D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 44:] The plural is there used for the singular, according to the custom of Scripture.

As in: “They are dead who sought the child’s life” (Matt. II, 2), though it speaks of Herod alone. Conversely, the singular is used for the plural, as in: “Pray therefore to God that he may remove the serpent from us” (Num. XXI), though the people suffered not from one serpent but from many.

Whether Adam’s actual sin was graver than all others. — Finally, [Col. 1064A] it seems necessary to ask whether Adam’s sin of transgression was graver than all other sins. It appears so because it changed and corrupted the entire human nature—which no other sin did—and harmed more than any other sin. For it subjected humanity to manifold misery and, finally, to both deaths, which no other sin did.

We answer that this sin should not be thought greater than sin against the Holy Spirit. It was not greater because it corrupted our whole nature, but because it was committed by a human being when the whole human nature was in him. Nor should it be thought greater because it caused more harm, since lesser evils sometimes harm more; and conversely lesser goods sometimes benefit more. Thus, when the Apostle was constrained between two alternatives, he chose the lesser [Col. 1064B] good, though it would benefit more people. Likewise, the sacrament of baptism benefits more people than the sacrament of the altar, but it is not therefore greater.

## DISTINCTION XXXIV. On actual sin according to its causality.

After the foregoing, let us discuss actual sin, considering what was the origin of sin, in what thing sin exists, what sin is, and in how many ways it is contracted. It must be understood that, since before sin no thing existed except a good thing, a good thing—namely, the nature of man or angel—is the origin of sin. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: [Col. 1064D] *Against Julian the Heretic*, Book I, ch. 3, in sense; but *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, ch. 28:] From what do you say that the evil will arose, if not from good? For if from an angel or a human being, what were those two before an evil will arose in them, except a good work of God and a praiseworthy [Col. 1064C] nature? Therefore evil arises from good, and it had no other source from which it could arise except good.

The evil will was the secondary cause of evils. In what thing evil exists. — Moreover, from an evil will, as from an evil tree, arise all evils that pertain to us, as evil fruits.

Similarly, evil exists in no thing other than a good thing; this is proved from Augustine. [Note: [Col. 1064D] *Enchiridion*, chs. 11 and 12.] Evil is nothing other than the corruption or privation of good, and this is found only in a good thing—that is, in a nature. Therefore, so long as a nature is corrupted, there is present in it a good of which it is deprived; and thus, if there were no good in which evil might exist, evil could not exist at all. Here the rule of the dialecticians fails, by which they say that two contraries cannot coexist in the same thing. For, although no one doubts that good and evil are contraries, not only can they exist together, but evils cannot exist at all without goods, nor except in goods. Hence a remarkable conclusion follows: since every nature, insofar as it is nature, is good, when a defective nature is called evil, nothing else seems to be said than that what is good is evil. Likewise, when a human being is called evil, what is said except “a good evil”? Good, because a human being; evil, because unjust. Certainly, in saying this we do not fall under that prophetic saying: “Woe to those who call good evil” (Isa. VIII), or evil good. For that must be understood of things of goodness and wickedness, by which human beings are good or evil: as if someone should call adultery good, or nature, insofar as it is nature, evil. [Col. 1065A]

## DISTINCTION XXXV. What sin is.

Sin, as Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 1065D] *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, bk. XXII.] is every word, deed, or desire which is done against the law of God. The same author says: [Note: [Col. 1065D] *On Two Souls*, ch. 27.] “Sin is the will to retain or attain what justice forbids.” Ambrose likewise says: [Note: [Col. 1065D] (322–323) In the book *On Paradise*.] “What is sin but transgression of the divine law and disobedience to the heavenly commandments?” From these statements it is evident that both an inward and an outward evil act—namely, evil thought, speech, and action—is sin. Yet sin consists chiefly in the will, from which, as from an evil tree, evil works proceed as evil fruits. [Col. 1065B]

## DISTINCTION XXXVI. On the variety of sins.

It must be known that certain sins are also punishments for sins. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1065D] On the passage in Psalm LVII, “Fire fell upon them.”] “Between the first sin of apostasy and the final punishment of Gehenna lie intermediate things which are both sins and punishments of sin.” Gregory likewise says: [Note: [Col. 1065D] On Ezekiel, Homily 21, near the words “but if he turns.”] “A sin that is not quickly removed through repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin, or at once sin, the cause, and the punishment of sin.” A sin is called a cause of sin with respect to a subsequent sin, but a punishment with respect to a preceding sin. For when sin is not washed away through repentance, it immediately draws one by its own weight into another sin, which is not only sin [Col. 1065C] but also the punishment of sin, because by a just judgment God darkens the sinner’s heart, so that by the merit of the preceding sin the sinner falls into others as well. Hence John says: “Let the one who is filthy become still more filthy” (Rev. XXII).

From this it appears that some sin—namely, that which is the punishment of sin—is just. For, as Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 1066D] *Retractations*, bk. I, ch. 9.] every punishment of sin is just. But it should be noted that sin is called a punishment, and a corruption or privation of good, not essentially but efficiently: just as riches are called joy, not because they are joy, but because they produce joy. So also in Peter’s Epistle unjust suffering is called grace, not because it is grace, but because it makes one pleasing to God (1 Pet. II)—that is, suffering patiently endured. Likewise, sin, as soon as it is committed by anyone, separates that person from God and darkens natural goods. [Col. 1065D] This separation or darkening is essentially the corruption and punishment of sin, and it is from God; but the sin is not. Augustine says this as follows: [Note: [Col. 1066D] *On the Predestination of the Saints*, bk. I, ch. 10.] “God foreknows but does not predestine those things which he will not do”—that is, all evils, which, although some are at once sins and punishments, according to the saying, “God gave them up to dishonourable passions,” etc. (Rom. I), are nevertheless not God’s sin but his judgment, that is, punishment.

[Col. 1066A]

## DISTINCTION XXXVII. That God is not the author of sins.

God is not the author of all these things, because a human being is not made worse with God as author. Evil is indeed called both guilt, which he by no means produces, and punishment, which he certainly does produce. Hence the prophet says: “There is no evil in a city which God does not do” (Amos III). Yet Augustine says of this: [Note: [Col. 1066D] In the book *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 21; explained in *Retractations*, bk. I, ch. 26.] that God is not the author of evil; rather, he says that the statement was made causally. For, he says, “I spoke this in the same way as it is said: ‘God did not make death’” (Wis. I), because he does not make that for which death is inflicted—that is, sin.

### That all things, insofar as they are, are good.

There are, however, those who think that every will and act is from God because they believe that, insofar as they exist, they are good. For Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1066D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 14.] “Everything which exists is good insofar as it exists.” And elsewhere: “He supremely is who is altogether unchangeable. Other things which exist cannot exist except from him; and they are good insofar as they have received being.” The reply according to Augustine is that this universality is to be attributed to the class of things. For it includes only substances and natures, as is clear from his own words. For he says: “If some things happen in the world by chance, the whole world is not governed by providence. But if this is so, then there is some substance or nature which does not belong to the work of providence.” Behold: by the name of the whole world he means natures or substances. By natures he understands those things which substances themselves naturally possess, such as intellect, memory, and so forth. [Col. 1066B]

Moreover, it is easily proved that an evil act, insofar as it exists, is not from God, because insofar as it exists it is a corruption of good. But whatever corrupts good is not from God, because, as has been said, nothing is done with God as author whereby a human being becomes worse. Again: everything God makes is a nature; but an evil act is not a nature, but an accidental act, which, through the defect of good, corrupts nature. Again: the works of the devil, called vices, are acts, not things. Again: an evil act is sin; but every sin is iniquity, and such an act is not from God, for iniquity was not made by him, but is a perversion made by man. Again: an evil act such as envy neither was, nor is, nor can be good from God; therefore it is not from him. For iniquity was not made by him. Again: if an evil act, which is sin, is not from God, then the assertion that it is made without him is false. For while it is committed, God gives it being; therefore it is not done without God. [Note: [Col. 1066D] Book *Eighty-Three Questions*, q. 3; *Expositions on Psalm* LXVIII, on the verse “There is no substance.”] [Col. 1066C–D]

### How sin is understood to be nothing.

Although we said above that sin is the act itself or the will, which are something, we perhaps seem to disagree with the saying that sin is nothing. But sin itself is called nothing, not because it is not something, but because of the defect to which it leads [Col. 1067A] and because it draws one away from true being, which is God. In this sense even human beings themselves, who undoubtedly are something, are sometimes said to be nothing. For Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1067D] On John, ch. 1.] “Sin is nothing, because human beings become nothing while they sin.” Likewise, an idol, although it is gold, is said to be nothing in the world.

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. On the will and the end by which it is judged.

It must be known that a will is weighed by its end: whether it is right or perverse. For a right end is charity, as the Prophet says: “I have seen an end of all perfection; thy commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII). The contrary of this is a perverse end. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1067D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 121.] “What God commands or counsels is then rightly done when it is referred to love of God and neighbour. But what is done in such a way that it is not referred to charity is not yet done as it ought to be done, and then is not rightly done.” There are also many other ends of the will, all of which are referred to one highest end. For example: “I wish to prepare food in order to refresh a poor person,” for this end, “that I may please God and possess eternal life,” which is the end of all good ends. But the end, as Augustine says, [Note: [Col. 1067D] On the passage, “Searching hearts.”] is the delight which someone strives to attain by care and thought. “Intention,” however, is sometimes taken for the will and sometimes for its end; wherever it occurs, the attentive reader should carefully distinguish these senses. [Col. 1067B]

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. How the will is understood to be evil.

It should be carefully noted that, when the will is said to be evil or to be sin, this is not understood of that natural power by which we will, but of its act, which is willing. That is, it means the evil use of the will, which, when directed toward evil things, can never be other than evil. This is not the case with the acts of the other powers. They are evil if they are contrary to charity—for example, remembering or understanding evil, not in order to avoid it but in order to do it. But the natural power itself, which is present even in little children, is always good. Thus Augustine says of the image in which we were created [Note: [Col. 1067D] *On the Trinity*, bk. XV, ch. 8.] that nature remains good even amid vices. [Col. 1067C]

## DISTINCTION XL. When works are good or evil.

We say that works must be weighed according to their end, whether they are good or evil, except for certain things which are so evil in themselves that they cannot be good for any reason. Augustine says this as follows: [Note: [Col. 1067D] *Against Lying*, ch. 7.] “Things which are not sins in themselves are now good, now evil, according as they have good or evil causes.” Thus providing food for a poor person is good if it is done from mercy and with right faith. Marital intercourse too is good if it is performed in the faith that children may be begotten for regeneration. These same things, again, are evil if a poor person is fed for the sake of boasting, or if one has intercourse with one’s wife out of lust. [Col. 1067D]

### One must consider not only why, but also what, is done.

But when the works themselves are sins in themselves, such as thefts, fornications, and blasphemies, who would say that they should be done for good reasons, or that they are not sins? For example, might theft be committed against a rich person in order that what is taken may be given to a poor one, or might false testimony be borne in order that an innocent person may be freed? What crime could not be rightly done if, once we granted in evil acts that one should ask not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is done for good reasons should not itself be judged evil? [Note: [Col. 1067D] Augustine has this in *Against Lying*.] [Col. 1068A]

## DISTINCTION XLI. Therefore, with the exception of those things which are evil in themselves, other things in general are judged by their end.

Of these Ambrose says: [Note: [Col. 1068D] *On Duties*, bk. II, ch. 30.] “Your disposition imposes the end upon your work.” And Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1068D] On Psalm XXXI.] “Let no one count his works good before faith, because where faith is not, there is no good work. For intention makes a work good, but faith directs intention. Do not pay great attention to what a person does, but to what that person intends in doing it.” [Col. 1068B]

Augustine nevertheless seems to contradict himself when elsewhere he says: [Note: [Col. 1068D] *On the Spirit and the Letter*, bk. XIV; *Book of Sentences*, prose ch. 272; and finally *Confessions*, bk. I, ch. 12.] “Sometimes good is not done well”; and, “No one does good unwillingly, even if what he does is good.” To this, distinguish the several meanings of the term *good*.

### “Good” is said in many ways.

For good is said by creation, as whatever God makes; by lawfulness, as whatever he commands or counsels; by signification, as the sacraments of the Old Testament; by usefulness, as whatever benefits anyone in any way; and by end, as what is done for obtaining eternal life—which alone is properly and truly called good. Thus, with this word so distinguished, someone sometimes does something which is rightly denied to be good in one of the foregoing senses and rightly affirmed to be good in another. For example, if someone offers sacrifice for the sake of gain, what that person does is good in respect of lawfulness; but it is not good in respect of its end. It is good by the rule of the classes, not by the privilege of individual cases. [Col. 1068C]

The common assertion, “Every sin is voluntary,” and “Sin is committed only by the will,” concerns mortal and actual sin. It is true for this reason: no such sin occurs without the will either of the sin itself or at least of that which is sin. [Note: [Col. 1068D] *On Free Choice of the Will*, bk. I, ch. 12; likewise *Retractations*, bk. I, ch. 9.]

## DISTINCTION XLII. Whether the will and its work are the same.

The will, as Augustine says in the first book of the *Retractations*, [Col. 1068D] is the first cause of sinning; and this will, together with its work, is one and the same sin, because the contempt is one in each. It is lesser when sin is committed in the will alone, but greater when a work is added to the will. Yet the will and its work are distinct. Thus loving God and loving one’s neighbour are one commandment, yet are themselves distinct. Likewise blood and flesh are one sacrament, yet are themselves distinct. And *I love* and *you love* are one word, [Col. 1069A] although there are two persons.

But a committed sin, if it is actual, passes away in act and remains in guilt—that is, in the obligation to punishment. Original sin, however, when remitted, passes away in guilt and remains in act. [Note: [Col. 1069D] In the questions on Leviticus, bk. III.]

### The difference between sin and offence. On the seven deadly sins.

Sin, properly speaking, as Augustine says, is the perpetration of evil. But an offence (*delictum*) is the abandonment of good, as it were a leaving behind (*derelictio*); nevertheless, the terms are used interchangeably.

Note also that there are seven principal vices, as Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1069D] Question 20, bk. XXXI of the *Morals*, ch. 31.] vain glory, anger, envy, sadness, avarice, gluttony (*gastrimargia*), and lust. As Chrysostom says, these were signified by the seven peoples occupying the land of promise. They are called capital or principal because all evils arise from them—not, of course, all of them in every person, but some in each person. [Note: [Col. 1069D] Lombard states this somewhat more clearly.] [Col. 1069B]

Yet all evils are said to arise from pride: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. X), and pride is the love of one’s own excellence. Likewise, all evils are said to arise from covetousness. Hence the Apostle says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). These statements seem contrary to one another unless one understands that the foregoing universality does not gather every individual sin into every person, but gathers individual or different sins into individual persons. For some become proud through covetousness, and some covetous through pride. Thus it is clear that pride is sometimes born from covetousness and covetousness sometimes from pride.

## DISTINCTION XLIII. On sin against the Holy Spirit. What obstinacy is. What despair is. What it means that this sin is not forgiven.

There is, moreover, a certain sin more damnable than the rest: sinning against the Holy Spirit. As Truth says, it will be forgiven neither here nor in the future. A person commits this sin when, after acknowledging God through the grace of Christ, that person attacks the brotherhood, driven by the flames of envy—provided that the person ends this life in that criminal perversity. For an unrepentant heart cannot be judged while anyone is still living here. This sin, as some say, is obstinacy or despair. Obstinacy is the stubborn persistence of a mind hardened in wickedness, through which a person becomes unrepentant. Despair is that by which someone utterly distrusts God’s goodness, thinking one’s own wickedness to exceed the divine goodness—as Cain did. [Col. 1069C–D]

This sin is said not to be forgiven, not because it should not be pardoned if the sinner repents (Gen. IV), but because the stain of that sin is so great that the sinner cannot submit to the humility of entreaty. Therefore John rightly says: “There is a sin unto death” (1 John V)—that is, a sin persisted in. “I do not say that anyone should pray for it,” because one who sins thus can be aided by no prayers either here or in the future. [Col. 1070A]

The statement that there is sin against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit must not be understood as though the offence against the three persons were divided. Rather, three kinds of sins are shown there; not all sins are thereby distinguished, but two are remissible and one is irremissible. To sin against the Father, to whom power is attributed, is to sin through weakness. To sin against the Son, to whom wisdom is attributed, is to sin through ignorance. These two are remissible. The third, which is irremissible, has been explained above.

### On venial sins. What removes venial sins.

There are also venial sins: that is, light sins which merit only temporal punishment. We commit them daily through ignorance or forgetfulness, surprise, necessity, the frailty of the flesh, unwillingly or willingly. Of these it is said: “The righteous person shall fall seven times” (Prov. XXIV), that is, shall sin frequently. Solomon says this of light sins, without which this life is not lived. Because of exceeding charity, they are forgiven immediately upon being committed. Hence the passage immediately adds, “and shall rise again.” In those less perfect, however, light repentance is needed. The Lord’s Prayer and mutual confession suffice; otherwise they burden the person after death, but are forgiven if by good works during life one has merited that they be forgiven. [Col. 1070B]

## DISTINCTION XLIV. That the power of sinning is from God.

Finally, it must be known that just as memory and understanding of evil are from God, so also is the power for evil. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1070D] *On Genesis according to the Letter*, bk. II, ch. 3.] “The will to harm can arise from a human mind, but the power only from God.” Therefore, before the devil took anything from Job, he said: “Put forth thy hand” (Job II), that is, give power. Every such power, as the Apostle says, is from God; whoever resists it resists God’s ordinance (Rom. XIII). [Col. 1070C]

### Whether one must ever resist authority.

Lest this seem to mean that the devil or some tyrant must not be resisted, it should be known that we ought not to resist when they do not abuse their authority. Hence the same passage says: “He resists God’s ordinance.” A just man who serves under a sacrilegious king rightly obeys him if it is certain that what is commanded is not contrary to God’s command, or if it is uncertain whether it is contrary. But if someone abuses authority, namely contrary to God’s command, that person must not be obeyed. Augustine proves this through the ranks of human affairs: [Note: [Col. 1070D] Sermon 6, *On the Words of the Lord*.] one must not obey a procurator if he commands contrary to the proconsul, nor the proconsul if he commands contrary to the emperor, nor even the emperor if he commands contrary to God. No one sins because one has authority, but because one abuses authority. [Col. 1070D]

[Col. 1069] End of the book on the creation of things, the fall of man, and other matters pertaining thereto: this is the second book of Bandinus’s *Sentences*.

[Col. 1071]

# MASTER BANDINUS’S BOOK ON THE INCARNATE WORD AND THE RESTORATION OF MAN, WHICH IS THE THIRD BOOK OF THE *SENTENCES*.

**Summary.**—Having set forth God’s nature in the first book, and the creation of the world and the fall of man in the second, he proceeds in this third book to teach, very briefly yet very clearly, the incarnation, passion, and death of Christ Jesus; the restoration of fallen humanity; and the recovery of humanity when lost. He teaches much concerning both the three theological virtues and the four principal moral virtues; likewise concerning the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which were present abundantly in Christ and which, through Christ’s benefit and gift, ought to be present in us, so that Christ’s death may be salutary and fruitful for us. At the end of the book he appends a brief exposition of the Decalogue, together with a discussion of lying and perjury.

[Col. 1071A]

## DISTINCTION I. On the incarnate Word.

Above, the fall of man was discussed; now let us consider his restoration.

When, therefore, the fullness of time came, the Son of God was sent into the world—that is, he visibly appeared to the world in the form of a human being (Gal. IV; Phil. II).

### Why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh.

The Father or the Holy Spirit was not sent, but the Son alone, so that he might be the Son of Man; lest the name “Son” should pass to another who was not Son by eternal generation, and there should thus be two sons in the Trinity. Therefore the Son was sent through the assumption of flesh, an act performed by the whole Trinity; yet neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh. Thus the whole Trinity descended upon Jesus in the appearance of a dove and produced the voice, “This is my beloved Son,” etc. (Matt. III); yet the Father alone uttered it, and the Holy Spirit alone descended upon Jesus (ibid.). [Col. 1071B]

## DISTINCTION II. Why the Son assumed humanity, and what is understood by the name humanity.

The Son assumed humanity, by which term I understand soul and flesh. For, as Jerome says: [Note: [Col. 1071C] In the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*.] “We confess in Christ two complete substances, namely divinity and humanity, the latter consisting of soul and body.” He therefore assumed this whole humanity with its properties. Hence John Damascene says: [Note: [Col. 1071C] *On the Orthodox Faith*, bk. III, ch. 6.] “The Word assumed everything that God implanted in our nature: namely, a body, a rational and intellectual soul, [Col. 1071C] and their idioms,” that is, properties. “For the whole Word assumed the whole of me, and the whole Word was united to the whole of me, so that he might grant salvation to the whole. For what is unassumed is incurable.” [Col. 1072A]

### That the Word assumed flesh and soul simultaneously.

Moreover, at the very moment of conception he took flesh and soul, in order that he might immediately be a complete human being. Hence Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1071C] *Morals*, bk. XVIII, ch. 27.] “At the angel’s announcement and the coming of the Holy Spirit, immediately in the womb the Word became flesh.” And John Damascene says: [Note: [Col. 1072C] *On the Orthodox Faith*, bk. III, ch. 2.] “Flesh at once; at once flesh of God the Word; at once flesh ensouled, rational, and intellectual.” Nor is this opposed by Augustine’s statement on the passage, “This temple was built in forty-six years”: [Note: [Col. 1072C] In the letter to Jerome.] “This number,” he says, “corresponds to the perfection of the Lord’s body” (John II). He did not say this as though the conceived flesh was animated only after that many days, in the manner of other conceptions. Rather, since it had been animated from the very beginning, as stated, it was within that number of days markedly differentiated into its members. [Col. 1072B]

## DISTINCTION III. On Christ’s conception.

Christ’s flesh was not sinful in Christ—that is, bound by any sin—because it was not born from fleshly pleasure, nor did it subsequently sin.

It was, however, sinful in his mother; but upon the coming of the Holy Spirit she was wholly cleansed. [Note: [Col. 1072C] Augustine, *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 36.] Indeed, as Augustine says, from that time it was granted even to the mother so to conquer sin that the saying, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John I), does not apply to her alone among all the saints. [Col. 1072C] Yet Christ’s flesh was like sinful flesh because it hungered, thirsted, and was subject to the other deficiencies. [Col. 1073A]

## DISTINCTION IV. How Christ’s incarnation is attributed to the Holy Spirit.

The work of the Incarnation is specially attributed to the Holy Spirit, as in the Creed: “And was incarnate by the Holy Spirit.” And in the Gospel: “She was found with child of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I). This does not mean that the Holy Spirit was seed for the Virgin, but that through the operation of the Holy Spirit that which was united to the Word was taken from the Virgin’s flesh. For what is from something is either from its substance, as the Son is from the Father’s substance, or from its power, as all things are from God; in the latter way the Holy Spirit is called the author of the Incarnation. And although this also belongs to the Father, it is attributed to the Holy Spirit, who is called kindness, because it is considered a work of exceptional kindness. [Col. 1073B]

### How Christ is said to have been conceived and born of the Holy Spirit.

Neither may it rightly be inferred that the Son is the Son of the Holy Spirit because he was born from him. For not everything born from something is its son, as a Christian is born from water; nor is everything that is someone’s son born from that person, as is an adopted son.

## DISTINCTION V. Who assumed, and what was assumed. That a person assumed a nature.

Finally, it must be known that both person and nature assumed nature, but neither person assumed person nor nature assumed person. For Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter* (ch. 2): “The only-begotten God assumed human nature in the unity of his person.” Again: “The only-begotten Son of God was incarnate through the assumption of flesh and a rational soul.” Behold: a person assumed a nature. [Col. 1073C]

### That nature assumed nature.

That nature assumed nature is stated by Augustine as follows (*ibid.*): “That nature which remains eternally begotten from the Father assumed our nature without sin.” Again: “The only-begotten Son of the Father is the same in the form of a servant and in the form of God, because the form of God received the form of a servant.” Now form is nature. For Hilary says: [Note: [Col. 1073D] *On the Trinity*, bk. XII.] “To be in the form of God has no meaning other than to remain in the nature of God.” Behold: nature assumed nature.

If elsewhere it is said that the form of a servant was assumed by the Son alone, it should be understood that not nature but another person is excluded there. Yet the Council of Toledo seems to say the contrary: “The Son alone received man in the singularity of person, not in the unity of the divine nature.” But how this should be understood is immediately explained in the same place: namely, as what is proper to the Son, not what is common to the Trinity—that is, the proper person of the Son assumed man, not the three persons collectively. This could have seemed otherwise to someone because it was said above that the whole Trinity made the formation of the assumed man. Therefore divine nature assumed flesh, and is consequently called incarnate. For John Damascene says: [Note: [Col. 1073D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, bk. III, ch. 6.] “We say that the divinity is united to flesh, and we confess one incarnate nature of God the Word.” [Col. 1073D]

### That the nature of God is not said to have become flesh.

Nevertheless, divine nature is not said to have become flesh, as the Word is said to have become flesh, because neither authority contains this expression nor ordinary usage admits it—perhaps lest a convertibility of one nature into another be signified thereby. [Col. 1074A]

### That a person was not assumed.

A person was never assumed, because no person joined to that flesh and soul existed for the Word to receive. Nor is it rightly said that a person was assumed because a soul was assumed. For a soul is not an individual nature or a person so long as it is personally united to another thing, but only when it exists by itself. If, however, it is said anywhere that “the man Christ Jesus,” or “that man,” was assumed by the Word of God—as the Psalm says, “Blessed is he whom thou hast chosen and assumed” (Ps. LXIV)—understand the statement thus: it is true of human nature but false of a person. [Col. 1074B]

## DISTINCTION VI. What is meant by “God is man.”

That it may more easily be understood what is asserted by propositions such as “God is man” and “man is God,” it should first be briefly stated that from the things which the Son of God assumed, namely soul and flesh, no human person was composed. For a person is composed from these two only when they come together principally in something which is not a person, as happens in other human beings apart from Christ. But if they come together in that which already is a person, as they did in Christ, they do not make a person; rather, they are merely possessed by it. Thus, if wall, roof, and foundation are added to a house already made, they do not make a house, but are merely possessed by that to which they are added. Likewise baptism does not cleanse one already baptized; and consecration, ordination, and dedication, when applied a second time to things already participating in them, do not increase them—that is, confer or alter nothing—but are merely applied. So soul and flesh were added to the Son of God as a garment is added to limbs. [Col. 1074C]

The Son of God was made man, not essentially and truly made man in the way that you are, who are the composite essence itself of your soul and body, but essentially and truly made man according to *habitus*, an external state or possession. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1074D] *On Faith to Peter*.] “God the Son was made true man for us, because he possesses true human nature.” Augustine treats this point in commenting upon the words, “Found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II). [Col. 1074D]

### Four kinds of *habitus*.

For he says that things may be added to something else in four ways, so that they are possessed by it. Something may be added to another thing so that it changes it and is not changed itself, as wisdom is added to a fool; or so that it changes and is changed, as food is added to the stomach; or so that neither changes nor is changed, as a ring is added to a finger; or so that it does not change but is changed, as clothing is added to a body. The last kind fits this comparison.

For God the Son “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II), without changing his own nature; and thus he was made in the likeness of man, by assuming a true human being, [Col. 1075A] and was “found in appearance as a man”—that is, in possessing a human being, he was found as a human being. He says “as a human being,” not “a human being.” Thus that flesh is called not sinful flesh but flesh like sinful flesh (Rom. VIII). Therefore, when it is said, “God is man,” *habitus* is predicated, so that the meaning is: God possesses a human being, or is one possessing a human being; or, again, the humanized person is predicated. Cassiodorus indicates this when he says: [Note: [Col. 1075D] In the gloss on Rom. I.] “The Son of God was made, so to speak, a humanized God.” But when it is said, “Man is God,” *habitus* is the subject and nature or person is predicated, so that the meaning is: “Man is God,” that is, the one possessing a human being is God. If *made* occurs in the proposition, as in “God was made man,” understand it thus: God began to possess a human being, or to be humanized God. Likewise, “Man was made God” means: that third person began, together with a human being, to be God. [Col. 1075B]

## DISTINCTION VII. On Christ’s predestination.

Accordingly, it is easy to understand: “who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. I). For the Son of God was predestined—that is, grace was prepared for him—not in order that he might be the Son of God, but in order that he might, together with a human being, be the Son of God; so that grace is attributed to him according to the nature of the person. It is as if we said: “A favour is granted to this advocate, not that he may speak before the judge, but that he may speak while seated”; thus the favour is granted to him not with respect to speaking, but with respect to sitting. So grace was granted to Christ not with respect to sonship, but with respect to his being called Son together with humanity. [Col. 1075C]

Augustine likewise says: “The name that is above every name was bestowed upon him according to the form of a servant”—that is, so that, together with the form of a servant, he might be called the only-begotten Son of God. Accordingly, that person is said to be predestined, or his human nature is said to be predestined, in order that it might be personally united to the Word of the Father. Then the saying is expounded thus: “who was predestined,” that is, whose nature was predestined. Similarly, understand Augustine’s statement: “So great is the union of the two natures that the whole is called God, the whole man”—that is, that this person, with this whole, namely divinity, soul, and flesh and their properties, is God and man.

## DISTINCTION VIII. That Christ is not something insofar as he is man. The several meanings of the word “according to.”

It must be known that the Son of God, by assuming a human being, was not made something—that is, a person or nature—because there is not a quaternity in the Trinity, nor is Christ two natures, although it is written, “Christ subsists in two natures and from two natures or substances.” He is not said to be two, but he was made of a nature which he did not formerly possess. Thus one must understand Origen’s statement: “He was without doubt made that which he was not before”—that is, of that nature. [Note: [Col. 1075D] Origen on the Epistle to the Romans.] Likewise: “One is the Son of God; another is the son of man”—that is, he is of one nature and another according as he was born of God or of a human being. [Note: [Col. 1075D] Augustine, *To Felicianus*.] [Col. 1075D–1076A]

Understand in this way all statements of this kind. Therefore the Son is not something insofar as he is man, unless “insofar as” denotes unity of person. For in this mystery the expression *according to* sometimes denotes person: “According to [his being] man,” that is, he who is man, “gave gifts to men.” Sometimes it denotes nature: “According to [his being] man, he suffered,” that is, humanity itself suffered. Sometimes it denotes state or *habitus*: “According to [his being] man, he was predestined,” or “a name was bestowed on him,” as stated above.

## DISTINCTION IX. On the adoration of Christ’s humanity.

Since humanity was assumed by the Word of God into one person, it is to be adored together with the Word. Hence John Damascene says: [Note: [Col. 1075D] *On the Orthodox Faith*, bk. III, ch. 8.] “We adore Christ with the Father and the Spirit in one adoration, together with his undefiled flesh.” And Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1075D] From the sermon of the Lord, “Let not your heart be troubled.”] “Therefore I adore the humanity in Christ, because it is united to the divinity.” Finally, if you separate the human being from God, I neither believe in nor serve that human being; just as, if someone finds royal purple or a royal diadem without the king, that person does not adore it, but adores it together with the king.

### Distinctions X and XI

[Note: [Col. 1076D] Distinction X is contained in VIII.] Whether Christ is a creature or made.—Although Christ is man, he nevertheless ought not simply to be called a creature or made. For, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1076D] *On the Trinity*, Book I], he through whom all things were made is not himself made. Nor is he a creature, since it would follow from this that he was not God. Augustine indicates that God and creature are immediately opposed with respect to substance, saying [Col. 1076C] [Note: [Col. 1076D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 6]: “Every substance which is not God is a creature; and whatever is not a creature is God.” Again: “If the Word is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father.” From this it is rightly inferred: if he is a creature, he is not God; and if he is God, he is not a creature; and if he is of the same substance as the Father, he is not a creature.

Therefore, we do not say simply that he was made, but in a certain respect—that is, according to his humanity. Hence Ambrose [Note: [Col. 1076D] *On the Trinity*, Book II]: “The Apostle said that the Son of God was made of a woman, so that being made may be attributed not to divinity but to the assumption of a body” (Gal. IV). For, when speaking of Christ, Augustine says that a distinction is necessary [Note: [Col. 1076D] *On the Trinity*, Book I, ch. 13]: “When we speak of Christ, [Col. 1076D] let the diligent and devout reader understand what is said, in what respect, concerning what, and for what reason.” Attending to this, therefore, he says: Christ, according as he is God, always was; but according as he is man, he began to be.

### Distinction XII. Whether Christ could sin

It is asked whether Christ could have sinned. This seems so because the ability to sin, as we proved above, belongs to the goodness of our nature; and Christ assumed that nature whole, except for sin, in order to heal it whole. But if this is so, it seems that he could have failed to be God, since being God and being able to sin are incompatible. To this we reply, according to the foregoing distinction, that Christ could sin according as he was man. Yet we do not say this simply, but add: naturally. For from the very conception, the assumed man was confirmed by grace—which he received not by measure—so that he could not sin; yet naturally he could.

#### Whether an angel can sin

The same is said of an angel, who received a lesser grace of confirmation: simply speaking, he cannot sin, but naturally he can. Much less, therefore, could the Lord of angels sin, who in the womb itself was a perfect man, not only in respect of soul and body, [Col. 1077B] but also in respect of wisdom and grace.

### Distinction XIII. How Christ advanced in wisdom

What is read in the Gospel appears contrary to this: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom, and in grace before God and men” (Luke II). Yet this also is to be understood according to what has been said. For Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1077D] In the gloss this is cited under Gregory’s name, but it is Bede’s eleventh homily on Luke]: “According to his human nature, he advanced in age, from infancy to youth. According to that same nature, he also advanced in wisdom and grace: not because, with the passage of time, he became wiser or fuller of grace, but because he gradually displayed more fully to others, in the course of time, that wisdom and grace with which he had been full from the first hour of his conception.”

Thus he advanced—that is, he caused advancement—just as a teacher is said to advance in his disciples. But when Ambrose says [Col. 1077C] [Note: [Col. 1077D] *On the Sacred Mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation*, ch. 7], “He advanced in a human respect, just as he hungered in a human respect,” this should be understood as said in this sense: with respect to human sight, Christ’s human understanding is said to have advanced. In the same sense, he is said by the prophet to have been ignorant of father and mother in infancy, because at that time he behaved and conducted himself as though he lacked knowledge (Isa. VIII).

### Distinction XIV. That Christ’s soul knows all that God knows

Furthermore, it must be known that Christ’s soul possesses knowledge of all things which Christ knows, because the spirit of knowledge was not given to him by measure (John III). For if he knew some things and did not know others, he would not have knowledge without measure. Fulgentius proves this by that authority [Note: [Col. 1077D] In a certain sermon]: “In whom [Col. 1077D] are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II). Reason also establishes it, because no one knows anything which his soul does not know.

But the following seems contrary: “In nothing is a creature equal to the Creator”; and the Prophet says: “Your knowledge has become wonderful” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Explaining this, Cassiodorus says: “The assumed man cannot be equalled to the divine substance in knowledge or in anything else.” But this must be understood as meaning in every respect, or perfectly. [Col. 1078A] For although Christ’s soul knows all that God knows, it does not comprehend all things as clearly and distinctly as God himself does. Or, “In nothing is a creature equal to the Creator” means that there is nothing which makes a creature equal to the Creator.

Nor is the following contrary: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II), who alone searches all things—that is, by himself—because he grants others to search them also. Hence the Apostle adds in the same place: “But we have the Spirit of God,” as if to say: through him we know the deep things of God. Much more, therefore, did that soul know all the deep things, since above all others it possessed the Spirit of God.

#### That Christ did not have all God’s power

But he did not have all power, lest by this he should be omnipotent and thus thought to be God. Yet what Ambrose says on the passage, “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke I), appears contrary [Col. 1078B] [Note: [Col. 1077D] Elsewhere, Bede, Homily 23 on Luke. In the gloss [Col. 1078D], however, it is cited under the names of Ambrose and Bede]: “He shall not be great because he was not great before the Virgin’s childbirth, but because, as man, he was in time to receive the power which the Son of God has naturally.” Since this does not seem capable of being said of the person, and the flesh could not receive it, it remains to understand it of the soul. But he spoke only of the person, which began through grace to possess with man the power which it had from eternity, as we said above concerning predestination.

### Distinction XV. That Christ assumed our defects

We add also that he assumed our defects, such as hunger, thirst, sadness, fear, [Col. 1078C] and the other general defects, none of which was sin. We say this because of the tinder of sin. Yet he did not assume all such defects, as Pope Leo says, but only those which it was fitting and necessary for him to assume for us. For he did not assume invincible ignorance or difficulty in doing good, which, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1078D] *On Free Will*, Book III, ch. 18], every human being suffers from the beginning of birth. He did not assume these also because they are contrary to what he possessed from humanity’s first state.

### Distinction XVI. Whether in Christ there was a necessity of suffering and dying

There are four states of man, from each of which Christ received something. From the first, before sin, he received freedom from sin. From the second, after sin and before grace, he received punishment. From the third, which was under grace, [Col. 1078D] he received fullness of grace. From the fourth, which will be in glory, he received inability to sin.

But he assumed these defects, like flesh itself and death, not by a necessity of condition—that is, not from the corrupt law of birth, which is the necessity of our condition—but by a merciful will. Understand accordingly what Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1078D] On Psalm XXI, “I shall cry, and you will not hear”]: “The Lord did not truly fear suffering, because he did not have a true cause for fear.” Hence Hilary [Note: [Col. 1078D] *On the Trinity*, Book X, before “me”]: “Christ had a body for suffering, [Col. 1079A] but not a nature for feeling pain.” Or, he did not truly fear—that is, not so that the fear of his soul dominated him by drawing him away from uprightness. For there was in him a preliminary emotion (*prop passio*), not a passion, as Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1079D] On Matthew, ch. 26]. Yet he truly feared—that is, with real, not feigned, fear.

#### Christ had a necessity of dying

He also had a necessity of dying; for just as it is appointed for all men to die once, so too Christ was offered once, by the same necessity and law of nature.

### Distinction XVII. Whether Christ’s will was always fulfilled

Moreover, it must be known that, just as Christ had two natures, so he had two wills. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1079D] On Psalm XXXIII]: “In his Passion Christ expressed in [Col. 1079B] himself two wills, according to the two natures.” For he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI). Behold the will of man, which he immediately directed to the divine will by saying: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.). Therefore, he asked that the cup might pass, but did not obtain it; and this seems contrary to the Psalm: “May the Lord fulfil all your petitions” (Ps. XIX).

#### The human will of Christ is twofold

But the human will of Christ must be distinguished according to the inclination of sense, by which he willed not to die, and according to the inclination of reason, by which he wholly willed to die, according to which he spoke by his spirit. Nor did Christ’s flesh in this desire lust against the spirit, [Col. 1079C] because according to the will of God and of his own spirit he asked this. He did not ask in order to obtain what he asked, but in order to express the reality of his humanity. He also asked this in order to give to his members, when placed amid tribulations, an example of crying out to God and subjecting their own will to the divine will. Therefore, both things which he willed were good, but that was better which he consigned to fulfilment.

#### Hilary’s opinion differs from those above
