Hilary [Note: [Col. 1079D] *On the Trinity*, Book X], however, understands by “the cup” the terror of death, to which all flesh except Christ’s was subject by a necessity of condition, and which, only after Christ’s death, was to be removed through the glory of virtues. Looking to this, he says that Christ prayed and feared not for himself but for his own people. For he himself, as was proved above [Col. 1079D], did not fear as others feared. Hence he did not say, “My soul is sorrowful because of death,” but “unto death” (Matt. XXVI), after he saw that the scandals caused by apostolic weakness would cease.

### Distinction XVIII. On Christ’s merit and what he merited for himself

After that death, and also through it, he merited for himself brightness and impassibility. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1080D] On the words, “Christ was made obedient for us”]: “In order that Christ might be glorified by resurrection, he was first humbled by suffering; humility is the merit of brightness, and brightness is the reward of humility.” By brightness he means the manifestation [Col. 1080A] of the bestowed name which is above every name (Phil. II). For that name was not then first bestowed on him. Yet it is said to have been bestowed then, according to that figure of speech by which a thing is said to come into being when it becomes known that it has come into being.

Through the same death he also merited impassibility of soul and body, though he had no less merited it, from the time when he became man, through charity and the other virtues. For Christ had nothing by which he could advance according to the merit of his soul—that is, according to the power of merit—although he advanced in the number of bodily merits, that is, of works.

#### Whether Christ was happier after death

If it is asked whether his soul was happier after death than before, we say that it was happier [Col. 1080B] with respect to immunity from misery, but not with respect to contemplation of God.

### Distinction XIX. On the manner of our redemption, and what Christ merited for us

But if the preceding merits were sufficient for these things, why then did he will to die? Certainly for you, not for himself: that he might instruct you in humility and thus bring you into paradise. For by his death he merited for us entry into paradise, which he had merited for himself by his previous acts, as well as redemption from sin, punishment, and the devil.

For when God was going to reconcile the world to himself through a sacrifice, no other sacrifice was sufficient to reconcile it, since all had sinned. God had decreed, as Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1080D] On the Epistle to the Hebrews], that no one should be admitted into paradise—that is, to contemplation of God—[Col. 1080C] and that no human being’s humility could avail as much as the pride of the first man had harmed. Therefore, no such person was found except the lion of the tribe of Judah, who, by dying, freed us from sin and the devil, while through that death charity is awakened in our hearts (Rom. V).

For, looking upon him as upon the bronze serpent (Num. XXI), and seeing how greatly he loved us, namely, so as to die for us, we are admonished and kindled to love him who did such great things for us; and thus, freed from sin and the devil, we are justified. Finally, bearing our sins upon the tree—that is, the punishment of sins—he redeemed us from eternal punishment, remitting the debt of temporal punishment in hope, though not yet in actuality. From this he will wholly free us when the last enemy, [Col. 1080D] death, is destroyed. Thus Christ properly became our redeemer by the display of humility; but the whole Trinity is called redeemer in a common sense, by the effect of power.

#### Christ alone is mediator

Yet Christ alone is mediator between mortal sinners and the immortal righteous one (I Tim. II). For he alone is God-man, made mediator according as he is man, approaching us by weakness, but approaching God by righteousness. Certainly, according as he is the Word, he is not intermediate, but is one God with the Father.

### Distinction XX. That God could have freed us in another way. Why Christ chose rather to free us in this way

Indeed, another way of our liberation was possible to God, but none was more suitable for healing our misery. For this manner most greatly frees us from the death of despair and raises our minds to things above, when we see that he accounted us so greatly worthy that he, unchangeably good, endured our evils by dying. It is also because in this way the devil is overcome by justice, not by power. By power God could have freed his servant, whom the devil had deceitfully led away and forcibly held; but he did not will this, lest man should appear to be taken away from him by force. But, humbled through death, he did this justly. For it is just that the debtors whom he held should be set free when they believe in him whom he killed without any debt.

[Col. 1081B] #### Christ’s death was brought about by the Trinity, Judas, the devil, and the Jews. Whether the Jews did good

Finally, it must be known that Christ’s death was the work of the Trinity, of Judas, of the devil, and of the Jews. It was the Trinity’s work because it occurred with God as author—that is, willing it (Rom. VIII); Judas’s, because he betrayed him (Matt. XXVI); and the Jews’ and devil’s, because they instigated it. Thus one event, namely Christ’s death, was performed by all these; but the actions from which that event resulted were different: the Father’s handing over, the Son’s voluntary encounter, Judas’s betrayal, and the instigation of the Jews and devil. Therefore the Jews did good with respect to what was accomplished, that is, the result, but evil with respect to the act.

### Distinction XXI. Whether the Word, once he became man, ever ceased to be man

It must firmly be held [Col. 1081C] that the Word, as was said above, is true man because he has soul and flesh in the union of one person. He is a living man because he has these two joined together. Therefore, from the time when he became man, he never ceased to be man, because he never ceased to have them. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1081D] On John X, “I lay down my soul”]: “From the time when the Word assumed man—that is, flesh and soul—he never laid down the soul, so that the soul should be separated from the Word.”

He also says concerning the flesh: “Thus even in the tomb Christ did not abandon his flesh by dying with it, just as in the Virgin’s womb he formed it by being born with it.” Therefore, divinity was not separated from humanity; but this must be understood with respect to union of person, not with respect to the protection of nature, according to which it was separated. [Col. 1081D] Hence Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1081D] In the exposition of Psalm XXI, “My God, my God”]: “The man about to die cries out because of the separation of divinity,” namely, with respect to protection. Divinity separated itself by withdrawing power, as is understood here (Matt. XXVI): “Why have you forsaken me?” But it did not dissolve the union. Outwardly it separated itself from protection, but inwardly it was present in union.

But when Athanasius says under an anathema that the whole man was assumed anew in the resurrection, understand this not with respect to possessing him, but with respect to rejoining those two, so that the flesh—which properly died—might live from the soul. In that flesh, [Col. 1082A] and not in himself, Christ is said to have died. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1082D] *Against Felicianus*]: “Far be it that Christ should have experienced death in such a way that, so far as he himself was concerned, life lost life.”

### Distinction XXII. In what sense God is said to have suffered

Certainly, whatever the flesh suffered, God cannot be said not to have suffered. Just as you cannot say that you did not suffer an injury if your garment is drenched or torn, although the garment is not you. Much more, therefore, whatever flesh united to the Word suffers must be said to be suffered by God, although the Word could neither die nor suffer.

Ambrose therefore says [Note: [Col. 1082D] *On the Holy Spirit*, Book III]: “The same one was dying and not dying; rising and not rising: he rose according to the flesh, not according to the Word.”

[Col. 1082B] ### Distinction XXIII. Whether Christ had faith and hope, as he had charity

Since Christ was full of grace, it is asked whether he had faith and hope. To explain this better, let us first see what faith and hope are [Note: [Col. 1082D] Augustine on John]. Faith, then, is believing what one does not see. For the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for by us, the evidence or conviction of things not apparent” (Heb. XI). For by faith things hoped for now subsist in us, and in the future they will subsist through experience.

### Distinction XXIV. On the faith of the ancients

If these things are doubted, they are established through faith, in this way: because the patriarchs and other saints believed thus. Properly speaking, therefore, faith concerns things not apparent. For concerning apparent things there is not faith but recognition. This faith is said by the Apostle to be one by resemblance, not by numerical singularity. Just as the will of persons willing the same thing is called one will, and two persons who are very alike are said to have one face. Therefore, our faith and that of the ancients are one faith. But the manner of believing is different. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1082D] *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 2]: “The same faith in the Mediator which saves us made the ancients safe. For as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe that he died, so they believed that he would die; as we believe that he rose, so they believed that he would rise and come to judgment.”

#### On the faith of the learned and the simple

These things, however, were distinctly revealed to the learned. But they were revealed to the simple in mystery. Hence Job says: “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them” (Job I), because [Col. 1082D] the simple adhered to the learned, believing in mystery what the learned taught in mystery.

### Distinction XXV. On hope. The difference between faith and hope

Finally, hope is the certain expectation of future blessedness, arising from God’s grace and merits preceding the thing hoped for, namely eternal life. It concerns things not seen, like faith. But hope differs from faith because hope concerns good things, future things, and things belonging only to the person who is said to possess that hope. Faith, however, concerns good things and evil things, present things, past things, [Col. 1083A] and future things, and things belonging both to the person who has that faith and to others—provided, however, that believing them pertains to religion.

These things advance in us until we know perfectly. For Augustine says: “We do not know in order to believe, but we believe in order to know.”

Accordingly, Christ did not have faith and hope, because he knew past and future things as fully as present things.

Hence the saints are not now said to believe or hope for the future resurrection, because they understand it most perfectly in the Word of God.

### Distinction XXVI. That the saints are not now said to believe or hope

Yet it is read that Christ believed and hoped. For through the prophet he says: [Col. 1083B] “I will be trusting in him” (Heb. II). And in the Psalm: “In you, Lord, I have hoped” (Ps. XXX). This must be understood with respect to the outward effect, not with respect to the inward act. For he prayed and performed other acts as one does who, not yet seeing, believes and hopes. Yet by hoping or believing he was not delayed from full knowledge.

Finally, in the same sense he says to the Father: “Your discipline itself will teach me” (Ps. XVII), namely by an outward effect, by which he exhibited the example of one well corrected, not by an inward act, because he never reformed himself from wrong things to right ones.

### Distinction XXVII. On Christ’s charity. The two commandments of charity

Christ had charity, which he displayed in the work of his Passion. Let us speak briefly of it. Charity, then, is the love by which God is loved for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. Its first and greatest commandment is: “You shall love God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Deut. VI; Matt. XXII)—that is, you should direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your understanding to him. This will not be fulfilled here, but in the future. Yet it is said so that we may not be ignorant of the goal toward which we must run.

The second is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (John XIII), that is, with the love by which, and for the reason for which, you love yourself. Understand “neighbor” to mean every human being, who is called neighbor in three ways: by common condition, by nearness in faith, and by a benefit bestowed.

[Col. 1083D] ### Distinctions XXVIII and XXIX. Angels are bound by the commandment of charity

Thus angels too are included under that commandment. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1083D] *On Christian Doctrine*, Book I, ch. 30]: “It is clear that the holy angels also are included under the commandment of love of neighbor, since they render us offices of mercy.”

#### There are four kinds of things to be loved

Finally, every kind of thing to be loved is comprehended in the aforesaid commandments. There are four, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1083D] *On Christian Doctrine*, Book I, chs. 23, 24, and 26]: one which is above us, namely God; another which is ourselves; a third which is beside us, [Col. 1084A] namely our neighbor; and a fourth which is below us, namely our own body and that of our neighbor. This is understood in those commandments, though not expressed. For Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1083D] *On Christian Doctrine*]: “If you understand that your whole self is to be loved—that is, soul and body—you ought also to love your neighbor, namely his soul and body.”

#### That we love God and neighbor with one charity

Although there are so many things which we love, we nevertheless love with one charity alone. Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1083D] Sermon on the Ascension of the Lord]: “Charity is one, and the commandments are two. For no charity loves the neighbor other than that which also loves God.” Therefore charity ought to be ordered both in inward affection and in outward effect. Concerning the order of affection Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1084D] *On Christian Doctrine*]: “Whoever wishes to have [Col. 1084B] ordered love must take care neither to love what ought not to be loved, nor fail to love what ought to be loved; neither to love equally what should be loved more or less, nor to love more or less what should be loved equally.”

#### The order of things to be loved

Every human being, insofar as he is a sinner, is not to be loved; insofar as he is human, he is to be loved. But God is to be loved more than every human being. Moreover, one’s neighbor is to be loved more than one’s own body, because he is loved for God’s sake and can enjoy God with us; but the body cannot.

Finally, all neighbors are to be loved with equal affection but unequal outward effect. Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1084D] *On Christian Doctrine*]: “All human beings are to be loved equally; but since you cannot benefit all, you must especially care for those who are more closely joined to you by the opportunities of place, time, or any other circumstances.” Ambrose also states this more distinctly [Note: [Col. 1084D] On Song of Songs 1]: “God is to be loved first; parents second; then children; afterwards members of the household. If these are good, they are to be preferred to bad children. Finally come enemies, whom God commands us to love neither with all our strength nor as ourselves, but simply. For it is enough that we love them and do not hate them.”

But Ambrose says this not because we ought not to love them as ourselves, since they are neighbors too, but to show that it is enough if we love them less than other neighbors—certainly with respect to outward effect.

#### On the degrees of charity

It must also be known [Col. 1084D] that charity is not perfect as soon as it is born. For in order to be perfected, it is born; once born, it is nourished; once nourished, it is strengthened; once strengthened, it is perfected. When perfect, it says: “I desire to be dissolved” (Phil. I), and so forth.

### Distinction XXX. Whether it is better to love friends than enemies, or conversely

It is also commonly asked whether loving a friend or an enemy is of greater merit. We say that both are of the same merit. For each is loved by the same charity, from which merit comes. With respect to the outward act, however, loving an enemy rather than a friend is a clearer sign of perfect charity. [Col. 1085A] Hence Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1085D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 73]: “This great good—namely loving one’s enemy, doing good to one who hates one, and praying for one who persecutes—is not found in so great a multitude as we believe is heard when it says: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors’” (Matt. VI).

### Distinction XXXI. Whether charity, once possessed, is lost

In saying this, we should understand him to have distinguished perfect charity from imperfect charity. Imperfect charity is often lost and recovered, and both good and evil persons share in it. Hence Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1085D] On Romans, ch. 9]: “Grace was given to some for use, as to Saul and Judas. For those who will be good are often first evil, and those who will be evil are first good.”

But rooted and perfect charity, once possessed, never ceases, [Col. 1085B] and only good persons share in it. Hence charity is the proper and singular fountain of the good, in which a stranger has no share. According to this, distinguish the apparent disagreement of many authorities.

#### How charity will not pass away

Perfect charity will remain in the future. Although it will be perfected in the future, it will nevertheless remain the same in substance and mode: toward God, more than oneself; toward neighbor, as oneself. Other things will either wholly cease, as faith and hope do—and some think the same of knowledge—or at least cease as to the mode, which in the future will be altogether different from that of the present.

#### Why charity is placed after faith and hope

It should also be noted [Col. 1085C] that charity is not placed after faith and hope because it arises from them, but because it will remain after them, increased. These three are now equal, not with respect to their scope, but with respect to the intensity of their acts. For if you believe more intensely, you also hope and love more intensely.

### Distinction XXXII. How Christ loved

Christ had charity not of the wayfarer, by which he loved every neighbor unto life, but of the homeland, by which he loved only the elect unto salvation. He also loved the reprobate, just as from eternity he loved them, insofar as they were going to be his work—that is, as those whom and such as he was going to make them. Accordingly, from eternity he loved some of the elect more and others [Col. 1085D] less, not according to the essence of love but according to its effect, because he prepared greater goods for these than for those. In this sense some are said to begin to be loved by God when they receive the effect of eternal love.

### Distinction XXXIII. On the principal virtues called cardinal

After the foregoing, let us consider the four principal virtues. The first is justice, which consists in assisting the wretched, who have less power against the strength of the more powerful. The second is prudence, in avoiding snares. The third is fortitude, [Col. 1086A] in enduring hardships. The fourth is temperance, in restraining disordered pleasures.

#### That these virtues remain in the future

These will exist in the future, but in a different use from that which they have here. Hence Bede says [Note: [Col. 1085D] On Exodus XXVI]: “The powers of heaven are distinguished by the four aforesaid virtues, which are exercised differently in heaven by angels and holy souls than here by the faithful.”

### Distinction XXXIV. On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit

The seven gifts are also virtues, and they are present in angels, as Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1085D] *On the Holy Spirit*, Book I, ch. 20 and final chapter]: “The Spirit of God gladdens the nature of angels with a more abundant richness of sanctifications.” Then, explaining “sanctifications,” he adds: “By these sanctifications is signified the fullness of the seven spiritual virtues which Isaiah enumerates (ch. XI), saying: ‘The spirit of wisdom,’ and so forth.”

[Col. 1086B] But Bede’s saying appears contrary [Note: [Col. 1086D] On the parables of Proverbs I]. Having dealt with servile and chaste fear, he added: “Both will cease in the future.” Augustine also says [Note: [Col. 1086D] On Psalm V]: “The fear of the Lord is a great safeguard for those advancing toward salvation; when they arrive, it is cast out. For they no longer fear their friend once they have been brought to what was promised.”

But we say that fear will exist in the future, not according to its present use, which is fear of separation, but according to reverence, which is mingled with the submission of love, and which existed in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “He was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. V).

#### Full distinction of fears: worldly fear; human or natural fear; servile fear; initial fear; chaste or filial fear

Here [Col. 1086C] it must be known that there are five fears. Worldly fear is guilt, by which we fear to lose worldly goods. Human or natural fear is punishment, and existed in Christ; by it we shrink from dangers to the flesh. Servile fear is that by which, from fear of Gehenna, a person restrains himself from sin and does what is good because it is useful; through it the habit of righteousness gradually develops, and it is insufficient. Initial fear follows, when what had been hard begins to be loved, and it is sufficient. Then comes chaste fear, also called friendly or filial fear, by which separation from the Bridegroom is feared, and it perfects.

According to this latter meaning, it remains until the end of the age; but according to the aforesaid meaning—that is, according to reverence mingled with filial submission—it exists both here and in the future (I John [Col. 1086D] IV). But the saying, “Fear is not in charity,” must be understood of perfect charity and initial fear. Of this Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1086D] On the First Epistle of John IV, Homily 9]: “As charity increases, fear decreases. And as charity becomes more inward, fear is cast out: greater charity, lesser fear; lesser charity, greater fear.”

It should be known, however, that in the usage of Scripture both servile and initial fear are called “the beginning of wisdom,” though for different reasons. Servile fear is called the beginning of wisdom because it prepares a place for the charity of God; initial fear, because it exists in charity that has begun.

[Col. 1087A] ### Distinction XXXV. The distinction between knowledge, understanding, and wisdom

Finally, the three gifts—knowledge, understanding, and wisdom—are distinguished from one another as follows. Knowledge serves the right management of temporal matters and good conduct among the wicked. Understanding serves contemplation of the Creator and of invisible creatures. Wisdom serves the contemplation and delight of eternal truth alone.

### Distinction XXXVI. On the connection and equality of virtues

Here it must be known that all virtues are so joined to one another that, when one is possessed, all are possessed. Hence Jerome says [Note: [Col. 1087D] On Isaiah X]: “All virtues cling to one another, so that whoever has one has all; and whoever lacks one lacks all.” Augustine also says [Col. 1087B] [Note: [Col. 1087D] *On the Trinity*, Book VI, ch. 4]: “Although the virtues which are in the human mind are severally understood in different ways, they are in no way separated from one another, so that whoever are equal, for example, in fortitude are equal also in prudence, justice, and temperance. For if you say that these persons are equal in fortitude but that one excels in prudence, it follows that the other’s fortitude is less prudent; and thus they are not equal even in fortitude, because the first one’s fortitude is more prudent. And you will find the same concerning the other virtues if you examine them all by the same consideration.”

When someone is said to excel in some virtue, as Abraham in faith and Job in patience, this should be understood with respect to outward uses or in comparison [Col. 1087C] with other human beings, because he especially displays the habit of humility, or chiefly performs the work of faith or of some other virtue.

### Distinction XXXVII. On the ten commandments of the Decalogue, and their reduction to the two commandments of charity

We must now consider the distinction of the Decalogue. The Decalogue has ten commandments: three on the first tablet, pertaining to God; seven on the second tablet, pertaining to neighbor.

The first on the first tablet is: “You shall have no strange gods. You shall not make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness” (Exod. XX). A graven image is that which has nothing similar to itself. A likeness, however, is that which bears the appearance of some thing (I Cor. VIII).

The second is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” [Col. 1087D] (Exod. XX). Literally, this means: “You shall not swear by God’s name for no purpose.” Allegorically, it commands that you should not think Christ, the Son of God, to be a creature.

The third is: “Remember to keep the Sabbath day holy” (Exod. 20). By the letter, this commands observance of the Sabbath. Allegorically, however, it commands that you await rest both here, from vices, and hereafter, in the contemplation of God. The first commandment pertains to the Father, in whom there is unity; the second to the Son, in whom there is equality; the third to the Holy Spirit, in whom there is the communion of the two.

[Col. 1088A] On the seven commandments of the second table.---On the second table there are seven commandments. The first of these concerns one’s earthly father: “Honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land” (Exod. 20), namely, the land of the living. The second is: “You shall not kill” (ibid.). Here, according to the letter, the act of homicide is forbidden; spiritually, the will to kill. The third is: “You shall not commit adultery” (ibid.), that is, you shall unite yourself with no one apart from the covenant of marriage. For the whole is understood from one part. Thus, under the name of adultery, every unlawful sexual union and every illegitimate use of those members must be understood to be forbidden. The fourth is: “You shall not steal” (ibid.). Here sacrilege and every kind of robbery are forbidden. For he who forbade theft did not permit robbery.

Whether the children of Israel committed theft in despoiling Egypt.---Here it is commonly asked whether the Israelites committed theft when they despoiled Egypt (Exod. 2). We say that they did not, because the perfect rendered service to God who commanded it. But the weak were permitted rather than commanded to do this to those who had justly incurred such treatment. [Note: [Col. 1088D] Augustine on that passage.] The fifth is: “You shall not bear false testimony against your neighbor” (Exod. 20). Here the crime of lying and perjury is forbidden.

## DISTINCTION XXXVIII. On lying

A lie, as Augustine says [Note: [Col. 1088D] *Enchiridion*, ch. 18.], is the expression of something false with the intention of deceiving. To lie, however, is to speak contrary to what one thinks in one’s mind. Hence, if a Jew says that Christ is God while not believing it, [Col. 1088C] he indeed lies, but he does not utter a lie.

Whether every lie is a sin.---Finally, every lie is a sin. Yet it makes a great difference with what intention, and concerning what matters, someone lies. For one who lies in order to help does not sin in the same way as one who lies in order to harm; nor does one who lies about an earthly road sin in the same way as one who lies about the way of life.

Threefold lying.---For someone sometimes lies solely for another person’s advantage, as did the midwives and Rahab (Exod. 1; Josh. 2); sometimes in jest, which does not befit the perfect; and sometimes out of malice, against which everyone must be most carefully on guard.

Whether Jacob, in calling himself Esau, lied.---Finally, Jacob, in saying that he was Esau, is excused from lying (Gen. [Col. 1088D] 27), since he intended only to obey his mother, who through intimate counsel with God knew that in this a mystery of the sacrament was being enacted. Or Jacob did not lie: for he himself was Esau by right, if not in person, because he had bought the birthright from him.

## DISTINCTION XXXIX. On perjury

Perjury is a lie confirmed by an oath. To swear is to render to God his due—namely, truth and not falsehood—that is, to call God as witness or to pledge something to him. This is what one does who swears by his children: he pledges them to God, so that what proceeds from his mouth may happen to them—if it is true, what is true; if false, what is false.

[Col. 1089A] Which oaths bind more strongly. What perjury is.---One swears by God, by the Gospels, and by created things. But the holier that by which one swears is, the more punishable is perjury. [Note: [Col. 1089B] Augustine, Letter 4 to Publicola.] Perjury, however, is lying after an oath has been invoked. It occurs when someone, in swearing, speaks with an intention to deceive—an intention which he either has immediately or later, before the time when what he swore ought to be done. For it is not a guilty tongue that makes one liable, unless the mind is guilty.

The companions of an oath. A careless oath is a sin.---It must also be observed that an oath has three companions: truth, judgment, and justice. Thus, with regard to oneself, one should swear discerningly; with regard to one’s neighbor, usefully; and, with regard to God, what one swears should be true, or believed to be true. [Col. 1089B] If these are lacking, there is perjury—that is, an oath made carelessly. This is a sin because an oath is not to be sought as though it were a good thing; yet neither is it to be avoided as though it were evil, when it is necessary.

When something is called perjury.---Perjury is properly spoken of when an oath can and, according to the terms in which it was sworn, ought to be fulfilled, but is disregarded. It should be disregarded by a sounder judgment when fulfilling the oath [Col. 1090A] would lead to a worse outcome—for example, when someone has sworn to persist in fornication. Such a person is plainly caught between fornication and the aforementioned perjury; in this case the pledged faith must be broken. For Isidore says: “In a shameful vow, change your resolution; do not do what you vowed carelessly.”

On one who swears through verbal trickery.---Accordingly, by whatever verbal artifice an oath is sworn, God understands it as the one who swears and the one to whom the oath is sworn understand it in their straightforward sense. [Note: [Col. 1090B] Augustine, in the sermon *On Perjuries*.]

On one who compels another to swear falsely.---If anyone knowingly demands a false oath, he is a murderer.

## DISTINCTION XL. On the sixth and seventh commandments of the second table

Finally, the sixth commandment is: “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20). The seventh: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor his servant, nor his maidservant” (ibid.). [Col. 1090B]

Whether these final commandments are included in the earlier ones.---But these two commandments seem to be included in the preceding ones, where it was said: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal.” Yet in those, deeds are forbidden; in these, desire is forbidden. The aforesaid commandments of the Law, therefore, are the ten strings of the psaltery, which must be struck with charity so that the beasts of vices may be slain.

[Col. 1089] End of the book *On the Incarnate Word and the Restoration of Man*, which is the third book of Bandinus’s *Sentences*.

[Col. 1089]

# MASTER BANDINUS’S BOOK ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL SACRAMENTS, WHICH IS THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE *SENTENCES*

*Periochē* [Summary].---Throughout almost the whole of this fourth book, Bandinus discusses, with remarkable clarity and very great brevity, the strengthening of man restored through Christ’s death—a strengthening consisting in the saving use and dispensation of the holy sacraments of the Church, which derive their power and origin from Christ’s Passion. Near the end he also touches upon the final, so to speak, blessedness of the man strengthened through ecclesiastical sacraments, explaining the resurrection of the dead and the Last Judgment, together with the punishments of the impious and the joys of the devout. With these matters Bandinus happily concludes his book, praying that the Lord may make us sharers in the joy of the righteous.

[Col. 1089C] ## DISTINCTION I. On sacraments in general. What a sacrament is

After the treatment of things which are to be enjoyed and used, and of those which enjoy and use, let us proceed to treat signs, which are called sacraments. A sacrament, therefore, is a visible form of invisible grace, or a sign of a sacred thing. A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance that it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into knowledge through itself.

How the sacraments of the old and new laws differ.---Finally, [Col. 1090C] a sacrament bears the likeness of the thing of which it is the sign; for example, the water of baptism bears the likeness of the cleansing of sins. Yet, properly speaking, that is called a sacrament which so signifies grace that it also confers it. By this the difference between the old and the new sacraments is clearly marked: the former only promised and signified; the latter signify and give grace.

Why sacraments were instituted.---They were instituted for a threefold [Col. 1091A] reason: namely, that we might be humbled, instructed, and exercised. For the person who despised one greater than himself pleases God when, at the Creator’s command, he humbly reverences visible things that are inferior even to himself. At the same time, through what is perceived in visible appearance, the mind is instructed to know invisible power. Through these sacraments also, one who could not remain idle avoids harmful occupation and is usefully exercised.

On circumcision.---Although the ancient sacraments did not give grace, circumcision nevertheless had the same efficacy against sin that baptism now has. Hence Bede says: [Note: [Col. 1091D] (398–399) On the Gospel of Luke, “And when they were fulfilled.”] “In the Law, circumcision provided against the wound of original sin the same aid of saving healing that baptism provides in the time of grace, [Col. 1091B] except that it did not open the gate of the kingdom.”

On the institution and purpose of circumcision.---Circumcision was first commanded to Abraham and afterward to his seed. It was commanded to him as proof of his faith and obedience, and so that this people might be distinguished from other nations by this sign.

Why it was in the flesh of the foreskin.---It was also commanded to be performed in the flesh of the foreskin because it was fitting that the sign of obedience should appear where the penalty of disobedience—that is, concupiscence—exercised the greater dominion.

Why on the eighth day and with a stone knife.---It was performed on the eighth day with a stone knife because, through Christ’s resurrection on the eighth day, the soul is cleansed from sins; and in the general resurrection, which will occur in the eighth age, all corruption will be taken away from the elect by the Rock, Christ. [Col. 1091C]

By what original sin was removed before circumcision.---Before circumcision, sins were forgiven to little children through the faith of their elders, but to adults through sacrifices. Hence Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1091D] *Moralia*, book 4, ch. 2.] “What the water of baptism accomplishes among us, that among the ancients either faith alone accomplished for little children, or the power of sacrifice for adults.”

Why circumcision was changed into baptism.---Circumcision was rightly changed into baptism because baptism is more universal and more perfect. Let us now consider it.

## DISTINCTION II. On baptism

It must be known that the baptism by which the faithful are regenerated was preceded by John’s baptism, which was useful in that it prepared people, through the practice of baptizing, for Christ’s baptism.

Why it is called John’s baptism.---It was called John’s baptism because it was only John’s operation: he washed outwardly, while God did not work inwardly. That baptism was administered in the name of the One who was to come.

Whether those baptized by John ought to be rebaptized.---Accordingly, those baptized with John’s baptism who did not believe that the Holy Spirit exists were rebaptized with Christ’s baptism. [Col. 1092A] Hence Jerome says: [Note: [Col. 1091D] In the letter to Oceanus *On the Husband of One Wife*.] “Those who did not know the Holy Spirit, when they received baptism from John in the name of the One to come, were baptized again, lest anyone suppose that water without the Holy Spirit suffices for salvation.” Let us therefore next consider what baptism is, what its form is, when it was instituted, and why.

## DISTINCTION III. What baptism is

Baptism is the washing of the body performed under the form of that word concerning which it is said: “The word comes to the element, and the sacrament comes into being.” [Note: [Col. 1092D] Augustine, on John, tractate 80.]

The form of baptism. Whether it is permissible to baptize in Christ’s name.---That word is the invocation of the Trinity. Accordingly Truth himself, setting forth the form of baptism, says: “Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and [Col. 1092B] of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). This word comes to the element not merely because it is spoken, but because it is also believed. We also read that the Apostles baptized in Christ’s name (Acts 8, 10). In this the whole Trinity is understood: namely, the Anointed One himself, the Father by whom he was anointed, and the Holy Spirit with whom he was anointed.

Whether it is permissible to baptize using the name of only one person.---Indeed, the sacrament is perfectly conferred even in the name of only one of the persons, provided one thinks rightly concerning the others. Conversely, though all are named, the mystery is void if one thinks wrongly concerning any of them. Hence Ambrose says: [Note: [Col. 1092D] *On the Holy Spirit*, book 1, ch. 2.] “Just as, if you comprehend by speech one—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—yet by faith deny neither Father nor Son nor Holy Spirit, the sacrament of faith is complete; so also, though you say Father and Son and Holy Spirit, if you diminish the power of any one of them, the mystery is void.” It is safer, nevertheless, to name the three persons in baptism, saying: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—not “in the names,” but “in the name,” that is, in the invocation or confession of the three persons.

Where baptism was instituted.---Baptism was instituted in the Jordan, when Christ, by the contact of his clean flesh, gave regenerating power to the waters, so that whoever afterward was immersed, with the name of the Trinity invoked, might be cleansed from sins.

Why baptism is performed only in water.---Baptism is celebrated [Col. 1092D] in water, not in any other liquid, lest anyone be excused by scarcity, and because of the sacramental likeness: just as water washes away the body’s filth, so baptism wipes away the stains of the soul.

How often the baptized person should be immersed.---Finally, according to the varying usage of churches, the person being baptized is immersed once or three times. Hence Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1092D] Letter 41, book 1 of the *Register*, to Bishop Leander.] “Within the one faith, diverse custom does no harm to the holy Church. Therefore it is by no means blameworthy to immerse an infant three times or once in baptizing; for by triple immersion [Col. 1093A] the Trinity of persons, and by single immersion the unity of the divinity, can be signified. But we, who immerse three times, also signify the sacrament of the three-day burial.”

## DISTINCTION IV. On the threefold effect of baptism. An error of some

After what has been said, it must be known that some receive both the sacrament and the reality, some the sacrament only, and some the reality only. Infants receive the sacrament and the reality, although some think otherwise about those who are to perish, wrongly relying on the statement of Augustine: [Note: [Col. 1093D] *On the Baptism of Infants*, ch. 2.] “The sacraments effect in the saints alone what they signify.” This must be understood thus: although the sacraments effect remission for all, they effect it unto salvation for the elect alone. Adults also who approach with faith receive the sacrament and the reality; [Col. 1093B] those who approach without faith receive the sacrament only. Hence Jerome says: [Note: [Col. 1093D] On Ezekiel 16.] “Those who receive baptism without full faith receive not the Holy Spirit, but water.” Augustine likewise says: [Note: [Col. 1093D] *On the Medicine of Penance*, ch. 2.] “Everyone who has already become master of his own will, when he approaches the sacrament of the faithful, cannot begin the new life unless he repents of the old.” What Augustine [Note: [Col. 1093D] *On the Baptism of Infants against the Donatists*, book 1, ch. 12.] seems to say—that sins are forgiven at that very instant to one who approaches deceitfully—he says not by asserting it, but by comparison and in disputing against others. This is shown by what he says there: [Note: [Col. 1093D] In the same book.] “If someone approaches baptism deceitfully, are his sins forgiven him, or are they not forgiven? Let them choose what they wish.” He also says: [Note: [Col. 1093D] There.] “Baptism then begins to avail for salvation, when that [Col. 1093C] deceit has departed from the heart through a subsequent truthful confession.” Therefore, one who approaches deceitfully receives not the reality, but the sacrament only.

What baptism benefits those who approach with faith.---But what does baptism confer upon those who approach with faith when they have been justified? We answer that it grants them release from outward satisfaction, assisting grace, an increase of every virtue, and a further weakening of the tinder of sin. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1093D] Homily 74 on John.] “The faith which makes believers is given or nourished in the waters of baptism, because there it is sometimes given to one who does not have it, and to one who has it it is given so that it may be possessed more fully.”

Who receive the reality but not the sacrament.---Those receive the reality but not the sacrament who shed their blood for Christ or hold his faith, [Col. 1093D] when help cannot be given to them because of the pressure of time. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1094D] *On the One Baptism*, book 4, ch. 22.] “Considering again and again, I find that not only suffering undertaken for Christ’s name supplies the place of baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart—provided only that not contempt for religion, but the exigency of necessity excludes the mystery of baptism.” Ambrose also says of Valentinian: [Note: [Col. 1094D] *On the Death of Valentinian*, shortly before the middle.] “I grieve from my inmost heart because I have lost the one whom I was about to regenerate; nevertheless, he did not lose the grace which he asked for.” [Col. 1094A]

What seem to conflict with the foregoing.---The Lord’s saying does not conflict with this: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit,” etc. (John 3). It must be understood of those who can be baptized and disdain to be. Likewise this saying must be understood in the same way: “We believe that no catechumen, however much he has died amid good works, has life.” [Note: [Col. 1094D] Augustine, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 74.]

Baptism relates variously to the remission of sins. What sponsors should do. Explanation of the words spoken by those receiving a child. What precedes baptism.---Finally, it must be known that, since baptism is the sacrament of remission of sins, it sometimes precedes that remission, as when a deceitful person is [Col. 1094B] baptized; sometimes follows it, as when a righteous person is baptized; and sometimes occurs together with it, as when infants are baptized. While they are baptized, infants receive as a gift, though not in actual use, the grace of acting rightly. They will possess it when they come to greater age unless by free choice they choose a wicked use. For them sponsors ask for faith and profess belief. [Note: [Col. 1094D] This is from the Master, Distinction 6.] All this must be understood as referring to the sacrament of baptism, so that the meaning is: “I ask for faith,” that is, “I am ready to receive the sacrament of faith”; “I believe,” that is, “I receive the sacrament of faith.” The sponsor says this for the infant, who is not old enough to speak for himself. By this, the infant too is bound to fulfill it when he has grown older, and the sponsor is likewise bound to take diligent care [Col. 1094C] that it is fulfilled. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1094D] *On the Creed, to Catechumens*, book 2, chs. 1–2, and book 4, ch. 10.] “You have issued the surest pledge, by which you promised to renounce the pomps of the devil.” Baptism is preceded by exorcism, that is, adjuration, and catechism, that is, instruction—not because baptism cannot exist without these, but so that the person to be baptized may be taught what to flee and may know to whom he becomes indebted. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1094D] *On the Creed, to Catechumens*, book 1, ch. 10.] “The infant is breathed upon and exorcized, that the devil may flee from him and that he may know to whom he henceforth becomes indebted.”

## DISTINCTION V. Baptism is equally efficacious whether administered by a good person or a bad one

Finally, since Christ alone baptizes, baptism is always equally good, regardless of whether it is administered by a good or a bad person.

## DISTINCTIONS VI and VII. Who may baptize

In brief, it must be known [Col. 1094D] that the ministry of baptism is permitted to priests alone. In a time of necessity, however, deacons and any person may administer baptism. Baptism administered by anyone is not repeated, provided there is no error in the form of the Church.

## DISTINCTION VIII. On the sacrament of the Eucharist. Why it is called Eucharist

After the sacrament of baptism follows the sacrament of the Eucharist, and rightly so: through [Col. 1095A] baptism we are cleansed; through the Eucharist we are strengthened in good. Eucharist means “good grace,” because in this sacrament that whole One is received who is the fountain and source of all grace. In this sacrament, then, let us consider its institution, form, and reality.

On the institution of this sacrament.---The Lord instituted this sacrament at supper, after the typical lamb, by which he signified that the sacraments of the old Law were ended by his death and that those of the new Law were established in their place.

On the form of this sacrament.---Its form is that which the Lord himself instituted, saying: “This is my body, which shall be given for you,” and: “This is my blood, which shall be shed for many” (Matt. 26). [Col. 1095B] The remaining words are spoken in praise of God. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1095D] Letter 59 to Paulinus.] “It must be believed that the sacraments are consecrated by those words of Christ; all the rest are praises, entreaties, and petitions.”

Three things to be distinguished in this sacrament.---In this sacrament three things must be distinguished. One is sacrament only: namely, the species of bread and wine. Another is both sacrament and reality: namely, Christ’s flesh, which he took from the Virgin, and the blood which he shed for us. The third is the reality only of the sacrament: namely, the unity of the Church, which is the Lord’s spiritual flesh, of which it is said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have eternal life in yourselves” (John 6).

[Col. 1095C] ## DISTINCTION IX. On two modes of eating

Just as there are two realities of this sacrament, so there are two modes of eating: the sacramental mode, by which the body that Christ took from the Virgin is received under the sacrament and his blood is drunk; and the spiritual mode, by which someone eats if he abides in God and God in him. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1095D] Homily 26 on John 6, and Sermon 11 *On the Words of the Lord*.] “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. If he abides in me and I in him, then he drinks. But whoever does not abide in me, nor I in him, even if he receives the sacrament, gains great torment.”

Likewise: “Why do you prepare stomach and tooth? Believe, and you have eaten.” According to these two modes is distinguished what Augustine says: the good person receives the sacrament [Col. 1095D] and the reality of the sacrament, while the bad person receives the sacrament only—that is, Christ’s body. In this sense also Augustine’s saying is understood: [Note: [Col. 1095D] There, homily on John, in meaning.] “The one who does not eat eats, and the one who eats does not eat.”

## DISTINCTION X. Christ’s body is on every altar

Finally, the body which Christ took from the Virgin is on every altar at the time of sacrifice. Yet it is visibly in only one place, namely at the right hand of the Father, according to its human form. This is what Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1096D] Tractate 50 on John.] “Christ’s body is visibly in one place, [Col. 1096A] namely, in human form; but his Truth is everywhere,” that is, his divinity. Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1096D] Likewise, Letter 57 to Dardanus.] “His Truth, that is, his true body, is everywhere,” that is, on every altar where it is celebrated, though invisibly, according to that same form. Similar statements must be understood in this way.

## DISTINCTION XI. On the conversion of bread into Christ’s flesh and wine into blood

Accordingly, true faith confesses that ordinary bread is on the altar before the sacred words set out above; after those words, bread becomes Christ’s flesh, or is made, or passes over, or is converted into flesh. The same holds for wine.

How this conversion occurs.---If the manner of conversion is asked about, we say that some hold that the conversion should be understood in this way: beneath the same [Col. 1096B] accidents under which the substance of bread and wine had been before, after consecration there is the substance of body and blood. Others say that the bread is substantially changed into flesh, yet does not increase. For everything that is there shines forth by the power of a miracle. But whether it is so or otherwise, we must maintain what Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1096D] In Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*.] “If you ask how this can occur, I answer briefly: the mystery of faith can profitably be believed; it cannot profitably be investigated.”

Why Christ’s body is received under another species.---Christ’s body is received under a species other than its own for a threefold reason: so that faith may have merit; so that the mind may not recoil from what [Col. 1096C] the eye sees; and so that unbelievers may not mock religion.

Why under two species. Why water is mixed in.---Under the two species, moreover, the whole Christ is received, so that it may be shown that Christ assumed the whole of human nature and redeemed it whole. Bread refers to flesh and wine to blood, as Moses says: “Flesh is offered for your body, but blood for the soul” (Deut. 12; Lev. 17). Water, signifying the people, is also mixed with wine, so that by this it may be shown that the multitude of believers is joined to him in whom it believes. If water is omitted through ignorance or negligence, what is done is not invalid. But if this is done in order to introduce heresy, nothing is done.

## DISTINCTION XII. In what those accidents subsist. On breaking and the parts

If it is asked in what those accidents subsist, it seems preferable to confess that they exist without a subject—something not impossible for him who created them. The Lord’s body is broken, not in its own essence, since it has become impassible, but in the sacrament, as Augustine says: “And indeed it happens in the sacrament that, in that sacrament, it is handled and broken and ground by the teeth of the faithful,” as Berengar swore before Pope Nicholas. [Note: [Col. 1096D] On Consecration, distinction 2, ch. *Ego Berengarius*.]

What those parts signify.---In the Church, three parts of the same sacrament are made in the daily rite, [Col. 1097A] not without significance, as Pope Sergius says. [Note: [Col. 1097D] On Consecration, distinction 2, ch. *Triformae*.] The part of the offering placed in the chalice shows Christ’s body which has already risen; the part eaten, his body still walking upon the earth; the part remaining on the altar until the end of Mass, his body lying in the tomb, because until the end of the age the bodies of the saints will be in tombs.

Why this sacrifice is called an immolation. Why it was instituted. How often one should communicate yearly.---This sacrifice is called Christ’s immolation. For Christ is immolated daily, not in his own essence—for he died once and now dies no more—but by sacramental representation. Yet this sacrament is not repeated, because the blessing is not repeated over the same thing, just as baptism is not repeated in the same person. [Col. 1097B] This sacrament was instituted as a remedy for daily weakness. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1097D] *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, ch. 10, and Sermon 28 *On the Words of the Lord*.] “This offering is repeated daily because we sin daily.” Likewise: “Because we fall daily, the mystery of Christ is immolated for us daily.” Each of the faithful, however, should communicate three times a year: at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas.

## DISTINCTION XIII. Who consecrates this sacrament

This sacrament is consecrated by any priest, according to the rite and with the intention of consecrating, provided that he remains in the unity of the Church. Therefore, those who have been excommunicated or publicly marked by heresy do not consecrate this sacrament. For no one consecrating says, “I offer,” but “We offer,” as though speaking in the person of the Church. Augustine says this as follows: [Note: [Col. 1097D] This passage is not found here, any more than in Lombard. In the sermon [Col. 1098D] *On the Body of Christ*.] “Recall the name and [Col. 1097C] observe the truth. For it is called a *missa* [Mass] because a heavenly messenger, that is, an angel, comes to consecrate the Lord’s body, when the priest says: ‘Almighty God, command this to be carried by the hands of your angel to your sublime altar.’ But when a heretic usurps this mystery, does God send an angel from heaven to consecrate his offering?” We have briefly set forth these matters concerning the heavenly mystery, which Catholics must faithfully maintain.

## DISTINCTION XIV. On penance. Why penance is so called. What it is to repent. Division of penance

After this let us consider penance, which, after the shipwreck of Adam and original sin, is the second plank. The first is baptism, in which the old person is put off and the new put on; once conferred, it is not repeated. [Col. 1097D] But penance often comes to our aid. John’s preaching began with it, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3). Penance is so called from punishing, by which one punishes the unlawful acts one has committed. For to repent is to hold to punishment, so that one may always punish in oneself, by taking vengeance, what one committed in sinning. Accordingly, the virtue of penance is conceived from fear. Hence Isaiah says: “From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived the Spirit of salvation.”

Solemn penance. Non-solemn penance. Confession.---Of penances, [Col. 1098A] one is solemn and another is not. Solemn penance, as Ambrose says, [Note: [Col. 1098D] Ambrose, *On the One Penance*, book 2.] is performed publicly outside the church, in ashes and haircloth. It is imposed only for notorious and horrifying offenses, and is not repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament. For it signifies the expulsion of the first man from Paradise. The other is not solemn: it is a virtue of the mind, performed in secret, and may repeatedly be undertaken by the same person unto salvation. This is proved by the example of David. After receiving pardon for adultery and homicide, he sinned grievously in numbering the people; and when the angel was striking the people, he offered himself, saying: “What has this flock done? Let your hand be upon me and upon my father’s house.” He at once became worthy to offer sacrifice and deserved absolution (2 Sam. 24). This is also what Augustine says: “I confess [Col. 1098B] sins even once to an earthly judge before death, but frequent confession to God brings life.” Likewise, on the Psalm, “He will spare the poor” (Ps. 71): “If one who has been delivered offends, he will spare him, because all sin.” Therefore, authorities which seem to forbid penance to be repeated must be understood either of the penance of the perfect or of solemn penance, such as this: “Penance is always vengeance, punishing what one has committed”; and this: “There are those who think that penance should be done more than once, who indulge themselves in Christ.” [Note: [Col. 1098D] The same, there.]

## DISTINCTION XV. Whether confession of one sin is effective while others remain

It seems that confession made concerning one sin alone is effective, especially if satisfaction has been made for it, because Scripture says: “God will not judge twice in the same matter, and a double [Col. 1098C] tribulation will not arise” (Nah. 1). But this must be understood of those whose present punishment is changed into good. If, however, they persist in evil, they join eternal punishments to present ones, according to the saying: “Crush them with a double destruction, O Lord our God” (Jer. 17). For Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 1098D] Gregory, on Ezekiel, book 1, homily 10.] “The Lord rains upon one city, and does not rain upon another; and he rains upon the same city in part and leaves it dry in part.” When someone who hates his neighbor corrects himself of other vices, one and the same city is rained upon in part and remains dry in part, because some people, while cutting off certain vices, persist gravely in others. But this should be referred not to the forgiveness of the sin, but to the abandonment of the act of sinning. Thus [Col. 1098D] one part of the city is said to be rained upon because it now abstains from the pleasure and act of sinning. This abstinence is called rain because it proceeds from the fountain of grace, so that the person may either gradually repent in this way or be punished less by God, since through a more prolonged pleasure in and practice of sin he would have accumulated greater torment for himself.

Whether satisfaction should be imposed for this sin confessed without the others.---As to the customary question whether satisfaction should again be imposed for that sin, we say that it should be imposed again, because at first he did not make fitting satisfaction, since his penance was false. For Innocent says: [Col. 1099A] [Note: [Col. 1099D] On Penance, distinction 5, ch. *Fratres nostros*.] “Penance is clearly false when, while several sins are disregarded, penance is done for one alone; or when it is done for one in such a way that one does not depart from another.” Nevertheless, it may be moderated at the priest’s discretion.

## DISTINCTION XVI. On the three things considered in penance

In penance three things must be considered: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. For as we offend in three ways, so we must make satisfaction in three ways: by heart, mouth, and deed.

On the three kinds of sin.---There are three kinds of sin, like three deaths: in the house, at the gate, and in the tomb. The Lord signified these in the three dead persons whom he raised. Contrition [Col. 1099B] is commended in the words: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2). Confession in the words: “The righteous man at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Prov. 8, 18). Satisfaction in the words: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3).

What one who confesses must attend to.---Finally, according to Augustine, one who confesses should disclose to the priest the nature of the crime, the place, time, his persistence in it, the condition and intention of the person with whom he sinned, and the temptation by which he committed it. For every such variation must be confessed and lamented.

Confession must not be divided among different priests.---He must also beware lest, led by shame, he divide his confession within himself and wish to disclose different matters to different priests. This is to praise oneself, to tend toward hypocrisy, and always to lack the pardon which he vainly supposes he will attain.

[Col. 1099C] On the three acts of penance.---There are also three acts of penance. Hence Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 1099D] Letter 108 to Seleucianus.] “People do penance before baptism for their former sins, provided that they are baptized. They also do penance after baptism if they have sinned so as to deserve excommunication. There is likewise an almost daily penance of good believers for sins without which this life is not lived, for which we beat our breasts, saying: ‘Forgive us our debts’” (Matt. 6).

### DISTINCTION XVII. To Whom Confession Is To Be Made

Finally, slight sins suffice to be confessed, with a contrite heart, to any fellow Christian; but grave sins must be confessed to a priest, unless he is absent and danger presses. Hence Bede says on the words, “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5): “We disclose daily and slight sins to equals, but grave sins to a priest. Yet grave sins too must be disclosed to equals when a priest is lacking and danger presses.” Therefore, if grave sins are secret, let them be confessed secretly; but if manifest, they require public medicine. Augustine teaches this through the likeness of those whom the Lord raised from the dead.

> [Note: Col. 1099D, in the cited book, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 11.]

For he says: “At the raising of the little girl, few were present who saw it” (Matthew 9). “[Col. 1100A] He raised within the house her whom he found within, leaving only Peter, James, John, and the girl’s father and mother” (Mark 5); by these the priests of the Church are signified. But those whom he found outside, he raised in this manner (Luke 7). The crowd wept after the widow’s son. Mary and Martha wept, entreating for their brother (John 11). In this we are taught that, for those who sin publicly, their own merit does not suffice, but that of the Church.

### DISTINCTION XVIII. When and What God Forgives, and What the Priest Forgives

God forgives sin in contrition of heart before oral confession. Hence the Prophet says: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Psalm 31). On this Cassiodorus says:

> [Note: Col. 1099D, On Psalm 31.] Great is God’s mercy, which forgives sins upon the promise alone.

Likewise Augustine: “He has not yet uttered it, and God forgives.” God forgives sin in this manner: he cancels the debt of eternal death and inwardly cleanses the soul. For God covers sin in the penitent, so that he does not punish it eternally. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1100D, Explaining the passage of Psalm 31, “Whose sins are covered.”] For God to see sins is to reckon them for punishment; but to turn his face from sins is not to reserve them for punishment.

#### On the Darkness of the Soul

Behold, in this way he forgives sin with respect to outer darkness; he also forgives it with respect to inner darkness when he illumines the soul, darkened by the cloud of sin, and restores it to its purity. Hence: “Arise, you who sleep” (Ephesians 5). And in the Psalm: “He scatters mist like ashes” (Psalm 147).

#### What the Priest Forgives

The priest, however, forgives sin in confession through the ministry of the office by which he can bind and loose.

> [Note: Col. 1100D. Bandinus is not followed here.]

For the evangelical priest alone both binds and looses: that is, by virtue of his office he shows a person to be bound or loosed by God, just as the legal priest of old pronounced the leper unclean or clean—that is, showed him to be unclean or cleansed (Leviticus 13). The authority which that priest had over the body, this priest has over the mind. He shows a person loosed by imposing temporal punishment upon one whom he judges truly penitent; he shows him bound if he acts otherwise. The priest also binds when he imposes temporal punishment; he looses when he remits it. Thirdly, he binds when he suspends someone from communion, and looses when he restores him to communion.

#### On the Keys of the Church

The priest may do this by the authority of the keys of the Church, which are entrusted to him at ordination, when the bishop says to him what the Lord said to Peter: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16). That is, as Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1100D, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 10.] “I, God, and all the orders of the heavenly host, and all the saints in my glory, praise and confirm with you those whom you loose and bind.” He did not say, “those whom you think you bind or loose,” but “those upon whom you exercise the work of justice and mercy.” “[Col. 1101A] But I do not acknowledge your other works upon sinners.”

Jerome likewise says:

> [Note: Col. 1101D, On Matthew 16, “I will give the keys.”] Some people, not understanding this passage, arrogate something to themselves from these words, after the manner of the pride of the Pharisees: they suppose that they may condemn the innocent and loose the guilty, whereas before God it is not the judgment of priests but the life of the accused that is considered—namely, whether it benefits or harms them.

#### On the Pastor’s Judgment. What the Two Keys Are

Moreover, whether the pastor’s judgment is just or unjust, it must rightly be revered, yet without prejudice to the truth. For sometimes one who is cast out is within, and one who seems even to be retained within is outside. These are the two keys: the knowledge of discerning sins and the power of judging sins.

### DISTINCTION XIX. When and To Whom Are These Keys Given?

Everyone ordained priest receives these keys. Even if he formerly possessed the knowledge of discerning, he did not possess it as a key: that is, he could not use it with the authority of a key-bearer, which only an ordained person can do. Yet it appears that not all priests possess these keys. For Origen says:

> [Note: Col. 1101D, in sense, Homily 1 on Matthew.] This power was granted to Peter alone and to his imitators—namely, the worthy, or those who imitate him in rank, even if not in life.

Therefore this dignity belongs to order, not to the person. Augustine proves this by the example of Caiaphas (John 11). He says:

> [Note: Col. 1101D, *Questions on the Old and New Testament*, question 11.] It was said concerning the utterly wicked Caiaphas: “He did not say this from himself, but because he was high priest that year.” By this it is shown that the spirit of graces follows not the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission; so that, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained.

#### Why Must a Sin Forgiven by God Be Confessed to a Priest?

But if God forgives sin in contrition, why must anyone afterward confess to a priest—that is, to the Church? I think that among the other reasons this is the chief: that through this sacrament the unity existing between Christ and the Church may be commended. Thus, just as the two are one flesh and one voice, so the two may be one in a single confession. This was not required in the Old Testament, but is required now, because now, not then, these two are one in one flesh.

#### On General Confession

Penance must be undertaken in the manner stated above, where sins are remembered. But because no one understands all his sins, it is necessary at least to confess them generally, as Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1102D, Book V of the *Hypognosticon*.] “If some sins have slipped from the mind, one confesses the truth to God when one says generally: ‘God, who know the secrets of hearts, my works and my offenses are not hidden from you; grant pardon for them.’” And this is the truthfulness of the confessor which God loves.

### DISTINCTION XX. On Those Who Repent at the End

Finally, since penance is always necessary, that penance is most praiseworthy which has not only fear but also freedom. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1102D, *On True and False Penance*, ch. 17.] Let no one wait until he is unable to sin. God seeks freedom of choice, so that he may blot out deeds committed; he seeks not necessity but love, not fear alone, because a human being does not live by fear alone.

Therefore, penance undertaken at the end is not so praiseworthy, because it seems to arise more from fear than love, when sins rather abandon you than you abandon them. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1102D, *Fifty Homilies*, Homily 41.] If you wish to do penance when you can no longer sin, sins abandon you, not you them.

Therefore assurance is not granted to one who thus repents. If, then, you wish to be freed from doubt, do penance while you are well.

### DISTINCTION XXI. Do Forgiven Sins Return?

It is also customary to ask whether forgiven sins return to one who sins again after having repented. We say that either position may be held without injury to faith. Approved teachers support both sides of the question: either that forgiven sins return when someone proves ungrateful for benefits—which the Gospel parable appears to explain—or that they do not return, but that there are as many acts of ingratitude in their place as there had been forgiven sins (Matthew 18). Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1102D, On Psalm 102.] “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses”: they are as many as the remissions; therefore the forgettings are also as many.

### DISTINCTION XXII. On Anointings

#### The Anointing of Catechumens; the External Anointing of the Sick; Anointing in Confirmation; What Oil and Balm Signify

Finally, it must be known that there are three kinds of anointing. The first is that by which catechumens and neophytes are anointed on the breast and between the shoulders, so that, as they approach Christ’s military service, they may be strengthened for right understanding and right action.

The second is the anointing of the sick, which began with the apostles, James saying: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they are forgiven him” (James 5). This anointing is repeated, or administered only once, according to the varying practice of churches.

There is a third anointing, more venerable than the others, by which the head is anointed: that of a bishop or king, or the forehead of one baptized or confirmed. By reason of the prerogative of the overflowing grace conferred in it, this is called *chrism*, a word interpreted “anointing.” By the privilege of more abundant grace, the general name claims for itself a proper meaning. It has, moreover, two principal liquids mixed in it—oil and balm—one of which excels in brightness, the other in fragrance. Thus, by oil is signified the glory of conscience, and by balm the most celebrated reputation, so that those anointed with chrism may be clear in conscience and glorious in reputation.

#### What Is the Sacrament, and What Is the Reality of the Sacrament?

In these, therefore, the sacrament is the anointing of the outward person; “[Col. 1103A] the reality of the sacrament” is the fruitfulness of the inward person, which is then given us through the Holy Spirit.

### DISTINCTION XXIII. On Ecclesiastical Orders

Let us now consider ecclesiastical orders, setting forth what force they have in us and how Christ bore them in himself.

#### What Order Is

Order is a seal: that is, a certain sacred thing by which spiritual power and office are conferred upon the ordained person.

#### How Many Orders of Clerics There Are

Finally, according to the prerogative of the sevenfold Spirit, there are seven orders: doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest.

#### Why They Are Called Clerics; What the Tonsure Signifies

> [Note: Col. 1103D, Isidore, Book VII.]

All clerics are called “clerics,” that is, “those chosen by lot,” because Matthias, whom the Church first ordained, was chosen by lot. The tonsure signifies this lot; it is a royal sign and a mark of dignity. Hence all ministers of the Church are not without reason called kings, as Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2).

#### Why He Is Called a Doorkeeper

The doorkeeper is so called because he presides over the doors of the temple. In the Old Testament he was called a gatekeeper, appointed to guard the temple lest any unclean person enter it (1 Chronicles 26). So now he guards the church, admitting the worthy and rejecting the unworthy. Hence the keys of the church are given him by the bishop when he is ordained.

#### Where Christ Exercised the Office of Doorkeeper

The Lord fulfilled this office in himself when he drove buyers and sellers from the temple with a whip (John 2).

#### On Readers; the Office of Readers

The second order is that of readers, who are so called from reading, because they chant and read in church in order to stir the minds of the hearers to compunction. It belongs to them by office to read prophecies and lessons in church. Hence the book of divine law is handed to them by the bishop at their ordination. They ought therefore to possess learning, so that they may pronounce and explain distinctly what they read.

Christ likewise fulfilled this office when, opening the book of Isaiah (ch. 61), he read distinctly in the midst of the elders: “[Col. 1103D] The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he sent me to preach the Gospel to the meek” (Luke 4).

The third order is that of exorcists, who in Latin are called “rebukers” or “helpers.” For they adjure or rebuke the unclean spirit over catechumens and the possessed—those, that is, rendered powerless. Therefore, by his office the exorcist ought to lay his hand upon the aforesaid persons with an exorcism. Hence he also receives from the bishop the book of exorcisms when he is ordained.

The Lord exercised this office when he touched and healed the ears and tongue of the deaf and mute man, and when “[Col. 1104A] he also drove away many demons by his command” (Mark 7).

The fourth order is that of acolytes, who in Latin are called candle-bearers, because they carry candles before them, especially when the Gospel is to be read. It belongs to the acolyte, therefore, to prepare and carry the light in the sanctuary, and to offer to the subdeacons the cruets for the Eucharist. When ordained, he receives from the archdeacon a candlestick with a candle and an empty cruet.

Christ fulfilled this office when he said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8; Mark 7).

The fifth order is that of subdeacons. They are so called because in ministries they are subject to the commands and “[Col. 1104B] offices of deacons. It belongs to the subdeacon to carry the chalice and paten to the altar and hand them to the deacons; likewise to hold the cruet and water, the towel and hand-cloth for priests and Levites to wash their hands before the altar. Therefore, when they are ordained, they receive the chalice and paten from the bishop, and the cruet, etc., from the archdeacon.

#### Where Christ Performed This Office

The Lord exercised this office when he girded himself with a linen cloth and washed the feet of his disciples (John 12).

#### On Deacons; the Office of Deacons; the Manner of Ordaining Deacons

The order of deacons is sixth, in which their perfection is commended. In Latin they are called “ministers,” because, as consecration belongs to the priest, so the dispensation of the mystery belongs to the deacon. “[Col. 1104C] It belongs to him to prepare the Lord’s table, carry the cross, preach, and always attend and minister at the celebration of the sacraments. They are also called Levites, after the tribe of Levi, because just as the ministry of the temple was entrusted to that tribe for all Israel, so the ministry of the altar is assigned to these men for the whole Church. The bishop lays his hand on them at ordination and gives them the stole on the left side, so that they may be unencumbered for ministry; and, spiritually, so that they may understand that they are to subject themselves to the divine yoke in all that belongs to the left side. He also gives them the text of the Gospel, declaring them thereby to be heralds of Christ.

#### Where Christ Performed the Office of Deacon

Christ exercised this office when he distributed to the disciples the sacrament of his body “[Col. 1104D] and blood, and when he exhorted them to pray, saying: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26).

#### On Priests; the Manner of Ordaining Priests; Where Christ Exercised This Power

The seventh order is that of presbyters, a word interpreted “elders,” not on account of age but dignity. For they ought to excel among the people in character and prudence, as it is written: “Venerable old age is not that which lasts long, nor is it reckoned by the number of years. For a person’s understanding is gray hair, and a spotless life is mature age” (Wisdom 4). When they are ordained, the bishop anoints their hands, by which they receive the grace of consecration. They also receive “[Col. 1105A] a stole which holds or presses both sides, so that, as more perfect persons, they may submit adversity and prosperity to the Lord’s yoke. The Lord exercised this office when he changed bread and wine into his body and blood and offered himself upon the altar of the cross.

#### On the Names of Dignities
