There are also certain other names, not of orders but of dignities, such as bishop, so called because he oversees and takes charge of his subjects: for ἐπί means “over,” and σκοπεῖν means “to observe” or “to direct one’s attention.”

The order of bishops is divided into four: patriarchs, metropolitans, archbishops, and bishops simply so called. “Patriarch” means the highest of fathers. A metropolitan is called from the “[Col. 1105B] measure of cities.” An archbishop is the chief of bishops. All these are called pontiffs and are styled high priests, for they make the other priests and Levites and arrange all the orders of the Church. So long as they remain in the unity of the Church, they may unquestionably do this.

### DISTINCTION XXIV. On Those Ordained by Heretics

#### Bandinus Reconciles the Contradiction of the *Sentences*

But if they have erred from the womb and speak falsehood, Innocent, Gregory, Cyprian, and Jerome say that only their baptism is valid; all else that they administer is false and empty. For those who have lost their office of honor cannot give it. From this it appears that the office must be conferred again upon those who return from heretics to the Church.

Augustine, however, seems to contradict this.

> [Note: Col. 1105D, Book II against the Letter of Parmenianus.]

He proves that heretics retain the right of conferring orders just as they retain baptism—though both are to their own destruction. They can therefore give what they have, and it must not be repeated for those returning, lest an injury be done to the sacrament. But this opposition is resolved in many ways. Either the authorities just mentioned speak of heretics cut off by sentence, while Augustine speaks of those divided from the purity of faith merely through the perversity of their own opinion; or the former speak of heretics celebrating sacraments under a different form, while Augustine speaks of those who preserve the Church’s form in celebrating; or the former regard the effect of the sacraments, which are empty for those handling them unlawfully, while Augustine calls them true and correct in themselves; or the former speak of those heretics “[Col. 1105D] who are outside the Church, while Augustine speaks of those who received orders within the Church.

#### On the Age of Those To Be Ordained

The canons have decreed concerning ordination that a subdeacon is not to be ordained before fourteen years of age, a deacon before twenty-five, nor a presbyter before thirty, even if he is very worthy.

### DISTINCTION XXV. On Marriage

Let us now consider marriage, which is said to have been instituted before all sacraments in paradise for the first human beings, when the Lord said: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1). Before multiplication, marriage was for the sake of office, according to the command; afterward it was for a remedy, according to indulgence, so that human weakness, inclined to the downfall of shamefulness, might be received into the honorableness of marriage.

### DISTINCTION XXVI. What Marriage Is

Marriage is a union between lawful persons, preserving an indivisible partnership of life. Though it is understood or consists in many respects, its chief point is that, while both remain alive, neither of them is joined matrimonially to another.

#### What Persons Are Lawful

Finally, lawful persons are those whom no vow of continence, sacred order, spiritual or carnal kinship, disparity of religion, servile condition, or natural frigidity prevents. “[Col. 1106B] But through the first four they are altogether unlawful; through the last two they are intermediate cases. For if such persons are joined unknowingly, because of certain circumstances that arise they may live together, and when these cease may separate—for example, if the known condition is acceptable and natural frigidity is not found intolerable.

#### What Cause Effects Marriage; the Effect of Marriage; Where Its Perfection Consists; the Twofold Union Understood in Marriage

The efficient cause of marriage is consent, not consent to the future but to the present, expressed in such words as: “I take you as husband,” and “I take you as wife.” In this human and divine laws agree. For the law says: “Marriages are contracted not by dowries but by affection.” And Isidore says: “Consent makes marriage; consent concerning the present, not the future, effects marriage.” Likewise Pope Nicholas: “The consent alone is sufficient according to the laws of those whose union is at issue; if this alone is absent, all the other things performed, even intercourse itself, are in vain.”

This consent is the mutual obligation to preserve an indivisible life and marital partnership. Marriage is begun by it and perfected in bodily union. For Ambrose says:

> [Note: Col. 1105D, *On Virgins*, ch. 16.] When marriage is begun, the name of marriage is assumed.

Likewise Isidore: “From the first pledge of betrothal they are more truly called spouses.”

> [Note: Col. 1106D, *Etymologies*, ch. 8.]

That it is perfected in bodily union, Ambrose says: “In every marriage a spiritual union is understood, which the bodily mingling of the united persons confirms and perfects.” “[Col. 1106D] Jerome likewise says: “The Lord [something is missing] future adulteries in marriages which are begun by a betrothal agreement and perfected by the mingling of bodies.”

From these things it can be understood that marriage is a sacrament: a sacred sign of a sacred reality, namely the union of Christ and the Church—according to the spirit in respect of its beginning, according to the flesh in respect of its perfection. Thus it is the sign of a twofold sacred reality: the union of the soul with God, signified in betrothal; and the union of our flesh with God, signified in bodily mingling, when husband and wife become “[Col. 1107A] one flesh.” Thus Christ and the Church were made one flesh in the virgin’s womb.

Finally, the authority speaks according to that latter sign: “There is no doubt that that woman does not belong to marriage”—that is, in respect of this sign—“with whom it is shown that there was no mingling of sex.”

> [Note: Col. 1107D, Leo, Letter 90.]

### DISTINCTION XXVII. Compulsion Excludes Consent

Moreover, the laws say that this consent must be free from compulsion: “Marriages ought to be free both in contracting and in dissolving.”

### DISTINCTION XXVIII. That Error Impedes Marriage

Error also impedes marriage, because nothing is so contrary to consent as error, which reveals ignorance. But we understand this of error concerning the person and condition, “[Col. 1107B] which wholly impedes marriage; not of error concerning fortune or quality, which is tolerated in marriage.

#### On the Final Cause of Marriage

The final cause of marriage is principally offspring, as the Lord says: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1); secondarily, the avoidance of fornication. There are also other causes: the restoration of peace, the beauty of a man or woman, gain and the possession of riches, and many others which anyone carefully considering the matter could easily discover.

#### On the Marriage of the Virgin and Joseph

According to the threefold good which will immediately be discussed below, marriage between the Virgin and Joseph was perfect. For Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1107D, Book I, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 1.] In Christ’s parents every good of marriage was fulfilled: for we recognize the offspring as the Lord Christ; fidelity, because there was no adultery; the sacrament, because there was no divorce.

### DISTINCTION XXIX. On the Threefold Good of Marriage

Finally, there are three goods of marriage, as Augustine says: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament.

> [Note: Col. 1108D, *On Genesis according to the Letter*, Book IX, ch. 7.]

Fidelity means that one does not cohabit with another man or woman; offspring, that it be lovingly received and religiously raised. If these are lacking, there is offspring without the good of offspring, as in the case of someone who rashly wishes to have an heir to property, not desiring offspring for the purpose of religious formation. But marriage frequently lacks these two goods; this never happens with the third, namely the sacrament: that “[Col. 1107D] marriage is not dissolved,” that is, while both are alive, neither is ever sacramentally joined to another.

#### What Marriage Separation Is, and How Many Kinds There Are

There is bodily and sacramental separation. Thus spouses may separate bodily because of fornication, without mutual consent; or by mutual consent, temporarily for the sake of religion, or permanently. Therefore, where these three goods exist, intercourse is excused from every fault if it takes place for the sake of offspring, or from a greater fault if it takes place because of incontinence. Hence Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1108D, *On the Good of Marriage*.] Marital intercourse for the purpose of generating has no fault; but intercourse for satisfying concupiscence, though with one’s spouse and for the faithfulness of the marriage-bed, has venial fault.

But when fidelity and the good of offspring are lacking, intercourse undertaken to satisfy a spouse’s lust is criminal. Hence Sextus Pythagoricus says in his *Sentences*: “Every excessively ardent lover of his own wife is an adulterer.”

### DISTINCTION XXX. On Those Things Which Impede Marriage; In What Order Marriage Cannot Be Contracted

Let us now return to the causes that impede marriage and examine them more fully. Not every ecclesiastical order impedes marriage, but only the priesthood, diaconate, and subdiaconate. Marriage is permitted in the other orders, unless they have taken on a religious habit or made a vow of continence. Hence Innocent says:

> In order that the law of continence and purity pleasing to God may be extended among the ecclesiastical orders, we decree that bishops, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons who have made profession and, transgressing their sacred undertaking, presume to take a wife for themselves, shall be separated.

Likewise the Synod of Ancharitana (otherwise Anchonitana) says: “Any deacons who, when asked concerning continence, have sworn and received the laying on of hands, thereby professing continence, must cease from ministry if they afterward enter into marriage.”

### DISTINCTION XXXI. On the Difference of Vows; Division of a Singular Vow

One vow is common, such as that which all make at baptism; another is singular, as when someone voluntarily promises continence. Again, a singular vow is either private, as when it is made secretly or without solemnity, or solemn, as when it possesses solemnity. Such solemnity is supplied in clerics by the aforementioned order, in virgins by a blessing, and in widows by a religious habit. This alone impedes marriage.

### DISTINCTION XXXII. On Disparity of Worship

Disparity of worship is disparity of religion, and it impedes marriage. For a Christian may not contract marriage with a pagan or a Jew. Yet if, while both were unbelievers, they entered marriage and one is converted to the faith, the marriage may stand in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her; and likewise concerning a woman” (1 Corinthians 7). In this the Apostle indicates that there is an opportunity for gain, although he may lawfully leave her. For a wife may lawfully be dismissed on account of both bodily and spiritual fornication.

#### Marriage Is Threefold: Lawful and Ratified; Ratified but Not Lawful; Lawful but Not Ratified

Here, therefore, it should be known that one marriage is lawful and ratified, as that contracted publicly between believers with solemnities observed according to custom; another is ratified but not lawful, as that contracted secretly between the same persons and without any solemnity. This is prohibited lest, when lawful spouses become displeased with one another, they separate when proof of marriage is lacking. Another is lawful but not ratified, as that entered publicly with solemnity between unbelievers.

### DISTINCTION XXXIII. On Kinship of the Flesh; How Far Consanguinity Impedes; the Impediment of Affinity

The kinship which impedes those wishing to marry is either of the flesh or of the spirit. Carnal kinship is called either consanguinity or affinity. Consanguinity impedes marriage to the sixth or seventh degree, according to differing methods of calculation. Affinity likewise impedes marriage, and indeed variously according to its many kinds. For in the first kind it impedes just as consanguinity does, namely to the seventh degree; in the second, to the fifth, but persons in the fourth are permitted; and in the third, to the second.

#### The First, Second, and Third Kinds of Affinity

The first kind of affinity consists, for you, in all the blood relations of your wife, and for her in yours. The second kind of affinity consists, for you, in every spouse of the male and female blood relatives of your wife, and similarly every spouse of your male or female blood relatives for her. The third kind, for you and your wife, consists in the spouse of persons related by second affinity, reciprocally. Thus, those who are relatives by first affinity to you and your wife are, among themselves, related by second affinity; finally, those who are related by second affinity to you and your wife are, among themselves, related by third affinity. For every person added through union changes the kind, not the degree; one added by generation changes the degree, but not the kind.

### DISTINCTION XXXIV. On the Degrees of Affinity

You shall calculate the degrees of affinity thus: since you and your wife, according to the divine pronouncement, are “[Col. 1109C] one flesh” and are reckoned as one person (Genesis 2), the degree in which her blood relative stands to her is the same degree in which that person stands to you by affinity, and conversely. Count all affinity in this way. Affinity is not erased in the surviving spouse when one spouse dies, because the Lord’s word remains valid and strong when he said: “The two shall be one flesh” (ibid.).

### DISTINCTION XXXV. On Spiritual Kinship

Spiritual kinship is that which a heavenly sacrament creates among certain persons through ministry—for example, between a godfather and godmother, and their sons and daughters. Through it spiritual proximity also arises between natural children and spiritual children. Therefore, as Pope Nicholas says, marriage cannot take place between the person through whom godparenthood was contracted and the natural children “[Col. 1109D] of the other; but between the others it may, although Paschal appears to prohibit marriage for those born after godparenthood.

#### Can Someone Marry Two Godmothers, One After the Other?

A man may also have two godmothers as wives, one after the other, if godmotherhood and bodily union with the first were never present together—for example, if he did not know the woman whom he married; or if, after he had formerly known her and repudiated her without reconciliation, she became someone’s godmother. Pope Paschal and the Council of Tribur say this. But if these “[Col. 1110A] two things were together, he cannot have both as wives, as Nicholas says.

### DISTINCTION XXXVI. On the Resurrection; What the Trumpet of the Last Judgment Is

Lastly, let us consider the resurrection and the manner of those who rise. The resurrection must be believed by all. For Isaiah says: “The dead shall rise, and those who were in the tombs shall rise” (Isaiah 26). And John: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth,” etc. (John 5).

The resurrection will take place at the sound of a trumpet—that is, a manifest sound—which will have the power of raising the dead (1 Thessalonians 4). Hence the Prophet says: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power” (Psalm 67). This trumpet is the cry of which it is said: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet “[Col. 1110B] him” (Matthew 25). This voice or trumpet is said to be that of the archangel, that is, Christ, which he will utter at midnight. This is not said of an hour of time, but because he will come when he is not expected; or it may be said of a time. For Cassiodorus says:

> [Note: Col. 1109D, On Psalm 118.] At this time the firstborn of Egypt were struck (Exodus 12), when the bridegroom also is to come.

This time is likewise called the day of the Lord, not on account of the character of the time, but because then the hidden things of every person will be made manifest. Hence Daniel says: “The Ancient of Days sat down, and the books”—that is, the consciences of each person—“were opened before him” (Daniel 7).

### DISTINCTION XXXVII. On the Age and Stature of Those Who Rise; How Will the Wicked Rise?

Every human being will rise at Christ’s age, as the Apostle says: “We shall all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4). Augustine says:

> [Note: Col. 1110D, *City of God*, Book XXII, ch. 14.] “Not to the measure of the body or stature, but of age,” because everyone shall receive the measure which he possessed in youth, if he died even as an old person, or which he would have possessed had he died before reaching it.

Among those who rise Christ will, with wonderful swiftness, restore all of which their bodies had consisted. It will make no difference whether hairs return to hairs and nails to nails, or whether whatever of them had perished is transformed into flesh and restored to other parts of the body, with the raiser providing that nothing unseemly occurs there; for nothing will be unseemly there. This is to be understood of the elect. But as for whether the wicked will rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies, what need is there to labor over investigation? Their uncertain form or beauty should not trouble us, since their condemnation will be certain and eternal.

### DISTINCTION XXXVIII. On Aid for the Dead

Meanwhile, before the resurrection occurs, let us consider what benefit comes from services performed in the Church for the dead. There are four classes of the dead. Some are very good, some very evil, some moderately good, and some moderately evil. Therefore, when sacrifices or offerings are made for them, for the very good they are acts of thanksgiving; for the very “[Col. 1111A] evil, even though they provide them with no help, they are nevertheless consolations of some sort to the living. But they benefit the other two classes: the moderately good, by producing remission of punishment for them; the moderately evil, by making their condemnation more tolerable.

### DISTINCTION XXXIX. On the order of those who are to be judged

There will be four classes of those present at the judgment. Some will be judged and will perish: those to whom it is said, “I was hungry and you did not give me food,” etc. (Matt. 25). Others will not be judged and yet will perish, such as those of whom the Lord says: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). Others will be judged and will reign, namely those who will hear: “I was hungry and you gave me food”; others will not be judged [Col. 1111B] and will reign, namely those to whom the Lord says: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

This is to be understood as said not only to the apostles, but to all who, having attained apostolic perfection, have left everything and followed Christ. These will judge both by comparison with the better deed and by judicial authority. Hence the “two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. 149): that is, judgment concerning the good and the wicked will be in their power. But whether the things then thought fit to be spoken will be uttered by voice, or will receive their effect solely through the power of the Judge, has nowhere been openly determined by authority.

### DISTINCTION XL. On the place of judgment and the sentence

The place of judgment, as authority says in its exposition of the prophet Joel, [Col. 1111C] will be in the region of this air, opposite [Col. 1112A] the Mount of Olives (Joel 2), whence he ascended. There the Lord will judge in the glorified form of a servant, appearing to both the good and the wicked.

Hence Augustine:

> When the good and the wicked see him judging in the glorified form of a servant, “the wicked man shall be taken away, lest he see the glory of God”; and then the angels will bear the sign of the cross before him, as he himself says: “Then shall the sign of the Son of Man appear in heaven” (Matt. 24).

[Note: [Col. 1111C] In his exposition of John; *On the Trinity*, book I, chapters 16 and 17, in substance.]

### DISTINCTION XLI. On the differing dwelling-places in heaven and hell

Moreover, the wicked will be tormented by diverse punishments. The devout, however, will differ in the brightness of their knowledge, because “in my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14). Yet the joy of all will be equal, either because each will rejoice in another’s good as though it were his own, or because, in every matter in which [Col. 1112B] one rejoices, all will rejoice. Thus equality is to be referred not to the intensity of their rejoicing, but to the number of things in which they rejoice.

### DISTINCTION XLII. On the vision of the good and the wicked

Finally, it should be known that the saints teach that, until the judgment, the good and the wicked see one another. After the judgment, however, the good will see the wicked, but the wicked will not see the good.

Hence Gregory:

> The unbelievers, placed in the depths before the day of judgment, behold the faithful at rest, whose joys afterward they are unable to contemplate.

[Note: [Col. 1112C] On Luke, chapter 16.]

Isaiah likewise says: “The elect shall go forth and see the corpses of the living who have transgressed against me” (Isa. 66). And the Psalmist: “The righteous man shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 58). May the Lord make us sharers in that joy. Amen.

*End of Bandinus’s fourth book of Sentences.*

## A.D. 1164. HUGH OF AMIENS, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

[Col. 1111]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. XI, col. 43)

[Col. 1111D] If we believe Orderic Vitalis, book XII, p. 889, Hugh was not made Archbishop [Col. 1112D] of Rouen before the year 1130. But it will shortly become clear that he was elected while Pope Honorius II was still alive, which must fall either at the [Col. 1113A] end of 1128, shortly after the death of his predecessor, or at least in 1129.

The learned author of the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. VI, p. 160, conjectures that the celebrated Matthew, bishop of Albano, was his full brother. More correctly, he proves that both were born in the territory of Laon and devoted themselves to letters in the school of Anselm of Laon. Finally, however, he professes himself unable to discover why Hugh is called “of Amiens” in both Orderic and Geoffrey of Vigeois.

Whatever may be the origin of this surname—which some think derived from Hugh’s descent from the counts of Amiens—Hugh first professed the monastic life at Cluny. In 1115 he became prior of Saint Martial at Limoges; then prior of Saint Pancras in England, [Col. 1113B] in the diocese of Chichester; and afterward abbot of the new monastery of Reading. After the death of Geoffrey, Archbishop of Rouen, all votes converged upon him when an election was held. The election was approved both by Henry, king of England, and by the bishop of Salisbury, in whose diocese Reading lay.

But because Hugh was unwilling to acquiesce in the election, the clergy of Rouen wrote to Pope Honorius, asking him to compel Hugh to undertake the archbishopric. We append their letter, drawn from *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 151:

> To the universal lord Pope Honorius, the Church of Rouen offers all obedience in Christ. By common election we have chosen our son Hugh, abbot of Reading, as bishop for us. In this matter we sought and obtained the assent of our lord Henry, king of England. From the bishop of Salisbury, under whose authority he exercised the office of abbot, we sought that he might be given to us free and released, and we received him with freedom.
>
> But because, as he himself disclosed, we learned that we could not have him without the assent of your authority—and because we read this written in your letters addressed to the aforesaid king of England: “Therefore, under the original right, we retain him without any lordship of ours, as a cleric especially belonging to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church”—we request of your highness that he be granted to us. We shall hold him so much dearer as we rejoice that he has been bestowed on us from the seat of your exalted dignity.
>
> With humble supplication we ask that he be granted to us by your grace on such terms that we may rejoice that he remains under the right or power of no one ever, save only under your gracious protection, dearest father and lord.

Released by the pontiff, Hugh was consecrated in 1130, according to the appendix to Robert of Torigni, where the following is read:

> Henry, king of England, was at Bec on the Nativity of Saint Mary, and brought with him Hugh, newly elected Archbishop of Rouen, who had been abbot of Reading. He was consecrated on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, on a Sunday, by Richard of Bayeux with his fellow bishops in the church of Saint Ouen.

In the same year he raised the church of Saint Martin of Aulcay to the rank of an abbey of Aumale.

In the following year Innocent II, acknowledged in France against the pseudo-pontiff Anacletus, came to Rouen in May, apparently to settle peace between the archbishop and the citizens. For Saint Bernard, writing letter 25 to the archbishop himself, indicates that some degree of quarrelling then existed between them. While the pope remained at Rouen, Hugh confirmed under his seal King Henry’s grant to Cluny of one hundred marks of silver from the London and Lincoln tolls for the support of the brethren.

In the same year Innocent II held a council at Reims in October. Hugh went there also, bearing letters from Henry, king of England, as tokens of filial obedience. Hugh likewise attended the consecration by the supreme pontiff of the great hospice of Saint John at Brussels. In that same year, on 6 October, the pope, in Hugh’s favour, confirmed the rights of the Church of Rouen; and on 26 July 1132 he wrote to Hugh that he should restrain the various offences against ecclesiastical discipline in his diocese.

About this time, when the king of England lodged complaints with the same pope that Hugh disturbed the duchy of Normandy by receiving professions and obedience from certain abbots, the pontiff wrote letter 16 to Hugh, directing him to yield something of ecclesiastical right to the king for the sake of peace. The entire letter may be read in *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 457, or in Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 133. [Note: [Col. 1113D] Or in *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, col. 669.]

[Col. 1114C] In 1133 the archbishop gave, or confirmed, to the monks of Tiron the priory of Bascheville, whose church the monks of Le Pin had relinquished to them. For this matter see the charter in Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 147. In the same year he attended the Council of Jort. When Peter the Venerable, book III, letter 17, requested Innocent II to confirm its acts, he added the following concerning Hugh:

> Moreover, there is no need to inform you how venerable in life, how faithful to your apostolate, the lord Archbishop of Rouen has been, or how he has laboured for your peace; for we believe that you are fully informed of all these things. We therefore beseech your fatherhood to provide for his peace and justice in such a manner that he may render [Col. 1114D] to God what is God’s and to Caesar what is Caesar’s; so that, if it be possible and divine judgment does not disapprove, he may neither displease the royal majesty nor offend it.

From these words it is clearly understood that certain disputes still existed at that time between Hugh and the citizens of Rouen, or even with the king of England himself.

We said in vol. I, col. 713, that in 1134 he solemnly absolved Guigues the Dauphin. In the same year, as legate of the Apostolic See, he attended the council held at Montpellier, and wrote Pope Innocent a letter concerning matters transacted in that assembly; it is found in vol. VI of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 666.

[Col. 1115A] In 1135 he dedicated the church of All Saints at Bellencumbre. In the same year, after a long delay, he consecrated Richard, son of the earl of Gloucester, bishop of Bayeux. [Note: [Col. 1115D] *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. III, p. 1012.] He also wished to attend the council held at Pisa. When the synod ended, he remained in Italy to assist the affairs of the Apostolic See. Thus Orderic, book XIII, p. 900, says:

> Occupied with the concerns of apostolic service, he for some time set aside the concerns of his own bishopric; remaining long in the regions of Italy, he diligently dispatched the affairs of others, which greatly displeased the king.

But when Henry I, king of England, died later that year, this hostility was stilled, while Henry devoutly and humbly begged forgiveness of the archbishop and received absolution. One should read, in William of Malmesbury, *Historia novella*, book I, fol. 100, or in Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 135, the letter which Hugh himself wrote to Pope Innocent regarding the Christian death of that king, to whom he had remained close until his final breath. [Note: [Col. 1116D] *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, col. 670.]

In 1136 he subscribed a charter of Stephen, king of England, for the foundation of the monastery of regular canons at Dover; and he received from the same king a charter concerning those who violated God’s Truce. By that charter, published by Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 145, all spiritual and synodal rights were confirmed to all the bishops of Normandy. But in the same year, in September, the city of Rouen was suddenly set ablaze, according to Orderic, book XIII, p. 905.

[Col. 1115C] In the following year Hugh settled a lawsuit between the canons of Saint-Évroult and the monks of Mortain concerning the burial rights of townspeople. He also restrained a serious conflict between the count of Boulogne and Robert, earl of Gloucester, as Malmesbury testifies, fol. 102. He bestowed the blessing of office upon Theobald, abbot of Bec. In the same year, 1137, he assigned mortmain (*mortuum mare*) to the Cistercian Order. In 1138 he confirmed the foundation of Ardenne in the diocese of Bayeux. In the same year he bestowed certain gifts upon Serlo, abbot of Saint-Lucien, and upon Joscelin, abbot of Augé.

In 1139, when another dispute arose between the bishops of England and the king himself, Archbishop Hugh pressed the entire affair at Rouen with fuller arguments and speeches; “as far as he could by eloquence, he was the king’s greatest defender,” says the same Malmesbury, fol. 103, against Henry, bishop of Winchester, legate of the Apostolic See and the king’s own brother. Certainly Hugh was most devoted to the king’s party. When the king’s brother Theobald had been routed, defeated, and captured at Lincoln in 1141, Hugh approached him with the Normans, offering him the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy, according to Orderic, book XIII, p. 923.

In that same year he consecrated Arnulf bishop of Lisieux; but in 1139 he had likewise consecrated Rotrou bishop of Évreux, and in 1140, at the invitation of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis in France, [Col. 1116A] he dedicated the lower portion of the basilica of Saint-Denis together with the bishops of Beauvais, Meaux, and Senlis, as we observed in Suger (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI). In 1141, with his consent, the Knights Templar were established at Le Petit-Quevilly; and he renewed the privilege of the monastery of Bec which William, formerly archbishop, had granted to Abbot Anselm.

In 1143 he confirmed for regular canons the church of Blessed Mary of Corneville. In the same year he confirmed the foundation of Bourg-Achard, made in the previous year, under the right and authority of the priors of Falaise. But afterward, when the canons of Falaise adopted the institute of Prémontré, the regular canons of Bourg-Achard began to be independent; and finally, in September 1685, they adopted the reform called that of Friardel. In that monastery, consecrated under the name of Saint Laud, the general superiors of this reform customarily established their seat.

In 1144 Hugh granted Létard, abbot of Bec, exemption from toll, and attended the dedication of the entire basilica of Saint-Denis, finally completed by Abbot Suger. He consecrated the altar of Blessed Mary. In 1145 he consecrated the church of the abbey of Mont-Calv, among the Vexin, handed over by the king of France to Abbot Suger and converted into a priory of twelve monks, as we have said in Suger. At about the same time he approved the foundation both of the Fontevrist nuns at Clairruisseau near Gournay-en-Bray [Col. 1116C] and of the Prémonstratensian nuns at Beaumont; the latter became extinct in 1185.

In 1146 he confirmed churches and other possessions to the monks of Marmoutier. On 3 September 1147 he dedicated the church of Corneville. In the same year he reconciled the monks of Caen and the canons of Bayeux. He attended the Council of Reims in 1148. In 1149 he blessed Roger as abbot of Bec. In 1150 he was chosen arbiter of peace between Philip, bishop of Bayeux, and the monks of Clairvaux. About this time he released sixteen parishes of the monastery of Fécamp, situated in the diocese of Rouen, from every episcopal jurisdiction.

In 1151 he attended the Council of Beaugency, where the divorce of King Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine was considered. In 1152 he confirmed tithes from several churches to the monks of Verley. On 3 May 1153, he gathered in the church of Saint Martin at Pontoise with the bishops of Paris and Senlis for the elevation of the relics of Saint Gautier, formerly the most devout abbot of that place. In the same year he removed the long-desolated church of Saint-Sidonius from the control of the lord of the castle and entrusted it to Roger, abbot of Fontenelle, to order and govern.

At about the same time, a serious dispute was active between the monks of Fontenelle and Saint-Étienne of Caen. John, bishop of Tusculum and legate of the Apostolic See, wrote to Hugh that, together with Rotrou, bishop of Évreux, and Gerard, bishop of Sées, he should put an end [Col. 1117A] to this dissension. That Hugh obeyed these commands is sufficiently clear from the letters by which he confirmed the agreement made between the two monasteries.

On 19 December 1154, he was present at the coronation of Henry II, king of England, at Westminster, performed by Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury. At about the same time Adrian IV, in a bull addressed to Hugh, confirmed the rights and estates of the Church of Rouen. Hugh celebrated the translation of Saint William Firmatus at Mortain in 1156, during the octave of Pentecost. In the same year he inspected the Lord’s tunic at the monastery of Argenteuil; on this matter he drew up an instrument, which may be read in Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 149. He also confirmed to the abbey of Saint-Denis in France all churches which it possessed [Col. 1117B] in his diocese. Two years earlier he had confirmed to the same monastery the market held every Friday at Neufchâtel near Saint-Clair.

In the same year, 1156, Henry II founded a priory of the Grandmontine Order in the forest of Rouvray, which he shortly afterward moved to his game-park near Rouen, on the left bank of the Seine. Hence the place acquired the name Blessed Mary of the Vivarium. But the prioral revenues of this house were assigned, under Henry IV, king of France and Navarre, to the college of the fathers of the Society of Jesus at Rouen.

In 1157 the same archbishop confirmed to the monks of Saint-Denis in France the church of Cergy, in which they established a priory subject, together with the church itself, to their complete jurisdiction. In 1158 he confirmed to the monks of Saint-Ouen the church of Ros, situated in the diocese of Bayeux and free from episcopal jurisdiction; and in 1159 he confirmed to the monks of Blessed Mary of the Valley whatever they possessed in his diocese.

About this time, at the command of H., king of England, he granted Robert, abbot of Saint Michael, permission to celebrate divine offices in the churches of Pontorson. In July 1160, or, according to others, 1161, with the consent of the king of England, a provincial council assembled at Neufmarché in Normandy. There all assented to Pope Alexander III and rejected Victor, the antipope. At about the same time the Knights Templar were established at Rouen on the site where the town hall was afterward built.

[Col. 1117D] In 1162 Hugh confirmed all possessions of the abbey of Le Vœu and the benefices of the priory of Mont-aux-Malades near Rouen. At about the same [Col. 1118A] time, he wrote to the king of England concerning the education of his son Henry, that he might learn both morals and letters from the best teachers, as may be inferred from Peter of Blois, letter 67. In 1163 he gave the church of Sorenc to Gerard, abbot of Flavigny. On 9 May 1164 he confirmed to Hugh, abbot of Saint Vincent of Senlis, the churches situated in his diocese.

He left many monuments of his learning. One is the *Treatise on Theological Matters*, dedicated to Matthew of Albano, which may be read in Martène, vol. V of the *Anecdota*. Another is the *Treatise on Heresies Arising in Armorican Territory*, dedicated to Alberic, bishop of Ostia, and printed at the end of the works of Guibert of Nogent. He also wrote three books *On Memory*, and a *Treatise on the Catholic Faith and the Lord’s Prayer*, published in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX; and a letter to Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, concerning persons who, in place of beasts of burden, drew carts for the building of churches. Written in 1145, it may be read in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. VI, p. 392.

He also wrote several letters to King Louis VII, published by Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, pp. 139 and 142; likewise others to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis in France, published in the *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 417 ff.; and letters to Rainard, abbot of Cîteaux, and to the count of Toulouse, which may be read in the same Pommeraye, ibid., pp. 140 ff. Finally, two letters in which he calls himself legate of the Apostolic [Col. 1118C] See occur in the appendix and in the *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 380. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, wrote to him in letter 15, published by Pommeraye, *Councils of Rouen*, p. 138; and Peter the Venerable wrote to him in letter 4 of book I and letter 33 of book VI.

This most deserving bishop died on 11 November 1164, according to his epitaph, which we shall not hesitate to transcribe after the Sammarthani:

> Among bishops, worthy of special honour,  
> Hugh here lays down the burden of our flesh.  
> His limbs, entrusted to a brief tomb, are enclosed;  
> yet neither hemisphere encloses the man’s deeds.  
> Whatever grace had bestowed upon the man,  
> he dispensed and shared among all.  
> Thus abundance made rich fruits of virtues,  
> and made him both more than man and a man made great.
>
> [Col. 1118D] At last, after the happy course of a renowned life,  
> a tearful hour carried off the deserving old man.  
> O Martin, destined to be your equal and companion,  
> by dying he received the same day as you.

[Col. 1117]

## SECOND NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, vol. XII, p. 647)

According to La Morlière, Hugh [Note: [Col. 1117] *Antiquities of Amiens*, p. 29.] was surnamed “of Amiens” because he belonged to the house of Boves, which descended from the counts of Amiens, if not in the direct line, at least through marriage. The seals of this prelate which remain to us appear to support that opinion, for on their counterseal is seen an ox grazing—arms corresponding to the name of the Boves family. [Note: [Col. 1119] *Defence of the Rights of the Abbey of Saint-Ouen*, p. 275; Pommeraye, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Ouen*, p. 425.]

What cannot be doubted is that he was of illustrious birth: *clarus avis*, “distinguished by his forefathers,” [Note:

> To Geoffrey [Col. 1119] succeeded Hugh, beloved of the people and a terror to the powerful,  
> distinguished by his ancestors, distinguished by his studies, a restorer of the needy.
>
> (In Alberic, under the year 1183.)
>
> Peter the Venerable (*On Miracles*, book II, chapter 4), speaking of Hugh of Amiens, says:
>
> “He was born of a family not obscure in the flesh, from the province of Reims, with both parents distinguished, as has been said, by nobility and rich in worldly resources. [Col. 1120] In childhood he was committed to learning; and, when he had grown up, he obtained clerical office in the Church of Laon.”]

says an ancient versifier speaking of him. His education matched the nobility of his birth. He studied at Laon in the school of the celebrated brothers Anselm and Ralph, where Matthew, his kinsman, was his companion. Matthew, after being a monk of Cluny and prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, became cardinal, bishop of Albano, and legate of the Holy See. Like Matthew, and perhaps at the same time, Hugh embraced religious life at Cluny.

A few years after his reception, Abbot Pons appointed him prior of Saint-Martial of Limoges in 1113. Hugh did not remain there long. When the priory of Saint Pancras of Lewes in England became vacant, he was selected to fill it. This new selection showed the great progress he had made in religious life. For a written agreement existed between the abbot of Cluny and William de Warenne, founder of Saint Pancras, that its superior should be the wisest and holiest religious of the order, with the exception of the grand prior of Cluny and the prior of La Charité.

Hugh in this office wholly fulfilled the expectations of those who had placed him there. His merit reached the court of King Henry I of England. When that monarch founded the abbey of Reading in the diocese of Salisbury in 1125, he judged no one more capable of being placed at the head of that house. Hugh established such good order there that in a very short time it surpassed the most celebrated monasteries of England.

After four years Providence drew him from this office in order to raise him to a ministry much more important, and one which he probably did not expect. Arriving at Rouen toward the end of 1129, he found the metropolitan see vacant since 28 November of the preceding year, the date of Archbishop Geoffrey’s death. The fine qualities which he displayed during his stay led the clergy of that city to elect him as their pastor. When the decree of election was taken to the king of England and the bishop of Salisbury, both approved it with praise. But the consent of the Holy See was further required, since Hugh, as a professed monk of Cluny, was immediately subject to it.

We have the letter which the Church of Rouen wrote to Pope Honorius on this matter, but his response is lacking. It is unknown whether it was Honorius, who died in February 1130, or his successor Innocent II who made the response. What is certain is that Rome granted the petition. Thus wholly free, the elect was brought to Rouen by the king of England and solemnly consecrated in his presence on 14 September 1130.

Saint Bernard, Hugh’s friend, wrote to him shortly afterward, not to congratulate him, but to exhort him to show much patience and discretion in his administration—virtues which, according to the saint, were more necessary for an archbishop of Rouen than for any other prelate. This was because the abbot of Clairvaux had, on what basis is unknown, a most unfavourable opinion of the people of Rouen:

> “Be patient, because you are among wicked people; be peaceable, because you are set over wicked people. Let charity possess zeal; but let severity apply moderation according to the occasion.”  
> *Esto patiens, quia es cum malis; esto pacificus, quia praees malis. Habeat charitas zelum; sed adhibeat pro tempore modum severitas.*

The virtues through which he had distinguished himself in the cloister followed him into the episcopate. On taking his see, in imitation of Saint Anselm, he chose three of his brethren—Elias, Ansgar, and Victor—as his chaplains, so that he might observe monastic practices with them. [Note: [Col. 1120] *History of the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés*, preliminary documents no. 53, p. XL.] These exercises did not diminish his pastoral functions. He was assiduous in distributing to his people the bread of the divine word. He regularly made visitations, not only of his diocese but also of his province, according to the immemorial custom of his predecessors, a custom whose traces are still observable [Note: [Col. 1120] The King’s Library preserves, under no. 1246, a manuscript containing the acts performed by Odo Rigault, Archbishop of Rouen, who died in 1275, not only in his diocese but throughout the whole extent of his province.] in later centuries.

The detailed account of his writings will show the care he took to keep from Normandy the errors which infected neighbouring regions, and the zeal with which he laboured to make religion flourish there in all its purity.

The schism of Innocent and Anacletus closely followed the election of our prelate. Having declared for the former along with the whole French nation, he had the honour of rendering him homage at Rouen, where the pontiff arrived in May 1131. Hugh joined him at the Council of Reims held toward the end of the same year, and brought letters from the king of England, by which that prince formally recognized him as the legitimate pope. They were read in the assembly with applause, and the eloquence of the man who brought them gave them new weight.

Innocent did not repay unjustly the zeal shown by the Archbishop of Rouen for his interests. When Hugh complained at the council that the abbots of his province refused him the oath, or profession, of obedience, the Holy Father immediately ordered a regulation to be made compelling them to render it. This was the first enactment on a matter long disputed between the metropolitans and bishops of Normandy on one side, and the abbots of that province on the other.

It would take too long to recount here the reasons upon which the latter relied in resisting the yoke which it was sought to impose on them. They may be seen fully set out in Father Mabillon’s preface (part I, no. 31) to the fourth century of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*. On his return, Hugh undertook to enforce the council’s decree and exerted all his authority to accomplish it. But he met with more obstacles than he had expected. Several abbots persisted in their refusal, yielding neither to the archbishop’s threats nor to those of the pope.

The king of England did not view this dispute with indifference. He took the abbots’ side and wrote to the pope to complain of the metropolitan’s conduct toward them, as an innovation equally [Col. 1121] harmful to the peace of the province and to the rights of his crown. This was indeed how he understood the oath Hugh demanded from the abbots. On the one hand, the ancient customs of the duchy offered him nothing similar; on the other, he regarded this oath of unlimited obedience as an act assigning to the metropolitan not merely spiritual jurisdiction but also the temporal right of feudal overlordship.

On the basis of this view, which he shared with the entire Norman nobility, the monarch asked the pope in his letter to restrain the Archbishop of Rouen’s undertaking. To induce him to do so, he represented all that he had already done in the pope’s service and all that he was prepared to do. These remonstrances had their effect. By the pope’s advice, Hugh deferred pressing his claims until another time and remained quiet during the rest of Henry I’s reign.

In 1134 he went to the Council of Pisa, [Note: [Col. 1121] Orderic Vitalis, book XIII, p. 900.] where he was honourably received and placed in the foremost ranks. The various questions discussed there gave him an opportunity to demonstrate both his learning and his attachment to the unity of the Church. After the close of the assembly, the pope retained him to employ him in several affairs of the Holy See with the title of legate.

Yet the length of his absence provoked murmuring in Normandy, and the king himself was offended, finding it very strange, he said, that the archbishop should prefer the pope’s interests to the care of his province. The prelate’s return in the following year caused fresh displeasure to the monarch because he refused to consecrate Richard, the natural son of the earl of Gloucester, whom Henry had appointed to the bishopric of Bayeux. The canons supported the metropolitan; but the prince, absolute as he was, recognized few laws that were not bound to bend to his will. The pope forestalled the unhappy consequences of this affair by granting Richard a dispensation, through which no difficulty remained concerning his consecration.

Amid his disputes with our prelate, the king nevertheless always retained a strong feeling of esteem and respect for him. These sentiments were strikingly displayed in Henry’s final illness. Seeing his end approach, he summoned the Archbishop of Rouen to console him and died in his arms on 1 December 1135.

After the death of Henry I, his dominions were disputed between his daughter Matilda, wife of Geoffrey, count of Anjou, and his nephew Stephen of Blois. Hugh attached himself to the latter, who was victorious and, during his reign, exercised considerable influence in governmental affairs. The abbots of Normandy soon felt the weight of his new influence. Hugh reopened the affair of professions of obedience and compelled Theobald, abbot of Bec and later Archbishop of Canterbury, to swear obedience to him, at least orally.

Hugh’s devotion to King Stephen’s interests was displayed on one of those delicate occasions which are, as it were, the touchstone of genuine attachment. For political reasons, the prince had taken possession of castles built by several English bishops on lands belonging to their churches. Those concerned raised loud protests and wished to obtain redress for what they regarded as a sacrilegious usurpation. The bishop of Winchester, the king’s brother, sacrificing the claims of blood to the pretensions of his order, joined their resentment. As papal legate, he assembled a council and had the boldness to summon the monarch before it.

Alberic de Vere, a learned man, appeared in Stephen’s name and vigorously pleaded the cause of the man he represented. In the meantime the Archbishop of Rouen arrived. He took his seat in the council; and, having had the matter under discussion explained to him, he asked the prelates whether they could prove that, in their capacity as bishops, they ought to possess fortresses.

> “But even if,” he added, “you could show that you may possess them without violating the canons, by what right can you refuse to place them in the king’s hands at a time when the kingdom is threatened with invasion? Is it not the king’s duty to watch over the security of the state? And can subjects deny him entry to their strongholds without making themselves guilty of rebellion?”  
> [Note: [Col. 1121] William of Malmesbury, ibid., fol. 102v.]

This speech halted the excommunication which was on the point of being pronounced against the king.

Hugh of Amiens had played only the politician in that assembly; he played the controversialist at the council held at Paris in 1147 [Note: [Col. 1121] Otto of Freising, *On the Deeds of Frederick*.] against the errors of Gilbert de la Porrée. He entered the contest with that subtle theologian and undertook to prove to him that one should not say that there are “three singular things,” *tria singularia*, in the Trinity—though in this he was not entirely right.

Normandy changed masters in 1150 when Stephen was compelled to cede it to Henry, Matilda’s son, who succeeded him four years later in the kingdom of England.

This revolution produced no change in the position of our prelate. Henry forgot that he had been the most zealous supporter of his rival, and continued to show him the same favour with which Stephen had honoured him. Upon his accession in Normandy, he addressed to him letters patent confirming the privileges of the inhabitants of Rouen. The king of France, Louis the Younger, also held his merit in high esteem, as is shown by the honour he did him in summoning him to the assembly held at Beaugency in 1152, to deliberate upon the annulment of his marriage with Eleanor. In the detailed account of Hugh’s writings we shall see further proofs of the correspondence between him and this monarch.

History passes very lightly over the last years of our prelate’s life. Beloved by his people, esteemed by all persons of merit, and honoured by the great, this worthy shepherd brought his career to a holy end on 11 November 1164. His epitaph, composed by Arnulf of Lisieux and reported in both the old and the new *Gallia Christiana*, magnificent though it appears, is merely the faithful expression of the lofty impression he left behind upon his death.

Hugh of Amiens left several works from his pen, scattered through various collections.

1. The earliest in date was published by Dom Martène in the fifth volume of his *Anecdotes* (vol. V, p. 895). It consists of seven books of *Dialogues*, treating various theological questions. Hugh was still abbot of Reading when he undertook this work. Its idea was suggested to him by his kinsman Matthew, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, to whom it was dedicated, through the various questions which Matthew proposed to him. Hugh completed the first six books in his monastery; later, after he had been raised to the metropolitan see of Rouen, he revised them and added a seventh. The dedicatory epistle likewise underwent some changes in this revision. For whereas Matthew was originally described only as prior of Saint-Martin, he was later called bishop of Albano, having meanwhile been promoted to that dignity.

[Col. 1123] These *Dialogues* proceed solely through questions and answers, without any names for the speakers.

The subject of the first book is the supreme good—that is, God and His absolute or relative attributes.

The second treats of creatures. The questions debated in it are: (1) Why does God, whose charity extends without distinction to all creatures, prefer certain ones, preserving them from evil, adorning them with virtues, and finally making them eternally happy in the life to come, while allowing the others to wallow in crime and reserving them to become one day the dreadful objects of His eternal vengeance? (2) How is it true that one who sins in one point is guilty of violating the entire law? (3) What are the seven gifts of grace?

The third book concerns free will. The author defines this faculty of the soul as follows: “Free will is a certain capacity of rational intelligence, possessing the ability to carry out what it judges” (*Liberum arbitrium est quaedam facultas intelligentiae rationalis, habens possibilitatem quod judicat exsequendi*). [Note: [Col. 1123] “Free will is a certain capacity of rational intelligence, possessing the ability to carry out what it judges.”] “But this judgment,” he adds, “is truly free only when the creature does what it soundly believes ought to be done. Now it does this when, loving its Creator, it knows His will through practice, preferring it to its own. But if it refuses to obey that will which it judges ought alone to be followed, it contradicts its own judgment and, by its transgression, justly loses the freedom to judge rightly. Once deprived of that freedom, it rightly remains given over to vice. Thus, losing its free will, it falls captive into the bonds of sin; for it cannot in any way restore to itself the liberty which it lost through its own fault, since He who gave it is alone able to restore it. Let those who insist with all their strength that free will was given by God equally for good and evil consider what they have to say to this. What is certain is that it is lost by sinning and can be recovered only through grace.” Hugh then proves that evil is merely a privation of good and that God is consequently not its author. His questioner raises several objections to this, which he resolves very clearly.

The fourth book concerns the fall of the angel and that of humankind. Hugh proves that pride was the origin of both.

The remedies for sin—that is, the sacraments—are the subject matter of the fifth book. The author speaks only of baptism and the Eucharist, but he treats them accurately.

The sixth book deals with the state of monks and eternal blessedness. The author maintains that monastic profession has the same efficacy as baptism; that both equally efface sins and confer the grace of regeneration. [Note: [Col. 1123] “For monastic consecration and baptismal regeneration bring about the same thing. For when he devoutly puts on this [monastic garment] through the hand of his spiritual father according to ecclesiastical custom, he is immediately released from sins and receives the grace which he had in baptism.”] From this Hugh proceeds to the other prerogatives of monks and applies himself to proving that they are clerics by status, that they are capable of receiving tithes, and, finally, that monastic profession is capable of all the advantages and all the functions of the clergy.

These six books, composed, as has been said, at Reading Abbey, were quickly circulated publicly and well received. Everything in them was approved except one passage in which the author maintained that deposed or excommunicated priests did not truly consecrate if they presumed in that state to ascend to the altar. “Therefore, he whom Christ, through the Church, has deprived of office by deposition or excommunication, if he presumes to minister in the sacraments of the altar—being now no minister—does nothing” (*Quem itaque Christus per Ecclesiam deponendo vel excommunicando destituit ab officio, si in sacramentis altaris ministrare praesumit, qui jam minister non est, nihil facit*). Matthew, his kinsman, having informed him from Saint-Martin-des-Champs of the criticism made of this proposition, Hugh replied in its defence. This response follows the sixth book. It consists in distinguishing title from exercise, priestly dignity from the functions of that dignity. The Church, he says, does not by deposition or excommunication remove the sacrament of order from the priest; it merely deprives him of the right to exercise it. It removes the office of priesthood without touching the character. He attempts to establish this by the words of the Gospel, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven,” etc., and by other texts no more conclusive. [Note: [Col. 1124] Gerohus says that he obtained it from the archives of the Roman Church: “The following letter, which we received from the archives of the Roman curia.”] This Letter is also reported in the work of Gerohus, provost of Reichersberg, who died in 1169, *Against Two Heresies*, among Dom Pez’s *Anecdotes* (vol. I, part II, pp. 297–300).

The seventh book is devoted to an exposition of the mystery of the Trinity, traces of which Hugh, following the taste of the age, claims to find in created things.

2. Three books on the Church and its ministers, against certain heresies then prevailing in Brittany. [Note: [Col. 1124] *Addenda to the Works of Guibert*, pp. 69, 715.] This work is dedicated to Cardinal Alberic. The author tells him that he remembers how, while they were together at Nantes for a new translation of the bodies of Saints Donatian and Rogatian, they observed a comet plunging into the sea: “A sure omen, according to your observation,” he adds, “of the approaching ruin of the heresy then prevailing in Armorica.” “Then,” Hugh continues, “the heretical people could not withstand the force of your preaching. Fear so seized even their leader that he did not dare appear. You therefore judged it appropriate that I should write something concerning these emerging heresies; and I now do so in obedience to you.”

The first of these three books is divided into fourteen chapters. The first ten explain the mysteries of the Trinity and the Incarnation; the unity, holiness, and authority of the Church; the necessity of baptism for all people; the excellence of the Eucharist; and the obligation of every adult believer to partake of this ineffable sacrament. In the following chapters certain objections of the heretics to infant baptism are refuted. They cited this Gospel passage: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). But, they said, children do not believe; therefore baptism is of no use to them. Hugh replies that this passage concerns only adults and those who have the use of reason. Nevertheless, he adds, baptism is necessary not only for them but for all people generally, according to these other Gospel words: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). “This,” he continues, “is a law that exempts no one, not even a child one day old. Let us therefore say that from children grace is required, not works: the grace of sanctification which comes from baptism, not meritorious works performed through the choice of the will. This grace is conferred upon them without their perceiving it. For just as they are unaware of the sin which they derive originally from our first father, so in Jesus Christ they receive through the sacraments a grace which they do not know. And just as children are not excused from original sin because they do not know it, so neither are they excluded from grace because they do not perceive it.” In answering the other objections of these heretics, our author says that the faith of the Church supplies the faith lacking in them, so that it becomes, as it were, their own faith.

The seven ecclesiastical orders are the subject of the second book. The author explains the nature and functions of each. Priests and deacons, he says, when canonically promoted, certainly possess the Holy Spirit, with whose help they live holy lives and worthily fulfill their ministry; but they cannot give by the laying on of hands the Holy Spirit they have received. This is a privilege reserved to the chief pastors. The bishop, he says later, is the foundation of the Church because through him the Church possesses the Holy Spirit. His functions are to make holy chrism; to bless the oil of catechumens and the oil of the sick; to consecrate basilicas and altars, chalices and corporals, ecclesiastical officers and their vestments, as well as all the vessels of the Church; to confirm the baptized; and to anoint emperors and kings. Concerning deacons, Hugh says that although they do not consecrate the body and blood of Jesus Christ, they receive these gifts from the hand of the consecrator in order to distribute them to the people.

In the third book our author pursues the other errors of the Bretons. Concerning the resurrection, one of their arguments ran as follows: Human bodies are often torn apart, dismembered, eaten by birds, devoured by beasts, or reduced to dust and carried away by the winds. It is impossible for parts thus dispersed or transformed into other substances to be reunited and to resume their former shape. Therefore the bodies to which they originally belonged cannot rise again. To this, Hugh says, we reply that, if the resurrection of bodies were the work of a human being or of any other creature, this objection might perplex us. But we believe and confess that it is the hand of the Almighty which gathers all these things, contains them all, and loses none of them. For however dispersed the parts of a human body may be, God contains and knows them all; and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, He can restore them to their first condition.

These heretics also seemed to make little account of marriage and not to reckon it among the sacraments. Hugh undertakes to prove to them the holiness and indissolubility of the marriage bond, after which he reproaches them for taking about with them women who were neither their wives nor their relatives, under the pretext of imitating the apostles but in reality to gratify their passions.

The vow of continence made by ecclesiastics and monks was likewise an object of derision for these heretics. Hugh justifies this vow by the authority of Saint Paul, who, following Jesus Christ, recommends continence as a state more perfect than marriage. Now, he says, it cannot be denied that one may vow what is most excellent in religion.

Finally, they asked why the Church had been instituted and what use it could be. Hugh replies that it was established to gather all believers together, instruct them, communicate to them the graces of the Holy Spirit through the channel of the sacraments, nourish them with heavenly bread, and dispose them, through the practice of the divine commandments, to enjoy eternal blessedness after this life.

Such, in substance, is the content of these three books, published by Dom d’Achéry after the Works of Guibert of Nogent. The heretics attacked in them appear to have been a branch of the Henricians or Petrobrusians, for they held nearly the same doctrines. But who was the heresiarch who brought these doctrines into Armorica? Hugh does not tell us, nor can we discover it elsewhere. [Note: [Col. 1125] Dom Mabillon (*Annals*, vol. VI, p. 421) thinks there can be no doubt that it was the famous Eon of the Star. Without seeking absolutely to reject this opinion, several reasons prevent us from accepting it: (1) none of the ancient writers attributes to this fanatic the errors which the archbishop of Rouen undertakes to refute; (2) ignorant and extravagant, as history portrays him, Eon scarcely appears capable of devising the subtle objections and arguments which the prelate puts into the mouths of his opponents; (3) Hugh says nothing of Eon’s remarkable madness, adopted by his disciples—the madness which led him to believe himself the Son of God through a crude play on his name and the word *eum* used in the conclusion of exorcisms, *per eum qui venturus est*, “through Him who is to come,” etc. [Col. 1126] It is true, however, that Robert of Mont reports that Eon appeared before the legate Alberic and did not fear to defy him during the mission which that prelate undertook in Brittany. Yet this very fact seems to prove that he was not the leader of the heretics whom Alberic was going to combat, since Hugh attests in the prologue to his work that this leader did not dare show himself. Be that as it may, we leave anyone free either to follow Dom Mabillon’s opinion or, with us, to regard it as doubtful.]

3. Three books *In Praise of Memory* (*in laudem Memoriae*), dedicated to a certain Philip, whom the author does not otherwise identify. It is a theological work treating God, the Trinity, the Incarnation, sin, its origin, its consequences, and the remedy supplied for it by the mercy of the Redeemer. The editor of these three books was Dom Martène, who published them in the ninth volume of his great collection.

4. An exposition of the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. It follows the preceding work in the collection just mentioned. Hugh dedicated it to Giles, his archdeacon, who later became bishop of Évreux.

5. A treatise on the work of the six days. As we have it, it is a fragment of a complete commentary on Genesis, divided into three books. Dom Martène, who published this fragment in the fifth volume of his *Anecdotes* (pp. 1002–1008), greatly regretted, when publishing it, that he did not then possess the whole work, as he had seen it among the manuscripts of Clairvaux. The dedicatory epistle is addressed to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, whom the author, in his capacity as metropolitan, calls his dear son. Hugh declares in this dedication that in his explanations [Col. 1127] of the sacred text he will adhere more closely to the literal and historical sense than to the allegorical and moral sense. Nevertheless, it can be seen that his natural inclination frequently carries him in the latter direction.

6. The *Life of Saint Adjutor, or Ajoutre*, monk of Tiron (Dom Martène, *Anecdotes*, vol. V, pp. 1012–1017). This saint, born at Vernon to noble parents, initially followed his father’s profession, that of arms. Having taken part in the First Crusade, he distinguished himself by bravery animated by Christian spirit and supported by the visible protection of heaven. Among his exploits the author recounts this one. One day, while leading a troop of two hundred men in the territory of Antioch, he fell into an ambush of fifteen hundred Saracens. Seeing that his men were unable to face this multitude, he invoked Saint Mary Magdalene and promised that, if she granted him victory, he would give Tiron Abbey his land of Mont, together with a chapel which he would cause to be built there. Then, full of confidence, he threw himself with his troop upon the enemy, killed a thousand, and put the rest to flight. This, says the historian, is a fact which we have from the illustrious knights Heliodorus of Blarru, Eudes of Porc-Mort, John of Bréhéval, Anselm of Chantemerle, Guy of Chaumont, Peter of Courtenay, Richard of Harcourt, Henry of Préaux, and others who were present at the battle. Ajoutre delayed fulfilling his vow because he did not think the service of the Holy Land permitted him to return so quickly to his native country. It happened that he was taken prisoner by the enemy. In his prison he again invoked Saint Mary Magdalene and also appealed to Saint Bernard of Tiron, who had been dead for some years. Both appeared to him in the night, broke his chains, and set him free. He immediately took the road to France and went to become a monk at Tiron. There he lived in the greatest fervour and worked several miracles during his lifetime, some of which had his historian as witness. It was our prelate who received his last breath on 29 April 1132. This *Life* is also found in the fifth volume of Dom Martène’s *Anecdotes*.

Besides the letters by our author of which we have already given an account, the following are still preserved:

1. Three letters to King Louis the Younger, published in the fourth volume of Duchesne (pp. 638–639). The first two contain nothing very interesting. The third is against the monks of Cluny, who wished to seize control of the election of the abbot of Saint-Martin of Pontoise. They claimed that this house belonged to their order because Saint Walter, its founder, had lived for some time at Cluny, and because the site on which it was built had been given by the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Hugh defends this abbey and begs the king to maintain it in possession of its right to be subject only to the archbishop of Rouen.

2. Three letters to Suger. The first, printed in the aforesaid volume of Duchesne (p. 527), and the other two in the first volume of Dom Martène’s *Anecdotes* (pp. 417–518), concern private matters.

3. A letter to Pope Innocent II, reported by William of Malmesbury [Note: [Col. 1127] Book I of the *New History*, fol. 100v. It is also found in the ninth volume of Dom Martène’s great [Col. 1128] collection, p. 1236.] and translated by Dom Pommeraye in his *History of the Archbishops of Rouen*. It contains the account of the death of King Henry I, at which, as has been said, our prelate was present.

4. A letter to Thierry, bishop of Amiens, placed in the supplement to the Works of Guibert of Nogent. It is too brief and at the same time too important for us not to reproduce it in full. Here it is, according to the translation supplied by Dom Pommeraye. We omit the beginning.

> “When the people of Chartres began to lead carts to assist in building their church, our Lord rewarded their humble zeal with miracles. The report of these, spreading everywhere, stirred the Normans to imitate the piety of their neighbours. Our diocesan people, having received our blessing, therefore went as far as Chartres and there presented their vows and offerings. Afterwards, several people from our diocese and from other districts of our province did the same, each for the principal church of his own locality. But they admit no one to their company unless he has first confessed and submitted to penance, renounced every animosity and every desire for vengeance, and been truly reconciled with his enemies. This done, the associates choose a leader from among themselves, under whose direction they themselves draw their carts in silence and humility, presenting their offerings while inflicting discipline upon themselves and shedding tears. Now these three matters which we have noted—confession with penance, reconciliation with enemies, humility in proceeding, joined to obedience toward their leaders—are so many necessary conditions which we require of all who come to us. When we see that they are willing to observe them, we receive them charitably, absolve them from their sins, and give them our blessing. Thereafter, when they set out in these good dispositions, it often happens that their faith is rewarded by miracles which God performs, especially in our churches, on behalf of the sick whom they bring with them; and these have the joy of returning to their country in full health. We permit our diocesan people to practise this devotion in other dioceses, but forbid them to enter places where there are excommunicated persons and where the celebration of divine office has been interdicted. These things occurred in the year of grace 1145. Farewell.”

This letter, whose original is no longer extant, agrees perfectly in the substance of its facts with that of Aimon, abbot of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dive, of which an account has been given above. [Note: [Col. 1128] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXI, col. 1703.] It was said, in connection with the latter, that its narrative was attested by Ralph de Diceto. We must further add the testimonies of Robert of Mont (under the year 1144), the *Chronicle of Normandy*, and an ancient manuscript. Thus, incredible as the account may appear, it nevertheless bears the marks of the highest authenticity.

5. A letter to Alfonso, count of Toulouse, excommunicated by Pope Innocent II for supporting the inhabitants of Montpellier in revolt against William VI, their lord. It is a reply to this prince, who had informed our prelate on 7 May 1143 that he was ready to go to Lyons, Vienne, or Valence, at Hugh’s choice, to receive absolution from his hand in his capacity as legate. After commending his good disposition, Hugh informs him that he will go to the last of these three cities to give him the satisfaction he requests. This letter, published in the original after the Works of Guibert of Nogent, is translated in the *History of the Archbishops of Rouen* (p. 339) and in the second volume of the *New History of Languedoc* (p. 436).

6. Letters of absolution issued to the dauphin Guigues for acts of violence he had committed [Col. 1129] against the Church of Romans. They are found in the first volume of Dom Martène’s *Anecdotes* (p. 380).

7. Two letters to Thibaut, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, inserted among the Documents (nos. 53, 54) of the history of that house.

8. A letter to Rainald, abbot of Cîteaux, published in the *Neustria pia* (p. 772), from Robert of Mont.

9. In 1134 Hugh of Amiens held at Montpellier a council, or an assembly of bishops, in which he decided in favour of Saint-Thibéry Abbey a lawsuit which it had with La Chaise-Dieu Abbey concerning the church of Bessan. [Note: [Col. 1129] *History of Languedoc*, vol. II, pp. 13 and 476.] Three legates presided: our prelate, the archbishop of Narbonne, and the archbishop of Arles. Hugh drew up the judgment, which he addressed in the form of a letter to the abbot of Saint-Thibéry and his successors. In another letter he informed Pope Innocent of this action. Both documents occur among the supporting records of the second volume of the *New History of Languedoc*.

10. A letter to Pope Eugenius III. It is reported in Hugh of Poitiers’s *History of Vézelay Abbey* and aims to induce the pontiff to uphold the exemption of that monastery against the encroachments of Stephen II, bishop of Autun.

7. In 1156 the seamless robe of Our Lord was discovered at the priory of Argenteuil. According to an ancient tradition, this relic had been sent by the Empress Irene to Emperor Charlemagne, who deposited it in the church of this monastery, then occupied by nuns. But at the beginning of the Norman incursions, about the year 845, the nuns, compelled to flee, enclosed it in a wall, where it remained hidden until the year just mentioned. Hearing of its discovery, Hugh of Amiens went to the place with a great number of prelates from different provinces. King Louis the Younger went there at the same time; and there, in the presence of that august assembly, our prelate authenticated the relic by means of the documents and attestations found in the shrine that contained it. The charter which he caused to be issued on this occasion is preserved in the original in the archives of Argenteuil. It was printed at the end of Dom Gerberon’s *History of the Seamless Robe*, and in M. du Saussay’s *Panoplia sacerdotalis*. M. Thiers declared the document, as well as the relic it attests, to be a forgery. It is not our purpose to undertake the defence of the latter; but we cannot refrain from examining the grounds on which the charter is attacked.

The critic first objects to the silence of contemporary writers concerning the event which it records. To this it is answered that the event is attested by Robert of Mont (under the year 1156), Nicholas Trivet, Matthew Paris, [Note: [Col. 1129] *Greater History*, under the year 1156.] Matthew of Westminster, [Note: [Col. 1129] *Flowers of History*, under the year 1156.] and John Brompton. [Note: [Col. 1129] *Chronicle*, under the year 1157.]

Secondly, he says, the archbishop of Rouen there assumes only the title of a simple priest, *humillimus sacerdos*, “most humble priest.” But for a former professor of humanities such as M. Thiers, this objection does him no credit. Does he not know that, in good Latin, *sacerdos* applies to priests of the first order as well as those of the second? But even if that term properly applied only to the latter, do we not have many examples of bishops calling themselves *presbyter*, “priest”? Finally, what wholly resolves the difficulty is that Hugh assumes in other charters, whose genuineness is beyond all suspicion, the same designation as in the charter now in question. [Note: [Col. 1129] See the *New Treatise on Diplomatics*, [Col. 1130] vol. V, p. 540, note 1, where, after observing that the subscriptions of this prelate’s charters vary greatly, one is reported in which he styles himself: *Sanctae sedis legatus et Rothomagensis sacerdos*, “legate of the Holy See and priest of Rouen.”]
