Thirdly, by what right, it is asked, did the archbishop of Rouen assemble outside his province prelates who did not belong to it? Answer: by his title of legate, which he certainly held, whatever the critic may say.

Fourthly, according to M. Thiers, this charter contains extraordinary graces unheard of until then. In order to understand what these graces consist of, the substance of the charter must be given. “All those,” it says after the preamble, “who shall come this year to offer their vows in this church in honour of the robe of Our Lord, we, through the confidence we have in divine goodness, remit one year of penance to them if they are entangled in grave sins; and, if they are guilty only of light offences, we remit half their penance. We likewise pardon the sins which they have forgotten (*oblita peccata*)—that is, by remitting to them half the penance deserved by such sins; this can only be understood of sins of inadvertence, which leave only faint traces upon the mind. … As for parents who, through negligence, have allowed their children under seven years old to die, whether they died baptized or unbaptized, we remit to them the entire penance, except that which they must perform on Fridays.”

To judge these clauses rightly, one must recall that this was the middle of the twelfth century, the century in which the Crusades gave rise to new kinds of indulgences unknown to all antiquity. Their use soon became so common that they were granted not only for the needs of the Holy Land, but for the most trifling reasons, and sometimes even without any reason. We have seen, in connection with Abelard, [Note: [Col. 1130] See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXVIII.] that there was scarcely a solemn ceremony at which bishops did not lavish such favours, without considering the injury they did to the discipline of the Church. What, then, is surprising in a legate of the Holy See distributing them with some profusion on an occasion among the rarest and most striking? Might one not even draw from the manner in which the indulgence is dispensed in the charter now under consideration a proof of the authenticity of that act? For canonical penance is still respected in it, and only a portion is relaxed; this is precisely characteristic of the twelfth century, with which this kind of penance appears to have almost entirely ended.

Hugh of Amiens may be counted among those theologians of the twelfth century who faithfully transmitted to us the doctrine of antiquity. With the exception of the point noted in his *Dialogues*, everything he teaches is drawn from the purest sources of tradition. None of those frivolous questions then debated with so much noise and so little usefulness in the public schools is found in his writings. He is a truly wise doctor, seeking to instruct soundly rather than vainly to display the subtlety of his intellect. His style is clear, simple, easy, suited to the subjects he treats, and almost equally removed from barbarism and affectation.

[Col. 1131]

# Letters of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen

## I. To Louis, King of the Franks—Concerning the Establishment of a Market at Gozengres

*(Duchesne, Writers of France, IV, 638.)*

[Col. 1131A]

To his most beloved lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, HUGH, his servant and archbishop of Rouen, greeting, honour, and prosperity.

It remains in our memory that we requested your nobility to establish a market at Gozengres, and that your royal magnificence said that inquiry should be made lest any impediment thereby arise to the neighbouring markets of the Vexin. Now, however, those who have made the inquiry report to us that it may be held on Monday without injury to the surrounding district. We therefore request your nobility to have this done, if it pleases you. May God preserve for you [Col. 1131B] life and health for a long time.

## II. To the Same

*(Ibid.)*

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, HUGH, his servant and archbishop of Rouen, greeting, honour, and prosperity.

God knows that in all synods, church consecrations, assemblies, and masses, we make remembrance of you in our prayers, because we love you greatly. Since it has pleased you to inform us where and when we ought to come to you, we ask you to await us until Wednesday. May God grant you life for long ages. [Col. 1131C] Amen.

### III. To the same.—On the liberty of the church of St Martin of Pontoise

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, HUGH, his own man and archbishop of Rouen, wishes health, honour, and prosperity.

From the beginning of its foundation, the abbey of Saint Martin of Pontoise has belonged in a special manner, after the primacy of your lordship, to the Church of Rouen and to its archbishop, in the election and consecration of its abbot and in every other right. But now the monks of Cluny, by I know not what novel contrivance, are attempting to claim it for their own subjection. [Col. 1132A] We therefore humbly entreat your royal highness to command that this church, which is yours, be maintained in its liberty—the liberty in which we have held it, and our predecessors in your time and in that of your forebears. May God preserve your life and health for long ages.

### IV–VI. To Suger, abbot of St Denis

(They are extant among Suger's letters, nos. 103, 173, 174, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, cols. 1399, 1430, 1431.)

### VI. To Innocent II, Roman pontiff.—On the death of Henry I, king of the English

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, col. 670.) [Col. 1132B]

### VIII. To the same.—On actions undertaken by him concerning the church of Beciano

(See ibid., col. 665.)

### IX. To the clergy and people of Romans.—On the absolution of Guigo the Dauphin. (Year 1132.)

[Marten, *Anecdota*, I, 380, from the archive of Romans.]

HUGH, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Rouen and legate of the apostolic see, to the venerable clergy and people of Romans: for ever.

The authority of the holy Fathers commands that the possessions and privileges of churches be preserved and defended alike with zeal. [Col. 1132C] Therefore, by these present letters, we commit to the knowledge of posterity that Saint Bernard, confessor of the Lord and archbishop of Vienne, formerly founded the Church of Romans; and that, together with the town adjoining it, called Romans, he granted it to the Roman pontiff for possession, free and exempt from every lay power. The present day clearly shows that it has thus been strengthened by ancient privileges and possessed without disturbance through the course of many years.

For when, through the exaction of sins, Count Guigo the Dauphin—fierce in spirit, mighty in arms, and surrounded by the heavy multitude of his armies—had violently entered the aforesaid town of Romans and ravaged it with hostile cruelty, yet the merciful God did not abandon the Church of Romans [Col. 1133A] so as not to preserve for it its former liberty, though he struck it in chastisement. When the blessed Pope Innocent, supreme Roman pontiff, heard that the church of Romans had been cruelly devastated by Count G. the Dauphin, he sent me from his side, though less fit for the task, to correct these and similar offences.

Accordingly we went down into those regions, and by apostolic authority summoned Stephen, archbishop of Vienne; the bishops Humbert of Le Puy, Eustace of Valence, Goceran of Viviers, Hugh of Grenoble, Ayrard of Maurienne, and Pons of Tricastin; John, abbot of Bonneval; and many other authoritative and religious men. Strengthened by their counsel and prayer, with the Lord’s assistance we at last received Count G. [Col. 1133B] the Dauphin, humbled and yielding to apostolic commands and to our own admonitions and those of our fellow bishops. As he promised peace for his sins and satisfaction for the sacrilege committed, we absolved him, etc.

### X. To Theodoric, bishop of Amiens.—On people who drew wagons in place of beasts of burden for the building of churches

(*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, appendix, p. 688.)

To the reverend father THEODORIC, bishop of Amiens, HUGH, priest of Rouen, may you ever prosper in Christ.

Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his purposes! At Chartres people began, in humility, to draw four-wheeled carts and wagons for the work of building the church. The report of their humility, shining also with miracles, spread far and wide. [Col. 1133C] At last it stirred our Normandy. Our countrymen, therefore, having received our blessing, went thither and discharged their vows. Then, in like fashion, they began to come to their mother Church in our diocese, throughout our bishoprics, under this condition: that no one should come in their company unless he had first made confession and undertaken penance; unless those who had formerly been enemies had laid aside anger and ill will, come together in concord, and established a firm peace.

When these things had been done, one of them is appointed leader. At his command they draw their wagons on their shoulders, in humility and silence; and they present their offering with discipline and tears. [Col. 1133D]

We require of them, when they come to us, the three things mentioned above: namely confession with penance; reconciliation from every ill will; and humility in coming with obedience. We receive them mercifully, absolve them, and bless them if they bring these three things. Since they come thus instructed upon the journey, very frequent miracles sometimes occur, especially in our churches. They also bring with them their sick, and take back healthy those whom they had brought infirm. We permit our people to go outside our bishoprics, but forbid [Col. 1134A] them to enter among the excommunicated or those under interdict.

These things occurred in the year 1145 of the incarnate Word. Fare well.

### XI. To Alfonso, count of Toulouse

[Note: [Col. 1133D] On this letter, see the Literary Notice on Hugh above, col. 1123.]

HUGH, archbishop of Rouen and legate of the apostolic see, to ALFONSO, most noble count of Toulouse, duke of Narbonne, marquis of Provence: whatever good we can and ought to command you.

Since God has made your person outstanding and exalted alike in honour and integrity, it is fitting in every way that you should please well him in whose hand your honour and integrity rest. Your liberality has written to us asking that we meet you either at Lyons, Vienne, or Valence; but out of respect for you [Col. 1134B] we shall rather come to meet you at Valence. On the Nones of March, with the Lord guiding us, we shall be at Valence in response to your request. For we hope that you intend to act in full faith, as you promised our venerable brother, the bishop of Troyes, and as you indicated by promising the same thing in your letter to us. Hasten to be reconciled with your mother the Church, that you may always increase in honour, illustrious prince and lord. Farewell.

### XII. To Rainard, abbot of Cîteaux.—He grants the church of Mortemer to the Cistercians

(*Neustria pia*, p. 772.)

To the reverend abbot RAINARD and the holy convent of Cîteaux, HUGH, priest of Rouen: greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Col. 1134C] In our time a monastery of Mortemer was built in our parish. At the request of the king of the English, we gave it to your order through the hand of Lord Waleran of Ourscamp. The abbot now presiding over the monastery of Mortemer, Alexander by name, had indeed been a monk of Abbot William of the monastery of Le Pin. But in the presence of our Church, this same William, holding the aforesaid Alexander’s hand, surrendered him with his own hand into our hand, to us; and I afterwards gave him to your order, under the hand of the aforesaid Abbot Waleran. Pray for me, my fathers and brothers, that the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world may forgive me my sins and have mercy upon me. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] From Robert of Torigni, *On the Change of Monastic Orders*, ch. 1.]

### XIII. To Ademar, abbot of St Thibéry. (Year 1134.)

[*History of Languedoc*, vol. II, Proofs, pp. 475–76.]

[Col. 1134D]

HUGH, by the grace of God archbishop of Rouen and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved son ADEMAR, abbot of St Thibéry, and to his successors, for ever.

The authority of the holy Fathers commands all those placed in governance to provide for religious persons and servants of God, and to preserve their possessions and ecclesiastical rights. Therefore, by apostolic authority, we undertook to settle the long-debated dispute concerning the church of Beciano.

[Col. 1135A] Accordingly, while the venerable archbishops B. of Arles and A. of Narbonne, legates of the apostolic see, the bishops of Agde and G. of Orange, P., abbot of Saint-Gilles, and many other religious persons were sitting with us at Montpellier, you appeared before us on the day fixed for you in the aforesaid place by apostolic authority and ours, prepared to receive justice. But the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, who had been summoned by us by apostolic authority to the same day and place, neither came himself, nor sent representatives on his behalf, nor offered any canonical excuse there.

Since he thus failed to appear, carrying out the justice commanded by our lord Pope Innocent, we asked the Church of Agde, in whose parish the church [Col. 1135B] of Béziers is situated, to declare truthfully before God and all of us assembled there to which, by canonical right, the aforesaid church of Beciano belonged: to yours or to the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu. They answered that, according to what they had truly received from their predecessors, it belonged by right and possession to St Thibéry, the monastery over which you preside by God’s favour.

You, Ademar, then produced the instrument of donation of the church of Beciano to the church of St Thibéry and to your predecessor Deodatus. This instrument had been made by Berengar, bishop of Agde of blessed memory, and was confirmed by the years of the Lord’s Incarnation and suitable witnesses. Next, you brought forward four old men as witnesses, who asserted that they had seen the church of St Thibéry peacefully possess the church of Beciano for many years before the monks of La Chaise-Dieu entered it. [Col. 1135C] Those canonically named then swore upon God’s Gospels that they had seen this and that it was true.

Four other witnesses also came forward. They said that they had been present at the hearing held at Corbian between the monks of St Thibéry and the monks of La Chaise-Dieu, in the presence of Aldebert, bishop of Agde, and in the presence of A., archbishop of Narbonne, and J., bishop of Nîmes. They declared that they had seen and heard suitable witnesses swear there that Bernard, bishop of Agde, who had introduced the monks of La Chaise-Dieu into the church of Beciano, upon receiving the testimony of authoritative persons of his church concerning the donation made by his predecessor Berengar to Abbot Deodatus and the monastery of St Thibéry of the church of Beciano, [Col. 1135D] had himself—[the text is defective here; apparently, “made restitution”]—before Bertrand, archbishop of Narbonne, at the hearing on that same case held at Cabrils, and in the presence of the monks of La Chaise-Dieu and St Thibéry. The aforesaid Aldebert of Agde, A. of Narbonne, and J. of Nîmes, having heard the sentence of restitution, judged it to be valid and to be maintained.

And just as the aforesaid four witnesses declared that they had seen and heard this, so, having been examined in our presence, they swore upon God’s Gospel the same thing. A., archbishop of Narbonne, Ermengald, archdeacon of Agde, R., sacristan, [Col. 1136A] and Master Dulcian, who was present at the aforesaid hearing at Corbian, declared orally before us that they had seen and heard it. All those who gave us this testimony attested that the same sentence concerning the aforesaid restitution had been confirmed at Loupian by the above-named A. of Agde and A. of Narbonne, P., bishop of Lodève, R., bishop of Maguelonne, and R., then archdeacon and now bishop of Agde, in the presence of the abbots of La Chaise-Dieu and St Thibéry.

For all these reasons, and moreover by the admonition and command of Guy, cardinal deacon and legate of the apostolic see, the aforesaid R., bishop of Agde, reinvested you and the church of St Thibéry with the church of Beciano. This reversal, made in this manner, as the same R., bishop of Agde, attests, [Col. 1136B] we and the above-named archbishops and legates of the apostolic see, bishops, and many authoritative and religious men sitting with us approve; and, in the apostolic capacity which we exercise in this affair, we confirm it as approved. By virtue of the canonical donation made by Berengar, bishop of Agde, and the lawful possession which followed, we adjudge to you, your successors, and the monastery of St Thibéry over which you preside, the aforesaid church of Beciano, with its tithes and all rights belonging to it, to possess for ever, all further dispute being silenced.

Done in the year 1134 of the incarnate Word, at Montpellier, in the universal pontificate of Pope Innocent and the reign of Louis, king of the Franks.

[Col. 1136C] I, Hugh, archbishop of Rouen and legate of the apostolic see.

### XIV. To Eugenius III, Roman pontiff.—That he should receive the monastery of Vézelay under the protection of the Roman see

(See under Eugenius III, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX, among the letters of various persons to Eugenius.)

### XV. To all the faithful.—On the seamless garment. (Year 1156.)

[Dom Gerberon, *History of the Seamless Robe*, p. 121.]

To all brothers of the Catholic Church, the most reverend [Col. 1136D] H., most humble priest of the Church of Rouen: greeting and the grace of divine propitiation.

We wish it to come to everyone’s knowledge that, prompted by heavenly mercy, we assembled at Argenteuil. With our humility were joined many authoritative and most reverend persons: the archbishop of Sens; Theobald of Paris; the bishops of Chartres, Orléans, Reims, Auxerre, Châlons, Évreux, Meaux, and Senlis; and also holy abbots—the venerable O., abbot of St Denis, [abbot] of St-Germain, G. of Lagny, [abbots] of Ferrières, Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, St Faron, St Maximin, St Magloire, Pontoise, and Marmoutier, together with many others.

We humbly inspected the garment of the child, the Lord Jesus, which from ancient times had been kept with fitting honour in the treasury of that same church for the salvation of the faithful. [Col. 1137A] We brought it forth openly; and, showing through solemn veneration the reverence due to its majesty, we offered it, in charitable concern, to the desire and devotion of the people. There was also present the eminent and exalted person of Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, with the nobles and magnates of the palatine dignity, while a vast multitude of common people stood by.

On account, therefore, of the outstanding token of heavenly grace—namely, that garment with which Wisdom made incarnate deigned to clothe itself—and on account of the most holy presence of the Fathers named above, it was decreed, by God’s favour and with salutary provision, that for all who came there seeking the grace of heavenly mercy, the reward and fruit of their devotion should be granted in the indulgence of pardon.

Therefore, whoever in this present year, in the place named above, has offered personal service and devotion in honour of the Lord’s garment: relying on the fullness of heavenly mercy, we remit for all such persons one year of penance if they are entangled in grave and very great sins. [Col. 1137B] But for those held by light sins, that is, venial sins, we remit half their penance. We likewise pardon forgotten sins.

Every year, moreover, from the feast of most holy Denis until its octave, we remit and grant forty days of their penance to those who devoutly visit the place and venerate the most sacred garment. Concerning little children who have been baptized, or who, through their parents’ negligence, have died without the remedy of baptism before reaching seven years: we remit all their penance, except on the sixth day of the week. On that day also, if the penitent has gone to church, let him receive such charity as the priest gives him. But if he is ill, or a pregnant or infirm woman unable to fast, let such a person say the *Our Father* seven times and perform whatever good work of piety is possible. [Col. 1138B] Upon all who observe these things and what is just, may there be the peace and salvation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

Done in the year 1156 of the incarnate Word, in the happy pontificate of Pope Adrian IV, of blessed memory.

[Col. 1137]

# THE SEVEN BOOKS OF DIALOGUES, OR THEOLOGICAL QUESTIONS, OF HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN

(Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, V, 891, from two manuscripts, one Colbert manuscript and the other a Rouen manuscript belonging to Monsieur Grebovald.)

## Preliminary Notice

I had the books of Dialogues of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, through the kindness of the distinguished Stephen Baluze. Having copied them in his own hand from Colbert manuscript 122 and already prepared them for publication, he freely offered them to me. As soon as I received them, I collated them with an old codex belonging to the distinguished Monsieur Grebovald, most worthy rector of the parish church of St Peter at Rouen. This codex, written five hundred years ago, seems to approach the author’s own time.

From the collation of the two codices I observed several matters which it is useful to record here. First, the entire seventh book is lacking in the Colbert manuscript; seven leaves are also missing at the end of the third book and the beginning of the fourth. Secondly, very many passages have been added here and there in the Grebovald manuscript which are absent from the Colbert manuscript. Thirdly, the division of the books is not the same in both. Fourthly, the prefatory letter to Matthew does not begin the same way in both.

For in the Colbert manuscript it reads: “Here begins the letter of Hugh, abbot of Reading.” But in the Grebovald manuscript it reads: “Here begins the letter of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, to Matthew, bishop of Albano.” Nor is the end of the same letter identical in the two manuscripts. For the Colbert manuscript has the following:

> For one kinship of family and the fellowship of the same profession in Christ have united us, whom the soil of Laon reared and instructed. But your native country retained you, while obedience made me an exile in England. Paris rejoices to have you as prior at Saint-Martin; Reading keeps me, unworthy as I am, as abbot, Brother Matthew.

But the Grebovald manuscript reads:

> For one kinship of family and the fellowship of the same profession in Christ have united us—us whom France bore, whom the soil of Laon reared and instructed, whom Cluny clothed in Christ’s garment; but afterwards the apostolic see chose you to be bishop of Albano, while it ordered me, sent into Normandy, to be priest of the people of Rouen, Matthew, dearest father and lord.

From all this I seem able to infer, first, that Hugh wrote the books of Dialogues while he was abbot of Reading in England; then, once made archbishop of Rouen and learning that they were acceptable to all and in everyone’s hands, he polished the same books, enlarged by various additions. To make these additions easier for readers to notice, we have taken care to enclose them in brackets, also noting in the lower margin the changes he made here and there.

From the end of this letter we learn who our Hugh was, what his homeland was, his profession, and his ranks: “France bore us,” he says. Therefore he was French by nationality, not English, as some have taught. Orderic Vitalis calls him an Amiénois at the end of Book XII of his *Ecclesiastical History*; Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, agrees in chapter 18 of his *Chronicle*, where he is called Hugh of Amiens, erroneously “Damian” in the printed editions. Yet it was the soil of Laon itself that reared and taught him, perhaps because he held some ecclesiastical benefice in the Church of Laon, as did Matthew, to whom he dedicated his work. He was a kinsman of this Matthew, of whom Peter the Venerable says in Book II, chapter 4, of the *Miracles*:

> This man was born of no obscure family according to the flesh, from the province of Reims, distinguished, as has been said, by the nobility of both parents and wealthy in worldly goods. In childhood he was given to letters, and when he had grown up he obtained clerical office in the Church of Laon.

From this you may infer that Hugh was distinguished not only in the Church but also in secular life.

He indicates his profession to us in these words: “One kinship of family and the fellowship of the same profession in Christ have united us … whom Cluny clothed in Christ’s garment.” Orderic Vitalis, in the passage cited, likewise teaches that he was a monk of Cluny; and Peter the Venerable confirms this in Book VI, in a letter to him, writing as follows:

> What could have had greater power either to draw my heart to love or to move my hand to write than your perseverance, so holy, so kindly, so long-lasting in its holy purpose, from almost the earliest years of youth to an old age broken more by divine labour than by the number of its years? What could have moved me, what ought to have moved me more, than that now ancient recollection, which I believe you have not forgotten, of the affairs of Cluny, known to me, to you, and to a few others? It has not slipped from my mind how, in the first season of your youth, I saw you distinguished among those old senators of our commonwealth.

From this community he was raised to various ranks in the cloister and the Church. His abbatial and archiepiscopal offices are made known to us by his letter. But Peter the Venerable, in the letter cited, teaches that he had earlier held the office of prior:

> I pass over—and while I live I shall not be able to forget—that, from the purpose of holy religion which you undertook, in the various grades of ecclesiastical honour, your countenance was not changed into different forms; but both among us and when removed from us, as prior, abbot, and finally supreme bishop of God, by the merit of virtue and knowledge you were always good, according to the Apostle, the fragrance of Christ in every place.

Whether he held the dignity of prior in the monastery of Cluny cannot be sufficiently determined from Peter the Venerable’s words. Yet in 1115 Hugh of Amiens was prior of St Martial of Limoges, and afterwards adorned the metropolitan cathedral church of Rouen by the renown of his religious life, as Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, writes. Not long afterward, at the command of Pons, abbot of Cluny, he crossed into England to govern there the notable monastery of St Pancras, subject to Cluny. He was administering it in 1123, when, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, Hugh, prior of St Pancras, became abbot of Reading, according to Matthew of Westminster. Yet the charter of foundation of the monastery of Reading which survives in the *Monasticon Anglicanum* was issued only in 1125. Before that, however, monks with their abbot could have been at Reading, labouring to construct and complete the regular buildings of the monastery before its foundation charter was drawn up.

At that time, encouraged by Matthew of Paris, prior of the monastery of St Martin in the Fields, Hugh, abbot of Reading, set his mind to writing six books of Dialogues. He dedicated them to this same Matthew before Matthew was created cardinal and bishop of Albano by the apostolic see, which, according to Ughelli in volume I of *Italia Sacra*, occurred in 1125. Matthew gladly received the books sent to him and made them available everywhere for everyone to read. Therefore, when Hugh was raised to the archiepiscopal mitre of the Church of Rouen in 1130, as Orderic Vitalis, Robert of Torigni, and Matthew of Westminster write, and learned that his books were generally approved by all, he revised and polished them, adding an entire seventh book.

In the first, indeed, he treats of the Supreme Good, that is, God himself; in the second, of creation; in the third, especially of free choice; in the fourth, of the fall of humankind; in the fifth, of remedies for sins, that is, the sacraments; in the sixth, of monks and eternal blessedness; and finally, in the seventh, he presents various traces of the Trinity in created things. The manuscripts bear no title; but Arnold Wion, who had seen the first six books in the monastery of St Benedict at Mantua, entitled them *Theological Questions*, perhaps because various theological questions are handled in them with no less learning than subtlety. Anthony Possevino gives them the same title in his *Sacred Apparatus*, as does Pits in *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, where he confuses our Hugh with another Hugh, abbot of Reading, who at the end of the twelfth century became the fifth abbot of Cluny bearing that name. But Hugh himself designated the true title of his books in his treatise on Genesis, where he cites what he had said in the second book of “our dialogue.” To reconcile these authors in some measure with Hugh himself, it has pleased us to prefix to his work the title: *Seven Books of Dialogues, or Theological Questions*.

What judgment should be made of these works you may learn from Bale, century III, chapter 20:

> Hugh of Reading, born long ago of an honourable family, left his fortunes and the tumult of his paternal house, and embraced the quiet of the cloister beneath monastic shades. Nor did he do so for any reason other than that he might give himself fittingly to good learning. While a monk, he chose as teachers men outstanding in learning; anxiously he followed in their footsteps, until he himself had acquired glory and renown equal to theirs. For through great and continual labour he became most learned in theology. “Both education and diligence,” says Leland, “made this ability outstanding in him.” He brought into ordered form many questions not drawn from the trivial arts but rather from the inner recesses of Scripture; and he penetrated them when ordered with such acuteness that he seems rather to have given them light than to have sought it elsewhere.

From this you may infer that Peter the Venerable did not write to our Hugh with a flattering mind: “It exceeds measure how greatly your learning and religious devotion adorned that sacred and great flock of Cluniac sheep.”

Besides these books of Dialogues, or Theological Questions, he also wrote some books on Genesis, dedicated to Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux. We shall give here a fragment of them from the Grebovald manuscript, where they were incomplete. He also wrote the *Life of St Adjutor*, monk of Tiron. When I had sought it long and fruitlessly from Bollandus, our Julian Belaise, a man plainly learned, supplied me with a carefully transcribed copy from the autograph itself. Moreover, he published three books on heresies, dedicated to Alberic, bishop of Ostia, and brought to public light by our Luc d’Achery in the appendix [Col. 1141] to Guibert’s works. From all these things it is clear that our Hugh possessed no ordinary learning and was fully worthy of all the praises with which the most renowned men of his age—Pope Innocent II, Bernard of Clairvaux, and Peter, abbot of Cluny—honoured him.

# HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO MATTHEW, BISHOP OF ALBANO

[Col. 1141]

[Col. 1141A] You ask about many matters and set forth still more; nor do you, importunately demanding that I answer, consider that I am less fit for this. I place before you the sacred volumes of learned doctors, full of exceedingly subtle judgments and clear in the elegance of their language. But I see you sluggish: you shrink from them because of their multitude and reject them because of their subtlety; yet, though I am slight in understanding, you harshly compel me to render payment.

What is especially astonishing is that you demand from me a brief answer on the greatest matters, a light answer on the weightiest. But what are you doing? Why do you insert so many things among the matters you had begun? You repeatedly interrupt what you have undertaken in the impetuosity of your will, and, wandering, you strike against the order of the questions. You inquire about creation, and how often you return to its creature. You compel me, though undeserving, to answer concerning rational creation, both that which fell [Col. 1141B] and that which stood; concerning what good and evil are; concerning freedom of choice and God’s ordering; concerning the grace of our Redeemer [Note: [Col. 1141B] Another reading: “of our redemption.”]; and concerning the sacraments.

These matters ought indeed to be proposed to great doctors, resolved not by opinion but by true assertions, or, what is stronger, proved by divine authorities. No righteous person opposes divine utterances; no sober-minded person assails reason; no faithful person provokes the Church. You say that many volumes ought to be produced by many persons, so that the same matter, in diverse expression but not in a different faith, may instruct very many people and lead them to truth by the way of charity.

Therefore, while I am compelled to comply with your affection, I feel detractors opposing me. I judged that they should be subdued by my silence, but your charity compels me to speak and write. Yet I think I must require this of you: whatever you find true in my answers, attribute to God; but whatever seems untrue, ascribe wholly to me, do not accept it, but in mutual charity kindly report it to me so that it may be corrected.

For both one kinship of family and the fellowship of the same profession in Christ have united us, [Col. 1142B] [whom France bore,] whom the soil of Laon reared and instructed [Note: [Col. 1141B] Colbert manuscript: “But your native country retained you, while obedience made me an exile in England. Paris [Col. 1142B] rejoices to have you as prior at Saint-Martin; Reading keeps me, unworthy as I am, as abbot, Brother Matthew.”], whom Cluny clothed in Christ’s garment. But afterwards the apostolic see chose you to be bishop of Albano; it ordered me, sent into Normandy, to be priest of the people of Rouen, Matthew, dearest father and lord.

# HERE BEGINS BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 1141D] Colbert manuscript: “Here begins the book of Hugh, abbot of Reading.”]

[Col. 1141]

## On the Supreme Good

[Col. 1141B]

### I.

God, supremely true and truly supreme, is a simple, perfect, unchangeable, and unique good. That which is begotten from the simple Good is equally simple. Therefore it must itself be the very same thing as that [Col. 1141C] from which it is begotten. We call these two Father and Son, from whom proceeds the Holy Spirit, likewise simple, unchangeable, and coeternal. These three, because they are distinguished neither by essence [Note: [Col. 1142D] Colbert manuscript: “differ.”] nor by difference, cannot be numbered. This Trinity is not greater than unity, nor is unity itself less than Trinity. For this Trinity remains altogether simple; consequently it cannot become multiple.

Rare knowledge of this most simple Trinity is handed down to us where, at the beginning of the book of Genesis, it is rightly stated first: “In the beginning God created” (Gen. 1:1); and then follows: “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over” (ibid., 2). For God created all things in the beginning—that is, the Father in the Son. That the Son is the Beginning he himself testifies when he says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). He is truly called the beginning of every creature, because by his omnipotent power he willed to make it from nothing. And when the Spirit of the Lord is said to be borne over it, [Col. 1142C] the Trinity is shown as cooperating.

Consider, then, Creator and creature, and weigh who made it, through whom, and why. The Father is he who makes; the Son is he through whom he makes; the Holy Spirit is the cause for which it pleased him that [all things] should be made. That supreme essence which is God, in his own wisdom consubstantial with himself, makes all things according to his unchangeable benevolence: lacking nothing, good [and making] good things, one [and making] all things.

Again, when Moses says, “God said: ‘Let there be light’” (Gen. 1:3), and likewise concerning the rest, and in each case there follows, “God saw that it was good,” the same Trinity, acting in each work, is signified. [Col. 1142D] As the Son of God is the beginning of every creature [Col. 1143A] so that it may exist, so he is also the Word to the same creature, so that, having been well made, it may remain good; thus he who was its beginning when it was to be made is also its Word now that it has been made.

For he creates, and, in creating, speaks, when he subjects each thing to its laws, distinguishes it by orders, and marks it by times. Hence it comes about that a creature, while it does not transgress his ordinances, is called beautiful and fitting; but when it transgresses those ordinances, it is immediately condemned as unfitting and guilty. Therefore he who is Beginning for things to be created is Word for things created. These two he shows to be one when he says: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

Likewise, as the Spirit of the Lord was said to be borne over the creature so that it might exist, so he sees it, now made, so that it may be well. But to see it is the same as to be pleased with it. For he who was pleased to make all things [Col. 1143B] good is pleased that things well made should remain good.

This author is more excellent than all things because he can do all things. The art by which he makes is superior to all things, for he knows each thing. The cause for which he makes is better than all things, for, remaining good, he always loves to make good things. These three are coeternal; together they are supreme; and they are one simple reality. They are three on account of the properties of the persons, one on account of the inseparable Godhead.

Accordingly, when something is said of each according to substance, it is at the same time predicated of all—not plurally, but singularly. Thus, when it is truly said, “The Father is God; the Son is God; the Holy Spirit is God,” we cannot say “three gods,” but proclaim simply one God, worshipping the divine essence as simply one and uniquely [Col. 1143C] simple.

### II. QUESTION.

What, I ask, do you mean by wishing to speak “according to substance,” when nothing can be said of God according to accident?

**ANSWER.** That supreme and perfect simplicity of essence which we call God neither admits increase nor suffers diminution. It does not undergo diversity, because it knows no changeability. For wherever there is changeability, there too is a manifold accumulated variety of accidental changes. Therefore, in every changeable thing, whatever is not said according to substance must be said according to accident—for example, when one asks of the substance which is a human being what sort it is, how great it is, or to what it is related; whether it stands or lies down; whether it is [Col. 1143D] helmeted or adorned; where it is placed; when it was born; whether it acts or suffers. Such things are known in the distinction of the categories: quality, quantity, relation, position, possession, place, time, acting, suffering.

But nothing is accidental to God, in whom there is no changeability. Yet the Father is related to the Son, and the Son to the Father, and the Spirit of both is related to both. This indeed is not said as an accident in God, because eternally this one is Father, that one is Son, and the Holy Spirit is of both: three persons without any changeability, one God. Hence it is said both plurally and singularly: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:13). [Col. 1144A] He says “one” and “are.” “One” according to the essence which is God; “are” according to relation, because this one is Father, that one Son, and that one the Holy Spirit, the gift of both.

**III. QUESTION.** Since many are reborn in time through the grace of God, and God begins in time to be called their Father, Lord, Teacher, or Friend, is not this relation—which indeed began in time—proved to be present in God accidentally?

**ANSWER.** We do not deny that God begins to be called, in relation to those reborn in grace, in time; but we declare it sacrilege to think that this is an accident in God. We begin to call him whom we know to have no beginning, to whom neither future things arrive nor past things pass away, but all things present endure. [Col. 1144B] Hence he does not gather his own by a new plan, nor love them by a new love. But when his own flee to him and turn toward him, while he himself is unchanged, they are changed for the better; just as, when they recoil from God, while he too remains unmoved, they themselves are changed for the worse. Thus God is called gentle toward the good and angry toward the evil, when they are changed, while he himself is not changed—just as one and the same brightness of radiance is pleasant to healthy eyes and harsh to diseased ones.

**IV. QUESTION.** Your answer pleases me. But how can God, who is simple goodness, be Trinity? For when I hear the Trinity of God, or the triune God, spoken of, I seem to hear of a threefold deity. Yet when I consider the Catholic faith itself, I confess—and blush—that I find myself thinking of God not as simple but as multiple on account of the Trinity.

**ANSWER.** I ask that your prudence consider that bodies are great by their bulk. Hence one body greater than another smaller one is sometimes double, sometimes triple, or manifold in whatever proportion of its parts. [Note: [Col. 1143D] Colb.: “whatever.”] But among spiritual things, which are great not by bulk but by power, when a good thing cleaves to a better—as a spiritual creature cleaves to the Creator, which happens through love—it becomes greater than it was before, but in power, not in bulk. To be greater, in this case, is to be better. For, as the Apostle testifies, one who cleaves to the Lord becomes one spirit with him, and so becomes greater because better. Therefore this greatness is not multiplicity, but simple love.

Since, then, that which God is is perfectly true and truly perfect, it is supreme by unchangeable truth and perfection. [Col. 1144D] Therefore, in the Trinity which is God, one is not greater than another, because one is not in the least truer or more perfect than another. Whatever God is, is perfect in itself by its own omnipotent power. Such perfection has no means by which it may grow or diminish. Hence it cannot be called threefold, but Trinity. For the simplicity of that nature is so true that the Trinity is not greater than the unity, nor the unity less than the Trinity. In it there is neither bodily bulk nor any alteration, but the perpetual stability of supreme perfection and wholeness.

Therefore Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are not greater than the Father alone, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone. I rightly said “alone.” For the Father is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. In that essence, while unity remains intact, the distinction of persons remains—not confusion; yet it is not such a distinction that one may be thought unequal to another in any respect.

**V. QUESTION.** I gladly listen to you. But I do not at all understand how the Trinity is in unity, or unity in Trinity.

**ANSWER.** There are certain things which in this mortal life we know neither through bodily senses nor through the reasoning of the mind, but see only by the apprehension of faith. The condition of faith is indeed truer insofar as it is more firmly supported by divine authority. In matters apprehended by bodily sense, we are very often deceived; and while the affliction of corrupt flesh continually strikes the eyes of our mind, there are few things which our reason rightly determines. But Catholic faith alone knows with the utmost certainty whatever Mother Church, taught by the Spirit of the Lord, has received.

It declares without doubt that God is one in Trinity and threefold in unity: unity does not make him solitary, nor does Trinity make him divided. We touch this in part through faith in the present life; afterward, when love is perfected, we shall see it perpetually. Hence the Apostle says: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:8). Do not therefore wonder that we struggle by seeing too little. For as long as we are in part, we see imperfectly. But when this imperfection is at last done away, in the other life, seeing perfectly, [Col. 1145C] we shall rest in the whole—that is, in God. Hear the Apostle’s testimony: “Then,” he says, “I shall know as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

There, through the very presence of unchangeable truth, we shall know God the Father with his only-begotten Word and the Holy Spirit of both so fully that, in comparison with that knowledge, we shall recognize ourselves in the present life only very slightly. When, therefore, we wish somehow to speak in this present life of that ineffable reality which is God—though we can by no means speak of it as it is, for it is truer than it is conceived by the mind, and truer as conceived by the mind than as uttered by the mouth—we speak, for the truth of faith, of three persons: not in order to expound it, but lest we remain silent.

For the sake of speech, when the usefulness of teaching at times compels us, or the necessity of disputing against heretics, we answer that, by saying “three persons,” we designate what is called Trinity in the Godhead. What the Greeks say of God as “three [Note: [Col. 1145D] Colb.: “substances.”] subsistences, one essence,” we Latins declare as three persons, one substance—or, more truly, one essence. [Note: [Col. 1145D] Colb.: “we utter three persons in words.”] By these words we utter what we conceive in the mind without words. Because of the poverty of speech, the Church chose, for answering, this Latin term *persona*, for which the Catholic Greek uses [Note: [Col. 1145D] Colb.: “substance.”] *subsistentia*. Thus we Latins speak of three persons in the Godhead [Col. 1146A], not in order to conceive diversity in so simple a nature, but because we do not wish to say “singularity,” since we worship Trinity in unity.

**VI. QUESTION.** I never cease to wonder that, in the essence of the Godhead, which is truly one, there is nevertheless a valid distinction of three persons, because I do not understand it.

**ANSWER.** As you marvel at God, whom you apprehend by faith and yet do not at all understand as he is, so, if you turned your attention to yourself, you would find yourself a marvel to yourself. You would indeed know this, yet could not define it.

**VII. QUESTION.** What is that?

**ANSWER.** Tell me: your body and your soul, though different in substance, how are they one in person? This body and this soul—of you I speak—are for you two individual things, different in nature. What makes them one individual—namely, you?

**VIII. QUESTION.** You have rightly checked me and shown me that I do not know myself. I feel that I know myself, as you said; but, to confess the truth, I do not know how to explain what it is that I know.

**ANSWER.** As you know that you possess yourself as diverse in substance but one in person, though you cannot define it, so Mother Church teaches you that God is one in essence and threefold in person. This, dearest friend, is what you must faithfully believe, even though in the present you cannot yourself explain it as it is. Walk by faith, that you may arrive at knowledge. “For now,” as the Apostle says, “we see [through a mirror] in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

**IX. QUESTION.** What is this mirror through which, according to the Apostle’s testimony, we now see God in an enigma?

**ANSWER.** Moses wrote in Genesis that God made humankind in his image and likeness. The Apostle, as we understand him, calls this image a mirror. For in this image, as in a mirror, we are able at present to behold God, though in an enigma—that is, in great obscurity. The rational soul, made in God’s image, possesses three things together: it understands itself, remembers itself, and loves itself, although it is one.

In it, that which is called understanding in a sense generates memory. For it remembers that it knows itself. How indeed does it remember unless it first knew or understood? From these two love proceeds fittingly, when it loves to understand what it remembers [Note: [Col. 1146D] Colb. adds: “and to love.”], and to remember what it understands [Note: [Col. 1146D] Colb. adds: “and to love.”]. Observe also that these three are equal in such a way that, just as it understands that it remembers and loves itself, so it remembers that it understands and loves itself, and likewise loves that it understands and remembers itself.

From this image [itself], consider in faith the one whom this image signifies. Thus, yet dissimilarly, God the Father eternally begot the Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeds everlastingly from both. But though the persons of the three are distinct, the essence of the three remains one; one omnipotence, the same honor, the same glory. Since that supreme blessedness eternally begets the Word consubstantial and co-omnipotent with itself, O what ineffable joy eternally proceeds from it! This Word, not made by God but begotten of God, eternally declares the Father, itself, and the Spirit proceeding from both. [Note: [Col. 1147D] Colb.: “proceeding.”]

**X. QUESTION.** What is it for the Father to beget the Son? What is the Word’s speaking? What is it for the Holy Spirit to proceed from both?

**ANSWER.** For the Father to beget the Son is the same as always to possess his wisdom, not from elsewhere but from himself. His creature, however, plainly possesses wisdom not from itself but from elsewhere; for it is one thing for it to exist, another to be wise. But for that supreme essence which is God, to exist is the very same thing as to be wise. Therefore we worship the Begotten together with the Begetter without distinction, as the Son coeternal and consubstantial with the Father.

The speaking of this Word is always to know all things together. Likewise, for the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and Son is the same as for them to love all things known together. He who always loves proceeds always from both. These three are together coeternal, together one in essence, and therefore together to be worshipped. They are three in person, not in essence; one in essence, not in person.

The Word born of God makes this known to angels; the Word made flesh proclaims the same to human beings. [Col. 1147C] Angels see and are made blessed; human beings believe and are justified. As the word of your heart, made vocal, sounds in my ears, so the Word of God appeared among us clothed in flesh—speaking to angels in essence, speaking to human beings in assumed flesh.

**XI. QUESTION.** How is the Word said to have been made flesh? Did it cease to be Word because it was made flesh?

**ANSWER.** The Word of God, dearest friend, is God. Therefore it is not one thing yesterday and another today, nor can it in any way change. Remaining what it eternally is with the Father, it was made from its mother what it received for us in time: made flesh, that is, [Note: [Col. 1148D] Alternative reading: “made human.”] human, as is said elsewhere: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” [Col. 1147D] (Luke 3:6). “All flesh,” that is, every human being.

Therefore let your faith hold firmly that the Word of God, one with the Father in essence yet distinct in person, is also one in person with the assumed human being, yet distinct in essence. Christ, God and human, consists of two natures and in two natures, but is one. For as flesh and a rational soul are one human being, so God’s Word and the assumed human being are one Christ. He received true flesh, in which for us he chose to suffer, die, and rise again. He also received a soul, concerning which he himself said: “I have power to lay down my soul, and power to take it again” (John 10:18). With it he descended into hell [Col. 1148A] and led his own out from there as free persons.

Thus in Christ there are together God’s Word, a rational soul, and human flesh: three unconfused and, in accordance with their nature, distinct, yet joined by supreme operative power into the unity of one person. Hence he is called wholly God because of God, and wholly human because of the human being. Thus he said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). And Paul says: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

The Son of Man rightly says that he descended from heaven because he is God, and while speaking on earth he testifies that he is in heaven. The Apostle rightly says that the Lord of glory was crucified because he is truly human and shares in our mortality. This same Christ, who suffered for us, was according to the flesh in the tomb, according to the soul in hell, and according to the divinity—which is everywhere—was not absent from paradise. Hence he promised the converted thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Wherever paradise is—a name signifying that rest in which life is blessed—whoever is in it is there with, through, and in him who is everywhere. For the supreme essence which is God is wholly everywhere; and, remaining unmoved, by its command it most rightly moves movable things.

**XII. QUESTION.** If, as you say, God is everywhere and moves individual things, it is necessary that he should sometimes be where he was not before, and sometimes do what he had not done before. I myself, since I now exist, had a time when I did not exist. Therefore, if he is now in me and moves me, he was not always in me and did not always move me, since I have not always existed. Hence I conclude that either he is not in me and does not move me, or, if, as you maintain, he is in me and moves me, he is in me temporally and moves me changeably.

**ANSWER.** It seems to me that you regard your being and God’s being as if they were alike. But you should know that your being is temporal, for you are a creature; and if temporal, certainly changeable. God’s being, however, is eternal. For he is always the same. What is always the same is certainly unchangeable. Therefore, when he who is unchangeable is in you, he is everywhere; he is in you not by your mode of being but by his own. By his own being he moves temporal things, and is not altered by time. By his own being he measures spatial things, and is not enclosed by place.

That which alone truly and unchangeably is must necessarily be everywhere, because whatever is changeable cannot in any way subsist through itself, but exists in him, through him, and in him who supremely is. For whatever is changeable is not eternal; and what is not eternal, though it exists, was probably made from nothing. For it does not always exist. But for something to be made from nothing, it must have an omnipotent maker. And what was made from nothing must have within it him through whom it exists, lest it return to nothing. Hence the Apostle says: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). And elsewhere: “From him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory” (Rom. 11:36).

**XIII. QUESTION.** Your answer pleases me. But how is God everywhere? Is he diffused or divided through every great or small thing?

**ANSWER.** You should know that, although God is everywhere, he is not diffused through all things by bodily bulk or spatial magnitude. He is not less in a part than in the whole, nor greater in the whole than in a part. Thus immortality, which Christ has entered into before us and which is promised to us at the end, will not be greater or less in one part of the body than in another. The quantity of a body is indeed greater in its larger parts and less in its smaller ones. But the bodily quality called immortality will be as great in the larger as in the smaller parts of the body subject to it. Quantity will differ in the unequal magnitude of members, but quality will be equal in things unequal, while one health or immortality is throughout the whole.

But this quality is in a subject body in a different way from God’s presence in every creature. For if you remove their subjects from qualities, the qualities will be nowhere, and thus will not exist. [Just as, if you take bodies away from the spaces of places, bodies will be nowhere; and because they will be nowhere, they themselves will not exist.] God, however, is indeed in things, wholly in all things together, and wholly in each individual thing, while remaining wholly everywhere in himself. I say “in himself” because, although everything in which he is cannot exist without him, he, needing nothing as though he could not be without it, remains perfect and blessed in himself alone.

**XIV. QUESTION.** I perceive that what you have said is true. But my mind is troubled by how the Word of God could become human in time, since, because he is God, he lives [Note: [Col. 1149D] Alternative reading: “unchangeably.”] unchangeably.

**ANSWER.** In the Word of God, all things which happen in time are without time. Therefore, in the Word of God there remains timelessly the time at which it was fitting for him to appear in flesh. “For,” as the Apostle says, “the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). He said “of a woman” because he wished to indicate the distinction of sex.

What is everywhere is sent precisely in that respect in which it is made. Flesh was made; it was not changed into flesh. In that respect in which it was made, it is less than the Father. But I want you to know that it is sent in one way in order to be with a human being, and in another way in order itself to be human. It is the Father’s wisdom, which the one who said, “Send her from the throne of your greatness, that she may be with me and labor with me” (Wisdom 9:10), desired to be sent to himself—that is, that she might teach me and make me perform what she has taught.

It transferred itself into human beings as it willed, making them friends of God and prophets; and so it dwells in holy angels, ordering them through fitting offices of love. It comes in a human being by whom it is known and loved, insofar as it is granted to be apprehended and loved by the mind. [Col. 1150A] But when it is in some measure apprehended by a person’s mind, it is said to be sent in time, though not into this world, since it is not sensibly presented to bodily senses—just as the mind itself, insofar as it apprehends divine things, does not perceive itself to be in this world.

But we say that the Son is sent in a far different manner, because he is begotten. Thus he says: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Sirach 24:5). As being born is for the Son to be from the Father [Note: [Col. 1150D] Colb.: “the Son.”], so being sent is for the Son to be known to be from the Father. Likewise, as it is for the Holy Spirit to be God’s gift to proceed from the Father and the Son, so being sent is for it to be known to proceed from both. Hence the Son says: “He proceeds from the Father.” And elsewhere: “Whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26). He also showed that the Spirit proceeds from himself when he breathed upon the disciples and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1150B] (John 20:24).

Observe that the Son breathed bodily; not because that bodily breath was the substance of the Holy Spirit, but because by breathing it was signified that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son. According to the Gospel, it is the very power which went forth from him and healed all. It is also sent by the Father, as we read: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). We read that the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent, but nowhere do we read that the Father is sent. For just as he has none from whom he exists, so he has none from whom he goes out or proceeds. Therefore he is not said to be sent, even though he is known in time by someone’s mind.

But when the fullness of time came, he sent his Son—not to be with angels or in angels, nor with human beings or in human beings, but himself to become flesh, that is, human. Therefore, when he was made human and lived among human beings, then he was sent into this world. In this act it is manifest that the holy Trinity worked together. For the Father sent the Son; the one sent put on humanity; the Holy Spirit made the Virgin fruitful. Thus the angel said to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). Hence we confess that Jesus Christ was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

**XV. QUESTION.** I am surprised that you said Jesus Christ was born of [Col. 1150D] the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. If he was born of the Holy Spirit, I do not know how to deny that he is the Holy Spirit’s Son.

**ANSWER.** From what was said before, you ought to have known that two natures remain in the one Christ: the divine nature, from God the Father, by which he is God; and the human nature, from the flesh of the Virgin, by which he is human. Yet he is said to be born of the Holy Spirit because the Spirit’s grace, not fleshly desire, made the Virgin fruitful. The Holy Spirit did not generate in the Virgin the substance of the one to be born from himself, but prepared from the Virgin’s flesh the material for the one to be born. Sexual intercourse was excluded; this remains the distinctive work of the Holy Spirit. Hence the angel said to Joseph: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). Because Mary conceived from him, she is both mother and remained a virgin.

**XVI. QUESTION.** How often we read that the ancient Fathers possessed the Holy Spirit, whom we know also worked more fully in Mary, from whose flesh we worship the Son of God as born. But what is meant by the passage elsewhere: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 7:39)?

**ANSWER.** We know indeed that the patriarchs and prophets possessed the Holy Spirit, through whom they longed to see the day of the Lord and were able to foretell many mysteries of things to come. John the Baptist was filled with this Spirit in his mother’s womb. Through it Zechariah, Anna the widow, and the aged Simeon were able to speak so many things about Christ. But no previous giving or sending of the Holy Spirit was ever such as shone forth abundantly at Pentecost after Christ’s glorification: “There came from heaven a sound as of a violent Spirit coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one sat upon each of them” (Acts 2:2).

This new and wonderful manifestation of the Holy Spirit had nowhere occurred before. In accordance with this new characteristic and distinctive newness, the Spirit had not yet been given; but it took place after Jesus was glorified, from whose fullness we have all received. For through this outpouring of the Holy Spirit people of every nation spoke wondrously in languages, and this sound went forth throughout all the earth. By it was signified that nations of every language would believe, because the Son of God assumed sinless human nature, so that the person of the one assuming and of the one assumed is one. [Note: [Col. 1151D] Colb. adds: “made.”]

Therefore, he who is equal to the Father in Godhead became less than the Father through assumed humanity—less than himself, less than the Holy Spirit, and, as the Psalm testifies, even less than an angel. For it says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8:6). The Holy Spirit, however, although he was sent in bodily form for a time, as was fitting, was not made, nor at any time changed into something else, nor united to any creature in one person, nor changed in any manner. Therefore he is not less, although he was sent.

Accordingly, when we read that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were sent, the Son was made less than the Father, but the Holy Spirit was not made less, though both were sent. The creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed in the same way as the human being in whom God’s Son appeared manifest to the world. The Holy Spirit did not unite to himself in unity of person the dove which appeared over the Lord, the breath by which the Lord breathed the Spirit, or the fire by which the same Spirit inflamed the disciples. Rather, these things appeared—creation serving the Creator—to demonstrate and signify the Holy Spirit, temporarily assumed, as it was fitting that the eternal should be signified and demonstrated to mortals.

Therefore we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is God and a dove, or God and breath, or God and fire, as we say that the Son of God is God and human. For that voice of the Father which bodily sounded over the Son, and the bodily form of the dove by which the Holy Spirit was there to be shown, were suddenly made and, when the mystery of their signification had been completed, immediately returned to that from which they had been taken. There Christ Jesus received the Holy Spirit, whom he gives as God, as a human being. Hence he was called full of grace and of the Holy Spirit.

Nor was he first anointed with the Holy Spirit when the Holy Spirit was seen descending upon him like a dove. For just as he came to baptism without any sin, so he did not come without the Holy Spirit, whom our humanity fully received when it was united in the Virgin’s womb with God’s Word. When the Holy Spirit descended upon Mary, through whom the Virgin supplied the substance of flesh to God’s Word, she immediately escaped every stain of original fault and afterward remained free from the impulses of vices; her perfect integrity gave birth to the Savior. Thus she was rightly called full of all grace: she gave birth in time to the Son whom God the Father eternally begot.

Do not wonder that the same Son of God and of man is signified in many ways: by the tree of life, which was in paradise; by the stone upon which Jacob slept; by Joseph, whom the envy of his brothers sold lest he should reign over them, though the one sold by them reigned over them; and by the rock which, struck in the wilderness, gave water. Of this the Apostle says: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1). While these things existed, an act of signification was added by which Christ had to be signified.

Christ was called the Lamb of God in another manner: both by John the Baptist, who said, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:29), and by the Evangelist, who in his Apocalypse saw the slain Lamb—something neither of them beheld bodily, but understood spiritually (Rev. 5:21). Those present did behold with their eyes the dove which appeared over Christ and heard with their ears the voice which sounded above him, just as Moses was shown the flame in the bush, Israel’s people were provided with the pillar of fire and cloud, and fire and thunder came upon Mount Sinai at the giving of the law [Col. 1152D], along with many similar things. The bodily form of all these things appeared in order to signify something and to pass away when its office of signification had been fulfilled.

Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the omnipotent Trinity, one God—work all these things inseparably. For the Son is not less than the Father in Godhead, nor does the Holy Spirit differ from both in any respect. Those whose essence is one have the same omnipotence without distinction.

**XVII. QUESTION.** I agree that the Holy Spirit is not less than the Father or the Son. Yet when I consider the Gospel’s words, I somehow perceive him to be unequal. For Truth says: “Whoever speaks a word against the Father or against the Son shall be forgiven. But whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

**ANSWER.** Whoever speaks, or sins, against the Father sins equally against the Son and the Holy Spirit. In the same way, whoever sins against the Son sins equally against [the Father and] the Holy Spirit. Likewise, whoever sins against the Holy Spirit sins equally against the Father and the Son. But observe that Mother Church received the Holy Spirit [to forgive sins], as the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20:23).

Hence Christ says to Peter, and through Peter to the Church: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in the heavens” (Matt. 16:19). This eminent judgment proceeds from Peter’s chair; because it signifies the priestly office, the Church judges that the feast of that chair is rightly to be celebrated. For this power is the key belonging both to Peter and to all who have care of souls. Therefore penitents must flee to those who, through the Holy Spirit, can forgive sins and open the heavenly kingdoms to the penitent, so that those who were able to bind themselves by sinning but cannot loose themselves may be loosed through Peter’s key and restored to the Catholic Church.

But the unbelieving or impious person despises the keys of the Church; and one who denies that sins can be forgiven through those to whom the Church has been entrusted blasphemes and sins against the Holy Spirit, whom Mother Church receives in order to forgive the sins of those subject to her. Thus it is rightly said: whoever sins against the Father or the Son—whom, because of identity of essence, we cannot separate from the Holy Spirit—shall be forgiven [Col. 1154A], provided, that is, that he flees to the Church of God, which forgives sins in the Holy Spirit. But if he despises the gift of the Holy Spirit, whom Mother Church has received for loosing sins, he remains condemned in his sins.

Hence it rightly follows: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” Here “the Holy Spirit” is understood not in his essence, but as that inestimable gift of the same Holy Spirit by which the Church looses sin. You must also know that this gift, as it belongs to the Holy Spirit, so it belongs to the Father and the Son. For the inseparable operation of the Trinity bestowed this gift upon the Church from the person of the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from Father and Son, is God and God’s gift. Therefore the one God with Father and Son brings about this effect by which the Church looses sin.

The first fratricide held an opinion contrary to this gift of the Holy Spirit when he said: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4:13)—as though to say, “There is no one who forgives.” The betrayer of the Lord likewise confessed his fault, but did not seek forgiveness. He too despised the Holy Spirit: though penitent, he did not flee to grace, but heaped sin upon sin, killed himself, and hanged himself with a noose.

We may also say that to sin against the Holy Spirit is the same thing as to offend against love. Whoever offends against love, however penitent he may be, cannot be absolved without love. For where love is absent, true repentance necessarily is absent. For concerning love we read: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Love makes the Church fruitful: she bears children for life, restores grace to penitents, and leads them to life, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns as God with God the Father for ages of ages. Amen.

**HERE BEGINS BOOK TWO.**

[Col. 1153]

[Col. 1153D] I. Supreme charity, which is God, wherever it is, is neither less nor more charity. For no substance and no essence is more or less substance or essence in one place than in another. John indeed says: “God is charity” (1 John 4:16). Since this is so essentially, he cannot fail to love anything. Therefore, just as wisdom, which is God, knows all things without distinction, so charity, which is God, loves all things without distinction. In the simple essence of the Godhead these are not divided; rather, charity and wisdom are altogether the same, and whatever is said of God according to substance—whether of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—is known to be that very same thing.

Yet the Word of God is properly called wisdom, certainly for this reason: because, appearing in flesh [Note: [Col. 1153D] Colb.: “having been received”], he restored wisdom to humankind. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God.” The Holy Spirit likewise is properly called charity. For through him charity is restored in us, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (1 Cor. 1:24). This love of God is present in a human being or an angel while the whole Trinity bestows it. But because the person of the Holy Spirit is bestowed, that same Spirit is properly called charity.

Although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are proclaimed essentially to be both charity and wisdom [Col. 1155A], a human being has no source from which to love unless charity comes to him from above. This occurs when the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God, kindles us in love of God and neighbour. Yet this is most wonderful: although God is certainly present, he is rightly known only where love is present [Note: [Col. 1155D] Colb.: “is absent,” correctly]. John indeed says: “Whoever does not love does not know God” (1 John 4:8). He is in all things by essence, but not in all things by knowledge. For although some people, as the Apostle says, knew God, nevertheless they became vain in their thoughts, and, claiming to be wise, became fools (Rom. 1:21). For this knowledge was not in them with charity, but with the presumption of knowledge. Whoever knows but does not love misuses the grace of so great a gift when he presumes to behold without love the Good which [Col. 1155B] is one and is the all of all things. Of such people John says: “Whoever does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). Therefore everyone devoid of love for God is plainly alien both from righteousness and from blessedness. Thus no one fares well who is without the love of God.

II. QUESTION. You have rightly commended charity, which you have truly shown to be God. But how did you say that God loves all things without distinction? Does he not love above others those whom he strips of evils, cultivates in virtues, and makes blessed?

RESPONSE. God does not know the whole creation because it exists; rather, it exists because he knows it. For he made it as he knew it, having ordained it to be created. Therefore he created it because he foreknew it, not because he had first created it [Col. 1155C] and then knew it. The created thing, therefore, added nothing to his knowledge, for he remained perfectly wise as he was. As he knows all things, so he loves them; as he loves, so he knows. For in him knowing is not one thing and loving another; knowing is the same as loving, and loving as knowing. Therefore, just as he is not more knowing in one place and less knowing here, so he is not less loving here and more loving elsewhere. God cannot be less or more God anywhere.

Accordingly, just as a created thing added nothing to his knowledge, so it neither increased nor diminished his charity. Charity neither needed things to be created, nor needs or will need created things; rather, by knowing all things without distinction it loves, and by loving it knows. When he bestows his good things on some, he does not incline toward them with a new love [Col. 1155D], for his eternal love undergoes no change. [He is said to love them more, however, by effect and not by affection.] For just as what he gives is his, so those to whom he gives are also his. They are better off from him; nothing is contributed to him by them. Yet he is properly said to love those to whom he has willed to reveal the love which he eternally possesses. These alone are blessed, who behold without end the ineffable joy of his love.

III. QUESTION. As I understand it, there is no new charity in God on account of creation; rather, creation itself is newly made in relation to the eternity of his charity. But if he loves everything equally [Col. 1156A], why does he punish some things? If he loves without distinction, why does he condemn certain things?

RESPONSE. That divine and perfect charity, which knows nothing except to act by loving, does not cease to do good to its creature by an undeserved gift. The devout mind receives this gratefully, and, receiving it, loves the giver; and at last, by the merit of love, it blissfully attains to the vision of him as he is. Concerning such people Truth testifies in the Gospel, where it says: “Blessed are the pure [Note: [Col. 1155D] Alternative reading: “of the world”] in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:2).

The rational creature is endowed with freedom of choice for this purpose: that, by loving its Creator rightly, it may know him, and, by knowing him rightly, may love him—the Creator who loved it beforehand without any obligation, in order to make it good and never to cease doing good to it once it had been made good. Hence the Creator requires this due return [Col. 1156B] from the creature: that it should rightly know by loving him who created it [without obligation], and rightly love by knowing him who does not cease to do good to it once created. When it diligently renders this, it finally deserves, by fully beholding him from whom it was created, to remain blessed.

On the contrary, an impious mind, remaining ungrateful to its lover, does not render the debt of love. Confused by desire, it rejects the order of righteousness; deprived of righteousness, it seeks misery. For by the ordering of supreme justice, which is God, every disordered will is its own punishment. God is indeed the Creator and arranger of all natural things. He is not the creator of sins, but only their arranger. Therefore he does not abandon the unrighteous person while he repeatedly calls and corrects him—while, in correcting him, he chastises him—and condemns the uncorrected person [Col. 1156C], so that, once condemned, he may learn even through torments how justly he bears punishment: he who, though created, despised the Creator, and, though loved, did not love God his lover.

Thus in those condemned he clearly makes known how greatly love must be esteemed: for love possessed he repays with blessedness, and for love not possessed he inflicts condemnation. Their very affliction grants them an understanding by which they know how rightly punishment strikes those who do not love, while the bosom of blessedness receives those who love. Hence that rich man, anxiously seeking a drop of water from Lazarus’s finger amid torments, deserved to be put to great shame by Abraham’s reply: “Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted, whereas you are tormented” (Luke 16:25).
