[Col. 1156D] IV. QUESTION. Why does Abraham call him “son” whom he knew to have been condemned for wickedness?

RESPONSE. You should know that another’s wickedness in no way diminishes the charity of the good. Thus Abraham, being a lover, called “son” the one whom he saw [Note: [Col. 1156D] Alternative reading: “sees”] in punishments. He by no means withdraws his charity from him when he reminds him amid torments that he ought to have loved God above all things, from whom he had received such great goods while living in the flesh. But he puts him greatly to shame when he shows him the poor man consoled, who indeed received evils from God in his lifetime; because he bore these patiently [Col. 1157A], he now rejoices forever, having received consolation. Just as that rich man, because he did not love God who bestowed goods upon him, is now, when reminded, made shamefaced by punishments.

The poor man, therefore, is mercifully comforted because he bore, in love, the evils inflicted upon him by the Lord. But the rich man, because he despised God even while God lavished goods upon him—as he showed by neglecting the poor man—is deservedly tormented. As for the assertion that a great chasm prevents him from obtaining what he asks, we may say that the great chasm is contempt for charity, which without doubt is hatred of God. Since that rich man lost life through this contempt in the present world, he is crushed beneath it in hell, so that he cannot return to life. Such great want also oppresses him that, just as Abraham did not heed him when he prayed for himself, so the same patriarch does not heed him when he pleads for his brothers [Col. 1157B], because, while he abounded in goods in this life, he disdained to listen to the poor man. When he is commanded to remember this, he is deservedly given over to punishments and openly put to shame.

Therefore the supreme lover, loving one who does not love, causes him even amid punishments to know that he ought to have loved the one whom he despised. For he despised God when, for God’s sake, he did not listen to the poor. God by no means despises such a person even in punishments; indeed, he loves him so greatly as to make him grieve because he neglected to preserve charity. Therefore he punishes the one whom he loves; if he did not love him, he would not punish him. For he does nothing except as one who loves, because, as we have already said and often wish to say, he knows how to do nothing except by loving.

He is the one who receives nothing from elsewhere, but solely from himself, through himself, and in himself knows, possesses, and can do [Col. 1157C] all things: he alone is perfectly wise, lacking nothing, perfectly sufficient to himself, the one almighty God. Therefore no necessity is a cause for him to act, but charity alone. By charity, as he foresaw things to be created, so he peacefully orders them once created. Although this has already been said, I wished to repeat it so that you might see more fully how greatly charity alone rightly surpasses all virtues.

V. QUESTION. Speak, I beg you, for I gladly listen to you speaking about charity.

RESPONSE. Our mediator, dearest one, rightly appeared to us as God and man, mercifully pouring into us the charity by which God and man ought to be loved. After his resurrection he poured out this gift more fully: upon earth, for love of neighbour; from heaven, for love of God [Col. 1157D]. This is the virtue by which a rational creature, if it retains it, becomes like its maker; but if it lacks it, remains unlike him. Whoever, therefore, in everything he thinks, does, or says, is moved by the cause of charity, is shown to be like his Creator, who likewise works all things solely by charity.

Therefore, as the Apostle testifies, a human being or angel who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him (1 John 4:16). But whoever performs anything without charity is shown to be unlike the supreme craftsman, since with a will turned away he does not imitate the charity [Col. 1158A] by which he was made [Note: [Col. 1157D] Alternative reading: “admires. This charity, my son”]. This one charity is established for us as the model for everything. For only by charity can we come to the kingdoms of heaven [Note: [Col. 1157D] Colb.: “of the poles,” i.e. heavenly], even if we do not speak in every tongue; if we lack prophecy; if we do not possess all mysteries or all knowledge; if, either because we have nothing or because some necessity prevents us, we give nothing to the poor; if we do not surrender our body to be burned, unless Christ’s cause requires this.

Faith also can exist without charity, but cannot profit. For demons too believe, but tremble because they do not love. Therefore faith which is joined with love is profitable. For the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything, but faith working through love” (Gal. 6:15). Nothing [Col. 1158B] is greater than charity. By it alone God and human beings are joined; by it the heavenly choir of virtues is firmly united to God. This charity grants blessedness to the inhabitants of heaven and justification to those on earth. By it sins are forgiven to the world; by it hell is despoiled; by it that turning sword is turned back; by it the gate of paradise is opened.

This, I say, is the charity which the devil lacked when he fell from heaven, and which the first-created human lacked when he fell from paradise. Since Christ Jesus possessed it uniquely, he could not be held by hell when he descended there; rather, his own charity brought him back free together with those for whom he had descended. For wherever charity is, freedom is likewise present. This alone must be possessed so that other goods may be possessed; if it is absent, none are possessed.

Thus the Lord speaks of it: “To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound” (Matt. 25:29). That is, to one who has charity the other goods will be given, and they will abound unto fullness. “But from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him” (ibid.). From one who does not have charity, whatever good he has for use through charity will be taken away; because he refused to use it through charity, he deservedly merits deprivation of it. For all things are good in charity [Note: [Col. 1157D] Colb.: “are made”]; but apart from charity, whatever things may exist are not good to the person who lacks charity. Hence it is written: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (James 2:10). Therefore seek charity through prayer, that he may give it who, coming from heaven, cries: “I came to cast fire upon the earth [Col. 1158D], and what do I will except that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).

VI. QUESTION. I beg you, do not pass over this [Note: [Col. 1158D] Colb.: “these matters”] so quickly; rather, explain sooner how one who offends in one point is guilty of all.

RESPONSE. [Note: [Col. 1158D] Colb.: “you ought to know that whoever in this ...”] Whoever offends against this one commandment, which is charity, is guilty of all, because one who lacks charity has kept none of them. We may also say otherwise: “Whoever offends in one,” namely, of the commandments, “is guilty of all,” namely, of the commandments (James 2:10). For one who neglects one has not kept them all. Beware the false opinion of those who say that one who offends in one sin is guilty [Col. 1159A] of every sin.

But leaving these matters aside, let us return to considering the excellence of charity. For charity covers a multitude of sins. Thus the Gospel testifies: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Charity has such power that anger, rebuke, punishment, condemnation, and whatever is similar are indeed evils in themselves when they occur without charity; but if charity is present, they are good through it. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ shall be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 3:22). Therefore, as Truth testifies, these things are evil and are rightly punishable.

So everything done without seeking there either God’s righteousness or a neighbour’s salvation is judged evil [Col. 1159B]. But if charity is involved in the matter, whoever is moved against sins is rightly angry, speaks rightly, and acts justly. Thus such things are good when governed by charity, though without charity they are nowhere free from sin—just as all sexual intercourse is always done wrongly wherever the remedy of marriage is absent.

Consider, therefore, how necessary charity alone is for us in all things, since whatever we do amid the misery of this present life remains culpable if it is done without charity. In the manner in which the supreme Creator knows how to work, since he does absolutely nothing except by loving, he commands his creature, whom he established as rational, to do whatever it does in charity. Thus it can keep what Truth commands [Col. 1159C]: “Be holy, for I am holy” (1 Pet. 1:16); and elsewhere: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48). This holiness and perfection exist nowhere except where charity exists.

Therefore you are commanded to love God above all things as God, and to love your neighbour—not as God, but in God—as yourself. I consider this especially worth remembering: just as the charity of God is the efficient cause of things, both of all things together and of each singly, so charity in the saints is the efficient cause of virtues, both of all together and of each singly. Thus it is itself their good, and without it they cannot be good; just as charity itself, which is God, so makes all things that without it absolutely nothing can exist. This is the almighty and supreme charity [Col. 1159D], which is known to have worked in that first sacred ordering of seven days through its sevenfold grace.

VII. QUESTION. Do not be troubled, I beg, to explain to us what that sevenfold grace is and how it worked in the first seven days.

RESPONSE. You have already heard above that the Holy Spirit is properly called charity. You have often read, if you recall rightly, of his sevenfold grace in the prophet Isaiah: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit [Col. 1160A] of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1, 3). You have heard “sevenfold”; do not suppose it to be multiple. For it is simple in essence but sevenfold in the grace of its gifts. With the charity by which he created all things, he fills created things with most abundant gifts.

Let us see how this was first done in the first [Note: [Col. 1159D] Colb.: “six”] seven days, through the inspiration of that grace. Moses indeed relates that God said: “Let there be light,” and so forth (Gen. 1:3). Thus the discourse proceeds through the order of the days as far as the seventh. By the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1159D] Colb.: “the Holy Spirit being omitted”] the sacred works are signified.

VIII. First. In the spirit of wisdom, the light first created is separated from darkness, having evening after it, then morning. It is made into day when that praiseworthy society of angels [Col. 1160B]—rightly called light because it was created rational and intellectual—is separated from darkness [Note: [Col. 1159D] Colb.: “because it did not consent to that same pride”]. For it did not consent to the pride that fell, but, humbly subject to the Lord, wisely clung to him. It has evening in the nature of its own mutability, for it is a creature. But it becomes morning when it receives the grace of the spirit of wisdom, because it is wholly inflamed with charity toward God and becomes wise by loving God singularly. Beholding the Creator not through the creature, but rather the creature through the Creator, it becomes one day, uniquely enjoying God’s wisdom.

Therefore, after the fall caused by our perversity, we who have been mercifully re-formed through Christ should seek this gift of wisdom from him, that we may deserve to become sharers in angelic blessedness.

IX. Second. In the spirit of understanding, God set the firmament [Col. 1160C] in the midst [Note: [Col. 1160D] Colb.: “placed”] of the waters, when, after the human being had been cast into exile through sin [Note: [Col. 1160D] Colb.: “by the merit of sin”], he established amid the waves of worldly errors the utterance of divine Scripture. It is rightly called heaven because it is diversified by the manifold abundance of mysteries. It has evening in the literal history, morning in moral teaching, and day in spiritual allegory.

Observe here that, whereas in the other days Scripture says, “God saw that it was good,” this was not said on the second day alone. I judge this to have occurred because the work of the second day was seen to be complete not on that second day itself, but rather on the third. For the waters are read to have been divided on the second day: those beneath the firmament from those above the firmament. But on the third day [Col. 1160D] it continues concerning those same waters, describing how they are separated from the land and called seas. Hence it is fitting that the words, “God saw that it was good” (Gen. 1:10), are said twice on the third day: first for the work of the waters then completed; second for the expanse of land adorned with herbs and trees.

And fittingly: because we have said that the divine utterance is signified by the firmament, “God saw that it was good” is not yet added until the earth begins to shine with herbs and trees through its saving doctrine. For it is not hearers only, but doers of the law who are righteous [before God]. Therefore it is rightly stated not at the reception of words but [Col. 1161A] at the performance of deeds: “God saw that it was good.” It should also be noted that in the fruitfulness of works, signified by the production of herbs and trees, “God saw that it was good” is read twice. For no work is good unless it comes from charity, which is twofold. Through it we are commanded to love God and neighbour. May divine charity grant that, within this firmament of sacred utterance, distinguished as history, morality, and allegory, we may so advance in conduct and life that we may also be able to teach others the same.

X. Third. In the spirit of counsel, God separates the land from the waters. Once separated, it produces trees and herbs, when certain persons pass from the flow of vices to the firmness of holy conduct and produce herbs—that is, the growth of good works—and trees—that is, the heights of virtues—from the root of charity. Evening comes upon them when they grieve that they had flowed away through fault. They have morning when restored to forgiveness, and become day when united to Christ through grace. May heavenly charity mercifully help us by its counsel, so that, withdrawn from the abyss of vices [Note: [Col. 1161D] Alternative reading omits “from the abyss of vices,” etc., through “does not cease”], it may make us for itself fruitful land which does not cease to bear the shoots of charity for the Church.

XI. Fourth. In the spirit of fortitude, God makes the lights of heaven: namely, those through whose teaching the Church shines like the sun and moon, and through whom miracles are at times performed. They have evening, in which they labour in the present world against scandals; they have morning, in which they triumph in Christ’s victory. They remain day, while they shine exceedingly with the brightness of virtues and thereby enlighten others [Col. 1161C]. Therefore let us always humbly worship the Holy Spirit, that by his fortitude the Church may be so formed that heresies and schisms may never prevail against it, but, the darkness of errors having been driven away, the catholic faith may shine everywhere and the lamp of charity glow on every side.

XII. Fifth. In the spirit of knowledge, fish and birds are created by the Lord from the waters. Thus some persons, though placed amid much ambition for worldly things, live in pious conduct like fish in waters and minister to the faithful by providing assistance. Others, rejecting worldly allurements, flee to Christ’s poverty and, on the wings of virtues, ascend from the waters to the heaven of charity’s breeze [Col. 1161D]. Their evening is the enticing glamour of worldly pomp, to which they were formerly accustomed. Their morning is the unfailing strength of faith. Their day is a free ascent into the upper air, after the burden of riches has been laid aside. Let us also pray to the Spirit of knowledge that he may instruct the rulers of the world and the powers of the age and take possession of their hearts, so that they may not be high-minded or trust in the uncertainty of riches, but may either use their possessions rightly for good according to God, or, leaving their possessions, freely serve God alone.

XIII. Sixth. In the spirit of piety, after cattle and the other animals had been made, the human being was formed in the image and likeness of God. All who are born in sins and serve sins, stripped of the robe of righteousness and cast out in a garment of skins—which signifies the desire of the flesh—are rightly called cattle, as the Psalmist testifies: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless cattle and made like them” (Ps. 48:13).

But for the restoration of human nature, Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin Mary in ineffable mercy. Made in the image of God, he did not depart from the likeness of him to whom all things are rightfully subject, over whom he rules with unbreakable command. He was prefigured by the first Adam, who, as the Apostle says, “is the figure of the one to come” (Rom. 5:14). And whereas concerning each individual [work] it was said, “God saw that it was good,” now one blessing common to them all was made in this instance, where it was said: [Col. 1162B] “God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). His evening is the Passion voluntarily undertaken for us. His morning is the glorious resurrection in the flesh. His day is the blessed ascension into the eternal confession of the Father’s glory. Therefore let us worship and glorify him, so that by his grace we may rise from death to life and ascend together after him.

XIV. Seventh. In the spirit of the fear of the Lord, God rested from every work that he had made and sanctified the seventh day alone above the others. This surely indicates to us that God does not rest in his work [Note: [Col. 1161D] Colb.: “alone”], but rests from work: he who needed nothing always rests in himself. Therefore let us also seek rest not in our own works, but let us strive to rest from our works in him who is always at rest in himself [Col. 1162C]. For there is no rest in any mutable thing, but only in him who rests in himself in perpetual blessedness.

And fittingly God is said to accomplish this in us in the spirit of fear, for he says: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). Through the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, which is called the beginning of wisdom, we who have fallen receive, through his lifting us up, the beginning of our return. Advancing from grace to grace, we complete our return in the holy fear of the Lord, which remains for ever and ever; and once made complete, we rest.

For there is another spirit of fear: namely, servile fear, not of the Lord but of sin. It loves sin but fears punishment; it hates righteousness but dreads the penalty. This is the fear which charity casts out. But there is another spirit, the fear of the Lord, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. By the working of its grace we begin, for love of God, to hate sins. It is, therefore, a fear belonging to charity, not to servitude. By this fear of the Lord, as love of God grows in the present life, hatred of sin likewise grows with it. You hate sin [Col. 1162D] as much as you love righteousness. They grow together in this life and will be perfected together in the life eternal. For charity begun, and that fear called the beginning of wisdom, advance together in the present life. Perfect charity, however, and the fear of the Lord, which remains holy for ever and ever, will be together eternally [Note: [Col. 1162D] Alternative reading: “in eternity”]. For we cleave to Christ through charity, not through fear of punishment.

It is good, therefore, to return from our sins through repentance in the fear of the Lord; better, through fear of him, to avoid sins lest we offend God; best, through the fear of the Lord, to advance so far that we can no longer be drawn down into fault. This will be fulfilled in the general resurrection, when God crowns the last of the elect, together with the rest, in incorruptible glory. That day, with no evening following, will remain without decline; in it we shall rest forever with the Lord, who will be all in all.

May this recent exposition of the first seven days remind you to consider that the book of Genesis was sealed at its beginning with these, as it were, seven seals. No one could loose them by himself until that Lamb who “shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts,” revealed to the hearts of the faithful this mystery concerning the sevenfold work of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1163B].

XV. QUESTION. I gladly receive your reflection upon that sequence of seven days. Yet I do not cease to wonder why it suddenly entered the Creator’s mind to make what he had not made before. For if he made all things from nothing, what was he doing before?

RESP. I see that in considering “before” or “suddenly” in God, you are being far too unreflective. For “before” and “suddenly,” if you weigh them properly, are marks of time. He who made times is not, dear friend, subject to time. For he who created all the things he willed, and co-created times with things, created all things together from formless matter—not temporally, indeed, but causally [Col. 1163C]—from which times run, places are filled, and ages roll on through the motions of temporal and spatial things.

We say that God alone is before the ages; that those things which were made together in the beginning, from which the ages proceed, are from the age; and that all things which run under time are into the age. Therefore, the Creator of things and times precedes neither things nor times in time, but in eternity.

For we say that one thing proceeds from another in four ways: by eternity, by origin, by time, or by choice. By eternity, as the Creator precedes every creature; by time, as the flower precedes the fruit; by choice, as the fruit precedes the flower; by origin, as sound precedes song, voice precedes word, and formless matter precedes the world. For when it is asked which is prior, sound [Col. 1163D] or song, we answer that sound is prior. Sound is the material of songs. Thus voice too is prior to word; for a word is formed voice. Yet sound precedes song and voice precedes word not in time, but by a certain origin. The singer does not first emit unformed sound and then gather and shape it into song; rather, both occur at once—sound and song—when someone sings. Yet we perceive naturally what is made from what: song is formed sound.

Thus God created both at once: the matter which he formed and the things into which he formed it. For as soon as he made anything, he made it formed. Yet that from which something is made is naturally prior to that which is made from it. Formless matter, therefore, is prior to the world, as voice is prior to word: not in time, indeed, but in origin. In the things we see, certainly, we understand matter and form to exist together. Yet when we wish to speak of both, we cannot speak of both at once. It is therefore proper that, in speech, that should be placed first which in action is prior only by origin. Hence Scripture divides by the times of speaking what it says was made—the world from formless matter—though God did not divide it by the times of making. For the world is preceded by formless matter through the cause of origin, not through any delay of time.

Formless matter, then, whatever it may be, is without time. I find also that those angels are without time who, as soon as they were created, were as quickly turned without any interval of time toward the supreme and unchangeable [Col. 1164B] good. Otherwise they would have been in fault if, even for a short time, they had been apart from him with whom they were made firm in unchangeable charity—unchangeable by grace, though not by nature. For they are creatures. They always behold God without time and place; from that contemplation of blessedness they never anywhere recoil or fall away. Yet they perform his commands in lower things and serve the members of the Church everywhere, as Truth testifies when it says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10).

When he says “their angels,” he indicates their temporal ministry concerning us. When he says “always see the face of the Father,” he indicates that they possess the unchangeableness of the divine vision, in which they see the unchangeable eternal principles of all creatures [Col. 1164C]. They also see all things made together without time, by causal reason alone.

[Note: [Col. 1163D] Colbert manuscript: “but by causal [reason].”]

For God made all things together originally and primordially, and from them things proceed in temporal succession. But among the things made together no one sees what ought to have been made earlier or later except that Wisdom which knows in itself both things and the order of things. Existing outside none of the things it made, finding nothing outside itself, and possessing all things principally within itself, it made all things as it knew them. For it would not make them unless it knew them within itself before making them. Hence Truth says: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3)—not as made, but in him as life. There, then, are all things, but not as made. In formless matter [Col. 1164D] all things were made together, but were not subject to time. In time, however, all things are ordered through the movements of their varieties or through the spaces of places.

[Note: [Col. 1164D] Colbert manuscript: “through spaces or intervals of places.”]

Accordingly, the causal principle of all things remains unmoved in the divine mind. Thus evangelical Truth testifies: “What was made in him was life. And the life was the light of men” (John 1:3–4). For the human being—that is, the rational creature—has no light except Wisdom, which is God, in whom everything made is life. The rational spirit, indeed, while it singularly preserves the image of God in which it was made, contemplates and loves him alone above itself; and nothing is higher or more blessed than he.

But insofar as all things were made together in the beginning, we read: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18:1). Insofar, however, as individual things proceed temporally, it is written: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17). Moses is believed to refer to all things created together materially where he says: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. When the day was made, God made heaven and earth, and every green thing of the field before it was upon the earth, and every grass of the field before it sprang up.” He made all things together in pre-existing matter before they visibly appeared and came forth temporally in act.

When, therefore, all these things were made together in the beginning, Scripture says that day was made. But understand that day as one day repeated seven times, without intervals of temporal delay [Col. 1165B]. To understand this clearly, answer me, I ask, concerning the seventh day. Tell me: was it made, or was it not made? But apart from God, whatever exists has altogether been made. Moses related with what works the first six days were made. He also writes that all things were completed within those six days and that God rested on the seventh. But how did he rest on a day which he did not create? Or, if he created it, how did he complete all things together on the sixth day? For he created nothing on the seventh day; rather, on it he rested from all that he had completed.

The statement is thus more plainly evident in this sense, if we say that one day was present for the works of God and for his rest from every work, in order to see [Col. 1165C]. It was not bodily but angelic or spiritual, having evening when it looks upon the nature or action of the lower creature; having morning when it is raised from knowledge of the creature to the praise of the Creator; and having day in contemplation of the most perfect truth. For it was then divided from darkness and formed into day, when it turned from the formlessness of its own mutability [Col. 1166A] to behold the unchangeable glory of the Creator.

The clearest vision, therefore, is to see all things in the height of unchangeable truth: to see the Son eternally begotten from the Father’s essence, and the ineffable gift of charity proceeding from both. Its obscure knowledge, however, is to see all things in the act in which they were made. Lest it be darkened by that knowledge, it is always made morning when it returns from the creature to the Creator’s praise. It praises the Creator, not in the creature, but, moving from the creature, praises him resting in himself: needing nothing, but fully and perfectly sufficient to himself in himself.

That day is read as repeated seven times because, when it is presented with stable knowledge both to God and to his works, it is distinguished not by variation of time but by an order of knowledge; not by bodily revolution but by spiritual contemplation [Col. 1166B].

There is likewise a commemoration of things arranged under intervals of time where Genesis reads: “But a fountain went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth” (Gen. 2:6). It is rightly believed to begin from that element from which kinds of animals, herbs, and trees arise. For all beginnings of seeds, from which all flesh and all shrubs proceed, are moist and grow together from moisture. Visible or actual nature drew this power and efficacy of most effectual generation from God’s works completed together, in which there were not times but the origin of times. For, from those things which he created together materially, he himself does not cease to work individual things formally in time—not by creating new things. Hence Truth [Col. 1166C] says in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work.” Therefore he always rests and yet does not cease to work. He rests because he needs nothing; he works by ordering individual things through ages of ages. Amen.

## THE THIRD BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1165]

[Col. 1165D] I. The eternal wisdom of God, in which abide the eternal principles of all rational and irrational things, in which live the unchangeable origins of all changeable things, created all things by eternal counsel and unchangeable will. And because it is uniquely and supremely good, whatever was made by it is itself good. I say good, but not supreme good, because it has been created. Therefore, to comprise in a brief sum all that exists: whatever exists is either Creator or creature. He is good; all his things are good. Thus Scripture concludes: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1:31). They are good because they are from him; mutable because they were not begotten from him but made from nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Colbert manuscript: “not indeed begotten.”]

[Col. 1166D] II. QUESTION. What are you saying? I know that the world has overflowed with evils from the beginning; I see evils everywhere, and experience how many things I endure. Yet, while you gather all things into two classes, you do not consider evil, but maintain that whatever exists is only good. What is more evident than evil, which we always wish to be absent and yet cannot avoid?

ANSWER. When evil is asked about and what evil is has not been properly considered, the proposed question is not easily answered. For “evil” is sometimes used of an inconvenience or defect of any body, and likewise of afflictions of a mind that does not feel them contrary to justice. Bodily evils include illnesses, punishments, penalties, labours, hunger, and the like. Evils of the mind include [Col. 1167A] anxieties, the labours of pursuits, fears, and the disturbances of desires. Souls suffer these because of mutability, as do bodies; ordinary speech customarily calls them evils, but they are not blameworthy. All the righteous endure them in this present life; although they suffer evils of this kind, they are not on that account called evil. Nor do we call irrational or insentient beings evil, although they too are subject to the inconveniences of suffering.

But we properly call evil those things which we judge blameworthy by the judgment of justice. What is blameworthy under the law of justice we certainly call sins. Whoever performs those things which are properly evil is therefore himself properly called evil. But if we wish to see where those things which are properly evil exist, we find that they exist nowhere except in rational will alone.

III. QUESTION. Speak, I beg you, of these evils.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Colbert manuscript: “show [them].”]

I desire only to hear in what manner they are in rational will.

ANSWER. The eternal and supreme essence, which is God—living, everlasting, and blessed in itself—out of the charity of its benevolence created an angel living and eternal, but not at all blessed unless he adhered to his Creator. He also made man living indeed, but, apart from the Creator’s benefaction, lacking eternity and blessedness. Therefore he who is essentially life, eternity, and blessedness, through his ineffable charity granted free choice to angel and human being, so that each might attain by grace what he had not received [Col. 1167C] by nature: the angel, blessedness; the human being, eternity and blessedness.

Since each had free choice, each both ought and was able uniquely to love above all things him from whom he is and to whom he owes his being, and through the merit of love to remain blessed—not in himself, but in him who supremely is, who is essentially living, eternal, and blessed. This love, this charity or affection, is properly said to be their good, in both human being and angel, by which they are humbly raised above themselves to God.

Accordingly, angel or human being, when they use well the free choice bestowed upon them, are rightly called good; and, adhering to him who is supreme, when they are raised to him in full charity and stripped of their mutability, they are joined to the unchangeable glory of God [Col. 1167D]. Conversely, if through undue desire a human being or angel turns away from him who is supreme, and by retrograde love bends toward that which is lesser, he at once misuses the grace of free choice. By the supreme justice, from which he cannot escape, he is deprived not of choice but of freedom of choice, so that he cannot do what he previously could, because he willed what he ought not to have willed.

By reason he perceives that he has fallen into fault and that he is not free to return. He could turn away from good through himself—if that ability was in fact an ability. For it is a falling away from what he was able to do well. He was able through the Creator’s grace; when he despised that grace, he came to inability. This contempt, this negligence or ill-will, is properly called his evil [Col. 1168A]. Hence he himself is properly called evil.

IV. QUESTION. How is it that you show a creature—of which, with all Scripture testifying, you had declared that it was very good—becoming evil? Does it cease to be what it was made and become another thing, namely evil? If God does this, then not all that he makes is good. If another makes this evil, then God is not creator of all things, nor were all things made through him.

ANSWER. It seems to me that you have attended carelessly to what we said above. For this evil of which we are now speaking, which we properly call sin, is nothing other than a defect of the rational creature. The creature which turns away from the good set before it by its Creator—the good which it ought to love, receive by loving, and by receiving remain blessed in, namely him who supremely is—does not turn into another thing. Rather, it is deprived of the freedom of its choice when it strives to put its own will, which a creature ought not to have, before its Creator.

Therefore this thing which we call evil is neither a nature nor any thing; rather, an abuse or negligence has acquired the name of evil. The privilege of having one’s own will belongs to the Creator alone, who owes nothing to anyone but does all things as he wills. The creature, however, which owes to the Creator everything that it has, can do, and is, ought in every way to owe even its own will to him through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3).

Thus the rational or intellectual creature is good because it was well created by the good Creator and enriched with freedom of choice. It ought by rightful obligation to love its Creator and diligently keep his ordinances. If it despises keeping them, it will deservedly lose freedom of choice through its contempt and will be unable to restore what it has lost. For it did not have this from itself; it received it from its Creator and lost it through misuse.

V. QUESTION. The free choice of which you speak is almost on everyone’s lips. Yet I confess that I myself do not know what it is.

ANSWER. As I understand it, free choice is a movement of rational intelligence having the ability to carry out what it judges. When both human being and angel, having received this free judgment of rational will, look to the Creator above all things and look upon the creature beneath them, they judge that the Maker must in every way be obeyed and that created things must be used in accordance with the Maker’s will [Col. 1168D]. But this judgment is not free unless it accomplishes what it knows ought to be done. It accomplishes this when it loves the Creator and, putting aside its own will, knows his will by keeping it.

But if it refuses to keep what it truly judges must uniquely be kept, it contradicts its own judgment and, as a transgressor, deservedly loses freedom of judgment. But when it abandons preserving freedom in justice, it is rightly handed over to vices. Having thus lost freedom of choice, it remains captive beneath sin’s fetter. It is in no way sufficient to restore to itself the freedom which it has abandoned through its own fault [Col. 1169A]. This freedom cannot be restored unless by him who was able to give it. Hence Truth says: “If the Son shall set you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36). Therefore after the fall they cannot be free unless they are set free through the only Son of God.

Let those see what they say—

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Colbert manuscript: “say.”]

—who loudly assert that free choice was given by God equally for good and evil. For it is lost by sinning, and, once lost, is not restored except by grace. Furthermore, when evil is proved to be nothing and good alone is proved to exist, how can freedom of choice be shown to have been given equally for something and for nothing? Yet we concede that it was given simply for both, not in order that it should follow both, but so that, with one rejected, the good may be chosen; as Isaiah says of the Virgin’s Son: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7:15).

VI. QUESTION. I gladly receive what you say concerning free choice. But I confess that I do not yet understand your claim that evil is nothing. For I see murders, robberies, arsons, acts of unchastity everywhere, and the like, constantly committed against the commandment of the divine law or the ordinances of omnipotent justice. Are these not plainly done? Who is so mad as to say that they are nothing?

ANSWER. Certainly no—

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Colbert manuscript: “dear friend.”]

—no variety of things or force of evils can overthrow the divine counsel. Nothing can obstruct the great works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills, possessing one counsel over works varied in many ways [Col. 1169C]. For the immovable moves movable things; the eternal, temporal things; the undivided, divided things; the just, unjust things; the good, evil things. In tranquil equity he orders the wills of rational creatures. He helps and rewards good wills; he restrains and condemns evil ones; he governs both well and orders both. Therefore this world is directed under his omnipotence in a most orderly course, and no injustice is found anywhere, since supreme equity always works good through both the evil and the good.

The power of the wicked is always just, because it is from the Lord; thus “she reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). Their will is always unjust, since it presumes against supreme justice [Col. 1169D]; hence it is in defect. For whatever exists either exists because it is the supreme good, or because it was created by the supreme good. But the supreme good cannot fail in any manner: it is supreme, and whatever exists is from it. What was made by the supreme good, however, is not itself that from which it was made; for it is from nothing. Hence it is in defect unless it adheres to him who supremely is.

Whatever turns away from him who supremely is, then, is itself nonexistent insofar as it falls short of the supreme good in which its being consists. For it to fail is for it not to love him who supremely is. This defect, this evil, belongs to the rational creature alone; and we say that it is not something, but nothing. For it is a falling away or negligence with respect to him whom it ought to love or worship. We properly call this defect, this fault, its evil.

[Evil is indeed committed in diverse ways and therefore receives diverse names, such as robbery, theft, unchastity, and the like. These are so called not because they are actions, but because they are not done rightly.]

VII. QUESTION. I accept well what you have said. But I do not agree that the just makes unjust things and the good makes evil things.

ANSWER. Have you not read that Truth says in the Gospel: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3)? Therefore, if we look to the supreme Maker, everything that is done is done well, whether the human being or angel through whom the Omnipotent works be good or evil [Col. 1170B]. But if the rational creature through whom God acts consents with a good will, it too acts well, and whatever it does is rightly called good.

[Conversely, if the rational will dissents, by refusing, from the supreme Maker who acts through it, it indeed acts badly; yet what it does is something, but because it acts unjustly, whatever it does is called evil.]

Yes, yes: if you remember well, you admit that your animal walks well when it goes where you command. But if it leaves the way upon which you intend it to go, you complain that it walks badly and goes astray—not because it does not walk, but because it deviates. Insofar as it walks, there is an action; insofar as it deviates, it is evil. It is evil because it does not consent to the master acting through it [Col. 1170C] and advancing the creature subjected to him according to his will.

Thus too the supreme—

[Note: [Col. 1170D] Colbert manuscript: “It is nevertheless established that the supreme [Maker].”]

—Maker always works well through whomever he chooses; but sometimes the subject through whom he works does not rightly concur with him. Therefore whatever is done through that subject is called unjust or evil with reference to that subject, although with reference to the supreme author of all things it is proved to be good.

VIII. QUESTION. As I hear you pursue these arguments, I understand that God both is good and does all good things. But when I attend to the holy Scriptures, I see very many things contrary to your assertions; indeed, I scarcely dare say it aloud, but I find that God is contrary to himself. For through the Prophet he says: “Making peace and creating evil: I am the Lord” (Isa. 45:7). Elsewhere: “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 9:12). And the Lord says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up” (Rom. 9:17). Elsewhere too it is written: “There is no evil in a city which the Lord has not done” (Amos 3:6). And other such passages.

ANSWER. We frequently say that he is supremely good, that he created all things well, and that he orders well the things he created. Hence whatever exists is good because it is from him. Every action, therefore, because it is well ordered by the supreme Author, is indeed called good. But because the intention of the agent—I mean of a human being or angel—discords from God, the action is called evil with respect to the evil agent, though it is good with respect to the supreme Maker, who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

He himself continually works good through evildoers, whom he orders well; and, though they act unjustly through an evil will, he who is good always uses them for good. Hence nothing is ever done except justly. Therefore whatever is done through them, though with reference to them it is rightly called evil, is rightly declared by the testimony of the prophets to be done by God himself. Thus, as evildoers are said to do the good which God does through them, so he who is good is said to do evils when he works through evildoers. It is therefore true that nothing whatsoever is done except good, since God works all things through both good and evil persons.

IX. QUESTION. If, as your position says, every action is good, why laws? Why judgments? What do priests correct, and what do authorities punish?

ANSWER. You must know what ought to be done, by whom, why, how, [Col. 1171B] where, and when. If anyone has undertaken something other than what has been established and commanded, that action is found blameworthy and is corrected by the proper office. Individual things are governed by private and public ordinances. The things concerning which an unjust action is undertaken, if you consider rightly, you will find free from fault. Hence you rightly rebuke not things themselves, but injustice in actions concerning things. Justice duly punishes the agent because he acted improperly; it would punish him improperly if the Author had acted properly.

It is surely a great proof of equity that evil nowhere remains unpunished. When unjust acts are justly punished, they themselves proclaim that God’s justice reigns everywhere; under it, those who perform what is just unjustly do not remain unpunished [Col. 1171C]. Remarkable though it is to say, even this is good in evil: that it does not go unpunished.

Your prudence should also know that human justice approves every work in which the ordinance of laws has been observed. For it judges only matters that are manifest, since it does not know the hidden things of hearts. But the supreme Judge judges very differently: he weighs hearts more than works, and approves no work which charity does not commend. Commandments, indeed, vary very often according to differing times and their needs.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] Colbert manuscript: “the commandments of the Son.”]

But in all things God seeks one charity; by it, whatever is done is accepted favourably by God, while without it whatever you do is disapproved.

X. QUESTION. When I consider God’s providence, I find myself thinking contrary to what you have said [Col. 1171D]. For what then? Does not God’s providence, which never errs, precede all things? Does he not make each thing just as he foresaw it? He made angel and human being, and not otherwise than he foresaw. But each fell in accordance with the truth of providence, which foresaw that angel and human being would fall. For God’s providence would not be true if anything happened otherwise than he knew. He therefore foresaw that they would fall. For it could not be otherwise than what was foreseen to be. This proposition is accepted by all without dispute, because God’s providence fails in nothing. Why, then, is the one who fell held guilty?

ANSWER. Divine providence is true, as you maintain; it is true, and individual things truly happen according to it. Therefore, according to God’s providence—

[Note: [Col. 1171] Colbert manuscript: “Therefore according to that same providence.”]

—the rational nature of angel and human being was made, and both were given the capacity for free choice. Thus, as God foresaw, he created each endowed with freedom of choice, a freedom by which angel and human being both ought and were able to act well. If either neglected so great a gift by misusing it, the one who could act well but willed evil is rightly blameworthy.

Having from God the ability for good, one ought not to add an evil will. Because the transgressor added it, he deservedly received, by God’s just judgment, that through willing evil he should lose the ability for good. Thus made captive under an evil will, he grieves that he cannot do what he wishes; if he had remained obedient under God, he could do whatever he wished. Therefore the one who despised the Lord rightly lost the ability for good granted him by the Lord [Col. 1172B], and miserably retained the inability to do what he wished, because he perversely conceived the will to do evil.

He did not therefore fall by necessity. God, who knows all things beforehand, foresaw him as falling not by necessity but by his own will. God’s providence does not make fall the one whom it foresaw as destined to fall through his own defect. He indeed foresaw angels and human beings who would sin, since nothing future is hidden from him. For future things would not be future if they were not in his foreknowledge. Therefore, whatever God foresees as future cannot fail to happen as foreseen; otherwise providence would be deceived.

But among all the things foreseen is the capacity for free choice. Just as God foresaw it, so he gave it to angel and human being. Accordingly, both human being [Col. 1172C] and angel proceed unfettered among all things made, by virtue of their free choice, as long as they use under God the capacity of free choice well. Thus, while retaining the freedom granted them by him, they are not compelled by necessity. But if through negligence they turn away from good, by their own fault they are stripped of freedom and remain slaves under the bond of fault.

XI. QUESTION. How do you say that angel and human being proceed without necessity by virtue of freedom of choice, when all things are under necessity according to the unchangeableness of divine providence? For nothing can happen otherwise than divine providence unfailingly determines.

ANSWER. Necessity is commonly assigned in two ways: one is called simple and the other conditional. Simple necessity is such as: every body is tangible. This is necessary simply, without any condition or qualification. Conditional necessity is such as: when I know someone to be reading, it is necessary that he be reading. I call it necessary not by the nature of the reader but by the addition of a condition. For what you certainly know cannot both be otherwise and be known by you then otherwise. No necessity makes the reader read voluntarily; nevertheless, when I know him to be reading, it is necessary, by the law of the condition, that he is reading.

In the same way, when divine providence beholds something as present, it is necessarily the case at that time, although in the thing seen there may be no necessity of nature. The rational creature [Col. 1173A] is established as free by the nature of its liberty; but if you refer it to the divine gaze, it becomes necessary by the certainty—

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Colbert manuscript: “most certain [constancy].”]

—of divine vision. Things, indeed, although by existing they occur as foreseen and are in no way able to depart from the law of Providence, nonetheless preserve the character of their own freedom: before they occur, they could either not occur or occur otherwise.

XII. QUESTION. What have you said? Can anything happen otherwise than God foresaw it?

ANSWER. Do you not know that a human being or angel who does good through a good will acts not necessarily but voluntarily? If he acts voluntarily, he could refrain from acting; he does not act by necessity. Therefore it could have happened otherwise, yet it does not happen otherwise. For providence remains secure, having foreseen that it would happen thus [Col. 1173B]. I say it happens voluntarily, not by necessity. Therefore it can happen otherwise than God foresaw, and yet it does not happen otherwise.

Accordingly, let no one excuse himself wickedly by saying, “I follow God’s providence. Let no one blame me if I sin. What God has foreseen must necessarily happen.” Rather, you ought to know that divine providence must be understood in such a way that the thing foreseen is also understood. See, therefore, that the freedom of your nature depends upon God’s providence; and do not say that it is altogether subject to necessity because of the certainty of divine providence, since we know that it was made free in its own kind by divine providence. Therefore your sin proceeds from the perversity of your will; Providence does not compel it. Hence you are deservedly blamed.

You should also know that he who created all things together enclosed within the world certain causal principles. He did not subject his power to them, but bound them beneath his power. You know that, by the causes of human nature, a person can proceed from childhood to youth and from youth to old age; but whether this happens depends upon the will above. But the causes which God retained with himself in his will do not depend upon the causes which he implanted in the world. For his counsel, remaining unmoved, sometimes changes the customary course of lower nature.

[This change is that repentance in God by which he says, “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6:6), and similar expressions. They indicate not a passion in God but a change in things, which he changes according to the unmoved firmness of eternal counsel [Col. 1173D].]

The causes which he always possessed in himself cannot be contrary to the causes which he arranged in things by his will. For the divine will, unchangeable and everlasting, cannot be contrary to itself. It so implanted causes in the world that from them that of which they are causes may be, but need not be; just as from a flower a certain fruit follows causally, but it need not follow. But the causes which he always possessed in himself, from which he makes lower things, are so unmoved that, from those higher causes, it must be that which he made possible from these lower causes [Col. 1174A] should be.

Thus the Creator’s omnipotence has, above the natural course of things, the power within itself to make from all things something other than that which the original course or customary principle of the creature contains within itself. Yet he does not make from things what cannot possibly be made from them. Hence Moses’ rod could suddenly become a serpent, and the serpent a rod. Hence Aaron’s rod, without shoot, soil, or moisture, could suddenly flower and bear fruit. Hence an old and barren woman is made fertile; hence an ass speaks. For in the things he created he reserves to himself the power to make these and like things from them, as he himself knows. He would not make such things from them unless he had ordained that they could be so made from them.

The Omnipotent, therefore, possesses within himself the free efficacies of his works; he does all that he wills and orders what he has made according to his will [Col. 1174B]. In this class is the grace by which sinners are saved. So far as concerns their iniquity, by which they voluntarily corrupt themselves, they have no means of return by which they may be healed unless divine medicine comes to their aid. Hence the Apostle says: “It is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”; and, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:16).

XIII. QUESTION. From this apostolic authority which you cite, my opinion—which you had weakened—has gained great strength. For I see, according to the Apostle, that freedom of choice is nothing, but only the will of God, which does good to whom it wills and rejects whom it wills.

RESP. Whom do I hear you say this? I strongly reproach you for having forgotten what we have said. Tell me, I pray, what does the authority of the divine utterances admonish and entreat us to do? What does it command and forbid, correct and rebuke, instruct and strengthen? In us, indeed, when we go astray and fall away from God through a contrary will, the fault weighs down the power of rational choice, but does not utterly take it away. Hence, because it errs, it is rightly blamed. Did you not hear above that, among all things made, the rational creature excels? It received free choice from its Creator, by which it ought to love above all things Him who formed it by His laws

[Note: [Col. 1173D] Colbert: “who loved it by His laws; and, since it is something other than Himself, it did not, by loving another, look away. Hence it does not turn aside toward itself, but in the constancy of love it perpetually loves that which is highest.” Then all that follows is wanting down to these words of Book IV, Question IX: “Hence it is that from the beginning fault did not touch [him],” etc.],

to whom the Lord gave commandments, which it itself, according to the reason by which it excels, judges ought to be kept; and which, having so judged, it ought to keep and was free to keep, with the help of Him who gave it, from whom it had both being and ability.

If we lose this freedom by sinning, we cannot restore it to ourselves; rather, we need the grace of God, which alone can raise those who have fallen and, once raised, restore their former freedom. Hence the Apostle rightly says: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” The rational power of choice remains for condemnation—I mean in those who, by sinning, lose its freedom. It itself indeed bears witness that a person is justly condemned by the God whom he unjustly deserted, since the very torments compel him to reckon what a difference there is between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.

But if heavenly grace at some time looks upon you in your sins, receive, so far as lies in you, the One who calls; present yourself as wretched to Him who has mercy. He will restore to you, if He wills, the freedom by which you may rise to justification. If you hear Him calling, He who called will not fail you; He has never failed anyone. He who called you while fleeing will receive you when you return. By stretching out His hand He raises the fallen, unless the fallen person turns himself away; He heals the sick, unless he flees; He glorifies the healthy, unless he falls away. But if we misuse His goods and remain ungrateful for His benefits, in a final just judgment He hardens us: we are abandoned by God. We find the cause of this in ourselves, for by sinning we ourselves have deserved it. But if we are lifted up by His mercy, we rightly marvel at the grace bestowed on us. For the cause by which we are saved freely lies in Him, not in ourselves; we did not deserve it.

According to these causes the Lord is recorded to have said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. IX.13), although, as the Apostle testifies (ibid. 11), before they were born they had done nothing either good or evil. Therefore, that He loves Jacob is grace; that He hates Esau is justice, since both were born under original guilt. But why grace chooses this one rather than that, the Apostle does not explain, but cries out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways!” (Rom. XI.33.) What then? “He has mercy on whom He wills”: this is grace. What? “Whom He wills He hardens”: this is justice. The cause by which we are condemned we have and bear within ourselves. But the cause by which we are saved we behold and praise not in ourselves, but in God. “[Col. 1175C] For He is the one who wills all people to be saved” (I Tim. II.4).

XIV. QUESTION. What is this that you have said? How does He will all people to be saved when He does not save all? We see a multitude of evil people perish; we scarcely find any good people.

RESPONSE. We understand this saying thus: all whom He wills are saved. For no one can be saved unless He wills it. Therefore one must pray to Him; for He will save if He wills. Accordingly the Apostle urges that prayer be made for all, especially for kings; and he says that this is good before God our Saviour. “For as all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ.” You must not say that all those dying in Adam are made alive in Christ; rather, just as all who remain in Adam—that is, in Adam’s transgression—die, so all who remain in Christ—that is, in Christ’s justification—shall be made alive. He said “all” and “all,” because no one comes into death except through the former, and no one comes into life except through the latter.

Thus understand that He saves all whom He wills to be saved. Yet if we refer the statement, “He wills all people to be saved,” to charity, it may be investigated more subtly. We read that God commands that a person love his neighbour as himself. Therefore he must first love himself; for one who does not love himself does not love his neighbour as himself. But he loves himself if he loves God. For he is from God, and he owes to his Creator the very fact that he is. If, then, he loves that which he himself is, he necessarily loves Him without whom that which he is cannot be, and, when that One is loved, that which he is is good; but when He is not loved, that which he is is not even good.

Before all things, therefore, he owes love to God, from whom, through whom, and in whom he has being; then to himself, yet not in himself but in Him from whom he has being and by loving whom he has a good being; afterward to his neighbour according to himself, since, by loving God, he loves himself. And according to the manner in which he loves himself, he is commanded to love his neighbour. Because of these degrees of love it is aptly said in the Song of Songs (II.4): “Set love in order within me.” For by the order of charity the true lover rightly proceeds from God down to himself, from himself down to his neighbour, and from his neighbour returns to God. This is the threefold cord which, as Solomon testifies, “is not quickly broken.” In this present life it is difficult to break; in the eternal life it will be impossible. For here charity is begun in us while we are subject to mutability; when this has at last been laid aside, charity will be perfected in us.

This is the ladder which the patriarch Jacob saw set up from earth to heaven: he recognizes it as begun here and to be completed there. He walks it rightly who loves God, himself, and his neighbour for God’s sake. If he loves for another reason, he has abandoned the ladder. The more vigorously he advances, the more deeply he falls. But the true lover who walks upon the straight ladder of charity does all things well by loving God, whatever he loves; and whatever the wicked do against God or concerning God is good for him. Hear the Apostle’s testimony: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. VIII.28). Therefore whoever has charity has all things cooperating toward salvation.

Accordingly, whoever loves himself with charity loves himself unto salvation; and when, at God’s command, he loves his neighbour as himself, he surely loves his neighbour also unto salvation. Since every human being is naturally our neighbour, when we love our neighbour, we love every human being unto salvation. Therefore whoever loves all unto salvation truly wills all people to be saved. And he rightly says that God wills this, since God has commanded him to will it. For God would not command it if He did not will it at all. It is also evident that God wills this because, by inspiring them, He makes His own people will the same thing. Hence Paul says: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. V.5).

The proto-martyr Abel possessed this love when he pleased God by offering worthily; but Cain, being devoid of it when he presumed to offer, deserved to be rejected. Nor did the man possess it who did not blush at his father’s nakedness but mocked it; therefore he was deservedly consigned, along with his descendants, to slavery. His brothers, however, having charity, knew how to cover their father’s shameful parts but did not know how to see them; and by their father’s blessing they rightly remained free. Joseph was destroyed by his brothers’ envy, but the charity of the one destroyed later saved his destroyers. Phinehas, in the fervour of charity, struck down the fornicators, and in anger appeased the Lord’s wrath. This charity, if you consider it carefully, is the fiery chariot in which Elijah was taken up to heaven. This charity is also that spirit which Elisha asked to receive twofold from Elijah.

XV. QUESTION. Elisha was neither so great nor did such great deeds that he should be thought Elijah’s equal, much less his superior. Tell me, then, if you know, in what manner Elijah’s spirit was twofold in Elisha.

RESPONSE. If carefully considered, Elijah’s spirit is believed to have been twofold in Elijah himself. For a twofold spirit is shown to exist in prophets and in all perfected persons, by which God and neighbour are loved by them. The disciple was therefore right to ask this twofold spirit from his master, and, having been proved by perseverance, he received it. For Elijah answered him thus: “If you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked shall be yours” (IV Kings II.10). But Elisha did not leave him even through the arduous pursuit. He persevered, saw, and received—not, we say, twice as much as Elijah, but such as Elijah had. The sons of the prophets said of this: “The spirit of Elijah has rested upon Elisha” (ibid. 15). Elijah had it twofold; Elisha received it twofold. We call it twofold because by it we love God and neighbour.

For if Elisha had presumed to be greater than Elijah and had asked that Elijah’s spirit be doubled within him, he ought rather to have been refused. But since he humbly desired to possess Elijah’s charity, he deservedly obtained what he sought by his devout request. But if, in devotion, Elisha wished the grace of Elijah to be doubled in himself, by devotion he deserved to receive twice what he sought. This is the Spirit which the Lord Jesus pours twofold into those who dwell on earth. Hence the giver of so great a gift—something which you must indeed confess most fully—is most rightly both God and man. Remaining God, one in essence with God the Father, He is one person with humanity. He is Emmanuel, born of Mary, whom not corruption of the flesh but the integrity of the Holy Spirit made fruitful. Thus she herself first received this twofold Spirit at the angel’s greeting, and in her integrity bore Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings.

He who was born of the Virgin is the stone cut out from the mountain without hands; not a fleshly embrace but the affection of charity begot Him. Hence the Virgin conceived; a virgin she remained whole in childbirth and after childbirth. Eve, a corrupted mother, bore a son of death; Mary, an intact mother, bore and brought forth the fruit of life. The former lost; the latter saved. The former consented to the devil and fell; the latter received the Holy Spirit and rose. For the true God, born of the Virgin together with assumed humanity, drew His origin from Adam—not the transmission of guilt; from our substance He took poverty, and from His own He gives us glory. He gave what was His and received what was ours.

The first human being received in paradise a commandment by which the created one ought to serve his Creator, so that by obeying he might retain righteousness, and, living in righteousness, pass into glory. But when by a hasty course he sought glory, he broke the righteousness of obedience and, falling into guilt, passed from guilt into the misery of death. The second man, whom the Virgin bore, the restorer of the world, descending from on high in order to raise us up, was found in lowliness. Hence the Apostle says: “Though He was in the form of God, He did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized; but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II.6).

When the author of death unlawfully seized Him, he was lawfully conquered through His undeserved death. For death could not hold Him whom guilt had not held. Our death, since we have sinned, is the penalty for sin; the Redeemer’s undeserved death is the sacrifice for sin, by which He frees from death those whom He releases from guilt. Sin is the way that draws to death; righteousness is the way that leads to life. The devil, the evil mediator who suggests sin and conveys into death, laid out the former; Christ, the good mediator who restores righteousness and leads to life, raises up the latter.

For in like manner the angel in heaven and the first-formed human being in paradise despised God through their own pride; hence the former deservedly lost heaven and the latter paradise. But he fell most grievously who not only cast himself down from heaven, but also, by deceiving humanity, drew it after himself down from paradise. For the former discovered sin; the latter received it from its discoverer. Therefore the supreme Judge condemned that plunderer forever, but mercifully raised up the plundered one in the manner He willed. The Son of God, who could not be plundered, took our nature, yet free from guilt; and He chose to become prey for us, in order to plunder the plunderer. Therefore, when the ancient plunderer unjustly seized Him, he deserved justly to be plundered by the mightiest plunderer, who held him fast, crushed him, and brought our captivity forth free from his impious hand. For by His passion we are redeemed, by His resurrection raised up, and by His ascension glorified. This mystery, ordained from eternity, entrusted to angels, hidden from the devil, revealed to prophets, was accomplished in Mary, received by the Church, and completed in glory. Amen.

## THE FOURTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1177]

[Col. 1177D] I. O wondrous immensity of the divine majesty! Since no exalted height can attain Your infinite loftiness, humility alone always ascends to You. For, in a marvellous manner, pride cannot find Him though He is everywhere, while humility comprehends Him though He is infinitely sublime. Hence only the humble receive His humble coming in the flesh; the proud do not recognize it. Pride and humility have always thought contrary things from the beginning and flee from one another. This is that irrevocable dissension which has separated angels from the world’s beginning. In some humility reigns; in others pride holds dominion. Some advance through humility; others fail through pride. They are distinguished neither by author, nor beginning, nor nature, but they think differently, are carried away from one another by different pursuits, and are drawn apart by different affections.

The charity of the humble seeks the Lord so exclusively that for His sake it even despises itself; but the covetousness of the proud loves itself so exclusively that it despises even the Lord before itself. Therefore, that we may be raised to the Lord, we must imitate the charity of the humble; but lest we fall from the Lord, we must utterly avoid the ambition of the proud. As the Gospel testifies, the tax collector advanced in the temple through humility, whereas the Pharisee fell away from good through pride (Luke XVIII).

II. QUESTION. How so? Did not that Pharisee acknowledge to the Lord, rather than to himself, the good things that he possessed and give thanks? Was he not glad that he differed from sinners? What did he lack, who both turned away from evils and did good, and for this gave thanks to the Lord?

RESPONSE. It is true that he lived rightly, and joyfully attributed this not to himself but to the Lord; hence he gave thanks. Yet, looking outside himself, he fell through pride when he presumed to judge the tax collector and proudly preferred himself to one whose character he did not know. Swollen with pride, he judged another’s servant; and the exalted man condemned as guilty one whom the Lord had justified when humble. You will see this plainly if you carefully consider at what degree of humility the tax collector stood and by what form of pride the Pharisee, lifted up, fell.

III. QUESTION. Please explain to me briefly what degrees humility has and what falls pride has.

RESPONSE. I have learned that there are four swellings of pride, by which, miserable as I am, I confess that I have very often fallen.

There are some arrogant people whom pride has so intoxicated that, although they themselves truly possess no trace either of knowledge or of any virtue, they utterly despise others who are wise and abound in virtues as though they were nothing, and falsely display themselves as alone having worth. This is mad pride, which has no ground at all for exalting itself. This is the first, utterly detestable fall of pride; Satan first discovered it when he falsely said: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.14). Against this grave precipice of swelling there comes the first and best remedy of humility: that a person pays no attention at all to the virtues he truly possesses, sets his own weaknesses before himself, and recognizes himself before the Lord as nothing but a sinner. From this valley of humility that tax collector rose, who was afraid even to lift his eyes to heaven. He knew only his sins in himself, and in repentance said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke XVIII.13).

Likewise, there are some who receive from the supreme Giver certain marks of virtue, but through the swelling of pride have arrived at such folly that they boast of what they have received as if they had not received it, and obstinately judge that it should be attributed to themselves rather than to the Lord. Of such people the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts; for, claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I.21). Humility expels such persons; although it possesses good things, it judges that nothing among what has been received is to be attributed to its own effort or nature, but humbly assigns them to God, the giver of every good. Hence Paul cries: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV.10).

Likewise, there are some who attribute their good things to God, not themselves, but who insolently maintain that God owed them these things on account of their merits. Against such people humility declares that from God’s fullness we have all received, and grace for grace. Even if among the good things received we have certain merits, they too are rightly called grace, since they too were given to us freely by God, who freely rewards His own gifts in the saints. Hence the Apostle says: “Who has first given to Him, and shall be repaid? For all things are from Him and through Him. To Him be glory” (Rom. II.35).

Likewise, there are some who, although they attribute all their good things and whatever merits of good they possess equally to God and give thanks, nevertheless, when they despise others before themselves and judge persons they do not know—persons who, as the Apostle says, stand or fall before the Lord (Rom. XIV.4)—fall back through presumption into pride and are stripped of their garment of righteousness. This is the fourth fall of pride, by which that Pharisee fell. He did possess good things and recognized that what he possessed came from God, and so rendered thanksgiving; but when he proudly presumed before God to judge a neighbour whom he did not know, he remained empty of righteousness and full of pride.

Humility, however, not only recognizes that its own good things and merits of good have been bestowed by God; it also thinks well of its neighbours, while setting before God nothing concerning itself but weakness. You too, warned by these matters, return devoutly to the Lord, that through Him you may return from the falls of pride and through the steps of humility come to Him—from whom pride always flees and to whom humility always approaches. The Saviour gives the latter from heaven, that we may ascend; the destroyer raises the former from hell, that we may fall.

IV. QUESTION. What are these things? What, I pray, is the pride that you blame? What is the humility that you praise? What is the charity that you commend? What is the covetousness that you detest?

RESPONSE. Charity is an advance of the mind by which it loves God and all things in God. Conversely, covetousness is a falling away from charity, by which it loves neither God nor anything in God. Charity, therefore, is the first of all virtues; covetousness the first of all vices. Humility and goodwill accompany charity; pride and envy follow covetousness. Humility is contempt for one’s own excellence out of love for God. Pride, on the other hand, is contempt for God out of love for one’s own excellence. Goodwill is love for another’s benefit, whereas envy does not cease to disparage the good things of others. As charity is the parent of all good things, so covetousness is the root of all evils. Accordingly, divine authorities command that charity alone be kept and show that covetousness alone must be fled. We are recalled from the latter and restored in the former. Whatever is done through the latter is condemned, while whatever you do through the former is approved.

For covetousness nourishes unbelief, induces despair, and, when the course of present wickedness is completed, remains unsatisfied unto destruction. Charity, by contrast, brings forth the virtue of faith, cherishes the firmness of hope, and, when the present time has passed, remains full unto blessedness. These two, opposed to one another from the beginning, establish two kingdoms. In the good angels charity obtained a kingdom; in the perverse, covetousness took its beginning. In its own, charity is the foundation of obedience, advance toward good, approach to God, garden of goodness, and fullness of happiness. Conversely, in its own, covetousness is the origin of transgression, falling away from good, fall from God, gathering of malice, and completion of misery.

In the holy angels, charity, making good use of free choice, steadfastly adhered to the Lord. Therefore the Psalm’s words pre-eminently apply to it: “But it is good for me to adhere to God and to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXII.27).
