And elsewhere: “That I may see the delight of the Lord” (Ps. XXVI.4). Thus the holy society of angels, made very good in nature by the supreme Good, is good; but when it wholly accords, by the free choice of charity, with the good will of its Creator, then by virtue it becomes better than itself. Through virtue it transcends nature and remains ordered with the Lord by grace. For in proportion as charity stretched out toward God raises each one, so the measured sublimity of rank bestowed by God lifts that one up.

Therefore it should be known that the nine orders of angels are distinguished by God according to the merit of charity. To them He added also the tenth drachma, namely human nature, which retained its order until, disordered by the disorderly, it fell. Yet He who created it sought it when lost, found it when sought, and carried it back on His shoulders when found. But he who was a liar from the beginning lacked charity: neglecting truth, he falsely said, “I shall be like the Most High.” Since he had no charity, he neither was an order nor fell from the orders, which are distinguished by the measure of charity. We nevertheless allow that it can be said that he fell from the order and fell from blessedness—not from those which he had, or among which he was, but from those which, by loving God, he could have had or among which he could have been.

For he could have done so because he was good in nature and received from God the good of free choice, by which he might be perfected in God. He received this good from the supreme Good in order that he might be good; but, abusing the capacity of the gift, he wished to have glory in himself rather than in God, and falsely said: “I shall set my throne toward the north; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV.14). This is covetousness, which flowed away from God and, an impious mother, brought forth her worst firstborn—pride, I mean—by which he presumed to become like the Most High. This is that firstborn of the Egyptians whom the Lord slew, and thus He was able to lead back His people.

So indeed, beloved, however many vices a person destroys within himself, unless this most evil firstborn, called pride, utterly perishes in him, he cannot freely go forth to God or depart from the regions of the north. But when the Lord kills the firstborn of Egypt within us, He requires that our firstborn be offered to Him. By our firstborn we mean Christ. For He is the firstborn of the dead, in whom we who died in Adam are reborn to life; without Him we rightly offer nothing.

V. QUESTION. You have well shown that the firstborn of the Egyptians must be put to death and that Christ, the firstborn of the Church, must continually be offered. But I wonder at your prudent opinion concerning the angel: that he was not an order or in an order. For the prophet Ezekiel, describing him, says: “You were the seal of the likeness of God, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of God’s paradise” (Ezek. XXVIII.12–13). How was he not in blessedness, when the same prophet says that he was in the delights of God’s paradise? How is he called a liar from the beginning, when the same prophet says of him: “You walked perfect in your ways from the day of your creation” (or, as it is said elsewhere, “in your days without fault”), “until iniquity was found in you”? (ibid. 15).

RESPONSE. Such words, and others like them, are sometimes spoken by the prophets concerning the king of Tyre, sometimes concerning the king of Babylon or Egypt. Yet ecclesiastical teachers, as you also think, wish them to be understood figuratively of Satan and his companions. In order to expound them more freely, let us refer them not so much to the prince of wickedness himself as to his members who apostasize from Christ and the Church.

For there are certain heretics who, after acknowledging the truth, openly fall away from Christ and from the Church. There are others who, though they are not bodily severed from the Church, are separated by their life: namely, those who, after Christ has forgiven their sins, fall back into vices and occupy themselves with crimes. These received the seal of God’s likeness in baptism and received the Spirit of wisdom through the bishop’s laying on of hands; they professed the perfection of apostolic life in God’s paradise—that is, in the present Church—and remained without fault from the day of their restoration in baptism, until, turning aside from righteousness, they returned to sins. Therefore they are rightly condemned, separated from the Church, and plunged into Tartarus.

There are also some who, not knowing how to discern how those prophetic words apply both to the head of wickedness and to his members, hastily turn to the opinion that two kinds of angels were created by God: one, supercelestial, from which none fell; the other, worldly, subject to those supercelestial beings for certain mysteries. Among these worldly angels, they say, some pass into blessedness for deeds rightly done, while others incur condemnation for evil deeds. But no authority of Holy Scripture tells us of these two kinds.

The divine utterances do indeed testify that the apostate angel is called “the beginning of the Lord’s creation,” not because God created him before all things. For we read: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. LXXXI.1). He is called “the beginning of the Lord’s creation,” not because God made him an evil beginning, He who made all things very good. He is called the beginning of the Lord’s creation as though it said: “The Lord made this creature in the beginning”; or thus: “This beginning—that is, this thing begun, for that which has a beginning is not eternal—belongs to the Lord’s creation.” That is: the Lord made it.

Therefore the Almighty nevertheless willed to create him good by nature, though destined to become evil by his own will, so that He Himself, being good, might use that evil being for the good of the good. For He foreknew that he would be useful to the saints, although ill-willed and unwilling. Hence the Psalmist testifies: “This dragon which You formed to be mocked by him” (Ps. CIII.26). That is, that he might be mocked by God’s angels. For that evil one is subjected by God to the good angels, so that they may mock his wickedness, since he cannot do as much as he strives to do, but only as much as he is permitted. Thus he serves God unwillingly, ministers to the good angels under compulsion, and renders service also to holy people, though hostilely.

A marvellous miracle concerning him is therefore evident, and a pleasing spectacle for the good. For while he strives to harm the saints, he is compelled to benefit them by tempting them. Yet he is evil to himself and good to others, since he does nothing but good and does nothing except wickedly. He is therefore rightly called a beginning made for mockery: God so formed—that is, ordered—him that his malice might be mocked; and because of his savagery he is called a dragon. He may also be called a beginning made for mockery because he is the beginning of all malice. This is rightly said because evil people follow him as evil members. He precedes them both by antiquity of time and by primacy in malice.

They too were made to be mocked, in God’s good providence for the benefit of the saints. When they wish to harm, their hostility provides the saints with caution; the more these people’s impiety oppresses the saints, the more godly humility under God lifts the saints up. While the former vomit heretical poisons, the latter shine with the grace of divine understanding; for the latter have a devout exercise through enduring evils and a holy trial through discerning enemies. Therefore Almighty God rightly created those whom He foresaw would become evil, since He knows and is able to make good use of their malice. He so ordered them by laws of justice that He makes them serve the saints and, according to the desert of their ill will, subjects them to everlasting punishments.

[Col. 1183D] VI. QUESTION. If you please, do not be unwilling to explain to us the prophetic words mentioned above, and how they apply to Satan himself.

RESPONSE. We read that the human being was made in the likeness of God, but that the angel was made the seal of the likeness of God. It is therefore evident that the angel possessed such excellence in nature that a human being could see in him, as in a seal, how much he owed to his Creator, who deigned to create him like Himself; the human could contemplate in the angel the exceeding dignity of that likeness. This seal remains whole for us in the angel who stood; in the one who fell we see it obscured. By the constitution of his nature, he was made full of wisdom and perfect in beauty. For, as regards the good constitution implanted in him by God—who made nothing imperfect—that rational or intellectual creature received fully from God every perfection which it ought to possess in the good nature in which it was created.

But it is one thing for God to make a creature full in nature and perfect according to the measure of a good constitution; it is another for a creature already perfect in nature to be raised above itself by charity and, through the merit of charity, be perfected in blessedness according to the measure of grace in Him who supremely is. Therefore that ill-willed being fell away from the perfection which he had in nature because he did not love his Creator; while the choir of heavenly citizens which uniquely loved the Lord ascended gloriously from it.

The perfection of that angelic creature, in the perfection in which it was created by God, is indeed itself complete; but its perfection, by which it adheres through charity to Him who supremely is, is most complete. Great indeed is the praise of the Creator, who made the intellectual creature so beautiful and also granted it the free capacity of choice, by which it could be raised to Him who supremely is and happily enjoy His charity. But it is a great disgrace to so excellent a creature that it refused to love Him who made it so good, so perfect, and so beautiful.

God is the universal good—full, perfect, singular, and supreme. Mad covetousness prefers some private thing to this universal good when it raises itself to seize what is not due and does not preserve what is its own. For it does not know how to preserve what it possesses, since it knows only how to covet what has not been granted. It forgets its own things while always pursuing what belongs to another. What it held slips from its hand while, intemperate, it hastens to seize other things. This fugitive from the light of charity always pursues wandering paths in darkness; and it is always liable to fall, since, always running, it does not know how to plant its foot anywhere.

Accordingly, it deservedly fell away from the perfection of blessedness, which is God—not a blessedness which it possessed, but one which it could have possessed and neglected. It also fell away from the perfection of the most excellent nature which it received in its creation, because it did not lovingly hold fast to Him who uniquely and truly is, and to whom it owes the fact that it is.

VII. QUESTION. What do you mean? How did he not possess blessedness, when, as the prophet testifies, he was in the delights of God’s paradise?

**Response.** Just as the first man was placed in the bodily paradise so that, by keeping there the justice of due obedience, he might afterwards enter the paradise of blessedness enjoyed by the blessed angels, having been proved in the justice of obedience: so that angel first received from God the Creator the whole fullness of a good created condition—which it befits an intellectual nature to possess—as the delights of the paradise of God, in order that, using freedom of choice well, he might by love attain to him who is the one and all-good of all things, as to the paradise of paradises. He is the supreme blessedness, which, once possessed, it is not lawful to lose. For it is altogether full and perfect. But he would not come to it by the way of love; scorning [Col. 1185A] what belongs in common to all, he presumed to possess something as his own. Hence he too is thrust back from the common good to what is his own—that is, from truth to falsehood.

Because he did not fear to lie to God, Truth rightly says of him in the Gospel: “He was a liar from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). Thus John also says: “The devil sins from the beginning” (1 John 3:2). Do not understand this to mean that the devil had an evil beginning, for God made him good, he who made all things very good. He was therefore not a liar from the beginning of creation, as though being evil belonged to him from creation, but from the beginning of sin. For he first committed sin; hence he is called a liar and its father—its, that is, falsehood’s—for he discovered falsehood when it did not exist.

Therefore do not suppose that this being was created evil by the good Creator; we know that he fell from good through his own iniquity. Otherwise he is falsely said to have fallen, if he was evil from his creation. For God does not condemn the nature which he created, but condemns the wickedness of the creature which he did not make. Indeed, it would be contrary to supreme truth if Truth itself condemned what it had created. Yet the authority of the Gospel shows that the devil is condemned together with all his followers, where we read most plainly: “Depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). It is therefore clear that he is justly condemned, whom the Lord knows must be punished for his own iniquity.

For he was created good by the good Creator, but at once turned away by his own will, corrupted by blind desire, swollen with pride and madness. He neither tasted the blessedness of angelic peace nor disdained a blessedness once possessed which he lost by refusing it; for he did not attain either the wisdom of God or that of the blessed spirits, blinded as he was by exalted desire. Thus, being immediately impious and consequently blind in mind as soon as he fell, he could neither have foreknowledge of his fall nor fall from a blessedness which he possessed. Rather, he failed to obtain that which he could have possessed, had he chosen in due love to submit to the Lord; because he refused it, he deserved condemnation.

Yet he did not escape, even unwillingly, the power of the Almighty, under whom in pride he had refused to be. In him there occurred a wondrous marvel: although he cannot at all hide from the light of justice, he does not rejoice in that justice which he cannot escape, and which he is rightly said not to see, since he is known not to love it though it is present everywhere. [Col. 1185D]

**VIII. Question.** If, as you say, he was not blessed, what is the meaning of what is read: “Every precious stone was his covering” (Ezek. 28:14)?

**Response.** The prophet wished, in order to show his fall to have been more grievous, to speak highly of his glory, saying what he could have been but perversely refused to be. By the precious stones we understand the holy angels. Had this one remained with them—as he certainly could freely have done under God—then without doubt all their glory would, through mutual love, have been his. But if every precious stone is said to have been his covering because God made him brighter than others in nature according to his created condition, then [Col. 1186A] he is the more blameworthy for lacking the grace of love. For the more he received from God, the more he ought to have loved him.

**IX. Question.** What do you mean? Did he not, as the prophet says, walk without blemish in his days?

**Response.** What is read, that he “walked without blemish in his days,” or what is elsewhere said, that he “walked perfect in his ways,” must be understood in the same sense: namely, that he first received from God a good day of his creation; and, immediately upon being created, he received from God a second day of freedom in rational choice, by which he could do all things with God and, bearing such great gifts of grace, could become a participant in eternal glory.

But he scorned his Creator without warrant and did not love the giver of such great gifts, when he presumed to set his own throne in the north [Col. 1186B]; thus he did not at all attain the order of love. Therefore God, who foreknew that he would become a sinner not by nature but through his own negligence, justly predestined him for punishment. God would punish him unjustly if he had predestined him to sin. Certainly, just as God is not the author of evils, so he predestines no one to sin. For he is the predestiner only of those things of which he is the author. Although he predestines sinners to punishment, he must not be thought to predestine them to guilt. For God’s foreknowledge is not the cause of sin; rather, the sinner’s desire is. Though, then, he foresees that someone will sin, he does not predestine that person to sin.

For God’s predestining his own things is the same as preparing them. As he predestines sinners to punishment, he is not to be thought to predestine them to fault. For if he were the author of fault, neither would he be a just inflicter of punishment. But he justly predestines for punishment those whom he foresees will become unjust through guilt. He also predestines his own to glory, just as he predestines them to righteousness. In the latter he glorifies his own gifts; in the former he condemns their evils.

For the predestination of heavenly glory, so that the elect person may attain it, has been arranged by the Almighty in such a way that whoever, during the time granted to him, passes by the way of righteousness to that glory, may receive what God foresaw before the ages that he would give to his own: by receiving the sacraments, praying, and doing good works. His will is the necessity of things. For whatever God wills to be cannot fail to be.

By his simple knowledge he sees all things in such a way that knowledge of individual things remains with him equally present and immovable. He does not therefore foresee them as future, since without change he sees all things together as present. Hence that knowledge which he has of things should more properly be called providence than foreknowledge: by it he looks without confusion upon things which are present and stable in himself, but future and changeable in the condition of time. He sees all things indeed with a surpassing gaze, not with temporal sight, but beholding each thing in his own eternity. [Col. 1186D]

The blessed company of angels chose before all else to behold this unchangeable knowledge of the Creator. Hence, although their nature is changeable, they do not incur the reproach of changeability: without any interval of time, as soon as they were made, so soon did they love their Maker with untiring love. Though each is something other than God, it loves nothing other than God; therefore it does not bend back toward itself, but loves perpetually, with the steadfastness of love, that which is supreme. Thus fault did not touch them from the beginning, nor did any stain of transgression darken them. Knowing no darkness by which to fall, but surpassing all things in the free course of love, they contemplate the Lord alone and embrace his will both for themselves and for all, glorying in his perpetual vision.

Conversely, the apostate angel, turning toward the depths from the beginning of his created existence, did not stand in the truth. He did not attain the blessed life of the blessed angels, but fell under the weight of his own desire and incurred the misery of everlasting calamity.

**X. Question.** What cause, I beg you, did this wickedness have? [Col. 1187B] Tell me, I pray, from where did it proceed? If I look to God, he is good. If I consider creation, it too is wholly good, as you yourself maintain. From this wickedness, whose cause I seek yet do not find, I see infinite evils arise.

**Response.** This cause which you seek, if you consider carefully, is none at all. It is not an effect but a defect: a falling away from that which is good to that which is not good, or from that which supremely is to that which is less. When the will fails in this way, it turns not toward evils but badly toward goods. For no thing is evil; every thing is good insofar as it is. But it turns badly because, contrary to the order of nature or to the ordinance of justice, it turns [Col. 1187C] away from him who supremely is and loves a lesser good.

You should know that when the will departs from the good, it inclines toward nothing. For you can find nothing if you neglect to hold the good apart from which there is nothing. One neglects to hold the good who, whatever he may hold, does not hold it for the good. This happens when a creature does not render to the Creator what is due, or when it neglects to hold what the supreme author commanded it to hold.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Colb. reads *actor*, “author/agent.”]

If you strive to find the cause of this negligence or defect, then you will be able to do so when you are able to see darkness [Note: [Col. 1187D] Another reading: “you seek.”] and hear silence. But darkness is not seen, nor silence heard, except by not seeing and not hearing. With the eyes one may in some manner perceive darkness, and with the ears silence, yet not as a form but as the deprivation of a form. Likewise, we behold with the understanding of the mind the forms of intelligible things which we know. But where these fail, we know as though by not knowing, and by knowing we do not know.

For example, when we perceive that a person’s soul has wisdom, we discern intellectually in it the form of wisdom. But if wisdom fails in that soul, when you call it foolish, you do not place anything in it through “foolishness”; rather, through “foolishness” you declare that wisdom is absent from it. [Col. 1187D]

**XI. Question.** What are you saying? Are “folly,” “silence,” “evil,” and similar words uttered in vain when someone speaks them? Why do they sound if they signify nothing?

**Response.** You should know that some words signify by naming or indicating some thing; others signify not by positing, but rather by removing, some thing. For example, the word “goodness” signifies its object by naming or indicating it. But “wickedness,” properly speaking, signifies that goodness is absent. Evil or wickedness, moreover, takes various names: falsehood, fornication, adultery, and very many such things. The things designated by these words are so called not because they exist, but because they are not goods; just as evil is called evil not because it is, but because it is not good.

Falsehood is called a deprivation of truth; fornication, a loss [Note: [Col. 1188D] Colb.: “absence.”] [Col. 1188B] of chastity; adultery, a violation of marital fidelity; and so forth. We cannot enumerate the words which we know signify not by positing but by removing: blindness, deafness [Note: [Col. 1188D] Colb. lacks “deafness.”], nakedness, poverty, “I am silent,” “I do not wish,” “I am foolish,” “I do not know,” and similar expressions.

You must therefore take the greatest care that, when someone disputes with you in pursuit or display of truth, you do not permit him to use such words to posit some thing. For if you permit this, he can quickly draw you into an absurdity.

**XII. Question.** If you please, demonstrate this by some example.

**Response.** Let someone set out an argument and say: “Whatever exists, God made.” Let him then add: “But evil exists.” Let him conclude: “Therefore God made evil.” And let him further infer that, if God made evil, then not all things which he made are good; or, if he made every good thing when evil exists, then he did not make all things.

From these few points you should infer that, if the word “wickedness” and similar utterances, with your assent, posit things by signifying them, they may prove infinite absurdities, though falsely. Yet from words which signify only by removal and name nothing—such as “wickedness,” “blindness,” “nakedness,” and the like—when we form derivatives, such as “wicked,” “blind,” and “naked,” these derivatives do name certain things; but in the things they name they principally represent that those things do not possess what their primitive terms indicate by removing rather than naming.

Thus “wicked,” when it names an angel or a human being, principally represents that goodness is not present in them—the goodness which “wickedness” indicates not by naming but by removing. For when I say “wickedness,” it is as though I said “not-goodness,” just as “man” and “not-man,” or “justice” and “injustice.” [Col. 1188D]

Observe also that, when someone asks whether “evil” signifies something, if he is discussing the primitive term, then insofar as it names nothing, it signifies nothing. [As with “blindness” and other such terms. But if he asks about the derivative term, it is true that it signifies that which it names.] Know, therefore, that all derivatives, in the things which they name, principally represent either the presence of what their primitive terms signify by positing, or the absence of what their primitive terms signify by removing. [Col. 1189A] For since “justice” signifies its object by positing it, “just,” too, in the things which it names principally represents justice as present. Conversely, since “blindness” signifies by removing sight, “blind,” in the things which it names, principally represents sight as absent. Thus derivatives, in the things which they name, represent either the presence or absence of something, just as their primitive terms indicate things by either naming or removing them.

[Note: [Col. 1189D] Colb.: “what”; another reading: “by indicating.”]

But we must return from these matters and raise our heart to him apart from whom everything that exists is insufficient and needy. Hence that angel, having turned away from God, became perverse; he is swept along by the weight of his own desire and, in excessive restlessness, opposes every good. From there [Note: [Col. 1189D] Colb.: “Hence.”] his grievous malevolence extended as far as humankind [Col. 1189B], whom he caused to stray from God’s commands.

**XIII. Question.** Why, I ask, did God command a human being what he foreknew that he [Note: [Col. 1189D] Another reading: “whom.”] would transgress? Why did he permit to be tempted one whom he foresaw would consent to the tempter?

**Response.** A human being, placed under the Lord, is rightly forbidden something [Note: Colb. reads: “something by right.”], so that it may be shown whether he loves the Lord. For how would he know that he had a lord if the lord commanded him nothing? The command showed that the human being, who was made, ought to be under his lord. But his transgression of the command proved that he was unwilling to be subject to his own lord.

Every rational creature, preserved in obedience, ought to be subject to the Lord. Therefore the command was good, because it showed what a rational creature owes to its Creator. It belongs to the Lord to see what and why he commanded; it belongs to the servant to do what the lord commanded. Since it is supremely beneficial for a human being to serve the Lord, whatever the Lord wishes to command is good for that person; for he neither commands nor does anything useless. [Col. 1189C]

It is also fitting that a permitted temptation follows the command, so that temptation may show whether the servant wishes to obey his lord. Thus, being permitted to be tempted, he heard: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3:5); but he would never have consented unless he had become proud against the Lord.

**XIV. Question.** Consider what you have said. For if human pride preceded temptation, then the human being fell before he was tempted. He therefore fell through himself, not through the devil. [Col. 1189D]

**Response.** No: human pride did not truly precede that temptation. Rather, after temptation had first permitted him to aspire to the height of divinity, pride swelled; on account of this swelling God forsook him, the tempter seized him when forsaken, and led him into what was forbidden. [Therefore temptation came first and deceived the human being,] whom it made to sin alike by suggestion, delight, consent, and defense.

**XV. Question.** It is clear that we sin when, after an evil suggestion is presented to us, we take delight in it; having taken delight, we consent; and, having consented, we sometimes defend the fault. But tell me: when do we sin by suggestion, unless when we suggest that others should sin? How did you say that Adam sinned by suggestion, when he himself suggested nothing to anyone, but rather a diabolical suggestion made to him brought him sin?

**Response.** When we are drawn to sin either by a demon’s temptation, by the desire of the flesh, or by worldly ambition, we sometimes do not proceed to delight, are not bound by consent, and are not held fast by obstinacy. Yet, if as soon as we perceive it we do not immediately reject it, oppose it, and detest it, we are shown to have sinned by suggestion alone: we perceived iniquity and did not immediately [Note: [Col. 1190D] Colb.: “nevertheless.”] resist it, even though we took no delight in it.

For example: if you tolerate a traitor to your lord or friend speaking with you about betrayal, and do not oppose him—though you have neither taken delight in nor consented to evil against your lord or friend—then because you were unwilling to contradict or resist what you immediately perceived, you are at once known to be guilty by that however slight assent to hearing him. [Col. 1190B] Thus one sins by suggestion alone, although one has not taken delight or given consent in act.

So too the first man did not fail to recognize the evil suggester, and answered that he had received the Lord’s command. When he knowingly gave a hearing to the evil suggestion, he at once sinned by accepting the very suggestion; then, taking delight and consenting, he incurred sin more fully [Note: [Col. 1190D] Colb.: “deserved.”]. Therefore, when temptation had been presented and he did not oppose it—as he certainly ought to have done—he saw iniquity and was silent. Consequently there followed in his heart the force of wrongful delight.

When he saw it, judged it beautiful to look upon and pleasant, and gave consent in action to the delight—when he took of the fruit and ate—and defended the deed by making excuses, then he shifted the blame onto God, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12). The woman likewise excused herself, saying: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid., 13). The excuse of both was proud. For no one’s persuasion ought ever to be preferred to God’s command. They refuse to confess their own sin in the matter, but with equal arrogance shift the blame to another; and while they put forward an excuse, they retain their iniquity.

Yet everyone born from them, but not imitating them, who is faithful and devoted to God, while being tried by many evils until the end of the age, continually flees to the Lord and says humbly: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5). Oh, if they too had said this after their fault—if, truly repentant, they had sought pardon from the Lord! Having fallen proud, they would have risen humble. But continual labor and the bitterness of death had not yet broken the necks of the sinners. To prevent people from presuming upon themselves, both the punishment which they endure in the present warns them, and the future judgment which they fear terrifies them. [Col. 1191A]

As for what is written of those transgressors, that “their eyes were opened” (Gen. 3:7), they were opened indeed—not merely for seeing, since it is written that they had seen the tree beautiful [to behold] and pleasant for food—but after the fault they were opened to feel [Note: [Col. 1191D] Colb.: “to know.”] the disturbance in their body [their own] which they had not previously felt. Ashamed, they could not endure to see the shameful parts implanted in their limbs through their fault, having in their pride abandoned the sight of divine things.

For, having lost that wonderful state in which, while living devoutly under the Lord and using the tree of life and the other health-giving trees, they neither wasted away through sickness nor grew old through age, they received after their fault intemperance and a most shameful, impetuous movement in their flesh. This death occurred on the day on which a human being presumed to transgress the Lord’s command. And one who had formerly rejoiced in the beauty of obedience at once suffered grievous shame in his flesh for disobedience, while the rational soul was ashamed to see in its members a bestial movement.

Moreover, the familiarity with the Lord previously enjoyed in security before sin increased their shame after sin. Seeking hiding places, the human being did not dare present his nakedness to the Lord when he came, for that nakedness was displeasing even to his own eyes. [Col. 1191B]

**XVI. Question.** What is this? Did not the human being sin through the ears by hearing a wrongful suggestion? Did he not fall into guilt through eyes covetously seeing what was not due, and through hands and mouth presuming what was forbidden? Why, then, was he struck in none of these, while vengeance was revealed only in those genital members?

**Response.** Do not say “only in those.” The whole human body was made so diseased by sin that the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (Rom. 17:10). But vengeance rages most severely, as it seems to me, in those genital members because from those members descends the propagation of the human race, which the violent law of sin originally bound. Thus each person may fear to offend God in himself when he bears in his own body so great a punishment for paternal crime. Whoever is born under it is held guilty under the bond of fault unless healed by Christ’s sacrament. [Col. 1191D]

Thus that son who mocked his father’s nakedness deserved to be condemned not only in himself but also in his posterity. Hence the father did not say, “Cursed be Ham,” but: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants” [Note: [Col. 1191D] Another reading lacks “of servants.”] (Gen. 9:25). For while he curses the son in the father, he extends the father’s fault to the son, and makes known to condemned descendants how grievous it is for a son to sin against his father.

Hence the Lord visits the iniquity of fathers upon children, as it is written, unto the third and fourth generation—namely, upon those who have not been reborn [Note: [Col. 1191D] Colb.: “even those who have been reborn.”] through grace. For [Note: Colb. adds: “certainly.”] in those whom the grace of baptism has regenerated, provided that they have not afterwards imitated their parents’ wickedness, Scripture testifies that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father that of the son.” [That is, one reborn in Christ will not be condemned for another’s sin, although he may be subjected to punishment.]

And one should know that the fact that wicked children [Note: [Col. 1191D] Another reading lacks “wicked.”] of any fathers after Adam bear iniquity, not indeed of all [Note: [Col. 1192D] Colb.: “all.”] their fathers, but nevertheless unto the third and fourth generation, is a great mercy of the Lord. His vengeance was not extended over their entire generation; yet the fault of the first father, as supreme justice required, rightly spread to the last son. For he who ought to have appeared as the first author of righteousness and, for righteousness, of glory to all his posterity, when he fell first [Note: [Col. 1192D] Colb. adds “of glory.”], became the first author of guilt, the first recipient of due punishment, and the first dispenser of evil throughout all his generation.

Blessed be the humility of our Savior, whose immense love sought the lost and mercifully raised up those found; this love leads the humble by the path of repentance to life [Col. 1192C] [Note: [Col. 1192D] Colb.: “leads back.”]. This grace of repentance raised David after his fall, restored Manasseh to his kingdom, and remade the weeping Peter into an apostle. It raises the fallen, heals the crushed, restores the lost.

The devil could not possess this grace after his fall, since he received no remedy from God. Hence Paul says: “He nowhere takes hold of angels, but takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16). Thus he remained lost in the iniquity which he had found, because he did not relinquish the pride by which he fell. For humility granted through Christ alone receives repentance; pride bestowed through the devil alone produces persistence in evil. Repentance raises the humble to heaven; persistence casts the proud down to hell. “For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6), through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] In the Colbert manuscript, the third book ends at this point.]

## THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 1191]

[Col. 1191D] **I.** God, Creator of all things, created among all the things he made, for the beholding of the glory of his blessedness, angel and [Col. 1192D] human being, whom he adorned with the grace of understanding. In them wisdom was first of all created [Note: [Col. 1193D] Colb.: “by which they look above themselves to God. Therefore whoever, etc.”], which says thus of itself in the Book of Wisdom (10:1): “From the beginning and before the ages I was created,” etc. Hence they know the creative Wisdom, creating all things together, [and indeed behold God above themselves.]

Therefore, those who through wisdom given by God understand God above themselves are at fault if they do not love him; and when they rebound from the highest light, they are darkened. Yet God’s omnipotence is wonderful: it works praiseworthily both from good things and from evil things. As it is aided by no one’s goodness, so it is hindered by no one’s wickedness. It makes the good fruitful and does not leave the evil unpunished; [Note: [Col. 1193D] Colb.: “because.”] nevertheless, it does not punish their evil will so as to destroy the dignity of their nature. For if good had not remained in nature, there would be no pain in punishment over lost good. A person grieves that he does not possess an inferior good, for the sake of which he scorned that which is supreme. [Col. 1193B]

For supreme justice, just as it does not benefit itself from the works of the good, so by a wonderful effect it benefits even the good from the punishments of the wicked. When the wicked attack, reverent fear is instilled in the good and the virtue of patience is increased. The wicked also, when they receive from God their deserved punishment, can serve as an example to others, so that they may strive to avoid sin. When certain persons are punished for iniquity, very many fear, and the wicked are corrected.

**II. Question.** Why is this so? Why this labor? Would not all be good if God willed it? God does not seem to have acted well: although he made all good, he does not keep them always [Col. 1193C] good; he not only permits them to fall but even punishes them after their fall.

**Response.** What are you saying? Do you wish to cast back upon God the guilt which he did not commit? Tell me, I ask: which do you choose for yourself? Does it seem better to you to be constrained by necessity than to live in freedom? But it is ridiculous to suppose that you wish to serve necessity and do not love freedom. Therefore God made better those to whom he gave freedom of choice, so that they might be able to be what they wish.

For all wish to be blessed, but not all seek blessedness where it truly is. When they seek it yet fail to reach where it is, they seek perversely and accept falsehood in place of truth. Yet in all these matters the most just ruler of all is rightly praised, who works praiseworthily from each individual thing. That nature is best which has advanced so far in God that it can now be bent toward no unlawful thing. That nature too is good which, living under the Lord, restrains the corrupt desire within itself and merits a triumph from victory. Therefore the good Author, who made both good, is rightly praised for both.

One kind is found in the good angels; the other in holy human beings. The former have been confirmed in good; the latter, by grace, have a return from evils and are sanctified through Christ. Even the wicked have their place for the benefit of the latter. God is also praised from the wicked, from whom he always works good. For, without their knowing it, the Church advances through them [Col. 1194A]; troubled by temptations, it is exercised more beneficially and grows more abundantly [their evil will is at last consigned to just punishments].

**III. Question.** When I consider the grace of our redemption present in the Church, and greatly rejoice that sins are forgiven in baptism and the devil is overcome by the faithful, I nevertheless grieve at the punishments of the good. Why does punishment remain where guilt has been forgiven?

**Response.** In all who are regenerated in Christ, every guilt is forgiven, and through grace freedom of rational choice to act well is restored. But he who freely restores us after our fall to good action, by a saving dispensation keeps us, though restored, under infirmity during the time of obedience, so that present infirmity may make us remember our former ruin and each person, chastened, may fear [Col. 1194B] lest by sinning again he fall more grievously.

Thus the supreme dispenser rightly deigns to train his own in the present life under the guarding discipline of punishment, so that, because the healthy human being had neglected to stand in paradise, even the infirm human being may strive by grace to return from exile. O admirable efficacy of heavenly mercy! The strong human being in paradise fell because in pride he forsook God. The weak human being in exile rises because in humility he serves God [Note: [Col. 1194D] Colb.: “will rise.”]. The former changed the good of strength into the evil of weakness by pride; the latter transfers the evil of weakness into the good of strength by humility. The former fails from strength without God; the latter advances from weakness with God.

Thus Paul’s thorn in the flesh, given long ago, is known to have been turned to good, even to be called grace. For the Lord answered him, humbled and praying: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). Therefore whoever rises by grace should strive to be humble, give thanks in present sufferings, learn when corrected to put trust not in himself but in the Lord, and seek by supplication that he who by propitiation forgives iniquity may heal sickness. Hence the Psalmist says to you: “Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities” (Ps. 102:3). First he remits sins to whom he wills; then he heals the infirmities contracted through sins.

Before sin, the human being had no infirmity; but after he willingly incurred sin, he unwillingly endured, by just judgment, punishment for sin. [Note: [Col. 1194D] Colb.: “of the one seeing.”] He did not fail to know the command given him by the Lord, nor did he have any weakness by which he could be hindered in observing it. Therefore, because he knowingly and able-bodied chose to transgress, he now, ignorant and weak, pays the penalties for his transgression. [Col. 1194D]

Proud transgression brought upon itself these two invincible disadvantages, from which it is never stripped except through Christ’s restoration. Everyone born of the desire of the flesh is born with these two invincible things. They remain as sin in infants and in all persons not reborn in Christ, and lead them to condemnation. But they are present in all regenerated through Christ, drawing them toward sin. When, though drawn by them, such persons do not consent, these things are not counted to them as sin because of baptism’s remedy.

Hence the Apostle says: “If I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. 7:20). The Apostle explains this sin to us where he says: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (ibid., 13). Thus the inner person renewed in Christ complains of his outer person. Therefore with the Apostle we cry: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid., 24). But taking breath with him, we gladly add: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (John 16:33). [Col. 1195A]

We also have the Lord himself, who consoles us who believe, when he says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (ibid.). Therefore, while we do not consent to sin but flee to Christ, grieving and lamenting this illustrious necessity which we endure, we make progress in humility and, through grace’s wonderful working, turn to the use of humility that evil in our members which we suffer unwillingly.

Hence the Apostle says: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, who do not walk according to the flesh. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 8:1). For believers, the law of the Spirit of life is in the inner person; but the law of sin and death is in the human members. Against this the Apostle cries: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (Rom. 8:13). Therefore, so long as the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, those reborn in Christ must resist the flesh and serve the spirit. [Col. 1195C]

**IV. Question.** Tell me, I ask, in what way does the flesh desire against the spirit, when without the spirit it has no sensation?

**Response.** In Adam, our father, before he had sinned, neither did the flesh resist the spirit nor the spirit the flesh. But after his spirit, led by pride, disdained to serve its superior, who is God, it immediately received in itself, by a just judgment, a reciprocal law from its inferior—namely, the flesh. For as long as the spirit obeyed in subjection to God, the flesh too served in subjection to it. But when it resisted God, the flesh resisted the resisting spirit; and so, as the penalty of sin, the spirit bears unruliness in its own body, and he who was unruly toward God now groans miserably beneath the unruliness of his own flesh.

Hence he endures a most grievous penalty while he carries his own flesh as an adversary. For the flesh, made alive by the spirit, ought to have been subject to the spirit that gave it life; but the spirit justly lost its subjection, because it refused to be subject to God, who had subjected to it the flesh to be made alive. Thus the spirit bears punishment in itself and from itself: abandoning God, from whom it lived, it grieves that the flesh which it itself gives life to resists it.

But you must take the greatest care not to suppose that there are two minds in one person in such a way as to believe, with heretics, that there are in one person two minds naturally different, one good and the other evil. The Apostle knew one mind in one person when he said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). For the mind that formerly possessed the darkness of sin has now received the light of grace. Indeed, while the Apostle delights in the law of his mind according to the inward person, by which he agrees with God, he grieves that, according to the outward person, he is led captive into the law of sin coming from Adam, by which he consents to transgression (Rom. 7:22).

Certainly there are not two souls proceeding from different beginnings, evil and good, since evil is altogether nothing, while good alone has being, as manifest reason proves. I remember that I have discussed this with you often. For the mind of each individual person is one and the same, and it is good and one. Each person has one mind. Yet the mind that is one, while subject to vanity, has not one will but very many. For it is subject to vanity while it dwells in the place in which it has been set—a place the Psalmist calls “the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:7).

Because it disdained to serve the One who is God, it deserved to become the handmaid of many masters—indeed, tyrants. Thus, when it strives to return to him from whom it derives its breath, so that it may rest in him who truly is, it is weighed down by the law of the members, which it contracted from Adam, not from the Creator. This is the law which it incurred voluntarily, but does not put off voluntarily. Therefore, when the nature which it received as good from God returns to God, while the defect contracted through transgression flows back into the flesh, it is not two minds but one mind that endures this penalty; and because it unjustly abandoned the One who is supreme, it scatters itself among many things. [Note: Colb.: “scatters itself.”]

I know one mind at the same time eagerly aspiring to commit many wrongful acts. Shall I then say that there are many minds in one? I certainly—I myself—am the one who, with one soul and one mind, simultaneously plans to do this and that, and who is at the same instant drawn in different directions, because with a feeble mind I desire nothing wholly, nothing perfectly. Now my mind is lifted to one thing; now I am drawn away by desires to another. This is the penalty which afflicted human misery suffers from the corrupted root of its offspring. [Note: Colb.: “misery.”]

Everyone descended from this concupiscence of the flesh does not have power over the flesh he bears, so that it should not contradict the spirit. The faithful, reborn through grace, fight against it, lest the violent law of the members, which they endure, should reign in them. It does not fight from outside; it is within, as long as this present life is lived. It is not wholly removed, but is fought against. For while it summons the elect, it is rejected rather than heeded. It embraces them in order to draw them back, but is restrained by the power of faith. Therefore, since the Apostle could not say, “Let it not be,” he said what he ought: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12). Though it is present by origin, let it not reign in the will. For where it reigns, it conquers and subjects one to condemnation. But where it does not reign, though present, it does not conquer; rather, since it is conquered, a crown remains for the victor.

But thanks be to our Redeemer, who, by taking our flesh, ordered our flesh aright: flesh which was free from original unruliness and in himself subjected to his spirit. [Note: Colb.: “freed … by subjecting it in himself,” etc.] For in him there are both: flesh from the flesh of the Virgin, and a rational spirit. These two the Son of God assumed for us, and with what he assumed he willed to become one person. Thus the assumed spirit was wholly subject to the assuming Word, so that the assumed flesh was most fully subject to it. He, God with God, man among us, and man between God and us, willed to be born of the Virgin not through the lust of the flesh but through the grace of love.

He is the expectation of the nations and the salvation of all. If we believe in him, through his grace we shall be delivered from the conflict of flesh and spirit, beneath which we groan in labor. The Apostle awaited this when he said: “We ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan inwardly, awaiting the adoption as sons of God, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23). Hence he also says above: “The creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption” (ibid., 21). This is the lamentable bondage of corruption: that the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

The flesh is said to desire in the same way that the tongue is said to speak or the eye to see. For who does not know that the soul speaks through the tongue, sees through the eye, moves the other senses, and acts through them? Bodily pleasure, therefore, comes from the soul, for pleasure is felt through it; but it comes from the flesh too, for without the flesh bodily pleasure is not felt. Thus, when it is said, “The flesh desires against the spirit,” this means only that pleasure which the spirit has from and with the flesh which it gives life to. Likewise, when it is said, “The spirit desires against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17), we understand only the pleasure which it has against the enticements of the flesh.

But when grace operates rightly in the elect, and the spirit commands the members of the body, the flesh does not stir up desire but renders obedience. Whoever in this mortal life grieves that he is often offended by his flesh should grieve still more that he himself, though made by his Maker, so often does not agree with him. While we live in a mortal body, we cannot by ourselves avoid sinning either through ignorance or through weakness, which we derive from Adam through the propagation of the flesh. The Apostle says: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25). See whence we are drawn to sin. But, showing whence justification comes, he says: “Christ was handed over for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25).

**V. Question.** How can this justification of which you speak be in us, when the apostolic voice says: “We know that we all stumble in many things” (Jas. 3:2)?

**Response.** Sin implanted in us by origin draws us toward sinning. Therefore the Apostle calls us back, saying: “As sin reigned unto death, so also let grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5:21). But, as we said above, weakness and ignorance, coming from the penalty of sin, constantly accompany us; consequently, even faithful persons are compelled to sin continually in this present life. Hence the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). Yet the saying of the same Apostle is true: “Whoever is of God does not sin” (1 John 3:6).

The person who is of God lives not for himself but for God. He lives for God, not for himself, who seeks not his own interests but those of God. And he seeks God’s interests whom love raises up to God (1 John 5:18). Therefore, the will possessed by love does not consent to sin, although it does not escape, while living here, the sin that comes from ignorance and weakness. Because it is not drawn into that sin by consent, it is freed through the remedy of love. For love performs this outstanding office in the elect: it always works good, and always covers the multitude of sins arising from ignorance and weakness. Where love perseveres, that person can by no means perish.

But whoever, abandoning love, gives his will over to sinning, despises God in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, [Note: alternative reading: “the Lord.”] when, by consent and deliberation, he willingly plunges into sin. Such a person no longer lives, because he has lost the righteousness by which he lived, since he has lost faith. He lost faith when knowingly and willingly, scorning the Lord, he fell into ungodliness. [Note: Colb.: “sin.”] When faith is lost, the righteousness which comes from faith is lost also; and when righteousness is lost, the life which comes from righteousness is lost as well.

Concerning such people there is a terrible cry in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no longer a sacrifice for sins.” Oh, how grievous is this loss, by which the sacrifice of our redemption is forfeited, and by a dreadful fall one is hurled into the lot of perdition! But whoever falls into such a profound abyss that, buried beneath the mass of despair, he does not remember from where he fell, is to be counted as dead among the dead. The Psalmist knew this when he prayed: “Let not the tempest of waters drown me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:26). He is drowned by the tempest of waters who is drawn into sin by waves of temptations. If the gift of repentance is not given to enable him to swim out, he is swallowed by the depth of crimes. But if iniquity advances so far as to be compounded by despair, the pit of his condemnation is shut over him from above.

On the other hand, the Apostle meets us and cries: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13).

**VI. Question.** What is the human temptation which the Apostle does not exclude, and what is that temptation which he does not permit?

**Response.** Human temptation, as it seems to me, is that which accompanies us invincibly and continually in this present life, while each person, however faithful, is held back from good through ignorance or weakness. Since we suffer these things unwillingly, we who have been reborn in Christ sin venially; and while we flee to him in humility, we are continually relieved of them.

But when a diabolical temptation is added to human temptation—as happens when sin is committed through deliberation, consent, or voluntary choice—the evil done is no longer a venial sin [Note: Colb.: “sin.”] but is rightly judged criminal. For there faith dies; when it is lost, condemnation is owed to the guilty person. From this principle of justice we know that civil law has established that, when someone is proved to have appropriated property of the Lord or anything whatsoever, if he defends himself by saying that he did it unknowingly, he restores what was appropriated according to custom and escapes uncondemned. But if he is convicted of having acted knowingly, he is deprived not only of what he appropriated but also of his own right, and is condemned for his contempt of his Lord. [Note: Colb.: “to appropriate.”]

On this reasoning we understand that light sins differ from grave sins, and venial from criminal sins. In light or venial sins, every believer is, as it were, touched by a serpent; but because he is not drawn by the will to sin, he is not held fast. Since he does not consent to sin, he does not die. For he has Christ as the unique and supreme remedy against every evil. In this present misery he groans and perseveringly flees to Christ, whom he loves.

But when someone knowingly receives an evil suggestion set before him and knowingly and willingly abandons the way of righteousness, he at once deserves, in the likeness of transgressing Adam, to be cut off from the Church as Adam was from Paradise. In place of the glory of the likeness of God, he incurs the shame of the likeness of cattle—the likeness of Adam’s transgression [Note: Colb.: “incurs the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”]—having given himself wholly over to sin, in body as well as spirit. No one can rise again from this by himself, unless raised by him who raises the dead and restores through repentance. These are those whose ruin Mother Church laments; if heavenly grace brings them back, she diligently helps and reconciles them, and the loving mother administers to them the remedies of the sacraments.

**VII. Question.** We wonder at the diversity of the sacraments: why is the Christian not bound by the same sacraments as the Hebrew people of old?

**Response.** Do you not know that the ancient people were drawn to Christ beneath the bond of the law and the light of prophecy? Do you not know that the Christian does not await Christ who is yet to be born, but worships Christ whom he has received?

Therefore there are rightly different sacraments for the time of those awaiting Christ’s coming and for those receiving him. The times indeed vary, and according to different times the life and conduct of the faithful are ordered; yet the unity of faith is not dissolved by the diversity of times. For after the fall of the first man it is impossible for anyone ever to be saved without faith in our Lord Jesus Christ—a faith which is present in infants in sacrament, but in adults together with the obligation of obedience.

At a younger age infants do not possess faith, but they receive the sacrament of faith. Just as the Rock which signifies Christ is called Christ—for the Apostle says, “The Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1)—so the sacrament of faith, because it signifies faith, is called faith. From Adam to Abraham there was faith without the visible sacramental remedy, concerning which the Epistle to the Hebrews reads: “For whoever approaches God must believe that he is and that he rewards those who seek him” (Heb. 11:6; citation printed as 2:16). From Abraham to Christ, however, the visible mystery of circumcision was added among the Hebrew people, but only for males. In Christ’s time, the sacrament of baptism is received with faith by women and men alike, in every nation.

For Truth says: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). And elsewhere: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16:16). In saying “whoever believes,” he indicates faith; in adding “and is baptized,” he shows the remedy. Therefore he commanded generally: “Go,” he said, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

What baptism now accomplishes among every nation, the faith of the elders alone formerly accomplished for infants; and for those descended from Abraham, the mystery of circumcision did so. Concerning them the Lord said: “The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17:14). And it must be known that sacraments of faith received for infants suffice for them; but for adults works of love and sacrifices instituted by God must be added—sacrifices which he altered, according to the diversity of times and as he willed, for the salvation of the faithful nations. [Note: Colb.: “nations.”]

We read the sacraments imposed upon the ancient people, which are now removed from practice, for instruction and strengthening of faith—not in order to observe them by performing them, but in order to reveal their mysteries to believers through spiritual interpretation.

**VIII. Question.** Tell me, please, why did this diversity arise? Why did Christ not come from the beginning?

**Response.** You must know that proud humanity first had to be left to itself under the natural law, so that in itself it might recognize that it had nothing of itself except sin, [Note: Colb.: “When it saw that of itself it could do nothing except sin, and, thus convicted, sought God not proudly but humbly.”] and could in no way cast off the habit it had acquired by itself. God further imposed upon it the discipline of commandments and written law, and supplied the teaching of prophecy, so that when it recognized that it could not avoid sin either by natural will, by the lash of the law, or by prophetic teaching, it might at last, convicted, return to Christ’s grace. Through Christ it would escape the condemnation it deserved, re-enter the paths of righteousness which it had unjustly abandoned, and return through obedience to blessedness.

For the law, by commanding, and prophecy, by teaching, show a person his weakness, so that the weakness thus shown may seek the Savior, by whom the will, once healed, may do what, weakened by itself, it could not do. The law therefore draws one to faith as a tutor; through faith the Spirit is obtained; the Spirit supplies love; love fulfills the law. The law heaps command upon the weak and a bond of punishment upon the negligent. The law is therefore good in rightly commanding: it does not heal the weak person, but increases transgression for the weak—not through any fault of its own, but through the fault of the weak person.

Thus humanity first had to be convicted by itself, then restrained by the authority of the law, instructed by prophetic teaching, renewed by the sacraments, nourished by obedience, and so, having put off the old person, clothed with the new person who would remain forever in Christ. And lest anyone despise the remedies of the sacraments, Jesus Christ himself, who instituted them and was foreshown by the oracles of the patriarchs and the voice of prophecy, himself received in his own person the circumcision which he instituted. And lest the servant reject the Lord’s baptism, the Lord received baptism from a servant—Christ from John.

Moreover, I want you to know that the holy bestowal of baptism, although it belongs properly to the office of priests, has nevertheless in necessity been entrusted to the hands of persons of any kind. For God so instituted it that no one can enter into life unless reborn of water and Spirit.

**IX. Question.** What do you say? Do not many attain eternal life when they have suffered for Christ, although they have not received the grace of baptism?

**Response.** Certainly, concerning those who die for Christ before they are reborn in Christ, the saying of Truth in Matthew’s Gospel can be understood: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matt. 10:39); according to Luke, “will save it” (Luke 9:24). Through this faith those were saved who, though they had not received the sacraments, were nevertheless overtaken by suffering for Christ. Under the sacrament of this faith, infants in Egypt under Pharaoh and in Bethlehem under Herod were crowned with martyrdom. For by the blood in which Christ was sought in them, they themselves were consecrated in Christ.

But what do those do who forcibly bring forward the holy thief on the cross against the remedies of the sacraments? They say that the thief was neither regenerated by baptism nor fixed to the cross for Christ’s cause. Why then, they ask, was Paradise promised him by the Lord? Could he not answer them in his own defense: “Why do you summon me against the grace of the sacraments, when I received grace? The very author of grace, freely hanging on the cross, looked upon me hanging beside him—hanging on a cross, but hanging because of a crime. He looked upon me and bestowed grace, because while dying I confessed to him the sins I had committed. And while the rest despaired at Christ’s death, I alone, if I may dare say so, sought life in one who was dying. Do you not know that to confess Christ, hanging and dying on the cross for us, is the same as to be crucified with Christ and to die with him?”

He who by his grace gave the remedies of circumcision and baptism has both public and private remedies. He sanctified Jeremiah in his mother’s womb by a hidden remedy, as he himself knew and willed. He also filled John, still enclosed in his mother’s womb, with the Holy Spirit and made him leap for joy when he was granted to perceive the Savior’s presence in the Virgin Mary. Why then are you astonished that, while I hung beside him and all the others denied him, he made me his confessor and, by a new remedy, made me both a participant in his suffering and a sharer in his glory? Therefore do not present me any longer against the remedies of the sacraments; for, if you believe the Gospel, you must confess me both a participant in the remedy and a possessor of Paradise. Tell me, please: what if I had been baptized previously? Because you do not know that I was baptized, do you prove that I was not baptized?”

**X. Question.** I greatly approve the answer you propose. But just as we know nothing certain concerning the thief’s baptism, so we doubt the baptism of the Apostles. For we read that they baptized others, but do not know that they themselves were baptized.

**Response.** It is true that we read of no Apostle except the Apostle Paul as having been baptized. But we hold with certainty that many things existed which we nevertheless have not seen written. How, then, can we doubt that the Apostles were baptized, when we know that they heard from the Lord and preached to the world: “Unless one is reborn of water and Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5)? [Note: Alternative reading: “To this is added also what the Lord [said] at the Paschal supper.”]

You should consider that at the Paschal supper the Lord answered Peter: “He who has bathed does not need except to wash his feet” (John 13:10). Thus he wished to wash one who had bathed, judging that he was to be washed not wholly but only in his feet. We understand “bathed” as baptized, [Note: alternative reading: “to be washed.”] and “washed” in respect of worldly conduct. Everyone reborn in Christ is wholly clean while preserving faith through works; yet because of worldly conduct he must have his feet washed, since he is not yet entirely free from sins arising through ignorance and weakness from propagation. [Note: Colb.: “from sins arising through ignorance and weakness from propagation.”] Therefore he washed only the feet of the one whom he knew to have bathed.

Accordingly, baptism is never to be repeated, because upon receiving it each person is wholly clean. But if one lives on after baptism and does not stray from the faith, one need only have one’s feet washed. Hence it is rightly judged heresy if anyone holds that one baptized once by anyone ought to be rebaptized. But for the filth of temporal actions, each of the faithful ought to be washed in the sacrament of repentance. The Lord both performed this sacrament, commanded his people to observe it, and the monastic order preserves it by celebrating it.

The Lord Jesus Christ imposed this sacrament upon his people to be observed; and whenever it is duly performed by the faithful, one must believe that in the sacrament of repentance their feet are washed—that is, that the faithful are cleansed from the defilement of this temporary way of life. This cleansing of remission truly occurs in those whom no iniquity that destroys faith has touched. Likewise, in accordance with apostolic tradition, the Church anoints sick believers. This anointing, as the Apostle James testifies (5:15), relieves the sick person of sins through the prayer of the presbyters.

Therefore the sacraments are to be revered and observed according to the manner in which God instituted them. They do not nourish the arrogant but purify the humble. They are not understood by worldly cleverness, but are grasped through divine obedience. Whoever approaches them should become foolish in order to become wise. Health, not the vanity of disputation, should be sought in them. For bodily sacraments are given to us, but endowed with heavenly power. In a wonderful manner, we who once fell in bodily things through the first father return from them to spiritual things through the second, who is also God.

Let no one therefore prejudge the sacraments, but let the devout person seek remedies in them. Let the sick person discern the trouble of his own disease, not impugn the healing antidote of the supreme physician. Let him recognize that his own things are weak, but that the things of God are strong. While he sees outwardly a bodily sacrament, let him weigh by faith the inward divine effect of God; for power works through the minister in the sacraments. The minister, however, is only a minister; God is the one who grants efficacy to the mysteries.

Therefore let no one despise the force of the sacraments because of the vices of ministers, for God’s omnipotence is not diminished by their wickedness. He who can neither do less in the wicked nor more in the good is able without distinction to work through all and in all. In God, indeed, the wicked person can do less and the good person more; but God can work omnipotently in both. Thus we know that many ministers, evil for themselves, have nevertheless been useful to others, because he works through them who always works well as he wills, through bad persons no less than through good persons.

Communion with evil persons in participation in the sacraments does not defile anyone; agreement with evil persons in their works does. Therefore let no one reject ministers, even bad ones, while the Church tolerates them. Let him hear the Apostle saying: “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14:4). They may be rejected only when the Church openly suspends or removes them. Yet the grace of ordination once conferred upon them remains; but it remains for judgment, not for office. If it should please the Church at some time to recall them, it absolves and reconciles them when recalled; it does not ordain them again.

Whomever it at some time separates from communion—may it never happen without judgment!—the Church condemns medicinally, and heals by pious cruelty, only if that person has been manifestly convicted or has publicly confessed; unless he stubbornly resists. But if, hardened, he despises the Church’s judgment, then, having been named by the Church, he receives the sentence of deserved condemnation; and with such a person, by apostolic authority, it is fitting not even to take food, [much less to pray, still less to perform acts in the sacraments.] But when crimes committed cannot be proved because witnesses are lacking, such persons must be tolerated and must not be condemned by a judge unless judgment has been given through proof. The Lord reserves them for himself when he says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). Yet we do not utterly despair even of these, though we fear for their danger. For we often see some such persons converted through grace visiting them, [Note: Colb.: “and we rejoice.”] and we rejoice that we once tolerated those whom we see at last living well.

**XI. Question.** I gladly hear you speak about the remedies of the sacraments and their ministers, and about either the just separation of evil persons or the dispensation of tolerating them. But I wish to hear you concerning suspended, excommunicated, or deposed ministers. If they at some time presume to minister, what do they do? Do those upon whom they lay hands receive the gift of the Holy Spirit through them? And if they come to the altar to minister, do they there consecrate the body of Christ?

**Response.** In these matters I want you to hold the Catholic view. It is not for everyone to celebrate the mysteries of the altar, perform consecrations, or ordain. For performing these things Christ Jesus consecrated the Apostles; from the Apostles the Church received the form of performing them and preserves it by solemn observance. Therefore no one is admitted to perform these acts unless, in the apostolic manner, he is consecrated to perform the mysteries.

But Christ, through the Church, entrusts the office of consecrating to the person to whom he gives it; and Christ, if occasion requires, withdraws that office through the Church and forbids him to minister. At times he also deposes him or casts him out from the company of the faithful by excommunication. Therefore, if one whom Christ has through the Church stripped of office by deposition and excommunication presumes to minister in the sacraments, he does nothing, since he is no longer a minister. For God so instituted these acts that they can be performed only through a minister. Consequently, one who is not a minister does nothing.

If anyone whatsoever could minister in the sacraments, the entire order of the Church, if you consider carefully, would perish. What could the key of the Church do if each person were able to act in the sacraments as he pleased? What would it bind? What would it loose? But whether the perversity of the wicked wishes it or not, Christ commands: the key entrusted to his Church looses and binds; it ordains, deposes, and reconciles ministers of the sacraments.

We nevertheless read that the Fathers made such dispensations concerning excommunicated persons. The universal Church, anathematizing, had condemned the Novatian heretics; but the Council of Nicaea permitted their clerics returning to the Catholic faith to retain the orders which they had received—indeed, it granted those orders. The Council of Carthage likewise decreed that Donatist clerics were to be received with their orders, granting them orders by a confirmed concession. It considered not what evil there had been in the ordainer, but what descended upon the person to be ordained through the words of the sacrament.

Let no one think against the Church; let no one contradict her keys, which loose and bind in the Holy Spirit and temper the office of binding and loosing with a discerning judgment. Whoever holds this key, let him hold it now until he is taken out of the midst. “Out of the midst,” that is, out of the common body, he will be when iniquity prevails openly and everywhere under Antichrist. Then the sacraments will be rejected and the keys of the Church despised. Then there will be such persecution against the Church that, if possible, even the elect themselves would be led into error. But thanks be to God: it will be a short time. The wicked one will be taken away, and the Church’s freedom will stand [Note: Colb.: “of glory.”] and will remain free with Christ.

This is the freedom which Christ, born of the Virgin, restored to the world. With it he entered hell as victor; with it, rising from the dead, he led his own free from the lower world; and he ascended gloriously into heaven. This freedom is that treasure hidden in the field, wisely sought by the purchaser. By the field we mean the commandments of the Lord, which he commanded to be diligently kept. For these the faithful person arms himself with a strong host, so that he may be able to obtain the treasure hidden in them.

Hence Paul says: “I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). Of this glory he says elsewhere: “The creation itself shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (ibid., 21). For this freedom the patriarch Jacob wrestled with the angel, whom he would not release until the bestowed blessing remained with him. Thus, to us also, when we wish to return from bondage to freedom, an angel comes—that is, the divine word, the messenger of the Lord’s will. While we wrestle with it in the devout exercise of labor, by the merit of perseverance we are perfected by a heavenly blessing.

You must first keep the commandments, so that by doing good you may advance to understand the freedom of the glory of the children of God, which the world does not know. Hence the Psalmist sings to the Lord: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118:104). Therefore the one who keeps the commandment boldly cries to the Lord: “I am your servant; give me understanding” (ibid., 125). Because the first man in Paradise refused to keep the Lord’s commandment, he justly lost freedom, and with it he also lost understanding. Hence the Psalmist says: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). This is the calamity of folly, which descends originally from Adam into every generation.

**XII. Question.** The propagation of the flesh, descending through the transmission of seed, is evident. But whether each of us has his soul from the same source as his flesh, I do not know. Nor do I know with certainty whether the soul thereby transmits sin and punishment, or contracts them from elsewhere.
