RESP. We have read that very many have discussed the soul, but we would not wish them to have erred. Some have even sought to prove their opinions by divine authorities; yet the testimonies they produce establish nothing except that God creates, forms, gives, or breathes souls into whom he wills, when he wills, and whence he wills—he who does all things as he knows how. But lest your devout simplicity, and their simple piety, agree with them in any error, we wish briefly to note for you certain errors against which you must be on guard.

He errs who says that God made souls, not from nothing or from something, but from himself. For we know that souls change and are often affected by errors; and unless they are restored by grace, they are condemned for their errors by the very one who created them. He errs who says that the soul is a body, when it is a spirit. For, being rational and intellectual, made in the image and likeness of God, it receives commandments and certainly distinguishes between good and evil—something which a body does not do. He errs who says that the soul had some good merit before it was united to the flesh but lost it through the flesh; likewise he who says that the soul had an evil merit for which it deserved to bear punishment in the flesh. But how can he show that the soul had good or evil merit before the flesh, when he does not prove that it existed before the flesh? Has he not read that the Apostle says that, while not yet born, they had done nothing good or evil?

He errs who says that little children who die without regeneration by the divine sacrament are not condemned, although the Apostle testifies that all are brought into condemnation through one, unless they are members of Christ. But no one becomes a member of Christ except by being reborn through faith in Christ or by suffering for Christ beforehand.

With these errors therefore excluded, you ought to know that the book of Genesis clearly shows how the first human being was made. It says that his body was made by God from the mud of the earth, and that the breath of life was breathed by the Creator into the one he had made. It calls this a breathed-in breath lest you suppose it made from God’s substance. For when we blow, we do not make breath from our own substance, but release air which has been drawn in. God is the creator of the breath; it is created. God is unchangeable; it is often changed.

God also formed from his rib a woman as a helper like himself. Scripture is silent about whence she received her spirit, just as it is silent concerning their descendants. But whether descendants have souls from the same source from which the first human being had his—that is, whether, just as God implanted a new soul in him, so descendants likewise receive new souls from God, not by propagation; or whether, just as subsequent bodies are propagated from the first body, so the souls of all others are formed from the first soul—reason has not yet made this clear to us, nor has prophetic or evangelical authority declared it to us.

But where am I being carried? When I suddenly return to the matter, I myself consider the opinion of the Catholic doctor Jerome, the presbyter; and I plainly see that the Apostolic See and the universal Church read and uphold it. He indeed writes that the individual souls are newly made by God, not propagated by transmission. He confirms this so strongly that he pronounces anathema upon those who think otherwise. The Church has likewise received this teaching generally.

We therefore, who are children of the Church, ought by no means to reject her judgment. Rather, with Jerome as witness, we grant that the soul is made by God, not transmitted from Adam: new and innocent, united to the flesh descended from Adam. The Apostle indeed says, as I have already quoted above, that those not yet born had done nothing good or evil. It is therefore certain that the soul, new and good, joined by God its author to the flesh, was created under no crime of its own or another’s. It is certainly settled before the supreme Judge that he gives no one over to condemnation who has had no sin.

“But,” someone says, “flesh transmitted from Adam contracts original sin.” What, I ask, does he say? Does he not know that sin is found nowhere except in rational will alone? It is certain that flesh was corrupted because of the disobedience of the rational soul. The soul has sin in the flesh and together with the flesh.

But he who says that flesh alone, because it comes from Adam by seed, has sin because, after it was corrupted in Adam, it was thereby made capable of sinning [Note: Colb. reads “toward sin” (*ad peccatum*)]—so that, as soon as a soul is united to that corrupted flesh, the soul immediately contracts from the flesh an inability to resist sin—let him say, I beg, whether the soul incurs this by necessity or by will. If God confines it under this necessity without any cause of evil merit, he acts unjustly. But it is wicked to say that God acts unjustly. Therefore God does not compel it to sin. Accordingly, if a new and good soul, arriving in the flesh or with the flesh, incurs sin, it sins not by necessity but by its own will. It sins, then, from itself, though not by transmission.

But what are we saying? Do we contradict the Apostle? “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Hear him testifying elsewhere: “From one,” he says, “all [came] into condemnation” (ibid., v. 16). It is therefore clear from apostolic authority that all incurred sin in Adam; they need the remedy of Christ, lest they die with sin and deserve condemnation. For this reason, in ecclesiastical practice, people hasten on behalf of little children lest they die unbaptized. For evangelical authority decrees that unless one is born again from water and the Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of heaven. [Note: Another reading: “of God.”]

Since, therefore, the Apostle says that all sinned in Adam, while the Church with Jerome holds that individual souls are not propagated by transmission but are newly made each day, how can both propositions simultaneously be true: namely, that all sinned, and that they are not made from Adam but each is new in each individual? Pressed by these difficulties, certain persons see both propositions but cannot reconcile them. Since they cannot answer those inquiring about these matters, yet are ashamed to confess that they do not know what they do not know, they throw themselves into one side so as to introduce prejudice against the other. And when they are accused of prejudicing the other and, once admonished, do not correct themselves—because they defend their error—they are called heretics.

### XIII. Question

Tell me, I pray, since the Church receives both propositions, how do they agree?

### Response

The rational soul which God infuses into each human being is not constrained by a necessity of sinning; rather, he makes it rational with freedom of choice. Therefore, when the soul first sins, though it is plainly endowed with freedom of choice, it incurs sin through no necessity—neither God’s, for he makes no one guilty, nor its own, for it was free—but through its own will. For just as God does not make one guilty, so neither does he condemn one who is innocent.

It is certain that, when the soul gives life to flesh coming from Adam by seed, as soon as the flesh lives through the soul, it immediately presses upon the life-giving spirit the impulses of desire which it contracted through corruption in Adam. When the spirit first consents to this voluntarily, it proceeds into habit; and, when habit has become ingrained, it incurs necessity. Hence at first it devotes itself wholly to bodily sensations, while reason lies dormant. Accordingly Adam is rightly spoken of, not by a property of nature, but by resemblance of guilt and participation in punishment. Thus the Lord says to certain people: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44), not indeed by nature, but only by wickedness.

[And although we do not know how the soul of a little child, generated by seed, sins as soon as it lives in the flesh, we nevertheless know that the Apostle confirms that everyone who sins needs grace.]

But because no soul sins before the flesh, none after the flesh, but sins solely when it gives life to corruptible flesh, in the flesh and together with the flesh, the Apostle rightly says that all sinned in Adam—that is, in flesh transmitted from Adam. Every soul united to flesh coming from Adam therefore incurs sin, according to the Apostle, and remains captive beneath the burden of sin unless, while it lives in the flesh, the mercy of Christ raises it up. For it is written: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

This miserable slavery does not permit human choice to be free. For, when it becomes subject to sin, it loses the ability to do good. Yet after freedom is lost, it retains its name and retains reason—not reason adequate in itself to attain divine things, but reason allotted for conducting the affairs of this present life, such as speaking of crafts, ploughing, building, and other such things. [How many things they can also discuss concerning the nature of spiritual or bodily things, yet destructively, since they do so without charity!]

These are goods arising from the goodness of nature, which God supplies, as he wills, to both good and evil people. But to seize, steal, destroy, indulge in lust, and the like, God has by no means instituted; and therefore they do not belong to the substance of this present life. They are not from God, but stain the life which is from God.

Evil, therefore, since it is not from God, is neither a thing nor an essence; hence it is only a name. For if it were some thing or essence, it would be good. For whatever exists exists precisely because it is from God, and goods are from the Good. But the highest Good, which was not made, truly exists because it is unchangeable. Things which have been made, however, neither altogether exist nor altogether do not exist. They altogether do not exist, inasmuch as they are by no means that very thing which God is; yet they do not altogether fail to exist, because, though changeable, they were nevertheless made by God.

We must therefore be recalled from those things which do not truly exist, so that we may cling faithfully and uniquely to him who truly is. [Note: Colb. reads “faithfully.”] But because we are weak for this, let us adore Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings, who joined his strength to our weakness and strengthened our weakness by his strength. Hence, in this present life, his truth is given to us for nourishment in the sacraments; but in eternal life it will be given to us itself, not in sacraments but openly; not in passing, but perpetually.

### XIV. Question

Since meanwhile we deal with sacraments, tell me, I pray, what the sacrament of the altar is. I myself do not doubt about it, but I wish you to answer me on behalf of those who doubt it.

### Response

No Catholic doubts concerning so well-known a matter. This thing about which you ask was done in this way by the one who instituted it. At the paschal supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it. “Take,” he said, “and eat of this, all of you; for this is my body.” He likewise blessed and gave the cup, saying: “Take and drink of this, all of you. This is the cup of my blood” (Matt. 26:26–28).

By the power of his word, through which all things were made from nothing, Christ here also made the substance of bread and wine become the substance of his body and blood. Christ was present among the apostles, sound and whole; with his own hand he gave his body and blood. And lest it be thought a figure, he said, “My body, which shall be given for you”; and, “My blood, which shall be shed for you” (ibid.). [Note: Colb. reads “given” in place of “shed.”]

The apostles heard the Lord speaking, saw bread and wine in appearance, but as believers trusted the Lord. Let us therefore also hold the apostolic faith; let us revere the efficacy of the almighty Word; let us believe that the substance of bread and wine has been changed by the word; let us hear him himself commanding thus: “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

At that hour Christ’s body was eaten; that same body suffered on the cross on the following day for the salvation of the world. At that hour Christ’s blood was drunk; that same blood was shed on the following day on the cross for the salvation of the world. There, having suffered for us, it is the price of our redemption; and it is received by the redeemed as nourishment unto life. Therefore, when the Church receives this from the altar, he himself working through her who commanded this to be done in remembrance of himself, she recalls by performing it that Christ, whom she eats, is both the price that redeems from death and the food that nourishes unto life.

Consider the sacrament: “Christ, having risen from the dead, now dies no more” (Rom. 6:9). But being immortal and impassible, he cannot be perceived by mortal and passible sense. Therefore, when by his command and gift we receive him from the altar of the present Church, the form and taste of his most merciful body remain there according to the manner of receiving. For he is received under the appearance of bread and wine, just as he was formerly received by the apostles at the paschal supper; yet there is neither bread nor wine there, but, as Truth itself testifies, the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Concerning this, the apostle Andrew replied:

> “Every day I sacrifice the spotless Lamb upon the altar of the cross. After the people of believers have eaten his flesh and drunk his blood, the Lamb who has been sacrificed remains whole and living. And although he has truly been sanctified, and his flesh has truly been eaten by the people, and his blood has truly been drunk, nevertheless, as I have said, he remains whole, spotless, and living.”

And he added:

> “If you believe with your whole heart, you will be able to speak; if you do not believe, you will never at all attain an investigation of this truth.”

Consider the sacrament. Christ is truly received upon the altar, whole and entire. Other bodies can indeed be cut, divided into parts, and reassembled; they can also be diminished or increased. But Christ’s body, now glorified and made impassible, while the people eat it with you, is wholly what you have received, wholly what that person has received, wholly what each person has received. Although the same body is received by many at intervals of time or across distances of place, there are not therefore many Christs, but one Christ in all those people.

### XV. Question

How can these things be?

### Response

What do you say? Do you wish these matters to be proved to you by human reason? Do you not know that this bread of which you speak is supersubstantial [daily] bread? This bread is not earthly—indeed, not even heavenly—but wholly above heaven. He asks for this [daily bread] in the Lord’s Prayer who, according to another translation, says: “Give us today our supersubstantial bread” (Matt. 6:11).

This bread is one and daily; but, if it were one and were wholly eaten continually, then according to the manner of ordinary bread it could not be daily once it had been consumed. But in order that it may be daily, it is both one and supersubstantial. It therefore transcends the ordinary manner of created substance, because it is united to the divine. It can consequently be received, not consumed.

That which is above every created substance cannot be defined by human reason. If you ask what it is, I answer that it is the body and blood of Jesus Christ. If you ask why I do not see it as it is, I answer: because it is a sacrament. Believe, therefore, what it is, although you cannot see it as it is. Sacraments require faith; they do not admit of definition.

Do you wish to know sacraments? Seek, child, someone to teach you. The world does not know; the Christian knows. The heretic contradicts; the Catholic defends. Pass beyond the world, trample down the heretic, question the Christian, listen to the Catholic. What does the Christian say? What does the Catholic teach? He replies that he knows; he replies truly. For he knows that very thing, but by the apprehension of faith, not by human reason. It is not known to everyone. For it is a sacrament.

### XVI. Question

What is a sacrament?

### Response

We call a sacrament a sign of a sacred thing. This sacrament, therefore, is a true thing, sacred and signified. Why are you astonished? Do you not know that, having fallen into sin, man lost the freedom of rational understanding and, entangled in earthly things, lost knowledge of divine things? But when, through merciful grace, he is brought back to divine things, he receives them meanwhile in sacraments while clothed in mortal flesh. This is that garment of skins with which the human being, expelled from paradise, was clothed in his pilgrimage.

Therefore, so long as he deals with sacraments, because he does not possess truth openly, he approaches through faith, and by faith surpasses reason. For he sees bodily sacraments, which through faith he understands to be divine; but human reason does not know them. He therefore uses sacraments by faith, not by reason; and while through them he is reborn by believing, he is endowed with wonderful power. Do you ask what that power is? The Evangelist says: “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). To whom? To those who know? No; rather, to those who believe. “To those,” he says, “who believe in his name” (ibid.). Believe, therefore, so that you may become a child. Accordingly, while you receive divine things through sacraments, faith, not reason, must be applied to understanding them.

### XVI. Question

What is faith?

### Response

The faith about which we are now speaking together is that disposition of the human mind by which the soul believes in God alone. While it believes uniquely in God, it apprehends—through God’s grace revealing it—what it holds as known and certain, though these things are unknown and doubtful to human reason.

This is the faith by which those baptized in Christ are called believers, distinct from faith in human agreements and contracts. We recognize and approve the fact that even unbelievers keep such agreements, but we disapprove of their swearing by unlawful things. This Christian faith of which we speak is therefore very different. This faith is the one, true, and Catholic faith in God, by which alone human beings are saved from the beginning of the age until its end. Seek through each age of the world, and you will find it so with Scripture as witness.

This faith is from God, not from earth. Thus Truth replied to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17). Peter saw the Lord: with his eyes, a human being; with faith, divinity. Faith therefore is that by which we believe, not that which we believe—[as the Apostle describes it thus: “Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 11:1).

With this faith one approaches the altar. When you receive the sacraments, outwardly you see the appearance of bread and wine; inwardly you believe the body and blood of Christ. There is truly eaten what was prefigured by the tree of life in paradise and by manna in the wilderness. But, the Apostle says, let the person who eats examine himself. For if he receives unworthily, he eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

### XVII. [Question

How will he examine himself?

### Response

Let him see whether he believes; for the answer given to one who believes is like the Lord’s answer to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). Thus he is forbidden to receive the body and blood of the Lord in whose heart Christ has not ascended—that is, one who does not believe that Christ, who is eaten upon the altar, remains alive and whole in the glory of God the Father. Therefore let one who approaches the Eucharist see] whether he lives by faith.

To live by faith is to believe God and not serve the desires of the flesh. For how does one dare to eat Christ [who does not believe, or] who despises Christ? He indeed despises Christ who despises his commandment. This happens when a person knowingly and willingly incurs sin. Therefore anyone [unbelieving, or] who, with a will to sin, dares to eat Christ eats judgment upon himself.

But whoever, through God’s grace, has laid aside the will to sin and approaches as a believer, eats unto life. For, having become a member of Christ, he has risen from death and lives Christ’s life. What is received or offered once [for the living] is sufficient, but for those whom subsequent fault does not touch. Yet for us, who already live by faith but still remain in danger—so that, as the Apostle says, “we all stumble in many things” (James 3:4)—it is necessary, against evils that return, to have the remedy of him who alone takes away sin. Therefore, because we wretchedly fall daily, we seek daily to be raised up by the saving remedy.

### XVIII. Question

What is this? Shall we therefore sin freely, because we can receive the saving remedy at the altar?

### Response

How do you understand it? Have you not heard that whoever receives it with a will to sin eats and drinks judgment upon himself? Know truly that no one eats it worthily unless he is a member of Christ. No one is a member of Christ unless he lives by faith.

Accordingly, the Church admits no one to communion except a believer. If she sees anyone straying from the faith, whether caught in word or deed, she first corrects that person with devout concern. Then, if he scorns correction, she formally and medicinally excludes him from the altar, lest he die guilty from that from which the righteous person lives. Finally, she removes the suspended person until, after satisfaction has been made, she reconciles him.

Therefore one must not sin securely because of the saving remedy: the Church removes from it one who persists in evil, and through it heals the sickness of penitents. Moreover, by the ancient and general custom of the Church, this saving remedy is offered for the salvation of deceased believers. For them a special prayer is poured forth in the sacred canon, which priests alone say over the Lord’s altar; and in the offering of the sacred oblation they are commended to the Lord, that he may forgive them their sins and grant them eternal rest.

### XIX. Question

Consider what you have said. God indeed forgives sins, but only in this present life. How then, as you said, does the Church ask God to forgive the sins of the dead?

### Response

When we ask that the dead—whom we believe to have departed this life as believers—be released from sins, we do not judge that they actually have sins; rather, by the name “sin” we designate the punishment of sin. For those whom we know to have departed this present life after making satisfaction through repentance, we in no way judge that punishments are reserved for them after death.

But when we see believers who have repentance but die before making worthy satisfaction, we confess that punishments are due to them—not condemnatory punishments, but purgatorial ones. For those who return, even late, to communion with Mother Church as penitents, and who depart after making a true confession and receiving absolution, the one common mother of all, the Church, offers prayers and alms to God that they may be released from the punishment due them after death; and she makes alive the mysteries of the Lord’s altar. These indeed would benefit the dead in no way unless they had died as believers in the fellowship of the Church. But now, by the merits of the Church, they are daily released from punishments.

For the mother whom they had in the sacraments while alive, they have as a merciful helper when dead. By a wondrous mercy of God they are daily released from punishment, while the present Church makes satisfaction for their received repentance. Thus the charity of the Church offers to God, publicly and privately, prayers, alms, and mysteries of the altar, pleading for deceased believers.

### XX. Question

Why is this so? Does not the Apostle say: “For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. 14:10)? In accordance with this, the Lord also says through the prophet: “Where I find you, there I will judge you” (Ezek. 24:14). Therefore, since after death people receive what they have earned while living in the body, whether good or evil, those things done for them after their death are useless.

### Response

It is indeed true that, according to the conduct of this present life, each person dying bears God’s judgment. But if, before death—even late—he had communion with the Church and remained in that communion to the end, then while living in the flesh he earned the benefit that the communion to which he belonged should protect him by its merits. Thus the dying person has the judgment that a member of the Church ought to have: that he may pay the punishment of due satisfaction, yet not know the fall of everlasting condemnation. He has a mother who releases him, since while he was alive in this present life Christ granted her that the gates of hell should not prevail against her.

Tell me, I pray: was not that sacrifice which the Son of God offered to the Father on the cross offered for deceased believers? That universal sacrifice expiated believers past, present, and future. Those whom he redeemed while dying on the cross, he himself, their redeemer, brought forth from hell. The Church has therefore retained this practice: that she offers him in the present for her dead, without whom neither living nor dead person can be absolved.

Let the wretched hasten, therefore; let them hasten from every side to the bosom of so great a mother, who prevails over hell, who absolves penitents from sins, and who, as a loving mother, sends the saving viaticum for her deceased children.

### XXI. Question

What do you call *viaticum*?

### Response

We call the sacrament of the altar *viaticum*, provision for the journey. For we are not yet in our homeland, but make our way toward it through faith. Therefore, while we are on the road, we are sustained by this viaticum. We also send it, by praying for them, to our dead, whom we believe have not yet received blessedness, so that God’s mercy may more quickly remit what punishment remains for them and graciously open to them Abraham’s bosom. By this bosom, sacred Scripture denotes the hidden rest of the blessed.

### XXII. Question

Why then is it called Abraham’s bosom alone, when it signifies the restful abode of all the elect?

### Response

It is called Abraham’s, not because it belongs to him alone, but because, possessing primacy in faith, he was made the father of many nations to be imitated. Thus also the Lord, though he is God of all, wished to be called the God of three. For he says in the Gospel: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” And shortly afterward follows: “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:32). For those who lived in the flesh by faith live without end after the flesh.

All their children—not, I say, by flesh, but by faith—escape death and shall enter blessedness with them. For those whose faith they imitate, with them they will obtain the reward of faith. This was known by that most steadfast Maccabee, who sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem to offer for the dead, considering that those who had fallen asleep with piety had an excellent grace laid up for them. [To sleep in piety is to persevere in the worship of God until the end.] This piety is at every time in faith; this faith is in Catholic fellowship. Whoever dies in it is not held by death but is granted everlasting life; and at the end, when bodies rise again, he will be enriched with glory.

And just as that offering was then made only for deceased believers who were circumcised, so in the present Church it is ordained that the Lord’s sacrament be offered upon the altar only for those regenerated in Christ. In accordance with what is written in the Gospel: they believed in Jesus, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them. Even if someone believes, unless he has been regenerated Jesus does not entrust himself to him; that is, he is not admitted to receive the body and blood of Christ. For this reception belongs only to the regenerate, who, if they persevere as believers, will be brought to the kingdom of God.

### XXIII. Question

Since God reigns everywhere, there is nowhere anyone who is not in his kingdom. What then do you promise when you say that they will enter the kingdom of God?

### Response

God truly is in all things and contains all things; he reigns everywhere and rules everywhere. He assigns rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked. His justice gathers all things together. Yet he is said to reign specially where he is known; he is known where he is loved. Therefore the kingdom of God is properly called that which the devout possess and the impious do not enter.

This is the kingdom for which the devout pray, saying in the Lord’s Prayer: “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10). If you weigh the matter rightly, charity makes this kingdom. Hence the present Church is rightly called the kingdom of God, because it loves him. In this sense it is said in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21). It is indeed founded in charity.

But where charity will be perfect, there will be the happiness of true and eternal peace; there, above all, the kingdom of God is said to be, in which there are many dwelling places, distinguished by degrees of charity. There God will be all in all. There blessed life consists in seeing God himself as he is. “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

Construe it thus: “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent to be the only true God.” That is: not two, but one; not many, but only one; not fabricated, but the true God in the unity of the Holy Spirit. This we believers now believe, which afterward, by the merit of faith, we shall see face to face. Believers now hold this, and are righteous. This faith is the foundation upon which the Church has been founded. For Christ founded her upon himself—he, the cornerstone who was made the head of the corner. With charity poured out from him, the one Church has grown in him out of diverse peoples: gathered from Jews and Gentiles, completed from angels and human beings, to remain with God and be blessed without end. Amen.

[Note: In the Colbert manuscript, the fourth book ends here.]

## THE SIXTH BOOK BEGINS

### I.

The Restorer of the human race, joining earthly things to heavenly and heavenly things to earthly, gives himself in heaven and gives himself also on earth: in heaven through open vision; on earth through sacraments. By his vision heavenly beings are made blessed; by his sacraments earthly beings are renewed. In heaven there is one blessedness; on earth, diverse sacraments.

For some sacraments are those by which we are generally renewed; others are sacraments by which some are ordained into the clergy. Ordination of clergy occurs for the governing of Christ’s people. But those among the faithful who are ordained to provide for others are promoted for this purpose: to serve in the Church, not to rule as masters; to serve in the place of Christ, who came to minister, not to be ministered to.

Among sacraments, then, some are necessary and others useful. In the necessary ones the whole fullness of human salvation consists; in the useful ones, concern of charity serves the people entrusted to it. But of those ordained to govern the people, some are ordained to govern them in earthly matters, while others are ordained to lead them to heavenly things.

Those ordained to govern God’s people in earthly matters are called collectively secular powers. Among them some are called emperors, others kings, dukes, consuls, and the like. The Apostle commands that they be humbly served. And lest anyone think otherwise, he says: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. 13:2).

Those ordained to direct God’s people from earthly to heavenly things are called collectively clerics. Among them, some are promoted for the offices to be carried out among the people entrusted to them. Hence there are those called apostolic men, pontiffs, abbots, and the like, whom the Church places over peoples to be governed through promotion in ranks.

Therefore those ordained into the clergy must consider the obligation both of their name and of their office. For *clerus* means “lot,” and *clericus*, “one chosen by lot.” Let him see that he himself belongs to the Lord and that the Lord is his lot. A cleric ought to live canonically in such a way that, entirely unencumbered insofar as possible and supported by divine grace, he preserves in himself and in others what is said of him.

For he is greatly disgraced who neglects to preserve what is entrusted to him and omits the office to which he is chosen: who delights in the name and is idle in the work; who bears the king’s sign upon his head but serves vices in his flesh; who goes about tonsured yet allows himself to be bound by the cords of desires. Clerics, however highly promoted, if they fall into sin, are by ancient authority judged to be deposed from the clergy, lest those whom, as superiors, they ought to have benefited receive from them examples for sinning.

Therefore the life of superiors which stains the souls of subjects by example must either be wholly removed or quickly corrected by canonical censure. The law of this kind suffers injury unless the honor of the order is defended. But heavenly censure corrects them better: it deposes them from office and confines those who have fallen badly under a stricter way of life. It accomplishes this more fully when it leads them through repentance to the monastic order.

### II. Question

What do I hear? Do you not know that they judge as guilty those whom you call monks, saying that they are dead and unworthy of ecclesiastical offices?

**RESP.** How, as you maintain, do they call monks dead? Whoever says they are dead in body plainly lies. For they speak, walk, eat, and do the other such things that none can do except those who live bodily. But if he says they are dead in spirit, let him explain what he means. For the human spirit sometimes dies to faith through sin, sometimes dies to sin through faith. Concerning the death of the spirit through sin, hear the Apostle saying: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5). For one devoted to worldly pleasures lives bodily, but dies in mind to the Lord. Of such persons the Lord says in the Gospel: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22). He meant that those dead in mind, not in body, should be left to bury those dead in body—would that they were not dead in mind as well.

But concerning the death of the spirit through faith, hear the Apostle thus speak to those living in body: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). If, therefore, they attack monks on account of death of spirit through sin, let them accuse them and prove them guilty, not with a slanderous mouth but in canonical fashion. Let them also pray, if they are Christians, that God may bring them to repentance and pardon them when they repent.

The monk, indeed—not merely a monk in name, but a monk in deed—then properly dies to himself when he is drawn not by his own will but by God’s, and is conformed to the Life which is God. Hence he is laudably called dead when Christ lives in him. And Christ lives in the person in whom the Holy Spirit is. Thus the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). Therefore, whoever belongs to Christ has his Spirit. From this unity of spirit he is called, by a special name, *unicus*, that is, monk (*monachus*), who publicly professes this unity by life and habit. For the monk’s profession has made a common word a proper designation, according to the merit of his life. From unity and the Spirit of Christ a monk ought properly to be called spiritual.

But the Apostle says that “the spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one.” Of such persons the Lord also says: “You who have left everything and followed me will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). Therefore do not call unworthy, do not style guilty, do not consider dead, one whom the Lord declares will be a judge of the world to come; who, as the Apostle says, judges all things and is judged by no one. Rather, take care lest one whom you judge falsely judge you.

Tell me, I ask, to whom does this authority to judge together with Christ belong more fittingly than to one who, denying not only his possessions but also himself, professes before a spiritual father the warfare of Christ, and, putting off the old man, receives with a blessing the new garment—which the Holy Spirit revealed to the ancient fathers to be a sacrament of Christ’s newness? One thing, my son—one thing among the sacraments in the Church—is the monastic garment. For monastic consecration and baptismal regeneration effect the same thing. Just as in baptism the oldness of sins is stripped off and the newness which is in Christ is put on, so in the monastic blessing, after the oldness has been stripped off, the *colobium* is received with a blessing: it is the sacrament of Christ’s newness. When the devout person puts this on, through the hand of his spiritual father, in the ecclesiastical manner, he is immediately released from sins and receives the grace which he had in baptism.

> [Note: Col. 1217D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “received.”]

Accordingly, holy baptism and monastic consecration effect the same thing, except that baptism, if it is kept, suffices without this; while this, when baptism has preceded it, does no harm.

**III. QUESTION.** Why do you commend this sacrament only in relation to monks? Do not those clerics who are called regular canons because of the linen tunics they put on do the very same thing? For to call them “regular canons” is the same as calling them “canonical canons.”

**RESPONSE.** That blessing of the linen tunic which you put forward was, as I hear, presumptuously adopted by clerics in modern times. If they considered their own order properly, they would recognize that it does not belong to them. For this consecration by a changed garment professes public penance. But public penance is not admitted among the clergy.

For a cleric ordained to govern the people is so formed by canonical order that he must be without the stain of crime before the people of God, and must appear without blame, since he is bound to correct the crimes of others. He who is ordained to teach others must also be thoroughly instructed in the pages of both Testaments. Hence I never cease to wonder when I see unlettered men admitted to the clergy by modern canons. And on what grounds, tell me, do they make public sinners clerics, when they do not permit this to be done by authority?

By your importunate questions you compel me to make such replies as, unless charity restrains them, will cause those clerics to rise against me. I do not wish to discuss clerical conduct with you any further, since I have no authority to judge the dignity of the clerical order. This order, indeed, is so pure and holy that it instructs others by wisdom and forms them by life. Clerics absolve crimes; they do not admit them. They cleanse sins; they do not take them upon themselves. They depose from the clergy those fallen into crime, but do not introduce criminals into the clergy.

For concerning them the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:12). This light, set before the world, must not be placed under a bushel. And elsewhere: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid., 13). This salt, dearest one, is the salt of wisdom. This light does not admit among itself the public darknesses of sinners, but steadfastly casts them out from the splendor of clerical order. This salt rejects the foolish and unlearned from the clergy.

But the bilge of the monastic order gathers up such persons everywhere and heals in its bosom those who could not stand in public because of their sickness; and it strengthens them with so salutary a remedy that it often restores them strong for governing churches, revives the weak, and renders the sound more useful.

> [Note: Col. 1218D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “moderation.”]

It is lesser in practical concern, greater in contemplation; less occupied, more free, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3:13). From any profession one may enter this order. So great is the authority of the monastic garment received with the blessing of a spiritual father that, once it has been received, it can in no way thereafter be laid aside, out of reverence for the sacrament.

For this sacrament, once received, if it is not abandoned, is crowned with blessedness. In this order every profession is brought to fulfillment. By this order, if one flees to it, the ruin of the other orders is raised up. For this reason the wise men of old—kings, bishops, and other faithful persons—built many monasteries with great zeal. Yet foolish modern men disparage them and condemn the monks whom they ought to imitate. But let them fear, I ask, what the Lord says through the prophet: “I will curse your blessings and bless your curses” (Mal. 2:2).

Yet, though they are envious, if they have eyes, let them see that monks use the clerical tonsure. For they properly belong to the Lord’s portion, and have as their portion that very one whom, leaving all things, they seek in a singular manner. They would therefore rightly be called clerics, and correctly canons, did they not deserve, by the right of a stricter excellence, to be called monks. For every monk is indeed a cleric, but the converse does not hold; just as every cleric is a Christian, but not every Christian is a cleric.

**IV. QUESTION.** What do you say? How do you prove that every monk is also a cleric?

**RESPONSE.** I see that you are untrained in recognizing the institutions of the holy Church, since I hear you ask what a monk is. Know that no one becomes a monk unless he has first been a cleric.

> [Note: Col. 1219D. The Colbert manuscript adds: “my son.”]

For when someone is received into monastic life, if he is a layman, he is first consecrated as a cleric by a Catholic blessing. Nor can one become a monk unless he has first followed the Lord. Thus he becomes a cleric, not in order to remain only at that stage, but to pass through that rank to higher things. Therefore, in order to become a monk, he first professes apostolic perfection: namely, that, leaving all things and denying himself, he may follow Christ in obedience.

Once the profession has been made, he is then stripped by his spiritual father, as one dying to the world, and clothed with the sacrament of Christ’s newness—that is, with the *colobium*—with Christ’s blessing. There the clerical order is not laid aside but is enhanced by monastic religion. Those who are both clerics and, having left their own possessions, live communally after the apostolic manner, are the more worthy to lead in Christ’s warfare and to govern others, the more unencumberedly they serve God; for they know how to govern themselves.

Monks ought therefore, on account of the merit of their more perfect life and when opportunity permits, to preach the kingdom of God among the people, rebuke sinners, receive penitents, absolve and bind. They ought diligently to serve the altar and to live from offerings and tithes. Tithes indeed belong properly to the poor; and the true poor are those who, according to the testimony of the Gospel, become poor in spirit. Such, plainly, are those who not only abandon possessions but also commit their wills to their fathers. The cenobites do this by a public profession.

Therefore, by the merit of true poverty and the rejection of private possession, the true poor of Christ ought to live from offerings and tithes. For they know how, after the apostolic manner, to distribute their goods to the poor and to pilgrims, not to squander the Church’s goods on feeding dogs and hawks, or on things which I am ashamed to mention.

> [Note: Col. 1219D. Another reading: “by apostolic tradition.”]

Since monks are suitable for carrying out ecclesiastical offices among God’s people, let no one prejudge them. For they are both of the clergy and live canonically, although, by reason of the distinction of their name and reverence for their sacred habit, they restrain themselves more strictly, keep silence in cenobitic cloisters, and diligently obey their spiritual fathers.

> [There is one rule for cenobites, another for anchorites. The former obey their fathers and do not seek what is their own; the latter live by their own judgment and gather possessions for themselves, from which they bring tithes and offerings to the altar. Scripture commends both and assigns rules of life to both. But we have said this by way of distinction, since we are concerned with cenobites.]

These are they who say with the Apostle: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial” (1 Cor. 10:22). Wherefore, denying themselves, they entrust their wills not to themselves but to their fathers; and when the bridegroom calls them to come out and open to him, they humbly excuse themselves, saying: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” (Song 5:3).

Let this preliminary treatment of the dignity of the monastic order suffice. I piously admonish you not to disparage the sacred order any further; do not rashly prefer clerics to monks, or monks to clerics. The same faith and the same grace in Christ unite them. Their habit is different, but Christ is one in them. Different members in one body do not have the same operation, but they have the same Spirit; because of that one Spirit we call those diverse members one body.

Therefore we ought to love, venerate, and honor the faithful in every class and every profession, not because they are diverse, but because they are one.

> [Note: Col. 1220D. Another reading: “I do not want you to say.”]

Do not say, “Christ is in these people” or “in those people,” lest you become a new Donatist. Let the one Christ be loved in all. And while you love all, do not love vices; rebuke them in others, I ask, in such a way that you first reject your own. I myself, while commending the monastic order, do not defend the vices of one who desires to appear a monk but neglects to be one. When I see someone wandering about as a vagabond, having cast off shame, seeking petty gifts, aspiring to honors, spreading lies, talkative and of disgraceful reputation, I grieve that he has fallen all the more deeply because he had been endowed with a holier order.

> [Note: Col. 1220D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “wandering.”]

We so abhor his crimes, however, that we do not in the least detract from the monastic order. Let us restrain a sword that cuts tyrannically without overthrowing royal dignity. Let us punish adulteries without condemning marriages. Let us remove a blemish from the eye without extinguishing the sharpness of sight. Thus let us pursue our brothers’ vices without dissolving charity, because we ought all to be one in Christ.

For if we live by charity, we live by charity alone. If we possess it, we love God not as much as ourselves but more than ourselves; while we love our neighbor neither more than ourselves nor equally with ourselves, but as ourselves. For it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, with your whole mind, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself” (Luke 10:27). You do indeed love yourself if you possess charity for loving God; otherwise, you do not love God wholly if you do not love yourself for the sake of loving God.

Your love is owed to your neighbor, not wholly, but in part. For the expression “as” signifies likeness, not equality of degree. To love one’s neighbor as oneself is indeed to love oneself and one’s neighbor for the sake of loving God. If therefore you love your neighbor for this end, you have kept the commandment, even though you love yourself with greater affection or care for yourself with greater effect.

For he who commanded that a needy person be given from two tunics or two foods said nothing concerning one. Know also that in both Testaments the Lord gave a command concerning love of neighbor. Therefore we owe the affection of love to all; if we withhold it from anyone, we transgress the Lord’s command. Yet we may at times withhold its effect. Thus in the Old Testament it was permitted to hate enemies—not in affection, lest this be against the commandment, but by withholding practical aid. Accordingly, they did not enter among the nations that had the foreskin—that is, the uncircumcised nations.

This also often occurs in the Church through the rigor of justice, not from the perversity of hatred but through the ordering of charity. For the Church sometimes suspends from office those whom she loves, and sometimes excommunicates those whom she loves. The Lord himself showed that this should be done: he “scourges every son whom he receives”; he kills in order to make alive, strikes in order to heal, humbles in order to exalt. Since he does this in charity, he does all things well.

> [Note: Col. 1221D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “loves.”]

Whoever shows charity to the needy from his possessions, as he would wish a neighbor to show it to himself were he in need, certainly keeps the Lord’s commandment, which he enjoins in both Testaments.

> [Note: Col. 1221D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “if he is in need.”]

But if one lays down his life for the salvation of his neighbor, he is known to imitate not so much the command of the author as the author of the command. The former is incipient charity, by which one serves the needy from one’s possessions; the latter is perfect charity, by which one’s life is laid down for a neighbor’s salvation. But one’s neighbor is not loved for God’s sake unless God is first loved.

**V. QUESTION.** Do you wish to oppose the authority which says: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 3:20). Therefore love of neighbor comes before love of God.

**RESPONSE.** In the outward performance of work, love of neighbor comes first, since God commanded that service be rendered to him; but unless the author of the command is first loved, his command is kept with no charity. For it is written: “Whoever says that he loves God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). Therefore, one who does not keep the command does not love God the commander. Love of God is thus the cause of that which follows. Love of neighbor follows from love of God.

But because love of God is not recognized unless it is shown through love of neighbor, the latter comes first in outward affection and the former in inward affection. Love of God therefore comes first through the devotion of the mind; love of neighbor follows through the zeal of action. But you ought to know that charity of mind, which loves God and neighbor, is not twofold but one. It begins from God and is nourished in one’s neighbor.

In the elect charity has its beginning in time; in those same persons it is perfected in eternity. Those who have already attained it in eternity are blessed with Christ. For he says: “Where I am, there my servant shall also be” (John 12:26). The Apostle desired this when he said: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Therefore, those whom we know to have passed to God in perfection through the merit of their life, we believe reign with Christ and can do all things in Christ. We do not pray for them; rather, we humbly ask them to pray for us and assist us, since at one and the same time we see their benefits bestowed upon those who seek them across different regions of the earth.

**VI. QUESTION.** What do you say? Are they present, at one and the same instant, when we invoke them though we are separated across such diverse regions of the earth? How can those who are not everywhere do this?

**RESPONSE.** It is altogether true that God alone is essentially everywhere.

> [Note: Col. 1221D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “dearest one.”]

But the saints, who live in him in supreme peace and do not fail us in charity, are not everywhere in their own essence. Yet it is manifestly certain that their benefits are present to the faithful at the same time in different regions of the earth. This may indeed occur through ministering angels, so that they themselves appear to people in the person of the saints and attend human needs in the saints’ stead.

Why are you surprised? We read that angels appeared to the fathers in the person of the Lord; they both spoke in the Lord’s stead and were worshiped in the Lord’s stead. Do you not know that those angelic spirits are ministering spirits, sent by the working of the supreme Craftsman for the service of the saints? Do you not know that, when Peter came from prison and knocked at the door, a maid came to meet him, but in her excessive joy did not open it; instead she ran back inside saying that Peter was at the gate, and she was answered that it was not Peter but Peter’s angel?

Concerning such persons Scripture says: “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. 18:10).

> [Note: Col. 1222D. The Colbert manuscript adds: “my.”]

But if you weigh the glory of the saints more attentively, you will sooner find what you seek. John says: “We shall be like God, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Seeing the one who sees all things, what will they not see? Knowing the one who knows all things, what will they not know? Like the Almighty, what will they be unable to do? “We shall be like him,” he says.

We know plainly that just as everyone is wretched or needy who cannot do what he wishes, so everyone is blessed and sufficient who can do all the things he rightly wishes. But Mother Church already confesses that the saints of whom we speak are blessed. Therefore, whatever they will, they can do. We also know that their whole will, wholly conformed to God, is charity. Just as charity knows all things in God, so it is present wherever it wills.

> [Note: Col. 1222D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “confirmed.”]

For by likeness to him it possesses, beyond the measure of our nature, that nothing is hidden from its knowledge of him and nothing hinders its power through him. Since therefore they can do all that they will, with supreme swiftness they are wherever they will. In moving, they do not leave God; rather, they run within him whom they always behold by loving him. Thus they move, because they are not everywhere, moved by charity rather than necessity; and they always stand, because they always love.

Therefore the Church, spread throughout the whole earth, rightly cries out to them in her needs, knowing herself to be heard by them wherever she is and experiencing their help on her behalf. In venerating and loving them, she honors, worships, and proclaims in the saints the Holy One who made the saints; and with certain hope she sighs for their peace, with whom she awaits the glorification of her bodies in the common resurrection. As the Apostle proclaims: “We await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20).

He who was awaited to redeem in the present is awaited in the future in order to glorify those whom he redeemed. Just as he was able to create them from whatever source he wished, so at the end of the world he will raise to life the ashes of his own, wherever they lie or are scattered. In hope of this, the ancient fathers carefully prepared tombs for themselves, that by this they might testify that their bodies would rise from death to life. They commanded their descendants to bury their bodies in the tombs of saints, so that in the resurrection they might be joined to those whom they had imitated in faith.

Hence Mother Church prepares sacred cemeteries for her departed faithful, among whom she especially venerates the holy relics which the Holy Spirit chose to use as instruments in the present life. Yet she especially buries her dead where the gathering of believers celebrates the divine office day and night, so that those entrusted to them may be specially commended to the Lord in remembrance and may be released from punishments by saving remedies. From this arose the offices established in holy communities, which the whole Church observes in the Catholic manner.

> [Note: Col. 1223D. The Colbert manuscript reads: “which.”]

Amid the pressures of the world, the Church frequently aids her own, living and dead alike, with remedies; and she will receive them all together in the general resurrection. Hence blessed Job says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior, whom I myself shall see, and not another; my eyes shall behold him. This hope is laid up in my breast” (Job 19:25–27).

Mother Church bears this hope now in her breast; and while she hopes for eternal things, she already begins to live through charity. Thus she is one with that heavenly Church which is already blessed in the eternity of charity. Therefore, since we are mutually members in the one body of our mother, which is the Church, let us beware of division, lest we wound our mother. Let us remain in charity, that we may live with our mother, serving the Lord, who also commands us to make friends from the mammon of iniquity.

> [Note: Here begins Book Six in the Colbert manuscript.]

**VII. QUESTION.** What? Is God unjust, who commands us to make friends from what is unjust?

**RESPONSE.** God is neither unjust nor does he require that an offering be made to him, or his poor be served, from what is unjust—that is, from robbery. Rather, he requires what he commanded when he said: “Honor the Lord your God from your substance, and give to the poor from the first fruits of your produce” (Prov. 3). “From your own,” he says, “not from another’s”; nor does he demand all the produce, but the first fruits of it.

The Lord indeed commands that friends be made from mammon—that is, from riches—which he calls “of iniquity” if they are superfluous, that is, possessed beyond what is necessary. For when any wealth is retained without necessity, it is reckoned unjust. Concerning such wealth the Lord commands that it should neither be accumulated superstitiously nor hoarded avariciously, but that from our abundance we should usefully provide friends for ourselves.

We do this when we extend it with the mighty hand of charity, offer it to the needy for the Lord’s sake, and give thanks, for all these things, to the giver of all good things—in whom we shall all rejoice in the one denarius of blessedness.

**VIII. QUESTION.** We know from the Gospel narrative that at the end of their labor the workers came to receive the reward for their work. But those who came first thought they would receive more, and, on receiving it, murmured against the householder (Matt. 20:10), and the rest that follows. As you know, these things are set down concerning the reward of all together at the end of the ages. But how, as you said, will charity at the end be one for all, and how shall we all rejoice in one denarius of blessedness, when some are shown to murmur against the householder? How do those agree who murmur over the good of others?

**RESPONSE.** Know that, after works are completed, no one entering to receive rewards at the end murmurs, and no murmurer enters. But in this Gospel pronouncement of truth, it seems to me that divine justice is especially commended.

Human justice judges according to work, considers merits, and pays a reward according to what is due. Divine justice, however, exceeds human justice, because it mercifully grants its goods to the ungrateful and undeserving, sometimes even to enemies. Therefore, when it restores the unjust and lost by grace, human justice, according to its own customary manner of judgment, on the other hand weighs the matter. Hence it is rightly said to murmur, because it does not restrict divine justice by its own laws, but, marveling, does not comprehend that justice as infinitely exalted above itself—a justice that does all things as it wills and freely bestows good things.

Divine generosity gives more abundantly even to those who deserved little or nothing, or had even done things worthy of condemnation; and human justice complains that this is more than their merits had earned. In defense of divine justice Paul said: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:15). Hence the Lord answered the murmurer: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will?” (Matt. 20:15). Hence the Apostle: “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18). And the Lord: “I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy” (ibid., 15).

But when he says, “Take what is yours and go” (Matt. 20:14), he sufficiently indicates that this murmuring is not blameworthy. It is only a consideration of human wretchedness. Otherwise, he would receive nothing and ought not to enter but to be cast out, if he murmured against God. Nor does the Lord say to him: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (ibid., 15), as an assertion—which indeed would be condemnable. Rather, it is said as a question: “Is your eye evil because I am good?”

We understand this eye to be the judgment of human reason. By this question he wishes to make it cautious, lest it impiously judge the higher good to be evil. One sins grievously who does not love the Lord’s works as always just; but one sins more grievously who stubbornly hates them. One does not love when one neglects; one plainly hates when one disparages. Negligence, therefore, is evil; disparagement is destructive.

Jonathan, son of King Saul but beloved of David, unknowingly did not observe the king’s prohibition and unwittingly incurred his father’s curse. When he learned of it, he did not humbly plead his ignorance, but said disparagingly: “My father has troubled the land” (1 Sam. 14:29). Hence it happened that the Lord would not answer Saul when he consulted him about whether he should pursue the Philistine. When the reason for this was sought, Jonathan was found guilty. When asked what he had done, it was discovered that he had broken his father’s prohibition by eating. He undoubtedly sinned both in refusing to confess that he had erred through ignorance and in adding disparagement of the king.

Therefore, as you well know, the commands of prelates must be obeyed with due acceptance. Even if they are transgressed unknowingly, they must be honored by humble satisfaction, not attacked by any rashness of subjects. Humility deserves ascent; pride, a fall; obedience, reward; contempt, punishment. Therefore, through humility let us rise again to the Lord, and, obedient to the Church, let us keep her commands; with her we shall then live blessedly, when God will be all in all.

**IX. QUESTION.** What? Will God become all things? What things? When we say “all things,” we are accustomed to think of wood, stones, and every creature, spiritual as well as bodily. Therefore God will be stone in a stone, or something else in each thing, if he is all in all.

**RESPONSE.** How rashly you proceed, how thoughtlessly you conclude. Who is so foolish as to say, according to your understanding, that the Lord becomes all things? God makes all things; he does not himself become them. Do you not know that every creature is from nothing and, according to its condition, subject to change? Every creature, therefore, insofar as it is in itself, is not what it is, because it is mutable.

But the Creator, because that which he is exists in himself without beginning or end and without any mutability, truly and immutably is what he is. The Gospel testifies of him that all things were made through him. But things that have been made cannot subsist in themselves in any way. Therefore, after saying, “All things were made through him,” it rightly adds: “And without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

I see this as requiring the following punctuation: “And nothing was made without him,” because, just as nothing can be made without him, so nothing made can subsist without him. For God did not create it from something, but from no thing—that is, from nothing. Therefore what has been made is nothing in itself. A creature exists only because it was created by God. The Creator truly is so fully that the creature, which is from him and through him remains what it is, though it is from nothing, nevertheless is life in him also, as the Evangelist testifies: “What was made in him was life” (ibid., 9).

Observe that this is said in such a way that you understand the cause through its effect. The cause is that art or wisdom of the Creator by which he makes all things. The effect is everything he created. That art, or wisdom, lives in God eternally and immutably. The effect—that is, the creature—both begins and stands mutable in itself. Therefore everything made is indeed nothing in itself; but whatever it is, it is in God, in whom its being is.

This is scarcely apparent to anyone in mortal life, but in eternal life it will be manifest to all. Hence it is rightly said: “God will be all in all.” He intended to say not “he is” but “he will be,” because then it will be clearly apparent that God is the being of all things. We can also say that it is especially promised to the saints that God will be all in all. Thus we understand “in all” to mean “in all the saints,” in whom he will then be all. As they behold one another, it will be evident that nothing besides God will remain in their desires. For while they lived amid the misery of the present life, many things were mingled with their wills through weakness and ignorance. Hence the Church daily cries to God: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). These will finally be none when eternity has been reached.

Once these have been excluded, God alone will be all in all the wills of the saints. For the one charity in them, which is God, will be manifestly seen and uniquely loved. There, through unity, the goods of each individual will be all the goods of all through charity. Yet, while we consider this by contemplation, we may call “all things” the virtues bestowed on us by God.

In the present we do not see God as he is; we seek him by faith, ascend to him by hope, touch him by charity, and grow by participation in him. Just as the human eye by itself cannot see unless it is illuminated by another’s light—a light which it neither increases by looking at it nor diminishes by turning away from it—so the rational soul or angelic mind, when it receives from God the power to be holy, becomes holy by participation; when it withdraws from him, it remains evil. Yet goodness, which is God, remains whole. It is not increased by your approach nor diminished by your withdrawal.

Whatever more you are—chaste, truthful, just, holy, or anything of that kind—you are not that essentially, but become it by participation. But God’s piety, chastity, truthfulness, justice, holiness, and whatever virtue of this kind is named do not come to him by participation; he is them essentially. Truth itself testifies to this in the Gospel: “No one is good except God alone” (Mark 10:18).

Therefore mercy, chastity, truth, justice, holiness, and every virtue of this kind are recognized as essentially one in God—indeed, as God. When many participate in him, that one reality is called many things and assigned many names because of the various effects which it produces in them. Paul says: “There are varieties of graces, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4). And, having listed certain effects of grace, he says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (ibid., 11).

For God gives the abundance of his gifts to his servants, to each according to his own capacity.

> [Note: Col. 1227B. The Colbert manuscript reads: “of his gifts.”]

All are certainly capable, according to their nature, of God’s gifts; some are more capable than others. All, unless they act foolishly, are without excuse.

> [Note: Col. 1227B. The Colbert manuscript reads: “unless they receive them.”]

And equally, whether unwilling or willing, they serve the will of him who is mighty in all things and able in all. For he is the almighty and highest Good, the one and all of all things. Therefore whoever participates in him is good; whoever turns away from him is not good.

> [Note: Col. 1228B. The Colbert manuscript has: “Uunde” [an apparent OCR or scribal form, uncertain].]

Remaining one in essence, he works diverse things in those who participate in him. In the same body, indeed, all members do not have the same function, but the same spirit works different things in those different members: sight in the eye, hearing in the ear, smell in the nostril, taste in the palate, touch in the hands. One spirit moves these, working various things in them, but remaining the same in essence.

So that highest goodness, which is God, gives itself as one to those who participate in it, whom it fills with different gifts of charisms. Its charisms are many in us while we are partial; in us they will be one only when we have come to perfection. Thus Paul says: “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be abolished” (1 Cor. 12:10). This is reserved for us in that life in which we shall see him as he is. There it will be made manifest that God was, is, and will be every good thing in all.

This charity will clearly see it: charity which will then be one in all, manifest as individuals perfectly see and love one another, wholly conformed to God—as creature to Creator—in perfect unity. Through all ages. Amen.

## Letter of Hugh, Abbot of Rading

> [Note: Col. 1227D. This letter exists only in the Colbert manuscript.]

[Col. 1227]

[Col. 1227B] To his dearest lord Matthew, Brother Hugh, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Rading, wishes sound understanding and right teaching.

I heard that the little book of ours which you wished to keep for yourself has, by your own wish and not by our permission, been circulated everywhere [Col. 1227C] and, as you yourself attest, gratefully received—except that they do not rightly accept what is there said (Book V) concerning a priest who has been deposed or excommunicated:

> “Therefore, the one whom Christ, through the Church, has deprived of office by deposition or excommunication—if he presumes to minister in the sacraments of the altar, though he is now no minister—does nothing. For God established that these things should be performed in such a way that they can be done only through a minister. Therefore, one who is not a minister does nothing in the sacrament of the altar.”

In this statement it seems rightly said—not merely according to ourselves, but according to all Catholics hitherto—that one who performs an act in the sacrament of the altar while not being a minister does nothing. For we read that it has been handed down by the Fathers, and we hold it established, that the Spirit of graces does not follow the person, whether worthy or wicked, but the order of transmission; so that, although someone may be of good merit, he cannot nevertheless consecrate unless he has been ordained so as to perform a minister’s office. It belongs to God, however, to grant the effect of consecration or blessing. Therefore what is there set forth, as the Catholic Church bears witness, ought not lightly to have been criticized.

Rather, this should have been asked by one in doubt: whether the Church, having once appointed someone a minister for the performance of some sacrament, can itself, when guilt merits it, depose or excommunicate him so that he cannot perform in the sacraments what he was formerly able to perform. To this it was necessary to reply that the word of the Lord is living and exceedingly powerful, and says to the Church’s key, which He established: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). From this the Apostolic See and Catholic teachers throughout the world, as ancient writings attest, customarily preach [Col. 1228C] that priests as well as every minister in clerical order retain, at the time of their deposition or excommunication, the grace once received, but lack the office.

They further add that those who are not ministers, yet presume to consecrate in the sacraments of the altar or in sacramental offices, indeed do nothing. Blessed Pope Innocent, with the assent of the Apostolic See, wrote that a certain Nezelon, ordained by heretics, had nothing, and therefore could give nothing to the man upon whom he laid hands. [Note: [Col. 1228D] Urban II, I, q. 7, c. 2, to Daibertus.]

If this man had been ordained by ministers who, though unworthy, had not been deposed or excommunicated, then he too, however unworthy, provided that he were a minister, would undoubtedly confer by virtue of his office upon the person on whom he duly laid hands. Grant a minister, however unworthy; grant a minister: we admit that he has an office. It is one thing to speak of a sacrament, another to speak of an office. Priestly office is forbidden to very many people, but the sacrament is not taken away from them. Hence, when it pleases the Church at some time to restore them, she absolves and reconciles those restored; she does not ordain them again.

It is also one thing to say of an evil office-holder that he ministers badly, though, so long as he is a minister, however evil he may be, he nevertheless ministers. It is another thing to depose him from office, lest he perform the ministry. Do we not know that some sacraments are necessary, while others are official? Baptism, indeed, is necessary for all; but every priestly or clerical dignity is entrusted to certain persons for an office [Col. 1229A]. No one is forbidden the work of the baptized person; for no baptized person is suspended from Christian practice. Rather, if he strays from it, he is recalled in many ways. But priestly or clerical office is very often cut off from many people because of fault, and some are repeatedly deposed from it.

By the former, all live in Christ; by the latter, some serve at the Church’s command. The former builds the house of the Church; the latter administers the house once built. This administration is carried on by anyone, but it is ministered by the official appointed through the Church. If he is deposed from office through the Church, the sacrament once conferred remains, but—as you read in our little work—it remains for judgment, not for office. Thus the sacrament of baptism remains also to any excommunicated Christian [Col. 1229B], not as a remedy but for judgment, not for salvation but for condemnation.

We say that it remains because, when he comes to repentance, he is reconciled through the Church, not baptized again. For if he lost the sacrament by sinning, then when he returned penitently to the Church he would unquestionably have to be baptized again. For the sacraments are divine. Therefore they cannot be taken from one who possesses them through a human being. The sacraments thus remain with ministers, but, when fault requires it, the offices of the sacraments are often taken away from them.

It must be understood, however, that the deposition of a Christian from the Church through excommunication is very different from the removal of some minister from office. The former constantly burdens; the latter often relieves. The former condemns; the latter disciplines. It is beneficial to a minister, if he acts unworthily, that he be deposed [Col. 1229C]. But it is deadly for a Christian to be separated from the Church. For while he is cut off from the Church, he is judged unbelieving—indeed, worse than an unbeliever. The Lord says: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Therefore to dissent from the Church is to fall away from Christ. To fall away from Christ is not to possess faith. But the person lacking faith has no good work. Hear the Apostle: “Everything,” he says, “which is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

A Christian, therefore, although he possesses the sacrament of baptism, while he strays from faith does no good. Not everyone who has a sacrament, then, also has the office belonging to the sacrament. We are therefore astonished that some say concerning an excommunicated or deposed priest that, because he retains the sacrament once received in his ordination [Col. 1230A], he also retains its effect whenever he presumes to consecrate.

Therefore, whoever undertakes to instruct others concerning the sacraments of ministers should distinguish in his teaching between the sacrament of ordination and the office of one ordained. Let him say that the sacrament once received remains in its recipient, but that the office of reception is often removed by the Church’s censure. Let him also say that the Church’s power is as true when it lawfully deposes a minister from office as when it rightly establishes him in office. And let him teach that he is a schismatic who does not agree with the Catholic Church, concerning whom authority says:

> “What a schismatic consecrates is not the body of Christ.”

And elsewhere:

> “Outside the Catholic Church there is no place for a true sacrifice.”

Therefore the Lord also commanded through Moses [Col. 1230B]: “You shall eat it in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside; and no uncircumcised person shall eat of it” (Exod. 12:46). Therefore it is received in unity, not in schism. It is neither obtained outside the Catholic Church nor from a foreigner.

Therefore do not believe windbags; do not yield to the proud. Believe the humble and obedient, who receive with reverence the sacraments of Mother Church—not by disputing, indeed, but by humbly reverencing the authority of their founder. From Him Mother Church has powerfully received the authority to loose and bind. By established power, not frivolous wordiness, she grants efficacy in the sacraments to one ordained, and sometimes also denies it.

There would not, moreover, be one prudence or power if the rites of consecration performed by schismatics or deposed persons were efficacious. Every see would today have countless bishops, and Rome very many supreme pontiffs, who, in dreadful confusion, would loose those bound by others and improperly bind those who had been loosed [Col. 1230C].
