Thus—yes, thus—if you weigh the matter well, valid acts would be annulled and invalid ones preferred. Thus nothing in ecclesiastical affairs would be certain, but everything would be frivolous; and, to confess the truth, there would be no Church at all.

But on these matters we have written this brief reply to you: we hold the acts of Mother Church not frivolous but valid; we have preferred to follow the authorities of the holy Fathers rather than our own opinions; we love you in Christ and wish to be loved by you. Therefore we gladly receive your writings, send ours to you, and entrust them to you for correction. Amen.

## Here Begins Book Seven

[Col. 1229D] I. Charity, mother of the virtues, magnificent everywhere, is nowhere solitary and never idle. Content with what is its own, benevolent toward all, it neither seizes what belongs to another nor wishes to possess private things. It reigns perpetually in that house which Wisdom raises upon the columns of sevenfold grace, illumines with the splendor of eternal light, and richly adorns with good works. Blessed concord preserves all its goods [Col. 1230D]; abundant goodwill distributes them; divine grace ministers them copiously: the more they are bestowed, the more they are increased.

Ever new and ever whole, it bears new children—all free, all of noble birth, distinguished in conduct and outstanding in strength. Humility nourishes them, patience advances them, obedience governs them. Their warfare, hostile to vices, takes the weapons of victory from Wisdom’s hand [Col. 1231A]. It proceeds steadfastly to battle, guarded by the unconquered strength of order. There prudence counsels, justice decides, courage carries out, and temperance orders.

As these advance, the tumult of vices, by a headlong rush, diverse clamor, and an unrestrained host, bursts forth in opposition and undertakes a reckless battle. Its own imprudence dissolves it, injustice casts it down, weakness breaks it, and intemperance destroys it. When such enemies have immediately been overthrown and destroyed, the choir of virtues advances in triumph beneath faith’s preceding banner; made stronger by hope’s firmness, it transcends all things, and soon reaches the joys of its mother, charity. There it rests by unceasingly beholding the essence of the supreme Trinity.

There neither bodily vision, companion to changeability, deceives; nor does spiritual imagination, variously conceived and assembled at will, mislead. Rather, the pure understanding of the mind—stable and certain, led from true things to Truth itself—beholds the Selfsame.

O Selfsame, one and every good of all things! You see; the eye which you have illumined sees, O eye of charity, that all things are in you. Yet you are neither enlarged by all things nor confined. Without all things you are not diminished. It numbers all things together in you without calculation; it measures you in all things without limit; it weighs you, without all things, as sufficient to yourself and supreme without an equal: one in Trinity, threefold in unity.

One, certainly, not derived from unity; threefold, likewise, not derived from Trinity; but simply the very same thing as Unity, altogether the same thing as Trinity. Unity, which in no way begins number; Trinity, which in no way presents number. Unity, which knows no limit; Trinity, which is distinguished by no measure. Unity, which is drawn by no weight; Trinity, which is weighed in no balance. Therefore unity possesses no less than Trinity by number, measure, or weight, nor does Trinity possess more than unity.

O heavenly Jerusalem! O house of charity, city of light, full of blessedness! You behold all things together in God without time; you marvel at God in all things without motion; you love God without all things, full and perfect in himself alone, without measure. To see and know these things has been granted, by ineffable goodness, to the citizens of the heavenly court. To us who still believe less fully and live within time, the merciful permission has been given to desire them through faith.

O God! And what do I say, “God”? God, I name you by faith, not yet by sight [Col. 1231D]. Wonderful to say: we cannot be silent about you, and we cannot speak you. For we do not yet see you; but by your gift, by your most merciful grace, we already believe in you and faithfully speak of you as one. We confess, adore, and follow you as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—not three gods, but one.

One, not merely in any fashion one. For we call many things one because they are gathered together, yet not simply one. But you are one in Trinity and threefold in unity: neither collected into unity nor divided by Trinity.

II. **Interlocutor.** I gladly hear the marvelous things you say; but if you draw me to them by reason or authority, I will follow more gladly.

[Col. 1232A] **Response.** At present, dearest friend, we proceed with so firm a rational basis for believing the settled Trinity of the one simple Godhead that, if we consider carefully, we clearly recognize in all created things the trace of the creating Trinity. Hence the Apostle says: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that are made and are seen: even his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1:20).

We construe these words as follows: “His invisible things, and his eternal power and divinity, are seen, being understood from the creation of the world through the things that are made.” Let us examine the Apostle’s words which we have set forth. “Invisible things” signifies the Father; “power,” the Son; “divinity,” the Holy Spirit, insofar as He who bears the key of knowledge grants us understanding.

The Father is from no one, but whatever exists has its being from Him [Col. 1232B]. Hence, because He is from no one, He has been seen by no one so as to be what He is. Therefore He is rightly said to be invisible. For all things are from Him: both those coessential and coeternal with Him, and those created from nothing and temporal. The Son and the Holy Spirit are coessential and coeternal; created from nothing and temporal are created things and all their properties.

“Eternal power” properly denotes the Son. “Christ,” says the Apostle, is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). Christ is God’s Wisdom, which God the Father did not receive from elsewhere but eternally begets perfect from himself. Through it He simultaneously orders all things immutably; through it He made all things from nothing, causally, materially, and naturally; through it He sets forth individual things visibly, actually, and temporally, and, himself unmoved, governs changing things.

He is the power of God by which all things, just as they were made from nothing, are also held lest they return to nothing. At no time and through no manner of change can they return to nothing—not through themselves, but through the Creator, who persists essentially in each thing. If you can remove the Creator’s essence from created things, then created things can fall back from nothing into nothing. As we were created without ourselves, so we are held by the Creator without ourselves.

Divinity is the Holy Spirit, and for this reason He is rightly called divinity. For when the reason is asked why God made all things, why He thus orders and governs what He made, the answer is that God did not lack, does not lack, and will not lack anything; rather, He made all things by charity alone, not by a new will. He reserved this divine singularity to himself [Col. 1232D].

When a creature does something, a need arises as the cause of its actions. Even if it sometimes presumptuously does what ought not to be done, reason discovers this to be a deficiency of understanding. But God, needing nothing and sufficient to himself alone, has in all that He does only the cause of his charity. Beholding this, the Prophet declares: “You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2).

That uniquely wonderful cause by which God makes all things without need is therefore rightly called divinity. For this cause, if one may so speak, remains properly and peculiarly God’s own. Thus the Father is invisible; the Word is the power through which the Father makes all things; the Holy Spirit is the one and same goodwill of Father and Son, in which all things were well made [Col. 1233A] and remain good.

Apostolic authority speaks of these three, and adds, “To him be glory.” It does not say, “To them,” but “To him be glory,” because unity remains in the Trinity. We, however, who reverence the Apostle’s words in a Catholic manner, neither confuse the Trinity nor divide the unity, because we preach these three in such a way as to hold fast to simple unity.

Therefore we number them without number, since with the Prophet we say: “There is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5). We measure them also without limit, and proclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). We likewise weigh them without weight, confessing with the Apostle: “May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds” (Phil. 4:7).

Let our hearts therefore hold and our understandings know that that highest reality is neither contained by number, measure, nor weight—that reality by which all things together are numbered, all things together measured, all things together weighed. If it could be numbered, measured, or weighed, it would surely be subject to number, measure, and weight; and therefore it would not be God.

What then do we do? He whom we seek is incomprehensible; He whom we desire to speak is ineffable. Let us therefore humbly confess our ignorance rather than rashly boast that we know what is unknown. But if we fail devoutly in ourselves, let us at last humbly seek the Apostle’s counsel, as he says:

> “I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person; that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; that, rooted and grounded in charity, you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, firmness, and depth, and also to know the splendor of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:14–19).

Moved by these words, let us first grieve because we do not comprehend Him in whose image and likeness we were made. Let us remove, by pursuing righteousness, that which prevents our comprehension, so that we may become one spirit with God—the one Spirit by whom alone the invisible God is seen, known, and comprehended [Col. 1233D].

O Holy Spirit, enlighten and draw us: you are weight without burden, charity without passion; breathe into us the new, yet not new, weight of love. Come to us, you who are unmoved; remain with us, you who depart nowhere and never. Breathe upon us so that we may perceive; come so that we may receive; remain so that we may love. Let us perceive by faith, receive by hope, and love by charity: the Father, namely, who begets the Son consubstantial with himself, without beginning and without end; the Son, begotten from the Father without separation and without time; and you, Holy Spirit, proceeding from both without motion and without division.

O unchangeable Unity! O inseparable Trinity! In you neither the generation from the Father nor the procession from both multiplies God, and therefore neither alters Him. The Father makes all things according to his knowledge [Col. 1234A]. His knowing is to number all things. The Father’s Son orders all things, assigning them to suitable times and offices, and measures each thing in them. The one Holy Spirit of Father and Son binds all things by his weight. For that is His goodwill, by which, just as it pleased Him that all things should be made, so it pleases Him that what has been made should remain. For all things depend on Him as effects upon their cause.

O God, who are my God: by your knowledge you number all things; by your power you measure all things; by your charity you weigh all things. Beholding this, that Wise Man spoke to you: “You have ordered all things by weight, measure, and number” (Wis. 11:21).

But someone says: “If all things are in these, are these not among all those things?” We know that the things which God ordered all have weights, measures, and numbers; and these would not exist at all if the things in which they subsist did not exist. For they too were created along with the things to which they belong; and therefore they too were ordered. They are among all things.

Thus things and the weights of things are equally weighed by a higher weight which itself is not weighed. Things and the measures of things are equally measured by a higher measure which itself is not measured. Things and the numbers of things are equally numbered by a higher number which itself is not numbered [Col. 1234B]. God’s knowledge numbers all things and is not contained by number; His eternal power measures all things and is limited by no boundary; the goodwill of both weighs the universe and is drawn by no balance.

These three, by which God ordered all things, are coeternal with Him and inseparable: one in essence, three in persons—not one in just any way, but Unity; not three in just any way, but Trinity. Unity does not constrict Trinity, and Trinity does not multiply Unity. Concerning number, measure, and weight in God, without the reasoning of calculation, without limitation of boundaries, and without the motion of a scale-beam, we have been able, as we received from Him, to set forth rather than to expound—according to our capacity—the innumerable in mutable terms, eternal things temporally, and incorporeal things in bodily words.

Now, however, let us consider weights, measures, and numbers in creatures; and let us first seek them in the rational spirit, so that in it we may recognize the trace of the creating Trinity. The rational spirit sees God above itself; it sees God’s power within itself; it sees below itself, after itself, in the irrational spirit. By rational understanding alone, without the body, it sees number, measure, and weight in God above itself—matters which, as we could, not as we should, we have touched upon timidly [Col. 1234D].

After God above it, the rational spirit ought, with the Lord’s gift, devoutly to meditate upon, speak of in a Catholic manner, and faithfully imitate that supreme, simple, and indivisible Trinity which that blessed choir of angels first knew, chose once known, and retained once chosen. O true knowledge! O just choice! O happy possession!

That blessed rational spirit, beholding God, gathers within itself the knowledge of all its things; and concerning all of them it rightly judges, by the free choice of reason, what it should do and to what end it should direct them. Weighing them according to its judgment, it loves them. Therefore by knowledge it numbers, by judgment it measures, and by love it weighs [Col. 1235A], by which it transcends itself and all things in singular love for God.

This drawing of weight, this weight of love, this love of charity preserves in the elect angels the seal of God’s likeness. O God, to be sought with every effort, worshipped with every strength, and held with every love: you created angel and human being, both rational, alone among all things able rightly to know, truly to judge, and fully to love, so that, lifted above themselves, they might ascend to you—not by bodily step, but by virtuous action.

No creature could ever cling to you by the weight of love unless helped by the drawing of the heavenly weight—that is, unless by the gift of the Holy Spirit, who abandons no one except one who flees Him. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32).

That fugitive angel did not wish to receive the Holy Spirit. Created good by God, he immediately conceived the spirit of pride; abandoning God by it, he kept himself for himself. Swollen only with himself, he remained altogether empty, and by deceiving us cast us down in the first father. Yet heavenly mercy looked upon us who had been deceived.

Do you ask the cause for which God calls sinners back? It is the same cause for which God creates all things from nothing. Above you heard that the one Holy Spirit of Father and Son is the unique and divine cause from which all things hang as effects from their cause; therefore all things must be referred to Him. Without Him, however much anyone does, all things are evil. Therefore, in everything you do, seek for yourself from the higher weight the weight of love—that is, from the Holy Spirit the gift of charity [Col. 1235C].

Pray to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. Do not divide by degrees Him whom we confess one in essence, whom will does not vary and action does not divide. Pray that charity may be given to you, which the Holy Spirit properly breathes forth, though the whole Trinity gives it to whom He wills. The unity of the supreme Trinity is indivisible, its efficacy inseparable, and its gifts common.

Pray that you may receive charity, and, having received it, say with the Apostle: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This charity, given by the Holy Spirit, because it is from above, lifts upward whatever you do through it. But cupidity, falsely striving to arise from low things, drags downward. Whatever you do through it, you lose entirely.

Therefore humbly seek the Holy Spirit, and through Him receive the remedies of repentance. The person whom the anointing of the Spirit has not touched has not received the remedy of repentance. That woman had received Him, whose charity the Gospel commends to us in the words: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). Know, therefore, that the love of God truly is the forgiveness of sins. Hence the Apostle John says: “Whoever does not love remains in death” (1 John 3:14). For the wages of sin is death.

Many people, indeed, instructed by reason alone—which is not removed even in punishments—grieve that they are in sins, from which they do not depart without the remedy of charity poured out by the Holy Spirit. So long as evil will remains, which alone strives against the Holy Spirit, they cannot be drawn, because the Holy Spirit does not descend into a malevolent soul [Col. 1236A].

III. **Interlocutor.** I perceive that what you say is true; but please prove it to me by some example.

**Response.** You know that the living creatures, all of which God had subjected to our first father Adam, were brought to him in Paradise. God had also granted him the trees of Paradise, except for one alone. Adam recognized all these things together; judging truly concerning what he recognized, he assigned proper names to each living creature. And, when tempted by the serpent, he answered with prudent mind when the woman said: “We eat of every tree of Paradise; but concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, God commanded us not to touch it, lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3:2).

But in order that we may retain some memory here of the Trinity, observe number in knowledge, measure in discernment [Col. 1236B], and the collapse of weight in cupidity. For charity did not draw them; cupidity pressed them down. Through it they departed from God when they ate what was forbidden and presumed to possess what was not lawfully theirs. By their evil will they were not drawn by the Holy Spirit, for they preferred not merely not to confess their sin, but even to defend it by excuses. For the defense of guilt is the closing-off of pardon.

See also that the first person born from the first parents, when he recognized all that God had given him, resolved rightly to offer his own goods to God, the giver. In knowledge of things he held and displayed number; in his offering, judgment. But he sinned in weight, being empty of charity: he offered his own things, yet did not divide rightly. He did not divide rightly, because, while offering his own things to God, he weighed himself down in sin through fratricide. Hence Scripture says: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4:7).

He offers rightly who strives lawfully to render back to God, the giver of all, what has been granted him by God. But he does not divide rightly who, while offering his own things, withdraws himself from God. The weight of love shows the direction in which one tends. Love itself either presses one down or raises one up. Good love is charity; bad love is cupidity. Good love raises up; bad love presses down. It presses down while loving things that ought not to be loved, and while loving oneself or anything else, neglects God.

But charity raises up: it urges those whom it can to love God, neglects private interests, and seeks common goods. God seeks the entire weight of love, receives it entire, and rejects it divided. “You shall love,” He says, “your God with all your heart, all your soul, all your strength, and all your mind” (Luke 10:27). Therefore love for God occupies the whole person, gathers everything, leaves nothing, and draws all things [Col. 1236D].

Without this, whatever you hold, you lose entirely, as Truth testifies: “He who does not gather with me scatters, and he who is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). Draw us, O God, by your weight. Raise us to yourself, O holy Trinity, with Elijah in the fiery chariot, in the Holy Spirit.

May our Trinity, which you created, be conformed to you, so that whatever it numbers by knowledge, whatever it measures by reason, it may draw altogether and wholly to you by charity’s strong weight, preserve it in you, and remain blessedly united to you, both by the honor of the image and by the likeness of charity. For your image possesses eternity; your likeness possesses blessedness.

But if, in place of the weight of love owed to you, we seek transient things while neglecting you—may it not be so!—then, having lost the likeness of your blessedness, we remain miserable. Yet because your image naturally remains in us, we endure under eternal misery. O blessed soul, which by due love seeks eternal things and holds the likeness of the supreme Trinity in glory! The Apostle John, drawing from the Lord’s breast, affirms this when he says: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

The Prophet also says concerning the image: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us.” And concerning the likeness he says: “You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). Certainly no image rejoices in God unless the likeness of God richly adorns it. The image of God is the nature of rational understanding, an image of eternity. The likeness of God is formed in us in the weight of charity [Col. 1237B], in the likeness of virtue.

The first human being lost this likeness by following the voice of his wife rather than the judgment of his own reason. When he believed the devil rather than God, he turned greedily toward what was unlawful and enslaved himself with his offspring to vices and demons. O wretched soul, fallen from the heights to the depths, wandering and straying in the region of likeness; naked and blind, empty of virtues, defiled by vices, subject to the flesh, companion of cattle!

Lamenting this, the Prophet cries: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). He was in honor because, possessing in himself the trace of the creating Trinity, he recognized God’s will in the commandments and judged that it ought to be kept; but he failed in love when he preferred to God things that belonged to God. Hence it rightly follows: “He did not understand.” Having lost understanding, he became an animal, like a beast of burden.

Paul says of such people: “The natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). Therefore our first parent Adam, because from intellectual he became animal-like, rightly had to be clothed in animal skins and driven down from the heights to the depths. From then on, human wisdom so perished, as sins demanded, that, like cattle, subject to bodily pleasure, humanity lost even knowledge of its own trinity. Forgetting the supreme Trinity, which is God, it shamelessly worshipped the creature.

The Apostle says of such people: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts [Col. 1237D], and their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1:21). And shortly afterward: “They exchanged the truth of God for falsehood, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (ibid., 25).

Having fallen from the light of truth into the darkness of errors, changed from the likeness of God into the likeness of cattle, wrapped in the filth of beasts instead of the garment of righteousness, these people recognize in neither themselves nor others the signs of the creating Trinity. Yet eternal Wisdom, not forgetting even such persons, clothed Himself with mercy and compassion. He took flesh from our race, but not fault from our transmission. “For,” says the Apostle, “he does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16).

His humility healed us; by his death He redeemed us. His resurrection sanctified us; by his ascension He raised us together with himself to the throne of eternal blessedness. For He says: “When I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

IV. **Interlocutor.** Who is this one, humbled and to be exalted again? Please make Him known to us, that we may follow Him—the one who, exalted, draws all things to himself.

**RESP.** He is, dearest friend, whom the oracles of the patriarchs, the mysteries of legal observance, and the prophecies of the prophets foretold; whom the angelic voice and the star from heaven revealed as present—the former to shepherds, the latter to kings. He is the Wisdom of the Father, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly.” The Father, indeed, as you have already heard above [Col. 1238B], eternally knows every creature with its distinctive property—not elsewhere, but within himself—without variation; he eternally numbers them without counting. You have heard that the Son of the Father, namely the Wisdom whom he begot from himself, not from another, perfect and without beginning, measures all things by fixed bounds according to the modes and operations of their natures. You have heard that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, holds all things in their own weight. For he is the cause whereby all things made from nothing through him are preserved.

Among created things, some are animated by natural motion; we often marvel at this in herbs and trees fixed only to the ground. Others are endowed with both natural and voluntary motion, as animals are: their bodies both grow naturally and move about in various ways. There are human beings who both grow naturally and direct themselves by voluntary motion, but who excel through rational intelligence, by which they know divine things above themselves. All other things, lacking reason, remain subject to those endowed with reason. Thus far does their nature extend. Humankind, as though placed midway between lower and higher things, ought both to hear God through the understanding of its reason and to judge lower things according to the measure of judgment granted it by God; it ought so to order lower things by the law of its judgment that, itself well ordered, it may continually please the Author of all things.

But this measure of human judgment failed when, abandoning God, to whom it ought to have been subject, humankind remained, in blindness of mind, subject to those things over which it had been set, both by God's gift and by the right of nature: companion of beasts, slave of demons. Yet the Wisdom of God—which is the higher measure and measures all things—appeared to us through the assumed humanity, as God and man: not two persons, but one; two natures, not one; God and man, one and not two; unconfused, undivided, full and perfect. For, with the property of each nature preserved, God made man did not cease to be God; man made God remained man. Therefore Christ is God and man from two natures and in two natures, one not by nature but by person; he is not newly God, but Christ from eternity.

Human nature, not a human person, was assumed by the Word of God; but the person of the Word and of the man—that is, of Jesus Christ—remains [Col. 1239A] eternal with the Father: not one of the things disposed within God, which have life. “What was made in him was life” (John 1:4); rather, he orders all things, creates each thing, and governs the universe. He is the third person in the Trinity, who is God—not third in the substance of deity, but abiding in one and the same essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

His humiliation for us is his assumption of human nature, whereby he became our Redeemer and our Lawgiver. He is the higher measure, who adorned with laws of obedience the measure of our judgment which had failed. Setting before us his own pattern, he says: “I have come not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). Having fulfilled this obedience even unto death, he returned victorious from the lower world and rose from death; he ascended into heaven, whence he poured out upon us more abundantly the Holy Spirit [Col. 1239B], by whose weight he draws us, his lowest members united to himself, upward to the things above. Therefore acknowledge and venerate him humbled for us; pursue by the steps of the virtues that same one now exalted, who by the weight of the Holy Spirit and the cord of charity draws all things to himself.

**V. INT.** What are “all things”? Do we not believe that many, whose wickedness persists until death, are condemned by an everlasting sentence?

**RESP.** “All things” was said, not indeed all things universally, but certainly all the elect: all from every nation, every condition, every age, every sex, and from all the ends of earth and sea; all the elect from the first righteous person to the last. In his humiliation he sought all these, and in his exaltation he draws them, gathered together, to himself.

By heavenly grace we, still oppressed by the weakness of the flesh, are stirred to know him amid the darkness of this age. Faith announces him; hope points him out; charity reveals him. Enlightened by these three, whatever we number by manifold knowledge, whatever we measure by the judgment of reason, whatever we weigh by fitting love, we rightly conform to the supreme Trinity, which gathers us and all things by its simple number, brings them forth by its simple measure, and preserves them by its simple weight.

The rational soul is one, and, conformed to the supreme Trinity, holds within itself, according to its capacity, three inseparable operations. In numbering, it measures and weighs; in measuring, it also numbers and weighs; in weighing, it at once numbers [Col. 1239D] and measures. But because its weight, in drawing, outweighs number and measure—and because the flame of charity, that very weight, carries them upward by drawing—the Lord especially commands charity to be kept, saying: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). And, that it may burn: “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. “This is the first and greatest commandment” (Matt. 22:37–38): first, because the others follow it; greatest, because by it they are perfected—or first and greatest because it belongs to the first tablet and concerns the worship of God. For the second and great commandment belongs to the second tablet and concerns love of one’s neighbor.

The love of God deservedly excels, by which the rational soul or spirit, strengthened, conforms itself to the supreme Trinity, weighing by love whatever it numbers for knowledge or judges by reason. It performs all things rightly, referring itself to him whose knowledge numbers without counting, whose wisdom measures without limit, and whose charity weighs without weight. We faithfully worship this supreme Trinity, who is God, and, with his own revelation, seek his image within ourselves; concerning this Trinity we have set down something above according to our limited measure, at your prompting. Now, because you press the matter, let us direct the gaze of the mind toward the irrational spirit, to seek that image there also.

**VI.** The irrational spirit is guided by no reason in its actions and raised by no intelligence above itself. It relies on the powers of the soul and is entangled in its own affections. It loves, hates, ventures, and fears—not according to an understanding of truth or a judgment of reason, but according to the appetite of its own pleasure and the habit of an ingrained attachment. Through its five bodily senses it has outward knowledge of bodily things; inwardly, through memory, it holds their images. For it remembers within itself, according to its memory, the bodies of those things which it knows outwardly through the senses. It occupies its will either with bodies or with images of bodies, and does not raise it above them, but holds and varies it among them.

By the senses it numbers in memory; by affection it measures; by desire it weighs. It discerns neither in itself nor in others these three things which reason apprehends and intelligence knows. These two—reason and intelligence—were bestowed by God only upon human beings and angels. Devoid of these, the irrational spirit is in no way made in the image and likeness [Col. 1240C] of God. It therefore does not possess blessedness by likeness to God or eternity by God’s image; lacking both, it is bounded by its own time. Hence that whatever-sort-of trinity which it has, and of which it is itself ignorant, in no way conforms itself to the supreme Trinity. For whatever lacks intelligence does not know eternal things; it indeed lacks intelligence. The Prophet, abhorring this in us who possess intelligence, cries out: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

**VII.** Consider now also the lowest bodies of things, that you may recognize in them certain signs of the Trinity. In every body you have number, because of the multitude of its parts; measure, because of their quantity; and weight, because of the nature of its substance: when moved, it returns, as it were, to its own place. For every body, wherever it may be, since it cannot lack parts, is numerable by its parts, measurable by the limit of its parts, and weighable by its own law.

For if even the smallest particle of earth is raised into air or water, you know that it does not rest until, by its natural weight, it returns to solid ground. So too a drop of water raised into the air does not remain there, by the law of weight, until it has returned to its own place. Moving air likewise, if it finds an outlet, does not endure confinement beneath water. This earthly fire too, in its nature, follows the inclination of the higher fire. So far as it can, it flies upward, unless the crowding together of the other elements confines it.

Each of these four things, which you perceive by bodily sense but distinguish by the touch of the incorporeal mind [Col. 1241A], has number in respect of its parts, a limit in respect of its measure, and a place in respect of its weight. These three—number, measure, and weight—are distinct and inseparable, naturally present in every body; and so, in unity, signs of the Trinity are set before intelligent beings—namely angels and human beings—to be known.

Therefore, whoever you are who understand, revere God for the understanding by which you excel, since you surely recognize signs of his Trinity in yourself and in every other created thing. You understand God, though neither what kind nor how great he is. You know that a spirit has been created by God, knowing what kind it is but not how great. You see bodies as both qualified and quantified. For God is altogether free from every quality, quantity, and any sort of variation. He is simple, the supreme true being, and one.

A created spirit, however, is varied by wills and changed by affections; hence it is known to be temporal. But, lacking parts, it is without local extension; therefore it cannot be proved either great or small. Bodies, finally, you see as colored; you feel them as smooth or rough, hot or cold; you measure them as great or small; you define them as long, broad, or high; you bear them as heavy or light; and you plainly apprehend that they are qualified and quantified. Having thus considered such things, you rightly understand that eternity belongs to God, time to spirit, and both time and place to body. But irrational beings do not know these things, nor do bodies perceive them.

**VIII.** Consider also the bodily senses which we use, five of which we know and often name sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. If you attentively observe their operations, considering three things in each act, you will preserve within yourself a recollection of the Trinity. The whole soul sees colors through the eyes, sounds through the ears, odors through the nostrils, flavors through the palate, and tangible things through the whole body.

When we see something with our eyes, you know that there is inwardly the soul which sees, outwardly the thing seen, and between them the eye through which the soul sees and the visible thing is seen. The things seen externally are presented in a number almost infinite; they are measured by the sight of the eye and weighed by the judgment of the seeing soul. Consider this small indication of the Trinity also in each operation of the other senses.

And see that your sight does not see itself, nor does it see hearing; just as your hearing does not hear itself or any of the other senses. But the soul sees the senses and sees bodies by means of the senses. For in the senses seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching are distinct; but in the soul they are not distinct, but are one in that one soul. The enlightened rational spirit understands this; the irrational spirit does not perceive it; bodily sense does not behold it; body does not feel it in any way.

**IX.** If you consider motion once more, you too may perceive in motions, viewed from highest to lowest, some knowledge of the Trinity. Every motion arises from what is unmoved; for if there were nothing from which it might arise, there would be no motion. God the Creator moves all things and is not moved. Bodily creation does not move, [Col. 1242A] but is moved. Spiritual creation both moves and is moved. He who moves all things holds all things moved in their own weight. Things which are moved are present to their mover in their own number. That which both moves and is moved is extended between the two, as though a middle measure. For it moves with what is above and is moved with what is below.

This middle thing, if it is rational and conformed to God, judges both itself and every other thing to be referred to what is higher: higher, I say, in excellence and supremacy, by which all things are moved together and which itself is moved by nothing. It is also worth observing that, if there were no motion of things, time would not come to be.

**X.** Time, as it appears to us, is not the motion of things nor the changeability of things moved, but the span of change in mutable things. Time, as you see, never stands still, while future things pass with all swiftness through the present into the past. We, who live within time and pass time temporally, are struck with awe at a wonderful sight: we cannot hold even time itself, which is ours, nor can we present or reveal what it is to those who ask. And in a marvelous way, although the past no longer exists, present memory nevertheless holds the past. In like manner, although the future does not yet exist, present expectation nevertheless grasps the future. Even the present itself, which does not stand still at all, is made to stand as it were by present awareness.

Therefore, while you number the past by remembering, measure the present by present attention, and weigh the future by expectation held in suspense [Col. 1242C], you diligently prepare yourself to gather from these three some image of the Trinity—one that scarcely admits of being grasped by hand. Assuredly, we number past things in memory, we scarcely measure present things in any manner whatever, and we stretch toward things to come. We try to assign these three, according to the change of things, as though by fixed spans of intervals; but in our continual deficiency we lose them as they flow away. We commonly call such spans, bounded by a definite division of interval, sometimes an age, a year, a month, a day, an hour, a moment, and the like.

Because of our mutability, we are carried along in time as a ship is usually borne upon sea-waves: whether we walk upon it or rest, the ship continually passes on or is tossed. In the same way, wherever we are in the world, our time, in which we are rolled along, passes, whether we act or are idle. The sun stood fixed in heaven at Joshua’s command; yet the sun’s time went on no less for that reason, nor was the sun any less mutable for it.

**XI.** Amid such revolutions of time, divine mercy, having compassion upon our misery, restores and regathers its faithful ones from the beginning to the end of the age, and leads them from the flowing-away of time to the steadfast glory of true blessedness. First, under the customs of natural capacity; second, under the bond of the law and the voices of the prophets; third, when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son.

The first period was when the human race was left to itself, so that it might live justly before the Lord according to the understanding of rational nature. The ancient fathers, from Adam to Moses, liberator of the Israelite people and giver of the law, maintained this time of natural righteousness with the help of grace. The second period was when, natural righteousness failing, the discipline of the written law and the teachings of the prophets were added, by which aided natural reason might walk in the way of truth, which by itself and without grace it could never keep. We know that this period was fulfilled from Moses to Christ, the Son of God.

The third period was when the fullness of grace entered, when the Son of God was born upon earth. By his blood he redeemed transgressors of natural righteousness and violators of legal observance and prophetic teaching, and enriched them with an abundance of heavenly gifts, as the truth of faith was made manifest to all the ends of the earth. Behold, in these three times we look upon signs of the Trinity which must always be contemplated. Whatever natural righteousness numbers by keeping, law and prophecy measure by teaching, divine Wisdom, born in flesh from the Virgin, restores by the weight of virtues, to be borne up to heavenly things.

Natural reason brings forth human conduct; the discipline of law and the authority of prophecy order it; the manifestation of the incarnate Word leads it onward even to the vision of divine things. With the aid of grace we ourselves live rightly in our conduct and instruct our neighbors, so that with them we may be brought before the divine vision face to face. We can number ourselves as though knowing ourselves; but we do not yet know our neighbors as ourselves. Yet, by forming them to love God, we measure them as though ourselves. But we set God, whom we seek uniquely, above ourselves and our neighbors with the entire weight of love; and we gladly behold the marks of his Trinity set before us both in these things and in others.

Since we have said something about conduct, it seems fitting to turn our attention briefly to the written law and to any sacred writings. Rational capacity begins our conduct, the authority of sacred speech confirms it, and the power of the sacraments brings it to everlasting completion.

**XI.** In the divine Scriptures we read through histories and parables; from these we sometimes draw a mystical sense, and, considering them wisely, we taste beforehand the sweetness of moral instruction. We are nourished by history and parables; we grow by allegory, which the intelligence of the mind alone perceives; we are perfected by morality, by which alone we are conformed to the Lord.

Even the unlearned and unbelievers number histories and parables by recounting them widely and reading them often. Teachers measure allegory according to the height of their understanding. But the faithful, even the simple, devoutly give moral instruction greater weight. Marked by these three under the remembrance of the Trinity, we perceive that the histories and parables which we retain in memory by reading or hearing, and the allegory which we see by intellect alone, remain useless to us unless they form our conduct. For this purpose divine Scripture is proposed for reading and hearing: that it may build up conduct and shape life.

Hence the Apostle says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience [Col. 1244A] and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). The Prophet saw this when he said: “The Lord guides me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a pasture-ground; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. 22:2). When the Lord, as Luke testifies, “opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45), they were wholly unable to recognize him until they rendered him the offices of charity, so that in the breaking of bread they at once beheld him with opened eyes. For, as the Apostle testifies, “it is not hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but doers of the law who shall be justified” (James 1:22).

**XIII.** Since we have touched briefly upon conduct and the Scriptures, let us also discuss the sacraments for the sake of the Catholic faith. By conduct we live naturally; by the Scriptures we are instructed; by the sacraments we are renewed. In the sacraments you outwardly see water, oil, balsams, and whatever else there may be. Unbelievers see these things along with believers. To these things the minister adds words divinely inspired, and they become sacraments. Unbelievers do not know this; believers alone recognize it, and in them recognize the power of the Holy Spirit wonderfully at work, both in themselves and in others to whom they have been duly administered.

These bodily things, visible to the eyes, consecrated by the word of faith through the ministers of the Church alone, grant eternal benefits to believers, although they themselves are not eternal but are supplied in time. See number in their administration, measure in their consecration, and weight in their efficacy together with eternity. For they are presented bodily, consecrated spiritually, and work eternally. These are divine things, not human; benefits of grace, not a power of nature; the work of the Holy Spirit, not human merit.

Therefore a minister of the Church ought to possess the Holy Spirit in performing these things. For all things are done in this Spirit; but by his special working the sacraments are valid and efficacious. Without him they are empty and useless. Let the minister, then, take care lest he be a minister in name alone. Let him be a minister of Christ, so that he may have the Spirit of Christ. Unless he has that Spirit, he cannot belong to Christ, as the Apostle testifies: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). But one who does not belong to Christ certainly does not have the Spirit of Christ, without whom sacraments cannot in any way be performed.

How then can the excommunicated, schismatics, the deposed, those who have risen up against the Catholic Church, or branches cut off from the vine, act in the sacraments? I know that some have said one thing and others another, and have written one thing and another. How can one bless whom Christ curses? How can one consecrate whom Christ execrates? How can one consecrate me with whom I cannot pray? How does one administer ecclesiastical things to whom the Church cries, “Let him who does not communicate go outside”? O Truth, teach us the judgment of truth; let the empty words of falsehood fall. Christ is the way, the truth, and the life. Therefore, whoever is cut off from Christ lacks life, does not hold the truth, and is in error. Whomever the ark did not hold, the flood destroyed. So everyone perishes who falls away from the Church.

This Church alone rightly binds and looses by heaven’s authority. From the first parent of humankind to the last child at the end of the age, it seeks the elect, whom it first finds scattered under the unhappy number of diversity; but by its teachings and the remedies of the sacraments it confines them within the measure of unity in Catholic faith, and by the weight of charity it leads them to behold divine things. For the attainment of this vision, that origin of the human race—which you ought to know—was brought forth in threefold fashion by the supreme Trinity, who is God.

**XIV. INT.** I have often heard of the origin of the human race, but I had not noticed that it was threefold.

**RESP.** You know that Adam, the first of human beings, was created by God with no preceding parents. Eve, we read, was formed from his rib, from the substance of the man alone, without the participation of a mate. From these two, Adam and Eve joined in one flesh, children are generated by the common law. In these three ways the origin of the human race is established, and by them it represents in itself a certain image of the creative Trinity.

For you know that God the Father is from no one; the Son is born from the essence of the Father; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, is the one Spirit of both. This Trinity of deity abides in unity, lacks an end, and knows no beginning. In it there is nothing earlier and nothing later. It cannot vary and therefore cannot change. It is always the same; it abides as that very same thing.

Human nature was made in its image and likeness; but through the transgression incurred by her who was brought forth from man without woman, that threefold origin of the race fell into sin. Yet heavenly grace did not abandon it in its sins. Amid the darkness of errors, grace caused the star of faith, shining more truly than the sun, to rise in such a way that no storms of persecutors and no floods of heresies could ever extinguish it. With this star thus firmly kindled, he who had been foretold and sought by all created beings came, that he might himself become Redeemer of the lost.

Therefore the eternal one came from the eternal Father, without a mother, and was made man from a temporal mother, without a temporal father: becoming the remedy from the very source whence guilt had arisen. For Eve is read to have been made from a man without a woman; he, from a woman without a man, holding the truth of our race without the stain of our crime: God with God, man among human beings; God and man between God and human beings; one God and man uniting God and human beings; one person [Col. 1245D] uniting God and human beings by grace.

He sent the Holy Spirit, through whom a new offspring springs from the earth. This is the one Spirit of Father and Son, the third person in the Godhead, not a third God. God proceeding from both, he wonderfully regenerates, by the power of both, those born from man and woman under the concupiscence of the flesh. He freely makes children of God out of children of flesh—freely, because by charity, not by merit and not by necessity. The concupiscence of the first mother made children of flesh; she ought to have preserved the measure of obedience to her husband, but, becoming excessive, she offered disobedience to her husband. The man, weighing wrongly, abandoned obedience and embraced disobedience; by it he remained condemned, a slave to his own concupiscence together with his posterity.

Thus all his posterity, generated by the fuel of the flesh, blotted out from the number of the good, bears the countless ruin of condemned evils. There is none to rescue, none to save, except you, our God. Truly born of a virgin woman, you alone can heal what the first mother—neither sound in mind nor a virgin in body—lost through the law of her own concupiscence. O merciful Lord, by the weight of your charity and through the measure of obedience, rescue us from the lot of the wicked; enroll us among the number of the righteous. O my God, because you, made man, are truly mine—made poor and needy for me in the land of my sojourn—make me, truly poor and needy, a possessor for ever of your eternal blessedness!

To obtain these things, you renew the human race by your sacraments: different according to differing times, but not differing in faith; different in effects, but not in powers. Of those reborn by whatever sacrament you have willed, many return to you clothed in grace alone, or clothed over with virtues appropriate to the time granted them; others, after dreadful crimes and neglected sacraments, are healed by the Church’s remedy of penance. The Church re-enrolls the latter, penitents, by numbering them; it raises the former, distinguished by pious works, on the wing of virtues; but others, after receiving the sacraments and with no subsequent stain, heavenly grace at once takes out of this present age—grace received whole and still whole, neither increased nor diminished.

Grace, therefore, saves those who die immediately after rebirth, heals penitents after their fall, and crowns those adorned with virtues. To these three orders, at the end, one denarius of eternal life is given, for the unity of faith. To the saints, who present the merits of virtues, it is owed on account of merits and rendered as a debt. But to those who fell after receiving grace, return through the Church by penance, and die at once without the fruit of virtues, that denarius is not owed; yet, because the Church heals and intercedes for them, it is granted after purgatorial sufferings, not rendered as a debt, because it is not owed. But those reborn in Christ who do not survive but depart more swiftly, because they are members of Christ, cannot fail to have the kingdom of Christ.

As these three distinctions of the good receive the unity of the denarius, a certain image of the supreme Trinity will remain marked in eternal blessedness: led from lowest things through middle things to highest things, gathered into one; the Trinity, full and perfect in unity, will remain full and perfect for ages of ages. Amen. Peace be with you.

**XV. INT.** What? Are you making an end of speaking, you who establish a progression from lowest things through middle things to highest, yet do not show what these things themselves are?

**RESP.** Lest I leave you dissatisfied, I shall explain them briefly. The highest things, as we understand them here, are the virtues which we have from God and in God, by which we ourselves are one spirit with God. The lowest things are bodies, spirits, and whatever we designate by the name of creature. The middle things, however, are the free choice and rational intelligence of human beings and angels. Although these too are created, we perceive them as middle things because they touch highest and lowest things alike.

For through them we are able to make use of highest and lowest things; through them we see that highest things should be set above lowest; through them we go before other creatures as though by a certain light. Of this light the Lord says in the Gospel: “See, therefore, lest the light that is in you be darkness” (Luke 11:35). For the light by which you excel irrational living beings becomes darkness precisely when you set lowest things above highest things in love. When you cast aside the virtues, the things you do without virtues cannot be done well.

He who says, “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35), intended these virtues to be understood as burning lamps. One girds the loins who restrains the lust of the flesh by the belt of chastity. To hold burning lamps in one’s hands is to possess virtues in action; when we hold them by acting, we act well in every respect concerning all lowest things. For no one commits adultery through chastity; no one lies through truth; no one commits fraud through justice; and so with the rest.

Therefore, when you perform all things by the virtues, you freely ascend from lowest things through middle things; and thus, in every action, you set forth before the eyes of a pure heart the venerable signs of the Trinity. In lowest things you bring forth number from multiplicity; in middle things rational intelligence measures judgment; in highest things heavenly truth draws all things with itself by its own weight [Col. 1248A]. Blessed is the action which proceeds in such an order and shines marked with the Trinity before devout eyes. Though earthly, such a human being now truly advances as a fellow-citizen of angels and one like the Lord; the person’s action, both bodily and spiritual, rises by the present honor of virtue in the sweetest fragrance to the heights of heaven.

Let your discernment therefore take care always to act with the virtues. For if you handle any lowest things without virtues, you will immediately sin without doubt; your action will immediately lack the beauty of the Trinity, and your reason and intelligence, plunged from light into darkness, will be neither middle things nor merely lowest, but rather most low. It is not that the lowest and middle things we have mentioned are evil—for God, being good, made all things good—but when we order any lowest things without virtues, we sin by misusing middle things. Then we call the lowest things evil because they are badly ordered; and the middle things most evil, because they misuse not only lowest things but themselves as well.

Receive this certain conclusion from these and the other matters set forth above: faithfully hold the Trinity whose image you possess; seek its signs in all things, know the signs you have sought, and love those you have known. Referring all lowest things rightly, through middle things, always to highest things, may you rest for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1247]

# Treatise on the Hexaemeron by Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen

*(Fragment.—Edited by Martène, **Thesaurus Anecdotorum**, vol. V, col. 1001, from the Rouen manuscript of Lord Grebovaldi.)*

[Col. 1247C] To the learned man Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, his most beloved son: Hugh, priest of Rouen, wishes the spirit of wisdom and the light of instruction.

With God’s permission, we undertake to contemplate the book of beginning, or of the creation of things. Moses, that great servant of the Lord, composed this cosmography. He was the first to receive from God the rod of power by which he performed miracles and governed the Church of God with magnificent episcopal authority. His book, the origin of the sacred volumes, contains heavenly and earthly things, divine laws and commandments, rewards of the righteous, punishments of sinners, and, above all, God almighty, ever working well both from evil and from good.

This author sets forth words that are plain and open, yet of the most profound depth of meaning, which the grace of the Holy Spirit alone discloses [Col. 1247D]. They can certainly be opened only by the Spirit in which they were written. Worldly wisdom, which human reason does not grasp, cannot investigate them. Therefore, invoking the Holy Spirit, let us consider them, so that, as he inspires, we may set forth the meaning of truth as he wills.

These are words of truth, uttered by the true Spirit. He who wrote them is truthful and understood truly what lay in them. Out of all the true things contained in them, we shall be able to know and say only those which he grants us to know—the same one who granted Moses to know what he willed. Yet Moses did not know in them everything which the Holy Spirit, who taught him, knew in them [Col. 1248C]. We therefore refer to the Holy Spirit what we say concerning these matters from him; without him neither Moses could speak nor can we.

In these things blind pride remains blind; in them humble people see with light. There the elephant swims dangerously; there the lamb walks safely. There the elephant’s head is submerged; there the lamb’s foot passes over. Therefore, in these things and in all things, may that supreme Teacher enlighten our minds from above—Jesus Christ, in whom “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,” and of whom the Apocalypse says: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to take the book and open its seven seals” (Rev. 5:5).

By these seven seals, this book of Genesis was marked in its seven first days, in its sevenfold work, under the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. I recall that I discussed these seven days and seals, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, in the second book of our dialogue. But now, in this little work, we treat history more by investigation than we touch upon allegorical or moral meanings. Accordingly, we proceed through this book as far as the place where our first parent, expelled from paradise, entered the valley of tears, entangled in sins and given over to punishments.

Read these things, my son; let whoever wishes read them, but on this condition: that all false things be imputed to my falsehood, and all true things to the Spirit of truth [Col. 1249A]—to me for correction, to him for thanksgiving—who, proceeding from the Father and the Son, lives and reigns forever and beyond, essentially one God with the Father and the Son [Col. 1250A].

# Book One

[Col. 1249]

[Col. 1249A] **1. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”** This celebrated and most familiar Scripture is spread throughout the whole world and proclaimed in every language; through the truth by which it surpasses all things, it offers itself to all. As you approach it, so you find it. By sweet speech it nourishes little ones; by devout teaching it refreshes the modest; by its height it mocks the proud; by its depth it terrifies the diligent. It treats of all things and shows God.

[Col. 1249B] 2. “In the beginning God created.” If perhaps you seek anything before the beginning of the creation of things, you will find absolutely nothing. Eternity alone precedes all things; God alone precedes all things—those things whose movement produced times and whose parts constitute places. The changeability of a creature proves that it had a beginning. As soon as you perceive the creation of things, you immediately find God the Creator. He who creates is himself the beginning for the things created, or by creating makes there be a beginning; thus they begin simultaneously to be made from nothing through him.

Therefore, when you say that there is a beginning, you must know that God precedes all things, not indeed in time, but in eternity. But when you say that, while God creates, all things simultaneously had a beginning, consider “the beginning of a thing” and “the thing of a beginning” without transitive force: that what was begun was created, and that what was created began. Therefore this writing did not receive its title among the Hebrews from so great a beginning of creation, or from so great a creation of beginning, because it would have been unworthy for anything to be placed before so universal a beginning; nevertheless, from the great beginning which it has, it received among us the name of “Beginning.”

3. “In the beginning God created.” Consider, you who read: consider the author of the work, the work of the author, the manner of the work, the author’s purpose. Recognize, then, as the author of the present work that holy Moses, who descended from Abraham both in faith and lineage; who was drawn from the water, prefiguring mysteries; who was reared in the royal court and adopted by the king’s daughter. You perceive that the royal court is Christ’s Church, and the king’s daughter divine grace. He freed his oppressed brother, destroyed an enemy, despised Egypt’s delights, and devoted himself to the Lord in the wilderness for forty years.

There, when the Lord appeared in a bush burning without being consumed, he received commandments. From there, by signs and wonders, he afflicted magicians and unbelievers; he celebrated the Passover; he protected God’s people by the blood of the lamb; he led them out in a pillar of cloud and fire; he divided the sea and destroyed the Egyptians. In the wilderness he received the Law written by the finger of God; from heaven he supplied manna, and from the rock streams, to the people whom he prepared to possess the land of promise. This man of such greatness, with his face glorified, spoke with the Lord as friend with friend. Thus he could rightly, though a man, speak of that which was before man existed—not from human wisdom, but through the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

4. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Behold: a man speaks to us concerning what man did not see, a prophet concerning the past. The same man, writing, handed down many mysteries and commanded that they be observed—a prophet concerning the present. Whoever reads and retains these has not understood them except through him who bears the key of knowledge. This prophet also shone forth concerning the future, when he said: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me” (Acts 7:37).

The Lord bears witness to him: “If you believed Moses,” he says, “you would perhaps also believe me, for he wrote of me” (John 5:46). The subject matter of the work must likewise be known—the subject which so great a prophet of the Lord, so pre-eminent a leader of the Israelite people, undertook—so that you may know what it concerns.

5. The subject matter of this work, then, is indeed God the Creator and his creature.

6. The manner of the work remains to be examined, so that you may recognize which things are there indicated as eternal, which temporal, which primordial, and which subsequent.

7. At one time he considers God, and all things in God, in the divine mind as in art itself. There all things are eternal, fixed, unchangeable. At another time he considers those same things made together in underlying matter: confused, undivided, invisible. At another time he considers those same things formed together in the beginning: distinct, clear, each with its own property. And from these primordial things all other things issue forth actually, temporally, and successively, never and nowhere transgressing God’s will. In reading, you will find these things and more besides, which the variety of method customarily contains.

8. In all these things alike, the author’s intention should be investigated, so that the fruit and usefulness of the author and of the recognized work may readily be grasped. Therefore, because all things together and individually are said to be from one, let all things together and individually likewise be referred to the one, so that the rational creature may seek in all things him who is uniquely one, and may not remain loving itself or other things; rather, from created things may it open itself with its whole love toward him who created it. These matters having thus been investigated briefly and moderately, let us listen.

[Col. 1250D] 9. “In the beginning he created heaven and earth.” From no existing things he created the things that he made in the beginning. For if he had made other things first, he would have produced these not in the beginning, but after the beginning. In the beginning he created not what existed, but altogether what did not exist. Do you seek the matter of primordial things? You find no pre-existing matter. God alone is he who makes them, creating from nothing, not from something, the things he willed.

Wondrous is the swiftness of the work. There is no delay of time there, no exertion of labor, no discipline of study, but the power of will and the will of power: in beginning he created; in creating he began. We recognize him as having wrought rather than as working, him whom we understand to have made in the beginning rather than to have begun. For “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.”

[Col. 1251A] 10. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” There have been people who, approving their own notions by their own opinions, said that three things were coeternal: namely God, matter, and all forms. They judged God not to be Creator but craftsman, one who had not created matter and forms, but knew how to join them and could fit them together. They said that something can be made from something, but not something from nothing.

God alone can equally make from nothing as well as from something. No creature, however, can create or make anything from nothing, although it can work from created things according to the capacity given it by the Lord. Accordingly, those aforesaid people, judging God as though by themselves, thought that God could do only what they knew themselves able to do: namely, make something from something and nothing from nothing.

But mutable things themselves, if you consider them by knowing them, plainly overthrow their errors. For every mutable thing must necessarily have been made from nothing. Its mutability proves this, whereas the divine eternity knows no mutability. For what is truly eternal is mutable neither in nature nor in act. It is always the same; it is not at one time or in one place otherwise. But a mutable thing does not always exist; hence, however far back you extend the matter, it must have proceeded from nothing. For if it had not arisen from nothing—that is, if it had remained without beginning—it would surely be eternal and would remain immutable.

Therefore let whatever changes be proved to have been from nothing. Yet a mutable thing could not make itself, nor could it subsist through itself. It must therefore have a maker through whom it is made and through whom, once made, it is preserved in being, lest, having been made from nothing, it return to nothing.

[Col. 1251C] 11. You ask concerning the Maker who always exists, who makes mutable things and is himself unmoved, what he was doing before he made them, and how it came into his mind suddenly to make what he does not always make. But you ought to know that “before” and “suddenly,” which you put forward, are marks of time; whereas God makes things and the times of things, and precedes these not in time but in eternity. If there were no things, indeed, there could be no movement of things; if there were no movement of things, there would certainly be no time. For time is said to be the bounded interval of the change of things.

Therefore he who made times is not subject to time, but precedes all things in eternity. Thus no mutable things are coeternal with God; rather, they were created by God and together have their beginning from nothing. They have being because they were made by God; they are mutable because they were made from nothing.

Therefore the holy Prophet, guide of truth, lofty leader over Israel, foreseeing that certain empty talkers either had already arisen in his own time or would arise later and would be found to have held heretical views concerning God and his works, shuts such persons out in the first chapter, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” You hear the beginning of things; you hear God the Creator; you hear the matter of created things. For heaven and earth, together with which air and water are included, are called the four elements, from which, as from matter, all bodily things are made. God did not find them coeternal with himself; rather, he is their beginning so that they may be, or he created them in the beginning so that they might begin to be made.

[Col. 1252A] 12. “God created.” You object and say: God is immutable and acts immutably. Therefore, if he created, he always creates; but he does not always create. Therefore he did not create. You must know that you argue thus because whatever can be said of God according to God must be understood not after our manner, but after the manner proper to God, with whom “there is no change nor shadow of turning.” Nothing is new in God; rather, he is always the same.

Thus the word “created” posits nothing in God; rather, by signifying God it posits something in what he created. This word “created” intimates the created thing by positing it. Our words, and any vocal expressions assumed in order to indicate him who supremely and truly is, do not posit action or passion, nor any kind of variation, in the Godhead itself. For this reason, understand prudently that words and any vocal expressions employed to signify God no longer belong to those eight parts established by grammarians, but signify according to a divine mode, not a grammatical, rhetorical, or dialectical one.

For God always is that which he is; he cannot be bounded, described, or defined, because he is incomprehensible. But things that have been made are apprehended and held; consequently, they are set forth as bounded, described, or defined. Every made thing begins to be what it is; yet it does not have from itself that which it is, but from, through, and in him who is essentially life, eternity, and blessedness. Hence it is written through Moses: “God created.”

[Col. 1252C] 13. For this word which we call “God,” *Eloym* is written in Hebrew. Now *Eloym* among the Hebrews is a plural word, but the idiom of the Latin language could not render this. For in Hebrew it is *Bara Eloym*, so that if you translate word for word, Latin usage would require one to say, “the gods created.” Hence it must be known that the word *Eloym*, signifying God in a plural expression, nevertheless cannot posit several gods, because among the Hebrews this is determined by the singular word added, namely *Bara*, which in Latin is *creavit*, “created.”

Our Catholics rightly and devoutly defend this Hebrew expression as so written, since they proclaim and adore the Trinity, which is God, in simple unity; this is represented for them by a singular word joined to a plural one, namely *Bara Eloym*.

[Col. 1252D] 14. “Heaven and earth”—not because they were called thus when they were created, but because afterwards those same things were so named by speakers. God also, and the things which in the beginning were either made or spoken, had to be designated by those words through which our customary usage presents them by signifying them.

15. He says here, “heaven and earth,” because Scripture, having providently said that heaven and earth were created, intimates by silence that air and waters were not created—although it carefully investigates the sequence of all created things. Know, therefore—know, my son—the manner of sacred speech: for it is accustomed to gather all created things together under the name of heaven and earth.

The Psalmist bears witness to this, when he summons the whole creation, from heaven and earth, to praise the Creator, first saying of the heavens: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights. Let all his angels praise him; let all his powers praise him. Let sun and moon praise him; let all stars and light praise him. Let the heavens of heavens and the waters above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:1–4).

Observe that angels, powers, the higher waters, and the rest are assigned to the heavens by their dwelling and co-creation, and are denoted by the name “heavens.” Of all these he immediately adds: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5). He also continued concerning the earth and said: “Praise the Lord from the earth: dragons and all deeps; fire, hail, snow, ice, storm-wind, which perform his word” (Ps. 148:7–8). For as he creates all things, so he moves and orders all things.

Therefore, the things which Moses comprehended as to be understood by “heaven and earth,” the Psalmist enumerated in distinction. We certainly see air, together with water, contained between heaven and earth; and from these two we know that the subtler things are assigned to the heavens and the more bodily to the earth, as we read in the aforesaid distinction of the Psalmist.

You, therefore, confess that air and waters were created, and devoutly sing to the Lord with the prophet: “You created the north wind and the sea” (Ps. 88:13). And elsewhere: “For the sea is his, and he made it” (Ps. 94:5). By “north wind” understand the winds, which arise in stirred air by the divine will; hence the Psalmist says: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. 134:7). But so that you may be unable to doubt further: “All things,” he says, “were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). And so that you may know how he made them: “You made all things,” he says, “in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24).

Now know that the Psalmist summons creation to God’s praise, first from the heavens and then, under distinct names, from the things assigned with the heavens and from the earth. Moses, however, proclaims in the beginning under the name of heaven and earth not distinct things but heavenly and earthly things made together materially, which he afterwards declares formed in a sixfold distinction—not because form can ever or anywhere exist without substance, or substance without form, but because he refutes those who said that substance and forms were joined by God as craftsman, rather than created by God.

Heretics, who do not know the sacred Scriptures and contradict the Holy Spirit, rave such things and the like. But the scribe of truth, whom God himself instructed thoroughly concerning the creation of things, knew and taught that both substances and their forms were created and joined by God. “He created,” he says, “heaven and earth.” Concerning heaven, because fire predominates in it and through it shines more beautifully and illuminates the rest, he passes on thus. Concerning the remaining things illuminated by fire so that they may be visible—namely earth, air, and water—because of the formlessness which they are shown to possess without the illumination of fire, he says:

16. “But the earth was empty and void.” Considered substantially, the earth was empty—not because it existed so in actuality, but because it can be considered so. For who does not know that substance and forms are naturally distinct? Although they are not found separated, nevertheless by the insight of reason they are perceived as naturally distinct within the same thing.

What we say of earth, we perceive likewise concerning heaven, air, and water, when we consider them only as substance, not as form, without those things called quality, quantity, relation, position, being, possession, action, passion, time, and place. This whatever-it-is is more capable of being thought than presented.
