The earth is called empty and void, not because it is so, but because it is formless and invisible, and does not yet have what it germinates or produces. For “empty” and “void” do not signify by positing, but name by removing.

A sound mind often considers what is to be made and from what it is to be made: first that from which something is made, and finally that which is made from it; first unformed matter, then formed matter. The former precedes by a kind of origin, though not bodily. In it, materially, was made whatever can actually be made from it, just as in soft wax there lies hidden causally whatever the craftsman’s skill can succeed in making from it.

Whoever can somehow apprehend this utterly empty thing without an image of forms apprehends something, almost nothing, yet material from which whatever is actual can proceed. This, if it can nevertheless be said, where all things are confused, blind, and insensible, some called *chaos* and named *hyle*—that is, an undigested mass and crude matter. “Empty and void,” he says, not because it was made so in the beginning, but because it had to be narrated so, in order that, although you see matter and form simultaneously, you may recognize them as distinct: empty of forms, plants, trees, living creatures, and all mortal beings.

[Col. 1254C] 17. “Darkness was upon the face of the deep.” Air too, like earth, when considered as substance abstractly and without form, and contemplated without light, is called a dark abyss—not only in itself, but also in the remaining things, namely earth and waters, which likewise are darkened unless the air is illuminated. Therefore we call the dark abyss, as it were, all things undistinguished and invisible in unformed matter, where, if you seek anything, you find almost nothing. I mean nothing composite, nothing visible. Or, “darkness was upon the face of the deep,” that is, it was darker than any abyss may be.

See that “darkness” names nothing, but indicates that light is absent. That is: I saw nothing; I apprehended nothing in appearance.

18. “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” Here too we understand “waters” not yet as those visible waters familiar to us, but as all things fluid and uncombined, formless and capable of formation, proceeding from nothing through God as author, bound under the designation of mutability. Hence they undergo the changes of accidents and decline through the vicissitudes of contingencies; but their failures, though infinite, are held under the omnipotence of their Creator, whose Spirit creates things to be formed, forms those created, and disposes those formed.

Therefore the things we call the elements of the world, and all things formed from them, are together subject to the divine will. And he fittingly designates bodily matter, formless and capable of formation, by water, because we see all things on earth cohere, increase, grow together, and take form in diverse species from moist nature. “The Spirit of God was borne over [them].” He is said to have been borne over them not in place but in power, surpassing and excelling all things. For God created all things not from need but from surpassing love; as he willed, so he created, and he does not cease to govern what he has created.

“The Spirit of the Lord.” See that he did not say “the heaven of God,” “the earth of God,” “the abyss of God,” or “the waters of God”; but he said, “the Spirit of God was borne over [them].” Therefore do not think that the Spirit of God is a creature, but understand that the Spirit of God is God.

Thus, at the beginning of the creation of heaven and earth—by which two the entirety of visible and bodily creation is comprehended—the cooperating Trinity of the Creator is shown and set forth for adoration, when it is said: “In the beginning God created.” In the name God, the Father; in the name beginning, the Son; but the Spirit … The remainder is missing.

[Col. 1255]

## Three Books of Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, Against the Heretics of His Time, or On the Church and Its Ministers

(*Works of Guibert of Nogent*, Appendix, p. 690.)

## Hugh’s Letter to Alberic, Bishop of Ostia

[Col. 1255B] To ALBERIC, bishop of Ostia, most frequent legate of the Apostolic See, son of the holy Roman Church: HUGH, sinner and, such as he is, priest of Rouen.

Reverend Father, for a time I delayed obeying your commands; yet I did not omit the matter. Grant pardon to one who asks it, you who are accustomed to grant grace. It is fitting for me to remember how, in the regions of Gaul near the Breton sea, in the city of Nantes, we were granted the privilege of attending you. There, before a great gathering of the faithful, you received and displayed the bodies of the holy martyr brothers Donatian and Rogatian; having displayed them, you replaced them with fitting honor and thanksgiving.

There, with you, we saw a comet falling in precipitous descent toward the west, which, as you declared, signified the downfall of the heresy then rampant in Armorica. There indeed the heretical people could not stand before your orthodox preaching. Their heresiarch was greatly afraid and did not dare appear. Therefore it pleased you that we should write something concerning the heresies that were arising. We undertook this by the authority of your command, but in a concise work and in a brief style. Let wide-ranging material, then, be drawn from a narrow sentence; let abundant dishes be taken from a small vessel, in Catholic fashion, in the Holy Spirit.

## Hugh’s Preface

[Col. 1255C] The Lord commands: let the servant obey. The Fathers enjoin; the brethren request; the children ask. By the command of charity, together and individually, they lay upon us the charge that against newly emerging heretics, and against their heresies—not new, but old—we should at last rise up, oppose to them the sincere purity of the Catholic faith, and, with the Lord’s aid, defend it against them.

Let therefore the almighty Father of the coeternal Word speak through us and for us; let the Word speak, which always and equally says all things; let the Spirit of Father and Word speak, one and coequal, who, containing all things, has knowledge of speech. The word of truth is set forth: let us hear. God is the issue: let us stand firm.

## Book One

[Col. 1257]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1257A] The rising sun, pouring out light, drives the darkness of night from the whole world. Sound doctrine, brighter than the sun and set forth everywhere, destroys heresy. Sound doctrine professes and proclaims that the Creator of all things, almighty God, is one and alone: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—an unconfused Trinity, an undivided Godhead.

This sublime and exalted truth transcends all things. Neither temporal understanding nor human reason comprehends it; it exceeds every height of both angelic and human mind. The Psalmist testifies to this, saying: “Man shall approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63:7); and elsewhere: “He mounted upon the Cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 17:11), that is, above the excellence of those who seek lofty things.

God is invisible and known to himself alone; no creature knows him completely except that creature which the wisdom of God the Father graciously illumines so that it may know. Hear the Evangelist: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). We therefore ask: how could John know what he proclaimed in the Gospel—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)—if no one has ever seen God? He immediately answered and said: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.”

Accordingly, with the Son declaring him, John could say that God was with God, the Son with the Father—the Son who gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name (John 1:12). Truth also says: “No one knows the Son except the Father; and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son has willed to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

He revealed it to the one who said: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9), and to the Apostle who said: “Do you seek proof of Christ, who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13:3). It was revealed also to Moses on Mount Sinai: concerning the creation of the world under the eternal threefold form of six; concerning the Lord’s rest when all things were completed, on the seventh day, without morning and without evening; concerning the Law and commandments, the tabernacle of the covenant, the rite of sacred things, and ceremonies, of all which he saw the pattern on the mountain.

Many things concerning God’s counsel, mercy, and judgment were also revealed to the Fathers and Prophets; but to pursue these is not presently our concern. The Son also reveals himself to us, saying: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:28). To the Jews he also said: “It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say is your God” (John 8:58). He then added elsewhere: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1). This would not follow unless Christ were God.

Therefore adore the Father, adore the Son, adore both alike as one God. The Father is one person, the Son another; yet the Father is not one God and the Son another God. Father and Son are distinct persons, but they are not two gods, but one. “Hear,” he says, “Israel: your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Truth bears witness to this: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He says “are,” because the person of the Father is one and that of the Son another. He says “one,” because the essence of Father and Son is one and the same.

The Holy Spirit likewise is the one Spirit of Father and Son, from the Father and the Son: the third person, not the third God. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). And: “There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5:6–7). He said “are” because they are three persons; “one” because of their inseparable divinity.

This Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:10). And John the Apostle says: “We abide in God, and he in us, because he gave us of his Spirit; and we have seen and bear witness that the Father sent his Son as Savior of the world” (1 John 4:13). This Holy Spirit, as he is the Father’s, is also the Son’s. The Son himself says of this: “He will receive of mine and declare it to you. All things whatsoever the Father has are mine; therefore I said that he will receive of mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14).

Therefore adore the Father, adore the Son, adore the Spirit of both—not three gods, but simply one. The Prophet knew this, who said: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:3). He said “him,” not “them,” in order to maintain one God, not three gods.

## Chapter II

But you who believe God and in God must know that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Son: “I,” he says, “will send to you from the Father the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). And elsewhere: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). This one sent also proceeds from the Son, whom after his resurrection he breathed upon the disciples, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22).

A bodily breath proceeded from him, by which the invisible procession of the Holy Spirit was signified—the Spirit whom he gave from himself. Concerning him the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:5). The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but is not born, and therefore is called not Son but proceeding. The Son, however, proceeds from the Father and is born, and is therefore called Son: “I came forth from God,” he says, “and came” (John 8:42).

The procession of the Son’s birth from the Father, and the procession without birth of the Holy Spirit from both, are faithfully believed and perpetually adored. Gospel truth taught this thoroughly; apostolic doctrine proclaimed it plainly. We set these things forward against heretics and establish them by divine authority. We do not scrutinize God, but believe as Catholics; for the divinity is not to be scrutinized, but worshipped in the simplicity of faith. As God the Father is from no one, so neither was he sent; but because the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit from both, each is rightly said to be sent by him from whom he exists.

## Chapter III

God the Son, sent by God the Father with the Holy Spirit cooperating, was born of the Virgin. He remained what he was, and willed to become what he was not: man. Perfect God, perfect man, one, not two. One with God the Father in essence; one with the assumed man in person. He was made from our race without the transmission of sin. From human beings, human; from sinners, without sin. Son of David, Son of Abraham, and Son of Adam. From the very source from which guilt had proceeded, he became its remedy.

God became man in order to make human beings gods: gods by grace, not by nature; gods by adoption, not by essence. Himself without sin, he suffered, died, and was buried for sinners; he descended to hell; freeing his own from there, on the third day he rose. Appearing manifestly to his disciples and blessing them, he ascended into heaven. Seated at the right hand of God the Father, he pours out the Holy Spirit more abundantly, whence the flame of love rises, as the Apostle testifies: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

## Chapter IV

When this gift has been given and received, there is one Church betrothed to one husband. Who is that bridegroom? Who is that bride? The teacher of the nations cries to the faithful: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). This betrothal is celebrated in the present through sacraments; in the future, through manifest vision. It is received by faith, strengthened by hope, perfected by love.

First, she is graciously washed by water and the Spirit, so that, her sins wiped away, she is released from guilt and, reborn through holy baptism, may be joined in holiness to her heavenly bridegroom. Reborn, therefore, through the font of enduring grace, she is sealed by the laying on of the paranymph’s hands with prayer and by heavenly chrism, so that she whom Christ’s baptism cleanses from all sins may be clothed in virtues by the surpassing anointing of chrism, duly celebrated through the bishop.

These virtues are the most excellent betrothal-gifts from the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which the heavenly Bridegroom wondrously bestows upon his bride. Then the life-giving participation of nourishment is prepared for her: the body and blood of her same bridegroom, Jesus Christ the Son of God. When these are received, human being and God, and God and human being, are united by an inexpressible unity of covenant. “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood,” he says, “abides in me and I in him; for my flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56–57).

Here we do not receive fruit from the tree of life which was in the earthly paradise, but receive from the Lord’s altar Life itself, who is Christ: “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). This life destroys in us the death that proceeded through the transgression of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

Attend, you who read. Venerate the bride of Christ: first cleansed by the water of baptism and reborn through the saving font; then adorned through royal chrism by the bishop’s laying on of hands, shining with sevenfold grace; afterwards led to the table of the heavenly banquet, where, under the covenant of eternal life, she receives the body and blood of her Bridegroom and rests blessedly, with John the son of love, upon the Lord’s breast.

See, therefore, faith in baptism; hope in confirmation performed with sacred chrism; love at the Lord’s table. For by faith she is renewed, by hope exalted, and by love glorified.

## Chapter V

Therefore, if you would understand the perfect Christian, first understand one reborn from water and Spirit; then adorned by the grace of charisms through the bishop’s hand; then admitted to the holy banquet of the Lord’s table. These three sacraments—namely baptism, the new regeneration in Christ; confirmation of the baptized person by the bishop’s hand through royal chrism in sevenfold grace; and participation at the heavenly table in the body and blood of Jesus Christ—begin indeed in faith unto eternal life, increase in certain hope, and endure in love.

These three constitute the city of God, of which the Psalmist sings and says rejoicingly: “Glorious things have been said of you, city of God” (Ps. 82:3). The same Psalmist professes that this city’s founder is both man and God, saying: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 82:5): God indeed, for he himself is the Most High; man, born in her under time. Of her blessedness he says in praise: “As the dwelling-place of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 82:4).

This city has God as Father, embraces God’s Son as her Bridegroom, and rejoices that the Holy Spirit is her Paraclete. Of this the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his tabernacle. God is in her midst; she shall not be moved. God has helped her at the morning dawn” (Ps. 45:6).

In this Church alone, so celebrated and so glorious, are forgiveness of sins, the efficacy of sacraments, the grace of charisms, communion of saints, resurrection, and the life of the blessed. Sound doctrine proclaims that this fixed and sacred creed of faith must uniquely be observed: by it ignorance is removed, error abolished, and heresy repelled.

## Chapter VI

[Col. 1261A] The first falling away from the light of truth immediately encountered the darkness of ignorance; the blindness of ignorance introduced error; ingrained error produced heresy. Heresy, moreover, is the name for an error proved to be obstinate. The Holy Spirit inspired sound doctrine, through which the way, truth, and life became known to us. Satan, the spirit of wickedness, scattered falsehood, by which he offered error, heresy, and death to the world.

Satan, the fountain of falsehood and origin of sin, was created good by the good Creator, but immediately, perverted by his own will, found within himself the fall of pride, the desire for plunder, and the defilement of idolatry, when he said: “I shall place my throne in the north; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14).

It was not his to set a throne for himself, occupy the north, or desire likeness to the Most High. “I shall place my throne”: behold pride. “In the north”: behold plunder. “I shall be like the Most High”: behold idolatry. See the fall of the impious one. The will which he owed to God, who made him from nothing, he held not for God but as his own. From this selfhood he generated falsehood. Of this Truth says: “When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources” (John 8:44). For he is a liar and its father—that is, this lying father, father of falsehood, fashioned an idol by falsehood.

From the first emergence of malignity, the abyss of falsehood burst forth: “And darkness,” it says, “was upon the face of the abyss” (Gen. 1:2). That Satan, the Lucifer created by God, bright and exalted, was immediately corrupted by his own will; [Col. 1261C] proud in presumption, blinded by greed, from lofty he became an abyss, from luminous dark. His darkness sends forth storms of presumption, weaves snares of covetousness, produces the foulness of lusts. From the mists of those darknesses are created nights of error and the tempest of the wicked. Concerning them and from them Truth replied in the Gospel: “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53).

## Chapter VII

You have heard of darkness upon the abyss; hear that “the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). This Spirit is God and Lord, as is read elsewhere: “The voice of the Lord is upon many waters; the God of majesty [Col. 1261D] has thundered; the Lord is upon many waters” (Ps. 28:3). “God,” it says, “made the firmament in the midst of the waters, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament” (Gen. 1:7). Those angels, indeed, who stood firm when others fell, were raised by humility, and from the waters of their mutability hardened into the crystal of eternal stability. They consented not to themselves but to the Holy Spirit; and they are blessed because they always seek not their own will but the Lord’s, continually behold it, and love it for ever.

Of these the Psalmist says: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148:4). These waters remain above the firm and immovable firmament, which is Christ Jesus, “upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). In him they have been made firm by perfect love, [Col. 1262A] and they cannot in any way fall from the blessedness which they received there.

But those waters that are beneath the firmament may plainly be understood as human beings, who have not yet escaped the snares of temptations and have not at all forsaken the world lying in wickedness. Over these also the Spirit of the Lord is sometimes borne, by whom they are stirred up, so that the life which was the light of human beings may destroy their darkness and transfer them into the light of the saints. There they hear the Apostle saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). These are the faithful waters which are gathered together into one by the word of the Lord; hence he says: “Let the waters which are beneath the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1:9). One, in the unity of faith, hope, and love: into the one [Col. 1262B] God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; into the one Catholic Church, gathered together by one Spirit. In this unity the dry land appears—that earth, namely, which, divinely watered by the Holy Spirit, gave its fruit and brought forth our Savior. Isaiah knew this and, seeing it, cried out: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above; and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). Blessed earth, the Virgin Mary, who gave her fruit: the life of angels and human beings, the Lord God Jesus Christ. “And let righteousness,” it says, “spring up together” (Isa. 45:8).

See that, whereas transgression descended by propagation together with the rest who are carnally born from flesh, with this one born of the Virgin, through the operation of the Holy Spirit, righteousness springs up: because guilt is loosed and the iniquity of those [Col. 1262C] who are reborn through the sacraments is abolished. Hence they are clothed with the grace of virtues and partake of the Lord’s table (Isa. 45:8). “I,” he says, “I the Lord created him,” not under the concupiscence of the flesh, but through the efficacy of divine power. Of this the angel answered the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

## Chapter VIII

From Adam, from Abraham, from David, and from the other fathers following in the same genealogy down to the Virgin’s childbirth, Jesus Christ, one God and man, descended; and through the closed gate of the Virgin, as befitted God and Lord, the almighty Prince chose to come forth to us in a true birth, without the wound [Col. 1262D] of guilt, without the crime of transgression. He was made from the Virgin, made from our race: not under the propagation of sin, but as the abolition of guilt, the bestowal of pardon, and the outpouring of everlasting grace. He is the sole mediator between God and us, the supreme pontiff reconciling God and us, a priest who remains for ever not according to the Levitical order but according to the order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek was priest of God Most High; Abraham paid him tithes, and Levi was there tithed in Abraham’s loins. As Levi was in Abraham’s loins, so he was in Adam’s loins, in whom all sinned. In Adam he sinned; in Abraham he was tithed. Because he sinned, he had to be tithed. What was tithed was what was being healed. But Christ, just as he did not sin in Adam, was likewise not [Col. 1263A] tithed in Abraham; for there was nothing in him needing healing, but he was the medicine and salvation by which all evils, and death itself, are destroyed. For Christ is a priest not according to Levi, who was tithed and received tithes from mortals, being himself destined to die, but according to the order of Melchizedek, who, as the Apostle testifies, gave a blessing to Abraham the victor as priest of God, and to whom Abraham apportioned tithes of all things (Heb. 7:2).

This Melchizedek, as the Apostle says, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, remains a priest for ever. “Consider,” he says, “how great this man was, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave tithes even from the choicest spoils” (Heb. 7:3–4). There, moreover, he testifies that he lives, and, so to speak, through Abraham even Levi, who received tithes, was tithed [Col. 1263B]—for he was still in his father’s loins when Melchizedek met him. Therefore it is fitting to consider that Levi was in Abraham’s loins in one way, and Christ in another. Levi was there under the law of transgression, because he needed to be tithed. Christ was there, to whom the Father says: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:1). To him all owe tithes, because he heals all and gives an eternal blessing.

This unique and ineffable priest, always offering himself to God the Father for us, gives himself also to us: God and man between God and us, one in essence with God the Father and one in person with the assumed humanity. He alone takes away the sins of the world; [Col. 1263C] as mediator of God and human beings, he makes complete peace, uniting himself to us and us to himself in the unity of the Holy Spirit, who is one—the Spirit of Father and Son—and one in all of us.

## Chapter IX

From this holy unity, wicked human beings sometimes fall by a manifest severance: corrupt in mind, shipwrecked concerning faith, having a seared conscience. Heretics of this kind are plagues: they scatter falsehoods, propound perversities, create schisms, and sow scandals. Wrapped in their own darkness and made foul by crimes, they persecute the light of faith: “Whoever does evil hates the light” (John 3:20). They detest the true light, which also shines in darkness, and sound doctrine; they embrace the intemperance of the flesh, the concupiscence of the spirit, [Col. 1263D] and the pride of the mind. Because they do not admit the light of faith, all their knowledge is darkness. Of such people Truth says: “See to it that the light which is in you is not darkness” (Luke 11:33).

Although these people are darkness because they are ungodly and criminal, yet by reason of the rational understanding which they received by nature, they sometimes know high things and apprehend sublime things. But their knowledge of bodily things, and their understanding or experience of incorporeal or divine things, they ascribe not to God but to themselves; they seek their own glory, not God’s. Thus their foolish heart has been darkened. The human intellect, by freedom of choice, by rational capacity, and by the understanding of the mind, ought always to seek, follow, and love him from whom [Col. 1264A] it has received so much, and humbly to be raised above itself toward God by power from above: by pure faith, unwearied hope, and abundant love.

On the other hand, all human knowledge which is governed neither by faith, raised by neither hope, nor joined to God by love, remains in darkness and does not know the light of truth. Hence Moses says: “God saw the light, that it was good, and divided it from the darkness; and he called the light day, and the darkness night” (Gen. 1:4). The light of human reason is good because it was well created by the good Creator. When it presents itself to him from whom it is, obeys him, and is preserved by the power received from God, it becomes better than itself. He calls this light day, because, whitened by a sound mind and clothed with the splendor of gifts of grace, it becomes the day of love, which God inhabits [Col. 1264B] and makes blessed. “Day utters speech to day” (Ps. 18:2): day to day—the Catholic to the Christian, the Christian to the Catholic, the faithful to the obedient, the obedient to the faithful—utters the Word who is with God, God the Word; all things were made through the Word; and because all things in the Word are life, life is the Word, and life is the light of human beings. Thus the Word is life and light. And so that humanity might be more fully united to God, “the Word was made flesh.” The Word made flesh is the same God and man, “and dwelt among us” (John 1:14): not as in angels or in all creatures, but as a human being made from us. Therefore the Word made flesh is life and the light of human beings. Blessed is the day that utters this Word to day; whoever loves him continually utters this Word.

“Day utters speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night” [Col. 1264C] (Ps. 18:2). Night to night—the erring person to the heretic, the heretic to the erring person, the criminal to the ungodly, the ungodly to the criminal—declares knowledge conceived in its own mind, slippery through false opinions and vaunted in obstinacy. This knowledge, because it depends on pride and advances through self-exaltation, seeks only to be puffed up rather than to build up. On the contrary, the Word of love grows through humility, stands firm through truth, proclaims day from day, illuminates those whom it fills, adorns them with sacramental grace, and builds them up by the hands of virtues. The Apostle affirms this, saying: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

## Chapter X

Love, therefore, patient and kind, builds the house of God, which supreme wisdom completes with a marvelous structure of the seven columns of gifts of grace, illuminates with the sun of righteousness, [Col. 1264D] and enriches with abundant stores of every good thing. Gazing from afar upon this house, the Psalmist sang in sweet melody: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). This psalmist sang, according to custom, in the transitory and perishable house of the Lord, in earthly Jerusalem; but in devout longing he stretched toward that heavenly, immovable, stable, and blessed Jerusalem. Those who said, “Our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2), especially intended to stand firm in this begun progress of their journey. But lest you should attend to that ruined and aged Jerusalem rather than behold the true and blessed heavenly one, he added: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same” (Ps. 121:3). Of [Col. 1265A] this he cries elsewhere: “Those who trust in the Lord are as Mount Zion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 124:1).

In this present, wretched, and shaken city, everyone who dwells therein is shaken; in that heavenly, glorious, and peaceful one, no inhabitant is shaken in any way. “Whose participation,” he says, “is in the same” (Ps. 121:3). It is as though he plainly said: That blessed heavenly city, Jerusalem, shares in “the same.” The phrase *eius in idipsum* (“of him in the same”) is expressed intransitively, set in the singular, divinely assumed, assigned solely and always to God as properly his own; for God neither begins nor ends nor changes. Yet to know or understand this fully, as it is, has never been permitted to any creature except one that has received the [Col. 1265B] Holy Spirit; having received him, it has itself merited to be one with God—one by grace through Christ, one by participation in “the same.” “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). At present we see him “through a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12), through sacraments, not yet in essence. Now, as the Apostle says, “our life is hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, our life, shall appear, then we also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3). There is not faith there, but the reward of faith; not hope, but the recompense of hope; there is love, which never fails and will see fully and perfectly what it has loved.

The courts of this heavenly and blessed Jerusalem are opened in this present and temporal Church; hence [Col. 1265C] the Psalmist sings: “Our feet stood in your courts, O Jerusalem” (Ps. 121:2). These courts are indeed in the Church which still labors in childbirth and travail. For it begets children through the sacraments, raises them through virtues, and continually assigns them, as conquerors through Jesus Christ, to heavenly Jerusalem.

Nevertheless, while it journeys in this valley of tears, it must suffer scandals. Here the snares of the faithless, the obscenity of crimes, the rapacity of robbers, the whirlwinds of errors, and the tempests of heresies break forth everywhere. Yet amid evils so utterly wretched and unbearable stands the faith of Peter, the Catholic faith, the highest tower. “A thousand shields hang from it, and all the armor of the mighty” (Song 4:4): the shields are the protection of the sacraments; the armor of the mighty, the missiles [Col. 1265D] of virtues. We are protected by sacraments and overcome through virtues. A thousand is a full and complete number; fittingly, therefore, there are a thousand shields, because there is perfection in the Church’s sacraments; fittingly, all the armor of the mighty, because in it is the fullness of virtues. The tower of Catholic faith, therefore, is a tower of strength; it is the tower of David that looks toward Damascus. David is understood as “strong of hand” or “desirable in appearance”; Damascus is interpreted as “mouth of blood.” Thus the tower of David, which is the fortified and strong Church of Christ, looks in opposition to Damascus: it stands against the savagery of that which devours blood, against heresies and every impiety.

[Col. 1266A] From this most fortified and excellent tower come forth armed men, strong and valiant, who slay the enemies of faith with the swords of virtues. “The mightiest of them guard Solomon’s bed” (Song 3:7); surrounded by these, the peaceful king rests in wondrous sweetness. For there the light of Catholic faith grows more brightly; hope, which does not confound, burns more strongly; the flame of love rises more abundantly; there are most delightful joy and peace. Conversely, out of the darkness of the abyss, the cold regions of the north, and the bloody face of Damascus emerge the ungodly, schismatics flow forth, and heretics speak. The ungodly neither worship God nor receive the sacraments. Schismatics neither obey their fathers nor consent to Catholic communion.

## Chapter XI

[Col. 1266B]

Heretics propound perversities and rage in disputation against the sacraments. “The sacraments,” they say, “benefit only those who understand; they benefit adult persons, but confer nothing upon little children.” They condemn the baptism of little children and infants; they draw from the Gospel against the Gospel, saying: “It is written in the Gospel: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned’” (Mark 16:16). Thus they set forth their premise and then infer: but little children do not believe; therefore, they immediately conclude, baptisms do not benefit little children.

Against this Catholics arise, fortified with all the armor of the mighty, and say that this cited passage [Col. 1266C] of the Gospel concerns not little children, but rather those who understand, adults. Adult persons, or persons possessing their faculties and memory, ought not to be baptized unless they have first given their own profession of the name and faith; such persons are at once commanded to keep in deeds what they promise in faith. For it is written: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:20, 26). Therefore it ought not to have been objected against little children—that which had been truly said of persons answering for themselves and openly professing. But since Truth says generally in the Gospel, “Unless a person be born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), and elsewhere, “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19), [Col. 1266D] no one is excluded, not even a newborn infant. Therefore their fraudulent conclusion is everywhere rejected; it does not hold, because it is plainly proved hostile to God’s grace. It concerns not little children or infants, but persons who understand and profess their own faith.

In little children, grace alone is sought, not yet works: the grace of sanctification from baptism, not yet the works of due action arising from free choice. As the sacrament of baptism is given to them now, so in ancient times the sacrament of circumcision was given to little children. Under the ancient fathers, little children were circumcised on the eighth day and then consecrated to the Lord with sacrificial offerings. For the stain of original guilt enclosed all those born from carnal concupiscence. [Col. 1267A] The Apostle says: “For all have sinned and need the glory of God” (Rom. 3:23). But just as little children do not know the guilt which they draw originally from Adam, so they do not know the grace which they receive in Christ through the sacraments. And as little children are not excused from guilt because they do not know it, so neither are they excluded from the grace whose bestowal they do not recognize.

Canaan did not know the guilt of his father Ham, who laughed at the nakedness of Noah his progenitor; yet Canaan remained a servant with his descendants on account of the guilt of Ham his father (Gen. 9:22). Nevertheless, because of the obedience of Abraham our father, a general blessing graciously flowed out to all nations, through no merits of theirs. Thus this regeneration of sacred baptism is a matter of grace alone, [Col. 1267B] not merit. “In your seed,” he says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). “In your seed,” that is, in Christ, who chose to become God and man in order to free humanity from sins. A human being could indeed sin, but the sinner could not forgive himself his own sin. Therefore everyone needs the glory of God, who became human for us and forgives sins, so that what a human being alone could not accomplish might be accomplished by the God-man, who “has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9:18): to whom he wills he grants grace, and whom he wills he condemns.

Concerning Jacob and Esau, not yet born and not yet knowing anything, the Apostle testifies that the Lord said: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13). Jacob did not know [Col. 1267C] the grace of love which he received; Esau did not know the sentence of hatred which he incurred. Jacob and Esau, indeed, like all others, sinned in Adam. But Jacob is granted gratuitous love for the glory of God; Esau, on account of the desert of original guilt, is rejected by God’s wrath. We behold mercy in Jacob and judgment in Esau alike, and with the Prophet say: “Mercy and judgment I will sing to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1). Evils are indeed ours, and on their account we are deservedly condemned; but we can have no good except from God, and we are undeservedly saved through grace bestowed upon us by God. The giver of this grace, Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin and full of grace and power, received in himself the sacrament of circumcision, sanctifying the sacraments, [Col. 1267D] not needing sacraments. He was offered in the Temple with victims, consecrating the victims, not consecrated by the victims. That he, greater than all yet made little for us, received the sacraments, shows us by his action that little children ought not to be deprived of sacraments. Concerning them he later replied: “Permit the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:14). And he, the Lord of all and Savior of all, baptized by his servant John, sanctified baptism; he was not sanctified by baptism.

This sacrament, unlike circumcision, is not bestowed only on males and on the eighth day, but once upon every person at every time, in either sex and at every age; without it no one is freed from guilt and no one is saved. [Col. 1268A] For the Son of God himself received baptism for us, lest what God bestows should be rejected by human beings, or what grace grants should be attributed to merits. Therefore all persons, of every sex, condition, and age, at every time, must be baptized once without repetition while they live here.

## Chapter XII

But although these matters have been briefly dealt with, heretics still rage and argue: “Christ received baptism when he was thirty years old; therefore little children ought not to be baptized, but those who have wished to be baptized at the age at which Christ was baptized.”

This heretical declamation, as pernicious as it is wicked, endeavors to exclude from baptism not only little children but also every person of lesser age. [Col. 1268B] Yet it must be known and professed in Catholic fashion that Christ’s baptism received sanctification from Christ; it did not sanctify Christ. But we who are baptized in Christ are sanctified by Christ’s baptism. Therefore Christ’s baptism, which he received in order to sanctify it, must not be set against our baptism, by which we are sanctified. The Lord Christ came to John to be baptized by him in the Jordan. John forbade him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” But Jesus answered and said to him: “Allow it for now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him (Matt. 3:14–15). Luke the Evangelist continues thus concerning this: “And it came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also having been baptized and praying, that heaven was opened to him, [Col. 1268C] and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased’” (Luke 3:21–22). Attend, therefore, and understand that in this baptism the Trinity itself, God, was manifested, whom we worship singly and inseparably. You hear the Father bearing witness concerning the Son; you see the Son coming out of the water; you behold the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove. Thus it also happens in every baptism of Christ. Whoever duly receives it is made a son of God; and the Father’s voice bears witness to him: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22); and the Spirit of God descends upon him. This is the whole righteousness which Jesus Christ came [Col. 1268D] to fulfill in every person reborn at the saving font.

The heavens are opened to one who is made a son of God in baptism. Such a person has God the Father and the Holy Spirit descending into him. Beholding this, the Psalmist sang devoutly: “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12). Truth sprang up from the earth: Jesus Christ was born from Mary. By his wondrous bestowal righteousness looked down from heaven, so that it might cleanse the children of iniquity from the stain of guilt, clothe them with heavenly grace, and thus, having justified them, lead them from earth to heaven. Those baptized in the present Church, our mother, become a new creation—sometimes by their own profession, sometimes by another’s attestation. Little children, indeed, while receiving through another’s action sacraments which they do not understand, put on through the faith [Col. 1269A] of the Catholic Church that aforesaid righteousness from heaven and become members of Christ. They are saved and justified by Christ’s baptism, not yet by their own faith, but by the sacrament of another’s faith.

Thus, indeed, the paralytic lowered through the roof before the Lord Jesus was saved not by his own faith but by that of another: “When he saw,” it says, “their faith, he said: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven you’;” and, “Rise and walk” (Matt. 9:2, 5). Thus the Canaanite woman, pleading for her daughter, found grace through her great persistence and deserved to hear: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you have asked” (Matt. 15:28). Thus the royal official acted for his son (John 4:46); thus the widow for her only son (Luke 7:12); thus another’s faith is accustomed to work for the deaf and mute, and for those overwhelmed by extreme infirmity—a faith which [Col. 1269B] wills all to be saved in Christ (1 Tim. 2:4). We have touched briefly upon these points concerning little children who are to be baptized, lest we be accused of having said nothing in reply to heretics on this subject.

## Chapter XIII

Furthermore, certain persons speak—though wishing to avoid being called heretics—raise a question, and say: “In the Old Testament we read written: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Gen. 15:6). “Finally, in the New [Testament] the sacrament of baptism has been joined to faith, where it says: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved’” (Mark 16:16). “Therefore, if justification comes from faith and salvation from baptism, what does the confirmation performed by the pontiff’s hand add over and above believers and baptized persons, justified and saved?”

[Col. 1269C] Let such persons hear that baptism, duly received once in Christ from any persons and through any persons, at every time, age, condition, and sex, truly suffices for the remission of sins, righteousness, the reception of grace, and eternal life. There grace is given without merits; from grace comes righteousness, and from righteousness life—if the person dies immediately, eternal and blessed life—and no sin is reckoned against him because of the remedy of baptism. But if one survives after baptism, having risen from baptism sanctified through Christ’s grace, he immediately endures the incitements of his flesh and meets the assaults of the devil; unless clothed with power from on high, he will not be able to stand, overcome by the desires of his flesh, the enticements of the world, and Satan’s temptations. [Col. 1269D] “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126:2). For this purpose the supreme pontiff, giver of graces and bestower of gifts of grace, after his ascension poured out the Holy Spirit mightily in fire upon his disciples, already purified and already sanctified. Having received the ruling Spirit, the warmth of power, and the fire of gifts of grace, those very persons who had previously fled when the Lord was abandoned, and he who had feared a maidservant accusing him, immediately came into the midst without fear, speaking the mighty acts of God and preaching the word of God with all confidence.

Therefore, as our pontiff and supreme priest, from the seat of majesty, poured out the Holy Spirit more fully in fiery tongues upon disciples who had first been baptized and sanctified by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1270A] so also those who hold preeminence in the pontifical office bestow by a heavenly work, in the place of Jesus Christ, upon children reborn in baptism: laying hands on them, with prayer, the sign of the holy cross, and the anointing of chrism, they bestow the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. These are the seven eyes upon one stone; the seven lampstands in the temple of God; the seven trumpets under the hand of Joshua triumphant; the seven stars in the pontifical order. These are overflowing treasures; these are surpassing riches.

These things are given to Christ’s faithful reborn in the saving washing, the perennial font, through the aid of the Holy Spirit, who from the beginning of the world was borne over the waters, as a sign that sacred baptism is to be rightly [Col. 1270B] celebrated in the Catholic Church. They are given not to persons being baptized, but after they have been baptized; not by just anyone, but by the hand of the pontiff alone. Concerning this Luke the Evangelist says in the Acts of the Apostles:

> When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them, that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Then they laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. But when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying: “Give me also this power, that upon whomever I lay hands he may receive the Holy Spirit.” But Peter said to him: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.” (Acts 8:14–20)

Luke also speaks thus of Simon Magus, who became an apostate:

> When in Samaria they had believed Philip preaching the gospel concerning the kingdom of God, men and women were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ; then Simon himself also believed, and, when he had been baptized, he attached himself to Philip. (Acts 8:12–13)

Philip, however, was not an apostle but a Levite, one of the seven upon whom the apostles, praying, had laid their hands. Therefore, seeing very great signs and miracles taking place through Philip [Col. 1270C], Simon was astonished and marvelled (Acts 8:13). Finally, when he saw the apostles Peter and John give the Holy Spirit through prayer and laying on of hands, he greatly coveted this surpassing dignity of pontiffs and sought, through money, to possess the episcopal eminence under the pretext of rapacity and avarice. From this Simon, simony received its name: it corrupts with mercenary dealing gifts of God and benefits freely received and to be freely bestowed. But Peter’s authority, the pontifical authority, and the purity of Catholic faith immediately destroyed and subjected to a curse this plague in Simon and his accomplices. Thus Simon Magus was destroyed with his followers because he wished to possess God’s gift by the intervention of money, so that he might sell to others what he had bought. Let those heretics who now speak against this likewise perish, saying that it is empty and superfluous that [Col. 1271A] Christ’s faithful are confirmed by the bishop after receiving sacred baptism.

For Peter and John were sent by the apostles from Jerusalem to Samaria so that they might confirm by pontifical authority those whom Philip the Evangelist had baptized, praying over them and laying hands upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit was given there not for cleansing from sins and sanctification, which they had received in baptism, but so that, against the recurring sins of the flesh, against this world’s pleasures, and against Satan’s dreadful conflicts, they might receive the divine and invincible sevenfold grace of wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. Whoever is reborn in Christ and clothed and fortified with these things goes forth victorious everywhere, secure from assault on every side; to this victor a crown is due, and for this triumphant person glory is prepared. Therefore let everyone baptized in Christ hasten to be sealed by the bishop’s prayer, the laying on of hands, and the heavenly anointing of chrism, so that, having received power from on high, he may advance victorious everywhere and shine for ever in the Christian name through the royal chrism.

## Chapter XIV

For such persons, while they live in the present life, it is necessary that life-giving refreshment be prepared: the bread of life, the cup of eternal blessing, the body and blood of our supreme Pontiff, Jesus Christ. This is altogether necessary, [Col. 1271C] and no Christian is permitted to abstain from participation in so great a mystery. The Lord says to this person: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves. Whoever,” he says, “eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. For my flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:54–56). Finally, at the Paschal supper, from the old he gave the new, from the earthly the divine, the living bread to his disciples. Thus Matthew says:

> While they were dining, Jesus took bread, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and eat: this is my body.” And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink from this, all of you, [Col. 1271D] for this is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins.” (Matt. 26:26–28)

By this communion of the true body and blood of Jesus Christ, we are joined to Jesus Christ and Jesus Christ to us in an inexpressible unity of covenant, as he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:55). This our supreme pontiff was alive and whole among his disciples, and with his own hands gave them his body and blood. “Do this,” he says, “in commemoration of me” (Luke 22:19).

Therefore, from this institution and command, upon the Lord’s altar and by the mouths and hands of priests, that same [Col. 1272A] body and blood of Christ are made present. It does not begin or come to birth; rather, that which remains wholly at the right hand of God the Father is wholly in the priest’s hand and wholly in the recipient’s mouth: one in many, the same in different persons. This inestimable benefit, this incomparable gift, was given to the universal Church, our mother, at that sacred banquet of the Paschal supper. In vain, therefore, did the traitor Judas sell the Lord Jesus to the Jews, whom Mother Church had received, through divine generosity, to possess perpetually as an eternal gift. Thus both the traitor who sold him and the faithless purchaser were frustrated. For “the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Rev. 5:5); he is the stone “cut out from the mountain without hands” (Dan. 2:34): God and man, born of a virgin, and without human agency, without embraces of the flesh, [Col. 1272B] one God and man, Jesus Christ. Made like us in all things except sin, he became for us a saving sacrifice and universal reconciliation. Offered upon the cross to God the Father, he redeemed all his faithful alike, both dead and living, from sin; cleansed them from guilt; and graciously released them from punishment. Christ our pontiff and priest, by his death redeemed and brought forth from hell the patriarchs, prophets, and all whom the mark of faith had designated from the beginning of the world; by rising he raised them up, and by ascending he glorified them.

Seated therefore at the right hand of God the Father, he gives himself upon the altar, suffering no loss, no diminution whatsoever, through the ministry of the priest: to his living faithful for the remission of sins; to holy departed persons, or to those absolved within the Church, [Col. 1272C] for the expiation of punishments; and to both as nourishment unto everlasting life. “I,” he says, “am the living bread which came down from heaven: if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever”; and: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:51–52). This is the living sacrifice which our Lord Jesus Christ both himself offered to God the Father for us and commanded us, as was fitting, to offer. “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Certainly in remembrance of him we do this very thing, when, just as he himself did and commanded us to do, we daily sacrifice him himself upon the Lord’s altar for departed believers and for those still living in this present world. For in every Mass which we celebrate, we both receive in sacrifice the Lamb [Col. 1272D] who always lives and takes away the sins of the world, and, having received him, do not consume him. “I am,” he says, “the bread of life,” etc. “I am the living bread,” not like the manna in the wilderness (John 6:48, 51), which could not bear the heat of the sun, which did not appear on the Sabbath, concerning which he says: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and died” (ibid., 31): evil fathers, unbelieving fathers, dead alike in body and soul. The manna they ate was no remedy against death. For the true and only medicine against death is he who says: “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). Amen.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1273]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1273A]

While Satan rages against the truth of the Catholic faith, the true light goes forth and the grace of the Holy Spirit becomes more clearly known: truth speaks, falsehood falls; sacraments are performed, sin fails. The open fountain in the house of David is poured out over the whole world: people are baptized and saved. The heavens are opened and powers work. The Church is betrothed to Christ and clothed with power from on high. Bishops prepare the bridal gifts and bestow the Spirit of sevenfold grace. The Church is marked with royal chrism; the queen stands at the bridegroom’s right hand in a garment of gold, gleaming with the radiance of charity. For this bride, so illustrious and beautiful, a Paschal banquet is prepared in the hall of wisdom. There the fatted calf, whole and perfect, and the year-old lamb, full and [Col. 1273B] spotless, are received with every sweetness, most delightful savor, and most welcome love. This food is known to be not earthly but heavenly beyond heaven; from him and through him and in him life, eternity, and blessedness are received. For this food is not transitory but daily, everlasting, always entire, always living: by it angels live in heaven and are blessed; by it human beings live on earth and are holy.

For this food is the Word—not transitory but eternal, not mutable but selfsame: with God, God the Word; with us, the Word made flesh, who dwelt among us. “And we saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full [Col. 1273C] of grace and truth” (John 1:14); and: “Of his fullness we have all received” (ibid., 17): namely, all bishops, deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, doorkeepers, and the rest under the clerical tonsure; likewise the princes and powers of this earthly government, and all others marked with the Christian name.

Bishops established throughout the whole world fulfil the office of Christ and, above all, build the house of God. For just as our supreme pontiff and universal bishop, Jesus Christ, chose twelve from among all his disciples, called them apostles by preferring them to the rest, and, though mere human beings, made them sharers in his office and participants in divine magnificence: so too he caused their successors—the prelates or pontiffs in episcopal grace—to excel with singular preeminence, [Col. 1273D] so that, after the apostolic manner, they bestow the Holy Spirit upon those on whom they duly lay hands. Those reckoned in a lower order—presbyters, deacons, and the rest advanced to a canonical rank in the Church—certainly possess the Holy Spirit, by whom they live rightly and serve day by day in the Church of God according to their office; but by laying on of hands they cannot give to others the Holy Spirit whom they have received. Bishops alone have received from the Lord this special prerogative: that, by their preeminent work, they bestow upon others the very Holy Spirit whom they possess, he who gave it enabling them to give it, upon those to whom they devoutly lay hands in fulfilment of their pontifical office, after prayers have been poured out to the Lord.

A marvelous miracle indeed, worthy of every reverence, yet neither new nor unusual. For we read that long ago the Lord acted thus with the Spirit of Moses in the book of Numbers: “And the Lord said to Moses: Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, and lead them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant; make them stand there with you, that I may come down and speak with you, and take from your spirit and give it to them, that they may bear with you the burden of the people and you may not [Col. 1274B] be burdened alone” (Num. 11:16–17). Moses therefore came and related the words of the Lord to the people, gathering seventy men from the elders of Israel and making them stand around the tabernacle. The Lord came down in a cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit which was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men. And when the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied and did not thereafter cease (ibid., 24–25). Moses alone had received the Holy Spirit by whom he was able to govern the people entrusted to him by the Lord. Therefore understand that this Spirit of Moses was not human but divine; for the Spirit whom Moses had from the Lord was God, and the Lord poured into the minds of others that which had been taken from Moses. The Spirit of the Lord was indeed in Moses [Col. 1274C] and was given also to others, whom he filled in a divine manner: wholly in Moses, wholly in them. Moses himself confesses this Spirit to be divine when he immediately replied, saying: “Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit” (Num. 11:29). Moses himself also, the Lord’s pontiff and priest, laid hands upon Joshua his minister and gave him the Holy Spirit. In Deuteronomy you read: “Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom, because Moses had laid his hands upon him; and the children of Israel obeyed him and did as the Lord commanded Moses” (Deut. 34:9). This is the Moses who consecrated Aaron, the first pontiff under the Law, and his sons, and who himself, as pontiff and priest, wondrously gave them the Holy Spirit for the performance of divine mysteries. Of his priesthood the Psalmist says: “Moses and Aaron were among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. 98:6).

Elijah also, if I remember rightly, not only possessed the Holy Spirit but gave it to Elisha as well. Elisha says to Elijah: “I pray, let your spirit be doubled in me” (4 Kings 2:9). But he replied: “If you see [Col. 1275A] me when I am taken away from you, what you have asked shall be granted” (4 Kings 2:10). Elisha persisted to this end: he saw and received. Accordingly the sons of the prophets said: “The spirit of Elijah has rested upon Elisha” (ibid., 15). Therefore they remained subject to Elisha as they had formerly been to Elijah.

But when the fullness of time came, in which God sent his Son, pontiff and bishop for ever according to the order of Melchizedek, the abundant and lavish sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit was poured forth from the throne of majesty; from this source pontifical authority and episcopal dignity grew more fully (Gal. 4:4). Hence he says to Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this Rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:13). For Peter is in the Church and the Church itself is in Peter: the bishop in the Church and the Church in the bishop. [Col. 1275B] The bishop is the foundation of the Church, because through the bishop the Church possesses the Holy Spirit. It belongs to bishops to prepare sacred chrism, holy oil, and oil for the sick; to consecrate God’s basilicas and altars, the chalice and corporals, ministers and their vestments, and all the Church’s implements; to confirm the baptized; and to anoint emperors and kings. From this rock, upon which mother Church has been founded, struck twice beneath the pastoral staff and stirred to the love of God and neighbor, waters flow most abundantly: saving waters, living waters. “He who drinks,” he says, “the water which I shall give shall become in him a fountain of water springing up to eternal life” (John 4:13). And elsewhere: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly”; and this he says “of the Spirit whom those believing in him were to receive” (John 7:38–39). “When,” he says, “the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13).

What a human being alone cannot know by his own understanding, a human being filled with the Holy Spirit can know. Accordingly he says: “Everything which I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15): made known in the Spirit of truth, made known in the fullness of charity. To such persons it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God (Mark 4:11). But lest anyone presume that they are not to be heard or that their commands may be annulled, he says: “He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me; but he who despises me despises him who sent me” (Luke 10:16). And elsewhere: “It is not,” he says, “you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10: [Col. 1275D] 20).

Therefore, possessing from the Lord the Spirit of truth and knowing the mysteries of the kingdom of God, they handed down for posterity to be maintained throughout the world what the apostles had likewise received together from the Lord Jesus. For after the apostles came apostolic men, pontiffs and bishops, who continually build by heavenly power the house of Christ, which they support with seven columns. For these are the seven most useful and necessary ranks, adorned by the bishop’s hand with sevenfold grace for supporting and preserving the house of God: men of the second order, namely presbyters; after them Levites or deacons; then subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers, according to the offices assigned them by the bishop. If these presume to act without the bishop’s direction or against the bishop, [Col. 1276A] they fall away from the number seven, recoil from the aforesaid seven columns, and, slipping from the house of wisdom, perish. But leaving these matters aside, let us continue what we have begun and say something briefly concerning the seven columns of God’s Church.

## CHAPTER II

First concerning presbyters, whom bishops, after invoking the Holy Spirit, consecrate to perform the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, just as the Lord himself did at the Paschal supper and commanded to be done—done only by bishops and by presbyters consecrated to the priestly office. The eminent power of this office and the surpassing dignity of its power were bestowed not upon angels nor upon any majesty of the heavenly citizens. God, made man, gave it to man—not by human help but by heavenly power; not as an acquisition by merit but as an election of mercy, from the graciously received gift of the Holy Spirit. Consecrated through this gift to this work in Christ, the priest has been granted to effect upon the altar precisely the same thing which Christ performed with his own hands at the Paschal supper. Therefore those hands—hands consecrated for this purpose, by which Christ’s body and blood are to be made upon the sacred altar—are indeed Christ’s hands, by which the Son is offered to the Father: he who takes away the sins of the world, frees departed believers from punishments, and makes them partakers of eternal blessedness.

The consecrated priest therefore stands in Christ’s place before the Father, supreme mediator of God and human beings, [Col. 1276C] when he brings forth and elevates from the altar the ineffable sacraments from heaven laid open, making the children of the Church partakers through communion; and when, in the Holy Spirit whom he has received, he both remits sins to penitents and reconciles to God those whom he absolves. In this work shines forth the Spirit of wisdom, by whom the Father’s name is sanctified in them, as every believer prays in the Lord’s Prayer (Matt. 6:9); and they become peacemakers and are therefore reckoned blessed, because they shall be called children of God (Matt. 5:9). In this present life they make peace between God and humanity, according to their rank, by sacraments duly celebrated, by their merits, and by their hands filled with heavenly medicine.

It must therefore be known and proclaimed with all reverence that the Spirit of wisdom sanctifies them as sons to our Father God—not just any persons, but peacemakers, and therefore blessed, both [Col. 1276D] in the present age and in the age to come.

## CHAPTER III

After presbyters, Levites or deacons are consecrated by the laying on of the pontiff’s hands, that they may attend the altar in the Church of God while the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are performed upon it. Although they do not themselves perform the consecration, they nevertheless receive from the consecrator the dispensation of the true body and blood of Jesus Christ. For from the hand of the pontiff or presbyter they receive that by which they refresh themselves and others, in generous distribution, with the food of life; and they administer the Church’s goods according to the bishop’s will. They are the eyes of pontiffs and presbyters, in order that, so far as they can, [Col. 1277A] they may secure rest and peace for those who keep watch for the performance of sacraments and labor more quietly to teach the peoples and pray.

In this work of Levites or deacons shines forth the Spirit of understanding: by it they understand the sacraments which they distribute; by it they devoutly administer matters entrusted to them; by it, as far as they are able, they provide peace and quiet for the preachers of God’s Word by removing disturbers and the restless. Adorned with chastity and blessed in purity of heart, they seek the kingdom of God, while through their diaconal ministries they make a way of teaching for bishops and report more certainly to the bishop what they know about each matter. Pontiffs also appoint these men as evangelists, and they diligently strive to carry out the duties of pontiffs according to their rank.

[Col. 1277B] By their exceeding charity these men earn, with Stephen, the sight of the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Likewise, when during the celebration of the Lord’s Mass they proclaim the holy Gospel to the Church assembled, they are answered, “Glory to you, O Lord,” in the harmonious voice of the faithful.

## CHAPTER IV

After deacons, subdeacons are promoted. After prayer has been offered, bishops lay upon them the charge that they obediently submit to Levites and presbyters, and prepare the sacred vessels in which Christ’s body and blood are made. According to custom, they prepare bread, wine, water, and the vessels suitable for them; likewise altar coverings and *prandea* [variant: *brandea*, cloths or relic-wrappers], with ready care and diligence.

[Col. 1277C] When they are consecrated by the bishop, an address concerning continence and chastity is delivered to them. If they then resolve henceforth to keep chastity, the bishop gives them the Lord’s chalice to hold in their hands, so that from that day they may attend to the Lord’s chalice in humility and chastity.

In this work appears the Spirit of counsel, which he receives particularly when he is consecrated by the pontiff’s prayer. Having received it, he strives to preserve himself pure and chaste, to prepare himself for the mysteries, and to present cleansed vessels for the sacraments. These men place no confidence whatsoever in themselves, but submit their own will to the Lord’s will and humbly say: [Col. 1277D] “Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth” (Matt. 6:11): as in our spiritual fathers, so also in us, their sons still upon earth, still fighting against the desires of the flesh. Thus they become merciful and pray with greater confidence for mercy from God.

## CHAPTER V

After subdeacons follow acolytes, ordained by bishops that in the Church of God they may carry cruets, ewers for hand-washing, and towels appropriate to their office; and that before the Gospel they may themselves bear lighted lamps, carefully set upon candle-bearers. Thus it appears in them that, by the light of true faith, the splendor of most certain hope, and the ardor of charity, they themselves seek the righteousness of God’s kingdom declared through the Gospel, [Col. 1278A] and by the example of their own light exhort others to seek it; and thereafter bring both themselves and others, by earnestly hungering, to receive the sacraments.

In this work appears the Spirit of fortitude, by which amid the storms of aerial power and the tempests of the world they now live by faith’s light, now advance in hope, now persevere in charity. They too are blessed in this, because “they hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6), because they devoutly taste at the Lord’s altar our daily bread, always living and always entire.

## CHAPTER VI

After acolytes follow exorcists, who are consecrated by bishops. The pontifical blessing makes exorcists commanders—not by earthly profit, not by carnal power, but by God’s power—by which, after invoking the name of Jesus and first offering prayer accompanied by exsufflation, they drive Satan and every wickedness from the possessed and all demoniacs; so that these may be able to come to the grace of holy baptism and receive the sacraments.

[Col. 1278B] In this work appears the Spirit of knowledge, lest they attribute this to themselves or become proud thereby, but that they may know what they were by nature, what they deserved by fault, and what they themselves, consecrated by the bishop, can accomplish by grace. Blessed are those who mourn their own former falling away from the good (Matt. 5:5), their lapse into evils; but they are comforted in the Lord Jesus Christ, who delivers them from evils and has powerfully made them commanders over Satan [Col. 1278C] for the driving away of his wickedness.

Therefore, most fittingly, these men—first redeemed for themselves by heavenly mercy, then delivering from demonic wickedness those whom they rescue by power bestowed upon them by God—humble themselves beneath the mighty hand of God, saying in a suppliant voice: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). In this Spirit of knowledge they have this help: although by office they are commanders, they nevertheless know, because of their own frailty, that they are sinners.

## CHAPTER VII

After exorcists, readers are blessed by bishops in order that, at the bishop’s command, they may read in the Church of God—either [Col. 1278D] in his presence or elsewhere—the words of the Old and New Testament; read according to custom, at the appointed time and suitable place; proclaiming the sacred pages of the New and Old Instrument, and the holy writings of the Fathers, as harmonious and fulfilled in one Lord, our Jesus Christ, and always to be heard with due reverence and observed as occasion requires.

In this work appears the Spirit of piety, because they presume neither from the pattern of pride, nor the exaltation of boasting, nor malignant cunning, nor heretical arrogance to read or dare to expound; but with a devout outlook and Catholic guidance they do not adapt the Scriptures to their own judgment but rather adapt their judgment to the Scriptures. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4): the solid truth [Col. 1279A] separated from the waters and waves of the sea at the beginning—that is, set apart from errors and the waves of errors. In order that they may escape these and be free, they pour out to the humble Lord this prayer: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13).

Therefore, possessing the Spirit of piety, they become meek in proclaiming the truth, avoid the snares of temptation, and advance in the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER VIII

After readers, pontiffs appoint doorkeepers, that, having received the blessing, they may keep the doors of the Church with diligent care and remind the faithful to come to God’s service at fixed hours by a suitable sound. In accordance with their office they admit those whom they know to be Catholics; they exclude unbelievers whom they perceive to be mockers or disturbers. They also firmly reject [Col. 1279B] those whom they certainly know to have been deprived of communion with the bishop.

In this work appears the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, which makes the poor in spirit blessed (Matt. 5:3). Having received it, doorkeepers exclude the evil from the good, from the kingdom of God which is Christ’s Church. Praying that this may already take place in the present and be wholly fulfilled in the future, they ask the Lord and say: “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). This Spirit of the fear of the Lord makes one chaste and humble and introduces wisdom. “The fear of the Lord,” he says, “is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). This fear of the Lord is not servile, nor is it of sin, but of charity, which serves freely. The doorkeeper receives it, so that he may be delivered from evil and, because of poverty of spirit, receive the kingdom of God.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1279C]

Take heed, you who read, if you possess the Spirit of God, who bears the key of knowledge: he closes and no one opens; he opens and no one closes. Consider these seven ranks, these seven columns, distinguished in order by the mouth of God’s wisdom through the bishop’s hands, strengthened by blessing, adorned with sacraments. The bishop raises these seven by the seven petitions of prayer, confirms them by the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and crowns them with the honor of the seven beatitudes. Jesus Christ himself taught those aforesaid seven petitions as full and perfect; in his magnificence he gave the wondrous seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and he bestows the seven beatitudes on his faithful for ever and beyond. By these seven petitions the seven gifts [Col. 1279D] of the Holy Spirit are obtained; by those seven gifts the seven beatitudes are acquired. Faith in the petitions, hope in the gifts, and charity in the beatitudes are assigned together; in the petitions is effort, in the gifts reward, in the beatitudes joy. If you seek devoutly, you will quickly find. Let us apply ourselves diligently to seeking such things and happily fulfill seven days upon these seven columns.

Behold: for the seven petitions, seven gifts, and seven beatitudes, you are truly blessed, mother Church. Most abundantly rich in divine sacraments, in you sins are fully forgiven, pardon is granted, grace is bestowed. All things are yours; for he who made all things is yours. Supreme wisdom ever dwells in you and enriches you with every good. Your good will [Col. 1280A] prepares good things; charity distributes them. Your ministers are bishops, vigorous overseers and most steadfast guardians. From you they beget for you strong and free-born sons; from those whom they approve, they choose and raise up; from them they create the seven ranks of honor, the seven columns of strength.
