They consecrate these with the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, illuminate them with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and glorify them with the seven beatitudes. These seven columns both uphold God’s Church and make it radiant with perpetual splendor.

The Lord Jesus Christ instituted that such columns should be ordained through bishops, and designated them by seven ranks. He also, possessing these ranks in himself, set them forth by his authority as ranks to be observed.

## CHAPTER X

[Col. 1280B]

This great doorkeeper of ours once and again drove sellers and buyers from God’s temple; to the blessed thief hanging upon the cross—confessing and asking mercy—he opened paradise (Luke 23:43). “I,” he says, “am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:9). By mighty power he broke the gates of hell and led his own out from there free. Then the veil of the temple was torn in the middle, and the Holy of Holies was opened (Matt. 2:51). At his resurrection the tomb was opened, the earth was shaken, the graves were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept arose. At his ascension heaven was opened, now and for ever.

Our Lord Jesus Christ was likewise always our great reader: the Word of God, God with God, who speaks all things together [Col. 1280C] and wrote in the book of life with a true character; who first dictated in paradise to the first human being the law of the decree. Of this reader the Apostle says: “God, who in many portions and in many ways formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us in the Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Heb. 1:1–2). This reader was writing with his finger on the ground for the woman caught in adultery, and said: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7). He was writing there with his finger on the ground—he who long before had given Moses, once and again, the two stone tablets written with his finger (Luke 4:17). At last, in the midst of the synagogue, the book [Col. 1280D] of the prophet Isaiah was given to this reader to read. He read from it; having returned the book, he expounded what he had read; and he taught that the passage of prophecy was plainly spoken truly of himself and truly fulfilled in himself.

Likewise our great exorcist was Jesus Christ, who utterly overthrew Satan—swollen with pride and wishing to reign above the north—by the mere command of his power: Satan who had cast down our first parents, transgressors, from paradise. This commander of ours, led up onto a high mountain, confronted that ancient tempter Satan. He first exposed him as an idolater and said: “Get behind me, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4:10). He also sent those demons whose name was Legion into swine. How many works of this kind you find when you read through the Gospels!

[Col. 1281A] Our great acolyte, moreover, was Jesus Christ when he said: “Let there be light,” and divided the light that had been made from the darkness (Gen. 1:3); and he says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). This light is the true light, of which the Evangelist says: “There was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). This acolyte wondrously led Israel in a pillar of fire from Egypt as far as the land of promise. He also says to those whom, coming in the flesh, he was enlightening: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:25). And: “So let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). [Col. 1281B] Concerning this, our acolyte commands thus: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12:35).

Moreover, our great subdeacon was Jesus Christ, most powerful of all. For forty years in the wilderness he supplied the children of Israel with manna from heaven (Deut. 2:7). At the torrent of Cherith he fed Elijah for a long time with bread and flesh, supplied by a raven (3 Kings 17:3, 15). At Cana of Galilee, turning water into wine, he gladdened the guests (John 2:1). At the Paschal supper he poured water into a basin and, as a subdeacon, humbly washed the disciples’ feet and wiped them with the linen cloth with which he was girded (ibid., 13).

Our same great deacon was Jesus Christ, “who reaches mightily from end to end and disposes [Col. 1281C] all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). Through Moses he arranged both the rites of sacred things and the duties of ministers. Under the customs of nature, under the governance of the Law, and under the remedy of grace, from the beginning of the world to the end of the age, he leads forward his Church by wondrous dispensation. This wondrous Levite at the Paschal supper, in order to make the new from the old and make truth appear from figures, set forth food that is always living. When he was placed upon the cross, he also devoutly arranged, under charity’s care, for his mother and the disciple whom he loved, saying: “Woman, behold your son.” But to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple took her into his own [home] (John 19:26–27): the son [received] as mother one entrusted to him by the supreme Levite. Concerning this disciple [Col. 1281D] the Lord answered Peter after his resurrection, saying: “Thus I will that he remain until I come” (John 21:23).

Our great presbyter was Jesus Christ, who with his own hands made his body and blood from bread and the cup at that sacred banquet, and gave them to his disciples to receive, without any ambiguity, in simple truth. “This,” he says, “is my body, which shall be given for you” (Matt. 26:26). “This is my blood, which shall be shed for you” (Mark 14:23). “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Concerning this sacrament of his body and blood, and concerning all the Church’s sacraments and their ministers, he fully instructed his disciples. As the disciples received from the Lord, so they passed on these things to their own followers to be maintained, [Col. 1282A] and commanded that posterity should continually observe them in the same form.

This great pontiff and bishop of ours, suffering on the cross for the salvation of the world, offered himself to God the Father for us as a holy, living, full, and perfect sacrifice. He fastened to the cross the written bond of our condemnation, blotting out upon it all our sins, both those transmitted from our origin and those added by our own will. His priesthood remains from eternity into eternity. At the beginning of the world, when all things had been created and completed, he gave blessing in his surpassing episcopal office and sanctified the day of his rest, in which he ever rests in himself from every work that he has made, with ineffable perpetuity. To the blessedness of this rest, after Satan and his followers had been cast out, the merciful pontiff raised by the hands of charity those nine orders [Col. 1282B] of heavenly citizens; and he looked upon us wretches, filthy with sins and foul with crimes, with ineffable compassion. The true light himself descended into our darkness: God made man, sent by the Father, born from a virgin, given as Abraham’s seed according to the promise, in whom all nations are blessed in endless fullness.

This supreme priest bore all our sins in his body. On this Isaiah says: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes” (Isa. 53:6). Hence through the same prophet God the Father testifies thus concerning his Son: “For the crime of my people I struck him” (ibid., 8). And the prophet says: “The Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all” [Col. 1282C] (ibid., 7). “The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (ibid., 5). And the good Shepherd himself says in the Gospel: “I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:15). Elsewhere concerning this he says: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (ibid., 18). He laid it down not for himself but for us, dying on the cross; he took it up again, rising from death. As he willed, so he did. For though he was in the form of God, as the Apostle says, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore [Col. 1282D] God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:6–10).

From this we see fulfilled what is said to him in the Song of Songs: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1:2). Solomon, however, says: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10:1). From the rising of the sun to its setting, from the heights of heaven to the uttermost darkness of hell, Christ’s name is everywhere poured out as the fragrance of life to all who are saved. Of this the Psalmist sings: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its height; and [Col. 1283A] none is hidden from his heat” (Ps. 18:6–7). This heat gives life to saints, burns the impious, and kills heretics.

Therefore the exalted conqueror and glorious pontiff pours forth the Holy Spirit in abundant blessing from the throne of majesty. And, when the dying flies—that is, heretics, pursuing every vain thing with inquisitive perversity—have been scattered far and wide and destroyed along with the darkness of their errors, [Col. 1284A] the heavenly anointing descends upon the humble and quiet, to the praise and glory of this same our Lord Jesus Christ, whose kingdom, dominion, and supreme priesthood remain for ever and unto all ages of ages.

## BOOK III

[Col. 1283]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1283B]

“The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). The Lord is gracious, reaching mightily from end to end and disposing all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). He said, “Let it be,” and it was made (Gen. 1). He saw what had been made, and it was good. “He said, Let it be”: the Word is in eternity, and it was made—the creature went forth with time. “He saw what had been made”: this is the regard of the Creator’s benevolence. “And it was good”: behold the magnificence of the divine gift. From the highest things to the lowest, if you look carefully, you see all things enriched with heavenly benefits. This Lord is gracious and does not cease to show mercy: “He makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and sends rain upon the just and unjust” (Matt. 5:45); “but his mercies are over [Col. 1283C] all his works” (Ps. 144:9). When you consider his works, if you are wise, you are not astonished. Almighty God has made everything whatsoever he willed, and there is none able to resist his will (Ps. 13:11).

He holds his peaceful kingdom, the kingdom of all ages (Ps. 144:13). He casts down the mighty and exalts the humble (Luke 1:32). By a mere nod he drove the transgressing angels out of heaven; he removed our first parents from paradise because they disobeyed. In the Church of this present exile, he removes from the faithful assembly vessels of falsehood, authors of wickedness, and defenders of heresy. In all these things and above all these things behold his most surpassing mercies, and consider devoutly: in order that human beings might become gods, God willed to become human. In a wondrous [Col. 1283D] manner he makes the unclean clean, the foul beautiful, the unworthy worthy, sinners righteous, the evil good, the very worst holy, and the wretched blessed: these are his mercies over all his works. Under this peaceful king, merciful toward all, and surpassing pontiff, the nine orders of angels in heaven carry out the offices of charity according to their humility; they are sent by God and are not separated from him. They always stand before him whom they always love.

In the earthly sphere, under Him and through Him, pontifical authority, adorned with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, advances the seven ranks of ministers in the Church beneath the clerical crown, with the discipline of obedience, for the performance of the divine mysteries. He also graciously administers princes and powers by the hand of the Most High. Of this the Apostle says: “Whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII, 2). And Peter: “Be subject,” he says, “to every human institution for God’s sake: whether to the king as pre-eminent, or to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good” (I Pet. II, 13). And, as Daniel testifies: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomsoever He wills” (Dan. IV, 14). Yet among all the kingdoms of the world the clerical crown shines more clearly: their life enlightens others; their teaching calls others to life, that they may abandon transitory things and desire eternal goods, avoid errors, and live by Christ’s sweet fragrance.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning this clerical crown, this royal form, this sign of Jesus Christ, heretics raise a question—especially those who have fallen away from the clergy and passed over to heresy. “Whence,” they say, “whence did this crown take its beginning? What have we to do with this crown?”

We reply not to them, since they are implacable, but to Catholics. Our Redeemer and Savior, moved by mercy for us, wretched as we were, oppressed by the slavery of sin, assigned to death, bound by Satan’s chains—our Samaritan, who is without sin—was made sin for us. Our Redeemer was offered as a sacrifice for sin; for us He took upon Himself sin’s punishment and bore the cross in His body. By dying He destroyed death, a glorious conqueror bearing a crown of thorns upon His head. From this crown of the Lord Jesus, assumed by our Redeemer for our sins [Col. 1284D], our present mother, the Church, the bride of the Crucified One, began to reign throughout the whole world under the thorny crown, defeating the powers of the air. Under this crown of our Redeemer the Apostle triumphs and cries: “But we must glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14). Concerning this kingdom of our crucified Lord Jesus, the Gospel records the answer: “Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer these things and so enter into His glory?” (Luke XXIV, 20). And elsewhere: “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20).

Ancient historiography often recounts that conquered and captured persons were sold beneath a crown by their victors. Such a sale was a manifest sign of servile disgrace [Col. 1285A]. Thus too our Christ, sold and captured for our sins, suffered upon the cross beneath a thorny crown. This crown, undeservedly assumed by the Lord, powerfully shattered the crown of condemnation due to us; and the excellent conqueror set over us, His redeemed and sanctified people, the crown of His victory, the crown of our freedom, the crown of everlasting glory.

Therefore the Catholic mother Church has chosen among her faithful certain persons to whom, because of steadfast faith, honorable life, and the splendor of learning, she gladly imparts the likeness of Christ’s crown: the head is shaved above, while the hair is retained in a circle and evenly trimmed. This sign of the crown, assumed in remembrance of Christian freedom, not taken indiscriminately but received by election [Col. 1285B], marked by pontifical blessing, took its beginning from the Apostles and is preserved throughout the world in the Church under apostolic authority. This crown of clerical tonsure is maintained in the religious habit without the stain of crime.

All such persons, because of the heavenly sign and the grace of blessing, are called by the common name “clerics,” because the Lord is their portion and they are the Lord’s portion, by a special prerogative, as a sign of holiness. Some of these, having renounced private ownership, possess all things in common in canonical unity: both regular clerics and cenobitic monks. Others, called seculars, are appointed to the service of the Church; and because they render together in churches, at the appointed hours, the canonical praises of God, they are also called canons. Yet they divide and distribute their prebends [Col. 1285C]; and if they live well, they are deservedly praised and are rightly raised to ecclesiastical honors for their life and learning.

Finally, episcopal authority, whenever it sees fit and judges it useful, ordains to ecclesiastical ranks and entrusts with the care of souls all those marked with the clerical crown, whatever their habit, provided it is religious and adorned by good conduct—so long as in themselves they exalt the Lord’s crown by their morals and glorify it by their life.

## CHAPTER III

We have said this because we see certain persons wear Christ’s crown, not for Christ but for themselves; and in the religious habit seek not virtues but gain. Not content with their own possessions, they covet those of others; pretending not to possess private property, through excessive ambition they seize what has not been granted them [Col. 1285D]. Some, moreover, having cast aside shame, invade episcopal rights, relying on false claims and perverse customs. Truth contradicts these madmen: “Do not overstep,” it says, “the boundaries which your fathers set” (Prov. XXII, 28). But they rage in opposition and leap with hasty foot over the bounds set them by their fathers. They lower their eyes from heaven; although they confess the future resurrection, they do not believe it at all. “They profess that they know God, but deny Him by their deeds” (Tit. I, 16); they follow their own desires and live for themselves (Ecclus. XVIII, 30).

No human being can call back such Epicureans, or vain pretenders, from their errors; He alone who can do all things can do so [Col. 1286A]. To such persons the Psalmist cried and said: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV, 3). Immediately he sets before them whom they ought to believe and follow, saying: “Know that the Lord has wonderfully exalted His holy one; the Lord will hear me when I cry to Him” (ibid., 4). This holy one the Lord wonderfully exalted: foreshadowed to the patriarchs through oracles, revealed beforehand to the prophets, born in the fullness of time from the Virgin by the Holy Spirit—one Jesus Christ, God and man. Him angels announced to shepherds; Him the star declared to kings; Him, glorified upon the holy mountain as the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father, Peter, James, and John were worthy to see. This conqueror, returning from the lower regions, rose wondrously alive from the dead and showed beforehand in Himself the glory of the true resurrection [Col. 1286B].

Concerning this glory of our resurrection and the life of eternal blessedness, many people—yet unbelievers—doubt; and in their doubt they ask, out of their vanity, what the same Psalmist cries on their behalf: “Who will show us good things?” (Ps. IV, 6). “We know,” they say, “these present goods, these temporal goods. We do not know those things which you call eternal, which you call goods without end.”

In reply that prophetic Psalmist exults in God, saying: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; You have given joy to my heart” (ibid., 7). According to the light of His countenance God made man in His own image and likeness. Man has eternity by reason of God’s image, and blessedness by reason of God’s likeness. God gave both these goods—eternity and blessedness—to the man whom He made in His image and likeness (Gen. I, 26). God made this distinguished and supreme good of man, He who is “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I, 9). Hence that Psalmist rightly sings: “The light of Your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV, 7) [Col. 1286C].

By reason of the image of God—which man does not lose even in wickedness—he will necessarily rise at the end of the world, in the general resurrection, so that the image may answer to its Maker and it may appear whether he has preserved by good living the likeness for which he was made [Col. 1286D]. There the wretched man who, having lost God’s likeness, has incurred the foulness of sin, if he rises without a remedy for sin, will depart from God as one unlike Him, condemned by an eternal sentence. This wretch, found without the wedding garment, without the clothing of God’s likeness—that is, without the grace of charity—will fall away from the light of the Lord’s countenance, delivered to outer darkness. While he had time, this wretch did not seek Him whom the Lord wonderfully exalted as His holy one, who is our mercy and refuge. “He will hear me,” he says, “when I cry to Him” (ibid., 4): this holy one of ours, then, who has been wonderfully exalted, hears those crying to Him, absolves them from sins, redeems them from death, and through the grace of the Holy Spirit restores His likeness in them [Col. 1287A], making them sharers in His resurrection. Therefore the Psalmist concludes: “In peace, in the selfsame [good], I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. IV, 9).

Blessed Job awaited this and said: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior. I myself shall see Him, and my eyes shall behold Him, and not another. This hope has been laid up in my bosom” (Job XIX, 25–27). Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good shall go forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29). And elsewhere: “This,” He says, “is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in Him may have eternal life; and I will raise him on the last day” (John VI, 39) [Col. 1287B].

If you read through the Gospels, investigate the Apostles, and examine the prophets, you cannot doubt the blessed resurrection of the saints, the common resurrection of all who live by faith. You live by faith if you hold to the righteousness of faith, for it is written: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17). Righteousness is from faith, and life from righteousness. Therefore, that you may live, offer to God, who is life, the righteousness of faith. This offering, this sacrifice, pleases Him who is life and who gives life. The Psalmist urges this when he says: “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness” (Ps. IV, 6). But because this sacrifice of righteousness is from faith, the hope of eternal life follows it. Therefore, after he had said, “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness,” he immediately added, “and hope in the Lord.” This hope is not empty or vain, but fulfilled; for charity, full toward God, preserves all things for it, and He rewards it with a generous hand [Col. 1287C]. In this hope he exulted with joy, saying: “You have given joy to my heart” (ibid., 7)—not in temporal things, but in God. “Others,” he says, “have been multiplied by the fruit of their grain, wine, and oil” (ibid., 8). Trusting in these things, they rejoice and perish. But I pass these things by and hope in God. Yet by what fruit, what reward? He says: “In peace, in the selfsame [good], I shall sleep and rest” (ibid., 9). Holy sleep in peace, which is always blessed, rests in the full charity which is God. Outside God you will not find that selfsame [good]; if you do not possess that selfsame [good], you tend toward nothingness [Col. 1287D], fall away from good, and fall into evil.

Therefore you who were created in God’s image and likeness, attend to yourself and cry to God. Draw near through faith; offer the sacrifice of righteousness; be renewed through the sacraments, so that, cleansed and purified by them, you may worthily offer the sacrifice of righteousness. Thus you will be able to hope in God, pass beyond mutable things, sleep in peace in that selfsame [good], and rest in the blessed resurrection. There, O human being, you who were created in God’s image and likeness, will be like God, because you will see Him as He is. The Evangelist John testifies to this: “We shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (I John III, 2). Then the likeness of God will be whole in holy human beings, whom God made in His image and likeness [Col. 1288A]. This will be the glory of the resurrection of all who are members of Christ, who says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die for ever” (John II, 25–26).

Accordingly, since those who are rational and believe God ought by no means to deny the resurrection, they nevertheless raise a question about it and frame it thus: “We see human bodies sometimes torn apart and scattered, or carried off and devoured by beasts and birds; moreover, reduced to dust, and at times dispersed into the air. These things can by no means be gathered together again; therefore they cannot be reassembled, and these very bodies of the dead will not rise again.” We answer and say without hesitation: if the resurrection of human bodies were accomplished by human action, or by that of any creature whatever, such objections and others like them could plainly be raised and could not easily be resolved. But we rightly believe and truly confess that the hand of the Lord, the almighty hand, gathers all things and loses none; it contains all things and seeks nothing outside itself. Thus it holds all human bodies together, however widely scattered; it knows each one, and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, restores them all as it wills [Col. 1288B]. Therefore one must not ask why or when He created human bodies, nor how or where He will restore them in the resurrection, since by His omnipotence, His complete knowledge, and His tranquil will, He disposes, orders, brings forth, and holds all things together and each thing individually by His nod.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1288C]

In His hand all heavenly and earthly things are held: spiritual and bodily, good alike and evil. Good things are good by reason of their Creator, their nature, and grace; evil things are evil by reason of defect, negligence, and wickedness. Yet in a wondrous way even the things we call evil are well ordered: worst for themselves, useful to the good, according to the decree of supreme Wisdom, which has placed its Church among evils, carries it forward amid scandals, and raises it amid adversities: “He founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (Ps. XXIII, 2). As the ark in the Flood, as Israel in the Red Sea, as the three children in the Babylonian fire: so also in the Church of God there are virgins, there are continent persons, and there are married persons. Virgins glory in the grace of integrity [Col. 1288D]; continent persons rejoice in victorious struggle; married persons are comforted by the remedy of sacred marriage. For marital chastity, under a priest’s blessing, is a remedy against the incitements of the flesh and the lust of fornication. In marriage, moreover, there is fidelity, which guards the marriage-bed, so that he is not with another woman nor she with another man. From this honorable offspring is received, preserved in dignity, and enriched with hereditary blessing.

There is also a sacrament in marriage, if it remains singular—that is, one. This sacrament, the Apostle says, is great in Christ and in the Church (Eph. V, 32), in a unity that is singular and perpetual. For the marriage of Christ and the Church, one and singular, began in time but remains in eternity. From the beginning of things, from the origin of time [Col. 1289A], woman is recorded to have been formed from the man’s rib; hence she was also called *virago*, “woman.” “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. II, 23–24). This law of marriage was given in Paradise and remained valid even outside Paradise after sin. In accordance with this law, at the time of the Flood the Lord preserved in the ark animals two by two, male and female. Righteous Noah, king of the ark, was there with his wife, and his three sons, each with his own wife. A single marriage was instituted in Paradise; a single marriage was preserved in the ark of the Flood.

This law of marriage is so just, so holy, that the very Creator of the world and Redeemer of humankind, when He was to become flesh from the flesh of a virgin, chose to be conceived and born not from a virgin merely, but from one who was betrothed [Col. 1289B]. He Himself, by the miracle performed at Cana of Galilee, changing water into wine, consecrated the marriage feast (John II, 1). Later He commanded concerning this sacred bond of marriage: “What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX, 6). The Church under Christ maintains this ordinance of marriage, divinely established in Paradise and preserved in the Flood.

But whenever, after the death of one spouse, a marriage has been repeated according to proper custom, it remains good indeed whenever it is one. Yet, because of its repetition, it is no longer singular and does not possess the sacrament of the one, singular heavenly marriage by which Christ is joined to the Church in perpetual stability [Col. 1289C]. Whoever, therefore, by repeated marriage passes from unity to number, from singularity to plurality, no longer represents in himself the most holy marriage of Christ and the Church, which remains singular for ever. Therefore a person of repeated marriage must not thereafter be promoted to ecclesiastical ranks or consecrated bishop. Nevertheless, however often his marriage may have been repeated following the death of a spouse, if it was lawfully contracted it is reckoned good and held honorable. But those do not maintain this honorableness of marriage who join women to their side without the law of marriage. The Church rebukes them for this and, by the authority in which it stands pre-eminent, commands them either to dismiss such concubines or, if it is permitted, to receive those same women, or others, by the lawful contracting of marriage in Christian fashion [Col. 1289D]. Christ’s Church rejects fornicators, strikes down the unchaste, overthrows the incestuous; it honors married persons, loves continent persons, and exalts virgins.

In opposition, heretics stand against the Church. They refuse to hear and refuse to submit. They keep with themselves little women hired from anywhere at all, not under the law of marriage or the obligation of kinship, but under the cohabitation of private lust. They say that in their dwellings they lead a common life and, in apostolic fashion, have women with them. They cite Paul’s saying: “Do I not have the right to lead about women, like Cephas and the other Apostles?” (I Cor. IX, 5). “Therefore we too preserve the form of apostolic life: we do not dismiss women, but lawfully gather them with ourselves in the same dwelling [Col. 1290A] and at the same table.”

But as they speak thus and cover the lurking places of their incontinence with the shadow of falsehood, Catholics answer and bishops declare: “The Apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ and His disciples continued to support, with due provision, those holy women whom they had lawfully taken before their conversion and honorably had under the bond of marriage, even after they became the Lord’s disciples. Thus their wives became sisters, serving not the flesh but the Lord in religious devotion. They also retained with just deliberation those women who were their mothers, daughters, or the like; and those holy women who had come from Galilee sometimes ministered to the Lord from their own resources. Therefore, if, as you pretend [Col. 1290B], you strive to follow the Apostles in this also and to imitate holy persons of every age, let the women whom you cause to dwell with you henceforth be your wives under priestly blessing and public attestation. Or, if you wish, let those women also be with you whom you ought to honor by reason of kinship and protect with irreproachable care, without the disgrace of fornication or the foulness of incest. Thus, according to Christian custom, have women with you if you please—either lawfully betrothed or near by blood—in holy conduct, so that, should mother Church at any time choose some of you and judge them worthy to be raised as Levites, presbyters, or bishops, this may be done without reproach. Then those whom you have as lawful wives, the marriage-bed having been set apart, shall remain your sisters under the honor of chastity [Col. 1290C]. Acting thus, you will remain irreproachable, honorable, and useful. The authority of the Fathers ordained that this custom be maintained in the Church, and their holy posterity undertook to preserve what had been ordained.”

Marital chastity, certainly, is recorded to have been instituted at the beginning. But we know that marital intercourse followed after sin and outside Paradise. For after our first parents had been expelled from Paradise, we read that Adam knew his wife, and the two became one flesh (Gen. IV, 1). This union of two in one flesh, if it is assumed without the remedy of marriage, is reckoned foul and is called by the common name fornication. The Apostle abhorred this and recalled every Christian from such contamination, saying: “Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Far be it!” (I Cor. VI, 15) [Col. 1290D]. If the lawful covenants of marriage proceed to unity of flesh, then the husband, although he rules in other matters, has no power over his own body, but the wife does. Husband and wife likewise exercise authority over each other’s flesh in the equal law of the marital obligation. Furthermore, a husband is judged an adulterer if he is with another woman, and a wife is judged an adulteress if she is with another man. For this cause a husband may dismiss his wife, and a wife her husband, if they do not keep the marriage-bed. Yet the husband is not therefore released from the law of his wife, nor the wife from the law of her husband, so long as either lives. Therefore she must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried; and he must either be reconciled to his wife or remain continent [Col. 1291A]. When one of them has died, the survivor may marry whomsoever he or she wishes, only in the Lord.

Accordingly, if it has been alleged and proved by judicial procedure that they have been joined within the seventh degree of consanguinity or closer, they must be separated from one another by the authority of the Apostolic See; and this applies to affinity arising from consanguinity as well as to kinship by blood. For neither may she marry a blood relative of her deceased husband, nor may he join to himself a blood relative of his wife.

## CHAPTER V

It must also be known that neither monks, nor canons, nor any persons who have publicly professed chastity before the Church can become married persons. If they attempt to act otherwise [Col. 1291B], they are reckoned concubinarians and fornicators. Mother Church condemns such fallen persons for their broken vow, and pontifical authority deprives them of communion. Some of them rush forward shamelessly and enlist heretics to dispute on their behalf. These cite the Apostle to us with clamorous talkativeness, where he says: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render to his wife her due, and likewise the wife to her husband” (I Cor. VII, 2–3). And shortly afterward: “I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not have self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (ibid., 8–9). “Look,” they say, “look at the Apostle; hear him. Thus we know that human beings were created by God from the beginning: He made them male and female [Col. 1291C], and, blessing them, said, ‘Increase and multiply’” (Gen. I, 28). “This plainly comes about through union of the flesh. Therefore, because of nature’s obligation and according to the Apostle, let every man have his own woman and every woman her own man.”

Catholics confront such arguments, bishops reply, and bring forward the Apostle himself speaking thus: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). And then: “I want you to be without anxiety. He who is without a wife is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But he who is with a wife is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided. And the unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body [Col. 1291D] and spirit; but she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband. I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what affords the ability to serve the Lord without impediment” (I Cor. VII, 32–35). From these words of the Apostle we answer especially our own people, sound in faith and not contentious, but those who have senses trained both to grasp the things of truth and to carry out all that God has commanded.

Paul the Apostle, teacher of the nations in faith and truth, has children who need milk rather than solid food. He makes them live in the waters, amid the waves of worldly life; he regulates them in works of the flesh under the law of marriage, keeping away the abyss of fornication [Col. 1292A] together with the shipwreck of immoderate lust. These are told to hold all that is theirs with righteousness; content with their own things, not to seize what belongs to others; and from the mammon of iniquity, from what is transient and deceptive, to make Christ’s poor their friends. “For the fashion of this world passes away” (I Cor. VII, 51). “The world passes away, and its desire” (I John II, 17). These, not yet leaving their possessions for God and not yet dedicating their own will to the Lord, hear from the Apostle that, against the impurities of fornications, if they do not have self-control, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, so that their act may not be imputed to them as sin because of the remedy of marriage contracted under blessing. Let them season their remaining deeds with almsgiving, govern them by obedience, and advance them by piety. Thus Christ’s Apostle has children raised from the waters of worldly pleasure to higher things [Col. 1292B].

These have not only left their possessions but have also vowed themselves to the Lord; and with the Prophet they say: “For You, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope” (Ps. IV, 10). And: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXIV, 4), “that I may behold the delight of the Lord and visit His temple” (ibid., 5). Of such persons Paul said: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17): one, certainly, not divided. “I want you,” he says, “to be without anxiety”—not indeed without that anxiety which concerns God, but without that which concerns the flesh. “He who is without a wife,” he says, “is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God. But he who is with a wife is anxious about the things of this world, how he may please his wife, and he is divided” (I Cor. VII, 32–33) [Col. 1292C]. Such a person is divided, not one; he is not raised to the Lord singularly in hope, but is bound by the work of the flesh. He does not glory with virgins in the hundredfold honor, nor rejoice in the sixtyfold palm of continence; but he is wearied by the thirtyfold labor of marriage and, because he is lawfully joined, is praised for the honorableness of marriage.

## CHAPTER VI

The Church of Christ receives, honors, and loves these three orders: virgins, continent persons, and married persons. But others—without virginal beauty, without the grace of continence, without marital comeliness—whose state is manifest by notorious disclosure [Col. 1292D], public confession, or judicial conviction, it finally anathematizes by pontifical censure, and the strength of the Church expels. While such persons perish, Noah, Daniel, and Job alone are delivered.

For Noah, at the Lord’s command, built the ark for one hundred years and steered it over the waters of the Flood. Into it, as the Lord brought them, he received male and female of every kind of earthly animal and bird flying through the air. Yet during this construction by day, during this steering amid things so innumerable and diverse, and even for three hundred and fifty years after the Flood, he is not recorded to have begotten children, but is said to have remained continent.

Daniel, one of the children of Judah, stood in the Babylonian king’s court unblemished and holy in body and spirit [Col. 1293A] before the Lord his God. Adorned with grace beyond others beyond measure, he knew the mysteries of visions and the sacraments of revelations, always resting before the Lord in his celibacy.

Job was great among all the peoples of the East. Of him the Lord said to Satan: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth—a simple and upright man, fearing God and withdrawing from evil?” (Job I, 8). The Lord gave him into Satan’s hand to test him; Satan took away all his substance and killed his sons and daughters, and struck him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head with a grievous sore. Over all these things Job blessed the Lord, replying to his reproaching wife: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not also endure evil things?” [Col. 1293B] (Job II, 10). But the Lord turned toward Job’s repentance when he prayed for his friends. The Lord also restored to Job all things double (Job XLII, 10) that he had possessed before, and blessed Job’s latter end more than his beginning in the wealth of his possessions, together with the restoration of his sons and daughters.

Thus righteous Noah, with all those entrusted to his care, is saved in the ark because of his obedience; holy Daniel lives among hungry lions because of his innocence; Job, simple and upright, fearing God and withdrawing from evil, is delivered from Satan and possesses more fully all that he had lost because of his penitence. Of these three, through whom are signified in the Church of God the three orders—virgins, continent persons, and married persons [Col. 1293C] living devoutly before the Lord—the Lord speaks thus to the prophet Ezekiel:

“Son of man, when a land sins against me by grievously transgressing, I shall stretch out my hand over it, break its staff of bread, send famine upon it, and destroy from it human being and beast. And if these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in its midst, they would deliver their own souls by their righteousness, says the Lord of hosts. But if I bring savage beasts upon the land, to lay it waste so that it becomes impassable because no one can pass through because of the beasts, and these three men are in it: as I live, says the Lord God, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they alone shall be delivered, while the land shall be desolated. Or if I bring a sword upon that land and say to the sword, ‘Pass through that land and destroy from it human being and beast,’ and these three men are in its midst: as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver sons, but they alone shall be delivered [Col. 1293D]. Or if I send pestilence upon that land and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, to remove from it human being and beast; and Noah, Daniel, and Job are in its midst: as I live, says the Lord God, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter, but by their righteousness they shall deliver their own souls” (Ezek. XIV, 13–20).

Therefore all who are signified by these three—virgins through Daniel, continent persons through Noah, and married persons through Job—are saved by their righteousness. The rest of humankind, who belong in no way to any one of these three orders [Col. 1294A], or who fall away from them by apostasy, do not escape the evils impending and deserved.

## CHAPTER VII

Because these backsliders desert their vows by transgressing them and render their first faith void, they are reckoned transgressors; and if, when admonished, they disdain to amend, they become infamous. If indeed they defend their error, they take upon themselves the name of heresy. The children of the Church confront them, set sound doctrine against them, rebuke the foolish, call back the erring, break heretics, and destroy the desperate. They follow the Apostle, who says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that one of this sort has been subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. III, 10) [Col. 1294B].

The more vigorously such plagues—heretics, subverted and desperate people—run, the more deeply they fall. Whoever is not held by truth is dragged along in error by falsehood. He loses the One, who is God, and descends into infinity. No one thing is sufficient for him because of the variety of different things; but as various things converge, he loses each one. Horrified by such precipices, the Prophet prayed to the Lord: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me; let not the deep swallow me; let not the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. LXVIII, 16). Whoever is dulled by the mists of ignorance is overwhelmed by the storm of waters; whoever is entangled in the cords of errors is swallowed by the deep. Whoever is suffocated by the foul accumulation of heresies is covered by the millstone of despair, the pit having been closed above him [Col. 1294C].

Nevertheless, even these utterly wicked persons, as pernicious as they are evil, are ordered by the hand of the almighty Craftsman. They are restrained from doing all that they attempt, and do only what they are permitted to do. In this evil age they retain their place: through them the present Church is more frequently roused, tested by anxieties, strengthened when tested, and, strengthened, reigns. But at last, when evils have been wholly excluded, the kingdom of the Catholic Church will stand firm and peaceful throughout the whole world, up to the heights of heaven; and God will be all in all (I Cor. XV, 39): all things in all the wills of the saints, all things in their powers, all things in every good, in unbroken eternity and divine blessedness.

These things are not considered by people who almost lack the intelligence of the mind and attend more fully to bodily things—beastlike people whose reason is truly asleep [Col. 1294D]. Since nothing concerning faith and the sacraments of the Church can adequately be communicated to such people as it ought, they are advised for their benefit not to follow their own judgments but to follow the Church of God in obedience. They reply, as though mocking our people: “You who propose that the Church of God ought to be followed, tell us what the Church of God is, where it is, and why it is. We wish,” they say, “to recognize it, find it when recognized, and, once found, preserve it for whatever usefulness it may have. We seek and approve visible things; invisible things, because we do not know them, we reject as unknown.”

Such Christians, living not by faith but as though dead, Mother Church abhors, and concerning them she now almost despairs; whereas she still patiently waits for Gentiles and Jews to be converted to the Lord. But because it is written, “Do not answer a fool, lest you seem like him yourself” (Prov. 26:4), we pass these people by, lest we cast pearls before swine; yet we are compelled to answer our own people who inquire devoutly. Let him therefore speak who said: “For in that hour you will be given what you are to say; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:19–20). May the Holy Spirit open the hearts of his faithful and close the mouths of the faithless; may the heavenly anointing descend, and the word of truth be heard.

## CHAPTER VIII

The true and Catholic Church, gathered into one, is indeed a full and perfect head and body: the supreme Trinity, the one God; Christ, one God and man; the unity of believers in one Spirit, one with God through the one Jesus Christ, our God and Lord. Although the ineffable mystery and wondrous sacrament of this unity cannot be explained by us, it nevertheless cannot be unknown.

The supreme Trinity—God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is three persons, yet is understood as one in such a Catholic manner that neither is the Trinity at all confused nor is the unity perceived as divided. The Trinity remains unconfused in unity; unity is always undivided in Trinity. For the Father alone is the Father of the Son; the Son is the Son of the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit is neither of the Father alone nor of the Son alone, but is one Spirit of both. In this one Spirit the Father and the Son are essentially one; hence the Son himself says: “I and the Father are one.” In this one Spirit Christ, God and man, remains personally one, born in time of the Virgin.

In this one Spirit, the unity of believers is one with God: uniquely gathered from Jews and Gentiles, joined to the assemblies of holy angels through the one mediator Jesus Christ. This unity, gathered from many and one out of a multitude, uniquely betrothed to the one man Jesus Christ, bears children in the one Holy Spirit. For by that Spirit through whom Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin, individual persons are reborn in holy baptism and made children of God: “Because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Of these children of God reborn in the Holy Spirit, the only-begotten Son says to the Father:

> “As you, Father, are in me and I in you, may they also be one in us”; and, “I have given them the love which you gave me, that they may be one as we also are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:21–23).

O unique and supreme One: within you are all goods; outside you, none! Whoever has been able by grace to know you—the One to be sought with every effort, held with all strength, and loved with complete charity—most certainly knows what the Church of God is.

Therefore whoever does not know this unity, or has withdrawn from it by apostasy, has lost every good by not possessing the Church of the faithful, which is one: subject to sin, entangled in evils, heaped with miseries—unless God’s mercy looks upon him, unless the mediator of God and men graciously rescues him, unless the unity of the Church devoutly gathers him back.

Thereafter they do not contentiously ask where the Church of God is. They can indeed know this if by pure faith they perceive the Church’s head, who is God and the light of the faithful. “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God” (John 1:12–13). These were made by grace children of God in Christ Jesus himself, the supreme cornerstone, “in whom the whole structure, built together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, into a dwelling-place of God in the Holy Spirit” (Eph. 2:21–22).

But, that you may know more fully and seek her when known, hear Truth speaking thus to the Father about this: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am” (John 17:24). O ineffable grace, abundant blessing, most complete blessedness! Beholding this, the Prophet exhorted the Church of God thus:

> “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house; and the king will desire your beauty, because he is the Lord your God” (Ps. 44:11–12).

Your beauty—not that which you had from the origin of your people or from your father’s ancient house, but that which you found with God when, by grace, you were made his daughter: you who, whitened by the sacraments, adorned by the sevenfold light of the Holy Spirit, and filled with the bread of life, hasten to behold the God of gods in Zion without end. The Apostle directed his attention to her when he said: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). There the king’s daughter already goes by faith, ascends by hope, and rests in charity. [Col. 1296C]

Thus the Church, joined to God in one Spirit, passes beyond all things on the wings of virtues. Raised by the breeze of charity, she rests in loving the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both; in loving, she rests. This rest is there, whence the Son says: “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be with me where I am” (John 17:24).

Where are you, Son of God the Father, Word of God, God the Word with God, life of all, light of men, Word made flesh, our redemption, salvation, and blessedness? “I,” he says, “am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11). This is so essentially, for the Spirit of both is one, coeternal and consubstantial. Sacred Scripture testifies that, when all things had been accomplished together in the beginning, God rested on the day that has neither evening nor morning—the blessed and sanctified seventh day—because “he rested on it from all his work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2:2).

This wondrous worker, neither wearied by labor nor refreshed by rest, made all things as he willed; and, needing none of the things he made, rested in himself from them all. He remains unmoved here: supported by none, aided by none; resting, he acts, and acting, he rests. He owes nothing to anyone; rather, all things owe themselves to him, through whom all things are and all things subsist. To this rest of the Lord the Church of the saints hastens, that from the storm of evils and the power of darkness she may return to her own beginning and rest where Christ is, in the glory of God the Father, in the Sabbath of rest, in the eternity of blessedness. [Col. 1297A]

## CHAPTER IX

Finally, our people inquire concerning the Church of God—not quarrelsomely like heretics, but with devout zeal like Catholics—why she exists. But no one could know this except one who has received the Holy Spirit within the unity of the Church, who has deserved to enter God’s sanctuary, Christ Jesus opening the way, and who has recognized his will in the commandments.

O how great he is, how sublime in charity, who is able to behold the origins of things and their immutable causes abiding with God! He perceives God’s eternal counsel, stable and unmoved, by which all things were created together from nothing at the beginning of things, without an interval of time. For immediately, from the movement of the Creator, times began to run, and the parts of bodies extended through spaces of place. Therefore no things were created in the beginning after times or places; for times proceeded from the movement of things, and places were divided from the spatial extension of bodies. But God, as he willed, both created all things together and formed each thing individually.

All things therefore come forth, and individual things are made together, from the divine will, as effects from a cause. It is thus not to be asked why, whence, or when God created the world, or where he placed it once created—he who according to his will brought forth all things together from nothing, from whose motion times flow, and whose bodily parts supplied the spaces of places. Rather, it should have been asked: who among all created things could know his Creator? Who held his will in the commandments? Who preserved his likeness in virtues? [Col. 1297C]

To this end, among all created things, you find only the angel in heaven and man upon earth endowed with rational intelligence: that they might seek the one true and supreme God and Lord according to reason, know him according to intelligence, and love him uniquely according to likeness. For man was created in the image and likeness of God; but the angel had within himself the seal of God’s likeness, so that both, through rational nature, God’s likeness, and the unity of charity, might alike obey the Lord God, love him alone, and remain blessed in him.

Let the angel, then, conformed to God, happy and blessed, acknowledge this; let man, restored by grace, acknowledge that God’s surpassing and ineffable charity willed to make them both for this purpose: that a twofold mutual charity in them might establish the Church of God, which loves God wholly and, loving itself mutually in one another, directs itself to God through mutual charity.

For this purpose, therefore, the Church of God was made: that she might be in God and God in her through the one Jesus Christ our mediator, who confirmed the angel in God and reconciled man to God; so that from both there might be one and unique Church of God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, in whom she will see God as he is, fully and perfectly, face to face.

Beholding this magnificence of divine charity, the Prophet said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30:20). It is hidden in time; in eternity it will be revealed. Hear the Son speak in the Gospel concerning this hidden thing: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (Matt. 11:25–26). And the Apostle says: “Now our life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). Thus, concerning what the Church of God is, where she is, and why she exists, we seem rather not to have been silent than to have given any worthy answer as we ought. [Col. 1298B]

If you inquire devoutly, you can discover that these three are from God, remain in God, and abide with God in unity. Apart from God, none of them exists. In these three behold together faith, hope, and charity. For faith arises from God; hope is raised up in God; charity works with God. In the present time, you believe in vain if you do not hope and love. You hope in vain unless you believe and love; you love in vain if you do not hope and do not believe. In this temporal life consider these three to be together in such a way that you do not rashly decide which of them is first, second, or third, but behold in them the signs of the unbounded Trinity.

From these three let that wondrous braid be woven of which Solomon bears witness: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4:12). You twist this one, three-knotted cord; if you are raised by it to God, you descend from God to your neighbor, and from your neighbor, taking yourself with him, you return to God. This is Jacob’s ladder in the Church of God, set up from earth to heaven, by which angels ascend and descend and return to God, who leans down upon the ladder from above. The patriarch Jacob saw this in God’s vision; awakening, he said: “This place is awesome; this is the house of God and the gate of heaven. Truly the Lord is in this place” (Gen. 28:17).

This indeed is the place in which the Lord is—not as he is everywhere, but as in the place of grace, where he is devoutly sought, found, and loved. It is recognized as an awesome house of God and gate of heaven: awesome to all ungodly persons, schismatics, and heretics; the house of God to all reborn through the sacraments, adorned by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, and filled with the one heavenly bread; the gate of heaven to all who walk with God like Enoch, who are raised up like Elijah in the fiery chariot, and who ascend to heaven with the Lord God Jesus Christ.

With God faith journeys, hope advances, charity ascends; with God faith conquers, hope triumphs, charity reigns. But at the end of time charity, with God, will hold a uniquely single sovereignty. In it, completed charity will bring into one the merit of faith, the reward of hope, and the due fulfillment of the other virtues—whose participation is in the One himself, who is one and every good of all, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1299]

# TREATISE OF HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, ON MEMORY, COMPRISING THREE BOOKS IN PRAISE OF MEMORY

(Mabillon extracted it from a manuscript codex of the Queen of Sweden; Martène published it in *Amplissima collectio*, vol. IX, p. 1186.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

We have already discussed Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, at greater length in the preliminary observation to his seven books of *Dialogues*, or *Theological Questions*. The extent of our Hugh’s learning is demonstrated by various treatises published by him, nearly all theological. Among these, three books *On Heresies*, dedicated to Alberic, Bishop of Ostia, were published in the appendix to Guibert’s works issued by Acherius. We inserted the seven books of *Dialogues*, or *Theological Questions*, together with the *Life of St. Adjutor* composed by him and a fragment of his work on Genesis, into volume V of our *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*.

Would that we could append here his work on Genesis, which we once saw, divided into three books, in the library of Clairvaux! In its absence, we bring to light two not insignificant works of our Hugh, hitherto shrouded in darkness: namely, the entirely theological treatise *On Memory*, consisting of three books in all; and an exposition of the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Mabillon extracted the first work, composed by Hugh in old age, from a manuscript belonging to the Queen of Sweden. We copied the second from a very ancient codex in the royal library, to which it seemed proper to add a letter to Pope Innocent on the death of King Stephen, found among Mabillon’s papers. Would that we possessed another letter of the same Hugh, addressed to Theoderic, Bishop of Amiens, concerning the construction of the Church of Blessed Mary at Chartres, mentioned by Robert of Torigni under the year 1144.

# LETTER OF HUGH, BISHOP OF ROUEN, TO HIS DEAREST PHILIP

[Col. 1299A] Philip, you gladly devote yourself wholly to the sacred Scriptures; but because you do not at once find in them everything you seek, you are troubled and humbly ask to be relieved by some consolation from us. At this present summer season I am greatly distressed by heat, worn down with old age, injured in the foot, and burdened with illness; nevertheless, I do not wish to disappoint your concern, which I have always resolved to honor.

What we send you is indeed narrow and brief, offered in compressed writing; yet it is exceedingly great and lofty in heavenly teaching, and we present it to you with the charity that is due. We have learned that these matters must be devoutly sought by Catholic faith, not human reasoning. Therefore attend to them more diligently, reread them thankfully, and retain them in memory. These are faithful, holy, and divine things, proposed to you through the revelation of the Holy Spirit; they are to be remembered, because “the merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders” (Ps. 110:4). We propose to speak concerning memory, which may God make sound within us.

# PREFACE OF HUGH, ARCHBISHOP OF ROUEN, TO THE BOOK DEDICATED TO SOUND MEMORY

[Col. 1299B] Everything which understanding discovers, study attains, and devout love desires, wise memory gathers together, considers prudently, and preserves with foresight. Whoever hastens to pursue, apprehend, and retain such things must diligently prepare for himself, through divine grace’s favor, a mind pure and unencumbered—not with empty presumption, but with submissive humility—and devoutly offer the vessels of his memory to receive God’s wisdom.

The apostle James shows how you may obtain it, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask it from God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them, and it will be given him” (Jas. 1:5). Once memory has received this, it also retains knowledge. “Memory,” he says, “is the key of knowledge”; it raises Jacob’s ladder from earth to heaven, because the best traveler advances strongly and progresses with sure step, loving God with his whole heart, and himself and his neighbor in God.

“A threefold cord is not easily broken”: the firm braid of charity is bound together. One who loves God in this threefold bond descends from God to himself, and from himself to his neighbor; lest the cord be broken, he returns to God from his neighbor, taking that neighbor with him. [Col. 1301A] This path, continually trodden, manifests within itself the perpetual Trinity, whom the aforesaid charity presents everywhere. Faithful memory watches here, holds this Trinity, and loves the supreme Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one God in essence. It endeavors to refer to the supreme Trinity the love of God, of oneself who loves, and of one’s neighbor whom it draws with itself to love God. In praise of this holy memory we intend to say a few things, for God’s glory, the unity of charity, and the benefit of us all.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 1301B]

1. Among all the powers of human reason, the power of memory flourishes most abundantly. It alone makes the past present, binds together the present, retrieves wisdom, and foresees the future. It adorns prudence, strengthens justice, fortifies courage, and illumines temperance. It establishes faith, raises hope, and brings forth charity. Called forth by faith, lifted by hope, and shining with charity, it marvels at God: one in Trinity and three in unity; not divided in Trinity, not assembled into unity, not begun, not new, not foreknown by anyone, but the provider for all; not one thing composed from all things, but singularly good and perfectly blessed; not of some particular quality or quantity, not moved through times, not situated through places, not changed by degrees, not many, but one—ever the same, ever self-identical. [Col. 1301C]

2. There are indeed three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—while one essence of deity remains, with inseparable will and the same power. But you say: “If there are three persons in the Godhead, there are three individual entities of the divine essence; therefore, when you assert three persons of deity, you necessarily confess three gods.” Whoever says this, being unlearned, attends to “person,” which is God, in a human manner. For these names, or any spoken terms adopted to signify God, are set forth in signifying not our manner but the divine.

We do not call Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three persons as though referring to substance with quality, word with action or passion, or something marked by any diversity; nor do we divide, delimit, or define God. We contemplate the truth of faith, not the rules or arguments of this world’s wisdom. The supreme Trinity, who is God, can neither be increased nor diminished, but must be adored inseparably. Therefore “person,” which in our ordinary usage names an individual rational being, does not signify God.

3. If you ask what the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are, the Catholic Christian answers you—not as an empty talker, not as a philosopher who, lest he seem ignorant, wanders in verbose chatter. He answers humbly: for the unity of faith, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are God; the Trinity in unity is presented as to be adored in itself.

4. Again, if you ask, “What is God?” do not wander or pour yourself out in speculation, but, as a Catholic, truly confess: God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Behold: unity in Trinity is always revered and adored—wondrous to say, incomprehensible to our understanding, something we cannot fail to know and cannot make manifest. Simple unity is God in Trinity; simple Trinity is God in unity. Unity in Trinity does not begin a number; Trinity in unity does not present a number. Unity does not enlarge Trinity; Trinity does not separate unity. Unity is not adored without Trinity, nor Trinity without unity.

This deep and ineffable mystery of deity is not attained by those who are wise in high matters in their own eyes, who refer their wisdom not to God but to themselves. Of these the Apostle testifies: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools and became vain” (Rom. 1:21). Concerning this Truth says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth, who have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because thus it was pleasing before you” (Matt. 11:25–26). [Col. 1302C]

5. Humble memory rejoices because it receives these things revealed to it by God. It considers God the supreme and unique Creator: he knows all things, possesses each thing, and can do all things. Nothing escapes his knowledge; no one can supplement his abundance; no one has assisted his omnipotence. He created all things together and each thing according to his will. No one taught him how to make; from no one did he receive the means to complete what was made; nowhere and never did he find anything from which to create.

He is the wondrous worker who worked and did not begin to work, who did not begin making and yet made all things together, because nothing existed from which he might create or from which he might begin. Therefore he made, though he did not begin making, because there was nothing from which he could begin. Things that were made have a beginning, because unless they began they would not be made; by the motion of their beginning they are changeable, and by their changeability they lie hidden beneath accidental variation. [Col. 1302D]

6. This unmoved Author moves movable things through intervals of time and spaces of place. These movable things, slipping through their changeability, flow away; yet they subsist through the power of the Creator, who is everywhere present in essence. They cannot return to nothing: “For he established them for age and for the age of ages; he gave a command and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148:11).

7. God the Creator is wholly everywhere: containing, not contained; enclosed by no boundary. But created things are held within their proper and fixed limits. God holds, governs, and preserves them—he “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1): mightily because omnipotent, sweetly because merciful. [Col. 1303A]

8. The Omnipotent casts down the mighty; the merciful exalts the humble. He caused Satan, swelling with pride and a liar from the beginning of his activity, immediately to fall headlong. “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). The angels who fell with him neglected humbly to behold God and refused to love him; they remained wretched. But the angels who stood continually behold God because of their humility, love him ardently, and remain blessed: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5).

Run through each age of the world, and you will always find him acting thus. He expelled our first parents from the place of delight because they were disobedient and defended their fault, and separated them from the tree of life. But because of Abel’s humility, he accepted Abel with the gifts he offered devoutly; and, while the rest perished, he saved Noah and those whom Noah’s ark contained in the flood. After the Egyptians had been struck with many disasters and destroyed by immense slaughter, Israel escaped under a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night.

Blessed is the pillar of cloud: the Holy Spirit’s overshadowing against the incitements of lust and against the burning heat of desire for the world that lies in evil. Blessed is the pillar of fire: the Holy Spirit against the darkness of lies, the storms of scandals, and the tempests of heresies. Thus Israel, protected by the pillar of power, crossed the sea with dry feet, traversed the vast solitudes of the wilderness, crossed the Jordan, and, after triumphing over the remaining enemies, entered to possess the better land of promise. There it had judges, kings, and leaders over very many people; there it very often gravely offended God and under God’s wrath most frequently endured evils; but sometimes, through repentance, it breathed again under God’s mercy.

9. “The scepter was not taken away from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he came who was to be sent.” He is the expectation of the Gentiles, the unique and supreme remedy against all evils, the true salvation and life of all: “whom God the Father appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages” (Heb. 1:2). This Son of God the Father was foreshadowed by the oracles of the patriarchs, announced by the proclamations of the prophets, and presented through the Gospel manifestation. He is also that Wisdom “which built her house and cut out seven pillars,” and which by its own power trampled the necks of the proud and lofty.

For he cast out Satan, who is called the prince of this world—the wicked and dark world. Exalted, he fell and remained foolish. On the other hand, Wisdom built her house, the holy Church, raised upon the seven pillars of the Holy Spirit. In her the hundredth sheep and the tenth drachma which had been lost are devoutly sought and joyfully restored. For in her penitents are admitted, renewed by the sacraments, and adorned by power from on high. In her they eat the bread of life and live Christ’s life: a life not earthly but heavenly, the life which is the Word of God. [Col. 1304A]

10. God is the Word; God is with God. The Son is one with the Father, always with the Father. He himself is God, the light of men, the Word made flesh—made flesh, made man—proceeding from Adam, Abraham, David, and the other fathers; born of the Virgin without a man’s seed, the Holy Spirit cooperating.

The Son of God, God made man for us, assumed not a human person but true and perfect human nature, without fleshly desire and without the root of sin. He is a new man, not a new God; God-man, not two but one; not two persons but one; one person not new but coeternal with God the Father. “I and the Father,” he says, “are one” (John 10:30). They are one because the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father: one essence, but not one person; one essence in the unity of the Holy Spirit, who is essentially one Spirit of Father and Son.

God the Father is Father of the Son alone; God the Son is Son of the Father alone. But the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone nor of the Son alone, but is one Spirit of both: other in person, yet entirely the same in essence with each. [Col. 1304B]

11. Upon this ineffable unity of the supreme Trinity—which we utter but are unable to expound—we say, praying to you, God the Father, that you may grant what we ask, as we conclude: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God.”

The Father distributes good things through the Son. The Son frees us from evils and reconciles us to the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit. He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world, slain from the beginning of the world. John the Apostle says this in the Apocalypse. From the beginning of the world, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was signified in the death of righteous Abel, who is a member of Christ, whose blood cried from the earth to God. Cain killed him because God looked not upon Cain but upon Abel and his gifts.

Isaac too, when offered, represented a type of Christ’s Passion: there it was not the son who was immolated by the father, but the ram that was slain. This one was slain in death, yet death did not touch him. In a similar manner, that paschal lamb, by the Lord’s command, was offered through the houses and families of Israel; its blood was placed on both doorposts and the lintel. By its blood the Hebrews were protected while the angel struck the firstborn of Egypt.

This was the mystery of our true Lamb, Jesus Christ, through whom the faithful redeemed in the Catholic Church are saved; while the rest remain under death, they enjoy the life which is Christ. Concerning this life, which is truth, he testifies: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26): in himself, as essential and divine life, not sought outside himself and not borrowed. The Father’s and Son’s life is one and the same, because the Father and Son have one essence. [Col. 1304D]

12. Therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father. The time of his assumed humanity, the Passion of his flesh, and his undergoing of death do not prejudice the eternity of the Son of God and our Lord Jesus Christ. Certainly, in Christ’s death his soul and body were separated from one another, so that death could occur; but the person of God and man, which neither began nor knows an end, remained whole. Without doubt, in Christ’s death his soul descended into hell and led his own out from there free. Meanwhile his body lay in the tomb, and he granted to the holy thief, his confessor, as he had promised him, the glory of Paradise.

These things were divided for a time, while the person of Jesus Christ, God and man, remained undivided. Do not wonder at the mystery of this integrity. He himself had foretold it to Nicodemus: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). See that while he speaks on earth, present among those present, he testifies that he is in heaven, so that the person of God and man may be recognized as one.

Yet the Trinity, who is God, is not faithfully adored as multiple or disjointed, but as simple and unmoved: enclosing all things in its palm and bearing the universe on three fingers. Observe that in the palm the unity of deity is signified, and in the three fingers the Trinity. Palm and fingers make up one hand. In the Trinity which is God, Christ the Son of God the Father, the third person, abiding before the ages, is not a third God; he is not a recent God, but perfect and omnipotent. He contains the flowing course of times, extends through the spaces of places, and encompasses all things. [Col. 1305B]

13. Therefore Christ is from eternity; Christ is everywhere; Christ is above all things. “All things,” he says, “were made through him” (John 1:3); without him nothing can exist. He distributes good things and preserves what has been distributed. Unless he had spoken, they would not have come to be; unless he held created things, they would cease. The good one made all good things; we, made good, made ourselves evil.

In his gratuitous mercy he descended to us, bore our evils, and freed us in his goodness; he restored us to goodness: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:9–11). He possesses this glory from the Father and with the Father in essence; he received it through the obedience of his assumed humanity. [Col. 1305C]
