14. In this obedience, he who owed absolutely nothing to sin bore all the sins of us all, gave us the remedies of the sacraments, and gave us the wondrous gifts of the Holy Spirit. He gave us the supper above the heavens, his body and blood. He grants it in the present time just as he did at the Paschal supper and commanded it to be done until the end of the age. This is the true sacrifice, given to us through the ministry of one consecrated for this purpose.

But outside the Catholic Church there is no place for true sacrifice: “You shall not carry any of its flesh outside,” he says (Exod. 12:46). He gives his whole self in the mouth and heart of the person who approaches faithfully, while he remains wholly at the right hand of God the Father. This food is food of redemption and salvation, food of life and peace, food of eternity and blessedness. At present it is given to us under the truth of faith, not yet under the light of manifest vision.

Meanwhile, in a manner of reception suited to our imperfection, it is given under the appearance of bread and wine; yet there is neither bread nor wine there, but the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—the very same body which was born of the Virgin, suffered on the cross, rose from death, ascended, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and abundantly poured out the one Holy Spirit. He is always present to his own: “Behold,” he says, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). He is everywhere by essence and is present to his own by grace: by the grace of blessing, by the grace of that ineffable unity concerning which he says thus to the Father concerning his chosen ones:

> “I have given them the glory which you gave me, that they may be one as we are one. I in them and you in me, that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:22–23).

O blessed unity, in which Father and Son are one; through which these people receive, as a gratuitous gift—not by nature or by merit—the glory which the Father gave the Son without beginning and without end! They are reborn to God in the one Holy Spirit; the Apostle testifies: “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

15. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father, the Son, and to these persons also. Whoever is reborn in this unity of the Holy Spirit becomes new from old, a son from a slave, a saint from a sinner. In this unity of the Holy Spirit, the unity of believers is betrothed to one husband, consecrated to Christ the bridegroom, and, being one, is perfected into one with the one God: one from Jews and Gentiles; one from angels and human beings. “He gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12), he who became the Son of man, uniting himself to us and uniting us also to himself. This wondrous unity [Col. 1306C] contains every good and absolutely no evil. That unity—the perfect unity—that liar Satan, the father of lies, did not touch; rather, he fell away with his own through his lie. But the humble angelic spirits, subject to God, held fast to the unity of eternal love with God; and when the evil fell, they remained good. Blessed is that fellowship which had no sin, incurred no guilt, but immediately undertook steadfastly to cleave to its Creator. To it rightly applies what is written: “But for me, it is good to cleave to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72:28): a hope free from confusion, a hope made complete by perfect love.

These are the good spirits, the ministering spirits, who carry out God’s commands everywhere; sent forth, they hasten, and they always stand before him whom they always love. [Col. 1306D] They openly behold the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both, the gift of Father and Son. This gift is poured forth from both and is not separated from either; it is offered openly and granted to good will. Let whoever wishes receive it; let no one turn himself away, let none make excuse, let none flee; let everyone run, provided that he holds fast. “For the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1:7); and, “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32:5). Mercy therefore calls sinners, grants pardon to the repentant, gathers them into the bosom of Mother Church, and sanctifies them in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

This holy unity Adam, the first man, refused to retain; through disobedience he fell away from it, because in excusing his sin he kept it for himself. Nor did Cain, the first [Col. 1307A] born among human beings, retain it at all. He refused to hear the Lord and was the first to stain himself with murder. Convicted by his brother’s blood crying out from the earth, he did not even then seek the Lord’s mercy. He spoke a word against the Holy Spirit: “My iniquity,” he said, “is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (Gen. 4:13), as though to say: God’s mercy is lesser and powerless; there is no one who takes away sin. He retained his sin for himself and did not seek a remedy from the Holy Spirit. This remedy is so abundantly bestowed that it has even been entrusted to human beings. Human beings remit sins when this has been granted them by grace. Jesus gave this authority to those consecrated to his service: “Receive,” he says, “the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you remit are remitted to them, and whose you retain are retained” [Col. 1307B] (John 20:22).

16. The Holy Spirit, then, was given for the remission of sins and for their retention: for remission to those who return in repentance and seek healing within the unity of the Church; for the retention of sins in those who always desire to sin and wish to persist in sins. Such people do not seek the keys entrusted to Peter; by neglect they despise the Church of God, which looses sins through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Such people sin against the Holy Spirit, a sin which is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come.

Mother Church received the Holy Spirit for the remission of sins. Those obstinate in sins, hardened and despairing, despise the Church of God and wish to perpetuate themselves in their sins. “There is,” he says, [Col. 1308A] “a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16). Concerning this the Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, sin that ought to have been remitted but was wickedly retained; of righteousness offered but despised; and of judgment not avoided (John 16:8). Therefore he who does not receive life within the unity of the Holy Spirit despises the Holy Spirit who convicts them—Satan having already become [such]. He does not receive life who despises the Church; he despises the Church who does not believe that it possesses the Holy Spirit; he does not believe that it possesses the Holy Spirit who says that it cannot forgive sin. This is blasphemy; this is a word against the Holy Spirit: blasphemers, schismatics, and heretics rage against the Church of God, say that there are no remedies for sins, and, as far as they can, rend the unity [Col. 1308B] of the Church. “This,” he says, “is their hour and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53).

Amid such people, the Church of God grows strong in the Holy Spirit. As Noah’s ark was borne up in the flood, so, in the exile of this failing age, the rising waters could raise the ark of God’s Church but could not sink it. Thus the rising storms of evil people can exalt the Church but cannot destroy it. From their evils the Church advances; through the Church’s goods malice falls. At last, when the wicked have been excluded, the whole Church shall possess, together with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let us make a pause (*sela*) in contemplating these things, so that, having drawn breath from the Holy Spirit, we may be able to speak faithfully.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1307]

[Col. 1307C] 1. Devout recollection therefore professes that the Father and the Son are one God in the unity of the Holy Spirit; that Christ Jesus, in that same Spirit, remains one true God and man; and that the unity of believers, in that same Spirit, remains one with God. For the sake of the full and perfect joy of this unity, to be wholly fulfilled in his own, he who gave himself for our redemption says: “When I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32): all things into this singular unity, in the love of the Holy Spirit, which is one love of Father and Son and of all whom the Church’s unity has gathered into one. Within this unity all live blessedly; outside it all perish under death.

2. Meanwhile, while we remain in the present life, [Col. 1307D] we very often see some persons, for whose peril we had feared, return to the Church’s unity through the regard of heavenly grace, and be healed and strengthened. King David the prophet sinned through adultery, sinned through murder, having carried out a treacherous stratagem; but the Lord warned him through the prophet. The king humbly heard him, returned to the unity of the Holy Spirit, and said in repentance: “Have mercy upon me, O God, according to your great mercy; and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my iniquity,” etc. (Ps. 50:3). Afterwards, praying, he said: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a ruling spirit” [Col. 1308C] (ibid., vv. 12–14).

You hear in the penitent’s prayer a right spirit, a holy spirit, and a ruling spirit named. The spirit is right in condemning sin; it is holy in the outpouring of the divine gift; it is ruling in the reception of perfect blessedness in simple unity with God. Behold, the humble sinner goes before the sentence of the judge, which by repenting he changes and averts. By repentance and exceeding humility he makes the judge whom he had feared into a father for himself. As repentance prevails, the sentence is changed; sin having been driven away, righteousness enters, and with a right spirit, a holy spirit, and a ruling spirit raises up the penitent. “You who lift me up,” he says, “from the gates of death, so that I may declare all your praises [Col. 1308D] in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:14).

But whoever puts on the right spirit, the holy spirit, and the ruling spirit receives God’s commandments, keeps those received, and loves those kept. Concerning this Truth itself says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 8:52). And, what is more glorious, he adds: “And my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Therefore, concerning David, made right through repentance, holy through pardon received, and ruling through the unity of the Holy Spirit—especially ruling because we devoutly look to the Father of Jesus Christ—we earnestly pray that through his Son, our Lord, pardon, grace, and blessing may be given to us. As we consider these matters, we rightly rejoice.

[Col. 1309B] 3. By contrast, Judas, that thief and betrayer of his Lord and teacher—indeed, of ours—the covetous seller, with conscience accusing, reason judging, and truth condemning, knew that he had sinned and could not conceal his sin. He said: “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). Yet he did not seek the Holy Spirit at all; rather, in despair, he killed himself by a noose. This Judas, one of the twelve, was one in number but did not rejoice in merit. He perished through greed, theft, and betrayal, and lost the height of the apostolic dignity. Concerning this most wicked man the Lord had foretold to them: “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:70).

What does this mean? On the witness of Truth, this wicked man too was chosen by God together with the good; he received from the Lord the allotted office of the apostolic name, but fell through his own wickedness.

[Col. 1309C] 4. It must therefore be understood that almighty God has chosen both good and evil persons. He acts almightily, because he is neither aided by the goodness of the good nor impeded by the wickedness of the evil; rather, from good and evil alike he always works well. Satan himself and the impiety of all evil persons serve the Church of God, which, exercised by their malice and crimes, continually advances, increases, and grows. These evil people serve God, but as broken and subjected servants. For God’s magnificence becomes more wonderfully known to us through them: while they always endeavor by their own wickedness to do harm, they are compelled by divine power to do good. The evils they do are certainly evil for them, [Col. 1309D] but God’s magnificence causes those very evils to become good, because they are useful to the good.

So too this Judas, through whom the blood of our Redeemer was sold and poured out for us on the cross: evil for himself by reason of his wickedness, he became useful to us through the operation of heavenly grace. He delivered him to his death whom the Father also delivered for our life. Behold, Judas’s evil became good for holy Church. He became a devil, as did those to whom Truth also said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8:44): children of the father devil, not by nature but by wickedness.

When we consider such sinners—fugitives and exiles from the unity of the Holy Spirit, obstinate in their evils and crimes—we see that Peter too truly sinned, denying the Lord himself, our Lord; but in anxious repentance and bitter weeping he sought the grace of the Holy Spirit. This is Peter who formerly, when the Lord asked, “But who do you say that I am?”, alone answered for all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” [Col. 1310A] (Matt. 16:15–16). To him the Lord said: “And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church” (ibid., v. 18).

There Peter, made a rock, shone forth on high; but during the Lord’s Passion he fell in ruin by denying him. Yet immediately, when the Lord looked upon him, he repented; reformed anew, Peter deserved through weeping to become Peter once more, and rose in the Holy Spirit. Having denied three times, he was questioned a third time, the Lord saying: “Peter, do you love me?” “Lord,” he said, “you know that I love you.” And by the merit of that love [Col. 1310B] which is from the Holy Spirit, he to whom all things belong said to him: “Feed my lambs; feed my sheep” (John 21:15). Behold, Peter is again placed over Christ’s Church.

In the one Peter the whole present Church is gathered. Therefore Peter’s successors, the Roman pontiffs, by pre-eminent authority through Christ’s power, hold, teach, and order the Catholic Church in the unity of the Holy Spirit. They hold it under the discipline of obedience, teach it under evangelical unity, and order it through the provision of offices. These things are done under Peter’s firm faith, concerning which Truth said to him: “Peter, I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail; and when you have once turned, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). From this, Peter’s faith is the foundation of the present [Col. 1310C] Church.

5. Thus the Church, at Christ’s command, is united to Peter and follows Peter. It walks upon the sea as it moves toward Christ; amid the waves of this age, over the billows of the stormy world, it proceeds faithfully. Meanwhile a mighty wind, full of malice, meets it, and it slips through fear. By the fall of fear it begins to sink; but, imitating Peter, it cries to Christ. Christ stretches out his hand to it as it cries, grasps it, and brings it to the stability of peace and blessedness. There no truth harasses anyone, no storm of evil people troubles anyone. This was signified by Peter’s little boat, when, with Christ entering it from the sea, the wind ceased and there was a great calm (Matt. 8:26). By this that full peace was prefigured, because God will be [Col. 1310D] all in all.

Behold with what joyful, behold with what blessed end the Church’s labor is concluded—grievous in the present life, and wholly unbearable unless Christ conquers. But those follow Christ who says to his own: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Therefore, through him, Mother Church, one in the Holy Spirit, conquers every evil; with Peter she overcomes the storms of the sea, that is, all evil persons. Thus Christ’s Church, remaining one with Christ and united to Peter, enters in the unity of the Holy Spirit into the peace of eternal blessedness. It sees the God of gods in Zion; what it believed, it beholds openly; what it hoped, it finds in that very reality; what it loved, it wholly grasps in fullness. Love gathers all things together. For when all other things have been emptied, passed away, and fulfilled, love never fails. The eye of love alone [Col. 1311A] shall see God; it alone shall bring to fulfillment within itself the merits of all the other virtues.

6. This is it: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This is the Holy Spirit who, through every age of the present world, has set forth sacraments of life for people to be saved. He has never failed anyone except one who never wished to leave sins or repent. The sacraments of life have been set forth, differing indeed according to different times, but with the same—not differing—effects; the same according to faith in Jesus Christ; the same in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

For in the earthly paradise the sacrament of life, which is Christ, was given to our first parents: namely, the tree called the tree of life. But our first parents passed from the tree of life [Col. 1311B] to the tree of desire, to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which they had been forbidden to touch. Yet they were neither hindered by ignorance nor compelled by the necessity of weakness; rather, knowing the command and able to keep it, drawn by their own desire, they became transgressors, seized what was not granted, and ate from it. Immediately they fell beneath the burden of sin and the law of death, and received knowledge of good and evil with eyes previously sound but now opened to evil. With the tree of life they knew and possessed good simply; with the tree of desire they came to know evils—addition and evil. They perceived that by transgressing they had lost the good of innocence. They perceived that through disobedience [Col. 1311C] they had lost the garment of righteousness. Ashamed and confounded in their own sight, they knew their nakedness; they did not flee to God in repentance, but went to the fig tree and presumed to cover their members with fig leaves. They adopted the practice of hypocrites, since they wished not humbly to confess their fault but to excuse it and cover it with false accusation.

Convicted again, condemned, and expelled, through the likeness of gods which they had wickedly desired—Satan saying, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:5)—they became like cattle, clothed in garments of skins. Once they had been cast out, the cherubim and flaming sword stood in the way, lest they return to the tree of life which they had lost by pride. This loss is grave, though imposed on them by just judgment. It is a remarkable loss to lose the tree of life. The tree [Col. 1311D] of life provided nourishment and presented a sacrament: nourishment for preserving present life; a sacrament granted so that, by the merit of obedience, they might pass from the earthly to the divine and afterwards live blessedly forever. Not through the earthly tree of life, but through the life which is Christ—who is heavenly life, the enduring life of all who truly live.

This nourishment was for earthly life, to avoid bodily death; this sacrament was for the supercelestial and divine life that remains with God. Both were lost through disobedience; when both had been lost, the necessity of sin spread abroad, and death, the wages of sin, entered.

7. But the merciful One, who never ceases to show mercy, had mercy upon us and, in place of the visible sacrament of the tree [Col. 1312A] of life in paradise which had been lost, prepared in this our exile of sin and death also the sacrament of faith. This sound and true faith, inspired by the Holy Spirit, leads back to Christ, who is truth essentially. We faithfully believe in him so that, united to him at last in the Holy Spirit through the merit of faith, we may live with an eternal course.

This faith first appeared to us in righteous Abel, who, kindled by faith, humbly offered God from what was his; for his faith God looked upon him and accepted his offerings. Because of this faith envy burned against him, and he first of all deserved from God the crown of martyrdom. In the unity of this same faith Enos began to invoke the name of the Lord. To invoke the Lord’s name is to assign both oneself and all things to God. This assignment is truly the invocation of the Lord’s name, which always blesses the Lord. [Col. 1312B] This blessing begins in faith, is raised up by hope, and is completed in love.

In this unity of faith, which proceeds first, Enoch, seventh from Adam, walked with God and did not appear. Such walking—believing faithfully, hoping firmly, loving singularly—always stands before God. In this unity of faith Noah, the restorer of the world, guided the ark in the flood and saved everything received within it. Whatever remained outside the unity of the ark the vast inundation of the flood destroyed. Finally, when the flood had subsided, he went out freely with his own; proved by faith, he received the world in his power to possess, and offered God a sacrifice as an odor of the sweetness of perfect faith. He offered from every kind of bird and cattle, from the clean [Col. 1312C] and not from the common.

In this faith, illuminated by the Holy Spirit, Abraham heard the Lord saying to him: “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” etc. (Gen. 12:1). “Abraham,” it says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6). He received the sign of circumcision as the seal of faith in himself and in his descendants. Thus a visible sacrament was added to Abraham’s faith, circumcision in the flesh, so that he who pleased the Lord through faith in his Holy Spirit might appear holy also in the flesh. This faith of Abraham received the promises: “In your seed,” he says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Abraham was first so named by God because through faith he was made father of many nations.

At the Lord’s command he unhesitatingly offered his beloved son Isaac for sacrifice; but, tested by faith, he received his son unharmed and heard the magnificent and surpassing blessings, to be fulfilled in himself and his seed, from the Lord who swore them. In this faith Isaac gave his son Jacob a blessing of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth; he established him above his brothers in dominion and above his enemies in power. Although this blessing was given by a father whose sight was dim, it remained firm through faith. Esau, the firstborn, though weeping and wailing before his father, could not annul it. Esau lost it through his own folly; Jacob held it through his simplicity, believing and devoted to his mother. Joyful recollection marvels at faith in Abraham, hope in Isaac, and love in Jacob, by a special prerogative. These three things appear gracious in these three patriarchs. For he who is God of all wished to be called the God of these three: “I,” he says, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” [Col. 1313A] (Matt. 22:32). He is their God because in these three faith, hope, and love were more illustrious in their respective times. “He is not,” he says, “the God of the dead but of the living.” These are living because they believed, hoped, and loved in him who is life.

Faith, hope, and love must all be possessed together in the present life. Abraham, servant of God; Isaac, beloved of God; and Jacob, saint of God, possessed them together, although they are marked out in each individual by the pre-eminent efficacy of certain works.

8. Thus the faith, hope, and love of the ancients and of these patriarchs were possessed together in the one Holy Spirit. Then circumcision was manifest in their flesh; afterwards the Law was given through Moses; there were also the sacred utterances of the prophets and the preceding holy mysteries. All these were together fulfilled wholly and truly in Christ Jesus our Lord, as the Apostle says of his person: “For in Christ dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” [Col. 1313B] (Col. 2:9), that is, not under a shadow or a figure, but essentially. He himself is the body of the shadows, the truth of the preceding figures, fitting together in himself all that gives life to the world. He is the one who creates a new creature, who makes a new world.

Up to Christ all human beings, born from flesh in a fleshly manner, all Adam’s children, were old. Christ is new from flesh, yet not carnally born, but born from the Holy Spirit and a virgin: the new man, the new condition of humankind. He is the one who answered Nicodemus: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless anyone is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” And again: “Unless anyone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God” (John 3:3–5).

You hear the Spirit together with water. Hence it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). Human beings are reborn from water and the Holy Spirit and are made new: from visible water and from the invisible Holy Spirit. In baptism both are reborn, namely soul and body: the body visible, the soul invisible. Both are purified; faith works in both; sins are loosed in both. Our ancient fathers, faithful and holy, did not actually receive this regeneration, but sought it [Col. 1313D] in Christ through faith and sacraments. They descended to hell because they had not been reborn. Christ descended to them and led out with himself, raising them to heavenly places, those whom he openly recognized in the sacrament of faith.

But those who in the present life have become one with Christ, reborn in the Holy Spirit, if they persevere in this unity, do not descend to the lower regions. When they die, they are not burdened by death; rather, they pass beyond it and freely ascend to heavenly things. “For God so loved the world,” he says, “that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life” (John 3:16). Behold the new world, his new creation. “God,” says James the apostle, “voluntarily begot us by the word of truth, that we might be some beginning of his creation” (Jas. 1:18): the wondrous and ineffable power of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1314A] by which the oldness of the old world is abolished, by which a new world is truly created in Christ and sanctified by perennial water.

9. From the origin of sin, darkness was upon the face of the abyss; when grace rose, the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters. “What is born of flesh,” he says, “is flesh; and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes; so is everyone who is born of the Spirit” (John 3:6, 8). The carnal person, not reborn in the Spirit who is God, is wholly flesh; darkness lies upon his face, and he is an abyss. He does not know the one reborn from the Spirit, because he is spirit. The former is dark; the latter illumined. The Apostle says: “The spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one; the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God” [Col. 1314B] (1 Cor. 2:15). Those reborn, therefore, are heavenly, not earthly.

To such people Christ speaks and says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way that, once every darkness and error has been dispelled, leads to truth; the truth, brighter than the sun and resplendent with every power, leads to life—life full of blessedness, without end, completed and perfected in God. This is God and the Son of God, sent by the Father, wholly in the Father. Having become man, the virgin’s son, he came to us: one person, wholly man and wholly God, inseparable, whole, undivided. To sanctify baptism, by which the whole world, renewed by faith and grace, is saved, he came to John and descended into the Jordan. John forbade him, saying: “I ought to be baptized by you, [Col. 1314C] and do you come to me?” And the Lord said to him: “Permit it now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15).

10. Therefore, when Christ had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened to him, and the Holy Spirit descended like a dove upon Jesus and remained over him; and the Father’s voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid., vv. 16–17). Behold, knowledge of the supreme Trinity, which is God, has been made manifest to us by sighted faith. The Father bears witness to the Son by a voice descending; the heavens are opened to the praying Son; the Holy Spirit is seen resting in the dove over the Son. This is knowledge of the supreme Trinity; it fulfills all righteousness and the magnificence of every virtue.

Within this Trinity the one reborn in the saving font stands in the middle, constantly meditates upon it, worships it, and loves it. Whoever neglects to know this Trinity, and despises it though it is manifest, remains devoid of all righteousness, guilty and unrighteous in sins. But whoever is reborn in the Holy Spirit through baptism is a son of God with our Lord Jesus Christ. The heavens are opened above him as he prays; the paternal voice speaks to him: “You are my beloved Son” [Col. 1314D] (Mark 1:11). The Holy Spirit appears over him; he is clothed over with all righteousness and has become a new creature in unity, consecrated with God in glory.

11. Holy recollection therefore rejoices, seeing the river flowing out in the present Church with spiritual efficacy, as it is written: “A river went forth from the place [Col. 1315A] of delight to water paradise” (Gen. 2:10). Concerning this the prophet Zechariah says: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing away of sin and of the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13:1). The prophet Ezekiel bears witness to it, through whom the Lord speaks thus to those whom he brings forth: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and I shall cleanse you from all your idols” (Ezek. 36:25).

This is the clean water prefigured by the water of expiation given through Moses, at the Lord’s command, to the children of Israel in the wilderness. Behold the new grace of baptism, washing away every sin of everyone. From it arises a new creature, an abundant adoption as children of God. These call God their Father, follow Jesus Christ their brother, and retain the Holy Spirit, given to them forever. Behold, the kingdom of God is within you and is continually being perfected.

That ancient treasure hidden in the field of the former fathers, wrapped in figures and mystical enigmas, is openly expounded. The precious pearl is openly offered to the buyer. Humble love buys it with whatever little it has; proud desire could not buy it with any of its magnificence, nor even attain it. Henceforth the net cast into the sea, filled with every kind of fish—namely the Church, which rejects no one but gathers all—will be brought to shore. There the evil will be cast out, but the good will be received into heavenly vessels: vessels overflowing with every good, vessels full [Col. 1315C] of God’s presence.

The Apostle, beholding this consummation of the present Church, says that Christ, pre-eminent and first among all the saints in rising again to life by ascension [lacuna], coeternal in glory with God the Father, ever one God in the unity of the Holy Spirit with that same God the Father and with the Spirit himself, says that, once every effect of the new creation has been fulfilled and all Christ’s works of obedience completed, then comes the end: the end of present works, the end of earthly gain, the end that brings every good to completion in the Good, [Col. 1316A] when he has delivered the kingdom to God the Father—the new kingdom that he himself created.

God, sent from God the Father and made the new man, when he has delivered the kingdom, we do not mean the kingdom of the old creation, the universal order of all things, which fell through sin and remained under death; but the kingdom of the new world, the new creation, holy regeneration, and divine adoption. This kingdom the Holy Spirit, who was borne over the waters, has cleansed, sanctified, and indwelt. This kingdom God the Son of God, having become man, will present to God the Father, that it may be completed, eternally one in the one Holy Spirit, transparent with divine brightness, blessed without end with God.

There will not be there the works of this present life, nor the merits of good works, but the rewards of merits and the glory of rewards: merits through cooperating grace; rewards through the Lord’s generosity; glory through enjoyment of the vision of God. The day of God’s vision endures happy and blessed. “On that day,” he says, “you shall know that I am in the Father, and you in me, and I in you” [Col. 1316B] (John 14:20). I am in the Father by one essence; you are in me, received by grace; I am in you as salvation and life.

On that day those shall rest in the seventh day, without morning and without evening. He who made all things and did not begin to make did so because there was certainly no source from which he might begin; nor had his rest any cause. He did not take on something from which he might begin, nor did he labor so as to rest. In acting he rests; in resting he acts. Thus that tranquil worker, the resting laborer, admonishes us to perform our works from him, through him, and in him, and to seek nothing outside [Col. 1316C] him. Let us not wish to rest in ourselves or in our works, but gladly rest from him, through him, and in him—him whom we know to rest not in his work but from work in himself, that is, on the seventh day, without beginning, without end, without evening, and without morning.

Taken into this inestimable blessedness of rest, the resting children of God bless the supreme Trinity in enduring unity, singing with joyful voice and continual praise, “alleluia” (“praise the Lord”), “hosanna” (“save, we pray”), “amen” (“truly”): the song known to the inhabitants of heaven.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 1315]

[Col. 1315D] 1. Faithful recollection, worthy of praise and proclamation, ranges through all things and beholds all things. Raised humbly to God, even to the vision of him, it sees God as the maker of all spiritual and bodily things. It sees them in the divine mind, in Wisdom itself, where they are eternally laid up; it sees them in their proper actuality, where created things subsist. Things past do not escape it, things present do not abandon it, things future do not hold it in suspense. It sees God present through all things, existing in all things: not contained, but containing; not in need of anything, but enriching all things.

Always illumined by heavenly Wisdom, it offers right speech in all its actions, provides sound counsel, and promises true judgment. It sees God as essentially good; it sees his works, according to their condition and nature, as without exception good; it sees some among the rest endowed with rational intelligence and adorned with a manifold diversity of virtues. Through grace bestowed by God, good is he who created them; good are the things well created by the Good, moving blessedly with God and under God.

2. Having contemplated these things, holy recollection rejoices; but looking in the opposite direction, it is suddenly troubled and marvels at things strange, unnatural, not created by God—things of which it had known nothing in God except what was good. How quickly it beholds evils, unexpectedly arising, spreading with tumultuous noise almost everywhere, in fury, obstinacy, and blasphemy. What are these things? [Col. 1317A] We know such things to be neither from God, nor through God, nor in God: not from God, because they were not created; not through God, because they lack form; not in God, because they are harmful.

What then are they? If I ask whether they are a substance, I find that they are not. The more attentively I consider whether they are some thing, the less I recognize them. Yet, to confess the truth, I perceive them to be contrary to unity and to overthrow peace. By their wickedness they throw all things into confusion and disturb all people; and, what is greatly to be lamented, they are almost everywhere throughout the whole world: without them I can scarcely find anything. What shall we say to this? Did God make them, or did he not make them? Since God made all things, one God made all things, the Good made good things: therefore, if these things are among the good things, then he who made all good things did not create everything; but if he created evils, not all the things he made are good. Yet God made all things well, and the Good created no evils.

If you seek devoutly, you find all things in God; apart from God you can find nothing. Therefore, when the things called evils are found not to subsist among all the things that are, sound recollection determines that they are named, as best one can, from the privation of good and the defect of virtue. For the defect of virtue and the privation of good give names to those things called most evil, harmful, and damnable. They are so called not because they are, but because they are not good: they disgrace bodies, stain souls, infect morals, and dull minds. If you strive to investigate them as they are, you will find them in the rational mind of angel and human being falling away from truth and falling away from God.

3. Those spirits indeed who are called the seal of the likeness of God [Col. 1317C], and human beings created in the image and likeness of God, ought and were able to see, follow, and love above all things him by whom they were made good and received grace. Thus, by the merit of charity, they could be raised above themselves to God; through virtues they could become better than their good nature, live happily, and remain good. But abusing the freedom of rational choice, they slipped from the One to the innumerable, from the unchangeable to mutable things, from the stable to vain things; perverted by desire and lavish in their ambition, they preferred the creature to the Creator, falsehood to truth. They embraced iniquity instead of justice and incurred death instead of life. The lying creature, not by nature but by transgression, conceived such utterly evil things and offered such monstrous, execrable things to the world.

[Col. 1317D] 4. Upon that twisting deceiver, Leviathan, God pronounced this sentence: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth; upon your breast you shall go, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. II, 14). He said, “all the days of his life”: all days according to his evil eternity, his life ever unhappy, wretched without end. Upon this one he also pronounced judgment upon the woman who had wickedly persuaded her husband: “In pain you shall give birth, and you shall be subject” (Gen. III, 16). He likewise passed sentence upon the man for disobedience, saying: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work” (ibid., 17). See, then, what falling away from God has found, what transgressive disobedience has found. Satan fell away from God [Col. 1318A] and remains cursed, feeding on earth’s food, though he ought to have enjoyed God. The first man, disobedient, found the earth cursed in his work and was given as food to him who eats earth. For he himself remained earth, when it was said to him, the transgressor: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (ibid., 19). This first man lost the dignity which he had received, having been made in the image and likeness of God; by transgressing the commandment he received a curse; by eating what had not been granted, he incurred death.

5. Behold plainly what turning away from God, what transgression of the commandment, produces in all that belongs to it. You see how the rational creature which departs from God subjects both itself and all its possessions to a curse, and places itself under the unbearable laws of death. Overwhelmed by these evils and bound by these shackles, they cannot at all [Col. 1318B] escape, return to their former freedom, or recover the goods they have lost. They have indeed the power of rational choice, but it is by no means free, because the good which they could do with God they cannot do without God, whom they abandoned by transgressing. They do not possess freedom of choice because they are not free, having become slaves under the law of sin. From this wretched slavery he alone can free them who alone can freely do all things, the Son from God the Father. Of this he himself says: “If the Son makes you free, you shall be truly free” (John VIII, 36). For they cannot be free unless they are sons; nor can they be sons except through God the Son, assigned together to the supreme Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit. Outside this unity of Mother Church no one has been able to do good; by grace one may work good, but without grace nothing but evil.

[Col. 1318C] The Apostle says: “It is not of the one who wills nor of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX, 16). However much you may will, however much you may strive to run, you cannot act rightly without God. Therefore the free choice of angel or human being, unless it stands with God, cannot avoid evils or do good. Isaiah says: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. VII, 14–15). Human skill makes butter from an animal’s milk; the ingenious, unfertilized bee gathers honey whole from heavenly dew. By these two, the animal and the spiritual are customarily understood. The Virgin’s Son, God-with-us, consumes both in the present Church—that is, incorporates them into himself—in order that he may know, and make them know, how to reject [Col. 1318D] evil and choose good. This is the work of free choice judging with God and preserving justice. Thus one judges rightly who rejects evil in oneself and in others, and chooses good. If one judges otherwise, one condemns oneself. Of such persons the Apostle says: “Seeking to establish their own justice, they are not subject to the justice of God” (Rom. X, 3). Thus the liberty of rational choice perishes; thus it loses grace; and, having lost the power of the highest good, it lurks with Satan in the recesses of the north. Satan reigns in such persons, having become an abyss from heavenly, darkness from luminous.

6. His kingdom is empty of virtues, filthy with vices; uncleanness defiles it, intemperance scatters it, discord destroys it, death overwhelms it. “The death of sinners,” he says, [Col. 1319A] “is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 22), because at the resurrection they shall be held under everlasting death. But “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. CXV, 15), because they shall rise from death, living with God in eternity. There death shall be swallowed up in Christ’s victory, because Christ, who owed nothing to death, took upon himself the death owed by us but not owed by himself, and freely gave us the life which he himself is, though we had not deserved it. O wondrous clemency of God! O infinite mercy! By his singular power he was able to destroy Satan’s kingdom within us: descending from the Father’s throne, he came humbly against pride, and by destroying sins overthrew Satan’s kingdom. “Now,” he says, “is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John XII, 31). He is cast out from the assembly [Col. 1319B] of the faithful and from the lot of the good; and the sins of the saints remain upon him. For he is himself the first inventor of sins and has remained ever their instigator. He is the depth of the sea into which all rivers descend, into which all evils of all persons flow together: “He shall cast,” it says, “all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Mic. VII, 19). The woman crushes his head, and he lies in wait for her heel; he bites the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward. He lies in wait for her heel who tries to infect the end of a good work with even the slightest self-exaltation. He bites the horse’s hoofs who crushes the beginning of a good work and makes its rider turn back.

A portion of the stars follows him, and he waits for the Jordan to flow into [Col. 1319C] his mouth. Like a roaring lion he goes about seeking whom he may devour; he circles the earth and walks through it. Nor did he leave even the Lord untempted: he sifted the apostles like wheat and swallowed Judas, his thief. But, thanks be to God, he lost the thief upon the cross; and in hell, conquered by Christ’s triumph, he fell defeated. There he lost the spoil of the good which he had violently seized, and remained broken. There, when the Lord appeared to his faithful who then dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, light rose for them. There the Lord, strong and mighty in battle, made the devil weak and laid the powerless one low. There the Lord of hosts is himself the King of glory; he placed ancient Leviathan, lord of vices and king of misery, under everlasting calamity. Alone, by the arm of his power, he descended and triumphed; [Col. 1319D] he released countless of his faithful from captivity and led them forth free with himself. When the Lord went forth and rose from the dead, “the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep arose” (Matt. XXVII, 52). The veil of the temple was rent, the mysteries of the old time were unveiled, the holy of holies appeared, the heavens of heavens were opened; the triumphant one ascended with an innumerable company of the faithful. By a wondrous miracle he made men pure, brought out from the lower world and gathered from every part of the earth, adorned by his grace, into new inhabitants of heaven, companions and fellow-citizens of the dwellers above.

7. Behold, a new kingdom and a new glory are established in heaven. No one resists those who enter. Prostitutes enter; tax collectors enter by that way, by that passage through which the camel too, [Col. 1320A] having laid aside its hump, enters through the eye of a needle. Here pride must be laid aside; here repentance must be undertaken and borne with humility. The true needle is Christ, wounded for our crimes: he penetrates all things, searches all things, “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII, 1). He is the way without whom no one comes to the Father. This way makes sons of perdition and vessels of wrath into sons of God and vessels of reconciliation, and brings them by the forceful hand of mercy to the kingdom which he builds anew in heaven. In the Gospel you read: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. II, 12).

That same wondrous conqueror makes daily, in this exile of the present life, new persons from old, saints from sinners. He frees them from Egypt’s fetters, leads them out of Babylonian captivity, and from these who are reborn, renewed, and sanctified in the Holy Spirit makes a new kingdom on earth, to be united with that new kingdom which he himself, ascending above the heights of heaven, has exalted in perpetual blessedness. Concerning the new kingdom on earth, however, the Apostle Peter speaks thus to the saints: “To you therefore who believe is honor” (I Pet. II, 7). And afterward: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his wonderful light” (I Pet. II, 9). And he introduced the prophet as saying: “You who once were not a people, but now are the people of God; who had not obtained mercy, but now [Col. 1320C] have obtained mercy” (ibid., 10).

Behold: Christ, the new man—not a new God, ever the same and ever whole—has built a new kingdom, a new Church. Not two, but one: one in the unity of person, with the property of each nature preserved; ever truly one, ever to be worshipped in a Catholic manner. “He founded her upon the seas; he prepared her upon the rivers”: upon the seas, upon the variety and defects of our mutability; upon the rivers, upon the surges of human desire and the assaults of heretical perversity. But his mercies are over all his works. It belongs to the Almighty to create all things at once; it belongs to him to form what is created, and always and everywhere to preserve what he has formed. This is divine and singular; yet his wondrous mercy is great over all [Col. 1320D] his works. “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III, 16), made man to redeem us. He redeemed us from the snares of darkness; he led us out from Ur of the Chaldeans; he drew us away from the muddy labor of the Egyptians. He sought out wicked, criminal, guilty people, wrapped in every kind of filth; he found none but evil persons. He washed them in his blood and made them white; by a new regeneration he made them new in the Holy Spirit. In Jericho he regarded Zacchaeus; he saw Matthew sitting at the tax-office; he called both. He himself and his disciples entered into the houses of such persons; he ate with tax collectors and sinners. The Pharisees grumble, and Jesus answers them that those in health have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do. “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not [Col. 1321A] sacrifice’; for I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matt. IX, 12–13). Those who make themselves righteous do not find him. If you confess yourself a sinner in true repentance, you immediately find him. She who was a sinner in the city sought him in Simon’s house; she hurried to kiss his feet, watered them with tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with ointment. Many sins were forgiven her because she loved much; and he said to her: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke VII, 50). She passed from intemperate sinning to the peace of the Holy Spirit and remained therein because she held fast to Christ’s charity.

8. Therefore let sinners arise, coming with repentance. Let them seek forgiveness of sins from him who came without sin and alone forgives sins; who, in an ineffable manner, as the Apostle testifies, made himself sin, when he gave himself as an offering for sin. He who is life received death. He who could not be held by death died; he redeemed us from the death which we deserved and gave us the life which we received not by merit but by grace. O sublime memory of the saints, which recalls such things and weighs matters so lofty! You see God and man not as a mixture, but as one person. Behold the magnificence of salvation: he destroyed evils and bestowed goods; he accomplished an inestimable work, who raised man so far that man became God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, in which the Father is one with the Son and the Son with the Father.

9. Therefore Christ, God and man, remains one in that majesty by which all things were made, by which the things made endure, by which they are seen to be good. But by a surpassing work God gave human beings “power to become children of God” (John I, 12), not because they were born of flesh, but because they were reborn from God through Christ Jesus in the work of the Holy Spirit, and became a new creation, a new world, a new kingdom of Christ. Behold, you see that human beings are exalted above all things. He who exalted them said to them: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). These great and most surpassing gifts God the Son of God, made man, bestowed upon human beings. He is Wisdom, “whose delights are to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII, 31), the humble and holy; and “his conversation is with the simple” (Prov. III, 32).

[Col. 1321D] This Wisdom assigned seven primordial days at the beginning for the sevenfold grace, according to which it causes seven days to run in time, and adorned the harmony of heaven with seven planets. In the present Church it raises seven pillars, which are the seven grades of honor conferred through the hand of the bishop in clerical promotion. These are doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, levites, and presbyters. The bishop, filled with Christ’s wisdom and Christ’s vicar, canonically consecrates these by the laying on of hands and grants them, with prayer, the sevenfold Holy Spirit. By these seven pillars he strongly exalts the holy Church. In her the faithful have been given seven prayers called the Lord’s Prayer; humbly sending these to the Father, they acquire the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. When these gifts are abundantly poured out, seven beatitudes are bestowed: in the prayers humility speaks to God; in the gifts God’s magnificence is extended to the humble; in the beatitudes everlasting peace with God is established for people of good will.

10. As these things thus proceed, memory rejoices in beholding God; it contemplates the sevenfold eye of the Holy Spirit in the one corner-stone, Christ Jesus. It sees that it is the work of the Holy Spirit that the Catholic Church is a garden enclosed, that in the enclosed garden there is a sealed fountain. The garden is enclosed so that the serpent which prevailed in the ancient paradise may not be able to enter the new garden enclosed by the power of the Holy Spirit. The fountain is sealed so that everyone reborn in it may always obtain eternal life. Behold, the treasures of wisdom are opened, inestimable delights are set forth. [Col. 1322B] In wisdom’s enclosed garden health-giving herbs spring up, flowers of innocence come forth, trees preeminent in grace ripen with multiplied fruit, and balsams overflowing with charity fill everything with a healing fragrance. He dies who dies to the good odor; he lives who delights in the good odor: an odor of life unto life for those who love, who confess the inseparable unity of the holy Trinity, who always bless Jesus Christ, God and man, as one, and the Catholic Church as one with God in the unity of the Holy Spirit—everlasting, blessed, possessing all things, and enjoying peace.

11. Behold the land of the living, the homeland of the blessed. In it sublime memory beholds human bodies proceeding from the resurrection, exalted above fellowship [Col. 1322C] with the wicked: bodies indeed, to each of which an individual rational soul was created together in the unity of person. But those which shall not rise in Christ shall not be changed, because they remain under sin. Hence the Apostle says: “Indeed, we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed. Then the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (I Cor. XV, 51). Human bodies shall rise, to be restored to the spirits to which they belonged, in that quantity and quality which, without the defect of corruption, they ought to have attained by natural development according to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age. All shall indeed rise: human beings whole in body, generated by resurrection. The Lord himself certainly calls this resurrection “regeneration” when he says: “You who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging” (Matt. XIX, 28). Human beings were made in the image and likeness of God, so that in respect of the image they may hold eternity with God, and in respect of the likeness may present charity to God—a charity which ever beholds the undivided and simple Trinity. Therefore they must rise again and stand before their maker, the ruler of all, so that it may openly appear whether they have retained the likeness of the supreme Trinity in the exercise of charity.

12. There books shall be opened, the revealed consciences of each person shall lie open; the hidden things of darkness and the secrets of hearts shall be manifest, while consciences accuse [Col. 1323A] or defend before all who behold. There shall be judgment; there shall be the end. Then the angels “shall separate the wicked from among the righteous” (Matt. XIII, 49). For very many wicked people had lived in the assembly of the faithful, yet hidden, in communion of the sacraments and participation in outward benefits. When these have been excluded and placed on the left, it shall be said: “Let the wicked person be removed, lest he see the glory of God.” But when the righteous have been placed at the right, exalted from death to life, from dishonor to glory, from misery to blessedness, they shall be given the robe of divine brightness. Hence, while laboring in the present life, the Apostle spoke consolation: “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who shall reform the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his brightness” (Phil. [Col. 1323B] III, 20). And elsewhere: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Those who think only of things of the flesh neither attend to such things nor accept divine utterances, but contradict them. They have seen human bodies torn apart and destroyed in various ways, scattered by driving winds, waters, and air. They say that they cannot be put together again: “There is no resurrection of the dead.” They love temporary life and do not seek eternal life. They do not heed the Gospels, the prophecies, the Law, or the sacred writings; they do not consider the hand of the supreme Craftsman, which, as it made all things, so holds each thing and gathers all things. That hand is most powerful in all things, most effective in restoring bodies: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet” (I Cor. XV, 52). From wherever it recalls them, it refashions them when recalled; when refashioned and separated from the wicked, it glorifies them. The Apostle says: “Now your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then we also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 4).

There the glory of brightness shall not empty out the reality of the body, just as in Christ Jesus our Lord the divinity of the one assuming did not diminish the human nature assumed. Rather, perfect God and perfect man subsists in divine majesty. He gave human beings reborn from God power to become children of God, so that what he himself, the Son of God, possesses with God the Father by essence, these too—made sons with God the Son by grace—may possess in the unity of the Holy Spirit. In this unity the universal Church ever remains one, in surpassing blessedness, happily through infinite, spotless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1323]

## Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, on the Catholic Faith and the Lord’s Prayer

(Edited by Martène from a manuscript codex of the Royal Library, *Amplissima Collectio*, IX, 1212.)

[Col. 1323C] Dearest son, Giles: you are called an archdeacon; may you be worthy to be one! I rejoiced with great joy because you investigate the divine books and gather the sacred writings from every place. If you seek devoutly, you find God in them. But if you neglect to seek God in them, you may read them, yet you will not be able to bring the reading to fulfillment. Therefore God must be sought in them so that he may be found. You will indeed find God if you believe in him. He who believes and confesses and says, “I believe in God,” etc., should observe that to believe that God exists is a matter of reason; to believe God is a matter of diligence; to believe in God is life. You must know that believing is faith. Since God is invisible, he must be sought by faith. Faith seeks him; hope finds him; charity grasps him.

Therefore, in the present life faith in God must be held fast. He who truly seeks God refers both himself and all things to [Col. 1323D] him and seeks nothing outside God: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. LXXII, 25). And shortly afterward: “But it is good for me to cleave to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (ibid., 28). This man lives by faith, who seeks nothing anywhere but God alone, saying: “I believe in God the Father,” etc. “I believe in God the Father.” Behold: through faith he deserves to have God for Father—not merely any father, but the Almighty. He proves him almighty who confesses him as creator of heaven and earth. Understand “heaven and earth” together with all things which we know to have been created from them and with them.

“And in Jesus Christ, his Son.” Join this to what precedes and say: “I believe in God the Father Almighty; I also believe in Jesus Christ, his Son.” Jesus himself says: “Do you believe in God? Believe also in me” (John XIV, 1). This follows truly because Christ is God. “His Son,” he says—not a son in any ordinary manner, but “our only Lord.” This Son of the almighty Father is our Lord, not like those who are called lords merely by assertion, but Lord alone by nature, because he is the one Son of the almighty Father, essentially almighty [Col. 1324D]. This one, who is God and Lord from the Father, was given to us and made man for us: “Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.”

Because of this miracle worthy of worship, I judge it worth remembering that God formed the first Adam from virgin earth; that same one created the second Adam from a virgin. Of this the angel answered the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I, 35). Observe that, just as the earth did not know when the first Adam was made from it, so neither did the Virgin’s flesh perceive when, through the working of the Holy Spirit, it conceived Christ. See the most surpassing magnificence of the divine work. He who is God from the Father was born as God and man from the Virgin, one person.

Made man, he suffered under Pontius Pilate: the judge of all was condemned under a human judge. Yet he who had no guilt owed no punishment. Why, then, did he receive punishment, who committed no sin? Because of this wrong: “What I did not seize, then I paid” (Ps. LXVIII, 5). Behold the mystery of our redemption: the impassible one suffered without obligation, in order to take from us the debt of ancient transgression. He was crucified, suspended on wood, in order to free us from the deadly taste formerly usurped from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. He who is life died for us upon the cross, so that our death may die within us and we may live in the life which is Christ, death having been swallowed up.

“And was buried.” He who is enclosed by no place was placed in a tomb, in order to draw us out of the narrow prison of our condemnation and raise us into the liberty of the glory of God’s children. He descended to the lower world, due to the guilty and captive, in order to draw his own out from there and to shut it forever, so that those who are his may not descend there: “I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell” (Hosea XIII, 14). Consider, then, that in Christ’s death his soul was separated from his body and his body from his soul, so that there could be death: they were separated from one another. Yet the person of God and man remained inseparable from each, though they were separated. For the person of the Word of God assumed human nature, not a human person. No new person was made when God was united to man; for two persons cannot become one, whereas two natures are properly united in one person. If the person of the Word had assumed a human person, Christ could be proclaimed not one but two. But Christ is one: not confused by a mingling of nature, but perpetually undivided in unity of person. “Everyone,” it says, “who dissolves the Lord Jesus, let him be anathema” (I John IV, 3). Nor was he dissolved in death, who is always one.

[Col. 1325D] The manhood was assumed by the Word of God in time, but the person of God and man remains in eternity. Time does not prejudice eternity; eternity surpasses time. No act is imputed to a nature, but only to a person. Therefore Christ is not a recent God, but from eternity full and perfect. By his eternity he orders all things; by his ordering he creates and governs them. Amid these very good things, wicked Satan and erring man inserted for themselves their own utterly evil evils. Entangled in these evils, Satan remained wretched and ruined. But our Samaritan, moved by compassion, descended by his grace to free the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, who, after inflicting wounds, left him half-dead. He cared for him, for whom he willed to suffer, be crucified, die, and be buried, and whom he freed from hell.

[Col. 1326A] Having thus endured these things in himself for us, he added the work of his magnificence. It follows: “On the third day he rose from the dead.” He suffered from the weakness which he assumed from us for our sake; he rose by the power which he possesses divinely from himself. “I have power,” he says, “to lay down my soul and to take it up again” (John X, 18). He rose on the third day—third, indeed, in time. We may also observe here that when a person is drawn out from the darkness of sins and renewed in baptism by the light of faith, he or she is raised into the day of divine knowledge. From this first day one advances into the second when, by episcopal authority, one is clothed with power from on high and confirmed by sevenfold grace. One ascends to the third [Col. 1326B] when one is freed from all iniquities and all infirmities in the resurrection of Jesus Christ and receives eternal life.

Of this liberation of the human being, liberated in Christ’s resurrection, the Prophet says of Christ: “Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your infirmities” (Ps. CII, 3). First iniquities are forgiven; afterward the infirmities contracted from iniquities are healed—not at any time whatever, but in the blessed resurrection, when the children are absolved from every debt; when we shall be freed from all our evil and also from Satan, evil and in every respect hostile to us; instructed by the Lord’s prayers, filled with the virtues of the Holy Spirit, to be glorified with Christ in Christ’s blessedness through the days of the eternity of the Lord’s rest. He rests not somewhere, but ever in himself, and makes those who share Christ’s resurrection rest with him.

“He rose from the dead”: from those dead under the law of sin and under the debt of death. Christ, the Son of God, who had no sin and paid without obligation death, the wages of sin, utterly destroys death in himself and in all his own, as the mightiest victor and most eminent conqueror. He ascended into heaven, from which he never departs; rather, he descended to us by assuming our humanity, and, having fulfilled the obedience of our salvation, ascended to the confession of the right hand of God the Father. Exalted according to our humanity, he received the name above every name and the name at which every knee bows—the glory which he always possessed. From there [Col. 1326D] he shall come to judge the living and the dead: he who came to be judged for us in humility shall come to judge all in majesty. The living are those found then alive in body; the dead, those previously released from bodily life. Or the living are certain persons alive in good but not yet revealed; the dead are those in evil but still hidden.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” Gather the whole together; hold it all at once. Say: “I believe in God the Father Almighty. I believe in God, Jesus Christ his Son. I believe in God, the Holy Spirit.” Behold: your faith confesses the Trinity when Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are named in your profession. But because you proclaim not gods, but God, as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you devoutly present for our worship the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are called three persons, not distinguished by temporal increase, not separated from one another by spaces of place, but inseparably abiding in one and the same majesty of God and Lord. It did not happen to God that he became Father; it was not added to the Word that he should be Son; the Holy Spirit did not assume it so as to proceed as one from both. Rather, without movement of time, without a limit of dimension, without any change of alternation—having no beginning and lacking no end—this is the true confession: God is Father, and Father is God. God is Son, and Son is God. God is Holy Spirit, and Holy Spirit is God. In this blessed and immutable truth neither does the Trinity divide the unity nor does the unity drive away the Trinity.

[Col. 1327B] You should know that the Lord God revealed this ineffable mystery of the Catholic faith to the human being made in the image and likeness of God. Hence he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI, 27). This revelation is from the Holy Spirit. Wisdom bestows this Holy Spirit, whose delights are to be with the children of men. Someone once dared to say: “I do not grant this proposition: ‘God is Father; God is Son; God is Holy Spirit.’ I reject this,” he said, “but I accept this: ‘Father is God; Son is God; Holy Spirit is God.’” He places *God* in the predicate and does not wish *God* to be placed in the subject. This man, made foolish by his predicamental construction and by the manner of the divisions of our secular teaching, [Col. 1327C] does not know that God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and conversely that Father and Son and Holy Spirit is always God. This truth is not subject to human reason, nor can temporal understanding see divine things; for they are not circumscribed for it, and hence cannot be defined or delimited. Names, verbs, and every sort of word invented by human beings cannot set forth for you these incomprehensible realities as they are.

God, indeed, if you speak after our manner, signifies substance with quality; likewise Father, Son, and Holy Spirit according to our customary usage. Propositions framed in this way are foreign to divine signification. For God is not substance with quality; he does not speak or act anything in himself through action or passion. There is nothing discordant there, [Col. 1327D] nothing variable. Therefore the Catholic faith holds firmly that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit do not signify an accidental difference or contingent property. God cannot fail to be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot fail to be God. We say these things because we wholly deny that there are many gods. For if there were many, they would certainly differ; if they differed, one would have more or less than another, and thus they would remain imperfect and insufficient. Therefore, even against the rules of philosophical disputation, when we speak of God we infer this: if there are many, there is none. God himself is simple and is essentially perfect gift. Nothing from the predicate is transferred back into the subject; nothing in the subject increases in [Col. 1328A] the predicate. The divine essence is not susceptible of contraries. Nothing there resembles our categories.

Finally, let us return to the apostolic creed of faith. There faith proposes for our continual consideration the effect of so great a confession: faith in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This undivided confession of the Trinity, which is God, builds within us the holy Catholic Church. Within this Catholic Church we receive and love the communion of saints. In her we receive forgiveness of sins. From forgiveness of sins we hope, with the saints, for the resurrection of our flesh unto eternal life, blessed without end. Amen. By God’s favor we have received the Catholic faith. From faith let us turn to the Lord’s Prayer. From prayer let us receive sevenfold grace; from grace [Col. 1328B] let us rise to fulfill the beatitudes on the day of eternity, in the presence of the supreme Trinity, which is God, who knows, can do, and possesses all things.

“I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88:2). The prophetic Psalmist looked upon us miserable human beings, and looked down from above upon the merciful God. He sees mercies and gives thanks. He rejoices and sings—he who formerly grieved and wept. He perceived attentively that all of us who are born amid the motion of temporal things, amid the fall of changeable things, are swept away in a temporal whirlpool and enclosed in the abyss of mutability. Entangled in these things, we lose everything that we gather, and gather it only to lose it. While we anxiously endure these things, we are shaken by a deeper grief, because we justly bear burdens so heavy and unbearable through a debt owed: both for our original sins and for voluntary and actual sins; for those inherited by descent and those completed in deed; from the offense of propagation and from the excess of crime. These two kinds—original and actual—make us guilty, consign us to condemnation, and subject us to death.

But, alas, neither by our own strength nor by our own resources can our guilt be wiped away or our punishment removed. While we suffer these things, we very often ask sorrowfully: “From where do these evils of ours arise?” The supreme and only God created every individual thing, all things, omnipotently; and in his goodness he created them good, among which no evils were created, nor are there any outside them. Therefore the things that we call evils are nothing. Yet this wickedness by which we are called wicked—which we call evil not by positing it, but by removing something—is so called not because it exists, but because good is absent. Therefore evil is nothing, because it was not created by God, the Creator of all things.

You do not find what evil is; yet, strangely, contrary to every apprehension of reason, you frequently find it in the rational mind of angel and human being. Apart from them, you can find evil nowhere and never. What, then, is it? Know, by subtle inquiry, that this is called evil because of a failure of good, or a privation of charity. Both human being and angel ought to have had charity toward God, so that each might devoutly know, follow, and love him by whom he was made good; and, by the merit of love, humbly raising himself above himself and transcending all things by free choice, might behold with the eye of charity the invisible, supreme, and omnipotent God [Col. 1329A], and thus, stripped of all mutability, remain blessed without end from him, through him, and in him.

Concerning this great and surpassing good, that theologian spoke when he said: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 1:2). From this vision, so holy and so exalted, that ancient Satan immediately fell away; he never even began to do any good. “He,” says the Lord, “was a liar from the beginning” (John 8:44): a liar from the beginning, not of his created condition, since the good Creator made him good, as he made all other things; but from the beginning of his own lie, by which he immediately fell when he said: “I will place my seat in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

“I will place my seat” is the exaltation of pride. “In the north” is the presumption of usurpation. “I will be like the Most High” [Col. 1329B] is the monstrous act of idolatry. Satan, puffed up and greedily pre-empting, set his mouth in heaven, falsely exalting himself as God. In pride he preferred not the Lord to himself, but himself to the Lord. By his lie he wished to establish for himself a seat in the north; he presumed to occupy what he had not created; weak and foolish, he undertook to make himself God when he was not God. On the contrary, the Lord says: “I am God, and there is no other; apart from me there is none besides” (Gen. 41:13).

Therefore Satan—the origin of schism, the fountain of avarice, the pit of heresy—standing against free choice, which he ought to have possessed but in fact never possessed, rightly fell, shattered by his own lie; and with his followers he was utterly excluded from the assembly of the blessed. [Col. 1329C] This falling away from God, this withdrawal from the choice of due charity, this fall from natural understanding: it is evil for him—execrable evil, inexpiable evil, Satan’s own evil. Thus the Lord says of him in the Gospel: “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things; for he is a liar and the father of it” (John 8:44)—that is, of the lie which he invented. Behold Satan’s evil, by which he fell.

Now see at last the evil of the human being, by which he withdrew from God. Adam, the first and greatest author of our transgression, was likewise distinguished by rational understanding. By the powers of free choice which God bestowed on him, he ought always to have blessed and loved the giver of such great gifts. But, ungrateful for benefits, he withdrew transgressively from the tree of life, which God had granted him to eat from, and disobediently approached the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which God had forbidden him to eat, listening falsely: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5).

When God’s command had been transgressed, those first man and woman, both called Adam, fell. They had wrongly desired the likeness of gods, and deserved to become like beasts; becoming animal-like, they were clothed in animal skins. Those who had been made in God’s image lost God’s likeness; they were expelled from the place of delight and fell into places of sorrow, into the valley of misery. Behold the evil of the human being who withdrew from God, who fell away from charity, who darkened the freedom of rational choice and, bound by his own desires, remained miserable and needy in the hand of Satan, whom he wickedly believed. [Col. 1330A]

Behold the fall of the human being; behold the ruin of the human race; behold the destruction of all flesh. But divine compassion looked upon this miserable person with its incomprehensible and ineffable goodness. Although he was a sinner, he did not invent sin, but received it ruinously from its inventor, namely Satan. To rescue him mercifully from Satan’s hand, the Son of God was sent by God the Father—co-omnipotent and co-eternal with the Father—and descended humbly against pride. Though God, he willed to become human: remaining what he had been, he assumed humanity, while both essences, divine and human, remained in the unity of his person. He clothed himself in mercy and compassion; he bore our sins in his body; he destroyed Satan’s kingdom within us; and, overthrowing the kingdom of pride, Wisdom, who is Christ, built within us the kingdom of humility by virtues bestowed from above.

Strengthened by this, the Prophet sang in the Holy Spirit: “I will sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88:2). Now, therefore, in Christ’s kingdom human beings are reborn in the Holy Spirit and are made new; they are clothed with power from on high and are holy.
