This kingdom does not consist in earthly possessions, deceitful and perishable, but in the virtues of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, eternal and blessed. The Apostle’s declaration stands firm, crying: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:10). There are indeed seven charisms of the Holy Spirit, within which are all good things; outside them there are absolutely no things but evils. Therefore these charisms [Col. 1330C] must be sought and obtained through prayers to Jesus Christ: “I,” he says, “will send the Spirit of my Father upon you. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:13).

That Spirit of truth Satan, the liar from the beginning, did not receive; Adam, our first parent, lost him by transgression. But in the humble, peaceful, spiritual kingdom—in the Catholic Church, from which the prince has been violently cast out—the wondrous gifts of the sevenfold Holy Spirit are given. To obtain these, Jesus Christ instituted for you seven petitions: that gifts may be obtained through petitions; that through the gifts the seven beatitudes may be acquired; and that they may be possessed everlastingly within the seven days of the divine vision.

1. “Thus,” he says, “you shall pray: Our Father,” etc. Those reborn in baptism, sanctified in the Holy Spirit—holy children of God praying with Christ—say these petitions, are heard, and receive gifts. The Son of God commanded that these petitions be spoken to the Father: that the children may be sanctified by his name; that his kingdom may come in those who are sanctified; that his will may be done in his kingdom by obedient children; that daily bread of life may be given to those obedient to his will; that debts may be forgiven to children of the highest Father who share his table, though they still live amid ignorance and weakness. “We know,” he says, “that in many things we all offend” (Jas. 3:2); and, once these are forgiven, that they may not be led into temptations, by which even the saints are afflicted in the present life. Thus they rightly pray to be delivered from evil as quickly as possible.

But why are these words, or any others, spoken to him who knows all things? He indeed knows all that is necessary to us, and he cares for us. “If you,” he says, “though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:16). Let us therefore ask, and hear the Father saying to us: “Ask and you shall receive; seek and you shall find; knock and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened” (ibid., 9).

Therefore the words which we say to the Father are useful to us, who are weighed down by weakness and delayed by ignorance while we live in the present under mutability. By holy words we are taught, stirred to ask, and receive gifts from the Almighty in prayer. Therefore let us say confidently: “Our Father.” Those who are not children cannot say this. The humble child who faithfully prays to God as his Father most certainly hopes that he will obtain all things.

“Our Father,” he says. He rightly adds “our,” being drawn by charity and rejoicing that children approach the goodness of so great a Father from every quarter. Thus the Son, essentially begotten in the Father’s bosom, did not wish to be alone, but descended humbly and willed that all humble people should become children of the highest Father. “To all who received him,” he says, “he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

2. “Our Father, who art in heaven.” Why is he said to be “in heaven,” when the same omnipotent and glorious God subsists everywhere? The Apostle says: “From him and through him and in him are all things.” Observe that, although God is everywhere, he is not known everywhere. And even where he is acknowledged, he is not loved by everyone. But in heaven, where people live happily with God, where no evil at all is found, where charity alone rejoices with charity, there God especially is: God is acknowledged and God is loved.

3. “Hallowed be thy name.” Nothing is holier or more blessed than the name of the highest Father. Its sanctification neither begins nor ends; it cannot be increased or diminished. The sanctification of the Father’s name is rather seen in his children. On the golden plate was written the sacred name *Tetragrammaton*, “holy to the Lord.” Aaron bore it on his forehead and thus appeared sanctified before the children of Israel. There the sanctification of children was prefigured, which, brought forth in us through the Holy Spirit, was displayed. [Col. 1331D]

On the other hand, children who preserve no likeness of their father either in life or in conduct do not sanctify their father’s name in themselves. Becoming unlike him, they fall away from so great a name and are justly deprived of the inheritance of children. “Because,” he says, “you did not sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I promised to your fathers” (Deut. 32:51). Then children who sanctify their Father’s name in themselves humbly say to him:

4. “Thy kingdom come.” Concerning this the Prophet says: “Thy kingdom, O Lord, is a kingdom of all ages” (Ps. 144:13). His kingdom remains indissoluble; it endures unmoved and stable. See, then, that although charity already makes the kingdom of God in the present Church—whence he says, “the kingdom of God is within you”—in very many of us it fails, and our iniquity very often resists the Holy Spirit. On the contrary, the humble child asks and prays that God’s kingdom may come, be strengthened, and advance in himself and in any weak children. Christ builds God’s kingdom not by bodily increase but by the growth of virtues. Humility guards this kingdom lest pride be able to enter. Thus it fittingly follows:

5. “Thy will be done.” What does he ask? Is he not the one who “has done whatever he willed”? Certainly no one can resist his will. Yet we must understand that he asks for it to be done in us—in our voluntary dispositions, namely in thoughts, words, and deeds alike—so that we may seek what he commands us and keep what he orders to be done. “As in heaven, so on earth.” The Psalmist says: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Ps. 113:16). In that heaven of heavens they both acknowledge and love the Lord. He earnestly desires the same to take place on earth: that here we may acknowledge him and, having acknowledged him, love him.

See that these three things set forth before us—name, kingdom, will—make known to us the supreme Trinity. The Father’s name is rightly first named and adored, whose fatherhood is named in heaven and on earth. The Father’s kingdom is the Son, who destroyed within us the kingdom of the ancient devil and made us new through the newness of the Holy Spirit: a kingdom not of this earthly mutability and perishing instability, but a kingdom planted with virtues and abiding in heavenly things. “My kingdom,” the Lord says to Pilate, “is not of this world” (John 18:36). Of those whom the Lord made his kingdom the apostle Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Pet. 2:9).

Therefore these people are the kingdom of the highest Father in Christ, and Christ is in them. Of this new king, the founder of the new kingdom, the patriarch foretold: “He who is to be sent will come, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Gen. 47:10). Those hoping in him will be his kingdom. Let us continue what we began. The will of God the Father and Son is the Holy Spirit [Col. 1332D], who is supreme charity, by whom God willed all things to be made, and they were made. God saw the things he made so that they should remain, and they are good: good indeed by reason of their author, their nature, and their condition, although some are called evil through deficiency of good, abuse of free choice, and privation of charity.

Leaving these things aside, faithful soul, always venerate and adore the ineffable *Tetragrammaton*, the Father’s name, “holy to the Lord,” prefigured on the forehead of the high priest. Adore the omnipotence of the kingdom, in which are enrolled children who shall reign for ever. Adore the unity of will, by which the Father’s name and the Son’s kingdom endure in indissoluble stability. “I,” says the Son, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30): one, because the Holy Spirit is always essentially one Spirit of Father and Son. The truly supreme Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is not three gods but one, singularly to be adored: not divided because of Trinity, but united because of unity; not extended through intervals of time, not dispersed through division of places, not separated by distinctions of rank. It reigns and rules through infinite ages of ages.

6. Having adored the Lord, let us now consider what follows and seek for ourselves those things necessary in the present: “Give us this day our daily bread.” What is this bread? The Lord says: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6:31); and: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 5:52). For the one who lives by this bread, all good things arise. Faith of the children dares, he says, to call this bread “our daily bread”; the evangelist Matthew calls it “substantial.” Beyond the nature of our earthly bread, the daily and supersubstantial bread is living and heavenly. For when our bread is eaten, it is itself consumed. But that supersubstantial and daily bread is continually eaten and is not consumed; it remains wholly and entirely living and true. It is wholly in the mouth of each person fed by it; they receive it whole, and it is not diminished.

“Give us.” It is ours, but not from us. We cannot have it unless he gives it; we shall not retain what has been given unless he preserves it. “Give us this day”: by continual bestowal. Hear the one who asks: “Lord, always give us this bread.” This bread is given to children, and they are made alive. By it they live and are made divine. We truly possess it already through faith; afterward we shall be made alive not in an enigma but by sight. We already eat it in the present and are conformed to him who is life; and in the future, with angels and all saints, we shall enjoy—not the fruit of the tree of life in the earthly paradise, but life itself, through which all things subsist, in the heavenly paradise.

7. Meanwhile, that we may eat the supersubstantial bread more peacefully, we beg the Father: “Forgive us our debts,” we who feed from the Lord’s table, lest, bound by debts, we be hindered from the delight of so great a banquet; “as we forgive our debtors.” Whoever desires to be free from liability should make his debtors free, as he would himself be.

8. “And lead us not into temptation.” It seems that he should more properly have said: “Defend us, lest we be led into temptation.” For God draws no one to evil and tempts no one so as to lead him into evil. He is the one who wills to save all human beings. Rather, we are tempted by our own wickedness and drawn to evil. Yet, if perhaps you consider it, he rightly asks: “Do not lead us.” For no devil or human being is able to do any evil unless the Lord brings it about. Apart from God, evil persons always intend to do evil; but without God, who continually works good through their evils, they cannot act.

Concerning this, the prophet says: “There is no evil in the city which the Lord has not done” (Amos 3:6). “The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. 10:1). And the Lord himself says to Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up” (Rom. 9:17). Likewise, the prophet replied concerning the one who cursed him: “The Lord commanded him to curse David” (2 Kings 16:10). The same prophet also says to the Lord: “With the holy you will be holy; with the innocent man you will be innocent; with the chosen you will be chosen; and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17:26).

The Lord becomes perverse whenever he cooperates with evil people. The Lord becomes perverse when he speaks thus to Satan concerning Job: “But you moved me to afflict him without cause” (Job 2:3). And, handing him over into Satan’s hand, he added: “Behold, he is in your hand; only preserve his life” (Job 2:6). Finally, a lying spirit is sent by God so that King Ahab may be deceived. “You shall deceive,” says the Lord, “and you shall prevail. Go out and do so” (3 Kings 29:22). And to his betrayer: “What you are doing,” he says, “do quickly” (John 13:27).

By the decree of supreme justice, though hidden from us, the Lord leads wicked people to do evil deeds, deeds which no one could ever have done in others unless the Lord had led him to do so. Behold how greatly the powerlessness of the wicked falls short: they are unable to do even those evils which are theirs until they receive from the Lord the power to perform them.

9. “Do not lead us into temptation.” Here one must be greatly afraid and say in humble supplication: “Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1:3), you who console and never cease to show mercy, do not, because our sins demand it, become justly perverse with us, who are wickedly perverse, against us. If you see that we are to be brought into temptation, grant repentance, change the judgment, and grant progress amid temptation. Do not cast us away, but hear your suppliant children; hear guilty persons who repent; have mercy on us. Deliver us from evil—both our own evil and evil Satan, the evil inventor of evils and the worst instigator of every evil.

10. Having heard from the Lord the seven petitions, let us also hear the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which ought to be merited through the seven petitions. He who taught the seven petitions likewise set before us the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, to be sought and found in himself, as Isaiah testifies when he says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11:1–3).

Behold gifts found in him, to be sought from him, and received through the Father’s generosity. The seven gifts are the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit. You hear that he is sevenfold, lest you suppose him to be multiple. “There are divisions of graces,” he says, “but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4). We adore the Holy Spirit, essentially one with Father and Son; yet through gratuitous generosity he pours out on us the seven gifts of charisms. The Holy Spirit is sought in prayers through his own inspiration, received in gifts, and known in their effect.

Therefore, as the Lord commands, let us humbly offer the aforesaid petitions, that we may receive gifts of charisms from the supreme giver, the most merciful Father. Let us pray, then, that God’s name may be sanctified in us; once sanctified by it, we shall receive within ourselves the spirit of wisdom, by which, made wise, we shall acknowledge the Father as essentially wise, adore him as omnipotent, and love him as the giver of all things to his children. Therefore let us supplicantly seek that the kingdom of the omnipotent Father, who gives all things, may come within us. There is given the spirit of understanding, by which we believe in the present that the children reign in the Father and the Father in the children; in the future we shall see it. “Your life,” he says, “is now hidden with Christ in God; but when Christ, your life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3).

To attain this, we ask that the Father’s will may be done in us, and we receive the spirit of counsel from the Father. For we, adopted as sons and supplicants, heard the chief counsel from the Father’s only-begotten Son: “I came not,” he says, “to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 5:30). Satan did not wish to follow God’s will, but held to his own; therefore he lost the dignity of heavenly glory, because he never received the spirit of counsel. Likewise our first parents lost the tree of life because they did not retain the spirit of counsel.

Accordingly, children who keep their Father’s will pray that daily and supersubstantial bread, bread which came down from heaven, may be given to them. In order to eat it, they must possess the spirit of fortitude, lest Satan be able to take away from them in the present time the living bread—he who long ago separated our first parents from the tree of life, and who also separated Christ’s disciples from the Lord’s food. For when the Lord said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you” (John 6:53), some said: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (ibid., 60). And many, blinded by the spirit of wickedness, went back and no longer walked with Jesus.

But to those remaining he said: “Do you also wish to go away?” Yet Peter, clothed in the spirit of fortitude, said: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (ibid., 68). Therefore this food must be received in the spirit of fortitude, which the person did not have who, called to this supper, excused himself: the one who proudly bought a farm, the one who greedily intended to test five yokes of oxen, and the one who took a wife, serving the enticements of the flesh. When these have been excluded, those strong guests become children of the highest Father.

11. But because, while we live in the present, we are weak and ignorant in many things, we must pray that our debts be forgiven, while flesh resists spirit and spirit flesh. For this purpose the spirit of knowledge is given to us by the Father, the giver of all good things, so that we may know how to forgive as we ask that we be forgiven. “Forgive,” he says, “and you shall be forgiven”; and: “If you do not forgive, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you” (Matt. 6:15).

For this reason we have recourse to the Father, supplicating him not to lead us into temptation but to provide the Holy Spirit of piety. Here we must understand piety not as mercy indiscriminately lavished upon anyone whatever, but as the constant service, uniquely owed, of divine obedience. “Whoever cleaves to God,” he says, “is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17). Therefore one who continually directs himself toward God in the spirit of piety cannot be cast down by temptation. “Pray,” he says, “that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41), from which no one escapes unless he preserves piety with the Lord.

The ancient tempter, as the Lord testifies, sought the apostles in order to sift them—that is, by temptation—and they were tempted, so that, abandoning the Lord, they fled. Peter not only fled but also denied him; Judas, however, becoming a traitor and a most wicked thief, was swallowed up wholly after falling from the apostolate. Therefore let no one presume; let no one trust in himself. “Let the one who stands take heed lest he fall”; rather, let him beseech the Lord in the spirit of fear and say: “Deliver us from evil.”

No human being can be altogether delivered unless he remains in the spirit of the fear of the Lord and is protected by the blood of the paschal Lamb, when the angel struck all the firstborn of Egypt. Under this fear of the Spirit of the Lord, having eaten the flesh of the paschal lamb with unleavened bread and lettuces, Israel crossed the depths of the Red Sea, passed through the vast wilderness, received the Lord’s commandments, overcame enemies, entered to possess the land of promise, excelling in good things, and everywhere proved victorious, so long as it served under the fear of the Lord.

This fear is not fear of sin but fear of the Lord; not the fear which charity casts out, but that which charity raises up. It is filial fear, which always fears to offend God the Father and always seeks to avoid sin. This fear is the beginning of wisdom; it is the fear that endures for ages of ages. It remains in the Lord Jesus and in all children of the Catholic Church. “He shall fill him,” he says, “with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11:3). He himself, God from God and one with God the Father, gives and infuses the spirit of fear as he does the other charisms. Having become human with us, he received them: like us by reason of the condition of our nature; unlike us by reason of the freedom of his righteousness.

For him the one formerly cried out in longing: “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise with him” (Isa. 45:8). We miserable people are born with sins; he was born without sin and bore our sins, not his own, because he had none. He arose with righteousness because he was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. “I,” says the Lord, “created him without the concupiscence of flesh, from virginal integrity.” For “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

12. This one was made in the image and likeness of God according to his humanity: perfect God and perfect human; not two, but one in unity of person, given for our redemption. In him flesh did not resist spirit, nor spirit flesh; but he is always holy and sanctifying. He redeemed us from sins and bestowed grace upon those redeemed. He instructed us by seven petitions; he enriched us with seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; he prepared for us the glory of seven beatitudes, to be received in the full days of God’s vision, made perfect in the eternity of likeness to the blessed Trinity. This Trinity is wholly known by the eye of charity in each individual, and one in all is adored.

Therefore, we who have learned the petitions through his teaching and received the gifts through his generosity, let us seek the beatitudes which he prepares for us and long for the days of God’s vision: “One day,” he says, “in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). The Lord’s day in the courts of the present Church is better than other days; but the Lord’s day in the eternity of blessedness abounds with unfailing goods. He himself set before us the beatitudes in the Gospel, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, because they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, because they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, because they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, because they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, because they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:3, 9).

13. Having heard these things from the Lord’s mouth, we must weigh and devoutly consider again the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, the seven beatitudes added above, and the days of the Lord made splendid by the Sun of righteousness. For we know that faith is active in the petitions, certain hope is raised up in the gifts, charity glories in the beatitudes, and the holy Trinity works all things in all in the days of the Lord. Those children who attend to these four things are overcome by no whirlwind of temptations. For they drive back their enemies through prayers, crush them with the weapons of charisms, transcend them by the beatitudes, and rest in enduring joy in the days of the Lord.

Happy is this progress, which climbs from the humility of petitions to the honor of gifts, is to be raised to the glory of beatitudes, and will abide within the days of eternal happiness in the presence of the divine majesty. In these things our wondrous leader is recognized—he who is named, adored, and loved as the Way, Truth, and Life; who holds the days of eternity at the right hand of God the Father. He himself is for us the Way in the petitions, Truth in the gifts, Life in the beatitudes, and glory in the seven enduring days.

Of him the Psalmist says: “Know that the Lord has made his holy one wondrous; the Lord will hear me when I cry to him” (Ps. 4:4). He himself says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). He draws them when he sanctifies the Father’s name in us, infuses the spirit of wisdom into us, and makes us peacemakers and blessed, because we shall be called children of God in the days of the eternal vision of God.

He likewise who draws all things to himself establishes his kingdom in you who are sanctified by the Father’s name, and infuses the spirit of understanding, by which he makes the pure in heart blessed through the vision of God within the days of divine contemplation. In those in whom he builds the kingdom, he also commands the Father’s will to be kept and adorns them with the spirit of counsel, so that, made merciful, they may remain blessed for mercy in the brightness of the Lord’s days. For those who keep the Father’s will, he prepares bread in return for merciful holy works and strengthens them with the spirit of fortitude, so that, hungering for righteousness, he may finally make them blessed in complete satisfaction and bring them to the days of eternal refreshment.

Those released from debts, as they themselves have forgiven their debtors, he will, through the spirit of knowledge, make blessed, comforted from every sorrow in the eternal joy of the Lord’s days. [Col. 1338A] So that they may not be led into temptation, he provides help to his falling children and grants advancement in temptation, saying to them: “Take courage, because I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). In the spirit of piety he makes them meek, so that he may enroll them as blessed possessors in the land of eternal blessedness, in the days of the fullness of God’s peace. Finally, this wondrous one delivers his children from evil, led forth under the spirit of fear, and makes them blessed, giving them, in exchange for the poverty of the present, the kingdom of heaven through the ages of eternal days.

14. Recognize, therefore, that the petitions of prayers and the merits of spiritual gifts obtain the rewards of beatitude and the glory of days without end. But because persecutions, hatreds, curses, and similar things pursue all good people living in the present life, he rightly added after the seven preceding beatitudes: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” etc. (Matt. 5:10). The Apostle says: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12).

For the flesh which we derive from Adam moves desire against the spirit; the desire of the eyes suggests vain glory; worldly ambition brings avarice. Ancient Satan pours out clouds of errors in order to obstruct the path of the elect; the cruel hand of rulers very often afflicts those who live devoutly with torments. But such people hear him who says: “Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you may follow in his footsteps—he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his life” (1 Pet. 2:21).

The Apostle strengthens those who suffer in Christ. “If,” he says, “we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12). And lest anyone despair in tribulations, the Apostle cries out: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us” (Rom. 5:3–5).

15. But neither should we pass over the fact that we must humbly consider how Jesus Christ, descending from the throne of majesty, sought us wretched and lowly people, and bestowed upon us the seven remedies of prayer, which he set forth as seven steps from his own height down to our lowest condition [Col. 1338D]. For, beginning with the hallowing of the name of the supreme Father and descending in sevenfold order as far as the evil of our confusion, from which he delivers us, he proceeds. Likewise, in a corresponding pattern, he has deigned to impart to us seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, sevenfold from the first to the last: he arranged seven charisms, from the Spirit of wisdom to the spirit of the fear of the Lord. But the beatitudes which he prepares for the future he orders from the lowest to the highest, just as he mercifully raises us from our low estate to his divine and blessed heights: he who, remaining God essentially, willed to become man, adopted human beings to himself through grace, and by gratuitous participation makes them gods.

Those deified by grace will no longer understand the invisible things of God through the things which he created, through the things which he made [Col. 1339A], but in the Creator himself they will know all things stable and immovable, as in the art itself. “What was made in him was life” (John 1:4). There the immutable principles of all mutable things are known, and the causes of mutable things persist immutably. The counsel of the Almighty remains unmoved over all things that flow and pass away in many ways, over good and evil alike; for God works through both good and evil people: through the good, for the good, unto good; through the wicked, for the wicked, unto evil. Wisdom indeed plays upon the circle of the earth; the saints see and love her, and, loving her, remain blessed on the day of the Lord, which is eternally clear and manifest. “On that day,” he says, “you shall know that I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:20).

This is that seventh day on which God’s rest from all his work is commended [Col. 1339B]. From Moses’ narrative we have learned that God the Creator made, formed, and completed all his works in six days: he made them together, formed them distinctly, completed them perfectly. Together in respect of substance; distinctly in respect of form; perfectly in respect of nature. We say these things successively in relation to time, because we understand that God, without time, brought them forth together in the beginning. Moses wrote concerning these matters and handed them down to us:

16. “And the Lord said: Let there be light; and there was light” (Gen. 1:3). And he continues in the same sixfold narrative concerning all the rest, to which we carefully relate and apply the things that we have said are to be brought about in God’s Church. He says: Let us assign prayers, gifts, and beatitudes to the primary days. Let us see, then, that God said: “Let there be light” [Col. 1339C]. This word remains eternal in the divine mind. “And there was light”: it was indeed made when it received its own being together with its own proper character. “And God saw the light, that it was good.” Behold the regard of divine mercy toward what had been created. “And God divided the light from the darkness” (ibid., 4), when rational intelligence, set aflame by love of the true light, did not consent to the fall of the proud, who remained as a dark night. “And darkness,” he says, “was upon the face of the deep” (ibid., 2). But that which stood with God in perfect charity deserved to be formed into day and called day, and lives perpetually blessed with God.

Those who are sanctified under the name of the Father are confirmed in this light, and they are seen to be good light, because they are illumined by the Spirit of wisdom; and they are separated from the fugitives who do not hallow the Father’s name in themselves—dark and blind people [Col. 1339D]—being peaceful and blessed, because, made children, they are day in the glory of the supreme Father.

17. We read also in Moses: “And the Lord said: Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters” (Gen. 1:6). This word stands perpetually in the divine mind; it remains unmoved. “And the Lord made the firmament” (ibid., 7). What he had disposed proceeded into actuality. “And God called the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1:8). Consider the firmament, because it signifies the kingdom whose coming the children ask for. This kingdom is called a firmament, rightly fortified by the Spirit of understanding; the pure in heart keep it, being blessed in seeing God, and divide waters from waters: namely, the waters that are above the heavens, which praise the name of the Lord, from the waters beneath the firmament of heaven [Col. 1340A], which are compressed and called seas because of the bitterness of unbelief and the flood of iniquities.

And the firmament, heaven, is blessed, because the kingdom of Christ, in the hand of the supreme Father, raised above earthly and mutable things by the power of the Holy Spirit, has become heaven. Of this heaven the Lord says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2): many, on account of different merits joined together by the unity of charity. This house is the kingdom of the supreme Father, the kingdom of life and peace. On the second day: “second,” not under the description of time, but under the grace of repeated contemplation.

18. And God said: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear” (Gen. 1:9). And subsequently he says: “Let the earth bring forth green grass bearing seed, and a fruit-bearing tree bearing fruit” (ibid., 11) [Col. 1340B]. These things were spoken in eternity; “and it was so”: they appeared as made things in time. This earth is Mother Church. God founded her upon the seas; he established her upon the rivers—upon the seas, that is, upon the unstable things that change; upon the rivers of attacking evils.

Among these, the children, since they cannot extricate themselves by their own strength, ask that the Father’s will may be done in themselves. Therefore the Spirit of counsel is given them; and they become merciful toward others, since they desire mercy to be granted to themselves by the Father, so that they may put forth seed-bearing herbs, growing in the fruits of good works, and fruit-bearing trees, producing fruit through the advance of virtues. Without the Father’s will, the Son’s help [Col. 1340C], and the counsel of the Holy Spirit, these cannot grow or multiply in the present Church.

Under the protection of the supreme Trinity the children do these things: hallowing the Father’s name, building his kingdom, pursuing his will, and, in freedom of will, faith, hope, and charity, presenting in themselves knowledge of the Trinity. Distinguished by the fruits of mercy, they shall remain blessed on the third day: “third,” not bound under time, but most excellent in the presence of the Trinity, who is God.

19. But God said: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven, to divide day and night; and let them be for signs and seasons, and days and years; and let them shine and give light upon the earth” (Gen. 1:14–15). These things, and all whatsoever has been made, remain in the divine mind before they come to be [Col. 1340D]. “And it was so.” They come forth, manifested with times and places. See the world arranged under the consideration of three days: one for the primordial light formed into day; two for heaven and earth, fitted and established. Then the world is adorned by the following three days: first heaven with sun, moon, and stars; then the waters with their fish and birds, together with every creeping aquatic creature; lastly the earth with its animals and all its moving things, with man pre-eminent among the things made.

Let us therefore consider the adornment of heaven: its lights illuminating the world and moving in their appointed course; signs governing temporal things, not by fatal necessity but by contingent service. The children see that life is not in these varieties. Therefore they ask the supreme Father [Col. 1341A] for bread from heaven which gives life to the world. For this they receive the Spirit of fortitude, by which they hunger for righteousness, which, against—as they say—the falsehoods of fate and against every opposing force, grants victory. These stand in the Church performing signs, namely powers and miracles. For they are the true lights of heaven. Satisfied in eternal life with full and perfect righteousness, they shall be blessed with the brightness of the heavenly lights amid the splendours of the saints. On the fourth day: “fourth,” not placed under time, but shining with the everlasting splendour of virtues, and among us repeated four times in the order of contemplation.

20. And God said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping creature having life upon the earth, under the firmament of heaven” (Gen. 1:20). Here also the Creator’s power, foreseeing all things, is considered. “And the waters brought forth,” etc. As they had been foreseen, so they appeared when manifested [Col. 1341B]. Knowing these things, the children, still dwelling amid the waters of this fluctuating life, recognize that they cannot advance altogether without offence. Therefore they pray that their debts may be forgiven them; and as though by a debt due in justice, because they forgive others. Hence they say, “as we forgive our debtors.” Because this is forgiven them, by reason of the added condition they receive the Spirit of knowledge, so that what they ask to be done for themselves, they may do for others.

This is done by those who desire to be released from debts: both those who remain amid the waves of worldly life, living in pious conduct and holy works so that they may not be swallowed up; and also those who, raised above the waters on the wings of virtues, having left all things behind, live in heavenly things. Of this sort is the Apostle when he says: “Our conversation is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20) [Col. 1341C]. In manner of life he dwelt on earth; in the desire of charity he lived in heaven. Both at last, having emerged from the waters of malice and iniquity in this temporal mode of life, escape the mourning of worldly remembrance, blessed on the day of eternal consolation, which here we call the fifth. “Fifth” on account of the number of repetition, without variation of blessedness.

21. God also said: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature,” etc. (Gen. 1:14). He added: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (ibid., 26). Observe that these things, and each particular thing, were foreseen, spoken, and predestined by the word of eternity, fixed by immutable stability; but when they were made, they were consigned to temporal operation [Col. 1341D], distinguished locally, separated among themselves by intervals of time, and ordered in spaces of place. God made man more excellent than the rest. And he said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” See and consider that here God did not say, “Let there be,” but “Let us make”; and “our image,” so that his image and likeness might be expressed.

Concerning the other things which the waters brought forth and which the earth brought forth, because they lack reason, he did not say “Let there be,” nor “Let us make”; but he said: “Let the waters be gathered,” “let the dry land appear,” “let the waters bring forth,” “let the earth bring forth the living creature,” etc. Even when instituting together the primordial light and heaven, he said only, “Let there be,” not “Let us make” [Col. 1342A]. But when he was to make man, he chose to say not “Let there be,” but “Let us make,” because he signified that the mystery of the Trinity was to be revealed to the rational creature, not to the irrational.

The waters brought forth and the earth brought forth a living creature endowed with the powers of animal activity but lacking rational intelligence, seeking earthly things only, not divine things. But Scripture has made known to us that God, when he made the human being rational and established him to know the ineffable Trinity of his majesty, used a plural expression in making him, saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” so that, because of the image in which he was made and the likeness which he ought to keep intact from him from whom he is, he may love the creating Trinity and show, not only by faith but also by the insight [Col. 1342B] of reason, that it is present in all things.

On this matter we treated explicitly in the seventh book of our *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 1341] You have these books of *Dialogues* in the fifth volume of our *Anecdota*.], which we sent to the venerable Matthew, bishop of Albano. Therefore the children, conformed to the image and likeness of God as the first Adam was, pray the Father that they may not be led into temptation, like him who fell when tempted and deserved to be deprived of God’s likeness. They pray and receive the Spirit of piety, by which, made gentle and humble, they escape the snares of temptation—snares which no one escapes unless he is devout toward God, gentle, and humble. For everyone devout and gentle before God shall possess the land of blessedness. On the sixth day: “sixth,” indeed, flowing with respect to time, but tranquil by reason of the perfection of six.

For the number six is perfect and complete [Col. 1342C], neither deficient nor superfluous. When its aliquot parts—which may be named within six—are gathered together, they restore the perfection of the six of which they are parts. For the parts by which six itself may be measured are these: one, two, three, distributed with the works of the six days: one with the primordial light created and formed; two, by which the world was made—namely heaven and earth; three, for the adornment of the world: first heaven, second the waters, third the earth. Look at the triangle: three, two, one. Gather them into one and you complete six. For God completed all his works, the ratio of six remaining in him fixed and everlasting; whence we know that none of his works can fail to be perfect. It follows:

[Col. 1342D] 22. “And God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished; and he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work” (Gen. 2:2–3). The children aspire to this rest of the Lord, sought not outside himself and received from no other source; that they may attain it, they pray to be delivered from evil—that is, they pray for the Spirit of the fear of the Lord, which remains for ever and ever. Having received this, they become poor in spirit; and thus, having cast aside all things, they are blessed, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven, as they see the Lord at rest.

They see him not wearied by his work, nor delighting in work completed. No one saw him working, but knows that he made both the days of the works [Col. 1343A] and the works of the days. He did not descend from rest into labour, nor rise from labour into rest. Resting, he acts; acting, he rests. There is no rest outside God; in him is the rest of all things. This rest is completed on the seventh day, full of the seven beatitudes, obtained through the sevenfold power of the Holy Spirit, and sought through the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer.

“Seventh,” not added by counting after the six days mentioned above, but extended, for rational intelligence, to those things which were made, though it itself was not made. For the things that were made are enclosed by evening and morning and confined within their own limits. But this is presented without evening and morning, without beginning and without end; it is known in the divine mind, abides inseparably in the bosom of Wisdom, and is essentially joined to God in peace and unity. This is the day [Col. 1343B] of the Lord’s rest, on which he rests in himself and on which the blessed, sanctified, happy children rest.

Therefore, having considered the number six as it applies to the six works of the days and the six days of the works, we proceed and ascend as far as seven, by which, Sacred Scripture narrating it, we have learned that God rested on the seventh day from all his work. Six alone, below ten, is a perfect number, the first among perfect numbers; but it is consummated on the seventh day, when everything enacted within it—both days and works—is completed in the seventh by the primordial institution. Hence Moses says: “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had done” (Gen. 1:2).

But since we see six raised to seven, in which it is completed [Col. 1343C], let us without hesitation raise seven itself to the perfect number which is found as the second perfect number below one hundred. For if seven is taken four times, when we gather the total, we find the number called twenty-eight. Let us accordingly investigate its perfection. Let us diligently consider its parts, which are called aliquot parts below the number itself, when measured by arithmetic reasoning, divided and gathered again. One, beyond doubt, measures twenty-eight itself, like the other numbers, by its first position; and fourteen, taken twice, does the same. Seven also, taken four times, attains the same result. Gather these parts therefore: fourteen, seven, four, two, one; taken together they restore twenty-eight whole and entire [Col. 1343D].

It must further be observed that the number seven, placed below ten, generates no number from one to ten. For unity is the limit of every number; the first is ten, the second a hundred, the third a thousand, the fourth . . . But lest you overflow in counting, set yourself a limit, lest you be carried away and fall into boundless immensity. For a multitude, if it does not fail in counting, grows into infinity; but magnitude decreases when divided by number. Let the curious apply their ingenuity to these matters. Let us return to seven: it has no measure of itself except unity alone; unity alone constitutes it and alone preserves it by measuring it. For these reasons seven, uniquely simple and simply one, is called a virgin number by a special prerogative; and rightly the undivided monad is joined to the virgin seven, since she alone begets and she alone measures that which she alone has generated.

Aged David, strong of hand and desirable in appearance, is warmed in a virgin’s bosom. Blessed is the rest within the sanctuary of virginity of the sevenfold Holy Spirit. Meanwhile the spiritual eye is exalted on high by God’s grace; it sees that the aforementioned six represents the works of this earthly world, created at God’s command, formed by God’s action, and preserved whole by God [Col. 1344A]. But the seven, rightly called virgin, reveals the marks of the heavenly kingdom and of the spiritual Church which rightly abides. It assigns to our contemplation the seven days of rational intelligence, the seven beatitudes of the children of the supreme Father, and the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit bestowed on the children and to be sought through the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer.

Since the children cannot yet obtain merit, they seek grace through prayer; helped by grace, they receive divine spiritual charisms. Adorned with these, they seek the beatitudes, which they find in the days abiding within the blessedness of the Lord’s rest. In these things, counted fourfold, the virgin number seven is found four times; and from the fourfold seven, gathered together, the number twenty-eight is presented—perfect in ratio and second among perfect numbers. We have assembled these considerations in commendation of seventy, who four times, that is, at every time, is always to be worshipped, and who is not multiple but one God with the Father and the Son.

In this faith, with grace cooperating, raised by certain hope, and re-formed in charity into the likeness of God, let us offer sanctified prayers to our Father; let us obtain virtues from our Father [Col. 1344C]; through virtues let us hold with our Father the beatitudes; let us make with our Father days of happiness, not temporal but eternal: days of the divine vision in which the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both are always beheld, happily loved, and glorified with perpetual praise—not several gods, but one essentially, full and perfect.

These ineffable things, to be sought by faith, attained by hope, and possessed by charity, we at times behold in the present age, full and perfect in the days of the Lord, through a wondrous sign and mystical mystery set forth for the Catholic Church. For on the holy mountain was made a holy manifestation of this holy sevenfold reality: there the Father’s voice bears witness from the cloud to the Son; there the Son appears with glorified face; there Moses and Elijah are seen in majesty [Col. 1344D]; there Peter, James, and John rejoice in unfamiliar amazement. Those three stand for the mystery of the Trinity; those two for the testimony of the Law and prophecy, attending Christ adorned with glory and honour. They receive the Father’s command always to hear the Son: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Luke 6:35).

Behold, you see the sevenfold Spirit especially commended. In this manifestation of Father and Son their equality is considered; in Moses and Elijah the Law and prophecy are present; in Peter, James, and John the Trinity, ever to be worshipped, is signified—essentially one in all, manifest in the days of eternity.

23. Finally, as we draw near, with the Lord’s inspiration, to the end of the work, let us recall the beginning of the present Church [Col. 1345A] as it arose, the progress of the Church as it advanced, and its consummation to be completed in everlasting glory. The present Church arose through faith, brought forth by the faith of the patriarchs and ancients, educated by the discipline of the Law and the teachings of the prophets, expanded throughout all lands by the virtues of apostles, evangelists, and doctors, and is to be adorned with the robe of blessedness alongside Christ Jesus, God and Lord of all, her bridegroom.

We, lastly, the children of so great a mother, liberated from Egyptian slavery by the finger of God, signs, and wonders, while in the straits of time we feed on the Paschal Lamb, are commanded to observe the seven days of unleavened bread. With the Apostle we profess that “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” whence he immediately continues, saying: “Therefore [Col. 1346A] let us keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness” (1 Cor. 5:7–8): of malice, in the committing of sins; of wickedness, in the stubborn defence of evil; “but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth”: of sincerity, because carnal desire has been put away; and of truth, because of perseverance in the Catholic faith.

Therefore let us supply to God the Father a sevenfold devotion of prayer; and, having obtained grace by prayer, let us be clothed with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and let us long for the seven beatitudes, which we ask to attain within the seven days through the blessed vision of the supreme and undivided Trinity, one and simple Godhead, in the unity of all the saints, unto infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1345]

# LIFE OF SAINT ADJUTOR, MONK OF TIRON

By HUGH, archbishop of Rouen, the third of that name, a contemporary of Adjutor himself.

(Edited by Martène from a Tironian manuscript codex, *Anecdota*, vol. V, col. 1012.)

[Col. 1345B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

To the most beloved brothers in Christ—the monks of the monastery of Tiron in Perche—venerable for their merits and to be embraced with the whole affection of the heart: HUGH, unworthy archbishop of the holy Church of Rouen, greeting and the affection of sincere love.

You have displayed the force of great charity and sweetness, earnestly requesting that we should commit to lasting memorials the foundation and origin of your place of Saint Mary Magdalene above the Seine, resplendent with great wonders and very many marvellous miracles, together with those miracles themselves, for the praise of the Church and the confirmation of the Catholic faith. Indeed, I would not dare, in response to your prayers—nay, commands worthy because of their merits—not to obey. Nor do I judge anything more worthy of being entrusted to written characters [Col. 1345C] than the deeds of the most glorious saints, especially of those who were so worthy as to merit seeing and touching our Lord Jesus Christ, associating with him, and hearing his saving counsels. Who could suppose anyone to be so ready to grant petitions, or so deserving of being heard in petitions, as one who, as has been said, was so near to the Lord? Let us therefore come to what was promised.

At the time when the Catholic faith, shining in the wheel of the world, was spreading through the Norman land, the glorious and most worthy man Adjutor came forth into this light of the world, his glorious life expressing both the force of his name and the grace of great salvation. For, while Adjutor overcame the various perils of this life [Col. 1345D], he conquered by his merits every worldly hindrance. For just as the Church stands upon the apostolic foundation, so that Peter, made firm rock by Christ, was appointed an invincible actor [Col. 1346B], so Adjutor, soldier of the eternal conqueror, is made a soldier through a twofold warfare.

No slight proofs show that he shone with the double endowment of martyrs and confessors; and assuredly his deeds must at least in part be recorded, lest the fame of so great a man should at some time be darkened by the cloud of doubt. Indeed, it is sufficient for his glory that in heaven he has Christ alone, whom he sought to please. He was born in the city called Vernon, his father being John, temporal lord of that place, and his mother Rosimund of Blarru, John’s wife—certainly, as we knew when we were younger, persons most devoted to God and most holy. Noble indeed in lineage, but nobler in faith; illustrious among his own people in worldly rank, but exceptional through the grace of divine gifts.

The childhood of this man sufficiently foreshadowed how great he would be in the future. For at the age when worldly youth is accustomed to indulge itself, he so mortified his body with vigils, fasts, and continual prayers that, with his flesh already wasted away, his skin seemed almost to cling to his bones [Col. 1346C]. As he grew older, by the providence of divine grace every good disposition increased in him. He was handsome in appearance, chaste in body, devout in mind, gracious in speech, and lovable in aspect.

At that time nearly all worshippers of Christ were engaged in the expedition to the Holy Land. The glorious man Adjutor himself, marked with the cross, took part in this expedition with almost two hundred armed men. It happened that one day, when he was going to a small place in the territory of Antioch called Jambuit, he and his aforesaid company fell into an ambush of more than fifteen hundred Ishmaelites [Col. 1346D]. Surrounded by them, he saw his men seeking flight, though they could not escape; and seeing that so few could not withstand such a multitude, he cast himself upon the ground, as was his custom when taking up arms, and poured forth both prayer and vow, saying:

“I vow to you, most blessed Mary Magdalene, that if you grant me victory in the imminent battle, I will give my house of Mont with its appurtenances to serve you in the monastery of Tiron in Perche; and in that very place I will give the monks of Tiron a chapel which, in your honour, I shall have built there as soon as I have returned to these regions, and which I shall endow from my own resources.”

And suddenly—slowly indeed, yet without any action by our men, who had despaired of safety—he charged against the enemies of the faith, so that all fled in every direction as best they could. But Adjutor, seeing that help had come to him from above, took strength with his men and vigorously wielded his sword against the enemy. For a thousand and more were slain in that battle, not by our men’s hands but through the help of blessed Mary Magdalene; the rest escaped by flight [Col. 1347B].

When victory had thus been achieved, the holy man Adjutor rejoiced in Christ in his triumph, because none of his men had fallen in the peril of so great a calamity. He who, after Pharaoh was drowned in the deep, saved the people of Israel without anyone perishing, could do this. Therefore, when the bitter barbarity had been overthrown, the glorious man Adjutor began, giving thanks to the Most High, to sing:

“O my most devout brothers, monks of Tiron, who continually pray to God for me! O most blessed Mary Magdalene, who hold me commended before God! O most high God, in whose hand all things are placed, what thanks can I, a wretch, render to you for such benefits? What praises can I, a sinner, utter for you? Your right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; your right hand has struck down the enemies, and in the multitude of your glory you have cast down our adversaries.”

We learned these things through the distinguished knights Heliodorus of Blarru, Odo of Porc-Mort, John of Breheval, Anselm of Cantamerula, Guy of Calvmont, Peter of Courtenay, Richard of Harcourt, Henry of Pratelles, and very many others who were present at the affair and the battle [Col. 1347D].

But we do not consider it fitting to omit that most renowned and utterly marvellous miracle: how he was captured by the enemies of our faith, committed to most dreadful prisons, bound in the tightest coats of mail and iron chains, and yet was set free. In the aforesaid Jerusalem expedition, he had already served for seventeen years, as few had done. By the unforeseen fortunes of war, by God’s hidden judgment, and perhaps because he delayed too long in fulfilling the vow that we have set forth above, it happened that the glorious man Adjutor was captured by the said enemies of Christ’s cross. The faithless Saracens bound him with thongs and cruel chains, crushed him harshly with every other contrived punishment, and afflicted him with the most savage tortures in order that he might deny Christ and his faith [Col. 1348A].

But he persevered in the faith and, a diligent suppliant, commended himself to the mercy of our Saviour, to his holy mother, to blessed Mary Magdalene, and to the prayers of holy, glorious, and God-devoted Bernard, formerly your father and that of your monastery of Tiron; he continually begged their aid. At last, after many courses of time had elapsed, when the most mighty God looked upon his athlete, he compassionately took pity on his miseries. For one night, when he had given himself to a little rest, he saw in a dream—or rather in a living vision—blessed Mary Magdalene on his right and glorious Bernard on his left, holding and lifting him and leading him with utmost speed. They left him, although freed from the bonds with which he had been bound, in the place mentioned above.

O wonderful event, unheard of in these regions, but an exceedingly celebrated miracle—and, as we discovered through most diligent inquiries made by us with Peter of Courtenay, Henry of Pratelles, Andrew of Feritate, Rofred of Puteaux, Odo of Porc-Mort, and many others who had seen him on the day preceding that night and had eaten and spoken with him, most certain!

He awoke from sleep and, seeing himself released from his chains and delivered from the faithless Ishmaelites in the place already mentioned, raised the loftiest cries from heart and voice to the Most High. He immediately sent to you, William, venerable abbot of your monastery of Tiron [Col. 1348C], and, asking admission among you, put off the old man together with secular knighthood and put on the new man: that is, he assumed there the habit of your holy Tironian religious order. He gave and granted himself and that place, with its lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, tithes, revenues, and all appurtenances, together with all his property wherever situated, to your Tiron monastery, to be assigned and distributed by the abbot of Tiron for provisions and necessities. Giving thanks to God, he said:

“From the ends of the earth I cried to you, when my heart was in distress; you raised me upon a rock. You led me, because you have become my hope, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. I shall dwell in your tabernacle for ever; I shall be sheltered beneath the covering of your wings, for you, O God, have heard my prayer; you have given an inheritance to those who fear your name” (Ps. 60:3–6).

Accordingly, the chapel was built. At last we dedicated it with three altars and consecrated the altars, consecrating the greater altar in honour of our Lord Jesus Christ and blessed Mary Magdalene, his apostle [Col. 1348D].

After he had left the world and entered your religious order as a monk, he led so holy and austere a life, as we know, that he took no food except bread, water, or oil seasoned with salt, unless perhaps affection for a feast day, a solemn celebration, or hospitality toward eminent visitors compelled him to take more. He kept from his presence not only the sight of women but even that of men, so that, withdrawn from human beings, he might look only for angelic visitations and might increase in divinity what was lacking in the human being [Col. 1349A].

From the time he became a monk he never had a bed; he knew no bedding; he never rested his head upon feathers. At night he was content only with the garment he had worn by day. Instead of soft wool, he clothed himself in rough haircloth, so that during the hours of sleep there might be no bodily rest, and, with the order reversed, after the day had passed the night might still follow in labour. His outer garment was so cheap and contemptible that the cowl, which was his ordinary garment and of little or no value, would by comparison have been a cloth of gold.

His daytime prayer and nightly rest were in a small cell behind the altar of the chapel which, as we have said, we dedicated at his request [Col. 1349B]. There were continual groans and tears; there continual vigils and prayers; there daily fasting. You would not know him to seek elsewhere or to receive elsewhere any refreshment for his body. Alas for me, a wretched sinner! When he was very often asked by us why he made himself so lowly and did not conduct himself somewhat according to the rank of his blood, or at least refresh his body somewhere other than that place, he answered at once: “My body was once too much refreshed according to the state of the world; now it is fitting that it repay what it received in excess.”

But since he gave no answer concerning that place, we certainly hope that there is something divine in it. Therefore, as long as we dwell in this fragile life, we hold that cell in the highest veneration; and whenever we approach it [Col. 1349C] and pour out prayers and petitions there, we perceive that some divine inspiration and much devotion toward God have come to us or increased in us. The ground in that little cell supplied his bed; where he laid his head, the earth, rising a little, supplied a pillow.

We saw many sufferers from fever and other sick persons come to his bed, sleep in it, and return home sound and unharmed; others, if not immediately, at least after a short time, recovered health. He nevertheless had a sufficiently respectable bed in his chamber, which served him only so that he might appear worldly like the rest. During these times he restored hearing to the deaf, and at times restored health to those suffering from many kinds of illness. As to the rest, since we are not fully certain about them, let us be silent; rather, we shall recount what was done under the protection of blessed Mary Magdalene in that chapel, and what we know through the testimony of many trustworthy persons [Col. 1349D].

For one day, while he was in that chapel with his aforesaid mother Rosimund and very many other people, a demoniac came upon them—his name was Hilgodus Ruffus—holding a drawn sword. With it he had wounded many men and women at that time. As this demoniac wandered here and there, he turned aside to the chapel itself, where the often-mentioned Adjutor, his mother Rosimund, and the said people were gathered. [Col. 1350A] Entering it, he compelled the people in terror to flee behind the altar. But the reverent Adjutor met him and said: “O my Lady, blessed Mary Magdalene, though this man has been brought here by a demon, yet now that he has come to this your chapel, shall he not experience something of your benefits?”

As soon as Adjutor uttered these words, the demon departed from Hilgodus with a great roar. Hilgodus himself, bending his knees to the ground, gave thanks to almighty God and blessed Mary Magdalene for his restored soundness. We know this most certainly through due testimony from Hilgodus himself and the others who were present.

Nor should another miracle, likewise most famous and astonishing to many, be passed over—a miracle which, as we maintain, [Col. 1350B] was wrought through the intercession of blessed Mary Magdalene before our own eyes and those of many people. Near the aforesaid place of blessed Magdalene, in the river Seine, there was a certain whirlpool of waters. It swallowed sailors passing by who were unaware of it, so that neither goods nor other equipment, nor persons—indeed, not even the ships themselves—ever returned at any time. Thus, from times long past, many people had perished, and ships and other possessions had been submerged.

When this happened once, after he had settled in that place upon assuming the habit of your religious order, he thought it fitting to summon us, that we might assist so great a calamity by help or counsel. Therefore, after we had celebrated there a Mass of the Holy Spirit, we and the venerable Adjutor boarded a little boat and hastened to the whirlpool, not without great tears and lamentation. [Col. 1350C] We, however, who were held in fearful dread lest we should be swallowed up by the whirlpool, urged Adjutor not to expose ourselves to this danger and hazard. But he said: “The Lord is able, through the merits of blessed Mary Magdalene, to deliver us now and the people hereafter, and on this day to work wonders in the sight of all.”

Trusting therefore in God and blessed Mary Magdalene, and in the assurance of the blessed man, we went together toward the place of the whirlpool. And when the current was already drawing us toward the river’s vortex, he said to us: “Bless, lord bishop, and make the sign of the cross, and cast the sprinkler of holy water into the place of the whirlpool.” This we immediately did.

[Col. 1350D] He himself cast into that place certain irons from which he had been delivered through the prayers of blessed Mary Magdalene and Saint Bernard, saying: “The Lord can, through the merits of blessed Mary Magdalene and most blessed Bernard, deliver his people, just as he delivered me through their prayers.” When these words had been spoken and these things done, that whirlpool, which had sought the deep places of the abyss, suddenly became a pleasant smoothness of water. We and the sailors who had stood at a distance then passed back and forth over it, amazed and bewildered in mind, yet rejoicing and glad; and we returned home. Thereafter, by the aid of divine grace and blessed Mary Magdalene, no one perished there, nor was the whirlpool seen again.

If we wished, we could recount many other miracles wrought in that place, [Col. 1351A] as we have heard from many trustworthy persons, through the merits and prayers of blessed Mary Magdalene, both during the life of the venerable Adjutor himself and after his death. But we include only those things which we ourselves saw or which we know with complete certainty through the testimony of many trustworthy people. And since many books, both by evangelists and by other saints, have appeared in praise and exaltation of blessed Mary Magdalene, our discourse is not worthy of her exaltation. Therefore an end shall be given to this page concerning our venerable Adjutor, to whom we have given its beginning and middle in the greater part, and concerning whom we have most often been questioned by you and others.

Let others praise him as an expeller of demons, a healer of corpses, and one powerful in other miracles. We [Col. 1351B] shall praise the rewards of patience of our Adjutor: the power of God; contempt for possessions; thereafter the gain of souls; the restoration of monasteries; the clothing and food of monks; the peace of churches; concord among kings and princes; the safeguarding of roads; earnestness in observing every commandment; perseverance in vigils and prayers; concern for the poor; correction of the young; honor for the old; reform of morals; love of virgins; consolation of the continent; mercy toward the wretched; undefiled observance of rules and commandments; and finally, an example of every virtue.

[Col. 1352A] At last, as the end of his life drew near and he knew that the dissolution of his body was imminent, he caused us and his abbot William of Tiron to be summoned to him. We aforesaid came to him with many others, weeping and groaning. Having heard his words concerning his end, we asked him: “Brother Adjutor, where have you appointed the burial of your body?” The man of God replied: “In this little chapel, if it please my lord abbot.”

The venerable man lay upon the ground on that little bed of which we wrote above, behind the altar of blessed Mary Magdalene. Strengthened by the divine sacraments and clothed as he always was, he departed to the Lord on the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April]. Although we were saddened by natural grief, we nevertheless rejoiced because we had sent before us to God so great and such a patron and helper on our behalf. Let the bishop triumph in spiritual rejoicing; let the priests exalt shining robes of righteousness; let monks rejoice in the strength of blessed works; and, girded with the beauty of virtues, let every ecclesiastical order resound with devout songs to almighty God. Let the lay multitude, with the female sex, answer in turn; and let young men and virgins, old men with the younger, all say in suppliant prayer: “Most holy Mary Magdalene, and you, holy man Adjutor, come to our aid.”

## BOOK ONE — On the Mystery of the Trinity

Distinction IV—The question whether it should be granted that God begot himself, 533. Distinction V—The question whether the Father begot the divine essence, or the essence itself begot the Son; whether essence begot essence; or whether the essence itself neither begot nor was begotten, 535. Distinction VII—The question whether the Father could or would beget the Son, 541. Distinction VIII—On the truth, propriety, immutability, [Col. 1384] and simplicity of God’s essence, 542.
